## Volume Front Matter

### Series Title Page

The Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal, Complete, Uniform, Convenient, Economical Library of all the Holy Fathers, Doctors, and Ecclesiastical Writers who flourished from the Apostolic Age up to the time of Innocent III; a chronological reprinting of all the monuments of Catholic tradition that have survived from the first twelve centuries of the Church, according to the most accurate editions, compared with one another and with certain manuscript codices, corrected with the greatest care; continually illustrated with dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged by all works discovered after the very extensive editions produced during the last three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indexes following each volume and each author of any importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with titles distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating the subject matter below; expanded by works both doubtful and apocryphal, and by works possessing some authority with respect to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which whatever each Father has written on any topic may be viewed at a glance; the other of Sacred Scripture, from which it may readily be learned which Fathers, and in which passages of their works, commented on the individual texts of the individual books of Scripture.

The most accurate edition, and one easily preferred to all others if the following are taken into account: the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the works reprinted, the highly convenient format of the volumes, consistently similar throughout the whole work, the low price, and above all this collection, which is unified, methodical, and chronological, of six hundred fragments and minor works previously scattered here and there, but gathered for the first time in our library from works pertaining to every age, place, language, and form.

### First Series

In which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and Writers of the Latin Church from Tertullian to Gregory the Great. Prepared by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Complete Courses in the several branches of ecclesiastical learning.

# [The Complete Works of Augustine]

## [Column 0009]

## Preface to the Sixth Volume

In this sixth volume are presented various minor works of Augustine that contribute to the formation of moral conduct. They are indeed distinguished works and intrinsically of immense value, but here they acquire a new splendor and illumination from being placed in a better order. In the editions previously published, these writings had been so scattered that some were read in the second and third volumes among the exegetical books, others in the sixth volume among the polemical works, and still others in the ninth volume after the *Tractates on John*. Although this arrangement had once been established through the care of Erasmus and was later adopted by the Louvain theologians, we decided to change it in this new edition, so that works of the same kind or of similar subject matter might be read continuously and in an orderly fashion, better understood by students, and more deeply impressed upon their minds.

We begin with certain books of Questions, among which the books addressed to Simplicianus deserve particular mention. Augustine was already a bishop when he published them, and they are thoroughly worthy of him. For although in some of his earlier writings he had not thought correctly about the gifts of faith and grace, in this work, written at the beginning of his episcopate, he came to his senses, corrected his position, and cast off his error, having been convinced especially by apostolic testimony, as he himself professes in the book *On the Predestination of the Saints*, from 1 Corinthians 4:7. Nevertheless, in that same place the holy man acknowledges that this too must be attributed to divine grace and revelation.

Although, therefore, in the discussion addressed to Simplicianus he sometimes turns the matter in both directions, appearing somewhat like one who doubts—a mode of argument that certainly requires a shrewd and attentive reader—he nevertheless says, in writing on the gift of perseverance, that even before the Pelagian heresy appeared he had argued in such a way that nothing remained which could cast doubt on the fact that the grace of God is not given according to our merits. He also established clearly enough that the beginning of faith is a gift of God, so that from what is said there it follows plainly that perseverance to the end is likewise bestowed only by him who predestined us for his kingdom and glory.

When the Questions have been completed, the series begins of the minor works that are more directly concerned with moral conduct. First among these is the book *On Faith in Things That Are Not Seen*, which we are restoring to Augustine, since the opinion of Erasmus and the Louvain theologians had wrongly taken it away from him. It is followed by the work *On Faith and the Creed*, which we must attribute to the bishops of the council of Hippo. At their command, Augustine, not yet adorned with the episcopal insignia, treated this subject in that plenary assembly of all Africa. He was then compelled, by the earnest insistence of his friends, to turn the discourse into a book.

Next is added the book *On Faith and Works*, published against those who held that everyone without distinction ought to be admitted to baptism; that moral precepts should be taught only after baptism; and finally that those who had been baptized should be saved by the merit of the Christian faith, even if they never changed their morals, however wicked they might be. Since the holy Doctor judged this third opinion exceedingly dangerous, he undertook to refute it not just once, but always with a friendly and peaceful hand, because it had undoubtedly proceeded from Catholic and devout authors. When he encounters them in Book 21, chapter 17, of *The City of God*, he says: “Now I see that we must deal with our merciful friends and argue peacefully.”

Here the *Enchiridion* could not be far away, for it teaches the doctrine of faith, hope, and charity: a truly golden work, to be handled by night and by day. The book *On the Christian Contest* aims at nearly the same goal, containing the rule of faith and precepts for living. These books on faith are followed by the work *On Instructing the Uneducated*, published at the request of Deogratias, a Carthaginian deacon, to whom those inexperienced in the sacred writings were frequently brought to be instructed in the first elements of faith.

There follow, together with the treatise *On Continence*, works joined to one another by the affinity of their subject and argument: *On the Good of Marriage*, *On Holy Virginity*, *On the Good of Widowhood*, and *On Adulterous Marriages*. Afterwards come *On Lying* and *Against Lying*. To avoid pursuing every individual item, all the works have been placed in a definite and appropriate order.

But, what we consider the principal point, the judgment of critics concerning the minor works has been brought under examination, in case anyone has been troubled by a question about their author. Some works that critics wished to regard as spurious are shown to be genuine; others, which they customarily added to the genuine works, are either rejected as spurious or separated with an indication that they are doubtful. The latter category includes the treatises *On the Creed for Catechumens* and certain other little books or sermons transferred here from the ninth volume, which we reproduce in smaller type in the final part of the volume.

Nor was slight care or useless labor expended in preparing the Appendix. In most cases the authors of the works falsely attributed to others have been sought and discovered. The little book *On the Substance of Love* is vindicated for Hugh of Saint Victor; to him likewise is returned the work *On the Seven Vices and Seven Gifts of the Holy Spirit*. The book *On the Ladder of Paradise* is restored to Guigo the Carthusian; *On Knowledge of the True Life* to Honorius of Autun; *On the Christian Life* to Fastidius the Briton; *On Salutary Instructions* and *On the Conflict of Vices and Virtues* to Paulinus of Aquileia; *On the Rectitude of Catholic Conduct*, and consequently also *On the Vanity of the World*, to Eligius of Noyon; *On the Good of Discipline* to Valerian, bishop of Cimiez; and so forth.

The little book *On Friendship* is shown to have been excerpted from Aelred, abbot of Rievaulx; the *Exposition of the Canticle Magnificat* from Hugh of Saint Victor; the book *On Contrition of Heart* from Anselm; and the treatise *On Antichrist* from Alcuin. We say nothing here of those works that we note in their proper places as having been excerpted and assembled from Augustine and other writers: some perhaps by John, abbot of Fécamp, such as the *Meditations* and others; others by Alcher, a Cistercian monk, or by an assemblage-maker not much earlier than he, namely *On Spirit and Soul*, the *Manual*, and *On Loving God*. Finally, in the Admonitions prefixed to the minor works, we indicate what is sound, what is learned, and what is worthy of reading.

# Saint Aurelius Augustine, Bishop of Hippo  
## One Book on Eighty-Three Different Questions

[Note: Begun toward the end of the year 388.]

[Note: The present Book on Eighty-Three Different Questions has been newly reviewed against fifteen manuscripts: namely, two Roman manuscripts of the Vatican Library; one Paris manuscript of the Royal Library; two of the Navarre College; one of the Sorbonne; one of the Augustinians of the great convent; one of the Abbey of Sainte-Geneviève; one of our monastery at Saint-Germain; likewise one each from Saint-Maur-des-Fossés, Saint-Bénigne of Dijon, and Saint-Michel in Peril of the Sea; two Cistercian manuscripts; and one belonging to the most illustrious lord D. de Saint-Georges, bishop of Clermont. Variant readings were also used, which the Louvain theologians collected from five Belgian manuscripts for the purpose of correcting this work. Finally, the older editions were collated: Rat., that is, the edition printed at Lyons by Johann Treschel under the care of Augustine of Regensburg in 1497; Er., the edition revised by Desiderius Erasmus and printed at Basel by Frobenius in 1528; and the Lov. edition, printed at Antwerp by the Plantin press in 1576 according to the recension of the Louvain theologians.]

[Note: In addition, we compared all the editions mentioned at the beginning of the *Retractions* and *Confessions*, volume 1. M.]

(C, S)

## I. Whether the Soul Exists from Itself

Everything true is true from truth; and every soul is a soul insofar as it is a true soul. Every soul, therefore, derives from truth the fact that it is altogether a soul. But the soul is one thing, and truth another. For truth never tolerates falsehood, whereas the soul is often deceived. Therefore, since the soul exists from truth, it does not exist from itself. Truth, however, is God. The soul therefore has God as its author, so that it may exist.

## II. On Free Choice

Whatever is made cannot be equal to the one by whom it is made. Otherwise justice, which ought to assign to each its due, must be removed from the world. Therefore, when God made the human being, although he made him excellent, he did not make him what God himself was. A person who is good by choice is better than one who is good by necessity. Free will, therefore, had to be given to the human being.

## III. Whether the Human Being Becomes Worse with God as Author

A human being does not become worse with any wise human being as author. For this is not a minor fault; indeed, it is so great that it could not befall any wise person. [Note: The editions Rat. and Er., and several manuscripts, read “although”; likewise the Venetian edition. M.] God, however, is superior to every wise human being. Still less, therefore, does a human being become worse with God as author. For God’s will is far superior to that of a wise human being. When someone is said to be the author of something, this means that he wills it. The cause of the human being’s deterioration is therefore a defect of the will. Since reason teaches that this defect is far removed from God’s will, we must ask where it is to be sought.

## IV. What the Cause Is That Makes the Human Being Worse

[Column 0012]

For a human being to become worse, the cause is either in the person himself, in something else, or in nothing. If it is in nothing, there is no cause. Or, if “in nothing” is taken to mean that the human being was made from nothing, or from things that were made from nothing, then the cause will again be in the person himself, since his matter, so to speak, is nothing.

If the cause is in something else, is it in God, in another human being, or in something that is neither God nor a human being? But it is not in God, for God is the cause of good things. If, then, it is in a human being, it must be either through force or through persuasion. But not through force in any way, lest that force be stronger than God. God made the human being so perfectly that, if he wished to remain perfect, nothing resisting could hinder him.

If we grant that a human being is corrupted by the persuasion of another human being, we must again ask by whom the persuader himself was corrupted. For one who persuades others to evil cannot fail to be evil himself. What remains is some entity that is neither God nor a human being; yet whatever it is, it either used force or persuaded. The answer concerning force is the one given above. As for persuasion, whatever that entity may be, since persuasion does not compel an unwilling person, the cause of the person’s corruption returns to that person’s own will, whether he was corrupted by someone’s persuasion or by no one’s.

[Note: Erasmus and eight manuscripts read: “but even this, whatever it is.” This is likewise found in the Lyons and Venetian editions. M.]

## V. Whether an Irrational Animal Can Be Blessed

An animal that lacks reason lacks knowledge. But no animal that lacks knowledge can be blessed. Therefore it does not belong to animals deprived of reason to be blessed.

## VI. On Evil

[Column 0013]

Everything that exists is either corporeal or incorporeal. The corporeal is contained by sensible form, while the incorporeal is contained by intelligible form. Therefore, everything that exists exists with some form. Wherever there is some form, there is necessarily some measure or order, and measure or order is something good. The highest evil, therefore, has no measure, for it lacks every good. It therefore does not exist, because it is contained by no form; and the entire term “evil” has been derived from the privation of form.

## VII. What Is Properly Called “Soul” in a Living Creature

The soul is sometimes spoken of in such a way that the mind is understood along with it, as when we say that a human being consists of soul and body. Sometimes it is spoken of with the mind excluded. But when the mind is excluded, the term is understood from those activities that we share with beasts. For beasts lack reason, which always belongs properly to the mind.

## VIII. Whether the Soul Is Moved by Itself

Anyone who perceives that there is will within himself perceives that the soul is moved by itself. For if we will something, no one else wills it in us. This movement of the soul is spontaneous, for it has been granted to the soul by God. Yet this movement is not movement from place to place, as bodily movement is. Local movement belongs properly to the body.

When the soul, by its will—that is, by a movement that is not local—nevertheless moves its body locally, this does not show that the soul itself is moved locally. We see, for example, that something can be moved from a hinge across a great distance of space, while the hinge itself does not move from its place.

[Note: Here Rat. and three manuscripts add: “since it is indivisible.”]

## IX. Whether Truth Can Be Perceived by the Bodily Senses

Everything touched by bodily sense, and therefore called sensible, is changed without any interruption of time. [Note: *Retractions* I.26.] Thus, when the hair of our head grows, or the body declines into old age, or blossoms into youth, this happens continuously and never entirely ceases to happen.

But what does not remain cannot be perceived. For that is perceived which is grasped by knowledge. What changes without interruption cannot be grasped. We must not, therefore, expect the purity of truth from the bodily senses.

But lest someone say that there are certain sensible things that always remain in the same condition, and bring forward the sun and stars, about which this cannot easily be demonstrated, there is at least one point that no one can avoid admitting: there is nothing sensible that does not have something resembling falsehood, so that it cannot be distinguished from it.

To leave other examples aside, everything that we perceive through the body, even when it is not present to the senses, nevertheless affects us through images as though it were completely present, whether in sleep or in madness. When this happens, we are entirely unable to distinguish whether we are perceiving the things themselves by our senses or whether they are images of sensible things.

If, therefore, there are false images of sensible things that cannot be distinguished by the senses themselves, and if nothing can be perceived except what is distinguished from falsehood, then the judgment of truth is not established in the senses. Accordingly, we are most beneficially warned to turn away from this [Column 0014] world—which is certainly corporeal and sensible—and to turn with complete eagerness toward God, that is, toward truth, which is grasped by the intellect and the inner mind, which always remains and is always of the same kind, and which does not have an image of falsehood from which it cannot be distinguished.

## X. Whether the Body Is from God

Everything good is from God. Everything beautiful is good insofar as it is beautiful; and everything that contains form is beautiful. Every body, however, is contained by some form in order to be a body. Therefore every body is from God.

## XI. Why Christ Was Born of a Woman

When God liberates, he does not liberate only one part; he liberates the whole that happens to be in danger. Therefore the Wisdom and Power of God, who is called the only-begotten Son, indicated the liberation of the human being by assuming humanity.

The liberation of humanity had to appear in both sexes. Therefore, since it was fitting that he assume a man, because that sex is more honorable, it followed that the liberation of the female sex should be shown by the fact that this man was born of a woman.

## XII. The Opinion of a Certain Wise Man

[Note: Namely, of Fonteius of Carthage, concerning the purification of the mind for seeing God. *Retractions* I.26.]

“Act, O wretched mortals,” he says; “act so that the evil spirit may never pollute this dwelling; so that, mingling with the senses, he may defile the holiness of the soul and obscure the light of the mind.

“This evil creeps through all the entrances of the senses. It presents itself in shapes, accommodates itself to colors, clings to sounds, lies hidden in anger, appears in the deceitfulness of speech, subjects itself to odors, pours itself into flavors, and, through the filth of turbulent movement and dark passions, darkens the senses. It fills with certain clouds all the passages of understanding through which the ray of the mind ordinarily spreads the light of reason.

“And because it is a ray of heavenly light, and in it is the mirror of the divine presence—for in it God, an innocent will, and the merit of right action shine forth—God is present everywhere. Yet he is with each of us only when the unblemished purity of our mind supposes itself to be in his presence.

“For just as the sight of the eyes, if it has been impaired, does not suppose that what it cannot see is present—for the visible image of things surrounds the eyes in vain if the eyes lack soundness—so God, who is absent nowhere, is present in vain to polluted minds, since the blindness of the mind cannot see him.”

[Note: Erasmus and seven manuscripts read: “the senses, having been darkened.”]

## XIII. By What Evidence Human Beings Surpass Beasts

Among the many things by which it can be shown that the human being surpasses beasts through reason, this is evident to everyone: wild animals can be tamed and domesticated by human beings, but human beings cannot in any way be tamed by wild animals.

## XIV. That Christ’s Body Was Not an Apparition

If Christ’s body was an apparition, Christ deceived; and if he deceived, he is not truth. But Christ is truth. Therefore his body was not an apparition.

## XV. On Understanding

Everything that understands itself comprehends itself. But [Column 0015] what comprehends itself is finite for itself. The intellect understands itself. Therefore it is finite for itself. Nor does it wish to be infinite, although it could be, because it wishes to be known to itself; for it loves itself.

## XVI. On the Son of God

God is the cause of all things that exist. But what is the cause of all things is also the cause of his own wisdom; and God has never existed without his wisdom. Therefore he is the eternal cause of his eternal wisdom; he is not earlier in time than his wisdom.

Furthermore, if being Father eternally belongs to God, and if he was never at any time not Father, then he was never without the Son.

## XVII. On the Knowledge of God

Everything past no longer exists; everything future does not yet exist. Therefore everything past and future is absent. But nothing is absent from God. Therefore, for God there is neither past nor future; everything is present to God.

## XVIII. On the Trinity

Everything that exists has one aspect by which it is constituted, another by which it is distinguished, and another by which it is brought into harmony. Therefore, if the whole of creation exists in some manner, is greatly distant from what is absolutely nothing, and is harmonious with itself in its parts, its cause must also be threefold: that by which it exists, that by which it is this particular thing, and that by which it is harmonious with itself.

We call the cause of creation—that is, its author—God. There must therefore be a Trinity, than which perfect reason can find nothing more excellent, more intelligent, or more blessed.

For this reason, even when truth is sought, there cannot be more than three kinds of questions: whether something exists at all; whether it is this thing or another; and whether it is to be approved or disapproved.

## XIX. On God and Creation

What is unchangeable is eternal, for it is always of the same kind. What is changeable, however, is subject to time, for it is not always of the same kind; and therefore it is not properly called eternal. What changes does not remain; what does not remain is not eternal.

The difference between immortal and eternal is this: everything eternal is immortal, but not everything immortal can, with sufficient precision, be called eternal. For although something may always live, nevertheless, if it undergoes change, it is not properly called eternal, because it is not always of the same kind. It may rightly be called immortal, however, because it always lives.

Sometimes what is immortal is also called eternal. But that which undergoes change and, although it is not a soul, is said to live through the presence of the soul, cannot be understood as immortal in any way, and still less as eternal.

For in what is eternal, when the term is used properly, there is neither anything past, as though it had passed away, nor anything future, as though it did not yet exist; rather, whatever is, simply is.

## XX. On the Place of God

God is not in any place. For what is in a place is contained by place; what is contained by place is a body. God, however, is not a body. Therefore he is not in any place.

Yet because he exists and is not in a place, all things are rather in him than he is anywhere. They are not in him in such a way that he himself is a place. For place exists in space, which is occupied by the length, [Column 0016] breadth, and height of a body; God is nothing of this kind.

Everything, therefore, is in him, but he is not a place. Nevertheless, the temple of God is called, improperly, the place of God—not because he is contained by it, but because he is present to it. Nothing is better understood by this than a pure soul.

## XXI. Whether God Is Not the Author of Evil

Whoever is the author of all things that exist, and whose goodness is concerned only with the fact that everything that exists should exist, cannot in any way be the cause of non-being. Everything that falls away falls away from what exists and tends toward non-being.

To exist and not to fall short in anything is good; to fall short is evil. But the one to whom non-being does not belong is not the cause of falling short—that is, of tending toward non-being—for, so to speak, he is the cause of existence.

He is therefore the cause only of good, and for that reason he himself is the highest good. Consequently, the author of all things that exist is not the author of evil, because insofar as things exist, they are good.

[Note: *Retractions* I.26.]

## XXII. That God Is Not Subject to Necessity

Where there is no need, there is no necessity; where there is no defect, there is no need. But there is no defect in God. Therefore there is no necessity.

## XXIII. On the Father and the Son

Everything chaste is chaste through chastity; everything eternal is eternal through eternity; everything beautiful through beauty; and everything good through goodness. Therefore everything wise is wise through wisdom, and everything similar through similarity.

But something is said to be chaste through chastity in two ways: either because it generates chastity, so that the thing is chaste through the chastity it generates and to which it is the origin and cause of being; or because something is chaste through participation in chastity, and therefore can at some time cease to be chaste. The same must be understood of the other qualities.

The soul, for example, is understood or believed to attain eternity, but it becomes eternal through participation in eternity. God, however, is not eternal in this way, but because he is the author of eternity itself. The same may be understood of beauty and goodness.

Therefore, when God is called wise, and is said to be wise through that wisdom without which it would be impious to believe that he either ever existed or could exist, he is not said to be wise through participation in wisdom, as the soul is, since the soul can be wise or not wise. Rather, he is wise because he himself generated the wisdom by which he is called wise.

[Note: *Retractions* I.26, and Book 6 of *On the Trinity*, chapter 2.]

Likewise, those things that are chaste, eternal, beautiful, good, or wise through participation receive, as has been said, the possibility of not being chaste, eternal, beautiful, good, or wise. Chastity, eternity, beauty, goodness, and wisdom themselves, however, in no way admit corruption or, so to speak, temporality, ugliness, or evil.

Therefore those things that are similar through participation admit dissimilarity; similarity itself, however, cannot in any way be dissimilar in any respect.

Hence, when the Son is called the likeness of the Father, because through participation in him whatever things exist are similar either to one another or to God—for he himself is the first [Column 0017] form by which all things are, so to speak, formed, and the pattern by which all things have been formed—he cannot be dissimilar to the Father in any respect.

He is therefore the same as the Father, in such a way that the one is Son and the other Father: the one is the likeness, the other the one whose likeness he is; the one is substance, the other substance.

[Note: The words “the one is substance, the other substance” are absent from nine manuscripts.]

Thus there is one substance. For if there were not one, likeness would admit dissimilarity; but every most certain principle of reason denies that this can happen.

## XXIV. Whether Sin and Right Action Belong to Free Choice of the Will

Whatever happens by chance happens randomly; whatever happens randomly does not happen through providence. If, therefore, some things happen by chance in the world, the whole world is not governed by providence. If the whole world is not governed by providence, then there is some nature or substance that does not belong to the work of providence.

But everything that exists is good insofar as it exists. For that good is supremely good through participation in which all other things are good. Everything changeable, moreover, is good insofar as it exists not through itself but through participation in unchangeable good.

That good through participation in which all other things that exist are good is good not through something else but through itself; and we also call it divine providence.

[Note: Rat. and eight manuscripts read “however much they exist.” Four others read “however great they are.”]

Nothing, therefore, happens by chance in the world.

Once this has been established, it seems to follow that whatever occurs in the world occurs partly through divine action and partly through our will. God is far and incomparably better and more just than any human being, however good and just.

A just ruler and governor of all things does not allow anyone to be punished undeservedly or to receive an undeserved reward. The merit of punishment is sin, and the merit of reward is right action.

Neither sin nor right action can justly be attributed to anyone who has done nothing by his own will. Sin and right action therefore belong to free choice of the will.

## XXV. On the Cross of Christ

The Wisdom of God assumed humanity as an example by which we should live rightly. It belongs to right living not to fear what ought not to be feared. Death, however, ought not to be feared.

Therefore this had to be demonstrated by the death of the man whom the Wisdom of God assumed. Yet there are people who, although they do not fear death itself, nevertheless dread some particular kind of death.

Nevertheless, just as death itself ought not to be feared, so no kind of death ought to be feared by a person who lives well and rightly. Therefore this too had to be shown through the cross of that man. For among all kinds of death, none was more accursed and more dreadful than that kind.

## XXVI. On the Difference among Sins

Some sins arise from weakness, others from ignorance, and others from malice. Weakness is opposed to virtue, ignorance to wisdom, and malice to goodness.

Therefore anyone who [Column 0018] knows what the virtue and wisdom of God are can judge which sins are venial. Anyone who knows what the goodness of God is can judge which sins deserve a definite punishment both in this age and in the age to come.

When these matters have been properly considered, it may reasonably be judged who should not be compelled to undertake grievous and tearful penance, although they confess their sins, and for whom no salvation at all may be hoped unless they offer God, through repentance, a spirit that is broken.

## XXVII. On Providence
It is possible that through an evil person divine providence both punishes and assists. For the impiety of the Jews both supplanted the Jews [Note: Erasmus and eleven manuscripts: “supplanted Judas.” Thus also the Lyons manuscript], and became a means of salvation for the Gentiles. Likewise, it is possible that through a good person divine providence both condemns and helps, as the Apostle says: “To some we are the aroma of life leading to life, but to others the aroma of death leading to death” (2 Corinthians 2:16).

But since every tribulation is either the punishment of the wicked or the discipline of the righteous—for the same threshing instrument crushes the chaff and strips the grain of its chaff, from which tribulation receives its name—and since, again, peace and relief from temporal troubles both profit the good and corrupt the wicked, divine providence regulates all these things according to the merits of souls. Nevertheless, the good do not choose for themselves the ministry of tribulation, nor do the wicked love peace. Therefore they too, through whom what they do not understand is brought about, receive the reward not of the justice that is referred to God, but of their own ill will.

Just as harm done to someone is not charged against the good when those who wish to benefit them cause it, but the reward of benevolence is assigned to their good intention, so also the rest of creation is either perceived or concealed, troublesome or beneficial, according to the merits of rational souls. For since the supreme God administers well everything that he has made, there is nothing disordered in the universe and nothing unjust, whether we know it or do not know it. The sinful soul is indeed offended in some particular part; yet because it is there according to its merits, and suffers what it is just for such a soul to suffer, it does not disfigure the universal kingdom of God by any ugliness of its own.

Therefore, since we do not know everything that the divine order does well on our behalf, we act according to the law in good will alone; in other matters we are acted upon according to the law, while the law itself remains unchangeable and governs all mutable things with the most beautiful ordering.

“Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2:14).

## XXVIII. Why God wished to make the world

Whoever asks why God wished to make the world is asking for the cause of God’s will. But every efficient cause is greater than what it produces. Nothing, however, is greater than God’s will. Therefore its cause must not be sought.

## XXIX. Whether there is anything above or below in the universe

“Set your minds on the things that are above” (Colossians 3:2). We are commanded to set our minds on the things that are above—namely, spiritual things—which are not to be understood as being above in the places and regions of this world, but by reason of their superior excellence, lest we fix our mind in some part of that world from which we ought to detach ourselves entirely.

Above and below do exist in the parts of this world. For the universe as a whole has neither above nor below. It is corporeal, since everything visible is corporeal. But in the whole of a body there is neither above nor below. For although motion appears to take place in six directions—the motion called rectilinear, that is, motion which is not circular—namely, forward and backward, rightward and leftward, upward and downward, there is absolutely no reason why the whole body should have front and back, right and left, but above and below.

Those who consider the matter in this way are deceived because it is difficult to resist the senses and customary ways of thinking. For bodily inversion is not as easy for us—when someone wishes to move with his head downward—as movement from right to left or from front to back. Therefore, once these words have been set aside, the mind must labor with itself so that it may be able to perceive this.

## XXX. Whether all things were created for human use

Just as there is a distinction between the honorable and the useful, so there is a distinction between enjoying and using. Although it can be subtly defended that everything honorable is useful and everything useful honorable, nevertheless, because “honorable” is more properly and ordinarily used of what is sought for its own sake, while “useful” refers to what is directed toward something else, we are now speaking according to this distinction, while carefully maintaining that the honorable and the useful can in no way oppose each other. They are sometimes mistakenly and popularly thought to be opposed.

We are said to enjoy a thing when we take pleasure in it. We use a thing when we refer it to that from which pleasure is to be obtained. Thus all human perversity—which is also called vice—is the desire to use things that should be enjoyed and to enjoy things that should be used. Conversely, all right ordering—which is also called virtue—is enjoying what should be enjoyed and using what should be used.

Things honorable should be enjoyed; useful things should be used. By “honor” I mean intelligible beauty, which we properly call spiritual; by “utility” I mean divine providence. Therefore, although there are many visible beautiful things, which are less properly called honorable, the beauty itself from which all beautiful things are beautiful is in no way visible. Likewise, many useful things are visible; but the utility itself from which whatever benefits us is beneficial—that is, what we call divine providence—is not visible.

It should be understood that everything corporeal is included under the term “visible.” We ought therefore to enjoy beautiful invisible things, that is, honorable things. Whether we ought to enjoy all of them is another question, although perhaps only those things that ought to be enjoyed deserve to be called honorable. We ought to use all useful things, according as any of them is needed.

Beasts are not thought wholly absurdly to enjoy food and every bodily pleasure; but no creature can use anything unless it participates in reason. For knowing what each thing should be referred to is not given to beings without reason—and not even to foolish rational beings. No one can use a thing if he does not know where it should be referred; and no one can know this unless he is wise. Therefore those who do not use things well are more correctly said to misuse them. For nothing benefits anyone if he uses it badly; and what does not benefit is certainly not useful. Whatever is useful is useful through use; therefore no one uses anything except what is useful. Whoever uses something badly, then, does not use it.

Perfect human reason, which is called virtue, first uses itself to understand God, so that it may enjoy him by whom it was also made. It uses other rational living beings for fellowship, and irrational beings for superiority. It also directs its own life toward enjoying God, for in this consists its blessedness. Thus it also uses itself; and it certainly begins misery through pride if it is directed toward itself rather than toward God.

It also uses certain bodies that are to be given life for acts of benevolence—for it uses its own body in this way; some things are taken up or rejected for health, some endured for patience, some ordered for justice, and some considered for learning a lesson of truth. It also uses the things from which it abstains for self-control. Thus it uses all things, both sentient and nonsentient; there is no third category.

It judges all the things it uses; it does not judge God alone, because it judges other things according to God. Nor does it use God; it enjoys him. For God must not be referred to anything else. Whatever is referred to something else is inferior to that to which it is referred. Nothing is superior to God—not in place, but in the excellence of his nature [Note: Erasmus and several manuscripts: “but in the excellence of his substance.” Thus also the Lyons and Venetian manuscripts].

Therefore all things that have been made were made for human use, because reason, which was given to humanity, uses all things by judging them [Note: Two manuscripts: “the reason for judging”]. Before the fall, humanity did not use things that had to be endured; after the fall, it does not use them except when converted. And although this is before bodily death, it is already, insofar as possible, a friend of God, because it is willingly a servant.

## XXXI. Cicero’s account of how the virtues of the soul are divided and defined by him  
*(Cicero, Book 2 of On Invention)*

### 1

Virtue is a disposition of the soul in agreement with the nature and rule of reason. Therefore, once all its parts have been understood, the entire power of simple honor will have been considered. It has four parts: prudence, justice, courage, and temperance.

Prudence is knowledge of good, evil, and neutral things [Note: Some manuscripts, as in Cicero: “knowledge of good and evil and of both kinds”]. Its parts are memory, understanding, and foresight.

Memory is that by which the soul recalls things that have been. Understanding is that by which it perceives things that are. Foresight is that by which something future is seen before it has happened.

Justice is a disposition of the soul that, while preserving the common advantage, assigns to each person his due dignity. Its beginning arose from nature; then certain things entered customary practice on the basis of usefulness; afterward, fear of the laws and religious observance sanctioned things that had arisen from nature and been approved by custom.

Natural right is what opinion did not generate, but what an innate force implanted—for example, religion, filial piety, gratitude, retribution, respect, and truth.

Religion is that which brings care and ceremonial observance toward some superior nature, which they call divine.

Filial piety is that by which a benevolent duty toward those joined to us by blood and toward our country, together with diligent reverence, is rendered.

Gratitude is that which contains remembrance of friendships and services, together with the willingness to repay the service of the other [Note: Here “of the other” was missing; it is restored from manuscripts and from Cicero].

Retribution is that by which force or injury, and altogether everything that is harmful, is driven away by defense or vengeance.

Respect is that by which we honor with a certain observance and distinction people who excel in some dignity.

Truth is that by which things that are, have been, or will be are spoken of without alteration.

Right by custom is what either, having been lightly derived from nature, has been strengthened and enlarged by usage, such as religion—and whenever we see that something arising from nature has been made greater through custom—or what antiquity has brought into practice with the approval of the populace.

Of this kind are agreement, equality, law, and judgment [Note: The word “law” is absent from the Ratian manuscript and three others].

An agreement is what has been settled among some people. Equality is what is equal for everyone [Note: Several manuscripts and Cicero: “what is equitable”]. A judgment is what has already been established by the decision of one person or of several.

Right by law is what is contained in a written document set before the people for their observance.

Courage is considered acceptance of dangers and endurance of hardships. Its parts are magnificence, confidence, patience, and perseverance.

Magnificence is the undertaking and administration of great and lofty matters with a certain broad and splendid conception of mind [Note: The printed editions have “thought.” But the better manuscripts and Cicero have “undertaking”].

Confidence is that by which the mind itself places great trust in itself, together with certain hope, in great and honorable matters.

Patience is the voluntary and prolonged endurance of difficult and arduous things for the sake of honor or usefulness.

Perseverance is steadfast and continuous persistence in a course of action carefully considered.

Temperance is the firm and moderate rule of reason over desire and over the soul’s other unruly impulses. Its parts are self-restraint, clemency, and modesty.

Self-restraint is that by which desire is governed through the direction of counsel.

Clemency is that by which the soul’s impulses, rashly drawn and stirred into hatred of someone, are held back by gentleness [Note: Several manuscripts and Cicero: “by which the soul’s impulses, stirred into an attack against someone and driven into hatred, are held back by gentleness”].

Modesty is that by which honorable shame acquires a clear [Note: The Ratian manuscript and three others: “dear”] and stable authority.

### 2

All these things are to be sought for their own sake alone, with no advantage added. Demonstrating this does not belong to our present purpose and is remote from the brevity appropriate to instruction.

Things are to be avoided for their own sake—not only those opposed to these virtues, such as cowardice opposed to courage and injustice opposed to justice, but also those that appear close and neighboring, while actually being very far away. Thus lack of confidence is contrary to confidence and is therefore a vice; daring is not contrary to it, but adjacent and close, and yet it too is a vice.

In this way, a vice neighboring each virtue will be found, either already designated by a definite name—such as daring, which is adjacent to confidence; stubbornness, which is adjacent to perseverance; and superstition, which is close to religion—or without any definite name. We shall likewise place all these among the things to be avoided, as opposites of good qualities.

Enough has been said about that kind of honor which is sought entirely for its own sake. Now we should speak about the kind to which usefulness is also added, although we nevertheless call it honorable.

### 3

There are many things that attract us both by their dignity and by their benefit. In this category are glory, dignity, greatness, and friendship.

Glory is frequent report about someone accompanied by praise.

Dignity is an authority that is honorable and worthy of respect, honor, and modesty [Note: Erasmus and Lovaniensis: “the authority of someone’s honorableness.” But the Ratian manuscript and several others, together with Cicero, have “honorable authority.” The Michaelinus manuscript has “with honor.” The Lyons and Venetian manuscripts have “the authority of someone’s honorableness,” as Erasmus and Lovaniensis].

Greatness is power, majesty, or great abundance of some resources [Note: Several manuscripts and Ciceronian books: “power or majesty”].

Friendship is goodwill toward someone concerning good things, for the sake of the very person whom one loves, together with a corresponding goodwill on his part.

Since we are speaking here about civil affairs, we add benefit to friendship, so that it may appear that friendship too is to be sought for their sake, lest those who think that we are speaking about every kind of friendship perhaps reproach us [Note: In some manuscripts and in Ciceronian books: “who think that we are speaking about every kind of friendship may begin to reproach us”; and below they have “be established” in place of “be appointed”].

There are some who think friendship should be sought only for usefulness, some only for its own sake, and some both for its own sake and for usefulness. Where the truth lies among these views will be considered elsewhere.

## XXXII. Whether one person understands anything more than another, and whether understanding of the same thing therefore proceeds to infinity

Whoever understands anything differently from the way that thing is, is mistaken; and everyone who is mistaken does not understand the matter about which he is mistaken. Therefore whoever understands anything differently from the way it is does not understand it. Nothing, then, can be understood except as it is.

Yet we understand something not as it is—for example, we understand this very proposition, “Nothing is understood,” which is not understood as it is. Therefore there is no doubt that perfect understanding exists, beyond which nothing more excellent can exist. Consequently, understanding of each thing does not proceed to infinity, nor can one person understand it more than another.

## XXXIII. On fear

There is no doubt that the only cause of fear is the possibility that we may either lose what we love after obtaining it, or fail to obtain what we hope for.

Therefore, if someone loves and possesses the state of not fearing itself, what fear is there that he might lose it? We fear losing many things that we love and possess, and so we guard them through fear; but no one can guard against fear by fearing.

Likewise, whoever loves not fearing and does not yet possess it, and hopes to possess it, ought not to fear that he will fail to obtain it. For by this fear nothing is feared except that same fear. Every fear, moreover, flees from something, and nothing flees from itself. Therefore fear is not feared.

But if someone thinks it incorrect to say that fear fears something, since the soul rather fears through fear itself, let him attend to what is easy to recognize: there is no fear except of an evil that is future and impending. Whoever fears must therefore flee from something. Hence whoever fears fear is utterly absurd, because in fleeing he possesses the very thing he flees.

Since one fears only that some evil may happen, fearing that fear may happen is nothing other than embracing what one rejects. If this is contradictory, as it is, then whoever loves nothing except not fearing does not fear at all. For this reason no one can love only this and not possess it. Whether this alone ought to be loved is another question.

Now the person whom fear does not dismay is not ravaged by desire, worn down by distress, or tossed about by eager and empty joy. If he desires something—for desire is nothing other than love of transient things—he must fear either losing them after obtaining them or failing to obtain them. But he does not fear; therefore he does not desire.

Likewise, if he is troubled by mental distress, he must also be agitated by fear, since anxiety concerns present evils, while fear concerns impending ones. But he is free from fear; therefore he is also free from anxiety.

Again, if he rejoices emptily, he rejoices over things that he can lose; therefore he must fear losing them. But he does not fear in any way; therefore he does not rejoice emptily in any way.

## XXXIV. Whether anything other than freedom from fear should be loved

If not fearing is a vice, it should not be loved. But no supremely blessed person fears, and no supremely blessed person is in vice. Therefore not fearing is not a vice.

Daring, however, is a vice. Therefore not everyone who does not fear is daring, although everyone who dares is without fear.

Again, every corpse does not fear. Thus not fearing is common to the supremely blessed person, the daring person, and the corpse; but the supremely blessed person possesses it through tranquility of soul, the daring person through recklessness, and the corpse because it lacks every sense.

Therefore not fearing should not be rejected, since we wish to be blessed; but it should not be loved alone, since we do not wish to be reckless and lifeless.

## XXXV. What should be loved

### 1

Since whatever does not live does not fear, and no one would persuade us to be deprived of life so that we might also be free from fear, what should be loved is living without fear.

But since a life without fear, if it also lacks understanding, is not desirable, what should be loved is living with understanding and without fear.

Should this alone be loved? Or should love itself also be loved? Indeed it should, since without it the other things are not loved. But if love is loved for the sake of other things that ought to be loved, it is not correctly said to be loved [Note: Thus the Ratian manuscript and eighteen others. Erasmus and Lovaniensis: “love is not correctly spoken of.” The Lyons and Venetian manuscripts: “to be loved”].

For loving is nothing other than desiring a thing for its own sake. Should love, then, be desired for its own sake, when, if what is loved is absent, there is unmistakable misery?

Moreover, since love is a kind of movement, and no movement exists except toward something, when we ask what should be loved, we are asking what that object is toward which one ought to move. Therefore, if love is to be loved, not every kind of love is to be loved.

There is also a shameful love by which the soul pursues things inferior to itself; this is more properly called desire, the root, of course, of all evils. Therefore what can be taken away from enduring and enjoying love should not be loved [Note: The Ratian manuscript and eight others: “from the lover”].

For what object should love be loved, except that which cannot be absent while it is being loved? That is what it means to have nothing other than to know [Note: Four manuscripts, together with Eugyppius: “to have nothing other than to know as it ought to be known.” Below: “No one therefore knows the blessed life as it ought to be known.” The addition is taken from Book 1, chapter 26 of the Retractations].

Possessing gold and every body is not the same as knowing it; therefore it should not be loved.

And since something can be loved without being possessed—not only among things that ought not to be loved, such as a beautiful body, but also among things that ought to be loved, such as the blessed life—and since, conversely, something can be possessed without being loved, such as fetters, it is rightly asked whether someone can fail to love what it means merely to know when he possesses it—that is, when he knows it.

Yet we see some people study numbers for no other reason, for example, than to become wealthy through that discipline or to please other people; and when they have learned it, they direct it toward the same end that they had set before themselves when they were learning it. Since possessing any discipline is nothing other than knowing it, it is possible for someone to possess something whose possession is identical with knowing it, and yet not love it.

Nevertheless, no one can perfectly possess or know a good that he does not love. For who can know how great is the good that he does not enjoy? He does not enjoy it if he does not love it. Therefore he does not possess what ought to be loved if he does not love it, even if someone who does not possess it might be able to love it.

No one, then, knows the blessed life and is miserable, because if it is to be loved as it is—and to know it is to possess it [Note: Book 1, chapter 26 of the Retractations].

### 2

Since this is so, what is it other than living blessedly to possess something eternal by knowing it? For what is eternal is the only thing on which one can rightly rely: it cannot be taken away from the person who loves it. And it is precisely what it means to possess nothing other than to know.

Of all things, what is eternal is the most excellent; therefore we can possess it only through that by which we are superior to other things, namely, the mind. Whatever is possessed by the mind is possessed through knowing; and no good is perfectly known unless it is perfectly loved.

But just as the mind alone can know, it cannot therefore love alone. Love is a kind of desire, and we see desire also existing in the other parts of the soul. If that desire agrees with the mind and reason, the mind will be free, in such peace and tranquility, to contemplate what is eternal.

Therefore the soul ought also, through its other parts, to love this great reality that must be known by the mind. And since what is loved must necessarily affect the lover from itself, it follows that when what is eternal is loved, it affects the soul with eternity.

Accordingly, that life is finally blessed which is eternal. What, however, is eternal and can affect the soul with eternity, except God?

Love of things that ought to be loved is better called charity or devotion. Therefore, with all the powers of thought, we must consider that most salutary commandment: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind” (Matthew 22:37); and what the Lord Jesus said: “This is eternal life: that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John 17:3).

## XXXVI. On nourishing charity

### 1

I call charity that by which things are loved that are not to be despised in comparison with the lover himself—that is, what is eternal, and what can love the eternal itself [Note: Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions have: “I call charity the movement of the soul by which…”].

God, therefore, and the soul by which he is loved [Note: Some manuscripts: “by which they are loved”], are properly called charity, most pure and consummated, if nothing else is loved [Note: Book 1, chapter 26 of the Retractations]. It is also pleasing to call this devotion.

But when God is loved more than the soul, so that a person prefers to belong to God rather than to himself, then the soul is truly and supremely cared for, and consequently the body as well—not because some desire is anxiously working for us, but because we simply take what is readily available and offered.

The poison of charity is hope of acquiring or retaining temporal things. Its nourishment is the diminution of desire; its perfection is the absence of all desire. The sign of its progress is the diminution of fear; the sign of its perfection is the absence of all fear. For desire is the root of all evils (1 Timothy 6:10), and “perfect love casts out fear” (1 John 4:18).

Whoever wishes to nourish charity should therefore apply himself to diminishing desires. Desire is love of acquiring or possessing temporal things. The beginning of its diminution is fear of God, who alone cannot be feared without being loved.

For one strives toward wisdom, and nothing is truer than what has been said: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ecclesiasticus 1:16).

No one fails to flee pain more than he seeks pleasure. We see even the most savage beasts deterred from the greatest pleasures by fear of pain; and when this has become habitual for them, they are called tamed and domesticated.

Therefore, since human beings possess reason, which, when it serves desire through a miserable perversion, suggests that people can avoid being detected by hiding what they have done and devises the cleverest deceits for concealing secret sins, it follows that people who are not yet delighted by the beauty of virtue are harder to tame than wild animals—unless they are deterred from sinning by punishments, which are most truthfully proclaimed through holy and divine men, and unless they acknowledge that what they conceal from human beings cannot be concealed from God.

To make God feared, one must persuade people that the universe is governed by divine providence—not so much through arguments, since whoever can grasp them can already perceive the beauty of virtue, but through examples, whether recent, if any arise, or drawn from history, especially those that, through the action of divine providence itself, have received the highest authority in religion, whether in the Old or the New Testament.

At the same time, one must speak both about the punishments of sins and about the rewards of right actions.

### 2

When some habit of not sinning has persuaded a person that what had seemed burdensome is easy, the sweetness of piety should begin to be tasted, and the beauty of virtue should be commended, so that the freedom of charity may stand out above slavery to fear.

Then the faithful, after receiving the sacraments of regeneration—which must necessarily move them deeply—should be instructed about the difference between two people: the old and the new, the outer and the inner, the earthly and the heavenly. That is, they should learn the difference between the person who pursues carnal and temporal goods and the person who pursues spiritual and eternal things.

They must be warned not to expect from God perishable and transient benefits, with which wicked people too may abound, but rather firm and everlasting benefits, for the sake of receiving which everything considered good or evil in this world must be utterly despised.

Here that preeminent and unique example of the Lord’s human being must be set before them [Note: Eugyppius in two manuscripts: “the example of the Lord must be set before them.” This corresponds to the passage corrected in Book 1, chapter 19 of the Retractations, where Augustine does not approve of his having at one time called Christ “the Lord’s human being”], who, while showing through so many miracles that he possessed such great power over things, both despised what the inexperienced consider great goods and endured what they consider great evils.

It must be shown, so that no one may be less willing to undertake this way of life because he honors that example all the more, both from his promises and exhortations and from the multitude of those who imitated him—the Apostles, martyrs, and countless saints—that these things are not to be regarded as hopeless.

### 3

But once the enticements of carnal pleasures have been overcome, care must be taken lest the desire to please people creep in and take their place—whether through some miraculous deeds, difficult self-restraint or endurance, some act of generosity, or under the name of knowledge or eloquence. The desire for honor belongs to the same category.

Against all these desires, the things written about the praise of charity and the emptiness of boasting should be brought forward. The person should be taught how shameful it is to wish to please those whom one would not wish to imitate.

For either such people are wicked, in which case there is nothing remarkable in being praised by the wicked; or they are good, in which case they ought to be imitated. But those who are good are good through virtue, and virtue does not desire what lies in the power of other people.

Therefore whoever imitates the good does not desire the praise of any human being; whoever imitates the wicked is not worthy of praise.

But if you wish to please people so that you may benefit them by leading them to love God, then you do not desire this any longer, but something else. Whoever desires to please still necessarily has fear: first, lest by sinning secretly he be counted by the Lord among hypocrites; then, if he desires to please through good deeds, lest, in seeking this reward, he lose what God is going to give.

### 4

Once this desire has been conquered, pride must be avoided. For it is difficult for someone who no longer wishes to please people and considers himself full of virtues to condescend to associate with them.

Fear is therefore still necessary, lest even what he appears to possess be taken away from him (Matthew 25:29), and lest, with hands and feet bound, he be cast into the outer darkness (ibid. 22:13).

Therefore fear of God not only begins wisdom but also perfects the wise person. The wise person is one who loves God supremely and his neighbor as himself.

What dangers and difficulties must be feared on this journey, and what remedies ought to be used, is another question.

## XXXVII. On what is always born

One who has always been born is better than one who is always being born. For one who is always being born has not yet been born; and if he is always being born, he has never been born and never will be born.

To be born is one thing; to have been born is another. Hence there is never a son if there has never been a birth. But because he has been born, he is always a son. Therefore he is always one who has been born.

## XXXVIII. On the formation of the soul

Since nature is one thing, discipline another, and habit another, and since these are understood in one soul without any difference of substance; and since talent is one thing, virtue another, and tranquility another, likewise within one and the same substance; and since the soul is of a substance other than God, although it was made by him, while God himself is that most sacred Trinity known by many through the word but by few in reality, we must investigate most carefully what the Lord Jesus said:

“No one comes to me unless the Father draws him” (John 6:44);

“No one comes to the Father except through me” (ibid. 14:6);

“He himself will lead you into all truth” (ibid. 16:13).

## XXXIX. On nourishment

What is it that receives the thing that it changes? An animal, for example, receives food.

What is it that is received and changed? The food itself, for example.

What is it that is received and not changed? Light by the eyes, and sound by the ears.

But the soul receives these things through the body. What, then, is it that the soul receives through itself and changes into itself? Another soul, for example, which, by receiving it into friendship, makes it like itself.

And what is it that the soul receives through itself and does not change? Truth, for example.

Therefore one must understand both what was said to Peter, “Kill and eat” (Acts 10:13), and what is said in the Gospel: “And the life was the light of human beings” (John 1:4).

## XL. If the nature of souls is one, whence do human beings have different wills?

From different visions arises a different desire of souls; from different desire, different success in obtaining; from different success, different habit; and from different habit, a different will.

The order of things produces different visions—an order indeed hidden, but nevertheless certain under divine providence. We must not therefore think that the natures of souls are different because their wills are different, since even the will of one soul varies according to differences of time.

At one time, for example, it desires to be rich; at another, having despised riches, it desires to be wise. Even in the desire for temporal things, at one time commercial activity pleases a person, and at another time military service does.

## XLI. Since God made all things, why did he not make them equal?

Because there would be no “all things” if they were equal. There would not be many kinds of things, by which the universe is composed, containing creatures arranged in first, second, and subsequent orders down to the last. This is what is meant by “all things.”

## XLII. How Christ was both in his mother’s womb and in heaven

Just as the word spoken by a human being is heard entirely by each of the many people who hear it.

## XLIII. Why the Son of God appeared in a man, and the Holy Spirit in a dove

The former came in order to show human beings an example of living; the latter appeared in the form of a dove in order to signify the very gift by which one attains that end through living well.

Both manifestations were made visible for the sake of carnal people, so that they might be transferred from things perceived by bodily eyes to things understood by the mind through the stages of the sacraments.

Words too sound and pass away; nevertheless, the things signified by words do not similarly pass away when something divine and eternal is expounded through speech.

## XLIV. Why the Lord Jesus Christ came so long afterward, and not at the beginning of human sin

Every beautiful thing derives from supreme beauty, which is God. Temporal beauty, however, is accomplished through the succession of things that decline and arise.

Each age in each human being, from infancy to old age, possesses its own beauty. Therefore, just as it would be absurd for someone subject to time to wish only the youthful age to exist in a human being—for he would begrudge the other beauties that have their own turns and order in the other ages—so it is absurd for someone to desire only one age in the whole human race, since the human race itself, as though it were one person, passes through its ages.

Nor was it fitting for the divine teacher, by whose imitation humanity was to be formed in the best practices, to come except at the time of youth [Note: Book 2, chapter 26 of the Retractations].

This is the point of what the Apostle says: that children were kept under the law as under a tutor (Galatians 3:23–24), until the one for whom they were being kept should come, the one who had been promised through the Prophets.

For one thing is what divine providence does privately with individuals, and another what it provides publicly for the whole human race [Note: Two manuscripts: “what it provides for public benefits”].

Indeed, all individuals who have attained a certain wisdom have been enlightened by the same truth, each at the appropriate time of his own age. And so, for the people to become wise, the human being was assumed by that truth at the appropriate age of the human race itself.

## XLV. Against the mathematicians
1. The ancients did not call those “mathematicians” whom people now call by that name, but rather those who investigated the numbers of time by observing the motions of heaven and the stars. Of them Scripture most rightly says: “Nor should they be forgiven. For if they were able to know enough to estimate the age of the world, how did they not more easily find its Lord?” (Wis. 13:8–9). The human mind, judging from visible things, can recognize that it is itself better than all visible things. Yet when, because of its deficiency and progress in wisdom, it acknowledges itself to be changeable, it discovers that above it there is an unchangeable truth. Clinging to that truth, as it is said, “My soul clung after you” (Ps. 62:9), it becomes blessed, finding within itself also the Creator and Lord of all visible things. It does not seek visible things externally, even though they are heavenly; for these either cannot be found, or are found in vain and only with great labor, unless from the beauty of things that are outside us one finds the craftsman who is within and who first works the higher beauties in the soul and then the lower beauties in the body.

2. Against those who are now called mathematicians—who wish to subject our actions to the heavenly bodies and sell us to the stars, while taking from us the very price for which we are sold—nothing truer or more concise can be said than that they give no answers except after receiving astrological configurations. In these configurations, they say, the zodiacal circle is marked out into 360 parts,

[Note: Thus the manuscripts; the printed editions read, “equal parts,” etc.] and the motion of heaven passes through fifteen parts in one hour, so that fifteen parts rise during as much time as one hour occupies. Each of these parts is said to contain sixty minutes. But they do not find minutes of minutes in the astrological configurations from which they claim to predict the future. The conception of twins, however, takes place through a single act of intercourse—as physicians attest, whose discipline is much more certain and evident—and occurs within so small a point of time that it does not extend even to two minutes of minutes. How, then, can there be such a diversity in the actions, outcomes, and wills of twins, who necessarily have the same configuration at conception, and for whom the astrologer assigns one configuration, as though they were one person?

[Note: Thus in the manuscripts; the printed editions read, “the astrologers assign.”]  
   
If they wish to adhere to configurations at birth, the twins themselves refute them. For twins are often delivered from the womb one after the other in such a way that the interval of time again falls within the minutes of minutes—yet they never accept such intervals as material to be handled in their configurations, nor can they handle them. When it is said that they have often predicted many things correctly, this happens because people do not retain in memory their falsehoods and errors. They pay attention only to what has occurred in accordance with their answers, forget what has not occurred, and recall events that come about not through that nonexistent art but through some obscure chance in the course of things. If they wish to attribute this to their skill, let them say that written, dead letters too can divine skillfully whatever the lot happens to produce, often according to one’s wishes. If a verse predicting the future often emerges from books without any art, why should it be surprising if some prediction of future events also emerges from the soul of a speaker—not by art, but by chance?

XLVI. On the Ideas

1. Plato is said to have been the first to call them “ideas.”  
   
[Note: Book 7 of *The City of God*, chapter 28.]

Yet if this name did not exist before he established it, it does not follow either that the things themselves that he called ideas did not exist, or that they were understood by no one. They may have been called by one name by some people and by another name by others. Anyone may assign whatever name he wishes to an unknown thing that has no customary name.

[Note: Four manuscripts read “known thing.”] For it is not plausible either that there were no wise men before Plato, or that they failed to understand whatever things Plato, as has been said, calls ideas—since such power is attributed to them that no one can be wise without understanding them. It is also believable that there were wise men among other peoples besides Greece. Plato himself sufficiently testifies to this not only by traveling for the sake of perfecting his wisdom, but also by mentioning it in his books. Therefore, if such men existed, we should not suppose that they were ignorant of ideas, although they may perhaps have called them by another name. But enough has now been said about the name; let us consider the reality, which is what must chiefly be examined and known, since names are subject to our power, so that each person may call the thing he has understood whatever he wishes.

2. In Latin, then, we may call ideas either *forms* or *species*, so that we appear to translate word for word. If we call them *reasons* (*rationes*), we depart from the proper manner of translation; for the Greeks call reasons *logoi* (λόγοι), not ideas. Nevertheless, whoever wishes to use this term will not depart from the reality itself.  
   
[Note: Almost all manuscripts read “will not recoil from it.”]

Ideas are therefore certain principal forms, or stable and unchangeable reasons of things. They themselves are not formed, and consequently are eternal and always remain in the same condition. They are contained in the divine understanding. Although they neither arise nor perish, everything that can arise and perish, and everything that does arise and perish, is nevertheless said to be formed according to them.

The soul, however, is said to be capable of beholding them only when it is rational, in that part of itself by which it excels—that is, by the mind and reason themselves—as though by a certain face or inner and intelligible eye. And even then it is not every rational soul indiscriminately that is suited to this vision, but the soul that is holy and pure. It must possess that very eye by which these things are seen in a sound, sincere, serene condition, and in a condition resembling the things it intends to see.

What religious person, instructed in true religion, even if he is not yet able to contemplate these things, would nevertheless dare to deny—or rather would not also profess—that all things which exist, that is, whatever are contained in their own kind by a particular nature so as to exist, have been created by God as their author; that all living things live by his authorship; and that the universal preservation of things, together with the very order by which changing things complete their temporal courses according to a fixed governance, is contained and governed by the laws of the supreme God?

Once this has been established and granted, who would dare say that God created all things irrationally? If this cannot rightly be said or believed, it remains that all things were created according to reason. Yet a human being was not created according to the same reason as a horse; for it would be absurd to think so. Each individual thing, therefore, was created according to its own proper reasons. Where are these reasons to be thought to exist, then, except in the very mind of the Creator? He was not looking at something placed outside himself in order to establish according to it what he was establishing; to think this is sacrilegious.

If, then, the reasons for creating all things, whether to be created or already created, are contained in the divine mind, and if nothing can exist in the divine mind except what is eternal and unchangeable; and if Plato calls these principal reasons of things “ideas,” then they are not merely ideas but are themselves true, because they are eternal and remain of such a kind, unchangeable. Through participation in them, whatever exists exists, in whatever manner it exists.

But the rational soul surpasses all the things created by God and is nearest to God when it is pure. To the extent that it is joined to him by love, to that extent it is in some manner filled and illuminated by that intelligible light of his. It sees these reasons—not through bodily eyes, but through its own principal faculty, by which it excels, that is, through its understanding. By their vision it becomes supremely blessed.

As has been said, one may call these reasons ideas, forms, species, or reasons; many are permitted to call them whatever they please.  
   
[Note: Thus most manuscripts. The printed editions instead read: “and many are permitted to call them by whatever names,” and so forth.]  
   
But very few are permitted to see what is true.

XLVII. Whether We Can Ever See Our Thoughts

It is customary to ask how, after the resurrection and transformation of the body promised to the saints, we shall be able to see our thoughts. A conjecture must therefore be drawn from that part of our body which possesses more light, since angelic bodies, such as we hope to have, must be believed to be exceedingly luminous and ethereal.

[Note: Book 10 of *The City of God*, chapters 5–6.]  
   
[Note: Book 10 of *The City of God*, chapters 5–6.]

If, then, many movements of our soul are now recognized in the eyes, it is plausible that no movement of the soul will remain hidden when the whole body has become ethereal, in comparison with which these eyes are flesh.

XLVIII. On Things That Are Believed

There are three kinds of things that are believed.

Some are always believed and are never understood, as is the case with all history, which recounts temporal and human events.

Others are understood as soon as they are believed, such as all rational principles of human knowledge, whether concerning numbers or any other disciplines.

A third kind is believed first and understood afterward. Such are the things concerning divine matters that cannot be understood except by those who are pure in heart. This occurs through observing the commands received concerning good living.

XLIX. Why Did the Children of Israel Sacrifice Visible Victims from the Herds?

Because there are also spiritual sacrifices, whose images the carnal people were required to celebrate, so that the prefiguration of the new people might be accomplished through the servitude of the old.  
   
[Note: *Retractationes* I, chapter 26, and *The City of God* XXII, chapter 29.]

The difference between these two peoples may also be observed in each one of us, since everyone must live as the old human being from his mother’s womb until he reaches youthful age.
