At that point it is no longer necessary to think in a carnal manner; one can turn by choice toward spiritual things and be regenerated inwardly. What therefore occurs in an individual properly educated, according to the order of nature and discipline, is most beautifully accomplished by divine providence in proportion throughout the whole human race.  
   
[Note: The Fossatensis manuscript reads, “what nature and discipline accomplish.” Some others read, “what occurs through the discipline of nature.”]

L. On the Equality of the Son

Since God could not beget one better than himself—for nothing is better than God—he had to beget one equal to himself. If he wished to do so but could not, he is weak; if he could but did not wish to, he is envious. It follows that he begot an equal Son.

LI. On the Human Being Made in the Image and Likeness of God

1. Since divine Scripture mentions an outward and an inward human being, and distinguishes them so clearly that the Apostle says, “Even if our outward human being is being corrupted, the inward one is renewed day by day” (2 Cor. 4:16), it may be asked whether one of these was made in the image and likeness of God. It would be foolish to ask, if only one was, which one it was. For who doubts that it is more appropriate to speak of the one who is renewed than of the one who is corrupted?

Whether both were made so is a serious question.  
   
[Note: *The Trinity* XI, chapter 1.]

For if Adam is the outward human being and Christ the inward, both are rightly understood in this way. Yet since Adam did not remain good as he was made by God, and became carnal by loving carnal things, it may reasonably appear that his fall consisted precisely in losing the image and likeness of God.

[Note: Thus the manuscripts; the printed editions read, “that this itself was for him to lack the image of God.”] Consequently, he himself is renewed, and he himself is the inward human being. How, then, is he also the outward human being?

Or is this according to the body, so that the inward human being is according to the soul, and the resurrection and renewal belong to the inward human being?

[Note: Erasmus and Lovaniensis read, “the inward human being is”; Ratramnus and the manuscripts more correctly read, “belong to the inward human being.” Lugdunensis and Venetiensis read as Erasmus and Lovaniensis.] This renewal now takes place according to the death of the former life—that is, sin—and according to the regeneration of a new life—that is, righteousness.

He likewise names these two human beings in such a way that he speaks of one as the old human being, whom we must put off, and of the other as the new human being, whom we must put on (Col. 3:9–10). Again, he calls the former the image of the earthly human being, because it is lived according to the sin of the first human being, Adam; and the latter the image of the heavenly human being (1 Cor. 15:49), because it is lived according to the righteousness of the second human being, Jesus Christ.

The outward human being, who is now being corrupted, will be renewed in the future resurrection when he has paid the debt of this death which he owes to nature, according to the law given in paradise.  
   
[Note: Here the printed editions add, “through the commandment.” The Navarrese manuscript has “after the commandment,” which is absent from nearly all the other manuscripts.]

2. How it is not incongruous to say that the body too was made in the likeness of God is easily understood by anyone who carefully considers the statement, “And God made all things very good” (Gen. 1:31). No one doubts that God himself is supremely good.

Things can be said to resemble God in many ways. Some were made according to virtue and wisdom, because in him there is uncreated virtue and wisdom. Others resemble him insofar as they merely live, because he lives supremely and first of all. Others resemble him insofar as they exist, because he supremely and first of all exists.

Therefore, things that merely exist but neither live nor possess wisdom are not perfectly but only slightly in his likeness. They are nevertheless good in their own order, since he is supremely good, from whom all good things proceed.

All things that live but do not possess wisdom participate somewhat more in his likeness. For whatever lives also exists, but not everything that exists also lives.

Those things that possess wisdom are so close to him in likeness that among created things nothing is nearer. Whatever participates in wisdom both lives and exists; whatever lives must exist, but need not possess wisdom.

Since, then, the human being can participate in wisdom according to the inward human being, according to that very inward human being he is so made in the image that no intervening nature forms him;

[Note: The printed editions read, “according to himself”; the manuscripts read, “according to it,” that is, the inward human being.] and therefore nothing is more closely joined to God. For he possesses wisdom, lives, and exists. No creature is better than this.

3. If the outward human being is understood as that life by which we perceive through the five familiar senses that we share with animals—for he too can be corrupted by the sensory afflictions inflicted through persecutions—then this human being is not without justification said to participate in the likeness of God. This is not merely because he lives, which is also evident in beasts, but more especially because he turns toward the mind that governs him, which wisdom illuminates—something impossible in beasts, which lack reason.

[Note: Lovaniensis reads, “turns the mind governing him, which,” etc.; the other printed editions and the manuscripts differ.]

The human body too, since among the bodies of earthly animals it alone is not prone and stretched upon its belly but, though visible, is raised upright to contemplate heaven, which is the principle of visible things, may rightly be considered more made in the image and likeness of God in this respect than the other bodies of animals. This is so even though it is known to live not by its own power but through the presence of the soul.

Nevertheless, it is good not only because it exists and insofar as it exists, but also because it is such that it is better suited to contemplate heaven. Yet since a human being is not rightly called a human being without life, the outward human being is perhaps more correctly understood to be not the body alone, nor the life that exists in bodily sensation alone, but both together.  
   
[Note: *Retractationes* I, chapter 26.]

4. It is also intelligently distinguished that one thing is the image and likeness of God, who is also called the Son, and another is the being made in the image and likeness of God, as we understand the human being to have been made.  
   
[Note: *The Trinity* VII, chapter 6, section 12, and *Retractationes* I, chapter 26.]

Some also reasonably understand the words “in the image” and “in the likeness” to refer to two things, since, they argue, if there were only one reality, one name would have been sufficient.

They wish the mind to have been made “in the image,” because it is formed by the truth itself without any intervening substance. It is also called spirit—not the Holy Spirit, who is of the same substance as the Father and the Son, but the spirit of the human being.

The Apostle distinguishes them in this way: “No one knows what is going on in a human being except the spirit of the human being; and no one knows what is going on in God except the Spirit of God” (1 Cor. 2:11). Likewise, concerning the human spirit he says: “May he preserve your spirit and soul and body” (1 Thess. 5:23).

This spirit too was made by God, just as the rest of creation was. For it is written in Proverbs as follows: “Know that the Lord knows the hearts of human beings, and he who formed the spirit for all knows all things” (Prov. 16:2).

Therefore this spirit is unquestionably understood to have been made in the image of God, since it contains the understanding of truth; for it clings to the truth without any intervening creature. They wish the other parts of the human being to be understood as made in the likeness, because every image is similar, but not everything that is similar is properly an image—although it may perhaps be called one improperly.

In such matters, however, care must be taken not to assert anything too forcefully. One salutary point must certainly be preserved: since every body is extended through spatial dimensions, we must not suppose that anything of this kind is the substance of God. For a thing that is smaller in a part than in the whole is incompatible with the dignity of the soul; how much less with the majesty of God?

LII. On the Statement, “It Repented Me That I Had Made the Human Being” (Gen. 6:6–7)

Divine Scripture, lifting us from an earthly and human understanding to a divine and heavenly one, descended even to the words used among themselves by the most foolish people. Thus the men through whom the Holy Spirit spoke did not hesitate to place in their books, with the greatest appropriateness, the names of those emotions that our soul experiences—emotions which anyone who understands better already recognizes as being very far removed from God.

For example, since it is extremely difficult for a human being to exact retribution without anger, they judged that the vengeance of God, which takes place entirely without such disturbance, should nevertheless be called anger.  
   
[Note: *The City of God* XV, chapter 25.]

Likewise, because husbands customarily guard the chastity of their wives through jealousy, they called that providence of God by which it is commanded and brought about that the soul not be corrupted or, by following other gods, commit adultery in a certain sense, the jealousy of God.

So too, they called the hand of God the power by which he acts; the feet of God the power by which he extends himself toward preserving and governing all things;

[Note: Ratramnus and seven manuscripts read, “toward establishing.”] the ears or eyes of God the power by which he perceives and understands all things; the face of God the power by which he manifests and makes himself known; and the other expressions of this kind.

They did so because we, to whom the speech is addressed, are accustomed to work with our hands, walk with our feet, arrive wherever the mind directs us, perceive bodily things with our ears, eyes, and other bodily senses, and make ourselves known by our face—and because anything else belonging to this sort of rule is understood in the same way.

Thus, since we ordinarily do not easily begin to change something and transfer it into another condition except by repenting, although divine providence appears to those who contemplate it with a tranquil mind to administer all things according to the most certain order, nevertheless, for the sake of humble human understanding, things that begin to exist but do not persist as long as they were expected to persist are most appropriately said to have been removed as though through God’s repentance.

[Note: Some manuscripts read, “for humble human understanding.”]  
   
[Note: Two manuscripts read, “we do not generally do so.”]

LIII. On the Gold and Silver That the Israelites Received from the Egyptians

1. Anyone who carefully observes how the dispensations of the two Testaments have been distributed in accordance with the periods of time and the ages of the human race understands, I believe, sufficiently what properly belongs to the earlier age of the human race and what belongs to the later.

For, with divine providence beautifully governing all things, the entire succession of generations from Adam to the end of the age is administered as though it were the life-span of one human being, proceeding from childhood to old age through successive stages of time.

Therefore, anyone who devotes a pious mind to the divine writings must also distinguish the stages of virtue in conduct, until one arrives at the highest and perfect virtue of the human being. Otherwise, when he finds that sometimes small things are commanded to the small and greater things to the greater, he may judge, by comparison with the greater things, that what is lesser is sinful, and may conclude that God ought not to have commanded such things to human beings.

But it would take too long now to discuss the stages of virtue. Nevertheless, enough for the present question is this: as far as deception is concerned, the highest and perfect virtue is to deceive no one and to exhibit what has been said: “Let there be in your mouth, ‘Yes, yes; No, no’” (Matt. 5:37).

Yet because this was commanded to those to whom the kingdom of heaven had already been promised, and because it is a great virtue to fulfill these greater commands to which that reward is owed—for “the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and those who use force seize it” (Matt. 11:12)—we must ask by what stages one reaches that summit and perfection.

Among these stages are those who were still being promised an earthly kingdom, so that, with this promise, they might play as children and, after obtaining from the one God, who is Lord of all, the earthly joys they still desired, might thereafter advance and grow in spirit and dare to hope even for heavenly things.  
   
[Note: The printed editions read, “and abundantly from the one God.” The word “abundantly” is absent from most manuscripts.]  
   
[Note: Erasmus and Lovaniensis read “growing further”; the manuscripts read “growing.” Lugdunensis and Venetiensis have “growing further,” as do Erasmus and Lovaniensis.]

Just as, then, the highest and almost divine virtue is to deceive no one, so the ultimate vice is to deceive anyone at all. For those moving from this ultimate vice toward that supreme virtue, there is an intermediate stage: not to deceive either a friend or a stranger, but sometimes to deceive an enemy.

Hence the poet’s line has already become nearly proverbial:

> Fraud or valor—who would ask which it is in an enemy?  
> (*Aeneid* II.390)

But since even an enemy can often be unjustly deceived—for example, when an agreement is made concerning a temporary peace, which they call a truce, and the pledge is not kept, or in other cases of this kind—the person who, although he wishes to deceive an enemy, does not deceive him except by divine authority is much more purified and much closer to that supreme virtue. For God alone, or certainly far more excellently and sincerely than human beings, knows what punishment or reward each person deserves.

2. God, therefore, does not deceive anyone by himself; for he is the Father of Truth, and Truth, and the Spirit of Truth. Yet, distributing what is appropriate to those who deserve it—for this too belongs to justice and truth—he makes use of souls according to their merits and dignities, which exist in their respective stages.

Thus, if someone deserves to be deceived, God not only does not deceive him by himself, but does not do so through a person who already appropriately loves and continues to preserve the command, “Let there be in your mouth, ‘Yes, yes; No, no,’” nor through an angel for whom the role of deception is unsuitable. Rather, he does so either through a person who has not yet cast off such desires, or through an angel who, because of the perversity of his will, has been assigned to the lowest stages of nature, either for the punishment of sins or for the testing and purification of those who are being reborn according to God.

For we read that a king was deceived by the false prophecy of pseudoprophets.  
   
[Note: Namely, Ahab.]

We read the account in such a way that we find that it happened neither without divine judgment—for he deserved to be deceived in this manner—nor through an angel to whom the task of deception ought not to have been assigned. Rather, it happened through an angel of error, who voluntarily and gladly requested that such a role be assigned to him (1 Kings 22:6–36).

In certain passages of Scripture, something is explained more openly, so that a diligent and pious reader may understand it also in other passages where it is less clearly revealed. For our God so governed the divine books through the Holy Spirit for the salvation of souls that he wished not only to nourish us with what is manifest but also to exercise us through what is obscure.

From this ineffable and sublime administration of things, which takes place through divine providence, a natural law has, as it were, been transcribed into the rational soul, so that in the conduct and earthly customs of this life human beings preserve images of such distributions.

This is why a judge considers it unworthy of his office and criminal to strike a condemned person himself; yet by his command the executioner does so. The executioner has been assigned to this office because of his own cupidity, so that he strikes the condemned under the regulation of the laws, although he could also strike an innocent person through his own cruelty.

The judge does not do this himself, nor through a ruler, advocate, or anyone else in whose office such a ministry is not appropriately placed.

This is also why we use irrational animals for things that it would be criminal to have done by human beings. A thief is certainly worthy of being torn by a bite, but a human being does not do this himself, or through his son, his household member, or even his servant. He does it through a dog, an animal for which such actions are suitable according to its place in nature.

When, therefore, it is fitting for some to suffer something that it is not fitting for others to do, there are certain intermediate ministries through which appropriate duties are assigned. Justice, using these ministries, not only commands that each person suffer what it is fitting for him to suffer, but also that those perform the actions for whom it is no less fitting to perform them.

Since, then, the Egyptians were worthy of deception, and the people of Israel, according to that stage of the human race, were still established at such a level of conduct that it was not improper for them to deceive an enemy, it came about that God commanded—or rather, in accordance with their desire, permitted—that they ask the Egyptians for golden and silver vessels, which those still longing for an earthly kingdom coveted, intending not to return them, and receive them as though they intended to return them (Exod. 3:22).

[Note: Thus Ratramnus and the manuscripts; Erasmus and Lovaniensis read, “of an earthly thing.” Lugdunensis and Venetiensis likewise read “of an earthly thing.”]

God wished this to be both a not-unjust reward for such a long period of labor and work, in view of the condition of those souls, and a punishment for those whom he rightly caused to lose what they ought to have returned.

God, therefore, is not a deceiver—as anyone can understand it would be criminal and impious to believe—but the most just distributor of merits and persons. He does some things by himself, things worthy of and appropriate to him alone, such as illuminating souls and making them wise and blessed by offering himself to them for enjoyment.

Other things he does through a creation that serves him and has been assigned by the most upright laws according to merits. Some things he commands, others he permits, extending even to the care of sparrows, as the Lord says in the Gospel, and even to the beauty of grass and the numbering of our hairs, with divine providence extending and reaching to all these things (Matt. 10:29–30; Luke 12:27–28).

Of this it has also been said: “She reaches from end to end mightily and orders all things gently” (Wis. 8:1).

3. That God punishes through the ministries of souls serving his laws and repays punishments appropriately to those who deserve them, while he himself remains perfectly tranquil, is written most openly as follows:

> You consider it strange to condemn even one who ought not to be punished, as though it were alien to your power. For your power is the beginning of justice; and because you are Lord of all, you make yourself merciful to all. You display your power when you are not believed to be consummate in power, and you convict the boldness of those who know it. But you, Lord of powers, judge with tranquility and govern us with great reverence.  
> (Wis. 12:15–18)

[Note: Ratramnus and Lovaniensis read: “you condemn one who ought to be punished and consider him strange.” The text has been emended in accordance with Erasmus and the manuscripts.]

4. The Lord also shows that what is first done in earthly matters becomes a stage toward heavenly justice, which is commanded to those who are already more firmly established, when he says:

[Note: Erasmus and Lovaniensis read, “which is commanded to those already weaker.” Several manuscripts more correctly read, “which is commanded to those already more firmly established”; one manuscript reads, “which is not commanded to the weaker.” Lugdunensis and Venetiensis read “weaker.”] “If you were not faithful in what belongs to another, who will give you what is yours?” (Luke 16:12).

He also demonstrates that souls are taught according to their respective stages when he says: “I have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now” (John 16:12).

And the Apostle says: “I could not speak to you, brothers, as spiritual people, but as carnal people. I gave you milk to drink, not food; for you were not able to receive it. Indeed, you are not yet able, for you are still carnal” (1 Cor. 3:1–2).

What was done in these cases according to their stages, we recognize as having been done throughout the human race, so that different things were commanded to the carnal people and to the spiritual people, in accordance with the appropriateness of the times.

It is therefore not surprising that those who were still worthy of deceiving an enemy were commanded to deceive an enemy who was worthy of deception.

[Note: Ratramnus and most manuscripts read, “worthy of deception.”] For they were not yet suited to being told, “Love your enemies,” but were such as could only appropriately be told, “You shall love your neighbor and hate your enemy” (Matt. 5:44, 43).

[Note: Erasmus and Lovaniensis read, “could be told”; Ratramnus and most manuscripts read, “ought to be told.”] For it was not yet the time to teach how broadly that neighbor was to be understood.

Thus a beginning was made under a pedagogue, so that perfection might be reserved for the teacher. Yet it was the same God who gave the pedagogue to children—namely, the law through his servant—and the teacher to the mature, namely, the Gospel through his Only Son.

[Note: Erasmus and Lovaniensis read, “the teaching to the mature.” The reading “the teacher” is restored from Ratramnus and several manuscripts; Lugdunensis and Venetiensis read as Erasmus and Lovaniensis.]

LIV. On the Statement, “But for Me It Is Good to Cling to God” (Ps. 72:28)

[Col. 0038]

Everything that exists either always exists in the same way or does not. And every soul is better than every body. For everything that gives life is better than that which is given life; and no one doubts that the body is given life by the soul, not the soul by the body.  
   
[Note: Some manuscripts read: “The body is given life by the soul, but the soul is not given life by the body. Therefore no one doubts that the soul is better than every body.”]

Whatever is not a body but nevertheless exists is either a soul or something better than a soul. Nothing is worse than every body, for if someone calls matter the source from which the body itself is made, it is rightly said to be nothing, since it lacks every form.

Again, between body and soul there is nothing that is better than body but worse than soul. For if there were some intermediate thing, it would either give life to the soul, be given life by the soul, or be neither; or it would give life to the body, be given life by the body, or be neither.

But whatever is given life by the soul is a body; and whatever gives life to the soul is better than the soul. Again, that by which the body is given life is the soul; and that which is given life by the body is nothing.

But what is neither—something that needs no life and gives no life—is either altogether nothing, or something better than both body and soul.

[Note: Lovaniensis reads “understanding,” corruptly and contrary to the other printed editions and the manuscripts.] Whether anything of this kind exists in nature is another question.

For now, reason has established that there is nothing between body and soul which is better than body and worse than soul. Whatever is better than every soul we call God.  
   
[Note: *Retractationes* I, chapter 25.]

Whoever understands him is joined to him. For what is understood is true, whereas not everything that is believed is true. Whatever is true and is separated from the senses and from the mind can be believed only; it cannot nevertheless be sensed or understood.

That which understands God is therefore joined to God. The rational soul does understand God, for it understands what is always of the same kind and suffers no change. But the body undergoes change through times and places, and the rational soul itself undergoes change, since at one time it is wise and at another foolish.

What always remains in the same condition is certainly better than what does not. Nothing is better than the rational soul except God.

When, therefore, it understands something that always remains in the same condition, it undoubtedly understands that very thing. This is truth itself. Since the rational soul is joined to it through understanding, and since this is good for the soul, the statement “But for me it is good to cling to God” is rightly understood to mean this.

LV. On the Statement, “There Are Sixty Queens, Eighty Concubines, and Maidens without Number” (Song 6:7)

The number ten can signify the complete knowledge of the whole. If this is referred to inward and intelligible things, which are signified by the number six, it becomes, as it were, ten times six, which is sixty. If it is referred to earthly and corruptible things, which can be signified by the number eight, it becomes ten times eight, which is eighty.

The queens, therefore, are souls reigning in intelligible and spiritual things.

The concubines are those who receive the reward of earthly things, concerning whom it was said, “They have received their reward” (Matt. 6:2).

The maidens without number are those whose knowledge is not determined and who may be endangered by various doctrines. Thus “number” signifies a certain and indisputable confirmation of knowledge.

LVI. On the Forty-Six Years in Which the Temple Was Built
Six, nine, twelve, and eighteen, added together, make forty-five [Note: The printed editions read, “these make forty-five altogether.” But most manuscripts read, “these make forty-five in sum.”]. Add one itself, therefore, and the result is forty-six; multiplied by six, this makes two hundred and seventy-six. Human conception is said to proceed and be completed in such a way that during the first six days it has, as it were, the appearance of milk; during the following nine days it is converted into blood; then, over twelve days, it becomes solid; during the remaining eighteen days it is formed until all the members have acquired their complete outlines; and thereafter, during the remaining time until birth, it increases in size. Thus, adding one to the forty-five days—a number signifying the total, since six, nine, twelve, and eighteen combined make forty-five—there are, as stated, forty-six. When these are multiplied by the number six itself, which holds the primary place in this ordering, they make two hundred and seventy-six: that is, nine months and six days, reckoned from the eighth day before the Kalends of April, on which day the Lord is believed to have been conceived, because on that same day he also suffered, until the eighth day before the Kalends of January, on which day he was born. It is therefore not without reason that the temple is said to have been built in forty-six years, since it signified his body (John 2:20–21): so that as many years as the temple took to construct, so many days were required for the perfection of the Lord’s body [Note: Book 4 of *On the Trinity*, chapter 5.].

LVII. On the one hundred and fifty-three fish

1. “All things are yours, and you are Christ’s, and Christ is God’s” (1 Cor. 3:22–23). If these are counted from the head, they are found to be one, two, three, and four. Again: “The head of the woman is man, the head of man is Christ, and the head of Christ is God” (ibid. 11:3). If they are counted in the same way, they likewise amount to one, two, three, and four. Moreover, one, two, three, and four taken together make ten. Therefore the number ten rightly signifies the discipline that reveals God the Creator and the created creature. And when the perfect and imperishable body is subjected to the perfect and imperishable soul, and the soul in turn is subjected to Christ, and Christ to God—not as someone unlike or of another nature, but as the Son to the Father—this whole order is again rightly signified by the same number ten, which is believed to be what will endure eternally after the resurrection of the body. Perhaps for this reason those who are hired for the vineyard receive a denarius as their wage (Matt. 20:2). And just as one, two, three, and four together make ten, so one, two, three, and four multiplied four times make forty.

2. But if the number four rightly signifies the body, on account of the four most familiar qualities of which it consists—dry and moist, cold and hot—and because progression from a point to length, from length to breadth, and from breadth to height produces the solidity of a body, which is likewise contained in the number four, then the number forty is not improperly understood to signify the temporal dispensation accomplished for our salvation, when the Lord assumed a body and deigned to appear visibly among human beings. For one, two, three, and four, which signify the Creator and the creature, multiplied four times—that is, demonstrated temporally through the body—make forty. The difference between four and fourfold is that four denotes a state, while fourfold denotes movement. Therefore, just as four refers to the body, so fourfold refers to time; and the mystery enacted bodily and temporally is conveyed for the sake of those who were entangled in love of bodies and subject to times [Note: Most manuscripts read, “and subject to temporal things.”].

Thus, as stated, the number forty is believed appropriately to signify the temporal dispensation itself. Perhaps this is what is signified when the Lord fasted for forty days (Matt. 4:2), displaying the poverty of this world, which is conducted through the movement of bodies and through time; and when he remained with his disciples for forty days after the resurrection, thereby, I believe, indicating to them this same temporal dispensation that he accomplished for our salvation. The number forty, when its parts by which it is measured are counted, reaches the number fifty, thereby commending the same point, since the parts by which it is measured are equal to one another: for when bodily and visible action is administered temporally with equity, it brings human beings to perfection. This perfection, as stated, is signified by the number ten; just as the number forty, when its equal parts are reduced to a sum, produces the number ten, since it reaches fifty, as was said above. For one, which is contained forty times in forty; two, which is contained twenty times; four, which is contained ten times; five, which is contained eight times; eight, which is contained five times; ten, which is contained four times; and twenty, which is contained twice—taken together—make fifty. No other number can measure forty by equal parts except those we have enumerated and, when counted, brought to the number fifty.

Therefore, after the Lord had completed forty days with his disciples after the resurrection—that is, after commending to them what had been accomplished temporally for our sake—he ascended into heaven; and after another ten days he sent the Holy Spirit (Acts 1:3, 9; 2:1–4), so that those who had believed in visible and temporal things might be perfected spiritually for the reception of invisible things. By those very ten days after which he sent the Holy Spirit, he indicated the same perfection conferred through the Holy Spirit by the number ten, which the number forty produces when its equal parts are counted, making fifty. In the same way, through a temporal dispensation administered with equity, one reaches the perfection signified by the number ten; and ten together with forty makes fifty.

Therefore, since the perfection brought about through the Holy Spirit, so long as we still walk in the flesh—even though we do not live according to the flesh—is joined to that temporal dispensation, the number fifty rightly appears to pertain to the Church, but to the Church already purified and perfected, which embraces in love the faith of the temporal dispensation and the hope of the future eternity [Note: The Navarricus manuscript reads, “which embraces in hope and love.”]—that is, as though joining the number forty to the number ten.

This Church, to which the number fifty pertains, reaches one hundred and fifty either because it is chosen from three classes of human beings—Jews, Gentiles, and carnal Christians—or because it is imbued with the mystery of the Trinity, the number being multiplied by three. For fifty multiplied by three makes one hundred and fifty. When the same three are added to this, because what is washed in the bath of regeneration in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit ought to be distinguished and eminent (Matt. 28:19), the result is one hundred and fifty-three. This is the number of fish that were found because the nets were cast on the right side; and therefore it contains large fish (John 21:6, 11), that is, those who are perfect and suited for the kingdom of heaven. For that likeness of a net which was not cast on the right side caught both good and evil together, who are separated on the shore (Matt. 13:48). At present, within the nets of God’s commandments and sacraments, in the Church that now exists, good and evil are found together. But there is a separation at the end of the world, as at the end of the sea, that is, on the shore; when the righteous first reign temporally, as it is written in the Apocalypse, and then eternally in that city described there (Rev. 21), where, once the temporal dispensation signified by the number forty has come to rest, the number ten remains—the reward that the saints who labor in the vineyard will receive.

3. If this number is also considered, it may suggest the holiness of the Church brought about through our Lord Jesus Christ. Since the creature is constituted by the number seven, when the number three is assigned to the soul and the number four to the body, the assumption of humanity itself may be understood as being carried to three times seven. For the Father sent the Son, and the Father is in the Son, and he was born from a virgin through the gift of the Holy Spirit. These are three: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Seven times over, humanity itself was assumed in a temporal dispensation [Note: The printed editions read, “was assumed.” The word “was” is absent from the manuscripts.], so that it might become everlasting. The total is therefore twenty-one, that is, three times seven.

This assumption of humanity served for the liberation of the Church, of which he is the head (Eph. 5:23), so that the Church itself, on account of soul and body, might be restored according to the same number seven [Note: So in the manuscripts. The printed editions read, “of which he is the head, Christ. But the Church itself, on account of soul and body, is found according to the same number seven.”]. Thus twenty-one is multiplied by seven, on account of those who are liberated through the Lord’s humanity, and together they make one hundred and forty-seven. To this is added the number six, a sign of perfection, since it is constituted by its own parts, which measure it, so that nothing less and nothing more is found. One measures it by being contained six times; two by being contained three times; and three by being contained twice. These, added together—one, two, and three—make six. Perhaps this also pertains to the mystery that God completed all his works on the sixth day (Gen. 2:2).

When six is therefore added to one hundred and forty-seven, since six is a sign of perfection, the result is one hundred and fifty-three. This is the number of fish found after, at the Lord’s command, the nets were cast on the right side, where sinners belonging to the left are not found.

LVIII. On John the Baptist

1. Considering the Scripture that is read about John the Baptist in the Gospel, it is not without reason, on the basis of many plausible indications, that he is believed to bear the figure of prophecy—especially because the Lord says of him, “More than a prophet” (Matt. 11:9). He represents the image of the whole of prophecy that was made concerning the Lord from the beginning of the human race until the Lord’s coming. In the Lord himself there is the figure of the Gospel, which was foretold through prophecy, and whose proclamation increases throughout the whole world from the Lord’s coming onward; but prophecy decreases after what it foretold has arrived. Therefore the Lord says: “The Law and the Prophets were until John the Baptist; from that time the kingdom of God is proclaimed” (Luke 16:16). John himself says: “He must increase, but I must decrease” (John 3:30).

This was also represented by the days on which they were born and by the deaths they suffered. John was born when the days begin to grow shorter; the Lord was born when the days begin to grow longer. John is diminished in the head when he is killed; Christ, however, is lifted up on the cross. Once prophecy itself, embodied in John, had pointed with its finger to the one whom it had sung as destined to come from the beginning of the human race, it began to decrease, and from that point the proclamation of the kingdom of God began to increase. For this reason John baptized for repentance (Matt. 3:11): the old life comes to an end in repentance, and from that point the new life begins.

2. It is understood by those who piously seek and are divinely assisted in investigating these matters that prophecy was not silent only among those who were expressly called prophets, but also in the history itself of the Old Testament. It appears most clearly, however, in those more evident figures of events: Abel the righteous is killed by his brother (Gen. 4:8), and the Lord by the Jews; Noah’s ark is governed through the flood of the world as the Church is governed (ibid. 7:1); Isaac is led to be sacrificed to God, and the ram in his place is recognized among the thorns as though crucified (ibid. 22:3–13); in Abraham’s two sons, one by a slave woman and the other by a free woman, the two Testaments are understood (Gal. 4:22–24); two peoples are prefigured in the twins Esau and Jacob (Gen. 25:23); Joseph, having suffered persecution from his brothers, is honored by strangers (Gen. 37; 41), just as the Lord, while persecuted by the Jews, was glorified among the Gentiles.

It would take too long to recall each example, since the Apostle concludes the matter in this way: “These things happened to them as a figure; but they were written for our sake, upon whom the end of the ages has come” (1 Cor. 10:11). The end of the ages, like the old age of the old human being, is marked by the sixth age, if the whole human race is constituted as one human being; in this age the Lord came. There are also six ages in a single human life: infancy, childhood, adolescence, youth, maturity, and old age.

The first age of the human race is therefore from Adam to Noah. The second is from Noah to Abraham; these divisions are especially clear and well known. The third is from Abraham to David, for this is how the evangelist Matthew divides them (Matt. 1:17). The fourth is from David to the deportation to Babylon. The fifth is from the deportation to Babylon to the Lord’s coming. The sixth, from the Lord’s coming to the end of the world, is to be awaited: in it the outward human being is corrupted as though by old age—he is also called the old human being—while the inward human being is renewed day by day (2 Cor. 4:16). After this comes everlasting rest, which is signified by the Sabbath.

This interpretation corresponds to the fact that the human being was made on the sixth day in the image and likeness of God (Gen. 1:27). No one is unaware that human life, once engaged in some administration, is supported by knowledge and action. For action without knowledge is rash, and knowledge without action is idle. But the first life of the human being, which is rightly believed to have no administration, is devoted to the five bodily senses: sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch. Therefore the first two ages of the human race are defined by ten generations each, like infancy and childhood—five doubled, since generation is propagated through both sexes. Thus there are ten generations from Adam to Noah, and another ten from Noah to Abraham; these are the two ages that we have called the infancy and childhood of the human race.

Adolescence, youth, and maturity—that is, the periods from Abraham to David, from David to the deportation to Babylon, and from there to the Lord’s coming—are represented by fourteen generations: seven doubled, according to the same principle of generation in both sexes, with action and knowledge added to the five bodily senses [Note: The *Ratio* and ten manuscripts read, “according to the same principle”; the printed editions read, “according to the same reasoning.”].

Old age, however, is also accustomed to last as long as all the other ages together. For since old age is said to begin at the sixtieth year, and human life can extend to one hundred and twenty years, it is clear that old age alone can last as long as all the preceding ages together. It is therefore uncertain by how many generations the final age of the human race, which begins with the Lord’s coming and continues to the end of the world, is to be reckoned. God wisely willed this to remain hidden, as it is written in the Gospel (Matt. 24:36), and as the Apostle testifies when he says that the day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night (1 Thess. 5:2).

3. Nevertheless, that the human race was visited in the sixth age through the humble coming of the Lord is demonstrated above by the generations distinguished there. Through this visitation, prophecy began to be revealed, although it had remained hidden during the preceding five ages. Since John bore the person of this prophecy, as stated above, he was born of aged parents, as though that prophecy were beginning to become known when the world was growing old; and his mother concealed herself for five months, as it is written: “Elizabeth concealed herself for five months.” In the sixth month she was visited by Mary, the mother of the Lord; and the infant leaped in the womb, as though prophecy were beginning to be revealed at the Lord’s first coming, when he deigned to appear in humility [Note: The Navarricus manuscript reads, “in humanity.”]—but as though still in the womb, that is, not yet so openly that everyone would acknowledge it as manifest in the light. We believe this will occur at the Lord’s second coming, when he will come in glory; the forerunner of that coming is expected to be Elijah, just as John was the forerunner of this one.

Therefore the Lord says: “Elijah has already come, and people have done many things to him; and if you wish to know, he is John the Baptist, who is to come” (Matt. 17:12; 11:14). For in the same spirit and with the same power, as though in the office of a herald who precedes him, this one has already come and the other is to come. For this reason it is also said that this John, through the spirit by which his father was filled as a prophet, would be the Lord’s forerunner in the spirit and power of Elijah.

After Mary had completed three months with Elizabeth, she departed (Luke 1). By this number, it seems to me, the faith of the Trinity and baptism in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are signified. Through the Lord’s humble coming the human race is imbued with this baptism, and through his future coming in glory it is raised up [Note: The *Ratio*, Erasmus, and eleven manuscripts read, “is cultivated.” Another Vatican manuscript reads, “is given to be cultivated.” The Lyon, Venice, and Lovanii editions read, “is raised up.”] [Note: On the six ages, see Book 1 of *Genesis against the Manichaeans*, chapter 23, sections 35–41.].

LIX. On the ten virgins

1. Among the parables spoken by the Lord, the one concerning the ten virgins commonly gives those who inquire about it much difficulty. Many have understood many things from it that are not contrary to the faith; but it is necessary to labor over how an interpretation may fit all its parts. I have also read in a certain writing, among those works called apocryphal—not because it is contrary to the Catholic faith, but because, when I consider all the parts of this parable together, it seemed to me less suited to this passage—that another interpretation is offered. Nevertheless, I do not dare rashly to judge anything about that interpretation, lest perhaps it is not its lack of correspondence that has caused me difficulty, but my own slowness in finding how it corresponds. I shall explain briefly and carefully, as far as I can, what seems to me not improperly to be understood here.

2. When our Lord was privately questioned by his disciples about the consummation of the world, among the many things he said he also said this: “Then the kingdom of heaven will be likened to ten virgins who took their lamps and went out to meet the bridegroom. Five of them were foolish, and five were wise. The five foolish, having taken their lamps, did not take oil with them; but the wise took oil in their vessels with their lamps. Since the bridegroom was delayed, they all became drowsy and slept. But at midnight a cry was made: ‘Behold, the bridegroom is coming; go out to meet him.’ Then all those virgins arose and prepared their lamps. And the foolish said to the wise: ‘Give us some of your oil, because our lamps are going out.’ But the wise answered, saying: ‘Perhaps there will not be enough for us and for you; go instead to those who sell it and buy some for yourselves.’ While they were going to buy, the bridegroom came; and those who were ready entered with him into the wedding feast, and the door was shut. Finally the remaining virgins came, saying: ‘Lord, Lord, open to us.’ But he answered and said: ‘Amen, I say to you, I do not know you.’ Therefore keep watch, because you do not know the day or the hour” (Matt. 25:1–13).

That ten virgins are divided so that five are admitted and five excluded signifies the distinction between the good and the evil [Note: Erasmus, the Lyon, Venice, and Lovanii editions present the passage as follows: “The number ten of the virgins, of whom five are admitted and five excluded, signifies the signification of the good and the evil.”].

Therefore, if the name “virginity” is honorable, why is it common to those who are received and those who are excluded? Further, what does the number five signify on both sides? And what the oil signifies seems remarkable. Likewise, why do the wise not share with those who ask, when it is not permissible for those who are so perfect that they are received by the bridegroom to be envious—and when they ought to be merciful in supplying what they have, in accordance with the saying of that same Lord: “Give to everyone who asks of you” (Luke 6:30)? What could there be that, when given, would not be enough for both? These matters especially increase the difficulty of the question; indeed, all the other details must also be carefully considered, so that everything converges in one interpretation and nothing said about one part obstructs another.

3. It seems to me, then, that the five virgins signify continence divided into five parts, from the enticements of the flesh. The mind’s appetite must be restrained from the pleasure of the eyes, from the pleasure of the ears, from the pleasure of smelling, from the pleasure of tasting, and from the pleasure of touching. But since this continence is practiced partly before God, so that one may please him in the inward joy of conscience, and partly only before human beings, so that one may be captivated by human glory, they are called five wise and five foolish. Yet both groups are virgins, because both possess continence, although each takes pleasure from a different source.

The lamps, since they are carried in the hands, are the works performed according to this continence. For it is written: “Let your works shine before human beings” (Matt. 5:16). All of them, therefore, took their lamps and went out to meet the bridegroom. It must be understood that those under discussion are counted under the name of Christ. For those who are not Christians cannot go out to meet Christ the bridegroom.

But the five foolish, having taken their lamps, did not take oil with them. Many, although they place great hope in Christ’s goodness, nevertheless have no joy while living continently except in human praise [Note: Erasmus and Lovanii read, “although they do not live.” The negative should be removed, since it is absent from the *Ratio* and the manuscripts. The Lyon and Venice editions likewise read, “although they do not live.”]. Therefore they do not have oil with them. For I think that joy itself is signified by oil. Hence it says: “God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of exultation” (Ps. 44:8). Whoever does not rejoice because he inwardly pleases God does not have oil with him.

But the wise took oil with them in their vessels along with their lamps; that is, they placed the joy of good works in their heart and conscience, as the Apostle urges: “Let each person test his own work,” he says, “and then he will have glory in himself and not in another” (Gal. 6:4).

While the bridegroom was delayed, they all became drowsy, because from both kinds of continent people—whether those who rejoice before God or those who rest in human praise—people die during this interval of time, until the resurrection of the dead takes place at the Lord’s coming.

But at midnight—that is, when no one knows or expects it, since the Lord himself says, “But concerning that day and hour no one knows” (Matt. 24:36), and the Apostle says, “The day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night” (1 Thess. 5:2)—a cry was made: “Behold, the bridegroom is coming; arise to meet him.” “In the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet, we shall all rise” (1 Cor. 15:52).

Therefore all those virgins arose and prepared their lamps—that is, they prepared to give an account of their works. For we must be presented before the tribunal of Christ, so that there each person may receive what he has done in the body, whether good or evil (2 Cor. 5:10).

And the foolish said to the wise: “Give us some of your oil, because our lamps are going out.” Those whose deeds are supported by the praise of others fail when that praise is withdrawn; and, according to its habitual practice, the mind always seeks what it is accustomed to enjoy. Thus they wish to have before God, who examines the heart, the testimony of human beings, who do not see the heart.

But what did the wise answer? “Perhaps there will not be enough for us and for you.” Each person will give an account for himself, and no one is assisted before God by another’s testimony, since the secrets of the heart are visible to him; indeed, each person scarcely suffices for himself, so that his conscience may bear witness on his behalf. For “who can say, ‘I have made my heart clean’?” (Prov. 20:9). Hence the Apostle says: “It is a very small thing for me to be judged by you or by a human day; indeed, I do not even judge myself” (1 Cor. 4:3).

Therefore, since each person can scarcely—or perhaps not at all—give a true judgment about himself, how can he judge another, when no one knows what is taking place in a human being except the human spirit within him (ibid. 2:11)?

“Go instead to those who sell it and buy some for yourselves.” They should not be thought to have offered advice, but rather to have indirectly recalled the foolish women’s crime. For flatterers sell oil: by praising either what is false or what they do not know, they lead souls into error; and by procuring empty joys for them as for fools, they receive some payment from them, whether food, money, honor, or some other temporal advantage. The foolish do not understand what is written: “Those who call you happy lead you astray” (Isa. 3:12) [Note: Erasmus and Lovanii read, “not understanding.” The reading of the *Ratio* and the manuscripts, “not understanding,” is better; the reference is plainly to the foolish women, from whom the flatterers receive their payment. The Lyon and Venice editions likewise read, “not understanding,” as Erasmus and Lovanii do.].

“It is better to be rebuked by the righteous than to be praised by the sinner. Let the righteous correct me in mercy and rebuke me; but let not the oil of the sinner fatten my head” (Ps. 140:5).

“Go therefore instead to those who sell it and buy some for yourselves”—that is, let us now see how those who are accustomed to sell you praises and lead you into error help you, so that you seek glory not before God but from human beings.

While they were going to buy, the bridegroom came—that is, when they were turning toward outward things and seeking their customary joys, because they did not know inward joys, the one who judges came. “And those who were ready”—that is, those whose conscience bore good testimony before God—“entered with him into the wedding feast”—that is, where the pure mind is joined to the pure, perfect, and everlasting Word of God so that it may be made fruitful [Note: Thus the better manuscripts read. The printed editions read, “so that it may be made fruitful,” as though the joining had already occurred.].

“And the door was shut”—that is, after those who have been transformed into an angelic life had been received [Note: Erasmus and Lovanii read, “who are to be transformed.” The *Ratio* and some manuscripts read, “who have been transformed.” The Lyon and Venice editions read, “who are to be transformed.”]. For, he says, “We shall all rise, but we shall not all be transformed” (1 Cor. 15:51). Access to the kingdom of heaven is shut. After the judgment there is no longer a place for prayers or merits.

Finally, the remaining virgins come, saying: “Lord, Lord, open to us.” It is not said that they bought oil; and therefore it must be understood that, with no joy from the praise of others remaining, they returned in distress and great affliction to imploring God. But great is his severity after the judgment, whose mercy before the judgment has been granted beyond expression.

Therefore he answered and said: “Amen, I say to you, I do not know you”—in accordance, that is, with the principle by which the art of God, namely, the wisdom of God, does not admit into its joy those who appeared to perform something according to his commandments not before God but in order to please human beings.

And so he concludes: “Therefore keep watch, because you do not know the day or the hour.” This refers not only to that final time when the bridegroom will come, but also to the day and hour of each person’s sleep, that is, death, which is owed to all. Whoever is prepared until sleep—that is, until death—will also be found prepared when that voice sounds at midnight, by which everyone will be awakened.

4. But when it says that the virgins went out to meet the bridegroom, I think this should be understood in such a way that the one called the bride is constituted from those very virgins. It is as though, when all Christians rush into the Church, one might say that children are rushing to their mother, although the one called the mother is constituted from the children gathered together.

At present the Church is betrothed, and she is a virgin who is to be led to the wedding, that is, so long as she restrains herself from worldly corruption. At that time she will marry, when all mortality in her has perished and she enjoys an immortal union [Note: The manuscripts nearly all read, “when all mortality in her has passed away.”]. “I betrothed you,” he says, “to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ” (1 Cor. 11:2). He says, “you, a virgin,” moving from the plural to the singular. Thus they may be called both virgins and a virgin.

Why they are said to be five has, I think, been explained above. But “now we see in a mirror dimly, and then face to face; now in part, and then fully” (1 Cor. 13:12). That we now see something in Scripture in a mirror and in part, yet in accordance with the Catholic faith, comes from the pledge received by the virgin Church at the humble coming of her bridegroom. At his final coming, when he comes in glory, she will marry him, when she will behold him face to face. For he has given us the Holy Spirit as a pledge, as the Apostle says (2 Cor. 5:5).

Therefore this interpretation does not claim to discern anything certain except that it accords with the faith; nor does it prejudice other interpretations that may likewise be in accordance with the faith.

LX. “But concerning that day and hour no one knows, neither the angels of heaven nor the Son of man, but the Father alone” (Matt. 24:36)

God is said to know even when he makes someone know, as it is written: “The Lord your God is testing you, to know whether you love him” (Deut. 13:3). This is not said as though God were ignorant, but so that they themselves may know how far they have progressed in love of the Lord—a matter that human beings cannot fully recognize unless through the temptations that occur. The word “tests” itself is used for “permits to be tested.”

So also, when he is said not to know, this either means that he does not approve; that is, he does not acknowledge something within his discipline and teaching, as it is said, “I do not know you” (Matt. 25:12); or it means that he usefully makes people ignorant of something whose knowledge would be useless. Therefore the statement that the Father alone knows is rightly understood to mean that he causes the Son to know; and the statement that the Son does not know is understood to mean that he causes human beings not to know—that is, he does not disclose to them what it would be useless for them to know.

LXI. On the passage in the Gospel where the Lord fed the crowds on the mountain with five loaves

1. The five barley loaves with which the Lord fed the crowds on the mountain signify the old law: either because it was not yet given to spiritual people but still to carnal people, that is, to those devoted to the five bodily senses—for the crowds themselves also numbered five thousand people (John 6:9–13)—or because the law itself was given through Moses, who wrote five books.

And the fact that the loaves were barley appropriately signifies either the law itself, which was given in such a way that the life-giving nourishment of the soul was covered by bodily sacraments—for the marrow of barley is covered by a very tenacious husk—or the people themselves, who had not yet been stripped of carnal desire, which clung to their heart like chaff; that is, they had not yet been circumcised in heart, so that even through the threshing of tribulations, when they were led through the wilderness for forty years, they would lay aside their carnal coverings through revealed understanding, just as barley is not stripped of its husk by the threshing of the threshing floor. Accordingly, such a law was given appropriately to that people.

2. The two fish, however, which gave the bread its agreeable flavor, seem to signify those two offices by which that people was governed, so that through them it might receive the direction of its councils: namely, the royal and the priestly offices, to which that most sacred anointing also belonged [Note: [Col. 0048] *Retractations*, chapter 26]. Their duty was never to be broken or corrupted by the storms and waves of the populace, and often to shatter the violent contradictions of the crowds like hostile waves, while at times yielding to them while preserving their own integrity—in short, to move among them as fish do in a stormy sea, so in the turbulent administration of the people.

These two offices, nevertheless, prefigured our Lord. He alone assumed both, and fulfilled them alone—not figuratively, but in reality. For our king also is the Lord Jesus Christ, who showed us an example of fighting and conquering: taking our sins upon himself in mortal flesh, yielding neither to the enticing nor to the terrifying temptations of the enemy; and finally, stripping off his flesh, he confidently stripped the principalities and powers [Note: [Col. 0049] Several manuscripts read *exemplans* (“setting forth an example”)], triumphing over them in himself (Colossians 2:15).

Therefore, with him as our leader, we are delivered from the burdens and labors of this pilgrimage of ours as from Egypt; and the sins pursuing us are overwhelmed when we escape through the sacrament of Baptism. And as long as we remain in hope of his promise, which we do not yet see, we are led as through the wilderness, consoled by the word of God in the Holy Scriptures, just as those people were by manna from heaven. With that same leader we presume that we can be brought into the heavenly Jerusalem, as into the land of promise, and that there, with him governing and guarding us eternally, we shall be preserved. Thus our Lord Jesus Christ is shown to be our king.

He is also our priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek (Psalm 109:4). He offered himself as a burnt offering for our sins, and entrusted to us the celebration of the likeness of that sacrifice in memory of his passion, so that we may now see what Melchizedek offered to God (Genesis 14:18) being offered throughout the whole world in the Church of Christ.

Therefore, since our king took our sins upon himself in order to show us an example of fighting and conquering, the evangelist Matthew, signifying both the assumption of those sins and the royal office, begins with Abraham the genealogy of Christ according to the flesh—Abraham being the father of the faithful people—and, enumerating the succession of his descendants downward, reaches David, in whom the establishment of the kingdom appears most clearly. From there, passing through Solomon, born of the woman with whom his father had sinned, he follows the royal line down to the generation of the Lord (Matthew 1:1–17).

Luke, however, another evangelist, since he too undertook to explain the Lord’s genealogy according to the flesh, but in its priestly aspect—a role to which the cleansing and abolition of sins pertain—does not begin at the start of his book, as Matthew does, but at the place where Jesus was baptized, where he prefigured the cleansing of our sins. From there he proceeds step by step through the origin of his ancestors, not downward, as does the one who displayed him as descending to assume sins, but upward, as does the one who presented him as ascending after the abolition of sins; nor does he name the same ancestors whom Matthew names (Luke 3:23–38).

For there was another, priestly, lineage which, through one of David’s sons, as was customary, by taking a wife from a priestly tribe, brought it about that Mary traced her ancestry through both tribes—that is, through the royal and priestly kinships. For when Joseph and Mary were registered in the census, it is written that they were of the house, that is, of the lineage, of David (ibid. 2:4). And Elizabeth, who is likewise written to have been related to Mary, was from the priestly tribe (ibid. 1:36, 5).

Just as Matthew, who presents Christ as the king descending to assume our sins, descends from David through Solomon, because Solomon was born of the woman with whom David had sinned, so Luke, who presents Christ as the priest ascending after the abolition of sins, ascends through Nathan to David, because the prophet Nathan had been sent, and through his rebuke David obtained by repentance the abolition of that very sin (2 Samuel 12:1, 13) [Note: [Col. 0050] *Retractations*, chapter 26].

Thus, after Luke has passed David, he does not differ from Matthew in the names of the ancestors. He names, ascending from David to Abraham, those whom Matthew names while descending from Abraham to David [Note: [Col. 0050] Most manuscripts read *generationum* (“of the generations”). Then: *eas*, etc.]. From David onward, that lineage was divided into two families, royal and priestly. As has been said, Matthew, descending, followed the royal family, while Luke, ascending, followed the priestly one. Thus our Lord Jesus Christ, our king and priest, could trace his kinship from the priestly stock and yet not belong to the priestly tribe—that is, to the tribe of Levi—but to the tribe of Judah, that is, to the tribe of David, from which tribe no one attends the altar.

For this reason he is especially called the Son of David according to the flesh, because Luke ascending and Matthew descending meet one another in David. It was necessary that, since he was to abolish the sacrifices performed according to the order of Aaron in the Levitical priesthood, he should not belong to the tribe of Levi, lest the cleansing of sins—which the Lord fulfilled by the offering of his burnt offering, prefigured in the ancient priesthood—seem to belong to that tribe and to that priesthood, which was temporarily a shadow of what was to come. And he gave the image of his burnt offering [Note: [Col. 0050] Three manuscripts—Regius, Navarricus, and Michaelinus—read *magnitudinem et imaginem* (“the greatness and image”). In Michaelinus the coordinating particle *et* is absent.] to be celebrated in the Church in memory of his passion, so that he might be a priest forever, not according to the order of Aaron, but according to the order of Melchizedek (Hebrews 6:20).

The sacramental meaning of this matter may still be considered more carefully. But because of the two fish, in which we have said that the two offices—the royal and the priestly—were prefigured, let what has been treated here suffice for the present.

3. The fact that the crowd reclined upon the grass signifies that those who had received the Old Testament had been placed in a carnal hope, because a temporal kingdom and a temporal Jerusalem were promised to them. For “all flesh is grass, and all the glory of man as the flower of grass” (Isaiah 40:6).

The fact that twelve baskets were filled with pieces from the fragments that remained signified that the Lord’s disciples, among whom the number twelve holds primacy, had been filled from the opening and discussion of the Law itself, which the Jews had abandoned and left behind. For the writing of the New Testament did not yet exist when the Lord, as though breaking and opening what was hard and closed in the Law, filled his disciples, when after the resurrection he opened the ancient Scriptures to them, beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, and interpreting for them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself. Indeed, it was then that two of them recognized him in the breaking of the bread (Luke 24:27–31).

4. Therefore the second feeding of the people, which was performed with seven loaves, is rightly understood to belong to the preaching of the New Testament. No evangelist says that these loaves were barley loaves, as John said of the five. This feeding, then, with seven loaves pertains to the grace of the Church, which is known to be nourished by that celebrated sevenfold operation of the Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 0051] The word *refecta* (“nourished”) has here been restored from several manuscripts].

For this reason, two fish are not recorded here, as in the Old Law, where only two were anointed—the king and the priest—but a few fish: that is, those who were the first to believe in the Lord Jesus Christ, who were anointed in his name and sent to preach the Gospel and to endure the turbulent sea of this age, so that they might act as ambassadors on behalf of the great fish, that is, Christ, just as the apostle Paul says (2 Corinthians 5:20).

Nor were there five thousand men in the crowd, as there were there, where those who receive the Law carnally—that is, those devoted to the five bodily senses—are signified. Rather, there were four thousand, by which number spiritual people are signified, because of the four virtues of the soul by which one lives spiritually in this life: prudence, temperance, fortitude, and justice.

The first of these is knowledge of the things to be pursued and avoided; the second, restraint of desire from things that delight temporarily; the third, firmness of soul against things that are troublesome temporarily; the fourth, which is diffused through all the others, is love of God and neighbor.

5. Certainly, both there and here, the five thousand men and the four thousand are mentioned as having been present apart from the women and children (Matthew 15:34–38). This seems to me to pertain to the following understanding: in the people of the Old Testament there were some who were weak in fulfilling the righteousness that is according to the Law, a righteousness in which the apostle Paul says that he lived without reproach (Philippians 3:6); and there were others who could easily be led astray into the worship of idols.

These two classes—weakness and error—are represented under the names of women and children. The female sex is weak for action, and childhood is readily given to play. What, however, resembles childish play more than the worship of idols, when the Apostle also referred this kind of superstition to it, saying: “Nor be worshipers of idols, as some of them were; as it is written, ‘The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play’” (1 Corinthians 10:7)?

Those, therefore, were like women who, not persevering manfully in the labors of expectation until they reached God’s promises, put God to the test; and those were like children who “sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play.” Such people are found not only there, but also among the people of the New Testament: those who do not persist in attaining “to the perfect man” (Ephesians 4:13), whether because of weakness of strength or lightness of mind, are to be compared with women and children.

To the former it is said: “If only we hold firm to the beginning of his substance to the end” (Hebrews 3:14); to the latter: “Do not become children in your understanding, but be infants in evil, so that you may be mature in understanding” (1 Corinthians 14:20).

And therefore such people are admitted to the number neither in the Old nor in the New Testament. Rather, whether five thousand there or four thousand here, they are said to have been present apart from the women and children (Matthew 14:21 and 15:38).

6. Although both there and here the two peoples were fed because of Christ himself, who is continually called a mountain in the Scriptures, so that both peoples might appropriately be fed on a mountain, here the people do not recline upon grass but upon the ground.

There, the exaltation of Christ is covered, on account of carnal people and the earthly Jerusalem, by carnal hope and desire; here, after every carnal desire has been removed, the guests of the New Testament were held—not with grass interposed—but by the firmness of enduring hope, as by the solidity of the mountain itself.

7. And since the Apostle says most rightly, “Before faith came, we were guarded under the Law” (Galatians 3:23), the Lord also seems to signify this when he says concerning those whom he was about to feed with the five loaves: “They do not need to go away; you give them something to eat” (Matthew 14:16).

Under these words they are figuratively held as though under guard [Note: [Col. 0052] Thus several manuscripts. The printed editions read *tanquam custodia* (“as though in custody”)], when the disciples had urged him to dismiss them.

But concerning this crowd, which pertains to the seven loaves, he said that he took pity on it of his own accord, because it had now been three days since they had remained with him fasting. For in the entire age of the human race, this is the third period, in which the grace of the Christian faith has been given. The first is before the Law, the second under the Law, and the third under Grace.

And since a fourth period still remains, in which we shall come to the fullest peace of the heavenly Jerusalem—the goal toward which everyone who rightly believes in Christ is directed—the Lord says that he is refreshing that crowd, lest they fail on the way.

For what else does this dispensation [Note: [Col. 0052] Erasmus and Lovaniensis read, “For this is the dispensation.” The same reading is found in Lugdunensis and Venetus M.] accomplish, by which the Lord deigned to appear to us temporally and visibly in a human being, and gave us the pledge of the Holy Spirit, by whose sevenfold operation we might be strengthened, joined with the flavor of a few fish through apostolic authority, than to enable us to reach, without our strength failing, the prize of the heavenly calling?

“For we walk by faith, and not by sight” (2 Corinthians 5:5, 7). The apostle Paul himself says that he has not yet apprehended the kingdom of God, but, “forgetting what lies behind and stretching forward to what lies ahead, I pursue,” he says, “according to my purpose, toward the prize of the heavenly calling. Nevertheless, let us walk by that to which we have attained” (Philippians 3:13–16). Because on the third day we cling to the Lord and are fed by him, we shall not fail on the way.

8. Here too, certainly, the eating could not be brought to an end, but food was left over. For it was not spoken without reason concerning the future: “Do you suppose that, when the Son of Man comes, he will find faith upon the earth?” (Luke 18:8) [Note: [Col. 0053] The Rationalist and several manuscripts read, “Do you suppose that the Son of Man will come and find faith?” The same reading occurs again below].

And I believe that this will happen because of the women and children. Nevertheless, the seven baskets were filled with the leftover fragments. To these belongs the sevenfold Church, which is also described in the Apocalypse (Revelation 1:4)—that is, everyone who perseveres to the end.

For the one who said, “Do you suppose that, when the Son of Man comes, he will find faith upon the earth?” did indeed signify that at the end of the feast it might be possible for his food to be left behind and abandoned [Note: [Col. 0053] The printed editions read *convivio* (“at the feast”). Most manuscripts read *convivii* (“of the feast”)]. But since he likewise said, “The one who perseveres to the end” [Note: [Col. 0053] Most manuscripts read, “Blessed is the one who perseveres to the end”], “this one will be saved” (Matthew 24:13), he signified that the Church would not fail: the Church which, under the sevenfold number, receives those same seven loaves in greater abundance and contains them in the breadth of heart [Note: [Col. 0053] The printed editions read *latitudinem cordis* (“breadth of heart”). The manuscripts more harmoniously read *latitudine cordis*. Several of these continue: “which itself seems to be signified by perseverance in the baskets”]. This breadth of heart itself seems to signify that perseverance in the baskets.

LXII. On what is written in the Gospel: “Jesus was baptizing more people than John, though Jesus himself was not baptizing, but his disciples were” (John 4:1–2).

The question arises whether those who were baptized at the time when it is written that the Lord, through his disciples, baptized more people than John, received the Holy Spirit. For elsewhere in the Gospel it is said: “For the Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified” (ibid. 7:39). A very easy answer is that the Lord Jesus, who also raised the dead, was able to allow none of them to die until, after his glorification—that is, his resurrection from the dead and ascension into heaven—they received the Holy Spirit.

But the thief to whom it was said, “Amen, I say to you, today you shall be with me in paradise,” comes to mind; he had not even received Baptism itself [Note: [Col. 0053] *Retractations*, chapter 26]. Although Cornelius and those Gentiles who believed with him received the Holy Spirit even before they were baptized (Acts 10:44, 47), I nevertheless do not see how that thief could have said without the Holy Spirit, “Remember me, Lord, when you come into your kingdom” (Luke 23:43, 42). For, as the Apostle says, “No one says, ‘Lord Jesus,’ except in the Holy Spirit” (1 Corinthians 12:3). The Lord himself showed the fruit of this faith when he said, “Amen, I say to you, today you shall be with me in paradise.”

Therefore, just as, by the ineffable power and justice of the sovereign God [Note: [Col. 0053] In some manuscripts, “God” is omitted], Baptism was reckoned even to the believing thief and regarded as received in his free mind, although it could not be received in his crucified body [Note: [Col. 0053] Seven manuscripts read “cannot be received”], so too the Holy Spirit was given secretly before the Lord’s glorification; but after the manifestation of his divinity [Col. 0054] he was given more manifestly. Thus it was said, “The Spirit had not yet been given”: that is, he had not yet appeared in such a way that everyone would acknowledge that he had been given.

Likewise the Lord had not yet been glorified among men, though his eternal glorification had never ceased. So too his advent is called that very manifestation in mortal flesh. For he came thither where he was, because “he came unto his own,” and “he was in the world, and the world was made through him” (John 1:11, 10). Therefore, just as the Lord’s advent is understood as a bodily manifestation, while before that manifestation he himself spoke in all the holy Prophets as the Word and Wisdom of God, so the advent of the Holy Spirit is the manifestation of the Holy Spirit even to bodily eyes, when divided fire was seen above them and they began to speak in tongues (Acts 2:3–4).

For if the Holy Spirit was not in human beings before the Lord’s visible glorification, how could David say, “Do not take your Holy Spirit from me” (Psalm 50:13)? Or how were Elizabeth and her husband Zechariah filled so that they prophesied, and Anna and Simeon, of all of whom it is written that, filled with the Holy Spirit, they spoke the things which we read in the Gospel (Luke 1:41–45, 60–79, and 2:25–38)?
