That God works some things secretly and others visibly through visible creation belongs to the governance of providence, by which all divine actions are performed in the most beautiful order and distinction of places and times [Note: [Col. 0054] The printed editions read *ordines*; on the authority of the Vatican manuscript we restore *ordine*, “order”], although divinity itself is neither contained nor moved by places, nor extended or varied by times.

Moreover, just as the Lord himself undoubtedly had the Holy Spirit with him in the manhood which he bore when he came to John to be baptized, yet after he had been baptized the Holy Spirit was visibly seen descending upon him in the form of a dove (Matthew 3:13–16), so we must understand that, before the manifest and visible advent of the Holy Spirit, any holy persons could possess him secretly. We have said this, however, so as also to understand that by that very visible manifestation of the Holy Spirit, which is called his advent, he was in an ineffable manner poured more abundantly into human hearts, even with an inconceivable fullness.

LXIII. On the Word.

“In the beginning was the Word” (John 1:1). What is called *logos* (λόγος) in Greek signifies in Latin both “reason” (*ratio*) and “word” (*verbum*). But in this place we translate it better as “Word,” in order that there may be signified not only its relation to the Father, but also the operative power directed toward those things which were made through the Word. “Reason,” however, is rightly called reason even if nothing is done through it.

LXIV. On the Samaritan woman.

1. The evangelical mysteries signified in the sayings and deeds of our Lord Jesus Christ are not open to everyone; and some, by interpreting them with too little care and sobriety, commonly bring destruction instead of salvation and error instead of knowledge of the truth. Among these is the mystery written concerning the Lord’s coming [Col. 0055] at the sixth hour of the day to Jacob’s well, sitting there weary from the journey, asking a drink from the Samaritan woman, and the other matters said in that same passage of Scripture which must be examined and discussed. On this subject, the first point to be maintained is that in all the Scriptures one must preserve the utmost vigilance, so that the exposition of the divine mystery may accord with faith.

2. Therefore our Lord came to the well at the sixth hour of the day. I see a dark depth in the well. Thus I am admonished to understand the lowest parts of this world—that is, its earthly parts—to which the Lord Jesus came at the sixth hour, that is, in the sixth age of the human race, as it were in the old age of the old man, whom we are commanded to put off so that we may put on the new man, created according to God (Ephesians 4:22–24). For the sixth age is old age: the first is infancy, the second childhood, the third adolescence, the fourth youth, the fifth maturity. Thus the life of the old man, which is lived according to the flesh under a temporal condition, is concluded in the sixth age, old age [Note: [Col. 0055] Thus the manuscripts; the printed editions read “the age of old age”]. In this old age of the human race, as I have said, our Lord came as both our creator and restorer, so that, with the old man dying, he might establish the new man in himself and transfer him, stripped of earthly defilement, into the heavenly kingdoms.

Therefore the well, as has been said, signifies by its dark depth the earthly labor and error of this world [Note: [Col. 0055] The printed editions read “signifies by depth and darkness”; “and darkness” is absent from the manuscripts]. And because the old man is outward and the new inward—for the Apostle says, “Though our outward man is decaying, yet the inward man is renewed day by day”—it is altogether most fitting that the Lord came to the well at the sixth hour, that is, at midday, from which point this visible sun begins to decline toward sunset. For, when we are called by Christ, delight in visible things diminishes, so that the inward man, refreshed by love of invisible things [Note: [Col. 0055] Erasmus and Lovaniensis read “outward,” against the manuscripts and the Rat. edition; Lugdunensis and Venetus follow Erasmus and Lovaniensis], may return to the inward light which never sets, according to apostolic teaching, seeking not the things which are seen but those which are not seen: for the things which are seen are temporal, but those which are not seen are eternal (2 Corinthians 4:16, 18).

3. His coming to the well weary signifies the weakness of the flesh; his sitting, humility. For he both took upon himself the weakness of the flesh for us and deigned to appear to human beings with such humility. Of this weakness of the flesh the Prophet says: “A man set in affliction and knowing how to bear weakness” (Isaiah 53:3). Of humility the Apostle speaks when he says: “He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death” (Philippians 2:8). Yet his sitting, since teachers customarily sit, may in another sense indicate not the modesty of humility but the office of a teacher.

4. But one may ask why he asked a drink from the Samaritan woman, who had come to fill her water jar with water [Note: [Col. 0055] Some manuscripts read “who had come to draw water”], when he afterward proclaimed that he could give the abundance of a spiritual spring to those who sought him. Certainly the Lord thirsted for that woman’s faith. Since she was a Samaritan, and Samaria is customarily understood to bear the image of idolatry—for, separated from the people of the Jews, they had devoted the honor of their souls to images of dumb animals, that is, golden calves—our Lord Jesus had come in order to lead the multitude of the Gentiles, who served images, to the stronghold [Note: [Col. 0056] Some manuscripts read “monument”; others also read “monument”] of Christian faith and uncorrupted religion. “For those who are well,” he says, “do not need a physician, but those who are ill” (Matthew 9:12). Therefore he thirsts for the faith of those for whom he shed his blood.

Jesus therefore said to her, “Woman, give me a drink.” And, so that you may know what our Lord thirsted for, shortly afterward his disciples came, having gone into the city to buy food, and said to him, “Rabbi, eat.” But he said to them, “I have food to eat which you do not know.” Therefore the disciples said to one another, “Has anyone brought him something to eat?” Jesus said to them, “My food is to do the will of him who sent me and to complete his work.” Is any will of the Father who sent him, and any work which he said he wished to complete, understood here other than that he should turn us from the destructive error of the world to faith in himself? Therefore, as is his food, so also is his drink. Accordingly, what he thirsted for in that woman was to do the Father’s will in her and complete his work.

But understanding carnally, she replied: “How do you, being a Jew, ask a drink from me, since I am a Samaritan woman? For Jews have no dealings with Samaritans.” Our Lord said to her: “If you knew the gift of God, and who it is who says to you, ‘Give me a drink,’ you would rather have asked him, and he would have given you living water.” By this he showed her that he had not asked for such water as she understood, but that, because he thirsted for her faith, he desired to give the Holy Spirit to her who thirsted. For we rightly understand this living water to be the gift of God, as he himself says: “If you knew the gift of God.”

And as the same evangelist John testifies elsewhere, saying that Jesus stood and cried out: “If anyone thirsts, let him come and drink. He who believes in me, as Scripture says, rivers of living water shall flow from his belly.” The sequence is entirely fitting: “He who believes in me,” he says, “rivers of living water shall flow from his belly,” because we first believe in order to merit these gifts. Therefore these rivers of living water, which he wished to give that woman, are the reward of the faith for which he first thirsted in her. He adds this interpretation of the living water: “This,” he says, “he spoke concerning the Spirit, whom those who were to believe in him would receive. For the Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified” (John 7:37–39). This, then, is the gift of the Holy Spirit which, after his glorification, he gave to the Church, as another Scripture says: “Ascending on high, he led captivity captive; he gave gifts to men” (Psalm 67:19; Ephesians 4:8).

5. But the woman still thinks carnally; for she replied: “Lord, you have neither a drawing-vessel, and the well [Col. 0057] is deep; whence do you have living water to give me? Are you greater than our father Jacob, who gave us this well, and himself drank from it, together with his children and his cattle?” But now the Lord explains what he had said. “Everyone,” he says, “who drinks of this water will thirst again; but whoever drinks of the water which I shall give will never thirst; rather, that water which I shall give will become in him a spring of water leaping up into eternal life.” But the woman still embraces the prudence of the flesh. For what did she reply? “Lord, give me this water, so that I may neither thirst nor come here to draw.” Jesus says to her, “Go, call your husband, and come here.” Since he knew that she had no husband, the reason why he said this is asked. For when the woman said, “I have no husband,” Jesus says to her: “You have spoken well in saying that you have no husband. For you have had five husbands, and the one whom you now have is not your husband; this you have said truly.” But these things must not be understood carnally, lest we appear to resemble this Samaritan woman herself, who still does so. Rather, if we have already tasted anything of that gift of God, let us consider these matters spiritually.

6. Some understand the five husbands as the five books administered through Moses. They understand the statement, “And the one whom you now have is not your husband,” to have been said by the Lord of himself, so that the meaning is this: First you served the five books of Moses, as though five husbands; but now the one whom you have—that is, whom you hear speaking with you—is not your husband [Note: [Col. 0057] Rat. and most manuscripts read “whom you hear is not your husband,” omitting “who speaks with you”], because you have not yet believed in him. But since, not yet believing in Christ, she was certainly still held by union with those five husbands—that is, the five books—one may wonder how it could be said, “You have had five husbands,” as though she no longer had them, although she was certainly still living subject to them. Further, since the five books of Moses preach nothing other than Christ, as he himself says, “If you believed Moses, perhaps you would believe me also; for he wrote of me” (John 5:46), how can a person be understood to depart from those five books in order to pass to Christ, when one who believes in Christ embraces those five books much more eagerly, not as books to be abandoned, but as books to be understood spiritually?

7. There is, therefore, another interpretation: the five husbands are the five bodily senses. One belongs to the eyes, by which we see this visible light and all sorts of colors and bodily shapes; another to the ears, by which we perceive the variations of voices and all sounds; a third to the nostrils, by which we take delight in the varied sweetness of odors; a fourth is taste in the mouth, which perceives sweet and bitter things and discerns every flavor; the fifth judges through the whole body by touch what is hot and cold, soft and hard, smooth and rough, and whatever else we perceive by touching.

By these five carnal senses the first age of a human being is formed through the necessity of the mortal nature in which, after the sin of the first human being, we have been born: until the light of the mind has been restored, we are subject to bodily senses and pass through a carnal life without any understanding of truth. Such must necessarily be [Col. 0058] infants and very young children, who cannot yet receive reason. Since these senses are natural, govern the first age, and have been bestowed upon us by God the maker, they are rightly called husbands—that is, lawful husbands—because nature contributes them not through the fault of error but through God’s craftsmanship.

But when anyone reaches the age at which he can now be capable of reason, if he can immediately apprehend truth, he will no longer use those senses as rulers. Rather, he will have as husband the rational spirit, to which he may reduce those senses into service, subjecting his body to slavery. Then the soul is no longer subject to five husbands, that is, the five bodily senses, but has the divine Word as its lawful husband. Joined and cleaving to him—and when the human spirit itself has cleaved to Christ, because “Christ is the head of man” (1 Corinthians 11:3)—it enjoys eternal life in a spiritual embrace without any fear of separation. “For who shall separate us from the love of Christ?” (Romans 8:35).

But because that woman was held by an error which [Note: [Col. 0058] Rat. and most manuscripts read “which” in the feminine. Of these, the Vatican manuscript then reads “signifies the multitude of the wicked of the age”; Navarricus, “the multitude of children”] signified the multitude of the age enslaved by vain superstitions, after those five periods of the bodily senses by which, as we have said, the first age is governed, the Word of God had not received her into marriage [Note: [Col. 0058] Erasmus and Lovaniensis read “as a wife”; Rat. and the manuscripts read “into marriage”; Lugdunensis and Venetus read “as a wife”], but the devil possessed her in an adulterous embrace.

Accordingly the Lord, seeing that she was carnal—that is, that she thought carnally—says to her: “Go, call your husband, and come here.” That is, withdraw from the carnal affection in which you now stand, and because of which you cannot understand what I say; and call your husband, that is, be present with the spirit of understanding [Note: [Col. 0058] Some manuscripts read “with an understanding spirit”]. For the human spirit is in some manner like a husband of the soul, governing the animal affection as though a wife. This is not the Holy Spirit, who remains immutable with the Father and Son and is given immutably to worthy souls; it is the human spirit, of which the Apostle says: “No one knows what belongs to a human being except the human spirit.” For the Holy Spirit is the Spirit of God, of whom he again says: “No one knows what belongs to God except the Spirit of God” (1 Corinthians 2:11).

Therefore when this human spirit is present—that is, attentive—and subjects itself to God in piety, a person understands what is said spiritually. But when the devil’s error rules in the soul, as though understanding were absent, it is an adulterer. “Call,” therefore, he says, “your husband,” that is, the spirit within you by which a person can understand spiritual things if the light of truth illumines it. Let it be present while I speak to you, so that you may be able to receive spiritual water. And when she said, “I have no husband,” he said, “You have spoken well. For you have had five husbands,” that is, the five bodily senses which ruled you in your first age; “and the one whom you now have is not your husband,” because the spirit that understands God is not in you, with whom you could have a lawful marriage; rather, the devil’s error rules and corrupts you with adulterous defilement.

[Col. 0059] 8. And perhaps, in order to indicate to those who understood that the five bodily senses mentioned above are signified by the name “five husbands,” after five carnal responses this woman names Christ in a sixth response. Her first response is: “How is it that you, although a Jew, ask me for a drink?” The second: “Lord, you have neither a vessel for drawing, and the well is deep.” The third: “Lord, give me this water, so that I may neither thirst nor come here to draw.” The fourth: “I have no husband.” The fifth: “I see that you are a prophet: our fathers worshiped on this mountain.” This response too is carnal. For an earthly place had been given to carnal people where they might pray; but the Lord said that spiritual people would pray in spirit and in truth. After he had said this, the woman’s sixth response acknowledges Christ to be the teacher of all these things. For she says: “I know that the Messiah is coming, who is called Christ; when he has come, he will announce everything to us.” Yet she is still in error, because she does not see that the one whose coming she hopes for has already come.

[Note: [Col. 0059] Four manuscripts read: “she spoke of as future the one whom she saw present.” “Nevertheless, mercy,” etc.]

Nevertheless, through the Lord’s mercy this error is now driven out like an adulterer. For Jesus says to her: “I am he who is speaking with you.”

When she heard this, she did not answer, but immediately left her water jar and hurried into the city, so that she might not merely believe the Gospel and the Lord’s coming, but also preach it. Nor should the fact that she departed after leaving her water jar be passed over carelessly. For the water jar perhaps signifies love of this present world—that is, desire—by which people draw pleasure for themselves from a dark depth, whose image the well bears: namely, from earthly conduct. Having experienced this pleasure, they again burn with desire for it, just as, concerning that water, he says: “Whoever drinks of this water will thirst again” (John 4:5–34). But once she had believed in Christ, it was necessary for her to renounce the world; and by leaving the water jar she demonstrated that she had left behind worldly desire—not merely believing in her heart for righteousness, but also confessing with her mouth for salvation and preaching what she had believed (Rom. 10:10).

LXV. On the resurrection of Lazarus.

Although we firmly accept in full faith, according to the Gospel account, that Lazarus was raised from the dead, I nevertheless do not doubt that the event also signifies something allegorically. When events that actually happened are interpreted allegorically, the historical reality of what was done does not thereby lose its credibility. Paul explains the allegory of Abraham’s two sons as signifying the two Testaments (Gal. 4:22–24); does that mean that Abraham did not exist or that he did not have those sons? Therefore, let us also understand Lazarus in the tomb as the soul buried under earthly sins—that is, the whole human race—which the Lord signifies elsewhere by the lost sheep, for whose liberation he says that he descended, leaving the ninety-nine on the mountains (Luke 15:4).

As for his asking, “Where have you laid him?” I think this signifies our calling, which takes place in secret. For the predestination of our calling is hidden; and the sign of this secret is the Lord’s question, as though he did not know, while we ourselves do not know—as the Apostle says: “That I may know, even as I also am known” (1 Cor. 13:12).

Or perhaps the Lord shows elsewhere that he does not know sinners when he says: “I do not know you” (Matt. 7:23). This is what was signified by Lazarus buried: sins are not found in the Lord’s discipline and commandments. A similar question occurs in Genesis: “Adam, where are you?” (Gen. 3:9). For he had sinned and hidden himself from God’s face. This concealment is signified here by the burial, so that the one who dies bears the likeness of the sinner, while the buried person bears the likeness of one hidden from God’s face.

As for the command, “Take away the stone,” I think it signifies those who wanted to impose the burden of circumcision upon Gentiles coming to the Church; against them the Apostle writes at length (Gal. 2). Or it signifies those who live corruptly in the Church and are an offense to those who wish to believe.

Martha says to him: “Lord, by now he has been dead four days, and he stinks.” The last of the four elements is earth. Thus the stench signifies the earthiness of sins, that is, carnal desires. “You are earth,” the Lord said to Adam after he had sinned, “and to earth you shall go” (Gen. 3:19).

When the stone had been removed, he came out of the tomb, his hands and feet bound, and his face covered with a cloth. His coming out of the tomb signifies the soul withdrawing from carnal vices. But that he was wrapped in bands signifies that even those who withdraw from carnal things and serve the law of God with their minds, while they still remain in the body, cannot be free from the troubles of the flesh, as the Apostle says: “With my mind I serve the law of God, but with my flesh the law of sin” (Rom. 7:25).

That his face was covered with a cloth signifies that in this life we cannot possess full knowledge, as the Apostle says: “Now we see through a mirror, in a riddle; but afterward face to face” (1 Cor. 13:12).

And Jesus said: “Release him and let him go” (John 11:1–44). This signifies that after this life all veils will be removed, so that we may see face to face.

The difference between the human being whom the Wisdom of God bore, through whom we have been liberated, and other human beings can be understood from this: Lazarus is not released until he has come out of the tomb. That is, even a soul reborn cannot be free from every sin and ignorance until the body has been dissolved, so long as it sees the Lord through a mirror and in a riddle. But the linen cloths and the face cloth of the one who committed no sin and was ignorant of nothing were found in the tomb (John 20:7). For he alone, in the flesh, was not merely unoppressed by the tomb, so that some sin might be found in him (Isa. 53:9), but was not even entangled in linen, so that anything might be hidden from him or delay him on his journey.

[Note: [Col. 0060] Rationales and Erasmus, “sees in a riddle.” But the Lord’s.]

LXVI. On what is written: “Are you ignorant, brothers—for I speak to those who know the Law—that the Law has dominion over a person for as long as he lives?” up to the passage: “He will give life even to your mortal bodies through his Spirit dwelling in you” (Rom. 7–8:11).

1. In this comparison, in which he speaks about a man and a woman, the Apostle commends three things for consideration: the woman, the man, and the law. The woman, namely, is subjected to the man by the bond of the law; by that bond she is released when the man dies, so that she may marry whom she wishes.

For he says: “The woman who is under a man is bound by the law to her husband as long as he lives; but if her husband dies, she is released from the law of her husband. Therefore, while her husband lives, she will be called an adulteress if she is with another man; but if her husband dies, she is freed from the law, so that she is not an adulteress if she is with another man.”

Up to this point the comparison extends. Then he begins to discuss the matter for whose explanation and proof he introduced the comparison. Here too three things must similarly be considered: the human being, sin, and the law. For he says that a person is under the law for as long as he lives in sin, just as the woman is under the law of her husband for as long as the husband lives.

[Note: [Col. 0061] Rat. and four manuscripts, “to the husband.”]

Here the sin must be understood as that which came through the law. He says that this sin becomes excessive, because when it has already become evident that it is sin, it nevertheless continues to occur and is heaped up by the addition of transgression.

[Note: [Col. 0061] Thus the better manuscripts. But the printed editions have “heaped up,” or “more abundantly heaped up.”]

“For where there is no law, there is no transgression” (Rom. 4:15). This is what he means when he says: “So that the sinner—or sin—might become beyond measure through the commandment.”

[Note: [Col. 0061] The printed editions have “or the sinner, sin.” The word “sinner” is absent from the manuscripts and from the Greek text of the Apostle.]

Therefore, although the law prohibits sinning, he does not say that it was given in such a way as to liberate from sin, but so as to reveal the sin to which the soul is enslaved, so that it may turn to the grace of the Liberator and be freed from sin. “Through the law comes knowledge of sin” (Rom. 3:21). Elsewhere he says: “But sin, so that it might appear to be sin, worked death in me through what is good.” Thus it was through the law, because “the law is good, if one uses it lawfully” (1 Tim. 1:8).

Where, then, the grace of the Liberator is absent, the prohibition of sins increases the desire to sin. This is useful in order that the soul may realize that it is not sufficient unto itself to draw itself out of sin’s slavery. In this way, with all pride swelling down and extinguished, it is subjected to its Liberator, and the human being sincerely says: “My soul has clung to you” (Ps. 62:9). This is no longer to be under the law of sin, but under the law of righteousness.

The law of sin is so called not because the law itself is sin, but because it is imposed upon sinners. It is therefore also called the law of death, because “the wages of sin is death” (Rom. 6:23); and “the sting of death is sin, while the power of sin is the law” (1 Cor. 15:56). For by sinning we slide toward death.

We sin more vehemently when the law prohibits us than if we were prohibited by no law at all. But when grace is added, we gladly and without burden fulfill the very thing that the law had commanded with difficulty. Thus the law of sin and death—that is, the law imposed upon those who sin and die—merely commands us not to desire; yet we do desire.

But the law of the Spirit of life, which belongs to grace and liberates from the law of sin and death, makes us cease to desire sin and enables us to fulfill the commands of the law. We are no longer servants of the law through fear, but friends through love, and servants of the righteousness from which that law was promulgated. Righteousness must be served not slavishly but freely—that is, through love rather than fear.

Therefore it was most truly said: “Do we then nullify the law through faith? By no means; rather, we establish the law” (Rom. 3:31). Faith accomplishes what the law commands. The law, therefore, is established through faith.

[Col. 0062] If faith is absent, the law merely commands; and, since they do not fulfill its commands, it holds them guilty, so that eventually, groaning and unable to fulfill what has been commanded, they may turn to the grace of the Liberator.

[Note: [Col. 0062] Some manuscripts read “groaning aloud.”]

2. Since, then, in that comparison we see three things—the woman, the man, and the law—and again, in the matter for which the comparison was employed, three things—the soul, sin, and the law of sin—the only difference here is that in the comparison the man dies so that the woman may marry whom she wishes and be released from the law of her husband. Here, however, the soul itself dies to sin so that it may marry Christ; and when it dies to sin, it also dies to the law of sin.

Thus he says: “Therefore, my brothers, you also have died to the law through the body of Christ, so that you may belong to another, to him who has risen from the dead, so that we may bear fruit for God.”

“For when we were in the flesh,” he says—that is, when we were held bound by carnal desires—“the passions of sins that come through the law were at work in our members, so that they might bear fruit for death.” When desire, which the law prohibits, was increased, and faith was absent, the crime of transgression was added to complete the heap of sins: “For where there is no law, there is no transgression.”

[Note: [Col. 0062] Eight manuscripts read: “so that they might bear fruit for death—increased desire, when the law forbids”; some read “forbade.”]

These passions, which come through the law, he says, were at work in our members so that they might bear fruit for death.

[Note: [Col. 0062] Erasmus and Lovaniensis have “worked.” The manuscripts have the better reading, “were at work.” Lyon and Venice have “worked,” following Erasmus and Lovaniensis.]

Under these passions, as under a ruling husband, the soul acted before grace came through faith. The person who now serves the law of God with the mind dies to these passions, although the passions themselves have not yet died, as long as he serves the law of sin with the flesh.

Something, therefore, still remains for the person who is under grace: something that does not conquer him or lead him captive, until all that has been strengthened by evil habit has been put to death—and from this the body is also now said to be dead, as long as it does not serve the spirit perfectly. But it will come to serve perfectly when the mortal body itself has been given life.

3. From this we understand that there are also four stages in one human being, through which, completed step by step, one will remain in eternal life. Since it was necessary—and just—that after our nature sinned, having lost the spiritual blessedness signified by the name “paradise,” we should be born as animal and carnal beings, the first stage is action before the Law, the second under the Law, the third under grace, and the fourth in peace.

The action before the Law occurs when we are ignorant of sin and follow carnal desires. The action under the Law occurs when we are already forbidden to sin, yet, overcome by the habit of sinning, we sin because faith does not yet assist us.

The third action occurs when we fully believe in our Liberator, attribute nothing to our own merits, and, loving his mercy, are no longer overcome by the pleasure of evil habit when it tries to lead us into sin. Nevertheless, we still suffer its assaults, although we do not surrender to it.

The fourth action occurs when there is absolutely nothing in the human being that resists the spirit, but all things, joined and bound together in harmonious unity, guard one reality in firm peace. This will happen when the mortal body has been given life, when “this corruptible body has put on incorruption, and this mortal body has put on immortality” (1 Cor. 15:54–55).

4. The following testimonies presently come to mind for demonstrating the first stage: “Through one human being sin entered this world, and through sin, death; and so death passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned. For until the law, sin was in this world. But sin was not reckoned when there was no law” (Rom. 5:12–13).

And again: “For without the law sin was dead; but I was once alive without the law.” What he says here, “was dead,” is what he says above, “was not reckoned”—that is, it was hidden. He makes this clear in what follows, saying: “But sin, so that it might appear to be sin, worked death in me through what is good”—that is, through the law; for “the law is good, if one uses it lawfully” (1 Tim. 1:8).

If he says here, “so that sin might appear,” it is clear that when he earlier said that sin was dead and not reckoned, he meant that it did not appear before it was shown through the law’s prohibition.

5. The following testimonies correspond to the second stage: “The law entered in addition, so that the offense might increase” (Rom. 5:20). For transgression was added, although it had not existed before.

There is also the passage already cited: “When we were in the flesh, the passions of sins that come through the law were at work in our members, so that they might bear fruit for death.”

And this passage: “What then shall we say? Is the law sin? By no means. But I did not know sin except through the law. For I would not have known desire unless the law said, ‘You shall not desire.’ But sin, taking an opportunity through the commandment, worked every desire in me.”

And shortly afterward: “When the commandment came, sin revived. But I died, and the commandment that was meant for life was found to be death to me. For sin, taking an opportunity through the commandment, deceived me and through it killed me.”

When he says, “I died,” he wants it understood that he discovered himself to be dead: for one who sees through the law what he ought not to do, and nevertheless does it, now sins even by transgression.

When he says, “Sin deceived me, taking an opportunity through the commandment,” this may mean either that the enticement of pleasure toward sin is stronger when prohibition is present, or that even if a person does something according to the commands of the law, if faith—which belongs to grace—is still absent, he wants to attribute the act to himself rather than to God, and by becoming proud sins still more.

He therefore continues and says: “So the law indeed is holy, and the commandment holy and just and good. Did what is good, then, become death to me? By no means. But sin, so that it might appear to be sin, worked death in me through what is good, so that the sinner—or sin—might become beyond measure through the commandment.”

[Col. 0063] “We know that the law is spiritual, but I am carnal”—that is, I consent to the flesh, not yet liberated by spiritual grace—

[Note: [Col. 0063] See *Retractationes* I.26.]

“sold under sin”—that is, sinning at the price of temporal pleasures.

“For what I do, I do not know”—that is, I do not recognize it as being among the precepts of truth, where true knowledge exists. In accordance with this manner of speaking, the Lord says to sinners: “I do not know you.”

[Col. 0064] For nothing is hidden from him; rather, because sins are not found within the rules of the commandments possessed by truth, Truth itself therefore says to sinners: “I do not know you.” Just as darkness is perceived by the eyes through their inability to see, so sins are perceived by the mind through ignorance.

I think that the following was spoken in the Psalms in accordance with this manner of speaking: “Who understands his transgressions?” (Ps. 18:13).

“For I do not do what I wish, but I do what I hate. But if I do what I do not wish, I agree with the law, that it is good. But now it is no longer I who do it, but sin dwelling in me.

“For I know that good does not dwell in me—that is, in my flesh. For to will is present with me, but to accomplish the good I do not find. For I do not do the good that I wish, but the evil that I do not wish, that I do. But if I do what I do not wish, it is no longer I who do it, but sin dwelling in me.

“Therefore I find this law for me who wish to do good: evil is present with me. For I delight in the law of God according to the inner human being; but I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind and taking me captive in the law of sin that is in my members.”

Up to this point these are the words of a person established under the Law, not yet under grace. Even if he does not wish to sin, he is overcome by sin. For carnal habit and the natural bond of mortality have grown strong—the bond through which we have been propagated from Adam.

[Note: [Col. 0064] Several manuscripts have “natal” rather than “natural.”]

Let the person placed in this condition, then, implore help, and let him understand that what fell was his own, but that what rises is not his own. Once liberated and acknowledging the grace of his Liberator, he says: “Wretched human being that I am, who will liberate me from this body of death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord.”

6. The words of the person established under grace now begin—of the third stage that we have described. In this stage the mortality of the flesh does resist, but does not conquer or lead him captive into consent to sin.

For he says: “Therefore it is I myself, with my mind, who serve the law of God, but with my flesh the law of sin. There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus. For the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus has liberated me from the law of sin and death.

“For what was impossible for the law, in that it was weakened through the flesh”—that is, through carnal desires—for the law was not fulfilled because the love belonging to righteousness was not yet present, the love that would hold the mind by an inward delight so that it would not be drawn toward sin by the pleasure of temporal things—

“God, sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, condemned sin in the flesh.” For it was not sinful flesh, since it was not born from carnal pleasure; nevertheless, the likeness of sinful flesh was present in it, because it was mortal flesh. Adam did not deserve death except by sinning.

[Note: [Col. 0064] The manuscripts have “through sin.”]

What, then, did the Lord do? “By means of sin he condemned sin in the flesh”—that is, by taking on the flesh of sinful humanity and teaching us how we should live, he condemned sin in that very flesh, so that the spirit, aflame with love for eternal things, would not be led captive into consent to lust.

“So that,” he says, “the righteousness of the law might be fulfilled in us, who do not walk according to the flesh but according to the spirit.”

[Col. 0065] Thus the commands of the law were fulfilled through love, which could not be fulfilled through fear. For “those who are according to the flesh set their minds on the things of the flesh”—that is, they desire carnal goods as the highest goods. “But those who are according to the spirit perceive the things of the spirit.”

“For the wisdom of the flesh is death, but the wisdom of the spirit is life and peace. For the wisdom of the flesh is hostile to God.” He shows what he meant by “hostile,” so that no one might suppose that some opposing principle was meant. For he adds: “It is not subject to the law of God; indeed, it cannot be.”

To act against the law, then, is to be hostile to God—not because anyone can harm God, but because whoever resists God’s will harms himself. This is what it means to kick against the goad, as was said divinely to the Apostle Paul while he was still persecuting the Church (Acts 9:5).

The statement “It is not subject to the law of God; indeed, it cannot be” is like saying: “Snow does not warm; indeed, it cannot.” As long as it is snow, it does not warm; but it can melt and boil so as to warm. When it does this, however, it is no longer snow.

Similarly, the wisdom of the flesh is so called when the soul desires temporal goods as great goods. As long as such desire is present in the soul, it cannot be subject to the law of God—that is, it cannot fulfill what the law commands. But when it begins to desire spiritual goods and despise temporal ones, it ceases to be the wisdom of the flesh and no longer resists the spirit.

For the same soul is said to possess the wisdom of the flesh when it desires lower things, and the wisdom of the spirit when it desires higher things. This is not because the wisdom of the flesh is a substance with which the soul is clothed or from which it is stripped, but because it is an affection of the soul itself, which will wholly cease when the soul has turned itself entirely toward higher things.

“Those who are in the flesh,” he says, “cannot please God”—that is, those who yield to the pleasures of the flesh.

[Note: [Col. 0065] Six manuscripts have “wills” (*voluntatibus*) rather than “pleasures” (*voluptatibus*).]

So that no one might think this was said of those who had not yet departed from this life, he most appropriately adds: “But you are not in the flesh, but in the spirit.” He is plainly speaking to people who are still established in this life. They were in the spirit because they rested in faith, hope, and love of spiritual things.

[Note: [Col. 0065] Two manuscripts have “in the faith, hope, and love of spiritual things they will rest.” Another of the Navarre manuscripts has “they rested in faith and hope and in love for spiritual things.”]

“If indeed,” he says, “the Spirit of God dwells in you. But if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to him. But if Christ is in you, the body is indeed dead because of sin, while the spirit is life because of righteousness.”

He calls the body dead as long as it is such that the lack of bodily things troubles the soul and, through certain movements arising from that lack, urges it anxiously toward earthly desires.

[Note: [Col. 0065] See *Retractationes* I.26.]

Although these movements exist, the mind does not consent to do unlawful things; it already serves the law of God and is established under grace. This is the force of what was said above: “With my mind I serve the law of God, but with my flesh the law of sin.”

The person now described as being under grace is therefore one who does not yet possess perfect peace, which will come through the resurrection and transformation of the body.

[Col. 0066]

7. It remains, then, for him to speak about that peace of the body’s resurrection, which is the fourth stage—if indeed it should be called a stage, since it is the highest rest.

For he continues and says: “If the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Jesus from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit dwelling in you” (Rom. 7–8:11).

Here there is also the clearest testimony concerning the resurrection of the body. It is sufficiently evident that as long as we are in this life, troubles do not cease through mortal flesh, nor do certain ticklings of carnal pleasures cease. For although the person established under grace does not yield, serving the law of God with his mind, nevertheless with his flesh he serves the law of sin.

When these stages have been completed in the perfected human being, no substance is found to be evil. Nor is the Law evil, since it shows the human being in what bonds of sin he lies, so that, by imploring the Liberator’s help through faith, he may deserve both to be released and raised up and firmly established.

In the first stage, therefore, which is before the Law, there is no conflict with the pleasures of this age. In the second, which is under the Law, we fight but are defeated. In the third, we fight and conquer. In the fourth, we do not fight, but rest in perfect and eternal peace.

[Note: [Col. 0066] Rat. and most manuscripts have “is added”; and below, “was not added.” Two other books have “is subjected,” and afterward, “was not subjected.”]

For what is lower in us is subjected to us, because previously we had abandoned the God who is higher than we are.

LXVII. On what is written: “For I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy of the future glory that will be revealed in us,” up to what is said: “For by hope we have been saved” (Rom. 8:18–24).

1. This chapter is obscure, because it is not sufficiently apparent what he now calls “creation.” According to Catholic teaching, however, creation means everything that God the Father made and established through his only-begotten Son, in the unity of the Holy Spirit. Therefore not only bodies but also our souls and spirits are included under the name “creation.”

The statement is: “Creation itself will be liberated from the slavery of decay into the freedom of the glory of the children of God,” as though we were not creation but children of God, and creation were to be liberated from slavery into the freedom of our glory. He also says: “For we know that every creature groans and suffers until now; and not only it, but we ourselves also,” as though we were one thing and every creature another.

The entire chapter must therefore be considered piece by piece.

2. “For I consider,” he says, “that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy of the future glory that will be revealed in us.” This is clear. For he had said above: “But if by the spirit you put to death the deeds of the flesh, you will live.” This cannot happen without hardship, for which patience is necessary.

This also relates to what he said shortly before: “If indeed we suffer with him, so that we may also be glorified with him” (ibid. 13, 17).

What, then, does he mean when he says: “For the expectation of creation awaits the revelation of the children of God”? I think he means this. That which suffers in us when we put the deeds of the flesh to death—that is, when we hunger or thirst through abstinence, when through chastity we restrain the pleasure of intercourse, when through patience we endure the wounds of injuries and the goads of insults, when, having neglected and rejected our own pleasures, we labor for the fruitfulness of Mother Church—whatever in us suffers in this and similar affliction is creation.

For the body suffers, and so does the soul, which is certainly creation; and it awaits the revelation of the children of God. That is, it awaits the time when what has been called will appear in the glory to which it has been called.

Since the only-begotten Son of God cannot be called creation—for through him all things whatsoever God made were made—we too are distinctly called creation before that clear manifestation of glory, and distinctly called children of God, although we merit this by adoption. For he is the Son by nature, the only-begotten Son.

Therefore the expectation of creation—that is, our expectation—awaits the revelation of the children of God. It awaits the time when what has been promised will appear, when it will be made evident in reality what we now are by hope.

For we are children of God, and what we will be has not yet appeared. But we know that when it appears, we will be like him, because we will see him as he is (1 John 3:2). This is the revelation of the children of God that the expectation of creation now awaits.

It is not that creation awaits the revelation of another nature that is not creation. Rather, creation, as it now is, awaits the time when it will become what it will be. It is as if one said that, while the painter is working with the colors placed before him and prepared for his work, the expectation of the colors awaits the manifestation of the image—not because then they will be other colors, or because they will cease to be colors, but because they will possess another dignity.

3. “For creation,” he says, “was subjected to vanity.” This is the meaning of: “Vanity of the vain, and all is vanity.”

[Note: [Col. 0067] The printed editions read “vanity of vanities” (*vanitatum*); the manuscripts read “vanity of the vain” (*vanitantium*). Augustine testifies in *Retractationes* I.7 that he had sometimes read the latter in Latin books.]

“What abundance does a person have in all his labor with which he labors under the sun?” (Eccl. 1:2–3). To him it was said: “In labor you shall eat your bread” (Gen. 3:19).

Creation, therefore, was subjected to vanity, not willingly. The addition “not willingly” is well made. For the human being sinned willingly, but was condemned unwillingly. Sin, therefore, was voluntary: to act against the commandment of truth. But the punishment of sin is subjection to deception.

Creation was not subjected to vanity willingly, but because of him who subjected it in hope—that is, because of his justice and mercy, who neither left sin unpunished nor wished the sinner to be incurable.

4. For creation itself—that is, the human being himself—when, after losing the seal of the image because of sin, only creation remained, will also be liberated from the slavery of decay.

[Note: [Col. 0067] See *Retractationes* I.26.]

When he says that creation itself will also be liberated, he makes us understand “itself” in the same way as “us”: even those must not be despaired of who are not yet called children of God because they have not yet believed, but are called merely creation. For they too will believe and will be liberated from the slavery of decay, just as we, who are already children of God, will be liberated, although what we will be has not yet appeared.

They will therefore be liberated from the slavery of decay into the freedom of the glory of the children of God. That is, they too will become free instead of slaves, and glorious instead of dead, in the perfect life that the children of God will possess.

5. “For we know that every creature groans and suffers until now.” Every creature is counted in the human being—not because all the angels, and the exalted Virtues and Powers, or heaven and earth and the sea and all that is in them, are in him, but because every creature is partly spiritual, partly animal, and partly corporeal.

To consider this from the lower levels upward: corporeal creation is extended through places; animal creation gives life to the corporeal; spiritual creation governs the animal. It governs well when it submits itself to be governed by God. But when it transgresses his commandments, it becomes entangled in labors and hardships through the very things it was able to govern.

Thus the person who lives from the body is called carnal or animal. He is carnal because he pursues carnal things; he is animal because he is carried along by the unrestrained wantonness of his soul, which the spirit does not govern or restrain within the limits of the natural order, because the spirit itself does not submit to be governed by God.

But the person who governs the soul by the spirit, and the body through the soul—for he cannot do this unless he himself has God as ruler, since “as the head of the woman is the man, so the head of the man is Christ” (1 Cor. 11:3)—is called spiritual.

This life is now lived with some hardship, but afterward it will suffer none.

And since the highest angels live spiritually, while the lowest live animal-like,

[Note: [Col. 0068] See *Retractationes* I.26.]

and beasts and all cattle live carnally, while the body does not live but is given life, every creature is in the human being: he understands by the spirit, senses through the soul, and moves bodily through place.

Thus every creature groans and suffers in the human being. For he did not say “the whole creature,” but “every creature.” It is as if someone were to say that all people who are healthy see the sun, but that they do not see it wholly, because they see only with their eyes.

So every creature is in the human being, because he understands, lives, and possesses a body; but the whole of creation is not in him, because outside him there are angels who understand, live, and exist; cattle that live and exist; and bodies that merely exist. To live is itself greater than not living, and to understand is itself greater than living without understanding.

Therefore, when the wretched human being groans and suffers, every creature groans and suffers until now. He rightly said “until now,” because even if there are some already in Abraham’s bosom (Luke 16:23) and the thief, established with the Lord in paradise, ceased to suffer on the day he believed (Luke 23:43), nevertheless every creature groans and suffers until now, because in those who have not yet been liberated, all creation is present through spirit, soul, and body.

[Col. 0069] **6.** “Not only,” he says, “does the whole creation groan and travail, but we ourselves also”: that is, not only do body, soul, and spirit together suffer in man because of bodily hardships, but we ourselves also, apart from our bodies, groan within ourselves, possessing the first fruits of the Spirit. And he rightly said, “possessing the first fruits of the Spirit”: that is, those whose spirits have already been offered to God like a sacrifice and have been seized by the divine fire of love. These are the first fruits of man, because truth first takes possession of our spirit, so that through it the other parts may be taken possession of also.

He therefore already possesses first fruits offered to God who says, “With the mind I serve the law of God, but with the flesh the law of sin” (Rom. VII, 25); and who says, “God, whom I serve in my spirit” (ibid. I, 9); and of whom it is said, “The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak” (Matt. XXVI, 41). But since he still says, “Wretched man that I am, who will deliver me from the body of this death?” (Rom. VII, 24), and to such persons it is still said, “He will give life even to your mortal bodies because of the Spirit dwelling in you” (ibid. VIII, 11), the whole offering has not yet become a burnt offering. It will be so when death is swallowed up in victory, when it is said to death, “Where is your contention, O death? Where is your sting, O death?” (1 Cor. XV, 54–55).

“Now therefore,” he says, “not only does the whole creation”—that is, together with the body—“but we ourselves also, possessing the first fruits of the Spirit”: that is, we souls, who have already offered the first fruits of our minds to God, groan within ourselves, that is, apart from the body, awaiting adoption, the redemption of our body. This means that the body itself, receiving the benefit of the adoption of sons by which we were called, may declare that we, in our entirety, have been freed, all troubles having passed away, and that we are in every respect children of God.

“For by hope we were saved. But hope that is seen is not hope.” What is now hope will then become reality, when what we shall be becomes manifest: namely, that we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is.

**7.** If this passage is opened up in the manner in which it has been explained, we do not fall into those difficulties which compel many to say that all the angels and exalted Powers are in pain and groaning until we are completely delivered, because it is said, “The whole creation groans and travails.” For although, by reason of their exalted rank, they assist us [Note: [Col. 0069] So Rat., Er., and eleven manuscripts. Lov. reads, “through their exalted ranks.”] while they obey God, who for our sake deigned even to send his only Son, we must believe that they do this without groaning and pain, lest they be thought miserable, and that Lazarus, who now rests in Abraham’s bosom, should be happier than those among their number.

This is especially so because he says that the very creation which groans and travails has been subjected to vanity; and it is impious to believe this of the highest and most excellent creatures among the Powers and Virtues. Further, he says that it is to be liberated from the slavery of corruption; yet we cannot believe that those who live a most blessed life in heaven have fallen into such a condition.

Nevertheless, nothing should be affirmed rashly; rather, the divine words must be handled again and again with devout diligence. Perhaps what groans and travails and has been subjected to vanity may in some other way be understood, so that it might not be impiously held of the highest angels, so long as, at our Lord’s command, they assist our weakness [Col. 0070]. But whether the exposition we have given, or some other exposition of this passage, is put forward, this alone must be guarded against: that the catholic faith not be violated or wounded. For I know that vain [Note: [Col. 0070] Florus and the Codex Regius read, “various.”] heretics have loudly proclaimed many impious and foolish things about this passage.

## LXVIII. On what is written: “O man, who are you that you answer back to God?” (Rom. IX, 20)

**1.** Although the Apostle appears to have rebuked the curious by saying, “O man, who are you that you answer back to God?”, they raise a question precisely about this statement and do not cease being curious in the very sentence by which that curiosity was rebuked. The impious do so with insult, saying that the Apostle failed to resolve the question and rebuked those who asked because he was unable to explain what was being asked.

Some heretics [Note: [Col. 0070] Manichaeans.]—since they deceive only when they promise knowledge which they do not provide, and since, as opponents of the Law and the Prophets, they accuse whatever the Apostle has inserted into his discourse concerning them of being false and introduced by corruptors—preferred to count this passage also among those which they claim were interpolated, and to deny that Paul said, “O man, who are you that you answer back to God?” For if this were said to them, when they slanderously seek to deceive people, they would certainly be silent and would not dare to promise ignorant people, whom they wish to deceive, any knowledge of the will of almighty God.

Others, however, who read the Scriptures with a good and devout mind, ask what answer can here be given to those who either curse or slander. But we, holding firmly and beneficially to apostolic authority, and in no way supposing that the books guarded by catholic discipline have been falsified [Note: [Col. 0070] Manuscripts read, “unfalsified.”], should recognize that we are unworthy and weak [Note: [Col. 0070] Er. and Lov. read, “that we are unworthy and weak.” The word “we” is absent from Rat. and the manuscripts.—Lugd. and Ven. agree with Er. and Lov. M.] for understanding the divine mysteries in which these matters are enclosed.

When they murmur and grow indignant that they do not learn God’s counsels, and begin to say, “Therefore he has mercy on whom he wills, and whom he wills he hardens. Why does he still find fault? For who can resist his will?” (ibid. 18–19), when by these words they begin either to slander the Scriptures or to seek a hiding place for their sins, so that they may despise the commandments by which one reaches the good life [Note: [Col. 0070] Rat. and the Cistercian Codex omit “good.” Most other manuscripts have, instead of “by which one reaches,” “to which one is invited.”], let us answer with complete confidence: “O man, who are you that you answer back to God?”

We should neither fear them and give what is holy to dogs nor throw our pearls before swine (Matt. VII, 6)—provided that we ourselves are no longer dogs and swine, and that, with the Holy Spirit revealing it, we discern at least partially and in a riddle something sublime and far removed from ordinary conjecture concerning the merits of souls.

**2.** The Apostle did not here forbid the saints to inquire, but those who are not yet rooted and grounded in love, so that they may be able, with all the saints, to comprehend the breadth, length, height, and depth, and the other matters which he explains in the same passage (Eph. III, 18–19). He therefore did not forbid inquiry when he says, “The spiritual person judges all things, but is himself judged by no one”; and especially when he says, “We have not received the spirit of this world, but the Spirit who is from God, so that we may know the things given to us by God” (1 Cor. II, 15, 12).

Whom, then, did he forbid, except those who are of clay and earthly, who, not yet regenerated and nourished inwardly, bear the image of that man who was first made from the earth, earthly (ibid. XV, 47, 49)? And because he refused to obey the one by whom he was made, he fell into that from which he had been made, and after his sin deserved to hear, “You are earth, and into earth you shall go” (Gen. III, 19).

To such people, therefore, the Apostle says, “O man, who are you that you answer back to God? Shall the thing formed say to the one who formed it, ‘Why did you make me thus?’” So long as you are a thing formed, you are not yet a perfected son, because you have not yet drawn in the fullness of grace by which the power was given to us to become children of God (John I, 12), so that you might hear, “I will no longer call you servants, but friends” (ibid. XV, 15). Who are you, then, that you answer back to God and wish to know God’s counsel? If you had wished to know the counsel of a human being equal to you, you would act shamelessly [Note: [Col. 0071] Rat. and most manuscripts read, “you would act imprudently.”] unless you had first been received into friendship.

Therefore, just as we have borne the image of the earthly, let us also bear the image of the heavenly (1 Cor. XV, 49), stripping off the old man and putting on the new (Col. III, 9–10), so that it may not be said to us, as to a thing formed from clay, “Shall the thing formed say to the one who formed it, ‘Why did you make me thus?’”

**3.** And to make it clear that these words are spoken not to a sanctified spirit but to carnal clay, see what follows: “Or does the potter not have power over the clay, from the same lump to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?” (Rom. IX, 21).

From the time our nature sinned in paradise, we have been formed by the same divine providence according to earth, not according to heaven—that is, not according to the spirit but according to the flesh—by mortal generation; and we have all become one lump of clay, which is the mass of sin.

Since by sinning we have lost our merit, and since, apart from God’s mercy, nothing but eternal condemnation is owed to sinners, what does a human being from this lump mean by answering God and saying, “Why did you make me thus?” If you wish to know these things, do not remain clay, but become a son of God through the mercy of the one who gave power to those believing in his name to become children of God—not, as you desire, to those who wish to know divine things before they believe [Note: [Col. 0071] We have corrected this passage according to the manuscripts. In the printed editions alone we found it corrupted as follows: “For it is not granted to those who wish to know divine things, as you desire, before they believe.”].

The reward of knowledge is given according to merits; but merit is acquired through believing. The grace itself, however, which was given through faith, was given without any preceding merits of ours. For what merit belongs to a sinner and an impious person? Yet Christ died for the impious and sinners (ibid. V, 6), so that we might be called to believe not by merit but by grace, while by believing we might also establish merit [Note: [Col. 0071] Several manuscripts read, “acquire merit.”].

Sinners are therefore commanded to believe, so that by believing they may be cleansed from sins [Note: [Col. 0071] Nine manuscripts read, “and by believing are cleansed from sins.”]. For they do not know what they will see by living rightly [Col. 0072]. Since they cannot see unless they live rightly, and cannot live rightly unless they believe, it is clear that one must begin with faith, so that the commandments by which believers are turned away from this world may make the heart pure, where God can be seen.

“For blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. V, 8); and it is sung prophetically [Note: [Col. 0072] Most manuscripts read, “And through the prophet it is sung.”], “Seek him in the simplicity of heart” (Wis. I, 1).

Therefore it is rightly said to people who remain in the oldness of life and consequently carry the soul’s darkened eye: “O man, who are you that you answer back to God? Shall the thing formed say to the one who formed it, ‘Why did you make me thus?’ Or does the potter not have power over the clay, from the same lump to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?”

“Cleanse out the old leaven, so that you may be a new lump” (1 Cor. V, 7), and in that new lump do not remain a little child in Christ, to be fed with milk (ibid. III, 2); but attain mature manhood, so that you may belong among those of whom it is said, “We speak wisdom among the mature” (ibid. II, 6). Only then will you rightly, and not perversely, hear whatever there may be concerning the most hidden merits of souls and the secrets of almighty God’s grace or justice.

**4.** For the case of Pharaoh is easily answered by the earlier merits through which he afflicted foreigners in his kingdom and became deserving that his heart should be hardened, so that he would not believe even the clearest signs of God’s command [Note: [Col. 0072] Two manuscripts here and below, in section 5, read “yield” instead of “believe.”].

From the same lump—that is, the lump of sinners—he therefore brought forth vessels of mercy, with which he would assist the children of Israel when they appealed to him, and vessels of wrath, through whose punishment he would instruct them: namely, Pharaoh and his people. For although both groups were sinners and therefore belonged to one lump, those who had been born for the one God had nevertheless to be treated differently.

He endured, therefore, with great patience the vessels of wrath, which were completed for destruction. By saying “with great patience,” he sufficiently indicated their earlier sins, in which he endured them, so that he might punish them at the fitting time, when their punishment would serve to assist those who were being delivered. And he did so “to make known the riches of his glory upon the vessels of mercy, which he prepared for glory.”

At this point perhaps, troubled, you return to that question: “He has mercy on whom he wills, and whom he wills he hardens. Why does he still find fault? For who can resist his will?” (Rom. IX, 18–23). Indeed, he has mercy on whom he wills, and he hardens whom he wills; but this will of God cannot be unjust. It proceeds from the most hidden merits. For although sinners, because of the general sin, have made one lump, there is nevertheless not no difference among them.

Something therefore precedes in some sinners by which, although they have not yet been justified, they become worthy of justification; and something likewise precedes in other sinners by which they become worthy of hardening [Note: [Col. 0072] Rat. and the manuscripts read, “blunting.” The same manuscripts below read “blunting” instead of “hardening.”]. You have the same Apostle saying elsewhere, “Because they did not approve of having God in their knowledge, God gave them over to a reprobate mind” (Rom. I, 28). His giving them over to a reprobate mind is the same as Pharaoh’s heart being hardened (Exod. IV, 21); and their not approving of having God in their knowledge is the same as their becoming worthy to be given over to a reprobate mind.

**5.** Nevertheless, it is true that salvation depends “not on the one who wills or the one who runs, but on God who shows mercy” (Rom. IX, 16). For even if someone, whether through lighter sins or certainly through very grave and numerous sins, should become worthy of God’s mercy through great groaning and the sorrow of repentance, it is not his own doing—he would perish if left to himself—but the doing of the merciful God, who comes to the aid of his prayers and sorrows.

It is not enough to will unless God shows mercy. Yet God does not show mercy to one whom he calls to peace unless the will has preceded [Note: [Col. 0073] *Retractations*, chapter 26], because “on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke II, 14).

And since no one can even will unless he has been admonished and called, either inwardly, where no human being sees, or outwardly through a spoken word or through some visible signs, it follows that God himself works even the willing within us (Phil. II, 13).

For not everyone who was invited wished to come to that supper which the Lord says was prepared in the Gospel; nor could those who came have come unless they had been called (Luke XIV, 16–26). Thus those who came ought not to attribute their coming to themselves, since they came because they were called; nor should those who refused to come attribute it to anyone else, but only to themselves, since they had been called to come by free choice.

Calling therefore produces the will before merit. Consequently, if anyone attributes to himself the fact that he came when called, he cannot attribute to himself the fact that he was called. But whoever was called and did not come, just as he had no merit of reward by which he should be called, so he begins to acquire merit for punishment when, having been called, he neglects to come.

Thus there will be those two things: “I will sing mercy and judgment to you, O Lord” (Ps. C, 1). Calling belongs to mercy; the blessedness of those who came when called and the punishment of those who refused to come belong to judgment.

Was Pharaoh, then, unaware how much good had come to those lands through Joseph’s arrival (Gen. XLI)? Knowledge of that event was his calling, so that by treating the people of Israel mercifully he would not be ungrateful. But because he refused to obey this calling and practiced cruelty against those to whom humanity and mercy were owed, he deserved punishment: his heart was hardened, and he suffered such blindness of mind that he did not believe in so many, such great, and such manifest signs of God. Through his punishment—whether the hardening or the final visible drowning—the people could be instructed; while through their affliction he acquired merit both for hidden dullness and for manifest drowning (Exod. V–XIV).

**6.** This calling, which operates in individuals, in peoples, and in the human race itself through the opportunities provided by the times, belongs to a high and profound ordering. To this also belongs the statement, “In the womb I sanctified you” (Jer. I, 5), and, “When you were in your father’s loins, I saw you” [Note: [Col. 0073] *Ibid.*], and, “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated” (Mal. I, 2–3), since this was said before they were born.

It cannot be comprehended except perhaps by those who love God with all their heart, soul, and mind, and love their neighbors as themselves (Matt. XXII, 37, 39). Grounded in such great love, they may perhaps already be able, with the saints, to comprehend the length, breadth, height, and depth (Eph. III, 18).

This, however, must be held with the most steadfast faith: that God does nothing unjustly, and that there is no nature which does not owe to God what it is. For all beauty, splendor, and harmony of parts are owed to God; and if you pursue this to its furthest extent [Note: [Col. 0074] So the manuscripts. The printed editions read, “if you follow this through.”] and remove from things all their remaining elements, nothing remains.

## LXIX. On what is written: “Then the Son himself also will be subject to the one who subjected all things to him” (1 Cor. XV, 28)

**1.** Those who maintain that the Son of God is not equal to the Father are accustomed to make especially familiar use of this testimony, where the Apostle says, “But when all things have been subjected to him, then the Son himself also will be subject to the one who subjected all things to him, so that God may be all in all.”

Their error could not be disguised under a Christian name unless it arose from Scriptures that were not understood. For they say, “If he is equal, how will he be subject to him?” This is certainly similar to that Gospel question: “If he is equal, how is the Father greater?” For the Lord himself says, “The Father is greater than I” (John XIV, 28).

The rule of catholic faith is as follows: whenever something is said in Scripture about the Son indicating that he is less than the Father, it is to be understood according to his assumption of humanity; but whenever statements are made by which he is shown to be equal, they are to be understood according to what he is as God.

It is therefore clear how these statements are to be understood: “The Father is greater than I,” and, “I and the Father are one” (ibid. X, 30); “The Word was God,” and, “The Word became flesh” (ibid. I, 1, 14); and, “He did not regard equality with God as something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Phil. II, 6–7).

But since many things are also said of him according to the particularity of his person, apart from what pertains to the assumption of humanity—so that the Father must be understood as nothing other than the Father and the Son as nothing other than the Son—heretics think that in statements made and understood in this way equality cannot exist.

For it is written, “All things were made through him” (John I, 3), clearly through the Son, that is, through the Word of God. Through whom, if not through the Father? Yet nowhere is it written that the Son made any creature through the Father. Likewise, it is written that the Son is the image of the Father (Col. I, 15); but nowhere is it written that the Father is the image of the Son.

Further, one is begetter and the other begotten, and there are other distinctions of this kind, which pertain not to equality of substance but to the particularity of the persons. Since they say that equality cannot exist in these matters, because they bring cruder [Note: [Col. 0074] Rat., Er., and the manuscripts read, “coarser.”—The same is found in Lugd. and Ven. M.] minds to penetrate them, they must be pressed by the weight of authority.

For if equality could not be understood in these matters—between the one through whom all things were made and the one by whom they were made, between the image and the one whose image it is, between the begotten and the begetter—the Apostle, closing the mouths of contentious people, would in no way have added the very word “equality,” saying, “He did not regard equality with God as something to be seized” [Note: [Col. 0075] The Navarricus Codex reads, “would have added the word ‘equality.’”].

**2.** Since the things written concerning the distinction between the Father and the Son were written partly because of the particularity of the persons and partly because of the assumption of humanity, while the divinity, unity, and equality of the divine substance of the Father and the Son nevertheless remain, it is rightly asked in this passage whether the Apostle said, “Then the Son himself also will be subject to the one who subjected all things to him,” according to the particularity of the persons or according to the assumption of humanity.

The context of Scripture often illuminates a statement when the surrounding passages, insofar as they bear upon the present question, are examined carefully. We find, then, that the argument has arrived at this point after he had said above, “But now Christ has risen from the dead, the first fruits of those who sleep.”

He was speaking of the resurrection of the dead, which took place in the Lord according to the assumption of humanity, although what follows makes the point completely explicit: “For since death came through a human being, the resurrection of the dead also came through a human being. For as all die in Adam, so also all will be made alive in Christ. But each in his own order: Christ the first fruits; then those who belong to Christ, at his presence (παρουσίᾳ); then the end, when he hands over the kingdom to God and the Father, when he has abolished every principality and every authority and power. For he must reign until he has placed all his enemies under his feet. The last enemy to be destroyed is death. For he has subjected all things under his feet. But when he says that all things have been subjected, it is clear that this excludes the one who subjected all things to him. But when all things have been subjected to him, then the Son himself also will be subject to the one who subjected all things to him, so that God may be all in all” (1 Cor. XV, 20–28).

It is therefore clear that this was said according to the assumption of humanity.

**3.** But they usually raise questions about other matters in this passage, the whole text of which I have recalled. First, about the statement, “When he hands over the kingdom to God and the Father,” as though the Father does not now possess the kingdom. Second, about the statement, “For he must reign until he has placed all his enemies under his feet,” as though he will not reign afterward, and as though the statement above, “Then the end,” meant the conclusion of his reign.

They understand this with sacrilegious opinion as though he had called the consummation of his kingdom “the end,” even though it is written in the Gospel, “And of his kingdom there will be no end” (Luke I, 33). Finally, concerning the statement, “But when all things have been subjected to him, then the Son himself also will be subject to the one who subjected all things to him,” they wish to understand it as though now either something is not subject to the Son or the Son himself is not subject to the Father.

**4.** The question is resolved by the manner of expression. Scripture often speaks in such a way that something which always exists is said to occur at a particular time when it is to be recognized in that time. Thus in prayer we say, “Hallowed be your name” (Matt. VI, 9), as though it had at some time not been holy.

Therefore, just as “hallowed be” means “let it be recognized as holy,” so also “when he hands over the kingdom to God and the Father” means “when he shows the Father reigning,” so that what is now believed by the faithful and not thought to be so by unbelievers may shine forth through its appearance and manifestation.

He will abolish every principality and authority by manifesting the Father’s kingdom, so that it may be known to all that no principality or authority, whether heavenly or earthly, possessed principality and authority by itself, but received them from the one from whom all things exist—not only so that they might exist, but also so that they might be ordered.

In that manifestation, no hope will remain for anyone in any ruler or in any human being. This too is now sung prophetically: “It is better to hope in the Lord than to hope in man; it is better to hope in the Lord than to hope in princes” (Ps. CXVII, 8–9). Through this meditation, the soul may already rise toward the kingdom of the Father, neither magnifying anyone’s power apart from him nor most ruinously flattering itself [Note: [Col. 0076] Rat., Er., and several manuscripts read, “flattering herself most ruinously.”—The same is found in Lugd. and Ven. M.].

He will therefore hand over the kingdom to God and the Father when, through him, the Father is recognized by manifestation. His kingdom consists of those in whom he now reigns through faith. The kingdom of Christ is spoken of in one way according to the power of his divinity, according to which every creature is subject to him; and in another way his kingdom is called the Church, according to the particularity of the faith which is in him, according to which the one who says, “Possess us,” prays (Isa. XXVI, 13, according to the Septuagint).

For it is not the case that he does not possess all things. In this sense, too, the statement is made: “When you were slaves of sin, you were free in regard to righteousness” (Rom. VI, 20).

He will therefore abolish every principality, authority, and power, so that when anyone looks upon the Father through the Son, there will be neither need nor desire to rest in the power of any creature or in one’s own power.

**5.** “For he must reign until he has placed all his enemies under his feet”: that is, his kingdom must be manifested to such an extent that all his enemies acknowledge that he reigns. This is what is understood by the enemies being under his feet.

If we take this as referring to the righteous, they are called enemies because they are justified from among the unjust and, by believing in him, are brought under his authority. Concerning the unjust, who do not belong to the future blessedness of the righteous, it must be understood that they too, confounded by the very manifestation of his kingdom, will acknowledge that he reigns.

Therefore, “He must reign until he has placed all his enemies under his feet” was not said as though, once he has placed his enemies under his feet, he will not reign afterward.
