Rather, it means: “He must reign,” he says, “until he brings his kingdom to such evident manifestation that his enemies in no way dare deny that he reigns.”

For it is written, “Our eyes are toward the Lord our God until he has mercy upon us” (Ps. CXXII, 2); yet when he has had mercy upon us, we must not turn our eyes away from him. Our blessedness consists precisely in the degree to which we enjoy his contemplation.

So here too, “until” is used to mean “no further.” Understand “until” here as meaning “not beyond that point.” For to what further or greater manifestation will the kingdom of Christ be manifested than that at which all his enemies acknowledge that he reigns?

Not being manifested any further is one thing; not continuing any further is another. The former means not becoming more manifest; the latter means not continuing longer. When will Christ’s kingdom be more manifest than when it has become clear to all his enemies?

**6.** “The last enemy to be destroyed is death.” There will be nothing else to destroy after this mortal nature has put on immortality.

“For he has subjected all things under his feet”: that is, so that he may also destroy death. But when he has said that all things are subjected—this, of course, was said by the prophet in the Psalms (Ps. VIII, 8)—it is clear that the one who subjected all things to him is excepted. He means that the Father subjected all things to the Son, just as the same Lord commends and proclaims this in many passages of the Gospel—not only because of the form of a servant, but also because of the principle from which he is and by which he is equal to the one from whom he is.

For, as his image, he loves to refer all things to one principle, but in him dwells all the fullness of divinity (Col. II, 9).

**7.** “But when all things have been subjected to him, then the Son himself also will be subject to the one who subjected all things to him.” This does not mean that it is not so now, but that it will then be manifest, according to the manner of expression discussed above.

“So that God may be all in all.” This is the end which he mentioned above, when he first wished to bring the whole matter briefly to a conclusion and then to explain and expound it as though part by part. He was speaking about the resurrection when he said, “Christ the first fruits; then those who belong to Christ at his presence; then the end.” The end itself is that God may be all in all.

For “end” can be understood in one way as completion and in another as consumption. A garment is brought to an end by weaving, whereas food is brought to an end by being eaten.

God is said to be all in all so that none of those who cling to him may love a will of their own against him, and so that it may become manifest to all what the same Apostle says elsewhere: “What do you have that you did not receive?” (1 Cor. IV, 7).

**8.** There are also those who understand the passage, “He must reign until he has placed all his enemies under his feet,” in this way: they say that “reign” is used here with another meaning, not the meaning of “kingdom” in the statement, “When he hands over the kingdom to God and the Father.”

They hold that the kingdom there refers to the way in which God rules the whole creation, whereas “to reign” here means something like leading an army against an enemy or defending a city. Thus he said, “He must reign until he has placed all his enemies under his feet,” because a kingdom of the kind possessed by military rulers will have no further purpose once the enemy has been so subjected that he cannot rebel.

For it is certainly said in the Gospel, “And of his kingdom there will be no end,” according to the way in which he reigns forever. But according to the way in which warfare is now carried on under him against the devil, this warfare will continue until he has placed all his enemies under his feet. Afterward it will no longer exist, when we enjoy perpetual peace.

**9.** These things have been said so that we may know that we must also consider more carefully in what sense the Lord now reigns through the dispensation of his mystery, by his incarnation and passion.

According to what he is as the Word of God, his kingdom is without end, without beginning, and without interruption. But according to the fact that “the Word became flesh” (John I, 14), he began to reign in believers through faith in his incarnation. Hence also the statement, “The Lord has reigned from the wood” (Ps. XCV, 10).

In this way he abolished every principality, authority, and power, while believers are saved not through his glory but through his humility. This was “hidden from the wise and understanding and revealed to little ones” (Matt. XI, 25), because “it pleased God through the foolishness of preaching to save those who believe” (1 Cor. I, 21).

The Apostle says that he knows nothing among the little ones except Jesus Christ, and him crucified (ibid. II, 2). This preaching is necessary until all enemies are placed under his feet: that is, until all worldly pride yields and is subjected to his humility, which I believe is signified by the name “feet.” This has already happened to a great extent, and we see it happening daily.

But to what end do these things happen? So that he may hand over the kingdom to God and the Father: that is, so that he may lead those nourished by faith in his incarnation to the vision in which he is equal to the Father.

He was already speaking to those who had believed when he said, “If you remain in my word, you are truly my disciples” [Note: [Col. 0078] Rat. and most manuscripts read, “you will be.”], “and you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free” (John VIII, 31–32).

He will hand over the kingdom to the Father when he reigns through that which is equal to the Father in those who contemplate the truth, and when through himself, the Only-Begotten, he makes the Father visible by manifestation.

For now he reigns in believers through that by which he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant (Phil. II, 7). Then he will hand over the kingdom to God and the Father when he has abolished every principality, authority, and power.

By what will he abolish them? By humility, patience, and weakness. For what principality would not be abolished when the Son of God [Note: [Col. 0078] The printed editions read, “the Son of man”; nearly all the manuscripts disagree.] reigns in believers precisely because the rulers of this world judged him?

What authority would not be abolished when the one through whom all things were made reigns in believers precisely because he was so subject to the authorities that he said to a human being, “You would have no authority over me unless it had been given to you from above” (John XIX, 11)?

What power would not be abolished when the one through whom the heavens were established reigns in believers precisely because he was weakened even to the cross and death?

In this way the Son properly reigns in the faith of believers. For the Father cannot be said or believed to have become incarnate, to have been judged, or to have been crucified.

By the manifestation in which he is equal to the Father, he reigns with the Father in those who contemplate the truth. In handing over the kingdom to God and the Father, leading those who now believe in him from faith in his incarnation to the vision of his divinity, he does not lose anything; rather, the two present themselves as one to those who contemplate them for their enjoyment.

It is necessary for Christ to reign in this way among human beings who are not yet able, by the clear light of the mind, to behold the equality of the Father and the Son: through that which such people can grasp and which he himself properly assumed, namely, the humility of the incarnation, until he places all enemies under his feet—that is, until all worldly pride is subjected to the humility of his incarnation.

10. It is true that the statement, “Then the Son himself will also be subject to him who subjected all things to him,” although it is said with reference to the assumption of humanity—for the question arose when he was discussing the resurrection of the dead—is nevertheless rightly questioned: was it said only with reference to him who is the head of the Church (Ephesians 5:23), or with reference to the whole Christ, including his body and members?

For when he says to the Galatians, “He does not say, ‘And to seeds,’ as though referring to many, but as referring to one, ‘And to your seed,’ which is Christ”; lest we should understand Christ in this passage to mean only the one born of the Virgin Mary, he later says, “For you are all one in Christ Jesus. And if you belong to Christ, then you are Abraham’s seed” (Galatians 3:16, 28–29).

And to the Corinthians, when he was speaking of love and drawing an analogy from the members of a body, he says: “For just as the body is one and has many members, and all the members of the body, though they are many, are one body, so also is Christ.” He did not say, “so also are Christ’s members,” but “so also is Christ,” showing that Christ may rightly be called the whole—that is, the head together with his body, which is the Church.

In many passages of Scripture we likewise find Christ called in this way, so that he is understood together with all his members, to whom it was said, “You are the body of Christ and members individually” (1 Corinthians 12:12, 27). We therefore understand the passage in this way without absurdity: “Then the Son himself will also be subject to him who subjected all things to him.” We should understand by “the Son” not only the head of the Church, but also all the saints with him, who are one in Christ, one seed of Abraham.

He will be subject according to the contemplation of eternal truth, for the attainment of blessedness, with no movement of the mind and no part of the body resisting; so that in that life, when no one loves his own power, God may be all in all.

## LXX. On the statement of the Apostle: “Death has been swallowed up in victory. Where, O death, is your contention? Where, O death, is your sting? The sting of death is sin, but the power of sin is the law” (1 Corinthians 15:54–56).

I think that by “death” in this passage the carnal habit is signified, which resists the good will through the pleasure of enjoying temporal things. For would it be said, “Where, O death, is your contention?” if it had not resisted and fought back? Its contention is also described in the passage: “The flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh. For these oppose one another, so that you do not do what you wish” (Galatians 5:17).

Through perfect sanctification, therefore, it comes about that every carnal appetite is subjected to our enlightened and enlivened spirit—that is, to the good will. And just as we now see ourselves deprived of many childish pleasures which, when we were children, tormented us most sharply if they were denied us, so we must believe that this will happen with every carnal pleasure when perfect holiness has restored the whole human being.

For now, however, as long as there is within us something that resists the good will, we need the help of God through good people and good angels, so that, until our wound is healed, it may not trouble us so much as to destroy even our good will.

We deserved this death through sin. Sin was previously, in every respect, within free choice, when in paradise no pain caused by a denied pleasure resisted the human being’s good will, as it does now. For example, if there were someone whom hunting had never pleased, he would be entirely free to choose whether or not he wished to hunt, and whoever forbade him this would not torment him. But if, having misused this freedom, he hunted contrary to the command of the one forbidding him, pleasure would gradually creep in and mortify his soul, so that, if he wished to abstain, he could no longer do so without distress and anguish, although previously, in complete health, he had not done this.

The sting of death, then, is sin, because through sin a pleasure was produced that could now resist the good will and be restrained only with pain. Since this pleasure arises from the soul’s decline and from its having become worse, we rightly call it death.

“But the power of sin is the law,” because what the law forbids is committed with far greater wickedness and shamefulness than it would be if it were forbidden by no law. Thus death will be swallowed up in victory when, through sanctification, the pleasure of carnal things is overwhelmed in every part of the human being by the perfect pleasure of spiritual things.

> **Note:** In the printed editions the seventieth question began as follows: “It is usually asked what is meant by the statement, ‘Then what is written will take place: Death has been swallowed up in victory,’ etc. I think that death is signified, etc.” The manuscripts correct this.

> **Note:** The printed editions add “of good things”; this word is absent from the manuscripts.

> **Note:** Sixteen manuscripts read *molestetur* (“be troubled”), rather than *molestet* (“trouble”).

> **Note:** Thus the Ratianus manuscript and the manuscripts. Erasmus and Lovaniensis read *denegata delectatione* (“a denied pleasure”). The Lyon and Venetian editions likewise have this reading.

> **Note:** Nearly all the manuscripts read “resist the will,” omitting the word “good.”

## LXXI. On the statement: “Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ” (Galatians 6:2).

### 1.

Since observance of the Old Testament involved fear, the fact that the gift of the New Testament is love could not be signified more clearly than in this passage, where the Apostle says, “Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ.”

This is understood as the law of Christ, by which the Lord himself commanded us to love one another, giving such weight to this commandment that he said, “By this it will be known that you are my disciples, if you love one another” (John 13:34–35).

The service of this love is to bear one another’s burdens. Yet this service, which is not eternal, will lead to eternal blessedness, in which there will be none of our burdens that we are commanded to bear for one another. But now, while we are in this life—that is, on this road—let us bear one another’s burdens, so that we may be able to reach the life that is free from every burden.

Some students of such matters have written that when deer cross a strait to an island in search of pasture, they arrange themselves so that they carry on one another the burdens of their heads, which they bear upon their antlers. The deer at the rear, placing its neck upon the one in front, rests its head upon it. Since there must be one who goes before the others and has no one ahead of him upon whom to lean his head, they are said to take turns: when the one leading becomes tired from the burden of his head, he withdraws to the rear and is replaced by the one whose head he had carried while he was in front. In this way, carrying one another’s burdens, they cross the strait until they reach solid land (Pliny, book 8, chapter 32).

> **Note:** Erasmus, the Ratianus manuscript, and the manuscripts read *redeat* (“returns”), rather than *recedat* (“withdraws”); the Lyon and Venetian editions likewise read *redeat*.

Perhaps Solomon had this nature of deer in mind when he said, “Let the deer of friendship and the young one of your graces converse with you” (Proverbs 5:19, according to the Septuagint). For nothing proves a friend so much as bearing a friend’s burden.

### 2.

Yet we would not bear one another’s burdens if both persons had the same period of weakness while bearing their burdens, or the same kind of weakness. Rather, different periods and different kinds of weakness make it possible for us to bear one another’s burdens.

For example, you will bear your brother’s anger when you are not angry with him, so that, in turn, when anger has overtaken you, he may support you by his gentleness and calm. This example concerns different periods in which people bear their burdens, although the weakness itself is not different: in both cases anger is borne by each on behalf of the other.

For a different kind of weakness, another example must be considered. Suppose one person has overcome loquacity in himself but has not yet overcome stubbornness, while another is still talkative but is no longer stubborn. The first ought to bear the second’s loquacity, and the second the first’s stubbornness, in love, until the former is healed in one and the latter in the other.

For if two people have the same weakness at the same time, they cannot tolerate one another when it is directed against each other. Against some third person, however, even two angry people can agree and tolerate one another. Yet they should not be said to tolerate one another so much as to console one another.

Similarly, people who are grieving over the same matter support one another and, as it were, lean upon one another more readily than if one were sad and the other joyful. But if they are sad in opposition to each other, they cannot tolerate one another at all.

Therefore, in such emotions, one should accept a little of the very distress from which one wishes to free another through oneself. It should be accepted in such a way that it serves as help, not as an equality of misery—just as one bends down when extending a hand to someone lying on the ground. One does not throw oneself down so that both may lie there; one bends only enough to raise the person who is lying down.

### 3.

Nothing makes us willing to undertake this dutiful labor of bearing the burdens of others except when we think how much the Lord endured for us. For this reason the Apostle, offering an admonition, says: “Have this mind among yourselves which was also in Christ Jesus, who, although he was in the form of God, did not regard equality with God as something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of human beings and found in appearance as a human being; he humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death—even death on a cross” (Philippians 2:4–8).

Earlier he had said, “Let each of you look not to his own interests, but to those of others.” He joined to this statement what follows: “Have this mind among yourselves which was also in Christ Jesus.”

The point is simply this: just as he, in that “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14), and, though he was without sin, took upon himself our sins, did not consider his own interests but ours, so we too, willingly and in imitation of him, should bear one another’s burdens.

> **Note:** Lovaniensis reads “obedient to the Father.” “To the Father” is absent from the other printed editions and the manuscripts.

### 4.

To this thought another should be added: he assumed humanity, whereas we are human beings. We must consider that the distress—whether of mind or body—which we see in another human being could also have been, or could now be, ours.

Therefore let us offer to the person whose weakness we wish to bear what we would wish him to offer us if we happened to be in that condition and he did not. This is related to what the Apostle himself says: “I have become all things to all people, that I might save all” (1 Corinthians 9:22)—by considering that he too might have been in the vice from which he wished to free another.

He acted in this way out of compassion, not by lying, as some suppose—especially those who, in defending their own lies, which they cannot deny, seek the protection of some great example.

### 5.

Furthermore, we must consider that there is no human being who could not possess some good that you do not yet possess, even if it is hidden—some good by which he could undoubtedly be superior to you.

This thought is useful for crushing and subduing pride, lest you suppose that because certain goods of yours are conspicuous and apparent, another therefore possesses no hidden goods, perhaps of greater weight, by which he surpasses you without your knowing it.

The Apostle does not command us to deceive ourselves, or rather to flatter ourselves, when he says, “Do nothing through rivalry or empty glory, but in humility of mind consider one another superior to yourselves” (Philippians 2:3).

> **Note:** Most manuscripts read “deceive us”; the printed editions read “deceives us.” We must not understand this as though we should not actually think so, but merely pretend to think so. We should truly think that something hidden may exist in another by which he is superior to us, even if the good by which we seem superior to him is not hidden.

These thoughts, which depress pride and sharpen love, make us bear the burdens of our brothers not only with equanimity but also most willingly.

> **Note:** Three manuscripts read “increase love,” rather than “sharpen love.”

No judgment should be passed in any way on a person who is unknown; and no one is known except through friendship. This is why we bear the faults of our friends more firmly: their good qualities delight us and hold us to them.

### 6.

The friendship of no one who offers himself for friendship should therefore be rejected—not so that he is immediately received, but so that he may be desired as someone who ought to be received, and treated in such a way that he can be received.

We may call someone received into friendship when we dare to pour out all our plans and counsels to him.

If someone is prevented from offering himself for friendship by some temporal honor or dignity of ours, we should descend to him and offer him, with a certain courtesy and humility of spirit, what he does not dare to ask for himself.

Although less frequently, it nevertheless sometimes happens that the faults of the person whom we wish to receive into friendship become known to us before his virtues. Offended and, as it were, repelled by these faults, we leave him and do not reach the investigation of his virtues, which may be more hidden.

The Lord Jesus Christ, who wishes us to become his imitators, therefore admonishes us to tolerate his weaknesses, so that through the endurance of love we may be led to certain healthy qualities in whose enjoyment we can rest. For he says, “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick” (Matthew 9:12).

Therefore, even if out of love for Christ we should not drive from our hearts someone who perhaps is sick in every respect—for he can be healed through the Word of God—how much less should we reject someone who may seem wholly sick to us merely because at the beginning of the friendship we could not endure certain wounded parts of him.

What is worse, we may have dared, in the offense of our own minds, to pass a rash preliminary judgment on the whole person, not fearing what was said: “Do not judge, so that you may not be judged”; and, “With the measure with which you measure, it will be measured back to you” (Matthew 7:1–2).

Often the good qualities appear first. Even then, rash judgment based on goodwill must be avoided, lest, when you have thought someone wholly good, the faults that later appear find you secure and unprepared, and offend you more severely. Thus you may hate more bitterly the person whom you had rashly loved—which is wicked.

For even if none of his good qualities had preceded, and the faults that later appeared had stood out first, those faults should nevertheless have been tolerated until you had dealt with him in all the ways by which such things are usually healed. How much more, then, when good qualities have preceded—qualities that ought to bind us, as pledges, to tolerate what comes later?

> **Note:** Seven manuscripts read “and to his good qualities”; shortly afterward they read “investigation.”

> **Note:** The printed editions read, “who is perhaps sick in part or wholly”; shortly afterward they have, “who may seem sick on our account.” The manuscripts read, “who is perhaps sick in every respect … who may therefore seem so to us.”

### 7.

This, then, is the law of Christ: that we bear one another’s burdens.

By loving Christ, we readily endure the weakness of another, even someone whom we do not yet love because of his good qualities. For we think that the Lord, whom we love, died for him.

The Apostle Paul impressed this love upon us when he said, “And the weak person will perish through your knowledge—the brother for whom Christ died” (1 Corinthians 8:11). If we love that weak person less because of the fault by which he is weak, we should consider him in relation to the one who died for him.

Not to love Christ is not weakness but death. Therefore, with great care and having implored God’s mercy, we must take thought lest we neglect Christ because of the weak person, when we ought to love the weak person because of Christ.

## LXXII. On eternal times

[Column 0084]

It may be asked how the Apostle Paul could have said, “Before eternal times” (Titus 1:2). For if they are times, how are they eternal? Unless perhaps he intended “before all times” to be understood.

For if he had said “before times” without adding “eternal,” it could be understood as meaning before certain times that themselves had other times preceding them. He preferred to say “eternal” rather than “all,” perhaps because time did not begin from time.

Or did he signify the age (*aevum*) by “eternal times”? The difference between the age and time is that the former is stable, whereas time is mutable.

> **Note:** Book 12 of *The City of God*, chapter 16.

## LXXIII. On the statement: “And found in appearance as a human being” (Philippians 2:7)

### 1.

We use the word “appearance” (*habitus*) in many ways. There is the appearance or disposition of the mind, such as the acquisition of some discipline strengthened and confirmed by practice. There is the appearance or constitution of the body, according to which we say that one person is more full-bodied and stronger than another; this is more properly called bodily condition (*habitudo*). There is also the appearance of things externally fitted to our members, according to which we speak of someone as clothed, shod, armed, or something similar.

In all these categories—if this word is indeed derived from the verb *habere*, “to have”—it is clear that “appearance” is said of something that happens to someone in such a way that he can also not have it.

Instruction happens to the mind; flesh and strength to the body; clothing and weapons to our limbs. Thus the mind can be unlearned if instruction does not happen to it; the body thin and weak without the nourishment of its organs and its strength; and a human being can be naked without clothing, unarmed without weapons, and barefoot without shoes.

“Appearance,” then, is said of something that happens to us so that it may be possessed.

There is nevertheless this difference: some of the things that happen to us in order to produce an appearance are not changed by us; rather, they change us into themselves, while remaining themselves whole and unshaken. Thus, when wisdom happens to a person, wisdom itself is not changed, but changes the person, making him wise instead of foolish.

Other things happen in such a way that they both change and are changed. Food, for example, loses its own form and is transformed into our body; and we, nourished by food, are changed from thinness and weakness into strength and vigor.

There is a third category, in which the things that happen are themselves changed in order to produce an appearance, and are formed, in a certain way, by those to whom they give an appearance. Clothing is an example. When it has been put away or thrown aside, it does not have the form it takes when it is put on and drawn over the limbs.

Thus, when clothed, it receives a form that it did not have when unclothed, while the limbs themselves remain in their own state both when they are clothed and when they are unclothed.

There may also be a fourth category, in which the things that happen to produce an appearance neither change those to whom they happen nor are themselves changed by them—such as a ring on a finger, if one does not examine the matter too finely.

Yet this category is either nonexistent, if one investigates carefully, or extremely rare.

### 2.

When the Apostle was speaking of the only-begotten Son of God, insofar as his divinity is concerned, according to which he is truly God, he said that he was equal to the Father. It was not robbery for him—that is, it was not like desiring something alien—if, while always remaining in that equality, he did not wish to be clothed with humanity and appear as a human being to human beings.

“But he emptied himself,” not by changing his own form, but by taking the form of a servant. He was not converted or transformed into a human being, losing his immutable stability; rather, although he truly assumed a human being, he himself—the one who assumed him—was made in the likeness of human beings. He was found in appearance as a human being, not for himself but for those to whom he appeared as a human being (Philippians 2:6–7); that is, by having a human being, he was found to be a human being.

God could not be found by those whose hearts were impure and who could not see the Word with the Father, except by his assuming what they could see and through which they could be led to that inner light.

This appearance does not belong to the first category. The human nature, remaining in itself, did not change the nature of God. Nor does it belong to the second, for the human being did not change God, nor was he changed by God. Nor does it belong to the fourth, for humanity was not assumed in such a way that it neither changed God nor was changed by him.

Rather, it belongs to the third category. Humanity was assumed in such a way that it was changed for the better and formed by him, ineffably more excellently and more closely than clothing is formed when it is put on by a human being.

By the word “appearance,” therefore, the Apostle sufficiently indicated how he said that Christ was “made in the likeness of human beings.” He was made not by transformation into a human being, but by appearance, when he was clothed with humanity, uniting and, in a certain way, conforming that humanity to himself, so that he might associate it with immortality and eternity.

The Greeks call the appearance that consists in the acquisition of wisdom and discipline **ἕξις** (*hexis*). The appearance according to which we speak of someone as clothed or armed they call rather **σχῆμα** (*schēma*).

From this it is understood that the Apostle spoke of this kind of appearance, since the Greek manuscripts have **σχήματι** (*schēmati*), which we have as *habitu* (“in appearance”) in Latin.

By this term we must understand that the Word was not changed by the assumption of humanity, just as limbs are not changed when clothed with garments. Nevertheless, that assumption united the one assumed to the one assuming him in an ineffable way.

But insofar as human words can be adapted to ineffable realities, so that God might not be understood as changed by assuming human weakness, it was chosen that this assumption should be called **σχῆμα** in Greek and *habitus* in Latin.

> **Note:** Eight manuscripts read as above. The printed editions read “but as though.”

> **Note:** The Cistercian codex omits “God”; several manuscripts have “so that he might be found a human being” in place of it.

> **Note:** The Ratianus manuscript, Erasmus, and most manuscripts read *assumptor* (“the one assuming”), rather than *assumptione* (“assumption”). The Lyon and Venetian editions likewise have the former reading.

## LXXIV. On the statement written in Paul’s Epistle to the Colossians: “In whom we have redemption and the forgiveness of sins, who is the image of the invisible God” (Colossians 1:14–15)

Image, equality, and likeness must be distinguished.

Where there is an image, there is immediately likeness, but not immediately equality. Where there is equality, there is immediately likeness, but not immediately an image. Where there is likeness, there is not immediately an image and not immediately equality.

Where there is an image, there is immediately likeness but not immediately equality. A human image in a mirror is an image because it has been reproduced from the human being. It is also necessarily a likeness, but it is not equality, because many things belong to the person from whom it has been reproduced that are lacking in the image.

Where there is equality, there is immediately likeness but not immediately an image, as in two equal eggs. Since equality exists between them, likeness also exists: whatever is present in one is present in the other. Yet there is no image, because neither has been reproduced from the other.

Where there is likeness, there is not immediately an image and not immediately equality. Every egg is like every other egg insofar as it is an egg. But although a partridge’s egg is like a hen’s egg insofar as it is an egg, it is not its image, because it has not been reproduced from it; nor is it equal to it, because it is smaller and belongs to another kind of animal.

When it is said “not immediately,” this of course means that it can sometimes be so. There can therefore be an image in which there is also equality. Such an image, equality, and likeness could be found in parents and children if an interval of time were absent. The likeness of the child has been reproduced from the parent, so that it is rightly called an image; and it can be so great that it is also rightly called equality, except that the parent preceded the child in time.

From this it is understood that equality can sometimes possess not only likeness but also an image, as is clear from the preceding example.

Likeness can also sometimes exist together with equality even though there is no image, as was said of two equal eggs.

Likeness and an image can also exist even though there is no equality, as we showed in the case of the mirror.

Likeness can also exist where there are both equality and an image, as we mentioned in the case of children, apart from the time by which parents precede them. Thus we call one syllable equal to another, even though one comes before and the other follows.

In God, however, because temporal condition is absent—for it cannot rightly be understood that God generated the Son in time, through whom he created time—it follows that the Son is not only his image, because he is from him, and his likeness, because he is the image (Colossians 1:15), but also so completely equal that not even an interval of time stands in the way.

## LXXV. On God’s inheritance

### 1.

As the Apostle says to the Hebrews, “A testament is confirmed by the death of the testator” (Hebrews 9:17). For this reason he asserts that, when Christ died for us, the New Testament was confirmed. The Old Testament was its likeness, in which the death of the testator was prefigured through a victim.

If, then, it is asked how, according to the words of the same Apostle, we are “coheirs with Christ, and sons and heirs of God” (Romans 8:17), since an inheritance is also held securely by the death of the predecessor and inheritance can be understood in no other way, the answer is that we became heirs when he himself died, since we are also called his children.

“The children of the bridegroom,” he says, “cannot fast while the bridegroom is with them” (Matthew 9:15).

We are therefore called his heirs because he left us possession of ecclesiastical peace through the faith of his temporal dispensation, which we possess in this life. He testified to this when he said, “My peace I give you; my peace I leave you” (John 14:27).

We will become his coheirs when, at the end of the world, death is swallowed up in victory (1 Corinthians 15:54). Then we will be like him, when we see him as he is (1 John 3:2).

We do not obtain this inheritance through the death of his Father, who cannot die. Indeed, he himself becomes our inheritance, according to what is written, “The Lord is the portion of my inheritance” (Psalm 15:5).

Rather, because when we were called while still children and less capable of contemplating spiritual things, divine mercy extended itself even to our lowliest thoughts, so that we might strive, however imperfectly, to see what we did not see clearly and distinctly, that which we saw in an enigma dies when we begin to see face to face.

It is therefore fittingly said that what will be taken away will die: “When the perfect comes, what is partial will be taken away” (1 Corinthians 13:10).

Thus, in a certain way, the Father dies for us in an enigma, and the same Father becomes our inheritance when he is seen face to face—not because he himself dies, but because our imperfect vision of him is destroyed by perfect vision. Nevertheless, unless that earlier vision had nourished us, we would not become capable of the other, fullest and clearest vision.

> **Note:** The word “his” is absent from the Ratianus manuscript and several manuscripts.

> **Note:** The Ratianus manuscript, Erasmus, and twenty manuscripts read “is possessed,” rather than “is seen.” The Lyon and Venetian editions likewise have this reading.

### 2.

If a devout understanding also admits the same point concerning the Lord Jesus Christ—not according to the Word who in the beginning was God with God (John 1:1), but according to the child who advanced in age and wisdom (Luke 2:40)—while preserving that unique assumption which he does not share with other human beings, it is clear whose death could give him possession of the inheritance.

For we cannot be his coheirs unless he himself is also an heir.

But if piety does not permit us to accept that the Lord’s humanity first saw partially and afterward wholly, although he is said to have advanced in wisdom, then let the heir be understood in his body—that is, in the Church, whose coheirs we are. In this way we are called children of his mother, although she consists of us.

> **Note:** *Retractations* 1.19.8.

### 3.

Again, however, it may be asked through whose death we too have become God’s inheritance, according to the statement, “I will give you the nations as your inheritance” (Psalm 2:8).

Perhaps it is through the death of this world, by which we were previously held as though it were ruling us. But afterward, when we say, “The world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Galatians 6:14), Christ possesses us, because the one who possessed us has died. When we renounce it, we die to it, and it dies to us.

> **Note:** Erasmus and Lovaniensis repeated “your inheritance” after the phrase, adding “But your inheritance”; this is absent from the Ratianus manuscript and the manuscripts. The Lyon and Venetian editions have the same reading as the editions of Erasmus and Lovaniensis.

## LXXVI. On what the Apostle James says: “But do you wish to know, O empty human being, that faith without works is useless?” (James 2:20)

### 1.

Because the Apostle Paul, preaching that a human being is justified by faith without works, was not well understood by those who interpreted the statement as though, once they had believed in Christ, they could be saved by faith even if they acted wickedly and lived criminally and shamefully, this passage in the Epistle of James explains how Paul’s meaning is to be understood (James 2:17–24).

For this reason James makes greater use of the example of Abraham, showing that faith is empty if it does not act well. The Apostle Paul also used Abraham’s example to prove that a person is justified by faith without works of the Law (Romans 4:2).

When James recalls Abraham’s good works, which accompanied his faith, he clearly shows that the Apostle Paul did not teach through Abraham that a person is justified by faith without works in such a way that, if someone believes, good works are irrelevant to him. Rather, Paul taught that no one should think he has attained the gift of justification, which exists in faith, through the merits of prior good works.

> **Note:** The printed editions, with several manuscripts, add “good.”

The Jews wished to place themselves above the Gentiles who believed in Christ because they said that they had reached evangelical grace through the merits of the good works contained in the Law. For this reason many who had believed from among them were scandalized because Christ’s grace was being granted to uncircumcised Gentiles.

Hence the Apostle Paul says that a person can be justified by faith without works—meaning without works that came before. For once justified by faith, how can a person fail to act justly thereafter, even though previously he had done nothing justly and had attained the justification of faith not through the merit of good works but through the grace of God, which can no longer be empty in him once he acts well through love?

> **Note:** Six manuscripts read “but through the grace of God, which cannot be idle in him.”

If, after believing, he immediately departs from this life, the justification of faith remains with him: not with preceding good works, because he reached it by grace and not by merit; nor with subsequent works, because he is not permitted to remain in this life.

> **Note:** The same number of manuscripts read *discesserit* (“departs”), rather than *decesserit* (“dies”).

It is therefore clear that what the Apostle Paul says—“For we hold that a person is justified by faith without works” (Romans 3:28)—must not be understood as though, once faith has been received, we should call someone just even if he lives wickedly.

The Apostle Paul therefore also uses Abraham’s example, because Abraham was justified by faith without the works of the Law, which he had not received. James uses the same example because he demonstrates that good works followed Abraham’s faith, showing how what the Apostle Paul preached is to be understood.

> **Note:** Two manuscripts, together with the Ratianus manuscript, read “faith without works, because …”

### 2.

Those who think that this statement of the Apostle James contradicts the statement of the Apostle Paul could also suppose that Paul himself contradicts himself, because elsewhere he says, “For it is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but the doers of the law will be justified” (Romans 2:13).

And elsewhere: “But faith working through love” (Galatians 5:6).

And again: “For if you live according to the flesh, you will die; but if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the flesh, you will live” (Romans 8:13).

What the deeds of the flesh are that must be put to death by spiritual works, he shows elsewhere when he says: “The works of the flesh are evident: fornications, impurities, indecency, the service of idols, sorceries, enmities, quarrels, jealousies, animosities, dissensions, heresies, envies, drunkenness, revelries, and things like these. I warn you, as I warned you before, that those who do such things will not possess the kingdom of God” (Galatians 5:19–21).

And to the Corinthians he says: “Do not be deceived: neither fornicators, nor those who serve idols, nor adulterers, nor the effeminate, nor men who have intercourse with males, nor thieves, nor the greedy, nor drunkards, nor slanderers, nor robbers will possess the kingdom of God. And such were some of you; but you were washed, but you were sanctified, but you were justified in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ and in the Spirit of our God” (1 Corinthians 6:9–11).

By these statements he teaches most clearly that they did not attain the justification of faith through a good work performed previously, nor was this grace given because of their merits, when he says, “And such were some of you.” But when he says, “Those who do such things will not possess the kingdom of God,” he sufficiently shows that, from the moment they believed, they ought to act well.

James says the same thing, and the Apostle Paul proclaims it clearly in many passages: all who have believed in Christ must live rightly, lest they reach punishment.

The Lord himself also recalls this when he says: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of my Father who is in heaven will enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 7:21).

And elsewhere: “Why do you call me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ and do not do what I say?” (Luke 6:46).

And: “Everyone who hears these words of mine and does them, I will compare him to a prudent man who built his house upon a rock,” and so forth. “But everyone who hears these words of mine and does not do them, I will compare him to a foolish man who built his house upon sand,” and so forth (Matthew 7:24–27).

The statements of the two Apostles, Paul and James, are therefore not contradictory when one says that a person is justified by faith without works and the other says that faith without works is empty. The former speaks of works that precede faith; the latter of those that follow faith, as Paul himself also shows in many passages.

## LXXVII. On whether fear is a sin
Every disturbance is a passion; every desire is a disturbance: therefore every desire is a passion. But whenever a passion is in us, we suffer through that very passion; and insofar as it is a passion, we suffer. Therefore, whenever desire is in us, we suffer through that very desire; and insofar as it is desire, we suffer. But every passion, insofar as we suffer through that passion itself, is not sin: so too, if we suffer fear, it is not sin. It would be as if one said, “If it is two-footed, it is not livestock.” If, then, this does not follow because there are many two-footed animals, for the same reason the other does not follow, because there are many sins that we suffer. For the contrary claim is that it does not follow that, if we suffer fear, it is therefore not sin. Yet you say that it follows that, if we suffer fear, it is not sin, although you nevertheless concede [Note: [Col. 0089] Rat. and six manuscripts: “although it is established.”] that there are some sins that we suffer.

## LXXVIII. On the beauty of images

That supreme art of almighty God, through which all things were made from nothing, which is also called his wisdom, [Col. 0090] itself works even through craftsmen, so that they make beautiful and well-proportioned things; although they work not from nothing but from some material, such as wood, marble, ivory, or any other kind of material subjected to the craftsman’s hands. But these men cannot fashion anything from nothing precisely because they work through the body; yet they receive in the mind from that supreme wisdom the proportions and harmony of lines that they impress through the body upon bodies—the wisdom that impressed those proportions and that harmony, with far greater artistry, upon the whole bodily world, which was fashioned from nothing. In that world there are also the bodies of animals, which are now fashioned from something already existing, namely, from the elements of the world—but far more powerfully and excellently than when human craftsmen imitate those same bodily figures and forms in their works.

For not all the proportionality of the human body is found in a statue; nevertheless, whatever of it is found there [Note: [Col. 0090] Erasmus and Lovaniensis read *inveniuntur* (“are found”) and below *trajiciuntur* (“are transferred”). But Rat. and the manuscripts more correctly read *invenitur* (“is found”) . . . *trajicitur* (“is transferred”). The understood subject is *numerositas* (“proportionality”). Lugd. and Ven. M. agree with Erasmus and Lovaniensis.] is transferred through the craftsman’s hand [Note: [Col. 0090] Five manuscripts: “is transferred through the craftsman’s mind.” Three others: “is transferred through the craftsman’s will.”] by that wisdom which naturally fashions the human body itself. Yet those who fashion or admire such works should not on that account be considered great, because the soul, occupied with lesser things that it makes bodily through the body, clings less closely to that supreme wisdom from which it possesses these powers. It misuses them while exercising them outwardly; for, loving the things in which it exercises them, it neglects their stable inner form and becomes emptier and weaker.

Those who have even worshiped such works [Note: [Col. 0090] Several manuscripts: “who worship such works.”]—how far they have strayed from the truth can be understood from this: if they were to worship the bodies of the animals themselves, which have been fashioned much more excellently and of which those works are imitations, what could we call them other than more miserable?

## LXXIX. Why did Pharaoh’s magicians perform certain miracles like Moses, the servant of God (Exod. VII–VIII)?

### 1.

Every soul exercises authority over part of its own private domain, while in part it is restrained and governed by the laws of the whole, as by public laws. Since, therefore, every visible thing in this world has an angelic power set over it, as divine Scripture testifies in several places, that power acts concerning the thing placed under it in one way as though by private right, and in another way as though compelled to act publicly.

For the whole is more powerful than the part, since that which it does privately is permitted to do only as much as the law of the whole allows. Each soul, therefore, is purer through piety to the extent that it takes less pleasure in what is private to it, looks to the law of the whole, and obeys it devotedly and willingly. The law of the whole is divine wisdom.

But the more a soul rejoices in what is private to it and, neglecting God—who presides beneficially and salutarily over all souls—wishes to be a god to itself or to others as far as it can, cherishing its own power over itself or others rather than his power over all, [Col. 0091] the more defiled it is, and the more it is compelled, as though by public laws, to serve the divine laws under punishment.

Therefore, the more a human soul, having abandoned God, takes pleasure in its own honors or power, the more it is subjected to such powers—powers that delight in what is private to them and desire to be honored by human beings as gods. By divine law they are often permitted to grant to those whom they have subjected to themselves according to their merits, by that private right, even some miraculous effects, to be displayed in matters over which they have been placed, at the lowest but nevertheless most orderly level of powers.

But wherever divine law, as a public law, gives an order, it certainly overcomes private license—although even that private license would be nothing without the permission of the universal divine power. Thus it happens that the holy servants of God, when it is useful for them to possess this gift, command inferior powers, according to public and in a certain sense imperial law—that is, by the authority of the supreme God—to perform certain visible miracles. For in them God himself gives the command: he whose temple they are and whom they love with the greatest ardor, having despised their own private power.

In magical imprecations [Note: [Col. 0091] Erasmus, Rat., and five manuscripts read *imperationibus* (“commands”). The Michaelinus manuscript reads *impetrationibus* (“requests”). Lugd. reads *imperationibus*. M.] they grant fulfillment to the prayers and services [Note: [Col. 0091] Fifteen manuscripts: “mysteries.”] of such persons, as a lure of deception, so that they may subject those to whom they grant such things. They do so by dispensing that private right which they are permitted to dispense to those who honor and serve them and who keep certain agreements with them in their sacramental rites.

And when magicians appear to command [Note: [Col. 0091] Two manuscripts: “obtain.”], they terrify inferior powers through the names of higher ones. They display to astonished people certain visible things which seem great to human beings unable to contemplate eternal realities—things which the true God himself grants to his lovers.

God permits all these things, however, while justly regulating everything, so that he distributes their servitude and freedom according to their desires and choices. And if at times, by invoking the supreme God, they obtain something for their evil desires, that is vengeance, not grace. For the Apostle does not say without reason, “God gave them over to the desires of their hearts” (Rom. I, 26). The ease with which certain sins are committed is punishment for earlier sins.

### 2.

When the Lord says, “Satan cannot drive out Satan” (Mark III, 23), lest someone, using the names of certain inferior powers and having driven out a demon, should suppose this saying of the Lord to be false, he should understand that Satan, even if he spares the body or the bodily senses, spares them in order to dominate the will of the person himself through the error of impiety with a greater triumph.

In this way Satan does not go out but rather enters into the innermost part, so that he may work in the person as the Apostle says: “According to the prince of the power of this air, who now works in the children of disobedience” (Eph. II, 2). He was not disturbing or tormenting their bodily senses, nor striking their bodies, but was reigning in their will—or rather, in their desire.

### 3.

When he says that false prophets will perform many signs and wonders, so as to deceive even the elect, if possible (Matt. XXIV, 24), he certainly admonishes us to understand that wicked people too can perform certain miracles, such as the saints cannot perform. Yet they should not on that account be considered to hold a higher place with God.

For the magicians of Egypt were not more acceptable to God than the people of Israel simply because that people could not do what they did, although Moses, through the power of God, was able to do greater things (Exod. VII–XII). But these things are not given to all the saints, lest the weak be deceived by a most destructive error and suppose that greater gifts are present in such deeds than in works of righteousness, by which eternal life is obtained.

Therefore the Lord forbids the disciples to rejoice in this, saying: “Do not rejoice in this, that the spirits are subject to you; but rejoice in this, that your names are written in heaven” (Luke X, 20).

### 4.

When magicians perform things of the sort that the saints sometimes perform, such things certainly appear visibly to be the same, but they are done with a different purpose and under a different right. The magicians act while seeking their own glory; the saints act while seeking God’s glory. The magicians act through certain powers granted to them in their own order, as through private transactions or sorceries [Note: [Col. 0092] So Rat. and three manuscripts. Erasmus, Lovaniensis, and other codices read *beneficia* (“benefits”). Lugd. and Ven. M. agree with them.]; the saints act through public administration, by the command of him to whom every creature is subject.

A possessor is compelled to give a horse to a soldier in one way, while he hands it over to a purchaser in another, or gives or lends it to anyone else. And just as many wicked soldiers, whom imperial discipline condemns, use the emperor’s standards to terrify certain possessors and extort from them something not publicly commanded, so sometimes wicked Christians, or schismatics, or heretics, through the name of Christ or through Christian words or sacraments, exact something from powers that have been ordered to yield to the honor of Christ.

When such powers yield to wicked commanders, they yield by their will in order to seduce human beings, whose error gives them pleasure.

Therefore magicians perform miracles in one way, good Christians in another, and wicked Christians in yet another: magicians through private agreements; good Christians through public justice; wicked Christians through the signs of public justice.

It is not surprising that these signs have power when they are employed by such people, since even when they are usurped by outsiders who have not at all enrolled themselves in this service, they have power on account of the honor of the most excellent Emperor. One of these was the man about whom the disciples reported to the Lord that he was casting out demons in his name, although he did not follow him with them (Luke IX, 49).

When such powers do not yield to these signs, God himself secretly prevents them when he judges it just and useful. For spirits in no way dare to despise these signs: wherever they have seen them, they tremble. But without human beings knowing it, something else is divinely commanded, either to confound the wicked when it is appropriate that they be confounded—as we read in the Acts of the Apostles concerning the sons of Sceva, to whom the unclean spirit said, “Jesus I know, and Paul I recognize; but who are you?” (Acts XIX, 14–15)—or to admonish the good to advance in faith, so that they may be able to perform such things not boastfully but beneficially, or to distinguish the gifts of the members of the Church, as the Apostle says: “Do all have powers? Do all possess gifts of healing?” (1 Cor. XII, 30).

For these reasons, then, as has been said, God often commands without human beings knowing it—that is, when such signs are applied, he commands these powers not to obey human beings’ will.

### 5.

The wicked are often granted power to harm the good temporarily, for the greater benefit of the good [Note: [Col. 0093] The printed editions read: “receiving power over them, for the greater benefit of the good it comes about.” But the manuscripts lack the word *fit* (“it comes about”); and in place of *accipientes* (“receiving”) they have *accipiunt* (“they receive”).], for the exercise of patience.

Therefore the Christian soul must always remain watchful in its tribulations to follow the will of its Lord, lest by resisting God’s ordering it acquire a more serious judgment for itself. What the Lord himself said, while acting as a human being before Pontius Pilate, Job too could have said to the devil: “You would have no power over me unless it had been given you from above” (John XIX, 11).

It is not the will of the one whose wickedness is granted power over the good, but the will of the one by whom this power is granted, that ought to be most precious to us. For “tribulation produces endurance, endurance produces proven character, and proven character produces hope; and hope does not disappoint, because God’s love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. V, 3–5).

## LXXX. Against the Apollinarists

### 1.

Certain heretics, who are said to be called Apollinarists after a certain Apollinaris, their founder, asserted that our Lord Jesus Christ, insofar as he deigned to become human, did not possess a human mind. Some people, adhering to them and listening to them attentively, took pleasure in that perversity by which Apollinaris diminished the human being in God, saying that he had no mind—that is, no rational soul, by which a human being differs inwardly from animals.

But when they themselves considered that, if this were so, it would have to be confessed that the only-begotten Son of God, the Wisdom and Word of the Father through whom all things were made, had assumed some kind of beast with the form of a human body, they became dissatisfied—not, however, so as to correct themselves, return to the way of truth, and confess that the whole human being had been assumed by God’s Wisdom without any diminution of nature. Instead, using even greater audacity, they alienated from him the soul itself and everything proper to a human being [Note: [Col. 0093] Most manuscripts: “but using even greater audacity, alienating from him even the soul and everything proper to a human being.” The Fossatensis book: “but using greater audacity toward themselves, alienating from him even the whole soul that other human beings possess.”] and said that he had assumed only human flesh.

They also brought forward testimony from the Gospel—or rather, failing to understand that statement, they perversely dared to contend against catholic truth, saying that it is written, “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John I, 14). By these words they wish the Word to have been joined and fused to flesh in such a way that there was present there not only no mind, but not even a human soul.

### 2.

They should first be answered that the Gospel expresses the matter in this way because the Lord’s assumption of human nature extended as far as visible flesh, and because, throughout that entire unity of assumption, the Word is primary, while flesh is the outermost and final element.

Thus, wishing to commend to us the abasement of God’s humility—expressing that he humbled himself and how far he humbled himself—the Evangelist named the Word and flesh, passing over the nature of the soul, which is inferior to the Word but superior to the flesh. For humility is commended more strongly by the statement “The Word became flesh” than it would be if it said, “The Word became human.”

For if they scrutinize these words too narrowly, another person, no less perversely, could use them to bring an accusation against our faith and say that the Word itself was converted and changed into flesh and ceased to be the Word, because it is written, “The Word became flesh”—just as human flesh, when it becomes ashes, is not both flesh and ashes, but ashes from flesh.

And according to the more familiar and widespread manner of speaking, whatever becomes something it was not ceases to be what it was. Yet we do not understand these words in that way. They themselves understand them with us in this way: while the Word remains what it is, the statement “The Word became flesh” was made because he accepted the form of a servant, not because he was changed into that form by some alteration.

Moreover, if wherever flesh is mentioned and the soul is left unmentioned the matter must be understood so that the soul is believed not to be present, then those too would have no soul of whom it is said, “All flesh shall see the salvation of God” (Isa. XL, 5; Luke III, 6); and in the Psalm, “Hear my prayers; to you all flesh shall come” (Ps. LXIV, 3); and in the Gospel, “As you have given him authority over all flesh, so that everything you have given him may not perish but have eternal life” (John XVII, 2).

From this it is understood that human beings are accustomed to be signified by naming flesh alone, so that according to this manner of speaking the statement “The Word became flesh” can also be understood to mean nothing other than “The Word became human.”

For just as the whole is often understood from a part when the soul alone is named—as in the statement, “So many souls went down into Egypt” (Gen. XLVI, 22, 27)—so again the whole human being is understood from a part when flesh alone is named, as in the passages we have cited.

### 3.

Accordingly, just as we answer their objection, which they raise from the Gospel, in such a way that no human being could be so foolish as to think that these words compel us to believe and confess that “the man Christ Jesus, the mediator between God and human beings” (1 Tim. II, 5), did not possess a human soul, so I ask how they themselves answer our very clear objections. We show from countless passages of the Gospel that the Evangelists narrated concerning him that he experienced those emotions which cannot exist without a soul.

I am not even adducing all the many things that the Lord himself mentions: “My soul is deeply grieved, even to death” (Matt. XXVI, 38); “I have power to lay down my soul, and I have power to take it up again” (John X, 18); and “No one has greater love than this, that someone lay down his soul for his friends” (John XV, 13). A stubborn contradictor could say that these words were spoken figuratively by the Lord, just as it is clear that he spoke many things in parables.

For even if these statements were not understood literally, there would still be no need to fight obstinately where we have the Evangelists’ narratives, through which we know that he was born of the Virgin Mary, seized by the Jews, scourged, crucified, killed, and buried in a tomb. No one can understand all these things as having happened without a body. Nor would even the most deranged person say that they should be taken fictitiously or figuratively, since they were stated by people who narrated events as they remembered them.

Therefore, just as these events testify that he had a body, so those emotions indicate that he had a soul—emotions that cannot exist except in a soul, and which we likewise read about in the narratives of the same Evangelists. “And Jesus marveled” (Matt. VIII, 10), “and was angry” (John XI, 15), “and was grieved” (Mark III, 5), “and rejoiced” (John XI, 15), and many other things of this kind without number.

The same is shown by those events that together display the functions of both body and soul: that he was hungry (Matt. IV, 2), that he slept (Matt. VIII, 24), that, wearied from his journey, he sat down (John IV, 6), and other such things.

They cannot argue that in the ancient Books God’s anger and joy, and certain other emotions of this kind, are also mentioned, and that it does not therefore follow that we must believe God to have had a soul. Those statements were made through prophetic imagery, not through the open narration of events. God’s limbs too are mentioned—his hands, feet, eyes, face, and similar things. And just as these do not indicate that he has a body, so neither do those statements indicate that he has a soul.

But just as a narrated event in which the hands and head of Christ are named, along with other things that indicate his body, points to his body, so too the things named in the same narrative manner concerning the emotions of his soul indicate his soul.

It is foolish to believe the Evangelist when he says that he ate but not to believe him when he says that he was hungry. It does not follow that everyone who eats is hungry—for we read that an angel ate (Gen. XVIII, 8–9; Tob. XII, 19), but we do not read that he was hungry—nor that everyone who is hungry eats, if he restrains himself for some duty or lacks food and the ability to eat.

Nevertheless, when the Evangelist narrates both things (Matt. IV, 2; IX, 11), both must be believed, because he recorded both as events that happened, as a reporter of facts. And just as the fact that he ate cannot be understood without a body, so the fact that he was hungry could not have occurred without a soul.

### 4.

Nor does that empty and foolish accusation frighten us, by which they maliciously resist and say: “Then he was subject to necessity, if he truly had these emotions of the soul.”

We answer easily: “Then he was subject to necessity because he was seized, scourged, crucified, and killed.” Let them at last, if they are willing, understand without obstinacy that he assumed the emotions of the soul—that is, the passions—truly, as he chose, by the will of his dispensation [Note: [Col. 0095] So ten manuscripts. The printed editions have only here: “by the dispensation of his will.”], just as by that same will of his dispensation, without any necessity, he assumed the passions of the body. We die without willing to do so, and likewise we are born without willing to do so; but he willingly underwent both, as was fitting, and underwent them most truly.

Therefore, just as no one uses the word “necessity” to tear us or them away from faith in the truly suffered passion by which his body is shown, so no one frightens us, by using that word, away from faith in the truly experienced emotion by which we recognize his soul. Nor should it frighten them away from assenting to catholic faith, unless they are frightened by the ruinous shame of changing an opinion that, although false, they have defended for a long time and with rashness.

## LXXXI. On Lent and Pentecost

### 1.

All instruction in wisdom that pertains to educating human beings consists in distinguishing the Creator from the creature, worshiping him as the ruler, and acknowledging the creature as subject. God is the Creator, from whom all things come, through whom all things exist, and in whom all things exist (Rom. XI, 36); and therefore he is the Trinity: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

The creature, however, is partly invisible, such as the soul, and partly visible, such as the body. The number three is assigned to the invisible; therefore we are commanded to love God in three ways: with all our heart, with all our soul, and with all our mind (Matt. XXII, 37). The number four is assigned to the body because of its most evident nature, namely, hot and cold, moist and dry.

The number seven, therefore, is assigned to the whole of creation. Consequently, all instruction that distinguishes and discerns the Creator and the creature is signified by the number ten. As long as this instruction is temporally signified through bodily movements, it consists in believing, and through the authority of events that have happened or will happen, it nourishes little ones as though with milk, so as to make them fit for contemplation—which does not come and pass but always remains.

In this contemplation, if someone perseveres in faith regarding the events divinely narrated to him as having happened temporally for the salvation of human beings, or regarding those still to happen that are proclaimed as future; if he hopes for what has been promised; and if he takes care to fulfill with indefatigable love what divine authority commands, he will rightly live the life of this necessity and this time, which is commended by the number forty.

For the number ten, which signifies the whole of instruction, multiplied by four—that is, multiplied by the number assigned to the body, because bodily administration is carried out through movement—produces the number forty, through which life is said to consist in faith [Note: [Col. 0096] Three manuscripts: “through bodily movements.” A little later Rat. and twelve manuscripts: “than which it was said to consist in faith.” Erasmus: “by which it was said that life consists.” Lugd. and Ven. M. agree with Erasmus and Lovaniensis.].

In this way he also obtains stable wisdom, which needs no time and is commended by the number ten, so that ten is added to forty, because the equal parts of the number forty, taken together, also reach fifty.

The number forty has the following equal parts: forty once, twenty twice, ten four times, eight five times, five eight times, four ten times, and two twenty times. Thus one, two, four, five, eight, ten, and twenty, taken together, produce fifty.

Therefore, just as the number forty, when its equal parts are calculated, produces an additional ten and becomes fifty, so [Col. 0097] the time of faith in the events accomplished and to be accomplished for our salvation, when lived with equity of life, obtains the understanding of stable wisdom, so that instruction is established not only through believing but also through understanding.

### 2.

And therefore the Church as it now exists, although we are sons of God, lives in labors and afflictions before what we shall be appears, and “the righteous lives by faith” in it (Rom. I, 17). “Unless you believe,” he says, “you will not understand” (Isa. VII, 9).

This is the time in which we groan and grieve, awaiting the redemption of our body (Rom. VIII, 23); this is what is celebrated in Lent. But we know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is (1 John III, 2), when ten is added to forty, so that we may deserve not only to believe what belongs to faith but also to understand manifest truth.

Such a Church—in which there will be no grief, no mixture of wicked human beings, and no iniquity, but joy, peace, and gladness—is prefigured by the celebration of Pentecost. Therefore, after our Lord rose from the dead, when forty days had been completed, he ascended into heaven with his disciples (Acts I, 3, 9). By this number, of course, was signified the same temporal dispensation belonging to faith. After another ten days had been completed, he sent the Holy Spirit (Acts II, 1–4): that is, ten was added to forty through a certain breath and burning of love and charity, so that we might look not toward human and temporal things but toward divine and eternal things.

Therefore, this whole period—the fifty days—is now to be marked by a celebration of joy.

### 3.

Our Lord also signifies these two periods—the one of labor and anxiety, the other of joy and security—by the nets cast into the sea.

Before the Passion, a net is said to have been cast into the sea, and they caught so many fish that they could scarcely drag it to shore, and the nets were breaking (Luke V, 6–7). It was not cast to the right side, for the Church of this present time has many wicked people; nor to the left, for it also has good people; but indiscriminately, to signify the mixture of the good and the wicked.

The fact that the nets broke signifies that, when charity was violated, many heresies emerged.

After the resurrection, however, when he wished to foreshadow the Church of the future age, in which all will be perfect and holy, he commanded the nets to be cast on the right side. They caught a great number of fish—one hundred and fifty-three—and the disciples marveled that, although the fish were so large, the nets did not break (John XXI, 6, 11).

Their size signifies the greatness of wisdom and righteousness. The number signifies the instruction perfected both through the temporal dispensation and through eternal regeneration, which we have said is commended by the number fifty.

Since at that time there will be no need for bodily aids, and faith and wisdom will be held in the mind—and since we have said that the number three is assigned to the mind—we multiply fifty by three, producing one hundred and fifty. The Trinity is added to that number, because the whole perfection has been consecrated in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Thus the total is one hundred and fifty-three, the number of the fish caught on the right side [Col. 0098].

## LXXXII. On what is written: “For whom the Lord loves, he disciplines; and he scourges every son whom he receives” (Heb. XII, 6)

### 1.

Many people, murmuring under God’s discipline, raise a question when they see the righteous often suffering serious troubles in this life—as though it were of no benefit to them that they serve God, since they endure either the common hardships, indiscriminately, of bodies, losses, insults, and all the other things mortals consider evils, or even greater hardships because of the word of God and righteousness, which, being burdensome to sinners, provokes tumultuous uprisings, plots, or hatred against those who preach it.

They are answered as follows: if this were the only life human beings had, it would not seem entirely unreasonable to suppose that a righteous life was either of no benefit or even harmful. Nevertheless, there have been people who so balanced the sweetness of righteousness and its inward joy against all the bodily labors and troubles that the human race suffers according to its mortal condition, and against all the injuries that are devised with the greatest injustice against those who live righteously for the sake of righteousness itself [Note: [Col. 0098] Three manuscripts: “that are provoked.”], that, setting aside hope for the future life, they would be tortured more pleasantly and joyfully by their love of truth than luxurious people feast through their desire for drunkenness.

### 2.

To those, however, who think God unjust when they see the righteous in pains and labors—or at least, if they do not dare to call God unjust, who think that he does not care for human affairs, or that he established the necessities of fate once and for all, against which he himself does nothing lest he appear to disturb through inconsistency the order of things arranged by him, or who hold some other opinion according to which God is in some respect too weak to prevent these evils from befalling the righteous—we must say that there would have been no future righteousness among human beings if God did not care for human affairs.

For all this human righteousness, which the human mind can both retain by doing rightly and lose by sinning, would not be impressed upon the soul unless there were some unchangeable righteousness, found intact by the righteous when they turned toward it and left intact by sinners when they turned away from its light.

That unchangeable righteousness is certainly God’s [Note: [Col. 0098] Three manuscripts: “God is.”], and he would not extend it to enlighten those who turn toward him if he did not care for human affairs.

But if he allowed the righteous to suffer hardships [Note: [Col. 0098] Erasmus and Lovaniensis read *non sineret* (“would not allow”); below, *servare non vult* (“does not wish to preserve”). At both places the manuscripts often lack the negative particle, as does Rat.] because he did not wish to depart from the order of things he had arranged, then he himself would not be just—not because he wishes to preserve his arrangement, but because he arranged the order of things in such a way that the righteous are afflicted by undeserved punishments.

And whoever thinks that God is in some respect too weak to repel the evils suffered by the righteous is foolish for this reason: he does not understand that just as it is impious to call God unjust, so it is impious to deny that he is almighty.

### 3.

Having briefly established these points for the question at hand—for it is a most destructive iniquity to doubt that God himself is both just and almighty [Col. 0099]—no more probable reason presents itself for why righteous people generally suffer in this life than that it is beneficial for them.

The righteousness now required of human beings in order to receive eternal salvation is one thing; the righteousness that the human being established in paradise ought then to have possessed in order to retain and not lose that same eternal salvation is another.

For just as God’s righteousness consists in giving beneficial commands and distributing punishments to the disobedient and rewards to the obedient, so human righteousness consists in obeying beneficial commands.

But since blessedness exists in the soul as health exists in the body, just as one kind of medicine is prescribed for the body so that good health may not be lost, and another so that lost health may be recovered, so in the whole condition of the human being one set of commands was then given so that immortality would not be lost, and another set is now prescribed so that it may be regained.

And just as, in bodily health, if someone falls into an illness by failing to obey the physician’s commands by which that same good health was to be preserved, he receives other commands by which he may be cured—commands that are often insufficient if the illness is serious unless the physician applies certain remedies, usually harsh and bringing pain, which nevertheless are effective for recovering health—so a person, having fallen through sin into the diseased and wretched mortality of this life because he did not wish to obey the first command by which he was to preserve and retain eternal health, has received second commands.
