By obeying these commands, he is rightly said not absurdly to live justly; yet the troubles he suffers arise either from the illness itself, which has not yet been cured, or from the remedy of medicine.

To this remedy belongs what is written: “For whom the Lord loves, he disciplines; and he scourges every son whom he receives.”

Those who live wickedly by refusing to obey the most salutary commands increase their illnesses more and more. They either suffer from those illnesses innumerable labors and pains even in this life, or, when punishments are also applied so that what is not healthy may be touched and made to hurt, they are mercifully warned of the evil in which they are, so that, turning toward medicine, they may be made healthy by God’s grace.

If they despise all these things—that is, the commands consisting in words [Note: [Col. 0099] In the margin of Rat.: “commands consisting in blows.”] and pains—they will deserve just and everlasting condemnation after this life.

Therefore, only someone who thinks that the mortal life we now live is the only life can say that these things happen unjustly; such a person does not believe what has been divinely foretold concerning the future and will bear the most severe punishments for his persistence in sin and his unbelief.

## LXXXIII. On marriage, concerning what the Lord says: “If anyone divorces his wife, except on the ground of fornication,” etc. (Matt. V, 32).

If the Lord admits only fornication as a reason for dismissing one’s spouse, and does not forbid the dismissal of a pagan marriage, it follows that paganism is to be counted as fornication. [Note: [Col. 0100] The printed editions read: “does not forbid dismissal; consequently paganism is not to be counted as fornication” (or “as fornication”). But the reading of several manuscripts is more polished: the negative particle is placed before *prohibet* (“forbids”), not before *deputetur* (“is counted”).]

That the Lord, when he speaks in the Gospel about dismissing a wife, makes fornication the sole exception, is evident. A pagan marriage, however, is not here forbidden to be dissolved because, when the Apostle gave counsel on this matter—that a believer should not dismiss an unbelieving spouse who wishes to remain with him—he said, “I say, not the Lord.” Thus the Lord is understood not indeed to command that the spouse be dismissed—for the Apostle would then seem to give counsel contrary to his command—but nevertheless to permit it, so that no one would be bound in this matter by the necessity of a command, but might act freely according to the will expressed in counsel.

Nevertheless, if someone maintains that the only fornication which the Lord admits as grounds for leaving a spouse is what is commonly called fornication—that is, what is committed through illicit intercourse—he may say that, when the Lord spoke of this matter, he was speaking of both believers, husband and wife: if both are believers, neither may leave the other except on account of fornication. Paganism cannot be understood here, because both parties are believers.

For the Apostle too seems to make this distinction when he says: “To those who are married I give this command—not I, but the Lord—that a wife should not separate from her husband; but if she has separated, she should remain unmarried or be reconciled to her husband.” Here it is also understood that, if the woman has left her husband for that one cause alone on account of which leaving the marriage is permitted, she ought to remain unmarried; or, if she does not exercise self-control, she ought rather to be reconciled to her husband—whether he has been corrected or is at least to be endured—than to marry another.

He then continues: “And a husband should not dismiss his wife,” briefly indicating for the husband the same rule that he had prescribed for the wife. After these matters have been conveyed as the Lord’s command, he continues: “To the rest I say, not the Lord: if any brother has an unbelieving wife and she consents to live with him, he should not dismiss her; and if any woman has an unbelieving husband and he consents to live with her, she should not dismiss her husband” (1 Cor. 7:10–13). Here he makes it understood that the Lord had spoken of cases in which both parties were believers, so that neither should dismiss the other.

# [On Various Questions for Simplicianus]

[Col. 0099]

[Note: [Col. 0099] See vol. 1, book 2 of the *Retractions*, chapter 1, from the words “Of the books which, as bishop,” col. 629, to the words “Most welcome indeed,” col. 631. M.]

## On the Subsequent Work

[Note: [Col. 0099] Augustine assumed the episcopate toward the end of the year 395. Ambrose, however, died on April 4, 397. Thus the subsequent work addressed to Simplicianus, the successor of Ambrose, belongs to the beginning of Augustine’s episcopate and was written in the year 397.]

### From *On the Predestination of the Saints*, chapter 4

“You certainly see what I then thought about faith and works, although I was laboring to commend the grace of God [Note: [Col. 0099] In the *Exposition of Certain Propositions from the Epistle to the Romans*, vol. 3.]; and I now see that these brothers of ours hold that same opinion, because, while they have taken pains to read my books, they have not likewise taken pains to make progress with me in them. For if they had taken care to advance, they would have found this question resolved according to the truth of the divine Scriptures in the first of the two books that I wrote to Simplicianus of blessed memory, bishop of the Church of Milan and successor of Saint Ambrose, at the very beginning of my episcopate.”

Further below in the same work:

“Behold why I said above that, especially by this apostolic testimony (1 Cor. 4:7), I myself had been convinced when I held a different opinion on this matter: God revealed this to me while I was resolving this question, when, as I said, I was writing to Bishop Simplicianus.”

### From *On the Gift of Perseverance*, chapter 20

“I began to understand more fully in the discussion that I wrote to Simplicianus of blessed memory, bishop of the Church of Milan, at the beginning of my episcopate, when I also recognized and affirmed that the beginning of faith is a gift of God.”

The same work, chapter 21:

“Let them see whether, in the later portions of the first book of those two books which I wrote to Simplicianus, bishop of Milan, at the beginning of my episcopate, before the Pelagian heresy appeared, anything remains that could cast doubt on the fact that God’s grace is given not according to our merits; and whether there I did not sufficiently establish that the beginning of faith too is a gift of God; and whether, from what is said there, it does not consequently become clear—even if it is not expressly stated—that perseverance to the end is also given only by him who predestined us for his kingdom and glory.”

### From volume 2, Letter 37

“To the most blessed lord and father Simplicianus, whom Augustine embraces with reverently sincere affection: greetings in the Lord.

“1. I have received, sent as a gift of Your Holiness, a letter full of every good joy: you remembered me, loved me as you usually do, and rejoiced greatly in whatever gifts the Lord in his mercy has deigned to bestow upon me—not because of my merits. In it I drank in the fatherly affection flowing from your most kindly heart, an affection that was not sudden or new to me, but one that I recognized again as fully tested and known, most blessed lord, whom I embrace with reverently sincere affection.

“2. But from where has such happiness arisen for our literary labor, in which we have toiled over the composition of certain books, that they should be read by Your Dignity? It can only be because the Lord, to whom my soul is subject, wished to console my cares and revive me from the fear with which I must necessarily be anxious in such works, lest somewhere I should stumble, through lack of learning or caution, even though I am walking in the broadest field of truth.

“For when what I write pleases you, I know whom it pleases, because I know who dwells in you. For he who distributes and bestows all spiritual gifts will, through your judgment, confirm my obedience. Whatever in those writings is worthy of your delight, God said in my ministry, ‘Let it be,’ and it was; while in your approval God saw that it was good.

“3. As for the little questions which you have deigned to command me to untangle: even if, because of my slowness, I did not understand them, assisted by your merits I would open them up. I ask only this: pray to God for my weakness; and whether in those matters with which you kindly and fatherly wished to exercise me, or in any others of ours that may perhaps come into your holy hands—for just as I recognize them as gifts of God, so I recognize them as my errors—not only extend the care of a reader to them, but also assume the judgment of one who corrects. Farewell.”

[Col. 0101]

# The Two Books of Saint Aurelius Augustine, Bishop of Hippo, *On Various Questions for Simplicianus*

[Note: [Col. 0101] The title in the most ancient Corbie manuscript is: “Aurelius Augustine, to Simplicianus’s questions.”]  
[Note: [Col. 0101] Written about the year 397.]  
[Note: [Col. 0101] These two books were corrected against the exceptionally fine Corbie manuscript, copied a thousand years ago; against an old book of the Church of Angers; against the Genovefan, Victorine, and Sorbonne manuscripts; against three Vatican manuscripts; against the variant readings of three or four Belgian manuscripts collected by the Louvain theologians; and also against the older editions, Am., Er., and Lov.—that is, those prepared through the work and scholarship of Johannes Amerbach, Desiderius Erasmus, and the Louvain theologians.]  
[Note: [Col. 0101] We also compared all the editions mentioned at the beginning of the *Retractions*, vol. 1. M.]

(C)

## Book One

In this book two of Simplicianus’s questions from Paul’s Epistle to the Romans are treated.

## Preface

You sent me, Father Simplicianus, a most welcome and exceedingly agreeable commendation of your questions. If I did not attempt to answer them, I would prove not only obstinate but also ungrateful. The matters concerning the Apostle Paul that you proposed for resolution had already been discussed by us to some extent and committed to writing [Note: [Col. 0103] After “and committed to writing,” the Victorine manuscript alone adds: “so that, apart from the text of this little book, I sent you what had already been prepared, for your wisdom to consider how these matters have been explained.” It then continues: “Nevertheless,” etc.]. Nevertheless, not content with my earlier investigation and explanation, I examined those same apostolic words and the sequence of their meaning with greater caution and attention, lest I had passed over anything in them too carelessly. For you would not have thought them worth questioning if their meaning were easy and straightforward.

# First Question

1. **Why the law was given. Concupiscence increased through the law. How sin was dead without the law. How it revived. Who misuses the law. The law is fulfilled only by spiritual people. The term “carnal” used in two ways. The punishment of original sin. What “the law of sin” in the members means. Passages in which the law might appear to be called evil. The law is good. The Manichaean error concerning the Old Law. Testimonies explained in which the law may appear not to be good.**

From the passage beginning, “What then shall we say? Is the law sin? Certainly not,” to the passage where he says, “Therefore the law is good for one who wishes to do good,” and so forth—I believe all the way to, “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Rom. 7:7–25)—you wished us to untangle the first question.

At this point it seems to me that the Apostle has represented in his own person the human being placed under the law, speaking in his own words as that person. And because shortly before he had said, “We have been released from the law of death in which we were held, so that we may serve in the newness of the spirit and not in the oldness of the letter,” and thus might appear through these words to have criticized the law, he immediately added: “What then shall we say? Is the law sin? Certainly not. But I did not know sin except through the law. For I would not have known covetousness unless the law said, ‘You shall not covet.’”

2. Here again the matter raises a difficulty: if the law is not sin but the revealer of sin [Note: [Col. 0103] Amerbach and Erasmus read “sower of sin.” The very ancient Corbie manuscript supports the reading “sower,” or perhaps “disseminator.”], nevertheless the law seems to be criticized by these words. We must therefore understand that the law was given for this purpose—not so that sin would be introduced, nor so that it would be uprooted, but only so that it would be revealed. By the very revelation of sin it would make the human soul, which had been secure as though innocent, guilty; and because sin could not be conquered without the grace of God, the anxiety of guilt would turn the soul toward receiving grace.

Thus he does not say, “I did not commit sin except through the law,” but, “I did not know sin except through the law.” Nor does he say, “I would not have had covetousness unless the law said, ‘You shall not covet,’” but, “I would not have known covetousness unless the law said, ‘You shall not covet.’” Hence it is clear that covetousness was not implanted through the law, but revealed.

3. It necessarily followed that, since concupiscence could not yet be resisted because grace had not been received, it would also increase. For concupiscence has greater force when the crime of transgression is added to it, since one then acts against the law, than when no law forbids it. Accordingly he adds: “But sin, finding an opportunity through the commandment, worked in me every kind of covetousness.”

Covetousness existed even before the law, but it was not yet “every kind,” since the crime of transgression was still absent. Hence he says elsewhere: “Where there is no law, neither is there transgression” (Rom. 4:15).

4. When he adds, “For without the law sin was dead,” this means the same as if he had said, “It was hidden”—that is, it was thought to be dead. He will make this clearer shortly.

“But I was once alive without the law,” he says—that is, I was not frightened by any death arising from sin, because, when there was no law, sin was not evident. “But when the commandment came, sin revived”—that is, it appeared. “And I died”—that is, I realized that I was dead; or because the guilt of transgression threatens the definite punishment of death.

When he says, “Sin revived when the commandment came,” he sufficiently indicates that sin had once lived in this sense: it had once been known [Note: [Col. 0104] The Corbie manuscript reads, “had once been born.”], as I believe, in the transgression of the first human being, since he too had received a commandment (Gen. 2:17). For elsewhere he says: “But the woman, being deceived, became a transgressor” [Note: [Col. 0104] So the manuscripts read, in accordance with the Greek. The printed editions read: “But the woman was deceived in transgression.”] (1 Tim. 2:14); and again: “In the likeness of Adam’s transgression, who is a type of the one to come” (Rom. 5:14).

For nothing can revive unless it once lived. But sin had been dead—that is, hidden—when mortals, born without the commandment of the law, lived by following the desires of the flesh without any knowledge, because without any prohibition. Thus he says, “I was once alive without the law.” This makes clear that he is not speaking strictly in his own person, but generally in the person of the old human being [Note: [Col. 0104] “Old” is absent from the Victorine manuscript and the very ancient Corbie manuscript].

“But when the commandment came, sin revived. But I died; and the commandment that was intended for life was found to be for death.” If the commandment is obeyed, it is certainly life. But it was found to be for death when it was violated, so that not only was the sin committed which had also been committed before the commandment, but it was committed more abundantly and harmfully: sin was now committed by one who knew and transgressed.

5. “For sin,” he says, “taking an opportunity through the commandment, deceived me and through it killed me.” Sin, not making legitimate use of the law, became sweeter because desire was increased by the prohibition, and therefore it deceived him. The sweetness is deceptive, for greater and more numerous bitterness of punishments follows it.

Since what is forbidden is more pleasantly admitted by people who have not yet received spiritual grace, sin deceives through a false sweetness. And because the guilt of transgression is also added, it kills.

6. “Therefore the law is holy, and the commandment is holy and just and good.” It commands what must be commanded and forbids what must be forbidden. “Did what is good, then, become death to me? Certainly not.” The fault lies in the one who misuses it, not in the commandment itself, which is good. “The law is good if one uses it lawfully” (1 Tim. 1:8).

But one misuses the law who does not submit to God in devout humility, so that the law may be fulfilled through grace. Therefore one who does not use the law lawfully receives it for no other purpose than that the sin which had previously lain hidden may begin to appear through transgression. And it appears beyond measure, because now sin is not merely committed but committed against the commandment.

He therefore continues: “But sin, so that it might appear as sin, worked death in me through what is good, so that sin—or the sinner—might become exceedingly sinful through the commandment.” Thus he makes clear the sense in which he earlier said, “For without the law sin was dead”: not that sin did not exist, but that it did not appear. He also makes clear how it was said, “Sin revived”: not that sin came into existence when it had existed before the law, but that it appeared because it was being committed against the law. For here he says, “But sin, so that it might appear as sin, worked death in me through what is good.” He does not say, “so that sin might exist,” but “so that sin might appear.”

7. He next gives the reason why this is so: “For we know,” he says, “that the law is spiritual, but I am carnal.” Here he sufficiently demonstrates that the law cannot be fulfilled except by spiritual people, and they become spiritual only through grace.

The more closely a person becomes like the spiritual law—that is, the more he himself rises into a spiritual disposition—the more fully he fulfills it. For he delights in it more and more, no longer afflicted by its burden but invigorated by its light: “The commandment of the Lord is bright, enlightening the eyes, and the law of the Lord is undefiled, converting souls” (Ps. 18:8–9). Grace forgives sins and pours in the spirit of love, through which righteousness is neither burdensome nor without delight.

When he had said, “But I am carnal,” he also explained what kind of carnal person he was. Those who are already established under grace, already redeemed by the Lord’s blood and reborn through faith, are called “carnal” in a certain sense. The same Apostle says to them: “And I, brothers, could not speak to you as spiritual people but as carnal, as infants in Christ. I gave you milk to drink, not food” (1 Cor. 3:1–2).

By saying this, he clearly shows that they had already been reborn through grace: they were infants in Christ and had to be nourished with milk, yet he still calls them carnal.

But one who is not yet under grace, but under the law, is carnal in such a way that he has not yet been reborn from sin, but has been sold under sin [Note: [Col. 0105] The printed editions read, “under the law, from sin.” The manuscripts read, “under sin” (*sub peccato*), or “under sin” (*sub peccatum*).]. He embraces the sweetness of the deadly pleasure that deceives him, and he takes delight in acting against the law—indeed, the more he is inclined to do it, the less it is permitted.

He cannot enjoy this sweetness as though it were the price of his condition unless he is compelled, like a purchased slave, to serve lust. He feels himself to be the slave of a ruling desire: he is forbidden, he recognizes that he is rightly forbidden, and yet he acts.

8. “For what I do,” he says, “I do not know.” Here “I do not know” does not mean that he is unaware that he is sinning. Otherwise it would contradict what he said: “But sin, so that it might appear as sin, worked death in me through what is good,” and also what he said earlier: “I did not know sin except through the law.”

For how can what he does not know appear, or how can he know what he does not know? Rather, the expression is like the Lord’s future statement to the wicked: “I do not know you” (Matt. 25:12). Nothing is hidden from God, since “the face of the Lord is against those who do evil, to destroy their memory from the earth” (Ps. 33:17). Yet we are sometimes said not to know what we do not approve.

Thus he says, “What I do, I do not know”—that is, I do not approve. He shows this in what follows: “For I do not do what I want, but I do what I hate.” Therefore, when he says “I hate,” he means “I do not know,” because of those to whom the Lord will say, “I do not know you,” it is also said: “You hate, Lord, all who work iniquity” (Ps. 5:7).

9. “But if I do what I do not want, I agree with the law, because it is good.” He does not want what the law does not want, for the law forbids that thing. He therefore agrees with the law not insofar as he does what it forbids, but insofar as he does not want what he does.

He is overcome because he has not yet been freed through grace, although through the law he already knows that he is doing wrong and does not want to do it.

When he continues, “But now it is no longer I who do it, but sin dwelling in me,” he does not say this because he does not consent to committing sin, even though he agrees with the law in condemning it. He is still speaking in the person of the human being established under the law [Note: [Col. 0106] See *Retractions*, chapter 1.], not yet under grace. Such a person is drawn into evil action by ruling concupiscence and by the deceptive sweetness of forbidden sin, although, in that part of him which possesses knowledge of the law, he disapproves of it.

He therefore says, “It is not I who do it,” because the action is performed by one who has been overcome. Desire performs the action, and one yields to it when it prevails. Grace, which he will discuss later, makes the human mind stronger against desire, so that it does not yield.

10. “For I know,” he says, “that good does not dwell in me—that is, in my flesh.” From what he knows, he agrees with the law; from what he does, he yields to sin.

If someone asks how he knows that good does not dwell in his flesh—that is, that sin dwells there—where does this knowledge come from except from the transmission of mortality and the continual practice of pleasure [Note: [Col. 0106] The Sorbonne and Corbie manuscripts read “will”]? The former comes from the punishment of original sin; the latter from the punishment of repeated sin. We are born into this life with the former, and by living we add the latter.

These two things—nature and habit, as it were—joined together, produce a desire of the greatest strength and most impossible to overcome. This is what he calls sin and says dwells in his flesh: it exercises a kind of domination and, as it were, holds a kingdom.

Hence the Psalm says: “I have chosen to be cast down in the house of the Lord rather than to dwell in the tents of sinners” (Ps. 83:11). The one who has been cast down there is not said to dwell there, even though he is there, wherever he may be. This suggests that dwelling is to be understood together with a certain authority. But if, through grace, what he says elsewhere is accomplished in us—“Let not sin therefore reign in your mortal body, so as to obey its desires” (Rom. 6:12)—then sin is no longer properly said to dwell in us.

11. “For to will,” he says, “is present with me, but to accomplish the good I do not find” [Note: [Col. 0107] The word “find” is absent from the manuscripts.]. To those who do not understand these words correctly, they seem to remove free choice. But how do they remove it, when he says, “To will is present with me”? Certainly this willing itself lies within one’s power, since it is present with us. But the fact that accomplishing the good is not within one’s power belongs to the merit of original sin.

This is not the human being’s first nature, but the punishment of sin, through which mortality itself came to be as a kind of second nature. From this the grace of the Creator frees us when, through faith, we submit ourselves to him.

These words, however, are spoken by a human being established under the law, not yet under grace. One who is not yet under grace does not do the good he wants; rather, he does the evil he does not want, because concupiscence prevails. It is strengthened not only by the bond of mortality but also by the weight of habit [Note: [Col. 0107] Erasmus and the better manuscripts read this way. The Louvain edition reads “of evil habit.”].

If he does what he does not want, then it is no longer he who does it, but sin dwelling in him, as was said and explained above.

12. “I discover, then,” he says, “a law for me who wish to do good: evil is present with me.” That is, I discover that the law is good for me when I wish to do what the law contains [Note: [Col. 0107] Perhaps “commands”]. Evil, however, is present with me for doing it easily.

When he earlier said, “To will is present with me,” he was speaking of ease. For what is easier for a person established under the law than to wish the good and do the evil? He wishes the good without difficulty, although he does not do it as easily as he wishes it; and he readily possesses what he hates, although he does not want it—just as someone who has been thrown headlong reaches the depths without difficulty, although he neither wants it nor hates it.

I have said this because of the word “present.” The human being placed under the law, not yet freed by grace, thus bears witness that the law is good. He bears witness to it precisely by condemning himself for acting against the law. He discovers that the law is good for him [Note: [Col. 0107] The Louvain edition reads, “he discovers that it is good for him.” The reading in Amerbach, Erasmus, and the manuscripts is, “he discovers that it is good for him.”] because he wishes to do what it commands but, overcome by concupiscence, cannot.

Thus he sees himself entangled in the guilt of transgression, so that he may implore the grace of the one who liberates.

13. “For I delight,” he says, “in the law of God according to the inner person”—that is, in the law which says, “You shall not covet.”

“But I see another law in my members,” he says, “warring against the law of my mind and making me captive under the law of sin which is in my members.”

By “law” in his members he means the very burden of mortality, under which “we groan, being burdened” (2 Cor. 5:4). “The corruptible body weighs down the soul” (Wis. 9:15). Through this it also often happens that what is not permitted becomes irresistibly pleasurable [Note: [Col. 0107] The Louvain edition reads, “what is permitted delights unwillingly.” We have partly restored the passage according to other editions and partly according to the manuscripts.].

He calls this oppressive and pressing burden a law because it was assigned and imposed as a punishment by the divine judgment, by the one who warned the human being: “On the day when you eat from it, you shall surely die” (Gen. 2:17).

This law wars against the law of the mind, which says, “You shall not covet,” and with which the human being delights according to the inner person. Before anyone is under grace, this law wars against him so as to make him captive under the law of sin—that is, under itself. When he says, “which is in my members,” he shows that this is the same law of which he had said above, “I see another law in my members.”

14. All this is said to demonstrate that a captive human being must not presume upon his own strength. Thus he argued against the Jews, who proudly gloried in the works of the law, even though concupiscence dragged them toward everything unlawful, while the law in which they gloried said, “You shall not covet.”

The person who has been overcome, condemned, and made captive—even overcome by the law he has received, so that he is not a victor but rather a transgressor—must therefore cry out in humility: “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord.”

In this mortal life, free choice has this remaining function: not that a person can fulfill righteousness whenever he wishes, but that he may turn with humble devotion toward the one whose gift enables him to fulfill it.

15. Throughout this entire sequence of the Apostle’s discourse that we have discussed, anyone who thinks that the Apostle regarded the law as evil because he says, “The law entered so that transgression might abound” (Rom. 5:20); “the ministry of death, engraved in letters on stones” (2 Cor. 3:7); “the strength of sin is the law” (1 Cor. 15:56); “you died to the law through the body of Christ, so that you might belong to another, who rose from the dead”; and “the passions of sins, which are through the law, were working in our members to bear fruit for death; but now we have been released from the law of death in which we were held, so that we may serve in the newness of the spirit and not in the oldness of the letter” (Rom. 7:4–6)—and if we find the Apostle saying anything else of this kind, let such a person observe that these statements are made because the law increases concupiscence through prohibition and binds a person as guilty through transgression. It commands what human beings cannot fulfill in their weakness unless they turn devoutly toward the grace of God.

For this reason those whom the law dominates are said to be under it. It dominates those whom it punishes; and it punishes all transgressors. Moreover, those who have received the law transgress it [Note: [Col. 0108] So Erasmus and the manuscripts read. The Louvain edition has, “transgress against it.”], unless through grace they obtain the ability to do what it commands.

Thus the law does not dominate those who are already under grace, because they fulfill it through love [Note: [Col. 0108] So the manuscripts read. The printed editions have, “through grace.”], though previously they had been condemned under its fear.

16. If those statements move someone to think that the Apostle is criticizing the law, what are we to do with his saying, “For I delight in the law of God according to the inner person”? By saying this he certainly praises the law.

When they hear this, however, they reply that here the Apostle is speaking of another law: the law of Christ, not the law that was given to the Jews. We therefore ask them about the law of which he says, “The law entered so that transgression might abound.” They reply that he is certainly speaking of the law received by the Jews.

Consider, then, whether this is the same law of which it is said, “Taking an opportunity, sin worked in me through the commandment every kind of covetousness.” For what else does “worked in me every kind of covetousness” mean than what is expressed there by “so that transgression might abound”?

Consider also whether the statement agrees with this: “so that the sinner or sin might become exceedingly sinful through the commandment.” For “so that sin might become exceedingly sinful” is the same as “so that transgression might abound.”

Therefore, if we show that the commandment through which sin, taking an opportunity, worked every kind of covetousness so that it became exceedingly sinful is good, we will at the same time show that the law which entered so that transgression might abound is good—that is, the law which caused sin to work every kind of covetousness and become exceedingly sinful.

Let them therefore hear the same Apostle saying: “What then shall we say? Is the law sin? Certainly not.” They say that this was spoken of the law of Christ—that is, of the law of grace.

Let them answer, then, of which law they understand the following words to have been spoken: “But I did not know sin except through the law. For I would not have known covetousness unless the law said, ‘You shall not covet.’ But sin, taking an opportunity through the commandment, worked in me every kind of covetousness.”

The actual sequence of the words sufficiently indicates which law he meant when he said, “Is the law sin? Certainly not.” He meant the law whose commandment provided an opportunity for sin to work every kind of covetousness. It was therefore the law that entered so that transgression might abound, which they regard as evil.

But what could be clearer than what he says shortly afterward? “Therefore the law is holy, and the commandment is holy and just and good.” Again they say that this was not spoken of the law given to the Jews, but of the Gospel.

This perversity is the Manichaeans’ blindness, beyond all expression. They do not observe what follows with complete openness and clarity: “Did what is good, then, become death to me? Certainly not. But sin, so that it might appear as sin, worked death in me through what is good, so that the sinner or sin might become exceedingly sinful through the commandment.”

That is, it became exceedingly sinful through the holy, just, and good commandment—the same commandment that entered so that sin might abound, that is, so that it might become exceedingly sinful.

17. Why, then, is it called the ministry of death if the law is good? Because “sin, so that it might appear as sin, worked death in me through what is good.”

Do not be surprised, since the same thing was said about the preaching of the Gospel: “We are the good odor of Christ to God among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing; to some, an odor of life unto life; to others, an odor of death unto death” (2 Cor. 2:15–16).

The law was called the ministry of death with respect to the Jews, among whom it was also written on stone, symbolizing their hardness—not with respect to those who fulfill the law through love. For “the fullness of the law is love.”

The law itself, which was represented in letters engraved on stone, says: “You shall not commit adultery,” “You shall not kill,” “You shall not steal,” “You shall not covet,” and so forth. The Apostle says that this law is fulfilled through love, speaking as follows: “Whoever loves another [Note: [Col. 0109] The printed editions read “neighbor.” The manuscripts read “another,” corresponding to the Greek *ton heteron*] has fulfilled the law. For, ‘You shall not commit adultery, You shall not kill, You shall not steal, You shall not covet’; and if there is any other commandment, it is summed up in this saying: ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself’” (Rom. 13:8–10). This too is written in the same law.

Why is the law called “the strength of sin” if the law is good? Because sin, through what is good, worked death, so that it might become exceedingly sinful—that is, so that it might acquire greater strength through transgression.

Why did we die to the law through the body of Christ if the law is good? Because we died to the law that condemned us [Note: [Col. 0110] Erasmus and many ancient manuscripts read “that dominated us.” Later in the same passage, five of these manuscripts have “dominates” instead of “threatens.”], and were freed from the disposition that the law punishes and condemns. The law is more commonly so called when it threatens, terrifies, and exacts punishment.

Thus the same commandment is law to those who fear it and grace to those who love it. Hence the Gospel says: “The law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (John 1:17). The very law that was given through Moses in order to be feared became grace and truth through Jesus Christ, so that it might be fulfilled.

Accordingly, “You died to the law” means the same as if it said, “You died to the punishment of the law through the body of Christ,” through which the sins that bound us to a deserved punishment were forgiven.

Why did the passions of sins that are through the law work in our members so as to bear fruit for death, if the law is good? Because by “the passions of sins” he wished to be understood here what has often been stated already: the increase of concupiscence through prohibition and the guilt of punishment through transgression. That is, through what was good, sin worked death, so that the sinner or sin might become exceedingly sinful through the commandment.

Why have we been freed from the law of death in which we were held, so that we may serve in the newness of the spirit and not in the oldness of the letter, if the law is good? Because the law is a letter to those who do not fulfill it through the spirit of love, to which the New Testament belongs.

Therefore those who have died to sin are freed from the letter by which the guilty are held because they do not fulfill what is written. For what else is the law, for those who know how to read it but cannot fulfill it, than mere letter? It is not unknown to those for whom it was written; but because it is known only insofar as it is read as writing, and not insofar as it is fulfilled through love, it is nothing else to such people than the letter.

That letter is not a helper to those who read it, but a witness against sinners. Therefore those who are renewed through the spirit are freed from its condemnation [Note: [Col. 0110] Erasmus and three manuscripts read “domination.”], so that they are no longer bound by the letter to punishment, but joined to understanding through righteousness.

Hence there is also the statement: “The letter kills, but the spirit gives life” (2 Cor. 3:6). The law, when merely read but not understood or fulfilled, certainly kills; then it is called “the letter.” But the spirit gives life, because “the fullness of the law is love,” which “has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. 5:5).

## QUESTION II

**Argument of the Epistle to the Romans.** The grace of faith precedes good works. The grace of faith is lesser in catechumens and greater in the reborn. The Apostle’s purpose in the examples of Jacob and Esau. Good works arise from grace, not grace from works. How Jacob’s election and Esau’s rejection are just. Whether Jacob was elected through foreknowledge of future faith. Election proceeds from the grace and purpose of God. Whether faith is to be counted among the gifts of grace. How Esau’s rejection is just. Faith is a gift of the merciful God. Why the gift of faith was withheld from Esau. Whether Esau was rejected and Jacob approved through foreknowledge of future will. Good will comes to be in us through God’s working. Whether calling produces good will. Congruent calling. Why Esau was not called congruently. What God’s hardening is. The solution to the question concerning Esau’s rejection. All human beings are one mass of sin. How God hated Esau, who hates nothing that he has made. What sin is. The vessels of destruction are made for the correction of others. Not all are called, but some from both Jews and Gentiles. The Apostle’s intention in the Epistle to the Romans. How hidden the election of grace is.

[Col. 0111]

### 1

But now, I think, it is time to proceed to another question, which you presented in this way: beginning from what is written, “And not only so” [Note: [Col. 0111] The printed editions, agreeing with the Vulgate, have: “And not only that.” But the manuscripts, agreeing with the Greek reading, do not add “that.” In place of this word, one can indeed find “that one” in ancient Latin Bibles; but Augustine seems to have read neither word, since here, in section 3, he thinks that the proposition “And not only so” is completed by supplying the words “Isaac was promised.”], “but Rebecca also, having conceived Isaac our father from one intercourse.” For the entire passage is to be explained, from “For when they had not yet been born and had done nothing good or evil” down to what is written, “Unless the Lord of hosts had left us offspring, we would have become like Sodom and would have been made like Gomorrah” (Rom. IX, 10–29); and certainly the whole connection is more obscure. But surely, knowing what sort of person you are toward me, you could not have commanded me to open these matters unless you were entreating the Lord that I might be able to do so [Note: [Col. 0111] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions, however, have *possem*, “I might be able.”]. Having been made more confident through that help, I undertake the task.

### 2

First, I shall hold to the Apostle’s intention, which prevails throughout the whole Epistle, and shall consult it. His purpose is that no one should glory in the merits of works—the very merits in which the Israelites dared to glory, because they had served the law given to them and on that account had received evangelical grace as though it were owed to their merits, since they served the law. For this reason they did not want the same grace to be given to the Gentiles, as though the Gentiles were unworthy unless they received the Jewish sacraments. This controversy, once it arose, is resolved in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts XV).

They did not understand that, precisely because it is evangelical grace, it is not owed to works; otherwise grace is no longer grace (Rom. XI, 6). The Apostle frequently bears witness to this in many passages, placing the grace of faith before works—not in order to abolish works, but to show that works do not precede grace; rather, they follow it. Thus no one should think that he received grace because he had acted well, but that he could not act well unless he had received grace through faith.

A person begins to receive grace when he begins to believe in God, moved to faith either by an inward or an outward admonition. Yet there is a difference in the stages of time or in the celebration of the sacraments through which grace is poured out more fully and more evidently. Catechumens do not, of course, fail to believe, nor did Cornelius fail to believe in God when, through almsgiving and prayers, he showed himself worthy that an angel should be sent to him (Acts X, 1–4). But he could not possibly have performed these acts unless he had first believed; and he could not possibly have believed unless he had been called either by secret admonitions through visions of the mind or spirit, or by more manifest admonitions through the bodily senses.

In some people, however, the grace of faith is so great that it is not sufficient to obtain the kingdom of heaven—as in catechumens, and as in Cornelius himself before he was incorporated into the Church through participation in the sacraments. In others it is so great that they are already reckoned among the body of Christ and the holy temple of God. “The temple of God is holy,” the Apostle says, “which you are” (I Cor. III, 17). And the Lord himself says, “Unless someone is born of water and the Holy Spirit, he will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (John III, 5).

Certain beginnings of faith therefore arise, resembling conceptions; yet it is necessary not only to be conceived but also to be born, in order to attain eternal life. Nevertheless, none of these things occurs without the grace of God’s mercy, since whatever good works there may be follow that grace, as has been said; they do not precede it.

### 3

Wishing to persuade us of this, the Apostle—since elsewhere he says, “For by the grace of God we have been saved; and” [Note: [Col. 0112] These words, “For by the grace of God we have been saved; and,” are absent here in Erasmus and most manuscripts.] “this is not from ourselves, but is God’s gift; not from works, lest anyone should boast” (Eph. II, 8–9)—gave an example from those who had not yet been born. No one could say that Jacob, who had not yet been born, had earned God’s favor through works, so that it might be divinely said, “And the elder shall serve the younger.”

Therefore, he says, “And not only so”: Isaac was promised when it was said, “At this time I will come, and Sarah shall have a son.” Isaac had certainly earned God’s favor through no works, so that he should be promised before his birth and so that Abraham’s offspring should be called in Isaac—that is, those should belong to the lot of the saints which is in Christ who understand themselves to be children of promise, not boasting in their merits but attributing to the grace of their calling [Note: [Col. 0112] Erasmus and four manuscripts read *gratiae vocationi*, “to the grace of calling.”] the fact that they are coheirs of Christ. For when it was promised that they would be such, those who did not yet exist had certainly earned nothing.

“But Rebecca also, having conceived Isaac our father from one intercourse.” He very carefully says “from one intercourse,” since twins had been conceived, lest someone attribute the matter to the parents’ merits and perhaps say, “This son was born of such a character because his father was disposed in that way at the time when he sowed him in his mother’s womb,” or, “because his mother was so disposed when she conceived him.” The father sowed both at the same time, and the mother conceived both at the same time. To emphasize this he says, “from one intercourse,” so that he would leave no room for astrologers—or rather, for those whom they called *genethliaci*, who infer the character and fortunes of those being born from their births.

What answer can they give as to why, from one conception, at one point in time, under the same arrangement of heaven and stars—so that no differing circumstance could possibly be recorded for each of them—there was such great diversity between the twins? They simply cannot discover one. And if they are willing, they easily recognize that those answers which they sell to wretched people are offered not through any exposition of an art but through random conjecture.

But, to speak rather about the matter at hand, these things are recalled in order to break and cast down the pride of people ungrateful for God’s grace and daring to glory in their own merits. “For when they had not yet been born,” [Col. 0113] “and had done nothing good or evil,” it was said—not from works but from the one who calls—“Because the elder shall serve the younger.”

Grace therefore belongs to the one who calls; good works, on the other hand, follow consequentially in the one who receives grace. They do not produce grace; they are produced by grace. Fire does not heat in order that it may be hot, but because it is hot; nor does a wheel run well in order to be round, but because it is round. So no one acts well in order to receive grace, but because he has received it.

For how can someone live justly who has not been justified? How can someone live holily who has not been sanctified? Or how can someone live at all [Note: [Col. 0113] The Corbeiensis and Victorinus manuscripts read: “How can he even live holily who has not been sanctified; or live at all,” etc.], who has not been given life? Grace justifies, so that the one who has been justified may live justly.

Grace therefore comes first, and good works second [Note: [Col. 0113] Lovaniensis has “the second good action.” But Em. Erasmus and the manuscripts have “the second good works.”], just as he says elsewhere: “But to the one who works, the reward is not reckoned according to grace but according to debt” (Rom. IV, 4). So too with immortality after good works, if even immortality itself is sought as a debt. The same Apostle says: “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith; henceforth the crown of righteousness awaits me, which the Lord, the just judge, will render to me on that day” (II Tim. IV, 7–8).

Perhaps, because he said “will render,” it is now owed as a debt [Note: [Col. 0113] In manuscript B: “then it is a debt.” We have followed Erasmus, the Lyon edition, the Venice edition, and Lovaniensis. Manuscript M has “then it may be a debt.”]. But when, ascending on high, he led captivity captive, he did not render gifts to human beings but gave gifts to them (Eph. IV, 8). From where could the Apostle presume that something was rendered to him as a debt, unless he had first received undeserved grace, by which he fought the good fight after being justified?

For he had been a blasphemer, a persecutor, and an insolent man; but he obtained mercy, as he himself testifies (I Tim. I, 13), believing in the one who justifies not the godly but the ungodly (Rom. IV, 5), so that by justifying him he might make him godly.

### 4

“It was said,” he says, “not from works but from the one who calls: ‘Because the elder shall serve the younger.’” This is connected with what he says: “For when they had not yet been born and had done nothing good or evil,” so that it could be said, “not from works but from the one who calls.”

This prompts the mind to ask why he said, “so that the purpose of God according to election might remain.” For how is there any just election—or any election at all—where there is no distinction? If Jacob, who had not yet been born and had done nothing, was chosen without any merit, he could not have been chosen at all, since there was no difference by which he might be chosen. Likewise, if Esau was rejected without any merit, since he too had not yet been born and had done nothing, when it was said, “And the elder shall serve the younger,” how can his rejection be called just?

By what distinction, by what standard of equity, then, are we to understand what follows: “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated”? This is indeed written in the prophet who prophesied long after they had been born and died. Nevertheless, the statement appears to recall the earlier saying, “And the elder shall serve the younger,” which was spoken before they had been born or had done anything.

Where, then, does this election come from—or what sort of election is it—if, before they were born and before they had done anything, there were no merits to consider? Or are there perhaps differences of nature? Who could understand that, when they came from one father, one mother, one intercourse, and one Creator?

Or did the same Creator, just as from the same earth he produced different kinds of animals and growing things, likewise produce from the same human marriage and union, in the case of the twins, one offspring whom he would love and another whom he would hate? There was therefore no election [Note: [Col. 0114] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions have: “There is no election.”] before there was anything to be elected.

For if Jacob was made good so that he might please God, how did he please God before he was made, so that he might become good? He was therefore not chosen in order to become good; rather, once made good, he could be chosen.

### 5

Was it perhaps “according to election” because God, who foreknows all things, saw Jacob’s future faith while he was not yet born? Thus, although no one deserves to be justified by his works—for no one can act well unless he has been justified—nevertheless, since God justifies the Gentiles by faith (Gal. III, 8), and since no one believes except by free will, God, foreseeing that future will of faith, chose by his foreknowledge the one whom he would justify, even though he had not yet been born?

If election occurs through foreknowledge, and God foreknew Jacob’s faith, how do you prove that he did not also choose him on account of works? If the reason is that they had not yet been born and had not yet done anything good or evil, then neither had either of them yet believed. But did foreknowledge see that he would believe [Note: [Col. 0114] The printed editions have: “But just as foreknowledge saw that he would believe.” Three Vatican manuscripts have: “If foreknowledge…” The Corbeiensis and Genovefaeanus manuscripts read: “But foreknowledge saw that he would believe,” omitting “just as.”]?

Then foreknowledge could also see that he would act, so that just as someone could say that Jacob was chosen because of the future faith God foreknew, another could say that he was chosen rather because of future works, which God likewise foreknew.

Therefore, how does the Apostle show that “the elder shall serve the younger” was said not from works? Is it because they had not yet been born [Note: [Col. 0114] Lovaniensis has: “But if it is because they had not yet been born.” Ambrosianus and Erasmus have “But because,” omitting “if.” The manuscripts have “If because,” omitting “but.”]? If so, it was said not only not from works but not even from faith, because neither existed in those who had not yet been born.

He therefore did not intend election to be understood as having been made through foreknowledge of the younger. For, wishing to show that it was not made from works, he added the words: “For when they had not yet been born and had done nothing good or evil.” Otherwise one could have said to him, “But God already knew what each of them would do.”

Why, then, did that election take place? For if it was not from works, which did not exist in those not yet born, nor from faith, since faith did not exist either, where did it come from?

### 6

Should we say that there was no election, since there was no difference in the womb of the mother—whether of faith, works, or any merits whatsoever? Yet it was said, “so that the purpose of God according to election might remain.” We ask this because it was said.

Unless perhaps the sentence should be distinguished in this way: we should not understand it as though “not from works but from the one who calls it was said, ‘The elder shall serve the younger,’ so that the purpose of God according to election might remain.” Rather, the example of those who had not yet been born and had not yet done anything should be understood to have been given precisely so that no election could be perceived here.

“For when they had not yet been born and had done nothing, whether good or evil, so that the purpose of God according to election might remain”—that is, they had done nothing good or evil, so that an election might be made on account of the action itself of the one who had acted well. Since therefore there was no election of one who had acted well according to which God’s purpose might remain, it was said—not from works but from the one who calls, that is, from the one who justifies the ungodly by calling him to faith through grace—“Because the elder shall serve the younger.”

The purpose of God therefore does not remain according to election; rather, election proceeds from his purpose. That is, God’s purpose of justification does not remain because he finds good works in human beings which he may choose. Rather, because his purpose remains to justify believers, he finds works which he may then choose for the kingdom of heaven.

For unless there were an election, there would be no elect, nor would it rightly be said, “Who shall bring an accusation against God’s elect?” (Rom. VIII, 33).

Yet election does not precede justification; justification precedes election. No one is chosen unless he is already distinct from the one who is rejected. Hence, concerning what is said, “God chose us before the foundation of the world” (Eph. I, 4), I do not see how it can be understood except as referring to foreknowledge.

But here, when he says, “not from works but from the one who calls it was said, ‘The elder shall serve the younger,’” he intended it to be understood not as an election based on merits—which arise after justification by grace—but as the generosity of God’s gifts, so that no one would boast of works: “For by the grace of God we have been saved; and this is not from ourselves, but is God’s gift; not from works, lest anyone should boast” (Eph. II, 8–9).

### 7

The question arises whether faith itself earns the justification of a human being, or whether even the merits of faith do not precede God’s mercy, but faith itself is also to be counted among the gifts of grace.

For here too, after saying “not from works,” he did not say, “but from faith it was said, ‘The elder shall serve the younger.’” Rather, he said, “from the one who calls.” No one believes who is not called. But the merciful God calls, granting this without any merits even of faith, because the merits of faith follow calling rather than precede it.

“For how shall they believe in him whom they have not heard? And how shall they hear without a preacher?” (Rom. X, 14). Unless God’s mercy precedes by calling, no one can believe, so as to begin to be justified through this and to receive the ability to act well.

Grace therefore precedes every merit. Indeed, “Christ died for the ungodly” (Rom. V, 6). The younger therefore received this from the one who calls, not from any merits of his works, so that the elder should serve him. Thus even the statement “Jacob I loved” comes from God who calls, not from Jacob who acts.

### 8

What, then, of Esau—that he should serve the younger, and that it is written, “But Esau I hated”? By what evils of his did he earn this, when he too had not yet been born and had done nothing good or evil, at the time when it was said, “And the elder shall serve the younger”?

Or, just as the statement concerning Jacob was made without any merits of good action, was Esau likewise hated without any merits of evil action? For if God foreknew that his future works would be evil and therefore predestined him to serve the younger, then for the same reason he predestined Jacob to have the elder serve him, because he foreknew his future good works—and the statement “not from works” is false.

But if it is true that it was not from works, and he proves this by saying that it was spoken concerning those not yet born and not yet acting, then it was not from faith either, since faith likewise did not yet exist in those not yet born. By what merit, then, is Esau hated before he is born?

There is no question that God made those things which he would love. But if we say that he made things which he would hate, that is absurd, since another passage of Scripture comes to mind and says: “For you would not have made anything if you hated it, and you hate none of the things that you have made” (Wis. XI, 25).

By what merit, then, was the sun made the sun? Or what offense did the moon commit that it should be so much inferior to the sun? Or what did it earn so that it should be created so much brighter than the other stars? Yet all these things were created good, each in its own kind.

For God would not have said, “I loved the sun, but hated the moon,” or, “I loved the moon, but hated the stars,” as he said, “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated.” He loved all those things, although they were ordered in different degrees of excellence, because God saw that they were good when they were established at his word (Gen. I).

But for him to hate Esau, unless it were on account of the merit of injustice, is unjust. If we grant this, Jacob begins to be loved on account of the merit of justice. And if that is true, then it is false that it was not from works.

Or perhaps it was on account of the justice of faith? What, then, does “For when they had not yet been born” help you, since in one not yet born there could not even be the justice of faith?

### 9

The Apostle therefore saw what might occur to the mind of the hearer or reader from these words, and immediately added: “What shall we say, then? Is there injustice with God? Certainly not.”

And as though teaching how this could not be so, he says: “For he says to Moses, ‘I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will show compassion to whom I show compassion.’”

Do these words solve the question, or rather bind it more tightly? For this is what chiefly troubles us: if he has mercy on the one on whom he will have mercy, and shows compassion to the one to whom he will show compassion, why was this mercy lacking to Esau, so that he too might become good through it, just as Jacob became good through it?

Or was it for this reason that it was said, “I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will show compassion to whom I show compassion”: that God will have mercy on the one to whom he shows mercy in order to call him; and he will have mercy on him in order that he may believe; and on the one to whom he has shown compassion so that he may believe, he will show compassion—that is, he will make him compassionate, so that he may also act well [Note: [Col. 0116] The printed editions have “in order to call him merciful.” The word “merciful” is absent from the better manuscripts.]?

From this we are warned that no one ought to glory or exalt himself even in works of mercy, as though he had earned God’s favor through what was supposedly his own, since God himself granted him the very mercy by which he might possess mercy—he who will show compassion to the one to whom he has shown compassion.

And if someone boasts that he earned this by believing, let him recognize that God granted him the ability to believe: it is God who, by inspiring faith, shows mercy to the one to whom he showed mercy in order to grant a calling even while he was still unbelieving.

For now the faithful person is distinguished from the ungodly. “What do you have,” he says, “that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (I Cor. IV, 7).

### 10

This is correct. But why was this mercy withheld from Esau [Col. 0117] so that he was not called in such a way that faith would also be inspired in him when he was called [Note: [Col. 0117] One of the Vatican manuscripts adds here: “so that he might believe.”] and that, believing, he would become compassionate and act well?

Or was it because he was unwilling? If Jacob therefore believed because he was willing, God did not give him faith; rather, by willing, he himself supplied it to himself, and he had something that he did not receive.

Or is the answer that no one can believe unless he is willing, and no one can be willing unless he is called, but no one can grant himself a calling? God grants faith by calling, because without calling no one can believe, although no one believes unwillingly.

“For how shall they believe in him whom they have not heard? Or how shall they hear without a preacher?” No one therefore believes without being called; but not everyone who is called believes. “For many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. XX, 16)—namely, those who did not despise the one calling them but followed him by believing. They certainly believed willingly.

What, then, is the meaning of what follows: “So then it is not of the one who wills or of the one who runs, but of God who shows mercy”? Is it because we cannot even will unless we are called, and our willing is of no value unless God helps us to complete what we will?

It is therefore necessary both to will and to run. For it would not be said without reason, “Peace on earth to people of good will” (Luke II, 14), and, “Run in such a way that you may obtain” (I Cor. IX, 24).

Nevertheless, “it is not of the one who wills or of the one who runs, but of God who shows mercy,” so that we may obtain what we will and reach the place to which we will go.

Esau therefore was unwilling and did not run. But even if he had been willing and had run, he would have reached the goal through God’s help—God who, by calling him, would also have granted him the will and the running—unless, despising the call, he had become rejected.

For God grants that we will in one way, and grants what we have willed in another. He willed that the act of willing should be both his and ours: his, in calling; ours, in following. But what we have willed—namely, the ability to act well and to live blessedly forever—he alone grants.

Nevertheless, Esau, who had not yet been born, could not yet will or refuse any of these things. Why, then, was he rejected while still in the womb? We are brought back to those difficulties, made more troubling not only by their obscurity but also by our own repeated treatment of them.

### 11

Why was Esau rejected before he was born, when he could neither believe the one calling him, nor despise the calling [Note: [Col. 0117] The Sorbonicus manuscript reads “the one calling him”], nor perform anything good or evil?

If it was because God foreknew his future evil will, why was Jacob not approved through God’s foreknowledge of his future good will?

If you grant once and for all that someone could be approved or rejected on the basis of what was not yet in him, but what God foreknew would be in him, it follows that he could also be approved on the basis of works which God foreknew would be in him, even though he had not yet done anything. In that case, the fact that they had not yet been born will not help you at all when it was said, “And the elder shall serve the younger,” as though this demonstrated that it was not from works, because he had not yet done anything.

### 12

If you carefully attend also to those words, “So then it is not of the one who wills or of the one who runs, but of God who shows mercy,” the Apostle does not appear to have said this merely because we reach what we will through God’s help. He also said it with the intention expressed elsewhere: “Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling; for it is God who works in you both to will and to work, for his good pleasure” (Phil. II, 12–13).

There he sufficiently shows that even good will itself comes to be in us through God’s working. For if the statement “it is not of the one who wills or of the one who runs, but of God who shows mercy” was said only because human will by itself is not sufficient for us to live justly and rightly unless we are helped by God’s mercy, then one could also say, “So then it is not of God who shows mercy, but of the human being who wills,” because God’s mercy alone is not sufficient unless the consent of our will is added.

But this is clear: it is useless for us to will unless God shows mercy. Yet I do not know how one could say that God shows mercy uselessly unless we are willing. For if God shows mercy, we also will; it belongs to that same mercy that we should will. “For it is God who works in us both to will and to work, for his good pleasure.”

If we ask whether good will is God’s gift, it would be astonishing if anyone dared to deny it. But because good will does not precede calling—rather, calling precedes good will—what we rightly will is attributed to God who calls, while the fact that we are called cannot be attributed to us.

It should not therefore be thought that the statement “it is not of the one who wills or of the one who runs, but of God who shows mercy” was made because we cannot attain what we will without his help. It was made rather because, without his calling, we do not will.

### 13

But if this calling produces good will in such a way that everyone who is called follows it, how will the statement “Many are called, but few are chosen” be true?

If that statement is true, and the one called does not necessarily obey the calling, and whether he obeys is left to his own will [Note: [Col. 0118] On the authority of the manuscripts, we have restored the negative particle, which had been omitted from the earlier editions.], then it can rightly also be said, “So then it is not of God who shows mercy, but of the human being who wills and runs,” because the mercy of the one who calls is not sufficient unless the obedience of the one called follows.

Or perhaps those who do not consent when called in this way could, when called in another way, apply the will of faith, so that both statements would be true: “Many are called, but few are chosen.” Although many are called in one way, nevertheless, because not all are affected in the same way, only those follow the calling who are found suited to receive it.

Then this statement would also be no less true: “So then it is not of the one who wills or of the one who runs, but of God who shows mercy”—the God who called in the manner suited to those who followed the calling.

In the case of others, calling indeed reaches them; but because it was of such a kind that they could not be moved by it and were not suited to receive it, they could be called but not chosen. In their case it is no longer equally true to say, “So then it is not of God who shows mercy, but of the human being who wills and runs.” For the effect of God’s mercy cannot be placed in human power, as though God should show mercy in vain if a person is unwilling. If he wished to show mercy even to those people, he could call them in a way suited to them, so that they would be moved, understand, and follow.

The statement is therefore true: “Many are called, but few are chosen.” [Col. 0119] Those are chosen who are called congruently [Note: [Col. 0119] Three Vatican manuscripts read: “who were congruent with the calling.”]. Those, however, who were not congruent with or adapted to the calling were not chosen, because they did not follow it, although they were called.

Likewise, this is true: “It is not of the one who wills or of the one who runs, but of God who shows mercy.” For although he calls many, he nevertheless shows mercy to those whom he calls in the way suited to them, so that they follow.

But it is false if someone says, “So then it is not of God who shows mercy, but of the human being who wills and runs,” because God shows mercy to no one in vain. And the one to whom he shows mercy he calls in the way he knows to be suited to him, so that he does not reject the one calling him.

### 14

Someone will say here: Why, then, was Esau not called in such a way that he would be willing to obey?

We see that different people are moved to believe in different ways by the same things when they are displayed or signified. For example, Simeon believed in our Lord Jesus Christ while he was still a little infant, recognizing him because the Spirit revealed him to him (Luke II, 25).

Nathaniel, after hearing from him the single statement, “Before Philip called you, when you were under the fig tree, I saw you,” replied, “Rabbi, you are the Son of God; you are the king of Israel” (John I, 48–49).

Because Peter confessed this much later, he deserved to hear that he was blessed and that the keys of the kingdom of heaven would be given to him (Matt. XVI, 16–19).

After the miracle at Cana of Galilee—which the evangelist John records as the beginning of Jesus’ signs, when water was changed into wine—his disciples believed in him (John II, 11).

He stirred many to faith by speaking [Note: [Col. 0119] Erasmus and most manuscripts have “invited.”]. Many did not believe even after the dead had been raised.

Terrified by his cross and death, the disciples themselves wavered; yet the thief believed at a time when he did not see him superior in works but equal to him in sharing the cross (Luke XXIII, 40–42).

One of the disciples, after his resurrection, believed not so much through his living limbs as through the fresh scars (John XX, 27).

Many of those who had crucified him—people who had despised him when they saw him perform miracles—believed when the disciples preached him and performed such things in his name (Acts II–IV).

Since one person is moved to faith in one way and another in another way, and since the same thing, when expressed in one way, often moves a person, but when expressed in another does not, and moves one person but not another, who would dare to say that God lacked a way of calling by which even Esau might have applied his mind to that faith and joined his will to it, the faith by which Jacob was justified?

But if the obstinacy of the will can be so great that an aversion of mind hardens against every manner of calling [Note: [Col. 0119] The Corbeiensis manuscript has “overturning”; Victorinus has “opposition.”], the question arises whether this hardness itself is a divine punishment, when God abandons a person by not calling him in the way by which he can be moved to faith.

For who would say that even the Almighty lacked the means by which he could persuade him to believe [Note: [Col. 0119] The printed editions have: “For when God abandons him . . . who would even say that the means,” etc. The Corbeiensis manuscript has: “When God abandons him,” followed, together with other manuscripts, by “who would say what means.”]?

### 15

But why do we ask this, when the Apostle himself adds: “For Scripture says to Pharaoh, ‘For this very purpose I raised you up, so that I might show my power in you and so that my name might be proclaimed throughout the whole earth’”?

The Apostle added this example to prove what he had said above: “So then it is not of the one who wills or of the one who runs, but of God who shows mercy.”

As though someone had said to him, “From where do you teach this?” he replies: “For Scripture says to Pharaoh, ‘For this very purpose I raised you up, so that I might show my power in you and so that my name might be proclaimed throughout the whole earth.’”

By this he certainly shows that it is not of the one who wills or of the one who runs, but of God who shows mercy.

And he concludes in this way: “Therefore he has mercy on whom he wills, and he hardens whom he wills,” although the two statements had not previously been made in the same form. For just as it was said, “It is not of the one who wills or of the one who runs, but of God who shows mercy,” so it was not also said, “It is not of the one who is unwilling [Note: [Col. 0120] Thus Erasmus and several manuscripts. Lovaniensis has “not of the one who wills.”] or of the one who despises, but of God who hardens.”

From this it is understood that the statement he placed below concerning both matters—“Therefore he has mercy on whom he wills, and he hardens whom he wills”—can be brought into agreement with the preceding statement in such a way that God’s hardening means his unwillingness to show mercy. Thus he does not inflict anything by which a person becomes worse; he merely fails to bestow what would make him better.

But if this occurs without any distinction of merits, who would not burst into the words which the Apostle himself posed as an objection: “You will say to me, then, ‘Why does he still complain? For who can resist his will?’”

God often complains about human beings, as appears throughout innumerable passages of Scripture, because they are unwilling to believe and to live rightly. For this reason the faithful, who do the will of God, are said to live without reproach (Luke I, 6), since Scripture does not complain about them.

But “Why does he still complain?” he says, “For who can resist his will?”—when he has mercy on whom he wills and hardens whom he wills?

Nevertheless, let us look at what precedes and, insofar as the Lord himself helps us, direct our judgment from there.

### 16

For a little earlier he says: “What then shall we say? Is there injustice with God? By no means.” Let this therefore be fixed and immovable in a mind sober in piety and steadfast in faith [Note: Printed editions have “steadfast faith,” omitting the preposition *in*, which we restore from the Corbie manuscript]: there is no injustice with God. And let this very thing be held with the utmost constancy and firmness: that God’s having mercy on whomever he wills and hardening whomever he wills—that is, having mercy on whomever he wills and not having mercy on whomever he does not will—is the expression of some hidden equity, impossible to investigate by human standards. This equity must be recognized in human affairs and earthly transactions; for unless we retained certain traces impressed upon them by heavenly justice, our feeble understanding would never look up toward, or aspire to, the innermost sanctuary and most chaste shrine of spiritual teachings.

“Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be filled” (Matt. 5:6). In this dryness of mortal life and condition, unless a very fine breath, as it were, of righteousness were sprinkled upon us from above, we would wither before we could thirst.

Since human society is therefore bound together by giving and receiving, and what is given and received may be either owed or not owed, who cannot see that no one can be accused of injustice if he demands what is owed him? Nor, certainly, can the person who wishes to give away what is owed to him. The matter lies not in the discretion of those who are debtors, but in the discretion of the one to whom the debt is owed. This image—or, as I said above, this trace of the highest equity impressed upon human dealings—has been set before us [Note: Three Vatican manuscripts read “highest.” A little later the same books have: “from whom the whole human race derives the origin of its offense against God”].

All human beings, then—since, as the Apostle says, “in Adam all die” (1 Cor. 15:22), from whom the origin of offense against God extends to the whole human race—are one mass of sin, owing punishment to divine and supreme justice. Whether that debt is exacted or forgiven, there is no injustice.

Debtors arrogantly presume to judge from whom the debt ought to be exacted and to whom it ought to be forgiven, just as those hired for the vineyard unjustly complained when as much was given to others as was paid to them (Matt. 20:11). Thus the Apostle bluntly rebuffs the insolence of this question: “O man, who are you to answer back to God?” A person answers back to God when he is displeased that God complains about sinners, as though God compelled anyone to sin merely because, when some people sin, he does not bestow upon them the mercy of his justification—and as though he were said to harden certain sinners because he does not have mercy on them, rather than because he impels them to sin [Note: The manuscripts read “but merely.” One of them, the Gonovefaeus, adds immediately before: “since he himself compels no one to sin.” Another Vatican manuscript below reads “he bestows and is said” for “he might bestow and be said”].

He does not have mercy on those whom, by a most hidden equity far removed from human understanding, he judges not to be recipients of mercy. “For his judgments are unsearchable and his ways inscrutable” (Rom. 11:33). Yet he rightly complains about sinners, as about those whom he himself does not compel to sin.

At the same time, this serves so that those on whom he has mercy may also receive this calling: when God complains about sinners, they may be pierced in heart and turn to his grace. He therefore complains justly and mercifully.

### 17

But if it troubles us that no one resists his will, because he helps whomever he wills and abandons whomever he wills—although both the one he helps and the one he abandons belong to the same mass of sinners, and although both deserve punishment, punishment is nevertheless exacted from one and forgiven the other—if this troubles us, then: “O man, who are you to answer back to God?”
