I think that the word “man” is used here with the same implication as in the statement, “Are you not human, and are you not walking according to human standards?” (1 Cor. 3:4). There the term designates carnal and natural people, to whom it is said: “I could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as carnal”; and again: “For you were not yet able; indeed, even now you are not able, for you are still carnal” (1 Cor. 3:1–4); and again: “The natural person does not receive the things of the Spirit of God” (1 Cor. 2:14).

To such people, then, it is said: “O man, who are you to answer back to God?” Shall the thing formed say to the one who formed it, “Why did you make me this way?” Or does the potter not have authority over the clay, from the same lump to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?

By this very comparison he perhaps makes it sufficiently clear that he is speaking to a carnal person, since the clay itself signifies the material from which the first man was formed. And because, as I have already mentioned, all die in Adam according to the same Apostle, he says that all belong to one lump.

Although one vessel is made for honor and another for dishonor, nevertheless even the vessel made for honor must begin by being carnal and rise from there into spiritual maturity [Note: Four manuscripts read “grace”]. For they had already been made for honor and had already been born in Christ; yet, because he is still addressing them as little ones, he also calls them carnal, saying:

“I could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as carnal. I gave you milk to drink, like infants in Christ, not solid food; for you were not able, and even now you are not able, for you are still carnal.”

Although, therefore, he says that they are carnal, they have already been born in Christ and are little ones in him, requiring to be fed with milk. And what he adds—“even now you are not able”—shows that, as they progress, they will become able, because grace had already begun in those who had been spiritually reborn [Note: The Victorinus manuscript reads “had begun,” masculine].

They were therefore already vessels made for honor, and yet it could rightly still be said to them: “O man, who are you to answer back to God?” If this is rightly said to such people, it is much more rightly said to those who have either not yet been regenerated in this way or have been made for dishonor.

Let this alone be held by unshaken faith: that there is no injustice with God. Whether he forgives a debt or exacts it, neither the one from whom he exacts it can rightly complain of his injustice, nor should the one to whom he forgives it boast of his own merits. The former does not repay anything except what is owed; the latter possesses nothing except what he has received.

### 18

At this point, if the Lord helps us, we must strive to see how both of these statements are true: “You hate nothing that you have made” (Wis. 11:25), and “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated” (Mal. 1:2–3).

If he hated Esau because he had been made a vessel for dishonor, and the same potter made one vessel for honor and another for dishonor, how is it true that he hated nothing that he made? For behold, he hates Esau, whom he himself made as a vessel for dishonor.

The difficulty is resolved if we understand God to be the maker of all creatures. “Every creature of God is good” (1 Tim. 4:4); and every human being, insofar as he is human, is a creature—not insofar as he is a sinner.

God is therefore the creator both of the human body and of the human soul. Neither of these is evil, and God hates neither; for he hates nothing that he has made. The soul, however, is superior to the body. God is the maker and creator of both soul and body, and he hates nothing in a human being except sin.

Human sin is disorder and perversity: that is, turning away from the superior Creator and turning toward created things that are inferior. God therefore does not hate Esau as a human being; God hates Esau as a sinner.

The same distinction appears in the statement about the Lord: “He came to his own, and his own did not receive him” (John 1:11). Yet to these same people he says: “For this reason you do not hear, because you are not of God” (John 8:47).

How are they “his own,” and how are they “not of God,” unless the former statement concerns the human beings whom the Lord himself made, while the latter concerns the sinners whom the Lord himself reproved? They are nevertheless the same people, both human beings and sinners: human beings by God’s creation, sinners by their own will.

What, then, did God love in Jacob? Was Jacob not a sinner? God loved in him not the guilt that he was removing, but the grace that he was bestowing. For “Christ died for the ungodly” (Rom. 5:6), not so that they might remain ungodly [Note: The printed editions read “so that dead ungodly persons might remain”; “dead” is absent from the manuscripts], but so that, justified from ungodliness, they might be converted [Note: The manuscripts read “might be changed”], believing in the one who justifies the ungodly (Rom. 4:5). God hates ungodliness.

Accordingly, in some he punishes ungodliness through condemnation; in others he removes it through justification, according to how he judges by those unsearchable judgments. And when, from the number of the ungodly whom he does not justify, he makes vessels for dishonor, he does not hate in them what he makes. For insofar as they are ungodly, they are accursed; but insofar as they are made vessels, they are made for some purpose, so that through the ordered punishments inflicted upon them the vessels made for honor may advance.

God therefore does not hate them either insofar as they are human beings or insofar as they are vessels—that is, he hates neither what he makes in them by creating nor what he makes in them by ordering. For he hates nothing that he has made.

Yet when he makes them vessels of destruction, he does so for the benefit of correcting others. He hates the ungodliness in them, which he did not make [Note: The manuscripts read: “Yet, in making them vessels of destruction for the benefit of correcting others, he hates the ungodliness in them,” and so forth].

Just as a judge hates theft in a person but does not hate what is committed to the prison—for the thief makes the theft, while the judge makes the imprisonment—so God does not hate what he makes from the lump of the ungodly as vessels of destruction: that is, the work of his ordering in the deserved punishment of those who perish [Note: Almost all manuscripts read “of those perishing”], in which those on whom he has mercy may find an occasion of salvation.

Thus it was said to Pharaoh: “For this very purpose I raised you up, that I might show my power in you, and that my name might be proclaimed throughout all the earth.” This manifestation of God’s power and proclamation of his name throughout the earth benefits those who, by fearing him, correct their ways and to whom such a calling is appropriate.

Accordingly, he continues: “But if God, desiring to show his wrath and to make known his power, endured with much patience vessels of wrath, which have been perfected for destruction”—the implied conclusion is: “Who are you to answer back to God?”

If the sentence is connected again with the preceding words, the meaning is: If God, desiring to show his wrath, endured vessels of wrath, who are you to answer back to God?

He endured them not only because he wished to show his wrath and make known his power, but also, as the following words say, “so that he might make known the riches of his glory upon vessels of mercy.”

For what benefit is there to the vessels perfected for destruction in God’s patiently bearing with them, so that he may destroy them in due order [Note: The manuscripts read this way; the printed editions have “so that he may destroy them in an orderly manner”], and use them as instruments of salvation for others on whom he has mercy?

It benefits, of course, those for whose salvation he uses them in this way, so that, as it is written, “the righteous shall wash his hands in the blood of the sinner” (Ps. 57:11)—that is, he is cleansed from evil works through the fear of God when he sees the punishments of sinners.

Thus, God’s enduring vessels of wrath because he wishes to show his wrath serves to instill useful fear in others, and his making known the riches of his glory upon vessels of mercy, which he prepared for glory, serves the same purpose.

The hardening of the ungodly therefore demonstrates both what must be feared, so that each person may turn to God in piety, and how great thanks must be given for God’s mercy, since through the punishment of some he shows what he gives to others.

But if the punishment that he exacts from some is not just, then he gives nothing to those from whom he does not exact it. Since, however, that punishment is just and there is no injustice in the God who punishes, who could sufficiently give thanks to him for remitting what, had he wished to exact it, no one could rightly say was not owed?

### 19

“And those whom he called,” he says, “us also, not only from the Jews but also from the Gentiles”—that is, the vessels of mercy that he prepared for glory.

For he did not call all Jews, but some from the Jews; nor all Gentiles without exception, but some from the Gentiles. There is one mass of sinners and ungodly people from Adam, in which Jews and Gentiles alike, apart from God’s grace, belong to one lump.

For if the potter makes from the same lump of clay one vessel for honor and another for dishonor, and it is evident that among the Jews there are some vessels for honor and others for dishonor, just as among the Gentiles, it follows that all are understood to belong to one lump.

Then he begins to cite testimonies from the Prophets [Note: The manuscripts read “from prophecy”] for each group, in reverse order. He first spoke of those from the Jews [Note: The printed editions have “those converted from the Jews”; most manuscripts lack “converted”], and afterward of those from the Gentiles; but he first offers testimony for the Gentiles and then for the Jews.

For, as Hosea says: “I will call those who were not my people, my people, and her who was not beloved, beloved; and in the place where it was said to them, ‘You are not my people,’ there they shall be called sons of the living God.”

This is understood to have been said about the Gentiles, because they did not have one appointed place for sacrifices, as the Jews had in Jerusalem. The Apostles, however, were sent to the Gentiles so that each might believe in his own place and, wherever they believed, offer a sacrifice of praise—those to whom he gave power to become sons of God (John 1:12).

“Isaiah,” he says, “cries out concerning Israel.” So that it might not again be thought that all Israelites had gone to destruction [Note: Lov. has “were thought to have been sent to destruction”; Am., Er., and our manuscripts more appropriately read “were thought to have gone to destruction”], he teaches that from Israel also some vessels were made for honor and others for dishonor.

“If the number of the children of Israel should be like the sand of the sea, the remnant shall be saved.” The rest, therefore, are vessels perfected for destruction.

“For, completing and abridging his word, the Lord will execute it upon the earth”—that is, by the brief summary of faith he saves believers through grace, not through the innumerable observances by which that multitude was burdened and oppressed in servitude.

Through grace God completed and abridged his word upon the earth, saying: “My yoke is easy and my burden light” (Matt. 11:30).

The same is said shortly afterward in this passage: “The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart” [Note: The most ancient Corbie codex adds “you” here, in agreement with the Greek]—that is, the word of faith that we preach: “because if you confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved. For with the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. 10:8–10).

This is the word that God completed and abridged upon the earth. Through this completion and abridgment [Note: Erasmus and the manuscripts read “brevity”] the thief was justified: although all his limbs were fastened to the cross, he still possessed these two free faculties—he believed with the heart unto righteousness and confessed with the mouth unto salvation. Immediately he deserved to hear: “Today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43).

His good works would have followed if, after receiving grace, he had lived longer among human beings. Yet they had not preceded grace, so that he might merit it: he was taken from robbery to the cross and from the cross to paradise.

“And as Isaiah foretold,” he says, “unless the Lord of hosts had left us a seed, we would have become like Sodom and would have been made like Gomorrah.”

What is said here—“had left us a seed”—corresponds there to “the remnant shall be saved.” The rest, like vessels of destruction, perished in deserved punishment.

And the fact that all did not perish as in Sodom and Gomorrah was not due to their merit, but to the grace of God, who left a seed from which another harvest might arise throughout the world.

The same is said shortly afterward: “So then, at this present time also, a remnant has been saved according to the election of grace. But if by grace, then not by works; otherwise grace would no longer be grace. What then? Israel did not obtain what it was seeking, but the elect obtained it; the rest were hardened” (Rom. 11:5–7).

The vessels of mercy obtained it; the vessels of wrath were hardened—from the same lump, as is also seen in the fullness of the Gentiles.

### 20

There is a passage of Scripture especially necessary for the matter now under discussion, confirming with wonderful testimony the points already treated. It occurs in the book called by some *Jesus Sirach* and by others *Ecclesiasticus*, where it is written:

“And all human beings are from the soil, and Adam was created from the earth” [Note: The printed editions have “from the earth from which Adam …”; the word “from which” is absent from the manuscripts and from the Greek text of the Septuagint].

“In the abundance of discipline the Lord separated them and changed their ways. And from among them he blessed and exalted; and from among them he sanctified and drew them to himself; and from among them he cursed and humbled; and he turned them toward their mutual dissension. Like clay in the hand of the potter, who forms and arranges it according to his will, so are all his ways according to his disposition; so is the human being in the hand of the one who made him, and he will repay him according to his judgment. The contrary of evil is good, and life is contrary to death; so also the sinner is contrary to the righteous man. And so look upon all the works of the Most High: two and two [Note: The printed editions have “two against two”; “against” is absent from the older books], one against one.”

First, God’s discipline is commended here: “In the abundance of discipline,” he says, “the Lord separated them.” From what else, unless from the blessedness of paradise? “And he changed their ways,” so that they would now live as mortals.

Then one mass of all human beings came into existence, deriving from the transmission of sin [Note: The Victorinus manuscript reads “from the root of sin”] and from the punishment of mortality, although God was forming and creating the things that are good.

In all human beings there is the beauty and structure of the body, with such harmony among its members that the Apostle drew from it an analogy for attaining charity (1 Cor. 12:12ff.). In all there is also the vital spirit that gives life to earthly limbs, and the whole nature of the human being is wonderfully ordered through the rule of the soul and the service of the body.

Yet carnal desire, already reigning as the punishment of sin, had confused the whole human race as one entire and single lump, with original guilt extending through everything.

And yet the passage continues: “From among them he blessed and exalted; from among them he sanctified and drew them to himself; from among them he cursed and humbled, and he turned them toward their mutual dissension”—as though the Apostle were saying: “Does the potter not have authority over the clay, from the same lump to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?”

For this reason, what follows is not unrelated to the same comparison: “Like clay,” he says, “in the hand of the potter, to form and arrange it, all his ways according to his disposition; so is the human being in the hand of the one who made him.”

But since the Apostle says, “Is there injustice with God?”, observe what is added here: “He will repay him,” he says, “according to his judgment.”

Although the condemned therefore receive just punishments, nevertheless, because this very thing is turned to the benefit of those who receive mercy, consider what follows:

“The contrary,” he says, “of evil is good, and life is contrary to death; so also the sinner is contrary to the righteous man. And so look upon all the works of the Most High: two and two, one against one”—so that, certainly, the better things may stand out and advance through comparison with the worse.

Yet because the better things are better through grace, the passage continues as though it were saying, “The remnant shall be saved” [Note: The manuscripts read “the remnant is saved”]. It then speaks in the person of the remnant:

“And I was the last to keep watch, and like one who gleans after the grape-gatherers.”

And how does he prove that this is not from his own merits but from God’s mercy?

“In the blessing of the Lord,” he says, “I too hoped; and like one who gathers grapes, I filled the winepress” (Ecclus. 33:10–17).

Although he kept watch as the last, nevertheless, because—as it is written—“the last shall be first” (Matt. 20:16), the people gathered as gleanings from the remnant of Israel, hoping in the blessing of the Lord, filled the winepress with the abundance of the harvest that arose throughout the whole world.

### 21

No intention, therefore, is held by the Apostle or by all those who have been justified, through whom the understanding of grace has been shown to us, except that “whoever boasts should boast in the Lord” (2 Cor. 10:17).

For who can scrutinize the works of the Lord, who from the same lump condemns one person and justifies another?

Free choice of the will is of great importance; indeed, it exists—but what can it do in those who are “sold under sin” (Rom. 7:14)? “The flesh,” he says, “desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh, so that you may not do the things you wish” (Gal. 5:17).

We are commanded to live rightly, with the reward set before us that we may deserve to live happily forever. But who can live rightly and do good works unless justified by faith?

We are commanded to believe, so that, through the gift of the Holy Spirit received, we may be able to do good works through love. But who can believe unless he is touched by some calling—that is, by some testimony of things?

Who has it in his power to have his mind touched by such a vision that his will is moved toward faith? And who embraces inwardly something that does not please him? Or who has it in his power either to encounter what can please him or to be pleased when he encounters it?

When, therefore, those things please us by which we advance toward God, this is inspired and supplied by God’s grace; it is not acquired by our own inclination, effort, or merits of works. For he grants and bestows the inclination of the will, the diligence of effort, and works fervent with love.

We are commanded to ask so that we may receive, to seek so that we may find, and to knock so that it may be opened to us (Matt. 7:7). Is our prayer not sometimes lukewarm—or rather cold and almost nothing [Note: Lov. reads “completely nothing”; Am., Er., and the manuscripts read “almost nothing”]—indeed, sometimes so utterly absent that we do not even notice this in ourselves with sorrow? For if we do sorrow over it, we are already praying.

What else is shown to us, then, except that the one who commands us to ask, seek, and knock also grants that we should do so? Therefore it is “not of the one who wills or of the one who runs, but of God who shows mercy,” since we can neither will nor run unless he moves and arouses us.

### 22

But if some election occurs here, so that we understand the statement, “The remnant has been saved according to the election of grace” (Rom. 11:5), not as an election of those already justified for eternal life, but as an election of those who are to be justified, then this election is certainly so hidden that it cannot at all be seen by us within the same lump. Or, if it is visible to some, I confess my weakness in this matter.

For if I am permitted to examine this election by some thought, I have nothing to observe in those chosen for saving grace except either greater intelligence, fewer sins, or both. Let us add, if one wishes, honorable and useful learning.

Whoever, then, is entangled and stained by the fewest sins—for who can be without any?—and is sharp in intellect and polished in liberal studies seems to be the one who ought to be chosen for grace.

But once I have made this judgment, the one who chose the weak things of the world to shame the strong, and the foolish things of the world to shame the wise (1 Cor. 1:27), will laugh at me. Looking upon him and corrected by shame, I will laugh at the many who are more chaste than certain sinners and at the orators who are more eloquent than certain fishermen.

Do we not observe many of our faithful who walk in God’s way, yet in no respect match—not to mention certain heretics—even actors in intelligence? Again, do we not see certain men and women living in conjugal chastity without complaint, yet either heretics or pagans, or even people within the true faith and the true Church so lukewarm that we are amazed to see them surpassed by suddenly converted prostitutes and actors, not only in patience and temperance but also in faith, hope, and love?

It remains, then, that wills are chosen. Yet the will itself cannot be moved in any way unless something occurs that pleases and invites the mind; and it is not in human power for such a thing to occur.

What did Saul will except to attack, drag away, bind, and kill Christians? What a savage will, how furious and blind! Yet, struck down by a single voice from above, when such a vision occurred that his mind and will, their savagery broken, might be turned back and corrected toward faith, he suddenly became a preacher more remarkable than he had been a persecutor of the Gospel (Acts 8:3; 9:1).

And yet what shall we say? Is there injustice with God, who exacts from whomever he pleases and gives to whomever he pleases? He certainly does not exact what is not owed, nor does he give what belongs to another.

“Is there injustice with God? By no means.” Why, then, does he act in this way toward one person and not toward another?

“O man, who are you?” If you do not repay what is owed, you have reason to be grateful; if you repay it, you have no reason to complain.

Let us simply believe—even if we cannot comprehend—that the one who made and established the whole spiritual and bodily creation disposes all things “by number, weight, and measure” (Wis. 11:21). But “his judgments are unsearchable and his ways inscrutable” (Rom. 11:33).

Let us say “Alleluia” and praise the song, and let us not say, “Why this?” or “Why that?” For all things were created in their proper time (Ecclus. 39:19, 26).

## BOOK TWO

### On the five or six remaining questions proposed by Simplicianus from the Books of Kings

[Col. 0127]

## PREFACE

I think that I have now answered sufficiently the matters you proposed concerning the Apostle. I shall next undertake another volume concerning the matters you asked about from the Books of Kings. These matters, like many—indeed nearly all—of the ancient books, are more figurative and wrapped in veils of mysteries.

Although, because we have passed over to Christ, the veil is removed (2 Cor. 3:16), nevertheless “now we see in a riddle, but then face to face” [Note: The most ancient Corbie book reads “face to face,” in agreement with the Greek].

The veil wholly shuts off the view; but a riddle, as through a mirror, as the same Apostle says—“Now we see through a mirror and in a riddle” (1 Cor. 13:12)—neither uncovers the form with complete clarity nor entirely conceals the truth.

I shall therefore undertake these matters too, with the Lord as guide, lifted up more by your prayers than burdened by your commands [Note: The older books read “let us undertake,” and accordingly below use the plural “lifted up” and “burdened”]. Especially since, from your letter, I understood that you were not asking what these things signify prophetically [Note: The passage has been restored with the help of the old codices. In earlier editions, the negative particle was omitted here, so that a little later the text stood: “in which I would indeed comply, if it were not most difficult for me.”]—for it would truly be difficult for me to comply in that matter, since one would have to pursue the meaning of the entire connected sequence of these books, and even if understanding were more readily available, the magnitude of the work would still be an obstacle. [Note: At the foot of column 129, the callout letter (a) is not printed in the text. Possibly: “led,” or “carried forward.”] If this task must be undertaken, it demands more leisure, time, and length. For now, however, you have been pleased to learn from my letters how I understand the actual properties of the events that are signified by those words whose mention you made.

## FIRST QUESTION

### Prophets are affected by the Spirit of God in different ways. Prophecy as a permanent disposition and as a transitory affect. The Spirit of God, without qualification, is understood to be good. Whether the Spirit understood by this name is the Holy Spirit, consubstantial with the Father and the Son. How the Spirit of God in Saul is both good and evil. Saul, while pursuing David, overcome by a prophetic and good spirit. Certain gifts of the Holy Spirit possessed without love. Other gifts of the Holy Spirit are of no benefit without love. Whether prophecy exists without love. Heretics and schismatics possess gifts of the Holy Spirit other than love. Why the evil spirit is called the spirit of the Lord.

### 1

The first matter you ordered me to explain from the First Book of Kings concerns the statement, “The Spirit of the Lord rushed upon Saul,” while elsewhere it says, “An evil spirit from the Lord was upon Saul” (1 Kings 16:14).

It is written as follows:

“And when he turned his shoulder to go away from Samuel, God changed Saul’s heart into another heart, and all those signs came to pass that day. And from there he came to the hill, and behold, a company of prophets met him; and the Spirit of God rushed upon him, and he prophesied among them” (1 Kings 10:9–10).

Samuel had foretold these things to him when, by command, he anointed him.

I do not think this presents any difficulty. “The Spirit blows where he wills” (John 3:8), and no contact with souls can defile the spirit of prophecy. “Because of his purity he reaches everywhere” (Wis. 7:24).

He does not affect everyone in the same way. He affects some by forming the spirit of those same human beings, when images of things are shown to them; others by producing understanding in the mind; others by both kinds of inspiration; and still others without their knowing it.

The formation of the spirit occurs in two ways: either through a dream, as when not only many holy people but also Pharaoh and King Nebuchadnezzar saw what none of them could understand, although both were able to see it (Gen. 41; Dan. 2–4); or through a manifestation in ecstasy, which some Latins interpret as “stupor” [Note: Eight manuscripts read “fear”]. The term is strange if taken literally, but approximately correct, since it means an alienation of the mind from bodily senses, so that the human spirit, taken up by the divine Spirit, is free to receive and contemplate images.

Thus it was shown to Daniel what he did not understand, and to Peter the vessel lowered from heaven by its four corners [Note: The principal manuscripts read this way; the printed editions have “by four sheets of linen”] (Acts 10:11). Peter himself later learned what that vision signified.

The mind is affected toward understanding in one way: when what is shown through images is also revealed—what it signifies and to what it refers. This is the more certain prophecy; for the Apostle more properly calls this prophecy itself (1 Cor. 13:2). Thus Joseph was granted understanding of what Pharaoh could only see [Note: Lov. has “what Pharaoh could do nothing but see”; the other printed editions and the manuscripts omit “could,” since it is understood from “was granted”]; and Daniel explained to the king what the king saw but did not understand.

When the mind is affected in such a way that it does not understand images of things through conjectural examination but contemplates the things themselves—as wisdom, justice, and every unchangeable and divine form are understood—that does not belong to the prophecy now under discussion.

Those are endowed with both prophetic gifts who see images of things in the spirit and simultaneously understand their meaning, or who are instructed through clear verbal statements in the very course of the vision, as certain things are explained in the Apocalypse.

The spirit of prophecy also affects people without their knowing it, as when Caiaphas, being high priest, prophesied about the Lord that it was expedient for one man to die for the whole nation (John 11:49–50), while attending to something else in the words he spoke and not knowing that he was speaking not from himself.

Examples abound in the holy books, and I am speaking of matters well known to your prudence. You do not state these questions because you are learning them from me; rather, by questioning me about them, you test me—eager to recognize progress and ready to correct error.

The phrase “the Spirit rushed upon him” signifies a sudden inspiration proceeding, as it were, from the hidden secret of divinity.

By which of these modes, then, should we understand Saul to have been affected? It is sufficiently clear from what is written there: “God changed Saul’s heart into another heart.” By changing it, God made a different disposition of heart, capable of receiving images that signified and prefigured things, for prophetic divination [Note: The printed editions have “because”; the manuscripts have “which”].

### 2

There is as much difference between the prophecy of prophets such as Isaiah, Jeremiah, and others of this kind, and the transient prophecy that appeared in Saul, as there is between human speech when human beings speak and that same speech when, because of a necessary prodigy, the she-donkey on which the prophet Balaam was riding spoke (Num. 22:28).

That animal received this capacity for a time, so that God might reveal what he had determined, not so that a beast might speak continually among human beings.

Or, if this example is too remote because of the greater difference, it is still far less astonishing that a reprobate human being was given prophecy for a moment through a transient affect, since the one who gave it also made a donkey speak when he wished.

A beast differs from a human being more than a reprobate human being differs from the elect—though both are still human beings.

If someone says something pertaining to wisdom, he should not immediately be considered wise. Likewise, if someone prophesies on one occasion, he should not immediately be counted among the prophets, since the Lord also says in the Gospel that some receive the word with joy but have no depth of root and are temporary (Matt. 13:20–21).

Therefore, as the following reading indicates, it became a proverb: “Is Saul also among the prophets?” (1 Sam. 10:12) [Note: The manuscripts read this way; the printed editions have “So is Saul also among the prophets?”].

Let us therefore cease to wonder when something divine appears in human beings that exceeds either their merit or their habitual condition, whenever God happens, for the sake of conveying some meaning, to wish such a thing to be revealed.

### 3

But if it is troubling that afterward Saul was being choked when an evil spirit invaded him, although previously he had received the spirit of prophecy, this too is not surprising. The former event took place as part of a dispensation intended to signify something; the latter as a deserved punishment. Nor should these alternations in the human mind—that is, in a mutable creature—trouble us, especially at a time when corruptible and mortal flesh is being borne.

Do we not see in Peter himself, as the Gospel indicates, that there was once so great a confession in him that he deserved to hear, “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jona, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven”; and shortly afterward he thought so carnally about the Lord’s passion that he immediately heard, “Get behind me, Satan; you are a stumbling-block to me, for you do not understand the things of God, but those of men” (Matt. 16:17, 23)?

And perhaps [Note: [Col. 0131] In the very ancient Corbie manuscript: “and perhaps.”], for those who understand these things somewhat more deeply, this distinction between those visions of the mind has as much significance as follows: Peter first understood, through God the Father’s revelation, that Christ was the Son of God, and afterward feared that he should die; similarly, for distinguishing the visions that arise imaginatively in the human spirit when the mind is estranged, it is significant that Saul was first inspired by the revelation of prophecy and afterward oppressed by the mingling of an evil spirit.

### 4

Now as for the fact that the evil spirit was also called “the spirit of the Lord,” this is understood in the same way as it is said, “The earth is the Lord’s” (Ps. 23:1), as a creature placed under his power.

Or, if this example of speech does not fit because the earth is not evil—for every creature of God is good (1 Tim. 4:4)—let the following example fit instead: Saul himself, already rejected, wicked, and ungrateful toward holy David, and even his persecutor, though driven by the flames of the fiercest envy, was nevertheless still called “the Lord’s anointed,” as David himself called him when he avenged his death (2 Sam. 1:14–15).

But I rather think that the evil spirit by which Saul was tormented was therefore called “the spirit of the Lord” because, by the Lord’s hidden judgment, it tormented Saul. For God uses even evil spirits [Note: [Col. 0131] Several manuscripts read “unclean spirits.”] as ministers, either to punish the wicked or to test the good—one way for the former purpose, another for the latter.

Although each evil spirit [Note: [Col. 0131] Louvain reads, “the spirit of the Lord.” “Of the Lord” is absent from Erasmus and the manuscripts.] is evil because it desires to do harm by an evil will, it does not receive the power to harm except from him under whom all things have been ordered by fixed and just degrees of merit. For just as an evil will is not from God, so power is not except from God (Rom. 13:1).

Although each person has it in his power what he wills, it is not therefore in each person’s power what he can either do to another or suffer from another. Even the only-begotten Son of God, when he was to suffer, said humbly to a proud man who was speaking to him and claiming that he had power to kill or release him, “You would have no power over me unless it had been given you from above” (John 19:11).

The devil too, wishing to harm the righteous man Job, had the will to harm him, but nevertheless asked power from the Lord, saying, “Stretch out your hand and touch his flesh” (Job 2:5), although, if permitted, he would have done this himself. In this way he was asking for that permission, and he called “the hand of the Lord” the hand that the Lord had permitted him to use—that is, the very power he wished to receive.

This corresponds to what the Lord says to his disciples in the Gospel: “This night Satan asked to sift you like wheat” (Luke 22:31).

The spirit was therefore called an evil spirit of God—that is, God’s minister for doing to Saul [Note: [Col. 0132] The printed editions read, “for doing evil to Saul.” The word “evil” is absent from the manuscripts.] what the all-powerful Judge judged that Saul should suffer. For in the will by which that spirit was evil, it was not God’s; but as a creature created by God, and in the power that it had received not from itself but from the Lord of all, according to his equity, it was God’s.

The very words of Scripture also read as follows:

> “And Samuel went and departed to Ramah; and the spirit of the Lord departed from Saul, and an evil spirit from the Lord seized him and suffocated him. And Saul’s servants said to him: ‘Behold, an evil spirit of the Lord is suffocating you’” (1 Sam. 16:13–15) [Note: [Col. 0132] The Vatican manuscripts read, “an evil spirit from the Lord.”].

How, then, the servants called it “an evil spirit of the Lord” is shown by the preceding words of the narrative Scripture, which says, “an evil spirit from the Lord.” It was according to this—that it was from the Lord—that it was called the Lord’s spirit [Note: [Col. 0132] The printed editions read, “According to this, then, he says, from the Lord.” The reading has been corrected from the manuscripts.]. For by itself it had the will to do harm—that is, to seize Saul—but it did not have the power unless supreme justice permitted it.

For if God justly punishes, as the Apostle himself says when he speaks of God handing people over to the desires of their hearts (Rom. 1:24), it is not surprising that, while justly punishing, he also hands them over to the desires of others who wish to do harm, always preserving his own unchangeable equity.

### 5

It should certainly be observed that the expression “evil spirit of God” is used with an additional qualification. When only “spirit of God” is said, even if “good” is not added, it is understood from this alone to be good. Hence it appears that a spirit is called God’s spirit according to its substance when it is good, but according to its ministry when it is evil.

Nevertheless, it may still be asked whether, when “spirit of God” is said, and from this alone it is already understood to be good even if nothing is added, the reference is to the Spirit who is consubstantial with the Father and the Son in the Trinity—the Holy Spirit, of whom it is said, “Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom” (2 Cor. 3:17)—and again, “God has revealed them to us through his Spirit”; and, “So also no one knows the things of God except the Spirit of God” (1 Cor. 2:10–11).

In many passages the Spirit of God is spoken of in this way, and the Holy Spirit is understood even when nothing is added, because the surrounding context sufficiently indicates whom it means. Sometimes even “of God” is not added, and yet that Spirit is understood, principally and preeminently holy.

For whom else does he mention when he says, “The Spirit himself bears witness to our spirit that we are children of God”; and, “The Spirit himself helps our weakness” (Rom. 8:16, 26); and, “All these things one and the same Spirit accomplishes, distributing to each one individually as he wills”; and, “There are distributions of gifts, but it is the same Spirit” (1 Cor. 12:11, 4)?

In all these statements neither “of God” nor “holy” is added, yet he himself is understood. But I do not know whether any clear example can be produced in which the spirit of God is mentioned without qualification and does not signify the Holy Spirit, but some other spirit, created and made, though good.

The examples commonly advanced are uncertain and require clearer proof, such as what is written: “The Spirit of God was hovering over the water” (Gen. 1:2) [Note: [Col. 0133] This is how the manuscripts read, in accordance with the Greek Septuagint. The printed editions read, “was borne over the waters.”].

For I do not see what prevents us from understanding the Holy Spirit there also. Since by the name “waters” that formless matter is indicated [Note: [Col. 0133] The Corbie and Vatican manuscripts read “was being indicated as formless.”] which was made from nothing, so that all things might be made from it, what prevents us from understanding the Holy Spirit of the Creator as hovering over this matter—not by stages of place and intervals of space, which cannot rightly be said of anything incorporeal, but by the excellence and eminence of the will that rules over all things, so that all things might be created?

This is especially so because that expression, in keeping with the custom of those Scriptures, also sounds somewhat prophetic and prefigures the mystery of the people who were to be born through the future Baptism from water and the Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 0133] This is how the manuscripts read. The printed editions instead read, “which prefigured the mystery whereby the people who were to be born from water and the Holy Spirit might be prefigured.”].

Thus the statement, “The Spirit of God was hovering over the water,” does not compel us to understand the spirit, as some wish, by which the entire bodily mass of the world is supposedly animated, for the service of all things that generate and the preservation in their form of bodily creatures. For anything of this kind is a creature.

There are also those who wish the same spirit to be understood in what is written: “For the Spirit of the Lord has filled the world” (Wis. 1:7)—namely, an invisible creature that gives life to and sustains all visible things through a kind of universal cooperation.

But here too I see nothing that prevents us from understanding the Holy Spirit, since God himself says through the prophet, “I fill heaven and earth” (Jer. 23:24). God does not fill heaven and earth without his Holy Spirit. What wonder, then, if it is said of his Holy Spirit, “He has filled the world”?

He fills in one way by sanctifying, as it is said of Stephen, “He was filled with the Holy Spirit” (Acts 6:5; 7:55), and of other such persons; in another way he fills with sanctifying grace [Note: [Col. 0133] This is how the manuscripts read. The printed editions read, “but he fills in another way with sanctifying grace.”], as he does certain holy people; and in yet another way by his attesting and ordering presence [Note: [Col. 0133] Six manuscripts read “foreknowledge” instead of “presence.”], as he does all things.

Therefore I do not know whether Scripture can establish by any definite proof that, when “the spirit of God” or “the spirit of the Lord” is said without any qualification, something other than the Holy Spirit is meant [Col. 0134]. But even if there is some example that does not presently occur to me, I certainly think this can safely be said: whenever the spirit of God is mentioned in the sacred utterances and nothing is added, whether the consubstantial Spirit, the Holy Spirit, who is with the Father and the Son, is understood, or some invisible creature is meant, it cannot be understood as evil unless “evil” is also added.

For because God makes good use of an evil spirit for the ministry of his judgment, it too is called God’s spirit, for the punishment of the wicked and the discipline or testing of the good.

### 6

Nor should it now trouble us that it is afterward written that Saul prophesied when the spirit of God came upon him—how, after the good spirit, there was an evil spirit, and again, after the evil spirit, a good one.

This does not happen through any mutability of the Holy Spirit, who is unchangeable with the Father and the Son, but through the mutability of the human mind, with God distributing all things either to the wicked according to the merit of their condemnation or correction, or to the good according to the generosity of his grace.

It might also appear that God’s spirit had always been the same in Saul, while it was evil to him because he was not capable of its holiness [Note: [Col. 0134] The older books read “holy”; perhaps this is a corruption of “of the holy one.”]. But this does not seem correct.

The safer and truer understanding is that, in accordance with the mutability of human affection, God’s good Spirit affects a person beneficially, whether for prophecy or for any other work belonging to the divine ministry; but the evil spirit affects him harmfully. Because of its ministry within God’s righteousness, by which he distributes all things and uses all things rightly, that spirit too is called God’s spirit.

This is especially so because it is said, “The Spirit of God departed from him, and an evil spirit from the Lord seized him.” For it cannot in any way be understood that the same spirit both departed and seized him.

Moreover, in some copies, especially those that appear to have been translated word for word from the Hebrew language, “Spirit of God” is found without qualification, and it is understood as evil from the fact that it seized Saul, while David restored him by playing the harp.

Yet it is clear that “evil” was not added because it had already been said shortly before and could be supplied and understood from the proximity of the Scripture. For in such copies the passage reads:

> “Therefore, whenever the spirit of the Lord seized Saul, David took the harp and played it with his hand, and Saul was refreshed and felt better; for the evil spirit departed from him.”

Thus, either because what is not said here—“the spirit of God”—but only “the evil spirit” appears to have been supplied in return for what had been omitted there, or because the earlier passage had read as follows:

> “And Saul’s servants said to him: ‘Behold, an evil spirit of God is troubling you. Let our lord command, and your servants who are before you will seek out a man skilled in playing the harp, so that when the evil spirit of God seizes you, he may play with his hand and you may feel better’” (1 Sam. 16:23, 15–16),

there was no need, when it was said again, “whenever the spirit of God seized Saul,” to add “evil,” because it was known which spirit was meant.

### 7

Nevertheless, the greater question is this, and it must not be examined with passing attention: when Saul was persecuting the innocent David, mad with envy and resentment, “the Spirit of God came upon him, and he went along as he entered, and prophesied.”

Here the spirit can only be understood as good, through which the holy Prophets saw images and visions of future things—not merely because it is said, “and he prophesied.” For in copies derived from the Hebrew this too is found said of the evil spirit:

> “On the following day, an evil spirit of God invaded Saul, and he prophesied in the midst of his house” (1 Sam. 18:10).

In other places of the divine Scriptures prophecy is often found to be spoken not only of good but also of evil; and the prophets were called Baals (1 Kings 18:19, 22, 25, 40); and certain people are reproached because they prophesied in Baal (Jer. 2:8).

It is therefore not necessary to understand the spirit that afterward came upon Saul as good merely because it is said, “he went along as he entered, and prophesied.” Rather, it is because the statement, “the Spirit of God also came upon him,” is made without qualification.

For it is not said here, as it had been said in the earlier passage, “an evil spirit of God,” so that the qualification might be supplied in what follows. On the contrary, the preceding circumstances testify more and more clearly that this was a good and genuinely prophetic spirit.

David was with Samuel, and Saul sent messengers to seize David. When Samuel was among the prophets and the company of prophets who were prophesying at that time, the messengers who had been sent, after receiving the same spirit, prophesied. The same thing happened when others were sent, and likewise when a third group was sent.

Afterward, when Saul himself had come, the Spirit of God also came upon him, and he went along as he entered, and prophesied. For when it is said, “The Spirit of God also came upon them, and they too prophesied,” it was clearly the same spirit that was in the prophets, among whom Samuel was found (1 Sam. 19:20–23). From this, therefore, it is necessary to understand that spirit as good.

Consequently, the question must be carefully examined: how did those men, when they had been sent to seize a man and bring him to his death, deserve to be affected by such a spirit? And how did Saul himself, who had sent them, when he came and was seeking to shed innocent blood, deserve to receive that spirit and prophesy?

### 8

Here surely what the Apostle Paul explains most clearly comes to mind, when he points out the way that surpasses all others:

> “If I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, but do not have love, I have become like sounding bronze or a clanging cymbal. And if I have prophecy [Note: [Col. 0135] The edition of Louvain reads, “and if I have all prophecy.” “All” is absent from the other editions and the manuscripts.], and know all mysteries and all knowledge, and if I have all faith, so that I move mountains, but do not have love, I am nothing. And if I distribute all my possessions, and if I hand over my body so that I may burn, but do not have love, it profits me nothing.”

Here it is clear that he mentioned those gifts that are given through the distributions of the Holy Spirit, as he says earlier:

> “To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good. To one, through the Spirit, is given the word of wisdom; to another, the word of knowledge according to the same Spirit; to another, faith in the same Spirit; to another, gifts of healings in one Spirit; to another, the working of miracles; to another, prophecy; to another, the discernment of spirits; to another, kinds of tongues. But one and the same Spirit works all these things, distributing to each individually as he wills [Note: [Col. 0133] The very ancient Corbie manuscript reads “to each one,” which corresponds more fully to the Greek *idia hekastō*; Augustine sometimes has “what is proper to each one.” So below, §7.].”

It is therefore sufficiently clear that prophecy is among the gifts of the Holy Spirit. Yet if someone possesses it and does not have love, he is nothing.

From this it is understood that some people who are unworthy of eternal life and the kingdom of heaven can nevertheless be sprinkled with certain gifts of the Holy Spirit, while lacking love, without which those gifts are not merely insignificant but profit them nothing.

For prophecy without love, as has already been shown, does not lead to the kingdom of God; but love without prophecy certainly does lead there. When he speaks of the members of Christ and says, “Are all apostles? Are all prophets?” he undoubtedly shows that someone who does not have prophecy can nevertheless be numbered among the members of Christ. What place would such a person have there if he did not have love, without which a human being is nothing?

He would in no way have spoken in this manner when discussing the members by which Christ’s body is completed: “Do all have love?” Instead he said, “Are all apostles? Are all prophets? Are all workers of miracles? Do all possess gifts of healing?” (1 Cor. 12:7–11, 29; 13:3), and other statements of this kind.

### 9

Someone may say that it can indeed happen that a person does not have prophecy and nevertheless has love, and so is counted among and remains attached to Christ’s members; but that it cannot happen that someone has prophecy and does not have love, since a person who has prophecy without love is nothing.

Perhaps this is like saying that a human being who has a soul without a mind is nothing—not because a person with a soul but without a mind can be found, but because, if such a person could be found, he would be nothing.

Similarly, one might say, “If a body had shape but no color, it could not be seen”—not because there is a body without color, but because, if there were one, it could not be seen.

In the same way, perhaps it was said that if someone has prophecy but does not have love, he is nothing—not because prophecy can exist in anyone without love, but because, if it did exist, it could be of no benefit.

To resolve this question, then, we must show that some reprobate person possessed the gift of prophecy. If we found no such person, this very Saul would sufficiently demonstrate it.

But Balaam too appears to have been reprobate; Scripture does not conceal that he was condemned by divine judgment. Yet he possessed prophecy. And because he lacked love, he had the will to curse the people of Israel—a will that the enemy had purchased by a price, hiring him for a fee to pronounce the curse. Yet, through the prophetic gift with which he had been endowed, he blessed them unwillingly (Num. 22–24).

The words written in the Gospel also strongly support this view. It says that many will say on that day:

> “Lord, Lord, in your name we ate and drank” [Note: [Col. 0136] The printed editions read, “we ate before you.” The manuscripts read, “in your name we ate,” as Augustine later does in *On Catechizing the Uninstructed*, chapter 16, and often elsewhere.], “and in your name we prophesied, and in your name we performed many miracles” [Col. 0137].

Yet he will say to them:

> “I do not know you; depart from me, workers of iniquity” (Matt. 7:22–23).

We do not suppose that they will be lying when they say these things at that judgment, where there will be no opportunity for deception. Nor do we read that any such people will say, “We loved you.”

They will therefore be able to say, “In your name we prophesied,” even though they are wicked and reprobate; but they will not be able to say, “We maintained the love that you commanded.” For if they say this [Note: [Col. 0137] “They say,” according to Erasmus’s manuscript.], the answer will not be, “I do not know you.”

“For by this,” he says, “it will be known that you are my disciples, if you love one another” (John 13:35).

### 10

This example of Saul therefore stands against certain proud heretics who deny that anything good from the gifts of the Holy Spirit can be given to those who do not belong to the lot of the saints.

We tell them that such people can possess the sacrament of Baptism, and that when they come to the Catholic Church it must in no way be violated in them or administered to them as though they did not possess it. Nevertheless, they should not therefore trust in their salvation because we do not reject what we grant that they have received.

Rather, they must recognize that the fellowship of unity is to be entered through the bond of love. Without love, whatever they may be able to possess—although holy and venerable in itself—makes them nothing. They become all the more unworthy of the reward of eternal life the more poorly they have used the gifts they received in this transitory life [Note: [Col. 0137] Most manuscripts read, “which is to pass away.”].

No one uses them rightly except through love. “Love endures all things” (1 Cor. 13:7), and therefore it does not divide unity, of which it is the strongest bond.

That servant too received a talent—or what else is the talent to be understood as except some divine gift? Yet it is said, “To everyone who has, more will be given; but from the one who does not have, even what he has will be taken away” (Matt. 25:29).

What he does not have cannot be taken away. Rather, he lacks something else, so that what he has may deservedly be taken away: he lacks the love by which he might use it, and therefore whatever else he possesses, which without love is of no benefit, is taken away.

### 11

It is therefore not surprising that King Saul received the spirit of prophecy when he was first anointed, and afterward, when he had been rejected because of his disobedience and the spirit of the Lord had departed from him, was seized by an evil spirit from the Lord.

That spirit too was called the spirit of the Lord because of its ministry, since the Lord makes good use even of evil spirits, either for the condemnation of some, or for their correction, or for their testing. Although wickedness is not from the Lord, power nevertheless comes only from God (Rom. 13:1).

The sleep of the Lord was also mentioned—the sleep that had overcome Saul’s soldiers when David removed the spear and cup from beside the head of the sleeping man (1 Sam. 26:12). This was not because the sleep was then in the Lord, as though he himself were sleeping, but because the sleep that had seized those men had been infused by God’s command, so that the presence of David his servant [Note: [Col. 0137] The printed editions read, “so that the presence of David and his servants might not be perceived.” The manuscripts read, “so that the presence of David his servant might not be perceived.” Perhaps the reading should be, “so that the presence of David and his servants might not be perceived,” namely, Abishai, who had gone down with David to Saul’s camp, as related in 1 Samuel 26:6.] would not be noticed in that place.

Nor is it surprising that Saul again received the spirit of prophecy when he was persecuting the righteous man and came to the place where the company of prophets was gathered, intending to seize him and put him to death.

For it has been sufficiently demonstrated that no one should now feel secure because of such a gift, as though he were especially pleasing to God, if he does not have love. That gift could be given to Saul because of the hidden purpose of some sacrament; yet it could still be given to one who had been rejected, envious, ungrateful, repaying good with evil, and not corrected or changed for the better even after receiving the spirit.

## Question II — Nothing Worthy Is Said of God

Whether Foreknowledge Properly Exists in God; What Knowledge Is and How It Exists in God; In What Sense God’s Anger, Mercy, and Jealousy Are Spoken Of; Human Terms Are Applied to Divine Matters but Must Be Understood There with Their Imperfections Removed; How Wisdom and Knowledge Differ; How Repentance Is Appropriate to God; Why Repentance and Jealousy Seem Less Suitable to God than Foreknowledge, Anger, and Similar Terms

### 1

Come, let us now see how the statement was made, “I repent that I made Saul king” (1 Sam. 15:11).

You are asking—not, of course, as someone untrained in understanding such words, but as one investigating my rudiments with a father’s diligence and kindly care—how God can repent of anything when all foreknowledge is in him.

For my part, when this is said of God, I would consider something unworthy to have been said if anything worthy could be found that was said of him. But since his eternal power and divinity wonderfully and unquestionably surpass all the words with which human conversations are conducted [Note: [Col. 0138] This is how the manuscripts read. The printed editions instead read “with which human conversations are conveyed”; below, where the manuscripts have *humanly*, the editions had *humanitus* (“in a human manner”).], whatever is said of him in human terms—even something that might appear contemptible to human beings—reminds human weakness that even those things it rightly considers to have been said of God in the sacred Scriptures are more suited to human capacity than to divine sublimity.

Accordingly, these expressions too must be transcended by a more serene understanding [Note: [Col. 0138] The printed editions read “sounder,” for which the manuscripts have “more serene,”] just as they have been transcended in whatever way was possible here.

### 2

Who is there among human beings to whom it would not occur that repentance cannot exist in God, who foreknows all things?

And yet these are two words: “repentance” and “foreknowledge.” Because we believe that one of them—foreknowledge—fits God, we deny that repentance exists in him.

But when someone else, examining the matter with clearer consideration, asks how foreknowledge itself can fit God, and discovers that even the meaning of this word is surpassed far and wide by God’s ineffable divinity, he is not surprised that both terms could be said of God for the sake of human beings, although neither could appropriately be said of him for his own sake.

For what is foreknowledge except knowledge of future things? But what is future for God, who transcends all times?

If God’s knowledge possesses the things themselves [Note: [Col. 0138] This is how the manuscripts read, except for one Vatican manuscript, which, in agreement with the earlier printed editions, reads, “if in knowledge God possesses the things themselves,”], they are not future for him but present. Consequently, it can no longer be called foreknowledge, but only knowledge.

But if, as in the order of temporal creatures, things that are future are not yet present with him, and he anticipates them by knowing them, then he experiences them twice: once according to foreknowledge of future things, and again according to knowledge of things that are present.

Something temporal would therefore be added to God’s knowledge [Note: [Col. 0139] The manuscripts read, “something temporal occurs to God’s knowledge.” Below they likewise have *occurs* and *will occur*, instead of *is added* and *will be added*.], which is utterly absurd and false.

For he cannot know what he foreknows will come to pass when it comes to pass unless it becomes known twice: first by foreknowing it before it exists, and then by knowing it when it already exists.

Thus it would follow—something far removed from the truth—that something temporal is added to God’s knowledge, since temporal things that are foreknown are also experienced as present, although they were not experienced before they came to be but only foreknown.

But if, when the things that were foreknown to come to pass have come to pass, nothing new is added to God’s knowledge, and that foreknowledge remains as it was even before the foreknown things came to be, how will it still be called foreknowledge when the things are no longer future?

They are now present, whereas shortly afterward they will be past. But knowledge of past things, just as of present things, cannot in any way be called foreknowledge.

We are therefore brought back to the conclusion that what was foreknowledge becomes knowledge of things that are already present. And when what was foreknowledge in God afterward becomes knowledge, it admits mutability and is temporal.

Yet God truly and supremely is neither mutable in any respect nor temporal through any novel movement.

It is therefore preferable not to speak of God’s foreknowledge, but only of his knowledge. Let us ask how this too can be understood.

For we do not usually speak of knowledge in ourselves except when we retain in memory what we have sensed and understood, when we remember that we sensed or understood something so that we may recall it whenever we wish.

If this is so in God, so that we can properly say, “He understands” and “He understood,” “He senses” and “He sensed,” then time is admitted, and that mutability also insinuates itself which must be removed far from God’s substance.

And yet God both knows and foreknows in an ineffable manner; in the same ineffable manner he also repents.

For God’s knowledge is so far removed from human knowledge that any comparison is ridiculous, yet both are called knowledge. Human knowledge is such that the Apostle even says of it, “Knowledge will be destroyed” (1 Cor. 13:8); but this cannot rightly be said of God’s knowledge.

Human anger is likewise turbulent and not without anguish of mind. But God’s anger, of which it is said in the Gospel, “But the wrath of God remains upon him” (John 3:36), and of which the Apostle says, “For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness” (Rom. 1:18), exercises punishment with marvelous equity in a creature subject to him, while he himself continually remains in tranquility.

Human mercy too contains a certain misery of the heart, from which it received its name even in the Latin language. Hence the Apostle urges us not only to rejoice with those who rejoice but also to weep with those who weep (Rom. 12:15).

But who in his right mind would say that God is touched by any misery? Yet Scripture everywhere bears witness that he is merciful.

In the same way, we understand human jealousy as never free from the infection of envy; but God’s jealousy is not so. The same word is used, but not in the same manner.

### 3

It would take too long to go through the rest, and there are innumerable examples showing that many divine realities are called by the same names as human realities, although they are separated from them by an incomparable difference.

The same terms are not nevertheless imposed on both kinds of things without reason. Rather, the things known to us, which are part of daily usage and become familiar through ordinary experience, provide some path toward understanding those lofty realities.

When I remove from human knowledge its mutability and its transitions from one thought to another—when we recall something so that we may behold mentally what had not been present to our contemplation a moment earlier, and thus leap repeatedly from one part to another through acts of recollection, which is why the Apostle says that our knowledge is partial (1 Cor. 13:9)—when I remove all these things and leave only the vitality of certain and unshaken truth, which surveys all things in one eternal contemplation [Note: [Col. 0140] This is how the principal manuscripts read. The printed editions read “which illuminates all things.”], or rather, when I do not leave it, since human knowledge does not possess this, but conceive of it according to my ability, God’s knowledge is somehow suggested to me.

Yet this name could be common to both things because, through knowing, something is not hidden from a human being.

Nevertheless, even among human beings knowledge is usually distinguished from wisdom, as the Apostle says: “To one is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom, and to another the word of knowledge according to the same Spirit” (1 Cor. 12:8).

In God, however, these are surely not two things but one.

Among human beings, the distinction is commonly made, and plausibly so, in such a way that wisdom concerns the understanding of eternal things, while knowledge concerns the things we experience through the bodily senses.

But even if someone proposes another distinction, unless they were different they would not be distinguished by the Apostle in this way.

Now if the name “knowledge” has been assigned to things that we experience through the bodily senses, then God has no knowledge at all. For God does not consist of body and soul, as a human being does.

It is better to say that God has a different kind of knowledge, not of the same kind as that called human knowledge—just as God, who is called God, is something altogether different from the one referred to when it is said that he “stood in the assembly of the gods” (Ps. 81:1).

Nevertheless, the very sharing of the word has to do in some way with the fact that something is not hidden.

In the same way, from human anger I remove turbulent movement, so that the strength of punishment remains; thus I rise, as best I can, toward some knowledge of what is called God’s anger.

Likewise, if from mercy you remove compassion—the sharing of misery with the one whom you pity [Note: [Col. 0140] The printed editions read corruptly, “when you have shared in the misery of the one whom you pity”; the manuscripts make the correct construction clear.]—so that the tranquil goodness of helping and freeing from misery remains, some sort of knowledge of divine mercy is suggested.

Nor should we reject or disdain God’s jealousy when we find it written [Col. 0141] [Note: [Col. 0141] This is how Erasmus and our manuscripts read. Louvain reads “when we shall find it written.”].

Rather, let us remove from human jealousy the pallid wasting sickness of grief and the diseased agitation of the mind. Let only that judgment remain by which corruption of chastity is not permitted to go unpunished, and let us rise so that we may begin in some way to grasp God’s jealousy.

### 4

Therefore, when we read that God too says, “I repent,” let us consider what the work of repentance ordinarily is among human beings.

Without doubt, a will to change is found [Note: [Col. 0141] The printed editions read: “Let us consider what the work of repentance ordinarily is. In human beings the work of repentance occurs when, without doubt, a will to change is found.”]. But in a human being this occurs with anguish of mind, for he reproaches himself for having acted rashly.

Let us therefore remove those elements that arise from human weakness and ignorance, and let only the desire that something not be as it was remain. In this way it can be suggested somewhat to our minds by what principle we are to understand God’s repentance.

For when God is said to repent, he wills that something not be as he had made it to be. Yet while it was so, it ought to have been so; and when it is no longer permitted to be so, it ought no longer to be so, by a certain perpetual and tranquil judgment of equity by which God orders all mutable things with an immutable will.

5. But since we are accustomed to speaking of foreknowledge and knowledge with praise when referring to human beings, and the human race usually fears anger itself in powerful persons [Note: [Col. 0141] Manuscripts: “tremble.”] rather than criticizing it, we think it appropriate that such things be said of God. But jealousy, and repentance over something, are usually either subject to blame or involve correcting a fault in oneself; and therefore such expressions are used of human beings with criticism. For this reason it is disturbing when we read that something of this kind exists in God. Yet Scripture, consulting the interests of all, includes these expressions for precisely this reason: so that those which please us may not be understood in God in the way they are customarily understood in human beings. For through those things which displease us, when we dare not understand them in God as they are found in human beings, we also learn to seek those other things in a manner that we had thought fitting and appropriate. For if it is not permissible to say that of God because it is displeasing in a human being, then let us not call God unchangeable, because it was said of human beings with reproof, “For there is no change in them” (Ps. 55:20).

Likewise, there are some things praiseworthy in a human being that cannot exist in God: such as modesty, which is a great adornment of youthful ages; and the fear of God—for it is praised not only in the ancient Books, but the Apostle also says, “Perfecting holiness in the fear of God” (2 Cor. 7:1)—which certainly does not exist in God. Therefore, just as certain things praiseworthy in human beings are not rightly said of God, so certain things blameworthy in human beings are rightly understood of God—not in the same way as in human beings, but only through terms common to both, with a wholly different reason and manner.

For a little later that same Samuel, to whom the Lord had said, “It repents me that I made Saul king,” says to Saul concerning God, “For he is not as a human being, that he should repent” (1 Sam. 15:29). There he clearly shows that even when God says, “It repents me,” this is not to be understood in the human manner, as we have already discussed as far as we have been able.

## QUESTION III.—How Samuel could be summoned through the medium. Perhaps it was Samuel’s apparition, not his spirit. How demons know the future.

1. You also ask whether the unclean spirit that was in the medium could have acted so that Samuel would appear to Saul and speak with him (1 Sam. 28:7–19). But it is a much greater miracle that Satan himself, the prince of all unclean spirits, was able to speak with God and ask that the most righteous man Job be put to the test (Job 1:11); he also asked that the Apostles be tested (Luke 22:31).

Or, if this does not pose a difficult question because, through whatever creature he chooses, the universal Truth speaks to whatever creature he chooses, wherever it may be—and because it is not therefore a sign of great merit in the one to whom God speaks, since what he says is what matters—for an emperor does not speak to many innocent persons whom he most providentially assists toward salvation, while he speaks to many guilty persons whom he orders to be killed—if, then, there is no question on that account, let there be no question about how an unclean spirit could also have spoken with the soul of a holy man. For God, the Creator and Sanctifier, is certainly far greater than all the saints.

But if it is troubling that an evil spirit was permitted to raise the soul of a righteous man and, as it were, summon it from the hidden dwellings of the dead [Note: [Col. 0142] The printed editions have “recall”; but the manuscripts have “summon,” and so does the book addressed to Dulcitius.], is it not more astonishing that Satan himself took up the Lord and set him upon the pinnacle of the Temple (Matt. 4:5)? Whatever the manner in which he did it, that manner too—by which Samuel was raised—remains hidden.

Unless perhaps someone should say that the devil had an easier permission to take up the living Lord from wherever he wished and set him wherever he wished than to raise the spirit of the dead Samuel from its abode. But if that Gospel event does not disturb us because the Lord wished and permitted it to happen without any diminishment of his power and divinity—just as he allowed himself, at the hands of the Jews, although they were perverse and unclean and were doing the works of the devil, to be seized, bound, mocked, crucified, and killed—then it is not absurd to believe that, through some dispensation of the divine will, it was permitted that the spirit of the holy Prophet should consent to appear before the king, not unwillingly or under the domination and subjugation of magical power, but willingly and obediently to God’s hidden dispensation, which was concealed both from that medium and from Saul, in order to strike him with the divine sentence.

For why should the soul of a good man, if summoned by evil living persons and if it comes, appear to lose its dignity, when good living persons are often summoned to the presence of evil people and conduct themselves toward them as the duty of justice requires, preserving and maintaining undiminished the dignity of their virtue, while dealing with the vices of those people according to the use or necessity of present circumstances?

2. Yet there may be another, easier and more straightforward solution in this matter: that we should not believe Samuel’s spirit itself to have been raised from its rest, but rather some apparition and imaginary illusion produced by the devil’s machinations. Scripture calls it by the name “Samuel” for the same reason that images are commonly called by the names of the things whose images they are.

Thus everything painted or fashioned from some material—metal, wood, or any other substance suited to such works—and everything seen in dreams, and nearly all images, are customarily called by the names of the things whose images they are. Who, after all, would hesitate to call a painted human being a human being? Indeed, when we look at paintings of particular persons, we readily apply their proper names—for example, when looking at a panel or wall we say, “That is Cicero; that is Sallust; that is Achilles; that is Hector; this is the river Simois; that is Rome”—although they are nothing other than painted images.

Hence, although the Cherubim are heavenly powers, the figures fashioned from metal at God’s command above the Ark of the Covenant, to signify a great reality, are nevertheless also called “Cherubim” (Exod. 25:18) [Note: [Col. 0143] The Corbie manuscript reads: “Although the Cherubim are heavenly powers, nevertheless fashioned …,” etc. The printed editions read “fashioned” in the feminine plural; in them, shortly afterward, one also finds “those figures of the Cherubim,” whereas the manuscripts and the book addressed to Dulcitius have “that figure,” or “that image.”].

Likewise, whoever sees a dream does not say, “I saw an image of Augustine or Simplicianus,” but “I saw Augustine or Simplicianus,” even though at the time when that person saw such a thing we would have no knowledge of it. So evident is it that not the people themselves, but their images, are being seen. Pharaoh too said that he saw ears of grain and cattle in a dream (Gen. 41:17–28), not images of ears of grain or cattle.

Therefore, if it is clearly established that images are themselves called by the names of the things whose images they are, it is not surprising that Scripture says Samuel was seen, even if perhaps an image of Samuel appeared through the contrivance of him who transforms himself into an angel of light and his ministers into ministers of righteousness (2 Cor. 11:14–15).

3. Now, if it is troubling how true predictions were also made to Saul by an evil spirit, it may likewise seem strange how the demons recognized Christ (Matt. 8:29), whom the Jews did not recognize. When God wishes someone to learn even through the lowest and infernal spirits certain truths—only temporal truths, that is, matters pertaining to this mortality—it is easy and not incongruous for the omnipotent and just God, for the punishment of those to whom these things are foretold, so that they may suffer in advance by foreknowing the evil that threatens them before it comes, to impart some power of divination even to such spirits through the hidden arrangement of his ministers [Note: [Col. 0143] The printed editions have “mysteries”; the better manuscripts have “ministers.” Augustine sometimes uses this term for angels.], so that they may foretell to human beings what they hear from angels.

Yet they hear only as much as the Lord and Ruler of all either commands or permits. Thus the pythonic spirit [Note: [Col. 0143] The printed editions have “pythonian”; the manuscripts have “pythonic,” or “of the pythoness.”] in the Acts of the Apostles bears witness to the Apostle Paul and attempts to act as an evangelist (Acts 16:17).

These spirits nevertheless mix deceptions into their predictions, and they foretell the truth they have been able to learn with the aim not so much of instructing as of deceiving. Perhaps this is what happened when that image of Samuel foretold to Saul that he would die and also said that he would be with him. That statement is certainly false.
