For we read in the Gospel that the good are separated from the wicked by a great interval after death, when the Lord testifies that a great chasm had been fixed between that proud rich man, who was already suffering torments in the underworld, and the man who had lain ulcerated at his gate and had already been placed in rest (Luke 16:26).

Or, if Samuel said to Saul, “You will be with me,” in order to refer not to equality of blessedness but to an equal condition of death—because both were human beings, both could die, and the dead man was foretelling death to the living—your prudence, I think, perceives that under either interpretation this passage has a meaning that does not conflict with the faith.

Unless perhaps, through a deeper and more intricate inquiry—one that exceeds the limits either of my abilities or of the time available—it should be discovered clearly whether or not a human soul, after departing this life, can be summoned by magical incantations to appear before the eyes of the living, even bearing the features of the body, so that it can not only be seen but recognized. And if this is possible, whether even the soul of a righteous person might not indeed be compelled by magical rites, but might deign to appear in obedience to the more hidden commands of the supreme law.

If it should become clear that this cannot happen, then both interpretations should not be admitted in the treatment and exposition of this Scripture; rather, with the one excluded, the imaginary imitation of Samuel, produced by a diabolical rite, should be understood. But since, whether this can happen or cannot, Satan’s deception and his cunning activity in fabricating apparitions nevertheless watch in many forms for the purpose of deceiving human senses, let us proceed cautiously—not wishing to impose a limit on more careful investigations—but nevertheless judge that something of this kind was done through the evil service of that medium, so long as we are not granted the ability to devise and explain anything further [Note: [Col. 0144] The particle “not” is restored here from the manuscripts. Compare the book on the Eight Questions of Dulcitius, at the end of Question 6.].

## QUESTION IV.—In what bodily posture one should pray.

As for your question about the meaning of what is written, “King David entered and sat before the Lord” (2 Sam. 7:18): what else should be understood except that he sat in the presence of the Lord? This may mean either where the Ark of the Covenant was, through which a more sacred and notable presence of the Lord may be understood, or that he sat in order to pray—for this is done rightly only in the presence of God, that is, in the innermost heart.

The phrase “before the Lord” may also be understood as referring to a place where there was no human being to hear him praying. Whether, therefore, on account of the Ark of the Covenant, or on account of a secluded place removed from observers, or on account of the innermost heart, where the affection of the person praying was located, it was appropriately said, “He sat before the Lord.”

Unless perhaps it is the fact that he prayed while sitting that causes difficulty, since the holy Elijah did this too when he obtained rain by praying (1 Kings 18:42–45). These examples teach us that no particular bodily posture is prescribed for prayer, provided that the mind, present to God, carries out its intention.

We pray standing, as it is written, “But the tax collector stood at a distance” (Luke 18:13); and on bended knees, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 7:59; 20:36); and sitting, as David and Elijah did here. But if we also prayed lying down, it would not have been written in the Psalms, “Every night I wash my bed; I water my couch with my tears” (Ps. 6:7).

Whenever someone seeks a time for prayer, he arranges his limbs according to whatever bodily posture occurs to him as suitable at that time for stirring the mind [Note: [Col. 0145] So the manuscripts. The printed editions have “the posture of the body.”]. But when the desire to pray is not sought out but arises spontaneously—that is, when something suddenly comes to mind by which the disposition to supplication is moved through inexpressible groanings—then, wherever it finds a person, prayer must certainly not be postponed while we look for somewhere to withdraw [Note: [Col. 0145] The printed editions have “where we may sit”; the manuscripts have “where we may withdraw.” Perhaps “and where we may sit” should be added here.], or somewhere to stand, or somewhere to prostrate ourselves.

For the mind’s attention creates solitude for itself, and often it even forgets toward which part of heaven, or in what bodily posture, that moment found its limbs [Note: [Col. 0145] The printed editions have “forgets itself”; “itself” is absent from the manuscripts.].

## QUESTION V.—On the words of Elijah complaining to God about the death of the widow’s son.

As for the words of blessed Elijah, in which he says, “O Lord, witness of this widow with whom I dwell in her house, have you done evil by killing her son?”—nothing would be troubling if the correct intonation were preserved.

For it is the voice of someone who does not believe that God had done such evil to that widow who had received the Prophet with such piety, especially at a time when she had brought him all her meager food amid such great and utter poverty. Thus the statement should be understood as though he were saying: “O Lord, witness of this widow with whom I dwell in her house, have you done evil by killing her son?” The implied meaning is certainly that the Lord, who was witness of the woman’s heart and saw how great her piety was—indeed, he himself had sent Elijah to her—had not killed her son in order to do evil, but in order to display a miracle for the glory of his name, by which he might commend such a great Prophet both to those then living and to posterity.

So the Lord says that Lazarus had not died for death’s sake, but so that God might be glorified in his Son (John 11:4). Accordingly, what follows confirms this, as does the confidence with which Elijah believed that this had not happened so that his hostess might be afflicted by bitter mourning, but rather so that God might show the widow more magnificently what kind of servant of God she had received.

Scripture continues and says [Note: [Col. 0145] More and better manuscripts read: “And what follows confirms this. For from the very confidence with which … she had received him, Scripture continues and says.” Perhaps the reading should be: “And this is confirmed by what follows,” etc.]: “And he breathed upon the child three times, and called upon the Lord and said, ‘O Lord my God, let the soul of this child return into him now.’ And it happened so” (1 Kings 17:21–22).

This prayer, in which Elijah asked so briefly and confidently that the child should rise again, sufficiently indicates with what feeling the preceding words were spoken. The woman herself also showed that her son had been killed for the very purpose Elijah had presumed it had occurred, when she had spoken those words not as an affirmation but as a repudiation.

For when she had received her son alive again, she said, “Now I know that you are a man of God, and that the word of the Lord in your mouth is truth” (1 Kings 17:24) [the citation is printed as III Reg. XVII–XX, 21–24].

There are many passages in Scripture that, unless they are pronounced in that manner, fall into the opposite meaning. Such is the statement, “Who will bring an accusation against God’s elect? God, who justifies” (Rom. 8:33). If you answer as though you were affirming it, you see how great a perversity arises. It should therefore be pronounced as though one were saying, “God, who justifies?”—with the implied answer, “Certainly not.” For this reason I think Elijah’s statement is clear enough; it was the failure to preserve its proper intonation that made it obscure.

## QUESTION VI.—On the spirit of falsehood sent to deceive Ahab.

As for the spirit of falsehood [Note: [Col. 0146] In Erasmus, Lyons, Venice, and Louvain, the sixth question is not treated separately from the fifth. Instead of “As for the spirit of falsehood,” one simply finds “On the spirit of falsehood,” and the entire book, with the fifth and sixth questions joined together, contains only five questions. M.] by which Ahab was deceived (1 Kings 22:20–23), let us understand this in the way I believe has already been explained sufficiently clearly above: namely, that God, almighty and just, the distributor of punishments and rewards according to merits, makes use not only of good and holy ministers for appropriate works, but also of evil ones for works suited to them.

When the latter desire to do harm according to their perverse desire [Note: [Col. 0146] So the manuscripts. The printed editions have “according to their perversity.”], they are permitted to do so only to the extent judged by him who orders all things by measure, weight, and number (Wis. 11:21).

The prophet Micaiah explained how this had been shown to him. For a hidden and exceedingly secret matter is shown to prophets in the manner that the human understanding can grasp, even when it is instructed in revelation through images of things as though through words.

How God carries out these things, being wholly and always present everywhere; how the holy angels, and all the exalted and most pure spirits created by the same God, consult his simple, unchangeable, and eternal truth, and temporally carry out what they see to be eternally just in him in accordance with the circumstances of lower things; how fallen spirits, who did not stand in the truth, unable on account of the uncleanness and weakness of their desires and punishments to behold and consult the present truth inwardly, await signs outwardly through creation and are moved by them either to do something or not to do it; and in what manner they are compelled by the eternal law by which the universe is governed, bound and constrained either to await God’s permission to act or to yield to his command—this is difficult to embrace and extremely lengthy to explain [Note: [Col. 0146] Thus the better manuscripts. The printed editions have: “either, with God permitting, to act, or to yield to the one commanding and compelling; difficult and extremely lengthy to explain.”].

But I fear that what I have said has neither satisfied your expectation nor become wearisome to your gravity; for although you wished one small book to be sent to you concerning all the matters you asked about, I sent two books, both exceedingly long, and perhaps did not answer your questions with sufficient care and efficiency. [Col. 0147] Therefore I ask that you offer many and continual prayers for my errors; but I earnestly request your judgment concerning this work—brief, but weighty—and, provided that it is entirely truthful, I do not decline an extremely severe one.

# [ON THE EIGHT QUESTIONS OF DULCITIUS]

[Col. 0147]

## NOTICE TO THE BOOK ON THE EIGHT QUESTIONS OF DULCITIUS

As for Dulcitius himself, who provided Augustine with the subject of this book, we have no doubt that he is the very tribune and notary praised in Book 2 of the *Retractions*, chapter 59. As can be understood from that same passage, around the year 420 he was active in Africa and had been appointed to execute the laws issued by the emperor Honorius against the Donatists.

When he wished to be instructed concerning what ought to be said in reply to those heretics, Augustine wrote to him Letter 204, prefaced with the title, “To the distinguished lord and honorable son Dulcitius.” Augustine believed the merchant to be very well known to Dulcitius—the merchant to whom, through Albinus, an acolyte of the Roman Church departing from Africa, Augustine sent the letters cited in this work at Question 3. He calls Laurentius, to whom the book called the *Enchiridion* is addressed as primicerius of the city of Rome, Dulcitius’s brother when answering Question 1 here.

As for the date of the work that follows, it is entirely certain that it was published after the year 419, indeed after 420, since the *Enchiridion*, cited in Question 1, did not appear before 421, as we shall state in its proper place. It is equally clear that the work was completed some time before the year 430, since it is listed in the books of the *Retractions*, completed around the year 427.

It is therefore not without reason that some think the Paschal date recorded at the beginning should be corrected, although all the manuscripts, both printed and handwritten, have the same reading. They report that in the year when Augustine composed this book, Easter Sunday fell on the third day before the Kalends of April. This occurred during Augustine’s episcopate only in the years 419 and 430, to neither of which, as can easily be conceded, this little work can be assigned.

For “the third day before the Kalends,” then, some would read “the seventh day before the Kalends of April,” assigning the work to the year 422; or else “the eleventh day before the Kalends of April,” on which day Bucherius asserts that Easter was celebrated by some Latins in the year 425.

[Col. 0147]

[Note: [Col. 0147] On the book *On the Eight Questions of Dulcitius*, see Book 2, chapter 65, of the *Retractions*, vol. 1, col. 656, from the words “The book which I have recorded” through the words “son of Dulcitius.” M.]

SAINT AURELIUS AUGUSTINE, BISHOP OF HIPPO,  
ONE BOOK ON THE EIGHT QUESTIONS OF DULCITIUS [Note: [Col. 0147] Probably written in the year 422 or 425.] [Note: [Col. 0147] In correcting this book *On the Eight Questions of Dulcitius*, three ancient Vatican manuscripts, two Corbie manuscripts, two Victorine manuscripts, the Royal, Sorbonne, Floriacian, and Michaelian codices, and one manuscript of the Church of Laon were used; also the variant readings of the Louvain editions from four Belgian manuscripts; and finally the editions of Ratisbon, Amerbach, Erasmus, and the Louvain theologians—that is, Augustine of Ratisbon, John of Amerbach, Desiderius Erasmus, and the Louvain theologians.] [Note: [Col. 0147] We also compared all the editions mentioned at the beginning of the *Retractions* and the *Confessions*, vol. 1. M.] (C)

## PREFACE

[Col. 0147]

As far as I can see, my dearest [Note: [Col. 0147] Several manuscripts have “most beloved.”] son Dulcitius, I have not been slow in answering your questions. For at Easter this year, in which Easter Sunday fell on the third day before the Kalends of April [Note: [Col. 0147] Most manuscripts have “in which Easter Sunday was celebrated.”], I received the letter your affection had sent me from Carthage. Immediately after those holy days I set out for Carthage, but in that city the excessive number of duties that cannot be absent from it did not permit me to dictate anything.

After I had returned from there, having spent fifteen days among our people—who, after my long absence, compelled me to attend to other matters, since I was permitted to return only after three months—I did not delay writing back. I drew from the same little works of mine either my answer or at least my discussion of the questions you had sent, questions that I had already treated in various works.

Finally, concerning only the matter in which you ask why the Lord, clearly foreknowing the future, said, “I have chosen David according to my heart” (1 Kings 8:16), although he had committed such grave and numerous offenses: I could not find where I had treated the matter or how I had explained it, and I do not know whether it exists in any of my books or letters.

Therefore, since you have imposed upon me the necessity of a new discussion, I placed that matter last in this reply, first wishing to set down what I already had prepared in my other volumes. In this way I would neither fail in the devotion owed to your holiness, which is most pleasing to me [Note: [Col. 0149] The better manuscripts have “which would fail.”], nor be forced to say the same things in another manner, which would be most laborious for me and would not help you any further.

## QUESTION ONE.—Whether baptized sinners will emerge from Gehenna. A difficult passage of the Apostle wrongly understood. The opinion of those who think that faith without works benefits salvation is refuted. How the Apostle’s passage should be understood. Another passage of the Apostle wrongly cited by those who teach that faith without works saves. What kind of faith was praised in the Canaanite woman. The opinion of some that baptized believers, however sinful, will be saved through fire. The fire that tests everyone’s work in this life. Purgatorial fire after this life.

[Col. 0149]

1. Your first proposition is this:

“Whether at some time those who are sinners after Baptism emerge from Gehenna. For, you say, some hold differing opinions on this matter, answering that just as the reward of the righteous has no end, so the punishment of sinners has no end. They wish to assert that the retribution remains just as perpetual as the reward. Against them that Gospel statement is brought forward which says, ‘You will not leave there until you have paid the last penny’ (Matt. 5:26). It follows, therefore, that once this has been paid, he can leave. We believe this also on the basis of the Apostle’s definition, which says, ‘He himself will be saved, but only as through fire’ (1 Cor. 3:15). But since, you say, we read elsewhere, ‘And he did not know her until she had given birth’ (Matt. 1:25), a statement that we cannot interpret in this way, we therefore wish to be made more certain about the matter.”

Up to this point, this is your proposition.

2. I answer you from my book entitled *On Faith and Works*, where I spoke about this matter as follows:

“James,” I said, “is so vehemently opposed to those who think that faith without works is effective for salvation that he even compares them with demons, saying, ‘You believe that God is one; you do well. Even the demons believe, and tremble.’ What could have been said more briefly, more truly, or more forcefully, when we also read in the Gospel that the demons said this, confessing Christ to be the Son of God, and were rebuked by him (Mark 1:24–25), while this confession was praised in Peter (Matt. 16:16–17)?

“‘What good is it,’ James says, ‘my brothers, if someone says that he has faith but does not have works? Can faith save him?’ He also says that ‘faith without works is dead’ (James 2:19, 14, 20). How long, then, will those be deceived who promise themselves everlasting life on the basis of dead faith?

3. “For this reason we must carefully consider how that statement of the Apostle Paul should be understood—a statement plainly difficult to understand—where he says:

‘For no one can lay any foundation other than the one that has been laid, which is Jesus Christ. But if anyone builds upon this foundation gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, or straw, the work of each person will become manifest. For the Day will disclose it, because it will be revealed in fire, and the fire will test what sort of work each person’s is. If anyone’s work that he has built upon it remains, he will receive a reward. But if anyone’s work is burned up, he will suffer loss; yet he himself will be saved, but only as through fire’ (1 Cor. 3:11–15).

“Some think this should be understood as follows: those who add good works to the faith that is in Christ are considered to build gold, silver, and precious stones upon this foundation; those who, while possessing the same faith, do evil works are considered to build hay, wood, and straw. Hence they believe that through certain punishments of fire these people can be purified so as to receive salvation on account of the merit of the foundation.

4. “If this is so, we must admit that these people are striving with commendable charity to admit everyone indiscriminately to Baptism—not only adulterers and adulteresses who, contrary to the Lord’s judgment, put forward false marriages, but also public prostitutes who persist in the most shameful profession, whom certainly not even the most negligent Church is accustomed to admit unless they have first been freed from that prostitution.

“But on this reasoning I do not see why they should not be admitted in every case. For who would not prefer that, once the foundation had been laid, even if they should pile up wood, hay, and straw, they should be purified by a somewhat longer fire rather than perish eternally?

“But then those statements would be false that contain no obscurity or ambiguity: ‘If I have all faith, so that I remove mountains, but do not have love, I am nothing’ (1 Cor. 13:2); and, ‘What good is it, my brothers, if someone says he has faith but does not have works? Can faith save him?’

“That statement too would be false: ‘Do not be deceived: neither fornicators, nor idolaters, nor thieves, nor the greedy, nor adulterers, nor the effeminate, nor men who lie with males, nor drunkards, nor slanderers, nor robbers will possess the kingdom of God’ (1 Cor. 6:9–10).

“And this too would be false: ‘The works of the flesh are manifest: fornication, impurity, shamelessness, licentiousness, idolatry, sorcery, enmities, strife, jealousy, anger, dissensions, factions, envy, drunkenness, revelries, and things like these, of which I warn you, as I warned you before, that those who do such things will not possess the kingdom of God’ (Gal. 5:19–21).

“These statements would be false. For if people merely believe and are baptized, even though they persist in such evils, they will be saved through fire; and therefore those baptized in Christ, even those who do such things, will possess the kingdom of God.

“In vain, then, is it said, ‘And such were some of you, but you were washed’ (1 Cor. 6:11), when those very things are still being done by the washed. In vain also would Peter have said, ‘In a corresponding form Baptism now saves you—not the removal of dirt from the flesh, but an appeal to God for a good conscience’ (1 Pet. 3:21), if people with the worst consciences, filled with every outrage and crime and not changed by repentance for those evils, are nevertheless saved by Baptism. For on account of the foundation laid in that same Baptism, they will be saved, even if through fire.

“I also do not see why the Lord said, ‘If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments’ (Matt. 19:17), and mentioned those things that pertain to good conduct, if life can be reached even without keeping them, through faith alone, which is dead without works.

“Moreover, how will this be true: that he will say to those whom he is going to place on his left, ‘Go into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels’? He does not rebuke them because they did not believe in him, but because they did not do good works.

“Indeed, so that no one might promise himself eternal life on the basis of faith that is dead without works, he said that he would separate all the nations that had been mixed together in the same pastures, so that it might become clear that those people would say to him, ‘Lord, when did we see you suffering this or that, and did not minister to you?’ They had believed in him, but had not taken care to do good, as though eternal life could be reached through that very dead faith.

“Or will those who did not perform works of mercy go into eternal fire, while those who seized other people’s property will not, or those who, by corrupting themselves as God’s temple, were merciless toward themselves? As though works of mercy were of any benefit without love, when the Apostle says, ‘If I distribute all that I have to the poor, but do not have love, it profits me nothing’ (1 Cor. 13:3). Or could anyone love his neighbor as himself who does not love himself? For ‘the one who loves iniquity hates his own soul’ (Ps. 11:6).

“Nor can the following argument be made here, by which some deceive themselves when they say that ‘eternal fire’ refers not to eternal punishment itself. They think that those whom they promise salvation through fire because of dead faith will pass through the fire that will be eternal, so that the fire will be eternal, but their burning—that is, the operation of the fire in them—will not be eternal.

“But the Lord foresaw this too, and, as Lord, concluded his sentence by saying, ‘Thus they will go into eternal burning, but the righteous into eternal life’ (Matt. 25:41, 44, 46). The burning, therefore, will be eternal, just as the fire is; and Truth said that those would go into it whose lack was shown to be not faith but good works.

5. “If, then, all these statements—and the countless others that can be found throughout all the Scriptures, spoken without ambiguity—are false, that interpretation concerning the wood, hay, and straw could be true: namely, that those who hold faith alone in Christ but neglect good works will be saved through fire.

“But if these statements are both true and clear, then without doubt another interpretation must be sought for that statement of the Apostle. It must be counted among those things that Peter says are difficult to understand in Paul’s writings, things that people should not twist to their own destruction (2 Pet. 3:16), so as to make the utterly wicked, who cling most stubbornly to their wickedness and have not been changed by correction or repentance, secure in the hope of receiving salvation, contrary to the clearest testimonies of Scripture.”

6. “Here perhaps I may be asked what I think about the very statement of the Apostle Paul, and in what way I believe it should be understood. I confess that I would rather hear more intelligent and learned men explain it in such a way that all those things remain true and unshaken which I mentioned above, as well as whatever other things I did not mention, by which Scripture most clearly testifies that faith is of no benefit unless it is the faith defined by the Apostle—that is, faith working through love (Gal. 5:6); and that without works it cannot save, neither apart from fire nor through fire: for if it saves through fire, it itself certainly saves. Yet it is stated absolutely and plainly: ‘What good is it if someone says that he has faith but does not have works? Can faith save him?’ I too shall state, as briefly as I can, what I think about that difficult-to-understand statement of the Apostle Paul—provided that what concerns my own profession is kept especially in view: namely, that I said I would rather hear better men on this matter. [Col. 0152]

“Christ is the foundation in the structure of the wise builder; this requires no explanation, for it is plainly said: ‘No one can lay any foundation other than the one that has been laid, which is Jesus Christ.’ But if Christ, then without doubt the faith of Christ; for through faith Christ dwells in our hearts, as the same Apostle says (Eph. 3:17). And if the faith of Christ, then certainly that faith which the Apostle defined as working through love. The faith of the demons cannot be understood as belonging to the foundation, since they too believe and tremble, and confess Jesus as the Son of God. Why not? Because it is not faith working through love, but faith expressed through fear. Therefore the faith of Christ, the faith of Christian grace—that is, the faith working through love—when laid in the foundation, permits no one to perish.

“But if I try to explain more subtly what it means to build upon this foundation with gold, silver, precious stones, and with wood, hay, and straw, I fear that the explanation itself may become more difficult to understand. Nevertheless, with the Lord’s help, I shall try to set forth briefly and as clearly as I can what I think. [Col. 0152]

“Consider the man who asked the good Teacher what good he should do in order to have eternal life. He heard that, if he wished to enter into life, he must keep the commandments. When he asked which commandments, he was told: ‘You shall not kill; you shall not commit adultery; you shall not steal; you shall not bear false witness; honor your father and your mother’; and, ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’ By doing these things in the faith of Christ, he would certainly possess the faith that works through love. Nor would he love his neighbor as himself unless he had received the love of God, without which he would not love even himself.

“Moreover, if he also did what the Lord added, saying, ‘If you wish to be perfect, go, sell everything you possess and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me’ (Matt. 19:16–21), he would build gold, silver, and precious stones upon that foundation. For he would think only about how to please God; and these thoughts, in my judgment, are gold, silver, and precious stones. [Col. 0153]

“But if he were held by a certain carnal attachment to his wealth, even though he gave many alms from it and undertook no fraud or robbery to increase it, nor, through fear of reducing or losing it, fell into any crime or disgraceful act—for otherwise he would already have withdrawn himself in this way from the stability of that foundation—but because of the carnal attachment I have mentioned, by which he could not bear to be deprived of such goods without pain, he would build wood, hay, and straw upon that foundation. This would be especially so if he had a wife in such a way that, even on her account, he thought about the things of the world, how to please his wife. [Col. 0153]

“Since such things, loved with carnal affection, are not lost without pain, those who possess them in such a way that they have in the foundation the faith that works through love, and do not in any way or through any desire place these things before that faith, suffer loss in their loss and reach salvation through a certain fire of pain. A person is safer from this pain and loss the less he has loved such things, or the more he has possessed them as though he did not possess them.

“But whoever, in order to retain or acquire such things, has committed murder, adultery, fornication, idolatry, or any similar offenses, will not be saved through fire because of the foundation. Rather, having lost the foundation, he will be tormented by eternal fire.

7. “For this reason, those who say this—as though wishing to prove how much mere faith is worth—when the Apostle says, ‘But if the unbelieving partner separates, let him separate; the brother or sister is not enslaved in such circumstances’ (1 Cor. 7:15), understand it to mean that, for the sake of faith in Christ, even a lawful wife united in marriage may be abandoned without any fault if she is unwilling to remain with her Christian husband precisely because he is a Christian. [Col. 0153]

“They do not observe that she is rightly dismissed in the same way if she says to her husband: ‘I will not be your wife unless you heap up wealth for me through theft, or unless, even as a Christian, you continue the customary practices of prostitution by which you maintained our household;’ or if she knew of any other criminal or shameful practice in her husband, by which she was pleased, satisfied her lust, obtained an easy livelihood, or even walked about more elegantly dressed.

“Then, if the man to whom his wife says this has truly repented of dead works when he approached Baptism, and has in the foundation the faith that works through love, he will certainly be bound more by love of divine grace than by conjugal flesh, and he will firmly cut off the member that causes him to stumble. Whatever pain of heart he suffers in this separation because of carnal affection for his wife—that is the loss he will endure; that is the fire through which he himself will be saved as the hay burns.

“But if he had such a wife as though he did not have her—not because of desire, but because of mercy, lest perhaps he might save her, giving rather than demanding the marital debt—then, when such a marriage is separated from him, he will certainly not grieve carnally. For he was thinking in her only about the things of God, how to please God (1 Cor. 7:29–34). Accordingly, insofar as he was building gold, silver, and precious stones upon the foundation through those thoughts, he would suffer no loss to that extent, and to that extent his structure, which was not made of hay, would not be consumed by any fire. [Col. 0154]

8. “Whether, therefore, people suffer these things only in this life, or whether certain such judgments also follow after this life, this understanding of the statement does not, in my judgment, depart from the reasoning of truth. Nevertheless, if there is another interpretation that has not occurred to me, it should be preferred. As long as we hold to this one, however, we are not compelled to say to the unjust, disobedient, wicked, defiled, parricides, matricides, murderers, fornicators, men who have intercourse with males, kidnappers, liars, perjurers, and anyone else who opposes sound doctrine, which is according to the gospel of the glory of the blessed God (1 Tim. 1:9–11): ‘If only you believe in Christ and receive the sacrament of his Baptism, you will be saved even if you do not change this most wicked life.’

9. “Therefore that Canaanite woman does not prescribe this for us, because the Lord granted her what she requested after first saying, ‘It is not right to take the children’s bread and throw it to the dogs.’ For he who examines the heart saw that she had changed when he praised her. Thus he did not say, ‘O dog, great is your faith!’ but, ‘O woman, great is your faith!’ (Matt. 15:26, 28). He changed the name because he saw that the disposition had changed, and he recognized that the correction had borne fruit.

“I wonder, however, whether he would have praised in her a faith without works—that is, a faith not of the kind already able to work through love, a dead faith, and, as James did not hesitate to say, not the faith of Christians but of demons. Finally, if they do not wish to understand that this Canaanite woman changed her depraved ways when Christ rebuked her by disregarding and correcting her, let them heal the children of all whom they find merely believing while living a most polluted life, not even concealing it but openly professing it and refusing to change—if they can—just as the daughter of the Canaanite woman was healed. Yet let them not make such people members of Christ, since they themselves do not cease to be members of a prostitute” (*On Faith and Works*, chs. 14–16).

10. Likewise, in the book entitled *On Faith, Hope, and Charity*, which I wrote to my son, your brother Laurence, these are my words on this subject:

“‘Some believe,’ I said, ‘that even those who do not abandon the name of Christ, and who are baptized in his Church with its washing, and are not cut off from it by any schism or heresy, will be saved through fire, no matter what crimes they commit—crimes which they neither wash away by repentance nor redeem by almsgiving, but in which they persist most obstinately until the final day of this life—although, on account of the magnitude and duration of their crimes and disgraces, they will be punished by fire that is long-lasting but not eternal. [Col. 0154]

“‘But those who believe this and nevertheless are Catholics seem to me to be deceived by a certain human benevolence; for, when consulted, divine Scripture gives a different answer. I have written a book on this question entitled *On Faith and Works*, in which, according to the holy Scriptures, insofar as I was able with God’s help, I demonstrated that the faith which saves is the one the Apostle Paul clearly expressed when he said: “For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision nor uncircumcision has any power, but faith working through love” (Gal. 5:6). [Col. 0155]

“‘But if faith works badly and not well, then, according to the Apostle James, it is certainly dead in itself. He says again: “If someone says that he has faith but does not have works, can faith save him?” Moreover, if a wicked person will be saved through fire on account of faith alone, and if the blessed Paul’s statement, “He himself will be saved, but only as through fire,” is to be understood in this way, then faith will be able to save without works, and what his fellow Apostle James said will be false.

“‘This also will be false, which that same Paul said: “Do not be deceived: neither fornicators, nor those who serve idols, nor adulterers, nor the effeminate, nor men who have intercourse with males, nor thieves, nor the greedy, nor revilers, nor drunkards, nor robbers will possess the kingdom of God.” For if those who persist in these crimes will nevertheless be saved because of faith in Christ, how will they not be in the kingdom of God?’

11. “But since these most manifest and explicit apostolic testimonies cannot be false, the obscure statement about those who build upon the foundation, which is Christ—not gold, silver, and precious stones, but wood, hay, and straw—must be understood in such a way that it is not found to contradict these clear testimonies. For wood, hay, and straw can reasonably be understood as desires for secular things, even when those things are lawfully permitted—desires of such a kind that the things cannot be lost without pain of soul. [Col. 0155]

“When this pain burns, if Christ has his place in the foundation of the heart—that is, if nothing is preferred to him—and if the person burned by such pain would rather be deprived of the things he loves in this way than of Christ, he is saved through fire. But if, at the time of temptation, he prefers to retain such temporal and secular things rather than Christ, he did not have Christ in the foundation, because he placed these things first, whereas in a building nothing can come before the foundation.

“For the fire of which the Apostle Paul spoke in that passage must be understood as such that both pass through it: both the one who builds gold, silver, and precious stones upon this foundation and the one who builds wood, hay, and straw. For after saying this, he added: ‘The quality of each one’s work will be tested by fire. If anyone’s work that he has built upon the foundation survives, he will receive a reward. But if anyone’s work is burned up, he will suffer loss; he himself, however, will be saved, but only as through fire.’ Therefore the fire will test the work of both, not of only one of them. [Col. 0155]

12. “There is a certain fire, the temptation of tribulation, about which it is plainly written elsewhere: ‘The furnace tests the potter’s vessels, and temptation by tribulation tests righteous people’ (Sir. 27:6).

“This fire, in the present life, does what the Apostle said if it comes upon two believers: one thinking about the things of God, how to please God—that is, building gold, silver, and precious stones upon Christ as foundation—and the other thinking about the things of the world, how to please his wife—that is, building wood, hay, and straw upon the same foundation.

“The work of the first is not burned, because he did not love the things whose loss would torment him. But the work of the second is burned, because the things possessed with love do not perish without pain. Yet since, under either condition, he would prefer to be deprived of them rather than of Christ, and does not abandon Christ through fear of losing such things, although he grieves while losing them, he is indeed saved, but only as through fire. For the pain of the things he had loved and lost burns him, but it does not overturn or consume him, since he is protected by the stability and incorruptibility of the foundation. [Col. 0156]

13. “It is not incredible that something of this kind also happens after this life, and the question may be asked whether it is so: whether some believers are saved sooner or later through a certain purifying fire, according as they have loved perishable goods more or less. Yet this does not apply to those of whom it was said that they will not possess the kingdom of God, unless those same crimes are forgiven to them after suitable repentance.

“I said ‘after suitable repentance’ so that they are not barren in almsgiving, since divine Scripture attributes such importance to almsgiving that the Lord foretells that he will reckon only its fruit to those on his right and only its barrenness to those on his left. To the former he will say, ‘Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom’; but to the latter, ‘Go into eternal fire’” (*On Faith, Hope, and Charity*, chs. 67–69).”

I think these statements from my two short works have provided a sufficient answer to your question.

14. As for the Lord’s statement, “You will not go out from there until you have paid the last quadrans,” I did not need to answer it, since you yourself resolved the question by a similar expression from the Gospel, where it is written [Col. 0156], “He did not know her until she gave birth.” [Textual note: The better manuscripts read “by a similar expression from the Gospel”; the printed editions, “by a similar expression from the Gospel reading.”] Certainly, so that I do not conceal my thoughts on this subject from you, I would like—indeed, if it is possible, I wish—to be overcome by the truth in this matter.

“For what is sometimes said, namely, that those who die in Catholic communion, even if they have lived most shamefully and wickedly until the end of this life, will eventually, though after a very long time, emerge from avenging punishments [Textual note: The printed editions read, “and if of a very long time”; corrected from the manuscripts.]—this touches more familiarly the affection I have toward those who share with us the sacraments of the body and blood of Christ, although we hate their depraved conduct, which we are unable to correct through ecclesiastical discipline or to exclude from the Lord’s table. But I wish to be conquered by that truth which does not resist the clearest testimony of the holy Scriptures. [Textual note: The manuscripts read “by that truth”; the printed editions, “from truth.” The printed editions also read “most plainly” below, where the manuscripts have “the clearest [testimonies].”] For what resists them cannot in any way be called or considered truth.

“In the meantime, until we hear or read some such thing, let us listen to him who says: ‘Do not be deceived: neither fornicators, nor those who serve idols, etc., will possess the kingdom of God.’ For if what is said against this is such that it cannot lead the manifest meaning of these apostolic words into other senses, then the same Apostle certainly instructed us against it and wished us to be prepared when he said: ‘But understand this: every fornicator, or unclean person, or greedy person—which is idolatry—has no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and God. Let no one deceive you with empty words’ (Eph. 5:5–6).

“Therefore, when we hear that certain fornicators, unclean persons, and greedy persons are saved through fire so that they may have an inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and God, let us not become deaf to this Apostle who cries out and says, ‘Every fornicator, or unclean person, or greedy person, has no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and God’; and let us not yield to those words, while he immediately adds, ‘Let no one deceive you with empty words.’” [Textual note: The printed editions read “let us not yield to his words.” Two manuscripts read more aptly, “let us not yield to any words”; other manuscripts, with the Ratian edition, read “let us not yield to those words.”]

## QUESTION II — Whether an offering made for the dead benefits them; the dwelling places of souls before the resurrection

1. Your second question is: “Whether an offering made for those who rest benefits their souls in any way, since we are clearly either helped or burdened by our actions. For we read that in hell no one can any longer confess to the Lord. To this many reply that, if some benefit can exist in this place after death [Textual note: Most manuscripts read “if some benefit can exist in this place”], would not the soul itself obtain refreshment for itself much more by confessing its sins there on its own than when an offering is arranged by others for its refreshment?” [Col. 0157]

2. I said something about this in the book I recently wrote to the holy bishop Paulinus of Nola, when he consulted me about whether burial in the memorial shrines of martyrs benefits the spirits of the dead in any way. This is what I insert here from that work:

“‘For a long time,’ I said, ‘venerable fellow-bishop Paulinus, I have been in your debt for a reply, ever since you wrote to me through the people of our most religious daughter Flora, asking whether it benefits anyone after death that his body be buried near the memorial of some saint.

“‘The widow mentioned above had asked this of you on behalf of her deceased son in those regions, and you had written back to console her, also reporting that what she desired in her maternal and pious affection concerning the body of the faithful young man Cynegius had been accomplished: namely, that it was to be placed in the basilica of the most blessed confessor Felix.

“‘On this occasion it happened that, through the same bearers of your letters, you also wrote to me, raising a question of this kind and asking me to explain what seemed to me to follow from it, while not concealing what you yourself thought. For you say that it seems to you that the religious and faithful people who arrange such things for their own dead are not moved in vain. You add that it cannot be without purpose that the whole Church is accustomed to pray for the dead. From this, one might also infer that it benefits a person after death if, through the faith of his family, a place of this kind is provided for the burial of his body, in which the assistance of the saints appears to have been sought in this way.

3. “‘But although these things are so, you indicate that you do not sufficiently see how this opinion is not contrary to what the Apostle says: “For we shall all stand before the tribunal of Christ, so that each may receive according to what he has done through the body, whether good or evil” (2 Cor. 5:10). This apostolic statement urges that, before death, whatever can benefit a person after death should be done—not at the time when each person is already to receive what he did before death. [Col. 0158]

“‘The question is resolved in this way: through a certain manner of life, acquired while one lives in this body, a condition is established in which these things can help the dead. Accordingly, on the basis of what they did through the body, they are helped by whatever is devoutly done for them after the body. For there are some whom these things do not help at all: either because they are done for people whose merits are so evil that they are not worthy of being helped even by such things, or because they are done for people whose merits are so good that they do not need such assistance.

“‘Thus it is the kind of life each person lived through the body that determines whether whatever is piously done for him after he has left the body is beneficial or not. For if no merit was acquired in this life by which these things might be beneficial, it is sought in vain after this life.

“‘Thus it happens that neither the Church nor the care of the living for the dead expends whatever devotion it can in vain, and yet each person receives according to what he did through the body, whether good or evil, since the Lord renders to each according to his works. For the fact that what is expended can benefit someone after death was acquired in the life he lived in the body’” (*On the Care to Be Taken for the Dead*, ch. 1).

4. I also said something similar to Laurence, as follows:

“‘The period,’ I said, ‘between a person’s death and the final resurrection holds souls in hidden dwelling places, according as each is worthy either of rest or of distress, in accordance with what each received in the flesh while living.

“‘Nor should it be denied that the souls of the dead are relieved by the piety of their living relatives when the sacrifice of the Mediator is offered for them or alms are given in the Church. But these things benefit those who, while they were alive, earned the right that such things might later benefit them.

“‘There is a certain manner of living that is neither so good that it does not require such things after death, nor so bad that such things do not benefit it after death. There is also a condition so good that it does not require them, and again a condition so evil that, when this life has passed, it cannot be helped by them.

“‘Therefore, all merit by which someone may be relieved or burdened after this life is acquired here. Let no one hope that, after death, he can obtain favor with God for what he neglected here.

“‘Accordingly, the practices that the Church regularly observes for commending the dead to God are not contrary to that apostolic statement which says, “We shall all stand before the tribunal of Christ, so that each may receive according to what he did through the body, whether good or evil.” For each person also acquired, while living in the body, the merit that these things might benefit him. They do not benefit everyone; and why do they not benefit everyone except because of the difference in the life each person lived in the body?

“‘Therefore, when sacrifices—whether of the altar or of any kind of almsgiving—are offered for all baptized dead, they are thanksgivings for the very good; propitiations for those who are not very bad; and, for the very bad, even if they provide no assistance to the dead, they are at least forms of consolation for the living. To those whom they benefit, they benefit either so that forgiveness may be complete or, at any rate, so that the condemnation itself may become more tolerable’” (*Enchiridion*, chs. 109–110).

## QUESTION III — Whether judgment will immediately take place at the Lord’s coming, or whether those who are caught up in the clouds to meet the Lord will die; the Creed as the rule of faith

[Col. 0159]

1. Your third question is: “Whether judgment should be believed to occur immediately at the Lord’s coming, or after an interval of time. For concerning the days of his coming, you say that we read that those who remain will be caught up in the clouds to meet Christ in the air, and so will always be with the Lord. I wish to know whether judgment immediately accompanies the coming, and whether those who are caught up into the clouds are released into death—unless perhaps we ought to understand the transformation itself as taking the place of death.”

2. To your question—whether judgment should be believed to occur immediately at the Lord’s coming—I think the faith of the Creed is sufficient, by which we confess that Christ will come from the right hand of the Father to judge the living and the dead. Since this is the very reason for his coming, what else will he do immediately upon coming except what he will come to do? [Col. 0159]

“As for those who will be caught up in the clouds, in a letter I wrote to my son Mercator, when he had consulted me about certain questions raised by the Pelagians, who deny that death was imposed as a recompense for sin, I undoubtedly made the following argument, as you know very well. [Textual note: The printed editions read “to my son Mercator,” and add that the letter begins “Undoubtedly well known to you.” Most manuscripts omit these words, rightly, since the letter cited begins “The letter of your Charity.”]

“‘Those of whom the Apostle spoke when he was discussing the resurrection of the dead—“And we who are alive, who remain, will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet Christ in the air; and so we shall always be with the Lord”—certainly raise a question, but on their own account, not because of these others. [Textual note: The manuscripts read “on their own account”; the printed editions, “because of themselves.”] For even if they themselves are not going to die, I do not see at all how they help these people, since things could be said about them such as were said about the two persons, Enoch and Elijah.

“‘But truly, insofar as the words of the blessed Apostle are concerned, he seems to assert that, at the end of the age, when the resurrection of the dead is to occur and the Lord is to come, some will not die but, being found alive, will suddenly be changed into that immortality which is also given to the other saints, and will be caught up together with them, as he says, in the clouds. Nothing else has seemed evident to me whenever I have wished to reflect on these words.

3. “‘But I would rather hear more learned men on this point, lest the Apostle should be found to say even to those who think that some will be brought to everlasting life without death preceding: “Fool, what you sow is not made alive unless it dies.” [Textual note: The printed editions add “first”; it is absent from the manuscripts and from the Apostle’s Greek text.]

“‘For how can the reading found in many manuscripts, “We shall all rise again” (1 Cor. 15:36, 51), be possible unless we all die? Resurrection, unless death has preceded, is no resurrection. And the reading found in some manuscripts, “We shall all sleep,” makes one understand this much more easily and plainly. If anything else of this kind is found in the holy Scriptures, it seems to press toward the conclusion that no human being is thought to attain immortality unless death has preceded.

“‘Therefore, when the Apostle said, “We who are alive, who remain until the coming of the Lord, will not precede those who have fallen asleep. For the Lord himself will descend from heaven with a command, with the voice of an archangel, and with the trumpet of God; and the dead in Christ will rise first; then we who are alive, who remain, will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet Christ in the air; and so we shall always be with the Lord” (1 Thess. 4:14–16), I would wish, as I said, to hear more learned men explain these words.

“‘And if they can explain them to me in such a way that it can be understood from them that all human beings who are alive, or who will live after us, will die, I would correct what I have at some time thought otherwise on this matter. [Textual note: The printed editions read “I would correct that which I at some time …”; the manuscripts support the present wording.] For we ought not to be unteachable teachers. Certainly, it is better for a crooked person to be corrected than for a stiff one to be broken [Textual note: Some manuscripts read “a small person” (*parvus*) for “a crooked person” (*pravus*)], when through what we write the weakness of ourselves or of others is exercised and instructed, provided that no kind of canonical authority is established in these writings.’ [Col. 0160]

4. “If no other meaning can be found in these words of the Apostle, and it becomes clear that he intended what the words themselves seem to proclaim—that at the end of the age and at the Lord’s coming there will be people who will not be stripped of the body but will be clothed over with immortality, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life (2 Cor. 5:4)—then this statement will certainly accord with what we confess in the rule of faith: that the Lord will come to judge the living and the dead.

“By ‘the living’ we should not understand righteous people and by ‘the dead’ unrighteous people, although both righteous and unrighteous will be judged. Rather, ‘the living’ are those whom his coming will find not yet departed from their bodies, and ‘the dead’ are those whom it will find already departed from their bodies.

“If this is established as the case, those words will have to be examined, so that we may understand ‘What you sow is not made alive unless it dies,’ and ‘We shall all rise again,’ or ‘We shall all sleep,’ in such a way that they do not conflict with the opinion that some are believed to live eternally with their bodies without tasting death. [Col. 0160]

5. “But whichever of these interpretations is found to be more truthful and clearer [Textual note: Some manuscripts read “may be found”], what will it matter to the case of these people, whether all are punished by the death they owe or whether some are spared this condition? [Textual note: Here the printed editions add “excepted,” which is absent from the manuscripts.] It nevertheless remains certain that, if sin had not preceded, neither the death of the soul nor even that of the body would have followed; and that it is through a more wonderful power of grace that the righteous return to life from death unto eternal blessedness than that they should not undergo death.

“Let this suffice concerning those about whom you wrote to me, although I no longer think that they maintain that, even if Adam had not sinned, he would nevertheless have died bodily.

6. “But as for the question of the resurrection, concerning those who are believed not to die but to pass from mortality to immortality without death intervening, a more careful investigation is required. If you have heard, read, or are still able to hear, read, or work out any reasoned and complete discussion that resolves and defines this matter, please do not hesitate to send it to me.

“For I confess to your Charity that I love learning more than teaching. We are reminded of this also when the Apostle James says: ‘Let every person be quick to hear, slow to speak’ (Jas. 1:19). The sweetness of truth should invite us to learn; the necessity of charity should compel us to teach. In this matter, we ought rather to hope that this necessity—by which one person teaches another—will pass away [Textual note: The manuscripts read “we ought rather to wish”; the printed editions, “we ought rather to pray”], and that we may all be teachable by God [Textual note: The manuscripts read “teachable to God.”], although we are also teachable in this sense when we learn what pertains to true devotion, even when a human being appears to teach it.

“For neither the one who plants nor the one who waters is anything, but God who gives the growth (1 Cor. 3:7). Since, if God did not give the growth, the Apostles who plant and water would be nothing, how much more am I, or you, or any people of this age, when we imagine ourselves to be teachers?” (*Letter* 193, ch. 4, nos. 9–13).

## QUESTION IV — How the children of the righteous are blessed in the Psalm

1. Your fourth question is: “Why did David say, ‘His offspring will be powerful on earth; the generation of the upright will be blessed’ (Ps. 111:2), when we know that the children of the righteous have both been and are accursed, and the children of the unrighteous have both been and are blessed?”

2. I answer this question from the exposition of the Psalm itself, which, when I was expounding it before the people, I stated as follows:

“‘Blessed is the man who fears the Lord; he will greatly delight in his commandments.’ Let God see—he who alone judges truly and mercifully—how much this person progresses in his commandments. For ‘human life upon earth is a time of testing,’ as holy Job says (Job 7:1). And again it is written: ‘The corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling burdens the mind with many thoughts’ (Wis. 9:15). [Col. 0161]

“‘But the one who judges us is the Lord; nor ought we to judge before the proper time, until the Lord comes, brings the hidden things of darkness to light, and reveals the thoughts of the heart. Then each person will receive praise from God’ (1 Cor. 4:4–5).

“‘Let him, therefore, see how much each person progresses in his commandments. Nevertheless, the person who has loved the peace of that mutual building will greatly delight in his commandments. He should no longer despair, because he will greatly delight in his commandments, and “on earth peace among people of good will”’ (Luke 2:14).

### 3

“From this comes: ‘His offspring shall be mighty upon the earth.’ That the offspring of the future harvest are works of mercy is attested by the Apostle, who says: ‘Let us not grow weary in doing good; for in due season we shall reap’ (Gal. 6:9) [Note: The printed editions, contrary to the manuscripts, add: “not failing.”]; and again: ‘Whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly’ (2 Cor. 9:6).

“What, then, brothers, is more powerful than this: that the kingdom of heaven should be purchased not only by Zacchaeus with half his possessions (Luke 19:8), but also by the widow with two small coins (Mark 12:42), and that each should possess the same amount there? What is more powerful than that the same kingdom should be of value both to the rich man with his treasures and to the poor man with his cup of cold water?

“Some do these things while amassing earthly possessions, either hoping for a reward from the Lord here, or desiring to please human beings. But ‘the generation of the upright shall be blessed’; that is, the works of those for whom the God of Israel is good, who are upright in heart. An upright heart is one that does not resist the Father when he corrects, and believes him when he makes a promise. It is not the heart of those whose feet are shaken, whose steps slip and falter, as is sung in another psalm, when they envy sinners, seeing the peace of sinners, and think that their own works are perishing because the reward given to them is itself destined to perish (Ps. 72:1–14).

“But this man who fears the Lord, and is fitted for the holy temple of God by the conversion of an upright heart, neither seeks human glory nor covets earthly riches; and yet, ‘Glory and riches are in his house.’ His house is his heart, where, praised by God, he dwells more richly in the hope of eternal life than, amid the flattery of human beings, in marble-covered and coffered halls with the fear of eternal death. ‘His righteousness endures for ever and ever’: this is his glory, these are his riches. But the other man’s purple, fine linen, and splendid banquets, while they are present, pass away; and when he has come to the end, his burning tongue will cry out, longing for a drop of water falling from a finger” (Luke 16:19–24).

These are the matters that I remember having expounded in the stated psalm (*Enarrationes in Psalmos* III, §§2–3), and I now consider them sufficient for the solution of the fourth point proposed in your question. [Note: The words enclosed here in parentheses are absent from five manuscripts.]

As the fifth point, however, you proposed the matter about which I promised to speak after everything else. [Note: See Question V below, col. 168, where it is treated.]

## QUESTION VI — Whether Samuel was truly summoned from the underworld by the witch of Endor. Perhaps Samuel’s phantom, not his spirit, appeared. How demons know the future

### 1

Your sixth proposition is: “Whether, according to the historical account in the Book of Kings, the witch of Endor summoned the prophet Samuel himself from the underworld” (1 Kings 28:7–19).

### 2

The blessed Simplicianus, bishop of Milan, once asked me this. Read below what I answered him. [Note: Manuscripts read *rescripserim*, “what I wrote in reply.”]

“You also ask,” I said, “whether the unclean spirit that was in the witch could have acted so that Samuel would be seen by Saul and speak with him. But it is a much greater miracle that Satan himself, the prince of all unclean spirits, was able to speak with God and ask that the most righteous man Job be put to the test (Job 1:11)—and he also asked that the Apostles be tested (Luke 22:31).

“Or, if this is not considered a difficult question because the truth that is everywhere present speaks through whatever creature it wishes to whatever creature it wishes, and because it is not for that reason a matter of great merit to the one to whom God speaks—for what matters is what he says, since an emperor does not speak with many innocent people whose welfare he carefully provides for, while he speaks with many guilty people whom he orders to be killed—if, then, there is no question here for that reason, neither should there be any question about how an unclean spirit could speak with the soul of a holy man. For God, the Creator and Sanctifier, is certainly far greater than all the saints.

“But if it is disturbing that an evil spirit was permitted to raise up the soul of a righteous man and, as it were, summon it from the hidden dwelling places of the dead, is it not still more astonishing that Satan himself took up the Lord and set him upon the pinnacle of the temple (Matt. 4:5)? For whatever the manner in which he did this, the manner in which Samuel was raised likewise remains hidden.

“Unless perhaps someone should say that the devil had an easier license to take up the living Lord wherever he wished and set him wherever he wished than to raise the spirit of the deceased Samuel from its dwelling place. But if that event in the Gospel does not trouble us because the Lord willed and permitted it to happen without any diminution of his power or divinity—just as he allowed himself, at the hands of the Jews, although they were perverse and unclean and doing the works of the devil, to be seized, bound, mocked, crucified, and killed—then it is not absurd to believe that, by some dispensation of the divine will, it was permitted that the spirit of the prophet, not unwillingly and not under the domination and subjugation of magical power, but willingly and in obedience to God’s hidden dispensation—which was concealed from both the witch and Saul—should consent to appear before the king’s eyes in order to strike him with the divine sentence.

“For why should the soul of a good man, if summoned by evil living people and if it comes, seem to lose its dignity, when good people who are still alive often come when summoned by evil people and do with them what the duty of justice requires, while preserving and keeping unshaken the dignity of their virtue, and dealing with their vices according to the use or necessity of present circumstances?”

### 3

“Nevertheless, in this event there may be another, easier solution and a more straightforward interpretation: we need not believe that Samuel’s spirit was truly raised from its place of rest, but rather that some phantom and imaginary illusion was produced by the devil’s contrivances. Scripture therefore calls it by the name of Samuel because images are customarily called by the names of the things whose images they are.

“Thus everything painted or fashioned from some material—metal, wood, or any substance suitable for such work—and everything seen in dreams, as well as almost all images, is customarily called by the names of the things whose images they are. Who, after all, would hesitate to call a painted human being a human being? Indeed, when we look at portraits of particular persons, we freely apply their proper names: when, for example, looking at a panel or wall, we say, ‘That is Cicero; that is Sallust; that is Achilles; that is Hector; this is the river Simois; that is Rome,’ although they are nothing more than painted images.

“Thus, although the cherubim are heavenly powers, those figures fashioned from metal at God’s command over the Ark of the Covenant, for the sake of signifying a great reality, are nevertheless called cherubim (Exod. 25:18). Likewise, whoever sees a dream does not say, ‘I saw an image of Augustine or Simplicianus,’ but, ‘I saw Augustine or Simplicianus,’ even though, at the time when he saw such a thing, we were unaware of it. So evident is it that the people themselves were not seen, but their images.

“Pharaoh likewise said that he saw ears of grain and cattle in a dream (Gen. 41:17–24), not images of ears of grain or cattle. If, then, it is clearly established that images are called by the names of the things whose images they are, it is not surprising that Scripture says that Samuel was seen, even if perhaps an image of Samuel appeared through the contrivance of him who transforms himself into an angel of light, and his ministers into ministers of righteousness (2 Cor. 11:14–15).

### 4

“But if it is troubling how true predictions were also made to Saul by an evil spirit, it may likewise seem surprising how the demons recognized Christ (Matt. 8:29), whom the Jews did not recognize.

“When God wishes someone to know the truth through even the lowest and infernal spirits—truths, that is, concerning temporal matters and things belonging to this mortal life—it is easy and not incongruous for the omnipotent and just God, as a punishment for those to whom these things are foretold, so that they may suffer in advance through foreknowledge the evil that threatens them, to grant even such spirits some power of divination through the hidden arrangement of his ministries, so that they may announce to human beings what they hear from the angels.

“They hear only as much as the Lord and governor of all either commands or permits. Thus the spirit of divination in the Acts of the Apostles also bears witness to the Apostle Paul and attempts to become an evangelist (Acts 16:17).

“Yet these spirits mix falsehoods with what they say, and they announce the truth they may have learned not so much for the purpose of teaching as of deceiving. Perhaps this is why, when that image of Samuel predicted to Saul that he would die, it also said that he would be with Samuel—for that is certainly false. For we read in the Gospel that the good are separated from the wicked after death by a great interval, when the Lord testifies that a great chasm has been fixed between the proud rich man, who was already suffering torments in the underworld, and the one who had lain ulcerated at his gate and was already established in rest (Luke 16:26).

“Or if Samuel said to Saul, ‘You shall be with me,’ so that this should refer not to equality of happiness but to a similar condition of death—since both were human beings, both could die, and the one already dead was announcing death to the living—your prudence, I think, perceives that this passage has an interpretation under either understanding that is not contrary to the faith.

“Unless perhaps, through a deeper and more intricate inquiry exceeding either my abilities or the limits of the present time, it should be established clearly whether or not a human soul, after departing this life, can be summoned by magical incantations and appear before the eyes of the living, even bearing the features of a body, so that it can not only be seen but also recognized. And if this is possible, whether even the soul of a righteous person might not indeed be compelled by magical rites, but might deign to appear in obedience to the more hidden commands of the highest law.

“If it should become clear that this cannot happen, then both interpretations should not be admitted in the treatment and exposition of this Scripture; rather, once that possibility has been excluded, the imaginary imitation of Samuel produced by a diabolical rite should be understood.

“Since, however, whether this can happen or cannot happen, Satan’s deception and his skillful operation in fabricating images are nevertheless constantly active in many forms for the purpose of deceiving human senses, let us proceed cautiously. We should not, indeed, prejudge more careful investigations; nevertheless, until we are granted the ability to devise and explain something more, let us rather suppose that something of this kind occurred through the evil service of that witch” (*Questions to Simplicianus* II.3).

### 5

These are the things I then wrote about the witch and Samuel. [Note: Rat., Am., Er., and two Vatican manuscripts omit the following thirteen lines and immediately continue, after the words “I wrote,” with “Your seventh proposition is.”]

That I did not without reason say that we should cautiously suppose that an imitation of Samuel had been presented through the evil service of the witch, lest we prejudge more careful investigations, was made clear by my subsequent inquiry. I found in the book of Ecclesiasticus, where the Fathers are praised in sequence, that Samuel himself is praised in such a way that he is said to have prophesied even after his death (Ecclus. 46:23).

But if this book too is rejected on the grounds that it comes from the Hebrews, since it is not in their canon, what will we say about Moses, who is certainly read as having died in Deuteronomy (Deut. 34:5), yet is also read in the Gospel to have appeared alive to living people with Elijah, who did not die (Matt. 17:3)?

## QUESTION VII — How Sarah escaped violation by Abimelech and Pharaoh

### 1

Your seventh proposition is: “How should one answer those who say that Sarah did not escape violation, since they say that Abimelech was turned back from intercourse with her by a dream (Gen. 20), while Pharaoh was admitted to intercourse with her (Gen. 12)?”

### 2

I do not see how they can say that Pharaoh was admitted to intercourse with her [Note: These words, “I do not see how they can say that Pharaoh was admitted to intercourse with her,” are restored from the manuscripts], since Scripture does not compel us to believe this. He did indeed receive her as his wife, and Abraham immediately became wealthy through many Egyptian gifts because of her; but it is not written that Pharaoh slept with her or had intercourse with her, because God prevented him from doing so by afflicting him with many severe calamities.

“For women who had been chosen for marriage by kings were not immediately joined to them in sexual intercourse. Rather, as we read in the book entitled Esther, for several months—or even for an entire year—their bodies were treated with ointments, cosmetics, and perfumes [Note: In the better manuscripts, instead of *pigmentis*, “cosmetics,” we find *lomentis*. Others read *linimentis*. Two Vatican manuscripts read *fomentis aromatum*, “applications of aromatics.”] before they were joined to the royal body (Esther 2:12).

“During this period, therefore, the events that are recorded took place, until Pharaoh, crushed and terrified, restored the wife to her husband. But because Abimelech was prevented from intercourse with her by a dream, those who maintain that Sarah did not avoid violation suppose that the king could not have gone to sleep and dreamed unless he had first slept with her. As though—quite apart from the period during which, as I said above, the women’s bodies were prepared for royal pleasure—God could not have plunged him into sleep and warned him in a dream before they came together!”

### 3

I shall relate something that happened in Mauretania Sitifensis. For the God of the holy Fathers is also our God.

A certain young catechumen named Celticius [Note: Rat., Am., and the Sorbonne manuscript read *Celcichius*. Two Vatican codices read *Celitichius*. The Corbie and Floriacensis manuscripts read *Celticius*. The Germanensis manuscript reads *Cletitius*. In the letter of the Council of Carthage to Celestine, an eleventh bishop is named Celticius.] abducted a widow who was committed to a life of continence, intending to have her as his wife. Before they had intercourse, he was overcome by sleep and terrified by a dream. When the bishop of Sitifis demanded her most insistently, he returned her untouched.

The people of whom I speak are still alive. After being baptized, the man was converted to the Lord by the miracle that had occurred in his own case, and he eventually attained the episcopate through venerable integrity. The woman continues in holy widowhood.

### 4

What I said against Faustus the Manichaean, when he slandered the patriarch Abraham by claiming that he had sold his wife to two kings for intercourse, is shown by what I added. [Note: Some manuscripts read as here; others, with the printed editions, read *indignansque subjeci*, “and in indignation I added.”]

“But in calling the righteous and faithful man,” I said, “the most infamous trafficker in his own marriage, and asserting that, for the sake of greed and his belly, he lied to two kings, Abimelech and Pharaoh, at different times, saying that his wife Sarah was his sister because she was extremely beautiful, and sold her for intercourse, he does not distinguish honesty from disgrace with truthful speech, but with slanderous speech turns everything into a crime.

“This deed of Abraham may appear similar to pimping, but those who cannot rightly distinguish righteous acts from sins in the light of the eternal law may mistake constancy for obstinacy, the virtue of confidence for the vice of recklessness, and whatever similar objections are made against those who are not acting wrongly by people who do not see correctly.

“For Abraham did not consent to the disgrace of his wife or sell her adultery. Rather, just as Sarah did not hand over her maidservant to her husband’s lust but freely brought her to him for the duty of begetting children, without in any way disturbing the natural order—in which she had the power to command one who obeyed rather than yielding to one who desired—so Abraham kept silent about his chaste wife, who was joined to him with a chaste heart and whose mind, where the virtue of chastity dwelt, he had no reason to doubt. He called her his sister so that, if he were killed by foreigners and impious men, she would not be possessed by them as a captive. He was certain of his God: he would not allow her to suffer anything shameful or disgraceful.

“His faith and hope did not deceive him. Pharaoh, terrified by portents and afflicted with many evils because of her, learned by divine revelation that she was Abraham’s wife and restored her unharmed and with honor. Abimelech, likewise warned and instructed by a dream, did the same” (*Against Faustus* XXII.33).

## QUESTION VIII — Finally, concerning the Spirit of God who was borne over the waters: whether this is the Holy Spirit

### 1

Finally, you ask that I explain the Spirit of God who was borne over the waters.

“Some,” you say, “assert that this was the Holy Spirit; others call it a worldly spirit, saying that the historian could not enumerate the Creator together with created things, nor assign him any place, since he is wholly everywhere, together with the Father and the Son.”

### 2

What I understood concerning these matters I have transferred into this little work from the first book of the twelve books on Genesis that I wrote as best I could—not according to allegories, but according to the truth of the events.

“God possesses,” I said, “the highest, holy, and righteous goodness, together with a certain love for his works that proceeds not from need but from generosity. Therefore, before it was written, ‘God said, “Let there be light,”’ Scripture first said, ‘And the Spirit of God was borne over the waters.’

“Whether by the name ‘waters’ he wished to designate all bodily matter, thereby indicating the source from which everything that we can now discern in its various kinds was made and formed—for we see everything on earth fashioned and growing together in various forms from a moist nature, and therefore he called it water—or whether he meant a certain spiritual life, as yet formless and, as it were, flowing about before its conversion into form, the Spirit of God was certainly borne over it.

“For whatever it was that had begun to be formed and perfected, it lay subject to the good will of the Creator. Thus, when God said in his Word, ‘Let there be light,’ what had been made remained according to its kind within his good will, that is, within his good pleasure.
