And therefore it is rightly said that what pleased God was good: ‘And light came to be; and God saw that the light was good.’

“Thus, just as at the very beginning of the creation that had been initiated—the creation which is mentioned under the name of heaven and earth because of what was to be perfected from it—the Trinity of the Creator is intimated, so also in the conversion and perfection of creation, as its various forms are arranged, the same Trinity is intimated.

“For when Scripture says, ‘In the beginning God made heaven and earth,’ we understand the Father by the name ‘God,’ and the Son by the name ‘Beginning’: he is not the beginning of the Father, but of the spiritual creature created first and above all through him, and consequently of the whole creation.

“When Scripture says, ‘The Spirit of God was borne over the waters,’ we recognize a complete mention of the Trinity. Likewise, when it says, ‘God said,’ it signifies the Word of God and the Begetter of the Word; and when it says, ‘God saw that it was good,’ it signifies holy Goodness, in which God takes pleasure in whatever, according to the measure of its nature, is perfected in a way pleasing to him.”

### 3

“But why, after the imperfect creation had first been mentioned, is the Spirit of God mentioned afterward, since Scripture first says, ‘The earth was invisible and unformed, and darkness was over the abyss,’ and then adds, ‘And the Spirit of God was borne over the waters’ (Gen. 1:1–4)?

“Was it because needy and indigent love loves in such a way that it becomes subject to the things it loves? For this reason, when the Spirit of God was mentioned—as signifying his holy goodwill and love—he was said to be borne over them, so that God would not be thought to love the works he was about to make through the necessity of need rather than through the abundance of his generosity.

“Mindful of this, the Apostle, when he was about to speak of love, said that he would show a way that surpasses all others (1 Cor. 12:31); and elsewhere he says, ‘The love of Christ surpasses knowledge’ (Eph. 3:19).

“Since, therefore, it was necessary to signify the Spirit of God in such a way that he would be said to be borne over the waters, it was more fitting that something already begun should first be signified, over which he could be said to be borne—not in a spatial sense, but by a power that surpasses and excels all things” (*On the Literal Interpretation of Genesis* I.5–7, §§11–13).

## QUESTION V — Treated last: How David was chosen according to God’s heart. Christ called David

### 1

Now give your attention for a little while to the matter whose discussion I postponed. You ask: “Why did the Lord, who certainly foreknew the future, say, ‘I have chosen David according to my heart’ (1 Kings 8:16), when David himself committed such great and numerous offenses?”

### 2

If we understand this as referring to David himself, who became king of Israel after Saul had been rejected and killed, then precisely because God foreknew the future, he foresaw in David such great devotion and such sincere repentance that David would belong to the number of those of whom God himself says: “Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven and whose sins have been covered. Blessed is the man to whom the Lord has not imputed sin” (Ps. 32:1–2).

Since God foreknew that David would sin and would erase his sins through devout humility and sincere repentance, why should he not have said, “I have found David according to my heart”—a man to whom he would not impute sin, since David performed so many good works, lived with such devotion, and in that very devotion offered a sacrifice of a contrite spirit for his sins?

Because of all this it was most truly said, “I have found David according to my heart.” For although what David did in sinning was not according to God’s heart, what was according to God’s heart was that he made satisfaction for his sins through fitting repentance.

The only thing in David that was not according to God’s heart was the thing that God did not impute to him. Once this has been removed—that is, once it has not been imputed—what remains except that for which it could most truly be said, “I have found David according to my heart”?

### 3

But if we wish to understand this as prophetically spoken of Christ, no difficulty in the question arises—unless perhaps we ask how Christ could rightly be called by this name. We answer that this was on account of the seed of David, from which Christ assumed flesh.

Nor do we lack an example for explaining this name as applied to Christ. We find Jesus Christ most plainly called David by the prophet Ezekiel, where we read in the person of God the Father:

“‘I will raise up over my sheep one shepherd who will feed them, my servant David. He himself will feed them, and he himself will be their shepherd. I, the Lord, will be their God, and my servant David will be prince in their midst. I, the Lord, have spoken.

“‘And there shall be one king ruling over all, and there shall no longer be two nations, nor shall they be divided any longer into two kingdoms. They shall no longer defile themselves with their idols, their abominations, or any of their iniquities. I shall save them from all their settlements [Note: One Vatican manuscript reads *sordibus*, “filth,” instead of *sedibus*, “settlements.” The Septuagint has *anomion*, “iniquities.”] in which they sinned, and I shall cleanse them. They shall be my people, and I shall be their God; and my servant David shall be king over them, and there shall be one shepherd for all of them’” (Ezek. 34:23–24; 37:22–24).

The prophet Hosea also, when he foretold the period of the Jews such as they now have and their subsequent belief in Christ, prophesied of the same Christ under the name David, saying:

“For the children of Israel shall sit for many days without a king, without a prince, without sacrifice, without an altar, without priesthood, and without manifestations” (Hos. 3:4).

No one doubts that the Jews are now in this condition. But after the Apostle Paul had said, speaking to the Gentiles, “For just as you were once disobedient to God, but now have received mercy through their disobedience, so they too have now been disobedient through the mercy shown to you, so that they too may receive mercy” (Rom. 11:30–31), this prophet, foretelling the same thing long beforehand, continued:

“Afterward the children of Israel shall return and seek the Lord their God and David their king; and they shall be astonished at the Lord and at his good things in the last days” (Hos. 3:4–5).

Here too Christ was prophesied under the name David, since when these things were being prophesied, David, the king of Israel, had long ago fallen asleep. The Lord Jesus, however, was to come in the flesh from David’s seed; for this reason he was called David according to the prophetic manner of speech.

The Apostle Paul seems to have placed this testimony in the Acts of the Apostles in such a way that it could be understood only of that king David who succeeded Saul. For among other things he says:

“After this they asked for a king, and God gave them Saul the son of Kish, a man of the tribe of Benjamin, for forty years. After removing him, he raised up David as king for them, and he bore witness to him, saying, ‘I have found David the son of Jesse, a man according to my heart, who will do all my will’” (Acts 13:21–22).

But since Paul immediately continues and says, “From this man’s seed, according to the promise, God brought Israel a Savior, Jesus” (Acts 13:23), he indicated more profoundly that this testimony should be understood rather of the Lord Jesus, who truly did all the will of God the Father, than of King David.

For although, according to the preceding discussion, David may not unjustly be said to have been found according to God’s heart because his sins were forgiven and not imputed to him, and also because of his devout repentance, how did he do all God’s will? Although Scripture praised him most highly when it narrated his times and deeds, it nevertheless censured him because he did not destroy the high places where God’s people sacrificed contrary to God’s command. God had ordered that sacrifices be offered to him only in the tabernacle of testimony, although on those same high places sacrifices were also offered to the same God.

Those high places were later destroyed by Hezekiah, a king descended from David’s seed, with the testimony of his great praise (2 Kings 18:4).

### 4

I have answered your inquiries as best I could. If you have found, or are able to find, something better concerning these matters, we shall be most grateful if you let us know. For, as I also mentioned above about myself, I prefer learning to teaching.

# ON FAITH IN THINGS THAT ARE NOT SEEN

## Prefatory Notice to the Following Book

We have taken care to restore to Augustine the following little work, which the Louvain theologians had rejected as his and relegated to the Appendix, prefacing it with the following judgment, borrowed from Erasmus:

“This little book has been patched together from various letters of Augustine, especially as regards its sentences.”

Erasmus added that it seemed probable that the work was by Hugh of Saint-Victor. His conjecture is refuted even by the fact that the writing of this very book in the Gemmeticensis manuscript predates Hugh’s time, and that the book bears Augustine’s name at its beginning.

The subject matter and style do not recall Hugh but are wholly Augustinian. Moreover—and this escaped Erasmus—in Letter 231 to the comes Darius, discovered after the Frobenian edition and first published in the Louvain edition of Plantin, Augustine claims the book as his own in these words (§4):

“I have also sent other books that you did not request, so that I might not do only what you requested: *On Faith in Things That Are Not Seen*, *On Patience*, *On Continence*, *On Providence*, and one substantial work *On Faith, Hope, and Charity*.”

That passage evidently also escaped Bellarmine, who, following the Louvain theologians, was all the more willing to count this book among the spurious works because it is not recorded in the *Retractations*. Yet he himself regarded the books now mentioned, *On Patience* and *On Continence*, as genuine, even though they are not mentioned there, because they are cited by Possidius and Bede.

These little works are evidently among those popular treatises that, as Augustine writes to Quodvultdeus in Letter 224 (§2), remained to be revised together with his letters after he had completed two volumes reviewing his books.

Bernard Vinding, in his *Augustinian Critic*, agrees with us. He also rightly judges that the title prefixed in the printed editions, *On Faith in Invisible Things*, should be corrected, since the subject here is not only faith in things that can never be touched by bodily eyes, but also in certain things that, if they were presented to those eyes, could be seen.

Everyone will recognize from what is said in §10 about the destruction of idols that this little work should be placed after the year 399, when Honorius issued laws against idols.

## One Book by Saint Aurelius Augustine, Bishop of Hippo, on Faith in Things That Are Not Seen

[Note: Written after the year 399.]

[Note: *The Book on Faith in Things That Are Not Seen* has been corrected against two Sorbonne manuscripts, one Vatican manuscript, and the Gemmeticensis manuscript, and also against the editions of Amerbach, Erasmus, and the Louvain theologians.]

[Note: We also compared all the editions mentioned at the beginning of volume 1 of the *Retractations* and the *Confessions*. M.] (C)

In this book it is demonstrated that, in the Christian religion, we believe things that we do not see with our eyes not through blameworthy rashness but through praiseworthy faith.

## CHAPTER ONE

### 1

Even in human affairs many things that are not seen with the eyes are believed. The good will of a friend is not seen but believed. Even the benevolence of a tested friend is not established for us without some faith.

There are people who think that the Christian religion should be ridiculed rather than embraced because in it no visible object is displayed, but human beings are commanded to believe things that are not seen.

To refute these people, who think themselves wise for refusing to believe what they cannot see, we shall show that, although we cannot display to human eyes the divine realities that we believe, we can nevertheless demonstrate to human minds that even things that are not seen must be believed.

First, those who have been made so subject to the foolishness of their bodily eyes that they think nothing should be believed unless those eyes perceive it must be reminded how many things they not only believe but also know that cannot be seen by such eyes.

These things are innumerable even within our own mind, whose nature is invisible. To say nothing of the rest, what is more exposed, more clear, or more certain to the inner vision of the soul than faith itself, by which we believe, or the thought by which we know that we either believe or do not believe something? Yet these are wholly alien to the sight of bodily eyes.

How, then, should we not believe what we do not see with bodily eyes, when we see without any doubt that we either believe or do not believe precisely where we cannot employ bodily eyes?

### 2

“But,” they say, “since we can perceive the things that are in the mind with the mind itself, we do not need to know them through the eyes of the body. But the things you tell us to believe you neither display outwardly, so that we may know them through the eyes of the body, nor are they within our minds, so that we may see them by thinking.”

They speak as though someone would be commanded to believe something if, once it had already been presented to him, he could see what he was being asked to believe.

For this very reason we must believe certain temporal things that we do not see, so that we may also deserve to see the eternal things that we believe.

But whoever you are who do not wish to believe anything except what you see: you see present bodies with bodily eyes, and you see your present will and thoughts with your mind itself, because they are in your mind. Tell me, I beg you: with what eyes do you see your friend’s will toward you? No will can be seen with bodily eyes.

Or do you also see with your own mind what is taking place in another person’s mind? If you do not see it, how do you return the favor of friendly benevolence if you do not believe what you cannot see?

Perhaps you will say that you see another person’s will through his actions. Then you will see his deeds and hear his words, but you will believe what cannot be seen or heard concerning your friend’s will.

That will is not a color or shape that can be presented to the eyes, nor a sound or melody that can enter the ears; nor is it your own, so that you can sense it through the affection of your heart.

It remains, therefore, that you must believe what you have neither seen nor heard nor perceived inwardly within yourself [Note: Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read *conscripta*, “written down,” instead of *conspecta*, “perceived”], lest your life be left desolate without any friendship, or the love shown to you go unreturned by you.

Where, then, is the claim you made that you should believe only what you see either externally with the body or internally with the heart? Here you believe your heart in someone whose heart is not your own, and you extend faith toward one to whom you direct neither the gaze of the flesh nor that of the mind.

You see your friend’s face with your body; you see your own faith with your mind. But your friend’s faith cannot be loved by you unless there is also in you a mutual faith by which you believe what you do not see in him.

A human being can indeed deceive by feigning benevolence and concealing malice. Or, even if he does not intend to harm you, he may pretend because he expects some advantage from you and lacks charity.

### 3

“But,” you say, “I believe my friend, whose heart I cannot see, because I have tested him in my trials and learned what kind of disposition he had toward me from the fact that he did not abandon me in my dangers.”

Do you therefore think that, in order for the love of friends toward us to be tested, calamity should be desired for us? Will none of our most trusted friends be happy unless he has been made unhappy by adversity, so that he cannot enjoy the love of another unless he is tortured by his own pain or fear?

And how can the happiness of having true friends be something to desire rather than fear, if it can be tested only through unhappiness?

Yet it is true that a friend can be possessed even in prosperous circumstances, although he is tested more certainly in adversity.

## CHAPTER TWO
With faith removed from human affairs, what dreadful confusion would follow! Yet, in order to test him, you would not entrust yourself to your friend’s dangers unless you believed him; and thus, when you entrust yourself in order to test him, you believe before you test him. Certainly, if we ought not to believe in things not seen, since we also believe in the hearts of friends before they have been more certainly tested [Note: Erasmus, the Lyon edition, the Venetian edition, and the Louvain edition read this passage as follows: “Certainly, if you do not wish to believe in things, we ought not at any time to believe in the hearts of friends not yet more certainly tested.” Morel, *Critical Elements*, pp. 367–368, thinks it should be read: “Certainly, if we ought not to believe in things not seen, how do we believe in the hearts of friends not yet more certainly tested? And when we have proved their goodness by our misfortunes, do we even then believe their goodwill toward us rather than see it?” M.]; and when we have proved their goodness by our misfortunes, even then we believe their goodwill toward us rather than see it—unless, indeed, faith is so great that we reasonably judge, with a certain kind of eyes, that we see what we believe, since for that very reason we ought to believe: because we cannot see.

## 4. The removal of faith would destroy human society

If this faith were removed from human affairs, who would fail to notice how great a disturbance of them, and how dreadful a confusion, would follow? For who would be loved by anyone with mutual affection, since love itself is invisible, if I ought not to believe what I do not see? Thus all friendship would perish, because it consists only in mutual love. What, then, could friendship receive from anyone, if it were not believed that any of it had been shown?

Moreover, when friendship has perished, neither the bonds of marriage nor those of kinship and affinity will be preserved in the heart, because in these too there is surely a friendly agreement. A husband, therefore, will not be able to love his wife in return, when he does not believe that he is loved, because he cannot see the love itself. Nor will they desire to have children whom they do not believe will in turn repay their affection [Note: The Vatican manuscript reads, “whom they do not believe will in turn believe in them.”]. If such children are born and grow up, they will love their parents still less, since they will not see their parents’ love toward them in their hearts, because it is invisible—if invisible things are believed not with praiseworthy faith but with blameworthy rashness.

What should I now say about the other relationships: those of brothers, sisters, sons-in-law and fathers-in-law, and of all who are joined by blood or affinity, if affection is uncertain and intention suspect—both for children toward parents and parents toward children—when the proper goodwill is not returned [Note: Several manuscripts read, “because what is owed to goodwill is not returned.”]? For it is not thought to be owed when one does not believe that what is not seen exists in another.

Further, if this caution is not ingenious but hateful—when we do not believe that we are loved because we do not see the love of those who love us, and do not return it because we do not think that we owe them a mutual love—then human affairs are so disturbed if we do not believe what we do not see that they would be utterly overthrown if we believed no human intentions, which we plainly cannot see.

I pass over saying how many things those who rebuke us because we believe what we do not see believe on the authority of reputation and history, or concerning places where they themselves have not been; nor do they say, “We do not believe, because we have not seen.” For if they say this, they are forced to admit that their own parents are uncertain to them, since they believed this too on the testimony of others who could not nevertheless demonstrate it, because the event had already passed; they retain no sensory memory of that time, and yet without hesitation they give assent to others speaking about it. Unless this is done, it is necessary to incur impious faithlessness toward one’s parents, while, as though avoiding rashness in believing what we cannot see, one falls into it.

# CHAPTER III

## Evidence that confirms faith. Prophecies fulfilled concerning the Church

If, then, human society cannot stand when we refuse to believe what we cannot see, since concord has perished, how much more must faith be given to divine realities, even though they are not seen! If it is not given, not merely the friendship of individual human beings but religion itself in its highest form is violated, and the greatest misery follows.

### 5. The Church’s visible growth is evidence

“But,” you will say, “although I cannot see my friend’s goodwill toward me, I can investigate it by many indications; but you cannot show by any indications the things you want us to believe though unseen.”

For the moment, it is no small point that you admit that certain things—even things that are not seen—ought to be believed because of the clarity of certain indications. For thus it is established that not everything unseen is unbelievable, and that the statement, “We ought not to believe what we do not see,” lies discarded and refuted.

Those who think that we believe in Christ without any evidence about Christ are greatly mistaken. For what evidence could be clearer than what we now see having been foretold and fulfilled? Therefore, you who think there is no evidence why you ought to believe in Christ concerning things you have not seen [Note: Several manuscripts add after “things you have not seen”: “or do not see.”], consider what you do see.

The Church herself addresses you with the voice of a mother’s love:

“I, whom you marvel to see bearing fruit and growing throughout the whole world, was not at one time what you now see me to be. Yet it was said: ‘In your seed all nations shall be blessed’ (Genesis 22:18). When God blessed Abraham, he was promising me; for I am spread among all nations through the blessing of Christ.

“The succession of generations bears witness that Christ is the seed of Abraham. To gather this briefly: Abraham begot Isaac, Isaac begot Jacob, and Jacob begot twelve sons; from these the people of Israel arose. Jacob himself was called Israel. Among these twelve sons he begot Judah, from whom the name ‘Jews’ derives; from them was born the virgin Mary, who bore Christ.

“And behold: in Christ—that is, in the seed of Abraham—you see all nations blessed, and you are astonished; yet you still fear to believe in him, in whom you ought rather to have feared not to believe!

“Do you hesitate or refuse to believe in the birth from a virgin, when you ought rather to believe that it was fitting for the God-man to be born in this way? For this too you must accept as having been foretold through the prophet: ‘Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and they shall call his name Emmanuel,’ which is interpreted, ‘God with us’ (Isaiah 7:14).

“You will not, therefore, doubt the virgin giving birth if you are willing to believe in God being born: that he did not abandon the governance of the world, yet came to human beings in the flesh; that he granted fecundity to his mother without taking away her virgin integrity. It was fitting for man to be born in this way, although he was always God [Note: The manuscripts read: “It was fitting for man to be born in this way, if he was always God.”], so that by being born he might become God for us.”

Again, concerning him the prophet says [Note: Several manuscripts read: “Again, concerning this God.”]:

“Your throne, O God, is for ever and ever; the scepter of righteousness is the scepter of your kingdom. You have loved righteousness and hated iniquity; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions.”

This anointing is spiritual: God anointed God, namely, the Father anointed the Son. Hence we know that he was called *Christ* from *chrism*, that is, from anointing.

“I am the Church, concerning whom it is said in the same psalm, and as something future is announced as though it had already happened:

‘The queen stood at your right hand, clothed in gold, surrounded with variety’—that is, adorned in the mystery [Note: The manuscripts read this way; the printed editions have “in the sanctuary.”] of wisdom and in the variety of languages.

“There I am told:

‘Listen, daughter, and see; incline your ear; forget your people and your father’s house. For the king has desired your beauty, since he is himself your Lord God; and the daughters of Tyre shall worship him with gifts, and all the rich among the people shall entreat your face. All the glory of the king’s daughter is within, clothed with golden fringes and surrounded with variety. Virgins shall be brought to the king after her; her companions shall be brought to you. They shall be brought with joy and gladness; they shall be brought into the temple of the king. Instead of your fathers, sons have been born to you; you shall appoint them rulers over all the earth. They shall remember your name throughout every generation and generation. Therefore the peoples shall confess you for ever and ever’ (Psalm 44:7–18).”

### 6. The prophecies are fulfilled in the Church

If you do not see this queen, now also fruitful in royal offspring; if you do not see fulfilled what she heard promised, to whom it was said, “Listen, daughter, and see”; if she has not abandoned the former rites of the world, to whom it was said, “Forget your people and your father’s house”; if she does not confess Christ the Lord everywhere, to whom it was said, “The king has desired your beauty, since he is himself your Lord God”; if you do not see the cities of the nations pour out prayers to Christ and offer gifts, concerning whom it was said to her, “The daughters of Tyre shall worship him with gifts”; if the pride of the rich is not also laid aside, and they do not seek help from the Church, to whom it was said, “All the rich among the people shall entreat your face”; if she does not recognize the king’s daughter, who was commanded to say, “Our Father, who are in heaven” (Matthew 6:9), and is renewed day by day in her saints, in the inner person (2 Corinthians 4:16), concerning whom it was said, “All the glory of the king’s daughter is within”—although she also strikes the eyes of outsiders with the splendor of the reputation of her preachers, in the diversity of languages, as though with golden fringes and the varied colors of a garment [Note: Perhaps “shining.”];

if, after she has been proclaimed in any place by the good fragrance of her, consecrated virgins are not also brought to Christ, concerning whom it is said, and to whom it is said, “Virgins shall be brought to the king after her; her companions shall be brought to you.” And lest they seem to be brought as captives into some kind of prison, it says: “They shall be brought with joy and gladness; they shall be brought into the temple of the king.”

If she does not bear sons from whom she may have, as it were, fathers whom she appoints as rulers everywhere, to whom it is said, “Instead of your fathers, sons have been born to you; you shall appoint them rulers over all the earth”—sons whose prayers she commends herself to as both mother and superior and subject; hence what follows: “They shall remember your name throughout every generation and generation”;

if, because of the preaching of these same fathers, in which they remember her name without interruption, such great multitudes are not gathered into her, and do not confess the praise of grace to her without end in their own languages, to whom it is said, “Therefore the peoples shall confess you for ever and ever.”

# CHAPTER IV

## What we now see fulfilled should move us to believe what we have not seen

If these things are not shown to be so clear that the eyes of enemies find no direction in which to turn without being struck by the same clarity, so that they are compelled openly to confess it [Note: The manuscripts read “openly.”], then perhaps you rightly say that no evidence is shown to you by which, once you have seen it, you may believe even what you do not see.

But if these things that you see were foretold long beforehand and are fulfilled with such great clarity; if truth itself declares itself through effects preceding and following you—O remnants of unbelief, be ashamed at the things you see, so that you may believe what you do not see!

### 7. The Church’s present existence confirms the prophecies

“Look at me,” the Church says to you; “look at me, whom you see, even if you do not wish to see me.”

Those who were faithful in those times in the land of Judea learned, while present, the miraculous birth from a virgin, the passion, resurrection, and ascension of Christ, and all his divine sayings and deeds. You did not see these things; for that reason you refuse to believe them.

Therefore look at these things; fix your attention on them; consider these things that you see. They are not narrated to you as past events, nor foretold as future ones, but demonstrated as present realities.

Does it seem empty or insignificant to you? Do you think it no miracle, or only a small miracle of God, that the whole human race runs in the name of one crucified man?

You did not see what was foretold and fulfilled concerning Christ’s human birth: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a son.” But you see what was foretold and fulfilled in God’s word to Abraham: “In your seed all nations shall be blessed.”

You did not see what was foretold concerning Christ’s miracles: “Come and see the works of the Lord, the wonders he has placed upon the earth” (Psalm 45:9). But you see what was foretold:

“The Lord said to me: You are my Son; today I have begotten you. Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as your possession” (Psalm 2:7–8).

You did not see what was foretold and fulfilled concerning Christ’s passion:

“They pierced my hands and my feet; they counted all my bones. They themselves looked and gazed upon me; they divided my garments among themselves, and for my clothing they cast lots.”

But you see what was foretold in the same psalm and now appears fulfilled:

“All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord, and all the families of the nations shall worship in his presence; for the kingdom is the Lord’s, and he himself shall rule the nations” (Psalm 21:17–19, 28–29).

You did not see what was foretold and fulfilled concerning Christ’s resurrection, when the psalm spoke beforehand in his person about his betrayer and persecutors:

“They went out and spoke together as one; all my enemies whispered against me; against me they devised evil. They determined an evil word against me.”

Then, to show that they had achieved nothing by killing the one who would rise again, it added:

“Will not he who sleeps rise again?”

A little later, after the same prophecy had foretold concerning his betrayer what is also written in the Gospel—“He who ate my bread has magnified his heel against me,” that is, has trampled upon me—it immediately added:

“But you, Lord, have mercy on me and raise me up, and I will repay them” (Psalm 40:7–11; John 13:18).

This was fulfilled: Christ slept and awoke, that is, he rose again. In another psalm, through the same prophecy, he says:

“I slept and took my rest; and I rose, because the Lord will receive me” (Psalm 3).

You did not see this, but you do see his Church, concerning which it was likewise said and fulfilled:

“Lord my God, the nations shall come to you from the ends of the earth, and they shall say: Truly our fathers worshiped lies, idols, and there is no profit in them.”

Whether you wish it or not, you certainly see this: for even if you think there is, or was, some usefulness in idols, you have nevertheless heard innumerable peoples of the nations say, after abandoning, casting down, or breaking such vanities:

“Truly our fathers worshiped lies, idols, and there is no profit in them: for if a man makes gods, behold, they are not gods” (Jeremiah 16:19–20).

Do not suppose, however, that the nations foretold were to come to one particular place of God, since it was said, “The nations shall come to you from the ends of the earth.”

Understand, if you can, that the peoples of the nations come to the God of Christians, who is the supreme and true God, not by walking but by believing. For the same matter was foretold by another prophet in this way:

“The Lord,” he says, “will prevail against them and destroy all the gods of the earth; and all the islands of the nations shall worship him, each from his own place” (Zephaniah 2:11).

What the one prophet says—“All the nations shall come to you”—the other says as, “Each shall worship him from his own place.” Therefore they will come to him without leaving their place, because by believing in him they will find him in their heart.

You did not see what was foretold and fulfilled concerning Christ’s ascension:

“Be exalted above the heavens, O God.”

But you see what immediately follows:

“And your glory is over all the earth” (Psalm 107:6).

You did not see all those things concerning Christ that have already happened and passed away; but you do not deny that you see these present realities in his Church. We show you that both were foretold. Yet we cannot demonstrate both as things to be seen as fulfilled, because we cannot bring past events back before your eyes.

# CHAPTER V

## Present evidence establishes faith in past and future events

### 8. The visible present confirms the invisible past and future

But just as the unseen intentions of friends are believed through visible indications, so the Church, which is now seen, is both an indication of all the things that are not seen but are shown in those writings in which the Church herself was also foretold, and a witness to past events and a herald of future ones.

For when both the past—which can no longer be seen—and the present—which at that time could not yet be seen [Note: The manuscripts read: “which can now be seen, together with all the things…”]—were being foretold, none of these things could then be seen. When the foretold events began to occur, those things that had been foretold concerning Christ and the Church proceeded in ordered sequence from what had happened to what is now happening. To this sequence belong the day of judgment, the resurrection of the dead, the eternal condemnation of the ungodly with the devil, and the eternal reward of the godly with Christ; these too have been similarly foretold as future events.

Why, then, should we not believe the first and last events, which we do not see, when we have as witnesses the intermediate events, which we do see? In the prophetic books we either hear the first, middle, and last events foretold before they occurred, or read of them.

Unless perhaps unbelieving people think that these writings were composed by Christians so that the things they already believed might have greater authority if they were thought to have been promised before they came.

# CHAPTER VI

## The Jewish Scriptures support our faith. Why the Jewish sect was not completely destroyed

### 9. The Jewish Scriptures bear witness to Christ

If they suspect this, let them examine the writings of our enemies, the Jews. There let them read the things we have mentioned, foretold concerning Christ in whom we believe and concerning the Church whom we see, from the arduous beginning of faith [Note: The Vatican and Gallican manuscripts read, “from the beginning of the faith that we hold.” Some of these have, “from the beginning of arduous faith.”] to the everlasting blessedness of the kingdom.

When they read these things, however, let them not be surprised that those whose writings they are do not understand them because of the darkness of their hostility. For it was foretold long beforehand by the same prophets that they would not understand them. As the other prophecies had to be fulfilled, so by the hidden and just judgment of God the punishment due to their deserts had to be repaid to them.

For the one whom they crucified, and to whom they gave gall and vinegar, although, hanging upon the wood, he said to the Father on behalf of those whom he was going to lead from darkness into light, “Forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34), nevertheless, on behalf of the others whom he was going to abandon for more hidden reasons, foretold through the prophet long beforehand:

“They gave me gall for food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink. Let their table become a snare before them, and a recompense and a stumbling-block; let their eyes be darkened, so that they may not see, and bend their backs continually” (Psalm 68:22–24).

Thus they walk about everywhere with their eyes darkened, surrounded by the clearest testimonies to our cause, so that these are proved through them, while they themselves are rejected.

For this reason it happened that they were not so destroyed that the same sect ceased entirely to exist [Note: The better manuscripts read this way. The printed editions have, “so that the same deeds ceased entirely to exist.”]. Instead, they were scattered throughout the earth, so that, carrying the prophecies of the grace bestowed upon us, they might everywhere benefit us by more firmly convicting unbelievers.

Understand how this very matter was prophesied:

“Do not kill them,” he says, “lest they at some time forget your law; scatter them by your power” (Psalm 58:12).

They were therefore not killed, insofar as they did not forget what they read and heard among themselves. For if the Jews had completely forgotten the sacred Scriptures, although they did not understand them, they would have been killed within the Jewish rite itself; for, knowing nothing of the Law and the Prophets, they could not benefit anyone.

Therefore they were not killed but scattered, so that, although they did not possess the faith by which they might be saved [Note: The Vatican manuscript reads, “although they did not possess faith…”], they might nevertheless retain in their memory what would assist us: in the books, our supporters; in their hearts, our enemies; in their writings, our witnesses.

# CHAPTER VII

## The faith of the whole world in Christ wonderfully established

### 10. The world’s conversion to Christ

Even if no testimonies concerning Christ and the Church had preceded them, who should not have been moved to believe when we see that divine illumination has suddenly shone upon the human race? False gods have been abandoned, their idols everywhere broken, temples overthrown or converted to other uses, and so many vain rites rooted out from the extremely ancient custom of humanity; one true God is invoked by all.

And this has been accomplished through one man who was mocked, seized, bound, scourged, struck in the face [Note: The printed editions have “stripped.” The manuscripts have *expalmatum*, a word familiar to Augustine.], reviled, crucified, and killed by human beings. His disciples—whom he chose to commend his teaching, though they were ignorant, untrained, fishermen, and tax collectors—announced his resurrection and ascension, which they said they had seen. Filled with the Holy Spirit, they proclaimed this Gospel in all the languages they had not learned.

Some of those who heard them believed; others, refusing to believe, fiercely resisted the preachers. Thus, while the faithful fought for the truth even to death—not repaying evil with evil but enduring it, and conquering not by killing but by dying—the world was changed to this religion, and the hearts of mortals—men and women, children and adults, learned and unlearned, wise and foolish, powerful and weak, noble and lowly, exalted and humble—were turned to this Gospel.

The Church spread throughout all nations and grew so greatly that even against the Catholic faith no perverse sect or kind of error arises that is so opposed to Christian truth that it does not seek and strive to glory in the name of Christ. It would not be allowed to spring up throughout the earth unless even this contradiction exercised a salutary discipline.

How much could that crucified man have accomplished if God had not assumed a human being—even if the prophets had foretold none of these future events? But since so great a mystery of piety had prophets and heralds who preceded it [Note: The printed editions have “and believing prophets.” The reading has been corrected with the help of the manuscripts.], whose divine voices foretold it, and since he came in the manner in which he had been foretold, who could be so insane as to say that the apostles lied about Christ? They proclaimed that he had come in the manner in which the prophets had previously foretold that he would come—and the prophets did not remain silent about the true things that would happen to the apostles themselves.

For concerning them they had said:

“There are no speech or words whose voices are not heard; their sound has gone out through all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Psalm 18:4–5).

We certainly see this fulfilled throughout the world, even though we have not yet seen Christ in the flesh.

Who, then, unless blinded by astonishing madness, or hardened and made ironlike by astonishing obstinacy, would refuse to trust the sacred Scriptures, which foretold the faith of the whole world?

# CHAPTER VIII

## Exhortation to steadfast observance of the faith

### 11. Perseverance in faith

But you, beloved, who possess this faith—or who have only now begun to possess it—may it be nourished and grow within you. For just as the temporal things foretold so long beforehand have come, so the eternal promises will also come.

Let neither vain pagans, nor false Jews, nor deceitful heretics deceive you; nor the evil Christians within the Catholic Church itself, who are all the more harmful because they are enemies from within.

For divine prophecy also did not remain silent about this, lest the weak be disturbed. In the *Song of Songs*, the bridegroom speaks to the bride—that is, Christ the Lord to the Church:

“As a lily among thorns,” he says, “so is my beloved among the daughters” (Song of Songs 2:2).

He did not say, “among strangers,” but “among daughters.”

Let anyone who has ears to hear, hear. And when the net cast into the sea, which gathers every kind of fish, as the holy Gospel says, is drawn to the shore—that is, to the end of the age—let each person separate himself from the bad fish in heart, not in body, by changing his evil conduct, not by tearing the holy nets. Otherwise those who now appear, as tested people, to be mixed with the rejected will find not eternal life but eternal punishment [Note: Some manuscripts read: “so that those who now appear, as tested people, to be mixed with the rejected, may find not punishment but life.”] when they begin to be separated on the shore (Matthew 13:9, 47–50).

[Col. 0181]

[Note: For the book *On Faith and the Creed*, see Book 1, chapter 17, of the *Retractations*, volume 1, column 612, from the words “At that same time” through the words in column 613, “For it is written.” M.]

## Saint Aurelius Augustine, Bishop of Hippo: One Book on Faith and the Creed

[Note: Written in the year 393.]

[Note: We corrected the book *On Faith and the Creed* with the aid of ancient exemplars from various Gallican libraries: namely, from the Colbert Library; the library of the Abbey of Saint Victor in Paris; likewise the Sorbonne College; the College of Navarre; the monastery of Saint-Germain-des-Prés; Saint Remigius of Reims; Saint Michael in Periculo Maris; Saint Arnulf of Metz; the Church of Laon; and two manuscripts from the Vatican Library. We were also aided by various readings from two Belgian manuscripts examined by the theologians of Louvain, as well as by previously published editions: the Frobenian edition of Erasmus and the Plantinian edition of the Louvain scholars.]

[Note: We also compared all the editions mentioned at the beginning of the *Retractations* and the *Confessions*, volume 1. M.]

(C)

The individual articles of the Creed are carefully explained, together with a refutation of heretics opposed to the Catholic faith, especially the Manichaeans.

# CHAPTER I

[Col. 0181]

### 1. The reason for and purpose of the present work

Since it is written and confirmed by the strongest authority of apostolic teaching, “The righteous person lives by faith” (Habakkuk 2:4; Galatians 3:11), and since this faith requires from us the duty of both heart and tongue—for the Apostle says, “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Romans 10:10)—we ought to be mindful both of righteousness and of salvation.

Since we are destined to reign in everlasting righteousness, we cannot be saved from the present evil age unless, striving also for the salvation of our neighbors, we confess with our mouths the faith that we carry in our hearts. We must provide for this with devout and careful vigilance, lest the faith be violated in us in any respect by the deceptive cunning of heretics.

The Catholic faith is known to the faithful in the Creed and committed to memory, expressed with as much brevity as the subject permits. Thus, for beginners and infants—those reborn in Christ who have not yet been strengthened by the most careful and spiritual study and understanding of the divine Scriptures—it was established in a few words what would have to be expounded in many words to those making progress and rising toward divine teaching with firm humility and charity.

Under the very few words established in the Creed, many heretics have attempted to conceal their poisons. Divine mercy has resisted and continues to resist them through spiritual men who have been worthy not only to receive and believe the Catholic faith in those words, but also, with the Lord revealing it, to understand and know it.

For it is written, “Unless you believe, you will not understand” (Isaiah 7:9, according to the Septuagint). The exposition of the faith, however, serves to fortify the Creed—not so that it should be committed to memory and recited instead of the Creed by those receiving the grace of God, but so that it may guard what is retained in the Creed against the snares of heretics with Catholic authority and a more secure defense.

# CHAPTER II

### 2. No nature coeternal with God existed from which he made the world. How the world was made from nothing if it was made from unformed matter

Some have attempted to persuade people that God the Father is not omnipotent—not because they have dared to say this, but because they are shown to think and believe it in their traditions.

When they say that there is a nature which omnipotent God did not create, but from which he fashioned this world, which they admit to be beautifully ordered [Note: The printed editions have “adorned.” The manuscripts have “ordered.”], they deny God’s omnipotence in this way: they do not believe that he could have made the world unless, in fashioning it, he used another nature that already existed and that he himself had not made. Their understanding is shaped by the bodily habit of seeing craftsmen, builders of houses, and artisans of every kind, who cannot bring their art to completion unless prepared material assists them.

Thus they understand the maker of the world not to be omnipotent if he could not fashion the world unless some nature not fashioned by him assisted him as matter [Note: Two manuscripts read, “who could not fashion the world…”]. Or, if they admit that God is the omnipotent maker of the world, they must necessarily confess that he made from nothing the things he made. For nothing can exist whose creator he would not be, since he is omnipotent.

Even if he made something from something else, as he made man from clay, he did not make it from something that he himself had not made; for he made the earth, from which clay comes, from nothing.

And if he made heaven and earth—that is, the world and all that is in it—from some matter, as it is written, “You made the world from invisible matter” (Wisdom 11:18), or from unformed matter, as certain copies read, it is in no way to be believed that that very matter from which the world was made—although unformed, although invisible, whatever its condition—could have existed by itself, as coeternal and coeval with God.

Rather, whatever mode of existence it possessed, by which it could in any way exist and receive the forms of distinct things, it possessed only from omnipotent God. Through his beneficence exists not only everything that has been formed, but also everything that can be formed.

The difference between the formed and the formable is that the formed has already received a form, whereas the formable can receive one. But he who grants things their form also grants them the capacity to be formed, because from him and in him is the most beautiful, unchangeable form of all things. Therefore he alone grants to every thing not only that it be beautiful but also that it be able to be beautiful.

Accordingly, we most rightly believe that God made all things from nothing. For even if the world was made from some matter, that same matter was made from nothing, so that, by God’s perfectly ordered gift, the first capacity for forms might be brought into being [Note: Four manuscripts read, “first,” rather than “first capacity,” in the corresponding construction], and afterward all formed things might be formed.

We have said this so that no one may think the statements of the divine Scriptures contradict one another, since it is written both that God made all things from nothing and that the world was made from unformed matter.

### 3. The Son is the Word through whom all things were made

Since we believe in God the Father Almighty, we ought to consider that there is no creature that was not created by the omnipotent God.

And because he created all things through the Word—which is also called Truth (John 14:6), and the Power and Wisdom of God (1 Corinthians 1:24), and is indicated by many other names by which Jesus Christ the Lord is commended to our faith—namely, as our liberator and ruler, the Son of God [Note: The Colbert manuscript reads, “creator”—the Son of God]—the Word through whom all things were created could have been begotten only by the one who created all things through him.

# CHAPTER III

## Why the Son of God is called the Word. The Word is identical with the Father

We also believe in Jesus Christ, the Son of God, the only-begotten—that is, the unique—Son of the Father, our Lord.

We must not understand this Word in the same way as our words, which, uttered by voice and mouth, pass through the struck air and remain no longer than they sound. That Word remains unchangeably, for concerning it was said, when Wisdom was being spoken of, “Remaining in herself, she renews all things” (Wisdom 7:27).

It is called the Word of the Father because through it the Father is made known. Thus, when we speak truthfully, we use our words to make our mind known to the listener, and whatever secret thing we carry in our heart is brought through such signs to the knowledge of another.

In the same way, that Wisdom whom God the Father begot is most fittingly called his Word, because through her the most secret Father makes himself known to worthy minds [Note: The Ambrosian and Louvain editions read, “the most secret mind of the Father makes itself known”; Erasmus reads, “the most secret Father makes himself known through signs.” Six manuscripts read, “the most secret Father makes himself known to worthy minds.” This reading is more likely partly because below, in section 4, it says that he indicates himself to minds, and partly because in the other manuscripts after the verb “makes known” there appears “the fire of the mind” or “the signs of the mind.”].

### 4. The Word is not the same as our words

There is, however, a very great difference between our mind and our words, by which we try to reveal that same mind. For we do not beget words that sound, but make them; and in making them, the body serves as their underlying material. There is, moreover, a very great difference between mind and body. But when God begot the Word, he begot what he himself is—not from nothing, nor from some already existing and fashioned material, but from himself, what he himself is.

We too attempt this when we speak, if we carefully consider the impulse of our will—not when we lie, but when we speak the truth. For what else do we strive to do than to bring our very mind, if possible [Col. 0184], into the mind of the hearer so that it may be known and perceived: while we ourselves remain in ourselves and do not depart from ourselves, yet bring forth such an indication by which our knowledge may be produced in another, so that, as far as ability permits [Note: Several manuscripts read, “as far as it permits.”], something like another mind may be brought forth from one mind, through which it may reveal itself?

We do this by striving with words [Note: Three manuscripts of better quality read, “with the sounding birth of the word.” Perhaps one should read, “striving with the birth of the word.” Morel, *Elem. crit.*, p. 94, reads: “with the sounding offspring of the word.” M.], with the very sound of the voice, with facial expression, and with bodily gesture—using so many devices, naturally, because we wish to display what is within us. For we cannot bring forth something of this kind, and therefore the mind of the speaker cannot become completely known; hence an opening is also left for lies.

But God the Father, who both truly willed and was able to reveal himself to minds that would come to know him, begot for the purpose of revealing himself that which is himself, namely, the one who begot it. He is also called his Power and Wisdom, because through him God worked and ordered all things. Concerning him, therefore, it is said: “He reaches mightily from end to end, and orders all things sweetly” (Wisdom 8:1).

## Chapter IV

### 5. The Son of God was neither made nor made lesser than the Father. “To create” and “to make” mean the same thing. Why the Son of God became man. Against the Manichaean heresy. The whole man assumed by the Word. Christ’s birth from a woman. Against the Manichaeans.

Accordingly, the only-begotten Son of God was not made by the Father, because, as the Evangelist says, “All things were made through him” (John 1:3). Nor was he begotten in time, since God, eternally wise, eternally possesses his Wisdom with him. [Note: The printed editions read *sempiternus* (“everlasting”); all the manuscripts read *sempiterne* (“eternally”).] Nor is he unequal to the Father—that is, lesser in any respect—for the Apostle also says: “Although he existed in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized” (Philippians 2:6).

By this catholic faith, therefore, those people too are excluded who say that the Son is the very same person as the Father. For this Word could not be “with God” unless he were with God the Father, and no one is equal to one who is alone.

Those too are excluded who say that the Son is a creature, even though not such as the other creatures are. For whatever creature they may say he is, if he is a creature, he has been made and created. For “to make” means the same as “to create,” although in ordinary Latin usage *creare* is sometimes used for “to beget”; Greek distinguishes the terms. What we call a creature they call *κτίσμα* or *κτίσις* (*ktisma* or *ktisis*); and when we wish to speak without ambiguity, we do not say “to create,” but “to make.” Therefore, if the Son is a creature, however great he may be, he has been made.

But we believe in the one through whom all things were made, not in one through whom the other things were made. For we cannot understand “all things” here in any other way than as meaning whatever has been made.

### 6. Why the Son of God became man

But because “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14), that same Wisdom which was begotten from God also deigned to be created among human beings. [Note: The Remigianus manuscript reads “among all things,” that is, “among all the things that have been made”; and this is not unreasonable.]

This is the meaning of the statement: “The Lord created me at the beginning of his ways” (Proverbs 8:22). For the beginning of his ways is the head of the Church, which is Christ [Col. 0185] [Note: This is how the manuscripts read. The printed editions have: “Christ is the beginning and head of the Church.”], clothed in human form. Through him an example of living was to be given to us—that is, a sure way [Note: The printed editions read, “this is a sure way.” The manuscripts instead read, “that is a sure way.” Four of them have, “a straight way.”] by which we might reach God.

For we could not return except through humility, since we fell through pride, as was said to our first creation: “Taste, and you will be like gods” (Genesis 3:5). Therefore our Restorer himself deigned to display in himself the example of this humility—that is, the way by which we had to return. He “did not regard equality with God as something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Philippians 2:6–7), so that man might be created at the beginning of his ways—the Word through whom all things were made.

Therefore, insofar as he is the only-begotten Son, he has no brothers; but insofar as he is the firstborn, he has deigned to call brothers all those who, after his primacy and through his primacy, are reborn by adoption as sons into the grace of God (Luke 8:21), as apostolic discipline commends [Note: The printed editions read “teaching,” in place of which the manuscripts have “discipline.”] (Hebrews 2:11).

The natural Son, therefore, was born alone from the very substance of the Father, existing as what the Father is [Note: This is how the manuscripts read. The commonly circulated editions have, “existing as the same as God the Father.”]: God from God, Light from Light. We, however, are not naturally light; rather, we are illumined by that Light so that we may shine with wisdom. For, he says, “There was the true Light, which enlightens every human being coming into this world” (John 1:9).

To our faith, then, in eternal realities we add the temporal dispensation of our Lord, which he deigned to undertake and administer for our salvation. For insofar as he is the only-begotten Son of God, he cannot be called “Was” or “Will be,” but only “Is”: for what was no longer is, and what will be does not yet exist. He therefore is unchangeable, without the conditions and variations of time.

I do not think that anything else is meant by the fact that he disclosed this name of his to his servant Moses. When Moses asked him what he should say if the people to whom he was being sent despised him and asked by whom he had been sent, he received the answer: “I am who I am.” Then he added: “Thus you shall say to the children of Israel: ‘He who is has sent me to you’” (Exodus 3:14).

### 7. Nothing can be contrary to God

From this, I trust, it is already clear to spiritual minds that no nature can be contrary to God. For if he is—and this word can properly be said of God alone—then God has nothing contrary to him. What truly is remains unchangeably; for what changes was something that is no longer, and will be something that is not yet.

If we were asked what is contrary to white, we would answer “black.” If we were asked what is contrary to hot, we would answer “cold.” If we were asked what is contrary to swift [Note: In B., “if one were asked what is contrary to swift.” Erasmus, the Lyons and Venetian editions, and Lovanius follow this reading; we have followed them. M.], we would answer “slow,” and so on with similar examples. But when we are asked what is contrary to that which is, the correct answer is “that which is not.”

### 8. The Son’s birth from the Virgin and the assumption of the whole human being

But since, as I have said, through a temporal dispensation [Col. 0186] for our salvation and restoration, with the goodness of God at work, our changeable nature was assumed by that unchangeable Wisdom of God, we add to our faith the temporal events beneficially accomplished for us. We believe in that Son of God who was born through the Holy Spirit from the Virgin Mary.

For by the gift of God—that is, by the Holy Spirit—such humility was granted to us on the part of so great a God that he deigned to assume the whole human being in the womb of the Virgin, inhabiting the maternal body while it remained intact and leaving it intact. [Note: Emmanuel Sa thought that *deserens* (“leaving”) should be read *deferens* (“bringing forth”). But all the manuscripts have *deserens*, a word signifying that nothing was taken away from the integrity of the Virgin mother by Christ’s birth.]

Heretics attack this temporal dispensation in many ways. But if someone holds the catholic faith and believes that the whole human being was assumed by the Word of God—that is, body, soul, and spirit—he is sufficiently armed against them. Since this assumption was carried out for our salvation, we must take care lest, by believing that something belonging to us did not pertain to this assumption, we conclude that it does not pertain to salvation.

Apart from the form of its limbs—which has been assigned differently to different kinds of animals—a human being differs from an animal only through the rational spirit, which is also called the mind. How, then, can the faith be sound which believes that God’s Wisdom assumed from us what we share with animals, but did not assume what is illumined by the light of wisdom and what is proper to the human being?

### 9. Christ truly had a human mother

Those too must be detested who deny that our Lord Jesus Christ had Mary as his mother on earth. That dispensation honored both sexes, male and female, and showed that both pertain to God’s care—not only the one whom he assumed, but also the one through whom he assumed humanity: by bearing a male and by being born from a woman.

Nor does what he said compel us to deny that Christ had a mother: “What is there between me and you, woman? My hour has not yet come” (John 2:4). Rather, it admonishes us to understand that, according to his divinity, he did not have a mother, since he was preparing to display the majesty of his person by changing water into wine.

But when he was crucified, he was crucified according to his humanity. That was the hour that had not yet come when he said, “What is there between me and you? My hour has not yet come”—that is, the hour at which he would recognize her. Then, as a human being crucified, he recognized the human being who was his mother and most humanely entrusted her to his beloved disciple (John 19:26–27).

Nor should the following disturb us: when he was told that his mother and brothers were seeking him, he replied, “Who is my mother, or who are my brothers?” and so forth (Matthew 12:48). Rather, this should teach us that in our ministry, by which we minister the word of God to our brothers, parents should not be acknowledged when they hinder that ministry.

For if someone should think that Christ therefore did not have a mother on earth because he said, “Who is my mother?”, he must also be compelled to deny that the Apostles had fathers on earth, since Christ commanded them: “Do not call anyone your father on earth; for one is your Father, who is in heaven” (Matthew 23:9).

### 10. The purity of Christ’s birth

[Col. 0187] Nor should reflection on a woman’s womb weaken this faith for us, so that our Lord’s birth might seem for that reason to be rejected, as though sordid people consider it sordid. For the Apostle says with complete truth that “the foolishness of God is wiser than human beings” (1 Corinthians 1:25), and that “to the pure all things are pure” (Titus 1:15).

Those who think otherwise should look at the rays of the sun. They certainly do not praise the sun as a creature of God, but worship it as a god [Note: The Manichaeans]. Yet its rays spread everywhere through the foulness of sewers and through every kind of horrible place, and work there according to their nature without becoming filthy through any contamination. Visible light is naturally more closely connected with visible filth; how much less, then, could the Word of God—neither bodily nor visible—be polluted by a female body, where he assumed human flesh together with soul and spirit, through the intervention of which the majesty of the Word dwells more secretly in the frailty of the human body [Note: This is how Lovanius and some manuscripts read. Others, with Erasmus, have “in the frailty of the human body.”].

It is therefore evident that the Word of God could in no way have been defiled by a human body, since not even the human soul itself was defiled by it. The soul is not defiled by the body when it governs and gives it life, but when it desires the body’s mortal goods. If those people wished to avoid the soul’s defilements, they should fear these lies and sacrileges instead.

## Chapter V

### 11. Christ’s passion and burial. Christ’s resurrection.

Our Lord’s humility in being born was small in comparison with what he did for us: he also deigned to die for mortals. “He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death—even death on a cross” (Philippians 2:8), so that none of us, even if he could cease to fear death, might shrink from some kind of death that human beings consider especially disgraceful.

We therefore believe in him who was crucified under Pontius Pilate and buried. The name of the judge had to be added for the sake of identifying the time.

When that burial is believed, it also recalls the new tomb [Note: The printed editions read “testament.” The manuscripts more correctly read “tomb.”], which would provide testimony to the one who was to rise to the newness of life, just as the virginal womb had provided testimony to the one who was to be born. For just as no other dead person was buried in that tomb, either before or afterward (John 19:41), so nothing mortal was conceived in that womb, either before or afterward.

### 12. The resurrection on the third day

We also believe that he rose from the dead on the third day, becoming the firstborn among the brothers who were to follow, whom he called to adoption as sons of God (Ephesians 1:5), and whom he deigned to make his fellow participants and coheirs.

## Chapter VI

### 13. The ascension into heaven

We believe that he ascended into heaven. He also promised us this place of blessedness, saying, “They will be like the angels in heaven” (Matthew 22:30), in that city which is “the mother of us all,” the eternal Jerusalem in heaven (Galatians 4:26).

What we believe—that an earthly body was taken into heaven [Col. 0188]—often offends either impious Gentiles or heretics. Gentiles frequently try to argue with us on the basis of philosophers’ arguments, saying that nothing earthly can exist in heaven. They do not know our Scriptures, nor do they understand how the statement should be taken: “It is sown an animal body; it rises a spiritual body.”

This was not said as though the body were changed into spirit and became spirit. Even now our body, which is called animal, has not been changed into soul and become soul. Rather, a spiritual body is understood as one so subjected to the spirit [Note: Erasmus and three manuscripts read, “because it must be so adapted.”] that it is suited to a heavenly dwelling, with all earthly fragility and corruption changed and transformed into heavenly purity and stability.

This is the change of which the Apostle also says: “We shall all rise, but we shall not all be changed.” The same Apostle teaches that this change is not for the worse but for the better when he says, “And we shall be changed” (1 Corinthians 15:44, 51–52).

But where and how the Lord’s body exists in heaven is a matter that is excessively curious and unnecessary to investigate. We must simply believe that it is in heaven. It is not our weakness to scrutinize heaven’s secrets; it is our faith to think exalted and honorable thoughts about the dignity of the Lord’s body.

## Chapter VII

### 14. His sitting at the right hand of the Father

We also believe that he sits at the right hand of the Father. Yet we must not therefore imagine that God the Father is bounded by a human form, so that when we think of him a right or left side comes to mind. Nor should we suppose that the Father’s being said to sit means that he sits with bent knees, lest we fall into the sacrilege for which the Apostle condemns those who “exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of corruptible man” (Romans 1:23).

For a representation of this kind may not be placed by a Christian in a temple dedicated to God; much more impious would it be to place it in the heart, where the true temple of God is, if it is cleansed of earthly desire and error.

Therefore, “at the right hand” should be understood to mean the highest blessedness, where justice, peace, and joy are found. In the same way, the goats are placed at the left hand (Matthew 25:33), that is, in misery, because of iniquities, labors [Note: Three manuscripts read, “because of the labors of iniquity.”], and sufferings.

When God is said to sit, therefore, this signifies not the position of limbs but judicial authority, a power of which that majesty is never deprived, always giving what is worthy to those who are worthy. In the final judgment, however, the unmistakable splendor of the only-begotten Son of God, judge of the living and the dead, will be much more openly displayed [Note: This is how the manuscripts read. The printed editions have, “will shine forth.”].

## Chapter VIII

### 15. His coming to judgment

We also believe that he will come from there at the most appropriate time and judge the living and the dead. These names may signify the righteous and sinners; or “the living” may refer to those whom he will find still on earth before our death [Note: The printed editions add “our”; the manuscripts reject it], while “the dead” refers to those who will rise at his coming.

This temporal dispensation is not merely—as is that generation according to God—but also was and will be. For our Lord was on earth, is now in heaven, and will be the judge of the living and the dead in glory. [Col. 0189] “He will come in the same way as you saw him go,” according to the testimony contained in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 1:11).

It is therefore with reference to this temporal dispensation that he speaks in the Apocalypse, where it is written: “Thus says he who is, and who was, and who is to come” [Note: The printed editions read, “who will be.” The manuscripts read, “who is to come.” In Greek: *ho erchomenos*, “the one who is coming.”] (Revelation 1:8).

## Chapter IX

### 16. Faith in the Holy Spirit. The mystery of the Trinity explained by analogies. The Christian confession of faith. The opinion of some concerning the Holy Spirit: that he is the very deity of the Father and the Son. Holiness derived from “sanctifying.”

After the faith in our Lord’s divine generation and human dispensation has been set forth and commended, the Holy Spirit is added to our confession in order to complete the faith we hold concerning God. He is of no lesser nature than the Father and the Son but, so to speak, consubstantial and coeternal, because this Trinity is one God.

This does not mean that the Father is the same as the Son and the Holy Spirit, but that the Father is Father, the Son is Son, and the Holy Spirit is the Holy Spirit, while this Trinity is one God, as it is written: “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one God” (Deuteronomy 6:4).

Nevertheless, if we are asked about each individually—“Is the Father God?”—we answer, “God.” If it is asked whether the Son is God, we give the same answer. When the same question is asked about the Holy Spirit, we must answer that he is God, taking great care not to understand this in the way in which it was said of human beings: “You are gods” (Psalm 81:6).

For those who have been made and created from the Father through the Son by the gift of the Holy Spirit are not gods by nature. The Trinity itself is signified when the Apostle says: “From him and through him and in him are all things” (Romans 11:36).

Although, therefore, when questioned about each one—whether Father, Son, or Holy Spirit—we answer that the one being asked about is God, no one should suppose that we worship three gods.

### 17. Analogies for the unity of the Trinity

Nor is it surprising that such things are said about an ineffable nature, since something similar occurs even in those things that we see with bodily eyes and distinguish by bodily sensation.

When asked about a spring, we cannot say that the spring itself is a river; nor, when asked about a river, can we call it a spring. Again, the drink that comes from a spring or river cannot be called either a river or a spring. Yet in this threefold relation we call them water; and when each is asked about individually, we answer “water.”

If I ask whether there is water in the spring, the answer is “water.” If we ask whether there is water in the river, nothing else is answered; and regarding the drink, no other answer can be given. Yet we do not call them three waters, but one water.

We must certainly take care not to imagine the ineffable substance of that majesty as though it were this visible and bodily spring, river, or drink. In these cases, the water that is now in the spring flows out into the river and does not remain in itself. [Col. 0190] When it passes from the river or spring into the drink, it does not remain where it was taken from.

Thus it is possible for the same water to belong now to the designation “spring,” now to “river,” and now to “drink.” In the Trinity, however, it is impossible for the Father at one time to be the Son and at another time the Holy Spirit.

The same may be seen in a tree. We can speak of the root only as root, of the trunk only as trunk, and of the branches only as branches. What is called the root cannot be called the trunk and branches; nor can the wood belonging to the root pass over and be now in the root, now in the trunk, and now in the branches. It is only in the root.

Yet the rule governing the names remains: the root is wood, the trunk is wood, and the branches are wood; nevertheless they are not called three woods, but one.

Or, if these have some dissimilarity so that they may not unreasonably be called three woods because of their differing degrees of firmness, everyone will nevertheless grant that if three cups are filled from one spring, they may be called three cups, but cannot be called three waters; they must be called one water. When asked about each cup, you answer that there is water in each, although no transfer takes place here as we learned takes place from the spring into the river.

These bodily examples have not been given because of a likeness to the divine nature, but because of the unity even of visible things. They show that some three things can receive not only individually but also together one singular name. Thus no one should be surprised or think it absurd that we call the Father God, the Son God, and the Holy Spirit God, yet do not call the Trinity three gods, but one God and one substance. [Note: The manuscripts read, “but that we worship one God and one substance.”]

### 18. The Father and the Son

Concerning the Father and the Son, learned and spiritual men have written many books. As far as human beings could explain to human beings, they have tried to indicate both how the Father and the Son are not one person but are one, and what properly belongs to the Father and what to the Son.

The Father is the begetter, the Son the begotten. The Father is not from the Son; the Son is from the Father. The Father is the Son’s beginning, and therefore is also called the head of Christ (1 Corinthians 11:3), although Christ too is called “beginning” (John 8:25), but not the beginning of the Father. The Son is the Father’s image (Colossians 1:15), although in no respect unlike him and entirely equal without distinction.

Those who wish to explain the whole Christian confession of faith less briefly than we do treat these matters more extensively. Accordingly, insofar as he is Son, the Son received from the Father that he should exist, whereas the Father did not receive this from the Son. And insofar as he assumed mutable human nature—destined to be changed for the better—in an ineffable mercy and through a temporal dispensation, many statements about him are found in Scripture which have led the impious minds of heretics, eager to teach before they understood, into error. They have therefore thought that he was not equal to the Father and was not of the same substance.

Such statements include: “The Father is greater than I” (John 14:28); “The husband is the head of the woman, Christ is the head of the man, and God is the head of Christ” (1 Corinthians 11:3); [Col. 0191] “Then he himself will be subject to the one who subjected all things to him” (1 Corinthians 15:28); “I am going to my Father and your Father, my God and your God” (John 20:17); and others of this kind.

All these statements were not made to signify an inequality of nature and substance, which would make the following statements false: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30); “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father” (John 14:9); “The Word was God”—for he was not made, since all things were made through him (John 1:1, 3); “He did not regard equality with God as something to be seized”; and other such statements.

Rather, the former statements were made partly because of the administration of the humanity he assumed, of which it is said, “He emptied himself” (Philippians 2:6). This does not mean that Wisdom was changed, since it is entirely unchangeable, but that he wished to make himself known to human beings with such humility.

Those statements were therefore written partly because of this administration, about which the heretics make their accusations; and partly because the Son owes to the Father what he is, including the fact that he is equal or comparable to the Father. The Father, however, owes what he is to no one.

### 19. The Holy Spirit
