Concerning the Holy Spirit, learned and eminent interpreters of the divine Scriptures have not yet discussed the matter so fully and carefully that his distinctive property can easily be understood—the property by which we cannot call him either the Son or the Father, but only the Holy Spirit.

They do, however, proclaim him to be the gift of God, so that we may believe that God does not give a gift inferior to himself. Yet they maintain that the Holy Spirit is not begotten as the Son is begotten from the Father, for Christ is the only Son; nor is he from the Son as a grandson from the supreme Father.

Nevertheless, they do not suppose that he owes what he is to no one, but say that he owes it to the Father, from whom all things are. Otherwise we would establish two principles without a principle, which is extremely false and absurd and belongs not to the catholic faith but to the error of certain heretics.

Some, however, have dared to believe that the very communion of the Father and the Son—and, so to speak, their deity, which the Greeks call *θεότης* (*theotēs*)—is the Holy Spirit. Since the Father is God and the Son is God, they say that the deity itself by which they are joined to each other—the Father by begetting the Son, and the Son by adhering to the Father—is equal to the one from whom the Son was begotten.

They therefore say that this deity, which they also want to be understood as the love and charity they have for each other, is called the Holy Spirit. Many scriptural testimonies support their opinion: for example, the statement, “Because the love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Romans 5:5), as well as many other testimonies of the same kind.

They also appeal to the fact that through the Holy Spirit we are reconciled to God. Since the Holy Spirit is called God’s gift, they wish this to signify sufficiently that the Holy Spirit is the love of God. For we are reconciled to him only through love, by which we are also called children (1 John 3:1), no longer under fear as slaves, because “perfect love casts out fear” (1 John 4:18), and we have received the Spirit of freedom, in whom we cry, “Abba, Father” (Romans 8:15).

Because, having been reconciled and restored to friendship through love (Romans 5:8–10), we shall be able to know all God’s secrets, the Holy Spirit is therefore said to “lead you into all truth” (John 16:13).

For this reason, too, the confidence with which the Apostles, filled with the Spirit at his coming, proclaimed the truth (Acts 2:4) is rightly attributed to love; for distrust is attributed to fear, which the perfection of love casts out.

The Holy Spirit is also called the gift of God (Ephesians 3:7), because no one enjoys what he knows unless he also loves it. To enjoy the wisdom of God is nothing other than to adhere to him through love; and no one remains in what he perceives except through love.

For this reason he is called the Holy Spirit: because whatever is made inviolable (*sancitur*) is so made for the sake of abiding. [Col. 0192] [Note: The printed editions read “is sanctified.” The manuscripts consistently read “is made firm.”] There is no doubt that holiness (*sanctitas*) derives its name from *sancire*, “to make firm.”

Those who assert this opinion rely especially on the testimony: “What is born from flesh is flesh, and what is born from Spirit is spirit” (John 3:6), since “God is Spirit” (John 4:24).

Here, they say, he speaks of our regeneration, which is not from flesh according to Adam but from the Holy Spirit according to Christ. Therefore, since the Holy Spirit is mentioned in this passage when it says, “God is Spirit,” they say we should note that it does not say, “Because Spirit is God” [Note: The printed editions and some manuscripts read, “Because the Spirit is of God.” The same manuscripts shortly afterward have, “Love is of God.” Other manuscripts read “God is” in both places, and this is no less satisfactory.], but “Because God is Spirit.” Thus, they say, the deity itself of the Father and the Son is called God here, and that deity is the Holy Spirit.

Another testimony is added by the Apostle John: “God is love” (1 John 4:16). Here too he does not say, “Love is God,” but “God is love,” so that the deity itself may be understood as love.

They also point to the fact that in the enumeration of realities joined to one another—“All things are yours, but you are Christ’s, and Christ is God’s” (1 Corinthians 3:22–23), and “The husband is the head of the woman, Christ is the head of the man, and God is the head of Christ” (1 Corinthians 11:3)—the Holy Spirit is not mentioned. They say this is because the connection itself is generally not numbered among the things connected to one another.

For this reason, they seem also to recognize the Trinity in the passage that attentive readers understand as saying: “From him and through him and in him are all things” (Romans 11:36). “From him” means from the one who owes what he is to no one; “through him” means through the mediator; “in him” means in the one who contains, that is, who joins things together through union.

### 20. The substance of the Holy Spirit

Those who think that this communion—which we call deity, love, or charity—is not a substance contradict this opinion. They seek an account of the Holy Spirit according to substance, yet they do not understand that the statement “God is love” could not have been made unless love were a substance.

They are led astray by their familiarity with bodily things. If two bodies are joined together by being placed next to each other, the joining itself is not a body. When the bodies that had been joined are separated, no joining is found. Yet the joining is not understood to have departed or migrated in the way those bodies do.

People of this kind should make their hearts as pure as they can [Col. 0193], so that they may be able to see that in God’s substance there is nothing of this sort—as though one thing there were substance and another something that happens to the substance without itself being substance. Whatever can be understood there is substance.

These matters can be stated and believed easily, but how they are so cannot be seen except by a pure heart. Therefore, whether this opinion is true or whether the matter is otherwise, we must hold an unshaken faith: we call the Father God, the Son God, and the Holy Spirit God; not three gods, but this Trinity one God; not different in nature, but of the same substance; not so that the Father is at one time the Son and at another time the Holy Spirit, but so that the Father is always Father, the Son always Son, and the Holy Spirit always the Holy Spirit.

Nor should we rashly assert anything about invisible realities as though we knew them, but only as believers. They cannot be seen except by a cleansed heart. Whoever sees them in this life only partially, “in part” and “in a riddle,” as it is said (1 Corinthians 13:12), cannot make the person to whom he speaks see them as well if that person is obstructed by the uncleanness of the heart.

“Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5:8).

This is the faith concerning God, our Creator and Restorer.

### 21. Love of God and neighbor

But since love is commanded to us not only toward God, when it is said, “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind,” but also toward our neighbor—for it says, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Luke 10:27)—if this faith does not preserve the gathering and fellowship of human beings, in which brotherly charity operates, it is less fruitful.

## Chapter X

### The catholic Church. The remission of sins. The transformation of the whole human being, to be completed in the resurrection. The resurrection of the flesh. The truth of the future resurrection confirmed.

We also believe in the holy Church, certainly the catholic Church. For heretics and schismatics, too, call their own gatherings churches.

But heretics violate the faith itself by holding false opinions about God; schismatics, on the other hand, break away through wrongful divisions from the brotherly charity that they nevertheless profess along with us.

Therefore heretics do not belong to the catholic Church, which loves God; nor do schismatics, because it loves its neighbor. For this reason the Church readily forgives the sins of its neighbor, because it prays to be forgiven by the one who reconciled us to himself, wiping away all our past sins and calling us to a new life.

Until we attain that life in its perfection, we cannot be without sins; nevertheless, it matters what kind they are.

### 22. Forgiveness of sins

It is not necessary at present to discuss the difference among sins. But we must believe absolutely that our sins can in no way be forgiven if we ourselves are inexorable in forgiving sins (Matthew 6:15).

Therefore, we also believe in the remission of sins.

23. And since there are three elements of which a human being consists—spirit, soul, and body—which are again spoken of as two, because the soul is often named together with the spirit—for a certain part of the same rational faculty, which beasts lack, is called “spirit”—our governing element is the spirit; then the life by which we are joined to the body is called “soul”; finally, the body itself, because it is visible, is our lowest element. Now all this creation [Note: [Col. 0194] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read: “Now all creation.”] groans and labors in travail until now (Rom. VIII, 22); yet it has yielded the firstfruits of the spirit, because it has believed God and already possesses good will.

This spirit is also called “my spirit,” of which the Apostle says, “With my mind I serve the law of God” (Rom. VII, 25). In another passage he likewise says, “For God is my witness, whom I serve in my spirit” (Ibid. I, 9). But when the soul still desires bodily goods, it is called “flesh.” For a certain part of it resists the spirit [Note: [Col. 0194] Four reputable manuscripts read, “is called and resists the spirit,” omitting “a certain part of it.”], not by nature, but through the habit of sins. Hence it is said, “With my mind I serve the law of God, but with the flesh the law of sin.” This habit has been turned into nature through mortal generation under the sin of the first human being. Therefore it is written, “And we too were once by nature children of wrath” [Note: [Col. 0194] Several manuscripts read, “we were by nature children of wrath.”] (Eph. II, 3), that is, of punishment, through which it came about that we serve the law of sin.

The nature of the soul is perfect when it is subject to its own spirit and follows that spirit as it follows God. Therefore “the natural person does not perceive the things of the Spirit of God” (I Cor. II, 14). Yet the soul is not brought under the spirit for good action as quickly as the spirit is brought under God for true faith and good will. Sometimes the soul’s impulse, by which it flows downward toward bodily and temporal things, is restrained only more slowly.

But since the soul itself is also cleansed, receiving the stability of its own nature under the rule of the spirit, which is its head, and whose head is Christ, we must not despair that the body too will be restored to its proper nature. This will indeed occur, though not as quickly as with the soul, just as the soul does not recover as quickly as the spirit; rather, it will occur at the proper time, at the last trumpet, when the dead will rise incorruptible and we shall be changed.

Therefore we believe also in the resurrection of the flesh—not merely because the soul is restored, which is now called “flesh” on account of its bodily affections, but because this visible flesh also, which is naturally flesh, has received the name “soul” not on account of its nature but on account of its bodily affections. Thus this visible substance, properly called flesh, must without doubt be believed to rise again.

The Apostle Paul seems to point to it as though with his finger when he says, “This corruptible must put on incorruption.” When he says “this,” he directs his finger, as it were, toward it. But what is visible can be pointed out with a finger, since the soul too could be called corruptible: for it is corrupted by moral vices. And when he says, “This mortal must put on immortality” (Ibid. XV, 52–53), the same visible flesh is signified, because the finger is again directed, so to speak, toward it. For the soul too can be called mortal, just as it can be called corruptible, on account of moral vices. The death of the soul is apostasy from God (Eccli. X, 14), and Sacred Scripture records this as its first sin in paradise.

24. The body, therefore, will rise according to the Christian faith, which cannot deceive. Whoever regards this as incredible considers what the flesh is like now, but does not consider what it will be like in the future, because at that time of angelic transformation it will no longer be flesh and blood, but only body.

For when the Apostle was speaking of flesh, he said, “There is one flesh of animals, another of birds, another of fish; and there are heavenly bodies and earthly bodies.” He did not say, “and heavenly flesh,” but “heavenly and earthly bodies.” For every flesh is also a body, but not every body is also flesh: among earthly things, wood is a body but not flesh, whereas a human being or an animal is both body and flesh. Among heavenly things there is no flesh, but simple and luminous bodies, which the Apostle calls spiritual; some call them ethereal.

Therefore the statement, “Flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God,” does not contradict the resurrection of the flesh; rather, it proclaims what that which is now flesh and blood will become [Note: [Col. 0195] I Retractations, chapter 17.].

Whoever does not believe that this flesh can be transformed into such a nature must be led to faith by stages. If you ask whether earth can be changed into water, it does not seem incredible to him because of their proximity. Again, if you ask whether water can become air, he does not answer that this is absurd; for they are near to one another. And if one asks about air, whether it can be changed into an ethereal body, that is, a heavenly body, proximity itself is already persuasive.

If, then, he grants that through these stages earth can be changed into an ethereal body, why does he not believe that, by the will of God—which enabled the human body to walk upon the waters—it can happen exceedingly quickly, “in the twinkling of an eye,” without any such stages, just as smoke is often changed into flame with marvelous speed? For our flesh is certainly from the earth. Yet the philosophers, whose arguments are so often used to resist the resurrection of the flesh, and who assert that no earthly body can exist in heaven, admit that any body can be converted and changed into every other kind of body.

When this resurrection of the body has taken place, freed from the condition of time, we shall enjoy eternal life with ineffable love and stability, without corruption [Note: [Col. 0196] Several manuscripts read: “when the body has been freed from the condition of time, it will enjoy eternal life with ineffable love.”]. Then what is written will come to pass: “Death has been swallowed up in victory. Where, O death, is your sting? Where, O death, is your contention?” (I Cor. XV, 39, 40, 50–54).

25. This is the faith given to new Christians to hold in the Creed in a few words. These few words are known to the faithful, so that by believing they may be subjected to God, by being subjected may live rightly, by living rightly may cleanse their hearts, and by having cleansed their hearts may understand what they believe.

[ON FAITH AND WORKS.]

[Col. 0195]

ADMONITION TO THE BOOK ON FAITH AND WORKS

This book should be assigned to the beginning of the year 413. For in chapter 14 Augustine mentions a book On the Spirit and the Letter, published toward the end of 412, as having been written by him shortly before: “Just now,” he says, “I published an extensive book on this question, entitled On the Letter and the Spirit.” Therefore, in the second book of the Retractations, after reviewing that same work On the Spirit and the Letter, he immediately added a retraction concerning the book On Faith and Works, in these words: “Meanwhile, some writings were sent to me by certain brothers . . .”—namely, those which he undertook to refute here.

The learned Garnerius, in the appendix to the first part of the works of Marius Mercator, p. 117, believes that those writings were none other than works which Jerome published either on Isaiah or on the Pauline Epistles; and he thinks that Jerome was the source of the three questions which Augustine here treats and refutes without naming him, out of reverence, as he says, for so great a man.

We do not dare affirm this opinion. As for the first question, concerning the admission of everyone without distinction to Baptism, so that even known and obstinate adulterers who refuse to change their lives should not be excluded, we have found nothing in Jerome consistent with this error. As for the second question, in which it was said to be perverse and contrary to proper order first to teach Christian morality and then to baptize, this could easily be inferred from what Jerome wrote on Matthew, chapter 28: “The principal order commanded the Apostles first to teach all nations, then to immerse them in the sacrament of faith, and after faith and Baptism to command what was to be observed.”

Perhaps, however, the pious interpreter was not concerned that moral teaching should precede Baptism, but only that it should not be omitted altogether—teaching which certainly had to be given even after Baptism and observed by the baptized.

Finally, concerning the third question, namely, whether baptized persons should be saved through faith even if they refuse to amend however wicked their conduct may be, the following passage is brought forward from Jerome’s dialogue Against the Pelagians, book 1: “If Origen says that all rational creatures are not to be destroyed, and attributes repentance to the devil, what does that have to do with us? For we say that the devil, all his followers, and all the impious and transgressors will perish forever, while Christians, if overtaken in sin, will be saved after punishments.”

And from the Commentaries on the last chapter of Isaiah: “Just as we believe that there are eternal torments for the devil and for all deniers and impious persons who said in their heart, ‘There is no God’ (Ps. XIII, 1), so we judge that there is a moderate sentence, mingled with clemency, for sinners and impious persons who are nevertheless Christians, whose works must be tested and purified in fire.”

Other theologians, however, explain these and similar passages, if there are any, in such a way as to defend Jerome from that error—a position which is gravely refuted in the Enchiridion and in book 21 of The City of God. Nor do we think that all the arguments refuted in the present work should be attributed to Jerome, especially since Augustine omits those scriptural testimonies which Jerome, in his work on Isaiah, notes as being used by those who wish the punishments of sins eventually to come to an end.

Augustine mentions the book On Faith and Works in the Enchiridion, chapter 67; in the book On Eight Questions of Dulcitius, question 1, no. 2; and in Letter 205 to Consentius, no. 18.

[Col. 0197]

[Note: [Col. 0197] On the book On Faith and Works, see book 2, chapter 38, of the Retractations, vol. 1, col. 646, from the words “Meanwhile, some writings were sent” up to the words “Some think.” M.]

ONE BOOK OF SAINT AURELIUS AUGUSTINE, BISHOP OF HIPPO, ON FAITH AND WORKS [Note: [Col. 0197] Written around the beginning of the year 413.] [Note: [Col. 0197] In correcting the book On Faith and Works, we used three Vatican manuscripts and thirteen Gallican manuscripts: one from the Royal Library; one from the Sorbonne; another from the Augustinian house of the greater Paris convent; another from the Paris College of the Bernardines; and others from the Church of Rheims, the Church of Laon, the Abbey of Corbie, Saint-Ouen at Rouen, Saint-Arnoul at Metz, Saint Michael in Periculo Maris, Casale Benedicti, Saint-Benignus at Dijon, and the Cistercian house. We also used variant readings extracted by the Louvain scholars from three Belgian manuscripts, as well as the older editions of Amerbach, Erasmus, and Louvain—that is, those of Johann Amerbach, Desiderius Erasmus, and the Louvain theologians.] [Note: [Col. 0197] We also compared all the editions mentioned at the beginning of volume 1 of the Retractations and Confessions. M.] (C)

The threefold error of certain persons is refuted, and the following is demonstrated against it: 1. That not everyone is to be admitted indiscriminately to Baptism, and that the wicked are to be tolerated in the Church in such a way that ecclesiastical discipline is not neglected; 2. That those being baptized must be given rules not only of faith but also of Christian life; 3. That baptized persons, unless they change their wicked life, will never attain eternal salvation by faith alone.

CHAPTER I

[Col. 0197]

1. The threefold error of certain persons. They think that everyone should be admitted to Baptism without distinction. Some believe that everyone should be admitted indiscriminately to the bath of regeneration which is in Christ Jesus our Lord, even if they refuse to change a wicked and shameful life marked by the most obvious crimes and scandals [Note: [Col. 0197] One Vatican manuscript reads, “devoted to.”], and even if they openly declare that they will persist in it [Note: [Col. 0197] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read, “even if they declare openly that they have confessed it.”].

For example, if someone is attached to a prostitute, he should not first be instructed to leave her and then come to Baptism; rather, even while remaining with her and confident that he will continue to remain with her [Note: [Col. 0197] Amerbach and Erasmus read, “remaining and confident that he will continue to remain.” Louvain reads, “remaining and confessing that he will continue to remain.”], or even openly professing this, he should be admitted and baptized. He should not be prevented from becoming a member of Christ, even if he persists in being a member of a prostitute (I Cor. VI, 15). Only afterward should he be taught how evil this is, and, once baptized, be instructed to amend his conduct for the better.

They consider it perverse and contrary to proper order first to teach someone how a Christian ought to live and then to baptize him. Rather, they think that the sacrament of Baptism ought to come first, followed by instruction in life and conduct. If he wishes to accept and observe this instruction, he will have acted beneficially; but if he refuses, retaining Christian faith—without which he would perish forever—and persists in any crime and impurity, he will nevertheless be saved, as through fire, like one who has built upon the foundation which is Christ, not gold, silver, or precious stones, but wood, hay, and straw (I Cor. III, 11–15)—that is, not righteous and chaste conduct, but wicked and unchaste conduct.

2. They think that moral instruction is to be given only after Baptism. They appear to have been driven to this argument because they were troubled that those who have divorced their wives and married others, or women who have left their husbands and married others, are not admitted to Baptism, since the Lord Christ unequivocally testifies that these are not marriages but adulteries (Matt. XIX, 9).

Since they could not deny that what Truth unambiguously confirms to be adultery is adultery [Note: [Col. 0198] Most manuscripts read, “without ambiguity.”], and since they wished to support the admission to Baptism of those whom they saw caught in such a snare—so that, if they were not admitted to Baptism, they would prefer to live or even die without any sacrament rather than be freed by breaking the bond of adultery—they were moved by a kind of human compassion to take up their cause in such a way that they judged all criminals and scandalous persons like them, even those corrected by no prohibition, reformed by no instruction, and changed by no repentance, should be admitted to Baptism. They believed that otherwise these people would perish forever, but that if they were admitted, they would be saved through fire even while persisting in those evils.

CHAPTER II

[Col. 0199]

3. The baptized are to be saved on account of Christian faith, even if they do not correct however wicked their conduct may be. The wicked are to be tolerated in the Church in such a way that correction and discipline are not omitted. In answering them, I say first of all this: no one should interpret those scriptural testimonies which either indicate the present intermingling of the good and the wicked in the Church or foretell it as meaning that the rigor or diligence of discipline should be entirely relaxed and abandoned. Such a conclusion would be based not on instruction from those Scriptures but on deception by one’s own opinion.

For although Moses, the servant of God, endured the intermingling of the first people with the greatest patience, he nevertheless punished many of them with the sword. Phinehas the priest also struck down adulterers whom he found together with an avenging weapon (Num. XXV, 5–8). This signifies what is to be done in the present age through degradations and excommunications, now that the visible sword in the discipline of the Church has ceased.

Nor, because the blessed Apostle laments with the utmost patience among false brothers (II Cor. XI, 26), and even permits some who are driven by the goads of diabolical envy to preach Christ (Phil. I, 15–18), does he therefore think that the man who had his father’s wife should be spared. Rather, he commands that, when the Church has assembled, he be handed over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord Jesus (I Cor. V, 1–5).

Nor did he therefore refrain from handing others over to Satan so that they might learn not to blaspheme (I Tim. I, 20). Nor does he speak in vain when he says:

“I wrote to you in my letter not to associate with fornicators—not meaning, of course, the fornicators of this world, or the greedy, or the robbers, or idolaters; otherwise you would have had to leave the world. But now I wrote to you not to associate with anyone who bears the name of brother if he is a fornicator, or an idolater, or greedy, or abusive, or drunkard, or robber; with such a one, not even to eat. For what have I to do with judging those who are outside? Are you not to judge those who are inside? Those who are outside God will judge. Remove the evil person from among yourselves” (I Cor. V, 9–15).

Some understand the words “from among yourselves” to mean that each person should remove evil from himself—that is, should himself be good. But however the statement is understood, whether it means that the wicked are to be corrected by the Church’s severity through excommunications, or that each person is to remove evil from himself by correcting and reforming himself, what was said above is nevertheless unambiguous: he commands that we not associate with those brothers who are known and notorious for any of the vices mentioned above.

CHAPTER III

The spirit in which sinners are to be corrected. The Lord’s command concerning the correction of the wicked. The spirit and love with which this merciful severity is to be applied are shown not only where he says, “so that the spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord Jesus,” but also elsewhere, where he plainly says: “If anyone does not obey our word through this letter, take note of that person, and do not associate with him, so that he may be ashamed; yet do not regard him as an enemy, but admonish him as a brother” (II Thess. III, 14–15).

4. The Lord himself, the singular example of patience, tolerated the devil even among the twelve Apostles until the Passion. He said, “Let both grow together until the harvest, lest while you gather the weeds you uproot the wheat along with them” (Matt. XIII, 29–30). He also foretold that the nets, in the likeness of the Church, would contain good and bad fish all the way to the shore—that is, to the end of the age—and spoke similarly elsewhere, whether openly or through parables, about the intermingling of the good and the wicked.

Yet he did not on that account judge that the Church’s discipline should be omitted. On the contrary, he instructed that it be applied when he said:

“Pay attention to yourselves. If your brother sins against you, go and correct him between you and him alone. If he listens to you, you have gained your brother. But if he does not listen to you, take with you one or two others, so that every word may be established by the testimony of two or three witnesses. If he refuses to listen to them, tell it to the Church. But if he refuses even to listen to the Church, let him be to you as a pagan and a tax collector.”

Then, in that same passage, he added the most grave terror of this severity, saying: “Whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven” (Ibid. XVIII, 15–18). He also forbids that which is holy to be given to dogs (Ibid. VII, 6).

The Apostle is not contrary to the Lord when he says, “Reprove sinners in the presence of all, so that the rest may have fear” (I Tim. V, 20), while the Lord says, “Correct him between you and him alone.” Both are to be done, as the diversity of the weaknesses of those whom we have undertaken not to destroy but to correct and heal requires: one person is to be healed in one way, another in another.

So too there is a proper way of overlooking and tolerating the wicked in the Church, and there is also a proper way of punishing and correcting them, of refusing them admission or removing them from communion.

CHAPTER IV

5. Errors of those who do not observe proportion in interpreting Scripture. The error opposed to that of the Donatists, arising from wrongly understood Scriptures. People go astray by failing to observe proportion. Once they begin to incline too readily in one direction, they do not consider the other testimonies of divine authority by which they might be recalled from that course and established in the truth and moderation composed from both sides—not only in this matter now under discussion, but also in many others.

Some, considering the testimonies of the divine Scriptures in which one God is presented as the object of worship, thought that the Father, who is the Son, was also the Holy Spirit. Others, suffering as though from the opposite disease, attended to the passages in which the Trinity is declared but could not understand how there could be one God when the Father is not the Son, the Son is not the Father, and the Holy Spirit is neither the Son nor the Father; consequently, they thought that differences of substances also had to be asserted.

Some, observing in Scripture the praise of holy virginity, condemned marriage. Others, pursuing the testimonies in which chaste marriages are praised, equated virginity with marriage. Some, when they read, “It is good, brothers, not to eat meat or drink wine” (Rom. XIV, 21), and similar passages, judged God’s creation and whatever foods they chose to be unclean. Others, reading, “Every creature of God is good, and nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving” (I Tim. IV, 4), collapsed into gluttony and drunkenness, unable to rid themselves of their vices unless they were replaced by vices equally great or greater.

[Col. 0201] 6. So too in the present matter, which is before us, some, observing the commands of severity by which we are instructed to correct the disorderly, not to give what is holy to dogs, to regard a despiser of the Church as a pagan, and to tear away from the structure of the body the member that causes scandal, disturb the peace of the Church so greatly that they attempt to separate the weeds before the proper time; blinded by this error, they themselves are instead separated from the unity of Christ.

This is the nature of our dispute with the schism of Donatus—not with those who know that Caecilianus was attacked by false and slanderous charges and, through a deadly shame, do not abandon their pernicious judgment, but with those to whom we say: Even if the people on account of whom you are not in the Church had been wicked, you nevertheless ought to have remained in the Church by tolerating those whom you were entirely unable either to reform or to separate.

Others, however, endangered in the opposite direction, perceive that the intermingling of the good and the wicked in the Church has been demonstrated or foretold, and learn the commands concerning patience—which make us so firm that, even if weeds appear to be in the Church, neither our faith nor our love is hindered, so that, because we see that there are weeds in the Church, we do not ourselves withdraw from the Church. Nevertheless, they think that the Church’s discipline should be abandoned [Note: [Col. 0201] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions, however, read: “they think that both the Church and discipline should be established.”], attributing to those in authority a most perverse security, as though it were not their concern to do anything except say what must be avoided or done, while caring nothing about what anyone actually does.

CHAPTER V

7. Sound doctrine requires that we neither withdraw from the Church because of the wicked nor neglect discipline toward the wicked themselves. We, however, believe that sound doctrine consists in moderating our conduct and judgment according to both sets of testimonies [Note: [Col. 0201] Amerbach and Erasmus read, “moderating a safe judgment.”], so that we tolerate dogs in the Church for the sake of the Church’s peace, but do not give what is holy to dogs where the Church’s peace is secure.

Therefore, when through the negligence of those in authority, or through some excusable necessity, or through secret infiltrations, we find wicked people in the Church whom we cannot correct or restrain by ecclesiastical discipline, then—lest an impious and destructive presumption rise in our hearts, leading us to think that we must separate ourselves from them lest we be defiled by their sins, and to attempt to draw after us disciples who are supposedly pure and holy, separated from the structure of unity as though from the company of the wicked—let those scriptural parables, divine utterances, and most certain examples come to mind by which it has been demonstrated and foretold that the wicked will remain mingled with the good in the Church until the end of the age and the time of judgment, and that they will harm none of the good who have not consented to their deeds through unity and participation in the Sacraments.

But when those through whom the Church is governed possess the authority, with the Church’s peace preserved, to exercise discipline against the wicked or depraved, then, lest we sleep through sluggishness and indifference, we must be roused by other goads of instruction belonging to the severity of restraint. Thus, directing our steps along the Lord’s way in accordance with both sets of testimonies, with Him as guide and helper [Col. 0202] [Note: [Col. 0202] The manuscripts read, “and as guide.”], we must neither grow numb under the name of patience nor become savage under the pretext of diligence.

CHAPTER VI

8. Whether an adulterer and an uncorrected sinner should be admitted to Baptism. Whether the commands for living well should be given before Baptism. With this moderation according to sound doctrine preserved, let us examine the matter at issue: namely, whether people should be admitted to receive Baptism in such a way that no diligence is exercised there to prevent what is holy from being given to dogs—even to the extent that the perpetrators of the most obvious adultery, and those who openly profess their persistence in it, appear not to be barred from the sacrament of such holiness.

They would certainly not be admitted if, during the very days in which they are to receive that grace, after registering their names and being purified by abstinence, fasting, and exorcisms, they professed that they would have intercourse with their lawful and genuine wives and would observe no continence during those few solemn days, although such intercourse is lawful at another time. How, then, is the adulterer who refuses correction admitted to those holy things, while the married man who refuses this observance is not admitted?

9. “But let him be baptized first,” they say, “and afterward let him be taught what pertains to good conduct and morals.” This is done when someone is perhaps pressed by the final day of his life, so that he believes in the very few words that nevertheless contain everything and receives the Sacrament, in order that, if he departs this life, he may leave freed from guilt for all his past sins.

But if he is healthy and has time to learn, what more suitable occasion can be found for him to hear how he ought to become and live as a believer than the time when, with a more attentive mind and with his religious concern itself suspended in expectation, he seeks the sacrament of the most wholesome faith?

Are we so far removed from our own experience that we either do not remember how attentive and anxious we were concerning what those who catechized us commanded us when we sought the sacraments of that font—and for this reason were even called “Competentes”—or fail to observe others who come each year to the bath of regeneration? What are they like during the days when they are catechized, exorcized, and scrutinized? With what vigilance do they gather, with what zeal do they burn, with what care do they remain intent?

If then is not the time to learn [Note: [Col. 0202] The manuscripts read, “to speak.”] what kind of life accords with so great a Sacrament, which they desire to receive, when will it be? Or, once they have received it, are they to remain in such crimes even after Baptism—not new people, but old people still guilty? In a wonderfully perverse order, they would first be told, “Put on the new person,” and once they had put him on, afterward be told, “Take off the old person,” whereas the Apostle, maintaining the proper order, says, “Take off the old person and put on the new” (Col. III, 9–10). The Lord himself cries out, “No one sews a new patch onto an old garment, and no one puts new wine into old wineskins” (Matt. IX, 16–17).

What else is accomplished throughout the entire period during which they hold the place and name of catechumens except that they hear what the faith and life of a Christian ought to be, so that, after testing themselves, they may eat from the Lord’s table and drink from the cup? For “whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself” (I Cor. XI, 28–29).

What is properly carried out throughout the entire period established in the Church for the salvation of those approaching the name of Christ, namely, that they pass through the stage of catechumens [Note: [Col. 0203] The printed editions read, “that they receive.” The manuscript reading, “that the stage of catechumens receive them,” is more coherent; the stage itself receives those who approach the name of Christ.], is done much more diligently and urgently during the days when they are called “Competentes,” after they have already registered their names to receive Baptism.

CHAPTER VII

10. Whether a virgin who unknowingly married another woman’s husband should be considered an adulteress. Neither the example nor the writings of the Apostles provide support for those who wish the candidates for Baptism to be instructed only in faith, while the baptized are instructed concerning conduct. “But what if,” they say, “a virgin unknowingly marries another woman’s husband?”

If she remains unaware forever, she will never thereby be an adulteress. But if she learns of it, she begins to be one from the moment she knowingly lies with another woman’s husband. Just as in the law of property a person is rightly called a possessor in good faith only so long as he does not know that he possesses what belongs to another, but once he knows and does not withdraw from another’s possession, he is held to be acting in bad faith and is rightly called unjust, so too here.

Far be it from us, therefore, with a judgment not merely inhuman but utterly foolish, to grieve when crimes are corrected as though marriages were being broken up—especially in the city of our God, on his holy mountain (Ps. XLVII, 2–3), that is, in the Church, where not only the bond of marriage but also its sacrament is so highly honored that a man is not permitted to give his wife to another. In the Roman Republic, Cato is said to have done this not only without blame but even with praise (Plutarch, Life of Cato the Younger).

There is no need to argue the point at greater length, since those to whom I am responding do not dare to assert that this is no sin, nor do they deny that it is adultery, lest they be openly convicted of opposing the Lord himself and the holy Gospel.

But when they are pleased that such people should first be admitted to receive the sacrament of Baptism and to the Lord’s table, even if they have refused correction in the clearest terms—indeed, that they should receive no warning whatever about this matter, but should be taught only afterward—so that, if they accept the observance of the command and correct their fault, they may be counted among the wheat, but if they disdain it, they may be tolerated among the weeds, they make it sufficiently clear that they are not defending these crimes or treating them as though they were light or nonexistent.

For what Christian of good hope would regard adultery as no crime or as a minor crime?

11. Nevertheless, they think that they derive from the Holy Scriptures the order by which such matters are either corrected or tolerated in other cases, since they say that the Apostles acted in this way. They bring forward certain testimonies from their writings in which the Apostles are found first to have presented the doctrine of faith and then to have given commands concerning conduct.

From this they wish it to be understood that only the rule of faith should be presented to those being baptized [Note: [Col. 0203] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read, “communicated.”], while afterward, once they have been baptized, instructions for changing their life for the better should also be given—as though they were reading some Epistles of the Apostles addressed to catechumens, in which they discussed faith alone, and others addressed to the baptized, containing commands for avoiding evil and establishing good conduct.

Since it is clear that they gave their writings to Christians who had already been baptized, why are those writings composed of both kinds of discourse—that which pertains to faith and that which pertains to a good life? Or perhaps they now approve of giving neither kind to those being baptized, and returning both kinds to the baptized?

If that is absurd to say, then let them acknowledge that the Apostles inserted the complete substance of their teaching in their Epistles, drawn from both areas. They generally presented faith first and then added what pertains to a good life because, in the human person himself, unless faith comes first, a good life cannot follow.

For whatever a person may appear to do rightly, if it is not referred to the piety owed to God, it ought not to be called right. If some foolish and extremely ignorant people were to think that the Apostles’ Epistles were addressed to catechumens, they would certainly admit that moral commands corresponding to faith should be communicated to those not yet baptized together with the rule of faith—unless, perhaps, these people are forcing us by their argument to accept the following necessity: that they want the first parts of the Apostolic Epistles, where faith is discussed, to be read to catechumens, and the later parts, where Christians are commanded how they ought to live, to be read to the faithful.

If it is foolish in the extreme to say this, then the Apostles’ Epistles provide no evidence for the opinion that those being baptized should be instructed only in faith, while the baptized should be instructed concerning conduct, merely because in the first parts of their writings they commended faith and afterward, in due sequence, exhorted the faithful to live well.

Although one matter comes first and the other afterward, both are nevertheless very often to be proclaimed in a single connected discourse to catechumens and to the faithful alike, to those being baptized and to those already baptized—whether so that they may be instructed, so that they may not forget, so that they may profess, or so that they may be strengthened—with the soundest and most diligent teaching.

Therefore, in the Epistles of Peter and the Epistles of John, from which they recall certain testimonies, let them add those of Paul and the other Apostles. What they have noticed—that faith is discussed first and conduct afterward—is to be understood in the manner which, unless I am mistaken [Note: [Col. 0204] The printed editions read, “which, unless I am mistaken.” The manuscripts read, “in the manner which, unless I am mistaken,” with “manner” understood.], I have explained most plainly.

CHAPTER VIII

12. Peter preached to those being baptized not faith alone but also repentance. Repentance was commanded not merely for unbelief but for changing the old life into a new one. “But in the Acts of the Apostles,” they say, “Peter addressed those who, after hearing the word, were baptized—three thousand in one day—in such a way that he preached to them only the faith by which they were to believe in Christ.”

When they said, “What shall we do?” he answered them: “Repent, and let each one of you be baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of sins, and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit.”

Why, then, do they not notice what was said: “Repent”? In that command lies the stripping off of the old life, so that those who are baptized may put on the new. But what benefit is repentance concerning dead works if a person persists in adultery and in other crimes by which love of this world is entangled?

[Col. 0205] **13. “They say that he wanted them to repent only of their unbelief, by which they had not believed in Christ.”** This is an astonishing presumption—I do not wish to say anything harsher—when, upon hearing the words “Repent,” they claim that only unbelief is meant, although the evangelical teaching was that life must be changed from the old to the new. Included here, certainly, is the Apostle’s statement: “Let the one who stole steal no longer” (Eph. 4:28), together with the rest, in which he explains what it means to put off the old person and put on the new.

Yet in Peter’s very words they have something by which they could have been warned, had they wished to pay careful attention. For after he had said, “Repent, and let each of you be baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of sins, and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit—for the promise is for you and for your children, and for all who are far away, whoever the Lord our God will call,” the writer immediately added and said: “And with many other words he bore witness, saying, ‘Save yourselves from this wicked age.’” But they eagerly received and welcomed the words, believed, and were baptized; and three thousand persons were added on that day (Acts 2:38–41).

Who would not understand here that, through the many other words which the writer omits because of their length, Peter urged them to save themselves from this wicked age, since the brief statement itself was inserted as the point he sought to persuade them of, and Peter pressed it upon them with many words? The summary itself is given when it is said, “Save yourselves from this wicked age.” Peter bore witness, with many words, so that this might be done. Those words contained condemnation of dead works, which the lovers of this age wickedly perform, and commendation of the good life which those who save themselves from this wicked age embrace and pursue.

Let them now, if they please, attempt to affirm that the person saves himself from this wicked age who merely believes in Christ, even if he persists in whatever crimes he wishes, right up to an open profession of adultery. If it is impious to say this, let them hear that those who are to be baptized must be taught not only what they ought to believe, but also how they are to save themselves from this wicked age. They must necessarily hear how believers ought to live.

**CHAPTER IX**

**14. The opponents misuse the example of the eunuch, who was baptized immediately after his confession of faith.** “That eunuch,” they say, “whom Philip baptized, said nothing more than, ‘I believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God’; and immediately, upon this confession, he was baptized.”

Are they then pleased that people should answer only this and be baptized immediately? Is nothing to be said by the catechist, and nothing confessed by the believer, about the Holy Spirit, the holy Church, the forgiveness of sins, or the resurrection of the dead? Finally, concerning the Lord Jesus Christ himself, is nothing to be said except that he is the Son of God—not about his incarnation from a virgin, his passion, death on the cross, burial, resurrection on the third day, ascension, and sitting at the right hand of the Father?

If, after the eunuch had answered, “I believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God,” Philip thought that sufficient for him to be baptized and depart immediately, why do we not follow this practice? [Col. 0206] Why do we not imitate it and remove the other matters which, even when the pressure of time makes it urgent that they be expressed in questioning for baptism, we nevertheless need to elicit, so that the person being baptized may answer all of them, even if he has not had time to commit them to memory?

[Note: [Col. 0206] The printed editions read, “was unable to commit to memory”; and shortly afterward, “left to be understood.” The manuscripts read better: “had no time … left to be understood.”]

But if Scripture remained silent and left the other matters to be understood—the matters which Philip dealt with when baptizing that eunuch—and if, in saying “Philip baptized him” (Acts 8:35–38), it intended us to understand that everything had been fulfilled which, although omitted from Scripture for the sake of brevity, we nevertheless know from the continuous tradition must be fulfilled, then similarly, where it is written that Philip preached the Lord Jesus to the eunuch, there can be no doubt that the matters belonging to the life and conduct of one who believes in the Lord Jesus were also stated in catechetical instruction.

For this is what it means to preach Christ: not merely to state what must be believed about Christ, but also what must be observed by the person who approaches incorporation into Christ’s body. Indeed, it means stating everything that must be believed about Christ—not only whose son he is, from whom he is begotten according to his divinity and from whom according to the flesh, what he suffered and why, what the power of his resurrection is, and what gift of the Spirit he promised and gave to believers, but also what members he seeks, establishes, loves, liberates, and brings to eternal life and honor, and of whom he is the head.

When these things are said, sometimes more briefly and compactly, sometimes more fully and expansively, Christ is preached. Yet nothing belonging not only to the faith but also to the conduct of the faithful is omitted.

**CHAPTER X**

**15. Paul’s statement that he professed to know nothing except Jesus Christ. The two commandments concerning love of God and neighbor are wrongly assigned, one to those being baptized and the other to those already baptized.** This may also be understood from what they recall the Apostle Paul to have said: “I resolved to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified” (1 Cor. 2:2). They think this was said as though nothing else had been taught them, so that they might first believe and then, after being baptized, learn whatever pertains to life and conduct.

They say that this was fully and sufficiently enough for the Apostle, who told them that although they had many pedagogues in Christ, they did not have many fathers, because he himself had begotten them in Christ Jesus through the Gospel (1 Cor. 4:15). If, then, the one who begot them through the Gospel—although he gives thanks that he baptized none of them except Crispus and Gaius and the household of Stephanas (1 Cor. 1:14, 16)—taught them nothing more than Christ crucified, what if someone should say that they had not even heard that Christ rose again when they were begotten through the Gospel? Why, then, does he say to them, “For I delivered to you in the first place that Christ died according to the Scriptures, that he was buried, and that he rose on the third day according to the Scriptures” (1 Cor. 15:3–4), if he had taught them nothing except the crucified Christ?

[Col. 0207] If they do not understand the statement in this way, but maintain that this too belongs to Christ crucified [Note: [Col. 0207] Thus the manuscripts; the printed editions read, “grant it.”], let them recognize that people learn many things in the crucified Christ, and above all that “our old person was crucified with him, so that the body of sin might be destroyed and we might no longer serve sin” (Rom. 6:6). Hence he also says of himself: “But far be it from me to boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Gal. 6:14).

Accordingly, let them pay attention and see how the crucified Christ is taught and learned, and let them understand that what we too are crucified to the world in his body belongs to his cross. Here every restraint of evil desires is understood. Therefore it is impossible that those who are formed by Christ’s cross should be permitted to persist in openly professed adultery.

The Apostle Peter also gives instruction concerning the mystery of that cross, that is, Christ’s passion, urging those who are consecrated by it to cease from sin. He speaks as follows: “Since therefore Christ suffered in the flesh, arm yourselves with the same intention; for whoever has died in the flesh has ceased from sin, so that he may live for the remaining time in the flesh no longer according to human desires but according to the will of the Lord God” (1 Pet. 4:1–2). In what follows he shows that the person belongs to the crucified Christ—that is, to Christ who suffered in the flesh—who lives well through the Gospel, with carnal desires crucified in Christ’s body.

[Note: [Col. 0207] Lov. reads, “crucified.” The reading is corrected from the other printed editions and the manuscripts.]

[Note: [Col. 0207] Lov. reads, “are fashioned in the cross of Christ.” The word “in” is absent from the other printed editions and the manuscripts; the principal manuscripts have “are fashioned,” not “are informed.”]

**16.** What of the fact that they also think the two commandments on which the Lord says that the whole Law and the Prophets depend support their opinion? They cite them in such a way that, since the first commandment is stated as, “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind,” while the second is like it, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Matt. 22:37–40), they believe the first belongs to those being baptized, where love of God is commanded, and the second to those already baptized, where the conduct of human life appears to be at issue.

Thus they have forgotten what is written: “If you do not love your brother whom you see, how can you love God whom you do not see?” (1 John 4:20); and also this other statement in the same Epistle of John: “If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him” (1 John 2:15). To what, then, do all the immoral acts of evil conduct belong, if not to love of this world? Consequently, the first commandment, which they think pertains to those being baptized, cannot in any way be observed without good conduct.

I do not wish to linger over this at length. For, when these two commandments are carefully considered, they are found to be so mutually connected that love of God cannot exist in a person who does not love his neighbor, nor love of neighbor in one who does not love God. But for the matter now under discussion, what we have said about these two commandments is sufficient.

**CHAPTER XI**

**17. Objection: the Israelites crossed the sea first and received the Law afterward.** “But,” they say, “the people of Israel were first led through the Red Sea, which signifies Baptism, and afterward received the Law, where they were to learn how to live. Why, then, do we deliver the Creed to those being baptized and require them to recite it back? Nothing of this kind was done for those whom God liberated from the Egyptians through the Red Sea.”

[Col. 0208] If they rightly understand that the preceding mysteries signify this—through the blood of the lamb smeared on the doorposts and through the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth (Exod. 12–14)—why do they not also understand, correspondingly, that separation from the Egyptians signifies the departure from sins which those being baptized profess?

This is the meaning of Peter’s words: “Repent, and let each of you be baptized in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ,” as though he were saying, “Depart from Egypt and cross the Red Sea.” Hence, in the Epistle entitled “To the Hebrews,” when the beginnings of those being baptized are recalled, repentance from dead works is placed among them. For it says:

“Therefore, leaving the elementary word of Christ, let us move toward maturity, not laying again a foundation of repentance from dead works and of faith in God, of the doctrine of washing, of the laying on of hands, of the resurrection of the dead, and of eternal judgment” (Heb. 6:1–2).

Scripture therefore bears sufficiently clear witness that all these things belong to the beginnings of neophytes. What is repentance from dead works except repentance from those things which must be put to death so that we may live? And if adulteries and fornications are not among them, what should be called a dead work?

Yet professing departure from such things is not sufficient unless, through the washing of regeneration, all past sins—which pursue them, as it were—are also wiped away. It was likewise not sufficient for the Israelites to depart from Egypt unless the mass of enemies pursuing them perished in the waves of that same sea, which opened for the passage and liberation of God’s people.

How, then, will the person who professes that he does not wish to change his adulterous conduct be led through the Red Sea, when he still refuses to depart from Egypt?

Furthermore, they do not notice that in the Law given to that people after the crossing of the Red Sea, the first commandment is: “You shall have no other gods besides me. You shall not make for yourself an idol or any likeness of anything that is in heaven above, or on earth below, or in the waters under the earth; you shall not worship them or serve them” (Exod. 20:4–5), together with the other matters belonging to this commandment.

Let them therefore affirm, if they wish, contrary to their own position, that concerning the worship of the one God and the avoidance of idolatry, instruction must be given not to those still being baptized but to those already baptized. And let them no longer say that those about to receive Baptism are to be told only of faith in God, while after receiving that Sacrament they are to be instructed in the conduct of life, as though this were a second commandment concerning love of neighbor.

The Law contains both, just as the people received it after the Red Sea, as after Baptism. Nor were the commandments distributed in such a way that before the people crossed that sea the multitude was taught to avoid idolatry, while after they had crossed it they were told to honor father and mother, not commit adultery, not kill, and the other requirements of good and innocent human conduct.

**CHAPTER XII**

[Col. 0209]

**18. The serious difficulty arising from the opposing position.** Suppose, then, that someone comes to request the holy washing in such a way that he professes he will not abandon sacrifices to idols except perhaps later, whenever he chooses, yet demands Baptism immediately and urgently pleads to become a temple of the living God—not merely remaining an idol-worshiper, but also persisting in some such utterly wicked priesthood.

[Note: [Col. 0209] Thus the manuscripts of better quality. Some add “sacrilegious”; others read “crime” instead of “priesthood.”]

I ask them whether they would consider him fit even to become a catechumen. They will undoubtedly cry out that he should not be admitted. For no other conclusion can be drawn from their own hearts.

Let them therefore give an account, according to the testimonies of Scripture which they think must be understood in their way, of how they dare contradict this man and affirm that he should not be admitted when he protests and says:

“I have learned about and revere Christ crucified; I believe that Christ Jesus is the Son of God. Do not delay me any longer; require nothing more of me. The Apostle wished those whom he begot through the Gospel to know nothing more at that time than Christ crucified. After the eunuch’s response that he believed Jesus Christ to be the Son of God, Philip did not delay to baptize him immediately. Why do you prohibit me from the worship of idols and refuse to admit me to Christ’s Sacrament before I have departed from it? I learned it in childhood and am held fast by a deeply rooted custom. I will do so when I can, when it is convenient. Even if I do not, I will not end this life without Christ’s Sacrament, lest God demand my soul from your hands.”

What do they think should be answered to him? Do they approve of admitting him? Far be it from us to believe that they would go so far.

What, then, will they answer when he says this and adds that he should at least have been told before Baptism that idolatry must be abandoned, just as that first people heard nothing about it before the Red Sea, since the Law containing this commandment was received only after they had already been liberated from Egypt?

They will surely say to the man: “You will become a temple of God when you have received Baptism.” But the Apostle says: “What agreement does the temple of God have with idols?” (2 Cor. 6:16).

Why, then, do they not see that the same must be said in the corresponding case: “You will become a member of Christ when you have received Baptism; but the members of Christ cannot be members of a prostitute”? For the Apostle says this too. Elsewhere he says: “Do not be deceived: neither fornicators, nor those who serve idols,” together with the other classes he enumerates there, “will possess the kingdom of God.”

Why, then, do we refuse to admit idol-worshipers to Baptism, while we think fornicators should be admitted, although he says both to them and to the other evildoers: “And such were some of you, but you were washed, but you were sanctified, but you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and in the Spirit of our God” (1 Cor. 6:15, 9–11)?

What reason is there, then, that when the power to prohibit both is evident, I should permit the person coming to Baptism to remain a fornicator, but not permit him to remain an idol-worshiper, when I hear both groups told, “And such were some of you, but you were washed”?

But they are moved by this consideration: they think the salvation of those who have believed in Christ and received his Sacrament—that is, have been baptized—is secure, even if it is [Col. 0210] “through fire,” although they are so negligent about correcting their conduct that they live wickedly. Therefore, with God’s help, I shall soon examine what ought to be thought about this according to the Scriptures.

**CHAPTER XIII**

**19. John gave moral commandments to those being baptized. Christ commanded that the commandments be observed for the attainment of eternal life.** I am still engaged in this question, in which it seems to them that those already baptized should be instructed concerning the conduct belonging to Christian life, while those being baptized should be taught only the faith.

If this were so, then, in addition to the many things we have mentioned, John the Baptist would not have said to those coming to his baptism: “Brood of vipers, who showed you how to flee from the coming wrath? Bear, therefore, fruit worthy of repentance” (Matt. 3:7–8), along with the rest, which plainly admonishes them not about faith but about good works.

Thus, when the soldiers asked, “What shall we do?” he did not say, “Believe for the time being and be baptized; afterward you will hear what you must do.” Rather, he spoke beforehand and warned them in advance, so that, as the Lord approached, he might cleanse the way into their hearts like a forerunner: “Extort from no one, accuse no one falsely; be satisfied with your wages.” Similarly, when tax collectors asked what they should do, he said: “Collect nothing more than what has been appointed for you” (Luke 3:12–14).

By briefly recalling these matters—for the Evangelist was not required to insert entire catechisms—he indicated clearly enough that it belongs to the one who catechizes a person being baptized to teach and admonish him concerning conduct.

If they had answered John, “We certainly will not bear fruits worthy of repentance; we will bring false accusations, extort, and demand what is not owed to us,” and if he had nevertheless baptized them after this profession, it still could not be said—contrary to the question now before us—that there is no time, when someone is being baptized, to address him beforehand about how he ought to lead a good life.

**20.** What of the Lord himself, to omit other examples? When that rich man asked him what good he should do to obtain eternal life, let them recall what he answered: “If you wish to enter life, keep the commandments.” The man asked, “Which ones?” Then the Lord recalled the commandments of the Law: “You shall not kill; you shall not commit adultery,” and the rest.

When the man replied that he had kept these from his youth, the Lord added a commandment of perfection: that, after selling all his possessions and distributing the proceeds as alms to the poor, he should have treasure in heaven and follow that same Lord (Matt. 19:17–21).

Let them therefore see that he was not told to believe and be baptized—which they think is the sole means by which a person comes to life—but was given commandments concerning conduct, which plainly cannot be kept and observed without faith.

Yet because the Lord here appears to have said nothing about communicating faith, we do not prescribe or insist that only commandments concerning conduct should be spoken to people who wish to attain life. Both are mutually connected, as I said earlier, because love of God cannot exist in a person who does not love his neighbor, nor love of neighbor in one who does not love God.

Therefore Scripture sometimes mentions one without the other—whether this one or that one—as a complete teaching, so that in this way too it may be understood that neither can exist without the other: the person who believes God must do what God has commanded, and the person who does something because God has commanded it must necessarily believe God.

**CHAPTER XIV**

**21. On the third question: faith is not sufficient for salvation without works.** Let us now examine what must be driven from religious hearts, lest people lose their salvation through a false security if they think that faith alone is sufficient for attaining it, while they neglect to live well and to walk in God’s way through good works.

Even in the time of the Apostles, because certain obscure statements of the Apostle Paul were not understood, some people thought he meant: “Let us do evil so that good may come” (Rom. 3:8), since he had said: “The Law entered so that transgression might increase; but where transgression increased, grace abounded all the more” (Rom. 5:20).

This is true because people who received the Law, arrogantly presuming upon their own powers and not obtaining through right faith divine assistance for overcoming evil desires, became burdened with many more serious transgressions by violating the Law itself. Thus, compelled by great guilt, they fled to faith, through which they might merit the mercy of forgiveness and assistance from the Lord who made heaven and earth (Ps. 120:2). Then, when love had been poured into their hearts through the Holy Spirit (Rom. 5:5), they would do with love what they were commanded to do against the desires of this age, in accordance with what had been foretold in the Psalm: “Their afflictions have multiplied; afterward they hastened” (Ps. 16:4).

When, therefore, the Apostle says that he considers a person justified by faith apart from works of the Law (Rom. 4), he is not doing this so that, once faith has been received and professed, works of righteousness may be despised. Rather, he teaches that anyone can know himself to be justified through faith even if works of the Law did not precede. They follow the justified person; they do not precede the one who is to be justified.

There is no need to discuss this more fully in the present work, especially since I have recently published a lengthy book on this question entitled *On the Letter and the Spirit*.

[Note: [Col. 0211] Six manuscripts, including the Corbie manuscript copied a thousand years ago, omit the word “recently.”]

Since this opinion had therefore arisen at that time, the other apostolic Epistles—those of Peter, John, James, and Jude—direct their chief force against it, emphatically asserting that faith is of no benefit without works. Paul himself likewise defined not every kind of faith by which one believes in God, but faith that is saving and fully evangelical, whose works proceed from love: “Faith,” he says, “which works through love” (Gal. 5:6).

Accordingly, he asserts that the faith which some think sufficient for salvation is so useless that he says: “If I have all faith, so as to move mountains, but do not have love, I am nothing” (1 Cor. 13:1).

[Note: [Col. 0211] The Casalinus manuscript reads, “Where faith exists and love works.”]

Where faithful love is at work, there is undoubtedly good living. For “love is the fullness of the Law” (Rom. 13:10).

[Col. 0211] [Col. 0212] **22.** Hence, in his Second Epistle, Peter plainly exhorts people to holiness of life and conduct and foretells that this world will pass away, while new heavens and a new earth are awaited, to be given as a dwelling to the righteous. From this they were to understand how they ought to live, so that they might become worthy of that dwelling.

Knowing that some wicked people had taken occasion from certain obscure statements of the Apostle Paul to neglect good living, as though secure in the salvation that comes through faith, Peter recalled that some things in Paul’s Epistles are difficult to understand, and that ignorant and unstable people distort them—as they do the other Scriptures—to their own destruction. Yet Paul, like the other Apostles, held the same view concerning eternal salvation, which is not given except to those who live well.

Thus Peter says:

“Since all these things are to be dissolved, what sort of people ought you to be in holy conduct and godliness, waiting for and hastening the coming of the day of the Lord, because of which the burning heavens will be dissolved and the elements will be melted by the heat of fire? But according to his promises we await new heavens and a new earth, in which righteousness dwells.

“Therefore, beloved, while you await these things, strive to be found by him undefiled and spotless, in peace; and regard the patience of our Lord as salvation. So also our beloved brother Paul, according to the wisdom given to him, wrote to you, as he does in all his Epistles when he speaks in them about these matters. In them there are some things difficult to understand, which the ignorant and unstable distort, as they do the other Scriptures, to their own destruction.

“You therefore, beloved, knowing this beforehand, beware lest, carried away by the error of the ill-omened, you fall from your steadfastness. Rather, grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. To him be glory, both now and to the day of eternity” (2 Pet. 3:11–18).

[Note: [Col. 0212] Thirteen manuscripts read this way. The printed editions read “the error of the false.” Perhaps the reading should be “the error of the foolish,” which better corresponds to the Vulgate’s *insipientium*. But the Greek text has *athesmōn*, “of the lawless” or “of the wicked.”]

**23.** James is so vehemently opposed to those who think that faith without works is effective for salvation that he even compares them with demons, saying: “You believe that God is one; you do well. Even the demons believe—and tremble” (Jas. 2:19).

What could be said more briefly, more truly, or more forcefully, since we read in the Gospel that the demons said this when they confessed Christ to be the Son of God and were rebuked by him (Mark 1:24–25), while the same confession was praised in Peter’s confession (Matt. 16:16–17)?

“What good is it,” James says, “my brothers, if someone says he has faith but does not have works? Can faith save him?” He also says: “Faith without works is dead” (Jas. 2:14, 20).

How long, then, will those who promise themselves everlasting life from dead faith continue to be deceived?

**CHAPTER XV**

**24. A difficult and misunderstood passage of the Apostle. The opinion of those who think that faith without works benefits salvation is refuted.** It is therefore necessary to consider carefully how that statement of the Apostle Paul—which is plainly difficult to understand—is to be taken. He says:

“For no one can lay any foundation other than the one that has been laid, which is Jesus Christ. [Col. 0213] Now if anyone builds upon this foundation with gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, or straw, each person’s work will become manifest. For the day will disclose it, because it will be revealed in fire, and the fire will test the quality of each person’s work. If anyone’s work that he built upon it remains, he will receive a reward. If anyone’s work burns up, he will suffer loss; but he himself will be saved, yet only as through fire” (1 Cor. 3:11–15).

[Note: [Col. 0213] The printed editions read, “For the day of the Lord.” “Of the Lord” is absent from the manuscripts and from the Apostle’s Greek text.]

Some think this should be understood as follows: those who add good works to the faith that is in Christ are the ones who build gold, silver, and precious stones upon this foundation; those who, while possessing the same faith, act wickedly build hay, wood, and straw. Hence they suppose that through certain punishments by fire these people can be purified and attain salvation by virtue of the foundation.

**25.** If this is so, we must admit that these people, out of commendable love, strive to admit everyone indiscriminately to Baptism—not only adulterers and adulteresses who pretend to false marriages contrary to the Lord’s teaching, but even public prostitutes who persist in the vilest profession, whom certainly not even the most negligent Church is accustomed to admit unless they have first been freed from that prostitution.

But on this reasoning I do not see at all why they should not be admitted in every case. Who would not prefer that, once the foundation had been laid, they should be purified by a somewhat longer fire, even while piling up wood, hay, and straw, rather than perish eternally?

Yet the following statements would be false, although they contain no obscurity or ambiguity: “If I have all faith, so that I move mountains, but do not have love, I am nothing”; and, “What good is it, my brothers, if someone says he has faith but does not have works? Can faith save him?”

This too would be false: “Do not be deceived: neither fornicators, nor those who serve idols, nor thieves, nor the greedy, nor adulterers, nor the effeminate, nor men who have sexual relations with males, nor drunkards, nor revilers, nor robbers will possess the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 6:9–10).

This also would be false: “The works of the flesh are manifest: fornications, impurity, licentiousness, the service of idols, sorceries, enmities, strife, jealousies, animosities, dissensions, factions, envy, drunkenness, revelries, and things like these. I warn you, as I warned you before, that those who do such things will not possess the kingdom of God” (Gal. 5:19–21).

All these statements would be false. For if people merely believe and are baptized, they will be saved through fire even if they persist in such evils; and consequently, those baptized in Christ, including those who commit such acts, will possess the kingdom of God.

But the statement “And such were some of you, but you were washed” (1 Cor. 6:11) would then be made pointlessly, since those who were washed are still such.

[Note: [Col. 0213] The printed editions read, “And such indeed were some of you.” The manuscripts of better quality read “some of you,” corresponding to the Greek *tines*. It is clear that this was formerly corrected in the Latin Bibles of the Vulgate edition, as appears from Lucas Brugensis, *Book on Passages of Roman Correction Ordered by Sixtus V*.]

Peter’s statement would likewise appear meaningless: “Thus Baptism likewise saves you by a similar pattern—not the putting away of filth from the flesh, but the inquiry of a good conscience” (1 Pet. 3:21), if Baptism saved even those who possessed the worst consciences, full of every crime and disgrace, and whose repentance had not changed them from these evils, because the foundation [Col. 0214] laid in that same Baptism would save them through fire.

Nor do I see why the Lord said, “If you wish to enter life, keep the commandments,” and recalled those pertaining to good conduct (Matt. 19:17–19), if life can be attained even without keeping these commandments through faith alone, which is dead without works.

Furthermore, how will this be true, which he will say to those whom he places on the left: “Depart into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels”? He does not rebuke them because they did not believe in him, but because they did not do good works.

[Note: [Col. 0214] Most manuscripts read, “Whom he does not rebuke,” or “Whom he does not reproach.”]
