For, plainly, lest anyone promise himself eternal life on the basis of faith that is dead without works, he said that he would separate all the nations, which had been mingled together and used the same pastures,

[Note: [Col. 0214] Three manuscripts of better quality read “shepherds.”]

so that it might become clear that those who had believed in him but had not taken care to do good would say to him: “Lord, when did we see you suffering this or that, and did not minister to you?”—as though eternal life could be reached through that dead faith alone.

Or perhaps those who did not perform works of mercy will go into the eternal fire, while those who seized what belonged to others, or who were merciless toward themselves by corrupting the temple of God within themselves, will not go there—as though works of mercy were of any benefit without love, when the Apostle says: “If I distribute all my possessions to the poor, but do not have love, it profits me nothing” (1 Cor. 13:3). Or could anyone love his neighbor as himself who does not love himself? “The one who loves iniquity hates his own soul” (Ps. 10:6).

Nor can the following defense be made here, by which some deceive themselves when they say that “eternal fire” refers not to eternal punishment itself: they suppose that those to whom salvation is promised through fire because of dead faith will pass through a fire that is eternal, while their burning—that is, the fire’s effect upon them—will not be eternal.

[Note: [Col. 0214] Most manuscripts read “eternal punishment”; the printed editions read “eternal burning.”]

But the Lord foresaw this as well and, as Lord, concluded his sentence in this way: “So these will go away into eternal burning, but the righteous into eternal life” (Matt. 25:32–33, 41–46).

The burning, therefore, will be eternal, just as the fire will be; and Truth said that those will go into it whose lack was shown to be not faith but good works.

**26.** If all these statements, and the countless others that can be found throughout the Scriptures expressed without ambiguity, are false, then that interpretation concerning the wood, hay, and straw could be true: namely, that those who held only faith in Christ and neglected good works will be saved through fire.

But if these statements are both true and clear, then without a doubt another interpretation must be sought for that statement of the Apostle. It must be counted among those matters which Peter says are difficult to understand in Paul’s writings, and which people must not distort to their own destruction by making the most wicked—those who cling most stubbornly to their wickedness [Col. 0215] and have not been changed by correction or repentance—secure in the expectation of receiving salvation, contrary to the clearest testimonies of Scripture.

**CHAPTER XVI**
### 27. How the Apostle’s passage is to be understood. Another passage of the Apostle brought forward by them in vain who teach that faith without works saves. What sort of faith the faith of the Canaanite woman was that was praised.

Here someone may perhaps ask me what I think about the very statement of the apostle Paul, and in what way I judge it ought to be understood. I confess [Note: [Col. 0215] In Er., Lugd., Ven., and Lov.: “here” (*hic*). M.] that I would rather hear this from more intelligent and learned men, if they explain it in such a way that all those things remain true and unshaken which I mentioned above, as well as whatever others I did not mention, by which Scripture most clearly testifies that faith is of no benefit unless it is the faith defined by the Apostle—that is, faith which works through love (Galatians 5:6)—and that it cannot save without works, neither apart from fire nor through fire: for if it saves through fire, then it is faith itself that saves.

The statement, however, is made absolutely and plainly: “What good is it, my brothers, if someone says he has faith but does not have works? Can faith save him?” (James 2:14). Nevertheless, I too shall say, as briefly as I can, what I think about that difficult passage in the apostle Paul, provided that what concerns my own profession [Note: [Col. 0215] The printed editions read “what concerns my own promise” (*promissionem*); the manuscripts more aptly read “what concerns my own profession” (*professionem*).] is kept especially in view: namely, that I said I would rather hear better interpretations of it from others.

“Christ is the foundation” in the structure of the wise architect. This requires no explanation, for it is plainly said: “No one can lay any foundation other than the one that has been laid, which is Jesus Christ” (1 Corinthians 3:11). But if Christ, then certainly the faith of Christ; for through faith Christ dwells in our hearts, as the same Apostle says (Ephesians 3:17). Moreover, if the faith of Christ, then assuredly that faith which the Apostle defined as working through love.

The faith of demons cannot be understood as the foundation, since they too believe and tremble, and confess Jesus as the Son of God. Why not, unless because theirs is not the faith that works through love, but one expressed through fear? Therefore the faith of Christ, the faith of Christian grace—that is, the faith which works through love—when laid as the foundation, permits no one to perish.

But if I try to explain more precisely what it means to build upon this foundation with gold, silver, precious stones, and with wood, hay, and straw, I fear that the explanation itself may become more difficult to understand. Nevertheless, with the Lord’s help, I shall endeavor to set out briefly and as clearly as I can what I think.

Consider the man who asked the good Teacher what good he should do in order to have eternal life. He heard that, if he wished to come to life, he must keep the commandments. When he asked which commandments, he was told: “You shall not kill; you shall not commit adultery; you shall not steal; you shall not bear false witness; honor your father and your mother”; and, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Matthew 19:16–19).

By doing these things in the faith of Christ, he would unquestionably hold the faith that works through love. For he would not love his neighbor as himself unless he had received the love of God, without which he would not love even himself.

Moreover, if he also did what the Lord [Col. 0216] added when he said, “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell everything you possess and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; then come, follow me” (Matthew 19:21), he would build upon that foundation with gold, silver, and precious stones. He would think only about the things of God—how he might please God—and, in my judgment, these thoughts are the gold, silver, and precious stones.

But if he were held by a certain carnal attachment to his wealth, even though he gave many alms from it, attempted no fraud or robbery to increase it, and did not fall into any crime or disgrace through fear of diminishing or losing it—for otherwise he would already be withdrawing himself in this way from the stability of that foundation—but, because of the carnal attachment I have mentioned, were unable to be deprived of such possessions without sorrow, he would build upon that foundation with wood, hay, and straw.

This would be especially so if he had a wife in such a way that, even because of her, he thought about the things of the world—how he might please his wife. Since these things, loved with carnal attachment, are lost only with sorrow, those who possess them in such a way that they have upon their foundation the faith which works through love, and who in no way or through no desire place these things above that faith, suffer loss in their destruction and reach salvation through a certain fire of grief.

The safer each person is from that grief and loss, the less he has loved such things, or the more he has possessed them as though not possessing them. But whoever, in order either to retain or acquire them, has committed murder, adultery, fornication, idolatry, or any similar offense will not be saved through fire because of the foundation; rather, having lost the foundation, he will be tormented by eternal fire.

### 28. 

For this reason, they also bring forward—apparently wishing to prove how much solitary faith can accomplish—the passage in which the Apostle says, “If the unbeliever departs, let him depart; the brother or sister is not enslaved in such circumstances” (1 Corinthians 7:15). They understand this as meaning that, because of faith in Christ, even a lawful wife united in marriage may be abandoned without any fault if she is unwilling to remain with her Christian husband precisely because he is a Christian.

But they have been unable to notice that she may most rightly be dismissed in the same way if she says to her husband: “I will not be your wife unless you pile up wealth for me through robbery, or unless, although you are now a Christian, you continue the customary procuring by which you used to support our household”; or if she knew him to engage in any other criminal or disgraceful activity [Note: The Reims manuscript reads, “if she knew her husband to engage in [it]” (*virum agere noverat*).], by which she took pleasure, satisfied her lust, secured an easy livelihood, or even went about more richly adorned.

For then, if the man to whom his wife says this has genuinely repented of dead works when he approached Baptism, and has upon his foundation the faith that works through love, he will unquestionably be held more by love of divine grace than by marital affection, and he will resolutely cut off the member that causes him to stumble.

Whatever grief of heart he suffers in this separation because of his carnal attachment to his wife is the loss he will endure; this is the fire through which, as the hay burns, he himself will be saved. But if he already possessed his wife as though not possessing her—not [Col. 0217] because of lust, but because of mercy, so that he might perhaps make her safe, giving the marital duty rather than demanding it—then, when such a marriage is separated from him, he will not grieve carnally. For he thought about her only in relation to the things of God: how he might please God (ibid. 29–34).

Accordingly, to the extent that he had built above those thoughts with gold, silver, and precious stones, to that extent he would suffer no loss; to that extent his structure, which was not made of hay, would not be consumed by any fire.

### 29. 

Whether, then, people suffer these things only in this life, or whether certain such judgments follow even after this life, this understanding of the passage does not, so far as I judge, depart from the reasoning of truth.

Nevertheless, even if there is another interpretation that does not occur to me and that ought rather to be chosen, as long as we hold this one we are not compelled to say to the unjust, the disobedient, the wicked, the defiled, parricides, matricides, murderers, fornicators, those who lie with males, kidnappers, liars, perjurers, and anyone else who opposes sound doctrine, which is according to the gospel of the glory of the blessed God (1 Timothy 1:9–11): “If only you believe in Christ and receive the sacrament of his Baptism, even if you do not change this very wicked life, you will be saved.”

### 30. 

Therefore that Canaanite woman does not prescribe this interpretation to us merely because the Lord granted her what she asked, after first saying, “It is not good to take the children’s bread and throw it to the dogs.” For the one who examines the heart saw that she had changed when he praised her.

That is why he did not say, “O dog, great is your faith!” but, “O woman, great is your faith!” (Matthew 15:26, 28). He changed the designation because he saw that her disposition had changed, and he recognized that the rebuke had reached its intended fruit.

I wonder, however, whether he would have praised in her a faith without works—that is, a faith not of such a kind that it could already work through love: a dead faith, or, as James did not hesitate to say, the faith not of Christians but of demons.

Finally, if they refuse to understand that this Canaanite woman changed her corrupt ways when Christ rebuked her by disregarding and correcting her, then let them, if they can, heal the children of anyone they find merely believing while living a most polluted life, not even concealing it but openly professing it and refusing to change—just as the daughter of the Canaanite woman was healed. Let them not, however, make such people members of Christ while they themselves continue to be members of a prostitute.

They do rightly understand that the person who refuses to believe in Christ until the end of life sins against the Holy Spirit and is guilty of an eternal sin without forgiveness. But they would understand correctly if they understood what it means to believe in Christ. For this is not to possess the faith of demons, which is rightly called dead, but the faith that works through love.

### CHAPTER XVII

### 31. The argument drawn in vain from the parables of the weeds and of those brought to the banquet, in order to admit people obstinate in sin to Baptism. The comparison of the servant unwilling to distribute the talent is likewise useless for this purpose.

Since these things are so, when we do not admit such people to Baptism, we are not trying to uproot the weeds before the proper time; rather, we do not wish, like the devil, to sow weeds in addition. Nor do we prevent those who wish to come to Christ; instead, by their own profession we prove that they do not wish to come to Christ. Nor do we forbid them to believe in Christ; we demonstrate that they do not wish to believe in Christ when they either say that adultery is not what he says adultery is, or believe that adulterers can be his members, although through the Apostle he says that such people will not possess the kingdom of God and that they oppose sound doctrine, which is according to the gospel of the glory of the blessed God.

Accordingly, such people are not to be counted among those who came to the wedding banquet, but among those who refused to come. Since they themselves dare openly to contradict Christ’s teaching and oppose the holy Gospel, they are not rejected after coming; rather, they disdain to come.

Those, however, who renounce the world at least in words, even if not in deeds, do come. They are sown among the wheat, gathered into the threshing floor, joined to the sheep, enter the nets, and are admitted among the banqueters. But whether they remain hidden inside or appear openly, they are to be tolerated when there is no power to correct them; nor should there be a presumption to separate them.

Let us certainly not understand the statement that those brought to the wedding banquet were “found both good and bad” (Matthew 22:2–10) to mean that the servants brought in those who professed that they would persist in being bad. Otherwise the servants themselves would have sown the weeds, and the statement would be false: “The enemy who sowed them is the devil” (Matthew 13:39).

But since this cannot be false, the servants brought in the good and the bad—whether those who remained hidden, or those who, after being brought and admitted, appeared openly; or “good and bad” was said according to a certain human manner of life, in which even those who have not yet believed are accustomed either to be praised or blamed.

The same applies to the instruction by which the Lord advises the disciples whom he first sends to preach the Gospel: in whatever city they enter, they are to seek out who there is worthy to stay with them until they depart (Matthew 10:11). Who, surely, will be worthy except one regarded as good by his fellow citizens? And who unworthy except one known to them as bad?

From both groups people come to faith in Christ, and thus the good and the bad are brought in, because even those who are bad do not refuse to repent of dead works. If they do refuse, they are not expelled as though wishing to enter; rather, by their open contradiction they themselves withdraw from entering.

### 32. 

That servant, therefore, will also be secure and will not be condemned among the lazy because he was unwilling to distribute his master’s talent, since those people were unwilling to receive what he distributed. For the comparison was proposed with them in view (Matthew 25:14–30): they refuse to undertake the office of steward in the Church, offering the lazy excuse that they do not wish to render an account for other people’s sins. They hear and do not act—that is, they receive and do not give back.

But when a faithful and diligent steward, fully prepared to distribute and eager for his Lord’s profits, says to an adulterer, “Do not be an adulterer if you wish to be baptized; believe in Christ, who says that what you are doing is adultery, if you wish to be baptized; do not be a member of a prostitute if you wish to become a member of Christ,” and the man replies, “I do not obey; I will not do it,” he himself does not wish to receive the true money of his Lord, but rather wishes to bring his adulterous money into the Lord’s treasury.

If he professed that he would do it but did not, and afterward could not be corrected in any way, it would be determined what should be done with him, so that he would not be useless to others when he could not be useful to himself. Thus, if he were a bad fish within the Lord’s good nets, he would not nevertheless entangle his Lord’s fish in bad nets—that is, if he had a bad life in the Church, he would not establish bad teaching there.

For when such people defend their conduct, or are admitted to Baptism while openly professing that they will persist in such behavior, nothing else seems to be preached [Note: Thus the manuscripts; the printed editions read, “they seem to preach nothing else.”] except that fornicators and adulterers who persist in that wickedness until the end of this life will possess the kingdom of God and, by the merit of faith—which is dead without works—will come to eternal life and salvation.

These are the bad nets which fishermen must especially avoid, if indeed bishops or ecclesiastical superiors of a lower order are to be understood by the fishermen in that Gospel comparison, since it is said, “Come, and I will make you fishers of men” (Matthew 4:19).

Good nets can catch both good and bad fish; bad nets, however, cannot catch good fish. For in good teaching, one who hears and does may be good, while one who hears and does not do may be bad. But in bad teaching, the person who considers it true, even if he does not obey it, is bad; and the person who obeys it is worse.

### CHAPTER XVIII

### 33. It is not a new practice to prohibit obstinately wicked people from Baptism.

What is truly astonishing is that brothers who think otherwise, although they ought to abandon this pernicious opinion, whether new or old, go further and say that the teaching by which the most wicked people—openly professing that they will persist in their crimes—are not admitted to Baptism is new.

As though I do not know where they wander when prostitutes, actors, and all other public practitioners of disgrace are not permitted to approach the Christian sacraments unless they have loosened or broken such bonds. According to their opinion, all such people would be admitted unless the holy Church retained an ancient and well-established practice, one arising from that utterly clear truth by which it is certain that “those who do such things will not possess the kingdom of God” (Galatians 5:19–21; 1 Corinthians 6:9–10).

Unless they repent of these dead works, they are not permitted to approach Baptism; and if they have entered by stealth, they cannot be saved unless afterward they change and repent [Note: Er., Lugd., Ven., and Lov. read, “do repentance” (*egerint poenitentiam*). M.].

But drunkards, greedy people, slanderers, and those guilty of any other condemnable vices that cannot be exposed and reproved through openly observable acts are nevertheless vigorously scourged by commandments and catechetical instruction; and all such people appear to approach Baptism with their will changed for the better.

But if they have noticed that adulterers—whom not human law but divine law condemns—that is, men who keep other men’s wives as their own, or women who keep other women’s husbands, are sometimes admitted somewhere with excessive negligence, they ought to try to correct what is right by means of those cases: that is, to ensure that such people too are not admitted. They ought not corrupt what is right by means of what is wrong, so that they judge that even the *Competentes* need not be catechized concerning correction of their conduct, and consequently conclude that all practitioners of those public disgraces and crimes—prostitutes, pimps, gladiators, and anyone else of this kind—ought to be admitted even while remaining in those evils.

For all the things the Apostle enumerates, concluding that “those who do such things will not possess the kingdom of God,” those who act more vigorously rebuke appropriately once they have been made manifest [Note: Most manuscripts read, “rebuke things made manifest to them, as appropriate” (*manifesta sibi congruenter increpant*)]; and those who resist and openly profess that they will remain in them are not admitted to receive Baptism.

### CHAPTER XIX

### 34. Three crimes are deadly and deserve punishment by excommunication even with the consent of more lenient people. Why adulterous marriages were not discussed in catechetical instruction. Marriage with unbelievers.

Those who think that the other sins can easily be compensated for by almsgiving nevertheless do not doubt that three are deadly and must be punished by excommunication until they are healed by more humble repentance: sexual immorality, idolatry, and murder.

There is no need now to ask what the quality of their opinion is, or whether it should be corrected or approved, lest we prolong the work undertaken because of a question that is in no way necessary for completing this one [Note: Am., Er., and two manuscripts read “for completing [it]” (*absolvendo*)]. It is enough that, if not everyone is to be admitted to the sacrament of Baptism, adultery is among those excluded; and if only those three are to be excepted, adultery is among those three. From this the present discussion arose [Note: The manuscripts read “arose” (*nata est*); the printed editions read “was moved” (*mota est*).].

### 35. 

But since the conduct of bad Christians, although previously very wicked, does not appear to have possessed this evil—that men should take other men’s wives, or women marry other women’s husbands—perhaps this negligence crept into certain churches, so that these vices were neither investigated nor attacked [Note: The printed editions read “struck back” (*repercuterentur*).] in the catechetical instruction of the *Competentes*. From this it happened that they also began to be defended.

Nevertheless, such unions are still rare among the baptized, provided that through our negligence we do not make them common [Note: The printed editions read “defend them” (*defensa*); the ancient books correct this evident error to “make them dense/common” (*densa*)]. For the Lord is plausibly understood to have signified such negligence in some people, carelessness in others, and ignorance in still others by the name of sleep, when he says: “While people were sleeping, an enemy came and sowed weeds over them” (Matthew 13:25).

It should therefore be judged that these practices did not first appear in the conduct even of bad Christians, since the blessed Cyprian, in his letter *On the Lapsed*, while lamenting and reproving many things which he rightly says provoked God’s indignation, so that he allowed his Church to be scourged by an intolerable persecution, does not mention these things there at all.

He does not even omit the practice of joining a marriage bond with unbelievers, and he confirms that this too belongs to bad conduct, asserting that it is nothing other than prostituting the members of Christ to the Gentiles. In our times this is no longer considered sinful, since nothing concerning it was expressly commanded in the New Testament; and so it has either been believed lawful or been left as doubtful.

It is likewise uncertain whether Herod took the wife of his dead brother or of his living brother. [Note: Josephus, *Jewish Antiquities*, book 18, chapter 7, reports that he took the wife of his living brother; this is also sung in the Roman Breviary on the feast of the Beheading of Saint John.] Therefore it is not entirely clear what John told him was unlawful (Matthew 14:3–4).

There is also reasonable doubt concerning a concubine who has declared that she will know no other man, even if she is dismissed by the man to whom she is subject: whether she ought to be admitted to receive Baptism.

Nor does anyone who has dismissed a wife caught in adultery and married another seem to be equated with those who dismiss and marry another except for the cause of adultery. Even in the divine statements it is so obscure whether this man—who is undoubtedly permitted to dismiss an adulterous wife—is nevertheless considered an adulterer if he marries another, that, in my judgment, anyone may be excused for erring about it.

For this reason, crimes of sexual immorality that are manifest must in every way be barred from Baptism unless they are corrected by a change of will and repentance. In doubtful cases, however, every effort must be made to prevent such unions from occurring. Why expose one’s head to so great a danger of uncertainty? But if such unions have occurred, I do not know whether those who contracted them should likewise be considered ineligible for Baptism.

### CHAPTER XX

### 36. The order of healing to be observed with those preparing for Baptism.

As far as the salutary teaching of truth is concerned, so that no one may be given the most destructive security in mortal sin, or even be granted the most pestilential authority, the order of healing is this: those preparing for Baptism must believe in God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, according to the form in which the Creed is handed down; they must repent of dead works; and they must have no doubt that in Baptism they will receive remission of all their past sins.

This is not so that they may be permitted to sin, but so that having sinned may not harm them: it is remission of what has been done, not permission to do it.

Then the saying may truly be applied, even spiritually: “See, you are well again; stop sinning now” (John 5:14). The Lord said this concerning bodily health because he knew that, in the case of the man whom he had healed, the sickness of the flesh had also resulted from the merits of his sins.

But I wonder how they think this can be said to a man who enters Baptism an adulterer and leaves Baptism an adulterer: “See, you are well again.” For what grave and deadly disease will there be if adultery is health?

### CHAPTER XXI

### 37. The action of the Apostles does not support those who wish adulterers to be admitted to Baptism. It is wrongly said that the Jews were destroyed solely because of unbelief. “The kingdom of heaven suffers violence” is not said of faith without love.

“But among the three thousand whom the Apostles baptized in one day, and among the many thousands of believers among whom the Apostle filled the region from Jerusalem to Illyricum with the Gospel” (Acts 2:41; Romans 15:19), “there must surely have been some joined to other men’s wives, or women joined to other women’s husbands. The Apostles ought to have established a rule concerning them, to be observed thereafter in the churches: whether such people were not to be admitted to Baptism unless they corrected those adulterous unions.”

As though it could not similarly be said against them that they do not find anyone mentioned who was admitted while in such a condition. Or could the crimes of individual people, which were infinite in number, really have been recorded, when the general rule is more than sufficient? Peter testifies to it in many words when he says to those preparing for Baptism, “Save yourselves from this crooked generation” (Acts 2:40–41).

For who could doubt that adulteries belong to the crookedness of this age, as do those who choose to persist in the same iniquity?

The same could be said of public prostitutes, whom no Church admits to Baptism unless they have been freed from that disgrace. Such women could certainly have been found among the many thousands then believing across so many nations; and the Apostles would therefore have had to establish examples concerning whether they should be received or prohibited.

Nevertheless, we may infer greater matters from certain lesser ones. If tax collectors coming to John’s baptism were forbidden to demand anything more than what had been appointed for them (Luke 3:13), I wonder whether adultery could be permitted to those coming to the baptism of Christ.

### 38. 

They also mentioned that the Israelites had committed many grave evils and shed much of the prophets’ blood, yet had not thereby deserved to be utterly destroyed, but only because of their unbelief, by which they refused to believe in Christ.

They failed to notice that their sin was not only that they did not believe in Christ, but also that they killed Christ. The one belongs to the crime of unbelief; the other to the crime of cruelty. The former is against right faith, the latter against a good life.

But the person who has the faith of Christ is free from both vices—not a dead faith without works, such as is also found in demons (James 2:19–20), but the faith of grace, which works through love (Galatians 5:6).

### 39. 

This is the faith of which it is said, “The kingdom of heaven is within you” (Luke 17:21). This kingdom they seize [Note: The printed editions read *Hanc enim diripiunt* (“For they seize this [faith]”); the manuscripts read *Hoc enim diripiunt* (“For they seize this [kingdom]”).] by believing, obtaining the Spirit of love, in whom is the fullness of the law (Romans 13:10)—the Spirit without whom the law in the letter made people guilty even of transgression.

Therefore it must not be thought that the words “The kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and those who use force seize it” (Matthew 11:12) were spoken because bad people, merely by believing and living most wickedly, enter the kingdom of heaven.

Rather, the guilt of transgression—which the law alone, that is, the letter without the Spirit, produced by commanding—is dissolved through believing; and by the violence of faith the Holy Spirit is obtained. Through him, love is poured into our hearts (Romans 5:5), and the law is fulfilled not through fear of punishment but through love of righteousness.

### CHAPTER XXII

### 40. What knowledge of God is true and leads to eternal life. Indulgence is to be hoped for not by those obstinate in sin, but by those who turn away from sin.

Let no unwary mind therefore be deceived into thinking that it has known God if it confesses him with a dead faith—that is, without good works—in the manner of demons. Nor should it therefore have no doubt that it will already come to eternal life merely because the Lord says, “This is eternal life: that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John 17:3).

It should also call to mind what is written: “By this we know that we know him, if we keep his commandments. Whoever says, ‘I know him,’ but does not keep his commandments is a liar, and the truth is not in him” (1 John 2:3–4).

And lest anyone think that his commandments concern faith alone—although no one has dared to say this, especially since he spoke of commandments which, so that their number might not scatter the mind [Note: The manuscripts read “might scatter the mind” (*cogitationem spargerent*); the printed editions read “might produce thoughts” (*cogitationes parerent*).], are summed up in the words, “On these two commandments depend the whole Law and the Prophets” (Matthew 22:40)—it may rightly be said that God’s commandments concern faith alone if faith is understood not as dead but as living: the faith that works through love.

Yet John himself later made clear what he meant when he said: “And this is his commandment: that we believe in the name of his Son Jesus Christ and love one another” (1 John 3:23).

### 41. 

It is therefore beneficial to believe in God with right faith, to worship God, and to know God, so that we may receive from him help for living well and, if we sin, may merit forgiveness from him—not while remaining secure in deeds that he hates, but by turning away from them and saying to him, “I said, Lord, have mercy on me; heal my soul, for I have sinned against you” (Psalm 40:5).

Those who do not believe in him have no one to whom they can say this; and those who are so far from him that they are alienated from the grace of the Mediator say it in vain.

This is the meaning of those words in the Book of Wisdom, which destructive security understands in some way I cannot fathom: “Even if we sin, we are yours” (Wisdom 15:2). We have, of course, a good and great Lord, who both wills and is able to heal the sins of those who repent—not one who scarcely dares to destroy those who persist in wickedness.

After saying, “We are yours,” the text adds, “knowing your power”: that is, the power from which the sinner cannot withdraw or conceal himself. It therefore continues: “But we will not sin, knowing that we are counted as yours” (Wisdom 15:2).

For who, thinking with due seriousness about dwelling with God—a dwelling to which all who are called according to his purpose are appointed by predestination—would not strive to live in a manner worthy of such a dwelling?

Thus, when John also says, “I write these things to you so that you may not sin; but if anyone does sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous; and he is the atoning sacrifice for our sins” (1 John 2:1–2), he is not encouraging us to sin with security [Note: The manuscripts read “he does/acts” (*agit*); the printed editions read “he says” (*ait*).]. Rather, he is teaching that, if we turn away from sin after something has been committed, we should not, because of that advocate whom unbelievers do not have, despair of forgiveness.

### CHAPTER XXIII

### 42. The passage of the Apostle is misunderstood by the opponents. “Judgment” in Scripture can mean eternal condemnation. Are only wicked believers to be understood as going to the resurrection of judgment, so that judgment does not mean eternal condemnation?

No milder condition, then, is to be promised on the basis of these words to those who wish to believe in God while persisting in corrupt conduct—still less on the basis of the passage in which the Apostle says: “Those who sinned without the law will also perish without the law, and those who sinned under the law will be judged by the law” (Romans 2:12).

It is as though there were some difference here between perishing and being judged, when the same thing is signified by another word. For Scripture commonly uses “judgment” even for eternal condemnation, as when the Lord says in the Gospel: “The hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear his voice and will come out: those who have done good to the resurrection of life, and those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgment” (John 5:28–29).

Nor does he say here [Note: Er., Lugd., Ven., and Lov. read “Nor does he say that” (*Neque illud*). M.], “Those who believed this,” and “those who did not believe that,” but “those who did good” and “those who did evil.” A good life cannot be separated from the faith that works through love; indeed, that faith itself is the good life.

We therefore see that the Lord spoke of the resurrection of judgment as the resurrection of condemnation. For, speaking of all who would rise again—which unquestionably includes those who do not believe at all, since they too are in the tombs—he divided them into two groups, declaring that some would rise to the resurrection of life and others to the resurrection of judgment.

### 43. 

But if they say that those who do not believe at all are not to be understood there, but rather those who will be saved through fire because they believed, even though they lived badly, and if they suppose that their temporary punishment is signified by the name “judgment,” this is said with the utmost impudence.

For the Lord plainly divided all who would rise again—which undoubtedly includes unbelievers—into two groups, life and judgment. He therefore intended judgment to be understood as eternal, even though he did not add the word “eternal,” just as he did not add it to “life.” For he does not say, “to the resurrection of eternal life,” although he certainly did not intend any other kind of life to be understood.

Let them nevertheless consider what they will answer when he says, “Whoever does not believe has already been judged” (John 3:18). Here, without doubt, they must either understand “judgment” as punishment without end, or dare to say that even unbelievers will be saved through fire. For he says, “Whoever does not believe has already been judged”—that is, already destined for judgment.

In that case, there will be no great benefit for them to promise to those who believe and live wickedly, since those who do not believe will not be destroyed either, but merely judged.

If they do not dare to say this, then they should not dare to promise anything milder to those of whom it is said, “They will be judged by the law,” since it is established that “judgment” is also customarily used for eternal condemnation.

What is more, we find that those who sin knowingly are not merely in a milder condition, but in a worse one. These are especially the people who received the law. For, as it is written, “Where there is no law, neither is there transgression” (Romans 4:15).

Hence also the statement, “I would not have known desire unless the law had said, ‘You shall not desire.’ But sin, seizing an opportunity through the commandment, produced in me every kind of desire” (Romans 7:7–8), along with many other things that the same Apostle says about this matter.

The grace of the Holy Spirit through Jesus Christ our Lord frees us from this more serious guilt. The Spirit, poured into our hearts through love, grants delight in righteousness [Note: Some codices read “love” (*dilectionem*) instead of “delight” (*delectationem*)], by which the immoderation of desire is overcome.

This confirms, therefore, that something not milder but more severe is to be understood concerning those of whom it is said, “Those who sinned under the law will be judged by the law,” than concerning those who sin without the law and will perish without the law. Nor does “judgment” here mean temporary punishment, but the judgment by which even those who do not believe will be judged.

44. For those who use this argument to promise salvation through fire to people who, although believers, live extremely wickedly—so that they say to them, “Those who have sinned without the Law will perish without the Law; but those who have sinned under the Law will be judged by the Law,” as though this meant that they will not perish but will be saved through fire—they have failed to observe that the Apostle said this concerning those who sinned without the Law and those who sinned under the Law, when he was discussing Gentiles and Jews, in order to demonstrate that the grace of Christ, by which they might be delivered, was necessary not only for the Gentiles but for both groups. The whole [Note: [Col. 0225] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read: “the whole.”] Epistle to the Romans clearly shows this.

Therefore, let them now promise salvation through fire, if they please, even to Jews who sin under the Law, of whom it was said, “They will be judged by the Law,” although the grace of Christ does not deliver them—for it was of these that it was said, “They will be judged by the Law.” But if they do not do this, let them beware of contradicting themselves [Note: [Col. 0225] The printed editions, omitting the particle *ne* (“lest”), read: “who contradict themselves.” The manuscripts correct this.], since they say that these people are bound by the most serious crime of unbelief. Why, then, do they transfer to unbelievers and believers, in what concerns faith in Christ, what was said concerning those who sinned without the Law and those who sinned under the Law, when Jews and Gentiles were being discussed, so that both might be invited to the grace of Christ?

## CHAPTER XXIV

### The freedom of faith must not be a veil for wickedness among believers

For it was not said, “Those who have sinned without faith will perish without faith; but those who have sinned in faith will be judged through faith.” Rather, it was said, “without the Law” and “under the Law,” so that it might be sufficiently clear that the subject is the distinction being made between Gentiles and Jews, not that between good and wicked Christians.

45. Even if they wish to take “Law” in that passage to mean “faith”—which is exceedingly inappropriate and absurd—they can nevertheless read here the Apostle Peter’s most explicit statement. He was speaking of those who had turned what is written—that we who belong to the New Testament are not children of the slave woman but of the free woman, and that Christ freed us by this freedom (Gal. IV, 31)—into an opportunity for the flesh and into a veil for wickedness. They had supposed that living freely meant that, secure as though because of so great a redemption, they might consider everything they pleased lawful for themselves, failing to heed the statement, “You were called to freedom, brothers; only do not use freedom as an opportunity for the flesh” (Gal. V, 13). Hence Peter himself says, “As free people, not using freedom as a veil for wickedness” (I Pet. II, 16).

He says of such people in his Second Epistle:

“These are dry springs and mists driven about by a whirlwind, for whom the gloom of darkness has been reserved. For, speaking boastfully of vanity, they entice through the lusts of the flesh, into shamelessness, those who have barely escaped from error, promising them freedom while they themselves are slaves of corruption. For by whatever anyone is overcome, to that he is enslaved. For if, after escaping the pollutions of the world through the knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, they are again entangled in these things and overcome, their latter state has become worse than the former. For it would have been better for them not to have known the way of righteousness than, after knowing it, to turn back from the holy commandment delivered to them. What has happened to them accords with the truth of the proverb: ‘The dog has returned to its own vomit,’ and, ‘The washed sow to wallowing in the mire.’”

What better condition is still being promised, contrary to this most manifest truth, to those who have known the way of righteousness—that is, the Lord Christ—and live recklessly, than they would have had if they had not known it at all [Note: [Col. 0226] The printed editions read “as though”; the manuscripts more correctly read “than if.”], when Scripture says with complete clarity, “It would have been better for them not to have known the way of righteousness than, after knowing it, to turn back from the holy commandment delivered to them”?

## CHAPTER XXV

### What the holy commandment is, and what punishment awaits those who know and transgress it; a temporary punishment must not be promised to the baptized who live wickedly

46. The holy commandment must not here be understood as the commandment by which we are ordered to believe in God, although the whole commandment is contained in that one if we understand it as the faith of believers that works through love. Rather, he plainly expressed what he meant by the holy commandment: namely, the commandment that, after turning away from the pollutions of this world, we should live in chaste conduct.

For he says:

“For if, after escaping the pollutions of the world through the knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, they are again entangled in these things and overcome, their latter state has become worse than the former.”

He does not say, “after escaping ignorance of God,” or “after escaping the unbelief of the world,” or anything of that kind, but “the pollutions of the world,” in which there is certainly every uncleanness of shameful acts. Speaking of such people above, he said, “Feasting with you, having eyes full of adultery and of unceasing sin” (II Pet. II, 13–22).

For this reason he also calls them “dry springs”: springs, clearly, because they have received the knowledge of the Lord Christ; but dry, because they do not live accordingly. The Apostle Jude likewise speaks of such people:

“These are the ones who are blemished in your love-feasts, feasting with you without fear, feeding themselves; clouds without water” (Jude 12), and so forth.

What Peter calls “feasting with you, having eyes full of adultery,” Jude calls “blemished in your love-feasts, feasting with you.” For they are mixed with the good at the feasts of the Sacraments and at the love-feasts of the congregations. What Peter calls “dry springs,” Jude calls “clouds without water,” and James calls “dead faith” (Jas. II, 20).

47. Therefore, let no temporary punishment by fire be promised to those who live shamefully and wickedly because they have known the way of righteousness, when Scripture, in its complete truthfulness, says that it would have been better for them not to have known it.

Of such people the Lord also says, “The last state of that man will be worse than the first” (Matt. XII, 45), because, having refused to receive the Holy Spirit as the inhabitant of his purification, he caused an unclean spirit to return to him in greater number.

Unless, perhaps, these people are to be regarded as better because they did not return to the uncleanness of adulteries, but did not depart from it; because they did not defile themselves again after being cleansed, but refused to be cleansed. For, so that they might enter Baptism with a relieved conscience, they do not even deign to vomit up their former uncleanness, only to swallow it again like dogs. Rather, in the holiness of the very font, they stubbornly strive to retain their undigested wickedness with an unyielding heart. Nor do they conceal it under a false promise; instead, they belch it forth through the shamelessness of their profession. Nor, when leaving Sodom, do they look back again at what lies behind them like Lot’s wife (Gen. XIX, 26); rather, they disdain altogether to leave Sodom and even attempt to enter Christ together with Sodom.

The Apostle Paul says, “I was formerly a blasphemer, a persecutor, and an insolent man; but I received mercy because I acted ignorantly in unbelief” (I Tim. I, 13). But to these people it is said: “Then you will receive mercy if, knowingly, you live wickedly in the very faith.”

It would be excessively lengthy, almost without end, to gather all the testimonies of Scripture by which it is evident that the condition of those who knowingly lead a most wicked and unrighteous life is not merely not milder than that of those who do so unknowingly, but is more serious precisely for this reason. Let this, therefore, suffice.

## CHAPTER XXVI

### Unless life corresponds to Baptism, the kingdom of heaven will not be obtained; sins of three kinds must be healed by three remedies

48. Let us therefore, with the help of the Lord our God, carefully avoid making people falsely secure by telling them that, if they have been baptized in Christ, they will attain eternal salvation however they may live in that faith. Otherwise we would make Christians as the Jews made proselytes, to whom the Lord says:

“Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who traverse sea and land to make one proselyte; and when he has been made, you make him twice as much a son of Gehenna as yourselves” (Matt. XXIII, 15).

Rather, let us uphold sound doctrine from God our teacher in both respects: Christian life must correspond to holy Baptism, and eternal life must not be promised to anyone if either of these is lacking.

For the one who said, “Unless anyone has been born of water and the Spirit, he will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (John III, 5) [Note: [Col. 0227] The old books read “of the Holy Spirit,” omitting “water and.”], also said, “Unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. V, 20).

Of the latter he says:

“The scribes and Pharisees sit on Moses’ seat. Do what they say; but do not do what they do, for they say and do not do” (Matt. XXIII, 2–3).

Therefore, their righteousness consists in saying and not doing; and by this he wished ours to exceed theirs by saying and doing. If this is absent, no one will enter the kingdom of heaven.

This does not mean that anyone ought to become so arrogant as to dare—not to boast before others, but even to think to himself—that he is without sin in this life. But unless there were certain sins so serious that they should even be punished by excommunication, the Apostle would not say:

“When you are assembled, and my spirit is present, deliver such a one to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord Jesus” (I Cor. V, 4–5).

Hence he also says:

“Lest, when I come, I should mourn over many who sinned before and have not repented of the uncleanness and fornication that they committed” (II Cor. XII, 21).

Again, unless there were certain sins not to be healed by the degree of repentance administered in the Church to those who are specifically called penitents, but by certain medicines of correction, the Lord himself would not say:

“Reprove him between you and him alone; and if he listens to you, you have gained your brother” (Matt. XVIII, 15).

Finally, unless there were certain sins without which this life cannot be lived, he would not have placed a daily remedy in the prayer that he taught us, so that we say:

“Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. VI, 12).

## CHAPTER XXVII

### Recapitulation of the foregoing

49. I have now explained, as I believe, sufficiently what I think about the whole of that opinion, in which three questions were raised.

The first concerned the mingling of the good and the wicked in the Church, like wheat and weeds. Here we must beware of thinking that these comparisons were proposed—this one, or the one concerning unclean animals in the ark, or any others with the same meaning—in order that the Church’s discipline should sleep. Of that discipline it was said, under the figure of the woman, “The ways of her household are severe” (Prov. II, 18, according to the Septuagint). Nor should rashness, which is rather madness than the severity of carefulness, proceed so far as to presume to separate the good from the wicked through wicked schisms.

These comparisons and prophecies did not give the good a pretext for indolence, by which they might neglect what they ought to prohibit; rather, they taught patience, by which they should endure, while preserving the soundness of the truth, what they are unable to correct.

Nor, because it is written that unclean animals also entered Noah’s ark (Gen. VII, 2), should leaders therefore fail to forbid those who are exceedingly unclean from wishing to enter Baptism while leaping about—something certainly milder than committing adultery. Rather, through this figure of an actual event, it was foretold that unclean people would be in the Church because of the necessity of endurance, not because of corruption of doctrine or dissolution of discipline.

For the unclean animals did not enter the ark wherever they pleased, breaking through its structure, but entered through the one same door, which the craftsman had made, while the ark remained intact.

The second question concerned their view that only faith should be handed on to those being baptized, whereas those already baptized should afterward be instructed concerning morals. But, unless I am mistaken, it has been sufficiently demonstrated that it is especially the concern of the watchman, when all who are seeking the Sacrament of the faithful are listening more attentively and earnestly to everything that is said, not to remain silent about the punishment that the Lord threatens to those who live wickedly—lest, in the very Baptism to which they come so that the guilt of all their sins may be remitted [Note: [Col. 0228] Several manuscripts read: “so that the guilt of all sins may be remitted.”], they become guilty of the gravest crimes. [Col. 0229]

The third question is the most dangerous. Since it was insufficiently considered and not treated according to the divine utterances, that entire opinion seems to me to have arisen in which salvation and eternal life are promised to those who live most wickedly and shamefully, even if they continue to live in that manner, provided only that they believe in Christ and receive his Sacraments. This contradicts the Lord’s most explicit statement. When someone who desired eternal life asked him, he replied, “If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments,” and he recalled which commandments (Matt. XIX, 17–19)—namely, those sins are avoided for which, somehow, eternal salvation is promised on the basis of faith that is dead without works.

I have discussed these three questions sufficiently, as I think, and have demonstrated that the wicked are to be tolerated in the Church in such a way that ecclesiastical discipline is not neglected; that those who seek Baptism are to be catechized in such a way that they hear and receive not only what they must believe, but also how they ought to live; and that eternal life is to be promised to believers in such a way that no one supposes he can attain it through dead faith, which cannot save without works, but through the faith of grace, which works through love.

Therefore, let not faithful stewards be blamed—not because of their own negligence or sluggishness, but because of the obstinacy of certain people who refuse to accept the Lord’s money and compel the Lord’s servants to distribute counterfeit money, while they are unwilling even to be the kind of wicked people whom Saint Cyprian recalls (*Sermon on the Lapsed*): those who renounce the world with words alone and not in deeds. For they do not even wish to renounce the works of the devil in words, since they openly profess that they will remain in adultery.

If they are accustomed to say anything that I may perhaps not have addressed in discussion, I have judged that my response was unnecessary—either because it did not pertain to the matter under discussion, or because it was so trivial that anyone could easily refute it [Note: [Col. 0230] The old books add: “Thanks be to God.”].

# [ON FAITH, HOPE, AND CHARITY]

[Col. 0229]

## EDITORIAL NOTICE TO THE FOLLOWING BOOK

Augustine listed the *Enchiridion to Laurentius* among his later works in the second book of the *Retractions*, placing it after the six books against Julian, which belong approximately to the year 421. Certainly, as the year 420 was drawing to a close, he had not yet completed this book. For he praised Jerome, who died in that same year 420—according to Prosper, on the day before the Kalends of October—as already dead in chapter 87, in these words: “Jerome the priest, of holy memory, left a written work.”

Laurentius, to whom the book was written, is called the brother of Dulcitius in the book *On Eight Questions of Dulcitius*, question 1, no. 10, because, as we suppose, he was connected with Dulcitius by natural kinship and family relationship, not merely by Christian fellowship. Augustine praises him highly for his learning and pious pursuits, but does not distinguish him from the body of lay believers. At the beginning of the work he calls him his son, and at the end he says that he loves him in the members of Christ.

Nor is Laurentius’s rank sufficiently established and confirmed by the book’s commonly transmitted title. Our older manuscripts have only: “Here begins the *Enchiridion*.” Those that add “To Laurentius the *primicerius*” are somewhat more recent, and do not entirely agree among themselves.

The Carcassonne manuscript has: “To Laurentius, *primicerius* of the notaries of the city of Rome.” One of the Vatican manuscripts has at the beginning of the work: “To Laurentius, *primicerius* of the Roman Church”; and at the end: “To Laurentius, *primicerius* of the Church of the city of Rome.” The Cistercian manuscript and certain others read: “To Laurentius the *primicerius.” The Royal manuscript and others read: “To Laurentius,” with nothing further, as do the editions of Amerbach and Erasmus. The Louvain edition, however, adds to the title: “*primicerius* of the city of Rome.” In an old Compendian manuscript one reads: “To Laurentius, notary of the city of Rome.” In another of the Colbert manuscripts: “To Laurentius the deacon.”

Although the book is correctly called the *Enchiridion*, by Augustine’s own concession in chapter 122—since Laurentius had requested an *enchiridion*, that is, a small work of limited size that could remain in his hands—Augustine nevertheless consistently calls it a book *On Faith, Hope, and Charity*, both there and in the *Retractions*, in the book *On Eight Questions of Dulcitius*, and in Epistle 231 to Darius. Possidius likewise calls it this in the *Index*, chapter 6.

For Augustine, the holy Doctor, thought it suitable to reduce all Laurentius’s questions to these three topics. Laurentius, inflamed by the love of wisdom and by devotion to the religion he professed, especially wished to receive from Augustine a firm and distinctive foundation of the Catholic faith, a summary of the whole of Christian doctrine, and, in general, everything that orthodox faith and religion hold from beginning to end, so that under this teacher he might be instructed and fortified against the various heresies then spreading.

In the first and by far the largest part of the book, Augustine teaches what must be believed, following the order of the Creed, and repeatedly refutes various heresies of the Manichaeans, Apollinarians, Priscillianists, Arians, and especially the Pelagians, without naming them explicitly. He devotes the second part, concerning those things that pertain to Hope, to a very brief exposition of the Lord’s Prayer. Finally, he adds a third part, also not lengthy, concerning Charity.

[Col. 0231] In the written manuscripts the work does not have the same chapter divisions and sections everywhere. In some it has 134, or 126, or, as in the printed editions, 122; in others it has 71; in some, 54; in others, fewer; and in some, none.

[Col. 0231]

[Note: [Col. 0231] On the *Enchiridion*, see book 2, chapter 63, of the *Retractions*, vol. 1, col. 655, from the words “I also wrote a book” through the words “I delight in your learning.” M.]

## THE *ENCHIRIDION* OF SAINT AURELIUS AUGUSTINE, BISHOP OF HIPPO, TO LAURENTIUS, OR ONE BOOK ON FAITH, HOPE, AND CHARITY

[Note: [Col. 0231] Written in the year 421 or shortly thereafter.]

[Note: [Col. 0231] We have collated the *Enchiridion*, or book *On Faith, Hope, and Charity*, against thirty-six ancient manuscripts: namely, four Roman manuscripts of the Vatican Library; twenty-two Parisian manuscripts; the manuscript of M. V. C. Antonius Faure, doctor of theology in the Faculty of Paris; and the others listed below in col. 275, note 3. We also used the variant readings of two Belgian manuscripts published by the Louvain editors, and finally the editions of Amerbach, Erasmus, the Louvain theologians, Lambert Daneau, and Antonius Arnauld—that is, those of Johannes Amerbach, Desiderius Erasmus, the Louvain theologians, Lambert Daneau, and Antonius Arnauld.]

[Note: [Col. 0231] We also compared all the editions mentioned at the beginning of the *Retractions* and the *Confessions*, vol. 1. M.]

(C)

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 0231]

### 1. He desires for Laurentius the gift of true wisdom

It cannot be said, dearest son Laurentius, how much delight I take in your learning and how earnestly I desire you to be wise—not among those of whom it is said, “Where is the wise man? Where is the scribe? Where is the investigator of this age? Has not God made the wisdom of this world foolish?” (I Cor. I, 20), but among those of whom it is written, “The multitude of the wise is the health of the world” (Wis. VI, 26), and such as the Apostle wishes people to become when he says, “I want you to be wise in what is good and innocent in what is evil” (Rom. XVI, 19).

[As no one can exist from himself, so no one can be wise from himself; rather, wisdom comes from the one who enlightens, of whom it is written, “All wisdom is from God” (Ecclus. I, 1).]

[Note: [Col. 0231] The old manuscript books lack the sentence enclosed in brackets.]

## CHAPTER II

### Human wisdom is piety

Human wisdom, however, is piety. You have this in the book of holy Job, for there it is written that Wisdom herself said to the human being, “Behold, piety is wisdom” (Job XXVIII, 28).

If you ask what kind of piety she meant in that passage, you will find more precisely in Greek the word *theosebeia* (θεοσέβεια), which means worship of God. In Greek, piety is also expressed by another word, namely *eusebeia* (εὑσέβεια), a term signifying proper or good worship, although this too refers chiefly to the worship of God.

But no term is more suitable than the one by which the worship of God is expressly indicated when the question is what wisdom is for a human being. Do you want something to be said more briefly, when you ask me to state great matters briefly? Or perhaps you yourself wish this very matter—how God should be worshiped—to be opened up briefly for you and gathered into a concise discourse?

## CHAPTER III

### God is worshiped through faith, hope, and charity

If I answer here that God must be worshiped through faith, hope, and charity, you will certainly say that this has been stated more briefly than you wished. Then you will ask that I briefly explain what pertains to each of these three: namely, what must be believed, what must be hoped for, and what must be loved.

When I have done this, everything you set forth by asking questions in your letter [Note: [Col. 0232] Thus Louvain and Arnauld; Amerbach, Erasmus, Daneau, and most manuscripts read “to be asked.”] will be included. If you have a copy of it, you can easily take it up and read it again [Note: [Col. 0232] Amerbach, Erasmus, Daneau, and three manuscripts read “so that you may take it up and read it again,” referring to the letter rather than the questions.]; but if you do not, you can recall it when I remind you of it.

## CHAPTER IV

### Laurentius’s questions; Augustine’s answers

You wish, as you write, that I make a book for you which you may possess as an *Enchiridion*—as people call it—and which will not leave your hands. It is to contain the things you request: namely, what above all must be pursued, what must chiefly be avoided because of the various heresies, how far reason contends on behalf of religion, and what does not fit within reason when faith alone is present [Note: [Col. 0232] The old German manuscript reads, “in religion, when faith alone is present, does not come.” The Colbert manuscript reads more suitably, “into reason, when faith alone is present, does not come.” This reading is supported by the Royal, Chartres, Gembloux, and two other manuscripts, which have, “in reason, when faith alone is present, does not come.” The Compendian manuscript, instead of “does not come,” has “finds.” Another Colbert manuscript and one of the Vatican manuscripts read, “in reason, when faith alone is present, fits.” Antonius Arnauld thought the text should be restored as: “in reason, when faith, if it is alone, does not fit.” Lambert Daneau, more boldly and without authority, restored it as: “in reason, when it does not fit with faith,” rejecting the words “if it is alone.”];

what must be held first and what last, what the summary of the whole definition is, and what the sure and distinctive foundation of the Catholic faith is.

You will undoubtedly know all these things if you carefully learn what ought to be believed, what ought to be hoped for, and what ought to be loved. For these are chiefly—or rather, in religion, the only things to be pursued [Note: [Col. 0233] Amerbach, Erasmus, and Daneau read “the only thing pursued in religion,” omitting *in*.]. Whoever contradicts these things is either wholly alien to the name of Christ or a heretic.

These matters are to be defended by reason, whether reason begins from the senses of the body or discovers them through the understanding of the mind [Note: [Col. 0233] Amerbach, Erasmus, Daneau, and four manuscripts read “which are either.”]. But whatever we have not experienced through bodily sense and have not been able, or are not able, to grasp by the mind must be believed without any hesitation on the testimony of those by whom Scripture, already worthy to be called divine, was composed. With divine assistance, whether through the body or through the soul, they were able either to see or even to foresee these things.

## CHAPTER V

### Response to questions 3 and 4

When the mind has been imbued with the faith that works through love, it proceeds through right living toward attaining vision, in which the ineffable beauty known to holy and perfect hearts is found, and the full vision of which is supreme happiness.

This is plainly what you ask: what must be held first and what last—namely, that it begins with faith and is perfected in vision. This is also the summary of the whole definition.

The sure and distinctive foundation of the Catholic faith is Christ. For the Apostle says, “No one can lay any foundation other than the one that has been laid, which is Christ Jesus” (I Cor. III, 11).

Nor should this be denied on the ground that some heretics might be thought to share this distinctive foundation with us. For if what pertains to Christ is considered carefully, Christ is found among all heretics who wish to be called Christians in name, but in reality he is not found among them.

To demonstrate this would take too long, since all heresies must be recalled—those that have existed, those that exist, and those that could exist under the Christian name—and it would be necessary to show, one by one, how true this is. Such a discussion would fill so many volumes that it might even seem endless.

## CHAPTER VI

### What is small in bulk can be held in the hand

You are asking us for an *Enchiridion*, that is, something that can be grasped in the hand [Note: [Col. 0233] The printed editions read, “something that can be grasped in the hands.” The manuscripts read, “something that can be grasped in the hand.” Among these, several have “held” instead of “grasped,” and some have “carried.”], not something capable of burdening bookcases.

Therefore, returning to those three things through which we said God is to be worshiped—faith, hope, and charity—it is easy to say what must be believed, what must be hoped for, and what must be loved. But defending these things against the accusations of those who think differently belongs to a more laborious and extensive kind of teaching. To acquire that teaching, the hand must not be filled with a brief *Enchiridion*; rather, the heart must be set aflame with great zeal.

## CHAPTER VII

### 2. The Creed and the Lord’s Prayer encompass faith, hope, and charity

For here [Note: [Col. 0234] Several manuscripts read, “For behold, there”; some, “For behold, there also.”] you have the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer: what is heard or read more briefly? What is more easily committed to memory?

Because the human race was weighed down by the grave misery of sin and needed divine mercy, the prophet, foretelling the time of God’s grace, said, “And it shall be that everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord will be saved” (Joel II, 32). For this reason there is prayer [Note: [Col. 0234] The printed editions read “the Lord’s Prayer.” Most manuscripts omit “the Lord’s.”].

But when the Apostle had recalled this prophetic testimony in order to commend that very grace, he immediately added, “But how will they call upon him in whom they have not believed?” (Rom. X, 14). For this reason there is the Creed.

In these two, observe the three things: faith believes; hope and charity pray. Yet they cannot exist without faith; and therefore faith itself also prays. For this reason it was said, “How will they call upon him in whom they have not believed?”

## CHAPTER VIII

### General explanation of faith, hope, and charity, and their connection

What can be hoped for that is not believed? Yet something that is not hoped for can be believed. For what believer does not believe in the punishments of the wicked, though he does not hope for them? Whoever believes that they threaten him and shudders at them in a fleeting movement of the soul is more properly said to fear than to hope.

Distinguishing these two, someone said:

> May the one who fears be permitted to hope.  
> (Lucan, *Pharsalia*, book 2, line 15.)

Yet this was not properly said by another poet, even though he was a better one:

> If only I could hope for so great a grief.  
> (Virgil, *Aeneid*, book 4, line 419.)

Finally, some grammarians use this verb as an example to demonstrate improper diction, saying, “He used *hope* for *fear*.”

Faith, then, concerns both bad things and good things, because both good and bad things are believed—and this is good faith, not bad faith. Faith also concerns past, present, and future things. We believe that Christ died, which is past; we believe that he sits at the right hand of the Father, which is present; we believe that he will come to judge [Note: [Col. 0234] The printed editions add after “he will come to judge”: “the living and the dead.”], which is future.

Likewise, faith concerns both one’s own affairs and those of others. Each person believes that he himself began to exist at some point and certainly was not eternal; and he believes that other people and other things [Note: [Col. 0234] The printed editions read, “and other things and other things.” The manuscripts read, “and other people and other things,” with the implied sense: other kinds of beings began to exist and were not eternal.] also began to exist and were not eternal.

We believe not only many things about other human beings that pertain to religion [Note: [Col. 0234] This phrase, “that pertain to religion,” is found in all the written and printed books. Lambert Daneau wished to treat it as a gloss; he disturbed this and many other passages with a notably ungenerous and unsympathetic spirit.], but also things about angels.

Hope, however, concerns only good things, only future things, and only things belonging to the person said to possess hope of them. Since this is so, faith must be distinguished from hope, not only by the word but also by a rational distinction [Note: [Col. 0235] Several manuscripts read, “faith was to be distinguished from hope.”].

As for the fact that the things believed or hoped for are not seen, this is common to faith and hope. For in the Epistle to the Hebrews, whose testimony the distinguished defenders of the Catholic Rule have used, faith is said to be “the conviction of things that are not seen” (Heb. XI, 1) [Note: [Col. 0235] Four manuscripts read, “of the Catholic faith and Rule.” In Augustine, the “Rule of faith” usually means the Creed, as below in chapter 56.].

Although, when someone says that he has believed—that is, placed his faith—not in words, witnesses, or any arguments, but in the evident presence of things, he does not seem so absurd that he should rightly be reproved for his wording and told, “You saw it; therefore you did not believe it.” From this it may be thought that it does not follow that whatever is believed must be unseen.

Nevertheless, we more properly call faith what the divine utterances have taught us to call faith: namely, faith concerning things that are not seen.

The Apostle also says of hope:

“Hope that is seen is not hope. For who hopes for what he sees? But if we hope for what we do not see, we await it with patience” (Rom. VIII, 24–25).

Therefore, when we believe that good things are in store for us in the future, we do nothing other than hope for them.

What, then, shall I say about love, without which faith profits nothing? Hope cannot exist without love. Finally, as the Apostle James says, “Even the demons believe—and tremble” (Jas. II, 19); yet they neither hope nor love. Rather, by believing, they fear that what we hope for and love will come.

For this reason the Apostle Paul approves and commends faith that works through love (Gal. V, 6), and such faith certainly cannot exist without hope. Therefore, neither is love without hope, nor hope without love, nor either without faith.

## CHAPTER IX

### 3. What must be believed is explained next, following the order of the Creed; there is no need for inquisitive investigation of natural things; it is enough for a Christian to believe that all things were created by the supremely good Trinity and are good

When, therefore, the question concerns what must be believed as pertaining to religion, nature must not be investigated in the manner of those whom the Greeks call physicists. Nor should it be feared [Note: [Col. 0235] Amerbach, Erasmus, Louvain, and Arnauld add here, “in the manner of those same people”; the old books do not contain this gloss.], lest a Christian be ignorant of anything concerning the power and number of the elements; the movement, order, and eclipses of the stars; the shape of the heavens; the kinds and natures of animals, shrubs, stones, springs, rivers, and mountains; the distances of places and times; the signs of impending storms; and six hundred other matters of this sort that those people either discovered or think they discovered.

For even they did not discover everything, although they excelled in talent, burned with zeal, possessed abundant leisure, investigated some matters through human conjecture, examined others through historical experience, and, among the things they boast of having discovered, often expressed more opinions than knowledge.

It is enough for a Christian to believe that the cause of created things—whether heavenly or earthly, visible or invisible—is nothing other than the goodness of the Creator, who is the one true God; and that there is no nature that is not either God himself or from him.

He is a Trinity: namely, the Father; the Son, begotten from the Father; and the Holy Spirit, proceeding from that same Father [Note: [Col. 0236] Two Vatican manuscripts read, “proceeding from the Father and the Son.”], yet the Spirit of the Father and of the Son is one and the same.

## CHAPTER X

### Against the Manichaean heresy concerning the origin of evil

From this supremely [Note: [Col. 0236] Louvain and Arnauld read “supreme.” The other printed editions and the manuscripts more suitably read “supremely.” The same reading occurs in the first book of the *Sentences*, distinction 46: “For it is.”] and equally and immutably good Trinity all things have been created. They are not supremely, equally, or immutably good, but each thing is nevertheless good; and taken together, all things are very good (Gen. I, 31), because the wondrous beauty of the universe consists of them all.

## CHAPTER XI
Why, then, does God permit evil to exist? Evil is nothing other than the privation of good. Even that which is called evil, when properly ordered and placed in its proper position, commends goods more impressively, so that they please more and are more worthy of praise when compared with evils. For surely almighty God—whom even unbelievers acknowledge to possess supreme power over all things (*Virgil, Aeneid* 10.100)—since he is supremely good, would in no way permit anything evil to exist in his works unless he were so almighty and good that he could bring good even out of evil [Note: In Am., Er., and Lamb. Dan., the following is added here: “God himself does good with the corrupted good of nature, by restoring or punishing what has been corrupted; and therefore evil will not even be a defect, because it is nothing when it is removed.” An inept gloss.].

What else, then, is that which is called evil except the privation of good? For just as, in the bodies of animals, to be afflicted by diseases and wounds is nothing other than to be deprived of health—for when treatment is applied, the purpose is not that these evils which were present, namely diseases and wounds, should depart from here and exist elsewhere, but that they should not exist at all—for a wound or disease is not any substance, but a defect of bodily substance; and since flesh itself is the substance, it is certainly some good to which these evils, that is, privations of the good called health, occur [Note: The printed editions have “is a good.” We have deleted *est* (“is”) on the authority of several and better manuscripts.]—so too all vices of souls are privations of natural goods. When these are healed, they are not transferred elsewhere; rather, what was there will nowhere exist when it is no longer present in that state of health.

## CHAPTER XII

### 4. All creatures are good, but because they are not supremely good, they are therefore corruptible

All natures, then, because the Creator of every nature is supremely good, are good. But because they are not, like their Creator, supremely and unchangeably good, good can therefore be diminished or increased in them. Yet the diminution of good is evil; however much it is diminished, something must necessarily remain, provided that the nature still exists, from which it derives its nature.

For no matter how considerable or how slight a nature may be, the good by which it is a nature cannot be consumed unless the nature itself is consumed [Col. 0236–0237]. An incorrupt nature is rightly praised; but if it is also incorruptible—that is, wholly incapable of corruption—it is without doubt much more praiseworthy. When it is corrupted, its corruption is evil because it deprives it of some good; for if it deprived it of no good, it would do no harm. It does harm, and therefore it removes good [Note: The printed editions have: “It does harm by removing good.” Corrected on the basis of the older books.].

As long, therefore, as a nature is being corrupted, there is in it a good of which it may be deprived. Accordingly, if something of the nature remains which can no longer be corrupted, the nature will certainly be incorruptible, and it will reach so great a good through corruption [Note: Am., Er., and Lov. have: “corruption will not reach it.” Several manuscripts have: “it will reach it through incorruption.” Arn. is more correct: “it will reach it through corruption.”]. But if it does not cease to be corrupted, neither will it cease to possess the good of which corruption can deprive it. If corruption consumes it wholly and entirely, no good will be present in it for the reason that no nature will exist. Therefore corruption cannot consume good except by consuming nature.
