Every nature, then, is a good: a great good if it cannot be corrupted, a small good if it can; yet it cannot be denied to be a good except by someone utterly foolish and ignorant. If it is consumed by corruption, the corruption itself will not remain either, since no nature will remain in which it can exist [Note: The passage has been corrected on the basis of the manuscripts. Am., Er., and Lov. otherwise had: “where it could exist, with nature remaining,” incorrectly. Danaeus had not corrected it more successfully when he added the negative particle: “where it could exist, nature not remaining.”].

## CHAPTER XIII

### There is no evil except what is also good

Accordingly, nothing that is called evil exists if there is no good. But good entirely free from every evil is sound good; good in which true evil is present is corrupted or defective good. Evil can never exist wherever there is no good at all.

Thus a remarkable conclusion follows: since every nature, insofar as it is a nature, is good, nothing else seems to be meant when a defective nature is called an evil nature than that what is good is evil; and there is no evil except what is good, because every nature is good, and no thing would be evil if the thing itself that is evil were not a nature. Evil, therefore, cannot exist except in something good.

Although this may seem absurd when stated, the connection of this reasoning compels us, as it were inevitably, to say it. We must take care, however, lest we fall into that prophetic declaration where it is written: “Woe to those who call evil good and good evil; who call darkness light and light darkness; who call bitter sweet and sweet bitter” (Isa. 5:20).

And yet the Lord says: “The evil person brings evil things out of the evil treasure of his heart” (Matt. 12:35). What is an evil person, then, except an evil nature, since a human being is a nature? But if a human being is some good because he is a nature, what is an evil person except an evil good?

Nevertheless, when we distinguish these two things, we find that a person is not evil because he is a human being, nor good because he is wicked, but good because he is a human being and evil because he is wicked. Whoever therefore says, “It is evil to be a human being,” or, “It is good to be wicked,” falls into that prophetic declaration: “Woe to those who call evil good and good evil.” He condemns God’s work [Col. 0238], which is the human being, and praises the human being’s vice, which is wickedness.

Every nature, therefore, even if it is defective, is good insofar as it is a nature and evil insofar as it is defective.

## CHAPTER XIV

### Good and evil, although contrary, can exist together in the same thing. Evils arise from goods and exist in goods

For this reason, in the case of those contraries called evils and goods, that rule of the dialecticians fails according to which they say that two contraries cannot exist simultaneously in any thing. No air is simultaneously dark and bright; no food or drink is simultaneously sweet and bitter; no body is simultaneously white where it is black; nothing is simultaneously deformed where it is beautiful. This is found in many, indeed nearly all, contraries: they cannot simultaneously exist in one thing.

But although no one doubts that good and evil are contraries, not only can they exist together, but evils cannot exist entirely without goods or except in goods, whereas goods can exist without evils. A human being or an angel can be not unjust; but an unjust being can be only a human being or an angel. The good is what belongs to the human being; the good is what belongs to the angel; the evil is what belongs to the unjust.

These two contraries exist together in such a way that, if good did not exist in that in which evil existed [Note: The Fathers of the Church manuscripts do not have *malum* (“evil”) in the text, but note in the margin that the word should be supplied. In Er., Lugd., Ven., and Lov., it is found in the text itself, and we have followed their reading.], evil could not exist at all. For corruption would have neither a place in which to remain nor a source from which to arise, unless there were something to be corrupted; and unless that thing were good, it would not be corrupted, since corruption is nothing other than the destruction of good.

Evils, therefore, have arisen from goods, and they exist only in certain goods. Nor was there any other source from which any nature of evil could arise. For if it existed, then insofar as it was a nature it would certainly be good; either an incorruptible nature would be a great good, or a corruptible nature could in no way exist unless it were some good which, when corrupted, corruption could harm.

## CHAPTER XV

### How the saying “A good tree cannot…” is to be understood

When we say that evils arose from goods, this should not be thought contrary to the Lord’s saying, “A good tree cannot produce evil fruits.” For, as the Truth says, “Grapes cannot be gathered from thorns” (Matt. 7:18, 16), because grapes cannot grow from thorns; yet we see that both vines and thorns can grow from good soil.

Likewise, an evil will cannot, like an evil tree, produce good fruits, that is, good works. But from the good nature of a human being both a good and an evil will can arise; nor was there any source from which an evil will could first arise except the good nature of an angel and a human being.

The Lord himself showed this most clearly in the same passage where he was speaking about the tree and its fruits. For he said: “Either make the tree good and its fruit good, or make the tree evil and its fruit evil” (Matt. 12:33), sufficiently indicating that evil fruits cannot indeed arise from a good tree, nor good fruits from an evil tree; nevertheless, both trees can arise from the very soil to which he was speaking.

## CHAPTER XVI

### 5. Whether knowing the causes of things pertains to happiness [Col. 0239]

Since this is so, when we enjoy that verse of Maro:

> Happy is the one who has been able to know the causes of things.  
> (*Georgics* 2.490.)

we should not think that knowing the causes of the great movements in the bodily world, which are hidden in the most secret recesses of nature, pertains to the attainment of happiness:

> Whence the trembling of the earth, by what force the deep seas swell,  
> when their barriers are broken, and then sink back into themselves.  
> (*Ibid.* 2.479–480.)

and other things of this kind. Rather, we ought to know the causes of good and evil things, and only to the extent that in this life, so full of errors and troubles, we are permitted to know them in order to escape those same errors and troubles.

For we must strive toward that happiness where no trouble shakes us and no error deceives us. If we ought to know the causes of bodily movements, we ought above all to know the causes of our own health. Yet when we do not know these causes, we seek physicians. Who does not see, then, how much patience is required in not knowing what is hidden from us concerning the secrets of heaven and earth?

## CHAPTER XVII

### What error is. Not every error is harmful. Augustine’s fortunate error at a crossroads

Although error must be avoided with every possible care, not only in greater matters but also in lesser ones, and although one can err only through ignorance of things, it does not follow that everyone who does not know something is immediately in error. Rather, it is whoever thinks he knows what he does not know. For he approves as true what is false, which is the distinctive feature of error.

Nevertheless, it makes a very great difference in what matter someone errs. For in one and the same matter, the person who knows is rightly preferred to the person who does not know, and the person who does not err to the person who errs. But in different matters—that is, when one person knows one thing and another knows something else, and one knows things more useful while the other knows things less useful or even harmful—who would not prefer the person who does not know to the person who knows, in matters known by the latter? There are indeed some things which it is better not to know than to know.

Similarly, it has sometimes benefited certain people to err, but on a path for the feet, not on the path of morals. This happened to us ourselves: at a certain crossroads we were misled and did not go by the place where an armed band of Donatists was lying in wait for our passage [Note: The armed Circumcellions ambushed Augustine several times, as Possidius reports in his *Life of Augustine*, chapter 12. There he also recalls this danger, which Augustine escaped because of an error by the guide.]. Thus it happened that we reached the place toward which we were traveling by a circuitous detour. Once we learned of their ambush, we rejoiced that we had erred and gave thanks to God for it.

Who, then, would hesitate to prefer a traveler who errs in this way to a robber who does not err? Perhaps for this reason, in the words of that supreme poet, a wretched lover says:

> “As I saw, I perished; evil error carried me away!”  
> (Virgil, *Eclogues* 8.41.)

For there is also a good error which not only does no harm but even benefits in some way.

Yet when the truth is considered more carefully, since to err is nothing other than to think what is false to be true and what is true to be false, or to hold the uncertain as certain or the certain as uncertain, whether the thing is false or true—and since this is as deformed and indecorous in the mind as we recognize “Yes, yes; No, no” to be beautiful and proper, whether in speaking or in giving assent (Matt. 5:37)—it is certainly also for this reason that the life we live is wretched: sometimes error is necessary for it not to be lost.

Far be it that the other life should be like this, where truth itself is the life of our soul, where no one deceives and no one is deceived. Here, however, human beings deceive and are deceived; and they are more wretched when they deceive by lying than when they are deceived by believing liars.

Nevertheless, rational nature so recoils from falsehood and avoids error as far as it can that even those who love to deceive do not wish to be deceived. For the liar does not think that he himself is in error, but believes that he is leading the person who trusts him into error. In the matter which he conceals by a lie, he does not err if he himself knows what is true; but he is deceived in thinking that his lie does him no harm, when every sin harms the one who commits it more than the one who suffers it.

## CHAPTER XVIII

### 6. Every lie is a sin, but one is more serious than another. One who unknowingly says what is false does not lie, but rather one who says what he thinks is false

Here there arises a very difficult and obscure question, concerning which we have already completed a substantial book when the necessity of answering compelled us: whether it belongs to the duty of a righteous person ever to lie. Some go so far as to contend that it can sometimes be a good and pious act to swear falsely, to say something false about matters pertaining to the worship of God, and even to say something false about God’s very nature [Note: The Priscillianists are being refuted.].

It seems to me, however, that every lie is indeed a sin, but that it makes a great difference with what intention and about what matters someone lies. The person who lies with the intention of helping does not sin in the same way as the person who lies with the intention of causing harm. Nor does the person who sends a traveler onto a different road by lying cause as much harm as the person who corrupts the way of life through a deceitful lie [Note: Am., Er., Lov., and Dan. have *haud vero* (“certainly not”), whereas the manuscripts and Arn. have *aut vero* (“or indeed”). The latter is more elegant but has the same sense, since the force of the preceding negative particle extends to this point.].

No one who says what is false but thinks it true should properly be judged a liar, because, insofar as it depends on him, he is not deceiving but is himself deceived. He should therefore be accused not of lying but sometimes of rashness, because he incautiously holds false things, once believed, to be true.

Conversely, insofar as it depends on him, the person who says what is true but thinks it false is the one who lies. For as far as his mind is concerned, since he does not say what he thinks, he does not speak the truth, even though what he says happens to be true. Nor is he in any way free from lying who unknowingly speaks the truth with his mouth but knowingly lies in his intention.

Therefore, if we do not consider the things themselves about which something is said, but only the speaker’s intention, the person who unknowingly says what is false because he thinks it true is better than the person who knowingly has the intention of lying, while not knowing that what he says is true. The former does not have one thing in his mind and another in his words; the latter, whatever the thing said may be in itself, has one thing concealed in his heart and another brought forth on his tongue [Col. 0240–0241]. This is the distinctive evil of the liar.

But when we consider the things themselves that are said, it makes a great difference in what matter a person is deceived or lies. Although, as far as human intention is concerned, being deceived is less evil than lying, it is nevertheless far more tolerable to lie about matters unrelated to religion than to be deceived about those without whose faith or knowledge God cannot be worshiped [Note: The printed editions Am., Er., and Dan. add here: “as will be investigated more clearly by one who pursues the matter in greater detail.”].

To make this clear by examples, let us consider the case in which someone, while lying, announces that a dead person is alive, while another, being deceived, believes that Christ will die again after however long a period of time. Is it not incomparably better to lie in the first way than to be deceived in the second, and is it not a much lesser evil to lead someone into the former error than to be led by someone else into the latter?

## CHAPTER XIX

### One error is more harmful than another, but every error is always evil

In some matters, then, we are deceived with great harm; in some, with little harm; in some, with no harm; and in some, even with a certain benefit. A person is deceived with great harm when he does not believe what leads to eternal life, or believes what leads to eternal death.

He is deceived with little harm when, approving something false as true, he falls into certain temporary troubles, which, when faithful patience is applied, he turns to good use. For example, someone may suffer harm from a person whom he thinks good but who is evil.

But someone who believes an evil person to be good in such a way that he suffers no harm from him is deceived with no harm [Note: Dan., Arn., and several manuscripts have “with no harm”; Am., Er., and Lov. have “in no way,” incorrectly.]. Nor does that prophetic condemnation apply to him: “Woe to those who call evil good.” For the statement is to be understood as referring to the very things by which evil people are evil, not to the people themselves.

Thus someone who calls adultery good is rightly accused by that prophetic utterance. But someone who calls a person good whom he thinks chaste, not knowing that he is an adulterer, is deceived not in the doctrine of good and evil things but concerning the hidden character of human conduct. He calls a person good because he thinks that person possesses what he knows to be good, and he calls adultery evil and chastity good; but in calling this person good, he does so in ignorance that he is an adulterer, not chaste [Note: The passage has been freed from a gloss by the aid of the older books. Earlier editions had: “but calling this person good, not knowing that he is an adulterer; calling the other evil, not knowing that he is chaste.”].

Moreover, if someone escapes danger through error, as I said above happened to us on our journey, then error also confers some good on a person.

But when I say that in some matters a person is deceived with no harm or even with some benefit, I do not mean that the error itself is no evil or some good. Rather, I mean the evil which he does not encounter, or the good which he reaches by erring—that is, what does not happen or what comes about as a result of the error itself.

For error in itself is either a great evil in a great matter or a small evil in a small matter, but it is always evil. Who, unless he is in error, would deny that it is evil to approve false things as true, to reject true things as false, to hold uncertain things as certain, or certain things as uncertain?

It is one thing to think good a person who is evil, which is an error; it is another thing, as a result of this evil, not to suffer some other evil, if the evil person who is thought good does no harm. It is likewise one thing to think that a road is the road when it is not; it is another thing to derive some good from this evil of error, as when one is freed from the ambushes of wicked people.

## CHAPTER XX

### 7. Not every kind of error is a sin. He refutes the Academics, who, in order to avoid error, wish all assent to be suspended

I do not know whether errors of this kind [Note: Am., Er., and Dan. have “whether this kind of error is.” Two manuscripts have “whether this manner of error exists.” Lov. has the better reading, “whether errors of this kind.” Refer it to the phrase below, “should be called sins.”] should also be called sins: when someone has a favorable opinion of an evil person without knowing what sort of person he is; when things similar to what we apprehend through the bodily senses occur, being perceived by the spirit as though by the body or by the body as though by the spirit—as the apostle Peter thought he was seeing a vision when he was suddenly released by an angel from chains and confinement (Acts 12:9); when something rough is thought smooth, or something bitter sweet, or something foul-smelling fragrant; when the passing of a wagon is thought to be thunder; or when one person is taken for another because two people are very similar, as often happens with twins. Hence the poet says:

> “A pleasing error to their parents.”  
> (Virgil, *Aeneid* 10.392.)

And should other such cases also be called sins?

I have not now undertaken to untie that most intricate question which tormented the keenest minds, the Academics: whether a wise person ought to approve anything, lest he fall into error by approving falsehoods as true, since, as they maintain, everything is either hidden or uncertain.

At the beginning of my conversion I composed three books on this subject, so that these arguments—which seemed to oppose us as though at the doorway—would not hinder us [Note: Several manuscripts have: “so that this question, which opposed us as though at the doorway, would not be…”; supply “question” as understood.]. Certainly the despair of discovering the truth had to be removed, since it seemed to be strengthened by their arguments.

Among them, therefore, every error is considered a sin, and they contend that it cannot be avoided unless all assent is suspended. They say that whoever assents to uncertain things is in error, and they argue with extremely subtle but shameless disputations that nothing is certain in human perceptions [Note: Several manuscripts have *visis* (“perceptions”), while the printed editions have *visu* (“sight”).], because of the indistinguishable likeness of falsehood—even if what appears to be the case should happen to be true.

But among us, “the righteous person lives by faith” (Rom. 1:17). If assent is removed, faith is removed, because nothing is believed without assent. There are truths, although they are not seen, which must be believed if one is to attain the blessed life, which is eternal and nothing else.

As for these people, I do not know whether we ought to speak with them, since they do not know that they are living in the present, much less that they will live forever—or rather, they say that they do not know what they cannot fail to know. For no one is permitted not to know that he is alive: if he is not alive, he cannot even be ignorant of anything [Note: The printed editions have “to know or not to know.” A little later they also have “it belongs only to one who is living.” The words “to know” and “only to one who is living” are absent from the manuscripts.], since not only knowing but also not knowing belongs to one who is alive.

Apparently, by refusing to assent to the fact that they are alive, they think they are guarding themselves against error, even though they are proved to be alive by their very error; for one who is not alive cannot err. Therefore, just as it is not only true but also certain that we are alive, so many things are true and certain. To refuse assent to them would be called dementia rather than wisdom.

## CHAPTER XXI

### Error is not always a sin, but it is always an evil

But in matters [Note: Am., Er., Lov., and Dan. read *In quibusdam* (“In some [matters]”). Corrected from the manuscripts, with which the text of *3 Sent.*, dist. 38, cap. *Illud*, agrees.] where it makes no difference for attaining the kingdom of God whether they are believed or not, or whether they are true—or merely thought true—or false, error, that is, taking one thing for another, should not be considered a sin; or, if it is a sin, it is a very small and slight one.

In any event, whatever its character and extent, it does not belong to that way by which we go to God. That way is faith in Christ, which works through love (Gal. 5:6).

For that pleasing error which benefited the parents in the case of the twin sons did not stray from this way. Nor did the apostle Peter stray from it when, thinking that he was seeing a vision, he took one thing for another, so that he did not distinguish the true bodies among which he was actually present from the images of bodies in which he thought he was, until the angel by whom he had been freed departed from him.

Nor did the patriarch Jacob stray from this way when he believed that his living son had been killed by a wild beast (Gen. 37:33). In these and similar false perceptions we are deceived while preserving the faith we have in God, and we err without abandoning the way that leads to him.

Although these errors are not sins, they must nevertheless be counted among the evils of this life, which is so subject to vanity that here false things are approved as true, true things rejected as false, and uncertain things held as certain. Although these errors are distant from that faith through which we strive toward true, certain, and eternal blessedness [Note: The manuscripts read *per quam veram certamque ad aeternam beatitudinem tendimus* (“through which we strive toward true and certain eternal blessedness”). The printed editions read *per quam ad veram certamque atque aeternam beatitudinem tendimus* (“through which we strive toward true, certain, and eternal blessedness”): less well.], they are not distant from the misery in which we still remain.

For we would in no way be deceived in any perception of mind or body if we were already enjoying that true and perfect happiness.

## CHAPTER XXII

### Every lie is a sin

Every lie must be said to be a sin because a person ought to say what he holds in his mind—not only when he himself knows what is true, but also when he errs and is deceived as human beings are—whether what he holds is true or merely thought true and is not.

Everyone who lies speaks voluntarily against what he feels in his mind, with the intention of deceiving. Words were instituted for this purpose: not so that people might deceive one another through them, but so that each person might convey his thoughts into the knowledge of another [Note: Most manuscripts have *proferat* (“bring forth”) rather than *perferat* (“convey”).].

To use words for deception rather than for the purpose for which they were instituted is a sin. Nor should any lie be considered not to be a sin because we can sometimes benefit someone by lying [Col. 0243–0244].

For we can also sometimes benefit someone by stealing: a poor person to whom something is openly given experiences the benefit, while the rich person from whom it is secretly taken does not experience the loss. Yet no one would therefore say that such theft is not a sin.

We can also benefit someone through adultery, if a woman appears likely to die from love unless someone consents to her, and if, should she survive, she might be cleansed through repentance. Yet adultery of this kind is not for that reason denied to be a sin.

But if chastity rightly pleases us, what has truth done wrong that, for another’s benefit, chastity should not be violated through adultery while truth is violated through lying [Note: The printed editions insert here: “A lie cannot therefore sometimes be praised because we sometimes lie for the salvation of certain people. It is therefore a sin, but a venial one, which benevolence excuses, and thus condemns deception.” These words are absent from nearly all manuscripts.]]?

It must not be denied that people who lie only for another person’s salvation have made considerable progress toward the good. Yet in such progress what deserves praise, or even temporal reward, is their benevolence, not their deception. Benevolence is enough to obtain forgiveness, not to deserve praise—especially among the heirs of the New Testament, to whom it is said: “Let your speech be, Yes, yes; No, no; whatever is more than this is from evil” (Matt. 5:37).

Because of this evil, which does not cease to creep into this mortal life, even Christ’s coheirs say: “Forgive us our debts” (Matt. 6:12).

## CHAPTER XXIII

### 8. The cause of good things is God’s goodness; the cause of evil things is a will deficient in mutable good

Having treated these matters as briefly as the present necessity required, since the causes of good and evil things must be known to the extent sufficient for the way that leads us to the kingdom, where there will be life without death, truth without error, and happiness without disturbance, we must have no doubt that the cause of the good things pertaining to us is nothing other than God’s goodness.

The cause of evil things, however, is the will of mutable good turning away from immutable good—first in the angel, and afterward in the human being.

## CHAPTER XXIV

### The secondary causes of evils: ignorance and desire

This is the first evil of a rational creature, that is, the first privation of good. Then ignorance of what ought to be done and desire for harmful things entered in, even against the will; and error and pain follow as their companions.

When these two evils are perceived as impending, the movement of the soul fleeing from them is called fear. But when the soul obtains what it desires, even if those things are harmful or empty, either it does not recognize this because of error, or it is overcome by diseased pleasure, or it is even tossed about by empty joy [Note: Here Am., Er., Dan., Arn., and several manuscripts omit *vel* (“or”).].

From these sources of disease, which are sources not of abundance but of want, every misery of rational nature flows.

## CHAPTER XXV

### Punishments inflicted for sins

Nevertheless, this nature could not lose, amid its evils, its desire for blessedness. These are common evils of human beings and angels, condemned by the Lord’s justice for their own wickedness.

But the human being also has a punishment proper to him, by which he has been punished with bodily death. God had threatened him with the penalty of death if he sinned, thus granting him free choice while nevertheless ruling him by command and terrifying him with destruction. He placed him in the happiness of paradise, as in the shadow of life, so that, if justice were preserved, he might ascend from there to better things (Gen. 2:17, 15).

## CHAPTER XXVI

### The punishment of Adam’s sin in his entire offspring. Against the Pelagians

After the sin, therefore, Adam became an exile and also bound his offspring—which, by sinning, he had corrupted in himself as in a root—with the punishment of death and condemnation [Note: Am., Er., Dan., and many manuscripts have “with the punishment of death and condemnation.” Lov. and Arn. have “with the punishment of death and by condemnation.”].

Thus whatever offspring was born from him and from the wife who was condemned with him, through whom he had sinned, through carnal desire—in which a similar punishment for disobedience was repaid—would contract original sin. Through that sin it would be drawn by various errors and pains to the final, endless punishment with the deserting angels, its corrupters, possessors, and companions.

“Through one human being sin entered the world, and through sin death; and so death passed to all human beings, in whom all sinned” (Rom. 5:12). In that passage the Apostle called the entire human race “the world.”

## CHAPTER XXVII

### The human condition after Adam’s sin. The restoration of humanity by God’s mercy alone

This, then, was the state of affairs: the condemned mass of the entire human race lay in evils, or was even rolled about in them, and was hurled from evils into evils. Joined to the portion of the angels who had sinned, it was paying the penalties fully deserved for its impious desertion.

For whatever the wicked do willingly through blind and uncontrolled desire, and whatever they suffer unwillingly through manifest and hidden punishments [Note: Am., Er., Dan., and nearly all manuscripts have “manifest and hidden punishments,” rather than “manifest and open punishments.”], belongs to God’s just anger.

Yet the Creator’s goodness does not cease to supply the evil angels with life and vigorous power—for if this provision were withdrawn, they would perish [Note: Several manuscripts have *intercidit* or *intercidet* (“it perished” or “it will perish”), and some have *intercidunt* (“they perish”).]—nor does it cease, in the case of human beings, although they are born from a corrupted and condemned stock, to form their seed, animate them, arrange their members, give vitality to their senses through the ages of time and the spaces of places, and provide them with nourishment [Note: The printed editions have “and to arrange their members.” Most manuscripts omit “and.” Several of these continue after “arrange their members” as follows: “through the regions of places, through the intervals of times.” The Cistercian and Fuliensian manuscripts have “through the variety of places.”].

For he judged it better to bring good out of evils than to permit no evils to exist.

Indeed, if he had not wished at all to restore human beings to something better, just as there is no restoration for the wicked angels, would it not rightly follow that the nature which abandoned God; which, misusing its power, trampled upon and transgressed the command of its Creator, which it could very easily have kept; which, stubbornly turning away from its Creator’s light, violated in itself the image of its Creator; and which, by a wicked exercise of free choice, tore itself away from the salutary servitude of his laws—would be abandoned by him forever in its entirety and would pay an everlasting penalty according to its deserts?

Certainly he would do this if he were only just and not also merciful. He would thereby show his undeserved mercy much more clearly in liberating the unworthy [Note: Danaeus wishes to emend the passage on the authority of an old manuscript to read “he would not show.” The negative particle prefixed to the immediately preceding clause is sufficient, however, and is not repeated here in our manuscripts.].

## CHAPTER XXVIII

[Col. 0246]

### 9. After the deserting angels were cast down, the others were established in blessedness

When certain angels had impiously abandoned God and had been cast down from their heavenly dwelling into the lowest darkness of this air, the remaining number of angels continued in eternal blessedness and holiness with God.

For the other angels were not generated from one angel who had fallen and been condemned, so that original evil might bind them, like human beings, in the chains of an inherited succession and drag them all to their deserved punishments. Rather, when the one who became the devil had been exalted along with his companions in impiety and had been cast down together with that very exaltation, the others remained joined to the Lord in pious obedience. They also received what the fallen angels did not possess: certain knowledge by which they could be secure concerning their own everlasting and never-failing stability.

## CHAPTER XXIX
In place of the expelled angels there succeeds a restored portion of the human race. It therefore pleased God, the Creator and Ruler of the universe, that, since not the entire multitude of angels had perished by deserting God, that part which had perished should remain in everlasting destruction, while those who had remained with God when the others deserted Him should rejoice in the certainly known and everlasting happiness that awaited them [Note: [Col. 0246] Here the printed editions add *secura* (“secure”); this word is absent from the better manuscripts.]. But since the other rational creature, which existed in human beings, had wholly perished through sins and punishments, both original and personal, a portion of it was restored, so that what that diabolical fall had diminished from the angelic society might be replenished [Note: [Col. 0246] Thus Am., Er., Dan., and most manuscripts. But Lov. and Arn. have *suppleret* (“might replenish”).]. For this was promised to the saints at the resurrection: they will be equal to the angels of God (Luke 20:36). Thus the heavenly Jerusalem, our mother, the city of God, will not be deprived of any number of her citizens [Note: [Col. 0246] The manuscripts read *nulla civium numerositate*, omitting *suorum* (“of her citizens”).], and perhaps will even reign with a more abundant multitude [Note: [Col. 0246] So Am., Er., Dan., and the manuscripts. But Lov. and Arn. have *sed uberiore* (“but with a more abundant [multitude]”).] [Note: [Col. 0246] See *On the City of God*, Book 22, chapter 1.]. For we do not know the number either of the holy human beings or of the unclean demons, in whose place the children of the holy mother [Note: [Col. 0246] The printed editions read *sanctae matris Ecclesiae* (“of the holy mother Church”). *Ecclesiae* is absent from the manuscripts.], who appeared barren on earth, will succeed and remain without end of time in that peace from which the others fell. But the number of those citizens—whether the number that exists now or that which is destined to exist—is known to that Craftsman who calls things that are not as though they were (Romans 4:17), and orders all things by measure, number, and weight (Wisdom 11:21).

## CHAPTER XXX

Human beings are restored neither by merits nor by free will, but by grace. But can this portion of the human race, to which God has promised liberation and an everlasting kingdom, be restored by the merits of its works? By no means. For what good does the lost person accomplish [Note: [Col. 0246] The printed editions read *operari potest perditus* (“can the lost person accomplish”). But the manuscripts have *operatur perditus* (“what does the lost person accomplish”). Ten of these manuscripts continue, *nisi quando fuerit* (“unless when he has been…”). One Vatican manuscript has *nisi quando vel quantum fuerit* (“unless when or to whatever extent he has been…”). Several manuscripts have *reparatus* (“restored”) where others read *liberatus* (“freed”).], except insofar as he has been freed from destruction? Is it by the free choice of the will? This too is impossible. For by using free will wrongly, a human being both lost himself and lost free will itself. [Col. 0247] Just as someone who kills himself certainly kills himself by living, but by killing himself does not live, nor can he raise himself again after he has killed himself, so, when free will sinned, free will itself was lost through the victorious power of sin. “For by whatever anyone is overcome, by this he is enslaved” (2 Peter 2:19).

This is certainly the judgment of the apostle Peter. Since it is true, what kind of freedom, I ask, can belong to one who has been enslaved, except when he takes pleasure in sinning? For one serves freely when he willingly does the will of his master. Thus the person who is a slave of sin is free to sin. Therefore he will not be free to do what is right unless, having been freed from sin, he begins to be a slave of righteousness. This is true freedom, because of the joy of right action [Note: [Col. 0247] So Am., Er., Dan., Arn., and some manuscripts. Most others, with Lov., read *propter recte facti licentiam* (“because of the license to do what is right”). Some have *propter recte faciendi licentiam* (“because of the license to do what is right”). The reading seems to be *propter recte facti libentiam* (“because of the delight in right action”).], and at the same time a devout servitude, because of obedience to the command. But from where will this freedom to do good come to a person who is enslaved and sold, unless he is redeemed by the one whose voice says, “If the Son sets you free, then you will truly be free” (John 8:36)?

Before this begins to take place in a person, how can anyone boast of free will in a good work, when he is not yet free to work well, unless he exalts himself, puffed up with empty pride? The Apostle restrains this pride when he says, “By grace you have been saved through faith.”

## CHAPTER XXXI

Faith and good works are gifts from God. And lest they should at least claim faith for themselves in such a way that they failed to understand that it too had been given by God, the same Apostle says elsewhere that he obtained mercy in order to be faithful (1 Corinthians 7:25). Here also he added and said, “And this is not from yourselves; it is the gift of God—not from works, so that no one may boast.” And lest it be thought that good works would be lacking in believers, he added again: “For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared beforehand so that we might walk in them” (Ephesians 2:8–10).

We therefore become truly free when God fashions us—that is, forms and creates us—not as human beings, which He has already done, but so that we may be good human beings [Note: [Col. 0247] The word *homines* (“human beings”) is absent here from several manuscripts.]—which He now accomplishes by His grace—so that we may be “a new creation in Christ Jesus” (Galatians 6:15), according to what has been said: “Create in me a clean heart, O God” (Psalm 50:12). For God had not failed to create his heart, insofar as the nature of the human heart is concerned [Note: [Col. 0247] Lov. adds: “but he asks for the renewal of the soul that dwells in the Prophet’s heart.” This is evidently a gloss, which we have removed on the authority of the ancient manuscripts and the editions of Am., Er., Dan., and Arn.].

## CHAPTER XXXII

Good will comes from God. Likewise, lest anyone, even if not boasting of works, should boast of free choice of the will itself, as though merit began from him and the freedom to do good were a reward owed to him, let him hear the same herald of grace saying: “For it is God who works in you both to will and to work, for his good pleasure” (Philippians 2:13). And elsewhere: “So then it depends not on the one who wills or on the one who runs, but on God who shows mercy” (Romans 9:16).

Without doubt, if a person is of an age at which he already uses reason, he cannot believe, hope, or love unless he wills to do so; nor can he attain the prize of God’s heavenly calling unless he has run willingly (Philippians 3:14). How then does it depend “not on the one who wills or on the one who runs, but on God who shows mercy,” unless the will itself, as it is written, is prepared by the Lord (Proverbs 8:35, according to the Septuagint)?

Otherwise, if it was said, “not on the one who wills or on the one who runs, but on God who shows mercy,” because both are involved—that is, the human will and God’s mercy—so that we understand the statement to mean, “It does not depend on the one who wills or on the one who runs, but on God who shows mercy,” as though it meant, “The human will alone is not sufficient unless God’s mercy is also present,” then God’s mercy alone is not sufficient unless the human will is also present. And consequently, if it is rightly said, “It does not depend on the willing human being, but on God who shows mercy,” because the human will alone does not accomplish this, why is it not also rightly said in the contrary form, “It does not depend on God who shows mercy, but on the willing human being,” because God’s mercy alone does not accomplish this?

But if no Christian will dare to say, “It does not depend on God who shows mercy, but on the willing human being,” lest he plainly contradict the Apostle, it remains that the statement, “not on the one who wills or on the one who runs, but on God who shows mercy,” should rightly be understood in such a way that everything is attributed to God. He both prepares the human being’s good will so that it may be helped and helps it once prepared.

A good will precedes many gifts of God, but not all of them; and where it does not precede, it is itself among those gifts. For both statements are found in the sacred writings: “His mercy will go before me” (Psalm 59:10), and “His mercy will follow me” (Psalm 23:6). He goes before the unwilling person so that he may will; He follows the willing person so that he may not will in vain.

Why are we instructed to pray for our enemies (Matthew 5:44)—who certainly do not wish to live devoutly—unless so that God may work in them to will [Note: [Col. 0248] Thus Am., Er., Dan., and the manuscripts. But Lov. and Arn. read, “unless God works in them so that they may will.”]? Likewise, why are we instructed to ask so that we may receive (Matthew 7:7), unless so that what we will may be brought about by the one who brought it about that we should will? We therefore pray for our enemies so that God’s mercy may go before them, just as it went before us; but we pray for ourselves so that His mercy may follow us.

## CHAPTER XXXIII

10. All human beings are born children of wrath and need Christ as reconciler. What the wrath of God is. The human race was therefore held under just condemnation, and all were children of wrath. Concerning this wrath it is written: “For all our days have failed, and in your wrath we have wasted away; our years will be meditated upon like a spider” (Psalm 90:9). Concerning this wrath Job also says: “For a human being born of woman is short-lived and full of wrath” (Job 14:1). Concerning this wrath the Lord Jesus also says: “Whoever believes in the Son has eternal life; but whoever does not believe in the Son does not have life [Note: [Col. 0248] The printed editions read, “does not have eternal life.” But the manuscripts agree with the Gospel and do not repeat *aeternam* (“eternal”) here. Some of these also have the future tense: “will not have life.”], but the wrath of God remains upon him” (John 3:36). He did not say, “It will come,” but “it remains.” For every human being is born with this condition. Hence the Apostle says: “For we too were by nature children of wrath, like the rest” (Ephesians 2:3).

Since human beings were in this wrath through original sin—and all the more grievously and harmfully insofar as they had added greater or more numerous sins besides [Col. 0249]—a mediator was necessary, that is, a reconciler, who would appease this wrath by the offering of a unique sacrifice, whose shadow was represented by all the sacrifices of the Law and the Prophets. Hence the Apostle says: “For if, while we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son, much more, having now been reconciled in his blood, shall we be saved from wrath through him” (Romans 5:10, 9).

When God is said to be angry, this does not signify a disturbance of the sort found in the mind of an angry human being. Rather, by a word transferred from human emotions, His vengeance—which is just and only just—has received the name “wrath.” Thus, by the mediator we are reconciled to God and receive the Holy Spirit, so that from enemies we may become children: “For all who are led by the Spirit of God are children of God” (Romans 8:14). This is the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord.

## CHAPTER XXXIV

Christ, the mediator, was born of Mary through the ineffable incarnation of the Word. Against the Apollinarians. Concerning this mediator, it would take a long time to say as much as is worthy of him, although such things cannot worthily be spoken by a human being [Note: [Col. 0249] In most manuscripts, *digna* (“worthy things”).]. Who, indeed, could explain in suitable words even this one fact: “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14), so that we might believe in the only-begotten Son of God the almighty Father, born of the Holy Spirit and the virgin Mary?

The Word became flesh in this way: divinity assumed flesh, not divinity being changed into flesh. Here we must understand “flesh” to mean “human being,” a part signifying the whole, just as it is said, “By works of the Law no flesh shall be justified” (Romans 3:20), that is, no human being.

For it is not permissible to say that anything belonging to human nature was lacking in that assumption, but it was a human nature entirely free from every bond of sin. It was not like the nature born from both sexes through the desire of the flesh with the burden of guilt, whose guilt is washed away by regeneration. Rather, he was such as ought to be born of a virgin—one whom his mother’s faith, not lust, had conceived. If her virginity had been corrupted even in giving birth, he would no longer have been born of a virgin; and the whole Church would falsely—God forbid—confess that he had been born of the virgin Mary. The Church imitates his mother: every day she gives birth to his members, and she is a virgin.

If you wish, read my letter on the virginity of holy Mary [Note: [Col. 0249] The printed editions read, “my letter sent to…” *missas* (“sent”) is absent from the manuscripts.] to the distinguished man whom I name with honor and affection, Volusianus (Letter 137).

## CHAPTER XXXV

Christ is both God and human being. Against the error that belonged to Leporius and later to the Nestorians. Accordingly, Christ Jesus, the Son of God, is both God and human being [Note: [Col. 0249] Am., Er., Lov., and Arn. read, “the Son of God is, and is God, and is human being.” We have altered the punctuation and deleted the second occurrence of *est* (“is”) on the authority of certain manuscripts.]. God before all ages, a human being in our age. He is God because he is the Word of God: “For the Word was God” (John 1:1). He is a human being because a rational soul and flesh were joined to the Word in the unity of one person. [Col. 0250]

Therefore, insofar as he is God, he and the Father are one (John 10:30); but insofar as he is human, the Father is greater than he (John 14:28). Although he was the only Son of God—not by grace but by nature—in order that he might also be full of grace, he became the son of a human being. The same one is both, and from both is one Christ.

For, though he was in the form of God, he did not deem it robbery to be equal to God, as he was by nature; yet he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant (Philippians 2:6–7), without losing or diminishing the form of God. Thus he both became lower and remained equal: one person, both realities, as it is written. One is so because of the Word, the other because of the human being: because of the Word, equal to the Father; because of the human being, lower.

One Son of God, and the same one the son of a human being; one son of a human being, and the same one the Son of God—not two Sons of God, God and human being, but one Son of God: God without beginning, a human being from a definite beginning, our Lord Jesus Christ.

## CHAPTER XXXVI

11. Grace is commended in Christ, who was raised to the dignity of the Son of God without any merits. Here the grace of God is commended in a particularly grand and evident manner. For what did human nature in Christ as a human being merit, that it should be uniquely assumed into the unity of the person of the only Son of God? What good will, what devotion to a good purpose, what good works preceded him, by which this human being might merit becoming one person with God? Was he previously a human being, and was this unique benefit granted to him because he had uniquely merited God [Note: [Col. 0250] So the excellent Remigianus manuscript and two Colbertine manuscripts together with one Vatican manuscript. Other manuscripts, as in the earlier editions, have “so that he might uniquely merit God.”]?

Certainly, from the moment he began to exist as a human being, he did not begin to be anything other than the Son of God [Note: [Col. 0250] Here the word *homo* (“human being”) is absent from Am., Er., Dan., and several manuscripts.]. He was the only Son, and because of the Word of God, which, having assumed him, became flesh, he was also God. Thus, just as any human being is one person—namely, a rational soul and flesh—so Christ is one person, the Word and the human being.

Whence came such glory to human nature [Note: [Col. 0250] The Fuliensis manuscript reads, “such grace.”], without doubt freely given and without any preceding merits? Only because here the great and singular grace of God is plainly shown to those who consider it faithfully and soberly, so that they may understand that human beings are justified from sins by that same grace by which it came about that Christ as a human being could have no sin.

Thus the angel also greeted his mother when he announced to her that this birth would take place: “Hail,” he said, “full of grace.” And shortly afterward: “You have found grace,” he said, “with God” (Luke 1:28, 30). She is said to be full of grace and to have found grace with God so that she might be the mother of her Lord—indeed, of the Lord of all.

But when John the Evangelist had said of Christ, “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us,” he continued: “And we saw his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth.” What he says, “The Word became flesh,” means “full of grace”; what he says, “the glory of the only-begotten from the Father,” means “full of truth.” For Truth itself, the only-begotten Son of God—not by grace but by nature—by grace assumed a human being in such unity of person [Col. 0251] that the same one was also the son of a human being.

## CHAPTER XXXVII

Christ’s birth from the Holy Spirit demonstrates grace. For this same Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God—that is, the only Son [Note: [Col. 0251] So several manuscripts with Am., Er., and Dan. Lov. and Arn. have “the same.”]—our Lord, was born of the Holy Spirit and the virgin Mary.

The Holy Spirit is certainly God’s gift, and this gift itself is equal to the one who gives it. Therefore the Holy Spirit is also God, not less than the Father and the Son. Since, then, Christ’s birth as a human being was from the Holy Spirit, what else is demonstrated except grace itself?

When the virgin asked the angel how what he announced to her could happen, since she did not know a man, the angel replied: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the holy one who will be born from you will be called the Son of God” (Luke 1:35).

And when Joseph wished to dismiss her, suspecting adultery because he knew that she was not pregnant by him, he received this answer from the angel: “Do not be afraid to take Mary your wife; for what has been born in her is from the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 1:20). That is: what you suspect to be from another man is from the Holy Spirit.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII

12. Christ was born from the Holy Spirit not as from a father, but from Mary as from a mother. Are we therefore to say that the Holy Spirit is the father of Christ as a human being, so that God the Father begot the Word, the Holy Spirit the human being, and from these two substances there would be one Christ—Son of God the Father according to the Word, and son of the Holy Spirit according to the human being—as though the Holy Spirit had begotten him from the virgin mother as his father?

Who would dare say this? There is no need to demonstrate through argument how many other absurdities would follow, since this itself is already so absurd that no faithful ears could endure it.

Accordingly, as we confess, our Lord Jesus Christ, who is God from God but was born as a human being from the Holy Spirit and the virgin Mary, is, in both substances—divine and human—the only Son of God the almighty Father, from whom the Holy Spirit proceeds.

How then do we say that Christ was born from the Holy Spirit if the Holy Spirit did not beget him? Is it because the Spirit made him? Our Lord Jesus Christ, insofar as he is God, is the one through whom all things were made (John 1:3); but insofar as he is human, he himself was also made, as the Apostle says: “He was made from the seed of David according to the flesh” (Romans 1:3).

But although the whole Trinity made that creature which the Virgin conceived and bore, even though it belonged solely to the person of the Son—for the works of the Trinity are not separable—why was only the Holy Spirit named in its making? Is it also the case that whenever one of the three is named in connection with some work, the whole Trinity is understood to have performed it? Indeed it is, and this can be demonstrated by examples. But there is no need to linger over this longer.

What troubles us is how it was said, “Born from the Holy Spirit,” when he is in no way the son of the Holy Spirit. For although God made this world, it is not permissible to call it God’s son or to say that it was born from God; rather, it was made, created, founded, or established by him—or whatever similar expression we can rightly use.

Here, then, when we confess that he was born from the Holy Spirit and the virgin Mary, it is difficult to explain how he is not the son of the Holy Spirit but is the son of the virgin Mary, since he was born from both. Certainly, he was not born from the Holy Spirit as from a father, but he was born from Mary as from a mother.

## CHAPTER XXXIX

Not everything born from something should be called its son. It must not therefore be granted that whatever is born from something should immediately be called the son of that thing. To omit the fact that a son is born from a human being in one way, while hair, a louse [Note: [Col. 0252] The older manuscripts have *peduculum* (“louse”).], or a worm is born in another way—and none of these is a son—to omit these examples, since they are an unbecoming comparison for so great a matter, certainly no one would rightly call those who are born from water and the Holy Spirit children of water. Rather, they are plainly called children of God the Father and of Mother Church.

Thus the Son of God was born from the Holy Spirit, but not as the son of the Holy Spirit. For the point of what we said about hair and the other examples is only to warn us that not everything born from something can also be called the son of that from which it is born.

Likewise, it does not follow that all who are called someone’s children must also be said to have been born from that person, as is the case with adopted children. People are also called children of Gehenna—not because they were born from it, but because they were prepared for it—just as they are called children of the kingdom who are prepared for the kingdom [Note: [Col. 0252] The pronoun *qui* (“who”) is absent from four Vatican manuscripts and from the older Gallican manuscripts.].

## CHAPTER XL

The manner in which Christ was born from the Holy Spirit signifies the grace of hypostatic union. Since, then, something may be born from something else without thereby being its son, and since not everyone who is called a son is born from the one whose son he is called, this manner in which Christ was born from the Holy Spirit—not as a son—and from the virgin Mary—as a son—indicates to us the grace of God.

Through this grace, without any preceding merits, a human being was joined to God the Word at the very beginning of his nature, when he began to exist, in such unity of person that the same one was the Son of God who was the son of a human being, and the son of a human being who was the Son of God. Thus, in the assumption of human nature, grace itself became, in a certain manner, natural to that human being, so that he could not commit any sin [Note: [Col. 0252] The Germanensis manuscript has *qui* (“which”). Two other manuscripts have *qua* (“by which”).].

This grace had to be signified through the Holy Spirit because the Holy Spirit is properly God in such a way that he is also called the gift of God (Acts 8:20). To speak of this adequately—if it can in fact be done—would require an exceedingly lengthy discussion [Note: [Col. 0252] Here Am., Er., Lov., and Arn. add, “would take a very long time”; this is absent from the manuscripts.].

## CHAPTER XLI

13. Christ was without sin, but was made sin. Having therefore been neither sown nor conceived through any pleasure of carnal desire, and thus drawing no original sin, he was also, by the grace of God, joined and united in a wondrous and ineffable manner to the Word of the Father, the only-begotten Son—not by grace, but by nature—in the unity of one person [Note: [Col. 0253] Some manuscripts have *in unitatem personae* (“into the unity of one person”).]. Therefore he himself committed no sin. Yet, because of the likeness of sinful flesh in which he came (Romans 8:3), he too was called “sin,” being destined to be sacrificed for the removal of sins.

For in the old Law, sacrifices for sins were called “sins” (Hosea 4:8). He truly became what those sacrifices prefigured. Hence, when the Apostle had said, “We beg you on behalf of Christ, be reconciled to God,” he immediately added: “He made him who knew no sin to be sin for us, so that we might become the righteousness of God in him” (2 Corinthians 5:20–21).

He did not say—as it is read in certain corrupt manuscripts—“He who knew no sin made [him] sin for us,” as though Christ himself had sinned for us. Rather, he said, “He made him who knew no sin”—that is, Christ—“sin for us”: God made him sin for us, to whom we were to be reconciled. That is, he made him a sacrifice for sins, through which we might be reconciled.

He himself, therefore, was sin, so that we might be righteousness—not ours, but God’s; not in us, but in him. Just as he displayed sin—not his own, but ours—as constituted not in himself but in us, by the likeness of sinful flesh in which he was crucified.

Since sin was not present in him, he therefore died, in a certain manner, to sin when he died to the flesh in which there was the likeness of sin. And since he himself had never lived according to the oldness of sin, by his resurrection he signified our new life rising from the old death in which we had been dead through sin [Note: [Col. 0253] The printed editions have *nova* (“new,” feminine/neuter). The manuscripts more correctly have *novam* (“new,” feminine), joining it with *vitam* (“life”); this preserves the antithesis with the preceding words, “from the old death.”].

## CHAPTER XLII

Baptism is given so that we may die and rise again. This is the great sacrament of Baptism celebrated in us: all who belong to this grace die to sin, just as he is said to have died to sin because he died to the flesh—that is, to the likeness of sin—and they live by being reborn from the washing, just as he rose from the tomb, whatever the age of their bodies may be.

## CHAPTER XLIII

In Baptism all die to sin, both infants and adults. From the newly born infant to the decrepit old man, just as no one is to be prevented from Baptism, so no one fails to die to sin in Baptism. Infants die only to original sin; adults die also to all those sins which they have added by living wickedly to what they brought with them at birth.

## CHAPTER XLIV

The figure *ἑτέρωσις* (*heterōsis*), in which one number is understood for another. For this reason they too are often said to die to “sin,” although without doubt they die not to one sin but to many—to all the sins they have already committed, whether in thought, speech, or deed. This is because a plural number is often signified by a singular number.

Thus Virgil says, “They fill the womb with armed soldiery” (*Aeneid* 2.20), although they did this with many soldiers. In our own Scriptures we read, “Pray therefore to the Lord, that he may take away the serpent from us” (Numbers 21:7, according to the Septuagint); it does not say “the serpents,” although this is what the people were suffering from when they said it. There are innumerable examples of the same kind.

When that one original sin is also signified by a plural number, as when we say that infants are baptized for the remission of sins, rather than “for the remission of sin,” the reverse figure is used: a singular number is signified by a plural [Note: [Col. 0254] Am., Er., Lov., and Arn. add *locutionem* (“expression”) here; this is superfluous, since in the manuscripts *numerum* (“number”) is more naturally understood.].

Thus in the Gospel, after Herod’s death, it was said, “For those who were seeking the child’s life are dead” (Matthew 2:20); it did not say, “He is dead.” And in Exodus it says, “They made gods for themselves out of gold,” although they had made one calf, concerning which they said, “These are your gods, Israel, who brought you out of the land of Egypt” (Exodus 32:31, 4). Here too a plural is used for a singular.

## CHAPTER XLV

Several kinds of sin are present in the first sin of the human being. Although even in that one sin which entered the world through one human being and spread to all human beings (Romans 5:12), and because of which infants too are baptized, several sins can be understood if that one sin is divided, as it were, into its individual parts.

It contains pride, because the human being preferred to be under his own power rather than under God’s power; sacrilege, because he did not believe God; murder, because he plunged himself into death; spiritual fornication, because the integrity of the human mind was corrupted through the serpent’s persuasion; theft, because he appropriated the forbidden food; greed, because he desired more than ought to have been sufficient for him; and whatever else may be found in this one offense through careful consideration.

## CHAPTER XLVI

It is probable that children are bound by the sins of not only their first parents. It is not improperly said that infants are bound by the sins of their parents—not only by those of the first human beings, but also by the sins of their own parents, from whom they themselves were born.

That divine sentence, “I will repay the sins of the fathers upon the children” (Deuteronomy 5:9), certainly holds them before, through regeneration, they begin to belong to the New Testament. This Testament was foretold when Ezekiel said that children would not bear the sins of their fathers and that the proverb would no longer exist in Israel: “The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children’s teeth have been set on edge” [Note: [Col. 0254] The older manuscripts have *obstipuerunt* (“were numbed”), a word derived from *stipes* (“stump”).] (Ezekiel 18:1–20).

For this reason each person is reborn: so that whatever sin there is in him with which he was born may be undone. The sins committed afterward through wrongdoing can also be healed through repentance, as we see happening even after Baptism.

Consequently, regeneration was instituted for no other reason than that generation is defective. Thus even one born of a legitimate marriage says, “In iniquities I was conceived, and in sins my mother nourished me in the womb” (Psalm 50:7). He did not say here “in iniquity” or “in sin,” although that too could rightly have been said; rather, he preferred to say “iniquities” and “sins.”

For even in that one sin which spread to all human beings and is so great that through it human nature was changed [Col. 0255] and transformed into the necessity of death, there are found, as I explained above, several sins. There are also the sins of parents, which, although they cannot change nature to the same extent, nevertheless bind their children by guilt unless free grace and divine mercy come to their aid.

## CHAPTER XLVII

The extent to which the sins of parents are transmitted to their children must not be defined rashly. But concerning the sins of other parents, through whom each person succeeds one another in his ancestral line from Adam down to his own father, it may reasonably be debated whether the one who is born becomes entangled in the evil acts and multiplied original offenses of all of them, so that each person is born in a worse condition the later he is born.

Or perhaps God threatens the descendants with the sins of their parents to the third and fourth generation because, in His merciful restraint, He does not extend His wrath further with respect to the guilt of their ancestors, lest those to whom the grace of regeneration is not granted should be weighed down by too great a burden in their eternal damnation if they were compelled to contract, from the beginning of the human race, the original sins of all their preceding parents and pay the punishments due for them.

Or perhaps something else concerning so great a matter can or cannot be discovered through more careful examination and treatment of the holy Scriptures. I do not dare to affirm anything rashly.

## CHAPTER XLVIII

14. Original sin is abolished only through Christ. Nevertheless, that one sin which was committed in a place and condition of such great happiness, and which was so great that, through one human being, the whole human race was condemned originally—and, so to speak, at its root—is not removed or washed away except through the one mediator between God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus (1 Timothy 2:5). He alone could be born in such a way that he did not need to be reborn.

## CHAPTER XLIX

John’s Baptism did not bring about regeneration. Why Christ wished to be baptized by John. Those who were baptized with John’s baptism were not reborn (Matthew 3:13)—the baptism with which he himself was also baptized. Rather, through the preliminary ministry of the one who said, “Prepare the way for the Lord” (Luke 3:4), they were being prepared for this one in whom alone they could be reborn.

His Baptism is not in water only, as John’s was, but also in the Holy Spirit (Mark 1:8), so that whoever believes in Christ may be regenerated by that Spirit from whom Christ was generated and did not need regeneration [Note: [Col. 0255] Lov. has *regeneratus* (“regenerated”). Am., Er., Dan., and the more authoritative manuscripts more correctly have *generatus* (“generated”).].

Hence the voice of the Father that came upon him after he had been baptized—“Today I have begotten you” [Note: [Col. 0255] This is not how it appears in the Gospel. For this reason Danaeus boldly adds, without manuscript authority, “You are my Son.”] (Psalm 2:7; Hebrews 5:5)—does not point to the single day on which he was baptized, but to the immutable eternity, in order to show that this human being belonged to the person of the Only-begotten. For where there is no day that begins with the end of yesterday or ends with the beginning of tomorrow, it is always today.

He therefore wished to be baptized in water by John, not so that any iniquity of his might be washed away, but so that great humility might be commended. Baptism found nothing in him to cleanse, just as death found nothing in him to punish. Thus, overcome and defeated by the truth of justice, not by force of power, the devil—because he had most unjustly killed one who had no sin—would justly lose through him those whom he held on account of sin.

Both things, therefore, were received by him—Baptism and death—for the purpose of a definite dispensation, not from pitiable necessity but rather from merciful will, so that one might take away the sin of the world, just as one had brought sin into the world, that is, into the whole human race.

## CHAPTER L

Through Christ not only original sin but also the other added sins are taken away. The one brought one sin into the world; this one, however, not only removed that one sin but also removed all the sins he found added to it.

Hence the Apostle says: “It is not as through one who sinned [Note: [Col. 0256] Arn. and six manuscripts have *per unum peccatum* (“through one sin”). We have retained the older reading, which corresponds to the Greek *di’ henos hamartēsantos*, which Augustine usually follows.] that the gift is also. For judgment indeed came from one offense for condemnation, but grace came from many offenses for justification.”

The one sin that is transmitted originally makes people liable to condemnation even if it is the only sin they have. Grace, however, justifies a person from many offenses: in addition to that one sin which he has inherited originally in common with everyone, he has also committed many personal sins.

## CHAPTER LI

No one is freed from Adam’s condemnation except by being reborn in Christ. Nevertheless, what he says shortly afterward—“As through one trespass there resulted condemnation for all human beings, so through one act of righteousness there resulted justification of life for all human beings” (Romans 5:16, 18)—clearly indicates that no one is born from Adam without being held under condemnation, and that no one is freed from condemnation except by being reborn in Christ.

## CHAPTER LII
## The likeness of Christ’s death and resurrection in baptism, equally in infants and adults

After speaking, as far as he judged sufficient for the place in his Epistle, of the punishment that came through one man and of the grace that came through one man, he commended the great mystery of holy baptism in the cross of Christ in such a way that we understand baptism in Christ to be nothing other than a likeness of Christ’s death, and the death of crucified Christ to be nothing other than a likeness of the remission of sins: just as true death occurred in him, so true remission of sins occurs in us; and just as true resurrection occurred in him, so true justification occurs in us.

For he says:

> What then shall we say? Shall we continue in sin, so that grace may abound?

For above he had said:

> Where sin abounded, grace abounded all the more. (Romans V, 20)

And therefore he himself posed the question whether one ought to remain in sin in order to obtain an abundance of grace. But he replied:

> By no means!

And he added:

> If we have died to sin, how shall we live in it?

Then, to show that we have died to sin, he says:

> Or do you not know that all of us who were baptized in Christ Jesus were baptized into his death?

If, therefore, we are shown by this to have died to sin, because we were baptized into Christ’s death, then surely infants also who are baptized in Christ die to sin, because they are baptized into his death. For no exception was made when it was said:

> All of us who were baptized in Christ Jesus were baptized into his death.

And this was said in order to prove that we have died to sin. But to what sin do infants die by being reborn, unless it is the sin which they contracted by being born?

Accordingly, what follows also pertains to them:

> Therefore we were buried with him through baptism into death, so that, just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too might walk in newness of life.

[Note: [Col. 0257] Thus the older manuscripts, in accordance with the Greek. The printed editions instead read, “For we were buried.”]

> For if we have been planted together in the likeness of his death, we shall also be in the likeness of his resurrection. Knowing this, that our old man was crucified together with him, so that the body of sin might be brought to nothing, and that we might no longer serve sin. For whoever has died has been justified from sin. But if we have died with Christ, we believe that we shall also live together with him, knowing that Christ, having risen from the dead, dies no more; death shall no longer rule over him. For the death he died, he died to sin once for all; but the life he lives, he lives to God. So you also must consider yourselves dead indeed to sin, but alive to God in Christ Jesus. (Romans VI, 1–11)

[Note: [Col. 0257] Several manuscripts read, “living.”]

He had begun from this point to prove that we must not remain in sin so that grace may abound, and he had said:

> If we have died to sin, how shall we live in it?

And in order to show that we had died to sin, he had added:

[Note: [Col. 0257] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions instead read, “he added.”]

> Or do you not know that all of us who were baptized in Christ Jesus were baptized into his death?

Thus he closed the whole passage in the manner in which he had begun. For he presented Christ’s death in such a way that he even said that Christ himself had died to sin. To what sin, unless to the flesh in which he was—though there was not sin in it, but the likeness of sin, and for that reason it was called by the name of sin?

[Note: [Col. 0257] The printed editions read, “of the flesh.” Most manuscripts read, “to the flesh.” Some omit the word altogether.]

Therefore, speaking to those baptized into Christ’s death, in which not only adults but also infants are baptized, he says:

> So also you—that is, just as Christ—must consider yourselves dead to sin, but alive to God in Christ Jesus.

## CHAPTER LIII

### The cross of Christ, his burial, resurrection, and so forth, as figures of the Christian life

Whatever, therefore, was accomplished in Christ’s cross, burial, resurrection on the third day, ascension into heaven, and sitting at the right hand of the Father was accomplished so that by these events, not merely spoken of mystically but also enacted, the Christian life lived here might be conformed to them.

For the sake of his cross it was said:

> Those who belong to Jesus Christ have crucified their flesh with its passions and desires. (Galatians V, 24)

[Note: [Col. 0257] The printed editions read, “with its vices.” The principal manuscripts read, “with its passions,” in accordance with the Greek, *sùn toîs pathêmasi*.]

For the sake of his burial:

> We were buried with Christ through baptism into death.

For the sake of his resurrection:

> Just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too might walk in newness of life.

For the sake of his ascension into heaven and his sitting at the right hand of the Father:

> If you have been raised with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God; set your minds on the things that are above, not on the things that are upon the earth. For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God. (Colossians III, 1–4)

## CHAPTER LIV

### The last judgment concerns the events to be accomplished at the end of the age

But what we confess will happen concerning Christ—that he will come from heaven to judge the living and the dead—does not pertain to the life lived here, because it is not among the events accomplished by him, but among those to be accomplished at the end of the age.

To this pertains what the Apostle subsequently added:

> When Christ, your life, appears, then you also will appear with him in glory. (Colossians III, 1–4)

## CHAPTER LV

### “To judge the living and the dead” understood in two ways

What is meant by his judging the living and the dead can be understood in two ways. Either we understand by “the living” those whom his coming will find here not yet dead, but still living in this flesh, and by “the dead” those who have departed from the body before he comes, or who will depart before he comes; or we understand the living to be the righteous and the dead to be the unrighteous, since the righteous too will be judged.

For sometimes God’s judgment is spoken of in relation to evil, as in:

> Those who have done evil will rise to the resurrection of judgment. (John V, 29)

At other times it is spoken of in relation to good, as it is said:

> O God, save me by your name, and judge me by your strength. (Psalm LIII, 3)

For by God’s judgment the very distinction between the good and the evil is made, so that the good, being freed from evil and not destroyed together with the wicked, may be separated to the right hand. (Matthew XXV, 32–33)

For this reason he cried out:

> Judge me, O God!

And, as though explaining what he had said, he added:

> Distinguish my cause from an unholy nation. (Psalm XLII, 1)

## CHAPTER LVI

### 15. The Holy Spirit and the Church are rightly mentioned in the Creed. The heavenly Church assists the earthly Church

When, for the sake of the brevity of the Confession, we have spoken of Jesus Christ, the only Son of God, our Lord, we add that we likewise believe in the Holy Spirit, so that the Trinity which is God may be complete; then the holy Church is mentioned.

[Note: [Col. 0258] Several manuscripts read, “we add that we believe in these things.” Others read, “we add, as is fitting, that we believe in this way.” A few read, “we add, as you know, that we believe in this way”; this is no less satisfactory.]

From this it is understood that rational creation, belonging to the free Jerusalem (Galatians IV, 26), was to be mentioned after the Creator, that is, after that supreme Trinity. For whatever is said about the man Christ pertains to the unity of the person of the Only-Begotten.

The proper order of the Confession therefore required that the Church be joined to the Trinity, as a house to its inhabitant, as a temple to God, and as a city to its founder.

Here the Church must be understood in its entirety—not only in that part [Note: [Col. 0258] Am. Er. Dan. and several manuscripts read, “which.”] which journeys on earth, praising the name of the Lord from the rising of the sun to its setting (Psalm CXII, 3), and singing a new song after the captivity of the old age, but also in that part which has always, from the time it was created, remained united to God in heaven and has experienced no evil through its fall.

This heavenly part remains blessed among the holy Angels, and assists its pilgrim part as is fitting; for the two will be one in the fellowship of eternity, and now they are one in the bond of charity. The whole Church has been established to worship the one God.

Therefore neither the whole Church nor any part of it wishes to be worshiped in place of God, nor does it wish to be God to anyone belonging to the temple of God—a temple built from gods whom the uncreated God makes.

Accordingly, if the Holy Spirit were a creature and not the Creator, he would certainly be a rational creature; for that is the highest kind of creature.
