[Note: [Col. 0259] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read, “For he himself would be the highest creature.”]

And therefore he would not be placed before the Church in the Rule of Faith, because he too would belong to the Church in that part of it which is in heaven. Nor would he have a temple; rather, he himself would be a temple.

But he has a temple, of which the Apostle says:

> Do you not know that your bodies are temples of the Holy Spirit, who is in you, whom you have from God?

And elsewhere he says of these same bodies:

> Do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ? (1 Corinthians VI, 19, 15)

How, then, can he not be God, who has a temple? Or how can he be less than Christ, whose members have a temple?

For his temple is not one thing and God’s temple another, since the Apostle himself says:

> Do you not know that you are God’s temple?

And to prove this he added:

> And the Spirit of God dwells in you. (Ibid. III, 16)

God therefore dwells in his temple—not the Holy Spirit alone, but also the Father and the Son. The Son, speaking of his own body, through which he became the head of the Church that exists among human beings, so that he himself might hold primacy in all things (Colossians I, 18), said:

> Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up. (John II, 19)

The temple of God, therefore—that is, of the entire supreme Trinity—is the holy Church, namely, the whole Church in heaven and on earth.

## CHAPTER LVII

### The stability of the heavenly Church

But what can we affirm concerning the Church that is in heaven except that there is no evil one in it, and that no one has fallen or will fall from it thereafter, from the time when God did not spare the angels who sinned, as the Apostle Peter writes, but cast them into the prisons of darkness and delivered them to be kept for punishment at the judgment? (2 Peter II, 4)

## CHAPTER LVIII

### What distinctions exist among the Angels, and whether the Angels are the stars, is uncertain

But how that most blessed and heavenly society is constituted, what distinctions of ranks exist there, so that although all are called Angels under a general name—as we read in the Epistle to the Hebrews:

> To which of the Angels did he ever say, “Sit at my right hand”? (Hebrews I, 13)

—for in this way he signified that all of them universally are called Angels—there are nevertheless Archangels there; and whether those same Archangels are called Virtues; and whether the statement

> Praise him, all his Angels; praise him, all his Virtues (Psalm CXLVIII, 2)

is equivalent to saying, “Praise him, all his Angels; praise him, all his Archangels”; and what difference exists among those four names by which the Apostle seems to have included the entire heavenly society when he says,

> Whether Thrones, or Dominions, or Principalities, or Powers (Colossians I, 16),

let those who can say so explain—if indeed they can prove what they say. I confess that I do not know these things.

But I do not even hold it as certain whether the sun, moon, and all the stars belong to that same society, although to some they appear to be luminous bodies without sensation or understanding.

[Note: [Col. 0260] See the book addressed to Orosius against the Priscillianists, chapter 11.]

## CHAPTER LIX

### It is difficult to explain what sort of bodies the Angels appeared in

Likewise, who can explain with what sort of bodies the Angels appeared to human beings, so that they were not only seen but also touched; and, again, how they may produce certain visions not through solid corporeal mass but through spiritual power—not upon bodily eyes but upon spiritual eyes or minds; or how they may say something not outwardly to the ear but inwardly in the human spirit, while themselves being present there?

[Note: [Col. 0260] The manuscripts read, “but inwardly in the soul of the human being.”]

As it is written in the Book of the Prophets:

> And the Angel who was speaking in me said to me. (Zechariah I, 9)

For he did not say, “who was speaking to me,” but “in me.”

Or they may appear in dreams and converse in the manner of dreams; for we read in the Gospel:

> Behold, an Angel of the Lord appeared to him in a dream, saying. (Matthew I, 20)

By these modes they seem to indicate that the Angels do not possess bodies that can be handled. And they create a very difficult question: how did the patriarchs wash their feet? (Genesis XVIII, 4; XIX, 2) How did Jacob wrestle with an Angel with such solid contact? (Ibid. XXXII, 24)

When these matters are investigated, and each person conjectures about them as he is able, minds are exercised profitably, provided that measured discussion is employed and the error of those who think they know what they do not know is avoided.

For what need is there to affirm, deny, or define these and similar matters at the risk of error, when they may be unknown without guilt?

## CHAPTER LX

### 16. Satan’s arts in transforming himself into an angel of light are more usefully discerned

It is more necessary to judge and discern when Satan transforms himself into an angel of light (2 Corinthians XI, 14), lest he lead someone through deception into something destructive.

For when he deceives the bodily senses but does not move the mind away from the true and upright judgment by which a person lives a faithful life, there is no danger in religion. Or when, pretending to be good, he does or says things that are consistent with good Angels, even if he is believed to be good, the error is not dangerous or morbid to the Christian faith.

But when through these alien things he begins to lead a person toward his own purposes, then discerning him and refusing to follow him requires great and necessary vigilance.

Yet how many human beings are capable of escaping all his deadly deceits unless God rules and protects them? The very difficulty of this matter is useful for this reason: that no one may place hope in himself or one human being in another, but that God may be the hope of all his people. No pious person doubts that this is entirely more advantageous for us.

## CHAPTER LXI

### The Church among Angels and human beings. Christ did not die for the Angels. How the redemption of human beings concerns the Angels

This Church, then, which exists among the holy Angels and Virtues of God, will become known to us as it truly is when we have been joined to it at the end, in order to possess everlasting blessedness together.

But the Church that journeys from it on earth is better known to us because we are in it, and because it consists of human beings, as we do.

This Church, through the blood of the Mediator who had no sin, has been redeemed from every sin. Its voice is:

> If God is for us, who is against us? He who did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all. (Romans VIII, 31–32)

For Christ did not die for the Angels.

Nevertheless, whatever among human beings is redeemed and delivered from evil through his death also benefits the Angels, because through it the human race in a certain manner returns to grace with them, after the enmity which sins created between human beings and the holy Angels. Moreover, through the redemption of human beings, the losses resulting from the fall of the angelic host are repaired.

## CHAPTER LXII

### How all things are restored and reconciled in Christ

The holy Angels, taught by God—blessed by the eternal contemplation of whose truth they live—certainly know how great a number must be supplied from the human race to complete that city.

For this reason the Apostle says that all things are restored in Christ:

> Both the things in heaven and the things on earth, in him. (Ephesians I, 10)

The things in heaven are restored when what fell from there among the Angels is restored from human beings. The things on earth are restored when the human beings predestined to eternal life are renewed from the oldness of corruption.

And thus, through that singular sacrifice in which the Mediator was offered—the one sacrifice prefigured by the many victims of the Law—the heavenly things are reconciled with the earthly, and the earthly with the heavenly.

For, as the same Apostle says:

> In him it pleased the whole fullness to dwell,

[Note: [Col. 0261] Here the printed editions add “of divinity”; most and the better manuscripts do not have it.]

> and through him to reconcile all things to himself, making peace through the blood of his cross, whether the things on earth or the things in heaven. (Colossians I, 19–20)

## CHAPTER LXIII

### How the peace of the heavenly kingdom surpasses all understanding

That peace surpasses all understanding, as it is written:

> The peace of God, which surpasses all understanding. (Philippians IV, 7)

It cannot be known by us except when we have reached those things.

For how are the heavenly things reconciled except to us—that is, by being brought into harmony with us? For there is always peace there, both among all intellectual creatures among themselves and between them and their Creator.

That peace surpasses, as was said, all understanding—but certainly ours, not the understanding of those who always see the face of the Father.

As for us, however great the human understanding within us may be, we know in part and now see through a mirror in a riddle. But when we have become equal to the Angels of God (Luke XX, 36), then, like them, we shall see face to face (1 Corinthians XIII, 12), and we shall have as much peace toward them as they have toward us, because we shall love them as much as we are loved by them.

Thus their peace will be known to us, because our peace will then be of the same kind and magnitude, and it will not surpass our understanding. But God’s peace, which exists there toward them, will without doubt surpass both our understanding and theirs.

For every rational creature that is blessed is blessed from him; he is not blessed from it. Accordingly, what is written is better understood in this sense:

> The peace of God, which surpasses all understanding.

When he says “all,” the understanding even of the holy Angels cannot be excepted; only God’s understanding is excepted.

[Note: [Col. 0262] The printed editions read, “exempted.” The manuscripts’ reading, “excepted,” is better.]

For God’s peace does not surpass God’s own understanding.

## CHAPTER LXIV

### 17. The remission of sins is explicitly expressed in the Creed. The life of the saints is without crime, but not without sin

The Angels also now agree with us when our sins are remitted. Therefore, after the commemoration of the holy Church, the remission of sins is placed in the order of the Confession.

For by this remission the Church that is on earth stands; through it what had perished and was found does not perish. (Luke XV, 24)

The gift of baptism was given against original sin, so that what was contracted by generation might be removed by regeneration; and baptism also removes whatever active sins it finds to have been committed in the heart, word, or deed.

Except for this great indulgence, then, from which the renewal of the human being begins and in which every guilt—both inborn and added—is dissolved, the rest of life, once the person has reached the age of reason, however greatly it may abound in righteousness, is not lived without the remission of sins.

For as long as the children of God live mortally, they contend with death. And although it is truly said of them:

> As many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are the children of God. (Romans VIII, 14)

they are nevertheless stirred by the Spirit of God and advance toward God as children of God, so that even by their own spirit—especially because the corruptible body weighs them down (Wisdom IX, 15)—they may, like children of human beings, fall back toward themselves through certain human movements and therefore sin.

[Note: [Col. 0262] The manuscripts read, “like children of man in certain …,” etc.]

There is, of course, a difference in degree. For although every crime is a sin, not every sin is therefore a crime.

Thus we say that the life of holy human beings, as long as they live in this mortal life, can be found without crime. But:

> If we say that we have no sin,

as that great Apostle says,

> we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us. (1 John I, 8)

[Note: [Col. 0262] The printed editions read, “the holy Apostle.” But the manuscripts’ reading, “that great Apostle,” is more apt for affirming the point emphatically.]

## CHAPTER LXV

### All crimes can be forgiven in the Church through penitence. Outside the Church sins are not forgiven

Nor should we despair of God’s mercy concerning the forgiveness of even very great crimes in the holy Church, provided that those who committed them perform penitence according to the measure of each person’s sin.

In the exercise of penitence, when something [Note: [Col. 0262] The printed editions read, “when such a crime has been committed.” The word “crime” is absent from the manuscripts.] has been committed of such a kind that the offender is separated even from the body of Christ, the measure of time should not be considered as much as the measure of grief.

> A contrite and humbled heart God does not despise. (Psalm L, 19)

But because one person’s grief is often hidden from another and does not come to the knowledge of others through words or any other signs, although it is before him to whom it is said:

> My groaning is not hidden from you (Psalm XXXVII, 10),

the leaders of the Churches rightly establish periods of penitence, so that satisfaction may also be made to the Church in which those sins themselves are forgiven.

[Note: [Col. 0263] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions instead read, “who preside over the Church.”]

For outside the Church they are not forgiven. For the Church has properly received the Holy Spirit as a pledge (2 Corinthians I, 22), without whom no sins are forgiven, so that those whose sins are forgiven may obtain eternal life.

## CHAPTER LXVI

### The remission of sins is oriented toward the future judgment

The remission of sins is more particularly granted with regard to the future judgment.

In this life, however, so powerful is what is written—

> A heavy yoke is upon the children of Adam, from the day they leave their mother’s womb until the day of burial in the mother of all (Ecclesiasticus XL, 1)—

that we even see infants afflicted and tormented by various evils after the bath of regeneration.

Thus we understand that everything accomplished through the saving Sacraments pertains more to the hope of future goods than to the retention or attainment of present goods.

Many things also appear to be forgiven here and not punished by any penalties, but their punishments are reserved for the future. For it is not without reason that the day on which the Judge of the living and the dead will come is specifically called the day of judgment.

Conversely, some things are punished here; nevertheless, if they are forgiven, they will certainly not harm people in the future age.

Therefore, concerning certain temporal punishments inflicted in this life upon those who sin, the Apostle says regarding those whose sins are blotted out, so that the punishments may not be reserved until the end:

> If we judged ourselves, we would not be judged by the Lord. But when we are judged by the Lord, we are corrected, so that we may not be condemned with the world. (1 Corinthians XI, 31–32)

## CHAPTER LXVII

### 18. Those who thought that all believers, however wickedly they had lived, would be saved through fire are refuted

Some people believe that even those who do not abandon the name of Christ, who are baptized in his Church through his washing, and who are not cut off from it by any schism or heresy, will be saved through fire no matter how many crimes they live in—crimes which they neither wash away through penitence nor redeem through almsgiving, but in which they persist with the greatest obstinacy until the final day of this life. They believe that such people will be punished by fire for a long time, in proportion to the enormity of their crimes and offenses, but not by eternal fire.

[Note: [Col. 0263] The manuscripts read, “Some people believe,” omitting “even.”]

[Note: [Col. 0263] Augustine consistently spared the name of these persons, whom he criticized several times, not only in the book *On Faith and Works*, but also in book 21 of *The City of God*, chapter 17 and those following. Johannes Garnerius believes that, when Augustine wrote this, he had Jerome in mind; see the first appendix to the first part of Mercator, p. 117. See above the Admonition to the book *On Faith and Works*.]

But those who believe this and are nevertheless Catholics seem to me to be deceived by a certain human benevolence. For divine Scripture, when consulted, gives another answer.

I have written a book on this question, entitled *On Faith and Works*, in which, according to the holy Scriptures and as far as I could with God’s help, I demonstrated that the faith which saves is the faith expressed clearly enough by the Apostle Paul when he says:

> In Christ Jesus neither circumcision nor uncircumcision has any power, but faith working through love. (Galatians V, 6)

But if faith works evil and not good, then, according to the Apostle James, it is certainly dead in itself. He says again:

> If someone says that he has faith but does not have works, can faith save him? (James II, 17, 14)

Moreover, if a wicked person will be saved through fire by faith alone, and if the blessed Paul’s statement is to be understood in this way:

> He himself will be saved, yet so as through fire,

then faith could save without works, and what his fellow Apostle James said would be false.

The same Paul’s statement would also be false:

> Do not be deceived: neither fornicators, nor idolaters, nor adulterers, nor the effeminate, nor men who lie with males, nor thieves, nor the greedy, nor drunkards, nor revilers, nor robbers will possess the kingdom of God. (1 Corinthians VI, 9–10)

For if those who persist in these crimes will nevertheless be saved because of faith in Christ, how will they not be in the kingdom of God?

## CHAPTER LXVIII

### How the Apostle’s passage about those saved through fire is to be understood. A certain fire in this life through which those building with wood are saved

But because these apostolic testimonies are exceedingly clear and cannot be false, the obscure statement about those who build upon the foundation, which is Christ, not with gold, silver, and precious stones, but with wood, hay, and straw—for it was said of these that they would be saved through fire, since they would not perish on account of the merit of the foundation—must be understood in such a way that it is not found to contradict these clear statements.

Wood, hay, and straw can reasonably be understood as desires for secular things, even things lawfully permitted, of such a kind that they cannot be lost without causing pain to the soul.

When this pain burns, if Christ has a place in the heart as its foundation—that is, if nothing is preferred to him—and the person burned by such pain would rather be deprived of the things he loves in this way than of Christ, he is saved through fire.

But if, at the time of trial, he prefers to retain such temporal and secular things rather than Christ, then he did not have Christ as his foundation, because he placed these things first, whereas in a building nothing comes before the foundation.

The fire of which the Apostle spoke in that passage must be understood as one through which both pass: both the one who builds upon this foundation with gold, silver, and precious stones and the one who builds with wood, hay, and straw.

For after saying this he added:

> Fire will test what sort each person’s work is. If anyone’s work which he has built upon it remains, he will receive a reward. But if anyone’s work is burned up, he will suffer loss; he himself, however, will be saved, yet so as through fire. (Ibid. III, 11–15)

Therefore the fire will test not the work of only one of them, but the work of both.

There is a certain [Note: [Col. 0264] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read, “indeed.”] fire of the trial of tribulation, concerning which it is plainly written elsewhere:

> The furnace tests the potter’s vessels, and the trial of tribulation tests righteous people. (Ecclesiasticus XXVII, 6)

For the present, in this life, this fire accomplishes what the Apostle said if it happens [Note: [Col. 0264] Lov. and Arn. read, “approaches.” Other manuscripts read, “happens.”] to two faithful people: one who is concerned with the things of God, how he may please God—that is, one building gold, silver, and precious stones upon the foundation of Christ—

[Note: [Col. 0265] Some manuscripts read, “upon Christ’s foundation.”]

—and another who is concerned with the things of the world, how he may please his wife (1 Corinthians VII, 32–33), that is, one building wood, hay, and straw upon the same foundation.

The work of the first is not burned, because he did not love those things whose loss would cause him pain. But the work of the second is burned, because the things possessed with love do not perish without pain.

Yet, when either alternative is placed before him, he would rather be deprived of those things than of Christ, and he does not abandon Christ out of fear of losing them, although he grieves when he loses them. He is therefore saved, yet so as through fire, because the pain of the loss of the things he had loved burns him; but it does not overthrow or consume him, since the foundation’s stability and incorruptibility protect him.

## CHAPTER LXIX

### There is also a certain purifying fire after this life

It is not incredible that something of this kind may also take place after this life, and the question may be asked whether it does. Some faithful people may be saved sooner or later through a certain purifying fire, according as they have loved perishable goods to a greater or lesser degree.

This does not apply, however, to those of whom it was said that they will not possess the kingdom of God, unless those same crimes are remitted to them after they have performed penitence in an appropriate manner.

I said “in an appropriate manner” so that they may not be barren in almsgiving. Divine Scripture attributes so much to almsgiving that the Lord foretells that he will reckon only its fruit to those on his right, and only its barrenness to those on his left.

To the former he will say:

> Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom;

but to the latter:

> Go into the eternal fire. (Matthew XXV, 34, 41)

[Note: [Col. 0265] Lovaniensis reads, “receive the kingdom of God;” and, “Go, accursed ones, into the eternal fire.” The words “of God” and “accursed ones” are absent from the manuscripts.]

## CHAPTER LXX

### 19. Crimes are not redeemed by almsgiving unless one’s life is changed

Certainly one must beware lest anyone think that those detestable crimes whose perpetrators will not possess the kingdom of God may be committed daily and redeemed daily by almsgiving.

Life must instead be changed for the better, and through almsgiving God must be appeased for past sins—not purchased, in a certain sense, so that it may always be permissible to commit those sins with impunity.

For God has given no one permission to sin (Ecclesiasticus XV, 21), although in his mercy he blots out sins already committed if appropriate satisfaction is not neglected.

## CHAPTER LXXI

### Lesser sins are expiated by the Lord’s Prayer

As for the daily, brief, and lesser sins without which this life is not lived, the daily prayer of the faithful makes satisfaction for them.

For those who have already been reborn to such a Father from water and the Spirit say:

> Our Father, who art in heaven. (John III, 5)

[Note: [Col. 0265] Here and in the similar passage below, chapter 75, the printed editions add “holy”; this word is absent from the manuscripts and from the Greek text of John III, 5, to which Augustine was referring.]

This prayer completely blots out these minimal and daily sins. It also blots out those sins from which the life of the faithful departs—even if they were wickedly committed—after repentance and a change for the better, provided that just as it is truly said,

> Forgive us our debts,

because there is no lack of things requiring forgiveness, so it is truly said:

> As we also forgive our debtors. (Matthew VI, 9, 12)

That is, provided that what is said is actually done.

[Note: [Col. 0266] The manuscripts and Am. Er. Dan. omit “provided that.”]

For it too is an almsgiving to forgive a person who asks for pardon.

## CHAPTER LXXII

### Many kinds of almsgiving

Accordingly, what the Lord says applies to everything done with useful mercy:

> Give alms, and behold, all things are clean for you. (Luke XI, 41)

Therefore, not only does the person who gives food to the hungry, drink to the thirsty, clothing to the naked, shelter to the traveler, a hiding place to the fugitive, visitation to the sick or imprisoned, ransom to the captive, support to the weak, guidance to the blind, consolation to the sorrowful, medical care to the sick, a way to the lost, counsel to the one deliberating, and whatever each needy person requires give alms;

[Note: [Col. 0266] Several manuscripts read, “whatever is needed.”]

the person who grants forgiveness to one who sins also gives alms.

Likewise, the person who corrects with a beating someone over whom he has authority, or restrains him through some discipline, while nevertheless forgiving from the heart the sin by which he was harmed or offended by that person, or praying that it may be forgiven him, gives alms—not only in what he forgives and prays for, but also in what he rebukes and in the corrective punishment he imposes, because he shows mercy.

For many benefits are conferred upon unwilling people when their welfare, not their wishes, is taken into account. They are found to be their own enemies, while their true friends are often those whom they think to be enemies; and in their error they return evil for good, although a Christian ought not to return evil even for evil.

There are therefore many kinds of almsgiving, and when we perform them, we are helped so that our sins may be forgiven.

## CHAPTER LXXIII
# The Greatest Kind of Almsgiving Is to Spare One’s Enemies

But nothing is greater than that by which we forgive from the heart whatever each person has sinned against us. For it is a lesser thing to be well-disposed, or even beneficent, toward someone who has done you no harm; but it is far greater and an act of the most magnificent goodness to love even your enemy, and always to wish good for the one who wishes you harm and, if able, does it—and to do good whenever you can. [Note: [Col. 0266] Most manuscripts read, “whatever you can.” Some then continue, “hearing God say,” or “hearing Jesus say”; this reading is also found in Ambrose, Erasmus, Daniele, and the third book of the *Sentences*, distinction 30, chapter “Here it is customary.” Lovaniensis and Arnoldus, however, after “whenever you can,” add: “Remembering the example of him who, hanging on the cross, prayed for his persecutors and admonished his own, saying, ‘Love,’ etc.”]—hearing God say, “Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who persecute you” (Matthew 5:44).

But since these are the acts of God’s perfected children, toward which every believer ought to strive, bringing the human spirit to this disposition by praying to God and struggling and contending with oneself; nevertheless, because this great good is not found in so great a multitude as we believe is heard when, in prayer, it is said, “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors”—without doubt the words of this pledge are fulfilled if a person has not yet advanced so far as to love an enemy, but nevertheless, when the person who has sinned against him asks him to forgive, he forgives from the heart. For he certainly wishes to be forgiven when he himself asks and says, “As we also forgive our debtors”: that is, “Forgive our debts as we ask, just as we forgive our debtor when he asks us.”

# Chapter LXXIV

## Those who do not forgive sins are not forgiven by God

Now, when the person against whom someone has sinned asks him for forgiveness, if he is moved by his sin to ask, he should no longer be regarded as an enemy, so that loving him would be difficult, as it was when he was practicing hostility. But whoever does not forgive from the heart the person who asks and repents of his sin should in no way suppose that the Lord forgives his own sins, since Truth cannot lie.

Who could be unaware of this among the hearers or readers of the Gospel, when he who said, “I am the truth” (John 14:6), has spoken? After teaching the prayer, he strongly commended this sentence contained in it, saying: “For if you forgive people their sins, your heavenly Father will also forgive you your sins. But if you do not forgive people, neither will your Father forgive your sins” (Matthew 6:14–15). One who does not awaken at such a great thunderclap is not asleep but dead; yet he is powerful even to raise the dead.

# Chapter LXXV

## 20. Almsgiving does not cleanse criminals and unbelievers unless they are changed

Certainly, those who live most wickedly, neither caring to correct such a life and character nor ceasing to give alms amid their very crimes and disgraceful acts, flatter themselves in vain because the Lord said, “Give alms, and behold, everything is clean for you.” They do not understand how broadly this statement applies. But in order to understand it, let them consider to whom he said it.

For it is written in the Gospel as follows: “While he was speaking, a certain Pharisee asked him to dine with him; and he entered and reclined at table. But the Pharisee began to think within himself and say why he had not washed before dinner. And the Lord said to him: ‘Now you Pharisees cleanse what is outside the cup and the dish, but what is within you is full of plunder and wickedness. Fools! Did not he who made what is outside also make what is inside?’” [Note: [Col. 0267] Lovaniensis adds here: “See that what is inside also becomes clean.” This is absent from Ambrose, Erasmus, Daniele, and most of the better manuscripts, as well as from the cited Gospel of Luke.] “Nevertheless, give alms, and behold, everything is clean for you” (Luke 11:37–41).

Are we therefore to understand this in such a way that everything would be clean for the Pharisees, who did not possess faith in Christ, even if they did not believe in him or were reborn of water and the Spirit, provided only that they gave alms, as these people suppose alms should be given? Yet all whom the faith of Christ does not cleanse are unclean, concerning which it is written, “Cleansing their hearts by faith” (Acts 15:9); and the Apostle says, “To the unclean and unbelieving nothing is clean, but both their mind and their conscience are defiled” (Titus 1:15).

How, then, could everything be clean for the Pharisees if they gave alms and were not believers? Or how could they be believers if they were unwilling to believe in Christ and be reborn by his grace? And yet what they heard is true: “Give alms, and behold, everything is clean for you.”

# Chapter LXXVI

## [Col. 0268] The first almsgiving is to have mercy on one’s own soul and live rightly

[Note: [Col. 0268] Thus the manuscripts; the printed editions read, “but whoever.”]

Whoever wishes to give alms in an orderly manner must begin with himself and give it first to himself. For almsgiving is a work of mercy, and it was said most truly: “Have mercy on your soul, pleasing God” (Sirach 30:24).

For this reason we are reborn, so that we may please God, who rightly displeases what we contracted by being born. This is the first alms that we gave ourselves, since through the mercy of the merciful God we sought out ourselves as wretched [Note: [Col. 0268] Three manuscripts read, “ourselves deservedly wretched.”], confessing his just judgment by which we became wretched. Of this the Apostle says, “The judgment from one offense brought condemnation”; and we give thanks for his great love, concerning which that same herald of grace says, “But God demonstrates his love for us in that, while we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:16, 8–9).

Thus we may judge our wretchedness truthfully, love God with the love [Note: [Col. 0268] The printed editions read, “and the love of God.” This is corrected from the manuscripts.] he himself has given, and live devoutly and rightly. When the Pharisees passed over this judgment and love of God, they nevertheless tithed even the smallest portions of their produce because of the alms they gave. And so they did not give alms beginning with themselves and first showing mercy to themselves. [Note: [Col. 0268] Ambrose, Erasmus, Lovaniensis, and Arnoldus add after “showing mercy to themselves”: “as these people suppose alms should be given.” These words have been wrongly transferred here from the preceding chapter.]

Because of this order of love it was said, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Luke 10:27). Therefore, when he rebuked them for washing themselves outwardly while inwardly they were full of plunder and wickedness, he admonished them through a certain almsgiving that a person ought first to give to himself, so that his inner parts might be cleansed. [Note: [Col. 0268] Ambrose, Erasmus, Lovaniensis, and Arnoldus read, “admonishing a certain almsgiving”; and below, after “give,” they have, “and cleanse the inward parts.” They are corrected here from the manuscripts.] “Nevertheless,” he said, “give alms, and behold, everything is clean for you.”

Then, to show what he had admonished them to do and what they themselves did not care to do—and so that they would not think he was unaware of their alms—he said: “But woe to you, Pharisees,” as though he were saying: “I did indeed admonish you to give the alms by which everything would be clean for you. But woe to you who tithe mint and rue and every herb! I know these are your alms, so do not suppose that I am now admonishing you about them; and you pass over the judgment and love of God. By this almsgiving you could be cleansed from every inner defilement, so that the bodies you wash would also be clean for you. For ‘everything’ means both inward and outward things, as it is read elsewhere: ‘Cleanse what is within, and what is outside will be clean also’” (Matthew 23:26).

But lest he appear to have rejected these alms, which are made from the fruits of the earth, he says: “These things you ought to have done”—that is, the judgment and love of God—“without neglecting the others” (Luke 11:42)—that is, alms from earthly produce.

# Chapter LXXVII

## Wickedness must be abandoned if almsgiving is to be beneficial

Therefore, let those who imagine that by the most lavish alms from their produce or from any money they can buy immunity for themselves while remaining in the enormity of their crimes and the wickedness of their disgraceful acts not deceive themselves. For they not only do these things but love them so much that they always wish to remain involved in them, provided only that they can do so with impunity.

“He who loves iniquity hates his own soul” (Psalm 10:6); and he who hates his own soul is not merciful toward it but cruel. For by loving it according to the world, he hates it according to God. If, then, he wished to give it the alms by which everything would be clean for him, he would hate it according to the world and love it according to God.

No one gives any alms unless he receives from the one who does not need anything what he is to give. Therefore it was said, “His mercy will go before me” (Psalm 59:10).

# Chapter LXXVIII

## 21. Some sins would not be judged sins by human judgment

Which sins are light and which are grave must be weighed not by human but by divine judgment. For we see that certain things were permitted even by the Apostles through indulgence. Such is what the venerable Paul says to married couples: “Do not deprive one another, except by mutual consent for a time, so that you may devote yourselves to prayer; and return again to the same, lest Satan tempt you because of your lack of self-control” (1 Corinthians 7:5). [Note: [Col. 0269] The word “venerable” is absent from only one of the Vatican manuscripts.]

[Note: [Col. 0269] The printed editions read, “return to it.” Most and better manuscripts read, “be again unto the same thing” (or, “unto it”). Augustine commonly follows this reading in Letter 262, Sermon 351, no. 5, and book 5, chapter 9, Against Faustus; the same reading was used by Origen in Homily 23 on Numbers, as though the earlier reading had been *ginesthe* instead of *sunerchesthe*. At the end of the same sentence, some codices read “intemperance” instead of “lack of self-control.”]

This could be thought not to be a sin: namely, to have intercourse with one’s spouse not for the purpose of producing children, which is the good of marriage, but also for bodily pleasure, so that the weakness of those lacking self-control may avoid the deadly evil of fornication, adultery, or any other impurity—which is shameful even to mention—and into which desire may be drawn by Satan’s temptation. As I said, this could be thought not to be a sin unless he had added: “But I say this by way of concession, not by command” (1 Corinthians 7:5–6).

Who, however, would deny that it is a sin when he acknowledges that those who do it are granted forgiveness by apostolic authority? [Note: [Col. 0269] The printed editions read, “apostolic authority acknowledges.” The better manuscripts read, “he acknowledges by apostolic authority”: that is, forgiveness is granted by the Apostle, in accordance with what was said shortly before, that certain things were permitted even by the Apostles through indulgence.]

Something similar occurs where he says: “Does any one of you, having a dispute against another, dare to be judged before the unrighteous and not before the saints?” And shortly afterward: “If, then, you have secular lawsuits,” he says, “appoint as judges those who are despised in the Church.” [Note: [Col. 0269] The printed editions add “to judge.” But neither the manuscripts nor the Apostle’s Greek text contain this. Again below, we follow the ancient manuscripts in agreement with the Greek, leaving aside the printed editions, which read “to judge between brother and brother”; instead, the brother contends in court with his brother.]

“I say this to your shame: is there no wise person among you who can judge between his brother? But brother is judged with brother—and this before unbelievers!”” For here too it could be thought that having a lawsuit against another was not a sin, but only wishing to have it judged outside the Church, unless he went on to add: “Indeed, it is already altogether a fault that you have lawsuits with one another” (1 Corinthians 6:1–7).

And lest anyone excuse this by saying that he had a just case but was suffering injustice, which he wished the judges’ sentence to remove from him, he immediately confronts such thoughts or excuses, saying: “Why not rather suffer injustice? Why not rather be defrauded?”

Thus we return to what the Lord says: “If someone wishes to take your tunic and contend with you in court, let him have your cloak as well” (Matthew 5:40); and elsewhere: “From anyone who takes away what is yours,” he says, “do not demand it back” (Luke 6:30).

He therefore prohibited his people from bringing lawsuits with other human beings over secular matters; and from this teaching the Apostle says that it is a sin. Yet when he allows such lawsuits to be settled within the Church, with brothers judging between brothers, while he sternly prohibits them outside the Church, it is clear that here too we see what is conceded to the weak by way of indulgence.

Because of these and similar sins, as well as others—though lesser—committed through offenses in words and thoughts, the Apostle James confesses and says, “For we all offend in many ways” (James 3:2). We ought therefore to pray to the Lord daily and frequently and say, “Forgive us our debts,” and not lie in what follows: “as we also forgive our debtors” (Matthew 6:12).

# Chapter LXXIX

## What seem light are sometimes exceedingly grave

There are certain things that would be considered extremely light unless the Scriptures showed them to be more serious than people think. For who would suppose that someone who says to his brother, “Fool,” is liable to hell, unless Truth said so? Yet immediately he applied medicine to this wound by adding the command of fraternal reconciliation: for he said at once, “Therefore, if you bring your gift to the altar and there remember that your brother has something against you,” etc. (Matthew 5:22–23). [Note: [Col. 0270] The manuscripts read *offers*. The Greek is *prospherēs* (“you bring” or “you offer”).]

Or who would estimate how great a sin it is to observe days, months, years, and seasons, as do those who, on particular days, months, or years, wish—or refuse—to begin something because, according to the vain teachings of human beings, they consider certain times auspicious or inauspicious, unless we gauged the magnitude of this evil from the Apostle’s fear when he says to such people, “I fear for you, lest I have labored over you in vain” (Galatians 4:11)?

# Chapter LXXX

## Horrible sins seem light through familiarity

To this must be added [Note: [Col. 0270] Lovaniensis and Arnoldus read, “hence it happened,” less well.] that sins, although great and horrible, are believed to be either small or nonexistent once they have become customary. Indeed, they seem not merely not to be concealed but even to be proclaimed and publicized, as it is written: “The sinner is praised in the desires of his soul, and the one who commits iniquity is blessed” (Psalm 9:24).

In the divine books such iniquity is called a “cry.” Thus, in the prophet Isaiah’s account of the evil vineyard, you have: “I expected it to produce judgment, but it produced iniquity; not justice, but a cry” (Isaiah 5:7). [Note: [Col. 0270] Two ancient manuscripts read, “but it produced crime.”] Hence also the statement in Genesis: “The cry of Sodom and Gomorrah has multiplied” (Genesis 18:20), because among them those disgraceful acts were not merely left unpunished but were publicly practiced as though by law.

In our own times, so many evils, though not of the same kind, have already become openly customary that, because of them, we not only do not dare to excommunicate a layman but do not even dare to depose a cleric.

Accordingly, when several years ago I was expounding the Epistle to the Galatians, at the very place where the Apostle says, “I fear for you, lest I have labored over you in vain,” I was compelled to exclaim:

“Woe to the sins of human beings, which we shudder at only when they are unusual! But when they are customary—sins for whose cleansing the blood of the Son of God was poured out—although they may be so great that they altogether close the kingdom of God against those who commit them, we are often compelled, by seeing everything, to tolerate it, and by tolerating it, sometimes even to do some of it! And would that, O Lord, we did not do all the things we have been unable to prevent!” (*Exposition of the Epistle to the Galatians*, no. 35). [Note: [Col. 0271] The reading in the *Exposition of the Epistle to the Galatians* differs somewhat; there it says, “but when they are customary, for whose cleansing the blood of the Son of God was poured out, however great they may be, and they altogether close the kingdom of God against those who commit them.” M.]

But I shall see whether excessive grief drove me to say something rash.

# Chapter LXXXI

## 22. The two causes of sin are ignorance and weakness; no one conquers them without divine help

I shall now say what I have already often said elsewhere in my smaller works. We sin for two reasons: either because we do not yet see what we ought to do, or because we do not do what we already see ought to be done. The former is the evil of ignorance; the latter, of weakness.

We ought indeed to fight against both. But certainly we are defeated unless we are divinely assisted, so that we not only see what must be done but also, when health is added, the delight of righteousness conquers in us the delights of those things in which, by desiring to possess them or fearing to lose them, we sin knowingly and consciously. Then we are not merely sinners—as we were even when we sinned through ignorance—but also transgressors of the law, since we fail to do what we know must be done or do what we know must not be done. [Note: [Col. 0271] One of the oldest Colbertine manuscripts reads, “when pleasantness is added,” which is not inappropriate. The other manuscripts and the printed editions more aptly read, “when health is added”: by it, namely, the evil of weakness is driven away.]

Therefore, we must ask him not only to forgive us if we have sinned, for which we say, “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors,” but also to govern us so that we may not sin, for which we say, “Do not lead us into temptation” (Matthew 6:12–13). He is the one to whom it is said in the Psalm, “The Lord is my light and my salvation” (Psalm 27:1), so that light may remove ignorance and salvation may remove weakness.

# Chapter LXXXII

## Repentance is God’s gift

Even repentance itself, when there is a worthy cause for performing it according to the custom of the Church, is often not performed because of weakness. For shame too is fear of displeasing, when the esteem of human beings is more pleasing than the justice by which each person humbles himself through repentance.

Therefore, God’s mercy is necessary not only when repentance is performed but also so that it may be performed. Otherwise the Apostle would not say of certain people, “Lest perhaps God may grant them repentance” (2 Timothy 2:25).

And when Peter was to weep bitterly, the Evangelist first wrote and said, “The Lord looked at him” (Luke 22:61).

# Chapter LXXXIII

## Sin against the Holy Spirit

Whoever does not believe that sins are forgiven in the Church, despises so great a bestowal of divine grace, and closes his final day in this obstinacy of mind, is guilty of that unforgivable sin against the Holy Spirit, in whom Christ forgives sins. On this difficult question I argued as clearly as I could in a certain short work written for this very purpose. [Note: [Col. 0272] We believe this refers to no other work than Sermon 71, formerly Sermon 11, *On the Words of the Lord*.]

# Chapter LXXXIV

## 23. The resurrection of the flesh

As for the resurrection of the flesh—not like that of certain people who came back to life and later died again, but into eternal life, just as Christ’s own flesh rose—I do not find that I can discuss it briefly and satisfy all the questions that are customarily raised about it.

Nevertheless, a Christian ought in no way to doubt that the flesh of all human beings who have been born and will be born, and who have died and will die, will rise again.

# Chapter LXXXV

## Whether aborted fetuses will rise

Thus the question of aborted fetuses arises first. They have indeed already been born in their mothers’ wombs, but not yet in such a way that they could already be reborn. If we say that they will rise, what is said concerning those that have already been formed can somehow be tolerated. But who would not more readily think that unformed abortions will perish, like seeds that have not been conceived? [Note: [Col. 0272] Ten manuscripts read, “abortive fetuses.”]

Yet who would dare deny—although he may not dare affirm—that the resurrection will bring about this: that whatever was lacking in bodily form will be completed? Thus perfection will not be absent, although it would have arrived with time, just as there will be no defects that had arrived with time. Nature will therefore neither be deprived of what the passage of days would have supplied, when it was fitting and appropriate, nor be disfigured by what the passage of days had brought about, when it was contrary and adverse. Rather, what was not yet complete will be completed, just as what had been damaged will be restored. [Note: [Col. 0272] See *The City of God*, book 22, chapters 12–13.]

# Chapter LXXXVI

## When a fetus in the womb begins to live

Accordingly, the most learned may indeed inquire and debate with the greatest precision when a human being begins to live in the womb, although I do not know whether this can be discovered by human beings. Is there perhaps some hidden life [Note: [Col. 0272] Ambrose, Erasmus, Daniele, Arnoldus, and a few manuscripts omit “and.”] that does not yet appear through the movements of a living creature?

For it seems excessively shameless to deny that the infants who are dissected limb by limb and expelled from the wombs of pregnant women—lest, if they remain there dead, they should also kill their mothers—have lived. From the moment a human being begins to live, he can already die. But once dead, wherever death could have occurred to him, I cannot discover how he would not belong to the resurrection of the dead.

# Chapter LXXXVII

## How monstrous fetuses will rise

Nor will the monsters that are born and live, however quickly they may die, either be denied resurrection or be believed to rise in their damaged condition. [Note: [Col. 0272] Ambrose, Erasmus, and Daniele add here “damaged,” a word absent from the manuscripts.] Rather, nature will be corrected and repaired.

For far be it from us to think that the two-bodied person who was recently born in the East—about whom very faithful brothers reported that they had seen him, and concerning whom the priest Jerome, of holy memory, left a written account—will rise as one double human being rather than as two, which he would have been if twins had been born. [Note: [Col. 0273] Jerome, in his *Letter to Vitalis*, writes: “‘Because,’ he says, ‘in our own age a double human being was born at Lydda, with two heads, four hands, one belly, and two feet, must all human beings therefore be born in this way?’ Compare *The City of God*, book 16, chapter 8.]

So too, the other offspring who are called monsters because each birth possesses something either greater or lesser than normal, or because of some excessive deformity, will be restored by the resurrection to the form of human nature. Each soul will thus possess its own body, with no conjoined parts, even those that had been born conjoined; instead, each will separately bear its own limbs, by which the integrity of the human body is completed.

# Chapter LXXXVIII

## The restoration of the flesh, however it may have perished

The earthly matter from which the flesh of mortals is created does not perish for God. Whether it is dissolved into any dust or ashes, scattered into any vapors or breezes, changed into the substance of other bodies or into the elements themselves, or becomes food for any animals, including human beings, and is changed into flesh, it returns in an instant to the human soul that originally animated it so that the human being might come into existence, live, and grow. [Note: [Col. 0273] Lovaniensis reads, “he returns it.”]

# Chapter LXXXIX

## How what is superfluous will return to the body

That earthly matter, then, which becomes a corpse when the soul departs, will not be restored in the resurrection in such a way that whatever has dispersed and been changed into the various kinds and forms of other things must return to the same bodily parts from which it dispersed and to the same bodily locations where it had been.

Otherwise, if what repeated cutting removed from the hair must return as hair, and what repeated trimming removed from the nails must return as nails, an excessive and indecorous deformity would present itself to those who think about it—and consequently do not believe in the resurrection of the flesh.

But suppose a statue made of some meltable metal were liquefied by fire, crushed into dust, or mixed into a mass, and the craftsman wished to restore it from the quantity of that material. For its integrity it would make no difference which portion of the material were returned to which limb of the statue, provided that he restored and recovered the whole amount from which it had been constituted.

So God, the marvelous and ineffable craftsman, will restore our flesh from the whole substance of which it had consisted, with marvelous and ineffable speed. It will not matter for its restoration whether hairs return as hairs and nails as nails, or whether whatever of them had perished is changed into flesh and recalled into other parts of the body, since the craftsman’s providence will ensure that nothing indecorous occurs. [Note: [Col. 0273] See *The City of God*, book 22, chapter 19.]

# Chapter XC

## Nothing indecorous will exist in the body’s stature or appearance

Nor does it follow that the stature of each person who rises again will therefore be different because the stature of the living had been different, or that thin people will rise again with the same thinness, or fat people with the same fatness.

But if it is the Creator’s plan that each person’s individual identity and recognizable likeness be preserved in his appearance, while all the other bodily goods are made equal, [Note: [Col. 0274] One Vatican manuscript reads, “in bodily limbs.”] then the matter in each person will be proportioned so that nothing of it is lost and he supplies whatever anyone lacked—he who was able to bring into being whatever he willed from nothing.

But if there will be a rational inequality in the bodies of those who rise, as there is among the voices by which a song is completed, then each person’s bodily matter will be arranged so that it both makes the human being equal to the angelic choirs and introduces nothing unsuitable to their senses. For nothing indecorous will exist there; whatever will exist will be fitting, since it will not exist if it is not fitting.

# Chapter XCI

## The bodies of the godly will rise with respect to the substance of the flesh, but without any defect

The bodies of the saints will therefore rise without any defect, without any deformity, just as they will be without corruption, burden, or difficulty; and in them there will be as much ease as there will be happiness. [Note: [Col. 0274] Ambrose, Erasmus, and three manuscripts read, “the ease of rising.” This is less correct, for the sentence should rather be understood as referring to ease of action.] For this reason they are also called spiritual, although they will undoubtedly be bodies, not spirits.

Just as the present body is called “animal,” although it is a body and not a soul, so then there will be a spiritual body, yet it will be a body and not a spirit. Therefore, insofar as corruption is concerned—which now weighs down the soul (Wisdom 9:15)—and insofar as the flesh lusts against the spirit through its defects (Galatians 5:17), then there will not be flesh but body, since heavenly bodies are also so called.

For this reason it was said, “Flesh and blood shall not possess the kingdom of God”; and, as though explaining what he had said, he adds, “nor shall corruption possess incorruption” (1 Corinthians 15:50). What he first called “flesh and blood,” he later called “corruption”; and what he first called “the kingdom of God,” he later called “incorruption.”

But insofar as substance is concerned, there will still be flesh. For this reason Christ’s body was called flesh even after the resurrection (Luke 24:39). Yet the Apostle says, “The animal body is sown; the spiritual body will rise” (1 Corinthians 15:44), because there will then be such harmony between flesh and spirit, with the spirit giving life to flesh that is subject to it without need of any support, that nothing within us will resist us. Just as outwardly we will suffer no enemy, so inwardly we will suffer none in ourselves.

# Chapter XCII

## What kind of bodies the condemned will rise with

Those who are not freed from that mass of perdition brought about through the first human being by the one Mediator between God and human beings will also rise, each with his own flesh, but in order to be punished with the devil and his angels.

Whether they will rise with the defects and deformities of their bodies—whatever defective and deformed limbs they carried—why labor to investigate? Their certain and eternal damnation should not be made burdensome for us by uncertainty about their bodily condition or appearance.

Nor should it trouble us how their body will be incorruptible if it can suffer, or how it will be corruptible if it cannot die. For there is no true life except where one lives happily, and no true incorruption except where health is not corrupted by any pain.

But where an unhappy being is not permitted to die, then, so to speak, death itself does not die; and where perpetual pain does not destroy but afflicts, corruption itself does not end. In the holy Scriptures this is called the second death (Revelation 2:11; 20:6, 14).

# Chapter XCIII

## Which of the condemned will have the mildest punishment

Neither the first death, by which the soul is compelled to leave its body, nor the second, by which the soul [Note: [Col. 0275] Lovaniensis and Arnoldus read “the soul” in the accusative; the other printed editions and the manuscripts read “the soul” in the nominative.] is not permitted to leave its body of punishment, would have come upon human beings if no one had sinned.

The mildest punishment of all will certainly be that of those who, apart from the original sin they inherited, added no further sin. Among the others who added sins, each will have a more tolerable condemnation there in proportion to the lesser iniquity he had here.

# Chapter XCIV

## 24. In eternal life the saints will know more fully what grace has conferred on them

When the rejected angels and human beings remain in eternal punishment, the saints will then know more fully what good grace has conferred on them. Then it will become clearer through the very facts themselves what is written in the Psalm: “I shall sing of mercy and judgment to you, O Lord” (Psalm 101:1), because no one is freed except through undeserved mercy, and no one is condemned except through deserved judgment.

# Chapter XCV

## God’s hidden judgments in the predestination of human beings will then be revealed

## God’s will is most efficacious

Then what is now hidden will not remain hidden: when, from two infants, one was to be taken up through mercy and the other left behind through judgment, the one who was taken up would recognize what was owed to him through judgment had mercy not come to his aid. Why was one taken up rather than the other, when the condition of both was the same? Why were works not performed among some people which, if they had been performed, would have led them to repentance, while they were performed among those who would not believe? [Note: [Col. 0275] Seven manuscripts read, “would certainly have led those people to repentance.”]

For the Lord says most openly: “Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida! For if the miracles that were performed among you had been performed in Tyre and Sidon, they would long ago have repented in sackcloth and ashes” (Matthew 11:21).

Certainly God did not unjustly refuse to save them, since they could be saved if they wished. [Note: [Col. 0275] Twenty-five ancient manuscripts—specifically, two from the Vatican Library in Rome; sixteen from Paris; one from the Royal Library; two from the College of Navarre; four from the Sorbonne; three from the Abbey of Saint Victor; one from Sainte-Geneviève; one from the monastery of Saint Bernard of the Feuillant Fathers; one from the Dominican Fathers on the Rue Saint-Jacques; one from the Franciscan Fathers of the principal convent; two from our monastery at Saint-Germain; and, in addition, one from the Church of Saint Martial at Limoges; one from the Abbey of Mont-Royal; one from Longpont; one from Bec; one from Saint Peter of Culture at Le Mans; one from Saint Remigius at Reims; and the very ancient Corbie manuscript—read, “if he wished.” The printed editions, except Arnoldus, read, “if they wished.” [Col. 0276] Eleven subsequent manuscripts agree with them: one Vatican manuscript and another; three Colbertine; one Royal; one belonging to Antonius Faure, Doctor of Theology of the Faculty of Paris; and one each from the Sorbonne, Saint Victor, Carcassonne, and Limoges. Nevertheless, in the Limoges manuscript, in another of the Colbertine manuscripts listed, and in one of the Vatican manuscripts, the penultimate letter had been erased, so that the reading became “if he wished.” The theologians of Louvain, in their edition of Augustine’s works, wrote in the margin, “Perhaps, ‘if he wished.’” Guillelmus Estius unhesitatingly asserts that this is the reading in *Sentences* I, distinction 46, paragraph 2; and Petrus Lombardus actually reads it this way in *Sentences* I, distinction 43, chapter “But these things.”]

Then, in the clearest light of wisdom, it will be seen what the faith of the godly now holds before it is seen through manifest knowledge: how certain, unchangeable, and efficacious God’s will is; how many things he can do yet does not wish to do, while he wishes for nothing that he cannot do; and how true is what is sung in the Psalm: “But our God is above, in heaven; in heaven and on earth he has done everything whatever he willed” (Psalm 113:11). [Note: [Col. 0276] Erasmus, Lovaniensis, and Arnoldus omit “above, in heaven.” The other printed editions and the manuscripts have it here and in the *Expositions on the Psalms*, Psalm 113.]

This would not be true if he willed some things and did not do them; and, more disgracefully still, if he did not do them because the human will prevented the omnipotent one from bringing about what he wanted. Therefore, nothing happens unless the omnipotent God wills it to happen, either by permitting it to happen or by doing it himself.

# Chapter XCVI
God does good even by permitting evil to occur. There can be no doubt that God does good even by permitting whatever evils occur. For he permits this only by a just judgment; and everything that is just is certainly good. Although, therefore, things that are evil are not good insofar as they are evil, nevertheless it is good that they should exist—not only the good, but also the evil. For unless it were good that evils should exist, the omnipotently good God would in no way permit them to exist; and for him, unquestionably, it is as easy not to permit what he does not will to exist as it is to do what he wills. Unless we believe this, the very beginning of our Confession [Note: [Col. 0276] The printed editions have *our Confession of faith*. “Of faith” is absent from the manuscripts. Elsewhere as well, the word *Confession* is used without the addition, in place of *the Creed*.] is put at risk, by which we confess that we believe in God the Father almighty. For he is truly called almighty for no other reason than that he can do whatever he wills, and that the accomplishment of the omnipotent will is not hindered by the will of any creature.

## CHAPTER XCVII

### Whether the will of God, who wills to save, is hindered by the human will

Accordingly, we must examine how it was said concerning God—for the Apostle also spoke this most truly—“who wills all human beings to be saved” (1 Tim. 2:4). Since, however, not all but very many fail to be saved, it appears that what God wills to happen does not happen, with the human will supposedly hindering God’s will. For when the question is asked why all are not saved, it is usually answered: because they themselves do not wish it. But this cannot be said of infants, who do not yet possess the capacity to will or not to will. For if what they do in infantile movement [Note: [Col. 0276] Am., Er., Dan., and several manuscripts read *infantuli* (“of little infants”); Lov. and Arn. read *infantili*.] were judged attributable to their will, then when they are baptized, resisting as much as they can, we would say that they do not want to be saved.

But the Lord speaks more plainly in the Gospel when he addresses the impious city: “How often,” he says, “I wanted [Col. 0277] to gather your children as a hen gathers her chicks, and you were unwilling” (Matt. 23:37)! It is as though God’s will had been overcome by the human will, and the most powerful One had been unable to do what he wished because the weakest had been unwilling. And where is that omnipotence by which “in heaven and on earth he has done whatever he willed,” if he willed to gather the children of Jerusalem and did not do so? Or rather, did that city refuse to have its children gathered by him, while he nevertheless gathered those of its children whom he wished? For in heaven and on earth he did not will and do some things, while willing and failing to do others; rather, “whatever he willed, he did.”

## CHAPTER XCVIII

### 25. Although God can convert whomever he wills, he does not act unjustly when he converts some and does not convert others. The original bond of condemnation

Who, then, would be so impiously foolish as to say that God cannot convert the evil wills of human beings, whenever and wherever he wishes, into good? When he does so, he acts through mercy; when he does not, he does not do so through judgment. For “he has mercy on whomever he wills, and he hardens whomever he wills.”

In saying this [Note: The printed editions have “when he said this.” The manuscripts read “in order that he might say this.” The sense is the same.], the Apostle was commending grace. In order to commend it, he had already spoken of the twins in Rebecca’s womb, who, before they were born and had done anything good or evil, were told—so that God’s purpose according to election might remain, not from works but from him who calls—“The elder shall serve the younger.” For this reason he added another prophetic testimony, where it is written, “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated.”

Recognizing how this statement might trouble those who cannot penetrate by understanding the depth of grace, he said, “What then shall we say? Is there injustice with God? Certainly not.” For it seems unjust that God should love one and hate another without any merits arising from good or evil works. If he had wanted this to be understood of the future good works of one or the future evil works of the other—works which God certainly foreknew—he would surely not have said “not from works,” but “from future works.” In that way he would have resolved the question, or rather would not have created any question requiring resolution.

But after answering, “Certainly not”—that is, “May there be no injustice with God”—he immediately demonstrated that this did not occur through any injustice of God, saying: “For he says to Moses, ‘I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will show mercy to whom I show mercy.’” For who but a fool would think God unjust, whether he inflicts punitive judgment upon one who deserves it or grants mercy to one who does not deserve it? Finally, he adds and says, “So then it depends not on the one who wills or on the one who runs, but on God who has mercy.”

Both twins, therefore, were born by nature children of wrath (Eph. 2:3), bound not indeed by any personal works but, originally, by the bond of condemnation inherited from Adam. But he who said, “I will have mercy on whom I have mercy” [Note: After “I will have mercy,” the printed editions add “and I will show mercy to whom I show mercy,” although this does not occur here in the manuscripts.], loved Jacob through gratuitous mercy, while he hated Esau through deserved judgment. Since this was owed to both, the one who was spared [Col. 0278] recognized that he had no ground for boasting in his own differing merits, because he had not suffered the same punishment in the same condition; rather, he had to boast in the abundance of divine grace. For “it depends not on the one who wills or on the one who runs, but on God who has mercy.”

In this highest and most salutary mystery, the whole appearance—and, so to speak, the countenance—of the holy Scriptures is found to admonish those who observe it rightly that “the one who boasts should boast in the Lord” (1 Cor. 1:31).

## CHAPTER XCIX

### As God has mercy through great goodness, so he hardens through no injustice. The apostate root

After commending God’s mercy in saying, “So then it depends not on the one who wills or on the one who runs, but on God who has mercy,” he then commended judgment as well—for where mercy is not shown, there is not injustice but judgment, since there is no injustice with God—and immediately added:

“For Scripture says to Pharaoh, ‘For this very purpose I raised you up, that I might show my power in you and that my name might be proclaimed throughout all the earth.’” [Note: Several manuscripts read “strength” instead of “power.”]

Having said this, and drawing a conclusion concerning both mercy and judgment, he says: “So then he has mercy on whomever he wills, and he hardens whomever he wills.” He has mercy, certainly, through great goodness; he hardens through no injustice, so that neither the one who is delivered may boast of his own merits, nor the one who is condemned complain except of his own merits.

Grace alone distinguishes the redeemed from the lost, whom the common cause inherited from the beginning had formed into one mass of perdition. But when someone hears this in such a way as to say, “Why does he still find fault? For who can resist his will?”—as though the evil person therefore should not be blamed because God has mercy on whomever he wills and hardens whomever he wills—far be it from us to be ashamed to give the answer that we see the Apostle gave:

“O man, who are you to answer back to God? Does the thing formed say to the one who formed it, ‘Why did you make me like this?’ Or does the potter not have authority over the clay, from the same lump to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?” (Rom. 9:11–21).

At this point some foolish people think that the Apostle failed in his answer and, lacking a reason to give, restrained the boldness of his opponent. But the words “O man, who are you?” carry great weight. In questions of this kind, by a brief word he recalls a human being to consideration of his own capacity [Note: [Col. 0278] Some manuscripts read: “And so that in questions of this kind . . . he might recall a human being, by a word brief indeed, but in reality, etc.”]; yet in reality this is a great presentation of the reason.

If he does not comprehend these things, who is he to answer God? If he does comprehend them, he finds even more clearly that he has nothing to answer. For if he comprehends, he sees that the whole human race was condemned by so just a divine judgment in the apostate root that, even if no one were delivered from it, no one could rightly reproach God’s justice. He also sees that those who are delivered had to be delivered in such a way that, from the many who were not delivered and were left in most just condemnation, it might be shown what the whole lump deserved, and where God’s deserved judgment would also lead those who are delivered, unless undeserved mercy came to their aid.

Thus “every mouth may be stopped” (Rom. 3:19) among those who wish to boast of their merits, and “the one who boasts may boast in the Lord.”

## CHAPTER C

[Col. 0279]

### 26. Nothing occurs apart from God’s will, even when it occurs against his will

“These are the great works of the Lord, sought out in accordance with all his wills” (Ps. 110:2). They are sought out with such wisdom that, when the angelic and human creature sinned—that is, when it did not do what God willed but what it itself willed—God nevertheless fulfilled what he willed through that same creaturely will by which what the Creator did not will was done. He makes good use even of evil, as supremely good, both for the condemnation of those whom he justly predestined to punishment and for the salvation of those whom he graciously predestined to grace.

As far as the creatures themselves are concerned, they did what God did not will; but as far as God’s omnipotence is concerned, they were in no way able to accomplish this. For precisely by doing what they did against his will, his will was accomplished through them. Therefore they are “the great works of the Lord, sought out in accordance with all his wills”: in a wondrous and ineffable manner, what occurs even against his will does not occur apart from his will. For it would not occur if he did not permit it; and he certainly does not permit it unwillingly, but willingly. Nor would the good God permit evil to occur unless he were omnipotent enough to bring good even out of evil.

## CHAPTER CI

### God’s good will is always fulfilled through both good and evil human wills

Sometimes a person wills something with a good will that God does not will, although God wills otherwise with a much better and much more certain will—for God’s will can never be evil. This would be like a good son wishing his father to live, while God, with a good will, wishes him to die.

Conversely, it can happen that a person wills with an evil will what God wills with a good one—for example, if a bad son wishes his father to die and God also wills this. The son wills what God does not will, while God wills what the son wills. Yet the son’s piety, although willing something else, is more in harmony with God’s good will than is the impiety of the other, who wills the same thing.

So much depends on what is fitting for a human being to will and what is fitting for God to will, and on the end to which each refers his will, that the will is either approved or condemned.

For God fulfills certain of his own wills—which are certainly good—through the evil wills of evil human beings. Thus, through the ill-willed Jews, Christ was killed for us by the good will of the Father. This was such a great good that when the Apostle Peter did not want it to happen, he was called “Satan” by the one who had come to be killed (Matt. 16:23).

How good appeared the wills of the devout faithful who did not want the Apostle Paul to go to Jerusalem, lest he suffer there the evils that the prophet Agabus had foretold (Acts 21:10–12)! Yet God willed him to suffer these things for proclaiming the faith of Christ, training him as Christ’s martyr.

Nor did God fulfill this good will of his [Note: [Col. 0279] Thus the manuscripts; Lov. and Arn. read, “for this good will.”] through the good wills of Christians, but through the evil wills of the Jews. Those who did not want what God wanted belonged more closely to him than did those through whom what he wanted was done willingly; for they did the same thing, but he did it through them with a good will, while they did it with an evil will.

## CHAPTER CII

### God’s will is always unconquered and never evil, whether he shows mercy or hardens

However great the wills of angels or human beings [Col. 0280] may be—whether good or evil, whether willing what God wills or something else—the will of the omnipotent God is always unconquered. It can never be evil, because even when it inflicts what is evil, it is just; and what is just is certainly not evil. [Note: Some books read “which is also.”] [Note: Lovaniensis reads “because it is just.” Other codices read “which is just.”]

Therefore God almighty, whether through mercy he has mercy on whom he wills or through judgment hardens whom he wills, does nothing unjustly and does nothing except willingly; and he does everything that he wills.

## CHAPTER CIII

### 27. The Apostle’s statement to Timothy, “Who wills all human beings to be saved,” is examined

Accordingly, when we hear and read in the sacred writings that God wills all human beings to be saved, although it is certain to us that not all human beings are saved, we must not for that reason detract anything from the most omnipotent will of God. Rather, we must understand what is written—“who wills all human beings to be saved”—as though it said that no human being is saved unless God himself wills that person to be saved.

This does not mean that there is no human being whom he does not will to save; it means that no one is saved unless he wills it. And for this reason he must be asked to will it, because if he wills it, it necessarily comes to pass.

The Apostle was speaking about praying to God when he said this. In the same way we understand what is written in the Gospel, “who enlightens every human being” (John 1:9): not because there is no human being who is not enlightened, but because no one is enlightened except by him.

Or the statement “who wills all human beings to be saved” may be understood in this way: not that there was no human being whom he did not wish to save—he who refused to perform miracles among those whom he says would have repented had he performed them—but that by “all human beings” we should understand the whole human race, distributed among every variety: kings and private citizens, noble and ignoble, exalted and humble, learned and unlearned, sound in body and weak, intelligent and dull-witted, foolish, rich, poor, and of middling condition; males and females; infants, children, adolescents, young men, older men, and the aged; people established in every language, every character, every art, every profession, and in an immeasurable variety of wills and consciences; and whatever other differences exist among human beings. [Note: Some manuscripts omit “the human race,” while some, with Danaeus’s edition, have “of human beings” in its place.]

For what sort of people are there whom God does not will to save through his only-begotten Son, our Lord, among all nations—and therefore does save them? [Note: One Vatican manuscript reads “may save them.”] For the omnipotent God cannot vainly will whatever he wills.

The Apostle had commanded that prayers be made for all human beings [Note: [Col. 0280] Am., Er., Dan., and Lov. read “for each individual”; most manuscripts, more correctly, read “for all,” as does the Apostle in the cited passage.], and had specifically added “for kings and all who are in high positions,” who might be thought, because of worldly arrogance and pride, to be alien to the humility of the Christian faith. Therefore, after saying, “For this is good and acceptable in the sight of God our Savior”—that is, that prayer should also be made for such people—he immediately added, to remove despair, “who wills all human beings to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth” [Col. 0281] (1 Tim. 2:1–4).

God judged this good: to grant salvation to the exalted through the prayers of the humble. We already see that this has been fulfilled.

The Lord also used this manner of speech in the Gospel when he said to the Pharisees, “You tithe mint and rue and every herb” (Luke 11:42). For the Pharisees did not tithe every herb that belonged to others, or all the herbs of foreigners throughout all lands. Therefore, just as “every herb” there means every kind of herb, so here “all human beings” may mean every kind of human being.

The statement may also be understood in any other way, provided that we are not compelled to believe that the omnipotent God willed something to happen and it did not happen.
