For if, as the Truth sings of him, “in heaven and on earth he has done whatever he willed” (Ps. 113:11) [Note: The manuscripts read “as the Truth sings.” The printed editions have “as the Truth also sings.”], he plainly did not will to do whatever he did not do.

## CHAPTER CIV

### 28. What God’s will was concerning Adam, whom he foreknew would sin

Accordingly, God would also have willed to preserve the first human being in the salvation in which he had been created, and, after children had been born, to bring him at the proper time, without the intervention of death, to a better state, in which he would not only no longer commit sin but could not even possess the will to sin [Note: [Col. 0281] *Non* (“not”) is absent from nearly all the manuscripts.], if God had foreknown that Adam would have a perpetual will to remain without sin, just as he had been created.

But because God foreknew that Adam would misuse his free will—that is, that he would sin—he prepared his will for this instead: that he himself might do good even through one who was doing evil, and that the good will of the omnipotent God might nevertheless be fulfilled rather than nullified by the evil will of the human being.

## CHAPTER CV

### The human will is free in different ways with regard to good and evil in the first and final states

The first human being therefore had to be made in such a way that he could will either good or evil, not without reward if he willed good and not without punishment if he willed evil. Later, however, he will be in such a state that he cannot will evil; yet for that reason he will not lack free choice.

For that choice will be much freer which cannot at all serve sin. We should not blame the will, or say that it is not a will, or deny that it is free, by which we wish to be blessed in such a way that we not only do not wish to be miserable, but are utterly unable to wish to be so.

Therefore, just as our soul even now will always possess the will not to be unhappy, so it will always possess the will not to be unrighteous.

But the order had to be preserved by which God wished to show how good a rational creature is when it can also refrain from sin [Note: Am., Er., Dan., and Lov. read “which can also sin,” and below “in which it could also die,” omitting the negative particle. We find the negative in both places in most manuscripts, as also in Arnaldus’s edition.], although better is the creature that cannot sin—just as the immortality was lesser, yet real, in which it was possible not to die, although greater will be the immortality in which it will be impossible to die.

## CHAPTER CVI

### Grace is necessary for free choice in the first and second states

Human nature lost the former immortality [Note: Lambertus Danaeus needlessly advises referring “that” to the human will discussed in the preceding chapter. Peter Lombard’s interpretation is more correct, as he cites the passage in *Sentences* II.29.1: “Human nature lost through free choice that immortality in which it could avoid dying; but it will receive through grace that immortality in which it cannot die.”] [Col. 0282] through free choice; it will receive the latter through grace, which it would have received through merit if it had not sinned—although even then no merit could have existed without grace.

For although sin consisted solely in free choice, free choice was not sufficient for retaining righteousness unless divine assistance were supplied through participation in the immutable Good. For just as it lies within human power to die whenever one wishes—there is no one who, to say nothing else, cannot kill himself by refusing to eat—so the will is not sufficient to preserve life if the aids of food or of any other protections are absent.

In paradise, therefore, the human being was capable, through the will, of killing himself by abandoning righteousness; but for the life of righteousness to be retained, it was not enough to will it unless the one who had made him assisted him.

After that fall, God’s mercy is greater, since even free choice itself [Note: The printed editions have “free choice.” “Free” is absent from the manuscripts.] must be freed from the slavery over which sin rules with death. It is not freed by itself at all, but solely by God’s grace, which is established in faith in Christ. Thus the will itself, as it is written, is prepared by the Lord (Prov. 8:35, according to the Septuagint), so that it may receive the other gifts of God through which one comes to the eternal gift.

## CHAPTER CVII

### Eternal life is a reward and yet also grace. God’s will concerning the sinful human being is fulfilled

For this reason the Apostle also calls eternal life—which is certainly the reward of good works—God’s grace: “For the wages of sin is death, but the grace of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Rom. 6:23). Wages are paid as what is owed for military service; they are not given as a gift. Therefore he said, “The wages of sin is death,” to show that death is inflicted upon sin not undeservedly but as something owed.

But unless grace is given freely, it is not grace. We must therefore understand that even human beings’ good merits are gifts of God; and when eternal life is given in return for them, what is given except grace in return for grace (John 1:16)?

The human being was therefore made upright in such a way that he could remain in uprightness, though not without divine assistance, and could become perverse through his own choice. Whichever of these two he chose, God’s will would be done—either by him or, at any rate, concerning him.

Since he preferred to do his own will rather than God’s, God’s will was done concerning him: from the same mass of perdition that flowed from Adam’s stock, God makes one vessel for honor and another for dishonor (Rom. 9:21)—for honor through mercy, for dishonor through judgment—so that no one may boast in a human being, and consequently not in himself either.

## CHAPTER CVIII

### Our salvation is from God, so that we would not be liberated through Christ if he were not God

For neither would we be liberated through him, the one Mediator between God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus (1 Tim. 2:5), unless he were also God.

When Adam was made, as an upright human being, there was no need for a mediator. [Note: Several manuscripts read, “He did not need a mediator.”] But when [Col. 0283] sins had separated the human race far from God, it was necessary for us to be reconciled to God through the Mediator, who alone was born, lived, and was killed without sin, all the way to the resurrection of the flesh unto eternal life.

Thus human pride might be rebuked and healed through the humility of God; it might be shown to the human being how far he had departed from God, when he was recalled through God incarnate; and an example of obedience might be offered to the rebellious human being through the human being who is God.

By the Only-begotten’s assuming the form of a servant, which had previously merited nothing, the fountain of grace was opened. The resurrection of the flesh promised to the redeemed was foreshadowed in the Redeemer himself. Through the very nature that had rejoiced in deceiving him, the devil was conquered. Yet the human being was not to boast, lest pride arise again.

And if anything else concerning so great a mystery of the Mediator can be seen and said by those who are making progress—or can at least be seen, even if it cannot be said—it belongs here.

## CHAPTER CIX

### 29. The dwelling places of souls before the resurrection

The period between a human being’s death and the final resurrection holds souls in hidden dwelling places, each according as it deserves rest or distress, in keeping with what it received in the flesh while it lived.

## CHAPTER CX

### The altar sacrifice and almsgiving for the dead: to whom and to what extent they are beneficial

Nor should it be denied that the souls of the dead are relieved by the devotion of the living who belong to them, when the sacrifice of the Mediator is offered for them or alms are given in the Church. But these things benefit those who, while they were alive, earned the possibility that such things might later benefit them.

There is a certain manner of life that is neither so good that it does not require these things after death, nor so evil that these things do not benefit it after death. There is also a manner of life so good that it does not require them, and again one so evil that, once a person has departed this life, not even these things can help him. Therefore all merit is acquired here by which someone may, after this life, be relieved or burdened.

Let no one hope to obtain favor with God after death for what he neglected here. [Note: Several manuscripts of good authority read, “Let no one prepare for himself what he neglected here.” The same manuscripts, together with most others, continue: “to win the Lord’s favor when he has died,” omitting “with God.”]

The practices that the Church regularly employs for commending the dead are therefore not contrary to the apostolic sentence: “We shall all stand before the tribunal of Christ, so that each may receive according to what he has done through the body, whether good or evil” (Rom. 14:10; 2 Cor. 5:10). For each person acquired this merit for himself while he lived in the body, so that these practices might benefit him.

They do not benefit everyone. Why do they not benefit everyone, except because of the difference in the life each person led in the body?

Thus, when sacrifices—whether of the altar or of any kind of almsgiving—are offered for all baptized dead, they are thanksgivings for the very good; expiations for the not very bad; and, for the very bad, even if they provide no assistance to the dead, they are at least consolations for the living.

For those whom they benefit, they benefit either so that there may be complete remission, [Col. 0284] or at least so that the damnation itself may become more tolerable. [Note: Many manuscripts omit “may become”; some replace it with “may be.”] [Note: Here Albert the Great taught that “damnation” should be understood as punishment for those who are to be saved after the pains of purgatory, in *Sentences* IV.45, article 3, response to objection 1; later masters approved this interpretation in the same place in the *Sentences*. Nevertheless, Peter Lombard, in that passage, IV.45, chapter “Nor should it be denied,” understood it as punishment for certain of the damned who will never be delivered, when he subsequently concluded: “They assist those who are moderately evil toward the mitigation of punishment.” For he entirely distinguishes these moderately evil persons from those who are released from purgatorial punishments, sooner or later, through the prayers of the Church, and calls all of the latter “moderately good.” This is clear from reading the chapters there entitled “A question commonly raised” and “But again.” Hence the Gloss on II, question 13, chapter “The time,” adds: “They benefit those who are moderately evil so that they may be punished less, but they will never be delivered.” Albert the Great cites Praepositivus in support of this opinion.

In the very old Gellone manuscript there is an inscription, “Mass for the soul of one concerning whom there is doubt,” in which the following prayer is found:

“Almighty and merciful God, who have power to put to death and again to give life, to lead down to hell and again to bring back, and who call things that are not as though they were; whose power is fully present in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in the lower regions: we, humble and trembling, beseech you for the soul of your servant, whom you have drawn from the present age without a period of repentance, that, if perhaps because of the gravity of his crimes he does not deserve to rise to glory, through these sacred offerings the torments themselves may at least become tolerable.”

Adrevaldus, in *The Book of the Miracles of Saint Benedict*, chapter 21, writes that the people of Fleury poured out prayers to the Lord for the souls of robbers killed in battle, “so that, even if they did not deserve to be released from everlasting sufferings, they might at least be punished by the strict Judge with lesser penalties.”]

## CHAPTER CXI

### Two cities after the judgment, in eternal blessedness or misery

After the resurrection, when the whole has been completed and judgment has taken place, the two cities will have their appointed ends: one belonging to Christ and the other to the devil; one of the good and the other of the evil. Each, however, will consist both of angels and of human beings.

The former will have no will to sin, the latter no capacity to sin; neither will have any condition of dying. The former will live truly and happily in eternal life, while the latter will endure unhappily in eternal death, without the power of dying, since both conditions will be without end.

Yet in blessedness one will remain more excellent than another, while in misery one will endure more tolerably than another.

## CHAPTER CXII

### The punishment of the damned will be eternal

It is therefore useless for some—or rather, very many—to pity the eternal punishment of the damned and their everlasting torments without interruption, moved by human feeling, and consequently not to believe that this will be so. They do not oppose the divine Scriptures, but soften whatever seems harsh according to their own feelings and bend toward a milder interpretation statements that they think have been expressed more terribly than is truly the case. [Note: Many manuscripts read “which they think are more terrible.”] [Note: See *The City of God* XXI.18 and 24.]

“God will not forget to be merciful,” they say, “nor will he restrain his mercies in his wrath” (Ps. 76:10). This is indeed read in the holy psalm, but without any difficulty it is understood of those who are called vessels of mercy, since they too are delivered from misery not according to their merits but through God’s mercy.

Or, if they think that this applies to everyone, it does not therefore follow that they must suppose the condemnation of those of whom [Col. 0285] it was said, “These will go away into eternal punishment,” can come to an end. Otherwise, by the same reasoning, the happiness of those of whom it was said, “But the righteous into eternal life” (Matt. 25:46), would also eventually be thought to end.

If they prefer, let them suppose that the punishments of the damned are mitigated to some extent at fixed intervals. Even then, “the wrath of God remains upon them” (John 3:36) may be understood—namely, the damnation itself, for this is called God’s wrath, not any disturbance of the divine mind—so that, in his wrath, that is, while his wrath remains, he nevertheless does not restrain his mercies, not by bringing eternal punishment to an end but by applying or inserting relief amid the torments.

For the psalm does not say “to bring his wrath to an end” or “after his wrath,” but “in his wrath.” Even if this were the only punishment, what can be imagined as least in it—exclusion from the kingdom of God, exile from the city of God, alienation from the life of God, deprivation of that great abundance of God’s sweetness which he has hidden for those who fear him, but which he has perfected for those who hope in him (Ps. 30:20)—would be such a great punishment that no torments known to us could be compared with it, if that exclusion were eternal while these torments lasted for however many ages.

## CHAPTER CXIII

### The death of the impious, like the life of the pious, is everlasting

That perpetual death of the damned, therefore—that is, alienation from the life of God—will remain without end and will be common to all, whatever human beings may conjecture, in accordance with their varying human feelings, about the diversity of punishments and the alleviation or interruption of sufferings. Likewise, the eternal life of the saints will remain common to all, even though they shine harmoniously with differing degrees of honor. [Note: The manuscripts read *quaelibet*; the printed editions read *quamlibet*. Likewise below, the manuscripts read *bonorum* (“of the good things”) instead of *honorum* (“of honors”).]

## CHAPTER CXIV

### 30. Having set out the faith, he proceeds to hope, showing that the matters belonging to hope are contained in the Lord’s Prayer. Cursed is the one who places hope in himself

From this confession of faith, which is briefly contained in the Creed and is, when conceived carnally, milk for infants but, when considered and treated spiritually, food for the strong, arises the good hope of the faithful, accompanied by holy charity.

But of all the things that must be believed faithfully, only those contained in the Lord’s Prayer belong specifically to hope. For, as the divine utterances testify, “Cursed is everyone who places his hope in a human being” (Jer. 17:5). Consequently, the one who places hope in himself is also caught in the bond of this curse.

We must therefore ask from the Lord God alone for whatever we hope either to do well or to obtain for good works. [Note: The particle “for” is absent from several manuscripts.]

## CHAPTER CXV

### The seven petitions of the Lord’s Prayer according to Matthew

Accordingly, the Lord’s Prayer appears, in the Evangelist Matthew, to contain seven petitions. In three of them eternal things are requested; in the remaining four, temporal things, which are nevertheless necessary for attaining the eternal.

For when we say, “Hallowed be your name; your kingdom come; your will be done [Col. 0286] on earth as it is in heaven”—which some have not absurdly understood as “in spirit and body”—these things are to be retained altogether without end. They are begun here and, to the extent that we make progress, increase within us; when perfected, as we hope will occur in the other life, they will always be possessed. [Note: Most manuscripts read, “and here they are begun insofar as we make progress.”]

But when we say, “Give us this day our daily bread; and forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors; and do not bring us into temptation, but deliver us from evil” (Matt. 6:9–13), who does not see that these petitions pertain to the needs of the present life?

In that eternal life where we always hope to be, the sanctification of God’s name, his kingdom, and his will will remain perfectly and immortally in our spirit and body. Daily bread is so called because it is necessary here, in whatever quantity must be supplied to soul and body, whether it is understood spiritually, bodily, or in both ways.

Here also is the forgiveness we ask for, where sins are committed; here are the temptations that entice or drive us to sin; here, finally, is the evil from which we desire to be delivered. There, however, none of these things exists.

## CHAPTER CXVI
Petitions only five in Luke, who is reconciled with Matthew. The evangelist Luke, in the Lord’s Prayer, comprised not seven petitions but five. Nor did he thereby disagree with this account; rather, by the very brevity of his wording he indicated how those seven are to be understood [Note: [Col. 0286] Am., Er., and the manuscripts: “but how those seven are to be understood.”]. For God’s name is sanctified in the spirit, while God’s kingdom is to come in the resurrection of the flesh. By showing, then, that the third petition is in a certain sense a repetition of the preceding two, Luke makes it understood more clearly by omitting it. Then he adds three others: for daily bread, for the forgiveness of sins, and for avoiding temptation (Luke XI, 2–4). But what Matthew placed last—“But deliver us from evil”—Luke did not include, so that we might understand it as belonging to the earlier statement concerning temptation. For this reason he says, “But deliver,” not “And deliver,” as though indicating that it is one petition (“not this” [Note: Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions have “not that.”], “but this”): so that each person may know that he is delivered from evil precisely in that he is not led into temptation.

## CHAPTER CXVII

### 31. On the charity that must be present together with faith and hope

Moreover, charity—which the Apostle declared to be greater than those two, namely faith and hope (I Corinthians XIII, 13)—is better in anyone in proportion to its greatness in that person. For when one asks whether someone is a good person, one does not ask what he believes or hopes, but what he loves. Whoever loves rightly undoubtedly believes and hopes rightly; but whoever does not love believes in vain, even if what he believes is true, and hopes in vain, even if what he hopes for is taught to belong to true happiness—unless he also believes and hopes that it can be granted to him, when he asks, that he may love.

Although no one can hope without love, it can nevertheless happen that a person does not love that without which he cannot attain what he hopes for. It is as if he hopes for eternal life—which who does not love? [Col. 0287]—but does not love justice, without which no one reaches it [Note: The printed editions, Am., Er., Dan., and several manuscripts have: “although he does not have it, and does not love justice.” Lov. and Arn. have: “although he does not love justice,” omitting “does not have it and.” The reading has been corrected with the help of the ancient books.].

This, then, is the faith of Christ that the Apostle commends, the faith that works through love (Galatians V, 6). What it does not yet possess in love, it asks to receive, seeks in order to find, and knocks so that it may be opened to it (Matthew VII, 7). Faith obtains what the law commands. For without God’s gift—that is, without the Holy Spirit, through whom charity is poured into our hearts (Romans V, 5)—the law can command but cannot help; indeed, it can make a person a transgressor who cannot excuse himself on the ground of ignorance. For carnal desire reigns where the charity of God is absent.

## CHAPTER CXVIII

### The four conditions, or ages, of the human being: before the Law, under the Law, under grace, and in peace

But when one lives according to the flesh in the deepest darkness of ignorance, with no reasoning resisting it, this is the human being’s first state. Then, when knowledge of sin has been produced through the law, if the divine Spirit does not yet provide help, a person who wishes to live according to the law is defeated; knowingly he sins, and, subjected to sin, serves it: “For by whatever a person is overcome, by this he is enslaved” (II Peter II, 19). The knowledge of the commandment causes sin to produce in the human being every form of desire, with an accumulation of transgression added, so that what is written may be fulfilled: “The law entered alongside, so that the offense might increase” (Romans V, 20). This is the human being’s second state.

But if God looks upon him, so that God Himself is believed to help him fulfill what He commands, and the human being begins to be directed by God’s Spirit, desire rises against the flesh with the stronger force of charity (Galatians V, 17). Thus, although there is still something arising from the human being that resists him, since his weakness has not yet been wholly healed, nevertheless “the just person lives by faith” (Romans I, 17), and lives justly insofar as he does not yield to evil desire, with the delight of justice prevailing [Note: Lov. and Arn. have “with the love of justice,” contrary to the other printed editions and nearly all the manuscripts.].

These are the third condition, the human being’s condition of good hope. If anyone advances in it with devoted perseverance, the final peace remains—a peace that after this life will be fulfilled first in the repose of the spirit and then, in the resurrection, also in the flesh.

Of these four distinctions, the first is before the Law, the second under the Law, the third under grace, and the fourth in complete and perfect peace. So too God’s people were ordered through the successive intervals of time, as pleased God, who arranges all things “in measure, number, and weight” (Wisdom XI, 21). At first there was the period before the Law; secondly, under the Law given through Moses; then, under grace, which was revealed through the Mediator’s first coming (John I, 17).

That grace, indeed, was not previously absent from those to whom it was fitting that it be given, although, in accordance with the dispensation of time, it was veiled and hidden. For none of the ancient righteous could find salvation apart from faith in Christ; nor, unless He had also been known to them [Note: Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions have: “But unless He had also been known to them, He could not have been proclaimed to us through their ministry,” and so forth.], could He have been prophesied to us through their ministry—sometimes more openly, sometimes more secretly.

## CHAPTER CXIX

### Regeneration abolishes all sins at every age [Col. 0288]. Some experience no servitude under the Law

But in whichever one of these four conditions, as it were ages, the grace of regeneration finds each human being, there all his previous sins are forgiven; and the guilt contracted by birth is dissolved by rebirth. So greatly does it matter that “the Spirit breathes where He wills” (John III, 8), that some have not known that second servitude under the Law [Note: The printed editions have: “have not known that there is that second servitude under the Law.” The manuscripts more correctly have “second,” without the verb “is.” He calls servitude under the Law “second” because it was preceded by servitude under sin.], but begin to have divine assistance together with the commandment.

## CHAPTER CXX

### Those regenerated who die before attaining the use of reason do not perish

Before a human being can be capable of receiving the commandment, he must live according to the flesh. But if he has already been imbued with the sacrament of regeneration, it will do him no harm if he then departs from this life. For Christ died and rose again for this purpose: that He might be Lord both of the living and of the dead (Romans XIV, 9); nor will the kingdom of death hold the one for whom He died, who is “free among the dead” (Psalm LXXXVII, 6).

## CHAPTER CXXI

### 32. Charity is the end of all the commandments

All the divine commandments, therefore, refer to charity, of which the Apostle says: “But the end of the commandment is charity from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith” (I Timothy I, 5). The end of every commandment is therefore charity; that is, every commandment is referred to charity.

Whatever is done either from fear of punishment or from some carnal intention, so that it is not referred to that charity which the Holy Spirit pours into our hearts (Romans V, 5), is not yet done as it ought to be, even though it may appear to be done. This charity is directed toward God and neighbor; and certainly “on these two commandments depend the whole Law and the Prophets” (Matthew XXII, 40).

Add the Gospel; add the Apostles. For the saying, “The end of the commandment is charity,” comes from no other source, and so does the saying, “God is charity” (I John IV, 16). Whatever God commands—including “You shall not commit adultery” (Exodus XX, 14; Matthew V, 27)—and whatever is not commanded but is recommended by spiritual counsel—including “It is good for a man not to touch a woman” (I Corinthians VII, 1) [Note: The manuscripts have “are vowed,” rather than “are recommended.”]—is rightly done when it is referred to loving God, and one’s neighbor for God’s sake, both in this age and in the age to come: now, God through faith; then, through sight; and now, one’s neighbor also through faith.

For we do not know the hearts of mortals while we are mortal. Then, however, “the Lord will bring to light the hidden things of darkness and disclose the counsels of hearts; and then each person will receive praise from God” (I Corinthians IV, 5). For what will be praised and loved by one’s neighbor in one’s neighbor is precisely what God Himself will illuminate so that it may not remain hidden.

Desire is diminished as charity grows, until charity comes here [Note: One manuscript from Germanus omits “here”; Arnaldus moved the word and transferred it there: “For here the greater charity …”] to such greatness that it cannot be greater: “Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends” (John XV, 13). But there—who could explain how great charity will be [Col. 0289], where there will be no desire for anything that charity must overcome even by restraint? For there will be perfect health, when there is no struggle with death [Note: Thus most manuscripts. Some, together with Dan., have “since perfect health will be present.” Lov. and Arn. have “when perfect health will be present.”].

## CHAPTER CXXII

### 33. Conclusion of the book

But let this volume at last come to an end. You yourself can judge whether you ought either to call it or to possess it as an *Enchiridion*. Nevertheless, since I did not think your studies in Christ should be despised, believing and hoping good things about you through the help of our Redeemer [Col. 0290] [Note: The printed editions have: “believing good things about you, trusting and hoping in the help of our Redeemer.” The word “trusting” is absent from most manuscripts, and their punctuation gives a different sense: “believing and hoping good things about you.”], and loving you greatly as one of His members, I have written this book for you, as best I could—may it be as useful as it is long—on Faith, Hope, and Charity.

# [ON CHRISTIAN COMBAT]

[Col. 0289]

## INTRODUCTION TO THE BOOK ON CHRISTIAN COMBAT

This book should be assigned to the year of our Lord 396 or 397. For it is found placed third in the second book of the *Retractations*, among those short works that Augustine completed soon after undertaking the episcopate, an office he obtained toward the end of the year 395. Indeed, in chapter 29, where he warns Christians against and turns them away from the schism of the Donatists—which he rightly observes to have been divided into various factions, so that, just as Donatus had attempted to divide Christ, Donatus himself was divided by his own followers through daily dismemberment—he does not there, for the usefulness of the case, bring forward the fact that the Donatists later received into their communion Praetextatus and Felicianus, both of whom they had expelled by the celebrated judgment of the Council of Bagai because of their crimes, although this reception occurred around the beginning of the year 397.

Nor is this point without significance for strengthening the opinion that, in the preface to volume 2, when discussing the date of Letter 31, written to Paulinus, we wished to keep independent of the books addressed to Simplicianus—books that are usually assigned to the year 397—the question whether those books could be brought back to the year 396, since they are listed in the *Retractations* before the work *On Christian Combat*.

Augustine called this work *On Christian Combat* because it trains Christians to fight against the devil. It teaches that the invisible enemy is defeated by right faith and upright conduct. Therefore it first urges us to struggle against our desires, to subject our body to servitude, and to subject ourselves to God. Then, because we begin to submit ourselves to God through faith, it exhorts us to hold fast to the Rule of Catholic Faith, rejecting the opposing heresies.

Here he names certain principal sects of heretics; but the book appears to have been directed especially against the Manichaeans, in order to turn the people away from that foolish as well as sacrilegious heresy. The first part of the book is directed against them, since it rejects their fantasies about a race of darkness rebelling against God; but so too is the second part, since it commends the simplicity and sincerity of the Christian faith, which those same heretics mocked.

Cassiodorus Senator mentions this work in book 16 of *On the Institution of Divine Literature*: “One book of the same Augustine, which he composed *On Christian Combat*, is especially necessary for you, who, having trampled upon the world, labor in Christian combat.”

[Col. 0289]

[Note: [Col. 0289] On the book *On Christian Combat*, see book 2, chapter 3, of the *Retractations*, volume 1, column 631, from the words “The book *On Christian Combat*” up to the words “the crown of victory.” M.]

### ONE BOOK OF SAINT AURELIUS AUGUSTINE, BISHOP OF HIPPO, ON CHRISTIAN COMBAT

[Note: [Col. 0289] Written in the year 396 or shortly thereafter.]

[Note: [Col. 0289] For correcting the book *On Christian Combat*, the following manuscripts were used, in addition to three Vatican manuscripts: seventeen Gallican manuscripts; above all, one manuscript worthy of praise, which the illustrious Lord D. Duke of Noailles gave as a gift to our Germanus library; also a manuscript of the Navarre College in Paris; manuscripts of the Abbey of Victor; Germanus; Corbie; Reims, Saint Remigius; Vendôme; Lérins; Utica, Saint Ebrulf; Saint Michael in Peril of the Sea; Angers, Saint Albinius; Angers, Saint Sergius; Casale Benedicti; two from the library of Fleury; and an equal number from the Colbert collection, formerly belonging to the Thuane library and the College of Foix; as well as the variant readings collected by the Louvain editors from three Belgian manuscripts; and the old editions: Parv., that is, John Parvus, 1513; Am., Amerbach; Er., Erasmus; and Lov., the Louvain editions.]

[Note: [Col. 0289] We also compared all the editions mentioned at the beginning of the *Retractations* and the *Confessions*, volume 1. M.] (C)

He exhorts and trains Christians to engage in combat against the devil. He teaches that the devil is conquered and subdued by us when desires are conquered and the body is reduced to servitude; and that the body itself is subjected to servitude if we subject ourselves to God, whom every creature serves either willingly or by necessity. He shows that human weakness is fortified by the help of faith, and that through the Son of God made flesh it has received an aid of the greatest appropriateness. Afterwards, reviewing one by one the articles of Catholic faith contained in the Creed, he exposes the various heresies that have arisen against it and commands that they be avoided.

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 0289]

### 1. The crown promised to those who conquer. The adversary, the devil, is conquered by Christ’s help. The crown of victory is promised only to those who fight

In the divine Scriptures we constantly find a crown promised to us [Col. 0291] if we conquer. But, so as not to recall many passages, it is stated most clearly in the Apostle Paul: “I have completed the work; I have finished the course; I have kept the faith. Now the crown of righteousness remains for me” (II Timothy IV, 7–8).

We must therefore learn who this adversary is: if we conquer him, we shall be crowned. For he is the one whom our Lord first conquered, so that we too, remaining in Him, might conquer. The Power and Wisdom of God, and the Word through whom all things were made—the only Son of God—always remains immutable above every creature. And since even the creature that has not sinned is beneath Him, how much more is every sinful creature beneath Him?

Therefore, since all the holy angels are beneath Him, much more are all the transgressing angels beneath Him, of whom the devil is prince. But because he had deceived our nature, the only-begotten Son of God deigned to assume that very nature of ours, so that the devil might be conquered through it, and so that He might cause the one who is always beneath Him to be beneath us as well.

This is signified when He says: “The prince of this world has been cast out” (John XII, 31). He does not mean that he was cast outside the world, as certain heretics think, but outside the souls of those who cling to the Word of God and do not love the world of which he is prince. For he rules those who love temporal goods, which are contained in this visible world—not because he himself is lord of this world, but because he is prince of those desires by which everything passing away is coveted. Through them, those who neglect the eternal God and love unstable and changing things become subject to him.

“For desire is the root of all evils”; by aspiring to it, “some have wandered from the faith and pierced themselves with many sorrows” (I Timothy VI, 10). Through this desire the devil reigns in a person and holds his heart. All who love this world are such people.

The devil is cast out when this world is renounced with the whole heart. For the devil, who is the prince of this world, is renounced when his corruptions, spectacles, and angels are renounced. Therefore the Lord Himself, already bearing the triumphant nature of humanity, says: “Know that I have conquered the world” (John XVI, 33).

## CHAPTER II

### 2. How the devil is conquered. Invisible powers are conquered when desires are conquered

Many say: “How can we conquer the devil, whom we do not see?” But we have a teacher who has deigned to show us how invisible enemies are conquered. Concerning Him the Apostle says: “Stripping off the flesh, He displayed the principalities and powers, triumphing over them openly in Himself” (Colossians II, 15).

The invisible powers hostile to us are therefore conquered where invisible desires are conquered. Since we conquer within ourselves the desires for temporal things, we must also conquer within ourselves the one who reigns in a person through those desires.

When it was said to the devil, “You shall eat earth,” it was said to the sinner, “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Genesis III, 14, 19). The sinner was therefore given to the devil as food [Note: [Col. 0291] Most manuscripts have “food of the devil.”]. Let us not be earth if we do not wish to be eaten by the serpent.

For just as we convert what we eat into our body, so that the food itself becomes, bodily, what we are, so through evil habits—through wickedness, pride, and impiety—each person becomes what the devil is, that is, like him; and he is subjected to the devil just as our body is subject to us. This is what it means to be eaten by the serpent.

Whoever, therefore, fears the fire prepared for the devil and his angels (Matthew XXV, 41), should strive to triumph over him within himself. We conquer within those who attack us from without by conquering the desires through which they dominate us. Those whom they find to be like themselves they drag with them to punishment.

## CHAPTER III

### 3. In what sense demons are in the heavens and are rulers of darkness

The Apostle likewise says that he fights within himself against external powers. For he says: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers, against the rulers of this world’s darkness, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places” (Ephesians VI, 12).

“Heaven” is also called this air, where winds, clouds, storms, and whirlwinds arise, just as Scripture says in many places: “The Lord thundered from heaven” (Psalm XVII, 14); “the birds of heaven” (Psalm VIII, 9); and “the flying creatures of heaven” (Matthew VI, 26), although it is clear that birds fly in the air. We too ordinarily call this air “heaven.” For when we ask whether the weather is clear or cloudy, we sometimes say, “What is the air like?” and sometimes, “What is the sky like?”

I have said this so that no one may suppose that evil demons dwell in the highest heaven, where God appointed the sun, moon, and stars. The Apostle calls these demons “spiritual” because the divine Scriptures also call evil angels spirits.

He calls them “the rulers of this darkness” because he calls sinful human beings darkness, over whom these beings rule. Thus elsewhere he says: “For you were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Ephesians V, 8), because they had been justified from among sinners.

We must not, therefore, suppose that the devil dwells in the highest heaven with his angels, from which we believe that he fell.

## CHAPTER IV

### 4. The error of the Manichaeans concerning a race of darkness rebelling against God

Thus the Manichaeans went astray. They say that, before the creation of the world, there existed a race of darkness that rebelled against God. In this war, the wretched believe that Almighty God could come to His aid in no other way than by sending a portion of Himself against it.

The princes of that race, as they say, devoured a portion of God and were tempered so that the world could be fashioned from them. Thus, they say, God achieved victory amid great disasters, tortures, and sufferings of His own members. They claim that these members were mixed with the dark entrails of those princes in order to temper them and restrain them from their fury.

They do not understand that their sect is so sacrilegious that they believe Almighty God fought against darkness not through a creature He had made, but through His very own nature. This is impious to believe. Nor is that all: they also say that those who were defeated were made better because their fury was restrained, while the nature of God that conquered was made most miserable [Col. 0293].

They further say that through this very mixture it lost its understanding and blessedness and became entangled in great errors and calamities. Even if they claimed that it would eventually be wholly purified, they would still assert great impiety against Almighty God, since they would believe that a part of Him had been tossed about for so long in errors and punishments without any guilt of sin.

But now, wretched men, they dare to say that it cannot even be wholly purified. They say that the very part that cannot be purified contributes to the binding, so that wickedness may thereby be wrapped up and bound in a tomb [Note: [Col. 0293] All manuscripts have “tomb,” in the masculine form.]; and thus that part of God itself, which has committed no sin, remains forever wretched there and is afflicted in an eternal prison of darkness [Note: [Col. 0293] Some manuscripts have “is fastened” or “is fastened to an eternal prison of darkness.”].

They say this in order to deceive simple souls. But who is so simple as not to perceive that these claims are sacrilegious—claims by which they assert that Almighty God was overpowered by necessity, so that He had to surrender His good and innocent portion to such disasters and pollute it with such defilement, and could not free it entirely; and that whatever He could not free He bound with eternal chains?

Who, then, would not abhor such doctrines? Who would not understand that they are impious and profane? But when those men capture people, they do not say these things first. If they did, everyone would laugh at them or flee from them [Note: Thus Parv. and many manuscripts. Other editions have “they would be driven away by everyone.” Three manuscripts have “they would be driven away by human beings.”].

Instead, they select passages from Scripture that simple people do not understand, and through them deceive inexperienced souls by searching for the origin of evil. They do this with the passage written by the Apostle: “the rulers of this darkness and the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places.”

Those deceivers ask and question a person who does not understand the divine Scriptures: “Where do the rulers of darkness in heaven come from?” When he cannot answer, they lead him astray through curiosity, because every uneducated soul is curious.

But one who has learned the Catholic faith well and is fortified by good conduct and true piety, even if he does not know their heresy, nevertheless answers them. For one who already knows what belongs to the Christian faith—which is called Catholic because it is spread throughout the world and, under the Lord’s governance, is secure against all the impious and sinful, including even its own negligent members [Note: The printed editions Am., Er., and Lov. have “while neglecting its own.” Parv., supported by seven manuscripts, more correctly has “while also against its own negligent members.” We understand “its own” to mean the Catholic faithful, against whom, when negligent, he says the secure faith is directed. Four manuscripts have “but from their negligent members,” though incorrectly.]—cannot be deceived.

## CHAPTER V

### 5. In what sense “the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places” is said

Since, then, we were saying that the Apostle Paul declared that we have a struggle against the rulers of darkness and the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places, and since we also established that this air close to the earth is called heaven, we must believe that we fight against the devil and his angels, who rejoice in our disturbances.

The Apostle himself also calls the devil elsewhere “the prince of the power of this air” (Ephesians II, 2) [Col. 0294].

Nevertheless, the passage in which he says “the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places” can also be understood in another way: perhaps he did not say that the transgressing angels themselves are in the heavenly places, but rather that we are there, of whom he says elsewhere, “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Philippians III, 20). Thus, established in the heavenly places—that is, walking in God’s spiritual commandments—we fight against the spiritual forces of wickedness that attempt to pull us away from there.

We must therefore inquire more carefully how we can fight and conquer those whom we do not see, lest foolish people think that we ought to fight against the air.

## CHAPTER VI

### 6. The body must be disciplined so that the devil and the world may be conquered

The Apostle himself teaches this when he says: “I do not fight as though beating the air; but I discipline my body and bring it into servitude, lest, after preaching to others, I myself should be found disqualified” (I Corinthians IX, 26–27).

He likewise says: “Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ” (the same, XI, 1). We must therefore understand that the Apostle himself triumphed within himself over the powers of this world, just as he had said of the Lord (II Corinthians II, 14, and Colossians II, 15), whose imitator he professes to be.

Let us therefore imitate him as he exhorts us, and discipline our body and bring it into servitude if we wish to conquer the world. For this world can dominate us through its unlawful pleasures, spectacles, and destructive curiosity—that is, through the things that lovers of temporal affairs gather through destructive delight and that compel them to serve the devil and his angels.

If we have renounced all these things, let us bring our body into servitude [Note: The printed editions have “if we renounce, let us bring into servitude.” All the manuscripts have “if we have renounced, let us bring into servitude.”].

## CHAPTER VII

### 7. So that our body may be subjected to us, let us subject ourselves to God, whom every creature serves, willingly or unwillingly. The distinction between the just and the unjust in the goods and evils of this life

But if someone should ask how it comes about that we subject our body to servitude, it can easily be understood and accomplished if we first subject ourselves to God with a good will and sincere charity. For every creature, willingly or unwillingly, is subject to the one God and its Lord.

We are admonished, however, to serve the Lord our God with our whole will. For the just person serves freely, while the unjust serves in chains. All serve divine providence; but some obey it as sons and do with it what is good, while others are bound as slaves, and what is just is done with them.

Thus Almighty God, Lord of the whole creation, who made all things “very good,” as it is written (Genesis I, 31), ordered them so that He might do good both through the good and through the evil. For whatever is done justly is done well. The good are blessed justly, and the evil suffer punishment justly. Therefore God does good both through the good and through the evil, because He does all things justly.

The good are those who serve God with their whole will; the evil serve Him by necessity, for no one escapes the laws of the Almighty. But it is one thing to do what the law commands and another to suffer what the law commands. Therefore the good act according to the laws, while the evil suffer according to the laws [Col. 0295].

### 8.

Nor should it disturb us that in this life the just, according to the flesh they bear, endure many difficult and harsh things. For those suffer no evil who can already say what that spiritual man, the Apostle, exults in and proclaims when he says: “We glory in tribulations, knowing that tribulation produces endurance, endurance produces proven character, and proven character produces hope; but hope does not disappoint, because the love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Romans V, 3–5).

If, then, in this life, where there are so many torments, good and just men, when they suffer such things, can not only endure them with equanimity but even glory in the love of God [Note: Thus Parv. and the manuscripts. Am., Er., and Lov. have “glory in God through love.”], what must we think of that life promised to us, where we shall feel no bodily distress?

For the body of the just will not rise for the same purpose as the body of the impious, as it is written: “We shall all rise, but we shall not all be changed.” And lest anyone think that this change is not promised to the just but rather to the unjust, and suppose that it is punitive, the text continues: “And the dead shall rise incorruptible, and we shall be changed” (I Corinthians XV, 51–52).

All who are evil have therefore been ordered in this way: each harms himself, and all harm one another. They desire what is ruinously loved and can easily be taken away from them; and they take this away from one another when they persecute one another.

They are therefore tormented when temporal things are taken from them, because they love them; while those who take them away rejoice. But such joy is blindness and utter misery. It entangles the soul still more and leads it to greater torments.

A fish too rejoices when, not seeing the hook, it swallows the bait. But when the fisherman begins to draw it in, its entrails are first tortured; then, through the very bait over which it rejoiced, it is dragged away from all its joy toward destruction.

So are all who think themselves blessed because of temporal goods. They have taken the hook and wander about with it; the time will come when they will experience how great the torments were that they greedily swallowed.

They do no harm to the good, because they take away from them what they do not love. What they do love, and from which they are blessed, no one can take away from them.

Bodily suffering miserably afflicts evil souls but bravely purifies good ones. Thus both the evil human being and the evil angel serve divine providence, though they do not know what good God accomplishes through them. They are therefore rewarded not according to the merits of their service but according to the merits of their wickedness.

## CHAPTER VIII

### 9. All things are governed by divine providence

Just as these souls, which possess the will to harm and the capacity to reason, are ordered under divine laws so that no one may suffer anything unjust, so all animals and bodily things, each according to its kind and order, are administered under the laws of divine providence.

Therefore the Lord says: “Are not two sparrows sold for an assarius, and not one of them falls to the ground without the will of your Father?” (Matthew X, 29). He said this to show that whatever human beings regard as most worthless is governed by God’s omnipotence [Col. 0296].

Thus Truth declares that the birds of heaven are fed by Him and the lilies of the field clothed by Him (Matthew VI, 26, 28–30), and says that even the hairs of our head have been numbered (the same, X, 30).

But since God Himself cares directly for rational souls that are clean—whether in the greatest and best angels or in human beings who serve Him with their whole will—while He governs other things through them, the Apostle could also say with complete truth: “For God is not concerned with oxen” (I Corinthians IX, 9).

In the holy Scriptures God teaches human beings how they should deal with human beings and serve God. How they should deal with their animals, they themselves know—that is, how they should care for the well-being of their animals through use, experience, and natural reason. All these abilities, indeed, they have received from the abundant resources of their great Creator.

Whoever, therefore, can understand how God, the Creator of the whole creation, governs it through holy souls that are His servants in heaven and on earth—for the holy souls themselves were also made by Him and hold the primacy within His creation—whoever can understand this, let him understand and enter into the joy of his Lord (Matthew XXV, 21).

## CHAPTER IX

### 10. An exhortation to taste the sweetness of God

But if we cannot do this while we are in the body and away from the Lord (II Corinthians V, 6), let us at least taste “how sweet the Lord is” (Psalm XXXIII, 9), because He has given us the pledge, the Spirit (II Corinthians I, 22, and V, 5), in whom we may experience His sweetness.

Let us desire the very fountain of life, where we may be flooded and watered with sober intoxication, like a tree planted beside streams of water, which yields its fruit in its season and whose leaves do not fall (Psalm I, 3).

For the Holy Spirit says: “But the children of human beings will hope in the shelter of Your wings; they will be intoxicated by the abundance of Your house, and You will give them drink from the torrent of Your delight. For with You is the fountain of life” (Psalm XXXV, 8–10).

Such intoxication does not overturn the mind; nevertheless, it carries it upward and grants forgetfulness of all earthly things. If we can already say with our whole affection: “As the deer longs for the springs of water, so my soul longs for You, O God” (Psalm XLI, 2)—

## CHAPTER X
## 11. The Son of God became human for our sake. Free will.

But if perhaps, because of the sicknesses of the soul that it has contracted from love of the world, we are still unable to taste how sweet the Lord is, let us at least believe the divine authority concerning what he wished to be written in the Holy Scriptures about his Son: that he was made for him from the seed of David according to the flesh, as the Apostle says (Rom. 1:3). For all things were made through him, as it is written in the Gospel, and without him nothing was made (John 1:3). He took pity on our weakness—which we deserved, not through his work, but through our own will. For God made humanity imperishable (Wis. 2:23) and gave it free choice of will. He would not be supremely good if humanity served God’s commands by necessity rather than by will.

This is altogether easy, as I understand it—though those who have abandoned the Catholic faith and still wish to be called Christians do not want to understand it. For if they admit with us that our nature is healed only by doing what is right, let them admit that it is weakened only by sinning. Therefore we must not believe that our soul is what God is. For if it were, it would be changed for the worse neither by its own will nor by any necessity [Note: Nearly all manuscripts read “would be moved”], since God is understood in every way to be immutable. [Col. 0297] This is understood by those who do not love, in contentiousness, rivalry, and desire for empty glory, to speak about what they do not know, but who, with Christian humility, think rightly about the Lord and seek him in goodness and simplicity of heart (Wis. 1:1).

The Son of God therefore deigned to take upon himself our weakness, and “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14)—not because that eternity was changed, but because he displayed a changeable creature to the changeable eyes of human beings, having assumed it in his unchangeable majesty.

## CHAPTER XI

### 12. How fitting was the way in which God’s Son incarnate liberated humanity.

There are foolish people who say, “Could God’s Wisdom not have liberated human beings in some other way, without assuming humanity, being born of a woman, and suffering all those things at the hands of sinners?” We answer them: Certainly he could; but if he had acted otherwise, it would likewise have displeased your foolishness. For if he had not appeared to the eyes of sinners, his eternal light—which is seen by the inner eyes—could not have been seen by defiled minds.

But now, because he deigned to admonish us visibly in order to prepare us for invisible things, he displeases the greedy because he did not possess a golden body; he displeases the unchaste because he was born of a woman—for the unchaste greatly hate the fact that women conceive and give birth; he displeases the proud because he endured insults with the greatest patience; he displeases the luxurious because he suffered; he displeases the timid because he died. And so that they would not seem to be defending their own vices, they say that this displeases them not in a human being but in the Son of God.

They do not understand what the eternity of God is, which assumed humanity, nor what the human creature itself is, which was being recalled through its changes to its former stability, so that we might learn—from the Lord himself as teacher—that the weaknesses we have accumulated by sinning can be healed by doing what is right. For it was shown to us to what fragility humanity had come through its own fault, and from what fragility it is liberated by divine help.

Thus the Son of God assumed humanity and suffered human things in it. This medicine for humanity is as great as it is impossible to conceive. For what pride can be healed if it is not healed by the humility of the Son of God? What greed can be healed if it is not healed by the poverty of the Son of God? What anger can be healed if it is not healed by the patience of the Son of God? What impiety can be healed if it is not healed by the love of the Son of God? Finally, what timidity can be healed if it is not healed by the resurrection of the body of Christ the Lord?

> [Note: The editions of Parv., Am., and Er., and the manuscripts omit “of Christ the Lord.” One manuscript, however, has “of the Son of God” in its place.]

Let the human race raise its hope and recognize its nature; let it see how much [Col. 0298] room it has among the works of God. Do not despise yourselves, men: the Son of God assumed a man. Do not despise yourselves, women: the Son of God was born of a woman. Yet do not love carnal things, because in the Son of God we are neither male nor female. Do not love temporal things, because, if they were rightly to be loved, the man whom the Son of God assumed would have loved them. Do not fear insults, crosses, and death, because, if they harmed humanity, the man whom the Son of God assumed would not have suffered them.

This whole exhortation—which is now preached everywhere and revered everywhere, and which heals every obedient soul—would not exist among human affairs if all those things that displease the very foolish had not happened. Whom will vicious boastfulness deign to imitate, so that it may be led to acquire virtue, if it is ashamed to imitate him of whom it was said before he was born, “He will be called the Son of the Most High” (Luke 1:32), and who is now called the Son of the Most High among all nations, something no one can deny?

If we think highly of ourselves, let us deign to imitate him who is called the Son of the Most High; if we think little of ourselves, let us dare to imitate the fishermen and tax collectors who imitated him. O medicine that cares for everyone, restrains everything swollen, restores everything wasting away, cuts away everything excessive, preserves everything necessary, repairs everything lost, and corrects everything distorted! Who can now exalt himself against the Son of God? Who can despair of himself, for whom the Son of God was willing to become so humble? Who can think blessed life consists in those things that the Son of God taught us to despise? To what adversities can one yield who believes that human nature was preserved through such great persecutions [Note: The editions read “by such great persecutions,” but all manuscripts lack “by”] in the Son of God? Who can think the kingdom of heaven closed to him when he knows that tax collectors and prostitutes imitated the Son of God?

> [Note: Parv. and some manuscripts read, “to be imitators of the Son of God.”]

What perversity would not be removed from one who looks upon, loves, and follows the deeds and words of that man in whom the Son of God offered himself to us as an example of life?

## CHAPTER XII

### 13. The Christian faith flourishes and triumphs everywhere.

Thus men and women alike, every age and every rank of this world, have now been stirred toward the hope of eternal life.

> [Note: Lov. reads “has been transformed.” Other editions and the manuscripts more correctly read “has been stirred.”]

Some, neglecting temporal goods, hasten toward divine things. Others yield to the virtues of those who do these things and praise what they do not dare to imitate. But a few still murmur and are tormented by empty envy: either those who seek their own interests in the Church, although they appear to be Catholics; or heretics who seek glory from the very name of Christ; or Jews who wish to defend the sin of their impiety; or pagans who fear losing the curiosity of a vain license.

> [Note: One Vatican manuscript reads “knowledge.”]

But the Catholic Church, spread far and wide throughout the whole world, has grown stronger and stronger, breaking the assaults of its opponents in earlier times—not by resisting, but by enduring. Now it laughs at their insidious questions by faith, examines them by diligence, and dissolves them by understanding. It does not concern itself with those who accuse its chaff, because it [Col. 0299] carefully and prudently distinguishes the time of harvest, the time of the threshing floors, and the time of the granaries. As for those who accuse its grain, it either corrects them when they are in error or counts them among the envious, amid thorns and weeds.

## CHAPTER XIII

### 14. Let faith be right and conduct good. The mind cannot grasp truth unless it is free from vices. The Church’s faith concerning the Trinity.

Let us therefore subject our soul to God if we wish to subject our body to servitude and triumph over the devil. Faith is the first thing that subjects the soul to God; next come the commandments of life. When these are observed, our hope is strengthened, love is nourished, and what previously was only believed begins to shine.

For since knowledge and action make a person blessed,

> [Note: The editions read, “and since action is a gift of God and makes a person blessed.” The manuscripts do not have “since action is a gift of God and.”]

just as error must be avoided in knowledge, so wickedness must be avoided in action. Anyone who thinks that he can know the truth while still living wickedly is in error. Wickedness is loving this world, considering highly the things that are born and pass away, desiring them and laboring to acquire them, rejoicing when they abound, fearing that they may perish, and grieving when they perish.

Such a life cannot see that pure, sincere, and unchangeable truth, cling to it, and no longer be moved forever.

> [Note: Several manuscripts read, “cannot see that sincere truth,” omitting “pure and.”]

> [Note: Most manuscripts read “and no longer die.”]

Therefore, before our mind is purified, we must believe what we are not yet able to understand, since it was said most truly through the prophet: “Unless you believe, you will not understand” (Isa. 7:9, according to the Septuagint).

### 15. The faith is transmitted very briefly in the Church.

In the Church, eternal things are commended—things that carnal people cannot yet understand—as well as the temporal things, past and future, that the eternity of divine providence has accomplished and will accomplish for the salvation of humanity. Let us therefore believe in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. These are eternal and unchangeable: that is, one God, an eternal Trinity of one substance—God from whom all things exist, through whom all things exist, and in whom all things exist (Rom. 11:36).

## CHAPTER XIV

### 16. Those who deny the three persons are not to be heeded.

Nor should we heed those who say that there is only the Father, that he has no Son, and that the Holy Spirit does not exist with him, but that the Father himself is sometimes called the Son and sometimes the Holy Spirit. They do not understand the Principle from whom all things exist, his Image through whom all things are formed, and his Holiness in whom all things are ordered.

## CHAPTER XV

### 17. Nor should those who introduce three gods be heeded.

Nor should we heed those who become indignant and angry because we do not say that three gods are to be worshiped. They do not understand what one and the same substance is. They are deceived by their own phantasms, because they are accustomed to see bodily either three animals or any three bodies separated in their respective places. Thus they think that God’s substance must be understood; and they greatly err because they are proud and cannot learn, since they do not wish to believe.

## CHAPTER XVI

### 18. Nor those who deny the equality [Col. 0300] and eternity of the persons.

Nor should we heed those who say that the Father alone is the true and eternal God, while the Son was not begotten from him but made by him out of nothing, and that there was a time when he did not exist, although he holds the first place in all creation; and that the Holy Spirit is of lesser majesty than the Son and was himself made after the Son; and that these three have different substances, like gold, silver, and bronze.

They do not know what they are saying, and they transfer to their arguments empty images drawn from those things they are accustomed to see with bodily eyes. For it is truly a great thing to contemplate mentally a begetting that does not take place from some point in time but is eternal, and that Love and Holiness themselves by which the Begetter and the Begotten are ineffably joined to one another. It is a great and difficult thing to contemplate these matters mentally, even when the mind is peaceful and tranquil.

It cannot therefore be that those people see these things who gaze too intently upon earthly begettings and add smoke to these darknesses—smoke that they continually raise for themselves through daily disputes and quarrels—having souls that flow away in carnal affections,

> [Note: Thus the manuscripts. The editions instead read “flow down.”]

like pieces of wood saturated with moisture, in which fire belches out only smoke and cannot possess bright flames.

> [Note: The Fuxensis manuscript reads “moves.”]

This can indeed be said most rightly of all heretics.

## CHAPTER XVII

### 19. The faith of Christ’s incarnation. Those who deny that Christ is God are not to be heeded.

Believing, then, in the unchangeable Trinity, let us also believe in the temporal dispensation undertaken for the salvation of the human race.

> [Note: Here the editions add “that he was born God,” which is absent from the manuscripts.]

Nor should we heed those who say that Jesus Christ, the Son of God, was nothing other than a human being, though so righteous that he deserved to be called the Son of God. The Catholic discipline has also expelled these people, because, deceived by a desire for empty glory, they wished to argue contentiously before understanding what the Virtue of God and the Wisdom of God are (1 Cor. 1:24), and what it means that “in the beginning was the Word,” through whom all things were made, and that “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:1, 3, 14).

## CHAPTER XVIII

### 20. Those who deny that Christ had a true body are not to be heeded.

Nor should we heed those who say that the Son of God did not assume a true human being and was not born of a woman, but displayed to those who saw him false flesh and a simulated image of a human body. They do not understand how the substance of God, which governs the whole creation, cannot possibly be defiled. Yet they declare that this visible sun scatters its rays through all the filth and dirt of bodies and preserves them everywhere clean and pure.

If visible clean things can touch visible unclean things without being defiled, how much more could invisible and unchangeable Truth, taking up spirit through a soul and a body through the soul, having assumed the whole human being, liberate him from all weaknesses without any contamination of itself?

Thus they suffer great perplexities. While fearing that something impossible might happen—that [Col. 0301] Truth might be defiled by human flesh—they say that Truth lied. Yet he commanded, saying, “Let what you say be ‘Yes, yes; No, no’” (Matt. 5:37), and the Apostle cries out, “There was not ‘Yes’ and ‘No’ in him, but ‘Yes’ was in him” (2 Cor. 1:19). These people insist that his entire body was false flesh, so that they may not seem to imitate Christ unless they lie to their own hearers.

> [Note: Some manuscripts read “to their own teachers.” This is wrong, for the Manichaeans are being criticized here; among them there were Elect and Hearers.]

## CHAPTER XIX

### 21. Those who deny that Christ had a human mind are not to be heeded.

Nor should we heed those who confess the Trinity in one eternal substance but dare to say that the human being assumed in the temporal dispensation did not have a human mind, but only a soul and a body. This is to say, “He was not a human being, but had human bodily members.” Animals too have a soul and a body, but they do not have reason, which belongs specifically to the mind.

But if those who deny that he had a human body—which is the lowest part of a human being—are accursed, I am amazed that these people are not ashamed, since they deny that he had what is best in a human being. The human mind must be greatly lamented if it is conquered by its own body; for in that human being it was not reformed in whom the human body itself had already received the dignity of heavenly form. But far be it from us to believe what reckless blindness and proud verbosity have fabricated.

## CHAPTER XX

### 22. Those who say that this human being was assumed by God’s Wisdom in no other way than the other saints, who become wise, are not to be heeded.

Nor should we heed those who say that the human being born of a virgin was assumed by that eternal Wisdom in the same way as other human beings become wise through it—those who are perfectly wise. They do not understand the particular mystery of that human being and think that the only thing he possessed beyond the other blessed ones was that he was born of a virgin.

If they consider this carefully, they may perhaps believe that he deserved this beyond the others because this assumption too possesses something distinctive beyond the others. For it is one thing merely to become wise through the Wisdom of God, and another to sustain the very person of God’s Wisdom.

Although the nature of the body of the Church is the same, who does not understand that the head differs greatly from the other members? If that man is the head of the Church, through whose assumption “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us,” then all the other saints are its members, through whom the Church is perfected and completed.

Just as the soul animates and gives life to our whole body, but in the head it also senses through seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, and touching, while in the other members it senses only through touching—and therefore all things are subjected to the head for action, while the head is placed above them for direction, because the head in a certain way sustains the person of the soul that directs the body; for every sense appears there—so the Mediator between God and humanity, the man Christ Jesus (1 Tim. 2:5), is the head of the whole people of the saints as of one body.

Therefore [Col. 0302] God’s Wisdom, the Word in the beginning through whom all things were made, did not assume that man in the same way as the other saints, but much more excellently and much more sublimely: in the way that it was fitting for that one alone to be assumed in whom Wisdom would appear to human beings, as it was fitting for it to be displayed visibly.

> [Note: Thus the manuscripts. The editions instead read “because it was fitting that he alone be assumed.”]

> [Note: The editions read “the Wisdom of God the Father.” “of God the Father” is absent from the manuscripts.]

Accordingly, all other human beings who are wise, or have been able to become wise, or will be able to become wise, are wise in one way; but that one Mediator between God and humanity, the man Christ Jesus, is wise in another way. He not only possesses the benefit of that Wisdom through which all human beings become wise, but also bears its person.

Of the other wise and spiritual souls it can rightly be said that they have within themselves the Word of God through which all things were made. But of none of them can it rightly be said that “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.” This is said most rightly of our Lord Jesus Christ alone.

## CHAPTER XXI

### 23. Those who say that only the body was assumed by the Word are not to be heeded.

Nor should we heed those who say that only a human body was assumed by the Word of God. They interpret the statement “the Word became flesh” in such a way as to deny that this man had either a soul or anything human besides flesh.

They are greatly mistaken and do not understand that flesh alone was named in the statement “the Word became flesh” because, for the sake of whose human eyes that assumption took place, only flesh could appear. For if it is absurd and utterly unworthy that this human being did not have a human spirit, as we discussed above, how much more absurd and unworthy it is that he had neither spirit nor soul, but only what is even baser and lowest in animals: a body?

Let this impiety therefore also be excluded from our faith, and let us believe that the whole and perfect human being was assumed by the Word of God.

## CHAPTER XXII

### 24. Those who deny that Christ’s body was formed from a woman, saying that it was made in the same way as the body in which the Spirit appeared as a dove.

### Through a woman came death; through a woman, life.

Nor should we heed those who say that our Lord had a body like that which appeared in the dove whom John the Baptist saw descending from heaven and remaining over him as a sign of the Holy Spirit. They try to persuade us that the Son of God was not born of a woman, saying that, if he had to be displayed to carnal eyes, he could assume a body in the same way as the Holy Spirit.

“For that dove too,” they say, “was not born from an egg, and yet it could appear to human eyes.” The first answer to them is what we read: that the Holy Spirit appeared to John in the form of a dove (Matt. 3:16) in the very Gospel in which we also read that Christ was born of a woman (Matt. 1:20, 25). We must not believe the Gospel in one part and refuse to believe it in another.

For what reason do you believe that the Holy Spirit was displayed in the form of a dove, unless because you read it in the Gospel? Therefore I too believe from that same source that Christ was born of a virgin, because I read it in the Gospel.

Why, then, was the Holy Spirit not born [Col. 0303] from a dove, as Christ was born from a woman? The reason is that the Holy Spirit did not come to liberate doves, but to signify to human beings innocence and spiritual love, which was visibly represented in the form of a dove.

But the Lord Jesus Christ came to liberate human beings, among whom both males and females belong to salvation. He did not disdain males, because he assumed a male; nor females, because he was born of a woman. A great mystery is also involved here: since death had come to us through a woman, life would be born to us through a woman; so that, from both natures—the female and the male—the devil, who had rejoiced in the overthrow of both, would be defeated and tormented. His punishment would have been insufficient if both natures had been liberated in us unless we were also liberated through both.

We do not say this in such a way as to claim that the Lord Jesus Christ alone had a true body, while the Holy Spirit appeared deceptively to human eyes. We believe that both were true bodies. For just as it was not fitting for the Son of God to deceive human beings, so it was not fitting for the Holy Spirit to deceive human beings.

But for almighty God, who fashioned the whole creation from nothing, it was not difficult to form a true body of a dove without the assistance of other doves, just as it was not difficult for him to form a true body in Mary’s womb without male seed, since bodily nature [Note: Parv. and the manuscripts read “bodily creature”] served the command and will of the Lord both in the woman’s womb for forming a human being and in the world itself for forming a dove.

But foolish and wretched people do not believe that even almighty God could do what they themselves cannot do or have never seen during their lives.

## CHAPTER XXIII

### 25. Those who call the Son of God a creature because he suffered are not to be heeded. The Son of God suffered without any change in his divinity.

Nor should we heed those who therefore wish to force us to number the Son of God among creatures because he suffered. They say: “If he suffered, he is changeable; and if he is changeable, he is a creature, because God’s substance cannot be changed.”

With them we too say both that God’s substance cannot be changed and that a creature is changeable. But it is one thing to be a creature and another to assume a creature. Therefore the only-begotten Son of God, who is the Virtue and Wisdom of God and the Word through whom all things were made, because he cannot be changed at all, assumed a human creature. He deigned to raise it after it had fallen and renew it after it had grown old.

He was not himself changed for the worse in it through suffering; rather, through the resurrection he changed it for the better. Nor should we therefore deny that the Father’s Word—that is, the only Son of God, through whom all things were made—was born and suffered for us.

We call the martyrs sufferers and dead because of the kingdoms of heaven; yet their souls were not killed in that suffering and death. For the Lord says: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot do anything to the soul” (Matt. 10:28).

Just as, therefore, we call the martyrs sufferers and dead in the bodies they carried, without the killing or death of their souls, [Col. 0304] so we call the Son of God a sufferer and dead in the human being he carried, without any change or death of his divinity.
