## CHAPTER XXIV

### 26. Those who deny that the Lord’s body rose again as it had been buried are not to be heeded.

Nor should we heed those who deny that the Lord’s body rose again in the same condition in which it had been placed in the tomb. For if it had not been such a body, he himself would not have said to his disciples after the resurrection: “Touch me and see, because a spirit does not have bones and flesh as you see me have” (Luke 24:39).

> [Note: Parv. reads “bones and sinews.” Most manuscripts likewise read this, and several of them below have “sacrilege” where the text has “sacrilegious.”]

It is sacrilegious to believe that our Lord, since he is himself Truth, lied in anything. Nor should we be troubled by the fact that he is written to have suddenly appeared to his disciples when the doors were shut (John 20:26), so that we might deny on that account that it was a human body because entering through closed doors appears contrary to the nature of this body.

For all things are possible for God (Matt. 19:26). It is plainly contrary to the nature of this body to walk upon water; yet not only did the Lord himself walk upon it before his passion, but he also caused Peter to walk upon it (Matt. 14:25, 29). Thus after the resurrection also he did with his body whatever he wished.

For if before the passion he could glorify it like the brightness of the sun (Matt. 17:2), why could he not after the passion also reduce it in a moment of time to whatever degree of subtlety he wished, so that it could enter through closed doors?

## CHAPTER XXV

### 27. Those who deny that Christ’s body was taken up into heaven are not to be heeded.

Nor should we heed those who deny that our Lord took that very body with him into heaven. They cite what is written in the Gospel: “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven” (John 3:13), and they say that, since the body did not descend from heaven, it could not ascend into heaven.

They do not understand that the body did not ascend into heaven. The Lord ascended; the body, however, did not ascend by itself, but was lifted into heaven by the one who ascended.

For if someone descends, for example, naked from a mountain, and after descending puts on clothing and ascends again clothed, we rightly say, “No one has ascended except the one who descended.” We do not consider the garment that he carried up with him; we say that only the person who was clothed ascended.

## CHAPTER XXVI

### 28. Those who deny that Christ sits at the Father’s right hand. What God’s right and left hand mean.

Nor should we heed those who deny that the Son sits at the Father’s right hand. They say: “Does God the Father have a right or left side, as bodies do?”

Nor do we understand God the Father in this way, for God is not defined or confined by any bodily form.

> [Note: Some manuscripts read “limited.”]

The Father’s right hand is the perpetual blessedness promised to the saints,

> [Note: The editions read “given.” Most manuscripts read “promised.”]

just as his left hand is most rightly understood as the perpetual misery given to the impious. Thus right and left are understood in this manner not in God himself, but in creatures.

For the body of Christ, which is the Church, [Col. 0305] will also be in that right hand—that is, in that blessedness—as the Apostle says: “He raised us up together and made us sit together in the heavenly places” (Eph. 2:6). Although our body is not yet there, our hope is already there.

For this reason the Lord himself, after the resurrection, ordered the disciples whom he found fishing to cast their nets on the right side. When they did so, they caught fish, all of them large (John 21:6–11); that is, they signified the righteous, to whom the right hand is promised.

This is also signified by the fact that he said he would place the sheep at his right hand and the goats at his left at the judgment (Matt. 25:33).

## CHAPTER XXVII

### 29. Those who deny that there will be a judgment are not to be heeded.

Nor should we heed those who deny that the day of judgment will come. They cite what is written in the Gospel: that the one who believes in Christ does not come into judgment, while the one who does not believe in him has already been judged (John 3:18).

They say: “If the one who believes will not come into judgment, and the one who does not believe has already been judged, where are those whom he will judge on the day of judgment?”

They do not understand that Scripture speaks in such a way as to indicate a future time by a past tense. As we said above, when the Apostle said of us that he made us sit together in the heavenly places, this has not yet happened; but because it will most certainly happen, it was stated as though it had already happened.

The Lord himself likewise said to his disciples: “All things that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you” (John 15:15). Yet shortly afterward he says: “I have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now” (John 16:12). How, then, could he have said, “All things that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you,” unless he spoke of what he was most certainly going to accomplish through the Holy Spirit as though he had already accomplished it?

Thus, when we hear, “The one who believes in Christ will not come into judgment,” we should understand that he will not come to condemnation. For “judgment” is used to mean condemnation, as the Apostle says: “Let the one who does not eat not judge the one who eats” (Rom. 14:3)—that is, let him not think badly of him. The Lord also says: “Do not judge, so that you may not be judged” (Matt. 7:1).

He does not thereby remove our ability to judge, since the prophet also says: “If indeed you love justice, judge rightly, children of men” (Ps. 57:2), and the Lord himself says: “Do not judge according to appearance, but judge a just judgment” (John 7:24).

But in the passage where he forbids judging, he warns us not to condemn someone whose thought is not open to us or whose future we do not know. Thus when he said, “He will not come into judgment,” he meant that he would not come into condemnation.

But when he said, “The one who does not believe has already been judged” (John 3:18), he meant that such a person has already been condemned in the foreknowledge of God, who knows what awaits those who do not believe.

## CHAPTER XXVIII

### 30. Those who say that the promised Spirit came upon Paul, or Montanus, and others are not to be heeded.

Nor should we heed those who say that the Holy Spirit whom the Lord promised his disciples came either upon the Apostle Paul, or upon Montanus and Priscilla, as the Cataphrygians say, or upon some unknown Manes or Manichaeus, as the Manichaeans say.

These people are so blind [Col. 0306] that they do not understand the manifest Scriptures—or so negligent of their salvation that they do not read them at all. For who, after reading, would not understand that the Holy Spirit came in the Gospel, where it is written after the Lord’s resurrection that the Lord said: “I am sending the promise of my Father upon you; but remain here in the city until you are clothed with power from on high” (Luke 24:49)?

And in the Acts of the Apostles, after the Lord had departed from the disciples’ sight into heaven, do they not observe that, after ten days had passed, on the day of Pentecost the Holy Spirit most clearly came? While they were in the city, as he had previously instructed them, he filled them so that they spoke in tongues. For the various nations that were present then each understood his own language among those who were listening (Acts 2:1–11).

But these people deceive those who are negligent in the Catholic faith

> [Note: The editions read “who are negligent in the Catholic faith.” The manuscripts read “who neglect the Catholic faith,” or “who are negligent toward the Catholic faith.”]

and do not wish to learn that very faith of theirs which is manifest in the Scriptures.

> [Note: Thus Parv. and many manuscripts. Am., Er., and Lov. read “to say.”]

And what is more serious and deeply lamentable, while they behave negligently within the Catholic Church,

> [Note: The editions add “faith,” which may be understood here in place of “Church.”]

they lend a diligent ear to heretics.

## CHAPTER XXIX
**31. The Donatists, who deny that the Church is spread throughout the world, are not to be heeded. Donatus himself divided from his own followers. Donatus proved nothing when pleading his case against Caecilian at Rome. The Donatists maintain that Baptism is invalid unless they themselves have administered it.**

Nor should we heed those who deny that the holy Church, which is one and catholic, is spread throughout the world, but think that it flourishes only in Africa, that is, in the party of Donatus. Thus they are deaf to the prophet who says: “You are my Son; today I have begotten you. Ask of me, and I shall give you the nations as your inheritance, and your possession to the ends of the earth” (Ps. 2:7–8). There are also many other passages, in both the books of the Old and of the New Testament, which were written to declare most plainly that the Church of Christ is spread throughout the whole world.

When we bring this objection against them, they say that all these things had already been fulfilled before the party of Donatus existed, but that afterward the whole Church perished and that its remnants remained only in the party of Donatus. O proud and impious tongue! And yet they would not live in this way if they at least afterward preserved peace among themselves.

But now they do not observe that, in Donatus himself, what was said has already been fulfilled: “With whatever measure you measure, it shall be measured back to you” (Matt. 7:2). For just as he attempted to divide Christ, so he himself is divided from his own followers by daily dismemberment. To this also pertains what the Lord says: “For whoever strikes with the sword shall perish by the sword” (ibid. 26:52). The sword in that passage, since it is used in an evil sense, signifies a contentious tongue, with which that wretched man then struck the Church, though he did not kill it.

For the Lord did not say, “Whoever kills with the sword shall perish by the sword,” but rather, “Whoever uses the sword shall perish by the sword.” Thus he struck the Church with a quarrelsome tongue, and now he himself is cut to pieces by that same tongue, so that he may utterly perish and die.

Yet at that time the apostle Peter had acted not out of pride, but out of love for the Lord, though it was still a carnal love. Therefore, when admonished, he put away the sword; this man, however, did not do so even when defeated. For when he pleaded his case against Bishop Caecilian before the bishops at Rome, whom he himself had summoned, he could prove nothing of the charges he had brought. Thus he remained in schism, so that he might die by his own sword.

As for his people, when they refuse to hear the Prophets and the Gospel—in which it is written most plainly that the Church of Christ is spread among all nations—but listen instead to schismatics who seek not God’s glory but their own, they show clearly enough that they are slaves, not free, and that their right ear has been cut off.

For Peter, while erring in his love for the Lord, cut off the right ear of a slave, not of a free man. This signifies that those who are struck by the sword of schism are slaves of carnal desires, not yet brought into the freedom of the Holy Spirit, so that they no longer place their confidence in man. They do not hear what is right—that is, the glory of the Lord, spread far and wide through the catholic Church—but hear instead the error of human conceit on the left.

Yet since the Lord says in the Gospel that the end will come when the Gospel has been preached among all nations (Matt. 24:14), how can these people say that all the other nations have already fallen away from the faith and that the Church remains only in the party of Donatus, when it is evident that, after this party was cut off from unity, some nations afterward came to believe, and that there are still others that have not yet believed, to whom the Gospel is preached daily without ceasing [Note: [Col. 0307] One of the Vatican manuscripts has “does not cease.”]?

Who would not be astonished that anyone should wish to be called a Christian and yet be so violently carried away against the glory of Christ by such impiety as to dare to say that all the peoples of the nations who are even now joining the Church of God and hastening to believe in the Son of God are doing so in vain, because no Donatist baptizes them?

Surely people would execrate such claims and abandon them without delay if they were seeking Christ, loving the Church, free, and retaining their right ear intact.

### CHAPTER XXX

**32. The Luciferians, who, although they do not rebaptize, cut themselves off from the Church because it received those who repented of the Arian heresy, are not to be heeded.**

Nor should we heed those who, although they rebaptize no one, nevertheless cut themselves off from unity and preferred to be called Luciferians rather than Catholics. In understanding that Christ’s Baptism must not be repeated, they act rightly. For they perceive that the Sacrament of the holy washing exists nowhere except in the catholic Church, but that the severed branches possess the same form which they had received in the vine itself before they were cut off.

These are the people of whom the Apostle says: “Having the appearance of godliness, but denying its power” (2 Tim. 3:5). For the power of godliness is great: it is peace and unity, because there is one God. They do not possess this, because they have been cut off from unity.

Therefore, if any of them come to the Catholic Church, they do not repeat the appearance of godliness which they possess, but receive the power of godliness which they lack. For the Apostle plainly teaches that even cut-off branches can again be grafted in, provided they do not remain in unbelief (Rom. 11:23).

When the Luciferians understand this and do not rebaptize, we do not condemn them. But that they themselves also chose to be cut off from the root—who would not recognize this as detestable? Especially since what displeased them in the catholic Church was precisely what belongs to true catholic holiness.

For nowhere should the inner compassion of mercy be so vigorous as in the catholic Church, so that, like a true mother, she neither proudly insults sinful children nor finds it difficult to forgive those who have been corrected.

It is not without reason that Peter represents this catholic Church among all the Apostles: the keys of the kingdom of heaven were given to this Church when they were given to Peter (Matt. 16:19). And when he is told, “Do you love me? Feed my sheep” (John 21:17), this is said to all.

The catholic Church ought therefore gladly to forgive children who have been corrected and strengthened in godliness. For Peter himself, who represented her, had wavered on the sea (Matt. 14:30), had attempted carnally to turn the Lord away from his Passion (ibid. 16:22), had cut off the servant’s ear with a sword, had denied the Lord three times (ibid. 26:51, 70–74), and afterward had fallen into hypocritical pretense (Gal. 2:12). Yet we see that forgiveness was granted him, and that, once corrected and strengthened, he reached the glory of the Lord’s Passion.

Accordingly, after the persecution carried out by the Arian heretics, when peace—which the Catholic Church indeed holds in the Lord—was restored even by the rulers of the world, many bishops who had joined the Arian perfidy during that persecution [Note: [Col. 0308] Some manuscripts have “disturbance.”] chose, after being corrected, to return to the Catholic Church, condemning either what they had believed or what they had pretended to believe.

The catholic Church received them into her maternal embrace, like Peter after the tears of his denial, when he had been admonished by the crowing of the rooster, or like that same Peter after his wicked pretense, when he had been corrected by the voice of Paul.

Receiving this motherly charity proudly and reproaching it impiously, they deserved to fall with Lucifer, who was rising in the morning, because they did not rejoice with Peter when he rose after the crowing of the rooster (Matt. 26:75; Isa. 14:12).

### CHAPTER XXXI

**33. The Cathari, who deny that the Church can forgive all sins and forbid widows to marry, are not to be heeded.**

Nor should we heed those who deny that the Church of God can forgive all sins. Thus, wretched people, because they do not understand the rock in Peter and refuse to believe that the keys of the kingdom of heaven were given to the Church, have themselves let those keys slip from their hands.

These are the people who condemn widows as adulteresses if they marry, and proclaim themselves purer than apostolic teaching (1 Tim. 5:14). If they wished to recognize their own name, they would call themselves worldly rather than pure.

For, unwilling to be corrected if they sinned, they chose nothing except to be condemned with this world. By denying forgiveness to sinners, they do not preserve them in any state of health [Note: [Col. 0308] Two manuscripts have “holiness.”]; rather, they take medicine away from the sick. And they force their widows to burn with desire, since they do not permit them to marry.

For they should not be considered wiser than the apostle Paul, who preferred that they marry rather than burn (1 Cor. 7:9).

### CHAPTER XXXII

**34. Those who deny the resurrection of the flesh are not to be heeded.**

Nor should we heed those who deny that there will be a resurrection of the flesh and cite what the apostle Paul said: “Flesh and blood shall not possess the kingdom of God,” without understanding what the Apostle himself says: “This corruptible body must put on incorruption, and this mortal body must put on immortality.”

When this has happened, it will no longer be flesh and blood, but a heavenly body [Note: [Col. 0309] See *Retractions* II, chapter 3.]. The Lord also promises this when he says: “They shall neither marry nor be given in marriage, but shall be equal to the angels of God” (Matt. 22:30). For then they will live no longer for human beings but for God, once they have become equal to the angels.

Flesh and blood, therefore, will be changed and will become a heavenly and angelic body. “The dead will rise incorruptible, and we shall be changed” (1 Cor. 15:50–53), so that both statements may be true: that the flesh will rise, and that flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God.

### CHAPTER XXXIII

**35. While we are little ones, we must be nourished with the simplicity of faith. Perfect love tolerates neither desire for the world nor fear of it. Knowledge of the truth is found in a purified heart.**

Nourished and fed by this simplicity and sincerity of faith, let us grow in Christ. While we are little ones, let us not desire the food of adults, but let us grow in Christ through the healthiest nourishment, accompanied by good morals and Christian righteousness, in which love of God and neighbor is perfected and established.

Thus may each of us triumph within himself over the enemy, the devil, and his angels, in Christ whom he has put on. For perfect love possesses neither desire for the world nor fear of the world—that is, neither the desire to acquire temporal things nor the fear of losing temporal things.

Through these two doors the enemy enters and reigns; he must first be driven out by the fear of God, and afterward by love.

We ought therefore to desire the most open and evident knowledge of the truth all the more eagerly as we see ourselves advancing in love and possessing a heart purified by its simplicity [Note: [Col. 0310] The printed editions have *in ejus simplicitate* (“in its simplicity”); the manuscripts omit *in*.], because truth is seen by the inner eye. For he says: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:8).

Being rooted and grounded in love, may we have strength to comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth and length and height and depth, and to know the surpassing knowledge of the love of Christ, so that we may be filled with all the fullness of God (Eph. 3:17–19). After these struggles with the invisible enemy, since Christ’s yoke is easy for those who willingly and lovingly bear it, and his burden is light (Matt. 11:30), may we deserve the crown of victory.

[Col. 0309]

[Note: [Col. 0309] For the subsequent book, *On Catechizing the Uninstructed*, see book 2, chapter 14 of the *Retractions*, vol. 1, col. 635, from the words “There is also our book” through the words “Brother Deogratias.” M.]

**ONE BOOK OF THE HOLY AURELIUS AUGUSTINE, BISHOP OF HIPPO, ON CATECHIZING THE UNINSTRUCTED** [Note: [Col. 0309] Written around the year 400.]

[Note: [Col. 0309] In collating the books *On Catechizing the Uninstructed*, we consulted fourteen manuscripts: the very fine Corbie manuscript, about 800 years old; another of the Church of Laon, about 700 years old; the manuscript of the Abbey of Saint Benignus at Dijon; those of Pratelles, Fécamp, Saint Michael, and Cîteaux; two from Fleury; two from Saint Victor; the Sorbonne manuscript; and two Vatican manuscripts. We also used variant readings drawn by the Louvain scholars from three Belgian manuscripts, and finally the first editions of Amerbach, Erasmus, and the Louvain scholars.]

[Note: [Col. 0309] We also compared all the editions mentioned at the beginning of *Retractions* and *Confessions*, vol. 1. M.]

(C)

Augustine, asked by a Carthaginian deacon to teach the art of catechizing, first gives instructions so that this duty may be fulfilled not only by a definite method and suitable procedure, but also without weariness and with cheerfulness. Later, having recalled these instructions for practical use, he himself provides as examples two discourses prepared for instructing someone who wishes to be a Christian: one longer and the other very brief.

### CHAPTER I

**1. Augustine writes, at the request of a Carthaginian deacon, about catechizing the uninstructed.**

You asked me, brother Deogratias [Note: [Col. 0309] This may perhaps be the same Deogratias to whom Augustine, around the year 406 after Christ, replied in the letter now numbered 102 concerning questions about the pagans that Deogratias had sent him from Carthage.], to write something for you about catechizing the uninstructed that might be useful to you.

For you said that often at Carthage, where you are a deacon, people are brought to you who are to be instructed in the Christian faith for the first time, because you are thought to possess an abundant ability to catechize, both in teaching the faith and in the grace of your speech [Note: [Col. 0310] The Louvain edition has “both the teaching of the faith and the grace of speech.”].

Yet you almost always find yourself in difficulty over how suitably to explain that very thing by which we are Christians through believing: where the account should begin, how far it should be carried, whether, once the account has been completed, we ought to add some exhortation, or merely give instructions by which the person to whom we are speaking may know that the Christian life and profession are maintained through their observance [Note: [Col. 0311] Thus in the manuscripts; the printed editions have “by which … he may know how to maintain.”].

You also confessed and complained that it often happened to you that, in a long and lukewarm discourse, you yourself seemed contemptible to yourself and became a weariness—not to mention the person whom you were instructing by speaking and the others who were present as hearers. This necessity compelled you to press me with the affection you owe me, so that I would not find it burdensome, amid my occupations, to write something to you about this matter.

**2. The duty of love toward the universal Church also compels Augustine to help.**

For my part, I am compelled not only by the love which I owe you as a friend, but also by the love and service which I owe universally to Mother Church. If the Lord commands that, through whatever service I am able to offer by the generosity of our Lord, those whom he has made my brothers should be helped, I must in no way refuse, but rather undertake it with ready and devoted willingness.

For the more I desire the Lord’s money to be distributed widely, the more I ought, if I discover that my fellow stewards and servants have difficulty distributing it, to do whatever lies within my power so that they may easily and efficiently accomplish what they wish to do eagerly and diligently.

### CHAPTER II

**3. A discourse that pleases the hearer often displeases the speaker; why this happens. The speaker should take care to speak cheerfully and without weariness.**

But, as far as your particular concern is concerned, I would not want you to be troubled by the fact that you have often seemed to yourself to possess a low and wearisome discourse. It may be that the person you were instructing did not think so, but because you wished something better to be heard, what you were saying seemed to you unworthy of the ears of others.

Even my own discourse almost always displeases me. I am eager for something better, which I often enjoy inwardly before I begin to express it in sounding words. When I have judged that it has turned out less well than it was familiar to me, I am saddened that my tongue could not be sufficient for my heart.

For I want everything I understand to be understood by the person who hears me, and I realize that I do not speak in such a way as to achieve this—especially because that understanding floods the mind like a swift flash of light, whereas speech is slow and extended and entirely unlike it. While speech is being unfolded, the understanding has already withdrawn into its own secret place.

Nevertheless, because understanding has left certain traces impressed upon the memory in a marvelous way, those traces remain along with the pauses between the syllables. From these same traces we produce sounding signs, whether the language is called Latin, Greek, Hebrew, or any other; whether these signs are merely thought or also uttered aloud.

Those traces themselves belong neither particularly to Latin nor to Greek nor to Hebrew nor to any other nation, but are produced in the mind in the same way that facial expressions are produced in the body. Anger, for example, is expressed one way in Latin, another way in Greek, and in still other ways in the diversity of other languages. But the face of an angry person is neither Latin nor Greek.

Thus not all nations understand when someone says, “I am angry”; only Latins do. But if the emotion of an inflamed spirit appears on the face and produces an angry expression [Note: [Col. 0312] Perhaps, “affects the face.”], everyone who looks at the angry person perceives it.

Yet it is not possible to bring out and, as it were, extend into the perception of hearers through the sound of the voice those traces which understanding impresses upon the memory in the same way that the open and visible face can be displayed. Those traces are within the mind, whereas the face is outward in the body.

We must therefore consider how far the sound of our mouth falls short of that stroke of understanding, since it does not even resemble the impression made upon the memory. Yet we, often burning intensely for the benefit of our hearers, wish to speak in the way in which we understand at that moment, although we cannot speak by means of that very act of understanding.

When this does not succeed, we become distressed and, as though we were wasting our effort in vain, grow languid with weariness. From that very weariness the discourse becomes more sluggish and duller than it had been, and thus it produces weariness.

**4. The speaker’s joy makes the discourse more effective.**

Yet the eagerness of those who wish to hear me often shows me that my speech is not as cold as it seems to me. From their enjoyment I recognize that they derive some benefit from it. I therefore apply myself diligently so as not to fail in performing this ministry, since I see that they receive well what is offered.

You too should understand, from the very fact that people are so often brought to you to be instructed in the faith, that your discourse does not displease others as much as it displeases you. Nor should you consider yourself fruitless because you do not explain what you see in the way you wish, since perhaps you are unable even to see it as you wish.

For who in this life sees except in a riddle and through a mirror (1 Cor. 13:12)? Nor is love itself so great that, once the darkness of the flesh has been torn apart, it can penetrate into the eternal brightness from which even these passing things shine in some fashion.

But because the good advance day by day toward seeing that day without the expanse of heaven and without the intrusion of night—a day which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor entered into the human heart (ibid. 2:9)—there is no greater reason why our discourse should become contemptible to us when we instruct the uninstructed than that we wish to see what is unfamiliar and grow weary of speaking in familiar ways.

And indeed we are heard with much greater pleasure when we ourselves take pleasure in the same work. The thread of our speech is affected by our own joy and flows forth more easily and more acceptably.

It is therefore not a difficult task to prescribe what is to be taught, where the account of the things to be believed should begin and how far it should extend, or how the account should be varied so that it is sometimes shorter and sometimes longer, yet always full and complete; nor is it difficult to say when a shorter account and when a longer one should be used.

The greatest concern is to determine by what means one may catechize joyfully—for the more one is able to do so, the more pleasing the discourse will be. The instruction concerning this matter is readily available. For if God loves a cheerful giver in material money, how much more in spiritual money (2 Cor. 9:7)?

But that this cheerfulness may be present at the proper moment is the work of the mercy of the one who gave this command. Therefore, first we shall discuss the manner of narration, which I know you wish to learn; then instruction and exhortation; and afterward whatever God may suggest concerning the acquisition of this cheerfulness.

### CHAPTER III

[Col. 0313]

**5. What a complete account should be when catechizing. The account must be directed toward the end of love. The ancient Scriptures were written to commend Christ’s coming, whose end is love.**

The account is complete when a person is first catechized from what is written, “In the beginning God made heaven and earth” (Gen. 1:1), up to the present time of the Church.

This does not mean that we must recite the whole Pentateuch, all the books of Judges, Kings, and Ezra [Note: [Col. 0313] The manuscripts have “Ezra.”], and the whole Gospel and Acts of the Apostles, either by heart, if we have memorized them word for word, or by unfolding and explaining in our own words everything contained in these volumes. Neither does the time permit this nor does any necessity require it.

Rather, we must embrace everything in summary and in general outline, selecting certain more remarkable events that are heard with greater pleasure and that occur at the principal divisions of time [Note: [Col. 0313] The five divisions of time are noted below, no. 6 and no. 39.], so that we do not merely display them as though in wrappings and immediately snatch them from view, but linger over them for a while, as though untying and unfolding them, and offer them to the minds of the hearers for examination and admiration. The remaining material should be woven into the account by passing over it rapidly.

In this way, the matters we especially wish to commend stand out more prominently through the subordination of the others. The person whom we wish to excite through narration does not reach them exhausted, nor is the memory of the person whom we must instruct through teaching confused.

**6. Everything must be referred to love, and the hearer’s attention must be directed toward it.**

In all things we must not only keep in view the end of the commandment, which is “love from a pure heart and a good conscience and an unfeigned faith” (1 Tim. 1:5), to which we must refer everything we say; we must also move and direct the attention of the person whom we instruct by speaking toward that same end.

For there is no other reason why everything we read in the holy Scriptures was written before the Lord’s coming than that his coming might be commended and the future Church might be foreshadowed—that is, the people of God among all nations, which is his body—together with all the saints who lived in this world before his coming, believing that he would come just as we believe that he has come.

For just as Jacob first extended his hand from the womb while he was being born, and by that hand held the heel of his brother who was being born before him; then the head followed, and afterward, necessarily, the remaining limbs (Gen. 25:25), yet the head precedes in dignity and power not only those limbs which followed but also the hand itself which came first in the birth, and precedes it in the order of nature though not in the time of appearing—

so also the Lord Jesus Christ, although before he appeared in the flesh, and in a certain sense came forth from the womb of his hidden purpose into the sight of human beings as the Mediator between God and humanity, a human being who is God over all, blessed forever (Rom. 9:5), sent ahead in the holy Patriarchs and Prophets a kind of portion of his body.

By it, as by a hand announcing beforehand that he would be born, he also trampled upon the preceding proud people with the bonds of the Law as though with five fingers [Note: [Col. 0314] Several manuscripts have *supplantaret*, “might trample upon.”] (for he did not cease to be announced and prophesied as the one who was to come through the five divisions of time; and, corresponding to this, the one through whom the Law was given wrote five books).

Those who thought carnally and wished to establish their own righteousness (Rom. 10:3) were not filled with blessing by the open hand of Christ; rather, they were held back by that hand clenched and closed. Thus their feet were bound, and they fell; but we have risen and have been set upright (Ps. 19:9).

Although, then, as I have said, the Lord Christ sent ahead a portion of his body in the saints who preceded him in the time of his birth, he himself is the head of the body, the Church (Col. 1:18). All of them adhered to that same body of which he is the head by believing in him whom they foretold.

They were not torn away by running ahead, but were rather joined to him by obedience. For although a hand can be sent ahead of the head, its connection remains beneath the head.

Therefore everything that was written beforehand was written for our instruction (Rom. 15:4), and they were our figures, and these things happened to them figuratively [Note: [Col. 0314] The printed editions have “these things happened to them,” omitting the word *in*, which is nevertheless found here in the manuscripts and in the Greek text of the Apostle]. They were written for us, upon whom the end of the ages has come (1 Cor. 10:11).

### CHAPTER IV

**7. The chief reason for Christ’s coming was to commend love. What is narrated from the Scriptures about Christ in catechizing must be referred to love.**

What greater reason is there for the Lord’s coming than that God might show and strongly commend his love toward us? For while we were still enemies, Christ died for us (Rom. 5:6–9).

This was because the end of the commandment and the fullness of the Law is love (1 Tim. 1:5; Rom. 13:10): so that we might love one another, and just as he laid down his life for us, so we too might lay down our lives for our brothers and sisters (1 John 3:16); and because God loved us first (ibid. 4:10) and did not spare his only Son but handed him over for us all (Rom. 8:32), if we were reluctant to love him, we should at least now not be reluctant to return his love [Note: [Col. 0314] Amerbach, Erasmus, and the manuscripts omit “now.”].

There is no greater invitation to love than to take the initiative by loving, and a spirit is exceedingly hard if, when it was unwilling to offer love, it is unwilling to return it.

If we observe this even in shameful and sordid loves, we see that those who wish to be loved in return do nothing else than reveal and show, by whatever proofs they can, how much they love. They strive to present a kind of image of justice, as though demanding from the minds they seek to entice that love be returned to them in some measure. They themselves burn more ardently when they already perceive that the minds they desire are being moved by the same fire.

If, then, a spirit that was sluggish is stirred when it realizes that it is loved, and one that was already burning is kindled more intensely when it learns that it is loved in return, it is clear that there is no greater cause by which love either begins or increases than when one who does not yet love learns that he is loved, or when one who loves first hopes that he can be loved in return, or already discovers that he is.

And if this is true even in disgraceful loves, how much more in friendship? For what else do we fear in offending a friend except that the friend may think that we do not love him or that we love him less than he loves us?

If he believes this, he will become colder in that love by which people enjoy mutual intimacy with one another. And if he is not so weak that this offense makes him grow cold toward all love, he remains in that love by which he loves not for enjoyment but for the friend’s welfare.

It is worthwhile to observe how, although superiors wish to be loved by their inferiors and take pleasure in their devoted service, and although the more they perceive this, the more they love them, nevertheless the inferior burns with how much greater love when he realizes that he is loved by the superior.

Love is more welcome where it does not burn with the dryness of need but flows forth from the abundance of beneficence [Note: [Col. 0315] The older books have “beneficence.”]. That love arises from misery; this one from mercy.

If, moreover, the inferior had despaired of being loved by the superior, he will be moved ineffably toward love if the superior has deigned of his own accord to show how much he loves one who would never have dared to promise himself so great a good.

What is higher than God, who judges, and what is more desperate than sinful humanity? The sinner had surrendered himself all the more to be guarded and subjected by proud powers, which cannot make him blessed, the more he had despaired that his care could be taken up by that power which does not wish to be exalted through wickedness but is exalted through goodness.

**8. Everything narrated about Christ should be referred to love.**

If, then, Christ came chiefly so that human beings might know how much God loves them, and so that, having come to know this, they might burn with love for the one by whom they were first loved and, at his command and by his example, love their neighbor—for by loving one who was not near but far away, he became a neighbor—and if all divine Scripture written beforehand was written to foretell the Lord’s coming, and whatever was afterward committed to writing and confirmed by divine authority narrates Christ and admonishes us to love, then it is clear that not only do the whole Law and the Prophets depend upon those two commandments of love of God and neighbor (Matt. 22:40), when these alone constituted the holy Scripture at the time the Lord said this, but so too does everything salutarily written afterward and committed to memory in the volumes of the divine Scriptures [Note: [Col. 0315] Amerbach, Erasmus, and many manuscripts have “followed” rather than “consecrated.” Two other manuscripts have “resulted.”].

Therefore, in the Old Testament there is the concealment of the New, and in the New Testament there is the manifestation of the Old. According to that concealment, carnal people who understand carnally were then and are now subjected by punitive fear. According to this manifestation, however, spiritual people—both then, when hidden things were opened to those who piously knocked, and now, when they do not proudly seek lest even what is open be closed—have been freed by the charity that has been given to them, understanding spiritually.

Since, therefore, nothing is more opposed to love than envy, and pride is the mother of envy, the same Lord Jesus Christ, God and human being, is both a sign of the divine love toward us and an example of human humility among us, so that our great swelling might be healed by an even greater medicine of the opposite kind.

Great is the misery of a proud human being, but greater still is the mercy of a humble God.

With this love, then, as the appointed end to which you refer everything you say, narrate whatever you narrate in such a way that the person to whom you speak may, by hearing, believe; by believing, hope; and by hoping, love.

### CHAPTER V

**9. The person approaching catechesis should be examined concerning the purpose for which he wishes to become a Christian.**

Even from the very severity of God, by which the hearts of mortals are shaken with salutary terror, love must be built up, so that the person who rejoices to be loved by the one whom he fears may dare to love him in return and may fear offending the love that God bears toward him, even if he could do so with impunity.

It very rarely happens—indeed, never—that someone comes wishing to become a Christian without having been struck by some fear of God. For if, in expectation of some advantage from people whom he does not think he could otherwise please, or in order to avoid some disadvantage from people whose offense or hostility he fears, he wishes to become a Christian, he wishes not so much to become one as to pretend.

For faith is not a gesture of the body that gives a greeting [Note: [Col. 0316] The printed editions of Erasmus and Louvain have “of saving.” Some manuscripts have “of salvation.” One has “of dancing.” But most manuscripts, and the better ones, together with Amerbach’s edition, have “of greeting,” that is, of one who signifies salvation or assent by a gesture.], but of a believing mind.

Yet the mercy of God is often present through the ministry of the catechist, so that a person, moved by the discourse, may now wish to become what he had decided to pretend to be. When he begins to wish this, we should regard him as having truly come.

It is hidden from us when he comes in spirit, though we already see him present in body. Nevertheless, we ought to deal with him in such a way that this will may arise in him, even if it is not yet there. For nothing is lost when it is there, since by such action on our part it is strengthened, although we do not know at what time or hour it began.

It is certainly useful, if possible, to be informed beforehand by those who know him what state his mind is in and what motives moved him to undertake the religion. If there is no one from whom we can learn this, he himself should be questioned, so that we may take the beginning of our discourse from his answer.

But if he has approached with a deceitful heart, desiring human advantages or fleeing human disadvantages, he will certainly lie. Even so, we must take our starting point from the very fact that he lies—not in order to refute his falsehood as though you were certain of it, but so that, if he says that he has come with a purpose which ought truly to be approved, whether he speaks truth or falsehood, we may approve and praise such a purpose as he claims to have brought him, and thereby make him glad to be what he wishes to appear to be.

If, however, he says something other than what ought to be in the mind of one who is to be instructed in the Christian faith, we should reprove him gently and mildly as an uninstructed and ignorant person, briefly and seriously demonstrating and praising the most truthful purpose of Christian teaching. In this way we neither occupy the time allotted to the future narration nor dare to impose that narration upon a mind not first prepared; rather, we make him wish for what, through error or pretense, he did not yet wish.

### CHAPTER VI
10. The beginning of the catechism, and the narrative from the history of the creation of the world down to the present time of the Church. If, perhaps, he answers that he was divinely admonished or frightened into becoming a Christian, he offers us a most welcome opening for beginning, namely, how great God’s care is for us. Certainly, his attention must be transferred from such miracles or dreams to the more solid path of the Scriptures and to more reliable oracles, so that he may understand how mercifully that admonition was granted to him before he clung to the Holy Scriptures. He must also be shown that the Lord Himself would not have admonished or compelled him to become a Christian and to be incorporated into the Church, nor instructed him by such signs or revelations, unless He had wished him to pursue more securely and safely the path already prepared in the Holy Scriptures, where he would not seek visible miracles but would become accustomed to hope for invisible things, and where he would be admonished not while asleep but while awake.

From this point the narrative should begin: from the fact that God made all things “very good” (Gen. 1), and it should be carried, as we have said, down to the present times of the Church. The causes and reasons of each of the events and deeds that we narrate should be explained, so that we relate them to that final purpose of love, from which the eye must not be turned away, whether in doing or in speaking.

For if good grammarians—those who are so called and regarded as good—try to refer to some useful purpose the fictitious tales of poets, invented for the pleasure of minds whose food is trifles [Note: [Col. 0317] Am. and most manuscripts read “for will” (*voluntatem*) instead of “for pleasure” (*voluptatem*).], although even that purpose is vain and greedy for worldly fattening, how much more careful ought we to be lest what we narrate as true, if arranged without an explanation of its causes, be believed either for empty sweetness or even from a destructive desire?

Yet we should not assert these causes in such a way that, abandoning the course of the narrative, our heart and tongue run off into the knots of a more difficult disputation. Rather, the very truth of the reasoning supplied [Note: [Col. 0317] So reads the old Corbie manuscript. Victorinus has “of the narrative supplied” (*adhibitae narrationis*). The editions of Am. and Er. read “the reason having been supplied” (*adhibita rationi*). Finally, Lov. has “of the reasoning supplied” (*adhibita rationis*).] should be like gold binding together a sequence of gems, without disturbing the line of the ornament by any excess.

## CHAPTER VII

### 11. The resurrection, judgment, and certain other matters to be conveyed after the narrative

When the narrative has been completed, the hope of the resurrection should be announced. According to the capacity and strength of the listener, and according to the limited time available, one should discuss the resurrection of the body against the empty mockery of unbelievers, and the goodness of the future final judgment toward the good, its severity toward the wicked, and its truth toward all. After recalling with abhorrence and horror the punishments of the ungodly, one should proclaim with longing the kingdom of the righteous and faithful, that heavenly city, and its joy.

Then human weakness must be instructed and encouraged against temptations and scandals, whether outside or within the Church itself: outside, against Gentiles, Jews, or heretics; within, against the chaff of the Lord’s threshing floor [Col. 0318]. This should not be done by arguing against each individual kind of perverse person and refuting all their erroneous opinions through proposed questions. Rather, within the short time available, it should be shown that these things were foretold, what benefit temptations provide for educating the faithful, and what remedy is found in the example of God’s patience, since He has determined to permit such things until the end.

When he is being instructed against those whose perverse crowds fill the churches bodily, the precepts of a Christian and honorable way of life should also be recalled briefly and appropriately. Otherwise he may be easily seduced by drunkards, the greedy, fraudsters, gamblers, adulterers, fornicators, lovers of spectacles, those who bind themselves to sacrilegious remedies, enchanters, astrologers, or diviners through any kind of vain and evil art, and by others of this sort; and he may suppose that such conduct will go unpunished because he sees many who are called Christians loving, practicing, defending, recommending, and persuading others to do these things. The divine Books must teach him what end has been appointed for those who persist in such a life, and how long they are to be tolerated within the Church, from which they will finally be separated.

He must also be told beforehand that, if he himself begins to be one, he will find in the Church many good Christians, true citizens of the heavenly Jerusalem. Finally, he must be earnestly warned not to place his hope in any human being. For it is not easy for one person to judge what another person is like; and even if it were easy, the examples of the righteous are not set before us so that we may be justified by them, but so that, by imitating them, we may know that we too are justified by the One who justified them.

From this will follow what must be especially commended: when the one who hears us—or rather, through us, hears God—begins to advance in conduct and knowledge and enters the way of Christ eagerly, he should not dare to attribute this either to us or to himself. Rather, he should love himself, us, and all other friends whom he loves in Him and for His sake—Him who loved him when he was an enemy, so that, by justifying him, He might make him a friend.

At this point, I do not think you need instruction on how, when your own time or that of those listening to you is limited, you should speak briefly, and when more time is available, more fully. Necessity itself teaches this without anyone’s advice.

## CHAPTER VIII

### 12. How educated people are to be catechized

This point certainly must not be omitted: if someone comes to you for cate instruction who has been cultivated in the liberal disciplines, has already decided to become a Christian, and has come for that purpose, it is exceedingly difficult that he should not know a great deal of our Scriptures and writings, having come already instructed merely to participate in the Sacraments. Such people ordinarily do not investigate everything carefully only when they become Christians, but beforehand; they also share and discuss the movements of their minds with those whom they can.

With such people, therefore, one should proceed briefly, not offensively inculcating what they already know, but touching upon it modestly [Note: [Col. 0318] Several manuscripts read “idly” (*otiose*)]. We should say that we believe they already know this and that, and in this way swiftly enumerate everything that must be impressed upon the uneducated and uninstructed. Thus, even if this educated person knows something, he will not hear it as though from a teacher; and if there is something he still does not know [Note: [Col. 0319] The editions read “and if he perhaps still does not know something.” “Perhaps” is absent from the manuscripts.], while we recall what we already believe he knows, he will learn it.

It is also by no means useless to ask him what moved him to wish to become a Christian. If you see that he has been persuaded by books [Note: [Col. 0319] The manuscripts read “if you see him persuaded by books” (*ut si libris eum persuasum*).], whether canonical books or those of useful interpreters, you should say something about them at the beginning, praising them according to the differing merits of canonical authority and the skillful diligence of their expositors [Note: [Col. 0319] Several manuscripts read “and for exposition” (*et ad exponendum*).]. Above all, commend in the canonical Scriptures the salutary humility of their astonishing profundity; and in the other writings, according to each author’s ability, commend a style of more resonant and, as it were, more polished eloquence, suited to minds that are prouder and therefore weaker [Note: [Col. 0319] Lov. reads “more ornate eloquence.”].

He should also be prompted to state which author he has read most, and to which books he has attached himself most familiarly—what persuaded him that he wished to join the Church. When he has said this, if those books are known to us, or if at least ecclesiastical reputation has informed us that they were written by some notable Catholic man, let us approve them gladly.

But if he has encountered the volumes of some heretic and, perhaps not knowing that the true faith rejects it, has retained it in his mind and thinks it Catholic, he must be carefully instructed, with the authority of the universal Church placed first, as well as that of other highly learned men who have flourished in its truth, both in their discussions and in their writings.

Even those Catholics who have departed this life and left some Christian writings to posterity have, in certain passages of their works, either because they were not understood or because, as human weakness dictates, they were less able to penetrate hidden matters with the sharpness of mind, and, led astray from the truth by resemblance to the truth, provided presumptuous and reckless people with an occasion for contriving and generating some heresy. This is not surprising, since even from the canonical Scriptures themselves—where everything has been spoken with perfect soundness—many have produced many destructive doctrines by defending with the fiercest stubbornness and arrogant obstinacy what they had perversely and wrongly believed, not merely by taking certain passages in a sense different from that intended by the writer or held by the truth itself. (For if that alone were the case, who would not readily forgive human weakness, prepared as it is to be corrected?)

All these matters should be treated in a modest exchange with someone who comes to join the company of the Christian people—not, as they say, an ignoramus, but polished and cultivated by the books of learned men. The authority of one who gives instruction should be assumed only as far as the humility that brought him can already be felt to accept it, so that he may beware of the errors of presumption.

The remaining matters, in accordance with the rules of salutary doctrine—whether those of faith, whatever must be narrated or discussed; those of morals; or those of temptations—should be surveyed in the manner I have described, with everything referred to that more exalted way.

## CHAPTER IX

### 13. How grammarians and rhetoricians are to be treated. The voice addressed to God is the disposition of the soul

There are also some who come from the most familiar schools of grammarians and rhetoricians. You would not dare to count them among the ignorant, nor among those most learned men whose minds have been exercised by investigations into great matters.

Therefore, when these people, who seem to excel other human beings in the art of speaking, come to become Christians, we should impart something more to them than to the uneducated. They must be carefully warned to learn, clothed in Christian humility, not to despise those whom they discover to avoid moral faults more than faults of speech; and they must not dare to compare an exercised tongue with a pure heart, though they had been accustomed to prefer the former [Note: [Col. 0320] The principal manuscripts read “an exercised tongue, and not compare it.”].

Above all, they must be taught how to listen to the divine Scriptures, lest solid eloquence seem mean to them because it is not inflated. Nor should they think that the sayings or deeds of human beings read in those books, wrapped and concealed in bodily coverings, are not to be unfolded and opened so that they may be understood, but are to be taken merely as the letters sound. They should learn by experience what benefit there is in the secrecy from which such passages are also called mysteries: how the hiding places of riddles sharpen the love of truth and shake off the sluggishness of boredom [Note: [Col. 0320] So read several manuscripts. The editions have “and break up the sluggishness.”]. This will happen when something that, lying openly before them, did not move them in the same way is brought forth through the unraveling of an allegory.

For such people it is especially useful to know that meanings are to be preferred to words in the same way that the soul is preferred to the body. Hence they should prefer to hear speeches that are truer rather than more eloquent, just as they should prefer to have wiser rather than more handsome friends.

They should also know that what reaches God’s ears is not the voice but the disposition of the soul. Thus they will not laugh if they happen to observe certain bishops or ministers of the Church invoking God with barbarisms and solecisms, or failing to understand the very words they pronounce and distinguishing them confusedly. This does not mean that such things should not be corrected, so that the people may say “Amen” to what they clearly understand; nevertheless, they should be piously tolerated by those who have learned that, just as one is blessed by sound in the marketplace, so one is blessed by intention in the Church.

Thus a piece of forensic eloquence may sometimes rightly be called good diction, but it can never be called a blessing. Concerning the Sacrament they are to receive, it is enough for the more perceptive to hear what that thing signifies. With the slower, however, one must use somewhat more words and comparisons, lest they despise what they see.

## CHAPTER X

### 14. On acquiring cheerfulness. Six causes that bring boredom to the catechist. Remedy for the first cause of boredom

Perhaps at this point you desire some example of a speech, so that by the work itself I may show you how these recommendations are to be carried out. I shall indeed do so, as far as I can with the Lord’s help; but first I must speak about acquiring that cheerfulness, as I promised.

I have now fulfilled my promise, insofar as seemed sufficient, concerning the precepts for explaining a discourse when catechizing someone who comes in order to become a Christian. It would be inappropriate for me also to do in this book what I prescribe should be done. If I did so, it would serve as an addition; but how could an addition be poured over by me before I had filled the measure of what is owed?

For I have heard you complain chiefly that your speech seemed to you cheap and insignificant when you were instructing someone in the Christian name. I know that this arises not so much from a lack of the matters to be discussed—for I know you are adequately prepared and equipped—nor from poverty of expression itself, but from weariness of spirit. This may arise from the reason I mentioned: that we are more delighted and occupied by what we see in silence with the mind, and do not wish to be called away from it to the very different clamor of words.

Or it may arise because, even when the discourse is pleasant, we prefer to hear or read what has been expressed better, and what is produced without our care and anxiety, rather than suddenly fit words to another person’s understanding, with an uncertain outcome—whether the words will occur appropriately, or whether they will be received usefully.

It may also arise because what is conveyed to the uneducated is so familiar to us, and no longer necessary for our own advancement, that we are annoyed at returning to it so often; nor does a somewhat mature mind now move with any pleasure among such familiar and almost childish matters.

The listener also causes boredom in the speaker—whether because he is not moved in feeling, or because he indicates by no movement of his body that he understands or approves what is being said [Note: [Col. 0321] The words in brackets are absent from most manuscripts and from Am. and Er.]. This is not because it is proper for us to crave human praise, but because what we administer belongs to God. The more we love those to whom we speak, the more we desire that what is offered for their salvation should please them. When this does not happen, we become sad, and in the very course of speaking we grow weak and are broken, as though we were wasting our labor in vain.

Sometimes, too, we are called away from something we desire to do, whose performance either delighted us or seemed more necessary to us, and we are compelled to catechize someone either by the command of one whom we do not wish to offend or by the unavoidable insistence of others. We approach an undertaking that requires great tranquility already disturbed, grieving that we are allowed neither to maintain the order of our activities as we wish nor to be sufficient for everything. Thus the speech proceeding from sadness is less agreeable, because it flows less abundantly from the dryness of grief.

At other times sorrow has occupied the heart because of some scandal [Note: [Col. 0321] The editions read “occupies”; the manuscripts read “has occupied.”], and then someone says to us, “Come, speak to this man; he wishes to become a Christian.” Those who do not know what burns within us say this [Note: [Col. 0321] Only the Lov. edition reads “it is unknown” (*nescitur*).]. If we ought not to disclose our feelings to them, we accept what they want with less goodwill; and certainly that speech will be languid and unpleasant when it passes through the channel of a heart that is fevered and smoking [Note: [Col. 0321] Several manuscripts read “we accept unwillingly what they want.”].

So, whenever any one of these causes clouds the serenity of our mind, remedies must be sought according to God’s will, by which that contraction may be relaxed, so that in the fervor of the spirit we may exult and rejoice in the tranquility of a good work. “God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Cor. 9:7).

### 15.

If the cause of our sadness is that the listener does not grasp our understanding, so that we are forced, as it were, to descend from its summit and linger in the slowness of syllables far beneath it, taking care to make what the mind absorbs in a swift draught proceed from the mouth of flesh through long and perplexed windings—and because it emerges so differently we are tired of speaking and wish to remain silent—let us consider what has been granted to us by Him who showed us an example, so that we might follow His footsteps (1 Pet. 2:21).

However much our articulated voice differs from the vitality of our understanding, the mortality of the flesh differs still more greatly from the equality of God. Yet, while He was in that same form, “He emptied Himself, taking the form of a servant,” and so forth, “even to the death of the cross” (Phil. 2:6–8) [Note: [Col. 0322] The words “and so forth, even to the death of the cross” are a scribe’s omission, as often happens, of the intervening words from the passage cited.]. Why did He do this, except because “He became weak to the weak, in order to win the weak” (1 Cor. 9:22)?

Hear His imitator saying elsewhere: “Whether we are beside ourselves, it is for God; or whether we are of sound mind, it is for you. For the love of Christ constrains us, judging this: that one died for all” (2 Cor. 5:13–14). How would he have been ready to be spent for their souls (ibid. 12:15), if he had been reluctant to stoop to their ears?

For this reason He became a little one in our midst, “like a nurse cherishing her own children” (1 Thess. 2:7). Does it delight anyone, unless love invites him, to mutter shortened and mutilated words? Yet people desire to have infants to whom they may offer such things; and it is sweeter for a mother to spit small chewed morsels into her little son’s mouth than to chew and swallow larger pieces herself.

Therefore let the thought of that hen also not depart from your heart: with languishing feathers she covers her tender offspring and calls her chirping chicks with a broken voice. When the proud flee from her gentle wings, they become prey for birds (Matt. 23:37).

If understanding delights us in the most sincere inner chambers, it is also delightful to understand that love, the more dutifully it descends to the lowest places, the more robustly it returns to the innermost places through a good conscience, seeking nothing from those to whom it has descended except their eternal salvation [Note: [Col. 0322] So read the manuscripts. The editions have “seeking nothing.”].

## CHAPTER XI

### 16. Remedy for the second cause of boredom

If we prefer to read or hear what has already been prepared and expressed better, and for that reason dislike fitting together what we say with an uncertain outcome, then, provided the mind does not depart from the truth of the matters themselves, it is easy to accept that, if something in our words has offended the listener, he may learn from the very occasion how little it matters if what was spoken in order that the matter might be understood sounded less complete or less precise.

If the attention of our human weakness has strayed even from the truth of the matters themselves—which is difficult in catechizing the uneducated, where the well-trodden path must be followed—nevertheless, should this perhaps occur and the listener be offended by it, we should regard it as having happened for no other reason than that God wished to test whether we would correct ourselves with a peaceful mind, lest we rush into a greater error by defending our own error.

If no one tells us, and the matter remains entirely unknown both to us and to those who heard us, there is no grief, provided it does not happen again. Usually, however, when recalling what we have said, we ourselves criticize something, without knowing how it was received when spoken. We grieve all the more when love burns within us, if something false was gladly accepted.

Therefore, when an opportunity is found, just as we criticize ourselves in silence, so we must take care that those who have slipped into some falsehood—not through God’s words but plainly through ours—are gradually corrected.

But if some people, blinded by insane envy, rejoice that we have erred—whisperers, slanderers, hateful to God (Rom. 1:30)—let them provide us with an occasion to exercise patience with mercy, since God’s patience also leads them to repentance. For what is more detestable, and what stores up greater wrath for itself on the day of wrath and the revelation of God’s righteous judgment (ibid. 2:4–5), than to rejoice in another’s evil by an evil resemblance to and imitation of the devil? [Note: [Col. 0323] Thus in the manuscripts. The editions have “mere resemblance.”]

Sometimes, even when everything is said correctly and truthfully, something either not understood or harsh because of its novelty, contrary to the listener’s opinion and former habit of error, offends and disturbs him. If this becomes apparent and he shows himself willing to be healed, he should be healed without delay by an abundance of authoritative texts and arguments. If the offense is silent and hidden, God’s medicine may help.

But if he recoils and refuses to be healed [Note: [Col. 0323] The editions read “if he should recoil”; the better manuscripts read “if he recoils.”], let us take comfort from that example of the Lord who, when people were offended by His word and, finding it hard, withdrew, said even to those who remained, “Do you also wish to go away?” (John 6:68).

It must be held firmly and immovably in the heart that, when the appointed times have run their course, captive Jerusalem will be freed from the Babylon of this age, and that none belonging to it will perish; for whoever perishes did not belong to it. “The firm foundation of God stands, bearing this seal: ‘The Lord knows those who are His,’ and, ‘Let everyone who names the name of the Lord depart from iniquity’” (2 Tim. 2:19).

Thinking of these things and invoking the Lord in our hearts, we shall fear less the uncertain outcome of our speech because of the uncertain responses of our listeners. Even the endurance of difficulties for a merciful work will delight us, provided we do not seek our own glory in it.

For the work is truly good when the intention of the one acting is launched forth from love and, as though returning to its proper place, comes to rest again in love.

The reading that delights us, or some hearing of more excellent eloquence, which we wish to place above our own speech when we reproduce it and therefore speak with reluctance or boredom, will make us more cheerful and prove more pleasant after the labor. We shall also pray with greater confidence that God speak to us as we wish, if we gladly accept that He speak through us as we are able. Thus “all things work together for good for those who love God” (Rom. 8:28).

## CHAPTER XII

### 17. Remedy for the third cause of boredom

If we are bored by often repeating familiar things suited to little ones, let us accommodate ourselves to them through brotherly, fatherly, and motherly love; and when their hearts are joined to ours, what is new to them will also seem new to us.

The feeling of one who sympathizes has such power that, when they are affected by us as we speak and we are affected by them as they learn, we dwell in one another. Thus they, in a way, speak within us what they hear, and we, in a way, learn in them what we teach.

Does this not commonly happen when we show people who have never seen them before some spacious and beautiful places, whether in cities or in the countryside, which we had already passed by many times without any pleasure? Our own delight is renewed in their delight at the novelty. This is especially so in proportion to their friendliness, because through the bond of love, to the extent that we are in them, things that were old become new to us.

But if we have made some progress in contemplating things, we do not merely wish those whom we love to rejoice and marvel when they look upon the works of human hands. We wish to raise them to the art or design of the maker [Note: [Col. 0324] The editions read “fortress” (*arcem*); the manuscripts more appropriately read “art” (*artem*),] and from there to rise to wonder and praise of God, the Creator of all things. This is the most fruitful end of love.

How much more, then, ought we to rejoice when people come to learn God Himself, for whose sake all that is to be learned must be learned, and to be renewed by their novelty, so that if our accustomed preaching is colder, their unaccustomed hearing may make it burn more warmly? It also contributes to acquiring joy that we think and consider from what death of error a person passes into the life of faith.

If we pass with benevolent cheerfulness through very familiar streets when we perhaps show the way to someone who had struggled in error, how much more eagerly and joyfully ought we to travel through the paths of salutary doctrine, even through those matters that we do not need to retrace for our own sake, when we lead a pitiable soul, wearied by the paths of worldly error, along the roads of peace, at the command of Him who granted that soul to us [Note: [Col. 0324] The Corbie manuscript reads “that” (*ea*) rather than “whom” (*eam*).]?

## CHAPTER XIII

### 18. Remedy for the fourth cause of boredom. How a listener wearied by listening or standing is to be refreshed. The practice of hearing the word of God while seated, accepted in certain churches

It is indeed very difficult to continue speaking until the appointed end when we do not see the listener moved. Perhaps he does not dare to indicate his approval by voice or by some movement of the body, constrained by religious fear; perhaps human modesty restrains him; perhaps he does not understand what is said or despises it. Since, when we cannot see his mind, we are uncertain, everything must be attempted in speech that may help to awaken him and, as it were, draw him out of hiding.

Excessive fear, which prevents him from declaring his judgment, must be driven away by gentle encouragement. His modesty must be moderated by suggesting a fraternal relationship. We should ask whether he understands and give him confidence to state freely anything that seems to him open to objection.

We should ask whether he has heard these things before and whether, perhaps, they fail to move him because they are familiar and widespread. According to his response, we should either speak more plainly and clearly, refute the contrary opinion, or avoid explaining at length what is already familiar to him. Instead, we should select some of the mystical sayings in the holy Books, especially in the narrative itself, so that our speech may become sweet by opening and revealing them.

If he is exceedingly slow and unresponsive and averse to all such sweetness, he must be endured mercifully. After briefly passing through the remaining matters, those that are most necessary—concerning the unity of the Catholic Church [Note: [Col. 0325] Lov. reads “of the Catholic faith”; the other editions and most manuscripts omit “faith,” which is to be understood as “Church.”], temptations, and Christian conduct in view of the future judgment—must be impressed upon him fearfully. More should be said to God on his behalf than said about God to him.

### 19.

It often also happens that someone who initially listened willingly, fatigued either by listening or by standing, no longer praises but opens his lips in a yawn and unwillingly shows that he wishes to leave. When we perceive this, we should either renew his attention by saying something seasoned with honest cheerfulness and suited to the matter at hand, or something very astonishing and marvelous, or even something sorrowful and mournful. We should speak especially about him, so that, touched by personal concern, he may awaken; yet this must not offend his modesty by any harshness, but should win him through familiarity.

Alternatively, we should come to his aid by offering him a seat [Note: [Col. 0325] Lov. adds “he should endeavor.” The phrase “it is necessary” is to be understood.]. Indeed, whenever it can decently be done, it is unquestionably better that he listen while seated from the beginning. It is much more advisable in certain churches overseas not only for the bishops to speak to the people while seated, but also for seats to be provided for the people themselves, lest someone weaker, wearied by standing, be turned away from a most salutary attentiveness or even forced to leave.

There is nevertheless a great difference between someone from a large crowd withdrawing to restore his strength after already being bound by participation in the Sacraments, and someone who is to be instructed in the first Sacraments leaving—something he is often unavoidably compelled to do, lest, overcome by greater weakness within, he also fall. He is too ashamed to say why he is leaving, and his weakness does not allow him to stand.

I speak from experience. A certain countryman did this while I was catechizing him, and I learned that one must take great precautions against it. For who could tolerate our arrogance if we do not allow our brothers—or, what must be cared for with even greater concern, those who are to become our brothers—to sit in our presence, when the Lord Himself, whom angels attend, was heard by a woman sitting (Luke 10:39)?

Certainly, if the speech will be brief or the place is unsuitable for sitting, they may listen standing. But this is appropriate when many are listening and they are not then to be initiated [Note: [Col. 0325] Only the Lov. edition has “are” (*sunt*) in place of “then” (*tunc*)]. For when one, two, or a few have come for the purpose of becoming Christians, it is dangerous to speak to them while they stand.

Nevertheless, if we have already begun in this way, then, as soon as we notice the listener’s weariness, a seat should be offered—or rather, he should be firmly urged to sit—and something should be said to renew him, so that any concern that may have suddenly invaded him and begun to distract him may also flee from his mind.

Since we do not know the causes of his now silently refusing to listen, something should be said to the seated listener against the intrusive thoughts of worldly affairs, either in a cheerful or, as I said, a sorrowful manner. If such thoughts are in fact occupying his mind, they will yield as though accused by name. If they are not, and he is merely tired from listening, then, since we do not know the truth, we speak in the manner I described about them as though they were the cause; his attention is renewed by something unexpected and extraordinary.

But this should be brief, especially because it is inserted out of sequence, lest the remedy itself increase the sickness of boredom that we are trying to relieve. The remaining matters should be hastened, and an approaching end should be promised and delivered.

## CHAPTER XIV

### 20. Remedy for the fifth cause of boredom. Remedy for the sixth cause of boredom. Again, concerning the sixth cause

If the omission of another activity, over which you had already been anxiously suspended as though it were more necessary, has broken your spirit, and for that reason you catechize sadly and without pleasure, you must consider—apart from the fact that we know we must act mercifully in everything we do with human beings and from the duty of the most sincere love—that it is uncertain what we are doing more usefully and what it is more appropriate either to interrupt or to omit altogether.

For we do not know what the merits are before God of the people for whom we are acting; and what is expedient for them at a particular time we suspect rather than comprehend, on no conjecture, or only a very slight or uncertain one. Therefore we should arrange the activities to be undertaken according to our capacity. If we are able to complete them in the order we have determined, let us not rejoice because the order is ours, but because it has pleased God that they be carried out in that way.

If some necessity arises that disturbs our order, let us bend easily so that we are not broken, so that the One whom God has placed before our order may Himself be our order [Note: [Col. 0326] “Our order” is to be understood.]. For it is more equitable that we follow His will than that He follow ours.

The order of activities that we wish to maintain according to our own judgment is indeed commendable when more important things come first.
