Why, then, do we grieve that human beings are preceded by the Lord God, who is so much more important, so that by loving our own order we desire to be disorderly?

No one orders what he should do better than the person who is more ready not to do what divine power forbids than eager to do what human thought has planned. “There are many thoughts in a man’s heart, but the counsel of the Lord remains forever” (Prov. 19:21).

### 21.

If, however, the mind has been disturbed by some scandal and cannot produce a serene and pleasant discourse, there ought to be such love for those for whom Christ died, wishing to redeem them by the price of His blood from the death of worldly errors, that the very fact reported to us in our sadness—that someone is present who desires to become a Christian—should serve to console us and dissolve our sorrow, just as the joy of profit usually eases the pain of loss.

A scandal does not make us sad on account of someone unless we either believe or see that someone is perishing, or that through someone a weak person is perishing. Let the person who has come to be initiated, while we hope that he can advance, wipe away the pain of the one who is failing.

Even if the fear is suggested that he may become “a proselyte son of Gehenna” (Matt. 23:15), while many such people are before our eyes and from them arise the scandals by which we burn, this should not serve to hold us back, but rather to rouse and sharpen us. We should warn the one whom we are instructing to avoid imitating those who are Christians not in the truth itself but only in name. He must not be disturbed by their multitude into wanting to follow them, nor into refusing to follow Christ because of them; nor should he refuse to be in the Church of God where they are, or wish to be there in the kind of condition in which they are.

Somehow, in such admonitions, the speech becomes more ardent, fed by the pain presently before us. Thus we are not merely less sluggish; we speak with greater intensity and force precisely what we would have said more coldly and slowly in safer circumstances. Let us rejoice that an opportunity has been given us in which the movement of our mind does not pass without bearing fruit [Note: [Col. 0327] The editions read “movement” (*motu*), a word omitted by the manuscripts; several other manuscripts have “admonitions” (*monitis*) in its place. Shortly afterward, instead of *subministrat*—or *sumministrat*, as is commonly written in ancient manuscripts—the editions read *suum ministrat*.].

22. But if distress over some error or sin of ours has seized us, let us remember not only that “a contrite spirit is a sacrifice to God” (Ps. 50:19), but also this: “As water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sin” (Sir. 3:33); and, “For I desire mercy rather than sacrifice” (Hos. 6:6). [Note: The printed editions read, “I desire mercy more than sacrifice.” The manuscripts consistently omit “more.”] Therefore, just as, if we were endangered by fire, we would certainly run for water by which it could be extinguished, and would be grateful if someone offered us some from nearby, so, if a flame of sin has risen from our hay, [Note: Erasmus, Lyons, Venice, and Louvain read *surrexerit*, “has risen.” Manuscript M reads *surrexit*, “rose.”] and we are consequently troubled, when an opportunity for a merciful work is given, let us rejoice as though a spring had been offered to us, so that what had flared up may be quenched from it.

Unless, perhaps, we are so foolish as to think that we should run more eagerly with bread to fill the stomach of someone who is hungry than with the word of God, by which we may instruct the mind of the one who eats this. [Note: The manuscripts read “the mind of the one who eats this”; the printed editions read “the mind of the one who is learning.”] Furthermore, if doing this were merely beneficial, while failing to do it did no harm, we would unhappily reject an offered remedy when our salvation—not now our neighbor’s, but our own—is in danger. But since the Lord’s words ring out so threateningly, “Wicked and lazy servant, you ought to have given my money to the money-changers” (Matt. 25:26–27), what madness is it that, because our sin troubles us, we should therefore wish to sin again by not giving the Lord’s money to one who wants it and asks for it?

When the darkness of our weariness has been driven away by these and similar thoughts and reflections, our purpose is made ready for catechizing, so that what flows freely and cheerfully from the abundance of charity may be received with pleasure. For it is not so much I who say this to you as charity itself, which “has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. 5:5). [Note: Almost only the printed editions read *dictat*, “dictates.”]

## CHAPTER XV

### 23. Speech must be adapted to the diversity of persons

But perhaps you now demand what, before I promised it, I ought not to have promised: that I should not be reluctant to explain some example of a discourse, as though I were catechizing someone, and set it before you for your consideration. Before I do so, I want you to consider that the intention of a person dictating is one thing when a future reader is in view, and the intention of someone speaking is another when an actual listener is attending. Even in this respect, the intention of someone giving private admonition, when no one else who might judge us is present, is one thing; that of someone teaching publicly, when an audience of people with differing opinions surrounds him, is another.

Within this latter kind, the intention is one thing when one person is being taught while the others listen as judges or witnesses to what they already know; another when everyone is waiting to hear what we have to say to them collectively. And here again it is one thing when people sit together almost privately, so that conversation may be exchanged; another when a silent crowd, suspended in expectation, watches one person from a raised place as he is about to speak.

It also makes a great difference, when we speak in this way, whether few or many are present; whether they are educated or uneducated, or a mixture of both; whether they are townspeople or country people, or both together; whether the crowd is composed of every kind of person.

For it is impossible that these circumstances should not affect the speaker in different ways, and that the speech delivered should not bear something like the face of the speaker’s disposition, and should not affect the listeners differently according to that same variety—since the listeners themselves also affect one another differently by their presence.

But since we are now dealing with the instruction of the uneducated, I call you as a witness concerning myself: I am moved in one way and in another when I see before me, ready to be catechized, an educated person, an inept person, a citizen, a foreigner, a rich person, a poor person, a private individual, a person of rank, someone holding a position of authority, a person of this or that nation, of this or that age or sex, coming from this or that sect, or from this or that popular error. According to the diversity of my own reaction, the speech itself proceeds, advances, and comes to an end.

And although the same charity is owed to all, the same medicine is not to be applied to all. That same charity gives birth to some, grows weak with others; it seeks to heal some so that they may be built up, while it fears offending others; it bends down toward some and raises itself up toward others; it is gentle toward some and severe toward others—an enemy to no one, a mother to all.

Someone who has not experienced what I am saying through this same charity sees that we take pleasure when some ability granted to us becomes commendably known in the mouths of the multitude, and therefore thinks us blessed. But may God, before whose sight “the groaning of the prisoners comes” (Ps. 79:11), look upon our humility and our labor, and forgive all our sins (Ps. 25:18).

Therefore, if something in us pleased you so that you sought to hear from us some guidance for your own speech, you would learn better by seeing and hearing us while we are doing these things than by reading us while we dictate them.

## CHAPTER XVI

### 24. A model of the catechist’s discourse

The beginning is drawn from the praiseworthy intention of undertaking the Christian religion because of the rest to come. Rest is not to be sought in restless things; nor in riches or honors. Those who seek rest in bodily pleasures and spectacles.

Nevertheless, let us suppose that someone has come to us who wishes to become a Christian. He is indeed from the class of the uneducated, though not a country person but a townsman—people of the sort whom you must often encounter at Carthage. Suppose that, when asked whether he wishes to become a Christian for some advantage in the present life or for the rest hoped for after this life, he has answered that it is for the future rest. We might instruct such a person with an address something like this:

“Thanks be to God, brother. I greatly congratulate you and rejoice over you, because amid the many and dangerous storms of this age you have thought about some true and certain security. In this life too, people seek rest and security through great labors, but they do not find them because of their perverse desires.

“For they wish to rest in things that are restless and impermanent. And because these things are taken away and pass with time, they are driven by fears and sorrows and are not permitted to be at rest.

“If a person wishes to rest in riches, he becomes more proud rather than more secure. Do we not see how many have suddenly lost them, and how many have perished because of them—either while desiring to possess them, or when, after they themselves have been overwhelmed by greedier people, those riches are taken away from them? [Note: Most manuscripts read, “or so that, when they had been oppressed by the more greedy, they might be taken away.”] Even if riches remained with a person throughout his whole life and did not abandon their lover, he would abandon them by his own death.

“For how long is a human life, even if a person grows old? Or, when people wish for old age, what else are they wishing for except a long illness?

“So too, what are the honors of this age except conceit, emptiness, [Note: Most manuscripts read, “conceit and emptiness.” The printed editions omit “and emptiness”; some manuscripts instead read “and vanity.”] and the danger of ruin? For holy Scripture says: ‘All flesh is grass, and human glory is like the flower of grass. The grass withers, the flower falls; but the word of the Lord remains forever’ (Isa. 40:6–8).

“Therefore, whoever desires true rest and true happiness must remove his hope from mortal and passing things and place it in the word of the Lord. Clinging to what remains forever, he too will remain with it forever.

### 25. Rest is not found in taverns, sexual immorality, theaters, or spectacles

“There are also people who neither seek to become rich nor strive to attain the empty display of honors. Instead, they want to rejoice and rest in taverns and sexual immorality, and in theaters and spectacles of frivolity that are freely available in great cities.

“But even these people either consume their poverty through extravagance and then advance from destitution to theft and burglary, sometimes even to robbery, and are suddenly filled with many great fears; those who shortly before were singing in a tavern now dream of the laments of prison.

“By devotion to spectacles they become like demons, inciting people with their shouting to kill one another, and making contentious contests for themselves out of people who have not harmed one another, while they desire to please a mad crowd. If they notice that the contestants are in agreement, they then hate and persecute them, shouting that they are colluders and ought to be beaten with clubs, and forcing even a judge who is supposed to punish wrongdoing to commit this injustice.

“But if they learn that the contestants are displaying dreadful hostility toward one another—whether they are those called *sintae*, [Note: Louvain reads, “whether they are athletes who are called *sintae*.” Most manuscripts, including the better ones, read *sintae qui appellantur*. The word may have been a common African term at that time. The Corbeiensis manuscript writes *sinthae*. Some manuscripts and Am. read *sint aequi appellantur*. Erasmus reads *sint qui appellantur*.] or performers and *thymelici*, or charioteers, or hunters—those wretched people whom human beings force into combat and struggle not only against other human beings but also against beasts—the more fiercely they perceive them raging against each other, the more they love and enjoy it. They applaud the contestants who have been provoked, and by their applause provoke them, so that the spectators themselves, maddened against one another on each other’s behalf, rage more than those whose madness they madly provoke, desiring to watch by means of their own madness.

“How, then, can a mind preserve the health of peace when it feeds on discord and contests? For the kind of food one takes determines the kind of health one has.

“Finally, although insane joys are not joys, whatever they are, and however much one may delight in the ostentation of riches, the swelling of honors, the maw of taverns, the wars of the theaters, [Note: Am., Erasmus, and most manuscripts read “the wars of the theaters.” Louvain reads “theatrical wars.”] the uncleanness of sexual immorality, and the itching of the baths, one little fever takes all these things away and, while people are still alive, removes their entire false happiness. An empty and wounded conscience remains, destined to experience God as judge, though it refused to have him as guardian; and destined to find a harsh Lord, though it scorned to seek and love him as a gentle father.

“But because you seek the true rest that is promised to Christians after this life, even here you will taste it as sweet and pleasant amid the bitterest troubles of this life, if you love the commands of the one who promised it. For you will quickly sense that the fruits of righteousness are sweeter than those of wickedness, and that a person rejoices more truly and pleasantly in a good conscience amid troubles than in a bad conscience amid pleasures.

“For you have not come to be joined to the Church of God in order to seek from it some temporal advantage.”

## CHAPTER XVII

### 26. Those who wish to be Christians for temporal advantage are reproved

A true Christian is one who professes the religion for the sake of future rest. The discourse turns to an account of the things that must be believed. Why the Son of God became human.

There are people who wish to be Christians so that they may win the favor of those from whom they expect temporal advantages, or because they do not wish to offend those whom they fear. But such people are rejected. If the Church bears with them for a time, as a threshing floor bears straw until the time of winnowing, then, if they do not correct themselves and begin to be Christians for the sake of future and eternal rest, they will be separated at the end.

Let them not flatter themselves that they can be on the threshing floor with God’s grain. They will not be with it in the granary, but are destined for the fire they deserve. [Note: Louvain reads *destinabuntur*, “will be destined.” Am., Erasmus, and the manuscripts have the present tense, *destinantur*, “are destined.”] (Matt. 3:12).

There are also others who have a better hope, but are nevertheless in no less danger. They already fear God, do not mock the Christian name, and do not enter the Church of God with a deceitful heart. Yet in this life they expect happiness, wishing to be more prosperous in earthly matters than those who do not worship God. Therefore, when they see certain wicked and impious people flourishing and excelling in the prosperity of this age, while they themselves either have less of such prosperity or lose it, they are troubled as though they worshiped God without reason, and they easily fall away from the faith. [Note: Am., Erasmus, and three manuscripts read *saeculari*, “worldly,” rather than *saeculi*, “of the age.”]

### 27. The true Christian seeks eternal blessedness and everlasting rest

But whoever wishes to become a Christian for the sake of eternal blessedness and everlasting rest, which is promised to the saints after this life, so that he may not go into everlasting fire with the devil but enter the eternal kingdom with Christ (Matt. 25:34, 41, 46)—he is truly a Christian. He is cautious in every temptation, so that he is not corrupted by prosperity or broken by adversity; in an abundance of earthly goods he is moderate and self-controlled, and in tribulations strong and patient.

As he advances, he will also reach such a disposition that he loves God more than he fears hell. Thus, even if God were to say to him, “Enjoy everlasting bodily pleasures and sin as much as you can; you will neither die nor be sent to hell, but only will not be with me,” he would shudder and not sin at all—not now to avoid falling into what he feared, but lest he offend the one whom he loves in this way.

In him alone is the rest “which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart, which God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Cor. 2:9).

### 28. The rest signified by the six days of creation

Scripture speaks of this rest and does not remain silent about the fact that, from the beginning of the world, after God made heaven and earth and everything in them, he worked for six days and rested on the seventh day (Gen. 1; 2:1–3).

For the Almighty could have made everything in a single moment of time. He had not labored so as to need rest, since “he spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created” (Ps. 148:5). Rather, he did this to signify that, after six ages of this world, he would rest in his saints in the seventh age, as on the seventh day. For they will rest in him after all the good works in which they served him—works that he himself performs in them, he who calls, commands, forgives past sins, and justifies the one who was previously impious.

Just as, when they work well by his gift, he is rightly said to work, so, when they rest in him, he is rightly said to rest. For, so far as he himself is concerned, he does not seek a pause, since he experiences no labor.

He made everything through his Word. His Word is Christ himself, in whom the angels and all the most pure heavenly spirits rest in holy silence.

But the human being, having fallen through sin, lost the rest that he had in God’s divinity, and receives it in God’s humanity. Therefore, at the appropriate time, when he himself knew it ought to happen, he became human and was born of a woman.

He could not be defiled by flesh; rather, he was to cleanse flesh. The ancient saints recognized through the revelation of the Spirit that he would come, and they prophesied him. Thus they were saved by believing that he would come, just as we are saved by believing that he has come.

We were to love God, who loved us so much that he sent his only Son, clothed in the humility [Note: Am. and Erasmus read “the humanity” rather than “the humility.”] of our mortality, to die at the hands of sinners and for sinners. From the very beginning of the ages, the depth of this mystery has never ceased to be prefigured and foretold.

## CHAPTER XVIII

### 29. What must be believed about the creation of humanity and other things

Humanity was placed in paradise. Why was one who was foreknown to sin created? The fall of humanity and the angel harmed God nothing.

For God is almighty, good, just, and merciful. He made all things good, whether great or small, whether highest or lowest; whether visible, such as heaven, earth, and sea, and in heaven the sun, moon, and other stars, and on earth and in the sea trees, shrubs, and animals of every kind, and all bodies, heavenly or earthly; or invisible, such as the spirits by which bodies are animated and given life.

He also made the human being in his own image, so that, just as God by his omnipotence rules over all creation, so the human being, through understanding—by which he also knows and worships his Creator—might rule over all earthly animals.

He also made woman as a helper for him—not for carnal desire, since at that time they did not yet have corruptible bodies, before mortality invaded them as the punishment for sin, but so that the man might also have glory from the woman when he led her toward God and offered himself to her as an example in holiness and devotion, just as he himself would be the glory of God by following his wisdom. [Note: Erasmus reads “dominion.” Other printed editions read “the Lord.”]

### 30. Humanity’s placement in paradise and fall

Accordingly, he placed them in a certain place of perpetual blessedness, which Scripture calls paradise. He gave them a commandment: if they did not transgress it, they would remain forever in that blessed immortality; but if they transgressed it, they would pay the penalties of mortality.

God knew beforehand that they would transgress. Yet, because he is the creator and maker of every good thing, he made them all the more when he also made the beasts, so that he might fill the earth with earthly goods. Certainly, even a sinful human being is better than a beast.

He gave a commandment that they would not keep, so that they might be without excuse when he began to punish them. Whatever a human being does, he finds God praiseworthy in his actions: if he acts rightly, he finds God praiseworthy through the justice of rewards; if he sins, he finds God praiseworthy through the justice of punishments; if, after confessing his sins, he returns to right living, he finds God praiseworthy through the mercy of forgiveness.

Why, then, would God not make the human being, even though he foreknew that he would sin, since he would crown him when standing, order him when fallen, and help him when rising—himself always and everywhere glorious in goodness, justice, and clemency?

This was especially so because he also foreknew that from the offspring of his mortality there would arise saints who would not seek glory for themselves but would give glory to their Creator; and, by worshiping him, would be freed from every corruption and deserve to live forever and happily with the holy angels.

For the one who gave human beings free will, so that they might worship God not under slavish compulsion but by free choice, gave it also to the angels. Therefore the angel who, together with the other spirits who served as his attendants, abandoned God’s obedience through pride and became the devil harmed God nothing, but himself.

For God knows how to order souls that abandon him [Note: *Retractationes* II.14] and adorn the lower regions of his creation with their just misery, according to laws of a wondrous administration that are entirely fitting and appropriate. [Note: Only the Louvain edition reads “to order.”]

Thus neither did the devil harm God in anything, whether he himself fell or seduced the human being into death; nor did the human being diminish in any respect the truth, power, or blessedness [Note: Most manuscripts omit “or blessedness.”] of his Creator, since he consented by his own will to his wife, who had been seduced by the devil, in doing what God had forbidden.

By the most just laws of God they were all condemned: God was glorified by the equity of his vengeance, while they were made shameful by the disgrace of their punishment (Gen. 2–3). Thus the human being, turned away from his Creator and overcome by the devil, was subjected to him; and the devil was set before the human being to be overcome when the human being turned back to his Creator.

Thus all who consent to the devil until the end will go with him into eternal punishments; but all who humble themselves before God and, through his grace, overcome the devil will deserve eternal rewards.

## CHAPTER XIX

### 31. The good and the wicked in the Church will be separated at the end

Two cities exist from the beginning of the human race. The flood and the ark as a sacrament. Abraham and the people of Israel. Their words and deeds were prophecy.

Nor should this trouble us: many consent to the devil, while few follow God. For grain too has a much smaller number in comparison with the chaff.

But just as a farmer knows what to do with a huge heap of chaff, so the multitude of sinners is nothing to God, who knows what to do with them, so that the administration of his kingdom is disturbed and dishonored in no respect.

Nor should the devil be thought to have won because he drew many along with himself, though he might be overcome along with them by the few.

Therefore two cities, one of the wicked and the other of the saints, are carried forward from the beginning of the human race to the end of the age. Now they are mingled in body but separated in will; on the day of judgment they will also be separated in body.

All human beings who love pride and temporal domination with vain conceit and the pomp of arrogance, and all spirits who love such things and seek their own glory through the subjection of human beings, are bound together in one society. Even if they often fight against one another over these things, they are nevertheless driven by an equal weight of desire into the same depth and joined by similarity of character and merits. [Note: The manuscripts read, “are bound together, and if they often,” omitting “but.”]

Again, all human beings and all spirits who humbly seek God’s glory, not their own, and follow him in devotion belong to one society.

Yet God, who is most merciful, is patient even with impious people and grants them an opportunity for repentance and correction.

### 32. The flood and the ark as figures of judgment and the Church

For when he destroyed everyone in the flood except one righteous man and those whom he wished to be preserved with him in the ark, he knew that they would not correct themselves. Nevertheless, while the ark was being built over a hundred years, the coming wrath of God against them was certainly proclaimed (Gen. 6–7). And if they turned to God, he would spare them, just as he later spared the city of Nineveh when it repented, after he had foretold its future destruction through the prophet (Jonah 3). [Note: Erasmus and Louvain read, “so that if they turned.” Ambrose and the manuscripts read, “and if they turned.”]

God does this even for those whom he knows will persist in wickedness, granting them time for repentance, so that he may exercise and shape our patience by his example. Thus we may learn how patiently we ought to endure the wicked, since we do not know what they will later become, when the one from whom nothing in the future is hidden spares them and allows them to live.

The sacrament of the flood was also foretold: through wood the righteous were saved, signifying the future Church, which its king and God, Christ, suspends from the drowning of this age through the mystery of his cross.

For God did not fail to know that even from those who had been saved in the ark there would be born wicked people who would again fill the face of the earth with iniquities. Nevertheless, he both gave an example of the future judgment and foretold the deliverance of the saints through the mystery of the wood.

After this, wickedness did not cease to sprout again through pride, lusts, and unlawful impieties. Human beings abandoned their Creator and fell not only toward the creature that God made, worshiping as God what God had made, but also bent their souls toward the works of human hands and the crafts of artisans. There the devil and demons could triumph over them all the more shamefully—those who rejoice to be adored and venerated in such images while feeding their errors on human errors. [Note: A Floriacensis manuscript reads “mixing their errors.”]

### 33. Abraham and the prophetic character of Israel

Nor were there then lacking righteous people who piously sought God and overcame the devil’s pride—the citizens of that holy city, whom the future humility of their king, Christ, revealed through the Spirit and healed.

Among them Abraham was chosen, a pious and faithful servant of God (Gen. 12), to whom the mystery of the Son of God was shown, so that, because of the imitation of his faith, all believers of every nation would be called his children.

From him was born the people by whom the one true God, who made heaven and earth, would be worshiped, while the other nations served images and demons. In that people the future Church was represented much more clearly.

For there was a carnal multitude that worshiped God because of visible benefits. But there were also a few who thought about the future rest and sought the heavenly homeland. To them the future humility of God, our king and Lord Jesus Christ, was revealed through prophecy, so that by faith in it they might be healed of all pride and swelling.

The words, life, marriages, children, and deeds of these saints who preceded the Lord’s birth in time were prophecy of the age in which, through faith in Christ’s passion, the Church is gathered from the nations.

Through those holy Patriarchs and Prophets, the carnal people of Israel—later also called Jews—received both visible benefits, which they desired carnally from the Lord, and punishments in the form of bodily afflictions, by which they were frightened for a time, as was appropriate to their hardness.

Yet in all these things spiritual mysteries were signified, pertaining to Christ and the Church. Those saints too were members of the Church, although they lived in this life before Christ the Lord was born according to the flesh.

For he himself, the only-begotten Son of God, the Word of the Father, equal and coeternal with the Father, through whom all things were made, became human for our sake, so that he might be the head of the whole Church as of a whole body.

But just as, when a whole human being is born, even if he presents a hand first at birth, that hand nevertheless remains joined and connected beneath the head to the entire body—just as some people, as a sign of this very reality, were born among the Patriarchs with a hand presented first (Gen. 25:25)—so all the saints who lived on earth before the birth of our Lord Jesus Christ, although they were born earlier, remained joined beneath the head to the whole body of which he is the head. [Note: Am. and the manuscripts read, “of which he himself is the head.”]

## CHAPTER XX

### 34. Israel’s slavery in Egypt, deliverance through the Red Sea, and the figures of baptism and Christ’s passion

The people of Israel were carried into Egypt and served a most harsh king. Trained through the heaviest labors, they sought God as their liberator. One of their own people, the holy servant of God Moses, was sent to them. By God’s power he terrified the impious nation of the Egyptians with great miracles, and led God’s people out through the Red Sea.

There the water parted and provided a path for those crossing. But when the Egyptians pursued them, the waves returned upon themselves, and the Egyptians were submerged and destroyed.

Thus, just as through the flood the earth was cleansed of the wickedness of sinners, who were then destroyed in that inundation while the righteous escaped through wood, so God’s people, leaving Egypt, found a path through the waters by which their enemies were consumed.

Nor was the sacrament of wood absent there. Moses struck with a staff so that the miracle might take place.

Both signs represent holy Baptism, through which believers pass into a new life, while their sins, like enemies, are destroyed and die.

The passion of Christ was represented more openly among that people when they were commanded to kill and eat a sheep, mark their doorposts with its blood, celebrate this every year, and call it the Lord’s Passover.

For prophecy most clearly says of the Lord Jesus Christ that “like a sheep he was led to the slaughter” (Isa. 53:7). With the sign of his passion and cross, you are to be marked today on the forehead as on a doorpost, and all Christians are marked in the same way. [Note: Only the printed editions read “the prophet says.”]

### 35. The law written by the finger of God

From there that people was led through the desert. For forty years it also received the law written by the finger of God on tablets. [Col. 0336] (Exod. 1–20; 32; 34; Num. 14:33; Deut. 29:5). By this name the Holy Spirit is signified, as the Gospel makes perfectly clear (Luke 11:20).

For God is not defined by bodily form, nor are bodily members and fingers to be imagined in him as we see them in ourselves. Rather, because the gifts of God are distributed to the saints through the Holy Spirit, so that although they possess different gifts they do not depart from the harmony of charity, and because a certain division is especially apparent in the fingers, though not a separation from unity, the Holy Spirit has been called the finger of God—whether for this reason or for some other.

Nevertheless, when we hear this, we must not imagine the form of a human body.

That people therefore received the law written by the finger of God on stone tablets, signifying the hardness of their hearts, because they would not fulfill the law.

For, desiring bodily gifts from the Lord, they were held more by carnal fear than by spiritual charity; but only charity fulfills the law.

Therefore they were burdened with many visible sacraments, so that they might be pressed under a slavish yoke: regulations concerning foods, sacrifices of animals, and countless other things. Yet these were signs of spiritual realities pertaining to the Lord Jesus Christ and to the Church. At that time, a few saints both understood them for the fruit of salvation and observed them as appropriate to the period; the carnal multitude, however, merely observed them without understanding them.

### 36. The promised land and the earthly image of the heavenly Jerusalem

Through many and varied signs of future things—which it would take too long to enumerate all, and which we now see being fulfilled in the Church—that people was led into the promised land. There it would reign temporarily and carnally, according to the measure of its desire. Yet that earthly kingdom bore the image of the spiritual kingdom.

There Jerusalem was founded, the most famous city of God, serving as a sign of the free city called the heavenly Jerusalem (Gal. 4:25–26). This is a Hebrew word and is interpreted as “Vision of peace.”

Its citizens are all sanctified human beings who have lived, who live, and who will live; and all sanctified spirits, including all those who in the heights of heaven obey God with devout piety and do not imitate the impious pride of the devil and his angels.

The king of this city is the Lord Jesus Christ, the Word of God by whom the highest angels are governed, and the Word assuming humanity so that human beings too might be governed by him. All of them together with him will reign in eternal peace.

As a prefiguration of this king in that earthly kingdom, David was especially prominent as king of the people of Israel. From his seed according to the flesh would come our most true king, the Lord Jesus Christ, who is “God over all, blessed forever” (Rom. 9:5).

Many things were done in that promised land as figures of the coming Christ and the Church, which you will gradually be able to learn in the holy books.

## CHAPTER XXI
### 37. What the Babylonian Captivity and the Events Connected with It Signify; What Kind of Freedom Was Restored after the Captivity

After several generations, another type was displayed that is especially relevant to the subject. For that city was captured, and a large part of it was led away [Col. 0337] into Babylon. Just as Jerusalem signifies the city and fellowship of the saints, so Babylon signifies the city and fellowship of the wicked, since its name is said to be interpreted as “Confusion.” Concerning these two cities, proceeding from the beginning of the human race to the end of the age amid an intermingling variety of times [Note: [Col. 0337] So the manuscripts. The printed editions, however, have *permixta*, “mixed.”], and to be separated at the last judgment, we have already said a little earlier (chap. 19).

Therefore, the Lord commanded through Jeremiah, the prophet of that time, that the captivity of the city of Jerusalem and that people led into Babylon should go into servitude. There arose kings of Babylon under whom they served; moved by what happened among them, these kings came to recognize and worship—and ordered others to worship—the one true God who created the whole creation (Dan. II–VI, XIV). They were also commanded to pray for those by whom they were held captive, and to hope for peace in their peace: to beget children, build houses, and plant gardens and vineyards. After seventy years, however, their liberation from that captivity was promised (Jer. XXV, XXIX).

All this signified figuratively that the Church of Christ, in all its saints who are citizens of the heavenly Jerusalem, would serve under the kings of this age. For apostolic teaching also says that every soul should be subject to the higher authorities, and that all dues should be rendered to everyone: tribute to whom tribute is due, taxes to whom taxes are due (Rom. XIII, 1, 7); and the other things which, without violating the worship of our God, we render to the rulers of human government. Even the Lord himself, in order to provide us with an example of this sound teaching, did not disdain to pay the tribute for the human head with which he was clothed (Matt. XVII, 26).

Christian servants and faithful believers are likewise commanded to serve their temporal masters with equanimity and fidelity (Eph. VI, 5). They will judge those masters if they find them wicked to the end; or they will reign equally with them if those masters too have been converted to the true God. Nevertheless, all are commanded to serve human and earthly authorities until, after the appointed period signified by the seventy years, the Church is liberated from the confusion of this age as from the captivity of Babylon, just as Jerusalem was.

On account of this captivity, even earthly kings, abandoning the idols for which they had persecuted Christians, came to know and worship the one true God and Christ the Lord. The apostle Paul commands us to pray for them, even when they were persecuting the Church. For he says:

“I urge, then, first of all, that supplications, adorations [Note: [Col. 0337] Lov. has *orationes*, “prayers.” The other printed editions and the manuscripts have *adorationes*. The Greek is *proseuchas*, “prayers.”], intercessions, and thanksgivings be made for kings, for all people, and for all who are in positions of authority, so that we may lead a peaceful and tranquil life with complete godliness and charity [Note: [Col. 0337] The Vulgate has *castitate*, “purity,” in accordance with the Greek *semnotēti*, “dignity” or “reverence.”]” (1 Tim. II, 1–2).

Thus, through those kings, peace was granted to the Church—although temporal peace, a temporal tranquility [Note: [Col. 0337] So the manuscripts. The printed editions instead have *temporis*, “of time.”]—for spiritually building houses and planting gardens and vineyards. For behold, even now, through this discourse, we are building and planting you. And this is done throughout the whole world in the peace of Christian kings, as the same apostle says: “You are God’s cultivation, God’s building” (1 Cor. III, 9).

### 38.

After the seventy years mystically prophesied by Jeremiah to prefigure the end of the ages, a restoration of the building of God’s temple did indeed take place in Jerusalem, so that the figure itself might be completed. But because everything was being enacted figuratively, firm peace and freedom had not been restored to the Jews. Therefore, afterward they were conquered by the Romans and made tributary.

From the time when they received the promised land and began to have kings, lest they think that what Christ the liberator was promised to them had been fulfilled in one of their kings, Christ was prophesied more openly through many prophecies—not only by David himself in the Book of Psalms, but also by the other great and holy prophets, down to the time of the captivity in Babylon. Even during the captivity there were prophets who foretold that the Lord Jesus Christ, the liberator of all, would come.

After the temple had been restored when the seventy years had elapsed, the Jews suffered such great pressures and calamities from the kings of the nations that they understood that the liberator had not yet come. They did not understand him as one who would liberate them spiritually, but desired him for a bodily liberation.

## CHAPTER XXII

### 39. The Six Ages of the World; the Sixth Age Beginning with Christ’s Coming; Christ, Manifesting the New Testament of the Eternal Inheritance, Teaches by His Example to Despise Earthly Things; His Birth, Life, and Death

Thus, after the five ages of the world had been completed—the first of which extends from the beginning of the human race, that is, from Adam, the first man created, to Noah, who built the ark during the flood (Gen. VI)—the second extends from then to Abraham, who was called the father [Note: [Col. 0338] The manuscripts have “was chosen.”] of all the nations (ibid. XVII, 4) that would imitate his faith, yet who was also the ancestor, through the descent of his flesh [Note: [Col. 0338] The manuscripts have “through the offspring of his flesh.”], of the future Jewish people.

Before the faith of the nations in Christ, this people alone among all the peoples of all the lands worshiped the one true God; from this people the Savior Christ was to come according to the flesh. These are the divisions of the first two ages that stand out in the ancient Books. The remaining three are also set forth in the Gospel when the bodily origin of the Lord Jesus Christ is recounted (Matt. I, 17).

The third age extends from Abraham to King David; the fourth from David to that captivity in which the people of God migrated into Babylon; the fifth from that migration to the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ. With his coming the sixth age is now unfolding, so that spiritual grace—which at that time was known to only a few patriarchs and prophets—might be revealed to all nations. Thus no one would worship God except freely, desiring from him not visible rewards for service or the happiness of the present life, but eternal life alone, in which he would enjoy God himself. In this sixth age the human mind is renewed according to the image of God, just as on the sixth day the human being was made in the image of God (Gen. I, 27).

Then the law is fulfilled, when everything it commands is done not out of desire for temporal things, [Col. 0339] but out of love for the one who gave the command. Who would not desire to love in return the most just and merciful God, who first loved the most unjust and proud human beings so greatly that for their sake he sent his only Son, through whom he made all things? Though he became human not by any change in himself but by assuming humanity, he was able not only to live among them but also to be killed for them and by them.

### 40.

Therefore, in manifesting the new testament of the eternal inheritance, in which the renewed human being would lead a new life through the grace of God—that is, a spiritual life—he showed what the old testament signified first. In it the carnal people, living as the old human being, except for the few discerning patriarchs and prophets and certain hidden saints, lived carnally, desired carnal rewards from the Lord God, and received them as figures of spiritual blessings.

Thus the Lord Christ, having become human, despised all earthly goods in order to show that they should be despised, and endured all earthly evils which he commanded should be endured, so that happiness would not be sought in the former, nor unhappiness feared in the latter.

He was born of a mother who, although she conceived without intercourse with a man and remained perpetually untouched—a virgin conceiving, a virgin giving birth, and a virgin dying—was nevertheless betrothed to a craftsman. In this way he extinguished all the arrogance of carnal nobility.

He was also born in the city of Bethlehem, which among all the cities of Judea was so small that even today it is called a village; he did not wish anyone to glory in the exaltation of any earthly city. He who possesses all things, and through whom all things were created, also became poor, lest anyone who believed in him dare to exalt himself because of earthly riches.

He did not wish to be made king by human beings, because he was showing the way of humility to the wretched, whom pride had separated from him—although the whole creation bears witness to his eternal kingdom.

He was hungry, though he feeds everyone; he was thirsty, though through him every drink is created and though he is spiritually the bread of the hungry and the fountain of the thirsty. He was wearied by an earthly journey, though he made himself the way for us to heaven. He was as though mute and deaf before those who reviled him, though through him the mute spoke and the deaf heard. He was bound, though he releases people from the bonds of infirmities. He was scourged, though he drove the scourges of every pain from human bodies. He was crucified, though he brought our torments to an end. He died, though he raised the dead.

Yet he also rose again, never to die, lest anyone learn from him to despise death as though he would never live again [Note: [Col. 0339] Am., Er., and nearly all the manuscripts have “would never be”; one Vatican manuscript has “would never rise again.”].

## CHAPTER XXIII

### 41. The Holy Spirit Sent on the Fiftieth Day after Christ’s Resurrection; Jews Converted through the Apostles’ Preaching and Burning with Zeal for Evangelical Life; Churches Established among the Nations through Paul

After this, having confirmed the disciples, he lived with them for forty days; then, while they watched, he ascended into heaven. When fifty days had been completed from his resurrection, he sent them the Holy Spirit—for he had promised it—[Col. 0340] so that, with love poured into their hearts, they might fulfill the law not only without burden but even with joy.

This law had been given to the Jews in ten commandments, which they call the Decalogue. These are reduced again to two: that we love God with all our heart, with all our soul, and with all our mind; and that we love our neighbor as ourselves. For the Lord himself both said in the Gospel that the whole Law and the Prophets depend on these two commandments (Matt. XXII, 37–40), and demonstrated it by his own example.

The people of Israel, from the day on which they first celebrated the Passover symbolically by killing and eating a sheep whose blood marked their doorposts for protection and salvation (Exod. XII), completed fifty days from that very day and received the law written by the finger of God (ibid. XIX, XX). As we have already said, this name signifies the Holy Spirit (above, chap. XX, no. 35).

In the same way, after the Lord’s passion and resurrection—which is the true Passover—the Holy Spirit himself was sent to the disciples on the fiftieth day. He no longer signified hard hearts by tablets of stone. Rather, while they were gathered together in one place in Jerusalem itself, suddenly there came from heaven a sound as of a powerful rushing wind; divided tongues appeared to them as though of fire, and they began to speak in languages, so that everyone who came to them recognized his own language. For Jews were coming to that city from every land in which they had been scattered, and they had learned the various languages of different nations (Acts II, 1–11).

Then, preaching Christ with complete confidence, they performed many signs in his name, so that, when Peter passed by, his shadow touched a certain dead man and he rose again (ibid. V, 15).

### 42.

When the Jews saw so many signs being performed in the name of the one whom some had crucified out of envy and others through error, some were provoked to persecute his preachers, the apostles. Others, however, were even more astonished that such miracles were being performed in the name of the one whom they had laughed at as though they had oppressed and conquered him. Repenting, thousands of Jews believed in him [Note: [Col. 0340] Lov. adds *multa*, “many,” after “thousands believed in him,” from one manuscript.]

They no longer desired temporal benefits and an earthly kingdom from God, nor did they expect the promised king Christ in a carnal way. Instead, they understood and loved him immortally—the one who had endured such great mortal sufferings for them and from them, who had forgiven their sins even to the shedding of his blood [Note: [Col. 0340] Lov. had added here *effusionem*, “outpouring”; this is less satisfactory.], and who had shown by the example of his resurrection that immortality should be hoped for and desired from him.

Thus, now putting to death the earthly desires of the old human being and burning with the newness of spiritual life, as the Lord had commanded in the Gospel, they sold all that they possessed and placed the proceeds of their goods at the apostles’ feet, so that they might distribute them to each person according to his need (ibid. II, 44; IV, 34). Living harmoniously in Christian love, they did not call anything their own; rather, everything was common among them, and they were one soul and one heart toward God (ibid. IV, 32–35).

Then they too suffered persecution from the carnal Jews, citizens of their own flesh, and were scattered, so that Christ might be preached more widely through their dispersion and so that they too might imitate the patience of their Lord. For the one who had meekly suffered them commanded those whom he had made meek to suffer for him [Note: [Col. 0341] Am. and Er. have “the one who had suffered before them”; Lov. has “the one who suffered for them”; some manuscripts have “the one who suffered through them,” others “the one who suffered because of them,” and most of the older manuscripts have “the one who suffered them.”].

### 43.

The apostle Paul himself had been among those persecutors of the saints, and he raged especially against Christians. But afterward he believed, became an apostle, and was sent to preach the Gospel to the nations. He suffered greater things for the name of Christ than he had inflicted against the name of Christ.

Establishing churches throughout all the nations where he sowed the Gospel, he earnestly commanded that, since those people were coming from the worship of idols and were inexperienced in worshiping the one God, and therefore could not easily serve God by selling and distributing their possessions, they should make offerings for the poor among the saints who were in the churches of Judea that had believed in Christ.

In this way, apostolic teaching constituted the former as soldiers and the latter as provincial tributaries, inserting Christ among them as the cornerstone, just as he had been foretold through the prophet. In him the two walls, coming from different directions—from the Jews and from the nations—would be joined together in genuine love (Ps. CXVII, 22; Isa. XXVIII, 16).

But afterward, more severe and more frequent persecutions arose from unbelieving nations against the Church of Christ, and each day the word of the Lord was being fulfilled: “Behold, I am sending you as sheep among wolves” (Matt. X, 16).

## CHAPTER XXIV

### 44. The Church Grows like a Vine and Is Pruned; From What Has Been Seen to Be Fulfilled, Let What Remains to Be Fulfilled Be Believed, Especially the Coming Judgment

But that vine which, as had been prophesied about it and foretold by the Lord himself, spread fruitful branches throughout the world was growing all the more vigorously the more abundantly [Note: [Col. 0341] Am. and Er. have *teneriore*, “more tenderly.”] it was watered by the blood of the martyrs. As these martyrs died innumerably throughout all lands for the truth of the faith, even the kingdoms that had persecuted them gave way; with the neck of their pride broken, they were converted to knowing and venerating Christ.

Yet this same vine had to be pruned, as the Lord had repeatedly foretold, and unfruitful branches had to be cut off from it (John XV, 2). From these arose heresies and schisms in various places, people seeking under Christ’s name not his glory but their own. Through their opposition the Church would be exercised more and more, and both its teaching and its patience would be tested and made manifest.

### 45.

Therefore, just as we read that all these things had been foretold so long beforehand, so we recognize that they have occurred. Just as the first Christians, because they did not yet see these things taking place, were moved by miracles to believe, so we, because all these things have been fulfilled as we read them in the Books written long before they were fulfilled—where all these events were declared as future and are now seen as present—are built up in faith, so that we may believe without doubt that the remaining things too will come, as we endure them and persevere in the Lord.

Indeed, the same Scriptures still speak of future tribulations, and of that final day of judgment when all the citizens of those two cities, having received their bodies again, will rise and give an account of their lives before the tribunal of Christ the Judge.

For he will come in the glory of his power, who previously deigned to come in the humility of his humanity; and he will separate all the godly from the ungodly. This will include not only those who entirely refused to believe in him, but also those who believed in him uselessly and without fruit. To the former he will give an eternal kingdom with himself; to the latter, eternal punishment with the devil.

Yet just as no joy in temporal things can in any respect be found comparable to the joy of eternal life, which the saints will receive, so no torment of temporal punishments can be compared with the everlasting torments of the wicked.

## CHAPTER XXV

### 46. Faith in the Resurrection Is Persuasively Taught; Perpetual Death in Torments; The Eternal Life of the Saints; One Must Beware Not Only of Pagans, Jews, and Heretics but Also of Bad Christians

Therefore, brother, strengthen yourself in the name and help of the one in whom you believe against the tongues of those who ridicule our faith. Through them the devil speaks deceptive words, wishing especially to ridicule belief in the resurrection.

But believe from your own case that you will be what you will be, since, although you previously were not, you now see that you are. For where, a few years ago, before you were born—or even before you were conceived in your mother’s womb—was this mass of your body, this shape and arrangement of your limbs? Where were this mass and this bodily stature of yours?

Did they not emerge into the light from the hidden secrets of this creation, invisibly formed by the Lord God, and rise through definite stages of life to this size and shape? Is it therefore difficult for God, who in a moment draws together from hidden places even masses of clouds and covers the sky in an instant, to restore this quantity of your body as it was, since he was able to make it when it did not exist [Note: [Col. 0342] So Am., Er., and several manuscripts. Lov. has “was able to make it when it did not exist.” The Corbeiensis manuscript, by a second hand, has “so when it did not exist.”]?

Believe, then, firmly and without wavering that all things which seem to be taken away from human eyes as though they were perishing remain safe and whole in the omnipotence of God. When he wills, he will restore them without delay or difficulty—only those things which his justice judges ought to be restored—so that human beings may give an account of their deeds in the bodies in which they performed them, and in those bodies may deserve either a change into heavenly incorruption according to the merits of their godliness, or the corruptible condition of the body according to the merits of their wickedness: not a condition dissolved by death, but one that supplies material for everlasting pains [Note: [Col. 0342] Several manuscripts have the adjective *corruptibilis*, “corruptible,” instead of the noun phrase “the corruptible condition.”].

### 47.

Therefore flee, through immovable faith and good conduct [Note: [Col. 0342] So the manuscripts. The printed editions instead have “toward good conduct.”]—flee, brother, those torments where neither the torturers cease nor those tortured die; where death exists without end, namely, the inability to die amid the sufferings.

Burn with love and longing for the eternal life of the saints, [Col. 0343] where activity will not be burdensome, nor rest idle; where the praise of God will be without weariness and without defect; where there will be no tedium in the soul and no labor in the body; no deprivation—neither your own, for which you would desire assistance, nor that of a neighbor, for which you would hasten to provide help.

God will be every delight and the fullness [Note: [Col. 0343] The printed editions have *societas*, “fellowship.” Five manuscripts more suitably have *satietas*, “fullness.”] of the holy city, which lives wisely and blessedly in him and from him. For we will become, as we hope and expect on the basis of his promise, equal to the angels of God (Luke XX, 36), and together with them we will enjoy that Trinity by sight, in which we now walk by faith (2 Cor. V, 7).

For we believe what we do not see, so that by the very merits of faith we may also deserve to see and cling to what we believe. Then we will no longer proclaim in the words of faith and resounding syllables the equality of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and the unity of the Trinity itself—how these three are one God—but will absorb it in the purest and most ardent contemplation, in that silence [Note: [Col. 0343] So two manuscripts. The printed editions have “so that we may be absorbed.”].

### 48.

Hold these truths fixed in your heart, and call upon the God in whom you believe to protect you against the temptations of the devil. Be watchful lest that enemy secretly approach you from some other direction—the one who, for the most evil consolation of his own condemnation, seeks those whom he may condemn with himself.

He does not dare to tempt Christians only through those who hate the Christian name, who grieve that the world is occupied by that name, and who still desire to serve idols and the occult practices of demons. He also attempts this through those whom we mentioned shortly before, who have been cut off from the unity of the Church like pruned branches and are called heretics or schismatics. Sometimes he also attempts to tempt and deceive through the Jews.

But one must be especially careful not to be tempted and deceived through people who are within the Catholic Church itself, whom God tolerates like chaff until the time of their winnowing. For God is patient with them so that, by exercising and strengthening the faith and prudence of his elect through their perversity, he may also bring many of them to progress; moved by pity for their own souls and wishing to please God, they turn with great force.

Not all of them are storing up wrath for themselves through God’s patience for the day of his just judgment. Rather, that same patience of the Almighty brings many to the saving sorrow of repentance (Rom. II, 5, 4). Until this happens, the patience—and also the mercy—of those who already hold to the right path is exercised through them.

You will therefore see many drunkards, greedy people, swindlers, gamblers, adulterers, fornicators, people binding sacrilegious remedies upon themselves, and people devoted to enchanters, astrologers, or diviners of every kind of impious art. You will also notice that those crowds fill the churches on the feast days of Christians who also fill the theaters on the solemn days of pagans. By seeing these things, you will be tempted to imitate them.

And what shall I say? You will see what you certainly already know: you are not unaware that many who are called Christians commit all these evils which I have briefly mentioned. Perhaps you also know that people whom you know to be called Christians sometimes commit still worse things [Note: [Col. 0344] The manuscripts have “somewhat worse.”].

But if you have come with the intention of doing such things as though you were secure, you are greatly mistaken. The name of Christ will not benefit you when he begins to judge with the utmost severity—the one who first deigned to come to your aid with the greatest mercy.

For he foretold these things and said in the Gospel: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of my Father. Many will say to me on that day, ‘Lord, Lord, in your name we ate and drank’” (Matt. VII, 21–22).

For all who persist in such works, condemnation is the end. Therefore, when you see many not only doing these things but also defending and recommending them, hold fast to the law of God and do not follow those who transgress it. You will not be judged according to their opinion but according to his truth.

### 49. Fellowship with the Good, but Hope Placed in God Alone

Join yourself to the good whom you see loving your king together with you. You will find many of them if you too begin to be such a person.

For if you wished to be with and cling to those in the theaters who loved with you either a charioteer, a hunter, or some actor, how much more should you delight in the fellowship of those who love God with you? His lover will never be ashamed of him, because he himself cannot be conquered and will also make his lovers unconquerable.

Yet even in the good themselves, who either precede you or accompany you toward God [Note: [Col. 0344] Er., Lugd., Ven., and Lov. omit “accompany you.” The manuscript tradition supports its inclusion.], you must not place your hope, just as you must not place it in yourself, no matter how far you may have progressed. Place it in the one who makes both them and you such people by justifying you.

You are secure concerning God, because he does not change; but concerning a human being, no one is wisely secure. If we ought to love those who are not yet just so that they may become just, how much more ardently ought those who already are just to be loved?

But loving a human being is one thing, and placing hope in a human being another. The difference is so great that God commands the former and forbids the latter.

If, after suffering insults or tribulations for the name of Christ, you do not fall away from the faith or deviate from the good path [Note: [Col. 0344] Am., Er., and several manuscripts have “life.”], you will receive a greater reward. Those who yield to the devil in such circumstances lose even the lesser reward. But be humble before God, so that he will not permit you to be tempted beyond your strength.

## CHAPTER XXVI

### 50. The Initiation of a Catechumen, with an Explanation of the Signs; A Shorter Sermon Should Sometimes Be Used; Another, Shorter Sermon Begins; The Son of God Was Sent So That We Might Be Freed from the Death That Entered through Adam

After these things have been said, he should be asked whether he believes them and desires to observe them. When he has answered, he should certainly be solemnly signed and instructed according to the custom of the Church.

Regarding the sacrament which he receives [Note: [Col. 0344] Perhaps the reading is “of salt.”], once it has been properly explained to him that the visible signs are signs of divine things, but that the invisible realities themselves are honored in them, and that this appearance, sanctified by blessing, must not be regarded in the same way as anything used ordinarily, it should also be explained what it signifies and what it seasons in him, of which that thing bears the likeness [Note: [Col. 0345] Er. and Lov. have “what is seasoned.” The manuscripts and Am. more correctly have “what it seasons,” since the subject here is the sacrament of salt by which the catechumen is initiated. The passage relates to Augustine, *Confessions* I.11: “I was already being signed with the sign of his cross and seasoned with his salt, even from the womb of my mother.” This is the appearance he here called sanctified by blessing; therefore, a little above, where the text reads “regarding the sacrament,” it seems preferable to read “regarding the sacrament of salt.”].

Then, on this occasion, he should be admonished that if he hears anything in the Scriptures which sounds carnal, even if he does not understand it, he should nevertheless believe that something spiritual is signified which relates to holy conduct and the future life.

He learns this briefly: whatever he hears from the canonical Books which he cannot relate to love of eternity, truth, and holiness, and to love of neighbor, he should believe to have been said or done figuratively. He should then try to understand it in such a way as to refer it to that twofold love.

He should understand “neighbor” not in a carnal sense, but as everyone who can be in that holy city with him, whether already present or not yet revealed. He should also despair of no one’s correction whom he sees the patience of God allowing to live—not for any other reason, as the Apostle says, than that the person may be led to repentance (Rom. II, 4).

### 51.

If this discourse seems long to you, by which I have instructed someone inexperienced as though he were present, you may say these things more briefly. I do not think it should be longer, although much depends on what the situation itself suggests when it is being handled, and on what the presence of the listeners shows that it can not only endure but also desire.

When speed is necessary, see how easily the whole matter can be explained. Imagine again that someone is present who wishes to become a Christian. Let him be asked the question, and let him give the answer which the person above gave; for even if he does not give that answer, it should be said that he ought to have given it. Then the rest should be joined together in the following way.

### 52.

Truly, brother, the great and genuine blessedness promised to the saints in the age to come is real. All visible things pass away, and all the splendor, pleasures, and curiosities of this age will perish and drag their lovers with them into destruction.

Wishing mercifully to free human beings from that destruction—that is, from eternal punishments—if only they are not enemies to themselves and do not resist the mercy of their Creator, God sent his only-begotten Son, that is, his Word, equal to himself, through whom he made all things.

Remaining in his divinity, not departing from the Father, and not changed in any respect, he nevertheless came to human beings by assuming humanity and appearing to them in mortal flesh [Note: [Col. 0345] Several manuscripts have the masculine adjective “mortal.”]. Thus, just as death entered the human race through one human being who was created first, namely Adam, because he consented to his wife, who had been deceived by the devil, so that they might transgress God’s command, in the same way, through one human being who is also God, the Son of God, Jesus Christ, all who believe in him would enter eternal life, with all past sins erased (ibid. V, 12–19).

## CHAPTER XXVII

[Col. 0346]

### 53. The Prophecies of the Old Testament Seen Fulfilled in the Church; From This, Faith in What Remains to Come Is Strengthened—the Last Judgment and the Resurrection; Temptations from the Wicked Found Even in the Church Must Be Avoided; Fellowship with the Good; All Hope in God

For all the things [Note: [Col. 0346] The Corbeiensis manuscript has “All things therefore.”] that you now see taking place [Note: [Col. 0346] The word *geri* (“taking place”) is absent from the manuscripts.] in the Church of God and throughout the whole world under the name of Christ were foretold before the ages. As we read them, so we see them, and from this we are built up in faith.

At one time a flood occurred over the whole earth so that sinners might be destroyed. Yet those who escaped in the ark were demonstrating the sacrament of the future Church, which now floats amid the waves of this age and is saved from submersion through the wood of Christ’s cross.

It was foretold to Abraham, God’s faithful servant, a single man, that a people would arise from him who would worship the one God among the other nations that worshiped idols. Everything that was foretold would happen to that people occurred just as it had been foretold.

Christ, the king of all the saints and God, was also prophesied among that people, destined to come from Abraham’s offspring according to the flesh which he assumed, so that all who imitated Abraham’s faith might also be his children. And so it happened: Christ was born of the virgin Mary, who belonged to that lineage.

It was foretold through the prophets that he would suffer on the cross at the hands of that same Jewish people, from whose lineage he came according to the flesh; and so it happened. It was foretold that he would rise again; he rose. And in accordance with the very predictions of the prophets, he ascended into heaven and sent the Holy Spirit to his disciples.

It was foretold not only by the prophets but also by the Lord Jesus Christ himself that his Church would exist throughout the whole world, spread through the sufferings and martyrdoms of the saints. This was foretold when his name was still hidden from the nations and was ridiculed where it was known.

Nevertheless, as the powers of his miracles were proclaimed and believed—whether the miracles he performed himself or those he performed through his servants—we now see that what was foretold has been fulfilled. We see that the very kings of the earth who previously persecuted Christians have been subjected to the name of Christ.

It was also foretold that schisms and heresies would emerge from his Church and would seek, under his name and wherever they could, their own glory rather than Christ’s. And these things too have been fulfilled.

### 54.

Are those things which remain, then, not going to come? It is clear that just as these foretold events came to pass, so those other events will also come: whatever tribulations of the righteous still remain; and the day of judgment, which will separate all the ungodly from the righteous in the resurrection of the dead.

That day will separate not only those who are outside the Church, but also the chaff of the Church itself, which it must endure with the utmost patience until the final winnowing, consigning it to the fire it deserves.

Those who ridicule the resurrection, thinking that this flesh cannot rise because it decays, will rise in it for punishment. God will show them that the one who was able to make these bodies before they existed is able to restore them in an instant as they were. [Col. 0347]

All the faithful who are to reign with Christ will rise in the same body, in such a way that they may also deserve to be transformed into angelic incorruption, so that they may become equal to the angels of God, as the Lord himself promised (Luke XX, 36). They will praise him without any defect or weariness, always living in him and from him, with such joy and blessedness as no human being can express or conceive.

55. Therefore, believing these things, beware of temptations (for the devil seeks those who will perish with him), so that this enemy may not deceive you—not only through those who are outside the Church, whether Pagans, Jews, or heretics, but also through those whom you see living wickedly within the Catholic Church itself. Do not imitate those who are immoderate [Note: The manuscripts read “immoderatis,” perhaps for “in immoderatis.”] in the pleasures of the belly and throat, or unchaste, or devoted to empty curiosities or unlawful pursuits—whether spectacles, remedies [Note: The printed editions read “sacrilegious remedies.” “Sacrilegious” is absent from the manuscripts, so that the word “diabolical,” which follows, may refer both to divinations and to remedies.] or diabolical divinations—or who are engrossed in the pomp and arrogance of avarice and pride, or in any way of life condemned and punished by the law [Note: The Corbie manuscript reads “the law of God”; but “of God” was added by a second hand.]. Rather, associate yourself with the good, whom you will easily find if you yourself are such, so that together you may worship and love God freely—for he himself will be our entire reward, so that in that life [Note: The printed editions read “in that eternal life.” “Eternal” is absent from the manuscripts.] we may enjoy his goodness and beauty.

But he must be loved not as something seen by the eyes, but as wisdom, truth, holiness, justice, charity [Note: The manuscripts omit “and holiness, and justice, and charity,”], and whatever else is so described are loved—not as these qualities exist in human beings, but as they exist in the very source of incorruptible and unchangeable wisdom. Therefore, join yourself to anyone whom you see loving these things, so that through Christ, who became human in order to be the Mediator between God and human beings, you may be reconciled to God.

As for wicked people, even if they enter the walls of the church, do not suppose that they will enter the kingdom of heaven; for in due time they will be separated, unless they change for the better. Imitate the good, tolerate the wicked, love everyone—for you do not know what tomorrow’s condition will be of one who is wicked today. Do not love their injustice; love the people themselves for this reason: that they may attain justice. For not only the love of God has been commanded to us, but also the love of our neighbor; on these two commandments the whole Law and the Prophets depend (Matt. 22:37–40).

No one fulfills this except one who has received the gift of the Holy Spirit, who is certainly equal to the Father and the Son, because the Trinity itself is God. In this God all hope must be placed. It must not be placed in a human being, whoever he may be. For the one by whom we are justified is one thing; those with whom we are justified are another.

The devil tempts not only through desires, but also through the terrors of insults, sufferings, and death itself. Whatever a person suffers for the name of Christ and for the hope of eternal life, and patiently endures to the end, a greater reward will be given him; but if he yields to the devil, he will be condemned with him. Yet works of mercy, together with devout humility, obtain from the Lord that he not permit his servants to be tempted beyond what they can bear (1 Cor. 10:13).

## [ON CONTINENCE]

[Col. 0347]

## EDITORIAL NOTICE TO THE FOLLOWING BOOK

Augustine himself acknowledges the book *On Continence* as his own in Letter 262, to Count Darius. Possidius mentions the same work in his *Index*, chapter 10, and Bede or Florus, as well as Eugippius—who is somewhat farther removed from Augustine’s time—quotes several passages from the same book in his collections. From this the judgment of Desiderius Erasmus is refuted: he prefixed it to the beginning of the book, stating that it seemed to him to be by Hugo and that its phrasing indicated that it was not Augustine’s. In our judgment, its style and diction are altogether similar to those of many of Augustine’s sermons, especially those which he delivered or dictated in his earlier years.

That this book is a sermon, which for that reason Augustine omitted from his *Retractions*, is made clear by its very beginning. The ancient books, as well as Possidius, Eugippius, and Florus, call it a sermon. Nor will anyone deny that it may appropriately be assigned to his earlier years, since it is a longer sermon and is largely directed against the Manichaeans, whose heresy Augustine was accustomed to attack especially at the beginning of his conversion.

[Col. 0349]

## ONE BOOK BY SAINT AURELIUS AUGUSTINE, BISHOP OF HIPPO, ON CONTINENCE

[Note: Written around the year 395 after Christ, when Augustine was a presbyter or a recently consecrated bishop.] [Note: The book *On Continence* was corrected against an old exemplar of the Church of Reims; against the manuscript of the Abbey of Saint Arnulf at Metz; against the Cistercian manuscript; against the Fuxian manuscript, now Colbertinus; against the manuscript of the monastery of Saint Bernard at Paris, Fuliensis; against the Genovefian, Michaelinian, and three Vatican manuscripts; also against the variant readings of three Belgian manuscripts used by the Louvain editors; and against the editions of Desiderius Erasmus and the Louvain theologians.] [Note: We also compared all the editions mentioned at the beginning of volume 1 of the *Retractions* and *Confessions*. M.] (C)

He explains two verses of Psalm 140: “Set, O Lord, a guard over my mouth, and a door of continence around my lips; do not incline my heart toward wicked words, to make excuses for sins.” Taking his subject from this passage, he teaches that the virtue of continence must, in accordance with its function, restrain the desires of both body and soul, and must generally watch over the restraint of those pleasures of desire which oppose the pleasure of wisdom.

He commands us not to trust in our own strength when fighting against desire, which is indeed recognized through the law, but is conquered only through grace. He rebukes the proud who offer various excuses for their sins. In this category he refutes the Manichaeans with particular care, since they attributed their sins to a nature of evil implanted within themselves. He also demonstrates from the Apostle himself that the passage in Galatians 5:17, “For the flesh desires against the spirit,” and so forth, by which they wanted to establish two natures, one good and one evil, was wrongly understood by those heretics.

## CHAPTER ONE

### 1. Continence from the desire of the flesh is God’s gift. Continence of the mouth is also God’s gift. The mouth of the body and the mouth of the heart.

It is difficult to discuss sufficiently and worthily the virtue of the soul called continence. But he whose great gift this virtue is will assist our weakness beneath the burden of so great a subject. For the one who grants it to his faithful people who practice continence himself gives speech to his ministers who speak about it.

Accordingly, concerning so great a matter, since we are about to speak of what he himself has granted, we first assert and establish that continence is God’s gift. In the Book of Wisdom we read that no one can be continent unless God grants it (Wis. 8:21).
