The Lord, speaking of that greater and more glorious continence by which one refrains from the marital bond [Note: The Cistercian manuscript reads, “by which the marital bond is despised.”], says: “Not everyone accepts this word, but those to whom it has been given” (Matt. 19:11).

And since marital chastity itself cannot be preserved unless it abstains from unlawful intercourse, the Apostle proclaimed that both are God’s gifts when he spoke of both ways of life—that is, the married life and the life without marriage—saying: “I wish that all people were as I myself am; but each has his own gift from God, one in this way, another in that” (1 Cor. 7:7).

### 2. Continence is also to be sought from the Lord in the desires of the mouth. The mouth of the body and the mouth of the heart.

And lest continence seem necessary to be sought from the Lord only in the desire of the body’s lower parts, it is also sung in the Psalm: “Set, O Lord, a guard over my mouth, and a door of continence around my lips.”

In this testimony of divine speech, if we understand “mouth” as we ought, we recognize how great a gift of God the continence placed there is. For it is not enough to restrain the mouth of the body, lest something unsuitable burst forth from it through the sound of the voice. There is within the mouth of the heart, and the one who spoke those words and had them written for us to say desired that a guard and a door of continence be placed there by the Lord.

We say many things neither with the mouth of the body nor aloud, but we cry out with the heart. Yet no word concerning any matter proceeds from the mouth of the body whose silence is not already present in the heart. Whatever does not flow from there does not sound outwardly; but whatever flows from there, if it is evil, pollutes the soul even if it does not move the tongue.

Therefore continence must be placed where the conscience of those who remain silent also speaks. The door of continence brings it about that nothing comes forth from there which, even when the lips of the flesh are closed, might pollute the life of the one who is thinking.

## CHAPTER TWO

### 3. The mouth of the heart, through which consent is expressed as an inward word. Continence of the heart commended under the name of the mouth by Christ. Continence of the heart sometimes violated without violation of the body. When continence of the heart is preserved, one does not sin against bodily continence.

Finally, to show more clearly the inward mouth signified by those words, after saying, “Set, O Lord, a guard over my mouth, and a door of continence around my lips,” he immediately added: “Do not incline my heart toward wicked words” (Ps. 140:3–4).

What is the inclination of the heart except consent? Whoever does not consent, by any inclination of the heart, to suggestions or images that arise within him has not yet spoken in his heart. But if he consents, he has already spoken with his heart, even if he has not uttered the words with his mouth; even if he has not acted with his hand or any other part of his body, he has nevertheless done what he has already determined in thought that he ought to do. He is guilty under the divine laws, although hidden from human senses: a word has been spoken in his heart, though no deed has been admitted through the body.

Nor would he have moved an outward limb in the deed whose beginning had not first occurred inwardly as a word. For it was not written falsely that “the beginning of every work is a word.” People do many things with their mouths closed, their tongues at rest, and their voices restrained; yet they do nothing through the work of the body that they have not first spoken in their hearts.

And so, since there are many sins in inward words that are not present in outward deeds, while there are no outward deeds that are not preceded by inward words [Note: Some manuscripts read this way. The printed editions instead read, “which do not proceed from inward words.”], innocence will be pure in both respects if a door of continence is placed around the inward lips.

### 4. What proceeds from the mouth and heart. The heart is polluted by evil thoughts even when bodily acts do not follow.

For this reason the Lord himself says with his own mouth: “Cleanse what is within, and what is outward will be clean” (Matt. 23:26). Elsewhere, when he was refuting the foolish talk of the Jews, who criticized his disciples for eating with unwashed hands, he said: “It is not what enters the mouth that defiles a person, but what proceeds from the mouth defiles a person.”

If this statement is understood entirely of the mouth of the body, it is absurd. For if food does not defile a person when it enters him, surely vomit does not defile him when it comes out of his mouth. Food enters the mouth, while vomit proceeds from the mouth.

But plainly the earlier words refer to the mouth of the flesh, where he says, “It is not what enters the mouth that defiles a person”; the later words refer to the mouth of the heart, where he says, “but what proceeds from the mouth defiles a person.”

Finally, when the apostle Peter asked him for an explanation, as though of this parable, he replied: “Are you also still without understanding? Do you not understand that everything which enters the mouth goes into the stomach and is expelled into the privy?” Here we certainly recognize the mouth of the flesh, into which food enters.

But in what he adds, so that we might recognize the mouth of the heart, our slowness of heart would not have understood unless Truth had deigned to walk with the slow. For he says: “But what proceeds from the mouth comes out of the heart,” as though he were saying, “When you hear ‘from the mouth,’ understand ‘from the heart.’ I am speaking of both, but explaining one from the other.”

The inward person has an inward mouth, and the inward ear distinguishes it. What proceeds from this mouth comes out of the heart, and these things defile the person. Then, abandoning the word “mouth,” which could also be understood of the body, he shows more openly what he means: “For out of the heart,” he says, “come evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, fornications, thefts, false testimonies, blasphemies: these are the things that defile a person” (Matt. 15:11–20).

Certainly, there is none of these evils—which can also be perpetrated through the limbs of the body—that is not preceded by an evil thought, which pollutes the person even if something prevents shameful and criminal bodily acts from following.

If the hand is free from killing a person because the power to do so is not granted, is the heart of the murderer therefore clean of crime? Or if one cannot take another person’s property as one wishes, is the thief therefore not a thief in his very will? Or if the woman whom the unchaste man wishes to commit adultery with is chaste, has he therefore not committed adultery with her in his heart? Or if a prostitute is not found in a brothel, does the one who seeks her therefore not commit fornication in his mind? Or if the person who desires to harm his neighbor by a lie lacks the time or place to do so, has he therefore not already spoken false testimony with his inner mouth? Or if someone, fearing other people, does not dare to utter blasphemy with the tongue of the flesh, is he therefore not guilty of this crime if he says in his heart, “There is no God” (Ps. 13:1)?

In the same way, other evil acts of human beings, which no bodily movement performs and which no bodily sense perceives, have their hidden guilty parties. Their only pollution is the consent of thought—that is, the wicked word of the inner mouth.

Fearing this, the Psalmist asks that the Lord place a door of continence around the lips of this mouth, which will restrain the heart so that it does not incline toward wicked words. It restrains it by not allowing thought to proceed into consent. Thus, in accordance with the Apostle’s command, sin does not reign in our mortal body, and we do not present our members as weapons of wickedness to sin (Rom. 6:12–13).

Those who refrain from moving their members to sin only because no power to do so is allowed are certainly far from fulfilling this command. If that power were present, they would immediately show, through the movement of their members as weapons, who reigns within them. Consequently, insofar as it depends on them, they present their members as weapons of wickedness to sin, because they desire what they do not present only because they cannot.

### 5. Bodily continence is not violated when continence of the heart is preserved.

Accordingly, that restraint of the genital members which is commonly and properly called continence is not violated by any transgression if the higher continence of which we have been speaking for some time is preserved in the heart.

For this reason, after the Lord had said, “From the heart come evil thoughts,” he then added what belongs to evil thoughts: “murders, adulteries,” and so forth. He did not name everything, but by giving certain examples he indicated that other things were also to be understood.

None of these things can be done unless an evil thought has preceded it, by which what is done outwardly is first established inwardly and which, proceeding from the mouth of the heart, already pollutes the person, even if no opportunity is granted for it to be carried out outwardly through the limbs of the body [Note: The Michaelinian manuscript reads “by which what is done outwardly is established.”].

Therefore, once the door of continence has been placed in the mouth of the heart, from which all the things that defile a person come forth, if nothing of this kind is permitted to emerge, cleanliness follows, so that the conscience may already rejoice—even though this is not yet the perfection in which continence will no longer struggle against vice.

For now, however, as long as the flesh desires against the spirit and the spirit against the flesh (Gal. 5:17), it is enough for us not to consent to the evils that we feel within us. When this consent occurs, what defiles a person comes out of the mouth of the heart. But when consent is not held through continence [Note: Two Vatican manuscripts and the Fuliensis read “when consent is held,” omitting “not.”], the evil of carnal desire, against which spiritual desire struggles, is not allowed to cause harm.

## CHAPTER THREE

### 6. Continence’s struggle against desires as long as we are in this life. The inward struggle of desires is experienced only by fighters for virtue. Desire is recognized through the law but conquered only through grace. We must fight so that the desire of sin does not reign. The works of the flesh must be put to death.

It is one thing to fight well, as happens now, when resistance is offered to the struggle of death [Note: The Michaelinian manuscript reads “when resistance is offered to death through struggle.” Two Vatican manuscripts read “when the mind resists through intention.” This is incorrect, for Augustine alludes to the Apostle’s words to the Corinthians: “Where, O death, is your struggle?” (1 Cor. 15:55). He regularly cites this passage with *contention* in place of *victory*, as in the Vulgate: the Greek *neikos*, written with the diphthong, means “contention”; otherwise it means “victory.”]; it is another thing to have no adversary, which will happen when death, the last enemy, is destroyed (1 Cor. 15:55, 26).

For continence itself, when it restrains and curbs desires, both seeks the good toward whose immortality we are advancing and rejects the evil with which we struggle in this mortality. It is the lover and observer [Note: The Vatican manuscripts read “seeker.” Perhaps “expectant observer” should be read.] of the former, but the enemy and witness of the latter: desiring honor and fleeing disgrace.

Continence would not labor to restrain desires if nothing pleased us contrary to what is fitting [Note: Erasmus and the Louvain edition read, “if nothing held us back from that against which we should contend.” But the manuscripts read, “if nothing pleased us contrary to what is fitting—or would be fitting.” Thus Augustine often joins the verb *libet*—which is usually construed with the dative—to the accusative.], if nothing from evil desire opposed our good will.

The Apostle cries out: “I know,” he says, “that good does not dwell in me, that is, in my flesh. For the will to do good is present with me, but I do not find the means to accomplish it.” For now it is possible to do good by not consenting to evil desire; good will be perfected when evil desire itself has come to an end.

The same teacher of the Gentiles also cries out: “I delight in the law of God according to the inward person, but I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind” (Rom. 7:18, 22–23).

### 7. Desire is conquered only through grace, not through the law alone.

Only fighters for virtue and conquerors of vice experience this struggle within themselves; and the evil of desire is conquered only by the good of continence.

There are people who know nothing at all of God’s law. They do not even count evil desires among their enemies, and in their pitiable blindness they serve them; indeed, they consider themselves blessed when they satisfy rather than subdue them.

Those who have recognized these desires through the law—for “through the law comes knowledge of sin” (Rom. 3:20), and, “I would not have known desire,” he says, “unless the law had said, ‘You shall not desire’” (Rom. 7:7)—are nevertheless defeated by their attack because they live under the law, which commands what is good but does not grant it. They do not live under grace, which through the Holy Spirit gives what the law commands.

For this reason the law entered, so that transgression might abound in them (Rom. 5:20). Prohibition increased desire and made it unconquerable, so that transgression might be added, which did not exist without the law, even though sin existed [Note: The Louvain edition reads “did not exist.” The word “not” is absent from Erasmus’s edition and from the manuscripts.]. “For where there is no law, neither is there transgression” (Rom. 4:15).

Thus, when grace does not assist, the law, by prohibiting sin, has itself become the strength of sin [Note: From the manuscripts we have restored the word “become,” omitted in the printed editions. Some manuscripts have “of the deed” in its place.]. Hence the Apostle says: “The strength of sin is the law” (1 Cor. 15:56).

Nor is it surprising that human weakness added strength even to a good law for evil, while relying on its own strength to fulfill that law. Ignorant of God’s righteousness, which he grants to the weak, and wishing to establish his own righteousness, which the weak person lacks, he is not subject to God’s righteousness; he is rejected and proud (Rom. 10:3).

But when the law makes a person a transgressor—wounded more grievously by this very process, so that he desires a physician—and leads him to grace like a tutor, the Lord gives, against the harmful sweetness by which desire was conquering, a beneficial sweetness by which continence may delight more, and “our land gives its fruit” (Ps. 84:13), by which the soldier who, with God’s help, conquers sin is nourished [Note: The Cistercian manuscript reads “by which continence is delighted.” The printed editions read “by which continence may be delighted.”].

### 8. The apostolic trumpet calls us to battle against sin.

The apostolic trumpet arouses such soldiers to battle with this sound:

“Therefore,” he says, “let not sin reign in your mortal body, so as to obey its desires; and do not present your members as weapons of wickedness to sin, but present yourselves to God as those who are alive from the dead, and your members as weapons of righteousness to God. For sin will not rule over you. For you are not under the law but under grace” (Rom. 6:12–14).

And elsewhere: “Therefore, brothers,” he says, “we are debtors not to the flesh, to live according to the flesh. For if you live according to the flesh, you will die; but if by the spirit you put to death the deeds of the flesh, you will live. For all who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God” (Rom. 8:12–14).

Therefore, as long as this mortal life of ours exists under grace, what is now being accomplished is that sin—that is, the desire of sin, for this is what he calls it here by the name “sin”—must not reign in our mortal body. It is shown to reign when its desires are obeyed.

The desire of sin is therefore within us, but it must not be permitted to reign. Its desires are present, but they must not be obeyed, lest it reign through those who obey them. For this reason, desire must not seize our members for itself; rather, continence must claim them for itself, so that they may be weapons of righteousness for God and not weapons of wickedness for sin. In this way sin will not rule over us.

For we are not under the law, which indeed commands what is good but does not grant it. We are under grace, which makes us love what the law commands and, having done so, is able to command free people.

### 9. The works of the flesh must be put to death.

When he also urges us not to live according to the flesh, lest we die, but by the spirit to put to death the deeds of the flesh so that we may live, the trumpet that sounds certainly reveals the war in which we are engaged. It stirs us to fight fiercely and to put our enemies to death, lest we be put to death by them.

He made it sufficiently clear who these enemies are. Those whom he wanted us to put to death are the works of the flesh. For he says: “But if by the spirit you put to death the deeds of the flesh, you will live.”

And so that we may know what these are, let us hear that same Apostle writing to the Galatians and saying: “The works of the flesh are manifest: fornications, uncleanness, licentiousness, the service of idols, magical practices, enmities, strife, jealousies, animosities, dissensions, heresies, envies, drunkenness, revelries, and things like these. I warn you, as I warned you before, that those who do such things will not possess the kingdom of God.”

There too he was showing the war itself when he said these things, and with the same heavenly and spiritual trumpet he was rousing Christ’s soldiers to put these enemies to death. For earlier he had said: “I say, walk by the spirit, and do not fulfill the desires of the flesh. For the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh. These oppose each other, so that you do not do the things you want. But if you are led by the spirit, you are not under the law.”

Thus he wants those established under grace to maintain this conflict against the works of the flesh. And to demonstrate these works of the flesh, he added the things I have mentioned above: “The works of the flesh are manifest: fornications,” and so forth—whether those he mentioned or those he indicated were to be understood, especially by adding, “and things like these.”

Finally, in this battle, as though bringing forward a spiritual army in another line against the army of the flesh, he says: “But the fruit of the spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, continence; against such things there is no law.”

He did not say, “against these,” lest they be thought to be the only ones. Even if he had said this, we ought to understand all the good things of the same kind that we could imagine. But he said, “against such things”—that is, against these and whatever things are similar.

Nevertheless, by placing continence last among the good things he mentioned—continence, which we have now undertaken to discuss and on account of which we have already said so much—he especially wished it to remain fixed in our minds. For it is particularly powerful in this battle, in which the spirit desires against the flesh, since in a certain manner it crucifies the desires of the flesh.

Accordingly, after the Apostle had said these things, he immediately added: “Those who belong to Jesus Christ have crucified their flesh with its passions and desires” (Gal. 5:16–24). This is the work of continence; in this way the works of the flesh are put to death [Note: The Cistercian manuscript reads: “This is the work of continence, if the works of the flesh are put to death.”]. They put to death those whom desire, when they fall away from continence, drags into consenting to the perpetration of such works.

## CHAPTER FOUR

### 10. To preserve continence, presumption concerning one’s own strength must be avoided. To live according to the human being and to live according to the flesh are the same.

To avoid falling away from continence, we must be especially vigilant against those snares of diabolical suggestion that lead us to presume upon our own strength. For “cursed is everyone who places his hope in a human being” (Jer. 17:5). And who is this, if not a human being [Note: The printed editions read “if not the human being himself.” The word “himself” is absent from the manuscripts.]?

Therefore, one who places hope in himself cannot truthfully say that he does not place his hope in a human being. For what else is living according to the human being than living according to the flesh? Let the person who is tempted by such a suggestion hear this—and, if he has any Christian understanding, let him tremble: let him hear, I say, “If you live according to the flesh, you will die.”

### 11. The Christian meaning of “flesh” and “human being.”

Someone may say to me that living according to the human being is one thing and living according to the flesh another, because the human being is a rational creature, possessing a rational soul by which he differs from an animal, whereas the flesh is the lowest and earthly part of the human being; therefore, to live according to it is vicious.

For this reason, the one who lives according to the human being does not live according to the flesh, but rather according to that part of the human being by which he is human—that is, according to the spirit of the mind, by which he surpasses animals.

Perhaps this argument has some force in the schools of philosophers. But if we wish to understand the Apostle of Christ, we must attend to the way in which Christian books customarily speak.

It is certainly the faith of all of us, for whom Christ is life, that the human being was assumed by the Word of God, and not without a rational soul, as certain heretics wish. Yet we read: “The Word became flesh” (John 1:14). What is to be understood here by “flesh” except a human being?

“And all flesh shall see the salvation of God” (Luke 3:6): what can this mean except “every human being”? “All flesh shall come to you” (Ps. 64:3): what does this mean except “every human being”? “You have given him authority over all flesh” (John 17:2): what does this mean except “over every human being”? “By the works of the law no flesh will be justified” (Rom. 3:20): what does this mean except “no human being will be justified”?

The same Apostle expresses this more clearly elsewhere: “A human being will not be justified by the works of the law” (Gal. 2:16).

He also rebukes the Corinthians, saying: “Are you not carnal, and do you not walk according to the human being?” (1 Cor. 3:3). Having called them carnal, he did not say, “you walk according to the flesh,” but “according to the human being.” For what else did he intend this to mean except “according to the flesh”? If walking—or living—according to the flesh were blameworthy but walking according to the human being praiseworthy, he certainly would not have said reproachfully, “you walk according to the human being.”

Let the human being recognize the reproach [Note: The Louvain edition alone reads, “Let the human being hear the reproach.”], let him change his purpose, and let him avoid destruction. Hear, human being: do not walk according to the human being, but according to the one who made the human being. Do not depart from the one who made you, nor turn toward yourself.

For a human being was speaking—yet he was not living according to the human being—when he said: “Not that we are competent to think anything from ourselves, as though from ourselves; our competence is from God” (2 Cor. 3:5). Consider whether the one who truthfully said this was living according to the human being.

Therefore, by warning the human being not to live according to the human being, the Apostle returns the human being to God. Whoever does not live according to the human being but according to God certainly does not live according to himself either, because he too is a human being.

But he is also said to live according to the flesh when he lives in this manner, because “flesh” alone can be used to mean “human being,” as we have already shown. Likewise, “soul” alone can be used to mean “human being.” Hence it is said: “Let every soul be subject to the higher authorities” (Rom. 13:1)—that is, every human being; and, “Seventy-five souls went down into Egypt with Jacob” (Gen. 46:27)—that is, seventy-five human beings.

Therefore, do not live according to yourself, O human being. You had perished, but you were sought. Do not, I say, live according to yourself: you had perished, and you were found [Note: Some manuscripts read this way. Erasmus reads, “if, because you had perished, you were found.” Louvain reads, “if you had perished, you were found.”].

Do not accuse the nature of the flesh when you hear, “If you live according to the flesh, you will die.” For it could be said, and said most truthfully, “If you live according to yourselves, you will die.”

The devil has no flesh, yet because he wished to live according to himself, he did not remain in the truth. What wonder, then [Note: Several manuscripts read this way. The printed editions instead read, “What is more truly the case, then?” They also read below “what he truly said” instead of “what he said as truth.”], if one who lives according to himself, when he speaks falsehood, speaks from what is his own (John 8:44)? This is what Truth said truthfully about him.

## CHAPTER FIVE

### 12. Whoever wishes to conquer the desire of sin must not trust in himself. The excuses of sins must be restrained through continence. Various excuses for sins: accusation of fate, fortune, the devil, and, among the Manichaeans, God himself.

When you hear, “Sin will not rule over you,” do not trust in yourself, as though sin will not rule over you through your own power. Rather, trust in the one to whom a certain holy person says in prayer: “Direct my ways according to your word, and let no iniquity rule over me” (Ps. 118:133).

For lest, when we heard, “Sin will not rule over you,” we should exalt ourselves and attribute this to our own strength, the Apostle immediately saw this danger and added: “For you are not under the law but under grace” (Rom. 6:14).

Grace, therefore, makes sin not rule over you. Do not trust in yourself, then, lest it rule over you all the more on that account.

And when we hear, “If by the spirit you put to death the deeds of the flesh, you will live,” let us not attribute this great good to our spirit as though it could accomplish it by itself. For lest we understand this carnal sense as referring to a spirit that is dead rather than one that puts to death [Note: The manuscripts read this way. The printed editions read “a spirit that gives life.”], he immediately added: “For all who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God” (Rom. 8:13–14).

Therefore, in order that we may put the works of the flesh to death by our spirit, we are led by the Spirit of God, who gives continence, by which we restrain, subdue, and conquer desire.

### 13. Continence must also restrain the proud excuses by which sinners evade responsibility.

In this great battle, in which a human being lives under grace and, when he fights well with divine assistance, rejoices in the Lord with trembling, even vigorous soldiers are not without certain wounds of sin—not even those who put the works of the flesh to death, though they may be unconquered. Because of these wounds, which must be healed, they truthfully say every day: “Forgive us our debts” (Matt. 6:12).

Against these same vices and against the devil, the prince and king of vices, they must fight through prayer itself with far greater vigilance and intensity, lest his deadly suggestions have any power. Through these suggestions he incites the sinner to excuse rather than accuse his sins; and thus the wounds are not only left unhealed but, even if they were not deadly, are inflicted severely and lethally.

Here too more cautious continence is necessary, by which the proud desire of the human being is restrained—the desire by which he pleases himself, does not wish to be found guilty, and, when he sins, disdains being convicted of having sinned. Instead of accepting the accusation of himself with salutary humility, he seeks an excuse through ruinous pride.

To restrain this pride, the Psalmist whose words I have already quoted and commended as best I could asked continence from the Lord. For when he had said, “Set, O Lord, a guard over my mouth, and a door of continence around my lips; do not incline my heart toward wicked words,” he explained more clearly why he said this: “to make excuses for sins” (Ps. 140:3–4).

For what is more wicked than these words, by which a wicked person denies that he is wicked, even when convicted by a wicked deed that he cannot deny? Since he cannot conceal what he has done, nor call it a good deed, and sees that it is plainly his own deed, he seeks to attribute to another what he himself has done, as though by doing so he could remove from himself what he has deserved.

Unwilling to be guilty, he adds instead to his guilt. By excusing rather than accusing his sins, he does not understand that he removes not punishment, but forgiveness. Among human judges, who can be deceived, any sort of deceptive defense by which a wrongful act seems to be cleared may appear temporarily useful. But before God, who cannot be deceived, one must not offer a deceptive defense, but a truthful confession of sins.

14. There are also others who customarily excuse their sins, complaining that they are driven to sin by fate, as though the stars had decreed this and heaven had first sinned by making such decrees, so that afterward human beings would sin by committing such acts. Others prefer to attribute their sins to fortune: they think that everything is stirred up by chance occurrences, yet they insist that they know and affirm this not through the rashness of chance, but by considered reasoning. What madness, then, is it to attribute their arguments to reason and subject their actions to chance? Others refer everything they do wrong to the devil; yet they do not wish to share any part of the blame with him, although they can suspect that he suggested evil to them through hidden promptings, while they cannot doubt that they consented to those suggestions, from whatever source they came.

There are also those who extend their excuse into an accusation of God—wretched in their view of divine judgment, but blasphemous in their own frenzy. For, proceeding from the opposite principle, they introduce a substance of evil rebelling against Him, which, they say, could not have been resisted unless He had mingled with that rebellious substance a portion of His own substance and nature, to be contaminated and corrupted by it. Then they say that they sin when the nature of evil prevails over the nature of God. This is the utterly filthy madness of the Manichaeans, whose diabolical contrivances are very easily overthrown by the undeniable truth that confesses God’s nature to be uncontaminable and incorruptible. What disgraceful contamination and corruption, indeed, should not rightly be expected from those who believe that God, supremely and incomparably good, is contaminable and corruptible?

## CHAPTER VI

### 15. Against others who, in order to excuse themselves, say that sins please God. God makes good things even from evil things. Human beings were made with the power to sin, and are to receive as a reward the inability to sin.

There are also those who, in the same manner of excusing their sins, accuse God by saying that sins please Him. “If they displeased Him,” they say, “His almighty power would certainly never permit them to occur.” As though God had permitted sins to remain unpunished—even in those whom He frees from everlasting punishment by forgiving their sins.

No one receives pardon for a deservedly heavier punishment unless he has paid some punishment, even though it be far less than he deserved; and thus the generosity of mercy is bestowed without abandoning the justice of discipline. Even the sin that seems to go unpunished has its punishment following after it, so that no one who has committed it either suffers grief in bitterness or, through blindness, fails to suffer grief.

Therefore, just as you say, “Why does He permit these things if they displease Him?” so I say, “Why does He punish these things if they please Him?” Accordingly, just as I confess that these things would not occur at all unless they were permitted by the Almighty, so you should confess that what is punished by the Just One ought not to be done. By not doing what He punishes, we may deserve to learn from Him why He permits things that He will punish.

“For the mature,” as it is written, “solid food” belongs (Hebrews 5:14). Those who have made good progress understand by this that it belonged rather to God’s almighty power to permit the evils arising from the free choice of the will. His goodness is so almighty (manuscripts: “so almighty” [tam quippe]) that He can make good things even from evil things—whether by forgiving, healing, adapting and turning them to the advantage of the devout, or even by punishing them with perfect justice.

All these things are good and supremely worthy of the good and almighty God; yet they arise only from evils. What, then, is better or more powerful than the One who does no evil, yet makes good even from evils?

Those who have done evil cry out to Him, “Forgive us our debts” (Matthew 6:12); He hears and forgives. Their evils have harmed sinners; He comes to their aid and heals their sicknesses. Their enemies rage against them; from the rage of those enemies He makes martyrs. Finally, He also condemns those whom He judges worthy of condemnation: although they suffer their own evils, He nevertheless does what is good. For what is just cannot fail to be good; and just as sin is unjust, so the punishment of sin is just.

### 16. God did not lack the power to make a human being unable to sin; but He preferred to make one who could sin if he wished and not sin if he did not wish—prohibiting the former and commanding the latter—so that at first the good merit would be not sinning, and afterward the just reward would be being unable to sin.

For He will also make His saints at the end such that they will be altogether unable to sin. Even now He has such angels, whom we love in Him in such a way that we fear none of them will become a devil by sinning. We do not presume this of any righteous human being during the mortality of this life. But we confidently believe that all will be such in the immortality of that life.

For the almighty God, who makes good things even from our evils—what good things will He give when He has freed us from every evil? Much more abundantly and subtly could be said about the good use of evil; but we have not undertaken that subject in this discourse, and its excessive length must be avoided.

## CHAPTER VII

### 17. The duties of continence and justice alike tend toward peace. Against the Manichaean madness concerning two natures fighting against one another. There is war in the human being because of the sickness contracted through fault; peace will come when the sickness has been healed.

Let us now return to the subject for which we said these things. We need continence, and we recognize it as a divine gift, so that our heart may not turn toward evil words “to make excuses for sins.” For what sin do we lack the necessary continence to restrain it from being committed, when continence itself also restrains us from defending it with wicked pride after it has been committed?

Thus, universally, we need continence in order to turn away from evil. But in order to do good, this seems to belong to another virtue, namely justice. The sacred Psalm admonishes us of this when we read: “Turn away from evil and do good.” And it immediately adds for what end we should do these things, saying: “Seek peace and pursue it” (Psalm 33:15).

For our peace will then be perfect when, with our nature inseparably clinging to its Creator, nothing within us resists us. This too, as I understand it, the Savior Himself wished to signify when He said: “Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning” (Luke 12:35). [One Vatican manuscript adds “in your hands,” which neither the printed editions nor other manuscripts contain; it is absent from the Greek Gospel text and from the Latin text of the ancient Corbie Bibles.] What does it mean to gird the loins? To restrain lusts—which is the work of continence. And what does it mean to have burning lamps? To shine and burn with good works—which is the work of justice.

Nor did He leave unstated the end for which we should do these things, adding and saying: “And you yourselves be like people waiting for their master, when he returns from the wedding” (Luke 12:35–36). When He comes, He will reward us: we have restrained ourselves from the things that desire suggested [the Cistercian codex adds “suggested”; Vatican manuscripts read “incited,” but “commanded” is understood], and have done the things that love commanded, so that in His perfect and everlasting peace we may reign without any conflict with evil and with the fullest delight in good.

### 18. All who believe in the living and true God—whose supremely good and unchangeable nature neither does nor suffers any evil, from whom all good comes, including good that can be diminished [the Lovaniensis edition reads “cannot be diminished,” wrongly and against the other editions and manuscripts], while He Himself, who is His own good, cannot be diminished at all—when we hear the Apostle saying, “Walk by the Spirit, and you shall not fulfill the desires of the flesh; for the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh; for these oppose one another, so that you do not do the things you wish” (Galatians 5:16–17), must not believe, as the madness of the Manichaeans does, that two natures arising from contrary principles are here being shown to fight against one another, one good and the other evil.

Both of these are entirely good: the spirit is good, and the flesh is good; and the human being, who consists of both, with one commanding and the other serving, is certainly good—but a changeable good. Yet this could not exist [printed editions: “it is evident that it cannot exist”; manuscripts: “it could not exist,” omitting “it is evident”] unless it came from the unchangeable Good, from whom every created good comes, whether small or great; however small, it was nevertheless made by the Great; and however great, it is in no way comparable with the greatness of its Maker.

But in this good human nature, created and established well by the Good, there is now war, because salvation has not yet arrived. When the sickness is healed, there will be peace. This sickness was deserved through fault; nature did not originally possess it. God’s grace has already forgiven this fault to the faithful through the washing of regeneration, but under the hands of the same physician nature still struggles with its sickness.

In such a battle, health will be the complete victory—not temporary health, but eternal health. There the present sickness will not merely come to an end; no sickness will arise thereafter. For this reason the righteous addresses his soul and says: “Bless the Lord, my soul, and do not forget all His rewards: He who is gracious to all your iniquities, who heals all your sicknesses” (Psalm 102:2–3).

He is gracious toward iniquities when He forgives sins; He heals sicknesses when He restrains wicked desires. He is gracious toward iniquities by granting pardon; He heals sicknesses by granting continence. The former occurred in Baptism for those who confessed; the latter occurs in the struggle for those who contend, in which our sickness must be conquered by us through His help.

Even now the former occurs when we are heard saying, “Forgive us our debts”; the latter when we are heard saying, “Do not lead us into temptation” (Matthew 6:12–13). For each person is tempted, as the apostle James says, when he is drawn away and enticed by his own desire (James 1:14).

Against this vice we ask medicinal help from Him who can heal all such sicknesses—not by separating us from another nature [printed editions: “by a separation from another [nature]”; manuscripts more correctly: “by separation from another [nature]”], but by restoring our own nature. Therefore the apostle mentioned above did not say, “Each person is tempted by desire,” but added, “his own,” so that whoever hears this may understand how he ought to cry out: “I said, Lord, have mercy on me; heal my soul, for I have sinned against You” (Psalm 40:5).

He would not have needed healing unless he had corrupted himself by sinning, so that his own flesh desired against him—that is, he himself, in the part in which he had been weakened in the flesh, resisted himself.

## CHAPTER VIII

### 19. The flesh desires against the spirit, not because it is an alien nature, but because it has been corrupted. The desires of the flesh arise from corruption; they can here be diminished, but cannot be wholly removed except in the life to come. Here the desire of the flesh is the punishment of sin; when the flesh has been healed, it will not exist among the blessed.

For the flesh desires nothing except through the soul. Yet the flesh is said to desire against the spirit when the soul, through carnal desire, resists the spirit. All this is what we are; and the flesh itself, which dies when the soul departs, is our lower part. It is not abandoned as something to be fled from, but laid down in order to be received again; and once received, it will never again be abandoned.

“It is sown an animal body; it will rise a spiritual body” (1 Corinthians 15:44). Then the flesh will no longer desire against the spirit, when it too will be called spiritual, because it will be subjected to the spirit and vivified eternally—not only without any resistance, but also without any need for bodily nourishment.

Therefore, since these two things now oppose one another within us, and we are present in both, let us pray and act so that they may be reconciled. We must not consider one of them an enemy, but the vice by which the flesh desires against the spirit. Once this vice has been healed, it will no longer exist; both substances will be preserved, and there will be no conflict between them.

Let us hear the Apostle: “I know,” he says, “that good does not dwell in me, that is, in my flesh.” He says this because the vice of the flesh is not good within a good thing. When that vice ceases to exist, the flesh will remain, but it will no longer be corrupted or vicious.

That the flesh belongs to our nature the same teacher shows by first saying, “I know that good does not dwell in me”; then, to explain this, he adds, “that is, in my flesh.” He therefore says that his flesh is himself. It is not, then, itself our enemy; and when its vices are resisted, it is loved, because it is being healed.

“For no one has ever hated his own flesh” (Ephesians 5:29), as the Apostle himself says. And elsewhere he says: “Therefore it is I myself who with the mind serve the law of God, but with the flesh the law of sin.” Let those who have ears hear: “It is I myself”—I with the mind, I with the flesh; but with the mind I serve the law of God, while with the flesh I serve the law of sin.

How does he serve the law of sin with the flesh? Surely not by consenting to carnal desire. Far from it. Rather, he has within himself the movements of desire that he does not wish to have, yet does have. By not consenting to them in his mind, he serves the law of God and restrains his members from becoming weapons of sin.

### 20. There are therefore evil desires within us, but by not consenting to them we do not live wickedly. There are within us desires for sins, but by not obeying them we do not complete evil; nevertheless, because we have them, we do not yet complete good.

The Apostle shows both points: that good is not completed here, where evil is desired in this way, and that evil is not completed here when such desire is not obeyed. He shows the former when he says, “To will is present with me, but to accomplish the good is not” (Romans 7:18, 25); the latter when he says, “Walk by the Spirit, and you shall not fulfill the desires of the flesh.”

For in the first passage he does not say that doing good is not present with him, but that completing it is not. Nor does he say here, “Do not have the desires of the flesh,” but “Do not fulfill them.”

Thus evil desires arise within us when we take pleasure in what is forbidden; but they are not fulfilled when lusts are restrained while the mind serves the law of God. And good is done when what is wrongly desired is not done because a good delight prevails; yet the perfection of good is not fulfilled so long as, while the flesh serves the law of sin [the Lovaniensis edition reads “while the flesh serves”; corrected from the other editions and manuscripts, most of which subsequently read: “unlawful desire, although restrained, nevertheless is stirred”], unlawful desire remains—and, although restrained, is still stirred. It would not need to be restrained unless it were stirred.

One day there will also be perfection of good, when evil is brought to an end: the former will be supreme, the latter nonexistent. But if we think this should be hoped for in our present mortality, we are deceived. It will be then, when death no longer exists; and it will be there, where eternal life exists.

In that age and in that kingdom there will be supreme good and no evil, when and where there will be supreme love of wisdom and no labor of continence.

The flesh is therefore not evil if it is without evil—that is, without the vice by which the human being has been corrupted. The human being was not made badly; rather, he himself made the evil by which he became bad. Made good by the good God from both parts—that is, from soul and body—he himself made the evil by which he became bad.

Although he has already been released from the guilt of that evil through pardon, so that he does not regard lightly what he has done, he still struggles against his vice through continence. Far be it from us to think that there will be any vices in the peace in which those who reign will dwell, since in this present warfare, as those who progress, they daily diminish not only their sins but also the desires themselves, with which they struggle by refusing consent and by which they sin when they consent.

### 21. The fact that the flesh desires against the spirit, that good does not dwell in our flesh, and that the law in our members resists the law of our mind does not result from a mixture of two natures made from contrary principles, but from the division of one nature against itself because of the desert of sin [some manuscripts read “as a result of sin”].

We were not such in Adam before human nature, having heard and followed its deceiver, despised and offended its own Creator. This is not the original life of the human being as created, but the subsequent punishment of the condemned.

Freed from this condemnation through the grace of Jesus Christ, those who are liberated struggle with their punishment, not yet possessing complete salvation but already having received its pledge. Those who are not liberated are both guilty of sins [the Michaelinus manuscript reads “of sin”; the Fuliensis and certain others read: “those not liberated from sins are guilty”] and entangled in punishments.

After this life, punishment for guilt will remain eternally for the guilty; but for the liberated, neither guilt nor punishment will remain eternally. The good substances of spirit and flesh will remain forever—substances that the good and unchangeable God created good, although changeable.

They will remain transformed for the better, never again to be transformed for the worse, when every evil has been utterly consumed: both the evil that human beings unjustly committed and the evil that they justly suffered.

When these two kinds of evil have entirely perished—the one consisting in preceding wickedness, the other in subsequent misery—the human being will possess a will that is right, without any perversity. There it will be clear and evident to all what many of the faithful now believe but few understand: evil is not a substance. Rather, as a wound in the body, so in the substance that corrupted itself [some manuscripts; printed editions read “so [it began] to corrupt the substance”], evil began as an infection and will there cease through perfect health.

When, therefore, every evil that arose from us has been removed from us, and our own good has been increased and perfected to the summit of the most blessed incorruption and immortality, what will our two substances be like?

Even now, in this corruption and mortality, while “the corruptible body weighs down the soul” (Wisdom 9:15), and while, as the Apostle says, “the body is dead because of sin” (Romans 8:10), he nevertheless bears this testimony to our flesh—that is, to our lower and earthly part—which I mentioned shortly before: “No one has ever hated his own flesh.” He immediately adds: “But he nourishes and cherishes it, just as Christ does the Church.”

## CHAPTER IX

### 22. The flesh is not evil by nature, since the Apostle exhorts husbands to love their wives by its example. The Apostle indicates three unions, all of them good, the third being that of flesh and spirit. Why no example of submission for the woman is drawn from the flesh.

By what error—or rather, by what utter madness—do the Manichaeans attribute our flesh to some fabulous race of darkness, which they wish to have possessed an evil nature eternally, without any beginning? The truthful teacher exhorts men to love their wives by the example of their own flesh, and also exhorts them to this by the example of Christ and the Church.

The whole relevant passage of the apostolic Epistle should finally be recalled:

“Husbands,” he says, “love your wives, just as Christ also loved the Church and gave Himself for her, so that He might sanctify her, cleansing her by the washing of water with the word, so that He might present the glorious Church to Himself, not having spot or wrinkle or anything of this kind, but so that she might be holy and without blemish. Thus,” he says, “husbands also ought to love their wives as their own bodies. He who loves his wife loves himself” (Ephesians 5:25–29).

Then he added what we have already mentioned: “For no one has ever hated his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it, just as Christ does the Church.”

What does the madness of this utterly filthy impiety say to these things? What do you say to these things, Manichaeans—you who attempt to introduce to us, as though from the apostolic writings, two natures without beginning, one good and the other evil, and who refuse to listen to the apostolic writings that would correct you from this sacrilegious perversity?

Just as you read, “The flesh desires against the spirit” (Galatians 5:17), and “Good does not dwell in my flesh,” so read also: “No one has ever hated his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it, just as Christ does the Church.” Just as you read, “I see another law in my members, resisting the law of my mind” (Romans 7:18, 23), so read also: “Just as Christ loved the Church, so husbands ought to love their wives as their own bodies.”

Do not be deceitful toward those testimonies of Holy Scripture and deaf toward these; then you will be corrected by both. For if you accept these in the manner they deserve, you will also strive to understand those as they are true.

### 23. The Apostle has suggested three unions to us: Christ and the Church, husband and wife, and spirit and flesh. The earlier members of these unions provide for the later, while the later serve the earlier. All are good when some preserve, with excellence, the beauty of order by being placed first, and others, with propriety, by being placed beneath.

Husband and wife receive both a command and an example concerning how they ought to be toward one another. The command is: “Let wives be subject to their husbands as to the Lord, because the husband is the head of the wife”; and: “Husbands, love your wives.” The example is given to wives from the Church and to husbands from Christ: “As the Church,” he says, “is subject to Christ, so also let wives be subject to their husbands in everything.”

Likewise, after giving husbands the command that they should love their wives, he added the example: “As Christ loved the Church.” But he also exhorted husbands by reference to what is lower, namely their own body, and not only by reference to what is higher, namely their Lord.

For he did not say only, “Husbands, love your wives as Christ also loved the Church,” which is an exhortation from what is higher; he also said, “Husbands ought to love their wives as their own bodies” (Ephesians 5:22–28), which is an exhortation from what is lower. For both what is higher and what is lower are entirely good.

Yet the woman did not receive from the body or flesh an example that she should be subject to her husband as the flesh is subject to the spirit. Either the Apostle intended us to understand what he omitted to say, or perhaps, because the flesh desires against the spirit in the mortality and sickness of this life, he did not wish to use it as an example of submission for the woman.

He wished to use it for men, however, because although the spirit desires against the flesh, even in this it provides for the flesh—not as the flesh, desiring against the spirit, provides for the spirit by such resistance [manuscripts; printed editions read “such resistance”], nor for itself. Nevertheless, the good spirit would not provide for it, either by nourishing and cherishing its nature through providence or by resisting its vices through continence, unless each substance indicated, by the beauty of this order, that the same God is the Maker of both.

What, then, is the matter with you? In your true madness you boast that you are Christians, yet with eyes closed—or rather, extinguished—you contend with such perversity against the Christian Scriptures [the Erfurt and Venetian editions omit “and”], asserting that Christ appeared to mortals in false flesh; that the Church belongs to Christ in soul but to the devil in body; that the male and female sexes are the work of the devil, not of God; and that flesh, as an evil substance, is joined to the spirit as a good substance?

## CHAPTER X

### 24. The Manichaean heresy denies that Christ had true flesh. It says that souls belong to Christ, bodies to the devil, and that both sexes come from the devil.

If what we have recalled from the apostolic writings seems to you insufficient as a reply [some manuscripts: “If replying seems too slight a thing to you”], listen to other things as well, if you have ears.

What does the utterly insane Manichaean say about Christ’s flesh? That it was not true, but false. What does the blessed Apostle say to this? “Remember Jesus Christ, risen from the dead, from the seed of David, according to my gospel” (2 Timothy 2:8). And Christ Jesus Himself says: “Touch Me and see, because a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see Me having” (Luke 24:39).

How can there be truth in their teaching, which proclaims that what was in Christ’s flesh was falsehood? How was there no evil in Christ, in whom there was such a great lie? Evidently, for people who are excessively pure, true flesh is evil, while false flesh in place of true flesh is not evil. True flesh born from David’s seed is evil, while a false tongue saying, “Touch Me and see, because a spirit does not have bones and flesh, as you see Me having,” is not evil!

What does the deceiver of human beings say about the Church in his deadly error? That it belongs partly to Christ in respect of souls and partly to the devil in respect of bodies. What does the Teacher of the Gentiles say to this, in faith and truth? “Do you not know,” he says, “that your bodies are members of Christ?” (1 Corinthians 6:15).

What does the son of perdition say about the male and female sexes? That neither sex comes from God, but both from the devil. What does the chosen Vessel say to this? “Just as the woman is from the man, so also the man is through the woman; but all things are from God” (1 Corinthians 11:12).

What does the unclean spirit say through Manichaeus about the flesh? That it is an evil substance, not God’s creation but the creation of the enemy. What does the Holy Spirit say through Paul to this?

“For just as the body is one and has many members, and all the members of the body, though many, are one body, so also is Christ.” And shortly afterward: “God has placed the members, each one of them [manuscripts; printed editions: “each of them”], in the body as He wished.” Again, shortly afterward: “God has composed the body, giving greater honor to the member that lacked it, so that there might be no division in the body, but that the members might have the same concern for one another. And if one member suffers, all the members suffer with it; if one member is glorified, all the members rejoice with it” (1 Corinthians 12:12–26).

How can the flesh be evil when souls themselves are urged to imitate the peace of its members? How can it be the creation of the enemy when the very souls that govern bodies take their example from bodily members, so that they may not have divisions of hostility among themselves, and may love to possess by grace what God has granted to the body by nature?

Rightly, when writing to the Romans, he says: “I appeal to you, brothers, by the mercy of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God” (Romans 12:1). If we present a living, holy, God-pleasing sacrifice from the bodies of the race of darkness, then we contend without cause [manuscripts; printed editions read “for” rather than “not”] that darkness is light and light is darkness.

## CHAPTER XI

### 25. The comparison between the flesh and the Church, and what it consists in.

“But,” they say, “how is the flesh compared with the Church by means of a certain likeness? Does the Church desire against Christ, when the same Apostle has said, ‘The Church is subject to Christ’?” (Ephesians 5:24).

Certainly the Church is subject to Christ. For the spirit desires against the flesh so that the Church may be subjected to Christ in every respect; but the flesh desires against the spirit because the Church has not yet received the promised perfect peace.

Accordingly, the Church is subject to Christ through the pledge of salvation, while the flesh desires against the spirit through the weakness of sickness. For the same people to whom it was said, “Walk by the Spirit, and you shall not fulfill the desires of the flesh,” were members of the Church. “For the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh; for these oppose one another, so that you do not do the things you wish” (Galatians 5:16–17).

These words were certainly addressed to the Church. If it were not subject to Christ, the spirit would not desire against the flesh within it through continence. For this reason they could indeed fail to fulfill the desires of the flesh, but while the flesh desired against the spirit they could not do what they wished—that is, they could not lack even the desires of the flesh themselves.

Moreover, why should we not confess that in spiritual people the Church is subject to Christ, while in those who are still carnal it continues to desire against Christ? Did those to whom it was said, “Christ is divided” (1 Corinthians 1:13), not desire against Christ? And did they not receive these words: “I could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as carnal, as infants in Christ? I gave you milk to drink, not food; for you were not yet able—and even now you are not able, for you are still carnal. Since there are jealousy and strife among you, are you not carnal?” (1 Corinthians 3:1–3).

Against whom does jealousy and strife desire, if not against Christ? Christ heals these desires of the flesh in His own, but He loves them in no one. Therefore, as long as the holy Church also has such members, it is not yet without spot or wrinkle.

To this are added those sins for which the daily voice of the whole Church says, “Forgive us our debts” (Matthew 6:12). Lest we think that spiritual people are alien to these sins, it was not just any one of the carnal, nor just any one of the spiritual, but the one who reclined upon the Lord’s breast and whom He loved more than the others (John 13:23), who said: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1:8).

In every sin—more in a greater sin, less in a smaller one—there is nevertheless desire against justice. And it is written of Christ: “He was made for us by God wisdom, and righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption” (1 Corinthians 1:30). Therefore, in every sin there is undoubtedly desire against Christ.

But when He who heals all our sicknesses (Psalm 102:3) has brought the Church to the promised healing of sickness, then there will not be in any of its members even the slightest spot or wrinkle. Then the flesh will in no way desire against the spirit, and therefore there will be no reason for the spirit to desire against the flesh either.

Then all this battle will end; then there will be complete harmony between both substances. Then there will be no carnal person there to such a degree that the flesh itself will be spiritual.

What each person living according to Christ now does with his own flesh—when he desires against its evil desire, restrains it because it must be healed [two manuscripts read “because” rather than “when”], and holds it because it has not yet been healed, while nevertheless nourishing and cherishing its good nature, since “no one has ever hated his own flesh” (Ephesians 5:29)—this Christ also does with the Church, insofar as it is permissible to compare lesser things with greater.

For by corrections He restrains it, lest, inflated by impunity, it burst apart [some manuscripts: “be dissolved”]; and by consolations He raises it up, lest, weighed down by weakness, it collapse. Hence the Apostle says: “If we judged ourselves, we would not be judged; but when we are judged, we are corrected by the Lord, so that we may not be condemned with the world” (1 Corinthians 11:31–32). And in the Psalm: “According to the multitude of my sorrows in my heart, Your consolations delighted my soul” (Psalm 93:19).

The perfect health of our flesh without any resistance is therefore to be hoped for when the Church of Christ possesses secure confidence without any fear.

## CHAPTER XII

### 26. The false continence of the Manichaeans and certain others, especially heretics. The unclean continence of some who seek to reach other men’s wives by magical arts.

It will have been sufficient to argue against the deceptively continent Manichaeans in defense of true continence, lest the fruitful and glorious labor of continence—when it restrains and curbs our lower part, namely the body, from immoderate and unlawful pleasures—be thought not to chastise it beneficially but to attack it with hostility.

The body is indeed different in nature from the soul, but it is not alien to human nature. For the soul does not consist of the body; nevertheless, the human being consists of soul and body. And certainly the God who liberates the whole human being liberates the whole human being.

Therefore the Savior Himself also assumed the whole human being, deeming it worthy to liberate in us the whole that He had made. What benefit is it to those who think contrary to this truth to restrain their lusts—if indeed they restrain any? What can be made clean in them through continence, when their continence itself is so unclean? It should not even be called continence.

To think what they think is the devil’s poison; continence, however, is God’s gift. Yet just as not everyone who suffers something, or endures any pains with the utmost endurance, possesses the virtue that is likewise God’s gift and is called patience—for many endure many tortures so that they may not expose either those who are privy to their crimes or themselves; many endure them to satisfy their most burning lusts, and to obtain or not abandon those things to which they are bound by the chain of a wicked love; many endure them because of various and destructive errors by which they are vehemently held; and far be it from us to say that all these possess true patience—so not everyone who restrains something, even if he extraordinarily restrains the lusts of flesh or soul, should be said to possess this continence whose usefulness and beauty we are discussing.

Some, indeed—something that may seem astonishing to say—are continent through incontinence, as when a woman abstains from her husband because she has sworn this to an adulterer. Some are continent through injustice, as when one spouse does not render to the other the marital due because either he or she is now able to overcome such bodily desire.

Again, some are continent because they have been deceived by false faith, hoping for empty things and pursuing empty things. These include all heretics and all who are deceived by some error under the name of religion. Their continence would be genuine if their faith were genuine also. But since that cannot even be called faith because it is false, this too is undoubtedly unworthy of the name of continence.

Are we really going to say that the continence [printed editions: “continence of faith”; “of faith” is absent from the manuscripts] which we most truly call God’s gift is a sin? Far be such detestable madness from our hearts. But the blessed Apostle says: “Whatever is not from faith is sin” (Romans 14:23). Whatever, therefore, does not possess faith must not even be called continence.

27. There are also those who, by openly serving wicked demons, abstain from bodily pleasures so that through them they may fulfill abominable pleasures whose force and ardor they do not restrain. To give one example, while omitting the rest for the sake of brevity: some do not even touch their own wives, while by magical arts they endeavor, as though they were pure, to gain access to the wives of others. O marvelous continence—or rather, extraordinary wickedness and uncleanness! For if it were true continence, it ought rather to have kept the desire of the flesh from marriage because of adultery than kept it from marriage in order to perpetrate adultery.

For continence within marriage usually relaxes this desire of the flesh and imposes restraint upon it through its reins, so that even within marriage unrestrained license does not run wild [Note: [Col. 0368] Two manuscripts read *diffluat* (“run wild”) instead of the printed *diffluatur*.], but moderation is preserved—either the moderation owed to the spouse’s weakness, to whom the Apostle grants this not as a command but as a concession (I Cor. VII, 6), or the moderation suited to the begetting of children, which was once the sole reason why holy fathers and mothers joined their bodies to one another. In doing this, continence—that is, moderating and in a certain way limiting the desire of the flesh in married persons, and ordering its restless and disordered movement within boundaries fixed, so to speak—makes good use of the human being’s evil, whom it makes good and wishes to make perfect; just as God also makes use of evil human beings for the sake of those whom he makes good.

## CHAPTER XIII

28. Continence restrains and governs not only bodily lusts but also the desires of the mind. The mind’s evil movements must be checked by continence, through withholding consent and rejecting even the pleasure of thought. Let us therefore not say that those also possess the continence of which Scripture says, “And this itself was wisdom: to know whose gift it was” (Wis. VIII, 21), who, by restraining themselves, either serve errors or overcome certain lesser desires only in order to satisfy others by whose greatness they are overcome. True continence, which comes from above, does not wish to suppress some evils by means of other evils, but to heal all evils with goods.

To summarize its activity briefly: the work of continence watches over the restraint and healing of every pleasure of desire that is opposed to the pleasure of wisdom. Hence those who define continence as the restraint of bodily lusts alone measure it too narrowly and without hesitation. They judge much better who do not add “bodily,” but say generally that the regulation of lust or desire belongs to continence. This desire is counted as a vice, and it is not bodily alone but also belongs to the mind. For if bodily desire is found in fornications and drunkenness, are not enmities, quarrels, jealousies, and finally hostilities exercised in bodily pleasures, rather than in the movements and disturbances of the mind?

Yet the Apostle called all these things works of the flesh, whether they properly belonged to the mind or to the flesh, evidently calling the human being himself by the name “flesh” (Gal. V, 19–21). For they are works of the human being that are not called works of God, since the person who does these things lives according to himself, not according to God, insofar as he does them. But there are other works of the human being that should more properly be called works of God. “For it is God,” says the Apostle, “who works in you both to will and to work, for his good pleasure” (Phil. II, 13). Hence also this statement: “For all who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God” (Rom. VIII, 14).

29. The spirit of the human being, therefore, cleaving to the Spirit of God, desires against the flesh—that is, against itself—but for its own sake, so that those movements, whether in the flesh or in the mind, which are according to the human being and not according to God, and which still exist because of an acquired weakness, may be restrained by continence for the sake of acquiring salvation. Thus the human being, no longer living according to the human being, may already say, “Yet I live—not I, but Christ lives in me” (Gal. II, 20).

For where there is no “I,” there is a happier “I”; so that whenever some blameworthy movement according to the human being arises, and the person who serves the law of God with his mind does not consent to it, he may also say, “It is no longer I who do it” (Rom. VII, 17).

To such persons are addressed those words which, as their companions and fellow members, we ought to hear: “If you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God. Set your minds on the things that are above, not on the things that are on earth. For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God. When Christ, your life, appears, then you also will appear with him in glory.”

Let us understand to whom he speaks—or rather, let us listen more attentively. For what could be clearer or more explicit? Certainly he speaks to those who had risen with Christ, not yet in the flesh, but in mind; whom he calls dead, and by this very fact more truly alive. “For your life,” he says, “is hidden with Christ in God.” The voice of such dead persons is: “Yet I live—not I, but Christ lives in me.”

Since their life was hidden in God, they are admonished and exhorted to put to death their members that are upon the earth. For what follows is: “Put to death, therefore, your members that are upon the earth.” And lest anyone who was too slow to understand should think that these visible bodily members were to be put to death by such persons, he immediately explains what he means: “Fornication,” he says, “uncleanness, lust, evil desire, and greed, which is the service of idols.”

Can it really be believed that these people, who had already died and whose life was hidden with Christ in God, were still committing fornication, still living in unclean habits and deeds, still serving disturbances, evil desire, and greed? What madman would think this of such people?

What, then, does he wish them to put to death by the work of continence, unless it is those very movements that still live in a certain way through their persistent appeal, without the consent of our minds and without the activity of the bodily members? And how are these movements put to death by the work of continence, unless the mind does not consent to them and the members of the body are not offered to them as weapons—and, what is more important and requires greater vigilance in continence, unless even our thought itself, although touched in a certain way by their suggestion and, as it were, their whispering, turns away from them rather than being delighted by them and turns instead to the more pleasurable consideration of things above? For this reason he names them in his discourse, so that one may not dwell in them but flee from them.

This takes place if we listen effectively, with the help of the one who gives this command through his Apostle: “Seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God; set your minds on the things that are above, not on the things that are upon the earth.”

## CHAPTER XIV

30. Faith without works does not save. The vices of the flesh must be steadfastly fought. In the battle of continence, strength and victory must be attributed to God. After he had recalled those evils, he added and said: “Because of these things the wrath of God is coming upon the sons of unbelief.” He thereby wisely terrified them, lest believers think that they could be saved by faith alone, even if they lived in these evils. The Apostle James protests against this notion in the clearest terms, saying: “If someone says that he has faith but has no works, can faith save him?” (Jas. II, 14).

Thus this Teacher of the Gentiles also said that the wrath of God comes upon the sons of unbelief on account of those evils. When he says, “In which you also once walked, when you lived in them,” he sufficiently shows that they no longer lived in them. For they had died to these things, so that their life might be hidden with Christ in God. Since, therefore, they no longer lived in them, they were commanded to put such things to death.

Those things were alive in them even though they themselves no longer lived in them, as I have just shown; and they were called their members—that is, the vices that dwelt in their members—by a manner of speaking in which the container is named for what it contains [Col. 0371] [Note: [Col. 0371] So read most manuscripts. Some, however, add “by which it is expressed.” The printed editions have “by which it is signified.”]. Thus one says, “The whole forum is speaking,” when it is the people in the forum who are speaking. In the same manner the Psalm says, “Let all the earth adore you” (Ps. LXV, 4), meaning all the people who are upon the earth.

31. “But now,” he says, “put away all these things, you also” (Col. III, 1–8), and he recalls several other evils of this kind. But why is it not enough for him to say, “Put away all these things,” and why, after adding the conjunction, does he say, “you also”? It is so that they would not think that they were doing these evils and living in them with impunity because their faith would free them from the wrath that comes upon the sons of unbelief who do such things and live in them without faith.

“Put away,” he says, “you also, those evils because of which the wrath of God comes upon the sons of disobedience; and do not promise yourselves immunity from them on account of the merit of faith.”

He would not say “Put them away” to those who had already put them away insofar as they did not consent to such vices and did not offer their members to them as weapons of sin, unless the life of the saints consists in this very action and remains engaged in this activity for as long as we are mortal.

While the spirit desires against the flesh, this matter is pursued with great intensity: evil pleasures, unclean lusts, and carnal and shameful movements are resisted by the sweetness of holiness, the love of chastity, spiritual vigor, and the beauty of continence. Thus these things are put away by those who have died to them and do not live in them by consenting to them.

They are put away, I say, while continued continence keeps them suppressed lest they rise again. Whoever, as though secure, ceases this putting-away of them, will immediately see them leap into the citadel of the mind [Col. 0372] and put the mind itself away from there [Note: [Col. 0372] So read the manuscripts. The printed editions have “and put it away from there.”], reducing it to their own service, shamefully and disgracefully captive.

Then sin will reign in the mortal body of the human being, so that it obeys its desires; then the person will offer his members as weapons of unrighteousness to sin (Rom. VI, 12), and “the last state of that person will be worse than the first” (Matt. XII, 45).

For it is much more bearable never to have begun such a struggle than to abandon a conflict once begun and to become a captive after having been a good fighter—or even after having been victorious. Hence the Lord does not say, “The one who begins,” but, “The one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. X, 22).

32. Whether we are engaged in a fierce struggle lest we be defeated, or whether we occasionally win—even with an unexpected or unforeseen ease—let us give glory to the one who grants us continence.

Let us remember that a certain righteous man said in his prosperity, “I shall never be moved”; and that it was shown to him how rashly he had spoken, as though he attributed to his own strength what had been granted to him from above. We learned this from his own confession, for he immediately added: “Lord, by your favor you had established strength for my beauty; but when you hid your face, I was troubled” (Ps. XXIX, 7–8).

Through a medicinal providence he was abandoned for a little while by his ruler, lest through deadly pride he himself should abandon his ruler. Whether, then, here, where we struggle with our vices in order to subdue and diminish them, or there, which will occur at the end, where we will be free from every enemy because we will be free from every plague [Note: [Col. 0372] So read the manuscripts. The printed editions have “where we will be free from every enemy and every plague.”], what is beneficially accomplished in us is that “the one who glories should glory in the Lord” (I Cor. I, 31).

# ON THE GOOD OF MARRIAGE

[Col. 0371]

## INTRODUCTION TO THE BOOK ON THE GOOD OF MARRIAGE
