[Note: [Col. 0371] On the book *On the Good of Marriage*, see also book 2, chapter 22, of the *Retractions*, vol. 1, col. 639, from the words “Jovinian’s heresy” through the words at col. 640, “is a part of the human race.” M.]

This book, together with the one that follows it immediately, is directed against certain remnants of the heresy of Jovinian. Augustine recalls the origin of this heresy in his own time in book 2 of *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, chapter 23: “Jovinian,” he says, “who a few years ago attempted to establish a novel heresy, used to say that Catholics were supporting the Manichaeans because they preferred holy virginity to marriage in opposition to him.” And in *On Heresies*, chapter 82: “This heresy arose in our own age from a certain monk named Jovinian, when we were still young.”

He adds that it was quickly suppressed and extinguished, probably around the year 390 after Christ: first condemned at Rome, and afterward at Milan. Concerning this matter there remain letters of Pope Siricius to the Church of Milan, as well as the letters sent to him by the Milanese synod under the presidency of Bishop Ambrose, reported by Baronius under the year 390.

Jerome had refuted Jovinian, but he was said to have attempted the defense of the excellence of virginity only by condemning marriage, and thus to have favored the Manichaean heretics incautiously. To avoid suffering a similar slander or complaint, Augustine judged that he should write about the good of marriage before speaking about the excellence of virginity. That he completed this work around the year 401 is understood not only from the sequence of the *Retractions* but also from the books *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, begun at approximately that time in 401.

Thus, in book 9 of *On Genesis*, chapter 7, where he commends the good of marriage, he says: “This good, however, is threefold: fidelity, offspring, and the sacrament. Fidelity requires that there be no intercourse with another man or woman apart from the marriage bond; offspring requires that children be lovingly received, kindly nourished, and religiously educated; and the sacrament requires that the marriage not be dissolved and that neither the husband nor the wife, after being dismissed, be joined to another even for the sake of producing children. This is, as it were, the rule of marriage, by which the fruitfulness of nature is ennobled and the depravity of incontinence is governed. Therefore, since we have discussed this sufficiently in the book that we recently published *On the Good of Marriage*, in which we also distinguished widowly continence and the excellence of virginity according to the dignity proper to their respective grades [Col. 0373], our pen should not be occupied here any longer.” This same work is noted in book 1 of *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, chapter 29.

[Col. 0373]

## ONE BOOK BY ST. AURELIUS AUGUSTINE, BISHOP OF HIPPO, ON THE GOOD OF MARRIAGE

[Note: [Col. 0373] Written around the year 401 after Christ.]

[Note: [Col. 0373] The book *On the Good of Marriage* has been collated against five Vatican manuscripts and eleven Gallican ones: namely, against the very ancient Corbie manuscript, written a thousand years ago; the German, Cistercian, Michaeline, and Sorbonne manuscripts; two Thuane or Colbertine manuscripts; the manuscript of the Royal Library; those of the Augustinian monastery of the Greater Convent in Paris; the manuscript of the Church of Reims; and that of the distinguished Emeric Bigot of Rouen; as well as against the variant readings of three Belgian manuscripts preserved at Louvain and against the editions of Erasmus and the Louvain editors.]

[Note: [Col. 0373] We also compared all the editions mentioned at the beginning of the *Retractions* and the *Confessions*, vol. 1. M.] (C)

In this work Augustine teaches that marriage is honorable in many respects, and that it is good not merely by comparison with fornication but in its own kind, and intrinsically free from every sin. He shows, however, that continence is far more excellent. Accordingly, although in former times the saints were obliged to make use of marriage as necessary for propagating the people of God, through whom Christ would be foretold and born, now, after it has been said, “Let the one who can receive it receive it,” marriage should be embraced only by those who cannot restrain themselves.

As for our continent persons, they can scarcely be compared with those ancient married people—Abraham and Sarah in particular—much less preferred to them. For those people, although married, possessed the virtue of continence in the disposition of their minds, and they excelled above all in the praise of obedience, which contains all the virtues as though in a womb.

## CHAPTER I

1. The first union of man and woman. Since each human being is a part of the human race, and human nature is something social and possesses a great and natural good, namely the power of friendship, God therefore willed to create all human beings from one person, so that they would be held together in their society not only by the likeness of their kind but also by the bond of kinship.

The first bond, then, of natural human society is man and woman. God did not create them separately and join them as strangers, but created one from the other, also signifying the force of their union in the side from which she was taken and formed (Gen. II, 21–22). For those who walk together and look together toward the place where they are walking are joined at the side.

The connection of society in children follows, and children are the one honorable fruit not of the union of male and female but of intercourse. For even without such mingling there could have been between the two sexes a certain friendly and kindred union, with one ruling and the other obeying.

## CHAPTER II

2. Different opinions concerning the propagation of children if the human being had not sinned. Nor is it now necessary for us to investigate or offer a definitive judgment on the question of how offspring could have existed from the first human beings, whom God had blessed when he said, “Increase and multiply, and fill the earth,” if they had not sinned—since by sinning their bodies incurred the condition of death, and intercourse can exist only among mortal bodies.

Many different opinions have arisen concerning this matter; and if it must be examined which of them most agrees with the truth of the divine Scriptures, that is the business of a lengthy discussion [Col. 0374]. Whether, if they had not sinned, they would have had children without sexual union, in some other way, by a gift of the almighty Creator—who was able to create them even without parents, who was able to form Christ’s flesh in a virginal womb, and, to speak even to unbelievers, who was able to give bees offspring without intercourse—or whether many things there were said mystically and figuratively, and “Fill the earth and rule over it” (Gen. I, 28) should be understood differently: namely, that this would occur through the fullness and perfection of life and power, and that the increase and multiplication expressed by “Increase and multiply” should be understood as the advancement of the mind and abundance of virtue, as it is written in the Psalm, “You will multiply me in my soul with virtue” [Note: [Col. 0374] The printed editions omit *me* and have *virtutem* (“virtue”) instead of *virtute* (“with virtue”). Augustine ordinarily reads, “You will multiply me in my soul with virtue,” in accordance with the Septuagint; and so do the manuscripts here, except that the very ancient Corbie manuscript has *in virtutem* (“into virtue”) instead of *virtute*.] (Ps. CXXXVII, 3);

or whether this succession of offspring was not given to the human being until, because of sin, departure in death was going to occur; or whether their body was made not spiritual but initially natural, so that afterward, by the merit of obedience, it might become spiritual in order to attain immortality—not after death, which entered the world through the devil’s envy (Wis. II, 24) and became the punishment of sin, but through that transformation of which the Apostle speaks when he says, “Then we who are alive, who are left, will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet Christ in the air” (I Thess. IV, 16);

so that we may understand the bodies of the first married couple to have been mortal in their initial formation, yet not destined to die unless they sinned, as God had threatened—just as if someone threatened a wound because the body was vulnerable, although the wound would not have occurred unless what he had forbidden came to pass.

Thus generations could also have continued through intercourse of such bodies, increasing up to a definite measure but not tending toward old age; or continuing into old age [Note: [Col. 0375] Only the Louvain edition omits “or continuing into old age.”], yet not into death, until the earth had been filled by that multiplication of blessing.

For if God preserved the garments of the Israelites in their proper condition for forty years without any deterioration (Deut. XXIX, 5), how much more would he have granted to the bodies of those obedient to his command a most blessed preservation of a fixed condition, until they were transformed into something better—not through the death by which the body is abandoned by the soul, but through a blessed transformation from mortality to immortality and from a natural to a spiritual condition!

## CHAPTER III

The manifold good of marriage. The first and second good of marriage. The third good of marriage. Which of these opinions is true, or whether one or more further opinions can still be drawn from those words, would take a long time to investigate and discuss.

3. For now we say that, according to this condition of being born and dying that we know and in which we were created, the union of male and female is in some respect good. Divine Scripture commends its covenant in such a way that a woman dismissed by her husband is not permitted to marry another as long as her husband lives, nor is a man dismissed by his wife permitted to take another wife unless the woman who departed has died.

The good of marriage, which the Lord also confirmed in the Gospel—not only because he forbade dismissing a wife except on account of fornication (Matt. XIX, 9), but also because he came when invited to a wedding (John II, 2)—is rightly a matter for inquiry. It seems to me to be good not solely because of the procreation of children, but also because of the natural society itself that exists between the sexes.

Otherwise marriage would no longer be called marriage among the elderly, especially if they had either lost their children or had never begotten any. But now, even in an aged marriage, although the ardor of youth between male and female has faded, the order of love between husband and wife still flourishes. For the better they are, the earlier they have begun, by mutual agreement, to abstain from the intercourse of their flesh—not because afterward they would be unable to do what they wished, but because it is a matter of praise that they first did not wish to do what they could.

If, then, fidelity in the honor and services owed mutually by each sex to the other is preserved, even when the limbs of both have grown weak and almost corpse-like, the chastity of rightly married souls perseveres all the more sincerely the more it has been tested, and all the more securely the more peacefully it endures.

Marriage also has this good: that carnal or youthful incontinence, even when it is vicious, is directed toward the honorable purpose of propagating offspring, so that the marital union makes something good out of the evil of lust. Moreover, desire of the flesh is restrained and burns, in a certain sense, more modestly because parental affection moderates it. For a certain gravity intervenes in ardent pleasure [Note: [Col. 0375] The Bigot manuscript reads *voluptati* (“for pleasure”) instead of *voluptatis* (“of pleasure”).], when, in the fact that a man and woman cling to one another, they are contemplating becoming father and mother.

## CHAPTER IV

4. The fourth good of marriage. What adultery is. Fidelity must be preserved even in lowly matters [Col. 0376] and preferred to this life. In addition, in the very act by which spouses discharge the marital debt to one another, even if they seek it somewhat intemperately and incontinently, they nevertheless owe each other fidelity. The Apostle attributes such great authority to this fidelity that he calls it a power, saying: “The wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband does; likewise the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife does” (I Cor. VII, 4).

The violation of this fidelity is called adultery, when, whether prompted by one’s own lust or consenting to another’s, a man or woman has intercourse with someone else against the marital agreement. Thus fidelity is broken; and fidelity is a great good of the mind even in bodily and lowly matters. Therefore it certainly ought to be preferred even to bodily salvation, by which our present life is preserved.

For although a little straw is almost nothing compared with much gold, fidelity is no less when it is sincerely preserved in a transaction involving straw than when it is preserved in one involving gold, merely because it is preserved in a lesser matter.

When fidelity is employed to admit a sin, it is surprising if it ought to be called fidelity; nevertheless, whatever its character, if it is violated, the wrong is worse. The exception is when it is abandoned for the purpose of returning to true and legitimate fidelity—that is, so that the sin may be corrected by reforming the perversity of the will.

It is as if someone were unable to rob a person alone, found a partner in iniquity, and made an agreement with him that they should commit the robbery together and divide the spoils, but, after the crime had been committed, took everything for himself. The other man is certainly distressed and complains that fidelity was not kept toward him. Yet in making this complaint he ought to consider that fidelity should rather have been preserved in a good life for the sake of human society itself, so that the person could not be made the object of an unjust robbery, if he understands how unjustly fidelity was not preserved toward him in a partnership of sin. The thief is manifestly faithless in both respects and must certainly be judged more criminal.

But if he had become displeased with what they had done wrongly and for that reason had refused to divide the spoils with his accomplice, so that they might be returned to the person from whom they had been taken, no one would call him faithless, nor would the faithless accomplice call him so.

Likewise, if a woman, after violating marital fidelity, keeps faith with an adulterer, she is certainly wicked; but if she does not keep faith even with the adulterer, she is worse. If, however, she repents of her crime and, returning to marital chastity, breaks off the adulterous agreements and arrangements, I wonder whether even the adulterer himself would consider her a violator of fidelity.

## CHAPTER V

5. When the union of man and woman is marriage, and when it is not. It is also customary to ask whether, when a man and woman—neither being the spouse of another—join themselves not for the procreation of children but solely for intercourse on account of incontinence, with this agreement between them, that neither he will do this with another woman nor she with another man, they should be called married.

Perhaps this can not unreasonably be called marriage if they have agreed that their arrangement will continue until the death of one of them [Note: [Col. 0376] Erasmus and the manuscripts read “until the death of either of them.”], and although they did not join for the sake of producing offspring, they have nevertheless not avoided generating children, by either not wishing children to be born to them or doing something evil to prevent their birth.

But if either or both of these conditions is absent, I do not see how we can call this marriage. For if a man takes a woman for a time, until he finds another worthy of his rank or wealth whom he can marry, he is an adulterer in his mind—not with the woman he hopes to find, but with the one with whom he has intercourse in such a way that he does not have marital fellowship with her.

And she too, knowing and willing this, certainly joins herself immodestly to a man with whom she has no marital covenant. Nevertheless, if she keeps faith with him concerning the marriage bed and, once he has married a wife, does not contemplate marrying herself but prepares to abstain altogether from such an act, I might perhaps hesitate to call her an adulteress readily; yet who would say that she does not sin, when he knows that she joins herself to a man whose wife she is not?

But if, as far as she is concerned, she wants nothing from that intercourse except children, and unwillingly endures whatever goes beyond the purpose of procreation, she is certainly to be preferred to many matrons. Although these women are not adulteresses, they nevertheless often compel their husbands—even when they wish to remain continent—to render the marital debt, not from a desire for offspring but from the ardor of lust, using their own right intemperately.

Yet in their marriages this very fact is good: that they are married. For they married so that desire, reduced to a lawful bond, would not flow forth deformed and unrestrained, possessing from itself the uncontrollable weakness of the flesh, but from marriage an indissoluble fellowship of fidelity; possessing from itself an immoderate impulse toward intercourse, but from marriage a chaste measure in procreation.

For although it is shameful to wish to use one’s husband lustfully [Note: [Col. 0377] The manuscripts read “to use even one’s husband.”], it is nevertheless honorable to refuse intercourse except with one’s husband and to bear children only by one’s husband.

## CHAPTER VI

Concerning the demanding and rendering of the marital debt. There are also husbands so extremely incontinent that they do not spare even their pregnant wives. Whatever married people do among themselves that is immodest, indecent, or sordid is therefore a vice of the human beings, not a fault of marriage.

6. Even in the more immoderate demand for the carnal debt—which the Apostle does not command them as a matter of authority, but grants by way of concession, so that they may have intercourse with one another even apart from the purpose of procreation—although corrupt habits drive them to such intercourse, marriage nevertheless protects them from adultery or fornication.

For the act is not permitted because of marriage; rather, it is forgiven because of marriage. Married people therefore owe each other not only fidelity in joining with one another sexually for the purpose of producing children, which is the first society of the human race in this mortal condition, but also, in order to avoid unlawful intercourse, a mutual kind of servitude in bearing with each other’s weakness. Thus, even if perpetual continence pleases one of them, it cannot be practiced without the consent of the other.

For this too, “the wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband does; likewise the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife does” (I Cor. VII, 4–6): so that what either husband or wife seeks—not for the procreation of children but because of weakness and incontinence—the other may not deny, lest through this they fall into damnable corruptions, with Satan tempting them on account of the incontinence of both or of either one.

Intercourse within marriage for the sake of procreation has no guilt; intercourse for the satisfaction of desire, though with one’s spouse and therefore on account of fidelity to the marriage bed, has venial guilt; but adultery or fornication has deadly guilt. Accordingly, continence from every form of intercourse is better even than marital intercourse undertaken for the purpose of begetting children.

## CHAPTER VII

The marriage covenant is not annulled by the separation of spouses. Whether it is lawful to take another wife after dismissing an adulteress. The taking of a second wife forbidden according to Roman custom. Divorce does not abolish the law of the marriage covenant among Christians. But since that continence has the greater merit, while rendering the marital debt is entirely free of crime, demanding it beyond the necessity of procreation is a venial fault, and committing fornication or adultery is a punishable crime, marital charity must take care lest, while seeking a means of receiving greater honor for itself, it provide the spouse with a means of condemnation.

“For the one who dismisses his wife, except on account of fornication, makes her commit adultery” (Matt. V, 32). So thoroughly is that marriage covenant, once entered into, a matter of sacrament that it is not annulled even by separation itself. For while her husband, by whom she was abandoned, is alive, she commits adultery if she marries another; and the man who abandoned her is the cause of this evil.

7. I wonder, however, whether, just as it is lawful to dismiss an adulterous wife, it is likewise lawful, after dismissing her, to take another wife. Holy Scripture makes a difficult knot of this matter when the Apostle says, by the command of the Lord, that a woman must not depart from her husband; but if she does depart, she must remain unmarried or be reconciled to her husband (I Cor. VII, 10–11).

Certainly she ought to depart and remain unmarried only from an adulterous husband, lest by departing from a husband who is not an adulterer she make him commit adultery. She may perhaps be reconciled to her husband either by tolerating him, if she herself cannot remain continent, or by his reforming himself.

But how a husband can have permission to take another wife if he has dismissed an adulteress, when a woman is not permitted to marry another if she has dismissed an adulterous husband, I do not see.

If this is so, the social bond of spouses has such force that, although it is contracted for the purpose of procreation, not even that purpose of procreation dissolves it. A man could dismiss a barren wife and marry one by whom he could have children, and yet this is not permitted. Indeed, in our own times and according to Roman custom, he may not even take another wife in addition, so as to have more than one living wife.

Certainly, after an adulterous wife had been dismissed, or an adulterous husband abandoned, more human beings could be born if she married another man or he took another wife. Yet if this is not permitted, as the divine rule appears to prescribe, who would not be compelled to consider what such great firmness of the marital bond means?

I do not think it could have had such force unless it contained a sacrament of some greater reality arising from the weakness of human mortality—a sacrament that would remain unshaken for the punishment of those who abandon it and wish to dissolve it.

For when divorce intervenes, the marriage covenant is not abolished, so that spouses remain married even when separated; and they commit adultery with those to whom they are joined even after their repudiation, whether the woman joins herself to a man or the man to a woman.

Yet such a situation with a wife exists only in the city of our God, on his holy mountain (Ps. XLVII, 2).

## CHAPTER VIII

The use of repudiation among the Gentiles and among the Jews. Marriage is wholly good, not good merely by comparison with fornication. Who does not know that the laws of the Gentiles operate otherwise? There, after a divorce has been issued, without incurring any penalty under human retribution, the woman marries whomever she wishes and the man takes whichever woman he wishes.

Because of the hardness of the Israelites, Moses appears to have permitted something resembling this custom through the bill of divorce (Deut. XXIV, 1; Matt. XIX, 8). In this matter, however, reproach of divorce appears more evident than approval of it.

## 8. Marriage, therefore, is honorable in all, and the marriage bed undefiled (Heb. 13:4). We do not call it good in such a way that it is good only by comparison with fornication; otherwise there would be two evils, one worse than the other. Or fornication would be good because adultery is worse; for violating another’s marriage is worse than cleaving to a prostitute. And adultery would be good because incest is worse; for lying with one’s mother is worse than lying with another man’s wife. And until one reaches those things which, as the Apostle says, it is shameful even to mention (Eph. 5:12), everything would be good by comparison with worse things. Who could doubt that this is false? Marriage and fornication, therefore, are not two evils, one of which is worse; rather, marriage and continence are two goods, one of which is better.

Just as temporal health and weakness are not two evils, one of which is worse, but health and immortality are two goods, one of which is better; and just as knowledge and vanity are not two evils, of which vanity is the worse, but knowledge and charity are two goods, of which charity is better. For “knowledge,” the Apostle says, “will be destroyed”; yet it is necessary for this present time, whereas “charity will never fail” (1 Cor. 13:8). So too this mortal generation, for the sake of which marriages are contracted, will be destroyed; but freedom from all sexual intercourse is both an angelic meditation here and remains forever.

Yet just as the meals of the righteous are better than the fasts of sacrilegious people, so the marriages of the faithful are to be preferred to the virginity of the impious [Note: [Col. 0379] Lov., “of the impious men”; other printed editions and manuscripts disagree.]. Nevertheless, in the former case it is not the meal that is preferred to fasting, but righteousness to sacrilege; nor in the latter are marriages preferred to virginity, but faith to impiety. The righteous eat when necessary, so that, like good masters, they may provide their servant bodies with what is just and fitting; but sacrilegious people fast in order to serve demons. So the faithful marry in order to be joined chastely to their spouses; but impious virgins are virgins in order to fornicate away from the true God.

Thus, what Martha was doing was good, occupied as she was in the service of the holy; but what her sister Mary was doing was better, sitting at the Lord’s feet and listening to his word (Luke 10:39–42) [Note: [Col. 0379] Only the Lov. edition adds here, “when both had received him as a guest.”]. In the same way, we praise Susanna’s goodness in marital chastity (Dan. 13), yet we place above it the goodness of the widow Anna (Luke 2:36–37), and still more that of the virgin Mary [Col. 0380] (Luke 1:27). What those women were doing was good when they supplied Christ and his disciples with what was necessary from their possessions; but those who left all their possessions so as to follow the same Lord more freely were doing better.

In these two kinds of good—the things done by these women, or by Martha and Mary—it would not be possible to do what is better without passing over or abandoning the other. From this it must be understood that marriage is not to be considered evil because, unless one abstains from it, widowed chastity or virginal integrity cannot be attained. What Martha was doing was not evil merely because, unless her sister abstained from it, she would not do what was better. Nor is it evil to receive a righteous person or a prophet into one’s home merely because someone who wishes to follow Christ to perfection ought not to have a home, so that he may do what is better.

## CHAPTER IX

### 9. Marriage is to be desired only for the sake of something else. The saints ought to have made use of marriage in the earliest times; now continence is to be preferred.

It must be observed that God gives us some goods which are to be desired for their own sake, such as wisdom, health, and friendship; and others which are necessary for the sake of something else, such as instruction, food, drink, sleep, marriage, and sexual intercourse. Some of these are necessary for wisdom, such as instruction; some for health, such as food, drink, and sleep; and some for friendship, such as marriage or sexual intercourse. For through these the propagation of the human race is maintained, and in that race social fellowship is a great good.

Whoever uses goods that are necessary for something else for a purpose other than that for which they were instituted sins—sometimes venially, sometimes damnably. Whoever uses them for the purpose for which they were given acts well. Therefore, if someone does not need them and does not use them, he acts better. Accordingly, when we need these goods, we rightly desire them; but it is better not to need them than to desire them, because we are better off when they are not necessary to us.

Thus it is good to marry, because it is good to beget children and to manage a household (1 Tim. 5:14); but it is better not to marry, because it is better that human society should not need this work. The human race is now in such a condition that, although some people practice continence, others are occupied with marriage, and many others indulge in illicit intercourse, the good Creator nevertheless brings good from their evils. Thus there is no lack of a multitude of offspring or an abundance of descendants from whom holy friendships may be gathered.

From this it follows that in the earliest times of the human race, especially for the propagation of God’s people, through whom the Prince and Savior of all nations would both be prophesied and born, the saints ought to have made use of this good of marriage, which was not desirable for its own sake but was necessary for something else. Now, however, since from every side and from all nations an abundance of spiritual kinship overflows for entering into a holy and sincere fellowship, those who wish to contract marriages merely for children should be admonished to make use instead of the greater good of continence.

## CHAPTER X

### 10. Objection against continence. Now only those should marry who do not practice continence. Marriage is not a sin. Only intercourse undertaken for procreation is marital intercourse.

But I know what some people murmur: “What if,” they say, “all human beings wished to abstain from all intercourse? From where would the human race continue?” Would that all wished this—provided only that they did so in charity from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith (1 Tim. 1:5)! The city of God would be filled much more quickly, and the end of the age would be hastened.

For what else does the Apostle appear to urge when, speaking on this subject, he says, “I wish that all were as I myself am”? Or in that passage: “But this I say, brothers: the time is short. It remains that those who have wives should be as though they had none; those who weep, as though they did not weep; those who rejoice, as though they did not rejoice; those who buy, as though they did not possess; and those who use this world, as though they did not use it. For the form of this world is passing away. I want you to be free from anxiety.”

Then he adds: “The unmarried man is concerned with the things of the Lord, how he may please the Lord. But the married man is concerned with the things of the world, how he may please his wife. And the unmarried woman and the virgin are distinct: she who is unmarried is concerned with the things of the Lord, so that she may be holy in body and spirit; but she who is married is concerned with the things of the world, how she may please her husband” [Note: [Col. 0381] This is the reading of almost all the ancient manuscripts, explained by Augustine in *On Holy Virginity*, chapter 22, and *On the Good of Widowhood*, chapter 2. In earlier editions it had been incorrectly emended as follows: “And the married woman and the virgin who is unmarried are distinct.” Jerome noted the disagreement among Latin manuscripts at this passage of the Apostle in Book 1 *Against Jovinianus*.].

Therefore, it seems to me that in the present time only those who do not practice continence ought to marry, in accordance with that same Apostle’s statement: “If they do not practice continence, let them marry; for it is better to marry than to burn.”

### 11.

Yet marriage is not a sin even for such people. If marriage were chosen in comparison with fornication, it would be a lesser sin than fornication; nevertheless, it would still be a sin. But what shall we say now against the Apostle’s most explicit statement: “Let him do what he wishes; he does not sin if he marries”; and, “If you take a wife, you have not sinned; and if a virgin marries, she does not sin” (1 Cor. 7:7, 28–36)?

There can surely no longer be any legitimate doubt that marriage is not a sin. The Apostle therefore does not grant marriage as a concession. For who could absurdly say that those to whom pardon is granted have not sinned? Rather, he grants as a concession that intercourse which occurs through lack of continence, not solely for the purpose of procreation, and sometimes with no purpose of procreation at all. Marriage does not compel such intercourse to take place, but obtains pardon for it—provided that it is not so excessive as to interfere with the times that ought to be set aside for prayer, and that it is not changed into the use which is against nature, concerning which the Apostle could not remain silent when he spoke of the excessive corruptions of unclean and impious people (Rom. 1:26–27).

Intercourse necessary for procreation is blameless, and it alone is properly marital. But intercourse which goes beyond this necessity already serves not reason but lust. Yet to refrain from demanding it and to render it to one’s spouse, lest the spouse sin damnably by committing fornication, belongs to the marital relationship. If both spouses are enslaved to such desire, they are doing something that is not entirely a work of marriage. Nevertheless, if in their union they love what is honorable more than what is dishonorable—that is, what belongs to marriage more than what does not belong to marriage—then, by the authority of the Apostle, this is granted to them as a concession. Their marriages do not encourage this fault but plead for mercy, provided that they do not turn God’s mercy away from themselves, whether by refraining on certain days so as to devote themselves to prayer and commending their prayers through this abstinence as through fasting, or by changing natural use into use against nature, which is more damnable in a spouse.

## CHAPTER XI

### 12. Use against nature is more detestable in a wife than in a prostitute. The greater holiness of the unmarried is commended, not the holiness of the married denied.

When natural use, in a wife, goes beyond the marital agreements—that is, beyond the necessity of procreation—it is venial; in a prostitute, it is damnable. But what is against nature is detestable in a prostitute and still more detestable in a wife.

The ordering of the Creator and the order of creation have such force that, even in things granted for use, an excess, when the limit is exceeded, is far more tolerable than either a single or a rare excess in things that have not been granted [Note: [Col. 0382] Manuscripts, “in it.”]. Therefore, in a permitted matter, a spouse’s immoderation is to be tolerated lest lust break out into a matter that is not permitted.

This is also why even someone who constantly approaches his wife sins far less than someone who goes to fornication even very rarely. But when a husband wishes to use a woman’s body for a purpose for which it was not granted, the wife is more shameful if she permits this to be done with her than if she permits it to be done with another woman.

Thus marital honor consists in chastity for procreation and fidelity in rendering the marital debt. This is the work of marriage; the Apostle defends it from every accusation when he says, “If you take a wife, you have not sinned; and if a virgin marries, she does not sin”; and, “Let him do what he wishes; he does not sin if he marries.” A more immoderate advance by either sex in demanding the debt is granted to married people as a concession because of what he said above.

### 13.

What he says, therefore—“The unmarried woman is concerned with the things of the Lord, so that she may be holy in body and spirit”—must not be understood as though we were to think that a chaste Christian wife is not holy in body. For it has been said to all the faithful: “Do you not know that your bodies are a temple of the Holy Spirit within you, whom you have from God?” (1 Cor. 6:19). The bodies, therefore, of married people who preserve fidelity toward one another and toward the Lord are also holy.

The same Apostle bears witness that this holiness is not hindered by an unbelieving spouse; rather, the holiness of a wife benefits an unbelieving husband, and the holiness of a husband benefits an unbelieving wife, when he says: “For the unbelieving husband is sanctified in the wife, and the unbelieving woman is sanctified in the brother” (ibid. 7:14) [Note: [Col. 0382] Printed editions have “in the faithful wife” and likewise below “in the faithful brother.” The word “faithful” is absent in both places from the manuscripts and from the Greek text of the Apostle, and Augustine commonly omits it, as in Book 1 of *On the Sermon on the Mount*, chapter 16.].

That statement, therefore, concerns the greater holiness of the unmarried over the married; and a greater reward is owed according to the degree in which the former good is better than the latter. For the unmarried woman considers only how she may please the Lord [Note: [Col. 0382] Lov. reads, “the woman considers.” “Woman” is absent from Er. and the manuscripts.]. A faithful woman who preserves marital chastity does not fail to consider how she may please the Lord, but she does so to a lesser degree, because she also considers the things of the world, how she may please her husband. He wished to say of those women that, in a certain manner, they may have—through the necessity of marriage—the concern to consider the things of the world, how they may please their husbands [Note: [Col. 0383] So the manuscripts. The printed editions instead read, “which.”].

## CHAPTER XII

### 14. Married women who think only of how to please God are exceedingly rare.

Whether he said this of all married women, or of women of such a kind as are so numerous that they can almost all be considered such, is not without reason doubted. For the statement he makes about the unmarried—“The unmarried woman is concerned with the things of the Lord, so that she may be holy in body and spirit”—does not apply to all unmarried women, since there are some widows who are dead while living in luxury (1 Tim. 5:6).

Nevertheless, with respect to a certain distinction and, as it were, characteristic feature of unmarried and married women, just as a woman is utterly detestable who, while abstaining from marriage—that is, from a permitted matter—does not abstain from sins of luxury, pride, curiosity, or talkativeness, so a married woman is rare who, even in the marital service itself, thinks only of how she may please God—not adorning herself with curled hair, gold, pearls, or costly clothing, but with what is fitting for women who profess devotion through good conduct (ibid. 2:9–10).

The Apostle Peter likewise describes such marriages in his instructions: “Likewise, women should be obedient to their husbands, so that, even if some do not believe the word, they may be won without a word through the conduct of their wives, when they see your reverence and chaste conduct. Let their adornment not be outward, with the curling of the hair, or with gold put around them, or with fine clothing, but the hidden person of your heart [Note: [Col. 0383] Only the Lov. edition reads, “of our heart.”] in the incorruptibility of a quiet and gentle spirit, which is precious before God.

“For in this way the holy women who hoped in the Lord once adorned themselves, being obedient to their husbands, just as Sarah obeyed Abraham, calling him lord. You have become her daughters by doing good and not fearing any vain fear.

“Likewise, husbands, live together with your wives in concord and chastity, and grant honor to them as to a weaker and subordinate vessel, as co-heirs of grace; and see that your prayers are not hindered” (1 Pet. 3:1–7) [Note: [Col. 0383] The Vulgate in the sacred Scriptures does not read this way, but has, “as also to co-heirs of the grace of life, so that your prayers may not be hindered.”].

Can such married women really fail to consider the things of the Lord, how they may please the Lord? But they are exceedingly rare. Who denies it? And among those who are such, almost all did not enter marriage in order to become such, but became such after they were already married.

## CHAPTER XIII

### 15. In the present time marriage is to be embraced only by those who do not practice continence; formerly it was also to be embraced by those who did. How rare it is to use marriage solely for the sake of children.

Why would Christians of our time, free from the marital bond and able to abstain from all intercourse, not choose to preserve either virginal or widowed continence when they perceived that the time had come—as it is written—not to embrace but to abstain from embracing (Eccles. 3:5), rather than endure the tribulation of the flesh, without which marriages cannot exist, to say nothing of the other things from which the Apostle spares us, when no duty toward human society now compels them to endure it?

But when such men have been joined in marriage while ruled by desire, and later overcome that desire, they cannot dissolve the marriage, since it is not permitted to undo a marriage once contracted as it was permitted not to contract it. They become the sort of people whom the form of marriage declares them to be, so that either by mutual consent they ascend to a higher degree of holiness, or, if both are not such, the one who is such is not a demander but a renderer of the marital debt, preserving chaste and religious concord in every respect.

In those earlier times, however, when the mystery of our salvation was still veiled under prophetic sacraments, even those who were such before marriage were joined in marriage for the duty of procreation—not conquered by lust but led by piety. If an option such as was given after the revelation of the New Testament had been offered to them, when the Lord said, “Let the one who can receive it receive it” (Matt. 19:12), no one who carefully considers how they used marriage will doubt that they would have accepted it with joy. At that time one man was permitted to have several wives, whom he possessed more chastely [Note: [Col. 0384] Lov. reads, “whom they possessed.” Er. and the manuscripts read, “whom he possessed.”] than any of those men now possess one wife, to whom we see what the Apostle grants as a concession (1 Cor. 7:6).

For they had their wives for the work of procreation, not in the sickness of desire, like the nations that do not know God (1 Thess. 4:5). This is such a great matter that many people today can more easily abstain from all intercourse throughout their entire lives than maintain the rule of not having intercourse except for the sake of children if they are joined in marriage.

We certainly have many brothers and companions, of either sex, in the heavenly inheritance, who practice continence—some having experienced marriage, others remaining untouched by any such union. Indeed, they are innumerable. Yet which of us has ever heard one of them, whether married or formerly married, tell us in ordinary conversation that he has never had intercourse with his spouse except in the hope of conception?

What the Apostles command married people is therefore the work of marriage. What they grant as a concession, or what interferes with prayer, is not compelled by marriage but tolerated by it.

## CHAPTER XIV

### 16. To use a concubine for the sake of children is a greater sin than to use a wife because of lack of continence.

Therefore, if perhaps—and I do not know whether this could happen, and rather think that it could not—but if, for a time, a man took a concubine and sought only children from that union, even this relationship is not to be preferred to the marriages of those who engage in that venial act.

What must be considered is what belongs to marriage, not what belongs to those who marry and use marriage immoderately. If someone seizes fields unjustly and unlawfully and uses them to give abundant alms from their produce, this does not justify his robbery. Nor, if another greedily occupies his paternal or legitimately acquired land, is the rule of civil law by which he became its lawful possessor thereby to be blamed.

Nor will the perversity of a tyrannical faction become praiseworthy if a tyrant treats his subjects with royal clemency; nor is the order of royal power blameworthy if a king rages with tyrannical cruelty [Col. 0385]. For it is one thing to wish to use an unjust power justly, and another to use a just power unjustly.

So neither do temporary concubines make their concubinage just if they have intercourse for the sake of children; nor do married people, if they indulge in lust with their spouses, impose a crime upon the order of marriage.

### 17.

That marriages can arise from unions wrongly formed, when an honorable decision subsequently follows, is clearly possible.

## CHAPTER XV

### Marriage cannot be dissolved on account of sterility. Whether it is permitted, with the wife’s consent, to take another woman so that common children may be born, he does not dare to decide.

Once a marriage has been entered into in the city of our God, where even from the first union of two human beings marriage bears a certain sacrament, it can in no way be dissolved except by the death of one of them. The marital bond remains even if the offspring for whose sake the marriage was entered into does not follow because of evident sterility. Thus, even when the spouses know that they will not have children, they are nevertheless not permitted to separate—even for the sake of children—and join themselves to others.

If they do so, they commit adultery with those to whom they join themselves; yet they themselves remain married.

Clearly, with the wife’s consent, it was lawful among the ancient fathers to take another woman from whom common children might be born through the union and seed of one man, but by the right and authority of the other woman. Whether it is lawful now, I would not rashly assert. For the necessity of propagation that existed then does not exist now. At that time, even while their wives were alive, they were permitted to take other wives for the sake of more abundant posterity; this is certainly not permitted now.

The hidden distinction of times provides so much opportunity for acting rightly or wrongly that now the better course is followed by one who does not marry even one woman unless he cannot practice continence. Then, however, men could marry several women without blame, even men who could have practiced continence much more easily, if piety had not demanded something else at that time.

For just as a wise and righteous person who now longs to be dissolved and to be with Christ, and delights more in this better state (Phil. 1:23), nevertheless now takes nourishment not from a desire to live here but from a duty of care, so that he may remain in the flesh because this is necessary for others, so at that time intercourse with women under the right of marriage was dutiful rather than lustful for holy men.

## CHAPTER XVI

### 18. The same principle of virtue and vice applies to intercourse and the use of food.

What food is for the health of a human being, intercourse is for the preservation of the human race; and neither is without bodily pleasure. Yet when this pleasure is moderated, restrained by temperance, and reduced to natural use, it cannot be lust [Note: [Col. 0385] *Retractations* II, chapter 22, no. 2.].

What illicit food is in sustaining life, fornication or adultery is in seeking offspring. What illicit food is in gluttony of belly and throat, illicit intercourse is in desire that seeks no offspring. What excessive appetite for permitted food is in some people, that venial intercourse is in married couples.

Therefore, just as it is better to die of hunger than to eat food sacrificed to idols [Note: [Col. 0385] In response to Publicola’s question about a Christian traveler who, overcome by hunger, finds nothing anywhere except food placed in an idol’s shrine, where no other human being is present, and asks whether it is better for him to die of hunger than to take it as nourishment, Augustine replies in the letter now numbered 47, no. 6 [Col. 0386]: “Either it is certainly food sacrificed to idols, or it is certainly not, or this is unknown. If it is certainly so, it is better to reject it with Christian virtue; but if it is known not to be so, or this is unknown, it may be taken for necessary use without any scruple of conscience.”], so it is better to die without children than to seek offspring through illicit intercourse.

However human beings may be born, if they do not follow the vices of their parents and worship God rightly, they will be honorable and saved. Human seed, from whatever sort of human being, is God’s creation; it will be evil for those who use it badly, but it will never itself become evil.

Just as good children of adulterers provide no defense for adulteries, so evil children of married people are no crime of marriage. Accordingly, just as the fathers of the time of the New Testament, taking nourishment out of a duty of care, received it with natural bodily pleasure but were in no way comparable either to those who ate food offered in sacrifice (1 Cor. 8:7) or to those who consumed even lawful foods immoderately, so the fathers of the time of the Old Testament had intercourse out of a duty of care. Their natural pleasure was not relaxed into irrational or abominable lust, and it is not to be compared either with the shamefulness of fornication or with the intemperance of married people.

It was through the same vein of charity that children were to be propagated—now spiritually, then carnally—for the sake of that mother, Jerusalem. The different works of the fathers were caused only by the difference of times. It was as necessary for the non-carnal prophets to have carnal intercourse as it was necessary for the non-carnal Apostles to eat bodily food.

## CHAPTER XVII

### 19. Those who marry in the present time are not to be compared with the holy married people of the earliest period. It was at times permitted for one man to have several wives, but never for one woman to have several husbands.

All those today to whom it is said, “If they do not practice continence, let them marry” (ibid. 7:9), are not to be compared with the holy people who married in those earlier times.

Marriage itself has the same purpose among all nations: the procreation of children. Whatever those children may later become, marriage was nevertheless instituted so that they might be born in an orderly and honorable manner. But people who do not practice continence seem to ascend into marriage by a degree of honor; whereas those who would certainly have practiced continence if the circumstances of that time had permitted it descended, in a certain sense, into marriage by a degree of piety.

Thus, although the marriages of both groups are equally good insofar as they are marriages, because they are for the sake of procreation, the married people of the present are not to be compared with the married people of that earlier time. The present have what is granted to them as a concession because of the honor of marriage, although it does not belong to marriage itself: namely, that advance which exceeds the necessity of procreation [Note: [Col. 0386] Lov. reads, “the cause or necessity of procreation.” Er. and the manuscripts do not have “cause or.”]. The earlier people did not have this.

Nor can those few who may now be found not seeking or desiring anything in marriage except what marriage was instituted for be made equal to those earlier people. In the former, the desire for children itself is carnal; in the latter, it was spiritual, because it corresponded to the sacrament of that time.

Now no one who is perfect in piety seeks to have children except spiritually; but then the very work of piety included propagating children carnally, because the generation of that people was a proclamation of future things and belonged to the prophetic dispensation.

### 20.

Therefore, just as one man was permitted to have several wives, so one woman was not permitted to have several husbands—not even for the sake of offspring, if she happened to be able to bear children while he was unable to beget them.

By a hidden law of nature, those who exercise authority love singularity; those who are subject, however, are subordinated not only one by one to one, but, if natural or social reason permits, several to one without disgrace. For one servant does not have several masters in the same way that several servants have one master.

We do not read that any holy woman served two or more living husbands. But we do read that several women served one man [Note: [Col. 0387] Understand, “served one man.”] when the social order of that people allowed it and the circumstances of the time advised it; for this is not contrary to the nature of marriage.

Several women can be made fertile by one man, but one woman cannot be made fertile by several men—such is the force of principles [Note: [Col. 0387] The printed editions add, “so that several women belong to one man”; these words are absent from all the manuscripts.]. In the same way, many souls are rightly subjected to one God. Therefore there is only one true God of souls, whereas one soul can fornicate with many false gods, but cannot be made fruitful by them.

## CHAPTER XVIII

### 21. The sacrament of marriage has now been reduced to one husband and one wife. A bishop may not be ordained unless he is the husband of one wife.

Since one city is to arise from many souls having one soul and one heart toward God (Acts 4:32)—the perfection of our unity which will exist after this pilgrimage, when no one’s thoughts will be hidden from another and they will not conflict among themselves in anything—for this reason the sacrament of marriage in our time has been reduced to one husband and one wife, so that an overseer of the Church may not be ordained unless he is the husband of one wife (1 Tim. 3:2; Titus 1:6).

Those who judged more perceptively understood this to mean that even a man who had possessed another wife while a catechumen or pagan ought not to be ordained [Note: [Col. 0387] Ambrose understood this in this way in his letter to the Church at Vercellae, and this interpretation was formerly accepted and approved by the custom of the Church. Jerome, however, argued sharply and harshly against it in his letter to Oceanus. At the end of Book 1 *Against Rufinus*, he states that Rufinus had raised this interpretation against him.].

The issue concerns the sacrament, not sin. For in baptism all sins are forgiven. But the one who said, “If you take a wife, you have not sinned; and if a virgin marries, she does not sin”; and, “Let him do what he wishes; he does not sin if he marries” (1 Cor. 7:28, 36), clearly demonstrated that marriage is no sin.

Because of the holiness of the sacrament, just as a woman who has been violated—even if she was only a catechumen—cannot, after baptism, be consecrated among God’s virgins, so it did not seem unreasonable that a man who had exceeded the singular number of wives had not committed some sin but had lost a certain norm of the sacrament—one necessary not for the merit of a good life but for the sign of ecclesiastical ordination.

Accordingly, just as the several wives of the ancient fathers signified the future Churches from all nations, subject to one husband, Christ, so our bishop, the husband of one wife, signifies the unity from all nations subject to one husband, Christ. This unity will be perfected when he reveals the hidden things of darkness and discloses the thoughts of the heart, so that then each person may receive praise from God (1 Cor. 4:5).

At present there are both manifest and hidden dissensions [Note: [Col. 0388] So the manuscripts. The printed editions read, “At present there are manifestly hidden dissensions.”], even among those who, while preserving charity, are destined to be one and in one. Then, of course, there will be none.

Therefore, just as the sacrament of plural marriages in that earlier time signified the future multitude subject to God among all the earthly nations, so the sacrament of singular marriages in our time signifies the future unity of all of us subject to God in one heavenly city.

Thus, just as it was not then permitted to serve two or more masters, so it is not permitted—nor was it then, nor will it ever be—to pass from a living husband into another marriage. To apostatize from the one God and go over to another’s adulterous superstition is always evil.

Nor did our holy men, for the sake of a larger number of children, do what Cato the Roman is said to have done [Note: [Col. 0388] Cato of Utica, according to Plutarch], namely, give his living wife to another household so that she might fill it with children. In our marriages the holiness of the sacrament has greater force than the fertility of the womb.

### 22.

If, then, even those who unite solely for the sake of generation—the purpose for which marriage was instituted—are not comparable with the fathers, still less are those who seek children far differently from the way those fathers did. For Abraham, when commanded to sacrifice his son, fearless and devoted, did not spare his only child, whom he had received after such great hopelessness, until the one at whose command he had raised his hand forbade him and made him lower it (Gen. 22:12).

## CHAPTER XIX

### Whether at least our continent people are to be compared with the ancient married saints

It remains to see whether at least those among us who practice continence are to be compared with those married fathers—unless perhaps these people are already to be preferred to those for whom we have not yet found anyone to compare with them.

There was a greater good in the marriages of those earlier people than the good proper to marriage, and the good of continence must certainly be preferred to that good. For they sought children from their marriages by a duty unlike that by which these people are led, through a certain sense of mortal nature that seeks succession to replace those who die [Note: [Col. 0388] Several manuscripts read, “those who seek.”].

Whoever denies that this is a good does not know God, the Creator of all goods, from heavenly to earthly, from immortal to mortal. Even beasts are not entirely without this impulse to beget, especially birds, whose care in building nests is obvious, and in whom there is a certain likeness to marriage for jointly producing and nourishing offspring.

But those human beings greatly surpassed this affection of mortal nature, whose chastity, when joined with the worship of God, is placed, as some have understood, in the thirtyfold fruit [Note: [Col. 0389] See *On Virginity*, chapter 45.]. They surpassed it with a far holier mind because they sought children from their marriages for Christ, so that his lineage according to the flesh might be distinguished from all nations. God was pleased to arrange that this should be especially useful for prophesying about him, because it was foretold from which lineage and from which nation he would come in the flesh.

The good possessed by the chaste marriages of our faithful people was therefore far surpassed by what the patriarch Abraham knew in his own thigh, when he ordered his servant to place his hand beneath it and swear concerning the wife who was to be taken for his son (Gen. 24:2–4). For when he placed his hand beneath a man’s thigh and swore by the God of heaven, what else did he signify except that the God of heaven would come in that flesh which would derive its origin from that thigh?

Marriage, therefore, is good; and married people are better in it the more chastely and faithfully they fear God—especially if they also nourish spiritually the children whom they desire carnally.

## CHAPTER XX
### 23. The law of purification after intercourse does not show that it was a sin

Nor does the fact that the Law commands a man to be purified even after marital intercourse declare it to be a sin—if that intercourse is not the act granted by way of concession, which, when excessive, also hinders prayers. Rather, just as the Law sets forth many things in sacraments and shadows of future realities, so a certain material formlessness in the seed, which is destined, once formed, to become the human body, was appointed as a sign of an unformed and uneducated life. Since a person must be cleansed from this formlessness by the form and instruction of teaching, that purification was prescribed as a sign of this reality after the emission of semen.

For even in sleep no sin is committed [Note: [Col. 0389] So the better manuscripts. The printed editions have *peccatum fit*, “a sin is committed.”]; yet purification is prescribed even in that case. Or if someone thinks that this too is a sin, supposing that it occurs only from some desire of this kind—which is undoubtedly false—are a woman’s ordinary menstrual periods also sins? [Note: [Col. 0389] The manuscripts read *et solita mensium*; or, as was customary in the oldest manuscripts, *mensuum*. Hence perhaps the reading *et solita menstruum* found in Erasmus’s edition.] Yet the same ancient Law commands women to be cleansed from them (Lev. 15), solely because of that material formlessness, which, when conception has taken place, is added as though to the construction of the body. Thus, when it flows in an unformed state, the Law intended it to signify an undisciplined soul flowing indecently and dissolutely; and it signifies that the soul ought to be formed when it commands such a bodily flow to be purified.

Finally, is dying a sin? Or is burying the dead not also a good work of human compassion? Yet purification is commanded even on that account (Num. 19:11), because the dead body, when life has departed from it, is not a sin, but signifies a soul deserted by righteousness.

### 24. Marriage is good and can be defended by sound reasoning

Marriage, I say, is good and can be defended by sound reasoning against every accusation. Yet when I compare the marriages of the holy fathers, I am not asking which marriages to compare, but which continence [Col. 0390]—indeed, not marriages with marriages, for the same institution has in every case been granted to mortal human nature. Rather, I must ask which men who use marriage should be compared with other men who used marriage in a very different way, since I do not find which continent persons are to be compared with those married men [Note: [Col. 0390] So the manuscripts. The printed editions read, “how continent persons are to be compared.”].

Unless perhaps Abraham was unable to abstain from marriage for the sake of the kingdom of heaven—he who, for the sake of the kingdom of heaven, was able without hesitation to sacrifice the one pledge of offspring for which marriage is dear.

## CHAPTER XXI

### 25. Continence, like the other virtues, must be distinguished as existing in disposition and in action. The example of Christ teaches that a virtue can exist in disposition even when it is not in action

Continence is a virtue not of the body but of the soul. The virtues of the soul, however, are sometimes manifested in action and sometimes lie hidden in disposition. Thus the virtue of martyrdom shone forth and became manifest through the endurance of sufferings. But how many possess that same virtue of soul without having the trial by which what is within, in God’s sight, also comes before human beings—and does not then begin to exist, but then becomes known?

Patience already existed in Job; God knew it and bore witness to it. But it became known to human beings through the testing of temptation, and what lay hidden within was not born through the things inflicted outwardly, but was revealed by them (Job 1).

Timothy certainly possessed the virtue of abstaining from wine. Paul did not take this virtue away from him when he advised him to use a little wine because of his stomach and his frequent illnesses (1 Tim. 5:23). Otherwise he would have taught perniciously that, for the sake of bodily health, a loss of virtue should be incurred in the soul. But because the advice could be followed while preserving that virtue, the bodily benefit of drinking was permitted in such a way that the disposition of continence remained in the soul.

For disposition is the state by which something is done when there is need; when it is not done, it can be done, but there is no need for it. Those who are told, “If they cannot contain themselves, let them marry” (1 Cor. 7:9), do not possess this disposition with regard to continence from intercourse. Those, however, to whom it is said, “Let him who is able to receive it receive it” (Matt. 19:12), do possess it.

In this way the perfect used earthly goods that were necessary for other purposes through this disposition of continence: they were not bound to those goods, and they could also refrain from using them if there were no need. No one uses them well unless he can also refrain from using them. Many more easily abstain from using them than exercise restraint in using them well; nevertheless, no one can use them wisely unless he can also refrain from using them continently.

From this disposition Paul also said, “I know how to abound and how to suffer want” (Phil. 4:12). To suffer want is within the capacity of any human being; but to know how to suffer want belongs to the great. Likewise, who cannot abound? But to know how to abound belongs only to those whom abundance does not corrupt.

### 26. The example of Christ makes it clearer how a virtue exists in disposition even when it is not in action

To make it clearer how a virtue can exist in disposition even when it is not in action, I shall speak of an example about which no Catholic Christian has any doubt. No one among those who believe the Gospel of Christ doubts that our Lord Jesus Christ truly hungered and thirsted, ate and drank. Was there therefore not in him the virtue of continence from food and drink, just as much as there was in John the Baptist?

For John came “neither eating nor drinking,” and they said, “He has a demon.” The Son of Man came “eating and drinking,” and they said, “Behold, a glutton and a wine-drinker, a friend of tax collectors and sinners” [Note: [Col. 0391] The most ancient Corbie manuscript, together with the Bigot manuscript, reads *et vinaria*. Erasmus’s edition, with several manuscripts, has *et vinarius*; in the margin it gives, “Elsewhere, *vinaurius*,” perhaps for *vinhaurius*.].

Are not similar things said about those members of his household, our fathers, with regard to another way of using earthly things—so far as intercourse is concerned: “Behold, lustful and unclean men, lovers of women and of wantonness”? Yet just as that was not true of him, although it was true that he did not abstain from eating and drinking as John did—for he himself said most clearly and truly, “John came neither eating nor drinking; the Son of Man came eating and drinking”—so neither is this true of those fathers.

Although the Apostle of Christ has now come unmarried and without begetting children, whom the pagans call a magician, and although the Prophet of Christ then came marrying and fathering children, whom the Manichaeans call a womanizer, nevertheless, “Wisdom,” he says, “is justified by her children” (Matt. 11:18–19). The Lord added this when he had spoken those words about John and himself: “Wisdom,” he says, “is justified by her children.”

Those who see that the virtue of continence ought always to exist in the disposition of the soul, but that it is manifested in action according to the suitability of circumstances and times, understand the matter correctly. Thus the virtue of patience appeared in action in the holy martyrs, while in the other equally holy people it existed in disposition.

Accordingly, just as the merit of patience is not unequal in Peter, who suffered, and John, who did not suffer, so the merit of continence is not unequal in John, who experienced no marriage [Note: [Col. 0391] Jerome is followed here. In the first book of *Against Jovinianus* he writes that John was perpetually a virgin, and that there was no other reason why he was loved by the Lord more than the other Apostles. Jerome maintains and proves that John was found by Christ a virgin and almost a boy, saying, “The ecclesiastical histories most clearly teach that he lived until the reign of Trajan, that is, that he fell asleep sixty-eight years after the Lord’s passion.” Compare Augustine, *Tractate 124 on John*, no. 7.], and in Abraham, who fathered children.

The celibacy of the one and the marriage of the other served Christ according to the distribution of the times. But John possessed continence both in action and in disposition, whereas Abraham possessed it only in disposition.

## CHAPTER XXII

### 27. Continence was held by the ancients in disposition, but must now be held in action. The Jovinianist objection is rejected

At that time, when the Law—which followed the days of the Patriarchs—called him accursed who did not raise up offspring in Israel (Deut. 25:5–10), the man who could refrain did not do so, but nevertheless possessed the disposition of continence.

But from the time when the fullness of time came (Gal. 4:4), so that it could be said, “Let him who is able to receive it receive it,” from then until now, and from now until the end, whoever possesses this virtue must exercise it; whoever refuses to exercise it must not pretend to possess it.

Accordingly, those who corrupt good morals by evil conversations (1 Cor. 15:33) say, with empty and vain cleverness, to the Christian man who is continent and refuses marriage: [Col. 0392] “Are you therefore better than Abraham?”

When he hears this, let him not be disturbed. Let him neither dare to say, “I am better,” nor abandon his purpose. The first statement would be untrue; the second would be wrong. Rather, let him say: “I am indeed not better than Abraham, but the chastity of celibates is better than the chastity of marriage. Abraham had one of these in use and both in disposition. He lived chastely in marriage; he could have been chaste without marriage, but at that time it was not appropriate. I, however, more easily refrain from using marriage, which Abraham used, than use marriage as Abraham used it. Therefore I am better than those who, through incontinence of soul, cannot do what I do—not better than those who, because of the difference of the times, did not do what I do.

“What I am doing now, he would have done better if it had been necessary to do it then; but what he did, I would not do, even if it were necessary to do it now.”

Or, if this man feels and knows himself to be such that, while the virtue of continence remained safe and enduring in the disposition of his soul, he would, if he descended to the use of marriage through some religious duty, be such a husband and such a father as Abraham was, let him boldly answer that deceitful questioner and say:

“I am indeed not better than Abraham in that particular kind of continence which he did not lack, even though it was not apparent. I am such as he was, possessing not something else, but doing something else.”

Let him say this plainly. Even if he wishes to boast, he will not be foolish, for he is speaking the truth. But if he exercises restraint so that no one may think that he possesses something beyond what is seen or heard in him (2 Cor. 12:6), let him remove the knot of the question from his own person and answer not about the man but about the matter itself. Let him say: “Whoever is able to attain this is such as Abraham was.”

It can happen that the virtue of continence is less in the soul of one who does not use marriage, which Abraham used, yet it is still greater [Note: [Col. 0392] The Louvain edition adds here, “in his action”; this is absent from Erasmus and the manuscripts.] than in the soul of one who preserved marital chastity because he was unable to attain anything greater.

Likewise, an unmarried woman who thinks about the things of the Lord, so that she may be holy both in body and spirit (1 Cor. 7:34), when she hears that shameless questioner saying, “Are you therefore better than Sarah?” should answer: “I am better, but only than those who lack the virtue of this continence—which I do not believe Sarah lacked. She did, with this virtue, what was appropriate to that time; I am exempt from it, so that what she preserved in her soul may also appear in my body.”

## CHAPTER XXIII

### 28. Continence is better than marital chastity, but married people can be better than continent people. The good of obedience is greater than that of continence. A more obedient married woman must be preferred to a less obedient virgin. Obedience is the mother of all virtues

If we compare the realities themselves, there is no doubt that the chastity of continence is better than marital chastity, although both are good. But when we compare people, the better person is the one who possesses the greater good.

Moreover, whoever possesses more of the same kind possesses what is less; but whoever possesses only what is less does not necessarily possess what is greater. Sixty contains thirty, but thirty does not contain sixty. Not exercising what one possesses belongs to the distribution of duties, not to poverty of virtues; for a person who does not find the miserable whom he might mercifully assist is not thereby lacking the good of mercy.

### 29. People should not rightly be compared with one another on the basis of a single good

Furthermore, people are not rightly compared with one another on the basis of a single good. It can happen that one person lacks something another possesses, but possesses something else that ought to be valued more highly.

Obedience is a greater good than continence. For nowhere in the authority of our Scriptures is marriage condemned, whereas disobedience is nowhere absolved. If, then, we are presented with a virgin who remains a virgin but is disobedient, and a married woman who could not remain a virgin but is obedient, which should we call better? Should we call the married woman less praiseworthy than she would have been if she were a virgin, or condemn her as we condemn the virgin?

Likewise, if you compare a drunken virgin with a sober married woman, who would doubt that the same judgment should be made? Marriage and virginity are two goods, one of which is greater. Sobriety and drunkenness, however, like obedience and defiance, are respectively good and evil.

It is better to possess all the good things, even the lesser ones, than to possess a great good together with a great evil. For even among bodily goods it is better to have Zacchaeus’s stature with health than Goliath’s stature with fever.

### 30. The proper comparison is not between an utterly disobedient virgin and an obedient married woman, but between a less obedient virgin and a more obedient married woman

The proper question is not whether an utterly disobedient virgin should be compared with an obedient married woman, but whether a less obedient virgin should be compared with a more obedient married woman. The latter possesses marital chastity, and therefore something good, but something less than virginal chastity.

Thus the virgin is as much inferior in the good of obedience as she is superior in the good of chastity. The person who judges which should be preferred, if one is compared with the other, must first compare chastity and obedience and recognize that obedience is, in a certain sense, the mother of all virtues.

Obedience can therefore exist without virginity because virginity is a matter of counsel, not of command. By obedience I mean obedience to commands. Obedience to commands can exist without virginity, but it cannot exist without chastity.

For chastity includes not committing fornication, not committing adultery, and not being defiled by any illicit intercourse. Those who do not observe these things act against God’s commands and are therefore excluded from the virtue of obedience.

Virginity, however, can exist without obedience because a woman may accept the counsel of virginity, preserve her virginity, and yet despise the commandments. We know many consecrated virgins who are talkative, inquisitive, drunken, quarrelsome, greedy, and proud. All these things are contrary to the commandments, and, like Eve herself, they perish through the crime of disobedience.

Therefore not only an obedient woman should be preferred to a disobedient one; a more obedient married woman should also be preferred to a less obedient virgin.

### 31. Through obedience Abraham was ready to be without his only son, though he had not been without a wife

Through this obedience that father who had not been without a wife was ready to be without his only son, even though he would have killed him [Note: [Col. 0393] *Retractations* II, chapter 22, no. 2.]. I may rightly call him his only son, since he heard from the Lord, “In Isaac shall your offspring be called” (Gen. 21:12).

How much more quickly, then, would he have obeyed if he had been commanded to be without a wife also? Hence we are often rightly astonished that some men and women who abstain from all intercourse are negligent in obeying the commandments, although they have so eagerly undertaken not to use what is permitted.

Who, then, doubts that the excellence of those holy fathers and mothers who fathered children should not rightly be compared with the men and women of our own time who are free from all intercourse but lesser in the virtue of obedience—even if those earlier people had lacked in the disposition of their souls what is manifest in the action of these later people?

Let the boys who follow the Lamb, singing a new song as it is written in the Apocalypse, “who have not defiled themselves with women” (Rev. 14:4), continue to follow him because they remained virgins. But let them not therefore suppose themselves better than the first holy fathers, who used marriage, so to speak, in a marital manner [Note: [Col. 0394] See also the reading, “did not use marriage in a marital manner,” despite the opposition of other printed editions and manuscripts.].

For the use of marriage is such that, if anything in it exceeds the necessity of begetting children—even if it is done with the indulgence granted to human weakness—it is a defilement.
