For what does indulgence cleanse if that extension does not defile at all? It would be astonishing if the boys following the Lamb were free from that defilement unless they remained virgins.

## CHAPTER XXIV

### 32. Among Christians the good of marriage is threefold. The ancient married people possessed obedience in action and continence in disposition

The good of marriage among all nations and all people consists in the purpose of begetting children and in fidelity of chastity. With regard to the people of God, it also consists in the holiness of the sacrament, by which it is unlawful for a woman who has left her husband, even by divorce, to marry another while her husband is alive—not even for the purpose of bearing children. Since this is the sole purpose for which marriages are formed, the marital bond is not dissolved when that purpose does not follow, except by the death of a spouse.

This is like the ordination of clergy for the gathering of a congregation. Even if the congregation does not subsequently gather, the sacrament of ordination nevertheless remains in those who were ordained. And if someone is removed from office because of some fault, he does not lose the sacrament of the Lord once it has been conferred, although it remains for judgment.

That marriage is undertaken for the sake of procreation is testified to by the Apostle: “I desire,” he says, “that younger women marry.” And as though someone had asked him, “For what purpose?” he immediately added, “to bear children and manage their households” (1 Tim. 5:14).

Fidelity of chastity is expressed in these words: “The wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband; likewise, the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife.”

The holiness of the sacrament is expressed in these words: “A wife should not separate from her husband; but if she does separate, she should remain unmarried or be reconciled to her husband; and a husband should not dismiss his wife.”

All these are good things, on account of which marriage is good [Note: [Col. 0394] The manuscripts read, “are a good”; that is, *bonum sunt*.]: offspring, fidelity, and the sacrament.

But no longer to seek carnal offspring at the present time, and therefore to retain a perpetual freedom from all such activity and to be spiritually subject to the one husband, Christ, is certainly better and holier—provided that people use this freedom in the manner prescribed in Scripture, so that they think about the things of the Lord and how they may please God (1 Cor. 7:4, 10–11, 32). That is, continence must think continually of obedience, lest it possess less of that virtue.

The holy fathers of old exercised obedience, as a kind of root and, as it is commonly said, matrix and universal virtue, in action; but they retained continence in the disposition of their souls. Through the obedience by which they were just and holy, and always ready for every good work, they would have been capable of abstaining from all intercourse if they had been commanded to do so.

For how much more easily could they have refrained from intercourse at God’s command or exhortation, when, through obedience, they were able to sacrifice the offspring whom they served by intercourse for the sole purpose of bringing forth?

## CHAPTER XXV

### 33. The Manichaeans’ accusations against the fathers of the Old Testament are refuted

Since these things are so, the response to the heretics—whether Manichaeans or any others—who bring numerous accusations against the fathers of the Old Testament on account of their several wives, treating this as an argument by which to convict them of incontinence, has been more than sufficiently given.

This is so, provided they understand that what was done was not a sin: it was not against nature, because those women were used not for wantonness but for begetting children; it was not against custom, because such things were practiced in those times; and it was not against a command, because no law prohibited them.

As for those who used women illicitly, either the divine judgment in Scripture condemns them, or Scripture presents them for us to judge and avoid, not to approve or imitate.

## CHAPTER XXVI

### 34. Those who are continent in the present age should not think contemptuously of the holy married fathers. Virginity must be guarded by humility

As far as we can, we admonish our people who have spouses not to dare judge those holy fathers according to their own weakness, comparing themselves with themselves, as the Apostle says (2 Cor. 10:12), and thereby failing to understand how great is the strength of a soul serving righteousness against lust, so that it does not yield to such carnal impulses and does not allow them to slip or advance into intercourse beyond the necessity of procreation, within the limits prescribed by the order of nature, the custom of morals, and the statutes of the laws.

People suspect this of those fathers because, through their own incontinence, they have either chosen marriage or used their spouses immoderately. But those who are continent—whether men whose wives have died, women whose husbands have died, or either sex who by mutual agreement have vowed continence to God—should know that a greater reward is owed to them than marital chastity requires.

Nevertheless, they should not merely refrain from despising the marriages of the holy fathers, who were joined prophetically, who sought in intercourse nothing except offspring, and in that offspring nothing except what would benefit Christ, who was to come in the flesh. They should, without hesitation, prefer those marriages to their own state.

### 35. Children and virgins should especially preserve their integrity with humility

We especially admonish boys and virgins who dedicate their integrity to God to know that the purity in which they live for the present on earth must be guarded with as much humility as the heavenly state they have vowed is greater.

For it is written: “The greater you are, the more you must humble yourself in all things” (Ecclus. 3:20).

It is our task, therefore, to say something about their greatness; it is their task to think about great humility.

Except for certain holy married fathers and mothers, whom these people are not better than merely because they are unmarried—for if they were married, they would not be their equals—let those who are unmarried in the present age, or who became continent after having experienced intercourse, have no doubt that they surpass all other married people of the present time—not as Anna and Susanna were surpassed, but as both Anna and Susanna are surpassed by Mary.

I am speaking with reference to bodily integrity itself; for who is unaware of Mary’s other merits?

Let them therefore join to this great vocation conduct that corresponds to it, so that they may possess firm assurance of the surpassing reward. Let them know that this great thing is granted in common to themselves, to all the beloved and chosen faithful who are members of Christ, and to the many coming from east and west who shine with the light of glory, although they differ among themselves in their merits: namely, that they will recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of God (Matt. 8:11)—those who were husbands and fathers not for the sake of this world, but for the sake of Christ.

[Col. 0395]

[Note: [Col. 0395] For the subsequent book, *On Holy Virginity*, see book 2, chapter 23 of the *Retractations*, vol. 1, col. 640, from the words “After I wrote” up to the words “We have recently published.” M. Saint Augustine also mentions this book in the immediately following book, *On the Good of Widowhood*, chapters 15 and 23, as well as in book 1 of *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, chapter 29.]

## One Book by Saint Aurelius Augustine, Bishop of Hippo, on Holy Virginity

[Note: [Col. 0395] Written about the year 401.]

[Note: [Col. 0397] We have corrected the book *On Holy Virginity* against two old Colbert manuscripts; the most ancient Corbie manuscript; the Bigot, Pratell, Michaelin, and Cistercian manuscripts; a manuscript of the Church of Reims; another of the Church of Laon; four Vatican manuscripts; the variant readings of the Louvain edition from three Belgian manuscripts; and finally the editions of Erasmus and Louvain.]

[Note: [Col. 0397] We also compared all the editions mentioned at the beginning of *Retractations* and *Confessions*, vol. 1. M.]

(C)

He speaks first about the excellence of holy virginity dedicated to God, demonstrating that no marital fertility can now be compared with it. He then confronts two contrary errors: one that condemns marriage, and the other that equates it with virginity. The first group thinks that marriage was indirectly and easily condemned by the Apostle when he said to the Corinthians, “Those who marry will have worldly troubles; but I am sparing you” [Col. 0397]. The second group relies on his writing to the same people, “I think that this is good because of the present necessity,” and contends that perpetual continence is commended for the sake of life in this age, not for the sake of the future one.

Afterward he commands Christ’s virgins to possess the humility by which their outstanding vocation is preserved, and he urges them with many serious words to pursue it above all.

## CHAPTER I

### 1. Virgins should not despise the married holy fathers

We recently published a book, *On the Good of Marriage*, in which we also admonished and continue to admonish Christ’s virgins not to despise, in comparison with themselves, the fathers and mothers of God’s people because of the excellence of the greater vocation they have received from God.

The Apostle commends those people as an olive tree, warning the grafted wild olive not to become proud (Rom. 11:17–18). They served the Christ who was to come also through the propagation of children. Virgins should not therefore think that these people possess an inferior merit because, by divine law, continence is preferred to marriage and holy virginity to married life.

In those people, future realities were prepared and brought forth—realities that we now see fulfilled with wonderful power. Their married life too was prophetic. Hence, not according to the customary pattern of human vows and joys, but according to the profound counsel of God, the fertility of some of them deserved to be honored, while the barrenness of others even deserved to be made fertile.

In the present age, however, those to whom it is said, “If they cannot contain themselves, let them marry” (1 Cor. 7:9), need consolation rather than exhortation. Those to whom it is said, “Let him who is able to receive it receive it” (Matt. 19:12), must be exhorted so that they are not frightened, and warned so that they do not become exalted.

Virginity therefore must not only be proclaimed so that it may be loved; it must also be admonished so that it may not become inflated with pride.

## CHAPTER II

### 2. Christ is the son of a virgin and the bridegroom of virgins. The Church, like Mary, is both mother and virgin

This is the subject we have undertaken in this discourse. May Christ help us—he who is the Son of a virgin and the Bridegroom of virgins, born bodily from a virginal womb and spiritually joined in marriage to a virginal union.

Since the whole Church is betrothed as a virgin to one husband, Christ, as the Apostle says (2 Cor. 11:2), how much honor do those members of his deserve who preserve even in the flesh what the whole Church preserves in faith? The Church imitates the mother of her husband and Lord.

For the Church too is both mother and virgin. Whose integrity are we protecting if she is not a virgin? Or whose offspring are we addressing if she is not a mother?

Mary bodily gave birth to the head of this body; the Church spiritually gives birth to the members of that head. In both, virginity does not prevent fertility; in both, fertility does not take away virginity.

Therefore, since the whole Church is holy in body and spirit, yet is not wholly a virgin in body but only in spirit, how much holier is she in those members in which she is a virgin both in body and in spirit?

## CHAPTER III

### 3. Spiritual kinship with Christ must be preferred to his bodily kinship

It is written in the Gospel that when Christ’s mother and brothers—that is, his relatives according to the flesh—were announced to him and were waiting outside because they could not approach him on account of the crowd, he replied: “Who is my mother, or who are my brothers?” And stretching out his hand over his disciples, he said: “These are my brothers; whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven is my brother, sister, and mother” (Matt. 12:46–50).

What else was he teaching us except to prefer our spiritual kinship to our carnal kinship? People are not blessed merely because they are joined by bodily relationship to the just and holy, but because they cling to them by obeying and imitating their teaching and conduct.

Mary, therefore, was more blessed in receiving the faith of Christ than in conceiving the flesh of Christ. For when someone said to him, “Blessed is the womb that bore you,” he replied, “Rather, blessed are those who hear the word of God and keep it” (Luke 11:27–28).

Finally, what benefit did his kinship according to the flesh provide his brothers, who did not believe in him? Likewise, his maternal relationship would have profited Mary nothing if she had not carried Christ more blessedly in her heart than in her flesh.

## CHAPTER IV

### 4. Mary’s virginity was dedicated to God by a vow before she heard that she would conceive Christ

Her virginity itself is therefore more pleasing and acceptable because Christ’s conception did not seize it in order to preserve it from a man who would violate it. Rather, before he was conceived, he chose as his mother one who had already been dedicated to God.

This is indicated by the words Mary gave the angel who announced the child to her: “How will this happen, since I do not know a man?” (Luke 1:34). She certainly would not have said this unless she had previously vowed herself a virgin to God.

But because Israelite customs still rejected this practice, she was betrothed to a righteous man—not one who would forcibly take away what she had vowed, but rather one who would guard it against those who might violate it.

Even if she had said only, “How will this happen?” without adding, “since I do not know a man,” she would not have been asking how she, as a woman, was to bear the promised son if she had married for intercourse. A virgin could have been commanded to remain a virgin, in whom the Son of God would receive the form of a servant through a fitting miracle.

But she was made an example for holy virgins to come, so that no one would think that only the woman who deserved to conceive offspring without intercourse ought to be a virgin. She dedicated her virginity to God while she still did not know what she was going to conceive, so that in an earthly and mortal body the imitation of heavenly life might be established by a vow, not by a command; by the love of choosing, not by the necessity of serving.

Thus, by being born from a virgin who had decided to remain a virgin before she knew who would be born from her, Christ preferred to approve holy virginity rather than command it. And so, even in the woman in whom he received the form of a servant, he willed virginity to be free.

## CHAPTER V

### 5. The birth of the one Virgin is the glory of all virgins. Virgins themselves are mothers of Christ in spirit

There is therefore no reason for God’s virgins to grieve because, while preserving their virginity, they cannot also be mothers in the flesh. Virginity could fittingly give birth only to the one who could not have an equal at his birth.

Nevertheless, the birth of that one holy Virgin is the glory of all holy virgins. They too are mothers of Christ together with Mary if they do the will of his Father.

For according to the saying quoted above, Mary is Christ’s mother more honorably and blessedly: “Whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven is my brother, sister, and mother.”

Among the people he redeemed, Christ spiritually displays all these forms of kinship. He has as brothers and sisters holy men and holy women, because they are co-heirs with him in the heavenly inheritance.

His mother is the whole Church, because the Church herself, by God’s grace, gives birth to his members—that is, to his faithful. Likewise, his mother is every devout soul that does the will of his Father with the most fruitful love in those whom it brings to birth, until Christ himself is formed in them (Gal. 4:19).

Thus Mary, by doing God’s will, is bodily only the mother of Christ, but spiritually she is also his sister and mother.

## CHAPTER VI

### 6. Mary alone is both virgin and mother in body and spirit

Accordingly, that one woman is not only a virgin in spirit but also, in body, both mother and virgin.

She is a mother in spirit—not of our head, which is the Savior himself, from whom she was spiritually born all the more because all who believe in him, among whom she herself is included, are rightly called the children of the bridegroom (Matt. 9:15). But she is plainly the mother of his members, which we are, because she cooperated through love so that the faithful might be born in the Church, and they are members of that head. In body, however, she is the mother of the head himself.

It was necessary for our head to be born bodily from a virgin through a remarkable miracle, thereby signifying that his members would be born spiritually from the virgin Church.

Therefore Mary alone is mother and virgin both in spirit and in body—both the mother of Christ and the virgin of Christ.

The Church, however, among the saints who will possess the kingdom of God, is wholly the mother of Christ and wholly the virgin of Christ in spirit; but in body she is not wholly either. In some she is the virgin of Christ, and in others she is a mother, though not the mother of Christ.

Married women who are faithful, as well as virgins dedicated to God, are spiritually mothers of Christ when, with holy conduct and love from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith (1 Tim. 1:5), they do the Father’s will.

Those who give birth bodily through married life, however, give birth not to Christ but to Adam. Therefore they hasten to have their offspring made members of Christ by being instructed in the sacraments, since they know what they have brought forth [Note: [Col. 0399] Some manuscripts read *curant*, “they take care,” instead of *currunt*, “they hasten.”].

## CHAPTER VII
### 7. No Fecundity of Marriage Can Be Compared with Virginity

I have said this lest the fecundity of marriage should dare to contend with virginal integrity and put forward Mary herself, saying to God’s virgins: “She possessed two things in the body worthy of honor, virginity and fecundity, because she both remained intact and gave birth. Since we could not both possess this happiness in its entirety, we divided it between us: you are virgins, we are mothers. What you lack in offspring is consoled by the virginity you have preserved [Note: [Col. 0399] The printed editions have *desit*; the manuscripts have *defit*, a word Augustine often uses.]; what we have lost in integrity is compensated by the gain of offspring [Col. 0400].”

This speech of faithful married women to holy virgins might in some fashion be tolerated if they bore Christians bodily. Then Mary’s fecundity of the flesh, apart from her virginity, would be superior only in this respect: she gave birth to the very Head of these members, whereas they give birth to members of that Head. But in fact, even if such women should contend in this way—women who join and unite themselves to men solely in order to have children, and who think of nothing else concerning their children except how to win them for Christ, and do this as soon as they are able—their children are not born Christians from their flesh. They become Christians afterward, when the Church gives birth to them by virtue of being spiritually the mother of Christ’s members, and also spiritually Christ’s virgin.

Mothers who have not borne Christians bodily cooperate in this holy birth, so that their children may become what they know they could not produce bodily. Yet they cooperate in it precisely where they themselves are both virgins and mothers of Christ—namely, in the faith that works through love (Gal. V, 6).

[Note: [Col. 0400] Perhaps better: “They are mothers of Christ,” with the particle *que* deleted.]

### CHAPTER VIII

#### 8. Virginity Is Honored Because It Is Dedicated to God

No fecundity of the flesh, then, can be compared even in the flesh with holy virginity. For virginity is not honored simply because it is virginity, but because it is dedicated to God. Although it is preserved in the flesh, it is preserved through the religion and devotion of the spirit. Accordingly, bodily virginity too is spiritual, for it is vowed and preserved by the continence of piety. [Note: [Col. 0400] The Louvain edition alone has *fovet* (“cherishes”) instead of *vovet* (“vows”).]

Just as no one uses the body immodestly unless wickedness has first been conceived in the spirit, so no one preserves chastity in the body unless purity has first been implanted in the spirit. Moreover, although conjugal chastity is guarded in the flesh, it is attributed to the mind, not to the flesh, since the mind presides and directs, and the flesh itself is joined to no one except one’s own spouse. How much more, and how much more honorably, should that continence be counted among the goods of the soul by which the integrity of the flesh is vowed, consecrated, and preserved for the very Creator of soul and body?

### CHAPTER IX

#### 9. Lost Virginity Is Not Compensated by Any Fecundity of the Flesh

Nor should we believe that the fecundity of those women who at this time seek nothing else in marriage except offspring to dedicate to Christ can compensate for lost virginity. In earlier times, when Christ was to come according to the flesh, the very propagation of the flesh was necessary within a certain extensive and prophetic nation. But now, since members of Christ can be gathered from every human kind and from all nations into the people of God and the city of the kingdom of heaven, let whoever can receive holy virginity receive it (Matt. XIX, 12), and let only she who cannot contain herself marry (I Cor. VII, 9).

What if a wealthy woman were to spend a great deal of money on this good work, buying slaves from various nations and making them Christians? Would she not thereby arrange for the birth of Christ’s members more abundantly and in greater numbers than any fertility of the womb could produce? Yet she would not dare to compare her money with the gift of holy virginity. But if fecundity of the flesh is rightly compensated for lost virginity because those who are born can be made Christians, then this undertaking would be more productive if virginity were lost for a large monetary price, by which [Col. 0401] many more children to be made Christians could be purchased than could be born from even one woman’s highly fertile womb.

### CHAPTER X

#### Marriage Must Not Be Set Against Virginity Because It Gives Birth to Virgins

If this is said foolishly, let faithful married women retain their own good, about which we have discussed as much as seemed appropriate in another volume; and let them honor still more, as they rightly and customarily do, that which is better in holy virgins and which we are discussing in this work.

#### 10.

For marriages should not even compare themselves with the merits of those who practice continence on the ground that virgins are born from marriages. This is not a good belonging to marriage, but to nature. Nature has been divinely instituted in such a way that from sexual intercourse between any human male and female—whether ordered and honorable or shameful and illicit—every female is born a virgin, although no one is thereby born a holy virgin. Thus a virgin may be born even from fornication, but a holy virgin cannot be born even from marriage.

### CHAPTER XI

#### 11. Virgins Are Praised Because They Are Dedicated to God

We do not praise this in virgins, that they are virgins, but that, as virgins dedicated to God, they are so through devout continence. For—and I would not say this rashly—a married woman seems to me happier than a virgin who is going to marry. The married woman already possesses what the other still desires, especially if the latter is not yet anyone’s betrothed. The married woman strives to please the one to whom she has been given; the other strives to please many, uncertain to whom she will be given. She protects the chastity of her thoughts from the crowd by seeking in the crowd not an adulterer but a husband.

That virgin, therefore, is rightly preferred to the married woman who does not offer herself to be loved by the multitude while seeking the love of one from among the multitude; nor does she already shape herself for one whom she has found, thinking about the things of the world and how to please her husband (I Cor. VII, 34). Rather, she has loved him who is beautiful beyond the sons of men (Ps. XLIV, 3) in such a way that, since she could not conceive him in the flesh as Mary did, she preserves her flesh intact for him whom she has conceived in her heart.

### CHAPTER XII

#### Holy Virgins Are Born to the Church Not by Bodily but by Spiritual Fecundity. The Good of Marriage Is Inferior to the Good of Holy Virginity

No bodily fecundity has produced this kind of virgin. This offspring is not of flesh and blood. If their mother is sought, it is the Church. Holy virgins are born only from a holy virgin—the one who was betrothed to one man, to be presented chaste to Christ (II Cor. XI, 2). From her, who is not wholly a virgin in body but wholly a virgin in spirit, holy virgins are born both in body and in spirit.

#### 12.

Let marriages retain their own good—not because they beget children, but because they beget them honorably, lawfully, chastely, and socially, and because they raise the children they have begotten together with soundness and diligence; because they preserve mutual fidelity in the marriage bed; and because they do not violate the sacrament of marriage.

### CHAPTER XIII

#### Against Those Who Think Continence Is Useful Only for the Present Life

All these, nevertheless, are duties belonging to human life. But virginal integrity, and freedom from all sexual intercourse through devout continence, is an angelic portion and a perpetual meditation on incorruption in corruptible flesh. Let all [Col. 0402] fecundity of the flesh and all conjugal chastity yield to this. The former is not within one’s power; the latter is not in eternity. Carnal fecundity does not belong to free choice; conjugal chastity does not belong to heaven. Surely those who already possess something not of the flesh within the flesh will have something great beyond the rest in that common immortality.

#### 13.

Thus those who think that the good of this continence is not necessary for the kingdom of heaven but only for the present world are astonishingly foolish. They say that marriage is weighed down by more numerous and more burdensome earthly cares, from which virgins and the continent are free—as though it were better not to marry only so that the pressures of this present time might be relaxed, and not because it contributes something to the world to come.

Lest they appear to have produced this empty opinion from the vanity of their own hearts, they bring forward the Apostle’s testimony, where he says: “Concerning virgins I have no commandment of the Lord, but I give counsel, as one who has obtained mercy from God to be faithful. I think therefore that this is good because of the present necessity, for it is good for a person to be thus” (I Cor. VII, 25–26).

“There,” they say, “the Apostle plainly shows that this is good because of the present necessity, not because of future eternity.” As though the Apostle would have considered the present necessity unless he were providing and giving counsel for the future, since his entire stewardship calls us only to eternal life.

[Note: [Col. 0402] Thus several manuscripts. The printed editions have *propria* (“of one’s own”), rather than *proprii* (“of his own heart”).]

[Note: [Col. 0402] The printed editions have *non providens* (“not providing”). The manuscripts have *nisi providens* (“unless providing”).]

### CHAPTER XIV

#### 14. Virginity Is Commended Not by Commandment but by Counsel, for the Attainment of a Special Glory in the Future Life

The present necessity, then, is to be avoided, but it is a necessity that impedes certain future goods. Through this necessity, conjugal life is compelled to think about the things of the world—how a husband may please his wife or a wife her husband. This does not separate them from the kingdom of God, as sins do; sins are restrained by commandment, not counsel, because it is damnable not to obey the Lord who commands. But what might be possessed more fully within the kingdom of God, if one thought more fully about how to please God, will necessarily be possessed less fully when the necessity of marriage causes one to think less about this very thing.

Therefore, he says, “Concerning virgins I have no commandment of the Lord.” Whoever does not obey a commandment is guilty and liable to punishment. Since taking a wife or marrying is not a sin—if it were a sin, it would be forbidden by commandment—there is therefore no commandment of the Lord concerning virgins.

But since, once sins have been avoided or forgiven, eternal life must be entered, and since within it there is a distinguished glory to be assigned eternally not to all who will live there but to some, it is not enough for attaining that glory to have been freed from sins. Something must also be vowed to the Liberator—something whose failure to vow is not a crime, but whose being vowed and fulfilled is praiseworthy. “I give counsel,” he says, “as one who has obtained mercy from God to be faithful.” I should not begrudge the faithful counsel, since I am faithful not through my own merits but through God’s mercy.

“I think therefore that this is good because of the present necessity.” [Col. 0403] What is this, he says, concerning which I have no commandment of the Lord but give counsel? It is this matter of virgins, which I think is good because of the present necessity. I know what the necessity of the present time, to which marriages are subject, compels: that the things of God be thought about less than is sufficient for attaining that glory which will not belong to everyone, even though all remain in eternal life and salvation.

“For star differs from star in glory; so also is the resurrection of the dead” (I Cor. XV, 41–42). It is good, therefore, for a person to be thus.

### CHAPTER XV

#### 15. The Counsel Is Not to Marry, Not a Commandment

The same Apostle then adds and says: “Are you bound to a wife? Do not seek release. Are you released from a wife? Do not seek a wife.” The first of these two statements, which he placed first, belongs to commandment, contrary to which one may not act. For it is not lawful to dismiss one’s wife except on account of fornication, as the Lord himself says in the Gospel (Matt. XIX, 9).

But what he added—“Are you released from a wife? Do not seek a wife”—is the judgment of counsel, not of commandment. It is therefore permitted to do so, but it is better not to do so. Accordingly, he immediately adds: “But if you take a wife, you have not sinned; and if a virgin marries, she has not sinned.”

When he had first said, “Are you bound to a wife? Do not seek release,” did he perhaps add, “And if you obtain release, you have not sinned”? For he had already said above: “To those who are married I give this command—not I, but the Lord—that a wife should not depart from her husband; but if she departs, let her remain unmarried or be reconciled to her husband.” For it may happen that she departs not through her own fault but because of her husband.

Then he says: “And let the husband not dismiss his wife” (I Cor. VII, 27–28, 10–11). This too he gives as a commandment of the Lord, and there he does not add, “And if he dismisses her, he has not sinned.” For this is a commandment, and not obeying it is sin; it is not counsel, such that if one does not wish to use it one obtains less good but commits no evil.

Therefore, when he had said, “Are you released from a wife? Do not seek a wife,” because he was not commanding that evil be avoided but advising that what is better be done, he immediately added: “But if you take a wife, you have not sinned; and if a virgin marries, she has not sinned.”

### CHAPTER XVI

#### 16. What the Tribulation of the Flesh in Marriage Is

He nevertheless adds: “But such persons will have tribulation in the flesh, and I am sparing you.” In this way he exhorts them to perpetual virginity and continence, also deterring them somewhat from marriage—not as from something evil or illicit, but as from something burdensome and troublesome.

For it is one thing to commit the shamefulness of the flesh, and another to have tribulation of the flesh. The former is to commit a crime; the latter is to endure labor, which people frequently do not refuse even for the most honorable duties.

But at the present time, when Christ is not served through the propagation of offspring by carnal generation, since he is not to come through such propagation, it would be utter folly to undertake and endure this tribulation of the flesh that the Apostle predicts for those who marry—unless those who cannot contain themselves feared that, when Satan tempted them, they might fall into damnable sins.

As for his saying that he spares those whom he says will have tribulation of the flesh, nothing more reasonable occurs to me for the moment than that he did not wish [Col. 0404] to disclose and explain in words the very tribulation of the flesh that he foretold for those who choose marriage: the suspicions of conjugal jealousy, the begetting and raising of children, and the fears and sorrows of bereavement. For who is there who, once bound by the ties of marriage, is not drawn and agitated by these emotions? We ought not to exaggerate them, lest we fail to spare those whom the Apostle thought should be spared.

### CHAPTER XVII

#### 17. Against Those Who Think Marriage Is Condemned There by the Apostle. How Harmful It Is to Attribute a Lie to Scripture

From the brief statement I have just made, the reader ought to have been warned against those who slander marriage on the basis of the words, “But such persons will have tribulation in the flesh, and I am sparing you,” claiming that this sentence indirectly condemns marriage. They imagine that the Apostle did not wish to state the condemnation itself when he said, “I am sparing you,” so that, while sparing them, he did not spare his own soul if he lied when he said, “If you take a wife, you have not sinned; and if a virgin marries, she has not sinned.”

Those who believe or wish others to believe this about holy Scripture seem to pave a way for themselves to license in lying, or to the defense of their perverse opinion, wherever they think differently from what sound doctrine requires. For whenever something plainly stated in the divine books is brought forward to refute their errors, they have this ready at hand as a shield with which, supposedly defending themselves against the truth, they expose themselves to be wounded by the devil. They say that the author of the book did not speak truth: sometimes to spare the weak, sometimes to terrify the contemptuous, or whatever explanation may present itself by which their perverse opinion can be defended.

Thus, while preferring to defend what they believe rather than correct it, they try to weaken the authority of holy Scripture, by which alone all proud and stubborn necks are broken.

### CHAPTER XVIII

#### 18. Virginity Must Be Preferred in Such a Way That Marriage Is Not Condemned

Therefore I admonish the followers, both men and women, of perpetual continence and holy virginity: let them prefer their own good to marriage in such a way that they do not judge marriage evil. Let them know that the Apostle spoke not deceptively but with complete truth: “He who gives his virgin in marriage does well; and he who does not give her in marriage does better. If you take a wife, you have not sinned; and if a virgin marries, she has not sinned.”

And shortly afterward: “But she will be happier if she remains thus, according to my judgment.” And lest this be thought a merely human judgment, he adds: “I think that I too have the Spirit of God.”

This is the Lord’s teaching, the Apostle’s teaching, true and sound doctrine: to choose the greater gifts without condemning the lesser. The truth of God in Scripture is better than human virginity in anyone’s mind or flesh. Let what is chaste be loved in such a way that what is true is not denied.

For what evil might those not imagine even concerning their own flesh who believe that the apostolic tongue, in the very passage where it commended bodily virginity, was not itself virgin—untouched by the corruption of falsehood? Therefore, first and above all, let those who choose the good of virginity hold most firmly that the holy Scriptures have lied about nothing. Accordingly, let this too be held true: “If you take a wife, [Col. 0405] you have not sinned; and if a virgin marries, she has not sinned.”

Nor should they think that the great good of integrity is diminished if marriage is not evil. Rather, let the woman who did not fear being condemned if she married, but desired to be crowned more honorably because she did not marry, confidently recognize that the palm of greater glory has thereby been prepared for her.

[Note: [Col. 0405] The Louvain edition alone has: “Let them be confident, who did not fear being condemned if they married, but desired to be crowned more honorably because they desired not to marry.”]

Those who wish to remain without marriage should therefore not flee marriage as though it were a pit of sin. They should rise beyond it as a hill of lesser good, so as to rest on the mountain of greater continence. This hill is inhabited under such a law that no one may leave it whenever he wishes. “A woman is bound as long as her husband lives” (I Cor. VII, 38–40).

Nevertheless, one ascends from it, as though by a step, to widowhood’s continence; but for virginal continence it must either be avoided by refusing suitors or crossed over by anticipating them.

### CHAPTER XIX

#### 19. Two Contrary Errors Concerning Virginity and Marriage

But lest anyone think that the rewards of the two works—the good and the better—would be equal, it was necessary to argue against those who interpreted the Apostle’s words, “I think that this is good because of the present necessity,” as meaning that virginity is useful not for the kingdom of heaven but for the present world, as though in eternal life those who had chosen this better course would possess nothing more than the others.

In the course of this discussion, when we came to the Apostle’s statement, “But such persons will have tribulation in the flesh, and I am sparing you,” we encountered other disputants who did not make marriage equal to perpetual continence but condemned it altogether.

Both errors are wrong: either to make marriage equal to holy virginity or to condemn it. Because they excessively flee from one another, these two errors clash face-to-face, refusing to hold the middle ground of truth. In that middle ground, by sound reasoning and the authority of holy Scripture, we find both that marriage is not a sin and that it is not equal to the good of virginal or even widowed continence.

[Note: [Col. 0405] The Louvain edition omits *nimis* (“excessively”) and, instead of *fugiendo* (“by fleeing”), has *fugiendi* (“of fleeing”), following Erasmus. The reading is corrected from the manuscripts.]

### CHAPTER XX

#### The Apostle’s Words, “I Am Sparing You,” Are Wrongly Twisted into a Condemnation of Marriage

Some, in their desire for virginity, have thought that marriage should be detested as adultery. Others, in defending marriage, have wished the excellence of perpetual continence to merit nothing more than conjugal chastity—as though Susanna’s good were Mary’s humiliation, or Mary’s greater good ought to be Susanna’s condemnation.

#### 20.

Far be it, then, that the Apostle should have said to married women or to those about to marry, “I am sparing you,” as though he did not wish to state what punishment was due to the married in the world to come. Far be it that Paul should send into hell the woman whom Daniel freed from a temporal judgment. Far be it that the marriage bed should be a punishment before Christ’s tribunal for her who, by keeping faith, chose to risk or suffer death under a false accusation of adultery.

What did that voice mean—“It is better for me [Col. 0406] to fall into your hands than to sin in the sight of God” (Dan. XIII, 23)—if God was going to free her not because she had preserved conjugal chastity, but to condemn her because she had married?

And now, whenever conjugal chastity is defended by the truth of holy Scripture against those who slander and accuse marriage, the Holy Spirit defends Susanna against false witnesses; each time she is freed from a false accusation, and this with a much greater burden. At that time one married woman was accused; now all married women and men are accused. Then the charge concerned a concealed and false adultery; now it concerns a true and manifest marriage. Then one woman was accused on the basis of what the wicked elders said; now all husbands and wives are accused on the basis of what the Apostle supposedly did not wish to say.

“They say that he concealed your condemnation when he said, ‘I am sparing you.’” Who said this? Surely the same one who had earlier said: “If you take a wife, you have not sinned; and if a virgin marries, she has not sinned.”

Why, then, do you suspect a crime against marriage in what he prudently left unsaid, while failing to recognize a defense of marriage in what he openly said? Does he condemn in silence those whom his words absolve? Is Susanna now accused more gently—not of marriage but of adultery—than apostolic teaching is accused of falsehood?

What would we do in such great danger if it were not as certain and clear that chaste marriage ought not to be condemned as it is certain and clear that holy Scripture cannot lie?

### CHAPTER XXI

#### 21. The Praise and Merit of Virginity Are Greater When Marriage Is Not Avoided as Evil

Someone may say: “What does this have to do with holy virginity or perpetual continence, the praise of which this work has undertaken?”

I answer first with what I mentioned above: the glory of that greater good is greater because, for the sake of attaining it, the good of marriage is surpassed, not because the sin of marriage is avoided. Otherwise it would be enough for perpetual continence not to be praised especially, but merely not to be blamed, if it were held because marriage was a crime.

Furthermore, since people must be exhorted to so excellent a gift not by human judgment but by the authority of divine Scripture, we must not act carelessly or pass over the matter lightly, lest anyone think that divine Scripture has lied in some respect.

Those who compel holy virgins to remain in virginity by condemning marriage discourage rather than encourage them. How can they trust that what is written is true—“He who does not give his virgin in marriage does better”—if they think false what is likewise written immediately beforehand—“He who gives his virgin in marriage does well”?

If, however, they believe without hesitation what Scripture says about the good of marriage, then, strengthened by the same supremely truthful authority of heavenly speech, they will hasten toward their better state with fervent and confident eagerness.

We have now said enough for the matter undertaken and have demonstrated as fully as we could that the Apostle’s statement, “I think that this is good because of the present necessity,” must not be understood as though holy virgins were better than faithful married people in this world but equal to them in the kingdom of heaven and in the world to come [Col. 0407].

Nor should his statement concerning those who marry—“But such persons will have tribulation in the flesh, and I am sparing you” (I Cor. VII, 38, 26, 28)—be understood as though he preferred to conceal the sin and condemnation of marriage rather than state them.

Two mutually opposed errors have failed to understand each of these two statements. Those who insist on equating married people with unmarried people interpret the statement about the present necessity in their own favor. Those who presume to condemn married people interpret in their own favor the statement, “I am sparing you.”

But in accordance with the faith of holy Scripture and sound doctrine, we say both that marriage is not a sin and that its good is placed below not only virginal but also widowed continence. We say that the present necessity of married people does not indeed prevent them from eternal life, but does prevent their attaining the distinguished glory and honor reserved for perpetual continence. We say that at this time marriage is expedient only for those who do not contain themselves, and that the Apostle neither wished to conceal the tribulation of the flesh arising from carnal desire—without which the marriages of the incontinent cannot exist—while warning of it, nor to explain it more fully, out of consideration for human weakness.

### CHAPTER XXII

#### 22. The Apostle Shows That Virginity Should Be Loved Not for This Life but for the Future Life

Now, by the clearest testimonies of the divine Scriptures that we have been able to recall according to the measure of our memory, it may become more evident that perpetual continence should be loved not for the present life of this world but for the future life promised in the kingdom of heaven. [Note: [Col. 0407] Thus the printed editions; the manuscripts have *diligendam*.]

Who would fail to notice this in what the same Apostle says shortly afterward? “He who is without a wife thinks about the things of the Lord, how he may please the Lord; but he who is joined in marriage thinks about the things of the world, how he may please his wife. And the unmarried woman and the virgin are divided: the unmarried woman is concerned with the things of the Lord, that she may be holy both in body and spirit; but she who is married is concerned with the things of the world, how she may please her husband” (I Cor. VII, 32–34).

He certainly does not say: “She thinks about the things of security in this world, so that she may pass her time without greater troubles.” Nor does he say that the unmarried woman and the virgin are divided from the married woman—distinct and separated from her—so that the unmarried woman may be secure in this life because she avoids temporal troubles from which the married woman is not free.

Rather, he says: “She thinks about the things of the Lord, how she may please the Lord,” and “she is concerned with the things of the Lord, that she may be holy both in body and spirit.”

Unless, perhaps, someone is so foolishly contentious as to attempt to claim that we wish to please the Lord not for the kingdom of heaven but for the present [Col. 0408] world, or that we are holy in body and spirit for this life rather than for eternal life. To believe this is nothing other than to be more miserable than all human beings. For the Apostle says: “If our hope in Christ is only in this life, we are more miserable than all human beings” (I Cor. XV, 19).

Is the person who breaks his bread for the hungry foolish if he does so only for this life, while the person who disciplines his body to continence, so that he does not even join himself in marriage, is prudent if this benefits him nothing in the kingdom of heaven?

[Note: [Col. 0407] The manuscripts omit “how he may please the Lord, and she is concerned with the things of the Lord.”]

[Note: [Col. 0407] Erasmus has: “And the married woman and the virgin are divided: the unmarried woman is concerned with the things of the Lord.” The Louvain edition, much more corruptly, continues after “how she may please her husband” as follows: “And he is divided. The unmarried woman also is concerned with the things of the Lord.” The passage is restored with the aid of very ancient manuscripts, both here and above, in *On the Good of Marriage*, chapter 10.]

### CHAPTER XXIII

#### 23. The Same Is Proved from the Words of the Lord

Finally, let us hear the Lord himself uttering this most evident judgment. When he was speaking in a divine and terrifying manner about not separating spouses except on account of fornication, the disciples said to him: “If such is the case of a man with his wife, it is not expedient to marry.”

To them he said: “Not everyone accepts this word. For there are eunuchs who were born so; there are eunuchs who were made so by men; and there are eunuchs who made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven. Let whoever can accept it accept it” (Matt. XIX, 10–12).

What could have been said more truthfully or more clearly? Christ says it; Truth says it; the Power and Wisdom of God says that those who, through a devout purpose, abstain from taking a wife make themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven. Yet human vanity, with impious recklessness, argues against this that those who do so merely avoid the present troubles of marriage and have nothing more than others in the kingdom of heaven.

### CHAPTER XXIV

#### 24. Likewise from the Words of Isaiah. Why the Church Is Called the Kingdom of Heaven

Of which eunuchs does God speak through the prophet Isaiah, to whom he says that he will give in his house and within his walls a named place, much better than that of sons and daughters, if not of those who make themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven?

Those whose male organ has been weakened so that they cannot beget children—such as the eunuchs of wealthy people and kings—need only become Christians and keep God’s commandments. Yet their intention is that, if they had been able, they would have had wives. Once they become Christians, they are to be made equal to the other married faithful in the house of God, who raise the offspring lawfully and chastely received in the fear of God and teach their children to place their hope in God. They are not, however, to receive a better place than that of sons and daughters. For they do not take wives through strength of soul but because of the necessity of the flesh.

Let anyone who wishes contend that the Prophet foretold these words about eunuchs who have been physically mutilated. This error too supports the case we have undertaken. For God did not prefer these eunuchs to those who have no place in his house, but to those who preserve the merit of married life in begetting children.

When he says, “I will give them a place much better,” he shows that a place is also given to married people, though much lower. Let us therefore concede that the eunuchs mentioned above who are eunuchs according to the flesh, and who were not among the people of Israel—for we see that even when they do not become Jews they nevertheless become Christians—will be in the house of God. And let us concede that the Prophet did not speak about those who, through a purpose of continence and by [Col. 0409] not seeking marriage, make themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven.

Is anyone so utterly deranged as to oppose the truth by believing that eunuchs made so in the flesh have a better place in the house of God than married people, while contending that those who practice continence through a devout purpose, disciplining their bodies even to the point of despising marriage, making themselves eunuchs not in the body but at the very root of desire, and meditating an angelic and heavenly life amid earthly mortality, are equal in merit to married people?

Can a Christian contradict Christ, who praises those who made themselves eunuchs not for the sake of this world but for the sake of the kingdom of heaven, by asserting that this is useful for the present life and not for the future?

What remains for such people except to assert that the kingdom of heaven itself belongs to this temporal life in which we now exist? Why should blind presumption not advance even to this madness? What could be more insane than such an assertion?

For although the Church, which exists in this time, is sometimes also called the kingdom of heaven, it is called this because it is being gathered for the future and everlasting life. Although it possesses the promise of the present life and of the future life (I Tim. IV, 8), in all its good works it nevertheless looks not to the things that are seen but to the things that are not seen. “For the things that are seen are temporal, but the things that are not seen are eternal” (II Cor. IV, 18).

### CHAPTER XXV

#### 25. Isaiah Speaks of the Eternal Reward Promised to Eunuchs

The Holy Spirit did not remain silent about what could stand openly and immovably against these shameless and senselessly obstinate people, repelling their bestial assault from his fold by an impregnable defense.

When he had said concerning eunuchs, “I will give them in my house and within my walls a named place, much better than that of sons and daughters,” lest anyone who was excessively carnal think that something temporal was to be hoped for in these words, he immediately added: “I will give them an everlasting name, and it shall never fail” (Isa. LVI, 4–5).

It is as though he were saying:

“What are you evading, impious blindness? What are you evading? Why do you cast the clouds of your perversity over the serenity of truth? Why do you search for darkness in so great a light of Scripture in which to lie in wait? Why do you promise the holy continent only temporal usefulness? ‘I will give them an everlasting name.’

“Why do you try to refer to earthly advantage those who are free from all sexual intercourse and who, precisely by abstaining from it here, think about the things of the Lord and how to please the Lord? ‘I will give them an everlasting name.’

“Why do you insist that the kingdom of heaven, for whose sake the holy eunuchs made themselves eunuchs, is to be understood as belonging only to this life? ‘I will give them an everlasting name.’

“And if perhaps you try to interpret ‘everlasting’ here as merely ‘long-lasting,’ I add, I pile up, I press the point: ‘and it shall never fail.’ What more do you seek? What more do you say?”

This everlasting name—whatever it is, and it plainly signifies a certain distinctive and excellent glory—will not be shared by the eunuchs of God with many others, even though they are established in the same kingdom and in the same house. Perhaps for this reason it is called a “name” [Col. 0410]: because it distinguishes those who receive it from the rest.

### CHAPTER XXVI
## CHAPTER XXVI

### 26. Objection concerning the denarius given to all, against the diversity of rewards

“What, then,” they say, “does that denarius signify, which, when the work in the vineyard has been completed, is given equally to all—both to those who worked from the first hour and to those who worked for a single hour?” (Matt. 20:9). What else, surely, except something that all will possess in common, such as eternal life itself, the kingdom of heaven itself, where all those whom God predestined, called, justified, and glorified will be?

For this corruptible body must put on incorruption, and this mortal body must put on immortality: this is that denarius, the reward of all. Yet star differs from star in glory; so also is the resurrection of the dead: these are the different merits of the saints. For if that denarius signified heaven, is it not common to all the stars to be in heaven? And yet one is the glory of the sun, another the glory of the moon, and another the glory of the stars (1 Cor. 15:53, 41–42).

If that denarius were understood as bodily health, is not health common to all the members when we are well, and, if it remains until death, present equally and in the same way in all? And yet God placed the members, each one of them, in the body as he willed (ibid. 12:18), so that the whole might not be an eye, nor the whole hearing, nor the whole smell; and whatever else there is has its own property, although it possesses health equally with all the others.

Thus, because eternal life itself will belong equally to all the saints, an equal denarius has been assigned to all; but because, within that eternal life itself, the lights of merit will shine distinctly, “there are many mansions in the Father’s house” (John 14:2). Accordingly, in the denarius—which is not unequal—one person does not live longer than another; but in the many mansions one is honored more gloriously than another.

## CHAPTER XXVII

### 27. The future glory of virgins will be greater, and they will have certain joys of their own

“To follow the Lamb wherever he goes” belongs specifically to virgins. Therefore proceed, holy men and women of God, boys and girls, males and females, celibates and unmarried women [Note: [Col. 0410] The Louvain edition alone reads, “and married women.”]; proceed perseveringly to the end. Praise the Lord more sweetly, since you contemplate him more abundantly; hope more happily in him, since you serve him more earnestly; love more ardently him whom you please more attentively.

With your loins girded and your lamps burning, await the Lord when he comes from the wedding (Luke 12:35–36). You will bring to the Lamb’s wedding a new song, which you will sing on your harps [Note: [Col. 0410] Two Vatican manuscripts add, “that is, dedicated to praise in your hearts.” Another Vatican manuscript reads, “that is, in your hearts.”]. It will certainly not be such a song as the whole earth sings, to which it is said, “Sing to the Lord a new song; sing to the Lord, all the earth” (Ps. 95:1), but such a song as no one will be able to sing except you.

For someone especially beloved by the Lamb, who was accustomed to recline upon his breast and drank and uttered [Note: [Col. 0410] The Louvain edition alone reads, “and had drunk and uttered.”] wondrous things concerning the heavenly Word of God, saw you in the Apocalypse. He saw you—twelve times twelve thousand holy harpists, possessing undefiled virginity in body and inviolate truth in heart—and because you follow the Lamb wherever he goes, he wrote about you (Rev. 14:2–4).

Where do we suppose this Lamb goes, where no one but you either dares or is able to follow him? Where do we suppose he goes? Into what forests and meadows? I believe there are herbage and joys there [Note: [Col. 0411] In place of “herbage,” the Louvain edition has “great things,” contrary to the manuscripts and Erasmus]; not the empty joys of this age and its deceitful madness, nor joys of the kind that the other non-virgins will have in the kingdom of God itself, but joys distinguished from the portion of all other joys.

The joy of Christ’s virgins is from Christ, in Christ, with Christ, after Christ, through Christ, and because of Christ. The particular joys of Christ’s virgins are not the same as those of non-virgins, although the latter also belong to Christ. For the joys are different for different people, but none are like these.

Enter into these joys; follow the Lamb, for the lamb’s flesh is also certainly virgin. In himself he retained what conception and birth did not take away from his mother. Rightly, therefore, you follow him in virginity of heart and flesh, wherever he goes.

For what is it to follow except to imitate? Since Christ suffered for us, leaving us an example, as the apostle Peter says, so that we might follow his footsteps (1 Pet. 2:21). Each person follows him in that in which he imitates him—not insofar as he is the one Son of God through whom all things were made, but insofar as he is the son of man, presenting in himself for imitation whatever was fitting.

Many things in him are set before everyone for imitation; but virginity of the flesh is not set before everyone. For those in whom it has already happened that they are no longer virgins have nothing they can do to become virgins.

## CHAPTER XXVIII

### 28. How far everyone can follow the Lamb

Therefore let the other faithful who have lost bodily virginity follow the Lamb—not wherever he goes, but as far as they are able. They are able everywhere except when he advances in the beauty of virginity.

“Blessed are the poor in spirit”; imitate him who, although he was rich, became poor for your sake (2 Cor. 8:9). “Blessed are the meek”; imitate him who said, “Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. 11:29). “Blessed are those who mourn”; imitate him who wept over Jerusalem (Luke 19:41). “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness”; imitate him who said, “My food is to do the will of him who sent me” (John 4:34).

“Blessed are the merciful”; imitate him who came to the aid of a man wounded by robbers, lying on the road half-dead and beyond hope (Luke 10:30–35). “Blessed are the pure in heart”; imitate him who committed no sin, and in whose mouth no deceit was found (1 Pet. 2:22). “Blessed are the peacemakers”; imitate him who said on behalf of his persecutors, “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34).

“Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake” (Matt. 5:3–10); imitate him who suffered for you, leaving you an example, so that you might follow his footsteps (1 Pet. 2:21).

Those who imitate these things follow the Lamb in them. But surely married people too can walk along these paths, even if they do not place their feet in exactly the same form; nevertheless, they walk along the same roads.

## CHAPTER XXIX

### 29. The ways in which the virgins alone follow him. There is no envy in heaven because of the difference of rewards

But behold, that Lamb walks along the virginal path. How will those follow him who have lost what they can in no way regain? Therefore, you—yes, you—go after him, his virgins; you go after him even there, because on account of this one thing [Note: [Col. 0412] The printed editions read, “one good thing.” The word “good” is absent from the manuscripts.] you follow him wherever he goes.

For every other gift of holiness by which married people may follow him, we can exhort them, except for this, which they have irreparably lost. Therefore follow him, holding steadfastly to what you have ardently vowed. Do what you can so that the good of virginity may not perish from you, since you can do nothing to make it return.

The rest of the faithful, who cannot follow the Lamb in this respect, will see you; they will see you and will not envy you. By rejoicing with you in what they do not possess in themselves, they will possess it in you. For they will not be able to sing that new song which belongs particularly to you; but they will be able to hear it and take delight in your exceptionally great good.

But you, who will both sing and hear it—since you will hear from yourselves what you sing—will rejoice more happily and reign more joyfully. Yet no sorrow will afflict those who lack this because of your greater joy. For that Lamb whom you follow wherever he goes will not abandon those who cannot follow him where you can.

We are speaking of the omnipotent Lamb. He will go before you, and he will not depart from them, when God is “all in all” (1 Cor. 15:28). And those who have less will not shrink from you. For where there is no envy, difference is harmonious.

Therefore be confident, trust, be strengthened, remain steadfast—you who vow and pay to the Lord your God vows of perpetual continence (Ps. 76:12), not for the sake of the present age, but for the sake of the kingdom of heaven.

## CHAPTER XXX

### 30. He urges virginity as a work of supererogation, not of precept

You also who have not yet made this vow—“if you are able to receive it, receive it” (Matt. 19:12); run perseveringly so that you may obtain the prize (1 Cor. 9:24). Each of you take your offerings and enter the courts of the Lord (Ps. 95:8), not under compulsion, since you possess authority over your own will.

For just as it is said, “You shall not commit adultery; you shall not kill” (Exod. 20:13–14), it cannot likewise be said, “You shall not marry.” The former are required; the latter are offered. If the latter are done, they are praised; if the former are not done, people are condemned.

In the former the Lord commands the duty you owe; but in the latter, if you perform anything beyond what is required, he will repay you when he returns (Luke 10:35). Consider whatever that may be: in his wall it has a designated place, much better than that of sons and daughters. Consider the eternal name there (Isa. 56:5). Who can explain what kind of name it will be? Whatever it is, it will be eternal.

By believing, hoping, and loving this, you have been able not merely to avoid forbidden marriages, but to soar beyond permitted ones.

## CHAPTER XXXI

### 31. Humility especially to be commended to virgins. The measure of humility given to each person. Pride is the mother of envy

The greater and more divine this gift is, which we have urged you to undertake according to our powers, the more it admonishes our concern to say something not only about most glorious chastity but also about the safest humility. When, therefore, those who profess perpetual continence compare themselves with married people and learn from Scripture that the latter are beneath them both in work and reward, in vow and recompense, let this immediately come to mind:

“However great you are, humble yourself in all things, and you will find grace before God” (Sir. 3:20).

The measure of humility given to each person corresponds to the measure of that person’s greatness. Pride is dangerous, since it lies in wait all the more for those who are greater. Envy follows it like a daughter and attendant; for pride immediately gives birth to it and is never without such offspring and companion.

The devil is associated with these two evils, namely pride and envy [Note: [Col. 0413] So read the manuscripts. Erasmus reads, “the devil presides over pride and envy.” The Louvain edition reads, “the devil presides over pride and envy.”].

Thus the whole of Christian discipline wages its chief battle against pride, the mother of envy. For it teaches humility, by which one acquires and preserves charity. When it had been said of charity, “Charity does not envy,” as though we were asking why it does not envy, the text immediately added, “It is not inflated” (1 Cor. 13:4), as if it said: “It has no envy for this reason, because it has no pride.”

Christ, therefore, the teacher of humility, first “emptied himself,” taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of human beings and found in appearance as a human being; he humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death—even death on a cross (Phil. 2:7–8).

But who could easily explain his teaching itself, how attentively it inculcates humility and how earnestly it insists upon prescribing it, or gather together all the testimonies for demonstrating this? Let whoever wishes to write separately on humility attempt or undertake that task. This work, however, has another purpose, since it was undertaken concerning so great a subject that it must be especially on its guard against pride.

## CHAPTER XXXII

### 32. The Lord’s commands and examples concerning humility

Accordingly, I shall recall a few testimonies which the Lord deigns to bring to mind from Christ’s teaching concerning humility, perhaps sufficient for the purpose I have undertaken.

His first longer discourse to the disciples began with these words: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:3). Without any controversy, we understand these to be the humble.

He especially praised the faith of that centurion and said that he had not found such faith in Israel, because the man believed so humbly that he said, “I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof” (ibid. 8:5–10).

Thus Matthew did not say that he approached Jesus for any other reason, when Luke makes it perfectly clear that he himself did not come to Jesus but sent his friends (Luke 7:6–7), except that through the most faithful humility he approached more truly than those whom he sent.

Hence also comes the prophetic statement: “The Lord is exalted, and he regards the humble; but the exalted he knows from afar” (Ps. 137:6)—as though they did not approach him.

For this reason he also says to that Canaanite woman, “O woman, great is your faith! Let it be done for you as you wish.” Earlier he had called her a dog and had answered that the children’s bread should not be thrown to her. She received this humbly and said, “Yes, Lord; for even the dogs eat from the crumbs that fall from their masters’ table.” Thus, what she did not obtain by persistent shouting, she earned by humble confession (Matt. 15:22–28).

For this reason two men are also presented praying in the temple, one a Pharisee and the other a tax collector, on account of those who seem righteous to themselves and despise others; and confession of sins is preferred to the enumeration of merits.

The Pharisee was certainly giving thanks to God for those things in which he took great pleasure. “I thank you,” he said, “that I am not like other people—unjust, robbers, adulterers—or even like this tax collector. I fast twice a week; I give tithes of everything I possess.”

But the tax collector stood at a distance and did not dare to raise his eyes toward heaven. Rather, he struck his breast, saying, “God, be merciful to me, a sinner.”

Then follows the divine judgment: “Amen, I say to you, the tax collector went down from the temple more justified than that Pharisee.” The reason why this is just is then shown: “For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke 18:10–14).

It can therefore happen that someone both avoids real evils, recognizes real goods in himself, and gives thanks for them to the Father of lights, from whom every good gift and every perfect gift comes (Jas. 1:17), and yet is rejected because of the vice of self-exaltation—if he proudly insults other sinners, especially those who confess their sins in prayer, whether openly or merely in the thought that is before God.

To such people not reproach accompanied by self-inflation is owed, but compassion without despair.

What of the occasion when the disciples were asking among themselves which of them was the greatest? He placed a little child before their eyes and said, “Unless you become like this child, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 18:1–3). Did he not especially commend humility and place the merit of greatness in it?

Or when the sons of Zebedee desired his sides in the exalted dignity of seats, he answered in such a way that they ought rather to consider drinking the cup of his passion (ibid. 20:21–22), in which he humbled himself unto death—even death on a cross (Phil. 2:8)—than to demand in proud ambition to be preferred to the others. What did he show except that he would be the giver of exaltation to those who first followed him as the teacher of humility?

And when, as he was about to go forth to his passion, he washed the disciples’ feet and very clearly instructed them to do for their fellow disciples and fellow servants what their Master and Lord had done for them (John 13:1–17), how greatly did he commend humility!

He chose that moment especially for commending it, when they were gazing upon him, soon to die, with great longing. They would surely retain above all in their memory what their Master had shown them to imitate for the last time.

Yet he did this at a time when he could certainly have done it on other days before, during which he had lived with them. If it had been done then, the same lesson would indeed have been handed down, but it would certainly not have been received in the same way.

## CHAPTER XXXIII

### 33. Humility to be preserved by Christians, but especially by virgins

Since humility must therefore be preserved by all Christians—inasmuch as Christians are named after Christ, and no one carefully regards his Gospel without finding him to be a teacher of humility—it is especially fitting that those who excel others in some great good should follow and preserve this virtue, so that they may take the greatest care over what I stated at the beginning:

“However great you are, humble yourself in all things, and you will find grace before God” (Sir. 3:20).

Since perpetual continence, and especially virginity, is a great good among the saints of God, the utmost vigilance is needed lest it be corrupted by pride.

### 34. The apostle Paul censures unmarried women who are curious and talkative, and says that this vice arises from idleness

“At the same time,” he says, “they learn to go around the houses while idle” [Note: [Col. 0415] The manuscripts read, “they learn to be curious, to go around the houses.”]; “and not only idle, but also curious and talkative, saying things that they ought not.”

Earlier he had said concerning them, “Avoid younger widows.” For when they have lived in pleasure, they wish to marry in Christ; they incur condemnation because they have invalidated their first faith—that is, they have not remained in what they first vowed.

## CHAPTER XXXIV

The present exhortation to humility does not concern unmarried women who live contrary to their purpose

Yet he does not say, “They marry,” but “They wish to marry.” Many of them are restrained from marrying not by love of their excellent purpose, but by fear of open disgrace—a fear which itself arises from pride, since they fear displeasing human beings more than God.

These women, then, wish to marry and therefore do not marry because they cannot do so with impunity. They would be better off marrying than burning—that is, than being consumed by the hidden flame of desire in their very conscience [Note: [Col. 0415] So read several manuscripts. The printed editions read, “in desire itself.”]. They regret their profession and are distressed by their confession.

Unless they direct their corrected hearts and once again conquer lust through the fear of God, they must be counted among the dead, whether they live in pleasure—for the apostle says, “She who lives in pleasure is dead while she lives” (1 Tim. 5:13, 11–12, 6)—or whether they live in labors and fasts which are useless because their hearts have not been corrected, and which serve display more than amendment [Note: [Col. 0415] Several manuscripts omit “more than amendment.”].

I do not impose a great concern for humility upon such women, in whom pride itself is disgraced and drenched in the blood of conscience. Nor do I impose this great concern of devout humility upon drunkards, misers, or those lying under any other kind of damnable disease [Note: [Col. 0415] The manuscripts read, “any damnable kind of disease”], even though they profess bodily continence and, by their perverse conduct, contradict their own name—unless perhaps, amid these evils, they will also dare to display themselves, for whom it is not enough that their punishments are being delayed.

Nor am I speaking of those in whom there is some desire to please others, whether through more elegant clothing than the necessity of so great a profession allows, or through a conspicuous headband, or through excessively puffed-up masses of hair, or through coverings so delicate [Note: [Col. 0415] The printed editions read, “they use coverings so delicate.” The words “they use” are absent from the manuscripts.] that little nets placed beneath can be seen. Such people must first be given instructions not about humility, but about chastity itself or the integrity of modesty.

Give me someone who professes perpetual continence and is free from these and all similar vices and blemishes of conduct: in that person I fear pride; in that person, possessing so great a good, I dread the swelling of self-exaltation. The more there is in that person to please himself, the more I fear that, by pleasing himself, he may displease the one who resists the proud but gives grace to the humble (Jas. 4:6).

## CHAPTER XXXV

### 35. Christ commands that humility be learned from him

Certainly the foremost teacher and example of virginal integrity must be contemplated in Christ himself. What more, then, should I command those who practice continence concerning humility than what he commands everyone:

“Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart”?

He had just mentioned his greatness, and, wishing to show the same thing—how very little he became for our sake [Note: [Col. 0416] Some manuscripts read, “he had mentioned it, wishing to show the same thing,” omitting “and.”]—he said:

“I confess to you, Father” [Note: [Col. 0416] The word “Father” is absent from the manuscripts; a little later they also omit “and to the prudent.”], “Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones. Yes, Father, because this was pleasing before you.

“All things have been handed over to me by my Father, and no one knows the Son except the Father; nor does anyone know the Father except the Son, and the one to whom the Son wills to reveal him.

“Come to me, all who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. 11:25–29).

He—he to whom the Father handed over all things, whom no one knows except the Father, who alone knows the Father, and to whom he wills to reveal him—does not say, “Learn from me to fashion the world,” or “to raise the dead,” but “because I am meek and humble of heart.”

O saving teaching! O Teacher and Lord of mortals, to whom death was offered and poured out in the cup of pride! He did not wish to teach what he was not; he did not wish to command what he himself did not do.

I see you, good Jesus, with the eyes of faith that you have opened for me, crying out as though in an assembly of the human race and saying, “Come to me, and learn from me.”

What, I beg you, Son of God, through whom all things were made, and who yourself became one among all things, Son of man—what do we come to you to learn from you?

“Because I am meek,” he says, “and humble of heart.”

Have all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge hidden in you (Col. 2:3) been reduced to this, that we must learn from you as something great that you are meek and humble of heart? Is it so great to be little that, unless it were done by you, who are so great, it could not be learned at all?

It is entirely so. For the soul finds rest in no other way than by dispersing the restless swelling by which it seemed great to itself, when it was not sound before you.

## CHAPTER XXXVI

### 36. The teaching of humility is readily heard by sinners; it must be heard much more by virgins
