Let those who seek your mercy and truth hear you, and come to you, and learn from you to be meek and humble—to live for you, not for themselves.

Let the laboring and burdened person hear this, the one weighed down by his load, who does not dare to raise his eyes toward heaven, that sinner who strikes his breast and approaches from a distance (Luke 18:13).

Let the centurion hear it, who was not worthy that you should enter under his roof (Matt. 8:8). Let Zacchaeus, the chief of the tax collectors, hear it, restoring fourfold the profits of his damnable sins (Luke 19:2, 8). Let the sinful woman in the city hear it, whose tears fell upon your feet all the more abundantly the farther she had been from your footsteps (Luke 7:37–38).

Let prostitutes and tax collectors hear it, who go before the scribes and Pharisees into the kingdom of heaven (Matt. 21:31). Let every kind of sick person hear it—those whose meals with you were brought forward as a crime, as though by healthy people who did not seek a physician, although you did not come to call the righteous but sinners to repentance (ibid. 9:11–13).

When all these turn to you, they readily become meek and humble before you, remembering their most wicked life and your most abundant mercy; for where sin abounded, grace abounded all the more (Rom. 5:20).

### 37. But look upon the ranks of holy virgins, boys and girls

This kind has been educated in your Church. There, from their mothers’ breasts, it has grown up for you; there, in your name, it has loosened its tongue to speak, and it has sucked your name as though it were the milk poured into its infancy [Note: [Col. 0417] The Louvain edition alone omits the particle “there.”].

No one from this number can say, “I was formerly a blasphemer, persecutor, and insolent man, but I obtained mercy because I acted ignorantly in unbelief” (1 Tim. 1:13). Rather, they seized and vowed what you did not command but merely proposed for those who wished to take it up, saying, “Let the one who is able to receive it receive it”; and for the sake of the kingdom of heaven they castrated themselves—not because you threatened them, but because you exhorted them (Matt. 19:12).

## CHAPTER XXXVII

### The example of humility set before virgins in the Lord himself

Call out to these; let these hear you, for you are meek and humble of heart. The greater they are, the more let them humble themselves in all things, so that they may find grace before you.

They are righteous—but are they righteous as you are, who justify the ungodly? [Note: [Col. 0417] Erasmus and some manuscripts read, “who justify the ungodly.”]

They are chaste—but their mothers nourished them in sins within the womb (Ps. 50:7). They are holy—but you are also the Holy One of holy ones. They are virgins—but they were not born from virgins. They are whole in spirit and flesh—but they are not the Word made flesh.

Nevertheless, let them learn—not from those whose sins you forgive, but from you yourself, Lamb of God, who take away the sins of the world (John 1:14, 29)—that you are meek and humble of heart.

### 38

I do not send you, devoutly chaste soul, who did not loosen your carnal desire even to permitted marriage, who did not indulge your body, destined to die, in the propagation of a successor, who raised your earthly and fluctuating members into the practice of heaven—I do not send you to tax collectors and sinners to learn humility, although they go before the proud into the kingdom of heaven.

I do not send you to them; for those who have been freed from the abyss of impurity are unworthy to be set before undefiled virginity for imitation.

I send you to the King of heaven, to him through whom human beings were created and who was created among human beings for human beings; to him who is “fairer in form than the sons of men” (Ps. 44:3), and who was despised by the sons of men for the sons of men; to him who, while ruling immortal angels, did not disdain to serve mortals.

Certainly it was not iniquity but charity that made him humble—charity that does not envy, is not inflated, and does not seek its own (1 Cor. 13:4–5). For Christ also did not please himself; rather, as it is written of him, “The reproaches of those who reproached you fell upon me” (Rom. 15:3).

Go, come to him, and learn that he is meek and humble of heart. You will not go to the one who did not dare to raise his eyes toward heaven under the burden of iniquity, but to him who descended from heaven under the weight of charity (John 6:38).

You will not go to the woman who watered her Lord’s feet with tears, seeking pardon for grave sins; rather, you will go to him who, while granting pardon for all sins, washed the feet of his servants (ibid. 13:5).

I know the dignity of your virginity. I do not set before you for imitation the tax collector humbly accusing his sins; but I fear for you the Pharisee proudly proclaiming his merits (Luke 18:10–14).

I do not say, “Be like the woman of whom it was said, ‘Her many sins are forgiven, because she loved much’”; but I fear that, when you think little has been forgiven you, you may love little (ibid. 7:38, 47).

## CHAPTER XXXVIII

### 39. Fear is necessary for virgins themselves—not worldly or servile fear, but the chaste fear of God

I fear greatly for you, I say, lest, while you boast that you will follow the Lamb wherever he goes, you may be unable to follow him through the narrow ways because of the swelling of pride.

It is good for you, virginal soul, that, just as you are a virgin, so you preserve wholly in your heart what you became through rebirth, and in your flesh what you became by birth; yet conceive from the fear of the Lord and bring forth the spirit of salvation (Isa. 26:18).

There is indeed no fear in charity; rather, as it is written, perfect charity casts out fear (1 John 4:18)—but this means fear of human beings, not fear of God; fear of temporal evils, not fear of the divine judgment at the end.

“Do not be high-minded, but fear” (Rom. 11:20). Love God’s goodness; fear his severity. Neither permits you to be proud. For by loving, you fear lest you gravely offend the one whom you love and who loves you.

What offense could be graver than displeasing through pride the one who, for your sake, displeased the proud? And where ought that chaste fear, which endures forever and ever (Ps. 18:10), to be more present than in you, who do not think about the things of the world—how to please a husband—but about the things of the Lord—how to please the Lord (1 Cor. 7:32)?

That other fear is not in charity; this chaste fear, however, does not depart from charity. If you do not love, fear lest you perish; if you love, fear lest you displease. Charity casts out the former fear; with the latter it enters together.

The apostle Paul also says: “For you did not receive the spirit of slavery again into fear” [Note: [Col. 0418] The printed editions read, “into fear” in the ablative. The older books read, “into fear” in the accusative, in accordance with the Greek *eis phobon*, to which the Vulgate in the ancient Corbie Bibles agrees.]; “but you received the Spirit of adoption as sons, by whom we cry, ‘Abba, Father’” (Rom. 8:15).

I believe he is referring to that fear which was given in the Old Testament, lest they lose the temporal goods that God had promised to his children—not yet under grace, but still under the Law, as servants.

There is also fear of eternal fire, because serving God in order to avoid it is not yet perfect charity. For the desire for a reward is one thing, and fear of punishment another.

Different are the words, “Where shall I go from your Spirit, and where shall I flee from your presence?” (Ps. 138:7), and these other words: “One thing I have asked of the Lord; this I will seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life, to behold the delight of the Lord and to be protected in his temple” [Note: [Col. 0419] The printed editions read, “to be protected by his temple.” But the manuscripts here and in the *Exposition of Psalm 26* read, “his temple”; and in place of “to be protected,” most have “to be protected” in the passive infinitive.]; and, “Do not turn your face away from me” (Ps. 26:4, 9); and, “My soul longs and faints for the courts of the Lord” (Ps. 83:3).

Let the person who did not dare to raise his eyes toward heaven and who watered the feet with tears to obtain pardon for grave sins have those former words [Note: [Col. 0419] The printed editions read, “had not had those words.” The manuscripts correct this to “had those words.”]. But let you have these words, since you are concerned with the things of the Lord, so that you may be holy both in body and in spirit.

The fear that contains torment accompanies those former words, and perfect charity casts it out; but these words are accompanied by the chaste fear of the Lord, which endures forever and ever.

Both kinds of people must be told, “Do not be high-minded, but fear,” so that a person may not exalt himself either through defending his sins or through presuming upon his righteousness.

For Paul himself, who says, “You did not receive the spirit of slavery again into fear,” nevertheless, with fear accompanying charity, says, “I was with you in fear and much trembling” (1 Cor. 2:3). And he himself used the statement I mentioned—“Do not be high-minded, but fear”—lest the wild olive, grafted among the broken branches of the olive tree, should become proud.

Addressing all the members of Christ generally, he says, “Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling; for God is the one who works in you both to will and to work according to his good pleasure” (Phil. 2:12–13), lest what is written, “Serve the Lord in fear, and rejoice before him with trembling” (Ps. 2:11), appear to belong only to the Old Testament.

## CHAPTER XXXIX

### 40. The place of the Holy Spirit is the humbled heart. The righteous have reason to humble themselves because of the danger of falling

And which members of the holy body, which is the Church, ought to take greater care that the Holy Spirit may rest upon it than those who profess virginal holiness?

But how does he rest where he does not find his own place? What else is that place than a humbled heart, which he may fill rather than be driven back from, which he may raise rather than press down? For it has been stated most clearly:

“Upon whom shall my Spirit rest? Upon the humble, the quiet, and the one who trembles at my words” (Isa. 66:2).

You are now living justly; you are now living devoutly, chastely, holily, with virginal purity. Yet you are still living here. Do you not humble yourself when you hear, “Is not human life upon the earth a trial?” (Job 7:1)

Does “Woe to the world because of scandals” (Matt. 18:7) not strike you from presumptuous self-exaltation? Do you not tremble lest you be counted among the many whose charity grows cold, because iniquity abounds (ibid. 24:12)?

Do you not strike your breast when you hear, “Therefore, let the one who thinks he stands watch” [Note: [Col. 0419] The manuscripts read, “let him beware.”] “lest he fall” (1 Cor. 10:12)?

Amid these divine warnings and human dangers, are we still striving to persuade holy virgins to humility?

## CHAPTER XL

[Col. 0420]

### CHAPTER XLI

41. **The just are mingled with those who will fall, so that fear may be increased by their fall.** Let the just person not think that little has been forgiven him, and therefore love little. Let him reckon as forgiven whatever evil he has not committed. Or is there any other reason to believe that God permits many men and women who will fall to be mingled among the number of your profession, except that, when these fall, your fear may increase and thereby restrain pride—a vice so hated by God that, in opposition to it alone, the Most High humbled himself so greatly?

Unless, perhaps, you will therefore fear less and become more inflated, loving less the one who loved you so greatly that he gave himself for you (Gal. 2:20), because little has been forgiven you—namely, because from childhood you have lived religiously, chastely, piously, with undefiled virginity. [Note: Col. 0420. The Louvain edition alone reads: “piously, chastely.”] As though you ought not to love much more the one who, after the immoral had turned to him, forgave them everything, while he did not permit you to fall into those sins!

Or was that Pharisee blind through this error for any other reason than that, being ignorant of God’s righteousness and seeking to establish his own, he was not subject to God’s righteousness (Rom. 10:3)—the Pharisee who loved little because he thought that little had been forgiven him (Luke 7:36–47)?

But you are a chosen race, and among the chosen the more choice: you follow the Lamb in the virginal choir. Yet you too have been saved by grace through faith; and this is not from yourselves, but is God’s gift—not from works, lest anyone should boast. For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared that we should walk in them (Eph. 2:8–10).

Will you therefore love him less the more richly you are adorned with his gifts? May he himself avert so dreadful a madness! Therefore, since Truth truly said that the one to whom little is forgiven loves little, in order that you may love with the greatest ardor the one whom you are free to serve in love, since you are released from the bonds of marriage, reckon as wholly forgiven whatever evil you have not committed under his guidance.

For your eyes are always toward the Lord, because he himself will draw your feet out of the snare (Ps. 24:15); and, “Unless the Lord guards the city, the one who guards it watches in vain” (Ps. 126:1). Speaking also of continence, the Apostle says: “I wish that all people were as I myself am; but each has his own gift from God, one this way, another that” (1 Cor. 7:7).

Who, then, gives these gifts? Who distributes them to each person individually as he wills (1 Cor. 12:11)? Surely God, with whom there is no injustice (Rom. 9:14). Consequently, by what equity he makes some one way and others another is either impossible or altogether difficult for a human being to know; yet one must not doubt that he does so equitably. What, then, do you have that you did not receive (1 Cor. 4:7)? Or by what perversity do you love less the one from whom you received more?

### CHAPTER XLII

42. **The first thought of humility: to recognize that virginity is possessed as God’s gift. The commandments are fulfilled only through the one who gives them and enables their fulfillment. Obedience and repentance are equally gifts of God.**

Let this, then, be the first thought with which the virgin clothes herself in humility: let her not think that she is such by her own power, but rather that this excellent gift comes down from above, from the Father of lights, with whom [Col. 0421] there is no change or shadow caused by turning (James 1:17).

Thus she will not think that little has been forgiven her and therefore love little; nor, being ignorant of God’s righteousness and wishing to establish her own, will she fail to submit to God’s righteousness. Simon was guilty of this fault, the man whom the woman surpassed—the woman whose many sins were forgiven because she loved much.

But she will think more cautiously and more truly, considering all sins as forgiven, insofar as God guards her from committing them. The prayers of devout people in the Holy Scriptures bear witness to this: they show that even those things God commands are not done unless the one who commands gives and assists their fulfillment.

For they would ask falsely if, without the aid of his grace, we could accomplish them. What is commanded more generally and especially than obedience, by which God’s commandments are kept? Yet we find this very obedience desired:

“You have commanded that your commandments be kept diligently.” Then follows: “Would that my ways were directed toward keeping your statutes! Then I would not be put to shame when I look upon all your commandments” (Ps. 118:4–6).

What he had stated above that God commanded, he now desired to fulfill in himself. [Note: Col. 0421. The manuscripts read, “that it might be fulfilled by himself”; the printed editions read, “that it might be fulfilled in himself.”] This is done, of course, so that one may not sin. But if sin has been committed, one is commanded to repent, lest the person who committed it perish through pride by defending and excusing the sin, refusing to perish through repentance from what he did.

This too is requested from God, so that it may be understood that it cannot be done unless he from whom it is requested grants it:

“Set a guard, Lord, over my mouth, and a door of restraint around my lips. Do not incline my heart toward evil words, to make excuses for sins, with those who work iniquity” (Ps. 140:3–4).

If, then, both obedience, by which we keep his commandments, and repentance, by which we do not excuse but accuse our sins, are desired and requested, it is clear that when they occur they are possessed because he gives them and completed because he assists them.

It is stated even more plainly concerning obedience: “The steps of a person are directed by the Lord, and he will delight in his way” (Ps. 36:23). And concerning repentance the Apostle says: “Lest perhaps God may grant them repentance” (2 Tim. 2:25).

43. And has it not been said most plainly of continence itself: “When I knew that no one could be continent unless God granted it—and this itself was wisdom, to know whose gift it was” (Wis. 8:21)?

### CHAPTER XLII

**Continence and wisdom likewise are granted only by God.**

But perhaps continence is God’s gift, while a person himself supplies the wisdom by which he recognizes that this gift is not his but God’s. No: “The Lord makes the wise blind” (Ps. 145:8); and, “The testimony of the Lord is trustworthy, giving wisdom to the simple” (Ps. 18:8); and, “If anyone lacks wisdom, let him ask God, who gives generously to all and does not reproach them, and it will be given him” (James 1:5).

Virgins ought to be wise, lest their lamps be extinguished (Matt. 25:4). How are they wise, unless they are “not wise in high things, but consenting to the lowly” (Rom. 12:16)? For Wisdom herself said to the human being: “Behold, piety is wisdom” (Job 28:28).

If, then, you have nothing that you did not receive, “do not be high-minded, but fear” (Rom. 11:20). And [Col. 0422] do not love little, as though little had been forgiven you by him; rather, love greatly the one from whom you received much.

For whoever remains chaste from the beginning is governed by him; whoever becomes chaste from being unchaste is corrected by him; and whoever remains unchaste to the end is abandoned by him. He can do this by a hidden judgment, but not by an unjust one. Perhaps it is hidden for this reason: that he may be feared more and pride may be diminished.

### CHAPTER XLIII

44. **Virgins should not exalt themselves over this gift of God.**

Once a person knows that by God’s grace he is what he is, he must not fall into another snare of pride, exalting himself because of God’s grace and despising others. That proud Pharisee was guilty of this fault [Note: Col. 0422. Some manuscripts read “proud.”]: he gave thanks to God for the good things he possessed, yet exalted himself over the tax collector who confessed his sins (Luke 18:10–14).

What, then, should a virgin do or think, so as not to exalt herself over those who lack this great gift? She must not pretend humility, but display it; for the pretense of humility is greater pride.

Therefore, wishing to show that humility must be genuine, Scripture says: “The greater you are, the more humble yourself in all things”; and immediately adds, “and you will find grace before God” (Sir. 3:20)—surely in the presence of one before whom she could not humble herself deceitfully.

### CHAPTER XLIV

45. **What a virgin should consider, so that she does not presume to prefer herself to a woman, even a married woman.**

What, then, shall we say? Is there something that a virgin of God can truly consider, so that she does not dare to prefer herself to a faithful woman—not merely a widow, but even a married woman?

I am not speaking of rejecting anyone; for who does not know that an obedient woman is to be preferred to a disobedient virgin? But when both are obedient to God’s commandments, will she hesitate to prefer holy virginity even to chaste marriage, and continence to wedlock—to place the hundredfold fruit before the thirtyfold?

Indeed, she should not hesitate to prefer one to the other. Yet this obedient and God-fearing virgin must not dare to place herself before that obedient and God-fearing woman; otherwise she will not be humble, and “God resists the proud” (James 4:6).

What, then, will she consider? The hidden gifts of God, which each person recognizes in himself only through the testing of temptation. [Note: Col. 0422. The printed editions read: “which, only by the inquiry of temptation, disclose even himself to each person.”] To say nothing of other matters: how does a virgin know—although she is concerned with the things of the Lord, how to please the Lord (1 Cor. 7:32)—that perhaps, because of some weakness of mind unknown to her, she is not yet mature for martyrdom, while the woman to whom she was eager to prefer herself may already be able to drink the cup of the Lord’s humility, which he first set before disciples enamored of greatness to drink (Matt. 20:22)?

How, I ask, does she know that she herself may not yet be Thecla, while that other woman may already be Crispina?

[Note: Thecla was the celebrated virgin who, under Nero, overcame fire and wild beasts for Christ. Crispina was a woman of Thagaste. She was beheaded at Thebeste in Africa under Diocletian and Maximian, with Anulinus as proconsul.]

### CHAPTER XLV

**The hundredfold, sixtyfold, and thirtyfold fruit understood in various ways. Certainly, unless temptation is present, there is no demonstration of this gift.**

46. [Col. 0423] This matter is so great that some understand this to be the hundredfold fruit. [Note: Jerome reports this opinion, but in Book 1 against Jovinian and in his commentary on Matthew 13 he chooses another: namely, he assigns the hundredfold fruit to virgins, the sixtyfold to widows, and the thirtyfold to chaste married persons.]

Ecclesiastical authority offers a distinguished testimony: the faithful know the place at which martyrs, and the place at which deceased consecrated women, are commemorated in the mysteries of the altar.

[Note: This is relevant to the statement in Sermon 159.1: “Martyrs are commemorated at God’s altar in a place where prayer is not offered for them; but prayer is offered for the other deceased persons who are commemorated.”]

But what that diversity of fruitfulness signifies, let those who understand these matters better than we do determine: whether virginal life is represented by the hundredfold fruit, widowhood by the sixtyfold, and marriage by the thirtyfold; or whether the hundredfold fruit is attributed rather to martyrdom, the sixtyfold to continence, and the thirtyfold to marriage; or whether virginity, when martyrdom is added, fulfills the hundredfold fruit, while by itself it is represented by the sixtyfold, and married people, bearing the thirtyfold, reach the sixtyfold if they become martyrs; or—what seems more probable to me—whether, since God’s gifts of grace are many, and one is greater and better than another, as the Apostle says, “Strive for the better gifts” (1 Cor. 12:31) [Note: All manuscripts read, “Imitate.”], we should understand that there are more gifts than can be distributed into three categories.

First, we must not place widow’s continence in no category of fruitfulness, or lower it to the merit of married chastity, or equate it with virginal glory. Nor should we suppose that the crown of martyrdom—whether established in the disposition of the soul, even when the test of temptation is absent, or established in the actual experience of suffering—can be added to any of those three forms of chastity without any increase of fruitfulness.

Furthermore, many men and women preserve virginal continence in such a way that they nevertheless do not do what the Lord says: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell everything you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me” (Matt. 19:21). Nor do they dare to join themselves to the fellowship of those among whom no one says that anything is his own, but all things are common to them (Acts 2:44; 4:32).

When virgins of God do this, are we to think that no increase of fruitfulness comes to them? Or that God’s virgins have no fruit even if they do not do this?

### CHAPTER XLVI

**The common life of consecrated women is more excellent.**

There are therefore many gifts [Col. 0424], some more distinguished and superior than others, with different gifts assigned to different people. Sometimes one person is fruitful through fewer but better gifts, another through more numerous but lesser ones. And who among human beings would dare judge how these will either be equalized or distinguished in the reception of eternal honors?

Nevertheless, it is certain that these gifts are many and diverse, and that the better ones are beneficial not merely for the present time but for eternity.

I think, however, that the Lord wished to mention three distinctions of fruitfulness (Matt. 13:8) and left the others for us to understand. Another evangelist mentioned only the hundredfold (Luke 8:8). Is he therefore to be thought either to have rejected or not known the other two, rather than to have left them for us to understand?

47. But, as I began to say, whether consecrated virginity is the hundredfold fruit, or whether that distinction of fruitfulness is to be understood in some other way—either one we have mentioned or one we have not mentioned—no one, I think, would dare to prefer virginity to martyrdom. Nor would anyone doubt that this gift remains hidden if the testing temptation that examines it is absent.

### CHAPTER XLVII

**Let a virgin consider that she may perhaps be unable to suffer for Christ what a married woman can suffer.**

A virgin therefore has something to consider that will help her preserve humility, so that she does not violate that love which surpasses all gifts, without which, whatever else she possesses—whether few or many things, great or small—is nothing.

She has, I say, something to consider so that she does not become inflated or jealous: she may rightly profess that the good of virginity is far greater and better than the good of marriage, yet she does not know whether this or that married woman may already be able to suffer for Christ, while she herself may not yet be able to do so. She may be spared this because her weakness is not tested by temptation.

“For God is faithful,” says the Apostle, “and he will not permit you to be tempted beyond what you can bear; but with the temptation he will also provide a way out, so that you may be able to endure it” (1 Cor. 10:13).

Perhaps, then, this or that married person, retaining within that way of life a praiseworthy moderation, may already be able to fight against the enemy who compels wrongdoing—even with the tearing of the flesh and the shedding of blood. Yet those who have lived continently from childhood and have made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven may still be unable to endure such things either for righteousness or for chastity itself.

For it is one thing not to consent to someone who persuades and flatters against the truth and a holy purpose; it is another not to yield even to one who tortures and strikes. These matters lie hidden in the capacities and powers of the soul; temptation reveals them, and experience makes them known. [Note: Erasmus and several manuscripts read: “when tested they are revealed; when experienced they are made known.”]

Therefore, so that no one may become inflated, let each person think humbly, from what he sees himself able to do, that he may perhaps be unable to do something more excellent that he does not know. Let him also consider that some people who neither possess nor profess what he is known to possess gloriously may nevertheless be able to do what he cannot.

Thus one will preserve not a false but a genuine humility: “Outdo one another in showing honor” (Rom. 12:10), and “considering one another superior to yourselves” (Phil. 2:3).

### CHAPTER XLVIII

48. **Another occasion for humility: no one here is without sin.**

What shall I say now about the very caution and vigilance required not to sin? “Who can boast that he has a pure heart?” Or “who can boast that he is clean from sin?” (Prov. 20:9).

Holy virginity is indeed intact from the womb of the mother. [Col. 0425] But no one, it says, is clean in your sight—not even an infant whose life upon earth is only one day (Job 25:4).

A certain virginal chastity is also preserved in inviolate faith, by which the Church is joined as a chaste virgin to one husband. But that one husband taught all Christians—both virgins in mind and body and all Christians without exception, from the spiritual to the carnal, from the Apostles to the latest penitents, from the heights of heaven to its farthest boundaries (Matt. 24:31)—to pray, and in that prayer instructed them to say:

“Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. 6:12).

By this petition he showed what we must remember ourselves to be. For he did not command us to pray for the debts of our entire past life, which we trust were forgiven us in Baptism through his peace, saying, “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.” Otherwise catechumens, rather than the baptized, ought to pray this prayer until Baptism.

But when the baptized pray it [Note: Col. 0425. The Louvain edition alone reads, “But when those already baptized pray it.”]—leaders and peoples, shepherds and flocks—it is clearly shown that in this life, which is wholly temptation (Job 7:1), no one should boast as though immune from every sin.

### CHAPTER XLIX

49. **Blameless virgins through the cleansing of sins and humble confession. The deadly security of those who sin in reliance upon the promised forgiveness of confession.**

Therefore the virgins of God, who are indeed blameless, follow the Lamb wherever he goes, both through the perfect cleansing of sins and through the preservation of virginity, which, once lost, does not return.

But because the same Apocalypse, where such persons are revealed in such a state, also praises them for this—that no lie was found in their mouths (Rev. 14:4–5)—they should remember that they must also be truthful in this respect: they must not dare to say that they have no sin.

For the same John who saw this also said:

“If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us. But if we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all iniquity. If we say that we have not sinned, we make him a liar, and his word is not in us.”

This is certainly said not to this group or that, but to all Christians, among whom virgins must recognize themselves. In this way they will be without falsehood, as they appeared in the Apocalypse. Therefore, as long as perfection in heavenly exaltation has not yet been attained, confession makes them blameless through humility.

50. But again, lest anyone should sin with deadly security on the pretext of this statement and allow himself to be dragged along as though sins could immediately be erased by an easy confession, he added at once:

“My little children, I write these things to you so that you may not sin. But if anyone sins, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous; and he himself is the propitiation for our sins” (1 John 1:8–11; 2:1–2).

Therefore let no one depart from sin as though intending to return to it, nor bind himself to iniquity by a kind of agreement, taking pleasure in confessing it rather than avoiding it.

### CHAPTER L

**The small sins that creep in upon the vigilant grow through pride and are destroyed by humility.**

[Col. 0426] If anyone is perhaps without sin here, the greater he is, the more he humbles himself.

But because, even among those who strive and remain vigilant not to sin, sins creep in through human weakness—though small, though few, yet not nonexistent—those very sins become great and serious if pride adds growth and weight to them. But if they are destroyed by pious humility before the priest whom we have in heaven, they are cleansed with complete ease.

51. I am not disputing with those who assert that a human being can live in this life without any sin. I do not dispute or contradict them. Perhaps, out of our misery, we measure great people and, comparing ourselves with ourselves (2 Cor. 10:12), fail to understand.

I know one thing: these great people—such as we are not, such as we have not yet experienced—are, the greater they are, all the more humble in everything, so that they may find grace before God. However great they may be, “the servant is not greater than his lord, nor the disciple than his teacher” (John 13:16).

And surely he is the Lord who says, “Everything has been handed over to me by my Father”; and he is the Teacher who says, “Come to me, all you who labor, and learn from me.”

What, then, do we learn? “Because I am gentle,” he says, “and humble in heart” (Matt. 11:27–29).

### CHAPTER LI

52. **God, who gave virginity, is its guardian and rests among the humble.**

Someone may say: “This is no longer writing about virginity, but about humility.” As though we had undertaken to praise every kind of virginity, rather than that which is according to God!

The greater I see this good to be, the more I fear for it the thief Pride [Note: Col. 0426. The printed editions read “the pride to come”; the manuscripts, “the thief Pride.”], lest it perish.

Therefore no one guards the good of virginity except God himself, who gave it; and “God is love” (1 John 4:8). Love, then, is the guardian of virginity; humility is the place of this guardian. For there dwells the one who said that his Spirit rests upon the humble, the quiet, and the one who trembles at his words (Isa. 66:2).

What, then, have I done that is irrelevant, if, wishing the good I praised to be guarded more securely, I have also taken care to prepare a place for its guardian?

I say this confidently, and I am not afraid that those whom I anxiously warn to fear for themselves along with me will become angry: humble married people follow the Lamb more easily—even if not wherever he goes, at least as far as they are able—than proud virgins.

For how can one follow the one to whom one does not wish to draw near? Or how can one draw near to the one who does not come to teach, “I am gentle and humble in heart”?

Therefore the Lamb leads wherever he goes those who follow him—those in whom he first finds a place where he can incline his head.

A certain proud and deceitful man had said to him: “Lord, I will follow you wherever you go.” He answered him: “Foxes have dens and the birds of the air have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to incline his head” (Matt. 8:19–20).

Under the name of foxes he condemned crafty deceit; under the name of birds he condemned windy arrogance. In that man he did not find the pious humility where he could rest.

Thus the man who had promised to follow the Lord—not merely to some point of progress, but wherever he went—did not follow him at all.

### CHAPTER LII

53. **How virgins should practice humility.**

Therefore do this, virgins of God—do this: follow the Lamb wherever he goes. But first come to the one whom you are to follow, and learn that he is gentle and humble in heart.

Come humbly to the humble one, if you love him; and do not depart from him, lest you fall. For the one who fears departing from him prays and says: “Let not the foot of pride come against me” (Ps. 35:12).

Travel the way of exaltation with the foot of humility. He himself exalts those who follow humbly—the one who was not reluctant to descend to those lying low.

Entrust his gifts to him for safekeeping; preserve your strength for him (Ps. 58:10). Whatever evil you do not commit because he guards you, reckon as forgiven by him, lest, thinking little forgiven you, you love little and, beating your breasts, despise tax collectors with ruinous boastfulness.

Beware of the powers you have tested, lest you become inflated because you have been able to endure something. Pray concerning those you have not tested, lest you be tempted beyond what you can bear.

Consider that there are some who are secretly superior to you, though in public you are better than they. [Col. 0427] When you kindly believe that the good qualities of others, perhaps unknown to you, exist in them, your own known qualities are not diminished by comparison but strengthened by love; and whatever qualities may still be lacking are more readily given in proportion as they are desired more humbly.

Let those who persevere in your number provide you an example; let those who fall increase your fear. Love the former, so that you may imitate them; mourn the latter, lest you become inflated.

Do not establish your own righteousness; submit yourselves to God, who justifies you. Grant pardon for the sins of others; pray for your own. Avoid future sins by vigilance; erase past sins by confession.

### CHAPTER LIII

54. **The holier virgins are to be the more humble.**

Behold, you are already such that your other conduct corresponds to the virginity you have professed and preserved.

Behold, you abstain not only from murders, diabolical sacrifices and abominations, thefts, robberies, frauds, perjuries, drunkenness, every form of lust and greed, pretense, jealousy, impiety, and cruelty, but even those things that are either lighter or thought to be lighter are neither found nor arising among you: no shameless expression, no wandering eyes, no unbridled tongue, no wanton laughter, no buffoonish jest, no indecent dress, no swollen or dissolute gait.

You no longer return evil for evil or curse for curse (1 Pet. 3:9). Finally, you fulfill that measure of love by which you lay down your lives for your brothers (1 John 3:16).

Behold, you are already such, because you ought also to be such. These virtues, added to virginity, offer human beings an angelic life and display the customs of heaven upon earth.

But however great you are—whoever among you is so great—the greater you are, the more humble yourselves in all things, so that you may find grace before God; lest he resist the proud, lest he humble those who exalt themselves, lest he fail to bring the inflated through the narrow gate. [Note: Col. 0427. The Louvain edition alone reads, “through the narrow gate.”]

Although the concern that humility might be absent where love burns fervently is unnecessary.

### CHAPTER LIV

55. **Let them love the Bridegroom with all their heart.**

If, then, you have despised marriage with the sons of men, from whom [Col. 0428] you would have begotten sons of men, love with all your heart the one who is more beautiful in form than the sons of men. You are free for him; your heart is free from marital bonds.

Look upon the beauty of your beloved: consider him equal to the Father, subject to his mother; ruling in heaven and serving on earth; creating all things and created among all things.

Look upon that very thing which the proud mock in him, and see how beautiful it is. With your inward eyes behold the wounds of the one hanging, the scars of the one rising, the blood of the one dying, the price of the one who purchased, the exchange by which he redeemed.

### CHAPTER LV

**With what happiness and security the Bridegroom is loved.**

Consider the worth of these things; weigh them on the scales of love. Whatever love you would have devoted to your marriages, repay to him.

56. It is good that he seeks your inward beauty, since he gave you the power to become children of God (John 1:12). He does not seek beautiful flesh from you, but beautiful conduct by which you restrain the flesh.

There is no one to whom someone can lie about you and make him, through jealousy, rage. See with what security you love him whom you do not fear offending through false suspicions.

A husband and wife love each other because they see each other; and what they do not see, they fear in each other. They do not rejoice with certainty in what is visible, while in secret they often suspect what is not there.

You, in the one whom you do not see with your eyes but perceive by faith, have nothing real to criticize, nor do you fear offending him through some false suspicion.

If, then, you would owe great love to spouses, how greatly must you love the one for whose sake you did not wish to have a spouse?

Let the one who was fixed upon the cross for you be fixed wholly in your heart. Let whatever you refused to occupy with marriage occupy your entire soul.

You may not love him little for whose sake you did not love even what would have been permitted. Since you love the one who is gentle and humble in heart, I have no fear of pride among you.

### CHAPTER LVI

57. **Conclusion of the work.**

According to our modest ability, we have spoken sufficiently both about the holiness by which you are properly called consecrated women and about the humility by which whatever great quality you possess is preserved.

More worthily, however, let those three young men, for whom the one they loved with their most ardent hearts provided refreshment in the fire, admonish you concerning this little work of ours—far shorter in number of words, but much greater in the weight of its authority—in the hymn by which God is honored by them.

For, joining humility to holiness in those who praise God, they taught most clearly that the more holy a profession a person makes, the more carefully he must guard against being deceived by pride.

Therefore you too should praise him who grants you that, amid the heat of this present age, although you are not joined in marriage, you are nevertheless not burned. And while praying also for us, say:

“Bless the Lord, holy and humble in heart; sing a hymn and exalt him above all forever” (Dan. 3:87).

## On the Good of Widowhood

### ADMONITION ON THE WORK *ON THE GOOD OF WIDOWHOOD*

[Col. 0429]

Desiderius Erasmus endeavors to remove this work from Augustine and to assign it to his opponent Julian. It is tiresome to refute the arguments he brings in Julian’s favor. Against Augustine he advances scarcely anything except the simplicity of the diction; but this very simplicity of diction loudly proclaims that the work is Augustine’s.

Jacobus Pamelius, in his notes on Tertullian’s *Against Hermogenes*, chapter 1, section 7, citing the work with the words, “The author of the little work *On the Good of Widowhood*, among the writings of St. Augustine,” seems to indicate that he believes it was not composed by Augustine at all.

In support of this opinion, Lindanus, in the *Panoplia*, book 4, chapter 98, thinks he has a substantial argument from canon 104 of the fourth Council of Carthage, to which Augustine is said to have subscribed. That canon decreed that widows who had devoted themselves to the Lord and assumed religious dress, if they later passed over to secular marriage, whether a second marriage or otherwise, should remain excluded from the communion of Christians and be branded with the crime of adultery.

On the contrary, the author of the following book, in chapters 10 and 11, rebukes those who think that the marriages of women who have fallen from a holy purpose, if they marry, are not marriages but adulteries, and who wish to restore them to continence by separating them from their husbands.

Augustine, however, does not disagree here with that canon. The canon does not allow the marriages of such women to be called adulteries, but nevertheless says that those who fall from a holy purpose are worse than adulterers. Thus it does not prohibit those who marry after taking a vow from being punished by some form of excommunication, just as adulteresses are, provided that their marriages, once contracted, are not dissolved.

No other command against the marriages of women who have fallen away is found in the decrees of the older councils. In this matter the sixteenth canon of the Council of Chalcedon is famous. Some years after Augustine’s death it defined as follows:

“If any virgin has dedicated herself to God, and likewise any monk, they may not be joined in marriage. If they are found to do this, let them remain excommunicated. We decree, however, that humaneness may be shown toward them if the bishop of the place approves it.”

For the rest, Cyprian in Letter 62 to Pomponius, Epiphanius in Heresy 61, that of the Apostolics, and others provide some support for Augustine’s teaching, which he gives here concerning marriage after a vow, as well as in *On Holy Virginity*, chapter 34, and in Letter 220 to Count Boniface, section 12.

Nor are there lacking those to whom the Council of Carthage mentioned above—since it does not appear in the code of canons of the African Church together with the other Carthaginian councils of that period—seems of doubtful authenticity.

Although the council is recorded as having been held in 398, when Augustine was still young and a newly appointed bishop, he subscribed to it second after Aurelius. This may have given Lindanus an opportunity for error, since he asserts that Augustine subscribed when he was already old.

Augustine did not mention this subsequent work in the books of the *Retractions*, because it was written in the form of a letter. For this reason Possidius lists it among the Letters in chapter 7 under the title: “To Juliana, on Holy Widowhood.”

Florus, or the commonly published Bede, also cites and transcribes almost the entire work in his comments on 1 Corinthians 2 and 7, Philippians 4, and 1 Timothy 5.

The inscription prefixed to the letter in all the ancient manuscripts attributes it to Augustine. He himself also indicates this in chapter 15, mentioning the books he published *On the Good of Marriage*, *On Holy Virginity*, and *Against Faustus*, and likewise in chapter 23, where he refers to the letter written to Proba on praying to God.

The book *On Widowhood* belongs approximately to the year 414. It was written after the consecration of the virgin Demetrias, praised here in chapter 19 as a recent event, “which has just begun.” We have observed that this took place toward the end of 413, in volume 2, in connection with Letter 150, addressed to Proba and Juliana.

In chapter 17 he commands his readers to beware of the error of the Pelagians, which he says had begun to spread, though he does not name them. Juliana perhaps gives thanks to Augustine for this very admonition in the letter cited in Letter 188, sent to the same Juliana, where Augustine reports her words:

“Certainly, because your Reverence urges me not to lend my ears to those people who often corrupt the venerable faith through perverse teachings, I offer abundant thanks for so pious an admonition.”

# Saint Aurelius Augustine, Bishop of Hippo: *The Book, or Letter, on the Good of Widowhood* [Note: [Col. 0429] In some manuscripts the title is: *On the Profession of Widowhood*; or: *On the Profession of Holy Widowhood*. In Erasmus and the Louvain edition: *On the Good, or Perfection, of Widowhood*.] to the Widow Juliana [Note: [Col. 0429] Probably written around the year 414.] [Note: [Col. 0431] In revising this book, we collated the old Gallican manuscripts with the printed editions of Erasmus and the Louvain scholars: twelve manuscripts—the Royal, Sorbonic, Victorine, Augustinian (that is, from the library of the Augustinians of Paris), the Chartres manuscript of the Abbey of Saint Peter, the Laon manuscript of the cathedral, the Cistercian, Cygirannian, Bec, Michaeline, Rouen, and the very old German manuscript, a thousand or more years old—as well as three Roman Vatican manuscripts and the variant readings of four Belgian manuscripts preserved in the Louvain edition.] [Note: [Col. 0431] We also compared all the editions mentioned at the beginning of *Retractations* and *Confessions*, volume 1. M.] (C)

Here he instructs and exhorts widows. First, by instruction, he proves that the profession of holy widowhood is to be preferred to marriage; yet that second marriages, indeed even third marriages and marriages of whatever number, are lawful and never wrong; and that women who marry after making a vow of widowhood or virginity are rightly condemned, but that the marriages themselves should neither be regarded as adulteries nor dissolved. He wishes the merits of widows to be weighed according to the strength of their continence and piety; and therefore demonstrates that a widow who has had two husbands may sometimes rightly be preferred to a widow who has had one. Afterwards, by exhortation, he urges Juliana above all to ascribe her continence to the grace of God, and to beware of the little speeches that have begun to spread among certain people who are hostile to the grace of Christ. He commands her to devote all her efforts, together with her virgin daughter and widowed mother-in-law, to pleasing God; to have spiritual delights in place of bodily pleasures; and finally not to neglect guarding their reputation.

Augustine, bishop, servant of Christ and of Christ’s servants [Note: [Col. 0431] So Erasmus and some manuscripts. The Louvain edition has: “Servant of the servants of Christ.” The very old Corbie manuscript has: “servant of Christ, servant of Christ.”], to Juliana, the religious servant of God: salvation in the Lord of lords.

## CHAPTER ONE

### 1. He writes to Juliana, at her request, about the profession of widowhood. He will explain the Apostle’s teaching on the subject.

So that I might no longer remain indebted, in respect of my promise, to your request and love in Christ [Note: [Col. 0431] The Cistercian manuscript has: “to your love in Christ.”], I have managed, amid my other extremely pressing occupations, to write something to you about the profession of holy widowhood. For when you asked me in person, you placed this burden upon me [Note: [Col. 0431] So the manuscripts. The printed editions have “honored me.”]; and when I could not refuse you this, you repeatedly demanded my promised work in letters.

When, in this work of ours, you read something that does not at all pertain to your situation, or to the situation of you all who live together in Christ, and that is not specifically necessary for the guidance of your life, you should not therefore judge it superfluous [Note: [Col. 0431] Thus Erasmus and the manuscripts; some read: “you [plural] should.”]. Although this letter was written to you, it was not written only for you; rather, since it could also benefit others through you, we certainly ought not to have neglected it. Whatever you find here that either was never necessary for you or is no longer so, but that you nevertheless see to be necessary for others, do not be unwilling either to possess it or to give it for reading, so that your charity may also become useful to others.

### 2. Both instruction and exhortation are necessary in questions concerning life and conduct.

Since, then, in every question relating to life and conduct, not instruction alone but also exhortation is necessary—so that by instruction we may know what ought to be done, and by exhortation may be stirred up not to shrink from doing what we have learned ought to be done—what more shall I teach you than what we read in the Apostle?

For Holy Scripture establishes the rule of our instruction, so that we do not dare to be wise beyond what we ought to be wise, but, as he himself says, that we should be wise with sobriety, according as God has allotted to each one the measure of faith (Romans 12:3). Therefore let it be my task to teach you nothing other than to explain to you the words of the teacher and to discuss from them whatever the Lord grants.

## CHAPTER TWO

### 3. In the Apostle, “unmarried women” means not only virgins but also widows.

The Apostle, therefore, teacher of the Gentiles and vessel of election, says: “But I say to the unmarried and to widows: it is good for them if they remain as I am.”

These words must be understood in such a way that we do not suppose widows ought not to be called unmarried because they have experienced marriage. For by the name “unmarried” he signifies those who are not bound by marriage, whether they have been married or have not been married.

He makes this clear elsewhere, where he says: “The unmarried woman and the virgin are divided.” Since he adds “the virgin” as well, whom does he wish to be understood by “the unmarried woman” except a widow? Hence, shortly afterward, he includes both conditions under the single name “unmarried,” saying: “The unmarried woman is concerned with the things of the Lord, how she may please the Lord; but she who is married is concerned with the things of the world, how she may please her husband” (1 Corinthians 7:8, 34).

Certainly, he did not wish “unmarried” to be understood only of one who has never married, but also of one who, having been freed from the bond of marriage through widowhood, has ceased to be married. For this reason, he calls no one “married” except one who has a husband, not one who had a husband and no longer has one.

Therefore every widow is unmarried; but because not every unmarried woman is a widow—for virgins also exist—he placed both terms here when he said, “I say to the unmarried and to widows,” as though he were saying: “What I say to the unmarried, I do not say only to those who are virgins, but also to those who are widows: it is good for them if they remain as I am.”

## CHAPTER THREE

### 4. Widowhood is better than marriage, though marriage is truly good. Marital fidelity and its other goods are inferior to widowhood.

Here is your good, compared with that good which the Apostle calls his own, if faith is present—or rather, because faith is present. This teaching is brief, but it is not for that reason to be despised; rather, because it is not worthless in its brevity, it is more easily and more dearly retained.

For the Apostle would not commend here just any kind of good, since he placed it, without any ambiguity, above the faith of married women. How great a good the faith of married women possesses—that is, of Christian and religious wives—can be understood from the fact that, when he was commanding the avoidance of fornication and was certainly addressing married people as well, he said: “Do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ?” (1 Corinthians 6:19).

So great, therefore, is the good of faithful marriage that its members themselves are members of Christ. Since the good of continence in widowhood is better than this good, the purpose of this profession is not to make a Catholic widow something greater than a member of Christ, but to give her a better place among the members of Christ than that occupied by a married woman.

For the same Apostle says: “Just as in one body we have many members, but all the members do not have the same activity, so we, though many, are one body in Christ, and individually members of one another” [Note: [Col. 0433] The printed editions have “are members of one another.” The word “are” is absent from the manuscripts.]—having different gifts according to the grace that has been given to us (Romans 12:4–6).

### 5. The Apostle’s concession to married couples.

For this reason also, when he warned married people not to defraud one another of the debt of bodily intercourse—and thus one of them, being denied the marital debt, might be tempted by Satan through lack of self-control and fall into fornication—he said: “But I say this by way of concession, not by command. I wish all people to be as I myself am; but each has his own gift from God, one in this way, another in that” [Note: [Col. 0433] The manuscripts have: “one in this way, another indeed in that way.”].

## CHAPTER FOUR

### The profession of widowhood does not condemn second marriages. Tertullian exposed the error of the Cataphrygians and Novatians.

You see that conjugal chastity and the marital fidelity of the Christian marriage-bed are also a gift, and a gift from God. Thus, when the desire of the flesh exceeds to some degree the measure of intercourse needed for the procreation of children, this is not an evil of marriage, but is pardonable because of the good of marriage.

For the Apostle was not speaking of marriage, which is joined together for the procreation of children, with the fidelity of conjugal chastity and the indissoluble sacrament of marriage so long as both spouses live—all of which are good—but of that excessive use of the flesh which is recognized in the weakness of married people and pardoned because of the intervention of the good of marriage, when he said: “I say this by way of concession, not by command.”

Likewise, when he says: “A woman is bound [Note: [Col. 0433] “By law” is not added; the word is taken from the Epistle to the Romans, chapter 7, verse 2. It is now read here in the Vulgate, but is absent from the handwritten Corbie and German Bibles.] as long as her husband lives; but if her husband dies, she is free: let her marry whom she wishes, only in the Lord. But she will be happier if she remains as she is, according to my advice,” he sufficiently shows that a faithful woman who marries again after her husband’s death is blessed in the Lord, but that a widow who remains in the same Lord is more blessed. In other words, to speak not only in the words but also in the examples of Scripture, Ruth is blessed, but Anna is more blessed.

### 6. Second marriages are not condemned by the good of widowhood.

Therefore, this is the first thing you must know: second marriages are not condemned by the good you have chosen, but honored as inferior. Just as the good of holy virginity, which your daughter has chosen, does not condemn your one marriage, so your widowhood does not condemn anyone’s second marriage.

It was especially on this point that the heresies of the Cataphrygians and Novatians became inflated. Even Tertullian, with sounding cheeks but without sound understanding, further inflated them, while he cut down second marriages with a slanderous tooth as though they were unlawful—marriages which the Apostle, with sober judgment, permits as entirely lawful.

Let no argument of any ignorant or learned person move you from this sound doctrine. Nor should you exalt your own good in such a way as to accuse another thing that is not evil as though it were evil. Rather, rejoice in your good all the more because you see that it not only avoids evils but also surpasses certain goods.

Adultery and fornication are evils.

## CHAPTER FIVE

### The good of widowhood is called honorable because it is more honorable, not because marriage is thought dishonorable.

But the woman who has bound herself by the freedom of a vow is very far removed from these unlawful things; she has made even what was lawful no longer lawful for herself, not by the command of the law but by the counsel of charity.

Conjugal chastity is good, but continence in widowhood is a better good. This better good is honored by the submission of the former good; the former good is not condemned by praise of the latter and better good.

### 7. “Honorable” does not mean that marriage is dishonorable.

When the Apostle commended the fruit of celibates and unmarried women, because they consider the things of the Lord and how they may please God, he added: “But I say this for your benefit, not to lay a snare for you”—that is, not to compel you—“but for what is honorable.”

We should not think that, because he called the good of unmarried women honorable, the bond of marriage is therefore dishonorable. Otherwise we would also condemn first marriages, which neither the Cataphrygians nor the Novatians, nor their most eloquent supporter, Tertullian, dared to call dishonorable.

Rather, when he says, “I say to the unmarried and to widows: it is good for them if they remain as I am,” he plainly uses “good” to mean “better,” since whatever is said to be better in comparison with something good is unquestionably itself good. For what else does “better” mean than “more good”?

Nor do we consequently suppose that he meant it to be evil if they married, merely because he said it was good for them if they remained as they were. Likewise, when he says, “but for what is honorable,” he did not show marriage to be dishonorable; rather, he commended what was more honorable than what was honorable by the general name of “honorable.” For what is “more honorable” except what is more honorable? And what is more honorable is certainly honorable.

He plainly declared that this was better than that good when he said: “He who gives his virgin in marriage does well; and he who does not give her in marriage does better.” And he declared that it was more blessed than the blessed when he said: “But she will be more blessed if she remains as she is” (1 Corinthians 7:5–8, 35–40).

Therefore, just as one thing is better than a good thing and more blessed than a blessed thing, so one thing is more honorable than an honorable thing—something he wished to call honorable.

Far be it from us to think that marriage is dishonorable, when the Apostle Peter says: “Husbands, likewise, grant honor to your wives as to a weaker vessel and one subject to you, as co-heirs of grace.” And when addressing the women, he exhorts them to be subject to their husbands, after the example of Sarah: “For in this way,” he says, “the holy women who hoped in God adorned themselves, obeying their husbands, as Sarah obeyed Abraham, calling him lord. You have become her daughters by doing good and not fearing any disturbance” (1 Peter 3:5–7).

## CHAPTER SIX

### 8. Married women are also holy in body, although less so than unmarried women. The good of widowhood is not diminished by praise of marriage but increased. Whether Anna the widow was more blessed than Ruth, who was married twice.

For this reason, what the Apostle Paul said about the unmarried woman—“so that she may be holy both in body and spirit” (1 Corinthians 7:34)—must not be understood as though a faithful and chaste married woman, subject to her husband according to the Scriptures, were not holy in body but only in spirit.

For it cannot happen that, when the spirit has been sanctified, the body also, which the sanctified spirit uses, is not holy. Yet, lest we seem to prove this by argument rather than by divine utterance, since Peter, when recalling Sarah, says only “holy women” and does not say “also in body,” let us consider the words of that same Paul.

When forbidding fornication, he says: “Do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ? Shall I therefore take the members of Christ and make them members of a prostitute? Certainly not.”

Let anyone dare, then, to say that the members of Christ are not holy; or let him dare to separate from the members of Christ the bodies of faithful married women.

A little later he also says: “Your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit within you, whom you have from God; and you are not your own, for you were bought at a great price” (1 Corinthians 6:15, 19–20).

He said that the body of the faithful is both members of Christ and a temple of the Holy Spirit, where surely believers of both sexes are understood. Married women are there, therefore, and unmarried women are there; but they are distinguished by their merits, and, like one member being preferred to another, one is placed before another, though neither is separated from the body.

When, therefore, speaking of the unmarried woman, he says, “so that she may be holy both in body and spirit,” he intended a greater sanctification of unmarried women in both body and spirit to be understood; he did not deprive the bodies of married women of all sanctification.

### 9. Differences among goods do not make the lesser good evil.

Learn, then, what your good is—or rather, remember what you have learned: your good is praised more because there is another good by which it is made better than it would be if it could exist only on the condition that the other good were evil or did not exist at all.

The eyes have great honor in the body, but they would have less honor if they were alone and there were no other members of lesser honor. In the heavens themselves, the sun surpasses the moon in light but does not condemn it; “star differs from star in glory” (1 Corinthians 15:41), but not in rivalry or pride.

Therefore God made all things, “and behold, they were very good”: not merely good, but very good; and this for no other reason than that they were all together. For with each individual work it was said, “God saw that it was good.” But when all things had been named, “very” was added: “God saw all that he had made, and behold, it was very good” (Genesis 1).

Some individual things are better than other individual things; but all things together are better than any individual thing.

Therefore may the sound doctrine of Christ make you sound in his body through his grace, so that the same spirit of yours, which rules the body, may not arrogantly exalt what you possess in body and spirit as better than what others possess, nor distinguish things foolishly.

### 10. Ruth’s blessedness does not mean that every widow is better than Ruth.

Nor, because I said that Ruth was blessed but Anna more blessed, since Ruth married twice whereas Anna, widowed soon after one husband, lived for a long time, should you immediately think that you are better than Ruth.

## CHAPTER SEVEN

### Holy women in the time of the Law married under the compulsion of obedience, not desire.

There was another dispensation in the prophetic times for holy women, whom obedience, not desire, compelled to marry, so that the people of God might be propagated, among whom the prophets of Christ would be sent ahead.

For that people itself, through the things that happened to them figuratively “for our instruction” (1 Corinthians 10:11), whether among those who understood them or among those who did not understand them, was nothing other than a prophet of Christ, from whom the flesh of Christ would also be born.

Therefore, so that that people might be propagated, the one who did not raise up offspring in Israel was regarded as accursed by the sentence of the law (Deuteronomy 25:5–10).

Hence holy women were inflamed not by a desire for intercourse but by devotion to bearing children. We should therefore believe with complete justice that they would not have sought intercourse if offspring could have come about in another way.

Men were also permitted to have several living wives. That this was caused not by lust of the flesh but by concern for procreation is shown by the fact that, while holy men were permitted to have several living wives, it was not likewise permitted for holy women to be joined to several living husbands. They would have been more shameful in proportion as they desired something that would not make them more fertile.

Accordingly, when the holy Ruth had no offspring of the kind that was necessary for Israel at that time, after her husband’s death she sought another husband from whom she might have such offspring.

Thus, although Ruth was married twice, Anna, a widow with one husband, was more blessed because she also deserved to be a prophetess of Christ. We must believe that, even if she had no children—which Scripture has left uncertain by saying nothing about it—she foresaw through the same Spirit by which she was able to recognize the child that Christ was soon to come from a virgin.

Therefore, even without children, if indeed she had none, she rightly refused a second marriage, because she knew that the time had already come when Christ would be better served not by the duty of bearing children but by the devotion of continence—not by making the wombs of marriage fruitful but by making the conduct of widows chaste [Note: [Col. 0436] Some manuscripts have “by disciplining” rather than “by making chaste.”].

But if Ruth also knew that through her flesh offspring would be propagated from which Christ would take flesh, and by marrying she rendered service to this knowledge, I would no longer dare to say that Anna’s widowhood was more blessed than Ruth’s fruitfulness.

## CHAPTER EIGHT

### 11. In the present time, first and second marriages are to be forgone unless lack of continence prevents it. Formerly marriage was obedience to the Law; now it is a remedy for weakness and a consolation of human life.

But you, who have children and live at the end of the age, when the time has come not for throwing stones but for gathering them, not for embracing but for refraining from embrace (Ecclesiastes 3:5), and while the Apostle cries out, “But I say this, brothers: the time is short; from now on let those who have wives live as though they had none”—

if you had desired a second marriage, it would certainly have been an indication not of obedience to prophecy or the Law, nor even of a carnal desire for offspring, but only of lack of continence.

For you would have done what the Apostle says after stating that it is good for them to remain as he is: “But if they do not exercise self-control, let them marry; for it is better to marry than to burn” (1 Corinthians 7:29, 8–9).

He said this so that the evil of unrestrained lust would not rush into the shamefulness of scandalous acts, while it was received within the propriety of marriage.

But thanks be to the Lord, because you have borne what you did not wish to be, and your daughter’s virginity has compensated for the loss of your own virginity.

For Christian teaching, when carefully consulted, answers that even first marriages in the present age are to be forgone unless lack of continence prevents it. The one who said, “If they do not exercise self-control, let them marry,” could have said, “If they have no children, let them marry,” if, after the resurrection and the proclamation of Christ, when such an abundance of children to be begotten spiritually among all nations is now available, the task of producing children from the flesh were still as necessary as it was in the earliest times [Note: [Col. 0437] So the manuscripts. The printed editions have “but after the resurrection”; and shortly afterward, “let such a task cease.”].

And when he says elsewhere, “Therefore I want younger women to marry, bear children, and manage households,” he commends the good of marriage with apostolic sobriety and authority; but he does not impose the duty of procreation even upon those who embrace the good of continence, as though it were an obligation of the Law.

Finally, he explains why he said this when he adds: “giving the adversary no opportunity for reproach; for some have already turned aside after Satan.”

From these words we understand that those whom he wished to marry could better have remained continent than married; but that it was better for them to marry than to turn back after Satan—that is, to look backward from that excellent purpose of virgin or widow chastity, fall away, and perish.

Accordingly, let those who do not exercise self-control marry before they profess continence, before they make a vow to God; for unless they fulfill what they vow, they are rightly condemned.

Elsewhere he says of such women: “For when they have grown wanton against Christ, they wish to marry, having condemnation because they have nullified their first faith”—that is, they have turned their will toward marriage away from their purpose of continence [Note: [Col. 0437] Several manuscripts have: “they have slipped in their will toward marriage away from their purpose of continence.”].

They nullified the faith by which they had previously vowed what they were unwilling to fulfill through perseverance (1 Timothy 5).

The good of marriage, therefore, is always indeed good; but among the people of God it was once obedience to the Law, whereas now it is a remedy for weakness and, in some cases, a consolation of human life.

To devote oneself to producing children—not in the manner of dogs through promiscuous use of women, but in the honorable order of marriage—is not an affection to be condemned in human beings. Yet even this is surpassed and overcome by the Christian mind that thinks upon heavenly things.

## CHAPTER NINE

### 12. To marry after a vow of continence is damnable; nevertheless, such marriages are not to be condemned.

But since, as the Lord says, “Not everyone can receive this saying” (Matthew 19:11), let the one who can receive it receive it; and let the one who does not exercise self-control marry. Let the one who has not begun deliberate; let the one who has begun persevere. Let no opportunity be given to the adversary; let no offering be withdrawn from Christ [Note: [Col. 0437] The manuscripts of Proba have: “let no offering of Christ be withdrawn.”].

If chastity is preserved within the marital bond, there is no fear of condemnation. But in widowhood and virgin continence, the excellence of a greater gift is sought. Once it has been sought, chosen, and offered as the obligation of a vow [Note: [Col. 0437] Several manuscripts have: “and offered as the obligation of a vow.” Bede, or Florus, in his commentary on Paul has: “and offered with a devoted vow.”], it is damnable not only to undertake marriage but even, if no marriage follows, to wish to marry [Note: [Col. 0437] The printed editions have “not to undertake marriage.” The word “not” is absent from the manuscripts and from Bede or Florus.].

For to demonstrate this, the Apostle did not say, “When they have grown wanton against Christ, they marry,” but, “they wish to marry,” having, he says, condemnation because they have nullified their first faith—even if they do not marry, but only wish to marry.

This is not because the marriages themselves of such women are judged condemnable, but because the betrayal of their purpose is condemned; the breaking of their vow is condemned; what is condemned is not their acceptance of an inferior good but their fall from a superior good.

Finally, such women are condemned not because they later entered into marital fidelity, but because they nullified the first faith of continence.

To indicate this briefly, the Apostle did not say that those who marry after adopting a purpose of greater holiness have condemnation—not because they are not condemned, but so that the marriages themselves might not be thought to be condemned—but after saying, “they wish to marry,” he immediately added, “having condemnation.”

And he said why: “because they have nullified their former faith.” Thus it becomes clear that the will which has fallen from its purpose is condemned, whether marriage follows or does not follow.

## CHAPTER TEN

### 13. Against those who say that the marriages of women who have fallen from a holy purpose are adulteries. The entire Church is a virgin.

Therefore, those who say that the marriages of such women are not marriages but rather adulteries do not seem to me to consider sufficiently keenly and carefully what they are saying. A resemblance to truth deceives them.

Because women who do not marry according to Christian holiness are said to choose the marriage of Christ, some argue in this way: “If a woman who marries another while her husband is alive is an adulteress, as the Lord himself defined in the Gospel (Matthew 19:9), then while Christ lives, and death no longer rules over him (Romans 6:9) [Note: [Col. 0438] Erasmus and most manuscripts have “husbands.”], a woman who had chosen his marriage is an adulteress if she marries a man.”

Those who say this are moved by an apparently subtle argument, but they pay too little attention to the absurdity that follows from it.

For when, even while her husband is alive and with his consent, a woman laudably vows continence to Christ, then, according to their reasoning, no woman ought to do this, lest she make Christ himself—something it is impious to think—an adulterer, since she would marry him while her husband was alive.

Furthermore, since first marriages have greater merit than second marriages, far be it from us to think that this is the view of holy widows: that Christ is, as it were, a second husband to them.

They already had him before, when they faithfully served their husbands in submission—not as a carnal husband, but as a spiritual one. The Church herself, whose members they are, is his spouse. Through the integrity of faith, hope, and charity, the whole Church is a virgin—not only in its holy virgins but also in its widows and faithful married women.

To the entire Church, whose members all these women are, the Apostle says: “I have betrothed you to one man, to present you as a pure virgin to Christ” (2 Corinthians 11:2).

He knows how to make a virgin spouse fruitful without corruption, since in the very flesh he was able to be born from a mother without corruption.

This poorly considered opinion—that the marriages of women who have fallen from a holy purpose are not marriages if they marry—produces no small evil: wives are separated from their husbands as though they were adulteresses rather than wives; and when people wish to return them to continence after separation, they make their husbands true adulterers [Note: [Col. 0438] Erasmus and most manuscripts have “husbands.”], since those husbands, while their wives are alive, have taken other women.

## CHAPTER ELEVEN

### 14. The fall from a holy purpose is evil, but the marriages of those who have fallen are nevertheless good.

Therefore, I cannot say that the unions of women who have fallen from a better purpose, if they marry, are adulteries rather than marriages. But I certainly would not hesitate to say that falls and ruin from a holier chastity, which is vowed to the Lord, are worse than adulteries.

For if—and this must not be doubted—it is an offense against Christ when his member does not keep faith with her husband, how much more grievously is he offended when faith is not kept with Christ himself in a matter that he requires once offered, though he had not required it to be offered?

When someone does not render what he vowed—not compelled by command but admonished by counsel—the iniquity of the violated vow is all the greater because the person had less necessity for making the vow.

I discuss these matters so that you may not think either that second marriages are a crime or that any marriages, insofar as they are marriages, are evil [Note: [Col. 0439] The words “or that any marriages, insofar as they are marriages, are evil” are absent from most manuscripts.].

Therefore, do not wish them to be condemned by you, but to be held in contempt. The good of widow continence is more splendidly fitting when women can vow and profess it by despising what is both pleasurable and lawful.

But after the profession of the vow, what is pleasurable must be restrained and conquered with perseverance, because it is now no longer lawful.

## CHAPTER TWELVE

### 15. No marriages, regardless of their number, are to be condemned.

People commonly raise questions about third, fourth, and still more numerous marriages. Therefore, to answer briefly, I dare neither condemn any marriages nor remove from them the modesty appropriate to their number.
