But lest anyone be displeased by the brevity of this answer, I am prepared to listen to my critic arguing at greater length. Perhaps he can offer some reason why second marriages should not be condemned but third marriages should be condemned.

For I, as I warned at the beginning of this discussion, do not dare to be wise beyond what one ought to be wise (Romans 12:3). For who am I to think that I should define what I do not see the Apostle having defined?

He says: “A woman is bound as long as her husband lives.” He did not say “first,” or “second,” or “third,” or “fourth” [Note: [Col. 0439] Some books have “or whatever number.”], but: “A woman,” he says, “is bound as long as her husband lives. But if her husband dies, she is free; let her marry whom she wishes, only in the Lord. But she will be more blessed if she remains as she is” (1 Corinthians 7:39–40).

As far as this matter is concerned, I do not know what can be added to or taken away from this sentence.

Furthermore, I hear the same Apostle, our teacher and Lord, responding to the Sadducees when they had proposed the case of a woman who was not married once or twice but, if one may put it so, seven times, asking whose wife she would be in the resurrection.

Rebuking them, he said: “You are mistaken, not knowing the Scriptures or the power of God. For in the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage; for they will not begin to die, but will be equal to the angels of God” (Matthew 22:29–30).

He was speaking of their resurrection who will rise to life, not of those who will rise to punishment.

He could therefore have said: “You are mistaken, not knowing the Scriptures or the power of God; in that resurrection these women who have married many times will not be able to exist as wives,” and then added, “because no one there marries either.”

But, as we see, he did not condemn that woman who had had so many husbands by any indication in his answer.

Therefore, without opposing the sense of human modesty, I do not dare to say that a woman may marry as often as she wishes after her husbands have died; nor, apart from the authority of Holy Scripture, do I dare, on my own judgment, to condemn marriages of whatever number [Note: [Col. 0440] So the manuscripts. The printed editions have “however many marriages.”].

What I say of a widow who has had one husband, I say of every widow: you will be more blessed if you remain as you are.

## CHAPTER THIRTEEN

### 16. A widow who has had two husbands may sometimes be preferred to one who has had one. The merits of widows are to be weighed according to the strength of their continence itself.

It is also customary to raise, not foolishly, the question of which widow ought to be preferred in merit. The question is whether it should be the widow who had one husband, lived with him for a longer time, bore children, and, after they had survived, became widowed and professed continence; or the woman who, as a young woman, lost two husbands within two years, had no children to console her, vowed continence to God, and grew old in that holiness with the greatest perseverance.

Let those who weigh the merits of widows by the number of their husbands rather than by the strength of their continence exercise themselves here in argument, if they can, and demonstrate something to us.

If they say that the widow who had one husband should be preferred to the widow who had two, unless they produce some special reason or authority, they will certainly be found to place before spiritual virtue not a greater spiritual virtue but the good fortune of the flesh.

For it belonged to the good fortune of the flesh both to live a long time with a husband and to bear children.

But if they do not prefer her because she had children, then surely the very fact that she lived a long time with her husband was nothing other than the good fortune of the flesh.

The merit of that Anna, however, is especially commended for this reason: although she had buried her husband very soon, she struggled with the flesh for a long period of her life and overcame it.

For it is written: “And there was Anna, a prophetess, the daughter of Phanuel, of the tribe of Asher. She had advanced in many days, and had lived with her husband for seven years from her virginity; and she was a widow until eighty-four years of age. She did not depart from the temple, serving with fastings and prayers night and day” (Luke 2:36–37).

You see how the holy widow is praised not only because she had one husband, but also because she lived only a few years with her husband from the time of her virginity and carried the gift of widow continence through such a long old age with such devoted service of piety.

## CHAPTER FOURTEEN

### 17. Another comparison among three kinds of widows. He desires for the widow Juliana the three goods that belonged to Anna.

Let us therefore place before our eyes three widows, each possessing one of all the qualities that belonged to Anna.

Let us posit one who had one husband but lacked both the great length of widowhood—because she had lived a long time with her husband—and the same degree of devotion to piety—because she did not serve with such dedication in fastings and prayers.

Let us posit a second who, after the very brief life of her first husband, also quickly lost a second husband and remained a widow for many years, but who likewise did not devote herself so greatly to the most religious service of fasting and prayer.

Let us posit a third who had not only had two husbands but had also lived for a long time with each separately, or with one of them [Col. 0441], and who, after being widowed at a later age—when, if she had wished to marry, she could also have borne children—embraced widow continence; but who, more intent upon God and more concerned to do what pleases him, served him day and night with fastings and prayers, like Anna.

If it is disputed which of these women is superior in merit, who would not see that in this contest the palm must be awarded to the greater and more fervent piety?

Likewise, if three other women are posited, each possessing two of those three qualities and lacking one [Note: [Col. 0441] The manuscripts have “of those three women.”], who could doubt that those would be better in whom devout humility was more powerful in their two goods, so that their piety was lofty?

### 18. None of these six widows conforms to your standard

None, indeed, of these six widows conforms to your standard. For if you carry this vow through to old age, you can possess all three qualities in which Anna excelled. You had one husband, and he did not live long with you in the flesh; and therefore, if you obey the words of the Apostle: “But she who is truly a widow and desolate has hoped in God and persists in prayers night and day” [Note: The better manuscripts read, in accordance with the Greek, *élpiken epì tòn Theòn, kaì prosménei* (“has hoped in God and persists”). The printed editions have: “She will hope in the Lord and will persist.”]; and if you avoid what follows, with sober vigilance: “But she who lives in pleasures is dead while she lives” (1 Tim. 5:5–6), then all those three good qualities that belonged to Anna will also be yours.

You also have children, whom perhaps she did not have. Yet you are not to be praised because you have them, but because you strive to nourish and educate them piously. That they were born to you is a matter of fertility; that they live is a matter of fortune; but that they be formed in this way is a matter of will and ability. In the former, let people congratulate you [Note: The Louvain edition alone reads, “they congratulate.”]; in the latter, let them imitate you.

By prophetic knowledge Anna recognized Christ in the virgin mother; the grace of the Gospel has made you the mother of Christ’s virgin. That holy virgin, therefore, whom you offered willingly and prayerfully to Christ, added to the merits of her widowed grandmother and mother something from the merit of virginity [Note: This is the virgin Demetrias, whose grandmother was Proba Faltonia and whose mother was Juliana. See Augustine’s Letters 130 and 150.]. For you do not have her for nothing; and in her you are what you are not in yourselves. Indeed, the reason that holy virginity was taken away from you when you married was so that she might be born from you.

### CHAPTER XV

#### 19. Summary of the foregoing

I would not have discussed in this work the different merits of different married women and widows if I were writing what I write to you only for you. But since there are certain exceedingly difficult questions in this kind of discussion, I wished to say something more than what specifically concerns you, because there are some who do not seem learned to themselves unless they attempt to examine the labors of others—not by judging them, but by tearing and rending them apart.

I wished also that you yourself might not only keep what you have vowed and make progress in that good, but might also know more carefully and firmly that your good is not separated from the goodness of marriage as though marriage were evil; rather, it is preferred to the goodness of marriage. Those who condemn the marriages of widowed women—even if they practice their continence [Col. 0442] wonderfully and fervently through abstinence from many things which you use—should not seduce you into thinking as they do, even if you are unable to do what they do. No one wants to be insane, even if he sees that the strength of an insane person is greater than the strength of the sane.

Sound doctrine, therefore, should especially adorn and protect the goodness of your resolve. That is why Catholic women who have married more than once are rightly preferred not only to widows who have had one husband, but even to the virgins of heretics.

There are, indeed, many recesses of questions and many perplexities concerning these three matters—marriage, widowhood, and virginity. To penetrate or resolve them by discussion requires both greater care and a fuller discourse, so that either we may think rightly about all of them, or, if we think otherwise about anything, God may also reveal that to us. Nevertheless, as the Apostle says in what follows: “Let us walk in the same direction to which we have attained” (Phil. 3:15–16).

With regard to the matter of which we are speaking, we have attained this: that we should prefer continence to marriage, and holy virginity even to widowed continence; and that we should not condemn marriages which are not adulteries but marriages, by praising any resolve of ours or of our own.

We have said many other things about these matters in the book *On the Good of Marriage* [Note: Erasmus’s edition alone omits “*On the Good of Marriage*, and in another book.”], in another book *On Holy Virginity*, and in the work that we composed, with as much labor as we could, against Faustus the Manichaean. For by attacking the chaste marriages of the Patriarchs and Prophets with extreme bitterness in his writings, he turned the minds of some unlearned people away from the soundness of the faith.

### CHAPTER XVI

#### 20. The second part of the work, concerning exhortation. Continence is a gift of God

Since at the beginning of this little work I had proposed two necessary matters and promised to carry them out—one concerning doctrine, the other concerning exhortation—and since I have discharged the first part as well as I could in accordance with the task I undertook, let us now come to exhortation, so that what is wisely known as good may also be loved ardently.

In this matter I first urge you to attribute to God whatever love of pious continence you feel to be present in you, and to give thanks to him who has bestowed so much upon you from his Spirit that, when his love was poured into your heart, your love of the better good took away from you the freedom to use what was lawful.

He gave you not to wish to marry when it was permitted, so that now you would not be permitted to do so even if you wished; and from this he gave you a firmer unwillingness, lest what would not be permitted should occur—something that did not occur even when it was permitted. He also granted you such merit as Christ’s widow that you might see your daughter too become Christ’s virgin [Note: Most manuscripts read in this way. The Louvain edition has: “and such merit that, while you were Christ’s widow, you might also see your daughter,” etc. The Vatican manuscripts read: “that, while you were Christ’s widow, your daughter too might become Christ’s virgin.”] For while you pray like Anna, she has become what Mary was.

The more you know that these are gifts of God, the more blessed you are through these same gifts; indeed, you are not blessed at all unless you know that what you have comes from him from whom you have it. Consider what the Apostle said about this: “We have not received the spirit of this world, but the Spirit who is from God, so that we may know the things given [Col. 0443] to us by God” (1 Cor. 2:12).

Many possess many gifts of God and, because they do not know from whom they have them, boast of them in impious vanity. No one is blessed by God’s gifts if he is ungrateful to the giver.

For even in the sacred mysteries, when we are commanded to lift up our hearts, we are able to do so only with the help of the one by whose command we are admonished. Therefore it follows that, for this great good of a heart lifted on high, we should not attribute glory to ourselves as though it were the result of our own powers, but should give thanks to the Lord our God. We are continually reminded of this, because it is fitting and just.

You remember where these words come from, and you recognize with what solemnity and holiness they are commended inwardly [Note: Most manuscripts read: “It is fitting and just.” The printed editions have: “It is fitting and just to remember.” Shortly afterward, the Cistercian manuscript and Florus, in his commentary on 1 Corinthians, chapter 2, read: “among which actions, and with what holiness.” The oldest Corbie manuscript reads: “among what sanction and with what holiness.” Three Vatican manuscripts and as many Gallican manuscripts read: “among which holy things and with what holiness.” Perhaps the reading should be: “from where they are, and with what sanction,” etc.]. Hold fast, therefore, and possess what you have received, and give thanks to the giver.

For although receiving and possessing are yours, you possess what you received. To the proud person who, because he possessed something, boasted impiously as though he possessed it from himself, Truth says through the Apostle: “What do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (1 Cor. 4:7).

### CHAPTER XVII

#### 21. Against the Pelagians, who defend free will in such a way as to deny God’s grace

These considerations compel me to warn against and avoid certain little discourses that have begun to creep through the ears into the minds of many. They are the enemies of Christ’s grace—a thing that must be said with tears—and through them people are persuaded that prayer to the Lord is not even necessary for us, lest we enter into temptation.

For they attempt to defend human free will in such a way that, by that alone, without the help of God’s grace, we are able to fulfill what is divinely commanded. It follows that the Lord said in vain, “Watch and pray, that you may not enter into temptation” (Matt. 26:41), and that each day, in the Lord’s Prayer itself, we say in vain, “Do not bring us into temptation” (Matt. 6:13).

If it is solely within our power not to be overcome by temptation, why do we pray not to enter or be brought into it? Let us instead do what belongs to our free will and absolute power, and mock the Apostle when he says: “God is faithful, who will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you are able” (1 Cor. 10:13). Let us resist him by saying: “Why do I ask the Lord for something that he has placed within my power?”

But may it be far from anyone who thinks soundly to think this. Let us therefore ask him to give what he commands us to possess. He commands us to possess what we do not yet have in order to show us what we should ask for; and when we discover that we are able to do what he has commanded, we should also understand from whom we received this ability, lest, puffed up and elated by the spirit of this world, we fail to know what has been given to us by God.

Therefore we do not destroy the choice of the human will when we proclaim God’s grace, by which that will is helped, not with ungrateful pride but with grateful devotion. It is ours to will; but the will itself is admonished so that it may rise, [Col. 0444] healed so that it may have strength, enlarged so that it may receive, and filled so that it may possess.

For if we did not will, we would certainly neither receive the things that are given nor possess them. Who, for example, would possess continence—and I speak especially of that among God’s gifts, since it is what I am discussing with you—unless he willed it? No one would receive it unless he willed it.

But if you ask from whom it comes, so that it can be received and possessed by our will, listen to Scripture—or rather, since you know it, recall what you have read: “I knew that no one can be continent unless God grants it, and this itself was wisdom, to know whose gift it was” (Wis. 8:21).

These are two great gifts: wisdom and continence. Wisdom is that by which we are formed in the knowledge of God; continence is that by which we are not conformed to this age. God commands us to be both wise and continent, for without these goods we cannot be just and perfect.

But let us pray that he may give what he commands, helping and inspiring us, just as he has admonished us by commanding and calling us to know what we ought to will.

Whatever he has given us, let us pray that he preserve it [Note: The manuscripts read this way. The printed editions have: “Whatever he has given here, let us pray.” The words “so that he may complete it” occur below.]. Whatever he has not yet given, let us pray that he supply. Yet let us both pray and give thanks for what we have received; and, because we are not ungrateful for what we have received, let us trust that we shall receive what we have not yet received.

For the one who gave faithful married people the ability to abstain from adulteries and fornications also gave holy virgins and widows the ability to abstain from every sexual union. In this virtue, the term “integrity” or “continence” is used in a proper sense.

Or have we received continence from him, but possess wisdom from ourselves? What then does the Apostle James say: “If any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask God, who gives generously to all and does not reproach anyone, and it will be given to him” (James 1:5)?

Concerning this question, we have already said much in other little works of ours, insofar as the Lord helped us; and on another occasion, when the opportunity is given, we shall say as much as we are able through him.

### CHAPTER XVIII

#### 22. The power of exhortation comes from grace

I wished to say something about this now because of certain brothers of ours, very dear friends whom we love deeply. They are not maliciously entangled in this error, but they are entangled in it nevertheless. They think that when they exhort people to justice and piety, their exhortation will have no power unless they place entirely within human power what they themselves urge a person to do—not assisted by God’s gift, but accomplished solely through the exercise of free will.

It is as though free will could exist for accomplishing a good work unless it had been liberated by God’s gift. They do not notice that they themselves possess, as a gift of God, the very ability by which they exhort others, so that they may rouse sluggish human wills to undertake the good life, kindle those that are cold, correct those that are perverse, turn back those that are estranged, and reconcile those that resist.

For in this way they are able to persuade others of what they themselves urge [Note: The printed editions read, “For if they are not able”; the manuscripts omit *not* and, in place of “if,” read “thus.”]. Or, if they do not accomplish these things in human wills, what do they accomplish? Why do they speak? Let them leave people to their own choice.

[Col. 0445] But if they do accomplish these things in them, does a human being accomplish so much in another human being’s will by speaking, while God does nothing there by helping? Rather, however great a person’s eloquence may be—so that through skill in argument and sweetness of speech he plants truth in the human will, nourishes love, removes error by teaching, and removes sluggishness by exhorting—“neither the one who plants is anything, nor the one who waters, but God who gives the growth” (1 Cor. 3:7).

The worker would labor in vain outwardly if the Creator were not secretly working inwardly.

I hope, therefore, that this letter of mine will deservedly soon come into the hands of people of that kind as well as into Your Excellency’s hands; for that reason I have thought it appropriate to say something about this. I also wish that you yourselves, and whatever other widows read or hear these words read, may know that you make more progress in loving and possessing the good of continence through your prayers than through our exhortations.

For if anything helps you, even when our conversations are supplied to you, everything must be attributed to that grace in whose hand, as it is written, “are both we and our words” (Wis. 7:16).

### CHAPTER XIX

#### 23. He exhorts them to the good of widowhood. Juliana’s entire attention should be directed toward pleasing God. Demetrias, her virgin daughter, and her grandmother should have one aim: to please God

If you had not yet vowed widowed continence to God, we would certainly exhort you to make the vow. But because you have already vowed it, we exhort you to persevere.

Nevertheless, I see that I must say such things as may cause even those who were still thinking of marrying to love and seize upon this way of life. Let us therefore incline our ear to the Apostle: “The unmarried woman is anxious about the things of the Lord, so that she may be holy in body and spirit; but the married woman is anxious about the things of the world, how she may please her husband” (1 Cor. 7:34).

He does not say, “She is anxious about the things of the world, so that she may not be holy.” But certainly, in that part of her concerns in which worldly pleasure is considered, conjugal holiness is less [Note: Nearly all the manuscripts read: “but certainly divine holiness is less.”].

Whatever attention of mind would be devoted to matters by which a husband might be pleased, the unmarried Christian woman ought in a certain way to gather together and direct toward that attention by which the Lord is pleased.

And see whom she pleases, she who pleases the Lord [Note: The manuscripts read “and see”; the printed editions, “and let her see.”]. Certainly, the happier she is, the more she pleases him; and the more she thinks about the things of the world, the less she pleases him.

Please, therefore, with your whole attention, him who is “more beautiful than the sons of men.” His grace is poured upon his lips, and it is by this grace that you please him. Please him also with that part of your thought which would have been occupied with the world in order to please a husband. Please him who displeased the world, so that those who please him might be freed from the world.

People saw this one, “more beautiful than the sons of men,” in the passion of the cross; yet “he had no form or beauty, and his appearance was rejected, and his posture was deformed” (Isa. 53:3). From this deformity of your Redeemer there flowed the price of your beauty—but of your inward beauty. “All the beauty of the king’s daughter is within” (Ps. 44:3, 14).

Please him by this [Col. 0446] beauty. Compose this beauty with diligent care and attentive thought. He does not love the cosmetics of falsehood; truth delights in what is true. And he is called Truth, if you recognize what you have read: “I am the way, and the truth, and the life” (John 14:6).

Run to him through him; please him from him; live with him, in him, and from him. In true affections and most holy chastity, love to be loved by such a husband.

#### 24.

Let the inward ear of your holy virgin daughter hear these words too. I shall consider how far she surpasses you in the kingdom of that King; that is another question. Yet you, mother and daughter, have found the one whom, by despising marriage—she despising all marriage, you a second marriage—you should both please through the beauty of chastity.

Certainly, if you had husbands whom you needed to please, you might perhaps now be ashamed to adorn yourself with your daughter. But do not be ashamed to do the things by which you are both adorned, for it is not criminal but rather glorious that you should both be loved by that one King.

Even if you had husbands, you would not employ an artificial whiteness and rouge applied with cosmetics, thinking neither that they were worthy to be deceived nor that you ought to deceive them. Now, therefore, truly please together and cling together to that King, who desired the beauty of his one bride, of whose members you are—she with virginal integrity, you with widowed continence, both with spiritual beauty.

In this beauty her grandmother, your mother-in-law, who has certainly grown old, is beautiful with you as well [Note: Proba was Demetrias’s grandmother and Juliana’s mother-in-law.]. As love extends the vigor of this beauty toward what lies ahead, age does not create a wrinkle in it.

You have with you a holy old woman, both in your household and in Christ, whom you may consult about perseverance: how to fight this or that temptation [Note: One Augustinian manuscript reads “that bestial temptation”; the printed editions read, “against the wars of the tempter.”], what should be done so that it may easily be overcome, and what defense should be adopted so that it may not easily lay an ambush again. If there is anything of this kind, she teaches you through her now-established experience, benevolent love, solicitous devotion, and secure age.

You especially—yes, you—should consult her in such matters, since she has experienced what you have experienced. For your daughter sings that song which, in the Apocalypse, virgins alone can sing (Rev. 14:3–4).

Nevertheless, she prays more anxiously for you both than for herself; but she is more anxious for her granddaughter, who has more years remaining in which to overcome temptations. She sees you as nearer to her own age, and as the mother of the daughter whom, if you had seen her married—which is no longer permitted, and may it never happen—you would, I think, have been ashamed to bear alongside her.

How much, then, of a dangerous age remains for you, who are not called a grandmother so that you may be fruitful with your daughter in the offspring of holy thoughts and works?

It is therefore not without reason that the grandmother is more anxious for her granddaughter, for whom you too are a mother: what the granddaughter has vowed is greater, and the whole of her course still lies before her [Note: The oldest Corbie manuscript and three others read: “and all that has only just begun remains for her.”].

May the Lord hear her prayers, so that you may submit to the merits of the holy woman who bore the flesh of [Col. 0447] your husband [Note: Olibrius, from Jerome’s Letter 8 to Demetrias.] in youth and now labors to bring forth your daughter’s heart in old age.

All of you, therefore, together and in harmony, please the one husband of the one spouse, in whose one body you live by one Spirit, through your conduct; devote yourselves to prayers.

### CHAPTER XX

#### 25. The fleeting attractions of the world, which quickly fail, are to be despised

The past day does not return to the future; after yesterday, today advances, and after today, tomorrow will advance. And behold, all times and temporal things pass away, so that the promise that remains may come; “and the one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. 10:22).

If the world is already perishing, what does a married woman bear children for? Or if she is to bear children in her heart but not in her flesh, why does she marry? But if the world is still going to last, why is the one through whom the world was made not loved more?

If the attractions of the world are already failing, there is nothing for a Christian mind to seek with desire. But if they will still remain, there is something for holiness to despise. Of these two alternatives, in the one there is no hope for lust; in the other, the glory of love is greater.

How many—or how great—are the years during which the flower of bodily youth seems to flourish? Some women, thinking about marriage and ardently desiring it, while they are rejected or delayed, suddenly grow old, so that they are now more ashamed to marry than they are willing to do so.

Many married women, after their very recent union, have become elderly while waiting for their husbands, who had gone far away, to return. As women widowed soon after marriage, they have sometimes not even been permitted, as old women, to receive back their husbands, who had themselves grown old.

If, therefore, when their suitors rejected or delayed them, or when their husbands were abroad, carnal desire could be restrained so that fornication or adultery would not be committed, why can it not be restrained so that sacrilege will not be committed? If it was restrained when it was inflamed by delay, why should it not be suppressed when, after being cut off, it has grown cold?

Those who do not despair of enjoying that same lust endure a more ardent desire [Note: The Louvain edition reads “ardently”; the other printed editions and the manuscripts read “more ardent.”]. But women who vow their unmarried chastity to God remove the very hope that is the fuel of love. Desire is therefore more easily restrained when it is kindled by no expectation; nevertheless, unless one prays that it be overcome, the forbidden object itself is desired more ardently.

### CHAPTER XXI

#### 26. Spiritual pleasures should take the place of carnal pleasures for widows

Let spiritual pleasures, therefore, succeed carnal pleasures in holy chastity: reading, prayer, the psalm, good thoughts, frequent good works, hope of the age to come, and the heart lifted on high. For all these things, give thanks to the Father of lights, from whom, as Scripture testifies, every good gift and every perfect gift descends without any doubt (James 1:17).

When, instead of the pleasures of married women who possess husbands in the flesh, other carnal pleasures are adopted as a kind of consolation, what evils follow? The Apostle has stated it briefly: “The widow who lives in pleasures is dead while she lives” (1 Tim. 5:6).

May it be far from you to be seized by a desire for wealth in place of a desire for marriage, so that money may take the place of a husband’s love in your hearts.

For, observing human conduct, we have often [Col. 0448] found that in some people, when wantonness has been restrained, avarice has grown. Just as those who do not see hear more sharply, and distinguish many things by touch—while those who use their eyes do not touch with such vividness—so that we understand that, when the attention of perception is restrained through one avenue, namely the eyes, it exerts itself more readily through the other senses [Note: The manuscripts read, “when the attention of perception is restrained, it exerts the power of perception more readily through the other senses.” Erasmus and some manuscripts have the incomplete variant, “more readily through the other senses”], as though it were attempting through one channel to make up for what is denied through another: so also carnal desire, when restrained from the pleasure of intercourse, often stretches itself with greater force toward the appetite for money, and, turning away from that, converts itself with more burning impulse toward this.

In you, however, let the love of wealth grow cold together with the love of marriage; and let the pious use of the things you possess be directed toward spiritual pleasures, so that your generosity may burn more brightly in helping the needy than in enriching the greedy.

For it is not the gifts of the covetous that are sent into the heavenly treasury, but alms given to the poor, which assist widows’ prayers in an immeasurable way.

Fasts and vigils also, insofar as they do not disturb bodily health, become spiritual pleasures when they are spent in prayer, psalmody, reading, and meditation on God’s law. The very things that seem laborious are thereby transformed into pleasures.

The labors of those who love are in no way burdensome; they themselves also give delight, as in the case of hunters, bird-catchers, fishermen, grape-harvesters, merchants, and those who amuse themselves with some game. What matters, then, is what is loved. In what one loves, either there is no labor, or even the labor itself is loved.

Consider how shameful and grievous it would be if labor gives pleasure when a wild animal is captured, a wine-jar or money-pouch is filled, or a ball is thrown, but gives no pleasure when God is acquired.

### CHAPTER XXII

#### 27. Care for a good reputation

In all the spiritual pleasures enjoyed by unmarried women, their holy conduct should also be cautious, lest, although their life is not evil through wantonness, their reputation becomes evil through negligence.

Nor should we listen to holy men or women who, when their negligence in some matter is reproved—negligence by which they come under evil suspicion, although they know that their life is far removed from such suspicion—say that their conscience before God is sufficient for them. They contemptuously disregard human opinion, not merely imprudently [Note: Most manuscripts read “shamefully.”] but cruelly, when they destroy the souls of others: whether of those who blaspheme the way of God because, according to their suspicion, the holy life that is chaste seems disgraceful to them, or of those who imitate them while making excuses—not what they see, but what they suppose.

Therefore, whoever guards his life from crimes, disgraceful acts, and wicked deeds benefits himself. Whoever also guards his reputation is merciful toward others.

Our life is necessary for us, but our reputation is necessary for others. And whatever we mercifully provide for the salvation of others also redounds to our own benefit.

Therefore the Apostle does not say without reason: “We provide what is good not only before God but also before human beings” (2 Cor. 8:21). He says again: [Col. 0449] “Please everyone in everything, just as I also please everyone in everything, not seeking what is useful to me but what is useful to many, so that they may be saved” (1 Cor. 10:33).

In another exhortation he says: “Finally, brothers, whatever things are true, whatever things are holy, whatever things are just, whatever things are chaste, whatever things are most dear, whatever things are of good repute—if there is any virtue, if there is any praise—think about these things, which you have both learned and received and heard and seen in me” (Phil. 4:8–9).

You see how, among the many things he urged by exhortation, he did not neglect to mention “whatever things are of good repute,” and how he concluded everything in two words when he said, “if there is any virtue, if there is any praise.” The good things he mentioned earlier belong to virtue; reputation belongs to praise.

I think the Apostle did not regard human praise as something very important when he said elsewhere: “It is a very small thing to me to be judged by you or by a human day” (1 Cor. 4:3); and elsewhere: “If I were pleasing human beings, I would not be Christ’s servant” (Gal. 1:10); and again: “For this is our glory: the testimony of our conscience” (2 Cor. 1:12).

Of those two things—good life and good reputation, or, more briefly, virtue and praise—he wisely retained one for its own sake and mercifully provided the other for the sake of others.

But since no matter how great human caution may be, it cannot entirely avoid malicious suspicions, once we have done whatever we rightly can for our reputation, if some attempt to stain it either by inventing evils about us [Note: The printed editions read: “by inventing evil.” The better manuscripts read: “by inventing evils.”] or by believing evil things, let the consolation of conscience be present—and plainly even joy—because our reward is great in heaven, even when people say many evil things about us while we are living piously and justly (Matt. 5:11–12).

That reward is like the pay of soldiers fighting with the weapons of righteousness, in the right hand as well as in the left: “through glory and dishonor, through ill repute and good repute” (2 Cor. 6:7–8).

### CHAPTER XXIII

#### 28. Those who practice continence should persevere and persuade others to practice it. Conclusion

Continue your course, therefore, and run with perseverance so that you may attain; and by the example of your life and by the word of exhortation draw into the same course as yourselves as many as you can.

Do not let the complaint of foolish people break your resolve—the complaint of those who say: “How will the human race continue if everyone practices continence?” It is as though this age were delayed for any other reason than that the predestined number of the saints might be completed. Once it has been completed more quickly, surely the end of the age will not be delayed.

[Col. 0450] Nor should this hold you back from urging your good upon others if someone says to you: “Since marriage too is good, how can all the goods—both the greater and the lesser—be present in the body of Christ if everyone imitates continence in praise and love of it?” [Note: The manuscripts read: “in praise and love of continence.” The printed editions have: “in praise and love.”]

First, because, when you strive for everyone to be continent, at least some will then be continent. For not everyone receives this word. But since it is written, “Let the one who can receive it receive it” (Matt. 19:11–12), those who can receive it will receive it if it is not kept silent even from those who cannot.

Moreover, we need not fear that perhaps everyone will receive it and that something of the lesser good—namely, married life—will be lacking in the body of Christ [Note: Erasmus and several manuscripts read: “married life”]. For if everyone hears and everyone receives it, we must understand that this too was predestined: that the goods of marriage would already be sufficient in the number of those members who have passed from this life, since so many have passed from it.

For even now, if everyone were continent, they would not be giving the honor of continence to those who have already brought the thirtyfold fruit into the Lord’s storehouses, if that fruit is understood to be present in the good of marriage (Matt. 13:8) [Note: The manuscripts read: “who have brought into the Lord’s storehouses the thirtyfold fruit, if it is understood in the good of marriage.” The printed editions have: “who have brought the thirtyfold fruit into the Lord’s storehouses, in which it is understood to exist in the good of marriage.”].

All these goods will therefore have their proper place there, even if thereafter no woman wishes to marry or no man wishes to take a wife.

Devote yourselves confidently, then, insofar as you can, so that others may become what you are. And pray watchfully and fervently that, by the help of the right hand of the Most High and the abundance of the Lord’s most merciful grace, you may both persevere in what you are and advance toward what you will be.

#### 29.

I beg you, therefore, by him from whom you have received this gift and from whom you hope for the rewards of this gift, to remember me also in your prayers, together with your entire household church.

It was entirely fitting that I should write a letter about prayer to your mother, now advanced in age [Note: Letter 130, to Proba]. For it is especially her task to contend in prayer on your behalf, since she is less concerned for herself than for you. It was also fitting that I should compose this little work on widowed continence for you rather than for her, because what remains for you to overcome has already been overcome by her age.

If your holy virgin daughter desires something about her profession from our labors, she has the substantial book *On Holy Virginity*, which she should read. I had also reminded you to read it, since it contains much necessary for both kinds of chastity, namely virginal and widowed chastity. Here I have touched on some of these matters lightly and omitted others entirely because I discussed them there at greater length.

Persevere in the grace of Christ.

[Col. 0451]

[Note: For the books *On Adulterous Marriages*, see Book 2, chapter 57, of the *Retractions*, vol. 1, col. 653, beginning with the words “I wrote two books” and ending with “You had written to me.” M.]

## Saint Aurelius Augustine, Bishop of Hippo: Two Books on Adulterous Marriages, addressed to Pollentius

[Note: Written around the year of Christ 419. In the second book of the *Retractions*, they are placed immediately after the work *On the Origin of the Soul*, which was composed in the year of Christ 419. Possidius calls them, in chapter 6, “On Inappropriate Marriages.”]

[Note: The books *On Adulterous Marriages* have been newly reviewed against the Royal, German, Bigotian, Pratellian, Michaeline, Ebrulphian, and Corbie manuscripts of the best quality; against three Vatican manuscripts; against the variant readings of three Belgian manuscripts cited by the Louvain editors; and against the editions of Erasmus and the Louvain scholars. The comparison was completed against the Amerbach edition, which agrees with the Erasmian edition.]

[Note: We also compared all the editions mentioned at the beginning of the *Retractions* and *Confessions*, vol. 1. M.]

(C)

## BOOK ONE

In this book chiefly two questions are treated.

The first concerns the passage in the Letter to the Corinthians: “But to those who are married I command . . . a woman . . . if she has separated, to remain unmarried,” and so forth. Pollentius thinks that this command of the Apostle concerns women who leave their husbands for a reason other than fornication, and that only these women are forbidden to marry another husband. Augustine, on the other hand, maintains that it concerns only those who have left their husbands because of fornication, and that departure is not permitted for any reason other than this.

The second question concerns the other passage in the Letter to the Corinthians: “To the rest I say—I, not the Lord,” and so forth. Augustine teaches that the Apostle said this as an admonition, namely, that faithful spouses should not make use of the permission granted to them to leave unbelieving spouses. Pollentius, on the contrary, holds that Paul forbids faithful spouses in that passage to dismiss even unbelieving spouses.

Finally, a question is touched upon concerning catechumens who are at the point of death: whether it benefits them to be baptized when they neither request baptism nor are able to answer on their own behalf.

### CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0451]

### 1. On the disagreement between Pollentius and Augustine concerning Paul’s passage: whether a spouse who wishes to remain unmarried may separate without the cause of fornication

The first question, dearest brother Pollentius, among those matters which you treated in your letter to me as though seeking my advice, concerns the Apostle’s statement: “To those who are married I give this command—not I, but the Lord—that a wife should not separate from her husband; but if she has separated, let her remain unmarried or be reconciled to her husband; and let the husband not dismiss his wife” (1 Cor. 7:10–11). Is this to be understood as meaning that he prohibited remarriage to a woman who separated from her husband without the cause of fornication? That is your view. Or is it to be understood as I judged in those books which many years ago I wrote on the evangelical discourse that the Savior delivered on the mountain according to Matthew: that he commanded those women to remain unmarried who had separated from their husbands for the one cause that is permitted, namely, fornication?

It seems to you that a woman separating from her husband ought not to marry if she was not compelled to separate by any fornication on her husband’s part. You do not consider that, if her husband had supplied no cause of fornication, she is not commanded to remain unmarried after separating, but is altogether forbidden to separate. For when a woman is commanded that, if she has separated from her husband, she should remain unmarried, permission to separate is not taken away from her, but permission to marry. If this is so, women who wish to live continently are therefore granted permission to await no consent from their husbands, so that the statement “let a wife not separate from her husband” appears to be a command directed to those women who could choose not continence, but a divorce by which they would be permitted to enter into another marriage.

Accordingly, women who have chosen to desire no intercourse and to bear no marriage will be permitted to leave their husbands even without any cause of fornication and, according to the Apostle, to remain unmarried. The same applies to men, since the rule is equal for both: if they wish to live continently, they will abandon their wives even against their wives’ consent and remain without any marriage. For, as you think, they would then be permitted to seek other marriages if the divorce arose from the cause of fornication. But when that cause is absent, it follows, according to your view, that either a spouse must not separate from the other spouse, or, if he or she separates, must remain without marriage, or must return to the former marriage.

Therefore, when no cause of fornication exists, either spouse may choose one of three alternatives: not to separate from the other spouse; or, if separated, to remain in that state; or, if not remaining so, not to seek another spouse but to restore himself or herself to the former one.

### CHAPTER II

#### 2. That a spouse may not separate except for the cause of fornication

And what becomes of the fact that the same Apostle did not wish spouses to deprive one another of the marital debt even for a time, so that they might devote themselves to prayer, except by mutual consent? How will what he says remain valid: “Because of fornications, let each man have his own wife, and let each woman have her own husband. Let the husband render the debt to his wife, and likewise the wife to her husband. The wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband does; likewise, the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife does” (1 Cor. 7:2–5)?

How can this be true unless it is because a spouse may not live continently against the other spouse’s will? For if a woman may dismiss her husband in such a way that she remains unmarried, then she, not he, has authority over her own body; and the same must be understood of the husband.

Moreover, when it is said, “Whoever dismisses his wife, except for the cause of fornication, makes her commit adultery” (Matt. 5:32), how are we to understand this unless it is forbidden for a man to dismiss his wife when no cause of fornication has arisen? The reason is also given: namely, lest he make her commit adultery. This is clearly because, even if she did not dismiss him but was herself dismissed, she will be an adulteress if she marries.

### CHAPTER III

#### The Apostle’s passage concerning a woman who separates from a fornicating husband is to be understood in this way

For this very great evil, therefore, a man may not dismiss his wife except for the cause of fornication. In that case, by dismissing her he does not make an adulteress; he dismisses an adulteress. But what if he says, “I am dismissing my wife without any cause of fornication, but I shall remain continent”? Shall we therefore say that he has done with impunity what he has done? Who would dare say this, if he understands the Lord’s intention in saying these things? For the Lord, who excepted the sole cause of fornication, did not wish a spouse to be dismissed even for the sake of continence.

#### 3.

Let us therefore return to the Apostle’s own words: “To those who are married I give this command—not I, but the Lord—that a wife should not separate from her husband; but if she has separated, let her remain unmarried.” Let us question him as though he were present, and consult him in a manner:

“Why did you say, Apostle, that if she has separated, she should remain unmarried? Is separation permitted, or is it not permitted? If it is not permitted, why do you command a woman who separates to remain unmarried? But if it is permitted, there must certainly be some cause for which it is permitted.”

When this cause is sought, none is found except the one cause which the Savior alone excepted: namely, the cause of fornication. Accordingly, the Apostle did not command a woman to remain unmarried if she separated except when she separated from her husband for that cause for which alone she was permitted to separate.

For when it is said, “I command her not to separate; but if she has separated, let her remain unmarried,” far be it from the woman who separates in such a way as to remain unmarried to act against this command. Unless the woman whom the command concerns is understood to be one who is permitted to separate—and she is not permitted to do so except from a fornicating husband—how is she commanded to remain unmarried if she separates?

Who would say, “If a woman separates from a husband who is not fornicating, let her remain unmarried,” when she is not permitted to separate from anyone except a fornicating husband? I think you now understand how greatly your interpretation conflicts with the bond of marriage, since the Lord did not wish even continence to be undertaken except by equal and harmonious consent.

### CHAPTER IV

#### 4. The Apostle misunderstood concerning a woman who separates because she has chosen continence

Let us explain the matter somewhat more clearly and, as it were, place it before our eyes. Suppose that continence pleases a woman but not her husband. The woman separates from him and begins to live continently, intending, of course, to remain chaste herself, but doing what the Lord does not wish: making her husband an adulterer, since, if he does not live continently, he will seek another woman.

What shall we say to the woman except what sound ecclesiastical teaching says? “Render the debt to your husband, lest, while you seek the means by which you may receive greater honor, he find the means by which he may be condemned.” We would say the same to him if he wished to live continently against her will. “You do not have authority over your own body, but she does; likewise, she does not have authority over her own body, but you do. Do not deprive one another, except by mutual consent.”

After we have said these and many similar things relevant to the matter, would you like the woman to answer us from your line of reasoning as follows?

“I hear the Apostle saying, ‘I command a wife not to separate from her husband; but if she has separated, let her remain unmarried or be reconciled to her husband.’ Look: I have separated; I do not wish to be reconciled to my husband, but I remain unmarried. For he did not say, ‘If she has separated, let her remain unmarried until she is reconciled to her husband’; rather, he said, ‘Let her remain unmarried or be reconciled to her husband.’ Let her do this or that, he says: he permitted a choice between two alternatives, but did not compel her to either one. I choose to remain unmarried, and thus I fulfill the command. Rebuke me, accuse me, denounce me; use whatever severity you wish, if I marry.”

### CHAPTER V

#### 5. That interpretation of the Apostle refuted

What can I say in response to her except, “You do not understand the Apostle correctly”? He would not have commanded a woman to remain unmarried if she had separated from her husband unless she were one whom it was permitted to separate—the one cause, namely, which is left unstated there because it is so well known: fornication.

For God the Teacher excepted this sole cause when he spoke about dismissing a wife, and he indicated that the same rule was to be observed in the case of a husband. For not only does the wife lack authority over her own body, but the husband does also; likewise, the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife does.

Since, then, you cannot accuse your husband of fornication, how do you suppose that you can excuse separating from him by not marrying, when you are not permitted to separate from him at all? When the woman hears these things from us, I think you would not wish her to answer that she remains unmarried because she separated without any fornication on her husband’s part. For if he had fornicated, she would have been permitted not only to separate but also to marry.

### CHAPTER VI

#### 6. Pollentius’s view that marriage to another man is not forbidden by command to a woman who separates from an adulterer, but should be avoided because of disgrace

She certainly would not say this, since you yourself have been embarrassed to grant such permission to women. You wrote:

“If a husband dismisses an adulterous wife and marries another, only the woman will suffer disgrace. But if the woman for the reason mentioned above dismisses her husband and marries another, not only the man but also the woman will suffer disgrace.”

In explaining the reasoning behind this opinion of yours, you say:

“For they will say that she separated in order to join herself to another husband, even if he should happen to be of the same kind as the man from whom she separated; for it is very easy for men to fall into this disease and vice. But if she dismisses that man also and marries another, they will say even more strongly that she desired a multitude of husbands.”

After giving this explanation, you conclude and say:

“Therefore, after these matters have been examined or even thoroughly discussed, the woman ought either to endure her husband or remain unmarried.”

You have certainly given women good advice: knowing that, if they dismiss adulterous husbands, they are permitted to marry others, they should nevertheless refrain from doing so because of disgrace, and should rather endure even adulterous husbands, lest they appear to wish to join themselves to many men on this pretext—since it is difficult for a woman not to find a husband of the same kind as the one she dismissed, because men are very prone to this disease.

When, therefore, we say that even the woman who has dismissed a fornicating husband may not marry another, while you say that she may marry but that it is not expedient, we both undoubtedly say that a woman who dismisses a fornicating husband ought not to marry. The difference is that, when both spouses are Christians, we say that a woman who separates from a fornicating husband may not marry another, and that she may not separate at all from a husband who is not fornicating. You, however, say that if a woman separates from a husband who is not fornicating, she may not marry another because of the command; but if she separates from a fornicating husband, it is not expedient for her to marry because of disgrace.

You therefore permit a woman who intends not to marry to separate from her husband, whether he is fornicating or not.

### CHAPTER VII

#### 7. The command that even a woman who separates from an adulterer should remain unmarried

But the blessed Apostle—or rather, through the Apostle, the Lord—does not permit a woman to separate from a husband who is not fornicating. It remains, therefore, that he forbids her to marry if she separates, while permitting her to separate from a fornicating husband.

For the woman of whom it is said, “If she has separated, let her not marry,” is permitted to separate on the condition that she does not marry. If, therefore, she chooses not to marry, there is no reason to prohibit her from separating. It is like the woman of whom it is said, “If she does not exercise self-control, let her marry” (1 Cor. 7:9): she is permitted not to exercise self-control on the condition that she marry. If she chooses to marry, she cannot be compelled to remain continent.

Therefore, just as this incontinent woman is compelled to marry, so that her failure to remain continent may not be condemnable, so the woman who separates from her husband is compelled to remain unmarried, so that her separation may not be culpable. But she separates culpably from a husband who is not fornicating, even if she remains unmarried.

The woman who is commanded to remain unmarried if she separates is therefore the woman who separates from a fornicating husband. If we understand the Apostle in the way that says to women, “Do not separate from your husbands, even if they are chaste; but if you wish to separate, remain unmarried,” all women who desire continence will think that they are permitted to separate even against their husbands’ consent.

Since we certainly ought not to permit this, it remains that the words “if she has separated, let her remain unmarried” must be taught to refer to the woman whom we have learned is permitted to separate—namely, from a fornicating husband. Otherwise, by using continence as a pretext, we would disturb Christian marriages and, contrary to the Lord’s most merciful command, drive incontinent husbands dismissed by continent wives, or incontinent wives dismissed by continent husbands, into adultery.

### CHAPTER VIII

#### 8. The rule concerning husband and wife is equal in this matter

The Lord said—not in the very discourse that we were explaining, but elsewhere—“Whoever dismisses his wife, unless for the cause of fornication, and marries another, commits adultery” (Matt. 19:9). If this is to be understood to mean that whoever dismisses his wife for the cause of fornication and marries another does not commit adultery, then the rule concerning husband and wife does not appear to be equal in this matter. For a woman, even if she separates from her husband for the cause of fornication and marries another, commits adultery; but a man, if he dismisses his wife for the same cause and marries another, does not commit adultery.

But if the rule is equal in both cases, both commit adultery if either joins himself or herself to another, even after separating from a fornicating spouse. The Apostle shows that the rule concerning man and woman is equal in this matter—something that must often be recalled—where, after saying, “The wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband,” he adds, “Likewise, the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife.”

### CHAPTER IX

#### 9. Pollentius’s objection from the passage in Matthew, refuted from a similar passage in James. The sins of the ignorant. Matthew is to be understood from Mark and Luke

“But why,” you ask, “did the Lord insert the cause of fornication instead of saying generally, ‘Whoever dismisses his wife and marries another commits adultery,’ if the man who, having dismissed a fornicating wife, marries another is also an adulterer?” [Note: Col. 0456: The manuscripts read, “if he too has committed adultery.”]

I believe it is because the Lord wished to mention what is the greater offense. [Note: Col. 0456: The manuscripts read “commend” rather than “mention.”] Who denies that it is a greater adultery to dismiss a wife who is not fornicating and marry another than to dismiss a fornicating wife and then marry another? This is not because the latter is not also adultery, but because the offense is lesser when another woman is married after a fornicating wife has been dismissed.

The Apostle James also uses a similar expression when he says, “Whoever knows how to do good and does not do it, for him it is sin” (James 4:17). Does this mean that it is not sin for the person who does not know how to do good and therefore does not do it? It is certainly sin; but it is more serious if he knows and does not do it. The former sin is not thereby nothing simply because it is lesser.

Thus, to express both cases in the same way: just as “whoever dismisses his wife, except for the cause of fornication, and marries another commits adultery,” so “whoever knows how to do good and does not do it sins.” But just as it cannot rightly be said here, “Therefore, if he does not know, he does not sin”—for there are also sins of the ignorant, although they are lesser than those of the knowledgeable—so neither can it rightly be said there, “Therefore, if he dismisses his wife for the cause of fornication and marries another, he does not commit adultery.” For those who marry another after leaving their former wives because of fornication also commit adultery, although their adultery is lesser than that of those who dismiss their wives without the cause of fornication and marry others.

For just as it has been said, “For the person who knows how to do good and does not do it, it is sin,” so the following may be said in the same way: “For the person who dismisses his wife without the cause of fornication and marries another, it is adultery.”

Accordingly, just as we say, “Whoever marries a woman dismissed by her husband apart from the cause of fornication commits adultery,” we undoubtedly speak the truth; yet we do not thereby absolve from this crime the man who marries a woman dismissed because of the cause of fornication. We have no doubt that both are adulterers.

No one is so absurd as to deny that the man who marries a woman whom her husband dismissed because of fornication is an adulterer, while calling the man an adulterer who marries a woman dismissed apart from the cause of fornication. Thus both men are adulterers.

Therefore, when we say, “Whoever marries a woman dismissed by her husband apart from the cause of fornication commits adultery,” we are speaking of one of the two; yet we do not thereby deny that the man who marries the woman whom her husband dismissed because of fornication also commits adultery.

Thus, since both are adulterers—the man who dismisses his wife apart from the cause of fornication and marries another, and the man who, after dismissing his wife because of the cause of fornication, joins himself to another—when we read of one of them, we must not understand the passage as though the other were denied to be an adulterer merely because the one is expressly named.

#### 10.

But if Matthew the Evangelist makes this difficult to understand because, by expressing one case, he leaves the other unmentioned, did not the other Evangelists state the same matter generally, so that it could be understood of both?

According to Mark it is written as follows: “Whoever dismisses his wife and marries another commits adultery against her; and if a wife dismisses her husband and marries another, she commits adultery” (Mark 10:11–12).

According to Luke: “Everyone who dismisses his wife and marries another commits adultery; and the man who marries a woman dismissed by her husband commits adultery” (Luke 16:18).

Who are we, then, to say, “There is a man who commits adultery by dismissing his wife and marrying another, and there is another who does not commit adultery by doing this,” when the Gospel says that everyone who does this commits adultery?

Accordingly, if everyone who does this—that is, everyone who dismisses his wife and marries another—commits adultery, then without doubt both cases are included: the man who dismisses his wife apart from the cause of fornication and the man who dismisses her because of the cause of fornication. For “whoever dismisses” means “everyone who dismisses.”

### CHAPTER X

#### 11. How the passage in Matthew stands in the books that Pollentius read

When I quoted the words of the Gospel according to Matthew, I did not, as I do not know why you thought, omit the words “and marries another” and then say “commits adultery.” Rather, I used the words found in that extended discourse which the Lord delivered on the mountain. I had undertaken to explain that discourse, and the words there are as I quoted them:

“Whoever dismisses his wife, except for the cause of fornication, makes her commit adultery; and whoever marries a woman released from her husband commits adultery.”

Although some copies express the same meaning in different words, they do not differ from what is understood. Some have “Whoever dismisses,” others “Everyone who dismisses.” Likewise, some have “except for the cause of fornication,” others “apart from the cause of fornication,” and others “unless on account of the cause of fornication.” Again, some have “whoever marries a woman released from her husband commits adultery,” while others have “whoever marries a woman dismissed by her husband commits adultery.”

I think you see that these differences make no difference to one and the same meaning. However, some Greek and Latin manuscripts do not contain the final clause—“whoever marries a woman dismissed by her husband commits adultery”—in the discourse which the Lord delivered on the mountain. I believe this is because the meaning could be considered already explained there in the preceding words, “he makes her commit adultery.” For how does the dismissed woman become an adulteress unless the man who marries her becomes an adulterer?

### CHAPTER XI

#### 12. Another passage in Matthew is somewhat obscure but is explained by the other Evangelists

The words that you yourself quoted, from which it seemed to you that the man who dismisses his wife because of the cause of fornication and marries another does not commit adultery, are indeed obscurely expressed. I am therefore not surprised that a reader has difficulty understanding them. But they do not occur in the Lord’s discourse which I was explaining when I wrote the books that disturbed you when you read them.

Elsewhere Matthew reports that the Lord said these words—not when he delivered that extended discourse on the mountain, but when the Pharisees asked him whether it was permitted to dismiss one’s wife for any cause. What is less clearly understood in Matthew can be understood from the other Evangelists.

Therefore, when we read in the Gospel according to Matthew, “Whoever dismisses his wife, unless for fornication,” or, as the Greek more clearly reads, “apart from the cause of fornication,” “and marries another commits adultery,” we must not immediately suppose that the man who dismisses his wife because of the cause of fornication and marries another does not commit adultery. We must remain in doubt until we consult the Gospels of the other Evangelists by whom this was reported.

For what if Matthew did not state everything relevant to this matter, but stated a part in such a way that the whole could be understood from the part, while Mark and Luke, explaining the matter and wishing the full meaning to be clear, preferred to state the whole?

When, therefore, we first accept without doubt as true what is read in Matthew—“Whoever dismisses his wife because of the cause of fornication and marries another commits adultery”—and then ask whether only the man who dismisses his first wife apart from the cause of fornication commits adultery by marrying another, or whether everyone who marries another after dismissing his wife does so, including the man who dismissed a fornicating wife, will not Mark answer us:

“Why do you ask whether one is an adulterer and another is not? Whoever dismisses his wife and marries another commits adultery.”

And will Luke not say to us:

“Why do you doubt whether the man who dismissed his wife because of the cause of fornication and married another commits adultery? Everyone who dismisses his wife and marries another commits adultery.”

Since it is not permissible for us to say that the Evangelists, although speaking of one matter in different words, disagree in meaning and in the same judgment, it remains that we understand Matthew to have intended to signify the whole by a part, while holding the same meaning: that we must have no doubt that everyone who dismisses his wife and marries another commits adultery.

### CHAPTER XII

[Col. 0459]

#### 13. A woman dismissed because of fornication does not cease to be the wife of the man who dismissed her

The following statement, which also occurs in Luke, must likewise be considered: “The man who marries a woman dismissed by her husband commits adultery.” How is this true? How does he commit adultery unless the woman he marries, while the man by whom she was dismissed is alive, remains another man’s wife?

For if she were now his own wife rather than another man’s, he would not be joining himself to another man’s wife and therefore would not commit adultery. But he does commit adultery; therefore, she is another man’s wife. If she is another man’s wife—that is, the wife of the man by whom she was dismissed—then, even if she was dismissed because of the cause of fornication, she has not yet ceased to be the wife of the man who dismissed her.

But if she has ceased to be his wife, she is now the wife of the man whom she subsequently married. And if she is his wife, he should not be judged an adulterer but a husband. Since Scripture does not call him a husband but an adulterer, she still belongs to the man by whom she was dismissed, even if she was dismissed because of the cause of fornication.

Consequently, any wife whom the dismissed woman herself takes is an adulteress, because she has intercourse with another woman’s husband. How, then, can he himself not also be an adulterer, when it is clear that the woman he married commits adultery?

### CHAPTER XIII

#### 14. Pollentius thinks that unbelieving spouses may not be dismissed; Augustine says that they may be dismissed, but that it is not expedient

Let us now examine what the Apostle says: “To the others I say—not the Lord.” He is speaking, of course, about unequal marriages, that is, marriages in which both spouses were not Christians.

It seemed to me that he said this as an admonition. Since a believing spouse could lawfully leave an unbelieving spouse, the Lord did not prohibit this; rather, the Apostle did. For whatever the Lord prohibits may not be done at all. The Apostle therefore admonishes them, so that he may provide an opportunity for the salvation of many, that believing spouses should not use the permission granted them to leave unbelieving spouses.

You, however, think that unbelievers may not be dismissed by believers because the Apostle forbids it. I say that it is permitted because the Lord does not forbid it, but that it is not expedient because the Apostle admonishes that it should not be done. He also gives the reason why it is not expedient, although it is permitted:

“What do you know, wife, whether you will save your husband? Or what do you know, husband, whether you will save your wife?”

He had also said above: “For the unbelieving husband is sanctified in the wife [Note: Col. 0459: The Louvain edition reads “in the believing wife”; “believing” is absent from the other editions and manuscripts.], and the unbelieving wife is sanctified in the brother,” that is, in the Christian; “otherwise your children would be unclean, but now they are holy” (1 Cor. 7:12–16).

In this way he appears to have encouraged the winning of spouses and children for Christ, even by examples that had already occurred. The reason why it is not expedient for believing spouses to dismiss unbelieving spouses is therefore clearly stated. The Apostle does not forbid separation from unbelieving spouses because the marital bond with such people must be preserved, but so that they may be won for Christ. [Note: Col. 0459: The Louvain edition reads “won to Christ.”]

### CHAPTER XIV

#### 15. Many things that are not commanded by law are to be done through the counsel of love

Many things are to be done not because the law commands them, but through free love. Those actions are more pleasing in the performance of our duties which, although we could lawfully refrain from them, we nevertheless undertake out of love.

Thus the Lord himself, after showing that he did not owe the temple tax, nevertheless paid it, lest he scandalize those whose eternal salvation he was seeking as one who had assumed human nature (Matt. 17:23–26).

The Apostle’s words testify to the way in which he commends this practice. He says:

“Although I am free from all, I made myself the slave of all, that I might win more.”

Shortly before this he had said:

“Do we not have the authority to eat and drink? Do we not have the right to lead about a sister as a wife, as do the other Apostles, and the brothers of the Lord, and Cephas? Or do only I and Barnabas not have the authority to do this? Who serves as a soldier at his own expense? Who plants a vineyard and does not eat of its fruit? Who tends a flock and does not partake of the milk of the flock?”

A little later he says:

“If others share in your authority, why not we even more? But we have not used this authority; rather, we endure everything, lest we cause any hindrance to the Gospel of Christ.”

Then, after a little more:

“What, then, will be my reward? That, in preaching the Gospel, I may present the Gospel without cost, so as not to make use of my authority in the Gospel” (1 Cor. 9:4–19).

Immediately afterward he adds what I mentioned shortly before:

“Although I am free from all, I made myself the slave of all, that I might win more.”

Elsewhere, concerning certain matters relating to food, he says:

“All things are lawful for me [Note: Col. 0460: “for me” is absent from the manuscripts here and in the following occurrence.], but not all things are expedient. All things are lawful for me, but I will not be brought under the power of anything. Foods are for the belly and the belly for foods, but God will bring both it and them to nothing” (1 Cor. 6:12–13).

Again, elsewhere on the same subject:

“All things are lawful for me, but not all things are expedient. All things are lawful for me, but not all things build up. Let no one seek his own advantage, but that of the other.”

And to show what he was speaking about, he says:

“Whatever is sold in the market, eat, asking no questions for the sake of conscience” (1 Cor. 10:22–25).

Yet elsewhere he says:

“I will never eat meat, so that I may not scandalize my brother” (1 Cor. 8:13).

And again elsewhere:

“Everything is clean, but it is evil for the person who eats through giving offense” (Rom. 14:20).

What is meant by “all things are lawful” is the same as “everything is clean”; and what is meant by “but not all things are expedient” is the same as “but it is evil for the person who eats through giving offense.”

Thus he shows that lawful things—that is, things not prohibited by any command of the Lord—are to be handled as expedient requires, not according to the constraint of law but according to the counsel of love.

These are the things that are given in addition to what is required to the wounded man who was brought to the inn to be cared for through the mercy of that Samaritan (Luke 10:33–35). They are therefore said not to be commanded by the Lord, although they are urged to be offered to the Lord [Note: Col. 0460: This is the manuscript reading; the printed editions read “by the Lord,” less well.], so that they may be understood to be more pleasing precisely because they are shown to be beyond what is owed.

### CHAPTER XV

#### 16. Certain things are lawful but not expedient

In matters of this kind, however, where something is lawful but not expedient, one cannot say, “This is good, but that is better,” as it is said: “He who gives in marriage does well, and he who does not give in marriage does better” (1 Cor. 7:38).

There, both alternatives are lawful, and sometimes one is expedient, sometimes the other. For women who do not exercise self-control are certainly better off marrying; what is lawful for them is also expedient. But those who have vowed continence may neither marry nor find it expedient to marry.

To leave an unbelieving spouse is permitted, but it is not expedient. To remain with that spouse, if he or she consents to live together, is both permitted and expedient; for if it were not permitted, it could not be expedient.

Something, then, may be permitted and yet not be expedient; but what is not permitted cannot be expedient. Accordingly, not everything permitted is expedient, but nothing forbidden is expedient.

Just as everyone redeemed by Christ’s blood is a human being, but not every human being has been redeemed by Christ’s blood, so everything that is not permitted is not expedient, but not everything that is not expedient is thereby forbidden. There are, as we have learned from the Apostle’s testimony, things that are permitted but not expedient.

### CHAPTER XVI

#### 17. What is lawful but not expedient differs from what is unlawful, so that doing the former is not sin, although it ought not to be done

It is difficult to define by any universal rule the difference between what is unlawful and therefore not expedient, and what is lawful but nevertheless not expedient.

Someone might more readily say: “Everything that is not expedient to do is sin; every sin is unlawful; therefore everything that is not expedient is unlawful.”

But where would those things be which the Apostle said are lawful but not expedient, if everything that is not expedient were unlawful? Since we cannot doubt that the Apostle spoke truly, and since we do not dare to say that some sins are lawful, it remains for us to say that something may be done which is not expedient and yet, if it is lawful, is not sin [Note: Col. 0461: The Louvain edition reads, “and yet it is lawful, nor is it sin.”]—although, because it is not expedient, it certainly ought not to be done.

If it seems absurd that something should be done which is not expedient and that the person who does it should be said not to have sinned, we must understand that this seems absurd because of ordinary usage. That usage is so broad that we often say even that beasts of burden, although they lack reason, ought to be beaten when they “sin.” Strictly speaking, however, only one who uses the rational freedom of the will can sin; and among all mortal animals, this has been divinely attributed only to the human being.

One matter arises when we speak properly, and another when we transfer or misuse words borrowed from other things. [Note: Col. 0461: The Louvain edition alone reads “we change” instead of “we borrow.”]

### CHAPTER XVII

#### 18. How what is permitted but not expedient differs from what is not expedient because it is not permitted

Christ neither forbids nor commands the dismissal of an unbelieving spouse; Paul admonishes that it should not be done.
