Therefore, if we can, let us strive to distinguish by some definite limit between what is permitted but not expedient and what is not permitted and therefore not expedient.

It seems to me that those things are permitted but not expedient which are allowed by the justice that stands before God, but which ought to be avoided because of the offense they may cause human beings, lest they be hindered from salvation on that account.

Those things, however, are not permitted and therefore not expedient which justice itself forbids in such a way that they ought not to be done, even if they are praised by those to whose knowledge they have come.

If this is so, the Lord prohibits only what is unlawful, so that things which are lawful but not expedient may be avoided not through the bond of law but through the free beneficence of love.

#### 19.

Accordingly, if it were not permitted to dismiss an unbelieving spouse, the Lord would prohibit this, and the Apostle would not say, while prohibiting it, “I say, not the Lord” (1 Cor. 7:12).

For if a person is permitted to separate from a spouse because of fornication of the flesh, how much more must fornication of the mind in a spouse be detested—that is, unbelief? [Note: Col. 0462: The manuscripts read “of unbelief.”] Concerning this it is written: “For behold, those who distance themselves from you will perish; you have destroyed everyone who fornicates away from you” (Ps. 72:27).

### CHAPTER XVIII

#### Why the Israelites were commanded to abandon foreign wives, whereas Christians are not similarly commanded to abandon unbelieving spouses. Paul’s counsel is to be accepted as Christ’s counsel. What is permitted is sometimes expedient and sometimes not. Separation from an unbelieving spouse is not prohibited by a legal command but discouraged by the counsel of love

Since dismissal is permitted in such a way that it is not expedient, the Apostle intervenes and, by admonition, forbids what is permitted but not expedient, lest people, offended by the separation of spouses, come to loathe the very teaching of salvation by which unlawful acts are prohibited, and thus remain in the same unbelief, becoming worse and perishing.

Thus believing men and women are not prohibited by the Lord from separating from unbelieving wives or husbands, but neither are they commanded to do so. For if they were commanded to dismiss such spouses, there would be no place for the Apostle’s counsel admonishing that this should not be done. For in no way would a good servant forbid what the Lord commands.

20. For the Lord once commanded this through the prophet Ezra, and it was done: the Israelites dismissed their foreign wives, whoever at that time was able to do so (1 Esdras 10:11–12). Through these wives it was happening that the Israelites themselves were being led astray to foreign gods, rather than that those women were being won for God through their husbands. For the Savior’s grace had not yet shone forth so abundantly, and the multitude of that people was still eagerly awaiting the temporal promises of the Old Testament. Therefore, when they saw that those who worshiped many false gods also abounded in the earthly goods which they awaited from the Lord as something great, they first feared to offend them because of their wives’ flatteries, and then were induced to worship those gods as well. Hence the Lord had commanded through holy Moses that no one should marry a foreign woman (Deut. 7:3). With good reason, therefore, they dismissed, at the Lord’s command, those whom they had married against the Lord’s prohibition.

But when the Gospel began to be preached to the Gentiles, the Apostle found Gentiles already married to Gentiles. If both did not believe, but one—the unbelieving husband or wife—consented to live with the believing spouse, the believer neither ought to have been forbidden by the Lord to dismiss the unbeliever, nor commanded to do so. The reason why the believer was not forbidden was that justice permits one to depart from a fornicator, and the fornication of an unbelieving person is greater in the heart; nor can that person’s chastity truly be called chastity in relation to the spouse, since “everything that is not from faith is sin” (Rom. 14:23). Nevertheless, a believer possesses true chastity even with an unbelieving spouse, who does not possess it. The reason why believers were not commanded to separate from unbelievers was that the Gentiles had not been joined in marriage against the Lord’s command.

21. Since, then, the Lord neither forbids nor commands a believer to depart from an unbeliever, the Apostle—not the Lord—says that the believer should not depart, possessing, of course, the Holy Spirit, through whom he could give useful and faithful counsel. Thus, after saying of a woman whose husband had died, “But she will be happier if she remains as she is, according to my counsel,” he added, lest anyone should think this counsel merely human, rather than divine and therefore to be disregarded: “But I think that I also have the Spirit of God.” Accordingly, we must understand that even those things which are not commanded by the Lord but are usefully urged by his holy servant are urged under the inspiration of that same Lord. Far be it from any Catholic to say that, when the Holy Spirit gives counsel, the Lord is not giving counsel—since the Holy Spirit is himself the Lord, and the works of the Trinity are inseparable.

Yet Paul says, “Concerning virgins I have no command of the Lord, but I give counsel.” This does not mean that we should regard the counsel as foreign to the Lord, since he immediately continues: “as one who has obtained mercy from the Lord to be faithful” (1 Cor. 7:40, 25). Therefore, he gives faithful counsel according to God, in the Spirit of whom he says, “But I think that I also have the Spirit of God.”

22. Nevertheless, the command of the Lord who gives orders is one thing; the faithful counsel of a fellow servant, given according to the mercy of charity which has been inspired and bestowed upon him by the Lord, is another. In the former case it is not permitted to act otherwise; in the latter it is permitted—though in such a way that what is permitted is sometimes advantageous and sometimes not advantageous.

It is advantageous when not only is it permitted by the justice that stands before the Lord, but no obstacle to salvation is thereby imposed upon human beings. For example, when the Apostle gives a virgin the counsel not to marry, thereby declaring that he does not have a command of the Lord, it is permitted to do otherwise—that is, to marry—and to embrace the good of marriage, which is inferior to continence. What is permitted is also advantageous in itself, since it thus receives the weakness of the flesh, which would otherwise rush into what is forbidden and unlawful, by the honorable provision of marriage, without hindering anyone’s salvation. Yet it would be more advantageous and more honorable if the virgin accepted the counsel which does not compel her, since the command does not compel her either.

What is permitted is not advantageous when it is indeed allowed, but the exercise of that permission can impede the salvation of others. Such is the matter about which we have been speaking for a long time: the departure of a believing spouse from an unbeliever. The Lord does not forbid this by a command of the law, since it is not unjust before him; but the Apostle forbids it by the counsel of charity, because it creates an obstacle to the salvation of unbelievers—not only because they are most dangerously scandalized and offended, but also because, when they enter into other marriages while the spouses from whom they were dismissed are still alive, they become bound by adulterous unions from which it is exceedingly difficult to be released.

[Note: [Col. 0463] Several manuscripts read: “from unbelief they are exceedingly difficult to release.” Other manuscripts of better authority agree with the printed editions.]

## CHAPTER XIX

23. The counsel not to marry concerns what is more advantageous; the counsel not to dismiss an unbeliever concerns what is not advantageous if done otherwise. Therefore, where what is permitted is not advantageous, one cannot say, “If he dismisses the unbeliever, he does well; if he does not dismiss her, he does better,” as it is said, “He who gives a virgin in marriage does well; and he who does not give her in marriage does better.”

For in that case both alternatives are equally permitted—hence no one is compelled to either by the Lord’s command—and both are also advantageous, one less so and the other more so. Therefore, by the Apostle’s counsel, whoever is able to accept it is urged toward what is more advantageous.

But where the question concerns dismissing or not dismissing an unbelieving spouse, both alternatives are equally lawful according to the justice that stands before the Lord, and therefore the Lord forbids neither. Yet both are not equally advantageous, because of human weaknesses; and therefore the Apostle forbids what is not advantageous. The Lord gives him room to forbid it, since the Lord neither forbids what the Apostle counsels, nor commands what the Apostle forbids. If this were not so, the Apostle would neither counsel anything against the Lord’s prohibition nor forbid anything against his command.

Accordingly, in these two matters—one concerning marrying or not marrying, the other concerning dismissing or not dismissing an unbelieving spouse—there is something similar and something dissimilar in the Apostle’s words. The similarity is that in both cases he says, “I have no command of the Lord, but I give counsel,” and here he says, “I say, not the Lord.” “I have no command of the Lord” is equivalent to “The Lord does not say”; and “I give counsel” is equivalent to “I say.”

The dissimilarity is that concerning marrying or not marrying one may say, “This is done well; that is done better,” because both are advantageous, one less and the other more. But concerning dismissing or not dismissing an unbelieving spouse, since one of these alternatives is not advantageous and the other is, one ought not to say, “He who dismisses does well; he who does not dismiss does better.” Rather, one ought to say, “Let him not dismiss her,” because although it is permitted, it is not advantageous.

Thus we may say that it is better not to dismiss an unbelieving spouse, although it is permitted to dismiss her, just as we rightly say that what is both permitted and advantageous is better than what is permitted but not advantageous.

## CHAPTER XX

24. The Apostle’s counsel concerning not dismissing unbelieving spouses is not a command. A warning here concerns a matter left free; the Apostle’s other admonitions concern matters commanded. For these reasons, when explaining the Lord’s sermon—the lengthy sermon he delivered on the mountain—I said, when I reached the question of dismissing or not dismissing spouses, and had also introduced apostolic testimonies, that the Apostle’s words were counsel, not the Lord’s command, where he says, “To the rest I say, not the Lord,” admonishing those who had unbelieving spouses not to dismiss them if they consented to live with them.

This had to be admonished rather than commanded because people should not be prohibited from doing what is lawful, even if it is not advantageous, with as much force as they are prohibited from doing what is unlawful. If the Apostle has sometimes deigned to admonish even matters that ought to be commanded, he did so out of consideration for weakness, not by prejudicing the command.

[Note: [Col. 0465] Two manuscripts read *parendo* (“by obeying”) instead of *parcendo* (“by sparing”).]

Thus, when he says, “I write these things not to shame you, but to admonish you as my most beloved children” (1 Cor. 4:14), what difficulty is there in the statement, “I say, not the Lord”? Likewise, when he says, “Behold, I, Paul, say to you that if you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing” (Gal. 5:2), did he also say here, “I say, not the Lord”? These matters are therefore not alike, because it is neither unworthy nor contrary for the Apostle to admonish the very things that the Lord commands. We admonish those whom we love to carry out the Lord’s precepts and commands. But when he says, “I say, not the Lord,” he sufficiently shows that the Lord does not forbid what he himself was forbidding. The Lord would have forbidden it if it were unlawful. Therefore, in accordance with what we discussed and examined at length above, it was lawful according to justice, but even though lawful, it was not to be done because of free benevolence.

## CHAPTER XXI

25. Pollentius’s position concerning marriages with unbelievers is examined. The question concerning those already married differs from that concerning those who are to be married. The Apostle’s cited passage concerns those already married, not those who are to marry. You, however, who wish it to be the case that what the Lord does not forbid but the Apostle does is unlawful, just as what the Lord forbids is unlawful, attempted to explain the meaning of the words, “I say, not the Lord,” when he was addressing believers who had unbelieving spouses. You said:

> “Because the Lord commanded that marriages between people of different religions should not be joined.”

You also brought forward the Lord’s testimony:

> “You shall not take a wife for your son from the daughters of foreigners, lest she lead him after her gods and his soul perish” (Deut. 7:3–4).

You added the Apostle’s words:

> “A woman is bound as long as her husband lives. But if her husband has died, she is free: let her marry whom she wishes, only in the Lord” (1 Cor. 7:39),

which you explained by adding:

> “That is, to a Christian.”

[Note: [Col. 0465] The Louvain edition alone reads, “and that to a Christian.”]

Then you continued:

> “This, therefore, is the Lord’s command, in both the Old and the New Testament: that marriages should remain joined only when the spouses share one religion and one faith.”

If this, then, is the Lord’s command in both the Old and the New Testament, and if the Lord commands this and the Apostle teaches it—that marriages should remain joined only when the spouses share one religion and one faith—why does the Apostle, against this command of the Lord, against his own teaching, and against the command of both the Old and the New Testament, command that marriages between people of different faiths should remain joined?

You reply:

> “Because Paul, preacher and apostle to the Gentiles, not only admonishes those already married, but also commands that if one husband or wife has come to believe while the other has not, the believer should not dismiss the unbeliever who consents to continue living with the believer.”

By these words of yours you clearly show that this matter and that matter are different. The one concerns marriages which are being contracted for the first time, so that a woman should not marry a man of another religion, nor a man marry such a woman.

> “For this,” you say, “God commands, the Apostle teaches, and both Testaments prescribe.”

Who, then, would deny that this matter is different, since it concerns not those who are to be joined, but those already joined? When they were joined, both belonged to one and the same unbelief. But when the Gospel came, one believed without the other, or the other without the one.

If this is a different matter—as plainly appears beyond any doubt—why does the Lord not command, just as the Apostle does, that a believer remain married to an unbeliever? Unless perhaps the statement which he makes so confidently is useless here: “Do you want to receive proof of Christ speaking in me?” (2 Cor. 13:3). And Christ is certainly the Lord.

Do you understand what I am saying? Or should I spend somewhat more time explaining it?

26. Attend, then, while we set the matter itself before our eyes in plainer speech. Here are two spouses belonging to one unbelief; they were like this when they were joined. No question concerning them pertains to that command of the Lord, to the apostolic teaching, or to the precept of the Old and New Testaments by which a believer is forbidden to enter into marriage with an unbeliever.

They are already spouses, and both are still unbelievers; they are still such as they were before they were joined, and such as they were when they were joined. A preacher of the Gospel arrives, and either the husband or the wife believes—but in such a way that the unbeliever consents to live with the believer.

Does the Lord command the believer not to dismiss the unbeliever, or does he not command this? If you say, “He commands it,” the Apostle objects: “I say, not the Lord.” If you say, “He does not command it,” I ask for the reason. You will not answer me with the reason which you included in your letter:

> “Because the Lord forbids believers to be joined to unbelievers.”

Here that cannot possibly be the reason, since we are speaking of those already joined, not of those who are to be joined.

If, then, you have not found the reason why the Lord does not forbid what the Apostle forbids—for by now, I think, you see that it is not the reason you had supposed—consider whether the reason might be the one that occurred to me, and which must now be brought forward and defended: namely, that we should understand the Lord to say that which justice, standing before him, in no way permits us to transgress. That is, he commands or forbids in such a way that it is altogether unlawful to do otherwise. But where he so leaves a matter to the will’s power that neither doing nor omitting it is unlawful, he also gives place to the counsel of his servants, so that they may advise what they see to be advantageous.

27. Let this therefore be held first and above all: unlawful acts must not be committed. But where something is permitted in such a way that doing something else would not be unlawful, let what is advantageous—or what is more advantageous—be done.

Therefore, where the Lord speaks as Lord—that is, not with the counsel of one giving advice, but with the command of one exercising authority—not to do what he commands is impermissible, and consequently it is not advantageous either.

[Note: [Col. 0466] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read “to do is not permitted,” omitting *non* before “to do.”]

Thus the Lord commands that a woman should not depart from her husband; and if she departs, for the very reason on account of which departure is permitted, she must remain unmarried or be reconciled to her husband (1 Cor. 7:10–11). For a woman is joined under the law to her husband while her husband lives, and while her husband lives she will be called an adulteress if she is with another man (Rom. 7:2–3), because “a woman is bound as long as her husband lives” (1 Cor. 7:39).

Hence, “If a wife dismisses her husband and marries another, she commits adultery” (Mark 10:12); and, “He who marries a woman dismissed by her husband commits adultery” (Matt. 19:9). For the same reason the Lord’s command also says, “And a husband must not dismiss his wife” (1 Cor. 7:11), because “he who dismisses his wife except on account of fornication makes her commit adultery” (Matt. 5:32). But if he dismisses her for this reason, he too must remain as he is:

> “For everyone who dismisses his wife and marries another commits adultery” (Luke 16:18).

## CHAPTER XXII

A man who dismisses an adulterous wife and marries another in order to make her a Christian commits adultery. These commands of the Lord must be observed without any reconsideration. For they contain the justice that stands before him, whether people approve or disapprove. Therefore one must not say, on account of people’s offenses, or lest people be hindered from the salvation that is in Christ, that these commands should not be observed.

[Note: [Col. 0467] The Louvain edition alone reads “should not be observed” in the singular.]

For what Christian would dare say, “So that I may not offend people, or so that I may win people for Christ, I will make my wife commit adultery, or I myself will become an adulterer”?

28. It can happen that, after a Christian has dismissed an adulterous wife, he is tempted by a woman who has not yet believed. Desiring to marry him, she promises that she will become a Christian—not deceitfully, but with the intention of doing so if she marries him.

To the man refusing this marriage, the tempter may suggest:

> “The Lord said, ‘Whoever dismisses his wife except on account of fornication and marries another commits adultery.’ But you dismissed your wife on account of fornication; if you marry another, you will not commit adultery.”

To this tempter, the man should reply with an instructed heart that the man who dismisses his wife for any reason other than fornication and marries another certainly commits the more serious adultery, but that the man who dismisses a fornicating wife and joins another woman to himself is not thereby free from adultery merely because he left the fornicator.

In the same way, the man who marries a woman dismissed for a reason other than fornication commits adultery; nor is the man who marries a woman whom he found dismissed on account of fornication thereby free from adultery.

For this reason, what is stated somewhat obscurely in Matthew—because the whole is signified by a part—has been explained in the other Evangelists, who expressed the whole generally.

[Note: [Col. 0467] The manuscripts read “because”; the printed editions read “how.” The Lyons and Venice editions read “has been explained” rather than “to have been explained.”] Thus we read in Mark:

> “Whoever dismisses his wife and marries another commits adultery.”

And in Luke:

> “Everyone who dismisses his wife and marries another commits adultery.”

They did not say that some men commit adultery and others do not when, after dismissing their wives, they marry other women. Rather, by saying “whoever dismisses,” they declared without any exception that absolutely everyone who dismisses his wife and marries another commits adultery.

## CHAPTER XXIII

29. It is not lawful to enter into an adulterous marriage in order to make a woman a Christian. But if the Christian man should answer the tempter, understanding that he was indeed permitted to dismiss an adulterous wife but not permitted to marry another, what if the tempter says:

> “Commit this sin in order to win a soul for Christ—the soul of a woman who is still in the death of unbelief and who is prepared, if she marries you, to become a Christian”?

What else should the Christian answer and say except that, if he does this, he cannot escape the judgment mentioned by the Apostle when he says:

> “And just as some claim that we say, ‘Let us do evil so that good may come’; their condemnation is just” (Rom. 3:8)?

But how could a woman be a Christian in a saving manner if she will be an adulteress with the man who marries her?

## CHAPTER XXIV

30. A vow of continence must not be broken for any hope of compensation. It is not only that the act committed by the man who dismisses his wife and marries another is adultery—not merely in some cases, but in every case—even if he marries her in order to make her a Christian. Whoever, while not bound to a wife, has vowed continence to God must likewise in no way commit this sin in expectation of such compensation, believing that he ought to marry a woman because she has promised that she will become a Christian if she obtains the marriage she desires.

What was permitted to someone before he made a vow will not be permitted after he has vowed never to do it—provided that he vowed what ought to have been vowed, such as perpetual virginity; or continence after an experienced marriage, once the person has been released from the marital bond; or continence vowed by mutual consent when faithful and chaste spouses release one another from their bodily obligations. Neither spouse may lawfully make such a vow without the other.

Therefore, when people have vowed these things, and any others which are rightly vowed, the vows must not be broken under any condition, since they were made without any condition. For we must understand that the Lord also commanded this, where it is written:

> “Make vows and fulfill them to the Lord your God” (Ps. 75:12).

Hence, concerning certain women who vow continence and afterward wish to marry—although marriage was certainly permitted to them before they made the vow—the Apostle says:

> “They have condemnation, because they have rejected their first faith” (1 Tim. 5:12).

31. Nothing that is unlawful is advantageous, and nothing that the Lord forbids is lawful.

## CHAPTER XXV

The Apostle’s counsel concerning matters that are not commanded must be heeded. The question concerning marriages is exceedingly difficult. Another question raised by Pollentius. In matters which have been left within our power because no command of the Lord binds us, the Apostle should be heard as he admonishes and counsels in the Holy Spirit, so that either better things may be chosen or things that are not advantageous may be avoided.

There he should be heard saying, “I have no command of the Lord, but I give counsel,” and, “I say, not the Lord.” There, if the hearer chooses the better course—“He who is released from a wife, let him not seek a wife,” because even if he takes a wife he does not sin—there the virgin should not marry. For “he who does not give a virgin in marriage does better, and he who gives her in marriage does well.”

There the woman will be happier by remaining as she is. After her husband’s death, she has the power to marry whom she wishes, only in the Lord. This can be understood in two ways: either that she remains a Christian, or that she marries a Christian.

I do not recall that, during the time of the revealed New Testament, it was declared without ambiguity in the Gospel or in any apostolic Letter whether the Lord prohibited believers from joining themselves in marriage to unbelievers. Although the most blessed Cyprian has no doubt about this, and does not place it among minor sins: he says that joining a marriage bond with unbelievers is prostituting the members of Christ to the Gentiles.

[Note: [Col. 0469] Cyprian, *On the Lapsed*.]

But because the question concerning those already joined is different, let the Apostle also be heard here saying:

> “If any brother has an unbelieving wife and she consents to live with him, let him not dismiss her; and if any woman has an unbelieving husband and he consents to live with her, let her not dismiss her husband” (1 Cor. 7:12–13, 25, 27, 38–39).

Let him be heard in such a way that, although the action is lawful because the Lord does not say otherwise, it should nevertheless not be done because it is not advantageous. For the Apostle teaches most plainly that not everything lawful is advantageous (1 Cor. 10:22), as we have already shown above.

Nevertheless, on account of every kind of fornication—whether of the flesh or of the spirit, in which unbelief is also understood—after dismissing a husband it is not lawful for a woman to marry another, nor after dismissing a wife is it lawful for a man to marry another. For the Lord says without making any exception:

> “If a wife dismisses her husband and marries another, she commits adultery,”

and:

> “Everyone who dismisses his wife and marries another commits adultery.”

32. Although I have treated and examined these matters as far as my ability permits, I do not fail to recognize that the question concerning marriages is exceedingly obscure and complicated. Nor do I dare to claim that I have yet explained all its recesses, either in this work or in another, or that I could explain them now if pressed.

As for the matter about which you likewise thought I should be consulted in another document, I would also have taken care to unravel it separately if my view had differed from yours. But since our opinion is the same, there is no need to argue about it at greater length.

## CHAPTER XXVI

33. Whether Baptism should be given at the end of life to catechumens who do not request it and cannot answer on their own behalf. The opinion of certain people who deny this is rejected, though they are not condemned. Therefore, if catechumens who are at the end of this life have been so overwhelmed by illness or some accident that, although they are still alive, they cannot request Baptism for themselves or answer the questions put to them, let the fact that their desire for the Christian faith is already known benefit them, so that they may be baptized in the same manner as infants, whose will has not yet become manifest.

[Note: [Col. 0469] See *Confessions*, book 4, chapter 4, §8.]

Nevertheless, we ought not for this reason to condemn those who act more cautiously than we think they should act, lest we be judged to have wished to assess more harshly than carefully the money entrusted to a fellow servant. In such matters we must sufficiently attend to the Apostle’s statement:

> “Each of us will give an account of himself to God” (Rom. 14:12).

Therefore, let us no longer judge one another.

There are some who think that, in this matter and even in others, we must observe what the Lord is recorded as saying:

> “Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor throw your pearls before swine” (Matt. 7:6).

Referring to these words of the Savior, they do not dare

[Note: [Col. 0470] Several manuscripts read “revering” instead of “referring to.”]

to baptize to baptize those who are unable to answer on their own behalf, lest they perhaps be acting contrary to the will of the person concerned. This cannot be said of little children, in whom there is as yet no use of reason.

But it is altogether incredible that a catechumen should not wish to be baptized at the end of this life; indeed, even if his will is uncertain, it is much better to give Baptism to one who may not want it than to deny it to one who may want it, when it is not apparent whether he wants it or not, but it is nevertheless more credible that, if he could, he would have said that he wished to receive those Sacraments without which he had already believed he ought not to depart from the body.

## CHAPTER XXVII

34. How the Lord’s saying, “Let what is holy not be given to dogs,” is to be understood. If, when the Lord said, “Do not give what is holy to dogs,” he intended the precaution which these people think should be understood, then he himself would not have given to his betrayer what that man, to his own destruction, received—without fault on the giver’s part—although he was unworthy to receive it.

Therefore, when the Lord said this, we should believe that he intended to signify that unclean hearts cannot bear the light of spiritual understanding. If a teacher thrusts upon them things that they do not rightly receive because they cannot comprehend them, they either tear them apart with the bites of criticism or trample them underfoot by despising them.

For if the blessed Apostle says that, although they had already been reborn in Christ, he gave even the little ones milk rather than solid food—“For you were not yet able,” he says, “and even now you are not able” (1 Cor. 3:2)—and if the Lord himself finally said to his chosen Apostles, “I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now” (John 16:12), how much less can the impure minds of the ungodly bear whatever is said concerning incorporeal light?

## CHAPTER XXVIII

35. In the case proposed, Baptism should also be given to catechumens who continue in adulterous unions. The same principle applies to granting reconciliation to penitents in danger of death. But so that our discussion may return to the point from which it began, I do not admit to Baptism while bodily healthy not only other catechumens, but even those who, while their spouses are still alive, retain adulterous unions. Nevertheless, if they lie in a hopeless condition and cannot answer on their own behalf, I think they should be baptized, so that this sin too may be washed away with the others in the bath of regeneration.

For who knows whether perhaps they had resolved to remain in the enticement of adulterous flesh until Baptism? But if, restored from that hopeless condition, they are able to live, they will either do what they had resolved, or, once instructed, they will obey, or what ought to be done even with such baptized persons will be done in their case as despisers.

[Note: [Col. 0470] In the printed editions the words *in his permanentes* (“remaining in these”) had been added unnecessarily; likewise, after *tamen si desperati* (“nevertheless, if they lie in a hopeless condition”), the words *et intra se poenitentes* (“and repenting within themselves”) were found. We have removed these words on the authority of the older books.]

The reason for reconciliation is the same as the reason for Baptism, if the danger of death should overtake a penitent before his life is ended. For Mother Church ought not to wish even such people to depart from this life without the pledge of their peace.

# BOOK TWO

[Col. 0471]

Pollentius is refuted for thinking that marriage is dissolved by adultery just as by death, and for applying to this the Apostle’s statement to the Corinthians, “But if her husband has died, she is free,” so that he wishes “dead” in this passage also to mean an adulterer. His remaining arguments are then dismantled, and the various difficulties which he fears would arise if a husband were not permitted to marry another woman after repudiating an adulterous wife are refuted.

## CHAPTER I

1. The occasion of this book. I had already written a fairly substantial volume in reply to what you had written to me, my religious brother Pollentius, concerning those who join themselves to other spouses while their own spouses are still alive. When this became known to Your Affection, you added some material to your little book, wishing me to answer these matters as well. I intended to do so by adding to my own work, so that it would be a single book containing my reply. But suddenly the work I had already completed was published, because the brothers were demanding it and our own people did not know that anything still remained to be added.

[Note: [Col. 0471] The printed editions read, “because our brothers were demanding it and our people did not know.” But the manuscripts place *nostris* after *et nescientibus*, so that by *nostris* they understand household members and companions, while by *fratribus flagitantibus* they understand outsiders.]

Thus it happened that I was compelled to respond to what you had added in a separate little work. The material you added was not attached to the end of your little book; rather, wherever it seemed appropriate, it was inserted into its body.

## CHAPTER II

2. Pollentius’s position: a wife is forbidden to marry another if she has separated from a husband who was not a fornicator, but not if she has separated from a fornicator. He thinks that “dead” in Paul’s passage should also be understood to mean “fornicating.” The first of your claims, to which I think I ought to respond, is this: in the Apostle’s words where he says, “To the rest I say, not the Lord: a woman should not depart from her husband; but if she departs, she should remain unmarried or be reconciled to her husband,” you do not think that “if she departs” means that she has departed from a fornicating husband—the only reason for which departure is permitted. Rather, you think that she has departed from a chaste husband and is therefore commanded to remain unmarried, so that she might be reconciled to him if he should be unwilling to remain continent, lest, by refusing reconciliation, she compel her husband to commit fornication—that is, to marry another while she is alive.

But if she has departed from a fornicating husband, you think that she is not commanded to remain unmarried. Rather, she may do this if she wishes to remain continent; she will not be found to be a violator of the command if she marries.

You think that the same arrangement must be observed by the husband: he should not dismiss his wife except on account of fornication; but if he dismisses her, he should remain without a marriage, so that he may be reconciled to his chaste wife, unless she perhaps chooses continence. Otherwise, by refusing reconciliation with his chaste wife, he would compel her to commit adultery if, unable to remain continent while he was alive, she married another.

But if he has separated from a fornicating wife, you think that he is no longer held by any command to remain continent, and that he does not commit adultery if, while she is alive, he marries another. For you think that the Apostle’s statement, “A woman is bound as long as her husband lives; but if her husband has died, she is free; let her marry whom she wishes” (1 Cor. 7:10–11, 39), should be understood in such a way that, if the husband has committed fornication, he is counted as dead, and the wife as dead; and therefore either of them may join themselves to another, as after the death of a spouse, so after the spouse’s fornication.

## CHAPTER III

3. Pollentius is refuted. Having considered these views of yours, I ask whether you regard as an adulterer anyone who marries a woman who has ceased to be bound to her husband. I think you do not regard him as such. For this is why a woman will be called an adulteress, if, while her husband is alive, she is with another man: because she is bound as long as her husband lives.

If this bond did not exist for her while her husband was alive, she could marry another without any charge of adultery. Therefore, if she is bound as long as her husband lives, she can in no way be said to be released from this bond except by her husband’s death.

Moreover, if this bond between husband and wife is dissolved by the death of either one, and fornication too is to be regarded as equivalent to death, as you say, then the woman will certainly be released from this bond when she has committed fornication. For it could not be said that she remained bound to her husband when the husband had been released from her.

Consequently, after she has ceased to be bound to her husband by committing fornication, whoever marries her will not be an adulterer.

## CHAPTER IV

How absurd it is to regard fornication as dissolving the marital bond as death does. Consider how absurd it is that he should not be an adulterer merely because he has married an adulterous woman. Indeed, what is more monstrous, the woman herself will not be an adulteress either, since she will not be another man’s wife but her later husband’s own wife.

For once the first marital bond has been dissolved by adultery, then, whoever she marries, if he has no wife, she will be a wife with a husband, not an adulteress with an adulterer.

How, then, will the statement be true, “A woman is bound as long as her husband lives”? Behold, her husband is alive, since he has neither departed from the body nor committed fornication—which you wish to count as death—and yet the woman is no longer bound to him.

Do you not see how contrary this is to the Apostle, who says, “A woman is bound as long as her husband lives”? Or perhaps you will say: “He is indeed alive, but he is no longer her husband, because he ceased to be her husband when she dissolved the marital bond through adultery.”

How, then, will she be called an adulteress, if, while her husband is alive, she is with another man, when that man is no longer her husband because the marital bond has already been dissolved through the woman’s adultery? For while which husband, unless her own, will she be called an adulteress if she is with another man?

But if he has ceased to be her husband, she certainly will not be called an adulteress while her husband is alive if she is with another man. Rather, having no husband, she will marry and be with her own husband.

Do you not see that anyone who thinks this thinks contrary to the Apostle? You yourself do not hold this view, but it follows from what you do hold. Change the premises, therefore, if you wish to avoid the consequences, and do not say that in this passage a fornicating husband or wife ought also to be understood as dead.

[Col. 0473] 4. Therefore, according to sound teaching, “A woman is bound as long as her husband lives”—that is, until he has departed from the body. For a woman is joined under the law to her husband while her husband lives; that is, while he remains in the body.

But if her husband has died—that is, departed from the body—she has been released from the law of her husband. Accordingly, while her husband lives, she will be called an adulteress if she is with another man. But if her husband has died, she is released from the law [Note: [Col. 0473] The printed editions read, “she is released from the law of her husband.” The word *viri* (“of her husband”) is not repeated here in the manuscripts], so that she is not an adulteress if she is with another man (Rom. 7:2–3).

These words of the Apostle, repeated and impressed upon us so many times, are true, living, sound, and plain. A woman does not begin to be the wife of a later husband unless she has ceased to be the wife of the first. She ceases to be the first husband’s wife if her husband dies, not if he commits fornication.

A spouse may therefore lawfully be dismissed on account of fornication; but the bond with the first spouse remains. For that reason, the man who marries a dismissed woman is guilty of adultery, even when she was dismissed on account of fornication.

## CHAPTER V
The bond of marriage is dissolved by death, but not by fornication and the separation of spouses. For just as, while the sacrament of regeneration remains in force, someone guilty of a crime is excommunicated and does not lose that sacrament even if he is never reconciled to God, so, while the bond of the marital covenant remains in force, a wife is dismissed on account of fornication and does not lose that bond even if she is never reconciled to her husband; she does lose it, however, if her husband has died. The excommunicated guilty person, moreover, will never lose the sacrament of regeneration—even if unreconciled—because God never dies.

It remains, therefore, that, if we wish to think according to the Apostle, we must not say that an adulterous husband is to be reckoned as dead, and that therefore his wife may marry another. For although adultery is a kind of death—not of the body, but, what is worse, of the soul—the Apostle was not speaking of this death when he said, [Note: [Col. 0473] Thus the manuscript codices. But the printed editions read: “he was not, however, speaking of this death.”] “But if her husband has died, let her marry whom she wishes”; he was speaking only of that death by which one departs from the body. For if the marital bond is dissolved by the adultery of a spouse, the following perversity results—the very perversity I have shown must be avoided: a woman, too, would be released from this bond through sexual immorality. If she is released, she will be free from the law of her husband; and therefore, as is most foolishly said, “she will not be an adulteress if she is with another man,” because she has been freed from her former husband through adultery.

But if this is so far removed from the truth that no human mind—not to say Christian—can accept it, then surely a woman is bound as long as her husband lives; or, to put it more plainly, as long as her husband is in the body. By the same principle, therefore, a husband is bound as long as his wife is in the body. Thus, if he wishes to dismiss an adulterous wife, he must not marry another, lest he himself commit what he condemns in her. Likewise, if a wife dismisses an adulterous husband, she must not join herself to another: she is bound as long as her husband lives, and she is freed from the law of her husband only when he has died, so that she is not an adulteress if she is with another man.

## CHAPTER VI

### 5. How fitting it is for a Christian that spouses should be reconciled after adultery when the offending spouse has repented

[Col. 0474] But what seems harsh to you—that after adultery one spouse should be reconciled to the other—will not be harsh if faith is present. For why do we still count as adulterers those whom we believe to have been cleansed by Baptism or healed through repentance? Under the old law of God these crimes were cleansed by no sacrifices; under the blood of the New Testament they are cleansed without question.

[Note: This is how Erasmus’s edition reads, agreeing here with most of our manuscripts and the better ones. But Lovaniensis has: “which are cleansed without question in the blood of the New Testament of Christ.”]

For that reason, at that time it was altogether forbidden to take back a wife who had been defiled by another man. Yet David, as a foreshadower of the New Testament, accepted without hesitation Saul’s daughter, whom her father had separated from him and given to another man (2 Samuel 3:14). But now, after Christ said to the adulterous woman, “Neither do I condemn you; go, and from now on do not sin,” who does not understand that a husband ought to forgive what he sees the Lord of both spouses has forgiven, and that he should no longer call her an adulteress whose repentant crime he believes has been erased by divine mercy?

## CHAPTER VII

### 6. Husbands who rage against adulterous wives, though they themselves are also adulterers

But this, evidently, is what the minds of unbelievers recoil from. Thus some men of little faith—or rather enemies of the true faith—fearing, I suppose, that their wives would be granted impunity for sinning, removed from their copies of the Scriptures what the Lord had done concerning the pardon of the adulterous woman.

[Note: In most Greek copies the story of the adulterous woman was not read. There is no mention of it in Chrysostom’s and Theophylact’s commentaries on the Gospel of John, although Chrysostom does acknowledge the story elsewhere, namely in Homily 60. Jerome, in the second book of his dialogue against the Pelagians, mentions it in these words: “In the Gospel according to John,” he says, “in many Greek and Latin copies there is found the story of the adulterous woman who was accused before the Lord.” Eusebius of Caesarea, in Book 3 of his Ecclesiastical History, says that this story of the adulterous woman was added to John from the Gospel entitled According to the Hebrews. Nevertheless, what Augustine conjectures may have happened: what originally stood in the more accurate copies of John may have been removed through the rashness of imprudent people, lest the Gospel be thought to grant adulterous women—against whom the secular laws were more severe—permission and impunity to sin.]

[Col. 0474] They acted as though the one who said, “From now on do not sin,” had granted permission to sin, or as though the woman ought not to be healed by God the physician through the remission of that sin lest the sick be offended. For those who are displeased by that deed of the Lord are not themselves chaste, nor does chastity make them severe. Rather, they belong to the class of men to whom the Lord said, “Let the one among you who is without sin be the first to throw a stone at her.” The difference is that those men, terrified by their consciences, withdrew and ceased tempting Christ and persecuting the adulterous woman (John 8:7–11); whereas these men criticize the physician while they themselves are sick, and, though adulterers, rage against adulterous women.

If they were told—not what those men heard, “The one among you who is without sin,” for who is without sin?—but, “The one among you who is without this sin, let him be the first to throw a stone at her,” then perhaps those who were indignant that the adulterous woman was not killed would consider how great God’s mercy was toward them in sparing them so that they themselves, though adulterers, might live.

## CHAPTER VIII

### 7. Adulterous husbands should be punished more severely than adulterous wives. The law of Antoninus, who wished unchaste [Col. 0475] men to be condemned equally with women. The unchastity of men is worse

But when we say these things to them, they not only refuse to diminish their severity; they also become angry with the truth and speak in reply:

“But we are men! Surely the dignity of our sex can bear no such insult as to make us equal to women in punishment when we commit some offense with women other than our wives?”

As though, precisely because they are men, they ought not to restrain unlawful desires with greater manliness; as though, precisely because they are men, they ought not to set themselves before their wives as examples of this virtue; as though, precisely because they are men, they ought not to be less easily overcome by lust; as though, precisely because they are men, they ought not to serve wanton flesh less readily.

And yet they are indignant when they hear that adulterous men are to suffer punishments like those of adulterous women, although they ought to be punished much more severely, in proportion as it pertains more to them both to conquer by virtue and to govern women by example.

I am speaking to Christians, who faithfully hear, “The husband is the head of the wife” (Ephesians 5:23). In this they recognize that they are leaders and that women ought to be their companions. Therefore a husband must take care not to live in such a way that he fears his wife may follow him by imitation.

But those who dislike equal standards of chastity for husband and wife, and who prefer—especially in this matter—to be subject to the laws of the world rather than to Christ, because the civil laws do not seem to bind men to the same obligations of chastity as women, should read what the emperor Antoninus established concerning this matter.

[Note: Erasmus’s edition has Antonius, incorrectly and against all the manuscripts.]

He ruled that a husband could not accuse his wife of adultery if he had not provided her with an example of chastity in his own conduct, so that both were to be condemned if he himself had shown that both were equally unchaste. For these are the words of the emperor mentioned above, found in the Gregorianus:

“Certainly,” he says, “my letter will in no respect prejudice the case. For if it was your fault that the marriage was dissolved and that your wife Eupasia married under the Julian law, my rescript will not for that reason condemn her for adultery unless it is established that adultery was committed. They will first inquire whether, while you were living chastely, you also encouraged her to cultivate good morals. For it seems exceedingly unjust to me that a husband should demand chastity from a wife to whom he does not himself display it. This circumstance can condemn the husband as well; it cannot settle the matter between the two on the basis of reciprocal guilt or remove the cause of the act.”

[Note: Hardly any fragments of the Gregorianus now remain. Among them is this constitution of Antoninus, word for word; we believe it was inserted there from this very book of Augustine. Part of it is also found in Ulpian, section 3, Book 13, *On Adulteries*.]

If these things must be observed for the honor of an earthly state, how much greater chastity does the heavenly homeland and the fellowship of angels require?

Since this is so, is the unchastity of men less—or rather not greater and worse—because it is accompanied by arrogant and licentious boasting? Let men, therefore, not recoil from the fact that Christ forgave the adulterous woman. Rather, let them recognize their own danger and, suffering from a similar disease, flee with humble devotion to the same Savior. [Col. 0476] Let them acknowledge that what they read was done for her is also necessary for themselves; let them receive the medicine for their adulteries, cease committing adultery, praise God’s patience toward themselves, practice repentance, accept forgiveness, and change their judgment concerning the punishment of women and their own impunity.

## CHAPTER IX

### 8. One who refuses reconciliation with an adulterous wife may not marry another

When these matters are considered and examined—when the common condition [Col. 0476], common evil, common danger, common wound, and common salvation are contemplated faithfully and humbly—the reconciliation of spouses, even after adulteries have been committed and cleansed, will not be shameful or difficult, where forgiveness of sins is certainly effected through the keys of the kingdom of heaven.

This is not so that an adulterous woman may be recalled after divorce from her husband, but so that, after entering into fellowship with Christ, she may no longer be called an adulteress.

But suppose this is not done. No one compels it, because perhaps some law of this age forbids it according to the practice of the earthly state, in which the abolition of crimes through holy blood was not considered. Let continence, therefore, be embraced, since no law forbids it; let no one proceed to other adulteries.

And what concern is it to us if the adulterous woman, not even cleansed by divine mercy, is not reconciled to her husband?

[Note: The printed editions have “is not reconciled by God.” The manuscripts do not add “by God.”]

Let it be enough that, while adulterous spouses are not reconciled, no other unions are formed that are demonstrably adulteries. “For the woman is bound as long as her husband lives” (1 Corinthians 7:39). Consequently, the husband too is bound as long as his wife lives. This bond makes it impossible for them to join themselves to others without adulterous intercourse.

Thus it is necessary that four adulterers arise from two spouses if both she marries another man and he marries another woman.

[Note: Only Lovaniensis has: “if she marries an adulterer and he marries an adulterous woman.”]

For although the man who dismisses his wife for a reason other than fornication and marries another commits adultery in a more criminal way—this is the kind of adultery Matthew mentioned—yet not only does he commit adultery himself, but, as it is written in Mark:

“Whoever dismisses his wife and marries another commits adultery against her; and if a wife dismisses her husband and marries another, she commits adultery” (Mark 10:11–12).

And as it is written in Luke:

“Everyone who dismisses his wife and marries another commits adultery; and the one who marries a woman dismissed by her husband commits adultery” (Luke 16:18).

I have already discussed these testimonies sufficiently in the preceding book.

## CHAPTER X

### 9. The complaints of the incontinent against Christ’s law, which forbids marrying another after dismissing an adulterous wife, are futile. If the complaints of the incontinent are admitted, adulteries must be permitted in many cases. The complaint of a woman dismissed for a reason other than fornication, who wishes to marry another, will seem more justified

But you reply to me:

“To live continently is the lot of few. Therefore those who have dismissed adulterous spouses, since they cannot be reconciled with them, find themselves in such danger that they declare Christ’s law to be not humane but savage.”

O brother, so far as the incontinent are concerned, they can have many complaints by which, as you say, they might call Christ’s law savage rather than humane. Nevertheless, we must not pervert [Col. 0477] or change Christ’s Gospel on their account.

You are moved only by the complaint of those who dismiss their spouses when fornication has occurred, if they are not permitted to marry others, since continence is the lot of few and they ought to be encouraged toward it by praise, not compelled to it by law.

Thus, if a man does not marry another after dismissing an adulterous wife, human incontinence will have, as you think, a just complaint. But consider how many situations there are in which, if we wished to admit the complaints of the incontinent, we would necessarily have to permit adulteries.

[Note: Only Lovaniensis has: “we would have to permit adulteries to be committed.”]

What if a spouse is afflicted by some prolonged and incurable bodily illness that prevents intercourse? What if captivity or some other force separates the spouses, so that the husband knows his wife is alive but is denied access to her? Do you think the murmuring of the incontinent should be admitted and adulteries permitted?

What about the very matter on which the Lord was questioned, and to which he replied that it ought not to be done, but that Moses permitted a writ of divorce and dismissal of one’s spouse for any reason because of the hardness of their hearts? Does Christ’s law not displease the incontinent who wish, by issuing a divorce, to cast off wives who are quarrelsome, abusive, domineering, irritating, or extremely unwilling to render the marital debt, and to marry others?

Since the incontinence of these people recoils from Christ’s law, must Christ’s law therefore be changed according to their judgment?

### 10.

Furthermore, if a wife leaves her husband, or a husband his wife, not on account of fornication but rather for the sake of continence, and the person to whom the divorce is given is incontinent, I ask whether that person will not be an adulterer if joined to another.

If it is said, “That person will not be an adulterer or adulteress,” then the Lord is contradicted, whose words are:

“It was also said, ‘Whoever dismisses his wife, let him give her a writ of divorce.’ But I say to you that everyone who dismisses his wife, except for the reason of fornication, makes her commit adultery; and whoever marries a dismissed woman commits adultery” (Matthew 5:31–32).

There she is the one who was dismissed, not the one who dismissed; and because continence is the lot of few, she yielded to incontinence and married. Yet the adulterer married an adulteress. Both are guilty; both must be condemned: both the woman who married while her husband was alive and the man who married a woman whose husband is alive.

Are we to call Christ’s law inhumane because by it a woman is made guilty of and punished for so great a crime—a woman whom her husband dismissed without any preceding fornication on her part, and whom, because continence is the lot of few, he compelled to marry by dismissing her?

Why do we not say here that the man who, by dismissing his wife unjustly, first broke the marital bond should be reckoned as dead? For on what grounds will you say that the man who, although an adulterer, did not dismiss his wife broke the marital bond, while the man who dismissed even a chaste wife did not break it?

I say that in both cases this bond remains: the bond by which a woman is bound as long as her husband lives, whether he is continent or an adulterer. Therefore the woman who has been dismissed and marries commits adultery, and the man who marries the dismissed woman commits adultery, whether she was dismissed by an adulterer or by a continent man, [Col. 0478] because the woman is bound as long as her husband lives.

But now we are discussing the complaints of the incontinent. For what complaint could seem more just than that of this woman who says:

“I was dismissed; I did not dismiss him. And because continence is the lot of few, I did not remain continent. So that I would not fornicate, I married; and yet I am called an adulteress because I married.”

Will we, because of this woman’s apparently just complaint, deem the divine law changeable so that we do not judge her an adulteress? Heaven forbid.

But you will reply that she ought not to have been dismissed, because no cause of fornication preceded. You speak truly, for the Lord explicitly identified her husband’s sin when he said, “Whoever dismisses his wife, except for the reason of fornication, makes her commit adultery.”

But did she therefore not sin by marrying afterward merely because he had first sinned by dismissing her? What benefit, then, does this incontinent woman gain from complaining about Christ’s law, except that she is punished for her complaint?

## CHAPTER XI

### 11. Another objection of Pollentius: that, at least for the sake of begetting children, it should be permissible to marry another after dismissing an adulterous wife

Let us now consider also what you introduced elsewhere and did not wish to answer, where you are moved and pity the man who is compelled to sleep with an adulterous woman—if not by incontinence, then certainly by the necessity of begetting children—if he is not permitted to dismiss her in such a way that, while she is alive, he may marry another.

You would rightly be moved if, while an adulterous wife was alive, it were not adultery to marry another. But if it is adultery, as the arguments already given have shown, what justification is there in the begetting of children?

The license of wicked acts must not be permitted for that reason. Or is it so necessary to avoid dying without descendants as it is to choose to live eternally? Adulterers will not be permitted this, since after their first death they must necessarily be condemned to the eternity of a second death.

This pretext of begetting children would also compel the dismissal not of adulterous women but of the most chaste women, if they happened to be barren, and the marriage of others in their place. I suppose you would not approve of that.

### 12.

Therefore, if adulteries are not to be excused on the grounds of incontinence, how much less are they to be excused on the grounds of begetting children?

## CHAPTER XII

### At the present time, marriage should be chosen for the sake of children only by those who cannot remain continent

The Apostle wished to assist that weakness—that is, incontinence—through the honorableness of marriage. For he did not say, “If she has no children, let her marry,” but, “If she cannot remain continent, let her marry” (1 Corinthians 7:9).

The propagation of children compensates for what is conceded to incontinence through marriage. For incontinence is certainly a vice, whereas marriage is not a vice. Thus, through this good, that evil becomes pardonable.

Since marriage was instituted for the purpose of procreation, this was the reason for which the Fathers married: they joined themselves to women only for the duty of begetting children, but not unlawfully. For at that time there was a certain necessity of propagation that no longer exists, since there was then, as it is written, “a time for embracing,” whereas now there is “a time for refraining from embrace” (Ecclesiastes 3:5). [Col. 0479]

Speaking of this latter time, the Apostle says:

“Moreover, brothers, the time is short. From now on, let those who have wives live as though they had none” (1 Corinthians 7:29).

Therefore it is now rightly said, “Let the one who is able to receive this receive it” (Matthew 19:12); but the one who cannot remain continent should marry.

At that time, therefore, even continence descended into marriage for the duty of propagating children.

[Note: The manuscripts of Germanus have: “descended into the duty of marriage.”]

But now the marital bond assists the weakness of incontinence, so that those who cannot remain continent may produce children not through the disgrace of sexual immorality but through the honorableness of marriage.

Why, then, did the Apostle not say, “If she has no children, let her marry”? Because, clearly, in this present time of refraining from embrace, it is not necessary to propagate children. And why did he say, “If she cannot remain continent, let her marry”? Certainly, so that she might not be compelled to commit adultery through incontinence.

Therefore, if she remains continent, let her neither marry nor beget children. But if she does not remain continent, let her marry lawfully, so that she may not beget children shamefully or, more shamefully, fail to beget them through unlawful intercourse.

Although some do this even while lawfully married. For intercourse even with a legitimate wife is unlawful and shameful when conception is deliberately avoided. This is what Onan, the son of Judah, did, and God killed him on that account (Genesis 38:8–10).

The propagation of children is therefore the first, natural, and legitimate purpose of marriage. Accordingly, those who marry because of incontinence ought not to restrain their evil in such a way that they destroy the good of marriage—that is, the propagation of children.

The Apostle was speaking of the incontinent when he said:

“I therefore want younger women to marry, bear children, manage their households, and give the adversary no occasion for slander. For some have already turned aside after Satan” (1 Timothy 5:14–15).

When he said, “I want younger women to marry,” he was certainly admonishing them in order to shore up the ruin caused by incontinence. But lest they think only of the weakness of carnal desire, which alone would need to be served by the work of marriage, while the good of marriage itself was despised or neglected, he immediately added, “to bear children, to manage their households.”

Those who choose to remain continent are choosing something better than the good of marriage, namely, the generation of children. Therefore, if continence is chosen so that something better than the good of marriage may be undertaken, how much more must it be preserved in order to avoid adultery?

For after the Apostle had said, “If she cannot remain continent, let her marry,” he continued, “For it is better to marry than to burn” (1 Corinthians 7:9). He did not say, “It is better to commit adultery than to burn.”

## CHAPTER XIII

### 13. Those unwilling to be reconciled with adulterous spouses should preserve continence

There is therefore no exhortation we can give to those who fear reconciliation with adulterous spouses healed through repentance except that they preserve continence.

For a woman is bound as long as her husband lives, whether he is an adulterer or chaste; if she marries another, she commits adultery. And a husband is bound as long as his wife lives, whether she is an adulteress or chaste; if he marries another, he commits adultery. [Col. 0480]

This bond is not dissolved even when, through divorce, one spouse is separated from a chaste spouse.

[Note: This is how the better manuscripts read. Lovaniensis has: “one spouse is separated from a chaste wife.” Erasmus has: “one spouse, chaste in body.”]

It is much less dissolved when a spouse who has not been separated commits adultery.

Accordingly, nothing dissolves it except the death of the spouse—not death through falling into adultery, but death through departing from the body.

Therefore, if a woman withdraws from an adulterous husband and does not wish to be reconciled with him, let her remain unmarried. And if a husband dismisses an adulterous wife and does not wish to take her back even after repentance, let him preserve continence—if not by choosing the greater good voluntarily, then certainly by the necessity of avoiding a destructive evil.

I would give the same exhortation even if the wife were suffering from a long and incurable illness, even if she were bodily separated somewhere so that her husband could not approach her. Finally, I would give the same exhortation even if a woman, wishing to live continently—though contrary to discipline, since it was not by mutual consent—dismissed a chaste husband.

For I think no Christian would object that a man is an adulterer if, while his wife is suffering for a long time, absent for a long time, or wishing to live continently, he joins himself to another woman.

Thus, even after dismissing an adulterous wife, he is an adulterer with another woman, because it is not this man or that man, but “everyone who dismisses his wife and marries another commits adultery” (Luke 16:18).

Therefore, if the life of the saints, free from the marital bond, is desired less, let the punishment of adulterers be feared; and let desire be restrained at least by fear, if continence is not chosen out of love.

For if labor operates where there is fear, love will also be present where labor was. We must not rely on our own strength; prayer must be joined to our efforts, so that the One who deters us from evil may fill us with good.

## CHAPTER XIV

### 14. Another objection: that this position excludes kindness, since husbands would wish adulterous wives to be punished so that they could marry others after their deaths

Let us also answer the point at which you suppose that husbands are compelled to punish adulterous wives without any compassion, since they want them to die if they are not permitted to marry others while those wives are alive.

Wishing to heighten the cruelty of this, you said:

“It does not seem to me, most loving father, that this is a divine attitude, where kindness and compassion are excluded.”

You speak as though husbands ought to spare adulterous women because they are permitted to marry others—so that, if they are not permitted to do so, they should not spare them in order to gain that permission.

On the contrary, they ought to show mercy to sinful women so that they themselves may obtain mercy for their own sins. They ought to do this all the more if, after dismissing adulterous wives, they wish to live continently.

They should be more merciful in proportion as they wish to be holier, so that they may receive divine assistance in preserving chastity in themselves, while they themselves do not, in human fashion, avenge the chastity violated by their wives.

Above all, that saying of the Lord must be recalled to them:

“Let the one among you who is without sin be the first to throw a stone at her” (John 8:7).

Not, “The one who is without this particular sin”—for we are speaking of chaste men—

[Note: The better manuscripts read this way. The printed editions have: “as though we were speaking of chaste men.”]

—but, “The one who is without sin.” If they say that they are [Col. 0481] without sin, they deceive themselves, and the truth is not in them (1 John 1:8).

But if they do not deceive themselves, and the truth is in them, there will be no bloody severity in them. Knowing that they are not without sin, they forgive so that they may be forgiven; nor are kindness and compassion excluded from them.

[Note: Lovaniensis has: “so that kindness and compassion may not be excluded from them.” The other manuscripts have “nor are they excluded from them,” though some read “may they be excluded”; others, with Ambrosius and Erasmus, have the singular “is excluded.”]

Indeed, these qualities are more truly excluded when they obtain forgiveness for their spouses’ sins through the license of lust rather than through concern for compassion—that is, when they spare them because they are permitted to marry others, rather than because they wish the Lord to spare them as well.

## CHAPTER XV

### Husbands should be led to spare adulterous wives not by the license of lust but by concern for compassion

How much better, I say, it is to tell them this than to say:

“Spare these adulterous women and do not seek their blood; whatever grief you suffer because of their crimes will be consoled by other women whom you marry. You would rightly wish to remove these women from the number of the living if their lives prevented you from marrying others. But now, since even while these women live you are permitted to arrange other marriages, why do you wish so desperately to kill them?”

If we say this, do you not see how far our persuasion is from the Christian character?

[Note: The Corbeiensis manuscript has: “from the charity of Christ.”]

For we would both be saying something false—that they are permitted to do what is not permitted, namely, to join themselves to others while these women live—and, if they spared them for that reason, they would not be sparing them out of compassion but because they had free authority to contract other marriages.

Finally, I ask you whether a Christian husband is permitted, either according to the old law of God or according to Roman law, to kill an adulterous wife.

[Note: All the manuscripts read this way. The printed editions have: “or according to Roman laws, to kill an adulterous wife.”]

If he is permitted, it is better for him to refrain from both: from the lawful punishment of the woman who has sinned and from the unlawful marriage contracted while she is alive.

But if he persists in choosing one or the other, it is better for him to do what is permitted—that the adulterous woman be punished—than what is not permitted—that, while she is alive, he himself commit adultery.

But if what is said more truly is the case—namely, that a Christian is not permitted to kill an adulterous wife but only to dismiss her—who is so mad as to say to him, “Do what is not permitted so that you may be permitted to do what is not permitted”?

Since both acts are unlawful according to [Col. 0482] Christ’s law—killing an adulterous wife and marrying another while she is alive—one must abstain from both; one unlawful act must not be committed in place of another.

If he is going to do what is not permitted, let him commit adultery rather than homicide: let him marry another while his wife lives rather than shed human blood. But if both acts are wicked, he must not commit one in place of the other; he must avoid both.

## CHAPTER XVI

### 16. It is objected that an incontinent man who secures the death of his adulterous wife by accusing her will obtain forgiveness through Baptism or reconciliation, whereas otherwise such forgiveness would forever be denied him as an adulterer

Graver objections can be devised against Pollentius’s position than those he himself raises.

Here I see what the incontinent may say: namely, that a man who dismisses an adulterous wife and allows her to live, then marries another, is a perpetual adulterer as long as the first wife lives. Since he does not withdraw from his disgraceful act, he does not perform fruitful repentance; and if he is a catechumen, he is not admitted to Baptism, because he does not change what prevents him from receiving it. Nor can a repentant person be reconciled while persevering in the same wickedness.

But if he kills the adulterous woman by accusing her, then, because the sin has been completed and he does not persist in it, that sin is cleansed by Baptism if it was committed by a catechumen, and, if committed by one already baptized, it is healed through repentance and reconciliation.

But are we for that reason going to say that adultery is not adultery when it is unquestionably committed by marrying another while an adulterous wife is alive?

You except this particular form of adultery; but surely you do not doubt that it is adultery if someone marries a living woman who was dismissed by her husband through a writ of divorce without any fornication on the woman’s part.

What, then, if a man sees that he will neither be admitted to Baptism, if he is a catechumen, nor perform useful repentance, if he is baptized, unless he corrects and abandons what he has done; and if he wishes and is able to kill the man whose wife he married, so that this crime may be washed away through Baptism or removed through repentance, and so that the other adultery too may not continue—since, after her husband’s death, the woman has been released from the law of her husband—and so that satisfaction may be made through repentance for what has been done, or it may be erased through regeneration:

Are we for that reason to accuse Christ’s law, as though it compelled homicide, when it says that marrying a woman dismissed without any charge of fornication is adultery?

### 17.

Here, if we pay even slight attention to what we are saying, much graver things can be said than what you have said. Since you do not want it to be adultery when other women are married after adulterous wives have been dismissed, you have discovered this argument:

“For if we call these acts adulteries, husbands will be compelled to kill the adulterous women whose lives prevent them from marrying others.”

And, to heighten the force of this, you said:

“It does not seem to me, most loving father, that this is a divine attitude, where kindness and compassion are excluded.”

Suppose, then, that someone unwilling to believe that it is adultery when a woman dismissed by her husband without any charge of fornication is married by another man finds this argument against you: that by your reasoning people are encouraged to commit homicide—to attack the husbands of women whom they have married after such a dismissal, whether by whatever ambushes they can devise, by calumnies, or by accusing them of some genuine crimes and killing them [Col. 0483]—so that, once those husbands are dead, unions that would have been adulteries while they lived may become marriages.

Would he not, exaggerating the matter, say to you:

“It does not seem to me, most loving brother, that this is a divine attitude, where not only kindness and compassion are excluded, but enormous malice and impiety are stirred up?”

For it is much lighter and more tolerable that husbands kill adulterous wives than that adulterers kill husbands.

Would it please you, on account of a most empty objection, to abandon the Lord’s defense of this position—or even to accuse it by saying that adultery should not be punished, even when a woman dismissed by her husband for a reason other than fornication is joined to another, lest he be compelled to kill her husband, by whom she was dismissed, while he wishes to turn adultery into marriage through the death of her former husband?

I know that this does not please you: that, because of such an empty objection, Christ’s law, although found to be true and sound, should be called harsh and inhumane.

In the same way, you ought not to think that adultery should be denied when a man marries another while his adulterous wife is alive merely because the husband may thereby be compelled to kill the adulterous woman, wishing that he might marry another after she has been killed, since he is not permitted to do so while she lives.

What if the detractors of the Christian faith also say that people are compelled to kill their wives by criminal plots—wives whom they cannot bear because they suffer from prolonged illness and cannot endure intercourse, or because they are poor, barren, or deformed—in the hope of marrying other women who are healthy, wealthy, fertile, and beautiful?

They might say this because men are not permitted to dismiss wives whom they cannot bear, except for the reason of fornication, and marry others, lest they remain perpetually bound to adultery and therefore be unable either to receive Baptism or to be healed through repentance.

Are we, for that reason, to say that, in order to prevent such crimes of homicide, it is not adultery for men, after dismissing wives for a reason other than fornication, to join themselves to other women?

## CHAPTER XVII
### 18. Another difficulty against Pollentius’s position

Now, from your view that it is not adultery if a man dismisses his wife on account of fornication and marries another, do you not think care must be taken lest husbands learn to compel their wives—whom they cannot endure for countless other reasons—to commit adultery, so that, once the marital bond has supposedly been dissolved through fornication, they may be permitted to marry others?
