And, because they compelled those wives to commit adultery, may they then be cleansed by Baptism or healed through repentance, since grace and medicine will be denied them as long as they live with adulterers, if, after dismissing their first wives for reasons other than fornication, they marry others?

Unless perhaps someone says that no one can make his wife commit adultery if she is chaste. Yet the Lord says: “Everyone who dismisses his wife, except on account of fornication, makes her commit adultery” (Matthew 5:33). This is certainly because, although she was chaste while living with her husband, once dismissed she is compelled through lack of self-control to join herself to another while her first husband is alive—and this is to commit adultery. Even if she does not do this, nevertheless, insofar as it lies within his power, he has compelled her to do it; and God will count this as a sin against him, even if she remains chaste.

[Col. 0484]

But who does not know how rare are those women who live so chastely with their husbands that, even if dismissed by them, they do not seek others? For incomparably greater is the number of women who, although they cleave chastely to their husbands, nevertheless, if dismissed by their husbands, do not delay marrying. When men therefore believe the Lord’s statement, “Everyone who dismisses his wife, except on account of fornication, makes her commit adultery,” and also believe your statement that, when a woman commits fornication, her husband is permitted to marry another, whoever wishes to be rid of the wife to whom he is joined on account of any other annoyance should first make her commit adultery by dismissing her without fornication, so that he may then marry another once she has become an adulteress through marriage. Thus, having been freed from the earlier sin by which he made her commit adultery—whether through Baptism or through repentance—he may imagine that he can have another wife without committing adultery himself, after marrying her following his first wife’s adultery, as though the marriage bond had thereby been dissolved.

But if he has contrived this, he will make his wife an adulteress, and he himself, although marrying another after his wife’s adultery, will be an adulterer; and it will profit him nothing that he believed you rather than the one who said without exception: “Everyone who leaves his wife and marries another commits adultery” (Luke 16:18).

## CHAPTER XVIII

### 19. Continence must be observed, whether conjugal or superior

After all these matters have been considered and examined, it remains for those who faithfully hear these things to say to us what was said to the Lord: “If such is the case of a man with his wife, it is not expedient to marry.” What answer can we give them except the answer he himself gave? “Not everyone grasps this saying, but those to whom it has been given. For there are eunuchs who were born so from their mother’s womb; there are eunuchs who were made so by men; and there are eunuchs who made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven. Let anyone grasp it who can” (Matthew 19:10–12).

Therefore, let whoever can grasp what not everyone grasps do so. Those who can grasp it are those to whom God’s hidden but just mercy grants this gift. [Note: The edition of Lovanienses has *sed non injusta* (“but not unjust”); the other editions and manuscripts have *sed justa* (“but just”).]

Among all those who have made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven, some have no knowledge of intercourse with either sex; others have experienced it and turned away from it—some having experienced it unlawfully, others lawfully. Among those who have experienced it lawfully, some have known only lawful intercourse, while others have known both unlawful and lawful intercourse. Some among them know only their marriages; others also know other women and every kind of illicit intercourse.

But those who, after intercourse within marriage, make themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven either lose their wives through death, or profess continence by mutual consent with them, or, compelled by separation, lest they commit adultery by joining themselves to others while their wives are alive, make themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven—not so that they may be more glorious there, but because otherwise they cannot be there. For those who practice continence not from this necessity but from desire for a better good could be there even while preserving conjugal chastity, though among lesser rewards, yet within the kingdom.

[Col. 0485]

Those, however, who practice continence because they fear marrying others while their first spouses are alive ought to take greater care for their salvation than those who chose continence as a more glorious reward. They will be there if they are not adulterers. If they do not practice continence, they will be adulterers, because while their former spouses are alive they will cleave not to other spouses but to adulterous unions. And if they will be absent from the kingdom of heaven, where will they be except where there is no salvation?

## CHAPTER XIX

### 20. He exhorts spouses separated from their spouses by divorce to continence

I therefore address these people: whatever they ought to do if they had spouses wasting away through prolonged illness, or absent in a place inaccessible to them, or maintaining an illicit separation through hostility, let them do this if they have spouses stained by adulterous defilement and have separated from their companionship on that account. [Note: The manuscripts have *divortientes* (“separating”); *divortiantes* (“divorcing”) appears in the printed editions.] Let them not seek other marriages, because they will not be marriages but adulteries.

Since there is an equal form of this bond between husband and wife, just as a wife is called an adulteress if, while her husband lives, she is with another man (Romans 7:3), so a husband also is called an adulterer if, while his wife lives, he is with another woman. Although the one who does so apart from the cause of fornication is more seriously culpable, nevertheless everyone who dismisses his wife and marries another commits adultery.

Let not the burden of continence frighten them: it will be light if it is Christ’s. It will be Christ’s if faith is present, and faith obtains from the one who commands the ability to do what he has commanded. Let them not be broken by the fact that their continence seems to arise from necessity rather than from the will. Those who chose it willingly made it necessary, since they can no longer depart from it without condemnation. Those who were driven into it by necessity make it voluntary if they place their confidence not in themselves but in the one from whom every good comes.

The former climbed to it for the sake of greater glory, seeking to find something more; the latter fled to it out of ultimate concern for salvation, lest they perish. Let both persevere; let both walk to the end in what they have attained; let them burn with zeal and beseech God with prayers. The former must also consider their salvation, so that they may fear falling from what their will has seized; and the latter must not despair of glory, if they choose to persist in what necessity has imposed. [Note: Erasmus and the manuscripts have *dilecta est* (“was chosen”); *delecta est* (“was delighted in”) appears in the printed editions.]

For it can happen that, with God frightening, exhorting, converting, and filling them, the human disposition may be changed for the better. They may then vow to live with the greatest perseverance without spouses, without any intercourse, and without the defiling touch of lust, so that even if the death of their separated spouses opens the opportunity for marrying others, what is open by lawful permission may be closed by their vow, and what began through necessity may be perfected through love.

Such people will certainly receive the reward given to those who either made this vow by mutual agreement with their spouses or, bound to no marriages, chose continence for the sake of a greater good. But if they practice continence in such a way that, should the women whose lives prevent them from marrying die, they intend to marry others, then even if they themselves should first depart from the body while maintaining such continence, it will be counted to them only as conjugal chastity, on account of which they do not do what they would do if it were permitted. To live continually with this intention is insufficient for receiving the rewards of that continence which is chosen more freely, but it is sufficient for avoiding adultery.

## CHAPTER XX

[Col. 0486]

### 21. Men ought to precede women in chastity. He proposes the continence of clergy who were chosen unwillingly to men unwilling to practice continence after divorce

Remember that I say these things about both sexes, but especially on account of men, who think themselves superior to women for the very reason that they do not deem it worthy to be equal to them in chastity—although in this they ought even to precede them, so that women might follow them as their heads.

When the law prohibits adulteries, if an excuse is admitted on the pretext of the flesh’s lack of self-control, an opportunity for many to perish under the name of false impunity is opened. Women have flesh as well; men who refuse to allow them such conduct behave as though, because they are men, it is permitted to them. But far be it from us that what detracts from modesty should be owed as an honor to the supposedly better sex. Just honor is owed to virtue, not to vice.

Indeed, since they demand from women—who certainly possess flesh—such great chastity that, when they are separated from their wives for very long periods, they want them to pass through the ardor of youth undefiled by adulterous intercourse—and very many do pass through it with the greatest chastity, especially Syrian women, whose husbands, occupied with the profits of commerce, leave their young wives in the bloom of youth and scarcely ever return to them except as old men to elderly women—by this very fact they are more clearly convicted that what they claim they cannot do is not impossible. For if human weakness could not do this, the weaker sex of women could do it even less.

### 22.

Hence, when we warn those who think masculine excellence consists in nothing but permission to sin that they will perish eternally by clinging to adulterous unions, we usually set before them also the continence of clergy, who are often compelled unwillingly to undertake the same burden and, once they have assumed it, carry it through to its proper end with the Lord’s help.

We say to them: “What if you too were seized by the violence of the people and compelled to undertake this? Would you not guard the office you had assumed chastely, suddenly turning to the Lord to obtain strength—strength of which you had never before thought?”

“But,” they reply, “honor greatly consoles those men.”

We answer: “Fear should govern you much more.” [Note: Only the Lovanienses edition has: “And may greater fear govern you.”]

If many ministers of God suddenly and unexpectedly accepted what had been imposed upon them, hoping to shine more illustriously in Christ’s inheritance, how much more ought you to live continently by avoiding adulteries, fearing not that you will shine less brightly in God’s kingdom but that you will burn in the fire of Gehenna?

We say these and similar things as best we can to those who, whenever their spouses depart from them for whatever reason or are dismissed because of adultery, wish to marry others and, when forbidden, plead the weakness of the flesh against us.

But now this book too must be brought to a close, and God must be asked either not to allow them to be tested by separation from their spouses, or to allow it in such a way that fear for their endangered salvation may become an opportunity for greater or more proven chastity.

[Col. 0487]

[Note: For the book *On Lying*, see book 1, final chapter, of the *Retractations*, vol. 1, col. 630, from the words “Also, *On Lying*” through the words “The question concerns lying.” M.]

# SAINT AURELIUS AUGUSTINE, BISHOP OF HIPPO, ONE BOOK ON LYING

[Note: The book *On Lying* belongs approximately to the year 395, since it occupies the final place in the first book of the *Retractations*, where the shorter works published by Augustine before his episcopate are reviewed; he attained the episcopate toward the end of 395. In the printed editions the book is entitled “On Lying, to Consentium.” But in the written manuscripts the name of Consentius—who many years later consulted Augustine on the same matter in opposition to the Priscillianists—is not attached to this earlier book; it belongs only to the book against lying that follows this one.]

[Note: The book *On Lying* was corrected with the help of the Colbertine manuscript, approximately eight hundred years old; the Germanensis and Corbeiensis manuscripts, contemporary in age with the Colbertine; and the old Regius, Sorbonicus, Victorinus, Bigotianus, Michaelinus, Pratellensis, Ebrulphensis, Regiomontanus, Vaticanus, and five Belgian manuscripts, or rather the variant readings that the Louvain editors drew from them; together with the assistance and comparison of the editions of Erasmus and the Louvain editors.]

[Note: We also compared all the editions mentioned at the beginning of the *Retractations* and *Confessions*, vol. 1. M.]

(C)

In this work it is investigated what a lie is and whether it may ever be admitted, weighing examples and the force of arguments on both sides. Eight kinds of lies are presented; after they have been examined and entirely rejected, it is established that one must never lie.

## CHAPTER I

### 1. The difficulty of treating the subject

The question of lying is a great one, and it often troubles us in the very actions of our daily lives, lest we either rashly condemn as a lie what is not a lie or suppose that one may sometimes lie with a certain honest, dutiful, and merciful lie. [Note: The manuscripts have this form. The printed editions have: “and dutifully, with a lie directed toward mercy.”]

We shall examine this question so carefully that we will seek together with those who seek. Whether we discover anything at all, without rashly affirming anything, the treatment itself will sufficiently indicate to an attentive reader. For the subject is exceedingly obscure and often eludes the attention of the inquirer through certain labyrinthine, cavernous twists, so that what had been found now seems to slip from the hands, now appears again, and again is swallowed up.

At last, however, a more certain investigation will grasp our judgment. If there is any error in it, since truth frees from every error and falsity entangles in every error, I consider that one can never err more safely than when one errs through excessive love of truth and excessive rejection of falsity. Those who criticize severely say that this is excessive; but truth itself may perhaps still say, “It is not yet enough.”

Whoever you are who read this, do not criticize anything until you have read the whole; and then you will criticize less. Do not seek eloquence. We have labored much over the matters themselves and over completing with speed a work so necessary to daily life; hence we have taken little or almost no care with words. [Note: Some manuscripts have this reading. Others have: “hence our concern has so far been properly…” The printed editions have: “hence our concern has so far been, and almost…”]

## CHAPTER II

[Col. 0488]

### 2. Jokes are not lies

With jokes excepted, therefore—for they have never been considered lies, since their meaning is made unmistakably clear by their pronunciation and by the very disposition of the one joking, whose intention is in no way to deceive even though he does not utter what is true—we may leave aside the further question whether such speech should be used by persons of perfected character, since we have not undertaken to resolve it now.

With jokes, then, excluded, our first task must be to ensure that someone who is not lying is not thought to be lying.

## CHAPTER III

### 3. What a lie is: whether the speaker must intend to deceive or whether this is sufficient

We must therefore see what a lie is. Not everyone who says what is false lies, if he believes or supposes that what he says is true.

The difference between believing and supposing is this: sometimes someone who believes recognizes that he is ignorant of what he believes, although concerning a matter that he knows he does not know he has no doubt at all, if he believes it with complete firmness. But someone who supposes thinks that he knows what he does not know. Whoever declares what he holds in his mind either as believed or as supposed, even if it is false, does not lie. For he owes this faithfulness to his statement: that through it he should express what he holds in his mind and possesses as he expresses it.

Nevertheless, he is not without fault, although he does not lie, if he either believes what should not be believed or thinks that he knows what he does not know, even if what he believes or thinks is true; for he treats the unknown as known.

Therefore, the person who lies is the one who has one thing in his mind and expresses another in words or by any other signs. Hence the liar is also said to have a double heart—that is, a double thought: one thought concerns the matter that he either knows or supposes to be true but does not express; the other concerns the matter that he expresses in place of it, knowing or supposing it to be false.

[Col. 0489]

Consequently, someone can say what is false without lying if he thinks that what he says is so, although it is not so; and someone can speak the truth while lying if he thinks it false and declares it as true, although it really is as he declares it. A person must be judged to be lying or not lying according to the judgment of his own mind, not according to the truth or falsity of the things themselves.

Thus someone who declares a falsehood as true, nevertheless supposing it to be true, may be called mistaken and rash, but he is not properly called a liar, because when he speaks he does not have a double heart, nor does he desire to deceive; rather, he is deceived.

The fault of the liar, however, is the desire to deceive in making a statement—whether he deceives when he is believed while uttering a falsehood, or does not deceive, either because he is not believed or because he utters the truth with the intention of deceiving, although he does not think it true. When he is believed, he certainly does not deceive, although he wished to deceive—unless he deceives to the extent that he is thought to know or suppose the matter to be as he declares it. [Note: The manuscripts have: “whether he deceives or does not, whether he is believed or whether he speaks the truth,” omitting the words “when he is believed while uttering a falsehood.”]

### 4.

Although the question is examined with the greatest subtlety, it remains to be asked whether, when the intention to deceive is absent, a lie is entirely absent.

## CHAPTER IV

### Whether lying may ever be useful or permissible

What if someone speaks falsely, believing it to be false, but does so because he thinks that he will not be believed, in order by this false statement to deter the person to whom he speaks, whom he perceives does not wish to believe him?

For if lying consists in declaring something otherwise than one knows or supposes it to be, this person lies precisely through his desire not to deceive. But if lying consists only in declaring something with the intention of deceiving, then this person does not lie: he speaks falsely, although he knows or supposes what he says to be false, so that the person to whom he speaks, by not believing him, will not be deceived, since he knows or supposes that the other will not believe him.

If it is therefore apparent that someone can speak falsely precisely so that the person to whom he speaks will not be deceived, another contrary kind of case arises: someone speaks the truth precisely in order to deceive.

For someone who speaks the truth because he realizes that he is not believed speaks the truth for the very purpose of deceiving. He knows or thinks that what is said can therefore be thought false because it is said by him. Accordingly, when he speaks the truth so that it will be thought false, he speaks the truth in order to deceive.

It must therefore be asked which of the two is lying: the one who speaks falsely so as not to deceive, or the one who speaks the truth in order to deceive—when the first knows or thinks that he is speaking falsely, and the second knows or thinks that he is speaking truly.

We have already said that the person who does not know that what he declares is false does not lie if he thinks it true; rather, the person who speaks the truth while thinking it false lies, because they must be judged according to the judgment of their own minds.

The question is therefore a substantial one concerning the two cases we have proposed. The first person knows or thinks that he is speaking falsely and does so in order not to deceive. For example, he may know that a road is being watched by robbers and, fearing that a man whose safety he seeks to protect might travel along it—and knowing that the man does not believe him—say that there are no robbers on that road, so that the man will not go that way, since he has decided not to believe the speaker and therefore thinks him a liar.

[Col. 0490]

The second person knows or thinks that what he says is true, but says it in order to deceive. For example, to a man who does not believe him, he may say that there are robbers on a road where he truly knows them to be, so that the man will travel along that road all the more readily and thus fall among the robbers, thinking that what the speaker said was false.

Which of these two, then, lies? Is it the one who chose to speak falsely so as not to deceive, or the one who chose to speak truly in order to deceive? Is it the one who, by speaking falsely, caused the person to whom he spoke to follow the truth, or the one who, by speaking truly, caused the person to whom he spoke to follow what was false?

Or perhaps both lied: the first because he wished to speak falsely, the second because he wished to deceive? Or rather, did neither lie: the first because he intended not to deceive, and the second because he intended to speak the truth?

For the question at present is not which of them sinned, but which lied. It quickly seems that the first person sinned—he who, by speaking the truth, caused the man to fall among robbers—while the other did not sin, or even acted well, by speaking falsely so that the man might avoid destruction.

But these examples can be reversed. The first person might wish the man whom he does not want deceived to suffer something more serious. For many, by learning certain truths, have brought destruction upon themselves when those truths were of a kind that ought to have remained hidden from them. And the second might wish some advantage for the man whom he wants deceived. Some people would have inflicted death upon themselves if they had learned something evil that had truly happened to those they loved; by thinking it false, they spared themselves. Thus deception benefited them, just as learning the truth harmed others.

The issue, therefore, is not the intention with which either the first spoke falsely so as not to deceive or the second spoke truly in order to deceive—whether the purpose was to help or to harm those to whom they spoke. Apart from the advantages or disadvantages of those addressed, the question concerns the truth or falsity itself: which of them lied, whether both did, or neither.

If a lie is a statement made with the intention of declaring what is false, then the one who wished to speak falsely lied rather than the one who, although he spoke falsely, did so in order not to deceive. If a lie is any statement made with the intention of deceiving, then not the first but the second lied, since he wished to deceive even by speaking the truth.

If a lie is a statement made with the intention that some falsehood be believed, then both lied: the first wished his statement itself to be false, while the second wished his true statement to be believed false. But if a lie is a statement made by someone wishing to declare what is false in order to deceive, then neither lied: the first intended, by speaking falsely, to persuade the other of the truth, while the second intended, in order to persuade him of what was false, to speak the truth.

All rashness and all lying will therefore be absent if, when necessary, we declare what we know or believe to be true and wish to persuade others of what we declare. But if, whether thinking what is false to be true, treating what is unknown to us as known, believing what ought not to be believed, or declaring something when there is no need to declare it, we nevertheless attempt to persuade others of nothing other than what we declare, there is indeed an error of rashness, [Note: The manuscripts have this form. The printed editions have: “rashness and error.”] but there is no lie.

None of those definitions need be feared when the mind is conscious that it declares what it either knows, supposes, or believes to be true, and that it wishes to persuade others of nothing except what it declares.

[Col. 0491]

### 5.

But whether a lie is ever useful is a much greater and more necessary question. It may be doubted whether someone who has no intention of deceiving—or who even acts so that the person to whom he makes a statement will not be deceived—lies, although he wanted the statement itself to be false because he wanted to persuade the other of the truth. It may also be doubted whether someone lies who wishes to make a true statement for the purpose of deceiving.

No one doubts, however, that the person lies who deliberately declares what is false in order to deceive. Therefore, a false statement made with the intention of deceiving is plainly a lie. But whether this alone constitutes a lie is another question.

## CHAPTER V

### The opinion affirming that one should sometimes lie. The opinion denying that one should ever lie. Examples in favor of lying drawn from the Old Testament are examined. No example of lying is supplied by the New Testament. Timothy’s circumcision was not performed through pretense. Peter willingly corrected by Paul. The authority for lying cannot be established by examples from ordinary life any more than by examples from Scripture

Let us meanwhile investigate the kind of case on which everyone agrees: whether it is ever useful to declare something false with the intention of deceiving.

Those who hold this view bring forward testimonies in support of their opinion. They recall that Sarah, when she laughed, denied to the angels that she had laughed (Genesis 18:15); that Jacob, when questioned by his father, replied that he was Esau, his elder son (Genesis 27:19); and that the Egyptian midwives, so that the Hebrew infants would not be killed at birth, lied, with God approving and rewarding them (Exodus 1:19–20). Selecting many similar examples, they mention the lies of people whom one would not dare to condemn, and thus admit that a lie may sometimes be not merely undeserving of blame but even deserving of praise.

They also add an argument by which they seek to press not only those devoted to the divine books but all human beings and common sense: “If someone takes refuge with you and could be saved from death by your lie, will you not lie? If a sick person asks about something that it is not good for him to know, and if, even without your answer, he could be afflicted more seriously, would you dare either to speak the truth to the man’s destruction or to remain silent rather than aid his health by an honest and merciful lie?”

By such arguments and others like them, they think they press their case most forcefully, so that, if concern for helping another demands it, we should sometimes lie.

### 6.

On the other hand, those who hold that one must never lie act with much greater force. They first employ divine authority, since the Decalogue itself says: “You shall not give false testimony” (Exodus 20:16). This expression embraces every lie, for whoever declares anything bears witness according to his own mind.

But lest anyone contend that not every lie should be called false testimony, what will he say about the statement: “The mouth that lies kills the soul” (Wisdom 1:11)? And lest anyone think this can be understood as referring only to certain liars, let him read elsewhere: “You will destroy all who speak lies” (Psalm 5:7).

[Col. 0492]

Hence the Lord himself says with his own mouth: “Let your speech be, ‘Yes, yes; No, no’; whatever is more than these is from evil” (Matthew 5:37). For this reason the Apostle, when commanding that the old person be put off—a term by which all sins are understood—then says, placing this first: “Therefore, putting away falsehood, speak the truth” (Ephesians 4:25).

### 7.

Nor do they say that they are frightened by the examples of lying brought forward from the ancient books, where everything that was done can be understood figuratively, although it really happened. Whatever is done or said figuratively is not a lie. For every statement must be referred to what it declares. Everything done or said figuratively declares what it signifies to those for whom it has been presented to be understood.

We must therefore believe that those people who are said to have been worthy of authority in prophetic times performed and said everything written about them prophetically; and that whatever happened to them happened no less prophetically, so that it was judged by that same prophetic Spirit to be committed to memory and writing.

As for the midwives, since they cannot say that through the prophetic Spirit they declared one thing instead of another to Pharaoh in order to signify a future truth, even if something was signified through what was done by them without their knowledge, they say that God approved and rewarded them according to their degree. For someone who is accustomed to lying in order to harm, if he lies for the sake of helping another, has made substantial progress.

But one thing is proposed as praiseworthy in itself; another is preferred in comparison with something worse. We rejoice in one way when a person is healthy, and in another when a sick person is improving. Indeed, in Scripture itself Sodom is said to have been justified in comparison with the crimes of the people of Israel (Ezekiel 16:52).

They apply this rule to all the lies presented in the ancient books that are not found, or cannot be found, to have been condemned: either they are approved on account of the character and hope of those making progress, or, because they signify something, they are not lies at all.

### 8.

For this reason, if, apart from the figurative meanings of the Lord’s actions and words, one considers the lives, conduct, deeds, and sayings of the saints in the books of the New Testament, nothing of this kind can be produced that invites imitation of lying.

Peter’s and Barnabas’s pretense was not only recorded but also censured and corrected (Galatians 2:12–13). For, contrary to what some think, the Apostle Paul did not circumcise Timothy because of the same pretense, nor did he himself celebrate certain sacraments according to Jewish ritual. [Note: Jerome, Letter 75 among the Augustinian letters, §§9–11.]

Rather, he acted from the freedom of his judgment, by which he preached that circumcision benefited neither Gentiles nor harmed Jews. Consequently, he judged that neither group should be compelled to adopt Jewish customs, nor the other deterred from the customs of their fathers.

Thus he says: “Was anyone called after being circumcised? Let him not draw back his foreskin. Was anyone called in uncircumcision? Let him not be circumcised. Circumcision is nothing, and uncircumcision is nothing, but the observance of God’s commandments. Let each person remain in the calling in which he was called” (1 Corinthians 7:18–20).

[Col. 0493]

For how can a foreskin be drawn back once it has been cut away? But by “let him not draw back” he meant, “Let him not live as though he had drawn back his foreskin”—that is, as though he had pulled the covering of flesh again over the part he had uncovered, and as though he had ceased to be a Jew. Elsewhere he says: “Your circumcision has become uncircumcision” (Romans 2:25).

The Apostle did not say this as though he were compelling either the Gentiles to remain uncircumcised or the Jews to remain in the customs of their fathers. Rather, he said it so that neither group would be compelled to enter the other’s way of life. [Note: Some manuscripts have: “so that neither person would be compelled to enter the other’s way of life.”] Each person was to have the freedom, not the necessity, of remaining in his own custom.

For if a Jew wished, where he disturbed no one, to withdraw from Jewish observances, the Apostle would not prohibit him, since he gave the counsel that they remain in those observances so that Jews, disturbed by superfluous matters, would not fail to come to what was necessary for salvation.

Nor would the Apostle have prohibited any Gentile who wished to be circumcised for the very purpose of showing that he did not detest circumcision as something harmful, but regarded it indifferently as a sign whose usefulness had already passed with time. For although salvation no longer came from it, it did not follow that destruction had to be feared from it.

Therefore, when Timothy had been called in uncircumcision, yet was descended from a Jewish mother and needed to show his relatives, in order to win them over, that he had not learned in Christian discipline to abominate the sacraments of the old Law, the Apostle circumcised him (Acts 16:1, 3). In this way they showed the Jews that Gentiles did not refuse to receive those sacraments because they were evil and had been dangerously observed by their ancestors, but because, after the coming of so great a sacrament—which the whole ancient Scripture had brought forth through prophetic figures over so many ages—they were no longer necessary for salvation. [Note: The manuscripts have: “so that in this way they might show.” The printed editions have: “so that in this way he might show.”]

He would also have circumcised Titus when the Jews pressed this upon him, unless the false brothers who had infiltrated the community had wanted it done for the purpose of spreading a report about Paul—as though he had yielded to their claim that the hope of evangelical salvation lay in circumcision of the flesh and similar observances, and that Christ was of no benefit to anyone without them (Galatians 2:3–4).

Yet Christ benefited nothing those who were circumcised with the intention of thinking that salvation lay there. Hence the saying: “Behold, I, Paul, say to you that if you are circumcised, Christ will be of no benefit to you” (Galatians 5:2).

From this freedom, then, Paul observed the customs of his fathers, taking care only to avoid and condemn the belief that Christian salvation was impossible without them. [Note: Only the Lovanienses edition has *christiano* (“for a Christian”); the other editions have *christiana* (“Christian salvation”).]

But by his pretense Peter, as though salvation lay in Judaism, was compelling the Gentiles to Judaize. This is shown by Paul’s words: “How can you compel the Gentiles to Judaize?” (Galatians 2:14). They would not have been compelled unless they saw Peter observing those customs as though salvation were impossible without them.

Peter’s pretense therefore must not be compared with Paul’s freedom. We ought to love Peter because he willingly accepted correction, not establish a lie even from Paul’s authority. Paul both recalled Peter publicly [Col. 0494] to the right path, so that the Gentiles would not be compelled by him to Judaize, and bore witness to his own preaching: although he was regarded as an enemy of the traditions of his fathers because he did not wish to impose them on the Gentiles, he did not disdain to observe them himself according to ancestral custom.

He thus sufficiently showed that, with Christ’s arrival, this remained in those traditions: they were neither harmful to Jews nor necessary for Gentiles, nor any longer salutary for anyone.

### 9.

If, then, authority for lying cannot be produced from the ancient books—either because what is accepted as having been done or said figuratively is not a lie, or because what is praised in comparison with worse behavior among those who have begun to improve is not proposed to good people for imitation—neither can it be produced from the books of the New Testament, since correction, rather than pretense, is to be imitated, just as Peter’s tears are to be imitated rather than his denial.

## CHAPTER VI
Mendacity is iniquity and brings death to the soul, and therefore it is not to be admitted even for anyone’s temporal salvation. With regard to those examples drawn from ordinary life, they assert this much more confidently. First, they teach from many testimonies of the holy Scriptures that lying is iniquity, and especially from what is written: “You hate, O Lord, all who work iniquity; you will destroy all who speak lies” (Ps. 5:7). Either Scripture, as it often does, explained the preceding verse in the one that follows, so that, since iniquity is usually a broader category, we should understand that, by naming lying, it intended to signify a species [Note: [Col. 0494] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions have “which species.”] of iniquity; or, if they think there is some distinction, lying is all the worse because “you will destroy” is more severe than “you hate.” For perhaps God hates someone with a certain mildness, so as not to destroy him; but whoever he destroys, he hates all the more intensely as he punishes more severely. He hates all who work iniquity, but he also destroys all who speak lies. Once this has been established, which of those who maintain these things will be moved by the examples in which it is said: “What if a person takes refuge with you whom your lie could free from death?” For the death that people foolishly fear [Note: [Col. 0494] Two manuscripts have “which fools fear.”], though they do not fear to sin, kills not the soul but the body, as the Lord teaches in the Gospel; hence he commands that it not be feared (Matt. 10:28). But the mouth that lies kills not the body but the soul. For it is written in the clearest terms: “The mouth that lies kills the soul” (Wis. 1:11). How, then, can it not be called utterly perverse to say that one person ought spiritually to die so that another may live bodily?

Even love of one’s neighbor receives its measure from each person’s own [Note: [Col. 0494] The printed editions have “from each person’s own love.” The word “love” is absent from the manuscripts.] love. “You shall love,” he says, “your neighbor as yourself” (Lev. 19:18; Matt. 22:39). How, then, does anyone love as himself someone for whose temporal life he himself forfeits eternal life? For if he were to lose even his own temporal life for that person’s temporal life, he would no longer be loving as himself but more than himself—a course that exceeds the rule of sound teaching. Far less, then, should he lose his own eternity by lying for another’s temporal life.

Certainly, a Christian will not hesitate to lose his own temporal life for the eternal life of his neighbor: for this example came first, so that the Lord himself might die for us. For this reason he also said: “This is my commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you. No one has greater love than this: that he lay down his life for his friends” (John 15:12–13). No one is so foolish as to say that the Lord, either by doing what he commanded or by commanding what he did, had any other purpose than to secure human beings’ everlasting salvation.

Since, therefore, eternal life is lost by lying, one must never lie for anyone’s temporal life. Indeed, these people who become angry and indignant if someone refuses to destroy his own soul by lying so that another may grow old in the flesh—what if someone could also be rescued from death by our theft, or by our adultery? Must one therefore steal or commit adultery? For they do not realize that this forces them to say that, if a man brings a noose and demands sexual intercourse, declaring that he will put it around his neck unless his demand is granted, one ought consent for the sake of saving his soul, as they themselves put it.

If that is absurd and wicked, why should anyone corrupt his own soul by lying so that another may live bodily, when, if he were to offer his own body to corruption for that purpose, everyone’s judgment would condemn him for wicked disgrace? Accordingly, in this question one must attend only to whether lying is iniquity. Since that is affirmed by the testimonies mentioned above, we must see that the question whether someone ought to lie for another’s salvation is equivalent to the question whether someone ought to be iniquitous for another’s salvation.

If the soul’s salvation rejects this—for it can be preserved only by righteousness—and commands us to place it before not only another’s temporal salvation but even our own, what remains, they ask, by which we should doubt that one must never lie at all? For it cannot be said that anything among temporal advantages, health, or bodily life is greater or more precious. Therefore, if even these must not be preferred to truth, what objection can be raised by which those who sometimes think that one ought to lie can maintain that lying is necessary?

## CHAPTER VII

### 10. One must not lie even for the sake of preserving bodily chastity. What lust is.

[Note: [Col. 0495] The manuscripts have “Chastity.” Below, most manuscripts, together with the Erfurt edition, have “a highly honorable person”; other manuscripts have “for a highly honorable person.” Morel, *Elem. Crit.*, p. 304, reads: “for bodily chastity indeed, since [it seems] very…”]

Since bodily chastity appears to involve a matter of great honor, and to demand a lie on its behalf—so that, if a rapist attacks and could be avoided by a lie, one should lie without hesitation—it can easily be answered that there is no bodily chastity unless it depends upon integrity of soul. Once that is shattered, bodily chastity must fall as well, even if it appears untouched; and therefore it must not be counted among temporal things, as though it could be taken away against one’s will.

The soul, then, must in no way corrupt itself by lying for the sake of its body, which it knows will remain uncorrupted if incorruption does not depart from the soul itself. For what the body suffers by force, without lust preceding it, should be called affliction rather than corruption. Or, if every affliction is corruption, not every corruption is shameful—only that which lust has brought about or to which lust has consented. And the more excellent the soul is than the body, the more criminally it is corrupted.

Chastity, therefore, can be preserved wherever corruption cannot be voluntary. Certainly, if a rapist attacks the body, and cannot be avoided either by opposing force or by any plan or lie, we must acknowledge that chastity cannot be violated by another’s lust. Since no one doubts that the soul is better than the body, the soul’s integrity must be preferred to bodily integrity—an integrity that can be preserved forever.

Who, however, would say that the soul of a liar is intact? For lust itself is rightly defined as “the soul’s desire by which any temporal things are preferred to eternal goods.” No one, therefore, can prove that lying is sometimes necessary unless he can show that some eternal good can be obtained by lying.

But since a person departs from eternity in proportion as he departs from truth [Note: [Col. 0496] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions have: “in proportion as he disagrees with truth; but whoever lies departs from truth; it is utterly absurd, etc.”], it is utterly absurd to say that, by departing from truth, someone can reach some good. Or, if there is some eternal good that does not include truth, it will not be true; and therefore it will not be good, because it will be false.

As the soul is to the body, so truth must be preferred to the soul itself, so that the soul desires truth not only more than the body but more than itself. In this way it will be more whole and chaste, when it enjoys truth’s immutability rather than its own mutability [Note: [Col. 0496] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions have “its own mobility.”].

If Lot, although so righteous that he was deemed worthy to receive even angels as guests, offered his daughters to the Sodomites to be violated, so that they would corrupt women’s bodies rather than men’s (Gen. 19:8), with how much greater care and steadfastness must the chastity of the soul be preserved in truth, since the soul itself is more truly preferred to its body than a male body is preferred to a female body?

## CHAPTER VIII

### 11. One must not lie in the effort to preserve others for eternal life.

If someone thinks that one ought to lie for another so that the other may live for the time being, or may not be offended in those things he loves greatly, and thus may be able to arrive through learning at eternal truth, he does not understand, first, that there is no disgraceful act which he would not be compelled to undertake on the same condition, as was already demonstrated above. Second, he does not understand that the authority of the teaching itself would be intercepted and utterly destroyed [Note: [Col. 0496] The Erfurt edition has “will intercept and utterly destroy”; Lovaniensis has “will begin utterly to destroy.” The readings are corrected from the manuscripts.] if, by our lie, we persuaded those whom we are trying to lead to it that one must sometimes lie.

Since saving doctrine consists partly in things to be believed and partly in things to be understood, and since one cannot arrive at what is to be understood unless what is to be believed is first believed, how can anyone believe a person who thinks that one must sometimes lie, lest he also lie at the very time when he commands us to believe? For how can it be known whether he too has some reason for an obliging lie, as he supposes, thinking that by a false account a frightened person can be restrained from lust, and imagining that in this way he can also promote spiritual welfare by lying?

Once this kind of lie is admitted and approved, the whole discipline of faith is utterly overturned. When it has been overturned, one cannot arrive at understanding either, for the sake of grasping which this discipline nourishes the little ones. Thus every doctrine of truth is removed, yielding to the most unrestrained falsehood, if a way is opened for a lie—even an “obliging” one [Note: [Col. 0497] The manuscripts have “as though obliging.”]—to enter from anywhere.

For either whoever lies places temporal advantages, whether his own or another’s, before truth—which could be more perverse?—or, by wishing to make someone capable of attaining truth with the aid of a lie, he blocks the way to truth. For while he wishes to be capable by lying, he becomes uncertain when he tells the truth [Note: [Col. 0497] Some manuscripts have “open.” Perhaps “covered” should be read.].

Therefore, either good people are not to be believed, or those whom we believe must sometimes lie are to be believed, or good people must not sometimes lie. Of these three, the first is destructive, the second foolish; it remains, then, that good people never lie.

## CHAPTER IX

### 12. Some think that a lie should be used to prevent the sexual violation which a person would himself suffer from another. Their argument and example are refuted. Another person’s sins are not to be imputed to someone who could have prevented them by a lesser sin of his own. Those who refuse to restrain sinners by sinning do not consent to their actions. Everyone ought to avoid the lesser sin that is his own rather than the greater sin that belongs to another. Whether one should lie to avoid bodily defilement. Lies that harm others must not be admitted to avoid bodily defilement.

Although this question has thus been considered and treated from both sides, a judgment cannot yet easily be reached. Those who say that no act is so evil that it should not be done to avoid something worse must still be heard carefully. They claim that human acts include not only whatever people do but also whatever they suffer with their consent.

Thus, if the situation arose that a Christian chose to burn incense to idols rather than consent to the sexual violation with which a persecutor threatened him unless he did so, they rightly seem to ask why he would not also lie to avoid so great a disgrace. For they say that the consent by which he preferred to suffer sexual violation rather than burn incense to idols is not a suffering but an act—one that he chose to avoid by burning incense. How much more readily, then, would he choose a lie if by lying he could remove such an enormous disgrace from his holy body?

### 13.

In this proposition, several matters may rightly be questioned: whether such consent should be counted as an act; whether consent should be called consent when it lacks approval; whether there is approval when one says, “It is better to suffer this than to do that”; whether he acted rightly by burning incense rather than suffering sexual violation; and whether, if the circumstance arose, he ought to lie rather than burn incense.

But if such consent is to be counted as an act, then even those who preferred to be killed rather than give false testimony are murderers—and, what is a more serious murder, murderers of themselves. For why should it not be said in this case that they killed themselves, because they chose this to be done to them rather than do what they were being compelled to do?

Or, if killing another is thought worse than killing oneself, what if this condition were proposed to a martyr: if he refused to give false testimony about Christ and sacrifice to demons, another person—not just anyone, but his own father—would be killed before his eyes, while even begging his son not to permit this by his persistence? Would it not be clear that, if he remained firm in his decision to give the most faithful testimony, only those who killed his father would be murderers, and not he a parricide?

Therefore, just as this man would not be a participant in so great a crime when he chose that his father be killed by others—even a sacrilegious man whose soul would be snatched away to punishment—rather than violate his faith by false testimony, so such consent would not make the other man a participant in so great a disgrace if he himself refused to do wrong, whatever others might do because he refused.

For what do such persecutors say except, “Do wrong, so that we may not do wrong”? Even if they would not have done it when we did it, we still ought not to assist them by our crime. But now, when they do it although they do not say this [Note: [Col. 0498] Thus the better manuscripts. The printed editions have “when they say this,” omitting “not.”], why should they be disgraceful and guilty together with us rather than alone?

It cannot be called consent, because we do not approve what they do. We are always wishing, and insofar as it lies within us preventing, them from doing it; and we not only do not join them in their act but condemn it with as much abhorrence as we can.

### 14.

“But how,” you ask, “does he not act together with them, when they would not do this if he did that?”

By this reasoning we break down a door with burglars, because if we did not close it, they would not break it. And we kill people with robbers if we happen to know that they are going to do so, because if we killed them before they could act, they would not kill others. Or, if someone tells us that he is going to commit parricide, we act together with him if, when we can kill him before he acts and cannot otherwise restrain or prevent him, we do not kill him.

For it can be said in exactly the same words: “You acted with him, because he would not have done this if you had done that.” I would wish neither evil to occur; but I could guard only against what lay within my power. The other evil, which was another person’s and which I could not extinguish by my command, I ought not to prevent by committing evil myself.

Therefore, the person who does not sin for another does not approve the other’s sin. Someone who would not wish either evil to be admitted approves neither; but he does not perpetrate, even by his own power, what pertains to himself, while what pertains to the other he condemns by his will alone.

And so, when those who propose that condition say, “If you do not burn incense, you will suffer this,” if he were to answer, “I choose neither; I detest both; I consent to none of this,” then, since these words and others like them would certainly be true, there would be no consent or approval on his part. Whatever he suffered at their hands would be counted as an injury received by him and as a sin committed by them.

“Should he, then,” someone may say, “have preferred to suffer sexual violation rather than burn incense?”

If you ask what he ought to have done, he ought to have done neither. For if I say that he ought to have done one of these things, I will approve one of them while disapproving both. But if the question is which of the two he ought rather to have avoided, when he could not avoid both but could avoid one, I will answer: his own sin rather than another’s, and the lesser sin that was his rather than the greater sin that was another’s.

For, to grant for the moment—subject to more careful inquiry—that sexual violation is graver than burning incense, the former was his own act, while the latter was another person’s act, even though he himself suffered it. And the act belongs to the person whose sin it is. For although murder is graver than theft, it is nevertheless worse to commit theft than to suffer murder.

Thus, if someone were told that he would be killed if he refused to commit theft—that is, that murder would be committed against him—since he could not avoid both, he would avoid what would be his own sin rather than what would be another’s. Nor would the latter thereby become his act because it was committed against him, or because he could avoid it by consenting to his own sin.

### 15.

The entire knot of this question therefore leads to the question whether no sin belonging to another—even if committed against you—is imputed to you if you could avoid it by a lesser sin of your own but do not [Note: [Col. 0499] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions have “so that you do not.”]; or whether every form of bodily defilement is excepted.

No one says that a person becomes unclean if he is killed, thrown into prison, held in chains, flogged, or afflicted by other torments and sufferings; if he is proscribed and subjected to the gravest losses, even to ultimate nakedness; or if he is stripped of his honors and receives enormous insults through every kind of abuse. Whatever of these things anyone suffers unjustly, no one is so insane as to say that he thereby becomes unclean.

But if he is covered with dung [Note: [Col. 0499] Four Gallican manuscripts have: “But if he says that he is made [unclean], or if such a thing,” etc. A little later, one Vatican manuscript has “or is thrust in.” But [another reading has], “if he suffers female things,” from which almost everyone’s sensibility recoils.], or if something of that kind is poured or thrust into his mouth, or if he suffers sexual violation, almost everyone’s judgment recoils, and they call him befouled [Note: [Col. 0499] The manuscripts have “sexually violated.”] and unclean.

The conclusion must therefore be this: of all sins belonging to others, except those that make the person against whom they are committed unclean, no one should avoid any by his own sins, either for his own sake or for anyone else’s, but should rather endure and bravely suffer them. And if he ought to avoid them by no sin of his own, then neither should he avoid them by lying.

But those acts that are committed against a person in such a way as to make him unclean, we ought to avoid even by our own sins; and consequently the acts done for the sake of avoiding that defilement should not be called sins. For whatever is done in such a way that, unless it were done, it would justly be condemned, is not a sin.

It follows that this too should not be called defilement when there is no possibility of avoiding it. Even then, the person who suffers it has something he can rightly do: patiently endure whatever he cannot avoid. No one acting rightly can be made unclean by any bodily contamination.

For every unrighteous person is unclean before God. Every righteous person, therefore, is clean—even if not before human beings, at least before God, who judges without error. Accordingly, even when a person suffers such a thing despite having the opportunity to avoid it, he does not become unclean by the contact itself [Col. 0500] but by the sin through which, although he could have avoided it, he did not [Note: [Col. 0500] The manuscripts have: “but by the sin, while he could have avoided it.”].

For whatever was done to avoid these things would not be a sin. Therefore, whoever has lied in order to avoid them does not sin.

### 16. Are some lies also to be excepted, so that it is better to suffer this than to commit that?

If this is so, it is not true that whatever is done to avoid that defilement is not a sin, since there are certain lies that would be graver to admit than to suffer that defilement. For if someone is being sought for sexual violation and could be concealed by a lie, who would dare say that one should not lie even then?

But if he could remain hidden by such a lie only if it harmed another person’s reputation—by falsely accusing that person of the defilement which the man being sought is about to suffer—as if one were to say to the searcher, naming some chaste man wholly unconnected with such crimes, “Go to him; he will arrange the person you can use more willingly, for he knows and favors such people,” and in this way the searcher could be diverted from the person he sought, I do not know whether one person’s reputation should be violated by a lie so that another person’s body may not be violated by another’s lust.

In no case should one lie for another by a lie that harms someone else, even if the person harmed is harmed less than the other would be harmed had you not lied. For one must not take another’s bread against his will, even if he is stronger, in order to feed someone weaker; nor may an innocent man be beaten against his will so that another may not be killed. Certainly, if they consent, let it be done; for they are not harmed when they wish it.

## CHAPTER X

### A lie must never be used in religious teaching.

But whether the reputation of a willing person should also be falsely damaged by an accusation of sexual misconduct so that sexual violation may be diverted from another’s body is a major question. I do not know whether it can easily be found how it could be just to stain the reputation of a willing person with a false accusation of sexual misconduct rather than to stain an unwilling person’s body by the sexual act itself.

### 17.

Nevertheless, if such a choice were offered to someone who preferred to burn incense to idols rather than suffer sexual violation, so that, if he wished to avoid the latter, he would violate Christ’s reputation by some lie, he would be utterly insane to do it.

I go further: he would be insane if, in order to avoid another person’s lust—so that he would not suffer in himself what he would not suffer through any lust of his own—he were to corrupt the Gospel of Christ by false praises of Christ, avoiding another’s bodily corruption more carefully than his own corruption of the doctrine of the sanctification of souls and bodies.

Therefore, all lies must be completely removed from religious teaching, and from all statements made for the sake of religious teaching when it is taught and learned. Nor should anyone believe that any reason at all can be found why one ought to lie in such matters, since one must not lie even in that doctrine in order to lead people more easily to the doctrine itself.

For once the authority of truth has been broken or even slightly diminished [Note: [Col. 0500] Some manuscripts have “removed.” Others have “diminished.”], everything will remain doubtful; and unless things are believed to be true, they cannot be held with certainty.

A speaker, disputant, preacher of eternal matters, narrator, or announcer of temporal matters that pertain to the building up of religion and piety may, therefore, conceal for a time whatever seems necessary to conceal [Col. 0501]; but he may never lie. Hence he may not conceal by lying.

## CHAPTER XI

### 18. Lies that harm either another person or the liar himself must also be rejected. A liar and a mendacious person differ.

Once this has been established first and most firmly, the other kinds of lies can be investigated with greater security. But it must also be considered next that all lies that unjustly harm someone must be rejected, because no injury, however slight, should be inflicted on anyone in order to ward off a greater injury from another.

Nor should those lies be admitted which, although they harm no one else, benefit no one and harm the very people who lie gratuitously. These are properly called “mendacious” persons. For there is a distinction between one who is lying and one who is mendacious.

A person who is lying includes someone who lies unwillingly; but a mendacious person loves to lie and dwells in his mind upon the pleasure of lying [Note: [Col. 0501] Some manuscripts have “in the love of lying.”].

Placed close to this group are those who wish to please people by lying—not in order to injure or insult anyone, for we have already excluded that kind—but in order to be agreeable in their speech. They differ from the group in which we placed the mendacious in this respect: the latter take pleasure in lying and rejoice in the deception itself; the former want to please through smooth speech, though they would rather please by telling the truth. But when they do not easily find truths that will gratify their listeners, they choose to lie rather than remain silent.

It is nevertheless difficult for such people ever to undertake an entirely false account. More often they weave falsehoods together with truths when their pleasantness deserts them.

These two kinds of lies do not harm those who believe them, because the believers are not deceived about religious and doctrinal truth, or about any advantage or benefit of their own. It is enough for them to judge that what is said could have happened and to place faith in a person whom they ought not rashly suppose to be lying.

For what harm is there if someone believes that another person’s father or grandfather was a good man, even though he was not, or that he reached as far as the Persians while serving in the army, even though he never left Rome?

But such lies greatly harm the liars themselves: the first group, because they abandon truth in such a way that they rejoice in deception; the second, because they prefer to please rather than tell the truth [Note: [Col. 0501] The Lovaniensis edition alone has: “to please people rather than to tell the truth.”].

## CHAPTER XII

### 19. Whether a lie that harms no one and benefits someone should be used. Whether there are honorable lies that benefit some and harm no one. Whether lying always means giving false testimony.

With these kinds of lies condemned without any hesitation, there follows, as though we were ascending step by step toward better things, the kind of lie commonly attributed to benevolent and good people: the lie by which the liar not only harms no one else but also benefits someone.

The entire dispute concerning this kind is whether the liar harms himself when he benefits another by acting against truth. Or, if only that truth is to be called truth which illuminates minds with its own intimate and immutable light, he certainly acts against some truth, because even if the bodily senses are deceived, the person who says that something is or is not so acts against truth when neither his mind, senses, opinion, nor faith tells him that it is so.

The great question, then, is whether someone does not harm himself by benefiting another in this way, or whether the benefit he provides another compensates for the harm to himself.

If this is so, then, consequently, a lie that harms no one ought also to benefit the liar himself. But these matters are connected, and once these points are granted, consequences follow that cause great confusion.

For if someone asks what harm it does to a man overflowing with abundant resources to lose one bushel from countless thousands of measures of grain—a bushel that could nevertheless provide necessary food to a thief—it will follow that theft can be committed without condemnation and false testimony spoken without sin. What could be more perverse than this?

Or, if someone else had stolen that bushel and you had seen it, and you were questioned, would you honorably lie on behalf of a poor person, while being blamed if you did it on behalf of your own poverty—as though you ought to love another more than yourself? Both alternatives, then, are disgraceful and must be avoided.

### 20.

But perhaps someone may think that an exception should be added, so that there are certain honorable lies which not only harm no one but also benefit someone—except those by which crimes are concealed and defended. Thus a lie would be disgraceful if, although harming no one and benefiting a poor person, it nevertheless concealed theft; but if it harmed no one and benefited someone without concealing or defending any sin, it would not be disgraceful.

For example, suppose someone hid his money while you watched, so that he would not lose it through theft or force, and, being questioned about it, you lied. You would harm no one and would benefit the person who needed that hidden thing to remain concealed [Note: [Col. 0502] Some manuscripts have “to be concealed.”], and by lying you would have covered no sin. For no one sins by hiding his own property when he fears losing it.

But if we do not sin by lying because we conceal no one’s sin, harm no one, and benefit someone, what are we to do with the sin of lying itself? For where it is written, “You shall not steal,” it is also written, “You shall not give false testimony” (Exod. 20:15–16).

Since each is separately prohibited, why is false testimony blameworthy when it conceals theft or some other sin, but not blameworthy when it is given by itself, without defending any sin, even though theft itself and the other sins are blameworthy in themselves? Is it not permitted to conceal sin, while it is permitted to commit it?

### 21.

If that is absurd, what shall we say? Is false testimony found only when someone lies in such a way that he either fabricates a crime against someone, conceals someone’s crime, or in some manner oppresses someone in court?

A witness appears to be necessary to the judge for knowledge of the case. But if Scripture used the word “witness” only in this sense, the Apostle would not say: “We are found to be false witnesses of God, because we testified concerning God that he raised Christ, whom he did not raise” (1 Cor. 15:15). In this way he shows that false testimony is a lie, even when it is spoken in someone’s false praise.

## CHAPTER XIII

### Whether one should lie so as not to betray either a murderer or an innocent person being sought for execution.

Firmus, bishop of Thagaste [Col. 0503], neither wishes to lie nor can be driven by torture to betray a person who is being sought. What someone who knows where the person being sought for execution is should answer when questioned.

Or does someone perhaps give false testimony when he lies only if he either fabricates or conceals someone’s sin, or harms someone in some way? For if a lie spoken against anyone’s temporal life is detestable, how much more so one spoken against eternal life—as is every lie told in religious teaching.

For this reason the Apostle calls it false testimony if someone lies about Christ, even when the lie appears to pertain to Christ’s praise. But if a lie is one that neither fabricates nor conceals anyone’s sin, is not sought by a judge, harms no one, and benefits someone, is it neither false testimony nor a blameworthy lie?

### 22.

What, then, if a murderer takes refuge with a Christian, or the Christian sees where he has taken refuge, and is questioned about this by someone seeking the murderer for punishment? Should he lie?

For how does he not conceal a sin by lying, when the person on whose behalf he lies has committed a criminal sin? Or is it because he is not questioned about the man’s sin but about the place where he is hiding?

Then is it evil to lie in order to conceal someone’s sin, but not evil to lie in order to conceal a sinner?

“Certainly,” someone might say. “For no one sins at the moment when he avoids punishment, but when he does something deserving punishment. It belongs to Christian discipline that we despair of no one’s correction and close the way of repentance to no one.”

What if, after being brought before a judge, you were questioned about the very place where the man is hiding? Will you say either, “He is not there,” when you know that he is, or, “I do not know and have not seen,” when you know and have seen?

Will you therefore give false testimony and kill your own soul so that the murderer may not be killed? Or will you lie until you come into the judge’s presence, but tell the truth once the judge asks, so that you may not be a false witness?

You yourself, then, will kill the man by betraying him. For divine Scripture also detests the betrayer. Or is a person not a betrayer if he tells the truth when questioned by a judge, but would be a betrayer if he voluntarily handed someone over to destruction?

What if you know where a righteous and innocent person is hiding and are questioned by a judge who has nevertheless been ordered by a higher authority to seize him for execution, so that the person questioning is an executor of the law rather than its maker? Will the lie you tell on behalf of the innocent therefore not be false testimony because the questioner is not himself the judge but only the executor?

What if the lawgiver himself questions you, or some unjust judge seeking an innocent person for punishment? What will you do? Will you be a false witness or a betrayer?

Will the person who voluntarily reveals a hidden murderer to a just judge be a betrayer, while the person who tells an unjust judge where the innocent person he seeks to kill is hiding, when the judge asks, not be a betrayer of the person who had entrusted himself to his loyalty?

Will you remain uncertain and undecided between the crime of false testimony and betrayal? Or, by remaining silent or declaring that you will not speak, will you certainly avoid both?

Why, then, should you not do this before coming before the judge, so that you may also avoid lying? For by avoiding lying, you will escape every false testimony—whether every lie is false testimony or not every lie is. But by avoiding only the false testimony that you recognize as such, you will not escape every lie.

How much more courageously and excellently, then, will you say: “I will neither betray nor lie”?

### 23.

This was done by a former bishop of the Church of Thagaste [Note: [Col. 0504] In an old Germanensis manuscript, “Thagasensis.” In the Colbertinus, “Tegasensis.”], named Firmus, whose will was firmer still.

When a man was being sought from him by order of the Emperor, through officials sent by the Emperor, and Firmus was concealing the fugitive, who had taken refuge with him, with all the diligence he could, he answered those who were searching that he could neither lie nor betray the man. He endured many bodily tortures—for the Emperors were not yet Christians—and remained firm in his decision.

Then he was brought before the Emperor and appeared so extraordinary that he obtained without difficulty the pardon of the man he had protected.

What could be stronger or more steadfast than this?

But someone more timid may say: “I can be prepared to endure any torture, even to undergo death, so as not to sin. But since it is not a sin to lie in such a way that you harm no one, give no false testimony, and benefit someone, it is foolish and a serious sin needlessly to endure torture and perhaps to throw away a useful life and salvation before those who rage against you.”

I ask him why he fears what is written, “You shall not give false testimony” (Exod. 20:16), but does not fear what is said to God: “You will destroy all who speak lies” (Ps. 5:7).

“It is not written,” he says, “ ‘every lie’; I understand it as if it were written, ‘You will destroy all who give false testimony.’”

But neither does it say there, “every false testimony.” “It is placed there,” he says, “among the things that are evil in every respect.”

And what of the command found there, “You shall not kill” (Exod. 20:13)? If killing is evil in every respect, how will the righteous be excused who, after the law was given, killed many people?

The answer is that the person who is a minister of a righteous commandment is not himself the killer.

I therefore understand their fear in this way: nevertheless, I think that the admirable man who was unwilling either to lie or to betray a person understood what was written better and more faithfully, and courageously fulfilled what he understood.

24. But sometimes a situation of this kind arises: we are not asked where the person being sought is, nor compelled to betray him if he is concealed in such a way that he cannot easily be found unless betrayed; rather, we are asked whether he is in that place or not. If we know that he is there, we betray him by keeping silent—or even by saying that we will in no way say whether he is there or not. For the questioner infers from this that he is there: if he were not, the only answer that someone unwilling both to lie and to betray a person could give would be that he is not there. Thus, through our silence or such words, the person is betrayed, so that the questioner, if he has the authority, may enter and find him—even though our lie could have turned him away from finding the man [Col. 0505].

Therefore, if you do not know where he is, there is no reason to conceal the truth; you must admit that you do not know. But if you know where he is, whether he is where he is being sought or elsewhere, then when asked whether he is there or not, you must not say, “I will not tell you what you are asking”; rather, say, “I know where he is, but I will never point him out.” For if you give no answer concerning one particular place and admit that you will not betray him, it is as though you pointed to that very place with your finger: a definite suspicion is aroused. If, however, you first admit that you know where he is but will not say, the investigator may perhaps be diverted from that place, and the burden will then fall upon you to betray where he is. For the sake of such fidelity and humanity, whatever you bravely endure is judged not merely blameless but praiseworthy—except only those things which, if a person suffers them, he is said to endure not bravely but immodestly and disgracefully. This is the final kind of lie, which must be examined more carefully.

## CHAPTER XIV

### 25. Eight kinds of lies

The first kind, which must be avoided and fled from far away, is the lie told in religious doctrine; no one should ever be driven to this lie under any condition. The second is told in order to injure someone unjustly; it is such that it benefits no one and harms someone. The third benefits one person in such a way that it harms another, although it does not harm him with respect to bodily impurity. The fourth is told merely from the desire to lie and deceive: it is a sheer lie. The fifth is told from the desire to please, through agreeable speech.

After all these have been utterly avoided and rejected, there follows the sixth kind, which harms no one and benefits someone: for example, if someone knows where another person’s money is hidden so that it may be unjustly taken, and, when anyone asks him, pretends not to know. The seventh likewise harms no one and benefits someone—except when a judge is asking: for example, when someone unwilling to betray a person sought for execution tells a lie, whether the person is just and innocent or even guilty, because Christian discipline requires that one despair neither of anyone’s correction nor close the door to anyone’s repentance [Note: [Col. 0505] The Lyon edition omits “except when a judge is asking” and encloses the following words in brackets; Erasmus omits them altogether: “for example, when someone unwilling to betray a person . . . close the door to anyone’s repentance.” M.].

We have dealt sufficiently with these two kinds, which commonly provoke considerable controversy, and have shown what our judgment is: that these kinds also should be avoided by brave, faithful, and truthful men and women, even when this requires them to accept hardships that can be endured honorably and bravely.

The eighth kind of lie harms no one and serves to protect someone from bodily impurity—specifically, the kind mentioned above. For the Jews even considered it impurity to eat with unwashed hands (Matt. 15:2, 20). Or if someone calls this impurity as well, it is nevertheless not the sort for the avoidance of which one ought to lie. But if a lie inflicts an injury upon someone, even if it protects a person from that impurity which all human beings reject and detest, the question whether one ought to lie in this case, when the lie causes an injury that does not belong to the kind of impurity now under discussion, is a separate matter. For the question is no longer about lying, but whether an injury should be inflicted upon someone—not by means of a lie—in order to drive away that impurity from another person. I would judge that this should never be done, although the injuries proposed may be very slight, such as the one I mentioned above concerning the loss of a single bushel; and although they may raise the troubling question whether we ought not to inflict even such an injury upon someone if by doing so another person could be defended or protected from suffering rape. But, as I said, that is a separate question.

## CHAPTER XV

### Divine authorities by which lying is prohibited, and other commands to be understood from the deeds of the saints. The command to offer the other cheek to one who strikes.
