The command not to swear at all. The command not to think about tomorrow. The command that the Apostles carry nothing with them on their journey

Let us now complete the undertaking we began: whether one ought to lie if even an unavoidable alternative is proposed, so that we must either do this or suffer rape or some other detestable defilement—even if by lying we injure no one.

### 26.

This matter will allow some room for consideration if we first examine carefully the divine authorities that prohibit lying. For if they themselves leave no room, we seek an escape in vain: God’s command must be obeyed in every way, and in whatever we suffer while keeping his command, God’s will must be followed with equanimity. But if some way out is permitted, lying in such a situation should not be refused.

For this reason, the divine Scriptures contain not only God’s commands but also the lives and conduct of the righteous, so that, if it should be unclear how a command is to be understood, this may be discerned from the deeds of the righteous. We must therefore set aside those deeds which anyone may refer to an allegorical meaning, although no one doubts that they actually occurred—as is generally the case with nearly everything in the books of the Old Testament. For who would dare to affirm that anything there does not belong to a figurative prophecy? The Apostle, after all, asserts that even the sons of Abraham—who plainly are said to have been born and to have lived according to the natural succession by which peoples are propagated, since they were not monsters or prodigies born to direct the mind toward some symbolic meaning—nevertheless signify the two Testaments (Gal. 4:22–24). He also says that the marvelous benefit God bestowed upon the people of Israel in rescuing them from the slavery under which they were oppressed in Egypt, and the punishment of vengeance when they sinned in the wilderness, occurred figuratively (1 Cor. 10:1–11). What deeds, then, can you find by which you could invalidate this rule and presume to assert that they should not be referred to some figure?

With these matters excepted, the deeds performed by the saints in the New Testament, where the commendation of imitable conduct is most evident, may serve as examples for understanding the commands arranged in Scripture.

### 27.

For example, when we read in the Gospel, “If you have received a slap, prepare the other cheek” (Matt. 5:39), we find no example of patience more powerful or excellent than that of the Lord himself. Yet when he was struck with a slap, he did not say, “Here is the other cheek,” but said, “If I have spoken wrongly, testify to the wrong; but if I have spoken rightly, why do you strike me?” (John 18:23). Here he showed that the preparation of the other cheek is to be made in the heart.

The Apostle Paul certainly understood this as well. For when he himself was struck before the high priest, he did not say, “Strike the other cheek,” but said, “God will strike you, whitewashed wall! You sit to judge me according to the law, and contrary to the law you order me to be struck” (Acts 23:3). He was perceiving with profound insight that the Jewish priesthood had by then become such that it shone outwardly in name but inwardly was filthy with muddy lusts. He saw in the spirit that it would pass away under the Lord’s vengeance when he said this. Nevertheless, his heart was prepared not only to receive other blows but also to endure any kind of torture for the truth, while still loving those from whom he suffered them.

### 28.

It is also written, “But I say to you, do not swear at all.” Yet the Apostle himself swore in his Letters (Rom. 9:1; Phil. 1:8; Gal. 1:20). In this way he showed how the command “I say to you, do not swear at all” should be understood: namely, so that by swearing one does not proceed to swearing easily, from ease into habit, and then from habit fall into perjury.

For this reason he is not found to have sworn except in writing, where more careful reflection does not have a hasty tongue. This too is “from evil,” as it is said, “Whatever is more than this is from evil” (Matt. 5:34, 37)—not, however, from his own evil, but from the weakness of those to whom he was trying in this way to establish the truth of what he said. I do not know whether any Scripture reports him swearing while speaking rather than writing.

Yet the Lord says not to swear at all; he did not grant permission for this to be allowed to writers. But since it is impious to call Paul guilty of violating the command, especially in Letters written and published for the spiritual life and salvation of peoples, we must understand the word “at all” as intended to mean that, insofar as it lies within you, you should neither seek nor love nor desire an oath as though it were a good, with any pleasure in it.

### 29.

The same applies to the command, “Do not think about tomorrow,” and, “Therefore do not think about what you will eat, or what you will drink, or what you will wear” (Matt. 6:34, 25). Yet we see that the Lord himself had a money box into which the contributions were placed, so that they could be kept for necessary uses at the appropriate time (John 12:6). We also see that the Apostles made provision for the needs of the brothers, not only for the next day but even for a more extended period of impending famine, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 11:28–30). It is therefore sufficiently clear that these commands are to be understood in such a way that we do nothing concerning the acquisition of temporal goods merely from love of them or from fear of want, as though compelled by necessity.

### 30.

The Apostles were also told to live from the Gospel, carrying nothing with them on their journey. In one passage the Lord himself indicated why he said this when he added, “For the laborer is worthy of his wages” (Luke 10:4, 7; Matt. 10:10). This sufficiently shows that the practice was permitted, not commanded, so that someone who accepted from those to whom he preached something for the necessities of this life would not think that he was doing something illicit in the work of preaching the word.

That it may nevertheless be more praiseworthy not to do so is clearly demonstrated by the Apostle Paul. When he said, “Let the one who is instructed in the word share all good things with the one who instructs him” (Gal. 6:6), and showed in many passages that this should beneficially be done by those to whom he preached the word, he nevertheless said, “I have not used this authority” (1 Cor. 9:12). Thus, in saying these things, the Lord granted authority; he did not impose it as a command.

In this way, since we are unable to understand many things in words, we gather from the deeds of the saints how we ought to interpret what might easily be taken in another direction unless their example recalled us to the proper one.

## CHAPTER XVI

### The two mouths, of the voice and of the heart: concerning which mouth it is said, “The mouth that lies,” and so forth. The mouth of the heart also demonstrated in the Gospel. Whether only that lie by which someone is slandered is forbidden. Three interpretations of the passage in Ecclesiasticus, chapter 7, verse 14

### 31.

Thus, concerning what is written, “But the mouth that lies kills the soul,” it must be asked of which mouth he spoke. Scripture often uses “mouth” to signify the very receptacle of the heart, where whatever is expressed through the voice, when we speak truthfully, is conceived and decided upon. Thus, a person lies in his heart when he approves of a lie; but someone may not lie in his heart if he expresses through his voice something other than what is in his mind, recognizing that he is admitting an evil in order to avoid a greater evil, while disapproving of both.

Those who maintain this say that the statement, “Who speaks truth in his heart” (Ps. 14:3), should likewise be understood in this way: truth must always be spoken in the heart, but not always with the bodily mouth, if some reason for avoiding a greater evil requires that something other than what is in the mind be expressed aloud.

That there is a mouth of the heart can already be understood from the fact that wherever there is speech, it is not unreasonable to understand a mouth to be present. Nor would it rightly be said, “Who speaks in his heart,” unless a mouth were also rightly understood to be in the heart.

Moreover, even in the passage where it is written, “The mouth that lies kills the soul,” if the context of the reading is considered, perhaps nothing other than the mouth of the heart should be understood. For the response there is obscure, whereas human beings cannot hear what lies hidden in a person unless the mouth of the heart corresponds with the bodily mouth. Scripture says that this mouth reaches the hearing of the Spirit of the Lord, who has filled the world; in that passage it even mentions lips, voice, and tongue. Yet understanding does not allow all of this to be taken as referring to anything except the heart, because it says that what is spoken is not hidden from the Lord, whereas what is spoken by that sound which reaches our ears is not hidden from human beings either.

The passage reads as follows:

> For the spirit of wisdom is kindly, and he will not free the blasphemer from his lips; for God is witness of his inward parts, the true searcher of his heart and hearer of his tongue. For the Spirit of the Lord has filled the world, and he who contains all things has knowledge of the voice. Therefore the one who speaks unrighteous things cannot remain hidden, nor will the judging condemnation pass him by. For there will be an inquiry into the thoughts of the ungodly, and the hearing of his words will come from the Lord, for the correction of his iniquities. For the ear of jealousy hears all things, and the tumult of murmuring will not be hidden. Therefore guard yourselves from murmuring, which profits nothing, and refrain from slanderous speech, for an obscure response will not go unnoticed. But the mouth that lies kills the soul. (Wis. 1:6–11)

He therefore appears to threaten those who think that what they devise and turn over in their hearts is obscure and secret. He wished to show that it is so clear to the ears of God that he even called it a tumult.

### 32.

We also plainly find the mouth of the heart in the Gospel, so that in one passage the Lord is found to mention both the bodily mouth and the mouth of the heart. He says:

> Are you also still without understanding? Do you not understand that everything entering the mouth goes into the stomach and is expelled into the sewer? But the things that proceed from the mouth come out of the heart, and these defile a person. For from the heart proceed evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, sexual immoralities, thefts, false testimonies, and blasphemies. These are the things that defile a person. (Matt. 15:16–20)

If here you understand only one mouth, namely the bodily mouth, how will you understand the words, “But the things that proceed from the mouth come out of the heart,” since spittle [Note: [Col. 0509] Lov. reads “sputum”; Erasmus and the manuscripts read “sputus.”] and vomit also proceed from the mouth? Perhaps a person is not defiled when he eats something unclean but is defiled when he vomits it up. Since that is utterly absurd, it remains for us to understand that the Lord explained the mouth of the heart when he said, “The things that proceed from the mouth come out of the heart.”

A theft can be—and often is—committed in silence, without bodily voice or mouth. It would therefore be the height of madness to understand the passage in such a way that we think someone is contaminated by the sin of theft only when he admits or reveals it, while considering him undefiled when he commits it secretly. But if we refer the statement to the mouth of the heart, then no sin at all can be committed silently; for it is not committed unless it proceeds from that inward mouth.

### 33.

Just as it is asked of which mouth he spoke when he said, “The mouth that lies kills the soul,” so it may be asked of which lie. He appears to be speaking particularly of the lie by which someone is slandered. For he says, “Therefore refrain from murmuring, which profits nothing, and spare yourselves slanderous speech.”

Such slander is produced by malice when someone not only utters through the bodily mouth and voice what he fabricates against another person, but also silently wishes that person to be believed to be such. This is indeed to slander with the mouth of the heart, which Scripture says cannot be obscure or hidden from God.

### 34.

For what is written elsewhere, “Do not desire to lie with every lie,” is not intended, according to some, to mean that no one should ever lie with any lie. Thus, when someone says that this testimony of Scripture so generally condemns every lie that, even if someone wishes to lie but does not actually lie, the will itself must already be condemned, he interprets the words as though they said—not, “Do not lie with every lie,” but, “Do not desire to lie with every lie”—so that no one would dare either to lie or even to desire to lie with any lie [Note: [Col. 0510] The manuscripts read, “but even to desire to lie.”].

## CHAPTER XVII

### Three interpretations also of Psalm 5:7. How the command forbidding false testimony is to be understood

Someone else says that the statement, “Do not desire to lie with every lie,” means that lying is to be expelled and kept away from the mouth of the heart. Thus, one should abstain with the bodily mouth from certain lies, especially those relating to religious doctrine; but from others one need not abstain with the bodily mouth if the avoidance of a greater evil requires it. With the mouth of the heart, however, we must utterly abstain from every lie.

Here the words “Do not desire” should be understood in this way. The will itself is taken as the mouth of the heart, so that lying does not belong to the mouth of the heart when, while avoiding a greater evil, we lie unwillingly.

There is also a third interpretation, according to which “every” is understood in such a way as to allow lying about certain matters. It would be as if he said, “Do not desire to believe every person”—not advising that no one be believed, but that not everyone be believed, while some are.

The following words, “For its persistence will not prosper” (Ecclus. 7:14), sound as though they prohibit not lying itself but persistent lying—that is, the habit and love of lying.

Anyone who thinks that every lie may be used will consequently fall into error; for then he will not avoid even the lie told in religious and pious doctrine, than which it is difficult to find anything more wicked—not merely among all lies but among all sins. The same is true of anyone who gives the assent of his will to some lie, however easy or harmless, so that he lies willingly and gladly rather than unwillingly for the sake of escaping a greater evil.

Thus, in this statement three interpretations are possible:

1. “Do not lie with every lie”: not only do not lie, but do not even desire to lie.

2. “Do not desire to lie,” but lie unwillingly when something more serious must be avoided.

3. “Do not lie with every lie,” so that, with certain lies excepted, the rest are permitted.

Of these, one is found on behalf of those who never approve of lying, while two are found on behalf of those who think that one may sometimes lie.

Yet I do not know whether the following words, “For its persistence will not prosper,” can support the first of these three interpretations—unless perhaps the command is addressed to the perfect, who must never merely lie or even desire to lie, while persistent lying is not permitted even to those who are making progress.

It would be as though, when it was commanded that one must never lie at all, nor even have the will to lie, someone objected by citing examples that had been approved by great authority as involving lies. The answer would be that those examples belong to people who are making progress and who possess, in accordance with this life, some measure of the ministry of mercy; but that every lie is so evil, and must be avoided in every way by perfect and spiritual souls, that even those who are making progress must not be permitted to persist in it.

We have already spoken of the Egyptian midwives, who were approved when they lied because they were progressing by disposition toward what is better: for there is some degree of progress toward loving true and eternal salvation when someone lies mercifully even for the sake of another person’s merely mortal safety (above, chap. 5, §§5–7).

### 35.

Again, concerning what is written, “You will destroy all who speak lies,” one person says that no lie is excepted here, but that every lie is condemned.

Another says: “Certainly—but those who speak a lie from the heart,” according to the preceding discussion. For the person who hates the necessity of lying—which he understands as the punishment of this mortal life—speaks truth in his heart.

Another says: “God will indeed destroy all who speak lies, but not every lie. For the Prophet was then indicating a certain lie in which no one is spared: namely, when someone refuses to confess his sins, instead defending them and refusing to repent. It is not enough that he practices iniquity; he must also wish to appear just and refuse to submit to the medicine of confession.”

Thus the distinction in the words themselves seems to convey something different:

> You have hated all who practice iniquity (Ps. 5:7),

but you will not destroy them if, by repenting, they speak truth in confession, so that by doing this truth they come to the light, as it is said in the Gospel according to John: “But the one who does the truth comes to the light” (John 3:21).

You will, however, destroy all who not only practice what you hate but also speak lies, pretending to possess a false righteousness and refusing to confess their sins in repentance [Note: [Col. 0511] The printed editions add “iniquity” here, but this word is absent from the manuscripts].

### 36.

Concerning false testimony, which is included among the Ten Commandments of the Law, it cannot in any way be maintained that one should preserve love of truth in the heart while uttering something false to the person before whom the testimony is given. When testimony is given to God alone, truth must be embraced in the heart alone; but when it is given to a human being, truth must also be spoken with the bodily mouth, because a human being does not inspect the heart.

Yet it is entirely reasonable to ask about the testimony itself: before whom is someone a witness? We are not witnesses whenever we speak with anyone, but before those who ought, and for whom it is useful, to know or believe the truth through us. Such a person is a judge, so that he may not err in judging; or someone being instructed in religious doctrine, so that he may not err in faith or waver in doubt because of the authority of the teacher himself.

But when someone asks you or wishes to learn from you something that does not concern him, or that it is not useful for him to know, he is seeking not a witness but a betrayer. Therefore, if you lie to him, you may perhaps avoid giving false testimony, but you will certainly not avoid lying.

## CHAPTER XVIII

### How another passage of Scripture is to be understood. What has so far been discovered by the preceding inquiry on both sides. Error in measuring evils according to desire and habit. Our twofold life. Whether lesser sins may be admitted, if not for temporal usefulness, at least for the preservation of holiness

Apart, then, from the fact that it is never lawful to give false testimony, the question is whether it is ever lawful to lie. Or, if every lie is false testimony, it must be considered whether compensation is permitted, so that one may say that it is done for the sake of avoiding a greater sin. Thus the command, “Honor your father and your mother” (Exod. 20:16, 12), is disregarded when a higher duty takes precedence [Note: [Col. 0512] Several manuscripts read “a stronger duty”]; consequently, the man who is called by the Lord himself to announce the kingdom of God is forbidden to pay his father even the final honor of burial (Matt. 8:22).

### 37.

Again, concerning what is written, “The son who receives the word will be far from destruction; but the one who receives it receives it for himself, and nothing false proceeds from his mouth” (Prov. 29:27), someone says that the phrase “the son who receives the word” should be understood as referring to no other word than the word of God, which is truth.

Therefore, “the son who receives truth will be far from destruction” refers to the statement, “You will destroy all who speak lies.” But what follows—“the one who receives it receives it for himself”—what else does it suggest than what the Apostle says: “Let each one test his own work, and then he will have glory in himself and not in another” (Gal. 6:4)?

For the one who receives the word—that is, truth—not for himself but to please human beings does not preserve it when he sees that they can be pleased by a lie. But the one who receives it for himself has nothing false proceeding from his mouth, because even when a lie pleases human beings, the person who has received for himself the truth that would please God, not them, does not lie.

There is therefore no reason to say here, “God will indeed destroy all who speak lies, but not every lie,” since every lie has been universally cut away in the statement, “Nothing false proceeds from his mouth.”

Another person, however, says that this should be understood in the same way that the Apostle Paul understood what the Lord said: “But I say to you, do not swear at all” (Matt. 5:34). Here too, every oath is cut away—but from the mouth of the heart, so that it would never be made with the approval of the will, but only from the necessity created by another’s weakness, that is, from the evil of another person, who seems unable otherwise to be persuaded of what is being said unless an oath establishes its credibility; or from that evil of our own by which, still enclosed in the skins of this mortality, we cannot display our heart. If we could do so, there would be no need for an oath.

Nevertheless, throughout this entire statement, if the words “the son who receives the word will be far from destruction” are understood as referring to the Truth itself, through which all things were made and which always remains unchanging—and if religious doctrine strives to lead us to contemplate that Truth—then the statement “nothing false proceeds from his mouth” may be understood as meaning that he says nothing false relating to doctrine. This kind of lie must not be undertaken under any compensation whatsoever; it must be avoided utterly and above all.

Or, if the words “nothing false” are absurdly understood unless they refer to every lie [Note: [Col. 0512] The Lyon edition alone reads: “Just as the statement ‘nothing false’ is absurdly understood unless it refers to every lie, so also the statement that follows,” which is inferior], someone who thinks that one may sometimes lie maintains that the words “from his mouth” should be understood, according to the preceding discussion, as referring to the mouth of the heart.

### 38.

Certainly, throughout this entire discussion, although it alternates between those who assert that one must never lie and cite divine testimonies to that effect, and those who contradict them and seek a place for lying among the very words of the divine testimonies, no one can claim to find either in the example or in the words of Scripture that any lie should appear lovable or not hateful, but only that one should sometimes do what one hates by lying, so that what is more detestable may be avoided.

People err in this matter because they subordinate what is precious to what is less valuable. Once you grant that some evil may be admitted to prevent another, more serious evil, each person measures evil not by the rule of truth but according to his own desire and habit. He considers more serious whatever he himself fears more, rather than what truly ought to be avoided more.

This entire vice arises from a perversion of love. For there are two lives of ours: one eternal, which is promised by God, and the other temporal, in which we now live. When someone begins to love this temporal life more than the eternal one, he thinks that everything must be done for the sake of the life he loves. He considers no sins more serious than those that injure this life, unjustly and unlawfully deprive it of some advantage, or take it away altogether by inflicting death.

Thus they hate thieves, robbers, abusers, torturers, and murderers more than the sexually promiscuous, drunkards, and the dissolute, provided that the latter do not trouble anyone. They do not understand—or care at all—that these people injure God, not to any disadvantage of his, certainly, but to their own great destruction, since they corrupt his gifts in themselves, including temporal gifts, and by those very corruptions turn away from eternal things.

This is especially so if they have already begun to be the temple of God. The Apostle says this to all Christians:

> Do you not know that you are the temple of God and that the Spirit of God dwells in you? Whoever corrupts the temple of God, God will corrupt that person. For the temple of God is holy, and that is what you are. (1 Cor. 3:16–17)

### 39.

All these sins, whether they inflict injury upon people in the advantages of this present life [Note: [Col. 0513] So the manuscripts; the printed editions read “in the disadvantages”], or whether people corrupt themselves while harming no one against that person’s will, all these sins, then, even if they seem to serve this temporal life in some pleasure or advantage—for no one commits any of them with another purpose or end—nevertheless hinder those entangled in them in every way from attaining the life that is eternal.

Some of these sins hinder only those who commit them; others hinder both those who commit them and those against whom they are committed. When advantages belonging to this life are preserved and then taken away by aggressors, only those who take them away sin and are hindered from eternal life, not those against whom they act.

Therefore, even if someone consents to having such things taken from him, either so that he may not do something evil or so that he may not suffer some greater harm in those very matters, he not only does not sin but acts bravely and praiseworthily in the former case, and usefully and without blame in the latter.

But when aggressors wish to violate those things preserved for the sake of holiness and religion, they should, if the circumstances and opportunity arise, be ransomed even by lesser sins—but not by injuries to others. In that case, the things undertaken to avoid more serious sins cease to be sins.

For just as, in matters of utility—such as money or some other bodily advantage—the loss incurred for the sake of a greater gain is not called a loss, so in sacred matters what is undertaken to prevent the commission of something more serious is not called a sin. Or, if what someone loses in order not to lose more is still called a loss, let this also be called a sin, provided that no one doubts that it must be undertaken in order to avoid a greater evil, just as no one doubts that, to avoid a greater loss, one must suffer the lesser.

## CHAPTER XIX

### Three things to be preserved for the sake of holiness: bodily modesty, purity of heart, and truth in doctrine

These, then, are the things that must be preserved for the sake of holiness: bodily modesty, purity of soul, and truth in doctrine.

No one violates bodily modesty when the soul neither consents nor grants permission. Whatever happens to our body against our will, when we grant it no power over us and it occurs through greater force, is not immodesty. There may, however, be a reason for permitting it; there can be no reason for consenting to it.

We consent when we approve and desire; but we permit something even unwillingly, for the sake of avoiding some greater disgrace. Consent to bodily immodesty certainly also violates purity of heart. Purity of heart consists in a good will and sincere love, which is corrupted only when we love and desire what truth teaches us ought not to be loved or desired.

We must therefore preserve the sincerity of our love for God and neighbor, for it is in this that purity of heart is sanctified. We must act with whatever strength we possess, and with devout supplication, so that when someone seeks to violate our bodily modesty, even the soul’s most remote sense—the part entangled with the flesh—may not be touched by any pleasure. If this cannot be achieved, at least the purity of the mind must be preserved by refusing consent.

In purity of heart, we must preserve innocence and benevolence insofar as these concern love of neighbor, and piety insofar as it concerns love of God. Innocence is the quality by which we harm no one; benevolence is the quality by which we also benefit whomever we can; piety is the quality by which we worship God.

Truth in doctrine, religion, and piety is violated only by a lie. The highest and innermost Truth, of which this doctrine is the expression, cannot in any way be violated. We shall not reach it, remain in it completely, or cling to it utterly until “this corruptible puts on incorruption, and this mortal puts on immortality” (1 Cor. 15:53).

But because all piety in this life is an exercise by which we strive toward that life, and because this doctrine guides that exercise by conveying and communicating the Truth itself through human words and the signs of bodily sacraments, this truth—which can be corrupted by lying—must therefore be preserved especially inviolate, so that, if something in the purity of the heart should be violated, there may be a source from which it can be restored.

For once the authority of doctrine has been corrupted, there can be no progress or return to purity of heart [Col. 0515].

## CHAPTER XX
41. One must not lie for the sake of bodily chastity. Whence “faith” is so called. Purity of soul.

From all this, then, the following conclusion is established: a lie that does not violate the doctrine of piety, nor piety itself, nor innocence, nor benevolence, nevertheless ought not to be admitted for the sake of bodily chastity. And yet, if someone proposed to himself that he should love truth in this way—not only the truth that is contemplated, but also the truth expressed in stating what is true in each particular sphere of things—and that he should utter with the bodily mouth [Note: [Col. 0515] Thus in the manuscripts. In the printed editions, “by bodily movement.”] no statement otherwise than it has been conceived and perceived in the mind, so that he would prefer the truthful beauty of faith not only to gold, silver, gems, and pleasant estates, but also to all temporal life itself and every bodily advantage, I do not know whether anyone could reasonably be said to be mistaken.

And if he rightly placed this above all such things of his own and valued it more highly, he would also rightly place it above the temporal goods of other people, whom by his innocence and benevolence he ought to preserve and assist. For he would love perfect faith—not only believing well what was told him by an excellent and trustworthy authority, but also faithfully stating what he himself judged ought to be said, and saying it.

For in the Latin language *fides* (“faith”) is so called from the fact that what is said is made to be so; and it is clear that a liar does not exhibit this. Even if faith is less seriously violated when someone lies in such a way that no inconvenience or injury results from his being believed, and when the intention is added of preserving either someone’s safety or bodily chastity, it is nevertheless violated; and what is violated is the purity and sanctity of soul that ought to be preserved.

Hence we are compelled to place perfect faith—even before bodily chastity—not according to human opinion, which is for the most part in error, but according to truth itself, which surpasses all things and alone is unconquerable. For purity of soul is ordered love, not subjecting greater things to lesser. Whatever can be violated in the body is certainly less than whatever can be violated in the soul.

Indeed, when someone lies for the sake of bodily chastity, he sees that it is not his own lust but another’s that threatens his body if it is violated; nevertheless, he takes care that he not at least become a participant by permitting it. But where can that permission exist except in the soul? Therefore bodily chastity too cannot be violated except in the soul. If the soul neither consents nor permits it, then whatever another’s lust may have perpetrated upon the body, bodily chastity is not rightly said to have been violated.

It follows that purity of soul must be guarded all the more carefully in the soul, in which the protection of bodily chastity resides. Therefore both things that are within our power must be fortified and enclosed by holy conduct and behavior, lest they be violated from another quarter. But when both cannot be preserved, who does not see what must be disregarded in place of what, when he sees what must be preferred to what: soul to body, or body to soul; purity of soul to bodily chastity, or bodily chastity to purity of soul; and what must be more carefully avoided in sins, permitting another’s act or committing one’s own?

## CHAPTER XXI

### 42. Epilogue to the preceding arguments. One must never lie in any of the eight kinds of lie enumerated. How blind are the defenders of lying.

When all the evidence has thus been examined, it becomes clear that those testimonies of Scripture give no other warning than that one must never lie at all—since, so far as concerns those Scriptures that refer to no figurative meaning, no examples of lying are found in the conduct and deeds of the saints that deserve imitation, as in the historical events recorded in the Acts of the Apostles. Everything in the Gospel concerning the Lord that appears to the less instructed to be a lie has a figurative meaning.

And when the Apostle says, “I have become all things to all people, that I might win all” (I Cor. IX, 22), it is rightly understood that he did this not by lying but by compassion: he acted with such love toward their liberation as if he himself were in the evil from which he desired to heal them.

One must not, therefore, lie in the doctrine of piety; for this is a great crime and the first kind of detestable lie.

One must not lie in the second kind, because no one is to be wronged.

One must not lie in the third kind, because no one’s interests are to be served through another person’s injury.

One must not lie in the fourth kind, because of the desire for lying, which is vicious in itself.

One must not lie in the fifth kind, because even the truth is not to be stated merely for the purpose of pleasing people; how much less a lie, which, simply because it is a lie, is certainly shameful in itself?

One must not lie in the sixth kind; for even the truth of a testimony must not rightly be corrupted for anyone’s temporal advantage or safety. No one is to be led to eternal salvation with the aid of a lie. A person is not to be converted to good morals by the evil morals of those converting him; for if he ought to act in this way toward another, then, once converted, he too ought to act in the same way toward others. Thus he is converted not to good but to evil morals, when he is offered for imitation, after his conversion, what was done for him in order to convert him.

Nor must one lie in the seventh kind; for no one’s temporal advantage or safety is to be preferred to the perfection of faith. Nor, if someone is so badly disturbed by our right actions that he becomes worse in soul and much farther removed from piety, should right actions therefore be abandoned. We must hold especially firmly to that by which we ought to call and invite those whom we love as ourselves. With the strongest courage we must drink in that apostolic saying: “To some we are the aroma of life unto life, to others the aroma of death unto death; and who is sufficient for these things?” (II Cor. II, 16).

Nor must one lie in the eighth kind; for among good things there are purity of soul and bodily chastity, while among evil things what we ourselves do is worse than what we permit to be done.

In these eight kinds of lying, therefore, a person sins less when he lies the more he rises toward the eighth, and sins more when he descends toward the first. [Note: [Col. 0516] The manuscripts of Corbie, the Royal Library, and the Sorbonne read, “the more he sinks toward the first.” The manuscript of Regiomontanus reads, “is sunk.” Those of Germanus, Ébrulphus, and Pratelles read, “rises.” The Vatican manuscript reads, “descends.”]

Whoever thinks that there is some kind of lie that is not a sin shamefully deceives himself, believing himself an honorable deceiver of others.

### 43.

Moreover, such blindness has taken possession of people’s minds that it is not enough for us to say that certain lies are not sins; they even say that it is a sin in certain circumstances if we refuse to lie. In defending lying they have gone so far as to say that the Apostle Paul made use of the first kind of lie, which is the most criminal of all.

In the Epistle to the Galatians—which, like the others, was certainly written for the instruction of religion and piety—they say that he lied in the passage where he speaks of Peter and Barnabas: “When I saw that they were not walking rightly according to the truth of the Gospel.” For while they wish to defend Peter from error and from the crookedness of the path into which he had fallen, they attempt to overthrow the very way of religion, in which salvation lies for all, by breaking down and reducing to fragments the authority of Scripture.

In doing so they fail to see that they are charging the Apostle not only with the crime of lying but also with perjury in the very doctrine of piety—that is, in the Epistle in which he proclaims the Gospel. For before relating this event he says: “As for the things I am writing to you, behold, before God, I am not lying” (Gal. II, 14, and I, 20).

But let this discussion now come to an end. Throughout its consideration and treatment, nothing deserves more thought and prayer than what the same Apostle says: “God is faithful, who will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you are able to bear, but with the temptation will also provide a way out, so that you may be able to endure it” (I Cor. X, 13).

[Col. 0517]

[Note: [Col. 0517] On the book *Against Lying*, see Book II, chapter 60, of the *Retractions*, vol. 1, col. 654, beginning with the words, “Then I also wrote *Against Lying*” [ [Col. 0517] From this we understand that the following book was written around the year of Christ 420. For after listing the books *Against an Adversary of the Law and the Prophets*, which belong to the beginning of the year 420, and mentioning below, in the next place, other books marked as having been written “at the same time”—the books *Against Gaudentius*—the present work is immediately mentioned in these words: “Then I also wrote a book *Against Lying*.” Augustine is to be understood as referring to this same book in the *Enchiridion*, chapter 18, where, concerning the very difficult and obscure question of lying, he testifies that, “when pressed by the necessity of replying, he had already completed a large book.” As for Consentius, to whom the book is addressed, it is, unless we are mistaken, his letter to Augustine, number 119; and Augustine’s letters numbered 120 and 205 are addressed to him. See the note on Letter 205 in the preface to volume 2.], ending with the words, “You sent me things to read.” M.]

## THE ONE BOOK OF SAINT AURELIUS AUGUSTINE, BISHOP OF HIPPO, AGAINST LYING, ADDRESSED TO CONSENTIUS

[Note: [Col. 0517] Written around the year 420.]

[Note: [Col. 0517] The book *Against Lying* was corrected against two ancient Vatican manuscripts and eleven Gallican manuscripts: namely, the Royal manuscript, approximately 900 years old; the Sorbonne manuscript; the Victorine manuscript; the manuscript of the abbey of Saint Peter at Chartres; that of Saint Benignus at Dijon; that of Saint Martin at Sées; the manuscript of Pratelles; those of Fécamp, Mont-Saint-Michel, Cygirannus; and that of the abbey of La Couture at Le Mans. It was also compared with the variant readings of the Louvain edition from five Belgian manuscripts, as well as with the editions of Amerbach, Erasmus, and the Louvain theologians.]

[Note: [Col. 0517] We also compared all the editions mentioned at the beginning of the *Retractions* and the *Confessions*, vol. 1. M.]

(C)

Augustine replies to the writings that Consentius sent him for consideration, concerning the use of lying to expose hidden Priscillianists who falsely claim to be Catholics. He teaches that neither liars are to be sought out by means of lies, nor blasphemers by means of blasphemies. He refutes the error of the Priscillianists, found especially in the book of Dictinius entitled *The Libra*, according to which they maintain that “in order to conceal religion, religious people ought to lie.” The testimonies and examples that they produce from the divine books in defense of this error, he argues, are partly not lies and partly, even where they are lies, not to be imitated. He resolves the difficulty concerning compensatory sins, rejecting as well the lie that may appear useful or necessary for preserving someone’s temporal or eternal safety. Finally, he commands Consentius to hold firmly that one must never lie at all, especially in matters pertaining to the doctrine of religion, and to defend this position against heretics.

## CHAPTER I

### 1. Those who use lies to remain hidden are not to be dragged from their hiding places by our lies.

You sent me many things to read, dearest brother Consentius; you sent me many things to read [Note: [Col. 0517] Several manuscripts omit the second occurrence of “you sent me many things to read.”]. While I was preparing a reply to them, and was being diverted by other occupations, each more pressing than the last, a year passed and thrust me into such straits that I had to reply somehow, lest, when the favorable season for sailing had already arrived, I detain longer the bearer who wished to return.

Accordingly, after examining and reading through everything that Leonas, God’s servant, brought me from you—both when I first received it and later, when I was about to dictate this—considering it as carefully as I could, I was greatly delighted by your eloquence, by your memory of the holy Scriptures, by your intellectual skill, by the grief with which you rebuke negligent Catholics, and by the zeal with which you gnash your teeth even against heretics who remain hidden.

But I am not persuaded that they should be dragged from their hiding places by our lies. Why, after all, do we search for and investigate them with such care, unless it is so that, once captured and brought into the open, we may either teach them the truth themselves, or at least, once convicted by the truth, prevent them from harming others? The purpose, then, is that their lie may be destroyed or guarded against, while God’s truth is increased.

How, then, can I rightly pursue lies with a lie? Are robberies to be pursued by robbery, sacrileges by sacrilege, adulteries by adultery? But if God’s truth will abound through my lie, shall we also say, “Let us do evil that good may come” (Rom. III, 7–8)? You see how the Apostle detests this.

For what else is it to say, “Let us lie in order to bring lying heretics to the truth,” than, “Let us do evil that good may come”? Is a lie ever good, or is a lie sometimes not evil? Why, then, is it written: “You hate, O Lord, all who work iniquity; you will destroy all who speak a lie” (Ps. V, 7)?

He did not except some, nor did he say indefinitely, “You will destroy those who speak lies,” in such a way as to allow some but not all to be understood. Rather, he stated a universal judgment, saying, “You will destroy all who speak a lie.”

Or is it because he did not say, “You will destroy all who speak every lie,” or “who speak any lie,” that we should therefore think that some room has been left for lying? That is, that there is some lie whose speakers God will not destroy, but that he will destroy all who speak an unjust lie—not every lie—because there is also a just lie, which ought indeed to be a matter of praise rather than accusation?

## CHAPTER II

### 2. The Priscillianist error concerning the use of lies to conceal oneself from outsiders. This position entirely removes martyrdoms.

Do you not see how much this argument helps those very people whom we are trying to capture by our lies as if on a great hunt? For, as you yourself have shown, this is the Priscillianist position. To prove it, they bring forward testimonies from Scripture, exhorting their followers to lie by appealing to the examples of Patriarchs, Prophets, Apostles, and Angels. They do not hesitate to add the Lord Christ himself, nor do they think that they can otherwise demonstrate their own falsehood to be truthful unless they say that Truth itself is a liar.

These arguments must be refuted, not imitated. We must not become participants in the evil of the Priscillianists in which they are shown to be worse than all other heretics. They alone—or at least they above all—are found to dogmatize that, in order to conceal what they think is their truth, one must lie. They consider this such a great evil to be just because they say that what is true must be retained in the heart, while to speak falsehood to outsiders with the mouth is no sin; and they claim that this is what is written: “He who speaks truth in his heart” (Ps. XIV, 3). As if this were sufficient for righteousness, even if someone speaks a lie with his mouth, provided that the hearer is not a neighbor but an outsider.

For this reason they also think that the Apostle Paul, after saying, “Putting away lying, speak the truth,” immediately added, “each one with his neighbor, because we are members of one another” (Eph. IV, 25). Thus, according to them, one may and ought to speak a lie to those who are not near to us in the fellowship of truth and are not, so to speak, our fellow members.

### 3. This position dishonors the holy martyrs, or rather removes holy martyrdoms altogether.

According to these people, the martyrs would be acting more justly and wisely if they did not confess to their persecutors that they were Christians and did not make them murderers through their confession. Instead, by lying and denying what they were, they would preserve both the advantage of their flesh and the purpose of their hearts, while preventing their persecutors from carrying out the crime they had conceived.

For their persecutors were not their neighbors in the Christian faith, so that they ought to speak with them by mouth the truth they spoke in their hearts; indeed, they were enemies of the truth itself.

If Jehu—whom they seem prudently to regard among their other examples of lying—pretended to be a servant of Baal in order to kill Baal’s servants, then, according to the perversity of their doctrine, how much more justly, during a persecution, would the servants of Christ pretend to be servants of demons, so that the servants of demons would not kill Christ’s servants? They might sacrifice to idols so as not to be killed, if Jehu sacrificed to Baal in order to kill people.

For what harm would it do them, according to the outstanding teaching of these speakers of lies, to pretend outwardly to worship the devil, when the worship of God was preserved in the heart?

But the true and holy martyrs did not understand the Apostle in this way. They saw and held fast to what is written: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. X, 10); and, “No lie was found in their mouth” (Apoc. XIV, 5). Thus they departed irreproachable to the place where they would no longer have to beware of being tested by liars, because among their heavenly assemblies they would no longer have liars as either outsiders or neighbors.

They would not have imitated that Jehu, who by an impious lie and sacrilegious sacrifice sought out the impious and sacrilegious to kill them—not even if the same Scripture had been silent about what sort of man he was. But since it is written that he did not have a right heart with God, what did it benefit him that, for the partial obedience he displayed in completely destroying the house of Ahab, driven by his desire for rule, he received some temporary reward in the form of a temporal kingdom (IV Kings X)?

Brother, I exhort you to defend the truthful judgment of the martyrs, so that you may be an advocate of truth against liars, not a teacher of lying. For, I beg you, attend more carefully to what I am saying, so that you may discover how much one must beware of what is thought to be taught with commendable zeal against the impious, in order that they may be captured, corrected, or avoided, but which is nevertheless taught without sufficient caution.

## CHAPTER III

### 4. The lie of Catholics in order to capture heretics would be more harmful than the lie of heretics in order to remain hidden from Catholics. The matter is demonstrated by an example. To wish to capture Priscillianists by lying is to be corrupted with them.

There are many kinds of lies, all of which we ought universally to hate. For there is no lie that is not contrary to truth. Just as light and darkness, piety and impiety, justice and iniquity, sin and right action, health and weakness, life and death are opposed to one another, so truth and lying are opposed to one another. Therefore, the more we love truth, the more we ought to hate lying.

Nevertheless, there are certain lies whose being believed does no harm, although even wishing to deceive by such a kind of lying is harmful to the liar, not to the one who believes him. Suppose, for example, that that brother Fronto, God’s servant, lied in some of the things he reported to you—which God forbid. He would certainly have harmed himself, not you, even if you believed everything he told you, without any iniquity on your part.

Whether those things happened in that way or not, they contain nothing such that, if someone believed them to have happened in that way when in fact they had not, he would be judged guilty in the rule of truth and the doctrine of eternal salvation.

But if someone lies about something such that anyone who believes it will become a heretic against the doctrine of Christ, the liar is more harmful in proportion as the believer is more wretched.

Consider, then, what it means if we lie against the doctrine of Christ: whoever believes us will perish, while we attempt to capture the enemies of that same doctrine and bring them to the truth by departing from it ourselves. Indeed, by capturing liars through lying, we would teach worse lies.

For what they say when they lie is one thing, and what they say when they are deceived is another. When they teach their heresy, they say things in which they are deceived; but when they claim to believe what they do not believe, or not to believe what they do believe, they say things in which they lie.

Whoever believes them in this, even if he does not discover what they are, does not himself perish. A person does not depart from the Catholic rule if he believes a heretic who falsely professes Catholic doctrines to be Catholic. Thus this is not harmful to him, because he is deceived in the mind of a human being—a mind about which he cannot judge while it remains hidden—not in the faith of God, which he ought to preserve implanted within him.

But when they teach their heresy, whoever believes them, thinking it to be the truth, will share not only in their error but also in their condemnation.

Thus, when they proclaim their wicked doctrines, in which they are deceived by a deadly error, whoever believes them perishes. But when we proclaim Catholic doctrines, in which we hold the true faith, whoever believes us is found, even if he had perished.

When, however, although they are Priscillianists, they falsely claim to be ours in order not to disclose their poisons, whoever among us believes them remains Catholic even while they remain hidden. But if, in order to investigate them, we pretend to be Priscillianists, and praise their doctrines as if they were ours, whoever believes those doctrines will either be confirmed among them or immediately transferred to them.

What the coming hour may bring—whether those who have been deceived by our lying will later be freed by our speaking the truth, and whether they will wish to listen to a teacher whom they have experienced as a liar—who can know with certainty? Who does not know that this is uncertain?

It follows that Catholics lie more harmfully—or, to speak more mildly, more dangerously—in order to capture heretics than heretics lie in order to remain hidden from Catholics. For whoever believes Catholics who lie in order to test them either becomes or is confirmed as a heretic; but whoever believes heretics who lie in order to conceal themselves does not cease to be a Catholic.

To make this clearer, let us propose some examples, especially from the writings that you sent me to read.

### 5.

Let us imagine before our eyes a clever investigator approaching someone whom he suspects of being a Priscillianist. He falsely praises either the life, if known to him, or the reputation, if unknown, of Bishop Dictinius [Note: [Col. 0522] The printed editions read, “and the saying of the bishop.” A little later they likewise read, “then the book of the saying, whose name is *The Libra*.” In these passages, as well as below in chapter 17, we have restored the name Dictinius on the authority of the ancient books. Dictinius was bishop of Astorga. As Hydatius writes in his *Chronicle*: “Turribius succeeded him after he had been expelled, along with other bishops of the same sect, on account of the Priscillianist heresy that he professed.” Nevertheless, Pope Innocent I testifies in his letter to the Council of Toledo that Dictinius was later received by the Church after condemning and abandoning his error. Pope Leo I also praises his correction in Letter 15 to Turribius of Astorga, chapter 16, while condemning “the fact that the treatises of Dictinius, which he composed according to the doctrine of Priscillian, were read by many with veneration, whereas, if they think that something ought to be attributed to the memory of Dictinius, they should rather love his restoration than his fall.” The Church of Astorga, moreover, celebrates the memory of Dictinius in Spain with an annual feast on June 2. See Ferrarius, *General Catalogue of the Saints*.].

This is at least somewhat more tolerable, because Dictinius is thought to have been a Catholic and to have been corrected from that error.

Next, following the art of lying, he will solemnly commemorate Priscillian, an impious and detestable man condemned for his wicked crimes and offenses. If, in this solemn commemoration of Priscillian, the person for whom such nets are being spread happens not to have been a firm Priscillianist, he will be made firm by this praise.

When the investigator’s speech has proceeded to other matters, and he says that he pities those whom the author of such great errors and darkness has enveloped in such darkness that they do not recognize the honor of their soul and the splendor of their divine lineage, he will then praise the book of Dictinius, whose title is *The Libra*—so called because, after twelve questions have been treated, it is unfolded, as it were, by twelve twelfths—with such extravagant praise that he will declare such a *Libra*, containing horrible blasphemies, to be more precious than many thousands of pounds of gold.

Surely this cunning of the liar kills the soul of the believer, or, if it has already been killed, sinks and buries it more deeply in the same death.

“But,” you will say, “he will later be freed.” What if that does not happen—whether because some obstacle intervenes and prevents the process from being completed, or because the heretical mind stubbornly returns to denying the very things it had begun to confess? This is especially likely because, if the person discovers that he has been tested by an outsider, he will be all the more boldly determined to conceal by lying what he believes, having learned from the example of the one who tested him that this can be done without blame.

For how, in a person who thinks that truth ought to be concealed by lying, shall we finally condemn or dare to denounce what we ourselves teach?

### 6.

It remains, therefore, that we should condemn with truthful piety whatever the Priscillianists believe concerning God, the soul, the body, and other matters according to the wicked falsehood of their heresy. But their belief that one must lie in order to conceal the truth must not, God forbid, become a doctrine shared by us and by them.

This is such a great evil that even if our attempt to capture and change them by lying should succeed—so that we capture them and change them—these gains cannot compensate for the losses by which we too are corrupted with them in the process of correcting them.

Through this lie, we shall be perverse in one respect, while they will be only half-corrected. For we do not correct in them the belief that one ought to lie for the sake of concealing truth, since we ourselves have learned and teach the same thing and command that it ought to be done in order that we may reach them for their correction.

Yet we do not correct them, because we do not remove from them the error [Note: [Col. 0523] Several manuscripts have “lie” here and below instead of “error.”] by which they think that truth must be concealed; rather, we ourselves become entangled in error when we seek them through such an error. Nor do we find how we can trust them once they have been converted, when we have lied to them while they were perverse. Perhaps they will do, once captured, what they endured in order to be captured—not only because they are accustomed to doing so, but also because they find this practice in us, to whom they come.

## CHAPTER IV

### 7. A person who lies in one matter is not trusted in others.

And what is more pitiable, once they have in a sense become ours, they cannot discover how they are to trust us. For if they suspect that we are also speaking the Catholic doctrines falsely in order to conceal something else that we consider true, you will certainly say to such a person, “I did that then in order to capture you.” But what will you answer if he says, “How do I know whether you are doing the same thing now, so that you will not be captured by me?”

Can anyone be persuaded that a person who lies in order to capture someone will not lie in order to avoid being captured? Do you see where this evil leads? It leads to the point that not only we appear with reason to be suspect to them, and they to us, but every brother appears with reason to be suspect to every brother.

Thus, while one stretches out a lie in order to teach faith, what is accomplished instead is that no one should be trusted. For if, when we lie, we also speak against God, what evil could be found in any lie so great that we ought to avoid it in every way as the most criminal of acts? [Note: [Col. 0523] Several manuscripts read, “what evil could be found in no lie?”]

## CHAPTER V

### 8. It is more tolerable for a Priscillianist to lie by concealing his heresy than for a Catholic to lie by concealing the truth. Catholics who pretend to be Priscillianists do worse than Priscillianists who pretend to be Catholics.

But now observe how much more tolerably the Priscillianists lie in comparison with us, when they know that they are speaking deceitfully, while we think that they ought to be freed by our lie from those false beliefs in which they are deceived through error.

A Priscillianist says that the soul is a part of God and of the same nature and substance as he. This is a great and detestable blasphemy. It follows that God’s nature is taken captive, deceived, misled, disturbed, and disgraced, condemned and tortured.

But if the person who wishes to free someone from such a great evil by lying also says this, let us see what difference there is between the two blasphemers.

“A very great difference,” you say. “For the Priscillianist says it while also believing it; the Catholic, however, does not believe it, although he says it.”

The one therefore blasphemes unknowingly, the other knowingly; the one against knowledge, the other against conscience. The one is blind in holding false beliefs, but at least in those beliefs he has the will to speak the truth; the other sees the truth while it remains hidden and willingly speaks falsehood.

“But,” you will say, “the former teaches this in order to make others share in his error and madness; the latter says this in order to free people from that error and madness.”

I have already shown above how much harm is done by what is believed to be beneficial. But for the moment, if we weigh the present evils in these two cases—for the future benefits that the Catholic hopes to obtain by correcting the heretic are uncertain—which of the two sins more gravely: the one who unknowingly deceives a human being, or the one who knowingly blasphemes God?

Certainly the person who places God above humanity with devout concern understands what is worse.

Moreover, if God must be blasphemed in order to bring people to praise him, then certainly by our example and teaching we invite people not only to praise God but also to blaspheme him. For when we seek to bring people to God’s praises through blasphemies against God, if we succeed in bringing them, they will learn not only to praise him but also to blaspheme him.

These are the benefits we confer on those whom we free from heretics by blaspheming knowingly rather than unknowingly. Although the Apostle handed people over even to Satan so that they might learn not to blaspheme (I Tim. I, 20), we endeavor to rescue people from Satan so that they may learn to blaspheme not through ignorance but through knowledge. And we ourselves, as their teachers, bring upon ourselves such a great ruin that, in order to capture heretics, we first become—what is certain—blasphemers of God, so that for the sake of those whom we hope—uncertainly—to free, we may become teachers of his truth.

### 9.

Since, then, we teach our people to blaspheme God so that Priscillianists may believe them to be their own, let us see what evil the Priscillianists themselves say when they lie in order that we may believe them to be ours.

They anathematize Priscillian and detest him according to our wishes. They say that the soul is God’s creature, not a part of God. They condemn the false martyrdoms of the Priscillianists. They praise highly the Catholic bishops by whom that heresy was stripped bare, attacked, and overthrown, along with other statements of this kind.

Behold: they speak truth when they lie—not in such a way that the very same thing can simultaneously be both truth and lie, but because, when they lie about one matter, they speak truth about another. When they falsely claim to be ours, they speak truth about the Catholic faith.

Thus, in order not to be discovered as Priscillianists, they speak truth deceitfully. But we, in order to discover them, not only speak deceitfully so that we may be thought to belong to them; we also speak falsehoods that we know belong to their error.

Therefore, when they wish to be thought ours, what they say is partly false and partly true. It is false that they are ours, but it is true that the soul is not a part of God. But when we wish to be thought to belong to them, both things we say are false: that we are Priscillianists and that the soul is a part of God.

They, therefore, praise God and do not blaspheme him when they conceal themselves; and when they do not conceal themselves but disclose their own beliefs, they do not know that they are blaspheming.

For this reason, if they are converted to the Catholic faith, they console themselves by being able to say what the Apostle said. After saying among other things, “Formerly I was a blasphemer,” he added, “I received mercy because I acted ignorantly” (I Tim. I, 13).

But we, in order that they may reveal themselves to us, if we put forward this supposedly just lie in order to deceive and capture them, certainly claim that we too belong to the blaspheming Priscillianists; and, in order that they may believe us, we blaspheme without the excuse of ignorance.

For a Catholic who wishes to be thought a heretic by blaspheming cannot say, “I acted ignorantly.”

## CHAPTER VI

### 10. It is never permissible to deny Christ before human beings, even deceitfully and as a pretense. Objection. Reply. The possible objections are likewise refuted. Believing in the heart is not enough unless Christ is also not denied with the mouth. How Psalm 14:3 is to be understood, where the one who speaks truth in his heart is praised. Likewise, the Apostle’s command that we speak truth with our neighbor. Those who preach truth without truth are tolerated, but not those who proclaim falsehood.

Brother, in such matters we must always recall with fear: “Whoever denies me before human beings, I also will deny before my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. X, 33).

But does the person who denies Christ before Priscillianists in order to expose and capture them while they remain hidden through a blasphemous lie not deny Christ before human beings? I ask you, who can doubt that Christ is denied when he is said not to be what he truly is, and when he is said to be what the Priscillianist believes him to be?

### 11

“But,” you will say, “we cannot discover the hidden wolves, clothed in sheep’s skins and secretly and grievously ravaging the Lord’s flock, in any other way.” How, then, did the Priscillianists become known before this hunting expedition of lies had been devised? How was the lair of their very author—surely a more cunning and therefore more concealed man—reached? How were so many, and so great a number, exposed and condemned, while the rest—countless in number—were partly corrected and partly gathered into the merciful Church as though corrected?

For when the Lord has mercy, he provides many ways by which they may be discovered; two of these are more successful than the others [Note: [Col. 0525] Only the Louvain edition reads, “more easily.”]: either they are revealed by those whom they tried to seduce, or by those who, having already been seduced, recover and are converted. This happens more readily if their impious error is overthrown not by deceitful stratagems but by truthful arguments.

You ought to devote yourself to composing these arguments, since the Lord has granted you the ability to do so. When these salutary writings—by which their deranged perversity is destroyed—become increasingly known, and are disseminated everywhere by Catholics, whether by bishops who speak among the people or by any devout persons filled with zeal for God, they will be holy nets by which such men are truly caught, rather than deceitfully sought.

For once caught in this way, they will either voluntarily confess what they have been, and will either correct in agreement with one another others whom they know to belong to their evil association or mercifully expose them; or, if they are ashamed to confess what they have concealed by prolonged dissimulation, they will be healed by the hidden hand of God as he applies his remedy.

### 12

“But,” you will say, “we penetrate their hiding places much more easily if we pretend to be what they are.” If this were permissible or expedient, Christ could have commanded his sheep to come to the wolves clothed in wolf skins, and to discover them by the deceptions of this art. But he did not say this to them, not even when he foretold that he would send them into the midst of wolves (Matthew 10:16).

But you will say: “They did not then need to be sought out, since they were completely open wolves; their bites and savagery simply had to be endured.” What, then, when, foretelling later times, he said that ravenous wolves would come in sheep’s clothing? Was that not the place to warn them and say: “And in order to discover them, you too should put on wolf’s clothing, while remaining sheep inwardly”? He did not say this. Rather, after saying, “Many will come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly they are ravenous wolves,” he did not add, “You will know them by your lies,” but, “You will know them by their fruits” (ibid. 7:15–16).

Lies must be avoided by truth, caught by truth, and destroyed by truth. Far be it from us to overcome the blasphemies of the ignorant by knowingly blaspheming; far be it from us to avoid the evils of deceitful people by imitating them.

For how shall we avoid them if, in order to avoid them, we possess the very things we are avoiding? If, in order to catch one who blasphemes unknowingly, I knowingly blaspheme, what I do is worse than what I catch. If, in order to discover one who unknowingly denies Christ, I knowingly deny Christ, the one whom I discover in this way will follow me to destruction; for in discovering him, I myself perish first.

### 13

Or perhaps the person who endeavors to discover the Priscillianists in this way does not deny Christ because he utters with his mouth what he does not believe in his heart? As though, as I already said shortly before, after it had been stated, “With the heart one believes unto righteousness,” the addition “and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Romans 10:10) were useless!

Did not nearly all those who denied Christ before persecutors retain in their hearts what they believed about him, and yet perish because they did not confess him with their mouths unto salvation—except those who came back to life through repentance?

Who could be so foolish [Note: [Col. 0526] The Cygirannian manuscript reads, “so insanely know.” Perhaps it should read, “so insanely think.”] as to suppose that the apostle Peter had in his heart, when he denied Christ, what he had on his lips? In that denial he inwardly held the truth, while outwardly uttering a lie.

Why, then, did he wash away with tears what he had denied with his mouth (Matthew 26:69–75), if what he believed in his heart was sufficient for salvation? Why, while speaking truth in his heart, did he punish with such bitter weeping the lie that he had uttered with his mouth, unless he saw that it was a great peril to believe in the heart unto righteousness but not confess with the mouth unto salvation?

### 14

Therefore, what is written, “He who speaks truth in his heart,” must not be understood as though, while retaining truth in the heart, one ought to speak a lie with the mouth. Rather, it was said because it can happen that someone speaks truth with his mouth, but that truth does him no good if he does not hold it in his heart—that is, if he does not believe what he himself says.

This is what heretics do, and especially these same Priscillianists: they do not believe Catholic truth, but nevertheless speak it so that they may be believed to be ours. They therefore speak truth in their mouth, but not in their heart. For this reason they had to be distinguished from the one of whom it was said, “He who speaks truth in his heart.”

A Catholic, however, speaks this truth in his heart because he believes it, and therefore ought also to speak it with his mouth, so that he may proclaim what he believes. He must have no falsehood either in his heart or in his mouth concerning this truth, so that he believes with the heart unto righteousness and makes confession with the mouth unto salvation.

For in that psalm, after it had been said, “He who speaks truth in his heart,” this too was immediately added: “He who has not practiced deceit with his tongue” (Psalm 14:3).

### 15

And when the Apostle says, “Putting away falsehood, speak the truth, each one with his neighbor, because we are members of one another” (Ephesians 4:25), far be it from us to understand this as though he permitted us to speak lies to those who are not yet members with us of the body of Christ.

It was said for this reason: each one of us ought to regard another as what we want him to become, even if he has not yet become so. Thus the Lord showed that the foreign Samaritan was the man’s neighbor because he acted toward him with mercy (Luke 10:30–37).

A person, therefore, is to be regarded as a neighbor, not as a stranger, when we are to act toward him so that he may no longer remain a stranger. And if, because he has not yet become a participant in our faith and sacrament, certain truths must be concealed from him, nevertheless falsehoods must not for that reason be told to him.

### 16

For even in the time of the Apostles there were people who proclaimed the truth not with truthfulness [Note: [Col. 0527] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions, however, read, “not sincerely.”]—that is, not with a truthful intention. The Apostle says that they proclaimed Christ not purely, but out of envy and rivalry.

Thus even then some people were tolerated who proclaimed the truth without a pure intention. Yet no one was praised as proclaiming falsehood with a pure intention. Accordingly, concerning those people he says, “Whether in pretense or in truth, Christ is proclaimed” (Philippians 1:15–18). But he would in no way have said that Christ should later be proclaimed after first being denied.

### 17

Accordingly, hidden heretics can be investigated in many ways, without disparaging the Catholic faith and without praising heretical impiety.

## Chapter VII

### Falsehood must not be admitted under the guise of any good intention

Some actions are made good or bad by their purpose, while others are sins in themselves; these latter must not be done under the pretext of any supposedly good purpose.

But if heretical impiety could not be brought out of its caves in any other way than by the Catholic tongue deviating from the path of truth, it would be more tolerable for that impiety to remain hidden than for the tongue to be driven from the path; it would be more tolerable for the foxes to lurk in their dens than for the hunters, in order to catch them, to fall into the pit of blasphemy; it would be more tolerable for the perfidy of the Priscillianists to be covered by a veil of truth than for the faith of Catholics to be denied by believing Catholics lest it be praised by lying Priscillianists.

For if blasphemous falsehoods are therefore just—not merely any falsehoods, but blasphemous ones—because they are uttered with the intention of exposing hidden heretics, then by the same reasoning, if committed with the same intention, adulteries could be chaste.

What if some immoral woman from the number of the Priscillianists were to cast her eyes upon the Catholic Joseph and promise him that she would betray their hiding places if she could obtain sexual intercourse from him, and it were certain that, if he consented to her, she would fulfill her promise? Would we judge that this should be done? Or would we understand that such a reward must not be obtained at such a price?

Why, then, do we not seek to draw out heretics to be captured by flesh lapsing into adultery [Note: [Col. 0528] The Amiens edition and the manuscripts read, “do we not buy”; below, they read, “to be bought.”], while we think them to be drawn out by a mouth fornicating in blasphemy [Note: [Col. 0528] Several manuscripts read, “fornicating into blasphemy.”]?

Either both practices may be defended on equal grounds, so that they are said not to be unjust because they were done with the intention of detecting the unjust; or, if sound teaching does not want us, even for the discovery of heretics, to mingle bodily—with the mind remaining chaste—with immoral women, surely it does not want us, even with the mind remaining sound, to proclaim an unclean heresy with our voice or to blaspheme the chaste Catholic faith.

For even the command of the mind, which every lower movement of the human being ought to obey, will not be without deserved reproach when something is done that ought not to be done, whether by a bodily member or by a word. Indeed, when it is done by a word, it is also done by a bodily member, since the tongue is the member by which the word is produced. And none of our acts is brought forth by any member unless it has first been conceived in the heart—or rather, unless it has already been brought forth inwardly through thought and consent and is then produced outwardly through action by the member.

The mind, therefore, is not excused from an act when it is said that something was not done intentionally, although it would not have been done unless the mind had decided that it should be done.

### 18

It makes a very great difference for what cause, purpose, or intention something is done. But actions that are known to be sins must not be done under the pretext of any good cause, any supposedly good purpose, or any apparently good intention.

Human actions that are not sins in themselves are good or bad according as they have good or bad causes. Thus providing food for the poor is a good work if it is done out of mercy with right faith; likewise, marital intercourse is good when it is undertaken for the purpose of begetting children, provided it is done with the faith that those begotten are to be regenerated.

Such works, and others like them, are good or bad according to their causes, because the very same acts become sins if they have bad causes: for example, if a poor person is fed for the sake of boasting; if intercourse with one’s wife is undertaken for lust; or if children are begotten not to be raised for God but to be raised for the devil.

But when the acts themselves are already sins—such as thefts, fornications, blasphemies, and other things of this kind—who would say that they should be done for good causes, either so that they would not be sins or, more absurdly, so that they would be just sins?

Who would say, “In order to have something to give to the poor, let us steal from the rich”? Or, “Let us sell false testimony, especially if this does not harm the innocent, but rather rescues the guilty from judges who would condemn them”? For two good things would supposedly result from selling this lie: money would be obtained with which to feed the needy, and the judge would be deceived so that a person would not be punished.

If we can do so, why should we not also suppress genuine wills and substitute false ones, so that undeserving people—who would do no good with their inheritances or bequests—may not receive them, but rather those by whom the hungry are fed, the naked clothed, strangers welcomed, captives ransomed, and churches built [Col. 0529]? Why should those evils not be done for the sake of these goods, if for the sake of these goods the evils themselves are not evil?
