Furthermore, if some immoral and wealthy women appear likely to enrich their lovers and seducers still more, why should not the merciful man undertake these roles and practices, using them for so good a purpose that he may have something to distribute to the needy, without hearing the Apostle say, “Let the one who stole steal no longer, but rather let him labor, working with his hands at what is good, so that he may have something to give to the one in need” [Note: [Col. 0529] Thus the manuscripts; the printed editions read, “so that he may give.”] (Ephesians 4:28)? For on this reasoning, not only theft itself, but also false testimony, adultery, and every evil act would not be evil but good if committed for the purpose of making possible some good.

Who would say such things except someone attempting to overturn human affairs, and all morals and laws? For what crime, however wicked; what disgraceful outrage, however shameful; what sacrilege, however impious, could not be said to be capable of being done rightly and justly—not merely with impunity but even gloriously—so that, in committing it, one would fear no punishment but hope for rewards, if we once conceded that in all human evil acts it is not what is done but why it is done that must be considered, so that whatever is found to have been done for good causes would not itself be judged evil?

But if justice rightly punishes a thief, it will also punish one who says and demonstrates that he took surplus property from a rich man in order to provide necessities for a poor person. If it rightly punishes a forger, it will also punish one who proves that he falsified another person’s will so that the heir who would have given abundant alms might inherit, rather than the one who would give none. If it rightly punishes an adulterer, it will also punish one who demonstrates that he committed adultery out of mercy, in order through the woman with whom he committed it to rescue a person from death.

Finally, to come closer to the matter under discussion: if justice rightly punishes the man who had intercourse in adultery with a Priscillianist woman who knew their depravity, in order to reach their hiding places, I ask you: when the Apostle says, “Do not present your members to sin as weapons of unrighteousness” (Romans 6:13), and therefore we ought not to present our hands, the sexual members of our body, or any other members to crimes so that we might discover the Priscillianists, what has our tongue offended us in? What has our entire mouth offended us in? What has the organ of our voice offended us in, that we should present these as weapons to sin—and to so great a sin—by blaspheming our God without any excuse of ignorance, in order to rescue captured Priscillianists from the blasphemies of ignorance? [Note: [Col. 0529] Only the printed editions read, “preserve.”]

## Chapter VIII

### One sin may be lighter than another in intention; nevertheless, the lighter sin must not be committed when it is often more serious than a sin of another kind

Someone may say: “Then is every thief to be equated with the thief who steals out of a desire to show mercy?” Who would say this? But of these two people, neither is good merely because one is worse.

The one who steals out of greed is worse than the one who steals out of compassion. But if every theft is a sin, all theft must be avoided. Who would say that one ought to sin, even if one sin is condemnable and another venial?

What we are now asking is this: if someone does this or that, will he sin or not? We are not asking who will sin more seriously or less seriously. The law certainly punishes thefts less severely than fornications; yet both are sins, although some are lighter and others more serious. Thus theft committed out of greed is considered lighter than fornication committed out of a desire to help.

Within its own category, one sin may be lighter than other sins of the same category when it appears to be committed with a good intention; yet it may still prove more serious than sins of another category that are lighter in themselves.

For it is more serious to commit theft out of greed than out of compassion; likewise, it is more serious to commit fornication out of lust than out of compassion. Yet it is more serious to commit adultery out of compassion than to steal out of greed.

The issue now is not what is lighter or more serious, but what is or is not a sin. No one would say that one ought to sin where it is established that there is sin. Rather, we say that, if something is a sin in one way or another, it should be determined whether it is to be forgiven or not forgiven.

## Chapter IX

### Compensatory sins must not themselves be admitted

### The act of Lot, who offered his daughters to the Sodomite violators

### The example of Lot, disturbed at that time by fear, is not to be imitated

### The example of David, who swore in anger, is likewise not to be imitated

### What David and Lot themselves ought to have done

### How Lot can scarcely be defended from sin

### Not everything done by saints is to be transferred into moral practice

To tell the truth, certain compensatory sins so disturb human minds that people even think they ought to be praised and called rightly done.

For who would doubt that it is a great sin if a father prostitutes his daughters to the fornication of wicked men? And yet there was a circumstance in which a just man thought he ought to do this, when the Sodomites were rushing upon his guests with an unspeakable assault of lust. For he says:

“I have two daughters who have not known a man. I will bring them out to you, and use them as you please; only do nothing wicked to these men, because they have entered under the shelter of my roof-beams” (Genesis 19:8).

What shall we say here? Do we not recoil so greatly from the crime that the Sodomites were attempting against the guests of that just man that we suppose anything should have been done to prevent it?

The person who acted also has considerable influence in this matter. He was rightly rescued from Sodom because of his justice. Since it is a lesser evil for women to suffer sexual violation than for men, it may even be said that this belonged to the justice of that just man: he preferred that it happen to his daughters rather than to his guests—not merely desiring this inwardly, but also offering it in words, and, if they had agreed, intending to carry it out in action.

But if we open this path to sins, so that we commit lesser sins to prevent others from committing greater ones, everything will enter and reign through a broad path—or rather, through no path at all, once every boundary has been torn up and removed, leaving unlimited space.

For when it has been determined that a person ought to commit a lesser sin so that another may not commit a greater one, then certainly our thefts will be used to prevent the fornications of others, and fornications to prevent incest; and if some impiety should appear worse even than incest, we will also be told to commit incest if it can be done in such a way that the impiety is not committed by others.

In each kind of sin, thefts will be thought necessary in place of thefts, fornications in place of fornications, incest in place of incest, sacrileges in place of sacrileges: our own sins in place of the sins of others—not only lesser sins in place of greater ones, but, if the very greatest and worst are reached, fewer sins in place of many, if circumstances should be so arranged that others will not refrain from sin unless we sin somewhat less, but still sin.

Thus whenever an enemy [Note: [Col. 0531] Perhaps, “an unjust man.”] who possesses such power [Note: [Col. 0531] Some codices read, “of this world.”] says, “Unless you become a criminal, I will be more criminal; or unless you commit this crime, I will commit many such crimes,” we would seem to commit a crime if we wished to refrain from crime.

What is this way of thinking except folly, or rather madness? I must guard against condemnation arising from my own iniquity, whether perpetrated against myself or against others, not from another’s iniquity. “The soul that sins, it shall die” (Ezekiel 18:4).

### 21

If, therefore, we certainly ought not to sin so that others may not sin more seriously either against us or against anyone else, we must consider whether what Lot did is an example that we ought to imitate or rather to avoid.

It seems more important to observe and note this: when a dreadful evil arising from the most outrageous impiety of the Sodomites threatened his guests, and he wished to avert it but could not, even the mind of a just man could have been so disturbed that he wished to do what not the obscure storm of human fear but the calm brightness of divine law would declare, if consulted by us, ought not to be done.

That law would instead command us to avoid our own sins in such a way that, out of fear of anyone else’s sins whatsoever, we commit no sin ourselves.

That just man, disturbed by fear of the sins of others—sins that cannot defile anyone except those who consent to them—did not attend to his own sin, by which he wished to subject his daughters to the lusts of wicked men.

When we read such things in the Holy Scriptures, we must not therefore believe that, because they happened, they should also be done, lest we violate commandments while indiscriminately following examples.

Or should we say that David is to be imitated because he swore that he would kill Nabal, but did not do so through more considered clemency [Note: [Col. 0531] Thus the manuscripts; the printed editions read, “through merciful consideration.”] (1 Samuel 25:22–35), so that we may rashly swear that we will do something which we later recognize ought not to be done?

Just as fear disturbed Lot, making him willing to prostitute his daughters, so anger disturbed David, making him swear rashly. If we were permitted to question both of them and ask why they had done these things, Lot might answer, “Fear and trembling came upon me, and darkness covered me” (Psalm 54:6); and David might say, “My eye has been troubled because of anger” (Psalm 6:8). We would then not be surprised that either, in the darkness of fear, or the other, with his eye troubled, failed to see what he ought to have seen, lest they do what ought not to have been done.

### 22

It could more justly be said of holy David that he ought not to have become angry, even though Nabal had been ungrateful and had returned evil for good. But even if anger crept upon him as a human being, it certainly ought not to have prevailed so far that he swore he would do something which he would either carry out by acting savagely or fail to carry out by perjury.

But who would dare say to Lot, standing amid the lustful madness of the Sodomites:

“Even if your guests, in your own house—into which you compelled them to enter through the most forceful hospitality—are seized and assaulted by shameless men and suffer what women suffer, do not fear anything, do not be concerned, do not be alarmed, do not recoil, do not tremble”?

What companion of those wicked men would dare say such things to a pious host?

Yet one could rightly say:

“Do whatever you can to prevent what you rightly fear from happening. But do not let this fear compel you to do something which, if your daughters are willing, they will themselves do with the Sodomites under your authority, while, if they are unwilling, they will suffer violence from the Sodomites under your authority.

“Do not commit your own great crime while recoiling from another’s greater one [Note: [Col. 0532] The Amiens edition and the manuscripts read, “a greater one.”]. However great the difference between your crime and another’s may be, this one will be yours and that one another’s.”

Unless someone should restrict himself to such narrow arguments in defense of this man as to say:

“Since it is better to suffer an injury than to inflict one, and those guests would not have inflicted an injury but would have suffered one, the just man preferred that his daughters suffer injury rather than his guests, under the authority he possessed as their father. He knew that they would not sin if this happened, because they would suffer, without personal sin, the actions of those who sinned and to whom they did not consent.

“Indeed, the daughters did not offer themselves to be violated, although women were offered in place of men and they in place of the guests, lest their guilt arise not from suffering another’s lust but from consenting to it. Nor did their father permit this to be done to them, since those who were attempting it were not handing over the guests to him.

“Although what happened to one would have been a lesser evil than what would have happened to two, he resisted as much as he could, lest any personal consent of his also stain him—consent which, even if lustful madness had prevailed by force upon his body, would not have stained him if he did not consent.

“Because his daughters did not sin, neither did he sin in their case, since he did not cause them to sin if they were assaulted against their will; rather, he caused them to endure the sins of others. It would be as though he offered his slaves to be beaten by wicked men so that his guests would not suffer the injury of being beaten in his house by violent criminals.”

I will not debate this matter, since it would take too long: whether even a master may rightly use his authority over a slave in such a way as to have an innocent slave beaten so that his equally innocent friend would not himself be beaten in the master’s house by violent and wicked men.

But certainly it cannot rightly be said of David that he ought to have sworn that he would do something which he would later recognize he ought not to do.

It is therefore clear that we ought not to transfer into our conduct everything we read as having been done by holy or just men. From this too we must learn how broadly applicable, and how far-reaching, is what the Apostle says:

“Brothers, if a person is overtaken in any transgression, you who are spiritual should restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness, keeping watch on yourself, lest you also be tempted” (Galatians 6:1).

Such episodes are instances of being overtaken, in which people sin because, at the moment, they either do not see what ought to be done or, even when they see it, are overcome—so that sin occurs either because truth is hidden or because weakness compels.

## Chapter X

### Examples sought in Scripture in defense of lying must be carefully weighed

### Concealing truth is one thing; uttering a lie is another

### Abraham and Isaac are defended from lying

### Jacob’s act was not a lie

### Figures of speech are not lies

### Metaphor

### Antiphrasis

### Why Scripture uses figures of speech

In all our actions, and especially in good actions, compensatory sins greatly disturb people, so that sins are not even considered sins if they have such causes for which they are committed and in which it seems that the sin would rather consist in failing to commit them.

This has prevailed especially concerning lies in human opinion: lies are not thought to be sins; indeed, they are believed to be rightly done when someone lies for the benefit of a person whom it is useful to deceive, or in order not to harm others who appear likely to cause harm unless avoided by lies.

Many examples from the Holy Scriptures are thought to support these kinds of lies. But concealing the truth is not the same as uttering a lie.

Although everyone who lies wishes to conceal what is true, not everyone who wishes to conceal what is true lies. Very often we conceal truths not by lying but by remaining silent.

For the Lord was not lying when he said, “I have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now” (John 16:12). He kept silent about truths; he did not speak falsehoods, since he judged them less capable of hearing those truths.

If he had not indicated even this to them—that is, if he had not said that they could not bear what he did not wish to tell them—he would nevertheless have concealed some truth; but we might not have known that this could rightly be done, or we might not have been strengthened by so firm an example.

Accordingly, those who assert that lying is sometimes necessary do not appropriately cite Abraham’s conduct concerning Sarah, whom he called his sister. He did not say, “She is not my wife”; he said, “She is my sister.” She really was so closely related to him that she could truthfully be called his sister.

Later, after the man who had taken her away had returned her, Abraham confirmed this by replying to him:

“Indeed, she is truly my sister by my father, though not by my mother” (Genesis 20:2, 12)—that is, she was of his paternal family, not his maternal family.

He therefore concealed something true; he did not say something false. He concealed that she was his wife and said that she was his sister.

His son Isaac did the same, for we know that he too took a close relative as his wife (ibid. 26:7; 24). It is not a lie when truth is hidden by silence, but when falsehood is expressed by speech.

### 24

As for what Jacob did at his mother’s direction, so that he appeared to deceive his father, if it is considered carefully and faithfully, it was not a lie but a mystery.

If we call these things lies, then all parables and figures that signify various realities—figures that are not to be understood literally but in which one thing is to be understood through another—will also be called lies. Far be such a thing from us.

For anyone who thinks this can bring the same accusation against all the many figurative expressions, so that even what is called a metaphor—that is, the transfer of a word from its proper object to an improper one—could for this reason be called a lie.

When we say that fields “wave,” vines “put forth gems,” youth is “flowering,” and gray hair is “snowy,” then, because we do not find waves, gems, flowers, or snow in the objects to which we have transferred these words from elsewhere, such expressions would plainly be judged lies.

Likewise, “Christ is the rock” (1 Corinthians 10:4), and “the stony heart of the Jews” (Ezekiel 36:26); “Christ is the lion” (Revelation 5:5), and “the devil is a lion” (1 Peter 5:8); and countless other expressions would be called lies.

What shall we say of the figure of speech called antiphrasis, in which what is not present is said to abound, what is sour is called sweet, a grove is called a place that does not give light, and the Fates are called those who do not spare?

Thus we read in the Holy Scriptures, “If he does not bless you to your face” (Job 2:5). The devil said this to the Lord concerning holy Job, and it is understood to mean, “If he does not curse you.” The same word was used by the accusers to describe the fabricated charge against Naboth. For it was said that he “blessed”—that is, cursed—the king (1 Kings 21:13).

All these modes of expression will be considered lies if figurative speech or action is counted as lying.

But if it is not a lie when things that signify one thing through another are referred to the understanding of truth, then not only what Jacob did or said to his father so that he might be blessed, but also what Joseph said to his brothers as though mocking them (Genesis 42), what David pretended when he feigned madness (1 Samuel 21:13), and other things of this kind must not be judged lies. Rather, they are prophetic expressions and actions to be referred to the understanding of realities that are true.

For this reason they are covered, as it were, with figurative garments, so that they may exercise the understanding of the person who seeks them piously, and so that, when exposed and readily apparent, they may not become cheap.

Although we have learned elsewhere that things plainly and openly stated are true, when those same things are drawn out from hidden places, they are in a certain way renewed in our knowledge, and, once renewed, become sweet.

They are not begrudged to learners because they are obscured in these ways; rather, they are commended, so that, as though withdrawn, they may be desired more ardently and, once desired, discovered more joyfully.

Nevertheless, true things, not false things, are spoken, because true things, not false things, are signified, whether by word or by deed. For the things that are signified are themselves certainly being spoken.

They are thought to be lies because people do not understand that the things signified are what is meant [Note: [Col. 0534] Only the Louvain edition reads, “truly”]; instead, they believe that false things have been spoken.

To make this clearer by examples, consider the very thing Jacob did. He certainly covered his limbs with the skins of goats. If we seek the immediate reason, we will think that he lied, for he did this so that he might be thought to be someone he was not.

But if this act is referred to the reality for which it was truly performed and signified, then the goat skins signify sins, while the one who covered himself with them signifies the one who bore not his own sins but those of others.

What is signified truthfully can in no way rightly be called a lie.

The same applies to words as to actions. When his father said to him, “Who are you, my son?” he replied, “I am Esau, your firstborn son” (Genesis 27:16–19).

If this is referred to those two twins, it will appear to be a lie. But if it is referred to the reality that these events and words were truly recorded to signify, then the one who is to be understood here is the one in his body, which is his Church, who speaks of this matter:

“When you see Abraham and Isaac and Jacob and all the prophets in the kingdom of God, but yourselves cast out, and people will come from the east and the west and from the north and the south and recline in the kingdom of God; and behold, those who were last will be first, and those who were first will be last” (Luke 13:28–30).

In this way, so to speak, the younger brother took away and transferred to himself the primacy of the elder.

Since, therefore, things so true are signified so truthfully, what is there here that ought to be thought to have been done or said falsely?

For the things that are signified are certainly not unreal; they either belong to the past, the present, or the future. The signification is therefore undoubtedly true, and there is no lie.

But it would take too long to examine in detail all the elements of this prophetic signification, in which truth holds the highest place, because just as they were foretold by being signified, so they were made clear by their fulfillment.

## Chapter XI
25. The threefold method of arguing against those who wish to enlist the divine Scriptures as patrons of their lies. I have not undertaken this in the present work with respect to you in particular—for you have exposed the hiding places of the Priscillianists insofar as their doctrines are false and perverse—lest they seem to have been investigated as though they ought to be taught, rather than refuted. [Note: Col. 0535. The Sorbonne manuscript reads, “and not rather refuted. Therefore,” etc.] Rather, make those things lie defeated which you have brought into the open by exposing them; for while we wish to track down deceitful people, we must not allow the falsehoods themselves to remain as though they were unconquerable. Indeed, we ought to destroy falsehoods in the hidden recesses of their hearts, rather than, by sparing falsehoods, discover deceitful people.

Among those doctrines of theirs that must be overthrown is certainly this: they teach that religious people ought to lie in order to conceal their religion, to such an extent that one must lie not only about other matters unrelated to religious instruction, but even about religion itself, lest it become known to outsiders; so that Christ must be denied, in order that a Christian may remain hidden among his enemies. Overthrow this impious and abominable doctrine also, I beg you, on account of which, in order to establish it, they gather testimonies from the Scriptures that seem to show that lies are not merely to be pardoned or tolerated, but even honored.

It is therefore your task, while refuting this detestable sect, to show how these testimonies of Scripture are to be understood: either teach that those things are not lies which are thought to be lies, if they are understood in the manner in which they ought to be understood; or show that even those things which plainly are lies are not to be imitated; or, finally, at least with regard to matters belonging to religious instruction, maintain that one must in no way lie. For they are truly overthrown from the foundations when the place where they lie hidden is overthrown, so that they are judged least worthy to be pursued and most necessary to be avoided precisely because they profess themselves liars in order to conceal their heresy. This is what must first be conquered in them; this, as though it were a suitable fortress, must be struck and cast down by the blows of truth.

Nor must another hiding place be provided for them, one that they did not possess and to which they might flee: namely, that if they are exposed by those whom they have tried but failed to seduce, they might say, “We wished to test them, since prudent Catholics have taught that this ought to be done in order to discover heretics.”

But I should explain somewhat more fully why this appears to me to be a threefold method of arguing against those who wish to enlist the divine Scriptures as patrons of their lies: first, that we show that some things which there are thought to be lies are not what they are thought to be, if they are rightly understood; next, that if there are manifest lies there, they are not to be imitated; third, that against every opinion of everyone who thinks that it sometimes belongs to the duty of a good man to lie, we must hold firmly that one must in no way lie in religious instruction. [Col. 0536] These are the three matters which a little earlier I commended to you for treatment, and in a certain sense imposed upon you [Note: Lov. reads “the three matters there”; other manuscripts read “to you”].

## CHAPTER XII

26. Some examples of lying in the Old Scriptures are truly such, but none can be produced from the New Testament. Peter’s and Barnabas’s dissimulation rightly censured by Paul. Certain observances of the Law were not hypocritically maintained by Paul. Paul became all things to all people, not by lying but by showing compassion. What a lie is.

In order to demonstrate that certain things which are thought to be lies in the Scriptures are not what they are thought to be, if they are rightly understood, it should seem to you no small point against these people that they find what appear to be examples of lying not in apostolic writings but in prophetic ones. For all those instances that they specifically mention, in which someone is said to have lied, are found in books in which not only many sayings but also many actions have been written down figuratively [Note: Col. 0536. Two manuscripts read *figurate conscripta sunt* (“have been written down in a figurative manner”).], because they too were performed figuratively. In figures, however, what is called a kind of lie is found, when rightly understood, to be true [Note: Col. 0536. Am., Er., and several manuscripts read “what is called a kind of error” (*velut mendum*)].

The apostles, on the other hand, spoke differently in their Letters, and the Acts of the Apostles were written differently, since the New Testament had by then been revealed, the prophetic figures having veiled it. In so many apostolic Letters, and in that very extensive book in which their deeds are related with canonical truth, no such person is found lying that these people might propose him as an example to justify permission to lie.

Indeed, Peter’s and Barnabas’s dissimulation—by which they were compelling the Gentiles to Judaize—was rightly censured and corrected, both so that it might not do harm at that time and so that it might not provide posterity with an example for imitation. When the apostle Paul saw that they were not walking rightly according to the truth of the Gospel, he said to Peter before them all: “If you, though a Jew, live like a Gentile and not like a Jew, how can you compel the Gentiles to Judaize?” (Gal. 2:13–14).

But as for what Paul himself did—retaining and practicing certain legitimate observances according to Jewish custom, so as not to show himself hostile to the Law and the Prophets—far be it from us to believe that he did this deceitfully. His opinion on this matter is well known: it had been established that Jews who at that time believed in Christ were not to be prohibited from following their ancestral traditions, nor were Gentiles, when they became Christians, to be compelled to follow them. Thus those rites which were clearly commanded by God were not to be avoided as sacrileges; yet, once the New Testament had been revealed, they were not to be regarded as so necessary that no one who turned to God could be saved without them.

There were people who thought and proclaimed this, even after receiving the Gospel of Christ, and Peter and Barnabas had pretended to agree with them; therefore they compelled the Gentiles to Judaize. For this was what compelling them meant: proclaiming those observances as necessary, as though, even after the Gospel had been received, there were no salvation in Christ without them. That was the error of certain people; that was what Peter’s fear pretended; that was what Paul’s freedom rebuked.

When, therefore, Paul says, “I have become all things to all people, that I might win all” (1 Cor. 9:20–22), he did this by showing compassion, not by lying. A person becomes, as it were, like the one whom he wishes to help when he assists with such compassion as he would wish to receive if he himself were placed in the same misery. Thus he becomes like that person, not because he deceives him, but because he imagines himself in his condition.

Hence that saying of the same apostle, which I mentioned above: “Brothers, if anyone is overtaken in any offense, you who are spiritual should restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness, considering yourself, lest you also be tempted” (Gal. 6:1).

For if, because Paul said, “I became to the Jews as a Jew, and to those who are under the Law as one under the Law” (1 Cor. 9:20–22), he is therefore to be thought to have adopted the sacraments of the old Law deceitfully, then he ought also, by lying in the same way, to have adopted the idolatry of the Gentiles, because he also said that to those who were without the Law he became as one without the Law, in order to win them. Yet he certainly did not do this. He did not sacrifice anywhere to idols or worship those images; rather, as a martyr of Christ, he freely showed that they were to be detested and avoided.

Thus these people produce no examples of lying to be imitated from any apostolic deeds or sayings. They think they have something to produce from prophetic deeds or sayings because they regard the prophetic figures that announce things beforehand as lies, on the grounds that they sometimes resemble lies [Note: Perhaps it should read, “because some of them are not unlike lies.”]. But when they are related to the things that they were performed or spoken to signify, they are found to be true significations and therefore in no way lies.

A lie is a false signification accompanied by the intention to deceive. But a signification is not false when, although one thing is signified through another, what is signified is nevertheless true, if it is rightly understood.

## CHAPTER XIII

27. Gospel passages that seem to support lying are examined. Christ figuratively pretended not to know what he knew. Likewise, prophetically and figuratively, he pretended that he was going farther.

There are also examples of this kind involving the Savior in the Gospel, since the Lord of the prophets himself deigned to be a prophet. Such are the passages in which, concerning the woman who suffered from an issue of blood, he said, “Who touched me?” (Luke 8:45), and concerning Lazarus, “Where have you laid him?” (John 11:34). He asked in such a way as though he did not know what he certainly did know. Thus he pretended not to know, so that by this apparent ignorance he might signify something else. Since that signification was true, it was certainly not a lie.

For the woman who suffered from the issue of blood and the man who had been dead for four days both signified those whom even the one who knew all things in a certain sense did not know. The woman represented the type of the people of the Gentiles, concerning whom the prophecy had been uttered beforehand: “A people whom I did not know served me” (Ps. 17:45). And Lazarus, removed from the living, lay there by a significant likeness as the one whose voice says, “I have been cast away from the sight of your eyes” (Ps. 30:23). Therefore, by Christ’s words of questioning, it was figuratively represented that Christ did not know who the woman was or where the man had been laid; and every lie was avoided through a truthful signification.

28. This is also the meaning of what you mentioned them saying: that after the Lord Jesus had risen, he walked along the road with two disciples; and when they approached the village to which they were going, he pretended that he was going farther. The evangelist says, “But he pretended that he was going farther” (Luke 24:28), using the very word with which liars are excessively fond of justifying their lies with impunity—as though everything that is pretended were a lie, when so many things are pretended truthfully in order that one thing may be signified through another.

If Jesus had signified nothing else by pretending that he was going farther, it would rightly be judged a lie. But if it is rightly understood and referred to what he wished to signify, it is found to be a mystery. Otherwise all the things would be lies that, because of a certain resemblance to realities to be signified, are narrated as though they had happened when they did not happen.

This is the case with the lengthy narrative about the two sons of one man: the elder who remained with his father and the younger who traveled far away (Luke 15:11–32). In this kind of fiction, human beings have also attributed human deeds or words to irrational animals and things without sensation, so that through such fictional narratives, but truthful significations, they might communicate more effectively what they wished to commend.

This is found not only among authors of secular literature—for example, in Horace, where a mouse speaks to a mouse and a weasel to a fox, so that through a fictional narrative a true signification may be directed toward the matter at hand (Horace, *Satires* 2.6; *Epistles* 1.7). Hence no one was so unlearned as to think that Aesop’s fables, related for this purpose, ought to be called lies. It is found also in the sacred writings, as when in the Book of Judges the trees seek a king for themselves and speak to the olive tree, the fig tree, the vine, and the bramble (Judg. 9:8–15).

All of this is certainly fabricated so that one may arrive at the intended matter by means of a fictional narrative—not a lying narrative, but a truthful signification.

I have said this because of what is written about Jesus: “He himself pretended that he was going farther,” lest anyone, like the Priscillianists, wishing on the basis of this word to establish that lying is permissible, should even claim that Christ lied. Whoever wishes to understand what he prefigured by pretending should consider what he accomplished by his deed.

For afterward he went farther, above all the heavens, yet did not abandon his disciples. To signify this future event, that present action was humanly fabricated. Therefore a truthful signification was set forth in that fiction, because the truth of that signification followed in his departure. Let the person who denies that Christ fulfilled by his action what he signified contend that Christ lied by his pretence.

## CHAPTER XIV

29. The examples of human lies narrated in the Old Scripture are not to be imitated. Just as Judah’s fornication is not to be imitated, neither is Tamar’s lie.

Since heretical people do not find examples of lying to be imitated in the writings of the New Testament, they think themselves abundantly supplied in this argument, by which they suppose that one ought to lie, when they find and produce many apparent lies in the old prophetic books. For only to a few who understand does it appear in those books to what the truthful, significant sayings or deeds are directed.

But while they wish to have examples of deception by which they may defend themselves as though they were examples to be imitated, they deceive themselves, and “their iniquity has lied to itself” (Ps. 26:12).

As for those persons whom we must not believe intended to prophesy, if they fabricated something by deed or word with the intention of deceiving, then, although something prophetic may also be drawn from their deeds or sayings—something sown and arranged by the omnipotence of the one who knows how to make good use even of human evils—nevertheless, insofar as the persons themselves are concerned, they unquestionably lied. But they should not therefore be considered worthy of imitation merely because they are found in books rightly called holy and divine.

Those books contain written accounts both of human evils and of human goods: the former are to be avoided, the latter pursued. Some things are presented in such a way that a judgment concerning them is explicitly given; others are left for us to judge by an unspoken judgment, because we needed to be nourished not only by clear matters but also exercised by obscure ones.

30. But why do these people consider Tamar, who lied, worthy of imitation, while they do not consider Judah, who committed fornication, worthy of imitation (Gen. 38:14–18)? They read both events there. That Scripture neither condemned nor praised either of them; it merely narrated both and left both for us to judge. But it would be astonishing if it permitted either to be imitated with impunity.

We know that Tamar lied not from a desire to engage in prostitution but from a desire to conceive. Yet fornication, even if Judah’s was not of this kind, can be something by which a person causes someone else to be delivered, just as Tamar’s lie was the means by which a person was conceived. Does it follow that one must also commit fornication if one thinks that one ought to have lied for that reason?

We must therefore consider not only lying but all human actions in which so-called compensatory sins occur, and determine what judgment we ought to pronounce. Otherwise we would open the way not merely to the lesser sins but to every crime, and no offense, disgrace, or sacrilege would remain in which a reason could not be found that made it seem right to commit it; and this opinion would overthrow the whole integrity of life.

## CHAPTER XV

31. A lie is always unjust, since it is a sin and contrary to truth. The Hebrew midwives and Rahab were not rewarded for deceit but for benevolence.

A person who says that some lies are just should be judged to be saying nothing other than that some sins are just, and consequently that some things which are unjust are just. What could be more absurd than this? For what is a sin except something contrary to justice?

Let them say, therefore, that some sins are great and others small; that is true, and we should not listen to the Stoics, who maintain that all sins are equal. But to say that some sins are unjust and others just is nothing other than to say that some iniquities are unjust and others just. Yet the apostle John says, “Everyone who commits sin also commits iniquity; and sin is iniquity” (1 John 3:4).

A sin therefore cannot be just, unless we use the word “sin” for something else, in which no one sins but either does or suffers something on account of sin. Sacrifices for sins have also been called “sins,” and punishments for sins are sometimes called “sins.” These can indeed be understood as just sins when sacrifices or punishments are called just.

But those things that are done contrary to the law of God cannot be just. It has been said to God, “Your law is truth” (Ps. 119:142). Therefore what is contrary to truth cannot be just. Who, moreover, could doubt that every lie is contrary to truth? No lie, then, can be just.

Again, who does not clearly see that everything just comes from truth? John cries out, “Every lie is not from the truth” (1 John 2:21). Every lie, therefore, is not just. Accordingly, when examples of lying are proposed to us from the holy Scriptures, either they are not lies but are thought to be because they are not understood, or, if they are lies, they are not to be imitated, because they cannot be just.

32. But what is written about God having acted well toward the Hebrew midwives (Exod. 1:17–20) and toward Rahab the prostitute of Jericho (Josh. 2; 6:25) does not mean that he did so because they lied, but because they showed mercy toward human beings. It was not deceit that was rewarded in them, but benevolence; goodness of mind, not the wickedness of the liar.

For just as it would not be astonishing or absurd if, at some earlier time, God wished to forgive certain evil deeds committed by them because of later good deeds, so it is not astonishing that, at one time and in one matter, God, seeing both things—that is, the deed done mercifully and the deed done deceitfully—rewarded the good and, because of that good, forgave the evil.

If sins committed because of carnal desire, rather than mercy, are forgiven on account of later acts of mercy, why should sins committed because of mercy itself not rightly be forgiven on account of that mercy? A sin committed with the disposition of one who harms is more serious than one committed with the disposition of one who helps. Therefore, if the former is erased by a subsequent act of mercy, why should the latter, which is less serious, not be erased by the person’s own mercy, both preceding the sin and accompanying it?

This may indeed seem so. Nevertheless, it is one thing to say, “I ought not to have sinned, but I will perform acts of mercy by which I may erase what I previously did,” and another to say, “I ought to sin, because I cannot otherwise show mercy.” It is one thing, I say, to say, “Since we have already sinned, let us do good,” and another to say, “Let us sin, so that good may come” (Rom. 3:8). In the former case it is said, “Let us do good, because we have done evil”; in the latter, “Let us do evil, so that good may come.” Accordingly, in the former case the sewer of sin must be emptied; in the latter, the doctrine of sinning must be avoided.

33. It remains, then, that we understand that those women, whether in Egypt or in Jericho, received a reward—certainly a temporal one—for their humanity and mercy. Yet this reward itself also prefigured, by prophetic signification and without their knowing it, something eternal for them.

Whether one may ever lie for someone’s salvation is a question on which even the most learned are exhausted in their efforts to find a solution. That question far exceeded the capacity of those little women, situated among those peoples and accustomed to those ways of life. Therefore God’s patience bore with their ignorance, just as with their ignorance of other matters that they likewise did not know but that must be known by the children not of this age but of the age to come.

Nevertheless, because of the human kindness they had shown toward his servants, God gave them earthly rewards, even though those rewards signified something heavenly. Rahab, after being delivered from Jericho, passed over into the people of God, where, as she advanced, she could attain eternal and immortal gifts—gifts that must not be sought through any lie.

## CHAPTER XVI

Whether it is ever permissible for a good person to lie for another’s salvation.

Nevertheless, when Rahab performed that good deed for the Israelite scouts, praiseworthy in view of her condition of life, she had not yet reached the state in which it could be demanded of her, “Let your speech be, ‘Yes, yes; No, no’” (Matt. 5:37).

As for those midwives, although they were Hebrews, if they had understood only according to the flesh, what or how much did their temporal reward profit them—that they made houses for themselves—unless, by making progress, they came to belong to that house of which it is sung to God, “Blessed are those who dwell in your house; forever and ever they will praise you” (Ps. 84:5)?

It must indeed be acknowledged that the person who never lies except with the intention of helping someone and harming no one comes very near to justice. Although not yet praiseworthy in deed, that person is already praiseworthy in hope and disposition.

But when we ask whether a good person may ever lie, we are no longer asking about someone who still belongs to Egypt, Jericho, or Babylon, or even to earthly Jerusalem itself, which is in bondage with her children. We are asking about a citizen of that city which is above, which is free and our eternal mother in heaven (Gal. 4:25–26).

And this is the answer given to us when we ask: “Every lie is not from the truth.” But the children of that city are certainly children of truth. They are the children of that city concerning whom it is written, “No lie was found in their mouths” (Rev. 14:5). The son of that city is also the one of whom it is written, “The son who receives the word will be far from destruction; but the one who receives it has received it for himself, and nothing false proceeds from his mouth” (Prov. 29:27).

If some kind of lie ever slips into the lives of these children of the heavenly Jerusalem and the holy eternal city, as it can happen to human beings, they humbly ask forgiveness; they do not seek glory from it.

## CHAPTER XVII

34. Whether the Hebrew midwives and Rahab would have done better by refusing to lie. The rule to which the alleged examples of lying brought from Scripture must be reduced.

But someone may say: “Then would those midwives and Rahab have done better if, by refusing to lie, they had shown no mercy?”

On the contrary, those Hebrew women, if they had been such as the people about whom we are asking whether they may ever lie, would neither have said anything false nor freely have refused the shameful service of killing infants. “But,” you will say, “they would have died.”

Consider, then, what follows. They would have died with a reward in their heavenly dwelling incomparably greater than those houses they were able to make for themselves on earth. They would have died for future eternal happiness, having suffered death for the sake of the most innocent truth.

What of the woman in Jericho? Could she have done this? If she had not deceived the citizens who were making inquiries by lying, would she not have betrayed the guests in hiding by telling the truth? Or could she have said to those asking, “I know where they are, but I fear God and will not betray them”? [Note: Col. 0542. Perhaps read: “Or could she not have said to those asking …?”]

She could indeed have said this if she were already a true Israelite, in whom there was no deceit (John 1:47)—the person she was destined to become through God’s mercy as she passed over into the city of God.

“But,” you will say, “when they heard this, they would have killed her and searched the house.” But did it necessarily follow that they would also find those whom she had carefully hidden? The very cautious woman had taken precautions and placed them where they could have remained concealed even if her lie had not been believed.

Thus, if she had nevertheless been killed by her fellow citizens for her act of mercy, she would have ended this life, which was to end, by a precious death in the sight of the Lord (Ps. 116:15) [Note: Several manuscripts read *feneam*, an uncertain reading], and her kindness toward them would not have been fruitless.

“But,” you will say, “what if those who were searching had also reached the place where she had hidden them?” One may answer in the same way: “What if they had refused to believe a woman so vile and disreputable—not only when she lied but even when she swore falsely?” Even so, she would have obtained what she sought through her fearful lie.

And where do we place the will and power of God? Could he not have protected both her—who neither lied to her fellow citizens nor betrayed God’s people—and those men of his from every danger? For the one by whom they were protected after the woman’s lie could also have protected them if she had not lied.

Unless, perhaps, we have forgotten what happened in Sodom, where males inflamed with an abominable desire for males were unable even to find the door of the house in which the men they sought were staying. At that time a righteous man, in an entirely similar situation, refused to lie for the sake of his guests, whom he did not know to be angels, although he feared that they might suffer violence worse than death.

Certainly he could have given the inquirers answers such as the woman in Jericho gave. For those men likewise sought them by asking questions. But the righteous man did not wish to stain his soul with a lie for the sake of the bodies of his guests, for whose sake he was willing that the bodies of his daughters should suffer violence through the wickedness of another’s lust (Gen. 19:5–11).

Let a person therefore do for the temporal safety of human beings whatever he can. But when the situation has reached the point at which he cannot provide for such safety without sinning, let him understand that there is nothing left for him to do, once he sees that the remaining course is not right.

Accordingly, Rahab in Jericho—because she received God’s people as guests, because she placed herself in danger by receiving them, because she believed in their God, because she carefully hid them where she could, and because she gave them the most faithful advice about returning by another route—should be praised as worthy of imitation even by the citizens of the heavenly Jerusalem.

But although she lied, and although something prophetic may be intelligently expounded in that lie, it is nevertheless not wisely proposed for imitation. God honorably commemorated those good deeds of hers, but mercifully forgave that evil.

35. Since these things are so, and since it would take too long to discuss everything contained in that book of Dictinius as alleged examples of lying to be imitated, it seems to me that not only these examples but also any others of the same kind must be reduced to this rule:

Either what is believed to be a lie must be shown not to be a lie—whether because the truth is left unspoken without a falsehood being uttered, or because a truthful signification wishes one thing to be understood through another. This kind of figurative saying or deed is abundant in the prophetic writings.

Or, where things are proved to be lies, they must be shown not to be imitated; and if such things should slip into our lives, like other sins, we must not assign them the status of justice but ask for forgiveness.

This is what seems right to me; and the arguments presented above compel me toward this conclusion.

## CHAPTER XVIII

36. Whether one should conceal from a sick person information that would bring about his death. Truth must not be feared as though it were a murderer. If lying is permitted in the proposed case, it becomes difficult to set limits to lies so that they do not grow into perjury and blasphemy. A pointed argument against teachers of lying.

But because we are human beings and live among human beings—and I confess that I am not yet among those whom so-called compensatory sins do not disturb—human feeling often overcomes me in human affairs, and I cannot resist when someone says to me:

“Look: a sick man is in danger from a grave illness, and his strength could no longer bear the news that his only and dearest son has died. He asks you whether his son is alive, though you know that he has died. What will you answer, when, whatever else you say apart from one of three answers—‘He is dead,’ ‘He is alive,’ or ‘I do not know’—he will believe nothing other than that his son is dead, since he understands that you fear saying so and do not wish to lie? The same result follows even if you remain completely silent.

“Of those three answers, two are false: ‘He is alive’ and ‘I do not know’; and you can say them only by lying. But if you say the one true thing—that he is dead—and the distressed man then dies, people will cry out that you killed him. Who could endure people exaggerating how great an evil it is to avoid a salutary lie, and how truth is to be loved as a murderer?”

I am deeply moved by these arguments, though it would be astonishing if they were also wise. For when I place before the eyes of my heart the intelligible beauty of that one from whose mouth nothing false proceeds, although, where truth shines ever more brightly, my trembling weakness recoils from its radiance, I am nevertheless so inflamed with love for such beauty that I despise everything human that draws me away from it.

But it is a great thing for this feeling to persist so strongly that action does not fail in temptation. Nor does it trouble me, as I contemplate that luminous good in which there are no shadows of lying, that when we refuse to lie and human beings die after hearing the truth, truth is called a murderer.

For if an unchaste woman seeks sexual violation, and, when you refuse to consent, she dies in the turmoil of savage passion, will chastity be a murderer? Or because we read, “We are the good fragrance of Christ in every place, both among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing; to some we are the fragrance of life leading to life, to others the fragrance of death leading to death” (2 Cor. 2:15–16), shall we also pronounce the fragrance of Christ a murderer?

But because we are human beings, and in questions and contradictions of this kind human feeling usually overcomes or exhausts us, Paul immediately added, “And who is sufficient for these things?” (2 Cor. 2:16).

37. Added to this, where we ought to lament even more pitifully, is the fact that if we concede that one may lie about the son’s being alive for the sake of the sick man’s health, this evil gradually and little by little increases. By short advances it slowly penetrates and leads to such a great heap of criminal lies that it becomes impossible ever to discover where resistance can be made to so great a plague, which grows immeasurably through the smallest additions.

Hence it was written with the greatest foresight: “The one who despises small things will gradually fall” (Sirach 19:1).

What of those who love this life so greatly that they do not hesitate to prefer it to truth, lest a person die—or rather, so that a person who is destined to die may die somewhat later? They want us not only to lie but also to swear falsely, so that, lest the empty safety of a human being pass away somewhat sooner, we may take the name of the Lord our God in vain.

Among them are learned people who even establish rules and set limits for when one ought or ought not to swear falsely. O where are you, fountains of tears? And what shall we do? Where shall we go? Where shall we hide ourselves from the wrath of truth, if we not only neglect to avoid lies but even dare to teach perjury?

Let the advocates and defenders of lying see what kind or kinds of lying they enjoy justifying. At least let them concede that one must not lie in the worship of God; at least let them refrain from perjury and blasphemy; at least where the name of God, where God as witness, where God’s sacrament is invoked, and where speech concerning divine religion is brought forth or exchanged, let no one lie, praise lying, teach it, prescribe it, or call a lie just.

As for the other kinds of lies, let the person who wishes to lie choose for himself what he thinks is the mildest and most innocent kind of lying.

This I know: even the person who teaches that one ought to lie wishes to appear to be teaching the truth. For if what he teaches is false, who would wish to devote himself to a false doctrine in which the teacher deceives and the learner is deceived? But if, in order to find a disciple, he claims that he is teaching the truth when he teaches that one ought to lie, how can that lie be from the truth, when the apostle John cries out, “Every lie is not from the truth” (1 John 2:21)?

It is therefore not true that one should sometimes lie; and what is not true must not be commended to anyone at all.

## CHAPTER XIX

38. Just as one must not commit sexual violation in order to help someone in danger, neither must one speak a lie. If lies are permitted in any way, there is a danger that they will progress to perjury and blasphemy. The difference between swearing falsely and blaspheming.

But human weakness performs its part and loudly declares that it has an irresistible case on the side of the crowd. It objects and says:

“How are people to be helped when they are in danger—people who, if they are certainly deceived, are turned away from danger, whether another’s or their own—if human feeling does not incline us to lie?”

If the crowd of mortals, the crowd of weakness, will patiently listen to me, I shall offer an answer on behalf of the cause of truth.

Certainly pious, true, holy chastity comes only from truth; and whoever acts against it certainly acts against truth. Why, then, if those in danger cannot otherwise be helped, do I not commit sexual violation, which is contrary to truth precisely because it is contrary to chastity, while, in order to help those in danger, I speak a lie, which is itself most plainly contrary to truth?

What has chastity done to deserve so much from us, and what has truth done to offend us [Note: Col. 0545. The printed editions read, “What has so greatly deserved this among us?”; *among us* is absent from the manuscripts], when all chastity comes from truth, and truth is chastity not of the body but of the mind, while the chastity of the body also dwells in the mind [Note: The manuscripts read this way. The printed editions have: “the chastity of the mind, and truth likewise dwells in the mind, just as the chastity of the body does.”]?

Finally, as I said a little earlier and say again: whoever contradicts me with any lie in order to persuade me or defend his position—what does he say if he does not speak the truth? But if he is to be heard because he speaks the truth, how does he wish to make me a liar by telling the truth? How does truth enlist a lie as its patron? Or does it conquer its adversary so that it may itself be conquered by him [Note: Almost only the Louvain edition reads, “so that it may itself be conquered by him,” rather than “by itself.”]?

Who could endure such an absurdity? We must therefore in no way say that those who assert that one must sometimes lie are truthful in making that assertion, lest—something most absurd and foolish to believe—truth teach us to be liars.

For what sort of thing would it be that no one should learn adultery from chastity, no one should learn to offend God from piety, no one should learn to harm anyone from benevolence, yet we should learn to lie from truth?

Moreover, if truth does not teach this, it is not true. If it is not true, it must not be learned. If it must not be learned, then one must never lie.

### 39. The solid food, he says, is for the mature (Hebr. 5:14)

For many things are relaxed by way of concession to weakness, although they in no way please the most sincere truth. Let whoever is not afraid of what consequences must be feared if certain lies are permitted in any way say this. Nevertheless, they must not be allowed to advance so far as to reach perjuries and blasphemies; nor should any reason at all be alleged why one ought to swear falsely, or—what is more execrable—why God ought to be blasphemed. For it is not the case that, because God is blasphemed through a lie, he is therefore not blasphemed. [Note: Am. and Lov. read, “because God is not blasphemed through a lie.” At this point *non* is absent from the manuscripts and from Erasmus, and it ought to be absent.] Indeed, one could similarly say that no false oath is sworn because a false oath is sworn through a lie. For who could be perjured through the truth? So also [Note: Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read, “if also.”], through the truth no one can be blasphemous.

Certainly, the person who swears falsely more mildly is the one who does not know that what he swears is false and believes it to be true, just as Saul blasphemed more excusably because he did it in ignorance (1 Tim. 1:13). But blasphemy is worse than perjury because, by swearing falsely, God is made a witness to a false matter, whereas by blaspheming, false things are said about God himself. And each person—whether perjured or blasphemous—is that much less excusable the more he knows or believes that the things he asserts by perjury or blasphemy are false. [Note: Am., Er., and four manuscripts read, “each person more inexcusably.”] [Note: Two Vatican manuscripts read, “or asserts by blasphemy, knows or believes [them] to be false.”]

Therefore, whoever says that for the temporal safety or life of a person in danger one ought to lie greatly deviates from the path of eternal salvation and life if he says that in such a case one ought also to swear by God, or even to blaspheme God.

## CHAPTER XX

### 40. Whether one ought at least to lie for a person’s eternal salvation

When a person’s eternal salvation is in danger, just as he ought not to be helped through sexual violation, so neither ought he to be helped through a lie, which is truly a sin. Yet sometimes the danger to that person’s very eternal salvation is also brought forward, and it is loudly declared that, if it cannot otherwise be averted, it must be averted by our lie. For example, suppose that someone who must be baptized is held in the power of wicked and unbelieving men, and that it is impossible to reach him so that he may be cleansed by the bath of regeneration unless the guards are deceived by lying.

From this most odious [Note: The Louvain edition alone reads “most treacherous.”] outcry—which compels us to lie not for anyone’s wealth or honors that pass away in this world, nor for life itself in the present age, but for a person’s eternal salvation—where shall I flee except to you, Truth? And from you chastity is set before me. For if these guards can be enticed by sexual violation to admit us to baptize the person, why do we not do what is contrary to chastity, while, if they can be deceived by a lie, we do what is contrary to truth? Without doubt, chastity would not be faithfully loved by anyone if truth did not command it.

Therefore, if truth commands that the guards be deceived by lying in order to reach the person who is to be baptized, let them be deceived. But how could truth command that a lie be told so that a person may be baptized, if chastity does not command that adultery be committed so that a person may be baptized? Why does chastity not command this, except because truth does not teach it? If, then, we ought to do nothing except what truth teaches, and truth teaches us not to do—even for the sake of baptizing someone—what is contrary to chastity, how will it teach us to do, for the sake of baptizing someone, what is contrary to truth itself?

But just as eyes that are not yet strong enough to gaze at the sun nevertheless willingly look upon the things illuminated by the sun, so souls that have already become capable of delighting in the beauty of chastity cannot immediately contemplate truth itself, from which chastity shines, by their own power. Thus, when they encounter something that must be done contrary to truth, they recoil and shudder from it in the way they recoil and shudder when something contrary to chastity is proposed as necessary.

That son, however, who, receiving the Word, will be far removed from perdition, and from whose mouth no falsehood proceeds (Prov. 29:27), considers himself shut off just as much if he is compelled to cross over into helping a person through a lie as if he were compelled to do so through sexual violation. And the Father hears the one who prays that he may be able to help without lying—the Father himself, whose judgments are unsearchable, wishes that person to be helped.

Such a son, therefore, guards himself from lying just as he guards himself from sin. For sometimes the word “lie” is used in place of the word “sin”; hence the statement: “Every human being is a liar” (Ps. 115:11). It is said as though one were saying: “Every human being is a sinner.” Likewise: “But if the truth of God abounded through my lie” (Rom. 3:7). Accordingly, when he lies as a human being, he sins as a human being, and he will be subject to the sentence in which it is said: “Every human being is a liar”; and: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1:8).

But when no falsehood proceeds from his mouth, he will belong, according to that grace, to which the statement refers: “Whoever is born of God does not sin” (1 John 3:9). For if this birth alone existed in us, no one would sin; and when it alone exists, no one will sin. But now we still bear what we received by being born corruptible, although, according to what we have been reborn, if we walk well, we are renewed inwardly day by day (2 Cor. 4:16). But when this corruptible nature has put on incorruption, life will swallow up everything, and no sting of death will remain. The sting of death, however, is sin (1 Cor. 15:53–56).

## CHAPTER XXI

### 41. Epilogue

Either, then, lies must be avoided by doing what is right, or they must be confessed through repentance; but when they abound through an unhappy way of life, they must not be increased further by teaching them. Let the person who thinks otherwise choose whatever lies he may use to help a person in danger toward any kind of salvation—provided that even among such people we maintain that no cause ought to compel us to perjure ourselves or to blaspheme.

Let us judge these crimes at least to be greater than sexual violations, or certainly no less than them. For it must be considered that husbands very often challenge wives whom they suspect of adultery to swear an oath; and they would certainly not do this unless they believed that even women who had not feared to commit adultery might fear perjury. Indeed, some shameless women who had not feared to deceive their husbands through illicit intercourse feared to call upon God deceitfully as a witness before those same husbands whom they had deceived.

What reason, then, is there for a chaste and religious person to refuse to help someone who is to be baptized through adultery, yet be willing to help him through perjury—something adulterers themselves commonly fear? Furthermore, if it is wicked to do this by perjury, how much more by blasphemy?

Far be it, then, for a Christian to deny and blaspheme Christ in order to make another person a Christian; and, while perishing, to seek someone to be found whom he will lose if he teaches him such things.

Thus you ought to refute and destroy the book entitled *The Balance*, so that you may first recognize that the principal argument by which they maintain that one ought to lie for the sake of concealing religion must be cut off. You must demonstrate that the testimonies by which they attempt to enlist the Holy Books as patrons of their lies are partly not lies at all, and that those which are lies are nevertheless not to be imitated.

And even if weakness claims so much for itself that it is permitted something venially which truth condemns, nevertheless hold and defend this firmly and without hesitation: in divine religion one must never lie at all. Those who are hidden, moreover, are not to be sought through lies any more than adulterers through adulteries, murderers through murders, or sorcerers through sorceries; nor are liars to be sought through lies, or blasphemers through blasphemies. This follows from the many arguments we have set out in this volume, so many that we have scarcely reached the conclusion which we have fixed at this point.

[Col. 0547]

[Note: Concerning the book *On the Work of Monks*, see book 2, chapter 21, of the *Revisions*, col. 638, beginning with the words “So that I might write *On the Work of Monks*” [Note: In the *Revisions*, Augustine places this book immediately before the work *On the Good of Marriage*, which, as noted above, was completed around the year 401.], through the words in col. 639, “Holy brother Aurelius.” M.]

# The One Book of Saint Aurelius Augustine, Bishop of Hippo, on the Work of Monks

[Note: Written around the year of Christ 400.]

[Note: For this book *On the Work of Monks*, nineteen manuscripts were collated: namely, three Vatican manuscripts, the others Gallican; specifically, the Colbertine manuscript, approximately 900 years old; the Royal, Victorine, Corbie, Rheims, Fleury, Vendôme, Michaeline, and Séez manuscripts; those of the Abbey of Saint Martin; of Saint Arnulf of Metz; of the Abbey of Casale Benedicti; of the Bernardines of the Mercy of God; of the Bernardine College of Paris; of the Cistercian Abbey; of the Church of Laon; and of the Augustinians of the principal convent of Paris. Also included were variant readings from four Belgian manuscripts collected by the Louvain scholars, as well as the editions of Erasmus and Louvain.]

[Note: We also compared all the editions mentioned at the beginning of the *Revisions* and the *Confessions*, volume 1. M.]

(C)

At the urging of Aurelius, bishop of Carthage, Augustine defended the cause of monks who supported themselves by the work of their own hands against certain others of the same profession. These others wanted to live from the offerings of religious people, claiming that, by doing no work, they were fulfilling the evangelical commands not to be concerned about food and clothing.

First, Augustine demonstrates that the apostle Paul gave God’s servants both a command and an example of doing bodily work by which they might provide themselves with food and clothing. Next, he shows that those evangelical commands—which some monks used to nourish not only their laziness but also their arrogance—are not contrary to the apostolic command and example. Finally, he reproves the long-haired monks and begs and exhorts them not to continue growing their hair contrary to the apostolic command.

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 0547]

### 1. He was prompted to write this work by Aurelius. The opinion of monks who refuse to work concerning the meaning of the Apostle’s command to work. They oppose the Gospel’s command not to be concerned about bodily food. They want the Apostle’s command to be understood as referring to spiritual work. They think that by not working they obey the Apostle and the Gospel.

Holy brother Aurelius, I ought to obey your command with all the greater devotion because it has become clearer to me that someone commands me through you. For our Lord Jesus Christ, dwelling within you [Note: The Louvain edition alone has “within your inner person.”], and inspiring you with the solicitude of paternal and fraternal charity as to whether this license ought to be allowed to our sons and brothers, the monks who neglect to obey the blessed apostle Paul when he says, “If anyone is unwilling to work, neither let him eat” (2 Thess. 3:10), assumed your will and tongue for his work and commanded me through you to write something to you on this matter.

May he himself also be present with me, so that I may obey in such a way that, through the useful outcome of this fruitful labor, I may understand that I obey him by his gift.

### 2. First, then, we must see what those people of that profession who refuse to work say; next, if we find that they do not think correctly, what should be said for their correction.

“They did not,” they say, “refer to this bodily work in which farmers and craftsmen labor when the Apostle said, ‘If anyone is unwilling to work, neither let him eat.’ For the Apostle could not be contrary to the Gospel, where the Lord himself says:

‘Therefore I tell you, do not be anxious about your life, what you will eat, nor about your body, what you will wear. Is not life more than food, and the body more than clothing? Look at the birds of the air: they neither sow, nor reap, nor gather into barns, and your heavenly Father feeds them. Are you not worth more than they? And which of you, by being anxious, can add one cubit to his stature? And why are you anxious about clothing? Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow: they do not labor, nor spin; yet I tell you that not even Solomon in all his glory was clothed like one of these. But if God so clothes the grass of the field, which is here today and tomorrow is thrown into the oven, how much more will he clothe you, people of little faith? Therefore do not be anxious, saying, “What shall we eat?” or “What shall we drink?” or “With what shall we be clothed?” For the nations seek all these things. But your heavenly Father knows that you need all these things. Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you. Therefore do not be anxious about tomorrow, for tomorrow will be anxious for itself. Sufficient for the day is its own trouble’ (Matt. 6:25–34).

“Look,” they say, “there the Lord commands us to be free from anxiety about our food and clothing. How, then, could the Apostle think contrary to the Lord, so as to command us to be so concerned about what we should eat, what we should drink, and what we should wear that he would even burden us with the occupations, cares, and labors of craftsmen?

“Therefore, when he says, ‘If anyone is unwilling to work, neither let him eat,’ we ought, they say, to understand him as referring to spiritual works. Concerning these he says elsewhere: ‘To each one as the Lord has given: I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth’; and shortly afterward: ‘Each will receive his own reward according to his own labor. For we are God’s fellow workers; you are God’s field, God’s building. According to the grace given to me, as a wise master builder I laid a foundation’ (1 Cor. 3:5–10).

“Therefore, just as the Apostle works by planting, watering, building, and laying a foundation, so ‘the one who is unwilling to work, neither let him eat.’ For what benefit is there in being spiritually nourished by eating the word of God [Note: Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions have: “to eat spiritually, that is, to be nourished by the word of God.”], if one does not thereby work for the building up of others? What benefit was there for that lazy servant in receiving a talent and hiding it, without working to gain profit for his lord? Was it not so that it would be taken away from him at the end and that he himself would be cast into the outer darkness (Matt. 25:24–30)?

“We do the same,” they say. “We read with brothers who come to us tired from the heat of the world, so that they may rest among us in the word of God, in prayers, psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs. We speak with them, console them, exhort them, and build them up whenever we see that something is lacking in their lives according to their station. If we did not perform such works, we would dangerously take spiritual nourishment from the Lord. This is what the Apostle meant when he said, ‘If anyone is unwilling to work, neither let him eat.’

“Thus these men think that they obey the apostolic and evangelical judgment, since they believe that the Gospel commands them not to care about the bodily and temporal necessities of this life, while the Apostle, they think, spoke about spiritual food and work when he said, ‘If anyone is unwilling to work, neither let him eat.’”

## CHAPTER II

### 3. They are refuted because, just as they derive the meaning of the Gospel from various sayings of the Lord, so they fail to observe that the Apostle’s passage must be understood from his other statements

They also fail to observe that if someone were to say that the Lord, speaking in parables and comparisons about spiritual food and clothing, warned his servants not to be anxious about them—as when he says, “When they bring you before tribunals, do not think about what you will say. For what you are to say will be given to you in that hour; for it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matt. 10:19–20)—since this is a saying about spiritual wisdom, and he did not want them to be anxious about it, promising that it would be supplied to them while they were not anxious about it; but that the Apostle, now speaking more openly in the apostolic manner and more literally than figuratively, as is the case with many, indeed almost all, passages in the apostolic Epistles, spoke literally about bodily work and food when he said, “If anyone is unwilling to work, neither let him eat”—then their position would be doubtful.

Yet, by considering the Lord’s other words, they might find something with which to prove that he spoke about not being concerned with bodily food and clothing [Note: The Louvain edition wrongly omits *curando* (“being concerned”), which appears in the other printed editions and in the manuscripts.] when he said, “Do not be anxious about what you will eat, what you will drink, or what you will wear,” if they paid attention to his statement, “For the nations seek all these things.” There he clearly showed that he was speaking about bodily and temporal things.

Thus, if the Apostle had said only this about the matter—“If anyone is unwilling to work, neither let him eat”—they could turn these words toward another meaning. But since in many other places in his Epistles he teaches with complete clarity what he thinks about this matter, they vainly try to envelop themselves and others in darkness, refusing not only to do what charity usefully commands, but even to understand it themselves or to allow others to understand it. They do not fear what is written: “He refused to understand, so as to act well” (Ps. 35:4).

## CHAPTER III

### 4. It is proved from the context of the passage that Paul’s command concerns bodily work. By his own example Paul taught what he commanded

First, therefore, we must demonstrate that the blessed apostle Paul wanted God’s servants to perform bodily works whose end would be a great spiritual reward [Note: The manuscripts have “whose end would be toward a great…”], so that they would need no one for food and clothing, but would provide these things for themselves with their own hands. Next, we must show that those evangelical commands, by which some people foster not only their laziness but also their arrogance, are not contrary to the apostolic command and example.

Let us therefore see how the Apostle came to say, “If anyone is unwilling to work, neither let him eat,” and what he connects with it afterward, so that the meaning may appear clarified from the very context of the passage.
