“We command you,” he says, “brothers, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, to withdraw yourselves from every brother who walks disorderly and not according to the tradition they received from us. For you yourselves know how you ought to imitate us, because we were not disorderly among you, nor did we eat anyone’s bread without paying, but in labor and toil, working night and day so that we would not burden any of you—not because we did not have the right, but so that we might give you an example for you to imitate. For even when we were with you, we commanded you this: if anyone is unwilling to work, neither let him eat. For we hear that some among you walk disorderly, doing no work but meddling. Now we command and exhort such people, in the Lord Jesus Christ, that by working quietly they should eat their own bread” (2 Thess. 3:6–12).

What can be said against this, since, so that no one afterward could interpret it according to his own will rather than according to charity, he taught by his own example what he had commanded?

The Lord had appointed him as a preacher of the Gospel, a soldier of Christ, a planter of the vineyard, and a shepherd of the flock, so that he might live from the Gospel; yet he himself did not demand the payment owed to him, so that he might provide an example for those who wanted to claim what was not owed to them. As he says to the Corinthians:

“Who ever serves as a soldier at his own expense? Who plants a vineyard and does not eat of its fruit? Who shepherds a flock and does not partake of the flock’s milk?”

Therefore, although what was owed to him he refused to accept, his example restrained those who thought that such things were owed to them without proper order in the Church [Note: Erasmus and most manuscripts read “those properly ordered.”].

What else does he mean when he says: “Nor did we eat bread from anyone without paying, but in labor and toil, working night and day so that we would not burden any of you—not because we did not have the right, but so that we might give you an example for you to imitate”?

Let those to whom he gave this command—that is, those who do not have the authority that he had—hear it. They were to eat bread free of bodily labor only while working spiritually. And when he says, “We command and exhort in Christ that, by working quietly, they should eat their own bread,” let them not argue against the Apostle’s most evident words. For this too belongs to the silence with which they ought to eat their bread while working.

## CHAPTER IV

### 5. Paul’s statement clarified from his other Epistles

I would consider and treat these words still more clearly and carefully if I did not have other passages in his Epistles that are much more explicit. When these are compared with the present passage, they make its meaning clearer; even if this passage did not exist, those others would be sufficient.

Writing to the Corinthians about this same matter, he says:

“Am I not free? Am I not an apostle? Have I not seen Jesus Christ our Lord? Are you not my work in the Lord? If I am not an apostle to others, yet surely I am to you. For you are the seal of my apostleship in the Lord. My defense to those who examine me is this: Do we not have the right [Note: Most manuscripts have “permission” in place of “right”] to eat and drink? Do we not have the right to take along a believing woman as a companion, as do the other apostles, the brothers of the Lord, and Cephas?” (1 Cor. 9:1–7).

Observe how he first shows what is permitted to him, and that it is permitted because he is an apostle. For he began with: “Am I not free? Am I not an apostle?” And he proves that he is an apostle by saying: “Have I not seen Jesus Christ our Lord? Are you not my work in the Lord?”

Once this has been proved, he shows that what is permitted to the other apostles is also permitted to him—that is, not to work with his hands but to live from the Gospel, as the Lord established. He demonstrated this most clearly in what follows. For faithful women who possessed earthly means also went with them and ministered from their possessions, so that the apostles would lack none of the things necessary for this life [Note: Almost all manuscripts have “the possessions necessary for this life.”].

The blessed Paul demonstrates that this was indeed permitted to him, as it was to the other apostles, but afterward states that he did not wish to use this power.

Some people, not understanding this, interpreted the phrase “Do we not have the right to take along a believing woman as a companion?” as referring not to a female companion but to a wife. The ambiguity of the Greek word deceived them, since the same word in Greek means both “wife” and “woman.” Yet the Apostle used the expression in such a way that they ought not to have been deceived: he says not merely “woman,” but “a believing woman”; and not merely “to lead,” but “to lead around.”

Other interpreters, however, were not deceived by this ambiguity, and translated it as “woman,” not “wife” [Note: The Louvain edition alone has “because he says ‘a believing woman.’”].

## CHAPTER V

### 6. By Christ’s example, the apostles were permitted to have women who ministered to them accompany them

Whoever thinks that it could not happen among the apostles that women of holy conduct should travel with them wherever they preached the Gospel, in order to minister necessary things to them from their own resources, should listen to the Gospel and learn how they did this by the example of the Lord himself.

Our Lord, in keeping with his merciful compassion for the weaker, although angels could minister to him, also had a money box into which the money contributed by good believers for the necessities of their support was put. He entrusted this money box to Judas, so that, even if we could not avoid thieves, we might learn to tolerate them in the Church. For Judas took away the things that were put into it, as it is written about him (John 12:6).

The Lord also wanted women to follow him in preparing and ministering necessary things. In this way he showed what was owed by the peoples of God, as though they were provinces, to evangelists and ministers of God, as though they were soldiers. If someone did not wish to use what was owed to him, as the apostle Paul did not, he would contribute more to the Church—not by demanding the payment owed to him, but by supporting himself through his own labors.

The innkeeper had heard the following words concerning the wounded man who had been brought to him: “Whatever more you spend, I will repay you when I return” (Luke 10:35). The apostle Paul therefore spent more, for, as he himself testifies, he served as a soldier at his own expense (1 Cor. 9:7–15; 2 Cor. 11:7).

For the Gospel says:

“After this, he himself went through cities and villages, preaching and proclaiming the kingdom of God; and the Twelve were with him, and certain women who had been healed of evil spirits and infirmities: Mary, who is called Magdalene, from whom seven demons had gone out [Note: Thus the manuscripts. The editions have “from whom he had cast out seven demons”]; and Joanna, the wife of Chuza, Herod’s steward; and Susanna; and many others, who ministered to them from their possessions” (Luke 8:1–3).

The apostles imitated this example of the Lord in receiving the food owed to them. The same Lord speaks about this most clearly:

“Go and preach, saying, ‘The kingdom of heaven has drawn near.’ Heal the sick, raise the dead, cleanse lepers, cast out demons. You received without payment; give without payment. Do not possess gold, silver, or money in your belts, nor a bag for the journey, nor two tunics, nor sandals, nor a staff; for the laborer is worthy of his food” (Matt. 10:7–10).

There the Lord established what the same apostle recalls. He told them not to carry all those things so that, wherever necessary, they might receive them from those to whom they proclaimed the kingdom of God.

## CHAPTER VI

### 7. Christ granted the right to live from the Gospel not only to the apostles but also to others

But lest anyone think that this was granted only to the Twelve, consider also what Luke relates:

“After these things the Lord appointed seventy-two others and sent them two by two before his face into every city and place where he himself was about to come. And he said to them: ‘The harvest is indeed plentiful, but the workers are few. Therefore ask the Lord of the harvest to send workers into his harvest. Go; behold, I send you like lambs among wolves. Do not carry a purse, nor a bag, nor sandals, and do not greet anyone on the road. Into whatever house you enter, first say, “Peace to this house.” And if a son of peace is there, your peace will rest upon him; but if not, it will return to you. Remain in the same house, eating and drinking what they have; for the laborer is worthy of his wages’” (Luke 10:1–7).

Here it is evident that these things were not commanded but permitted. Whoever wished to use them could use what was permitted to him by the Lord’s ordinance; whoever did not wish to use them did not act contrary to a command, but surrendered his right, conducting himself [Note: Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read “would conduct himself.”] more mercifully and laboriously in the Gospel and refusing to accept the wages due to him.

Otherwise, the Apostle acted contrary to the Lord’s command when, after showing that this was permitted to him, he immediately added: “Nevertheless, I have not used this authority.”

## CHAPTER VII

### 8. The authority granted to the apostles not to work is to be understood as concerning bodily work

But let us return to the order of the argument and carefully consider the entire passage of the Epistle.

“Do we not,” he says, “have permission to eat and drink? Do we not have permission to take along a believing woman as a companion?” What permission did he mean except that which the Lord gave to those whom he sent to preach the kingdom of heaven, saying, “Eat what is provided by them” [Note: The editions have “among them.” The manuscripts have “from them.” The Greek is *par’ autōn*]; “for the laborer is worthy of his wages”? He also presented himself as an example of the same authority, while faithful women ministered such necessities from their own possessions.

The apostle Paul did still more, using his fellow apostles as evidence of this permission granted by the Lord. For he did not add by way of reproach, “As do the other apostles, the brothers of the Lord, and Cephas,” but showed by this that he had not wished to accept what, by the practice of his fellow soldiers, he proved was permitted to him to accept.

“Or are Barnabas and I alone without the authority not to work?”

Here he removed every doubt, even from the slowest minds, so that they might understand what kind of work he meant. Why else would he say, “Or are Barnabas and I alone without the authority not to work?” unless all evangelists and ministers of the word of God had received authority from the Lord not to work [Note: The word “work” is absent from most manuscripts.] with their hands, but to live from the Gospel, working only spiritually in preaching the kingdom of heaven and building up the peace of the Church?

No one can say that the Apostle was speaking about spiritual work itself when he asked, “Are Barnabas and I alone without the authority not to work?” All of them possessed this authority not to work. Let the person who attempts to twist and distort the apostolic commands into his own meaning say—if he dares—that all evangelists received from the Lord the authority not to evangelize.

But if it is absurd and insane to say this, why do they refuse to understand what is obvious to all: that those men received the authority not to work, but not to perform the bodily works by which they would obtain food, since “the laborer is worthy of his food and his wages,” as the Gospel says?

Therefore, it was not Paul and Barnabas alone who had the authority not to work; all of them equally had this authority. Paul and Barnabas did not use it, contributing more to the Church, as they judged appropriate for the weak in the places where they preached.

And so, lest he appear to have reproached his fellow apostles, he adds and says:

“Who ever serves as a soldier at his own expense? Who shepherds a flock and does not partake of the flock’s milk? Am I saying these things merely from a human point of view? Or does the Law not say the same? For it is written in the law of Moses: ‘You shall not muzzle an ox while it is treading out the grain.’ Is God concerned with oxen? Or does he say this entirely for our sake? It was written for our sake, because the one who plows ought to plow in hope, and the one who threshes in hope of sharing in the harvest” [Note: The manuscripts have “in hope of sharing,” omitting the word “harvest.”].

By these words the apostle Paul sufficiently indicates that his fellow apostles had usurped nothing beyond what was owed to them, since they did not work bodily to obtain the necessities of this life, but, as the Lord had established, lived from the Gospel, eating free bread from those to whom they preached free grace.

They received their wages like soldiers; from the fruit of the vineyard they had planted, they freely took what was necessary; from the flock they tended, they drank milk; and from the threshing floor they threshed, they took food.

## CHAPTER VIII

### 9. The Apostle clearly speaks about the work of the hands

He connects the remaining points more clearly and completely removes every ambiguity of doubt.

“If we have sown spiritual things in you,” he says, “is it a great thing if we reap your carnal things?” What are the spiritual things he sowed except the word and the mystery [Note: The Cistercian manuscript has “ministry”] of the sacrament of the kingdom of heaven? And what are the carnal things that he says he is permitted to reap except these temporal things granted for the life and necessities of the flesh?

He makes clear that, although these things were owed to him, he neither sought nor accepted them from the Corinthians, so as not to place any obstacle in the way of the Gospel of Christ.

What remains, then, except that we understand him to have worked in order to obtain food through bodily work performed with his bodily and visible hands? For if he had sought food and clothing through spiritual work—that is, if he had received these things from those whom he was building up in the Gospel—he would not consistently have said:

“If others share in your authority, why not we even more? But we have not used this authority; rather, we endure everything, so that we may place no obstacle in the way of the Gospel of Christ.”

What authority does he say he did not use except the authority he had received from the Lord over them, so that he might reap their carnal things for the food of this present life, which is lived in the flesh? Others also shared in this authority—those who had not first preached the Gospel to them but later came to their Church preaching the same Gospel.

Therefore, after saying, “If we have sown spiritual things in you, is it a great thing if we reap your carnal things?” he added: “If others share in your authority, why not we even more?”

And after showing what authority they possessed, he said: “But we have not used this authority; rather, we endure everything, so that we may place no obstacle in the way of the Gospel of Christ.”

Let these men say, then, how the Apostle obtained bodily food through spiritual work, when he himself plainly says that he did not use this authority. But if he did not obtain bodily food through spiritual work, it remains that he obtained it through bodily work, and that he referred to this when he said:

“Nor did we eat bread from anyone without paying, but in labor and toil, working night and day so that we would not burden any of you—not because we did not have the authority [Note: The Vulgate and Augustine himself read *quasi* (“as if”) in place of *quia* (“because”); Morel strongly supports this reading, *Elem. Crit.*, p. 104. M.], but so that we might give you an example for you to imitate” (2 Thess. 3:8–9).

“We endure everything,” he says, “so that we may place no obstacle in the way of the Gospel of Christ.”

## CHAPTER IX

[Col. 0556]

10. That this is more evident and clearer from what follows. He returns again and, in every possible way, repeatedly emphasizes what he is permitted to do, and yet does not do. “Do you not know,” he says, “that those who work in the temple eat what comes from the temple? Those who serve the altar share with the altar” [Note: [Col. 0556] The Cistercian codex has *comparticipantur* (“participate with”). “So also the Lord ordained that those who proclaim the Gospel should live from the Gospel; but I have used none of these things.” What could be more evident? What could be clearer? I fear that, when I undertake to explain something that is already self-evident, what is bright and clear by itself may become obscure [Note: [Col. 0556] Erasmus and several manuscripts read *clamat* (“cries out”).]. Those who do not understand these words—or pretend not to understand them—understand my words much less, or claim much less to understand them; unless perhaps they quickly understand ours because they are permitted to ridicule what they have understood, whereas the same permission is not granted concerning the Apostle’s words. Therefore, whenever they cannot interpret them according to their own opinion in some other way, they reply that even clear and manifest statements are obscure and uncertain, because they do not dare to call what is perverse and distorted by its proper name.

The man of God cries out: “The Lord ordained that those who proclaim the Gospel should live from the Gospel; but I have used none of these things.” Yet flesh and blood attempts to distort what is straight, to close what is open, and to cloud what is serene. “He was performing a spiritual work,” they say, “and lived from it.” If that is so, he lived from the Gospel. Why, then, does he say, “The Lord ordained that those who proclaim the Gospel should live from the Gospel; but I have used none of these things”? Or, if they wish to interpret even the expression “to live” here according to spiritual life, the Apostle had no hope in God, since he did not live from the Gospel, for he said, “I have used none of these things.”

Accordingly, so that his hope of eternal life might be certain, the Apostle certainly lived spiritually from the Gospel. But when he says, “I have used none of these things,” he plainly means by this the life conducted in the flesh: the life which, as he said, the Lord ordained that those who proclaim the Gospel should live from the Gospel—that is, to pass this present life, which requires food and clothing, by means of the Gospel. Thus above, speaking of his fellow apostles, he said—whence the Lord Himself declares, “The laborer is worthy of his food,” and, “The laborer is worthy of his wages”—that he did not receive from those to whom he preached the Gospel this food and this wage due for sustaining the present life, rightly saying, “But I have used none of these things.”

## CHAPTER X

11. Why Paul does not live from the Gospel. He continues and adds this, lest anyone should think that he had not received it because they had not given it to him: “I have not written these things so that they should be done in my case; for it is good for me rather to die than that anyone should deprive me of my glory.” What glory could this be except the glory he wished to have before God, sharing in Christ’s sufferings for the sake of the weak, as he is about to state most plainly?

“For if I preach the Gospel,” he says, “it is no glory to me; for necessity is laid upon me”—that is, the necessity of sustaining this present life. “Woe to me,” he says, “if I do not preach the Gospel”—that is, I shall not preach it to my own harm [Col. 0557], because I shall be tormented by hunger and will have nothing from which to live.

For he continues and says: “If I do this willingly, I have a reward.” He says that he does it willingly if he is not compelled to do it by any necessity of supporting this present life; and for this he has a reward, certainly with God, namely, eternal glory. “But if unwillingly,” he says, “I have been entrusted with a stewardship.” That is: if I am unwillingly compelled to preach by the necessity of getting through this present life, a stewardship has been entrusted to me—so that, through my stewardship, because I preach Christ and the truth, although by opportunity, although seeking my own interests, although compelled by the necessity of earthly gain, others may advance, while I do not receive from God that glorious and everlasting reward.

“What, then,” he says, “will my reward be?” He asks this question, and therefore the statement must be suspended until he supplies the answer. To make it easier to understand, let us imagine that we ask him: “What, then, will your reward be, Apostle, when you do not accept that earthly reward which is due even to good evangelists—not evangelizing for this reason, but nevertheless receiving what follows and is offered to them by the Lord’s ordinance? What, then, will your reward be?”

See what he answers: “That, when preaching the Gospel,” he says, “I may offer the Gospel without expense”—that is, so that the Gospel may not be costly to believers, lest they think that it is preached to them for the purpose of making the evangelists appear to sell it. Yet he returns again and again to show what he is lawfully permitted to do by the Lord’s authority, and that he himself does not do it: “That I may not abuse,” he says, “my authority in the Gospel.”

## CHAPTER XI

12. In this matter, as in others, Paul adapts himself out of compassion to the weak. How he became as one under the Law and as one without the Law without pretense or deceit. He fears that, if he lives from the Gospel, the weak may think it is being sold. Since he did this out of compassion for human weakness, let us hear what follows:

“For although I am free from all, I made myself the servant of all, so that I might win the more. To those who are under the Law, I became as one under the Law, although I myself am not under the Law, so that I might win those who were under the Law; to those who are without the Law, as one without the Law, although I am not without the law of God but am in the law of Christ, so that I might win those who are without the Law.”

He did this not by the cunning of pretense, but by the mercy of compassion—that is, not in order to pretend to be a Jew, as some have thought, because he observed the ancient legal practices at Jerusalem [Note: [Col. 0557] Jerome, in the letter numbered 75 among the Augustinian letters, §§ 9–11.]. For he did this in accordance with his free and explicit statement, in which he says: “Was anyone called after being circumcised? Let him not bring on the foreskin” [Note: [Col. 0557] Here and in the immediately following passage, the word *praeputium* (“foreskin”) is absent from the manuscripts, as it is also absent from the Greek text of the Apostle.]. That is, let him not live as though he had brought on the foreskin and covered what he had uncovered. As he says elsewhere: “Your circumcision has become uncircumcision” (Rom. II, 25).

In accordance, therefore, with this statement of his—“Was anyone called after being circumcised? Let him not bring on the foreskin. Was anyone called in uncircumcision? Let him not be circumcised” (I Cor. VII, 18)—he did those things which, to those who did not understand and paid little attention, he was thought to have pretended. He was a Jew and had been called while circumcised; he did not wish to bring on the foreskin [Col. 0558]—that is, he did not wish to live as though he were not circumcised. For this was already within his power.

He was not under the Law in the manner of those who served it slavishly; yet he was in the law of God and of Christ. For that Law was not one thing and the law of God another, as the wretched Manichaeans are accustomed to say. Otherwise, if he acted in that way with respect to the Law, he ought to be thought to have pretended; and he also pretended to be a pagan and sacrificed to idols, because he says that he became to those without the Law as one without the Law. By these he clearly wishes the Gentiles—whom we call pagans—to be understood.

To be under the Law, therefore, is one thing; to be in the Law, another; and to be without the Law, another. Carnal Jews are under the Law; spiritual Jews and Christians are in the Law. Hence the former preserved that ancestral custom, but did not impose unusual burdens upon believing Gentiles; and therefore they too were circumcised [Note: [Col. 0558] The printed editions read *nec illi* (“nor they”). The manuscripts, however, have *et illi* (“and they”), namely, the spiritual Jews who preserved the ancestral custom.]. Those without the Law, on the other hand, are the Gentiles who have not yet believed. The Apostle testifies that he accommodated himself to them through compassionate mercy, not through deceitful pretense—that is, in order to help a carnal Jew or pagan in the manner in which he himself would have wished to be helped, if he were in that condition: bearing their weakness in the likeness of compassion, not deceiving them through a fabricated falsehood.

This follows immediately when he says: “I became weak to the weak, so that I might win the weak” (I Cor. IX, 1–22). It was from this point that he was speaking, so that he might also say all those other things. Therefore, just as his becoming weak to the weak was not a lie, so neither were the other statements made above.

For what weakness does he say that he had toward the weak, except compassion for them—to such an extent that, lest he appear to be a seller of the Gospel and obstruct the course of God’s word by causing it to fall under suspicion among the uninstructed, he did not wish to accept what was owed to him by the Lord’s authority? If he had wished to accept it, he certainly would not have been lying, because it was truly owed to him; and because he did not wish to accept it, he certainly did not lie.

For he did not say that it was not owed to him. Rather, he showed that it was owed, and declared that he had not used what was owed, nor wished at all to use it. He thus became weak precisely by refusing to use his authority, clothed in such a compassionate disposition that he considered how he would wish others to deal with him if he himself were so weak that, on seeing those through whom the Gospel was preached to him accept financial support, he might suspect them of turning it into a marketplace of merchandise.

## CHAPTER XII

13. Shaken by the dangers threatening the weak, he chooses to work rather than live from the Gospel. Concerning this weakness of his he says elsewhere: “We became little children in the midst of you, as a nurse cherishes her own children.” The context of the passage makes this clear:

“For never,” he says, “did we come with a word of flattery, as you know; nor with an occasion of greed—God is witness; nor seeking glory from human beings, either from you or from others, although we could have been a burden to you as apostles of Christ. But we became little children in the midst of you, as a nurse cherishes her own children” (I Thess. II, 5–7).

What he says to the Corinthians—that he possessed the authority of his apostleship, as did the other Apostles, but testifies that he did not use that authority—he also says here to the Thessalonians: “Although we could have been a burden to you as apostles of Christ,” in accordance with what the Lord says: “The laborer is worthy of his reward” [Col. 0559].

That he says this is indicated by the statement he made above: “Nor with an occasion of greed—God is witness.” Through what was owed by the Lord’s authority to good evangelists—not because they evangelized for this purpose, but because they sought the kingdom of God, so that all these things might be added to them—others found an occasion for greed. Of such people he says: “For such do not serve our Lord, but their own belly” (Rom. XVI, 18). The Apostle wished to remove this occasion from them, and therefore omitted even what was justly owed to him.

He makes this clear in the Second Epistle to the Corinthians, where he says that his needs were supplied by other churches. For, as is evident, he had come into such great need that necessary provisions were sent to him from distant churches, while he accepted nothing of the sort from those among whom he was [Note: [Col. 0559] Some manuscripts read *praedicabat* (“was preaching”).].

“Did I commit a sin,” he says, “by humbling myself so that you might be exalted, because I preached the Gospel of God to you without charge? I robbed other churches by accepting support for your service; and when I was with you and was in need, I was a burden to no one. For the brothers who came from Macedonia supplied what was lacking to me; and in every respect I kept myself from burdening you, and will continue to do so. The truth of Christ is in me: this glory of mine will not be silenced in the regions of Achaia. Why? Because I do not love you? God knows. But what I do, and what I will continue to do, is to cut off the opportunity from those who seek an opportunity, so that in the matter of which they boast they may be found to be like us” (II Cor. XI, 7–12).

Thus, concerning this opportunity which he says he cuts off here, he wished the statement there—“Nor with an occasion of greed—God is witness”—to be understood. What he says there, “Humbling myself so that you might be exalted,” is what he says in the First Epistle to the same Corinthians, “I became weak to the weak,” and what he says to the Thessalonians, “I became little in the midst of you, as a nurse cherishes her own children.”

Accordingly, attend to what follows: “So,” he says, “being affectionately desirous of you, we were pleased to share with you not only the Gospel of God but also our own souls, because you had become very dear to us. For you remember, brothers, our labor and toil, working night and day so that we might not burden any of you” (I Thess. II, 8–9).

This is what he said above: “Although we could have been a burden to you as apostles of Christ.” Therefore, shaken by the dangers threatening the weak—lest, agitated by false suspicions, they should hate the Gospel as though it were for sale—he did this as though trembling with paternal and maternal affection.

He speaks in the same way in the Acts of the Apostles, when he sent from Miletus and summoned the elders of the Church from Ephesus. Among other things he said to them:

“I coveted no one’s silver or gold or clothing; you yourselves know that these hands served my needs and those who were with me. In everything I showed you that, by laboring in this way, we ought to help the weak, remembering also the words of the Lord Jesus, for He Himself said: ‘It is more blessed to give than to receive’” (Acts XX, 33–35).

## CHAPTER XIII

14. What the Apostle’s bodily work was. Honest occupations for obtaining a livelihood. At this point someone may perhaps say: If the Apostle performed bodily work, from what source did he sustain this life? What was that work, and when did he have time both to work and to preach the Gospel?

I reply: Suppose that I do not know. Nevertheless, the statements made above testify without any doubt that he worked bodily and lived in the flesh from that work, while he did not use the authority which the Lord had given the Apostles, so that the one proclaiming the Gospel might live from the Gospel.

For this was not said in just one place or briefly, so that it could be twisted and perverted into another meaning by the evasions of even the most cunning person. Since, then, the opposition of those who contradict such authority, with such great and repeated forces, is crushed, what do they ask of me? What work did he perform, or when did he perform it?

I know one thing: he was neither a thief, nor a burglar, nor a robber; neither a charioteer, nor a hunter, nor an actor, nor one who seeks shameful profit. Rather, he worked innocently and honestly at things suitable for human use, such as the work of smiths, builders, shoemakers, farmers, and similar occupations.

Honesty itself does not condemn what the pride of those who love to be called respectable condemns, although they do not love to be respectable in reality. The Apostle, therefore, would not disdain either to undertake some agricultural work or to engage in the labor of craftsmen.

For he says, “Be without offense to Jews and Greeks and the Church of God” (I Cor. X, 32). I do not know whom they could revere in this matter. If they name the Jews: the patriarchs tended flocks. If the Greeks, whom we also call pagans: even philosophers considered shoemakers highly honorable. If the Church of God: that just man, chosen as a testimony to a virginity that was always to remain within marriage, to whom the virgin Mary—who gave birth to Christ—was betrothed, was a craftsman (Matt. XIII, 55).

Whatever work people perform innocently and without fraud is therefore good. The Apostle himself takes care to prevent anyone from falling into evil occupations out of the necessity of sustaining life. “The one who stole,” he says, “must steal no longer; rather, let him labor, working with his hands at what is good, so that he may have something to give to the one who is in need” (Eph. IV, 28).

This, then, is sufficient to know: even in bodily work itself, the Apostle performed what is good.

## CHAPTER XIV

15. When the Apostle was accustomed to work. The leisure of monks. When he was accustomed to work—that is, during what periods of time, so that he would not be hindered from evangelizing—who could determine? He himself did not fail to say that he worked during both the daytime and the nighttime (I Thess. II, 9; II Thess. III, 8).

Yet what are these people doing who inquire about the time of his work as though they were greatly occupied and busy? Have they themselves filled the lands with the Gospel from Jerusalem and around as far as Illyricum? Or have they undertaken, from the peace of the Church, whatever barbarian nations still remain to be visited and brought to completion?

We know that they have gathered together in some holy fellowship in the utmost leisure. The Apostle did something remarkable: although he was genuinely burdened with such great concern for all the churches—both those already established and those still to be established—that came under his care and labor, he also worked with his hands. Yet, when he was in Corinth and in need, he was a burden to none of those among whom he was; rather, what he lacked was fully supplied by the brothers who came from Macedonia (II Cor. XI, 9).

## CHAPTER XV

16. In commanding God’s servants to work, Paul nevertheless does not wish their needs to be cared for less by the faithful. The labor to be chosen by God’s servants should be undertaken with a free mind, without anxiety and greed.

For he himself, because of the needs of the saints—who, although they obeyed his commands to eat their own bread while working quietly, could nevertheless, for many reasons, need some supplementary support—after teaching and warning them as follows, “To such persons we command and exhort in the Lord Jesus Christ that, working quietly, they should eat their own bread,” immediately added, lest those who had the means to provide what was necessary for God’s servants should grow idle on this pretext: “But you, brothers, do not grow weary in doing good” (II Thess. III, 12–13).

And when he wrote to Titus, saying, “Send Zenas the lawyer and Apollos diligently on their way, so that they lack nothing,” he immediately added, to show from what source they ought to lack nothing: “And let our people learn to excel in good works for necessary uses, so that they may not be unfruitful” (Tit. III, 13–14).

He also knew that Timothy, whom he calls his most genuine son, was physically weak, as he shows when he advises him not to drink water but to use a little wine for the sake of his stomach and his frequent illnesses (I Tim. V, 23). Since Timothy could not labor at bodily work, Paul feared that, if he did not wish to be in need of daily food from those to whom he ministered the Gospel [Note: [Col. 0561] The printed editions read: “when he was in need and did not wish to use daily food,” and so forth. The manuscripts read: “when he did not wish to be in need of daily food,” and so forth, although some have: “when he was in need and did not wish to be supported by daily food from those to whom he ministered the Gospel.”], he might seek some business that would entangle the focus of his mind.

For it is one thing to labor bodily with a free mind, as a craftsman does if he is not fraudulent, greedy, or eager for private gain; it is another thing to occupy the mind itself with the cares of acquiring money without bodily labor, as do merchants, agents, or contractors. They preside through anxiety rather than labor with their hands, and therefore occupy their minds with the concern of possessing.

Because Timothy could not work with his hands on account of bodily weakness, Paul therefore exhorts, admonishes, and consoles him in this way:

“Labor,” he says, “as a good soldier of Christ Jesus. No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in worldly business, so that he may please the one to whom he has proved himself. Moreover, the one who competes in the contest is not crowned unless he has competed lawfully.”

Here, lest Timothy suffer the distress of saying, “I cannot dig; I am ashamed to beg” (Luke XVI, 3), he added: “The farmer who labors ought to be the first to receive a share of the fruits” (II Tim. II, 6), in accordance with what he had said to the Corinthians:

“Who ever serves as a soldier at his own expense? Who plants a vineyard and does not eat of its fruit? Who tends a flock and does not partake of the milk of the flock?” (I Cor. IX, 7).

Thus he made the chaste evangelist secure—not one who preached the Gospel in order to sell it, but one who was nevertheless unable with his own hands to provide himself with what was necessary for this life. Timothy was to understand that what he received as necessary from those to whom he ministered as to provincial subjects, and whom he cultivated like a vineyard or tended like a flock, was not begging but an exercise of authority.

## CHAPTER XVI

17. Paul wishes the needs of God’s servants to be supplied by the faithful when, because of their occupations or infirmities, they cannot obtain a livelihood for themselves. The ministry to the saints, by which material goods are supplied to those from whom spiritual goods are received in return. Let God’s servants obey Paul by working, and let good believers supply their needs.

Because of these occupations of God’s servants, or their bodily infirmities—which cannot altogether be absent—the Apostle not only permits the needs of the saints to be supplied by good believers, but also most beneficially urges this.

Apart from that authority which he says he himself did not use, although he commands the faithful to serve it, saying, “Let the one who is instructed in the word share in all good things with the one who instructs him” (Gal. VI, 6)—apart, then, from this authority, which he often testifies that preachers of the word possess over those to whom they preach—he also commands and urges that the necessities of the saints who had sold all their possessions and lived at Jerusalem in a holy community of life, claiming nothing as their own, but having everything in common, with one soul and one heart directed toward God (Acts II, 44; IV, 32), be supplied by the churches of the Gentiles.

Hence also his statement to the Romans: “Now, therefore, I am going to Jerusalem to minister to the saints. For Macedonia and Achaia have been pleased to make some contribution for the poor among the saints who are in Jerusalem. For they have been pleased to do so, and they are their debtors. For if the Gentiles have shared in their spiritual goods, they ought also to minister to them in material goods” (Rom. XV, 25, 27).

This resembles what he said to the Corinthians: “If we have sown spiritual things among you, is it a great matter if we reap your material things?” (I Cor. IX, 11).

Likewise, in the Second Epistle to the Corinthians he says:

“We make known to you, brothers, the grace of God that has been given in the churches of Macedonia: that amid much testing through tribulation, the abundance of their joy and their profound poverty overflowed into the riches of their generosity; for, according to their means, I bear witness, and beyond their means they were willing, with many entreaties begging us for the grace and fellowship of the ministry that is carried out for the saints. And not as we hoped, but they gave themselves first to the Lord and then to us by the will of God, so that we might exhort Titus that, just as he had begun, he might also complete this grace among you.

“But just as you abound in everything—in faith, in speech, in knowledge, in all earnestness, and in the love that comes from you toward us—so also abound in this grace. I do not say this as a command, but, by the earnestness of others, testing the genuineness of your love as well. For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ: that although He was rich, He became poor for your sake, so that you might become rich through His poverty.

“And in this matter I give my advice, for this is beneficial for you, who began not only to do but also to will from the previous year. Now, therefore, complete the deed as well, so that, just as there is readiness of will, there may also be completion according to what each person has. For if there is readiness, a person is acceptable according to what he has, not according to what he does not have. This is not so that others may have relief while you have distress, but that there may be equality at the present time: that your abundance may supply their need, and that their abundance may also supply your need, so that there may be equality, as it is written: ‘The one who had much did not have too much, and the one who had little did not lack.’

“But thanks be to God, who has given the same earnest care for you in Titus’s heart. For he received the encouragement, but, being even more earnest, he went to you of his own accord. We sent with him the brother whose praise in the Gospel is throughout all the churches. And not only that, but he was also appointed by the churches as our traveling companion with this grace that is administered by us for the glory of the Lord and our ready willingness [Note: [Col. 0563] Perhaps: “your ready willingness.”], avoiding this, lest anyone should reproach us in this abundance that is administered by us. For we take care to do what is good not only before God but also before human beings.”

In these words it is evident how greatly he wished not only that the holy congregations should be cared for, but also that they should minister what was necessary to the holy servants of God. He gives his advice in this matter because it benefited more those who performed this service than those toward whom they performed it. For the latter benefited in another way: by making holy use of this service of their brothers toward them, neither serving God for this reason nor accepting these things except to supply their needs, not to nourish their idleness.

“But the blessed Apostle also says that his own care in this ministry—which was now being conveyed through Titus—was so great that, for this purpose, he mentions that the churches appointed as his traveling companion a man of God of good reputation, whose praise, he says, is in the Gospel throughout all the churches. He says that this man was appointed as his companion for the purpose of avoiding human criticism, lest, without the testimony of holy companions in this ministry, he should be thought to accept for himself and turn into his own pockets what he received from the weak and ungodly, when in fact it was being received to supply the needs of the saints and to be carried to or distributed among the needy.

18. Shortly afterward he says:

“Now concerning the ministry that is carried out for the saints, it is superfluous for me to write to you. For I know your readiness, of which I boast about you to the Macedonians, because Achaia has been prepared since the previous year, and the zeal arising from you has stirred up many. But we sent the brothers so that our boasting about you might not be emptied in this matter, so that, as I said, you may be ready. Otherwise, if Macedonians come with me and find you unprepared, we—we will not say you—would be put to shame in this confidence.

“Therefore I considered it necessary to urge the brothers to go to you in advance and prepare this blessing of yours, promised long ago, so that it may be ready as a blessing and not as an act of greed. Now this: ‘The one who sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and the one who sows with blessings will also reap with blessings. Each person should give as he has resolved in his heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver.’

“God is able to make every grace abound toward you, so that, always having all sufficiency in everything, you may abound in every good work. As it is written: ‘He scattered; he gave to the poor; his righteousness remains forever.’

“He who supplies seed to the sower will also supply bread for food, and will multiply your seed and increase the fruits of your righteousness, so that, having been enriched in everything [Note: [Col. 0564] The printed editions read, “having been enriched, you may abound.” The word *abundetis* (“you may abound”) is absent from the manuscripts and is not expressed in the Greek.], you may abound in complete generosity, which through us produces thanksgiving to God. For the ministry of this service not only supplies what is lacking to the saints, but also causes abundant thanksgiving to God through many. By the testing of this ministry, they glorify God for your obedience in confessing the Gospel of Christ, and for the generosity of your contribution to them and to all, while they themselves pray for you and long for you because of the surpassing grace of God in you. Thanks be to God for His indescribable gift” (II Cor. VIII–IX).

With what richness of holy joy the Apostle is filled when he speaks of the reciprocal supply of the needs of Christ’s soldiers and provincials—material goods going from one side to the other, and spiritual goods from the other to the first—so that he might exclaim and, as though bursting forth from the fullness of holy joys, say: “Thanks be to God for His indescribable gift”!

19. Therefore, just as the Apostle never ceased—or rather, as the Spirit of God, possessing, filling, and directing his heart, never ceased—to exhort faithful people who had such worldly resources [Note: [Col. 0564] One Vatican manuscript reads, “the resources of this world.”], so that nothing might be lacking for the needs of God’s servants who had chosen to hold a higher degree of holiness in the Church, cutting every bond of worldly hope and dedicating their free minds to divine service, so they too ought to obey his commands: they should show compassion to the weak; not be bound by love of private property; labor with their hands for the common good [Note: [Col. 0564] So the manuscripts. The printed editions read, “in common labor.”]; and obey their superiors without murmuring. In this way, whatever they have judged lacking—because of the bodily infirmities of some who labor and perform some work by which they maintain their livelihood, or because of ecclesiastical occupations or instruction in saving doctrine—may be supplied from the offerings of good believers.

## CHAPTER XVII

20. The idle claim that they devote themselves to prayer, psalms, reading, and the word of God. It is permissible to sing psalms while working. Reading is of no benefit unless one does what is read. What, then, do those who refuse to work bodily do? I wish to know what they devote themselves to.

“To prayers,” they say, “and psalms, and reading, and the word of God.” Certainly this is a holy life, praiseworthy for the sweetness of Christ [Note: [Col. 0564] The printed editions read, “and in the sweetness of Christ.” The word *in* is absent from the manuscripts.]. But if we are not to be called away from these things, then neither should we eat, nor should the food itself be prepared every day so that it can be set before us [Col. 0565] and consumed.

If the necessity of weakness itself compels God’s servants to devote themselves to these things at fixed intervals of time, why do we not also assign some portions of time to observing the apostolic commands? “The prayer of one who obeys is heard more quickly than that of ten thousand who despise.”

They can also easily sing divine songs while working with their hands, and console the labor itself as though with a divine *kéleuma*—a sailors’ and rowers’ song by which they encourage one another to work [Note: [Col. 0565] *Kéleuma*: a song of sailors and rowers by which they encourage one another to labor.].

Or do we not know how many vanities, and often even obscenities from theatrical performances, craftsmen pour into their hearts and tongues while their hands do not cease from their work? What, then, prevents a servant of God, working with his hands, from meditating on the law of the Lord (Ps. I, 2) and singing psalms to the name of the Most High Lord (Ps. XII, 6)—provided, of course, that he set aside times for learning those things which he will recall by heart?

For this reason, the good works of the faithful and their support for supplying what is necessary ought not to be lacking: the hours devoted to educating the mind, during which bodily work cannot be performed, should not oppress anyone with poverty [Note: [Col. 0565] Several manuscripts read, “should not be oppressed.”].

But those who say that they devote themselves to reading—do they not find there what the Apostle commands? What kind of perversity is this, to refuse to obey reading while wishing to devote oneself to it, and, in order that what is good may be read for a longer time, to refuse for that reason to do what is read? For who does not know that a person progresses all the more quickly when reading good things, the more quickly he does what he reads?

## CHAPTER XVIII
**21. Those who refuse to work under the pretext of distributing the word of God are corrected.** Paul appointed definite times for distributing the word and others for working. Excellent administration requires that everything be done in its proper order.

But if a discourse must be delivered to someone and it occupies a person so fully that he has no time to work with his hands, can everyone in the monastery do this when brothers come to them from another way of life—either expound the divine readings or engage in beneficial discussion of various questions? Since not everyone can do so, why do they all wish to be free from work on this pretext? Even if everyone could, they ought to do it in rotation [Note: [Col. 0565] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions have *vicissim facere deberent*, “they ought to do it alternately.”], not only so that the others would not be prevented from necessary tasks, but also because it is sufficient for one person to speak when many are listening.

Furthermore, how would the Apostle himself have had time to work with his hands unless he had appointed definite times for distributing the word of God? God did not wish this to remain unknown to us. For Scripture has not been silent either about what craft he practiced or about the times he set aside for dispensing the Gospel.

When the day of his departure was pressing upon him while he was at Troas, and the brothers had gathered on the first day of the week to break bread, his attention and the discussion’s necessity were so great that the discourse continued until midnight (Acts 20:7), as though they had forgotten that on that day there was no fast. But when he remained in some place [Note: [Col. 0565] Several manuscripts read, “when he remained in another place”; and most have, “when he was going to remain.”] for some time, disputing daily, who could doubt that he had hours assigned to this duty [Col. 0566]?

When he was at Athens, because he had found people exceptionally eager to investigate matters, it is written of him: “So he disputed in the synagogue with the Jews, and with the resident Gentiles in the marketplace throughout the day” [Note: [Col. 0566] Lovaniensis has, “with Gentiles in the alleys and marketplace.” Erasmus has, “with individual Gentiles in the marketplace.” Several manuscripts have, “with Gentiles in the villages, in the marketplace.” More correctly, the old Floriacensis codex has, “with resident Gentiles in the marketplace.”] “with those who were present” [Note: [Col. 0566] The printed editions have, “with everyone.” Several manuscripts have, “with those who were present.”].

He did not spend the entire day in the synagogue, where it was customary to preach on the Sabbath; rather, he says, “in the marketplace throughout the day,” clearly because of the Athenians’ intellectual interests. For the passage continues: “But some Epicurean and Stoic philosophers conversed with him.” A little later it says: “Now all the Athenians and the resident foreigners spent their time doing nothing other than saying or hearing something new” (Acts 17:17–18, 21).

Let us suppose that the Apostle did not work during all the days he was at Athens. His needs were supplied from Macedonia for this very reason, as he says in the Second Epistle to the Corinthians (2 Cor. 11:9), although he could also have worked at other hours and during the nights, since he was strong both in mind and body.

But when he had left Athens, let us see what Scripture says: “He disputed in the synagogue every Sabbath.” This took place at Corinth. At Troas, however, where, because of the necessity of his impending departure, the discourse continued until midnight, it was the first day of the week, which is called the Lord’s Day. From this we understand that he was not with the Jews but with Christians, since the narrator himself says that they had gathered to break bread.

This, then, is the best administration: that everything be distributed among its proper times and carried out in an orderly manner, lest the human mind be disturbed by being entangled in confused complications.

### CHAPTER XIX

**22. Paul performed truly bodily work.** The work the Apostle did is also stated there. “After this,” it says, “he departed from Athens and came to Corinth. Finding a certain Jew named Aquila, a native of Pontus, recently arrived from Italy, together with his wife Priscilla—for Claudius had ordered all Jews to leave Rome—he went to them. Because he had the same trade, he stayed with them and worked; for they were tentmakers” [Note: [Col. 0566] In Greek, *skēnopoioi*, “tentmakers.”] (Acts 18:1–4).

If they attempt to interpret this allegorically, they show how much progress they have made in the ecclesiastical writings to which they boast of devoting themselves. Certainly, as for the statements already mentioned—“Do we alone, Barnabas and I, have no right not to work?” and “We have not made use of this right” (1 Cor. 9:6, 12); “Although we could have been a burden to you as Christ’s apostles” (1 Thess. 2:7); “Working night and day so as not to burden any of you” (2 Thess. 3:8); and “The Lord commanded that those who proclaim the Gospel should live from the Gospel; but I have used none of these rights” (1 Cor. 9:14–15)—let them either explain these and similar passages differently, or, if they are pressed by the brilliant light of truth, understand and obey them. If they neither wish nor are able to obey, let them at least acknowledge that those who wish to obey are better, and those who are able to do so are happier.

For it is one thing either truthfully to plead bodily weakness or to pretend a false one; it is another to be so deceived and to deceive others so that, on this account, greater righteousness seems to exist among God’s servants because idleness has been able to rule among the inexperienced.

The person who demonstrates a genuine bodily infirmity should be treated humanely. The one who claims a false infirmity and cannot be proved false should be left to God. Neither, however, establishes a pernicious rule. The good servant of God serves his visibly infirm brother; and when he believes the one who deceives, because he does not think him evil, he does not imitate him so as to become evil. If he does not believe him, he considers him deceitful and nevertheless does not imitate him.

But whoever says, “This is true righteousness: that we imitate the birds of the sky by doing no bodily work, since whoever has performed such work acts against the Gospel”—if any weak-minded person hears and believes this, he is to be mourned.

### CHAPTER XX

**23. The objection: did the other Apostles sin by not working and by living from the Gospel? The response. The command to work applies to those who do not evangelize.** From this arises another question. Someone may perhaps say: “What, then? Did the other Apostles, the brothers of the Lord, and Cephas sin because they did not work? Or did they hinder the Gospel, since blessed Paul says that he did not use this right so as not to place any obstacle in the way of the Gospel of Christ?”

If they sinned because they did not work, then they had not received the right not to work but to live from the Gospel. But if they had received this right, since the Lord ordained that those who proclaim the Gospel should live from the Gospel, and since he said, “The worker is worthy of his food” (Matt. 10:10), while Paul, who distributed something more, refused to use that right, then they certainly did not sin. If they did not sin, they caused no obstacle. For it is not the case that hindering the Gospel is no sin. If this is so, they say, then we too are free either to use or not to use this right.

**24.** I could resolve this question briefly by saying—and I would say it justly—that the Apostle must be believed. He himself knew why, in the Churches of the Gentiles, the Gospel ought not to be carried about as something for sale. He was not blaming his fellow Apostles but distinguishing his own ministry, because they had undoubtedly divided the provinces for evangelization among themselves at the prompting of the Holy Spirit: Paul and Barnabas were to go to the Gentiles, while the others were to go to the circumcised (Acts 13:2; Gal. 2:9).

That he nevertheless gave this command to those who did not possess such a right is demonstrated by the many things already said.

### CHAPTER XXI

Those who wish to be free from work have, for the most part, been converted from a poor and laborious life. These brothers of ours, as I believe, rashly claim for themselves that they possess such a right. For if they are evangelists, I admit that they possess it. If they are ministers of the altar and dispensers of the sacraments, they do not wrongly claim this right for themselves but plainly vindicate it.

**25.** If only they had possessed something in this world by which they could easily support this life without practicing a craft, and had distributed it among the needy when they turned to God, then their weakness should be believed and endured. Such people are accustomed—not because they were better brought up, as many think, but, in truth, because they were raised more delicately—to be unable to bear the strain of bodily work.

Perhaps many such people were in Jerusalem. For it is written that they sold their estates and placed the proceeds at the Apostles’ feet, so that distribution might be made to each according to his need (Acts 2:45; 4:34). Because they were found nearby and were useful to the Gentiles [Note: [Col. 0568] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions have: “Therefore they were found faithful and were useful to the Gentiles.”], who were being called from far away from the worship of idols, in accordance with what was said, “The law shall go forth from Zion, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem” (Isa. 2:3), the Apostle called the Gentile Christians their debtors: “They are their debtors,” he says; and he added why: “For if the Gentiles have shared in their spiritual goods, they ought also to minister to them in material things” (Rom. 15:27).

### CHAPTER XXII

**Against the idle and talkative, who by example and speech draw others away from work.** Now, however, people often come to this profession of service to God from a servile condition, or as freedmen, or because they have been—or are to be—freed by their masters; also from rural life, from the practice of crafts, and from plebeian labor. They are all the more fortunate because they have been raised all the more vigorously. If such people are not admitted, it is a grave offense. For many truly great and exemplary people have arisen from their number.

Indeed, God chose the weak things of the world to confound the strong; he chose the foolish things of the world to confound the wise; and the lowly things of the world, and things that are not, as though they were, to abolish the things that are, so that no flesh might glory before God (1 Cor. 1:27–29).

This pious and holy consideration therefore causes even those to be admitted who bring no evidence of a life changed for the better. For it is not apparent whether they have come with the purpose of serving God, or whether, fleeing a poor and laborious life, they have wished to be fed and clothed while idle, and even to be honored by those by whom they had been accustomed to be despised and trampled.

Since such people cannot excuse their refusal to work by bodily weakness—for the habits of their former life convict them—they conceal themselves under the shelter of bad discipline, intending, through a wrong understanding of the Gospel, to overturn the apostolic commands: they are truly the birds of the sky, but because of pride they lift themselves up on high; and they are the grass of the field, but because they think carnally.

**26.** What the same Apostle says must be avoided in the case of undisciplined younger widows happens to them: “At the same time they learn to be idle; and not only idle, but also inquisitive and talkative, saying things they ought not to say” (1 Tim. 5:13).

He said this about wicked women, but we grieve and lament that it also occurs among wicked men, who, against the very person in whose Epistles we read these words, speak idly and talkatively about things they ought not to say.

If there are some among them who have come to the holy service with the purpose of pleasing the one to whom they have pledged themselves (2 Tim. 2:4), and who possess such bodily strength and sound health that they can not only be instructed but also work, according to the Apostle, then—apart from the idle and corrupt speeches of these men, which they cannot judge because of their inexperienced condition—they are changed by a fatal contagion into the same corruption [Note: [Col. 0569] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions have “they imitate,” less suitably.].

They not only fail to imitate the obedience of the saints who work quietly, and of those living in other monasteries according to the apostolic norm and in the most salutary discipline; they also insult their betters, praising idleness as the guardian of the Gospel and accusing mercy as its transgressor.

For the person who looks after the good reputation of God’s servants works with far greater mercy toward the souls of the weak than the person who breaks bread for the hungry works toward the bodies of the needy.

Therefore, would that those who wish to be free from work with their hands were entirely free from work with their tongues as well! They would not invite so many to imitate them if they offered not only lazy examples but also silent ones.

### CHAPTER XXIII

**27. The idle misunderstand the Gospel. The lazy are mockingly ridiculed. Monks shut themselves away so that they may be seen by no one for many days. The Gospel command not to think about tomorrow agrees with the Apostle.** Now they recite the Gospel of Christ against the Apostle of Christ. The works of the idle are so astonishing that they wish to hinder the Gospel, which the Apostle both commanded and practiced precisely so that the Gospel itself would not be hindered.

Yet if we force them to live according to their understanding of the very words of the Gospel, they will be the first to try to persuade us that those words should not be understood in the way they understand them.

Certainly they say that they ought not to work because the birds of the sky neither sow nor reap, and the Lord gave us them as an example so that we would not concern ourselves with such necessities. Why, then, do they not attend to what follows? For it was not said only that they neither sow nor reap; it was also added, “nor gather into storehouses” (Matt. 6:26).

Storehouses, granaries, or *repositoria*—repositories—may be so called, word for word [Note: [Col. 0569] The printed editions have, “word for word from the Greek.” The words “from the Greek” are absent from the manuscripts.] [Note: [Col. 0569] Most manuscripts have *repostoria*.].

Why, then, do these men wish to have idle hands and full repositories? Why do they store and preserve what they receive from the labors of others, so that it may be brought out day by day? Why, finally, do they grind and bake? Birds do not do these things.

Or, if they find people whom they can persuade to perform this work as well, so that prepared food may be brought to them each day, do they at least fetch water for themselves from springs, cisterns, or wells, and draw and store it? Birds do not do this.

But if this pleases them, let good and most devoted provincial believers in the eternal King strive to serve his bravest soldiers even in these matters, so that they are not forced to fill even their water vessels—if indeed they have now surpassed those who were then in Jerusalem by a new degree of righteousness.

When famine threatened them, good believers from Greece sent grain to those who were in Jerusalem at that time, through the prophets who had foretold these events (Acts 11:28–30). I believe that those men made bread for themselves from it, or at least arranged for it to be made—something birds do not do.

But if these people, as I had begun to say, have now surpassed even those men by some degree of righteousness and act like birds in everything that concerns sustaining this life [Col. 0570], let them show us human beings serving birds, as they wish to be served, except for captured and confined birds, which are not trusted lest they fail to return when they fly away. And yet birds prefer to enjoy their freedom and take as much as they need from the fields rather than receive what human beings set before and prepare for them.

**28.** Accordingly, those who have trained themselves to go daily into the fields as though to pasture, and to pluck whatever they find at whatever time [Note: [Col. 0570] The old Casalensis codex has, “and whatever is available at the time.”] and return once their hunger has been quieted [Note: [Col. 0570] The Cistercian manuscript has, “once their hunger has been satisfied.”], will again surpass these men by another, more exalted degree of righteousness.

But, plainly, for the sake of the field-guards, how good it would be if the Lord also deigned to give them wings, so that the servants of God found in other people’s fields would not be seized as thieves but driven away like starlings.

For now, the person whom the hunter cannot catch will imitate a bird [Note: [Col. 0570] The printed editions have *quam*, “which.” The better manuscripts have *quem*, “whom.” Two Vatican manuscripts have *vinitor*, “vine-dresser,” instead of *venator*, “hunter.”].

But let us grant all servants of God permission to go into their fields whenever they wish and depart from them safely and refreshed. Thus the law commanded the people of Israel that no one should treat as a thief someone in his fields unless that person wished to carry something away with him; if he had touched nothing except what he had eaten, they were to let him depart free and unpunished (Deut. 23:24–25).

For this reason the Jews accused the Lord’s disciples, who plucked ears of grain, of violating the Sabbath rather than of theft (Matt. 12:1–2).

But what will be done during those seasons of the year when food that can immediately be eaten is not found in the fields? Whoever attempts to carry home something that he can prepare by cooking will, according to these men’s understanding, hear the Gospel say: “Put it down; birds do not do this.”

**29.** Let us grant, moreover, that throughout the turning year something can be found in the fields—on a tree, among herbs, or in various roots—that can be taken as food uncooked; or let such vigorous bodily exercise be undertaken that whatever must be cooked will not harm them even if eaten raw; and let it be possible to go out for food despite every winter hardship. Let everything then be arranged so that nothing is carried away for preparation and nothing stored for tomorrow.

Even so, those who shut themselves away alive for many days from human sight and admit no one to them, devoting themselves intensely to prayer, will not be able to preserve these practices. They are accustomed to shut away with themselves foods that are certainly simple and worthless, but sufficient for the days during which they have decided that no one should see them [Note: [Col. 0570] The Venetus manuscript has *consuescunt*, “they become accustomed”; M.].

Since they have leisure for such practices, and since they present themselves for imitation not with arrogant pride but with merciful holiness, I not only do not criticize their discipline of such astonishing continence, but cannot praise it as much as it deserves.

What, then, according to their understanding of the Gospel words, are we to say about these men? Are they perhaps more unlike the birds the holier they are, because unless they store food for many days they will be unable to shut themselves away as they do? Yet they hear along with us: “Therefore do not think about tomorrow” (Matt. 6:34).

**30.** To sum up briefly: these men, who attempt through a perverse understanding of the Gospel to overturn such clear apostolic commands, must either not think about tomorrow, like the birds of the sky, or obey the Apostle, like beloved children. Indeed, they should do both, because the two agree. Paul, the servant of Christ Jesus (Rom. 1:1), would not give counsel contrary to his Lord.

We say this plainly to them: If you understand the birds of the sky in the Gospel to mean that you should not provide food and clothing for yourselves by working with your hands, then store nothing for tomorrow either, just as the birds of the sky store nothing.

But if storing something for tomorrow can be consistent with the Gospel, where it says, “Look at the birds of the sky: they neither sow, nor reap, nor gather into storehouses,” then it can also be consistent with the Gospel—and with the likeness of the birds of the sky—to pass this bodily life in the labor of physical work.

### CHAPTER XXIV

**31. The Gospel does not prohibit storing something for tomorrow.** If they are pressed by the Gospel to store nothing for tomorrow, they answer quite correctly: “Why, then, did the Lord himself have a money box in which he kept the money that had been collected?” (John 12:6). “Why, when famine was threatening so long beforehand [Note: [Col. 0571] Several manuscripts have, “when impending famine threatened.” Two Vatican manuscripts below have, “sent to the holy brothers.”], was grain sent to the holy fathers?” (Acts 11:28–30).

“Why did the Apostles provide what the saints needed in such a way that it would not be lacking in the future, so that the most blessed Paul wrote to the Corinthians in his Epistle: ‘As for the collection for the saints, as I directed the Churches of Galatia, so you also are to do. On the first day of every week, let each of you put something aside privately, storing up whatever he has decided, so that collections will not be made when I come. When I arrive, I will send by letter those whom you approve to carry your gift to Jerusalem. If it is fitting that I go as well, they will travel with me’” (1 Cor. 16:1–4)?”

They bring forward these and many other statements, most abundantly and most truly. We answer them: “You see, then, that although the Lord said, ‘Do not think about tomorrow,’ you are not compelled by these words to reserve nothing for tomorrow. Why, then, do you claim that you are compelled by the same words to be free from work? Why are the birds of the sky not your example for reserving nothing, while you want them to be your example for doing no work?”

### CHAPTER XXV

**32. What benefit there is in abandoning former occupations if one must still work. The charity of common life. Those who convert from a higher social condition ought also to work, but much more those who come from a lower one.** Someone may say: “What benefit does it bring a servant of God that, after abandoning the occupations he had in the world, he turns to this spiritual life [Col. 0572] and service, if he must still engage in occupations like a craftsman?” [Note: [Col. 0572] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions have *opifices*, “craftsmen.”]

As though it could easily be explained in words how much benefit there is in what the Lord said to the rich man who asked for advice about attaining eternal life: if he wished to be perfect, he should sell what he possessed, distribute it to the poor in their need, and follow him (Matt. 19:21).

Or who followed the Lord with such swift progress as the one who said, “I have not run in vain, nor labored in vain” (Phil. 2:16)? Yet he both commanded and performed these very works.

Having been taught and formed by such great authority, we ought to have been satisfied with this example for abandoning our former possessions [Note: [Col. 0572] Two Vatican manuscripts have: “This authority ought to have been sufficient for us to abandon them.” Some others have, “nor ought we,” and so forth.] and working with our hands.

But with the help of the Lord himself, we can perhaps understand, to some extent, what benefit it brings servants of God to have abandoned their former occupations even while they work in this way.

If someone converts to this life from wealth and is not prevented by bodily weakness, are we so lacking in Christ’s wisdom that we do not understand how great a swelling of former pride is healed when, after the superfluous things that previously inflamed his mind destructively have been cut away [Note: [Col. 0572] Several manuscripts have *inflabatur*, “was puffed up.”], he does not refuse the humility of a craftsman in the small things that remain and are naturally necessary for this life?

But if someone converts to this life from poverty, he should not think that he is doing what he used to do if he has transferred himself from loving or enlarging even the smallest private possession—no longer seeking his own interests but those of Jesus Christ (Phil. 2:21)—to the charity of common life, intending to live in the company of those whose soul and heart are one in God, so that no one says that anything is his own, but everything is held in common (Acts 4:32).

For if the ancient rulers of this earthly state are regularly praised in the eloquence of their learned writers because they placed the commonwealth of their entire people above their private affairs, so that one of them, a conqueror who had triumphed after subduing Africa, had nothing to give his daughter when she married except that, by decree of the senate, a dowry was provided for her from public funds [Note: [Col. 0572] Scipio, in Valerius, book 4, chapter 4; Zonaras, book 2; and Seneca, *To Albinus*, chapter 12]—with what spirit should a citizen of that eternal city, the heavenly Jerusalem, regard his commonwealth? Surely he should ensure that whatever he produces with his own hands is held in common with his brother, and, if he lacks anything, receive it from the common fund, saying with the one whose command and example he has followed, “As having nothing, yet possessing everything” (2 Cor. 6:10).

**33.** Therefore even those who, after abandoning or distributing possessions—whether extensive or of whatever degree of wealth—have wished, with pious and salutary humility, to be numbered among Christ’s poor should work with their hands if they are physically able and free from ecclesiastical occupations.

Although, when they bring such great evidence of their spiritual commitment and contribute much or at least a substantial amount from the possessions they formerly had toward meeting the needs of that same community, the common reality and fraternal charity ought to support their livelihood [Col. 0573], nevertheless, if they themselves also work with their hands in order to remove the excuse of the idle who come from a humbler—and therefore more laborious—life, they act with far greater mercy than when they distributed all their possessions to the needy.

If they do not wish to work, who would dare compel them? Nevertheless, occupations must be found for them in the monastery, even if they are less demanding physically, but require vigilant administration, so that they do not eat their bread for nothing merely because it has now become common [Note: [Col. 0573] This relates to the blessed Benedict’s command in chapter 48 of the Rule, concerning manual labor: “Let work or a craft be assigned to sickly or delicate brothers such that they are neither idle nor oppressed by the violence of labor, so that they may avoid it. Their weakness is to be considered by the abbot.”].

Nor should it matter in which monasteries or in what place each person distributed what he had to needy brothers. All Christians have one commonwealth. Therefore, whoever supplies what Christians need anywhere, wherever he himself receives what he needs, receives it from Christ’s goods [Note: [Col. 0573] The word *bonis* was restored on the authority of Erasmus, the Lyon edition, the Venetian edition, and the Lovaniensis edition. The Benedictine Fathers, omitting it from the text, add in the margin: “Supply *rebus*, ‘things.’” M.].

For wherever he himself gave to such people, who received anything except Christ?

But those who, even outside this holy fellowship, used to pass their lives by bodily labor—and many come to monasteries from their number, since such people are also more numerous among humanity—if they do not wish to work, should not eat.

For it is not so that the rich are humbled to piety in the Christian service of arms that the poor may be exalted to pride. It is wholly unfitting that in a life where hardworking senators are formed, idle craftsmen should be formed; and that where men who had been owners of estates come after abandoning their luxuries, delicate peasants should be found.

### CHAPTER XXVI

**34. How the command not to be anxious about food and clothing is to be understood.
