How the statement about the birds of the sky and the lilies of the field is to be interpreted.** But the Lord says: “Do not be anxious about your life, what you shall eat, nor about your body, what you shall wear.”

This is rightly said, because he had previously stated: “You cannot serve God and Mammon.” Whoever preaches the Gospel in order to have food and clothing thinks that he serves both God, because he preaches the Gospel, and Mammon, because he preaches for the sake of those necessities. The Lord says that this is impossible.

Accordingly, the person who preaches the Gospel for the sake of those things is shown to serve not God but Mammon, even if God uses him for the advancement of others in a way unknown to him.

For to this statement the Lord adds: “Therefore I say to you, do not be anxious about your life, what you shall eat, nor about your body, what you shall wear.” He does not mean that they should not provide these things insofar as necessity requires, and by whatever honorable means they can; rather, they should not fix their attention upon these things or do whatever they are commanded to do in proclaiming the Gospel for their sake [Note: [Col. 0573] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions have *praeconio*, “preaching.”].

He calls the intention behind an action its “eye.” For shortly before, speaking in order to reach this point, he said: “The lamp of your body is your eye. If your eye is simple, your whole body will be luminous; but if your eye is evil, your whole body will be dark” (Matt. 6:22–23)—that is, your actions will be such as the intention behind your actions has been.

To arrive at this point, he had earlier given instructions concerning almsgiving, saying: “Do not store up treasures for yourselves on earth, where rust and moth destroy, and where thieves break in and steal. But store up treasures for yourselves in heaven, where neither moth nor rust destroys, and where thieves do not break in and steal. For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.”

Then he added: “The lamp of your body is your eye” (Matt. 6), so that those who give alms would not do so with the intention of pleasing human beings or of seeking on earth a return for what they do.

Thus, when the Apostle commanded Timothy that the rich should be admonished, he said: “Let them give easily, share, and store up for themselves a good foundation for the future, so that they may take hold of true life” (1 Tim. 6:18–19).

Therefore, when the Lord directed the eye of those who give alms toward the future life and heavenly reward, so that their deeds too might be luminous when their eye was simple—for the following applies to that final recompense: “Whoever receives you receives me, and whoever receives me receives him who sent me. Whoever receives a prophet in the name of a prophet will receive a prophet’s reward; whoever receives a righteous person in the name of a righteous person will receive a righteous person’s reward; and whoever gives one of these least ones only a cup of cold water in the name of a disciple—amen, I say to you, his reward shall not be lost” (Matt. 10:40–42)—lest perhaps, after correcting the eye of those who provide necessities to the needy, prophets, righteous persons, and the Lord’s disciples, the eye of those for whom these things were done should become corrupted, so that they would wish to serve Christ in order to receive these things.

“No one,” he says, “can serve two masters.” And a little later: “You cannot,” he says, “serve God and Mammon.” Immediately he connected this with the words: “Therefore I say to you, do not be anxious about your life, what you shall eat, nor about your body, what you shall wear.”

**35.** As for what follows concerning the birds of the sky and the lilies of the field, the Lord says it so that no one may think that God does not care for the necessities of his servants, since his most wise providence extends even to creating [Note: [Col. 0574] Manuscripts of good quality have “restoring.”] and governing these things.

For he himself also feeds and clothes those who work with their hands. But so that they may not distort Christian service into a means of acquiring these things, the Lord warns his servants that, in the ministry owed to his sacrament, we should seek not these things but his kingdom and righteousness.

All these things will be added to us—whether we work with our hands, are hindered by bodily weakness, or are so occupied by the duties of that service that we are unable to do anything else.

### CHAPTER XXVII

We must use our own resourcefulness, lest we appear to tempt God. For because God said, “Call upon me in the day of trouble; I will deliver you, and you will glorify me” (Ps. 49:15), the Apostle ought not therefore to have refrained from fleeing and being lowered through a wall in a basket so that he might escape the hand of his persecutor (Acts 9:25), but rather have waited to be captured and for God to free him from the midst of the fires as he had freed the three young men (Dan. 3:50).

Nor, for this reason, should the Lord have been forbidden to say, “If they persecute you in one city, flee to another” (Matt. 10:23), because he himself said, “If you ask the Father for anything in my name, he will give it to you” (John 16:23).

Thus, if someone raised such a question against the disciples of Christ who were fleeing persecution—asking why they had not stood their ground and, after calling upon God, been rescued by his miracles as Daniel was from the lions (Dan. 6:23; 14:40) and Peter from his chains (Acts 12:7)—they would answer that they ought not to tempt God. He would perform such deeds if he wished, but only when they had no other course of action available to them. When he granted them the power to flee, even if they were delivered through flight, they would still be delivered by him alone.

In the same way, if someone uses the Gospel to question servants of God who are free from other duties and able, by the Apostle’s example and command, to support themselves by working with their hands—raising the issue of the birds of the sky, which neither sow, reap, nor gather into storehouses, and of the lilies of the field, because they neither labor nor spin—they will readily answer:

“If we are unable to work because of some illness or occupation, he will feed and clothe us in the manner of the birds and lilies, which do none of this kind of work. But when we are able, we ought not to tempt our God. For the very ability we possess comes from his gift; and when we live by it, we live by the provision of the one who granted us the ability.

Therefore we are not anxious about these necessities. When we can perform these tasks, he feeds and clothes us—the one by whom human beings are fed and clothed. When we cannot perform them, that same one feeds and clothes us—the one by whom the birds are fed and the lilies clothed, because we are worth more than they.”

Therefore, in this service of ours, we do not think about tomorrow, because we have pledged ourselves to please him not for the sake of these temporal things, to which tomorrow belongs, but for the sake of eternal things, where it is always today, remaining free from involvement in worldly occupations (2 Tim. 2:4).

### CHAPTER XXVIII
36. He graphically describes idle and wandering monks. Since this is so, allow me, holy brother—for through you the Lord grants me great confidence—to address those very sons and brothers of ours whom I know you bring forth with such great love together with us, until apostolic discipline has been formed in them. O servants of God, soldiers of Christ, do you really so disregard the snares of the most cunning enemy? He has scattered everywhere, under the appearance of monks, so many hypocrites who go about the provinces—sent by no one, settled nowhere, standing nowhere, sitting nowhere—eager by every means to obscure your good reputation, that good fragrance of Christ, lest good souls say, “We will run after the fragrance of your ointments” (Song 1:3), and so escape his snares.

Some of them peddle the relics of martyrs—if indeed they are relics of martyrs; others magnify their fringes and phylacteries; others falsely claim that they have heard that their parents or relatives are living in this or that region and that they are going to visit them. They all beg, all demand either the expenses of profitable poverty or the price of pretended sanctity. Meanwhile, whenever they are caught in their evil deeds, or in any way become known, your way of life is blasphemed under the general name of “monks”—a way of life so good and holy that, in the name of Christ, we desire it to flourish throughout all Africa just as it does in other lands.

Are you not therefore inflamed with zeal for God? Does your heart not grow warm within you, and does fire not burn in your meditation (Ps. 38:4), so that by good works you may pursue the evil works of these men, cutting off their opportunity for shameful commerce, by which your reputation is injured and a stumbling-block is placed before the weak? Have pity, then, and suffer with them; show people that you seek the kingdom of God not through idleness and easy sustenance, but by the narrow and constricted way of this calling.

Your situation is the same as the Apostle’s, so that you may cut off the opportunity of those who seek an opportunity (2 Cor. 11:12), and so that those who are choked by their foulness may be refreshed by your good fragrance.

## CHAPTER XXIX

37. Augustine’s occupations. He would prefer to work at fixed hours in the manner of monks. We do not bind up heavy burdens and place them on your shoulders, while refusing to touch them with a finger (Matt. 23:4). Seek out and recognize the labors imposed by our occupations, as well as the bodily illnesses of some among us, and the established custom of the churches that we serve—such a custom that it does not allow us leisure for the tasks to which we exhort you.

Although we can say, “Who ever serves as a soldier at his own expense? Who plants a vineyard and does not eat of its fruit? Who tends a flock and does not receive milk from the flock?” (1 Cor. 9:7), nevertheless I call upon the Lord Jesus, in whose name I say these things with confidence, as witness over my soul: so far as my own advantage is concerned, I would much rather work with my hands each day for a fixed number of hours, as is established in well-regulated monasteries [Note: [Col. 0576] Some manuscripts read, “and fixed hours.”], and have the remaining hours free for reading and prayer or for attending to something from the divine Scriptures [Note: [Col. 0576] Hence this was established by Blessed Benedict in the Rule, chapter 48: “At fixed times the brothers must be occupied in manual labor, and again at fixed hours in sacred reading.” Fulgentius, a follower of Augustine, maintained the same manner of life. Ferrandus writes of him in his Life, chapter 14: “He took delight in working with his own hands. He practiced the art of writing with distinction, and very often wove fans from palm leaves; even when he had become abbot, he devoted himself to this work in his monastery. In his cell he also frequently devoted himself to reading in the presence of the brothers.” And in chapter 27: “He had less affection for brothers who labored and tirelessly performed manual tasks but did not devote themselves to reading, and he did not consider them worthy of the highest honor.”], than to endure the most tumultuous complications of other people’s lawsuits arising from secular affairs, whether by judging cases that must be settled or by intervening to bring them to an end. The Apostle imposed these burdens upon us—not by his own judgment, but by the judgment of the one who spoke through him [Note: [Col. 0576] Several manuscripts read “afflicted” (*afflixit*)]—although we do not read that he himself endured such burdens. For the course of his apostleship was otherwise [Note: [Col. 0576] In many manuscripts, “their apostolic journeys were otherwise” (*se habebant*)].

He did not say, “If you have secular lawsuits, bring them to us,” or, “Appoint us to judge.” Rather: “Those who are held in low esteem in the church, appoint these,” he says. “I say this to your shame: is there no one wise among you who can judge between his brother? But brother goes to law with brother—and that before unbelievers!” (1 Cor. 6:4–6). Thus he wanted faithful and holy men who remained settled in their places—not men who went here and there for the sake of the Gospel—to examine such matters. That is why it is never written of him that he devoted himself at any time to these affairs, from which we cannot excuse ourselves, even if we are held in low esteem; for he preferred that even such men be appointed, if wise men were lacking, rather than that Christian affairs be brought before the secular courts.

Nevertheless, we undertake this labor with the Lord’s consolation, for the hope of eternal life, so that we may bear fruit with endurance. We are servants of his Church, especially of its weaker members, whatever kind of members we may be in that same body [Note: [Col. 0577] So the manuscripts. The editions instead read, “however great members we may be.”]. I omit the countless other ecclesiastical cares, which perhaps no one believes unless he has experienced them.

We therefore do not bind up heavy burdens and place them on your shoulders while refusing to touch them with a finger, since, if we could do so without violating the order of our office—as the one who tests our hearts sees—we would prefer to do what we urge you to do rather than what we are compelled to do.

Certainly, for all of us—both you and us—who labor according to our rank and office, the way is narrow, marked by labor and hardship. Yet for those who rejoice in hope, his yoke is easy and his burden light: he who called us to rest, who first passed through the valley of weeping, where he himself was not without afflictions.

If you are brothers, if you are our sons, if you are fellow servants—or rather, if in Christ we are your servants—listen to what we advise, acknowledge what we command, and accept what we distribute. But if we are Pharisees who bind heavy burdens and place them on your shoulders, then do what we say, even if you disapprove of what we do (Matt. 23:3).

For us it is a very small matter to be judged by you or by a human day (1 Cor. 4:3). Let the one who gave us something to offer for his inspection see how genuine our care for you is. Finally, think of us as you wish: the Apostle Paul commands and entreats you in the Lord “to eat your own bread in quietness,” that is, working in an orderly, peaceful, and obedient manner (2 Thess. 3:12). Nor, I suppose, do you believe anything evil about him; and you have believed in the one who speaks through him.

## CHAPTER XXX

38. He fears that the good may be corrupted by growing sluggish through the idleness of the wicked. My dearest and most reverend brother Aurelius, in the depths of Christ, I have not delayed writing this, insofar as the one who commanded me through you to do so granted me the ability, concerning the work of monks. My chief concern was that good brothers who obey the apostolic commands should not be called transgressors of the Gospel because of the idle and disobedient, but that those who do not work should at least have no doubt that those who work are to be preferred to them.

But who could tolerate stubborn men who resist the Apostle’s most salutary admonitions being not merely tolerated as weaker persons, but even praised as holier, so that monasteries founded upon sounder teaching are corrupted by a twofold enticement: by the unrestrained license of idleness and by the false name of sanctity?

Therefore, let the other brothers and sons of ours also know—those who are accustomed to favor such people and, through ignorance, to defend this sort of presumption—that they above all must be corrected, so that those men may be corrected and not weakened in doing good. Certainly, in that they promptly and cheerfully provide the necessities of God’s servants, we not only do not rebuke them but embrace it most warmly. Yet they must not, through a misguided mercy, harm those men's future life more than they assist their present life.

39. For there is less sin if the sinner is not praised in the desires of his soul and if the one who practices iniquity is blessed (Ps. 9:24).

## CHAPTER XXXI

Against long-haired monks. What is more unjust than to want one’s juniors to obey while refusing to obey one’s seniors? I speak of the Apostle, not of myself—so much so that some even grow their hair long. Concerning this he did not wish the matter to be debated at all, saying: “If anyone wishes to be contentious, we have no such custom, nor the Church of God.”

This is what I command: the matter calls not for the ingenuity of an arguer, but for attention to the authority of the one who commands. For what does it mean, I ask, to wear one’s hair so openly against the Apostle’s command [Note: [Col. 0578] Some manuscripts read “to strive” (*conari*). Several others read “to be idle” or “to be at leisure.”]? Is one to be so free from work that even barbers do not work? Or do they claim to imitate the birds of the Gospel, fearing, as though they might be plucked, that they would be unable to fly?

I fear saying more on this subject because of certain long-haired brothers, whose other qualities—and almost all their qualities besides this one—I deeply honor. But the more we love them in Christ, the more carefully we admonish them. We do not fear that their humility will reject our admonition, since we ourselves desire to be admonished by such men whenever we perhaps stumble or go astray.

This, then, is what we admonish these holy men: let them not be moved by the foolish arguments of vain people or imitate in this perversity those from whom they are otherwise so entirely different. Those men, carrying their hypocrisy about for sale, fear that shorn sanctity will be considered inferior to long-haired sanctity, so that whoever sees them may think of those ancient figures whom we read of—Samuel and the others who were not shorn (Num. 6:5).

They do not consider the difference between that prophetic covering and the revelation of the Gospel, concerning which the Apostle says: “When you turn to Christ, the veil will be taken away” (2 Cor. 3:16). For what the veil placed between Moses’ face and the sight of the people of Israel signified (Exod. 34:33), the hair of the holy men also signified in those times. Indeed, the same Apostle says that hair is a covering, by whose authority these men are pressed. He plainly says: “If a man wears his hair long, it is a disgrace to him.”

“We accept this disgrace,” they say, “deservedly because of our sins.” In this way they offer the shelter of a pretended humility, so that beneath it they may display a vanity put up for sale [Note: [Col. 0579] Several manuscripts read “type” (*typum*) instead of “vanity” (*typhum*).], as though the Apostle taught pride when he says: “Every man praying or prophesying with his head covered dishonors his head”; and, “A man ought not to cover his head, since he is the image and glory of God” (1 Cor. 11:4–16).

The one who says “ought not” perhaps does not know how to teach humility. But if, during the time of the Gospel, they seek this disgrace—which was a sacrament in the time of prophecy—as a sign of humility, let them be shorn and cover their heads with sackcloth. Yet then that appearance will not be put up for sale, because Samson was covered not with sackcloth but with his hair (Judg. 16:17).

## CHAPTER XXXII

40. The perverse interpretation of Scripture by long-haired monks. The Apostle Paul professed the highest chastity. The command to men not to cover the head. The mind represented by the man, desire by the woman. What they have once again invented in defense of their long hair is, if it may be said, tragically ridiculous. “The Apostle prohibited a man from having long hair,” they say; “but those who have castrated themselves for the sake of the kingdom of heaven (Matt. 19:12) are no longer men.”

O singular madness! The man who says this, as he deserves, arms himself by a counsel of unspeakable impiety against the clear proclamations of Holy Scripture. He persists on a crooked path and attempts to introduce a pestilential doctrine, because he is not the blessed man who has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly, nor stood in the way of sinners, nor sat in the seat of pestilence (Ps. 1:1).

For if he meditated on God’s law day and night, there he would find the Apostle Paul himself, who, having certainly professed the highest chastity, says: “I wish that all people were as I myself am” (1 Cor. 7:7). Yet he shows himself to be a man not only by living in this way but also by speaking in this way. For he says: “When I was a child, I spoke as a child, I understood as a child, I reasoned as a child; but when I became a man, I put away the things of a child” (1 Cor. 13:11).

But why should I mention the Apostle, when those who say these things do not know what they think about our Lord and Savior himself? For of whom else is it said: “Until we all attain to the unity of faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God, to a perfect man, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ, so that we may no longer be children, tossed and carried about by every wind of doctrine, by the deceit of men and by their craftiness for the machination of error” (Eph. 4:13–14)?

By this deceit they deceive the inexperienced; by this craft and these machinations of the enemy they themselves are carried about, and, clinging together in their wandering, they attempt in some way to make the minds of the weak whirl around with them, so that all alike may not know where they are.

They have heard or read what is written: “For as many of you as were baptized in Christ have put on Christ: there is neither Jew nor Greek; there is neither slave nor free; there is neither male nor female” (Gal. 3:27–28). They do not understand this to have been said according to the concupiscence of bodily sex [Note: [Col. 0579] Lov. reads “not according to”; “not” is absent from the edition of Erasmus and from most manuscripts.], because in the inner person, where we are renewed in the newness of our mind (2 Cor. 4:16), there is no such sexual distinction.

They should not, therefore, deny that they are men simply because they accomplish nothing by means of the male sex. Married Christians who engage in this activity are not Christians on account of what they share with other non-Christians and even with beasts. One thing is what is conceded to weakness or paid to mortal propagation; another is what is signified by a faithful profession for the attainment of incorruptible and eternal life [Note: [Col. 0580] The manuscripts read “is signified” (*signatur*).].

The command given to men not to cover their heads is indeed represented in the body, but the words themselves indicate that it is to be enacted in the mind, where the image and glory of God are. “A man,” he says, “ought not to cover his head, since he is the image and glory of God.” He himself explains where this image is when he says: “Do not lie to one another; strip off the old man with his deeds, and put on the new man, who is renewed in knowledge according to the image of his creator” (Col. 3:9–10).

Who could doubt that this renewal takes place in the mind? But if anyone does doubt it, let him hear the clearer statement. Giving the same admonition elsewhere, he says: “As the truth is in Jesus, put off, according to your former way of life, the old man, who is corrupted according to the desires of deceit; be renewed in the spirit of your mind, and put on the new man, who according to God was created” (Eph. 4:21–24).

What, then? Do women not possess this renewal of the mind, where the image of God is? Who could say so? But they do not signify it by the sex of their body; for this reason they are commanded to be veiled. By the very fact that they are women, they signify that part which may be called the desiring part, over which the mind rules and which itself is subject to its God whenever life is lived rightly and in proper order.

Therefore, what in one human being are mind and desire—the former ruling, the latter being ruled; the former exercising dominion, the latter being subjected—is represented in two human beings, man and woman, according to the sex of the body. Speaking of this sacrament, the Apostle says that a man ought not to be veiled, but that a woman ought to be.

For the more gloriously the mind is raised toward higher things, the more diligently desire is restrained from lower things—until the whole human being, together with the mortal and fragile body it now possesses, is clothed in incorruption and immortality at the final resurrection, and death is swallowed up in victory (1 Cor. 15:54).

## CHAPTER XXXIII

41. He asks certain good long-haired men to cut their hair. Therefore, let those who refuse to do what is right at least cease teaching what is wrong. But there are others whom we rebuke in this address [Note: [Col. 0580] The manuscripts read “correct” (*corrigimus*).]: those who, by this one fault—wearing their hair long contrary to the apostolic command—offend and disturb the Church.

Some people, unwilling to think evil of them, are forced to twist the Apostle’s plain words into a perverse meaning; others prefer to defend the sound understanding of Scripture rather than flatter any human beings [Note: [Col. 0580] So the manuscripts. Lov. reads, “rather than flatter any people.”]. Thus the weaker and the stronger brothers become involved in the bitterest and most dangerous disputes. If those men knew this, they would doubtless correct this fault also—men whose other qualities we admire and love.

We do not rebuke them, but we ask and entreat them, by the divinity and humanity of Christ and by the love of the Holy Spirit, not to place this stumbling-block before the weak any longer, those for whom Christ died. Nor should they increase the pain and anguish of our hearts when we consider how much more readily wicked people can imitate this evil in order to deceive others when they see it in men whom, because of their many other good qualities, we honor with the duties owed by Christian love.

If, after this admonition—or rather, entreaty—of ours, they decide that they must persist in this practice, we shall do nothing other than grieve and groan. Let them know this; it is enough. If they are servants of God, they will have compassion. If they do not, I do not wish to say anything harsher.

Therefore, if you approve, make all these matters—on which I may perhaps have been more talkative than your occupations and mine would have wished—known to our brothers and sons, for whose sake you deemed it appropriate to impose this burden upon me. But if anything seems to you to need to be withdrawn or corrected, let me learn this through a letter from Your Blessedness.

[Col. 0581]

[Note: [Col. 0581] Concerning the book *On the Divination of Demons*, see Book 2, chapter 30, of the *Retractations*, col. 643, beginning with the words, “About this same time, the necessity arose for me from a certain discussion” [Note: [Col. 0581] Augustine indicates that this book belongs to the same period in which he published the brief works against the Donatists that he had just reviewed—works belonging to a period somewhat before the Conference of Carthage, and therefore to be placed between the years 406 and 411] and continuing to the words, “the holy days of the Octaves.” M.]

# THE ONE BOOK OF SAINT AURELIUS AUGUSTINE, BISHOP OF HIPPO, ON THE DIVINATION OF DEMONS

[Note: [Col. 0581] Written between the years 406 and 411.]

[Note: [Col. 0581] The book *On the Divination of Demons* was reviewed against three Vatican manuscripts and seven Gallican manuscripts: namely, two belonging to the Dominicans of Paris on the Rue Saint-Jacques; one from the College of Navarre; and also the Royal, Remigian, Michaeline, and Fleury manuscripts; against the variant readings of three Belgian manuscripts cited by Lov.; and against the editions of Amerbach, Erasmus, and Lov.]

[Note: [Col. 0581] We also compared all the editions mentioned at the beginning of *Retractations* and *Confessions*, vol. 1. M.]

(C)

The divinations of demons, and the practices pertaining to their worship, are not thereby rightly performed merely because they do not occur without God’s permission. What is the source of those divinations of demons, and why are they sometimes true, although they are usually false?

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 0581]

1. The occasion for writing this book. What God permits is not immediately right. Even in matters pertaining to religious worship, God permits things that displease him. One day during the holy days of the Octaves [Note: [Col. 0581] The solemn Octaves of the baptized at Easter are mentioned elsewhere. See the note on Sermon 260, vol. 5.], when many Christian lay brothers were present with me in the morning and we had taken our customary seats, a discussion arose concerning the Christian religion in opposition to the presumption of the pagans and their supposed extraordinary and profound knowledge.

I remembered this discussion and thought that it ought to be completed in writing, without identifying the persons who had contradicted me, although they were Christians and seemed, by their very opposition, rather to be seeking what ought to be answered to the pagans.

When, therefore, the question was raised concerning the divination of demons, and it was asserted that someone or other had foretold the destruction of the temple of Serapis that took place in Alexandria, I replied that it was not surprising if the demons were able both to know and to foretell that the destruction of their temple and image was imminent [Note: [Col. 0581] So the manuscripts. The editions instead read, “the destruction of the temple and its images was imminent.”], just as they know and foretell many other things, insofar as they are permitted to know and foretell them.

2. When someone replied to me, “Then such divinations are not evil, nor do they displease God; otherwise the all-powerful and just God would not permit them to occur if they were evil and unjust,” I answered that such things ought not therefore to be considered just merely because the all-powerful and most just God permits them to occur.

For many other things that are manifestly unjust—such as murders, adulteries, thefts, robberies, and other acts of this kind—certainly displease the just God because they are unjust. Nevertheless, the same all-powerful God permits them to occur according to a definite rationale of his judgment—not with impunity, but for the condemnation of those by whom the things that displease the just God are committed.

3. When, conversely, it was said that there was indeed no doubt that God is all-powerful and just, but that he did not care about human sins committed against human society while they were occurring, and that for this reason they could occur—for certainly they could not occur if the all-powerful God had not permitted them—yet that it was in no way to be believed that he disregarded matters pertaining to the worship of religion itself; and consequently that such things could not have occurred unless they had pleased him, and therefore ought not to be considered evil, I replied as follows:

“Then do they now displease him, when temples and images are destroyed and the sacrifices of the nations, if they have been performed, are punished? For just as it is said that these things could not have occurred unless they had pleased God, and that they must therefore be considered good because they pleased the just God, so it can be said that they could not now be prohibited, destroyed, and punished unless they displeased God. Accordingly, if they were then rightly performed because they were shown to please the just God by the fact that he allowed them to be performed, they are now performed wickedly because they are shown to displease God by the fact that he either commands or permits them to be destroyed.”

## CHAPTER II

4. The sacrifices of the pagans are not to be considered good merely because God did not prevent them from being performed. Things permitted by the all-powerful God but disapproved by that same just God. The pontifical books of profane rites. What has so far been established, and what must be considered next.

It was objected that these practices are indeed not now performed justly, but that they are not evil; and that they are unjust because they are performed contrary to the laws that prohibit them, but not evil because, if they were evil, God would certainly never have been pleased by them. Moreover, if he had never been pleased by them, they would never have occurred, since he who can do all things would not have permitted them—and he would not have disregarded them when they were so important that, if they were evil, they would have been performed against the very religion by which God is worshiped.

I replied: “If they are not evil for this reason—that they are proved to have pleased God by the fact that the all-powerful God permits them to occur—how will that be good which is prohibited and destroyed? If it is not good that things pleasing to God are destroyed, the all-powerful God would not permit this to happen, since it too is done against the religion by which God is worshiped, if human beings destroy things that please God. But if the all-powerful God permits this to happen as an evil, then those earlier things are not to be considered good merely because the all-powerful God permitted them to occur.”

5. It was objected that it must be granted that these practices are no longer rightly performed—or rather, that they are now entirely no longer performed—because they now displease the all-powerful God; nevertheless, they pleased him when they were being performed. We do not know why they pleased him then or why they displease him now; yet it remains certain that they could not then have been performed unless they had pleased the all-powerful God, nor have ceased now unless they had displeased the all-powerful God.

I replied: “Why, then, are such things still secretly performed—either remaining concealed forever or being punished when discovered—if the all-powerful God permits none of these things to occur except what pleases him as a just God, since what is unjust cannot please the just God?”

It was objected that such things are not now performed at all. “For those sacred rites,” he said, “that were written down in the pontifical books are not performed. Those rites were rightly performed then, and they were shown at that time to please God precisely by the fact that the all-powerful and just God permitted them to be performed. But if any of the now-prohibited sacrifices is performed secretly and unlawfully, it is not to be compared with that class of pontifical sacrifice; rather, it must be assigned to the category of what is done at night, since it is certain that all such unlawful practices are prohibited and condemned in the pontifical books themselves.”

I replied: “Why, then, does God permit even such things to occur, if he disregards none of these evil deeds that are committed against religion? In particular, those who attach great value to the pontifical books are compelled to admit from this very fact that God cares about them, since they assert that the things prohibited by these books are certainly prohibited by divine authority. How, then, are they prohibited by divine authority unless they displease God? By prohibiting them, God shows not only that they displease him but also that he cares about them and does not disregard them entirely. From this it follows that God, as the just one, disapproves of something and yet, as the all-powerful one, permits it.”

6. When these points had been made, it was conceded that something is not therefore to be considered just and good merely because the all-powerful God, although displeased by it, nevertheless permits it to occur [Note: [Col. 0584] Two manuscripts read, “because God, although just and all-powerful, nevertheless permits it to occur.”]. It had to be acknowledged that even those evils committed against the religion by which God is worshiped both displease the just God and are permitted by the all-powerful God according to the rationale of his judgment.

But another matter now had to be considered: the source of the divinations, whether of demons or of whatever beings the pagans call gods. For it had to be examined whether perhaps these things should not be considered good merely because the all-powerful God permits them to occur, but rather because they are so great that they seem attributable only to the power of God.

I promised that I would answer this later, since at that time the hour for going out to the people was already pressing upon us. I did not delay when time was granted for writing [Note: [Col. 0584] The manuscripts read “for writing” (*scribendo*).]: I both unraveled those earlier arguments and appended these further ones.

## CHAPTER III

7. The divination of demons has three causes. They surpass human beings in keenness of perception, speed of movement, and long experience of things. Demons are not therefore to be preferred to human beings.

The nature of demons is such that, through the perception of an aerial body, they easily surpass the perception of earthly bodies. Because of the greater mobility of that same aerial body, they also surpass beyond comparison not only the running of any human beings or animals but even the flight of birds.

Endowed with these two qualities so far as the aerial body is concerned—that is, keenness of perception and speed of movement—they announce or foretell many things learned beforehand, which human beings marvel at because of the sluggishness of their earthly senses. To this was added, through the very long period over which their life extends, a much greater experience of things than can accrue to human beings because of the brevity of life.

Through these capacities [Note: [Col. 0584] Several manuscripts read “efficiencies” (*efficientias*).] that the nature of an aerial body has acquired, demons not only foretell many future events but also perform many marvelous deeds. Since human beings cannot say or do such things, some judge demons worthy of serving and honoring with divine worship, chiefly under the impulse of the vice of curiosity, through love of a false and earthly happiness and of temporal excellence [Note: [Col. 0584] Most manuscripts read: “under the strongest impulse of the vice of curiosity, through love of false happiness and of earthly temporal excellence,” omitting the conjunction “and.”].

But those who cleanse themselves of these desires, and do not allow themselves to be deceived and captured by them, but seek and love something that is always the same, through participation in which they may be blessed, first consider that demons are not to be preferred to them merely because they prevail through a keener bodily sense—an aerial sense, that is, of a subtler element.

For even among earthly bodies they do not think that animals should be preferred to themselves merely because animals perceive many things more keenly. Thus, they do not prefer a clever dog because, through its exceptionally acute sense of smell, it finds a hidden beast and in this way provides a kind of guidance to a human being in capturing it—not through a more prudent understanding of the mind, but through a sharper bodily sense. Nor do they prefer a vulture because, when a corpse has been thrown out, it flies to it from an unexpected distance. Nor do they prefer an eagle because, flying high, it is said to see from a great distance a fish swimming beneath the waves and to seize it with its extended feet and talons after plunging heavily into the water.

Nor do they prefer the many other kinds of living creatures that wander among plants harmful to their health, feeding without touching anything that would injure them, while a human being can scarcely learn through experience to avoid such things and fears many harmless things simply because they are unfamiliar.

From this it is easy to infer how much keener perception may exist in aerial bodies. Yet no prudent person would on that account consider demons, who possess this quality, preferable to good human beings.

I would say the same about speed of body. By this excellence, human beings are surpassed not only by birds but also by many four-footed animals, so that in comparison with them they must be considered leaden. Yet they do not for that reason think that these kinds of animals should be preferred to themselves, since they govern them—not by bodily force but by reason—in order to capture them, tame them, and turn them to the use and advantage of their own will.

## CHAPTER IV

Certain marvelous things performed by demons are nevertheless to be despised. As for that third power of demons—namely, that through their long experience of things they have learned how to foresee and foretell many events—those who carefully distinguish such matters from the truth of the truest light despise it so completely that they do not consider wicked old men who have experienced more and therefore seem more learned to be superior to good young men. Nor do they think that physicians, sailors, or farmers whom they have seen to be wicked in will and unjust in character should therefore be preferred to themselves merely because the first foretell many things about illnesses, the second about storms, and the third about kinds of trees and crops, so that to someone inexperienced in these matters they may seem to be divining.

8. But since demons not only foretell certain future events but also perform certain marvelous things—because of the excellence of their bodies—why should this not be despised by the prudent, when wicked and abandoned human beings often exercise their bodies in such ways and can accomplish so much through various arts [Note: [Col. 0585] The editions read, “can accomplish so much by practicing their arts.” The words “by practicing” are absent from the manuscripts.] that those who do not know of such things and have never seen them scarcely believe them even when they are reported?

How many marvelous things have rope-walkers and other theatrical performers accomplished? How many have craftsmen, especially mechanics, accomplished? Are they therefore better than human beings endowed with goodness and holy piety?

I have mentioned these things so that anyone who considers them without obstinacy and without the vain contentiousness of resistance may also reflect that, if certain human beings can accomplish so much with the underlying, denser material of their own bodies or of earth, water, stones, wood, and various metals—so that those who cannot do such things are often struck with amazement and call them divine in comparison with themselves—while some of those people are more powerful in their arts and some of these are better in character, then demons, by the capacity and facility of their most subtle body, that is, an aerial body, can accomplish how much greater and more marvelous things!

Yet they are unclean and perverse spirits because of the depravity of their will, and especially because of the arrogance of pride and the malice of envy [Note: [Col. 0586] So the manuscripts. The editions instead read, “and evident malice.”].

How powerful the element of air is—the element by which their bodies prevail—in invisibly grinding, moving, changing, and manipulating many visible things would take too long to demonstrate now. I think that it readily occurs to anyone who considers the matter even moderately carefully.

## CHAPTER V
### 9. How demons foretell the future

Since this is so, it must first be understood that, when the question concerns demonic divination, demons generally foretell what they themselves are going to do. For they often receive the power both to inflict diseases and to make the air unhealthy by corrupting it, and to suggest evil deeds to depraved people and to lovers of earthly advantages—people whose character assures them that such persons will consent when these things are suggested to them. They make these suggestions by astonishing and invisible means, penetrating the bodies of people who do not perceive it through the subtlety of their own bodies, and mingling with their thoughts through certain imaginary apparitions, whether the people are awake or asleep.

Sometimes, however, they foretell not what they themselves do, but what they foresee will happen from natural signs—signs that cannot enter into human perception. A physician’s foreseeing what someone ignorant of his art does not foresee does not therefore make him a diviner. What is surprising, then, if, just as a physician foresees future good or bad health from the condition of the human body, whether disturbed or well-regulated, so a demon foresees future storms from a condition and arrangement of the air known to him but unknown to us? [Note: [Col. 0586] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions, however, read: “known to them, unknown to us.”]

Sometimes they also learn with complete ease the dispositions of human beings—not only those expressed in speech, but also those conceived in thought—when certain signs are expressed from the mind in the body. [Note: [Col. 0586] *Retractations* II, chapter 30. See also *Against the Academics*, book I, chapters 6 and 7, §§16–21.] From this too they foretell many future events, which seem astonishing to others who do not know that these things have been arranged. For just as a more agitated movement of the mind appears in the face, so that human beings too can recognize outwardly something that is taking place inwardly, so it should not be thought incredible that even milder [Note: [Col. 0586] The Venetian edition reads *leviores* (“lighter”). M.] thoughts give certain signs through the body—signs that cannot be perceived by the duller human senses, but can be perceived by the sharper senses of demons. [Note: [Col. 0586] In the manuscripts, *obtunso*; the reading *obtuso* is printed.]

### Chapter VI

### 10. How far demonic divination falls short of the height of divine prophecy. Demons are usually both deceived and deceivers. How they are deceived. How they deceive

By this and similar abilities demons foretell many things, although they are far removed from the height of that prophecy which God brings about through his holy Angels and Prophets. For if they foretell anything concerning God’s plan, they hear it in order to foretell it; and when they announce what they hear from it, they neither deceive nor are deceived, since angelic and prophetic oracles are utterly truthful.

People react with indignation, however, [Note: [Col. 0586] Thus the manuscripts. But Amerbach and Erasmus print: “People do not react with indignation.” Lovaniensis reads: “But let it not be received with indignation.”] that demons also hear and proclaim some things of this kind—as though it were unworthy that what is said in order to make it known to human beings should be kept silent not only by the good but also by the evil. Even among human beings we see the precepts of a good life sung alike by the just and the depraved; and this does not hinder, but rather contributes to, a greater knowledge and reputation of the truth, when even those who oppose it by their depraved conduct declare whatever they know about it.

In their other predictions, however, demons are generally both deceived and deceivers. They are deceived because, when they foretell their own plans, something is suddenly commanded from above that disrupts all their schemes. It is as though human beings subject to various authorities should make some plan which they suppose their superiors will not prevent, and should promise that they will carry it out; but those who possess greater power should suddenly prohibit the whole plan, which had been arranged and prepared according to some higher decision.

They are also deceived when they foresee certain things from natural causes—as physicians, sailors, or farmers do, though far more keenly and with much greater skill, owing to the more alert and more practiced perception of their aerial bodies. For these things too are suddenly and unexpectedly changed by the Angels who piously serve the supreme God, according to another disposition unknown to the demons. It is as if something external should happen to a sick man [Note: [Col. 0587] Only the Lovaniensis edition reads “internal.”] and cause him to die, although the physician had promised that he would live on the basis of the preceding signs of recovery; or if, after foreseeing the condition of the air, some sailor had predicted that a certain wind would blow for a long time, but the Lord Christ, sailing with his disciples, commanded it to cease, and a great calm arose (Matthew 8:26); or if a farmer, skilled in the nature of the soil and the cycles of seeds, should promise that a particular vine would bear fruit that year, but in that same year either an unexpected storm should dry it up or some more powerful command should uproot it. In the same way, many things belonging to the demons’ foreknowledge and predictions, which are foreseen as future by lesser and customary causes, are altered when greater and hidden causes intervene and prevent them.

They also deceive deliberately, through the envious will by which they rejoice in human error. But, so that they may not lose the weight of their authority among their worshipers, they arrange matters so that blame is assigned to their interpreters and to those who conjecture the meaning of their signs whenever they have been deceived or have lied. [Note: [Col. 0587] The printed editions add: “Sometimes, however, the evil spirits themselves, who deceive human beings and assault their salvation, are accustomed to predict the destruction of their worship and idols, so that they may appear to be foreknowers of what is going to happen in particular kingdoms or places, and of what may befall their faction as an adversity—something that even those who read the histories of the Gentiles know.” These words are absent from all the manuscripts.]

### 11. Why, when the overthrow of the temples and images was already imminent, the demon Serapis announced this to one of his worshipers

What wonder, then, if, when the overthrow of the temples or images was already imminent—an event that the Prophets of the supreme God had foretold so long beforehand—the demon Serapis disclosed this impending event to one of his worshipers, so that, as though withdrawing or fleeing, he might commend his supposed divinity?

### Chapter VII

### Why demons either keep silent about their own defeats or sometimes foretell them

For these beings are driven away, or, bound by superior commands, are even dragged away and removed from their places, so that God’s will may be done concerning the things over which they ruled and by which they were worshiped. God had foretold long beforehand through all the nations that this would happen, and had commanded that it be brought about through his faithful servants.

Why, then, should the demon not have been permitted to foretell this, when he already foresaw that it threatened him? This prediction both bore witness to the Prophets, by whom these things were written, and enabled prudent people to understand how watchfully the demons’ deception and worship had to be avoided. For, although the demons could not have been ignorant of these events, since they had been foretold by the Prophets, they had kept silent about them in their temples for so long; but once the events began to approach, they wished to appear to foretell them, so that they would not be thought ignorant and defeated.

Since it had therefore been foretold and written so long beforehand—to say nothing for the moment of other passages—that which the prophet Zephaniah says:

> The Lord will prevail against them,  
> and will destroy all the gods of the nations of the earth;  
> and they will worship him, each one from his own place,  
> all the islands of the nations.  
> (Zephaniah 2:11)

Either those who were worshiped in the temples of the nations did not believe that this would happen to them, and therefore did not wish to repeat it frequently through their prophets and fanatics—as their poet represents Juno as not altogether believing what Jupiter had said about Turnus’s death. Juno, moreover, is described by them as an aerial power, and in Virgil she speaks as follows:

> Now a grievous end awaits the innocent man—or I am vainly carried away from the truth.  
> Would that I might be deceived by a false fear,  
> and that you, who have the power, might turn your undertaking toward a better outcome!  
> (*Aeneid* 10.630–632)

Or else the demons—that is, the aerial powers—doubted that what they knew had been foretold through the Prophets could happen to them, and for that reason did not celebrate the Prophets’ prediction; and from this we must understand what sort of beings they are. Or, although they knew with absolute certainty that these things would come to pass, they kept silent about them through their temples so that, even then, people who understood might not begin to abandon and despise them—since the Prophets who bore witness to the future overthrow of their temples and images were the very ones who prohibited their worship.

But now that the time had arrived when the prophecies of the one God’s Prophets were to be fulfilled—the Prophets who call these beings false gods and most emphatically command that they not be worshiped—why should the demons not also have been allowed to announce that they had discovered this, so that it might become still clearer that previously they had either not believed these things at all or had been afraid to announce them to their worshipers, while at the end, as though they had nothing further to do, they wished to display their divination even there, where they were already exposed as having long pretended to be divine?

### Chapter VIII

### 12. Demons could have foretold certain true things from the oracles of the Prophets, but never dared to say anything against the true God

As for what the rest of their worshipers say—that some of their books also contain foreknowledge of these events—those statements should be regarded as inventions based on events that had already occurred. If they had been true, such predictions ought to have been made known to their peoples in their temples so long beforehand, just as our own prophecies are recited not only in our churches but also—as a weightier testimony against all our enemies—in the synagogues of the Jews, where they are ancient and widely known.

Nevertheless, even these statements, which are brought forward only rarely and secretly, should not disturb us if some demon was forced to disclose to his worshipers what he had learned from the utterances of the Prophets or from the oracles of Angels. Why should this not happen, since such disclosure is not an attack but a testimony to the truth?

The one thing that ought to be demanded of them—and which they have never previously declared, nor will they ever afterward attempt to declare unless it is fabricated—is that their gods, through their seers, dared to foretell or say anything against the God of Israel. Concerning this God, their most learned authors, who were able to read and know all those writings, sought rather to discover who he was than to deny that he was God.

This God, whom none of them dared deny to be the true God—for even if anyone denied it, he would not only suffer the penalties due to him but would also be refuted by unmistakable results—this God, then, whom, as I have said, none of them dared deny to be the true God, openly foretold through his prophets that their gods were false and had to be abandoned altogether; by manifest power he commanded that their temples, images, and sacred rites be overthrown; and by his manifest truth he fulfilled it.

Who, then, could be so foolish as not to choose to worship the one whom those whom he worshiped do not prohibit from being worshiped? Once he begins to worship him, he certainly will not worship those whom the one he worships prohibits from being worshiped.

### Chapter IX

### 13. The Prophets foretold that the worship of demons would yield to the worship of the one God

That the nations themselves would worship him after the false gods whom they had formerly worshiped had been destroyed was, as I mentioned shortly before, foretold by his Prophets; and I repeat it now:

> The Lord will prevail against them,  
> and will destroy all the gods of the nations of the earth,  
> and they will worship him, each one from his own place,  
> all the islands of the nations.

Not only the islands, but all the nations—including all the islands of the nations. Elsewhere, indeed, he does not mention islands but the whole world, saying:

> All the ends of the earth will remember and turn to the Lord,  
> and all the families of the nations will worship in his presence.  
> For the kingdom belongs to the Lord,  
> and he will rule the nations.

That these things were to be fulfilled through Christ is sufficiently evident from many other testimonies and from the very psalm from which I have quoted this passage. For shortly before, when he himself was speaking through the Prophet of his future Passion, he said:

> They pierced my hands and my feet;  
> they counted all my bones.  
> They themselves looked upon and observed me;  
> they divided my garments among themselves,  
> and over my clothing they cast lots.  
> (Psalm 21:17–19)

Shortly afterward he adds the passage I quoted:

> All the ends of the earth will remember and turn to the Lord, etc.

Moreover, the testimony I cited earlier—“The Lord will prevail against them, and will destroy all the gods of the nations of the earth”—also clearly shows, in the word “will prevail,” that this too was foretold: the Pagans would first attack the Church and persecute the Christian name as far as they could, so that, if possible, it might be entirely erased from the earth. But because the Lord was going to overcome them through the endurance of the martyrs and the greatness of the miracles, followed by the faith of the peoples, it was therefore said: “The Lord will prevail against them.” For it would not be said, “He will prevail against them,” unless they resisted him by attacking.

Accordingly, it was also prophesied in the Psalm:

> Why did the nations rage,  
> and the peoples devise empty things?  
> The kings of the earth stood forth,  
> and the rulers gathered together  
> against the Lord and against his Christ.

A little later it says:

> The Lord said to me: You are my Son;  
> today I have begotten you.  
> Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance,  
> and the ends of the earth as your possession.  
> (Psalm 2:1–2, 7)

Here is the source of the statement I inserted above from another Psalm:

> All the ends of the earth will remember and turn to the Lord.

Through these and similar prophetic testimonies it is shown to have been foretold that, through Christ, the God of Israel—whom we understand to be the one true God—would be worshiped not only in that one nation called Israel but among all nations; and that all the false gods of the nations would be torn down both from their temples and from the hearts of their worshipers. [Note: [Col. 0590] In the manuscripts, *amoliretur*; the printed editions read *demoliretur*.]

### Chapter X

### 14. The remnants of the Pagans vainly boast of their learning and wisdom

Let these people now go on and dare still to defend their former vanities against the Christian religion and against the true worship of God, so that they may perish amid their shouting. For this too was foretold concerning them in the Psalm, where the Prophet says:

> You sat upon the throne, judging righteousness.  
> You rebuked the nations, and the wicked perished;  
> you blotted out their name forever and ever.  
> The weapons of the enemies have failed completely,  
> and you destroyed their cities.  
> Their memory perished amid the shouting,  
> but the Lord remains forever.  
> (Psalm 9:5–8)

All these things must therefore be fulfilled. Nor should we be disturbed by the fact that the few who have remained still dare to display their empty doctrines and mock Christians as though they were completely ignorant, while we see those prophecies being fulfilled in them. For the very supposed ignorance and foolishness of Christians—which appears to the humble, the holy, and those who diligently study it as lofty and as the only true wisdom—has, as I say, reduced them to this small number, because, as the Apostle says:

> God made the wisdom of this world foolish.

He then adds something remarkable, if one understands it, and continues:

> For since, in the wisdom of God, the world did not know God through wisdom, it pleased God through the foolishness of preaching to save those who believe. For Jews ask for signs, and Greeks seek wisdom; but we preach Christ crucified, to the Jews indeed a stumbling-block, but to the Gentiles foolishness; yet to those who are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the Power of God and the Wisdom of God. For the foolishness of God is wiser than human beings, and the weakness of God is stronger than human beings.  
> (1 Corinthians 1:20–25)

Let them therefore mock our supposed ignorance and foolishness as much as they can, and boast of their own learning and wisdom. I know this much: these mockers of ours are fewer this year than they were last year.

From the time when the nations raged and the peoples devised empty things against the Lord and against his Christ—when the blood of the saints was being poured out by them and the Church was being devastated—until now and from now on, they are daily diminishing in number. Against their insults and proud mockery, the oracles of our God make us exceedingly strong, since we see and rejoice that these things too are being fulfilled.

For he addresses us through the prophet in this way:

> Hear me, you who know judgment, my people, in whose heart my law is:  
> Do not fear the reproach of human beings,  
> and do not be overcome by their abuse;  
> do not consider greatly what they now despise you for.  
> For as a garment, so they will be consumed in time,  
> and as wool, so a moth will eat them;  
> but my righteousness remains forever.  
> (Isaiah 51:7–8)

Let them read these writings of ours, if they deign to do so; and when their objections reach us, we shall answer as far as the Lord helps us.

[Col. 0591]

[Note: [Col. 0591] On the book *On Care for the Dead*, see book II of the *Retractations*, chapter 64, volume 1, column 655, beginning with the words “The book *On Care*” and continuing through the words “Venerable Paulinus” in column 656. One may conjecture when Augustine wrote this book from the sequence of the *Retractations*, where he places this same book immediately after the *Enchiridion to Laurentius*, a work which he did not complete before the year 421. See above, columns 229–230, the Admonition prefixed to that work, and also the other Admonition, columns 147–148, to the book of the eight Questions of Dulcitius, into question 2 of which Augustine inserted the beginning of the following book addressed to Paulinus. M.]

## Saint Aurelius Augustine, Bishop of Hippo: One Book on Care for the Dead, addressed to Paulinus

[Note: [Col. 0591] Written approximately in the year of Christ 421.]

[Note: [Col. 0591] The book *On Care for the Dead* has been newly corrected by collating fifteen Gallican manuscripts: namely, two Colbertine manuscripts, two Pratellian manuscripts, one Corbie manuscript approximately 900 years old, and one belonging to the Church of Reims, another belonging to the Church of Laon, as well as the Regius, Bigotian, Victorine, and Fossatensis manuscripts of the Abbey of Saint-Maur; the Metensis of Saint Arnulf; the Divionensis of Saint Benignus; the Uticensis of Saint Ebrulf; the Michaelinus; and, in addition, four Roman manuscripts from the Vatican Library. Variant readings from five Belgian manuscripts held by Lovaniensis were also consulted, together with the principal editions: Bad., that is, Joannes Badius, published by Joannes Parvus at Paris in 1502; Am., Joannes Amerbachius; Er., Erasmus; and Lov., the Lovaniensis theologians.]

[Note: [Col. 0591] We also compared all the editions mentioned at the beginning of volume 1 of the *Retractations* and the *Confessions*. M.]

(C)

When Bishop Paulinus of Nola asked whether burial in the memorial shrines of martyrs benefits the spirits of the dead, Augustine first shows that nothing harms the dead themselves, even if burial is entirely denied to their bodies. The place of burial does not benefit them in itself, but only incidentally, insofar as the memory of that place moves and increases the affection of those who pray for the dead. He explains that concern for burial arises from the human heart’s affection for its own flesh, and that the holy martyrs rightly despised it, since it makes no difference to blessedness or misery. From this he discusses the dead who are said to have appeared to the living so that burial might be provided for their bodies. He explains by various examples how such apparitions occur. Finally, he investigates whether the dead take an interest in the concerns and affairs of the living.

## Chapter I

[Col. 0591]

### 1. Paulinus’s question: whether it benefits a dead person to be buried near the memorial of a saint. His own view is that it does benefit the dead. The difficulty raised by Paulinus is examined. What is done for the dead benefits or fails to benefit them according to the kind of life each person led

For a long time, my venerable fellow bishop Paulinus, I have been indebted to Your Holiness for a reply, ever since you wrote to me through the men of our most religious daughter Flora, asking whether it benefits a person after death that his body be buried near the memorial of some saint.

That widow had asked this of you for her son, who had died in those regions, and you wrote back to console her. You also informed her that the matter concerning the body of the faithful young man Cynegius [Note: [Col. 0591] The manuscript of the Abbey of Saint Ebrulf has *Cynegri*.], which she had desired with maternal and devout affection, had been completed—namely, that it should be placed in the basilica of the most blessed confessor Felix. On this occasion it happened that, through the same bearers of your letter, you also wrote to me, presenting a question of this kind and asking me to state what I thought about it, while not concealing your own opinion.

For you say that it seems to you that the movements of religious and faithful hearts, when they take care of these matters for their own dead, are not empty. You add that it cannot be without significance that the whole Church is accustomed to pray for the dead. From this, you suggest, it may also be inferred that it benefits a person after death if, through the faith of his relatives, a place is provided for the burial of his body in which the help of the saints may appear to have been sought in this way as well.

[Col. 0593]

### 2. How Paulinus’s difficulty is resolved: the benefit or lack of benefit of what is done for the dead depends on the kind of life each person led

But although this is so, you indicate that you do not sufficiently see how it is not contrary to the Apostle’s statement:

> For we shall all stand before the tribunal of Christ, so that each one may receive according to what he has done through the body, whether good or evil.  
> (2 Corinthians 5:10)

This apostolic statement, you think, admonishes us that before death one should do what may benefit a person after death—not at the time when each person is already to receive what he did before death.

The question is resolved as follows: through a certain kind of life, lived while one is in this body, a person acquires the condition that these things may help the dead. Consequently, according to what they did through the body, they are helped by what is religiously done for them after the body. For there are people whom these things help not at all: either because they are done for those whose merits are so evil that they are not worthy of being helped even by such means, or because they are done for those whose merits are so good that they do not need such assistance.

Thus it is according to the kind of life each person led through the body that whatever is piously done for that person after he has left the body benefits or fails to benefit him. For if the merit by which these things might benefit him was not acquired in this life, it is sought in vain after this life.

It follows that the Church, or the care of the survivors for the dead, does not spend its religious devotion in vain; and yet each person receives according to what he did through the body, whether good or evil, as the Lord repays each according to his works. For the fact that what is offered can benefit a person after the body is due to what was acquired in the life he lived in the body.

### 3. Sacrifice for the dead and the Church’s authority in praying for them

This brief reply might have been sufficient for your inquiry, but for a little while attend to the other matters that I think ought to be answered.

In the books of the Maccabees we read that a sacrifice was offered for the dead (2 Maccabees 12:43). But even if this were found nowhere at all in the ancient Scriptures, the authority of the universal Church, which shines forth in this practice, is no small thing. [Note: [Col. 0593] The editions of Badius, Amerbach, and Erasmus read: “the authority that shines forth in this practice is not small”; the manuscripts and Lovaniensis resist this reading.] In the prayers of the priest poured out to the Lord God at his altar, the commending of the dead also has its appointed place.

## Chapter II

### What honor in burial contributes

### Burial of Christian bodies, if denied, takes nothing away

But whether the place of a dead person’s body benefits the soul must be investigated more carefully. First, we must consider whether, after this life, it makes any difference to inflict or increase misery upon human spirits if their bodies have not been buried—not according to some widespread popular opinion, but rather according to the sacred writings of our religion.

We must not believe, as one reads in Maro, that the unburied are prevented from sailing and crossing the infernal river because:

> They are not allowed to cross the dreadful banks and hoarse waters  
> before their bones have rested in their dwelling-place.  
> (*Aeneid* 6.327–328)

What Christian heart would yield to these poetic and fabulous inventions, when the Lord Jesus, so that Christians might lie down securely amid the hands of enemies who had power over their bodies, asserts that not even a hair of their heads will perish, exhorting them not to fear those who, when they have killed the body, have nothing more that they can do?

For this reason, in the first book of *The City of God*, I spoke sufficiently, as I believe, to blunt the attack of those who, by attributing the barbarian devastation—especially the devastation that Rome recently suffered—to Christian times, also bring this charge: that Christ did not come to the aid of his own there. When they are answered that the souls of the faithful were received by him according to the merits of their faith, they mock their unburied corpses. I therefore explained the whole matter of burial in that place in words such as these.

### 4. The care of burial is a consolation for the living rather than assistance for the dead

> “But surely,” I said, “amid such a slaughter of corpses they could not even be buried? Yet pious faith does not fear this excessively, holding fast to what was foretold: that the beasts which consume them will not harm the bodies destined to rise, and that not a hair of their heads will perish.
>
> “Nor would the Truth in any way say, ‘Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul,’ if anything whatever that enemies might wish to do to the bodies of the slain could harm the life to come. Unless, perhaps, someone is so absurd as to argue that those who kill the body should not be feared before death, lest they kill the body, but should be feared after death, lest they prevent the dead body from being buried.
>
> “It is therefore false if Christ says, ‘Those who kill the body, and afterward have nothing more that they can do’ (Matthew 10:28, 30; Luke 12:4, 7), if they have so much that they can do to corpses. Far be it that what the Truth said should be false. It is said that they do something when they kill because, while the body is being killed, there is sensation in it; afterward, however, they have nothing more that they can do because there is no sensation in a dead body.
>
> “Many bodies of Christians, therefore, were not covered by the earth; but no one separated any of them from heaven and earth, which is wholly filled by the presence of the one who knows from where to raise up what he created.
>
> “It is indeed said in the Psalm:

> ‘They gave the dead bodies of your servants as food to the birds of heaven,  
> the flesh of your saints to the beasts of the earth;  
> they poured out their blood like water around Jerusalem,  
> and there was no one to bury them.’  
> (Psalm 78:2–3)

> “But this was said rather to intensify the cruelty of those who did these things than the unhappiness of those who suffered them. For although these events appear harsh and dreadful in human eyes, ‘the death of his saints is precious in the sight of the Lord’ (Psalm 115:15).
>
> “Accordingly, all these things—the care of the funeral, the provision of burial, and the procession of the funeral rites—are more consolations for the living than aids for the dead. If a costly burial benefits the wicked, a cheap or nonexistent one will not harm the pious.
>
> “That rich man clothed in purple was given a splendid funeral in the eyes of human beings, with a crowd of servants in attendance; but in the sight of the Lord, far more splendid service was given to that poor man covered with sores by the Angels, who did not carry him to a marble tomb but lifted him into Abraham’s bosom (Luke 16:19–22).
>
> “Those against whom we have undertaken to defend the City of God laugh at these things. Yet even their philosophers despised concern for burial; and often whole armies, while dying for an earthly homeland, did not care where they would afterward lie or what beasts would become their food. Poets were even permitted to speak approvingly on this subject:

> ‘He is covered by the sky who has no urn.’  
> [Note: [Col. 0595] Lucan, *Pharsalia* 7.819, concerning those killed in the battle of Pharsalus.]

> “How much less ought they to mock Christians over unburied bodies, when Christians are promised that the restoration of the flesh and all its members will be returned and renewed in an instant—not only from the earth but also from the most hidden recesses of the other elements into which dissolved corpses have withdrawn?”

## Chapter III

### 5. Why care for a funeral and burial is praiseworthy

> “Yet for this reason the bodies of the dead are not to be despised and cast aside, especially the bodies of the just and the faithful, which the spirit used as instruments and vessels for every good work in holiness. [Note: [Col. 0595] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read: “which the Holy Spirit used in holiness.”]
>
> “For if a father’s garment and ring, or anything of this kind, is dearer to descendants in proportion to their greater affection for their parents, the bodies themselves must certainly not be despised—bodies that we wear much more familiarly and closely than any garments. They belong not to adornment or external assistance but to the very nature of the human being.
>
> “For this reason the funerals of the ancient righteous were attended to with dutiful piety, their obsequies were celebrated, and burial was provided. While they were alive, they themselves instructed their sons concerning the burial or even the transfer of their bodies (Genesis 23; 25:9–10; 47:30).
>
> “The angel also commends Tobias as having pleased God by burying the dead (Tobit 2:9; 12:12). [Note: [Col. 0595] In ancient manuscripts, *Tobis*.]
>
> “The Lord himself, destined to rise on the third day, praises and commands to be praised the good work of the religious woman who poured costly ointment over his limbs and did this for his burial (Matthew 26:7–13). The Gospel also commendably recalls those who took his body down from the cross and carefully and honorably arranged for it to be covered and buried (John 19:38).
>
> “These authorities do not, however, teach that corpses possess any sensation. Rather, they indicate that the bodies of the dead also belong to God’s providence, which is pleased by such duties of piety, because they establish faith in the resurrection.
>
> “Here one also learns profitably how great the reward may be for the alms we provide to living and conscious people, if even the service and care performed for the lifeless limbs of human beings is not lost before God.
>
> “There are also other things that the holy Patriarchs, by prophetic inspiration, wished to be understood as having been said concerning the burial or transfer of their bodies (Genesis 47:30; 50:24); but this is not the place to discuss them, since what we have said is sufficient.
>
> “If the necessities required to sustain the living—such as food and clothing—do not break the virtue of those who endure and tolerate their absence, even when they are lacking amid severe affliction, nor uproot piety from the heart, but make it more fruitful through exercise, [Note: [Col. 0595] The printed editions read “make it more aroused.” The manuscripts’ *exercitatam* is better; the same reading occurs in book I of *The City of God*.] how much less does the absence of those things customarily used to care for funerals and bury the bodies of the dead make miserable those who are already at rest in the hidden abodes of the pious?
>
> “Consequently, when these things were lacking for the bodies of Christians during the devastation of that great city, or even of other towns, neither were the living at fault, since they were unable to provide them, nor was it punishment for the dead, since they were unable to feel it.”  
> (*The City of God*, book I, chapters 12 and 13)

This is my view concerning the cause and purpose of burial. I have therefore transferred it from another book of mine into this one, because it could more easily be reviewed by me in this form than expressed anew in another manner.

## Chapter IV

### 6. The place of burial benefits the dead not in itself but incidentally, by prompting prayer for them

If this is true, then a place provided for burying bodies near the memorials of saints is likewise an expression of the good human affection shown toward the remains of one’s relatives. For if there is some religious significance in their being buried, there cannot be none when attention is paid to where they are buried.
