But when such consolations for the living are sought—consolations by which their pious affection toward their own becomes evident—I do not see what assistance they provide to the dead except that, when people remember where the bodies of those they love have been placed, they commend those beloved dead in prayer to the same saints, as patrons received into the presence of the Lord.

They could indeed do this even if they were unable to bury them in such places. But the tombs of the dead are called either “Memorials” (*Memoriae*) or “Monuments” (*Monumenta*) for no other reason than that they bring back to memory those who have been taken away from the eyes of the living by death, lest they also be taken away from their hearts by forgetfulness, and by reminding people cause them to be thought of. The name “Memorials” (*Memoriae*) makes this perfectly clear, and “Monument” (*Monumentum*) is so called because it admonishes the mind—that is, reminds it.

For this reason the Greeks call such a place μνημεῖον (*mnēmeion*), which we call a “memorial” or “monument,” since in their language memory itself, by which we remember, is called μνήμη (*mnēmē*).

When the mind recalls where the body of a dearly loved person was buried, and the place associated with it bears the name of a venerable martyr, the affection of the person remembering and praying commends the beloved soul to that martyr. When this is done for the dead by their faithful loved ones, there is no doubt that it benefits those who, while they lived in the body, earned the right for such things to benefit them after this life.

But even if some necessity or lack of opportunity prevents bodies from being buried, or from being buried in such places, prayers for the spirits of the dead must not be omitted. The Church has undertaken to offer these prayers for all the dead within the Christian and Catholic community, even when their names are not spoken, under a general commemoration, so that those whose parents, children, or any relatives or friends are absent to perform these duties may receive them from the one common pious mother.

If these prayers, offered with right faith and piety for the dead, were absent, I think that it would benefit their spirits nothing at all, no matter how their lifeless bodies were placed in holy places.

## Chapter V
### 7. How much the place contributes on occasion [Col. 0597]

When, therefore, a faithful mother desired that the body of her faithful deceased son be placed in a martyr’s basilica, if indeed she believed that his soul would be helped by the martyr’s merits, that belief itself was a kind of supplication; and this was beneficial, if anything was beneficial. [Note: [Col. 0597] Bad., Am., and Er. read *commendandus* (“to be commended”) rather than *commendatus* (“had been commended”).] The fact that she returned in her mind to the same tomb and commended her son more and more earnestly to the prayers of the martyr helped the spirit of the deceased—not the place where the dead body lay, but the living affection of the mother, awakened by the memory of the place. For both who he was and to whom he had been commended touched the religious mind of the one praying, and certainly did not do so without benefit.

Those who pray likewise use parts of their bodies in ways appropriate to supplication: they bend their knees, stretch out their hands, or even prostrate themselves on the ground, and perform whatever other visible actions they may perform. Yet their invisible will and the intention of their heart are known to God, nor does he need such signs in order that the human mind may be disclosed to him. Rather, through these actions a person stirs himself to pray and groan with greater humility and fervor. And somehow, since these bodily movements cannot occur without a movement of the mind preceding them, when they are again performed outwardly and visibly, that inner and invisible movement which produced them is increased. Thus the affection of the heart, which preceded these actions so that they might be performed, grows because they have been performed.

Nevertheless, if someone is held or even bound in such a way that he cannot perform these actions with his bodily members, that does not mean that the inward person does not pray, or that before God’s eyes—in the innermost chamber where he is pierced with compunction—he does not prostrate himself.

So too, although it makes a very great difference where someone places the body of his dead person when he beseeches God for the person’s spirit—for the preceding affection chose a holy place, and, once the body has been placed there, the memory of the holy place renews and intensifies the affection that preceded it—nevertheless, even if a religious mind cannot bury the one it loves where it has chosen, it must in no way cease the necessary supplications made on the person’s behalf. [Note: [Col. 0597] The manuscripts read *religiosus animus* (“a religious mind”); the printed editions read *amicus* (“a friend”).]

For wherever the flesh of the deceased lies—or does not lie—rest must be obtained for the spirit. When the spirit departed from the flesh, it carried away with it the capacity by which it can know how each person is situated, whether among the good or among the evil. Nor does it expect its life to be helped by that flesh to which it itself had given life, which it removed in departing and will restore in returning. For it is not the flesh that secures merit for the spirit, but the spirit that secures merit even for the flesh at the resurrection, determining whether it will rise again for punishment or for glory.

### Chapter VI

### 8. The bodies of the martyrs burned, and their ashes scattered in the Rhône

We read in the *Ecclesiastical History*, written in Greek by Eusebius and translated into Latin by Rufinus, that the bodies of martyrs in Gaul were exposed to dogs, and that the remains and bones left by the dogs were burned in fires until entirely consumed; and that their ashes were scattered in the river Rhône, so that nothing whatever might remain for any kind of memorial. [Note: [Col. 0597] Eusebius relates that the bodies of these martyrs of Lyons lay exposed in the open air for six continuous days [Col. 0598], and were afterward burned and thrown into the Rhône (*Ecclesiastical History* 5.1).] [Note: [Col. 0597] One Vatican manuscript reads *carniumque* (“and pieces of flesh”). The other manuscript codices and printed editions read *canumque reliquias* (“the remains left by the dogs”).]

This must be believed to have been permitted by divine providence for no other reason than that Christians might learn, while confessing Christ and despising this life, to despise burial all the more. If what was done to the martyrs’ bodies with such savage cruelty had harmed them by preventing their most victorious spirits from resting in blessedness, it certainly would not have been permitted to happen. [Note: [Col. 0598] Some manuscripts read *beati* (“blessed”) instead of *beate* (“in blessedness”).] The event itself therefore made clear that the Lord did not say, “Do not fear those who kill the body and afterward have nothing more that they can do” (Luke 12:4), because he would not permit them to do anything to the bodies of his dead; [Note: [Col. 0598] Several manuscripts of good authority read *martyrum* (“of the martyrs”).] rather, whatever they were permitted to do would accomplish nothing that diminished the blessedness of Christian dead or affected the awareness of those living after death. It would not even harm their bodies in such a way as to prevent them from rising again intact.

### Chapter VII

### 9. Care for burial arising from natural affection for the body

Nevertheless, because of that affection of the human heart by which no one has ever hated his own flesh (Ephesians 5:29), if people know that after their death something will be lacking to their bodies which the custom of their own nation or homeland requires in burial, they grieve as human beings. [Note: [Col. 0598] The manuscripts read *suis corporibus defuturum* (“will be lacking to their bodies”); Lov. reads *suis corporibus defunctis deesse*, and Am. and Er. *suorumque defunctorum deesse* (“will be lacking to their deceased persons”).] Before death they fear for their bodies what will not concern them after death.

Thus we find in the books of Kings that God, through a prophet, threatened another prophet who had transgressed his word that his corpse would not be brought into the tomb of his fathers. Scripture reads as follows:

“Thus says the Lord: Because you were disobedient to the word of the Lord and did not keep the commandment which the Lord your God commanded you, and you returned and ate bread and drank water in the place in which he commanded you not to eat bread or drink water, your corpse shall not be brought into the tomb of your fathers” (3 Kings 13:21–22).

If we consider this punishment according to the Gospel, where we have learned that, once the body has been killed, there is nothing to fear lest the lifeless limbs suffer, it should not even be called a punishment. But if we consider the human affection for one’s own flesh, the living man could have been terrified or saddened by what he would not feel when dead. That was the punishment: his spirit grieved that this would happen to his body, although it would feel no grief when the event occurred.

The Lord wished to chastise his servant to this extent—not because he had contemptuously refused to fulfill God’s command, but because he believed that he was obeying when he was in fact deceived by another’s fraudulent trickery. We must not suppose that he was killed by the beast’s bite in such a way that his soul was afterward carried off to infernal punishment. The very lion that had killed him guarded his body, while the animal on which he had been riding remained unharmed; and, together with that savage beast, it stood fearlessly present at the funeral of its master.

By this remarkable sign it is evident that the man of God was restrained temporally, even unto death, rather than punished after death. Concerning this matter the Apostle, after mentioning the illnesses and deaths of many on account of certain offenses, says: “For if we judged ourselves, we would not be judged by the Lord. But when we are judged, we are chastened by the Lord, so that we may not be condemned with the world” (1 Corinthians 11:31–32).

The very man who had deceived him buried him quite honorably in his own tomb and arranged that he too should be buried beside his bones. He hoped in this way that his own bones might also be spared when the time came for King Josiah of Judah, in accordance with the prophecy of that man of God, to remove the bones of many of the dead from that land and defile with those bones the sacrilegious altars that had been established for carved images.

For Josiah spared the tomb in which the Prophet lay, who had foretold these things more than three hundred years earlier; and because of him the burial of the man who had deceived him was not violated either (3 Kings 13:24–32; 4 Kings 23:16–18). The man who had killed his own soul by a lie had, through that affection by which no one has ever hated his own flesh, provided for his corpse.

Thus, because each person naturally loves his own flesh, it was a punishment for the first man to learn that he would not be in the tomb of his fathers; and it was a concern for the second to ensure that his bones would be spared if he lay beside the one whose tomb no one would violate.

### Chapter VIII

### 10. The martyrs disregarded concern for burial

The martyrs of Christ, contending for the truth, overcame this affection. It is not surprising that they despised what they would not feel after death, since they could not be overcome by tortures inflicted upon those whom they perceived while alive.

God could certainly have prevented dogs from approaching the bodies of his slain servants, just as he did not permit the lion to touch the body of the Prophet whom it had killed, and made the killer its guardian. I repeat, he could have restrained by countless means the savagery of those men, so that they would not dare to burn the corpses or scatter the ashes. But this trial also had to be included among the manifold varieties of temptation, [Note: [Col. 0599] Bad., Am., and Er. read *experimentum multiplicium tentationum deesse* (“this trial be lacking from manifold temptations”).] so that the strength of their confession—which would not yield to the savagery of persecution for the sake of bodily preservation—would not tremble for the honor of a tomb; and finally, so that faith in the resurrection would not fear the destruction of the bodies.

These things therefore had to be permitted, so that, even after examples of such horror, the martyrs, fervent in confessing Christ, might also become witnesses to this truth which they had learned: those who killed their bodies afterward had nothing more that they could do. Whatever they did to dead bodies, they did nothing at all, since the one who had departed from the flesh, now deprived of all life, could feel nothing, and the one who created it could lose nothing through it.

Yet while these things were being done to the bodies of the slain, and the martyrs endured them with great courage without fear, there was nevertheless immense grief among the brethren because no opportunity was given to perform the proper rites for the holy dead, nor even secretly to remove anything, as the same history testifies that the watchfulness of the cruel guards prevented (Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* 5.1).

Thus, although those who had been killed suffered no misery in the tearing apart of their limbs, the burning of their bones, or the scattering of their ashes, those who could not bury any part of them were nevertheless tormented by great compassion. They in a certain way felt themselves what the dead could in no way feel; where there was no longer any suffering for the martyrs, there was a pitiable fellow-suffering for the survivors. [Note: [Col. 0600] The printed editions read: “misery tormented them, because they felt nothing at all.” This is less satisfactory than the manuscripts, which read: “because those who felt nothing at all were concerned”; some manuscripts have *dissentientibus* (“those who differed”), which is inferior.]

### Chapter IX

### 11. Why the duty of burial is praised in Scripture

In accordance with the pitiable compassion I have described, those men are praised and blessed by King David who showed the mercy of burial to the dry bones of Saul and Jonathan (2 Kings 2:5).

But what mercy is shown to those who feel nothing? Should this perhaps be referred to the opinion that the unburied could not cross the infernal river? (*Aeneid* 6.327–328.) Far be this from Christian faith. Otherwise, the fate of the great multitude of martyrs whose bodies could not be buried would be wretched indeed, and Truth would have spoken falsely to them in saying, “Do not fear those who kill the body and afterward have nothing more that they can do,” if they were able to inflict such evils upon them that the martyrs were prevented from reaching their desired places.

But since this is without any doubt utterly false, and since the denial of burial to the bodies of believers does them no harm, while its provision to unbelievers does them no good, why are those who buried Saul and his son said to have shown mercy, and for this reason blessed by the pious king? It can only be because the hearts of the compassionate are rightly moved when, in the bodies of the dead belonging to others, they grieve over what they do not want done to their own bodies after death, because of that affection by which no one has ever hated his own flesh. What they wish to have done for themselves when they will no longer feel anything, they take care to do for others who feel nothing, while they themselves still feel.

### Chapter X

### 12. Some dead appear so that burial may be provided for them: how such apparitions occur

Certain apparitions are reported which seem to introduce into this discussion a question that must not be neglected. It is said that some dead have appeared either in dreams or in some other way to the living, who did not know where their bodies lay unburied; after revealing the places, they reminded them or urged them to provide the burial that had been lacking.

If we answer that these reports are false, we may seem impudently to oppose the writings of certain faithful people and the testimony of those who affirm that such things have happened to them. But we must answer that we should not therefore suppose that the dead experience these things because they appear in dreams to say, indicate, or request them.

Living people often appear to other living people who are asleep, while the living persons themselves do not know that they are appearing; and they hear from those who tell them what they dreamed, namely, that they saw them doing or saying something in a dream. [Note: [Col. 0600] Er., Lugd., Ven., and Lov. read *nesciunt* (“do not know”); the manuscripts read *nesciant* (“may not know”). See Sermons 322 and 323.] If, therefore, someone can see me in a dream indicating something that has happened, or even foretelling something that will happen, although I am entirely unaware of it and have absolutely no concern—not only with what he dreams, but whether, while I am asleep, he is awake, or, while I am awake, he is asleep, or whether we are both awake or both asleep at the same time when he sees me in his dream—why should it be surprising if the dead, though unaware and feeling none of these things, nevertheless appear in dreams to the living and say something which the living, once awake, recognize as true?

I would therefore believe that such things occur through angelic operations, whether they are permitted from above or commanded, so that the dead may appear in dreams to say something about the burial of their bodies, although those to whom the bodies belong know nothing whatever of it.

This sometimes happens beneficially, either for some kind of consolation to the living who are related to those dead persons whose images appear to the dreamers, or so that, through these reminders, humane concern for burial may be commended to the human race. Although burial does not help the dead, it is nevertheless culpably neglected through irreligious disregard.

At other times, however, people are led into great errors by deceptive apparitions, and it is just that they should undergo such experiences. For example, someone may see in a dream what poetic falsehood reports Aeneas saw among the dead; the image of some unburied person may appear to him and speak words such as those said to have been spoken to Aeneas by Palinurus (*Aeneid* 6.337–383). When he awakens, he may find that person’s body in the place where, while dreaming, he heard that it lay unburied, having been warned and asked to bury the body he had found. Because he discovers that this is true, he may believe that the dead are buried so that their souls may pass to places from which, as he dreamed, the law of the underworld prevents the souls of the unburied from departing.

Would he not, by believing this, stray very far from the path of truth? [Note: [Col. 0601] Bad., Am., Er., and two Vatican manuscripts read: “would he not, by believing thus, stray very far.”]

### Chapter XI

### 13. Two examples of visions in dreams. A deceased father appears to his son. Augustine himself, while still alive, appears in a dream to the rhetorician Eulogius and explains a passage of Cicero

Human weakness is such that when someone sees a dead person in a dream, he supposes that he is seeing the person’s soul; but when he similarly dreams of someone living, he has no doubt that not the person’s soul, nor the body, but merely the likeness of a human being has appeared to him. Yet why should likenesses of dead people, who are unaware of it, not appear to sleepers in the same way, without their souls appearing?

Certainly, [Note: [Col. 0601] Two manuscripts read *Porro certe* (“moreover, certainly”); seven others read *Porro* (“moreover”), omitting *certe*.] when we were at Milan, we heard that a man was being presented with a claim for a debt, supported by his deceased father’s written acknowledgment. The debt, however, had already been paid by the father, without the son’s knowledge. The man began to be deeply distressed and to wonder why his father, when dying, had not told him what he owed, especially since he had also made a will.

Then, when he was extremely anxious, his father appeared to him in a dream and indicated where the document had been deposited by which the acknowledgment had been canceled. [Note: [Col. 0601] Bad. and Lov. read: “where the document had been placed by which the acknowledgment had been annulled.” Erasmus and the manuscripts more correctly read *recautum quo*, that is, “the document by which that acknowledgment had been revoked or, as the text says, voided.”]

When the young man found and produced it, he not only repelled the charge of a false debt but also recovered his father’s written acknowledgment, which his father had not retrieved when the money was paid.

It is therefore thought that the man’s soul had taken care of his son and had come to him while he slept, so that, by teaching him what he did not know, it might free him from great distress.

But at almost the same time when we heard this, while we were likewise staying at Milan, Eulogius, a rhetorician of Carthage who had been my student in that discipline, later reported the following to me after we had returned to Africa. While he was assigning Cicero’s rhetorical works to his students and reviewing the passage he was to teach the following day, he encountered a difficult passage. Unable to understand it, he could scarcely sleep because of his anxiety. That night, while he was dreaming, I explained to him what he did not understand—or rather, not I, but my image, without my knowledge, while I was doing something else or dreaming somewhere far across the sea, and was entirely unconcerned with his difficulties.

I do not know how these things occur. But however they occur, why should we not believe that a dead person can appear in a dream in the same way as a living person? In both cases, those concerned are unaware and unconcerned about who is dreaming of their images, or where or when the dream occurs.

### Chapter XII

### 14. Visions of the delirious. The vision of Curma, a municipal official

Some waking visions are also similar to dreams, namely those experienced by people whose senses are disturbed, such as the delirious or those raging in any other way. They too speak to themselves as though they were speaking with people truly present, and they speak both with absent people and with those present, whose images they see, whether the people are living or dead. [Note: [Col. 0602] Eight manuscripts read: “For they too often speak with those truly present, and they also speak with absent people as though they were present, whose images they see.”]

But just as the living persons do not know that they are seen by such people or that they are conversing with them—for they are not actually present, nor are they themselves speaking, but people with disturbed senses are undergoing such imaginary visions—in the same way those who have departed this life appear to people in such a condition as though they were present, while they are absent and entirely unaware whether someone is seeing them imaginatively.

### 15.

Something similar also occurs when people are withdrawn from bodily sensation more deeply than in sleep and are occupied by such visions. Images of the living and the dead appear to them as well. But when they have been restored to their senses, whoever they say they saw dead is believed actually to have been with them. Those who hear these reports do not consider that, in the same way, images of certain living people who were absent and unaware may also have appeared to them.

A man named Curma, [Note: [Col. 0602] Bad. and Lov. read *de turma Curina nomine* and consistently use *Curina* below. The manuscripts almost everywhere read *Curma*, as do Am. and Er.; these latter two editions add *de turma* after *Homo quidam*, which is absent from the manuscripts and seems to have entered from a marginal annotation, perhaps “On Curma.”] a poor municipal official from the town of Tullium, which is near Hippo, scarcely of the rank of a former duumvir [Note: [Col. 0602] *Duumviralitius* means the same as *duumviralis*, that is, one who had held the office of duumvir. Duumvirs were called municipal magistrates because there were two of them, as Brissonius says.], and a simple countryman, fell ill and, withdrawn from his senses, [Note: [Col. 0602] The better manuscripts read *ablatus a sensibus* (“withdrawn from his senses”); the printed editions read *ablatis sensibus* (“with his senses removed”).] lay almost dead for several days. A very faint breath in his nostrils, perceptible to some extent when a hand was placed near them, was the only slight indication that he was alive and prevented him from being buried as lifeless. [Note: [Col. 0603] Lov. reads *indicium quod illum sepeliri* (“an indication which [prevented] him from being buried”); *quod illum* has been deleted as a superfluous addition and is absent from the manuscripts.] [Col. 0603] He moved none of his limbs, took no nourishment, and felt nothing with his eyes or any other bodily sense, no matter what discomfort was inflicted upon him.

Yet he saw many things as if in dreams. At length, after many days, when he seemed to awaken, he related what he had seen. First, as soon as he opened his eyes, he said: “Let someone go to the house of Curma the blacksmith and see what is happening there.”

When someone went there, Curma the blacksmith was found to have died at the very moment when this man had been restored to his senses and had almost returned from death. Then, as those present listened attentively, he indicated that Curma the blacksmith had been ordered to be brought in when he himself was released. He said that, in the place from which he had returned, he had heard that not Curma the municipal official but Curma the blacksmith had been ordered to be brought to those regions of the dead.

Among these visions, therefore, which were like his dreams, he recognized among the dead—who were treated in different ways according to the diversity of their merits—some people whom he knew to be alive. [Note: [Col. 0603] The printed editions read *fuit inter eos* (“he was among them”); *fuit* is absent from most manuscripts.] I might perhaps have believed that those whom he saw were truly dead [Note: [Col. 0603] The printed editions read *vere mortuos* (“truly dead”); *mortuos* is redundant and absent from the manuscripts.] if, among these things that were like his dreams, he had not also seen certain people who are still alive, namely some clerics from his own district. From their presbyter there he heard that he was to be baptized by me at Hippo, and he said that this had also happened.

Thus, in that vision he had seen the presbyter, the clerics, and me myself, although we were certainly not yet dead; afterward, in the same vision, he also saw dead people. Why should we not believe that he saw the living in the same way as he saw us—both the living and the dead being absent and unaware—and therefore that he saw not the people themselves but their likenesses, just as he saw likenesses of places?

For he also saw the estate where the presbyter was with the clerics, and Hippo, where he was supposedly baptized by me. Clearly he was not in those places when he seemed to himself to be there. He did not know what was happening there at that time; beyond doubt, he would have known if he had truly been there.

These things were therefore visions that were not presented [Note: [Col. 0603] The manuscripts read *praesentantur* (“are presented”); the printed editions read *praestantur* (“are supplied”).] in the things themselves as they exist, but were represented in certain images of things.

Finally, after seeing many other things, he also reported that he had been brought into paradise and that, when he was sent away from there, he was told that he would return to his own people: “Go, be baptized, if you wish to be in this place of the blessed.”

Then, when he was reminded that he should be baptized by me, he replied that it had already been done. Again the one who was speaking with him said: “Go, be truly baptized, for what you saw was a vision.”

After this he recovered and went to Hippo. Easter was already approaching. Without our knowing him, he enrolled with the other candidates for baptism, together with many others. He did not tell me or any of our people about his vision. He was baptized, and after the holy days had been completed he returned home.

Two years or more passed before I learned all these things. At first I learned them from one of my friends and his friend at a dinner in my house, while we were discussing matters of this kind. Then I persisted and arranged for Curma himself, who was present, to relate the story to me. His respectable fellow citizens testified both to his remarkable illness—that he had lain almost dead for many days—and to the other Curma, the blacksmith, whom I mentioned above. As he related all these matters to me, they also recalled and confirmed that they had heard them from him at the time.

Therefore, just as he saw his baptism, myself, Hippo, the basilica, and the baptistery not in the things themselves but in certain likenesses of things, so too he saw certain other living people while those living people were unaware:

### Chapter XIII

### The souls of the dead do not participate in the affairs of the living. Why, then, should they not similarly see the dead without the dead knowing it?

### 16.

Why should we not believe that these are angelic operations, [Note: [Col. 0604] One Vatican manuscript reads *credimus fieri per dispensationem* (“believe to be done through the administration”).] carried out through the administration of God’s providence, which makes good use of both the good and the evil, according to the inscrutable depth of his judgments? Through them the minds of mortals may be instructed, deceived, consoled, or terrified, according as mercy must be shown or punishment inflicted upon each person by him whom the Church not without reason praises in the words, “Mercy and judgment I will sing, O Lord” (Psalm 100:1).

Let everyone accept what I am going to say as he wishes. If the souls of the dead participated in the affairs of the living, and if, when we saw them, they themselves spoke to us in dreams, then—to say nothing of others—my devout mother would never leave me during the night. She followed me by land and sea so that she might live with me. Surely she did not become cruel by attaining a happier life, so that, when something troubles my heart, she would not console her sorrowful son whom she loved uniquely and whom she never wished to see sad.

But certainly what the sacred Psalm proclaims is true: “For my father and my mother have abandoned me, but the Lord has taken me up” (Psalm 27:10). If our parents have abandoned us, how do they participate in our concerns and affairs? If parents do not participate in them, what other dead people know what we do or what we suffer?

The prophet Isaiah says: “For you are our father; because Abraham did not know us, and Israel did not recognize us” (Isaiah 63:16). If those great patriarchs did not know what was happening to the people begotten from them—although that people was promised to those who believed in God through their lineage—how are the dead involved in knowing and helping the affairs and actions of the living?

How can we say that those who died before the evils that followed their death came upon them were spared, if after death they experience whatever occurs amid the calamity of human life? Or are we mistaken in saying these things, and do we suppose that those are at rest whom the troubled life of the living agitates?

What, then, is the meaning of the great benefit God promised to the most devout King Josiah, namely that he would die before seeing the evils that he threatened would come upon that place and people? These are God’s words:

“Thus says the Lord God of Israel: The words that you heard, and because you feared before my face when you heard what I spoke concerning this place and those who dwell in it—that it would be deserted and accursed—and because you tore your garments and wept before me, I also have heard, says the Lord of hosts: behold, I will add you to your fathers, and you shall be added to them in peace; and your eyes shall not see all the evils which I am bringing upon this place and upon those who dwell in it” (4 Kings 22:18–20). [Note: [Col. 0605] Almost the sole exception, the Louvain edition reads *inducam*, “which I shall bring.”]

Terrified by God’s threats, Josiah had wept and torn his garments. He was made secure from all the future evils by his approaching death, since he would rest in peace in such a way that he would not see any of them.

The spirits of the dead are therefore in a place where they do not see whatever is done or happens to people in this life. How, then, do they see their tombs or their bodies, whether they lie discarded or buried? How do they participate in the misery of the living, when either they themselves suffer their own evils, if they have acquired such merits, or rest in peace, as was promised to Josiah, where they endure no evils either by suffering them or by suffering with others—freed from all the evils that, while living here, they endured by suffering and fellow-suffering?

### Chapter XIV

### 17. An objection to the foregoing

Someone may say: If the dead have no concern for the living, how did the rich man who was tormented in hell ask Abraham his father to send Lazarus to his five brothers, who were not yet dead, and warn them not to come themselves to that same place of torment?

But did the rich man’s saying this mean that he knew what his brothers were doing or suffering at that time? He had concern for the living, although he had no knowledge whatever of what they were doing, just as we have concern for the dead although we certainly do not know what they are doing.

For if we had no concern for the dead, we would certainly not beseech God on their behalf. In the end, Abraham did not send Lazarus; he replied that they had Moses and the Prophets here, whom they ought to hear so that they would not come to those punishments. [Note: [Col. 0605] This wording agrees with Bad., Am., Er., and most manuscripts: “nor did he send Lazarus, but Moses.”]

Here the question arises again: How did Abraham himself know what was being done here, when he knew that Moses and the Prophets were here—that is, their books, by obeying which people might avoid infernal torments? And how, finally, did he know that the rich man had lived in luxury while the poor Lazarus had lived in toil and suffering?

For he also said to him: “Remember, son, that you received good things in your life, while Lazarus received evil things.” He therefore knew these matters, which had certainly occurred among the living, not among the dead.

Yet he could have learned them from Lazarus after both of them had died, not while they were occurring during their life. Thus the prophet’s statement, “Abraham did not know us,” is not false.

### Chapter XV

### 18. How the dead may know what is happening here

We must therefore admit that the dead do not know what is happening here while it is happening. Later, however, they may hear from those who go from here to them by dying—not everything, but whatever those who are permitted to do so are permitted to disclose, and whatever they are permitted to remember, and whatever those to whom they disclose these things ought to hear.

The dead may also hear something from angels who are present at the affairs taking place here, according to what the one to whom all things are subject judges that each of them ought to hear.

For if there were no angels capable of being present both in the places of the living and in those of the dead, the Lord Jesus would not have said: “It happened that the poor man died and was carried by angels into Abraham’s bosom” (Luke 16:22–29). Those whom God wished to carry from here to there could therefore be present now here and now there.

The spirits of the dead may also learn, through the revelation of God’s Spirit, certain things occurring here which it is necessary for them to know and which it is necessary for certain of them to know—not only past or present things but also future things. While they lived here, the Prophets knew such things, though not all of them, but only those which God’s providence judged ought to be revealed to them.

Divine Scripture also testifies that some dead may be sent to the living, just as, conversely, Paul was caught up from among the living into paradise (2 Corinthians 12:2). For the deceased prophet Samuel foretold future events to Saul, who was alive and was also a king (1 Samuel 28:7–19).

Some, however, think that it was not Samuel himself who could have been summoned by magical arts, but that another spirit, suited to such evil practices, assumed Samuel’s likeness. [Note: [Col. 0606] See above, Book 2, to Simplicianus, Question 4.] Yet the book of Ecclesiasticus, traditionally said to have been written by Jesus son of Sirach and attributed to Solomon because of a certain similarity of style, [Note: [Col. 0606] See *Retractations* 2.4 and *On Christian Doctrine* 2.8.13.] includes among its praises of the ancestors the statement that Samuel prophesied even after his death (Ecclesiasticus 46:23).

But if this book is rejected on the authority of the Hebrews, because it is not included in their canon, what shall we say about Moses? He is certainly read as having died in Deuteronomy (Deuteronomy 34:5), and in the Gospel he is read as having appeared to the living together with Elijah, who did not die (Matthew 17:3).

### Chapter XVI

### 19. Martyrs are present to help some people. He says that he cannot determine how martyrs are present to those in danger

This also resolves the question of how martyrs, through the benefits granted to those who pray, indicate that they participate in human affairs, if the dead do not know what the living are doing.

We have heard—not through uncertain rumors but through reliable witnesses—that Felix, the confessor whom you devoutly love as a fellow citizen or resident, appeared to people not only through the effects of his benefits but also visibly, when Nola was being attacked by the barbarians. [Note: [Col. 0606] The Louvain edition reads: “that Felix appeared to citizens or residents who were devoutly loved by him”; this is less satisfactory and is opposed by the other printed editions and most manuscripts.]

But such events are provided by divine action, in a manner altogether different from the ordinary order assigned to each kind of creature.

The fact that water was suddenly changed into wine when the Lord wished it (John 2:9) does not mean that we should fail to distinguish what water is capable of doing in its proper order among the elements from the rarity—or rather the uniqueness—of that divine work. Nor, because Lazarus rose again (John 11:44), should we suppose that every dead person rises whenever he wishes, or that a lifeless person is awakened by a living person in the way that a sleeping person is awakened by someone who is awake.

The limits of human affairs are one thing, and the signs of divine power another. Some things occur naturally, others miraculously. Yet God is present to nature so that it may exist, and nature is not absent from miracles.

We must not therefore suppose that any dead people can participate in the affairs of the living merely because martyrs are present to heal or help certain people. Rather, we should understand that martyrs participate in the affairs of the living through divine power precisely because, by their own nature as dead, the dead cannot participate in the affairs of the living.

20. Although this question exceeds the powers of my understanding—namely, how martyrs assist those whom it is certain they assist through them—whether they themselves are present by their own agency at one and the same time in places so different and so far apart, either wherever their memorials are or wherever else they are perceived to be present; or whether, while they themselves are withdrawn to a place befitting their merits and removed from all human intercourse, yet praying generally for the needs of those who entreat—as we pray for the dead, to whom we are certainly not present, nor know where they are or what they do—almighty God, who is present everywhere, neither joined to us nor remote from us, hears the prayers of the martyrs and, through angelic ministries diffused everywhere, grants human beings these consolations, which in the misery of this life he judges ought to be granted; and whether he commends the merits of his martyrs, wherever, whenever, and however he wishes, especially through their memorials, because he knows this to be useful to us for building up the faith of Christ, for whose confession they suffered, by a wondrous and ineffable power and goodness.

This matter is too lofty for me to reach and too hidden for me to investigate. Therefore I do not dare to determine which of these two alternatives is the case—or whether perhaps both are: whether sometimes these things occur through the martyrs’ own presence, and sometimes through angels assuming the person of martyrs. I would rather inquire of those who know such things. For there is certainly someone who knows them—not someone who merely seems to himself to know and does not. These are gifts of God, who bestows different gifts on different people, according to the Apostle, who says that “the manifestation of the Spirit is given to each for the common good: to one, indeed, through the Spirit, is given a word of wisdom; to another, a word of knowledge according to the same Spirit; to another, faith in the same Spirit; to another, gifts of healings in the one Spirit; to another, workings of miracles; to another, prophecy; to another, discernment of spirits; to another, kinds of tongues; to another, interpretation of tongues. But one and the same Spirit works all these things, distributing to each one individually as he wills” (1 Cor. 12:7–11). Whoever among all these spiritual gifts mentioned by the Apostle has received discernment of spirits knows these matters as they ought to be known.

## CHAPTER XVII

### 21. On John the Monk

We should believe that the monk John whom the elder Theodosius consulted about the outcome of the civil war was such a man; for he also possessed the gift of prophecy. I do not doubt that one person can possess not merely one of these gifts, but several.

This John, when a certain most devout woman ardently desired to see him and her husband [Col. 0608] pressed him very insistently to grant this request, refused, since he had never permitted women to visit him. “Go,” he said, “tell your wife that she will see me next night—but in a dream.” And so it happened. He instructed her in whatever a faithful married woman ought to be instructed. When she awoke, she told her husband that she had seen such a man of God as he knew John to be and reported what she had heard from him. A serious and noble man, fully worthy of belief, learned this from them and reported it to me.

But if I myself had seen that holy monk—who, as is said, was questioned with the greatest patience and answered with the greatest wisdom—I would have asked him, concerning the question before us, whether he had himself come to that woman in a dream, that is, whether his spirit had appeared in the likeness of his body, just as we dream of ourselves in the likeness of our bodies; or whether, while he was doing something else—or, if he was asleep, dreaming of something else—the vision of such a man had been produced in the woman’s dream, whether through an angel or in some other way; and whether he had foreseen that it would happen because the Spirit of prophecy had revealed it to him.

For if he was present to the woman as she dreamed, he could certainly have done so by wondrous grace, not by nature, and by God’s gift, not by his own power. But if, while he was doing something else—or sleeping and occupied with other visions—the woman saw him in her dream, then assuredly something occurred like what we read in the Acts of the Apostles: the Lord Jesus speaks to Ananias about Saul and tells him that Saul had seen Ananias coming to him, although Ananias himself did not know this (Acts 9:10–15).

Whatever answer that man of God might have given me, I would then have gone on to ask him about the martyrs: whether they are present in dreams or in some other way to those who see them in whatever form they wish—especially when demons confess that they are being tormented by them in human beings and beg them to spare them; or whether these things occur at God’s command through angelic powers, for the honor and commendation of the saints and for the benefit of human beings, while the martyrs themselves rest in complete tranquility, occupied apart from us with other and far better visions and praying for us.

For at Milan, at the shrines of the holy martyrs Protasius and Gervasius, demons expressly confessed Bishop Ambrose to be still alive, naming him just as they named the dead whom they commemorated in the same manner, and they begged him to spare them, although he was engaged in something else and was entirely unaware that this was happening.

Or would these things sometimes occur through the martyrs’ own presence and sometimes through angels? Could these two possibilities be distinguished by us, and, if so, by what signs? Or can no one perceive and discern them except one who possesses that gift through the Spirit of God, who distributes his own gifts to each as he wills? I think John himself would have explained all this to me as I wished—so that either I might learn from his instruction and recognize what I heard as true and certain, or might believe what I did not know because he was telling me what he knew.

If perhaps he had answered me from holy Scripture and said, “Do not seek what is too high for you, and do not investigate what is too difficult for you; but always consider what the Lord has commanded you” (Ecclus. 3:22), I would also have received that answer gratefully. For it is no small gain if, concerning certain obscure and uncertain matters that we cannot comprehend, at least this becomes clear [Col. 0609] and certain to us: that they are not to be sought. And whatever each person wishes to learn, thinking that knowledge would be useful, he should learn that ignorance is not harmful.

## CHAPTER XVIII

### 22. Solemn services for the dead: sacrifices of the altar, prayers, and almsgiving. The duty of burial

Since these things are so, let us not think that anything reaches the dead for whom we care except what we solemnly petition on their behalf through sacrifices of the altar, prayers, or almsgiving—although these do not benefit everyone for whom they are offered, but only those for whom it has been arranged during life that they should benefit.

But because we do not know who these are, we ought to perform these acts for all the regenerate, so that none of those to whom these benefits can and ought to come may be omitted. It is better that these things remain in excess for those whom they neither harm nor benefit than that they be lacking to those whom they benefit.

Nevertheless, each person performs these acts more diligently for those close to him, so that they may likewise be performed for him by his own people. Whatever is expended on burying the body, however, is not a safeguard of salvation but an act of human decency, according to the affection by which no one ever hates his own flesh (Eph. 5:29). Therefore one ought to care as much as possible for the flesh of one’s neighbor after the person who cared for it has departed.

[Note: The manuscripts read this way. The printed editions, however, read “ruled” rather than “cared for.”]

[Col. 0610]

And if those who do not believe in the resurrection of the flesh perform these duties, how much more ought those to perform them who do believe, so that the service rendered to a dead body—which nevertheless will rise again and remain for eternity—may also in some way be a testimony to that same faith?

As for being buried near the memorials of martyrs, this alone seems to me to benefit the dead: that, by commending him also to the martyrs’ protection, it increases the devotion of the supplication offered for him.

### 23

You have here the answer I was able to give to the questions you thought ought to be asked of me. If it is more extended than is necessary, forgive me; this happened because I enjoyed speaking with you at greater length.

I ask that you let me know by your reply how your Reverence has received this book. Its bearer will undoubtedly make it more welcome to you: our brother and fellow presbyter Candidianus, whom, having come to know through your letters, I welcomed with all my heart and dismissed unwillingly. By his presence he greatly consoled us in the charity of Christ; and, as must be admitted, by his insistence he made me comply with your request. For so many things distract my heart that, unless he had continually reminded me and not allowed me to forget, my answer would certainly have been lacking to your question.

# [ON PATIENCE]

[Col. 0609]

## Notice concerning the book *On Patience*

Erasmus expressed his judgment concerning the author of this little work in these words: “The phrasing shows that it is not Augustine’s, being consonant with that of the preceding little works.” In Erasmus’s edition, the preceding little works are *On Continence*, *On the Substance of Love*, *On Faith in Invisible Things*, and so forth; he likewise judged that these little works should be rejected on account of their phrasing and attributed to Hugh of Saint-Victor.

We admit that the style of this little work is the same as that of the book *On Continence*, and that its ideas and passages are often very similar. Yet it is demonstrated above, in the notice prefixed to that book, pp. 347–348, that the aforementioned book *On Continence*, to which Erasmus immediately appends the little work *On Patience*, is Augustine’s.

What we observe there—that the book *On Continence* is a sermon—we may also note concerning the following little work. At its beginning Augustine speaks as follows, in chapter 1: “Now, then, I shall explain, insofar as the Lord grants and the brevity of the present discourse permits, what human patience is like, the patience that we can and ought to possess . . . .” And below, in chapter 3: “Let us therefore consider, beloved . . . .”

From this it is understood why Augustine did not include such little works in the books of the *Retractions* that we possess: evidently, he was contemplating another work of *Retractions* in which he would review his sermons and letters. Concerning this, in Letter 224 to Quodvultdeus, section 2, he writes: “I had already completed two volumes, reviewing all my books, and so forth. The letters remained, and then the popular treatises, which the Greeks call homilies.”

Nevertheless, Augustine mentions both little works, *On Continence* and *On Patience*, and acknowledges them as his own in Letter 231, section 7, to Darius. This testimony of Augustine himself especially prevents us from numbering among the doubtful little works the book that follows. Its style did indeed trouble us to no small degree, particularly the form of expression that usually ends, and very deliberately concludes, with a similar sound of words. An example occurs in chapter 12, where Adam is compared with Job:

“This man was more cautious amid sufferings than that one amid the groves; the one was overcome in pleasures, the other conquered in punishments; the one yielded to delights, the other did not yield to torments.”

For the rest, this book conveys Augustine’s genuine doctrine and contains absolutely nothing contrary to it or less consistent with it.

In chapter 13, the Donatists who inflicted death upon themselves are censured without their name being mentioned. If, in that passage, no response is made to the example of Razis, which they began to produce from the Second Book of Maccabees in the year 420, one may infer that this sermon was delivered before that time. Later, in chapter 15, where the opponents of divine grace are refuted, the name of the Pelagians is still spared, although from the year 418 Augustine customarily attacked them openly and by name.

In chapter 26, we understand that some people hesitate because it is said that the patience of a schismatic is praiseworthy: he suffers not from charity but from fear of Gehenna, lest he deny Christ; and this patience is thought to benefit him somewhat, so that his condemnation may be more tolerable.

But this is certainly not alien to Augustine. Concerning the unbelieving Fabricius himself, in book 4 *Against Julian*, chapter 3, he says: “Fabricius will be punished less than Catiline—not because this man was good, but because the other was worse; and Fabricius was less impious than Catiline, not because he possessed true virtues, but because he did not depart very far from true virtues.”

And in *On the Spirit and the Letter*, chapter 27, explaining the Apostle’s passage in Romans 2:14, he says: “But if those who naturally do what belongs to the law are not yet to be counted among those whom the grace of Christ justifies, but rather among those of whom—even though they are impious and do not truly and rightly worship the true God—we nevertheless read, know, or hear that certain actions have been performed which, according to the rule of justice, we can not only not censure but rightly and deservedly praise, although, if the purpose for which they are done is examined, scarcely any are found that deserve the praise or defense due to justice,” and so forth.

[Col. 0611]

## The One Book of St. Aurelius Augustine, Bishop of Hippo, *On Patience* (C)

[Note: Possibly written before the year 418.]

[Note: The book *On Patience* was reviewed in fifteen Gallican manuscripts: the Colbertine, Sorbonne, Victorine, Augustinian Hermits of the Great Convent at Paris, Cistercian, Regiomontan, Floriacensian, Vendôme, Pratellian, Michaeline, Audoenian, Dijon manuscript of Saint-Benignus, Angers manuscript of Saint-Albinus, Metz manuscript of Saint-Arnulfus, and a codex from the abbey of Casal Benedetto. It was also reviewed in four Roman manuscripts of the Vatican Library, together with which the variant readings of four Belgian manuscripts seen by the Louvain scholars were collated, as well as the principal editions of Erasmus and Louvain.]

[Note: We also compared all the editions mentioned at the beginning of volume 1 of the *Retractions* and *Confessions*. M.]

Augustine first distinguishes true patience from false patience. He then urges the embrace of that patience which is true, by which evils are endured for eternal life and out of love of God. Finally, he teaches that this virtue of patience is to be attributed not to the powers of free will but to the help of divine grace.

## CHAPTER I

### 1. What God’s patience is like

The virtue called patience is so great a gift of God that even the patience of the one who bestows it upon us is praised—his patience by which he waits for the wicked to be corrected. Thus, although God cannot suffer anything [Note: Twelve manuscripts read, “cannot suffer anything evil”], and although patience takes its name from suffering, we nevertheless both faithfully believe and profitably confess that God is patient.

But who could explain in words what God’s patience is like and how great it is—God whom we call one who suffers nothing and yet is not impatient, indeed, supremely patient? That patience is therefore ineffable [Note: Here eleven manuscripts add, “yet it is not non-existent”], just as are his jealousy, his anger, and anything else of this kind.

For if we conceive of these qualities in him as though they were like ours, they do not exist in him. We experience none of these things without distress; but far be it from us to suppose that God’s impassible nature undergoes any distress.

As he is jealous without envy, angry without disturbance, merciful without pain, and repents without correcting any perversity in himself, so he is patient without any suffering.

Now, then, I shall explain, insofar as the Lord grants and the brevity of the present discourse permits, what human patience is like—the patience that we can and ought to possess.

[Col. 0612]

## CHAPTER II

### 2. What right patience is and how useful it is

Human patience that is right and praiseworthy and worthy of the name of virtue is understood to be that by which we endure evils with an even mind, lest with an evil mind we abandon the good things through which we may reach better things.

[Note: Louvain, with only one manuscript, reads “lest with an evil mind we desire good things,” which is less satisfactory.]

Therefore the impatient, because they do not wish to suffer evils, do not bring it about that they are rescued from evils; rather, they bring it about that they suffer more serious evils.

But the patient, who prefer to endure evils by not committing them rather than to commit them by refusing to endure them, both make lighter the things they suffer through patience and escape the worse things into which they would be submerged through impatience.

[Note: Louvain reads “than the things which”; “than” is absent from the other printed editions and manuscripts.]

They do not lose eternal and great goods because they do not yield to temporal and brief evils, since “the sufferings of this present time are not worthy of comparison with the future glory that will be revealed in us,” as the Apostle says (Rom. 8:18). And again he says: “Our momentary and light tribulation is producing for us, in an immeasurable way, an eternal weight of glory” (2 Cor. 4:17).

[Note: The printed editions read “in us.” The word “in” is absent from the manuscripts and from the Greek text of the Apostle.]

## CHAPTER III

### 3. How great is the patience of the wicked

Let us therefore consider, beloved, how much hardship and suffering people endure for things that they love viciously, and how much more unhappy their desires become the happier they think these things will make them.

How many exceedingly dangerous and painful things are endured with the greatest patience for false riches, empty honors, and frivolous pleasures! We see those who desire money, glory, and lust endure, in order to reach what they desire and not be deprived of what they have obtained, the sun, rain, ice, waves, and the most violent storms; the harsh and uncertain conditions of war; the blows of monstrous wounds; and dreadful injuries—not from unavoidable necessity but from culpable will.

Yet these are, in a certain sense, regarded as permissible forms of madness.

## CHAPTER IV

### Such patience is praised by vanity

For avarice, ambition, luxury, and the pleasures of various games are thought to belong to innocence unless, for their sake, some crime is committed or some disgrace prohibited by human laws.

Indeed, when someone, without defrauding anyone, endures great labors and pains either to acquire or increase money, to obtain or retain honors, or to compete in an athletic contest, hunt, or present something theatrical to popular applause, it is not merely the case that popular vanity restrains him with no reproach; he is even exalted with praises.

“For the sinner is praised,” as it is written, “in the desires of his soul” (Ps. 9:3).

The force of desire produces endurance of labor and pain; no one willingly undertakes to bear what torments him except for something that delights him.

But these desires, as I have said, for the fulfillment of which those who burn with them patiently endure many harsh and bitter things, are considered lawful and permitted by the laws.

## CHAPTER V

### 4. The savage endurance of Catiline and robbers

What shall we say of those who endure many very grievous things even for manifest crimes—not in order to punish such crimes but in order to commit them?

Do not the authors of secular literature tell us, concerning a certain most noble parricide of his country, that he could endure hunger, thirst, and cold, and that his body was capable of fasting, exposure to cold, and sleeplessness beyond what anyone could believe (Sallust, *Catiline*, chapter 5)?

What shall I say of robbers? Whenever they lie in wait for travelers, they all endure sleepless nights and, in order to intercept innocent passersby, expose their guilty minds and bodies to every severity of the weather.

[Note: Only three manuscripts read “who all.”]

Some of them are even said to torture one another, so that training against punishments scarcely differs from punishment itself. For perhaps they are not tortured by a judge as much, in order that truth may be extracted from those who suffer, as by their accomplices, so that the truth may not be betrayed by those who suffer.

[Note: The manuscripts read this way. The printed editions read “so that they may not be betrayed.”]

And yet in all these cases their patience is more astonishing than praiseworthy—or rather, it is neither astonishing nor praiseworthy, since it is not patience at all. What is astonishing is their hardness; what must be denied is their patience. Nothing there is rightly to be praised, and nothing usefully to be imitated.

[Note: Some manuscripts read, “praised where nothing is usefully to be imitated.”]

The more an animus subjects the instruments of virtue to vices, the more rightly you will judge it worthy of a greater punishment.

Patience is the companion of wisdom, not the servant of desire; patience is the friend of a good conscience, not the enemy of innocence.

## CHAPTER VI

### 5. The cause of suffering distinguishes true patience from false

When, therefore, you see someone patiently suffering something, do not immediately praise the patience, which is shown only by the cause of the suffering.

When that cause is good, then the patience is true; when the cause is not polluted by desire, then patience is distinguished from falsity. But when the cause is bound up with crime, the name of patience is being greatly misused.

For just as not everyone who knows participates in knowledge, so not everyone who suffers participates in patience. Rather, those who use suffering rightly are praised for the truth of patience; they are crowned with the gift of patience.

## CHAPTER VII

### 6. How much the godly ought to suffer for eternal salvation, if the wicked suffer so much for temporal life

Not only the soul but also the body itself is cared for by enduring death and pains.

Yet when people endure many dreadful things with astonishing determination for lusts, or even for crimes, and finally for this temporal life and its safety, they sufficiently remind us how much must be suffered for a good life, so that afterward it may also be eternal—secure in true happiness, without any limit of time and without loss of any benefit.

The Lord says: “By your patience you will possess your souls” (Luke 21:19). He does not say, “your estates,” “your praises,” or “your luxuries,” but “your souls.”

If, then, the soul suffers so much in order to possess that by which it may perish, how much ought it to suffer so that it may not perish?

Then, to mention something that is not blameworthy: if a person suffers so much for the health of his flesh at the hands of physicians who cut or burn, how much ought he to suffer for his salvation amid the fury of any enemies?

Physicians, so that the body may not die, care for the body through painful treatments. Enemies, by threatening the body with pain and death, drive a person to act so that both soul and body may be killed in Gehenna.

### 7

Even the body itself is more wisely cared for when its temporal safety is despised for the sake of justice, and its pain or death is endured with the greatest patience for the sake of justice.

The Apostle speaks of the redemption of the body that will occur at the end when he says: “And we ourselves groan within ourselves, awaiting the adoption of sons, the redemption of our body.” Then he adds: “For in hope we were saved. But hope that is seen is not hope; for who hopes for what he sees? But if we hope for what we do not see, we await it with patience” (Rom. 8:23–25).

[Note: The printed editions omit “for your salvation.” It is restored from the manuscripts.]

## CHAPTER VIII

### The use of patience in soul and body

When evils torment us but do not extort evil deeds from us, the soul is possessed through patience. And when, through patience, the body itself is afflicted or lost for a time, it is restored to eternal stability and salvation; through pain and death, inviolable health and blessed immortality are secured for it.

Therefore the Lord Jesus, exhorting his martyrs to patience, promised that the integrity of their bodies would in the future remain complete, without the loss of so much as a member—or, I do not say, a member, but even a hair.

“I tell you,” he said, “not a hair of your head will perish” (Luke 21:18).

Since, as the Apostle says, no one has ever hated his own flesh (Eph. 5:29), the faithful person should therefore watch over the condition of his flesh more through patience than through impatience, and compensate whatever present losses it may suffer with the immeasurable gain of future incorruption.

### 8

Although patience is a virtue of the soul, the soul nevertheless uses it partly in itself and partly in its body.

It uses patience in itself when, while the body remains unharmed and untouched, it is urged by the goads of any adversity or by the ugliness of circumstances or words to do or say something improper or unbecoming, and patiently endures every evil so that it may not itself commit anything evil in deed or word.

[Note: The manuscripts read, “or is urged as though by the goads of words.”]

## CHAPTER IX

### Patience of the soul

Through this patience we endure, even while we are physically healthy, the postponement of our blessedness amid the scandals of this age. Hence the statement I recalled shortly before: “If we hope for what we do not see, we await it with patience.”

By this patience holy David endured the insults of the man who cursed him. Although he could easily have taken revenge, he not only did not do so, but restrained another who was grieving and angered on his behalf (2 Sam. 16:5–12). He employed royal power more by forbidding vengeance than by exercising it.

[Note: The Casalinus manuscript reads “by displaying vengeance.”]

His body was not then afflicted by any disease or wound. Rather, a time of humility was recognized and endured, and God’s will was obeyed; for its sake the bitterness of insult was drunk with the greatest patience.

The Lord taught this patience when the servants, disturbed by the mixture of weeds and wishing to gather them, and the master of the household was said to have answered: “Let both grow until the harvest” (Matt. 13:30).

What ought not to be removed hastily must be endured patiently.

He himself also provided and demonstrated an example of this patience when, before the suffering of his body, he endured the disciple Judas as a thief before revealing him as a betrayer (John 12:6; 13:29), and, before experiencing bonds, the cross, and death, he did not refuse the kiss of peace from his deceitful lips (Matt. 26:29).

[Note: Seven Gallican manuscripts read *diabolum*, “the devil,” while three Vatican manuscripts read *diabolus*, also “the devil,” with a different grammatical form.]

All these things—and any others whose enumeration would be lengthy—belong to that form of patience by which the soul patiently endures in itself not its own sins but whatever evils come from outside, while its own body remains wholly unharmed.

## CHAPTER X

### Patience in external hardships. Both forms of patience in the martyrs. The greater struggle of patience when the devil rages

There is another form of patience, by which that same soul endures whatever is painful and difficult in the suffering of its body—not as foolish or wicked people do, for the sake of acquiring vanities or committing crimes, but, as the Lord has defined it, for the sake of justice (Matt. 5:10).

The holy martyrs contended in both ways. They were filled with the insults of the ungodly, while the soul, with the body unharmed, bore its wounds, as it were, intact. They were also bound in their bodies, imprisoned, afflicted by hunger and thirst, tortured, cut, torn apart, burned, and slaughtered. With unshaken devotion they subjected their minds to God while suffering in the flesh whatever the cruelty that sought to torment them could devise.

[Note: The Casalinus manuscript reads “they subjected their minds with unshaken devotion.”]

### 9

The struggle of patience is certainly greater when the enemy is not visible—when he does not openly and visibly drive someone into wickedness by pursuing and raging against him, so that he can be defeated by one who refuses consent—but when the devil himself, through the children of unbelief as through his own vessels, pursues the children of light and secretly attacks them directly, pressing on with rage so that something may be done or said against God.

## CHAPTER XI

### The patience of holy Job

Holy Job experienced such an attack. He was afflicted by both forms of temptation, yet in both he remained unconquered through the steadfast strength of patience and the weapons of devotion.

First, while his body remained unharmed, he lost everything he possessed, so that before the torment of his flesh his soul might be broken by the removal of the things that people ordinarily value highly, and might say something against God when the things for whose sake it was thought that he worshiped him were lost.

He was also struck by the sudden bereavement of all his children, so that those whom he had received one by one he might lose all together—as though their multitude had arisen not to adorn his happiness but to increase his calamity.

But when, after suffering these things, he remained immovable in his God, he clung to the will of him whom he could lose only by his own will. In place of what he had lost, he retained the one who had taken them away, in whom he would find what could never perish.

For it was not the one who had the will to harm who had taken them away, but the one who had granted the power to do so.

## CHAPTER XII

### Job more cautious than Adam

The enemy then attacked the body as well. He did not strike merely at the things that belonged externally to the man, but struck the man himself in whatever part he could.

From head to foot, pains burned; worms swarmed; pus flowed. Within the corrupt body the soul remained whole, enduring the dreadful tortures of wasting flesh with inviolate devotion and incorrupt patience.

His wife was present, but she offered her husband no help; rather, she urged him to blaspheme God. The devil had not left her behind, even after taking away his children, through ignorance of how to cause harm. He had already learned in Eve how useful she was to a tempter (Gen. 3:1–6). But now he had not found another Adam whom he could capture through a woman.

This man was more cautious amid sufferings than that one amid the groves; the one was overcome in pleasures, the other conquered in punishments; the one yielded to delights, the other did not yield to torments.

Friends were present too—not to console him in his evils, but to suspect him of evil. They did not believe that a man who suffered such things was innocent, and their tongues did not keep silent about what his conscience did not possess. Thus, amid the monstrous tortures of his body, his soul was also struck by false reproaches.

But he, enduring his own bodily pains in his flesh and the errors of others in his heart, rebuked his wife’s folly, taught his friends wisdom, and preserved patience everywhere.

## CHAPTER XIII

### 10. The impatience of the Donatists who lay hands upon themselves when they are sought by Catholics

Let those who inflict death upon themselves when they are being sought for life look upon this man. By taking away the present life from themselves, they also deny the future life.

If they were compelled, like true martyrs, either to deny Christ or to do something against justice, they ought to endure everything patiently rather than impatiently inflict death upon themselves.

If this could rightly be done in order to escape evils, holy Job would have killed himself so that he might escape such great evils in his possessions, his children, and his limbs, all caused by the devil’s cruelty.

But he did not do so. Far be it from that wise man to commit against himself what even a foolish woman did not suggest.

For even if she had suggested it, he would rightly have heard the same answer that she heard when she suggested blasphemy: “You have spoken as one of the foolish women. If we have received good things from the hand of the Lord, shall we not endure evil things?” (Job 1–2, etc.)

He too would have lost patience—either by blaspheming, as she had wished, or by killing himself, which she had not dared to suggest—and would have died. He would have been among those of whom it is said: “Woe to those who have lost patience!” (Ecclus. 2:16).

Rather than escape punishment, he would have increased it, being swept away after the death of his body into the punishment not only of blasphemers but also of murderers, or even of those worse than parricides.

For if a parricide is more criminal than any other murderer because he kills not merely a human being but also a relative, and among parricides each person is judged more monstrous the closer the relative he has killed, then without doubt the one who kills himself is worse, because no one is closer to a human being than he himself.

What, then, do wretched people accomplish when, after inflicting suffering upon themselves here, they later pay the due penalties not only for impiety against God but also for the cruelty they exercised against themselves—and yet additionally seek the glory of martyrs?

Even if they were suffering persecution for the true testimony of Christ and killed themselves so as not to suffer anything at the hands of their persecutors, one would rightly say to them: “Woe to those who have lost patience!”

For how can a just reward for patience be given if impatient suffering is also crowned?

Or how will one be judged innocent to whom it was said, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Matt. 19:19), if he commits against himself the homicide that he is forbidden to commit against his neighbor?

## CHAPTER XIV

### 11. The patience of the good

Let the holy hear the commands concerning patience from the sacred Scriptures:

“My son, when you come to the service of God, stand in justice and fear, and prepare your soul for temptation. Humble your heart and endure, so that your life may increase at the end. Accept whatever comes upon you, and endure in suffering; and in your humiliation have patience. For gold and silver are tested in fire, but acceptable people in the furnace of humiliation” (Ecclus. 2:1–5).

And elsewhere we read:

“My son, do not reject the discipline of the Lord, and do not grow weary when you are rebuked by him. For whom the Lord loves, he disciplines; and he scourges every son whom he receives” (Prov. 3:11–12).

What is stated here as “the son whom he receives” is expressed in the passage cited above as “acceptable people.” For it is just that we who were dismissed from the former happiness of paradise because of our rebellious desire for pleasures should be received again through humble endurance of hardships: fleeing by doing evil, returning by suffering evil; there doing what is contrary to justice, here suffering for the sake of justice.

## CHAPTER XV

[The supplied source ends here.]

12. Patience does not arise from the powers of free will, but from divine assistance

But true patience, which is worthy of the name of this virtue, must be examined as to where it is obtained. For there are those who attribute it to the powers of the human will—not to the powers they possess through divine assistance, but to those they possess through free choice. This error, however, is proud; it belongs to those who abound, of whom it is said in the Psalm: “Reproach to those who abound, and contempt for the proud” (Ps. 122:4). This, then, is not the patience of the poor, which does not perish forever (Ps. 9:19).

These poor receive it from that rich one to whom it is said, “You are my God, for you have no need of my goods” (Ps. 15:2); from him comes “every good gift and every perfect gift” (Jas. 1:17). To him cries out the needy and poor person who praises his name and, asking, seeking, and knocking, says: “My God, deliver me from the hand of the sinner, and from the hand of the transgressor of the law and of the unjust; for you are my patience, Lord, my hope from my youth” (Ps. 70:4–5).

But those who abound and disdain being needy before God, lest they receive true patience from him, boast of their own false patience and wish to frustrate the counsel of the poor, “because the Lord is his hope” (Ps. 13:6). They do not consider that, although they are human beings, by attributing so much to their own— that is, human—will, they fall under what is written: “Cursed is everyone who places his hope in man” (Jer. 17:5).

Therefore, even if it happens that they endure certain harsh and difficult things—whether in order not to displease other people, or in order not to suffer worse things, or because they take pleasure in and love their own presumption—and endure those very things by that exceedingly proud will, what must be said to them about their patience is what blessed the Apostle James says about wisdom: “This wisdom is not descending from above, but is earthly, natural, demonic” (Jas. 3:15). Why, then, should there not be a false patience of the proud, just as there is a false wisdom of the proud?

[Note: Cyprian, in *On the Good of Patience*: “If true wisdom is not there, true patience cannot be there either.”]

From the one, however, from whom true wisdom comes, true patience also comes. To him that poor in spirit sings: “My soul is subject to God, for from him is my patience” (Ps. 61:6).

## CHAPTER XVI

13. Objection: why the powers of the will are not sufficient for suffering on behalf of justice, as they are for injustice
