But they respond and say: If the human will, without any assistance from God, by the powers of free choice, endures so many grievous and dreadful things, whether in mind or in body, in order to enjoy this mortal life and the pleasure of sins, why does that same human will not, in the same way and by those same powers of free choice, without waiting to be divinely assisted for this purpose, but sufficient for itself by its natural capacity, endure with the greatest patience whatever labor or pain is imposed for the sake of justice and eternal life?

Or, they say, is the will of the wicked capable, without God’s assistance, of exercising itself amid tortures for the sake of iniquity, even before it is tortured by others? Is the will of those who love the continuation of this life capable, without God’s assistance, of persevering amid the most atrocious and prolonged torments in a lie, lest, by confessing their crimes, they be ordered to be killed? And is the will of the righteous not capable, unless strength is supplied from above, of enduring whatever punishments, whether because of the beauty of justice itself or because of love for eternal life?

## CHAPTER XVII

14. Solution: the wicked derive hardness from desire, the godly derive strength from love. Human will is sufficient for false patience, but not for true patience

Those who say these things do not understand that each wicked person is harder in enduring any evil in proportion as the desire for the world is greater in him, and that each righteous person is stronger in enduring any evil in proportion as the love of God is greater in him.

But desire for the world begins from the choice of the will, advances through the pleasure of delight, and is strengthened through the bond of habit. “The love of God, however, has been poured into our hearts,” not from ourselves, certainly, but “through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. 5:5). Accordingly, the patience of the righteous comes from him through whom their love is poured out.

[Note: Two manuscripts read, “in their hearts.”]

Praising and commending this love, the Apostle said among its other goods that it endures all things. “Love,” he says, “is magnanimous.” A little later he says: “It endures all things” (1 Cor. 13:4, 7).

Therefore, the greater the love of God is in the saints, the more they endure everything for the sake of what they love; and the greater the desire for the world is in sinners, the more they endure everything for the sake of what they crave. Hence the true patience of the righteous arises from the same source as the love of God in them; and the false patience of the wicked arises from the same source as the desire for the world in them.

For this reason the Apostle John says: “Do not love the world, nor the things that are in the world. If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him; for everything that is in the world is the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the ambition of the age. This is not from the Father, but is from the world” (1 John 2:15–16).

This desire, therefore, which is not from the Father but from the world, the more vehement and ardent it is in a person, the more patiently that person endures every hardship and pain for the sake of what he desires. Thus, as we said above, this is not “patience descending from above.” The patience of the godly, however, is from above, descending from the Father of lights.

Accordingly, the former is earthly, the latter heavenly; the former natural, the latter spiritual; the former demonic, the latter divine. For the desire by which sinners are made to endure everything obstinately is from the world, whereas the love by which those who live rightly endure everything bravely is from God.

Therefore human will can suffice for that false patience without God’s assistance—being harder in proportion to its greater desire, and enduring evils more tolerably in proportion as it becomes worse itself. But for this patience, which is true patience, human will is not sufficient unless it is assisted and inflamed from above, because the Holy Spirit is its fire. Unless it is kindled by him to love the good that cannot suffer, it cannot endure the evil that it suffers.

## CHAPTER XVIII

15. As love is from God, so true patience, which flows from love, is from him

For, as the divine utterances testify, “God is love, and whoever remains in love remains in God, and God remains in him” (1 John 4:16). Therefore, whoever contends that the love of God can be possessed without God’s assistance is contending for nothing else than that God can be possessed without God.

What Christian would say this—something that no insane person would dare to say?

Thus true, godly, and faithful patience exults through the Apostle and says by the mouths of the saints:

“Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or danger, or the sword? As it is written: ‘For your sake we are put to death all day long; we are counted as sheep for slaughter.’ But in all these things we overwhelmingly conquer through him who loved us”—not through ourselves, but through him who loved us.

Then he continues and adds: “For I am certain that neither death nor life, nor angels nor principalities, nor powers, nor things present nor things to come, nor height nor depth, nor any other creature will be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Rom. 8:35–39).

[Note: The Casalinus manuscript reads, “the patience of the saints says,” omitting “by the mouths.”]

This is that love of God which has been poured into our hearts—not from ourselves, but through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us. The desire of evil people, however, because of which they possess false patience, is not from the Father, as the Apostle John says, but is from the world.

## CHAPTER XIX

16. If desire is from the world, how is it from the human will? Not being of the world is a matter of grace, not of nature

Here someone may say: If the desire for evil things is from the world, through which they endure every evil for the sake of what they desire, how is it said to be from their will?

As though they themselves were not also of the world when they love the world, having abandoned him through whom the world was made. “For they serve the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed forever” (Rom. 1:25).

Therefore, whether the Apostle John, by the term “world,” meant the lovers of the world, the will that comes from them is certainly from the world; or whether, by the name “world,” he embraced heaven and earth and whatever is in them—that is, the whole creation—the will of the creature, which is not the Creator’s, is undoubtedly from the world.

For this reason the Lord says to such people: “You are from below; I am from above. You are of this world; I am not of this world” (John 8:23).

But to the Apostles he says: “If you were of this world, the world would love what is its own.” Yet, lest they claim more for themselves than their measure permitted, and lest they think that his statement that they were not of the world referred to nature rather than grace, he immediately adds: “But because you are not of the world, and I chose you from the world, therefore the world hates you” (John 15:19).

Therefore they were of the world.

[Note: Lovaniensis reads, “they were not.” The word “not” is absent from Erasmus and from many manuscripts.]

For in order that they might not be of the world, they were chosen from the world.

## CHAPTER XX

17. The election of grace precedes all good merits. Grace gives merits; it is not given on the basis of merits. It precedes faith

Demonstrating that this election is not an election based on preceding merits in good works, but an election of grace, the Apostle says: “At this present time a remnant has been saved by the election of grace. But if by grace, then not by works; otherwise grace is no longer grace” (Rom. 11:5–6).

This is the election of grace—that is, the election by which human beings are chosen through the grace of God. This, I say, is the election of grace by which all good human merits are preceded.

For if it is given on the basis of any good merits, it is no longer given freely but is repaid as something owed; and consequently it is not called grace in the true sense, since, as the same Apostle says, a reward “is not reckoned according to grace but according to debt” (Rom. 4:4).

But if, in order that it may truly be grace—that is, gratuitous—it finds nothing in a person to which it is owed by merit, this is well understood also in what is said: “You will save them for nothing” (Ps. 55:8). Clearly, grace itself gives merits; it is not given on the basis of merits.

It therefore precedes even faith, from which all good works begin. “The righteous,” as it is written, “lives by faith” (Hab. 2:4). Grace, moreover, not only assists the righteous but also justifies the ungodly. And therefore, even when it assists the righteous and appears to be repaid for his merits, it does not cease to be grace, because it assists what it itself has bestowed.

Because of this grace, which precedes all human good merits, Christ was not only killed by the ungodly but also died for the ungodly (Rom. 5:6). Before he died, he chose as Apostles not the righteous but those who were to be justified, saying to them: “I chose you from the world.”

For when he said to them, “You are not of the world,” and lest they think that they had never been of the world, he immediately added, “But I chose you from the world,” it was clearly through his election of them that they were made not to be of the world.

Accordingly, if they were chosen through their own righteousness and not through his grace, they would not have been chosen from the world, since they would no longer have been of the world if they were already righteous.

Furthermore, if they were chosen because they were already righteous, they themselves would have chosen the Lord first. For who can be righteous except by choosing righteousness?

But “Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Rom. 10:4). He “has become for us wisdom from God, and righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption, so that, as it is written, ‘Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord’” (1 Cor. 1:30–31). He, therefore, is our righteousness.

## CHAPTER XXI

18. Through the gift of grace and faith, the ancients too were justified before the Incarnation. No one was ever righteous without faith

Hence the righteous of ancient times, before the Incarnation of the Word, were justified in this faith in Christ and in this true righteousness, which is Christ for us. They believed that what we believe has happened would take place; and they too were saved by grace through faith, not from themselves but as God’s gift, “not from works, lest they should boast” (Eph. 2:8–9).

Their good works did not precede the mercy of God but followed it. They themselves heard and wrote, long before Christ came in the flesh: “I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will show compassion to whom I show compassion.” Many ages later the Apostle Paul would say on the basis of these words of God: “So then it is not of the one who wills or of the one who runs, but of God who has mercy” (Exod. 33:19; Rom. 9:15–16).

Their voice also is heard, long before Christ came in the flesh: “My God, his mercy will precede me” (Ps. 58:11).

How could they have been strangers to the faith of Christ, when Christ was foretold to us even through their love? Without faith in him, no mortal ever was, is, or can ever be righteous.

Therefore, if the Apostles were already righteous when they were chosen by Christ, they themselves would have chosen him first, so that they could be chosen as righteous; for without him they could not be righteous.

But this did not happen. He himself said to them: “You did not choose me, but I chose you.” Hence the Apostle John says: “Not that we loved God, but that he first loved us” (1 John 4:10).

## CHAPTER XXII

19. Before the election of grace, all were unrighteous

Since this is so, what is a human being, using his own will in this life before choosing and loving God, except unrighteous and ungodly?

What, I ask, is a human being who has wandered from the Creator toward the creature, unless his Creator remembers him (Ps. 8:5), chooses him freely, and loves him freely?

For he cannot choose or love unless he is first chosen and loved and cared for—he who, through blindness, does not see what ought to be chosen, and through sickness finds distasteful what ought to be loved.

But perhaps someone may say: How does God first choose and love the wicked in order to justify them, when it is written, “You hate all who work iniquity” (Ps. 5:7)?

How are we to understand this except in a wonderful and ineffable way? Yet even we can think of the good physician who both hates and loves the sick person: he hates him because he is sick, and loves him in order to drive away his sickness.

[Note: Thus read two Vatican manuscripts. Most others, together with the printed editions, read, “we cannot.”]

## CHAPTER XXIII

20. As love is the source of true patience, so desire is the source of evil patience

Let this much be said concerning love, without which true patience cannot exist in us: for in the good there is the love of God, which endures all things, just as in the wicked there is desire for the world.

But this love is in us through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us. Therefore, from the one from whom we receive love, we receive patience as well.

When the desire for the world patiently endures the burdens of any calamity, it boasts of the strength of its own will, as though boasting of the insensibility of disease rather than the strength of health. This boasting is insane; it belongs not to patience but to madness.

This will appears more patient in enduring bitter evils in proportion as it is more avid for temporal goods, because it is emptier of eternal goods.

## CHAPTER XXIV

21. A wicked will can exist even without the instigation of an evil spirit

But if a demonic spirit, joined to it in evil conspiracy, agitates and inflames it with deceptive visions and impure persuasions,

[Note: Several manuscripts read, “with deceptive appearances.” In a very similar passage in *On Continence*, chapter 2, section 3, we read: “Whoever has consented in his heart to the suggestions of whatever visions occur . . .”]

and makes the human will either foolish through error or ardent through desire for any worldly pleasure,

[Note: A few manuscripts read, “an impure and demonic spirit.” Immediately afterward, two Vatican manuscripts read, “joined to it in a malicious conspiracy.”]

so that, when it appears remarkably to endure intolerable things,

[Note: Thus read manuscripts of good quality. The printed editions read, “whatever things appear.”]

it does not follow that a wicked will, without the instigation of another impure spirit, cannot exist, any more than a good will can exist without the assistance of the Holy Spirit.

That a wicked will can exist even without some spirit either deceiving or inciting it is sufficiently shown in the devil himself, who is found to have become a devil through his own will, not through another devil.

Thus a wicked will, whether it is carried away by desire, restrained by fear, expanded by joy, or contracted by sadness, and whether amid all these disturbances of the mind it despises and endures things that are more grievous to others or at another time,

[Note: Most manuscripts read, “or at that time.”]

can, even without the impulse of another spirit, deceive itself and, by falling through its own defect from higher things into lower ones, endure all the more tolerably for the sake of what is less to be suffered than that thing is to be enjoyed, the more pleasantly it judges what it seeks to attain, fears to lose, rejoices in having attained, or grieves at having lost.

For whatever that thing may be, it is from the creature, whose pleasure is known.

[Note: The printed editions read, “whose will is known.” The manuscripts more correctly read, “whose pleasure is known.”]

In a certain manner, through familiar contact and connection, the creature loved lies close to the creature that loves, so that the latter may experience its sweetness.

## CHAPTER XXV

22. A good will comes only from God

But the pleasure of the Creator, of which it is written, “You will give them drink from the torrent of your pleasure” (Ps. 35:9), is of an entirely different kind. For he is not a creature, as we are.

Unless love for him is given to us from him, there is no source from which it can exist in us. Consequently, a good will—by which God is loved—cannot exist in a human being unless God is at work in that person “both to will” (Phil. 2:13).

This good will, therefore—that is, a will faithfully subject to God; a will kindled by the holiness of heavenly ardor; a will that loves God and neighbor for God’s sake—whether through the love of which the Apostle Peter responds, “Lord, you know that I love you” (John 21:15); or through the fear of which the Apostle Paul says, “Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling” (Phil. 2:12); or through the joy of which he says, “Rejoicing in hope, patient in tribulation” (Rom. 12:12); or through the sadness which he says he had for his brothers, “great sorrow” (Rom. 9:2)—whatever bitter and harsh things it may endure, it is the love of God that “endures all things” (1 Cor. 13:7), and this love is poured into our hearts only through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us (Rom. 5:5).

## CHAPTER XXVI

The patience of the godly is God’s gift. Is the patience of schismatics for Christ to be praised?

Therefore, with pious confidence, just as the love of those who love in holiness is God’s gift, so the patience of those who endure in godliness is God’s gift.

For divine Scripture neither deceives nor is deceived. In the ancient Books it bears witness to this matter when it says to God, “You are my patience” (Ps. 70:5), and, “My patience is from him” (Ps. 61:6). Elsewhere another prophet says that we receive “the Spirit of fortitude.” And in the apostolic Letters we read: “To you it has been granted for Christ not only to believe in him but also to suffer for him” (Phil. 1:29).

Therefore, no one should become elated as though this were his own possession when he hears that it has been granted to him.

23. But if someone does not possess the love that belongs to the unity of the Spirit and the bond of peace by which the Catholic Church is gathered and joined together, and, being situated in some schism, suffers tribulations, distress, hunger, nakedness, persecution, dangers, prisons, chains, tortures, the sword, flames, wild beasts, or even the cross itself, through fear of hell and eternal fire, in order not to deny Christ, these things are in no way to be condemned. Indeed, this patience too is to be praised.

For we cannot say that it would have been better for him to deny Christ and suffer none of the things that he suffered by confessing him. Rather, it must perhaps be judged that his sentence will be more tolerable than it would have been if, by denying Christ, he had avoided all those things.

Thus the Apostle’s statement, “If I deliver my body to be burned but do not have love, it profits me nothing” (1 Cor. 13:3), should be understood to mean that it profits him nothing for obtaining the kingdom of heaven, not that it does nothing to make him undergo the punishment of the final judgment more tolerably.

## CHAPTER XXVII

24. Whether this patience of theirs is God’s gift

It may rightly be asked, therefore, whether this patience too is God’s gift or whether it should be attributed to the powers of the human will: namely, when someone separated from the Church suffers temporal punishments, not for the error that separated him but for the truth of the sacrament or word that has remained with him, because of his fear of eternal punishments.

For care must be taken lest, if we call this patience God’s gift, those who possess it be believed also to belong to the kingdom of God; whereas, if we deny that it is God’s gift, we are forced to admit that something good can exist in the human will without God’s assistance and gift.

For it is certainly good that a person believe he will be punished with eternal punishment if he denies Christ, and that for this faith he endure and despise whatever human punishment may be imposed.

25. Therefore, just as it must not be denied that this is God’s gift, so it must be understood that there are other gifts of God belonging to the children of that Jerusalem which is above and is our free mother.

## CHAPTER XXVIII

The gifts of the children who are heirs and the gifts of the disinherited children are different

For these gifts are, in a certain sense, hereditary gifts, through which we are heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ. But there are other gifts that can also be received by the children of concubines, to whom carnal Jews, schismatics, and heretics are compared.

Although it is written, “Cast out the slave woman and her son; for the son of the slave woman will not be heir with my son Isaac” (Gal. 4:26, 30; Gen. 21:10), and although God said to Abraham, “In Isaac shall your offspring be called” (Gen. 21:12; Rom. 9:7–8)—which the Apostle interpreted as follows: “That is, it is not the children of the flesh who are children of God, but the children of the promise are counted as offspring”—so that we might understand that Abraham’s offspring according to Isaac belongs, because of Christ, to the children of God, who are Christ’s body and members, that is, the one, true, genuine, Catholic Church, holding the godly faith—not the faith that works through pride or fear, but the faith that works through love (Gal. 5:6).

Nevertheless, when Abraham sent away the children of his concubines from his son Isaac, he gave them certain gifts, so that they would not be left entirely empty-handed, though not so that they would be made heirs.

For thus we read: “Abraham gave all that he possessed to his son Isaac; but to the sons of his concubines Abraham gave gifts, and he sent them away from his son Isaac” (Gen. 25:5–6).

Therefore, if we are children of the free Jerusalem, let us understand that the gifts of the disinherited are one thing and those of the heirs another. For these are the heirs to whom it is said: “You did not receive the spirit of slavery again for fear, but you received the Spirit of adoption as sons, in whom we cry, ‘Abba, Father’” (Rom. 8:14–17).

[Note: In this passage and the following one, the printed editions read “divided.” The manuscripts consistently read “sent away,” in accordance with the Greek Septuagint of Genesis 25:6, καὶ ἐξαπέστειλεν αὐτούς (“and he sent them away”). The Hebrew verb means “he sent out.”]

## CHAPTER XXIX

26. The eternal reward of Christ’s poor in patience

Let us therefore cry out in the spirit of love; and until we come to the inheritance in which we shall remain forever, let us endure through free love, not servile fear.

[Note: Nearly all manuscripts read “enduring”; in some, the words are punctuated as follows: “not in servile fear. Enduring, let us cry out,” and so forth. In the printed editions, with the same punctuation, the reading is “Patiently,” and so forth.]

Let us cry out as long as we are poor, until we are enriched by that inheritance. For we have received great pledges from it: in order to enrich us, Christ became poor; and, when he had been exalted to heavenly riches, the Holy Spirit was sent to inspire holy desires in our hearts.

The patience of these poor—still believing and not yet contemplating; still hoping and not yet possessing; still sighing with desire and not yet reigning in happiness; still hungering and thirsting and not yet satisfied—this patience of the poor will not perish forever (Ps. 9:19).

This is not because patience will exist there, where there will be nothing to endure; rather, “it will not perish” is said because it will not be fruitless. It will have an eternal fruit, and for that reason it will not perish forever.

For one who labors in vain, when the hope for which he labored has deceived him, rightly says, “I have lost so much labor.” But whoever reaches the promises of his labor says joyfully, “I have not lost my labor.”

Labor is therefore said not to have perished, not because it remains forever, but because it was not poured out in vain.

So too the patience of Christ’s poor—who are to be enriched as Christ’s heirs—will not perish forever. This is not because we shall also be commanded to endure patiently there, but because, in return for what we patiently endured here, we shall enjoy eternal blessedness.

The one who grants temporal patience to the will will not bring an end to everlasting happiness, because both gifts are bestowed upon the love that has been given.

# SERMONS ON THE CREED. ON CHRISTIAN DISCIPLINE. ON THE NEW SONG. ON WEDNESDAY. ON THE CATACLYSM. ON THE TIME OF THE BARBARIANS. ON THE BENEFIT OF FASTING. ON THE DESTRUCTION OF THE CITY

## [SERMONS ON THE CREED]

[Col. 0625]

## Editorial Notice on the Sermons on the Creed for Catechumens

These four sermons were formerly published together in volume nine and, in the old manuscript codices as well as in the printed editions, are called four books on the Creed and attributed to Augustine.

The first sermon certainly resembles Augustine in every respect; the other three do not. In these three, the style of speech is uncultivated and low, lacking sufficient intellectual force and dignity, as can be seen in the second sermon, chapter 2, where we read: “We too have our spiritual charioteer, the holy prophet Elijah, who, mounted upon a fiery chariot, ran so far that he might seize the boundaries of heaven.”

Scriptural passages are sometimes cited with unusual wording and explained in a manner and with a meaning that we do not dare attribute to Augustine, as in the same sermon, chapter 5, sections 13 and 14.

Moreover, we suspect that this sermon was delivered during the time of the Vandal persecution, after Augustine had already died, when the Arians were attempting by every means to draw Catholics away from the faith, through benefits no less than through injuries. We suspect this from the words at its conclusion: “Let the Arian heretic not insult the Church. He is a wolf; recognize him. He is a serpent; crush his heads. He flatters, but he deceives. He promises much, but he cheats,” and so forth.

In the third and fourth sermons, there are also many and weighty reasons for doubt. Possidius, in the *Index*, chapter 10, lists three treatises on the Creed; but these are found in the preceding volume of the *Sermons*, numbers 212, 213, and following.

At the end of volume nine of the edition prepared by the Louvain editors, fourteen treatises are likewise included, which, with only a few exceptions, we regard as doubtful and spurious. Some of them have been relegated to the Appendix, while others are printed here in their proper place in smaller type.

Among them is the sermon on Wednesday, or “On the Cultivation of the Lord’s Field,” in which, in chapter 3, the passage from Acts 1:18 is cited, and in chapter 6 the passage from John 6:51, neither quite accurately. Moreover, in chapter 7 the Vandal persecution seems to be mentioned.

There is also the sermon on the Cataclysm, in which chapter 2 says that through baptism the body was restored to the condition of the first man before sin.

There is also the sermon on the Time of the Barbarians, which, especially in chapter 4, contains several things less consistent with the sacred history of the Bible, as well as an exhortation at the end to strengthen Catholics against the persecution of the Arians.

The style of these three sermons is certainly equally crude, low, and wholly un-Augustinian.

Finally, both these sermons and the three others on the Creed mentioned above seem to have the same author—perhaps one of Augustine’s disciples, who sometimes presents Augustine’s opinions without mentioning the holy Doctor’s name. An example is the statement in the sermon on the Cataclysm, chapter 3: “Take away the word, and what is water except water? The word is added to the element, and it becomes a sacrament.” This was evidently drawn from *Tractate 80 on John*, section 3.

We also hesitated somewhat over the sermon on the New Song, and only with some reluctance allowed it to be printed again under the name of Augustine, which it has borne from ancient times.

In chapter 3 it contains several statements taken from the sermon that follows shortly afterward, “On the Benefit of Fasting,” chapter 3, namely: “If you were sitting on an animal that wanted, by plunging about, to throw you down,” and so forth. At its conclusion the preacher says to those about to be baptized: “Our reward is that, in that holy font, you help us with your prayers.” The author of the immediately following sermon similarly asks those about to be baptized: “As our reward, pray for us in that most holy font.”

[Col. 0627]

# Sermon of Saint Aurelius Augustine, Bishop of Hippo, on the Creed, for Catechumens

[Note: In earlier editions this was called “Book One,” in volume 9.]

[Note: The sermons on the Creed were corrected against the manuscript of the abbey of Saint Benignus at Dijon, approximately eight hundred years old; against the Gemmeticensis manuscript; against the manuscript of the church at Laon; against the manuscript of the Fathers of the Fulian monastery of Saint Bernard at Paris; and against the editions of Erasmus and Louvain. The first sermon was also found in the manuscript of Saint Albinus at Angers, eight hundred years old; the other three were not found there.]

[Note: We also compared all the editions mentioned at the beginning of the *Retractations* and the *Confessions*, volume 1. M.]

(C, G, S)

## CHAPTER I

1. The Creed is the rule of faith. The Creed is collected from the Scriptures. Almighty God. Little children are breathed upon and exorcized

Receive, children, the rule of faith, which is called the Creed. And when you have received it, write it in your heart, and say it every day to yourselves: before you sleep, before you go out, fortify yourselves with your Creed.

No one writes the Creed so that it may be read. Rather, so that it may be recited, lest forgetfulness perhaps erase what diligence has handed down, let your memory be your book.

What you are about to hear, you will believe; and what you believe, you will also return with your tongue. For the Apostle says: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. 10:10).

This, then, is the Creed that you will recite and return. These words that you have heard are scattered throughout the divine Scriptures, but they have been gathered from there and brought together into one statement, so that the memory of slow-witted people would not be burdened, and so that every person might be able to say and retain what he believes.

Have you only now heard that God is almighty? But you are beginning to have him as Father when you have been born through the Church as mother.

2. Therefore you have already received it, meditated upon it, and retained it through meditation, so that you may say: “I believe in God the Father almighty.”

God is almighty; and although he is almighty, he cannot die, he cannot be deceived, he cannot lie, and, as the Apostle says, he cannot deny himself (2 Tim. 2:13).

How many things he cannot do, and yet he is almighty! Indeed, he is almighty precisely because he cannot do these things. For if he could die, he would not be almighty; if he could lie, be deceived, deceive, or act unjustly, he would not be almighty. If such things existed in him, he would not have been worthy to be almighty.

Our Father, absolutely almighty, cannot sin. He does whatever he wills; this is omnipotence. He does whatever he wills rightly and justly; whatever is done wrongly, he does not will.

No one resists the Almighty so as to prevent him from doing what he wills.

He made heaven and earth, the sea and all that is in them, things invisible and visible: invisible things such as the Thrones, Dominions, Principalities, Powers, Archangels, and Angels in heaven—if we live well, they are our fellow citizens.

In heaven he made visible things: the sun, moon, and stars. He adorned the earth with its terrestrial animals; he filled the air with winged creatures, the earth with walking and creeping creatures, and the sea with swimming creatures. He filled everything with its proper creatures.

He also made the human being according to his image and likeness in the mind. For the image of God is there; and therefore the mind itself cannot be grasped even by itself, since the image of God is there.

We were made for the purpose of ruling over the other creatures. But through sin we fell in the first human being, and all came into the inheritance of death. We became lowly mortals, filled with fears and errors. This was the fitting consequence of sin, together with whose guilt every human being is born (Gen. 1–3).

Therefore, as you saw today and as you know, little children are breathed upon and exorcized, so that the hostile power of the devil—which deceived the human being in order to possess human beings—may be driven away from them.

It is not God’s creature in the infants, then, that is exorcized or breathed upon, but the one under whom are all who are born with sin; for he is the prince of sinners.

And consequently, because one who fell cast everyone into death, one without sin was sent to lead all who believe in him into life, freeing them from sin.

## CHAPTER II
### 3. That the Son of God, our Lord, is truly God and omnipotent

The Father and the Son are not two gods, but one God. The Son, omnipotent and equal, was begotten by the Father. Therefore we believe also in his Son, that is, in the only Son of God the almighty Father, our Lord. When you hear “the only Son of God,” acknowledge that he is God. For the only Son of God could not be non-God. What he is, that he begot—even though he is not the one whom he begot. If he is truly a Son, then he is what the Father is; if he is not what the Father is, he is not a true Son.

Consider mortal and earthly creatures: whatever each thing is, that it generates. A human being does not generate an ox; a sheep does not generate a dog; nor does a dog generate a sheep. [Col. 0629] Whatever the thing that generates is, that is what it generates. Hold firmly, steadfastly, faithfully, therefore, that God the Father begot what he himself is: the omnipotent one. These mortal creatures generate through corruption. Does God generate in this way? A mortal generates what is mortal; an immortal generates what is immortal; a corruptible being generates a corruptible being, an incorruptible being an incorruptible being; a corruptible being generates corruptibly, an incorruptible being incorruptibly—so completely is the offspring what the begetter is, that one begets one, and therefore an only one.

You know that when I recited the Creed to you I said it in this way, and this is how you ought to believe: “We believe in God the almighty Father, and in Jesus Christ, his only Son.” Now, when he is called “only,” believe him omnipotent.

[Note: Manuscripts read: “When he is called only, believe him omnipotent.” The printed editions read: “And when he is called only, believe him omnipotent.”]

For God the Father does not do what he wills while God the Son does not do what he wills. The Father and the Son have one will, because they have one nature. Nor can the Son’s will be separated in any degree from the Father’s will. God and God: both are one God. Omnipotent and omnipotent: both are one omnipotent.

### 4.

We do not introduce two gods, as some do when they say: “God the Father and God the Son—but God the Father is greater, and God the Son lesser.” What are they both, then? Two gods? You are ashamed to say it; be ashamed to believe it. You call the Father Lord God, and the Son Lord God; yet the Son himself says, “No one can serve two masters” (Matthew 6:24).

Will we be in his household in such a way that, just as in a great house where there is a master and he has a son, we should say, “The greater Lord, the lesser Lord”? Reject such a thought. If you entertain such things in your heart, you set up idols in your one soul. Drive them out completely.

Believe first; afterward understand. If God grants someone that, after believing, he quickly understands, that is God’s gift, not the achievement of human frailty. Nevertheless, if you do not yet understand, believe: God the Father is one God; Christ, the Son of God, is God. What are they both? One God.

And how is it said that both are one God? How? Are you astonished? In the Acts of the Apostles it says, “The company of believers was of one heart and one soul” (Acts 4:32). There were many souls, but faith had made them one. There were many thousands of souls; they loved one another, and many became one. They loved God in the fire of charity, and from multiplicity they came to the unity of beauty.

If charity made one soul out of so many souls, what sort of charity is there with God, where there is no difference but complete equality? If such great charity could exist on earth and among human beings that it made one soul out of so many souls, where the Father was always inseparable from the Son and the Son from the Father, could both of them be anything other than one God?

Those souls, however, could be called both many souls and one soul. But God, where there is ineffable and supreme union, can be called one God, not two gods.

### 5.

The Father does what he wills; the Son does what he wills. Do not suppose that the Father is omnipotent and the Son is not omnipotent. That is an error: erase it from yourselves; let it not cling to your memory or be swallowed into your faith. And if perhaps one of you has swallowed it, let him vomit it out.

The Father is omnipotent; the Son is omnipotent. If the omnipotent did not beget [Col. 0630] the omnipotent, he did not beget a true son.

What are we saying, brothers, if the greater Father begot a lesser son? What did I say—“begot”?

[Note: The manuscripts read “is said.”]

A greater human being does indeed generate a lesser son; that is true. But the father grows old, while the son grows, and by growing reaches the form of his father. The Son of God, if he does not grow—for God cannot grow old—was born perfect.

[Note: According to Erasmus, Lyon, Venice, and Louvain, the text reads, “The Son of God does not grow,” with *si* omitted. M.] Born perfect, then, if he does not grow, he did not remain lesser; he is equal.

To show you that the omnipotent was born from the omnipotent, listen to him who is the Truth. What the Truth says about himself is true. What does the Truth say? What does the Son, who is the Truth, say? “Whatever the Father does, the Son does likewise” (John 5:19).

The Son is omnipotent, doing everything he wills. For if the Father does some things that the Son does not do, the Son spoke falsely when he said, “Whatever the Father does, the Son does likewise.” But because the Son spoke truly, believe: “Whatever the Father does, the Son does likewise.” And by believing this, you have believed in the omnipotent Son.

Although you did not say this particular word in the Creed, this is what you expressed when you believed in him as the only God. Does the Father have anything that the Son does not have? The blasphemous Arian heretics say this, not I.

But what do I say? If the Father has something that the Son does not have, then the Son is lying when he says, “Everything that the Father has is mine” (John 16:15). There are many and innumerable testimonies proving that the Son is the true Son of God the Father.

[Note: The manuscripts read “God” rather than “the Son of God.”]

The Father, God, truly begot the Son, God; and the Father and the Son are one God.

## CHAPTER III

### 6. The Son of God’s human birth from a virgin. His passion under Pontius Pilate. Christ’s eternal birth from the Father. Why Christ chose the punishment of the cross. The reward of patience is not temporal in the present but eternal in the future age

But let us see what this only Son of God the almighty Father did for us and what he suffered for us.

[Note: The Louvain edition reads “God of God the almighty Father,” and so forth. The word “God” is absent from the other printed editions and the manuscripts.]

He was born of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary. That great God, equal to the Father, was born humbly of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary, thereby to heal the proud. A human being exalted himself and fell; God humbled himself and raised him up.

What is Christ’s humility? God extended his hand to fallen humanity. We fell; he descended. We lay prostrate; he bent down. Let us grasp his hand and rise, so that we do not fall into punishment.

His bending down, then, is this: he was born of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary. And this human birth was both humble and exalted. Why humble? Because he was born human from human beings. Why exalted? Because he was born of a virgin. The virgin conceived; the virgin gave birth; and after giving birth she remained a virgin.

### 7.

What follows? “He suffered under Pontius Pilate.” Pontius Pilate was exercising the office of governor and was himself the judge when Christ suffered. The mention of the judge marks the time when he suffered: under Pontius Pilate; when he suffered, was crucified, died,

[Note: The word “died,” here and in the following passage, is absent from the manuscripts.]

and was buried.

[Col. 0631]

Who? What? For whom?

Who? The only Son of God, our Lord. What? Crucified, dead, and buried. For whom? For the ungodly and sinners.

Great condescension! Great grace! “What shall I render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to me?” (Psalm 115:12).

### 8.

He was born before all times, born before all ages. Born before—before what, when there is no “before”? Do not imagine any time before Christ’s birth from the Father; I am speaking of that birth by which he is the only Son of God the omnipotent, our Lord. I am speaking first of that birth.

Do not imagine the beginning of time in this birth. Do not imagine any interval of eternity in which the Father existed and the Son did not. From when there is a Father, there is a Son. And what does “from when” mean where there is no beginning? Therefore the Father is always without beginning, and the Son is always without beginning.

“And how,” you will say, “was he born if he has no beginning?” He is coeternal with the eternal. There was never a time when the Father existed and the Son did not, and yet the Son was begotten by the Father.

Where can any likeness be found? We are among earthly things, among visible creation. Let earth provide me with a likeness: it cannot. Let the element of water provide me with some likeness: it has none. Let some animal provide me with a likeness: it cannot do so either. An animal does generate, and both the one that generates and the one generated exist; but the father is first, and afterward the son is born.

Let us find something coeval, and believe in what is coeternal. If we can find a father coeval with his son and a son coeval with his father, let us believe that God the Father is coeval with his Son and God the Son coeternal with his Father. On earth we can find something coeval; we cannot find anything coeternal. Let us contemplate what is coeval and believe in what is coeternal.

Perhaps someone will challenge you and say: “When can a father be found coeval with his son, or a son coeval with his father?

[Note: The manuscripts read: “He will make you attentive. Perhaps someone says.”] For the father to generate, he is older in age; for the son to be born, he comes later in age. How, then, can this father be coeval with his son, or the son with his father?”

Let fire the father and radiance the son come before you: behold, we have found something coeval. From the moment fire begins to exist, it immediately generates radiance. Fire does not precede radiance, nor does radiance follow fire.

And if we ask which generates which—fire radiance, or radiance fire—your natural understanding and the wisdom implanted in your minds immediately respond, and you all cry out: “Fire generates radiance, not radiance fire.”

Behold a father beginning; behold a son beginning at the same time, neither preceding nor following. Behold, then, a father beginning and a son beginning simultaneously. If I have shown you a father beginning and a son beginning at the same time, believe in the Father who does not begin and, with him, in the Son who also does not begin: the one eternal, the other coeternal.

If you are making progress, you understand. Make every effort to progress. You must be born, but you must also grow, because no one begins in a perfected state. The Son of God was permitted to be born perfect, because he was born outside time, coeternal with the Father, preceding all things—not in age but in eternity.

This one, therefore, born coeternal with the Father, is the one of whose generation the prophet said, “Who shall declare his generation?” (Isaiah 53:8). Born from the Father outside time, he was born from a [Col. 0632] virgin in the fullness of time.

Times had preceded this birth. He was born at the appropriate time, when he willed and when he knew; for he was not born unwillingly. None of us is born because he wills it, and none of us dies when he wills it. He was born when he willed; he died when he willed. As he willed, he was born of a virgin; as he willed, he died on the cross.

He did whatever he willed, because he was human in such a way that God was hidden. God was the one who assumed; humanity was what was assumed: one Christ, God and human.

### 9.

What shall I say about his cross? What shall I say? He chose the most extreme kind of death, so that his martyrs would fear no kind of death. He displayed teaching in the human being and demonstrated an example of patience on the cross.

There was the work, because he was crucified; the cross was the example of the work; the resurrection was the reward of the work. On the cross he showed us what we ought to endure; in the resurrection he showed us what we ought to hope for.

Just as the supreme director of the contest, he said: “Do it and receive; perform the work and receive the reward; compete in the contest and you will be crowned.”

What is the work? Obedience. What is the reward? Resurrection without death. Why did I add “without death”? Because Lazarus rose and died; Christ rose and now does not die: “Death no longer rules over him” (Romans 6:9).

### 10.

Scripture says: “You have heard of the patience of Job, and you have seen the end of the Lord” (James 5:11). When we read how much Job endured, we are horrified, terrified, and tremble.

[Note: According to Erasmus, the Lyon edition, and the Venetian edition, the text should read: “When we read how much Job endured, we are horrified, terrified, and tremble.” According to the Louvain edition: “When we read how much Job endured, we are horrified, terrified, and tremble.”]

And what did he receive? Twice as much as he had lost.

Therefore, let no one endure patiently for the sake of temporal rewards and say to himself: “I will tolerate this loss; God will give me twice as many children.” Job received everything else doubled, but he fathered as many children as he had buried.

Are they not therefore doubled? They truly are doubled, because the others were alive. Let no one say, “I will endure evils, and God will repay me as he repaid Job,” so that what is no longer patience may become greed.

For if that holy man had not possessed patience and had not bravely endured what befell him, where would he have obtained the testimony that the Lord gave him? The Lord says: “Have you noticed my servant Job? For there is none like him on earth: a blameless man, a true worshiper of God.”

What a testimony, brothers, did this holy man merit from the Lord! Yet an evil woman tried to deceive him by her persuasion. She too represented that serpent who, just as he deceived the first human being made by God in paradise (Genesis 3:1–6), so now thought he could deceive a man pleasing to God by suggesting blasphemy.

How much did he suffer, brothers! Who could endure so much in his possessions, in his house, in his children, in his flesh, and even in the wife who had remained to tempt him? Yet the devil would long ago have taken away even the woman who remained, had he not kept her as his helper; for he had defeated the first man through Eve and had preserved Eve.

How much, then, did he suffer! He lost everything he possessed; his house fell—if only it had been alone! It crushed his children also. And because patience held a great place [Col. 0633] in him, listen to what he replied:

“The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away; as it pleased the Lord, so it has happened. Blessed be the name of the Lord.”

He took away what he had given. Did the giver perish? He took away what he had given, as though Job were saying: “Let him take everything away; let him leave me naked, provided that he preserves himself for me. For what shall I lack if I have God? Or what do other things profit me if I do not have God?”

Then the affliction reached his flesh. He was struck with a wound from head to foot; he streamed with corruption and swarmed with worms, yet he showed himself immovable in his God and fixed himself upon him.

The woman—an ally of the devil, not a comforter of her husband—wanted to persuade him to blaspheme: “How long,” she said, “will you endure these and these sufferings? Say some word against the Lord and die.”

Therefore, because Job had been humbled, he was to be exalted. The Lord did this to show it to human beings; for he himself had reserved greater things for his servant in heaven. Thus he exalted the humbled Job and humbled the exalted devil, “because he humbles one and exalts another” (Psalm 75:8).

But when you suffer some such tribulations, dearest brothers, do not expect your reward here. For example, if you suffer some losses, do not say with that intention, “The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away; as it pleased the Lord, so it has happened. Blessed be the name of the Lord,” so that you may receive twice as much.

Let patience praise God, not greed. If you seek to receive double what you lost and therefore praise God, you praise him out of desire, not out of charity. Do not bring forward the example of that holy man; you are deceiving yourself.

When Job endured everything, he was not hoping for double. This can be observed both in his first confession, when he suffered his losses and buried his children, and in his second, when he was already enduring the torment of wounds in his flesh.

These are the words of his first confession: “The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away; as it pleased the Lord, so it has happened. Blessed be the name of the Lord.”

He could have said: “The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away; the one who took away can give again, and he can restore more than he took.” He did not say this. Instead, he said, “As it pleased the Lord, so it has happened.” What pleases the good Lord should please me; what pleases the physician should not displease the sick person; what pleases the master should not displease the servant subject to him.

Hear another confession of his. He said to his wife: “You speak as one of the foolish women speaks. If we have received good things from the hand of the Lord, why should we not endure evils?” (Job 1–2).

He did not add what would have been true had he said it: “The Lord is able to restore my flesh to its former state and to multiply what he has taken from us.” He did not seem to have endured these things in hope of that; he did not say it, and he did not hope for it.

But so that we might be instructed, the Lord granted this to a man who was not hoping for it, in order that we might learn that God was with him. For if those things had not also been restored to him, we could scarcely have seen his hidden crown.

And therefore what does divine Scripture say when exhorting us to patience and hope for future things, not to a present reward? “You have heard of the patience of Job, and you have seen the end of the Lord.”

Why “the patience of Job,” and not “you have seen the end of Job”? You would open your mouth for the double reward and say: “Thanks be to God; I will endure, and I will receive twice as much as Job.”

It says: “The patience of Job, the end of the Lord.” We know the patience of Job, and [Col. 0634] we know the end of the Lord.

What is the end of the Lord? “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Psalm 22:2). These are the words of the Lord hanging on the wood. It was as though he had abandoned him with respect to present happiness, but he did not abandon him with respect to eternal immortality. That is the end of the Lord.

The Jews seize him; the Jews mock him; the Jews bind him; the Jews crown him with thorns; they dishonor him with spittle; they scourge him; they overwhelm him with insults; they hang him on the wood; they pierce him with a spear; finally, they bury him. He seems to have been abandoned.

But abandoned to whom? To those who were mocking him. Therefore, have patience so that you may rise and not die—that is, so that you may never die, as Christ does. For this is how we read: “Christ, rising from the dead, dies no more” (Romans 6:9).

## CHAPTER IV

### 11. What it means to sit at the right hand of the Father. The Father’s right hand is blessedness. He ascended into heaven: believe it. He sits at the right hand of the Father: believe it

To sit means, understand, to dwell. Thus we say of some person, “He dwelt in that country for three years.” Scripture also says that someone sat in a city for a certain length of time (1 Kings 2:38, according to the Septuagint). Did he sit and never rise? This is why human dwellings are called “seats.” When there are seats, does one always remain seated? Is there no rising, walking, or lying down? And yet they are called seats.

Believe, then, that Christ dwells at the right hand of God the Father: he is there. Let your heart not say to you, “What is he doing?” Do not seek to discover what you are not permitted to discover. He is there; that is enough for you.

He is blessed; and “the Father’s right hand,” which is called blessedness, is the very name of that blessedness. For if we understand it carnally, since he sits at the Father’s right hand, the Father will be at the left. Is it right to arrange them in this way—to place the Son at the right and the Father at the left? There everything is right, because there is no misery.

### 12. From there he will come to judge the living and the dead

The living: those who will remain; the dead: those who have gone before. It can also be understood in this way: the living are the righteous; the dead are the unrighteous. For he judges both, repaying each according to his deserts.

At the judgment he will say to the righteous: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.” Prepare yourselves for this; hope for this; live for this; live in this way; believe for this purpose; be baptized for this purpose, so that it may be said to you: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.”

And what will he say to those on the left? “Go into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matthew 25:34, 41).

Thus the living and the dead will be judged by Christ. Christ’s first birth was spoken of as outside time; another birth of Christ, from a virgin, was spoken of in the fullness of time; Christ’s passion was spoken of; Christ’s judgment was spoken of.

Everything that had to be said about Christ, the only Son of God, our Lord, has been said. But the Trinity has not yet been fully explained.

## CHAPTER V

### 13. That the Holy Spirit is God

The Creed continues: “And in the Holy Spirit.”

This Trinity is one God, one nature, one substance, one power, supreme equality, no division, no difference, [Col. 0635] perpetual charity.

Do you wish to know that the Holy Spirit is God? Be baptized, and you will be his temple. The Apostle says: “Do you not know that your bodies are the temple of the Holy Spirit within you, whom you have from God?” (1 Corinthians 6:19).

God has a temple. For King and prophet Solomon was also commanded to build a temple for God. If he had built a temple for the sun alone, or the moon, or some star, or some angel, would God not have condemned him? Since he built a temple for God, he showed that he worshiped God.

And from what did he build it? From wood and stones, because God deigned, through his servant, to make for himself a house on earth where he might be entreated and remembered.

[Note: Several manuscripts read “where he might dwell.”]

Thus blessed Stephen says: “Solomon built him a house, but the Most High does not dwell in temples made by hands” (Acts 7:47–48).

If, then, our bodies are the temple of the Holy Spirit, what kind of God is the one who built a temple for the Holy Spirit? God. For if our bodies are the temple of the Holy Spirit, the one who built a temple for the Holy Spirit is the one who also built our bodies.

Listen to the Apostle: “God has arranged the body, giving greater honor to the part that lacked it” (1 Corinthians 12:24), when he was speaking of the different members, so that there might be no division in the body.

God created our body. God created grass; who created our body? How do we prove that God creates grass? The one who clothes it also creates it. Read the Gospel: “If then God so clothes the grass of the field, which is here today and tomorrow is thrown into the furnace” (Matthew 6:30).

Therefore, the one who clothes it creates it. And the Apostle says: “Foolish one, what you sow is not made alive unless it dies”; and, “What you sow is not the body that is to be, but a bare grain, perhaps of wheat or one of the other kinds. But God gives it a body as he wills, and to each of the seeds its own body” (1 Corinthians 15:36–38).

If, then, God builds our bodies; if God builds our members; and if our bodies are the temple of the Holy Spirit, do not doubt that the Holy Spirit is God. And do not add a third God, as though he were separate, because the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God. Believe this.

## CHAPTER VI

### 14. On the holy Church

After commending the Trinity, the Creed continues with the holy Church. God and his temple have been demonstrated. “The temple of God is holy,” the Apostle says, “and you are that temple” (1 Corinthians 3:17).

This is the holy Church, the one Church, the true Church, the catholic Church, fighting against all heresies. It can fight, but it cannot be conquered. All heresies have gone out from it, like useless branches cut from the vine; but it remains in its root, in its vine, in its charity. “The gates of hell will not prevail against it” (Matthew 16:18).

## CHAPTER VII

### 15. Even enormous sins are forgiven in Baptism, and venial sins in the Lord’s Prayer. Public penance is undertaken for enormous sins, not [Col. 0636] for trivial ones

“Forgiveness of sins.”

You possess the Creed perfectly within you when you are baptized. Let no one say, “I did that; perhaps it will not be forgiven me.” What did you do? How great was your deed? Name something enormous that you committed—something grave and horrifying, something that you shudder even to think about. Whatever you may have done, surely you did not kill Christ?

Nothing is worse than that deed, because nothing is better than Christ. How great a crime it is to kill Christ! Yet the Jews killed him, and afterward many believed in him and drank his blood. The sin they committed was forgiven them.

When you have been baptized, maintain a good life according to God’s commandments, so that you may preserve your Baptism to the end. I am not telling you that you will live here without sin; but there are venial sins, without which this life does not exist.

Baptism was instituted for all sins; prayer was instituted for the lesser sins without which we cannot be. What does the prayer contain? “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matthew 6:12).

We are washed once in Baptism; every day we are washed in prayer. But do not commit the sins for which it is necessary that you be separated from Christ’s body. May that never happen to you.

Those whom you see doing penance have committed crimes, adulteries, or some enormous deeds; that is why they do penance. For if their sins were minor, daily prayer would be sufficient to erase them.

## CHAPTER VIII

### 16. Sins are forgiven in three ways

Therefore, sins are forgiven in the Church in three ways: in Baptism, in prayer, and in the greater humility of penance.

[Note: The manuscripts read “in greater humility.” The printed editions read “in the humility of greater penance.”]

Yet God does not forgive sins except to the baptized. The sins he first forgives, he forgives only to the baptized. When? When they are baptized.

The sins that are afterward forgiven to those who pray and repent are forgiven by him to baptized people. For how can those who have not yet been born say, “Our Father”? As long as catechumens remain catechumens, all their sins remain upon them. If this is so with catechumens, how much more with pagans? How much more with heretics?

But we do not change the Baptism of heretics. Why? Because they possess Baptism as a deserter possesses his military mark. These people likewise possess Baptism; they possess it as the basis of their condemnation, not as the means of their crowning.

And yet, if the deserter himself, once corrected, should begin to serve again, would anyone dare to change his military mark?

## CHAPTER IX

### 17. On the resurrection of the flesh unto eternal life

We also believe in the resurrection of the flesh, which has already taken place in Christ, so that the body may also hope for what has already occurred in the Head.

Christ is the Head of the Church, and the Church is Christ’s body (Ephesians 5:23). Our Head has risen and ascended into heaven: where the Head is, there also are the members.

What kind of resurrection of the flesh? Perhaps someone might think it will be like Lazarus’s. So that you may know that it is not so, the Creed adds: “unto eternal life.”

May God regenerate you; may God preserve and protect you; may God lead you to himself, who is eternal life itself. Amen.

[Col. 0637]

[Note: Three other sermons on the Creed follow. They do not at all represent Augustine, to whom they were attributed in earlier editions, but rather an orator much inferior to him in style of expression, learning, and talent.]

# SERMON ON THE CREED TO THE CATECHUMENS

[Note: In other editions, “The Second Book,” in volume 9 of the earlier editions.]

*(C, G, S)*

## CHAPTER I

### 1. The rites celebrated concerning the catechumens. The sign of the cross. Examination and scrutiny. Weapons against the devil: the Creed and the Cross. The catechumens’ profession that they renounce the devil and his spectacles. The devil’s weapons: pleasure and fear. Our spiritual weapons: chaste fear of God and the faith of prayer

We have undertaken to explain to your Holiness the meaning of the sacraments, both those of the past night and those of the present holy Creed, by the gift of him who gives generously to all and does not reproach anyone (James 1:5). For he is rich toward all who call upon him (Romans 10:12).

He himself can assist our purpose, making your prayer acceptable on our behalf. Receive, then, you who desire the word of God with faith, as though it were suitable food from which the Lord may bring about your growth.

You have not yet been reborn through holy Baptism, but through the sign of the cross you have already been conceived in the womb of holy mother Church. Let this mother therefore first nourish with fitting food those whom she carries, so that after giving birth she may rejoice that she has received such children to nourish spiritually.

What is it, dearly beloved, that has been celebrated among you? What is it that was done concerning you this night and not during the preceding nights, when each of you was brought out from hidden places into the sight of the whole Church, and there, with your necks humbled that had previously been lifted up wrongly, with humility celebrated through sackcloth spread beneath your feet, an examination was carried out among you, and the proud devil was driven out from you while the humble Most High, Christ, was invoked over you?

You were all humble, and you humbly asked, praying, singing psalms, and saying: “Test me, Lord, and know my heart” (Psalm 139:23). He tested you; he examined you; he touched the hearts of his servants with his fear; he drove away the devil by his power; and he freed his household from the devil’s domination.

This act was not performed here one way for the poor and another way for the rich, one way for the master and another way for the servant, because there is one entrance into life for all (Wisdom 7:6).

[Note: The Louvain edition alone reads “was carried out.”] And if this is so for this fragile and fleeting life, how much more for that immortal and everlasting life?

### 2.

After the household of the Redeemer had been purified and had sung the song of salvation, it received the remedy of the Creed against the serpent’s venom.

[Note: The Louvain edition adds “ancient”: “against the venom of the ancient serpent.”]

Thus, if the adversary, the devil, should again wish to lie in wait, the redeemed person will know that he must confront him with the sacrament of the Creed and the banner of the cross. Armed with such weapons, the Christian will easily conquer the wicked devil, who had previously triumphed over him in his oppression.

From what else has the devil become our adversary except from this: he sees free people whom he had previously held captive; he sees healthy those whom he had struck down and wounded with his arrows; he sees those whom he had stripped naked by offering them iniquity clothed again in immortality; his traps have been shattered, and we have been rescued: “Our help is in the name of the Lord” (Psalm 124:7–8).

If our help is in his name, let us renounce the devil, his spectacles, and his angels. You heard this, and you yourselves professed it: that you renounce the devil, his spectacles, and his angels.

See, dearly beloved, that you carry this profession of yours before the heavenly court. The names of those making the profession are entered in the book of life, not by any human being but by a higher power from heaven.

Now excellent recruits of God, strong soldiers of Christ, while you receive the weapons of the sacraments, you declare war against the devil. While [Col. 0638] you renounce his works, you provoke his fury against you all the more intensely.

But let Christ’s soldier not be afraid. You will put on Christ himself, so that through him you may swiftly overcome the adversary, the devil.

With what weapons does he fight? With seductive and deceitful ones. There are two very powerful kinds of weapons of his, against which every soldier of Christ who wishes to triumph and overcome the devil’s power must stand watchfully and bravely.

What are these two kinds of weapons? Pleasure and fear. He captures some by pleasure and breaks others by fear.

Let our battle line also be strengthened; let spiritual weapons be brought forth. Against the devil’s fear, let there be the chaste fear of the Lord, enduring forever and ever (Psalm 19:10). Against the pleasure of the most shameful delight, let the faith of prayer not be lacking.

And what should a Christian fear when he is taught to pray, presume, and trust in such a way as to say: “The Lord is my helper, and I will look down upon my enemies” (Psalm 118:7)?

Nevertheless, know, dearly beloved, that the adversary captures more people through pleasure than through fear. Why else does he set before them every day the trap of spectacles, the madness of contests, and shameful pleasures, except to capture through these delights those whom he had lost, and to rejoice that he has found again those whom he had destroyed?

## CHAPTER II

### 3. The spectacles of the circus are to be avoided; the Church offers other spectacles that can be seen there and are salutary. He deters from the theater of the Scandalist. The bloody contests of the amphitheater. Hunters competing with bears

Why should we go through many things?

[Note: The printed editions here add “must.”]

You must be briefly admonished about what you ought to despise and what you ought to love.

Flee, dearly beloved, the spectacles; flee the devil’s most shameful cages, lest the bonds of the evil one hold you. But if the mind is to be entertained and you take pleasure in watching, holy mother Church presents you with venerable and salutary spectacles. They entertain your minds with their delight, and in you they do not corrupt but preserve the faith.

Is someone a lover of the circus? What delights him in the circus? Seeing charioteers competing,

[Note: The Louvain edition has in the margin: “Alternatively, racing.”]

people panting with insane excitement, one swift driver overtaking another and breaking his opponent’s horse.

This is the whole delight: to shout because the one whom the devil has conquered has won; to exult and jeer because the opposing side has lost its horse, while the person who delights in such a spectacle has already lost his own mind to vanity.

Look instead at our holy, healthy, and most delightful spectacles. Look in the book of the Acts of the Apostles at the man lame from his mother’s womb, who had never walked, whom Peter made able to run. See suddenly made healthy the one whom you had previously seen as infirm (Acts 3:2–8).

And if there is health of mind in you, if the reason of justice shines in you, together with the delight of salvation, see what you ought to hope for and where you ought to shout: there, where healthy horses are broken, or here, where broken human beings are saved?

But if that procession delights you—the appearance of the horses,

[Note: The manuscripts read “the appearances of the horses.”]

the arrangement of the chariots, the adornment, and the charioteer standing above and guiding the horses, wishing to win—if this procession, as I said, delights you, then the one who commanded you to renounce the devil’s spectacles has not denied you this either.

We too have our spiritual charioteer, the holy prophet Elijah, who, placed upon a fiery chariot, ran so far that he seized the boundaries of heaven (2 Kings 2:11).

And if you wish to see the adversaries whom true virtue conquered, whom he passed in flight, and from whose victory he received the palm of heavenly exaltation: [Col. 0639] “He cast Pharaoh’s chariots and all his army into the sea” (Exodus 15:4).

## 4. Another perhaps should be warned, if he is a lover of the theater, what he ought to flee and in what he ought to delight, so that he does not lose his desire to watch spectacles but changes it. In the theaters there is moral pollution: learning shameful things, hearing dishonorable things, seeing things that bring destruction. But with the Lord’s help let us firmly drive these things from your hearts. Let us compare each thing with its counterpart.

There spectators gaze upon some fictitious god, Jupiter, committing adultery and hurling thunderbolts; here we behold the true God, Christ, teaching chastity, destroying impurity, and proclaiming what brings salvation. There it is invented that Jupiter has Juno as both sister and wife; here we proclaim holy Mary, at once mother and virgin. There amazement is imposed upon the sight by the spectacle, familiar through use, of a man walking on a rope; here there is a great miracle: Peter crossing the sea on foot (Matt. XIV, 29). There chastity is violated through mimed indecency; here lust is restrained by the chaste Susanna and the chaste Joseph (Gen. XXXIX and Dan. XIII); death is despised, God is loved, and chastity is exalted.

There the chorus and the pantomime’s song entice the hearing but conquer healthy feeling. And what could be compared with our song, in which the one who loves and sings says: “Sinners have told me of their delights, but not as your law has, O Lord; all your commandments are truth” (Ps. CXVIII, 85–86)? For there everything is fabricated by vanity.

Who there, perhaps, would not admire the skill of the stage performers, seeing little children playing in the arena and presenting various stories? But look at the games of our children. In Rebecca’s womb two children struggle; as the elder emerged, the hand of the younger, thrust out from the womb, seized the elder’s heel (Gen. XXV, 22, 25). In their struggle the figure of a great sacrament was displayed: the younger was to supplant the elder and afterward take away his primacy and blessing. In these little ones, as though playing and, as I have said, presenting a great sacrament, the Jews—rejected—are shown in Esau, while Christians—predestined—appear in Jacob. For that one little Jacob, chattering in this way, represented in himself the many predestined, even infants, who are received from the womb of their mother into the hands of the faithful—not so that they are shaken off and left hanging in the air, but so that, reborn, they may live in heaven.

Let the mind take delight, then, in these entertainments; let the Christian soul be nourished by them. Holding fast to this sobriety of mind, let it flee the drunkenness of the devil.

## 5. Nor should the combats of the amphitheater seduce or draw the Christian along. Indeed, people run there with greater eagerness the longer the spectacle is delayed. But even there, what is not dangerous thrust before the eyes, what is not bloody? There, as the most blessed Cyprian says, “a culpable desire condemns men without any crime to the wild beasts” (Cyprian, *Epistle 2 to Donatus*).

Therefore, beloved, do not let that cruel spectacle invite you to watch two hunters contending with nine bears; rather, let it delight you to see one of our number, Daniel, overcome seven lions through prayer. Distinguish the spiritual combats, lover of such contests: see two guilty men guilty by their will [Note: [Col. 0639] Erasmus and the manuscripts: “by pleasure.”]; see one innocent and full of faith. See those men, for the sake of an earthly prize, offering their souls to beasts; see this man crying out in prayer: “Do not hand over to the beasts the souls that confess you” (Ps. LXXIII, 19).

In that spectacle the sponsor is saddened if the hunter escapes unharmed, after killing several beasts for him. In this spectacle of ours, the battle is fought without iron: Daniel is not injured, nor is the beast killed. Yet he conquers in such a way that the king marvels and is changed, the peoples are afraid, and the enemies perish (Dan. XIV, 30–42).

Our spectacle is marvelous—truly marvelous—in which God gives help, faith obtains strength, innocence fights, holiness conquers, and the victor receives such a reward that the one who wins receives it, while the one who grants it loses nothing.

Desire these spiritual gifts [Note: [Col. 0639] That is, spectacles.]; come eagerly to the church to behold and watch them in complete security. Withdraw the purpose of your heart from every carnal desire; entrust all your anxiety to God’s governance. Thus the adversary may be afraid, finding nothing of his own in you. When you reject him and renounce his pomps, after your freedom has been rescued from his snares, do not let that wicked one find you empty—the one whom we know even to desire to hold those who are not his own.

# CHAPTER III

## 6. God’s omnipotence proved from the creation of things out of nothing. The Trinity. The Son also is God, omnipotent, eternal, and equal to the Father.

“Believe faithfully in God the Father almighty.”

We believe in God almighty, who, while making all things, was himself not made. He is therefore almighty because he made whatever he made out of nothing. No material substance assisted him from which he might demonstrate the power of his craft; rather, as I have said, he created everything out of nothing.

For this is what it means to be almighty: that not only the structure itself, but also the material, is found to exist from him who had no beginning in order to exist; and that he who is everlasting created not something that he himself was, but created things that received their existence from him [Note: [Col. 0640] A perplexing passage, in which the Fuliensian codex omits *sed ut ab illo essent, jam accepisse* (“but that they had already received existence from him”).].

Everything that exists is from him; he, however, is from himself, since he was not made by anyone. Thus he made things that were made, without himself being made; he created a creature, without himself being created. He also established powers for that creature through different arrangements and suitable degrees.

Anyone—angel or human—may indeed be called powerful according to the power granted to him. But can anyone be called omnipotent? A person may be called king or emperor because he can do many things that he wishes; yet no one of sound judgment would dare call him omnipotent. If he wished to praise him in this way through flattery, he would begin by deceiving both that man and himself.

For how would he dare call omnipotent one whom he sees greatly desiring to live, yet ending his life when death follows? If he is omnipotent, let him not die; let him be excluded from death [Note: [Col. 0640] The manuscripts read: “let him not be excluded from death.”]. But if death will bring him to an end, death itself will show that he was not omnipotent.

No one, therefore, would dare call any creature—whether heavenly or earthly—omnipotent, except the Trinity alone: namely, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

## 7. For when we say that we believe in God the Father almighty, we do not, like the Arian heretics, deny that the Son is almighty, nor do we deny that the Holy Spirit is almighty. If you deny that the Son is almighty, you will also deny that the Father is almighty.

“But he is greater,” they say. “The Father is greater; the Son is lesser.”

That is true among human beings, true in all such matters—and you are confused about everything. Consider the divine nature; attend to God; think of the everlasting one. For you are being disturbed in vain.

If the Father is eternal, then certainly the Son is also eternal. For if there was a time when the Son was not the Son, there was also a time when the Father was not the Father. But if at some time the Father was not the Father, he was not omnipotent, since he lacked that which he afterward became when he became Father. If you give the Son a beginning, you also give a beginning to the Father. For the Father was called Father by the Son. If, however, he was always Father, then the Son was always Son.

And if the Father is God, the Son is also God; for nothing other than God could have proceeded from God. If the Father is God, then the Son is God; and if the Father is eternal, then the Son is eternal.
