He did not diminish in equality the Son whom neither age nor dignity preceded [Note: [Col. 0640] The manuscripts read *non enim* (“for not”). The edition of Erasmus likewise has this reading, and alone continues by diminishing equality.].

Hear what the Apostle says about God the Son: “Though he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be grasped” (Phil. II, 6). He did not seize it, because he possessed it by nature.

Thus the omnipotence of the Father is in the Son, and the omnipotence of the Son is in the Father, because the Father was never without the Son, nor the Son ever without the Father. We cannot explain that divine birth by which the Son proceeded from the Father, by which God was born from God—without beginning, without time, without a mother, without any frailty, without any diminution of himself. “Who shall declare his generation?” the prophet says (Isa. LIII, 8). And truly, who can comprehend or say how he was born who is always in the Father and never departs from the Father?

As I have said, we cannot worthily declare it. But we must prepare our hearts for the Son himself, so that by enlightening us and guiding us through faith he may bring us to the vision of his truth. Let us not remain in the darkness of our unbelief; let us not think of the Son as being other than what the Father is, lest the Son himself, not teaching but rebuking us, admonish us as he admonished Philip, saying: “Philip, whoever has seen me has seen the Father. Do you not recognize that I am in the Father and the Father is in me?” (John XIV, 9–10) [Note: [Col. 0641] Thus the manuscripts of better quality, in accordance with the Greek. The printed editions twice read *videt* (“sees”).]

Therefore, just as God was born from God, light from light, and day from day, so also the Almighty was born from the Almighty.

In our mortal birth, the one who is a father was at some time not a father, and the one who is a son is not always a son. For when a son, with the passage of time, loses his father, takes a wife, and begets offspring, he will no longer be called a son but will himself be called a father; and any father, before he has a son, will not be called a father. Thus something arises in time that did not previously exist.

Let us not, then, suppose that this is so in that substance of divinity, in that everlasting generation. There the Father does not die through decline, so that the Son may arrive at the Father’s dignity by growing; nor are there times there, since times themselves were made through him.

# CHAPTER IV

## 8. The same point confirmed against the Arians. The whole Trinity is God almighty. The Trinity is judge. The whole Trinity is omnipotent, immortal, and invisible. The idols of the heart.

In what respect, then, do you dare, heretic, to call the Son lesser, whom we confess to be equal? In age? There are no times there. In divinity? The Father is God, and the Son is God. In work? All things were made through the Son.

Scripture does indeed say that God made the world, as it is written in the book of Genesis: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth” (Gen. I, 1). But when we hear “God the Father,” we recognize the Son and the Holy Spirit.

Perhaps you say, “God the Father made the world.” But hear what John the Evangelist says: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John I, 1–2).

Behold: he says that nothing was made without the Son, since all things were made through him. If nothing was made without the Son, what did the Father make that the Son did not make, when the Evangelist says that nothing was made without the Son?

But if, as the true Catholic faith holds, you establish the Father as working in the Son and the Son as working in the Father—for the Son is in the Father and the Father is in the Son—the Son will be found to be omnipotent if the Father is omnipotent in him. If, however, the Son is not omnipotent, as the Arian heretic proclaims, the Father is not omnipotent in him, and what the Son himself said will be false: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me.”

But far be it that what the Truth says should be false. Let the Arian be confounded, since he contradicts the truth.

## 9. Let us nevertheless demonstrate from the Scriptures that the Son is called omnipotent, just as the Father is, so that not only true reasoning but also divine testimonies may strike the shameless brow of the heretics.

The Father is called omnipotent, as the prophet says: “Thus says the Lord omnipotent” (I Cor. VI, 18). The Son is also called omnipotent, as the apostle John says in the Apocalypse: “From Jesus Christ our Lord, who is, and who was, and who is to come, the omnipotent one” (Apoc. I, 5, 8). The Holy Spirit is also called omnipotent, as Solomon prophesies: “The Spirit of the Lord has filled the inhabited world, and he who contains all things has knowledge” (Wis. I, 7).

Is he not omnipotent who contains all things?

Scripture says that God is judge, as the Apostle says: “We shall all stand before the tribunal of Christ, so that each may receive according to what he did through the body, whether good or evil” (II Cor. V, 10). But when we hear “God the judge,” we understand the whole Trinity.

You, however, heretic, say who this God the judge is: the Father or the Son. If you say, “The Father,” you deny that the Son is judge, although even you confess in the Creed that he will come to judge the living and the dead.

You also contradict the Gospel, which says: “When the Son of Man comes in his glory, all the nations will be gathered before him, and he will separate them from one another, as a shepherd separates sheep from goats.” In this passage the Evangelist more explicitly shows that the judge is the Son, so that the sentence of that same judge might also be made known: “The wicked will go into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life” (Matt. XXV, 31–32, 46).

If, unwilling to oppose such great authority, you say that the Son is judge, will you then deny that the Father is judge?

“No,” you say, “I do not deny that the Father is judge.”

How do you not deny it?

“Because,” you say, “the Father gave authority, and the Son received it.”

I see, heretic, where you are directing your eyes and toward what object you are turning the gaze of your perverse mind. For you are about to recite to me from the Gospel: “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John V, 22). In this, you say, the Father gave and the Son received; therefore the one who gives is certainly greater than the one who receives: the Father is greater, the Son lesser.

Let your vanity not boast on the basis of this statement, for divine authority itself now convicts you through it. “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son.” We understand this; sound faith knows how to understand it.

That man who was assumed, who himself was also called the Son of God, received authority—but the Father and the Son gave it, because the Son is in the Father and the Father is in the Son.

But if you, heretic, according to that perverse doctrine of yours, wish to assign this to the divinity in which the Son is equal to the Father, I ask you more carefully—and I insist that you answer me quickly—who it was who said to Moses in the book of Deuteronomy: “On the day of judgment I will repay them.”

You cannot say, “The Father,” because, according to the Gospel statement you have produced, the Father judges no one. Therefore it is the Son who said: “On the day of judgment I will repay them.”

Is it the Son? Answer. Why do you hesitate? Did the Son say this, or did he not? There is nothing you can say except that the Son said, “On the day of judgment I will repay them,” because the Father judges no one.

But see what follows in this book, how it challenges you and how it convicts you. For after saying, “On the day of judgment I will repay them,” he shortly afterward added: “See, see, I am God, and there is no other besides me” (Deut. XXXII, 35, 39).

What are you doing, Arian? There is no way out for you. If you dare, say that the Son alone said this, and you will deny that the Father is either God or judge.

Lay aside your stubbornness now that you have been convicted. Hear the truth: understand that the Trinity is God the judge.

Hear that the Holy Spirit too is judge. The Lord himself says in the Gospel: “When the Paraclete comes, he will convict the world concerning sin, righteousness, and judgment” (John XVI, 8). What more do you seek?

Divine Scripture likewise shows that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit dwell together in a human being as in their own temple. In the Gospel the Son says: “If anyone loves me, he will be loved by my Father; and we will come to him, I and the Father, and we will make our dwelling with him” (ibid. XIV, 23).

There are the Father and the Son. What of the Holy Spirit? Hear the Apostle: “Do you not know that you are God’s temple and that the Spirit of God dwells in you?” (I Cor. III, 16)

Scripture likewise shows that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit together depart from the wicked. The prophet Solomon says: “Perverse thoughts separate from God.” There is God the Father departing from perverse thoughts. What of God the Son? It continues: “For wisdom will not enter a malevolent soul.” For Christ is the Power of God and the Wisdom of God (ibid. I, 24). There too the Son departs from the malevolent soul in which are the perverse thoughts from which the Father departed.

What remains concerning the Holy Spirit? Hear what follows shortly afterward: “The holy Spirit of discipline will flee deceit and withdraw from thoughts that lack understanding” (Wis. I, 3–5).

Hear that the Holy Spirit departs from a person who lacks understanding. When that same Holy Spirit was saying these things through the prophet, he was foreseeing you.

Behold, that inseparable Trinity is now demonstrated by testimonies from the divine Scriptures to dwell together, reign together, possess together, and depart together. But you, Arians, by separating it and inflicting insults upon the Son and the Holy Spirit through your various gradations, do not allow it to dwell in you [Note: [Col. 0643] The manuscripts read: “does not dwell in you.”]. For God the Father also withdraws from the perverse thoughts that are in you; and wisdom will not enter a malevolent soul. Through the malice of your soul, just as you separate the Son from the Father, so you separate the flock from the supreme shepherd. And the Holy Spirit will flee deceit—that is, the falsehood of your perverse doctrine—in which it has been shown that neither the Father, nor the Son, nor the Holy Spirit remains.

## 10. Since, then, the subject is the unity of the Trinity—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—we dare not call this unity three gods, or three omnipotent beings, or three invisible beings, or three immortal beings, but one God, of whom the Apostle says: “To the immortal, invisible, incorruptible, only God, be honor and glory” (I Tim. I, 17).

Let us not therefore fabricate for ourselves different dignities of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; separable and unequal ages; greater and weaker powers. Otherwise, what our Lord and Savior eradicated by his power and majesty—the idols and temples—the devil will again build as idols in the hearts of Christians.

The Catholic faith, then, is this: to believe God the Father to be omnipotent, immortal, and invisible; to believe God the Son, according to his divine birth, to be omnipotent, immortal, and invisible, but according to the humanity he assumed to have been made visible and mortal, and made lower than the angels; to believe the Holy Spirit, according to his equal divinity, to be omnipotent, immortal, and invisible, but to have been seen in the form of a dove for the testimony concerning the Son (Matt. III, 16).

And this is the Trinity: a simple, inseparable, ineffable unity, always abiding, always present, reigning everywhere, one God, of whom the prophet David says: “You alone are the great God” (Ps. LXXXV, 10).

# CHAPTER V

## 11. The Son’s birth from a virgin. Signs at Christ’s birth. The slaughter of infants. The boy Jesus found among the teachers. Water changed into wine.

“We believe in his Son Jesus Christ, born of the Holy Spirit from the virgin Mary.”

Why, unbeliever, are you terrified by this birth? Do not believe it if the one who was born was merely human. But if he was God and human, he was born from whatever mother he wished, because he was born as he wished.

Rather marvel at this: that the Word took flesh. He was not changed into flesh, because, remaining God, he assumed humanity. For the rest, why do you marvel that the mother gave birth to her own creator, that the creature brought forth the one who made her?

The Most High wished to be born humble, so that in that very humility he might display his majesty. An untouched mother carried her son; she herself marveled at the sight of her offspring, whom no marital embrace had enclosed.

But, unbeliever, hear what was foretold; recognize what has been fulfilled. The prophet David says: “A man will say, ‘Mother Zion’; and a man was made in her, and the Most High himself founded her” (Ps. LXXXVI, 5).

The one who founded her, the Most High, was himself made man in her: the Most High because he created such a mother; the Most High because he formed himself in her in such a way that, proceeding from her womb, he both rendered himself her son and did not corrupt her integrity.

What is the grace of this mother and virgin? What is the grace of this woman who, knowing no man, carries a son? What is the grace? Hear the angel Gabriel greeting her: “Hail,” he said, “full of grace; the Lord is with you” (Luke I, 28).

When the angel greeted this virgin in such a way, then the Holy Spirit made her fruitful; then that woman conceived a man without a man; then she was filled with grace; then she received the Lord, so that he who had made her might be in her.

For, beloved, it must not be believed that corruption could rule over that woman while he was already present and protecting her, in whom there was no burning lust.

## 12. Let the virgin mother know whom she carried; let her know, and let amazement depart while faith approaches. Behold, the one whom she carries is born; he does not yet speak, and he shakes the whole world.

Heaven cries out, radiant with the brightness of a new star. Earth cries out, disturbed by Herod. The Magi come, having been warned; the Jews, disturbed, inquire. They seek where the one who is wholly everywhere might be; the maker of the world is sought in the world.

He was sought not in order to be recognized, but in order to be killed (Matt. II), because “the world was made through him, and the world did not recognize him” (John I, 10).

O unclean world, the one who will redeem you has come, and you are disturbed! You wish to destroy him at the very time when he has resolved to set you free!

O impious land of the Jews, you do not agree with heaven. Heaven points him out so that he may be worshiped; you seek him so that, as an infant, he may be killed. Heaven announces to you that God has assumed humanity for your sake, and you wish to destroy the one who has come to redeem you.

Wait a little. He has indeed come in order to fulfill even your most evil will; but endure, so that he may gather his own inheritance.

Gather, gather, Redeemer; let the disperser not boast. Take vengeance on those who persecute you as a little child; let their little children die for you. If they are cruel toward you, let their little children die for you. Take vengeance—take vengeance in this way.

Let children, not yet speaking, insult their parents; let them convict those raging against you. Let infants bear witness to your innocence, because there is no wickedness in you; and let this happen to those who wish to kill you innocent: may you cause their own little children to be separated from them.

You may mourn and lament, Jews, for your children, but they do not die, because they are received into life. The punishment of bereavement is inflicted upon you; but glory of immortality is offered to them.

You told Herod where the Son of God could be found to be killed. But by killing your children for the Son of God, he punished you, as traitors, with the penalty of bereavement, though he did not realize it, and he made your children heirs of God.

This was how he mocked you—he who, dwelling in heaven, lay upon the earth. This was how he derided your madness and that of your king, when he turned your evils back upon you and made many good things arise from your evils.

## 13. You have recognized, virgin mother, the infancy of your son; recognize his childhood as well. The Gospel speaks:

“His parents,” it says, “went with the boy Jesus to Jerusalem to offer a sacrifice for him according to the law. And when they were returning, the boy Jesus remained in the temple. He was disputing with the elders and scribes; and everyone marveled at the wisdom that was in him, and he disturbed many.

“But when they had returned in search of him, they found him sitting in the midst of the elders, questioning them and answering them. And his mother said to him: ‘Son, what have you done to us? For behold, we have been seeking you in anxiety and distress.’

“Then he said to her: ‘Why were you anxious? Did you not know that I must be engaged in the matters that belong to my Father?’” (Luke II, 43–49)

When the mother heard such words from her boyhood son, she was terrified in her heart. For he was not naming as father the one whom he did not know on earth, but the one who made heaven and earth.

## 14. Let her recognize his adolescence as well; let her behold the many great miracles, the changing of water into wine.

In this first miracle that woman attempted to command her son, as a mother who could exercise authority over him, though she recognized herself to be a servant. “Son,” she said, “they have no wine. Make the water be changed into wine again.”

But he, distinguishing between God and human being—because according to his humanity he was lesser, according to his humanity he was subject, but according to his divinity he was above all—said: “What have I to do with you, woman? My hour has not yet come” (John II, 3–4).

It was as though he were saying to her: “The hour will come when that which was born from you, hanging upon the cross, will acknowledge you and entrust you to the beloved disciple. But in this miracle, what have I to do with you? For this did not proceed from you, but from the one who made you” [Note: [Col. 0644] Thus the Fuliensian codex. The Divionensis reads: “but in him he made you.” The printed editions read: “but from him who made you.”].

It is not fitting for you to command God; it is fitting for you to be subject to God.

But let the devout mother, who did not take harshly the rebuke of her son, who said, “What have I to do with you?”, behold God working in the other miracles as well, whom she was looking upon as her adolescent son. Let her behold the illumination of the blind, the cleansing of lepers, the running of the lame, the hearing of the deaf, the expulsion of demons—and, greater than all these, the resurrection of the dead.

But let this mother still recognize these things and be terrified at even the youth of her son.

# CHAPTER VI

## 15. The passion and resurrection of Christ

What remains for a young man except to come forth like a bridegroom from his chamber? Let the bridegroom receive a bride; let the one who is to be joined to him be sought and found.

He is not merely human, but God and human being. Let the one who is to be joined to him be sought. Let one like the woman from whom he was born be found for him—one who will both make her mother fruitful and preserve her as an untouched virgin. Let the Son of a virgin who remained a virgin receive a virgin who will remain a virgin.

Behold, the time has come. Now let the Jews fulfill their will, when he himself deigns to grant them the power. Act, Jews, who do not know the wedding of the Lamb; give the reward of money to the evil rogue Judas. Act so that the one born from a virgin may be hung upon a cross by Pontius Pilate.

Let our bridegroom ascend the wood of his bridal chamber; let our bridegroom ascend the bed of his bridal chamber. Let him sleep in dying; let his side be opened, and let the virgin Church come forth. Just as Eve was made from the side of the sleeping Adam, so let the Church be formed from the side of Christ hanging upon the cross.

For his side was pierced, as the Gospel says, and immediately blood and water flowed forth (John XIX, 34), which are the Church’s two sacraments: water, in which the bride was purified; blood, by which she is found to have been endowed.

In this blood the holy martyrs, the bridegroom’s friends, washed their robes and made them white. Invited to the wedding of the Lamb, they came; they received the cup from the bridegroom, drank, and gave him to drink. They drank his blood; they poured out their own blood for him.

What did the mad impiety of the Jews accomplish? They had been invited, yet not only did they refuse to come, they also killed the bridegroom. What did the wickedness of Judas accomplish, who sold the one by whom he ought to have been redeemed?

Behold, neither Judas kept the price, nor did the Jews retain the Christ whom they had purchased. To Judas I say: “Where is what you received?” To the Jew I say: “Where is what you purchased?” To Judas I say: “When you sold him, you deceived yourself.” To the Jews I say: “What you purchased, you could not possess.”

Rejoice, Christian: in the transaction of your enemies, you have won. What Judas sold and the Jew bought, you have acquired.

Rejoice, rejoice, bride Church, because if these things had not happened in Christ, you would not have been formed from him. The one who was sold redeemed you; the one who was killed loved you. And because he loved you exceedingly, he wished to die for you.

O great sacrament of this marriage! O how great the mystery of this bridegroom and this bride! It cannot worthily be explained in human words.

The bride is born from the bridegroom, and as soon as she is born she is joined to him. The bride marries when the bridegroom dies; he is joined to the bride when he is separated from mortals. When he is exalted above the heavens, she becomes fruitful throughout the whole earth.

What is this? Who is this bridegroom both absent and present? Who is this bridegroom present and hidden, whom the bride Church conceives by faith alone [Note: [Col. 0645] The manuscripts read *conspicit* (“beholds”).], and without any embrace gives birth to his members every day?

Who is this one who was born in this way, grew in this way, and died in this way? Who is this one who, as an infant, terrified a king; as a boy, convicted the Jews; and as a young man, troubled Pontius Pilate?

Who is he? Do you wish to know? “The Lord of hosts, he is the King of glory” (Ps. XXIII, 10).

If the Lord of hosts is himself the King of glory, then he feared neither the Jews when they came armed, nor the judge judging unjustly, nor the soldiers mocking, nor the enemies jeering, nor those placing upon him a crown of thorns, nor those dividing his garments, nor gall, nor vinegar, nor the cross, nor the spear, nor death.

For when the Jews and Pontius Pilate were doing these things, the Lord of hosts was conducting our business; he was then repaying what he had not stolen. He did not steal iniquity, yet for the iniquitous he accepted death, so that what was written about him might be fulfilled: “What I had not stolen, I then repaid” (Ps. LXVIII, 5).

Finally, so that you may know that he repaid on our behalf what he did not owe—for “Christ died for the ungodly” (Rom. V, 6)—as soon as he loosed the purse of his flesh upon the wood of the cross [Note: [Col. 0645] Erasmus and the manuscripts read *persolvit* (“paid in full”).] and handed over our price to the one who demanded it, he immediately made that thief a confessor (Luke XXIII, 42), so that through him he might restore the ruin of the ungodly.

Behold the redeemed one whom the devil had possessed as a murderer; behold the Lord of hosts performing miracles even in death. The thief confessed when Peter was troubled; this man recognized him when that man denied him.

But did the Lord’s acquiring the thief mean that he lost Peter, the denier? Far from it, far from it. The one who poured out the price was enacting a mystery, showing in Peter that no one ought to presume upon his own righteousness, and in the thief that no converted sinner can perish.

Let the good person fear lest he perish through pride; let the wicked person not despair because of his great wickedness. Let those who presume be gathered [Note: [Col. 0646] Thus Erasmus and the manuscripts. Lovaniensis reads: “let those who presume be shattered.”]; let those who despair be gathered.

We recognize that a great price was given for us, because we have been redeemed by Christ’s blood. Let us act so as not to displease such a Lord.

Behold, he loved servants and made those whom he redeemed servants free. Behold, this is little: he grants them his freedom; he offers them brotherhood; he even promises an inheritance.

Do you have anything greater to expect? By coming, he assumed your death; by rising, he gave you his life. Do you have anything greater to expect?

He—the one, the one who was crucified for you—rising from the dead on the third day, exalted you above the heavens; he made you a son of God.

Do you have anything greater to expect?

“What shall we repay the Lord for all that he has repaid to us?” (Ps. CXV, 12)

He made us before we existed; he gave us life; he gave us our age; he gave us free will; he gave us substance; he gave us talent; he gave us reason; he gave us knowledge; he gave all that was his so that it might be yours. We have misused all these good things, become proud, and offended the Creator who lavishly granted such gifts—rightly, because of our transgression. We perished, and he sought us; we were led away captive, and he came to our aid; we were being led to everlasting death, and he set us free.

What less did he offer you, who handed himself over for you? And do you doubt that he will give you his life, when he shared his death with you?

What shall we repay him? If we have nothing with which to repay him, let us receive from him what we may offer him.

This is what Christ asks of you; this is what he says to you: “What I did for you, do also for me. I laid down my life for you; you too lay down your life for your brothers.”

Do not fear death. Since you could not conquer it, I died so that you might conquer. You would conquer not through yourself but through me, because my death too was not for my sake but for yours.

You knew how to die, but you did not know how to rise. I accepted the death you knew and demonstrated the resurrection you did not know. By believing, love the one who rose, so that through him you too may rise.

We have spoken, and, insofar as he granted it, we have explained these three statements: that he was born from the virgin Mary, crucified under Pontius Pilate and buried, and rose from the dead on the third day. For if we could speak about each of them as fully as would be fitting, the length of the sermon would produce more weariness than delight in you.

# CHAPTER VII
### 16. On the Lord’s Ascension and His Sitting at the Right Hand of the Father

Since, then, we have said how far that Most High descended for our sake, let us now say how he raised to heaven what he had assumed from us, placed it at the right hand of the Father, and gave our faith a sure pledge, so that the members might be secure concerning so great a Head and might faithfully hope that they can reach him whom they already believe to be sitting at the right hand of the Father.

“He was taken up into heaven.” Beloved, do not understand this sitting as referring to human limbs, as though the Father were seated on the left and the Son on the right; rather, understand “the right hand” as the power which that man, assumed by God, received, so that he who had previously come to be judged might come as judge.

For this reason he ascended into heaven: so that faith might fulfill its proper place. This had indeed been foretold through the prophet David, for he says: “The assembly of peoples will surround you, and on account of it return on high; the Lord judges the peoples” (Ps. 7:8–9). This is what he says: Because you humbled yourself in the form of a servant even to the shame of the cross (Phil. 2:6), and some of those who saw you crucified believed, while many doubted, return on high, deign to ascend above the heavens [Col. 0647]; so that the assembly of the faithful people may be gathered together in unity through faith, and faith may lead them to sight.

This is the power of your omnipotence: that you can accomplish more in those faithful people when you are perceived as absent from them in that man whom you assumed. Otherwise, by the presence of your majesty, you never depart from the hearts of your faithful.

But see, beloved, what he who ascended on high gave: “He led captivity captive; he gave gifts to men” (Ps. 67:19; Eph. 4:8). See what he gave. He came wondrously, grew wondrously, performed many miracles, which we mentioned above, and bestowed eternal salvation upon many. He who took upon himself our weaknesses healed many and various weaknesses.

At that time, too, he was surrounded by a multitude of people, whom curiosity of the eyes, not faith, had brought together. Finally, when they saw the miracles, many praised him, while others reviled him. Hence came that word of reviling by those who said that he cast out demons by Beelzebub, the prince of demons (Luke 11:15).

Although he performed such great miracles, he was despised. Not only was he not regarded as worthy of honor, but he was even killed. Why was it not then brought about that this number of people should be gathered by his presence, except because everything that had been written about him had to be fulfilled? For when those things were taking place, their captivity had already been prepared for them by him; their captivity had already been taken captive. It was awaited that the Savior should ascend and give gifts.

What gifts? The gifts which the disciples received; which Peter received, so that he might die for the one who was absent, whom in despair he had denied when he was present. See what this same Peter says in his Epistle, what he pours forth from that gift of the Holy Spirit: “Believing in him whom you do not see, rejoice with unspeakable joy” (1 Pet. 1:8).

Let us also rejoice by believing in him whom we do not see, so that we may see him securely when we have reached him. He himself will also come, but not in the same manner as he came before.

### 17. In What Form Christ Will Come for Judgment

For he will come to judge the living and the dead. He will come as judge who stood beneath a judge; he will come in the form in which he was judged, so that they may see the one whom they pierced. Let the Jews recognize the one whom they denied; let that man, assumed by God and crucified by them, convict them.

Perhaps, beloved, since the gospel truth did not conceal that he rose with scars—although, if he had wished, he could have removed every mark of every scar from his risen and glorified body—he knew why he preserved the scars on his body: to heal the wounds of doubt in the hearts of the disciples. Perhaps, then, as I have said, just as he showed them to Thomas, who would not believe unless he touched and saw, so also he will show his wounds to his enemies.

For this reason it was said through the prophet: “They will look upon him whom they pierced” (Zech. 12:10). Not so that he may say to them, as he said to Thomas, “Because you have seen me, you have believed” (John 20:25–29), but so that Truth, convicting them, may say: “Behold the man whom you crucified; behold the God and man in whom you were unwilling to believe. You see the wounds which you inflicted [Note: [Col. 0647] Erasmus and the manuscripts read *infixistis*, ‘pierced’; the printed editions read *inflixistis*, ‘inflicted.’]; you recognize the side which you pierced. For it was opened both by you and on account of you, yet you were unwilling to enter.”

“You who were not redeemed by the price of my blood are not mine. Depart from me into the eternal fire which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25:41).

But may their death contribute to our salvation. If they despised him, let us fear him who will come in this way to judge. While each person is alive, let him hasten so that he may live; let him run so that he may be redeemed by his precious blood, lest, when he is not found among the number of the redeemed, he remain among the number of the lost.

Here—here, while one is alive—let him choose the better place. This is the time of faith. But “in hell,” says the prophet, “who will confess you?” (Ps. 6:6). Whoever wishes always to live and not to fear death, let him hold fast to life, so that death may be overcome by life. Whoever does not wish to fear the just Judge when he judges, let him now appoint that same Judge as his advocate.

### 18. On the Holy Spirit

Against the Arians, who say that the Father is greater, the Son lesser [Col. 0648], and the Holy Spirit much lower still. The Arians are refuted further.

We also believe in the Holy Spirit. We believe the Holy Spirit to be God, equal to the Father and the Son, because he is simultaneously in the Father and in the Son.

How is he in the Father? Hear the Son: “The Spirit,” he says, “who proceeds from the Father, he will lead you into all truth” (John 15:26; 16:13).

How is he in the Son? After the resurrection, the Son himself, sending his disciples to preach the Gospel, breathed upon their faces and said to them: “Receive the Holy Spirit” (John 20:22).

How is he the Spirit of the Father? The Lord himself says in the Gospel: “For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matt. 10:20).

How is he also the Spirit of the Son? The Apostle says: “If anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to him” (Rom. 8:9).

How does this same Spirit, the Spirit of the Father and the Son, proceeding from the Father and the Son, testify that the Son assumed flesh? The evangelist John says: “The Spirit,” he says, “had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified” (John 7:39).

But when the Son had been glorified, he himself says: “The heavens were opened,” he said, “and the Holy Spirit descended upon Jesus when he had been baptized in the form of a dove, and a voice came saying: ‘This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased’” (Matt. 3:16–17).

### 19.

When you hear or read this, Arian heretic—namely, that the Son was glorified and that the Holy Spirit was sent from heaven in the form of a dove—your carnal reasoning, and the fantasy of the evil spirit who works in the children of unbelief, leads you to say that the Father is greater because he was not seen; that the Son is lesser because he was seen in a man; and that the Holy Spirit is much lower than the Son because he appeared in the form of a dove.

For you say to yourself and reason perversely: “As much as the visible differs from the invisible, so much does the Son differ from the Father; and as much as the form of a man differs from the form of a dove, so much does the honor of the Son differ from the honor of the Holy Spirit.”

Thinking such things, you are close to the precipice of error [Note: [Col. 0648] The manuscripts read: “Thinking such things, he is greatest at the precipice of error.”].

For there have not been lacking those who held this view concerning the human soul which you wish to assert concerning the divine substance. Some have maintained that souls are given to bodies according to their merits and that there are revolutions and cycles. The prophet David, shattering this with a divine utterance, says: “The wicked walk in a circle.” Those who believe or preach such things are wicked.

And as though God were saying to him, “What do you think concerning the generation of human beings?” he continued: “According to your greatness you have multiplied the children of men” (Ps. 11:9).

But this is another question, on which there is no need to dwell longer now. Nevertheless, since our dispute with you, heretic, concerns the form of a man and of a dove—for you say that the Son is greater than the Holy Spirit because, according to the rank proper to each, just as there is a great difference between the nature of a man and that of a dove, so you wish there to be a corresponding difference between the Son and the Holy Spirit—I could indeed answer you that the dove possesses an innocence which the human being does not possess. But I will not say this, for we are speaking of that man who came without sin.

But if this troubles you, because the Son assumed a man while the Spirit appeared in a dove, this also ought to trouble you: that this same man assumed by the Son of God is called a lamb by divine Scripture. For John the Baptist says: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sin of the world” (John 1:29). And the prophet Isaiah says: “He was led like a sheep to the slaughter, and like a lamb before its shearer, so he did not open his mouth” (Isa. 53:7). And the apostle John says in the Apocalypse: “I saw a Lamb standing as though slain” (Rev. 5:6).

Tell me, if you are able to explain why the Son of God was called a lamb; then I too will explain to you the form of the Holy Spirit as a dove. If you say to me, “The Son of God is a lamb because of innocence,” I will say the same to you concerning the Holy Spirit: “The Holy Spirit is a dove because of innocence.”

If Christ is a lamb because of innocence, and the Holy Spirit is a dove because of innocence, then you too must preserve innocence and “behold uprightness” (Ps. 36:37). You see uprightness if you understand the unity of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

### 20.

But let Catholic teaching still undermine your empty devices and your various comparisons concerning the substance of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, so that it may overthrow your building—which you are building upon sand, not upon a rock—by the blast of the winds, namely, the divine utterances, and by the rain of grace descending, and so that, once overthrown, it may become a great ruin.

Although we know, believe, and hold that the whole Trinity is invisible, tell us, heretic, who was the one who appeared to Moses in a flame of fire on Mount Sinai, whose back Moses saw when the Lord himself showed it to him.

For when Moses asked to see the face of God, saying, “If I have found favor before you, show me your face,” the Lord answered him: “Go up to Horeb and stand upon the rock; my glory will pass before you, and you will see my back, but my face will not be seen by you” (Exod. 33:13–23).

Who was the one who provided guidance to the children of Israel as they came out of Egypt? “God,” says the Book of Exodus, “went before them: by day in a pillar of cloud, and by night in a pillar of fire” (Exod. 13:21).

Who was this one? Was he the Father or the Son? If you say, “The Father,” then the Father too was seen in some form. But you do not dare to say, “The Son,” lest once again you be overwhelmed by Moses’ own testimony: “You are God alone, and we know no other besides you” (Deut. 32:39).

Therefore you will assign to God the Father what appeared in the pillar of fire or cloud. If you assign this to God the Father, now return to that reasoning of yours and tell me which nature is better: that of fire, cloud, or man.

And if you say “fire,” or “cloud,” you will be mocked not only by human beings endowed with sound reason—not by those who have been deceived by your empty seduction—but even by the beasts themselves. For although they do not possess rational understanding, they do possess natural sensation, which has not been attributed to fire or clouds.

But if you say, “The nature of man is better,” then you demonstrate that the Son is greater than the Father, because the Son appeared in a man while the Father appeared in fire.

Let this be said, Arians, according to your position. According to the sound and true teaching, however, just as the Son is not greater than the Father because the Son appeared in a man and the Father in fire, so the Holy Spirit is not lesser than the Son because he appeared in the form of a dove.

That divine substance of the Trinity, remaining in itself as it is, visibly manifested itself according to human capacity and according to the suitability of each thing, in order to renew what had been lost and restore our ruin [Note: [Col. 0649] The manuscripts read: “and according to the suitability of each of its own things he manifested himself invisibly.” Erasmus’s edition likewise reads “invisibly manifested himself.”]. It did not lose its unity and equality.

God was in the fire, but he is not fire. The Son was in a man, but he was not merely what was seen; he was also what was hidden. For if he was wholly what was seen, what is the meaning of his saying to his disciples: “Whoever loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and manifest myself to him” (John 14:21)? What would he have had to manifest if he was wholly what was seen? Therefore he was also what was hidden.

In the same way, the Spirit appeared in a dove, but the Spirit was not a dove.

### 21.

All this, human being, was done for your sake. Do not wrong the one who made you, so that you may receive from him what follows in this holy Creed:

## CHAPTER X

### On the Forgiveness of Sins

**The forgiveness of all sins.**

Do not proclaim as lesser the one who leads you to the kingdom of heaven through the forgiveness of sins. If anyone approaches Baptism without this faith, he himself closes the door of pardon against himself.

For no other reason, beloved, did it happen that the Father sent the Son, that the Son himself assumed a man to be healed, and that the Holy Spirit poured forth this gift, except so that our souls might be freed from the burdens of sins.

He assumed the whole human being in order to heal him, but he showed that greater care had to be applied to the soul than to the body. For when the Savior himself saw, among the other miracles he performed while present, a paralytic afflicted by an ancient illness, he judged that his soul first had to be healed; only then did he deign to grant health also to his body.

“Son,” he said, “take courage, for your sins are forgiven you” (Matt. 9:2). Great salvation must not be despised. Whoever desires to be saved inwardly and outwardly ought to seek it.

“Cleanse,” the Lord himself says, “the things that are within, and the things that are outside will be clean” (Matt. 23:26).

Nevertheless, the perverse intention of the Jews—which did not follow Christ faithfully, but frequented him because they deceitfully prepared deceitful ambushes for him—when they heard the Lord say to the paralytic, “Your sins are forgiven you,” immediately produced that worst whispering of thought. The one who searched their hearts heard them saying: “Who is this who forgives sins? He blasphemes; for no one can forgive sins except God alone.”

But in order to show them that he was God, expose their wickedness, and demonstrate his power, he said to them: “Why are you thinking evil [Note: [Col. 0650] The manuscripts read this. The printed editions read: ‘Why are you thinking something evil?’] in your hearts? Which is easier, to say, ‘Your sins are forgiven,’ or to say, ‘Rise and walk’? But so that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins”—he said to the paralytic—“rise, take up your bed, and go to your house.” And immediately he rose, took up his bed, and went away (Matt. 9:2–7).

Oh, how much better it would have been for him if, after receiving the forgiveness of sins, he had not risen from his bed to sin again, but had risen from the grave to true life, freed and secure!

For it is not without significance, beloved, that he was told: “Take up your bed and go to your house.” For the Lord wished him to be healed inwardly in such a way that he would no longer labor [Note: [Col. 0650] The manuscripts read this. The printed editions instead read: “He wished him to be healed outwardly, so that he would no longer be inwardly ill.”].

But what does “Take up your bed” mean except “Carry again the burden of your sins”? Your shoulders will not be free; you will carry what weighs you down; you will be bent beneath the burden; your head, now freed, will again be weighed down by servitude. For, says the Lord, “Everyone who commits sin is the slave of sin” (John 8:31).

If that paralytic had departed from this life after the forgiveness of sins, he would have received complete freedom. But since he was permitted to live afterward—even if he did not sin, which is difficult to believe—he was in great danger, because “the whole of this life is a trial” (Job 7:1).

Therefore, whoever faithfully believes, beloved, and holds and embraces without doubt this profession of his faith, in which all sins are forgiven, should prepare his will for the will of God. If God should deign to keep him for a little while in this life after Baptism, let him not cease praying and saying: “Be my helper; do not forsake me” (Ps. 26:9–10).

But if God should deign to call him to himself, free and cleansed from every sediment of sin, let him go to him without hesitation and without sadness, with whom and through whom he too may begin to reign. Let him not fear the vehicle of death, in which the one who calls him first ascended.

For just as he led him to the Father by rising again, so through the resurrection he also presented you to him. For in order to invite you to heaven, he descended to earth, but he did not abandon heaven.

## CHAPTER XI

### 22. On the Resurrection of the Flesh

**The resurrection of the flesh.**

Let us faithfully hold that all flesh—that is, every rational creature—will rise again. This is the summit of our faith, which separates us from unbelievers.

For it is not right for us to discuss cattle or the other living creatures to which the image of the Creator has not been assigned. We know that all these things were created for our use.

Let anyone read what God said to the human being when he formed and blessed him, and he will find it written in the Book of Genesis: “God made man; he made him in his own image; male and female he made them, and he blessed them, saying: ‘Increase and multiply, fill the earth and rule it; and have authority over the fish of the sea, the animals of the land, and the birds of the sky’” (Gen. 1:27–28).

All these things, then, were created for the uses of our weakness, as I have said. But just as our corruption does not rise with us, nor our weakness, so neither will those things that are now necessary for our weakness [Col. 0651] rise with us.

The Apostle Paul says what our bodies will be like: “It is sown in corruption; it will rise in incorruption. It is sown in weakness; it will rise in power. It is sown in dishonor; it will rise in glory. It is sown an animal body; it will rise a spiritual body” (1 Cor. 15:42–44).

This incorruption, power, glory, and life-giving spirit will make us, as the Lord himself has deigned to promise, “equal to the angels of God” (Matt. 22:30), so that we may live with them in eternal life, in one immortality and everlasting homeland.

In that homeland, Christ himself will be our eternal life: “For he is the true God and eternal life” (1 John 5:20).

## CHAPTER XII

### 23. On Eternal Life

This also follows in this holy Creed, namely, that we believe after the resurrection of the flesh:

**And in eternal life.**

Corruption will no longer rule over us, as we live immortally and remain with eternal life itself. We will not need clothing there, where we will be clothed with immortality; nor will food be lacking for us, when the living bread itself, which for our sake descended from heaven even to earth, will satisfy our souls by its presence; nor will drink be lacking for us, when the fountain of life is present.

“For he will satisfy us with the abundance of his house, and water our hearts with the stream of his delights.” We will suffer no heat there, for there is our refreshment—he who sheltered and shelters us beneath the shadow of his wings (Ps. 35:8–10).

We will suffer no cold there, for there is the sun of righteousness, which warms our hearts with its love and illumines our eyes with the rays of its divinity, so that they may see the divinity and equality of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

We will not grow weary there, for our strength will be with us, to whom we now say: “I will love you, Lord, my strength” (Ps. 17:2).

We will not sleep there, for there are no darknesses capable of excluding the day that remains forever. There will be no business there, no servitude, no work.

And what will we do there? Perhaps what is written: “Be still, and know that I am God” (Ps. 45:11). This stillness of contemplation will be the work of our activity, so that, contemplating, we may delight, and in delight may contemplate seeing.

What will we see? “The good things of the Lord” (Ps. 26:13). What good things? Can we express what “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man” (1 Cor. 2:9)? Can we explain how God will be all in all?

Can we explain how the Son himself, when he has handed over the kingdom to God the Father (1 Cor. 15:28, 24)—that is, the holy assembly of the faithful—will not abandon that man whom he assumed and further glorified, and yet will not delay showing those same faithful the glory which he has with the Father before the world existed?

Can we explain how the bride, the Church, which consists of men and women, will all be transformed into a perfect man and thus receive manly dignity, while nevertheless not losing the name of bride?

Can we explain from what glory into what glory the resurrected bodies of the saints will pass?

Can we explain where the virgins will follow Christ, and where non-virgins will be unable to follow him, and how he will lead those virgins with him—I do not know where, remaining everywhere [Note: [Col. 0651] The manuscripts read: “remaining where”]—without nevertheless abandoning those who are not virgins?

Who, placed in this mortal flesh, which weighs down the soul (Wis. 9:15), dares to say anything about these matters, when the Apostle Paul himself could not explain them, although, while remaining in this body, he was able by grace to ascend as far as the third heaven (2 Cor. 12)?

Let us not be curious to investigate what the Apostles themselves were entirely unable to express. Certainly, no one should ask me to know what I know that I do not know—unless perhaps he wishes to learn not to know what must be known to be incapable of being known.

But through faith and patience, and through the holy mother Church, let us hope to receive whatever he deigns to grant to the great and the small.

## CHAPTER XIII

### 24. He Commands the Sons of the Catholic Church to Beware of the Arians

The holy Church—in which the whole authority of this sacrament reaches its conclusion—the mother and virgin, chaste in body, fruitful in offspring, declared above to be the bride of Christ, lovingly nourishes the children whom she strives to present as worthy to God the Father.

Good children, love so great a mother. Good children, do not abandon her who daily seeks you. Repay her due; love the one who loves you. She is so great, so excellent, noble, fruitful in royal offspring.

Do not allow her to be tormented by the injuries and ambushes either of wicked children or of utterly evil servants. Defend your mother’s cause; display her most exalted dignity.

Let an evil servant not insult his mistress; let the Arian heretic not insult the Church.

He is a wolf—recognize him. He is a serpent—crush his heads. He flatters, but deceives; he promises much, but betrays.

“Come,” he says, “I will defend you. If there is need, I will feed you; if you are naked, I will clothe you. I will give money; I will establish what each person is to receive each day.”

O wicked wolf! O unjust serpent! O most evil servant! You trample your mistress, attack your true mother, contemptuously blow upon Christ, rebaptize the Catholic. And what is worst in your craft: you oppress some by force so that you may destroy them, and purchase others with money so that you may kill them.

So, heretic, is this why you clothe the naked—that you may strip from within the one who is clothed with Christ? Is this why you feed the hungry—that you may take away the soul’s heavenly food? Is this why you give money—that these people may sell you Christ to be rebaptized, just as Judas sold Christ to the Jews to be crucified?

“May your money perish with you” (Acts 8:20).

You do worse things, heretic, than the Jew did. For behold, although the Jew purchased Christ to be put to death for a reward, he pierced the side of the one hanging on the cross only once, but preserved his whole body intact. You, however, purchase him daily with money for this purpose: to tear apart the various members of the one seated in heaven.

But you, beloved, who from the beginning were nourished at the breasts of the holy mother Church and have been led by her to solid food, remain in her.

If anyone has taken harshly some discipline or admonition of hers and departed in anger, let him recognize his mother and return to her willingly. She receives those whom she seeks, and she will rejoice that her lost son has been converted.

But although she greatly rejoices that her lost son has been converted, she does not cease to proclaim the dignity of the steadfastness of the children who remain with her.

[Col. 0651]

## ANOTHER SERMON ON THE CREED FOR THE CATECHUMENS  
[Note: [Col. 0651] In earlier editions, volume 9: “Another, or third, book.”] (C,G)*

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 0651]

### 1. The Devil’s Pageantry, Which Those Being Baptized Renounce

The sacrament of the Creed which you have received and committed to memory, retaining it for your salvation—know that this is the foundation of the Catholic faith, upon which the building of the Church has arisen, constructed by the hands of the Apostles and Prophets.

For the stones of the house of God are living stones—and you are those stones. Thus the Apostle writes to believers: “Do you not know,” he says, “that you are the temple of God and that the Holy Spirit dwells in you?” (1 Cor. 3:16).

The Apostle Peter also addresses the faithful: “You,” he says, “like living stones, are being built into a spiritual house” (1 Pet. 2:5).

Whoever desires to be joined to this building must renounce the devil, his pageantry, and his angels.

The devil’s pageantry consists of every unlawful desire—those desires that disfigure the soul, not those that adorn it: the desires of the flesh, the desires of the eyes, and the ambitions of the world.

The allurements of pleasures belong to the desire of the flesh; the triviality of spectacles belongs to the desire of the eyes; and insane pride belongs to worldly ambition. There is the inflated smoke by which a human being placed in some position of power does not acknowledge that he is a human being when he judges another human being.

Therefore, whoever wishes to conquer the world must conquer these three things that are in the world. Through them he also conquers the one who, by persuading through pride, deceived the world.

## CHAPTER II

### 2. The Worship of Idols Is Reproved

After a human being, by renouncing the devil, excludes the worst invader, let him admit the best possessor: let him believe in God the almighty Father, and so forth.

It is a great gift of grace to believe and understand God. But what does the prophet say? “Unless you believe, you will not understand” (Isa. 7:9). Let us therefore believe so that we may understand, but let us pray that we may deserve to see what we believe.

For sins, and the author of sin, the devil, separated the soul from God. While the creature followed its seducer, it abandoned its own Savior; and a great ruin resulted. The soul went astray, so that instead of worshiping the true God it worshiped idols and adored the very things it had made, abandoning the one by whom it had been made.

By worshiping a stone that possesses no life, the soul itself perishes, abandoning God, who is its true and eternal life.

Hence comes every error and abandonment of good things; hence the worship of the pagans and the perversity of heretics. Souls wandered through various and perverse pleasures, so that some worshiped the sun, others the moon and stars, others mountains, others stones and every kind of shrubbery, each believing that he had found for himself not God as helper but the devil as deceiver.

Thus the soul wandered away from its Creator in various directions, so that it worshiped as God everything that God had given it for service.

Were not all things created for the human being? Let anyone read the holy Scriptures, and he will find that God said to the human being whom he formed from the clay of the earth: “Increase and multiply, fill the earth and rule it; and have authority over the fish of the sea, the birds of the sky, and the animals of the land.”

And shortly afterward: “Behold,” he says, “I have given you all things for use and for food” (Gen. 1:28–29).

But those who refuse to read the holy Scriptures are themselves convicted by the nature of things and by the world, which serves them through its works, speaking in its own voice. Rebuking the perverse soul, it says:

“What is this, wretched one, that you go astray in me and, having become degenerate, have forgotten by whom and how greatly you were created, for whom heaven and earth—so beautiful a house—were constructed without any preceding merits?”

And the individual elements also reply, crying out and demonstrating their craftsman through their own works.

The sky cries out: “I am not God. For if I were God, no clouding could have cast a shadow over me, nor would darkness have succeeded my light. My light would have remained whole, incorrupt and inviolate, as that true light remains which created this temporal light in me for your sake.”

The sun also cries out: “Why do you worship me, human being, as God, when you see me bounded by rising and setting? God has neither rising nor setting; but by abandoning him you have incurred a great fall.

“You consider me great and wondrous; but I recognize that there is one above me who created both me and you. Since the works of my brightness and heat serve you, how can you regard me as worthy of worship as God, unless you do not know how to worship the true God?”

In the same way the moon and stars utter this similar voice: “Do you not see, human being,” they say, “that we spend the night in our appointed course, are excluded by the light, and do not cross the boundaries established by the almighty Craftsman for the solace of your rest?

“We are not God. We convict your falsehood by serving you for your punishment.”

The sea and everything in it cry out: “We are not God. For I offer service as I have been commanded: receiving the ship’s passage, providing suitable movements and the breath of the winds, directing its course so that I may bring it to the desired harbor without delay, even when greed drives you on.

“You know that the animals born from me have been given to you as food. Since I recognize my proper measure in everything, why do you abandon your proper order by abandoning God, the Creator of all?”

The earth cries out [Col. 0654]: “So, human being, do you assign to me the name of divinity? This is because you do not recognize what I am: you have forgotten who you are.

“You do not recognize your material; you do not recognize that you are my clay, formed from me, yet animated—which I am not. You do not recognize that among all the animals produced from me, you alone have been established under God as almost the lord of the world.

“Rightly you do not understand, because when you were in honor you did not understand. You have been compared with foolish beasts and made like them” (Ps. 48:13).

## CHAPTER III

### 3. The True God Is to Be Worshiped After False Gods Have Been Rejected

But we, beloved, to whom it has been granted to believe, must not believe that the sun is God or the king of heaven; nor the sea, nor some king of it named Neptune, whom vanity, not truth, invents; nor the earth and Pluto.

Rather, let us believe in God the almighty Father, Creator of all things, King of heaven. For he who made all things from nothing because he willed to do so himself rules what he made.

Those so-called immortals whom we mentioned above are not gods because they can be grasped and seen here with the eyes. As for the others whom the foolish foolishly worship—Jupiter, Saturn, Mars, Juno, Minerva, Venus, and the other monstrosities—their own writings, which delight in such errors, cry out that they were mortal human beings, not good divinities but evil names [Note: [Col. 0654] According to Erasmus: “not good names, but evil names.” According to the Lyon and Venice editions: “not good divinities, but evil divinities.” In B. a note is added in the margin: “For *nomina*, perhaps *omina* should be read.” M.].

But hear the Apostle Paul concerning the kind of God our sacred Scriptures proclaim: “To the immortal, invisible, incorruptible, only God be honor and glory” (1 Tim. 1:17).

Our God is not seen by the eyes of the flesh, but he is seen by the eyes of the heart. He is not seen for a time, but he is seen forever.

But the pagan says: “Show me the one whom you worship.” I reply: “I do indeed have one whom I can show you even now, but you do not have eyes with which to see.”

“For blessed,” says our Savior, “are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:8).

Does an impure heart, wrapped in the darknesses of sins, seek to see God? “The light shines in the darkness, but the darkness did not comprehend it” (John 1:5).

Is it the case that because a blind person does not see, therefore the light does not shine? If you knew, unbeliever, how to say to the true God, “Illumine my eyes” (Ps. 12:4), you would now see with us “through a mirror in a riddle,” so that you might be able to see “face to face” (1 Cor. 13:12).

If you understood the craftsman from his works, you would infer the Creator from the creature. If you were astonished at yourself, because you do not entirely comprehend yourself, you would recognize the God who made you.

For you do not see your soul, although your soul sees everything through your flesh. Or, if you do see your soul, tell me what kind or how large it is: whether square or round; smooth or rough; hot or cold; of some color or without any color.

I see that you fail. You cannot show what your soul is like.

Behold, your soul is immortal and gives life to your mortal flesh. I call your soul immortal in both respects: if it believes, it is immortal for life; if it does not believe, it is immortal for punishment.

Let us therefore believe in the immortal and invisible God—not in the god whom you unbelievers invent, committing adultery and thundering at once, but in the true God, the maker and ruler of the whole world.

## CHAPTER IV
## 4. Christ’s Birth from a Virgin According to Isaiah’s Prophecy

### Signs at Christ’s Birth

### The Infants Slain at Herod’s Command Become Christ’s Martyrs

### Humanity Restored by the Same Steps by Which It Had Perished

And in his Son Jesus Christ, formerly promised through the Prophets: we hold to what we now know has already been fulfilled. But we are also commanded to believe this because, when it happened, we were not present. The Jews were present then; from their race the Savior himself chose the Apostles, through whom this faith has reached us.

Among that very people, from whom he deigned to be born, the prophet Isaiah had long before foretold:

> Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a Son, and you shall call his name Emmanuel, which is interpreted, “God with us” (Isa. 7:14).

[Col. 0655] And elsewhere:

> A rod shall go forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root (Isa. 11:1).

The rod signifies the virgin Mary, and the flower of the rod signifies the Son of the Virgin, the Lord Jesus Christ.

Before these things happened, the Jews read them but did not understand them. What had been promised began to be fulfilled, and they did not rejoice, but rather grew jealous.

Christ is born from a virgin, like a flower from a rod, without any mingled seed. A small infant is born, a great king. Certain indications and signs of the great King appear: Angels announce him to shepherds; through a star, as through a new language, the heavens cry out. Magi are brought from afar; they come to adore him who still lies in a manger, but already reigns in heaven and on earth.

When the Magi announce that a king has been born, Herod is troubled. He wants to kill him lest he lose his kingdom—although, if he believed in him, he would reign securely both here and in the life without end. Herod asks the Jews where Christ is to be born. They seek him together, not in order to adore him like the Magi, but to kill him once he has been found.

Why are you afraid, Herod, because you hear that a king has been born? He has not come to exclude you, but to conquer the devil. But you, not understanding these things, are troubled and rage; and, in order to destroy the one whom you seek, through the deaths of so many infants you become a cruel magus. [Note: According to the Erfurt, Louvain, and Venetian editions, “you become a great cruel man.” In B it is noted in the margin: “For *magus*, perhaps *magis* [‘more’] should be read.” M.]

No pity for the mothers who mourn, no grief of fathers lamenting the deaths of their children, no lowing and groans of the infants turns you back. [Note: GG suspect that *vagitus* [‘wailing’] should perhaps be read here, a word in fact more fitting for little children. M.] You kill the little ones in body, because fear kills you in heart; and you think that, if you accomplish what you desire, you can live for a long time, although you are seeking to kill life itself.

But that fountain of grace, small and great, who lies in the manger, frightens your throne. Through you, though you are unaware of his purposes, he acts and frees souls from the captivity of the devil. He receives the children of his enemies into the number of the adopted. The little ones die for Christ without knowing it; their parents mourn martyrs who are dying. He makes those who cannot yet speak suitable witnesses of his own.

Behold how he reigns who came in order to reign in this way. Behold, the Liberator is already liberating, and the Savior is granting salvation. But you, Herod, not knowing this, are troubled and rage; and while you rage against the little one, you are already rendering him service, though you do not know it.

[Col. 0657] For that great King who came for this purpose—to gather his own from here through you and through others—you are the first to send before him to the kingdom of heaven an innumerable army of so many thousands of infant candidates. That crowd was shown by the Apocalypse of the blessed Apostle John, which says:

> I saw a great multitude that no one could number, from every tribe, standing in the presence of God; and they were clothed in white garments, and there were palms in their hands (Rev. 7:9).

O great gift of grace! By what merits of theirs was it granted to these infants that they should conquer in this way? They do not yet speak, and they confess Christ. They do not yet have the strength, through the movements of their limbs, to take up the battle, and already they carry away the palm of victory.

How do you reign, Herod, when you are conquered in this way? That little one did not overcome you by the hand of armed and mighty men, but conquered you through an innumerable multitude of dying infants.

Do you wish to know what you accomplished for the infants whom you slaughtered? You hastened upon their lives so that they would not, together with their parents, kill the true Life. In this, he acted through you who knows how to use even your evils well. He freed their souls from sharing in the destruction of their parents and left you alone empty in your crime.

Grace has acted and acts for its own purposes, both through its enemies and through them and in them. For even those who were dying were by nature children of wrath, like the rest (Eph. 2:3). But what did grace grant them except that it should rescue them from the power of darkness (Col. 1:13)? Christ granted them that they should die for Christ; he granted that by their own blood they should be cleansed from original sin. They were born for death, but death immediately restored them to life.

Beloved, human nature was restored by the Lord Jesus Christ through the same steps by which it had perished. Adam was proud; Christ was humble. Through a woman came death; through a woman, life. Through Eve came destruction; through Mary, [Col. 0656] salvation. The one, corrupted, followed the seducer; the other, remaining undefiled, gave birth to the Savior. The one gladly accepted the cup offered by the serpent and gave it to her husband, so that together they might deserve to be killed. The other, with heavenly grace poured upon her from above, brought forth life, through which dead flesh might be raised again.

Who is it that accomplished these things except the Son of the Virgin and the Bridegroom of virgins? He brought fertility to his mother but did not take away her integrity. What he conferred upon his mother, he also gave to his bride. Finally, holy Church, which is joined to him in her own integrity, daily gives birth to his members and remains a virgin.

# CHAPTER V

## 5. Christ’s Passion

### The Antidote Made from Christ’s Blood

Crucified under Pontius Pilate and buried.

We believe this, and we believe it in such a way that we glory in it. For, says the Apostle Paul, teacher of the Gentiles:

> Far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world (Gal. 6:14).

Let us also glory in this, hope in him, and cling to him. For our old man was crucified together with him on the cross (Rom. 6:6). Unless he had been crucified, the world would not have been redeemed. That punishment is our salvation. What the Jew and the Gentile detest is the means by which the Christian is saved.

But why does the Jew detest it? Because, as the Apostle says, through their transgression salvation has come to the Gentiles (Rom. 11:11). What transgression did the Jews commit? They seized Christ, bound him, handed him over to Pilate, and cried out, “Crucify him, crucify him.”

Why? For what reason? Because he had raised a dead man.

Pilate hears this, finds him innocent, sees the people raging, and excuses himself, saying: “I find no cause in this man. Take him yourselves and crucify him.” When Pilate said, “I find no cause in this man; take him yourselves,” what else was he saying but this: “You have come to the judge with a defendant, but you have handed over an innocent man to the laws, against whom you have been unable to prove any crime. I shall not be just if I kill an innocent man according to your desire. I shall be free from this deed and from your revolt if I hand him over to you. Take him,” he says, “yourselves, and crucify him according to your law.”

And they said: “We know that he is liable to death.”

What does the blind man in heart know, though not blind in body? He cries out what he does not know, and, in order to accomplish what he rages for, says that he knows what he does not know.

Again Pilate hears Jesus; and, struck with fear by his answers, he devises a way to release him. He went out to the Jews and said: “It is customary that I release one to you at the Passover. Do you therefore wish me to release the King of the Jews?” They cried out and said: “Do not release him, but Barabbas” (John 18:30; 19:15).

Barabbas, as the Evangelist relates, was a notorious robber.

O blindness of the Jews! O madness of the frenzied! “Do not release him, but Barabbas”—what else was this than saying: “Let Christ the Savior be killed because he raised a dead man; let the robber be released so that he may commit homicide again”?

But cry out: what are you crying out without knowing it? Let Christ be killed by you, and let the nations be redeemed.

That physician of souls, who saw that you were suffering from madness, was putting you into a saving sleep; and therefore he himself also wished to sleep for us. It was as though he were saying: “I am a physician; you are sick. Your illness is so great that it recoils from the sleep of salvation. Behold, I sleep for your sake, so that, when you see me, you may also take delight in sleeping, and I may free you from a death of punishment.”

But he was saying this to them and concerning those whom he knew would later believe in him, and for whom, while hanging on the cross, he prayed to the Father, saying:

> Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing (Luke 23:34).

Among them was also that madman, first Saul and afterward Paul; first proud, afterward humble. He too was suffering from madness and rejected the sleep of salvation.

But what did the physician do for him? He struck down the raging man and raised up the believer; he struck down the persecutor and raised up the preacher (Acts 9). Struck down upon the earth, the madman slept; he arose and became a physician.

He began to heal in others the disease from which he himself had suffered. Having become a disciple of the heavenly chief physician, he drank the antidote prepared from the physician’s blood. He himself drank it first, and offered it for drinking to those who loved him.

This antidote, prepared from the blood of the crucified one, was also drunk by the kings of the earth; and those who had been persecutors of the Church became its defenders.

# CHAPTER VI

## On His Burial

### How the Resurrection Took Place on the Third Day

The holy Gospel indicates the burial of this crucified man: he was received by Joseph, wrapped in linen cloths, and placed with spices in a new tomb. For the new man, created from a virgin without any corruption, was placed in a new tomb in which no dead man had yet been placed, so that the holiness of the virgin womb might everywhere be adorned by the correspondence of the inviolate tomb (John 19:38–42).

## 6. On the Third Day He Rose from the Dead

Although many holy men have understood and spoken many things about this—for some, wishing to express three days and three nights up to the Lord’s day, counted the preceding night together with Friday itself as one day, then the night of the Sabbath and the Sabbath, and the night of the Lord’s day together with the day of resurrection itself.

Others, however, beginning with Friday itself and the night that occurred in the middle of the day, wished to explain the three days and three nights up to the Lord’s day on the basis of that saying of the Lord recorded in the Gospel:

> For just as Jonah was in the belly of the sea-monster three days and three nights, so the Son of Man must be in the heart of the earth three days and three nights (Matt. 12:40).

But without invalidating either of their interpretations, let us nevertheless, if it pleases you, seek in these matters a spiritual understanding: how the Son of Man was in the heart of the earth for three days and three nights.

Let us take the three days as the three periods of the world: before the Law, under the Law, and under Grace. Let us take the three nights as three deaths—that is, the three dead whom the Lord raised while present in the flesh: the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue, in the house (Matt. 9:18–25); the son of the widow, outside the gate; [Note: According to the Erfurt, Louvain, and Venetian editions: “outside at the gate.” M.] and Lazarus, who had been four days in the tomb (John 11:14–44).

For where does death come from except through sin? And what are sins except great darknesses that create a heavy night?

Thus the correspondences fit together: one day is the period before the Law, when sin was hidden; joined to it is that night in which the dead girl lay in the house, as sin lay hidden within the conscience.

The second day is the period under the Law, when it was said to man, “You shall not covet” (Exod. 20:17), and sin came out into public. Joined to it is that night in which the widow’s son was outside the gate, as the sin of the soul that had been hidden within came out into public.

The third day is the period under Grace, when the soul sins all the more because it knows the will of its Lord and does things deserving of blows (Luke 12:47); and, under such an abundance of grace, through the merit of its sins it already lies putrefying. Joined to it is that night of the death of Lazarus lying in the tomb, as the soul is overwhelmed and foul with sins.

In these three days and nights Christ was in the heart of the earth—that is, the faith of Christ lay in the hearts of those who dwell on earth. Therefore, in these days and nights souls possess both the commandments of the Law and the voices of repentance, so that they may rise again with Christ.

For the day and night of hidden sin, the general law is:

> What you do not want done to you, do not do to another (Tob. 4:16).

Its voice of repentance is:

> Do not remember the sins of my youth and my ignorance (Ps. 24:7).

For the following day of manifest sin, the law is:

> You shall not covet (Exod. 20:17).

Its voice of repentance is:

> Against you alone I have sinned, and I have done evil before you (Ps. 50:6).

For the third day and night, when the soul has already been buried through the habit of sin, the law is:

> Behold, you have been made well; now sin no more (John 5:14).

Its voice of repentance is:

> Lord, deliver my soul from death (Ps. 114:4);

and:

> You have brought my soul up from the underworld (Ps. 29:4).

Through these three periods, as through three days, souls rise with Christ. To them the prophet says:

> The dead shall rise, and those who are in the tombs shall be raised, and all those who are upon the earth shall rejoice (Isa. 26:19).

And through the Apostle it is said to them:

> Rise, you who sleep, and arise from the dead, and Christ will enlighten you (Eph. 5:14).

And to those already rising—[Col. 0658] that is, those freed from sins—he says:

> If you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, sitting at the right hand of God (Col. 3:1).

For the Lord Jesus, rising from the dead, was taken up into the heavens and sits at the right hand of God the Father.

# CHAPTER VII

## 7. As Man, Christ Sits at the Right Hand of the Father; as God, He Is Everywhere

Who is it who sits at the right hand of the Father? Christ as man. For insofar as he is God, he is always with the Father and from the Father; and when he came forth to us, he did not depart from the Father.
