For this is what it means to be God: to be wholly everywhere. Therefore the Son is wholly with the Father, wholly in heaven, wholly on earth, wholly in the virgin’s womb, wholly on the cross, wholly in the underworld, and wholly in the paradise into which he led the thief.

We do not mean that he is wholly everywhere at different times or in different places, so that now he is wholly there and at another time wholly elsewhere, but that he is always wholly everywhere.

For if God granted this to the light that is visible to our eyes—that it should be wholly everywhere at once—for when it is here, it is not absent in the East or in other parts of the earth; rather, it is wholly everywhere and wholly in all things, satisfying the eyes of all while itself remaining undivided—if creation can do this, how much more can the Creator himself?

But when it is said that the Son sits at the right hand of the Father, it is shown that the very man whom Christ assumed received the power of judging.

# CHAPTER VIII

## 8. The Nature of Christ’s Coming for Judgment

For from there he will come to judge the living and the dead. The book of the Acts of the Apostles indicates his coming. After he rose from the dead, he lived with his disciples for forty days and forty nights, entering and going out, eating and drinking—not because he had any weakness, but in order to teach the truth.

On the fortieth day, while they watched him and in a certain manner escorted him into heaven with their eyes, two men in white garments stood beside them and said:

> Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into heaven? This Jesus, who has been taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven (Acts 1:3–11).

He will come, therefore, my brothers; he will come. He who first came hidden will come manifest in power. He who was judged will come to judge. He who stood before a man will judge every human being.

God will come manifest. What does “God will come manifest” mean? Not as before, as a humble man, but as God-man, exalted in majesty.

> And he will judge (Ps. 49:3).

How will he judge? He will not, like an earthly judge, seek witnesses in order to convict you, or seek the truth through torture in order to punish you after confession. The judge himself is justice, and the evil conscience itself is the witness.

That Judge, beloved, is not anticipated by grace, nor is he now moved by mercy; he is not corrupted by money, nor is he appeased by satisfaction.

Here—here, while there is time—let the soul do whatever it can for itself, where there is a place for mercy. For there it will have nothing to do for itself, because there will be room for justice alone.

Here let the soul repent, so that he may be able to change the sentence. Here let it give bread, so that afterward it may receive salvation. Here let it show mercy, so that there it may find forgiveness.

# CHAPTER IX

## 9. The Three Persons Are One God

We believe also in the Holy Spirit. We call the Holy Spirit God, and yet we do not say that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are three gods, but one, because there is one eternity, one majesty, and one power.

The Father is not the Son, but the Father is the Son’s Father. The Son is not the Father, but the Son is the Father’s Son. The Holy Spirit is neither the Father nor the Son, but is the Spirit of the Father and the Son: three persons, but one God.

“How,” you ask, “do you name three and say one? Show this either by reason or by some likeness through which what this may be can be understood.”

What reason or likeness can be compared with that invisible reality? Nevertheless, let its majesty pardon us, because our weakness offers some likeness that occurs to us from his creation, through which your Charity may be able to understand.

For unless he permitted it, who among us would dare to speak about his divinity?

It is not without significance that every creature is subject to the Creator. [Col. 0659] Yet God our God wished to appear in no other form than fire. He appeared to holy Moses in a flame within the bush (Exod. 3:2), gave the children of Israel guidance in a pillar of fire (Exod. 13:21), and poured out upon the assembled disciples the gift of the Holy Spirit in tongues of fire (Acts 2:3).

This element possesses a great sacrament through which it exercises the intelligence of the one who seeks.

Behold, in fire we observe three things: fire, brightness, and heat; and although they are three, there is one light. They arise together and stand together. Neither does fire precede brightness, nor brightness heat.

These are not confusedly one, nor are they separately three; but while they are one, they are three. They work together, and although they work inseparably, one operation is attributed to fire, another to brightness, and another to heat.

For when burning is attributed to fire, brightness and heat also operate there. When illumination is attributed to brightness, fire and heat operate together. When warming is attributed to heat, fire, heat, and brightness operate together.

Thus, when it is said that God made the world, the Father is understood as acting with the Son, through the Son, and with the Holy Spirit. And when we say that the Son suffered for us, we understand that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit all effected the Son’s passion.

When the forgiveness of sins is attributed to the Holy Spirit, we understand that the whole Trinity works this gift inseparably as well.

These things have been said for your Charity on account of the Arian heretics and others who think about God in a manner unworthy of him. But that which is ineffable and incomprehensible [Note: In B: “that which is, is ineffable, is incomprehensible.” We have followed Erfurt, Louvain, and Venetian. M.] cannot be explained by angelic words—how much less by human ones?

# CHAPTER X

## 10. Baptism Removes All Sins

### The Forgiveness of Sins

Holy Baptism completely removes all offenses, both original and personal: things said, things done, things thought, things known, things unknown—all are forgiven.

He renews the human being who made the human being; he grants forgiveness who does not seek merits. Grace anticipates even infancy itself, so that those who had been held captive in Adam by the devil may be free, liberated through Christ.

# CHAPTER XI

## 11. Faith in the Resurrection Is Persuaded by the Likeness of Seed

### The Resurrection of the Flesh

The whole hope of our faith is this: that we shall be raised. “We shall all rise,” says the Apostle, “but we shall not all be changed” (1 Cor. 15:51).

The good will rise, and the wicked will rise. The good, so that they may enjoy everlasting blessedness; the wicked, so that they may be punished by everlasting fire. There the faithful will be distinguished from the unfaithful, so that faith may receive its reward and faithlessness may obtain its place of punishment.

Let unbelievers not flatter themselves in vain when they hear in the Psalm:

> The ungodly do not rise in the judgment (Ps. 1:5).

“In the judgment” is what is meant: they do not rise in order to be judged, because they were long ago condemned through unbelief, according to that saying of the Lord:

> Whoever does not believe has already been judged (John 3:18).

But the Apostle, in order to remove every doubt from the hearts of unbelievers, proposed the likeness of sowing and said:

> Fool! What you sow is not made alive unless it dies (1 Cor. 15:36).

I think none of you is unaware of what happens with seed—how grains, after being threshed, cleaned, and stored, are brought out, scattered, and covered over.

Unless the fertility of the harvest were known, this would be thought madness. Yet when the seeds are covered and removed from sight beneath the earth, they lie as dead.

Now, if curiosity demands that one see them before the rain descends, one sees that what had been put into the ground whole has become rotten and decayed. But if hope of the harvest is absent, grief burns the heart; one thinks that one has lost what had been stored away.

When the rain arrives, however, how delightful it is to look again upon the green grass, the rising stalk, the plant reaching its joints, producing its stem, and putting forth its ears!

Is it not delightful to see what had lain dead come to life again in this way?

But let the earth not claim the fertility for itself, since:

> The Lord will give goodness (Ps. 84:13).

For if rain does not descend from above, even good earth produces not ears of grain but thorns, to be handed over to the fire rather than stored in the granary.

Likewise, let our earth—that is, our flesh—whether here or there, not claim merits for itself, but acknowledge that even there it will receive grace for grace.

# CHAPTER XII

## 12. The Happiness of Eternal Life Cannot Be Expressed in Words

### We Must Cling to the Church of God

### In Eternal Life

All that good—our being raised, our being freed from sins—will be everlasting, and therefore it will be everlasting good because it will remain in eternal life.

But what is the good that God promises to his saints? Who could explain it in his own words? It is easier, nevertheless, for us to say what will not be there in that eternal life than what will be there.

There will be no death there, no mourning, no weariness, no weakness, no hunger; no thirst, no heat, no corruption, no want, no distress, no sadness.

Behold, we have said what will not be there. But do you wish to know what will be there?

> What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart, these things God has prepared for those who love him (1 Cor. 2:9).

If it has not entered into the human heart, let the human heart ascend there. Let the heart be cleansed from every impurity, so that it may bear God, who is true and everlasting justice.

For God remains in the heart of the believer and of the one who loves him; and the human being remains in God—that is, in eternal life, which is the reward of the one who loves God.

## 13. No One Can Love Who Is Not in His Church

No one can love or cherish him who is not in his Church, because everyone who is outside it is not with God, who is eternal life.

Therefore the conclusion of this sacrament ends with the Church, because she is the fruitful, intact, and chaste mother, spread everywhere. She spiritually gives birth to children for God; she spiritually nourishes little ones with the milk of his words; she teaches children wisdom; she guards adolescents from their own luxury and impurity through her holy chastity; she arms young men with the strength of virtue against the devil; she teaches the elderly prudence; and she makes those advanced in years venerable.

Through her, young men and virgins, elders with the younger, every age and both sexes praise the name of the Lord (Ps. 148:12).

She calls back her wandering children; she grieves deeply over the dead; she feeds without failing those who persevere with her.

Let us all love her, beloved. Let us cling inseparably to such a mother, who loves us, watches over us, and cares for us, so that together with her and through her we may deserve to be joined perpetually to God the Father.

---

# [Col. 0659] ANOTHER SERMON ON THE CREED FOR THE CATECHUMENS [Note: In earlier editions: “Another, or fourth, book.”]

## CHAPTER I

### 1. Catechumens Are Prepared for Baptism by the Sign of the Cross and Various Sacraments

### The Profession of Renunciation

When holy mother Church received you into her womb through the most sacred sign of the cross, she—who will spiritually give birth to you, as also to your brothers, with the greatest joy—received you as a new offspring destined for so great a mother. Until she restores you, regenerated through the holy bath, to the true [Col. 0660] light, she nourishes in her womb those whom she carries with suitable food and brings them joyfully to the day of her birth.

For she is not held by that sentence imposed upon Eve, who gives birth to children in sadness and groaning (Gen. 3:16), nor to children who themselves rejoice, but rather to those who weep. This mother loosens what the other had bound, so that the offspring whom the former, through her disobedience, gave over to death, the latter may restore to life through obedience.

All the sacraments that have been and are being performed in you through the ministry of God’s servants—exorcisms, [Col. 0661] prayers, spiritual songs, breathings, sackcloth, the bowing of your necks, humility of your feet, and that very fear which must be sought above every security—all these things, as I have said, are food that refreshes you in the womb, so that, once reborn from Baptism, your mother may present you joyful to Christ.

You have also received the Creed, the protection of the woman in labor against the serpent’s poisons. In the Apocalypse of the Apostle John it is written that a dragon stood before a woman who was about to give birth, so that, when she had given birth, it might devour her child (Rev. 12:4).

None of you is unaware that the dragon signifies the devil. That woman signified the virgin Mary, who, remaining intact, gave birth to our intact Head; she also displayed in herself a figure of holy Church: just as, giving birth to her Son, she remained a virgin, so the Church gives birth to his members at all times without losing her virginity.

With the Lord’s help, we have undertaken to explain the very statements of the most sacred Creed, so that we may make known to your understanding what each of them contains.

Your hearts are prepared, because the enemy has been expelled from your hearts. The house has been cleansed; let it not remain empty. Otherwise, when the deserter finds it vacant, he may bring with him seven other spirits more wicked than himself, and the latter state of that person may become worse than the former, as the Gospel says (Luke 11:26).

As soon as the worst invader has been expelled, let the best possessor be brought in.

Who is the invader? The devil.

What did he invade? The human being whom he did not make, and whom he moreover deceived. He promised immortality and offered iniquity.

You have professed to renounce him. In this profession, not to human beings but to God and to his angels who record it, you said, “I renounce.”

Renounce him not only with your words but also with your conduct; not merely with the sound of your tongue but with the action of your life; not only with lips that speak but with works that proclaim.

Know that you have entered into combat with a crafty, ancient, and long-worn enemy. After your renunciation, let him not find his works in you, lest he rightfully draw you into servitude.

For you will be exposed and revealed, Christian, when you do one thing and profess another: faithful in name, but demonstrating something else in your conduct, not keeping faith with your promise; now entering the Church to pour out prayers, and shortly afterward shouting shamelessly in the theaters, actors. [Note: The printed editions read “with actors”; *with* is absent from the manuscripts. M.]

What have you to do with the pomp of the devil, to which you renounced?

Why do you limp on both sides? If God is God, follow him. If the world is the world, follow it. If God is chosen, let him be served according to his will. If the world is chosen, why is a deceitful heart offered to God as though it were sincere?

Whoever, having despised God, follows the world, will find that the world itself abandons him.

You, evil as you are, do not wish to fulfill God’s will, and God’s will is fulfilled concerning you as an evil person. Continue to follow the fugitive as far as you can; if you can, seize him and hold him. But I see that you cannot—you are deceiving yourself.

For, rushing along through its slippery movements with the force of a torrent, while the world sees you clinging to it and holding it, it drags you along not in order to save you but to destroy you.

What have you to do with the pomp of the devil, lover of Christ? Do not deceive yourself. God hates such people and does not count among his professors those whom he sees to be deserters from their own life.

Behold, the world is collapsing. Behold, God has filled the world with such great calamities. Behold, the world is bitter—and yet it is loved!

What would we do if it were sweet? O unclean world, you wish to be held while perishing; what would you do if you remained? Whom would you not deceive, if, being bitter, you pretended to provide sweet nourishment?

Do you wish, beloved, not to cling to the world? Choose to love the Creator of the world, and renounce the worldly pomps, whose prince is the devil with his angels.

# CHAPTER II

## 2. Faith Must Precede, So That the Reward of Vision May Follow

### We Are All Evil

Believe. Believe in such a way that you desire to see what you believe.

Someone says: “Behold, I believe, and I desire to see what I believe. If only it were shown to me, so that my faith itself might rejoice in vision!”

If you saw now, you would not believe. You believe because you do not see; but believe in such a way that you may see.

Faith is the work; the vision of God is the reward. You wish to receive the reward in the wrong order, though you have not labored in the work. [Col. 0662] Does not every worker rightly receive a reward from you only when the work has been completed?

What you do with your servant, ask from your Lord. [Note: Several manuscripts read: “with your fellow servant.”] He is granting you this: he exercises you through faith. By postponing his vision, he commends his gift; he does not deny it. He does this so that you may desire more greatly what has been delayed, lest what is given quickly become cheap.

Yet he does not abandon you when, for your benefit, he now withholds his vision. Your eyes cannot grasp him. Nevertheless, he himself attends to you at all times.

Apply the eyes of faith. Do you not look upon his face when you believe in his only-begotten Son? Do you not see his hands when you contemplate the whole of creation? Do you not hear his mouth when you observe his commandments being recited?

How do you pour out your prayer unless you know that you are reaching him of whom the prophet says:

> Behold, the eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and his ears are toward their prayers (Ps. 33:16).

But if you seek to know his feet as well, hear whom he wished to be his feet:

> How beautiful are the feet, he says, of those who announce peace, who announce good things (Isa. 52:7).

We have listed the members, but God is not contained in these human limbs, because he is not in a place; rather, he is wholly everywhere.

We have spoken according to the measure of human understanding, not according to the ineffable power of the divine majesty.

Do you wish to know what he is like? Look at the work of creation, and you will understand the maker. Examine what he has made, and you will understand him who created all things.

Behold, the prophet says to God:

> The heavens of heavens do not contain you (2 Chron. 6:18).

And the one whom the expanses of heaven do not contain is contained by the narrowness of the human heart, since he himself says:

> I will walk among them, and I will dwell in them (2 Cor. 6:16).

And the Lord Jesus says:

> Whoever loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and manifest myself to him; and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him (John 14:21, 23).

Behold what the Almighty who created you has made you. First recognize who you are, and you will recognize who he is who made you.

An earthly king is mortal because he is visible. The heavenly King is immortal and invisible. Although an earthly king has created nothing, he has nevertheless received everything under his power. And you do not believe that the King who created all things governs and rules everything?

“How,” you ask, “does he govern and rule everything?”

Behold, so many evils occur in the world, and he does not punish them!

O human being, do you deny his power because he displays great patience? He does not leave the sinner unpunished; he preserves him either to be corrected through repentance or to be punished at the final judgment.

Believe me, whoever you are who complain about evils: we are all evil. If God immediately repaid the wicked with evils, as you wish, no one would remain to complain about another.

But that great King, who knows how to rule what he created, does not fulfill perverse desires; rather, he accomplishes his own righteous will, so that he may teach you his patience.

Do not wish to turn God toward your rages. Let him who made you rule you; for if you wish to be ruled by yourself, you immediately fall through yourself.

That first human being stood as long as he clung to God. He left God, and God left him. He wished to test his own strength and discovered both his own misery and ours.

How good it would have been for him if he had done what the Psalm admonishes:

> Cast your care upon the Lord, and he himself will nourish you (Ps. 54:23).

If that human being was unwilling to be cautious then, let the human being now beware, having learned by experience.

## 3. Let Us Confess and Understand That We Have an Immortal and Invisible King

No human being has seen him, nor can see him with these eyes (1 Tim. 6:16). These are the words of the Apostles.

# CHAPTER III
## On the Vision of God

### How Moses Saw God

If no human being has ever seen God, how did he speak with Moses face to face, as one speaks with a friend? A considerable question arises. For the Lord says: “I will not speak with Moses as with others through riddles; I will speak with him face to face.” And Scripture added what we mentioned above: “For Moses was speaking with God face to face, as one speaks with a friend.” If he spoke with him face to face and saw him, how is that apostolic statement true, that no one has ever seen God, nor can see him? [Col. 0663]

But if Moses did see him, what is the meaning of the fact that shortly afterward Moses himself asks for something as a great favor and says, “If I have found grace before you, show me your face”; and the Lord says to him, “My face indeed shall not be seen by you; for no one shall see my face and live”? Where is that which he saw? And if he saw him, why did he desire to see what he was seeing? Yet how was that which was already being shown to him denied to him? This exercises the understanding of the questioner.

Moses saw God not with bodily eyes but with the eyes of the mind. And because that perpetual light, which is God, had illumined him more than the others, therefore it was said, “He spoke with him face to face,” as though it had been said: “He was manifested to him more than to all others.” But in the statement, “For no one shall be able to see my face and live,” it was shown that no one can see God with these bodily eyes.

But what was granted to Moses, God’s most faithful servant, so that so great a desire of his would not be frustrated in every respect, your Charity ought to know. The Lord said to him, as the same Scripture relates: “Go, climb upon the rock in Horeb, and stand there; and my brightness shall pass before you, and you shall see my back; but my face shall not be seen by you” (Num. XII, 8, and Exod. XXXIII, 13–23).

Lest a perverse understanding or heretical interpretation insinuate itself, and anyone suppose that God is corporeal, let devout faith and catholic doctrine remain vigilant. Divine Scripture speaks in mystical figures, reserving matters for their proper times, so that, once they have been recognized, it may exercise us in manifest truth. For it is not without mystery that Moses was commanded to climb upon the mountain of Horeb, upon the rock, and to stand there. This is that rock which, when struck, brought forth water for the thirsty people (Exod. XVII, 6), of which holy David says, “He split the rock, and waters flowed” (Ps. LXXVII, 20).

But the Apostle, explaining this, says: “Our fathers ate spiritual food, and drank the same spiritual drink. For they drank from the spiritual rock that followed them; and the rock was Christ” (I Cor. X, 4–5). Those “back parts” of God are Christ, God’s Christ. Moses saw this prophetically, which Paul explains by saying: “When the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, made from a woman” (Gal. IV, 4).

Here he uses “woman,” following the customary Hebrew manner of speaking, which calls all females “women.” For it is written, “Keep alive the women who have not known a man” (Num. XXXI, 18); and of Eve it is said, “He formed her into a woman” (Gen. II, 22). Before he joined her to the man, he called her “woman.”

# CHAPTER IV

## 4. Christ’s Nativity

Faith and truth proclaim this: that Christ was born of a virgin. Thus you received it; thus you declared that you believed it: “I believe.” This birth of God and man took place for the sake of humanity, so that that sublime Majesty, proceeding from the heart of the Father, might pour itself into the mother’s womb. The cause was the demand of mercy: humanity had to be found lost and, once found, restored to God the Father through the Mediator.

Yet this second birth is wondrous, most beloved brothers. Who, moreover, can recount that first birth by which he was born from the Father without any mother? If we cannot explain this one, when can we even begin to approach the other? If this one exercises us so greatly that it makes room for faith, when shall we reach that one, which even the hearts of the prophets could not comprehend?

Let us nevertheless say something about this second, wondrous and ineffable birth, which took place for our sake, “so that the Word might become flesh and dwell among us” (John I, 14). Who would not be terrified when he hears that God was born? You hear that he is being born; observe him working miracles at his very birth. The virgin’s womb swells, yet the enclosure of her chastity remains. The mother’s womb is filled without any embrace of a father; she experiences a child though she had not known a husband. An angel speaks to the virgin; the virgin’s heart is prepared; Christ is conceived through faith.

Do you marvel at this? Marvel still further. The mother gives birth, and she is a virgin—fruitful and untouched. A son is born without a human father, the one who made the mother herself. The maker of all things becomes one among all things. The ruler of the whole world is carried in his mother’s hands. He suckles at the breast while governing the stars. He is silent, and he is the Word.

He had not yet revealed through his tongue who he was, yet all creation declared its Creator newly born. Angels announce him to shepherds; a star invites the Magi. The rustic simplicity of the shepherds requires the angels’ announcement; the curiosity of the Magi is instructed by the language of heaven.

The Magi proclaim the king of the Jews; the Jews deny him. The former seek to worship; the latter seek to kill. The Magi tell King Herod which king they seek, the one who has been born; the Jews tell him from which city Christ will arise to reign. Both proclaim; both confess—but in different ways: the former so that, once found, he may be worshiped; the latter so that, once captured, he may be killed.

O Jews, carrying in your hands the lamp of the Law for this purpose: to show the way to others and bring darkness upon yourselves! Behold, the Magi, the first fruits of the Gentiles, offer gifts to Christ—not only gold, frankincense, and myrrh, but also their own souls. Yet your own wickedness rejects you, so that, having become mad, you seek to kill the one who came to free you from your bondage!

What benefit did you gain by telling Herod where Christ would be born? Did you not harm yourselves more than you harmed Christ? For when he heard from you where Christ could be found, he immediately ordered the infants of your people to be killed. Herod rages so that, among many, he may destroy one; by killing so many, he makes himself guilty, yet he does not kill the man whom he seeks—the God-man.

O Herod, great is your wickedness! You kill infants and heap up witnesses to your depravity; yet Christ is not found by you, because his hour had not yet come for him to suffer. You are indeed held as Christ’s persecutor and guilty of his death, though you accomplished nothing against him. But while doing many things against him, you destroyed yourself.

Why do you fear such a king, who came to reign in such a way that he did not wish to exclude you? The one whom you seek is the King of kings. If you wished to possess your kingdom securely, you would plead with him to receive an eternal kingdom from him.

Let Christ reign as he came to reign: let him receive believers, mock persecutors, make strong those who struggle, help those who labor, and crown those who conquer. Let him grant holiness, love chastity, and reward virginity.

Rejoice, holy virgins: a virgin has given birth to Christ. Let not barrenness grieve you whose faith is great fruitfulness; and do not sorrow that you are not mothers, since you give birth spiritually, remain virgins, receive children, and do not lose your integrity. You have received from him the name of motherhood, so that the glory of chastity may remain eternal in you.

Love what you are; preserve what you have received. Imitate the faithful mother of your Head and Bridegroom. He who was born of the virgin Mary has not denied you pledges of motherhood. What he bestowed upon that great mother and preserved in his own flesh, he has also given to you: the virgin mother, the holy flesh of Christ, intact from every contamination.

Nor was his flesh itself barren, since through it, by preaching, he regenerated spiritual children for life, and after his passion it bore fruit throughout the whole world, though it had been slain.

# CHAPTER V

## 5. The Passion: The Crucified One

From this, the Christian soul should take up complete freedom and confidence. It ought not to be ashamed to have believed in Christ crucified. That cross is not a reproach to the faithful but a triumph.

That cross is our standard against our adversary, the devil. For our King fought on our behalf against our adversary. The adversary, the devil, terrified us by threatening death; Christ promised eternal life. The adversary, the devil, said that he would destroy the flesh. But our King, to teach how his army might conquer, demonstrated in himself that bodily death was not to be feared, since he himself first deigned to die for all, so that his army might not be slain in soul by the devil.

This was what the devil was doing in that battle, if anyone consented to him: he desired to destroy souls and promised safety to bodies. Christ taught that one should die for a time and live forever, both in soul and in body.

The devil said, “If you consent to me, I will give you this temporal life.” Christ said, “If you do not depart from me, you will not lose even temporal life, and you will receive eternal life.” The devil said, “Do not lose this light.” Christ said, “I who made this light will give you a better one.”

“What he promises,” our Christ says, “he does not have the power to give. This light also is mine, and this life was created by me. But the life for which I came to instruct you is far more excellent and better. Pass from good to better, lest by consenting to the devil you remain in what is worse.”

In this great struggle, while the devil takes captive, Christ liberates; the devil deceives, Christ redeems; the devil kills, Christ restores.

Amid all this, the adversary, the devil, supposed that our King himself could be destroyed in the flesh, as though, once the head had been struck down, he could more easily subjugate the remaining members. Deceived by what he saw, he gave no thought to the fact that God was concealed in the flesh. He was ignorant of so great a mystery: that Christ was the Mediator and so tempered God [Note: [Col. 0665] The printed editions read: “to tempt God.” Corrected from the manuscripts.] in man as to unite man to God.

The devil killed him as though he were a powerful man defending human beings, but he encountered God liberating all the human beings he had created.

Finally, observe in the passion itself the spectacle of so great a conflict. Judas arms himself to sell his master for a price; he who had belonged to the number of the disciples becomes a participant in the Jews’ counsel. He gives a false kiss, in which there was a sign of wickedness; he feigns peace while full of malice in his heart.

The Jews are stirred up. They come with torches, lanterns, and weapons. Many seek one, and the children of darkness come carrying light in their hands—the light by which they might show others the true light, which they themselves, blinded in heart, could not retain.

But the Lord Jesus, knowing everything that was to come upon him—for he who had come for this purpose was ignorant of nothing—went out to them and said, “Whom do you seek?” They answered, “Jesus the Nazarene.” He said to them, “I am he.” When he said to them, “I am he,” they went backward and fell to the ground (John XVIII, 4–6).

Behold, a ray of the true light, still hidden beneath the cloud of flesh, looked upon the darkness and struck it down upon the ground. How will the Jews then dare to look upon that brightness when they were entirely unable to endure this weakness?

But in order to fulfill the purpose for which he had come, the darkness rises again. He gives them power; the darkness seizes the light—not to follow it but to kill it. The light permits itself to be seized, led away, hung up, and killed, so that, stripped of the cloud of flesh, it might restore the radiance of its majesty.

What, then, took place in that struggle? How much stronger the servants of the devil seemed to themselves as they gnashed their teeth, mocked him, shook their heads, placed a crown of thorns upon him, tore his garments, saw hanging there the one whom they had seen performing miracles, gave him gall and vinegar, and pierced him with a lance!

What kind of victory-song was their cry: “If he is the Son of God, let him come down from the cross” (Matt. XXVII, 40)? Yet through them this was shouted by the one who wanted to take Christ’s patience from him, so that, provoked by the Jews’ insults, he might display his power but lose his patience.

But that strong King—and that unique counsel through which every sound counsel is born and governed—looked upon both lines and preserved both lines: both patience and power. What he preserved, he displayed. He preserved patience, for he did not come down from the cross; and he demonstrated power when he rose from the tomb.

While he hung upon the cross, the Jews possessed a false victory; when he rose from the tomb, the Jews suffered true shame and Christians gained eternal victory.

While he hung upon the cross, the disciples were sorrowful, distressed, and scattered; when he rose from the tomb, they rejoiced and were gathered together in one house.

While he hung upon the cross, there was the disciples’ distrust; when he rose from the tomb, there was the gathering of the Gentiles.

While he hung upon the cross, Peter denied him out of fear; when he rose from the tomb, the whole world believed through love.

This struggle did not take place only then; it is taking place now. The members of Christ fight and labor while the adversary presses upon them; they resist him, because our Head now sits in heaven. He wished to fight for this purpose: to teach you how to conquer.

But if your strength is small, call upon him as Savior; call upon him as Helper. When he sees you faithfully calling upon him—he who hung upon the wood for you—he will prepare for you both victory here and the crown of victory in heaven.

# CHAPTER VI

## 6. The Resurrection on the Third Day

The Lord’s three-day death was foretold, promised, and fulfilled through the prophets. For the prophet Hosea says, “After two days he will revive us; on the third day we shall come, and we shall find him prepared, as it were, before the light” (Hos. VI, 3). He shows that we shall rise in him, because he deigned to receive from us the flesh in which he would die.

What more shall I say about the figure of the prophet Jonah, whom the Lord himself more clearly indicated when he said to the Jews: “This generation is an evil generation. It seeks a sign, and no sign shall be given it except the sign of the prophet Jonah. For just as Jonah was in the belly of the sea-monster three days and three nights, so must the Son of Man be in the heart of the earth three days and three nights” (Matt. XII, 39–40)?

Let us briefly trace the prophetic figure by comparison. Jonah was sent to the city of Nineveh to proclaim its destruction; Christ was sent by the Father to reveal the end of the world to all.

Jonah fled to Tarshish from the presence of the Lord; Jonah’s flight signifies Christ’s swift passage, of whom the prophet says, “He rejoiced as a giant to run his course” (Ps. XVIII, 6).

The fleeing prophet boarded a ship; Christ mounted the wood, passing across the sea of this age.

A great storm arose upon the sea; the storming of the sea signifies the Jews’ faithlessness.

A lot was cast so that the fugitive prophet might be thrown into the sea; a lot was cast over Christ’s garments, so that unity might be proclaimed to the whole world.

Jonah was thrown from the ship into the sea; Christ’s death was placed in the hearts of the Gentiles.

The prophet was received by the beast, to be guarded, not eaten. Hear here Christ’s own voice through holy David: “You will not abandon my soul to the underworld, nor permit your holy one to see corruption” (Ps. XV, 10).

When holy Jonah was placed in the belly of the sea-beast, he prayed; when Christ descended into the underworld, he raised the dead.

On the third day the prophet was returned unharmed to the shore; on the third day Christ rose from the tomb and was exalted above the heavens.

At Jonah’s preaching the city was saved through repentance; through Christ’s preaching the holy city Jerusalem was redeemed.

# CHAPTER VII

## 7. The Ascension: Taken Up into Heaven

“The one who descended,” the Apostle says, “is also the one who ascended above all the heavens, so that he might fulfill all things” (Eph. IV, 10).

Who is the one who descended? God the man. Who is the one who ascended? That same God-man. Let every human being recognize that God became man for humanity’s sake.

What he assumed for you, he raised into heaven; he made an earthly body heavenly. If you also believe that you can rise and ascend into heaven, then, because you are certain of so great a pledge, you will be secure concerning so great a gift.

The man who has been assumed now reigns, sitting at the Father’s right hand; and he calls, invites, and urges his own to receive a kingdom from him. Let every soul eager for glory hasten to him; let it go to such a king. To receive authority from him, it will not offer him a price in money; but when it brings him complete and perfect faith, it will even judge angels.

# CHAPTER VIII

## 8. The Second Coming for Judgment: From There He Will Come

Who is this one who is expected to come to judge the living and the dead, except that man who deigned to hang upon the cross for us? The man assumed by God is expected to come.

But insofar as he is God and equal to the Father, he always judges and is always present. Our Redeemer will come in the form in which he was taken up, so that what the prophet Zechariah says about him may be fulfilled: “They will look upon the one whom they pierced” (Zech. XII, 10; John XIX, 37).

The Jews, therefore, will see the God-man reigning forever—the one whom, by denying him, they had despaired of as a dying man. He will judge those dead in soul, he who is to come to raise the dead.

For this statement is understood in two ways: the living and the dead in soul, and likewise the living and the dead in body. According to the first interpretation, he will judge the living in soul, namely believers, and the dead in soul, namely those who have no faith. According to the second, he will judge the living in the flesh, those whom his coming finds present; and he will also judge the dead in the flesh, whom the Most High God will raise.

Let us choose, most beloved, that his coming find us alive in soul, lest, by sinning, both flesh and soul be condemned by him together.

The end of the world is near; and if, as some think, it is not near, the last day of each one of us is uncertain. Why do we delay, if we are striving toward blessed life? Let us be corrected while there is time; let us be amended. Let us have good causes, so that we may not fear the future day of judgment.

# CHAPTER IX

## 9. On the Holy Spirit

“I believe in the Holy Spirit.” The Holy Spirit is God, not less than the Father and the Son: one majesty, one power, inseparable Trinity, indivisible holiness, wholly present everywhere at once. God the Father, God the Son, God the Holy Spirit—not three gods, but one God, the Trinity.

Nor is the Son separated from the Father by time, since he is the eternal Word of the Father. Nor is the Father greater than the Son, since God begot God, equal to himself, without time—through whom he made time.

Nor is the Holy Spirit less than the Father and the Son, since he is the love and concord of the Father and the Son. For how is the Son less than the Father, as the heretic Arius teaches, when the Apostle calls him “the Power of God and the Wisdom of God” (I Cor. I, 24)? If the Son is the Power and Wisdom of the Father, whoever calls him lesser insults God the Father, since he asserts that the Father possesses in himself a lesser wisdom and a weakened power.

Or how does he also proclaim the Holy Spirit lesser than the Son, when the Apostle says that the members of Christ are the temple of the Holy Spirit? “You,” he says, “are the body of Christ and members” (ibid. XII, 27). And elsewhere: “Do you not know,” he says, “that your members are the temple of the Holy Spirit within you?” (ibid. VI, 19).

How is he not God who has a temple? Or how is he less than Christ, whose members he has as his temple? There are no different degrees where there is one Trinity and a threefold eternity. For whoever establishes different degrees cuts himself off from unity.

How do you exult, Arian, that you possess the truth, when evil error, separating you from catholic doctrine and declaring you a heretic, has excluded you from communion with the whole world and condemned you to remain in one corner?

Beware, brothers, of the doctrines of heretics, as of wolves’ ambushes. Sheep of Christ, hear the voice of your shepherd. “The one who enters through the door into the sheepfold of the sheep is the shepherd,” he says; “but the one who climbs in by another way is a thief and a robber” (John X, 1–2).

Beware thieves; beware robbers. The shepherd does not cease to cry out; he does not even permit his own dogs to remain silent. Let not the sheep withdraw from the chief shepherd, lest it offer itself to the plundering of the most wicked wolf.

# CHAPTER X

## 10. On the Remission of Sins

“Into the remission of sins.” Hold firmly, hope faithfully, and wait patiently. Renewal will be given to you through Baptism, with the old condition passing away. The soul will be relieved of the burdens of sins, so that, clothed in the freedom of new life, it may be able, with divine assistance, to fight bravely against the devil and so overcome the one by whom it was defeated that, transferred into the kingdom of God and secure in the defeat of its enemy, it may reign with its Head, Christ.

# CHAPTER XI

## 11. On the Resurrection of the Flesh

“The resurrection of the flesh.” Great faith is necessary, because a great reward is promised. Do not consider what happens now, but what will happen then [Note: [Col. 0667] In the manuscripts: “what is now, but what now happens.”]: for what happens now moves many people.

Who is not moved when he sees such form, such beauty, and such loveliness—the human being formed and then dissolved into dust, bones scattered, earth committed to earth?

Do not let these things frighten you, Christian. The human being has been sown, not lost. When the soul departs, its dwelling is dissolved; for that mistress who cares for the clay house and restores its ruins is no longer present. She goes away in order to purchase an everlasting kingdom at a great price.

Why, then, are you afraid, O soul? You have been dedicated to Christ the Lord; and because he grants it, you live well and strive to reach the kingdom of God. Why do you fear the vehicle of death? You are indeed departing, and your flesh will suffer injury for a time; but you will return reigning with the supreme King, and such a body will be restored to you that it cannot decay and will remain with you forever.

If you are going on in order to become better, do you not believe that better lodging will in some manner be prepared for you in the kingdom of heaven, for the one who has become better and is administering it there? If this earthly, clay-like, fragile body has displayed such beauty to you, what loveliness will it display when restored and made heavenly?

If you love this body so greatly, although it remains only a little while and passes away in time, how much will you love that body which will never lack its beauty, since its life will remain forever?

# CHAPTER XII

## 12. On Eternal Life

This follows in the holy Creed: that we may receive in eternal life all that we believe and hope for.

Eternal life, most beloved, must never become cheap in our eyes; it must always grow sweeter. If life is loved, why is true life not sought? If life is loved, let the kind of life that never ends be sought. And if it is loved, why is it not sought? Or if it is sought because it is not here, why do we not hasten to the place where it is?

What is more, life itself has thrust itself upon us freely. For Christ is the true God and eternal life. He came to us who were lost and redeemed us when he had found us. True life itself came here, to the region of mortals. It gave us a taste of its flavor; we tasted and saw that it is sweet.

It went before us and invited us to follow. Yet, having received a taste of so great a gift, do we fear to follow? Life came to you; repay the favor—come, you also, to it. It took up the vehicle of death so that, passing through it, it might free you. Take up death yourself, so that when you come to it, it may receive you in such a way that you will never die.

# CHAPTER XIII

## 13. On the Holy Church

“The holy Church.” For this reason the conclusion of this sacrament ends with the holy Church: if anyone is found outside it, he will be a stranger to the number of the children. Nor will he have God as Father if he has refused to have the Church as mother. Nothing will benefit him—not what he believed or what he did, however many good works he performed—without the supreme Good.

The Church is a spiritual mother. The Church is Christ’s bride, whitened by his grace and endowed with a dowry of precious blood. She possesses everything that she received as a dowry from her husband.

I read her marriage documents; I shall recite them. Hear, heretics, what is written: “It was necessary that Christ should suffer and rise from the dead, and that repentance and remission of sins should be preached in his name among all nations” (Luke XXIV, 47). “All nations” means the whole world.

The Church possesses everything that she received as a dowry from her husband. Whatever assembly of any heresy sits in corners is a concubine, not a matron.

O Arian heresy, why do you insult? Why do you hiss? Why do you even temporarily usurp so much? The mistress suffers injury at the hands of the slave-woman; you heap many insults upon her. Although she grieves at this, the holy Catholic bride of Christ does not greatly fear you.

For when that Bridegroom looks upon her, you will be expelled as a slave-woman with your children, because “the children of the slave-woman will not be heirs with the children of the free woman” (Gen. XXI, 10).

Let the one holy and true queen, the Catholic Church, be recognized. Christ has given her such a kingdom that, spreading her throughout the whole world and cleansing her from every stain and wrinkle, he has prepared her entirely beautiful for his coming.

[Col. 0669]

## Sermon of Saint Aurelius Augustine, Bishop of Hippo, on Christian Discipline

[Note: [Col. 0669] In most manuscripts it is called Augustine’s Book or Booklet on Christian Discipline, or on the Discipline of Christians. In the printed editions of Erasmus and Louvain there is added: “or on the Gift of Discipline.”]

[Note: [Col. 0669] The Sermon on Christian Discipline has been corrected against the Corbie manuscript, written approximately 800 years ago; against the German, Gemmetic, and Bigotian manuscripts; against the manuscript from the Fossatense Abbey of Saint Maur; against two Cistercian manuscripts; and against the editions of Erasmus and Louvain.]

[Note: [Col. 0669] We also compared all those editions mentioned at the beginning of the Retractations and the Confessions, volume 1, marked M.] (C, G, S)*

# CHAPTER I

## 1. The Subject of the Sermon

The word of God has been spoken to us and brought forth for our exhortation, as Scripture says: “Receive discipline in the house of discipline” (Ecclus. LI, 31, 36).

“Discipline” derives its name from learning; the house of discipline is the Church of Christ.

What, then, is learned here, and why is it learned? Who are those who learn, and from whom do they learn?

What is learned is how to live well. The reason for learning to live well is that one may arrive at living forever. Christians learn; Christ teaches.

First, therefore, what it means to live well; then, what the reward of a good life is; third, who true Christians are; fourth, who the true teacher is. We shall say only a little, as the Lord grants, and you will kindly listen.

We are all in the house of discipline, but many do not wish to have discipline. And what is more perverse, they do not even wish to have discipline in the house of discipline. Since they ought to receive discipline in the house of discipline so that they may preserve it in their own homes, they instead wish not only to have indiscipline in their homes but also to carry it with them into the house of discipline.

Therefore, there are those in whom the word of God finds no room, who join their hearts to gold; those who are not the road, where the seed, once it has fallen, is gathered up by the birds; those who are not the rocky places, where the seed cannot take deep root, springs up for a time, and withers in the heat; those who are not the thorny field, where, once the seed has germinated and begun to rise into the air, it is choked by the density of the thorns.

But there are also those who are good soil, prepared to receive the seed and return a harvest—either a hundredfold, sixtyfold, or thirtyfold. Remember, you who do not enter the school of discipline without reason, that I have recalled these comparisons from the Gospel (Matt. XIII, 3–23).

Those who are such should receive what the Lord deigns to say through me. For since he is the one who sows, what am I? Scarcely the basket of the sower. He deigns to place in me [Note: [Col. 0669] Some manuscripts: “may deign.”] what he may scatter among you.

Do not therefore attend to the lowliness of the basket, but to the love of the seed and the power of the sower.

# CHAPTER II

## 2. What It Means to Live Well

### The Precepts of Good Living Contained in One Short and Clear Commandment

What, then, is living well, which is learned here? There are many precepts in the Law, and the good life itself is contained, commanded, and taught in them. There are altogether many precepts—innumerable ones. Scarcely anyone can count the pages of the precepts themselves, much less the precepts themselves.

Yet God wished, for the sake of those who might excuse themselves either because they have no time to read, or because they do not know how to read, or because they cannot easily understand, that no one should have an excuse on the day of judgment. He wished, as it is written, “to complete and abbreviate the word upon the earth,” as the prophet had foretold concerning it: “For the Lord shall make a word that completes and abbreviates upon the earth” (Isa. X, 23).

God also wished this completed and abbreviated word not to be obscure. It is brief so that no one may say there was no time to read it; it is clear so that no one may say, “I was unable to understand.”

The treasury of the divine Scriptures is therefore great, containing within itself many wondrous precepts, like many gems, precious necklaces, and immense vessels of great metal. But who can search out this treasury, make use of it, and reach everything that is in it?

When the Lord gave this comparison in his Gospel and said, “The kingdom of heaven is like a treasure found in a field,” lest anyone should declare himself unequal to searching out the treasure, he immediately gave another comparison: “The kingdom of heaven,” he said, “is like a merchant seeking good pearls, who, having found one precious pearl, sold everything he had and bought it” (Matt. XIII, 44–46).

Thus, if you were too lazy to search out the treasure, do not be too lazy to carry one pearl beneath your tongue and walk securely wherever you wish [Note: [Col. 0670] Most manuscripts: “and walk securely wherever you wish.”].

# CHAPTER III

## 3. The Commandment to Love God and One’s Neighbor

### Who Is One’s Neighbor?

What, then, is the word that completes and abbreviates? “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind; and you shall love your neighbor as yourself. On these two commandments depend the whole Law and the Prophets” (ibid. XXII, 37–40).

Behold what is learned in the house of discipline: to love God and to love one’s neighbor—to love God as God, and one’s neighbor as oneself.

You cannot find an equal to God, so that it could be said to you, “Love God as you love him.” But in the case of your neighbor, a rule has been found for you, because you have been found to be equal to your neighbor—you yourself.

Do you ask how to love your neighbor? Attend to yourself; and just as you love yourself, so love your neighbor. There is no place for you to go wrong.

I now wish to entrust your neighbor to you, so that you may love him as yourself. I wish to, but I am still afraid. I wish to say to you, “Love your neighbor as you love yourself,” and I am afraid; for I still wish to examine how you love yourself.

Do not therefore take offense. You yourself cannot easily be dismissed, since so many neighbors are to be entrusted to you. You cannot be dealt with superficially. You are one person, but your neighbors are many.

You must not initially understand “neighbor” as merely brother, kinsman, or relative by marriage. Every human being is the neighbor of every human being. A father and son, a father-in-law and son-in-law are called one another’s neighbors. Nothing is so close as one human being to another.

But if we think that only those who are born from the same parents are neighbors, let us consider Adam and Eve: we are all brothers. And indeed, if we are brothers according to our humanity, how much more are we brothers according to our Christianity?

As a human being, you have one father, Adam, and one mother, Eve. As a Christian, you have one Father, God, and one mother, the Church.

# CHAPTER IV

## 4. How One Must Love Oneself When Commanded to Love One’s Neighbor as Oneself

See, therefore, how many neighbors one person has. All the human beings whom he encounters and to whom he can be joined are his neighbors.

How, then, must the person be examined as to whether he loves himself, when so many neighbors are to be entrusted to him, so that he may love them as himself? Let no one therefore become angry if I examine how he loves himself.

Certainly, I am examining him so that he may discover himself. Why am I examining him? Is it because I am going to find him? I examine him so that he may question himself, appear to himself, not remain hidden from himself, not conceal himself from himself, and place himself before his own eyes rather than behind his back.

Let him do this while I am speaking; let him do it without my knowing.

How do you love yourself? Whoever hears me—or rather, whoever hears God through me in this house of discipline—attend to yourself: how do you love yourself?

If I ask you whether you love yourself, you will surely answer that you do. For who hates himself? You will say, “Who indeed hates himself?”

Then you do not love wickedness, if you love yourself. For if you love wickedness, I am not the one saying this; listen to the Psalm: “Whoever loves iniquity hates his own soul” (Ps. X, 6).

Therefore, if you love wickedness, hear the truth—not truth flattering you, but openly saying to you, “You hate yourself.” The more you say that you love yourself, the more you hate yourself: “Whoever loves iniquity hates his own soul.”

What shall I say about the flesh, which is the baser part of the human being? If he hates his soul, how does he love the flesh? Finally, those who love iniquity and hate their own souls practice every disgrace upon their own flesh.

So now, you who love iniquity, how did you wish a neighbor to be entrusted to you, so that you might love him as yourself? Human being, why are you destroying yourself? For if you love yourself in such a way that you destroy yourself, you will certainly destroy the one whom you love as yourself.

Therefore, I do not want anyone to love another: let him perish alone. Either correct your love or reject companionship.

# CHAPTER V
## 5. How One May Love One’s Neighbor to His Harm: The Bestial Man

You will say to me: “I love my neighbor as myself.” I hear you plainly; I hear you. You want to become drunk with the one whom you love as yourself. “Let us do ourselves some good today; let us drink as much as we can.” See how you love yourself: you draw him toward yourself and invite him to what you love. It is necessary that the one whom you love as yourself be drawn there—to what you yourself love.

You are a human being—or rather, a bestial one, because you love the things beasts love. God made beasts with their faces bowed down, seeking food from the earth; but he raised you from the earth onto two feet. He wanted you to direct your face upward. Let your heart not disagree with your face. Do not have your face above and your heart below; rather, hear the truth and do the truth: “Lift up your hearts,” so that you do not lie in the house of instruction. For when you hear this, respond—but let what you answer be true.

Love yourself in this way, and you will love your neighbor as yourself. What does it mean to have your heart above, except what was said earlier: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind”? Since there are therefore two commandments, would one alone be insufficient if it were stated? One is sufficient, if it is understood. For Scripture sometimes speaks as the apostle Paul does: “You shall not commit adultery; you shall not murder; you shall not covet”; and if there is any other commandment, it is summed up in this saying: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself. Love does no harm to one’s neighbor. Therefore love is the fulfillment of the Law” (Romans 13:9–10).

What is charity? Love. He seems to have said nothing about love of God, but to have said that love of one’s neighbor alone is sufficient for fulfilling the Law. Whatever other commandment there is is summed up in this saying; in this saying it is fulfilled. In what? “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.” There it is: one commandment. Certainly there are two commandments on which the whole Law and the Prophets depend.

# CHAPTER VI

## God Must Be Loved by Man So That He May Be Blessed; Money Must Not Be Loved in Such a Way That One Is Unprepared to Share It with One’s Neighbor

See how much has been abbreviated, and yet we are still sluggish. These two have become one. Love your neighbor absolutely, and that is sufficient. But love him as you love yourself—not as you hate yourself. “Love your neighbor as yourself”; but first you must love yourself.

### 6.

You must ask how you are to love yourself, and you must hear the answer: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind.” For just as man could not make himself a man, so he cannot make himself blessed. One thing made him man, and that thing is not man himself; another thing will make him blessed, and that thing is not man himself.

Finally, the one who is wandering sees for himself that he cannot become blessed through himself, and he loves something else from which he may become blessed. Whatever he thinks will make him blessed, that he loves. What, we may ask, does he love as the thing from which he supposes he will become blessed? Money, gold, silver, estates—in short, money. Everything that people possess on earth, everything of which they are masters, is called money. A slave, a vessel, a field, a tree, livestock—whatever of these it may be, it is called money.

And why was it first called *pecunia*? It is called *pecunia* because the ancients possessed everything they had in livestock. *Pecunia* derives from *pecus*, “livestock.” We read that the ancient patriarchs were wealthy shepherds.

Therefore you love money, O man. What you think will make you blessed is money, and you love it greatly. You wanted to love your neighbor as yourself; share your money with him.

I was examining what you were like; you have been found out. You have revealed yourself to yourself; you have seen and considered yourself. You are not prepared to share your money with your neighbor.

But what does kindly avarice answer me? What does it answer me? “If I share with him, there will be less for both him and me. What I love will be diminished; neither will he have everything nor will I have everything. But because I love him as myself, I wish him to have as much as I have, so that what is mine is not diminished and he is made equal to me.”

# CHAPTER VII

## Envy, a Diabolical Vice Arising from Pride; Wishing Well to the Needy but Giving Nothing

You wish for something that costs you nothing—and would that you were speaking or wishing truthfully! For I fear that you may be envious. How can your happiness be shared, when another’s happiness torments you? When your neighbor begins to grow wealthy, and begins, as it were, to rise and follow after you, do you not fear that he may catch up with you? Do you fear that he may surpass you? Certainly you love your neighbor as yourself.

But I am not speaking of the envious [Note: [Col. 0673] According to Erasmus, Lyons, and Venice: “But I shall not speak of the envious.” M.]. May God avert this plague from the hearts of all human beings, much more from those of Christians: a diabolical vice, for which the devil alone is guilty, and guilty beyond all pardon. For the devil is not told, in order to condemn him, “You committed adultery; you stole; you seized another’s estate,” but, “You envied a human being who was standing upright when he fell.” Envy is a diabolical vice, but it has a mother of its own. Its mother is called pride. Pride makes people envious. Strangle the mother, and the daughter will not exist.

This is why Christ taught humility. I am not speaking, then, to the envious; I am speaking to those who wish others well. I am speaking to those who wish their friends well, wishing them to possess as much as they themselves possess. They wish the needy well, wishing them to have as much as they do, but they do not want to give them anything from what they possess.

Do you boast, Christian man, because you wish others well? A beggar who wishes you more good, while possessing nothing, is better than you. You are willing to wish well to one who receives nothing from you; give something to the one who wishes you well. If wishing well is good, repay the favor.

A poor man wishes you well—why are you afraid? I add something: you are in the house of instruction. I add something to what I have said [Note: [Col. 0673] According to Erasmus, Lyons, and Venice: “I add another point to what I said.” M.]: Give to the one who wishes you well; it is Christ. The one who asks this of you is the one who gave you what you have. Be ashamed. Though rich, he wished to become poor, so that you would have poor people to whom you might give.

Give something to your brother; give something to your neighbor; give something to your companion. You are rich; he is poor. This life is a road, and you are walking together.

# CHAPTER VIII

## The Burden of Riches Must Be Reduced by Giving to the Poor; the Cruel Excuse of the Avaricious Concealed under the Name of Piety

But perhaps you say: “I am rich; he is poor.” You are walking together, are you not? What does “I am rich; he is poor” mean except “I am burdened; he is unencumbered”? “I am rich; he is poor.” You are calling attention to your burden; you are praising your weight. And what is worse, you have tied your burden tightly to yourself; that is why you cannot extend your hand.

You load yourself, you bind yourself—and what do you boast about? What do you praise yourself for? Loosen your bonds; reduce your burden. Give to your companion: you help him and lighten yourself.

While you praise your burden in these words, Christ is still asking and receiving nothing. You put forward the name of piety in cruel words and say, “What about my children? What am I to preserve for them?” I set Christ against this objection; he sets his children before me. Is this great justice—that your son should have something with which to indulge himself while your Lord is in need?

“For whatever you did for one of the least of mine, you did for me.” Have you not read this? Have you not paid attention? “Whatever you did not do for one of the least of mine, you did not do for me” (Matthew 25:40, 45). Have you not read it? Have you not been afraid?

Look: someone is in need, and you are counting your children. Finally, count your children and add one among them—your Lord. You have one: let him be second. You have two: let him be third. You have three: let him be fourth. You want none of this.

See how you love your neighbor, whom you would make your companion in this destruction.

### 9.

What shall I say to you—“You love your neighbor”? What will you whisper into his ears, avaricious man, except this: “My son, or brother, or father, it is good for us that, while we live here, things go well for us. As much as you have, so much will you be. Break the moon and make your fortune”? These are the things you will whisper to your neighbor, things you did not learn in the house of instruction and did not hear here.

# CHAPTER IX

## The Harmful Conversations of the Avaricious Must Be Avoided

I do not want you to love your neighbor in this way. If only I could arrange matters so that you were joined to no one! “Bad conversations corrupt good morals” (1 Corinthians 15:33). But I cannot prevent you from joining yourself to anyone into whose ears you whisper these evil things—things you do not wish to unlearn, and which you not only refuse to have unlearned but even desire to teach.

I do not want to—or rather, I do want to—but I cannot separate you from the ears of others. I must warn those whose ears you seek, whose ears you strive to penetrate, and through whose ears you intend to enter their hearts.

O you who receive sound teaching in the house of instruction: “Fence your ears with thorns” (Sirach 28:28). Bad conversations corrupt good morals: fence your ears with thorns. Fence them—and fence them with thorns—so that anyone who dares to enter improperly may not merely be repelled but also pricked.

Repel him from yourself. Say: “You are a Christian; I am a Christian. We did not receive this in the house of instruction; we did not learn this in that school which we entered freely. We did not learn this under that teacher whose chair is in heaven. Do not say such things to me, or do not come near me.” This is what it means to fence your ears with thorns.

### 10.

I shall turn to that man. You are avaricious; you love money. Do you wish to be blessed? Love your God. Money does not make you blessed; you make it adorned, not it you blessed.

But because you love money greatly, and I see that you are proceeding wherever desire commands, lazy man, proceed wherever love commands. Look back and see how great the difference is between your money and your God.

This sun is more beautiful than your money, and yet this sun is not your God. Moreover, if this light is more beautiful than your money, how much more beautiful is the one who made this light? Or do you perhaps wish to compare your money with the light?

Look: the sun has set. Show me your money. It shines, and I remove the lamp during the night; now, rich man, show me your riches. If you are deprived of light, if you have no means by which to see what you possess, where are your riches?

# CHAPTER X

## A Sharp Rebuke of Certain Blind Avaricious Men; How God Is to Be Loved as Money Is Loved; Beating the Breast without Reforming Oneself Strengthens Sin Rather Than Removing It

And yet the dreadful depth of avarice is not visible to the eyes, and it teems in the hearts [Note: [Col. 0674] Manuscripts: “It is not visible to the eye, and it teems in the heart.”].

We have seen blind avaricious men. Let it be explained to me how the avaricious are blind, since they do not see. One who has and does not have is nevertheless blind through avarice. Why? Because he believes that he possesses; he is avaricious. Faith makes him rich: he is rich by believing, not by seeing.

How much better would it be to turn that faith toward God [Note: [Col. 0675] The Cistercian manuscript: “How much better does faith turn toward God?”]! You do not see what you possess, and I preach God to you in the same way. You do not yet see; love, and you will see.

You love money, blind man, though you will never see it. You possess it blindly; you will die blindly; what you possess you will leave behind here. You did not hold it even while you were alive [Note: [Col. 0675] The printed editions add: “how much more do you lose,” which is absent from the manuscripts], because you did not see what you had.

### 11.

What is said to you about God? Wisdom itself says this to you: “Love him as money” (Proverbs 2:4). It is unworthy and insulting to compare wisdom with money; but love is being compared with love.

I see that you love money here in such a way that, at money’s command, you undertake labors, endure fasts, cross the sea, and entrust yourselves to winds and waves. I have something by which I may choose what you love, but I do not have anything to add to the love with which you love.

“Love me in this way; I do not want to be loved more,” says God. I speak to the wicked; I speak to the avaricious: “You love money; love me just as much.” Certainly I am incomparably better. I do not want a greater love from you; love me as much as you love money.

Let us at least be ashamed, confess, and beat our breasts—not so that we may make a pavement over our sins. For whoever beats his breast and does not reform strengthens his sins rather than removing them.

Let us beat our breasts, strike ourselves, and reform ourselves, lest the one who is the teacher strike us later. For we have said what is learned here; now let us consider why it is learned [Note: [Col. 0675] Erasmus, Lyons, and Venice: “For we have already said what is learned here and why it is learned.” In Leuven, the final words “why it is learned” are absent from the text. M.].

# CHAPTER XI

## How Common and How Vain It Is to Learn Letters in Hope of Temporal Advantage; Fear of Death

### 12.

Why did you go to school? Why were you beaten, brought there by your parents, sought when you ran away, found and dragged back, and brought there stretched out? Why were you beaten? Why did you endure so many hardships in childhood?

“To learn.”

What would you learn?

“Letters.”

Why?

“So that money might be obtained, or honor acquired, and high rank and status maintained.”

See: for something destined to perish, you learned a perishable thing with such great effort and amid such great punishments. And the one who dragged you to your punishments loved you. The very one who loved you dragged you to your punishments; he did it out of love so that you would be beaten, so that you would learn. What would you learn? Letters.

“Are letters good?”

“They are good.”

I know what you will say to me: “Then why have you bishops learned letters? Why do you now expound the divine Scriptures through that very learning?” [Note: [Col. 0675] According to Erasmus, Lyons, and Venice: “Have you not read? Have you not expounded?” M.]

Indeed—but we did not learn letters for this purpose. For when our parents sent us to school, they did not say to us, “Learn letters so that you may have the means to read the Lord’s books” [Note: [Col. 0675] Erasmus, Lyons, Venice, Leuven, and the Benedictine editions do not have *possitis* in the text; a marginal note indicates that it should be supplied. M.] [Col. 0676]. Nor do Christians themselves say this to their children. What do they say? “Learn letters.”

Why?

“So that you may be a man.”

What? Am I now an animal? When I say, “So that you may be a man,” I mean, “So that you may be distinguished among men.” Hence the proverb: “As much as you have, so much will you be.” You should have as much as others, or as much as the few; more than others, or more than the few. From this you should have honor; from this, status.

And where will all these things be when death comes? How it goads us! How this fear interrupts us! How the very name I have mentioned has struck every heart! How you have shown your fear by your groaning! I heard it; I heard it. You groaned; you fear death.

If you fear it, why do you not take care? You fear death. What are you afraid of? It will come. Whether I fear it or do not fear it, it must come; sooner or later, it will come. If you fear it, you will not make the thing you fear cease to exist.

# CHAPTER XII

## Death Is Good If a Good Life Has Preceded It

Fear instead what, if you do not wish it, will not occur.

What is that?

Sin.

Fear sin, because if you love sins, you will rush into another death—a death to which you could have avoided coming if you had not loved sins.

But now, in your perversity, you love death more than life.

“God forbid,” you say. “Who is there who loves death more than life?”

Perhaps I can prove that you love death more than life. Here is how I prove it.

You love your tunic and want it to be good. You love your estate and want it to be good. You love your son and want him to be good. You love your friend and want him to be good. You love your house and want it to be good.

What is this, then? You also want to have a good death. Every day you pray that, since death is coming, God may grant you a good death, and you say, “May God avert a bad death from me.”

Therefore you love your death more than your life. You fear dying badly, but you do not fear living badly. Reform your bad living; fear a bad death. But do not be afraid: the one who has lived well cannot die badly.

I firmly affirm this; I dare to say, “I believed, and therefore I spoke”: the one who has lived well cannot die badly.

Now you say to yourself: “Have not many just people perished in shipwreck?” [Note: [Col. 0676] Erasmus, Lyons, and Venice read *num* three times here and below, instead of *non*. M.]

Certainly, the one who has lived well cannot die badly.

“Have not many just people been killed by the sword of an enemy?”

Certainly, the one who has lived well cannot die badly.

“Have not many just people been killed by robbers? Have not many just people been torn apart by beasts?”

Certainly, the one who has lived well cannot die badly.

And I answer: Do you think these deaths are bad—perishing in shipwreck, being struck by the sword, being torn apart by beasts? Does such a death seem bad to you? Did not the martyrs undergo these deaths, whose anniversaries we celebrate? What kind of death did they not undergo?

And yet, if we are Christians, if we remember that we are in the house of instruction—whether we are here or whether we are listening here—if, when we leave this place, we do not forget, if we remember what we hear here, do we not call the martyrs blessed?

Examine the deaths of the martyrs with the eyes of the flesh: they died badly. Ask the eyes of faith: “Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints” (Psalm 115:10, 15) [Col. 0677].

Whatever it is that you dread in death, do not dread it at all if you imitate them. Act so that you may have a good life; and whatever occasion comes for you to depart from this body, you will go out to rest, you will go out to blessedness—a blessedness that has neither fear nor end.

It may seem that the rich man in purple and fine linen had a good death, but the death of the thirsty man longing for a drop of water amid torments was bad. It may seem that the poor man lying before the rich man’s gate, among the tongues of dogs, in hunger and thirst and longing for crumbs from the table, had a bad death—a bad death, a death to be avoided.

Look to the end. You are a Christian; direct the eye of faith. It happened that the poor man died and was carried by angels into Abraham’s bosom.

What benefit was the marble tomb to the rich man thirsting in hell? What harm were the poor man’s rags, covered with the discharge of his sores, to him as he rested in Abraham’s bosom? From far away he saw the one whom he had despised when he saw him lying there (Luke 16:19–24).

Now choose death. Tell me: who died well, and who badly? I think the poor man did better than the rich man.

Or do you wish to be buried amid spices and thirst in hell?

You answer: “God forbid.”

I think that is what you will say. Therefore you will learn to die well if you have learned to live well. For the reward of a good life is eternal.

# CHAPTER XIII

## Some Hearers Learn from the Word; Others Receive It Badly

### 14.

Those who learn are Christians. Those who hear and do not learn—what concern are they to the sower? The sower’s hand is not frightened by the road; stones do not frighten it; thorns do not frighten it. He casts what is his.

Whoever fears that the seed may fall on bad soil never reaches good soil. We too say this: we cast seeds; we scatter seeds. There are those who despise, those who criticize, and those who mock. If we fear them, we have nothing to sow and will be hungry at harvest.

Therefore let the seed reach good soil. I know that the one who hears and hears well both fails and advances: he fails with respect to iniquity and advances toward truth; he fails with respect to the world and advances toward God.

# CHAPTER XIV

## Who the True Teacher Is

### 15.

Who is the teacher who teaches? Not just any man, but an apostle. Clearly, an apostle—and yet not an apostle. “Do you wish to receive proof of the one who speaks in me, namely Christ?” (2 Corinthians 13:3).

It is Christ who teaches; he has his chair in heaven, as I said shortly before. His school is on earth, and his school is his body. The head teaches its members; the tongue speaks to its feet.
