It is Christ who teaches. Let us listen, fear, and act.

And do not despise Christ himself, who for your sake was born in the flesh and wrapped in the garments of mortality; for your sake he hungered and thirsted; for your sake, wearied, he sat at the well; for your sake, tired, he slept in the boat; for your sake he heard unworthy insults; for your sake he did not turn away the spittle of men from his face; for your sake he received blows upon his face; for your sake he hung upon the wood; for your sake he poured out his soul; for your sake he was placed in the tomb.

Do you perhaps despise all these things in Christ? Do you wish to know who he is? Recall the Gospel you heard: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30).

### 16.

Let us turn toward the Lord and entreat him for ourselves and for all his people standing with us in the courts of his house. May he deign to guard and protect them through Jesus Christ, his Son, our Lord, who lives and reigns with him forever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 0677]

## Saint Aurelius Augustine, Bishop of Hippo: On the New Song, the Return to the Heavenly Homeland, and the Dangers of the Journey—a Sermon to Catechumens

[Note: [Col. 0677] The sermons *On the New Song*, *On Wednesday*, *On the Flood*, and *On the Barbarian Time* were found and edited in the same manuscripts that contain the four sermons on the Creed addressed to catechumens.]  
[Note: [Col. 0677] We also compared all the editions mentioned at the beginning of *Retractions* and *Confessions*, volume 1. M.]  
(C, G, S)*

# CHAPTER I

[Col. 0677]

## 1. Passing from the Oldness to the Newness

Everyone who desires Christ’s baptism longs for a new life. Therefore let him pass from oldness so that he may arrive at newness.

There was first an old covenant, an old song, and an old man. Now there is a new covenant, a new song, because there is a new man.

Let us demonstrate what we are saying by testimonies from the holy Scriptures. The prophet Jeremiah says: “Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, and I will establish a new covenant with the house of Judah” (Jeremiah 31:31).

The prophet David also says: “O God, I will sing a new song to you” (Psalm 143:9), and again: “Sing to the Lord a new song” (Psalm 95:1).

The apostle Paul likewise says: “Strip off the old man and put on the new” (Colossians 3:9–10), and elsewhere: “The old things have passed away; behold, new things have come to be” (2 Corinthians 5:17).

What old things have passed away? What new things have come to be?

If a spiritual hearer is present, he not only understands but also sees what has come to be new. But if a fleshly hearer is present, one who understands everything through the eyes of the flesh and nothing through the mind’s vision, he responds mockingly:

“Please tell me what new things have come to be. Do I see any other heaven than before, or stars shining with a new brilliance? Does not the sun complete the day along the same courses, and the moon complete the night along the same paths? Has the sea crossed its boundaries and limits, or has the face of the earth been changed so as to produce unfamiliar plants? Is not the day completed in twelve hours as it was from the beginning, with summer passing through the same increases and winter through the same decreases? The human race itself, with some dying and others succeeding them, brings its allotted days to an end.

“Since everything proceeds just as it was established from the beginning, preserving its movements and limits, what is the meaning of what is preached to us: ‘The old things have passed away; behold, new things have come to be’?”

Answer the one who asks us such things, O Paul. Since I am less able to answer, I beg you: answer on my behalf.

Listen to the apostle: “Why do you seek, fleshly hearer, to look through the eyes of the flesh? Raise the vision of your mind so that you may understand what is said: ‘The old things have passed away; behold, new things have come to be.’”

What old things have passed away? What new things have come to be?

“The first man,” he says, “was from the earth, earthly; the second man is from heaven, heavenly” (1 Corinthians 15:47).

Adam has passed away—the old man made from clay. Christ has come—the God-man sent from heaven. The oldness of minds has passed away; the newness of believers has arrived. Carnal life has passed away; spiritual life has succeeded it.

Is this a small newness, demonstrated in the God-man in such a way that, by dying, he took upon himself your oldness; by rising, he displayed your newness; and by ascending, he confirmed your glory?

“The old things have passed away.” What old things have passed away? You were children of Adam, carnal children.

“New things have come.” What new things? You are being made children of God, spiritual children.

“The old things have passed away”: you were earth. “Behold, new things have come to be”: you have now almost become heaven. “The heavens declare the glory of God” (Psalm 18:1).

Do not think it impossible that, although you are earthly, you may become heavenly. Can the one who made earth and heaven from nothing not make heaven from earth?

“The old things have passed away”: you worshiped stones. “New things have come”: you worship the true God.

“The old things have passed away”: mortality has passed away. “New things have come”: immortality has been promised.

“The old things have passed away”: all flesh had perished through the woman together with the man who sinned. “New things have come”: flesh has been restored, with a virgin giving birth without a man.

“The old things have passed away”: the region of oldness has passed away. “New things have come”: Jerusalem, the heavenly city of newness, succeeds it.

You desire to arrive at this new city, you who have given your names to be enrolled.

# CHAPTER II

## 2. Let Us Hurry toward the Homeland: The Fitting Out of the Ship

Come, my brothers, let us ardently desire our own homeland. Let us endure this pilgrimage, which still keeps us away from it; let us not love it. Nevertheless, let us hurry.

There is no reason to remain here, nor can you find anything in this world that you are now able to love. For the love of parents, spouses, children, and possessions either imposes great labor upon some or produces great fear. There is no reason to remain here.

For it is better to hasten toward eternal things than, by remaining here, to be overtaken by the world’s ruin [Col. 0680].

Let us prepare provisions, seize and board the ship—faith together with the cross [Note: [Col. 0680] Thus the manuscripts. Erasmus has “faith together with the cross”; Leuven has “the faith together with the cross.”]. Let the anchor of our hope of salvation not be absent. Let us stretch out the ropes of various virtues. Let us gather the sails of love [Note: [Col. 0680] The Divion manuscript has “let us place them,” and somewhat later, “he was placing the sails.” The Gemmeticensis manuscript has “let us cultivate,” and below, “he cultivated the sails.”]. Let us invoke the favorable wind, the word of God. Let us pump out the bilge of sins; through almsgiving let conscience be cleansed.

Let nothing impede the course of our ship; let us work with our hands as we are able [Note: [Col. 0680] In the manuscripts: “so that we may be able to do this.”]. The one who said, “With my hands before him through the night, and I was not deceived” (Psalm 76:3), was pumping out the bilge with his own hands.

Let us not neglect our sins. They are small, but they are many. A single powerful wave breaking in can overwhelm the ship and threaten shipwreck; but water flowing in through cracks and reaching the bilge does the same thing if it is not repeatedly drained.

Therefore let the bilge be pumped out; let mercy not be neglected, because “almsgiving frees from death, and it itself cleanses sins” (Tobit 4:11).

May Christ’s grace be our protection. Let us sweetly sing our sailors’ song, “Alleluia,” so that joyful and secure we may enter our eternal and most blessed homeland.

Let the soul not fear this great sea—namely, the world, whose waves and storms we experience as the hostile powers of the world. Many saints, trusting in God, have already despised these waves; many have trampled them; many, walking securely upon its waters, have reached their homeland.

But a strong wind and great storm arise: each person’s own desire. Faith wavers on the sea. Let Peter cry out within you, “Lord, I am perishing!” He will give his hand to the one who is sinking, and the one who for our sake deigned to walk upon the waters will not allow him to perish (Matthew 14:25–32).

Look at the apostle Paul, not only demonstrating this ship but also boarding it and inviting very many others aboard.

When he said, “Having food and clothing, let us be content with these” (1 Timothy 6:8), what else was he showing than that suitable provisions should be loaded?

When he said, “Far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me and I to the world” (Galatians 6:14), he was boarding the ship.

When he said, “Clothe yourselves, as God’s chosen ones, with kindness, humility, patience, and gentleness” (Colossians 3:12), what else was he doing than stretching out the ropes?

When he said, “Faith, hope, and love remain; and the greatest of these is love” (1 Corinthians 13:13), he was gathering the sails.

When he said, “Let the word of God dwell in you richly” (Colossians 3:16), he was invoking a favorable wind.

When he said, “Therefore, while we have time, let us do good to all without growing weary” (Galatians 6:10), and, “Work with your own hands” (1 Thessalonians 4:11), what else was he commanding than that the bilge be pumped out?

When he said, “By grace you have been saved” (Ephesians 2:8), he was imploring protection.

When he said, “Singing in your hearts to the Lord with psalms and hymns” (Ephesians 5:19), he was teaching the holy sailors’ song.

When he said, “In hope we were saved” (Romans 8:24), he was fastening the anchor in the hearts of believers.

When he said, “Jerusalem above is free, and she is our mother” (Galatians 4:26), he was pointing out the homeland itself.

When he said, “Where, O death, is your contest? Thanks be to God, who has given us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Corinthians 15:55, 57), he was no longer in danger at sea but was already rejoicing in his own homeland.

O excellent pilot, O most beautiful master and teacher! You taught and you acted; and for that reason you arrived quickly, because you yourself first did what you taught.

# CHAPTER III

## 3. The Overland Road to the Homeland and the Appropriate Beast of Burden

If someone, as often happens, avoids sailing, dreads the unfamiliar waves of the sea, and desires to complete the journey by a route through which he may reach his homeland—even if more slowly—I shall show him the way. Indeed, the way itself shows itself.

Look: in the Gospel the Savior cries out, “I am the way” (John 14:6). You have the way; walk. Yet be vigilant and tame your beast of burden, your flesh, for your soul rides upon it.

If, on this mortal road, you were riding an animal that wanted to throw you down by bucking, would you not, in order to travel safely, withhold food from the raging beast and tame by hunger what you could not control with the bridle?

Our flesh is our beast of burden. We are traveling to Jerusalem. Often the flesh carries us away and tries to drive us from the road [Note: [Col. 0681] Perhaps “throw us off.”].

Let us therefore restrain such a beast with fasts. Look at that pilot and traveler, the apostle Paul; see him taming his beast. “In hunger and thirst, in frequent fasts,” he says (2 Corinthians 11:27); “I chastise my body and bring it into servitude” (1 Corinthians 9:27).

So you also, who desire to walk, tame your flesh and walk. For you walk if you love. We do not run toward God with our feet but with our affections.

# CHAPTER IV

## 4. The Various Kinds of Travelers

This road of ours seeks travelers. It hates three kinds of people: one who remains behind, one who turns back, and one who wanders off.

With the Lord’s help, may our steps be rescued and defended from these three evil kinds. When we are traveling, one walks more slowly and another more quickly, but both are walking.

Those who remain behind must be stirred up; those who turn back must be recalled; those who have gone astray must be led onto the road; the slow must be encouraged; the swift must be imitated.

Whoever does not advance has remained on the road. Whoever perhaps turns away from a better purpose toward what he had previously abandoned as worse has gone back. Whoever abandons the faith has wandered from the road.

Let us have concern both for the slow and for the swifter, provided that they are traveling.

Who is the one who does not advance? The one who thinks himself wise; the one who says, “What I am is sufficient for me”; the one who does not heed him who says, “Forgetting what lies behind and stretching toward what lies ahead, I pursue the goal for the prize of God’s call in Christ Jesus” (Philippians 3:13–14).

He said that he was running; he said that he was pursuing. He did not remain behind; he did not look back. Far be it that he should have gone astray, since the one who both held and showed the way himself was teaching it.

And so that we might imitate his speed, he says: “Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ” (1 Corinthians 11:1).

Therefore, beloved, we think that we are traveling along the road with you. If we are slow, pass us; we are not jealous—we are looking for people whom we may follow. But if you think that we are proceeding quickly, run with us. There is one destination toward which we are all hurrying, both those who walk slowly and those who walk quickly.

Who are those who turn back? Those who return from self-restraint to impurity; those who turn away from the holy and singularly good purpose of virginity toward the degradations of pleasure, corrupting both their minds and their flesh.

The apostle Peter rebukes them, saying: “It would have been better for them not to know the way of salvation than, after knowing it, to turn back” (2 Peter 2:21).

O evil of looking back! Lot’s wife, who had been rescued from the Sodomites, looked back against the commandment; she lost what she had escaped. And not undeservedly was she suddenly changed into a pillar of salt (Genesis 19:26), unless it was so that she might preserve fools by her example as well.

Who are those who wander? All heretics, who have abandoned the road of truth and, wandering through the desert, act as robbers, capture souls in sins, and prevent anyone from reaching the homeland. They have become wolves along the paths, clothed in sheep’s clothing, though inwardly they are ravenous wolves; they preach Christ as the way, but lead those who follow them to death.

# CHAPTER V

## 5. How False Preaching Can Be Distinguished from True Preaching

If someone says here, “What am I to do? I cannot determine. Here is a man preaching Christ and preaching the way; he says that he is Christ’s disciple and that he announces the truth. Why should I not follow someone who preaches such things?” I answer: Because his tongue says one thing and his conscience another.

“How do I know that?” you ask. “Can I examine consciences? I hear Christ from him; what I hear, I believe; what I hear, I hold.”

Do not let the son of falsehood deceive you, if you are a son of truth. Learn now, Christian, since you desire both to hear and to see Christ.

If someone preaches Christ to you, pay attention and consider what kind of Christ he preaches and where he preaches him. For Christ is the truth (John 14:6), and he is preached through the holy Scriptures—not in corners, not secretly, but openly and publicly.

“For he placed his tent in the sun” (Psalm 18:6); that is, he established his Church in the open. Now look at the one who preaches Christ to you, and let him say what kind of Christ he preaches.

# CHAPTER VI
### 6. The Error of the Manichaeans

Behold the Manichaean heretic, who by his teaching promises to lead you into the truth, yet declares Christ himself to be deceptive. “He did not have,” he says, “a true body; he was a phantom, he was a spirit.” And the most wicked Manichaean denies that a true body was in him.

O most wicked Manichaean heretic, if you do not wish to believe the Truth saying to his disciples, “Touch me and see, because a spirit does not have bones and flesh, as you see me having” (Luke 24:39), then, as I have said, if you do not wish to believe the Truth, believe the Jew who crucified him. For when you say, “Christ was God, not man,” the Jew says, “He was not God, but man.” The Catholic Church, convicting both, says: “I hold the truth: Christ is both God and man.”

But you, Manichaean, on what grounds do you prove that Christ was a spirit? Did a spirit receive slaps? Did a spirit wear a crown of thorns? Did a spirit carry his own cross? If he was a spirit, whose garments did the soldiers divide? If he was a spirit, how, when he gave up his spirit, did his body hang lifeless on the cross for nearly half a day [Col. 0683]? If he was a spirit, how was his side pierced by a lance? How was he received by Joseph for burial? How was he placed in a tomb? A spirit cannot undergo any of these things.

Just as these things were foretold about him earlier through the Prophets, so also they came to pass. You err exceedingly, falsehood; in everything truth surpasses you. So then, heretic: according to your teaching, has Truth lied, while you preach the truth? And where do you preach this? In hiding, in secret. If your preaching is supported by truth, let your doctrine be public. Show me your Church.

But we know what you do, deceived and deceivers. The Apostle Paul exposed you when he said: “For the things they do secretly, it is shameful even to mention” (Ephesians 5:12). It is shameful for us to mention them, but you do not cease to do them. Your disgrace is manifest; your shame has been stripped bare. Through both your confession and your own writings, your shameful doctrine has been made public to all. Would that your hearts might at some time be corrected!

## CHAPTER VII

### 7. The Error of the Arians

There are other heretics, the Arians, who do not wish Christ himself—the way by which one goes to the Father—to be equal to the Father according to his divinity. And although he himself says, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30), they say: “If Christ was sent, he is lesser; surely the one who sends is greater than the one who is sent.”

This argument is human, not divine authority. The operation of the Trinity is something else—something you, heretic, do not comprehend because you think according to the flesh. For you do not have a pure heart, nor one directed toward God.

Christ is said to have been sent insofar as he assumed humanity; insofar as he is God, he is equal to the Father. For where would the Father send him if he himself were not with the Son? Or where would the Son have come if he who says, “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me,” and, “Philip, whoever has seen me has seen the Father” (John 14:10, 9), were not there together with the Father? He is the one who says through the Prophet, “I fill heaven and earth” (Jeremiah 23:24), and of whom Solomon says, “He reaches mightily from end to end and orders all things sweetly. He reaches everywhere because of his purity” (Wisdom 8:1; 7:24).

But you, heretic, say that the one who sends is greater and the one who is sent lesser because you reckon in terms of intervals of time. Yet you err greatly in assigning temporal sequence to the one through whom times were made. If you confess the Father as God, the Son as God, and believe both Father and Son to be eternal, do not make the Son lesser in that which made you. He was made lesser for this reason: that he might redeem you.

“But he himself,” you say, “said, ‘The Father is greater than I’” (John 14:28). Understand this according to the humanity he assumed, and you will put aside your error. According to this humanity he says, “The Father is greater than I,” in accordance with what the Prophet says of him: “You made him a little less than the angels” (Psalm 8:6).

But tell me: according to what do you assert that he is lesser? If according to power, “the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5:22). If according to works, “all things were made through the Son.” If you believe this of your God according to time—because just as you are greater than your son, so he is greater than his Son—may God turn such a thought away from the ears of the faithful. Such things are unworthy to believe of God.

For if the Son, according to his divinity, is the Word of God, as the Evangelist John relates, “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1, 3), was there ever a time when the Father was without the Word? Or was there some beginning before that beginning, since the Son himself said that he was the beginning? For when the Jews asked, “Who are you?” he answered, “The Beginning” (John 8:25).

Therefore that which is written in Genesis, “In the beginning God made heaven and earth” (Genesis 1:1), is understood as referring to the Son, who said that he was the Beginning. Thus the Father is always God, and the Son is always God, because the Father was never at any time not Father, nor the Son at any time not Son.

When the Father begot the Son, he did not diminish himself; rather, he begot from himself another who was such as he, in such a way that he remained wholly in himself. The Holy Spirit, moreover, does not precede the one from whom he proceeds [Note: [Col. 0684] In the Dijon manuscript, a second hand has substituted *divisit* (“divided”). Perhaps read *praecidit* (“cut off”).], but comes forth whole from the whole; by proceeding he neither diminishes the one from whom he proceeds nor increases him by adhering to him.

And these three are one God, of whom the Prophet says: “You alone are the great God” (Psalm 85:10). But you, heretic, arrange degrees, divide the Trinity: make the Father greater, the Son lesser, and the Holy Spirit subsequent.

But we have already said something about the Son, that he is equal to the Father, and we have said what has occurred to us. Hear also about the Holy Spirit, whom you wish to be lesser than the Father and the Son. Surely the Holy Spirit himself is the Spirit of God. Hear also that he is together with the Father and the Son and is wholly everywhere.

“The Apostle John says, ‘God is Spirit’” (John 4:24). The Son himself also says through the Prophet, “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me” (Isaiah 61:1). He does not say “after me,” as though making the Spirit subsequent to himself or lesser, but says “upon me.” Hence the angel Gabriel also says to Mary: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you” (Luke 1:35).

The Prophet David likewise says: “Where shall I go from your Spirit, and where shall I flee from your presence? If I ascend into heaven, you are there; if I descend into the abyss, you are present” (Psalm 138:7–8). Therefore, if the Spirit of God is present in heaven, on earth, and in the underworld, together with him who says, “I fill heaven and earth” (Jeremiah 23:24), then the Trinity is one God.

But hear still further, heretic, by what you may be convicted—that the Trinity is one God. At the very beginning of the book of Genesis, which we mentioned, it is written: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth.” Behold God the Father, and the Son as the Beginning, in accordance with his saying that he was the Beginning.

But if you also seek the Holy Spirit: “The Spirit of God,” it says, “was borne over the waters.” When, then, it subsequently reads, “God said, ‘Let there be light,’” and “God formed from the earth,” and “God made,” this demonstrates that the works of the Trinity are inseparable.

This is demonstrated still more clearly in what follows. For when the time came for the human being to be formed, Scripture says: “And God said, ‘Let us make man according to our image and likeness.’” It did not say, “Let me make [man] according to my image and likeness,” so that only the Father would be understood; nor did it say, “Let it be made,” as though he were commanding the Son, through whom all things were made; nor is it said, “They made,” as though each person contributed a separate work to it. Rather, when it said, “Let us make man according to our image and likeness,” it indicated that the Trinity is one God. Immediately it adds: “And God made man; according to his image he made him” (Genesis 1) [Col. 0685].

Behold, through the holy Scriptures the Trinity is proclaimed as one God. May the Arian, at last convicted, be confounded.

But hear still further, heretic, the Apostle Paul convicting you and teaching me. Hear what he says about God the Son: “Although he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized” (Philippians 2:6). He proclaims him equal; you assert him to be lesser. Whom should one believe—the Apostle or you? You, whom the whole world has rejected, or him, whom the whole world has received?

Let your perversity, convicted at last, therefore yield, because evangelical and apostolic doctrine has already possessed the whole world.

## CHAPTER VIII

### 8. The Heresy of the Pelagians

Another den of robbers, not of good men—the heretics called Pelagians—must also be pointed out and avoided, for this is their perverse doctrine.

When Scripture says, “Cursed is the man who places his hope in man” (Jeremiah 17:5), and, “Let the one who glories, glory in the Lord” (1 Corinthians 1:31), these men, on the contrary, promise that a person will not incur this curse if he relies upon himself or glories in himself.

But why should we say much against them? Their father, the devil, made the same promise to that first man: “You will certainly not die; you will be like gods.” He despised God, believed the serpent, and lost what he had received.

If that man was not cautious then, let humanity now be cautious, having learned by experience. God hates those who presume upon their own strength. What free will unaided can accomplish was demonstrated in Adam himself. It is sufficient for evil; for good it is not sufficient unless it is aided by God.

For that first man received upright free will, and God placed before him, as Scripture says, fire and water: “Stretch out your hand to whichever you wish” (Sirach 15:17). He chose fire and abandoned water.

Behold the just Judge. What the human being freely chose, he received: he desired evil, and evil followed him.

Behold again that just Judge showing mercy. When he saw that humanity had condemned its entire stock in itself, as in its root, by misusing the freedom of its will, he himself, unasked, descended from heaven and healed the human being perishing through pride [Note: [Col. 0685] The manuscripts read: “the human race perishing through pride,” or “as it perished.”] by his humility. He led the wandering to the way; he leads exiles to their homeland.

Let human nature, therefore, not glory in itself, but let it glory in him who made it.

## CHAPTER IX

### 9. The Heretics Are Confounded with One Voice

Now, moreover, the other sects of heretics, who preach Christ as the way but wander far from the way, are convicted and confounded by one utterance of that true Way himself, who says:

“Many will say to me on that day, ‘Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, and in your name cast out demons, and in your name perform many mighty works?’ And then I will say to them, ‘I do not know you; depart from me, all you who have worked iniquity’” (Matthew 7:22–23).

You worked iniquity because you disturbed the unity of my Church.

## CHAPTER X

### 10. He Exhorts Those Who Are to Be Baptized to Strive Straight toward Their Homeland

But you, faithful offspring of the holy mother Catholic Church, spread throughout the whole world, flee all heresies. “If anyone preaches to you a gospel contrary to what you received, let him be anathema” (Galatians 1:9).

Make straight paths for your feet. Do not turn aside either to the right by presumption or to the left by despair. Run swiftly along the straight way, for it leads you to your homeland—that homeland whose citizens are angels, whose temple is God, whose splendor is the Son, whose love is the Holy Spirit; the holy city, the blessed city; the city where no friend perishes and no enemy is admitted; where no one dies, because no one is born; where no one grows weak, because everyone rejoices in incorruptible health.

When we have arrived there, we shall not hunger or thirst. The vision itself will be our satisfaction. We shall not sleep there, because we shall not labor there. No refreshment of any kind will be necessary where there will be no decline.

We shall live, reign, and rejoice. If it is so delightful merely to speak about it, what will it be to see it? To see God, to live with God, to live from God. For our life will be to praise God and to love without failing.

“For blessed are those,” says the Prophet, “who dwell in your house, Lord; forever and ever they will praise you” (Psalm 83:5).

Most beloved brothers, if we have labored with those who sail and provided guidance for travelers; if we have carefully pointed out the treacherous jaws of robbers—that is, of heretics; if you already see with the eyes of your hearts that heavenly homeland declared and shown to you—give us the fruit of our labor.

Give it back to us, brothers; give it back. We demand it of you. Such is our reward that we ask it of you, so that we are not ashamed to request it, nor you reluctant to bestow it.

By bestowing what we demand, you will increase it rather than suffer loss by failing to bestow it. What, then, is our reward? We do not seek your gold, your silver, your money, or anything belonging to you. Our reward is that, in that holy font, you assist us by your prayers.

---

## DOUBTFUL SERMONS

[Note: [Col. 0685] The following sermons—“On Wednesday,” “On the Cataclysm,” and “On the Barbarian Age”—are doubtful to us and appear to be interpolated. [On these matters, see above, cols. 625–626, the Admonition to the sermon “On the Creed.”]]

[Col. 0685]

# SERMON ON WEDNESDAY, OR ON THE CULTIVATION OF THE LORD’S FIELD (C, G, S)*

[Note: [Col. 0686] The old books likewise call it this, although at the end they add: “Here ends the sermon on the last Wednesday.”]

## CHAPTER I

### 1. The Cultivation of the Lord’s Field: What the Five Yokes of Oxen Signify

The field of the Church must be prepared for heavenly grace and spiritual rain, because the divine shower is near. Let us work, beloved, in this field entrusted to us [Col. 0687]. For we have been appointed to plant, water, plow, and cultivate new growth; but it belongs to God to give the increase.

The Apostle Paul, teacher of the Gentiles in faith and truth, taught us to carry out this cultivation of the Lord both by his own example and by his work and admonition, saying: “I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the increase”; and shortly afterward: “We are God’s fellow workers; you are God’s field, God’s building” (1 Corinthians 3:6, 9). Elsewhere he says: “Be my fellow workers, brothers, and observe those who so walk, as you have our example” (Philippians 3:17).

In this cultivation of the Lord, therefore, brothers—in which the Lord commanded us to work—let us work in such a way that we may deserve to receive the promised reward as a gift of grace. It is time: let us work, let us labor.

### 2. The Five Yokes of Oxen

Those five yokes of oxen which the man invited in the Gospel said he wanted to test and on that account excused himself from the supper (Luke 14:19)—because he had purchased them for himself, not for the cultivation of the Lord—we should yoke together in the field of the Lord. Let us plow the very hard earth with spiritual furrows; let us cast out the seed of God’s word; whatever thorns of evil desires we find, let us pull up, uproot, and set on fire with divine fire. Then, laboring in such a work, we may confidently say to the Lord our God:

“Lord, master of the household, since with your help we have completed the work you commanded, give back the reward you promised.”

What are those five yokes of oxen? The five yokes of oxen are the five bodily senses: sight in the eyes, hearing in the ears, smell in the nostrils, taste in the throat, and touch in the hands.

And these yokes are as follows: two eyes, two ears, twin nostrils, and two hands. Even in taste something twofold is found, since the flavor itself is distinguished by the judgment of the throat and palate.

These five yokes, then, turn over the earth when, serving their functions, they prepare the mind and the flesh either for rich crops, if the heavenly dew has poured down, or for dry thorns, if the earth remains parched; and their work will have consequences in the future.

[Note: [Col. 0687] Thus the Fulda manuscript. But Erasmus and several manuscripts have, instead of *parant* (“they prepare”), *peractam* (“completed”). Then, following Lovaniensis, they continue as follows: “either fertile, etc., or dry, etc.”, omitting *ad* (“for”).]

## CHAPTER II

### 3. The Sowing, Plowing, and Watering of the Lord’s Field

But since our Lord and master of the household has commanded us to scatter the seed of his word everywhere and without distinction over every clod of earth—for in the Gospel he introduces the likeness of this servant and says: “Behold, a sower went out to sow. And as he sowed, some fell among thorns, some on the way, some on rocky ground, and some on good soil”—and when he explained what the thorny soil was, namely, people who choke the seed of God’s word with the thorns of their desires and do not produce fruits of righteousness; and likewise gave the explanation corresponding to the likeness he had set forth concerning the other soil, the rocky ground and the trampled path [Note: [Col. 0687] According to Erasmus, Lyon, Venice, and Louvain, *reddens* (“giving back”) is read here. M.]—he came to the good soil and said:

“But what fell on good soil: these are those who, when they have heard the word of God, hold on to it and produce fruit” (Matthew 13:3, 23); “for it is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but the doers of the law will be justified” (Romans 2:13).

Therefore, beloved, let neither fear of thorns, nor stones and rocks, nor the hardest road frighten us, provided that, while sowing the word of God, we may at last reach good soil.

Receive the word of God, every field, every human being, whether barren or fertile. I scatter the seed; you must see how you receive it. I distribute it; you must see what kinds of fruits you return.

For it is better that you yourself give an account on your own behalf for what you have received than that, when we have not distributed it, it should rightly be said to us: “Wicked and lazy servant, you should have distributed it, and when I came I would have exacted it with interest” (Matthew 25:26–27).

But if you feel that you are barren, thorny, or dry soil, have recourse to your Creator. For this is now being done: that you may be renewed, made fertile, and watered by him who “made the desert into pools of water, and the dry land into outlets of water, and caused the hungry to dwell there; and they established a city as a dwelling place, and sowed fields, and planted vineyards, and produced a harvest of grain” (Psalm 106:35–37).

From what kind of earth? From that which was barren, thorny, and without water.

And you, every soul that approaches Christ, are thorny and dry soil. How do we prove that you are such? Recall the sentence that you received in your first parents, and you will discover what you have drawn from them: “Thorns and thistles it shall bring forth for you” (Genesis 3:18).

Or will you answer that you are not thorny soil? If you had no thorns, you would not place a crown of thorns upon the head of your Creator.

Since you too are such—burdened by a multitude of thorns, that is, of sins—this cultivation is therefore applied to you. For this reason you are plowed by the wood of the cross; for this reason you are prepared for heavenly rain, so that, once you have become fertile, you may not rejoice in your own merits, which are nothing, but, returning good fruits, may proclaim the grace of Christ.

Do you wish to know what kind of cultivation is applied to you, and what grace pours down upon you from above? Behold and recognize it: you are plowed by Christ’s cross when you are marked on the forehead with his sign; you are watered by his blood when you are baptized into his death. “For all of us,” says the Apostle, “who were baptized in Christ Jesus were baptized into his death” (Romans 6:3).

## CHAPTER III

### 4. How We Are Watered by Christ’s Blood; What “Amen” Means When Those Who Receive Christ’s Blood Respond

Much has been said in the statement, “You are watered by his blood.” Let us see how we can prove what we have said by means of some analogy. Faith must be given not to our words but to divine testimonies.

Behold, pay attention, beloved: that wicked and false disciple Judas, venal and a seller, thief and betrayer, purchased by the Jews so that he might be the devil’s slave together with them, receiving a price from the one who has no price—the seller of Christ’s blood—bought himself, as Scripture relates, a potter’s field with that very price, wishing to have some portion in this world, since he did not possess Christ as his complete inheritance in heaven.

He did not even possess that portion, because, conscious of such a great crime, he fastened a noose around his neck and, falling on his face, burst apart in the middle. Yet that field which he purchased was called the Field of Blood (Acts 1:16–19), because it was bought with the price of such blood.

The disciple sold the Master’s blood and with it bought a potter’s field. What does this mean? Do we suppose, beloved, that this action in that sale and purchase, or in Christ’s mystical Passion itself, is without significance?

Scripture says that Judas bought a potter’s field, and that field was called the Field of Blood. The earth itself cries out with what, and at what price, it was purchased; indeed, the price itself cries out, the blood itself cries out—Abel, that righteous man killed by his wicked brother, cries out.

For, beloved, when this likeness of Christ’s Passion and the wickedness of Judas and the Jews was displayed in those first two brothers, Cain and Abel, after the younger had been killed by his elder, after the innocent had been slain by the envious and the pious had been killed by the criminal, God questions Cain as though unaware and ignorant, and says: “Where is Abel, your brother?”

This voice does not belong to one who is ignorant, but to one who places the sin before the eyes of the wicked person, so that every human being who, even when admonished, does not wish to repent of evil may be without excuse.

“Where is Abel, your brother?” This was as though to say to him: “Acknowledge, Cain, that what you thought could be hidden from me could not be hidden from me. Acknowledge what you have done. At once repent, so that you may receive forgiveness.””

But he, hardened in understanding, obstinate in crime, wounded in soul by his perverse character, responds to God, who says, “Where is your brother?” and says, “I do not know. Am I my brother’s keeper?”

What are you saying, Cain? To whom are you saying, “I do not know”? You are speaking with the one whose eyes see everything. What is this that you say, “Am I my brother’s keeper?” By committing such acts you have driven the fear of God entirely away from you.

And the Lord says to him: “What have you done? The voice of your brother’s blood cries out to me from the earth.”

For if you had been your brother’s keeper, you would not have been his murderer. If you had recognized brotherhood, you would not have committed such a monstrous deed. If you had feared my judgment, you would not have committed parricide against your brother.

“The voice of your brother’s blood cries out to me from the earth. And now,” says the Lord, “you are cursed by the earth”—not “cursed is the earth,” but “you are cursed by the earth,” which has received your brother’s blood from your hand (Genesis 4:1–11).

Acknowledge now, earth, that you have been watered by the blood of the innocent. Convict the voice of the one who denies; receive the blood of the one who confesses.

Let Judas and the Jews now be questioned—or rather, let all the Jews be questioned in Judas. Let the Lord question Judas and say to him: “Judas, where is Christ, your brother?”

Or perhaps, wicked brother, you will say that Christ was not your brother? Let the Lord himself first convict you that he was your brother.

Tell us, Lord Jesus Christ, whether Judas was your brother. He answers: “If he was, he was; for he is not what he was, and if he was, he was. I said generally concerning all of them to my Father, ‘I will proclaim your name to my brothers’” (Psalm 21:23).

Behold, Judas: you have been convicted that Christ was your brother. Where is your brother? Answer; speak; follow; say what he also said: “I do not know. Am I my brother’s keeper?”

For neither were you his keeper, since you became both betrayer and seller. Say, “Am I my brother’s keeper?” so that the answer may also be given to you: “The voice of your brother’s blood cries out to me from the earth.”

For what does every human being say who is earth? The first human being was from earth, earthly; and “as was the earthly, so are the earthly” (1 Corinthians 15:47–48).

What does every human being who is earth say when he receives Christ’s blood? He says, “Amen.”

What is “Amen”? “It is true.”

What is true? That Christ’s blood was poured out.

Through whose action? Through the disciple Judas, who betrayed him.

By saying “Amen,” by crying out “It is true,” every human being who is earth says this.

Behold, Judas: the voice of your brother’s blood cries out to me from the earth.

We have proved that you are watered by his blood.

## CHAPTER IV

### 5. How Christ’s Blood Must Be Received: Stephen, Cyprian, Laurence, Perpetua, and Felicity

See, earth, how you receive this blood. For whoever receives it rightly receives a blessing, but whoever receives it wrongly acquires judgment for himself by drinking it.

This was also prefigured in that field of Judas, of which it was said that it was the Field of Blood. For it followed that it should be said: “Let his dwelling become desolate” (Acts 1:20).

If you belong to Judas, if you imitate his deeds, if you do not receive Christ’s blood with fear and trembling, you will be a desolate dwelling, accursed, rejected, and thorny.

But if you receive Christ’s blood with complete reverence, you will recognize that through it your sins are forgiven you, because the field which Judas bought was called the potter’s field: “Has the potter no power over the clay, from the same lump to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?” (Romans 9:21).

O earth watered by so great a blood, answer this great blood—not with words of excuse, as Cain and Judas did, but with words of confession, as the holy martyrs did.

Answer as blessed Stephen answered. In this field of the Lord, as a good cultivator, he labored greatly, bent his knee, and, wounded by stones from the rocky earth, gathered the stones into his body as though into his lap. Sweating in his labor and watering the earth with holy blood, he presented to the Lord a hundredfold harvest from his martyrdom.

Answer as Cyprian, Laurence, and the other holy boys and girls answered—every age and both sexes—who, receiving Christ’s blood, bearing witness and not denying Christ’s name, did not hesitate to pour out their own blood for the blood they had drunk. Together with Perpetua and Felicity, they deserved to reign forever.

When the angel revealed this in the Apocalypse, John saw a great multitude that no one could count. When he asked who they were, he received this answer: “These are,” it was said, “those who washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb” (Revelation 7:9, 14).

## CHAPTER V

### 6. The Soul Is Whitened and Adorned by Christ’s Blood; Christ Denied by Peter in His Passion

Now you recognize, Christian soul, how you too are made white by that blood, so that, beautiful in body and heart, you may ascend from Christ’s font, consecrated in blood.

For what flowed from the side of the crucified man? Blood and water: from the blood, redness; from the water, radiance [Col. 0690]. In these two sacraments individual souls are adorned, and from them that one beautiful bride, the Church, is made. To her it is said in the Song of Songs: “How beautiful you are, my sister, my beloved; how beautiful are your cheeks” (Song of Songs 4:1, 3).

And when he himself has made her such, and himself has given her this beauty, seeing her as she is, he exclaims as though in wonder and, asking those standing around, says: “Who is this who ascends whitened?” And they answer him: “Righteousness has loved you” (Song of Songs 8:5).

She is the queen who stood at your right hand, in a garment of gold, clothed round about with variety (Psalm 44:10), adorned with the varied languages of different nations.

Hearing the voice of her bridegroom saying, “Who is this who ascends whitened?” she herself is compelled modestly to answer and says to her bridegroom:

“You ask about me—who I am who have ascended whitened. I am the one whom you found ugly and made beautiful. I am the one whose prayers you heard when you caused me to sing in the Psalm, ‘You shall wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow’” (Psalm 50:9).

“Why, then, do you marvel at my beauty, when you know that it is your work? Why do you ask about what you yourself have done? You see me whitened: you washed me and made me white above snow.

“To see me ascending, I recognized you descending from heaven; I loved you hanging on the cross. Your humility became my exaltation; your ugliness became my beauty.

“For unless you, wounded, had descended from the cross, I, whitened, would not have ascended from the font.

“Truly it was said: ‘Love is strong as death’” (Song of Songs 8:6). How far did this bridegroom stoop, who, loving the ugly so greatly that he might make her beautiful, came even to the exit of death? “And the exits of death belong to the Lord,” it says (Psalm 67:21).

“For we saw him,” says the Prophet, “and he had no form or beauty” (Isaiah 53:2). Why do you marvel? Through love he became such.

### 7. Peter’s Fear of Christ’s Loss of Beauty and His Denial

Yet Peter feared this loss of beauty when, as the Lord foretold his Passion, he said: “Far be it from you, Lord; may God be gracious to you—this shall certainly not happen.”

But he rebuked the one who thought such thoughts and called the Apostle “devil,” saying: “Get behind me, Satan; for you do not think the things of God, but the things of men” (Matthew 16:22–23).

Peter supposed that all that beauty of divinity could somehow be swallowed up in the appearance of a human body, and he did not know that the great mystery was being accomplished: for this reason he would in a certain manner strip himself of that beauty, so that he might clothe with that very beauty the Church, the bride whom he deigned to unite to himself.

For by giving he did not lose what increased through being bestowed. He gave; she received. She found what she had not possessed, and he, by giving what he gave, did not lose it, because he rose from the dead with that same beauty.

Why are you terrified, Peter, as though Christ had lost that beautiful garment when you watched him hanging naked on the wood? Do not be terrified, do not fear, do not deny. Christ did not lose that garment of divinity and immortality on the cross, because he entrusted it as a dowry to his bride.

You saw him, Peter, without form or beauty, and immediately denied him—the one whom you had loved after abandoning all that was yours. And not merely once: standing in the high priest’s courtyard, questioned three times by a servant girl, you denied him.

But when, at the crowing of the rooster, he convicted you of presumption—he who had earlier foretold you would deny him—he looked upon you inwardly in your heart, and so that you might weep bitterly (Matthew 26:69–75), his very divinity was speaking silently with you within, as it were, and saying to you:

“Where is it, Peter, that ‘if you possess a friend, possess him in temptation’” (Sirach 6:7)? Where is it that “in his time of tribulation remain faithful to him, so that you may also be his fellow heir” (Sirach 22:29)? Where is it, Peter, that you said, “I will lay down my life for you” (John 13:38), and “I will go with you even to death” (Luke 22:33)?

How quickly you denied as though dead the one whom earlier you had confessed to be the living Son of God!

While he was speaking these things with you in your heart, divinity looked upon you, and humanity wept. Sweetness was recognized, and bitterness perished; love was received, and iniquity was erased; love returned, and fear was driven away.

Behold, suddenly the one whom he had denied because he had no form or beauty, he recognizes as risen, beautiful beyond the sons of men. He sees the bride joined to him, sees that garment of immortality—which Peter had earlier feared would perish—clothed upon her.

He recognizes that she is surrounded with such a garment, and Peter addresses that very bride, urging her to preserve the dignity of this garment. He says to the human soul: “Christ suffered for you, leaving you an example, so that you might follow his footsteps” (1 Peter 2:21).

Follow, bride; follow the footsteps of your bridegroom. Let no fear call you back from fellowship with your beloved. Love the one who loves you, because he first loved the one who did not love. Seek the one who seeks you, because he first sought the one who did not seek.

Seek him, and say to your bridegroom: “Where do you pasture your flock? Where do you lie down at midday? Otherwise I may become like one veiled among the flocks of your companions” (Song of Songs 1:6).

You whom she has loved thus, for whom you shed your blood, whose tabernacle you set in the sun (Psalm 18:6): “Let me not become like one veiled among the flocks of your companions.”

## CHAPTER VI
## 8. On Avoiding Heretics, Especially the Arians

Behold, while I ask you where you feed and where you lie down at noon, noon is Africa, which lies in the setting of the sun; and yet, because your name is praised from the rising of the sun to its setting (Ps. CXII, 3), there are those who proclaim you impurely, seeking what is theirs, not what is yours. While I seek you at noon—that is, in Africa—behold, the flocks of your companions, the most wicked schools of heretics, the fraud of the Manichaeans, the wickedness of the Pelagians, the proud assembly of the Arians, insult me as though they were covered—that is, as though they were unknown—and say to me, “Whom are you seeking? Are you seeking Christ? Behold, he is here; behold, he is there.”

But because you warned me, saying, “If they say, ‘Behold, he is here,’ or, ‘Behold, he is there,’ do not go after them” (Matt. XXIV, 23), and because I know that you are wholly everywhere, that you defend not parts but love unity, I have become unknown and, as it were, covered to them; and they mock me because they do not know you. And what is it of great consequence that I endure such an insult from them, when you continue to endure their insulting speech—those who do not wish you to be one with the Father, but, by dividing the Father and the Son, the bride and the bridegroom, incur great sacrilege and inflict great sickness upon their own soul? For they desire neither to have you as the one and only bridegroom, nor as a faithful and whole physician.

But you, Christian soul, who are about to rise from the most sacred font, drenched with radiance and beauty, exceedingly beautiful and white, preserve your beauty. Recognize what you were and what you will be; see that you do not abandon the table of your bridegroom. To remain beautiful, you shall eat his flesh daily; to possess eternal life, you shall drink his blood. See that you do not abandon this table.

Flee the many banquets of the heretics. And if many things are set out there through wicked disputations, they are either foul or half-eaten. For nothing there is whole, where the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit are not one. The table of your bridegroom has whole bread and a holy cup. Although we saw that this bread was broken and crushed in the Passion, it nevertheless remained whole in that indivisible unity of his with the Father.

Concerning this bread and this cup the Lord himself said: “The bread that I shall give is my flesh for the life of the world; and the cup that I shall sanctify is my blood, which shall be poured out for you for the remission of sins.” For earlier he had said: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you shall not have life in yourselves.” Hearing this saying but not understanding it, the disciples said: “This is a hard saying; who can hear it?” And many, scandalized by this saying, departed.

When Jesus saw this, he said to the others: “Do you also wish to go away?” Then Peter, who bore the figure of the holy Church, answered on behalf of all: “To whom shall we go? You have the word of life, and we leave you?” (John VI, 52–69.)

You see, beloved, what it means to go out and what it means to remain. Those who went out, because they did not understand the word of Christ, [Col. 0692] remained no longer disciples but heretics; those who persevered held fast to the word of life. Recognize your departure, heretics, because you preach our Christ as lesser. You also refused to stand with him, because you did not understand that Christ is one with the Father. Therefore you went outside, because you abandoned the word of life.

He does not remain in you who remains equal with the Father. Hear him himself, because he remains together with the Father. “If anyone loves me,” he says, “he will be loved by my Father, and I shall love him, and I and the Father shall come to him and make our dwelling with him” (John XIV, 21, 23).

Tell me, I beg you, Arian heretic: does this Trinity—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—dwell together in your one soul? For the Holy Spirit also dwells in us: “Do you not know,” says the Apostle, “that you are the temple of God and that the Holy Spirit dwells in you?” (I Cor. VI, 19.)

Or do you prepare separate dwellings in your heart for the Trinity, so that the greater Father may occupy the greater portion, the lesser Son the smaller, and the lower Holy Spirit the lowest? Then you no longer have one heart, but a double or triple one. Therefore the Trinity does not dwell there. Why? Because it is said: “Woe to the double-hearted” (Ecclus. II, 14)!

Senseless, foolish, witless man: fire, radiance, and heat dwell together and inseparably—not distinctly, but equally—in one lamp; and one Trinity, God, cannot dwell together in a human soul? If a dwelling worthy of the equal and indivisible unity of the Trinity is not found with you, it will be said to you: “Behold, your house shall be left to you desolate” (Matt. XXIII, 38).

For you do not build a temple for God from living stones, whom, by rebaptizing, you choke, dishonor, reject, lay waste, condemn, and exterminate. Nor do you follow the foundations of the Apostles, since they themselves are the pillars of the living God, upon which Wisdom built her house, so that the true temple might be constructed, in which there was the great sacrament of godliness. Concerning this temple he said to the Jews: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I shall raise it up” (John II, 19).

In your fathers *[Note: At [Col. 0692], Morel, *Elem. Critic.*, pp. 291–292, thinks that perhaps “parts” (*partibus*) should be read here. M.]* you do not have the cornerstone, whom you do not believe to be equal to the Father according to his divinity. Nor do you demonstrate that you possess with yourself, from the two wings of charity, love of God and neighbor, because you love neither God as he ought to be loved, nor your neighbor as yourself. For it is said: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your strength” (Matt. XXII, 37).

Give your heart to the Father, your soul to the Son, your strength to the Holy Spirit. Behold, you have offered three things to the Trinity, and from the three you have offered one human being as a sacrifice to the one Trinity; you have overcome the Arian heresy, since the Lord your God is not three gods but one Lord.

This is the holy structure; this is the true hall *[Note: Perhaps “sheepfold” (*caula*).]*, in which are Christ’s sheep, not the devil’s wolves.

## CHAPTER VII

### 9. He urges them to love the Church and to pray for peace and the liberation of their homeland

Beware, beloved, of the deceits of heretics; sheep of Christ, fear the ambushes of wolves. See that nothing has been withheld from your benefit, insofar as the Lord himself has granted it through the proclamation of the word of God. You have heard, approved, and proclaimed what Christ is and what the Church is. But why we should suffer such great evils, or for what merits of our sins we have been handed over into the hands of those who afflict us, we recognized and wept together when we spoke a very few days ago.

Even now the sound of our voice still rings in your ears concerning what you are to receive and what you are to become. We admonish you as brothers, entreat you as fathers, exhort you as sons. Do not lose so great a good. Let the love of Christ not grow cold in your hearts; let the love of this mother toward you not become sluggish—she who gives birth to you, who takes great care for the salvation of your soul, who directs your hope, who daily receives you when you return into her motherly embrace, who prepares spiritual food for you, and who desires to lead you to eternal fullness.

She wishes to present to God the Father [Col. 0693] sons without blemish, whom she deigns to nourish with such great care and solicitude. Love her with your whole heart; by loving her, love your fellow servants and your brothers with pure love, the ministers of God; and in return for our labor, pray for us at that most sacred font.

Pray for peace; pray for the liberation of this land; pray that he who is justly indignant may have mercy. New sons, while the Father rejoices in your holy [Col. 0694] birth, calm by your prayers and tears the one who is angry, whom we have felt taking severe vengeance.

In short, using the words of the holy Apostles, we commend you to God in the word of his grace, who is able to preserve in you what he himself has given (Acts XX, 32). To him be glory with the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

*[Note: Perhaps from the sermon “On the Barbarian Times.”]*

[Col. 0693]

## SERMON ON THE CATACLYSM FOR THE CATECHUMENS  
*(C, G, S)*

## CHAPTER I

### 1. After baptism, labor and warfare against vices remain

Since the day of your redemption is near, receive, beloved, those things that may instruct you, nourish your hearts, raise them up, and strengthen them for the fear of God. Let this fervor of so great a love not grow sluggish in your hearts.

Let no one think that it is enough to be a Christian merely because, having been instructed in these mysteries, he is reborn from water and the Spirit, and afterward abandons himself to various pleasures; and, made secure because he has fortified his soul with the sacrament of Baptism, fails to guard it against the deceits of the enemy. Rather, let him guard it himself as much as he can, and ask that it be guarded, lest it perish amid the storms and tempests of this world.

Someone has been baptized: the ship has been restored, caulked, fitted with sails, and sent out to sea; it needs a helmsman until it reaches the desired harbor. The sea—namely, this age—is dangerous not only because of storms and reefs, but also because it abounds in beasts lying in wait amid the passions. Let the sailors, already aroused to vigilance, now keep watch with every concern, every care, and every effort. Let Christ the helmsman also be invoked frequently, so that he himself may bring the ship, rescued from such great dangers, to the harbor of safety.

You have been baptized; you have been sealed with the royal mark; you have begun to receive provisions from the table of your King. Do not become a deserter, nor, like a delicate soldier, dissolve in pleasures, so that the enemy, the devil, may find you unarmed and relaxed. Rather, as a brave soldier, do whatever you can in this warfare, so that your valor—Christ—may not only protect you but may also advance others toward salvation.

Ask your King for spiritual weapons. “War,” he says, “is declared against you, in which you are to shine by fighting, so that through triumph you may reach complete peace.” You will not fight against one alone; for many adversaries will come out against you. You will fight against vices, and, as the blessed martyr Cyprian says, “If you have struck down avarice, lust will arise; and if you overcome lust, ambition will follow; and if ambition has been conquered by you, anger, jealousy, rivalry, envy, pride, drunkenness, together with their other destructive companions, will form a camp against you as one united force” (Cyprian, in the book *On Mortality*).

## CHAPTER II

### 2. The aids of the Christian soldier

But do not be afraid; you have something to do. Invoke the Lord of hosts. May he clothe you from on high with strength, so that you may utter this cry: “Though armies encamp against me, my heart will not fear; and though battle rise against me, in him I shall hope” (Ps. XXVI, 3).

In whom, unless in the Lord of hosts, who awaits his soldier as he fights in order to help him in his labor? You have been baptized, cleansed, anointed with oil; your body has been restored to the former condition of that first man before sin. Do not afterward become falsely secure.

You are brought forth to the contest; you will fight against the devil, the prince of vices, in the arena of this world. An immense multitude of people, belonging to both sides—Christ’s and the devil’s—awaits you as you wrestle. See every crowd hanging in intense attention to discover who will win.

Let the devil’s side not triumph over you. If you wish to win, do not presume upon yourself, but assign the glory of victory to him who grants you that you may carry away the palm of victory.

Do you wish to win? First crush the head of the enemy by excluding the devil’s suggestions from your heart.

Do you wish to win? Let your hands be found strong in [Col. 0694] good works.

Do you wish to win? Fix your feet; do not let your steps waver by frequenting spectacles and abandoning the church.

But so that you may accomplish this victory even in so great a contest and struggle, may the Lord send you help from the sanctuary, and from Zion protect you (Ps. XIX, 3).

## CHAPTER III

### 3. The power of water in Baptism. The effect of Baptism foreshadowed where Christ walked upon the waters. Another figure of Baptism in the deliverance of the people through the Red Sea

Behold, beloved, you are about to come to a fountain of water. Do not say in your hearts, “Is this all that we desired so greatly?” This visible fountain is a likeness of the eternal fountain. You will be reborn from water and the Spirit. That water cleanses not only the filth of the body, but also frees the soul from sins.

You ought to know, however, why the power of that water benefits both soul and body. For not every water cleanses: this water is sanctified through the consecration of the word. Take away the word, and what is water except water? The word is added to the element, and it becomes a sacrament. *[Note: From the Treatise 80 on John, no. 3.]*

The power of the Word cleansed us through water, because he walked upon the waters. But so that he might free you from the storm of this age, behold the power of the Word of God, how he rules over all his creation. You know what I am about to say.

It is read in the Gospel: When the Lord Jesus came to his disciples during the fourth watch of the night, walking upon the waters of the sea, and found them fishing—those whom he had already made fishers of men—the disciples, terrified, thought that they saw a phantom. But Jesus approached and said to them: “Do not be afraid; it is I.”

Then one of them, that Peter who was presumptuous, afterward a denier, and later a confessor and lover, said: “If it is you, Lord, command me to come to you upon the waters.” And the Lord said: “Come.”

Peter descended and began to walk upon the sea, full of confidence. While he was walking, weakness trembled, but divinity immediately came to his aid. He began to sink and cried out: “Lord, I perish!” The Lord stretched out his hand, raised up the sinking man, strengthened the one who was losing confidence, and said to him: “You of little faith, why did you doubt?” (Matt. XIV, 25–31.)

You see, beloved, how much faith helps and how much unbelief weighs down. For if someone comes to the waters of Baptism full of faith, he is lifted up; if someone is unbelieving, he sinks. But let the Lord stretch out his hand even to unbelievers who are sinking, and let him bring about complete faith in their hearts.

### 4. The sacrament of water and what it will accomplish in you

Hear further what the sacrament of water will accomplish in you. I shall set forth a figure, so that from it the truth may shine forth for you.

When the Egyptians were oppressing the Hebrew people with harsh labor, the cry of the people arose in the ears of God; and they pleaded that he free them from the domination of that wicked nation. Moses was sent to lead them out of their Egyptian slavery.

Before Pharaoh, the ruler of the Egyptians, the most faithful servant of God presented the command of his Emperor and made known to the most hardened king what the King of all nations had ordered. Pharaoh hardened his heart and said that he did not know God; and, rejecting his ministers, he afflicted the people with heavier punishments.

From the people’s greater distress a greater cry arose. The servant of God, Moses, undertook the struggle; he confronted Pharaoh without any weapon or sword, wearing no visible arms, but fortified with divine power.

[Col. 0695] Ten plagues were inflicted upon Egypt, and avenging wrath rose against the rebellious people, so that the necks of the proud might fall before the smallest creatures—worms, frogs, and locusts. Among these plagues, the final one was the death of all the firstborn of the Egyptians, so that those who unjustly detained others might justly lose their own.

Pharaoh released the people, compelled not by his will but by overwhelming necessity. The rescued people hurried toward the Red Sea, so that those who had been freed from the worst enemy might be saved through the waters. The Egyptians followed and threatened the fleeing people.

The Israelites saw the enemies above them and awaited the sword of their foes. Death was before their eyes; fear and trembling were in the hands of each one, lest they fall into the jaws of their pursuers.

Moses, the servant of God, arose, carrying the staff he had received from the Lord, through which he had already performed many signs. He struck the sea, and it was divided.

Where is that power—not of gods, but of demons? Where is the empty superstition of the pagans? Was Neptune invoked so that the sea might be divided—the one whom they wish to be king of the sea, while they refuse to acknowledge the true God as their king?

Moses stretched out his hand with the staff and struck the waters; immediately the waves were forced into a heap, and the surge, driven back upon itself, curved over. The liquid received solidity, and the bed of the sea dried into dust.

Some entered to be saved, others to be condemned. One element of water, at the command of the author of all creation, judged both groups: it separated the godly from the ungodly; it washed the former and overwhelmed the latter; it cleansed the former and killed the latter (Exod. I–XIV).

Moses was a figure of the Lord Christ, since he was the leader of the people. Recognize the cross in the staff. Recognize the Red Sea as Baptism, reddened with Christ’s blood. Recognize the king of Egypt and his people as the author of sins, the devil, together with all his ministers.

The devil rages when he sees us freed from his oppression through the water of Baptism. Cry out to your Moses, the Lord Christ, and let the staff of the cross strike the sea of Baptism; let the water return and cover the Egyptians, so that, just as not one of the Egyptians remained, so none of your sins may remain either.

May he cleanse everything who made everything; may he restore what was lost who created all things whole; may he extinguish Pharaoh, the devil, the author of death, and free his people through the water of salvation.

## CHAPTER IV

### 5. On the mysteries of the Paschal lamb

You have heard, beloved, how those figures passed over into the form of truth. It remains for you to know how the people freed from Egypt celebrated the Passover, having been baptized, as the Apostle says, “in the cloud and in the Red Sea” (I Cor. X, 1).

They received the Lord’s command through Moses: at the slaying of the lamb they were to celebrate the Passover; from its blood each person was to smear the doorposts of his house, and they were not to fear the destroying angel if they had upon the front of their house the sign of the blood of the slain lamb.

“His bone,” he says, “you shall not break, nor shall you leave anything of it until morning. You shall eat the lamb with picridia and unleavened bread” (Exod. XII).

The children of Israel did what had been commanded. And you, spiritual Israel, son of Abraham according to faith, not according to the flesh, demonstrate how you celebrate the Passover. You have a slain lamb; demonstrate it. “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sin of the world” (John I, 29).

Smear the doorposts of your house with his blood. Demonstrate it and say: “Behold, the cross of Christ’s blood is upon the foreheads of our modesty.” Say with Paul: “God forbid that I should glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Gal. VI, 14).

“It shall not be broken,” it was said. This was fulfilled in the Lord’s very Passion, in the immolation of that holy Lamb, when, crucified with two robbers, he hung in the middle, that perfect righteousness freeing one who confessed and punishing the other who blasphemed (Luke XXIII, 39–43).

Thus three crosses and three causes came to be. One of the robbers insulted Christ; the other, confessing his own deserts, commended himself to Christ’s mercy. Christ’s cross in the middle was not a punishment but a tribunal.

As soon as he had completed everything that had been written concerning him, having received gall and vinegar—for it had been foretold, “They gave me gall for food, and in my thirst they gave [Col. 0696] me vinegar to drink” (Ps. LXVIII, 22)—he bowed his head and gave up his spirit.

The soldiers came and broke the legs of the robbers hanging on the cross. But when they came to Jesus, they did not break his legs, so that, as the Evangelist says, what had been written might be fulfilled: “You shall not break any of his bones” (John XIX, 28, 36).

But one of the soldiers opened his side, and immediately blood and water came out, which are the two sacraments of Mother Church. The persecutor struck his side with a lance, and the Redeemer poured out the price.

This blood intoxicates the mind so that it forgets its love of the world. This water cleanses the soul, so that the body may be free from the filth of the devil.  
*[Note: Thus the manuscripts: “so that the body may lack the devil’s filth” (*ut corpus sordes careat diaboli*). But the printed editions have: “so that the body may be free from the devil’s filths” (*sordibus careat diaboli*).]*

“Nor shall you leave anything of it until morning.” This is now being enacted: the lamb is eaten during the night of this age, so that when that morning comes which will have no evening, we may no longer offer the sacrifice of the lamb’s image, but may find there the Lamb himself whom we eat daily  
*[Note: Here only the Louvain edition adds “whom we sacrifice.”]*  
and whose blood we drink—the perfect priest whom we know to have been slain here for our salvation.

What are these *picridia*, bitter herbs, which spiritual Israel eats, except that bitter voice uttered for a time by the holy martyrs through the holy David, who say, “You will feed us with the bread of tears, and give us drink in tears, in measure” (Ps. LXXIX, 6), and through the Apostle Paul: “In everything we suffer tribulation, but we are not distressed” (II Cor. IV, 8)?

And you, holy Paul, demonstrate the unleavened bread, having become spiritual from carnal Israel. For you celebrated the Passover with the ancient people, and you taught and demonstrated how the new people would convert the figures into truth. Therefore show the new kneading of unleavened bread.

“Not in the old leaven,” he says, “nor in the leaven of malice and wickedness, but in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth” (I Cor. V, 8).

## CHAPTER V

### 6. Moses’ staff devouring the magicians’ serpents, a figure of Christ’s cross, by whose power heresies are crushed. The Donatists are defeated; the Maximianists, Manichaeans, Pelagians, and Arians are refuted

O slain Lamb, O holy Christ crucified for us, who hung upon the cross in order to restore what had fallen: this is that staff of your kingdom, the cross itself, I say, through which power is made perfect in weakness. This is that staff—the cross; this is that staff which flowered from the root of Jesse; this is that staff which Moses carried, which, when changed into a serpent, swallowed the magicians’ serpents: the doctrine of Christ, spread through all nations, overcoming the deranged heretics.

For in that people, brothers, among whom Moses performed many miracles through the staff, Pharaoh’s magicians arose, performing wonders against God’s servant Moses themselves. But they were permitted to perform certain marvels for this purpose: that they might be defeated more wondrously.

What else did Pharaoh’s magicians signify except all heretics, ministers of the devil, who, under the name of Christ, desire to devour Christ’s people? Heresies now swarm over this land like the magicians’ serpents, whom that serpent lifted up upon the wood has swallowed and continues to swallow.

But since there is no time to go through many of them, let the heads of each be crushed: just as they arise, so let them be devoured.

There was here, as you know, beloved, the viper-like teaching of the Donatists: it has been crushed, it has been consumed. Soon the serpentine fraud of the Maximianists sprang up: it has been crushed, it has been consumed. The poison of the Manichaeans had crept in like that of an asp: it has been crushed, it has been consumed. The new doctrine of the Pelagians, raised up by ministers of the devil like Pharaoh’s magicians, challenged our serpent: it is being crushed, it is being consumed.

### 7. The Arian serpent refuted

When Catholic teaching has crushed, scattered, and consumed the heads of so many serpents, behold, for us one Arian snake, long since dead, insults us. It raises its head and tries to show itself as though alive, although it is established to have been killed long ago.

Return, our Moses; return, staff; return, serpent, holy Christ, possessing equal power with the Father. Return; crush the heads of dragons upon the waters. Break the head of the great dragon, which claims to be alive but does not possess true [Col. 0697] life.

Say what you are, since he teaches something other than what you are. Speak—speak, so that we may hear how we can convict the heretics.

Hear what he says: “I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me” (John XIV, 6). According to his humanity, he is the way; according to his divinity, the truth and the life.

But you, Arian heretic, who wish the life and truth to be lesser in divinity, it follows that you do not come through him to the Father.

But still, Lord Jesus, crush the head of the dragon. Say what you are with the Father. Let us hear you teaching, not the heretic blaspheming. Say what you are with the Father.

“I and the Father,” he says, “are one” (John X, 30).

Say further: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me.” Say further: “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father” (John XIV, 10, 9).

Do you believe such authority now, heretic? Or do you not accept his testimony concerning himself, but seek other witnesses about him?

Behold, they are brought forward against you; they speak, you are convicted, you are refuted, and you are caught in the snares of Scripture.

Speak, Paul, witness of God, who advanced even to bloodshed for this testimony and laid down your soul lest you yield to false doctrine. Speak. Let him hear who fears conviction; let him be convicted who does not change even when convicted.

“Let each of you,” he says, “have this mind in yourselves which was also in Christ Jesus, who, being in the form of God, did not consider it robbery to be equal with God” (Phil. II, 5, 6).

You hear “equal”; you hear “the form of God”; and you dare to say that the Son of God is lesser!

Let another witness also come, so that the equity of the truth may be confirmed by two or three. Speak also, holy Peter, concerning what was revealed to you—not by flesh and blood, but by the heavenly Father.

“You are,” he says, “the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matt. XVI, 16, 7).

And in his Second Epistle to the Gentiles: “We make known to you,” he says, “the power, foreknowledge, and greatness of our Lord Jesus Christ.”

You hear power; you hear greatness; you hear foreknowledge. In what respect, heretic, do you say that Christ is lesser?

But hear further what this witness says against you concerning both the Son and the Holy Spirit.

“Prophecy,” he says, “was not brought by human will; but men of God spoke, moved by the Holy Spirit. Yet there were also false prophets among the people, just as there will be false teachers among you, who will secretly introduce destructive sects, and who, denying the master who bought them” (II Pet. I, 16, 21; and II, 1).

You see that you are both demonstrated and convicted by powerful testimonies. “Denying,” he says, “the master who bought them.” Whom do you deny to be the master except the Son whom you say is lesser? And who bought us except he who redeemed us with his own blood?

But let a third witness also enter, so that three may speak one true testimony to the one Trinity and the threefold divinity.

Speak, holy John, who reclined upon the breast of the Savior and saw the heavenly wonders of the Lord’s Word. Speak, I say, concerning what you know of the Son of God.  
*[Note: See the book *On Holy Virginity*, chapter 27.]*

“In the beginning,” he says, “was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John I, 1).
