And in his Epistle: “We know,” he says, “that the Son of God has come and has given us understanding, so that we may know what is true and may be in his true Son. For this is the true God and eternal life” (I John V, 20).

But by saying that the Son who is the true God is lesser, you do not have eternal life.

But to refute the stubbornness of the perverse heresy, and to swallow you as a serpent magically made, not accepted by truth, let the Father himself bear witness concerning the Son, so that you seek and believe nothing further.

Through the Prophet: “With you,” he says, “is the beginning in the day of your power. In the splendors of the saints, from the womb, I have begotten you” (Ps. CIX, 3).

The beginning is the Father; the beginning is the Son. Therefore the Father and the Son are the beginning without any beginning.

“With you is the beginning in the day of your power; in the splendors of the saints, from the womb I have begotten you,” as though he were saying: “You proceeded from me so that the holy might be illumined.”

There was no other reason, beloved, why the very names of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit appeared to be separated, except that holy people might be instructed. Otherwise, what was said to Moses by the very substance of the Trinity was: “I am who I am”; and: “Thus shall you say: ‘He who is has sent me’” (Exod. III, 14).

Therefore the Son was begotten from the womb in the splendors [Col. 0698] of the saints. But lest you understand this begetting carnally or temporally as having taken place, hear how he begot him.

“My heart,” he says, “uttered the Word” (Ps. XLIV, 2). John the witness says: “In the beginning was the Word.” God the Father says: “My heart uttered the Word.” Habakkuk says: “The Word walked” (Hab. III, 5, according to the Septuagint).

You hear that God is the Word, that the Word is in the beginning with God, and that the Word is God. The voice of the testimonies and the unity of the Trinity itself cry out against you throughout the whole world; and you bark like a rabid dog against the whole world.

But hear further by what you may be more fully convicted: that the Trinity is one God.

The Father’s voice is spoken through the Prophet to the Son: “In the splendors of the holy places, from the womb I begot you.” The Father’s voice is spoken to the prophet Isaiah concerning the Holy Spirit: “The Holy Spirit,” he says, “will go forth from me.”

And the Son’s voice is heard in the Gospel, showing that the Father is in him and he in the Father, where he says: “The Father who remains in me, he performs the works” (John XIV, 10).

The Son’s voice is heard concerning the Holy Spirit, showing that just as he proceeds from the Father, so he proceeds from the Son himself, where he said to his disciples after the resurrection: “Receive the Holy Spirit.” And the Evangelist says that he breathed upon them, giving them the Holy Spirit, and saying: “Whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven” (John XX, 22, 23).

Hence also there is that saying of the Apostle Paul: “If anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he is not his” (Rom. VIII, 9).

Therefore, if the Son is in the Father and from the Father, the Holy Spirit is likewise in both the Son and the Father. The Trinity is not divided where there is perfect unity.

Let the confused and guilty Arian depart, because the Trinity is one God.

## CHAPTER VI

### 8. He continues the mysteries of the staff and cross of Christ. Examples of the saints set before every kind of person

But when, perverse heresy, do my words benefit you, since you are a deaf asp, stopping your ears so that you may not hear the voice of those who enchant?

Nevertheless, know that you are to be devoured by the serpent, when that shepherd has led the sheep whom you hold captive back to their own fold, so that there may be one flock and one shepherd.

That shepherd of ours, beloved, who feeds and rules with an iron staff, breaks and restores, is himself our shepherd, our ruler, our maker, and our architect.

I see you as a great shepherd, Lord Jesus, feeding the sheep, seeking the straying, and carrying the found sheep back to the flock with joy upon your shoulders. I see you as a great architect, carrying the staff, hanging upon the staff, and performing many miracles through this staff.

I greatly dread the exposition of this staff, beloved, as I consider the passages of divine Scripture. The staff is holy Mary; the staff is Christ himself; the staff is the cross.

And what great and wondrous things this architect has made from this staff! He made the tree of the cross, upon which the cornerstone himself hung, and the ladders of heaven, by which he raised fallen humanity to the Father.

What a miracle, brothers, of this architect: that from his staff he should make ladders, and ladders whose top he should set in heaven; that by them he should himself ascend and descend; and that, for their strengthening, he should himself lean upon them!

Ascend securely, you who desire heaven. Let neither their narrowness, their length, nor their height frighten you. Fear nothing. Its steps do not waver; that architect strengthened them in such a way that he willed his hands to be fastened with nails to its wood.

See the disciple of this architect, the Apostle Paul, both demonstrating these ladders, counting their steps as it were, ascending them, and inviting very many to them: “I bend my knees,” he says, “to the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, that he may grant you to comprehend with all the saints what is the height and breadth, the length and depth” (Eph. III, 14, 18).

He set four steps in the cross. Therefore these ladders are not laborious: they have four steps and lead to heaven.

At the height of the cross was placed the head of the crucified. Let the Christian have his heart raised upward to the Lord, to whom he responds daily when questioned; and he ascends the first step.

Across the breadth of the cross the hands of the crucified were fastened. Let the Christian’s hands persevere in good works; and he ascends the second step.

Along the length of the cross the body of the crucified hung. Let each person discipline his body through observances and suspend it by fasts, [Col. 0699] so that he may subject it to the service of the soul; and he ascends the third step.

In the depth of the cross there is hidden what you do not see, but from which all that you see arises. Let Christian faith be present. Let it believe with the heart what it cannot comprehend; let hope nourish it; and then it ascends the fourth step.

### 9. Examples of the saints for every condition of life

By these steps all the saints ascended: the continent, the married faithful. They escaped the ruins of the world and migrated to the safest places, where they now neither fear barbarians nor dread the frail accidents of human life, nor fear corruptions, nor suffer illnesses, nor are afflicted by tribulations. They no longer even fear death itself, but live with God and from God.

Let us love, seek, and desire this life, beloved. Whoever runs toward it does not walk by the way of the feet, but by the way of conduct. Let good morals therefore be sought and be found in everyone.

Both sexes and every age have in this an example for imitation from holy men. Let old men imitate the conduct of Tobias, who, though blind in body, demonstrated the way of life to his son in his heart. The son led him by the hand on earth, and the father, by admonishing him, led him onward to heaven.

Let young men imitate holy Joseph, beautiful in body and more beautiful [Col. 0700] in mind, whom chastity so possessed that the threats of the shameless woman rushing upon him could not violate him, neither in mind  
*[Note: “nor in mind” is absent from Erasmus and from the manuscripts.]*  
nor in body, whose mind God had already possessed.

Let holy virgins imitate holy Mary, the mother of their Lord.

Let widows imitate the devout widow Anna; and let married women imitate the chaste Susanna.

The virgin mother fulfilled what she had vowed. The widow Anna persevered in prayers and fasts to the end. The chaste Susanna advanced even to the danger of death for marital modesty.

Pay attention, married women, to the kind of imitation that Holy Scripture sets before you. For it does not praise her because she was outwardly adorned with gold, necklaces, or costly clothing, since inwardly she was adorned with the modesty of chastity.

He gave life to all who established good conduct. For this reason he himself deigned to be born from a woman, because through him each sex has been set free.

We have said much; you have listened most attentively; you have gladly eaten the Lord’s feast. Repay your minister, so that, if not by the word, at least by your prayers, you may feed me.

[Col. 0699]

## SERMON ON THE BARBARIAN TIMES  
*(C, G, S)*

## CHAPTER I
## Chapter I

### 1. Repentance must be embraced when God scourges on account of sins. All are deservedly crushed by God’s scourge

God our Lord warns us that we must not neglect our sins when he displays such anger. He himself justly punishes the guilty, because he finds no one repentant. How often, beloved, have the divine trumpets sounded and continue to sound: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near to you” (Matt. 4:17)? Yet, with the ears of our hearts closed, we pursue evil more earnestly and ask that good things come to us. But the Apostle says that the judgment of such people is just. In the very fact that such people think that they can receive good things from evil deeds, they have become hardened and seek no opportunity for repentance. They are rightly and justly judged, because they are found to have condemned themselves.

Although this sermon of ours does not touch everyone, the divine word nevertheless binds everyone, saying: “All have turned aside; together they have become worthless. There is no one who does good, not even one” (Ps. 13:3). How are all included, and how are they not all included?

How are they not all included? Because there are many who groan and grieve over the iniquities committed among them, wishing to resist them, but who do not dare to do so out of fear of worldly things—things which human frailty still either desires to acquire or fears to lose. Insofar as they grieve, they are not all included; insofar as they fear what ought not to be feared, “all have turned aside; together they have become worthless.” For the fear of human beings is valued more highly than the fear of God, and people prefer the things they have received from God to God himself. So that an evil person may not take them away, God, through whom the human being was made, is despised.

I would indeed like to warn you who are still like this, who are bound by love of worldly things and either spare or favor those who sin, through certain exhortations, about what you ought to prefer to what. But the river of tears compels us to mourn those who sin and refuse to repent. If we possessed ordinary human feeling, if we possessed a sense of compassion, we ought to weep, grieve, and mourn the death of one person. With what tears, with what groaning, with what lamentation are we shaken when we mourn either the greater part or almost the whole city?

A beloved person is ill, and his pulse announces danger; all who love him are sick in spirit along with him. If they see him laughing even on the threshold of death, when they recognize that every hope of recovery has been taken from him, do they not rightly mourn him as though he were already dead? Amid such great anguish, and at the very end of things, the whole province lies stricken, while spectacles are held every day: human blood is shed daily throughout the world, and the cries of the maddened resound in the circus.

O lament more welcome than every sadness! O lament afflicting the heart more than every sorrow! It is a pleasure to weep. For we mourn both them and ourselves, beloved, because we too are worthy to be scourged together with such people. For when we accuse others, [Note: [Col. 0700] Perhaps “we excuse ourselves” should be added.] “all have turned aside; together we have become worthless”—absolutely all of us. No one is excused, because the judge is such that every human being is found guilty before him. For when the just King sits upon the throne, “who will boast that he has a pure heart? Or who will boast that he is clean from sin?” (Prov. 20:8–9).

### 2. Faith and the coming judgment

That time has arrived which the Lord foretold: “When the Son of Man comes, do you think he will find faith on earth?” (Luke 18:8). Who has faith? Who believes the words? Would any one of us dare to claim faith for himself when he hears the Lord saying to his disciples: “If you had faith like a grain of mustard seed, you would say to this tree, ‘Be uprooted and planted in the sea,’ and it would obey you” (Luke 17:6)?

Who would dare to claim for himself that he does everything God has commanded? No one—absolutely no one. We preach, but we do not act; you listen, but you do not take care to act. All are rightly under the scourge: teacher and doer, hearer and despiser alike. We are eager to criticize one another, but we are not eager to examine our own works. Neighbor slanders neighbor, cleric slanders cleric, layperson slanders layperson. I see people accusing one another, but I see no one justly excusing himself.

For each person, beloved, bears his own burden. “Do not slander one another, brothers,” says the Apostle James. “Whoever slanders a brother or judges his brother slanders the law and judges the law. But if you judge the law, you are not a doer of the law but a judge. There is one lawgiver and judge, who is able to destroy and to save. But who are you to judge your neighbor?” (James 4:11–13).

## Chapter II

### 3. Repentance must be practiced before the tree is cut down

Nor can the voices of slanderers impose silence upon the word of God. He cries out through [Col. 0701] the good and through the wicked: “Repent; the kingdom of God has drawn near to you.” “Do not be merely hearers of the law, but doers” (James 1:22). “Bear fruits worthy of repentance.” For, as the Evangelist says, “the axe is already laid at the roots of the trees. Every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire” (Matt. 3:2, 8, 10).

I see, he says, that all people are different trees, possessing different fruits as well; but a good fruit is sought that may nourish, not one that may wound. For there are also thorny trees, assigned to the fire and rightly destined to burn, because they possess no fruit for the soul.

Do you think, beloved, that we are all such people, since we have been abandoned in these evils on account of our sins? The farmer sharpens the iron, cuts away the useless wood, and keeps what has been cut off to be consumed by fire. This is now being done by the true farmer.

The wicked seem to themselves still to stand and still to flourish. Whoever you are who are like this, whoever you are who are wicked, whoever you are who refuse to be corrected, let your height not console you, because a greater fall and a greater flame await you. Because this axe has not yet come to you, do you therefore think that you can stand forever, when you see or hear that other trees greater than you have fallen?

The fact that this farmer delays with you is due to his patience, so that perhaps an opportunity for repentance may intervene before him. For that laborer in the Gospel who interceded for the tree which its master wanted to uproot because it had borne no fruit for three years—see what he says: “Lord, leave it this year also; I will dig around it and apply a basket of manure. If it bears fruit, well and good; but if not, you shall cut it down” (Luke 13:8–9).

This barren tree is the human race that bears no fruit of repentance. Its Lord is its creator. The intercessor for this tree is the Apostle Paul. How do we prove this? Hear how he interceded for such people in one of his Epistles: “I bend my knees,” he says, “to the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, that he may grant you strength” (Eph. 3:14–16). Thus he was asking for them to receive what they did not possess.

“I will dig around it; I will apply a basket of manure.” The trench is the place of humility; the basket of manure is the penitent’s tears. Whoever despises this place will endure greater torment when he feels the sharpest instrument of that farmer.

Repent, wicked people; be corrected, wicked people, because the good too are scourged together with you.

## Chapter III

### 4. Why the good are punished together with the wicked

Someone may say: If the wicked are rightly scourged, why do the good suffer such things together with and at the hands of the wicked?

Why? Because they are called good in a certain sense; but according to the true and upright good, “No one is good except God alone” (Luke 18:19). Therefore even those who are good—whoever they are—are not such as the good ought to be. They are not perfect goodness; for they advance from day to day. If they advance, they advance through exercises.

Let no one justify himself as though he were already perfect. Let the Pelagian who justifies himself wrongly withdraw from our midst; let the Arian heretic be confounded: “No one is good except God alone.”

What then? Is Christ not God? Certainly he is God. For divine Scripture says of him: “This is the true God and eternal life” (1 John 5:20). What of the Holy Spirit—is he not God? Certainly he is God. How do we prove that he too is God? Hear Peter reproving Ananias for his deceit in the Acts of the Apostles: “Ananias,” he says, “why has Satan filled your heart, so that you should lie to the Holy Spirit? You have not lied to human beings but to God” (Acts 5:3–4). Behold, the Holy Spirit too is God.

Therefore the Trinity is one God, and it is true that “no one is good except the one God.” Be patient, good people, so that you may truly be good; be patient until the coming of the Lord. Endure the evils that you suffer from the wicked together with the wicked, because this trial is your testing.

If you are gold, why fear straw? Why fear fire? You will indeed be together in the furnace, but the fire turns the straw to ashes while it removes your impurities. If you are grain, why fear the threshing floor? You will not appear as you were before in the ear unless the threshing, by crushing, separates the chaff from you. If you are oil, why fear the pressure of the press? Your nature will not be revealed unless the weight of the stone [Col. 0702] also separates the dregs from you.

Nevertheless, let each soul question itself and see whether it suffers unjustly. Let the scales of justice be brought forth; let the love of the world be weighed against the love of God; see how the love of the world outweighs it. Let the mirror of divine Scripture be brought forth. This mirror flatters no one: whatever you are, it shows you to yourself. Pay attention and look; and if there is anything offensive, depart ashamed and return corrected.

Will you not be ashamed and glory in your evils? For you will be perfect evil, not some kind of good. Are you unwilling to be scourged with the world, or do you grumble under the scourge after being scourged?

Wicked servant, have you done what the Lord commanded? Do not complain about being beaten; he foretold these scourges to you. Who commanded this? The Lord commanded it; your Creator commanded it.

What did he command? “Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me.” See what he commanded. Or again: “Whoever loves son or daughter more than me is not worthy of me” (Matt. 10:37). See what he commanded.

And who, he says, is the one who hates father or mother or children? He did not command that one hate them; rather, he commanded that he be loved as much as they are loved. You ought indeed to love the Creator more than the creature; but if you are unable to prefer him, at least deign to place him on an equal footing.

You would truly love your children if you preferred Christ to your children and entrusted the children themselves to him. You would truly love your children if you loved them in the one who gave them to you to love.

Or do you think you love them because you favor their pleasures? You hear them blaspheming, and you endure patiently, Christian, what the foreign king Nebuchadnezzar could not endure, saying: “If anyone speaks blasphemy against the God of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, he shall be put to death” (Dan. 3:96).

You see them frequenting spectacles and do not call them back. You see them indulging in luxury and do not chastise them. Nor are you able to show yourself such a father as would be prepared either to disinherit or cast away undisciplined children, although you ought to be prepared, like Abraham, even to sacrifice your son.

For everyone who slaughters the pleasures of his children offers God a sacrifice like Abraham’s. But while these things are not done, and while those who use this world are badly raised in these depraved ways, the world is shaken. Not without reason does the prophet say: “The earth languished, and all its inhabitants with it” (Isa. 24:4).

Even now people do not cease to murmur, praise past times, and accuse the Christian times. “The times of our fathers were great,” they say; “O how good were the times our fathers had!”

## Chapter IV

### 5. Each person should chastise and punish vices in his own household, following the example of the ancients

But see what our fathers did. Phinehas killed with his own hand the man who was sacrificing to idols, in order to appease God’s anger (Num. 25:8). Moses restrained the wandering people who were worshiping the cast idol in such a definitive correction that, calling to himself one tribe out of the twelve—the one that wished to follow God—he commanded them, after taking swords in their hands, that sons strike down their parents and parents kill their sons (Exod. 32:26–28).

No affection recalled them; no place was reserved for human tenderness, because the fear and love of God were placed before every love of carnal desires.

Jephthah, in order to overcome enemies who sacrificed to gods and demons, offered his only daughter in sacrifice (Judg. 11). Samson, after long crushing and exhausting the demon-worshiping nations in wars by the strength he had received from God in his head, was later deceived by a woman and lost both his eyes and the strength of his head. Afterward, when he learned that all those people had gathered in the temple of their idols to his disgrace, magnifying their gods because they had delivered their fiercest enemy into their hands, and when the strength had grown together with the growth of his hair, he asked the boy who guided him to give him his hand and requested that he be led to that temple.

When he arrived there, he seized with each hand one of the two columns upon which the entire building rested, and wished that both he and the others would be crushed in the collapse, so that he would not willingly tolerate the praises of demons being heard to the insult of his God by anyone (Judg. 16).

Daniel, so that he would not ask any request from a human king but from the living God, who grants all good things to his people, was given as food to fasting lions so that he might perish. But the Lord, not abandoning his faithful servant, both preserved him unharmed and fed him and the lions through the prophet Habakkuk (Dan. 14:30–40).

What shall I say about the three boys who, because they refused to worship the royal image, mocked the fires? In those boys grace shone forth so brightly that, after being bound and thrown into the furnace, they appeared to walk about, opening their mouths and praising God. They did not admit the flames to themselves but drove them away, so that they were worthy to have the Son of God with them before he appeared in human form to the world; so that the flame might become their defender, while the furnace devoured and consumed the Chaldean ministers; and so that, brought unharmed from the furnace, they might make the peoples marvel at them and change the king, making him a worshiper of their God, whom they had previously experienced as their persecutor (Dan. 3).

But faith, fear, and love of God accomplished all these things. These people hated not only everything they possessed for God’s sake but even their own souls; and God made them renowned here and enriched them with the reward of eternal life.

What have we done like this, beloved—or rather, what evil have we not done? They did not sacrifice to demons, though they were assailed by neither threats nor tortures. Did the person who eagerly watched the images of idols performing at night—what they call the “Nocturnal”—not sacrifice? He sacrificed, indeed he sacrificed; and, what is worse, he sacrificed not a bull or some animal victim but the precious soul of a human being.

In this most wicked sacrifice, not one or a few are accused; the entire city did this, since the entire city consented. Not by enemies or barbarians, but by himself, each person inwardly killed himself in his soul by watching, consenting, and failing to prohibit it. We all remained guilty. And while we do not wish the city’s perverse peace to be disturbed, we do not receive the true peace that we desire.

We despise preserving the peace of good morals, and the peace of our times has perished. Learn even now, beloved, what you ought to prefer to what. Do not love vices in your children, friends, servants, or anyone you know.

Let the singular power be preferred to every power. Let us show honor to Caesar as Caesar, but fear to God. Let the Creator be preferred to the creature. Let us love God, because he loves us—and in the very fact that he scourges us in this way, he loves us.

For what son is there whom his father does not discipline? (Heb. 12:6–7). Whoever has sound understanding, whoever believes the words of God, fears eternal fire more than the sword of any savage barbarian; he fears everlasting death more than any death, however terrible it may be here.

Let unbelievers mock these things; let fools mock them; let them refuse to believe, even when events themselves have proved them. Behold, they are crushed; behold, everything is perishing; behold, the world they loved cannot stand together with them; behold, they are being dragged to God, whose commands they despised. For one who dies blaspheming does not go willingly.

Behold, we are going. When we have arrived there, what will be done? Where are we going? By whom will we depart? Who will be forced to return here again? It is finished—and it is finished for him to amend what he did wickedly.

“Return, children, return; return to your heart, transgressors” (Isa. 46:8). Make joy from your conversion; let your hearts be corrected; let your deeds become displeasing to you. Be strong; let the world’s tribulation not break you. The Lord is near; be anxious about nothing (Phil. 4:5–6).

## Chapter V

### 6. The courage of the martyrs, especially Perpetua and Felicity

You have great examples of courageous men. The martyrs conquered the world. Among them, women too were found stronger than men. A few days ago we celebrated the anniversaries of the martyrs Perpetua and Felicity and their companions. Since so many men were present there, why are these two named above all others, unless because the weaker sex either equaled or surpassed the courage of men?

One of them was pregnant; the other was nursing. Felicity was giving birth; Perpetua was nursing. But Perpetua nursed only so long as she received from that shepherd and father a morsel of milk; after receiving it, the sweetness of perpetual felicity made her despise her son, reject her father, cling no longer to the world, and lose her life for Christ.

Felicity, who had Perpetua as her companion, was giving birth and suffering; when exposed to the beasts, she rejoiced rather than feared. What courage in women! What grace this is, which, when it pours itself forth, judges no sex unworthy!

Thanks be to grace, for it restored the female sex. Woman had remained in great disgrace, because from the beginning sin came through a woman, and because of her we all die. The devil cast down one Eve; but Christ, born of a virgin, exalted many women.

Perpetua and Felicity trampled the head of the serpent, which Eve had admitted inwardly into her heart. The serpent deceived Eve by making false promises; it could not overcome Perpetua and Felicity by raging against them. It deceived Eve amid the happiness of paradise; it could not approach these women, placed as they were under the power of so many sufferings. [Note: [Col. 0704] Some manuscripts read thus. Erasmus has: “nor, having been deprived of the power of substances.” Lovaniensis has: “nor, having been deprived of the power of substances.”]

The devil rejoiced in Eve’s fall amid the delights of paradise; amid their sufferings, he himself in a certain way feared the steadfastness of these women’s courage. Rightly were they thus exalted; rightly were they either made equal to men or preferred to them.

Although in Christ Jesus there is neither slave nor free, neither male nor female (Gal. 3:28), but all are one as they come to maturity into a perfect man (Eph. 4:13), this gift nevertheless descended from great grace. For Perpetuity and Felicity—the names of these holy women—are the reward of all the holy martyrs.

## Chapter VI

### 7. Job’s patience

Job too, known to everyone, conquered the world: so often tested, but never overcome. He fulfilled the Lord’s command. He despised his children so as not to blaspheme the one who had given him children. He rejected his wife, who urged him to blaspheme; the devil had left her alone because he knew that he needed her.

For he had not left the husband a comforter but an accomplice in his temptation. He had made her a new Eve, but Job was not the old Adam. The devil thought that, as he had deceived Adam through a woman, he could deceive Job in the same way. But Job, rejecting the wife who suggested the worst things, was divinely assisted and was even able to overcome the devil himself through her.

Job was stronger in sufferings than Adam in the groves: Job did not yield to tortures, whereas Adam was overcome amid delights. [Note: [Col. 0704] From *On Patience*, chapter 83.]

You see, beloved, what temptation accomplishes, how useful the pressures of this world are, and how earthly pleasures corrupt. Job despised his wife, his children, all that was his, and afterward even his own flesh. He loved more the one who had given these things than what had been given. He used what he had received like a good traveler: he possessed it but was not possessed by it.

But when it pleased the one who had given these things to take them away, Job blessed him and did not blaspheme: “The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away; as it pleased the Lord, so it has happened. Blessed be the name of the Lord” (Job 1–2).

Imitate such a man; imitate such children even when scourged, so that you may deserve to be received. For he scourges every son whom he receives. Endure his discipline: God treats you as sons.

## Chapter VII

### 8. The parable of the prodigal son. Christ’s side opened so that all may enter through it

This is proved by the younger son presented in the Gospel. He despised his father’s discipline, squandered his property among prostitutes, fed pigs, was crushed by hunger, and could not fill his stomach with the pigs’ pods. At last he returned to himself and found himself—the one who had lost himself.

He remembered that many hired servants of his father had an abundance of bread, while he himself was perishing from hunger. Immediately he rose and returned to his father. He asked not to be counted as a son but as one of the servants.

Humility bends low; mercy is stirred. The voices of the repentant son shake the father’s heart. The son declares himself unworthy, so that the father may judge him worthy. He asks to be received among the servants, and the father orders that the first robe be brought to him, kills the fattened calf, gathers the choir, summons his friends, and prepares a great feast.

Why? [Col. 0705] “Because this son of mine was dead and has come to life again; he was lost and has been found.”

The Lord presented this likeness in the Gospel, and he himself explained it, saying that such joy takes place in heaven over a sinner who repents. Now, since the time has come to exhort everyone to repentance, so that wandering children may return and a feast of the fattened calf may be prepared for them by the father, let us too, beloved, be prepared to attend this feast as friends and members of the household—especially because, approaching the table of this head of the household with him every day, he no longer deigns to call us servants but friends.

Let us, if you please, go through the very parable presented by the Lord in the Gospel, in which he showed us both the father’s loving affection, indicated the return of the lost son, and related the troubled spirit of the elder son, who had not departed from his father’s house. This is what the text of the reading itself contains.

“When his elder son was coming from the field,” it says, “and heard music, he asked the servants what it meant. They told him, ‘Your brother has returned, and your father has killed the fattened calf, because he has received him back safe and sound.’ And he became angry and refused to enter. His father went out to him and urged him to enter. But he reproached his father because he had always worked with him and he had never provided him with such things, whereas, when this son of his had come—the one who had wickedly squandered all his father’s property—he had killed the fattened calf for him.”

The father gives an account of his action, consoles his son who remained with him and did not leave the house, and says to him: “Son, you are mine, and you are always with me, and everything I have is yours. But we had to do this, because your brother was dead and has come to life; he was lost and has been found” (Luke 15:11–32).

This presentation by the Lord is not without purpose. May he who presented it grant us to demonstrate that he himself fulfilled what, through a certain likeness, he stirred us in a certain way to investigate.

No Christian doubts that our Lord Jesus Christ displayed a father’s affection toward his own. Let us inquire more closely who the younger son is, who lived prodigally and squandered his father’s property, and who the elder son is, who became angry because the fattened calf had been killed for the returning lost son and refused to enter.

Who is this lost son, who squandered all his father’s property among prostitutes, except that thief who, dissipating through crimes the substance of his soul given to him by God, even hung upon the cross? He fed pigs when by his deeds he filled the pleasures of demons. Perhaps he fed those pigs which the devil had asked the Lord for, saying: “Command us to enter the herd of pigs” (Matt. 8:31).

He was crushed by hunger because he could not find the bread of God’s word. He desired to fill his stomach with pods when he was filling his soul with twisted thoughts.

But let him return to himself. Let the thief see himself hanging on the cross; let him run to the father; let him say while hanging on the cross: “Lord, remember me when you come into your kingdom. Lord, remember me; I am not worthy to be called your son; receive me as one of your servants. Lord, remember me.”

For the thief, considering his merits, despaired of himself; but the Lord, like a merciful father, offered the thief, as though he were a son, what he had despaired of. Let the father bring forth for him that first robe; let him clothe with immortality the son whom he sees hanging with him on the cross; let him bring him into the house. Let Christ say to the thief: “Amen I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:42–43).

Let him kill the fattened calf—the human being received and even crucified for the sake of thieves. Let him summon his friends, his disciples, to whom he said: “If you do what I command you, I no longer call you servants but friends” (John 15:14–15).

Let that heavenly feast be prepared; let the choir of angels stand by, sweetly proclaiming: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2:14).

Let that elder son also come and refuse to enter. Who is this elder son who refused to enter, except the first of the Apostles, Peter, who, in response to a single servant girl in the high priest’s courtyard, dared three times to deny the Lord?

You did say, O Peter, as to your father Christ: “I have labored with you,” when you said to the Savior, “I am with you even unto death” (Matt. 26:69–74, 35); “I will lay down my life for you” (John 13:37).

Where is what you promised? You are questioned once, and you deny; you are questioned a second time, and you deny; a third time, and you deny. You do not wish to enter the feast, and therefore you dared three times to deny the Lord. Where is “I will lay down my life for you”? The claw did not terrify you when you denied three times, but a single little woman overcame you. Surely you said, “I am with you even unto death.” Look, look, then, Peter, how presumptuously you previously thought of yourself. Behold, now, by denying three times, you are convicted, with the rooster as witness.

But let the father go out to the elder son who refuses to enter. Let Christ say to Peter: “Enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matt. 25:21). Let him look upon the denier and make him a confessor; let him pierce the one who weeps and make him a lover.

Let the father exhort him with a father’s voice: “Son,” he says, “you are mine. You are Peter; although you denied me, you are mine. You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church. You are mine, and everything I have is yours. I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 16:18–19).

The keys are with you, Peter; now deign to enter the feast. These things had to happen, because your brother, the thief, was dead and has come to life; he was lost and has been found.

If Peter received the keys of the kingdom of heaven before Christ was crucified for all, by what means did that thief enter there, now no longer guilty, except through the side that the Jew opened?

### 9. All may enter through Christ’s open side

And now let all who love paradise come—the place of rest, the place of security, the place of perpetual happiness, the place where you need not fear a barbarian, where you suffer no adversary and have no enemy. Come, all of you; enter, all of you. There is a way by which you can enter. [Note: [Col. 0706] Thus according to Erasmus, Lyons, Venice, and Louvain. The Benedictine editions do not have the word *possitis* in the text, but the marginal note indicates that it should be supplied.]

The side is open. For that thief showed where everyone ought to enter; by his example he taught no one to despair.

## Chapter VIII

### On avoiding the Arian heresy

“Strive,” says the Lord, “to enter through the narrow gate” (Luke 13:24). What is narrower than that opening which one of the soldiers made by striking the side of the crucified man? And yet through these narrow passages almost the whole world has already entered.

Come, you Jews as well; the Son of God whom you crucified calls you. Strive to enter through the narrow gate, for through this gate your fathers entered. Those who cried out for him to be crucified, who saw him hanging on the wood, who mocked him, who shook their heads—through these narrow passages they nevertheless entered.

For the one hanging on the cross was not crying out in vain: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34). Through these narrow passages, then, as I have said, through the narrow gate of Christ’s side, the changed thief entered, the repentant Jew entered, every converted pagan entered, and from it the wicked Arian heretic went out.

He went out because he was not among those who remained. He belonged to those of whom John says: “They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would certainly have remained with us” (1 John 2:19).

O Arian heretic, the thief recognizes the one hanging on the cross; the very Jewish enemies trembled at him when he rose again; and you treat with contempt the one reigning in heaven!

### 10. Against rebaptism and schism

Beware, beloved, of the Arian pestilence. Let it not separate you from Christ by promising earthly things; because of a tunic, let it not strip you of faith. Members of Christ, preserve the unity and wholeness of the one tunic, which even Christ’s persecutors did not dare to tear.

Do not inflict injuries upon your own head. He died for you so that you would not die. Since Christ gave life to someone through Baptism, why does the Arian kill him by baptizing him again? Be ashamed, be ashamed, heretic.

Peter denied Christ, but he returned and by weeping erased what he had denied through fear. Paul persecuted Christ in his members, but at Christ’s voice he fell and rose again. He fell in one way and rose in another: he fell as a persecutor and was raised as a preacher.

Kings persecuted Christ in Christians, but they did Christ great service when his members swiftly passed over to their head. No one inflicts upon Christ losses such as you do, for you desire to kill the souls of many for whom Christ came in the flesh to be killed.

Be ashamed, be ashamed, heretic. Why do you repeat what is given only once? Christ is already within his members; do not wish to rebaptize Christ himself in them. For once, on behalf of all, he himself deigned to descend into the water with John (Matt. 3:16).

Christ redeemed souls; guard what he redeemed. Assign to the whole Christ an undivided estate. Let no one invade it; let no one consent to the invader. Let no one erase the Lord’s mark; let no one remove Christ’s titles.

You will have to render an account to the Lord and King. Good servants, an opportunity for doing good has been given to you. There are many strangers, captives, and dispossessed people. “Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of unrighteousness, so that they may receive you into eternal dwellings” (Luke 16:9).

---

# Sermon of Saint Aurelius Augustine, Bishop of Hippo, on the Benefit of Fasting

[Col. 0707]

[Note: [Col. 0707] Possidius lists it in chapter 8 of the *Index*. It has been found only in printed editions.]

## Chapter I

### 1. Fasting is offered to God by human beings, not by angels

We are urged to say something about the benefit of fasting, and God urges us, and the season urges us. For this observance, this virtue of the spirit, this deprivation of the flesh and profit of the mind, is not offered to God by angels. There everything is abundance and everlasting security, and therefore there is no deficiency, because affection is full toward God.

There is the bread of angels; so that man might eat the bread of angels, he became man. Here, all souls bearing earthly flesh fill their bellies from the earth; there, rational spirits presiding over heavenly bodies fill their minds from God. Here too there is food, and there too there is food. But this food, when it refreshes, diminishes, and fills the belly in such a way that it itself is reduced; the other both fills and remains whole.

Christ commanded us to hunger for this food, saying: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied” (Matt. 5:6). It therefore belongs to human beings living this mortal life to hunger and thirst for righteousness; to be filled with righteousness belongs to the other life.

The angels are full of this bread, this food. But while human beings hunger, they stretch themselves out; while they stretch themselves out, they are enlarged; while they are enlarged, they become capable; once they have become capable, they will be filled in due time.

What then? Do those who hunger and thirst for righteousness receive nothing of it here? They certainly receive something. But it is one thing when we are speaking about the refreshment of travelers, and another when we are speaking about the perfection of the blessed.

Hear the Apostle hungering and thirsting—and certainly for the righteousness that can be received and practiced in this life, as much as can be received and practiced here. For who among us would dare to compare himself with him, much less to prefer himself to him?

But what does he say? “Not that I have already received it, or am already perfect.” See who is speaking: the vessel of election, and in a certain way the very edge of the Lord’s garment; yet the edge that heals the one who touches it because he believes. For he was the last and least of the Apostles, as he himself says: “I am the last of the Apostles,” and, “I am the least of the Apostles”; and again: “I am not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God. [Col. 0708] But by the grace of God I am what I am, and his grace toward me was not in vain; rather, I labored more than all of them—not I, however, but the grace of God with me” (1 Cor. 15:8–10).

Hearing this, you seem to yourself to hear someone full and perfect. You have heard what he belches forth; hear also what he hungers for. “Not that I have already received it, or am already perfect,” he says.

“Brothers, I do not consider that I have apprehended it. But forgetting what lies behind and stretching forward to what lies ahead, according to my intention I pursue the prize of God’s heavenly calling in Christ Jesus” (Phil. 3:12–14).

He says that he is not yet perfect, that he has not yet received and apprehended it. He says that he stretches himself out; he says that he pursues the prize of the heavenly calling. He is on the way; he hungers, he wishes to be filled, he strives, he longs to arrive, he burns with longing: nothing seems to him so great a delay as the delay before he may depart and be with Christ (Phil. 1:23).

## CHAPTER II

### 2. Human fasting occupies a middle position between carnal human beings and angels

Therefore, dearly beloved, since there is earthly food by which the weakness of the flesh is nourished, and there is also heavenly food by which the piety of the mind is filled; and since this earthly food has its own life, and that food has its own: the life of this food is the life of human beings, while the life of that food is the life of angels.

Faithful human beings, already separated in heart from the multitude of unbelievers, suspended upon God, to whom it is said, “Lift up your hearts,” possessing another hope and knowing that they are pilgrims in this world, occupy a certain middle position. They are not to be compared with those who think that nothing is good except to enjoy earthly pleasures, nor yet with those heavenly inhabitants whose only delights are the very bread by whom they were created.

Those human beings, bent toward the earth and seeking nourishment and joy from the flesh alone, are compared with cattle. They are far removed from the angels both by condition and by conduct: by condition, because they are mortal; by conduct, because they are pleasure-seeking.

Between that people of heaven and that people of earth, the Apostle hung, as it were, in the middle: he was going there, and from here he was raising himself up. Yet he was not still with those others, for then he would have said, “I am already perfect”; nor was he with these—sluggish, torpid, withered, drowsy, thinking that nothing exists except what they see, what passes away, what they were born for, and what they are going to die for. For if he had been with them, he would not have said, “I pursue toward the prize of the heavenly calling.”

We must therefore govern our fasts. This, as I said, is not an angelic duty; yet neither is it the duty of those who serve their belly. It belongs to our intermediate condition, by which we live separated from unbelievers while longing to be joined to the angels. We have not yet arrived, but we are already on our way; we do not yet rejoice there, but here we already sigh.

What, then, does it profit us to abstain for a while from fleshly nourishment and pleasure? The flesh forces us toward the earth; the mind strains upward. It is carried away by love, but held back by weight. Scripture speaks of this matter as follows: “For the corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks of many things” (Wis. IX, 15).

If, therefore, the flesh inclining toward the earth is a burden to the soul, and a weight oppressing it as it flies upward, then the more each person delights in his higher life, the more he lays aside of his earthly burden. Behold what we are doing when we fast.

## CHAPTER III

### 3. Fasting is necessary for subduing the flesh

Therefore, let this not seem to you a trivial or superfluous matter, lest someone perhaps, doing this according to the custom of the Church, think to himself and say, or hear the tempter suggesting inwardly: “Why are you fasting? You are defrauding your soul; you are not giving it what delights it. You are inflicting punishment upon yourself; you are yourself your own torturer and tormentor. Does God, then, take pleasure in your torment? Then he is cruel, since he delights in your punishments.”

Answer such a tempter: “I certainly torment myself so that he may spare me; I suffer punishment in myself so that he may come to my aid, so that I may please his eyes and delight his sweetness. For a victim too is tormented so that it may be placed upon the altar. My flesh will weigh less heavily upon my mind.”

And answer such a wicked dissuader, a servant of the belly, by means of this comparison, saying: “If you happened to be sitting upon a beast, if you were using a horse that, in its eagerness, could throw you headlong, would you not, in order to travel safely, take food away from the enraged animal and tame by hunger the one whom you could not control with the bridle?

“My flesh is my beast. I am traveling to Jerusalem; often it drags me away and tries to drive me from the road [Note: [Col. 0709] Perhaps, ‘throw me off.’]. But my road is Christ. Shall I not restrain it by fasting when it is so exuberant?”

If anyone understands this, he also proves by experience itself how beneficial fasting is. For will this flesh, which is now being subdued, always be subject to discipline? While it fluctuates in time, while it is weighed down by the condition of mortality, it has its obvious and dangerous excitements, dangerous to our mind. For the flesh is still corruptible; it has not yet risen again. It will not always be so, since it does not yet possess the proper condition of heavenly existence. For we have not yet been made equal to the angels of God.

## CHAPTER IV

### 4. The Manichaean error concerning the struggle between the flesh and the spirit. The struggle of the flesh is the punishment of sin

Therefore, let Your Charity not suppose that the flesh is hostile to the spirit, as though one were the author of the flesh and another the author of the spirit. Many, thinking this, were truly carried away by the flesh itself and went astray; they assigned one author to the flesh and another to the spirit.

They use as though it were an apostolic testimony something they do not understand: “The flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh” (Gal. V, 17). This is true; but why do you not also attend to the other statement: “No one has ever hated his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it, just as Christ does the Church” (Eph. V, 29)?

In that first statement, which I mentioned, there appears to be a kind of struggle between two enemies, the flesh and the spirit, because the flesh desires against the spirit and the spirit against the flesh. But in this other statement there is something like a marital union: “No one has ever hated his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it, just as Christ does the Church.”

What, then, shall we do between these two statements? If they are contradictory, which shall we reject and which shall we retain? But they are not contradictory. Let Your Charity attend: for the moment I accept both, and I shall show, insofar as I can, that both agree.

But you, whoever establishes one author of the flesh and another of the spirit—what will you make of this? “No one has ever hated his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it, just as Christ does the Church.” Does the comparison not frighten you? For he says, “he nourishes and cherishes it, just as Christ does the Church.”

Do you think the flesh is a shackle? Who loves his own shackle? Do you think the flesh is a prison? Who loves his own prison? “No one has ever hated his own flesh.” Who does not hate his own chain? Who does not hate his punishment? And yet: “No one has ever hated his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it, just as Christ does the Church.”

You, then, who posit one author for the flesh and another author for the spirit, will have to posit one author for the Church and another for Christ. Anyone who thinks this is out of his mind.

Therefore each person loves his own flesh, as the Apostle says, and apart from the Apostle’s statement each person proves this in himself. However much you may be a disciplinarian of the flesh, however fiercely you may be inflamed against it, I do not know whether you would not close your eye if some blow threatened it.

### 5. There is therefore something like a marriage between the spirit and the flesh

How, then, does the flesh desire against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh? From where comes this punishment, which has been derived from the succession of death? Whence was it said, “All die in Adam” (1 Cor. XV, 22)? And whence does the Apostle say, “We too were once by nature children of wrath, like the rest” (Eph. II, 3)?

That one from whom we were born received the punishment of death, and we draw along with us what we must overcome. Therefore we desire against the flesh so that we may subject the flesh, once subdued, to ourselves and draw it toward obedience.

Do we therefore hate the one whom we desire to obey us? Each person often imposes discipline in his own household upon his wife; he subdues her when she resists, but does not persecute her as an enemy. You discipline your son so that he may obey you: do you therefore hate him? Do you regard him as an enemy?

Finally, you love your slave and punish him, and by punishing him you make him obedient. Concerning this matter you have the Apostle’s own clear and complete statement: “I therefore run not as uncertainly; I fight not as one beating the air. But I discipline my body and bring it into servitude, lest perhaps, after preaching to others, I myself should be found disqualified” (1 Cor. IX, 26–27).

The flesh, then, by its mortal condition, has certain earthly desires. Over these you have been granted the authority of the bridle. Let the one set over you rule you, so that the one subject to you may be able to be ruled by you.

Your flesh is beneath you; your God is above you. When you wish your flesh to serve you, you are reminded how you ought to serve your God. You attend to what is beneath you; attend also to what is above you. You have no authority over what is lower unless you receive it from what is higher.

You are a slave, and you have a slave; but the Lord has two slaves. Your slave is more under the power of your Lord than under yours. Therefore you wish the flesh to obey you: can it obey in everything? It obeys your Lord in everything; it does not obey you in everything.

“How so?” you ask. You walk, you move your feet, and it follows. But will it go with you as far as you wish? It is animated by you, but will it be so for as long as you wish? Will you suffer whenever you wish? Will you be healthy whenever you wish? For your Lord often disciplines you through your slave, so that, because you have been contemptuous of the Lord, you may deserve to be corrected through the slave.

## CHAPTER V

### 6. The pleasure of the flesh must be restrained somewhat even from what is lawful. Our fasting differs in purpose from the fasting of pagans, Jews, and heretics. Heretics must return to the Church if fasting is to benefit them

But what does this concern you? Not to relax the pleasure of the flesh all the way to what is unlawful, and to restrain it somewhat even from what is lawful. For whoever restrains himself from nothing lawful is close to what is unlawful.

Therefore, brothers, marriage is lawful, adultery is unlawful; and yet temperate men, in order to remain far from unlawful adultery, restrain themselves somewhat even from lawful marriage.

Satiety is lawful, drunkenness is unlawful; nevertheless modest people, in order to keep themselves far from the disgrace of drunkenness, discipline themselves somewhat even in the freedom of satiety.

Let us act in this way, then, brothers; let us exercise restraint, and let us know why we do what we do. By ceasing from fleshly pleasure, one acquires the pleasure of the mind.

### 7. The purpose of our fasts concerns our journey

Therefore, the purpose of our fasts concerns our journey. What that journey itself is, and toward what we are heading, must be considered. For pagans too sometimes fast, yet they do not know the region toward which we are heading. Jews too sometimes fast, yet they have not grasped the road on which we walk.

It is like someone taming a horse while wandering astray upon it.

Heretics fast. I see what kind of people they are; I ask where they are going. “You are fasting: in order to please whom?” “God,” they reply. “Do you think he accepts the offering?”

But first see what he says: “Leave your offering, and go; first be reconciled to your brother” (Matt. V, 24). Do you properly discipline your own members when you tear apart the members of Christ?

“Your voice is heard in clamoring,” he says, “and you goad and strike with fists those who are under your yoke. I have not chosen such a fast,” says the Lord (Isa. LVIII, 4–5).

Would your fasting therefore be disapproved if you were excessively severe toward your slave, but approved when you do not acknowledge your brother? I am not asking what food you abstain from, but what food you love. Tell me what food you love, so that I may approve your abstaining from this food.

“Do you love justice?” “Perhaps,” you say, “I do.” Then let your justice appear. For I think it is just that you serve the one who is greater, so that the one who is lesser may obey you.

We were speaking about the flesh, which is less than the spirit and which has been subjected to discipline and governance. You deal with it so that it may obey you, and you take food away from it because you love it subject to you. Acknowledge the greater; acknowledge the higher, so that what is lower may properly yield to you.

## CHAPTER VI

### The harmony of the bodily members recalls them to unity

What if your flesh obeys you, but you do not obey your God? Are you not condemned by that very flesh when it obeys you? Does it not, by obeying you, give testimony against you?

### 8. Christ’s commandment of mutual love

“And whom,” he says, “should I obey as the greater?”

Behold, Christ speaks. You had called yourself a lover of justice: “I give you a new commandment, that you love one another” (John XIII, 34). Hear, then, your Lord giving the command that we love one another.

Since he makes from all of us, as from members, a body for himself, a body whose one head is the Lord and Savior himself, you nevertheless tear yourself away from the members of Christ; you do not love unity.

Would you not be alarmed by this in your own members? If you had a crooked finger, would you not run to a physician to correct your finger? Certainly your body is healthy when its members agree with one another. Then you are called healthy; then you are well.

But if some part of your body disagrees with the others, you seek someone to correct it. Why, then, do you not seek to be corrected, so that you may be recalled to the structure of Christ’s members and fit harmoniously within that body and within your own?

Surely the hairs of your head are less valuable than the other members? What is less valuable in your body than your hair? What is more despised? What is more insignificant? And yet, if a barber cuts your hair badly, you become angry with the barber because he has not preserved equality in your hair. And you do not preserve unity among Christ’s members?

What, then, are your fasts, or what good do they do? Do you think God unworthy of being served in unity by all who believe in him, and yet you want unity preserved among your members, in your body, and in your hair?

Your inward parts speak; your members give true testimony against you—and you give false testimony against Christ’s members?

### 9. The pagans’ fasting and the unity of Christ

“Have you separated yourself from the fasting of the pagans?” You think so, and therefore you seem secure to yourself. “I fast for Christ,” you say, “while they fast for idols and demons.”

I accept what you say, and in truth I do not deny that there is a distinction. But behold how, when I mentioned this a little earlier, your members gave testimony against you, so that I might remind you what you ought to be among the members of Christ your God. Let the pagans themselves, from whose fasting you separate your fasting, also teach you something about the unity of your Christ.

## CHAPTER VII

### The unity of the pagans themselves in the worship of gods who quarrel

Behold, they worship many false gods without being divided. Did we therefore find one true God so that we might not be united under the one?

They have many false gods, while we have one true God. Yet they have no division under many false gods, while we do not preserve unity under the one true God. Do you not grieve, groan, or blush with shame?

I add something else. The pagans not only worship many false gods; they worship many who are opposed and hostile to one another.

For example, let us recall some of their stories, if we cannot recall them all. Hercules and Juno were enemies, for they were human beings: he was the stepson, she the stepmother. Yet the pagans built temples to both of them, to Juno and to Hercules. They adore him; they adore her. They go together to Juno; they go together to Hercules. Though those deities are angry with one another, the worshipers are united.

Vulcan and Mars are enemies, and Vulcan has a just cause. But let someone who will hear the case judge it. The wretched husband hates his wife’s adultery; nevertheless he does not dare to prevent his worshipers from entering the temple of Mars. They adore both him and the other together.

If they imitate their gods, then they too quarrel. They go from the temple of Mars to the temple of Vulcan. What a great disgrace! Yet they do not fear that the husband will be angry with them because they come to him from the temple of the adulterer Mars.

They have understanding; they know that a stone cannot feel.

Behold: though they worship many, false, diverse, and hostile gods, they nevertheless preserve among them, in their worship, some sort of unity. Behold, the pagans themselves, from whose fasting you have separated your fasting, give testimony against you.

Come, then, to unity, brother. We worship one God. We have never seen the Father and the Son quarreling.

Nor should the pagans be angry with me because I have said these things about their gods. Why should they be angry with my words, and not rather with their own writings? Let them first erase those writings, if they can—or rather, if they wish. Let grammarians no longer hang out their curtains for teaching them. He is angry with me because I say these things, although he pays a fee so that his son may learn them.

## CHAPTER VIII

### 10. Christians’ discord should not deter pagans from the Christian religion. Charity is life; dissension is death

Therefore, dearly beloved, those people indeed have—or rather, had—such gods. Since they themselves did not wish to abandon them, they have been abandoned by them. Many have abandoned them, and many still abandon them; in their hearts they tear down their temples.

But let us rejoice over them, because they are coming to unity, not to division.

Let no pagan find an excuse for refusing to become a Christian. Let us agree, brothers, in worshiping one God, so that by our own agreement we may in some way urge them also to abandon their many gods and come to the peace and unity of worshiping one God.

And if perhaps they are disgusted and reproach us on this account, saying that we Christians do not possess unity among ourselves, and if because of this they are slow and sluggish about coming to salvation, I shall address them also for a little while and say what you should say to them.

Let them not place their supposed agreement before us; let them not pride themselves as though their own unity were something to admire. They do not suffer the enemy whom we suffer. He possesses them, even while they do not act in this way or that. He sees them worshiping false gods; he sees them as slaves—and slaves of demons. What profit is it to him that they quarrel, or what loss is it that they do not quarrel? Even while they think alike concerning one false and empty thing and agree among themselves, he possesses them in this way.

But when he saw himself being abandoned, when many were hastening to the one God, abandoning his sacrilegious rites, overturning temples, breaking idols, and prohibiting sacrifices; when he saw that he had lost those whom he held, that they had withdrawn from his household and come to know the true God—what could he do? How could he lay his ambush?

He knows that he cannot possess us if we are united. He cannot divide the one God among us; he cannot substitute false gods for us. He recognizes that our life is charity and our death dissension. He therefore introduced quarrels among Christians, because he could not manufacture many gods for Christians. He multiplied sects, sowed errors, and established heresies.

But whatever he has done, he has done it from the Lord’s chaff.

Behold, we have security, even though he rages, even though he lies in wait, even though he sows various dissensions among Christians. If we acknowledge our God, hold fast to him in harmony, and preserve the faith, we are secure.

Brothers, the grain either does not leave the threshing floor or returns to it. The wind of temptation carries away some chaff—not so that it may make for us a road of destruction, but an exercise in endurance.

How much chaff it does not carry outside, though even that must be winnowed at the end; and the entire chaff does not go anywhere except into the fire.

Therefore, my brothers, while there is time, we must strive with all the strength we can, with all the earnestness we can, so that, if possible, the chaff too may return while the grain does not perish.

Our charity is being tested here; a great task of our life is set before us. We would not discover how much we love our brothers if no one were in danger. The extent of the love involved in seeking would not appear if no one were held by the abyss of perdition.

## CHAPTER IX

### 11. Every effort must be made so that heretics may return to unity. The different duties of fishermen and hunters

Let us labor, brothers; let us not cease. Let us act with every work and every sweat, with devoted affection toward God, toward them, and toward one another, lest, while wishing to quiet their old quarrel, we create new quarrels among ourselves.

Above all, let us be careful to maintain the firmest charity among ourselves.

They have grown frozen in their iniquities. How will you melt the ice of iniquity in them if you do not burn with the flame of charity?

Let us not worry that we seem troublesome to them when we compel them. Let us attend to where we are leading them; in this let us be secure. Are we leading them to death, or rather away from death?

By whatever means we can, but with moderation, let us handle their old wounds. Let us be careful lest the one being healed fail while in the physician’s hands.

Why, then, should we care if the child cries when he is being taken to school? Should we think about the fact that he resists the physician’s hand when he is being cut?

The Apostles were fishermen, and the Lord said to them, “I will make you fishers of human beings” (Matt. IV, 19). Through the prophet it is said that God would first send fishermen, and afterward hunters (Jer. XVI, 16).

First he sent fishermen; afterward he sends hunters. Why fishermen, and why hunters?

Believers were fished out from the abyss and the depths of the sea of superstitious idolatry by the nets of faith.

But where were the hunters sent? When those people wandered through mountains and hills—that is, through the pride of human beings and the swellings of earthly things.

One mountain was Donatus, another Arius; one mountain was Photinus, another Novatus. They wandered through these mountains; their error needed hunters.

Therefore the duties of fishermen and hunters were distributed, lest these people perhaps say to us: “Why did the Apostles compel no one or force no one?”

Because a fisherman casts his nets into the sea and draws out whatever enters them.

But a hunter surrounds the forests, shakes the thorns, and, with terrors multiplied on every side, drives the quarry into the nets. “Do not go this way; do not go that way. Attack from there; strike from there; frighten from there. Let it not get out; let it not escape.”

But our net is life, provided only that charity be preserved.

Do not consider how troublesome you are to them; consider how dear they are to you. What kind of piety is it if you spare them and they die?

## CHAPTER X

[Col. 0715]

### 12. A comparison showing that it belongs to piety not to spare obstinate heretics, lest they perish

Brothers, consider this comparison and likeness as well. One thing can have many comparisons.

Human beings are born under this condition: every person wants his children to succeed him, and there is no one who does not either desire or hope for this order in his household—that those who beget children should yield, and those who are begotten should succeed them.

Yet if an old father should fall ill—I do not mean if the son whose father is present, whom he expects to be his heir, whom he desires as his successor, and whom he therefore begot so that, when the father has died, the son himself may live; I do not mean such a case. Rather, if an old father should fall ill, on his way out, already near death, already approaching the order of nature, already having nothing further to hope for—if, nevertheless, he should fall ill and his devoted son should be present, and a physician should see him oppressed by a deadly and harmful sleep, the son is patient with the old man who is about to die for the sake of the few days during which the father can still live.

The son stands by and remains anxiously present to his father. When he hears the physician say, “This man may be lethargic and may die from it if he is allowed to sleep; if you want him to live, he must not sleep,” that harmful sleep presses upon the old man—a sleep that is both harmful and sweet.

His son, warned by the physician, stands anxiously beside him and troubles his father. He knocks; and if his knocking is overcome, he pinches; and if pinching accomplishes nothing, he pricks.

Certainly he is troublesome to his father; and he would be impious unless he were troublesome.

But the man who delights in dying strikes back at his troublesome son with a sorrowful look and voice: “Leave me alone. Why are you troubling me?”

But the physician says, “If you sleep, you will die.”

And the old man says, “Leave me; I want to die.”

The old man says, “I want to die”; and the son is impious if he does not say, “I do not want that.”

And that life is temporal, of course; nor will the man whose son troubles him in order to awaken him remain in it forever, nor will the one who succeeds his departing and dying father. Both pass through it; both fly through it temporarily. Yet they are impious unless, even while they trouble one another, they care for that temporal life itself.

Shall I therefore see my brother oppressed by the sleep of a harmful habit and not awaken him, because I fear being troublesome to one who is sleeping and perishing? Far be it from me to do this, even if our inheritance were diminished while he lived.

But now, since what we are to receive cannot be divided, since it cannot be diminished by an increase in the number of its possessors, shall I not raise him up—even by troubling him—so that he may keep watch and, deprived of the sleep of the most ancient error, rejoice with me in the inheritance of unity?

I will certainly do so. If I am awake, I will do so; if I do not do so, then I too am asleep.

## CHAPTER XI

### 13. Against heretics who divide the Church

Dearly beloved, a certain man interrupted the Lord while he was speaking to the crowds and said to him: “Lord, tell my brother to divide the inheritance with me.”

And the Lord replied: “Man, who appointed me a divider of an inheritance between you?” (Luke XII, 13–14).

He was not, of course, disdaining to restrain greed; but he did not wish to become a judge for the purpose of division.

But we, dearly beloved, should not seek him as judge of such matters, for our inheritance is not of that kind. With pure face and good conscience let us appeal to our Lord, and let each one of us say to him: “Lord, tell my brother not to divide the inheritance, but to hold it with me.”

What do you want to divide, brother? What the Lord has left us cannot be divided. Is it gold, so that he may bring out a balance for dividing it? Is it silver, money, slaves, cattle, trees, or fields? All these things can be divided.

But he says, “My peace I give you; my peace I leave you” (John XIV, 27).

Finally, even in earthly inheritances division makes the inheritance smaller. Place two brothers under one father: whatever the father possesses belongs to both; all of it belongs to one, and all of it belongs to the other.

Therefore, if either of them is asked about the possessions, he answers as follows: “Whose is that horse, for example?” “It is ours.” “Whose is that estate, that slave?” In every case he answers: “It is ours.”

But if they divide, the answer is now different. “Whose is that horse?” “Mine.” “Whose is this one?” “My brother’s.”

Behold what division has done to you. You have not acquired one thing; you have lost one thing.

Therefore, even if we possessed such an inheritance as could be divided, we still ought not to divide it, lest we diminish our riches.

And certainly nothing is more offensive to sons than wanting to divide an inheritance while their father is alive. Finally, if they attempt to do this, if they devote themselves to quarrels and disputes in order to claim their portions for themselves, the old man cries out: “What are you doing? I am still alive. Wait a little for my death; then cut up my household.”

But we have God as our Father. Why do we go toward division? Why do we go toward quarrels? Certainly let us wait. If he can die, let us divide.

[Col. 0715]

## SERMON OF SAINT AURELIUS AUGUSTINE, BISHOP OF HIPPO, ON THE DESTRUCTION OF THE CITY

[Note: [Col. 0715] Cited by Bede on 1 Corinthians X.]

[Note: [Col. 0715] The Sermon on the Usefulness of Fasting has not been found except in printed editions. The Sermon on the Destruction of the City was checked against an old manuscript of the Abbey of Saint Michael at Peril of the Sea (in Periculo Maris), and against the editions of Erasmus and Louvain.]

[Note: [Col. 0715] In addition, we compared all the editions mentioned at the beginning of the Retractations and the Confessions, vol. 1. M.]

(C, G, S)*

## CHAPTER I

### 1. By the example of Daniel confessing his sins, he rebukes those who complain against God about the destruction of the City. What Noah, Daniel, and Job signify

Let us consider the first reading from the holy prophet Daniel, in which we heard him praying and marveled that he confessed not only the sins of his people but also his own.

For after that prayer—whose words certainly indicated that he was not only one who pleaded for mercy but also one who confessed—after that prayer, he says: “While I was praying and confessing my sins and the sins of my people to the Lord my God” (Dan. IX, 20).

Who, then, is there who can profess himself to be without sin, when Daniel confesses his own sins?

For it was said to a certain proud man through the prophet Ezekiel: “Are you wiser than Daniel?” (Ezek. XXVIII, 3).

Likewise, among certain holy men through whom God signifies three classes of human beings whom he will deliver when great tribulation is about to come upon the human race, he also placed this Daniel. And he said that no one would be delivered from it except Noah, Daniel, and Job (Ezek. XIV, 14).

It is indeed clear that in these three names God signifies, as I said, three particular classes of human beings.

Those three men have already fallen asleep, their spirits are with God, and their bodies have decayed in the earth. They await the resurrection and their placement at the right hand, and they fear no tribulation in this world from which they desire to be delivered.

How, then, will Noah, Daniel, and Job be delivered from that tribulation?

When Ezekiel said these things, perhaps Daniel alone was still in the body. For Noah and Job had long ago fallen asleep and been gathered to their fathers in the sleep of death.

How, then, could they be delivered from an impending tribulation, when they had long ago been delivered from the flesh?

In Noah are signified good leaders who rule and govern the Church, just as Noah governed the ark during the Flood. In Daniel are signified all holy persons living in continence; in Job, all married people who live justly and well.

These three classes of human beings God delivers from that tribulation.

Nevertheless, how highly Daniel is commended appears from the fact that he was worthy to be named as one of those three—and yet he confesses his sins.

When Daniel therefore confesses his sins, whose pride does not tremble? Whose swelling does not subside? Whose arrogance and exaltation are not restrained?

“Who can boast that he has a chaste heart, or who can boast that he is clean from sin?” (Prov. XX, 9).

## CHAPTER II

### Why God did not spare the City for the sake of the righteous. The righteous in two senses

People marvel—and would that they only marveled and did not also blaspheme—when God chastises the human race and agitates it with the scourges of loving correction, exercising discipline before judgment and often not choosing whom to scourge, because he does not wish to find someone whom he must condemn.

For he scourges the righteous together with the unrighteous. Yet who is righteous, if Daniel confesses his own sins?

### 2. Abraham’s intercession for the city

A reading from the Book of Genesis was read a few days ago which, unless I am mistaken, made us very attentive. There Abraham says to the Lord whether, if he finds fifty righteous people in the city, he will spare the city for their sake, or destroy the city together with them.

And the Lord answered him that if he found fifty righteous people in the city, he would spare the city.
