Then Abraham continued his questioning and asked whether, if there were five fewer and forty-five remained, he would likewise spare it. God answered that he would spare it for the sake of the forty-five.

Why say more? Gradually, by questioning and subtracting from that number, he came down to ten. He asked the Lord whether, if he found ten righteous people in the city, he would destroy them with the rest of the innumerable wicked, or would rather spare the city for the sake of the ten righteous.

God answered that he would not destroy the city even for the sake of ten righteous people (Gen. XVIII, 23–32).

What, then, shall we say, brothers? A strong and pressing question confronts us, especially from people who maliciously attack our Scriptures rather than investigate them with reverence. They say, particularly concerning the recent destruction of so great a city:

“Were there not fifty righteous people in Rome? In such a large number of faithful people, such a large number of holy women and celibates, such a large number of male and female servants of God, could not even fifty righteous people be found—nor forty, nor thirty, nor twenty, nor ten?

“If this is incredible, why did God not spare that city for the sake of fifty, or even ten, righteous people?”

Scripture does not deceive, unless a human being deceives himself. When the question concerns righteousness, and God answers concerning righteousness, he seeks righteous people according to the divine standard, not according to the human standard.

I answer quickly, therefore: either he found that many righteous people there and spared the city, or, if he did not spare the city, he did not find righteous people there.

But I am answered that it is obvious that God did not spare the city.

I reply: No, it is not obvious to me. For the destruction that took place there was not like the destruction that took place in Sodom.

The question concerning Sodom arose when Abraham questioned God. But God said, “I will not destroy the city”; he did not say, “I will not scourge the city.”

He did not spare Sodom; he destroyed Sodom. He completely consumed Sodom with fire. He did not postpone it for judgment, but exercised upon it what he reserves for other evils until judgment.

Absolutely no one escaped from Sodom. Nothing human remained, nothing of the cattle, nothing of the houses; fire entirely swallowed everything.

Behold how God destroyed a city.

But from the city of Rome, how many people went out and will return? How many remained and escaped? How many were in holy places where they could not even be touched?

“But many were led away captive,” they say.

So too was Daniel—not for his punishment, but for the consolation of the others.

“But many were killed,” they say.

So too were all those righteous prophets, from the blood of Abel to the blood of Zechariah (Matt. XXIII, 35). So too were the Apostles as a whole; so too was the Lord himself, the Lord of the prophets and Apostles.

“But many were tortured with various torments,” they say.

Do we suppose that anyone suffered as much as Job?

### 3. The calamities reported from the city

Horrifying events have been reported to us: slaughter, fires, plundering, killings, and the torturing of human beings.

It is true. We have heard many things; we have groaned over everything; we have often wept; we have scarcely found consolation. I do not deny or reject it: we have heard many things, and many things were committed in that city.

## CHAPTER III
In the devastation of the City, nothing more grievous occurred than Job’s calamity. Yet, my brothers (let your Charity attend to what I say), we have read in the Book of holy Job that, when his possessions had been destroyed and his children lost, he could not even preserve the flesh that alone remained to him; struck by a grievous wound from head to foot, he sat upon dung, rotting with an ulcer, flowing with discharge, swarming with worms, tortured by the most bitter torments of pain. If it were reported to us that the entire city was sitting—sitting, I say, the whole city, with no one there sound, covered with the gravest wounds, and rotting with living worms just as the dead rotted—what would be more grievous: this, or that war? I think iron would rage less harshly against human flesh than worms; blood would flow more tolerably from wounds than discharge would drip from putrefaction. You see a corpse corrupting and shudder; yet the punishment is for that reason less severe, because the soul is absent. But in Job the soul was present and felt all this—bound so that it could not flee, subjected so that it would suffer, pierced so that it would blaspheme [Note: Some passages here have been restored from the Michaelinus manuscript]. Yet Job endured the tribulation [Note: Erasmus, the Lyons edition, Venice edition, and Louvain edition: “nevertheless Job endured”; M.], and it was reckoned to him as great righteousness. Therefore no one should consider what he suffers, but what he does. In what you suffer, man, your power is not involved; in what you do, your will is either guilty or innocent.

Job was suffering; his wife stood there, left alone—not for consolation, but for temptation; not to bring medicine, but to urge blasphemy: “Say something against God,” she said, “and die.” See how dying was a benefit to him, and no one offered him such a benefit. But in all that the holy soul endured, patience was exercised, faith was tested, the woman was refuted, and the devil was defeated. What a great spectacle—and, amid that foul putrefaction, what a splendid beauty of virtue! The enemy secretly lays waste; the female enemy openly counsels evil: an aid to the devil, not to her husband; a new Eve, but he was not the old Adam: “Say something against God, and die.” By blaspheming, wrest away what you cannot obtain by praying.

“You have spoken,” he said, “like one of the foolish women.” Attend to the words of a strong and faithful man; attend to the words of one rotting outwardly but sound within: “You have spoken,” he said, “like one of the foolish women. If we have received good things from the hand of the Lord, shall we not endure evil things?” (Job I and II). He is a father; is he to be loved when he caresses us and rejected when he corrects us? Is he not a father who both promises life and imposes discipline? Have you forgotten: “My son, when you approach the service of God, stand in righteousness and fear, and prepare your soul for temptation”? “Accept everything that is brought upon you; and in your sorrow endure, and in your humility have patience, because gold and silver are tested in the fire, but acceptable men in the furnace of humiliation” (Eccli. II, 1–5). Have you forgotten: “For whom the Lord loves, he corrects; moreover, he scourges every son whom he receives” (Prov. III, 12; Hebr. XII, 6)?

## CHAPTER IV

**4. Temporal torments are light when compared with Gehenna.** Consider any torments you please; extend your mind to whatever human punishments exist in this life; compare them with Gehenna, and everything you contemplate is light. Here, both the one who torments and the one who is tormented are temporal; there, they are eternal. Are those who suffered at the time when Rome was devastated still suffering? But that rich man is still suffering in the underworld (Luke XVI, 19–26). He burned, he burns, and he will burn; he will live until the judgment. He will receive his flesh, not for benefit, but for punishment.

Let us fear those punishments, if we fear God. Whatever a person suffers here, if he is corrected, is amendment; if even then he is not corrected, it is a double condemnation. Here he has suffered temporal punishments, and there he will experience eternal ones.

I say to your Charity, brothers: certainly we praise, glorify, and admire the holy martyrs; we celebrate their days with devout solemnity, venerate their merits, and, if we can, imitate them. Indeed, the glory of the martyrs is great; but I do not know whether the glory of holy Job was less. Yet he was not told, “Place incense before idols, sacrifice to foreign gods, deny Christ”; he was told, nevertheless, “Blaspheme God.” Nor was he told, so as to imply, “If you blaspheme, all the putrefaction will withdraw and health will return”; rather, the foolish and senseless woman said, “If you blaspheme, you will die, and by dying you will escape the torments.” As though eternal pain would not follow a blasphemer upon death!

The foolish woman shuddered at the distress of present putrefaction and gave no thought at all to the eternal flame. He bore the present evil so as not to fall into what was future. He kept his heart from evil thought and his tongue from cursing; he preserved the soul’s integrity amid the body’s putrefaction. He saw what he was escaping in the future; therefore he bore what he was suffering.

Thus, thus should every Christian, whenever he suffers some bodily affliction, contemplate Gehenna and see how light is what he suffers [Note: The Michaelinus codex reads: “and he will perceive more clearly how light is what he suffers,” and so forth]. Let him not murmur against God or say, “God, what have I done to you? Why am I suffering these things?” Rather, let him say what Job himself, although holy, said: “You have examined all my sins and marked them as if in a bag” (Job XIV, 16–17). He who suffered did not dare to say that he was without sin—not because he was being punished, but because he was being tested. Let everyone say this when he suffers.

## CHAPTER V

**5. Whether there were righteous people in Rome, for whose sake the City might be spared. All possess sins which they should confess sincerely.** There were fifty righteous people in Rome—or rather, if you consider the human standard, thousands of righteous people; but according to the rule of perfection, no righteous people exist. Whoever in Rome dares to call himself righteous will not hear that from me [Note: In the same manuscript: “No righteous people exist. Let whoever in Rome dares to call himself righteous come forward. From me he will hear: ‘Are you wiser than Daniel?’”]: “Are you wiser than Daniel?” (Ezech. XXVIII, 3). Hear him, then, confessing his sins (Dan. IX, 20). Or perhaps, when he confessed, he was lying? He therefore had this sin: he was lying to God about his sins.

But people sometimes argue and say, “A righteous person ought also to tell God that he is a sinner; although he knows that he has no sin, nevertheless he should say to God, ‘I have sin.’” I wonder whether this should be called sound counsel. Who makes you have no sin? Is it not God, who heals your soul? That is, if you have no sin. For consider, and you will find not one sin but sins.

Yet if you truly have no sin, is this not the benefit of the one to whom you said, “I said, Lord, have mercy on me; heal my soul, for I have sinned against you” (Ps. XL, 5)? If, therefore, your soul is without sin, your soul has been healed in every respect. If your soul has been healed in every respect, why are you ungrateful to your physician, saying that a wound still exists where he has already brought complete healing?

If you showed your sick or wounded body to a physician and asked him to apply his healing care, and he did so, restoring you sound and unharmed, while you still said, “I am not well,” would you not be ungrateful to the physician? Would you not be insulting him? If God has healed you, do you dare to say, “I still have a wound”? Do you not fear that he may answer you, “Then I have done nothing, or everything I did has been wasted; I accept no payment and deserve not even praise”?

May God turn away this madness and this empty argument. Let a person say, “I am a sinner,” because he is a sinner; let him say, “I have sin,” because he has sin. For if he does not have sin, he is not wiser than Daniel.

Therefore, my brothers, let me settle that question once and for all. If people are called righteous in the way they are presently called righteous according to a human standard—according to a certain manner of life in which they live among human beings blamelessly—there were many such people in Rome, and for their sake God spared it; many escaped. But God also spared those who died. Those who died in a good life and true righteousness, in good faith—were they not freed from the troubles of human affairs and brought to divine refreshment? They died after tribulations, as did the poor man before the rich man’s gate. But did they suffer hunger? He suffered it too. Did they suffer wounds? He suffered them too—perhaps the dogs licked them less. Did they die? He died too. But hear the end: “It came to pass,” he says, “that the poor man died and was carried by the angels into Abraham’s bosom” (Luke XVI, 20–22).

## CHAPTER VI

**6. How God spared the City for the sake of the righteous. Constantinople, corrected and saved by divine means through fear of the impending fire.** Would that we could see with our eyes the souls of the saints who died in that war! Then you would see how God spared the city. For thousands of saints are in refreshment, rejoicing and saying to God: “Thanks to you, because you have rescued us from the troubles and torments of the flesh. Thanks to you, because now we fear neither barbarians nor the devil. On earth we fear neither hunger, nor hail, nor the enemy, nor the executioner, nor the oppressor; but we are dead on earth and with you, God, never to die, safe in your kingdom—not by our merit, but by your gift.”

What sort of city of the humble is it that says these things [Note: Erasmus and the Michaelinus manuscript read: “of thousands”]? Do you think a city should be reckoned by its walls? A city consists in its citizens, not in its walls. Finally, if God had said to the Sodomites, “Flee, because I am about to burn this place,” would we not say that they possessed great merit if they fled, while a flame descending from heaven destroyed the walls and fortifications? Would God not have spared the city because the city had moved away and escaped the destruction of that fire?

**7.** Did not, a few years ago, during the reign of the emperor Arcadius at Constantinople (what I am saying may be heard by some who know of it, and there are people here who were also present there), God, wishing to frighten the city, and by frightening it to correct, convert, purify, and change it, appear in a revelation to one of his faithful servants, a military man, as they say? He told him that the city would perish from a fire soon to come from heaven, and instructed him to tell the bishop.

The message was delivered. The bishop did not disregard it, but addressed the people. The city was turned toward the mourning of repentance, just as ancient Nineveh once had been (Jonah III, 5). Yet, lest people think that the one who had spoken had either been deceived by falsehood or deceived them through fraud, the day arrived that God had threatened. While everyone watched and awaited the outcome in great fear, and the beginning of night was already darkening the world, a fiery cloud appeared in the east, small at first, then gradually growing as it approached the city, until fire terribly threatened the entire city [Note: The editions read “a great fire.” The Michaelinus manuscript more suitably reads “fire”]. A dreadful flame seemed to hang above them, and there was no lack of the smell of sulfur.

Everyone fled to the church; the place could not contain the crowd. Each person sought baptism from whoever could administer it. Salvation through the sacrament was demanded not only in the church but also throughout the houses, alleys, and streets—not, of course, so that the present wrath might be escaped, but the future wrath.

After that great tribulation, when God had shown the truth of his words and of the revelation given by his servant, the cloud began to diminish as it had grown, and little by little it was consumed. The people, having become somewhat secure, heard again that everyone had to migrate, because the city would perish on the following Saturday.

The entire city migrated with the emperor. No one remained in his house; no one locked his home. Moving far from the walls, and looking back at their beloved roofs, they bade farewell in mournful voices to their dearest dwellings. After that vast multitude had advanced several miles, it gathered in one place to pour out prayers to God. Suddenly it saw a great smoke and raised a loud cry to God. At last, when calm was observed, they sent people to report what had happened. The appointed hour passed without incident, and the messengers announced that all the walls and roofs remained safe and standing. Everyone returned with immense rejoicing. No one had lost anything from his house; each person found it open just as he had left it [Note: Marcellinus and Prosper mention this in their Chronicles, as does Paul the Deacon, book 13. Baronius refers to it under the year 396].

## CHAPTER VII

**8. Rome, like Constantinople, was chastised by God rather than destroyed.** What shall we say? Was this the wrath of God, or rather his mercy? Who would doubt that the most merciful Father wished to correct the city, and to punish it by frightening rather than destroying it, when the great impending calamity harmed nothing—neither people, nor houses, nor walls [Note: The same manuscript reads thus. The editions have “the presence of the calamity”]?

It happened exactly as hands are accustomed to be raised for striking and then, when the person about to be struck is terrified, are withdrawn out of pity. So it happened to that city. Nevertheless, if, at the time when the entire abandoned population had departed, devastation had fallen upon the place and destroyed the whole city like Sodom, leaving not even ruins behind, who would even then doubt that God had spared that city, since, after it had been warned and terrified and its people had departed and migrated, that place would have been consumed?

Thus there is no reason to doubt that God also spared the city of Rome, which, before the hostile fire, had in large part migrated in many ways. Those who fled migrated; those who departed from the body migrated. Many who were present hid themselves somehow; many were preserved alive and unharmed in holy places. Therefore that city was seized by the hand of God correcting it rather than destroyed—like a servant who knows his master’s will and does things deserving of blows: “He shall be beaten with many stripes” (Luke XII, 47).

## CHAPTER VIII

**9. The usefulness of temporal tribulation.** May it serve as an example to awaken fear; and may the evil desire that thirsts for the world and longs to enjoy its most pernicious pleasures—when the Lord demonstrates how unstable and transitory are all the vanities and deceitful insanities of the age—be restrained rather than murmur against the Lord beneath deserved scourges.

A threshing floor undergoes one tribulation, so that the straw may be crushed and the grain cleansed. A refiner’s furnace undergoes one fire, so that the chaff may pass into ashes and the gold be freed from its impurities. So Rome too endured one tribulation, in which the devout person was either corrected or freed, while the impious was condemned—whether he was snatched from this life, where he would have paid more fully the penalties most justly due, or remained here, where he would have blasphemed more damnably; or whether, in his ineffable clemency, God reserved for repentance those whom he knew would be saved [Note: Some passages omitted in the editions have here been restored from the Michaelinus manuscript].

Therefore let the toil of the devout not disturb us; it is exercise, not condemnation. Unless perhaps we shudder when we see some righteous person suffer unworthy and grievous things on this earth, and forget what the Righteous One of the righteous and Holy One of the holy endured. What that entire city suffered, one man suffered. But see who that one man was: the King of kings and Lord of lords (Apoc. XIX, 16), seized, bound, scourged, subjected to every insult, hung and nailed to the wood, and killed.

Weigh Rome with Christ; weigh the whole earth with Christ; weigh heaven and earth with Christ. Nothing created can be weighed with the Creator; no work can be compared with its Craftsman. “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John I, 3); and yet he was reckoned as nothing by his persecutors.

Let us therefore endure whatever God wishes us to endure. He knows, as a physician knows, what pain is useful for treating and healing us. Certainly it is written: “Patience has a perfect work” (James I, 4). But what work would patience have if we suffered nothing adverse? Why, then, do we refuse to endure temporal evils? Is it perhaps because we fear being perfected?

But let us plainly pray, groan, and weep before the Lord, so that what the Apostle says may be preserved for us: “God is faithful, who will not permit you to be tempted beyond what you can bear, but with the temptation will also provide a way out, so that you may be able to endure it” (I Cor. X, 13).

# APPENDIX TO VOLUME SIX OF THE WORKS OF SAINT AUGUSTINE, CONTAINING

[Col. 0723]

CERTAIN SPURIOUS LITTLE WORKS, NAMELY:

The Twenty-First Book of Sentences. The Dialogue of Sixty-Five Questions. The Book on Faith to Peter. On Spirit and Soul. On Friendship. On the Substance of Love. On Loving God. Soliloquies. Meditations. On Contrition of Heart. The Manual. The Mirror. Another Mirror, called the Sinner’s Mirror. On the Threefold Dwelling. On the Ladder of Paradise. On Knowledge of the True Life. On the Christian Life. [Col. 0724] On Salutary Teachings. On the Twelve Degrees of Abuse. On the Seven Vices and the Seven Gifts of the Holy Spirit. On the Conflict of Vices and Virtues. On Sobriety and Chastity. On True and False Repentance. On Antichrist. The Psalter, which Augustine is said to have composed for his mother. An Exposition of the Canticle *Magnificat*. A Treatise on the Assumption of Blessed Mary. On Visiting the Sick. Sermons on the Consolation of the Dead. Certain Other Sermons to the People. Finally, Sermons to the Brothers in the Desert.

## [BOOK XXI OF SENTENCES]

[Col. 0725]

### PREFATORY NOTICE TO THE FOLLOWING BOOK

Here you have some sentences taken from Augustine and others collected from various authors, rashly and without any fixed method reduced to the number of twenty-one sentences or questions. As a result, under the same title one frequently finds matters that are different and entirely irrelevant to the subject. Some material is also repeated twice in this very short book. Nor are there lacking solecisms and unlearned definitions and distinctions of matters, as the Louvain theologians observed after Erasmus. We possessed only one manuscript copy of this book, discovered in the Michaelinus monastery.

[Col. 0725]

# ONE BOOK OF TWENTY-ONE SENTENCES OR QUESTIONS (C, G, S)*

## FIRST SENTENCE.—“Blessed is he who…”

Everyone who wishes to live blessedly is blessed if he lives as he wishes. Every human being, however, wishes to live blessedly. Therefore every human being who lives as he wishes is blessed. From this it follows that no one who wishes to live disgracefully lives as he wishes, because no one who lives disgracefully is blessed. The reason he does not live as he wishes is that, although he does many things according to his will, more things nevertheless happen against his will.

## SENTENCE II.—On the Jews

Since the Apostle says that everything happened to the Jews in a figure (I Cor. X, 11), and that all past things were shadows—for the body is Christ—I can maintain that the Passover was celebrated only once, when Christ, the body signified, was killed.

For even if the sheep described by the Law for the Passover cannot be found, so that it is composed of sheep and goats—for the very nature of these animals contradicts their producing a common offspring—how could the true Passover have been celebrated when that particular lamb which is the Passover was lacking?

But if Christ is born according to the flesh from the righteous, that is, from sheep, and from sinners, that is, from goats, he alone is the lamb that is sought. Since he is killed no more than once, it is shown that, according to the truth, that perfect Passover was celebrated no more than once.

The figures, therefore, existed at that time, as we have said. The lamb is chosen to signify simplicity and innocence; a male is sought to demonstrate strength; one without blemish, to signify freedom from crime; one year old, to signify the completion of the time of preaching; perfect, to signify one equipped with every kind of virtue; in the first month, so that the whole year might be consecrated from its own beginning; on the fourteenth day of the month, so that, when filled with the light of truth, the night of error might be covered; toward evening, to signify that the setting of the world was approaching; with the leaven removed, so that the corruption of malice might be taken away from the heart of a perverse mind; with the lintels of the houses smeared with blood, so that the thresholds of the houses might be marked with blood as a figure of the Lord’s Passion; roasted in fire—for the Gospel and the word of Christ are strong food; not soaked in water—for it must not be dissolved in the watery weakness of a delicate interpretation.

Nothing is omitted, for absolutely nothing in Christ is rejected. Its bones are not broken, because Christ cannot be weakened—that is, overcome—in any respect. Whatever remains is committed to the divine fires: whatever someone cannot comprehend, he entrusts to Christ’s divine knowledge, while devoting himself, according to his strength, only to what is manifest [Note: Other editions read *epulatur*, “feasts”].

The fact that they eat standing is also a figure, lest anyone fall or prostrate himself in the Gospel out of necessity; rather, with the strength of a vigorous spirit, undefeated in the battles of persecution, that is, lofty and upright, he should stand firm [Note: Other editions read “of a mighty spirit”]. The girded loins signify evangelical continence, since the place of generation is restrained and bound. The staffs signify the Holy Spirit, on whom one relies. The shod feet signify the expulsion of the slipperiness of error, since, by advancement toward faith in heavenly things, everything in the Gospel is fixed as though by iron defenses and made solid with the firmest truth [Note: The manuscript and Erasmus read “by testing”].

They also eat in haste: for those who are fervent are proved by faith, while the lukewarm and negligent are rejected and vomited out. They eat it with unleavened bread: for Christ is received with the pure simplicity of an entirely simple spirit. They eat it with bitter herbs [Note: *Picridiae* are bitter vegetables, wild lettuces], for this Passover resulted in the bitterest bitterness for the condemnation of the Jews.

It was given only to the circumcised (Exod. XII), for the ability to receive the sacred food of Christ’s body is offered only to those who have been cleansed and purified by the bath of heavenly forgiveness [Note: The manuscript and Erasmus read “the food of the sacrament of Christ’s body”].

Thus the things that had been figured among the Israelites have been strengthened in us, and what were images for them are realities themselves in us. They practiced celebrating the Passover by means of likenesses, while Christ’s disciples alone would celebrate the true Passover.

> Not those who handle the entrails, the heart and liver of animals,  
> > but those whose prudent virtue cleanses their inmost parts,  
> > excluding the stain of vices laid beneath,  
> > will be able, with favorable oar-strokes, to penetrate heaven  
> > and race through the now-empty ether on joyful wings.

## SENTENCE III.—On the question of fate and fortune

Because I noticed, when I was present, that your mind was not lightly moved, and have now learned more agreeably and certainly from your letters, I owe you a reply of no small length, and so forth. I shall nevertheless be more eager if your Charity does not grow weary of frequently remembering me in your letters and if you inform me by reply what you think of this letter [Note: Augustine, Letter 246 to Lampadius].

## SENTENCE IV.—On magical miracles

One should not be disturbed when miracles produced by magical arts are generally similar to miracles performed through the holy servants of God. Thus it is written in Exodus that Pharaoh’s magicians did certain things in a similar manner to those performed by Moses (Exod. VII and VIII).

These things, therefore, should not cause wonder, since everything that happens visibly is believed, not unreasonably, to be capable of being performed even by the lower powers of this air. But there is this difference: when the saints perform such things, the lower creature is commanded by higher authorities in the name of God, the Lord of all things. When evil people perform similar things by magical arts, they are given into the demons’ power when the demons heed them.

They are worthy of being deceived by such an answer, so that what they appear to obtain as a benefit becomes a punishment for them, when certain aerial powers display miracles to them as though privately, in order to keep them subjected—yet by permission of divine providence [Note: The manuscript reads “divine,” omitting the word “providence”], so that, according to the merits of souls, each may receive what is assigned to him.

## SENTENCE V.—On the one hundred and fifty-three fish

When this number is considered, it can also suggest the holiness of the Church, and so forth … where sinners, who belong to the left, are not found [Note: From Question 57 among the Eighty-Three Questions].

## SENTENCE VI.—In what respect the human being is superior to beasts

No one doubts that a human being consists of soul and body, with the soul being a certain power by which the body is given life; and that these are two things, so that one is superior to the other, one ruling and the other serving.

But again, in the soul itself two things seem to be found: one, which loves divine things, understands and participates in reason, and is called rational; the other, which enjoys sensible things, shares with beasts, and is irrational.

Again, two things must be observed in these: one by which it desires to resist those who oppose it [Note: Louvain edition: “those who persist”]; the other by which it seeks to obtain what is fitting—which beasts also plainly do.

When these things are gathered together, it will be evident that a human being consists indeed of soul and body, but with their functions divided in this way. Over all these presides that first part, which is close to reason. When it takes delight in itself and in what belongs to it through the power and strength of its Maker—not through itself, since of itself it is nothing, but through the kindness of God, through which the soul exists—it frees the lower part of its nature by restraining it and drawing it away from temporal things, from the poverty of pains, the difficulty of need, and the troubles of illnesses; and it restores it to its own good through a beneficent generosity, so that firmness in justice remains in it, as it rules according to its nature and provides for what serves it.

But if the serving part delights in life and loves temporal things, it will be judged—not as ruling but as serving, not as providing for the inferior part but as obeying it—and in the end it will experience more grievous punishments, abandoned by all those things it loved against the commands of God.

But when it returns to heavenly things and wholly recovers itself through God’s benefits, it will be like the one by whom it was made, and it will be blessed, possessing the likeness according to which it was made. For it is written: “And God made man in the image of God” (Gen. I, 27).

The likeness that we are to receive by that very vision is expressed through the Apostle John: “Beloved, we are children of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be. We know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (I John III, 2).

Concerning the division of the soul it is said: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind” (Deut. VI, 5; Matt. XXII, 37). And the Apostle Paul says: “May the Lord keep your spirit, soul, and body safe” (I Thess. V, 23).

Therefore the human being is superior to beasts in nothing except that he has an intellectual soul. He is superior to other human beings when he understands God and, corrupted by vanity, does not pursue temporal goods. For this too is most truly said: “Do not be like the horse and the mule, which have no understanding” (Ps. XXXI, 9). And this: “Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord” (I Cor. I, 31), which is understood as: “For I am the Lord.” And this: “Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity. What abundance does a person have in all his labor with which he labors under the sun?” (Eccl. I, 2–3).

## SENTENCE VII.—On the resurrection of the body

Apart from the fact, entirely worthy of faith, that nothing is impossible for God, it can also be concluded by such reasoning that it is not contrary to nature for this body to rise again.

The whole body—which is also signified by the name of the sensible heaven and earth of this world—exists in some manner. Everything that exists in some manner, yet not in the supreme manner, exists by participation in that form which exists in the supreme manner; insofar as it exists, it can undergo whatever ordered changes it is capable of undergoing while that form is retained.

But it cannot cease altogether to be a body. For if it will not be a body at all, it will either be nothing or something better. But it is not permitted to be nothing, since the form that always remains and truly exists in the highest degree prevails. Nor can it be something better than a body, because the entire universe of bodies has a fixed measure, and the number of incorporeal things that have been made does not need to be increased.

Nor is there any need for a new nature to be made, as though all things had not been made or another thing had to be substituted for something that had perished. Everything has been made perfectly, and all things are governed by providence according to a form that always remains, so that sensible nature, through ordered mutability, and thereby through a certain permanence within change, may proceed and thus remain within its own kind and preserve its proper measure.

It follows that every body is one thing at one time and another at another time, yet does not cease to be a body. Thus the whole of nature remains intact, even though the things perceived by our senses depart and are thought to perish completely.

Therefore it is not surprising if this body receives its own measure, in which it now exists insofar as it exists, or acquires some better measure, since what is called destruction is a departure into other modes, not complete annihilation.

## SENTENCE VIII.—On faith, hope, and charity

Faith without hope and charity exists if you say: “I believe that the things to which you call me are true, but I cannot and do not wish to attain them.”

Faith without hope, but with charity, exists if you say: “I believe that the things to which you call me are true, and I wish to attain them, but I cannot.”

Faith with hope but without charity exists if you say: “I believe that the things to which you call me are true, and I can attain them if I wish, but I do not wish to.”

Charity without hope and faith exists if someone says that he very much wishes to live eternally without the enticements of his body, but neither believes that eternal life exists nor, if it exists, believes that he can attain it.

Charity with faith but without hope exists if someone says that he both desires eternal life and believes that it exists, but denies that he can attain it.

But how hope could exist without faith, I do not see. No one hopes to attain what he does not believe exists.

All three must therefore be present in the mind—faith, hope, and charity—so that a person believes that the things to which he is called are true, hopes that he can attain them, and loves them altogether.

## SENTENCE IX.—That philosophy is divided into three parts

Philosophy is divided into three parts: moral, natural, and rational.

Moral philosophy is divided into two parts: knowledge and administration. Knowledge is divided into two parts: exhortation and the treatment of good and evil. Administration is divided into two parts: duty and the end. Duty concerns what we ought to do; the end is that to which we refer everything we rightly do, while the end itself is referred to nothing else.

Natural philosophy is divided into two parts: corporeal and incorporeal. The division of corporeal things is fivefold: into the cause, which makes something; the matter, from which it makes it; the motion, by which it makes it; the causation, why it makes it; and the effect, which it makes.

The division of incorporeal things is fourfold: into place—for place is not a body but the space occupied by a body; into time; into extremities—for the extremities of bodies are not bodies, since they have no thickness; and into things sayable (*dicibilia*)—for things sayable, which we conceive in the mind in order to express them in words, are not bodies. They are properly called “sayables” when they are impressed upon the mind through things by means of words.

Rational philosophy is divided into three parts: directing, which exists in the perception of the senses or is said to be existence; defining, by which we define whatever a thing is; and distinguishing, by which we reason and bring an argument to its conclusion.

## SENTENCE X.—What state Adam was in before he sinned

Before Adam sinned, his soul was rational, perfect, and blessed. He had a body—not such as our fragile and mortal body is now, but one suited to such a soul, which had not yet corrupted within itself the likeness of God by a perverse will; such as we too shall have after the resurrection, when the same soul has received that same likeness of God through perfect holiness.

But after he sinned, the rational soul became corrupted by desire, and he had a body such as we now see in ourselves.

## SENTENCE XI.—On the fall of the one who sins

We are seeking the cause of the sinner’s fall, which proceeds from free choice, although no deprivation and no desire was driving him to it. I seem, however, to suspect that it was caused by the quality of matter.

But the work of God and the perfection of God arise as an objection: it was from him that such a being, so great, deserved to be made. This confounds all our explanations, lest we suppose that God, despairing of that matter according to a better plan, therefore granted free choice so that, if sin should creep in, he would rightly be free from blame.

## SENTENCE XII.—One must beware of thinking that anything is truer than that everything which exists derives from that which exists through itself

And that which exists supremely exists with him and from him [Note: Erasmus: “That which exists supremely exists”; M.]. But that which does not exist supremely receives from him who exists supremely, out of nothing, the fact that it exists.

In this nature, therefore, what can rightly be attributed to God is only what it has in itself as existence—that is, all its goodness. But whatever pertains to sins and death undoubtedly inclines toward non-being. Whatever its source, it certainly does not come from that which exists supremely, nor from that which exists in any manner. It is therefore neither from God nor from any work of God.

It will therefore be from that which is contrary to the one who exists supremely. What you ask, then, as to where it comes from, has no source from which it comes.

## SENTENCE XIII.—What human beings have in common

The first animals are mortal, without sensation, and irrational, such as trees and the rest with which human beings have in common growing, generating, being nourished, and dying.

The second are mortal, irrational, and sensory, such as livestock, with which human beings have in common growing, generating, being nourished, dying, sensing, desiring, and fleeing.

The third are sensory, rational, and mortal, such as human beings.

The fourth are immortal, sensory, and rational, such as angels, with whom human beings have in common hearing, sensing, and understanding.

## SENTENCE XIV.—What is the will?

The will is a movement of the soul, compelled by no one, toward acquiring or not losing something [Note: From *On Two Souls*, chapter 10].

## SENTENCE XV.—Three kinds of virtues

The first are civic virtues, belonging to political life; the second are purgative virtues, by which the soul is stripped of vices; the third are exemplary virtues, which are impressed by God upon the mind that already contemplates, where everything lives, where everything always lives, where everything always lives blessedly.

Intelligible things are those that are understood. God is called intelligible because he is understood; intellectual because he understands through himself; the soul is intelligible because it is understood, and intellectual because it too understands.

## SENTENCE XVI.—On the beauty of the world
Now, if it pleases you, receive with unbiased ears and a pure mind

the first works of God—which you deny are good,

and cry out that all these things ought not to have been made;

for [the transmitted wording is unclear]: as God, the highest, [is] all things, the highest things were not made.

The first four elements of the good world are good.

Light fire, sharp and mobile above;

heavy, blunt, and sluggish earth is opposed to it below.

Therefore three things are hostile to the three highest as well as to the lowest [Note: [Col. 0729] The manuscript reads *quod ima*, “that the lowest.”],

while the two that come in the middle, air and water, bind

the extremes together, friendly to each again insofar as each is friendly to itself.

Air joins lightness and mobility to fire;

water joins blunt weight below to the earth;

it is a dull and mobile bond by which air and water cling together.

But what is dull and speaks from above, air ought to [join] the earth;

what is mobile and flows into the lowest, water ought to [join] the flames [uncertain; Note: [Col. 0729] Other printed editions read *unum*, “one,” instead of *imum*, “the lowest.”].

The middle elements take two things from their neighboring extremes [Note: [Col. 0729] Other printed editions read *bona*, “good,” instead of *bina*, “two”],

and from the things placed far away they have each taken one for themselves.

Thus this world is squared by diverse elements;

thus there is harmonious discord, thus things far apart are joined.

In this way all these things are duly balanced by their movements, so that

beauty may be proportionate in unequal numbers.

What each element bears, and what things suited to it it produces,

I shall relate as I am able, in verse [Note: [Col. 0729] Other printed editions read *numeros*, “numbers,” instead of *numeris*, “in verse”]; listen kindly:

so that, when in these things you see the covenants of the world established by the firm law of truth,

you may believe that these things were made in a definite order.

In these four elements—air, water, fire, and earth—

certain animals are created, suited to their proper place, and

possessing uses and movements appropriate to one another.

Those that walk and those that are fixed—we see two kinds—

are animals belonging to the two lowest elements.

Come now, look down upon the lowest things of earth, and compare the lowest with the highest:

every tree clings fixedly to the earth by its roots;

just as the fixed stars revolve high in the lofty heavens [Note: [Col. 0730] The manuscript reads *alta*, “high,” instead of *alto*, “lofty.”].

Whatever creeps along the earth leaves tracks here [Note: [Col. 0730] Other printed editions read *his*, “these,” instead of *hic*, “here.”];

the globe is such that the seven stars likewise set their courses for each [creature].

What swims in the waters and flies, moving through the surrounding air,

seeks alternately upward and downward among living creatures,

balancing the middle well by an effort exerted in either direction.

There is another corresponding feature, in turn, present in these four elements:

a double contrary quality. Attend briefly, and I shall explain, for these are no small matters.

Thus the first is contained in the third, and the fourth is as the second:

I want you to discern in these things their oppositions and the force of each.

Fire is hot and dry, possessing what is above;

the third, water, creeps along intensely cold and wet.

Air, placed between the two and mixed from both, is opposed to the fourth and is second from last,

partly similar to both, yet wholly dissimilar.

For it melts through the moisture of the waters [Note: [Col. 0730] The manuscript reads *liquescit quid aquarum*, “what of the waters melts.”], and fire boils with heat.

Earth takes rigidity from the waters and becomes dry through the sky.

Thus, through varying changes, the whole year is tempered by the four elements,

bound together through seasons that bring movement.

Rainy winter waters the earth with rain and constricts it with cold [Note: [Col. 0730] Lovaniensis reads *frigora*, “colds,” instead of *frigore*, “cold.”].

Dry, fiery summer ripens everything and scorches it.

Spring takes from both of these a pleasant tempering:

from fire and water it gently holds a warm air flowing softly.

Autumn grows numb with cold and gapes open with dryness.

Thus our four bodily elements are joined from these.

They also regulate the span of night and the hours of the days.

The middle part, which burns and dries with fire, belongs here to the day.

The middle part, cold and wet with waters, belongs there to the night.

The ends of night are wet; now the first light is warm.

From each side a gentle morning is tempered for you:

the last hours of day are dry; the first shadow is cold.

Take the law from both, and temper the evening [Note: [Col. 0730] The manuscript reads *et temperari vespere*, “and to be tempered in the evening.”].

And, envious one, [consider] so many such things: the shining stars of heaven,

heaven and the form of heaven and its perpetual movements,

the fixed weight in the middle, which is also the single weight of all the earth,

the blue-green Ocean sea, and the rivers, the hoofs of the nourishing world,

the clear airs, now dense, then soon serene [Note: [Col. 0730] The manuscript reads *orbi alma, Aura*, apparently “the nourishing world, Air.”],

so many winged bodies, colored, pleasing, gentle,

add the varied beauty and splendor of so many swimming creatures,

so much multiform beauty adorned with things born from earth:

and cry out that, envious of so many such things, you do not wish to be,

with the swift alongside the slow, and the steady wheel running as it wanders this way and that;

with stationary things remaining [Note: [Col. 0730] The manuscript reads *aestatisque moventia*, “and things moving with summer,” instead of *statisque manentia*, “and stationary things remaining.”], the rare among the dense, the great among the small;

things aflame among the obscure [Note: [Col. 0730] The manuscript reads *flammicerata*, “made flame-bearing,” instead of *flammiferata*, “aflame”], the black among the luminous;

things perishing among things born, and things born among those yet to be born;

the middle with the extremes, those with the middle, and the lowest with the highest,

agreeing according to the law above—I mean the law of truth—

they sound one song and sing together as one:

everything whatsoever that exists strives after a certain unity.

And cry out, if you dare, that, envious of so many such things, you do not wish to be.

## SENTENCE XVII.—That the clearer knowledge of good is the experience of evil.

Likewise, good things would not be sweet if they did not undergo adversities. Likewise, the good that one loved less when obeying, one loves more ardently by comparison. A person will not be great if he thinks it a great thing that logs and stones fall and mortals die [Note: [Col. 0730] Possidius, *Life of Augustine*, chapter 28.]. But if an artisan makes something from such material that is better than the material itself, has he not fashioned something better than himself? In no way: for the material can be neither better than nor even equal to the art. For material is subject to the artisan in this way: if it is subject, it must necessarily be inferior.

## SENTENCE XVIII.—What the prophet means when he says that the Lord has ordered all things by measure, number, and weight.

This concerns the Son: the eternally begotten; the Only-Begotten; the Word. “Measure” can be understood as one. For numbers are measured by it: thus the Father may be understood as measure, the number itself as the Son, and weight as the Holy Spirit—for he is love. For one who loves is said to be dependent upon love; and one who depends is on his way toward something. There will therefore be number from measure, and from this the order itself follows. “He depends” is said from weight. It belongs to the striving toward order. For order can also be understood as weight: weight can be an effort toward a place; the effort, or the desire of one striving toward a place, encounters that place. Weight, therefore, belongs to order.

It is clear that this light of the sun is a substance, not a quality. For a quality exists in a body, and where the body is, there the quality is. The body of the sun is in heaven; therefore its quality is there. A quality is such things as shape, color, hardness, or softness. But this light extends as far as the earth, and it is clear that it is a body: for it passes from place to place. These, then, are two infinite things: the light of the sun and the earth. A quality moves with that of which it is the quality.

Therefore the substances of the sun’s light and of the air, possessing their own natures, remain intermingled with one another without any constriction or expulsion of one by the other, so that one does not alter the other; and they are bodies.

Now apply this to incorporeal things that are coeternal, such as light and fire; to things equal, such as one human being from another. Coeternal is better than non-coeternal; equal is better than unequal. In that divine nature, therefore, there are both coeternity and coequality.

“With you is the beginning on the day of your power, in the splendors of the holy ones; from the womb, before the morning star, I begot you” (Psalm 109:3).

The highest good is not unfruitful or barren. Whatever is begotten from it is equal to it, especially in this respect: that one comes from one. And the highest limit of generation is one, whence “Only-Begotten” especially confirms equality. A limit is the end of each thing. But lest anyone think that the Son also ought to beget—for if that were so, there would be no end to begetting—what is measured is better than what is immoderate; because of equality, the end is more properly something measured.

One may be two infinite things, and these may be bodies, such as air and light, which extend through places without constricting one another. If this is so in bodily things, how much more in spiritual things? In the Lord there ought to be nothing mutable. If he begot in time [Note: [Col. 0731] Other printed editions read *ex parte*, “in part,” instead of *ex tempore*, “in time.”], he is mutable; a quality exists in a mutable substance.

In the Wisdom of Solomon: “All wisdom is from the Lord God, and it has always been with him, and it is before the age” (Ecclesiasticus 1:1). Likewise, in Solomon: “For she is a breath of the power of God, and a certain pure emanation of almighty God” (Wisdom 7:25). Again: “The fountain of wisdom is the word of God in the highest” (Ecclesiasticus 1:5).

A reason proceeding forth is rightly called a word. A voice is something; silence is nothing. If the One existed alone, he would be in himself, barren, and would produce nothing. But because he is good, proceeding forth in order to make something, he proceeded into another who is himself. This is the generation of the Only-Begotten, because the one who makes exists, and the one through whom he makes exists, and the two have effected [what they effect].

One precedes two; and between these two there is a certain order, and three come to be, which is called the Trinity.

The Father is understood as the hinge of all things. For although a hinge is immovable, nevertheless the motion—which is understood as the Son himself—is said to be one, and all the worthy enjoy it, though not all in the same manner. For the more divinely a human being is taken up by divine Wisdom, the more divinely he understands.

Although there is one body, nevertheless all the members do not have the same health. The health of the eye is spoken of in one way, that of the head in another, and that of the rest of the body in another. A human being escaping from sin strives to understand; but the one taken up is taken up by that same understanding. Yet the hand will never be the foot, nor the foot the eye; so too a human being will never be what he is who was taken up by the Wisdom of God.

God is said to be finite externally as far as the soul, and internally as far as himself; for he contains all things in himself. The soul, however, is finite as far as the body and as far as God. The body too is finite externally as far as nothing, but internally it is infinite: for by dividing it never reaches an end.

## SENTENCE XIX.—On ideas.

Every passage from one place to another occurs through a line, because everything extended is joined to itself by a line, and every body is joined to itself by a line—which line is certainly not a body. So too every transition in the soul—that is, every change or affection by which it is now foolish and now wise—takes place through certain lines [Col. 0732], that is, through certain intermediate passages, just as the soul itself was made from nothing.

If a human being knows the truth, he is almost God; if God does not know the truth, he is not almost but truly a stone.

The human mind ought to be carried along by the best movement. By what circuit, then, should it be moved? The mind’s best circuit is rational thought, which proceeds from what is sought and returns more certain to its starting point through the circle of succeeding arguments.

Therefore likenesses are also suited to the intellect, because through the very movement that nature desires they are presented to the mind. For they seem to carry minds away from what is being done and then bring them back to it: what they carry away is directed against sluggishness; what they bring back is directed against error.

For this reason the ancient sages also chose to mark certain things by the images of myths, so that when attention is carried toward them and then brought back to what they signify, the mind, even while it plays, might be exercised in discussion through its movement. One must take care that no one lie.

Every soul is changed by affections, for it is also changeable in its functions. God and the angels alone are immutable; therefore they are always unchangeable when they perform their functions.

The worm is born from death and consumes death; born from corruption, it consumes corruption.

All mutable things change even in a moment of time, and especially bodies, which do not remain wholly at all, but are moved without interruption through their ages. For every thing has its own ages, so that in relation to a short age every greater age is, as it were, eternity. Even while they are still living, they undergo certain deaths of those ages; and the final death is in a certain way a greater death, so that the very growths of the ages undergo deaths.

When mountains collapse, and when islands collapse and arise, these are, as it were, deaths occurring in the whole universe, so that the final death for the world too is what is called the conflagration.

There are three things: one that is always immutable, such as God; one that is always mutable, such as the body; and a middle thing, such as the soul, which can be mutable and can also be immutable. But after the change the body does not change.

That, finally, is true and genuine freedom by which it comes about that wherever you are, it is well with you.

God alone is never absent from those for whom he alone is the source of pleasure [Note: [Col. 0732] Lovaniensis reads *sola*, “she alone,” instead of *solus*, “he alone.”].

But the merciful Father made mortal bonds for them [Note: [Col. 0732] A saying of Plotinus, from Book 9 of *The City of God*, chapter 10.].

The descent of the soul is such that, when it thinks it desires something beneficial to itself, it is drawn toward other things necessary to that object, as though what it wanted were entangled in many things; and it says, “Unwillingly I came before what I wanted” [Note: [Col. 0732] The manuscript reads *ac si id quo volebat*, “as though that by which he wanted,” and, for the quotation, *quo nolebam*, “where I did not want.”]; but it returns through the grace of God.

There are three kinds of virtues: the first are the civic virtues of political life, and so forth.

## SENTENCE XX.—On evil.

For a clearer knowledge of good is the experience of evil for those who possess inward power, so that through instruction they may know evil before experiencing it.

Good things would not be sweet if they did not undergo adversities. Likewise, the good that one loved less through observance, one loves more ardently by comparison.

A person will not be great if he thinks it a great thing that logs and stones fall and mortals die.

Does God exist before the ages according to time, or according to excellence? Not according to time before the ages; otherwise he begins to precede the ages in time, and the one who precedes them in time no longer precedes the ages.

## SENTENCE XXI.—On free will.

By God’s command we do what we wish, because we wish what we are able to do—provided that it is good. For evil is within our power, though it ought not to be within our will.

This, moreover, is both the greatest and the sole feature of free will: to will completely everything that you can rightly do [Note: [Col. 0732] In the manuscript, the following is added in the margin: “and to will nothing that you cannot avoid.”]. If you cannot do what you rightly wish to do, make yourself willing to do what you can rightly do.

It is clear that one who sins against the Holy Spirit cannot obtain forgiveness, for he is punished. When he is afflicted, the deed itself is punished in the very act of repentance, and the penalty is discharged. Therefore he is not forgiven, because he is punished.

## [DIALOGUE OF SIXTY-FIVE QUESTIONS.]

[Col. 0733]

## PREFATORY NOTICE TO THE FOLLOWING BOOK.

This book survives in very ancient copies under the title “Orosius Asking Questions and Augustine Answering.” Nevertheless, just as the style of the preface and of the questions differs from Orosius’ manner of expression, so the remaining discourse is not consistent with Augustine, except where his own words are quoted.

Questions have been gathered here from various places. The first twelve are found in the short work *On the Trinity and the Unity of God*, which is included among the spurious books in volume 8. Several of those that follow belong to the *Commentaries on Genesis* published under the name of Eucherius. Quite a few have also been excerpted from Augustine’s books *On Genesis Literally*.

Finally, the dialogue closes with an opinion of Augustine quoted in these words: “For concerning one who hastens to preside, one of the Fathers elegantly expressed the matter by saying: Let him know that he is not a bishop who desires to preside, not to be of benefit.” The passage is in Book 19 of *The City of God*, chapter 19: “Let him understand that he is not a bishop who has loved to preside, not to be of benefit.”

We compared the work with the Corbie manuscript, written nearly eight hundred years ago; with the manuscripts at Vendôme and Saint-Michel, at least six hundred years old; with four Roman manuscripts of the Vatican Library; and with the older editions.

In the Corbie and Saint-Michel manuscripts it is prefaced as follows: “Questions of Orosius and answers of Saint Augustine the bishop.” In one of the Roman manuscripts it is called “The Book of Dialogues of the blessed Augustine the bishop, with the priest Orosius asking questions.” It is inscribed not much differently in the other books.

[Col. 0733]

## DIALOGUE OF SIXTY-FIVE QUESTIONS UNDER THE TITLE “OROSIUS ASKING AND AUGUSTINE ANSWERING.” (C, G, S)*

[Col. 0733] Although many highly reputable men, differing indeed in style but not in faith, have published innumerable short works, so that it is difficult to read them all, nevertheless the works that are read are scarcely understood, because of the elegance of their expression and the extreme intricacy of their questions.

For in truth, while they are compelled by the profundity of divine Scripture to follow a hidden path, they have left our small understanding with no small degree of ambiguity. There are also plainly spiritual men who attain their eloquence and penetrate their meaning. But while we satisfy our desires, we do not equal their distinguished knowledge, so that we are able to understand these things as they did.

Therefore I ask you to answer me when I question you, and to clarify whatever causes obscurity.

## QUESTION I.

First of all I ask you whether God is a Trinity, and I desire to know by what testimonies you prove it.

### ANSWER.

The beginning of Genesis clearly demonstrates this. For it says: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth.” What other beginning should we understand except the Son? For when the Jews asked him who he was, he answered concerning himself: “The Beginning, because I am also speaking to you” (John 8:25). Therefore the Beginning is the Son.

Through the Son God made heaven and earth: “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made,” as the evangelist John relates (John 1:3). Without doubt, in the name of God the Father is to be understood, and in the name of the Beginning the Son.

Indeed, after saying, “In the beginning God made heaven and earth,” he immediately added, “And the Spirit of God was borne over the waters” (Genesis 1:1–2), who is the third person in the Trinity.

Therefore, if the Trinity did not exist, our Lord Jesus Christ would never have said to his disciples, “Go, baptize all nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19). Nor, when the Lord was baptized in the Jordan by John, would a voice from heaven have said, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased”; nor would it be said that the Holy Spirit descended upon him in the form of a dove and remained upon him (Matthew 3:17, 16).

I am astonished at the wretched Sabellian heresy, that is, the heresy of the Patripassians, because they are so blind in mind that they do not attend to such illustrious and unmistakable testimonies [Col. 0734]. They assert that there is one person: that is, that the very one who is the Father is himself the Son, and himself the Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 0734] Two Vatican manuscripts add *unam tantum*, “only one.”].

But leaving aside their blindness, let us understand three persons according to the holy Scriptures: one is the Father who begot, another the Son who was begotten by the Father, and another the Holy Spirit—not another thing, because they are one in substance. We distinguish the persons; we do not separate the deity.

Therefore the Son of God is Son by nature, not by adoption. For it is written: “From the womb,” he says, “before the morning star, I begot you” (Psalm 109:3). This is not because God the Father has a womb as we do, or is to be believed corporeal; rather, he wished “womb” to be understood as the substance from which the Son was born.

What the Father is, that he begot: God from God, light from light. Thus, just as a human being begets a human being, and a dog a dog, it has never been seen that a human being begot a dog. Therefore he begot the Son not from nothing, nor from some other substance, but from himself.

## QUESTION II.

I believe that I have been satisfied concerning the distinction of the persons and concerning the person of the begotten Son. Now I ask what you believe about the Holy Spirit: is he also unbegotten, or begotten?

### ANSWER.

A sure faith declares that the Holy Spirit is neither unbegotten nor begotten. For if we say that he is unbegotten, we seem to affirm two fathers; but if begotten, we will be accused of believing two sons.

But what the sure faith maintains is that he is neither unbegotten nor begotten, but proceeds from both—that is, from the Father and from the Son.

And to confirm this with testimonies, let us hear our Lord Jesus Christ himself teaching his disciples: “When the Paraclete has come,” he says, “whom I will send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father, he will bear witness concerning me” (John 15:26).

And again our Lord Jesus Christ, after his resurrection, wishing to show that the Holy Spirit proceeds from him just as from the Father, breathed upon his disciples and said, “Receive the Holy Spirit” (John 20:22). Likewise: “I will send the promise of my Father upon you” (Luke 24:49).

Therefore the Spirit of the Father and of the Son is one [Col. 0735], the Spirit of both is one. And that he is the Spirit of the Father, our Lord and Savior himself says to his disciples: “For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matthew 10:20).

And that he is also the Spirit of the Son, the apostle Paul bears witness: “But if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ,” he says, “he is none of his” (Romans 8:9).

## QUESTION III.

From the holy Scriptures we have observed concerning the individual persons that the Father is one, the Son another, and the Holy Spirit another; and that the Son is begotten while the Holy Spirit proceeds. Now I wish to know whether the Son or the Holy Spirit is God, and whether there is one substance or essence, which the Greeks call *homousian* (ὁμουσίαν, “of the same substance”).

### ANSWER.

Attend with an intent mind: I shall more willingly demonstrate what troubles you.

The blessed apostle Paul, writing to the Romans concerning the Israelites, says that their fathers are those “from whom Christ is according to the flesh, who is over all, God blessed forever” (Romans 9:5).

And again in the Gospel according to John: “That they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John 17:3). The order of the words is: “That they may know you, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent, the only true God.”

And again another Scripture says: “That we may be in his true Son Jesus Christ; he is the true God and eternal life” (1 John 5:20).

And to show his equality, the Lord himself says: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30). They are one, that is, in nature, not in person.

And again: “Therefore,” he says, “the Jews sought to kill Jesus, because he not only broke the Sabbath, but also called God his own Father, making himself equal with God” (John 5:18).

And again the blessed apostle Paul says: “Although he was in the form of God, he did not consider equality with God something to be seized” (Philippians 2:6). For it could not be seizure where the nature was equal; it had not been usurped, but born. He did not seize it, because he possessed it—and there are many other innumerable testimonies that do not occur to me at this moment.

The Acts of the Apostles teach most clearly that the Holy Spirit is true God. “Ananias,” Peter says, “why has Satan tempted your heart, so that you should lie to the Holy Spirit?” And below: “You have not lied to human beings, but to God” (Acts 5:3–4).

And in the Gospel according to John: “The Lord is Spirit” (John 4:24).

The apostle Paul, writing to the Corinthians, says: “Do you not know that your bodies are a temple of the Holy Spirit who is in you, whom you have from God, and that you are not your own? For you were bought at a great price; glorify and bear God in your body” (1 Corinthians 6:19–20).

The Father is God, I say; the Son is God; the Holy Spirit is God—not three gods, but one God.

For if the Father is greater, the Son lesser, and the Holy Spirit more than lesser, as heretical perversity asserts, then there will no longer be one God but three gods, which it is impious to believe.

And divine Scripture strongly refutes them: “Hear, O Israel,” it says, “the Lord your God is one God” (Deuteronomy 6:4).

Accordingly, just as we do not say three gods or three essences, so neither do we say three wisdoms or three spirits.

For when asked concerning the individual persons whether the Father is wisdom or the Holy Spirit is wisdom, we answer: the Father is wisdom, the Son is wisdom, and the Holy Spirit is wisdom—not three wisdoms or three spirits, but one wisdom and one spirit, just as there is one substance or one essence, because for him to be is the same as to be wise or to be spirit.

## QUESTION IV.

If the Father and the Son are equal, how does the Son himself say, “The Father is greater than I” (John 14:28); and, “I have not come to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me” (John 6:38); and, “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matthew 26:39); and, “My teaching is not mine, but his who sent me” (John 7:16)?

### ANSWER.

All these things, and others that you have not mentioned, were said according to the form of a servant which he assumed.

Therefore, when the first human being had been created by God, endowed with free will, and given a command [Col. 0736], if he had kept what God had commanded him, he would not have been punished with the death either of body or of soul [Note: [Col. 0736] In B, *ut si custodisset*, “so that if he had kept it.” We have followed Erasmus, the Lyon edition, the Venetian edition, and the Louvain edition. M.].

But he disobeyed God’s command, and, lifted up by pride, obeyed the serpent’s persuasion and despised God’s commands. This became the cause by which he incurred the danger of death, and by which all human nature, from that one human being, became corrupt, subject to sin, and mortal.

The apostle Paul says: “Through one human being sin entered the world, and through sin death, and so death passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned. For just as through one human being all human beings came into condemnation, so also through the righteousness of one all human beings come to justification of life” (Romans 5:12, 18).

And again: “The first human being was from the earth, earthly; the second human being was from heaven, heavenly” (1 Corinthians 15:47).

This, I say, is the heavenly human being. I call him heavenly because he was not conceived from human seed, but was assumed from the Virgin Mary by the Son of God for our salvation, as the evangelist John bears witness: “And the Word,” he says, “became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14).

The Word became flesh, not was changed into flesh, so that he did not cease to be what he was, but began to be what he was not. For he assumed flesh; he did not transform himself into flesh.

By “this flesh” we understand the whole human being by a part standing for the whole—that is, flesh and a rational soul. And just as the first human being had died both in flesh and in soul, so it was also necessary that through the mediator between God and human beings, the man Jesus Christ, he should be made alive both in flesh and in soul.

Therefore, as we said above, “The Father is greater than I” was said according to the form of the assumed human being.

## QUESTION V.

I see that, while you were investigating the one Son of God, you wanted to introduce two, so that you could speak of the Son of God and the son of man.

### ANSWER.

There are not two sons, but one. For he who was the Son of God became the son of man in the unity of person. Just as soul and flesh are one human being, so the Word and the human being are one Christ.

We understand two substances in the one Son of God: one of divinity, the other of humanity—not two persons. Therefore, if we say that there are two persons, we introduce two sons; and it will no longer be a Trinity but a quaternity.

Certainly, insofar as he is God, he is always equal to the Father, present everywhere, wholly in heaven, wholly on earth, and contained by no place.

Insofar as he is human, he both suffered and died, rose again, ascended into heaven, and sits at the right hand of the Father. Thus he will come to judge the living and the dead, just as he was seen to go into heaven, in the same form and substance of flesh; to that flesh he certainly gave immortality, but he did not remove its nature.

## QUESTION VI.

If the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one substance, how did the Son assume flesh without the Father and the Holy Spirit?

### ANSWER.

It was not the person of the Father or of the Holy Spirit, but only the person of the Son, who assumed flesh.

And so that you may understand this, I shall use comparisons, so that you may understand the Creator from the creature. Certainly there is reason in the soul, and although they are one, the soul does one thing and reason another: by the soul we live; by reason we are wise.

Thus, although the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one substance [Note: [Col. 0736] B reads *cum sit una substantia*, “since it is one substance.” We have followed Erasmus, the Lyon edition, the Venetian edition, and the Louvain edition. M.], the whole Trinity made the human being; yet the whole Trinity did not assume him, but only the person of the Son.

## QUESTION VII.

Did the Father beget the Son by will or by necessity?

### ANSWER.

Neither by will nor by necessity, because there is no necessity in God. But will cannot precede wisdom, which is the Son. Therefore it is rationally prior to know wisely than rationally to will.

For it is reported that when a heretic asked one of our people whether the Father begot the Son willingly or unwillingly, he gave this praiseworthy answer: “Tell me, heretic: is God the Father God by necessity or by will?” [Col. 0737]

If he had said “By necessity,” a great absurdity would have followed for him. But if he said “By will,” the reply was made to him: “Then he is God by will, not by nature.” Thus he himself fell into the snare he had wished to lay, and, seeing himself defeated, fell silent.

## QUESTION VIII.

How is that passage to be understood which says: “Just as the Father has life in himself, so he also gave the Son to have life in himself” (John 5:26)?

### ANSWER.

We know that the Son of God is not from himself, but was begotten by the Father; the Father, however, was begotten by no one and received life from no one.

The Father gave life to the Son by begetting him—not because the Son previously existed without life and afterward received life, as we, who lost life through sin, receive it again through the grace of the Savior. Rather, he is said to have received life because he was not begotten from himself; he did not give it by existing, but by begetting.

## QUESTION IX.

Since by reasoning and by testimonies you have persuaded me concerning the Son’s subordination—that he is not lesser according to substance, but according to the form of a servant which he assumed—I therefore ask what you think concerning the sending of the Holy Spirit. Did he too assume a human being, so that he may be said to have been sent?

### ANSWER.

Just as the Son is not said to have been sent or to be lesser according to substance, so neither is the Holy Spirit.

Finally, just as the Son was lesser or sent for the sake of the human being, so the Spirit is said to have been sent for the sake of the dove or the fire (Matthew 3:16; Acts 2:2), because he did not appear in that substance in which he is equal to the Father, but, as has been said, through a created thing placed beneath him.

For the Holy Spirit did not assume a dove or fire in the way the Son assumed a human being, so that he might remain in that form forever. Rather, those visions were made from an inferior creature for the manifestation of the Holy Spirit, and afterward ceased.

For that incomprehensible and immutable divinity, which is the triune God, can never be seen by bodily eyes except, as has been said, through a created thing placed beneath it.

## QUESTION X.

You have explained how the Son of God was born from the Father, while the Holy Spirit proceeds from both. Therefore I ask what difference there is between the birth of the Son and the procession of the Holy Spirit.

### ANSWER.

The Son belongs to the Father alone, not to the Holy Spirit; the Spirit belongs to both, that is, to the Father and the Son.

If the Holy Spirit were called a son, however, no son exists except from two, father and mother. Far be it from us to suspect anything of this sort between God the Father and the Son.

For even a human son does not proceed simultaneously from his father and from his mother: when he proceeds from his father, he does not then proceed from his mother; and when he proceeds from his mother into this light, he does not then proceed from his father.

The Holy Spirit, however, does not proceed from the Father into the Son and from the Son to sanctify creation; rather, he proceeds simultaneously from both.

## QUESTION XI.

How is that passage to be understood which the evangelist John says concerning the Holy Spirit, that he will not speak from himself? For he says: “For he will not speak from himself, but whatever he hears he will speak” (John 16:13).

### ANSWER.

He will not speak from himself because he is not from himself. The Father is born from no one; the Son is begotten from the Father; the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son.

Therefore he does not speak from himself, but whatever he hears, he speaks. For him, hearing means being; but being is not from himself, rather from the Father. Therefore whatever he hears, he speaks.

## QUESTION XII.

What does the apostle Paul mean when, writing to the Romans, he says: “For we do not know what we ought to pray for, but the Spirit himself pleads for us with unutterable groanings. But he who searches hearts knows what the Spirit desires, because he pleads for the saints according to God” (Romans 8:26–27)?

### ANSWER.

This manner of speaking is frequently found in the holy Scriptures, as when the Lord says to Abraham: “Now I know that you fear God” (Genesis 22:12)—that is, “I have caused you to know.” So the Apostle says: “Now knowing God—or rather, now being known by God” (Galatians 4:9).

All things are always present to God; before they happen, they are present, and future things are already accomplished. How, then, are we now said to be known by God, unless God causes us to know God?

So here too the Holy Spirit is said to groan for us—that is, to make us groan. For he pours into us love for God and neighbor.
