Just as a day is called joyful because it makes people joyful, or sad because it makes people sad, or a letter joyful because it makes people joyful, so here the Holy Spirit is said to groan because he makes us groan.

## QUESTION XIII.

When the Jews asked a sign from our Lord and Savior, he answered them: “This adulterous generation seeks a sign, and no sign will be given to it except the sign of the prophet Jonah. For just as Jonah was in the belly of the sea creature three days and three nights, so also will the Son of Man be in the heart of the earth three days and three nights” (Matthew 12:39–40).

Explain, therefore, how he was in hell for three days and three nights, since on the sixth day of the week, which is the day of preparation, at the ninth hour he gave up his spirit, and on the first day of the week, before dawn, which is the Lord’s Day, he rose again. Behold, there are neither three complete days nor three nights.

### ANSWER.

Our ancient fathers understood this to mean that the first day, which is the day of preparation, should be counted in its final portion, and the last day, which is the Lord’s Day, in its first portion, with each day counted together with its night. Thus, by naming the whole from a part, there were three days: the final part of Friday, the whole of the Sabbath, and the first part of the Lord’s Day, together with their nights.

## QUESTION XIV.

Our Lord Jesus Christ promises the saints that at the resurrection they will shine like the sun (Id. XIII, 43). Why, then, did the Lord himself not shine in this way at his resurrection?

**RESP.**

He certainly rose with his flesh glorified; but he did not wish to appear to his disciples in that glorification, because they would not have been able to endure such radiance with their eyes. For if, before he died for us and rose again, when he was transfigured on the mountain, his disciples could not look upon him but fell to the ground from fear, how much less could they look upon the Lord’s flesh when it had been glorified?

**QUESTION XV**

The evangelist Mark says that the Lord was crucified at the third hour (Mark XV, 25), while John says, at the sixth hour (John XIX, 14–18). Which of these two should be believed?

**RESP.**

Each of them spoke the truth, and likewise the other. For at the third hour the Jews cried out to Pilate, “Crucify him, crucify him” (Luke XXIII, 21). The soldiers, however, crucified him at the sixth hour. Thus what the Jews accomplished with their tongues, the soldiers accomplished with their hands. But so that the Jews would not appear not to have crucified the Lord, the evangelist stated that the Lord was crucified at the third hour, because those who carried out the execution were not the only ones who crucified him, but also those who cried out. In them was fulfilled what the Psalmist says: “The sons of men: their teeth are weapons and arrows, and their tongue a sharp sword” (Psalm LVI, 5). You see what kind of sword they had, with which they killed the Lord at the third hour.

**QUESTION XVI**

Since God created all things good, and since nothing exists that was not created by him, where does evil come from?

**RESP.**

Evil is not a nature; rather, the privation of good has received this name. Indeed, good can exist without evil, but evil cannot exist without good, nor can there be evil where good has not existed. Accordingly, we speak of a good angel and an evil angel, and of a good person and an evil person: the angel’s nature is good, while his corruption is evil; the human being’s nature is good, while his corruption is evil. Therefore, when we say “good,” we praise the nature; when we say “evil,” we condemn not the nature but the vice, which is contrary to a good nature.

**QUESTION XVII**

Were all the angels created equal or unequal? If equal, why were they not all firm and stable? But if unequal, by what merit did some deserve to receive stability in their foreknowledge, while others were entirely unable to foresee their future fall?

**RESP.**

[Col. 0739]

All the angels were indeed created equal. But when some fell through pride, the others adhered to the Lord in devout obedience, receiving certain knowledge of their own stability—a knowledge those others never possessed. Thus they are surrounded on every side by the grace of God, so that they can never fall away from the blessed life they enjoy while adhering to the Lord.

**QUESTION XVIII**

How should we understand what God says in Genesis: “Let us make the human being in our image and likeness” (Gen. I, 26)?

**RESP.**

There is reason and understanding in the mind. Therefore, when the mind thinks about eternal things, it should truly be called the image of God. In thinking about eternal things, it is masculine, as the apostle Paul says: “A man ought not to cover his head, since he is the image of the glory of God” (I Cor. XI, 7). The more it stretches itself toward what is eternal, the more it is formed according to the image of God; and for this reason it is not to be restrained, so that it may contain and moderate itself thereby. But when it does and thinks about temporal things, it is called feminine. At that point it should not be called the image of God, and therefore it ought to cover its head, lest its advance toward lower things become excessive and, while doing what is permitted, it desire what is forbidden.

[Note: [Col. 0739] See the book *On Spirit and Soul*, chapter 34.]

**QUESTION XIX**

Was the first human being made mortal or immortal?

**RESP.**

He was both mortal for one reason and immortal for another. The first human being had a body like ours, but without sin. He did not yet have a law in his members resisting the law of his mind; he acquired that only after his transgression. Adam therefore had an animal body, but through the power of that tree by which he was sustained—the tree that in paradise received the name “of life”—he would not grow old or waste away. Consequently, if he had kept God’s commandments, by the merit of his obedience he would afterward have been changed into that spiritual body which is promised to the saints at the resurrection. Thus he could have avoided death if he had adhered to God’s commandments in devout obedience. He had not been made in such a way that he could not die, as are the other natures that absolutely cannot die; rather, he had been made so that obedience would make him immortal and disobedience mortal.

**QUESTION XX**

What does the apostle Paul mean when he says, “Flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God”?

**RESP.**

On the basis of this testimony, many who understand it inadequately—and consequently make a heretical assertion—claim that a human being cannot rise again in the same flesh in which he died. Instead, removing true flesh, they attribute to the human being after the resurrection some kind of airy body that he never possessed. This is shown to be highly absurd when the actual statement is considered. “Flesh and blood,” he says, “will not possess the kingdom of God.” Then the same apostle Paul, explaining this in a certain way, continued and added: “Nor will corruption possess incorruption.” To whom was the Apostle writing? To those, certainly, who said, “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die” (Id. XV, 50, 32). Blessed Paul the apostle rebukes them, saying that flesh and blood—that is, the works of flesh and blood—cannot attain the kingdom of God.

For if “flesh” must here be understood as the substance itself, what will they say about those to whom the same apostle writes: “But you are not in the flesh, but in the spirit”? Did the Romans to whom the Apostle was writing not have flesh? “You are not in the flesh,” he says; that is, “you are not carnal; you do not perform the works of the flesh, which are hostile to God and are not subject to the law of God.” “Those who are in the flesh,” he says, “cannot please God” (Rom. VIII, 9, 8). Behold the kind of flesh that will not possess the kingdom of God.

But that the human being will rise again in the same flesh in which he dies, our Lord Jesus Christ demonstrated after his resurrection. When his disciples doubted and thought they were seeing a spirit, he answered them: “Touch and see, because a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see me have” (Luke XXIV, 39). Accordingly, we believe that the human being will rise again not only with flesh and bones but also with blood, and with whatever belongs to his nature; but without any corruption, [Col. 0740] he will possess everlasting life and eternal happiness, contemplating the Triune God. Thus, just as the righteous will rise with their flesh to eternal happiness, so the impious will rise to eternal misery.

**QUESTION XXI**

The beginning of Genesis says: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth” (Gen. I, 1). Were the angels made afterward, or not? For if the angels were made before them, God did not make heaven and earth first of all.

**RESP.**

“When the stars were made together,” Scripture says, “all my angels praised me with a loud voice” (Job XXXVIII, 7, according to the Septuagint). The stars were made on the fourth day, and the angels already existed. They were not made on the third day or on the second. For what was made on those days is evident. On the third day the dry land—that is, the earth—was separated from the waters. On the second day the firmament was made, where the sun, moon, and stars move. The first day itself, however, is the angelic nature, which was first called by the name “heaven.”

[Note: [Col. 0740] Two Vatican manuscripts add here: “in which it was made.”]

Thus it is clearly shown that the spiritual—that is, the angelic—nature was made on the first day, and then this heaven that we perceive with our eyes. For when he says, “In the beginning God made heaven and earth,” he does not mean “first of all,” as you say, but “in the beginning”—that is, in the Son; indeed, through the Son God made every spiritual and bodily creature, which has been called by the names “heaven” and “earth.”

That the Son himself is the Beginning is shown when the Jews asked him who he was and he replied: “The Beginning, because I am also speaking to you” (John VIII, 25). Therefore, first he wished to speak of heaven and earth as a kind of spiritual and bodily matter, and then to weave together in order how they were made individually. For by “heaven,” he seems to me to have meant the dark abyss of waters and, in a certain sense, a fluctuating life which, unless it turns toward the Creator, becomes light, and contemplates the Triune God as God in God.

We do not say this in such a way that this matter precedes its form as wood precedes a chest, but as the voice precedes the word—not in time, but in origin. Therefore, the first creature is not this light that was made on the fourth day, but the spiritual—that is, the angelic—nature.

**QUESTION XXII**

“The Spirit of God was borne over the waters” (Gen. I, 2). Was he borne locally, like the sun, moon, and other stars, or in some other way?

**RESP.**

The Holy Spirit is God. Therefore he is not contained in a place or extended through space, nor is he subject to the movements of time; rather, he is wholly present everywhere. Since Scripture has just named the creature over which the Holy Spirit was said to be borne, this is said not locally but potentially. God did not make his works out of need but out of benevolence, nor does he need the things he made. For love that is needy and impoverished is subject to the things it loves. Thus the Holy Spirit is said to have been borne over creation because he did not work upon that creation out of need.

**QUESTION XXIII**

“God said, ‘Let there be light’” (ibid., 3). Did he say this during the day, or before every day? If he said it during the day, he spoke temporally; if he spoke temporally, he spoke through some creature. Therefore, light is not the first creature.

**RESP.**

He did not speak during the day, nor did he speak temporally, because before every creature he begot his Word, and through the Word he created every creature. God’s speech, therefore, is God’s Word.

But divine Scripture, accommodating itself to little ones and, in a certain sense, nursing them so that they may advance and receive spiritual nourishment, chose to call God’s speech by the name “speech” throughout the formation of every creature. For example, if you ask, “How was light made?” you hear the answer: “It was in the Word of God that it should be made.” “How was heaven made?” “It was in the Word of God that it should be made.” And if you ask in order how the other things were made, they were in the Word of God that they should be made.

This is what is meant by, “God said, ‘Let there be light.’” The divine nature does not speak in bodily ways, nor, whenever it is said “He said,” does it form words each time. For he begot one Word, coeternal and consubstantial with himself, in which he spoke all things ineffably and outside time.

**QUESTION XXIV**

If God suddenly saw that the light was good (Gen. I, 4), did he previously not know this, and did seeing it give him knowledge?

**RESP.**

Every work is preceded by our will, when we think about what we ought to do. No one does anything while ignorant, when he considers how the things he has decided should be done through thought are to be made. And since it is impossible for a human being to do something while ignorant, how much less is this possible for God, who made everything he wished by his eternal and unchanging plan, and who did not see things as having been made one way and as needing to be made another? Thus he saw things as made in the same way he had seen them as needing to be made.

**QUESTION XXV**

“And he divided,” Scripture says, “the light from the darkness” (ibid.). Everything that is divided can also exist. Therefore, just as there is a substance of light, so there is a substance of darkness. And why did Scripture not say, “God saw that the darkness was good,” as it said concerning the light?

**RESP.**

God created all the angels good, by a good and unchangeable will. And because through the unchangeability of his foreknowledge he knew that some of them would fall through pride, he divided between the good and the evil. Calling the evil “darkness” and the good “light,” he said of the good, “God saw that they were good”; of the evil he said nothing of the kind, lest he appear to approve sins, which are darkness.

**QUESTION XXVI**

You assert that the first day is the spiritual creature. How, then, did it have evening and morning (ibid., 5)?

**RESP.**

Before every creature came to be in its own time, it first existed in the Word of God to be known by the angels, and then it was to be made in its own time. Therefore, the knowledge of the creature in itself was evening, while in God it was morning, because the creature is seen more fully in God than it is seen in itself. A creature is seen more fully in the art by which it was made than in itself, once it has been made. For this reason the evangelist John says: “What was made, in him was life” (John I, 3, 4).

Therefore, all things that have been made and do not possess life are life in the Word of God, but are not life in themselves. Heaven, earth, and a stone do not possess life, yet in God they are life. Thus all the principles of creatures live in God without beginning and unchangeably. Accordingly, they are seen more fully by the holy angels in the Word of God, where they are life, than in themselves, because the knowledge of the angels, in comparison with God, grows dim in a certain sense and becomes evening.

Thus, in the knowledge of the spirits [Note: [Col. 0741] Two Vatican manuscripts add here: “of light.”] there was the first day; in the knowledge of the firmament, the second; in the knowledge of the separation of earth and sea, the third; in the knowledge of the sun, moon, and stars, the fourth; in the knowledge of reptiles and birds, the fifth; in the knowledge of beasts of burden, wild animals, and the human being, the sixth. The knowledge of the one day that we understand as the nature of spiritual creatures—that is, of the angels—was not made six times so as to produce six days, on account of the perfection of the number six.

But I will gather for you something from the sacred Scriptures concerning the perfection of the number six. Attend willingly, and prepare yourself entirely for listening. One cannot be divided in numbers, for every number arises from it. Two, therefore, can be divided, but one is a part of it. Thus the division of two into two ones is one; the division of three into three ones is one. What else does this number show here except the Trinity, which is God? Although there are three persons, they are believed to be one in the unity of nature.

Four has two parts: its fourth part is one, and its middle is two. One and two make three. Here are its parts; yet it neither increases beyond them nor is completed by them, and therefore it is an imperfect number.

Five has only one part, which is its fifth. Six, then, is a perfect number, because it is completed by its parts. It has one, which is its sixth part; two, which is its third; and three, which is its half. One, two, and three therefore make six. For this reason, on account of the perfection of this number, God worked all creation in six days.

These three parts of the number six show us that the Triune God, in the trinity of number, measure, and weight, made all creation. We frequently find the great importance of the perfection of the number six in the sacred Scriptures, especially in the Lord’s single death and single resurrection, and in our double death and double resurrection.

[Note: [Col. 0742] This sentence, namely from the words “and in the death” through the words “our double resurrection,” is absent from the manuscripts.]

The death of our Lord Jesus Christ was not in the soul but in the flesh alone. Our death, however, is not only in the flesh but also in the soul: in the soul because of sin, and in the flesh because of the punishment of sin. But because he had no sin, he did not die in the soul, but only in the flesh—and this because of the likeness of sinful flesh that he had drawn from Adam.

Thus his single death benefited our double death, and his single resurrection benefited our double resurrection. For there are the death of his flesh and his resurrection; the death of our flesh and his resurrection; and the death of our soul and his resurrection. The death of his flesh and his resurrection signify our two deaths and our two resurrections.

Therefore, if you add the one death of the Lord and his one resurrection—which together make two—to our two deaths and two resurrections, which make four, the result is six. Thus the Lord’s single reality twice, and our double reality twice, make three twice; and three twice, as we said above, are the parts from which the number six is formed.

The thirty-six hours during which the Lord was in hell also correspond to this single and double reality. Twelve hours were therefore daylight, and twenty-four were night. Likewise, the twenty-four hours correspond to our double death, and the twelve hours to the Lord’s single death.

Indeed, his birth also has the number six. The Jews say in the Gospel that the temple was built over forty-six years, which is understood as referring to the Lord’s body (John II, 20–21). The forty-six years are reckoned as days. They say that an infant is formed in the womb over forty-six days and thereafter grows until the day of birth. For forty-six times six make 276, which comprise nine months and six days [Note: [Col. 0742] The manuscripts read “ten” days.].

Count, then, from the eighth day before the Kalends of April, when the Lord suffered—for he is also believed to have been conceived at that time—up to the eighth day before the Kalends of January, and you will find 276 days, which are constituted according to the number six.

What shall we say about the woman in the Gospel whom Satan had bent double for eighteen years and whom the Lord healed (Luke XIII, 11–13)? Those years too have the number six, for three times six is eighteen. That woman is understood to represent the human race, which our Redeemer, the Lord Jesus, freed from the captivity of the devil in the sixth age of the world.

The first age is from Adam to Noah. The second age is from Noah to Abraham. The third is from Abraham to David. The fourth is from David to the Babylonian exile. The fifth is from the Babylonian exile to the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ. The sixth, which is now in progress, will continue until the Most High comes for judgment.

Thus, in the sixth age of the world, the human race is restored according to the image of God. Indeed, the eighteen years clearly signify not only the six ages but also three periods: one before the Law, another under the Law, and a third under grace.

The year itself, then, is also contained within the number six. It has 365 days. Six times sixty make 360. There remain five days and a quarter. Five days taken six times make a month. Yet even if you count that quarter as a day, taking the part for the whole, they make six. Behold how much the Lord has helped me to give an account of the perfection of the number six: not as much as I wished, but as much as I could.

**QUESTION XXVII**

The order and weight of the elements do not permit water to exist above the heavens. Water yields to earth, air yields to water, and fire yields to air. It is entirely impossible for the second element, water, to be above the fourth, fire. How, then, does Scripture say, “Let there be a firmament in the midst of the waters, and let it divide waters from waters” (Gen. I, 6)?

**RESP.**

Whatever those waters may be, and whatever their nature, which Scripture teaches to be above the heavens, we should have no doubt that they are there. For just as these clouds, which are certainly water, are borne above the air, the third element, so I think it possible that thin and subtle waters are borne above the heaven.

Many philosophers, relying on this weight of the elements, mock the resurrection of the flesh and say that it cannot happen that a human being, who was certainly made from earth, should be in heaven. But truth refutes them: it makes many earthly animals fly through the air, places water above the air, and causes fire—which is certainly the fourth element—to exist in the earth. Therefore, God’s power, which is shown to accomplish these things, also causes both the human being and water to be above heaven.

**QUESTION XXVIII**

Did water not cover the whole earth? How, then, does Scripture say, “Let the waters that are under heaven be gathered into one place, and let the dry land appear” (ibid., 9)?

**RESP.**

Water covered the whole earth like an exceedingly thin mist, which afterward was brought together and gathered into one place, so that the appearance of the earth could also become visible. Although the earth sank down far and wide, it could provide hollow places that would receive the waters as they flowed together, so that the dry land might appear.

**QUESTION XXIX**

Since God created all things good, as Scripture says, “And behold, everything that God made was very good” (ibid., 31), why does the Lord again say in the Gospel, “No one is good except God alone” (Mark X, 18)?

**RESP.**

That the human being is good, the Lord himself says in the Gospel: “The good person brings good things out of the good treasure of his heart” (Matt. XII, 35). But when he said, “No one is good except God alone,” he was answering the man who was seeking eternal life from him, a man who regarded him as merely human when he said, “Good Teacher.”

Therefore he answered him: “Why do you call me good? No one is good except God alone.” That is: “This form that I have assumed, which you see and which the good and the evil, the devout and the impious, will see, will not be good for those who do evil. Therefore, do not call me good according to this form, which those who pierced me will see. There is another form that the impious will not see, which only the righteous will see; according to that form I am good to those who will have been worthy to see me.”

**QUESTION XXX**

“Now a spring,” says Holy Scripture, “went up from the earth, watering the entire surface of the earth” (Gen. II, 6). If it watered the entire earth, then it also watered the mountains, since the mountains too are certainly earth. But if it watered the mountains as well, there was a flood. How, then, had the earth produced green grass bearing seed? Or how did a human being live on the earth if water covered the whole earth?

**RESP.**

The singular “spring” is used in place of the plural. If we carefully investigate this, we frequently find it in the sacred Scriptures. For example, in the Psalm you have: “He sent among them the dog-fly, and it devoured them; and the frog, and it destroyed them” (Psalm LXXVII, 45), although there was certainly neither one dog-fly nor one frog. Elsewhere in the Psalm he said, “And the locust came” (Psalm CIV, 34); he did not say “locusts,” but “the locust.” Here you have the singular number used for the plural.

This accords with what a certain most distinguished poet said: “And they fill both wombs with armed soldiery” (Virgil, *Aeneid* II, verse 20).

Moreover, “one spring” was said because of the unity of nature, so that we may understand all the springs that are on the earth, since in a certain sense they all flow from the nature of one abyss. When he says, “It watered the entire surface of the earth,” he does not mean that it watered the whole earth, but a part. He signified a part by the whole, just as we say, “Christ died; Christ rose,” although he died and rose only according to the flesh.

**QUESTION XXXI**

“Therefore the Lord God took the human being,” Scripture says, “and placed him in the paradise of pleasure, to cultivate it and guard it” (Gen. II, 15). What, I ask, was he to cultivate and guard: the paradise, or something else?

**RESP.**

This statement gives rise to a twofold interpretation. If the human being was cultivating the paradise—that is, if he was doing some work in the paradise—he was not working out of necessity for sustenance but for pleasure [Note: [Col. 0744] Two Vatican manuscripts read “with pleasure”; the Corbie manuscript, “for love.”].

For he had not yet sinned, and the earth had not yet brought forth thorns and thistles for him, so that he would eat his bread in the sweat of his face. He deserved that only after sin. Before sin, therefore, he cultivated the paradise through agriculture and guarded it through discipline—not from need or necessity, but solely, as we have said, for pleasure [Note: [Col. 0744] Four manuscripts read “by will”]—not from beasts or any animals, but for his own sake—namely, so that he would not lose through sin what he could preserve through obedience.

Alternatively, God placed the human being himself in paradise so that he might cultivate and guard him: he was to cultivate him so that he would be good, and guard him so that he would be safe. Whichever interpretation is given—whether the human being cultivated the paradise through agriculture and guarded it through discipline, or whether God cultivated the human being so that he would be good and guarded him so that he would be safe—either interpretation accords with reason.

**QUESTION XXXII**

Since God threatened the human being with death on the day he touched the forbidden food, why did he not die on that day? Scripture says: “On whatever day you eat from it, you shall surely die” (Gen. II, 17).

**RESP.**

Holy Scripture clearly shows that there are four deaths. The first death is of the soul, when it abandons its Creator; for when it abandons him, it sins. “Let the dead,” the Lord says in the Gospel, “bury their own dead” (Matt. VIII, 22). Here you have the dead according to the soul, namely those burying the dead; and those whom they bury are dead according to the flesh. This statement therefore teaches two deaths most clearly: one of souls and the other of bodies.

The third belongs to the soul alone, which it suffers after it has departed from this body, according to what we read in the Gospel concerning the rich man. “Father Abraham,” the rich man says, “send Lazarus, so that he may cool my tongue with his finger, because I am tormented in this flame” (Luke XVI, 24).

The fourth death occurs when the soul has received its body so that it may be cast into eternal fire, according to what the Lord says in the Gospel concerning the future judgment: “Go into the eternal fire that has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. XXV, 41).

On the day Adam sinned, therefore, he died in his soul. For just as the body lives through the soul, so the soul, in order to live more blessedly, lives through God. Therefore, when Adam’s soul was abandoned by God, it is rightly said to have died the first death, from which the three deaths that followed afterward proceeded. For in order that these might follow, the abandonment of God first occurred; accordingly, Adam died on the day he sinned.

**QUESTION XXXIII**

How could Adam fear death, when he had no knowledge of it whatsoever?

**RESP.**

Just as we know about the resurrection, which we have never experienced and never seen, so he knew about death. We also know that when the soul leaves the body, it produces death, and that when it returns to its body, it will produce resurrection. Behold, we know about the resurrection, which we have never experienced. In the same way, he certainly knew about death—not yet through experience, but through knowledge.

He knew what it was to live, and through the privation of life he certainly knew what death was. Just as darkness is known through the privation of light, silence through the privation of sound, and emptiness through the privation of body, so he knew death through the privation of life.

**QUESTION XXXIV**

“The Lord brought all the animals and birds to Adam,” Scripture says, “and when he had seen them, he gave them names” (Gen. II, 19). Shortly afterward, concerning the woman, it says: “The woman, therefore, seeing that the tree was good for eating,” and so forth. Behold, Scripture most clearly shows that the eyes of both were open. For it is not permissible to say that the first human beings were made blind. Why, then, shortly after touching the forbidden tree, does the same Scripture say: “The eyes of both were opened” (ibid. III, 6, 7)? If their eyes had not been open, he could not have given names to the animals, nor could she have seen the beauty of the tree.

**RESP.**

This is indeed true: they had open eyes. Yet unless their eyes had been closed with respect to something, Scripture would never have said, “The eyes of both were opened.” They were opened, that is, for no other reason than to desire one another, so that there might be a law in their members resisting the law of the mind (Rom. VII, 23). Thus there was also in their very members a movement that was not voluntary—a just vengeance from God—so that the human being who had refused to be subject to God would not have a body subject to him. Therefore, their eyes were opened in this respect: so that their members would be moved by desire.

**QUESTION XXXV**

“When Adam and Eve had heard the voice of the Lord God walking in the paradise,” Scripture says, “they hid themselves” (Gen. III, 8). I ask, what is this walking?

**RESP.**

Far be it from us to believe that God, who is the Trinity, is corporeal or local because his “walking” is mentioned. Every body is local, and everything local is certainly a body. God, however, is incorporeal; he does not move temporally, is not contained by a place, and is not transferred from one place to another. His walking must be understood as having taken place through some creature. From the surrounding context of Scripture, I recall that our predecessors understood this creature to have been the human being.

[Note: [Col. 0745] One of the Vatican manuscripts reads “angel” here; the others read “human being.”]

**QUESTION XXXVI**

Since God is one, as Scripture says, “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one God” (Deut. VI, 4), how did he himself say, “Behold, Adam has become like one of us” (Gen. III, 22)? “Us” appears to indicate plurality.

**RESP.**

Although God is one, he is nevertheless a Trinity: namely, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. “One of us” was said not because of a plurality of gods, but because of a plurality of persons.

**QUESTION XXXVII**

We often see many animals born from the corruption of bodies, especially dead bodies. Were they created at the same time as those bodies?

**RESP.**

Far be it from us to say that they were created when the bodies themselves were created. Rather, they were somehow implanted in the bodies, and were to emerge at their proper time. For just as the seed of any tree possesses a certain power, so that when it has been buried in the earth it sprouts and produces a shoot, which then expands, closely set with branches and foliage [Note: [Col. 0745] The Corbie manuscript reads “made visible”; three Vatican manuscripts, “made dense.”], and afterward, adorned with flowers, bears fruit, so there is also in the body, so to speak, a kind of seedbed from which, at its proper time and under the care of God’s providence, certain kinds of animals arise.

**QUESTION XXXVIII**

Since God said, “Let the earth bring forth green grass bearing seed and fruit-bearing trees” (ibid. I, 11), when did he make trees without fruit, or thorns and thistles?

**RESP.**

God made everything at once, as Scripture says: “He who lives forever created all things together” (Eccli. XVIII, 1). Therefore, trees that in some way provide human beings with assistance should by no means be called fruitless. For even if we do not find in them something to eat, we certainly find something useful as medicine, and something useful for assistance. Consider for yourself how many benefits are found in them.

Since “fruit” is named from “enjoyment,” and we can receive some assistance from every tree, we rightly say that no tree is fruitless. As for thorns and thistles, although they grow for human toil after sin, as Scripture says, “The earth shall bring forth thorns and thistles for you” (Gen. III, 18), we should nevertheless not say that they first arose from the earth at that time. They had already been made for the nourishment of cattle or birds, not produced to increase the human being’s punishment.

**QUESTION XXXIX**

If God arranged all things in number, measure, and weight, as Holy Scripture testifies (Wis. XI, 21), where did he arrange number, measure, and weight themselves?

**RESP.**

Number, measure, and weight are God himself. He is number without number, from whom every number comes. He is measure without measure, from whom every measure comes. He is weight without weight, from whom every weight comes.

Thus he arranged everything in number, measure, and weight, as though he were saying, “He arranged everything in himself.” He did not see creation outside himself or somewhere else, as human beings retain in memory what they are going to make. Therefore, the entire cause of creation is the will of the Creator. In him, will is what nature is. Yet his nature is eternal for him, and his will is likewise eternal. No new thought arose in God for forming creatures.

Thus the Trinity, God, arranged all things in himself, because he possessed in himself everything he made. The passage may also be understood in another way: he arranged everything in number, measure, and weight; that is, everything he made possesses number, measure, and weight.

**QUESTION XL**

Did God bring all the animals of the earth and all the birds of heaven to Adam (Gen. II, 19) in the way that bird-catchers or hunters bring them to nets? Or perhaps a voice of command came from a cloud, which they understood as rational souls, and when they heard it they all obeyed?

[Note: [Col. 0746] Erasmus, Lyon, Venice, and Louvain read: “and nevertheless, when they heard it, they obeyed.” M.]

**RESP.**

The animals and birds of heaven did not receive the capacity for reason by which they could obey their Creator. Yet within their own kind they obey God—not by the rational choice of the will, but as he moves all things at suitable times, without himself being moved temporally.

Thus he moves himself without time and place; he moves a created spirit without place but within time; and he moves bodily creation temporally and locally. Therefore, the substance that is moved only temporally precedes the substance that is moved both temporally and locally. The substance that is moved neither temporally nor locally precedes the substance that is moved only temporally.

The created spirit moves itself through time without place, and moves the body through time and place. The Creator Spirit moves himself without time and place. Therefore, both the rational spirit found in human beings and the irrational spirit found in beasts are moved by his commands. But the rational spirit possesses understanding, by which it can judge whether it should consent to his commands or not consent. Animals, reptiles, and birds did not receive this judgment; nevertheless, according to their kind and nature, they are driven onward by a command.

Thus the angelic nature, carrying out God’s commands, moves every kind of animal by those commands, teaching what does not know. For if human beings can tame certain kinds of animals so that they appear to carry out certain human wishes, how much more can angels do this?

**QUESTION XLI**

What caused God, whom you assert to move, not to be moved in time, while a created spirit, which is moved in time, is not also moved in place?

**RESP.**
God, who instituted times and exists before times, has nothing in him that is past or future, no new plan and no new thought; for, obviously, if there were something new, it would be an accident. But if anything happens to God, he is no longer immutable. Therefore God is immutable: nothing happens to him, no new thought, no new plan; and for this reason he is not moved in time. Therefore God is immutable. A created spirit, however, such as the spirit of the angels, although it contemplates God’s eternity, truth, and charity without time, is nevertheless rightly believed to be moved in time, because it fulfills God’s commands in lower things within time. It moves its own bodies in place when they descend from heaven and ascend into heaven. Thus the spirit of human beings is moved in time by remembering the past, awaiting the future, and learning something new. For when I remember some lesson or some city, just as my spirit is moved in thought [Col. 0747] so as to recall these things in time, it is not thereby moved in place. If it were moved in place, it would be moved either in heaven or on earth, since there is no place apart from heaven and earth. Where, then, was the spirit itself—in heaven or on earth—when it saw that lesson or that city? Therefore, if it saw in no place in order to remember, it saw within itself. And because thought has a beginning, and everything that has a beginning also has time, a created spirit, according to the reasoning given above, can be moved through time, but not through place; the creating Spirit is moved neither through time nor through place; whereas a body is moved both in place and in time.

## QUESTION XLII

Since rest occurs only after labor, why is God said to rest? Was he also wearied by his work, so that he is said to rest?

## ANSWER

God did not rest in any creature as though he needed that creature as his good, but in himself. Indeed, he is read to have rested not on one of the days, but after the works of the sixth day. Hence it plainly appears that God made no creature out of need, but solely out of goodness. If he rested in some creature, he would have made some creature out of need. Therefore, because he made no creature out of need, he rested in no creature.

For when Scripture says that God rested on the seventh day from all his works that he had made (Gen. 2:2), I think this can be understood to mean that he did not rest on that day as though he needed its good in order to become more blessed; rather, he brought the seventh day itself—that is, the angelic nature—into his rest. Thus, just as they might see in God every creature that was to be formed [two Vatican manuscripts: “form and creature”], so they might also see him to have made no creature out of need, but solely out of goodness. This, I think, may be understood as God’s rest.

God’s rest can also be understood in another way: namely, when he causes us to rest after good works, according to the meaning of God’s words to Abraham, “Now I know that you fear God” (ibid. 22:12), which is understood as “I have caused you to know.” So here also God is understood to rest when he grants rest to his saints.

Again, God is said to rest from creating new creatures because, after the completion of the works of the six days, he created no creature thereafter. For when he says, “My Father is working until now, and I am working” (John 5:17), this is not understood as creating a new creature, but as governing what he created.

## QUESTION XLIII

How could the serpent speak in paradise (Gen. 3:1), when it plainly appears to be an irrational animal?

## ANSWER

The serpent could not speak by itself, because it had not received this power from the Creator. The devil took it into his service, using it like an instrument through which he could emit articulate sound. Through it he uttered words, although even the serpent itself did not know this. Thus a nature devoid of reason is subjected to a rational nature; yet the latter does not do in or through it as much as it wishes, but only as much as it has received from the Creator.

## QUESTION XLIV

And if serpents do not understand, how do they hear the words of the Marsi, so that they come out of their holes at their incantation?

## ANSWER

Although they have no understanding, they are by no means lacking bodily senses. They have sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch. Therefore, although they hear the words of the Marsi, they do not understand them at all. They do not obey through understanding; rather, so that they may come out of their caves at the words of the Marsi, they are compelled by the devil, with God’s permission. Hence testimony is given concerning that first event: the devil deceived the first human being in paradise through the serpent.

## QUESTION XLV

Since Adam needed a wife, could this not have been done in another way, without a rib being taken from him while he slept, from which the wife would be built (ibid. 2:20–22)?

## ANSWER

God could have done this in another way also, but he judged it more fitting to do it in this manner, so that something might be signified. For just as a rib is taken from the sleeping Adam [Col. 0748] so that a wife may be made, so also, from the dying Christ’s side, blood is poured out so that the Church may be built. By sharing in Christ’s body and blood, the Church becomes Christ’s wife.

## QUESTION XLVI

How should we understand what Adam says: “Therefore a man shall leave his father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh” (Gen. 2:24)?

## ANSWER

The blessed apostle Paul explained this passage by taking it as his text, saying: “This mystery is great; but I speak of Christ and the Church” (Eph. 5:32).

But how did Christ leave the Father, since he is of one substance with the Father? Or where could the Father be without the Son, when it is said of the Son himself, who is Wisdom, that he “reaches mightily from end to end and orders all things sweetly” (Wis. 8:1)? Therefore, if the Son is wherever the Father is, the Father cannot be without the Son, nor the Son without the Father, since, just as they are inseparable in nature, so also they are inseparable in persons. For the Son himself says of the Father in the Gospel: “He who sent me is with me” (John 8:29).

How, then, did he leave the Father in order to cling to his wife, that is, to his Church, unless in the manner described by the Apostle: “Although he was in the form of God, he did not consider being equal with God something to be seized; but he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Phil. 2:6–7)? The taking of the servant’s form is therefore the emptying; and although this emptying is not the abolition of divinity or the loss of nature, nevertheless, because he is recognized as having appeared in the form of a servant, the Apostle rightly says that he left the Father.

He also left his mother, namely, the Synagogue, which clung carnally to the Old Testament; and he clung to his wife, that is, to his holy Church, so that through the peace of the New Testament the two might be one flesh.

## QUESTION XLVII

Why are Cain’s offerings from the fruits of the earth rejected, while Abel’s offerings from the fat of his flock [manuscripts: “from the sheep”] are accepted (Gen. 4:3–5)?

## ANSWER

Cain represented the Jews, who practiced those bodily sacraments according to the Old Testament. With the coming of faith in the New Testament, their sacrifices were despised and nullified; whereas the sacrifices of Christians, which consist in the innocence of Christ, the innocent Lamb, are praised. These were signified by Abel’s offerings from the sheep. Cain’s offerings, therefore, are not accepted. Hence it is also said in the Psalm: “You did not desire offerings and burnt offerings,” and so forth (Ps. 39:7).

## QUESTION XLVIII

What does it signify that Cain killed his brother Abel in the field (Gen. 4:8)?

## ANSWER

We have already said above that Cain signifies the Jews, who killed Christ. Abel, therefore, the younger by birth, is killed; Christ, the head of the younger people, is killed by the Jewish people, older by birth: Abel in the field, Christ in the place of Calvary.

## QUESTION XLIX

How should we understand the statement that Abel’s blood is read as having cried out to God from the earth (ibid. 10)?

## ANSWER

Abel’s blood signifies the blood of Christ, which the whole Church receives and over which it says, “Amen.” If you can, consider for yourself what kind of cry the whole Church makes when it is given to drink of Christ’s blood and says, “Amen.”

The Jews, therefore, who are understood under the person of Cain, because they do not believe in Christ and do not drink Christ’s blood, are cursed upon the earth—upon that earth, namely, which opened its mouth through confession and drank the blood of its brother, that is, of its Christ. Because the Jews do not drink it, they are therefore accursed.

## QUESTION L

What does it signify that Enoch, the seventh from Adam, walked with God and did not appear (ibid. 5:24)?

## ANSWER

Enoch, the seventh from Adam, is transferred to God, and rest is promised to the saints on the seventh day, because in the sixth age of the world they are restored to the knowledge of God so that they may be transferred into rest.

## QUESTION LI

What does it signify that Noah was saved through water and wood (ibid. 6–8)?

## ANSWER

Water signifies Baptism, and wood signifies the cross. Just as Noah was saved through water and wood, so also the Church is saved through Baptism and the sign of Christ’s passion.

[Col. 0749]

## QUESTION LII

What does it signify that the ark, built of squared timbers, was coated inside and outside with pitch (Gen. 6:14)?

## ANSWER

Just as the ark is built of squared timbers, so the Church is built from holy people. A square stands firmly no matter which side one places it upon; so the saints remain steadfast amid every kind of temptation. They do not yield to adversity or prosperity.

Pitch signifies charity. Through charity the saints yield neither to the scandals caused by those who are inside nor to those caused by those who are outside; they preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace, bearing with both wicked Christians who are in the Church and heretics who are outside the Church.

## QUESTION LIII

What does it signify that the ark was three hundred cubits long, fifty cubits wide, and thirty cubits high (ibid. 15)?

## ANSWER

The holy Church, in order to carry out God’s commandments, is assisted by the Spirit of God, as the Psalmist says: “I ran in the way of your commandments, when you enlarged my heart” (Ps. 118:32). If his heart had not been enlarged, he would certainly not have run in the way of the Lord. And from what is the heart enlarged, unless through spiritual charity?

For this reason the blessed apostle Paul also agrees with the Psalmist’s voice: “Our mouth is open to you, O Corinthians; our heart is enlarged” (2 Cor. 6:11). How was it enlarged? “The grace of God,” he says, “has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. 5:5).

Therefore, having received the Holy Spirit, the Church performs God’s commandments with enlargement [one Vatican manuscript: “with love”; the Corbie manuscript: “with delight”], which it could by no means perform without the grace of the Holy Spirit. Holy Scripture mentions and commends this Spirit as sevenfold (Isa. 11:2–3).

Seven times seven makes forty-nine; adding one to complete the number makes fifty. Hence, when the Lord ascended into heaven, on the fiftieth day he sent the Holy Spirit (Acts 1:9 and 2:1–4), so that he might enlarge the hearts of believers.

The thirty cubits signify the ten commandments of the Law. Ten times thirty makes three hundred. But these commandments cannot be fulfilled except through charity, that is, through the Holy Spirit, who is signified by the fifty cubits of width. For this reason the ark has both numbers.

The Church also performs good works for the sake of the higher end; this is signified by the thirty cubits of height. In truth, the Spirit is our height; it is he, namely, the number thirty [two Vatican manuscripts: “the number represented by thirty,”] who consecrated evangelical teaching. He is also the higher end, and he unquestionably fills the Church with every good work.

## QUESTION LIV

What does it signify that, seven days after Noah entered the ark, the Lord caused rain to fall upon the earth for forty days and forty nights (Gen. 7:10–12)?

## ANSWER

The fact that the Lord caused rain to fall upon the earth after seven days signifies that all who are baptized are baptized in hope of the future rest, which was signified by the seventh day.

All the guilt of sins committed throughout the whole world—which is contained by its four regions—under the ten commandments of the Law, and from which ten multiplied by four produces forty, is washed away by the sacrament of heavenly Baptism. This includes either the guilt belonging to the “days,” arising from prosperity, or that belonging to the “nights,” contracted through adversity.

## QUESTION LV

What does it signify that Noah was six hundred years old when the waters of the flood inundated the earth (ibid. 11)?

## ANSWER

The six hundred years signify the six ages of the world. The first age is from Adam to Noah. The second, from Noah to Abraham. The third, from Abraham to David. The fourth, from David to the Babylonian captivity. The fifth, from the Babylonian captivity to [Col. 0750] the coming of the Lord. The sixth is the age now in progress.

The flood occurred in the six-hundredth year of Noah’s life; so, in the sixth age of the world, the human being is restored to the knowledge of God through Baptism.

## QUESTION LVI

What does it signify that of every kind of animal and bird, two unclean creatures were brought into the ark, and seven clean ones (Gen. 7:2–3)?

## ANSWER

The unclean signify those people who are inclined toward schism; the clean signify holy people who, having received the sevenfold Spirit, live by faith.

For this reason a certain poet also says:

> “God delights in the odd number.”  
> (Virgil, *Eclogue* 8, line 75)

## QUESTION LVII

What does it signify that the water rose fifteen cubits above all the high mountains (Gen. 7:20)?

## ANSWER

Eight and seven make fifteen. Eight signifies the resurrection, and seven signifies rest. Thus this mystery of resurrection and rest rose above all the knowledge of proud sages, and they were entirely unable to investigate the knowledge of resurrection and rest.

## QUESTION LVIII

Why, when Noah entered the ark, is he told, “Enter, you and your sons, your wife, and your sons’ wives with you” (ibid. 1)? Men and women are therefore placed separately. But when he came out of the ark, he is told, “Go out, you and your wife, your sons and your sons’ wives” (ibid. 8:16). At the entrance they are said to be separated, but at the exit joined together.

## ANSWER

Their entrance signifies this present life, in which “the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh,” so that we do not do whatever we wish (Gal. 5:17). Their exit signifies that life in which the flesh will no longer have any desire against the spirit, and nothing within us will oppose us.

## QUESTION LIX

What does it signify that the raven sent out from the ark did not return (Gen. 8:7)?

## ANSWER

The raven did not return either because it was seized by the waters or because it was attracted by some corpse and settled upon it. It signifies those people who, devoted to carnal things, despise God’s commandments and never make satisfaction to the Church through repentance; hence, through evil works, they have withdrawn.

Alternatively, if that raven was seized by the waters, it signifies those who leave the Church and are polluted by the Baptism of heretics.

Although there is one Baptism both among heretics—namely, those who baptize in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit—and in the Catholic Church, nevertheless, because they are baptized outside the Church, they do not receive Baptism for salvation but for destruction. They have “the appearance of piety but deny its power” (2 Tim. 3:5); and again, Scripture says, they are “natural, not having the Spirit” (Jude 19).

For this reason the Church does not rebaptize them, since they were baptized in the name of the Trinity. That is indeed the form of the sacrament. Therefore, when they have returned, they receive the power of the Holy Spirit, which those baptized outside the Church do not yet possess.

## QUESTION LX

What does it signify that Noah, a righteous man, planted a vineyard, became drunk from drinking wine, and was uncovered in his tent (Gen. 9:20–21)?

## ANSWER

In a certain way, God planted the Jewish nation by separating it from all the nations. Hence he also imposed the sign of circumcision, gave the Law, instituted sacrifices, and foretold in the Law that he himself would come in the flesh.

But because they did not believe him [Col. 0750: The sense is defective here; something appears to be missing. M.], he was crucified, having suffered the wine of his vineyard—that is, the wickedness of his people [Col. 0750: the Corbie manuscript reads, “having suffered wine, that is, wickedness”; two Vatican manuscripts, “having drunk wine, that is, wickedness”]—being smeared with spittle and mocked. He suffered this in his tent, that is, among his own people.

## QUESTION LXI

What does it signify that Ham, the father of Canaan, saw his father’s nakedness, went outside, and told his brothers (ibid. 22)?

## ANSWER

In the two sons, the eldest and the youngest, two peoples [Col. 0751] are represented. Carrying one garment on their backs—the mystery, namely, of the Lord’s passion, already past and completed—they cover their father’s nakedness without looking at it. These are those who do not consent to Christ’s death and honor him by covering him, as though they knew from whom they had been born.

The middle son, that is, the Jewish people—middle because it neither held the primacy of the Apostles nor was the last among the nations to believe—saw his father’s nakedness because he consented to Christ’s death. And he told his brothers. Through him what had been the secret of prophecy was revealed and, in a certain way, made public. For this reason he becomes his brothers’ servant.

For what else is that nation today except the Christian people’s keeper of the archives, carrying the Law and the Prophets as testimony to the Church’s claim, so that we may honor through the sacrament what they announce to us through the letter?

## QUESTION LXII

What does God’s command to Abraham signify: “Go out from your land, from your kindred, and from your father’s house” (Gen. 12:1)?

## ANSWER

Abraham represented Christ. Just as Abraham left his land and his kindred and his father’s house and went into a land he did not know, so Christ left his own nation, namely the Jews, and came to the people of the Gentiles.

This is the temporal explanation. Morally, however, we go out from our land when we despise riches and the resources of this world; from our kindred, that is, from our former vices, which cling to us from our birth and are joined to us as though by a kind of affinity and blood relationship; and from our father’s house, that is, from every memory of this world that presents itself to our eyes.

[Note: Erasmus, the Lyon edition, and the Venice edition read this passage as follows: “Here another explanation also has this: ‘We go out from our land.’”]

## QUESTION LXIII

How many kinds of vision are there?

## ANSWER

Three. The first vision is bodily; the second spiritual; the third intellectual.

Bodily vision is what takes place through the body. Spiritual vision occurs when we store in memory the images of the things we see. Intellectual vision occurs when, through understanding, we distinguish the things we see bodily and retain imaginatively in memory—namely, that one thing is a body and another is the likeness of a body.

Beasts, cattle, and birds have no such understanding at all. They see through the body, and an image-like form is produced in them from the things they see. [Col. 0752] Thus cattle recognize their mangers, and birds return to their nests; but they do not understand either what they themselves are or what they see with their eyes.

Finally, bodily vision cannot exist without spiritual vision. As soon as we turn our eyes away from the things we see, we retain in memory the images of what we have seen.

Spiritual vision, however, can exist without bodily vision. Thus we remember people who are absent, and in darkness we see imaginatively the things we have seen.

Intellectual vision requires neither bodily nor spiritual vision. Through the intellect we see neither a body nor an image of a body. Through it we see justice, charity, God himself, and the human mind itself, which possesses no body and no likeness of a body.

For this reason the apostle Paul was also “caught up into the third heaven” (2 Cor. 12:2), that is, into intellectual vision, so that he might see God not through a body or through the likeness of a body, but as he is, in his very truth.

The three heavens, therefore, are the three kinds of vision of which we are speaking. Paul had indeed reached the point at which, in this life, he saw God in the manner in which the saints will see him after this life.

## QUESTION LXIV

How many kinds of apostleship are there, or what sort of name is “apostle”? I wish to know.

## ANSWER

“Apostle” means “one who is sent.” There are four kinds of apostles: from God, not through a human being; from God, but through a human being; through a human being alone; and from oneself.

Moses was sent from God. Joshua, son of Nun, was sent from God and through a human being. In our own times many have been appointed to the priesthood through a human being alone, by popular favor. Those who are from themselves are the false prophets.

## QUESTION LXV

How can we know who has been sent by God?

## ANSWER

Recognize as sent by God not the person chosen by the praise—or rather, the flattery—of a few people, but the one adorned both by an excellent life and character and by the scrutiny of apostolic priests [the editions read: “commended by the action of apostolic priests”; the Corbie manuscript has *exagio*, that is, “examination,” and lacks the verb “commended”], or even the one approved by the judgment of all peoples; one who does not seek to preside and does not give money in order to acquire the honor of the episcopate.

For concerning the person who hastens to preside, one of the Fathers expressed the matter elegantly, saying: “Let him know that he is not a bishop who desires to preside, not to benefit” (Augustine, *City of God*, book 19, chapter 19).

# [ON THE RULE OF TRUE FAITH]

[Col. 0751]

## NOTICE CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING BOOK

[Col. 0751] The book *On Faith to Peter* was formerly printed among Augustine’s works on the authority of several old manuscripts that assign it to him. Erasmus, however, clearly demonstrated that it is not Augustine’s, on the basis of the diction itself and other arguments, which we consider unnecessary to reproduce here. For no one now fails to recognize its unquestioned author: Fulgentius.

Certainly the very ancient writing of the Corbie codex, copied a thousand years ago and reproduced at the end of the work, asserts this, in these words: “Here ends the book of Fulgentius, bishop of the holy Catholic Church of Ruspe, *On the Rule of True Faith*.” Nor should the title be dismissed, although it was added there at the beginning of the work by a later hand: “Letter of Fulgentius, bishop, *On the Catholic Faith*.”

Moreover, Ratramnus cites it under Fulgentius’s name in his book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*. Isidore also, in his *Catalogue*, and Honorius of Autun, in his *Chronicles*, testify that Fulgentius wrote the *Rule of True Faith*. The deacon Ferrandus requests that Rule from the same Fulgentius in the thirteenth letter among the letters of the new edition of Fulgentius.

It was formerly entitled *On Faith to Peter the Deacon*. But we readily believe that this Peter was someone other than the deacon Peter to whom Fulgentius’s book *On the Incarnation* was written, for the reasons set forth in the new edition of Fulgentius, which is now being issued in Paris from the workshop of Guillaume Desprez, revised, enlarged, and corrected through the study and labor of the learned man Luca Mangeant, a Parisian cleric.

The word “deacon” has rightly been removed from the title, since at the beginning Fulgentius calls this Peter “son,” not, as he usually addresses deacons, “brother” or “fellow deacon.”

We have collated this work with four Roman manuscripts of the Vatican Library, two English manuscripts, the oldest Corbie manuscript, and the Sorbonne, Victorine, Bec, and several other manuscripts. In the Corbie manuscript and other manuscripts of better quality, the work ends at the end of chapter 44; chapter 45, which is written in a different style and addressed to a military man, is nowhere found in them.

[Col. 0753]

# ON FAITH TO PETER, OR ON THE RULE OF TRUE FAITH

One Book. (C, G, S)*

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 0753]

### 1

I have received, my son Peter, the letter of your Charity, in which you indicated that you wished to travel to Jerusalem and requested instruction from my writings concerning the rule of true faith that you ought to maintain in those regions, so that no idea of heretical falsehood might creep into you.

I rejoice that you are concerned to preserve the true faith without any taint of disloyalty; for without faith no conversion can be of benefit—or rather, no conversion can exist. The apostolic authority says, “Without faith it is impossible to please God” (Heb. 11:6).

Faith is the foundation of all good things; faith is the beginning of human salvation. Without it no one can belong to the number of God’s children [Louvain edition: “reach the number of God’s children”]. For without faith no one in this age receives the grace of justification, nor will anyone possess eternal life in the age to come. And if someone here does not walk by faith, he will not attain to vision.

Without faith all human labor is empty. For it is as though someone wished to please God by despising the world but, while journeying toward his homeland, where he knows he will live in blessedness, abandoned the straight path and heedlessly followed a wrong one. He would not reach the blessed city but would fall into a precipice, where the one arriving would receive no joy, but the one falling would suffer destruction.

### 2

Nevertheless, sufficient discourse concerning the faith cannot be produced within the available time, since you desire to have my reply quickly; and this work of discussion is so great that it could scarcely be completed even by great men [one Vatican manuscript: “that it could scarcely be completed by extensive discourses”].

For you did not ask to be instructed in the faith in such a way that you would identify one particular heresy against which the purpose of our discussion might be specifically directed. Rather, when you ask indefinitely for a definition of the faith and wish it to be brought within a brief compass, you plainly see how impossible it is for us to encompass fully in a short space so great a subject, for which we cannot be adequate—even if we had enough time and such ability that we could compose many volumes on the matter you seek from us [manuscripts: “that we may compose many volumes”].

But because “God is near to all who call upon him in truth” (Ps. 144:18), and because he “finishes and abbreviates his word upon the earth” (Rom. 9:28), I hope that, just as he gave you the holy concern for this faith, so also he will grant me sufficient ability to serve your desire, so good and praiseworthy.

Thus, even if I cannot say everything by which every heretical error might be recognized, and, once recognized, either refuted or avoided, nevertheless, in the name and with the help of the holy Trinity, who is the one and only true and good God, I will state those things in which, at least in large part, the reason of the Catholic faith is plainly contained without any obscurity of error.

If you retain these things, you will also be able to detect and flee those teachings which, although they do not appear to be specifically refuted in this work, nevertheless become apparent from what will be set forth here generally and absolutely: teachings that unbelieving people whisper into the ears of the faithful, not handed down by the rule of divine truth, but invented by the wickedness of human error [other editions: “which they are accustomed to whisper”].

# CHAPTER ONE

### 3. The Trinity Is One God

Wherever you may be situated [Col. 0754], because according to the rule promulgated by the command of our Savior you know that you were baptized in the one name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, hold firmly and without doubt, with your whole heart, that God the Father, God the Son, and God the Holy Spirit—that is, the holy and ineffable Trinity—are naturally one God.

Concerning this it is said in Deuteronomy: “Hear, Israel: The Lord your God is one God” [manuscripts: “The Lord is one”]; “and you shall adore the Lord your God, and serve him alone” (Deut. 6:4, 13).

Nevertheless, because we have said that this one God, who alone is naturally the true God, is not the Father alone, nor the Son alone, nor the Holy Spirit alone, but together the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, we must take care that, just as we truthfully say that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one God with respect to their natural unity [the Corbie manuscript: “truth”], so we do not dare personally to say or believe that the one who is Father is the same as the Son or the Holy Spirit; or that the one who is Son is either the Father or the Holy Spirit; or that the one who is properly called the Holy Spirit in this confession of the Trinity is either the Father or the Son. That would be wholly impious.

### 4

For the faith divinely received by the holy Patriarchs and Prophets before the incarnation of the Son of God, and heard by the holy Apostles from the Lord himself when he was present in the flesh, which they not only proclaimed in speech after being instructed by the teaching of the Holy Spirit but also left written in their writings for the saving instruction of posterity, proclaims one God, the Trinity—that is, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

But the Trinity would not be true if the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit were said to be one and the same person. For if, just as the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit have one substance, they also had one person, there would be nothing at all in which the Trinity could truthfully be called a Trinity.

Conversely, the Trinity would indeed be true, but the Trinity itself would not be one God, if, just as the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are distinct from one another by the particularity of their persons, they were likewise distinguished by diversity of natures.

But because in that one true God who is Trinity it is naturally true not only that he is one God but also that he is Trinity, the true God is therefore Trinity in persons and one in nature.

Through this natural unity, the whole Father is in the Son and in the Holy Spirit, and the whole Son is in the Father and in the Holy Spirit, and the whole Holy Spirit is in the Father and in the Son. None of them is outside any of the others, because none precedes another in eternity, surpasses another in greatness, or exceeds another in power.

For, insofar as the unity of the divine nature is concerned, the Father is neither earlier nor greater than the Son or the Holy Spirit. Nor can the eternity and immensity of the Son, as though earlier or greater, naturally precede or exceed the eternity and immensity of the Holy Spirit.

Therefore, just as the Son is neither later nor less than the Father, so the Holy Spirit is neither later nor less than the Son. Eternal and without beginning is the fact that the Son has come forth, born from the Father’s nature [six manuscripts and the *Master of the Sentences*, book 1, distinction 19, read this way; the editions read: “exists”]; and eternal and without beginning [Col. 0755] is the fact that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the nature of the Father and the Son.

Therefore we rightly believe and say that the three are one God, because the three persons possess one eternity, one immensity, and one divinity by nature.

### 5

Let us therefore hold that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are naturally one God. Yet let us not hold that the Father himself is the Son, that the Son himself is the Father, or that the Holy Spirit himself is the Father or the Son.

For the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit have one essence, which the Greeks call *οὐσία* (*ousia*, “essence”); in this essence the Father is not one thing, the Son another, and the Holy Spirit another, although personally the Father is one, the Son another, and the Holy Spirit another.

This is demonstrated to us especially at the very beginning of the holy Scriptures, where God says: “Let us make the human being in our image and likeness.” When he says “image” in the singular, he shows that there is one nature in whose image the human being was to be made. But when he says “our” in the plural, he shows that the same God in whose image the human being was made is not one person.

For if in that one nature of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit there were one person, he would not have said, “in our image,” but “in my image”; nor would he have said, “Let us make,” but “Let me make.”

If, however, three substances were to be understood or believed in those three persons, he would not have said, “in our image,” but “in our images”; for one image of three unequal natures would be impossible.

But when the human being is said to have been made in the one image of the one God, the essential divinity of the holy Trinity is indicated. Then, shortly afterward, in place of what God had earlier said, “Let us make the human being in our image and likeness,” Scripture described the human being as having been made by saying: “And God made the human being; in the image of God he made him” (Gen. 1:26–27).

### 6

The prophet Isaiah did not keep silent about this Trinity of persons and unity of nature when he said that he had seen Seraphim crying out: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of hosts” (Isa. 6:3).

In the fact that “Holy” is said three times, we clearly recognize the Trinity of persons; in the fact that “Lord God of hosts” is said once, we recognize the unity of the divine nature.

In that holy Trinity, therefore—and this is repeated by us so that it may be impressed more firmly upon your heart [Louvain edition: “which is repeated so often by us so that it may be impressed upon our heart,” and so forth]—there is one Father, who alone essentially generated one Son from himself; one Son, who alone was essentially born [Louvain edition: “begotten”] from the one Father; and one Holy Spirit, who alone essentially proceeds from the Father and the Son.

A single person could not do all of this—that is, both generate himself, be born from himself, and proceed from himself. Since, therefore, to have generated is different from having been born, and to proceed is different from having generated or having been born, it is manifest that the Father is one, the Son another, and the Holy Spirit another.

The Trinity, then, refers to the persons of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; unity refers to the nature.

# CHAPTER TWO
## 7. Christ’s Humanity. What the Emptying of the Son of God Was

Therefore, just as, according to that divinity by which the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one, we believe that neither the Father nor the Holy Spirit was born, but only the Son, so also, according to the flesh, the catholic faith both believes and proclaims that only the Son was born. For in that Trinity it would not be the peculiar property of the Father alone that he himself was not born but begot one Son; nor the peculiar property of the Son alone that he himself did not beget but was born from the Father’s essence; nor the peculiar property of the Holy Spirit that he himself was neither born nor begot, but alone proceeds from the Father and the Son [Note: [Col. 0755] The printed editions read, “but alone”; “alone” is absent from the manuscripts. The Corbie manuscript reads, “proceeds in unchangeable eternity.”]—if, according to the divine nature, God the Father were born from no God, but according to the flesh he himself were born from a virgin.

For if the Father were born from a virgin, [Col. 0756] the Father and the Son would be one person. But since this one person would be born not from God but only from a virgin, he would truly be called not the Son of God but only the son of a human being. Yet the Son of God himself says [Note: [Col. 0756] One Vatican manuscript reads, “Nor would the Son of God himself say,” contrary to the other books.]: “God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son.” And again: “For God did not send his Son into the world to judge the world, but so that the world might be saved through him” (John 3:16–17). Nor would blessed John have said: “Whoever loves the Begetter loves also him who has been born from him” (1 John 5:1). Nor would the Son himself have said: “My Father is working until now, and I am working” (John 5:17). For he who is called the Son, if he were the same person as the Father, would not truly be called the Son of God, since he would be born not from God but from the virgin alone.

Finally, the Father himself would not have borne witness from heaven and indicated his Son with a bodily voice, saying: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” [Note: [Col. 0756] The printed editions read, “in whom I am well pleased indeed.” The word “indeed” is absent from the manuscripts.] (Matthew 3:17). The apostle Paul likewise would not have said of God the Father: “He did not spare his own Son, but handed him over for us all” (Romans 8:32) [Note: [Col. 0756] The printed editions read, “his own Son.” The more authoritative manuscripts omit “his.”]

## 8.

But since all these things were spoken divinely for our instruction, and since they were spoken by God, they are certainly true. What the catholic faith proclaims is therefore true: that, according to his divinity, only the Son was born from the Father, eternal with the Father, immortal, impassible, and immutable God; and that, according to the flesh, it was not the Father but his only-begotten Son who was born temporally, without surrendering his eternity; who suffered, without surrendering his impassibility; who died, without surrendering his immortality; and who was truly raised, without surrendering his immutability, by which he is true God and eternal life [Note: [Col. 0756] Lovaniensis reads, “without surrendering his immutability, because …”].

He possesses in common with the Father everything that, as eternal, he naturally possessed without beginning; but he possesses nothing in common with the Father of those things that the eternal and exalted one assumed temporally and humbly in his own person.

## 9.

Again, if it were not he who is the proper and only-begotten Son of God the Father, but the Holy Spirit, who were born from a virgin, the holy Church would neither believe in her heart for righteousness nor confess with her mouth for salvation that the very Son who was made from a woman, made under the Law, was born from the Holy Spirit of the Virgin Mary, as received in the Creed.

And if the Holy Spirit himself, who is the Spirit of the Father and the Son, were to assume the form of a servant, the Holy Spirit himself would not come from heaven upon himself, made man, in the appearance of a dove.

## 10.

God the Father, therefore, begotten from no God, once begot from his own nature, without beginning, God the Son, equal to himself and coeternal with him in the same divinity by which he himself is naturally eternal.

Yet this same Son of God, being eternal and true God, and naturally one God with the Father according to his divinity, as he says, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30), was also made, for our sake, a true and complete human being: true, because that God truly possesses human nature; complete, because he assumed both human flesh and a rational soul.

Nevertheless, the same only-begotten God was born a second time [Note: [Col. 0756] Lovaniensis had omitted “a second time”]: once from the Father, once from his mother. For he was born from the Father as God the Word, and he was born from his mother as the Word made flesh.

## 11.

There is therefore one and the same Son of God, born before the ages and born in the world; and both births belong to the one Son of God. His divine birth is that by which, as Creator in the form of God, he is God coeternal with the Father. His human birth is that by which, emptying himself and taking the form of a servant, he not only formed himself, as he became human, in the conception of his mother’s womb through that same assumption of the servant’s form, but also, having become the God-man, came forth from that same maternal womb; having become the God-man, hung upon the cross [Col. 0757]; having become the God-man, lay in the tomb; and having become the God-man, rose from the dead on the third day.

Yet in the tomb the same God lay according to the flesh alone, and into the underworld he descended according to the soul alone.
