When the soul returned from the underworld to the flesh on the third day, the same God rose from the tomb according to the flesh in which he had lain in the tomb. On the fortieth day after his resurrection, the same God-man ascended into heaven and sat at the right hand of God [Note: [Col. 0757] Four manuscripts read, “sits.”] From there he will come at the end of the age to judge the living and the dead.

## 12.

The Word made flesh is therefore one Son of God, the Lord Jesus Christ, mediator between God and human beings. He is mediator because he is the same true God and true human being, possessing with the Father one divine nature and with his mother one substance of humanity; possessing from us, even unto death, the penalty of our iniquity, and possessing from God the Father immutable righteousness [Note: [Col. 0757] The Corbie manuscript reads, “substance.”]

He died temporally because of our iniquity, while because of his righteousness he himself is always living and will bestow immortality upon mortals. He preserved his perfect humanity within the very perfection of his divinity; but through the assumption of death he absorbed the reality of his mortality into the reality and immutability of his immortality [Note: [Col. 0757] So the Corbie manuscript and several others. Lovaniensis reads, “the reality of our mortality.”]

## 13.

This is what blessed Peter testifies: that Christ swallowed up death so that we might be made heirs of eternal life (1 Peter 3:22). Blessed Paul likewise teaches that Christ swallowed up death but brought life and incorruption to light (2 Timothy 1:10).

Christ therefore tasted death because he is true man; and the same Christ swallowed up death because he is true God. For the same one, as the Apostle says, “was crucified from weakness, but lives by the power of God” (2 Corinthians 13:4): one and the same, who, according to the prophecy of blessed David, both became human in Zion and himself founded it, the Most High (Psalm 86:5).

## 14.

Thus Christ’s divinity is not foreign to the nature of the Father, according to what is said: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made.” Nor is his humanity foreign to the nature of his mother, according to what is said: “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:1–3, 14).

For that nature which remains eternally begotten from the Father assumed our nature without sin, so that it might be born from a virgin. The eternal and divine nature could in no way be conceived and born temporally from human nature unless, by assuming the reality of humanity, the ineffable divinity within itself had accepted a true temporal conception and birth.

Thus the eternal and true God was truly conceived and born from a virgin in time. “When the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, made [Note: [Col. 0757] Lovaniensis reads, “born.”] from a woman, made under the Law, so that he might redeem those who were under the Law, so that we might receive adoption as sons” (Galatians 4:4–5)—that is, the God who was naturally made the son of a human being, who is naturally the one Son of God the Father.

The evangelist John confirms this. After saying, “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us,” he immediately adds: “And we saw his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth.”

Thus the Creator and Lord of all spirits and all bodies—that is, of all natures—created the virgin, in order to be created from the virgin. He who himself is her Maker made her his mother when the immense and eternal God received from her flesh, in order to be conceived and born, the true material of flesh. Thus, according to the truth of the servant’s form, God mercifully became man; and, according to the form of God, [Col. 0758] the same God-man remained by natural truth [the final wording is grammatically elliptical in the source].

## 15.

Believe Christ, the Son of God—that is, one person of the Trinity, true God—in such a way that you do not doubt that his divinity was born from the Father’s nature. And believe him to be true man in such a way that you do not suppose his flesh to be heavenly, aerial, or of any other nature, but of that nature which is the flesh of all human beings: the flesh that God himself formed for the first human being from the earth and forms for other human beings, whom he creates through generation from human beings.

Although Christ’s flesh and the flesh of all human beings are of one and the same nature, this flesh, which God the Word graciously chose to unite to himself from the Virgin Mary, was conceived without sin and born without sin. For according to this flesh the eternal and righteous God was mercifully both conceived and born, and the Lord of glory was crucified.

## 16.

What words could explain the singular excellence of that flesh whose person is divine from the very moment of its conception, whose origin in birth is extraordinary, and through which the Word became flesh in such a way that the only-begotten and eternal God was one person with his flesh—himself conceived in the conception of his flesh? [Note: [Col. 0758] After “of his flesh,” the margin of the Corbie manuscript adds: “which he did not have in the first birth.”]

It is certain that the flesh of other human beings is born through ordinary human intercourse: the man sowing, and the woman conceiving and giving birth. And because, when man and woman unite with one another in order to beget children, their intercourse is not without lust, the conception of children born from their flesh cannot be without sin. For it is not propagation but lust that transmits sin to infants; nor does the fecundity of human nature cause human beings to be born with sin, but rather the foulness of lust, which human beings possess as a result of the just condemnation of that first sin.

Therefore blessed David, although he was born from a lawful and righteous marriage—in which there could be found neither the guilt of infidelity nor the stain of fornication—nevertheless, because of original sin, by which children are naturally bound under wrath, cries out and says: “For behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother bore me” [Note: [Col. 0758] Lovaniensis reads, “my mother conceived me.”] (Psalm 50:7).

Holy Job also says that a human being is not clean from defilement, even if his life upon the earth is only one day (Job 14:4, according to the Septuagint).

## 17.

The only-begotten Son of God, who is in the bosom of the Father, became incarnate through the assumption of flesh and a rational soul in order to cleanse the flesh and soul of humanity. He who is true God became true man—not so that one would be God and another man, but so that the same one would be God and the same one man.

In order to remove the sin that human generation contracted through the intercourse of mortal flesh, he was conceived in a new manner: God became incarnate in a virgin mother, without intercourse with a man and without lust in the virgin who conceived. Thus, through the God-man whom the inviolate womb of the virgin brought forth, conceived without lust, the sin inherited by all human beings at birth would be washed away. For all human beings are born under such a condition in this body of death that their mothers cannot perform the work of generation without first losing the virginity of their flesh.

The only-begotten God therefore alone removed the sin of human conception and birth. In his conception he received the reality of flesh from the virgin; in his birth he preserved the integrity of virginity in his mother.

This is why God became the son of the Virgin Mary, and the Virgin Mary became the mother of the only-begotten God: so that the one whom the Father begot from eternity the virgin might bring forth, conceived in time. She was the virgin whom God—he who was to be born from her—so anticipated and filled with singular grace that she bore as the fruit of her womb the one whom the universe has had as its Lord from the beginning; and she saw subjected to herself in the solemnity of birth the one whom, in the unity of the Father’s substance, not only human but also angelic [Col. 0759] creation knows and worships as the Most High.

## 18.

Thus sin and the punishment of sin, which entered the world through the crime of a corrupted woman, are removed from the world through the childbirth of an inviolate virgin. And because, in the condition of the human race, it happened through a woman who was made from a man alone that we became bound under the chain of death, divine goodness brought this about in the redemption of the human race: that through a man who was born from a woman alone, life might be restored to human beings.

There the devil joined human nature to himself through the likeness of sin by the most wicked deception; here God assumed human nature into the unity of his person. There the woman was deceived so that she might become the devil’s daughter; here the virgin was filled with grace so that she might become the mother of the supreme and immutable only-begotten God. There the angel cast down through pride seized the mind of the deceived woman; here God, humbling himself through mercy, filled the womb of the incorrupt virgin in order to be born from her.

For Jesus Christ, the Son of God, who was in the form of God—for he could not be so unless he had been born from the Father’s nature [Note: [Col. 0759] The printed editions of Lovaniensis read “because.” This has been corrected according to the Corbie manuscript]—according to apostolic teaching, “emptied himself, taking the form of a servant.”

God therefore took the form of a servant—that is, the nature of a servant—into his own person. Thus the Maker of human beings, having become like human beings, was found in appearance as a human being. He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross (Philippians 2:6–8).

## 19.

Consider this statement of the Apostle attentively, so that through it you may understand how to believe the Lord Jesus Christ to be the same God and human being, while nevertheless neither confusing nor dividing in him the reality of both natures in one person.

When you first hear of the Lord Jesus Christ that he was in the form of God, you must recognize and hold most firmly that by the name “form” the fullness of nature is to be understood. The Lord Jesus Christ was therefore in the form of God because he was always in the nature of God the Father, from whom he was born.

He is of one nature with the Father and equally eternal and immeasurable with him; equally immortal and immutable; equally invisible and indescribable; equally good and just; equally compassionate and merciful, patient, abundantly merciful, and truthful; equally powerful and gracious; equally wise and omnipotent.

## 20.

Holding all these things that we have said about the Son of God with the firmest faith [Note: [Col. 0759] The printed editions read, “hold.” This has been corrected according to the ancient books]—for since he possesses all these things in the unity of nature with the Father, he is undoubtedly equal to the Father—the Apostle immediately adds: “He did not consider it robbery to be equal with God.” For the equality of the Son’s divinity with the Father was not robbery but nature [Note: [Col. 0759] Lovaniensis reads, “robbery”; shortly afterward, “but by nature.”]

You must also take personally all those things that the Apostle next adds, saying that he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of human beings and found in appearance as a human being; and that he humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross.

Take all these things personally as referring to that only-begotten God, the Son of God; to that Word who is God, of whom the evangelist says: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God”; to that Power of God and Wisdom of God, of whom it is said to God: “You made all things in Wisdom” (Psalm 103:24); to that Beginning with which the Father himself, the Beginning, is one, and in which, coeternal with himself, he made heaven and earth—that is, every spiritual and bodily nature; to the only-begotten God who, as I said, is in the bosom of the Father.

Receive all these things as belonging personally to him, while preserving the eternity, immensity, immortality, immutability, and invisibility of his divinity. God the Son [Note: [Col. 0759] Other printed editions read, “the Son of God.”] possesses these things naturally and equally in common with God the Father, so that, although he truly became human for our sake, he nevertheless remained equal to the true God the Father, from whom the true God, God who is Truth, [Col. 0760] was born [Note: “The true God” is absent from the Corbie manuscript and several others].

He therefore emptied himself, but from his fullness we have all received. If, when emptied, he had lost his fullness, he would have nothing to give us from it. If he had nothing, we could certainly receive nothing. Yet “from his fullness we have all received.” From what he gave us of his fullness, he thus also showed that, when he emptied himself, he did not lose the fullness that he possessed; for if he lost his fullness, he could in no way give from it.

He therefore took the form of a servant. For that emptying of the supreme God was nothing other than the assumption of the servant’s form—that is, of human nature.

## 21.

Both forms therefore exist in Christ, because in Christ both substances are true and complete. For this reason the holy evangelist proclaims him full of grace and truth (John 1:1, 16, 14): he is full in the divine nature, in which God is Truth, and he is full in the human nature, in which he became true man, Grace.

In that fullness he is God, equal to God in the form of God; in this fullness he is a servant, in the form of a servant, because he was made in the likeness of human beings and found in appearance as a human being.

Emptying himself, therefore, he took the form of a servant in order to become a servant; but he did not lose the fullness of the form of God, in which he is eternally and immutably Lord. Having become true man according to the form of a servant, he is of the same nature as his servant mother; remaining true God in the form of God, he is of the same nature as the Lord Father also.

In the form of God, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, he is the one and only God who formed all things. According to the form of a servant, he alone was formed through the operation of himself, the Father, and the Holy Spirit. What he is as Creator he possesses naturally in common with the Father and the Holy Spirit; what he is as created [Note: [Col. 0760] The printed editions add here, “the form of a servant according to which he was created.” This is a gloss absent from the manuscripts], he possesses personally in himself alone.

The Law and the Prophets never ceased to foretell his future birth according to the flesh, his death, resurrection, and ascension into heaven, obeying [Note: [Col. 0760] Lovaniensis had omitted “obeying,” which is present in the manuscripts] his commands in both words and deeds.

## 22.

For in the sacrifices of bodily victims, which the holy Trinity itself—one God of the New and Old Testaments—commanded our fathers to offer, the most pleasing gift of that sacrifice was signified by which God the Son alone, according to the flesh, would mercifully offer himself for us.

For, according to apostolic teaching, “he offered himself for us as an offering and sacrifice to God for a fragrant aroma” (Ephesians 5:5). He is the true God and true High Priest who, not in the blood of bulls and goats but in his own blood, entered once for all into the holy places (Hebrews 9:12). That earlier high priest signified him when he entered the Holy of Holies each year with blood.

This, then, is the one who in himself alone presented everything that he knew to be necessary for accomplishing our redemption. He is at once priest and sacrifice; God and temple: priest, through whom we have been reconciled; sacrifice, by which we have been reconciled; temple, in which we have been reconciled; God, to whom we have been reconciled.

Yet he alone is priest, sacrifice, and temple because all these things belong to God according to the form of a servant—not to God alone, because according to the form of God he possesses this together with the Father and the Holy Spirit.

## 23.

We have therefore been reconciled through the Son alone according to the flesh, but not to the Son alone according to his divinity. For the Trinity reconciled us to itself through this: that the Trinity itself made only the Word flesh.

In him the unchangeable truth of the human and divine nature remains, so that just as his divinity is always true—divinity that he has immutably from the Father—so also his humanity is always true and immutable, humanity that the supreme divinity bears united to itself.

## 24.

I have inserted these few points concerning the faith of the holy Trinity, which alone [Col. 0761] and naturally is the true God, insofar as the brevity of time and discourse permitted. Now I shall explain what you ought to believe without hesitation concerning creation.

# CHAPTER III

## 25. Created Things Are from God. From What Created Natures Derive Their Growth and Decline. God Is Everywhere. God Is Life by Nature. The Origin of Evil Life. Sin against the Holy Spirit

Hold this as the principal point: every nature that is not God the Trinity was created from nothing by the holy Trinity itself, which alone is the true and eternal God. Thus everything in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible—whether Thrones, Dominions, Principalities, or Powers—is the work and creation of the holy Trinity (Colossians 1:16). It is one God, Creator and Lord of all things, eternal, omnipotent [Note: [Col. 0761] Lovaniensis adds here, “just”], and good, naturally possessing the condition of always existing and of never being able to change.

This God, who is always without beginning because he exists supremely, gave the things created by him existence. Yet they are not without beginning, because no creature is of the same nature as the Trinity, the one true and good God, from whom all things were created.

And because he is supremely good, he gave all the natures he made the quality of being good—not as good as the Creator of all good things, who is not only supremely good but also the supreme and immutable Good. He is eternal Good, possessing no deficiency because he was not made from nothing, and possessing no growth because he has no beginning.

Created natures can therefore grow because they began to exist; they can decline because they were made from nothing. The condition of their origin leads them toward decline, while the Creator’s operation advances them toward growth.

In this first aspect of the Trinity, which is the true God, its natural eternity without beginning is recognized: it made certain things in such a way that, although they began to exist, they can never cease to exist. Its omnipotence is understood in this, that it made every visible and invisible creature—that is, every bodily and spiritual creature—from nothing. In these creatures, the very diversity of things commends still more the goodness and omnipotence of the Creator.

For unless he were omnipotent, he would not have made the highest and lowest things with one and the same ease; and unless he were supremely good, he would not have applied himself even to governing the lowest things.

## 26.

Therefore, in both the great and the smallest created things, the goodness and omnipotence of the Creator are great. For he made all things wisely, by the highest and true Wisdom, for whom being is naturally the same as being wise, and making is the same as making wisely.

The simplicity of God’s manifold wisdom commends the greatness of his sublimity not only in the greatness of exalted creatures but also in the smallness of the lowest ones. All the good things he created are not only far beneath and unlike their Creator—since they were not brought forth from him but made entirely from nothing—but are also unequal among themselves. Each thing remains as it received from God the gift of existing: one in this way, another in that.

For bodies did not receive existence in the same way as spirits received it. Even bodies themselves are not equal, and among heavenly and earthly bodies there is found a certain diversity. Heavenly and earthly bodies differ not only in unequal magnitude but also shine with dissimilar brightness.

“For one is the glory,” as the Apostle says, “of heavenly bodies, and another of earthly bodies. There is one glory of the sun, another glory of the moon, and another glory of the stars; for star differs from star in glory” (1 Corinthians 15:40–41).

The diversity of bodily natures therefore shows that each of them is not what it could always have possessed from itself, but what it received through the arrangement and work of the almighty, immutable, and wisest Creator.

## 27.

[Col. 0762] If any bodily creature were of the same nature as the holy Trinity, which is one God, it would neither be located locally in a place, nor ever experience temporal change, nor pass from place to place, nor be bounded by the measure of its bulk.

All these things show that the maker of such natures is one for whom no place is wide or narrow, because he is wholly present no less in narrow places than in wide ones. Nor is he changed by time, because he alone can wonderfully order the cycles of time—not through temporal flux but through eternal stability [Note: [Col. 0762] The Corbie manuscript reads, “will,” rather than “motion”].

For he does not think within time about how the succession of times proceeds through the departure and succession of things; nor is he bounded by any quantity of bulk, because he is confined by no bulk [Note: [Col. 0762] Lovaniensis reads, “by no limit.” The more authoritative manuscripts read “no,” with “bulk” understood].

Nor is he diffused through the parts of the world by parts of himself, so that he might fill the larger parts of the world with his larger parts and the smaller parts with his smaller parts, yet nowhere pour himself forth as wholly present. For he is the God who says: “I fill heaven and earth” (Jeremiah 23:24).

Therefore the Lord God, wholly and ineffably present everywhere, both fills and sustains all the things he made: spirits and bodies, highest and lowest, heavenly and earthly, living things and those to which he did not grant the capacity for life. He is not divided in things that are divided, nor altered by any change in things that are changed.

For unless he were immutable by nature, the immutable order of his purpose and arrangement would never remain in mutable things.

## 28.

The immense God, Creator of corporeal and incorporeal things, first shows that he is not a body by the fact that he did not give life to certain bodies, although he himself created all bodies.

He is naturally life, because if he were not life, he would not have made nonliving bodies. For nothing nonliving makes a nonliving thing; only a living thing does so.

Bodies that cannot live at all are therefore not of one nature with God. Nor are those bodies of one nature with God into which he inserted individual irrational and mindless spirits, so that those bodies might be enlivened and endowed with sensation.

Nor are those mindless spirits themselves of one nature with God. Although it is recognized that he inserted them into bodies in order to enliven and endow them with sensation, he nevertheless granted those spirits no light of understanding by which they could know or love their Creator.

## 29.

Who would dare, with blasphemous spirit and blind heart, either to think or say that those spirits who are unquestionably rational and intellectual are of the same nature as God, when God is naturally altogether immutable and immense?

Although God cannot possess any diversity within himself, he nevertheless displays the diversity of his operation in those same spirits whom he made rational and intellectual. Among them—namely, those inserted into earthly and mortal bodies—there is no local movement, because, while they are in bodies, they are not distributed in portions through the parts of bodily places, but just as they are wholly in whole bodies, so they are wholly in the parts of those same bodies.

Yet the variety of their thoughts shows in them a diversity of a certain temporal movement and change: at one time they do not know something, at another they know it; at one time they will, at another they do not will; at one time they are wise, at another foolish; at one time they are unjust from being just, at another just from being unjust; at one time they are illumined by the light of piety, at another they are corrupted by the dark error of impiety.

## 30.

[Col. 0763] Who cannot see that those who are not burdened by the muddy material of earthly bodies—namely, angelic spirits—are not of one nature with God but were made from nothing?

Their natural mutability is recognized in this: that a part of their nature has been changed for the worse.

Furthermore, those who have not been corrupted—although, through the gift of him by whom they were made when they did not exist, they continually partake of the abundance of the Lord’s sweetness in tireless and, insofar as it has been freely granted to angelic creatures, perfect love, contemplation, and rejoicing [Note: [Col. 0763] Lovaniensis reads, “perceive”]—do not, by the condition of their nature, fall away from him.

Nothing of temporal variation exists in those who cling to God, because, through the gift of eternal incorruption and immutability bestowed upon them, they experience no change within themselves. Nevertheless, each possesses a natural boundary by which they are distinguished from one another: none of them is in another, and whenever some task is assigned to one of them, another is appointed by the will of divine power to carry out another task.

All these things show that even the holy angels are creatures of the holy Trinity. In each of the things he made as he willed, there appears the wondrous wisdom of his arrangement and the power of his work.

## 31.

God created certain spirits so that they would always exist; others he created so that, at some point, they would cease to be spirits. Of those destined to cease, he produced some from water and others from earth, because the Omnipotent willed it so.

But he made the higher spirits have no natural association with bodily elements. He created them eternal and implanted in them the capacity and understanding to contemplate, know, and love the divinity.

Yet he created them in such a way that they would love above themselves the one whose work they recognized as having made them such, even though no merits had preceded their becoming such. And so that this love might receive a just and fitting praise, he also granted them freedom of will. Thus it was possible for them either to raise the intention of holy love toward him who is above them, or to incline themselves downward, under the weight of perverse desire, toward themselves or toward the things beneath them.

## 32.

There is therefore no nature that can continue forever, whether in misery or in blessedness [Note: [Col. 0763] Lovaniensis reads, “happily”], unless it is able, by God’s gift, to contemplate God.

This intellectual nature exists in human beings and in angelic spirits. For God granted the capacity to know and love him only to angels and human beings.

Because of the freedom of choice that, by the Creator’s kindness, ought especially to be granted to an intellectual creature, he gave them the capacity and will to know and love him in such a way that each could possess it and lose it. Yet if anyone voluntarily lost it, he could not thereafter recover it by his own choice.

Thus it belonged to him, whose gratuitous gift it was at the beginning of creation to arrange spirits and bodies, places and dispositions, wondrously according to his wisdom and will, to infuse anew into those whom he willed the beginnings of holy thought, renewed by a freely given gift of goodness.

Angels and human beings, therefore, because they were made rational, received by divine gift the possibility of eternity and blessedness in the very creation of their spiritual nature. They would have remained both eternal and blessed if they had continually clung to the love of their Creator. But if, by the choice of their own freedom, they attempted to make their own will prevail against the command of their supreme Creator, blessedness would immediately depart from the rebellious, and miserable eternity would be left to them as punishment, to be tormented thereafter by errors and pains.

With regard to the angels, he established and fulfilled this arrangement: if any of them lost the goodness of their will, they would never restore it through a divine gift.

### 33.

And so that part of the angels which, by a wholly voluntary turning away, departed from God its Creator, by whom alone it had been blessed, found in that very turning of its will the beginning of its damnation, according to the judgment of supreme justice. Thus, for it, to begin already to be punished was nothing other than to be deprived of love for that blessed Good. God ordained that this deprivation should remain wholly subject to punishment, and also prepared eternal fire for it; in that fire all those transgressing angels can never be without either the evil of their wicked will or punishment. Rather, as the evil of their unjust turning away remains in them, so too the eternal condemnation of just retribution remains.

The devil, prince of these evils, enviously led the first human beings into participation in sin and implanted the deserving of death—not only in them but also in their entire posterity—together with the fault of sin. But God, merciful and just, just as he established the other angels in the eternity of his love when the devil and his angels fell by their own will, so also did not permit the whole human race to perish forever. Instead, those whom his gratuitous goodness willed, after driving away the darkness in which every human birth is enveloped by the condemnation of original sin, he predestined to be brought back to the light. In this he demonstrated above all that these persons would be freed by the undeserved grace of the Liberator from the bonds of original sin, while others—and especially infants, in whom no merits of their own will, whether good or evil, can exist—would be held by an indissoluble bond in eternal condemnation.

[Note: [Col. 0764] The Corbeiensis manuscript of excellent quality reads *praecipitium* (“a precipice”) instead of *participium* (“participation”).]

[Note: [Col. 0764] The Corbeiensis manuscript reads *sed si quis* (“but if anyone”); corrected by a second hand to *sed si quos* (“but those whom”).]

[Note: [Col. 0764] Thus three Vatican manuscripts. The Corbeiensis omits *propriae* (“of their own”). Lov. has *propria merita* (“their own merits”). One of the Vatican manuscripts has *propriae merito* (“by their own merit”).]

### 34.

God also clearly shows that the beginning of good will and thought does not arise in a human being from the person’s own resources, but is both prepared and bestowed by God. For neither the devil nor any of his angels, from the time when by the deserving of their ruin they were thrust down into this lower darkness, has been or can be able to recover a good will. If it were possible for human nature, after turning away from God and losing the goodness of its will, to possess it again from itself, this would be much more possible for angelic nature, which, the less it is burdened by the weight of an earthly body, would possess this capacity all the more abundantly. But God shows from where good will is given to human beings—a will which the angels lost when they possessed it, so that thereafter they cannot possess it again.

### 35.

Since, therefore, that same good will is worthy, through the grace of God, of the reward of eternal blessedness, while angelic and human wickedness ought not to remain unpunished, we faithfully await, according to the rule of the catholic faith, that the Son of God will come to punish all sinful angels and to judge the living and the dead.

For blessed Peter testifies that God did not spare the angels when they sinned, but cast them into the prisons of the darkness of hell and handed them over to be kept for punishment at the judgment (II Peter 2:4). Concerning the judgment of the living and the dead, blessed Paul also says: “I testify before God and Christ Jesus, who is going to judge the living and the dead, and by his coming [Note: [Col. 0764] Lov. and the manuscripts read *et adventum ejus* (“and his coming”), omitting *per* (“by”), which is found in one of the Vatican manuscripts.], and by his kingdom” (II Timothy 4:1).

At his coming, he will raise up everything—from the body of the first human being, which God fashioned from the earth, to the bodies of all human beings that at some time began to live when animated by him—from whom they were created through his working. In the resurrection each individual body will be restored to its own individual soul, which it began to possess in the maternal womb so as to begin living. Thus, at the tribunal of the just Judge, souls will receive their retribution in those same individual bodies, whether the reward of the kingdom or punishment, in which they possessed either the good or the evil quality of their present life.

### 36.

The quality of an evil life begins with unbelief, which takes its beginning from the guilt of original sin. Whoever begins to live in such a way that life ends before the person is released from that guilt—whether that soul has lived in the body for one day or one hour—must endure, together with that same body, the unending punishments of Gehenna. There the devil will burn eternally with his angels: he who both sinned first and persuaded the first human beings to sin. There also, together with him, fornicators, idol-servants, adulterers, the effeminate, those who lie with males, thieves, the greedy, drunkards, the abusive, the rapacious, and all who practice the works of the flesh will be burned in eternal fires if they are not turned from their evil ways before the end of this life. Of these blessed Paul the Apostle says that they will not inherit the kingdom of God (I Corinthians 6:9–10; Galatians 5:19–21).

For every person who remains in this world to the end in delight in iniquity [Note: [Col. 0765] The Corbeiensis and four other manuscripts read *dilectione* (“love”) instead of *delectatione* (“delight”). A little later they likewise read *dilectio* (“love”).] and hardness of heart will be held by eternal torment without end, just as the harmful delight in crimes held that person here.

### 37.

There will also be a resurrection of the wicked, but without the transformation that God will give only to the faithful and to those who live justly by faith. For this is what blessed Paul says: “We shall indeed all rise, but we shall not all be transformed.” Showing that the just will be changed by divine gift, he says: “And we shall be transformed.”

The wicked, therefore, will share with the just a common resurrection of the flesh, but they will not have the grace of transformation, which will be given to the just. For corruption, dishonor, and weakness will not be removed from the bodies of the ungodly, in which they are sown. These will not be extinguished by death either, so that they may constitute for body and soul the continual torment of eternal death.

But the just souls whom God the Redeemer freely justified here through faith, and to whom he granted perseverance in living well to the end after their justification, will attain the eternal blessedness of the heavenly kingdom in those very bodies in which they received the grace of justification from God here, and in which, justified through faith, they lived in the love of God and of their neighbor. Their bodies, too, will be glorified. The nature of the flesh that God created will certainly remain truly present in them, but they will then possess bodies that are spiritual rather than animal, as they are here. “The body is sown an animal body; it will rise a spiritual body” (I Corinthians 15:44).

In these persons, through that transformation which will be given only to the just, what the Apostle says must happen will be fulfilled: “This corruptible body must put on incorruption, and this mortal body must put on immortality” (I Corinthians 15:51, 52, 44, 53). In them the male or female sex will remain, just as those bodies were created. Their glory, however, will differ according to the diversity of their good deeds. Nevertheless, all bodies, whether of males or females, that will be in that kingdom will be glorious. The Judge knows how much glory he is to give each person, because in this life, by mercy, he freely justifies those whom he has determined to glorify there by justice.

### 38.

God gave human beings the time for acquiring eternal life only in this life, in which he also willed fruitful repentance to exist. Repentance is fruitful here because a person can lay aside wickedness, live well, change an unjust will [Note: [Col. 0765] The Corbeiensis and four other manuscripts omit *injusta* (“unjust”).], change merits and deeds together with it, and perform, in the fear of God, those things that please God.

Whoever does not do this in the present life will indeed have repentance for his evils in the age to come, but will not find forgiveness in the sight of God. For although the goad of remorse will be present there, there will no longer be any correction of the will. Such people will condemn their iniquity in such a way that they will in no manner be able either to love or to desire righteousness. Their will will be such that it will always contain within itself the punishment of its wickedness, yet will never be able to receive an affection for goodness.

For just as those who will reign with Christ will have no remnants of an evil will within themselves, so those who are assigned to the punishment of eternal fire with the devil and his angels will have no rest thereafter and will in no way be able to have a good will. And just as the coheirs of Christ will be given the perfection of grace for eternal glory, so the very wickedness of the devil’s companions will heap up their punishment, when, assigned to the outer darkness [Col. 0766], they will not be illumined by any inner light of truth.

### 39.

Therefore repentance can be useful to every person in this life. Whenever a person undertakes it—however wicked or advanced in years—if he renounces his past sins with his whole heart, sheds before God not only tears of the body but also tears of the heart on their account, and takes care to wash away the stains of evil deeds by good deeds, he will immediately receive forgiveness for all his sins.

For the Lord promises this to us in prophetic speech, saying: “If you turn and groan, you will be saved” (Isaiah 30:15, according to the Septuagint). And elsewhere it is said: “My son, you have sinned; do not add again, but pray concerning your past sins, that they may be forgiven you” (Sirach 21:1). Repentance for sins would never have been prescribed for one who sins if forgiveness were not to be granted to the one who repents.

But repentance benefits a sinner only if he performs it within the catholic Church. To the Church God granted, in the person of blessed Peter, the power of binding and loosing, saying: “Whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven” (Matthew 16:19).

Therefore, at whatever age a person performs true repentance for his sins and, with God illuminating him, corrects his life, he will not be deprived of the gift of forgiveness. For, as God says through the prophet, he does not desire the death of the dying, but rather that he turn from his evil way and that his soul live (Ezekiel 33:11) [Note: [Col. 0766] Thus six manuscripts. Lov. reads *mortem peccatoris sive morientis, sed magis ut* (“the death of the sinner or of the dying, but rather that…”).]

### 40.

Nevertheless, no human being ought, in the hope of God’s mercy, to remain longer in his sins, since even in the body no one wishes to remain sick longer in the hope of future health. For those who neglect to withdraw from their iniquities and promise themselves forgiveness from God are sometimes overtaken by God’s sudden wrath in such a way that they find neither time for conversion nor the benefit of forgiveness.

Therefore sacred Scripture kindly warns each one of us, saying: “Do not delay turning to God, and do not put it off from day to day. For suddenly his wrath will come, and at the time of vengeance he will destroy you” (Sirach 5:8–9). Blessed David also says: “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts” (Psalm 94:8).

Blessed Paul likewise agrees with him in these words: “See, brothers, that perhaps there is in any one of you an evil heart of unbelief, causing departure from the living God. But exhort one another each day, as long as it is called ‘Today,’ so that none of you may be hardened by the deceitfulness of sin” (Hebrews 3:12–13).

A person therefore lives with a hardened heart [Note: [Col. 0766] Thus the manuscripts of good quality. Lov. reads *Obduratus igitur vivit* (“A hardened person therefore lives”).] either when he does not turn back because he despairs of forgiveness for his sins, or when he hopes in God’s mercy in such a way that he remains in the perversity of his crimes until the end of his present life [Note: [Col. 0766] Lov. reads *permaneat* (“remains”) instead of *remaneat*.]

### 41.

Therefore, while loving God’s mercy and fearing his justice, let us neither despair of the forgiveness of sins nor remain in sin. We know that the equity of the most just Judge will demand payment for all that the mercy of the most compassionate Redeemer has not forgiven.

For just as mercy receives and absolves those who turn back, so justice will reject and punish those who are hardened. These are the people who, by sinning against the Holy Spirit, will receive forgiveness of sins neither in this age nor in the age to come (Matthew 12:31–32).

The human soul is therefore an intellectual spirit so that it may seek, recognize, and distinguish both the time of its deeds, for which it will receive in judgment what divine justice has ordained, and the time of that same retribution, when it will no longer be possible either to change one’s deeds or profitably to ask divine mercy for forgiveness of one’s sins.

But the other spirits of all animals, which have no understanding—because some of them originate from the earth and some from the waters (for reptiles and birds are from the waters, while from the earth arise some creatures that crawl and others that walk)—are spirits only as long as they live in bodies.

For an animal soul, which was not divinely made capable of reason, begins and ends its life together with its flesh. When it no longer gives life to the body, it too does not live. Thus, in a remarkable way, although the soul is the cause of life for every flesh, an irrational spirit lives only as long as it is able to remain in the flesh; and when it is separated from its flesh, it is extinguished.

Thus, although it is itself the life of its flesh, it cannot live when it has ceased to supply life to the flesh. And if there is no flesh to which it can give life, it too immediately ceases to have life. For this reason neither eternity has been given to irrational spirits, nor is any judgment prepared for them in which blessedness for good works or condemnation for evil works will be repaid to them.

No distinction of works is required of them because they have received from God no capacity for understanding. Therefore their bodies will not rise again, because their souls possessed neither righteousness nor unrighteousness for which eternal blessedness or punishment could be repaid to them.

### 42.

Those animals of the present age therefore complete the course and adornment of the world according to the incomprehensible will of the Creator. They will render no account of their deeds because they are not rational. “Is God concerned about oxen?” (I Corinthians 9:9).

Human beings, however, because they were made rational, will render an account to God both of themselves and of all the things they received for the use of their present life; and according to the quality of their actions they will receive either punishment or glory.

For “we must all be revealed before the tribunal of Christ, so that each may receive what is proper to the body, according to what he has done, whether good or evil” (II Corinthians 5:10). This will be when, according to the words of our own Creator and Redeemer, “all who are in the tombs will hear his voice and will come forth: those who have done good, to the resurrection of life; but those who have done evil, to the resurrection of judgment” (John 5:28–29).

Thus those who have done evil will go into eternal fire, always burning with the devil, the prince of all evils; but those who have done good will go into eternal life, reigning without end with Christ, the King of all ages.

Those will reign with Christ whom God, by his gratuitous goodness, predestined for the kingdom. For by predestining them he prepared them to be such that they would be worthy of the kingdom; he prepared them to be called according to his purpose, so that they might obey; he prepared them to be justified, so that, having received grace, they might believe rightly and live well; and he also prepared them to be glorified, so that, made coheirs of Christ, they might possess the kingdom of heaven without end.

### 43.

Those whom God saved freely, with no preceding merit of good will or good work, reached that kingdom at different times through the sacraments that Christ instituted for faith in his incarnation.

From the time when our Savior said, “Unless one is reborn from water and the Holy Spirit, one cannot enter the kingdom of God” (John 3:5), no one can receive the kingdom of heaven or eternal life without the sacrament of Baptism, except those who, in the catholic Church, shed their blood for Christ without Baptism.

For if anyone receives the sacrament of Baptism in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, whether in the Catholic Church [Note: [Col. 0767] Lov. reads *in catholica fide* (“in the catholic faith”). The word *fide* is absent from the better manuscripts; in its place one Vatican manuscript has *Ecclesia* (“Church”), but this has been added unnecessarily, since among the ancients the name “Catholic” itself sufficiently designates it.] or in any heresy or schism, he receives the complete sacrament. But he will not have the salvation that is the power of the sacrament if he possesses the sacrament itself outside the catholic Church.

Therefore he must return to the Church, not in order to receive the sacrament of Baptism again—for no one ought to repeat it in any baptized person—but so that he may receive eternal life in the catholic fellowship [Col. 0768]. No one can ever be fit to obtain that life who remains alienated from the catholic Church while possessing the sacrament of Baptism.

Even if such a person gives abundant alms and sheds his blood for the name of Christ, he will not have eternal salvation, because in this life he did not maintain the unity of the catholic Church. For where Baptism can benefit a person, there almsgiving can also benefit him. Baptism, however, can exist outside the Church, but it cannot benefit anyone unless it is within the Church.

### 44.

Therefore, only in the catholic Church can the reception of Baptism, works of mercy, and the glorious confession of Christ’s name benefit anyone—provided that one lives well in the catholic Church.

For just as, without fellowship with the catholic Church, neither Baptism nor works of mercy can benefit anyone, except perhaps so that the person may be tormented less severely but not counted among the children of God, so within the catholic Church eternal life is not acquired through Baptism alone if one lives badly after Baptism.

Indeed, even those who live well must devote themselves continually to works of mercy, knowing that, although they may be slight, they nevertheless contract certain sins every day. For these sins even the saints and the just must always say to God in this life: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matthew 6:12).

### 45.

Because these sins frequently creep upon human beings even in matters that are lawful and granted by God [Note: [Col. 0768] Thus the Corbeiensis manuscript. Lov. reads *quando* (“when”) instead of *quoniam* (“because”).], and because the more the body is filled with substantial foods and the human heart is entangled in carnal acts and affections, the more frequently guilt is contracted in this mortal life, humble servants of Christ who desire to serve their Lord without hindrance and without harmful occupation of mind do not seek marriage at all, and abstain from meat and wine insofar as bodily health permits.

This is not because it is a sin to have a spouse or to consume wine or meat. For blessed Paul the Apostle says: “Every creature of God is good, and nothing is to be rejected that is received with thanksgiving; for it is sanctified by the word of God and prayer” (I Timothy 4:4–5).

God also both instituted and blessed marriage among the first human beings (Genesis 2:22–24). For this reason the Apostle says: “Marriage is honorable in all, and the marriage bed undefiled” (Hebrews 13:4).

Therefore, when servants of God abstain from meat and wine, they do not reject them as unclean things but follow the practices of a purer life. And when they do not marry, they do not consider the goodness of marriage blameworthy; rather, they do not doubt that continual continence is better than a good marriage—especially at this time, when it is said concerning continence, “Let anyone who is able to receive it receive it” (Matthew 19:12), but concerning marriage it is said, “If they cannot contain themselves, let them marry” (I Corinthians 7:9).

In the one case virtue is raised up by exhortation; in the other weakness is supported by a remedy. Therefore, since one must always provide for infirmity, if someone first happens to be deprived of a spouse, and wishes to enter a second or even a third marriage, he will have no sin on their account if he preserves them chastely—that is, if one man and one woman, joined lawfully, keep faith, so that neither he has intercourse with any woman besides his wife nor she with any man besides her husband.

In such marriages, even if some excess of marital conduct occurs, provided that it does not violate the legitimate marriage bed, the person will have some sin, but a venial one.

[Note: [Col. 0768] The Lov. edition reads *in una enim ratione* (“for in one consideration”). The text is corrected according to the Corbeiensis manuscript.]

### 46.

But these matters concern those who have made no vow of continence to God.

Whoever, however, has made himself a eunuch for the sake of the kingdom of heaven and has vowed continence to God in his heart will incur condemnation not only if he is stained by the deadly crime [Note: [Col. 0768] Alternatively, “wound.”] of fornication, but also if a man wishes to take a wife or a woman wishes to marry, because he has nullified his first commitment (I Timothy 5:12).

Therefore, just as, according to the Apostle’s judgment, it is right for a husband to render the marital debt to his wife, and likewise a wife to her husband—for if anyone takes a wife he does not sin, and if a virgin marries she does not sin—so, according to the same Apostle’s statement, whoever has firmly resolved in his heart, without necessity, but with power over his own will, and has vowed continence to God (I Corinthians 7:3, 27, 37), ought to guard it with the utmost care of mind to the end, lest he incur condemnation by nullifying his first commitment.

Likewise, married men or married women who, by mutual agreement, vow perpetual continence to God should know that they are held bound by their vow [Note: [Col. 0769] One Vatican manuscript reads: “that they are held bound by the bond of their vow.”] and that they no longer owe one another sexual intercourse, which they previously possessed lawfully; rather, they owe God the continence that they vowed.

Each person will then possess the kingdom of heaven, which is promised to the saints, if, forgetting what lies behind and stretching forward to what lies ahead (Philippians 3:13), he acts according to what is said in the Psalms: “Vow and fulfill your vows to the Lord your God” (Psalm 75:12). Whatever he recognizes as lawful and belonging to the progress of a better life, let him willingly vow, quickly fulfill, and, in fulfilling his vow, advance ever more earnestly.

For to everyone who vows to God and fulfills what he has vowed, God himself will also give the rewards of the heavenly kingdom that he promised.

## CHAPTER IV, OR RULE I

### 47. The Divine Nature

[Note: [Col. 0769] Here begin the Rules of Faith, forty in number, marked by numerical headings in the Corbeiensis book and several other manuscripts.]

Hold most firmly, therefore, and have no doubt whatever, that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are naturally one God, in whose name we were baptized.

Although “Father” is one name, “Son” another, and “Holy Spirit” another, this is nevertheless the one name of the nature of these three: “God.” Of him it is said in Deuteronomy: “See, see [Note: [Col. 0769] Thus most manuscripts. Lov. has *videte* only once.], that I am God, and there is no other besides me” (Deuteronomy 32:39). And of him it is said: “Hear, O Israel: the Lord your God, the Lord is one; and you shall adore the Lord your God and serve him alone” (Deuteronomy 6:4, 13).

## CHAPTER V, OR RULE II

### 48. One God

Hold most firmly, and have no doubt whatever, that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—that is, the holy Trinity—are the one naturally true God.

Although we are not permitted to worship three gods, but only one true God, just as the Apostle bears witness that the Father is called the true God, saying, “You turned to God from idols, to serve the living and true God, and to await his Son from heaven, whom he raised from the dead, Jesus” (I Thessalonians 1:9–10), so the Apostle John also commends the Son as the true God, saying: “We know that the Son of God has come and has given us understanding, so that we may know the true God and be in his true Son Jesus Christ. This is the true God and eternal life” (I John 5:20).

Since he is certainly the true God, he is also Truth, as he himself teaches us, saying: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6). The Apostle John also says of the Holy Spirit: “The Spirit is truth” (I John 5:6). And he who is Truth cannot by nature fail to be the true God.

The Apostle Paul also confesses him to be God, saying: “Your members are a temple of the Holy Spirit, who is in you, whom you have from God, and you are not your own. For you were bought at a great price: glorify and bear God in your body” (I Corinthians 6:19–20).

## CHAPTER VI, OR RULE III

### 49. The Eternal God

Hold most firmly, and have no doubt whatever, that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—that is, the holy Trinity—are one true God, eternal without beginning.

For this reason it is written: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and God was the Word; he was in the beginning with God” (John 1:1–2). This eternity is again made known in the Psalm, where it says: “But God our King is before the ages” (Psalm 73:12); and elsewhere: “His eternal power and divinity” (Romans 1:20).

## CHAPTER VII, OR RULE IV

### 50. The Immutable God

Hold most firmly, and have no doubt whatever, that the holy Trinity, the one true God, is, just as eternal, also naturally the only immutable one.

For this is signified when he says to his servant Moses: “I am who I am” (Exodus 3:14). Hence [Note: [Col. 0770] The Corbeiensis manuscript reads *huic* (“to this one”) instead of *hinc* (“hence”).] it is also said in the Psalms: “In the beginning, Lord, you founded the earth, and the heavens are the works of your hands. They will perish, but you remain; and all of them will grow old like a garment, and like a covering you will change them, and they will be changed; but you are the same” (Psalm 101:26–28).

## CHAPTER VIII, OR RULE V

### 51. God, Creator of All

Hold most firmly, and have no doubt whatever, that the holy Trinity alone is the true God, Creator of all visible and invisible things.

Of him it is said in the Psalms: “Blessed is he whose God is Jacob’s helper, whose hope is in the Lord his God, who made heaven and earth, the sea and all that is in them” (Psalm 145:5–6). The Apostle also says of him: “From him, through him, and in him are all things; to him be glory forever” (Romans 11:36).

## CHAPTER IX, OR RULE VI

### 52. The Trinity in Unity

Hold most firmly, and have no doubt whatever, that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit have one nature, but are three persons.

The Father alone is the one who said, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” [Note: [Col. 0770] Lov. reads “in whom I am well pleased” with *bene* (“well”) added. The better manuscripts omit *bene*.]. The Son alone is the one over whom that voice of the Father alone resounded when, according to the flesh, the Only-Begotten God was baptized in the Jordan—the one who alone assumed flesh. And the Holy Spirit alone is the Spirit of the Father and the Son who descended in the form of a dove upon Christ after he had been baptized and was ascending from the water (Matthew 3:17, 16), and who, on the fiftieth day after Christ’s resurrection, came and filled the faithful gathered in one place in the division of fiery tongues [Note: [Col. 0770] Thus the Corbeiensis manuscript. Lov. reads *visione* (“vision”) instead of *divisione* (“division”).] (Acts 2:3–4).

But that voice through which God the Father alone spoke, that flesh through which God the Only-Begotten alone became human, that dove in whose form the Holy Spirit descended upon Christ, and those fiery tongues in whose division he filled the faithful [Note: [Col. 0770] Lov. reads “the faithful Apostles.” The word *Apostolos* (“Apostles”) is absent from the manuscripts.] gathered in one place—these are works of the whole holy Trinity, that is, of the one God who made all things in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible.

## CHAPTER X, OR RULE VII

### 53. The Distinction of the Persons

Hold most firmly, and have no doubt whatever, that God alone the Son—that is, one person of the Trinity—is the Son of God the Father alone; but that the Holy Spirit, himself also one person of the Trinity, is the Spirit not of the Father alone but simultaneously of the Father and the Son.

Showing that he alone was begotten from the Father, God the Son said: “God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son”; and shortly afterward: “Whoever does not believe has already been judged, because he has not believed in the name of the only-begotten Son of God” (John 3:16, 18).

The Apostle teaches that the Holy Spirit is the Spirit of both the Father and the Son, saying: “You, however, are not in the flesh but in the Spirit, if indeed the Spirit of God dwells in you”; and he follows with: “If anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to him” (Romans 8:9).

## CHAPTER XI, OR RULE VIII

### 54. The Holy Spirit

Hold most firmly, and have no doubt whatever, that the same Holy Spirit, who is the one Spirit of the Father and the Son, proceeds from the Father and the Son.

For the Son says: “When the Spirit of truth comes, who proceeds from the Father” (John 15:26). There he taught that the Spirit is his own, because he himself is the Truth [Col. 0771] (John 14:6).

That the Holy Spirit also proceeds from the Son is commended to us by prophetic and apostolic teaching. Isaiah says of the Son: “He will strike the earth with the rod of his mouth, and with the Spirit of his lips he will kill the wicked” (Isaiah 11:4). Of him the Apostle also says: “The Lord Jesus will kill him with the Spirit of his mouth” (II Thessalonians 2:8).

The only-begotten Son of God himself also signified that the Spirit is the Spirit of his mouth when, after his resurrection, he breathed upon the disciples and said: “Receive the Holy Spirit” (John 20:22). John says in the Apocalypse concerning the mouth of the Lord Jesus himself that a sword sharpened on both sides proceeded from it (Revelation 1:16). Therefore the Spirit of his mouth is himself the sword that proceeds from his mouth.

## CHAPTER XII, OR RULE IX

### 55. The Trinity Circumscribed by No Limits

Hold most firmly, and have no doubt whatever, that God the Trinity is immense in power, not in bulk, and that every spiritual and bodily creature is contained by his power and presence.

For God the Father says: “I fill heaven and earth” (Jeremiah 23:24). It is also said of the Wisdom of God, who is his Son, that “she reaches mightily from one end to the other and orders all things gently” (Wisdom 8:1). We also read of the Holy Spirit: “The Spirit of the Lord has filled the world” (Wisdom 1:7). And the prophet David says: “Where shall I go from your Spirit, and where shall I flee from your presence? If I ascend into heaven, you are there; and if I descend into hell, you are present” (Psalm 138:7–8).

## CHAPTER XIII, OR RULE X

### 56. The Person of the Son

Hold most firmly, and have no doubt whatever, that one person of the Trinity—God the Son, who alone was born from the nature of God the Father and is of one and the same nature with the Father—was, in the fullness of time, according to his assumption of the form of a servant, voluntarily conceived in a virgin and born from a virgin, the Word made flesh.

He is also the one who was essentially born from the Father and essentially conceived and born from the virgin; he is one and of one nature with the Father and of one nature with the virgin [Note: [Col. 0771] Lov. lacked “and of one nature with the Father”; it is restored from the Corbeiensis manuscript.]. Concerning God the Father he says: “Before the ages he founded me, and before all the hills he begot me” (Proverbs 8:22, 25). Of him the Apostle also said: “When the fullness of time came, God sent his Son, made from a woman, made under the law” (Galatians 4:4).

## CHAPTER XIV, OR RULE XI

### 57. The Humanity of Christ

Hold most firmly, and have no doubt whatever, that Christ the Son of God, just as he was born from God the Father as fully and perfectly God, was born from the virgin mother as fully and perfectly human [Note: [Col. 0771] The Corbeiensis manuscript reads “from the virgin Mary as fully and perfectly God and human.”].

That is, he is the Word who is God, possessing, without sin, true flesh of our race and a rational soul. The Son of God himself clearly demonstrated this when he said concerning his flesh: “Touch me and see, because a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see me have” (Luke 24:39).

He also showed in these words that he possessed a soul: “For this reason the Father loves me, because I lay down my soul, and I will take it up again” (John 10:17). He showed that he possessed understanding in his soul in saying: “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble in heart” (Matthew 11:29). And God says of him through the prophet: “Behold, my servant will understand, and he will be exalted and will be very high” (Isaiah 52:13).

Blessed Peter also confesses, according to the prophecy of holy David, that Christ possessed flesh and a soul. Speaking of him, blessed David, Peter says: “Since he was a prophet and knew that God had sworn to him with an oath that he would set one from the fruit of his loins upon his throne, he foresaw and spoke about the resurrection of Christ: that neither was his soul abandoned in hell, nor did his flesh see corruption” (Acts 2:30–31).

## CHAPTER XV, OR RULE XII

### 58. The Divinity of Christ

Hold most firmly, and have no doubt whatever, that it is one and the same God the Word [Note: [Col. 0772] Thus the manuscripts. Lov. reads “that it is one and the same Son, true God.”] who, together with God the Father and God the Holy Spirit, made all times and gave the law to Moses on Mount Sinai, arranged through angels (Exodus 20; Galatians 3:19).

And it is the same Word who is God made flesh: when the fullness of time came, he was sent by the Father and the Holy Spirit, and alone was made from the woman whom he had made; alone he was made subject to the law that he had given (Galatians 4:4).

## CHAPTER XVI, OR RULE XIII
### 59. On the Two Natures in Christ

Hold most firmly, and in no way doubt, that the two natures of the Word of God who became flesh remain without confusion and without separation: one truly divine, which he shares with God the Father, according to which he says, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30); and, “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father” [Note: [Col. 0772] So the Corbie manuscript. But in Lovaniensis twice, *sees*.]; and, “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (John 14:9–11); according to which the Apostle calls him “the radiance of the glory and the form of God’s substance” (Heb. 1:3). The other is truly human, according to which God himself, incarnate, says, “The Father is greater than I” (John 14:28).

### CHAPTER XVII, or RULE XIV

### 60. The Unity of the Person in Christ

Hold most firmly, and in no way doubt, that the Word of God made flesh has one person of his divinity and flesh. For God the Word graciously united to himself the complete human nature in such truth, and, while his divinity remained, the Word so became flesh, that although the Word is not naturally the same as flesh, since the truth of the two natures remains in Christ, nevertheless, according to one person, the same Word became flesh from the beginning of his mother’s conception. For God the Word did not assume the person of a human being, but a nature; and into the eternal person of his divinity he assumed the temporal substance of flesh. Therefore there is one Christ, the Word made flesh (John 1:14), who is both descended from the patriarchs according to the flesh and “God blessed above all forever” (Rom. 9:5).

There is one Jesus, to whom the Father also says, “From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you” (Ps. 109:3): by this is signified an eternal birth without beginning, before all time. [Note: [Col. 0772] In Lovaniensis, “There is one Jesus” is repeated.] Of him the Evangelist also says that “his name was called Jesus,” as the angel had said, before he was conceived in the womb (Luke 2:21).

### CHAPTER XVIII, or RULE XV

### 61. The Union of the Word and the Flesh

Hold most firmly, and in no way doubt, that Christ’s flesh was not conceived in the Virgin’s womb without divinity, before it was assumed by the Word; rather, God the Word himself was conceived through the taking on of his flesh, and that very flesh was conceived through the incarnation of the Word.

### CHAPTER XIX, or RULE XVI

### 62. Sacrifices. The Sacrifice of Bread and Wine

Hold most firmly, and in no way doubt, that God the only-begotten Word, made flesh, offered himself for us as a sacrifice and offering to God for a pleasing aroma (Eph. 5:2). To him, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, animals were sacrificed by the Patriarchs, Prophets, and priests in the time of the Old Testament; and to him now—that is, in the time of the New Testament—the holy Catholic Church throughout the whole world does not cease to offer, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, with whom he has one divinity, the sacrifice of bread and wine in holy faith and charity.

For in those carnal victims there was a sign [Note: [Col. 0772] Lovaniensis: “representation.”] of the flesh of Christ, which he himself, though without sin, was to offer for our sins, and of the blood which he was to pour out for the remission of our sins. In this sacrifice, however, there is thanksgiving and a commemoration of the flesh of Christ, which he offered for us, and of the blood which the same God poured out for us.

Concerning this, blessed Paul says in the Acts of the Apostles: “Pay attention to yourselves and to the whole flock, in which the Holy Spirit has placed you as bishops to govern the Church of God, which he acquired with his own blood” (Acts 20:28). [Col. 0773] In those sacrifices, therefore, what was to be given to us was symbolically signified; but in this sacrifice what has already been given to us is clearly displayed. In those sacrifices the Son of God was foretold as one who would be killed for the ungodly; in this one he is proclaimed as having been killed for the ungodly, the Apostle testifying that “while we were still weak, at the proper time Christ died for the ungodly,” and that “while we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son” (Rom. 5:6, 10).

### CHAPTER XX, or RULE XVII

### 63. The Humanity of Christ

Hold most firmly, and in no way doubt, that the Word made flesh always possesses that same true human flesh in which God the Word was born of the Virgin, in which he was crucified and died, in which he rose again and ascended into heaven, and in which he sat at the right hand of God [Note: [Col. 0773] Lovaniensis: “sits.”], in which also he will come to judge the living and the dead.

For this reason the Apostles heard from the angels: “He will come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven” (Acts 1:11). And blessed John said: “Behold, he will come with the clouds, and every eye will see him, even those who pierced him” [Note: [Col. 0773] Lovaniensis: “crucified him.”]; “and all the tribes of the earth will see him as such” (Rev. 1:7).

### CHAPTER XXI, or RULE XVIII

### 64. Nature Is Entirely Good. What Evil Is

Hold most firmly, and in no way doubt, that God the Trinity—that is, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—is by nature the supreme and unchangeable good; and that all natures were created by him, good indeed because they were made by the supreme good, but changeable because they were made from nothing. There is no nature of evil, because every nature, insofar as it is a nature, is good.

But because the good in a nature can be diminished or increased, it is called evil insofar as its good is diminished; for evil is nothing other than the privation of good. Hence it is clear that rational creation has a twofold evil: one by which it voluntarily fell away from its supreme good, its Creator [Note: [Col. 0773] The manuscripts read “which voluntarily”; and shortly afterward, “which against its will.”]; the other by which, against its will, it will be punished by the penalty of eternal fire. It will suffer the latter justly because it committed the former unjustly; and what did not preserve within itself the order of divine institution will not escape the order of divine retribution. [Note: [Col. 0773] Lovaniensis: “and because.”] [Note: [Col. 0773] Lovaniensis: “an evil nature.” But most manuscripts: “a nature of evil.”]

### CHAPTER XXII, or RULE XIX

### 65. No Creature Is the Same as God

Hold most firmly, and in no way doubt, that neither the angels nor any other creature is of the same nature as that which, according to its natural divinity, the supreme Trinity is: one God by nature, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. For the one who made and the things he made could not be of one nature. [Note: [Col. 0773] The manuscripts read “could not be”; another reading is “could not have been.”]

### CHAPTER XXIII, or RULE XX

### 66. The Angels Made Firm

Hold most firmly, and in no way doubt, that every creature, naturally changeable, was made by the unchangeable God; yet none of the holy angels can now be changed for the worse, because they received eternal blessedness, in which they stably enjoy God, in such a way that they cannot be deprived of it.

But the fact that they cannot at all be changed for the worse from the state of blessedness in which they are is not implanted in them by nature; rather, after they were created, it was bestowed upon them by the generosity of divine grace. For if the angels had been made naturally unchangeable, the devil and his angels would never have fallen from their company.

### CHAPTER XXIV, or RULE XXI

### 67. Rational Creatures

Hold most firmly, and in no way doubt, that in every creature—spiritual and bodily—which the supreme Trinity made, only angelic and human spirits received from God the capacity for understanding; but that the other spirits, those of irrational animals, did not receive reason and understanding, and are wholly unable to possess them. For this reason it is said to human beings, “Do not become like the horse and the mule, which have no understanding” (Ps. 31:9).

Therefore the souls of human beings and the souls of animals are not of one nature; nor can the souls of animals at any time pass into human beings, nor the souls of human beings into animals. [Col. 0774] [Note: [Col. 0774] Lovaniensis: “into human souls”; and below, “into animal souls.”]

### CHAPTER XXV, or RULE XXII

### 68. Adam’s Free Will

Hold most firmly, and in no way doubt, that the first human beings—that is, Adam and his wife—were created good, upright, and without sin, with free will, by which, if they wished, they could always serve and obey God with humility and good will [Note: [Col. 0774] Lovaniensis omits “always serve God.”]; and by that same will, if they wished, they could sin by their own choice.

They sinned not from necessity but by their own choice; and through that sin human nature was so changed for the worse that not only did death gain dominion through sin in those first human beings themselves, but the dominion of sin and death also passed to all human beings.

### CHAPTER XXVI, or RULE XXIII

### 69. Original Sin

Hold most firmly, and in no way doubt, that every human being conceived through the intercourse of man and woman is born with original sin, subjected to ungodliness and placed under the power of death, and therefore is born a child of wrath by nature. Concerning this the Apostle says: “For we too were by nature children of wrath, like the rest” (Eph. 2:3).

No one is freed from this wrath except through faith in the Mediator between God and human beings, the man Jesus Christ, who was conceived without sin, born without sin, died without sin, and was made sin for us (2 Cor. 5:21)—that is, he was made a sacrifice for our sins.

For in the Old Testament, the sacrifices offered for sins were called “sins”; in all of them there was a sign of Christ, because he is “the Lamb of God who takes away the sin” [Note: [Col. 0774] So the Corbie manuscript. Lovaniensis reads “sins.”] of the world (John 1:29).

### CHAPTER XXVII, or RULE XXIV

### 70. The Punishment of the Unbaptized

Hold most firmly, and in no way doubt, that not only human beings who have already attained the use of reason, but also infants—whether they begin to live in their mothers’ wombs and die there, or, having already been born from their mothers, depart from this world without the sacrament of holy Baptism, which is given in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit—will be punished with the everlasting punishment of eternal fire.

For although they have no sin of their own action, they have nevertheless contracted the condemnation of original sin through carnal conception and birth.

### CHAPTER XXVIII, or RULE XXV

### 71. Judgment

Hold most firmly, and in no way doubt, that Christ the Son of God will come to judge the living and the dead in order to raise up at his coming the human beings whom here he freely justifies through faith by the gift of his grace, and to whom, once justified, he grants perseverance in faith and the charity of holy Mother Church to the end; to glorify them; to make them equal to the holy angels according to his promise (Matt. 22:30); and to bring them to that state in which they will be perfectly good, insofar as God grants this to each one, and from that perfection will no longer be able to change.

There the glory of the saints will be diverse, but the eternal life of all will be one.

The devil and his angels, however, are to be sent by Christ into eternal fire, where they will never be without the punishment prepared for them by divine justice. Together with the devil, ungodly and unrighteous human beings—of whom Scripture says, “They imitate him who are on his side” (Wis. 2:25)—because they imitated him in evil works and did not perform fitting repentance before the end of the present life, will, after receiving their bodies again, burn in the punishment of eternal fire.

### CHAPTER XXIX, or RULE XXVI

### 72. The Resurrection of the Flesh

Hold most firmly, and in no way doubt, that at the Lord’s coming there will be a common resurrection of the flesh for all human beings, both good and evil, but that God’s just retribution will be unlike for the good and the evil, according to what the Apostle says: “For we shall all rise, but we shall not all be changed.”

The righteous, however, who will go into eternal life, will be changed. The Apostle shows this when he says: “And the dead will rise incorruptible, and we shall be changed.” Showing what this change will be, he added: “For this corruptible body must put on incorruption, and this mortal body must put on immortality.”

In their bodies [Note: [Col. 0775] Understand: “the bodies of the righteous.”] what the Apostle himself says will take place: “It is sown in corruption, it will rise in incorruption; it is sown in dishonor, it will rise in glory; it is sown in weakness, it will rise in power; it is sown an animal body, it will rise a spiritual body” (1 Cor. 15:51–53, 42–44).

He called it spiritual not because the body itself will be spirit, but because, made immortal and incorruptible by the life-giving Spirit, it will remain. A body will then be called spiritual when it is not spirit but remains a body, just as now it is called animal although it is found to be not a soul but a body.

### CHAPTER XXX, or RULE XXVII

### 73. Faith and Baptism

Hold most firmly, and in no way doubt, that, except for those who are baptized in their own blood for the name of Christ, no human being will receive eternal life who here has not been turned from his evils through repentance and faith, and liberated through the sacrament of faith and repentance—that is, through Baptism.

For adults it is necessary both to repent of their evils, to hold the Catholic faith according to the rule of truth, and to receive the sacrament of Baptism. But for infants, who can neither believe by their own will nor repent for the sin which they bear from their origin, the sacrament of faith and repentance, which is holy Baptism, is sufficient for salvation for as long as their age is incapable of reason.

### CHAPTER XXXI, or RULE XXVIII

### 74. Grace
