Hold most firmly, and in no way doubt, that no human being here can repent unless God has enlightened that person and converted him by gratuitous mercy. For the Apostle says: “Lest perhaps God may grant them repentance for the knowledge of the truth, and they may recover from the devil’s snares” (2 Tim. 2:25–26).

### CHAPTER XXXII, or RULE XXIX

### 75. Nothing Is Done without Grace

Hold most firmly, and in no way doubt, that a human being whom neither ignorance of letters nor any weakness or adversity prevents can indeed either read the words of the holy Law and Gospel or hear them from the mouth of some preacher.

But no one can obey the divine commandments unless God has first come to that person with his grace, so that what he hears with the body he may also receive with the heart [Note: [Col. 0775] The Corbie manuscript reads “receive”]; and, having received from God good will and strength, may both desire and be able to fulfill God’s commandments.

“For neither is the one who plants anything, nor the one who waters, but God who gives the growth” (1 Cor. 3:7); he also “works in us both to will and to accomplish, according to his good will” (Phil. 2:13).

### CHAPTER XXXIII, or RULE XXX

### 76. Nothing Is Hidden from God

Hold most firmly, and in no way doubt, that to the unchangeable God not only all past and present things but also all future things are unchangeably known, to whom it is said: “O God, knower of hidden things, who know all things before they come to be” (Dan. 13:42).

### CHAPTER XXXIV, or RULE XXXI

### 77. Predestination

Hold most firmly, and in no way doubt, that God the Trinity, unchangeable and the most certain knower of all things and works, both his own and human, knew before all ages to whom he would grant grace through faith [Note: [Col. 0775] In the margin of the Corbie book is added: “inspired by him”]. Without this grace no one, from the beginning of the world to its end, could be absolved [Note: [Col. 0775] The editions of Erasmus, Lyons, Venice, and Lovaniensis read “can be.”] from the guilt both of original and of actual sin.

“For those whom God foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son” [Note: [Col. 0775] The manuscripts read “his image.”] (Rom. 8:29).

### CHAPTER XXXV, or RULE XXXII

### 78. The Blessed through Predestination

Hold most firmly, and in no way doubt, that all whom God makes vessels of mercy by his gratuitous goodness [Note: [Col. 0775] The Corbie manuscript reads: “whom God made freely”], whom God predestined before the foundation of the world for adoption as his children [Note: [Col. 0775] In Lovaniensis, “and of repentance” had been omitted; it is found in the manuscripts], [Col. 0776] cannot perish if God predestined them for the kingdom; and that none of those whom God did not predestine for life can be saved by any means.

For that predestination is the preparation of a gratuitous gift, concerning which the Apostle says that we were predestined for adoption as sons through Jesus Christ, for himself (Eph. 1:5).

### CHAPTER XXXVI, or RULE XXXIII

### 79. Baptism

Hold most firmly, and in no way doubt, that the sacrament of Baptism can exist not only within the Catholic Church but also among heretics who baptize in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit; but that outside the Catholic Church it cannot be beneficial.

Indeed, just as salvation is conferred through the sacrament of Baptism upon those who rightly believe within the Church, so those baptized outside the Church, if they do not return to the Church, are by that same Baptism burdened with destruction. For the unity of ecclesiastical fellowship has such value for salvation that one is not saved by Baptism when it is not given there where it ought to be given.

Nevertheless, Baptism is present in a person baptized even outside the Church, but it is present for judgment in one separated from the Church. And since it is clear that wherever this Baptism has been given, it is to be given only once, therefore, even if it has been given by heretics in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, it must be reverently acknowledged and for this reason never repeated.

For the Savior says: “The one who has bathed once does not need [Note: [Col. 0776] Here the Corbie manuscript adds “to wash”] anything except to wash his feet” (John 13:10).

### CHAPTER XXXVII, or RULE XXXIV

### 80. There Is No Salvation outside the Church

Hold most firmly, and in no way doubt, that no one baptized outside the Catholic Church can become a participant in eternal life if, before the end of this life, that person has not been restored and incorporated into the Catholic Church.

For, says the Apostle, “If I have all faith and know all mysteries, but do not have charity, I am nothing” (1 Cor. 13:2). For in the days of the Flood also, we read that no one outside the ark could be saved.

### CHAPTER XXXVIII, or RULE XXXV

### 81. Those Who Must Be Condemned

Hold most firmly, and in no way doubt, that not only all pagans but also all Jews, and all heretics and schismatics who end their present life outside the Catholic Church, will go into the eternal fire “which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25:41).

### CHAPTER XXXIX, or RULE XXXVI

### 82. Heretics

Hold most firmly, and in no way doubt, that any heretic or schismatic baptized in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, if he has not been joined to the Catholic Church, cannot be saved by any means, however many alms he may have given, even if he has shed his blood for the name of Christ.

For no human being who does not maintain the unity of the Catholic Church can receive any benefit toward salvation from Baptism, however abundant an almsgiving, or death undertaken for the name of Christ, so long as the heretical or schismatic perversity that leads to death persists in that person. [Note: [Col. 0776] Lovaniensis: “as long as.”]

### CHAPTER XL, or RULE XXXVII

### 83. Christians Who Live Badly

Hold most firmly, and in no way doubt, that not all who are baptized within the Catholic Church will receive eternal life, but only those who live rightly after receiving Baptism—that is, those who have abstained from vices and the desires of the flesh.

For just as unbelievers, heretics, and schismatics will not possess the kingdom of heaven, so criminal Catholics cannot possess it.

### CHAPTER XLI, or RULE XXXVIII

### 84. No One Lives without Sin

Hold most firmly, and in no way doubt, that no one, even among righteous and holy people except for infants who have been baptized, can live here without sin; and that it is always necessary for every human being to wash away his sins until the end of the present life through almsgiving [Col. 0777] [Note: [Col. 0777] In the margin of the Corbie book the manuscript adds: “fasts, prayer, or tears”], and humbly and sincerely to ask God for forgiveness.

### CHAPTER XLII, or RULE XXXIX

### 85. Food and Drink. Marriage. Second Marriages Permitted

Hold most firmly, and in no way doubt, that every creature of God is good, and that nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving (1 Tim. 4:4). God’s servants who abstain from meat or wine should not reject as unclean things that were made by God, but should abstain from stronger food and drink solely for the chastening of the body.

Marriages too were instituted and blessed by God. It is indeed better if someone is without marriage, so that he may think more freely and fully about the things of God and how to please God; nevertheless, for those who have not vowed continence, there is no sin whether a woman marries or a man takes a wife (1 Cor. 7:34, 28).

Nor did God institute only first marriages; he also permitted second and third marriages because of the weakness of those who cannot remain continent. But for those who, whether married or free from marriage, have vowed continence to God, it is exceedingly condemnable if the former wish to seek the marital act, which they professed by their free choice they would not approach, or if the latter wish to return to that from which they professed, by their common choice, that they would withdraw.

### CHAPTER XLIII, or RULE XL

### 86. The Wicked Are Mixed with the Good in the Church

Hold most firmly, and in no way doubt, that the Catholic Church is God’s threshing floor, and that within it, until the end of the age, chaff will remain mixed with the grain—that is, the wicked will be mixed with the good through participation in the sacraments. In every profession—whether of clergy, monks, or laypeople—there are both good and wicked.

The good are not to be abandoned because of the wicked; rather, the wicked are to be tolerated for the sake of the good, insofar as the order of faith and charity requires this—that is, provided that they either scatter no seeds of unbelief in the Church or do not lead their brothers to some evil deed through deadly imitation.

Nor can anyone within the Catholic Church who rightly believes and lives well ever be stained by another’s sin, if he neither gives consent nor favor to anyone who sins. It is beneficial for the wicked to be tolerated by the good within the Church, provided this is done by living well with them and admonishing them well, so that, seeing and hearing what is good, they may reject their evil deeds and tremble at the thought that God will judge them for their evil works. Thus, with the gift of grace going before them, they may be ashamed of their iniquities and, through God’s mercy, be converted to a good life.

For the present, the good ought to be separated from the wicked within the Catholic Church only by the dissimilarity of their works, so that, although they share the divine sacraments with those who are criminal, they do not share their evil works. [Note: [Col. 0777] So the manuscripts. The printed editions read: “ought not to be separated except by.”]

At the end of the age, however, the good will also be separated bodily from the wicked, when Christ will come holding a winnowing fan in his hand, will thoroughly cleanse his threshing floor, and will gather his wheat into the granary [Note: [Col. 0777] So the Corbie manuscript. Lovaniensis reads: “the wheat into his granary”], but will burn the chaff with unquenchable fire (Matt. 3:12).

Then by a just judgment he will separate the righteous from the unjust, the good from the evil, the upright from the perverse. He will place the good at his right hand and the wicked at his left; and from his mouth will proceed the sentence of eternal and unchangeable judgment: all the unrighteous will go into eternal burning, but the righteous into eternal life (Matt. 25:45). The unrighteous will burn forever with the devil, but the righteous will reign without end with Christ.

### CHAPTER XLIV

### 87. Perseverance in the Faith

Believe faithfully, hold firmly, and defend truly and patiently these forty chapters, which in the strongest manner pertain to the rule of the true faith. If you discover anyone teaching doctrines contrary to them, flee from him as from a plague and reject him as a heretic.

For the things we have set forth agree so closely with the Catholic faith that if anyone wishes to oppose not only all of them but even individual points, then, in the matter in which he obstinately resists any one of these and does not hesitate to teach what is contrary to it, he will appear a heretic and an enemy of the Christian faith [Col. 0778], and therefore is to be anathematized by all Catholics. [Note: [Col. 0778] So the Corbie manuscript and the older manuscripts. Lovaniensis reads “to be placed under anathema.”]

Although, therefore, both the pressure of time and the haste of the bearer compelled us to pass over in silence certain matters that ought to have been inserted for recognizing and avoiding various heresies, nevertheless, if you do not neglect to review and regard as thoroughly known everything contained in this little work, you will be able, with prudent discernment, to judge specifically even concerning the remaining matters.

For the Apostle says that “the spiritual person judges all things” (1 Cor. 2:15). Until each of us reaches this point, let each walk in what he has attained—that is, let him persevere faithfully in what he has certainly received. “And if you think otherwise about anything, God will reveal this also to you” (Phil. 3:15). Amen. [Note: [Col. 0778] Here the work ends in the manuscripts. What follows does not belong to Fulgentius and is absent from the better manuscripts, indeed from all the old books that we have seen.]

### CHAPTER XLV

### 1. Another Rule

The true and firm foundation of faith is principally to believe that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are by nature one God: so that we believe the only-begotten Son to have been truly born from the nature of the Father, and the Holy Spirit to proceed truly and naturally from the Father and the Son. We should also believe that the holy Trinity itself is one, alone, true, eternal, and unchangeable God.

It is also fitting for salvation to believe that one person of the Trinity—that is, God the Only-Begotten—became completely human for our salvation; and that this same one is true God and true human being. According to his divinity, he has one nature with the Father and the Holy Spirit; according to his humanity, Christ’s rational soul is of the same nature as the souls of all human beings, and Christ’s flesh is of the nature of all those who derive their origin from the first human being.

Therefore neither Christ’s soul nor his flesh is of one and the same nature with his divinity, because according to his humanity he was truly created. But just as his divinity shares the divine nature with the Father and the Holy Spirit, so his soul and body naturally share a communion with our souls and bodies.

By his divinity he freely rescued the flesh and soul of those who believe in him both from the dominion of sin and from the punishment of eternal death, by taking away sin.

### 2.

Strengthened by this belief, do not forget to implore divine mercy day and night, beseeching the blessed hope of all who believe in him, who is Christ the Lord, to hold firmly to the truth of this faith and preserve it inviolate.

For the Holy Spirit supplies abundant help to the faithful who pray to him, as the Prophet says: “The Lord is near to all who call upon him in truth. He will do the will of those who fear him, and he will hear their prayers and save them. The Lord guards all who love him, but he will destroy all sinners” (Ps. 144:18–20).

And again he says to God himself: “Behold, all who depart far from you will perish; you have destroyed all who commit fornication away from you.” But of himself he says: “For me, it is good to cling to God, to place my hope in the Lord” (Ps. 72:27–28).

### 3.

Therefore cling to God, dearest son, and place your hope in him with your whole heart, in faith and charity.

In the service of the world, render faithful service to the earthly king, because God loves this and the Apostle commands it. But in the cause of faith, through which Christ redeemed us in his blood, let all fear depart from our hearts.

We owe our souls to him by whose blood we were redeemed. We ought to love above all the one whom we know to be the most merciful Redeemer of our souls. We ought above all to fear the eternal and true power of the one whom we hope will come as the most just judge. We ought to desire with the whole affection of our hearts his promises, for he can grant eternal life to soul and body.

We ought to fear the anger of the one who can cast soul and body into Gehenna; in whose judgment, without respect of persons and without the influence of power, masters and servants, kings and soldiers, rich and poor, humble and exalted will be judged equally.

There, every servant who has kept the faith of God in truth here will possess an eternal kingdom; but the unfaithful master will be consumed by everlasting fire. There the life of faithful servants and masters will neither end nor their joy cease; but of the unfaithful, whether servants or masters, according to the truth of the prophetic word, “their fire will not be quenched, and their worm will not die” (Isa. 66:24).

For the unrighteous will go into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels.

### 4.

Let us consider whom the Savior declared would go there: surely those to whom he will say:

“I was hungry, and you did not give me food; I was thirsty, and you did not give me drink; I was naked, and you did not clothe me; I was a stranger, and you did not receive me; I was sick and in prison, and you did not come to me” (Matt. 25:41–43).

If the one who did not give bread to Christ, hungry in his least ones, will rightly be sent into eternal fire, what will happen to the one who, through the vice of unbelief, deprives himself of that very bread which came down from heaven?

And if the one who did not give Christ, thirsty in his least ones, a cup of cold water will be burned in everlasting flames, what will that person suffer who, having been reborn from water and the Holy Spirit, allows holy Baptism [Col. 0780] to be repeated in him, although he received it once for salvation and as the sacrament of holy regeneration?

And if we believe that the one who neglects to welcome Christ, a stranger in his least ones, with charitable hospitality is to be subjected to everlasting torments, what will the person think he will suffer who, excluding the Lord Christ from the house of his heart and receiving the devil into himself in utterly blind unbelief, departs from the holy Church—which is “the pillar and foundation of the truth” (1 Tim. 3:15)—having been surrounded by heretical falsehood?

And if the one who does not visit Christ’s servants who are sick and imprisoned is assigned to everlasting fire, what shall we say is owed to those who violently afflict God’s servants, in whom they persecute only the truth of the faith, whether through the squalor of prisons or through exile and deportation?

Yet in all these matters, although unbelievers rage, God supplies help to his own. While the enemies of the faith seek to corrupt each person either by cunning seduction or by violent compulsion, Christ, who is the Power and Wisdom of God, grants strength, so that they may despise the promises of deadly persuasion and withstand human terrors with the strength of divine fear.

The only requirement is that the will not be turned away from God and that it obtain the reward of faith. For it is the will itself for which either eternal punishment is inflicted because of unbelief or everlasting joy becomes the reward of preserved faith.

## [ON THE SPIRIT AND THE SOUL]

[Col. 0779]

## NOTICE CONCERNING THE BOOK *ON THE SPIRIT AND THE SOUL*

This work, as Erasmus correctly judged, is the product of a man of varied and extensive reading. In it one sees not so much art or ingenuity as, so to speak, sand without lime: merely sayings and excerpts copied from different sources, namely from Augustine, Gennadius, Boethius, Cassiodorus, Isidore of Seville, Bede, Alcuin, Hugh of Saint Victor, Bernard, Isaac, abbot of Stella, and others.

The abbot Johannes Trithemius lists this book in his catalogue of the writings of Hugh of Saint Victor. Vincent of Beauvais cites it under the same name throughout *The Natural Mirror*, books 23 and 25, and in book 24, chapter 1, and book 27, chapter 73. Moreover, in *The Historical Mirror*, book 18, chapter 55, where he observed that this little work does not at all exhibit the style of Augustine, to whom some attributed it, he says that it seems to him to have been excerpted from Augustine’s books, with Master Hugh of Saint Victor reported as its author.

Finally, it is included among the published minor works of Hugh, where it is the second book *On the Soul*, prefaced in a Victorine manuscript with his name. Nevertheless, the numerous excerpts found in it from Hugh’s own books, together with the significant alteration of their statements, compel us to seek another author for the work.

Thomas Aquinas, in his single question *On the Soul*, article 12, response to objection 1, attributes it to an anonymous member of the Cistercian order. We suspect that this was Alcher, to whom his intimate friend Isaac, abbot of Stella and a member of the Cistercian family, wrote a letter *On the Soul*. Alcher had apparently asked him to teach him more about the essence and powers of the soul, having heard him discuss this subject at a conference.

Indeed, in volume 6 of the Cistercian library, immediately after the aforementioned letter, this book *On the Spirit and the Soul* is printed with the following inscription: “The book of the same blessed Isaac, abbot of Stella, or, as he himself preferred it to be entitled, Alcher’s book *On the Soul*.” The latter part of this inscription will rightly seem true, while the former is false, especially because most of Abbot Isaac’s letter has been inserted into this book by the compiler.

Furthermore, Alcher is read in Possevinus, under Isaac, to have been a monk of Clairvaux: a man eager for learning and distinguished in natural philosophy, as Isaac himself testifies in the aforementioned letter to Alcher.

We have collated the work with four Roman manuscripts of the Vatican Library, with one from the abbey of Saint-Médard at Soissons, and with the Victorine, Sorbonic, and other manuscripts.

[Col. 0779]

# ONE BOOK ON THE SPIRIT AND THE SOUL (C, G, S)*

## PREFACE
[Note: *On the Quantity of the Soul*, chapters 14 and 28. Here and in the chapters that follow, we have indicated before the chapters themselves the books from which the passages are drawn—passages which sometimes constitute the whole sequence of a chapter and sometimes are interwoven with the author’s own statements. M.]

Since I have been told to know myself, I cannot endure remaining unknown to myself. For it is a great negligence not to know what that is by which we think so deeply about heavenly things, [Col. 0780] investigate natural things with such subtle inquiry, and desire to know such sublime truths about our Creator himself. It is not something foreign, nor is it to be sought far away: it is the mind by which we understand these things. But it is always with us, [Col. 0781] present, handling matters, speaking, and moving within us [Note: [Col. 0781] Two Vatican manuscripts read “and among these it is unknown.”]. It has been granted to the mind to know the secrets of such immense things, yet it cannot know itself. Indeed, only a few are permitted to behold the mind by the mind itself—that is, for the mind itself to see itself. Yet by a certain divine providence it cannot happen that the capacity for discovering themselves and their God should be lacking to religious minds that seek them piously, chastely, and diligently. Therefore I shall restore myself to myself—or rather to my God, to whom I owe myself above all—and I shall see what the mind is and what its homeland is.

## CHAPTER ONE. What the Mind Is. Reason. Reasoning.

[Note: *On the Quantity of the Soul*, chapters 13 and 27; and Hugh of Saint-Victor, book 1 of *The Didaskalion*, chapter 2.]

The mind is a certain substance endowed with reason and suited to govern the body. The mind illumined by wisdom looks back to its own origin, knows itself, and understands how unbecoming it is to seek outside itself what it can find within itself. But when lulled to sleep by bodily passions and carried outside itself by sensible forms, it has forgotten what it was. And because it remembers having been nothing else, it believes itself to be nothing other than what it appears to be. It occupies itself solely with the senses in relation to bodies and with imagination in relation to the likenesses of bodies and places; and in these it is distracted, whether awake or asleep [Note: [Col. 0781] The Medardus manuscript reads “wanders.”]. But when, rising from this distraction through pure understanding, it gathers itself into unity, it is called rational. For reason is the mind’s mode of seeing, by which it beholds truth through itself. Reasoning, however, is the inquiry of reason. Thus the former is needed for seeing, the latter for investigating.

## CHAPTER TWO. The Mind Understands Itself. [Note: [Col. 0781] Augustine, on Psalm 41, no. 7.]

The mind is invisible. For it could not otherwise perceive invisible things. Through the body it sees visible things; through itself it sees invisible things, and in this it sees itself: that it sees itself to be invisible. Yet it is seen in the body through the body, just as the sense remains in a letter and is seen through the letter. The mind, ruler, governor, and inhabitant of the body, sees itself through itself: through itself it sees itself. It does not seek the assistance of bodily eyes; rather, it withdraws from all the senses of the body, as from obstacles and disturbances, toward itself, so that it may see itself in itself and know itself with itself. And when it wishes to know God, it raises itself above itself by the mind’s sharp vision. For God is not such as the mind is; yet he cannot be seen except by the mind, nor can he be seen in the way the mind can see. For truth is unchangeable, without any defect in substance. The mind is not such: it fails and progresses, knows and is ignorant, remembers and forgets; sometimes it wills, sometimes it does not will. Scattered among thoughts and plans, it wanders here and there; it considers and observes all things. It sees what is absent; with its sight it encompasses things overseas and traverses them in its vision; it searches out hidden things. In a single moment it carries its senses through the boundaries of the whole world and the secrets of the universe. It descends to the underworld and rises from there; it moves through heaven, clings to Christ, and is joined to God. For God himself is its homeland and dwelling, in whose likeness it was made. Therefore whoever desires to be restored to what he was made by God to be—that is, to be made like God—should return to himself, remain within himself, and thus seek within himself and see of what the human being consists, and from which part of himself he was made in the image of God.

## CHAPTER THREE. Of What the Human Being Consists. [Note: [Col. 0781] From Gennadius, *On the Dogmas of the Church*.]

The human being consists of two substances, soul and flesh: soul with reason, flesh with its senses. Yet the flesh does not move these senses without the soul’s partnership, whereas the soul retains its rational faculty without the flesh.

## CHAPTER FOUR. The Powers of the Soul. Four Affections. Four Virtues. Five Powers of the Mind. [Note: [Col. 0781] From Isaac of Stella, letter to Alcher.]

The soul is rational, concupiscible, and irascible. Through rationality it is capable of being enlightened so as to know something beneath itself and above itself, within itself and beside itself. It knows God above itself, itself within itself, the angel beside itself, and whatever is contained within the circuit of heaven beneath itself. Through concupiscence and irascibility it is capable of being affected toward seeking or avoiding, loving or hating something. Therefore every perception of the soul arises from rationality, while every affection arises from the other faculties.

Affection is recognized as fourfold: when we already rejoice in what we love, or hope to rejoice in it; and when we already grieve over what we hate, or fear that we shall grieve over it. Thus joy and hope arise from concupiscence, while grief and fear arise from irascibility. These four affections of the soul are, as it were, the principles and common material of all vices and virtues. For affection gives its name to an act. And since virtue is a habit of a well-ordered mind, the affections of the mind must be composed, formed, and ordered toward what they ought to desire and in the way they ought to desire it, so that they may advance into virtues; otherwise they will easily decline into vices.

Therefore, when love and hatred are formed prudently, temperately, courageously, and justly, they rise into the virtues—namely prudence, temperance, fortitude, and justice—which are, as it were, the origins and hinges of all virtues. And when all these things are established in the soul with affection and virtue [Note: [Col. 0782] The manuscripts read “are formed.”], through hatred of the world and of itself the soul advances into love of God and neighbor; through contempt for temporal and inferior things it grows in desire for eternal and higher things.

There is one sense in the soul, and it is what the soul itself is; and although it is not a body, it is called corporeal because it does not transcend the body, or because it is exercised through bodily instruments. Hence, on account of the number of its instruments, it is said to be fivefold, although inwardly it is only one. Nevertheless, because of its various exercises it varies and receives various names. It is called sense, imagination, reason, intellect, and intelligence. All these in the soul are nothing other than the soul itself: different properties among themselves because of different exercises, but one essence of reason and one soul. The properties are diverse, but the essence is one. According to their exercises they are many; according to their essence they are one and the same in the soul and are the soul itself.

And just as this visible world is ordered by a certain fivefold distinction—namely earth, water, air, and ether or the firmament, together with the highest heaven, which they call the empyrean—so the soul, wandering as a pilgrim through the world of its body, has five advances toward wisdom: sense, imagination, reason, intellect, and intelligence. For through five advances rationality is exercised toward wisdom, and through four affections toward charity, so that by these nine advances the soul, progressing within itself through sense and affection, may walk by fourfold feet, as it lives by the spirit, all the way to the Cherubim and Seraphim—that is, to the fullness of knowledge and the kingdom [Note: [Col. 0782] Isaac has “the pyre,” apparently an erroneous reading for “kingdom.”] of charity—and may possess through exercise the virtues whose capacities it possesses by nature.

## CHAPTER FIVE. The Comparison of the Soul’s Virtues with the Choirs of Angels. [Note: [Col. 0782] From Isaac of Stella, letter to Alcher.]

I leave it to the prudent reader to compare these advances with the names and orders of the angels. It will easily be done if he knows how to adapt sense—which is the soul’s first messenger—to the Angels, who are called messengers; imagination to the Archangels, since it perceives more than sense; fear to the Virtues; and grief to the Powers. For one who is terrified by fear of punishments and pierced with grief over sins, and who despises the world and himself, performs miracles with the Virtues and drives out demons with the Powers. For it is greater to despise oneself than the world, which many have despised because of its vanity.

We assign reason to the Principalities. For just as they rule and govern subordinate spirits, so reason governs the senses and affections. We assign love of neighbor, or joy, to the Dominions: those who love everyone and rejoice in everyone’s progress rightly rule over others. We assign intellect to the Thrones. Thrones are called seats because God sits in them. You must also understand that God dwells in our hearts through faith (Ephesians 3:17), through sanctification, through peace, and through love, because God is a God of peace and love (2 Corinthians 13:11).

We assign intelligence to the Cherubim. For those spirits are filled with knowledge all the more perfect because they contemplate God’s divinity in the innermost depths. Intelligence is the power of the soul that is immediately subject to God: it sees him himself and the things that are in him. We assign hope, desire, or love of God to the Seraphim. For God is the hope of all the ends of the earth (Psalm 64:3), whose face the whole earth desires; and he whom the Seraphim desire to behold is our whole hope and desire.

Hatred of the world belongs to the Virtues; hatred of oneself to the Powers; reason to the Principalities; love of neighbor to the Dominions; intellect to the Thrones; intelligence to the Cherubim; love of God to the Seraphim. Fear of punishments and grief over sins produce contempt for the world and for oneself, so that with the Virtues they perform miracles and with the Powers expel demons. Hope in the promises and joy over the rewards produce love of neighbor and of God.

## CHAPTER SIX. From Whom the Traces of the Trinity in the Soul Derive. [Note: [Col. 0783] From Isaac of Stella, letter to Alcher; and from the *Manual*, chapter 26.]

The soul, made in the likeness of all wisdom, bears within itself the likeness of all things. Hence it was defined by a philosopher as “the likeness of all things.” For it possesses within itself powers by which it apprehends everything, or investigates everything, and it exists as the likeness of everything, although it is one. It is like earth through sense, like water through imagination, like air through reason, like the firmament through intellect, and like the heaven of heavens through intelligence. It is like stones through essence, like trees through life, like animals through sense and imagination, like human beings through reason, like angels through intellect, and like God through intelligence.

And just as God can be apprehended and participated in by all things, so the soul is capable of all things. God can be apprehended and participated in by all things because, through his natural gift—that is, the Holy Spirit—and through the use that proceeds from the gift of grace, he is participated in by all things according to the essence by which they exist; according to that essence, in the suitable form by which they differ from others; and according to both, in the fitting use by which they advance. These three are present in every existing human being as certain traces of the highest essence, image, and gift—that is, of the Trinity of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Eternity is in the Father, form in the image, and use in the gift [Note: [Col. 0783] The printed editions omit this sentence, from the word “Eternity” through the word “gift.”].

[Note: [Col. 0783] From Augustine, book 6 of *On the Trinity*, no. 11.]

Eternity is in the Father [Note: [Col. 0783] Lovaniensis reads “being.”], because the Father does not have a father from whom he derives his being. The Son derives being from the Father, and from him also derives coeternity with the Father. For if an image perfectly fulfills that of which it is the image, it is coequal with it.

Form is in the image—that is, beauty, proportion, equality, the first and highest likeness, the first and highest life, and the first and highest intellect. Use is in the gift. The gift of the Father and Son is the Holy Spirit. Therefore use is in the gift—that is, delight, joy, gladness, happiness, and sweetness. For that ineffable union of the Father and the Image is not without perfection, charity, or joy. Thus in that highest Trinity there is the highest origin of all things, the most perfect beauty, and the most blessed love [Note: [Col. 0783] Some manuscripts read “delight.”]. For us, however, every use of divinity comes from the gift.

In a certain way the Holy Spirit seems to be nearer to us, as the gift of the Father and Son. From him, together with the Father and Son, comes every use of grace. For he governs and instructs, consoles and leads the Church to Christ; and he himself will present her, without spot or wrinkle (Ephesians 5:27), to God and the Father as his kingdom (1 Corinthians 15:24).

Thus from the Father, through the Son and the Holy Spirit—or rather, in the Holy Spirit—divine things have descended to us. The Father gave his Son to redeem servants; he sent the Holy Spirit to adopt servants as sons. He gave the Son as the price of redemption, the Holy Spirit as the privilege of adoption, and finally keeps himself wholly as an inheritance for those whom he has adopted.

Therefore let no one distrust God’s mercy, for his mercy is greater than our misery; and whoever cries out to him with all his heart, he will hear, because he is merciful. For it seems to the sinner that God is slower to grant forgiveness than the sinner is to receive it. Thus he hastens to release the guilty person from the torment of his conscience, as though compassion for the miserable person tormented him more than compassion for himself torments the miserable person.

## CHAPTER SEVEN. The Soul Is Capable of All Things. [Note: [Col. 0784] Isaac of Stella.]

The soul is capable of all things because through rationality it is found capable of knowing the whole universe, and through concupiscence of loving it. For there are two things in the soul, and these are what the soul is: natural sense, which knows everything and judges among all things; and natural affection, by which the soul loves everything according to its proper order and degree.

Nevertheless, it possesses by nature the capacities and, as it were, instruments for knowing and loving; but it possesses neither knowledge of truth nor the order of love except from grace. For when the rational mind was made by God, it received knowledge and love just as it received his image. The vessels that creative Wisdom forms so that they may exist, assisting grace fills so that they may not be empty, if it finds a diligent worker.

## CHAPTER EIGHT. What the Soul Is Again.

The soul is a rational and intellectual substance, made spiritual by God—not from God’s nature, but rather a creature made from nothing—capable of turning toward good or evil. Therefore it is mortal in some respect, insofar as it can be changed for the worse and alienated from the will of God, by participation in whom it becomes good; and it is immortal in some respect, since it cannot lose the awareness by which it will fare well or badly after this life.

This is not because it earned, through deeds performed before entering the flesh, to be enclosed in the flesh, as some have wished to claim. Nor, for that reason, can it exist in a human being without the stain of sin unless it has been liberated by Christ. For by God’s command the soul comes to the body, so that if it wishes to act according to his command, it may receive the reward of eternal life and fellowship with the angels; but if it despises him, it may suffer the most just and bitter punishments, whether continuous anguish or eternal fire.

## CHAPTER NINE. The Human Being’s Twofold Sense. [Note: [Col. 0784] From Gennadius, *On the Ecclesiastical Dogmas*, chapter 19; from Hugh of Saint-Victor on Luke 1, verse 47; and from the *Manual*, chapter 26.]

The soul is so called because it animates the body for living—that is, because it gives it life. It is called spirit because of its spiritual nature, or because it breathes into the body. Soul and spirit are the same in a human being, although “spirit” signifies one thing and “soul” another. Spirit refers to substance, while soul refers to animation. The essence is the same, but the property is different. For one and the same spirit is called spirit in relation to itself and soul in relation to the body.

It is spirit insofar as it is a rational substance endowed with reason; it is soul insofar as it is the life of the body, of which it was said: “Whoever loses his soul for my sake will save it” (Luke 9:24)—that is, whoever willingly despises, for God’s sake, this present life, which is temporally mortal because it is constituted by the soul’s animation of the body, will in the future receive that same life of the body—and not merely of the soul—eternal and immortal [Note: [Col. 0784] The manuscripts read “and immortal.”].

The human soul, because it exists in the body and outside the body, can equally be called soul and spirit. There are not two souls, one sensual and the other rational, one by which the human being lives and another by which, as some suppose, he understands; rather, there is one and the same soul, which lives in itself through intellect and gives life to the body through sense.

For the human body can neither live nor be born without a rational soul. Yet before it receives a rational soul, it is nourished, moved, and grows, and receives human form in the womb. In the same way we see shrubs and herbs move and grow without a soul [Note: [Col. 0785] The Medardus manuscript adds “that is, a rational soul.”].

The soul’s life is twofold: one by which it lives in the flesh, and another by which it lives in God. There are likewise two senses in the human being, one interior and one exterior, and each has its own good in which it is restored. The interior sense is restored in contemplation of divinity; the exterior sense in contemplation of humanity.

For this reason God became human: so that he might bless the whole human being in himself, so that the whole human conversion might be toward him, and so that all human love might be in him, since he is seen by the sense of the flesh through the flesh and by the sense of the mind through contemplation of divinity.

This was the whole good of the human being: whether entering or departing, to find pastures in his Creator (John 10:9)—pastures outside, in the flesh of the Savior, and pastures within, in the divinity of the Creator.

This great good was followed by evil. For when the good that was within was lost, the soul went out toward alien goods that were outside, and made a pact with the delights of the world, resting upon them and paying no attention to the absence of its inner good, because it saw its consolations in alien goods.

For when the exterior, carnal sense uses its own good, the interior sense of the mind seems to fall asleep. It does not recognize the goods of the interior sense because it is captivated by the pleasantness of exterior goods. For one who lives in the flesh senses in the flesh and flees the pains of the flesh insofar as he can, but is wholly ignorant of the wounds of the soul and seeks no medicine for them.

When, however, the sense of the soul by which it lives in the flesh has died, that sense by which it senses itself will begin to be made alive. Then it will know its pains and begin to feel its wounds, all the more grievously because they are nearer. For evil that is nearer does greater harm, and good that is more inward does greater good.

## CHAPTER TEN. The Spirit. [Note: [Col. 0785] From book 12 of *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, chapters 7 and 23; from book 1 of the *Soliloquies*, chapter 6, numbers 12 and 13; and from Hugh, *On the Sacrament of Faith*, part 6, chapter 2.]

“Spirit” is said in many ways. God is called Spirit, as are this air and the breath of air which, received by the heart and sent from there through the whole body, sustains the life of mortals by necessary breathing. Yet this spirit cannot properly be called soul, because it is dissolved by variations of the air [Note: [Col. 0785] Some manuscripts read “of life.”].

The soul, whether human or animal, is called spirit. The rational mind is called spirit, where there is a certain spark, as it were the eye of the soul, to which the image [Note: [Col. 0785] The printed editions read “imagination.”] and knowledge of God belong.

The eye of the soul is the mind pure from every stain of the body; the mind’s mode of seeing is reason; vision is intellect. These three are necessary for every soul: that it have healthy eyes, that it look, and that it see. It has healthy eyes when it has been cleansed and removed from the desires of mortals. It looks when it fixes the eyes of contemplation upon God’s light. It sees when, in that contemplation, it perceives how great are the joys, how great the gladness, how great the security, how great the serenity, and how great the delight.

Health makes it secure, looking makes it upright, and vision makes it blessed. For when it has been freed from every impurity and washed clean from stains, then at last it holds itself within itself most willingly [Note: [Col. 0785] The printed editions read “holds itself most freely.”], fears nothing for itself, and is not troubled by any fault of its own. Then, with immense and incredible confidence, it proceeds toward God—that is, toward the contemplation of truth itself. For the vision of God, which is the goal of looking, follows an upright act of seeing.

Thus the soul is first healed; once healed, it is led inside; once led inside, it is restored [Note: [Col. 0785] The Medardus manuscript adds “namely, through wisdom.”].

Spirit is also a certain power of the soul, lower than the mind, in which the likenesses of bodily things are represented. Nor is this spirit itself a body, but it is like a body. For the things seen through the spirit are not bodily, but similar to bodily things.

The face of a human being is known to us externally, and it has its own image in our memory—incorporeal, certainly, but similar to a body. The marvelous beauty of this world is likewise present to us outside, and it has its own image in our memory—incorporeal, certainly, but similar to a body—which we return to when we think of it with our eyes closed.

What a body in a place is in relation to bodily sense, the likeness of a body in memory is in relation to the mind’s vision. And what the intention of the will is in relation to joining a body that is seen to the act of seeing, that same intention of the will is in relation to joining the image of the body, which exists in memory, to the vision of the one who thinks.

That spirit is said to have been made in the image and likeness of God in which there is knowledge of truth and love of virtue. The image is in knowledge, and likeness is in love: image because it is rational, likeness because it is spiritual. For it clings to truth without any intervening substance.

We call our rational faculty, by which we reason, understand, and comprehend, spirit [Note: [Col. 0786] Some manuscripts read “But our rational faculty.”]. The Apostle calls this spirit “mind” when he says, “Be renewed in the spirit of your mind” (Ephesians 4:23)—that is, in the mind; for the spirit of the mind is nothing other than the mind, just as the body of the flesh is nothing other than flesh.

## CHAPTER ELEVEN. Whence the Mind Is Named. Sense and Imagination Differ. The Dimension of the Soul. Wisdom. Prudence. [Note: [Col. 0786] From Cassiodorus, *On the Soul*, chapters 1 and 7; Isaac of Stella; from Hugh’s *On the Union of Body and Spirit*; and from *Micellanum*, book 1, title 159.]

The mind is said to derive its name from μήνη (*mēnē*). Greek μήνη is called *luna*—“moon”—in Latin. And just as the moon waxes and wanes and changes through varying alternation, yet restores itself by a certain perfect renewal to what it was, so the mind sometimes inserts its head among the highest things, sometimes falls into the lowest, sometimes bringing itself back to itself [Note: [Col. 0786] The printed editions read “bringing in.”], refutes falsehoods with truths. At one time it bends down to govern bodily things; at another it clings to the examination or consultation of eternal principles.

Reason is the mind’s mode of seeing, by which it distinguishes good from evil, chooses virtues, and loves God. The mind, capable of all things and marked by the likeness of all things, is said to be all things by a certain natural power and natural dignity. Therefore through intelligence it comprehends the invisible causes of things, and through the passions of the senses it gathers the visible actual forms of things.

Whether it goes out through the senses toward sensible things or rises through intelligence toward invisible things, it draws the likenesses of things back to itself. It knows what is present, understands what is absent, investigates what is unknown, and occupies itself with what it has discovered.

We call rational and intellectual light—the light by which we reason, understand, and comprehend—the mind. It was made in the image of God in such a way that it is formed by the truth itself without any intervening nature. The mind is so called because it stands out in the soul. For it is the soul’s more excellent power, from which intelligence proceeds. Through intelligence it understands truth itself; through wisdom it loves it.

Wisdom is love of the good, or taste of the good; indeed, it is called wisdom from “savor” or “taste.” The vision of the mind is intelligence; its taste is wisdom. The former contemplates; the latter delights.

When we wish to ascend from lower things to higher things, sense first meets us, then imagination, then reason, intellect, and intelligence; and at the summit is wisdom. For the highest wisdom is God himself. Human wisdom is piety, that is, worship of God.

Sense is that power of the soul which perceives the bodily forms of bodily things present [Note: [Col. 0786] Here and shortly afterward, the printed editions read “receives.”]. Imagination is that power of the soul which perceives the bodily forms of bodily things that are absent. Sense perceives forms in matter; imagination perceives them outside matter. The power that, when formed externally, is called sense is called imagination when carried inward to the innermost part.

For imagination arises from sense, and its variation corresponds to the variations of sense. The soul sees many things with bodily eyes and conceives many things through phantasmal imagination. Everywhere it seems to spread itself, move, rise, and fluctuate [Note: [Col. 0787] The manuscripts read “is extended.”]. It does not go outside itself; rather, it wanders within itself as through a great space. It does not go out to those things, but represents them to itself through its own processes.

It possesses within itself, as it were, breadth, length, and height. Through charity it embraces God and all the faithful; through meditation it meditates on all that God has done for our salvation from the beginning of the world to its end; through contemplation it contemplates the heavenly things above.

Reason is that power of the soul which perceives the natures, forms, differences, properties, and accidents of bodily things: all of these are incorporeal, but do not subsist outside bodies except through reason. For it abstracts from bodies those things that are grounded in bodies—not through action, but through consideration. The nature of body itself, insofar as every body is body, is certainly not any particular body.

Intellect is that power of the soul which perceives invisible things, such as angels, demons, souls, and every created spirit. Intelligence is that power of the soul which is immediately subject to God. For it beholds the highest truth itself, which is truly unchangeable.

Thus the soul perceives bodies through sense, the likenesses of bodies through imagination, the natures of bodies through reason, created spirit through intellect, and uncreated Spirit through intelligence.

Whatever sense perceives, imagination represents; thought forms; ingenuity investigates; reason judges; memory preserves; intellect separates; intelligence comprehends and leads it to meditation or contemplation.

Ingenuity is that power or intention of the soul by which the soul extends and exercises itself [Note: [Col. 0787] Elsewhere, “exerts” or “rouses itself.”] toward knowledge of the unknown. Ingenuity seeks out unknown things; reason distinguishes what has been discovered; memory stores away what has been judged and offers it again for judgment.

Thus an ascent is made from lower things to higher things, and the lowest depend upon the highest. Intellect is, as it were, an image and likeness of intelligence; reason is an image of intellect; and the phantasmal spirit is an image of reason. To this spirit even the highest body of the body—that is, fire—is joined by a certain likeness; air is joined to fire, water to air, and earth to water.

Sense informs imagination; imagination informs reason and makes knowledge or prudence. Again, divine prudence, meeting reason, informs it and makes intelligence or wisdom.

Thus in reason there is something directed toward heavenly and celestial things, and this is called wisdom; and there is something directed toward transient and perishable things, and this is called prudence. These two arise from reason and consist in reason.

Reason divides itself into two, namely upward and downward: upward into wisdom, downward into prudence, as into a man and a woman, so that the man may be superior and rule, and the woman inferior and ruled. Hence it was said: “Better is the iniquity of a man than a woman doing good” (Sirach 42:14). For the one inflamed by heavenly desire, who afflicts the flesh even by withholding what is necessary from it, is better than one loosened by carnal affection who strives to satisfy himself in everything that is comfortable for him.

## CHAPTER TWELVE. Sense and Its Work. [Note: [Col. 0787] From Isaac of Stella and Hugh on Luke 1, verse 47.]

Sense is assisted externally. For although the eye of the flesh has by nature the capacity for seeing, it never achieves vision by itself; nor does the ear achieve hearing except through the benefit of external light and sound.

Imagination is assisted externally [Note: [Col. 0787] In B: “Imagination is assisted from below.” We have followed Erasmus, Lyon, Venice, and Louvain. M.], because it is conceived from sensible things.

Reason is assisted internally. For although the rational spirit, by the Creator’s gift, is capable of knowing truth and loving good, unless it has been suffused by the ray of an interior light and kindled by its warmth, it never attains knowledge of wisdom or the affection of charity.

Intellect and intelligence are assisted from above, because God is fire and light (1 John 1:5). Light, therefore, sending forth from itself a radiance that it retains within itself, illuminates intelligence [Col. 0788] for knowledge of the truth. Fire, sending forth heat from itself without losing it, inflames affection toward love of virtue.

And just as the eye does not see the sun except in the sun’s light, so intelligence cannot see true and divine light except in that light itself. “Lord,” says the prophet, “in your light we shall see light” (Psalm 35:10).

When this mortal nature has put on immortality and this corruptible nature has put on incorruption (1 Corinthians 15:54), then, made spiritual in mind and body alike, we shall know all things according to our measure through the illumination of the mind, and through the lightness of an incorruptible body we shall be able to be everywhere. We shall fly in mind through contemplation and in body through incorruption. We shall discern with the mind and discern with the body, when our bodily senses are changed into reason, reason into intellect, intellect into intelligence, and intelligence into God [Note: [Col. 0788] Here the Medardus manuscript inserts these words: “Claudianus, on ‘number, weight, and measure’: Measure exists in the soul according to its capacity; number according to the number of its powers or virtues; weight according to its appetite for that toward which it is directed. And every rational soul subsists through three powers—memory, judgment, and will—by which it is capable of number, measure, and weight.”].

Visible things are perceived by sense. In imagination are contained the images and likenesses of visible things. To reason belong the principles and definitions of visible things and the investigations of invisible things. To intellect and intelligence belong the comprehensions and contemplations of spiritual and divine things.

Sense and imagination do not ascend to reason. Yet, remaining below it, they can in some measure lead it and, as it were from a distance, show certain things to which they cannot attain. In a similar proportion reason can assist intellect and intelligence, but it cannot ascend to their condition, because they have their own boundaries and proper limits, which it cannot transcend.

We share sense and imagination with the other animals. They see visible things and remember what they have seen. In certain senses they even surpass us, since it was just that brute animals, to whom nothing was to be given in intellect, should be given something more in sense. Conversely, the greater the deficiency suffered by our sensuality, the greater the necessity imposed upon the human being to exercise reason.

Reason begins where something occurs that we do not share with animals. Some things, therefore, are beneath reason, some alongside reason, and some above reason.

Beneath reason are the things we perceive through sense, such as hard and soft, hot and cold, white and black, sweet and bitter. Alongside reason, and accessible to reason, are the things we perceive through reason, such as advantageous and disadvantageous, true and false, just and unjust.

Reason is a certain movement of the mind, sharpening its vision [Note: [Col. 0788] Some manuscripts read “sense.”] and distinguishing truths from falsehoods.

Above reason are those things that neither sense teaches nor reason persuades, but which are either grasped through divine revelation or believed on the authority of the divine Scriptures—for example, that God is three in one substance and substantially one in three persons.

For God is the universe of things, in such a way that he is none of the individual things. Therefore he is not subject to the movements of reason, since reason concerns only some particular thing.

## CHAPTER THIRTEEN. The Definition of the Soul. Its Actions. Its Simplicity. Its Powers. Its Faculties. [Note: [Col. 0788] Alcuin, *On the Reason of the Soul*; Hugh, *The Didaskalion*, book 2, chapter 5; and Isaac of Stella.]

The soul is an intellectual spirit, rational, ever-living, ever in motion, capable of both good and evil willing. According to the Creator’s benevolence and according to the function of its activity, it is called by various names. It is called “soul” (*anima*) when it gives life; “spirit” (*spiritus*) when it contemplates; “sense” (*sensus*) when it perceives; “spirit” or “mind” (*animus*) when it is wise; “mind” (*mens*) when it understands; “reason” (*ratio*) when it distinguishes; “memory” (*memoria*) when it remembers; and “will” (*voluntas*) when it consents. Yet these do not differ in substance as they do in name, for all these are one soul: the properties are indeed diverse, but the essence is one.

There can nevertheless be a distinction between spirit and soul, because every soul is a spirit, but not every spirit is a soul. The soul’s activities are of two kinds. For by one disposition it is raised toward God, and by another it is inclined toward the flesh. It is inclined in the following way. Since it is subtle and invisible, it cannot be seen, but through its powers it extends and manifests itself. Through desire (*concupiscibility*) it seeks; through irascibility it rejects or despises; through rationality it distinguishes between the two. The whole essence of the soul consists in these powers of its own, and it is not divided into parts, since it is simple and indivisible. If it is sometimes said to have parts, this is to be understood as a matter of likeness rather than of actual composition.

The soul is a simple substance. Reason is neither another thing nor anything less in substance than the soul; nor are irascibility and concupiscibility either other than, or less than, the soul. Rather, one and the same substance receives different names according to its different powers. It possesses these powers before it is joined to the body. They are natural to it, and are nothing other than the soul itself. For the whole substance of the soul consists fully and perfectly in these three, namely, rationality, concupiscibility, and irascibility, as in a kind of trinity of its own. This entire trinity is a certain unity of the soul, and is itself the soul.

God is all that is his, and the soul is in a certain sense all that is its own. It possesses natural properties, and is all of them. Its powers and strengths are therefore identical with itself. It possesses accidental properties, and is not those properties. It is its own powers, but it is not its own virtues. For it is not its prudence, temperance, fortitude, or justice. The powers of the soul are rationality, concupiscibility, and irascibility. Its strengths are sense, imagination, reason, memory, intellect, and intelligence. Yet the powers may also be called strengths, and the strengths powers.

## CHAPTER XIV. The friendship of soul and body. Three wondrous unions. What belongs to the body and what belongs to the soul.

[Note: [Col. 0789] Cassiodorus, *On the Soul*, chapters 4 and 5; Isaac of Stella, *De Alcherum* [title uncertain as printed]; Hugh, book 2 of the *Instructional Handbook*, chapter 5; the same, book 1 of *On the Sacraments*, part 6, chapters 3, 5, and 6; the same, *Miscellany*, book 1, titles 122 and 120; the same, *On the Vanity of the World*, book 2; and *On the Substance of Love*, chapter 6.]

By certain affections and by a certain friendship the soul is joined to the body. According to this friendship, no one hates his own flesh. Although associated with it and weighed down by its companionship, the soul nevertheless loves it by an ineffable condition. It loves its prison, and therefore cannot be free. It is deeply affected by the body’s pains. It fears destruction, although it cannot die. It fears decline, although by nature it cannot decline. It feeds upon the sight of the eyes, delights in melodious sounds, rejoices in the sweetest fragrances, and is refreshed by abundant feasting. Although it does not itself make use of these things in any way, it is nevertheless afflicted by deep sorrow if they are taken away.

Hence vices contrary to reason sometimes creep in, when the soul, by indulging its beloved body too freely, is known to provide an opportunity for sin. Through the senses also the soul advances toward moving and giving life to the body. For there are nine openings in the human body through which, according to a natural balance, everything by which that body is enlivened and governed flows in and out.

There are also certain likenesses between the two: namely, the body’s highest element and the spirit’s weakness. In these, without confusion of natures but by personal union, they can easily be joined together. For like things rejoice in like things. Thus the soul, which is truly spirit, and the flesh, which is truly body, are easily and suitably united at their extremities: that is, in the soul’s phantastic faculty, which is not body but is similar to body; and in the flesh’s sensuality, which is almost spirit [Note: [Col. 0789] Two manuscripts: “which is corporeal spirit.”].

For just as the highest part of the soul, namely intelligence or mind, bears the image and likeness of its superior, namely God—and therefore could be receptive of him and, even for personal union, was assumed when he himself willed it, without any alteration of nature—so the highest part of the flesh, namely sensuality, bearing a likeness to the soul, can receive its essence for personal union. Nor is this surprising, since even in the sense and memory of an animal there is a certain imitation of rationality, and in the appetite of its will, and in the things from which it recoils, an imitation of rejection.

The corporeal spirit, which is certainly truly body [Note: [Col. 0790] Two manuscripts: “which is certainly not of corporeal life.”], distinguishes many things by natural sense, chooses by the power of concupiscibility, and rejects by the nature of irascibility. Corporeal life possesses certain degrees of increase by which it advances toward the image of the highest life.

The first degree of corporeal life is sensation. The second is imagination, entering through sensation. The third is memory of what has been conceived, through imagination. The fourth is a certain foresight, according to the passions of the senses, without the discernment of intelligence—a foresight in which there is, as it were, an image of reason, but no reason. In all these respects corporeal life imitates spiritual life: first, in sensing; second, in conceiving what is sensed; third, in retaining what has been conceived; fourth, in bending itself, whether toward things imagined or toward sensations, according to a certain likeness of reason, either to pursue or to flee.

The most suitable intermediaries between flesh and soul are the sensuality of the flesh, which is most like fire, and the spirit’s phantastic faculty, which is called fiery vigor. Hence someone speaking of souls said:

> Fiery is their vigor, and heavenly their origin.  
> *(Virgil, Aeneid, book 6, verse 730.)*

Wondrous is the fellowship of flesh and soul, of the spirit of life and the clay of earth. For it is written: “God made man from the clay of the earth, and breathed into his face the breath of life” (Genesis 2:7). He gave him sense and understanding, so that through sense he might give life to the clay joined to him, and through understanding govern it; so that through understanding he might enter within and contemplate God’s wisdom, and through sense go outward and contemplate the works of wisdom. By understanding he enlightened him within; by sense he adorned him outwardly, so that in both he might find refreshment—within for happiness, outwardly for delight.

But because external goods cannot long endure, man was commanded to return from external things to interior things, and from interior things to ascend to higher things. For human nature is of such dignity that no good except the highest can suffice for it.

It was a great miracle that things so diverse and so divided from one another could be joined to one another. No less wondrous was it that God joined himself to our clay, so that God and clay might be united to one another—such sublimity, such lowliness. Nothing is more sublime than God, and nothing is more lowly than clay. The first union was wondrous; the second was wondrous also; and no less wondrous will be the third, when human being, angel, and God will be one spirit.

Man is good by the same good by which the angel is good, and both are blessed by the same good, provided that both desire that very thing with the same will and the same spirit. If God could join the natures of flesh and soul, so unequal to one another, in a single fellowship and friendship, it will certainly not be impossible for him to raise the rational spirit—which was humbled even to fellowship with an earthly body—together with that body glorified, so that what was once its burden may become its glory, to the fellowship of the blessed spirits who have remained in their purity, and to exalt it to participation in his own glory.

The Most High created it for this purpose by love alone, without any necessity: to make it a participant in his blessedness. If, therefore, there is so much joy and such delight in this temporal life, which consists in the presence of spirit within a corruptible body, how great will be the delight and how great the joy in eternal life, which will consist in the presence of the Godhead within a rational spirit?

Let the body therefore be subject to the mind, and the mind to God; and there will be one spirit with him—provided, however, that it remains in humility and acknowledges the grace of its Creator, through which it is to be exalted and glorified. [Col. 0791]

Man consists of flesh and soul, and each possesses its own good, in which it rejoices and exults. The good of the soul is God, together with the abundance of his sweetness. The good of the flesh is the world, together with the abundance of its delight.

But this world is external, whereas God is interior. Nothing is more interior than he, and nothing is more present. He is interior to every thing, because all things are in him; he is exterior to every thing, because he is above all things. Returning, then, from this world to God, and ascending as though from below upward, we must pass through ourselves.

For to ascend to God is to enter into oneself—and not merely to enter into oneself, but in an ineffable manner to pass beyond oneself in one’s inmost depths. Whoever, entering inwardly and penetrating within, transcends himself truly ascends to God.

Let us therefore gather our heart away from the distractions of this world and recall it to interior joys. And if we cannot always hold our heart firmly, let us at least restrain it from unlawful and empty thoughts, so that we may at some time be able to fix it in the light of divine contemplation.

This is the rest of our heart: when it is fixed by desire in the love of God. This is the life of our heart: when it contemplates its God and is sweetly refreshed by that very contemplation. It is sweet for the heart always to consider what is always delightful to love and praise.

For nothing seems more excellent for the blessed life than, as though the bodily senses were closed and one had become external to flesh and world, to turn inward upon oneself and, having become alien to the desires of mortals, speak only to oneself and to God.

## CHAPTER XV. The body governed by the soul. The composition of the body. What follows from its balance or disorder.

[Note: [Col. 0791] From book 7 of *On the Literal Interpretation of Genesis*, chapters 15 and 20; from *On the Greatness of the Soul*, chapter 31, no. 62; and from Isaac of Stella.]

Although the soul is incorporeal, it governs the body through the body’s subtler nature, namely fire and air, which in this world too are superior bodies and therefore more akin to spirit. These, being closer to incorporeal nature than moisture and earth, first receive the commands of the soul that gives life, so that the whole mass of the body may be administered through their immediate service.

Without these two, there is neither sensation in the body nor any spontaneous movement of the body by the soul. For fire and air, which are light, move water and earth, which are heavy. Therefore we see bodies move even after the soul’s departure, because fire and air—which, through the soul’s presence, are held within the earthly and moist body so that all four elements may be balanced—escape upward and release themselves after the soul’s departure.

The body is composed as follows. The body consists of functional members; the functional members of similar parts; the similar parts of humors; the humors of foods; and foods of the elements. None of these is the soul, but the soul acts in them as in instruments, and through them provides for the body and for this life in which man was made a living soul.

When these things are balanced and ordered, they are suited to the giving of life, and the soul does not depart. But if they become disordered and confused, the soul departs unwillingly, drawing everything with it: namely, sensation, imagination, reason, intellect, intelligence, concupiscibility, and irascibility. According to their merits it is affected by these toward delight or pain.

The body, which had previously been whole, like a balanced and arranged instrument designed to contain a musical melody and resound when touched, then lies broken and useless. When the elemental parts return to their own regions, the soul, having no place in which to exercise its powers, rests from those movements by which it moved the body through time and place, while itself having been moved through time without location.

For although the instrument has perished, the melody has not, nor has that which moved the instrument. The soul, placed between God and the body, is moved through time, either by remembering what it had forgotten, learning what it did not know, or willing what it did not will. It is not moved through place, because it is not extended through the intervals of space.

God [Note: [Col. 0792] The Medard manuscript adds here: “like the soul.”] does not need a body in order to exist; nor a place in order to be somewhere; nor time in order to be at some time; nor a cause in order to be from something; nor a form in order to be something; nor any kind of subject in which to subsist or beside which to stand. [Col. 0792]

## CHAPTER XVI. The excellence of the soul adorned with love.

[Note: [Col. 0792] *Manual*, chapter 21, and Hugh of Saint-Victor, *On the Praise of Charity*.]

The soul possesses a certain proper nature superior to all the elements of this worldly mass. It cannot truly be conceived through any imagination of bodily images that we perceive through the senses of the flesh; it must be understood by the mind and experienced through life. It can be understood, but it cannot be sensed.

For it is neither body nor God, nor life without sensation, such as exists in trees, nor life without a rational mind, such as exists in animals. Rather, it is life—and everlasting life. At present it is less than the angels, but it will be like the angels if it lives according to the command of its Creator. [Note: [Col. 0792] In the Medard manuscript and in Hugh: “Indeed, it is not less than the angels” (Hugh adds: “it is future”), “if it lives according to the command,” and so forth. See Alcuin, *On the Reason of the Soul*.]

His command is that we remain in his love: “Remain,” he says, “in my love” (John 15:9). Through love he joined the rational creature to himself, so that it might always possess him and remain in him, delighting, rejoicing, and exulting in him and from him.

Through love the rational creature is joined to its Creator and to itself. For the bond of love alone binds both together in unity. Through love of God we all cling to him; through love of neighbor we are all one with one another, so that the common good of all may become the possession of each, and what one person does not have in himself may be possessed in another.

Charity is God’s way to human beings, and the way of human beings to God. Through charity God came to human beings, came into human beings, and became man. Through charity human beings love God, choose God, run toward God, and reach God.

Charity is so familiar to God that he does not wish to dwell where charity is absent. If, therefore, we have charity, we have God, because God is charity.

## CHAPTER XVII. An exhortation to the love of God.

[Note: [Col. 0792] Anselm, *Meditations*, chapter 7, no. 2, and Hugh, *On the Soul’s Earnest* (*De Arrha Animae*).]

Wretched that I am, how greatly ought I to love my God, who made me when I did not exist and redeemed me when I was lost! I did not exist, and he made me from nothing—not a stone, not a tree, not a bird, nor any other animal, but he willed me to be a human being. He gave me life, sensation, and discernment.

I was lost, and he descended to mortality, assumed mortality, endured suffering, conquered death, and thus restored me. I was lost and had gone astray, for I had been sold into my sins. He came after me to redeem me, and he loved me so greatly that he offered the price of his blood for me. In this way he brought me back from exile and redeemed me from slavery.

He also called me by his own name, so that his memorial might always be with me. He anointed me with the oil of gladness with which he himself had been anointed, so that I might be anointed by the Anointed One and be called Christian from Christ.

Thus his grace and mercy always went before me. My Redeemer often rescued me from many dangers: when I was wandering, he led me back; when I was ignorant, he taught me; when I was sinning, he rebuked me; when I was sorrowful, he consoled me; when I was despairing, he strengthened me; when I fell, he raised me; when I stood, he upheld me; when I went, he guided me; when I came, he received me.

My God did these and many other things for me. It will always be sweet for me to speak of them, to think of them, and to give thanks, so that for all his benefits I may always be able to praise and love him.

Although he presides over all, fills all things, is present everywhere, cares for all, and provides for both individuals and the whole, I see him wholly occupied with guarding me, as though I myself stood above my own protection—as though he had forgotten everyone else and wished to attend to me alone.

For he always shows himself present and always offers himself ready, if he finds me ready. Wherever I turn, he does not abandon me unless I abandon him first. Wherever I may be, he does not depart, because he is everywhere, so that wherever I go I may find him, with whom I can be.

Whatever I do, he stands beside me, as the perpetual observer of all my thoughts, intentions, and actions. When I consider these things carefully, I am overwhelmed equally by fear and immense shame, because I behold him present to me everywhere and seeing all my hidden things.

For there are many things in me of which I am ashamed before his eyes, and for which I fear greatly that I displease him. For all these things I have nothing with which to repay him except to love him. For nothing better or more fitting can repay what was given through love than love itself.

I seem to have said these things beside the point, but perhaps they are not beside the point for my benefit and for the benefit of those who share my feelings.

## CHAPTER XVIII. The soul as the life of the body. In what sense the soul is immortal and mortal, incorporeal and corporeal. How the soul is in the body.

[Note: [Col. 0793] Cassiodorus, *On the Soul*, chapters 6–8; from Gennadius, *On Ecclesiastical Dogma*, chapters 11 and 12; and Hugh, book 1 of *On the Sacraments*, part 3, chapter 18.]

By its presence the soul gives life to the body, and it is so bound to the body that it can neither separate itself from it when it wishes nor retain itself when it has heard the command of its Creator.

The life of the body consists in the life of the soul, and the death of the soul descends from the death of the body. For just as the soul makes the flesh living by its own life and irrigates it by animating it from the fountain of its own nature, so the flesh, through the corruption of its own material, kills the soul if it binds it to unlawful desires.

And when one nature is conquered and another nature conquers [Note: [Col. 0793] So the Medard manuscript. Others read: “when the nature of the other seems to pass,” and so forth.], each passes into the nature of the victor: that is, either the soul bestows a spiritual character upon the flesh through its virtues, or the victorious flesh makes the soul carnal.

Yet the soul can have nothing from death except what has been offered to it through vices; nor can the flesh retain anything of life unless it has been irrigated by the soul; nor can one pass into the nature of the other unless the former has been infected by vices or the latter has been abandoned by virtues [Note: [Col. 0793] Four manuscripts: “unless it has been wiped away.”].

The soul is distinguished by reason, through which it is taught excellent arts and instructed in eminent disciplines, so that it may understand divine things and deal with human things. Thus it appropriately surpasses the other animals, being a rational substance.
