For this is properly what the soul is: a rational substance, that is, a rational spirit. The soul is immortal, lest it appear unlike the likeness of its Creator. For it could not be the image and likeness of God if it were confined by the limit of death.

According to a certain mode of life, which it can in no way lose, it is immortal. According to a certain mutability, by which it can become better or worse, it is mortal. And just as it is mortal when it loses blessed life, although it cannot lose miserable life, so in relation to incorporeal God it is corporeal.

Nothing invisible and incorporeal is to be held to exist by nature except God alone—that is, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. He is called incorporeal and invisible because he is infinite and uncircumscribed, simple and wholly sufficient to himself, sustaining himself and remaining identical with himself. Since he is everywhere in himself, he is recognized as invisible and incorporeal.

Every rational creature, however, is corporeal. The angels and all the virtues are corporeal, although they do not subsist in flesh. We call intellectual natures corporeal because they are bounded by place, as is also the human soul, which is enclosed by flesh. For this reason it can be said both to exist in a place and to be local: “in a place,” because it is present here or somewhere; “local,” because what is wholly present somewhere is not elsewhere.

Yet it does not possess bodily dimension or bodily circumscription, because it is without bodily quantity. But because it is confined in a place through its presence and activity, it too is called local. Nevertheless, it is not so in the manner of a body, to which beginning, middle, and end are assigned according to place.

In relation, however, to incorporeal nature—which is supremely unchangeable and everywhere—the soul is corporeal, because it is not such a thing. Yet it is not positioned or moved through the space of place in such a way that a greater part of it occupies a greater place, a smaller part a smaller place, or that it is smaller in a part than in the whole.

For it is wholly present at once in every portion of the body: neither smaller in smaller portions nor greater in larger ones. Yet it is more intensely present in some places and less intensely in others, while it is wholly present in all and wholly present in each.

For just as God is wholly everywhere in the whole world and in every creature of his, so the soul is wholly everywhere in its entire body, as in a certain world of its own, though more intensely in the heart and in the brain, just as God is said to be especially in heaven.

## CHAPTER XIX. It acts wholly in whatever it acts.

The soul is invisible and incorporeal. For if it were visible, it would be corporeal. And if it were corporeal, it would be divisible and would have parts, nor could it be wholly present at once in one place.

For no body can either be touched wholly at once or touch another thing wholly at once. The soul, however, is wholly present at once in all its movements and activities.

It sees wholly, and wholly remembers what it has seen. It hears wholly, and wholly recalls sounds. It smells wholly, and wholly remembers odors. Through the tongue and palate it wholly senses and distinguishes flavors. It wholly touches hard or soft things. It wholly approves and rejects at once.

It distinguishes hot and cold with its entirety even through the tip of a single finger. It is wholly sight; it is wholly hearing; it wholly remembers. When it remembers wholly, it is wholly memory; when it wills wholly, it is wholly will; when it thinks wholly, it is wholly thought; when it loves wholly, it is wholly love.

For it can think in part and love in part.

## CHAPTER XX. The soul’s powers directed toward virtues and against vices. Sacramental virtues. Through what it clings to God and through what it clings to the body. The soul’s natural power.

The soul possesses affections by which it is exercised toward virtue. Sorrow over sins, fear of punishments, desire for promises, and joy over rewards are certain exercises of virtue.

It also possesses virtues by which it is instructed and armed against vices. Through prudence it knows what it ought to do; it possesses temperance against prosperity, fortitude against adversity, and justice, by which it knows what it ought to render to each person.

Prudence is knowing what one can do; fortitude is doing what one can; temperance is not presuming to do what one cannot; justice is not wishing for more than one can have.

Prudence concerns choosing; temperance, using; fortitude, enduring; justice, distributing.

It belongs to prudence to desire nothing that one must regret and to wish to do nothing except what is just. It belongs to temperance to fear nothing except what is shameful and to direct everything we do or think according to the rule of reason. It belongs to fortitude not merely to restrain earthly desires but to forget them completely. It belongs to justice to direct every thought of the soul toward God alone and to contemplate him with the sole focus of the mind, as though nothing else existed.

The soul also possesses sacramental virtues by which it is initiated: faith, hope, the sacrament of Baptism, anointing, Confirmation, and the other things by which it is consecrated to God.

It also possesses virtues through which it advances and by which it is joined to God, such as humility, purity, and charity. Humility subjects it to God; purity joins it to him; charity unites it with him.

The soul also possesses powers by which it is mingled with the body. The first is natural, the second vital, and the third animal.

And just as the triune and one God, true and perfect, holds all things, fills all things, sustains all things, surpasses all things, and encompasses all things, so the soul is diffused throughout the entire body by these three powers—not by local extension, but by vital intensity.

The natural power works in the liver to produce blood and the other humors, which it sends through the veins to all the body’s members, so that they may thereby grow and be nourished.

This power is fourfold. It is divided into the appetitive, retentive, expulsive, and distributive powers.

The appetitive power desires what the body needs. The retentive power retains what has been taken in until useful digestion has been produced from it. The expulsive power drives out harmful and superfluous matter. The distributive power distributes the good humors of good foods among all the members, according to what is beneficial to each.

All animals possess these powers, and therefore they seem to belong to the body rather than to the soul.

## CHAPTER XXI. The vital power.

The vital power is in the heart. By drawing in and expelling air in order to regulate the heart’s heat, it grants life and health to the whole body.

With pure air it drives purified blood through the entire body by the pulsating veins called arteries. From their movement physicians recognize the balance or disorder of the heart.

## CHAPTER XXII. The animal power. The animal power is threefold.

[Note: [Col. 0795] *On the Literal Interpretation of Genesis*, book 7, chapter 18, and book 12, chapter 16.]

The animal power is in the brain, and from there it gives strength to the body’s five senses. It also commands the emission of voices and the movement of the limbs.

There are three ventricles of the brain. One is anterior, from which all sensation proceeds; another is posterior, from which all movement proceeds; the third is intermediate between the two, namely the rational ventricle.

The senses of the body are produced as follows. What is most subtle in the body, and therefore more similar and closer to the soul [Note: [Col. 0795] The Medard manuscript: “more intimately.”] than other things—namely, light—is first diffused through the eyes themselves and flashes forth in the rays of the eyes for the purpose of looking at visible things. Then, through a certain mixture, it completes the five senses together with the sense of sight itself: first with pure air, second with dark and cloudy air, third with denser moisture, and fourth with earthly thickness, in which it alone excels.

Because these senses are situated only in the face, I think it was therefore written that God breathed into man’s face the breath of life, and he became a living soul (Genesis 2:7).

The anterior part is rightly placed before the posterior, because the former leads and the latter follows; from the former comes sensation, from the latter movement, just as deliberation precedes action.

These powers may be called both those of the soul and those of the body, because they are produced by the soul in the body and cannot be produced without both.

In the first part of the brain the animal power is called phantastic, that is, imaginative, because the likenesses and images of bodily things are contained there; hence it is called the phantastic faculty.

In the middle part of the brain it is called rational, because there it examines and judges what is represented through imagination. In the final part it is called memorial, because there it commits to memory what has been judged by reason.

## CHAPTER XXIII. How many powers of perception there are in the soul. Lustful dreams.

[Note: [Col. 0795] The same work, book 12, chapters 20, 32, 23, 12, and 15.]

There is one faculty in us by which we sense bodies, which we do through the five bodily senses. There is another by which we perceive not bodies but things similar to bodies, and in which we also behold ourselves as similar to bodies.

There is another by which we perceive neither bodies nor likenesses of bodies, but those things that do not possess images resembling themselves, such as God and the rational mind itself, or intelligence, or reason. The same is true of the virtues—prudence, justice, chastity, charity, piety, and all the others—which we enumerate, distinguish, and define by understanding or thinking.

The soul, moreover, is not a body [Note: [Col. 0795] Manuscripts: “not corporeal.”], because not every likeness of a body is itself a body. When you are asleep, something like a body will appear to you in dreams [Note: [Col. 0795] Two manuscripts: “corporeal.” Two others: “corporeal” in the feminine form.]. Yet this is not your body, but your soul; nor is it a true body, but a likeness of your body.

Your body will lie still, while that likeness walks. The tongue of your body will be silent, while it speaks. Your eyes will be closed, while it sees. And thus the likeness of your flesh will be perceived in the soul, whole and undiminished.

In this likeness it runs about, as it were, through known or unknown places, and experiences things joyful or sorrowful. The soul of a dead person, like that of a sleeping person, experiences good or evil in the likeness of its own body. These experiences are not corporeal, however, but similar to corporeal things; through them souls stripped of their bodies are affected well or badly, while they themselves appear to themselves as resembling their bodies. Nevertheless, the joy and distress are real, produced from spiritual substance in spiritual substance.

It is certain that there is in us a spiritual nature in which likenesses of corporeal things are either formed or introduced once formed. This happens either when we touch present things through some bodily sense, and their likeness is immediately formed in the spirit and stored in memory, or when we think about absent things already known or things we do not know, so that a certain spiritual understanding may be formed from them.

We also invent innumerable things according to our choice and opinion, whether they do not exist or are not known to exist. Innumerable and varied forms of things also move about in our mind, either when we are doing something or when we are about to do something. Sometimes, too, the soul is carried away by some spirit and lifted up to see such things, whether good or evil.

Through excessive concentration of thought, through some force of illness—as commonly happens to those delirious with fever—or through the mingling of some other spirit, whether good or evil, images of corporeal things are so impressed upon the spirit as though bodies themselves were presented to the bodily senses. Thus absent things seem present as though actually there, and things that do not exist appear to stand before the eyes.

Many things also appear to sleepers, signifying either nothing or something. Hence images of corporeal things are often presented to them in dreams with as much vividness as bodies themselves are presented to those who are awake, so that no distinction is made between the vision of sleepers and the actual intercourse of the awake. Their flesh is immediately moved, and they appear to have intercourse against their intention or against lawful conduct; what has been naturally gathered is emitted through the genital passages.

Those who are awake and chaste restrain and control this movement. Sleepers, however, cannot do so because they do not have control over the expression of the bodily image [Note: [Col. 0796] Two manuscripts: “suppression”], by which the flesh is naturally moved. What ordinarily follows that movement then follows, although it cannot take place without sin among those who are awake.

Thus in the spirit images of corporeal things appear, and many things are invented according to one’s will or displayed contrary to one’s will. For the soul itself, which is always in motion by its own movement, is prevented by the body—or not wholly prevented—from sensing corporeal things or directing the force of its attention toward corporeal things. When the body is asleep, the spirit either itself produces likenesses of corporeal things, just as it usually turns images of bodies about within itself by thinking, or it contemplates images presented to it when it is taken up by some spirit to see them.

## CHAPTER XXIV. What the soul is and what it is not. Three kinds of vision. What is liable to falsity. On ecstasy. Other kinds of vision.

[Note: [Col. 0796] Isidore, book 2 of *Differentiae*, chapters 26 and 23; following Augustine, book 12 of *On the Literal Interpretation of Genesis*, chapters 11, 14, and 18–26, and chapter 30.]

The soul is a spiritual substance, simple and indissoluble, invisible and incorporeal, subject to suffering and change, devoid of weight, shape, and color. It is not to be considered a part, but a creature of God, nor as deriving from God’s substance or from the matter of any element, but as created from nothing. For if God had made it from himself, it would in no way be flawed, changeable, or miserable. If, however, it had been made from the elements, it would be corporeal. Since, then, it is incorporeal and its origin is unknown, it has a beginning but no end. And since it is of a spiritual nature, it contains nothing mixed or compounded with earth, nothing moist, airy, or fiery; it has no color, is contained in no place, bounded by no limbs, and limited by no space. Rather, it must be conceived and understood in the same way as wisdom, justice, and the other virtues created by the Almighty.

The nature of the soul is invisible; therefore it remains invisibly in the body and invisibly departs from the body. Through the body it sees bodies, such as heaven and earth and the things in them that are visible to our eyes. Through the spirit, however, it perceives the likenesses of bodies. For whatever is not a body and yet exists is rightly called a spirit. Therefore, by a certain hidden and spiritual power, the soul is carried away so that, in place of bodies, it may see in the spirit the expressed likenesses of corporeal things. But by the intellect it perceives those things that have neither bodies nor the forms of bodies, such as justice and wisdom, or the mind itself and every good affection of the soul.

These three kinds of vision are clear. The first is bodily, by which bodies are perceived through the bodily senses. The second is spiritual, by which likenesses of bodies are perceived through the spirit, not through the mind [Note: [Col. 0797] The Medardus Manuscript reads “through the spirit or mind.”]. The third is intellectual, by which those things that have neither bodies nor the forms of bodies are perceived.

In intellectual vision the soul is never deceived: either it understands, and the thing is true; or, if it is not true, it does not understand. In bodily vision, however, the soul is often deceived, when it thinks that what occurs in the bodily senses occurs in the bodies themselves. Thus, to those who are sailing, things that are stationary appear to move on land; and to those looking at the sky, stars that are moving appear to stand still. When the rays of the eyes are spread apart, one object appears to have two forms, one man two heads, and an oar in water appears broken; and there are many similar cases.

The soul is also deceived and deluded in spiritual vision, because the things it sees are sometimes true and sometimes false, sometimes confused and sometimes tranquil. Even the true things are sometimes wholly like future events; sometimes they are openly stated, and sometimes foretold through obscure signs or figurative expressions.

In ecstasy, however, when the soul is estranged and turned away from all the bodily senses—more fully than in sleep, but less than in death—it is not deceived. When the mind itself is divinely assisted, or when someone interprets what has been seen—as the great revelation in the Apocalypse was interpreted to John—it is a revelation. For when the soul is taken up by a good spirit, it cannot be deceived, because the holy angels, in wondrous ways and through a certain easy and overpowering union or mingling, make their visions our own and, in an ineffable manner, imprint their vision upon our spirit. They preside over the judging and administering of these corporeal things, and so distinguish their significant likenesses in the spirit, handling them with such power that they can even mingle them with human spirits by revealing them.

Hence the angel of the Lord appeared to Joseph in a dream, saying, “Do not be afraid to take Mary as your wife”; and again, “Take the child and his mother and flee into Egypt” (Matthew 1:20; 2:13). God also says through the prophet: “I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh; and your young men shall see visions, and your old men shall dream dreams” (Joel 2:28).

There are also other customary and human visions, which arise in various ways either from our own spirit or are, in a certain manner, suggested to the spirit by the body, according to the condition of our flesh or mind. For people who are awake do not merely turn their concerns over in thought through likenesses of bodies; those who are asleep also often dream of what they need. They conduct their business out of desire, and eagerly long for meals and drinks if they have gone to sleep hungry and thirsty.

We also know that thoughts which they would later divine are introduced into those who are awake by a certain hidden impulse. Thus Caiaphas the high priest prophesied (John 11:51), although he had no intention of prophesying.

The soul sees many things, and the nature of all visions is the same, whether they occur in those who are awake, asleep, or ill, since the things that are seen derive from no other kind of source than the nature of the spirit, in which or through which likenesses of bodies are formed. The visions of the delirious are therefore like the visions of dreamers, for they have the pathways of sensation blocked, so that they see what dreamers see. The visions of dreamers are likewise like the thoughts of those who are awake. In sleepers, the pathway of sensation in the brain, which directs attention toward the eyes, is lulled to sleep. Thus, with attention turned elsewhere, the soul sees dream-visions as though bodily appearances were present, so that sleepers seem to themselves to be awake and think that they are looking not at things resembling bodies, but at the bodies themselves.

I, however, am much more astonished and deeply amazed at the speed and ease with which the soul fashions within itself images of bodies that it has seen through the bodily eyes than at the visions of the delirious, dreamers, or even those in ecstasy. Whatever the nature of these visions may be, it is unquestionably not bodily. For the bodies that are seen do not themselves produce those images in the spirit, nor do they possess the power to form something spiritual; rather, the spirit itself, being intellectual and rational, produces them within itself with wondrous speed.

## CHAPTER XXV. The Five Kinds of Dreams. Why Dreams Differ.

Of all the things that sleepers seem to see, there are five kinds: the oracle, the vision, the dream, the anxiety-dream (*insomnium*), and the phantasm [Note: [Col. 0798] Following Macrobius, *Commentary on the Dream of Scipio*, book 1, chapter 3.].

An oracle occurs when a parent or some holy and distinguished person, or a priest, or even God, announces in a dream that something will or will not happen, or that something must be done or avoided.

A vision occurs when someone sees something that will happen in exactly the way in which it appeared.

A dream is veiled in figures and cannot be understood without interpretation.

An anxiety-dream (*insomnium*) occurs when something that exhausted a person while awake intrudes upon the sleeper—for example, concern about food or drink, or some studies, skills, or illnesses. For each person dreams according to the studies in which he has been engaged, and the likenesses of his customary arts, impressed upon the presence of his mind, appear in dreams. Dreams also vary according to differences in illnesses. They vary as well according to differences of character and bodily humors. The sanguine see one kind of thing, the choleric another, the phlegmatic another, and the melancholic another. The former see red and variegated things; the latter, black and white.

A phantasm occurs when someone has only just begun to sleep and still thinks that he is awake, yet seems to see forms—different and various, cheerful or turbulent—rushing upon him or wandering about indiscriminately. The *ephialtes* belongs to this category, which popular belief supposes to attack resting people and to weigh upon and oppress them with its burden. It is nothing other than a kind of vapor rising from the stomach or heart to the brain and there suppressing the vital power.

## CHAPTER XXVI. The Nature of Apparitions.

Human opinion also says that, through a certain art of women and the power of demons, human beings can be changed into wolves and beasts of burden, and can carry whatever loads are necessary [Note: [Col. 0798] The Medardus Manuscript reads “to carry certain burdens.”], and afterward return to themselves once the tasks have been completed; and that their minds do not become bestial, but remain rational and human.

This is to be understood as follows: demons do not create natures, but they can do something that makes them appear to be what they are not. No art or power can truly transform the mind—or even the body—into bestial limbs and features. But the human phantasm—which, whether through thought or dreaming, is varied among innumerable kinds of things and, although it is not a body, takes on forms resembling bodies with wondrous speed—can, when the bodily senses of a human being have been lulled or oppressed, be led into the bodily forms of other senses. This occurs in such a way, however, that the human bodies themselves lie somewhere, alive but with their senses closed far more heavily and oppressively than in sleep; while that phantasm, as though formed [Note: [Col. 0798] Hugo reads “embodied.”] into the image of some animal, appears to other people’s senses, and such a person seems to himself to be what he might seem to be in a dream—and to carry burdens.

If those burdens are real bodies, they are carried by demons, so that human beings may be deceived: some seeing genuine human bodies, others false beasts of burden [Note: [Col. 0798] Elsewhere, “burdens.”].

## CHAPTER XXVII. What Angelic Spirits Can Do to the Human Spirit [Col. 0799]. [Note: [Col. 0799] From *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, book 12, chapters 13–14, and Bede on Acts 5.]

Sometimes a good spirit, sometimes an evil spirit, takes possession of the human spirit. It cannot easily be discerned by which spirit it is possessed, except that the good spirit instructs and the evil deceives. The evil spirit often deceives through things that are manifestly good, so that, once trust has been placed in those things, it may lead a person toward its own purposes.

Thus it often carries off the human spirit in such a way that, through a certain hidden mixture, the possessing spirit seems to be the same as the spirit that is possessed, just as we see in those afflicted by demons.

No creature, however, can fill the human soul—that is, the mind—in its substance, except the Trinity alone. Satan is said to fill someone’s mind and the ruling faculty of the heart, not by entering into that person and into his understanding, but by enticing and seducing him through fraud, iniquity, and every form of wickedness. Through an inclination toward evil, Satan draws him through thoughts and incitements to vices, with which Satan himself is filled, being a deceitful, wicked, and fraudulent deceiver of souls [Note: [Col. 0799] Three Vatican Manuscripts read “transports him.”].

The devil does not fill anyone through participation in nature or substance, as some think, nor does he become the inhabitant of the person. Rather, he is said to dwell in the one whom he fills through fraud, deception, and wickedness. For it belongs to the Trinity alone to enter into and fill the nature or substance that it created.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. The Demons’ Experience and Arts of Deception. [Note: [Col. 0799] From *On the Divination of Demons*, chapter 3, and from the Appendix to the Council of Ancyra.]

Through the keenness of their perception and the speed of movement of their airy bodies, demons easily surpass the senses of earthly bodies, and they announce certain thoughts in advance—thoughts that amaze human beings because of the slowness of the earthly body.

Moreover, through the very long period by which their life is extended, demons have acquired a far greater experience of things than can come to human beings because of the brevity of human life. Therefore they foretell certain future events and perform certain marvels by which they attract and lead people astray.

Thus certain little women who have turned to Satan, seduced by demonic illusions and phantasms, believe and profess that during the night they ride with Diana, the pagan goddess, or with Herodias and Minerva, and with an innumerable multitude of women, obeying their commands.

For Satan himself, who transforms himself into an angel of light (2 Corinthians 11:14), when he has seized the mind of any such woman and subjected her to himself through unbelief, immediately transforms himself into the forms and likenesses of various persons. Deceiving the mind that he holds captive in dreams, showing it now joyful, now sorrowful, now familiar, now unfamiliar persons, he leads it through every kind of byway.

And because only the unbelieving spirit suffers this, while the body does not, the person thinks that it occurs in the body. Therefore anyone is exceedingly foolish and dull who believes that all these things, which occur in the spirit, also happen in the body, when Ezekiel and the other prophets, as well as John the Evangelist and the other apostles, saw visions in the spirit, not in the body.

## CHAPTER XXIX. The Apparitions of the Dead. Their Ignorance of What Happens Here. How They Learn of It. [Note: [Col. 0799] From *On the Care to Be Taken for the Dead*, chapters 12–16.]

When dead or living human beings appear to people who are asleep or awake, they are not seen in the things themselves as they are, but in certain likenesses of things. We believe that this happens through angelic operations, by the dispensation of God’s providence, which makes good use of goods and evils according to the inscrutable depth of its judgments—whether the minds of mortals are thereby instructed or deceived, consoled or terrified—just as mercy is to be shown or justice inflicted upon each person by the one to whom the Church does not vainly sing of mercy and judgment (Psalm 100:1).

The spirits of the dead are indeed in a place where they do not see or hear what human beings do or what happens in this life. Yet they are concerned about the living, although they have no knowledge at all of what the living are doing, just as we are concerned about the dead, although we certainly do not know what they are doing [Col. 0800].

The dead do not know what happens here while it is happening. Later they may hear from those who, by dying, go from here to them—not everything, but as much as those who depart are permitted to tell them and as much as the dead ought to hear.

They may also learn from the angels who are present with us here and carry our souls to them. Through the revelation of God’s spirit they may also learn what happens here and what it is necessary for them to know.

Some of the dead may also be snatched back to the living—not by their own nature, but by divine power. Whether this happens through their presence or through angels who assume their persons, I do not dare to affirm. For almighty God, who is present everywhere, can through angelic ministries spread everywhere provide such consolations to human beings as he judges should be provided amid the misery of this life.

## CHAPTER XXX. The Soul Does Not Grow. Where It Is and What It Does When Stripped of the Flesh. [Note: [Col. 0800] Isaac of Stella, *Letter on the Soul*, and *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, book 12, chapters 33 and 32.]

The powers and virtues of the soul grow through long exercise and the passage of time. The soul itself, however, neither grows nor diminishes; but, impeded either by the unequal proportion of the limbs or by the thickness and corruption of the humors, it cannot exercise its powers.

The soul, stripped of the flesh, lives, sees, hears, and vigorously retains all its senses and faculties, being pure, subtle, swift, and everlasting. And just as God is everywhere in himself, so the soul is in a certain way everywhere in itself. Hence, after the body, the soul is there where it was while acting in the body.

God is now where he was before the world existed, and where he would be if the world ceased to exist.

As has often been said, the soul is incorporeal. Yet it can possess a likeness of a body—not something corporeal, but something resembling a body and its corporeal limbs—when it departs from the body. Thus it is either carried, according to its merits, toward spiritual things, or toward places of punishment resembling bodies, such as have often been shown to those who have been snatched away from their bodily senses and lain as though dead. In such cases, they themselves retained within themselves a certain likeness of their body, through which they could be carried to those places and experience such things through corresponding senses.

For souls that, while living in bodies, are affected by corporeal images through love of visible things suffer torment in those same images when they depart from their bodies. They can be held there in corporeal sufferings because here they were not cleansed from the corruption of corporeal affections, which they acquired through the bodily enjoyment of corporeal pleasure [Note: [Col. 0800] One Vatican Manuscript reads “love.”].

Some souls, moreover, are punished in the same places in which they committed their sins; others are confined in hidden receptacles until the final resurrection, each according to whether it is worthy of rest or misery.

## CHAPTER XXXI. Man Is Mortal. The Senses Prevent Him from Knowing Himself. [Note: [Col. 0800] Thus Anselm, *Meditations*, 7; Augustine, *On Order*, book 2, chapter 11, section 31.]

I have said much about the soul, but I have not yet said when it was made or when it will depart from the body. I shall discuss the former later; the latter I cannot state, because I do not know my end.

This much I plainly know: we are mortal, and whether we wish it or not, we shall all die. Nothing is more certain than death, and nothing more uncertain than the hour of death. For we do not know when, or how, or where we shall die, since death awaits us everywhere.

Therefore we must always be ready, so that when the body returns to the earth from which it was taken, the spirit may return to the one who gave it.

We should be moved especially by the fact that human beings were defined in this way by the ancient sages: “Man is a rational, mortal animal.” Once the genus “animal” has been posited, we see that two differences were added, by which a human being was to be admonished—both where he should return and from where he should flee.

For just as the soul’s advance toward mortality was a fall, so its return must be toward reason, by which it may resist the vices that attack it [Col. 0801], so that it may live according to its nature and desire to be ordered beneath the one by whom it ought to be governed, and above those things that it ought to govern.

In one word, by being called rational, man is separated from beasts; by another, by being called mortal, he is separated from divine beings. If he does not retain the former, he will be a beast; if he does not turn away from the latter, he will not attain the divine.

Therefore, in order that a human being who is unknown to himself may come to know himself, he greatly needs the practice of withdrawing from the senses, so that he may gather his mind toward itself and retain it within itself. For the soul is hindered by these senses from being able to perceive itself and its Creator, whom it ought to behold alone and in its simplicity, without these eyes.

## CHAPTER XXXII. Nothing Is More Known to the Mind Than Itself. The Soul’s Union with the Body. How the Soul Descends to the Body. How It Rises from the Body. Meditation. Contemplation. [Note: [Col. 0801] *On the Trinity*, book 10, chapters 8–10; *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, book 7, chapters 21 and 14; *On the Quantity of the Soul*, chapter 33, sections 70–71; and Hugh of Saint-Victor, *On the Union of Body and Spirit*.]

The rational soul surpasses all things created by God, and it is closest to God when it is pure. To the degree that it adheres to him through charity, it is in a certain way filled and illumined by that intelligible light—not through bodily eyes, but through its own ruling faculty, that is, through the intellect. In that light it beholds God, in whom there is perfect beauty and the most blessed vision; through that vision it becomes blessed.

Let it therefore remove from its consideration all knowledge acquired externally through the bodily senses. All corporeal things, their likenesses, and the sensations and imaginings fixed in the memory, when recalled in remembrance, belong to the exterior human being, although through these messengers the soul perceives external things.

The mind, then, to which nothing is more present than itself, sees itself within itself through an inward presence that is not feigned but true. For the mind knows nothing so well as what is present to it, and nothing is more present to the mind than the mind itself. It knows that it lives, remembers, understands, wills, thinks, knows, and judges. It knows all these things in itself; it does not imagine them as though it had touched them outside itself through some bodily sense, as bodily things are touched.

If, from its thoughts of these things, it forms no image of itself, imagining that it is something of that kind, then whatever remains to it concerning itself is simply what it itself is. For nothing is so present in the mind as the mind itself, and nothing knows the mind as the mind does.

When the mind asks what the mind is, it certainly knows that it is seeking itself, and that it is itself the mind that seeks itself. For it seeks itself from nowhere other than itself. When, therefore, it knows itself as the seeker, it certainly knows itself. And whatever it knows, it knows wholly; thus it knows itself wholly.

Even if, having found a part, it does not seek itself as a whole, nevertheless, because it seeks itself wholly, it is wholly present to itself. For nothing can be more present to it than itself.

What it seeks concerning itself is what it was before, what it will be in the future, or what it is now—that is, how similar or dissimilar it is to God; how humble and devoted, how pure, how holy.

But because it is among these corporeal things, which it thinks about with love and to which it has become accustomed through love, it cannot see itself or exist within itself without their images. For these external corporeal things have clung to it with such a bond of love that, even when they are absent, their images are present to the mind that thinks of them. Therefore it cannot separate them from itself so that it may contemplate and see itself alone.

Let it therefore return to itself and remain within itself. Let it not seek itself as though absent, but take care to perceive and discern itself as present. Let it establish within itself the attention of the will, which had wandered through other things, and think of itself, so that it may know and love itself.

In this way it will see that it has never failed to love itself and has never failed to know itself; but, by loving other things along with itself, it became confused with them, so that it cannot separate itself from those things without great effort, since it adhered to them through love.

For this reason it is disfigured by the phantasms of corporeal images, and, even when freed from the body, it is not stripped of those images, because they have been deeply impressed upon it. If here it is not cleansed from the corruption of corporeal affections [Col. 0802], then, once stripped of the body, it will be held by corporeal sufferings.

Therefore, in this life, it should strive to cleanse itself from such filth, so that when it departs from here it may carry nothing corporeal with it and may exist free from corporeal suffering.

The soul descends to the body by giving it life and sensation. By its presence it vivifies the body, gathers it into unity, and keeps it unified; it does not permit it to disperse and waste away, and it preserves its proportion and order—not only in beauty, but also in growth and generation.

The soul also directs itself toward touch, and through it perceives and distinguishes hot and cold, rough and smooth, hard and soft, heavy and light. Then, by tasting, smelling, hearing, and seeing, it judges innumerable differences of flavors, odors, sounds, and forms. In all these things it desires what accords with the nature of its body and flees what is contrary to it.

At certain intervals it withdraws from these senses, as though restoring their movements through periods of rest, and turns over with itself, in groups and in many forms, the images that it has absorbed through them.

When, therefore, it wishes to understand either divine things, or God, or itself, or to consider its own virtues, it withdraws from all the bodily senses, which assist it only in perceiving corporeal forms and colors. Through spirit and reason it beholds itself, and through meditation and contemplation it ascends to God.

God, however, descends to it through revelation and divine inspiration.

Meditation is the diligent investigation of hidden truth. Contemplation is the joyful wonder at manifest truth. Divine revelation illumines meditation so that it may know the truth; divine inspiration kindles contemplation so that it may love the truth.

The body, however, ascends to the spirit through sensation and imagination.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. The Matter of the Body. How the Senses and Imagination Are Formed. What Imagination Is. The Corporeal Spirit. [Note: [Col. 0802] *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, book 7, chapter 13; and Hugh, *On the Union of Body and Spirit*.]

The human body is composed of the four elements. Earth appears most clearly in the flesh and bones because of their earthly solidity. Water is present in the humors; air is contained in the lungs. For this reason the air is always in motion: it is the bellows of the heart, so that the heart may not be consumed and dissolved by excessive heat.

The seat of fire is in the heart. Therefore its lower part is broad and its upper part pointed, because it retains the shape of fire.

A certain fiery force tempered by air rises from the heart to the brain, as though to the heaven of our body. There it is purified and strained through the eyes, ears, nostrils, and the other instruments of the senses; it proceeds outward and, through contact with external things, is formed into the five bodily senses—sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch.

The sense of touch passes from the front part of the brain to the rear, and from there descends through the neck and spinal cord and spreads throughout the body.

Moreover, that fiery force which, once formed externally, is called sensation is, after being formed [Note: [Col. 0802] Elsewhere, “form.”] through the very instruments of the senses through which it emerges and in which it is formed, drawn and led back inward by the operation of nature as far as the imaginative chamber; and it becomes imagination.

Afterward this same imagination passes from the front part of the head to the middle, touches the substance of the rational soul itself, and awakens discernment. By then it has become so purified and subtle that it is immediately joined to the spirit, while nevertheless truly retaining the nature and property of the body.

In brute animals this imagination does not pass beyond the imaginative chamber. In rational beings, however, it becomes purer and is carried and advances far enough to touch the rational and incorporeal substance of the soul.

Imagination, then, is a likeness of the body, conceived externally through the bodily senses from contact with bodies, and through those same senses led inward to the purer part of the corporeal spirit and impressed upon it—at the summit of the corporeal spirit and at the lowest point of the rational spirit—informing the corporeal and touching the rational.

By “corporeal spirit” I mean air, or rather fire, which cannot be seen because of its subtlety and gives life to bodies inwardly by animating them.

Some things it merely animates and does not give sensation, such as trees, plants, and everything that germinates in the earth. Some things it both animates and gives sensation, such as all brute animals. Among these, some possess sensation alone and do not possess imagination; others possess both sensation and imagination.

Since to possess sensation is more than merely to be animated [Note: [Col. 0803] Elsewhere, “greater.”], it is plainly established that this power is more subtle; and where it is more subtle, it is more truly spirit. It approaches incorporeal nature more closely when it forms imagination than when it produces sensation.

For nothing in the body can be higher or closer to spiritual nature than that point at which, after sensation or above sensation, the power of imagination is formed. This is so sublime that whatever lies above it is nothing other than reason [Note: [Col. 0803] Here the book ends in one Vatican Manuscript. In the Medardus Manuscript there is: “According to some, the second book ends.” Then: “Another book, according to some.”].

## CHAPTER XXXIV. Sensation. Memory. Mind. Spirit. The Spirit Is the Same as the Soul. Reason. How the Soul Raises Itself to God. The Marvelous Division of the Soul. The Mind as the Image of God.

[Note: [Col. 0803] Ambrose, *On the Dignity of the Human Condition*; Isidore, *Etymologies*, book 11, chapter 1; the same, *Differences of the Spirit*, book 2, chapter 19; Augustine, *On the Trinity*, book 10, chapter 9.]

The soul is called the whole inner human being, by which that mass of clay is given life, governed, and held together—moistened by juices so that it may not dry out and disintegrate.

When it gives life to the body, it is called the soul (*anima*); when it wills, it is called the mind (*animus*); when it knows, it is called the mind (*mens*); when it recalls, it is called memory; when it judges, it is called reason; when it breathes or contemplates, it is called spirit; when it perceives, it is called sensation.

The body also has five senses. They are so called because through them the soul, by the power of sensation, moves the whole body with the utmost subtlety. For the soul is called *sensus* (“sensation”) from the things it perceives; hence *sententia* (“judgment”) too takes its name.

All these faculties are joined to the soul in such a way that they are one thing. Yet, according to the effects of their causes, the soul has received different names. In its essence it is simple; in its functions it is manifold.

Memory is also mind; hence we call those who are forgetful “mindless.” Memory is the treasury and guardian of all things, and its vast complexity cannot be described. It is also the mind (*animus*).

When I say “mind,” I signify nothing other than the soul, but I call the soul “soul” for one reason and “mind” for another. For everything that lives is the human soul. But when the soul acts upon itself, within itself, from itself, and through itself [Note: [Col. 0803] In manuscript B: “But when the soul acts upon itself, from itself, and through itself.” We have followed the readings of Erasmus, Lyons, Venice, and Louvain. M.], it is customarily called the mind alone.

In carrying out its ministries, it is more usually called the soul in relation to sensation.

The Evangelist declares that spirit is the same as soul when he says: “I have power to lay down my soul, and again I have power to take it up” (John 10:18). Concerning that same soul of the Lord at the time of his Passion, the Evangelist likewise says: “And he bowed his head and gave up his spirit” (John 19:30). For what is it to give up the spirit except to lay down the soul?

The soul is called soul because it lives; spirit, however, is so called either because of its spiritual nature or because it breathes in the body.

Likewise, we say that the mind (*animus*) is the same as the soul. But the soul is concerned with life, while the spirit is concerned with counsel. Hence philosophers say that life can remain without the spirit, and the soul endure without the mind, as in those who are mentally deficient [Note: [Col. 0803] As Lactantius testifies, *On the Workmanship of God*, chapter 18.].

It appears to belong to the mind (*mens*) to know and to the mind (*animus*) to will. Children live in their mother’s womb without knowledge or will.

The mind (*mens*) is so called because it rises above the soul or because it remembers. Therefore it is not the soul as such, but what excels in the soul, that is called the mind, like its head or eye [Col. 0804]. Hence the human being himself is called the image of God according to the mind.

The mind is so called because it rises above the soul; for it is the soul’s superior power, from which understanding proceeds.

Reason is the movement of the spirit or mind, sharpening the mind’s vision and distinguishing truth from falsehood.

Therefore let the rational mind return to itself and gather itself within itself, so that it may be able to contemplate itself, without bodily images, and the invisible nature of almighty God. Let it reject the phantasms of earthly images and whatever earthly thing may occur to its thought; and let it seek and see itself within as it is without these things. Let it consider itself as it was created beneath God and above the body. Then let it rise above itself, abandon itself, and, as it were, come into forgetfulness of itself [Note: [Col. 0804] Elsewhere, “of itself.”], and let it humbly and devoutly submit itself to the contemplation of its Creator.

For when the mind begins, through pure understanding, to surpass itself [Note: [Col. 0804] Thus one of the Vatican manuscripts. Other books read, “to exercise itself.”], and to enter wholly into the clarity of that incorporeal light [Note: [Col. 0804] Printed editions read, “to gaze upon it.”], and to draw from what it sees inwardly a certain taste of intimate sweetness, seasoning its understanding with it and transforming it into wisdom, then, in this great ecstasy of the mind, that peace which surpasses all understanding is found and attained. Thus there comes to be silence in heaven for about half an hour; the soul of the contemplative is disturbed by no tumult of contending thoughts, finding nothing at all that it either seeks through desire, censures through disgust, or accuses through hatred. Rather, it gathers itself entirely within the tranquility of contemplation and is admitted into a certain very unusual inward affection and into I know not what sweetness—which, if it were always experienced in this way, would assuredly be great happiness.

The sensual faculty does nothing; the imagination does nothing. Rather, every lower power of the soul is temporarily deprived of its proper function. The purer part of the soul, however, is introduced with joyful delight into that secret place of deepest quiet and that mystery of supreme tranquility.

“For the word of God is living and effective, and sharper than every two-edged sword, reaching even to the division of soul and spirit” (Hebr. IV, 12). Therefore nothing more wondrous than this division is perceived among created things: that which is essentially one and indivisible is split within itself, and that which is simple in itself and constituted without parts is divided, as it were, by a kind of partition.

For the spirit of one human being is not one essence and his soul another; rather, they are altogether one and the same substance of a simple nature. The twofold expression does not signify a twofold substance. Instead, when the expression is used for distinction, a twofold power of the same essence is designated: one superior, through “spirit,” the other inferior, through “soul.” In this division, the soul and whatever is animal remain below, while the spirit and whatever is spiritual soar upward. It is divided from the lowest things so that it may be raised to the highest; it is cleft away from the soul so that it may be united to the Lord: “For whoever is joined to the Lord is one spirit” (I Cor. VI, 17).

Blessed and wondrous is the separation in which what is corporeal and turbid remains below, while what is spiritual and subtle is raised even to the contemplation of divine glory and transformed into the same image. The lower part is composed for supreme peace and tranquility; the higher part is raised to glory and joy.

Although the human mind is not of the nature that God is, nevertheless the image of that nature—than which no nature is better—is to be sought and found in us precisely where our own nature has nothing better. But first the mind itself must be considered within itself, and in it the image of God must be found.

When the mind turns back upon itself in thought, it understands and knows itself. When, through contemplation, it rises toward God in order to understand and love him, it must be called the image of God. By thinking upon eternal things, it is a man, as the Apostle says: “A man ought not to veil his head, since he is the image and glory of God” (I Cor. XI, 7). That is, the more it extends itself toward what is eternal, the more it is formed according to the image of God; and therefore it must not be restrained, as though it ought to hold itself back and limit itself from that ascent.

But when it does or thinks what belongs to temporal things, it is called a woman. At that point it is not to be called the image of God, and for that reason it ought to veil its head, lest its advance toward lower things become excessive, and lest, while doing what is permitted, it desire what is forbidden.

## CHAPTER XXXV. The dignity of the human condition. In what respect man is made according to the image of God. Again, how the image of God is in the soul. In what respect the soul bears the likeness of God.

[Note: [Col. 0805] This is elsewhere Treatise 13 in the Appendix to volume 9, where it is also found among the works of Ambrose and Alcuin; much of it is contained in Hugh’s work, likewise published in the Appendix to Bernard, Book 3, *On the Soul*, chapters 46 and 47. Compare the book *On Salutary Instructions*, presented later here. The passages enclosed in brackets are not found in Ambrose, Alcuin, or Treatise 13 of volume 9.]

The dignity of the human condition is recognized as so great that man was created not merely by the word of command, as were the other works of the six days, but by the counsel of the Holy Trinity and by the work of divine majesty. Thus, from the honor of his first creation, he might understand how much he owed his Creator, since the Creator immediately bestowed upon him so great a privilege of dignity in his creation; and he might love his Creator all the more, the more wondrously he understood himself to have been created by him.

Nor was this so only because he was created so excellently by the Creator through the counsel of the Holy Trinity, but also because the Creator of all things made him according to his own image and likeness—something he granted to no other creature. This image must be considered more carefully in the dignity and nobility of the inner man.

First, just as the one God is always wholly present everywhere, giving life, moving, and governing all things—as the Apostle says, “In him we live and move and have our being” (Acts XVII, 28)—so the soul is wholly active everywhere in its body, giving it life, moving it, and governing it. It is not greater in the larger members of its body and smaller in the smaller members; rather, it is wholly present in the smallest and wholly present in the greatest.

[It is infused into the body in such a way that it is not divided part by part according to the parts of the members. Wherever a part of the body is struck, the whole soul suffers. Yet, in a wondrous manner, while presiding over the members through one and the same act of vivification, although it is not diverse in its own nature, it performs diverse actions through the body. It is the soul that sees through the eyes, hears through the ears, smells through the nostrils, tastes through the mouth, and touches through all the members; and by touching it distinguishes what is smooth from what is rough. Although it is not diverse in itself, it nevertheless performs diverse operations through the senses.

From this it is understood that the soul, in its own manner, is in its body as God is in his world. It is inward and outward, above and below: ruling what is above, bearing what is below, filling what is within, surrounding what is without. It is within in such a way as to be outside; it surrounds in such a way as to penetrate; it presides in such a way as to bear; it bears in such a way as to preside. And just as God neither grows when creatures grow nor diminishes when they diminish, so the soul is neither diminished by smaller members nor increased by enlarged ones.]

This is the image or likeness of almighty God that the soul possesses within itself.

It also possesses in itself a certain image of the Holy Trinity. First, just as God is, lives, and knows, so the soul, in its own manner, is, lives, and knows. There is also another trinity in it, because it was created according to the image of the perfect and supreme Trinity, which exists in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

Although the soul is of one nature, it nevertheless possesses three powers [Note: [Col. 0805] Ambrose, Alcuin, and Treatise 13 elsewhere in volume 9 have “dignities” here and below]: understanding, will, and memory. The same thing, though expressed in other words, is indicated in the Gospel when it says: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind” (Matt. XXII, 37)—that is, with all your understanding, with all your will, and with all your memory.

For just as the Son is generated from the Father, and the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, so the will is generated from the understanding, and memory proceeds from both of them, as anyone who is wise can readily understand. Nor can the perfect soul exist without these three, nor can any one of these three remain complete without the other two, so far as its proper relation is concerned [Note: [Col. 0806] In most books, “so far as its blessedness is concerned.”].

And just as God the Father, God the Son, and God the Holy Spirit are not three gods but one God and three persons, so the soul is understanding, the soul is will, and the soul is memory—not, however, three souls in one body, but one soul and three powers.

In these three, then, our inner man wondrously bears the divine image in his own nature. Through these, as through the soul’s more excellent powers, we are commanded to love the Creator: to love him insofar as he is understood, and insofar as he is loved, always to hold him in memory. It is not enough to have understanding of him unless the will is brought into his love. Indeed, these two are not enough unless memory is added, so that God may always remain present in the mind of the one who understands and loves him. Just as there can be no moment in which a human being does not use or enjoy God’s goodness and mercy, so there should be no moment in which he does not possess God as present in his memory. Therefore it seems to me rightly said that our inner man is the image of God.

[Note: [Col. 0806] Ambrose has inserted more material here.]

Now let us speak of some likeness. Just as God the Creator, who created man according to his image (Gen. I, 27), is charity, good and just, patient and gentle, pure and merciful, and possesses the other marks of holy virtues that are read of him, so man was created to possess charity, to be good and just, patient and gentle, pure and merciful.

The more each person possesses these virtues within himself, the closer he is to God and the greater likeness of his Creator he bears. But if—God forbid—someone degenerates and strays from this most noble likeness of his Creator through the byways of vices and the side paths of evils, then what is written about him will come to pass: “Man, when he was in honor, did not understand” (Ps. XLVIII, 13), and so forth.

What greater honor could there be for man than to be created according to the likeness of his Creator and adorned with the same garments of virtue with which the Creator too is adorned? Of him it is written: “The Lord has reigned; he is clothed with beauty” (Ps. XCII, 1)—that is, he is adorned with the splendor of every virtue and the beauty of complete goodness.

Or what greater disgrace or more unhappy misery could there be for man than, after losing the glory of this likeness of his Creator, to fall into the shapeless and irrational likeness of beasts and cattle?

Therefore let each person attend more carefully to the excellence of his first creation, recognize in himself the venerable image of the Holy Trinity, and strive to possess the honor of the divine likeness according to which he was created through nobility of conduct, the practice of virtue, and the dignity of merits. Thus, when what he is shall be revealed, he may appear like the one who wondrously created him according to his likeness in the first man and, more wondrously still, re-formed him in the second—that is, in himself.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. Comparison of the soul with God.

[Note: [Col. 0806] Bernard, Sermons 80–82 on the *Song of Songs*, and *Confessions*, Book 10, chapter 6.]

There is a great correspondence between God and the soul. God is life, spirit, wisdom, and love. The soul too is life and spirit, in which spirit there are wisdom and love.

God is life, and the soul too is life—similar, but different. It is similar in that it is life, in that it lives through itself, and in that it not only lives but also gives life, just as he is all these things. It is different because he is the Creator and the soul is a creature. For unless it had been created by him, it would not exist; and unless it had been given life by him, it would not live.

The soul lives by natural life even if it does not live spiritually; but such life is rather death than life, because “the death of sinners is most evil” (Ps. XXXIII, 22). The soul that lives according to the flesh is dead while living; and therefore it would have been better for it not to live than to live in this way.

The soul is life, living indeed, but not from another source than itself; and for this reason it is not so much living as it is life. Hence, when infused into the body, it gives life to it, so that the body, through the presence of life, is not life but living.

The soul was created by God—life from life, the simple from the simple, the immortal from the immortal—so that it might not be far from its Creator, to whom it appears to draw near through the simplicity of its essence and the perpetuity of its life. Although it does not live spiritually, it must nevertheless live immortally.

The soul was created great from the great and upright from the upright: great insofar as it is capable of eternal things; upright insofar as it desires things above; blessed [Note: [Col. 0807] The Medard manuscript reads, “good.”] insofar as it is united to God. For the soul upon which God’s kindness looks, humility subjects, repentance brings back, justice leads, obedience conducts, perseverance brings through, devotion introduces, purity joins, and charity unites.

The soul possesses within itself love, by which it can always remain with God—or return to him if, having been moved away with its affections, or rather its failings, it has departed from him. Of all the soul’s affections and perceptions, love alone is that in which the soul can answer its Creator, though not on equal terms, or return a reciprocal response resembling his. And if it loves less because it is lesser, nevertheless, if it loves with its whole self, nothing is lacking where the whole is present.

Renouncing all other affections, therefore, let it devote itself entirely to love alone, pouring itself wholly into love of the one to whom it must respond by returning love. For God loves in order to be loved; and when he loves, he wants nothing other than to be loved, knowing that those who love him are blessed by that very love.

Through love he comes to human beings, comes into human beings, and becomes man; and “his delights are to be with the children of men” (Prov. VIII, 31). Our delight, however, will be when we come to him, see him as he is, and become like him (I John III, 2).

Then there will be manifest vision, full knowledge, true love, firm union, undivided fellowship, perfect likeness, and blessed life, forever and beyond, through everlasting ages.

For just as the body in its resurrection will receive life and sensation, so the soul in its resurrection will receive life and sensation—that is, knowledge and love of God. That knowledge is eternal life, Truth itself affirms when it says: “This is eternal life, that they know you, the true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent” (John XVII, 3).

Love too is a sense. For just as the outer man is affected by temporal things through five senses—sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch—so the inner man in blessed life will be affected by the five ineffable things of God through ineffable love.

When he loves his God, he will love a certain light, a certain voice, a certain fragrance, a certain food, and a certain inner embrace. There shines what space cannot contain. There sounds what time cannot carry away. There is fragrant what the breeze cannot disperse. There is tasted what appetite cannot diminish. There clings what satiety cannot tear apart.

There God is seen without interruption, known without error, loved without offense, and praised without weariness.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. The soul as the city of God. Its citizens. Its counselors. Its soldiers. Its common people. The three powers of the soul according to Plato and the physicians. Reason. Understanding. Memory. Appetite.

[Note: [Col. 0807] Bernard, Sermon 5 on the Dedication, no. 9.]

The soul is a noble creature. It is the city of God, of which such glorious things have been spoken (Ps. LXXXVI, 3), because it was made according to the image and likeness of God.

This city ought rightly to be called Jerusalem, because it was created to enjoy the vision of that supreme peace “which has made both one” (Eph. II, 14). Its mind is a paradise, in which, when it meditates upon heavenly things, it delights as in a paradise of pleasure.

The soul is also the house of the supreme head of the household, because of unity of conduct; the bride of Christ, through love; the temple of the Holy Spirit, through sanctification; and the city of the eternal King, because of the peace and harmony of its citizens.

And because no city exists without a people, our Creator arranged within it a people of three ranks: the wise, to give counsel; soldiers, to defend it; and craftsmen, to serve.

The citizens of this city are the soul’s natural and innate powers, like native inhabitants. Their ranks are distinct: some are higher, some lower, and some intermediate. The higher are intellectual senses, the middle rational senses, and the lowest animal senses.

Their difference is as follows. The animal or sensual power desires visible things. The rational power distinguishes them and rejects them with the eye of discernment. The intellectual power draws the soul toward divine things.

The intellectual senses are therefore like the soul’s counselors, saying to it: “Fear God and observe his commandments. For this is the whole of man” (Eccles. XII, 13). The rational powers are like soldiers who attack enemies—namely, desires—by the weapons of justice. The animal or sensual powers are like peasants and craftsmen who occupy themselves with bodily rudiments and provide what the body requires.

Philosophers called this threefold power of the soul—sensual, rational, and intellectual—its parts, not integral parts but powers, because they are its capacities.

Sensuality is that power of the soul by which it nourishes the body and perceives and distinguishes these external things through the bodily senses. All the senses, both external and internal, are referred to the soul, since they proceed from it; for they all receive from the soul the ability to sense.

Reason is the power of the soul placed above corporeal things and below spiritual things. It separates the true from the false, which belongs to Logic; virtues from vices, which belongs to Ethics; and investigates the natures of things through experiments, which belongs to Physics. In these three consists the whole of Philosophy. Reason therefore comprehends the whole of Philosophy.

Intellect or understanding is that power of the soul by which divine things are known insofar as this is possible for man. Reason by itself is not sufficient to penetrate heavenly mysteries unless it is aided by God. When, if it is vigorous in the right way, it reaches knowledge of the secrets it has sought through long investigation, it is called intellect or understanding.

Boethius, however, says that understanding belongs to God alone and to very few human beings; nevertheless, one term is often used in place of the other.

Memory is also a companion and co-worker of reason, since without it reason can neither proceed toward what is unknown nor retain knowledge of what has been learned. Memory is the power of the soul that retains what it has received, revisits the past, and gathers up what has slipped away.

Human appetite, placed between the highest and the lowest, is often divided between both and thus opposed to itself. When it passes wholly into one side or the other, it rightly takes the name of that side.

If it feeds upon the pleasures of the flesh, it is called carnal or animal. If it delights in spiritual desires, it is called spiritual. Appetite is a natural power implanted in a living creature for moving its senses eagerly.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. Definitions of the powers of the soul.

[Note: [Col. 0808] Hugh of Saint-Victor, *On the Union of Body and Spirit*; likewise *The Didascalicon*, Book 2, chapter 6, and Book 3, chapters 11 and 8.]

Since I have often mentioned the powers of the soul, I ought to define them, so that what has been said or is to be said about the soul may be understood more clearly.

Sensuality, sense, and imagination may be predicated both of the body and of the soul. Bodily sensuality is a certain fiery power. The sensuality or animality of the soul is its lower power, which, drawing sensuality of the flesh along with it like a servant and subordinate, produces senses and imaginings and stores them in the ark of memory.

In sense there is the instrument of sensuality [Note: [Col. 0808] Elsewhere, “sensuality.”] and the origin of imagination. For the very fiery power that, when formed externally, is called sense is called imagination when the same form has been conveyed inward to the deepest part.

Sense therefore gives birth to imagination, imagination to thought, and thought to meditation. Meditation sharpens ingenuity, ingenuity sharpens reason; reason leads to intellect, intellect to understanding; understanding, through contemplation, marvels at truth itself and, through charity, delights in it.

Sense is a passion of the soul in the body arising from qualities that occur externally. Imagination is the power of the soul that recognizes the form of corporeal things when the corporeal object is absent and without external sense.

Thought is the mind’s occupation with any matters whatsoever. Consideration is attentive thought. Meditation is frequent thought that investigates the manner, cause, and reason of each thing.

Ingenuity is a certain power naturally implanted in minds and capable of acting by itself. Reason is a certain power of the soul that distinguishes and judges all things, but especially when it longs for spiritual things and preserves the image of God within itself.

Intellect is perception of things that truly exist. Understanding is pure and certain knowledge of the principles of things alone—that is, of God, ideas, matter (*hyle*), and incorporeal substances.

Contemplation is joyful wonder at evident truth. Charity is harmony among minds and fellowship among the elect, the life of blessed souls and angels, because neither souls nor angels live except through charity.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. For what purpose the soul was made according to the image and likeness of God.

[Note: [Col. 0809] Hugh, Book 1 of *On the Sacraments of the Christian Faith*, part 6, chapter 3.]

The rational and intellectual soul was made according to the image and likeness of God so that it might know its maker by way of image and love him by way of likeness. From the image of God it possesses reason, and from likeness it possesses charity.

Charity itself represents the Trinity. Reason perceives it and seeks it in peace; charity finds it and, seeing it, rests in blessedness. In the present life faith follows it, hope accompanies it as far as heaven, and charity embraces it eternally.

Therefore let the spiritual mind, or rational understanding, first look upon its Creator; then let it see his creature; and, through the mediation of free choice, let it refer both itself and all other things to him who created everything.

Thus may the Trinity appear in man, which charity makes manifest, so that man may always display charity and may always contemplate the one whom the image of the Trinity adorns. In this way man will preserve the likeness of the one whose image he naturally bears within himself.

Let the image of God therefore appear in rational understanding, in the spiritual mind, and in the dignity of free choice. Let the likeness of God appear in conduct as regards nature, in works as regards justice, and in virtues as regards grace: so that nature may be adorned by conduct, justice demonstrated by works, and grace completed by virtues, and so that man may always present himself before the Lord.

The soul wholly and equally gives life to the entire human body. It is life breathed into man by God, not made from preexisting matter but made by him from nothing. Concerning other living creatures Scripture says: “Let the waters bring forth,” and so forth; “Let the earth bring forth the living soul” (Gen. I, 20 and 24).

But the soul was produced neither by water nor by earth; God breathed it in. Yet he did not breathe in something alive or living, but “the breath of life” (Gen. II, 7)—rational, from the image of God, made according to the likeness of God.

## CHAPTER XL. The misery of the soul that departs from God. It departs from the likeness, not from the image, of God. Souls are not generated.

The soul is not a part of God. Its mutability proves this. God is immutable; the soul, however, is often changed, sometimes condemned on account of guilt, and made miserable also as a punishment.

Yet nothing could harm it unless it had departed from God. It departed when it sinned. Therefore it is tortured in misery as a fugitive from God. Separated from the One, it is scattered among many things; and through its lack of self-control it becomes diseased and troublesome.

For this reason, when the bodily senses are disturbed and the memory unsettled, they become dull, withered, and sluggish. Hence the flesh suffers, illnesses arise, and violent death spreads abroad.

A human being turned away from God and perverted through sin, because he disagrees with God, is also at odds with himself, and bears within himself punishment from himself.

The soul is not formed from unformed matter; rather, at its creation it received the form according to which it was made in the image and likeness of God. If it turns away from him, it remains formless because it is guilty and unlike him [Note: [Col. 0809] Elsewhere, “it remains formless because it is unlike God.”]; yet it does not thereby become irrational, because it bears the image of God and can therefore be re-formed.

Nor, even if it is completely enclosed by sin and, on account of its folly, compared to a beast, does it thereby become the soul of cattle or of another body. It will always possess the very body it now has and will have at the end, with which it was made one person.

Nor does it thereby become a body, even if it is utterly dulled. It is not divided into parts or confined to a place. It is not greater in the larger parts of its body, nor smaller in the smaller parts capable of sustaining life. For the rational soul is spirit, however much evil may bury it; and wherever it is, it is wholly present.

The soul is not transferred from father to son, lest one soul belong to both. “As the soul of the father is mine,” says the Lord, “so also the soul of the son is mine” (Ezek. XVIII, 4). Nor does part of the father’s soul pour itself into the son when he begets him.

To be divided or partitioned, increased or diminished, is unknown to spirit according to its substance. It cannot become greater, but it can become better. For if it were transferred in parts, it would be proved to be corporeal.

If, as some deliriously claim, the soul’s seed were transferred in generation along with the seed of the flesh, many shameful and impossible consequences could be alleged from this—things that ought neither to be said nor imagined concerning rational spirit. For it is indecent to uncover obscenities and expose the ill-scattered seeds of the flesh.

## CHAPTER XLI. Souls are created day by day. No new creation of matter occurs after the first creation. Original sin is contracted through the flesh. The necessity of baptism.

We say that rational souls, as regards their essence, are newly made each day from nothing; but, as regards their likeness of nature, they are not new, since they arise from the divine institution. For such as God gave to the male and female at the beginning on the sixth day (Gen. I, 27), such he breathes into each person daily: a new creation from nothing, but not a new institution.

“My Father,” he says, “is working until now, and I am working” (John V, 17). The Father and the Son work until now—through a new operation, indeed, but not through a new institution—acting in accordance with the former while the latter remains at rest.

After their first creation, no new corporeal things are created; rather, those established together at the beginning are propagated through temporal formation. Souls, however, were not all made together in essence, but, because they are made according to a similar nature in the image and likeness of God, they are considered to have been made together, though they are judged not to have been brought forth together.

They were not brought forth together in essence, but they were made together with respect to the equal form granted according to the image and likeness of God. Flesh is transferred from flesh through generation, but spirit is by no means propagated from spirit.

We hold it as certain that flesh contracted from flesh, through the law of concupiscence, is burdened with the bond of original guilt as soon as it is given life; and the soul, which gives life to the flesh, is weighed down by the flesh’s affections.

Under this bond of sin are plunged infants who die without the remedy of baptism. For they possess original sin, contracted not through the soul but through the flesh and poured back upon the soul. The soul is so joined to the flesh that it is one person with the flesh.

By God’s authorship, the soul and flesh become one individual, one human being. Thus, while the proper character of each nature is preserved, what belongs to the soul is added to the flesh, and what belongs to the flesh is added to the soul—not because the natures are diverse, but because the person is one.

What is proper to each individually therefore becomes common to both: proper according to nature, common according to person. Hence the soul becomes subject to original guilt, which the flesh contracts and pours back upon the soul with which it is united in person, although it is distinct from it in nature.

For this reason an infant must, while it lives, be renewed by Christ’s sacrament, lest the fellowship of sinful flesh harm its soul. Even when separated from the body, the soul remains burdened by that fellowship unless, while it lives in the body, it has been cleansed by a saving remedy.

Let adults therefore run—let them run for themselves. Let them also administer the sacraments of faith to infants; let them receive Christ’s faith together with the sacraments, so that the faith of the Church may protect infants reborn in Christ, and works of faith may accompany adults together with the sacraments.

When these too have been renewed through grace [Note: [Col. 0810] The Medard manuscript reads, “renewed through the grace of faith.”], it will finally be completed in the general resurrection: the flesh itself will rise in glory, restored to its soul, living and eternal, happy and blessed.
