## CHAPTER XLII. Why the soul is given to the unbaptized. What nature is. The breath of life.

If it is asked why [Col. 0811] God gives souls to those who happen to die without a saving remedy, we answer that the divine institution by which things and the natures of things are created is neither removed by sin nor hindered by violence.

For this reason the law of carnal union is not deprived of its own power even among the wicked. Adulterers, fornicators, and profane people beget children; yet the natural institution does not perish even in such cases.

Nature, insofar as God instituted it, performs what belongs to it. Nature is a certain power and capacity implanted by God in things for their creation, which grants each thing its own being. By this power, whoever uses a good thing badly is judged to be evil.

For those who misuse what is permitted are rightly punished. Those who attempt to seize what is not permitted are rightly punished as well. Thus Satan lost heaven, and thus the first-formed man lost paradise.

Those who stain God’s good things through forbidden uses misuse what is permitted. They stain God’s good things who, with the ardor of lust, perform the acts of carnal union. From these, children are generated, whose bodies are formed by the creature serving the Creator and are animated, as God breathes into them the breath of life.

Understand the breath of life as the human soul, which is produced neither by earth nor by water, but breathed in by God. Through it the bodily senses are animated, and hence man is said to have been made into a living soul.

In these matters and in others the Almighty acts according to the order he established. No good things assist him, nor do evil things impede him. He advances the good through his grace; he terrifies the wicked through his justice [Note: [Col. 0811] The Medard manuscript reads: “He indeed goes before the good; and afterward, he restrains the wicked.”]

We servants, while misusing the good things of the Lord, are found at once guilty and miserable. But the Lord himself, who makes good use of the evils of his servants, is worshiped as holy and almighty.

He breathes a soul, according to his institution, into the earthly body propagated from the transmission of sin [Note: [Col. 0811] The Medard manuscript reads, “from the path”], making good use of our inborn transgression—which, if it were natural, could be charged to the Creator.

But the Creator prepares sacraments at every time and mercifully proposes commands of obedience, so that the sacraments may be a remedy against sin and observance of temporal commandments may bring eternal rewards.

Therefore, if some infants born under sin die without a saving remedy, fear the justice of God, who owes nothing to anyone but condemns in each person the evil he did not himself commit in them.

But if he renews infants through the sacraments, marvel at God’s mercy. Just as they do not know the guilt with which they are born from the flesh, so they do not know the grace by which they are renewed through Christ.

Their ignorance does not excuse infants from guilt; nor does their ignorance exclude grace from them. Do you seek guilt in them? You find it transmitted from the flesh. Do you seek grace in them? You find it bestowed by God.

The former is justly condemned; the latter is freely granted. The former proclaims judgment; the latter displays mercy. In both, God is recognized, to whom mercy and judgment are sung in perpetual praise (Ps. C, 1).

But in contemplating these things, let our mind—our feeble mind, weighed down by sins—return more quickly to itself and seek a remedy for itself, so that what fell in Adam may rise again in Christ.

## CHAPTER XLIII. On the nature of the soul. The death of man.

[Note: [Col. 0811] Thus Hugh of Saint-Victor, *The Didascalicon*, Book 1, chapter 11, and Book 4, chapter 12.]

The ancients are found to have said many things about the nature of the soul, but nothing in such a way that something does not still seem to remain unsaid. I have therefore carefully gathered from their statements, as far as I could, this brief and certain account and tried to reduce it to a single whole that might be committed to memory.

For human memory is weak and delights in brevity; and if it is divided among many things, it becomes weaker in each.

Man consists of body and soul. Whatever is seen by bodily eyes was made for the sake of the body; the body was made for the sake of the soul; and the soul for the sake of God.

The life of the body is the soul; the life of the soul is God. The soul is immortal because it lacks flesh; nor does it have anywhere to fall so as to require resurrection after ruin, unless it has fallen through sin.

Therefore, in death our life does not perish; rather, the soul abandons the body. As it departs, it does not lose its power, but leaves behind what it had given life to and, insofar as it is concerned, brings about the death of another without itself receiving death. It brings it about, I say, by not giving life to what it abandons, not by losing that by which it lives.

The death of man, therefore, is nothing other than the decline of the flesh. When the power of the soul that gives life has departed from it, the flesh returns to the earth from which it was taken, having lost the senses that it did not possess through itself.

The soul gives life to the flesh, when it comes to it, no otherwise than the sun gives light to the day; and when it departs, it brings about death. Yet death does not consume what was joined; it divides it, returning both to their origin.

And lest anyone think that the soul is consumed by the death of the body, let him hear what the Lord says in the Gospel: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul” (Matt. X, 28).

The body is wearied by the thoughts of the mind; the mind is affected in the body by the pains of the body.

## CHAPTER XLIV. The soul is invisible. Reason is the mirror in which it sees God.

[Note: [Col. 0812] From Hugh, *On the Sacraments*, book 1, part 3, chapters 6 and 7.]

The body consists of the four elements. The soul is neither an element nor made from the elements, but was created from nothing and is known only to its Creator. From all these things, therefore, that it sees visibly in itself—that is, in its body—it sees that it is not, and cannot be, any of them. Let it therefore separate and distinguish itself by itself from that whole which it sees visibly within itself; and in what it sees itself to be, yet sees itself unable to be seen, let it recognize that it is altogether invisible. Then let it raise itself above itself and contemplate the invisible God in that which is first and principal among mirrors for contemplating God, and which has been made most nearly and congenially akin to His image and likeness. This is reason itself, and the mind using reason, which was made according to the first likeness of God so that it might discover by itself the One by whom it was made, and sweetly rest in His love and contemplation. For those things reveal their maker more perfectly which approach more closely to His likeness. This, moreover, is the rational creature itself, which was made both especially and properly according to His likeness. It recognizes and loves its Creator, whom it does not see, all the more readily when it understands that it was made according to His image.

[Note: [Col. 0812] In the manuscripts the following material, up to chapter 45, is absent. In its place, the Medardus manuscript has: “Therefore the love of God is the efficient cause of the rational creature, and participation in divine goodness is its final cause.”]

The rational mind understands itself by thinking, and possesses an image of itself born from itself; this image is its word. For the word of a thing is the thing’s very cognition, formed according to its likeness from memory. In this way it clearly appears that the supreme Wisdom, when it understands itself by expressing itself, generates a likeness consubstantial with itself—that is, its Word. The rational mind, however, since it does not always think of itself, although it always remembers itself, evidently gives birth to its word from memory whenever it thinks of itself. Hence it is clear that, if it always thought of itself, its word would always be born from memory. But concerning the supreme Wisdom, which always expresses itself in the way in which it is always mindful of itself, it is clear that its coeternal Word is born from eternal memory. For just as the supreme Wisdom is eternal, so it is eternally mindful of itself; it eternally understands itself and eternally expresses itself, since for it to express itself is the same as to understand itself. And since it eternally expresses itself, its Word is eternally with it.

Let the rational mind, therefore—the only one among all creatures capable of rising to investigate supreme Wisdom, and likewise the only one capable of advancing toward its discovery—always strive to remember, understand, and love it. It was made for this purpose: to live forever, provided that it always loves the supreme Life, the supreme Wisdom, the supreme Being, to whom it owes the very fact that it is. But it cannot love Him unless it remembers Him and strives to understand Him. Let it therefore do that for which it was made, so that it may live well.

## CHAPTER XLV. The threefold condition of rational beings. The threefold power of the soul. What love is

[Note: [Col. 0812] Hugh of Victor, book 1 of *The Sacrament of Faith*, part 6, chapter 1; likewise *On the Union of Body and Spirit* and *On the Substance of Love*, chapter 2.]

Almighty God, whose blessedness can neither increase, because it is perfect, nor diminish, because it is eternal, created rational spirits solely through love, without any necessity of His own, in order to make them participants in His blessedness. Some He confirmed in heaven in their purity; others, because of their pride, He hurled into hell; and still others He joined to earthly bodies in an earthly dwelling, so that, to test their humility and obedience, they might animate clayey matter to the perception of life.

For in their nature they possess a certain mutability by which they draw near to bodies in order to give them life, and in this they lay aside something of their own purity. When they are affected by bodily pleasure, they draw from it, as it were, a kind of corporeality, which corrupts their purer nature. The more deeply this fault has clung to them while they remain in bodies, the more difficultly does it leave them when they depart from their bodies, since a passion is not removed when the cause of the passion is removed unless, during this life, they have striven to cleanse themselves of such defilement.

We, therefore, who are placed between good and evil, ought often to consider both the joy of those above and the punishment of those below, as well as our own misery. Our soul is rational, so that it may know how to distinguish between good and evil. It is also desiring and spirited—that is, capable of desire and anger—so that it may love good and hate evil. Love arises from desire; from love arise desire and joy. Love is the delight of a heart directed toward something for the sake of something, running forward through desire and coming to rest through joy: through desire when seeking, and through joy when enjoying.

The human heart is good, if it is good, for no other reason than that it loves well what is good. It is evil, if it is evil, for no other reason than that it loves badly what is good. Everything that exists is good; vice lies only in loving it wrongly.

Hatred arises from the irascible power. Anger generates hatred, and from hatred come sorrow and fear. When we grow angry at our sins and begin to hate them, we grieve because we have sinned and fear the punishments due for our sins.

## CHAPTER XLVI. The differing lot of the rational creature. For what purpose the soul was given four affections. The purpose of reason

Thus God, the Creator of all things, chose to illumine the rational nature more fully than the other things, and above the other things, that He created. He made it distinguished by His likeness and wished it to share in His blessedness. Although the origin of this rational creature appears similar, its condition became diverse: one part of it was established in eternal happiness; another, dragged down by the ropes of hell and handed over to Tartarus, is kept for judgment and punishment (II Peter 2:4); and a third part, joined to earthly bodies, is known to have received an intermediate place.

At first this intermediate part, being nearer to the highest, had been placed amid the delights of paradise; now, because of the guilt of disobedience, it has been humbled in a place of affliction and is nearer to the lowest. The highest place among all these has complete joy; the lowest has only sorrow. There is complete happiness in the former; in the latter there is only utter misery. In the middle, however, the highest things are to be hoped for, but nevertheless the lowest are to be feared. Hence we have now greater reason for fear than for hope, since we, cast down into the very shadow of death, live nearer to those lowest regions.

Since God knew that the human soul could become a participant both in that blessedness and in that eternal condemnation, according to the quality of its merits, He implanted in it four natural affections, so that it might have the means both to desire those good things and eventually rejoice in them, and conversely to fear those evil things or even to be continually saddened by sorrow in them.

Meanwhile, the present condition is all the more grievous because it not only displays present sadness and distress, but fear itself has its punishment, and hope deferred afflicts the soul. The most merciful Father and terrible Judge, who has prepared those true and everlasting joys for His children and equally everlasting sufferings for the guilty at the end, nevertheless wished us to receive in the present some experiences of joy or sorrow, so that those future realities might not only be believed with greater certainty but also desired and feared with deeper feeling.

Yet present joys are not joys in comparison with those joys, nor is present sadness sadness in comparison with that sadness. Nor would someone be foolish if, in the meantime, he preferred to devote all his efforts to making himself able to desire those joys and fear those pains rather than to avoiding the troubles of this life and seeking its pleasures. Nevertheless, even in the present one can find reasons for useful joy and salutary sorrow: one may rejoice in God’s benefits while giving Him thanks and exulting in devotion to Him, and one may lament one’s own sins or those of one’s neighbors.

Therefore, by divine arrangement, reason was established in the human heart between these affections, so that through it a person might discern and judge what he should rejoice or grieve over, and even what he should desire or fear. Those who taught that the soul has three powers—rational, irascible, and concupiscible—seem to have included the diverse affections, joined by a certain kinship, under the irascible power as fear and sadness, and under the concupiscible power as desire and joy.

## CHAPTER XLVII. Man between the world and God

[Note: [Col. 0814] Hugh, book 2, *On the Vanity of the World*.]

Meanwhile, as the human soul fluctuates among various affections, it must eventually receive a fixed dwelling either in the depths or in the heights, and thereafter persist in joy alone or in sorrow alone. God is in the heights; the world is in the depths. God always remains in the same state of His eternity. The world, unstable always in its course of mutability, continually flows onward.

The human spirit, placed, as it were, in the middle by a certain excellence of its condition, rises above this mutability below, yet has not reached that true immutability which is with God. If it plunges itself through desire into the things below that pass away, it will immediately be swept along through endless distractions and, divided from itself in a certain way, will be scattered. But if it raises itself from this endless distraction below, abandons these lowest things, and gradually gathers itself into unity, learning to be with itself, then it will be gathered into unity all the more as it is raised upward in thought and desire, until at last it becomes altogether immutable and reaches that true and unique immutability which is with God, where it rests forever without any changeability or variation.

## CHAPTER XLVIII. The origin of souls. Free choice. Election

[Note: [Col. 0814] Gennadius, *On Ecclesiastical Dogma*, chapters 14–18.]

We believe that souls did not exist from the beginning together with the angels, nor were they created simultaneously, as Origen imagines. Nor are they sown through sexual intercourse together with bodies, as the Luciferians [Note: [Col. 0814] Three Vatican manuscripts read *Lucifer*; others, *Luciferianus*.] and Cyril, along with certain presumptuous Latins, assert. Rather, we say that only the Creator of all knows their creation; that only the body is sown through the union of marriage; that by God’s judgment it is coagulated in the womb and joined together and formed; and that, once the body has been formed, the soul is created and infused, so that a human being composed of soul and body may live in the womb and emerge alive from the womb, complete in human substance.

Nor do we believe that there are two souls in one human being, as many write: one animal soul, by which the body is animated and which is mixed with the blood, and another spiritual soul, which supplies reason. Rather, we say that there is one and the same soul in a human being, which both gives life to the body through its association with it and orders itself through its reason. It possesses freedom of choice, so that in the thought of its own substance it may choose what it wills.

Man has indeed been entrusted to the freedom of his own choice. After he fell through the serpent’s deception by means of Eve (Genesis 3:6), he lost the good of nature and likewise the strength of free choice, but not choice itself, lest what he had to correct—the sin—not belong to him. The freedom of choice therefore remains for seeking salvation, that is, the will of reason, but only after God has first admonished and inspired him toward salvation.

To consent to saving inspiration lies within our power; to attain what we desire to attain is a divine gift [Note: [Col. 0814] The Medardus manuscript adds, “and partly a matter of our own concern.”]. Not to fall away after receiving the gift of salvation depends on our diligence and equally on heavenly assistance; to fall away depends on our power and laziness.

We believe that only human beings possess a substantial soul, which, once separated from the body, lives and vividly retains its senses and faculties. It does not die together with the body, as Aratus [Note: [Col. 0815] Two manuscripts read *Arabs*; another, *Arabes*.] asserts, nor does it later perish, as Zeno says, because it lives substantially.

The souls of animals, however, are not substantial. They are born together with the flesh through the vitality of the flesh itself and come to an end with the death of the flesh. Therefore they are not governed by reason, as Plato and Alexander suppose, but are driven by every impulse of nature.

The human soul does not die with the flesh, because neither, as we said above, is it sown with the flesh. Rather, once the body has been formed in the mother’s womb, we have said that it is created and infused by God’s judgment, so that the human being may live within the womb and thus proceed by birth into the world.

The soul, having its beginning from the Creator, is perfect in its own kind from the moment it exists. Consequently, from the moment it exists it would know everything that can be known by a human being, were it not for the heaviness of the flesh. This can be demonstrated by the first human being, who, before the corruption of humanity, possessed perfect human knowledge from the moment he came into existence.

But now, with humanity corrupted, the soul is corrupted from the moment it is joined to that corruption. It cannot exercise its own properties until, stimulated by use, experience, and someone’s instruction, it begins to distinguish—just as someone with a keen power of sight, if thrust into darkness, cannot see there until he first becomes accustomed to the darkness or a light is kindled.

Hence Virgil writes:

> “How much harmful bodies impede.” (*Aeneid* 6.731)

Although the body has some actions and the soul other actions, the vices or virtues of the body can nevertheless belong to the soul. For the soul was given for this purpose: to correct the unlawful movements of the flesh. When these occur through ignorance or negligence, the soul is implicated. Just as, if a pupil or servant sins through the negligence of his teacher or master, the teacher or master is not free from blame, so the soul is not free from blame when such things occur, since it ought to command while the body ought to obey.

## CHAPTER XLIX. The senses also exist in the inner man. Devotion to meditation

[Note: [Col. 0815] From Gennadius, *On Ecclesiastical Dogma*, chapters 19 and 20; Hugh, *On the Method of Prayer*, chapter 1. This material also appears in Anselm’s *Meditations*, 7; some passages in that meditation are found in Hugh’s *Book on the Soul’s Earnest Money*.]

Man consists of only two substances, soul and flesh: the soul with its reason, and the flesh with its senses. Yet the flesh does not move these senses without the soul’s association, whereas the soul retains its rational faculty even without the flesh.

It must nevertheless be noted that the very senses described in the outer man are likewise manifested, in their own manner, in the inner man, because spiritual things must be examined not by bodily senses but by spiritual ones. Thus the divine voice says in Deuteronomy: “See that I am God, and there is no other besides me” (Deuteronomy 32:39). And in the Apocalypse: “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches” (Revelation 2:29). And in the Psalter: “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet” (Psalm 33:9). And the Apostle says: “We are the good odor of Christ, both among those who are perishing and among those who are being saved” (II Corinthians 2:15). And in the Gospel the Lord shows that the woman touched Him by faith rather than bodily, saying: “Someone touched me, for I too perceived that power had gone out from me” (Luke 8:46).

Thus, with every precaution, we must observe what pertains to the senses of the body and what pertains to the dignity of the soul, lest a confused order and irrational judgment should anywhere appear to conflict with the truth. There is no third spirit in the substance of man, as Didymus contends; rather, the spirit is the soul itself. It is called “spirit” either because of its spiritual nature or because it breathes within the body. The soul, however, is so called because it animates the body for living or gives it life.

As for the third element, which the Apostle introduces together with soul and body—“spirit” (I Thessalonians 5:23)—let us understand it as the grace of the Holy Spirit. The Apostle prays that this grace may remain complete in us, lest through our fault it be diminished or driven away from us, because “the Holy Spirit will flee from deceit and will withdraw from thoughts that are without understanding” (Wisdom 1:5).

Let us therefore exercise our mind in constant meditation and consider our miseries and necessities, our labors and sorrows. We entered this life mourning; we live with labor; and we shall depart with sorrow and fear. Let us consider how brief our life is, how slippery the way, how certain death, and how uncertain the hour of death.

Let us consider with how many bitter things anything sweet or pleasant that beguiles us in its encounter along the way of this life is mixed; and how how deceptive and suspect, how unstable and transitory, is everything that the love of this world brings forth, and everything that temporal appearance or beauty promises.

Let us also consider the beauty, sweetness, and delight of our heavenly homeland. Let us attend to and weigh from where we have fallen and where we lie; what we have lost and what we have found, so that from both we may understand how greatly we ought to mourn in this exile. Hence Solomon says: “He who increases knowledge increases sorrow” (Ecclesiastes 1:18), because the more a person understands his evils, the more deeply he sighs and groans.

## CHAPTER L. What meditation is. Knowledge. Compunction. Devotion. Prayer. Affection

[Note: [Col. 0816] This material also appears in the appendix to Bernard, *On Conscience*, chapter 29.]

Knowledge of oneself must be preferred to other kinds of knowledge. Meditation gives birth to knowledge, knowledge to compunction, compunction to devotion, and devotion perfects prayer.

Meditation is frequent thought: investigating obscure things with curiosity and insight, and bringing hidden things into awareness. Knowledge exists when a person is enlightened concerning self-knowledge through continual meditation. Compunction exists when, through consideration of one’s evils, the heart is touched by inward sorrow. Devotion is a pious and humble affection directed toward God: humble through awareness of one’s own weakness, pious through consideration of divine clemency. Prayer is devotion of the mind—that is, turning toward God through a pious and humble affection. Affection is a spontaneous and sweet inclination of the spirit itself toward God. Nothing inclines God so strongly toward pity and mercy as a pure affection of the mind.

People usually praise and love knowledge of heavenly and earthly things, but those are much better who place before such knowledge the knowledge of themselves. The mind that knows its own misery is more praiseworthy than one that, without considering that misery, investigates the courses of the stars and the natures of things.

But when someone has already awakened to God, stirred by the warmth of the Holy Spirit, and has become contemptible in his own sight before God and, wishing to enter into Him but unable to do so, attends to himself because God’s light shines upon him, he discovers himself and recognizes that his sickness cannot be brought into harmony with God’s purity. He finds it sweet to weep and to pray that God may have mercy on him and strip away his entire misery.

Knowledge does not puff up this needy and sorrowful person, because love builds up. He has preferred one knowledge to another: to know himself and his weakness rather than to know the powers of herbs and the natures of animals. By adding this knowledge, he has added sorrow—the sorrow, namely, of his pilgrimage [Note: [Col. 0816] Erasmus, Lyons, Venice, and Louvain read this passage as follows: “And by adding this knowledge, he added sorrow, that is, the deficiency of his pilgrimage.”] arising from his desire for his homeland and for the vision of God, whom to behold is the end [Note: [Col. 0816] Here the book ends in all our manuscripts, as it does in Hugh and Alcher. Nevertheless, what follows does not indicate another author.]: “to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen.” [Note: [Col. 0816] Erasmus and Venice omit “whom to behold is the end: to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen.” In Lyons these words are enclosed in brackets, with the marginal note: “The old copies ended here with these words.”]

The one who is held in exile grieves because he is kept from the kingdom. He grieves when he remembers what and how many evils he has committed and how intolerable the punishments are that he will suffer for them.

## CHAPTER LI. Attention to and examination of oneself. Faulty considerations

[Note: [Col. 0816] See the cited book *On Conscience*, chapter 43; see also *Mecapp.*, 6.3; and Hugh, *On the Formation of a Novice*, chapter 9.]

Since no knowledge is better than that by which a person knows himself, let us examine our thoughts, words, and deeds. What does it profit us if we investigate the natures of all things with subtlety and comprehend them effectively, yet do not understand ourselves?

Let us examine what we have done, to see whether we did it as we ought; and let us consider what we are going to do, to see whether it is according to God. Careful self-examination is extremely necessary for us, so that through experience of what we have done we may become more cautious about what must be done.

Often the work that we believe was begun with good intention plunges us all the more quickly into the snare of deception because, secure about the beginning of our intention, we do not watch the end of the action. Thus, unwisely, we run along what seems a level path toward a pit: we see what we are doing, but we do not attend to what ought to follow as the outcome [Note: [Col. 0817] In Hugh: “what has been done.”] of our action.

For the affection of the mind is so ambiguous that we cannot distinguish the quality of its intention unless we examine the end of the work. Moreover, we must summon our life to judgment every day and examine what we have done through night and day: how much more readily than usual we have been inclined to do good, and how much more steadfastly than usual to overcome evil; whether in any action we have been tripped by the enemy’s snares; and how, finally, by the evidence of the deception already experienced, we may guard against his future fraud. Thus neither a temptation that suddenly arrives may cast us unprepared into an evil deed, nor may present negligence deceive us, undiscerning, in a good work.

Whoever exercises his heart in this kind of discipline should hear what a certain wise man says: “Know yourself.” Know where you came from and where you are going; how you live; how much you are advancing or declining; how far you are from God or how near—not by distance of place, but by the likeness or unlikeness of your conduct.

Know how you are a human being, whose conception is guilt, whose birth is misery, whose life is punishment, and whose death is necessity. It is certain that you will die, but uncertain how, when, or where. Since death awaits you everywhere, if you are wise you will await it everywhere.

Pay close attention, therefore, to what you do and what you ought to do: whether you do what must be done; whether you mix any evil with a good work; whether you complete the good you do with as much devotion as is required; whether you love another’s good as your own; whether you rebuke your own evil as though it belonged to another; and whether you turn away from evil in such a way that you do good.

Some people pay attention only to the evils they do not commit. Fearfulness keeps these people from good works, lest evil should steal upon them. Others pay attention only to the good things they do. They take such pleasure and comfort in their good work that they are not at all frightened by the admixture of wickedness.

Others are wise enough to do evil but do not know how to do good. These worst of all rejoice when they have done evil and exult in the most wicked things. Still others seek God through external things while abandoning their interior selves, in which God is interior.

## CHAPTER LII. The three degrees of knowledge. Expansion of the mind. Elevation of the mind. Ecstasy of the mind. The human mind as a mirror, darkened by sin. How it is to be wiped clean

[Note: [Col. 0817] From Hugh of Victor, *On the Moral Ark*, book 3, chapter 6.]

Let us therefore return to ourselves, so that we may be able to ascend to ourselves. There are three ascents.

In the first, we ascend from these external and lower things to ourselves. In the second, we ascend to the deep heart (Psalm 63:7); for the more we advance, the higher we ascend. Whoever does not ascend descends, and whoever does not advance falls back. In the third ascent, we ascend to God.

The first ascent takes place through consideration and contempt of the world. By considering how perishable and transitory earthly things are, we despise them and return to ourselves. The second ascent takes place through knowledge and contempt of ourselves. When we recognize how inclined we are toward evil and how weak we are toward good, we despise ourselves and ascend above ourselves.

The third ascent takes place through knowledge and love of God. This third ascent occurs through expansion of the mind, elevation of the mind, and ecstasy of the mind.

Expansion of the mind occurs when, within a single act of mental vision, we perceive many things—whether concerning God’s wisdom, His power, or His complete goodness. We ought to contemplate how powerfully God created all things from nothing, how wisely He governs them, and how kindly He dispenses everything. He made the whole world, so beautifully ordered, for the sake of bodies; bodies for the sake of souls; and souls for His own sake.

Therefore we must carefully guard our souls, so that we may be able to return them clean and holy to God, from whom we have received such great goods for their sake.

Elevation of the mind occurs when we are raised from visible things to invisible things. When we consider human dignity, we marvel at God’s condescension, by which He created the rational spirit so wonderfully according to His image and likeness.

The ecstasy of the mind occurs when the mind is carried above itself. No one can be instructed about this excess of mind, because there it has nothing of itself. But it can be instructed about the expansion and elevation of the mind, because there it retains something of itself. It is instructed sometimes by human effort, sometimes by divine revelation or inspiration.

At times a person beholds himself and God in the mirror of his heart—that is, in the rational mind. For the human heart was formed in such a way that the Lord might dwell in it as in a temple and shine back in it as in a kind of mirror, so that He who could not be seen in Himself might appear visibly in His image.

Great indeed is the dignity of man: to bear the image of God, continually behold His countenance within himself, and always have Him present through contemplation. But after we scattered our delight upon the earth by sinning, the dust of sin was thrown over our heart. Therefore, falling from that inner mirror of contemplation [Note: [Col. 0818] In Hugh: “those mirrors . . .”], we slip into the miserable darknesses of this present life, where we cannot worthily serve God, because we are wrapped in the filth of iniquity and the darkness of ignorance and, to a great extent, no longer see what we ought to do or avoid.

Let us therefore wipe our mirror clean of love of vanity and love of iniquity—that is, of dust and filth—so that in it we may be able to behold both ourselves and our Creator, whom by sinning we have placed behind our backs. We have indeed turned away from God; our sins separate us from Him. Therefore let us say with the prophet: “Turn us, O God our Savior” (Psalm 84:5).

If women, when they lose the mirror in which they look at their faces, diligently seek it and carefully wipe it clean of dust and filth, how much more ought we both to find, wipe clean, and inspect the mirror of the inner man, so that in it we may be able to detect all our ugliness and thus arrive through knowledge of ourselves at knowledge of God.

## CHAPTER LIII. Two things necessary for self-knowledge. Man is dust and ashes. How great our thanks to God ought to be. This knowledge produces humility, love,

and so forth.

[Note: [Col. 0818] See Augustine, *Confessions*, book 2, chapter 7; see also *Manual*, chapter 25.]

Two things are necessary for us to know ourselves: namely, what we are like with respect to evil and what we are like with respect to good. We are inclined toward evil, and if God’s mercy did not hold us back, we could fall into every vice and could not rise from it unless God’s mercy followed after us and lifted us up.

The prophet knew this well when he said: “O Lord, your mercy is before my eyes” (Psalm 25:3)—the mercy that guards me—and, “Your mercy shall follow me” (Psalm 23:6)—the mercy that raises me up.

We are weak with respect to good, and without God’s grace we cannot do good or persevere in any good. The Apostle also knew this when he said: “By the grace of God I am what I am,” and, “His grace toward me was not in vain” (I Corinthians 15:10): His grace remains in me.

Abraham possessed this twofold knowledge of himself when he said: “I shall speak to my Lord, although I am dust and ashes” (Genesis 18:27).

Man truly is dust. For just as dust is driven by whatever part of the wind pushes it and is cast onto another patch of ground, where it remains, so man can fall into every vice and cannot rise again unless God’s mercy comes to his aid.

Man is also ashes, because just as ashes produce no shoot from themselves and do not make the seed they receive germinate, so man can neither do good nor persevere in any good without God’s grace.

Therefore we ought to give the greatest thanks to God, because He has both granted us many good things [Note: [Col. 0819] Erasmus, Lyons, and Venice read this way. In B., “many good things have been granted.”] and forgiven us many evils that we have committed, and has preserved us from many evils that we could have committed, just as we committed many others.

For whatever evil we did not commit, we did not commit because He had mercy on us. If He Himself had permitted it, we would certainly have committed those evils, either in deed or in will. Therefore I do not know whether we ought to love Him more for the things He has forgiven us or for the things from which He has kept us free.

Although we did not commit those things, we ought to consider ourselves as having committed them and Him as having forgiven them, since we would certainly have committed them in will if He had permitted it.

Whoever truly knows himself in this way is humble before God and human beings. He loves God for God’s sake and all human beings for God’s sake. If he possesses perfect love, he judges no one, accuses no one, condemns no one; he does not preserve anger, stir up quarrels, sow discord, support wrongdoers, persecute the innocent, or hate those who rebuke him. He commits no theft, bears no false witness, swears no false oath; he slanders no one, harms no one, hates no one, but loves everyone.

It is written: “Owe no one anything, except to love one another” (Romans 13:8). Love is so closely united to God that it does not wish to dwell in anyone in whom love is absent. Whoever therefore has love has God, because “God is love” (I John 4:16). And whoever hates even one person loses God and the good that he does.

Therefore let each person take care not to lose God and every good thing because of hatred for one person.

## CHAPTER LIV. Man’s twofold good. The twofold sense. The purpose of his actions. Knowledge of the Trinity guided by reason
[Note: [Col. 0819] From Hugh of Saint-Victor, *On the Sacraments of the Christian Faith*, book 1, part 6, chapters 5 and 6, and part 3, chapter 21. See also the same author, *Summary of Sentences*, treatise 1, chapter 6; likewise *The Instruction of Scholars*, book 7, chapters 21 and 23, and *Manual*, chapter 26.]

Now let us return to our mirror and see how, through knowledge of ourselves, we may ascend to knowledge of God himself. Human nature is twofold. One part is interior, which is the human being himself, since each person’s mind is that person; the other is exterior, namely, the body. Humanity is composed of these two natures, and therefore, so that the whole person might be blessed, God prepared two goods for him from the beginning: one visible, the other invisible; one corporeal, the other incorporeal. Thus, in the one, the sense of the flesh might be nourished for enjoyment; in the other, the sense of the mind might be filled for happiness.

For this reason the rational soul was endowed with a twofold sense, so that it might apprehend visible things through the sense of the flesh and invisible things through the sense of the mind, so that visible and invisible things might stir it to knowledge and love of the Creator. For the intention of all human actions ought to run toward this end: either that the likeness of the divine image in us may be restored, or that provision may be made for the necessities of this life.

Those things, however, that restore the divine likeness in us are two: the contemplation of truth and the practice of virtues, because a human being is like God in being wise and just. Those things manifest their author more perfectly that approach more closely to his likeness. This is especially true of the rational mind, which was made properly and preeminently in his likeness. It recognizes its Creator, whom it does not see, more quickly when it understands that it itself was made in his likeness.

Here, then, the first trace of the Trinity is discovered: when the mind began to recognize what it was in itself, and from this considered what was above itself. For it saw that wisdom, which is in it, arises from itself; and it loves its own wisdom. Love proceeds from the mind and its wisdom, by which it loves what was generated from itself and, remaining in itself, does not divide it from itself. Thus three things appear in one: mind, wisdom, and love.

Wisdom is from the mind, and from the mind and wisdom love proceeds. A trinity arises, yet unity does not depart; trinity and unity exist together.

So it is in us. But reason teaches us that it is far better so in God. Since God is the source of all wisdom, he has always possessed wisdom, has always loved it, and, because he has always loved it, has always possessed love. He himself generated the wisdom he possesses, and it has always been with him, because what is generated does not divide itself from its generator. It is always being generated because it is eternal; it is always generated because it is perfect. It neither begins when it is generated nor ceases when it has been generated.

He who generated is the Father; he who was generated is the Son; and he who proceeds from both is the Holy Spirit. The Father is from no one; the Son is from the Father alone; the Holy Spirit is from the Father and the Son together. We must confess that these three exist substantially as one in God. [Note: [Col. 0820] Hugh has *unum*, “one.”]

But since he who is generated cannot be the one from whom he was generated, and since he who proceeds from the generator and the generated cannot be both the one who generates and the one who is generated, we are compelled by an unconquerable reasoning of truth to recognize in the Godhead a trinity of persons, a unity of substance, and equality of majesty.

The Father, the Son, and the love of the Father and the Son are one God, and they love one another with one love, because they are one. Nor is there anything that each loves in the other except what each loves in himself. Nor is there anything that each is except what the other is. Therefore each must love himself, and each must love the other in return. [Note: [Col. 0820] Hugh has: “Because there is nothing else.”]

God the Father manifested this love and this Trinity to us when, because of his great love with which he loved us (Eph. 2:4), he sent his Son in the likeness of sinful flesh (Rom. 8:3) to save us. He also sent the Holy Spirit, by whom he would adopt us as sons. He gave the Son as the price of redemption and the Holy Spirit as the privilege of love; finally, he keeps himself as an inheritance for those whom he has adopted.

## CHAPTER LV. The Names of the Trinity Are Names of Loving-Kindness. The Happiness of Eternal Life

[Note: [Col. 0820] Thus in *On Loving God*, chapter 10, from Hugh’s *On the Soul’s Earnest Money*; likewise in Bernard’s or Hugh’s *Meditations*, book 1, *On the Soul*, chapter 4; and in book 7 of *The Instruction of Scholars*, chapter 21.]

Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are names of loving-kindness, names of sweetness, names of gentleness and love. For what is sweeter than the Father—and such a Father, so sweet and merciful? What is gentler than Jesus Christ? Our Savior is entirely anointed, entirely compassionate, entirely sweet and gentle. What is more lovable, sweeter, or holier than the Holy Spirit? He is the love of the Father and the Son, through whom all who are holy are holy.

Consider, then, how great is that glory, how ineffable the joy, when we come to God the Father and he places us in his kingdom as sons and heirs; Jesus Christ receives us as brothers and co-heirs; and the Holy Spirit makes us one spirit with them. For he is the indissoluble bond of the Trinity and of love.

Then we shall enter into the powers of the Lord (Ps. 70:16), and shall see that city of which such glorious things have been spoken (Ps. 86:3). The life of that city is peaceful rest, tranquil peace, perpetual happiness, wondrous beauty, praiseworthy splendor, desirable delight, glorious honor, everlasting joy, continual festivity, and sweetest songs.

There are found there all the things that transform the hearts of everyone into an ineffable sweetness and delight. There are eternal joys that pour forth gentleness without bringing corruption; they continually restore and never fail, nourish and remain whole. They offer themselves to be enjoyed and remain incorruptible. The sweetness of that city pours itself forth as gentleness, its beauty as delight, and its vision as pleasure.

All beauty is there, where supreme beauty is. For how great is the beauty where the forms of all things flourish without defect, remain without passing away, endure without corruption, and are eternal without mutability? If that which is not truly beautiful is so beautiful, what is that which is beautiful?

O holy city, beautiful city, whatever is in you is altogether beautiful, sweet, delightful; it is one good, and every good is in it. Whatever good I can name is all there, because all goods are in one, and all are one.

When love and desire for so great a good touch me at times, they affect me profoundly and sweetly, and somehow draw me away from myself. Suddenly I am renewed and wholly transformed; I am carried away by affection, drawn by desire, and I begin to feel well beyond what I can express. Conscience is gladdened, the memory of all former sorrows passes into oblivion, the spirit exults, understanding grows bright, affection is kindled, the heart is illuminated, and desires rejoice.

Already I see myself somewhere else—I do not know where. For I see, though as if still from far away, choirs of Angels and Archangels singing psalms and praising God. There the work of all is one: to contemplate the wonders of God and praise him in his works. All contemplate, all rejoice, all delight in God, whose gaze is compassionate, whose face is beautiful, whose speech is sweet. He is delightful to behold, pleasant to possess, sweet to enjoy. It is always pleasing to look upon him, always to possess him, always to enjoy him, and to delight in him.

He is pleasing in himself and for his own sake; he is sufficient as merit and sufficient as reward. Nothing is sought outside him, because everything that is desired is found in him, and everything is loved in him. He is one good, and every good is in him. Only the good possess and see this good; they love and praise it with everlasting praise.

## CHAPTER LVI. The Intellectual Spirit. The Soul’s Life and Death. The Severity of Eternal Punishments. The Principal Punishment

[Note: [Col. 0821] From *Meditations*, chapter 27. Likewise Hugh of Saint-Victor, *On the Sacraments of the Christian Faith*, book 2, part 18, chapter 4; and Bernard’s *Meditations*, chapter 3.]

When I consider the nature of the soul—how it can give life to the flesh, yet cannot restrain itself in good thoughts as it desires—I discover an intellectual spirit living through the Creator’s power and giving life to the body that it sustains, yet subject to vanity and exposed to mutability. Joy often raises it up, fear afflicts it, iniquity kills it, and justice gives it life.

God is indeed the soul’s life; sin is the soul’s death. The soul that sins shall itself die (Ezek. 18:20), but the soul that judges rightly and practices justice shall live and shall not die. The soul is so immortal that it can die; so mortal that it cannot die. It is mortal through immortality and immortal through mortality.

Therefore, for the wretched there is death without death, an end without end, decay without decay, because death will always live, the end will always begin, and decay will never cease to decay. Death will destroy but will not extinguish; pain will torture but will not drive away fear; flame will burn but will not dispel darkness. There will be darkness in the fire, fear in the darkness, and pain in the burning.

Thus the reprobate, handed over to the fires of hell, will feel pain in their punishments and will be struck with fear in the anguish of pain. They will always endure and always fear, because they will live forever in endless torment, without hope of pardon or mercy—which is misery upon misery.

If, after as many thousands of years as there are hairs on all who have existed and will exist, they hoped that their punishments would end, they would endure them much more lightly. But because they have not and will not have hope, they will fail through despair and will not have the strength for their torments.

Of them it is written through Isaiah: “Their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be quenched” (Isa. 66:24), because they themselves will not be consumed. The worm will gnaw the conscience; the fire will burn the flesh, so that those who offended their Creator in heart and body may be punished in heart and body together.

When the soul has been separated from blessed life and the body has been subjected to eternal punishments, there will be fear and sorrow, mourning and pain. Then there will truly be nothing left to mourn except to weep, because repentance will then be of no benefit to anyone. There will be an executioner striking, a worm gnawing, and a fire consuming. Sins will be exposed, the guilty will be punished, and all this will be everlasting. Whoever goes to those torments will never depart.

The pain of burning will torture them outwardly; the punishment of blindness will darken them inwardly. They will see those most dreadful monsters, the demons, and their ghostlike faces. They will also see the torments of hell, and among those torments their followers whom they loved with disordered love against the commandments of God, so that the destruction of those followers may afflict them by increasing their own condemnation.

But they will not see God—which is the most wretched of all miseries. For who can say how great a punishment it will be not to see the Creator and Fashioner of all things, the Redeemer and Savior, the Son, the King of heaven and earth, and the Lord of the universe, through whom we exist, live, and possess understanding (Acts 17:28)?

## CHAPTER LVII. Prudence in Pursuing Good and Avoiding Evil. Meditating on Eternal Joys. The Mutual Joy of the Blessed. Perfect Happiness. Its Activities and Endowments

[Note: [Col. 0822] *On the Magnitude of the Soul*, chapter 34; and from *Meditations*, chapter 27.]

Therefore we must look around us on every side and guard ourselves everywhere, lest we either do what is wrong or fail to do the right things that have been commanded; and, after completing good works, lest we become puffed up in our thoughts. For many have fallen into hell through pride because of their virtues.

Let us desire good things eagerly and avoid evil things carefully, lest we do evil under the appearance of good, since vices often pretend to be virtues. Whoever remembers having committed unlawful acts should strive to abstain from what is lawful; and whoever has committed what was forbidden should cut himself off even from what is permitted.

Let him who still mourns his sin fear committing vices, and let him who remembers having transgressed in great matters rebuke himself even in small ones. However strong the mind may be in virtue, however firm in seriousness, carnal [Note: [Col. 0822] Perhaps “senses” should be added here.] senses nevertheless make a childish clamor outwardly; and unless they are restrained by a kind of youthful fervor, they drag the weakened mind toward every fleeting and frivolous thing. If the mind has been held there by long habit, when it wishes to rise it will not be able to do so, weighed down by the burden of bad habit.

Therefore, “let anyone who thinks that he stands take heed lest he fall” (1 Cor. 10:12); and if he falls, let him rise quickly through contrition of heart, confession of mouth, and sanctification of conduct. Let him be humbler within his own conscience, more fervent and ready to do penance, and more careful in guarding himself.

Whoever, from the sole desire for heavenly blessedness, despises these temporal things, loves nothing of this world, and desires only the eternal homeland is sustained by great tranquility of mind. In that tranquility a person sees God more purely when he finds himself alone with the One who alone is.

Nothing is more present than God, and nothing is more hidden than he. Let us therefore seek an inner retreat from the crowd of earthly desires, and, driving out from the secret of our heart the tumult of unlawful thoughts, let us pant with longing for intimate rest through our attention to the heavenly homeland and raise ourselves into the heights of contemplation of God.

Let us contemplate what those choirs of Angels are, what the fellowship of the blessed spirits is, what the majesty of the vision of God is, and how God will refresh his saints with the sweetness of his eternal vision. No one in this life can worthily estimate how great is the happiness of seeing God face to face, how great the sweetness of hearing that angelic melody, or how great the delight of possessing the fellowship of all the saints.

Each person will rejoice in another’s blessedness as much as in his own ineffable joy; and as many companions as he has, so many joys will he have. In that glory I see nothing more pleasing and find nothing more delightful to contemplate than the affection of intimate love, by which each person will love the other as much as himself, and will love God more than himself and all others along with himself; while God will love them more than they love themselves—and this in everlasting joy.

We shall see nothing foreign there, love nothing unsuitable, and hear nothing that offends our ears. Everything there is harmonious, everything joyful, everything peaceful. Since all heavenly ordinances are harmonious, all are secure.

There is every happiness, every gentleness, every delight and pleasantness, every beauty, and every sweetness. [Col. 0823] Whatever is useful and whatever delights is there: all riches and pleasures, all rest and every consolation. There is constant tranquility, pleasant serenity, eternal joy, joyful and beautiful praise, and complete knowledge of all good things.

For what can be lacking where God is, to whom nothing is lacking? All who are there are gods; nor is it necessary for one to say to another, “Know the Lord” (Jer. 31:34). For all know and see him; all praise and love him. They know without error, see without end, praise without weariness, and love without disgust.

They always see him and always desire to see him, for he is so desirable to behold. They always love him and always desire to love him, for he is so sweet to love. The more they love him, the more they wish to love him, for he is so delightful to enjoy.

In this delight they rest, filled with God, filled with every blessing and sanctification. Always clinging to blessedness, they are blessed; always contemplating eternity, they are eternal; joined to the light, they have become light; always gazing upon immutability, they have been changed into immutability.

With all the greater willingness, because of all the greater sweetness, they look upon him whose gaze is compassionate, whose face is beautiful, whose speech is sweet. O blessed vision—to see the King of Angels in his beauty (Isa. 33:17), to see the Holy of holies, through whom all are holy! To see him is supreme happiness, supreme delight, eternal life, and blessed life.

## CHAPTER LVIII. He Rejoices for the Godly Who Enjoy God. They Cannot Describe Their Joy to Those Who Have Not Experienced It

Rejoice and exult, you righteous, because you see the one whom you loved, possess the one whom you long desired, and hold the one whom you never fear losing. Therefore sing and exult to him, for he is your glorious and beautiful Lord God; he is salvation and life, honor and glory, peace and every good.

How great is the peace there, where none of you is opposed by anything, either by another or by himself, but the Lord himself governs you, and you shall lack nothing (Ps. 22:1)? He has appointed a kingdom for you, so that you may eat and drink at his table in his kingdom (Luke 22:29–30).

Taste, then, and see that the Lord is sweet (Ps. 34:9). He is sweet to see and sweet to taste. It cannot be said how much pleasure there is in tasting him, how much delight in his flavor, how much sweetness in his fragrance. You who have experienced it cannot communicate to us, who have never tasted such a thing, the greatness of that sweetness.

It is as though someone wished to describe the sweetness of honey in words to one who had never tasted anything sweet. Surely the one who had never received that flavor’s sweetness in his mouth would not grasp it with his ears; nor could the sweetness that the righteous person has recognized through delight be communicated in words.

## CHAPTER LIX. He Laments His Miseries. He Invokes the Saints. The Mutability of the Mind: Its Cause and Its Lesson

[Note: [Col. 0823] Hugh, book 2 of *On the Sacraments of the Christian Faith*, part 18, chapter 21. Likewise Bernard’s *Meditations*, which is found in Hugh, book 1, *On the Soul*, chapter 10.]

Woe to me, wretched man, who never feel what you feel and am not where you are! You are in a place of refreshment, light, and peace, where your existence will have no death, your knowledge no error, your love no offense, and your joy no sorrow.

But I am in the region of the shadow of death. I do not know my end; I do not know whether I am worthy of love or hatred (Eccl. 9:1); I do not know when I shall leave the body. I shall leave it, but I do not know when, and perhaps this day is the last. Therefore, trembling and afraid, I await death each day. It threatens me everywhere; I distrust the devil, who lies in wait for me everywhere; I fear and dread the final examination and the anger of the strict Judge, lest, because of my sins, he send me into the fire of Gehenna.

Just as you cannot communicate to me your joy and gladness at the vision of God, so I cannot adequately set before you the necessities and weaknesses that I suffer, the iniquities and sins that I have committed, the faults and countless negligences that I have carried out—and that I carry out daily and without ceasing—in heart, word, deed, and nearly every way in which human frailty can offend God. [Col. 0824]

You, therefore, who have deserved to become companions of the citizens above and to enjoy the glory of eternal brightness, pray for me to the Lord, that he may lead me out of this prison in which I am held captive and bound (Gen. 40:14).

For the mind is blind and restless, changing according to the quality of the things at which it looks; and according to what it beholds, its thought and perception change. When it strives to stand within itself, it nevertheless somehow departs from itself, even without knowing it; and it is driven away by weariness from each thing to which it gives its attention.

While it eagerly desires things to be considered and suddenly grows weary of the things it has considered, it learns that it depends upon something else and does not rest where it has been placed. For it is suspended from God alone, by whom it was formed.

But because everything it desires below is less than God, whatever is not God rightly does not satisfy it. Hence it is scattered here and there and distracted among innumerable things, seeking rest where rest is not. It seeks pleasant delights in which it may pause. But because it abandoned the one God, whom it could possess sufficiently, it is now led through many things, so that, since it cannot be satisfied by the quality of things, it may at least be satisfied by their variety.

## CHAPTER LX. The Necessity of Calling the Mind Back to Heavenly Things. Aspiration Toward This Task. The Glory of Heaven. The Joys of the Heavenly Citizens

Therefore we must gather our mind, which has been scattered among diverse things, and settle it upon one desire for eternity. In contemplation of the Creator we shall attain this above all: that we may enjoy steadfastness of mind. This means that, by laboring now, we should strive to imitate what we shall afterward receive with joy as a gift.

Let us therefore strive to withdraw our years from earthly cares, to withdraw them from sorrows, so that for one hour or half an hour we may be permitted to dwell in thought and longing in the city of the Lord of hosts.

Let us consider, and estimate as far as we can, what that glory is, how great the joy, what solemn celebration, what veneration, what exultation belongs to the citizens above, who continually offer praise and honor to their Ruler, offer devotion, and bring forth a new song, a song of joy, with an indescribable cry: with the most fervent love, ineffable song, wondrous affection, heavenly exultation, and spiritual melody.

For he himself is their true food, complete satisfaction, eternal dwelling, supreme blessedness of eternal joy, eternal salvation, unfailing strength, and immortal life.

I meditate on these things often; I strive to ascend there.

I sigh, I gnash my teeth; by prayers and vows I strive toward that place;

And in wondrous fashion I revolve what things are there and how great they are.

The mind clings to Christ; the heart delights in him.

There it turns, rejoices, marvels, and reveres—now all the more sweetly, the more often; with great eagerness, but no satiety—for the hour is so rare and the stay so brief.

If only I might ever sleep in peace and rest in the same place (Ps. 4:9), so that I might dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life (Ps. 27:4)! If only I might ever see him so desirable, into whom the Angels long to look (1 Pet. 1:12), so that I might say: “Behold, I see the one whom I desired; I now hold the one whom I longed for!”

When shall I come and appear before the face of the Lord (Ps. 42:3), to see him in the goodness of his chosen ones, to rejoice in the joy of his people, and to be praised with his inheritance (Ps. 106:5)? When shall I see that city of which it was said: “Your streets, Jerusalem, shall be paved with pure gold, and in you a song of joy shall be sung, and throughout all your streets all shall say, Alleluia” (Tob. 13:22)?

O holy city, beautiful city! From afar I salute you; to you I cry; I seek you. For I desire to see you and rest in you, but I am held back by the flesh and am not permitted.

O desirable city! Your wall is one stone, your guardian is God himself, and your citizens are always joyful, for they continually rejoice in the vision of God. There is no corruption in you, no defect, no old age, no anger; but everlasting peace, solemn glory, eternal joy, continual celebration. [Col. 0825] Truly there are immense joy and exultation, the flower and adornment of youth and perfect health.

There is no yesterday or former day in you, but the same present day. For your yesterday is tomorrow, and what was long ago is everlasting and the same. Salvation is yours, life is yours, infinite peace is yours; God is everything to you.

“Glorious things are spoken of you, city of God.” For the dwelling of all who rejoice is in you (Ps. 86:5, 7). There is no fear in you, no sadness; every desire passes into joy, while whatever is desired is present and whatever is longed for abounds.

All your citizens will receive an overflowing measure of joys, so that all may openly rejoice in common and rejoice without limit. All will rejoice as one, when brothers dwell together as one, when all meet together as one. Finally, all will become one, as he prayed for his family who is worthy to obtain this through his reverence:

“As you, Father, are in me and I in you, may they also be one in us” (John 17:21).

Therefore the whole of that city will rejoice; its unity will rejoice; the city will rejoice, whose fellowship is in oneness. The bride will rejoice in the kisses and embraces of the bridegroom; she will rejoice and exult in gladness, praising him forever and ever.

So also the bridegroom will rejoice over the bride (Isa. 62:5), and the Lord will rejoice in all his works (Ps. 104:31), seeing the things he made, and that they were indeed very good (Gen. 1:31). The Father too will rejoice and, through the Only-Begotten, gain many adopted sons. The Son also will rejoice as the firstborn among many brothers (Rom. 8:29), whom he will graciously admit into communion with the Father’s inheritance. Nor will the Holy Spirit, through whom they were adopted, take less pleasure in them.

With new joys and ineffable vows, those neighboring powers, the Angels, will also sing in celebration to the supreme Shepherd and supreme Good over the sheep that was found and marvelously brought back—the hundredth sheep (Luke 15:5–6).

In these the Father’s glory rejoices; in these the Spirit’s will rejoices; in these the Son exults; heaven is filled with joys. [Note: [Col. 0825] From the hymn concerning the Apostles.]

Because they have been redeemed by the Lord, they will confess with devotion and say: “For he is good, for his mercy endures forever” (Ps. 106:1). Everlasting joy will be upon them (Isa. 61:7), and the exultations of God will be in their throats forever (Ps. 149:6), and forever and ever, through perpetual eternities (Dan. 12:3).

“Blessed are all who dwell in your house, O Lord; forever and ever they will praise you” (Ps. 84:5). “They shall be inebriated with the abundance of your house, and you shall give them drink from the torrent of your delight. For with you is the fountain of life, and in your light we shall see light” (Ps. 36:9–10), when we shall see you in yourself, and ourselves in you, and you in us, in continual vision and perpetual happiness.

## CHAPTER LXI. The Seven Grades of Activity in the Soul. Contemplation of Truth. True Religion

[Note: [Col. 0825] *On the Magnitude of the Soul*, chapter 33, nos. 70–76, and chapter 36, nos. 80–81.]

The soul is simple in essence and manifold in its activities. For it has seven grades of activity by which it displays its powers and capacity. The first is giving life; the second, sensation; the third, art; the fourth, correction; the fifth, tranquility or purity; the sixth, contemplation; the seventh, rest.

At the first grade or activity, through its presence the soul gives life to the body, gathers it into one, and holds it together as one. At the second, it extends itself through the senses to arrange these external things. At the third, it comprehends various arts. At the fourth—which is where goodness and all true praise begin—it cleanses itself from defilement and prepares itself for purity.

Then, when it has been cleansed from every stain and washed free of blemishes, it possesses purity. For it is one thing to produce purity and another to possess it. Then, with immense and incredible confidence, it advances toward God—that is, toward the contemplation of truth—and this is the sixth grade.

In that vision or contemplation, which is the seventh grade, the soul remains; it rejoices, exults, and delights. For it is one thing to direct the eye of the mind toward what is to be seen [Col. 0826] and another to keep it fixed there.

We share the first grade with plants; the second with beasts; the third with the learned and the unlearned. At this third grade God binds the soul to himself—that is, he begins to lead it; he purifies it at the fourth, strengthens it at the fifth, introduces it at the sixth, and feeds it at the seventh.

But what shall I say about the pleasure in contemplating truth, the endless solemnity of the vision of God, the joy without failure of love, the ardor that does not torment but delights, the greatness of the desire for vision together with satiety, and of satiety together with desire; about the fruit of the true and supreme good, the serenity, pleasantness, delight? Certain great and holy souls, whom we believe have seen and do see these things, have spoken of them.

But if we hold with complete steadfastness to the course of life that God has set before us and that we have undertaken to follow, through God’s grace we shall reach that true and supreme good. Let us therefore devote ourselves with the utmost religious devotion, steadfastness, and vigilance to fulfilling God’s commandments, since there is no other escape from such great evils to such a great good.

True religion is that by which the soul binds itself again to God through reconciliation, from whom it had broken away, as it were, through sin.

The power of our soul claims seven activities for itself:

It gives life, senses, embraces various arts,

Corrects excesses, applies itself to virtues, and directs

Its gaze toward the Godhead itself, rejoicing in it.

The first is also present in seeds; brute animals

Share another; two belong properly to us;

Three belong to those above, though the heavenly are preferred.

From the first activity bodies are nourished and grow;

From it arise vigor, connection, structure, movement,

Position, form, and a certain harmony.

From the second it touches, sees, hears, tastes, and smells;

It hates and loves; seeks what suits it and avoids what opposes it;

It is dissolved in sleep and wanders in dreams through the mind;

It remembers the past, presses toward what is to come, and performs

Many things that are carried out by sense, but not by reason.

The third traverses various liberal arts;

Whatever either natural talent or instruction supplies,

It gathers, and through varied progress clings to minds.

The fourth recalls it from what is unlawful and teaches

The mind to renounce its guilt; then it begins

To recognize itself and learns to pass into a new beauty.

From the fifth we learn to be held by nature’s law,

To avoid forbidden things through love of virtue,

And even to abstain from some permitted things without a witness.

The sixth carries the immaculate soul into the sight

Of the sun and heavenly light, making it almost equal to those above.

The seventh binds it and gives it an earnest through steadfast [Note: [Col. 0826] A term of Late Latin meaning “to give earnest money.” M.]

Love, and joins it to God, whose dowry it now contemplates.

Who could describe the bridal chamber, the adornment,

The celebrations that make it radiant? “My bride, come,”

The blessed and the greater souls have said;

Yet they had neither the power nor the language

By which they might disclose these things;

The hidden reward surpasses sense and merit.

## CHAPTER LXII. What the Soul Ought to Be

[Note: [Col. 0826] From Bernard, sermon 83 on the *Song of Songs*, no. 1; from the same author’s sermon 85, nos. 10, 11, 12, and 1. See also his *Meditations*, chapter 8.]

Behold, my soul, you have heard what you are and what you can do. Now hear what you are and what you ought to be.

You are burdened with sins, entangled in vices, captured by allurements, a captive in exile, imprisoned in the body, clinging to mud, fixed in clay, fastened to your members, nailed to cares, stretched out by activities, constricted by fears, afflicted by pains, wandering through errors, disturbed by suspicions, anxious with worries, a stranger in the land of enemies, defiled among the dead, and assigned to those who are in hell.

If, condemned and despairing as you are, you wish to breathe again in the hope of pardon and mercy and to bear with the King of Angels the gentle yoke of love, you must be chaste, modest, truthful, fearful, watchful, admitting absolutely nothing that empties your conscience of its glory.

Let your conscience contain nothing for which you would blush before the presence of truth or be compelled to turn your face away from the light of God. And so that this beauty may delight the divine gaze, let it come forth and spread through the limbs and senses of the body, so that every action, word, look, walk, and laugh may shine forth from it. [Col. 0827]

Yet let the laugh be mingled with seriousness and full of honorable [Note: [Col. 0827] Erasmus, the Lyon edition, the Venice edition, and the Louvain edition read this passage: “and full of honorable movements.” Actions and habits, etc. M.] movement. When the movement, actions [Note: [Col. 0827] Elsewhere, “gestures.”] and habits of the whole body appear, let the conduct be pure, modest, and wholly free from insolence, wantonness, frivolity, and laziness.

Let speech be less frequent, the face more cheerful, the gaze more modest, and the walk more restrained. Such beauty of soul and nobility of mind is so careful, with a good conscience, to preserve the integrity of its reputation that, according to the Apostle, it provides what is good not only before God but also before human beings (2 Cor. 8:21).

Such beauty, having abandoned all other desires, clings to God, lives for God, and loves nothing except God and what ought to be loved for God’s sake. It diligently strives to keep the Lord always in its sight (Ps. 16:8): to whom it may consent for correction, by whom it may be illumined for knowledge; upon whom it may rely for virtue, by whom it may be restored to wisdom; to whom it may be conformed for beauty, and from whom it may enjoy delight.

Blessed is the soul to which it has been given from above both to will and to know and to be able to do good, so that the will may be present and the ability not be lacking.

Woe to me, wretched man, who preserve these things in memory and write them on paper but do not possess them in life! Not because I, who wrote these things, am such, but because I would wish to be such—and I am not ashamed that I am not. 

## CHAPTER LXIII. Seeking God. What God Is. God’s Image in Our Mind
[Note: [Col. 0827] From Anselm’s *Proslogion*, chapters 1, 22, 14, and 23.]

You have heard, my soul, what you ought to be. Flee, then, for a little while, from your occupations, and hide yourself briefly from your tumultuous thoughts. Enter the chamber of your mind, and shut out everything except God and those things that help you to seek him; and when you have found him, rest in him for a little while.

Say, then, my soul, to God: “Who are you, Lord, and as what am I to understand you?” Certainly, you alone are what you are, and you are the one who is. You are that than which nothing greater, better, or more delightful can be conceived. You are life, wisdom, light, truth, goodness, eternity, the highest good; wholly sufficient to yourself, needing nothing, while all things need you in order to exist and to exist well.

You have found, my soul, what you were seeking. For you were seeking God, and you have found him to be something supreme over all things, than which nothing greater can be conceived; and you have found that he is life, wisdom, light, truth, goodness, eternal blessedness, blessed eternity, and every true good.

This good are you, God the Father. This good is your Word, that is, your Son. You are so simple that nothing other than what you are can be born from you. This very thing is the one and common love belonging to you and your Son, that is, the Holy Spirit proceeding from both. For from supreme simplicity nothing other than what its source is can proceed.

I give you thanks, Lord my God, who have given me this grace: that I might be able to seek you and find you. For in my mind—which in your goodness you created in your image and likeness—I find three things, namely memory, understanding, and love, by which I may remember you, understand you, and love you.

For you remain in my memory from the moment when I came to know you; and in it I find you when I remember you and take delight in you. Remain, then, within it, most merciful God, so that there I may be able to find you and also rest in you. For this is my glory, these are my delights, this is the joy of my heart: when I can devote myself to you and see what you are.

For you are supreme being, supreme life, supreme wisdom, supreme salvation, supreme light, supreme truth, supreme goodness, supreme eternity, supreme greatness, supreme beauty, supreme blessedness, supreme immortality, supreme immutability, supreme unity, the highest good—in whom is every good, or rather, who is every good: the one, whole, and only good.

## CHAPTER LXIV. An awakening to reflection upon the highest good. All good things are in it.

[Note: [Col. 0827] From the same *Proslogion*, chapters 24 and 25; Bernard’s *Appendix*, *On Conscience*, chapter 14; and *The City of God*, book 22, chapters 29 and 30.]

Awaken now, my soul, and raise your whole understanding; think, as far as you can, how excellent and how great God’s goodness is. For if individual good things are delightful, consider attentively how delightful that good must be which contains the delight of all good things—not a delight of the kind we have experienced in created things, but one differing from them as greatly as the Creator differs from the creature.

If created life is good, how good is the Life that creates? If created salvation is so delightful, how delightful is the Salvation that made every salvation? If wisdom in the knowledge of created things is lovable, how lovable is the Wisdom that created all things from nothing? Finally, if there are many great delights in delightful things, what sort and what magnitude of delight are found in him who made the delightful things themselves?

O what will the person who enjoys this good be, and what will he not have? Certainly, whatever he wishes will be, and whatever he does not wish will not be. For there will be there bodily and spiritual goods such as “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor the human heart conceived” (Isaiah 64:4).

Why, then, do you wander through many things, little man, seeking goods for your soul and your body? Love the one good in which all goods are found, and it is enough. Desire the simple good that is every good, and that is sufficient.

For what do you love, my flesh? What do you desire, my soul? Whatever you love is there; whatever you desire is there.

If beauty delights you: “The righteous will shine like the sun” (Matthew 13:43). If speed, strength, or bodily freedom delights you—freedom that nothing can resist—“they will be like the angels of God” (ibid. 22:30), because “the natural body is sown, and a spiritual body will rise” (1 Corinthians 15:44), possessing power, certainly, but not possessing a different nature.
