If a long and healthy life delights you, there is healthy eternity and eternal health, because “the righteous will live forever” (Wisdom 5:16), and “the salvation of the righteous is from the Lord” (Psalm 36:39).

If satiety delights you, “they will be satisfied when the glory of the Lord appears” (Psalm 16:15). If drunkenness, “they will be intoxicated by the abundance of your house” [Psalm 35:9]. If melody, the choirs of angels sing there to God without end. If any pure pleasure, “the Lord will give them drink from the torrent of his delight” in his divinity (Psalm 35:9).

If wisdom, “all will be taught by God” (John 6:45): in what manner wisdom itself will show itself to them. If friendship, they will love God more than themselves, and one another as themselves; and God will love them more than they love themselves, because they will love him, themselves, and one another through him, while he will love them through himself.

If harmony, they will all have one will, because they will have no will except the will of God. If power, “they will enter into the powers of the Lord” (Psalm 70:16), and they will be all-powerful in regard to their own will, as God is in regard to his. For just as God will be able, through himself, to do whatever he wishes, so they will be able, through him, to do whatever they wish. Since they will wish nothing other than what he wishes, whatever they wish he will wish; and what he wishes cannot fail to exist.

If honor and riches, God will set his good and faithful servants over many things (Matthew 25:23); indeed, they will be called and will be sons of God and gods. “Where his Son will be, there they will also be” (John 17:24), heirs indeed of God and coheirs with Christ (Romans 8:17).

If true security, they will be so certain that this—or rather, that this good—will never fail them, as they will be certain that they will not lose it of their own accord, nor will God, whom they love, take it away from those who love him against their will.

[Note: [Col. 0828] Add from Anselm: “nor will anything more powerful than God separate God and them against their will.”]

But what sort and what magnitude of joy will there be where such a great good is found? Human heart, needy heart, heart acquainted with troubles—or rather, overwhelmed by troubles—how greatly would you rejoice if you abounded in all these things? Ask your inmost self whether it could contain its joy at such blessedness.

But certainly, if someone else whom you loved altogether as yourself possessed the same blessedness, your joy would be doubled, because you would rejoice for that person no less than for yourself. If two or three, or many more, possessed the same thing, you would rejoice for each one as much as for yourself, if you loved each one as yourself.

Therefore, in that perfect charity of countless blessed angels and human beings, where no one will love another less than himself, there will be countless joy.

[Col. 0829] [Note: [Col. 0829] Anselm has instead: “there will be immeasurable joy”; he adds: “each one will rejoice for every other no differently than for himself.”]

If, then, the human heart can scarcely contain its joy over its own great good, how will it be capable of containing so many and such great joys in that perfect happiness? There, just as each person will love God incomparably more than himself and all others together, so each will rejoice beyond measure in God’s happiness more than in his own and that of all others together.

They will love God with all their heart, all their mind, and all their soul, so that the whole heart will not suffice for love; and they will rejoice with all their heart, so that the whole heart will not suffice for the fullness of joy. Such is the joy.

God of infinite mercy, source of all goodness and compassion, make us participants in such great joy. For you are complete joy, supreme blessedness; you are that than which nothing better can be desired, nothing happier or more useful possessed.

## CHAPTER LXV. In the blessed, a threefold enjoyment of God. In the blessed, the soul’s threefold capacity is fulfilled. The four qualities of the glorified body: immortality, impassibility, agility, and beauty.

In that eternal and perfect blessedness, we shall enjoy God in three ways: seeing him in all creatures, possessing him within ourselves, and—and this will be incomparably more delightful and blessed than all these things—knowing the Trinity itself in itself and contemplating that glorious Trinity without any riddle, with the eye of a pure heart.

For this is perfect and eternal life: that we know the Father and the Son with the Holy Spirit (John 17:3), and see God as he is (1 John 3:2)—that is, not in the way in which he is present in us or in creatures, but as he is in himself.

But how great is that blessedness, and how hidden from our eyes! The eye has not seen, the ear has not heard, nor has it entered the human heart, how much love, sweetness, and delight await us in that knowledge. There is the peace of God, which surpasses every sense and understanding (Philippians 4:7)—and how much more does it surpass all our speech?

Therefore, since no one has been granted the experience of it, let no one attempt to express it. “The Lord will give a good measure into your lap, pressed down in the inner person, shaken together in the outer person, overflowing in God himself” (Luke 6:38). There is the heap of happiness, there the surpassing glory, there the overflowing blessedness.

For how he is to be seen in creatures and how he is to be possessed in us, we can to some extent conjecture, especially from those in whom we have already received “the firstfruits of the Spirit” (Romans 8:23). But that knowledge of God himself is still unknown to us: it “has become wondrous; it has been strengthened,” so that we cannot attain it (Psalm 138:6).

How he is to be seen in creatures, however, we can understand to some degree, since even now he is seen in them. Hence, as the apostle Paul testifies, “the invisible things of God are perceived through the things that have been made” (Romans 1:20). Therefore, however far anyone may advance in understanding and perceiving how powerfully, benevolently, and wisely the eternal majesty made all things, governs everything, and orders the universe, it is still exceedingly little compared with what he will comprehend.

But the time will come when, through vision, contemplation, and ineffable joy, we shall follow the Lamb wherever he goes; and we shall follow him in all creatures (Revelation 14:4), so that we may rejoice in all things—not, certainly, from anything other than him, just as he himself does not enjoy other things but enjoys himself. How he is to be possessed in us, too, we can consider in part.

For it is clear that souls have a threefold nature. Hence the wise men of this world have taught that the human soul is rational, desiring, and spirited [or irascible]; and nature itself, together with daily experience, teaches us of this threefold power of the soul.

Moreover, just as knowledge and ignorance belong to our rational faculty, as habit and privation, so desire and contempt belong to the desiring faculty; and joy and anger belong to what is called the spirited faculty.

The Lord, then, will fill our rational faculty with the light of wisdom, so that nothing at all will be lacking to us in any knowledge (1 Corinthians 1:7). He will fill our desiring faculty [Col. 0830] with the fountain of justice, so that we will desire it completely and be filled with it entirely, as it is written: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for justice, for they will be satisfied” (Matthew 5:6).

For no other thing can fulfill the soul’s desire; nothing other than justice can make the soul blessed. When God has filled our desiring faculty with justice, the soul will reject whatever it ought to reject, desire whatever it ought to desire, and, among all these things, desire most what ought most to be desired. It is rightly, therefore, that we attribute justice to our desiring faculty, since by it we are reckoned either just or unjust.

But when God has filled what is called our spirited faculty, there will certainly be tranquility within us, and we shall be filled with divine peace unto the highest joy and delight.

Consider whether perfect blessedness, insofar as it concerns the soul, does not truly consist in these three things: knowledge will no longer puff up because of justice, nor will it grieve because of joy; thus that proverb will cease: “Whoever increases knowledge increases sorrow” (Ecclesiastes 1:18). Justice will be neither indiscriminate because of knowledge nor burdensome because of joy; joy will be neither suspect because of knowledge nor impure because of justice.

But in all these things our outer person has received nothing. Therefore, so that glory may dwell even in our land (Psalm 84:10), and, according to another prophet [Note: [Col. 0830] Perhaps “psalmist.”], the whole earth may be filled with the majesty of the Lord (Psalm 71:19), four things must be sought, since it is clear that the outer person is composed of the four elements.

Do not be surprised that the body seems to require more, since it is now the place of need. Hence the prophet says in the Psalm: “My soul thirsts for you; how manifoldly my flesh longs for you” (Psalm 62:2).

Our “earth,” then, will have immortality, so that it will no longer fear being reduced to dust again. For when our body rises, it will no longer die, and death will no longer rule over it (Romans 6:9).

But what good would that do [Note: [Col. 0830] Perhaps: “What would it profit?”] if it happened to live amid the miseries and troubles of this state of susceptibility, by which this incorruptible body is continually afflicted? Even if it does not die once, it is nevertheless always dying.

Certainly it will have from God, in every respect, impassibility. For they say that the causes of suffering arise from disordered humors.

But now our body also desires lightness, corresponding to the portion it has from the air, so that it may not be burdensome through its very weight. The lightness and agility of the bodies of the good must therefore be believed to be so great in the future that, if we wish, they will be able to follow the speed of our thoughts to everything, without any delay or difficulty.

What more is lacking for perfect bodily blessedness? Only beauty. Since we shall possess this in the highest perfection, we may rightly attribute it to that part which we have from fire.

For, as the Apostle says, we await the Savior, who “will reform the body of our lowliness, conforming it to the body of his glory,” fulfilling what he promised (Philippians 3:20–21), since “the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (Matthew 13:43).

Therefore, just as God will fill our souls when they possess perfect knowledge, perfect justice, and perfect joy, so our whole “earth” will be filled with his majesty when the body is immortal, impassible, agile, and finally conformed to the body of his glory.

Then it will truly be possible to say what a certain poet said: “O thrice and four times blessed” (Virgil, *Aeneid* 1.98)!

No one can adequately weigh how great that joy and glory will be when we see God present everywhere and governing all things. He will be so known and evident to us that he will be seen in spirit by each of us, seen by one in another, seen in himself, seen in the new heaven and the new earth (Revelation 21:1), and in every creature that will then exist.

Freed from every evil and perfectly filled with every good, we shall rest and see that he is God (Psalm 45:11), and we shall be full when he is “all in all” (1 Corinthians 15:28).

He himself will be the end of our desires: we shall see him without end, love him without weariness, and praise him without fatigue.

[Col. 0831] But who is fit for these things? Without doubt, the one who is found faithful over the few things he received during the time of his service—that is, over his senses, actions, and appetites, which he undertook to govern, so that in these things his faithfulness to his Lord might be proved (Matthew 25:21).

Therefore, let Christ’s servant know how to possess his vessel in sanctification and honor (1 Thessalonians 4:4), and let him glorify and bear God in his body (1 Corinthians 6:20); let him pursue peace (Hebrews 12:14). Amen.

# [ON FRIENDSHIP]

[Col. 0831]

## NOTICE CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING BOOK, ON FRIENDSHIP

This is a short work by Aelred, Abbot of Rievaulx in England, written in dialogue form and arranged by him into three books. Among his other works published in print, it is presented in an authentic and complete form; here, however, it has been abridged by an idle person who not only failed to preserve the author’s style and method, but also repeatedly and conspicuously altered and corrupted his judgments.

For sometimes what Aelred, speaking as one of the interlocutors, proposes by way of a question—intending shortly either to explain or refute it himself—is here put forward absolutely and asserted contrary to his intention.

Thus, for example, at the end of the first chapter, where the cited saying of Tully is followed by: “Who has expressed toward this pagan a strong affection of charity and works of benevolence?” In Aelred it is arranged so that the interlocutor says: “I do not see what that pagan meant by the name of charity or benevolence.” Then Aelred himself replies: “Perhaps by the name of charity he expressed an affection of the mind, and by benevolence the effect of a work.”

And in the fourth chapter, the statement “But many abuse wisdom” is so alien to Aelred’s teaching that he himself, on the contrary, explicitly and admirably proves that no one abuses wisdom.

Peter of Blois, almost Aelred’s contemporary, made better use of Aelred in his treatise *On Christian Friendship*, which was at one time attributed to Cassiodorus. From Aelred’s books he transferred a considerable amount into this treatise, without naming him, but nevertheless openly acknowledging his procedure and intention in the preface with these words:

“Gathering, as it were, flowers from various writers in order to make honey for myself, I have compressed the opinions of many, both ancient and modern, concerning friendship and the love of God and neighbor into a single compendium of concise reading.”

Nor should it be passed over in silence that the passage expressly cited by Peter of Blois from Augustine in chapter 8 belongs not to the following book *On Friendship*, as it is incorrectly marked in the margin of the final edition of Peter of Blois, but to book 4, chapter 8, of the *Confessions*.

We compared each word with Aelred’s genuine and authentic books, and wherever anything had been altered or corrupted, we took care to note it.

[Col. 0831]

# ONE BOOK ON FRIENDSHIP (G, S)

## CHAPTER I. The occasion for writing this book

[Col. 0831]

When I was still a boy at school, and was greatly delighted by the affection of my companions, amid the customs and vices by which that age is usually endangered, my whole mind gave itself over to affection and devoted itself to love. Nothing seemed to me sweeter, nothing more delightful, nothing more useful than to be loved and to love.

Thus, wavering among various loves and friendships, my spirit was carried here and there; and, ignorant of the law of true friendship, it was often deceived by something resembling it.

At last a book came into my hands that Tully had written *On Friendship*. It immediately appeared to me useful because of the gravity of its judgments and sweet because of the charm of its eloquence. And although I saw that I was not suited to that kind of friendship, I nevertheless rejoiced that I had found a certain formula of friendship to which I might recall the wanderings of my mind [Note: [Col. 0831] In Aelred: “of my loves.”] and affections.

But when it pleased my good Lord to correct one who had gone astray, raise up one who had been cast down, and cleanse a leper by a healing touch, I abandoned hope in the world and entered a monastery. At once I devoted myself to reading the sacred Scriptures, where the honey-sweet name of Christ claimed my entire affection for itself [Note: [Col. 0831] Up to this point from Aelred’s prologue; from here through chapter 5, from his first book.], so that nothing else can be pleasing or luminous to me.

## CHAPTER II. Among whom true friendship exists

[Col. 0831]

It is clear to me [Col. 0832] that Tully did not know the virtue of true friendship, since he entirely failed to know Christ, its beginning and end—Christ who is the Alpha and Omega, the beginning and end of all good things.

What is friendship? Tully says: “Friendship is agreement concerning human and divine matters, joined with goodwill and charity.” Who has expressed toward this pagan a strong affection of charity and works of benevolence?

But this true friendship cannot exist among those who are without Christ.

As I think, *amicus* [friend] is derived from *amor* [love], and *amicitia* [friendship] from *amicus*. Love is a certain affection of the rational soul, through which it seeks and desires something with longing in order to enjoy it; through which, moreover, it enjoys it with a certain inward sweetness, embraces what it has obtained, and preserves it.

An *amicus* is said to be, as it were, the guardian of love or of the soul itself, because my friend ought to be the guardian of our mutual love—or of my very soul—so that he may preserve all its secrets in faithful silence. Whatever he sees to be vicious in it, he should, as far as he can, guard against and remove [Note: [Col. 0832] In Aelred: “take care of and tolerate.”]. He should rejoice with it when it rejoices, grieve with it when it grieves, and share everything of his own with it, since friends [Note: [Col. 0832] In Aelred: “and consider everything his own that belongs to his friend.”] are those who agree in all things.

Friendship itself, therefore, is the virtue that is joined to a friend by such a covenant of sweetness and love that many become one [Note: [Col. 0832] In Aelred: “by which souls themselves are joined and become one from many.”].

For this reason even the philosophers of this world placed friendship not among accidental or transitory things, but among the virtues themselves, which are eternal. Hence Solomon says in Proverbs: “The one who is a friend loves at all times” (Proverbs 17:17), clearly declaring that friendship is eternal if it is true. If it ceases, it was never true.

I want you to know this: the person who injures one whom he has once received into friendship was never a friend; nor has the person who, once injured, ceases to love the one he once loved ever tasted the delights of true friendship. Even if he is accused, handed over to the flames, or crucified, “the one who is a friend loves at all times.”

Hence Jerome says: “Friendship that can cease was never true, since friendships ought to be immortal” (*Letter* 41, to Rufinus).

Since there is such perfection in true friendship, it is not surprising that those whom antiquity commends as true friends have been rare.

“For scarcely,” as Tully says, “does fame celebrate three or four pairs of friends throughout so many past ages” (*On Friendship*, §15).

“A great thing,” someone said, “and even the attempt itself is great” [Note: [Col. 0833] Aelred has: “A great undertaking, someone said, and even the attempt is great.”].

It is therefore characteristic of a virtuous mind always to meditate on lofty and difficult things, so that it may attain what it desires, or understand and recognize more clearly what ought to be desired. For the person who has learned through knowledge of virtue how far he is from virtue must be considered to have made no small progress.

Were not Pylades and Orestes prepared to die for one another? But those about whom it is written were stronger in their love of virtue: “The multitude of believers had one heart and one soul” (Acts 4:32). And the holy martyrs laid down their lives for their brothers; they spared neither labor nor bodily torments.

But it is not surprising that divine authority has ordained that far more people be received into the embrace of charity than into the embraces of friendship, since it embraces not only friends but also enemies under the law of charity (Matthew 5:44).

We call only those people friends to whom we do not fear to entrust our heart and everything within it, while they in turn are bound to us by the same law and security of faith.

Those among whom there is an agreement in vices therefore falsely assume the illustrious name of friendship, because whoever does not love is not a friend. But the person who loves iniquity does not love a human being; such a person hates his own soul and cannot love another.

When, however, in such a friendship—whether lust stains it, greed defiles it, or sensuality pollutes it—so great and such sweetness is experienced, it is pleasing to conjecture how much sweetness belongs to that friendship which, the more honorable it is, is also the more secure; the chaster it is, the more delightful; the freer it is, the happier.

## CHAPTER III. Three kinds of friendship: carnal, worldly, spiritual and true

Friendship, then, is of one kind carnal, of another worldly, and of another spiritual. Carnal friendship is created by agreement in vices; worldly friendship is kindled by hope of gain; spiritual friendship is cemented among good people by similarity of life, character, and pursuits.

The beginning of carnal friendship proceeds from an affection that, like a prostitute, spreads its legs to every passerby, following its ears and eyes as they fornicate through various things. Through these entrances, the image of beautiful bodies or pleasurable objects is carried into the mind itself; it thinks that to enjoy these things at will is blessed, but considers the pleasure less without a companion.

Then, by movement, gesture, words, and services, one spirit is taken captive by another; one is inflamed by the other, and they are fused [Note: [Col. 0833] Aelred has: “are molded together.”] into one, so that, after entering into a wretched covenant, each one performs and suffers every crime and sacrilege for the other. They consider nothing sweeter than this friendship, nor judge anything more just, thinking that to will and not to will the same things is commanded by the laws of friendship.

This friendship is undertaken neither after deliberation, approved by judgment, nor governed by reason; rather, according to the impulse of affection, it is swept through various directions. It observes no measure, seeks no honorable things, considers neither advantages nor disadvantages, but advances toward everything thoughtlessly, indiscriminately, lightly, immoderately, and without restraint.

Therefore, after being driven by such madness, it consumes itself and dissolves with the same fickleness by which it was formed.

Worldly friendship, which is born from desire for possessions or temporal goods, is always full of fraud and deception. Nothing in it is certain, constant, or secure. It always changes with fortune and follows the purse.

Hence Solomon says: “There is a friend according to the occasion, and he will not remain in the time of trouble” (Ecclesiasticus 6:8). Remove the hope of gain, and he will immediately cease to be a friend.

Hence someone wrote:

> He is not a friend of the person, but of prosperity;  
> whom sweet fortune holds, bitter fortune drives away.

Spiritual friendship, which we call true friendship, is desired not with a view to any worldly advantage, nor because of any external cause that arises, but from the dignity of its own nature and from the feeling of the human heart; so that its fruit and reward is nothing other than friendship itself.

Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “I appointed you to go and bear fruit” (John 15:16)—that is, to love one another. For in true friendship itself one progresses by advancing, and its fruit is gathered by experiencing the sweetness of that perfection.

True charity is called friendship, so that every vice may be excluded. When it is called goodwill, the very agreement [Note: [Col. 0834] Aelred has: “feeling.”] of loving—which is moved inwardly with a certain sweetness—is expressed.

Where such friendship exists, there is one willing and one refusing the same things: the sweeter, the more sincere; the more pleasing, the more sacred. There, those who love in this way can will nothing dishonorable, nor refuse anything beneficial.

Prudence directs this friendship, justice governs it, courage guards it, and temperance moderates it.

## CHAPTER IV. The origin and development of friendship

Friendship’s affection was first, as I think, impressed upon human minds by nature itself; experience then increased it; finally, the authority of law ordered it.

For God, supremely powerful and supremely good, is sufficient to himself and has no need of our goods. He willed that peace should harmonize all his creatures and that fellowship should unite them.

Thus, from the very beginning, nature impressed upon human minds by God himself an affection for friendship and charity; the inner sense of character then increased it through a certain taste of the sweetness of love [Note: [Col. 0834] In Aelred: “the inner sense immediately.”].

It is clear that friendship is natural, just as virtue, wisdom, and the other virtues are. But many misuse wisdom, whether by accepting something in return for it or by selling it. In the same way, some misuse friendship, seeking something in return for it or seeking something along with it.

## CHAPTER V. The fruits of friendship

[Note: [Col. 0834] From Aelred’s second book.]

What benefit does friendship possess, when among human affairs nothing more sacred is desired, nothing more useful is sought, nothing more difficult is found, nothing sweeter is experienced, and nothing more fruitful is held?

For it bears fruit for the present life and the future. It seasons all virtues with its sweetness and pierces vices with its strength; it moderates adversity and arranges prosperity. Thus, without a friend, almost nothing among mortals can be pleasant. A person is compared to a beast if he has no one to rejoice with him in prosperity and grieve with him in sadness; no one to whom he may unburden whatever troubling thought his mind has conceived, and with whom he may share whatever unusual, exalted, or spiteful [Note: [Col. 0834] Aelred has: “luminous.”] thing has arisen.

“Woe to the one who is alone, because when he falls he has no one to raise him up” (Ecclesiastes 4:10). A person who is without a friend is entirely alone.

What happiness, security, and delight it is to have someone with whom you dare to speak as openly as with yourself; to whom you are not afraid to confess if you have done wrong; to whom you are not ashamed to reveal if you have made progress in spiritual matters; to whom you entrust all the secrets of your heart and with whom you share your plans!

What, then, is more delightful than to unite one person’s spirit to another’s [Note: [Col. 0834] In Aelred: “spirit to spirit.”] and make one from two, so that no boastfulness is feared, no suspicion dreaded; so that when one reproves the other, the other does not grieve; and so that neither accuses or brands the other’s praise as flattery?

“The friend,” says the Wise Man, “is a medicine of life” (Ecclesiasticus 6:16). No medicine is stronger or more effective for our wounds than to have someone who compassionately meets every misfortune and joyfully meets every good fortune, so that, joining their shoulders, they bear one another’s burdens, except that each person carries his own injury more lightly than his friend’s injury [Note: [Col. 0835] In Aelred: “so that they might bear one another’s burdens, except that each person carries his own more lightly than his friend carries it.”].

Friendship therefore makes prosperity more splendid, while by dividing and sharing adversity it makes it lighter.

This was pleasing even to philosophers. We do not use water, sunlight, or fire in more places than we use a friend: in every action, every pursuit, in certainties, in doubts, in every event, in every kind of fortune, in private, in public, in every consultation, at home and abroad—everywhere friendship is welcome, everywhere a friend is necessary, everywhere the benefit of friendship is found.

“Therefore,” says Tully, “friends are present to one another even when absent; in need they abound; in weakness they are strong; and, what is more difficult to say, the dead live” (Cicero, *On Friendship*, §23).

Friendship, then, is an alms to the rich, a homeland to exiles, wealth to the poor, medicine to the sick, life to the dead, favor to the healthy, virtue to the weak, and a reward to the strong.

Such honor, remembrance, praise, and longing attend friends that their life is judged praiseworthy and their death precious. And, higher than all these things, friendship is a certain degree near to the perfection that consists in the love and contemplation [Note: [Col. 0835] In Aelred: “knowledge.”] of God, so that through friendship with a human being a person may become a friend of God.

In the Gospel: “I will no longer call you servants, but my friends” (John 15:15).

In friendship there is nothing dishonorable, nothing false, nothing feigned. Whatever it is, it is holy, voluntary, and true; and this is precisely what belongs properly to charity.

In friendship, honor and sweetness, truth and delight, tenderness and will, affection [Note: [Col. 0835] Words added from Aelred: “truth” and “affection.”] and action are joined together. All these things begin from Christ, advance through Christ, and are perfected in Christ.

Thus a friend, cleaving to a friend in the spirit of Christ, becomes with him one heart and one soul. And so, ascending by the steps of the songs of love [Note: [Col. 0835] Aelred: “the steps of love”] toward the friendship of Christ, he becomes one spirit with him in one kiss.

“Let him kiss me,” it says, “with the kiss of his mouth” (Song of Songs 1:1).

## CHAPTER VI. When a bodily kiss should be used. The spiritual kiss

There is a bodily kiss, made by the pressing of the lips, which should be offered only for certain and honorable reasons: as a sign of reconciliation, when those who were enemies become friends; as a sign of peace, as when those who are about to receive communion in church demonstrate interior peace by an exterior kiss.

It is permitted as a sign of love between bridegroom and bride, or as it is both offered and received by friends after a long absence. It is also used as a sign of Catholic unity, as when a guest is received.

But just as many abuse water, fire, iron, food, and air—which are naturally good things—in the service of their cruelty or pleasure, so perverse and shameful people attempt in some way to season their crimes with this good thing as well. They defile the kiss itself with such depravity that to kiss in this way is nothing other than to commit adultery.

The spiritual kiss, moreover, properly belongs to friends who are held together under one law of friendship. It is not made by the touch of the mouth but by the affection of the mind; not by the joining of lips but by the mingling of spirits. The Spirit of God makes everything chaste and, through participation in himself, sends in a heavenly savor.

For he himself inspires this most sacred affection, so that one person seems to have one soul in different bodies.

The Psalmist says: “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity” (Psalm 132:1).

A soul affected in this way sighs for the intellectual kiss and, crying out with the greatest desire, says: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.” Thus, with earthly affections soothed and all thoughts and desires belonging to the world put to rest, it takes delight in Christ’s kiss alone and rests in his embrace, exulting and saying: “His left hand is under my head” (Song of Songs 2:6).

## CHAPTER VII. What friendship is
[Column 836]

I believe friendship [Note: [Col. 0836] Aelred thinks and believes otherwise.] to be nothing other than such a partnership of wills between two people that one wants nothing which the other does not want; but such agreement between them in good and evil that neither appearance, nor wealth, nor honor, nor anything belonging to one is denied to the other for enjoyment according to his will and for use [Note: [Col. 0836] Aelred: “for abuse”]; so that each is disposed toward his neighbor as toward himself, in every duty and service which they render in turn, and that honors are shunned. Friendship can arise among the good, advance among the better, and be perfected among the perfect.

For as long as someone takes pleasure in the pursuit [Note: [Col. 0836] Aelred: “in the pursuit.”] of evil, prefers dishonorable things to honorable ones, and finds pleasure dearer than purity, rashness than moderation, flattery than correction, how may he be permitted to aspire to friendship, when its origin proceeds from a reputation for virtue?

A compact is base, and unworthy of the name of friendship, by which something disgraceful is demanded of a friend; and this must be done by one who, with his vices not yet subdued or suppressed, is either enticed or compelled toward every unlawful act. There is no excuse for sin if you have sinned for a friend’s sake. Jonadab, Amnon’s friend, would have done better to prevent his incest than to give him counsel by which he might obtain what he desired [Note: [Col. 0836] Aelred: “than that he might obtain.”] (2 Samuel 13:5). We call a good man one who lives soberly, justly, and devoutly in this world, asks nothing dishonorable of anyone, and does not grant such a request even when asked. Among such people friendship can arise and be preserved.

## CHAPTER VIII. Friendship Has Its Faults. Is It Therefore to Be Rejected?

Some say that friendship ought to be avoided: that it is a matter full of anxiety and cares, not free from fear, exposed to many pains, and that nothing is more difficult than to preserve it to the very last day. Thus [Note: [Col. 0836] Aelred adds “more safely” and does not have “with Cicero.”], with Cicero, they judge that one should love in such a way that one may hate whenever one wishes; thus they approve loving today so that they may hate tomorrow; being a friend in such a way as to be faithful to no one—now praising, now blaming, now flattering, now biting; ready for kisses today, for insults tomorrow. The love of such people withdraws at the slightest offense.

Cicero says of them: “They seem to take the sun from the world who take friendship from life; and we possess nothing better from God, nothing more delightful” (*On Friendship*, §47).

What sort of wisdom is it to detest friendship so that you may avoid anxiety, be free from cares, and strip yourself of fear, when no virtue fights without anxiety—prudence against errors, temperance against lusts, justice against wickedness, or courage against cowardice? Who, then, especially among the young, can preserve chastity without pain or fear, or restrain an affection that is running riot?

Was Paul foolish, who did not wish to live without others’ [Note: [Col. 0836] Add from Aelred: “others’.”] care and anxiety, but, considering charity—which he believed to be the greatest virtue—became weak with the weak and burned with those who were scandalized (2 Corinthians 11:28–29)? He also had grief and continual pain in his heart for his brothers according to the flesh (Romans 9:2).

I should call those who say that one ought to live in such a way as to be a consolation to no one and a burden or grief to no one, not so much human beings as beasts: people who derive no pleasure from another’s good, cause no bitterness to others by their own perversity, care to love no one and to be loved by no one.

## CHAPTER IX. Childish Friendship

There is a childish friendship, created by a wandering and wanton affection, without reason, weight, or measure, and without consideration of any advantage or disadvantage. For a time it affects and binds one intensely, and attracts one with great sweetness. But affection without reason is a bestial impulse, inclined toward every unlawful thing.

And although affection promotes friendship [Note: [Col. 0836] Aelred: “anticipates”], it is not to be followed [Column 837] unless reason guides it, propriety moderates it, and justice governs it. Such affection reigns more strongly in children. Let those whom spiritual love delights beware of an affection that is faithless and unstable and always mingled with impure loves; for it is poison.

## CHAPTER X. Spiritual Friendship. True Friendship. The Fountain of Friendship. The Origin of Love

The beginnings of spiritual friendship must first possess purity of intention, the guidance of reason, and the bridle of temperance. Then, when the sweetest affection approaches, it will certainly be felt as so pleasant that it will never cease to be well ordered.

He does not yet know what true friendship is who wants any reward other than friendship itself. For although faithful friendship among good people produces many great benefits, we do not doubt that these proceed from friendship, not friendship from them. Since friendship always precedes among the good and benefit follows, it is surely not so much what has been obtained through a friend that delights as the friend’s love itself.

Nothing is to be denied to a friend; everything must be endured for him, and one’s bodily life must be laid down for a friend, as divine authority has decreed (John 15:13).

[Note: The remainder is excerpted from the third book of Aelred.]

Love is the fountain and origin of friendship: love can exist without friendship, but friendship never without love. Love proceeds sometimes from nature, sometimes from duty, sometimes from reason alone, sometimes from affection alone, and sometimes from both together.

From nature, as when a mother loves her son.

From duty, when people are joined by a certain special affection through the reasoning involved in giving and receiving.

From reason alone, as when we love our enemies not from a spontaneous inclination of mind but from the necessity of a commandment (Matthew 5:44).

From affection alone, when someone draws to himself the affection of certain people solely because of bodily qualities—for example, beauty, strength, or eloquence.

From reason and affection together, when the person whom reason advises us to love because of the merit of virtue enters another’s mind through the sweetness of his character and the charm of a praiseworthy life. Thus reason is joined to affection, so that love is chaste through reason and sweet through affection.

## CHAPTER XI. The Foundation of Friendship

The foundation of friendship is the love of God. Everything suggested either by love or by affection, everything which some spirit secretly or some friend openly recommends, must be referred to this love. It must be carefully examined whether whatever is built upon it agrees with the foundation; and whatever is found to exceed it must be recalled to its pattern and wholly transformed according to its quality—this you should not hesitate to do.

## CHAPTER XII. Choosing a Friend

Yet not everyone whom we love is to be admitted into friendship, because not everyone is suitable for it. For since a friend is a sharer of your soul, to whose spirit you join and attach your own, mingling them so that you wish two to become one; since he is someone to whom you entrust yourself as to another self, hiding nothing from him and fearing nothing from him—first, certainly, one must choose someone thought suitable for these things, then test him, and only then admit him.

Friendship ought to be stable and to display something resembling eternity, always persevering in affection; one must not change or injure friends in a childish manner. No one is more detestable than the person who has injured a friend, and nothing torments the soul more than either being abandoned by a friend or being attacked by him [Note: Elsewhere, “or being attacked by the friend”]. Yet a friend must be chosen, tested, and endured.

There are four stages by which one ascends to the perfection of friendship: the first is choice; the second, testing; the third, admission; the fourth, complete agreement in divine and human matters, together with a certain charity and highest goodwill.

There are certain vices which, if someone is entangled in them, will prevent him from long preserving the laws and rights of friendship. Those who are excessively angry, unstable, suspicious, or talkative are not suited to friendship. These four things must be noted when choosing a friend.

It is difficult for one whom the fury of anger often agitates not at some point to rise up against a friend. Hence Ecclesiasticus says: “There is a friend who will reveal hatred, strife, and insults” (Sirach 6:9). [Column 838] “Do not be a friend to an angry man, nor walk with a furious man, lest you incur a scandal to your soul” (Proverbs 22:24–25).

Some are angry by natural constitution, yet are so anxious to restrain and moderate this passion [Note: Elsewhere, “accustomed to restrain and moderate”] that they never break forth in the five ways by which, according to Scripture, friendship is dissolved and corrupted, although they may sometimes offend a friend by word, deed, or excessive zeal. Such people are to be tolerated. When we are certain of their affection, if there has been some excess of speech or action, the friend should be forgiven; or certainly he should be admonished about his excess without any pain, and even pleasantly.

## CHAPTER XIII. The Reasons for Dissolving Friendship

But whoever insults a friend dissolves the friendship. If he has drawn a sword against a friend [Note: [Col. 0838] Aelred: “even if he has drawn.”], do not despair; if he has shown a sad countenance, do not fear. There is a return to friendship. Except for insult, reproach, pride, the revelation of a secret, and a treacherous wound, in all these cases the friend will flee (Sirach 22:25–27).

Insult injures reputation and extinguishes charity. Human wickedness is so great that whatever, under the prompting of anger, has been hurled by a friend against a friend is proclaimed to be true—even if it is not believed—on the grounds that it came from one acquainted with his secrets [Note: [Col. 0838] Supply from Aelred: “uttered.”]. Many people take pleasure in the praise of others just as they do in their own praise.

What is more wicked than reproach? Even a false accusation covers the face of an innocent person with pitiable shame. And what is less bearable than pride? It excludes the remedy of humility and confession, which alone could have helped a broken friendship, making a person bold in injury and swollen against correction.

The revelation of secrets—nothing is more disgraceful, nothing more detestable, nothing leaves less love or goodwill between friends, but it fills everything with bitterness, indignation, hatred, and the gall of grief, sprinkling all things with its poison. Solomon says: “He who reveals the secrets of a friend loses faith” [Note: Some additions and changes are to be made here from Aelred]. What is more wretched than the person who loses faith and languishes in despair? Hence, “To reveal a friend’s secrets is the despair of an unhappy soul” (ibid. 27:17, 24).

A treacherous wound is secret detraction; it is the wound of a serpent and the deadly wound of an asp. Solomon says: “If a serpent bites without enchantment, there is nothing less in him who secretly defames” (Ecclesiastes 10:11).

Whenever you find someone persistent in these vices, you must beware of him, and he must not be chosen until he is healed. Let us renounce insults, whose avenger is God. Shimei, who attacked David with insults, was killed by Solomon (1 Kings 2:44–46). Unhappy Nabal of Carmel, who reproached David with servitude and flight, deserved to be struck down and killed by the Lord (1 Samuel 25:38).

Let us also avoid pride and anticipate the favor of a friend by the benefit of humility [Note: Elsewhere, “recover the favor of a friend”]. For this reason David’s sword and fire consumed the people and cities of the Ammonites (2 Samuel 10).

To reveal the secrets of friends is sacrilege; through it faith is lost and the despair of captive souls is brought about, as is evident in the traitor Ahithophel (ibid. 16:23). Let us regard defaming a friend as the poison of friendship—the poison that disfigured the body of Miriam, Moses’ sister, with leprosy and caused her to be expelled from the camp for six days (Numbers 12).

## CHAPTER XIV. Those Less Suited to Friendship

The unstable and suspicious must also be avoided. Since security is the fruit of friendship, how can you trust and entrust yourself to a friend? How can there be any security in the love of one who is carried about by every wind and yields to every counsel; whose affection, like soft clay, receives and forms throughout the day whatever different and contrary images anyone chooses to impress upon it?

What is more suited to friendship than peace and tranquility of heart? Yet the suspicious person is always deprived of these. He never rests. Curiosity always accompanies him, sharpening continual goads and supplying material for unrest and [Column 839] disturbance.

If he sees his friend speaking privately with someone, he will think it treachery. If the friend shows goodwill or cheerfulness toward another, he will proclaim that he is loved less. If the friend corrects him, he will interpret it as hatred.

Nor do I think that a talkative person should be chosen, because “a man of many words shall not be justified.” Solomon says: “Do you see a man hasty in his words? A fool has more hope than he” (Proverbs 29:20).

## CHAPTER XV. Those Suited to Friendship. Friendship Is to Be Loosened, Not Broken

You should therefore choose as a friend someone whom the fury of anger does not disturb, instability does not divide, suspicion does not crush, and talkativeness does not dissolve from due seriousness. It is especially useful to choose someone whose character agrees with yours and whose qualities correspond to your own. For firm friendship cannot exist between dissimilar characters [Note: Ambrose, *On Duties*, book 3, chapter 21]. Therefore the goodwill of both must be mutually compatible.

Many are moved by these passions, but are found superior to them: they restrain anger through patience, control fickleness by maintaining seriousness, and overcome suspicions through consideration of love. I would say that such people, as if trained through struggle [Note: In Aelred, “more thoroughly exercised”], should be admitted to friendship. Having conquered vices through virtue, they are possessed with greater security because they have also learned to resist the vices that test them more vigorously.

In the very choice or love of a friend, care must be taken not to love too quickly, especially those who are unworthy. Those are worthy of friendship in whom there is a reason why they should be loved.

Yet among those who are considered tested and worthy, vices often break out, both against friends themselves and against strangers. When the resulting disgrace reaches their friends, diligence must be applied so that they may be healed. And if this is impossible, friendship should not immediately be broken but loosened. As someone says: “Friendships should be loosened, not entirely broken” (Cicero, *On Friendship*, §76).

Friendship is eternal; hence, “He who is a friend loves at all times” (Proverbs 17:17). If the person whom you love has injured you, still love him. If he is such that friendship must be withdrawn, love must never be withdrawn. Care as much as you can for his welfare and look after his reputation [Note: Add “his”]; never betray the secrets of his friendship, even if he has betrayed yours.

## CHAPTER XVI. Injury to Those Who Should Be Loved

To the five things mentioned earlier—insult, reproach, pride, revelation of secrets, and hidden bites of detraction [Note: In Aelred, an interlocutor asks: “What are those vices, I ask, for which you say friendship should gradually be loosened?” Aelred replies: “Those five which we described above, especially the revelation of secrets and hidden bites,” etc.]—we add a sixth: if he injures those who should be loved and provides an occasion of scandal, where the disgrace of those very vices touches you.

For love must not outweigh religion, faith, the charity of many, or salvation. Know this: among the perfect, wisely chosen and carefully tested, whom true and spiritual friendship has joined together, dissension cannot arise. For when friendship has made two people one, just as what is one cannot be divided, so friendship cannot be separated from itself.

But virtue is proved by loving the person who does not love you; honoring the person who despises you; blessing the person who curses you; and doing good to the person who devises evil against you.

## CHAPTER XVII. Four Things Are Required for Friendship

Four things seem especially to belong to friendship: love, affection, security, and joy.

Love concerns the bestowal of benefits together with goodwill.

Affection concerns an inward delight that proceeds from it.

Security concerns the revelation, without fear or suspicion, of all counsels and secrets.

Joy concerns a certain sweet and friendly exchange about everything that happens, whether it brings happiness or sadness; everything that is thought, whether harmful or useful; and everything that is taught or learned.

Whoever dissolves friendship loses these things.

## CHAPTER XVIII. Four Things to Be Tested in a Friend

[Column 840] Four things must be tested in a friend: faith, intention, discretion, and patience.

Faith, so that you may entrust yourself to him securely.

Intention, so that you expect nothing from friendship except God and the natural good belonging to it.

Discretion, so that you are not ignorant of the measure, time, and place for what should be done for a friend, what should be asked of him, when one should grieve for him, when one should rejoice with him, and for what he should be corrected.

Patience, so that when corrected he does not grieve, does not despise or hate the person correcting him, and is not reluctant to endure any adversity for his friend.

## CHAPTER XIX. Faithfulness in Friendship

There is nothing in friendship more excellent than faithfulness, which seems to be its nurse and guardian. It presents itself as equal in all adversity and prosperity, in joy and sadness, in pleasant and bitter things. It looks with the same eye upon the lowly and the exalted, the poor and the rich, the strong and the weak.

A faithful friend looks at nothing in his friend that lies outside the friend’s soul. He embraces virtue in its proper place, while regarding everything else as placed outside him: he neither greatly approves of these things when they are present nor seeks them when they are absent.

Faith itself lies hidden in prosperity but stands out in adversity. A friend is proved in need. “The rich have many friends” (Proverbs 14:20), but adversity, when it intervenes, proves whether they are true friends.

Solomon says: “He who is a friend loves at all times, and a brother is proved in distress” (ibid. 17:17). And rebuking the faithless person, he says: “A rotten tooth and a slipping foot is one who hopes in the faithless on the day of distress” (ibid. 25:19).

## CHAPTER XX. Intention

We have also said that intention must be tested. There are many who know nothing good in human affairs except what is profitable in temporal terms. They love their friends as they love their oxen, from whom they hope to obtain some benefit. Such people are entirely without genuine and spiritual friendship, which is to be sought for God’s sake and for its own sake. Nor do they look within themselves at the natural model, where its force and magnitude can easily be recognized according to the form prescribed by the divine word: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Matthew 22:39).

The person whom you love will then be another self if you pour your charity into him. “For friendship,” as Ambrose says, “is not a tax, but full of beauty and full of grace” (*On Duties*, book 3, chapter 21). It is virtue, not profit: money is not brought forth, but grace; and it is not through bidding up prices but through a contest of goodwill. It ought not to be mercenary but freely given.

The friendships of the poor are more trustworthy than those of the rich, since poverty removes the hope of gain in such a way that it increases charity. Many flatter and ingratiate themselves with the rich; no one pretends toward the poor. Whatever honor is shown to the poor is genuine; their friendship is free from envy.

[Note: [Col. 0842] The word “to assist” is superfluous and is not in Aelred.]

## CHAPTER XXI. Discretion

Some perversely and indiscreetly wish to have friends of a kind they themselves cannot be. These are people who impatiently tolerate their friends’ minor transgressions, correct them harshly, and, lacking discretion, neglect great matters while rising up against the smallest things. They confuse everything, observing neither the proper place, where, nor the proper time, when, nor the persons to whom anything ought either to be disclosed or concealed.

With regard to the person whom you choose, discretion must be tested, lest you take an improvident or imprudent person for yourself and thereby seek out daily quarrels and disputes. If someone lacks discretion, he will always be carried about like a ship without a helmsman, driven by his own unstable motion.

## CHAPTER XXII. Patience. What Must Be Considered in Choosing a Friend

Patience must be tested when it becomes necessary to correct the person you love. At times this must be done deliberately and more harshly, so that his endurance may thereby be tested or trained.

One should never grow weary of being careful in choosing friends, since the fruit of this labor is the medicine of life and the foundation of immortality. A certain impulse of love must be avoided—one that outruns judgment and removes the ability to test. It is therefore the mark of a prudent man to restrain this impulse once it has arisen, to set a limit to goodwill, and to advance gradually in affection, until, once he has been tested, he gives and entrusts himself entirely to his friend.

This is the great happiness which we await through God’s working and infusing: that between himself and his creature, and among the very [Column 841] ranks and orders he has chosen, there may be such friendship and charity that each loves the other as himself; that each rejoices in the happiness of another as in his own; and that the blessedness of each may be the blessedness of all, and the totality of all blessedness belong to each.

There no thoughts are hidden, no affections disguised. This is true friendship: what begins here is perfected there; what is here possessed by a few is there possessed by all, where all are good. Here testing is necessary, where there is a mixture of the wise and the foolish.

## CHAPTER XXIII. Not Everyone Is to Be Admitted Equally

We embrace many people with every affection, yet do not admit them to the secrets of friendship or to the disclosure of our counsels.

In the Gospel Christ says of his disciples, whom he made friends instead of servants: “I will no longer call you servants, but friends” (John 15:15).

Ambrose [Note: In Aelred: “Concerning these words, as the holy Ambrose says, he gave,” etc.] says: “He gave us the pattern of friendship which we should follow: that we should do the will of our friends, reveal to them all our secrets, whatever we have in our hearts, and not be ignorant of their secrets” (*On Duties*, book 3, chapter 21).

A friend hides nothing. If he is a true friend, he pours out his soul, just as our Lord Jesus Christ poured out the mysteries of his Father.

## CHAPTER XXIV. The Cultivation of Friendship

Let us see how friendship ought to be cultivated. Faith is therefore the foundation of stability and constancy in friendship; for nothing that is faithless is stable. A varied and crooked disposition cannot be faithful; nor can those who are not moved by the same things or agree about the same things possess a stable friendship or faithfulness.

Above all, suspicion must be avoided, since it is the poison of friendship. Let us never think evil of a friend, nor believe someone who speaks evil of him. Let pleasantness enter our speech, cheerfulness our face, sweetness our manners, and serenity even the movement of our eyes.

Sadness and a sterner expression possess a certain honorable gravity. But friendship, as though somewhat relaxed, ought sometimes to be freer and sweeter, inclined toward courtesy and ease without frivolity or dissolution.

It is also a law of friendship that the superior should make himself equal to the inferior. Often people of a lower rank and order, dignity and learning, are taken into friendship by those who are more eminent, so that the exalted descends, the humble rises, the rich becomes needy, and the poor grows rich. Thus each shares his condition with the other, so that equality is created. Hence “he who had much did not have too much, and he who had little did not have too little” (2 Corinthians 8:15).

Never put yourself above your friend. If perhaps you are found superior in the matters mentioned, then submit yourself all the more to your friend. Do not hesitate to offer him confidence, raise up the modest, and confer upon him so much more honor than his condition or poverty prescribes.

Jonathan made a covenant with David and, treating his servant as equal to his master in friendship, preferred to himself a man driven out by his father, condemned to death and destined for execution. He humbled himself and exalted David: “You shall be king,” he said, “and I shall be second after you” (1 Samuel 23:17).

If it seems harsh to you to prefer the one whom you love to yourself as a master [Note: Read: “If it seems harsh to you to prefer him as a master”], do not neglect to make him your equal. For friendship is not properly cultivated by those who do not preserve equality. Treat your friend as an equal, and do not be ashamed to anticipate him in service [Note: See Ambrose, *On Duties*, book 3, chapter 21]. Friendship knows no pride. A faithful friend is indeed the medicine of life.

## CHAPTER XXV. The Law of Friendship in Asking and Giving

This, then, is the law of friendship: that we ask our friends for honorable things and do honorable things for them, without waiting to be asked. Delay must always be absent; zeal must always be present.

“Spend your money,” says Solomon, “for the sake of a friend” (Sirach 29:13). If money must be spent for a friend, much more must it be devoted to his benefit or needs.

Therefore give to a friend in such a way that you do not reproach him, expect payment, cloud your brow, turn away your face, or lower your [Column 842] eyes; but with a serene face, cheerful expression, and pleasant speech, interrupt the words of the person asking. Meet him with goodwill, so that you seem to provide what is requested without having been asked.

A noble spirit considers nothing more shameful than asking. Since, therefore, you and your friend ought to have one heart and one soul, it is unjust if you do not also have one purse. Let them devote themselves and their possessions to one another in such a way that the giver preserves cheerfulness and the receiver does not lose security.

## CHAPTER XXVI. What Friends Owe One Another

There are certain ways in which friends can assist one another in friendship. First, they should be concerned for one another, pray for one another, be ashamed on one another’s behalf, rejoice for one another, and grieve over the other’s fall as over their own.

[Note: Addition by the compiler.]

[The beloved belongs to the one who loves him. Amid the variable chances of fortune and the shifting variety of changing things, nothing is judged by the wise to be more desirable, more kindly, sweeter, or more honorable than to find true friendship. What we love to hold, we burn with the desire to see. Such is the power of love that the eye of the mind presents what the mind desires more ardently. Your familiar features and your words, seasoned with honey, come before me. The pleasantness of happy nights comes before me—nights that steal me from myself, from study and work. In the midst of reading I dream of you; in dreams I embrace you; in embraces I lose you; and both you and the dream depart with their deception. Therefore heal my longings, heal my absence; love one who loves you, and let this be the remedy for our madness: let those who love you know that I love [you]. For love contains less love when the one who loves feels that he is not loved. It belongs to friends to know one another’s affairs and to provide mutual assistance according to their needs. He is not a friend who does not help his friend, nor is he a good companion who does not grieve sufficiently over his companion’s adversity or regard the other’s progress as his own.]

By these means one may assist a friend: lift up the fainthearted, support the weak, console the sad, and endure the angry person. One should be so mindful of a friend’s eyes that one dares do nothing dishonorable or say anything unbecoming. For whatever he himself does wrong rebounds upon his friend.

## CHAPTER XXVII. Correcting a Friend

Whatever must be advised is more readily received from a friend and more readily retained. His authority in advising ought to be great, since his trustworthiness is not doubtful and his flattery is not suspect.

Friends are not merely to be admonished [Note: Aelred has “instructed”], but, if necessary, rebuked. A friend must be rebuked if he spurns the truth and is summoned into guilt through services and flatteries. But admonition must be free of harshness, and rebuke of insult.

Ambrose says: “If you discover some vice in a friend, correct him privately; if he does not listen to you, correct him publicly” (*On Duties*, book 3, chapter 21).

There are good corrections, and they are often better than silent friendship. Even if a friend thinks himself injured, correct him nevertheless. “The wounds of a friend are more tolerable than the kisses of flatterers” (Proverbs 27:6).

A friend ought to sympathize with and accommodate his friend, considering his vice as his own, and correcting him humbly and compassionately. Let a more sorrowful expression and a lowered voice correct him. Let tears interrupt the words, so that he may not only see but also feel that the correction proceeds from love and not resentment.

A friend should conform himself to his friend so that he corresponds to his quality [Note: Aelred has “corresponds”]; and just as he ought to be present to him in external adversity, so much more ought he to meet him in spirit.

To be admonished and to admonish are not incompatible [Note: The passage is corrupt], provided this is done neither flatteringly nor deceptively, but truly. “A deceiver deceives his friend with his mouth” (ibid. 12:9).

## CHAPTER XXVIII. Epilogue

Let us offer a friend whatever belongs to love, whatever belongs to goodwill, whatever belongs to sweetness, and whatever belongs to charity. Let us impose subtle honors [Note: Aelred has “trivial honors”] and burdens upon those whom reason prescribes, knowing that no one truly loves when the friend himself is not sufficient to him, unless he has cast away these worthless and contemptible things [Note: Aelred has “unless he has added these things”].

[Column 843] Care must be taken lest a tenderer affection hinder greater benefits, while we neither wish to send away nor to burden those whom we embrace with fuller charity, even when there is hope of more abundant fruit. For this is ordered friendship: that reason govern affection, and that we attend not so much to what their sweetness demands as to what the benefit of many requires.

He who does not love himself cannot love another. He does not love himself who either demands something shameful or dishonorable from himself, or grants it to himself. First, therefore, each person must purify himself, indulging himself in nothing indecent and withholding from himself nothing useful.

But since this love loves many [Note: Elsewhere, “gathers many together”], from among them let him choose one whom he may admit by the law of intimate friendship to its secrets, into whom he may pour his affection abundantly, laying bare his breast even to the inspection of his entrails, marrow, thoughts, and the intentions of his heart.

Let him not be chosen according to the wantonness of affection, but according to the discernment of reason, the similarity of character, and the contemplation of virtues. Let him devote himself to his friend in such a way that all frivolity is absent, cheerfulness present, and the ordered services and duties of goodwill and charity not lacking.

Let his faithfulness, honesty, and patience be tested. Let there be a sharing of the friends’ counsels, constancy in [Column 844] equal pursuits, and a certain conformity of faces.

Thus, once chosen and tested, he should neither wish to ask a friend for anything unbecoming nor provide anything unbecoming when asked. He should regard friendship as virtue [Note: Read: “when it has been established that he regards friendship as virtue”], not profit; flee flattery and detest obsequiousness; be free in discretion, patient in correction, firm and stable in affection.

Then it is useful to grieve for one another, labor, carry one another’s burdens, neglect oneself for the other, prefer the other’s will to one’s own, attend to his need more than to one’s own, oppose and expose oneself to adversity on his behalf; it is sweet to converse with one another and mutually disclose one’s pursuits [Note: Aelred has “how sweet it is to converse with one another”].

Prayer for one another is added. In the memory of a friend, prayer is admitted with all the greater efficacy the more ardently it is offered, with tears flowing—tears which fear forces out, affection draws forth, or grief brings forth.

Thus, when praying for a friend, he looks attentively and lovingly toward Christ himself. Then, as affection suddenly passes into affection and touches the sweetness of Christ himself, he begins to taste how sweet he is and to feel how gracious he is.

Thus, ascending from that holy love by which he embraces a friend to the love by which he embraces Christ, he receives the spiritual fruit of friendship.

# [ON THE SUBSTANCE OF LOVE]

[Column 843]

## NOTICE CONCERNING THE BOOK ON THE SUBSTANCE OF LOVE

This little book is clearly made up of two short works confused together. In manuscript books they are not joined in this place without being separated from one another at least by the title prefixed to each.

The first short work, entitled *On the Substance of Love*, ends with the final words of chapter four, and in manuscript copies it bears the name of Augustine only very rarely, but that of Hugh most often. Indeed, it exists among works published under Hugh’s name, being attached to the book called *Catholic Institutions on the Decalogue*.

The second work begins with the words of chapter five, “Love is the life of the heart,” and so forth. It bears, without the author’s name, this or a similar title: *That Love Is the Life of the Heart*. This work, too, was published with Hugh’s works in book 1 of the *Miscellanies*, title 170 or 171 of the theological teachings.

Bernard Vinding criticizes several points in this little book in his *Augustinian Critic*, but these are certainly not foreign to Hugh of Saint-Victor. For example, the point which he considers worthy of censure—that God performed the works of human restoration partly through human beings, partly through angels, and partly through himself—Hugh repeats several times in book 4 of *The Moral Ark*, chapters 3, 5, and 9, and in book 2 of *The Vanity of the World*, and elsewhere.

Finally, Abbot Trithemius counts the book *On the Substance of Love* among Hugh’s works.

[Column 843]

# ONE BOOK ON THE SUBSTANCE OF LOVE. (S)*

## CHAPTER ONE. The Two Streams of Love: Charity and Desire. From Love Comes Every Good and Every Evil. Love Is One Movement and Many
We shall sow a daily discourse on love, lest perhaps [Note: [Col. 0843] In Hugh is added, *without our noticing*.] a spark should glow in our hearts and the fire blaze up, making a flame that either consumes everything or purifies everything. For from it comes all that is good, and from it comes all that is evil. One fountain of love, springing up within, pours forth two streams: one is love of the world, cupidity; the other is love of God, charity. The human heart is the middle point from which the fountain of love bursts forth: when it flows outward through appetite, it is called cupidity; but when it directs its desire inward, it is called charity. Thus there are two streams issuing from the fountain of love: cupidity [Col. 0844] and charity; cupidity is the root of all evils, and charity the root of all good things. From it, therefore, comes everything that is good, and from it comes everything that is evil. Whatever it is, then, it is a great thing that is within us; and from it comes everything that proceeds from us [Note: [Col. 0844] In Hugh, *that which is within us*]. This, however, is love. What is love, how great is love, and whence is love? And the word of God speaks of love. Is this business not rather the concern of those who are accustomed to prostitute chastity? Behold how many willingly undertake its ministries [Note: [Col. 0844] The Victorine manuscript and Hugh read *mysteries*], and how few are not ashamed to bring its words forth publicly! What, then, are we doing? Perhaps through great shamelessness we have a battered brow, since we are not ashamed to give utterance to love that has been dictated [Note: [Col. 0845] The Victorine manuscript reads *to form*; Hugh, *to formulate what has been dictated*], which even the shameless are sometimes unable to express in words without embarrassment. But it is one thing to investigate vice so that it may be uprooted, and another to encourage vice so that virtue and truth may not be loved. We, therefore, investigate and inquire in order to know, and, knowing, to avoid what they investigate in order to know, but know in order to practice: namely, what it is within us that divides our desires in so many ways and leads one heart into different directions. We find, however, that this is nothing other than love. In itself, as the motion of the heart according to nature, it is singular and one; but according to its operation it is divided. When it moves in a disordered way—that is, toward things toward which it ought not—it is called cupidity; but when it is ordered, it is called charity. By what definition, then, shall we be able to signify this very motion of the heart, which we call love? It is useful for us to look more closely at it, lest it remain hidden in some way and go unrecognized, and consequently neither be avoided when it is evil nor desired or discovered when it is good—for from it, when it is evil, such great evils arise, and when it is good, such great goods proceed.

## CHAPTER II. What Love Is. What Evil Is.

How, then, shall we define it? Let us investigate and consider, because what is sought is hidden; and the more deeply it is situated, the more completely it rules the heart in both respects. It seems, then, to be this: love is the delight of a heart in something for the sake of something; desire in seeking, and joy in enjoyment—running through desire and coming to rest through joy [Note: [Col. 0845] Hugh reads here and below *love* (*dilectio*)]. From this comes the goodness, and from this the evil, of the human heart; for you are good for no other reason, if you are good, nor evil for any other reason, if you are evil, except that you love well or badly what is good. For everything that exists is good; but when what is good is loved badly, that good is not [Note: [Col. 0845] Hugh omits *not*], and this is evil. Therefore neither is the one who loves evil, nor is what he loves evil, nor is the love by which he loves evil; rather, what he loves badly is evil, and this is the whole of evil. Order charity, therefore, and there is now no evil at all.

## CHAPTER III. Those Capable of Blessedness through God’s Grace. They Become Partakers through Love.

We wish to commend a great matter, if only we are able to accomplish what we wish. Almighty God, who needs nothing because he himself is the highest and true good; who can receive nothing belonging to another by which he might increase, since all things are from him; and who can lose nothing of his own by which he might decline, since all things subsist immutably in him—he created the rational spirit through charity alone and through no necessity, so that he might make it a partaker of his blessedness. Moreover, so that it might be fit to enjoy so great a blessedness, he formed spiritual love within it, in a certain way making the palate of the heart sensitive through this love to the taste of inward sweetness, so that through this very love it might taste the delight of his happiness and cling to him with tireless desire.

Through love, therefore, God joined the rational creature to himself, so that, by always clinging to him, it might in some way draw through affection the good by which it was to be made blessed from him, drink of him through desire, and possess him through joy. Suck, little bee, suck; suck and drink the inexpressible sweetness of your honey. Plunge in and be filled, for he knows no failing unless you begin to find him tedious. Cling, therefore, and hold fast; take and enjoy. If the taste is everlasting, everlasting too will be the blessedness. Let us no longer be ashamed or regret having spoken of love: let there be no regret where there is such usefulness, no shame where there is such nobility.

## CHAPTER IV. On the Double Cord of Charity.

Through love, therefore, the rational creature was joined to its Maker; and the bond of love alone binds both together into one, the more happily the more strongly. For this reason, too, so that an undivided fellowship and perfect harmony might be maintained on both sides, the bond was doubled in love of God and love of neighbor: so that through love of God all might cling to the One, and through love of neighbor all might become one with one another; so that whatever each person could not contain in himself from that One to whom all clung, he might possess more fully and perfectly through love of neighbor in another, and the good of all might become wholly the good of each individual. Order charity, therefore. What does it mean to order charity? If love is desire, let it run well; if it is joy, let it rest well. For love is, as has been said, the delight of a heart in something for the sake of something: desire in seeking, and joy in enjoyment; running through desire and resting through joy, running toward that thing and resting in it. Toward what, or in what?

## CHAPTER V. Ordered Charity: With Respect to God, Neighbor, and the World.

Listen, if perhaps we can explain toward what our love ought to run, or in what it ought to rest. There are three things that can be loved well or badly: God, neighbor, and the world. God is above us, neighbor beside us, and the world beneath us. Order charity, therefore. If it runs, let it run well; if it rests, let it rest well. Desire runs; joy rests. Hence joy is uniform, because it is always in one thing and cannot be varied by alternation. Desire, however, admits the mutability of motion, and therefore does not remain in one thing but presents various forms.

For every course is either from that thing, or with that thing, or in that thing toward which it is directed. How, then, ought our desire to run? There are three objects: God, neighbor, and the world. Let God have three modes, neighbor two, and the world one in the course of our desire; and thus charity is ordered in desire.

Love can run in an ordered way through desire from God, with God, and toward God. It runs from God when it receives from him the reason for loving him. It runs with God when it contradicts his will in nothing. It runs toward God when it desires to rest in him. These are the three things that pertain to God.

There are two things that pertain to neighbor. Desire can run from neighbor and with neighbor, but it cannot run into neighbor. From neighbor, so that it may rejoice in his salvation and progress. With neighbor, so that it may desire to have him as a companion on God’s way and a partner in reaching the goal. But it cannot run into neighbor, namely, so as to place its hope and confidence in a human being [Note: [Col. 0846] *Namely* is absent from the Victorine manuscript and from Hugh]. These are the two things that pertain to neighbor: from him and with him, but not into him.

There is one thing that pertains to the world: to run from it—not with it or into it. Desire runs from the world when, having looked outwardly upon God’s work, it turns inward more ardently toward him through wonder and praise. It would run with the world if, because of the mutability of temporal things, it conformed itself to them, whether by being cast down in adversity or lifted up in prosperity. It would run into the world if it wished always to rest in its pleasures.

Order charity, therefore, so that through desire it may run from God, with God, and toward God; from neighbor, with neighbor, and not into neighbor; from the world, neither with the world nor into the world, so that through joy it may rest in God alone. This is ordered charity; and apart from it, everything that is done is not ordered charity but disordered cupidity [Note: [Col. 0846] Hugh omits *through*].

## CHAPTER VI. Love Is Never Idle. The True Rest of the Heart. Whether It Is Perfect Here.

Love is the life of the heart, and therefore it is altogether impossible for a heart that wishes to live to be without love. Consider what follows from this. If the human mind cannot be without love, it must love either itself or something else. But since it does not find perfect good in itself, if it loved only itself, its love would not be happy. Therefore, if it desires to love happily, it must seek something other than itself to love. But if it begins to love something imperfect outside itself, it frustrates its own love but does not exclude misery. It therefore does not love happily until, through the desire of love, it turns toward the true and highest good.

Since God alone is the highest and true good, the person loves happily who loves God, and the more happily the more abundantly. This, then, is the true rest of our heart: when it is fixed in the love of God through desire and seeks nothing further, but takes delight in what it holds with a kind of happy security. For because neither appetite draws it farther onward nor fear drives it away, it rests, in a certain way, in the same thing, in enjoyment without disturbance.
