But because the weakness of the human mind can scarcely ever—let alone always—be fixed in that sweetness of divine contemplation, it must meanwhile be trained by a certain practice toward that stability which it is not yet capable of attaining. That is, if we cannot always think of God, let us at least keep our heart from illicit and empty thoughts and hold it in consideration of God’s works and wonders, so that, while we continually strive to be less unstable, we may at last, by God’s gift, become truly stable.

## CHAPTER VII. How It Is to Be Acquired. Faith as a Ship amid the Waves of This World. From What It Is to Be Built.

To offer you some example of this progress: the whole of this world is like a kind of flood, because everything that is in this world flows along, fluctuating through uncertain events like water. True faith, however, which promises not transitory but eternal things, lifts the soul toward higher things from the desire of this world as though from certain waves. It can indeed be carried by the waters, but it cannot possibly be submerged, because it uses this world for necessities but is not entangled in its desires through affection.

Whoever, therefore, does not believe in eternal things but seeks only what passes away is like a person struggling in the waves without a ship; the force of the flowing water carries him away with it. But whoever believes in eternal things yet loves transitory things suffers shipwreck beside the ship. Whoever both believes in and loves eternal goods, however, passes safely through the waves of the surging sea, placed in the ship. And because through the desire of faith he does not cross beyond the ship, he already imitates, in a certain way, stability amid the waves of the earth.

First, then, if we wish to cross this great sea unharmed, let us build a ship, so that we may have an unbroken faith. Then let us inhabit the ship of faith through charity, so that we may both believe what we ought to love and love what we believe. Thus the law of God will be in our heart through knowledge of right faith, and our heart will be in the law of God through love.

But so that you may more easily understand how or from what you ought to build in your heart the ship or ark of which I have spoken, by which you may be brought out of the shipwreck of this flood and reach the harbor of rest, consider two works of God: namely, the work of creation and the work of restoration. The work of creation is the creation of heaven and earth and of all that they contain, which was accomplished in six days. The work of restoration is the incarnation of the Word and everything that, from the beginning of the world to its end, either preceded it in order to foretell it or will follow it in order to confirm it. All these things take place over six ages.

The works of restoration, however, pertain more directly to the Catholic faith; for this reason the saints love them more deeply, because in them they recognize the remedies of their salvation. God accomplished these works partly through human beings, partly through angels, and partly through himself, so that in the spiritual ark the first dwelling might be the work of human beings, the second the work of angels, and the third the work of God—the highest cubit being God, the author of all things.

# [ON LOVING GOD]

[Col. 0847]

## NOTICE ON THE FOLLOWING BOOK

The book *On Loving God* is pious, in the judgment of Erasmus and the theologians of Louvain, and not unlearned; yet they rightly considered it spurious, if only because its phraseology differs so greatly from Augustine’s. Its author certainly reveals himself sufficiently as belonging to a later age by citing a saying of Jerome from Book 3 of his *Commentary on Matthew* XVIII in this form: “Hence, a certain holy man says, ‘Great is the dignity of souls,’” and so forth.

The author gathered here statements intended to kindle the love of God from various books, especially those of Hugh of Saint Victor, Bernard, and Anselm. Indeed, from Chapter 4 through Chapter 11 he offers us nothing else to read than what Hugh wrote, in the *Soliloquy on the Earnest-Money of the Soul*, in the same words and almost the same number of words. There are likewise passages excerpted from other minor works of Hugh, many more from various sermons of Bernard, and some from the sixteenth *Meditation* in Anselm’s final edition; these we indicate throughout by notes placed alongside them [Note: [Col. 0847] Before the individual chapters, we indicated with alphabetical notes the books from which various passages were excerpted here and there. M.].

Finally, in Chapter 18, a notable passage from Anselm’s own *Proslogion* is presented. This work suggests the same author as the book *On Spirit and Soul*. One might perhaps also more suitably attribute to that author the *Manual* and certain other minor works represented below, as well as the first and third books *On the Soul* attributed to Hugh, which Bernard calls *Meditations* and *On Conscience*. Vincent of Beauvais, moreover, in Book 23 of the *Natural Mirror*, Chapter 1, cites under the name of Peter Comestor something that may be read in Chapter 3 of this book. We compared the book with two royal manuscripts in which it is falsely prefaced with Augustine’s name.

[Col. 0847]

# ONE BOOK ON LOVING GOD (G, S)*

## CHAPTER I. Charity Is the Way to Life. The Manner of Loving God and Neighbor.

With vigilant care, an attentive mind, the greatest effort, and continual solicitude, we ought to seek and learn how and by what way we can avoid infernal punishment and obtain heavenly joy, since neither can that punishment be avoided nor that joy acquired unless the way by which the former is to be avoided and the latter obtained is known.

Let us therefore listen more willingly and examine more carefully the words of the Apostle, by which he himself points out two things: namely, that the life of heavenly glory is ineffable, and what the way is that leads to life. For he says: “Eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man what God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Cor. 2:9). Behold: by saying that God has prepared good things for those who love him, he shows that love is the way by which one reaches those good things [Col. 0849]. But love of God cannot be possessed without love of neighbor, as blessed John testifies when he says: “He who does not love his brother whom he sees, how can he love God whom he does not see? And we have this commandment from God, that whoever loves God should love his brother also” (1 John 4:20–21).

Behold: in this twofold love true charity consists, concerning which the Apostle says: “I show you a still more excellent way” (1 Cor. 12:31). Behold: charity is the most excellent way that leads to the heavenly homeland, and without it no one can arrive there. But who is on this way? Who knows it? The one who loves God and neighbor.

How is God to be loved, and how is neighbor to be loved? We ought to love God more than ourselves, but our neighbor as ourselves. We love God more than ourselves if in all things we place his commands before our own will. We are not commanded to love our neighbor as much as ourselves, but as ourselves—that is, to will and desire for him every good thing that we ought to will and desire for ourselves, especially eternal blessedness, and to assist him in attaining it, both in bodily and spiritual matters, as reason requires and ability permits.

Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Whatever you wish that people would do to you, do the same to them” (Matt. 7:12); and the Apostle John says: “Let us not love in word or speech, but in deed and in truth” (1 John 3:18). But who are the neighbors whom we ought to love in this way? Certainly all human beings: Christians, Jews, pagans, friends, and enemies.

## CHAPTER II. Why and How God Is to Be Loved. Love of God Is Stirred by Contemplation of Creation. The Rational Creature Is Twofold. For What It Was Made.

[Note: [Col. 0849] From Hugh of Saint Victor, Book 1 *On the Sacraments*, Part 2, Chapter 4, and from the same author’s *Summa of Sentences*, Tract 2, Chapter 1.]

Since our entire salvation consists in love, we must carefully consider why and how our Lord is to be loved by us. To stir up, nourish, and increase the love of God within us, nothing is so effective as frequent and careful consideration of his benefits. For he has bestowed and repaid so many things upon us that our soul fails—indeed, utterly fails—in contemplating the greatness of his benefits. Although we cannot render him as much love, service, and thanksgiving as we ought, nevertheless we must return as much and as many as we can.

Behold why he is to be greatly loved by us: because of his benefits, which the Lord, in his great mercy and gratuitous goodness, conferred upon us without any of our merits demanding them. How God is to be loved by us is shown by that commandment of his which he commanded with such insistence and wished to be observed so carefully (Ps. 118:4). Listen, then, O human being, to that greatest and first of all commandments. Listen, I say, attentively; retain it in memory; meditate upon it continually; and fulfill it earnestly, constantly, and perseveringly, according to your strength.

This is the commandment: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart”—that is, with your entire understanding—“and with all your soul”—that is, with your entire will—“and with all your mind” (Deut. 6:5; Matt. 22:37)—that is, with your entire memory: so that you preserve all your thoughts, your whole life, and your entire understanding for him.

But because perhaps you consider yourself little loved by God, you are not afraid also to love him little. Search out and turn over in your mind what gifts and benefits he has bestowed upon you and what he has promised, and you will be convinced that you ought to love him intensely.

To stir up and increase the love of God in you still further, carefully consider by whom, why, and for what purpose human beings were created, and what God created on account of humanity. You should know, then, that the cause of created things—heavenly and earthly, visible and invisible—is none other than the goodness of the Creator, who is the one true God. His goodness is so great that he wished others to share in the blessedness in which he is eternally blessed, since he saw that it could be communicated without being diminished at all. He wished, through goodness alone and not through necessity, to communicate to others that good which he himself was and by which he himself was blessed, because it belonged to the supreme good to will to benefit, and to the almighty good it was impossible to harm.

Since no one can become a partaker of his blessedness except through understanding—and the more fully something is understood, the more fully it is possessed—God made the rational creature to understand the highest good, to love it through understanding, to possess it through loving, and to enjoy it through possessing. He distinguished it in this way: one part was to remain in its own purity and not be joined to a body, namely, the angel; the other part was to be joined to a body, namely, the soul. The rational creature was thus divided into incorporeal and corporeal. The incorporeal is called an angel; the corporeal is called a human being, subsisting from a rational soul and flesh.

The rational creature, therefore, had the goodness of God as its first cause. The human being or angel was created on account of the goodness of God [Note: [Col. 0850] In another reading, *so that*]. For because God is good, we exist; and insofar as we exist, we are good. For what purpose, however, was the rational creature created? To praise God, to serve him, and to enjoy him—in all of which the creature progresses, not God. For God, perfect and full of supreme goodness, can neither increase nor diminish.

That the rational creature was made by God must therefore be referred to the goodness of the Creator and the benefit of the creature. When it is asked why or for what purpose the rational creature was made, the answer should be: for the goodness of God and the benefit of the creature. For it is beneficial to the creature to serve God and enjoy him.

## CHAPTER III. All Things Belong to Humanity.

[Note: [Col. 0850] These words are cited under the name of Comestor by Vincent of Beauvais, *Natural Mirror*, Book 23, Chapter 1; by Hugh of Saint Victor, Book 1 *On the Sacraments*, Part 2, Chapter 1; and by Bernard, Sermon 1 *On Saint Michael*.]

An angel or a human being is therefore said to have been made on account of God—not because God, the Creator and supremely blessed one, needed the service of either, since he has no need of our goods, but so that the creature might serve and enjoy him, for serving him is reigning. In this, the servant progresses, not the one whom he serves.

And just as the human being was made on account of God—that is, to serve him—so the world was made on account of the human being, namely, to serve him. The human being was therefore placed in the middle, so that service might be rendered to him and so that he himself might serve; so that he might receive both, and that everything might flow back to the good of the human being, both the service he received and the service he rendered.

For God wished to be served by the human being in such a way that through this service not God but the human being who served would be helped [Note: [Col. 0850] The excerpt from Comestor and Hugh add here: *the one who serves*]. He also wished the world to serve humanity, so that humanity might likewise be helped by it. Everything, therefore, was for the good of humanity: both what was made on its account and the purpose for which it itself was made.

“For all things are ours,” says the Apostle (1 Cor. 3:22): the higher, the equal, and the lower. The higher things are ours for enjoyment, such as God the Creator, the Trinity. The equal things are ours for companionship, namely, the angels, who, although they are now superior to us, will in the future be equal to us (Matt. 22:30). The lower things are ours for use, just as the possessions of masters are said to belong to servants—not by ownership, but because they are for their use [Note: [Col. 0850] The printed editions read: *not because they are deprived of their master*].

The angels themselves are said in certain passages of Scripture to serve us, since they are sent to minister on our behalf. Hence the Apostle says: “Are they not all ministering spirits, sent out to minister for the sake of those who are to inherit salvation?” (Heb. 1:14). Nor should this seem incredible to anyone, since the Creator and King of angels himself came not to be served but to serve and to give his soul for many (Matt. 20:28).

The angels are said to offer our prayers and vows to God—not because they teach God, who knows everything before it happens just as he knows it afterward [Note: [Col. 0850] The Royal Manuscript reads: *and knows more fully than before it happens*], but because they consult his will concerning these things and report to us, openly or secretly, what they have learned to have been accomplished at God’s command. Hence the angel says to human beings: “When you prayed, I offered your prayer to God” (Tob. 12:12).

Likewise, when we pray, we do not teach God, as though he did not know what we desire and what we need. Rather, it is necessary for the rational creature to refer temporal causes to eternal truth, whether by asking what should be done concerning it or by seeking counsel about what it should do.

From the lofty dwelling of heaven, therefore, surpassing charity draws the angels to console, visit, and assist us—for God’s sake, for our sake, and for their own sake. For God’s sake, certainly, because they too fittingly imitate his great compassion toward us; for our sake, because they have pity on us on account of our likeness to them; and for their own sake, because they await with complete desire the restoration of their orders from among us.

## CHAPTER IV. The Dignity of the Soul. It Is Recognized from God’s Love for It. To It All Things Serve through God’s Gift. How Created Things Are to Be Loved, and How the Creator Is to Be Loved.

[Note: [Col. 0851] Words of Hugh of Saint Victor, *On the Earnest-Money of the Soul*.]

First, then, everyone must consider himself; and when he has recognized his own dignity, he must not wrong his Creator by loving what is beneath himself. For things that are beautiful when considered in themselves become worthless when compared with more beautiful things; and just as it is foolish to join deformed things to beautiful ones, so it is altogether unfitting to equate things that possess only a very low and imaginary beauty with the most beautiful things.

Attend, then, O soul, to your beauty, and understand what sort of beauty you ought to love. But if your inward vision has perhaps been darkened through your negligence, and you are not capable of contemplating yourself as you ought and as is expedient, why do you not at least judge from another’s judgment what you ought to think about yourself?

You have a bridegroom, but you do not know him. He is the most beautiful of all, yet you have not seen his face. He has seen you, because if he had not seen you, he would not love you. He has not yet wished to present himself to you; instead, he sent gifts, gave a pledge, the earnest of love, the sign of affection. If you could know him, if you could see his appearance, you would no longer doubt your own beauty. For you would know that one so beautiful, so fair, so graceful, so unique would not have been captivated by your appearance if a singular beauty, admirable beyond all others, had not drawn him.

What, then, will you do? You cannot now see him, because he is absent; and for that reason you neither fear nor blush to wrong him, because you despise his singular love and shamefully and immodestly prostitute yourself to another’s lust. Do not act in this way. If you still cannot know what he is like who loves you, at least consider the earnest-money he gave you. Perhaps in the very gift of his that you possess you will be able to recognize with what affection you ought to love him and with what care and diligence you ought to preserve yourself for him.

His pledge is remarkable, his gift noble; for it would not have been fitting for one who was great to give something small, nor would one wise have given something great for what was small. Great, then, is what he gave you; but greater is what he loves in you. Great, therefore, is what he gave you.

What did your bridegroom give you, O soul? Look upon this entire world and consider whether there is anything in it that does not serve you. All nature [Note: [Col. 0851] Alternatively, *every creature*] directs its course toward this end: that it may serve your needs, minister to your benefit, and likewise meet your pleasures and necessities according to an inexhaustible abundance. Heaven, earth, air, and seas, with all that is in them, never cease to fulfill this purpose. The cycle of the seasons, renewing what is ancient through annual renewal and recurring births, restoring what has fallen apart and rebuilding what has been consumed, continually supplies nourishment.

Who, then, do you think established this? Who commanded nature to serve you in such unanimous agreement [Note: [Col. 0851] Alternatively, *with a single reckoning*; or *with a single perception*]? You receive a benefit but do not recognize its author; the gift is manifest, the giver hidden. Yet your own reason does not allow you to doubt that this is not something owed to you but a benefit bestowed by another.

Whoever, then, he may be, he has bestowed much upon us; and the one who wished to give so much has loved greatly. By his gift he shows himself to have loved greatly and to be greatly worthy of love [Note: [Col. 0852] Alternatively, *to have given so much*]. How foolish it is not spontaneously to desire the love of one so powerful! How impious and perverse it is not to love one who loves so greatly!

If you love these things, love them as things subject to you; love them as things that serve; love them as the pledge of the bridegroom, the gifts of a friend, and the benefits of a lord. Yet always remember what you owe to him. Do not love these things for their own sake, but for his sake; not these things together with him, but these things because of him; and through these things love him, and above these things love him [Note: [Col. 0852] Thus also Peter of Blois, *On the Charity of God and Neighbor*, Chapter 21].

## CHAPTER V. The Benefits of God Are Enumerated.

Beware, O soul, lest—God forbid—you be called a prostitute if you love the gifts of the giver more than the affection of the one who loves you. You do greater injury to his charity if you both accept his gifts and fail to return love in exchange. Either reject his gifts, if you can; or, if you cannot reject his gifts, return love in exchange.

Love him for his own sake; love yourself for his sake. Love him so that you may enjoy him; love yourself so that you may be loved by him [Note: [Col. 0852] Hugh reads: *because you are loved by him*]. In his gifts, love what has been given by him. Love him for you, and yourself for him. This is pure and chaste love, containing nothing sordid, nothing bitter, nothing transitory.

Consider, then, O my soul, what things you have received in common with everyone, what things specially with some, and what things uniquely by yourself alone. In all these he has loved you: in what he has granted to you either commonly with everyone, specially with some, or uniquely to you alone. He loved you again together with all those with whom he joined you through a share in his gift. Above all those to whom he preferred you by the singular gift of grace, he loved you [Note: [Col. 0852] The passage has been restored from Hugh and from the Royal Manuscript].

In every creature you have been loved; with all good people you have been loved; above all evil people you have been loved. And lest this seem little to you—that you have been loved above all evil people—consider how many good people there are who received less than you.

## CHAPTER VI. The Benefit of Creation. The Benefit of Restoration. The Value of the Human Being.

First consider, O soul, that once you did not exist, and that you received existence as a gift from God. It was therefore his gift that you should come to be. But had you given him anything before you came to be, so that what you received from him in coming to be might be repaid to you? Nothing at all; you had given nothing, nor could you have given anything before you came to be.

Even if he had given nothing more, he would nevertheless always deserve to be praised and loved by us for this alone. But now he gave more, because he gave not only existence but also beauty and form. Yet the munificence of the best of givers could not end even there: he gave still more and drew us more closely into his likeness [Note: [Col. 0852] The Royal Manuscript reads: *and he gave still more; we*]. He wished to draw to himself through likeness those whom he was drawing to himself through love.

He therefore gave us existence and beauty; he also gave us life, so that through essence we might surpass those things that do not exist, through form those that are disordered, incomplete, or uncomposed, and through life those that are without life.

You are bound by a great debt, my soul. You have received much and possessed nothing from yourself; and for all these things you have nothing to give in return except that you love. For what was given through love can be repaid neither better nor more fittingly than through love; and you received this through love.

Now I shall begin to tell you how greatly this bridegroom of yours, who appeared so exalted when he created you, deigned to humble himself when he restored you. There he was so sublime; here, so humble—yet here he is no less lovable than there, because here too he is no less wonderful than there. [Note: [Col. 0852] We supply from Hugh the words “lovable, because here too he is no less than there.”] There he powerfully bestowed great things upon you; here he mercifully endured dreadful things for you. For in order to raise you back to the place from which you had fallen, he deigned to descend himself to this place where you lay; and so that what you had lost might justly be restored to you, he mercifully deigned to suffer himself what you were enduring. He therefore descended, assumed, endured, conquered, and restored. He descended to mortal man, assumed mortality, endured suffering, conquered death, and restored humanity.

Behold, my soul: stand amazed at so many wonders, so many benefits displayed for your sake. Consider how greatly he loves you, who has deigned to do so much for you. You had been made beautiful by his gift; you became foul through your own iniquity. Yet again you were cleansed and made beautiful by his mercy, though in both cases his love was at work. Long ago, when you did not yet exist, he loved you so that he might create you; afterward, when you were foul, he loved you so that he might make you beautiful. And to show you how greatly he loved you, he willed to free you from death only by dying, so that he might not merely bestow such a great benefit of mercy, but also display the affection of his love.

Thus, with great condescension, the merciful Fashioner first breathed the breath of life from above into the first man; but with far greater love, for that same man he no longer gave something belonging to himself, but bestowed and surrendered himself. It is a great thing concerning God that I recognize myself to be his work; but it is far greater that I see him himself having become my price, since redemption is accomplished by so costly a gift that a human being seems to have been valued at God.

O happy fault of mine! While he is drawn by love to wipe it away, his love itself is disclosed to me as I desire it and long for it with all my inmost heart. I would never have known his love so well if I had not experienced it amid such great dangers. O how happily I fell, since after my fall I rose again more happily! There is no greater love, no purer affection, no holier charity, no more ardent devotion. The innocent one died for me, finding nothing in me that he could love. What, then, did you love in me, Lord—and love so greatly that you died for me? What did you find in me for which you wished to endure such great and such harsh things?

## CHAPTER VII. On the benefit of being called to the faith

And what if you begin to consider, O my soul, how many and what kinds of people were rejected in comparison with you, who were unable to attain the grace that was given to you? Surely you have heard, from the beginning up to this day, how many generations have passed away, all of which slipped into everlasting destruction without knowledge of God and of the price of their redemption. Your Redeemer preferred you to all of them when he bestowed upon you this grace, which none of them deserved to receive. You alone were chosen from among them all; and why this was done in your case, you will be unable to find any reason except the love of your Savior alone.

Your bridegroom, therefore—your lover, your God, your Redeemer—chose and fore-chose you. He chose you among all, took you from among all, and loved you above all. He called you by his own name, so that his memory might always be with you. He wished you to share in the name and to share in the reality of the name, since he anointed you with the oil of gladness (Ps. 44:8), with which he himself had been anointed, so that, because you are anointed by the Anointed One, you are called Christian from Christ.

But were you stronger, wiser, nobler, or richer than all those others, so that you deserved to receive this special grace above them all? How many strong, wise, noble, and rich people were there among them—and yet all were abandoned and rejected and perished? Much, I confess, has been bestowed upon you. For although you had previously been foul, polluted, deformed, filthy, torn apart and scattered, and full of every horror and monstrosity, God your Lord loved you so much that he enriched you with such great gifts of his grace.

Therefore, unless you have first been cultivated with great care and ardent diligence and suitably adorned, you will not be worthy to be introduced into the chamber of your heavenly bridegroom. Now, then, while there is time, O my soul, cultivate your appearance, adorn your face, arrange your clothing, wipe away your stains, restore your purity, correct your conduct, preserve discipline, and, when all things have finally been changed for the better, make yourself by every effort a worthy bride for a worthy bridegroom. Prepare yourself, therefore, as befits the bride of an immortal bridegroom, the bride of the heavenly kingdom.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the gift of the virtues. To acquiesce in God’s ordering of all things

[Col. 0854]

Know also that this pertains to love: you possess something with which you can adorn yourself—something you would certainly not possess from yourself unless you received it from him. From him you received the ability to put on the clothing of good works and to be adorned or embellished with the fruit of almsgiving, together with fasts and prayers, holy vigils, and other works of piety, as though with a kind of varied ornament. Whatever is recognized as useful for health, for restoration, for repairing one’s appearance, or for increasing beauty, he has abundantly bestowed.

See with what abundant provision you are everywhere assisted. You did not have it, and it was given to you; you lost it, and it was restored to you. You are never abandoned, so that you may know how greatly he loves you, by whom you are loved. He does not wish to destroy you; and therefore he awaits you with such patience, and mercifully permits you, again and again if you wish, to restore what you have so often carelessly lost.

O how many have already perished who received these things together with you, but did not deserve to receive them again with you after losing them! You are loved more than all of them, because what is restored to you with such kindness, after being lost, is denied to them with such strictness. Through the generosity of the giver, the grace of doing good has never been denied you.

If you perform great works, you are mercifully exalted; if you do not perform great works, you are beneficially humbled. [Note: [Col. 0854] The passage has been restored from Hugh and from the Regius manuscript.] For he knows better than you what is beneficial for you. Therefore, if you wish to think rightly about him, understand that everything done to you by him is done rightly. Such indeed is God’s love in us: human weakness endures absolutely nothing which he, insofar as his goodness permits, does not order for our good.

Perhaps you do not possess the grace of the virtues; but while you are shaken by the impulse of vices, you are more firmly established in humility. For weak humility gives off a sweeter fragrance to God than exalted virtue. Do not dare to prejudice the divine ordering in anything; rather, always pray to God with fear and reverence that, in the manner he knows, he may come to your aid; that if any evils still remain in you, he may mercifully wash them away; that if any good things have been begun, he may graciously bring them to completion; and that he may lead you to himself by whatever path he wills.

## CHAPTER IX. On illumination and other benefits

O soul, what shall we do for the Lord God, from whom we have received so many good things? For he was not content merely to bestow upon us the same good things as upon others; even in our evils we recognize his singular love, so that we may love him uniquely for all our good things as well as for our evils.

You gave me, Lord, the ability to know you and, above many others, to understand what was revealed concerning your secrets. You abandoned other people of my own age in the darkness of ignorance, but poured into me, above them, the light of your wisdom. [Note: [Col. 0854] Another reading: “of your grace.”]

You gave me an understanding capable of receiving, an intellect that grasps readily, a tenacious memory, effectiveness in action, graciousness in conduct, progress in study, accomplishment in undertakings. [Note: [Col. 0854] Another reading: “progress in what had been conceived.”] You gave me consolation in adversity and caution in prosperity. Wherever I turned, your grace and mercy went before me.

Often, when I seemed exhausted, you suddenly delivered me; when I was wandering, you led me back; when I was ignorant, you taught me; when I sinned, you reproved me; when I was sorrowful, you consoled me; when I fell, you raised me up; when I stood, you sustained me. You gave me to know you more truly, to love you more purely, to believe in you more sincerely, and to follow you more ardently.

O Lord my God, sweetness of my life, light of my eyes, what shall I render to you for all that you have rendered to me? You wish me to love you. And how shall I love you? How greatly shall I love you? Who am I, that I should love you? And yet I shall love you, Lord, my strength, my support, my refuge and my deliverer, my God, my helper, my protector, the horn of my salvation, and my sustainer. And how much more shall I say? You are, Lord, my God.

## CHAPTER X. On God’s care for us. What his presence produces in the author

You have done many and innumerable good things for me, Lord my God. It will always be sweet for me to think about them, always to speak of them, always to give thanks, so that I may praise and love you for all your benefits.

Behold, my soul, you have your pledge; and in your pledge you recognize your bridegroom. Preserve yourself, therefore, untouched for him; preserve yourself undefiled, preserve yourself uncontaminated, preserve yourself whole. If once you were a prostitute, you have now become a virgin, just as his love customarily restores integrity to the corrupt and preserves chastity in the intact. [Note: [Col. 0855] Add: “and so.”]

Always consider how great a mercy he has shown you, and weigh in this how greatly you are loved by him: you recognize that his benefit has never been absent from you. Certainly, when I attend to his mercies toward me, it seems to me that, if one may say so, God does nothing else than provide for my salvation. I see him wholly occupied with guarding me, as though he had forgotten everyone else and wished to devote himself to me alone.

God always presents himself to me as present; he always offers himself as ready. Wherever I turn, he does not abandon me; wherever I am, he does not depart; whatever I do, he assists me equally. In the end, he plainly shows by the effect of his work that he stands beside all my actions as their perpetual observer and, insofar as his goodness is concerned, as an inseparable fellow-worker.

From this it is clear that although his face cannot yet be seen by us, his presence can never be avoided. But what is that sweetness which, in remembering him, usually touches me and affects me so powerfully and gently, so that I begin to become wholly alienated, in a certain way, from myself and to be carried away I know not where?

Suddenly I am wholly renewed and wholly changed, and I begin to feel better than I am able to express. Conscience is gladdened; all the misery of past sorrows passes into oblivion; the spirit exults; the intellect grows bright; the heart is illuminated; desires rejoice.

Already I see myself existing elsewhere—I do not know where—and as though I were holding something within me in the embraces of love, though I do not know what it is. Nevertheless, with all my strength I strive always to retain it and never to lose it. The soul struggles, in a kind of delightful way, not to withdraw from what it always desires to embrace; and as though it had found in it the end of all its desires, it exults supremely and ineffably, seeking nothing more, desiring nothing further, always wishing to remain so.

Is that beloved one? Truly it is my Lord who visits me. But he comes invisible, he comes hidden, he comes incomprehensible. He comes to touch me, not to be seen by me; he comes to admonish me, not to be grasped by me; he comes not to pour himself into me completely, but to offer himself for tasting—not to fulfill desire, not to display the fullness of his perfect satisfaction.

And this is what pertains most of all to his pledge of betrothal: that he who in the future will give himself to you to be seen and possessed forever now offers himself to you in some manner to be tasted, so that you may recognize how sweet he is. [Note: [Col. 0855] Here end Hugh’s words from *The Pledge of the Soul*.]

## CHAPTER XI. On the gift of life preserved from birth. On granted sensory pleasures. On other privileges

[Note: [Col. 0855] From Anselm, *Meditations* 16; Hugh of Saint-Victor, *The Instruction of the Scholar*, book 7, chapter 13.]

Your God, therefore, must be loved greatly by you, since he has bestowed such great benefits upon you. But in order that you may be kindled more greatly by the flame of his love, consider carefully, O soul, whether, besides those things mentioned above, he has bestowed any other benefits upon you.

When you see that the good things mentioned here have been bestowed upon you, you owe it to him from whom they were bestowed to be very grateful and devoted, and, giving thanks, to say:

“My God must be loved exceedingly, since, making good use of the evil of my parents, he created me from their flesh and breathed into me the breath of life. He distinguished me from those who were either cast away as miscarriages from the womb or suffocated within the maternal entrails, seeming to have been conceived for punishment rather than for life.

“I received existence; I received the condition of being human; I received understanding, by which there is a distinction between me and cattle. I received the form of the body; I received in the body the differentiation of the senses: eyes for seeing, ears for hearing, nostrils for smelling, hands for touching, the palate for tasting, feet for walking, and bodily health itself.

“It was also a great thing that God created many beautiful and fitting objects for the delight of these same senses of mine—things that shine beautifully, delight with harmonious sound, emit a pleasant fragrance, taste sweetly, and please the touch. For this reason the Creator’s providence endowed things with such varied qualities, so that all the senses of human beings might find their pleasures.

“Sight perceives one thing, smell another, hearing another, the sense of scent another, taste another, and touch another. Beauty of colors nourishes sight; the sweetness of song soothes hearing; fragrance nourishes the sense of smell; sweetness of flavor nourishes taste.

“And who could enumerate all the delights of the senses? They are so manifold in each individual sense that, if anyone considered any one of them by itself, he would think that each had been endowed separately with abundant riches.

“As many delights of the eyes as we display in the variety of colors, so many delights of the ears do we hear in the variety of sounds. Among these, the first are the sweet exchanges of speech, by which human beings communicate their intentions to one another, recount past things, indicate present things, announce future things, and reveal hidden things. Indeed, if human life lacked these, it would seem comparable to that of beasts.

“What shall I say of the concert of birds, the pleasant melody of the human voice, or the sweet measures of every kind of sound? There are so many kinds of harmony that thought cannot run through them, nor speech easily explain them. Yet all of them serve hearing and were created for its delight.

“The same is true of smell. Incense has its fragrance, as do all things that provide a pleasant odor and breathe forth sweet scents. They serve the sense of smell and were created for its delight. In the same way, taste and touch have various pleasures, which can be sufficiently appreciated from the similarity of the preceding examples.

“It is certainly also a great thing that God created my limbs sound and whole, so that I would not be a pain to myself or a reproach to others.

“I received still more: namely, a mind able to understand, able to grasp truth, able to distinguish the just from the unjust, able to investigate, desire, praise, and cling to the Creator.

“I also consider it a great benefit that God wished me to be born at such a time and among such people that through them I might come to his faith and sacraments. I see that what was denied to countless people was granted to me, for which I rejoice, although our condition was one and the same. [Note: [Col. 0856] In Anselm: “was.”] They were abandoned through justice, while I was called through grace.

“I shall proceed further, also recognizing that it was his gift that I was raised by my parents; that flame did not injure me; that water did not swallow me; that I was not tormented by a demon; that I was not struck by beasts; that I was not killed by a fall; and that I was nourished in his faith and good will until a suitable age.”

## CHAPTER XII. On God’s long-suffering. Three ways in which we are preserved from sinning. On the guardian angel. The sinner stirs every creature against himself. How generously God forgives

[Note: [Col. 0856] From *Meditations*, chapter 2; from Hugh of Saint-Victor, book 3 of *On the Manner of Praying*, chapter 1; Bernard, sermon 3 for the sixth Sunday after Pentecost, §§1–4; and from Anselm’s *Meditations* 16.]

You have shown great mercy toward me, Lord God. Although you are wonderful in all your works, you are believed to be even more wonderful in the depths of your mercy. For you despise no one, reject no one, shrink from no one—unless perhaps someone, out of madness, shrinks from you.

These, then, are your gifts, Lord, mercifully granted to me: that when I was often placed in dangers, you graciously rescued me; and that you could never be overcome by my sins so as to cease having mercy on me. You reminded me of yourself when I had forgotten you; you called me back when I had turned away from you; you kindly received me when I came to you; and when I repented, you forgave not only the sins I had committed, but also those which, under your protection, I did not commit.

Whatever evil I did not commit because you protected me must all be reckoned as forgiven by you. For just as I fell into many sins, so I would have fallen into many more if you had not preserved me.

I remember that I was preserved from sins in three ways: by the removal of opportunity, by the strength given to resist, and by the soundness of my affection. I would have fallen into many sins if opportunity had been given; but by God’s mercy no such occasion overtook me.

I would also have fallen into many sins, almost grievously, driven by the violence of temptation; but you gave me strength, Lord, so that my desire was subject to me and I did not at all consent to the concupiscence I felt.

But from certain sins your mercy kept me so far away, Lord, that I utterly abhorred them, and no temptation toward them troubled me at all. This too is surely a sign of great goodness.

Lord God, it is also a sign of great goodness that I, wretched as I am, provoked you, did evil before you, aroused your fury, and deserved your anger; that I sinned, and you endured it; that I transgressed, and you still bear with me. If I repent, you spare me; if I return, you receive me; moreover, while I delay, you wait for me.

You call back the one who wanders, invite the one who resists, await the one who is sluggish, embrace the one who returns, teach the ignorant, and soothe the sorrowful. You raise me from ruin, restore me after my fall, give generously to the one who asks, allow yourself to be found by the one who seeks, and open to the one who knocks. You show me the path of right living and give me knowledge of how to walk.

It is also a great thing, Lord, that before I could ask, wish for, or know them, you bestowed many good things upon me. Not only this, Lord: after I learned and was able to ask you, seek you, desire you, and cling to you, by your gratuitous goodness you bestowed your good things upon me when I did not ask, did not seek, did not desire—but even when I regarded them as insignificant or actually despised them.

I also consider it the greatest benefit that from the beginning of my birth you gave me an angel of peace to guard me until the end of my life. Hence a certain holy man says: “Great is the dignity of souls, that each one has an angel assigned to guard it from the beginning of its birth” (Jerome, on Matthew 18).

It was also a great act of mercy, Lord, that your wondrous patience endured my iniquities. To whom should I give thanks because you did not repay me according to my iniquities; because the earth did not swallow me; heaven did not strike me with lightning; lightning did not burn me; rivers did not drown me; and you did not punish me with any other penalty or death as I deserved?

When by sinning I departed from you, I not only deserved your anger, but also stirred every creature against me. For if a servant were to depart from his master, he would not only provoke the master himself, but would also justly anger his entire household.

Since, therefore, I offended you, God and Creator of all, I stirred every creature to anger against me, insofar as my merit was concerned, so that the whole world would rightly fight against me on your behalf.

The earth could say to me: “I ought not to support you, but rather to swallow you, since you did not fear departing in sin from my Creator and clinging to his enemy, namely the devil.”

The sun could likewise say: “I ought not to shine upon you for salvation; rather, for vengeance on behalf of my Lord, who is light of light and fountain of brightness, I ought to hide my rays from you completely.”

So too every creature would serve to avenge such an injury to its Creator, unless he himself who made it restrained its assault—he who does not desire the death of the sinner, but rather that he should turn and live.

Therefore, Lord, I must humble myself beneath your powerful hand all the more, and become all the more grateful, devoted, and ready to serve you, the more I see myself bound to give an account for such great benefits. Otherwise, vengeance long delayed may punish my evils all the more harshly when it comes, the longer it has endured what could have been punished.

Consider, then, O my soul, the long-suffering of God, which he displayed while waiting for you; the choice of his predestination, which he wished to fulfill; and the excessive love with which he loved us.

For this reason the Lord waited and waited, and turned his attention toward me; but he turned his eyes away from my sins, as though unwilling to notice how greatly I was transgressing. For this reason, I say, he concealed his displeasure: to commend his patience, fulfill his election, and confirm his love.

For this reason, as I well remember, he shook my heart, rousing it to notice the wounds of its sins and to feel the pain of those wounds. He also terrified me, leading me to the gates of hell and showing me the punishments prepared for the wicked. And, so that no harmful pleasure might remain, [Note: [Col. 0858] One of the Regius manuscripts reads “thought”; the printed editions read “reason.”] he inspired me with a better consolation and gave me hope of forgiveness; then he bestowed forgiveness itself.

He forgave everything so completely and pardoned the whole injury so generously that he no longer condemns by taking vengeance, shames by reproaching, or loves any less by imputing it. For some people forgive an injury without taking vengeance, yet frequently reproach the offender; others, although they remain silent, still retain something stored deep in their minds and hold resentment in their hearts. Neither kind of forgiveness is complete.

Far removed from these is the most kindly nature of the divinity, which acts generously and forgives fully, so that, not on account of the confidence of sinners but of penitents, where sin abounded grace also customarily abounds. [Note: [Col. 0858] The Regius manuscript adds here: “not.”]

Peter is a witness: after his threefold denial, the pastoral care of the whole Church was entrusted to him. Paul is a witness: from a persecutor of the Church he became a chosen vessel and teacher of the Gentiles. Matthew is a witness: from the tax office he was chosen as an Apostle, and was also granted the honor of being the first writer of the New Testament.

## CHAPTER XIII. On the gift of continence. Its threefold enemy

[Note: [Col. 0858] Bernard, sermon 3 for the sixth Sunday after Pentecost, §5, and [lacuna] *Meditations*, chapter 15.]

After this, the Lord God gave me continence. By continence I mean not merely abstinence from lust, but also, as is necessary, from other vices and sins. There was a time when I scarcely managed to abstain for three days; afterward, with God’s grace assisting me, I was able to remain continent for a long period. From this I find grounds to exclaim rightly: “For he who is mighty has done great things for me” (Luke 1:49).

Perhaps someone considers continence a small matter; but I do not. For I know what opponents it has and how great its virtue must be in order to resist such enemies.

The first enemy of our continence is our own flesh, lusting against the spirit. What a familiar enemy, what a dangerous struggle, what an internal war! This most savage enemy we can neither flee nor drive away, O my soul; we must carry it about, because it has been bound to us.

What is more dangerous and miserable than being forced to sustain our enemy, when we are not permitted to destroy it? You see, therefore, how carefully you must guard yourself against the one who sleeps in your bosom. [Note: [Col. 0858] Another reading: “see.”]

Yet this is not my only adversary. I still have another, who has surrounded and besieged me on every side. This enemy is the present wicked age, which wounds me with its darts through five gates—namely, the five bodily senses—and death enters through my windows.

The third enemy is the ancient foe of the human race, the ancient serpent, more cunning than all living creatures. This is an enemy whom we cannot see—how much less can we guard against him? This enemy attacks and pursues us, sometimes openly and violently, sometimes secretly and deceitfully, but always maliciously and cruelly.

And who is capable of enduring these things, not to mention overcoming them? I have said this so that the difficulty of continence might become known, and so that we might know the things given to us by God (1 Cor. 2:12). Thus we may love more greatly him who bestowed this virtue upon us.

For we exercise this virtue entirely in the Lord, and he brings to nothing all those who trouble us. He is the one who crushes beneath our feet not only our flesh with its vices and desires, and the present wicked age with its curiosities and vanities, but even Satan himself with his temptations.

Was I not right to say that in continence I would find grounds to cry out, “For he who is mighty has done great things for me”?

## CHAPTER XIV. Eternal life rests upon three things

[Note: [Col. 0859] Bernard, *Meditations*, chapter 15, §6, and from Anselm’s *Meditations* 16.]

After this, the Lord God gave me the grace of meriting the good things of eternal life. I believe that this grace rests chiefly upon three things: hatred of past evils, contempt for present goods, and desire for future goods.

Then he gave me hope of attaining those same things. This hope consists in three things—three things which strengthen and confirm my heart so firmly that neither any lack of merits, nor any consideration of my own worthlessness, nor any estimation of heavenly blessedness can cast me down from the height of hope in which I am firmly rooted.

Do you wish to know what these things are, O my soul? I consider three things upon which my entire hope rests: the love of adoption, the truth of the promise, and the power of fulfillment.

Let my foolish thought murmur as much as it wishes, saying: “Who are you, or how great is that glory, and by what merits do you hope to obtain it?” And I shall answer confidently: “I know whom I have believed, and I am certain that in his immense love God adopted me, that he is truthful in his promise, and that he is powerful in granting its fulfillment. He is able to do whatever he wishes.”

For these reasons, therefore, my God rightly deserves to be loved.

## CHAPTER XV. On benefits bestowed. God must be confessed in good things and in evil things

It was a great grace that God pursued me when I was fleeing from him and spoke gently to me when I was afraid; that he raised me to hope when I had despaired so many times; that he overwhelmed me with his benefits when I was ungrateful; that by the taste of inward sweetness he drew and enticed me, accustomed as I was to filthy pleasures; that he dissolved the unbreakable bonds of evil habit; and that he kindly received me when I had been withdrawn from the world.

Even now, O my soul, look upon those gifts of divine goodness of which you alone are conscious. With what joyful face Christ met you when you renounced the world; with what delicacies he fed you when you were hungry; what riches of his mercies he displayed; what affections he inspired; with what cup of love he intoxicated you.

It was also a great thing that, although I was fleeing from him as his servant and rebel, and was called solely by his mercy, he did not leave me deprived of spiritual consolations. If I was tempted, he sustained me; if I was in danger, he raised me up; if I was sorrowful, he strengthened me; if I was wavering, he made me firm.

Whenever I dried up with fear, he, the merciful Comforter, stood beside me; whenever I burned with fear, he poured himself into my inmost being. I also consider how often, while I was singing psalms or reading, he illumined me with the light of spiritual perceptions; how often, while I was praying, he carried me away into an ineffable desire for him; how often, withdrawing my mind from earthly things, he transported me to heavenly delights and the pleasures of paradise.

I am silent about many great works of his mercy toward me, lest some glory—which belongs entirely to him—seem to pass over to me. For according to human judgment, the grace of the giver and the happiness of the recipient adhere so closely to one another that not only is the giver praised, who alone ought to be praised, but the recipient too.

For what does anyone possess that he has not received? Or why is one who received freely praised as though he had earned it? To you, therefore, be praise, my God, and my glory; to you be thanksgiving. To me, however, belongs shame of face, since I have done so many evils and received so many good things.

See, therefore, O my soul, how much God’s goodness is commended not only by his generosity but also by our iniquity. For if it is a great thing to bestow many things upon those who deserve nothing, how great and extraordinary must it be to repay those who deserve evil with good?

O what mercy, which no impiety can surpass! There are things which God mercifully forgives, and other things which he lavishly bestows. He forgives our evils and grants his good things; always ready to forgive, always ready to give—merciful in the one respect, generous in the other, kind in both, good everywhere.

Let us therefore confess our evils to him, and let us confess our good things as well. Let us confess that our evils come from us, so that he may mercifully forgive them; let us confess that our good things come from him, so that he may preserve and increase them.

Let us do this without ceasing, lest we appear ungrateful either for forgiveness granted or for grace bestowed. Let the person who believes—or desires—to be a lover of God do this. For true love always confesses.

What do all these things, when carefully considered, accomplish, except that they wonderfully carry away the mind of the one who considers them, wholly withdrawn from every other love, toward loving God, who has bestowed them, and affect it powerfully?

But if anyone does not see that all these good things have been bestowed upon him by God, and therefore does not hesitate to love him little, let him know for certain that there is no one who, if he seeks, cannot easily find reasons why he is greatly indebted to God—reasons why he ought to love him with all his strength and with all the depths of his heart, and also to give continual thanks.

Therefore, let the person who lacks some good things necessary for salvation neither murmur against God nor accuse him, because God does everything according to the most certain and most just reason. He has mercy on whom he wills, and he hardens whom he wills (Rom. 9:18). He is powerful both to bestow his gifts whenever he wishes and to take away what he has bestowed whenever he wishes. Let the one who does not possess these things grieve, strive, and pray to possess them; but for the good things he has received, let him show himself grateful to God.

## CHAPTER XVI. On the benefit of redemption. Earthly and heavenly good things
[Note: [Col. 0860] It imitates Bernard, Sermon 20 on the Song of Songs, no. 2.]

Great, therefore, and many—indeed, certainly innumerable—are the benefits that you, Lord God, have bestowed upon me; for these you rightly deserve to be loved by me and always praised. For what good do I have, or have had, or shall have, that is not from you, the supreme Good, from whom everything that is good is both called good and proceeds? Yet there is one thing that inflames, urges, moves, and advances me toward loving you more than all these others: above all, I say, it makes you lovable to me, O good Jesus—the most disgraceful and bitter death that you endured, the work of our redemption. This alone wholly claims for itself with ease our entire life, our entire labor, our entire service, and finally our entire love. This, I say, is what best arouses our devotion, nourishes it most sweetly, and increases it most greatly.

For the author of the world labored greatly in this work, and did not endure such exhaustion in the whole construction of the world. Concerning the world and the things that are in the world, he spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created (Ps. 32:9). But for the redemption of the human race he endured great, numerous, and prolonged labors and sufferings. Behold how he loved us: not from any necessity of his own, but solely from love for us, he endured things so harsh and so unworthy. I may therefore rightly say that this one benefit surpasses all the others. For although it is a great thing for someone freely to bestow something of his own upon another, it is certainly much greater to expend himself. And although it is an act of great love to give one’s life for one’s friends, it is a sign of far greater love to lay down one’s life for one’s enemies—which the Son of God did for us. For while we were enemies of God, we were reconciled through the death of his Son. Yet scarcely does anyone die for a righteous person; but he died for the ungodly, the righteous one for the unrighteous, so that he might offer us to God—exiled from heaven so that he might bring us back to heaven.

O what ineffable compassion, what ineffable sweetness of love, what astonishing condescension of love it was for God to become human for the sake of humanity; for God to put on flesh for humanity, to die, and to be tempted in every respect, apart from sin! Behold at what price and with what labor the human being was redeemed—one who rightly belonged to the devil, and who, if not redeemed, would undoubtedly have been condemned eternally with the devil.

I have said these things so that a person may understand how much he ought to love God; how patiently—indeed, willingly, and not only that, but ardently—he ought to endure labors and sufferings for him who endured such great and such terrible things for his sake. For through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of heaven (Acts 14:21).

Let my soul, therefore, embrace you, Lord Jesus, crucified; let it drink deeply of your most sweet blood. May this sweet meditation occupy my memory, lest forgetfulness entirely obscure it. May I judge that I know nothing except Jesus Christ, and him crucified, lest empty error draw my knowledge away from the solidity of faith. May this wondrous love of yours claim all my love for itself, lest worldly desire swallow it up.

For the mind that your sweetness, Lord, of love has filled is not cramped by fear, stained by lust, torn apart by anger, lifted up by pride, or blown about by the empty smoke of vainglory; it is not harassed by rage, disemboweled by the spur of ambition, constricted by greed, cast down by sadness, or consumed by envy. In short, no vice corrupts it while it remains immovable in that same sweetness.

If, then, he bestows such great things upon his own in the present, what and how great are the things he reserves for them in the future? What he gives in the present is temporal; but what God promises to give his own in the future age is eternal, and incomparably better than temporal goods. Temporal goods are difficult to acquire, and once acquired easily slip away. Even when possessed, they are guarded with great anxiety, lost with grief, and recovered after great toil. But the goods of the future age are never lost or diminished; they are possessed with joy and peace, always held, always desired, and never become wearisome. Once someone has received them, he will be as secure that he will never lose them as he is—or will be—certain that he will never wish to lose them.

## CHAPTER XVII. God’s promises. They cannot be desired excessively.

God, therefore, is greatly to be loved in his promises: he has given us great things, but has promised greater things. He promised us rest from labor, freedom from servitude, security from fear, consolation from sorrow, resurrection from death, and in the resurrection complete joy—supreme and unfailing joy. Finally, he promised us himself, just as he swore to our fathers that he would give himself to us (Luke 1:73).

Great, therefore, are the promises of God, and ineffable; and for their sake, and in them, he wishes to be loved by us in some measure. If you ask what measure, intense desire for the promise is the measure of love. However greatly God’s promise may be desired, it is desired less than it ought to be. For however much one has advanced, one ought to desire it more. Intense desire, therefore, in a certain sense has no measure, since it cannot be excessive. While impatience is ordinarily censured in other matters, in awaiting so great a promise an intense impatience with delay is praiseworthy. When impatience with delay torments more greatly the one who loves more and desires more, hope deferred afflicts the soul; yet all these good things are possessed in the heavenly homeland.

Concerning that good, therefore, which is the supreme good of all goods, we must first say what it is and what it is like.

## CHAPTER XVIII. The nature and greatness of the joy of the elect. The minds of the blessed will be open to one another. Their bodies will be whole.

[Note: [Col. 0861] From Anselm’s *Proslogion*, chapters 22–25; from the *Book of Meditations*, chapters 17 and 22.]

Let us therefore rouse and raise our entire understanding, insofar as God grants it, and consider what kind and how great is this unique and singular joy of the elect—namely, the one supreme good, which is life, light, blessedness, wisdom, eternity, and many such goods; and yet it is only one and supreme good, wholly sufficient to itself, needing nothing, while everything needs it in order to exist and to exist well.

This good is God the Father; this is the Word, that is, the Son of the Father; this same good is the one common love of the Father and the Son, namely, the Holy Spirit proceeding from both. What each one individually is, the whole Trinity is together—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—for each individually is nothing other than supremely simple unity and supremely one simplicity, which can neither be multiplied nor be one thing and another.

Moreover, “one thing is necessary” (Luke 10:42). This, then, is that one necessary thing, in which every good exists—or rather, which is every good, the one, the whole, and the only good. If individual goods are delightful, consider attentively how delightful that good must be which contains the pleasantness of all goods—not, however, as we have experienced it in created things, but differing from them as greatly as the Creator differs from the creature. If created life is good, how good is the Life that creates? If made salvation is delightful, how delightful is the Salvation that made salvation? If wisdom accompanied by knowledge of created things is lovable, how lovable is the Wisdom that created all things from nothing? Finally, if there are many great pleasures in pleasant things, what kind and how great is the pleasure in him who made all pleasant things?

O what will the one who enjoys this good have, and what will he not have? Certainly whatever he wills will exist, and whatever he does not will will not exist. For there will be bodily and spiritual goods such as “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the human heart” [Note: [Col. 0862] In Anselm: “nor has the human heart conceived.”] (1 Cor. 2:9).

Why, then, do we wander among many things seeking goods for our body and soul? Let us love the one good in which all goods exist; and it is sufficient. Let us desire the simple good that is every good; and that is enough. For what do you love, O flesh? What do you desire, O soul? There is there whatever you love and whatever you desire.

No one clothed in flesh can speak of, think of, or understand the goods of the heavenly kingdom as they are; for they are far greater and better than anything we think or understand. The kingdom of God is greater than every report, better than every praise, more numerous than every knowledge, and more excellent than every glory that is imagined.

The kingdom, I say, of God is full of light and peace, love and wisdom, honor and glory, sweetness and affection, joy and everlasting blessedness, and every ineffable good that can neither be spoken nor imagined. Nevertheless, I ought not on that account to remain silent, but to speak as much as I can, because I cannot speak as much as I wish. For although we believe God to be ineffable, we ought not for that reason to refrain from saying about him what we can.

Indeed, more should be believed about that life than is written, because as much of it cannot be put forward in speech as the mind can embrace; and however profound the human mind’s grasp may be, it conceives less than the greatness of the reality itself.

Let the future life, therefore, be believed to be blessedly eternal and eternally blessed: where there is certain security, secure tranquility, tranquil delight, happy eternity, eternal happiness; where love is perfect, fear nonexistent, the day eternal, movement joyful, and there is one spirit of all, secure in the contemplation of its God and in remaining with him; where the city itself, blessed by the gathering of all the angels and saints, shines with radiant merits; where eternal salvation abounds and truth reigns; where no one deceives and no one is deceived; from which no blessed person is expelled; where no wretched person is admitted.

This is the blessed contemplative life. Those who reach it through the completion of good works will be like the blessed and will reign with God without end. What they believed here they will see there. Contemplating the substance of their Creator with the purest hearts, they will rejoice with eternal exultation; possessing divine love and mutual affection, they will cleave forever to their God and to one another. Having received their bodies in incorruption and immortality, they will receive citizenship [Note: [Col. 0862] Royal manuscript: “an unfailing gift.”] in the heavenly homeland, and, made its citizens forever, they will carry away its promised rewards.

There such great joy and such an abundance of heavenly delights will overflow for them that they will both give thanks to their rewarder for such great gifts and suffer no weariness from the very abundant reception of graces and goods.

There the minds of individuals will be open to one another just as bodily faces are exposed to bodily eyes. For there will be such great and perfect purity in human hearts that they will have reason to give thanks to their purifier, not reason to blush at any stains of sins by which they have been defiled [Note: [Col. 0863] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read: “ancient.”]. For there will be neither sins nor sinners there; and those who are there will no longer be able to sin.

Nor will anything hidden remain unknown to the perfectly blessed, who—something far more excellent—will see God himself with pure hearts. For the human creature will then be so perfected that it can no longer be changed either for the better or for the worse. In this human substance, raised to the likeness of its Creator, all the goods that it had naturally received but corrupted by sinning will be restored for the better: understanding without error, memory without forgetfulness, thought without wandering, love without deceit, perception without injury, soundness without weakness, health without pain, life without death, ease without impediment, fullness without satiety, and complete health without disease.

For whatever bodily losses our corrupted bodies suffer here—whether from the bites of wild beasts, unforeseen accidents, various kinds of illness, human cruelty, fire, or any other cause that inflicts weakness, or from old age, burdensome even to the healthy—these and similar bodily losses will there be repaired by a single resurrection, and incorruptible health will possess bodies restored in all their members.

Therefore, whoever will be there, although they will differ from one another in their merits, will nevertheless all be blessed with one perfection, because each will have rewards sufficient for himself. Just as bodily satiety makes all who are filled equally satisfied, although individuals do not take equal amounts of food but as much as their capacity permits, so all the saints, even though distinguished by some diversity in their ranks, will be perfected in one blessedness, because they will be blessed in one perfection.

Moreover, in that region of such great blessedness, those of greater merit will not claim anything for themselves, because there will be no arrogance there; nor will those below envy those above, because no one there will be able to be envious. Therefore, although there will be a difference among the dwelling places, there will be in them all the supreme equality of one perfection, and they will share one happiness of the heavenly kingdom.

# SOLILOQUIES OF THE SOUL TO GOD

[Col. 0863]

## NOTICE CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING BOOK

[Col. 0863] Possidius mentions *Soliloquies* composed by Augustine in his *Index*, chapter 6; Augustine himself also discusses them in *Retractions*, book 1, chapter 4. From their method of composition and the character of their argument, it is sufficiently clear that they are very different from the work that follows, and are precisely the same as those that appear in the first volume among his earliest writings.

After these had been divided into two books and written in dialogue form, Augustine explains in the same chapter of the *Retractions* why he gave them the name *Soliloquies*: “I wrote two volumes . . . concerning those matters that I most wished to know, questioning myself and answering myself, as though we were two persons, Reason and I, although I was alone; hence I called this work *Soliloquies*.”

He then explicitly states what questions he raised in the first book and what questions in the second, as well as what statements he found in them less acceptable; all these matters are found in the aforementioned *Soliloquies* of the first volume and apply to those alone. Florus, or the commonly circulated Bede, cites one of these same books of the *Soliloquies* in connection with 1 Corinthians 13.

As for the following book, which—if not inappropriately, at least not for the same reason—was given the name *Soliloquies*, no ancient writer before perhaps five hundred years ago, and certainly not Augustine himself, could have mentioned it anywhere. It was collected more recently by an unknown author, not only from Augustine—especially from his *Confessions*—but also from Hugh of Saint-Victor, from his book *On the Soul’s Pledge*. It also contains, in its thirty-second chapter, the first chapter of the Fourth Lateran Council, held around the year 1198, with a few words omitted.

[Note: [Col. 0863] We have indicated passages taken from the holy Doctor or from other authors by alphabetic notes enclosed in parentheses and placed at the beginning of the excerpted passage. M.]

You will find in it a strong agreement and affinity with most of the collected little works of this Appendix—namely, with the books *On the Spirit and the Soul* and *On Loving God*, with the *Manual*, and so forth. Above all, however, it is designed to kindle love of God and is filled with devout affections toward him.

This book is now presented in a more accurate form through the assistance of ancient manuscripts from the Royal Library, the Colbert Library, the monastery of Saint-Médard at Soissons, and Saint Peter of La Couture at Le Mans.

[Col. 0863]

# ONE BOOK OF THE SOLILOQUIES OF THE SOUL TO GOD (C, G, S)

## CHAPTER I. Aspiration to the knowledge and love of God. Desire for the vision of God. Causes of the deficiency of love of God. The human being’s divergence from God.

[Col. 0863]

Let me acknowledge you, Lord, my knower; let me know you, strength of my soul. Show yourself to me, my comforter; [Col. 0864] let me see you, light of my eyes. Come, joy of my spirit; let me see you, gladness of my heart; let me love you, life of my soul. Appear to me, my great delight, my sweet consolation, Lord my God, the entire life and glory of my soul. Let me find you, desire of my heart; let me hold you, love of my soul. Let me embrace you, heavenly bridegroom, my supreme exultation within and without. Let me possess you, everlasting blessedness; let me possess you in the midst of my heart, blessed life, supreme sweetness of my soul.

Let me love you, Lord, my strength; “the Lord is my firmament, my refuge, and my deliverer” (Ps. 17:2–3). Let me love you, my God, my helper, my tower of strength, and my sweet hope in all my tribulation. Let me embrace you, the good without which there is no good; let me enjoy you, O best [Note: [Col. 0865] In another manuscript, “the best.”], without whom there is nothing best.

Open the inner chambers of my ears, O Word more penetrating than any two-edged sword (Heb. 4:12), so that I may hear your voice. Thunder from above, Lord, with a great and powerful voice. Let the sea and its fullness thunder; let the earth and all that is in it be shaken (Ps. 95:11–12). Enlighten my eyes, incomprehensible light; flash forth your radiance and scatter them (Ps. 143:6), so that they may not see vanity. Multiply your thunderbolts and disturb them, so that the springs of waters may appear and the foundations of the world may be revealed (Ps. 17:16).

Grant sight, invisible light, to one who may see you. Create a new sense of smell, O fragrance of life, so that it may run after you, after the fragrance of your perfumes (Song 1:3). Heal the sense of taste, so that it may savor, know, and discern how great is the abundance of your sweetness, Lord, which you have hidden from those who are filled with your love (Ps. 30:20). Give me a heart that thinks of you, a soul that loves you, a mind that remembers you, an understanding that comprehends you, and a reason that always clings firmly to you, supreme sweetness; let it love you wisely, O wise love.

O life in whom all things live; life that gives me life; life that is my life; life through which I live, without which I die; life through which I am raised again, without which I perish; life through which I rejoice, without which I am afflicted—[Note: [Col. 0865] From the *Speculum*, chapter 30.] living life, sweet and lovable, always to be remembered. Where, I ask, are you? Where shall I find you, so that I may fail in myself and subsist in you? Be near to me in my soul, near in my heart, near in my mouth [Note: [Col. 0865] The printed editions add here: “near in my ears.”], near in my help; for I languish with love, for without you I die, for by remembering you I am raised again.

Your fragrance revives me; your memory heals me. But I shall be satisfied when your glory appears, life of my soul. My soul longs and languishes for the memory of you. When shall I come and appear before you, my joy? Why do you turn your face away, joy through which I rejoice? Where are you hidden, beautiful one whom I desire? I draw in your fragrance; I live and rejoice, but I do not see you. I hear your voice, and I revive. But why do you hide your face? Perhaps you say, “A human being shall not see me and live” (Exod. 33:20). Come, Lord, let me die so that I may see you; let me see you so that I may die here. I do not wish to live; I wish to die. I long to depart and be with Christ (Phil. 1:23). I desire to die so that I may see Christ; I refuse to live so that I may live with Christ.

O Lord Jesus, receive my spirit. My life, receive my soul. My joy, draw my heart to yourself; my sweet food, let me eat you. My head, direct me; light of my eyes, enlighten me; my melody, attune me; my fragrance, give me life; Word of God, restore me. My praise, gladden the soul of your servant. Enter into it, true joy, so that it may rejoice in you; enter into it, supreme sweetness, so that it may taste sweetness; eternal light, shine upon it, so that it may understand, know, and love you.

For this is why it does not love you, Lord—if it does not love you—because it does not know you; and it does not know you because it does not understand; and it does not understand because it does not grasp your light. “The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it” (John 1:5).

O light of the mind, O shining truth, O true brightness, which enlightens every human being coming into this world (coming, indeed, but not loving; for whoever loves the world is made an enemy of God [Col. 0866] [James 4:4]), drive away the darkness from the face of the abyss of my mind, so that it may see you by understanding, know you by comprehending, and love you by knowing. For whoever knows you loves you; he forgets himself and loves you more than himself; he abandons himself and comes to you in order to rejoice in you.

This, then, Lord, is why I do not love you as much as I ought: because I do not know you fully. But because I know you little, I love you little; and because I love you little, I rejoice little in you.
