Yet, withdrawing from you, the true inner joy, through outward things, while I lack you alone, I seek adulterous friendships in these external things. Thus I, wretched that I am, have given to vanities the heart that I ought to have devoted to you alone with all love and affection; and I have become vain because I loved vanity.

## CHAPTER II. The various relations of God to the human being.

This, too, is why I do not rejoice in you or cling to you: because I am in outward things, while you are in inward things; I am in carnal things, while you are in spiritual things. I spread myself in mind among transitory things, I turn among them in thought, and I am entangled in speech, while you, Lord, dwell in eternity.

You are in heaven, I on earth; you love what is high, I what is low; you love heavenly things, I earthly things. And when will these opposites be able to come together? Wretched that I am, when will my crookedness be made equal to your uprightness?

You, Lord, love solitude; I, crowds. You love silence; I, clamor. You love truth; I, vanity. You pursue purity; I, impurity. What more can I say, Lord? You are truly good; I am evil. You are devout; I am impious. You are holy; I am wretched. You are just; I am unjust. You are light; I am blind. You are life; I am dead. You are medicine; I am sick. You are joy; I am sadness. You are supreme truth; I am utter vanity, like every living human being (Ps. 38:6).

Alas! What shall I say, O Creator? Hear me, O Creator. I am your creature; I have already perished. I am your creature; I am already dying. I am your work; I am already being reduced to nothing. I am your fashioned work: your hands, Lord, made me and fashioned me (Ps. 118:73)—those hands, I say, that were fastened with nails for me. Do not despise the work of your hands, Lord; I beg you to look upon the wounds of your hands.

Behold, you have inscribed me upon your hands; read that very writing and save me. Behold, your creature sighs toward you; you are the Creator—recreate me. Behold, your work cries out to you; you are life—restore me. Behold, your fashioned work looks toward you; you are the former—restore me. Spare me, Lord, for my days are nothing (Job 7:16).

What is a human being, that he may address God his maker? Spare me as I speak with you; forgive the servant who presumes to speak with the Lord. Necessity has no law. Pain compels me to speak, and the calamity I suffer forces me to cry out. I am sick; I cry to the physician. I am blind; I hasten toward the light. I am dead; I sigh toward life.

You are the physician, you are the light, you are life. Jesus of Nazareth, have mercy on me; Son of David, have mercy on me (Matt. 20:30). Fountain of mercy, hear the sick man who cries out to you. O light that passes by [Note: [Col. 0866] The manuscripts read “who passes by.”], wait for the blind man. Extend your hand, so that he may come to you and see light in your light (Ps. 35:10). Living life, call back the dead.

What am I, that I speak with you? Woe to me, Lord; spare me. I am a rotting corpse, food for worms, a foul vessel, fuel for fires. What am I, that I speak with you? Woe to me, Lord; spare me. I am an unhappy human being—human, I say, born of woman, living a short time and filled with many miseries (Job 14:1); human, I say, made like vanity (Ps. 143:4), compared with foolish beasts and already made like them (Ps. 48:13).

What am I again? A dark abyss, a land of misery, a child of wrath, a vessel suited for dishonor, begotten through impurity, living in misery, destined to die in anguish. Wretched that I am, what am I? Alas, what shall I become? And what am I? A vessel of filth, a shell of corruption, full of stench and horror; blind, poor, naked, subjected to innumerable necessities, ignorant of my own coming in and going out.

Wretched and mortal, my days pass like a shadow; my life vanishes like the shadow of the moon. It grows like a flower on a tree and immediately withers; now it blooms, and immediately it dries up (Ps. 101:12). My life, I say, is fragile life, fleeting life, a life that, the more it grows, the more it diminishes; the farther it proceeds, the nearer it comes to death: deceptive and shadowy life, full of snares of death.

Now I rejoice, and immediately I am saddened; now I am strong, and already I am weak; now I live, and immediately I die; now I appear happy, and always I am wretched; now I laugh, and immediately I weep. Thus everything is subject to change, so that scarcely one hour remains for me in one condition.

Hence fear, hence trembling; hence hunger, hence thirst; hence heat, hence cold; hence weakness, and from there pain abounds. After these comes troublesome death, which daily snatches wretched human beings away in a thousand ways. One it crushes with fevers, another with pains; one it consumes with hunger, another thirst extinguishes. One it suffocates in water, another it kills by the noose; one it destroys with flames, another the teeth of savage beasts devour; one it slaughters with iron, another it corrupts with poison; still another it forces to end his wretched life through sudden terror.

And now, beyond all these things, there is great misery: although nothing is more certain than death, the human being nevertheless does not know his own end; and when he thinks he is standing firm, he is taken away and his hope perishes. For no one knows when, where, or how he will die; yet he is certain that he must die.

Behold, Lord, how great is the misery of humanity in which I am, yet I do not fear; how great the calamity that I suffer, yet I do not grieve and do not cry out to you. I shall cry out, Lord, before I pass away—if perhaps I may not pass away, but remain in you.

I shall speak, then; I shall speak of my misery. I shall confess, and I shall not be ashamed before you of my lowliness. Help me, my strength, by which I am lifted up. Come to my aid, my power, by which I am sustained. Come, light by which I see. Appear, glory by which I rejoice. Appear, I say, and I shall live.

## CHAPTER III. The misery and fragility of the human being.

[Note: [Col. 0867] From book 10 of the *Confessions*, chapter 34.]

O light that Tobias saw when, with his eyes closed, he taught his son the way of life (Tob. 4:2–20); light that Isaac saw inwardly when, with his outward eyes growing dim, he foretold future things to his son (Gen. 27:28); invisible light, I say, to which every abyss of the human heart is visible; light that Jacob saw when, as you taught inwardly, he foretold future things outwardly to his sons (Gen. 49:1–28)—behold, darkness lies upon the face of the abyss of my mind; you are light. Behold, dark gloom lies over the waters of my heart; you are truth.

O Word through which all things were made, without which nothing was made; Word that exists before all things, before which nothing exists; Word creating all things, without which nothing is anything (John 1:3); Word governing all things, without which things do not exist; Word that you spoke in the beginning, “Let there be light,” and light was made (Gen. 1:3), say also now, “Let there be light,” and let light be made. Let me see the light, and know whatever is not light; for without you, darkness is placed for me as light, and light as darkness.

Thus without your light there is no truth, but error is present; vanity is present, truth is absent; discernment is absent, confusion is present; ignorance is present, knowledge is absent; blindness is present, vision is absent; there is no way, but a pathless condition is present; death is present, life is absent.

## CHAPTER IV. The necessity of God’s light and an appeal for it.

Behold, Lord: where there is no light, there is death—or rather, there is no death, because death is nothing. For through it we tend toward nothingness, since by sinning we do not fear to make ourselves nothing. And this is just, indeed, Lord, for we receive what our deeds deserve, as we come to nothing like flowing water. For without you nothing was made, and by making nothing we have become nothing, because without you we are [Note: [Col. 0867] In the printed editions alone, “nothing” is added here]—you through whom all things were made and without whom nothing was made.

O Lord Word, O God Word, through whom all things were made, without whom nothing was made [Col. 0868] (John 1:3)! Woe to me, wretched that I am, blinded so many times, because you are light and I am without you; wounded so many times, because you are salvation and I am without you; made foolish so many times, because you are truth and I am without you; wandering so many times, because you are the way and I am without you; dead so many times, because you are life and I am without you; annihilated so many times, because you are the Word through which all things were made, and I am without you, without whom nothing was made.

O Lord Word, O God Word, who are the light through which light was made; who are the way, the truth, and the life (John 14:6); in whom there are no darkness, error, vanity, or death; light without which there is darkness, way without which there is error, truth without which there is vanity, life without which there is death—speak the word, speak, Lord: “Let there be light,” so that I may see the light and avoid darkness; see the way and avoid the pathless condition; see the truth and avoid vanity; see life and avoid death.

Shine upon me, Lord, my light, my illumination and my salvation—whom shall I fear? My Lord, whom I shall praise; my God, whom I shall honor; my Father, whom I shall love; my Bridegroom, to whom I shall devote myself. Shine upon me, I say, shine upon this blind man of yours who sits in darkness and in the shadow of death, and direct his feet into the way of peace, through which I may enter the place of the wondrous tabernacle, even to the house of God, amid the voice of exultation and confession.

Truly, confession is the way by which I shall enter to you, the way by which I shall depart from the pathless condition and return to you, the way, because you are the true way of life [Note: [Col. 0868] The manuscripts do not have the words “because you are the true way of life.”].

## CHAPTER V. Our misery from sin. That sin is nothing. That the one who sins becomes nothing.

Let me confess, then; let me confess to you, Lord Father, King of heaven and earth, my misery, so that I may be permitted to come to your mercy. I have become wretched and have been reduced to nothing, and I did not know it, because you are truth and I was not with you. My iniquities wounded me, and I did not feel pain, because you are life and I was not with you. They brought me down to nothing, because you are the Word and I was not with you—through whom all things were made, without whom nothing was made. And therefore, without you, I became nothing, because that which leads to nothing is nothing [Note: [Col. 0868] Royal manuscript: “because.”].

All things that have been made were made through the Word. And what sort of things were they made? “God saw everything that he had made, and it was very good” (Gen. 1:31). Everything that exists was made through the Word; and everything made through the Word is very good. Why is it good? Because it was made through the Word.

“And without him nothing was made” (John 1:3), because nothing is good without the supreme Good. But where good is absent, there is evil, which is nothing; for evil is nothing other than the deprivation of good, just as blindness is nothing other than the deprivation of light.

Evil, therefore, is nothing, because it was made without the Word, without whom nothing was made. That is evil which deprives one of that good through which all good things were made, namely, the Word through which everything that exists was made [Note: [Col. 0868] The printed editions and the Royal manuscript read: “is deprived.”]. But those things that do not exist were not made through him, and therefore they are nothing.

And therefore those things are evil that were not made, because everything that exists was made through the Word, and all things were made good through the Word. Since, then, all things were made through the Word, evils do not exist through it. It follows, therefore, that everything that was not made is not good, because everything that was made is good.

And therefore evils are not, because they were not made [Note: [Col. 0868] Two manuscripts read this way. The Royal manuscript, however, reads: “Rather, evils are those things that were not made.” The printed editions read: “And therefore they are evils that were not made,” and so forth.], and therefore they are nothing, because without the Word nothing was made.

Evil, therefore, is nothing, because it was not made. But how is it evil if it was not made? Because evil is the deprivation of the Word, through which good was made. To be without the Word is therefore evil; yet it is not being, because without him there is nothing.

But what does it mean to be separated from the Word? If you wish to know, hear what the Word is. The Word of God says, “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6). To be separated from the Word, therefore, is to be without the way, without truth, and without life; and therefore without him there is nothing, and therefore evil, because it is separation from the Good [Note: [Col. 0869] Thus the manuscripts, except that the Royal manuscript reads: “separating from the Good.” The printed editions read: “is separated from the Word.”] through which all things were made very good.

To be separated from the Word through whom all things were made is nothing other than to fail, and to pass from being made into deficiency, because without him there is nothing. Whenever, therefore, you turn away from the good, you separate yourself from the Word, because he is the Good; and therefore you become nothing, because you are without the Word, without whom nothing was made.

Now, Lord, you have enlightened me so that I might see you. I saw you and came to know myself, because I became nothing as often as I was separated from you; for I forgot the good that you are, and therefore became evil.

Woe to me, wretched that I am! Why did I not recognize this—that by abandoning you I was becoming nothing? But why do I ask this? If I was nothing, how could I wish to understand? We know that nothing is nothing; and what is nothing does not exist; and what does not exist is not good, because it is nothing.

If, therefore, I was nothing when I was without you, I was, as it were, nothing, like an idol that is nothing. It has ears, but does not hear; it has nostrils, but does not smell; it has eyes, but does not see; it has a mouth, but does not speak; it has hands, but does not touch; it has feet, but does not walk—and all the features of limbs without their sensation.

## CHAPTER VI. The misery of the sinner. Without the Word nothing exists or is preserved.

Since, then, I was without you, I was not; because I was nothing. And therefore I was blind, deaf, and insensible: for I neither discerned good nor avoided evil, neither felt the pain of my wounds nor saw my darkness, because I was without you, the true light that enlightens every person coming into this world (John 1:9). Woe is me! They wounded me, and I felt no pain; they dragged me along, and I perceived nothing: because I was nothing, because I was without the life that is the Word through whom all things were made. Therefore, Lord, my light, my enemies did with me whatever they wished: they struck me, stripped me, defiled me, corrupted me, wounded me, and killed me, because I withdrew from you and became nothing without you. Ah, Lord, my life, who made me; my light, who guided [Note: [Col. 0869] Manuscripts: “loved” me.] me. Defender of my life, have mercy on me and raise me to life [Note: [Col. 0869] The Regius manuscript adds, “and I shall repay myself.”]. Lord my God, my hope, my strength, my might, my consolation in the day of my tribulation, look upon my enemies and rescue me. Let those who hate you flee from your face, and let me live in you through you.

For they, Lord, considered me, and when they saw me without you, they despised me. They divided among themselves the garments of the virtues with which you had clothed me (Psalm 21:18–19); they made a road for themselves through me and trampled me beneath their feet. With the filth of sins they polluted your holy temple; they left me desolate and worn out with sorrow. I followed after them blind and naked, entangled in the cords of sins. They dragged me behind them, going round and round from vice to vice and from mud to mud; and I went without strength before the face of the one pursuing me.

I was a slave, and I loved slavery. I was blind, and I desired blindness. I was bound, and I did not dread my bonds. I believed bitter to be sweet, and sweet to be bitter. I was wretched, and I did not know it; and this because I was without you, the Word, without whom nothing was made, through whom all things are preserved, and without whom all things are annihilated.

For just as all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made, so through him all things that exist are preserved, whether in heaven, on earth, in the sea, or in all the depths. No part adheres to another part in a stone, nor does anything adhere within any created thing, except because they are preserved by the Word through whom all things were made. Let me therefore cling to you, O Word, so that you may preserve me; for where I withdrew from you, I perished in myself—except that you, who had made me, remade me. I sinned, and you visited me; I fell, and you raised me up; I was ignorant, and you taught me; I did not see, and you enlightened me.

## CHAPTER VII. Love of God is aroused by consideration of his benefits. The benefit of creation. In what respect human beings are inferior to angels.

Wretched that I am, my God, show me how greatly I am bound to love you; demonstrate to me how greatly I ought to praise you; make known to me how greatly I ought to please you. Thunder, Lord, with a great and mighty voice into the inner ear of my heart: teach me and save me, and I shall praise you together with others—you who created me when I was nothing; who enlightened me when I was in darkness; who raised me to life when I was dead; who have fed me from my youth with all your good things.

You nourish this useless worm, foul with sins, with all your choicest gifts. Open to me, O key of David, who open and no one shuts for the one to whom you open, and shut and no one opens for the one to whom you shut. Open to me the door of your light, so that I may enter, see, know, and confess you with all my heart, because your mercy is great over me, and you have rescued my soul from the lowest hell.

Lord my God, how wonderful, how praiseworthy is your name throughout the whole earth! And what is a human being that you remember him, or a son of man that you visit him (Psalm 8:2, 5)? Lord, hope of the saints and tower of their strength; life of my soul, through which I live and without which I die; light of my eyes, through which I see and without which I am bereft; joy of my heart and gladness of my spirit—I shall love you with all my heart, with all my soul, with all my marrow and inward parts, because you loved me first (1 John 4:10).

And from where is this granted to me, O creator of heaven, earth, and the abyss, who have no need of my good things? From where is this granted to me, that you loved me? O Wisdom who opens the mouths of the mute, O Word through whom all things were made, open my mouth and give me a voice of praise, so that I may recount all your benefits, which, Lord, you bestowed upon me from the beginning.

For behold, I exist because you created me; and that you should create me and count me among your creatures, you ordained from eternity. Before you made anything in the beginning, before you stretched out the heavens—when the abysses did not yet exist, when you had not yet made the earth or founded the mountains, when the springs had not yet burst forth (Proverbs 8:22–27)—before you made all these things that you made through the Word, by the utterly certain providence of your truth you foresaw that I would be your creature, and you willed me to be your creature.

And from where is this granted to me, most gracious Lord, most high God, most merciful Father, most powerful and ever most gentle Creator? What merits of mine, what grace of mine moved you to create me, so that I might please the sight of your magnificent majesty? [Note: [Col. 0870] See the book *On the Spirit and the Soul*, chapter 17.]

I did not exist, and you created me; I had been nothing, and from nothing you made me something. But what sort of something? Not a star, not fire, not a bird or fish, not a serpent or any of the brute animals, not a stone or a piece of wood; not of the kind that merely exist; nor of the kind that merely can exist and grow; nor of the kind that can merely exist, grow, and feel. Rather, above all these, you willed me to belong among those that exist, because I exist; among those that exist and grow, because I exist and grow; and among those that exist, grow, and feel, because I exist, grow, and feel.

## CHAPTER VIII. When equal. In what respect the creature is most excellent. The great benefit of being able to become a son of God. This capacity comes from pure grace.

And you created me only a little lower than the angels, because you gave me with them in common the faculty of knowing you. Yet I said “only a little lower,” for they already possess your blessed knowledge by direct vision, whereas I possess it through hope; they face to face, I through a mirror in an enigma; they fully, but I in part. But when what is perfect has come, what is partial will be done away, when with face already unveiled we shall see your face.

What will then prevent us from being no longer even a little lower than the angels, whom you, Lord, crowned with the crown of hope adorned with glory, and crowned with glory and honor; whom you honored exceedingly as your friends—indeed, whom you made in all respects equal and like to the angels? Surely your truth also says this: “They are equal to the angels, and are sons of God” (Luke 20:36). Why should they not be sons of God, if they will be equal to the angels? Truly they will be sons of God, because the son of man became the Son of God.

As I consider this, I have confidence to say: Human beings are not merely a little lower than the angels, nor simply equal to the angels, but superior to the angels, because the human being is God and God is human, not an angel. And for this reason I shall say that the human being is the most excellent creature: because the Word who was in the beginning, God with God—the Word through whom God said, “Let there be light,” and there was light (Genesis 1:3), namely, the angelic nature; the Word through whom God created all things in the beginning—that same Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we saw his glory (John 1:1, 14).

Behold the glory through which I glory, when I glory in health. Behold the joy through which I rejoice, when I rejoice in health, Lord my God, the whole life and glory of my soul.

I confess, therefore, Lord my God, that when you created me capable of reason, you created me in a certain way equal to the angels, because I can be perfected through your Word, so that I may attain equality with the angels and receive adoption as a son through your only-begotten Word, Lord, through your beloved Son, in whom you were well pleased; through the man who clings to you [Note: [Col. 0871] So the manuscripts. The printed editions have: “through the only co-heir.”], consubstantial and co-eternal with you, Jesus Christ, our one Lord and Redeemer, our enlightener and consoler, our advocate with you and the light of our eyes. He is our life and Savior, our one hope; he loved us more than himself. Through him we have confidence placed before you, firm hope in you, and access by which to come to you, because he gave power to become children of God to those who believe in his name (ibid., 12).

I shall give praise to your name, Lord, who by creating me in your image and likeness (Genesis 1:27) made me capable of such great glory that I might become a son of God. Trees cannot do this; stones cannot; nor, in general, can all things that move or grow in the air, sea, or earth, because your Word did not give them the power to become children of God, since they do not possess reason. This power consists in reason, through which we know God. He gave this power to human beings, whom he created rational, in his own image and likeness.

And I, Lord, by your grace, am a human being; and by grace I can be your son, which they cannot.

From where is this granted to me, Lord, supreme Truth and true Sublimity, beginning of all creatures? From where is this granted to me, Lord, that I can become your son, which they cannot? For you, remaining eternal, created all things at once. At once you created human beings and animals, stones and the green things of the earth. Their merits did not precede; no grace of theirs came beforehand, because you created all things solely by your goodness, and all creatures were equal in merits, since none of them possessed any merits.

How, then, did your goodness appear more greatly in this creature of yours, whom you made rational, than in all the others that lack reason? Why am I not like all those, or why are they not all like me, or why am I alone like them? What were my merits, what was my grace, that you should create me capable of becoming a son of God [Note: [Col. 0871] The Regius manuscript has: “of the sons of God.”], while denying this to all the others? Far be it from me, Lord, to think this. It was solely your grace, solely your goodness, that made me a sharer in its sweetness. Therefore, that grace by which you created me from nothing, grant me, I ask, the grace to give you thanks for it.

## CHAPTER IX. On the omnipotence of God. Why we were not made a stone, a tree, and so forth.

Your omnipotent hand, always one and the same, created angels in heaven and worms on earth: neither greater in the former nor lesser in the latter. For just as no hand but yours could create an angel, so none could create a worm; just as none could create heaven, so none could create the smallest leaf of a tree; just as none could create a body, so none could make a single hair white or black. But your omnipotent hand can do all things in equal fashion.

For it is no more possible for you to create a worm than an angel; nor is it more impossible for you to stretch out the heavens than a leaf; nor is it easier for you to form a hair than a body; nor is it more difficult for you to establish the earth upon the waters than the waters upon the earth [Note: [Col. 0872] Erasmus, the Lyon edition, the Venetian edition, and the Louvain edition present the passage thus: “Nor is it more difficult to establish the earth upon the waters than the waters upon the earth.” Manuscript M.]. But whatever you willed, you did, in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in all the depths; and among all these things you made me as you willed, were able, and knew.

Your hand, Lord, could have created me as a stone, a bird, a serpent, or some beast, and it knew how; but it did not will this, because of its goodness. Why am I not a stone, a tree, or some beast? Because your goodness ordained it so. And when it ordained this, my merits did not precede.

## CHAPTER X. Human insufficiency for praising God. Who praises God. True human praise. Again concerning insufficiency for the praise of God. From where it is supplied.

From where is this granted to me, Lord? From where do I have praises with which to praise you? Just as you made me without me, as it pleased you; so praise is offered to you without me, as it pleases you. Your praise, Lord, is you yourself. Let your works praise you according to the abundance of your greatness.

Your praise, Lord, is incomprehensible: it is not grasped by the heart, measured by the mouth, or received by the ear, because these things pass away, while your praise remains forever. Thought begins and thought ends; the voice sounds and passes away; the ear hears, and hearing ceases [Note: [Col. 0872] Manuscripts: “passes away.”]; but your praise stands forever.

Who, then, is the one who praises you? What human being announces your praise? Your praise is perpetual; it is not transitory. The one who praises you here is the one who believes that you yourself are his praise. The one who praises you here is the one who knows that he cannot reach your praise by himself. Perpetual praise, which never passes away, is in you our praise; in you my soul shall be praised.

We do not praise you, but you praise yourself, through yourself, and in yourself; and for us also there is praise in you. We have true praise when we receive praise from you, when light approves light; because you, the true praise, bestow true praise. Whenever we seek praise from anyone other than you, we lose your praise, because theirs is transitory, but yours is eternal. If we seek the transitory, we lose the eternal. If we desire the eternal, let us not love the transitory.

Eternal praise, Lord my God, from whom all praise comes, without whom there is no praise—I cannot praise you without you. Let me possess you, and I shall praise you. For who am I, Lord, that I should praise you by myself? I am dust and ashes; I am a dead and stinking dog; I am a worm and corruption. Who am I to praise you, Lord God, strongest of the spirits of all flesh, who dwell in eternity?

Will darkness praise light, or death life? You are light; I am darkness. You are life; I am death. Will vanity praise truth? You are truth; I am a human being made like vanity.

What, then, will praise you, Lord? Will my misery praise you? Will stench praise fragrance? Will human mortality, which exists today and is removed tomorrow, praise you? Will corruption and the son of man, a worm, praise you? Will the one born and brought forth in sins praise you, Lord?

May your omnipotent power praise you, Lord my God; your unbounded wisdom; your ineffable goodness. May your surpassing clemency praise you, your overflowing mercy, and your eternal power and divinity as well. May your all-powerful strength praise you, and your supreme kindness and love, for the sake of which you created us, Lord God, life of my soul.

## CHAPTER XI. The hope of salvation rests upon the goodness that created us.

But I, your creature, shall hope under the shadow of your wings in your goodness, by which you created me. Help your creature, whom your goodness created. Let what your goodness has wrought not perish in my wickedness; let what your supreme clemency has made not perish in my misery.

For what benefit is there in your creation if I descend into my corruption? Surely you did not establish all the children of human beings in vain? You created me, Lord; rule what you created. Do not despise the work of your hands, O God. You made me from nothing; if you do not rule me, Lord, I shall return again to nothing.

For just as I did not exist, Lord, and you made me something from nothing, so if you do not rule me, I shall again be reduced within myself to nothing. Help me, Lord, my life, lest I perish in my wickedness. If you had not created me, Lord, I would not exist; because you created me, I now exist; if you do not rule me, I shall no longer exist.

It was not my merits or my grace that compelled you to create me, but your most gracious goodness and clemency. May that love, Lord my God, which compelled you to create me, itself, I ask, now compel you to rule me. For what benefit is it that your love compelled you to create me if I perish in my misery and your right hand does not rule me?

May this clemency compel you, Lord my God, to save what has been created—the clemency that compelled you to create when it did not yet exist. May that same love conquer you for salvation which conquered you for creation, because it is not now less; for that love is you yourself, who are always the same.

Your hand has not been shortened so that it cannot save, nor has your ear become heavy so that it cannot hear (Isaiah 59:1); but my sins have made a division between me and you, between darkness and light, between the image of death and life, between vanity and truth, between this moonlike life of mine and your everlasting life.

## CHAPTER XII. A prayer against the snares of desires. Who can escape these snares?

These are the shadows with which I am covered in this dark abyss of this prison, in which I lie prostrate until day breathes forth, the shadows incline, and a voice arises in the firmament of your power: the voice of the Lord in power, the voice of the Lord in majesty. Let it say, “Let there be light,” and let the darkness be driven away; let the dry land appear, and let the earth bring forth green plants producing seed and the good fruit of the justice of your kingdom.

Lord Father and God, life through which all things live and without which all things are reckoned dead, do not abandon me to an evil thought, and do not give me over to the haughtiness of my eyes. Take away desires from me, and do not hand me over to an irreverent and unrestrained mind (Sirach 23:4–6); rather, possess my heart, so that it may always think of you.

Enlighten my eyes, so that they may see you and not become exalted before you, eternal glory, but may think humbly, not of great things beyond them; and may they see what is at your right hand, not what is at your left. May my eyelids go before my steps, for your eyelids also examine the children of human beings (Psalm 10:6).

Strike down my desire with your sweetness, which you have hidden for those who fear you, so that I may desire to desire you with everlasting desires. Let not my inward taste, enticed and deceived by empty things, place bitter for sweet and sweet for bitter, darkness for light and light for darkness, amid so many traps prepared everywhere by the enemy across the face of this road to capture souls. The whole world is full of them, so that the one who saw them did not pass by in silence, saying: “Whatever is in the world is either the desire of the flesh, or the desire of the eyes, or the pride of life” (1 John 2:16).

Behold, Lord my God, the whole world is full of the snares of desires that they have prepared for my feet. And who will escape these snares? Surely the one from whom you have removed the haughtiness of his eyes, so that the desire of the eyes may not capture him; the one from whom you have removed the desire of the flesh, so that the desire of the flesh may not capture him; and the one from whom you have removed an irreverent and unrestrained mind, so that the pride of life may not cunningly deceive him.

O how blessed is the one for whom you do this! He will indeed pass through unharmed.

Now I beseech you through yourself: help me, lest I fall before the sight of my adversaries, captured by the snares they have prepared for my feet in order to bend down my soul. But rescue me, power of my salvation, lest your enemies who hate you make me an object of their laughter.

Arise, Lord my God, my strong one, and let your enemies be scattered; let those who hate you flee from your face (Psalm 68:1). As wax melts before fire, so may sinners perish before the face of God. And let me be hidden in the hiding place of your face, and rejoice with your children, satisfied with all your good things.

And you, Lord God, father of orphans, and you, mother of your wards, hear the wailing of your children. Spread out your wings, so that we may flee beneath them from the face of the enemy, tower of strength of Israel, who neither slumbers nor sleeps while guarding Israel, because the enemy who attacks Israel does not slumber.

## CHAPTER XIII. On the wondrous light of God. That human beings are well only in God alone. On God’s various benefits.

Light that no other light sees; brightness that no other brightness sees; light that darkens every light, and brightness that blinds every foreign light; light from which all light comes, brightness from which all brightness comes; brightness for which every other brightness is darkness, for which all light is obscurity; light to which all darkness is light, to which all obscurity is brightness; supreme light that blindness does not cloud, gloom does not dull, darkness does not obscure, no obstruction closes [Note: [Col. 0874] The Colbertinus manuscript has “doors.”], and no shadow ever separates—light that enlightens all things wholly, simultaneously, once and forever, absorb me into the abyss of your brightness, so that I may see you everywhere in yourself, myself in you, and all things beneath you.

Do not abandon me, lest the shadows of my ignorance increase and my sins multiply. For without you everything is darkness to me, everything evil, because nothing is good without you, the true, sole, and highest good.

This I confess; this I know, Lord my God, because wherever I am without you, it is bad for me apart from you—not only outside me but also within me—because every abundance that is not my God is poverty to me. I shall be satisfied only when your glory appears (Psalm 16:15).

Indeed, Lord, my blessed life, as I confess my misery to you: ever since I fell from unity with you, the highest and one good, the multiplicity of temporal things has battered me, fallen as I am, through the bodily senses and divided me from you, the one, into many. And a laborious abundance and an abundant poverty came to be mine, while I pursued one thing and another and was filled by none; while I was not found in you, the unchangeable, singular, indivisible one good, which, when I follow it, I do not go astray; when I attain it, I do not grieve; when I possess it, my entire desire is satisfied.

Alas, great misery! Alas for me! Lord, my wretched soul flees from you, with whom it is always full and rejoices, and follows the world, with which it is always needy and sorrowful. The world cries, “I fail”; and you cry, “I restore.” And my wretched soul follows the one who fails more than the one who restores.

This, plainly, is my infirmity. Healer of spirits, heal it, so that I may confess you, salvation of my soul, with all my heart above all your benefits, with which you feed me from my youth even to old age and gray hairs. I beseech you through yourself: do not abandon me.

[Note: [Col. 0874] See the book *On the Spirit and the Soul*, chapter 17; the book *On Loving God*, chapters 6 and 7; and Anselm, *Meditations*, 7.]

You made me when I did not exist; you redeemed me when I had perished. I had perished; I had died. You descended to the dead; you assumed mortality; the King descended to the servant. To redeem the servant, you handed yourself over. So that I might live, you accepted death; you conquered death; you restored me when you humbled yourself.

I had perished, had gone away, and had been sold into sins. You came for me to redeem me, and you loved me so greatly that you gave your blood as the price for me. You loved me more than yourself, because you were willing to die for me.

By such an agreement and at so dear a price, you brought me back from exile, redeemed me from slavery, and recalled me from punishment. You called me by your name; you marked me with your blood, so that your memorial might always be with me and never depart from my heart—you who never withdrew from the cross for me. You anointed me with your oil, with which you yourself were anointed, so that through you, Christ, I might be called Christian.

And in your hands you inscribed me, so that my memory might always be before you—provided that your memory is continually before me. Thus your grace and mercy always went before me. From many dangers you often rescued me, my deliverer. When I went astray, you brought me back to the road; when I was ignorant, you taught me; when I sinned, you rebuked me; when I was sad, you consoled me; when I despaired, you strengthened me; when I fell, you raised me; when I stood, you upheld me; when I went, you led me; when I came, you received me; when I slept, you guarded me; when I cried out, you heard me.

## CHAPTER XIV. That God continually observes the deeds and intentions of human beings.

[Note: [Col. 0875] Compare this chapter with the books *On the Spirit and the Soul*, chapter 17; *On Loving God*, chapter 10; and Hugh of Saint Victor’s book *On the Soul’s Earnest*.]

These and many other benefits you have bestowed upon me, Lord my God, life of my soul. It would be sweet for me always to speak of them, always to think of them, and always to give you thanks, so that I may praise you for all your good things and love you with all my heart, with all my soul, with all my mind, and with all my strength, together with all the innermost marrow of my heart and all my joints, blessed sweetness, Lord my God, of all who delight in you.

But your eyes saw my imperfection (Psalm 139:16)—your eyes, I say, far brighter than the sun, surveying all the ways of human beings and the depth of the abyss, always contemplating the good and the evil in every place (Proverbs 15:3).

For although you preside over all things, filling each one, wholly present everywhere at all times, and caring for everything you created, because you hate nothing that you have made, so you consider my steps and paths and watch day and night over my keeping, carefully noting all my paths, an eternal watcher—as though, having forgotten all your creation of heaven and earth, you considered only me and cared for nothing else.

Nor does the unchangeable light of your vision increase if you look upon only one thing, nor diminish if you see innumerable and diverse things. For just as you consider one whole thing perfectly and all at once, so your vision, wholly and entirely, sees each individual thing—although diverse—perfectly, all at once.

But you consider all things as one, and one as all things; so you consider each individual thing wholly and simultaneously, without division, alteration, or diminution [Note: [Col. 0875] Thus one of the Regius manuscripts. The printed editions have: “But just as all things, so one; just as one, so each individual thing.”]. Thus you, wholly present in the whole of time without time, consider all of me simultaneously and always, as though you had nothing else to consider.

Therefore you stand over my keeping as though you had forgotten all else and wished to attend to me alone [Note: [Col. 0875] Manuscripts: “Thus therefore I shall stand …,” and so forth.]. For you always show yourself present everywhere; you always offer yourself ready, if you find me ready. Wherever I go, you, Lord, do not abandon me—unless I first abandon you. Wherever I may be, you do not depart, because you are everywhere; so that wherever I go, I may find you, through whom I may exist and not perish without you, since without you I cannot exist.

I confess indeed that whatever I do, whatever it may be that I do, I do before you; and whatever that thing is that I do, you see it better than I who do it. For whatever I am always doing, you are always present beside me, as the perpetual observer of all my thoughts, intentions, delights, and actions.

Lord, all my desire is always before you; all my thought is before you. You see from where the spirit comes, where it is, and where it goes, because you are the weigher of all spirits.

Whether the root is sweet or bitter, from which beautiful leaves are sent forth outwardly, you, the inward judge, know me better than I do [Note: [Col. 0875] That is, “better than I do.”], and you search more subtly even the marrow of the roots. You gather, observe, and mark not only the intention but also the innermost marrow of its root, with the most discerning truth of your light, so that you may repay each person not merely according to deeds or intention, but also according to the hidden inward marrow of the root from which the intention of the one acting proceeds.

Toward what do I strive when I act? Whatever I think, whatever I take delight in—you see it; your ears hear it; your eyes observe it; you carefully mark, note, and write it in your book, whether it is good or evil [Col. 0876], so that afterward you may give rewards for good and punishments for evil, when the books are opened and we are judged according to what has been written in your books (Revelation 20:12).

Perhaps this is what you have already said to us: “I will consider their end” (Deuteronomy 32:20); and what is said of you, Lord: “He himself considers the end of all things” (Job 28:3), because in everything we do you attend more to the end of the intention than to the act of the deed.

When I consider these things carefully, Lord my God, terrible and strong, I am overwhelmed equally by fear and great shame, because a great necessity has been imposed upon us to live justly and rightly, since we do everything before the eyes of the Judge who sees all things.

## CHAPTER XV. That a human being can do nothing by himself. That he has nothing in which to glory. Who deserves the riches of grace. What a human being is by himself. It is by grace that we do not fall into sins.

[Note: [Col. 0876] Boethius, *Consolation of Philosophy*, book 5, prose 6. See Bernard, *Book of Meditations*, chapter 2, no. 19.]

Most powerful, almighty God of the spirits of all flesh, whose eyes are over all the ways of the children of Adam, from the day of their birth to the day of their departure, to repay each according to his good or evil works, show me, so that I may confess to you, my poverty. For I said that I was rich and needed nothing, and I did not know that I was poor, blind, naked, wretched, and miserable (Revelation 3:17).

I believed that I would be something, when I was nothing. I said, “I shall become wise,” and I became foolish. I thought I was self-controlled, but I was deceived. And now I see that this is your gift, without which we can do nothing, because unless you guard the city, the one who guards it keeps watch in vain (Psalm 127:1).

Thus you taught me, so that I might know myself, because you abandoned me and tested me—not for your sake, so that you might know me, but for my sake, so that I might know myself. For, as I said, Lord, I believed that I would become something from myself; I thought I was sufficient by myself and did not perceive that you were ruling me, until you withdrew from me for a little while, and I immediately fell into myself. Then I saw and knew that you were ruling me: my falling was from myself, and my rising was from you.

You opened my eyes, O light; you awakened and enlightened me. And I saw that human life upon earth is a temptation, and that no flesh can glory before you, nor can any living person be justified, because if there is any good, small or great, it is your gift, and what is ours is nothing but evil.

In what, then, will all flesh glory? Surely in evil? That is not glory, but misery. But will it glory in good? In what belongs to another? The good is yours, Lord; the glory is yours.

For whoever seeks glory for himself from your good, and does not seek it for you, is a thief and robber, and is like the devil, who wished to steal your glory. Whoever wishes to be praised by human beings for your gift, and does not seek your glory in it but his own—although he may be praised by human beings because of your gift, he is nevertheless condemned by you, because from your gift he sought not your glory but his own.

[Note: [Col. 0876] Augustine, *Confessions*, book 10, chapter 36.]

The one who is praised by human beings while you condemn him will not be defended by human beings when you judge him, nor freed when you condemn him. But you, Lord, my fashioner from my mother’s womb, do not allow me to fall into that reproach, that I should be reproached for having wished to steal your glory.

To you be glory, to whom all good belongs; but to us shame of face and misery, to whom all evil belongs, unless you choose to have mercy. For you have mercy, Lord, you have mercy on all that you have made, and you hate nothing that you have made. You give us from your good things and enrich us, who are needy, with your choicest gifts, because you love the poor and make them rich with your riches.

Behold, now, Lord, we your children are poor, and your little flock. Open your doors to us, and the poor will eat and be satisfied, and those who seek you will praise you.

I also know, Lord, and confess, because you teach me, that only those who know themselves to be poor and confess their poverty to you will be enriched by you, because those who consider themselves rich while they are poor will be found excluded from your riches.

Therefore I too confess to you, Lord my God, my poverty; and may your glory be wholly yours [Note: [Col. 0877] The Colbertinus manuscript has: “my whole glory.”], because all good is yours.

For by myself, Lord, I confess, as you have taught me, I am nothing other than complete vanity and the shadow of death, a kind of dark abyss, and an empty and desolate earth, which without your blessing produces nothing and bears no fruit except shame, sin, and death.

If I have ever had any good, I received it from you; whatever good I have is yours [Note: [Col. 0877] The Regius manuscript has: “I have it from you.” Both readings occur in the printed editions.]. If ever I stood, I stood through you; but when I fell, I fell through myself. I would always have lain in the mud if you had not raised me; I would always have been blind if you had not enlightened me. When I fell, I would never have risen unless you had extended your hand to me. After you raised me, I would always have fallen unless you had sustained me; I would have perished more often unless you had guided me.

Thus always, Lord, thus always your grace and mercy went before me: freeing me from all evils, saving me from those of the past, raising me from those of the present, and fortifying me against those of the future; even cutting off before me the snares of sins and removing their occasions and causes.

For unless you had done this for me, I would have committed all the sins of the world, because I know, Lord, that there is no sin ever committed by one human being that another human being could not commit, if the Creator by whom the human being was made were absent.

But that I did not do, you accomplished; what I abstained from, you commanded; and that I should believe in you, you infused by grace. For you, Lord, were ruling me for yourself, preserving me for yourself and for me, so that I would not commit adultery or any other sin.

## CHAPTER XVI. On the devil and his temptations. The devil’s snares everywhere.

The tempter was absent; and that he might be absent, you brought it about. Place and time were absent; and that these might be absent, you brought it about. The tempter was present, place was not lacking, time was not lacking; but so that I might not consent, you held me fast. The dark tempter came, as he is; and so that I might despise him, you strengthened me. The strong, armed tempter came; and so that he might not overcome me, you restrained him and made me strong. The tempter came transformed into an angel of light; and so that he might not deceive me, you rebuked him, and so that I might recognize him, you enlightened me.

For he is that great, red dragon, Lord, that ancient serpent called the devil and Satan, having seven heads and ten horns (Rev. 12:3), whom you created to sport in this great sea, broad in its expanse, in which are reptiles without number, and animals both small and great (Ps. 103:25–26)—that is, the various kinds of demons, who do nothing else day and night except roam about seeking whom they may devour, unless you rescue them.

For he is that ancient dragon who arose in the paradise of delight, who with his tail drags a third of the stars of heaven and casts them upon the earth (Rev. 12:4); who with his poison corrupts the waters of the earth, so that those who drink them die; who spreads gold beneath himself as though it were mud (Job 41:21), and trusts that the Jordan will flow into his mouth (ibid. 40:18); he was made so as to fear no one. And who will defend us from his bites, who will snatch us from his mouth, unless you, Lord, who have crushed the heads of the great dragon?

Spread your wings over us, Lord, so that we may flee beneath them from the face of this dragon who pursues us, and by your shield deliver us from his horns [Note: [Col. 0877] The Regius Manuscript reads, “from his bites.”]. For this is his continual occupation, this his sole desire: to devour the souls whom you created.

And therefore we cry out to you: deliver us from our daily adversary, who, whether we sleep or keep watch, whether we eat or drink, or perform whatever work, presses upon us in every way, day and night, with deceits [Col. 0878] and stratagems—now openly, now secretly—directing poisoned arrows against us in order to kill our souls.

And yet, Lord, such is our utterly wretched madness that, although we continually see the dragon before us, mouth open and ready to devour, nevertheless we sleep and indulge ourselves in our laziness, as though secure before him who desires nothing other than our destruction. The enemy is always awake, without sleep, in order to kill us; and we, in order to guard ourselves, do not wish to awaken from sleep.

Behold, he has spread countless snares before our feet and filled all our paths with traps for capturing our souls. And who will escape? He has set snares in wealth, snares in poverty; he has stretched snares in food, in drink, in pleasure, in sleep, in wakefulness. He has set snares in word and deed, and in every path of our life.

But you, Lord, deliver us from the snare of the hunters and from the harsh word (Ps. 90:3), so that we may confess to you, saying: “Blessed is the Lord, who has not given us over as prey to their teeth. Our soul, like a sparrow, has been rescued from the snare of the hunters; the snare has been broken, and we have been set free” (Ps. 123:6–7).

## CHAPTER XVII. The Necessity of God’s Light for Avoiding Them. The Devil’s Cunning.

And indeed, Lord, my light, open my eyes, so that I may see the light, walk in your light, and not stumble into his snares. For who will escape these many snares unless he sees them? And who will see them unless you enlighten him with your light?

For the father of darkness hides his snares in his darkness, so that all who are in his darkness may be caught in them—those who are children of these darknesses and do not see your light, in which whoever walks will not fear. Whoever walks in the day does not stumble; but whoever walks in the night stumbles, because the light is not in him (John 11:9–10).

You are light, Lord; you are the light of the children of light; you are the day that knows no setting, in which your children walk without stumbling. Without you, all who walk are in darkness, because they do not possess you, the light of the world.

Behold, every day we see that the farther someone withdraws from you, the true light, the more he becomes entangled in the darkness of sins; and the more he is in darkness, the less he sees the snares in his path. Therefore he recognizes them less, is caught in them more often, and falls into them; and, what is more dreadful, he does not even know that he has fallen. Whoever does not know his fall is all the less concerned to rise, since he supposes that he is still standing.

But now enlighten my eyes, Lord my God, light of the mind, so that I may see and recognize him, lest I fall before my adversaries. For our enemy labors for our destruction; we ask you to make him melt away from before us as wax melts before fire (Ps. 67:3).

For, Lord, he is the first and last thief, who plotted to seize your glory when, puffed up and exalted, he burst apart and fell into his own pit. You cast him out from your holy mountain and from the midst of the fiery stones, in whose midst he walked.

And now, my life, my God, ever since he fell he has not ceased to persecute your children. Out of hatred for you, O great King, he desires to destroy this creature of yours, whom your almighty goodness created in your image, so that he may not possess your glory, which he himself lost through his pride.

But crush him, our strong defender, before us, your lambs; and enlighten us, so that we may see the snares he has prepared and escape to you, the joy of Israel.

And all these things you know better, Lord, for you know his contentiousness and his exceedingly hard neck. Nor do I say this to inform you, who see all things and from whom no thought is hidden. Rather, before the feet of your majesty I bring a complaint against my enemy, eternal Judge, so that you may condemn him and save us, your children, whose strength you are.

This enemy is cunning and crooked, Lord: [Col. 0879] the circuits of his path cannot easily be detected, nor the appearance of his face recognized, unless you enlighten us. For now here, now there; now as a lamb, now as a wolf; now as darkness, now as light, he shows himself. Yet, according to the various changes of circumstances, he presents various temptations through every possible quality, place, and time.

For in order to deceive the sorrowful, he too becomes sorrowful; in order to mock the joyful, he pretends that he too is joyful; in order to defraud the spiritual, he transforms himself into an angel of light; in order to suppress the strong, he appears as a lamb; in order to devour the gentle, he appears as a wolf.

All these things are effected according to the likeness [Note: [Col. 0879] One of the Regius Manuscripts reads “likenesses,” omitting “according to the likeness of.”] of various temptations: some are from the terror of night, others from the arrow that flies by day, others from the business that walks about in darkness, others from assault, and others from the demon of noonday (Ps. 90:5–6).

And who is fit for these things, so as to recognize them? Who will reveal the appearance of his clothing, and who has recognized the circuit of his teeth? Behold, he hides his arrows in his quiver, and he also hides snares beneath the appearance of light. This is more difficult to discern unless, Lord, our hope, we receive light from you so that we may see [Note: [Col. 0879] The Regius Manuscript reads “appearance.”].

For he hides subtle snares not only in the works of the flesh, which are easily recognized, and not only in vices themselves, but even in spiritual exercises themselves. Beneath the color of virtues he clothes the vices themselves, and he transforms himself into an angel of light.

Our enemy, this son of Belial, this Satan, Lord our God, strives against us in these and many other ways. Now as a lion, now as a dragon, openly and secretly, within and without, day and night he lies in wait to seize our souls.

And rescue us, Lord, you who save those who hope in you, so that he himself may grieve because of us, and you may be praised in us, Lord our God [Note: [Col. 0879] The Regius Manuscript adds “amen.”].

## CHAPTER XVIII. The Evils of Ingratitude. Description of God’s Benefits. Thanksgiving for Those Same Benefits. We Are Bound Always to Love God, and Cannot Do So Unless He Grants It.

But I, the son of your handmaid, who entrusted me to your hand, let me now confess to you, my deliverer, with all my heart, in these poor confessions of mine; and let me recall to my mind the good things you have done for me from my youth throughout my whole life.

For I know that ingratitude displeases you. It is the root of all spiritual evil and a certain wind that dries up and burns every good thing, closing the fountain of divine mercy over a person. Through it, dead evils arise, living works die, and no further progress is made.

And I will give you thanks, Lord, so that I may not be ungrateful to you, my deliverer, because you have delivered me. How often that dragon had already swallowed me, and you, Lord, drew me out of his mouth! When, or how often, have I sinned, and he was ready to devour me; but you defended me? When I acted wickedly against you, when I broke your commandments, he stood ready to snatch me into hell; but you prevented him.

I offended you, and you defended me; I did not fear you, and you guarded me. I was withdrawing from you and presenting myself to my enemy; you deterred him from taking me. You were conferring these benefits upon me, my God, and I did not recognize them.

Thus many times you freed me from the jaws of the devil, snatched me from the lion’s mouth, and brought me back from hell on many occasions, although I did not know it. For I descended even to the gates of hell, and so that I might not enter there, you held me back; I approached even to the gates of death, and so that death itself might not seize me, you intervened.

You also often rescued me from bodily death, my Savior, when severe illnesses held me, when I was in many dangers by sea and land; you freed me from fire and sword and every danger, always standing by me and mercifully saving me.

You knew, Lord, that if death had then overtaken me, hell would have received my soul and I would have been condemned forever. But your mercy and your grace went before me, rescuing me from the death of the body and from the death of the soul, Lord my God.

You bestowed these and many other benefits upon me, [Col. 0880] and I was blind and did not recognize them until you enlightened me.

Now therefore, light of my soul, Lord my God, my life through whom I live, light of my eyes through which I see, behold, you have enlightened me, and I know you, because I live through you. And I give you thanks, although what I offer is paltry, slight, and unequal to your benefits, as my frailty permits.

For you alone are my God, my gracious Creator, who love souls and hate nothing that you have made (Wis. 11:25). Behold, I am the first among the sinners whom you have saved, so that I may offer others an example of your most gracious compassion and confess your great benefits: for you have snatched me from hell once, twice, three times, a hundred times, a thousand times, while I was always heading toward hell and you were always bringing me back.

And although you could justly have condemned me a thousand times, if you had wished, you did not wish to do so, because you love souls and overlook my sins for the sake of repentance, Lord my God, for your mercies are many in all your ways.

Now therefore I see these things, Lord my God, and know them through your light, and my soul fails before your great mercy toward me, for you have rescued my soul from the lowest hell and brought me back to life. I was wholly in death, and you resurrected me wholly; therefore let everything by which I live be yours.

I offer my whole self, wholly, to you: let my whole spirit, my whole heart, my whole body, my whole life live for you, my life. For you freed my whole self so that you might possess my whole self; you restored my whole self so that you might have me wholly again.

Therefore I will love you, Lord, my strength; I will love you, my ineffable exultation. Let my whole life, which had perished in my misery and has been resurrected in your mercy, now live not for me but for you—you who are a merciful and compassionate God, rich in mercy to thousands who love your name.

Therefore, Lord my God, my sanctifier, you commanded me by your law to love you with all my heart, all my soul, all my mind, and all my strength (Deut. 6:5; Matt. 22:37), and with all my powers, even from the inmost marrow of my heart, at all the hours and moments in which I enjoy the goods of your mercy.

For I would always perish unless you always governed me; I would always die unless you always gave me life; and at every moment you bind me to yourself by granting me your great benefits at every moment. [Note: [Col. 0880] See the book *On the Spirit and the Soul*, chap. 35, and the *Manual*, chap. 39.]

Therefore, just as there is no hour or instant throughout my whole life in which I do not make use of your benefit, so there ought to be no moment in which I do not have you before my eyes in my memory and love you with all my strength.

But I cannot do even this unless you grant it to me, for every good gift and every perfect gift comes down from the Father of lights, with whom there is no change or shadow of alteration (James 1:17). For it is not of the one who wills or the one who runs, but of you who show mercy (Rom. 9:16), that we love you.

This gift is yours, Lord, for every good thing is yours. You command that you be loved; grant what you command, and command what you will. [Note: [Col. 0880] From Book 10 of the *Confessions*, chapters 29 and 37.]

## CHAPTER XIX. Fervent Desire for Love. Recapitulation of God’s Benefits.

[Note: [Col. 0880] These words are not found in the manuscripts. See the *Manual*, chap. 10.]

I love you, my God, and I desire always to love you more, because you are truly sweeter than every honey, more nourishing than every milk, and brighter than every light. Therefore you are dearer to me than all gold, silver, and precious stones.

For everything I did in the world displeased me in comparison with your sweetness and the beauty of your house, which I loved. [Note: [Col. 0880] From Book 10 of the *Confessions*, chap. 29.]

O fire that always burns and is never extinguished, O love that always boils and never grows lukewarm, divine charity, my God, kindle me. Kindle me, I say, entirely, so that I may love you alone with my whole being.

For the one who loves something together with you, but does not love it for your sake, loves you less. I will love you, Lord, because you first loved me (1 John 4:10).

And from where shall I find words to explain the signs of your love, especially toward me, on account of your innumerable benefits by which you have nurtured me from the beginning?

After the benefit of creation, when in the beginning you created me from nothing in your image, honoring and exalting me among the creatures you made, and ennobling me with the light of your face, with which you marked the lintel of my heart; by this you distinguished me alike from insensible things and from sensible beasts, and made me a little lower than the angels (Ps. 8:6).

This was little in the sight of your goodness, because through the daily, singular, and very great gifts of your benefits you have continually nourished me without interruption. Like a tender little son of yours, you nursed and strengthened me at the breasts of your consolation.

For, so that I might serve you wholly, you entrusted everything you made to my service.

## CHAPTER XX. All Things Serve Humanity So That Humanity May Serve the Creator.

You subjected all things beneath the feet of human beings (Ps. 8:8), so that the human being alone might be wholly subject to you; and so that the whole human being might belong to you, the human being exercised dominion over all your works.

You created all exterior things for the body, the body itself for the soul, and the soul for you, so that it might be free for you alone and love you alone, possessing you for consolation and all lower things for service.

For whatever is contained within the circuit of heaven is lower than the human soul, which was made so that it might possess the highest good above and become blessed through possessing it. If it clings to that good, rising above the necessities of all mutable things below, it will rejoice in the immortality of eternity, with serenity, in that supreme majesty whose likeness it strives to imitate.

Then it will enjoy those supremely good things in the house of the Lord, in comparison with which everything we see here is counted as nothing. These are the things [Note: [Col. 0881] The manuscripts read, “namely, those things.”] that eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor have entered into the human heart, which God has prepared for those who love him (Isa. 64:4; 1 Cor. 2:9).

And these things, Lord, you will give to the soul. With these also you daily gladden the souls of your servants, you who love souls.

Why should I marvel at these things, Lord my God? You honor your image and your likeness, according to which they were created. For even to our body, although it is still corruptible and lowly, you gave the splendor of heaven for seeing, through the hands of your tireless ministers, the sun and moon, which continually serve your children day and night at your command.

For breathing, you generously gave the purity of the air; for hearing, varieties of sounds; for smelling, the sweetness of scents; for tasting, the qualities of flavors; for touching, the solidity of all bodily things.

You gave beasts of burden to assist its needs; you also provided the birds of heaven, the fish of the sea, and the fruits of the earth for its refreshment. You created medicines from the earth for each of its various disorders and prepared particular remedies to meet particular illnesses, because you are merciful and compassionate, and you know our formation—you, our potter—and we are all like clay in your hand.

## CHAPTER XXI. From Temporal Goods the Greatness of Heavenly Goods Is Inferred.

Behold, your great mercy is opening before me; enlighten me, I beg you, with your light still more, so that it may be opened to me more fully.

For from these small things we comprehend your great things, and from these visible things your invisible things, Lord our holy God and good Creator.

If, then, my Lord, for this lowly and corruptible body you bestow such great and innumerable benefits from heaven and air, earth and sea, light and darkness, heat and shade, dew and rain, winds and showers, birds and fish, beasts and trees, the abundance of grasses and plants of the earth, and the service of all your creatures, which successively minister to us in their appointed times in order to relieve our weariness—what, I ask, and how great and innumerable will be those goods that you have prepared for those who love you in that homeland of heaven, where we shall see you face to face?

If you do such great things for us in prison, what will you do in the palace? [Col. 0882] Great and innumerable are your works, Lord, King of heaven.

Since all these things that you have given in common to the good and the wicked are exceedingly good and delightful, what will those things be like that you have stored up for the good alone?

If your gifts, now so innumerable and varied, are bestowed alike upon friends and enemies, how great and innumerable, how sweet and delightful, will those be that you will lavish upon your friends alone?

If there are such great consolations in this day of tears, how many will you bestow on the day of the wedding feast? If prison contains so many delights, how many, I ask, does the homeland contain?

Eye has not seen, O God, apart from you, what you have prepared for those who love you (Isa. 64:4). For according to the great multitude of your magnificence is also the great multitude of your sweetness, which you have hidden for those who fear you (Ps. 50:3; 30:20).

For you are great, Lord my God, and immeasurable; there is no end to your greatness (Ps. 144:3), no number to your wisdom, no measure to your goodness, no end, number, or measure to your recompense. But just as you are great, so are your gifts great, because you yourself are the reward and gift of all your lawful warriors.

## CHAPTER XXII. Eternal Consolation Must Not Be Expected Together with the Present. The Sweetness of God Soothes the Bitterness of the World.

These are your great benefits, Lord God, sanctifier of your saints, with which you will fill the poverty of your hungry children; for you have become the hope of the despairing and the consolation of the desolate. You are the crown of hope, adorned with glory and prepared for those who conquer; you are the eternal satisfaction of the hungry, to be given to those who hunger; you are everlasting consolation, which you grant only to those who despise the consolation of this world for the sake of your consolation [Note: [Col. 0882] Two manuscripts read, “which you will grant.”].

For those who are consoled here are considered unworthy of your consolation. But those who are afflicted here are consoled by you; and those who share in sufferings also share in consolations.

No one can be consoled in both worlds, nor can anyone rejoice both here and in the future; rather, whoever wishes to possess one must necessarily lose the other.

When I consider these things, Lord my consoler, I refuse to console my soul, so that it may be deemed worthy of your eternal consolations. For it is just that whoever chooses to be consoled in something else rather than in you should lose you.

And I beg you, supreme Truth, by your own self, do not permit me to be consoled in any empty consolation rather than in you. Instead, let everything become bitter to me, so that you alone may appear sweet to my soul—you who are immeasurable sweetness, through which all bitter things are sweetened.

For your sweetness sweetened the stones of the torrent for Stephen (Acts 7:58); your sweetness made the gridiron sweet for Lawrence. Because of your sweetness the Apostles went away rejoicing from the presence of the council, since they were deemed worthy to suffer dishonor for the name of Jesus (ibid. 5:41).

Andrew went confidently and joyfully to the cross, because he was hastening toward your sweetness. This sweetness of yours so filled the chief Apostles that one chose the cross as his gallows, while the other did not fear to offer his head to the striking sword.

To purchase this sweetness Bartholomew gave his own skin; and in order to taste it, John fearlessly drank the cup of poison.

When Peter tasted it, he forgot all lower things and cried out as though drunk, saying: “Lord, it is good for us to be here; let us make three tents here” (Matt. 17:4). “Let us remain here and contemplate you, because we need nothing else. It is enough for us, Lord, to see you; it is enough,” he said, “to be satisfied with such great sweetness.”

For he tasted one drop of sweetness and grew weary of every other sweetness. What do you think he would have said if he had tasted that great multitude of the sweetness of your divinity which you have hidden for those who love you?

Your ineffable sweetness had also been tasted by that virgin [Note: [Col. 0882] Agatha.], of whom we read that she went most joyfully and triumphantly to prison, as though she had been invited to a banquet.

He too, I think, had tasted it who said: “How great is the multitude of your sweetness, Lord, which you have hidden for those who fear you!” (Ps. 30:20); and who urged us: “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet” (Ps. 33:9).

This is that blessedness, Lord our God, which we await you to give us; for its sake we continually serve as soldiers for you, and for its sake we are put to death all day long, so that we may live in your life.

## CHAPTER XXIII. Aspiration to the Enjoyment of God. It Is Obtained Only as a Gift from God.

But you, Lord, are the expectation of Israel (Jer. 14:8), the desire toward which our heart sighs every day. Hasten; do not delay. Arise, make haste, and come, so that you may lead us out of this prison to confess your name, so that we may glory in your light.

Open your ears to the cries of the tears of your little ones, who cry out to you: “Our Father, give us today our daily bread” (Matt. 6:9, 11), in whose strength we may walk day and night until we reach your mountain, Horeb.

And I, a little one among the little ones of your household, God my Father and my strength, when shall I come and appear before your face, so that I who now confess you for a time may from then on confess you forever?

I shall be blessed if I am admitted to see your glory. Who will grant me this, that you may permit me to come to it? I know, Lord, I know and confess that I am unworthy to enter under your roof; but do it for the sake of your honor, and do not put to shame your servant who hopes in you.

And who will enter your sanctuary to contemplate your powers unless you open it? But who will open it if you have closed it [Note: [Col. 0883] The manuscripts read, “if you have shut it up”?]. For if you destroy, no one can build; and if you shut a person in [Note: [Col. 0883] The Regius Manuscript reads, “to a person.”], no one can open.

If you hold back the waters, everything will dry up; and if you release them, they will overthrow the earth. If you reduce to nothing everything that you have made, who will oppose you? (Job 11:10).

Moreover, eternal goodness of your mercy, by which you willed and made all things whatsoever you willed: you made us, Maker of the world—govern us; you created us—do not despise us, for we are your work.

Indeed, Lord our God, we, who are clay and worms, cannot enter into your eternities unless you lead us in, you who created all things from nothing.

## CHAPTER XXIV. We Can Do Nothing without God’s Grace.

But I, the work of your hands, confess to you in your fear, because I will not hope in my bow, nor will my sword save me (Ps. 43:7), but your right hand, your arm, and the light of your face.

Otherwise I would despair, were you not my hope, you who created me and will not abandon me, because you do not abandon those who hope in you.

For you are, Lord our God, sweet and gentle, patient, and ordering all things in mercy (Wis. 11:21). And if we have sinned, we are yours [Note: [Col. 0883] So read the manuscripts. The printed editions have “we are not yours”; shortly afterward, “we are yours.”]; and if we have not sinned, we know that we have been counted among those who are with you.

We are a leaf of the universe, and every living human being is vanity (Ps. 38:6); our life upon the earth is a breath (Job 7:7). Do not be angry if we, your little orphans, fall, for you know our formation (Ps. 102:14), Lord our God.

Will you, God of immeasurable strength, display your power against a leaf carried away by the wind and pursue a dry straw (Job 13:25)? Will you condemn, eternal King of Israel [Note: [Col. 0883] The printed editions add here, “a dead dog”], will you condemn a single flea? (1 Sam. 24:15).

We have heard of your mercy, Lord, that you do not make death, nor rejoice in the destruction of those who die (Wis. 1:13). For your sake we pray to you: do not permit what you did not make to dominate this creature of yours, whom you did make.

If you grieve over destruction, what prevents you, Lord, who can do all things, from rejoicing always over our salvation? If you will, you can save me; but although I may wish it, I cannot [Note: [Col. 0883] So read the manuscripts. The printed editions have, “although I might wish it, I could not.”], so great is the multitude of my miseries that is with me.

For to will is present with me, but I do not find how to accomplish it (Rom. 7:18). I cannot will what is good unless you will it; nor can I do what I will unless your power strengthens me.

And sometimes I do not will what I can, unless your will is done on earth as in heaven; and what I will and can, I do not know unless your wisdom enlightens me.

And even if I know, sometimes unwilling [Note: [Col. 0884] The Regius and Colbertinus Manuscripts read here, “being able.” Another Regius Manuscript has, “sometimes willingly, sometimes unwillingly.” The printed editions have, “sometimes willingly, sometimes being able.”], sometimes unable, my imperfect and empty wisdom passes away unless I am aided by your true wisdom.
