My life produces fear, but your compassion inspires confidence; your kindness encourages me, while my wickedness holds me back. And, to confess more truthfully, the phantoms of my vices come to mind and beat back the boldness of my presumptuous spirit. For when someone deserves hatred, with what face does he seek favor? When punishment is owed, with what recklessness is glory requested [Note: Er., Lyon, Venice, and Leuven print this passage as: “When punishment is owed to whom, with what recklessness does he demand glory?” M.]? He challenges the judge who, having postponed satisfaction for his offense, seeks to be honored with rewards. A person liable to punishment insults the king when he demands an undeserved reward; and a foolish son aggravates his father’s tender affection when, after inflicting insults and before repentance, he usurps the eminence of an heir.

What do I remember having done, my father? I deserved death, and I ask for life. I angered my king, whose protection I now shamelessly invoke. I despised the judge whom I ask to hold as my helper. Insolently I refused to hear the father whom I now presume to have as my guardian. Alas for me, how late I come! Alas, how slowly I hasten! Alas for me, who run after the wounds, scorning to guard against the arrows while I was unharmed! I neglected to look ahead at the weapons; now I am anxious about approaching death. I drove wounds into wounds, because I did not fear adding crimes to crimes. I sprinkled fresh scars with corruption, because I repeated former offenses through modern pollutions, and my frenzied itching loosened what divine medicine had made firm. The skin that had grown over the wounds and concealed the disease rotted when pus burst forth, because repeated iniquity emptied out the mercy that had been granted. For I know that it is written, “On whatever day the righteous person sins, all his righteousnesses will be forgotten” (Ezek. 18:24). If the righteousness of a righteous person who falls is erased, how much more the repentance of a sinner who returns to the same things? How often have I returned like a dog to its vomit and, like a sow, gone back to the mud in which it wallows (2 Pet. 2:22). It is impossible for me to confess—and to remember—how many mortals I taught to sin while they were ignorant of sinning [Note: In Anselm: “Therefore it is difficult for me to confess, because it is also difficult to remember”]; how many unwilling to offend I persuaded to do wrong; how many who resisted I compelled; how many who desired it I joined in with.

How many travelers did I ensnare; for how many seeking the road did I uncover a pit? I did not shrink from committing such deeds, nor fear forgetting them. But you, just Judge, “sealed them up as though in a purse”; you observed all my paths and counted all my steps. You were silent, always silent; you were patient. Woe to me: at last you will speak “like a woman in labor” (Isa. 42:14).

## CHAPTER IV. Fear of the Last Judgment; The Reason for Fear; The Reason for Trust

Lord, God of gods, surpassing all malice, I know that you will come openly; I know that you will not always be silent, when fire blazes before you and a mighty storm gathers around you, when you summon heaven above and earth to judge your people (Ps. 49:3–4). Behold, before so many thousands of peoples all my iniquities will be exposed; before so many ranks of angels all my crimes will be revealed—not only those of my actions, but also those of my thoughts and words. I will stand helpless before as many judges as there have been people who preceded me in good works; I will be confounded before as many accusers as have offered me examples of good living; I will be convicted by as many witnesses as have admonished me with useful words and given themselves to be imitated in righteous deeds.

My Lord, I have nothing to say, and no answer comes to me. And as though I were already present at that judgment, conscience torments me, the secrets of my heart torture me: avarice constricts me, pride accuses me, envy consumes me, lust inflames me, luxury attacks me, gluttony dishonors me, drunkenness refutes me, detraction tears me apart, ambition trips me up, greed reproaches me, discord scatters me, anger disturbs me, fickleness casts me down, sluggishness oppresses me, hypocrisy deceives me, flattery breaks me, favor exalts me, and slander pricks me.

Behold, my deliverer from angry nations; behold those with whom I have lived from the day of my birth, those whom I cultivated and to whom I kept faith. The very pursuits I loved condemn me; those I praised reproach me. These are the people to whom I listened as friends; whom I obeyed as teachers; whom I served as masters; the counselors in whom I trusted; the citizens with whom I lived; the members of my household with whom I grew old [Note: Alternatively, “with whom I agreed”]. Woe is me, my king and my God, because my sojourn has been prolonged. Woe is me, my illumination, because I have dwelt with those who dwell in Kedar (Ps. 119:5). And when the holy man said “too long,” how much more may I, the wretched one, say, “My soul has been a sojourner exceedingly long” (ibid., 6)?

My God, my firm support: “No living person will be justified in your sight.” My hope is not in human beings; if you judge anyone after withdrawing your compassion, whom will you find righteous? And unless you anticipate the ungodly with mercy, there will be no one whom you may glorify as godly. For I believe, my salvation, what I have heard: that your kindness leads me to repentance (Rom. 2:4). Tower of strength, honeyed lips have proclaimed: “No one can come to me unless my Father who sent me draws him” (John 6:44). Indeed, because you have instructed me and, in your mercy, formed me through such teaching, with all the marrow of my heart and the full exertion of my mind I invoke you, almighty Father, together with your most beloved Son [Note: The Metz manuscript reads, “your child, and you,” etc.]; and you also, sweetest Offspring, together with the most serene Paraclete. Draw me, so that I may delight to run after you, toward the fragrance of your ointments [Note: More is added here in Anselm and in the Metz manuscript].

## CHAPTER V. How Effective Is the Invocation of the Father through the Son?

I invoke you, my God; I invoke you because you are near to all who invoke you—but to those who invoke you in truth, for you are truth. Teach me, I beg, holy Truth, to invoke your mercy in you; for I do not know how this ought to be done, but I humbly ask to be taught by you, blessed Truth. To have wisdom apart from you is folly; to know you is perfect knowledge. Instruct me, divine Wisdom, and teach me your law. Indeed, I believe that blessed is the person whom you instruct and whom you teach from your law. I desire to invoke you, and I ask that this be done in truth.

What is it to invoke truth in truth except to invoke the Father in the Son? Therefore, holy Father, your word is truth; the beginning of your words is truth. For this is the beginning of your words: “In the beginning was the Word.” In that beginning I adore you as the highest Beginning. In that Word of truth I invoke you, perfect Truth, so that in that same truth you may direct and teach me.

For what is sweeter than to entreat the Begetter in the name of the Only-Begotten, to incline the Father to compassion by remembering the Son, and to soften the king by naming his dearest offspring [Note: Alternatively, “by the designation”]? Thus defendants are accustomed to be snatched from prison; thus those bound in chains are freed; thus those who have received the sentence of death obtain not only life but also extraordinary favor, provided that they make known to angry rulers the love of their beloved offspring. Thus offending servants escape their masters’ punishments when the sweetness of sons intervenes on their behalf.

Thus, almighty Father, I ask you through the love of your almighty Son: “Bring my soul out of prison, that I may confess your name” (Ps. 141:8). By your co-eternal and only-begotten Son I implore you: free me from the bonds of sin; and, being gracious, restore me to life through the intercession of your most precious offspring, seated at your right hand, while my own merits threaten me with a sentence of death.

I know no other intercessor whom I may direct to you except this one, who is “the expiation for our sins” (1 John 2:2), who sits at your right hand and “also intercedes for us” (Rom. 8:34) [Note: The Metz manuscript adds, “whence glory to him and …,” omitting “Behold.”] Behold my advocate with you, God and Father. Behold the high priest who does not need to be cleansed by another’s blood, because he shines, drenched in his own blood. Behold the holy offering, pleasing and perfect, both offered and accepted as a fragrance of sweetness. Behold the spotless lamb, who was silent before those shearing him (Isa. 53:7), who, struck with blows, smeared with spittle, and subjected to insults, did not open his mouth. Behold the one who committed no sin, who bore my sins and healed my sicknesses by his bruising (1 Pet. 2:22, 24).

## CHAPTER VI. The Son’s Passion Is Set Before the Father

Look, gracious Father, upon your most gracious Son, who suffered so impiously for me. Look, most merciful King, upon him who suffers, and kindly remember for whom he suffers. Is this not, my Lord, that innocent one whom you handed over as your Son in order to redeem your servant? Is this not the author of life, who, led like a sheep to slaughter (Isa. 53:7), and obedient to you even unto death (Phil. 2:8), did not fear to undergo the most atrocious kind of death? Remember, disposer of all salvation, that this is the one whom, although you begot him from your own power [Note: Alternatively, “with him”], you nevertheless willed to make a participant in my weakness. Truly this is your divinity, which clothed itself in my nature and ascended the gallows of the cross; which, in the flesh it assumed, endured a grievous punishment.

Bring back, Lord my God, the eyes of your majesty to the work of ineffable compassion. Look upon your beloved Son stretched out with his whole body; see his innocent hands flowing with sacred blood, and, appeased, forgive the crimes committed by my hands. Consider his defenseless side pierced by a cruel spear, and renew me in that sacred font which I believe flowed from it. See his immaculate footprints, which did not stand in the way of sinners (Ps. 1:1) but always walked in your law, fastened with dreadful nails; and perfect my steps in your paths, graciously making me hate every way of iniquity. Mercifully remove from me the way of iniquity, and graciously make me choose the way of truth. I ask you, King of the saints [Note: Alternatively, “King of the ages, through this Redeemer”], through this Holy of Holies, through this Redeemer of mine: make me run along the way of your commandments, so that I may be united in spirit with him who did not shrink from clothing himself in my flesh.

Do you not look, gracious Father, upon the head of your dearest young Son, bowed upon his snow-white neck and released into precious death? Look, gentlest Creator, upon the humanity of your beloved offspring, and have mercy upon the weakness of your frail creature. His bared breast gleams white; his bloodied side is red; his stretched entrails are parched; his beautiful eyes grow faint; his royal face is pale; his tall arms are rigid; his marble-like legs hang down; a stream of blessed blood moistens his feet pierced through.

Look, glorious Begetter, upon the mangled limbs of your most beloved offspring, and kindly remember what my substance is. Behold the punishment of the God-man, and raise up the misery of created humanity. See the Redeemer’s suffering, and forgive the sin of the redeemed. This is he, my Lord, whom you struck because of the sins of your people, although he is the beloved Son in whom you were well pleased (Matt. 3:17). This is that innocent one in whom no deceit was found, and yet he was numbered with the wicked (Isa. 53:9, 12).

## CHAPTER VII. God’s Wonderful Arrangement in Christ’s Passion; How a Human Being May Repay Grace Received from It

What did you do, sweetest child, to be judged in this way? What did you do, most beloved young man, to be treated so harshly [Note: Anselm adds, “so cruelly”]? What was your crime, what your offense? What was the cause of your death, what the occasion of your condemnation? For I am the wound of your pain; I am the guilt of your slaughter. I am the bruise of your passion, the labor of your torment. I am the cause deserving your death, the crime deserving your vengeance.

O marvelous condition of this judgment, ineffable arrangement of this mystery! The wicked sins, and the just is punished; the guilty transgresses, and the innocent is beaten; the ungodly offends, and the godly is condemned. What the evil person deserves, the good person suffers; what the servant commits, the master pays; what the human being does, God endures.

To what depths, Son of God, has your humility descended? To what lengths has your love burned? How far has your compassion proceeded? How greatly has your kindness grown? How far has your love reached? To what extent has your sympathy gone? I acted wickedly, and you are punished; I committed a crime, and you are chastised in retribution; I produced guilt, and you are subjected to torture. I was proud, and you are humbled; I swelled up, and you are diminished; I was disobedient, and you, obedient, pay the penalty for my crime of disobedience. I obeyed gluttony, and you are afflicted by hunger. Desire for the tree carried me toward what was unlawful [Note: Thus the Metz manuscript. In Anselm: “Desire carried me toward the unlawful tree”; or, “Desire carried me toward unlawful ardor.” The printed editions have: “The tree carried me toward unlawful desire.”], while perfect love leads you to the cross. I presumed to take what was forbidden, and you submitted to the instrument of torture. I delight in food, and you labor on the gallows. I enjoy delights, and you are mangled by nails. I taste the sweetness of the fruit, and you taste the bitterness of gall. Eve laughs and rejoices with me; Mary weeps and suffers with you. Behold, King of glory, behold my impiety, and your compassion shines forth. Behold my injustice, and your justice is clear.

What, my King and my God, what shall I repay you for all that you have given me? Nothing can be found in the human heart that could worthily return such rewards. Can human ingenuity devise anything comparable to divine compassion? Nor can any creature undertake a service by which it might justly repay the protection of the Creator.

Yet, Son of God, in this marvelous arrangement of yours there is something through which my frailty may contribute in some measure: if, moved to compunction by your visitation, my mind crucifies its flesh with its vices and desires (Gal. 5:24). And if this is granted by you, it begins already, as it were, to suffer with you, since you too deigned to die for sin. Thus, under your guidance, through an inward victory [Note: Thus the Metz manuscript; the printed editions read, “through [the victory] of the inward man”] it will be armed for an outward triumph, so that, after conquering spiritual persecution, it will not fear being subjected to the material sword for love of you. In this way the smallness of the creature, if it pleases your compassion, will be able, according to its strength, to answer the greatness of the Creator.

This is the heavenly medicine, good Jesus; this is the antidote of your love [Note: “your” is absent from the Metz manuscript]. I ask you, by your ancient mercies, pour into my wounds [Note: Alternatively, “into my inward parts”] what, once the bile of the serpent’s contagion has been rejected, will restore me to my former health. Let the nectar of your sweetness, once tasted, make me utterly despise the seductive prosperity of the world and fear none of its adversities for your sake. Remembering my perpetual nobility, let me always disdain the winds of this passing arrogance.

Let nothing, I beg you, be sweet to me without you; let nothing please me, let nothing seem precious, let nothing beautiful smile upon me apart from you. At your prompting, I beg, let everything become worthless to me and all things be defiled. What is opposed to you, let it be grievous to me; and what pleases you, let it be my unfailing desire. Let me grow weary of rejoicing without you, and let me delight in grieving for you. Let your name be my refreshment and your memory my consolation. Let my tears become my bread (Ps. 41:4) as I seek your ordinances day and night. Let the law of your mouth be good to me above thousands of gold and silver pieces (Ps. 118:72). Let obedience to you be lovable and resistance to you detestable.

I ask you, my hope, by all your powers, to be gracious toward my impieties. Open my ears to your commandments; and, by your holy name, I implore you, do not incline my heart to words of malice, to make excuses for sins. I ask you also, by your marvelous humility, do not let the foot of pride come upon me, nor let the hand of the sinner move me.

## CHAPTER VIII. How Great Is the Confidence of the One Who Prays through the Merit of Christ’s Passion

Behold, almighty God, Father of my Lord, graciously determine how you will have mercy on me, since whatever I found most precious I have devoutly offered, and whatever I found most dear I have humbly presented. I have left nothing for myself without laying it before your majesty; nothing remains that I could add, because I have entrusted my entire hope to you. I have directed to you my advocate, your beloved Son; I have sent your glorious offspring as mediator between me and you. I have sent, I say, an intercessor through whom I trust in forgiveness. I sent in words what I said had been sent for me in deeds [Note: The printed editions have: “I sent the Word in words, whom I said had been sent for my sins in deeds.” We follow the manuscripts]. And I have reckoned to you the death of your most holy offspring, which I believe he endured for me.

I believe that the divinity sent by you assumed my humanity; in it he considered it worthy to endure bonds, blows, spittle, and mockery, and also to receive the cross, nails, and spear. Having once been wearied by the cries of infancy, bound in the clothing of childhood, harassed by the labors of youth, weakened by fasts, afflicted by vigils, and exhausted by journeys, he was afterward scourged, torn by punishments, counted among the dead, and then enriched with the glory of resurrection. He led it into the joys of heaven and placed it at the right hand of your majesty. Behold my appeasement and your propitiation.

Here, graciously, look upon the Son whom you begot and the servant whom you redeemed. Here look upon the Maker, and do not despise his handiwork. Serenely embrace the Shepherd, and mercifully receive the sheep brought back on his own shoulders. This is that most faithful Shepherd who long sought the wandering sheep through the mountain crags and the precipices of the valleys, through many and various labors. When it was already dying and failing after long exile, he rejoiced at finding it, placed himself beneath it, and, with wondrous exertion of love, lifted it from the abyss of confusion. Binding it in loving embraces, he carried back the one that had been lost to the ninety-nine (Luke 15:4–7).

Behold, my Lord and King, almighty God; behold the good Shepherd returns to you what you entrusted to him. By your arrangement he received, in order to save humanity, the one whom he restored to you free from every stain. Behold, your dearest Son reconciles to you your creature, which had wandered far from you. Behold, the gentle Shepherd restores to your flock what the violent robber had carried away. He returns to your presence the servant whom his own conscience had made a fugitive, so that the one who deserved punishment by himself may, through such a benefactor [Col. 0908] [Note: In Anselm, “through the Maker of the world.” The printed editions have “through the action of this one,” etc.; corruptly], deserve forgiveness; and the one for whom Gehenna remained because of his sins [Note: In the Metz manuscript: “the one who hoped for Gehenna because of his sins”], may now, under so great a leader, confidently hope to be recalled to his homeland.

By myself I was able to offend you, holy Father, but by myself I could not appease you. Your beloved Son, my God, became my helper, sharing my humanity in order to heal my weakness. Thus, from the very place where the guilt of offense had arisen, he might offer you a sacrifice of praise; and through this make me acceptable to your compassion, while, seated at your right hand, he continually showed himself to be a sharer in my substance. Behold my hope; behold my entire confidence.

If, because of my iniquity, you despise me as I deserve, at least look upon me in pity because of the love of your beloved offspring. Look upon the Son, so that you may be gracious toward the servant; behold the sacrament of the flesh, and forgive the guilt of the flesh. Whenever the wounds of your blessed offspring are displayed before you, I beg that my crimes may be hidden. Whenever precious blood flows red from his gracious side, I beg that the stain of my pollution may be washed away. And because flesh provoked you to anger, I implore you, let flesh incline you to mercy; so that, if flesh seduced me into guilt, flesh may lead me to forgiveness.

My impiety surely deserves much; but far greater is what the mercy of my Redeemer rightfully claims. Great is my injustice, but the Redeemer’s justice is greater still [Note: Thus the Metz manuscript. The printed editions have “I confess; but it is greater”; in Anselm, “but much greater”]. For just as God is higher than humanity, so my wickedness is lower than his goodness, both in quality and in quantity. What could a human being do wrong that the Son of God, made human, could not redeem? What pride could swell so greatly that such humility could not bring it low? What power of death could exist that the punishment of the Son of God’s cross could not destroy?

Surely, my God, if the sins of the sinful human being and the grace of the redeeming Creator are weighed on equal scales, the distance between them is no greater than that between east and west, or between the lower regions and the highest point of heaven [Note: The Metz manuscript has “surpasses”]. Now, best Creator of light, now forgive my sins for the sake of your beloved Son’s immense labors. Now, I beg, let my impiety be pardoned because of his compassion; my perversity because of his restraint; my ferocity because of his gentleness. May his humility overcome my pride, his patience my impatience, his kindness my harshness, his obedience my disobedience, his tranquility my restlessness, his sweetness my bitterness, his gentleness my anger, and his love redeem my cruelty.

## CHAPTER IX. Invocation of the Holy Spirit

[Note: Prayer 14 in Anselm.]

Now, holy communion of the divine love of the almighty Father and of his most blessed offspring, almighty Paraclete Spirit [Note: The Metz manuscript consistently has “Paraclite”], most merciful consoler of the grieving: now, with powerful force, flow into the innermost chambers of my heart. As a gracious inhabitant, make every dark hiding place of my neglected dwelling glad with the radiance of shining light; and, by visiting it with abundant dew, make fruitful whatever has withered through the long dryness of desolation.

Wound the secret places of the inner person with the arrow of your love; penetrate and kindle the tepid marrow of my liver with saving flames; and, illuminating its depths with the fire of holy fervor, consume everything within my mind and body. Give me to drink from the torrent of your delight, so that I may no longer desire to taste any worldly sweetness, poisoned as it is.

“Judge me, Lord, and distinguish my cause from an unholy nation” (Ps. 42:1). “Teach me to do your will, for you are my God” (Ps. 142:10). I therefore believe that whoever you inhabit, you make a dwelling for the Father and likewise for the Son. Blessed is the person who deserves to have you as a guest, for through you the Father and the Son will make their dwelling with him (John 14:23).

Come now, come, most gracious consoler of the sorrowful soul, helper in times of need and tribulation. Come, cleanser of crimes, healer of wounds. Come, strength of the weak, lifter of those who are falling. Come, teacher of the humble, destroyer of the proud. Come, merciful father of orphans, gentle judge of widows. Come, hope of the poor, refreshment of those who are failing. Come, star of voyagers, harbor of the shipwrecked. Come, singular glory of all the living, only salvation of the dying.

Come, most holy one of spirits; come, and have mercy on me. Make me fit for you, and graciously bend down to me, so that my smallness may please your greatness and my weakness your strength, according to the abundance of your mercies, through Jesus Christ my Savior, who with the Father lives and reigns as God in your unity, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## CHAPTER X. A Prayer of One Who Thinks Humbly of Himself

[Note: Anselm, Prayer 21.]

I know, Lord, I know and confess that I am not worthy for you to love me; but surely you are not unworthy of being loved by me. I am indeed unworthy to serve you, but you are not unworthy of the service of your creature. Therefore, Lord, give me that by which you are worthy; and I shall be worthy of what now makes me unworthy. Make me cease from sins as you will, so that I may serve you as I ought.

Grant me to guard, govern, and complete my life in such a way that I may sleep in peace and rest in you. Grant me, at the end, that sleep may receive me with rest, rest with security, and security in eternity [Note: Alternatively, “so that at the end sleep may receive me”]. Amen.

## CHAPTER XI. Confession of the Trinity

[Note: From the end of the book On the Mirror.]

You, God the unbegotten Father; you, the only-begotten Son; you, the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete: the holy and undivided Trinity we confess, praise, and bless with our whole heart and mouth. To you be glory throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## CHAPTER XII. Contemplation of God’s Perfections

[Note: The first part of John of Fécamp.]

Highest Trinity, one power and undivided majesty, our God, almighty God: I, the least of your servants and a small member of your Church, confess you. [Note: Words of Alcuin, p. 135.] I confess you and honor you with the sacrifice of praise that is your due, for the knowledge and ability that you have deigned to grant to one so insignificant as I. And because I lack external gifts that I might offer, behold, from the gift of your mercy I gladly and joyfully offer you the vows of praise that are within me, from an unfeigned faith and a pure conscience.

Therefore I believe you with my whole heart, Lord, King of heaven and earth, and with my mouth I confess you: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, three in persons and one in substance; the true, almighty God, of one simple, incorporeal, invisible, and uncircumscribed nature [Note: This also occurs in the book On the Mirror, chapter 24]; possessing nothing in yourself that is greater or lower, but perfect in every way without deformity; great without quantity; good without quality; everlasting without time; life without death; strong without weakness; true without falsehood; wholly everywhere without place; present everywhere without position; filling all things without extension; meeting all things everywhere without contraction; transcending all things without movement; remaining within all things without fixed location; creating all things without need; governing all things without labor; giving all things a beginning without having a beginning yourself; making all mutable things without undergoing change yourself.

Infinite in greatness, almighty in power, supreme in goodness, immeasurable in wisdom, terrible in counsels, just in judgments, most hidden in thoughts, truthful in words, holy in works, abundant in mercies; most patient toward transgressors, most tender toward penitents; always the same, eternal and everlasting, immortal and unchangeable [Note: The Metz manuscript and Alcuin have “the same”].

You are neither expanded by spaces nor confined by the narrowness of places; no receptacle constrains you; no will alters you; no necessity corrupts you; sad things disturb you not, nor do joyful things soothe you. Forgetfulness does not take anything from you, nor does memory restore anything to you; past things do not pass away from you, nor do future things arrive. Neither origin gives you a beginning, nor time an increase, nor chance an end. Rather, before the ages, in the ages, and through the ages, you live forever.

To you belong enduring praise and eternal glory, supreme power and singular honor, perpetual kingship and endless rule, throughout infinite, unwearied, immortal ages of ages. Amen.

## CHAPTER XIII. On the Mystery of the Incarnation; In This Mystery We Have Strong Hope

[Note: From part 2 of Alcuin’s Confession, nos. 1 and 5.]

Thus far, almighty Trinity, one God, inspector and searcher of my heart, I have confessed the omnipotence of your majesty and the majesty of your omnipotence. Now, how you deigned to help the human race at the end of the ages, I confess before you with my mouth for salvation, just as I believe it in my heart for righteousness.

You, God the Father, alone are nowhere read of as having been sent. But concerning your Son the Apostle writes: “When the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son” (Gal. 4:4). By saying “he sent,” he clearly shows that the Son came into this world as one sent, when, born from Mary, ever-virgin, he appeared in the flesh as a true and perfect human being [Note: The Metz manuscript omits “blessed”].

But what is the meaning of what that foremost of the Evangelists says about him: “He was in the world, and the world was made through him” (John 1:10)? He was therefore sent there through his humanity where he always was and is through his divinity. I believe with my whole heart and confess with my mouth that this mission was the work of the entire holy Trinity. [Note: This too is from Augustine, Confessions, book 10, chapter 43, no. 69.]

How you loved us, holy and good Father! How greatly you loved us, gracious Creator, that you did not even spare your own Son but handed him over for us ungodly people! He was subject to you unto death, “even death on a cross” (Phil. 2:8), taking the record of our sins and fastening it to the cross (Col. 2:14); he crucified sin and killed death. He alone was “free among the dead” (Ps. 87:6), having the power to lay down his life and to take it up again (John 10:18): for us he was victor and victim, and therefore victor because victim; for us he was priest and sacrifice, and therefore priest because sacrifice.

I rightly have strong hope in him, because you will heal all my illnesses through him who sits at your right hand and intercedes for us (Rom. 8:34). My illnesses, Lord, are great and many; they are many and great. The prince of this world has much in me, I know and confess. But I ask you: free me through our Redeemer who sits at your right hand, in whom he could find nothing of his own [Note: Thus the Metz manuscript. Alternatively, “nothing of his own evil”].

Justify me through him who committed no sin and in whose mouth no deceit was found (1 Pet. 2:22). Through him, our head, in whom there is no stain, free his member, however small and weak. I beg you, free me from my sins, vices, faults, and negligences. Fill me with your holy virtues and make me abound in good conduct. Make me persevere in your holy works to the end, for the sake of your holy name and according to your will.

## CHAPTER XIV. Thanksgiving for the Benefits Granted through This

[Note: See part 2 of Alcuin’s Confession, no. 5.]

I could surely have despaired because of my excessive sins and countless negligences, unless your Word, O God, had become flesh and dwelt among us. But now I dare not despair, because, when we were enemies, we were reconciled through the death of your Son; how much more, now having been saved, shall we be saved from wrath through him?

For all my hope and the certainty of my entire confidence lie in his precious blood, which was poured out for us and for our salvation. In him I breathe again; and, trusting in him, I desire to come to you—not possessing my own righteousness, but that which is in your Son, our Lord Jesus Christ.

[Col. 0911] [Note: [Col. 0911] From Alcuin’s *Confession*, part 4, no. 11.] Hence, most merciful and most kindly lover of mankind, God, who through Jesus Christ your Son, our Lord, powerfully made us when we did not exist, and wondrously restored us when we had been ruined by our own fault, I give thanks to your loving-kindness and render you abundant thanks from the depths of my heart: you who, because of your ineffable love, by which you graciously chose to love us wretched and unworthy ones with wondrous goodness, sent your only-begotten Son [Note: [Col. 0911] See Alcuin, p. 133; and *On the Mirror*, chap. 15.] from your bosom into our common plight, to save us sinners, then sons of wrath and sons of perdition. I give you thanks for his holy incarnation and birth, and for his glorious Mother, from whom he graciously assumed flesh for us and for our salvation, so that, just as he was true God from God, so he might be true man from man.

I give you thanks for his passion and cross, for his death and resurrection, for his ascension into heaven, and for his seat of majesty at your right hand. For on the fortieth day [Note: [Col. 0911] From the Preface for Pentecost.] after his resurrection, ascending above all the heavens in the sight of his disciples (Acts I, 9), and sitting at your right hand, he poured out the Holy Spirit upon the children of adoption according to his promise (ibid. II, 4). [Note: [Col. 0911] From Alcuin’s *Confession*, part 4, no. 11.]

I give you thanks for that most sacred outpouring of his precious blood, by which we have been redeemed; and likewise for the holy and life-giving mystery of his body and blood, by which every day in your Church we are fed and given drink, washed and sanctified, and made participants in the one supreme divinity. I give you thanks for this wondrous and ineffable charity of yours, by which you so loved and saved us unworthy ones through your only and beloved Son. For you so loved the world that you gave your only-begotten Son, so that everyone who believes in him should not perish but have eternal life (John III, 16). And this is eternal life: that we should know you, the true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent (ibid. XVII, 3), through right faith and works worthy of faith.

## CHAPTER XV. The immeasurable charity of God in restoring humanity. That we are incapable of repaying grace. How great a confidence we have because of the man assumed by God.

O immeasurable compassion, O inestimable charity! To free a servant, you handed over your Son. God became man so that ruined humanity might be rescued from the power of demons. How supremely kind a lover of mankind was your Son, our God, whose merciful heart was not satisfied that, having become man, he should humble himself from the true virgin Mary, unless he also underwent the punishment of the cross, shedding his blood for us and for our salvation. The merciful God came; he came because of his compassion and goodness; he came to seek and save what had perished. He sought the lost sheep; he sought it, found it, and carried it back on his shoulders to the folds of the flock (Luke XV, 4–5)—the merciful Lord, and truly a very gentle shepherd.

O charity, O compassion! Who has heard such things? Who would not be astonished at such great depths of mercy? Who would not marvel, who would not rejoice together? Because of your exceedingly great charity, by which you loved us, you sent your Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, so that, on account of sin, he might condemn sin; so that we might become your righteousness in him (Rom. VIII, 3–4). [Note: [Col. 0911] From the Preface for Easter.] For he himself is the true lamb, the spotless lamb, who took away the sins of the world; who by dying destroyed our death, and by rising restored life.

But what can we repay you, our God, for such great benefits of your mercy? What praises, what thanksgivings? Even if we possessed the knowledge and power of the blessed angels, we would still be entirely unable to recompense anything worthy of such compassion and goodness of yours. If all the members of our body were turned into tongues, our smallness would still in no way suffice to render you the praises due to you. [Col. 0912] For your inestimable charity, which you have shown to us unworthy ones solely because of your goodness and compassion, surpasses all knowledge. For your Son, our Lord, did not take hold of angels but of the offspring of Abraham (Hebr. II, 16), being made like us in all things except sin.

Thus assuming a human, not an angelic, nature, and glorifying it with the robe of holy resurrection and immortality, he raised it above all the heavens, above all the choirs of angels, above the Cherubim and Seraphim, placing it at your right hand. The angels praise this; the Dominions adore it; and all the heavenly Powers tremble at the man who is God above them. This, indeed, is my entire hope and all my confidence. For in Jesus Christ our Lord there is a portion of each one of us: flesh and blood. Where, therefore, my portion reigns, there I believe that I shall reign. Where my flesh is glorified, there I know that I shall be glorious. Where my blood rules, there I feel that I shall rule. Although I am a sinner, I do not despair of this communion of grace. And if my sins [Note: [Col. 0912] The manuscript of Mettensis here and shortly afterward has *me*, “me,” instead of *mea*, “my.”] hinder me, my substance claims me. And if my offenses exclude me, the communion of nature does not reject me. For the Lord is not so harsh as to forget humanity and not remember the one whom he himself bears; so that he would not seek, for my sake, the one whom he assumed for my sake. Certainly the Lord our God is gentle and exceedingly kind, and he loves his own flesh, his own members, his own inward parts, in that most sweet, kind, and merciful God and Lord of ours, Jesus Christ: in whom we have already risen, in whom we have already ascended the heavens, and in whom we already sit in heavenly places.

Our flesh loves us; and in him we possess the privilege of our blood. We are his members and his flesh. Finally, he is our head, from whom the whole body comes, as it is written: “Bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh”; and, “The two shall be one flesh” (Gen. II, 23–24); and, “No one has ever hated his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it.” “This mystery is great: I speak,” says the Apostle, “with reference to Christ and the Church” (Eph. V, 29, 32).

## CHAPTER XVI. Thanksgiving is rendered for this. That there are two natures and one person in Christ. Petition in view of this mystery.

[Note: [Col. 0912] From Alcuin’s *Confession*, part 2, nos. 11–12.] Therefore I give you thanks with lips and heart and with every power I possess, Lord our God of infinite mercy, for all your compassions, by which you graciously chose wondrously to aid us, who had been ruined, through that same Son of yours, our Savior and Restorer, who died for our sins and rose for our justification (Rom. IV, 25); and now, living without end, sits at your right hand and intercedes for us (ibid. VIII, 34), and together with you has compassion, because he is God from you, the Father, coeternal and consubstantial with you in all things, and therefore able to save us forever.

But according to that by which he is man, in which respect he is less than you, all authority in heaven and on earth was given to him by you (Matt. XXVIII, 18), so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth, and every tongue should confess that the Lord Jesus is in your glory (Phil. II, 10–11), God the almighty Father. He has indeed been appointed by you as judge of the living and the dead. You, however, judge no one, but have given all judgment to your Son (John V, 22), in whose breast all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden (Col. II, 3).

He is both witness and judge—judge and witness (Jer. XXIX, 23)—whom no sinful conscience will be able to escape; for all things are naked and open to his eyes (Hebr. IV, 13). He who was unjustly judged will indeed judge the world with equity and the peoples with justice (Ps. XCV, 13). Therefore I bless your holy name and glorify you with all my heart, almighty and merciful Lord, for that wondrous and ineffable union of divinity [Col. 0913] and humanity in the unity of one person: so that there would not be one God and another man, but one and the same God and man, man and God.

But although by wondrous condescension the Word became flesh, neither of the two natures was thereby changed into the substance of the other. A fourth person was not added to the mystery of the Trinity. The substance of the Word and of man was united, not confused, so that what had been assumed from us might reach God, while that which had never not been remained what it had always been. O wondrous mystery! O ineffable exchange! O the wondrous and ever-marvelous kindness of divine reconciliation! We were not worthy to be servants, and behold, we have been made sons of God—indeed, heirs of God and coheirs with Christ (Rom. VIII, 17). From where has this come to us, and what are we in relation to such things?

But I ask you, most merciful Father God, by this your inestimable compassion, goodness, and charity, to make us worthy of the many and great promises of that same Son of yours, our Lord Jesus Christ. Command your power, and confirm what you have wrought in us (Ps. LXVII, 29). Perfect what you have begun, so that we may deserve to reach the fullness of your gracious compassion. Grant that through the Holy Spirit we may understand, merit, and always venerate with the honor due to it this great mystery of piety, which was manifested in the flesh, justified in the Spirit, appeared to angels, proclaimed among the nations, believed in the world, and taken up in glory (I Tim. III, 16).

## CHAPTER XVII. What we owe to God. That we serve him from what belongs to him. Petition for further gifts on the basis of those already bestowed.

O how greatly we are indebted to you, Lord our God, redeemed at so great a price, saved by so great a gift, and aided by so glorious a benefit! How greatly must we wretched people fear and love, bless and praise, honor and glorify him who loved us so, saved us so, sanctified us so, and exalted us so! To you, indeed, we owe everything we can do, everything we know, everything by which we live. And who has anything that is not yours? You, Lord our God, from whom all good things proceed, for your sake and for the sake of your holy name, give us from your goods, so that from your gifts and bestowals we may serve you, please you in truth, and render you each day the praises due to you for such benefits of your mercy. For we cannot serve or please you from any other source than your gift. Every good bestowal and every perfect gift is from above, descending from you, the Father of lights, with whom there is no change or shifting shadow (James I, 17).

Lord our God, compassionate God, good God, almighty God, [Note: [Col. 0913] Words from Alcuin’s *Confession*, part 2, no. 6, and part 4, no. 12; also Alcuin, p. 133e.] ineffable God of uncircumscribed nature, creator of all things, and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who sent that same beloved Son of yours, our most sweet Lord, from your bosom into our common plight to take up our life, so that he might give us his, and might be perfect God from you the Father and perfect man from his mother—wholly God and wholly man, one and the same Christ, eternal and temporal, immortal and subject to death, creator and created, strong and weak, victor and vanquished, [Note: [Col. 0913] Neither the Mettensis manuscript nor Alcuin has “victor and vanquished.”] nourisher and nourished, shepherd and sheep, temporally dead and living with you forever—he gave those who love him the citizenship of life as he promised, and said to us: “Whatever you ask the Father in my name, he will give you” (John XV, 16).

Through that supreme priest, true pontiff, and good shepherd, who offered himself to you as a sacrifice, laying down his life for his flock, I ask you; through him who sits at your right hand and intercedes for us, our Redeemer and Advocate, I beseech your compassion and goodness, most merciful, most loving, and most kind lover of mankind, God, [Note: [Col. 0913] From Alcuin’s *Confession*, part 2, no. 7.] to grant me, together with that same Son of yours and [Col. 0914] your Holy Spirit, to bless and glorify you in all things, with great contrition of heart and a fountain of tears, with great reverence and trembling; for where there is one substance, there is also one gift.

But since the body that is corrupted weighs down the soul (Wis. IX, 15), stir up, I ask, my sluggishness with your goads, and make me persevere vigorously day and night in your commandments and praises. Grant that my heart may grow warm within me, and that in my meditation the fire may burn (Ps. XXXVIII, 4). [Note: [Col. 0914] Alcuin, p. 134; and *Confession*, part 2, no. 10.]

And because your only-begotten Son himself said, “No one comes to me unless the Father who sent me draws him”; and, “No one comes to the Father except through me” (John VI, 44; XIV, 6), I beg and humbly entreat you: draw me ever toward him, and may he at last lead me to you, there where he sits at your right hand; where life is eternal and eternally blessed; where love is perfect and there is no fear; where there is eternal day and one spirit among all; where there is supreme and certain security, secure tranquility, tranquil delight, delightful happiness, happy eternity, eternal blessedness, and the blessed vision and praise of you without end; where you, with him, and he, with you, live and reign eternally and forever in the communion of the Holy Spirit, God, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## CHAPTER XVIII. Prayer to Christ. What he is to us. The necessity of cleaving to him through love. Love of Christ is kindled by remembrance of the house of God.

[Note: [Col. 0914] From John of Fécamp, part 2.]

My hope, Christ God, sweet lover of mankind,

Light, way, life, salvation, peace, and every honor of your own,

All these things you were willing to endure for the salvation of your own:

Flesh, bonds, cross, wound, death, and tomb;

Then, after three days, rising again, death defeated,

Appearing to the disciples and restoring their wavering hearts,

On the fortieth day you sought the heights of heaven:

You live forever, now and throughout the ages reigning.

[Note: [Col. 0914] Alcuin, p. 293b; p. 138d.]

You are my living and true God, my holy Father, my compassionate Lord, my great King, my good Shepherd, my one Teacher, my timely Helper, my most beautiful Beloved, my living Bread; my priest forever, my guide to the homeland, my true light, my holy sweetness, my straight way, my splendid wisdom, my pure simplicity, my peace-bringing harmony, my safe protection, my good portion, my everlasting salvation, my great mercy, my most steadfast patience, my spotless victim, my holy redemption, my future hope [Note: [Col. 0914] Elsewhere, “firm hope.”], my perfect charity, my holy resurrection, my eternal life, my exultation and most blessed vision, destined to endure without end.

I beseech, implore, and ask you that through you I may walk, reach you, and rest in you, who are the way, the truth, and the life (John XIV, 6), without whom no one comes to the Father. For you are the Lord whom I desire, most sweet and most beautiful.

O splendor of the Father’s glory, who sits above the Cherubim and gazes upon the abyss, true light, light that illuminates, unfailing light, into which the angels long to look (I Pet. I, 12), behold, my heart is before you; scatter its darkness, so that it may be more fully flooded with the brightness of your love. [Note: [Col. 0914] Augustine, *Confessions* XIII, 8, 3, 9.]

Give me yourself, my God; restore yourself to me. Behold, I love you; and if that is too little, let me love you more strongly. I cannot measure, so as to know how much of your love is lacking in me for what is sufficient—that my life may run into your embraces and not turn away until it is hidden in the secret place of your face. This alone I know: that apart from you, Lord, all is evil for me, not only outside me but within me; and every abundance that is not my God is poverty for me.

For you alone are the good that cannot be changed either for the better or for the worse, because you alone simply are; for you there is not one thing to live and another to live blessedly, since your blessedness is yourself. But your creature, for whom living and living blessedly are different things, owes everything that lives and everything that lives blessedly to your grace alone. Therefore we need you, not you us; for if we did not exist at all, nothing would be lacking to you for the good that you are.

Therefore we must always cleave to you, our Lord, so that through the continual help of your grace we may be able to live holily, devoutly, and rightly. Indeed, by the weight of our frailty we are dragged downward; but by your gift we are kindled and carried upward. We burn, and we go; we ascend the ascents in our heart, and sing the Song of Ascents. By your fire, your good fire, we burn, and we go. Where do we now go upward? To the peace of Jerusalem; “because I rejoiced at the things that were said to me: We shall go into the house of the Lord” (Ps. CXXI, 1). There a good will has placed us, so that we desire nothing other than to remain there forever.

But since, while we are in the body, we are absent from you (II Cor. V, 6), Lord, and here we have no lasting city but seek the one that is to come (Hebr. XIII, 14), while our citizenship is in heaven, therefore, guided by your grace, [Note: [Col. 0915] Augustine, *Confessions* XII, 16.] I enter the chamber of my heart and sing love-songs to you, my King and my God, groaning with inexpressible groanings in the place of my pilgrimage (Ps. CXVIII, 54), where your ordinances have become songs for me.

And remembering Jerusalem, with my heart stretched upward toward her—Jerusalem my homeland, Jerusalem my mother—and you reigning above her, illuminating her, her father, guardian, patron, ruler, shepherd, chaste and powerful delights, solid joy, and all ineffable goods, all together, because they are one supreme and true good, I shall not turn away until you gather into the peace of that dearest mother, where the first fruits of my spirit are, all that I am from this dispersion and deformity, and conform and establish me forever, my God, my mercy.

## CHAPTER XIX. The house of God, created wisdom. Its distinction from uncreated wisdom. How there is no time in it. How it is the heaven of heaven. God’s eternity.

[Note: [Col. 0915] The same book, chap. 15, nos. 19–21.] This is your house, God—not earthly, nor any bodily mass of heaven, but spiritual and sharing in your eternity, because it remains without stain forever. You established it for ever and ever; you gave a command, and it shall not pass away (Ps. CXLVIII, 6). Yet it is not coeternal with you, God, because it was not without a beginning; for created wisdom was created before all things (Ecclus. I, 4).

This is not that Wisdom, plainly coeternal and equal with God the Father, through whom all things were created, and in which Beginning heaven and earth were made (Gen. I, 1). Rather, it is the wisdom that was created: a spiritual nature, namely, which through contemplation of the light is itself light. It too is called wisdom, although created. But as much as light that illuminates differs from light that is illuminated, so much does you, supreme Wisdom who creates, differ from this wisdom that was created; just as the justifying righteousness—which you, our God, are—differs from the righteousness that has been made through justification.

For we too are called “the righteousness of God the Father in his Son, our Lord” (II Cor. V, 21), as the Apostle testifies. Therefore, since a certain created wisdom was created before all things (Ecclus. I, 4)—the rational and intellectual mind of your chaste city, our mother, which is above and free (Gal. IV, 26), and eternal in the heavens—which heavens could these be except those that praise you, the heaven of heavens? For this too is “the heaven of heaven for the Lord” (Ps. CXIII, 16).

Although we do not find time before it, since it precedes the creature of time and was created before all things, yet before it you exist, eternal God, creator of all things, from whom it received the beginning of its existence—not in time, since time did not yet exist, but in the order of its creation. Thus it is from you, our God, while plainly being something other than you.

Although we find no time either before it or within it—for it is able always to behold your face and never turns away from it, with the result that it is changed by no alteration—there is nevertheless within it that mutability by which it would grow dark and cold unless, cleaving to you with great love, it shone and burned from you as an everlasting noon. [Note: [Col. 0916] Thus Augustine and the Mettensis manuscript; the printed editions have “above noon.”] Finally, it cleaves to you, the true and truly eternal God, with such chaste love that, although it is not coeternal with you, it nevertheless neither dissolves nor flows away from you amid the changes and vicissitudes of any time, but rests in the truest contemplation of you alone. For you, God, show yourself to the one who loves you as much as you command, and you are enough for it. Therefore it does not turn away from you or from itself, but always remains in the same state, continually seeing you and unfailingly loving you, the true light and chaste love.

O blessed and exalted creature, greatest among creatures, [Note: [Col. 0916] Augustine, *Confessions* XII, 11, nos. 12–13.] blessed because it always clings to your blessedness! Happy—indeed, exceedingly happy—is this creature, with you as its eternal indweller and illuminator. Nor do I find anything I would more gladly call “the heaven of heaven for the Lord” than your house, contemplating your delight without falling away [Note: [Col. 0916] In the printed editions, a gloss had crept in: “and without affection.”] into something else; a pure mind, most harmoniously one, the foundation of peace for blessed spirits, in the heavenly places above these heavens.

From this let the soul whose pilgrimage has become long understand whether it now thirsts for you, whether its tears have already become its bread (Ps. XLI, 4), whether it now asks for one thing and seeks this alone: to dwell in your house all the days of its life (Ps. XXVI, 4). (And what is its life except you? And what are your days except your eternity, like your years, which do not fail? [Ps. CI, 28].)

From this, then, let the soul that can understand realize how far beyond all times you are eternal, when your house—which has not been on pilgrimage, although it is not coeternal with you—nevertheless, by clinging to you without interruption or failure, suffers no change of times; and, continually drinking in you with most steadfast purity, never and nowhere displays its mutability [Note: [Col. 0916] Elsewhere, “immutability.” And shortly afterward, “has gone forth from you.”]. With you present to it, to whom it holds fast with its whole affection, it has no future to await, nor does it transfer anything into the past for remembrance; it is altered by no succession and extends itself into no times.

## CHAPTER XX. Aspiration toward the house of God, and that it should pray for us.

[Note: [Col. 0916] From the same book XII, chap. 15, no. 21.]

O luminous and beautiful house, I have loved your beauty and the dwelling-place of the glory of my Lord, your creator and possessor. May my pilgrimage sigh for you; may my heart, night and day, long intensely for you; may my mind be directed toward you; may my soul desire to reach fellowship in your blessedness. I speak to the one who made you, asking that he may possess me in you, since he made me also.

Rather, you speak; you ask that he make me worthy to share in your glory. For I do not seek your holy fellowship and wondrous beauty by merit, but I do not despair of attaining them through the blood by which I was redeemed. May your merits assist me; may your holy, most devout, and pure prayers aid my perversity—prayers that can in no way be ineffective before God.

I have gone astray, I confess, like a lost sheep (Ps. CXVIII, 176), and my sojourn has been prolonged (Ps. CXIX, 5); and I have been cast far from the face of the Lord my God into this blindness of exile. There, expelled from the joys of paradise, I daily lament with myself over the miseries of my captivity, singing a mournful song and uttering great lamentations, while I remember you, mother Jerusalem; while I set my feet in your courts, holy and beautiful Zion, still unable openly to behold your inner places.

But I hope to be carried back to you on the shoulders of my shepherd, your builder, so that I may rejoice in you with him in that ineffable joy with which those who are with you rejoice before our God and Savior, who abolished hostilities in his flesh and made peace between all things in heaven and all things on earth through his blood. For he is our peace, who made both one (Eph. II, 14); joining together in himself the two who came from opposite sides, he promised that he would give himself to us likewise and in the same measure in the abiding happiness of your blessedness, saying: “They will be equal to the angels of God in heaven” (Matt. XXII, 30).

O Jerusalem, eternal house of God, after the love of Christ [Note: [Col. 0917] The words “after the love of Christ” are absent from the manuscripts.], be our joy and consolation; may the sweet memory of your blessed name be the lifting of our grief and weariness.

## CHAPTER XXI. The misery and weariness of this life.

For I am greatly wearied, Lord, with this life and this sorrowful pilgrimage. This life is a wretched life, a fleeting life, an uncertain life, a laborious life, an unclean life, the mistress of evils, the queen of the proud, full of miseries and errors. It should not be called life but death, in which at every moment we die through various failures of mutability, by different kinds of death.

Can we call what we live in this world life? [Note: [Col. 0917] From *On the Mirror*, chap. 30.] Its humors swell, pains wear it down, fevers dry it out, airs make it sick, foods inflate it, fasts weaken it, amusements dissolve it, sorrows consume it, anxiety constricts it, security dulls it, riches inflate it, poverty casts it down, youth exalts it, old age bends it, weakness breaks it, and grief depresses it.

And furious death follows upon all these evils, and at the same time brings such an end to all the joys of this most wretched life that, when they have ceased to be, they are thought never to have been. This life-giving death and mortal life, although it is sprinkled with these and other bitterness, alas, captures very many by its allurements and deceives how many by its false promises!

And although it is in itself so false and bitter that it cannot remain hidden even from its blind lovers, nevertheless, with the golden cup that it holds in its hand, it gives drink to and utterly intoxicates an infinite multitude of fools. Happy are those—and they themselves are few—who avoid its familiarity, despise its superficial joys, and reject its companionship, lest one day they be compelled to perish with the perishing deceiver.

## CHAPTER XXII. The happiness of eternal life and desire for it.

O you life whom God has prepared for those who love him, vital life, blessed life, secure life, tranquil life, beautiful life, pure life, chaste life, holy life, life ignorant of death, unaware of sorrow, life without stain, without corruption, without pain, without anxiety, without disturbance, without variation or change, life filled with every elegance and dignity; where there is no adversary or attacker, where there is no enticement to sin, [Note: [Col. 0917] Alcuin, p. 134d.] where love is perfect and there is no fear, where there is eternal day and one spirit among all, where God is seen face to face and the mind is fed without failing on the food of this life!

I delight to direct my attention to your brightness; I rejoice to consider your goods with eager heart, as much as I can, within myself. For I languish with love for you, burn intensely with desire for you, and take great delight in your sweet memory. I delight, then, to raise the eyes of my heart toward you, to lift up the posture of my mind, and to conform the affection of my soul.

Indeed, I delight to speak of you, to hear of you, to write of you, to converse about you, to read every day of your blessedness and glory, and to turn what I have read over repeatedly beneath my heart. Thus, at least in this way, may I pass from the heat, dangers, and labors of this mortal and perishing life into the sweet coolness of your life-giving breeze; and, having passed over, may I recline my weary head in your bosom, there to sleep, if only for a little while.

For this reason I enter the pleasant meadows of the holy Scriptures. By writing I pluck the greenest grasses of their sentences; by reading I eat them; by frequent practice I ruminate them; and at last, gathering them together, I store them in the lofty seat of memory. In this way, having tasted your sweetness, may I feel less keenly the bitterness of this most wretched life.

O most happy life, O truly blessed kingdom, [Note: [Col. 0917] From *On the Mirror*, chap. 30.] lacking death and free from an end, to which no times succeed throughout the ages; where continuous day without night knows no time; where the victorious soldier, joined to the hymn-singing choirs of angels, sings to God without ceasing the song of the songs of Zion,

with a noble crown perpetually embracing his head.

Would that, once pardon for my sins had been granted and this burden of flesh laid down, I might enter your joys to possess true rest; would that, would that I might enter the splendid and spacious walls of your city, destined to receive the crown of life from the hand of the Lord; so that [Note: [Col. 0918] From Gregory, homily 37 on the Gospel.] I might stand among those most holy choirs; so that I might stand with the blessed spirits in the presence of the glory of the Creator; so that I might behold the face of Christ present; so that I might always gaze upon that supreme, ineffable, and uncircumscribed light; and thus, affected by no fear of death, but rejoicing forever in the gift of perpetual incorruption [Note: [Col. 0918] The Mettensis manuscript has “rejoicing in the perpetual incorruption of glory.”], might live without end!

## CHAPTER XXIII. The happiness of the saints who depart from this life.

Happy the soul that, released from its earthly prison, freely seeks heaven! It is secure and tranquil; it fears neither enemy nor death. For it always has present, and continually beholds, the most beautiful Lord whom it served and loved, and to whom at last it has happily and gloriously come. No day will diminish the glory of such great blessedness; no wicked person will be able to take it away.

The daughters saw her and proclaimed her most blessed; queens and concubines praised her (Song VI, 8), saying: “Who is this who comes up from the wilderness, overflowing with delights, leaning upon her beloved?” (ibid. VIII, 5). “Who is this who advances like the rising dawn, beautiful as the moon, chosen as the sun, terrible as an army drawn up in battle array?” (ibid. VI, 9).

How joyfully she departs, how swiftly she runs [Note: [Col. 0918] Erasmus, Lyon, Venice, and Louvain: “she hastens, runs.” M.], when with astonished ears she hears her beloved saying to her: “Arise, my beloved [Note: [Col. 0918] Erasmus, Lyon, Venice, and Louvain: “Arise, hasten, my beloved.” M.], my beautiful one, and come; for winter has now passed, the rain has gone and departed, the flowers have appeared, the season of pruning has arrived. The voice of the turtledove has been heard in our land; the fig tree has put forth its green figs, and the flowering vines have given their fragrance. Arise, hasten, my beloved, my beautiful one, my dove in the clefts of the rock, in the hiding-place of the wall; show me your face; let your voice sound in my ears. For your voice is sweet, and your face is beautiful” (ibid. II, 10–14).

Come, my chosen one, my beautiful one, my dove, my spotless one, my bride. Come, and I will set my throne in you, because I have desired your beauty. Come, so that you may rejoice in my presence with my angels, whose fellowship I have promised you. Come, after many dangers and labors, enter into the joy of your Lord, which no one will take from you.

## CHAPTER XXIV. Invocation of the saints.

[Note: [Col. 0918] From *On the Mirror*, chap. 29.] Blessed are all the saints of God, who have already crossed the sea of this mortality and have deserved to reach the harbor of perpetual rest, security, and peace. You are secure and tranquil, and always joyful and glad.

I beseech you by the mother Charity: secure for yourselves, be concerned for us; secure in your unfading glory, be concerned for our manifold misery. By him who chose you, who made you such, whose beauty now satisfies you, whose immortality has made you immortal, whose most blessed vision continually gives you joy, I ask you: remember us constantly. Help us wretched ones, who are still tossed amid the storms surrounding us on the sea of this life.

You most beautiful gates, who have risen to great height, help us, the vile pavement lying far below. Give your hand and raise to their feet those who lie fallen, so that, recovering from weakness, we may become strong in battle. Intercede and pray constantly and without ceasing for us, wretched and exceedingly negligent sinners, so that through your [Col. 0919] prayers we may be joined to your holy fellowship; for otherwise we cannot be saved.

For we are exceedingly frail little men, possessing no virtue: animals enslaved to belly and flesh, in whom scarcely any trace of goodness appears. Yet we are placed under the confession of Christ and carried by the wood of the cross, sailing across this great and spacious sea, where there are reptiles without number, where there are small animals together with great ones (Ps. CV, 25), where there is a most savage dragon, always ready to devour, where there are dangerous places—Scylla and Charybdis—and countless others in which the unwary and those uncertain in faith suffer shipwreck.

Pray to God, pray, most holy ones; pray, all ranks of the saints and every assembly of the blessed, so that, aided by your prayers and merits, [Note: [Col. 0919] See *On the Mirror*, chap. 30.] we may deserve to reach, with the ship safe and the cargo intact, the harbor of perpetual rest, continual peace, and security that will never end.

## CHAPTER XXV. Ardent desire for heaven. The glory and joys of heaven.

Mother Jerusalem, holy city of God, dearest bride of Christ, my heart loves you, my mind greatly desires your beauty. How beautiful, how glorious, how noble you are! You are altogether beautiful, and there is no blemish in you. Rejoice and be glad, beautiful daughter of the prince, because the king desired your beauty and loved your loveliness, being more beautiful in form than the sons of men. But what is your beloved like among the beloved, O most beautiful one? Your beloved [Note: [Col. 0919] Erasmus, Lyons, Venice, and Louvain, here and shortly below: “My beloved.” M.] is white and ruddy, chosen out of thousands (Song 5:9–10). As an apple tree among the trees of the forest, so is your beloved among the sons. Beneath his shade, whom I desired, behold, I sit in joy; and his fruit is sweet to my throat (ibid. 2:3). Your beloved put his hand through the opening, and my belly trembled at his touch (ibid. 5:4). On my bed by night I sought your beloved [Note: Erasmus, Lyons, Venice, and Louvain: “I sought him whom my soul loves.” M.], I sought him and found him (ibid. 3:1); I hold him and will not let him go until he brings me into your house and into your chamber [Note: Erasmus, Lyons, Venice, and Louvain: “into his house and into his chamber.” M.], my glorious mother. For there you will give me your sweetest breasts (ibid. 7:12) more abundantly and perfectly, and you will satisfy me with wondrous fullness, so that I shall never hunger or thirst. Happy is my soul, and happy forever through the ages, if I shall have deserved to gaze upon your glory, your blessedness, your beauty, your gates and walls, your streets, your many dwellings, your most noble citizens, and your strongest king, our Lord, in his beauty.

For your walls are made of precious stones, your gates of the finest pearls, and your streets of purest gold; in them a joyful alleluia is sung without interruption. Your many dwellings are founded on squared stones, built of sapphires, and covered with golden bricks; no unclean person enters them, no polluted person dwells there. You have been made beautiful and sweet in your delights, mother Jerusalem. Nothing in you is like what we suffer here or what we see in this wretched life. There are no darknesses in you, nor night, nor any variation of times. The light of a lamp does not shine in you, nor the radiance of the moon, nor the beams of the stars; rather, God from God, light from light, the sun of righteousness, always illuminates you. The white and spotless Lamb, radiant and most beautiful, is your light [Note: [Col. 0919] Erasmus, Lyons, Venice, and Louvain present the passage thus: “The white and spotless Lamb is your radiant and most beautiful light.” M.]. Your sun, your brightness, and all your good is the unfailing contemplation of this most beautiful King. The King of kings himself is in your midst, and his children around him [Note: So the book *On the Mirror*, chapter 30, following Gregory]. There are the singing choirs of angels; there is the fellowship of the heavenly citizens. There is the sweet solemnity of all who return from this sorrowful pilgrimage to your joys. There is the prophetic choir, wise in foreknowledge; there is the twelvefold number of the Apostles as judges [Note: Elsewhere, “the twelvefold judge.”]; there is the victorious army of countless martyrs [Col. 0920]; there is the sacred assembly of holy confessors; there are true and perfect monks; there are holy women who have overcome the pleasures of the world and the weakness of their sex; there are boys and girls who have surpassed their years in character. There are all the sheep and lambs who have already escaped the snares of this pleasure. All rejoice in their own dwellings. The glory of each is different, but the joy of all is common. There perfect and complete charity reigns, because God is all in all (1 Cor. 15:28); they see him without end, and by always seeing him they burn with love for him. They love and praise; they praise and love. Their whole work is the praise of God, without failure and without labor.

Happy am I, and truly happy forever, if, after the dissolution of this little body, I shall have deserved to hear those songs of heavenly melody which are sung to the praise of the eternal King by the citizens of that heavenly homeland and by the hosts of blessed spirits. Exceedingly fortunate and blessed am I if I myself shall have deserved to sing them, to stand before my king, my God, my leader [Note: Manuscript of Metz: “my sweet one.”], and to behold him in his glory, just as he himself deigned to promise when he said, “Father, I will that those whom you have given me be with me, so that they may see my glory which I had with you before the foundation of the world” (John 17:24); and elsewhere, “Whoever serves me, let him follow me; and where I am, there my servant will be also” (ibid. 12:26); and again, “Whoever loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and manifest myself to him” (ibid. 14:21).

## CHAPTER XXVI. A Rhythm on the Glory of Paradise

[Note: This hymn is missing from the manuscripts of Metz and the Royal manuscript. It is by Peter Damian, vol. 4, p. 226.]

To the fountain of everlasting life  
my parched mind thirsts;

the soul seeks at once to break  
the enclosed barriers of the flesh;

as an exile it burns, longs, and struggles  
to enjoy its homeland,

while it laments that it is subject  
to pressures and hardships,

and contemplates the glory  
it lost when it sinned.

For the memory of the lost good  
increases the present evil.

Who could express how great  
is the joy of supreme peace?

There buildings rise  
with living pearls;

lofty roofs gleam with gold,  
banquet halls shine,

this structure is joined  
with precious gems of the sun,

and the city’s road is paved  
with pure gold, like glass.

No mud is present, no filth remains;  
no disease is seen.

There raging winter  
and scorching summer never prevail.

A purple flower of roses [Note: In B., “everlasting.” We corrected it on the authority of Peter Damian, to whom this hymn belongs. M.]  
maintains perpetual spring;

the lily shines white, the crocus glows red,  
and balsam exudes its fragrance;

meadows are green, fields are ever in bloom,  
and streams of honey flow;

the scent of perfumes breathes forth,  
with liquid fragrances;

the fruits of flowering groves hang there,  
never to fall.

The moon does not alternate its phases,  
nor the sun, nor the courses of the stars:

the Lamb is the unfailing light  
of the blessed city.

Night and time are absent from it;  
it bears continuous day;

for every saint shines like a brilliant sun,

and, crowned after triumph,  
they rejoice together in mutual jubilation,

and, now secure, count the battles  
of the prostrate enemy.

Purified from every stain,  
they know nothing of the wars of the flesh.

The flesh, made spiritual,  
and the mind perceive one thing.

Enjoying abundant peace,  
they suffer no scandals.

Stripped of mutability,  
they return to their origin,

and contemplate the present vision  
of truth:

from it they draw  
the sweetness of the living fountain.

Thence they receive forever  
the same state of being [Note: Elsewhere, “going forth”; and shortly afterward, “they fall through accidents.”],

bright, lively, joyful,  
exposed to no accidents.

Diseases are absent from the always healthy;  
old age from the young.

Thus they possess everlasting being,  
for passing away has passed away.

Thence they are green, strong, and flowering;  
corruption has fallen,

and the strength of immortality  
has swallowed the power of death.

Those who know all things with knowledge  
cannot be ignorant of anything [Note: In all printed editions except the GG edition, this verse ends with a question mark; corruptly. M.].

For they also penetrate  
one another’s secrets;

they will one thing and reject one thing;  
there is unity of minds.

Although each person’s merit  
may differ according to his labor,

this charity makes what one loves  
in another his own [Note: Elsewhere, “while loving another.”].

Thus what belongs to individuals  
becomes common to all.

Where the body is,  
there the eagles are rightly gathered.

[Col. 0921] There, with the angels,  
holy souls are refreshed [Note: In B., “There, with the angels, the holy souls are refreshed.” We have followed Erasmus, Lyons, Venice, and Louvain. M.];

the citizens of both homelands  
live by one bread.

Hungry, yet always full,  
they desire what they possess.

Satiety causes no distaste,  
nor does hunger torment them;

always yearning, they eat,  
and eating, they yearn.

The melodious voice resounds  
with ever-new harmonies.

The organs, extended in jubilation,  
charm the ears,

and give worthy praises  
to the king through whom they are victorious.

Happy is the soul  
that sees the present king of heaven,

and beneath his high throne  
watches the world’s mechanism revolve:

the sun, the moon,  
and the spherical stars with the planets.

Christ, crown of warriors,  
bring me into this commonwealth,

once my military belt has been removed;

make me a sharer in the gift  
of the blessed citizens;

grant strength to one laboring  
in unending battle,

so that after the girding  
you may grant me deserved rest,

and I may deserve to possess you  
as my reward without end. Amen.

## CHAPTER XXVII. To Celebrate the Praises of God with the Blessed. The Glory of the Blessed Is Incomprehensible to Us. The Soul’s Amazement and Insight. To Fly Away from Created Things into God. The Uncreated Light

[Note: John of Fécamp, part 3.]

Bless the Lord, my soul, and all that is within me bless his holy name. Bless the Lord, my soul, and do not forget all his recompenses. Bless the Lord, all his works; in every place of his dominion, bless the Lord, my soul. Let us praise the Lord, whom the angels praise, whom the Dominions adore, before whom the Powers tremble, and to whom the Cherubim and Seraphim proclaim with unceasing voice, “Holy, holy, holy.” Let us join our voices to the voices of the holy angels, and praise together the common Lord according to our capacity. For they praise the Lord most purely and without ceasing [Note: Manuscript of Metz: “blamelessly.” Reims: “without ceasing.” M.], because they always cling to the contemplation of God, not through a mirror and in a riddle, but face to face.

But who could be sufficient to say or think [Note: [Col. 0921] From Gregory the Great, Homily 8 on Ezekiel.] what that innumerable multitude of blessed spirits and heavenly Powers is like in the presence of the omnipotent Lord; what endless festival of the vision of God exists among them; what joy without failure; what ardor of love—not tormenting but delighting; what desire for the vision of God together with satisfaction, and what satisfaction together with desire, in which neither desire produces pain nor satisfaction breeds disgust; how, by clinging to supreme blessedness, they are blessed; how, joined to the true light, they have become light; how, always gazing upon the immutable Trinity, they have been changed into immutability?

But when shall we be able to comprehend the height of that angelic dignity, when we cannot investigate even the nature of our own soul? [Note: From the cited passage of Gregory. See the book *On Spirit and Soul*, chapter 56.] What is this soul like, which can give life to the flesh but cannot restrain itself in holy thoughts as it wishes? What is it like—so strong, yet so weak; so small, yet so great—which searches out secrets [Note: The printed editions have “the secrets of God.”] and contemplates heavenly things, and is shown by its discerning intelligence to have discovered skill in many arts for human advantage?
