What, then, is this soul like, which knows so much about other things and is utterly ignorant of how it was made? For although some people put forward various uncertainties about its origin, we nevertheless find that it is an intellectual spirit made by the Creator’s power, living immortally according to its mode, giving life to the mortal body it supports, subject to mutability, given over to forgetfulness, often afflicted by fear and lifted up by joy. O wondrous reality, worthy of every astonishment! Concerning God, the Creator of all, who is incomprehensible and ineffable, we read, speak, and write lofty and exceedingly marvelous things, removed from every ambiguity; but whatever we say about angels and souls, we cannot affirm with equal clarity.

[Col. 0922] But let the mind pass beyond these things and transcend everything that has been created; let it run and ascend, fly and pass through, and direct the eyes of faith, as far as it can, toward him who created all things. “I will make steps of ascent in my heart, and through my very soul I will ascend to my God” [Note: Thus the manuscripts. But the printed editions have: “through them I will ascend to my soul, and through my soul I will ascend to my Lord.”], who remains above my head. Whatever is seen visibly, whatever is imagined spiritually, let it be removed far from the mind’s gaze by a strong hand; let the pure and simple intellect alone, moving in swift flight, reach him, the Creator of angels and souls and all things. Blessed is that mind which leaves low things and seeks high things; which establishes the seat of its dwelling in lofty places and from the highest rocks contemplates the sun of righteousness with eagle eyes. For nothing is so beautiful and delightful as to contemplate God himself with the mind’s gaze and the heart’s desire, and in a wondrous manner invisibly to behold the invisible; thus to taste another sweetness, not this one, and to behold another light, not this one. For this light, which is confined to a place, ended by time, varied by the interruption of nights, and which we share with worms and beasts, in comparison with that supreme light ought not to be called light, but night.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. No One Can Behold Him in This Life, and in What Manner He Is Seen. An Exhortation to Praise God

Although that supreme and immutable essence, the true light, the unfailing light, the light of angels, cannot be seen by anyone in this life—for this is the one reward reserved for the saints in heavenly glory—nevertheless, to believe, understand, and feel it, and to yearn eagerly for it, is in a certain manner to see and possess it.

Let the voice, then, resound above the angels, and let a human being contemplate God with an attentive mind and offer him such praises as he can in words. For it is right that the creature should praise the Creator; he made us to praise him, although he has no need of our praises. He is an incomprehensible power, needing nothing and sufficient to himself. “Great is our Lord, and great is his power, and his wisdom is without number” (Ps. 146:5); “great is the Lord, and greatly to be praised” (Ps. 95:4). Let the mind therefore love him, the tongue sing of him, the hand write of him, and let the faithful spirit exercise itself wholly in these holy pursuits. Let the man of desires and contemplator of heavenly things be continually refreshed by the sweetest nourishment of this heavenly contemplation, so that, fattened on this heavenly food, he may cry out with a great cry, cry out from the depths of his heart, cry out in jubilation, and say with the most ardent desire of his mind:

## CHAPTER XXIX. A Prayer Explaining Many of God’s Perfections

[Note: From the book *On the Mirror*, chapters 3 and 5–9.]

Most high, almighty, most merciful and most just, most hidden and most present, most beautiful and most powerful: you are stable and incomprehensible, invisible, seeing all things [Note: Same work, chapter 4], immutable, changing all things, immortal, not confined to place, without limit, uncircumscribed, bounded nowhere, beyond estimation, ineffable, inscrutable, immovable, touching all things, investigable, unspeakable, to be feared and dreadful, to be honored and terrible, venerable and reverend, never new, never old, renewing all things and bringing the proud into old age though they do not know it, always active, always at rest, gathering and needing nothing, bearing all things without burden, filling all things without being enclosed, creating, protecting, nourishing, and perfecting all things, seeking when nothing is lacking to you.

You love without agitation; you are jealous and secure; you repent and do not grieve; you grow angry and remain tranquil; you change your works but do not change your counsel. You receive what you find, though you never lost it; you are never needy, yet you rejoice in gains; you are never greedy, yet you demand interest; what is given beyond obligation is reckoned to you as a debt, and who has anything that is not yours? You repay debts while owing nothing; you forgive debts while losing nothing.

You alone give life to all things; you created all things; you are everywhere and wholly everywhere; you can be felt but cannot be seen; you are absent nowhere, yet you are far from the thoughts of the wicked; you are not absent even where you are far away, because where you are not present by grace, you are present by vengeance. You touch all things, yet you do not touch all things equally. For you touch some things so that they may exist, but not so that they may live and feel; others so that they may exist and live, but not so that they may feel and discern; others so that they may exist, live, and feel, but not so that they may discern; and others so that they may exist, live, feel, and discern. Although you are never unlike yourself, you touch unlike things in unlike ways.

You are present everywhere and can scarcely be found; we follow you while you stand still, but cannot grasp you; you hold all things, fill all things, encompass all things, surpass all things, and sustain all things. For you do not sustain on one side and surpass on another [Note: [Col. 0923] The printed editions have “are surpassed.”], nor fill on one side and encompass on another; rather, by encompassing you fill, and by filling you encompass; by sustaining you surpass, and by surpassing you sustain.

You teach the hearts of the faithful without the clamor of words. You reach strongly from end to end and dispose all things sweetly (Wis. 8:1). You are not spread out in places, nor varied by times. You have neither approaches nor withdrawals, but dwell in inaccessible light, which no human being has seen or can see (1 Tim. 6:16). Remaining at rest in yourself, you encompass the whole everywhere [Note: Erasmus, Lyons, Venice, and Louvain add, “everywhere wholly.” M.]. For you cannot be split or divided, because you are truly one; nor can you be made into parts, because wholly you hold, fill, illuminate, and possess the whole.

The human mind cannot comprehend the immense depth of this mystery, nor can an eloquent tongue recount it, nor can the volumes of libraries, however extensive their discourse [Note: Thus the manuscript of Metz and the book *On the Mirror*. Elsewhere, “discourses cannot,” etc.], explain it. Even if books filled the whole world, your ineffable knowledge could not be narrated. Since you are truly unspeakable, you can in no way be written down or enclosed, for you are the fountain of divine light and the sun of eternal brightness.

For you are great without quantity, and therefore immeasurable; you are good without quality, and therefore truly and supremely good. No one is good except you alone, whose will is your work, for you to will is to be able; whatever you created from nothing, you made by will alone. You possess your whole creation without need, govern it without labor, rule it without weariness, and nothing disturbs the order of your command, whether in the highest or the lowest things. You are held to be in all places without place, contain all things without circumference, and are present everywhere without position or movement. You are not the author of evil, and cannot do evil—the very thing you cannot do—though there is nothing you cannot do.

You have never repented of having done anything, nor are you disturbed by any storm of emotional agitation, nor is the kingdom of the whole earth your portion [Note: Thus the manuscripts and the book *On the Mirror*. But the printed editions have: “the dangers are your loss.”]. You approve or command no disgrace or crime. You never lie, because you are eternal truth. By your goodness alone we were made; by your justice we suffer punishment; by your mercy we are freed. Nothing heavenly, nothing fiery, nothing earthly, and nothing touched by bodily sense is to be worshiped in your place.

You truly are what you are, and you do not change. To you above all and especially belongs what the Greeks call ὤν (*ōn*), and the Latins *Est* (“He is”), because you are always the same, and your years shall not fail (Ps. 102:28).

[Note: From the book *On the Mirror*, chapters 23–24.]

These and many other things holy mother Church has taught me, whose member I have become through your grace. She has taught me that you alone are the living and true God, not corporeal, passible, or tangible; and that nothing of your substance or nature can in any way be violated, changed, composed, or fabricated [Note: The printed editions have “made.”]. Therefore it is certain that you cannot be perceived by bodily eyes; [Col. 0924] nor could you ever have been seen by any mortal in your own essence. From this it is plainly understood that from the same place from which the angels behold you, we too shall see you after this life. But even they cannot see you perfectly as you are; finally, no one else knows the whole of you except you alone, almighty Trinity.

## CHAPTER XXX. Further Discussion of God’s Properties. On the Unity and Plurality of the Persons in God

[Note: From the book *On the Mirror*, chapters 20–22.]

You, unity of the Godhead, manifold in the plurality of persons, are numerically innumerable; and therefore measurably immeasurable and ponderably imponderable. We do not profess the origin of the supreme goodness—which you yourself are, from whom, through whom, and in whom all things exist—but we say that all good things are good by participation in it. For your divine substance has always lacked and lacks matter, although it does not lack form: form informed, the form of forms, the most beautiful form. When you impress it upon individual things like a seal, you undoubtedly cause them to differ far from you without any mutability involving an increase or diminution of you.

Whatever exists in the nature of creatures is your creature, O one Trinity and triune unity, God, whose omnipotence possesses, rules, and fills all that it has created. We do not say that you fill all things so that they contain you, but rather so that they themselves are contained by you. You do not fill all things piecemeal, nor should it be thought that each creature receives you according to the size of its portion—more, if it is greater, and less, if it is smaller—since you are rather yourself in all things, or all things in you.

Your omnipotence encloses the universe, and no one can find a way of escaping your power. For whoever does not have you propitiated will by no means escape you when angry, as it is written: “Neither from the east, nor from the west, nor from the desert mountains, for God is judge” (Ps. 75:7–8); and elsewhere: “Where shall I go from your spirit, and where shall I flee from your face?” (Ps. 139:7).

The immensity of your divine greatness is such that we understand you to be within all things but not enclosed; outside all things but not excluded. [Note: From the same work, chapter 23.] Therefore you are interior, so that you may contain all things; and you are exterior, so that by the immensity of your uncircumscribed greatness you may enclose all things. By the fact that you are exterior, you are shown to be the Creator; by the fact that you are interior [Note: Thus the manuscripts and the book *On the Mirror*. But the printed editions have: “By the fact that you are interior, you are shown to be the Creator; by the fact that you are exterior,” etc.], you are demonstrated to govern all things. And so that created things might not exist without you, you are within all things; but so that they might not exist apart from you, you are exterior, so that all things may be enclosed by you—not by local magnitude, but by the presence of your power. You are present everywhere, and all things are present to you, although some understand this and others do not.

The unity of your inseparable nature cannot have separable persons. For just as you are Trinity in unity and unity in Trinity, so you cannot have separation of persons. Those persons are sometimes named individually; but you, God the Trinity, willed to show yourself inseparable in the persons, so that no name belonging to any one person should not, according to the rule of relation, refer to another: as the Father refers to the Son, and the Son to the Father, or the Holy Spirit most truly refers to the Father and the Son.

Those names that signify your substance, power [Note: The printed editions add, “or person.”], or essence, or whatever is properly said of God, apply equally to all the persons: God, great, almighty, eternal, and all that is naturally said of you as God. There is therefore no name of nature that can belong to you, God the Father, in such a way that it could not belong to your Son or to the Holy Spirit. We say that you, the Father, are naturally God; but naturally the Son is God, and naturally the Holy Spirit is God—not three gods, but one God by nature: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. [Col. 0925]

Therefore you are inseparable, holy Trinity and God, to be understood as persons in sense, although you have names separable in speech, because you in no way admit a plural number in the names of nature. In this it is shown that the persons cannot be divided in the holy Trinity, which is the one true God, because the name of any person always looks toward another person. If I say “Father,” I indicate the Son; if I name the Son, I proclaim the Father; if I call upon the Holy Spirit, it must be understood that he is the spirit of someone—that is, of the Father and the Son. This is the true faith that comes from sound doctrine; this certainly is the catholic and orthodox faith, which God, by your grace, taught me in the bosom of mother Church.

## CHAPTER XXXI. Invocation of the Holy Trinity

[Note: From the book *On the Mirror*, chapter 1.]

My faith, which you gave me through your goodness for my salvation, invokes you, O Lord. The faithful soul lives by faith and holds in hope what it will see in reality. My pure conscience invokes you, my God, and the sweet love of my faith, which, after dispelling the darkness, you led to understanding the truth, and which, after removing the foolish bitterness of the world [Note: Thus the manuscript of Metz and the book *On the Mirror*, where *tulta*, from *tollo*, is used in place of *ablata*. Erasmus, Lyons, Venice, and Louvain: “and which you rescued from the foolish bitterness of the world, and having supplied,” etc. M.], and applying the love of your sweetness, you made joyful and honey-flowing for me.

The blessed Trinity invokes you: a clear voice and the sincere love of my faith, which, as you nourished it in me from my earliest cradle, you have always illumined by the illumination of your grace, and which, increasing it, you have strengthened in me through the teachings of mother Church.

I invoke you, O blessed, benedict, and glorious one Trinity [Note: From the cited book, chapter 30, after Alcuin, in the *Invocation of the Holy Trinity*], Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; God, Lord, Paraclete; charity, grace, communion; begetter, begotten, regenerating; true light, true light from light, true illumination; fountain, river, irrigation; from one are all things, through one are all things, in one are all things; from whom are all things, through whom are all things, in whom are all things; living life, life from the living one, vivifier of the living; one from himself, one from one, one from both; ὤν (*ōn*, “being”) from himself, ὤν from another, ὤν from both; truthful Father, truth the Son, truth the Holy Spirit. Therefore Father, Logos, and Paraclete are one in essence, one in power, one in goodness.

## CHAPTER XXXII. Invocation of God with Praise. That God Ought to Be Praised

[Note: Thus also the book *On the Mirror*, chapter 32, after Augustine, *Soliloquies* book 1, chapter 1.]

God, supreme and true blessedness, from whom, through whom, and in whom all things that are blessed are blessed. God, true and supreme life, from whom, through whom, and in whom all things that truly and happily live have life. God, good and beautiful, from whom, through whom, and in whom all things that are good and beautiful are good and beautiful. God, whose faith awakens us, whose hope raises us up, whose charity joins us together. God, who commands us to ask you, makes yourself found, and opens to those who knock. God, from whom to turn away is to fall, toward whom to turn is to rise, in whom to remain is to stand firm. God, whom no one loses except by deception, no one seeks except after being admonished, and no one finds except after being purified. God, to know whom is life, to serve whom is to reign, and to praise whom is salvation and joy of the soul: I praise, bless, and adore you with lips and heart and with every power I possess; I give thanks to your mercy and goodness for all your benefits, and sing a hymn to your glory: “Holy, holy, holy.”

I invoke you, O blessed Trinity, that you may come into me and make me a temple worthy of your glory. [Note: Thus the book *On the Mirror*, chapter 1.] I ask the Father through the Son; I ask the Son through the Father; I ask the Holy Spirit through the Father and the Son, so that all vices may be driven far from me and all holy virtues planted in me.

Immense God, from whom, through whom, and in whom all things visible and invisible have been made [Note: From Alcuin’s *Confessions*, part 3, no. 16], who surround your works outside, fill them within, cover them above, and bear them below—[Col. 0926] guard me, the work of your hands, who hope in you and trust solely in your mercy. Guard me, I beg you, here and everywhere, now and always, within and without, before and behind, above and below, and all around, so that no place in me may lie open to the snares of enemies.

You are the almighty God, guardian and protector of all who hope in you; without you no one is safe, no one is freed from dangers. You are God, and there is no other besides you, neither in heaven above nor on earth below, who does great, marvelous, and inscrutable things, whose number is without end.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. The One Eager to Praise Asks for the Means to Praise Worthily. He Flies Away into God. How the Angels Surpass Us in Praising God. An Ardent Prayer for the Perpetual Praise of God

Praise is fitting for you, a hymn is fitting for you. To you all the angels, to you the heavens and all the Powers, sing hymns and unceasingly chant praises, as creatures to their Creator, servants to their Lord, soldiers to their king. Every creature magnifies you, holy and undivided Trinity; every spirit praises you. To you the saints and those humble in heart, to you the spirits and souls of the righteous, to you all the heavenly citizens and all the orders of blessed spirits, sing glory and honor while humbly adoring you, without end. Those heavenly citizens praise you, O Lord, magnificently and wondrously [Note: See Augustine, *Confessions* book 1, chapter 1]; let a human being, a great portion of your creation, praise you [Note: Thus the manuscript of Metz. The printed editions have “praises you.”].

But I too, a sinful little human being, greatly desire to praise you and long to love you with a special love. My God, my life, my strength and my praise, deign to let me praise you. Give light to my heart and a word to my mouth, so that my heart may meditate on your glory and my tongue sing your praises all day long. But because praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner (Ecclus. 15:9), and because I am a man of unclean lips (Isa. 6:5), cleanse my mouth, I beseech you, from every defilement. Sanctify me, almighty sanctifier, inwardly and outwardly, and make me worthy of your praises.

Kindly and acceptably receive from the hand of my heart, from the love of my mind receive the sacrifice of my lips. Let it be acceptable in your sight and rise to you as an odor of sweetness. Let the memory of your holiness and your most blessed sweetness possess my whole soul and seize it into the love of invisible things. Let it pass from visible things to invisible, from earthly things to heavenly, from temporal things to eternal; let it pass through and behold a wondrous vision.

[Note: Augustine, *Confessions* book 7, chapter 10; book 13, chapters 14–15.]

O eternal truth, true charity, and beloved eternity, you are my God. To you I sigh night and day; I yearn for you; I direct myself toward you; I desire to reach you. Whoever knows you knows truth; he knows eternity. You are truth, presiding over all things; we shall see you as you are (1 John 3:2), when this blind and mortal life has passed, in which it is said to us, “Where is your God?”

And I say, “My God, where are you?” [Note: The manuscript of Metz adds: “Behold where you are, behold where you are, behold where you are.”] I draw breath in you for a little while, when I pour out my soul over myself in a voice of exultation and in the sound of confession celebrating a festival; yet it is still sad, because it slips back and becomes an abyss—or rather, because it perceives that it is still an abyss.

My faith, which you kindled in the night before my feet, says to it: “Why are you sad, my soul, and why do you trouble me? Hope in the Lord; his word is a lamp for my feet. Hope and persevere until the night, mother of the wicked, has passed; until the wrath of the Lord has passed, whose children we once were—for once we were darkness; until these things have wholly passed away [Note: Thus the manuscript of Metz. Elsewhere: “until this rush of waters has passed through.”], whose remnants we still drag about in the body that is dead because of sin; until the day breathes forth and the shadows are removed [Note: Elsewhere, “incline.”]. Hope in the Lord.”

“In the morning I will stand and contemplate,” and I shall always confess to him. “In the morning I will stand and see” (Ps. 5:5) the salvation of my face, my God, [Col. 0927] who will give life to our mortal bodies because of the Spirit who dwells in us (Rom. 8:11), so that we may now be light, although we have been saved as yet in hope, and sons of light and sons of day, not of night or darkness (1 Thess. 5:5). For once we were darkness, but now we are light in you, our God (Eph. 5:8)—and yet still through faith, not yet through sight. Hope that is seen is not hope (Rom. 8:24).

The immortal peoples of your Angels praise you, Lord, and the heavenly Powers glorify your name—those who have no need to read this writing of ours or to come to know you, holy and undivided Trinity. For they always behold your face, and there they read, without the syllables of time, what your eternal will desires. They read, choose, and love. They read always, and what they read never passes away. By choosing and loving, they read the unchangeability itself of your counsel. Their book is not closed, nor will their scroll be folded, because you yourself are this for them, and you will be so forever.

O supremely blessed heavenly Powers, who can praise you in holiness and perfect purity, with immense sweetness and ineffable exultation! They praise you from the very source of their joy, because they always see the source from which they can rejoice and praise. But we, weighed down by the burden of the flesh, placed far from your countenance in this pilgrimage, and distracted among the changing things of the world, cannot praise you worthily; for we walk by faith, not yet by sight [Note: [Col. 0927] The printed editions read: “Yet we praise by faith, not by sight.”]. Those angelic spirits, however, walk by sight, not by faith. This is the reason [Note: [Col. 0927] The printed editions read: “For this flesh is the reason.”] why we praise in a very different manner from them. Yet although we utter praise in different ways, you are nevertheless the one God, creator of all, to whom the sacrifice of praise is offered in heaven and on earth. By your mercy, however, we shall eventually join the company of those with whom we shall always see you and praise you without end.

Grant, Lord, that so long as I am placed in this fragile body, my heart may praise you, my tongue may praise you, and all my bones may say, “Lord, who is like you?” You are the almighty God whom we worship and adore as three in persons and one in the substance of divinity: the unbegotten Father, the only-begotten Son from the Father, and the Holy Spirit proceeding from both and remaining in both—the holy and undivided Trinity, one almighty God [Note: [Col. 0927] From Alcuin’s *Confession*, p. 4, nos. 11–13]. When we did not exist, you powerfully made us; and when we had been lost through our own fault, you wondrously restored us through your compassion and goodness. Do not, I beg you, allow us to be ungrateful for such great benefits or unworthy of so many mercies.

I implore, entreat, and beseech you: increase faith, increase hope, increase love. By your grace make us always steadfast in faith and effective in action, so that through right faith and works worthy of faith, by your mercy, we may attain eternal life. There, seeing your glory as it is, may we adore your majesty and say together—those whom you have deemed worthy to see your immeasurable beauty [Note: [Col. 0927] So in Anselm, *Prayer* 1]:

“Glory to the Father, who made us; glory to the Son, who redeemed us; glory to the Holy Spirit, who sanctified us; glory to the supreme and undivided Trinity, whose works are inseparable and whose rule remains without end. Praise is fitting for you; a hymn is fitting for you; all glory is owed to you. To you belong blessing and splendor, thanksgiving, honor, power, and strength, our God, forever and ever. Amen.”

## CHAPTER XXXIV. The Humble Confession of a Sinner and Unworthy Praiser

[Note: [Col. 0927] This chapter is absent from the Royal Manuscript and does not occur in this order in the Mettensis codex; it is, however, Anselm’s *Prayer* 5.]

Forgive, Lord, forgive in your goodness; forgive and have mercy. Spare my ignorance and my great imperfection. Do not reject me as presumptuous because I, a servant—if only a good one, and not also useless and wicked, indeed wicked and exceedingly wicked—dare to praise, bless, and adore you, our almighty God, terrible and greatly to be feared, without contrition of heart, without a fountain of tears, without due reverence and trembling.

For if the Angels who adore and praise you tremble, filled with wondrous exultation, why do I, a sinner, when I stand before you, utter praises and offer sacrifice, not tremble in heart, grow pale in face, quiver in my lips, shudder throughout my body, and so lament before you continually with tears springing forth? I desire this, but I cannot. And because I cannot do what I desire, I am greatly astonished at myself when I behold you, so exceedingly terrible, with the eyes of faith. But who can do this without the help of your grace? For our entire salvation is your great mercy.

Wretched me! How has my soul become so senseless that it is not seized with immense terror while it stands before God and sings his praises? Wretched me! How has my heart become so hardened that my eyes do not continually pour forth rivers of tears while a servant speaks before his Lord, a human being before God, a creature before the creator—one made from clay (Gen. II, 7) before him who made everything from nothing?

Behold, Lord, I place myself before you, and I do not conceal from your fatherly ears what I feel secretly about myself [Note: [Col. 0928] The Mettensis Manuscript reads “brotherly ears.”]. You are rich in mercy and generous in rewards: give me some of your good things, so that from them I may serve you; for we cannot serve or please you from any other source than your gift. Pierce my flesh, I beg you, with your fear; let my heart rejoice so that it may fear your name. Would that my sinful soul feared you as did that holy man who said, “For I always feared God as though waves were swelling over me” (Job XXXI, 25).

God, giver of every good thing, give me amid your praises a fountain of tears together with purity of heart and jubilation of mind, so that, loving you perfectly and praising you worthily, I may taste, savor, and know by the palate of my heart how sweet you are, Lord, as it is written: “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet; blessed is the man who hopes in him” (Ps. XXXIII, 9). “Blessed is the people that knows jubilation” (Ps. LXXXVIII, 16). “Blessed is the man whose help is from you; he has set ascents in his heart, in the valley of tears, in the place he has established” (Ps. LXXXIII, 6–7). “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. V, 8). “Blessed are those who dwell in your house, Lord; forever and ever they shall praise you” (Ps. LXXXIII, 5).

## CHAPTER XXXV. Prayers Burning with Love for Jesus. The Character of Two Loves

[Note: [Col. 0928] John of Fécamp, part 4, and in Anselm, *Prayer* 17.]

Jesus, our redemption, love, and desire, God from God, be present to me, your servant. I invoke you; I cry out to you with a great cry, with my whole heart. I invoke you into my soul: enter it and join it to yourself, so that you may possess it without stain or wrinkle. For a habitation is owed to the most pure Lord that is itself clean.

Therefore sanctify me, your vessel, which you have made; empty it of wickedness, fill it with grace, and preserve it full, so that I may become a temple most worthy of your dwelling, here and forever. Most sweet, most kind, most loving, dearest, most precious, most desired, most lovable [Note: [Col. 0928] The Mettensis Manuscript here and below reads *amabillime* (“most lovable”)”], most beautiful: sweeter to me than honey, whiter than milk and snow, more pleasing than nectar, more precious than gems and gold, dearer to me than all the riches and honors of the earth.

What am I saying, my God, my one hope, my immense mercy? What am I saying, my unfailing sweetness, my blessed and secure sweetness? What am I saying while I say such things? I say what I can, but I do not say what I ought [Note: [Col. 0928] From the *Book of the Mirror*, ch. 33].

Would that I could say things like those angelic choirs that sing hymns! O how willingly I would pour myself out entirely in your praises! O how devoutly, in the midst of the Church, I would proclaim without weariness the songs of that heavenly melody to the praise and glory of your name! But because I cannot say such things, shall I therefore be silent? Woe to those who are silent about you, who loosen the mouths of the mute and make the tongues of infants eloquent! Woe to those who are silent about you, for when they utter your praises, they are eloquent mutes!

Who can praise you worthily, ineffable power and wisdom of the Father? And because I find no words with which I can sufficiently express you, all-powerful and all-knowing Word [Col. 0929], I shall say for now what I can, until you command me to come to you, where I shall be able to say what becomes you and is required of me. Therefore I humbly ask you not to look so much at what I now say as at what I desire to say. For I greatly desire to speak about you what is fitting and becoming, because praise and hymn are fitting for you, and all honor is owed to you.

You know, God who knows hidden things, that you are dearer to me not only than the earth and everything in it, but also more acceptable and more lovable to me than heaven itself and everything in it. For I love you above heaven and earth and all else that is in them—indeed, unless it is for love of your name, things that pass away certainly ought not to be loved [Note: [Col. 0929] The word “unless” is absent from the manuscripts]. I love you, my God, with great love, and I desire to love you more. Grant me always to love you as much as I wish and as much as I ought, so that you alone may be my entire intention and all my meditation. May I meditate on you throughout the days without ceasing; may I sense you in sleep during the night; may my spirit speak to you; may my mind converse with you; may my heart be illumined by the light of your holy vision [Note: [Col. 0929] The Mettensis Manuscript reads “visitation”], so that under your governance and guidance I may walk from virtue to virtue and at last see you, God of gods, in Zion (Ps. LXXXIII, 8)—now indeed through a mirror and in an enigma, but then face to face, when I shall know you as I am known (1 Cor. XIII, 12).

“Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. V, 8). “Blessed are those who dwell in your house, Lord; forever and ever they shall praise you” (Ps. LXXXIII, 5).

I therefore ask you, Lord, by all your mercies, through which we have been freed from eternal death [Note: [Col. 0929] Alcuin, *Confession*, part 2, no. 4], soften my hard, stony, rocky, and iron heart with your most holy and powerful anointing. By the fire of compunction make me before you at every hour a living sacrifice. Make me always have in your sight a contrite and humbled heart, with an abundance of tears [Note: [Col. 0929] Alcuin, col. 133b]. Make me, out of longing for you, be utterly extinguished to this world and forget passing things because of the greatness of your fear and love, so that with regard to temporal things I neither grieve nor rejoice, neither fear nor love anything temporal, am neither corrupted by flattering things nor shaken by adverse ones [Note: [Col. 0929] *Ibid.*, 134c, and *Confession*, part 2, no. 7].

And because your love is full and strong as death, let the fiery and honey-sweet power of your love, I beg you, absorb my mind away from everything beneath heaven, so that I may cling to you alone and feed only on the memory of your sweetness.

Descend, Lord—descend, I beg you, descend into my heart, your most sweet fragrance. Let your honey-sweet love enter. May the wondrous and ineffable fragrance of your savor come to me, awakening in me eternal desires and bringing forth from my heart streams of living water flowing into eternal life. You are immense, Lord, and you ought to be loved and praised without measure by those whom you have redeemed with your precious blood, most gracious lover of humankind.

Most merciful Lord and most just judge, to whom the Father has given all judgment (John V, 22), by the most wise authority of your justice you determine [Note: [Col. 0929] Another reading: “you discern by judgment”] that it is right and just that the children of this age—of night and darkness—should love and seek perishable riches and fleeting honors with greater desire, strength, and zeal than we, your servants, love you, our God, through whom we were made and redeemed.

For if one human being loves another with such love that each scarcely tolerates the other’s absence; if a bride is joined to her bridegroom with such ardor of mind that, because of the greatness of her love, she can enjoy no rest, bearing the absence of her beloved only with great sorrow—then with what love, zeal, and fervor ought the soul whom you have betrothed to yourself in justice and faith, in mercy and compassion, to love you, the true and most beautiful bridegroom, who have loved and saved us so greatly and done such great and wondrous things for us?

Although these lowly things have their pleasures and their loves, they do not delight in the manner that you do, our God. The righteous person delights in you, because your love is sweet and tranquil; it fills the hearts it possesses with sweetness, gentleness, and peace. The love of the world and of the flesh, by contrast, is anxious and troubled; it does not allow the souls it enters to remain at rest, for it continually harasses them with suspicions, disturbances, and various [Note: [Col. 0930] The Mettensis Manuscript reads “empty”] fears.

You, therefore, are the delight of the upright, and rightly so; for with you there is powerful rest and undisturbed life. Whoever enters into you, good Lord, enters into the joy of his Lord and will fear no more, but will be exceedingly well in the highest good [Note: [Col. 0930] The printed editions read “in the best place”], saying: “This is my rest forever and ever; here I shall dwell, for I have chosen it” (Ps. CXXXI, 14); and: “The Lord governs me, and I shall lack nothing; he has placed me in a place of pasture” (Ps. XXII, 1–2).

Sweet Christ, good Jesus, fill my heart always, I beg you, with your unquenchable love and your continual remembrance, so that, like a burning flame, I may burn entirely in the sweetness of your love, which even many waters may never extinguish in me. Make me, sweetest Lord, love you [Note: [Col. 0930] The Mettensis Manuscript reads “love of you”] and, through desire for you, lay down the burden of all carnal desires and the very heavy load of earthly cravings that attack and weigh down my wretched soul [Note: [Col. 0930] The same manuscript reads “that hinder wretched souls”].

Running freely after you in the fragrance of your ointments, until I am effectively satisfied by the vision of your beauty, may I, with you as my guide, deserve to arrive there as quickly as possible. For two loves—one good and one evil, one sweet and one bitter—cannot occupy the same breast at once. Therefore, if anyone loves something besides you, your love, God, is not in him.

Love of sweetness and sweetness of love; love that does not torment but delights; love sincere and chaste, lasting forever and ever [Note: [Col. 0930] From Augustine’s *Confessions*, book 10, ch. 29]; love that always burns and is never extinguished—sweet Christ, good Jesus, my God and my love—kindle me wholly with your fire, your love, your sweetness and delight, your joy and exultation, your pleasure and desire, which are holy and good, chaste and pure, tranquil and secure. Thus, filled entirely with the sweetness of your love and wholly kindled by the flame of your charity, may I love you, my Lord, with all my heart and all the marrow of my inmost being, having you in my heart and on my lips and always and everywhere before my eyes, so that no place in me may be open to adulterous loves.

Hear, my God; hear, light of my eyes; hear what I ask, and grant what I shall ask you to hear. Merciful and easily entreated Lord, do not become inexorable to me because of my sins. Rather, because of your goodness, receive the prayers of your servant and grant me the fulfillment of my petition and desire, through the intercession, prayer, and advocacy of your glorious mother, my lady, together with all the saints. Amen.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. Prayer to Christ Arising from the Desire for Love and Tears. Tears as Signs of Love. The Soul Seeking God Is Stirred to Tears by the Example of Hannah. It Is Also Stirred by the Example of Magdalene. The Continual Grace of Tears Is Entreated

[Note: [Col. 0930] John of Fécamp, p. 5, and in Anselm, *Prayer* 16.]

Christ the Lord, Word of the Father, who came into this world to save sinners, I ask you, through the most forgiving depths of your mercy [Note: [Col. 0930] From Alcuin, *Confession*, part 2, no. 4], correct my life, improve my deeds, reform my conduct, and remove from me what harms me and displeases you. Give me what you know pleases you and benefits me.

Who can make clean what has been conceived from unclean seed, unless you alone? You are the almighty God of infinite compassion, who justifies the ungodly and gives life to the dead, who changes sinners, and they are no more. Therefore remove from me whatever in me displeases you; for your eyes see my many imperfections. Send, I beg you, the hand of your compassion and remove from me whatever in me offends the eyes of your goodness [Note: [Col. 0931] From the *Book of the Mirror*, ch. 1 after Augustine].

Before you, Lord, are my health and my sickness; preserve the one, I beg you, and heal the other. Heal me, Lord, and I shall be healed; save me, and I shall be saved—you who heal the weak and preserve what has been healed, who by a single command restore what has been ruined and fallen. For if you deign to sow good seed in your field, it is necessary that the hand of your compassion first uproot the thorns of my vices.

Most sweet, most kind, most loving, dearest, most precious, most desired, most lovable, most beautiful: pour, I beseech you, the abundance of your sweetness and love into my breast, so that I may desire or think of nothing earthly, nothing carnal, but love you alone and have you alone in my heart and on my lips.

Write upon my breast with your finger the sweet memory of your honey-sweet name, never to be erased by forgetfulness. Write your will and your ordinances upon the tablets of my heart, so that I may always and everywhere have before my eyes you, the Lord of immeasurable sweetness, and your commandments. Kindle my mind with that fire of yours which you sent upon the earth and wished to be intensely kindled (Luke XII, 49), so that each day, with tears breaking forth, I may offer you the sacrifice of a troubled spirit and a contrite heart.

Sweet Christ, good Jesus, as I desire, as I ask with my whole mind, give me your holy and chaste love, which may fill me, hold me, and possess me entirely. And give me a visible sign of your love: an irrigating fountain of tears continually flowing, so that the tears themselves may testify to your love in me; may themselves reveal and speak how much my soul loves you, while, because of the immense sweetness of your love, it cannot restrain itself from tears.

I remember, merciful Lord, that good woman [Note: [Col. 0931] The printed editions add “Hannah” here] who came to the tabernacle to pray for a son, of whom Scripture reports that after her tears and prayers her face was no longer changed in different directions [i.e., no longer sorrowful] (1 Kings I, 18). But when I remember such virtue and steadfastness, I am tormented by sorrow and confounded by shame, because I see that I, wretched as I am, lie exceedingly low.

If that woman wept in this way and persisted in weeping while she sought a son, how ought the soul to mourn and persist in mourning that seeks and loves God and desires to reach him? How ought such a soul to groan and weep night and day when it wishes to love nothing besides Christ? It is indeed astonishing if its tears have not already become its bread day and night.

Look upon me, therefore, and have mercy, because the sorrows of my heart have multiplied. Give me your heavenly consolation, and do not despise the sinful soul for which you also died [Note: [Col. 0931] Alcuin, *Book on the Sacraments*, ch. 1]. Give me, I beg you, inward tears arising from your affection, which may loosen the bonds of my sins and continually fill my soul with heavenly joy, so that, if I cannot attain even a small portion in your kingdom together with true and perfect monks, whose footsteps I cannot imitate, at least I may attain it with devout women [Note: [Col. 0931] The Mettensis Manuscript reads “your servants” instead of “monks”].

Another woman’s remarkable devotion also comes to mind: she sought you, lying in the tomb, with devoted love. When the disciples departed from the tomb, she did not depart; she sat there sad and mourning, and wept for a long time and intensely. Rising with many tears, she examined the tomb’s recesses again and again with watchful eyes, to see whether she might perhaps behold you somewhere—the one she sought with burning desire.

Certainly, she had already entered the tomb once and again, but for one who loved so greatly that was not enough [Note: [Col. 0931] Gregory, *Homily 25 on the Gospels]; for the strength of a good work is perseverance. And because she loved you more than the others, and by loving wept, and by weeping sought, and by seeking persevered, she deserved to be the first of all to find you, see you, and speak with you (John XX, 11–17). Not only this, but she also became the herald to the disciples of your glorious resurrection, when you commanded and mercifully instructed her: “Go, tell my brothers to go to Galilee; there they will see me” (Matt. XXVIII, 10).

If, then, that woman wept and persisted in weeping while she sought the living among the dead, while she did not touch you with the hand of faith [Note: [Col. 0932] We add “not,” from the Mettensis Manuscript], how ought the soul to mourn and persist in mourning when it believes in its Redeemer, who now presides in heaven and reigns everywhere, and confesses him with its mouth? How ought such a soul to groan and weep when it loves you with its whole heart and longs with its entire desire to see you?

The sole refuge and unique hope of the wretched, to whom no one ever pleads without hope of mercy, grant me this grace for your sake and for the sake of your holy name: whenever I think of you, speak of you, write of you, read of you, converse about you, remember you, stand before you, offer you praises, prayers, and sacrifice, may I each time weep abundantly and sweetly in your presence, with tears breaking forth, so that my tears may become my bread day and night.

You, King of glory and teacher of every virtue, taught us by word and example to groan and weep, saying: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matt. V, 5). You wept over your dead friend and shed tears over the city destined to perish (John XI, 35; Luke XIX, 41). I ask you, good Jesus, by those most blessed tears of yours and by all your mercies, through which you graciously deigned to help us who were wondrously lost: give me the grace of tears, which my soul greatly desires and asks of you, because without your gift I cannot have it.

Through your Holy Spirit, who softens the hard hearts of sinners and pricks them toward weeping, give me the grace of tears, as you gave it to my fathers, whose footsteps I ought to imitate, so that I may mourn myself throughout my whole life, as they mourned themselves night and day. For the merits and prayers of those who pleased you and served you most devoutly [Note: [Col. 0932] So in Alcuin’s *Confession*, part 4, no. 16], have mercy on me, your most wretched and unworthy servant, and give me the grace of tears.

Give me the lower irrigation and the upper irrigation, so that my tears may be my bread day and night. In your sight, my God, through the fire of compunction, may I become a rich and marrow-filled burnt offering. May I be wholly slaughtered upon the altar of my heart and, like the richest burnt offering, be consumed for you as a pleasing fragrance. Give me an irrigating fountain, a clear fountain, in which this defiled burnt offering may continually be washed.

Although, with your grace assisting [Note: [Col. 0932] The Mettensis Manuscript reads “working”], I have offered myself entirely to you, nevertheless I offend you daily in many ways because of my excessive frailty. Therefore give me the grace of tears, blessed and lovable God, especially tears arising from the great sweetness of your love and the remembrance of your mercies.

Prepare this table for your servant in the sight of your servant, and give it into my power, so that whenever I wish I may be satisfied from it. In your compassion and goodness grant that this, your inebriating and glorious cup, may satisfy my thirst, so that my spirit may yearn for you and my mind burn with your love, forgetful of vanity and misery.

Hear, my God; hear, light of my eyes; hear what I ask, and grant what I shall ask you to hear. Merciful and easily entreated Lord, do not become inexorable to me because of my sins; rather, because of your goodness, receive the prayers of your servant and grant me the fulfillment of my petition and desire, through the prayers and merits of the glorious virgin Mary, my lady, and of all the saints [Note: [Col. 0932] The Mettensis Manuscript does not contain the words “of the glorious virgin Mary, my lady, and”]. Amen.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. Prayer to Christ Burning with Desire for God. A Human Being Needs Two Kinds of Food. The Groaning of a Soul Thirsting for God. For the Present He Asks for the Wings of Contemplation and That Everything Created May Be Silent to Him. He Prays for the Wound of Love. Here He Rejects Every Consolation

[Col. 0933]

[Note: [Col. 0933] John, p. 6, and in Anselm, *Prayer* 18.]

Lord Jesus, merciful Jesus, good Jesus, who deigned to die for our sins and rose again for our justification, I ask you by your glorious resurrection: raise me from the tomb of all vices and sins, and give me daily a share in the first resurrection, so that in your resurrection I may truly deserve to receive my portion.

Most sweet, most kind, most loving, dearest, most precious, most desired, most lovable, most beautiful: you ascended into heaven in the triumph of glory and sit at the right hand of the Father. Most powerful King, draw me upward to yourself. I shall run after you in the fragrance of your ointments; I shall run and not grow faint, with you drawing me, you leading me, and me running [Note: [Col. 0933] The Mettensis Manuscript does not contain “and me running”].

Draw the mouth of my soul, which thirsts for you, toward the heavenly streams of eternal satiety; indeed, draw it to yourself, the living fountain, so that from there I may drink according to my capacity and from there live forever. My God, my life! For you said with your holy and blessed mouth: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink” (John VII, 37).

Fountain of life, grant the thirsty soul always to drink from you, so that, according to your holy and truthful promise, living waters may flow from my belly (ibid., 38). Fountain of life, fill my mind with the torrent of your delight and intoxicate my heart with the sober intoxication of your love, so that I may forget what is vain and earthly and have you alone continually in my memory, as it is written: “I remembered God, and I was delighted” (Ps. LXXVI, 4).

Give me your Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 0933] The Mettensis Manuscript reads “give through your Holy Spirit”], whom those waters signified that you promised to give to the thirsty. Grant, I beg you, that with all desire and every effort I may strive toward the place to which we believe you ascended after the resurrection on the fortieth day [Note: [Col. 0933] From the *Book of the Mirror*, ch. 18], so that in the present misery I may be held only in body, while in thought and longing I may always be with you; so that my heart may be where you are, my desirable, incomparable, and greatly lovable treasure.

For in this great flood of the present life, where we are driven about by encircling storms, no trustworthy anchorage and no higher place can be found where the foot of the dove may rest even for a little while. Nowhere is safe peace, nowhere secure rest; everywhere there are wars and quarrels, everywhere enemies [Note: [Col. 0933] The Mettensis Manuscript reads “enemies on every side”]; battles outside, fears within.

[Note: [Col. 0933] *Ibid.*, ch. 3.]

And because we are partly of heaven and partly of earth, the body that decays weighs down the soul. Therefore my mind, my companion and friend, weary from the road, comes languishing and lies prostrate; torn and lacerated by the very vanities through which it has passed, it is exceedingly hungry and thirsty. I have nothing to set before it; I am poor and a beggar.

You, Lord my God, rich in all good things and most abundant giver of the food of heavenly satiety, give food to the weary, gather together what has been scattered, and restore what has been torn apart. Behold, it stands at the door and knocks. I beseech you, by the depths of your mercy with which, rising from on high, you visited us: open to the wretched one who knocks with the hand of your compassion [Note: [Col. 0933] The printed editions read: “extend the hand of your compassion to the wretched one”], and command in your merciful condescension that it enter into you, rest in you, and be refreshed by you, the living and heavenly bread. Once satisfied and its strength restored, may it ascend to higher things; and, snatched from this valley of tears on the wing of holy desire, may it fly toward heavenly joys.

Let my spirit, Lord, take up wings like an eagle’s; let it fly and not grow faint; let it fly and reach the beauty of your house and the place of your glorious dwelling. There, upon the table of refreshment of the citizens above, may it be fed on your hidden things in the place of your pasture, beside waters in their fullness.

Let my heart rest in you, my God, my heart that is a great sea swelling with waves. You who commanded the winds and the sea, and there was a great calm (Matt. VIII, 26), come and walk upon the waves of my heart, so that everything within me may become calm and serene. Thus may I embrace you as my one good and contemplate you, the sweet light of my eyes [Col. 0934], without the blind darkness of tumultuous thoughts.

Let my mind, Lord, flee beneath the shadow of your wings from the heats of this world’s thoughts, so that, hidden in the moderation of your refreshment, it may sing joyfully and say: “In peace, in the same place, I shall sleep and rest” (Ps. IV, 9). Let my memory, I beg you, my God, sleep concerning everything beneath heaven while remaining awake in you, as it is written: “I sleep, but my heart is awake.”

Let my soul, my God, be safe and always secure beneath the wings of your protection. Let it remain in you and always be warmed by you. Let it contemplate you in an ecstasy of mind and sing your praises in jubilation. May these sweet gifts of yours be my consolation amid these storms for the present, until I come to you, true peace, where there is no bow, shield, sword, or war, but supreme and certain security; secure tranquility and tranquil security; joyful happiness and happy eternity; eternal blessedness; and the blessed vision and praise of you forever and ever. Amen.

[Note: [Col. 0934] John of Fécamp, p. 7, and in Anselm, *Prayer* 19.]

Christ the Lord, power and wisdom of the Father, who make the cloud your ascent, who walk upon the wings of the winds, who make your Angels spirits and your ministers a burning fire, I beseech and humbly ask you: give me swift wings of faith; give me speedy wings of the virtues, by which, carried aloft, I may be able to contemplate eternal and heavenly things.

Let my soul cling to you, I beg you, and let your right hand receive me. Let it lift me above the heights of earth and feed me with that heavenly inheritance for which my pilgrimage sighs day and night. And because these dying limbs blunt the vigor of the soul—

[Note: [Col. 0934] From the *Book of the Mirror*, ch. 3.]

Disperse the clouds and burdens of the earthly mass.

Stop the wandering mind that rushes through many byways,

and grant the mind to climb to the heavenly seat, so that, illumined by the light above, it may look down upon earth, look up toward heaven, hate sins [Note: [Col. 0934] The printed editions omit the words enclosed in parentheses; we have restored them from the Mettensis Manuscript, which reads: “let my memory sleep concerning all evils, let it hate iniquity.”], and love justice.

For what is more beautiful, or sweeter, than amid the darkness of this life and its many bitterness to yearn for divine sweetness and sigh for eternal blessedness, and to hold the mind there where it is most certain that true joys are possessed?

Most sweet, most kind, most loving, dearest, most precious, most desired, most lovable, most beautiful: when shall I see you? When shall I appear before your face? When shall I be satisfied with your beauty? When will you lead me out of this dark prison, so that I may confess your name and thereafter no longer be pricked with remorse? When shall I pass into that wondrous and most beautiful house of yours, where the voice of joy and exultation resounds in the tents of the righteous?

“Blessed are those who dwell in your house; forever and ever they shall praise you” (Ps. LXXXIII, 5). Blessed, truly blessed, are those whom you have already chosen and received into that heavenly inheritance.

Behold your saints, Lord; they flourish before you like lilies. For they are filled from the abundance of your house, and you give them drink from the torrent of your delight (Ps. XXXV, 9), because you are the fountain of life, and in your light they see light, so that they themselves—light illumined by you, God the illuminating light—shine like the sun in your sight.

How wondrous, how beautiful, how pleasing are the dwelling places of your house! Lord of hosts, my sinful soul longs to enter them. “Lord, I have loved the beauty of your house and the place where your glory dwells” (Ps. XXV, 8). “One thing I have asked of you; this I shall seek: that I may dwell in your house all the days of my life” (Ps. XXVI, 4).

As the deer longs for the springs of water, so my soul longs for you, O God. When shall I come? When shall I appear? When shall I see my God, for whom my soul thirsts (Ps. XLI, 2)? When shall I see him in the land of the living? For in this land of the dying he cannot be seen by mortal eyes [Col. 0935].

What shall I do, wretched as I am, weighed down by the fetter of my mortality? What shall I do? “While we are in the body, we are away from the Lord” (2 Cor. V, 6). “Here we have no lasting city, but we seek the one that is to come” (Heb. XIII, 14); but our citizenship is in heaven.

Alas for me, because my sojourn has been prolonged! I have dwelt with the inhabitants of Kedar; my soul has been a sojourner for a long time (Ps. CXIX, 5–6). “Who will give me wings like a dove’s, and I shall fly away and rest?” (Ps. LIV, 7). Nothing is as sweet to me as to be with my Lord. “But it is good for me to cling to God” (Ps. LXXII, 28).

Grant me, Lord, as long as I remain in these fragile limbs, to cling to you; as it is written: “He who clings to the Lord is one spirit” (1 Cor. 6:17). Give me, I beg, the wings of contemplation, clothed in which I may fly upward to you. And since everything sinister lies below, hold my mind lest it fall into the depths of the dark valley; lest, with the earth’s shadow intervening, it be separated from you, the true sun of justice, and, covered by the darkness of mist, be prevented from looking upward. Therefore I strive upward toward the delightful and most serene state of peace, joy, and light. Hold my heart in your hand, because without you it cannot be borne upward to higher things. I hasten there, where supreme peace reigns and continual tranquility shines. Hold and govern my spirit, and take it according to your will, so that, with you as guide, it may ascend into that region of abundance where you feed Israel forever on the nourishment of truth; so that there, even by swift thought, it may reach you, the supreme Wisdom abiding above all things, knowing all things [Note: [Col. 0935] Alternatively, “passing.”], and governing all things.

But many things obstruct the soul as it flies toward you. At your command, Lord, let everything be silent for me; let the soul itself be silent for me; let everything created pass away; let it pass beyond itself also, and reach you, and fix the eyes of faith upon you alone, the Creator of all things. Let it yearn for you, attend to you, meditate upon you, contemplate you, set you before its eyes, revolve you within its heart as the supreme and true good, and as joy that will remain without end.

[Note: [Col. 0935] From *The Book of the Mirror*, chapter 33.] There are, finally, many contemplations by which the soul devoted to you is wonderfully nourished; but in none of them does my soul rest and delight itself as much as when it thinks of and contemplates itself alone. “How great is the abundance of your sweetness, Lord” (Ps. 30:20), how wonderfully you breathe it into the hearts of those who love you! How marvelous is the sweetness of your love, which those enjoy who love nothing besides you, seek nothing, and desire even to think of nothing else! Happy are those for whom you alone are hope, and every work is prayer. Blessed is the one who sits alone and is silent, and stands continually upon his watch, night and day, so that, while still placed in this frail little body, he may be able in some measure to taste beforehand your sweetness.

I beg you by those life-giving wounds of yours, which you suffered on the cross for our salvation, from which flowed that precious blood by which we were redeemed: wound this sinful soul, for which you also deigned to die; wound it with the fiery and most powerful arrow of your excessive love. You are living, Word of God, effective and sharper than every two-edged sword (Heb. 4:12). You are the chosen arrow and the keenest sword, which by your power can pierce the hard shield of the human heart. Fix my heart with the dart of your love, so that my soul may say to you: “I have been wounded by your love”; so that from that very wound the richest tears of your love may flow night and day. Strike, Lord, strike, I beg you, this exceedingly hard mind of mine with the mighty point of your love; penetrate more deeply into its innermost places by your powerful virtue; and thus give my head an immeasurable supply of water, and pour into my eyes a true fountain of tears that continually flows, arising from my excessive affection and desire to see the beauty of your face. Let me mourn night and day, receiving no consolation in the present life, until I deserve to see you, my beloved and most beautiful Bridegroom, my God and my Lord, in the heavenly bridal chamber. Then, seeing your glorious [Col. 0936] and wondrous and most beautiful face, filled with every sweetness, may I adore your majesty humbly with those whom you have chosen; and there, at last, filled with heavenly and ineffable joy, may I exclaim with those who love you, saying: “Behold, now I see what I desired; now I possess what I hoped for; now I have what I longed for. I am now joined in heaven to the one whom, while placed on earth, I loved with all my strength and embraced with all my love.” To him I clung with total love; him I praise, bless, and adore, who lives and reigns, God, forever and ever. Amen.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. Prayer in Affliction

[Note: [Col. 0936] John of Fécamp, *Prayer* 8.] Have mercy, Lord, have mercy, merciful one; have mercy on me, the most wretched sinner, doing what is unworthy and suffering what is deserved; continually sinning and daily enduring your scourges. If [Note: [Col. 0936] The Mettensis manuscript reads *sed*, “but.”] I consider the evil I have done, it is not as great as what I suffer; what I committed is heavier, what I endure is lighter. You are just, Lord, and your judgment is right; all your judgments are just and true. You are just and upright, Lord our God, and there is no iniquity in you. For you do not afflict us sinners unjustly or cruelly, almighty and merciful Lord; [Note: [Col. 0936] From Alcuin, *Confessions*, part 4, no. 11.] when we did not exist, you powerfully made us, and when we had been lost through our own fault, by your compassion and goodness you wonderfully restored us [Note: [Col. 0936] Alternatively, “renewed us.”]. I know and am certain that our life is not driven by random impulses, but is ordered and governed by you, Lord God. Therefore you care for all things, especially for your servants, who have placed all their hope in your mercy alone. For this reason I beg and humbly entreat you not to deal with me according to my sins, by which I deserved your anger, but according to your great mercy, which surpasses even the sins of the whole world. You, Lord, who inflict scourges outwardly, always grant inwardly unfailing patience, so that your praise may not depart from my mouth. Have mercy on me, Lord, have mercy on me, and help me as you know I need in body and soul. You know all things; you can do all things, for you live forever.

## CHAPTER XXXIX.—Prayer to God mingled with fear and confidence. Confession of sins. Turning to the Father that he may forgive. Humble petition to the Son for pardon. Horror of judgment. He flees to God’s mercy. The name of Jesus gives confidence.

Lord Jesus Christ, Son of the living God, who, with your hands extended on the cross, drank the cup of suffering for the redemption of all mortals, deign today to grant me your help.

[Note: [Col. 0936] From Anselm, *Proslogion*, chapter 1.] Behold, poor, I come to you who are rich; wretched, to you who are merciful, lest I depart empty or despised. Hungry, I begin to seek you, lest I be abandoned fasting; famished, I approach, lest I depart unfed. And if I sigh before I eat, grant that after my sighs I may at least eat. First of all, sweetest Jesus, before the magnificence of your sweetness I confess against myself my injustice. Behold, Lord, I was conceived and born in sins, and you washed and sanctified me, while afterward I stained myself with greater sins. [Note: [Col. 0936] Thus in Anselm, *Prayer* 62.] I was born in necessary sins and afterward wallowed in voluntary sins; but, mindful of your compassion, Lord, you took me from the house of my carnal father and from the tents of sinners, and inspired me to follow you among the generation of those who seek your face, who walk along the straight path, who dwell among the lilies of chastity, and who recline with you in the upper room of the highest poverty. Yet I, ungrateful for so many benefits, after entering religious life [Note: [Col. 0936] Thus in the Ambrosian, Atrebatensian, Erfurt, and Louvain witnesses: “after receiving Baptism.”] committed many unlawful acts and perpetrated many abominable deeds; and where I ought to have corrected sins, I added sins to sins. These are my evils, Lord, by which I dishonored you and stained myself, whom you created in your image and likeness [Col. 0937] (Gen. 1:27): pride, vainglory, [Note: [Col. 0937] From Anselm, *Prayer* 4.] and many other things by which my unhappy soul is harassed and afflicted, torn apart and destroyed. Behold, Lord, my iniquities have risen above my head and, like a heavy burden, have weighed upon me (Ps. 38:5); and unless you, whose proper work it is always to have mercy and spare, place beneath me the right hand of your majesty, I am miserably compelled to sink into the depths.

Attend, Lord God, and see, for you are holy; and behold, my enemy insults me, saying: “God has abandoned him; I will pursue and seize him, for there is no one to deliver him” (Ps. 70:11). And you, Lord, how long? Turn and deliver my soul; save me for the sake of your mercy (Ps. 6:5). Have mercy on your son, whom you brought forth with no small sorrow; and do not regard my evil in such a way that you forget your goodness. What father does not free his son? Or what son is there whom the father would not correct with the rod of compassion? Therefore, Father and Lord, although I am a sinner, I cannot fail to be your son, because you made me and remade me. As I have sinned, correct me, and, after correcting me with your scourge, hand me over to your Son. Can a mother forget the infant of her womb? And certainly, even if she should forget, you, Father, promised that you would not forget (Isa. 49:15). Behold, I cry out, and you do not hear me; I am tormented by sorrow, and you do not console me. What shall I say or do, most wretched that I am? Deprived of so much consolation, I have been cast away from the sight of your eyes (Ps. 30:23). Woe is me! From what great good have I fallen into what great evil! Toward what was I striving, and where have I arrived? Where am I, and where am I not? For whom did I aspire, and for what do I now sigh? I sought good things, and behold, confusion. Behold, I am already dying, and Jesus is not with me. Certainly it is better for me not to exist than to be without Jesus; better not to live than to live without life.

And you, Lord Jesus, where are your ancient mercies (Ps. 88:50)? Will you be angry with me forever (Ps. 84:6)? Be appeased, I beg you, and have mercy on me, and do not turn your face away from me (Ps. 26:9)—you who, in redeeming me, did not turn your face away from those who reviled and spat upon you. [Note: [Col. 0937] Anselm, *Meditation* 3.] I confess that I have sinned, and my conscience deserves condemnation, and my repentance is not sufficient for satisfaction; but it is believed [Note: [Col. 0937] In Anselm: “it is certain.”] that your mercy surpasses every offense. Do not, I beg you, most merciful Lord, write my bitter things against me (Job 13:26), so that you may enter into judgment with your servant (Ps. 142:2); but according to the multitude of your mercies blot out my iniquity (Ps. 50:3). Woe to me, wretched that I am, when the day of judgment comes and the books of consciences are opened; when it is said of me: “Behold the man and his works.” What shall I do then, Lord my God, when the heavens reveal my iniquity and the earth rises against me? Behold, I shall be able to answer nothing, but with bowed head, out of shame, I shall stand before you trembling and confused. Woe to me, wretched that I am! What shall I say? I shall cry out to you, Lord my God. Why am I consumed in silence? Yet if I speak, my pain does not rest; and if I remain silent, I am inwardly tormented by the bitterest bitterness. Weep, my soul, like a widow over the husband of your youth; howl, wretched one, and weep, because your bridegroom, that is, Christ, has left you.

[Note: [Col. 0937] From the same author’s *Meditation* 2.] Anger of the Almighty, do not rush upon me, for you could never be contained by me. Certainly there is nothing in all of me capable of enduring you. Have mercy, lest I despair, but let me revive through hope. [Note: [Col. 0937] From the same author’s *Meditation* 3.] And although I have committed what gives you power to condemn me, you have not lost what you habitually use to save. Lord, you do not desire the death of sinners (Ezek. 33:11), nor do you rejoice in the destruction of the dying; rather, so that the dead might live, you died, and your death killed the death of sinners. And if they lived while you were dying, I beg you, Lord, let me not die while you live. Send your hand from on high and deliver me from the hand of my enemies, lest they exult over me and say: “We have devoured him” (Ps. 34:25). Who could ever distrust your mercy, good Jesus? When we were your enemies, you redeemed us in your blood and reconciled us to God (Rom. 5:10). Behold, protected beneath the shadow of your mercy, I run to the throne of glory, seeking pardon, crying out and knocking until you have mercy on me. For if you called us to pardon when we were not seeking pardon, how much more shall we obtain pardon when we ask for it?

[Note: [Col. 0938] Anselm, at the end of *Meditation* 3.] Do not remember, sweetest Jesus, your justice against your sinner; but remember your kindness toward your creature. Do not remember your anger against the guilty; but remember your mercy toward the wretched. [Note: [Col. 0938] Now from the end of *Meditation* 2.] Forget the proud man who provokes you, and look upon the wretched man who calls upon you. For what is Jesus except Savior? Therefore, Jesus, rise up through yourself to help me, and say to my soul: “I am your salvation” (Ps. 34:3). Lord, I presume greatly upon your goodness, because you yourself teach us to ask, seek, and knock (Matt. 7:7); and therefore, instructed by your prayer, I ask, seek, and knock. And you, Lord, who command us to ask, make me receive; you counsel us to seek, grant that I may find; you teach us to knock, open to the one who knocks. Strengthen me, the weak; restore me, the lost; raise me, the dead; and deign to direct and govern all my senses, thoughts, and actions according to your good pleasure, so that henceforth I may serve you, live for you, and surrender myself to you. I know, my Lord, that because you made me, I owe myself to you; and because you redeemed me and became human for me, I would owe you more than myself, if I had more to give, since you are greater than that which you gave—your very self. Behold, I have neither anything more nor even what I have can I give you without you; but take me yourself and draw me to yourself, so that I may be yours through imitation and love, just as I am yours by my created condition; for you live and reign forever.

## CHAPTER XL. He commends all that is his to God. He prays that vices be removed and virtues granted. He invokes the saints. He supplicates for all. Again he prays for himself and others.

Lord God almighty, who are three and one, who are always in all things, who were before all things and will always be in all things, blessed God forever: to you today and at all times I commend my soul, my body, my sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch, all my thoughts, afflictions, words, actions, all outward and inward things, my senses and understanding, my memory, my faith and belief, and my perseverance, into the hands of your power, so that you may guard them by days and nights, by hours and moments.

Hear me, holy Trinity, and preserve me from every evil, every scandal, and every mortal sin; from all the snares and assaults of demons and of visible and invisible enemies; through the prayers of the Patriarchs, the merits of the Prophets, the intercessions of the Apostles, the steadfastness of the martyrs, the faith of confessors, the chastity of virgins, and the intercession of all the saints who have pleased you from the beginning of the world. Drive from me the boasting of the mind and increase contrition of heart; lessen my pride and perfect true humility in me; awaken in me weeping; [Note: [Col. 0938] See above, chapter 35.] soften my hard and stony heart. Deliver me, Lord, and my soul from all the snares of the enemy, and preserve me in your will. Teach me, Lord, to do your will, because you are my God (Ps. 142:10). [Note: [Col. 0938] From Alcuin, *Book on the Sacraments*, chapter 1.] Give me, Lord, perfect sense and understanding, so that I may be able to receive your profound goodness. Give me the ability to ask for what it pleases you to hear and benefits me. Give me tears arising from my whole affection, which can dissolve the bonds of my sins. Hear, my Lord and my God, hear what I ask, and grant what I ask, that you may hear me. If you look away, I perish; if you look upon me, I live; if you seek my justice, I stink as one dead; if you look upon me with mercy, you raise the stinking one from the grave. Whatever you hate in me, remove far from me [Note: [Col. 0939] Add from Alcuin: “Drive away from me the enemy of lust.”], and implant in me the spirit of chastity and continence, so that in whatever I ask I may not offend you even in the asking. Take from me what harms me, and provide what helps me. Grant me, Lord, medicine by which my wounds may be healed. Give me, Lord, your fear, contrition of heart, humility of mind, and a clean conscience. [Note: [Col. 0939] Alcuin, column 295, under Jerome’s name.] Grant me, Lord, always to be able to maintain brotherly love, and not to forget my own evils or seek those of others. [Note: [Col. 0939] Alcuin, column 289, under Augustine’s name.] Spare my soul, spare my evils, spare my sins, spare my crimes. Visit me in my weakness, care for me in my sickness, heal me in my languor, and raise me, the dead. [Note: [Col. 0939] Again, column 232.] Give me, Lord, a heart that fears you, a mind that loves you, a sense that understands you, ears that hear you, and eyes that see you. Have mercy on me, God, have mercy on me, and look upon me from the holy seat of your majesty; illuminate the darkness of my heart with the ray of your splendor. Give me, Lord, discernment to distinguish between good and evil, and grant that I may possess an alert understanding. I ask you, Lord, for remission of all my sins, from whom and through whom propitiation may be made for me in the time of my need and distress.

Holy and immaculate Virgin Mary, Mother of God and Mother of our Lord Jesus Christ, deign to intercede for me with him whose temple you deserved to become. Holy Michael, holy Gabriel, holy Raphael, holy choirs of Angels and Archangels, Patriarchs and Prophets, Apostles, Evangelists, martyrs, confessors, priests, levites, monks, virgins, and all the righteous: through him who chose you and whose contemplation brings you joy, I dare to ask you to deign to supplicate God himself for me, the guilty one, so that I may deserve to be delivered from the jaws of the devil and from everlasting death. Deign, Lord, to bestow on me everlasting life, according to your clemency and most gracious mercy.

Grant, Lord Jesus Christ, concord to priests, and tranquility and peace to kings, bishops, and princes who judge justly. I pray, Lord, for the entire holy Catholic Church; for men and women; for religious and secular persons; for all rulers of Christians; and for all believers in you who labor for your holy love, that they may obtain perseverance in good works. Grant, eternal King, chastity to virgins, continence to those dedicated to God, holiness to the married, pardon to penitents, support to widows and orphans, protection to the poor, return to travelers, consolation to those who mourn, everlasting rest to the faithful departed, and to those at sea arrival in the harbor of salvation; [Note: [Col. 0939] Thus in Anselm, *Prayer* 1.] grant the best that they may always remain in goodness; the good and the mediocre, that they may become better; and those acting wickedly and offending, that they may quickly correct themselves.

O sweetest and most merciful Lord Jesus Christ, Son of the living God, Redeemer of the world, among all and in all things I confess myself a wretched sinner; but you, most merciful and supreme Father, who have mercy on all, do not allow me to become alienated from your mercy. And you, Lord, King of kings, who grant a reprieve for living, grant me the devotion to correct myself; awaken in me a mind that seeks you, desires you, and always loves you above all things—you who are everywhere wholly three and one—fears you, and does your will. Above all, [Col. 0940] therefore, I beseech you, holy Father, who are blessed and glorious forever, to deign mercifully to govern all who remember me in their prayers; those who have commended themselves to me in my unworthy prayers; those who have shown me any service of love or devotion of piety; and those who are close to me by blood and kinship—both those who now remain in the body and those who are covered by burial—so that they may not perish. Also deign to grant help to all living Christians, and absolution and everlasting rest to the faithful departed, throughout eternal ages.
