And I earnestly entreat this also, Lord, who are Alpha (α) and Omega (ω): when my final day and the end of my life arrive, may you yourself be a merciful judge for me against the wicked accuser, the devil; may you be my perpetual defender against the snares of the ancient enemy; and may you cause me to persevere in the fellowship of all the Angels and saints in your holy paradise, you who are blessed forever and ever. Amen.

## CHAPTER XLI. Thanksgiving and desire for love. He recalls God’s benefits in order to kindle love. Meditation on Christ’s passion and resurrection. Burning thirst for God.

[Note: [Col. 0940] Anselm, *Prayer* 20.] Lord Jesus Christ, my redemption, my mercy, my salvation, I praise you and give you thanks. Although greatly unequal to your benefits, although far from worthy devotion, although excessively thin from the desired fullness of your sweetest affection, nevertheless my soul offers you whatever praises and whatever thanks it can—not such as I know I ought to give, but as it is able to strive to give. Hope of my heart, strength of my soul, help of my weakness, may your most powerful goodness complete what my exceedingly lukewarm frailty attempts. My life, the end of my intention: although I have not yet deserved to love you as much as I am bound to love you, at least I desire to love you as much as I ought. My illumination, you see my conscience, for, Lord, before you is all my desire (Ps. 37:10), and you give whatever my conscience desires rightly. If what you inspire is good, Lord—indeed, because it is good that I wish to love you—give what you make me desire; grant that I may deserve to love you as much as you command. I praise and thank you for the desire you inspired. I offer praise and prayers lest your gift, which you freely gave, be fruitless for me. Perfect what you began; grant what, graciously going before me, you made me desire. Most merciful one, turn my tepidity into the most ardent love of you.

To this end, most merciful one, my prayer, my remembrance, and my meditation on your benefits are directed: that I may kindle your love within me. Your goodness, Lord, created me; your mercy cleansed me, once created, from original sin; your patience, after that cleansing in Baptism, has until now tolerated, nourished, and awaited me as I wallowed in other filth of sins. You, good Lord, await correction; my soul awaits the inspiration of your grace, so that I may repent sufficiently and live well. My God, my Creator, my Sustainer, and my Nourisher, be my helper. I thirst for you, I hunger for you, I desire you, I sigh for you, I long for you. And just as an orphan deprived of the presence of a most loving father, weeping and wailing, continually embraces his beloved face with his whole heart, so I too—though not as much as I ought, but as much as I can—remembering your passion, remembering your slaps, remembering your scourges, remembering the cross, remembering your wounds, remembering how you were killed for me, how you were taken down, how you were buried, and at the same time remembering your glorious resurrection and wondrous ascension, hold all these things by unwavering faith. I lament the sorrows of my exile, hope for the sole consolation of your coming, and ardently desire [Note: [Col. 0940] The manuscripts read: “I burn for the consolation of your coming,” etc.] the glorious contemplation of your face.

Woe is me, for I could not see the Lord of Angels humbled to share the life of human beings, so that he might exalt human beings to share the life of Angels, while the offended God died so that the sinner might live! Woe is me, for I did not deserve to be present and overwhelmed by such wondrous and immeasurable compassion! Why, my soul, did the sword of the sharpest grief not pierce you when you could not bear to see the side of your Savior wounded by the lance; when you could not endure seeing the hands and feet of your Creator violated by nails; when [Note: [Col. 0941] The Mettensis manuscript reads “why.”] you shuddered to see the blood of your Redeemer poured out? Why were you not drenched in the bitterness of tears when he was made to drink the bitterness of gall? Why did you not suffer with the most chaste Virgin, his most worthy mother, your most gracious Lady? My most merciful Lady, what fountains shall I say burst forth from your most modest eyes when you saw your only innocent son bound, scourged, and slaughtered before you? What weeping [Note: [Col. 0941] The Mettensis manuscript reads “floods.”] shall I believe washed over your most devout face when you saw that same one, both your God and Lord, stretched upon the cross without guilt, and flesh from your flesh cruelly cut apart by the wicked? With what sobs shall I estimate that your most pure breast was afflicted when you heard: “Woman, behold your son”; and to the disciple: “Behold your mother” (John 19:26–27)—when you received the disciple in place of the Master, the servant in place of the Lord? Would that, with blessed Joseph, I had taken my Lord down from the cross, embalmed him with spices, and placed him in the tomb—or at least followed or caught up with him, so that something of my service might not be absent from so great a funeral! Would that, with the blessed women, I had been terrified by the radiant vision of the Angels and had heard the announcement of the Lord’s resurrection, the announcement of my consolation, the announcement so long awaited, so greatly desired! Would that, I say, I had heard from the Angel’s mouth: “Do not be afraid. You seek Jesus the crucified; he has risen, he is not here” (Mark 16:6)! Most kind, sweetest, most serene one, when will you restore me, since I did not see that blessed incorruption of your flesh; since I did not kiss the places of your wounds and the marks of the nails; since I did not sprinkle with tears of joy the scars that testify to your true body? Wondrous, immeasurable, incomparable one, when will you console me and restrain me from my sorrow? For my sorrow cannot be contained within me as long as I am a pilgrim away from my Lord. Woe is me, Lord; woe to my soul! [Col. 0942] You have departed, comforter of my life, and did not say farewell to me! As you entered upon your ways, you blessed your own, but I was not present; you were received into heaven by a cloud with hands raised, but I did not see it (Luke 24:50–51); the Angels promised that you would return, but I did not hear it.

What shall I say? What shall I do? Where shall I go? Where shall I seek him? Where or when shall I find him? Whom shall I ask? Who will announce to the beloved that I am faint with love? The joy of my heart has failed; my laughter has turned into mourning. My flesh and my heart have failed; God is the God of my heart and my portion forever. My soul refuses to be consoled except by you, my sweetness. For what is there for me in heaven, and what have I desired from you upon earth? I desire you, I hope in you, I seek you. My heart has said to you: “I have sought your face; your face, Lord, I shall seek. Do not turn your face away from me.” Most gracious lover of humanity, to you the poor man is abandoned; you will be the helper of the orphan. My most secure advocate, have mercy on the abandoned orphan: I have become fatherless; my soul is like a widow. Look upon the tears of my bereavement and widowhood, which I offer to you until you return. Come now, Lord [Note: [Col. 0942] Alternatively: “Come now, Lord, come.”], appear to me and I shall be comforted; show your face and I shall be saved; present your presence and I shall obtain my desire; reveal your glory and my joy will be complete. My soul thirsted for you; how greatly my flesh thirsted for you (Ps. 62:2)! My soul thirsted for God, the living fountain: when shall I come and appear before the face of my God (Ps. 41:3)? When will you come, my comforter, whom I await? O, if only I might one day see the joy I desire! O, if only I might be satisfied when your glory appears (Ps. 16:15), for which I hunger! O, if only I might be intoxicated by the abundance of your house, for which I sigh; if only you might give me to drink from the torrent of your pleasure (Ps. 35:9), for which I thirst! Meanwhile, Lord, let my tears be my bread day and night, until it is said to me: “Behold your God” (Ps. 41:4); until I hear: “Soul, behold your bridegroom.” Meanwhile feed me with my sighs, give me drink with my weeping, refresh me with my sorrows. In the meantime perhaps my Redeemer will come, because he is good; and he will not delay, because he is merciful. To him be glory forever and ever. Amen.

## [ON CONTRITION OF HEART]

[Col. 0941]

## INTRODUCTORY NOTICE TO THE BOOK ON CONTRITION OF HEART

After examining the manuscript codices, we found in place of this little book a somewhat longer work which in them is falsely entitled *The Meditations of Blessed Augustine*. It begins with these words: “Come now, little man, flee for a while from earthly occupations”; and contains thirty-nine chapters, all extracted from works of Anselm, whether certainly or doubtfully his. In that work of the *Meditations*, this little book—which earlier editions of Augustine call *On Contrition of Heart*—is included in such a way that it begins with chapter eight of those *Meditations* and ends with chapter twenty-nine, seven initial and ten final chapters being omitted. We call these excerpted chapters selections from Anselm’s works, whether certainly or doubtfully his. For the work from which we have discovered that the aforementioned eighth chapter of the *Meditations* was taken—that is, Anselm’s *Meditation*, now numbered seventh, which Theophilus Raynaudus first published under Anselm’s name—is by no means sufficiently confirmed as Anselm’s by the authority of ancient codices, and contains certain sayings of Hugh of Saint-Victor from the books *On the Method of Praying* and *On the Earnest-Money of the Soul*. The rest, however, are drawn from Anselm’s *Proslogion* and from those works of his in which that distinctive character shines forth by which Anselm’s writings are commended by Durand, abbot of La Chaise-Dieu, in a letter among the Anselmian letters, book 1, 61: namely, that they are “published or derived from a contrite spirit and from the piety of a contrite heart.” In the very words of Durand, therefore, one would more appropriately call the following little book *Of the Contrite Heart* than *On Contrition of Heart*. Here you have it cleansed of countless errors with the aid of the manuscripts of the Royal Library, the Victorine Library, and the College of the Bernardines in Paris.

[Col. 0943]

# ONE BOOK ON CONTRITION OF HEART. (G, S)

## CHAPTER ONE. That contrition arises from consideration. Consideration of God’s benefits. Concerning the call to the Christian faith.

[Col. 0943]

[Note: [Col. 0943] From *Meditation* 7, no. 1, in Anselm; *On Spirit and Soul*, chapter 50; following Hugh of Saint-Victor, *On the Method of Praying*, chapter 1.] Nothing is more certain than death, nothing more uncertain than the hour of death. Let us therefore consider how brief our life is, how slippery the path, how certain death and how uncertain the hour of death. Let us consider how much bitterness is mixed into whatever sweetness or pleasure, on its passing, plays before us along the road of this life; how deceptive and suspect, how unstable and transitory is everything that the love of this world gives birth to, everything that temporal appearance or beauty promises. Let us also consider what sweetness and delight the heavenly homeland possesses; and let us observe and weigh from where we have fallen and where we lie, what we have lost and what we have found, so that from both we may understand how greatly we ought to mourn in this exile. For Solomon says: “He who adds knowledge adds also pain” (Eccles. 1:18), because the more a person understands his evils, the more he sighs and groans. Meditation indeed produces knowledge, knowledge contrition, contrition devotion, and devotion commends prayer. Through continual meditation a person is enlightened unto knowledge of himself; in contrition, through consideration of his evils, the heart is touched by inward sorrow.

[Note: [Col. 0943] Thus cited in Anselm, *Meditation*, no. 2; *On Spirit and Soul*, chapter 17; following Hugh, *On the Earnest-Money of the Soul*.] Wretched am I: how greatly ought I to love my God, who made me when I did not exist and redeemed me when I had perished? I did not exist, and he made me from nothing—not a tree, not a bird, not one of the animals, but he willed that I should be a human being; he gave me life, sensation, and discernment. I had perished, and the immortal one descended to mortal life; he underwent suffering, underwent death, and conquered, and thus restored me. Thus his grace and his mercy always went before me. My Deliverer also often freed me from many dangers. When I was wandering, he led me back; when I was ignorant, he taught me; when I was sinning, he corrected me; when I was sorrowful, he consoled me; when I was despairing, he strengthened me; when I fell, he raised me; when I stood, he held me; when I went, he guided me; when I came, he received me. These things and many others my God did for me, and it will always be sweet for me to speak of them, always to think of them, always to give thanks, so that for all his benefits I may be able to praise and love him. For all these things I have nothing with which to repay him except to love him; indeed, nothing better or more fitting can repay, through love, what was given through love.

[Note: [Col. 0943] From Anselm’s *Meditation* 11.] Consider, O man, what you were and what has been done for you; and weigh who did these things for you, and how worthy he is of love. Look upon your need and his goodness; and see what thanks you render and how much you ought to honor [Note: [Col. 0943] Elsewhere, “love.”] him. In darkness, on slippery ground, in a descent over the irretrievable chaos of hell, an immense and almost leaden weight hanging from your neck was dragging you downward, and an unbearable burden was pressing upon you from above. Invisible enemies were pushing you with all their might. Thus you were without any help, and you did not know that you had been conceived and born in such a condition.

I was in darkness, because I knew nothing—not even myself; on slippery ground, because I was weak and prone to the fall of sin. I was in descent, because over the chaos of hell the weight of original sin was pressing me downward, [Col. 0944] and my enemies, the demons, were violently assailing me in order to make me more liable to damnation through other sins. Thus, when I was deprived of every aid, you shone upon me, my God: you displayed the lead that was dragging me and the burden that was weighing me down, and you drove back the enemies who were pushing me. For you removed the sin in which I had been born and conceived, and the damnation [Note: [Col. 0944] Anselm adds, “its damnation.”]; and you prevented the evil spirits from doing violence to my soul.

You caused me to be called a Christian, from your name, by which I both confess you and you recognize me among your redeemed. You raised me up and lifted me to the knowledge and love of you; you caused me to trust in the salvation of my soul, for which you gave your own soul and promised me your glory if I should follow you. And behold, although I do not yet follow you as you instructed, and have even committed many sins that you forbade, you still wait for me to follow you and grant what you promised.

## CHAPTER II. That we owe ourselves wholly, and more than wholly, to God. A Petition for Love

[Note: [Col. 0944] From Anselm’s *Meditation* 11.] Consider, my soul; attend, all my inward parts, how much my whole substance owes him. Certainly, Lord, because you made me, I owe my entire self to your love; indeed, I owe your love more than myself, insofar as you are greater than I, and for me you gave yourself and promised yourself. Grant me, I beseech you, Lord, to taste through love what I taste through recognition; let me feel through affection what I perceive through understanding. I owe you more than my whole self; but I have nothing more, nor can I repay even what I have by myself in its entirety. Draw me, Lord, into your love; and make this whole being that I am—yours by creation—yours also by love.

Behold, Lord, my heart is before you; it strives to approach you [Note: [Col. 0944] In printed editions, *conatur* is absent; in the manuscripts, however, as also in Anselm, *accedere ad te* is absent.], but by itself it cannot. Do what it itself cannot do. Admit me into the chamber of your love: I ask, I seek, I knock. You who make me ask, make me receive; you give me to seek, grant me to find; you teach me to knock, open to the one who knocks. To whom do you give, if you deny the one who asks? Who finds, if the seeker is frustrated? To whom do you open, if you close to the one who knocks? What do you give to one who does not pray, if you deny your love to the one who prays?

From you I have the power to obtain this; I wish my soul to cling to you. Good Lord, my soul languishes from hunger for your love; revive it. May your affection heal it, your tenderness enrich it, your love fill it; may it occupy me wholly and possess me entirely.

[Note: [Col. 0944] Now from *Prayer* 21 and *Book of Meditations* 10.] I know, Lord—I know and confess—that I am not worthy for you to love me; but certainly you are not unworthy of the service of your creature. Therefore, Lord, give me that by which you are worthy, and I shall be worthy of that by which I am unworthy. Make me cease from sins in whatever way you wish, so that in whatever way I ought [Note: [Col. 0944] The manuscripts read, “wish.”] I may serve you. Grant that I may guard, govern, and complete my life in such a way that I may sleep in peace and rest in you. At the end grant me that sleep may receive me with rest, rest with security, security [Note: [Col. 0944] Anselm reads, “fullness,” and “fullness.”] with eternity. Amen.

## CHAPTER III. Desire for God

[Note: [Col. 0944] Anselm, *Prayer* 2, which is the same as *Prayer* 20; *Book of Meditations* 41, but in a more abbreviated form.] Lord Jesus Christ, my redeemer, my mercy, my salvation, I praise you; I give you thanks. Your goodness, Lord, created me; your mercy cleansed me from original sin; your patience, after that cleansing, has until now endured, nourished, and awaited me as I wallowed in the other filth of sins. [Col. 0945]

Lord my God, my creator, my helper, I thirst for you, I hunger for you, I desire you, I sigh for you, I long for you. Most kind, most sweet, most serene, I want you, I seek you, I hope in you. My soul refuses to be consoled by anything except you, my sweetness. Come now, Lord, appear to me, and I shall be comforted; show me your face, and I shall be saved; make your presence manifest, and my desire shall be fulfilled; reveal your glory, and my joy shall be complete.

My soul thirsted for you; how greatly my flesh thirsted for you (Ps. 62:2). When will you come, my comforter, whom I await? O that I might someday see my joy, which I desire! O that I might be satisfied when his glory appears (Ps. 16:15), for which I hunger! O that I might be intoxicated by the abundance of your house, for which I sigh! O that you might give me drink from the torrent of your delight (Ps. 35:9), for which I thirst!

Give me, Lord, in this exile, the bread of sorrow and tears, which I hunger for above every abundance of delights. Let my tears, Lord, meanwhile be my bread day and night, until it is said to me, “Behold your God” (Ps. 41:4); until I hear, “Behold your bridegroom.” Feed me, Lord, meanwhile with my sobs; revive me with my sorrows.

## CHAPTER IV. The Misery of a Depraved Conscience. Humble Confession. The Foulness and Fruit of Sin

[Note: [Col. 0945] From Anselm’s *Prayers* 62 and 72.] My God, what sort of person have I made myself? What was I like? God, what sort of person did you make me, and what sort of person have I made myself again? For I was conceived and born in sins, and you washed me; you sanctified me, and I defiled myself with worse sins. I was then born under necessity; now I have wallowed in voluntary sins.

Woe to me, wretched and exceedingly wretched! Exceedingly wretched is the one whom his conscience torments and from which he cannot flee! Exceedingly wretched is the one whose damnation awaits him and which he cannot escape! Exceedingly unhappy is the one who is horrible to himself; still more unhappy is the one for whom eternal death will be perceptible. Exceedingly miserable is the one whom continual horrors concerning his unhappiness terrify [Note: [Col. 0945] Anselm reads, “foulness.”]; still more miserable is the one whom eternal pains for his iniquity will torment.

This is evil, and this is evil; but this is exceedingly so, and this exceedingly so [Note: [Col. 0945] Elsewhere, “this is lesser and that is greater.”]. How bitter and evil a thing it is to sin! O sins, how easy your entrances, how difficult your exits! While you persuade, you anoint; after you have persuaded, you go on pricking even unto the death of the soul. The sinners whom you lead in, you shut up within yourselves as though in skins [Note: [Col. 0945] Anselm: “Sinners, into whom do you lead them? Within what bars do you shut them?”—Erasmus, Lyons, Venice, and Louvain read this passage as follows: “O sins, how easy your entrances are while you persuade, and how difficult your exits will be! While you persuade, you anoint; but after you have persuaded, you prick even unto the death of the soul. The stinking things whom you lead in, you shut up into skins of iniquity.” M.].

Understand, you who sin, that it is evil and bitter to abandon God; return, and do not sin; do not, I say, do not. Truly it is evil and bitter: I have experienced it; I am in this very condition. For either continual pains will torture my penitent life, or eternal torments will afflict my soul when it is punished. Certainly both are evil and bitter; free me from both.

My soul, above all things, and as the mother of virtues, I warn you: beware lest, in recalling your evils, you fall into any of the devil’s snares, into which many unwary people fall. While they bring their evils back before the eyes of the mind as though weeping over them, through those very recollections they foolishly fall into the pleasures of the evils themselves.

[Note: [Col. 0945] Anselm, *Prayer* 15.4.] More often, when I begin speaking with someone without any useful purpose, I immediately fall into slander; or thoughtlessly swear about some matter; or succumb to the vice of foolish curiosity; or endure within my inmost self the foulness of evil thoughts and illicit, shameful impulses. Alas, [Col. 0946] for such great unhappiness, such great ruin! For while I wish, forgetting what lies behind, to stretch toward what lies ahead, I suddenly see myself, through some misery I do not understand, slipping back into empty and harmful things. And as though sudden death intervened, or like a rabid dog that does not restrain itself from tearing a man even after being struck, carnal pleasure pierces my mind; and instead of the sweet fragrance of virtues I sense the intolerable and most dreadful stench of inward vices.

I confess, sweetest Lord Jesus, and I lay before you all the iniquities that I endure within my soul. These, then, are my eleven evils: anger, impatience, hateful discord—hostile to God and all the saints—indignation, resentment of spirit, weariness of mind, ravenous gluttony, murmuring, desire for pleasure, delight of the flesh, and the storm of lust; together with many similar things by which my unhappy soul is harassed and afflicted, torn and mangled.

[Note: [Col. 0946] Anselm’s *Meditation* 2 and *Prayer* 72.] O how much more tolerably does a putrid dog stink to human beings than a sinful soul does to God—and how much more unhappily does this soul stink to God than that dog to human beings! My soul, fruitless tree, where are your fruits? Such a tree is worthy of the axe and fire, worthy to be cut down and burned (Matt. 3:10). What are your fruits? Surely they are pricking thorns and bitter sins. Would that, by repenting, they might prick you so that they pierced you [Note: [Col. 0946] Anselm reads, “so that they might be broken.” But the manuscripts read, “thus to those confessing.”]; might become so bitter that they vanished.

Perhaps you think some sin is a small thing. But alas! Does not every sin dishonor God through transgression? How depraved, then, is what dishonors God? Will the sinner dare to consider any sin small? Good Lord Jesus, why did you come from heaven? What did you do for the world? Why did you give yourself over to death? Was it not to save sinners, of whom I am the greatest?

## CHAPTER V. An Appeal for Divine Mercy. The Enemies of Man

[Note: [Col. 0946] Again from *Meditation* 2 and 3, and *Prayer* 63.] Breathe, then, O sinner, breathe; do not despair. Hope in the one whom you fear; flee to the one from whom you fled; call insistently upon the one whom you arrogantly provoked. Jesus, for the sake of your name, deal with me according to your name. Jesus, forget the proud man who provokes you; look upon the wretched man who invokes your sweet name, your delightful name, the name that strengthens the sinner, and the name of blessed hope.

For what is “Jesus” but “Savior”? Therefore, for your own sake, be Jesus to me; be my gracious savior. Do not, Lord, do not regard my evil in such a way that you forget your own goodness, O good Lord. And if I have committed what enables you to condemn me, have you then lost what enables you to save? For if I have deprived myself of my chastity, have I destroyed your mercy?

It is true that my conscience deserves damnation, and my repentance is insufficient for satisfaction; but it is certain that your mercy surpasses every offense. Therefore spare me, Lord, who are salvation; and since you do not desire the death of the sinner, have mercy on my sinful soul, loose its bonds, and heal its wounds.

Behold, merciful Lord, I present my soul before you: loosened from the sinews of virtues, bound with chains of vices, weighed down by the burden of sins, befouled by the filth of offenses, split open by the wounds of demons, putrid and foul with the ulcers of crimes; overwhelmed, oppressed, surrounded, and enveloped by these and other grave evils, which you see better than I do, and deprived of every relief from good things. Behold how great a misery constricts me: help, succor me, O all-encompassing mercy!

[Note: [Col. 0946] From *Prayers* 3 and 70.] Alas, wretched man that I am, alas, wretched, always and everywhere wretched! How great is the captivity of miserable man! If a man lives badly, damnation is open before him; if he appears indeed to live rightly, but guards himself carelessly and takes pride in it, once again certain death and eternal damnation await the wretched man.

These are the enemies of miserable man: pride, envy, and empty glory, which defile and attack the unhappy man; [Col. 0947] and unless God’s mercy protects him, he is often wounded even unto death. Free me, Lord, from these enemies of mine, from whom I cannot free myself.

For my heart is perverse and exceedingly wicked: toward lamenting my sins already committed it is stony and dry; toward resisting present assaults [Note: [Col. 0947] So Anselm. But the manuscripts read, “insults.” The printed editions read, “those who insult.”] it is soft and muddy; toward handling useless and harmful things it is swift and tireless; toward thinking about what is salutary it is disgusted and immobile.

My soul, twisted and depraved, is exceedingly ready and eager to plunge and wallow in vices; toward remembering salvation it is exceedingly difficult and sluggish. It would take too long to enumerate each vice: gluttony, sleepiness, frivolity, impatience, vainglory, slander, disobedience, and the other vices by which my unhappy soul has become the daily object of mockery, by which it is distracted, trampled, and destroyed.

Free it, Lord; unload it, buried beneath the mass of sins. Loosen it, bound with the ropes of offenses; release it, entangled in crimes; raise it when it lies fallen; support it when it totters; equip it with spiritual arms when it is unarmed by virtues; cover and protect it when it fights; overcome the one who attacks it.

Good Jesus, see my humiliation and my labor, and forgive all my offenses. Be my helper; do not abandon me or despise me, but teach me to do your will. May my soul testify to what my mouth willingly confesses. Help me, merciful, kind, and compassionate Lord, more than I am able to imagine, so that I may feel this no less than I presume to hope.

## CHAPTER VI. The Perils of the Sinner

[Note: [Col. 0947] Anselm, *Prayer* 67.] O my sins, you are exceedingly great; you are exceedingly many [Note: [Col. 0947] Erasmus, Lyons, Venice, and Louvain present this passage as follows: “O my sins, you are very great; you are exceedingly many!” M.]! The judge is terrifyingly strict, unevenly severe, immoderately offended, vehemently angry; the sentence is unchangeable; the prison is inescapable; the torments are without interruption and without mitigation; the torturers are horrifying, never growing weary and never showing mercy. Fear disturbs the guilty; conscience confounds him; thoughts reproach him. There is no permission to flee.

Behold the danger in which I constantly stand—except that I do not always think about it; and I am all the more wretched and pitiable because I can forget it [Note: [Col. 0947] The Royal Manuscript adds, “not.”]. For God always sees me and my sins; the strict sentence is always pronounced against me; hell is always open and torments prepared; invisible plotters are always ready to snatch my wretched soul there.

Such am I when I am awake; such am I when I sleep; such am I when I laugh; such am I when I rejoice; such am I when I am proud; such am I when I slander; such am I when I grow angry; such am I when I grieve; such am I when I embrace the bodily pleasures of the wretched flesh! In short, such am I always and everywhere. Alas, wretched me—and where am I, and where am I not [Note: [Col. 0947] Two manuscripts read, “now.”]—since I do not know where I am safe?

## CHAPTER VII. The Bonds, Prison, and Darkness of Sins

[Note: [Col. 0947] What follows through chapter 10 is from Anselm’s *Prayer* 69.] Woe to me, wretched man, what shall I do? Alas, how long my mind has languished; how greatly my heart has been hardened by stupor; how greatly my soul has been blocked by torpor! What is it that hinders me so? What is it that presses my neck so heavily?

My soul wishes, Lord, wishes to lift its face toward you, but burdened with a leaden weight it is weighed down; it strives to free itself, but is bound by iron chains; it attempts to escape, but is shut up in a bronze prison; it desires to direct its gaze toward you, but is darkened by murky shadows.

What are these things, my God, that thus darken and weigh down my soul, close and bind it? Perhaps these are my sins; indeed, these truly are my sins—certainly these are. Carnal affection has dulled in me the taste for spiritual things; attention to lower things has bent my soul away from contemplating higher things; love of earthly things has extinguished in me delight in heavenly things; the practice of vices has emptied [Note: [Col. 0947] The manuscripts read, “has vanished.”] from me the perception of true gifts [Note: [Col. 0948] Anselm reads, “goods”; and shortly afterward, “goods.”].

I have been distanced from those gifts and occupied with these evils; shut out from the former and enclosed in the latter; rolled away from the former and wrapped up in the latter. Hence come that prison and those bonds; hence those darknesses and weights. Woe to me, for the day of wrath is near—near, I say! It has suddenly come unknown, and perhaps it will be today.

## CHAPTER VIII. That the Sinner Is a Blind Man Who Sees

My sins, were you destined to be so harmful when you watered my soul with your sweetness, when you anointed my heart with your sweetness? Why did you conceal these things from me, and why did you hand me over? No, you did not hand me over; I handed myself over, because I trusted you. You did not deceive me; I deceived myself, because I welcomed you within me.

Alas, why did I place faith in you? Why did I trust you? No, I neither had faith in you nor trusted you; but, in a dreadful way, being blind though seeing, I handed myself over to you. Seeing, because I recognized you and knew the evils that follow you; blind, because I did not beware of you.

O sin, horrifying name, detestable reality, incomparable with any evil! A blind man does not see the pit into which he falls; a madman thinks he ought to do what he does. Whoever commits sin willingly, seeing and knowing, delivers himself over to ruin.

Death and every kind of torment are merely torments, and are not foul in themselves, because they are ordered; sin possesses its own foulness and draws eternal unhappiness along with it. For it would have been better to choose a torment [Note: [Col. 0948] Add from Anselm, “eternal.”] that does not in itself attract eternal foulness than sin, which joins eternal pains to its own foulness.

And certainly, O wretched man, the foulness of sin itself is more to be avoided than any enormity of torments. For in sinning, with the foulest perversity, you placed yourself before your Creator—nothing could be more unjust. In enduring the torments of sins, created being submits itself, in the fairest order, to its Creator—nothing could be more just.

O man, where has your humanity vanished? Where has your reason gone? You had learned that whoever commits sin is a slave of sin (John 8:34), and yet you committed sin. O unheard-of insanity, to sin knowingly! You knew that you are a spirit going away and not returning (Ps. 77:39), and you cast yourself into the irretrievable and bottomless abyss of sin.

## CHAPTER IX. On the Threefold Abyss

Truly, my sins are an abyss, because they are incomprehensible in weight and depth and immeasurable in number and vastness. “Abyss calls to abyss”! O my sins, the torments that you keep in store for me are also an abyss, because they are infinite and wholly incomprehensible.

There is also a third abyss, and it is exceedingly terrible: “the abyss of the judgments of God is great” (Ps. 35:7), because it is hidden beyond human understanding. Woe upon woe [Note: [Col. 0948] The manuscripts read, “to me.”], fear upon fear, pain upon pain. “Abyss calls to abyss at the sound of your cataracts” (Ps. 41:8), because the abyss of sin merits the abyss of torments, as God’s judgments declare.

The abyss of God’s judgments is above me; the abyss of hell is beneath me; the abyss of sins is within me. I fear that the one above may fall upon me and overwhelm me, together with my abyss, in the one that lies open beneath me—where torments will never erase sins, but sins will hold torments over me.

Wretched am I, against whom I have sinned! Where have I gone from your Spirit, and where have I fled from your face? Certainly, even though I wickedly fled from you and hid myself in my damnable abyss, there too you see me. For who but you moved my soul to repentance [Note: [Col. 0948] Elsewhere, “to resistance.”]?

Good Lord, you knocked upon it and awakened it in the abyss of its offenses, as though it were sleeping in a bed [Note: [Col. 0948] The manuscripts read, “in mud.”]; you shook it when it was torpid; you stirred it when it was negligent; you made it repent of what had delighted it and grieve over what had pleased it. Good God, you did all these things in the abyss.

Hear, then, the one crying out from the abyss. Most kind Lord, I do not hide my sins from you; I do not defend them before you, but display them; I do not excuse them, [Col. 0949] but accuse them. I am the guilty one; I myself am my accuser. Do not accuse me, you who made me. I alone was sufficient for sinning; I alone shall suffice for accusing myself, and I alone for repenting.

## CHAPTER X. The Feelings of the Penitent

[Note: [Col. 0949] Up to this point from the said *Prayer* 69; now from *Meditations* 3 and 2.] But from where, my God, shall correction for such great crimes come, and from where satisfaction for such great offenses against you? Hurl yourself, then, wretched little man, into the depths of immoderate sorrow—you who willingly hurled yourself into the abyss of dreadful wickedness. Bury yourself, unhappy man, beneath the mass of terrible grief—you who gladly fell into the filth of infernal stench. Wrap yourself, miserable man, once more in the horrifying darkness of inconsolable mourning—you who willingly rolled yourself into the chasm of so foul a torrent [Note: [Col. 0949] Anselm reads, “luxury.”].

Roll about in the whirlpool of bitterness—you who took delight in the mire of disgrace. Horrifying terror, terrible pain, inconsolable grief: gather over me, rush upon me, overwhelm me, disturb me, envelop me, possess me. It is just, it is just: torment the guilty man; avenge God. Let the fornicator feel the torments of hell that he deserved; let him taste in advance what he prepared, drink what he nourished, become accustomed to what he is going to suffer.

Consolation, health, joy—I do not want you, unless perhaps forgiveness of sin should bring you back. Keep far away before death, unless indulgence should call you back to me before death. It is impossible for a sinner not to weep, either here or in the future. Let repentance therefore be continual, the bitter companion of my life; continual pain, the insatiable torturer of my life. Let sorrow and bitter mourning be tireless torturers [Note: [Col. 0949] The Royal Manuscript reads, “terrors”; Anselm, “tribulations.”] of my youth and old age.

Would that it were so; I pray and desire that it be so. For if I am not worthy to lift my eyes toward heaven in prayer before you, Lord God, certainly I am not unworthy [Note: [Col. 0949] Elsewhere, “worthy.”] to blind them even by weeping. If my mind is confounded by the shame of conscience, it is right that it be confounded by the storm of mournful pain and sadness. If it fears being presented before the sight of the Lord its God, it is just that it have before its own sight the torments of its crime.

Breathe, O sinner, breathe at last, and flee to the very God whom you offended. Flee, I say, from the angry one to the appeased one.

## CHAPTER XI. An Appeal for God’s Mercy

[Note: [Col. 0949] Again from *Meditations* 3, 11, and 2; see *Book of Meditations* 40 and Anselm’s *Prayer* 72.]

Remember, just and kind God, remember that you are merciful and my creator. If you are judge in judging your guilty one, you are also Lord in protecting your servant; you are creator in preserving your work; you are God in saving your believing and baptized servant. Do not, then, good Lord, remember only your justice against your sinner; but remember your kindness toward your creature. Do not remember your anger against the guilty; but remember your compassion toward the wretched.

I know and confess that it is true: my conscience deserves damnation, and my repentance is insufficient for satisfaction. Therefore spare me, good Lord, who are salvation, who do not desire the death of a sinner (Ezek. 33:11); spare my sinful soul, God.

In you I place my hope, and to you I entrust my soul. Guard it while I sleep; preserve it while I do something else; and watch over it. Remember it while I forget it. I am a sinner; I am wretched. But I grieve that I have sinned, and I recognize that I am wretched. Merciful God, have mercy on me in my humility.

To sin is to dishonor God—something a man ought not to do, even if it were necessary for everything that is not God to perish. Alas, alas! I have sinned; I have dishonored God; I have provoked the Almighty. Sinner, what have I done? What evils have I done? Woe to the one who does evil; woe to the one who neglects good! Woe, woe!

Anger of almighty God, do not rush upon me. Anger of the Almighty, where could you be contained in me? There is nothing in all of me that could endure you. God, whose goodness is not exhausted, whose mercy is not emptied, whose knowledge does not fail, whose power accomplishes whatever he wills: from where shall I be able to breathe, since because of my sins I am forced to despair?

For even if you are angry with sinners, you nevertheless customarily give kind counsel to those who ask. Teach me, Lord, from where I ought to hope, so that I may be able to pray [Note: [Col. 0950] The printed editions add here, “to be saved.”]. For I wish to; but I neither know how, because of my ignorance, nor can I, because of my hardness [Note: [Col. 0950] Here the Royal Manuscript adds, “I am prevented from hoping.”]; because of my iniquity I am forced to despair.

I know and confess that I deservedly suffer what I willingly undertook, and that I am rightly not heard because I did not obey. Certainly, good Lord, I have sinned; I have gone astray. Yet I neither hate you nor detest your goodness. Therefore [Note: [Col. 0950] Here the Royal Manuscript adds, “I am prevented from hoping.”] deal with me according to your mercy, you who are blessed forever and ever [Note: [Col. 0950] These final words—from “therefore” through “forever and ever”—are absent from the manuscripts.]

# [MANUALE]

[Col. 0949]

## NOTICE CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING BOOK

This *Manual* has been circulated under the name not only of Augustine but also, in part, of Anselm and of Hugh of Saint-Victor. The first twenty-four chapters, in particular, are found in Hugh’s fourth book *On the Soul*. In Anselm, the first nine chapters constitute *Prayer* 14, to which the title *Manual* itself has been prefixed.

An uncertain author collected this little work from various places, perhaps the same author whose effort we think produced several of the books above—namely, *On the Spirit and the Soul* and *On Loving God*—so far as one may conjecture from comparing the works with one another. Here he employs many sayings of Augustine, as well as some of Cyprian, Gregory, and Isidore; but he drew them not from their genuine sources, rather from less pure streams.

The first part of the *Manual*, namely the prologue and chapters one and two, the author copied from the book that follows immediately here, called the *Mirror*. He extracted the second part, from chapter three to approximately the middle of chapter twelve, from an unpublished prayer in the old Metz manuscript mentioned above in the notice concerning the book of *Meditations*. In that manuscript, which contains the prayers of John of Fécamp and of Abbot William, the prayer appears under this title: “A beautiful prayer compiled through contemplation, or a theoretical meditation.”

Certainly, in this prayer the sentences are fuller than in the *Manual* that follows here and are more closely connected with one another. This is evidence that the prayer was not taken from the *Manual* itself, but rather the reverse. For example, what is stated here briefly in chapter 4—“May my heart rest in you,” and so forth—is explained better and more fully in the said prayer as follows:

“May my heart rest in you, my heart, a great sea swelling with the waves of pride. Because you commanded the winds and the sea, command it so that all my inward parts may become tranquil, so that I may contemplate you, my sweet joy, for which I hunger and thirst, without the noise of the inner man and without the tumult of worldly concerns. Behold my mind, my friendly mind, weary as it comes from the road of thoughts, divided by many things from the very vanities it had passed through, suffering a dangerous hunger. I have nothing to place before it; I am poor and needy. O rich giver of all good things and most abundant bestower of the food of heavenly satiety, and so forth.”

Likewise, concerning the statement in chapter 12, “Let the soul itself also be silent to itself and pass beyond itself, not thinking about itself,” the aforementioned prayer continues more appropriately:

“You, my God, speak to me alone—not through the things you have made—so that apart from these I may hear you,” and so forth.

This part of the *Manual* contains several words of Bernard that are absent from the prayer in the Metz manuscript, which, unless we are mistaken, was written before Bernard. Because of these words of Bernard, as well as certain others of Alcuin, the fourteenth prayer of Anselm itself, which we mentioned above and in which these words occur, will not unjustly appear spurious and interpolated.

The remaining parts of this *Manual* were drawn from various sources: some, such as chapters sixteen and seventeen, from sermon 209 of the appendix to volume five; others, namely the following eight chapters, from Bernard’s sermons; then, from Hugh of Saint-Victor, what is found from chapter twenty-six through chapter thirty; finally, the last part was taken from Anselm’s *Proslogion*.

Moreover, the old manuscript codices—which we have examined in considerable number—by no means agree sufficiently either with the printed editions or with one another. Some contain more, others fewer passages; most, however, insert certain material absent from the printed editions, extracted from Augustine, Bernard, Hugh of Saint-Victor, or from the books *On the Spirit and the Soul* and *On Loving God*, as well as from the *Meditations* circulated under Bernard’s name. In the end, scarcely one manuscript contains the final chapters: the Royal Codex. Yet even it omits almost the whole of chapters twenty-six and twenty-seven.

[Col. 0951]

# MANUAL, ONE BOOK. (G,S)

## PREFACE. The Purpose of This Work. Invocation of God

[Note: [Col. 0951] From the end of the book *On the Mirror*; see the book of *Meditations*, chapter 22; Augustine, *Confessions* 1.2.] Because we are placed in the midst of snares, we easily grow cold toward heavenly desire. Therefore we constantly need a reminder, so that, awakened to our true and highest good, God, we may return when we have drifted away. For this reason, not through the rash presumption of self-confidence, but rather through love for my God, I devoted myself to this little work in his praise, so that from the more elegant sayings of the holy Fathers I might always have with me a brief and portable word concerning my God, and so that, whenever I grow lukewarm, I might be kindled to his love by the fire of reading it.

Now be present to me, my God, whom I seek, whom I love, whom I confess with heart and mouth, and whom with whatever strength I possess I praise and adore. My mind, devoted to you, kindled by your love, sighing for you, yearning for you, desiring to see you alone, finds nothing sweet except speaking about you, hearing about you, writing about you, conversing about you, and frequently turning your glory over in its heart, so that the sweet memory of you may be some rest for me amid these storms.

Therefore I invoke you, most greatly desired one; to you I cry out with a great cry in my whole heart. And when I invoke you, I invoke you within myself, for I would not exist at all unless you were in me; and unless I were in you, you would not be in me. You are in me because you remain in my memory: from it I came to know you, and in it I find you when I remember you, and in you I delight because of you, from whom all things exist, through whom all things exist, and in whom all things exist.

## CHAPTER I. God’s Attributes

[Note: [Col. 0951] From the book *On the Mirror*, chapters 4–8, 21, and 22; from Augustine, *Confessions* 1.4.] You, Lord, fill heaven and earth, carrying all things without burden, filling all things without confinement, always active, always at rest, gathering and needing nothing, seeking although nothing is lacking to you, loving without agitation, jealous and secure, repenting without sorrow, [Col. 0952] growing angry while remaining tranquil. You change your works but do not change your plan; you receive what you find and have never lost anything; you are never needy, yet you rejoice in gains; you are never greedy, yet you demand interest. You give more than is owed to one to whom you owe nothing, or more is always given to you so that you become a debtor—and who possesses anything that is not yours?

You repay debts while owing nothing; you give gifts without losing anything. You who are everywhere and wholly everywhere; who can be sensed but cannot be seen; who are absent nowhere, yet are far from the thoughts of the wicked; who are not absent even where you are far away, because where you are not present by grace, you are present by vengeance.

You who are present everywhere and can scarcely be found; whom we follow while you stand still, yet cannot grasp. You who hold all things, fill all things, embrace all things, surpass all things, and sustain all things. You who teach the hearts of the faithful without the noise of words. You who are not extended through places, nor varied by times, nor subject to coming and going. You who dwell in inaccessible light, which no human being has seen or can see (1 Tim. 6:16).

Remaining quiet in yourself, you encompass the whole everywhere. For you cannot be cut up or divided, because you are truly one; nor are you made into parts. Rather, wholly you hold the whole, and wholly you fill, illumine, and possess the whole.

## CHAPTER II. On the Same Subject
If books filled the whole world, your ineffable knowledge could not be narrated. Since you are unspeakable, you can in no way be written down or confined. You are the fountain of divine light and the sun of eternal splendor. You are great without quantity and therefore immeasurable; good without quality and therefore truly and supremely good. No one is good except you alone, whose will is the work, whose willing is power, who by your sole will made all things that you created from nothing. You possess your entire creation without any need, govern it without labor, and rule it without weariness; and there is nothing that disturbs the order of your dominion, whether in the highest or in the lowest things. You are found in every place without being located, contain all things without spatial enclosure, and are present everywhere without position or movement. You are not the author of evil, which you cannot do, though you can do all things; and you have never regretted having done anything. By your goodness we were made; by your justice we suffer punishments; by your mercy we are freed. Your omnipotence governs, rules, and fills all that it has created.

Nor do we say that you fill all things because they contain you; rather, they themselves are contained by you. You do not fill all things piece by piece, nor should it be thought in any way that each thing receives you according to the size of its portion—that the greatest receives more and the smallest less—since you yourself are rather in all things, and all things are in you. Your omnipotence encloses all things, and no one will be able to find a way of escape from your power. For whoever does not have you reconciled to him will by no means escape you when you are angry.

## CHAPTER III. The Desire for God and Its Effects

[Note: [Col. 0953] Here begins an excerpt from an unpublished prayer in the manuscript of Metz.]

Therefore I call upon you, most merciful God, within my soul, which you prepare to receive you through the desire that you inspire in it. Enter it, I beg you, and fit it to yourself, so that you may possess the soul that you made and remade; so that I may have you like a seal upon my heart. I beseech you, most holy Lord, do not abandon me as I call upon you—you who, before I called upon you, called me and sought me—so that I, your servant, might seek you, find you by seeking, and love you once found.

[Note: [Col. 0953] Up to the note marked (d), these words do not belong to the cited prayer.]

I sought you and found you, Lord, and I desire to love you. Increase my desire and grant what I ask; for even if you were to give me everything that you have made, it would not be enough for your servant unless you gave yourself.

[Note: [Col. 0953] Augustine, *Confessions*, Book 13, chapter 8.]

Give yourself, then, to me, my God; give yourself back to me. Behold, I love you; and if that is too little, let me love you more strongly. I am held by your love, I burn with desire for you, and I delight in the sweet memory of you. Behold, while my mind sighs for you and meditates upon your ineffable goodness, the burden of the flesh weighs less heavily, the tumult of thoughts ceases, and the burden of mortality and misery no longer dulls me as usual. All things are silent; everything is tranquil. The heart burns, the spirit rejoices, memory is vigorous, understanding shines, and the whole spirit, kindled by the desire to see you, sees itself carried away by love of invisible things.

[Note: [Col. 0953] Likewise in the *Book of Meditations*, chapter 37.]

May my spirit take the wings of an eagle; may it fly and not grow weary, fly and reach the beauty of your house and the throne of your glory, so that there, above the table of refreshment of the heavenly citizens, it may feed upon your hidden things, in a pastureland beside the fullest-flowing streams. Be our exultation, you who are our hope, salvation, and redemption; be our joy, you who are to be our reward. May my soul always seek you, and grant that it may not grow weary in seeking.

## CHAPTER IV. The Misery of the Soul That Does Not Love Christ

Woe to the wretched soul that neither seeks nor loves Christ; it remains dry and miserable.

[Note: [Col. 0953] Up to “I shall reign and be blessed,” these words are absent from the cited prayer. They are largely taken from Bernard, *Sermon 20 on the Song of Songs*, no. 1.]

He loses the life he lives who does not love you, God. Whoever cares to live not for you, Lord, is nothing and is for nothing; whoever refuses to live for you is dead; whoever does not taste you is without understanding. Most merciful Lord, to you I commend, restore, and surrender myself, through whom I am, live, and understand. In you I trust and hope, and in you I place all my hope, through whom I shall rise again, live, and rest. I desire, love, and adore you, with whom I shall remain, reign, and be blessed.

The soul that does not seek or love you loves the world, serves sins, and is subject to vices; it is never at peace, never secure. May my mind always serve you, most holy Lord; may my pilgrimage always sigh for you; may my heart burn with your love; may my soul rest in you, my God; may it contemplate you in spiritual ecstasy and sing your praises with jubilation. May this be my consolation in this exile of mine.

[Note: [Col. 0953] See the *Book of Meditations*, chapter 37.]

May my mind flee beneath the shadow of your wings from the heats of the thoughts of this age. May my heart rest in you—my heart, a great sea swelling with waves. O rich possessor of all good things, most lavish giver of the abundance of heavenly satisfaction,

[Col. 0954] God,

[Note: [Col. 0954] Erasmus, Lyons, Venice, and Louvain read: “O rich possessor of all good and heavenly delights, most lavish giver, God!” Manuscript M.]

give food to the weary, gather up what is scattered, free the captive, and restore what has been torn apart. Behold, he stands at the door and knocks. I beseech you, by the depths of your mercy with which you visited us, rising from on high, command that the wretched man who knocks be allowed to enter, so that with free steps he may come in to you, rest in you, and be refreshed by you with heavenly bread. For you are the bread and fountain of life; you are the light of eternal splendor; you are all things from which the righteous who love you live.

## CHAPTER V. A Prayer Inviting God into Oneself

God, light of hearts that see you, life of souls that love you, and strength

[Note: [Col. 0954] In the prayer of the Metz manuscript, the words “marrying minds and bosoms” are added here; shortly afterward it reads “may they cling,” with the verb “make” omitted.]

of thoughts that seek you, make me cling to your holy love. Come, I beg you, into my heart, and intoxicate it with the abundance of your delight, so that I may forget these temporal things. I am ashamed and distressed to suffer the things that this world inflicts. What I see is grievous to me; everything I hear concerning transitory things is burdensome. Help me, Lord my God, and give joy to my heart; come to me, so that I may see you.

But

[Note: [Col. 0954] Augustine, *Confessions*, Book 1, chapter 5; see the *Book of Meditations*, chapter 35.]

the house of my soul is too narrow for me until you come to it and enlarge it through yourself; it is ruined—restore it. It has very much that offends your eyes, I confess and know it; but who will cleanse it? Or to whom else besides you shall I cry, “Cleanse me from my hidden faults, Lord, and spare your servant from those of others” (Psalm 18:14)?

Make me, sweet Christ, good Jesus, make me, I beg you, lay down, through love and desire for you, the burden of carnal desires and earthly cravings. Let the soul rule the flesh, reason rule the soul, and your grace rule reason; subject me inwardly and outwardly to your will. Grant that my heart, my tongue, and all my bones may praise you. Expand my mind and lift up the gaze of my heart, so that my spirit, at least in swift thought, may reach you, eternal Wisdom who abides above all things. Release me, I beg you, from the bonds by which I am held fast, so that, leaving all these things behind, I may hasten to you, cling to you alone, and attend to you alone.

## CHAPTER VI. How Blessed Are the Saints Who Depart from This Life

[Note: [Col. 0954] See the *Book of the Mirror*, chapter 30, and the *Book of Meditations*, chapters 23 and 25.]

Blessed is the soul which, released from its earthly prison, seeks heaven in freedom; which sees you, sweetest Lord, face to face; which is affected by no fear of death but rejoices in the incorruption of perpetual glory. It is tranquil and secure; it fears neither the enemy nor death. It already possesses you, its gracious Lord, whom it sought for a long time and always loved. Joined to choirs of singers, it sings forever, to the praise of your glory, O good King Christ Jesus, the honey-sweet songs of perpetual celebration.

For you give it drink from the abundance of your house and make it drink from the torrent of your delight (Psalm 35:9). Blessed is the fellowship of the heavenly citizens, and glorious the solemn assembly of all who return to you, from the sad labor of our pilgrimage to the pleasantness of beauty, to the loveliness of complete splendor, and to the dignity of perfect elegance, where your citizens continually behold you, Lord.

Nothing at all that could disturb the mind is permitted to be heard there. What songs, what instruments, what chants, what melodies are sung there without end? There the honey-sweet instruments of hymns always resound, together with the sweetest melody of the angels and the wondrous songs of songs, which the heavenly citizens sing forever to your praise and glory.

Bitterness and every harshness of gall have no place in your realm. There is no evil or wickedness; no adversary or attacker; no enticement to sin; no want; no disgrace; no quarrel; no reproach; no accusation; no fear; no unrest; no punishment; no doubt; no violence; no discord. Rather, there is supreme peace, complete charity, eternal jubilation and praise of God, secure rest without end, and joy always in the Holy Spirit.

[Col. 0955] O how fortunate I shall be if I hear the most delightful chants of your citizens, honey-sweet songs bringing forth praises to the Most Holy Trinity with due honor! But I shall be exceedingly blessed if I myself should merit singing to the Lord Jesus Christ a song from the sweet songs of Zion.

## CHAPTER VII. The Goods of Eternal Life

O life that truly lives, eternal life, eternally blessed life, where there is joy without sorrow, rest without labor, dignity without trembling, riches without loss, health without weakness, abundance without failure, life without death, perpetuity without corruption, blessedness without calamity. Where all goods are found in perfect charity; where there are beauty and vision face to face; where there is complete knowledge in all things and through all things; where the supreme goodness of God is seen, and the illuminating light is glorified by the saints; where the majesty of God is seen present, and the minds of those who gaze upon it are satisfied without defect by this food of life.

They always see, and desire to see; they desire without anxiety and are satisfied without disgust. There the true sun of righteousness, by the wondrous vision of its beauty, refreshes everyone and illuminates all the citizens of the heavenly homeland so that they themselves shine—

[Note: [Col. 0955] See the *Book of Meditations*, chapter 37.]

that is, they are illuminated light through God, illuminating light beyond all the splendor of our sun and the radiance of all the stars, clinging to the immortal Godhead. Thus made immortal and incorruptible, according to the promise of the Lord and Savior: “Father, those whom you gave me, I desire that where I am, they also may be with me; that they may see my glory; that they may all be one, just as you, Father, are in me and I am in you, and that they also may be one in us” (John 17:24, 21).

## CHAPTER VIII. The Miseries of the Present Life

The kingdom of heaven, the supremely happy kingdom, the kingdom without death and free from an end, to which no times succeed throughout eternity; where continuous day without night knows no passage of time; where the victorious soldier is heaped with ineffable gifts,

> A noble head embraced by an everlasting crown:

Would that, once the burden of sins had been removed, divine mercy might command me, the least of Christ’s servants, to lay down this burden of flesh, so that I might pass over to rest amid the eternal joys of its city;

[Note: [Col. 0955] An allusion to Gregory’s *Homily 37 on the Gospel*.]

so that I might take my place among the most holy choirs of the heavenly citizens, stand with the most blessed spirits in the glory of the Creator, behold the face of God present, be touched by no fear of death, rejoice secure in the incorruption of perpetual immortality, and, joined to the one who knows all things, cast off all the blindness of ignorance; so that I might regard all earthly things as insignificant and no longer deem it worthy to look upon or remember this valley of tears.

Whereas here there is a laborious life, a corruptible life, a life full of every bitterness, a life mistress of evils and handmaid of hell; a life which bodily humors inflate, pains weaken, fevers dry out, the air makes diseased, foods puff up, fasts waste away, amusements dissolve, sorrows consume, anxiety constricts, security dulls, riches scatter, poverty casts down, youth exalts, old age bends, weakness breaks, and grief depresses;

[Note: [Col. 0955] The words “where the devil lies in wait, the world flatters, the flesh delights, the soul is blinded, and the whole person is troubled” do not occur in the cited prayer in the Metz manuscript.]

where the devil lies in wait, the world flatters, the flesh delights, the soul is blinded, and the whole person is troubled—and after so many and such great evils comes raging death, imposing an end upon empty joys in such a way that, once they have ceased to exist, they are thought never to have existed.

## CHAPTER IX. In These Things Consolation from God Is Not Absent

But what praises and what thanksgivings can we offer you, our God, who, even amid such great troubles of our mortality, never cease to console us through the wondrous visitation of your grace?

Behold me, wretched and full of many sorrows: while I fear for my life, while I consider my sins, while I dread your judgment,

[Col. 0956] while I think of the hour of death, while I shudder at the punishments of Tartarus, while I do not know with what strictness you weigh my works, while I utterly do not know with what end I shall close

[Note: [Col. 0956] The Metz manuscript adds “life.” Read shortly before this, “it.”]

them, and while I turn these and many other thoughts over within my heart, you are present to console me in your customary goodness, Lord God. Amid these complaints, excessive weeping, and the deep sighs of my heart, you lift my sad and anxious mind over the lofty ridges of the mountains to the beds of spices, and place me in a pastureland beside streams of sweet waters. There you prepare before me a table with a manifold array, to restore my weary spirit and gladden my sad heart. At last refreshed by these delights, forgetting my many miseries and lifted above the height of the earth, I rest in you in true peace.

[Note: [Col. 0956] Here *Meditation* 14 ends in Anselm.]

## CHAPTER X. A Petition for the Love of God

I love you, my God; I love you, and I desire to love you more and more. Grant me, Lord Jesus, beautiful beyond the sons of men, to desire you and to love you as much as I wish and as much as I ought. You are immeasurable and must therefore be loved without measure, especially by us whom you loved and saved in such a manner, and for whom you did things so great and so excellent.

[Note: [Col. 0956] See the *Book of Meditations*, chapter 35.]

O love that always burns and is never extinguished! Sweet Christ, good Jesus, God my charity, kindle me wholly with your fire, your love, your sweetness, your affection, your desire, your charity, your delight and exultation, your goodness and gentleness, your pleasure and desire—which is holy and good, chaste and pure—so that, wholly filled with the sweetness of your love and wholly enveloped in the flame of your charity, I may love you, my sweetest and most beautiful Lord, with all my heart, with all my soul, with all my strength, and with all my intention; with great contrition of heart and a fountain of tears; with great reverence and trembling; having you always and everywhere in my heart, on my lips, and before my eyes; so that no place may remain in me for adulterous loves.

## CHAPTER XI. Likewise, on the Grace of Tears and Divine Help, Especially During the Sacred Mysteries

Most beautiful Jesus Christ, I ask you by that most sacred outpouring of your precious blood by which we were redeemed: grant me contrition of heart and a fountain of tears, especially while I offer prayers and supplications to you; while I sing psalmody to you in praise of you; while I recall or proclaim the mystery of our redemption, the manifest sign of your mercy; while, although unworthy, I stand at the sacred altars, desiring to offer that wondrous and heavenly sacrifice worthy of all reverence and devotion, which you, Lord my God, immaculate priest, instituted and commanded to be offered in commemoration of your charity (Luke 22:19)—namely, of your death and passion, for our salvation and for the daily restoration of our frailty.

May my mind be strengthened amid such great mysteries by the sweetness of your presence; may it perceive that you are present to it, and may my heart rejoice before you. Fire that always shines, love that always burns, sweet Christ, good Jesus, eternal and unfailing light, bread of life that refreshes us and does not fail in you—you are eaten daily, yet always remain whole: shine upon me, kindle me, illuminate and sanctify your vessel; empty it of wickedness, fill it with grace, and preserve it full, so that for the salvation of my soul I may eat the food of your flesh; so that, by eating you, I may live from you, go through you, reach you, and rest in you.

O sweetness of love and love of sweetness, may my belly eat you, and may my inward parts be filled with the nectar of your love, so that my mind may utter a good word. Charity, my God, who are sweet honey, milk white as snow, and food for the mature, make me grow in you, so that you may be eaten by me with a sound palate.

## CHAPTER XII. To Direct Every Thought toward Christ; In Him We Already Reign

You are my life, by which I live; my hope, to which I cling; my glory, which I desire to attain.

[Note: [Col. 0956] The same work, chapter 37.]

Hold my heart, rule my mind, direct my understanding, raise up my love, lift up my spirit, and draw the mouth of my thirsting spirit toward the heavenly streams. Let the tumult of the flesh be silent, I beg; let the fantasies of earth and water, of air and the heavens, be hushed. Let dreams and imaginary revelations, every tongue, every sign, and whatever comes into being in passing be silent. Let the soul itself be silent to itself and pass beyond itself, thinking not of itself but of you, my God, for you are truly

[Note: [Col. 0957] Up to this point, an excerpt from the unpublished prayer. What follows is from the *Book of Meditations*, chapters 15, 14, and 13.]

my entire hope and trust. For in you, my God and our most sweet, kind, and merciful Lord Jesus Christ, there is a portion, blood, and flesh of each one of us. Where, then, my portion reigns, I believe that I reign; where my blood rules, I trust that I rule; where my flesh is glorified, I know that I am glorious.

Although I am a sinner, I do not despair of this communion of grace. Even if my sins prohibit me, my substance demands it; even if my own offenses exclude me, the communion of nature does not repel me.

## CHAPTER XIII. Confidence in Christ

For the Lord is not so harsh as to forget the human being and fail to remember the one whom he himself bears; as not to love his own flesh, his own members, and his own inward parts.

[Note: [Col. 0957] Thus in the *Appendix to Bernard*, *On Conscience*, chapter 20. See Augustine, *Confessions*, Book 10, no. 69.]

I certainly might have despaired because of my excessive sins and vices, faults and countless negligences, which I have committed and continue unceasingly to commit each day in heart, word, deed, and in every way by which human frailty can sin—if your Word, my God, had not become flesh and dwelt among us.

But now I do not dare despair, because he, subject to you even unto death, and death on a cross, took away the record of our sins and fastened it to the cross (Philippians 2:8; Colossians 2:14), thereby crucifying sin and death. In him I breathe securely: he sits at your right hand and intercedes for us (Romans 8:34). Trusting in him, I desire to come to you—in him we have already risen and come to life again, already ascended into heaven, and already sit in the heavenly places.

To you be praise, to you glory, to you honor and thanksgiving.

## CHAPTER XIV. How Great Is the Delight That Comes from This

Most holy Lord, who loved, saved, justified, and exalted us in this way; most holy Lord, how sweet is the memory of you! The more I meditate upon you, the sweeter and more lovable you are to me. Therefore

[Note: [Col. 0957] See the *Book of Meditations*, chapters 22 and 37.]

it gives me great delight, with a pure gaze of the mind and the sweetest affection of devout love, to contemplate your goods in the place of my pilgrimage, according to my measure, for as long as I remain in these fragile limbs.

[Note: [Col. 0957] Erasmus, Lyons, Venice, and Louvain read this passage as follows: “Therefore your goods delight me greatly, with a pure gaze of the mind and the sweetest affection of devout love, in the place of my pilgrimage, according to my measure. Meanwhile, for as long as I remain in these fragile limbs, I desire continually to desire and contemplate your wondrous love and beauty.” Manuscript M.]

For I have been wounded by the dart of your charity; I burn intensely with desire for you; I long to reach you and desire to see you. Therefore I shall stand upon my watch and, with vigilant eyes, sing psalms in spirit; I shall sing with my mind and with all my strength praise you, my maker and restorer. In mind I shall pierce the heavens, and in desire I shall be with you, so that in the present misery I may be held by my body alone, but may always be with you in thought, longing, and every desire; so that my heart may be where you are, my desirable, incomparable, and greatly beloved treasure.

But behold, my most holy and merciful God, when I wish to contemplate the glory of your immeasurable goodness and mercy, my heart is not sufficient. Your beauty, loveliness, power, glory, magnificence, majesty, and charity surpass every understanding of the human mind. Just as the splendor of your glory is beyond estimation, so the goodness of your eternal charity is ineffable—the charity by which you adopt as children those whom you created from nothing and join them to yourself.

## CHAPTER XV. Nothing Is Too Harsh to Obtain the Glory of Heaven

[Col. 0958]

O my soul,

[Note: [Col. 0958] From a sermon in the *Appendix*, volume 5, page 209, no. 3.]

if we had to endure torments every day, if we had to tolerate hell itself for a long time in order to see Christ in his glory and be joined to his saints, would it not be worth suffering everything that is grievous so that we might share in so great a good and so great a glory?

Let the demons lie in wait, then; let them prepare their temptations;

[Note: [Col. 0958] Alternatively: “Let the demons prepare unceasingly,” and so forth.]

let fasts break the body; let clothing press upon it;

[Note: [Col. 0958] Erasmus, Lyons, Venice, and Louvain read, “let clothing press upon the flesh.” Manuscript M.]

let labors weigh it down; let vigils dry it out; let one cry out against me and another trouble me; let cold bend me; let conscience murmur; let heat burn; let my head ache; let my breast burn; let my stomach swell; let my face grow pale; let me grow entirely weak; let my life fail in pain and my years in groaning (Psalm 30:11); let decay enter my bones and bubble beneath me, so that I may rest in the day of tribulation and ascend to our girded people (Habakkuk 3:16).

[Note: [Col. 0958] Thus in the sermon cited immediately afterward, no. 4; following Cyprian, *On Works and Almsgiving*.]

For what will be the glory of the righteous, how great the joy of the saints, when each face shines like the sun; when the Lord begins to enumerate his people in the kingdom of his Father according to their distinct orders, and to restore to each according to his merits and works the promised rewards—heavenly things in place of earthly, eternal things in place of temporal, great things in place of small?

Truly, it will be the summit of happiness when the Lord brings his saints into the vision of the Father’s glory and makes them sit in the heavenly places, so that he may be all in all.

## CHAPTER XVI. Its Price

O happy delight and delightful happiness: to see the saints, to be with the saints, and to be holy; to see God and possess God forever and beyond!

Let us think upon these things with diligent minds; let us desire them with the whole longing of our hearts, so that we may be able to reach them quickly. If you ask how this can happen, or by what means, by what merits, or by what assistance, listen:

[Note: [Col. 0958] From the same sermon.]

this matter has been placed in the power of the one who acts, because the kingdom of heaven suffers violence (Matthew 11:12). The kingdom of heaven, O man, seeks no price other than yourself. It is worth as much as you are; give yourself, and you will have it. Why are you troubled about the price? Christ gave himself in order to acquire you as a kingdom for God the Father; so give yourself, that you may be his kingdom, and let sin not reign in your mortal body, but let the spirit reign in the acquisition of life.

## CHAPTER XVII. The Happiness of Paradise

O my soul,

[Note: [Col. 0958] From the same sermon in the *Appendix*, nos. 2 and 3; and also from Gregory’s *Homily 37 on the Gospel*.]

let us return to the heavenly city in which we are enrolled and appointed citizens. Therefore, as citizens with the saints, members of God’s household, and heirs of God—co-heirs, moreover, with Christ—let us consider, as far as it is possible to consider, the renowned happiness of our city.

Let us say with the Prophet: “O how glorious things have been spoken of you, city of God! The dwelling place of all who rejoice is in you” (Psalm 86:3, 7). For you are founded upon the exultation of the whole earth. There is no old age in you, nor the misery of old age; no maimed person, no lame person, no hunchback, no deformity, since all attain to the perfect man, to the measure of the fullness of the age of Christ (Ephesians 4:13).

What life is more blessed than this, where there is no fear of poverty, no weakness of sickness; where no one is harmed, no one grows angry, no one envies; where no desire burns, no longing for food exists, and no ambition for honor or power knocks at the door?

There is no fear of the devil there, no ambush of demons, no terror of hell nearby; there is neither death of body nor death of soul, but a joyful life through the gift of immortality. There will be no discord anywhere then; all things will be harmonious and fitting, because there will be one concord among all the saints. Peace and joy contain everything; all things are tranquil and at rest.

There is perpetual splendor—not the kind that exists now, but so much brighter as it is more blessed—

[Col. 0959] because that city, as it is written, will have no need of the light of the sun, but the Lord Almighty will illuminate it, and its lamp is the Lamb (Revelation 21:23). There the saints will shine like stars forever and ever, and like the splendor of the firmament, those who instruct the many (Daniel 12:3; Wisdom 3:7).

Therefore there will be no night there, no darkness, no gathering of clouds, and no harshness of cold or heat; rather, the conditions of things will be such as eye has not seen, ear has not heard, nor has entered into the human heart (1 Corinthians 2:9; Isaiah 64:4)—except in the case of those who are found worthy to enjoy them, whose names are written in the book of life.

But above all these things is fellowship with the choirs of angels and archangels and with all the heavenly Powers; beholding the patriarchs and prophets, seeing the apostles and all the saints, and seeing our parents as well. These things are glorious, but far more glorious is to behold the face of God present and to see the unbounded light. The surpassing glory will be this: when we see God in himself, and see and possess him within ourselves—him whose vision has no end.

[Note: [Col. 0959] Alternatively: “him whose vision is an end without end,” or “whose vision will have no end.”]

## CHAPTER XVIII. The Sufficiency of Love and the Degrees of Love

The soul, marked by the image of God and distinguished by his likeness,

[Note: [Col. 0959] Bernard, *On the Song of Songs*, sermon 83, nos. 2, 1, 3, and 4.]

possesses within itself from God something by which it is always admonished either to stand with him or to return to him, should it be moved by its affections—or rather, by its failings. It possesses not only the means of breathing again in hope of pardon and hope of mercy, but also the means of daring to aspire to the marriage of the Word, to enter into a covenant of fellowship with God, and to bear with the King of angels the easy yoke of love.

Love accomplishes all these things if the soul makes itself like God through the will, to whom it is like by nature: loving as it has been loved.
