For love alone, among all the soul’s movements, senses, and affections, is that in which the creature, though not equally, can respond to the Creator or return a mutual counterpart from likeness.

When love comes, it draws all the other affections into itself and captivates them. Love is sufficient in itself; it pleases in itself and for its own sake. It is itself merit, reward, cause, fruit, and use. Through love we are joined to God. Love makes one spirit from two; love makes one will and one refusal.

Love first orders one’s conduct; afterward it enables one to regard all present things as though they were not present; and, thirdly, with a pure vision of the heart, it enables one to behold heavenly and inward things. Through love, at first the honorable things of this age are rightly performed; afterward even the honorable things of this age are despised

[Note: [Col. 0959] The Royal Manuscript adds here, “in place of eternal things.”]

and finally the innermost things of God are seen.

## CHAPTER XIX. We Are Joined to God by Love; How the Lover Should Conduct Himself; What Love Accomplishes in Him

God the Father is charity; God the Son is charity; the Holy Spirit is the love of the Father and the Son. This charity requires something similar in us—namely, charity, by which, as though through a certain kinship of blood, we may be associated and joined to it.

[Note: [Col. 0959] The same source, sermons 64, 83, and 74, nos. 6 and 7.]

Love is unaware of rank and therefore knows no reverence. Whoever loves approaches God confidently on his own and speaks with him familiarly, fearing nothing and hesitating over nothing. He loses what he lives for who does not love; but whoever loves always keeps his eyes upon the God whom he loves, whom he desires, in whom he meditates, in whom he delights, by whom he is nourished and made rich.

Such a devoted person sings and reads in this way and is so prudent and watchful in all his works as though God were present before his eyes—as indeed he truly is. He prays as though he had been taken up and presented before the face of the majesty upon the lofty throne, where thousands upon thousands minister to him and ten thousand times a hundred thousand stand before him (Daniel 7:10).

Love, when it visits a soul, awakens it from sleep, moves and softens it, wounds its heart, illuminates dark things, opens what is closed, sets cold things aflame, calms a harsh, irascible, and impatient mind, drives away vices,

[Col. 0960] restrains carnal affections, corrects and reforms conduct, renews the spirit, and restrains the impulses and frivolous actions of an unstable age. Love does all these things when it is present; but when it has departed, the soul begins to lie languid, just as though you had removed the fire from a boiling pot.

## CHAPTER XX. The Nature of Love

Great is the power of love,

[Note: [Col. 0960] Bernard, *On the Song of Songs*, sermons 83, no. 3; 79, no. 1; 69, no. 7; 83, nos. 4 and 6; 84, no. 6; 74, no. 4; 85, no. 13; and 74, no. 3.]

by which the soul confidently approaches God on its own, steadfastly clings to God, and familiarly questions God and consults him about everything. The soul that loves God can think of nothing else and speak of nothing else. It despises what remains and is disgusted by everything else. Whatever it meditates upon, whatever it says, tastes of love and smells of love; so completely has the love of God claimed it for itself.

Whoever wishes to know God should love. In vain does one approach reading, meditation, preaching, or prayer without loving. The love of God gives birth to the soul’s love and makes it direct itself toward him. God loves in order to be loved. When he loves, he wants nothing else but to be loved, knowing that those who love him are blessed.

The loving soul renounces all its own attachments and devotes itself wholly to love alone, so that it may respond to love by returning love. And when it has poured itself out entirely into love, what is that compared with the perpetual outflow of the fountain? Love and lover, soul and God, Creator and creature do not flow together with equal abundance; yet if the soul loves with its whole being, nothing is lacking where everything is present.

Let the soul that loves not fear; let the soul that does not love be afraid. The loving soul is carried by vows, drawn by desires; it disregards merits, closes its eyes to majesty, opens them to delight, placing itself in salvation and acting confidently in God.

Through love the soul withdraws from and rises above bodily senses, so that it does not sense itself, while it senses God. This happens when the mind, enticed by the ineffable sweetness of God, in a certain way steals itself away from itself—or rather, is carried away and slips away from itself—so that it may enjoy God in delight.

Nothing is so delightful, if only it were not so brief. Love gives familiarity with God; familiarity gives boldness; boldness gives taste; taste gives hunger. The soul touched by the love of God can think of nothing else and desire nothing else, but often sighs, saying: “As the deer longs for the springs of water, so my soul longs for you, God” (Psalm 41:2).

## CHAPTER XXI. The Love of Christ; The Fruit of Christ’s Passion and Death

God came to human beings through love; he came into human beings and became human. Through love, the invisible God made himself like his servants; through love, he was wounded for our sins.

[Note: [Col. 0960] The same source, *On the Song of Songs*, sermon 61, nos. 3 and 4.]

For the weak and sinful, secure and firm rest is found in the wounds of the Savior. There I dwell securely; through the wounds, his inward parts are open to me. Whatever is lacking in me, I take for myself from the inward parts of my Lord, for they abound in mercy, and there is no lack of openings through which it may flow out.

Through the openings in his body, the secrets of his heart are open to me; the great mystery of his loving-kindness is open; the inward parts of the mercy of our God are open, in which the Dawn from on high visited us. The wounds of Jesus Christ are full of mercy, full of goodness, full of sweetness and charity.

They pierced his hands and feet, and pierced his side with a lance. Through these cracks it is permitted me to taste how sweet the Lord my God is, for he is truly sweet, gentle, and rich in mercy to all who call upon him in truth, to all who seek him, and especially to those who love him.

Abundant redemption has been given to us in the wounds of our Savior: a great multitude of sweetness, the fullness of grace, and the perfection of virtues.

## CHAPTER XXII. How Useful Remembrance Is in Temptations and Adversities
When some shameful thought strikes me, I run back to the wounds of Christ. When my flesh oppresses me, I rise up through remembrance of the wounds of my Lord. When the devil lays snares for me, I flee to the merciful heart of my Lord, and he withdraws from me. If the heat of lust stirs my limbs, it is extinguished by remembrance of the wounds of the Son of God. In all adversities I find no [Col. 0961] remedy so effective as the wounds of Christ: in them I sleep secure and rest without fear. Christ died for us. Nothing so pertains to death that the death of Christ cannot save from it.

## CHAPTER XXIII. And Against Despair

All my hope is in the death of my Lord. His death is my merit, my refuge, my salvation, my life, and my resurrection. [Note: [Col. 0961] From the same sermon, 5.] My merit is the Lord’s compassion. I am not without merit so long as he has not forgotten his mercies. And if the Lord’s mercies are many, I too am rich in merits. The more powerful he is to save, the more secure I am.

I have committed a great sin, and I am conscious of many offenses; yet I do not despair, because where offenses abounded, grace also abounded exceedingly. Whoever despairs of the forgiveness of his sins denies that God is merciful. He does a great injury to God who distrusts his mercy: insofar as it lies within him, he denies that God possesses charity, truth, and power, [Note: [Col. 0961] Also in the book *On Loving God*, chapter 14, from Bernard.] in which my entire hope consists—namely, in the charity of adoption, in the truth of the promise, and in the power of restoration [Note: [Col. 0961] Elsewhere, “redemption.”].

Let my foolish thought murmur as much as it wishes, saying, “Who are you, and how great is that glory, and by what merits do you hope to obtain it?” And I will answer confidently: “I know whom I have believed, because in his great love he adopted me as a son; because he is truthful in his promise, powerful in its fulfillment, and it is permitted him to do whatever he wills.” I cannot be terrified by the multitude of my sins if the Lord’s death comes to mind, because my sins cannot overcome him. [Note: [Col. 0961] Bernard, *On the Song of Songs*, sermon 61, sections 4 and 3; and sermon 62, section 7.]

The nails and the lance cry out to me that I have truly been reconciled to Christ, if I have loved him. Longinus opened Christ’s side with a lance (John 19:34), and I entered, and there I rest secure. Let the one who fears, love, because love casts out fear (1 John 4:18).

No medicine is so powerful and effective against the heat of lust as the death of my Redeemer. He stretched out his arms upon the cross and spread his hands, ready to embrace sinners. Between the arms of my Savior I both wish to live and desire to die. There I shall sing securely: “I will exalt you, O Lord, for you have received me, and have not gladdened my enemies over me” (Psalm 29:2).

Our Savior bowed his head in death in order to give kisses to his beloved. As often as we are pierced with compunction in his love, so often do we kiss God.

## CHAPTER XXIV. The Soul Awakened to the Love of Christ

O my soul, marked with the image of God, redeemed by Christ’s blood, betrothed by faith, endowed with the Spirit, adorned with virtues, appointed to dwell with the angels: love him by whom you have been so greatly loved; attend to him who attends to you; seek him who seeks you; love your lover, by whom you are so greatly loved, whose love has anticipated you, and who is the cause of your love.

He himself is the merit, he himself the reward, he himself the fruit, he himself the enjoyment, he himself the end. [Note: [Col. 0961] Following Bernard, *On the Song of Songs*, sermon 69, section 7; likewise the book *On Conscience*, in the Appendix to Bernard, chapter 1; afterward Hugh of Saint-Victor, *Miscellany*, book 1, title 52; and Augustine, *Confessions*, book 10, chapter 6.]

Be diligent with the diligent, at leisure with the one at leisure, pure with the pure, holy with the holy. As you have prepared yourself for God, so he must appear to you. God is gracious and gentle, and rich in mercy (Psalm 85:5); he seeks those who are gracious, gentle, sweet, humble, and merciful.

Love him who led you out of the pit of misery and the mire of filth. Choose him as your friend above all your friends: when everything else has been taken away, he alone will remain faithful to you. On the day of your burial, when all your friends withdraw from you, he will not abandon you. Rather, he will protect you from the roaring creatures prepared for food, lead you through an unknown region, and bring you to the streets of heavenly Zion. There he will place you with the angels before the face of his majesty, where you will hear that angelic melody: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of hosts.”

There is the song of joy, [Col. 0962] the voice of exultation and salvation, thanksgiving, and the voice of praise, and alleluia forever. There is an accumulation of blessedness, surpassing glory, overflowing joy, and every good thing.

O my soul, sigh ardently and desire vehemently, so that you may be able to reach that heavenly city of which such glorious things have been spoken, in which, as it is written, “the dwelling of all who rejoice” is found (Psalm 86:3, 7).

You can ascend by love; for one who loves, nothing is difficult, nothing impossible. The soul that loves often ascends and familiarly runs through the streets of heavenly Jerusalem, visiting patriarchs and prophets, greeting the apostles, admiring the armies of martyrs and confessors, and gazing upon the choirs of virgins. Heaven, earth, and all that is in them never cease saying to me that I should love the Lord my God. [Note: [Col. 0962] Up to this point the text is identical in Hugh, book 4 *On the Soul*; from here onward it is entirely different.]

## CHAPTER XXV. The Highest Good Alone Suffices for the Soul. The Value of a Good Will

The human heart, when it is not fixed in the desire for eternity, can never be stable, but is more changeable than anything changeable. It passes from one thing to another, seeking rest where rest is not found. In these fleeting and transitory things, in which its affections are held captive, it cannot find true rest, because it is of such dignity that no good apart from the highest good can suffice for it; and it is also so free that it cannot be compelled against its will to pursue anything else. [Note: [Col. 0962] Hugh of Saint-Victor, *Miscellany*, book 1, title 7; likewise *On the Praise of Charity*.]

Therefore each person’s own will is the cause of his damnation or salvation; and for that reason nothing richer is offered to God than a good will. A good will brings God down to us and directs us toward him. Through a good will we love God, choose God, run toward God, reach God, and possess God.

O good will, through which we are reshaped according to the likeness of God and made like him! A good will is so beloved by God that he does not wish to dwell in a heart in which there is no good will. A good will inclines the Trinity of that supreme majesty toward itself. Wisdom illuminates it for the knowledge of truth; charity inflames it for the desire of goodness; fatherhood preserves in it what it created, lest it perish.

What is the knowledge of truth? First, to know yourself and what you ought to be, so that you may strive to be what you ought to be, and to know what must be corrected, so that you may correct it; then to know and love your Creator. For this is the whole good of the human being.

## CHAPTER XXVI. Knowledge of Truth. God’s Benefits to Humanity. The Causes of the Incarnation

Consider, then, how ineffable is the love of divine charity toward us. He created us from nothing and gave us everything we possess; but because we loved the gift more than the giver, the creature more than the Creator, we fell into the devil’s snare and became his servants. But God, moved by mercy, sent his Son to redeem the servants; he also sent the Holy Spirit to adopt the servants as sons. He gave the Son as the price of redemption, the Holy Spirit as the privilege of love, and finally kept himself wholly as the inheritance for those adopted. [Note: [Col. 0962] It should read, as in the book *On the Spirit and the Soul*, chapter 54, “for those adopted.”]

Thus God, as the most loving and most merciful lover of humanity, out of desire for or love of the human being, expended not only what was his but even himself, in order to recover the human being—not so much for himself as for the human being himself. So that human beings might be born from God, God was first born from them.

Who is so hard that the love of God, which thus anticipates humanity, would not soften him? I mean such a vehement love that God deigned to become human for humanity’s sake. Who can hate the human being whose nature and likeness he sees in God’s humanity? Truly, whoever hates that person hates God, and thus loses whatever he does. [Note: [Col. 0962] Hugh of Saint-Victor, *Miscellany*, book 1, title 87.]

For God became human for humanity’s sake, so that the one who is Creator might also be Redeemer, and so that the human being might be redeemed from what belonged to him. [Col. 0963] And so that God might be loved more intimately by humanity, he appeared in the likeness of a human being; and so that both senses of the human being might be blessed in him, the eye of the heart might be refreshed by his divinity and the bodily eye by his humanity, so that whether entering or departing, human nature, created by him, might find pasture in him.

## CHAPTER XXVII. The Effects of the Holy Spirit. Joy in Iniquity, Vanity, and the Holy Spirit

[Note: [Col. 0963] The same Hugh, *Miscellany*, book 1, title 103.]

Our Savior was born for us, was crucified, and died for us, so that by his death he might destroy our death. And because a cluster of flesh had been carried to the winepress of the cross, and the must of divinity had begun to flow after the pressing, the Holy Spirit was sent, so that the vessels of hearts might be prepared and the new wine placed in new wineskins: first, so that hearts might be cleansed, lest what was poured in be polluted; and afterward so that they might be bound, lest what had been poured out be lost. They were to be cleansed from the joy of iniquity and bound against the joy of vanity.

For what is good could not come unless what is evil first departed. The joy of iniquity pollutes, and the joy of vanity pours out. The joy of iniquity makes the vessel filthy, and the joy of vanity makes it leaky. The joy of iniquity exists when sin is loved; the joy of vanity exists when transitory things are loved.

Cast out, then, what is evil, so that you may be able to receive what is good. Pour out bitterness, so that you may be filled with sweetness. The Holy Spirit is joy and love. Cast out the spirit of the devil and the spirit of this world, so that you may receive the Spirit of God.

The spirit of the devil produces the joy of iniquity, and the spirit of the world produces the joy of vanity. These joys are evil, because one contains guilt and the other provides an occasion for guilt. But the Spirit of God will come when the evil spirits have been cast out; he will enter the tabernacle of the heart and produce good joy and good love, by which love of the world and love of sin are expelled.

Love of the world attracts and deceives; love of sin pollutes and leads to death. Love of God illuminates the mind, cleanses the conscience, gladdens the soul, and reveals God.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. The Mind and Conduct of One Who Loves God

[Note: [Col. 0963] Hugh of Saint-Victor, *On the Praise of Charity*; *Miscellany*, book 1, title 120.]

Where the love of God is present, one always thinks about when one will reach God, when one will abandon the world, when one will escape the corruption of the flesh, and when [Note: [Col. 0963] Elsewhere, “so that;” and shortly afterward, “his heart.”] one will find true peace. The heart is always raised upward, and its desire is lifted to heavenly things.

When such a person sits, walks, rests, or does anything else, his heart does not depart from God. He exhorts everyone to the love of God, commends the love of God to everyone, and demonstrates by heart, speech, and action how sweet the love of God is and how evil and bitter the love of the world is.

He mocks the glory of this world and censures its anxious care; he shows how foolish it is to place confidence in things that pass away. He marvels at the blindness of people who love these things; he also marvels that all people do not abandon these transitory and perishable things. He considers sweet for everyone what tastes sweet to him, believes that everyone should be pleased by what he loves, and supposes that what he knows is evident to everyone.

He frequently contemplates his God and is sweetly refreshed in that contemplation—more happily the more frequently. For God is always sweet to contemplate and always pleasant to love and praise.

## CHAPTER XXIX. Rest of the Heart. Attentive Prayer

Truly, [Note: [Col. 0963] Book *On the Substance of Love*, chapter 6; *On the Spirit and the Soul*, chapter 35; and the already cited book *On Conscience*, chapter 3.] this is the heart’s true rest: when the whole heart is fixed by desire in the love of God and desires nothing else, but delights in what it holds with a certain happy sweetness and rejoices in its delight.

If, however, it is drawn away from there even briefly by some vain thought or by involvement in worldly affairs, it hastens to return there with the greatest speed, considering it exile to remain anywhere other than there. For just as there is no moment in which a human being does not enjoy or make use of God’s goodness or mercy, so there ought to be no moment in which he does not have God present in his memory.

Therefore anyone who, while speaking with God in prayer, is suddenly drawn away from his sight—as though from the eyes of one who neither sees nor hears—is bound by no small fault. This occurs when he follows his evil and intrusive thoughts and prefers to God some most worthless creature, toward which the mind’s gaze is easily distracted: repeatedly turning it over or thinking about it in his mind more than about God, whom he ought continually to remember, adore as Creator, await as Savior, or fear as Judge. [Note: [Col. 0964] The printed editions read: “to remember the Creator, adore the Redeemer, await the Savior, or fear the Judge.”]

Whatever therefore draws the sight away from him must be entirely fled and detested.

Whoever loves the world, look to yourself, where you must go.

This way on which you walk is a most evil way, full of ruin.

## CHAPTER XXX. Fleeing Whatever Turns the Mind Away from God. What Humanity Lost Through Sin and What It Found

[Note: [Col. 0964] From this point onward, the words are purely those of Anselm, *Proslogion*, chapter 1.]

Flee, then, O human being, for a little while from your occupations, and hide yourself briefly from your tumultuous thoughts. Cast aside your burdensome cares now, and postpone your laborious distractions. Give some time to God, and rest for a little while in him.

Enter the chamber of your mind; shut out everything except God and what helps you seek him. With the door closed, seek him, and give your whole heart to God, saying, “I seek your face; your face, O Lord, I require.”

Come now, then, O Lord my God: teach my heart where and how to seek you, where and how to find you. Lord, if you are not here, where shall I seek you in your absence? But if you are everywhere, why do I not see you present? Yet surely you dwell in inaccessible light (1 Timothy 6:16).

But how shall I approach inaccessible light? Or who will lead me and bring me into it, so that I may see you in it? Then by what signs, with what appearance, shall I seek you? I have never seen you, Lord my God; I have never known your face.

What shall this distant exile of yours do, O most high Lord? What shall your servant do, anxious with love for you and cast far away from your face? He longs to see you, yet your face is far from him. He desires to approach you, yet your dwelling is inaccessible. He longs to find you, yet he does not know your place. He strives to seek you, yet he does not know your face.

Lord, you are my God and my Lord, and I have never seen you. You made me, restored me, and bestowed all my good things upon me; yet I have not seen you, nor do I yet know you. Finally, I was made to see you, and I have not yet done what I was made for.

O miserable fate of humanity, when it lost that for which it was made! O harsh and grievous fall! Alas, what did it lose, and what did it find? What departed, and what remained? It lost the blessedness for which it was made, and found the misery for which it was not made. That without which nothing is happy departed, and what is in itself nothing but miserable remained.

Then humanity ate the bread of angels, for which it now hungers; now it eats the bread of sorrows, of which it knew nothing then.

## CHAPTER XXXI. Aspiration toward Knowledge of God. Why We Were Made in the Image of God

And, O you Lord, how long? How long, O Lord, will you forget us? How long will you turn your face from us (Psalm 12:1)? When will you look upon us and hear us? When will you illumine our eyes and show us your face? When will you restore yourself to us?

Look upon us, Lord; hear us; illumine us; show us yourself. Restore yourself to us, so that it may be well with us, without whom it is so ill with us. Have mercy on our labors and efforts toward you, for without you we can do nothing.

You invite us [Note: [Col. 0964] Elsewhere, “invite”]; help us. I beg you, Lord: do not let me despair in sighing, but let me breathe again in hope. I beg you, Lord: my heart has been embittered by its desolation; sweeten it with your [Col. 0965] consolation.

I beg you, Lord: hungry, I have begun to seek you; do not let me be abandoned by you fasting. Famished, I have approached you; do not let me depart unfed. Poor, I have come to the rich; wretched, to the merciful; do not let me depart empty and despised.

Lord, I am bowed down and can look only downward; raise me up, so that I may be able to look upward. My iniquities have risen above my head; they have wrapped me around and, like a heavy burden, weighed me down (Psalm 37:5). Unwind me and unload me, lest their pit press its mouth over me.

Let me look up toward your light, whether from far away or from the depths. Teach me to seek you, and show yourself to the one who seeks you; for I cannot seek you unless you teach me, nor find you unless you show yourself.

Let me seek you by desiring; let me desire you by seeking. Let me find you by loving; let me love you by finding.

I confess, Lord, and give thanks that you created in me this image of yourself, so that I might remember you, think of you, and love you. But it has been so effaced by the abrasion of vices and so darkened by the smoke of sins that it cannot do what it was made to do unless you renew and reform it.

I do not attempt, Lord, to penetrate your heights, because in no way do I compare my understanding with them. I desire to understand in some measure your truth, which my heart believes and loves. For I do not seek to understand in order to believe, but I believe in order to understand. [Note: [Col. 0965] From Anselm’s *Proslogion*, chapter 2.]

Therefore, Lord, who grant understanding to faith, grant me to understand, insofar as you know it to be beneficial, that you are as we believe, and that you are what we believe.

## CHAPTER XXXII. What God Is. He Who Is Entirely Good

Indeed, we believe you to be something than which nothing greater or better can be conceived. [Note: [Col. 0965] In Anselm, here and below, “better” is omitted.] [Note: [Col. 0965] From chapters 5 and 9.]

What, then, are you, O Lord God, than whom nothing greater or better can be conceived? What is this except the highest of all things, existing alone through itself, which made everything else from nothing? Whatever is not this is less than that than which nothing greater can be conceived; but this cannot be conceived of you.

What good, then, is lacking in the highest good, through which every good exists? You are therefore just, truthful, blessed, and whatever it is better to be than not to be.

But how do you spare the wicked, if you are entirely and supremely just? Is it because your goodness is incomprehensible and lies hidden in the inaccessible light in which you dwell? Truly, in the highest and most secret depth of your goodness there lies hidden the fountain from which the river of your mercy flows.

For although you are entirely and supremely just, you are nevertheless kind even to the wicked, because you are entirely and supremely good. You would be less good if you were kind to no evil person. For the one who is good to both the good and the wicked is better than the one who is good only to the good. And the one who is good to the wicked both by sparing and by punishing is better than the one who is good only by punishing.

Therefore you are merciful because you are entirely and supremely good. O immeasurable goodness, which surpasses all understanding: let that mercy which proceeds from such abundance come upon me; let what flows forth from you flow into me. Spare me through clemency, lest you punish me through justice.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. How Great and What Kind of Good

[Note: [Col. 0965] What follows consists of chapters 24, 25, and 26 of the *Proslogion* mentioned above, reproduced here in full.]

Awaken now, my soul, and raise your whole understanding. Consider, as far as you can, what kind and how great is that good which God is.

If individual good things are delightful, consider attentively how delightful that good must be which contains the delight of all things—not the kind of delight we have experienced in created things, but one as different from them as the Creator differs from the creature.

If created life is good, how good is the creating Life? If created salvation is delightful, how delightful is the Salvation that made every salvation? If wisdom is lovable when it consists in knowledge of created things, how lovable is the Wisdom that made and created all things from nothing?

Finally, if there are many and great delights in delightful things, what kind and how great is the delight [Col. 0966] in the one who made those very delightful things?

O whoever will enjoy this good, what will belong to him, and what will not belong to him? Certainly whatever he wishes will belong to him, and whatever he does not wish will not be there. For there he will have goods of soul and body such as “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of humanity.”

## CHAPTER XXXIV. All Goods Are in Him

Why, then, do you wander through many things, little human being, seeking goods for your soul and your body? Love the one good in which all goods exist, and it will suffice. Desire the simple good that is every good, and that is enough.

What do you love, my flesh? What do you desire, my soul? It is there; it is there: whatever you love, whatever you desire, is there.

If beauty delights you, “the righteous will shine like the sun” (Matthew 13:43). If speed, strength, or bodily freedom delights you—freedom such that nothing can resist it—“they will be like the angels of God” (Matthew 22:30), because “what is sown as an animal body will rise as a spiritual body” (1 Corinthians 15:44), with power, certainly, though not by nature.

If a long or healthy life delights you, there will be healthy eternity and eternal health, because “the righteous will live forever” (Wisdom 5:16), and “the salvation of the righteous is from the Lord” (Psalm 36:39).

If satiety delights you, “they will be satisfied when the glory of the Lord appears” (Psalm 16:15). If drunkenness, “they will be intoxicated by the abundance of your house” (Psalm 35:9). If melody, there the angels sing together to God without end. If any pleasure that is not impure but pure, “the Lord will give them drink from the river of his pleasure” (ibid.).

If wisdom, the Wisdom of God itself will show itself to them. If friendship, they will love God more than themselves, and one another as themselves, and God will love them more than they love themselves—for they will love him, themselves, and one another through him, and he will love himself and them through himself.

If harmony, they will all have one will, because none will be in them except the supreme will of God. [Note: [Col. 0966] In Anselm, “only.”]

If power, they will be all-powerful in regard to their own will, as God is in regard to his. For just as God will be able to do through himself whatever he wills, so they will be able through him to do whatever they will, because just as they will not will anything other than what he wills, so he will will whatever they will; and what he wills cannot fail to exist.

If honor and riches, God will set his good and faithful servants over many things (Matthew 25:23). Indeed, they will be called and will be sons of God and gods; and where his Only-Begotten One is, there they also will be, heirs indeed of God and fellow heirs with Christ (Romans 8:17).

If true security, they will certainly be so assured that this good will never in any way fail them, just as they will be certain that they will not lose it by their own will, that God, who loves them, will not take it from those who love him against their will, and that nothing more powerful than God will separate God and them.

And what sort and how great will the joy be where such a great good exists?

## CHAPTER XXXV. How Great the Joy Will Be for Those Who Enjoy It

Human heart, needy heart, heart that has experienced hardships and miseries—indeed, overwhelmed by miseries—how would you rejoice if you abounded in all these things? Ask your inmost self whether it could contain its joy over such great blessedness.

But certainly, if someone else whom you loved exactly as yourself possessed the same blessedness, your joy would be doubled, because you would rejoice for him no less than for yourself. If two or three, or many more, possessed the same thing, you would rejoice as much for each one as for yourself, if you loved each one as yourself.

What, then, will there be in that perfect charity of countless blessed angels and human beings, where no one will love another less than himself? For each person will rejoice for every other person no differently than for himself.

If, then, the human heart can scarcely contain its joy over so great a good of its own, how will it be capable of so many and such great joys? Certainly, the more anyone loves another, the more he rejoices in that other’s good.

And just as in that blessed happiness each person will love God incomparably more than himself and all the others with him, so he will rejoice beyond measure more in God’s happiness than in his own and that of all the others with him.

And if they love God with their whole heart, whole mind, and whole soul, while their whole heart, whole mind, and whole soul are still insufficient for the dignity [Col. 0967] of their love, surely they will rejoice with their whole heart, whole mind, and whole soul, while their whole heart, whole mind, and whole soul are still insufficient for the fullness of their joy.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. Whether It Can Be Fully Conceived Here. Here We Must Always Grow in Knowledge, Love, and Joy in God

My God and my Lord, my hope and the joy of my heart, tell my soul whether this is the joy of which you say to us through your Son, “Ask, and you will receive, so that your joy may be full” (John 16:24).

For I have found a certain joy that is full, and more than full. Even when the heart, mind, soul, and whole person are filled with that joy, joy will still remain beyond measure. Therefore all that joy will not enter into those who rejoice; rather, all those who rejoice will enter into that joy.

Tell me, Lord, tell your servant within my heart whether this is the joy into which your servants will enter, those who will enter into the joy of their Lord. Certainly, that joy with which your elect will rejoice is such as “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of humanity” (Isaiah 64:4; 1 Corinthians 2:9).

Therefore I have not yet conceived or said, Lord, how greatly your elect will rejoice. [Col. 0968] Certainly, they will rejoice as greatly as they love; they will love as greatly as they know. And how greatly will they know you, Lord, and how greatly will they love you? Certainly, in this life eye has not seen, ear has not heard, nor has it entered into the heart of humanity how greatly they will know and love you in that life.

I beg you, my God: let me know you, love you, so that I may rejoice in you. And if I cannot do so fully in this life, let me at least advance day by day until fullness comes.

Let knowledge of you increase in me here, so that there it may be complete; let your love grow in me here, so that there it may be full; so that here my joy may be great in hope, and there full in reality.

Truthful God, I ask to receive what you promise, so that my joy may be full. In the meantime, let my mind meditate on it, my tongue speak of it, my heart love it, my mouth converse about it, my soul hunger for it, my flesh thirst for it, and my whole substance desire it, until I enter into the joy of my Lord, who is the blessed Triune and One God forever. Amen.

# [THE MIRROR]

[Col. 0967]

## PREFATORY NOTICE TO THE BOOK ENTITLED *THE MIRROR*

The following book does not bear one single title in the ancient manuscripts. In most it is called *The Mirror* or *The Manual*, perhaps deriving its title from the author’s words when, near the end, he addresses God as follows: “I have devoted myself to this little flower-gathering so that I might always have with me a brief and manual word about you, from whose reading, whenever I grow lukewarm, I might be rekindled in your love.”

A little later the author says that he extracted this little discourse so that, just as he believes God in his heart for righteousness, he might confess him with his mouth for salvation. Hence it is not inappropriately entitled in the manuscript of the Paris College of Bernardines, *A Little Book of Catholic Faith*.

In that Bernardine manuscript another short work is also attached immediately afterward, with the title *A Confession of How Much Christ Deigned to Aid the Human Race*. It begins as follows: “In the preceding little discourse, the confession of my faith, etc.”

These two little works are no different from the first and second parts of the *Confession of Faith*, which, under the name of Alcuin, were published in four parts through the care of Peter Francis Chifflet from the Boherian copy.

The writing of this Boherian copy seems to approach the time of Charlemagne and not to be later than the ninth century. This is attested by men of outstanding expertise in literary matters, who, in order to establish this very point, signed the instrument published in volume 1 of the *Ancient Analecta*, where more is discussed on this matter.

Therefore, whatever is found in the following *Mirror*—which is nothing other than the first part of the aforementioned *Confession*—to be shared with the *Meditations* printed shortly above should be thought to have passed not from the *Meditations* into the *Mirror*, but rather from the *Mirror* into the *Meditations*, which are clearly later than the tenth century.

For the rest, we observe that words and sentences have been excerpted here not only from the books of Augustine, Gregory, and Isidore, but also from other writings of Alcuin himself. This is chiefly why we hesitate to affirm without qualification that the work belongs to Alcuin.

In correcting the *Mirror*, besides the Parisian manuscripts of the Colbert Library and the College of Bernardines, we also used a copy of the Boherian exemplar.

[Col. 0967]

# THE MIRROR, ONE BOOK (G, S)

## CHAPTER I. Invocation of the Holy Trinity

[Note: This is how Alcuin’s invocation begins after the books *On the Trinity*.]

Be present to me, true light, God the almighty Father. Be present to me, true light from light, Word, Son of God, almighty God. Be present to me, true illumination, Holy Spirit, unity, holiness, and love of the Father and the Son, almighty God. Be present to me, O one Trinity and threefold unity, Father and Son and Holy Spirit, one almighty God.

My faith invokes you, Lord, which in your goodness you gave me for my salvation. My pure conscience invokes you, my God, and the sweet love of my faith, which, after shaking off the darkness of ignorance, you led to an understanding of the truth; which, after removing the foolish bitterness of the world and applying the sweetness of your charity, you made flavorful and honey-sweet for me. [Note: The better manuscripts read *tollo*, “I remove.” Others—Erasmus, Lyon, Venice, and Sixtus—give this passage as follows: “which, after you had shaken off the darkness of ignorance, you led to an understanding of the truth; after the foolish bitterness of the world had been removed and the sweetness of your charity applied, you made it flavorful and honey-sweet for me.” Thus also the Louvain edition, which nevertheless reads *qua stulta* rather than *quam stulta*.]

O blessed Trinity, the clear voice and sincere cry of my faith invokes you; nourishing that faith in me from my very cradle, you have always illumined it [Col. 0969] through the inspiration of your grace; which, increasing it, you strengthened me through the ministry of the preaching of Mother Church.

How sweet it has become in the ear [Note: Erasmus, Lyon, and Venice read “in the mouth”; Louvain, “in the ears.”] of my heart; how sweetly it tastes on the very palate of the joys of my soul; how powerfully and how frequently it strikes my mind and admonishes it, moving all my senses and the inner regions of my spirit, so that it delights me to praise you, because you made us for praising you!

But my mind is restless until it rests in you. It reproaches me for my laziness and gathers me back from the dispersion by which I am torn apart piecemeal, as I turn away from you, the One, and dissipate myself among many things. Thus, returning to myself, rising above myself, and transcending all things to reach you, may I exult in you with the joy of my heart and bring forth praises through the service of my mouth, so that in meditation on the confession of your glory my heart may grow warm, my spirit yearn for you, and my mind burn in your love, having forgotten vanity and misery, while it attends to you alone and, astonished and awestruck, clings to the unchangeableness of your glory.

With the eyes of faith it gazes upon you, the sun of righteousness, as it is written: “Whoever clings to God is one spirit with him” (1 Corinthians 6:17).

I shall flee, then, Lord—and gladly flee—the clamorous uproar of all vanities. But where shall I flee, so as to avoid them, trample them beneath my feet, and drive them far from the serenity of joyful contemplation? To you, who are the sole refuge and only hope of the wretched; to you, my glory and the one who lifts up my head (Ps. 3:4); to you I shall flee from the pit of misery and the filth of mire (Ps. 39:3). Let me cling to you, insofar as you yourself grant it, honey-sweetness, so that you may become sweet to me—a sweetness that does not deceive, a sweetness blessed and secure. [Note: [Col. 0969] Alcuin, col. 171, e.]

I shall seek you, therefore, Lord, calling upon you; and I shall call upon you, believing in you, so that in seeking you I may find you, and in finding you bless you, who have blessed us with every blessing. [Note: [Col. 0969] Augustine, *On the Trinity*, book 15, chapter 28.]

My God, my only hope, hear me, lest, wearied, I should be unwilling to seek you; rather, let me always seek your face ardently. You grant the strength to seek, you who have made yourself findable and have given ever greater hope of finding you. Illuminate, Lord, the eye of my heart with the clear light of inward vision; for it is veiled and blinded by the dreadful darkness of sins and ignorance. Illuminate it with the light of your grace, so that with the sincere eyes of faith and the pure light of the heart I may contemplate the mysteries of your kingdom. Yet because praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner (Sir. 15:9), and faith without works worthy of it is not praised, [Note: [Col. 0969] Alcuin, col. 273, c., in the *Prayer Attributed to Gregory.] I ask the Father through the Son; I ask the Son through the Father; I ask the Holy Spirit through the Father and the Son: may all vices be driven far from me and all holy virtues planted within me, so that the sacrifice of praise offered by my faith may be acceptable to you, my God, and rise to you as an odor of sweetness.

I beseech you, and as a suppliant implore your mercy, fountain and source of all things, God who bestows and preserves the virtues: increase in me hope [Note: [Col. 0969] The Bohairian Manuscript reads *faith* instead of *hope*.], holy faith, upright and undefiled, learned, catholic, and most prudent faith, fervent, unconquerable, and orthodox faith; faith which, through love and humility, may work in me everything that pleases you, and which cannot be overcome amid contentious words in a time of persecution or on a day of need. God who searches hearts and kidneys (Ps. 7:10), [Note: [Col. 0969] Augustine, cited above, *On the Trinity*, book 15, chapter 28.] before you are my health and my weakness: preserve the former, I pray, and heal the latter. Before you are my knowledge and my ignorance. Where you have opened to me, receive me as I enter; where you have closed, open to me when I knock, so that, hearing, I may understand you; understanding, love you; loving, praise you; and with my whole heart desire always to behold the beauty of your vision. I hear what your Scripture—which you sanctified and sent into the world—wishes to make known to us; I hear it, and I believe it.

## CHAPTER II  
### That God is spirit and wholly present everywhere

For it says: “God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship and believe in spirit and truth” (John 4:24).

[Col. 0970]

But the Spirit is incomprehensible, incorporeal, immutable, unbounded, wholly everywhere, divided nowhere, according to the true testimony of Scripture itself. In this way, Creator, you are distinguished from the creature, among whom there are those who are also called spirits. If this is so—indeed, because it is so—how shall I call upon my God and my Lord? For surely, when I call upon him, I shall call him into myself. And what place is there in me into which my God may come—into which he may come who made heaven and earth? Is there, then, something in me that can contain you, my God? Or do heaven and earth, which you made and in which you made me, contain you? Or, since without you nothing would exist, does whatever exists come to be so that it may contain you? Why, then, do I ask you to come into me, when I would not exist unless you were in me? For I am not now in the underworld [Note: [Col. 0970] Elsewhere, *in the underworld*.], and yet you are there; for even if I descend into hell, you are present (Ps. 138:8). I would not exist, therefore, my God—I would not exist at all—unless you were in me. Or rather, I would not exist unless I were in you, from whom, through whom, and in whom all things are (Rom. 11:36). Yes, Lord, even so.

Where, then, do I call upon you, when I am in you? Or from where will you come into me? Where can I withdraw, where can I go? Perhaps outside heaven and earth, so that from there my God may come into me—he who said, “I fill heaven and earth” (Jer. 23:24)? Do heaven and earth, then, contain you because you fill them? Or do you fill them, and yet there remains something by which they do not contain you? And where do you pour out whatever remains of you after heaven and earth have been filled? Do you need to be contained by anyone, you who contain all things? For you fill what you contain by containing it. The vessels that are full of you do not make you stable; even if they are broken, you are not poured out. And when you are poured out upon us, you do not fall down, but raise us up; nor are you scattered, but gather us together.

Since you fill all things, do you fill all things with your whole self? Or, because all things cannot contain you wholly, do they contain a part of you, and do all things together contain that same part? Or does each individual thing contain an individual part, larger things larger parts and smaller things smaller parts? Is one part of you, then, greater and another smaller? Or are you wholly everywhere, while no thing contains you wholly?

What, then, are you, Lord God of mine—what, then, except the Lord my God? For who is God besides the Lord, or who is God besides our God (Ps. 17:32)? No one, certainly, no one. There is no other besides you, triune and one, one and triune, neither in heaven above nor on earth below. Who is like you? Who is majestic in holiness, fearful and praiseworthy in every virtue, like you, our God, who do great and wondrous things, and things unsearchable beyond number (Exod. 15:11)?

All things magnify you; every spirit praises you; all those hosts of blessed spirits and heavenly citizens worship and bless you. Throughout the whole world, Mother Church offers prayers to you and unceasingly sings your praises. I, the least of your servants, praise and bless you. My mind rejoices to you; all my bones cry out to you, “Who is like you, Lord?” (Ps. 88:9). And rightly so: all that you have made obeys, serves, and trembles before you alone, its Creator; at your command you do whatever you will.

## CHAPTER III  
### That God made all things by his sole command and is wholly in all things

For you truly are the one Lord, the invisible, inestimable, unbounded, nonlocalized, immeasurable, incomprehensible God, wholly everywhere, everywhere present, penetrating all things ineffably, containing all things, knowing all things, seeing all things, powerful over all things, and governing the universe; wholly in heaven, wholly on earth, wholly also everywhere. There is no other God besides you, our God, in whom the apostolic and universal Church believes and whom it worships.

You truly are to be worshiped and venerated, feared and loved with all devotion always, Lord our God. When we did not exist, you powerfully made us; and when we had been lost through our own fault, by your piety and goodness [Col. 0971] you wondrously restored us. [Note: [Col. 0971] Alcuin, col. 135.] Therefore I confess you, King of heaven and earth, and honor you with the sacrifice of praise. And because external gifts are lacking, I return to you the vows of praise with all the marrow of my heart that is within me.

But since nothing can be acceptably offered to you except what comes from you, you, God, in whose light we see light, give, I beg you, light to my heart, give a word to my mouth, give my mind the power to ascend to the heavenly seat:

> Grant that I may behold the fountain of goodness; grant that, once the light is found,  
> I may fix the eyes of my mind upon you, clearly seen.

[Note: [Col. 0971] Boethius, *The Consolation of Philosophy*, book 3, meter 9.]

And since we are partly of heaven and partly of earth, whereby the body that decays weighs down the soul and an earthly dwelling depresses the sense that thinks on many things (Wis. 9:15):

> Scatter the clouds and burdens of the earthly mass, and, I beg you, illuminate by your splendor the dark face of the inner person:

> Halt minds that wander, rushing through many byways.

Subject the flesh to the spirit, desire to reason, vices to virtues, the body to the soul; subject me inwardly and outwardly, in all things, to your will, so that when everything has been rightly ordered in its proper arrangement, by your grace I may be worthy both to love you perfectly and to praise you worthily with lips and heart, crying out to you with every virtue within my power, and saying thus:

## CHAPTER IV  
### On the essence of the Godhead

[Note: [Col. 0971] Thus also Alcuin, col. 172, a, b, c, following Augustine, *Confessions*, book 1, chapter 4.]

Most high, best, most powerful, most merciful, most just, most hidden, most present, most beautiful, most mighty, most sweet, most unconquerable, most true Lord our God: you are steadfast and incomprehensible; immutable, yet changing all things; invisible, yet seeing all things; immortal, nonlocalized, without end, unbounded, nowhere finite, ineffable, inestimable, unspeakable, unsearchable, unmoved, touching all things, investigable, to be feared and dreadful, venerable and awe-inspiring, honorable and terrifying; never new, never old, making all things new, and bringing the proud into old age, though they do not know it; always active, always at rest; gathering and needing nothing; bearing all things without burden; filling all things without being enclosed; creating and protecting all things, nourishing and perfecting them; seeking, though nothing is lacking to you.

You love, yet do not burn with passion; you are jealous, yet secure; you repent, yet do not grieve; you grow angry, yet remain tranquil; you change your works, but never your counsel. You receive what you find, though you never lost it; you are never needy, yet rejoice in gains; you are never greedy, yet demand interest. An excess payment is made to you, as though you owed it—and who has anything that is not yours? You repay debts while owing nothing; you give what is owed while losing nothing.

## CHAPTER V  
### How God is far and near, and wholly in all things

[Note: [Col. 0971] Gregory the Great, *Homily 8 on Ezekiel*.]

You alone give life to all things; you created all things. You are everywhere and wholly everywhere. You can be sensed, but cannot be seen. You are absent nowhere, and yet you are far from the thoughts of the wicked. You are not absent even where you are far away, because where you are not present by grace, you are present by judgment.

You touch all things, yet you do not touch all things equally. You touch some things so that they may exist, but not so that they may live and sense; some so that they may exist, live, and sense, but not so that they may discern; and some so that they may exist, live, sense, and discern. Although you are never unlike yourself, you touch unlike things in unlike ways. You are present everywhere, yet can scarcely be found; we follow you as you stand still, but cannot lay hold of you.

## CHAPTER VI  
### That God touches all things, yet is not moved

You hold all things, fill all things, encompass all things, surpass all things, and sustain all things. You do not sustain from one side and surpass from another; nor do you fill from one side and encompass from another. Rather, by encompassing you fill, and by filling you encompass; by sustaining you surpass, and by surpassing you sustain.

You teach the hearts of the faithful without the noise of words. You reach from end to end mightily and order all things sweetly (Wis. 8:1). You are not extended through places, nor varied by times; you have neither comings nor goings. You dwell in inaccessible light, which no human being has seen or can see (1 Tim. 6:16–17); remaining at rest in yourself, you encompass the whole everywhere.

## CHAPTER VII  
### That God is not divided into parts

You cannot be cut apart or divided, for you are truly one. You do not become parts; rather, wholly holding the whole, you fill the whole, illumine the whole, and possess the whole. The human mind cannot grasp or conceive this mystery, nor can an eloquent tongue narrate it, nor can the volumes of libraries explain it through extended discourse. Even if books filled the entire world, your ineffable knowledge could not be narrated.

For you are truly unspeakable; in no way can you be written down or enclosed—you who are the fountain of divine light and the sun of eternal brightness. You are great without quantity, and therefore immeasurable; good without quality, and therefore truly and supremely good. No one is good except you alone.

## CHAPTER VIII  
### That for God, to will is to do

You whose will is your work, and for whom to will is to be able; you who made all things that you created from nothing by your will alone; you possess your entire creation without any need, govern it without labor, and rule it without weariness. Nothing disturbs the order of your rule, whether among the highest or the lowest. You are held in all places without being in a place; you contain all things without circumference; you are present everywhere without position or movement.

You are not the author of evil—for you cannot do evil, though you can do all things. You have never regretted having done anything, nor are you disturbed by the storm of any agitation of soul. Nor is your kingdom merely a portion of the whole earth. You approve or command no disgrace or crime. You never lie, because you are eternal truth: by whose goodness alone we were made, by whose justice we suffer punishments, and by whose clemency we are freed.

## CHAPTER IX  
### That nothing is to be worshiped except God

For nothing heavenly, nothing earthly, nothing fiery, and nothing touched by bodily sense is to be adored or worshiped in your place—you who truly are what you are and do not change. [Note: [Col. 0972] Alcuin, col. 119, b.] To you above all and especially belongs what the Greeks say, **ὤν** (*ōn*), which the Latins render *Est*, “He is,” because you are always the same, and your years shall not fail (Ps. 101:28).

From this it is plainly understood that you, our God whom we worship, the true and almighty God, are without doubt invisible, although you may be seen by devout understanding; incomprehensible, although you may be represented through grace; inestimable, although you may be devoutly believed and holily contemplated by human senses; ineffable, although, through the customary words of human speech, you may somehow be named by way of accommodation. Therefore you are true and so great.

Whatever can be known, comprehended, thought, or said about you is less than you. But what is incomprehensible and immeasurable, unspeakable and infinite, is known to you alone. For this is what surpasses every understanding; this also is what causes you to be regarded, certainly believed, and called the universal God, since you cannot be found all the way to perfection, nor wholly understood or contained. Thus the magnitude of your greatness presents you to us both as known and unknown.

And this is the height of the offense of those who despise knowing you and refuse to serve you, their Creator. They have what they may worship knowingly; they have what they may wonder at unknowingly. They have what they may fear and what they may love. For if you were wholly exposed to our knowledge, you could not be believed to be the living and true God. So completely false were those found to be who were thought to be gods, since they could be known in every respect—who they were, what they were like, and how great they were.

## CHAPTER X  
### That God made all things in the Word alone

[Col. 0973]

But you, our wondrous and powerful God, who brought forth from nothing the entire mass of this world, with all the equipment of the elements, bodies, and spirits, by the word with which you commanded, by the reason with which you ordered, and by the power with which you were able, as an adornment of the majesty of your glory; you who, ordering time to proceed from that very first age while remaining steadfast, grant all things to move; you who adorned the earth with the manifold growth of fruits and heaven with the beautiful light of the stars, whose names, signs, powers, courses, and seasons you alone know.

You are gentle, you are kind; strong, jealous, and unconquerable Sabaoth, visiting the sins of the fathers upon the children to the third and fourth generation, and showing mercy to thousands of thousands who love you (Exod. 20:5) and fear your name.

If your works are so great and unsearchable, beautiful and astonishing, let those who wish say how you, their most beautiful Creator, can be comprehended. For it is evident that the maker of all things exists in a very different manner from the things he willed to be made. Yet from the beauty of circumscribed nature and the wondrous appearance of worldly things, your beauty—which you yourself are, because you are simple—and the excellence of your glory, which cannot be circumscribed, can to some extent be understood, although no sense can reach the infinite and incomprehensible greatness of your divinity—not even [Note: [Col. 0973] Elsewhere, *even*.] that of those heavenly citizens. [Note: [Col. 0973] Isidore, *Sentences*, book 1, chapter 3.] Yet in a wondrous way your essence is known when it is believed to exist.

## CHAPTER XI  
### On the two syllables of God

Whenever I recall or hear the two short syllables and four letters by which *Deus*—“God”—is written—for this name is rightly owed to you alone, Almighty—and when I contemplate the mighty works of your power and the wondrous creation of the world, that is, when I consider the beauty of the world’s making; and when I silently reckon within myself your mercies, which are from eternity—for let those who wish marvel at your power, but I am even more astonished when I observe your mercies—then, in these four letters and two short syllables, I contemplate with the vision of my mind and the sincere eyes of faith something infinite and incomprehensible, immeasurable and ineffable, insofar as you deign to grant such knowledge and ability to me, so small a human being.

For are you, our God, two short syllables? Or do we worship two short syllables, or desire to reach two short syllables—syllables that almost cease to sound before they have begun, and in which there is no place for the second unless the first has already passed? Surely something great remains, and it is great and supreme: that which is incomparable and preeminent over all things [Note: [Col. 0973] The Bohairian Manuscript adds, “and unlike all things”], which is called *Deus*, even though the sound does not remain when *Deus* is spoken.

## CHAPTER XII  
### That God is not seen in his own nature

But because flesh does not know spirit, and invisible things are not seen by visible things—for we walk by faith and not by sight—[Note: [Col. 0973] From Isidore, *Sentences*, book 1, chapter 5, with notable variation. See also Alcuin, col. 273.] you, our exceedingly good and devout God, in consideration of human weakness, deign to make yourself known to us, not according to your own nature, but through a certain likeness. Hence you are also described as having the qualities of our bodily members, since you wish unworthy passions to be attributed to yourself for this purpose: because, as we cannot know you as you are in our present misery, you draw us from our own things to yours, so that, while you condescend to us, we may more easily rise up to you.

## CHAPTER XIII  
### On the image of God made in the human being

In many ways, in order to signify you to human beings, you draw forms from lower things toward yourself, although it is established that according to your own nature you are invisible and incorporeal, incomprehensible and unbounded. Accordingly, we believe that you never appeared to anyone according to your essence, but that, in the forms of creatures which you assumed as you willed, you appeared for the accomplishment of your purposes.

The followers of the heresy of the Anthropomorphites are therefore deceived. When they read that the human being was made in the image and likeness of God, they assert with foolish presumption that you possess a human form, although in that passage you are said or believed to have created the mind, not the flesh, in your image.

## CHAPTER XIV  
### On the breadth, length, height, and depth of God

[Note: [Col. 0974] From Isidore, *Sentences*, book 1, chapter 2.]

Indeed, human speech says nothing worthy of you, because nothing concerning you can rightly be said according to quality or quantity, position or appearance, or movement. And yet breadth, length, height, and depth are read as existing in you in some manner.

Breadth is the charity by which you gather us from error and hold us in truth. Length is the patience with which you bear us, though we are evil, until, once corrected, you restore us to our future homeland. Height is that by which, through the immensity of your knowledge, you surpass every understanding of human beings and angels. Depth is that by which you arrange those destined for condemnation below, and as the just Judge predestine them by righteous judgment.

Therefore, whoever wishes to taste something of your nature, supreme good Godhead, should transcend every creature and direct the gaze of the mind beyond all things. [Note: [Col. 0974] The Bohairian Manuscript reads, “the goodness of God.” The printed editions read, “the Godhead of the good.”]

## CHAPTER XV  
### On the knowledge of the Holy Trinity

A human being, placed far from vanity, is held more fully in truth when God is devoutly believed and holily contemplated in his heart in peace, with all other things removed from his gaze. Yet although no one in this valley of tears can effectively comprehend or define you, it is nevertheless a great and exceedingly wondrous gift granted to our age to know concerning you, the supreme good, through your grace, which has revealed it to us.

Who before us, upon whom the ends of the ages have come (1 Cor. 10:11), could hear or know such clear things concerning the Trinity and unity, persons and substance? Concerning you, God the Father, that you are from no one and are therefore called unbegotten; concerning your Son, that he is begotten and is from you, not from himself; and concerning the Holy Spirit, that he proceeds and is not from himself, but from you and the Son, whose Spirit he is.

In such a way that, just as you, Father, cannot be called begotten or proceeding, so the Son cannot be called unbegotten or proceeding, and likewise the Holy Spirit cannot be called unbegotten or begotten, so that the properties of the persons may plainly show us that you are one Father together with one Son and one Holy Spirit.

Who in earlier ages understood so wisely, professed so openly, and truly knew that you are one God and triune, neither separating the substance nor confusing the persons? Your Son, indeed, sent [Note: [Col. 0974] A manner of expression customary with Alcuin. See col. 133, e.] from your bosom into our public sphere, made this rule of faith more clearly known to this final age.

Before you showed the creature its Creator, you were known only in Judea, God, and in Israel the great renown and worship of your name were heard (Ps. 75:2). But was it then as plainly, or as fully, as among us who have been established under grace? Concerning the undivided Trinity, only a very few at that time perceived a little.

For the children of the lawmakers, struck by a fitting blindness, still do not know what they ought to know concerning the one Trinity or the triune unity. In their misery they refuse to confess anything besides one God and chatter malicious words against us when we say that you, the Father, have a Son.

But how much and how truly it has been granted to us who came from the Gentiles to understand concerning the triune and one God is proved by hearts that believe and mouths that confess, and no less by the very scourges and death inflicted for this confession. For it is written: “I have understood more than the elders” (Ps. 118:100).

## CHAPTER XVI  
### That the Trinity is undivided; creation belongs to God alone; how the Word is in the Father

[Note: [Col. 0974] Alcuin, col. 148, following Augustine, *On the Trinity*, book 10, chapter 28. See also Augustine, *Tractates on John*, tractate 29.]

Lord our living and true God, unless you were Trinity, the voice of Truth would not have said: “Go, baptize all nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. [Col. 0975] 28:19). For we would not be commanded, Lord God, to be baptized in the name of one who was not the Lord God.

And again, unless you, Trinity, were one God, your voice would never have said: “Hear, O Israel: the Lord your God is one God” (Deut. 6:4). Therefore, unless you, God the Father, were yourself God, and your Son, your Word Jesus Christ, were himself God, and your gift were the Holy Spirit himself, we would not read in the writings of truth, “God sent his Son” (Gal. 4:4).

Nor would you, Only-Begotten, have said concerning the Holy Spirit, “Whom the Father will send in my name” (John 14:26), and “Whom I will send to you from the Father” (John 15:26), and elsewhere, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30), and “Whoever sees me sees the Father. For I am in the Father, and the Father is in me; and the Father who remains in me himself does the works” (John 14:9–10).

What else do you teach us through these words, except to believe in the triune and one God—you, the teacher of truth, in whose heart the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden?

You also say, “My teaching is not mine” (John 7:16), and “The word that you heard is not mine, but the Father’s who sent me” (John 14:24). A wondrous matter, an astonishing matter.

Speak, then, speak, Word of the Father; answer, I beg you, Power and Wisdom of the supreme Principle. You yourself are principle from Principle, yet not two principles, but certainly one Principle. Speak, Word who always remains; teach the servant who humbly asks.

For what is so much yours as you yourself? Yet you are your own and not your own, because you are not from yourself, as you often testify in many passages, but from the Father, whose mouth is the Word—not a sound uttered in syllables and carried away, but eternally living and remaining immovably.

And therefore you are the Word—not one that ceases once spoken, but one that remains when born; not transitory, but eternal; not made, but begotten; not only begotten, but also only-begotten. Reason is present to the one who orders, and power is ready to the one who accomplishes, for you are true God and supreme Lord.

The Father begot you, the only-begotten Word, from himself, through whom he created all things from nothing. For this reason we believe without doubt: unless you, the Word God, were all-knowing and almighty, all things could in no way have been made through you. How can a creature create anything? Certainly only God can create, he who was not created; for nothing except God is uncreated. Let it be far from our understanding that we should confess anything to be born from the Father except the Son; and therefore only God could be born from God.

Thus, for me who desire to contemplate you, Word of the Father, no words are sufficient by which I might explain you. When shall I ever be able to speak adequately or worthily? Who speaks of whom? A human being of God, a work of its maker, a creature of its Creator, a small thing of the immeasurable, the temporal of the eternal—whose venerable power is all-powerful, by which you made us through gratuitous goodness, and whose grace is no less venerable, by which you saved us through all-powerful mercy.

You freely made us the work of your creative omnipotence, and omnipotently completed us as the work of saving grace, possessing perpetual power both to establish what had not been established and to restore what had been lost.

Therefore that foremost of theologians, who contemplated more deeply than the others with eagle-like eyes and wrote, “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God; he was in the beginning with God” (John 1:1–2), would not have spoken forth these words unless you, God the Word, had always been with the Father, always with the Father, always from the Father, and always in the Father—not as a vessel in a vessel, or a city beside a city, but as wisdom within the wise, truth in the truthful, goodness in the good, eternity in the eternal; for nothing other than God, equal and coeternal with the Father from whom you were begotten, can exist in the substance of the Father.

Therefore let every heretical perversity fall silent and perish with its authors—the perversity that, ever hostile through contentious strife, now divides the substance and now confuses the persons.

May Mother Church, instructed in heavenly disciplines, increase in faith, I pray, and be ever more abundantly fruitful in devout works. She judges it profane and exceedingly impious to worship three gods or not to distinguish the Trinity in its persons. Finally, taught by heavenly instruction, she believes, confesses, and teaches beyond doubt one substance and three persons, knowing everything that pertains to the rule of faith.

Instructed from childhood by her teaching and doctrine inspired from heaven, I believe in my heart and confess with my mouth that you, O supreme Trinity, are one power and undivided majesty.

## CHAPTER XVII  
### On the knowledge of the incorporeal divine essence

[Note: [Col. 0976] Alcuin, col. 156, a; 151, a.]

I confess you, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, triune in persons and one in substance, the one true and almighty God, creator of visible and invisible things—not a body or existing in a body, nor composed by the mixture of different forms, nor fashioned by the joining together of limbs, but of one simple and incorporeal, invisible and unbounded nature.

I believe and confess that you are truly the Father, the source of supreme goodness and of the whole Godhead, God of unbounded and unbegotten majesty, deriving your beginning from no one but giving beginning to all things. You beget the Son not through bodily generation, nor from outside yourself, nor by necessity or will, but by nature.

[Note: [Col. 0976] From Pelagius. See *Sermon* 236, no. 2, Appendix, volume 5.]

I also confess that you are truly the Son, ineffably born from the Father without beginning, true God, the only-begotten, through whom all things were made, and the true Word of the Father—not made, not created, not adopted, but begotten and of one substance with the Father. Thus in every respect you are equal to God the Father, so that you cannot be inferior in time, rank, or power.

I confess that you, who were begotten, are as great as the one who begot you. But when I say that the Son was begotten by the Father, I do not assign any time to the divine and ineffable generation. Nor do I say that the Father once began to exist, nor that you, his Son, did. Since he was always Father, you therefore were never not the Son. For we cannot confess an eternal Father without also confessing an equally eternal Son. The Father is called father from the Son; and since he was always Father, there is no doubt that he always had a Son.

## CHAPTER XVIII  
### On the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son

I also believe that you are the Holy Spirit, true God, not made, nor created, nor begotten, nor unbegotten, but proceeding ineffably from the Father and the Son, and remaining substantially in both the Father and the Son.

Thus you proceed from both in such a way that you remain inseparably in both; and in every respect you are equal, coeternal, and consubstantial with God the Father and the Son, so that you cannot differ from them or be cut off from them—in power, will, eternity, or substance—from whom you proceed. [Note: [Col. 0976] Elsewhere, *precede*.]

Therefore I believe in my heart and confess with my mouth, and love in my mind, the eternal Father without birth; the eternal Son with birth; the eternal Holy Spirit with procession but without birth; the whole Father remaining in the Son and the Holy Spirit; the whole Son in the Father and the Holy Spirit; the whole Holy Spirit remaining in the Father and the Son; and the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit as one almighty God, with one power and one kingdom, one majesty and one eternity, reigning everywhere from then and now and forever.

Directing my attention toward this rule of faith, I sought you, my God, insofar as you made me able, and desired through understanding to see what I had believed. For this reason I entered the storehouse of many delights by which Mother Church is nourished; there I considered many things and began to examine them one by one.

And as I anxiously and eagerly ran about here and there, you, being good and wishing to aid the desire that you had given me, stretched out your hand of mercy and loosened the knot of my uncertainty. Therefore it greatly delights me to think about you, to speak about you, and, according to the measure of my smallness, to bring forth your praises with a desiring heart, so that amid my present misery I may be held only in body, but be with you in mind and with every desire, O my Lord.

## CHAPTER XIX  
### On the comparison of the three persons; and on the venerable mysteries of the Trinity and the Eucharist

[Col. 0977]

God, three and one, kindle the light of knowledge within me, by which I may deserve to understand you as the triune and one God, just as you are the triune and one God. Remove from me more and more, as you have begun to do, the darkness of ignorance, so that I may see spiritual things spiritually, insofar as human frailty permits. On this road along which I walk with you as my guide, grant me understanding; inspire me and continually teach me by your grace how one must believe in you irreproachably: so that I may apprehend you as one God essentially and grasp you as incomprehensibly three personally—the unbegotten Father, the Only-Begotten from the Father, and the Holy Spirit proceeding from both and remaining in both; with no moment of priority or posteriority intervening among the three, and with no divided sovereignty; no divided counsel in creating, no divided assistance or work in governing and perfecting creatures. Whatever is natural in them is undivided; whatever is personal is unconfused.

O ineffable mystery, and more difficult than all others to understand! The remaining sacraments which are held in your Church, Lord, are wondrous and venerable; but this sacrament of yours surpasses them all. This mystery of your undivided Trinity, and that Sacrament of the heavenly table which feeds faithful and devout souls with flesh and gives them drink of blood, lest they hunger or thirst forever—grant that I, my God, may especially perceive and believe, receive and retain these things with a pure and simple conscience above all else. Do not permit, I beg you, Lord, that my faith in them should waver in the least; but by your goodness grant me always to believe and understand in them and concerning them as their truth requires.

Let your grace enter my heart—a grace that resounds without sound or noise and speaks there the whole truth of such great mysteries; let that teacher of virtues and judge [Note: [Col. 0977] Elsewhere, “index,” that is, “indicator.”] of all truths pour light and sweetness inwardly everywhere and outwardly on every side over my soul. Thus, by illuminating and making it taste, establish and confirm it in the very center of truth, so that I may neither wish nor be able to think otherwise about such great mysteries than is proper and fitting [Note: [Col. 0977] Codex Boherianus adds: “It is wondrous that I long to say it, but the tongue does not express what the mind desires.”].

Almighty Goodness, whose merciful ears are open to the very desires of your poor, understand the cry of my heart and favor my prayers. Grant, Lord, that with the palate of my mind I may feel, taste, and savor these ineffable sacraments: for they are great and exceedingly wondrous, and I, a little one, fail in contemplating them whenever I raise the eyes of faith to gaze upon them.

But since both are necessary for our salvation in one way, God, author of all things, invisible Creator, who are one divinity in supreme substance and a true and perfect Trinity personally: I entreat you as God the Father, from whom are all things; and your Son, through whom are all things; and likewise the Holy Spirit, in whom are all things. I humbly beg you, my Lord, whom I confess as the one and true God in Trinity, by whom we were created, redeemed, and enlightened: eager for such great mysteries, nurse me, nourish me, and extend my littleness to the measure of mature manhood, so that I may be able to receive this solid and perfect food. For your eyes saw my imperfection (Psalm 138:16).

## CHAPTER XX. That the divine substance is indivisible
