God the Father, giver of all good things, to whom no one ever prays without hope of mercy, together with your Son and the Holy Spirit, grant what my soul desires and asks of you. For since their substance is one, their gift is also one, their operation one, their gift one, and their power one, so that even in the distinct property of the persons some unity may be perceived according to a deeper understanding. [Note: [Col. 0977] Alcuin, *On the Faith of the Holy Trinity*, book 1, chapter 14.]

Indeed, the unity of your inseparable nature cannot have separable persons: for just as you are Trinity in unity and unity in Trinity, so you cannot have separation of persons. Those persons are sometimes named individually; but you, Trinity God, willed to show yourself inseparable in the persons in such a way that no name belonging to you in any person is not referred, according to the rule of relation, to another person—as the Father is most truly referred to the Son, the Son to the Father, and the Holy Spirit to the Father and the Son.

Those names, however, which signify your substance, power, or essence—or whatever is properly said of God—belong equally to all the persons: God, great, good, eternal, almighty, and all things that are naturally said of you as God. There is therefore no name of nature that can belong to you, God the Father, in such a way that it cannot belong to your Son or to the Holy Spirit. We say that you, God the Father, are naturally God; but the Son is also naturally God, and the Holy Spirit is naturally God—not, however, three gods, but one God: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

Therefore you are inseparable, holy Trinity God, understood as three in the persons, although in speech you have names that can be separated; for you admit no plural number in the names of nature. This shows that the persons cannot be divided in the Holy Trinity, which is the one true God, because the name of each person always looks toward another person. If I say “Father,” I indicate the Son; if I name the Son, I proclaim the Father; if I call upon the Holy Spirit, it must be understood that he is the spirit of someone—that is, of the Father and the Son.

You, however, unity of divinity multiplied by the plurality of persons, are numerically innumerable, and therefore measurably immeasurable and ponderably imponderable. For we do not profess the origin of that supreme Goodness—which you yourself are—from which are all things, through which are all things, and in which are all things; rather, we say that all good things exist by participation in it.

## CHAPTER XXI. That there is no matter in the divinity

For your divine substance has always been without matter and remains without matter, although it is not without form. When you impress this form upon individual things, as upon them all a kind of seal, you undoubtedly cause them to differ from you without any alteration through your increase or diminution. [Note: [Col. 0978] Alcuin, *On the Faith of the Holy Trinity*, book 1, chapter 4, after Isidore, *Sentences*, book 1, chapter 2.]

Whatever exists in the nature of creatures is your creature, O God, triune unity and one Trinity, whose omnipotence governs, rules, and fills all that it has created. We do not say that you fill all things because they contain you, but rather that they themselves are contained by you.

## CHAPTER XXII. That there is no part or division in God

You do not fill all things piecemeal, nor should it in any way be supposed that each thing receives you according to the size of its portion—that the greatest receives more and the smallest less. Rather, you yourself are wholly in all things, or all things are in you. Your omnipotence encloses everything, and no one will be able to find a way by which to escape its power. Whoever does not have you placated will by no means escape you when you are angry.

For the immensity of your divine greatness is such that we understand you to be within all things, but not enclosed; outside all things, but not excluded.

## CHAPTER XXIII. That God contains all things

You are therefore inward, so that you may contain all things; you are outward, so that by the immensity of your unbounded greatness you may surround and govern all things. In that you are outward, you are shown to be the Creator; in that you are inward, you are demonstrated to govern and rule all things.

And lest created things exist without you, you are within all things; but lest they exist outside you, you are outward, so that all things may be enclosed by you—not by local magnitude, but by the presence of your power. For you are present everywhere, and all things are present to you, although some understand this and others do not.

## CHAPTER XXIV. That the deity is not corporeal

These and many other things the Church has taught me—the holy, universal, and orthodox mother whom, by your grace, you willed me to become a member of. Through the continual illumination of your inspiration, you have graciously made me so certain and secure in all matters concerning her heavenly teaching, Lord, as though I were gazing face to face—not through a mirror—upon many things that lie hidden, closed within mysteries.

She has therefore taught me that you alone, the living and true God, are not corporeal, passible, or tangible; that no part of you can be perceived by bodily eyes; that nothing of your substance or nature can in any way be violated, compounded, fabricated, [Note: [Col. 0979] Alcuin, column 136a.] greater, or lesser; but that in every respect and on every side you are perfect without deformity, great without quantity, good without quality, everlasting without time, life without death, strong without weakness, truth without falsehood, wholly everywhere without place, present everywhere without position, filling all things without extension, meeting all things everywhere without contraction, transcending all things without motion, remaining within all things without fixed location, creating all things without need, ruling all things without labor, giving all things a beginning without yourself having a beginning, making all mutable things without yourself undergoing change, and reigning always and everywhere, remaining without end.

Lord God, one; Trinity God, who incomparably surpasses all things: you are so ineffable, infinite, and incomprehensible that everything that can be said of you is exceedingly little. We say many things, but we cannot fully say what you are. And since you yourself are the consummation of all speech, when we have reached you, many of these things that we say will undoubtedly cease, and you will remain one, all in all; and without end we shall say all things as one, praising you as one, and having ourselves also become one in you: continually seeing you, without end, as the incorporeal and unchanging Trinity; knowing all things in you; possessing in you joy that will remain forever; healed from every sickness and transformed into that glory of immortality.

## CHAPTER XXV. On the vision of God. The one Trinity

When this vision comes, which is promised to be given face to face; when everything concerning the mysteries is announced openly, and the appearance of faith and the substance of hope take their place; then, knowing and seeing more clearly and more certainly, we shall behold that in you, one Trinity, there is nothing created or servile, nothing unequal, nothing equal by grace, nothing earlier or later, nothing greater or lesser, nothing foreign or subordinate to another, nothing inserted by persuasion [Note: [Col. 0979] Perhaps, “by intrusion.”] or stealth, nothing diverse in character or will, nothing singular in office or communicable to another, nothing [Note: [Col. 0979] Elsewhere, “nothing confused.”] confused, but everything perfect—because everything is in one and one is in everything, though not in solitude.

For we worship and adore you, holy Father, as the supreme Good, supreme Wisdom, and supreme Goodness, one source of all things; and your Truth, through which we understand you, in no respect unlike you, which is the form of all things and which alone fills what all things desire; and at the same time the Gift of both, by which all things that are blessed are blessed. We worship and adore one immutable Trinity.

## CHAPTER XXVI. An example from fire and the soul

When it is repeated three times that something is one, a number is not heaped up; rather, its unity is asserted. [Note: [Col. 0979] From Isidore, *Differences of the Spirit*, book 2, chapter 2.] Begetter, begotten, and proceeding: three persons indeed, but one substance. Just as fire, brightness, and heat are three names but one reality, so memory, understanding, and will are three, but one soul; they are shown to be inseparable and operate inseparably.

If this is found in creatures, what should be understood concerning you, the Creator? For the nature of your divinity is in every way immovable and unchangeable; the persons, however, are mobile according to relation, not according to their property. Therefore, in the relation of the persons there is Trinity, but in the substance of nature there is unity.

There is unity because of the inseparable essence of the divinity; Trinity, however, because of the diversity of names. For we confess not merely the names, but also the properties of the names—that is, the persons—or, as the Greeks express it, ὑποστάσεις (*hypostaseis*), that is, substances.

## CHAPTER XXVII. On the immutability of God. The incomprehensible mystery of the Trinity

Nevertheless, we say these things about you, our God, insofar as human understanding can grasp them. But who, situated in this life, even with a breast of crystal, would be sufficient to penetrate the inner mysteries of your Trinity itself: how you, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, are three persons and one nature; how you, Father, are called unbegotten, the Son begotten, and the Holy Spirit neither begotten nor unbegotten, but proceeding; how the Son was born from you, the Father, and the Holy Spirit proceeds from you and from the Son; how the Son, being born, does not proceed, while the Holy Spirit, proceeding, is not born; how the Son is not from himself but from you, and yet is not later than you, from whom he is; how the Holy Spirit proceeds from you and from the Son, and yet is not preceded by you and the Son, from whom he proceeds [Note: [Col. 0980] Elsewhere, “separated from.”]; how you are three as one and one as three; how you are three relatively to one another and one essentially; how you, triune and one God, are not locally but everywhere; and how you are not everywhere piecemeal, but wholly everywhere, present everywhere without position, place, or motion?

Who, I ask, could contemplate these things? Who could comprehend them, endowed with however much goodness or knowledge? Yet this has been reserved in the hope of the promise, because we shall see you, Lord—and each person will see more clearly the purer the life he has lived here. For, as Scripture testifies, the pure in heart shall see God (Matthew 5:8).

Then it will plainly be seen, when the darkness of the mind has been wiped away, how the Son, who exists by being born, is not subsequent to you, O Father, from whom he is born; and how the Spirit of both, who is produced by procession, is not preceded by you and the Son, who bring him forth; and how you are one divisibly as three, and three indivisibly as one.

For the vision of the brightness, seizing and raising the pure loving gaze of our mind to the unveiled appearance of your majesty, will lift us up. But that brightness is itself nature, and that nature is itself brightness. This vision is begun now by faith, but then it will be perfected in appearance, when we drink at the very source the Wisdom coeternal with you, which we now receive through the mouths of teachers.

Then all the sacraments and all the hidden things will appear to us—not through the words of teachers, for we shall need no mysteries when we see you face to face—but, if I am not mistaken, from the place from which the angels see you. What could remain hidden from us then, when you, our God, the life of the living, the cause of causes, the form of forms, the most beautiful form, the unformed form, will disclose yourself to us in clear vision?

## CHAPTER XXVIII. That the deity lacks matter

It does not seem unworthy of you when we call you form. For your essence can also be called appearance and form—it is not without reason that “most splendid” and “most beautiful” are included among your praises. But this is a form without matter, motion, time, or place; and therefore it is one and is what it is, whereas other things are not what they are.

This alone can most truly say, “I am who I am” (Exodus 3:14). It is so great and such that the human mind dares not claim for itself in this life anything from the vision of its beauty; you reserve this alone for your elect as their reward in the recompense to come.

## CHAPTER XXIX. On thirst without necessity. The blessed see God unequally

When, therefore, we have reached you, the fountain of life, the eternal light, and the sweetest beauty, the thirst and satisfaction impressed upon us will arise delightfully from your vision. But necessity will be far removed from thirst, and disgust far from satisfaction; for while thirsting we shall be satisfied, and while satisfied we shall thirst.

Finally, you will be eternal life, joy, and crown for us. Your blessed vision will be the reward of our labor, so that after the darkness of this mortality we may rejoice, kindled by the light of your glory. We shall therefore see the unchangeableness of your essence, so that through it we too may become unchangeable—but not as you see yourself.

For in us we shall be able to know whatever we shall be; but in you, who cannot be comprehended, whatever you are, when shall we be able to know it? And if we shall be able to know it, we cannot yet do so; and when we can, will we be able to know you as you know yourself, God?

Even rational and elect creation will not enjoy your vision equally [Col. 0981]; each person will receive according to the reward of his labor, yet what is given to each will be fully sufficient for him to behold.

How great is the abundance of your sweetness, Lord (Psalm 30:20)! Blessed are those who dwell in your house, Lord (Psalm 83:5). Happy are those who have already crossed the sea of this mortality and reached the harbor of perpetual security. Unhappy are we, who are still tossed amid the storms surrounding the sea of this life, and who, amid many dangers and various misfortunes, uncertainly struggle to drag along our vessel.

## CHAPTER XXX. On eternal life

[Note: [Col. 0981] From Gregory, *Homily 37 on the Gospels*.]

Lord, with you as our ruler and guide, grant that we may hold our course midway between Scylla and Charybdis, so that with our vessel intact and our cargo safe we may reach you, the safest harbor.

Blessed is the soul which, released from its earthly prison, seeks heaven in freedom; which, already joined to the blessed spirits, stands before your majesty; which sees you, the unbounded light; which is affected by no fear of death or enemy; which rejoices in the gift of perpetual incorruption.

O life that is life indeed, sweet, lovable, and always to be remembered—where there is no enemy attacking, no enticement, but supreme and certain security, secure tranquility, tranquil delight, delightful happiness, happy eternity, eternal blessedness, and the blessed vision and praise of you without end, O God!

Would that this might follow, and that this mortal nature might be clothed with immortality! Would that this life might cease and quickly come to an end—this uncertain life, blind life, wretched life—which humors swell, pains destroy [Note: [Col. 0981] Elsewhere, “weaken.”], fevers dry out, air makes sick, food inflates, fasts weaken, amusements dissipate, sorrows consume, anxiety constricts, security dulls, riches make arrogant, poverty casts down, youth exalts, old age bends, weakness breaks, grief depresses; and after all these things death destroys, bringing an end to every joy, so that when they have ceased to exist, they are scarcely thought ever to have existed.

May that kingdom now, even now, come, Lord—may it fly to us, I beg—the kingdom without death, free from an end, to which no periods of time succeed throughout the ages; where continuous day without night knows no passage of time; [Note: [Col. 0981] This is from *Homily 14 on the Gospels*.] where there are the hymn-singing choirs of angels and the fellowship of the citizens above; where there is the sweet solemn celebration of those returning from the sad labor of pilgrimage; where there are the prudent choirs of prophets, the judicial company of apostles, the victorious army of innumerable martyrs, and likewise the steadfastness of confessors, consoled by receiving their reward; where there are faithful men whom the pleasure of this age could not soften from the strength of their manhood, and holy women who, together with the world, conquered their sex; where there are children who, while still in the flesh, surpassed their years in character, and old men whom age made weak but did not deprive of the power of good works.

To the holy assembly of all these, and to the joy that will remain forever as your beauty is contemplated, make me, Lord God, direct my whole heart, run bravely, and arrive happily. Meanwhile, while I remain in this body, let the one who instills goodness continually exercise my mind in these meditations.

Cleanse, therefore, the sight of my heart; sharpen the understanding of my mind; kindle my spirit with heavenly fire, so that I may think of you alone, love you alone, and hold you alone in my heart and on my lips—you who are to be our reward without end.

And that I may bear the weight of my mortality more lightly, give light to my heart and a word to my mouth; open the secrets of the holy Scriptures and pour the depths of the mysteries of your kingdom into my inward parts. Give me tears born of your love [Note: [Col. 0981] Alcuin, *Invocation of the Holy Trinity*, column 756.]; give me the wings of faith and virtue, clothed in which I may fly upward to you and, hating the earth, seek heaven.

This faith I confess through you, concerning you, and in you, O blessed, holy, and glorious Trinity; O true, supreme, and everlasting unity: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; God, Lord, Paraclete; love, grace, communion; true light, light from light, true illumination; living life, life from the living one, vivifier of the living; fountain, river, irrigation; one from himself, one from one, one from both; from one are all things, through one are all things, in one are all things—that is, the Father from himself, the Son from another, that is, from the Father, and the Holy Spirit from both, that is, from the Father and the Son: ὤν (*being*) from himself, ὤν (*being*) from another, ὤν (*being*) from both; and every ὤν (*being*) is always in the three, and every ὢν (*being*) is equal in each. The true Begetter, the begotten Truth, the Holy Spirit, the love of both. One power, equal majesty, equal glory, one and the same essence. The wise Begetter, the begotten Wisdom, and the Holy Spirit, love.

## CHAPTER XXXI. On the divine light

Triune and one God, almighty God, with whom there is no change or shadow of alteration (James 1:17), and therefore with you the course of time is not at all varied by the alternation of day and night.

God, true light, who without approaching illuminate what you choose, and without withdrawing abandon what you reject; therefore no deficiency or change comes upon you.

God, who remain immutable in yourself, have created transitory things in such a way that with you they cannot pass away; therefore, in your sight, time does not flow away as it runs to its end among us [Note: [Col. 0982] The Colbertinus manuscript has “to an end”; Bernard has “an end”; Boherianus has “outside.”].

God, in whose eternity those things remain fixed which, not fixed outwardly, flow forth through the cycles of the ages; therefore your eternity is one day, which is closed by no end and opened by no beginning.

## CHAPTER XXXII. That God is immutable

God, who without any change in yourself simultaneously behold all things, comprehend without extension both the good things that you assist and the evil things that you judge, both those whom you reward as you assist them and those whom you condemn as you judge them; in the things you arrange in different orders, you are not yourself different.

God, who surround your works externally and fill them internally, cover them above and sustain them below; and although you are above through power, below through support, outside through greatness, and within through subtlety, nevertheless you are above and below without place, vast without breadth, subtle without diminution.

Therefore, through the mass of a body you are nowhere; but through your unbounded substance and the immensity of your unchanging nature you are absent nowhere. Yet because the Creator is far removed from the creature, who can think how you are in a place, when you are not contained in a place?

You cannot be in a place at all, since you are everywhere and not in a place. The unbounded spirit itself is believed to be your placeless place; hence it is difficult to discover where you are, but much more difficult to discover where you are not.

Who can subsist or exist without you? Yet not everyone can be with you. For all things are from you and subsist through you.

## CHAPTER XXIII. On the infinity of God. Thanksgiving to God. The purpose of this little book

[Note: [Col. 0982] Alcuin, at the place cited.]

God, true and infinite blessedness, from whom, through whom, and in whom all things that are blessed are blessed.

God, true and supreme life, from whom, through whom, and in whom all things that truly and supremely live have life.

[Note: [Col. 0982] From Augustine, *Soliloquies*, book 1, chapter 1, sections 3 and 4.]

God, good and beautiful, from whom, through whom, and in whom all things that are good and truly beautiful are good and beautiful.

God, above whom there is nothing, outside whom there is nothing, without whom there is nothing, beyond whom there is nothing, beneath whom there is nothing.

God, beneath whom is everything, with whom is everything, in whom is everything.

God, from whom are all things, through whom are all things, in whom are all things.

God, whose faith awakens us, whose hope raises us up, whose love unites us.

God, who command us to ask, make us find, and open to those who knock (Matthew 7:7).

God, from whom to turn away is to fall; toward whom to turn is to rise again; in whom to remain is to stand firm.

God, whom no one loses except through deception, whom no one seeks except when admonished, whom no one finds except when pure or purified.

God, not to know whom is to die, to know whom is to live, to despise whom is to perish, to serve whom is to reign.

God, through whose merciful help the subject serves well and the superior rules well; therefore without you none of them proceeds along the right path or in the right order.

Invisible and immense God, ineffable and eternal, incomprehensible and incorporeal, immortal and perpetual, immutable and unbounded, wondrous and blessed, unspeakable—of whom to be is to live, to be wise and to understand, to know and to be able, to become beautiful and to shine, all one and the same, because you are simple and cannot be divided.

You are my living and true God, merciful God, my great King. I worship you as one God, one principle of natures, from whom the universe both begins, is perfected, and is contained: one God from whom we are, through whom we are, in whom we are; from whom we have departed and to whom we have become unlike; the principle to which we return, the form we follow, and the grace by which we are reconciled; one by whose authorship we were created, the likeness through which we are restored to unity, and the peace by which we cling to unity; one God, through whose creation we live, whom we love, and by enjoying whom we live blessedly.

I praise, bless, and adore you; I offer thanks to your clemency and goodness for all your gifts and endowments, and for all the benefits of your mercy that you bestow upon my soul and body, and have always bestowed from my childhood and from my cradle, for your sake and for the sake of your holy name.

From this experience I have learned that you, our God, are a God of infinite mercy, immense majesty, and freely given compassion: you who wondrously direct and protect your servants amid adversity and prosperity, and so order their life in both conditions that adversity follows prosperity, and prosperity follows adversity.

Let all your works therefore give thanks to you, Lord, and let your holy ones bless you (Psalm 144:10); and so that by giving thanks they may come to their senses, let even sinners not cease from your praises. I am one of them, although more prone to sin; yet with a desirous heart I sing your praises. If I do not do so with the praise or dignity I ought, I do so with the ability I possess.

Look, I beg you, with a serene face upon this service of my littleness, and with merciful condescension accept this tiny sacrifice of the confession of my faith, so that what came from you may return to you. Do not look so much at what I, your devotee, offer as at what I most devoutly wished and wish to say. For whatever is dishonorable or offensive to you, my soul abhors.

Would that I could offer such things as those hymn-singing choirs of angels offer! O how diligently I would pour myself out entirely in your praises, and how brightly I would proclaim the hymn of your glory, untiring, in the midst of the Church! But because I cannot do as they do, should I remain completely silent?

Woe, Lord, to those who are silent about you—you who loosen the mouths of the mute and make the tongues of infants eloquent (Wisdom 10:21). But since even little ones may stammer your praises, receive, I beg you, a sacrifice from the hand of my tongue and from the love of my heart.

But forgive me, I ask, Lord, your most unworthy and unhappy servant, for speaking so long with you about you. Forgive me in your goodness, because I devoted myself to this little selection not through the rashness of presumption, but through eagerness for my desire for you: so that I might always have with me a brief and portable word concerning you, from whose reading, whenever I grow lukewarm, I may be rekindled in your love.

For we are placed amid snares, and therefore we easily grow cold toward the heavenly desire. Hence we need a continual reminder, by which, awakened, we may return to you, our true and supreme good, whenever we drift away.

There are, indeed, many contemplations by which the soul devoted to you is exercised and advances; but none delights me or engages my mind as much as that which concerns your own property. Therefore I judged it necessary to pluck for myself this little discourse alone, in which, just as I believe in my heart for righteousness, so I confess with my mouth for salvation (Romans 10:10), that you are God the unbegotten Father, God the only-begotten Son, God the Holy Spirit the Paraclete; the holy and undivided Trinity, one God [Note: [Col. 0984] Alcuin’s words, column 136a]: infinite in greatness, almighty in power, supreme in goodness, beyond estimation in wisdom, fearful in counsels, just in judgments, most secret in thoughts, truthful in words, holy in works, abundant in mercies; most patient toward transgressors, most merciful toward penitents; always the same, eternal and everlasting, immortal and unchangeable.

You are not enlarged by distances, narrowed by the shortness of places, confined by any receptacles, altered by will, corrupted by necessity, disturbed by sad things, or softened by joyful things. Neither does forgetfulness remove anything from you, nor memory restore anything; past things do not pass away from you, nor do future things succeed to you. Neither origin gives you a beginning, nor times an increase, nor chance an end. Rather, before the ages, in the ages, and through the ages, you live eternally; and to you belong perpetual praise and eternal glory, supreme power and singular honor, everlasting kingship and dominion without end, through infinite, unwearied, and immortal ages of ages. Amen.

---

# [THE MIRROR OF THE SINNER]

[Col. 0983]

## ADMONITION TO THE BOOK CALLED *THE MIRROR OF THE SINNER*

This other *Mirror* is by an uncertain author and is considerably later than the time of Augustine. This is evident from the words in chapter 7: “And Satan dared, in fury, to make an assault upon the most holy soul of blessed Martin, who was, as it is said, a jewel among priests.” These words plainly refer to the praises of Martin composed by Odo, abbot of Cluny.

Add also the word *praebenda* in chapter 7, used for an ecclesiastical benefice—a meaning which, as we suppose, was unknown before the tenth century. Moreover, what is read in chapter 5 seems to presuppose Hugh of St. Victor’s book *On the Manner of Praying* and to have much agreement with the book printed above, *On the Spirit and the Soul*, as well as with the little work *On Conscience* in the Appendix to Bernard.

This little book was compared with two manuscripts: one from the Royal Library and the other from Saint-Medard of Soissons, in which Pope Leo is cited.

[Col. 0983]

# *THE MIRROR OF THE SINNER*, ONE BOOK (G, S)

## CHAPTER I. What the sinner is taught by “Would that they were wise,” etc.

Since, dearest one [Note: [Col. 0983] The Medardensis manuscript has “dearest brothers” here and below, but not consistently.], we are on the road of this fleeting age, our days pass away like a shadow. It is therefore necessary, with an anxious heart, to remember frequently what our frailty and mortal weakness so often compel us to forget.

What is this? It is that the almighty Lord himself, wishing by his grace to bring about our progress, gave us counsel through blessed Moses, saying: “Would that they were wise and understood, and provided for their final end” (Deuteronomy 32:29).

Come, my brother: see how happily we shall be able to escape the danger of death if we diligently strive to follow the divine counsel that the Lord makes known to us, saying, “Would that they were wise,” and so forth.

O happy and useful counsel, remedy of death, antidote of salvation, mirror of the sinner: “Would that they were wise,” and so forth!

O saving sentence of our Redeemer, from which instruction in wisdom, admonition to self-restraint, a mirror of foresight, exaltation of repentance, and acquisition of divine grace are given to us!

He says, therefore, “Would that they were wise,” and so forth.

O wondrous goodness of our Creator! O ineffable love of our Redeemer! O praiseworthy kindness of our Savior!

We are wicked servants, negligent servants, useless servants, who by the demands of our merits deserved death rather than life. And behold, the merciful author of life, the very giver of forgiveness, the very bestower of grace, invites us to salvation, saying, “Would that they were wise,” and so forth.

Who, unless he is a doomed human being, on hearing and considering these things, would not rejoice most intensely and exult beyond what speech could express in the joy of his spirit within him, because the almighty God himself, the King of the ages himself, the Lord of the angels himself, the Creator of all creatures himself, cares for us who are weak, wretched, and mortal?

Great care, therefore, ought to be ours, so that before all things and above all things we may diligently obey his sacred commandments, love them devoutly, and earnestly fulfill them.

Woe to us forever, for, as the Apostle testifies, we shall be more pitiable than all human beings (1 Corinthians 15:19), or worse than they, if we do not do these things.

Truly, we are idle and empty in carrying out God’s commands unless, first of all, we hate everything that we know is displeasing to the Lord himself and love with faithful hearts those things that we believe please his dread majesty.

Therefore, by day and by night, that merciful and compassionate God and Lord must be entreated to grant us assistance—he who offers such saving counsel, saying, “Would that they were wise,” and so forth.

That sentence is exceedingly wondrous and useful, and should be repeated not once only but frequently: “Would that they were wise,” and so forth.

## CHAPTER II. What consideration of this sentence accomplishes. It belongs to few. Hence the falls of Samson, David, and Solomon. Why their falls are read in the Church. Scripture has no savor except to one who loves ardently.

My dearest brother, understand, I beg you, what you are reading. For consideration of this sentence is the destruction of pride, the extinguishing of envy, the remedy for malice, the driving away of lust, the emptying out of vanity and boasting, the construction of discipline, the perfection of holiness, and the preparation for eternal salvation. He therefore says: “Would that they were wise,” etc.

Alas, alas! How few possess this virtue! Few are those who wisely apprehend this saving teaching of our Savior; few are those who keep before their eyes knowledge of their own frailty, the corruption of corruptible flesh, remembrance of sins, meditation on approaching death, and consideration of the stinking [Note: [Col. 0985] Elsewhere, “burning.”] pit of Gehenna. Behold how useful a mirror of sinners this is. Truly, good brother, if you look upon yourself frequently in such a mirror, you will undoubtedly be stronger than Samson, more cautious than David, and wiser than Solomon. Yet those men neglected to examine themselves frequently in this mirror; therefore, blinded by the desires of their flesh, they fell.

If such great men fell so horribly into sin, although they possessed such strength and wisdom, with what caution and diligence must we keep watch, in whom there is such weakness and such inexperience? These three mighty men are therefore read in the holy Church so that, for the faithful, their downfall may serve not as an example to imitate but as a mirror of caution: so that none of us may trust in his own strength, none presume upon his own wisdom; rather, let us always be fearful, always conscious of our guilt, always concerned for our salvation, and never forgetful of our corruption and mortality.

Those, however, who attend carelessly to such words are neither wise nor understanding, nor do they foresee what is to come; and thus they go to death and damnation. Therefore, so that our mind may awaken to the pursuit of prudence, the Lord’s sentence urges us, saying: “Would that they were wise,” etc. Consider this saving admonition with the eye of reason, dearest one—not in passing, but by turning it over most frequently with diligence and deliberation. For just as incense gives off no fragrance unless it is placed in fire, so no sentence of Sacred Scripture gives off its savor unless it has been cooked in the heart.

## CHAPTER III. What knowledge, understanding, and foresight are required there. Consideration of life’s brevity produces contempt for the world.—“Would that they were wise,” etc.

Behold, my brother, three things are proposed in this verse: namely, knowledge, understanding, and foresight. The Lord therefore wishes you to know, to understand, and also to foresee.

He wishes you to know that the present life is fleeting, dangerous, brief, wasting away in misery, subject to every kind of vanity, polluted by the filth of sins, corrupted by desire, and soon to perish; so that, the more wretched this world is seen to be, the more easily it may be despised for love of the heavenly homeland.

The Lord therefore wishes you to understand your fragile condition, meditating in this way: that you came forth naked from your mother’s womb, and naked you shall return there (Job 1:21); that you are earth, and into earth you shall go; that you entered naked into the misery of this life, passed your days in grief, pain, and hardship, and will depart from here with lamentation and labor. Understand, then, how tearful your entrance and departure are, how feeble your progress, and how dreadful your exit. Understand how much you are an exile and a sick person in this valley of misery, poor and insignificant in virtues [Note: [Col. 0986] Elsewhere, “a beggar.”], unstable and weak, and soon to die.

Brother, you will be happy if you understand such an admonition, write it in your heart as in a book, and strive to keep this one rule that I hand on to you:

> Live gratefully to God, buried to the whole world,  
> Cleansed from crime, ever ready to depart.

O how blessed is the man whose soul is awake to such a pursuit! How wisely he tastes and understands, and foresees what is to come! Dearest one, do the same.

You have already read in this mirror of the sinner what you should wisely apprehend and what you should understand; it remains for you to foresee what is to come. Pray, then, and say with the Prophet: “Make known to me, Lord, my end, and what is the number of my days, so that I may know what is lacking to me” (Psalm 38:5).

O useful prayer, O blessed contemplation, O necessary petition! You are not asking to know beforehand the times or moments that the Father has placed in his own authority; rather, understand and recognize that you are a stranger and a pilgrim in the exile of this sorrowful pilgrimage, a weak human being of brief duration upon the earth.

Therefore: “Would that they were wise”—namely, that they might know how bitter past sins are. Hence Jeremiah says: “See how bitter and evil it is to have abandoned your God” (Jeremiah 2:19). The fault is evil, and the punishment is bitter.

“And that they might understand”—namely, how vain present things are. Ecclesiastes says: “Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity” (Ecclesiastes 1:2).

“And that they might foresee what is to come”—namely, the eternity of glory for the good and the eternity of death for the wicked; so that they might provide for themselves against future barrenness, like Joseph (Genesis 41:33). Hence Solomon says: “In all your works remember your last things, and you will never sin” (Sirach 7:40).

Indeed, dearest brother, if you attend to the brevity of your present life, and to what is lacking in you for performing repentance worthy of God, for observing his commandments with discipline, and for perfecting holiness before him; if you were wise and understood these things and kept death before your eyes, then without doubt, immediately and without delay, rejecting worldly pageantry, setting aside worldly cares, despising the enticements of the flesh, casting away pleasures, and scorning luxuries, you would keep watch over yourself and prudently foresee what is to come.

For it belongs to the wise person not so much to look to the beginning of anything as to foresee its end and outcome. Finally, the person is proved happy who thinks about punishment before punishment, so that afterward he may escape the danger of punishment. [Col. 0987]

## CHAPTER IV. Consideration of death subdues the flesh. Meditation as enrichment of the mind.

You say to me, then: “I am prepared above all to submit to the divine counsel, so that I may be wise and understand, and foresee what is to come. But what are my last things?”

Those, certainly, about which the Holy Spirit speaks to you through Solomon, saying: “My son, in all things remember your last things, and you will never sin.”

The lustful flesh cannot be subdued more effectively than by meditating beforehand upon what it will be when dead; and if you maintain such meditation continually, all generations will call you blessed. For meditation is nothing other than enrichment of the mind. Your mind is therefore enriched most excellently when the knowledge of foresight illuminates it against all adversities.

We read in the poet that

> “Argus had a head encircled by a hundred lights”  
> (Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, Book 1, line 625).

This can be understood to mean that, within the watchfulness of his mind, he possessed prudence [Note: [Col. 0987] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions have: “which possessed the watchfulness and prudence of his mind.”] on every side of himself. Therefore, if the pagan poet possessed such power through the diligence of caution, a Christian cleric ought much more to possess a purer eye of foresight [Note: [Col. 0987] The Medard manuscript adds here, “the people or”; the Regius manuscript has “the monk or.”].

Be another Argus, then—indeed, more cautious than he, more diligent than he, more prudent than he—so that you may taste and understand, and prudently foresee what is to come.

## CHAPTER V. What the last things are. With what benefit they are foreseen.

But what are your last things, which it is the sum of all foresight to foresee with care? They are, certainly, that terrifying hour in which your wretched soul will depart in fear from this little corruptible body.

Brother, believe me: for the fearful consideration of this matter you ought to have wished more to possess foresight than dominion over the whole world. Would that you therefore knew the things of God, understood the things of the world, and foresaw the things of hell! You would surely fear God, not desire pride [Note: [Col. 0987] Elsewhere, “you would desire heavenly things.”], despise the world, and dread hell.

In that exceedingly fearful final hour of yours, which friend or parent of yours, coming with swords and weapons, will be able to bring you help? “There will be no one then to comfort you from all your dear ones” (Lamentations 1:2). You will look for human assistance and aid, but your refuge will be with God alone.

Think with yourself, dearest one, with what fear the Lord Jesus Christ our God ought to be feared, with what love loved, and with what honor revered—he who alone will be able to provide the protection of salvation after death.

Therefore, dearest one, bring that final day of your departure back to mind frequently; and before your wretched soul leaves the prison of the flesh, let it foresee where it is going. [Note: [Col. 0987] See *On the Spirit and the Soul*, chapter 50.]

Such remembrance conceives contrition; contrition gives birth to compunction; compunction gives birth to contemplation—that is, a devout and humble affection toward God: devout, namely, through trust in the help of divine goodness and mercy; humble, through consideration of one’s own frailty and misery.

Here, reader, pay attention. What is there in all knowledge that can more easily urge a person to guard himself, to drive out every injustice, and to perfect holiness in the fear of God than consideration of his own corruption, certain knowledge of his mortality, and, finally, remembrance of his dreadful death?

For when a person becomes not a person—that is, when he falls ill; when, as he grows ill, his illness increases; when the sinner is terrified, the heart trembles, the head grows numb, the senses vanish, strength withers, the face pales, the countenance blackens, the eye darkens, the ear grows deaf, the nose rots, the tongue fails, the mouth falls silent, the body wastes away, and the flesh decays—then the beauty of the flesh becomes stench [Col. 0988] and putrefaction; then the human being is dissolved into ash and changed into a worm.

[Note: [Col. 0988] These verses are absent from the manuscripts; they are found in Bernard’s *Book of Meditations*, chapter 3.]

> After the human being, a worm; after the worm, stench and horror.  
> Thus every human being is changed into a non-human being.

Behold, my dearest brother, a sufficiently horrifying spectacle—but it is an exceedingly useful mirror. For no medical art and no instruction overcomes pride so effectively, conquers malice so effectively, extinguishes lust so effectively, or tramples upon the vanity of the world so effectively as remembrance of such a dreadful death.

Would that they were wise! And what becomes so worthless in this world as a human being whose body, once lifeless, is not permitted to remain inside a house for three days because of its stench, but is thrown outside like vile dung, hidden in the depths of the earth, handed over to decay, given as food to worms, and made into a corpse?

## CHAPTER VI. On vain studies. On the discipline that must be undertaken here.

Let the proud and wretched sinner blush, then, and let him fear—blinded by arrogance, inflamed by anger, disfigured by the vice of impatience, inflated by knowledge—when he prefers the art of Aristotle to knowledge derived from the Apostles, the book of Plato to the divine book; when no reading delights him, no knowledge builds him up, and no speech has savor for him unless it has been conceived grammatically, imagined dialectically, and adorned rhetorically.

You are foolish because you do not know these things, and you are in error. For those who do such things and consume their days in such pursuits generate sin for themselves and prepare death, because from a similar study they conceive a similar kind of knowledge: that is, they gather leaves, not fruits; words, not virtues. They utter words into the wind and beat the air with words; they make a sound of wordiness and display their boasting. Of such people it is said through the Psalmist: “They were troubled and shaken like a drunken man, and all their wisdom was swallowed up” (Psalm 106:27).

For just as a drunken person does not know what he is doing or where he is going, because he does not know himself, so foolish secular clerics [Note: [Col. 0988] The Regius manuscript adds, “monks and,” which does not seem to fit what follows.] disturb themselves by drinking in such knowledge. They devour books and multiply opinions, but they are utterly ignorant of what they are doing, because in their misery they do not consider toward what wretched end they are heading.

O would that such people were wise! If they had weighed the brevity of their fleeing life, if they had turned the losses of their days before their eyes, if they had foreseen how fearfully they would be required to answer at the judgment—not only for their dead works but even for every idle word—then, immediately terrified by fear and struck by divine love, they would have abandoned the vain studies of this life. They would have come from the study of vanity to the study of truth, from the study of folly to the study of wisdom—that is, from the study of curiosity to the study of holy humility; from the school of lust and depravity to the school of purity and holiness, or chastity; from a life of iniquity to a life of holiness—that is, from a life of fornication to a life of blessed religious observance; in other words, from the house of worldly conduct to the house of holy discipline.

Hence the blessed Holy Spirit commands sinners through the Prophet, saying: “Take hold of discipline, lest the Lord become angry and you perish from the righteous way” (Psalm 2:12).

O how terrible and greatly to be feared is this sentence for those who do not take hold of discipline! From this sentence of the Holy Spirit it is clear that they will perish.

This is why the Lord says through Moses: “Every soul that is not afflicted on this day shall perish from among my people” (Leviticus 23:29). These words must be noted with the greatest attention. “The soul,” he says, “shall perish that is not afflicted”—understand, through discipline, correction of morals, the satisfaction of repentance, contrition of heart, and purification of conscience.

And he said, “on this day”—that is, in the present time of grace, on the day of this life—for whoever does not accept the time of repentance now will find no place of pardon after death.

Therefore fear, sinner; you proud flesh; you vile corpse—while still alive, you are daily gnawed by worms generated from your corruptible little body. Tremble at pride, cast away vanity, flee lust, take hold of discipline, lest you perish.

See in this mirror what you are and what you will be: your conception, menstrual decay; your origin, mud; your end, putrefaction.

Would that they were wise, etc. Behold, wretched one: you have a thousand causes of sorrow, and still you are proud. Again, brother, I address you:

> Whatever others may do, keep yourself in mind;  
> let the world become more worthless to you than you are to the world.

Considering more attentively the misery of such great calamity, and groaning with the Prophet, say:

> “I will declare my iniquity, and I will think upon my sin.  
> For I am ready for scourges, and my sorrow is ever before me”  
> (Psalm 37:19 and 18).

And again say with the Apostle, who laments the sorrowful condition of humanity:

> “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death?”  
> (Romans 7:24).

This saving sentence of the Apostle requires a prudent reader. The Apostle was still living in the body when he nevertheless called the body dead; for the wise person already considers death before his eyes and already counts himself dead, since he knows with certainty that he will die.

## CHAPTER VII. On the dreadful departure of the soul condemned. How dreadful the devil’s presence will then be.

Attend, then, in that terrible hour of which we are speaking, wretched soul of the sinner, when you are about to leave the world and where you are about to go.

The evil ministers will immediately be present—those accursed ones, those infernal devils, those dreadful spirits, savage lions roaring to seize their prey, namely, your sinful and wretched soul. Then suddenly the dreadful places of punishment will be revealed: chaos and the darkness of gloom; the horror of misery and tribulation; the terror and trembling of anguish and confusion; the terror of a dreadful vision; the trembling of a terrifying dwelling.

There will be the place of those who weep, the gnashing of teeth, the biting of worms, the cry of those in pain, the lamentation of those who groan, and the voice of sinful criers saying:

> “Woe, woe, woe to us, the children of Eve!”

When the wretched soul—or rather, the most wretched soul—about to leave the body has heard, seen, and sensed these things and things like them, indeed things a thousand times worse than can be expressed, what and how great and immense will its terror, fear, and trembling be? What tongue can say it? What book can set it forth?

What benefit then will come from the boasting of knowledge, the pageantry of the world, worldly vanity, or desire for earthly dignity? Will the appetites of lust help? Will exquisite food, delicate drink, elaborate clothing, handsome footwear, softness of the flesh, gluttony of the belly, excess of food, drunken surfeit, the construction of houses, the acquisition of benefices, or the accumulation of riches help? Will all these things be able to snatch the wretched human soul from the mouth of the dreadful and terrible lion and from the jaws of the accursed dragon?

Would that someone entangled in sins, drunk and blinded by love of the world and the flesh, read this lesson, taste it, understand it rightly, and retain it in his heart—someone who prefers the poisonous pleasure of a lustful corpse to the health of his soul, who devotes more attention to Martha than to Mary [Note: [Col. 0989] Thus the Regius manuscript. The Medard manuscript has, “more to the mark than to the mark.” The printed editions have, “more to the ark than to Martha.”], who cares more for the world than for Christ, and more for bovine law than for divine law.

Let such a foolish person read this lesson and contemplate his own appearance in this mirror of the sinner. Let him consider carefully where he comes from, what he is, and where he is going. Let him weigh, from what has already been said, along what greatly fearsome path, by what dark road, and through what dreadful hands his wretched soul will pass.

O foolish sinner, because you do not know how to consider these things—or do not wish to meditate upon them! Because you neglect to foresee them, pride often assails you, anger harasses you, malice torments you, envy wounds you, lust inflames you, sloth exhausts you, and avarice binds you.

And because you do not prudently foresee the dreadful torments that threaten you, you therefore often become rebellious, injurious, and obstinate; you approach the divine work sluggishly and listlessly. You perform it carelessly and negligently. Why? Because you do not wish to foresee where you are going. [Col. 0990]

Would that you were wise and understood, etc.

“Terrible is his appearance,” as Pope Leo says, “for whom every solid thing is passable, every secret open; to whom obscure things shine, the mute respond, silence confesses, and the mind speaks without a voice” [Note: [Col. 0990] From the Medard manuscript we add the words from “Would that” through “speaks.”].

If that poisonous serpent, the devil and Satan, dared furiously to attack the most holy soul of blessed Martin—who was, as is said, [Note: [Col. 0990] In the Office concerning him.] “the jewel of priests”—and sought to hinder that blessed soul, in the presence of Angels, as it went to heaven, how greatly must you, sinner, fear, and how tremblingly must you meditate upon the way in which that artificer of deceit, that son of iniquity, that most bitter enemy of souls, will horribly confront your wretched soul?

Come, dearest brother, think beforehand of this, and let it never depart from your heart: how much that most blessed perpetual virgin, the mother of our Lord Jesus Christ, provided for her soul. For, as we read, she entreated her Son that evil spirits might not be present at her departure.

If one so great and so holy, dear to God—indeed, most dear—doubted the vision of wicked spirits [Note: [Col. 0990] Perhaps, “trembled at it.”], what will the sinful soul do [Note: [Col. 0990] From the same manuscript we add: “Come, dearest brother … the sinful soul.”]?

How will it be able to stand before the dreadful sight of his terrifying face, the intolerable stench of his mouth, and the sulfurous flames of his eyes? Be certain that fear of this dreadful beast surpasses every kind of torment by more than can be imagined in this world.

The frightened and trembling Prophet, fleeing to prayer, says:

> “Hear, O God, my prayer when I plead;  
> deliver my soul from fear of the enemy”  
> (Psalm 63:2).

He does not say, “from the power,” but “from the fear.” Why? To indicate how great the punishment is, how dreadful and intolerable the terror of that enemy is.

Alas, alas, my brother! If the sinful soul experiences such great trembling from Satan’s mere appearance, how great will be the confusion, horror, affliction, and lamentation caused by his touch?

## CHAPTER VIII. How God will laugh and mock at the destruction of the wicked. The origin of various vices. The difference between the senseless and the foolish.

O foolish children of men! “You vain children of men, why do you love vanity and seek falsehood?” (Psalm 4:3).

For whoever loves vanity hates his own soul. “The ungodly and his ungodliness are hateful to God” (Wisdom 14:9). Hence the Psalmist says: “Do I not hate those who hate you, Lord?” etc. “With perfect hatred I hate them” (Psalm 138:21–22).

Again: “The Most High hates sinners and has mercy on those who repent” (Sirach 12:3).

Why do you not contemplate such a dreadful and terrible misery? Why do you not cast away pride? Why do you not extinguish avarice? Why do you not despise lust? Why do you not correct your ways? Why do you listen carelessly to God’s commandment and his saving counsel? Why do you not taste and understand, and foresee what is to come?

This is why God addresses you sinners terribly:

> “I will laugh at your destruction and mock when what you feared comes upon you”  
> (Proverbs 1:26).

O how greatly that sentence of the Lord is to be feared! Would that the reader tasted in the palate of his heart how much bitterness and dread it contains. For truly, if he knew, he would guard his life more cautiously every hour of every day.

But perhaps you will say that laughter and mockery cannot be attributed to almighty God himself, nor can his venerable and most holy simple nature admit such passions or ironies. Why, then, is it said by almighty God to sinners, “I will laugh at your destruction”?

Attend, you who ask, to how the sentence must be explained when it says, “I will laugh at your destruction.” This means: “When your end has come, I will proclaim you worthy of mockery; and when that sudden calamity has rushed upon you, I will mock”—that is, when bitter death has bitten you, I will condemn you as worthy of eternal mockery.

Hear, sinner, the terrible sentence. If you understood it, you would undoubtedly be terrified. But you read the Holy Scriptures carelessly; you do not wisely consider the actions of your life, the evil you do, the sins you commit, or your evil deeds, words, and works.

You are quick to the table, slow to church; powerful for drinking, but weak for chanting; wide awake for stories, but sleepy for vigils; bold [Note: [Col. 0991] Elsewhere, “ready.”] in speaking, but slow and silent in singing; quick to anger and slander, but sluggish in prayer; a lover of envy, a persecutor of Christ’s poor; looking at the speck in another’s eye, but not seeing the beam in your own; condemning the deeds of others, but neither considering nor abandoning your own.

You rebuke others but do not correct yourself; you blame others and praise yourself; an inventor of malice, a destroyer of discipline; a friend of vices and an enemy of virtues.

These are the things that blind a person and separate him from God; these are the things that make a monk demonic, a convert perverse, a cleric heretical, and a Christian antichristian. For whoever is not a Christian is an antichrist. He is not a Christian whose life and conduct are opposed to Christ.

Alas, alas! “The senseless person will not know, and the foolish will not understand these things” (Psalm 91:7); and therefore, as the same Prophet says: “The senseless and the foolish will perish together” (Psalm 48:11).

But what is the difference between the senseless person and the foolish person?

Every foolish person is senseless. For “senseless” means, as it were, “not wise.” Many remain who are not wise and yet are not foolish. Many are just, and many are not just, yet they are not wicked.

Do you wish to know who is senseless and who is foolish?

The senseless person is one who does not consider that he is an exile from the joys of paradise, who does not recognize that he is an exile in this exile. The foolish person is one who, although he has recognized these things, nevertheless does not strive to be freed from the misery of the world through the merit of his life.

Again, the senseless person is one who does not believe that the future punishments of the rejected are everlasting and that the joys of the just are eternal. The foolish person, however, is one who, although he believes these things, does not strive to escape everlasting death and acquire eternal glory by living chastely and conducting himself devoutly.

Therefore, by the just judgment of God, the senseless and the foolish will perish together. Yet this would not happen if they were wise and understood, and foresaw what is to come.

Behold, my brother, you have now read and seen in this mirror of the sinner what you should taste, what you should understand, and how you ought to foresee what is to come. It remains, therefore, for you to learn diligently and establish these things in your heart, so that you may taste wisely and understand rightly how prudently to foresee your last things, in order that through them you may escape eternal damnation and possess eternal life with our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.

[Col. 0991]

# ONE BOOK ON THE THREE DWELLINGS, BY AN UNKNOWN BUT NOT UNLEARNED AUTHOR (C, G, S)

## CHAPTER I. On the three dwellings: the kingdom of God, the world, and hell. The blessings of God’s kingdom and the evils of hell.

There are three dwellings under the hand of almighty God: the highest, the lowest, and the middle. The highest is called the kingdom of God, or the kingdom of heaven; the lowest is called hell; the middle is called the present world, or the globe of the earth.

The two extremes are entirely opposed to one another and joined by no fellowship. For what fellowship can there be between light and darkness, or between Christ and Belial (2 Corinthians 6:14–15)?

The middle, however, has some likeness to the extremes. Hence it has light and darkness, cold and heat, pain and health, joy and sorrow, hatred and love, good and evil people, just and unjust people, masters and servants, kingship and subjection, hunger and satiety, death and life, and countless things of this kind.

Of all these, one part bears the image of the kingdom of God, and the other part of hell. For the wicked and the good are mixed together in this world; in the kingdom of God there are no wicked people, but all are good; in hell there are no good people, but all are wicked. Each place is filled from the middle.

For among the people of this world, some are raised to heaven and others dragged down to hell. Like are joined to like: the good to the good, and the wicked to the wicked; just people to just Angels, and transgressing people to transgressing angels; servants of God to God, and servants of the devil to the devil.

The blessed are called to the kingdom prepared for them from the foundation of the world; the accursed are driven into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels (Matthew 25:34, 41).

[Note: [Col. 0991] The same material appears in *On Loving God*, chapter 18, having been taken from here.]

No one clothed in flesh can speak of, think of, or understand the blessings of the heavenly kingdom as they truly are. They are far greater and better than can be thought or understood. Hence it is written that “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the human heart what God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Corinthians 2:9). For the kingdom of God is greater than every report, better than every praise, more countless than all knowledge, and more excellent than all the glory that is imagined.

Nor can anyone speak of or think of the evils of hell as they truly are; for they are far worse than can be thought.

The kingdom of God is therefore full of light, peace, love, wisdom, glory, honor, sweetness, affection, melody, joy, everlasting blessedness, and every ineffable good that can neither be spoken nor imagined.

But the place of hell is full of darkness, discord, hatred, folly, misery, shame, bitterness, offense, pain, burning [Note: [Col. 0992] The Victorinus manuscript has “stench.”], thirst, hunger, unquenchable fire, sadness, everlasting vengeance, and every ineffable evil that can neither be spoken nor imagined.

The citizens of heaven are just people and Angels, whose king is almighty God. In contrast, the citizens of hell are ungodly people and demons, whose prince is the devil.

The vision of holy people and Angels satisfies the just, and above all the vision of God himself. The vision of condemned people and demons torments the ungodly and sinners, and above all the vision of the devil himself.

Nothing is desired in the kingdom of God that is not found there; but in hell nothing is found that is desired. In the kingdom of God nothing is found except what pleases, delights, and satisfies. In contrast, in the everlasting lake of misery nothing is seen and nothing is felt except what displeases, offends, and torments.

[Note: [Col. 0992] The words “In the eternal kingdom” through “disturbance” are absent from the manuscripts; they are from Augustine’s *Enchiridion*, chapter 23.]

In the eternal kingdom there will be life without death, truth without error, and happiness without disturbance. Every good abounds in the kingdom of God, and no evil; every evil abounds in the devil’s prison, and no good.

No unworthy person is received into the kingdom of God; no worthy person, no just person, is dragged into hell.

## CHAPTER II. On the punishments of hell.

[Col. 0993]

There are two principal torments in hell: intolerable cold and the heat of unquenchable fire. Hence we read in the Gospel: “There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matthew 13:42; 22:13; 25:30).

Weeping and melting of the eyes arise from heat; gnashing of the teeth arises from cold. Hence blessed Job also says: “They pass from waters of snow to excessive heat” (Job 24:19).

From these two proceed countless kinds of punishment: intolerable thirst; the punishment of hunger; the punishment of stench; the punishment of horror; the punishment of fear; the punishment of anguish; the punishment of darkness; the severity of torturers; the presence of demons; the ferocity of beasts; the cruelty of those administering punishment; the tearing apart by immortal worms; the worm of conscience; fiery tears; sighs; miseries; pain without remedy; bonds without release; eternal death; punishment without end; and the absence of Christ after his vision [Note: [Col. 0993] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions have, “as regards his vision.”]—which alone surpasses all the punishments mentioned above and is more intolerable than them all.

## CHAPTER III. On those whom the eternity of punishment does not deter from worldly pleasure. The twofold punishment of hell. One hundred years are no portion of eternity.

Perpetual woe, therefore, to those who deserve to undergo all these evils without end in exchange for the pleasing dream of a single hour. For such and so great is all the glory of this world when compared with eternal glory.

It would have been better for them, as was said of the wretched Judas, not to have been born (Matthew 26:24), than to endure the punishments of hell because of their evil merits.

What is more foolish, what more insane, than to be deceived and overcome, like infants, by the shadow, image, and likeness of true glory, true pleasure, true beauty, true splendor, and true honor, while not seeking or desiring the true glory itself?

Who would choose the image of gold in water while neglecting the gold itself, and not immediately be considered foolish and insane by everyone? Who would love the disk of the sun reflected in a mirror, or formed in some material, more than the sun itself, and not be mocked by everyone?

Thus, indeed he deserves to be mocked, or rather pitied, whoever loves, seeks, and pursues the fleeting fragility of this world and the useless pleasure of the flesh, while despising eternal glory and neglecting the ineffable joys of the heavenly kingdom.

This is a very foolish bargain, characteristic of miserable people who do not possess a sound heart—even if the punishments of hell did not follow, punishments that can neither be spoken nor imagined.

There are, in fact, two punishments: to be absent from the kingdom of God and always to be in hell, that is, to be condemned with the devil; to lose the presence of the Angels and always suffer the terrible presence of demons. How greatly this ought to be avoided, escaped, and feared cannot possibly be expressed.

Who with sound judgment would choose a punishment of one hundred years in exchange for the pleasures of a single day? Yet miserable people without any wisdom, following the pleasure [Note: [Col. 0993] Two manuscripts have “will,” rather than “pleasure.”] of the flesh, do not avoid or escape intolerable punishments—not punishments of one hundred years, nor of a thousand thousand years, but punishments lasting through all the ages without end—in exchange for forty or sixty years of pleasure, or for any corruptible delight.

The difference between one day and one hundred years is great; but the difference between forty, sixty, or one hundred years and eternity—whether eternity in good or in evil—is not merely as great, but greater.

For one day is in some measure a portion of the span of one hundred years, however small a portion it may be. But the span of one hundred years is no portion at all of that eternity. For if, for example, a hundredth or thousandth part were eternity, that span would cease to be eternal after one hundred times or one thousand times its duration. Reason does not permit this of eternity; for if it were to end in any way, at any time, it would not be eternity at all.

## CHAPTER IV. Migrating from the broad way to the narrow. The happiness of the blessed. Knowledge. Love of one’s lot. On the ineffable sweetness of the vision of the Lord.

Resist carnal pleasure, therefore, with all your strength; fight valiantly against the deceptive allurements of this world, and keep watch against Satan’s manifold suggestions. With every effort, the broad way of the world must be avoided, for it leads to death; but with every desire of the heart, the narrow way, which leads to life, must be entered and sought (Matthew 7:13–14). This narrow way is the way of abstinence, chastity, humility, and every form of religious devotion—the way which Christ trod before us, by which he migrated to his kingdom. Let us also follow his footsteps until, by that same way after him, we reach the royal city in which he reigns. Whatever a person may say about that city is like a drop from the sea or a spark from the fire. In that city, as the Lord says, the righteous will shine like the sun (Matthew 13:43). There will be supreme peace, supreme rest, no labor, no pain, no poverty, no old age, no death, and no night; no craving for food and no burning thirst. Rather, the food and drink of all will be the vision of Christ and of the Holy Trinity, and the contemplation, with the pure eye of the heart, of divinity itself, as well as the continual reading, so to speak, of the book of life—that is, of eternal truth, supreme wisdom, and the Word of God, which is the vision of Jesus Christ. There, whatever is now hidden from us will be manifest.

There it will be clear why one person was chosen and another rejected; why one was received into the kingdom and another reduced to servitude; why one dies in the womb, another in infancy, another in youth, and another in old age; why one is poor and another rich; why the son of an adulteress is baptized, while at times the son of a lawful wife dies before baptism; why one who begins to live well sometimes ends badly, while one who begins badly often ends well. All these things and many others of this kind will be plain and open in the book of life.

In that same city, the reward of each will belong to all, and the reward of all will belong to each through charity. There the good of all [Note: [Col. 0994] In one manuscript, “an abundance of all good things”; in the editions, “every good thing.”] will be evident to everyone. There all will know one another’s thoughts. No superior will be proud, and no inferior envious. For how could one who loves everyone as himself envy anyone, when no one envies himself? No one there will desire to be better or higher than he is, since it would not be fitting to be other than what he has deserved; nor will anyone desire to be other than what he will be, because to be as he will be will be beautiful—not only for himself, but also for the whole body of the heavenly Church.

Just as any bodily member, if placed higher or lower than nature has ordained, makes the body misshapen and ugly, so likewise, if someone were placed in God’s kingdom higher than the skill and will of the almighty craftsman require, he would produce deformity—not only for himself, but for the whole assembly. In that assembly, the least will without doubt possess greater glory than one who possessed the whole kingdom of the world, even if that kingdom were eternal. For it is exceedingly worthless to enjoy the elements compared with enjoying and rejoicing in God himself, and to delight in visible and bodily things.

[Note: [Col. 0994] Words of Augustine, *On Free Will*, book 3, no. 77. They are absent from the manuscripts.]

For so great is the beauty of justice, so great the delight of eternal light—that is, of unchangeable truth and wisdom—that even if one were not permitted to remain in it longer than the space of a single day, for that reason alone innumerable years of this life, full of pleasures and surrounded by bodily goods, would rightly and deservedly be despised. For it was not falsely or with little feeling that it was said: “For one day in your courts is better than thousands” (Psalm 83:11).

Nothing can be compared with the delight and joy that arise from invisible and incorporeal things, from the fellowship of all the angels and righteous, from certain knowledge and understanding of the divine nature itself, and from seeing God himself face to face. The angels marvel at his beauty; at his command the dead are raised; his wisdom is beyond numbering (Psalm 146:5); his kingdom knows no end; his glory cannot be told. His light so eclipses the sun that, by comparison with it, the sun has no light at all; his sweetness so surpasses honey that, compared with it, honey is like the bitterest wormwood.

If all who are confined in the prison of hell were to see his face, they would feel no punishment, no pain, and no sadness. If his presence appeared in hell together with the holy inhabitants [Note: [Col. 0995] One manuscript reads, “his own.”], hell would immediately be transformed into a delightful paradise. Without his nod, not even a leaf falls from a tree. His flame-spewing eyes penetrate the depths of hell. His ear hears the silent voice of the heart—that is, thought. His eye hears no less than it sees, and his ear sees no less than it hears, because they are not bodily organs, but supreme wisdom and certain knowledge.

His delights satisfy without inducing disgust. When the blessed find them, they nevertheless always desire them; they produce hunger and thirst without pain, and delight them with an ever-burning desire. His hidden mysteries are always new and wonderful to those who see them. They do not produce greater amazement in those who behold them when they first begin to be seen than they do after a thousand years or a thousand thousand years. Although the angels have been accustomed to see them from the beginning of the world, they marvel at them no less today than on the first day; otherwise, long ago, through continual familiarity, they would have grown cheap in the sight of the angels. To his knowledge, past and future are not past and future, but present. [Note: [Col. 0995] The manuscripts omit “not past and future, but.”]

## CHAPTER V. All things present without prejudice to human freedom. God’s speech and praise. Existence before time. Light. True evil worse than false evil. What the vision of God confers upon the blessed. God’s eternity. God’s knowledge.

Thus he will see neither the day of judgment nor the first day of the world—and yet he sees both. His foreknowledge compels no one to sin, as many who err say. “If God,” they argue, “foreknew that Adam would sin, he could not refrain from sinning.” From this error arises the claim that God is the cause of sin, which it is impious to say. Yet they are also bound by their own words. If what God’s foreknowledge contains must necessarily occur, then man sinned by his own will and not under any compulsion, because God’s foreknowledge included the fact that he would sin by his will and free choice, not under the pressure of necessity.

If, then, God’s foreknowledge cannot be avoided, man could not have sinned otherwise than willingly, with no other force compelling him, because God foreknew that he would sin in this way. If he sinned willingly, he was not compelled. If he was not compelled to sin, he could certainly have refrained from sinning if he had wished; and therefore he deserved punishment, because he did not sin unwillingly. Otherwise he would not receive from God the punishment of death.

God’s speech is a hidden inspiration by which he invisibly reveals his will and his love to minds. By seeing this, the angels obey God in all things. God’s praise is that by which he will praise the elect: it is the manifestation by which he will show everyone the good deeds of his chosen. The continual praise by which the elect will praise him is their perpetual wonder at him.

In a wondrous manner he did not precede the world and time in time—for he was not before the world by the duration of any hour—and yet he always existed without beginning. There was no time before time; rather, time was created together with the world. If time therefore began to run from the beginning of the world, it did not exist before the world was made. Thus God did not, at any time, as we have said, precede the times and the world coeval with them—indeed, the world slightly prior to them, for the times began to run by its motion. Whatever is moved precedes its own motion. God preceded the world by ineffable eternity, not by time. There was no time before the world.

His light drives away the darkness of ignorance. By some particle of that light we know that all the things we have said are true and certain. By the same light we see that what is true is better than what is false, and yet that true evil or true sin is worse than false evil or false sin—not because it is true, but because it is evil or sin. Rather, it is evil or sin because it is truly evil or truly sin.

[Col. 0996] [Note: [Col. 0996] The manuscripts lack the words “but it is evil or sin because it is truly evil or truly sin.”]

Otherwise it could not be evil or sin unless it were truly evil or sin; for false evil is not evil, just as false silver is not silver. Someone might say that evil or sin arose or was made from truth, and that, in a certain sense, the evil of truth is its work. This is wholly false. Everything true is from truth, and everything true, insofar as it is true, is good. Therefore, it is from truth that something is true in such a way that it is evil or sin; but the evil or sin itself is not from truth. For the evil itself is one thing, and its being true is another.

Although evil itself is not good, it is good that it truly exists as that evil. For unless it were good for evil to exist, God would in no way permit it to occur. The Almighty makes many good things from evils, just as from human adultery he forms and makes good human beings.

If by some particle of that light, infused as if through narrow cracks, we have recognized that these and all the other things we know are true, with what and how great a light of knowledge and wisdom will we be illuminated there, where we shall see the very sun of truth face to face—that is, where we shall know certain and true wisdom? Its presence makes those who are present like it. Whoever clings to true wisdom, true beauty, and true eternity will be wise, beautiful, and eternal. In the same way, its absence makes those who lack it wholly unlike it.

Its eternity is without beginning and without end. For if there were a time when it did not exist, who would have made it? He alone is God, and before him there was no other God, nor is there, nor will there be. He did not perhaps create himself, since nothing creates itself. By what power could one who did not exist at all make himself? It remains, therefore, that God was not made at all. Since God was in no way made, he existed without beginning before all things.
