Whatever has been made has a beginning, and whatever has a beginning has undoubtedly been made—not by anyone other than the uncreated God, who makes all things.

His knowledge, without any variation in cognition [Note: [Col. 0996] The word “cognition” is absent in the manuscript of Victorinus.], and without any movement back and forth, comprehends and understands, simultaneously and all at once, the innumerable variety of all creatures: angels, human beings, stars, grains of sand, hairs, words, thoughts, and every moment. God is therefore the source and origin of all knowledge. The more anyone drinks from him, the more he thirsts.

## CHAPTER VI. The knowledge of the blessed. On the threefold vision: bodily, spiritual, and intellectual.

As we said above, the kingdom of the whole world, even if it were eternal, is incomparably inferior to the fellowship of the angels and saints and to being present before the vision of God himself. From that vision arises a threefold knowledge: namely, the human being who sees, God who is seen, and all the others who will see and understand everything.

Just as a threefold vision is afforded to us through a glass mirror—for we see ourselves, the mirror itself, and whatever is present—so through the mirror of divine splendor we shall see God himself as he is, insofar as this is possible for a creature; and we shall know ourselves and all the others by true and certain knowledge.

Then, by seeing God, we shall see the hidden things of creatures and of hell itself. Then it will be clear to the righteous how God is invisible, incomparable, without beginning and without end, before all things and after all things; what distinction there is between being born, which pertains to the Son, and proceeding, which pertains to the Holy Spirit—except that one is born from one, while the other proceeds from two; how the Father did not precede the Son in time, but in origin, nor did he precede the Holy Spirit; and how all things belonging to God are one in God, except insofar as relation is concerned.

For God’s wisdom, truth, and eternity are not different from one another, but are one, just as all the other things belonging to God are one. God’s wisdom is no more wisdom than it is truth, and it is no more truth than wisdom, eternity, or anything else belonging to God. For all are one in God. And not only are these things identical with one another in God; they are nothing other than God himself.

Then it will be clear how the world was in God before it existed in itself—not as the world, but as God; how he is wholly everywhere without a place, great without quantity, good without quality; and how he penetrates all things, clean and unclean, without being polluted by them.

For if this visible light illuminates every place and penetrates even dung heaps without smell and without being polluted by them, how much more does God, who is invisible and unchangeable light, penetrate, govern, sustain, surround, and illuminate all things without any alteration or pollution—not only heavenly and earthly things, but also those of hell?

Then God’s elect will have a threefold vision: bodily, by which bodies will be seen—some shining like the sun, some like the moon, and others like the stars; spiritual, by which they will behold the likenesses of bodies in the spirit and not in deceptive fantasy [Col. 0998]; by this vision the spirits of the righteous also enjoy it today, after the confinement of their bodies; and intellectual, by which, with the pure eye of the mind, they will see God in the spirit, as well as their own souls, their inner virtues, and the angelic spirits.

Then they will give God double thanks: for their deliverance from perpetual damnation and for the ineffable recompense of good things. Then the devil, the common culprit and enemy of all, will be condemned in the sight of God’s elect. His condemnation and intolerable punishment will provide the elect with a delightful spectacle. Then they will love their deliverer and the giver of all good things with the most ardent love, and without end or weariness they will praise almighty, kind, and merciful God with the cry of their hearts. To him be honor and glory, now and throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

# THE LADDER OF PARADISE

[Col. 0997]

## NOTICE ON THE FOLLOWING BOOK

This little work also circulated among the works of Bernard, entitled *The Ladder of the Cloister*, or *Treatise on the Way of Prayer*; but the Louvain scholars judged, quite rightly, that it was not his. For in the manuscript codex of the Carthusian house of Cologne—as is noted in the latest edition of Bernard—it has prefixed an epistle bearing this title: “Letter of Lord Guigo the Carthusian to Brother Gervasius, on the contemplative life.”

“To his beloved brother Gervasius, Brother Guigo: delight in the Lord.

“I am bound to love you as a duty, because you began to love me first; and I am compelled to write back to you because your letter first invited me to write. I have therefore decided to send you certain things that I had devised concerning the spiritual exercise of those in the cloister, so that you, who have learned such things better through experience than I through discussion, may be the judge and corrector of my thoughts.

“Rightly do I offer you the beginnings of our work first, so that you may gather the first fruits of a new planting, since you stole yourself away from the service of Pharaoh by a laudable theft into a secluded life, placed yourself in the ordered battle line of the camps, and prudently grafted a branch skillfully cut from the wild olive onto the olive tree.”

Then the book begins: “One day, while …” After the final words, “peace in unity,” the book closes as follows:

“Therefore, my brother Gervasius, if it should ever be granted you from above to climb the heights of the steps mentioned above, remember me; and pray for me when all is well with you, so that curtain may draw curtain, and the one who hears may say, ‘Come.’”

[Col. 0997]

# THE LADDER OF PARADISE, BOOK ONE (G, S)*

## CHAPTER I. Description of the four stages of spiritual exercise: Reading, meditation, prayer, contemplation.

One day, while I was occupied with the bodily labor of my hands and had begun to think about the exercise of the spiritual person, four spiritual stages suddenly presented themselves to my mind as I reflected: namely, reading, meditation, prayer, and contemplation.

This is the ladder of those in the cloister, by which they are raised from earth to heaven. It is distinguished by few steps, yet is of immense and incredible size. Its lower end rests upon the earth, while its upper part penetrates the clouds and searches out the secrets of heaven.

These steps, just as they differ in name and number, are also distinguished in order and function [Note: [Col. 0997] Elsewhere, “merit.”]. If anyone carefully examines their individual properties and duties—what each accomplishes in us, how they differ from and surpass one another—he will consider whatever labor or effort he expends upon them brief and easy, in view of their great usefulness and sweetness.

Reading is the diligent examination of the Scriptures with focused attention. Meditation is the purposeful activity of the mind investigating, under the guidance of one’s own reasoning, knowledge of hidden truth. Prayer is the devout intention of the heart [Note: [Col. 0997] Elsewhere, “of the mind.”] directed toward God for the removal of evils and the attainment of good things. Contemplation is a certain elevation of the mind suspended in God, tasting the joys of eternal sweetness.

## CHAPTER II. Description of the functions of the four stages.

Having therefore set out descriptions of the four stages [Col. 0998], we must now examine their functions. Reading seeks the sweetness of blessed life; meditation finds it; prayer asks for it; contemplation tastes it. Hence the Lord himself says: “Seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you” (Matthew 7:7). Seek by reading, and you will find by meditating. Knock by praying, and it will be opened to you by contemplating.

Reading places solid food before the mouth; meditation chews and breaks it down; prayer obtains its flavor; contemplation is the sweetness itself, which gives delight and refreshment. Reading is in the outer shell, meditation in the fat, prayer in the asking of desire, and contemplation in the delight of the sweetness obtained.

To make this clearer, I will give one example from many. In reading, I hear: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5:8). Behold a brief saying, but sweet and filled with many meanings, offering the soul nourishment like a grape. After the soul has carefully examined it, it says within itself:

“Something good may be present here. I will return to my heart and test whether I might perhaps understand and discover this purity. For this is a precious and desirable thing, whose possessors are called blessed, and to whom the vision of God—which is eternal life—is promised and commended by so many testimonies of Holy Scripture.”

Desiring this to be explained more fully, the soul begins to chew and break down this one saying, placing it, as it were, in a winepress. Then it stirs its reason to inquire what this purity, so precious and desirable, is and how it may be possessed.

## CHAPTER III. The function of meditation. Knowledge in evils, not wisdom.

[Col. 0999]

Diligent meditation therefore approaches. It does not remain outside or cling to the surface of the letter; it plants its foot more deeply, penetrates the interior, and examines each detail. It carefully considers that he did not say, “Blessed are the pure in body,” but “in heart,” because it is not enough for the hands to be innocent of evil deeds unless we are also cleansed in mind from wicked thoughts.

This is confirmed by the authority of the Prophet, who says: “Who shall ascend the mountain of the Lord, or who shall stand in his holy place? The innocent in hands and pure in heart” (Psalm 23:3–4). It also considers how greatly that same prophet desired purity of heart when he prayed: “Create in me a clean heart, O God” (Psalm 50:12). And again: “If I had regarded iniquity in my heart, the Lord would not have heard” (Psalm 65:18).

It thinks how careful blessed Job was in this guardianship when he said: “I have made a covenant with my eyes, that I would not even think about a virgin” (Job 31:1). Behold how strictly the holy man restrained himself: he closed his eyes so that he would not see vanity, lest he should perhaps carelessly look upon what he would later desire unwillingly [Note: [Col. 0999] Instead of “he would look … unwillingly,” Erasmus, the Lyon edition, and the Venetian edition read “he would look back … inwardly.” M.]

After it has considered these and similar matters concerning purity of heart, it begins to think about its reward: how glorious and delightful it is to see the desired face of the Lord, who is beautiful beyond the sons of men (Psalm 44:3); no longer rejected and contemptible, possessing no beauty such as his mother, the synagogue, clothed him with, but dressed in the robe of immortality and crowned with the diadem with which his Father crowned him on the day of resurrection and glory, the day that the Lord has made.

It thinks that in that vision there will be the satisfaction of which the Prophet says: “I shall be satisfied when your glory appears” (Psalm 16:15). Do you see how much liquid has flowed from this tiny grape, how great a fire has arisen from this spark, how far this small mass—“Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5:8)—has been stretched out upon the anvil of meditation?

Yet how much further could it be extended if someone experienced in such matters were to approach? I feel that the well is deep, but I, inexperienced in such things [Note: [Col. 0999] In Bernard, “a novice”; and the word “vessel” is absent.], have scarcely found a vessel with which to draw a little water.

With these torches the soul is set aflame, and with these desires it is stirred. Having broken the alabaster jar, it begins to sense the fragrance of the ointment—not yet by tasting it, but as though by the smell of the nostrils. From this it concludes how sweet it would be to experience this purity, whose meditation it knows to be so delightful.

But what will it do? It burns with the desire to possess it, yet does not find within itself how it may possess it (John 4:11); and the more it searches, the more it thirsts. As it adds meditation, it adds pain, because it thirsts [Note: [Col. 0999] Elsewhere, “does not sense”; and shortly afterward, “provides,” in place of “pre-tastes.”] for the sweetness that meditation shows to exist in purity of heart, but does not pre-taste.

For it does not belong to the reader and meditator to experience this sweetness unless it has been given from above. Reading and meditation are common to the good and the wicked alike. The philosophers of the nations themselves discovered, by the guidance of reason, in what the highest true good consisted. But because, although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God (Romans 1:21), and instead, trusting in their own powers, said, “With our tongue we will prevail; our lips are our own” (Psalm 11:5), they did not deserve to receive what they were able to see.

They became futile in their thoughts, and all their wisdom was swallowed up—the wisdom supplied to them by human study and discipline, not by the spirit of wisdom, who alone gives true wisdom: namely, a knowledge made flavorful, which delights and refreshes the soul that clings to it with an inestimable savor. Of this it was said: “Wisdom will not enter into a malevolent soul” (Wisdom 1:4).

This wisdom comes from God alone. Just as the Lord granted the ministry of baptizing to many, but retained for himself alone the power and authority to forgive sins in baptism—hence John spoke of him antonomastically and distinctly: “This is he who baptizes in the Holy Spirit” (John 1:33)—so we may say of him: “This is he who gives the flavor of wisdom and knowledge made flavorful to the soul” [Col. 1000] [Note: [Col. 1000] In Bernard, “the soul”; shortly afterward, the word “knowledge” is omitted.]. For speech is given to many, but wisdom to few, distributed by the Lord to whomever he wishes and in whatever manner he wishes.

## CHAPTER IV. The function of prayer.

When the soul sees that by itself it cannot attain the desired sweetness of knowledge and experience, and that the more it approaches the deep heart, the more God is exalted, it humbles itself and takes refuge in prayer, saying:

“Lord, who are seen only by pure hearts, I have investigated by reading and sought through meditation how true purity of heart may be possessed, so that through it, even if only in small measure, I might know you. I was seeking your face, O Lord; your face, O Lord, I was seeking” (Psalm 26:8).

“I have meditated for a long time in my heart, and in my meditation the fire and desire to know you more deeply have burned within me” (Psalm 38:4). “While you break for me the bread of Holy Scripture, there is great knowledge in the breaking of the bread” (Luke 24:30–31). The more I know you, the more I desire to know you—not now in the outer shell of the letter, but in the experience of its meaning.

“I do not ask this, Lord, on account of my merits, but because of your mercy. For I confess that I am unworthy and sinful; yet even the little dogs eat of the crumbs that fall from the table of their masters” (Matthew 15:27). Give me, Lord, the pledge of the inheritance to come, or at least a drop of heavenly rain with which I may cool my thirst, for I am burning with love.

## CHAPTER V. The function of contemplation.

With these and similar fiery words, the soul inflames its desire. In this way it reveals its affection; by these incantations it summons the bridegroom.

But the Lord, whose eyes are upon the righteous and whose ears are directed not only to their prayers but even to the prayers themselves, does not wait until they have finished speaking. Interrupting the course of the prayer midway, he hastens to enter and hastens to meet the desiring soul, surrounded by the sweetness of heavenly dew. Anointed with the finest perfumes, he refreshes the weary soul, restores the hungry, enriches the dry, and makes it forget earthly things, strengthening, enlivening, and intoxicating it wonderfully with the memory of himself, while also making it sober.

Just as in certain bodily activities carnal desire is overcome to such an extent that a person loses all use of reason and becomes almost wholly carnal, so rightly, in this heavenly contemplation, carnal impulses are consumed and absorbed by the soul to such an extent that the flesh in no way contradicts the spirit, and the person becomes almost wholly spiritual.

## CHAPTER VI. Signs of the Holy Spirit’s coming to the soul.

O Lord, how shall we know when you do this, and what sign will there be of your coming? Are sighs and tears perhaps the witnesses and messengers of this consolation and joy? If so, this is a new use of antiphrasis and an unusual meaning. For what agreement is there between consolation and sighs, or between joy and tears? That is, if these should be called tears, rather than an overflowing abundance of inner dew infused from above and an outward cleansing of the human being as a sign of the inner washing.

Just as in the baptism of children the inner washing of the soul is signified and represented by outward washing, so here, conversely, inner cleansing precedes outward washing. O happy tears, through which inward stains are cleansed, through which the fires of sins are extinguished! “Blessed are you who mourn in this way, for you shall laugh” (Matthew 5:5).

In these tears, O soul, recognize your bridegroom; embrace the one you desire. Now let the torrent of pleasure intoxicate you (Psalm 35:9); draw from his breast the milk and honey of consolation. These are the wondrous gifts and consolations your bridegroom has given you—namely, sighs and tears. In these tears he brings you drink in due measure. These tears are your bread day and night (Psalm 41:4), bread that strengthens the human heart (Psalm 103:15), and sweeter than honey and the honeycomb.

O Lord, if these tears, stirred up by memory and desire for you, are so sweet, how sweet will the joy be that will be received from the manifest vision of you? If it is so sweet to weep for you, how sweet will it be to rejoice in you?

But why do we bring such secret conversations into public? Why do we attempt to express ineffable and indescribable affections in ordinary words? Those without experience of such things do not understand them unless they read them more clearly in the book of experience, where the anointing itself teaches them. Otherwise, the external letter provides no benefit to the reader. Reading the outer letter has little flavor unless it receives its gloss and inner meaning from the heart.

## CHAPTER VII. On the concealment of grace.

O soul, we have prolonged our conversation. It was good for us to be here, with Peter and John contemplating the glory of the bridegroom, and to remain with him for a long time, if he wished not two or three tabernacles to be made here, but one in which we might be together and rejoice together.

But now the bridegroom says, “Let me go.” The dawn has already risen; you have already received the light of grace and the visitation you desired. After giving his blessing, weakening the sinew of the thigh, and changing the name from Jacob to Israel, the long-desired bridegroom withdraws for a little while, having quickly slipped away. He withdraws both from the vision mentioned above and from the sweetness of contemplation; yet he remains present with respect to governance, glory, and union [Note: [Col. 1001] These words—“with respect to glory and union”—are absent in Bernard.]

## CHAPTER VIII. Why it is concealed for a time.

But do not fear, O bride; do not despair; do not think that you are despised if the bridegroom withdraws his face from you for a little while. All these things work together for your good, and from both his approach and his withdrawal you gain profit. He comes for you, and for you he also departs. He comes for consolation and departs for caution: lest the greatness of the consolation exalt you; lest, if the bridegroom were always with you, you should begin to despise your companions; and lest you attribute this continual visitation not to grace but to nature.

The bridegroom grants this grace to whom he wishes and when he wishes; it is not possessed as though by hereditary right. There is a common proverb that excessive familiarity breeds contempt. He therefore withdraws, lest perhaps, through being too constantly present, he should be despised; so that, being absent, he may be desired more, being desired, sought more eagerly, and, after being sought for a long time, found with greater gratitude.

Moreover, if this consolation never failed—which, in comparison with the future glory that will be revealed in us, is enigmatic and partial (1 Corinthians 13:12)—we might perhaps think that here we possessed a permanent city and would seek the future one less eagerly (Hebrews 13:14).

Therefore, lest we mistake exile for our homeland or the pledge for the full price, the bridegroom comes and departs in turn: now bringing consolation, now changing our entire bed in sickness. He permits us to taste for a little while how sweet he is, and before we fully feel him, he withdraws himself. Thus, as though flying above us with outspread wings, he urges us to fly.

It is as if he says: “Behold, you have tasted a little how sweet and delightful I am. But if you wish to be fully satisfied with this sweetness, run after me into the fragrance of my perfumes, with your hearts lifted upward, where I am at the right hand of God the Father. There you will see me, not through a mirror in an enigma, but face to face; and your heart will rejoice fully, and no one will take your joy from you.”

## CHAPTER IX. How carefully each person should conduct himself at that time.

But take care, O bride. When the bridegroom withdraws himself, he will not go far away. Although you do not see him, he nevertheless always sees you, full of eyes before and behind; you can never be hidden from him.

He also has around you his messengers, spirits like extremely shrewd spies, to see how you conduct yourself in the bridegroom’s absence. They accuse you before him if they detect in you any signs of wantonness or frivolity.

This bridegroom is jealous. If you should accept another lover, or if you should strive to please others more, he will immediately depart from you and cling to other young women. This bridegroom is delicate, noble, and rich; he is beautiful beyond the sons of men (Psalm 44:3), and therefore he deigns to have no bride unless she is beautiful.

If he sees a stain or wrinkle in you, he will immediately turn his eyes away. For he can tolerate no impurity. Therefore be chaste, modest, and humble, so that you may deserve to be frequently visited by your bridegroom.

I fear that this conversation has detained us too long; but a subject both fertile and sweet compelled me to continue. I was not prolonging it willingly, but was drawn along involuntarily by some sweetness of its own.

## CHAPTER X. Recapitulation. How the foregoing stages are linked together.

So that what has been said at greater length may appear better when joined and brought together, let us collect the substance of the foregoing by recapitulating it.

As was indicated in the examples above, it can be seen how the foregoing stages are connected and how they precede one another both temporally and causally. Reading comes first, like a foundation, and, once it has supplied its material, sends us on to meditation. Meditation more carefully investigates what ought to be desired and, as though digging up a treasure, discovers and displays it; but since it cannot obtain it by itself, it sends us on to prayer.

Prayer, rising toward the Lord with all its strength, obtains the desired treasure: the sweetness of contemplation. When it arrives, contemplation rewards the labor of the preceding three stages by intoxicating the thirsty soul with the sweetness of heavenly dew.

Reading, therefore, is the first outward exercise; meditation concerns the inner understanding; prayer concerns desire; contemplation transcends every sense. The first stage belongs to beginners. The second to those making progress. The third to the devout. The fourth to the blessed.

These steps, however, are so interconnected and serve one another by reciprocal assistance that the preceding steps are of little or no benefit without the subsequent ones, while the subsequent ones can be attained only rarely, or never, without the preceding. For what does it profit a person to occupy time in continuous reading, passing through the deeds and writings of the saints, unless by chewing and ruminating on them we extract their juice and, swallowing it, send it into the innermost recesses of the heart, so that from these things we may carefully consider our own condition and strive to do the works of those whose deeds we desire to read? But how shall we think about these things, or how shall we be able to take care lest, while meditating on certain false or empty notions, we overstep the boundaries established by the holy Fathers, unless beforehand we have been instructed about such matters through reading or hearing? Hearing, indeed, in a certain way pertains to reading. Hence we are accustomed to say that we have read not only the books themselves that we read either to ourselves or to others, but also those that we have heard from teachers.

Likewise, what does it profit a person if through meditation he sees what ought to be done, unless through the help of prayer and the grace of God he grows strong enough to attain it? For every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, descending from the Father of lights (James 1:17), without whom we can do nothing; yet he himself works deeds in us, though not altogether without us. For we are God’s fellow workers (1 Cor. 3:9), as the Apostle says. God indeed desires us to pray to him, and, when he comes and waits at the door, to open to him the embrace of our will and consent to him. He required this consent from the Samaritan woman when he said, “Call your husband,” as though he were saying: “I wish to pour grace into you; apply your free will.” He required prayer from her when he said, “If you knew the gift of God, and who it is who says to you, ‘Give me a drink,’ perhaps you would have asked him for living water.” Having heard this, as though instructed through reading, the woman meditated in her heart that it would be good and useful for her to have this water. Thus, kindled by the desire to possess it, she turned to prayer, saying, “Lord, give me this water, so that I may thirst no more, nor come here to draw water” (John 4:16, 10, 15). Behold: hearing the Lord’s word, followed by meditation upon it, moved her to pray. For how would she have been eager to ask unless meditation had first kindled her? Or what would the meditation that preceded have contributed to her unless the prayer that followed had obtained what it showed to be desirable? Therefore, for meditation to be fruitful, it is necessary that the devotion of prayer follow it; [Col. 1003] the sweetness of contemplation is, as it were, its effect.

## CHAPTER XI. How imperfect they are without one another. The happiness of contemplatives.

From these things we can gather that reading without meditation is dry, meditation without reading is erroneous, prayer without meditation is lukewarm, meditation without prayer is fruitless; prayer with devotion acquires contemplation; and the attainment of contemplation without prayer is either rare or miraculous. For God, whose power has neither number nor limit, and whose mercy is over all his works, sometimes raises up children for Abraham from stones, compelling the hard and unwilling to consent so that they may become willing; and thus, as the saying commonly goes, like a prodigal, he pulls the ox by the horn when, though not summoned, he pours himself into us. Although we read that this has sometimes happened to certain people, such as Paul and some others, we should nevertheless not presume upon divine things by testing God, but do what belongs to us: namely, read and meditate on the law of God; pray [Note: [Col. 1003] Some copies add here, “or love.”] to him to help our weakness and to regard our imperfection. He himself teaches us to do this, saying, “Ask, and you shall receive; seek, and you shall find; knock, and it shall be opened to you” (Matt. 7:7). “Now the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it” (ibid. 11:12). From these distinctions already indicated, the characteristics of the aforementioned steps can be perceived: how they are connected with one another and what each of them produces in us.

Blessed is the person whose mind, free from other concerns, always desires to occupy itself with these four steps; who, having sold all that he possessed, bought that field in which the desirable treasure lies hidden (ibid. 13:44)—namely, to be at leisure and see how gracious the Lord is; who, exercised in the first step, circumspect in the second, devoted in the third, and lifted above himself in the fourth, ascends through these elevations that he has arranged in his heart, going from strength to strength until he sees the God of gods in Zion. Blessed is the one who is permitted to remain for even a short time in this highest step; who can truly say: “Behold, I feel the grace of the Lord; behold, with Peter and John I contemplate his glory on the mountain; behold, with Jacob I am often delighted by Rachel’s embraces.” Yet let such a person beware, lest after this contemplation, by which he has been raised even to the heavens, he fall through a disorderly collapse all the way to the depths; and lest, after seeing God [Note: [Col. 1003] Another reading: “after the visitation that has taken place.”] he turn back to the wanton deeds of the world and the allurements of the flesh. When the sight of the human mind, being weak, can no longer endure the illumination of the true light for long, let it descend gently and in orderly fashion to one of the three steps by which it had ascended; and let it remain alternately, now in one and now in another, according to the measure [Note: [Col. 1003] Another reading: “movement.”] of free will and as the place and time require—already nearer to God in proportion as it is farther removed from the first step.

But alas, the fragile and wretched condition of humanity! Behold: by the guidance of reason and the testimonies of Scripture, we plainly see that the perfection of the good life is contained in these four steps, and that the spiritual person’s discipline ought to be occupied with them. But who is there who follows this path of life? [Col. 1004] Who is this person? And we shall praise him. Many find it easy to will, but few to accomplish. Would that we were among those few!

## CHAPTER XII. Four causes that draw us away from these steps.

There are four causes that usually draw us away from these steps: unavoidable necessity, the usefulness of honorable activity, human weakness, and worldly vanity. The first is excusable, the second tolerable, the third pitiable, and the fourth blameworthy. Why blameworthy? For those whom this last cause draws back from a holy purpose would have been better off never to have known the glory of God than to turn back after having come to know it. What excuse, indeed, will such a person have for his sin? Will the Lord not justly be able to say to him:

“What ought I to have done for you that I did not do? You did not exist, and I created you; you sinned, and had made yourself a servant of the devil, and I redeemed you; you were running in the course of the world with the impious, and I chose you; I had given you grace in my sight and wished to make my dwelling with you, but you despised me and cast behind you not only my words but me myself, and walked after your desires.”

But, O good God, sweet and gentle, dear friend, wise counselor, strong helper—how inhuman, how reckless is the person who rejects you, who drives from his heart so humble and so gentle a guest! O what an unhappy and destructive exchange: to reject one’s Creator and admit wicked and harmful thoughts! To hand over to be trampled upon that secret chamber of the Holy Spirit, the secret place of the heart, which only a little while before was intent upon heavenly joys, and so suddenly to surrender it to filthy thoughts and sins! The bridegroom’s footprints are still warm in the heart, and adulterous desires are already being admitted.

It is ill-fitting and unbecoming for ears that have just heard words that it is not permitted for a human being to speak (2 Cor. 12:4) so quickly to incline themselves to hear fables and slanders; for eyes that have just been baptized with sacred tears suddenly to turn toward seeing vanities; for the tongue that has just sung a sweet wedding song, that by its fiery and persuasive words reconciled the bride to the bridegroom and led her into the wine cellar (Song 2:4), to turn again to vain speech, buffoonery, contriving deceit, and slander. Far be it from us, Lord.

But if, through human weakness, we should slip into such things, let us not therefore despair; rather, let us return again to the merciful physician, who raises the needy from the dust and lifts the poor from the dung heap (Ps. 112:7), and who does not desire the death of the sinner (Ezek. 33:11). He will again care for us and heal us.

Now it is time to bring the letter to an end. Let us therefore pray to God that, in the present, he may lessen for us the obstacles that draw us away from contemplation of him, and in the future remove them from us completely; that through the aforementioned steps he may lead us from strength to strength until we see the God of gods in Zion (Ps. 83:8). There the elect will not receive the sweetness of divine contemplation drop by drop or intermittently; rather, continually filled from the torrent of delight, they will possess a joy that no one shall take from them, and an unchanging peace, peace in unity.

# [ON THE KNOWLEDGE OF TRUE LIFE]

[Col. 1003]

## EDITORIAL NOTICE TO THE FOLLOWING BOOK

Honorius of Autun, in his book *On the Luminaries of the Church*, lists among his published works a book entitled *Knowledge of Life*, concerning God and eternal life. This is precisely the subject of the following book, which, although it is wholly about God and eternal life, is called either simply *Knowledge of Life*, as in the old Audun manuscript, which appears to have been written approximately in Honorius’s time, or, as in the printed editions, *On the Knowledge of True Life*, although the title in one edition of Jodocus Badius lacks the word “true.”

No one who has seen other works by Honorius of Autun can fail easily to recognize him here. In particular, he is accustomed to follow the method observed in this book: to treat matters in the form of a dialogue and introduce disciples conversing with their teacher, who always receive their good wishes at the end of the dialogue. Here, indeed, *Brothers* had everywhere been substituted for *Disciples*; but we have corrected the error on the basis of the Audun exemplar. Moreover, Honorius likes to imitate Anselm, transmitting not only his teaching but sometimes even using certain of his expressions—for example, when here he calls the supreme Spirit God, or the Holy Spirit; and when he so often employs the particle “further” (*amplius*) whenever the argument proceeds to additional proofs, and so forth. You will find the same ideas, and Anselm’s very doctrine, expressed in his *Monologion* and transferred here.

The little work also bears the scent of the schools, and for that reason is not unworthy of Honorius, who calls himself a scholastic in his book *On the Luminaries of the Church*. In addition, the book is furnished with a preface of the same kind as those of nearly all Honorius of Autun’s books. It is characteristic or customary for him, at the beginning of his works, both to complain about his detractors—as he does in the books *On the Image of the World*, *On the Luminaries of the Church*, and *On Predestination and Free Will*—and to present and explain the title of each work, as in the books *On the Gem of the Soul*, *On the Image of the World*, and *On the Seal of Blessed Mary*. He did this at least at the end of the book *On Predestination* as well.

It must further be admitted that the work called *Elucidarium* in the Anselm Appendix can, on the same indications and arguments, be attributed to this same Honorius, although that work contains certain things not sufficiently consistent with his other writings. One such matter is the definition of free will given in Book 2, chapter 2: “The freedom to choose good and evil,” a definition that Honorius by no means approves in the book *On Predestination and Free Will*. He must presumably be thought to have advanced, or to have changed his opinion, after writing the *Elucidarium*, which he himself lists first among his works.

Furthermore, this treatise *On the Knowledge of True Life* was known even to the Greeks. A fragment of it, together with excerpts from certain other Latin writers—such as Leo the Great and Hilary, likewise found in Greek—was published at Basel in 1578 under the care of Leunclavius, who recovered these fragments from the library of John Sambucus and restored them to Latin. That same fragment of *On the Knowledge of True Life* survives in manuscript 115 of the Munich library, joined with works by Bessarion, as can be seen in the catalogue of that library published at the end of Possevinus’s *Apparatus*. The fragment begins with these words:

“Brothers, just as the weight of the flesh burdens the soul” (Ἀδελφοὶ ὥσπερ τὸ τῆς σαρκὸς βάρος πιέζει τὴν ψυχήν), “and so forth.”

It is drawn from chapter 10 of the following book and ends near the conclusion of chapter 18, omitting chapter 15. The Greek title of the fragment is:

“Of Saint Augustine, *On the Trinity*, from the book entitled *On the Knowledge of True Life*, in which, as in a dialogue, the Brothers ask questions and the Teacher answers” (Τοῦ ἁγίου Αὐγουστί́νου περὶ Τριάδος, ἐκ τοῦ βιβλίου τοῦ περὶ τῆς γνώσεως τῆς ἀληθοῦς ζωῆς ἐπιγραφομένου, ἐν ᾧ ὡς ἐν διαλόγῳ ἐρωτῶσι μὲν οἱ ἀδελφοί, ἀποκρίνεται δὲ ὁ διδάσκαλος).

“Of Saint Augustine, *On the Trinity*, from the book entitled *On the Knowledge of True Life*, in which, as in a dialogue, the Brothers ask questions and the Teacher answers.”

You can see that the Greeks encountered a Latin exemplar already corrupted, in which the work was not only attributed to Augustine, but *Disciples* had also been changed into *Brothers*. This change, in turn, became the cause and occasion of another corruption in the title—unless one prefers to suppose that the changes were made at the same time. For in a somewhat recent manuscript of the Royal Library, numbered 4546, this title is found prefixed to the work:

“Here begins the book of blessed Augustine, *On the Knowledge of True Life*, which he made for the hermit brothers on Mount Pisano, while he himself was a brother, in the thirty-first year of his age.”

And just as *Brothers* was substituted for *Disciples*, so *Augustine* was everywhere substituted for *Teacher*.

[Col. 1005]

# KNOWLEDGE OF LIFE, OR ONE BOOK ON THE KNOWLEDGE OF TRUE LIFE (G, S)*

## CHAPTER I. For what purpose rational nature was made. The plan of the work undertaken. Its title.

The Wisdom of God, which opened the mouth of the mute (Matt. 9:33) and granted a braying animal to form human words (Num. 22:28), impels even me, inexperienced not only in speech but also in knowledge, to speak, and compels me to make known piously to others what has been understood through it and concerning it. Therefore, at its prompting, for the benefit, as I hope, of many, I once again expose myself to be gnawed by the teeth of the envious, and perhaps to be cherished [Note: [Col. 1005] So the Audun manuscript. The Medard manuscript has “to be built”; the printed editions, “to be pierced.”] in the hearts of those who love life, since Christ, who is truth and life, says, “This is eternal life: that they know you, the only true God” (John 17:3).

It is certainly established that rational nature was made for this one purpose: to understand its Maker, the true God; by understanding him, to love him; and by loving him, to live eternally and blessedly in him, who is eternal life. Therefore, to investigate rationally the essence of divinity is to hasten toward eternal life; while to neglect and thus not know it is plainly to hurry toward unending death, because that person will be unknown by it when he is eventually separated from the blessed life.

Accordingly, although many of the holy Fathers have written much that is glorious about this splendid subject and have in a certain way made the matter itself more obscure to simpler minds, I wish through these dense thickets to smooth out, as it were, a path with my pen, so that those of weak understanding, leaving behind the trackless ways of error, may be able to walk freely along the level ground of truth.

But perhaps some envious person now confronts me with a clouded face and bitterly spits at me the venom long congealed in his jaundiced heart:

“What are you attempting? Are you trying to carry wood into the forests, or to pour a drop of water into the overflowing sea?”

Let this rock blunt the biting tooth of such a biter and pour the maliciously spat-out poison back into the very inward parts of the one who must again be tormented by it [Note: [Col. 1006] The printed editions have “by turning it back.”]. “Through the envy of the devil death entered the world, and those who belong to his faction imitate him” (Wis. 2:24–25).

O unhappy envious person, tormented by another’s happiness and feeding upon another’s misfortune! By the very facts you prove that you belong to the one whose faction you share, since you envy others for knowing what you do not know; and you groan with sickly sighs over the pious labor bestowed upon me, although you recognize that it has been denied to you because of your laziness—or rather, because of your envy. Come, wretch: instead of vomiting forth the deadly poison with which you are swollen, receive the wholesome antidote of love. Otherwise, wasting away with black bile, favor your father’s faction.

But I have no dealings with envy as it wastes away. Entering eagerly into the noble forest of the Scriptures, I shall not, as you assert with your poisonous tongue, carry wood into it; rather, I shall endeavor to carry out from it the precious wood of life—righteousness—for those who hunger, and I shall not delay to draw from the sea of Scripture a sweet draught of life for those who thirst for life. Let us therefore all the faithful run to the tree and fountain of life, by whose taste we may live blessedly forever.

Let the little book receive the title *Knowledge of Life* [Note: [Col. 1007] So Badius and the Audun manuscript. Other books add “true.”], since in it true life appears to be made knowable to those of slower understanding.

## CHAPTER II. The carnal conception of the heavenly kingdom. How difficult it is to present knowledge of God. By what method this is attempted. Why it is requested. The difficulty of the work.

**DISCIPLES.** We give thanks to God, by whose gift we can be plainly assured in matters of doubt. Since you see us gathered here for this very purpose, lest, as we make our way toward our homeland, we should fail from weariness along the road, refresh us, as you are accustomed to do, with the food and drink of life; and, fastening the time that slips away in an irreversible course with the bonds of questions, make it stable for us, lest its own revolving motion engulf us while we sit idle, but let your graciousness raise us, as we labor in divine things, into the ever-enduring age.

**TEACHER.** Come eagerly with me to the fruit of the tree of life hanging from the branches of the cross, and together drink from the fountain of life flowing from the Father of life [Note: [Col. 1007] The printed editions omit the word “Father.”] as from a place of delight, watering Paradise—that is, the Church, the garden of delights. If its flavor sweetens the palate of your hearts, I assure you that he will one day satisfy you from his torrent of delight, you who will remain with him throughout the ages.

**DISC.** Since, being carnally minded, we cannot think about spiritual things, we form in our minds the kingdom of heaven as a most brilliant region, overflowing with every kind of wealth, in which we imagine the splendid city of heavenly Jerusalem, renowned for its merits and riches, and in it God as a glorious king, with Angels appearing like soldiers in varied attire. Therefore we ask you to bring the truth, hidden as though in darkness, into the light while reason searches out the matter and arguments crush every obstacle; and to place before the eyes of our hearts, made visible in some fashion, the God whom, as you assert, we shall one day see.

**MAG.** Since almighty God, alone immortal, alone invisible, alone incomprehensible, dwells in inaccessible light, while I, covered with the darkness of vices, dwell in foul gloom, unfit for the light of virtues, how shall I be able to bring ineffable light into the wounded eyes of others, when, struck blind in the eye of my heart and dazzled by the splendor of such majesty, I cannot in any way behold it myself?

**DISC.** Nevertheless, strive with all your power to be swept into that light, so that, once the darkness has been scattered, you may deserve to be illuminated by it and we may be enlightened through you—just as we often see valleys illuminated by the sun’s radiance shining from the mountains.

**MAG.** I shall endeavor to the best of my ability, while you pray, and, with logic leading the way and arguments accompanying me, I shall follow the truth as it flees into the hiding place of that inaccessible light; and, with its permission, I shall bring it forth for you as you investigate it and it reveals itself.

**DISC.** Our prayer will certainly not be lacking to you, provided that reason, the guide of truth, goes before you. For we greatly desire to hear from you how we ought to think about God in our prayers, lest our weak mind perhaps imagine for itself a handsome human being and, deceived, venerate this image instead of the true God.

**MAG.** I confess that, overcome and crushed by the greatness and height of the task undertaken, I falter, because I can scarcely explain in words what I grasp in any way with my mind. For it far surpasses the entire distinguished intellect of the greatest philosophers, since the sublimity of the subject being treated exceeds every understanding. Indeed, the more I try to enter into every creature and contemplate it with attentive gaze [Note: [Col. 1008] The printed editions have “to transcend,” less appropriately.], the more I feel it receding from the sight of my understanding. Nevertheless, I shall do my best to satisfy your inquiry according to my capacity, insofar as the one about whom we are speaking deigns to make himself known to the soul that desires knowledge of him. But when your strength, weighed down by the burden of such eminence, gives way, you must forgive weakness.

**DISC.** The more carefully we weigh the height of this matter, the more ardently we desire that it be made knowable to us in whatever way may be possible, and that we behold its beauty in whatever manner we can. Therefore, we willingly forgive you if you explain by gestures at least what you cannot express in words.

## CHAPTER III. God cannot properly be expressed. None of the categories applies to him.

**MAG.** It must therefore be understood that God cannot properly be expressed in any words and cannot be comprehended by any thought. For how would he be called immeasurable and incomprehensible if he were enclosed within human speech or meditation? Yet it is now evident how wondrous he is, since he is unsayable in every language and unthinkable in every heart.

Dialectic, powerful in argument, decisively defining every doubt, shaking out and dissecting all writings, annihilating all human wisdom—when it turns its attention to divinity, struck by the light of such majesty, turns back its trembling head in fear, flees, and hides in the secret recesses of worldly wisdom; and, once the bonds of syllogisms have been dissolved, it falls silent in foolishness.

Indeed, everything that is conceived by the human heart under the ten categories is expressed by a name and a word. But reason clearly proves that none of these applies properly to God. For if we say that God is substance, which grants subsistence to all things and through which all things have being, immediately universals and particulars, of which substance is predicated, and the genera and species in which it is found, together with the nine accidents that necessarily inhere in it, come to mind. Yet it is evident that none of these belongs in any way to God.

If we predicate that God is magnitude itself, which orders all things according to measure, number, and weight, immediately smallness sets itself against this quantity and diminishes by its own littleness what is greatest above all. If we call him goodness itself or the highest good, who makes all things exceedingly good, evil, contrary to this quality, immediately confronts him and does not hesitate to oppose such goodness.

But if he is called Creator or Lord—both of which are relative terms, namely, relative to the world—relation immediately objects that before the world’s establishment he lacked this name, and that this relative property accrued to him through the creation of the world, even though reason asserts that nothing accidental belongs to God, but that everything predicated of him is essential to him.

Further, if he is said to be wholly everywhere and at the same time to fill all places, locality immediately creeps in secretly and confines within a place the one who encloses all things in his hand. If he is called eternal and said to order all times, the present immediately hastens to succeed the past, and the future to succeed the present, and does not fear to assign a beginning and an end to eternity.

If it is said that he possesses all things and shines clothed in light as in a garment, thought immediately strips him of this clothing, separating the garment of light or the possession of things from him. If he is affirmed to be always present, the position of standing or sitting is immediately imagined. If he is said to rule the universe, the activity of labor tries to cancel eternal rest. Further, if he is declared to be capable of suffering and to endure our evils, suffering immediately intrudes and strives to make the impassible suffer.

All human condition is enclosed within these ten categories, and the property of the highest essence is clearly excluded from all of them by evident reasoning. For whatever admits opposition, contrariety, or accident cannot properly belong to God in any way. Therefore, since contrary to reason we cannot speak properly about God, let us at least strive to speak about him improperly and through enigmas.

## CHAPTER IV. The mind as the soul’s mirror. From where knowledge comes to us. Spiritual things are reached by faith, not reason. The word “spirit” has six meanings in Scripture. Air. Wind. The life of brute animals.

**DISC.** Clear reason indeed teaches that God is unsayable in human words, but the intellectual mind eagerly desires that he be made knowable to it in whatever way may be possible. This mind seems like a mirror of the soul, in which it may contemplate the very image of its Creator.

**MAG.** Everything that we know among created things, we have come to know through bodily senses. And those things that we have learned neither by sight nor by experience, we learn through comparisons with things seen or experienced—for example, what we read about beasts or unknown people. But things wholly unknown to us, which are not signified through familiar comparisons, are never made known to our understanding at all. Therefore, because spiritual things are invisible to us and incomparable with bodily senses, they will never be made probable to us by any reasoning. Since, however, it is established that these things exist but cannot be taught through likenesses, they require only the faith of believers.

**DISC.** Whatever reason proves by arguments, even if it fails in comparison, every rational person must necessarily not refuse to believe. You need only state what reason suggests to you that we ought to know about spirits.

**MAG.** You surely know that in Scripture “spirit” is used substantially in six ways. First, God, supreme over all, is called Spirit, as in: “God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit” (John 4:24). Second, angels are called spirits, as in: “He makes his angels spirits” (Ps. 103:4). Third, souls are called spirits, as in: “His spirit shall go forth, and the flesh shall return to the earth” (Ps. 145:4). Fourth, the life of brute animals is called spirit, as in: “Who knows whether the spirit of beasts goes downward?” (Eccles. 3:21). Fifth, winds are called spirits, as in: “Storm winds” (Ps. 148:8). Sixth, air is written of as spirit, as in: “I opened my mouth and drew in the spirit” (Ps. 118:131).

Their definition is as follows: air is a sensible but not sentient spirit—that is, one that we feel when we draw it in, though it feels nothing itself, while nevertheless providing breath to all living things beneath the heavens. Wind is air that is spirit, agitated by some movement at God’s command, intensified by storms of water, raised up through angelic ministries, and calmed through the same ministries. The life of brute animals is a vital spirit consisting of air and blood, animal in nature, invisible but sensible, possessing memory but lacking understanding, dying with the flesh and dissipating into the air.

## CHAPTER V. What the intelligent soul is. It is a sensible, changeable, nonlocal, passible life, without quantity, shape, or color.

The soul, however, is a spirit, an incorporeal substance, the life of its body, invisible, sensible, changeable, nonlocal, passible, incapable of receiving either the measure of quantities or the form or color of qualities [Note: [Col. 1009] In the manuscripts: “incapable of receiving quantity … quality … color.”]; possessing memory, reason, and understanding, and immortal.

And lest this definition waver, let reason strengthen it with proofs. The soul is a spiritual substance. For whatever supplies life to another must itself necessarily subsist; but the soul grants life to the body; therefore the soul truly subsists. That it is life itself is proved by the fact that through its presence it gives life to the body and through its absence brings the same body to death.

It is invisible to us, but visible to spirits. It is also clearly sensible, since it enables the eyes to sense colors, the ears sounds, the nostrils odors, the palate flavors, and the hands rough or smooth things. It is also changeable: whatever becomes worse or better is changeable; but the soul becomes worse through vices and better through virtues; therefore it is changeable.

It is also nonlocal. Whatever is enclosed within a place and bounded by the height, breadth, and [Col. 1010] length of space is a body; but reason has taught that the soul is incorporeal—that is, that it is neither a body nor possesses any bodily member. Therefore it is clear that it is nonlocal. It does not occupy a space of air as a body does, nor fill a body as water fills a wineskin; rather, just as heat is nonlocally present throughout a fire, so the soul fills the whole body nonlocally.

Fire is visible, but heat is invisible and sensible, and in a certain way gives life to the fire; so the soul is invisible but sensible, and by a hidden power makes the visible body sentient and alive.

It is also passible. Whatever is affected by sorrow is passible; but when the soul does not become master of its own will, it is affected by painful grief. Therefore it is proved to be passible.

Quantity is excluded from it, since it is measured neither by height, breadth, nor length, nor does it allow the six spatial directions—front and back, right and left, above and below—to enclose it. The quality of shape and color is also separated from it, since no form either of the human body or of any colored thing is attributed to it.

It possesses memory because it recalls the past [Note: [Col. 1010] Two manuscripts read “gathers together again.”]. It possesses reason because it discerns the present. It possesses understanding because it understands the future. It is clearly immortal from the fact that it strives to make its memory endure perpetually among later generations.

## CHAPTER VI. What angels are. That they exist. What they do. The difference between their knowledge and ours.

An angel is a spirit, an incorporeal substance, invisible, sensible, rational, intellectual, and immortal; bright and impassible in the case of the good, dark and passible in the case of the evil.

But it must be considered whether any such substance is believed to exist among created things, since it is by no means seen by us. The very insensible things prove that angels exist, because they observe so fixed a law of their movement. For whatever moves either has movement from itself or from elsewhere; but whatever has movement from itself is sensible, like the soul, while whatever has it from elsewhere is insensible, like a body.

If the sun, moon, and stars move by themselves, they appear to possess sensation or reason, since they observe such fixed times and such fixed spaces of heaven, and in a certain way signal their own understanding to this world through light or signs. But whoever thinks that they are rational or at least sentient bodies, being himself devoid of sense, is rightly counted among irrational beings.

Since they are truly visible bodies, insensible and lacking motion of themselves, and yet they move, it is certainly established that they are moved from elsewhere. It remains, therefore, that they are moved through angelic ministries.

Likewise, whoever doubts that winds, rains, hailstorms, lightning, thunder, storms, and breezes are governed at God’s command through the angels thinks that these things are sentient; but reason proves such a person foolish together with the insensible things [Note: [Col. 1010] Two manuscripts read “refutes.”]. Those who do not believe that brute animals obey or resist human purposes through the angels, or who believe that they do these things through the understanding of reason, depart far from reason. And whoever doubts that all that occurs among insensible things or sentient creatures is administered through the angels is very far from the light of truth.

It is therefore established that angels truly exist and plainly know all things hidden from us. But the difference between their knowledge and ours is this: they foresee all the causes of things before they happen, whereas we investigate them only with difficulty and great labor, after things have been established in actuality.

## CHAPTER VII. What God is. That he exists. That he is truth, life, wisdom, justice, and eternity.

Furthermore, just as the supreme Spirit cannot properly be conceived by any understanding, so he cannot properly be determined by any definition. But because the intellectual mind longs to know him in whatever way it can, let this enigmatic definition suffice for the time being:

God is a Spirit, an invisible essence incomprehensible to every creature, possessing essentially and simultaneously all life, all wisdom, and all eternity; or, rather, existing as life itself, wisdom itself, truth itself, justice itself, and eternity itself, containing every creature within himself as though it were a point.

[Col. 1011] But if some fool is so foolish as to doubt that God exists, let him arrive at the conclusion by this reasoning that God alone truly exists and that all other things have their existence from him. Every substance either subsists through itself or through another; but whoever contends that this world does not subsist is a fool rushing toward nothingness. That the world does not subsist through itself is clear from the fact that reason teaches that it began; for it consists of parts. Now whatever is joined together from parts or resolved into parts necessarily undergoes joining or dissolution from some cause. Therefore the world does not subsist through itself; and consequently it follows that it is a creature. A creature, however, is related to something—namely, to the Creator. The Creator alone, therefore, exists through himself and in himself; every creature subsists through him. For if he received being from another, then that from which he received it would be greater than God, which is incompatible with God. And since nothing exists apart from the Creator and the creature, if God does not have being through himself, it necessarily follows that he exists through the creature—which is utterly absurd.

Furthermore, the substance of the world is divided into diverse genera and different species, and goodness is found in each of these. For everything useful is good; indeed, all things are considered useful, and therefore each is proved to be good. Now every good is either good through itself or through another. But diverse goods must be good by participation in one good, since diversity admits of more and less. Thus, with respect to genus, a stone is a lesser good, since it merely exists and does not live [Note: [Col. 1011] See Anselm, *Monologion*, chapter 4]; wood is a greater good, since it lives by growing; a horse is better than wood, since it lives and senses; and a human being is more excellent than a horse, since he lives, senses, and distinguishes by reason. There therefore remains that which is supremely and incomparably good, from which goodness flows to all inferior things. This good is God, from whom, as from a fountain, all good things flow and into whom they all flow back.

He alone truly exists; and therefore he is truth. For everything that exists is true, whereas what does not exist is false. But God truly exists; therefore he is truth [Note: [Col. 1011] See the same work, chapter 28]. A creature, when compared with him, is as though it did not exist; and for this reason it is as though falsehood in relation to truth. For everything that began to exist from nothing can be reduced to nothing; but every creature, produced by God from nothing, has been brought into being. Therefore, when compared with him, it is proved to be nothing.

No mind, then, doubts that God exists, since it considers that all other things exist through him. His essence is life. For everything that exists either lives or lacks life; and everything that lives either lives through itself or through another. But God lives through himself and in himself, and grants life to all other things. Therefore he is true life and living truth. He also knows and understands himself and his entire creation; for knowing is nothing other than living and existing. Therefore he is wisdom. He also loves himself and every creature, because he is justice; and he does not receive this justice from elsewhere [Note: [Col. 1011] The printed editions add, “uncreated”]. Therefore he exists as justice and love. He has neither beginning nor end and possesses neither past nor future; therefore he is eternity.

## CHAPTER VIII. The brightness that must be known. Every soul is greater than the whole world. Intellectual magnitude. The brightness of God that must be contemplated.

Since reason has thus proved that God truly exists and has taught by true assertions that he is essentially life, wisdom, truth, justice, and eternity, it remains now to open some window toward seeing him, through which the mind, ascending by certain steps, may look out far enough to behold the King of glory in his beauty. Let reason proceed gradually through bodily things, lest the feeble intellect, striving through difficult heights, be broken by the effort and fall back.

First, therefore, let us consider in the mind this bodily sun, by whose magnitude we see the whole world warmed and by whose brightness the entire globe illuminated. After this, let us attend to the thousands upon thousands of angels who minister to God. Guided by reason, let us know that each of them is seven times—or rather a hundred times—brighter than the sun; for the sun is the servant of the world, whereas the angels are [Col. 1012] the temples of God. As far, then, as the temple of God surpasses the servant of the world, so far does the brightness of the angels surpass the brightness of the sun.

Next, let us ponder the ten thousand times a hundred exalted angels who stand before God, and let us know with certainty that each of them is a hundred times—or rather a thousand times—brighter than the sun. For just as the moon is seen to surpass the stars in brightness, and the sun the moon, so each higher order of angels is believed to surpass the lower in glory, dignity, and brightness, from the angels up to the seraphim.

Afterward, let us contemplate the innumerable thousands of holy souls, each of which, we do not doubt, is far more luminous than the sun and equal to the angels in blessedness and brightness. Having considered individually so many and such great lights, let us also contemplate the magnitude of each, so that we may be more easily raised toward that which we long to behold.

Let us therefore imagine the soul as a splendid fire, whose smallest spark, instructed by reason, surpasses this sun. For whatever is enclosed by something else is necessarily proved to be smaller than that which encloses it. But the soul’s thought—which is its spark—not only encloses this sun within a brief span, but also the entire circuit of the world; and the whole globe does not at all circumscribe it. Therefore it is clear that every soul is far greater than the whole world.

The angels, moreover, differ from souls not only in blessedness but also in magnitude. Here let no one understand magnitude of bodily quantity; rather, let him understand that intellectual magnitude which reduces this bodily world, and all the bodies within it, to smallness.

At this point let the mind raise itself on high. Let it expand its heart as far as it can, and look beneath itself upon all these lights, shining with immeasurable brightness and incomparable magnitude. Above itself, let it direct its attention toward a certain wondrous light that is the light of all those lights, shining so far above and beyond so many great lights as the sun shines above all the stars. Let those many great lights continually marvel at the ineffable magnitude and wondrous beauty of this light, and let them delight in gazing without weariness upon its overflowing sweetness.

This, assuredly, is the inaccessible light in which the essence of God dwells (1 Tim. 6:16), visible only to the pure in heart. Let no one here imagine God as a man surrounded by light as by a tabernacle, as though God, who inhabits the light, were one thing and the light he inhabits another. Rather, let him understand that the light itself is the essence of God, in which all good things are understood to be located together.

This is the light that satisfies angels and souls in heaven through its vision. This is the light that illuminates the pure in heart through contemplation. This is the light that has supplied those dwelling in the world with the sun’s lamp, just as the light of a candle is supplied to those confined in prison, so that through it they may return from darkness to light, from death to life, and from exile to their homeland.

Therefore, in prayer let your mind meditate upon God in this manner; let your attention contemplate his image in this manner—namely, as such a light that it shines above the sun as the sun shines above a candle; an immortal light that shines above the countless thousands of angels and souls, each a hundred times brighter than the sun, as the sun shines above the stars.

Hence he is called the Father of lights in the Canonical Letter of James: “Every good gift and every perfect gift is descending from above, from the Father of lights” [Note: [Col. 1012] The manuscripts do not contain these words, “Hence he is called … from the Father of lights”] (James 1:17). For one who holds such an image of God before the eyes of his heart in prayer does not depart far from the truth.

## CHAPTER IX. The reason for the various names of the blessed vision of God. How the saints should be contemplated in prayer.

This present vision of God face to face is called the kingdom of heaven, because outside this bodily heaven—or rather, outside every place—the angels and the righteous, who are called “heavens,” enjoy this vision. For this reason, although God is believed to dwell essentially in all creatures, he is properly proclaimed to dwell in heaven, that is, [Note: [Col. 1012] The manuscripts omit “in heaven, that is”] in the righteous, because they experience his indwelling by enjoying it and rejoice to behold that he is present in all things. Those who love earthly things know him to be absent from themselves.

For just as a sighted person and a blind person may both stand in the sun, the sighted person enjoying the sun’s brightness by seeing, while the blind person is deprived of its light—and although the sun’s presence is equally present to both, neither experiences that presence equally—so God is said to dwell only in those who enjoy his presence by seeing him face to face, like the angels, or by contemplating and beholding him, like the righteous in this life. He is said not to be in those who are deprived of his vision.

Hence the kingdom of heaven is also proclaimed to be within us (Luke 17:21), because the vision of almighty God—which is called the kingdom of heaven, that is, of the righteous—is contemplated in angels and the righteous.

This is also called eternal life, because the blessed are completely suffused with the presence of unfailing life and are never permitted to be subject either to death or to any of the pains that serve death. For they were created to live eternally and to behold eternal life eternally.

This is likewise called the heavenly city, because the harmony of those citizens is gathered together to behold the King of glory in his beauty. It is also called Jerusalem, because they are satisfied by the vision of ever-abiding peace. It is called paradise, because they rejoice in the abundance of every kind of delight. It is also called the heavenly homeland, because all the righteous, as sons of God, are believed without doubt to inherit this vision.

When, therefore, you invoke the saints in prayer, you ought to think of them as established in the glory of eternal brightness: as exceedingly splendid lights shining far more brightly than the sun’s radiance, possessing all good things fully in the vision of God, and powerfully assisting all who invoke them.

**DISCIPLE.** May the eternal Sun, whose vision your sweet prayer has led us to behold, and whose serene light has shone into our hearts through your words, establish you, freed from darkness, in the region of light; and among the lights that you proclaim, may he grant you to enjoy forever, shining with the light of his vision.

**MASTER.** If anything credible is brought forth through me, I do not want thanks for it to be given to me, but to God, whose gift it is. He often summons his sons to the inheritance of his vision through despised servants, and through enemies he marks out for his friends the saving path from exile to their homeland. And you know well that at times a misshapen person has held up a mirror for the handsome—or rather, a blind person has held up a light for those who see—and a lame person has shown the way to those in sound health.

## CHAPTER X. That the Trinity of persons and the unity of essence are necessary in God.

**DISCIPLE.** Because of what we have heard, we too give perpetual thanks to the eternal God, whose vision has become known to us through you and who has brought forth for us through you such a treasure hidden from the carnal. But [Note: [Col. 1013] The Greek version begins here] because the weight of the flesh burdens the soul, behold, carnal thought once again assails the mind contemplating divine things. Since reason above has demonstrated most truly that there is one God and has proved that he alone made all things from nothing, how are we taught to worship, as it were, three gods, when we are instructed to confess the Father as perfect God, the Son as perfect God, and the Holy Spirit as perfect God? For when three distinct persons are distinguished in this way, what else do we understand than three gods?

**MASTER.** With truth itself demonstrating and reason proving it, you will soon see the necessary Trinity of persons in one essence, and likewise the necessary unity in every respect of the undivided substance in three persons. When I was speaking above about God in an enigmatic way, since I could not speak properly, what did I say the essence of God is?

**DISCIPLE.** Light.

**MASTER.** What is generated from light?

**DISCIPLE.** Splendor.

**MASTER.** What is considered together in light and splendor?

**DISCIPLE.** Heat.

[Col. 1014] **MASTER.** [Note: [Col. 1014] See *Elucidarium*, book 1, chapter 1] Is there diversity in the substance of light, splendor, and heat?

**DISCIPLE.** No, but identity.

**MASTER.** Is identity proclaimed in their names or functions?

**DISCIPLE.** Not at all, but diversity. For the name “light” seems to express the substance itself; the name “splendor,” the grace of light; and the name “heat,” the efficacy of light.

**MASTER.** It is therefore clear that three different names constitute one undivided essence.

**DISCIPLE.** It is entirely clear.

**MASTER.** You have it from the Apostle that the supreme Spirit is called the Father “light”: “God is light, and in him there is no darkness at all” (1 John 1:5). You also have it from the Apostle, in another passage, that the supreme Spirit is called the Son “splendor”: “Who is the splendor of his substance” (Heb. 1:3). No less, you have it from Moses that the supreme Holy Spirit is called “heat”: “Our God is a consuming fire” (Deut. 4:24).

Since, then, light, splendor, and heat are one nature and one undivided substance, though different in name, it is entirely clear that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one nature and one undivided essence. For in what signifies what something is, the Spirit is named substantially; and likewise there is a necessary diversity among the persons, since the Father is proclaimed as begetting, the Son as being born, and the Holy Spirit as proceeding from both.

**DISCIPLE.** Clearly we see the Trinity in the persons, and we firmly grasp the necessary unity in the substance.

## CHAPTER XI. Why the names “substance” and “person” are applied to God. Why the Father is called thus and not “mother.” Why he is called begetting.

**MASTER.** These two names—namely, substance and person—are most carefully fitted to the divine essence for this reason: substance is always predicated of individuals existing in plurality, whereas person is predicated of an individual rational nature. We customarily use “persons” to designate plurality, but “substance” to designate unity of essence.

**DISCIPLE.** In what likeness is the eternal light called Father?

**MASTER.** Because from himself he begot offspring [Note: [Col. 1014] The Greeks read “splendor”] equal to himself.

**DISCIPLE.** Would not the name “mother” seem more appropriate to him?

**MASTER.** [Note: [Col. 1014] From Anselm, *Monologion*, chapter 42] In a father there is always the principal cause of offspring, and therefore by right this name ought to be applied according to the principal sex.

**DISCIPLE.** In what likeness is he called “begetting”?

**MASTER.** It is certain that the mind begets thought. When the mind thinks about itself, it generates, as it were, another thing like itself. Thus, when the supreme God thought about himself as he is, he undoubtedly generated an image entirely like himself. And just as the one who begets is rightly called Father, so the one begotten is most rightly called Son.

## CHAPTER XII. That he never existed without the Son.

**DISCIPLE.** If God begot the Son, it seems that at some time he existed without having the Son and acquired this name accidentally. But if that is so, the preceding statement is undermined, according to which nothing accidental, but everything essential, was predicated of God.

**MASTER.** Reason has already taught that God’s essence is eternal life, knowing neither beginning nor end. If this singular true life always existed without beginning, it is clear that it also always understood itself to live without beginning. If it did not understand itself to live, it was not wise—which it is impious to say of God. If at some point it received wisdom from elsewhere, because it previously lacked it, then that from which it received so great a good existed as something better than God—which is utterly absurd.

But if eternal life always understood itself to live, this wisdom of understanding did not accrue to it from elsewhere; it was always coessential with it, although it ineffably begot it from itself as its offspring. Therefore the Father never existed without the Son.

## CHAPTER XIII. Why this is Son, not daughter.

**DISCIPLE.** In what likeness is the splendor of eternal light called Son and not daughter?

**MASTER.** Because the Father’s likeness is expressed in him in every respect; hence he is also called his likeness [Note: [Col. 1015] Anselm, *Monologion*, chapter 39]. For nothing among created things preserves in full the likeness of that from which it is born. Hair born from the head is unlike the head; apples born from trees are unlike the trees; wool is unlike the sheep; the offspring of animals, and even human children, are not entirely like their begetters in quality. But he is in every respect most like the one who begets him; therefore he is most truly not daughter but Son.

## CHAPTER XIV. Why he is called Word. The etymology of “word.”

**DISCIPLE.** By what relationship, then, is the Son called Word?

**MASTER.** [Note: [Col. 1015] Same work, chapter 10] “Word” is understood in three ways. For example, when the word “man” is uttered by the mouth; or when the same word, “man,” is formed in the heart without movement of the tongue; or when the thing itself signified by the word “man” is considered in the intellect as it is.

It was in this third way that God begot his Word, when he spoke himself by thinking. And because he spoke the entire form of the world by this same thought [Note: [Col. 1015] Thus the manuscripts; the printed editions read “created”], he is said to have made all things in his Word. Hence it is read concerning the creation of the world: “He spoke, and they were made” (Ps. 32:9).
