For the Son, or Word, of God is nothing other than his thought, art, or wisdom. Indeed, when we think of some thing, we form an image of that thing in our thought. Thus, when God thought of himself, he formed an image entirely like himself. Therefore this Word is called the image or likeness of God, although nothing other than the same essence is expressed. Hence it is called “word” as though it were “truly good.”

## CHAPTER XV. How every created thing is life in the Word.

**DISCIPLE.** How is it said that everything that has been made was life in him [Note: [Col. 1015] Erasmus, Lyons, Venice, and Louvain: “Why is it said, ‘Everything that was made was life in him?’”]? Do stones, which are senseless, live in the Word of God?

**MASTER.** Every creature is said to subsist in three ways [Note: [Col. 1015] Same work, chapters 34–36]: in God, in itself, and in us. In God it is immutable life; in itself, mutable substance; in us, an imaginably represented likeness of things.

For example, a stone in itself is mutable substance, since it can be converted into lime; in our thought it is the likeness of a stone; in God’s art it is the essence of an unending and enduring life. When an artisan thinks of making a house, the house already lives in the art itself, which the hand afterward builds. But the house that the hand raises will collapse; the one that lives in the art endures.

For art is nothing other than soul, and soul is nothing other than life [Note: [Col. 1015] Thus the manuscripts; the printed editions read, “than his art, and his art is nothing other than life itself”]. Thus the Word of God is nothing other than his art, and art is nothing other than life itself. In this Word all things will remain immutable, although in the substance of themselves they are mutable and perish.

## CHAPTER XVI. How only the Word could become incarnate.

**DISCIPLE.** Since evident reason has proved beyond refutation that the same Word shares one undivided substance with the Father and the Holy Spirit, how could he alone become incarnate? For if he was separated from the essence of the Father and the Holy Spirit and was thus alone made human, it is plainly established that the substance of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is not undivided, since it could undergo the division of separation.

**MASTER.** Just as the everlasting power of divinity can be understood through the things that are seen to have been made (Rom. 1:20), so this exceedingly hidden depth may be examined by reason through what takes place in us.

[Col. 1016] It is known that the human mind, by thinking, begets from itself the word of ordinary speech, and that this same word exists simultaneously in the mind and memory as one essence. When the mind wishes to make its word known to others, it arranges, with the same thought—which is nothing other than its word—and with memory, that this word assume the body of a voice and proceed audible to the ears and perceptible to the hearts of those who hear. It also permits its body to be bound in letters and made visible. Yet, while remaining invisible, it does not depart from the essence of the mind and memory.

Therefore it is not the mind or the memory, but only the word, that sounded forth individually through the perceptible body of the voice; nevertheless, it remained inseparably and invisibly in the essence of the mind and memory.

So the supreme Father begot his Word by thinking of himself. The Word subsists coessentially and simultaneously in the essence of the Father and the Holy Spirit; nevertheless, neither the Father nor the Holy Spirit, but only the Word who is the Son of the Father, individually assumed a human body, presented himself sensibly to human beings, and permitted the body he had assumed to suffer unworthy things. He himself remained inseparably invisible and incapable of suffering in the essence of the Father and the Holy Spirit.

## CHAPTER XVII. Why the love of God is called Spirit, and why it is called Holy.

**DISCIPLE.** In what likeness is the love of God called Spirit?

**MASTER.** I said that God’s essence is life. True life understands itself to live; and if it understands itself as life, it certainly loves itself. But God’s living, understanding, and loving are nothing other than existing. Therefore the love of God is life, and life is spirit. And because God grants being or life to all things through love, he is therefore called Spirit.

The word “holy” is added because all things are sanctified through him.

## CHAPTER XVIII. How the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son. How he appeared in the form of a dove or fire.

**DISCIPLE.** How is it proved that this Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son?

**MASTER.** The Holy Spirit is understood to be nothing other than the love of God; hence God is called love (1 John 4:16). It is clear that the Father loves the Son as himself, and likewise the Son loves the Father as himself. For life loves itself as knowing, and wisdom loves itself as living; and life and wisdom have been proved to be one essence.

Therefore love or affection or charity—which is the Holy Spirit—exists coessentially in the substance of the Father and the Son, and therefore proceeds equally from both.

**DISCIPLE.** If the Holy Spirit exists coessentially with the Father and the Son, how could he be separated from the undivided substance when he appeared in the form of a dove over the Lord (Matt. 3:16) or in the form of fire over the Apostles (Acts 2:3)?

**MASTER.** The substance of the Holy Spirit was not transformed into a dove or fire, just as the substance of the Word was not transformed into flesh. Rather, the Holy Spirit formed the body of a dove [Note: [Col. 1016] Here the Greek version ends], in which he made himself visible for a time to human beings as a testimony above the body of the Word, while he himself remained invisibly and inseparably in the essence of the Father and the Word.

By possessing the souls of the disciples inwardly, he also displayed outwardly to human eyes the appearance of fire or light as a sign. Yet he did not depart from the substance of the Father and the Son. He plainly signified that the Father and the Son consume sins through him and kindle human hearts through him to their love, and that through him they will judge the ungodly by fire, while they will glorify the righteous in him by the light of life.

## CHAPTER XIX. On the equality of the persons. Why the deity is not worshiped under the names of the virtues.

**DISCIPLE.** How is it established that these persons are equal?

**MASTER.** God is supreme life, supreme wisdom, and supreme love. As much, therefore, as life lives, so much does it understand itself [Col. 1017] and so much does it love itself. For if it did not understand itself as much as it lives, it would in no way be supreme wisdom; and if it did not love itself as much as it understands itself, it would not at all be supreme love.

But since his substance is most truly the supreme good, and since supreme life, supreme wisdom, and supreme love can be found only in the supreme good, it necessarily follows that the three persons—the Father who begets, the Son who is begotten, and the Holy Spirit who proceeds—are equal in every respect and exist as the supreme good in one and the same undivided substance.

**DISCIPLE.** Why is the deity more especially venerated under these names [Note: [Col. 1017] The printed editions add here, “than under the names of the other virtues”], when mercy, justice, and the other virtues are also assigned to his essence?

**MASTER.** Because those qualities are substantial to him properly and according to himself, whereas the others are accidental to him according to us. He is called merciful not because he has a miserable heart; rather, reason proves that all misery is far from God. Human speech calls “just” the one who repays good people with good things and evil people with evil things.

Since God, however, assists the miserable in their miseries, he has received the name “merciful” or “mercy.” Yet even if no one had ever been miserable to whom he might show mercy, mercy itself would nevertheless exist no less in his substance.

Because he grants rewards to the just and inflicts just punishments on the unjust, he is rightly called just or justice. Yet if there were no one to whom he might grant glory or inflict punishment, he himself would nevertheless subsist no less as justice. The same must be understood concerning the other virtues.

## CHAPTER XX. Whether some are necessarily miserable; whether God is the author of evil. That the justice and mercy of God can be manifested without the miserable.

**DISCIPLE.** From this a very serious question seems to arise. If God’s mercy could not be recognized except through the miserable, nor his justice known except through those destined for damnation, it seems inevitably to follow that some had necessarily to be made miserable, through whom God’s mercy might be revealed, and some necessarily condemnable, through whom his justice might be manifested.

But if this is so, it will now be preached in vain that evil is nothing, since nothing worse than misery and damnation can be imagined. And if this is not weakened by the strongest arguments of reason, God will no longer be understood as the supreme good; indeed, he will be proved the author of so great an evil.

Moreover, if he neither wished nor was able to display his mercy except in the miserable, and his justice except in those destined for damnation, who would not see that he must be either malevolent or powerless—malevolent in having refused to display the good except through evil, and powerless in having been unable to act otherwise?

**MASTER.** Who, even if insane, would dare say that God’s mercy and justice could not be manifested except through the miserable and the condemned, when it is plainly evident that we can demonstrate hidden riches not only through the needy but also through the wealthy?

If I possess money secretly, it will not therefore be necessary for someone to be poor so that I may make it known by giving to him, since I can do the same by giving it to a rich person. But if some poor person comes to me, I ought to show him mercy from my hidden money. His experience thus proves me generous and wealthy. The same thing can plainly be done with a rich person, although the knowledge or experience of a poor or rich person contributes nothing useful to me, since I possess every good; for them, however, it is greatly useful, indeed necessary, to know and experience that I possess these things.

In this way, if no one had ever been miserable or condemnable, almighty God could nonetheless have manifested his mercy and justice in angels and human beings, mercifully bestowing upon them from his abundance what they did not possess—especially since every creature has absolutely nothing from itself, but receives everything from him, the fountain of all good, and since he would justly preserve in his creatures the gifts they had received from him.

Therefore it was not necessary for either an angel to fall into damnation so that God’s justice might be manifested, or a human being into misery so that God’s mercy might be declared. He manifested both in the angels who stood: mercy, by preserving them from falling; justice, by granting them rewards.

But because an angel or a human being apostatized from God by free will, they clearly experienced mercy and justice, previously hidden, when justice justly condemned the one and mercy mercifully freed the other from misery.

And since God gained no advantage from this experience—for the fullness of all good existed in him before every created creature—it follows that no necessity, but only will, compelled them to misery.

## CHAPTER XXI. That God is not the author of evil but its ordainer. The goodness of God. Omnipotence.

That God is not the author of evil is plainly evident from the fact that he condemns every evil. Moreover, evident reason proves that evil does not subsist. Every substance is good, but evil is not good; therefore evil is not a substance, but a deprivation of good.

Evil appears to be a separable accident of acting or suffering: in action, when one acts disorderly; in passion, when a disordered action is brought into proper order [Note: [Col. 1018] Thus the *Elucidarium*, book 1, chapter 16]. For in the kingdom of the one who orders all things, nothing disordered is left.

The proper order of a rational creature is to reject things that perish and desire things that endure; to love human beings, who are immortal in soul; and, loving God, the supreme good, above all things, to obey his will. But those who despise the supreme good, love the perishable good of the world, scorn their fellow souls, and obey the desires of the flesh live disorderly lives and thus do evil.

This evil, however, will be ordered when the action is changed into suffering. For when such people are deprived both of the supreme good and of the perishable good of the world, they must be afflicted with harsh things, which are contrary to pleasant ones. These things, however, are not evil in themselves, but seem bitter to those who suffer them. Therefore by nature nothing is evil.

That God is the supreme good is clear from the fact that he gives his mercy to the wicked and guilty, as though contrary to justice. From the fountain of the supreme good such justice flows that God ought rightly to show mercy to those undeserving of it. He is also proved benevolent in this respect: he did not wish to enjoy so many goods alone, but brought forth from nothing so many substances to which he distributed the goods of glory.

That he is omnipotent—or rather, that he is omnipotence itself—is declared by the fact that he was able to form from nothing so great a structure of things, together with all that exists, and that no creature bends him toward what is unfitting; rather, whatever exists obeys his command.

Behold, the entire fortification of your proposition lies overthrown by the battering ram of manifest reason [Note: [Col. 1018] The printed editions read, “by the fortress of manifest error”].

## CHAPTER XXII. From where created things come. Not from God’s substance. Not from matter but from nothing. How, nevertheless, they are not from nothing.

**DISCIPLE.** It is useful to overthrow the rampart of error and build the citadel of truth. Since you have firmly placed its foundation upon the one who creates above all things, it remains for you to consolidate the structure upon the origin of creation, to build by joining the end of the world to its beginning, and to complete its summit on high in the kingdom of heaven.

Therefore, with reason proving it, explain to us whether the universe of creation was made from the Creator’s substance, from some preexisting [Note: [Col. 1018] The manuscripts read “existing”] matter, or from nothing.

**MASTER.** The architect has strengthened the framework of this structure, and no effort to enlarge the work will shake it. Creation itself denies that it is from the substance of the Creator, and evident reason resists this with all its weapons.

God is immutable, whereas every creature is mutable. If creation had proceeded from an immutable nature, it too would consequently remain immutable. Moreover, if corruptible nature proceeded from God’s substance, it would follow that God’s essence could be corrupted. The darts of reason pierce this madness of a blind mind and cast it far from the presence of truth.

That creation was made from no substantial matter is clear from the fact that nothing besides God existed. It therefore remains that [Col. 1019] the universe was created from nothing—not in the sense that nothing was or is something, but in the sense that what was not something the Creator made into something [Note: [Col. 1019] See Anselm, *Monologion*, chapters 9 and 11].

Nevertheless, before the creation of the whole of creation, its image existed in the Word—that is, in God’s art—and according to its model the universe burst forth in creation. Just as a painter first forms the variety of a painting in his mind, and afterward paints a visible picture according to its likeness, so God had first formed the universe of creation in his wisdom, according to which form he created all things in their manifold species.

But a painter brings the picture conceived in his mind, which does not yet exist in reality, into existence through colors and external instruments. God, however, produced the universe in his wisdom—without any existing substance and through no instruments—into so many substances. Therefore he made all things from nothing; and yet, as though the visible world had proceeded not from nothing but from something, it emerged by taking on the forms of the archetypal world.

## CHAPTER XXIII. Questions concerning the presence of God.

**DISCIPLE.** Now, as the excellent tower rises high, let discriminating reason drive away the darkness of error on every side, illuminate the splendid structure with the clear light of truth, and open to us, as we marvel at the work of this renowned edifice, whether the Creator exists in the creature, or the creature in the Creator, or each in the other; or whether rather the Creator dwells substantially somewhere outside creation, in some glory, while he fills the self-existing creature potentially; whether he is half in heaven and half in the world; whether at one time he subsists wholly in heaven and at another wholly in the world; whether he is divided among individual places or exists wholly in every place; whether he is sometimes in one place and sometimes in another—for example, whether he should be thought to remain yesterday in Jerusalem, today in Carthage, and tomorrow in Rome; or whether he is always and everywhere outside every place and outside all time.

**MASTER.** Just as the rising sun illuminates by its presence innumerable forms of things buried in darkness, so powerful reason, although your propositions are many and exceedingly complicated, distinguishes each of them with perceptive insight and clearly elucidates the deepest matters drawn forth from the darkest hiding places.

## CHAPTER XXIV. That God is in every creature. That each creature senses him to be in itself.

That the Creator exists in the whole of creation is proved by every creature, which proclaims that it is nothing from itself, but is from God and possesses goodness. For God is supreme being and supreme good; every creature subsists through him, and every substance is good because it is from the supreme good. Wherever God is not, there is nothing; wherever anything substantial exists, there God is. Therefore God exists in every creature, since every creature subsists.

At this point perhaps a weak-minded person says to himself: “If God is in every creature, then he is also in mud, in hell, and in brute animals; indeed, he is even in demons, which are certainly creatures.” Clear reason finds no inconsistency here, since it considers the good in all these things. Mud, indeed, is a thing mixed with another, as earth with water or something else of that kind. Earth is good because it is a substance, and water is good because it is a substance. Hell too is said to be fiery; and fire is good because it is a substance. Brute animals individually are useful for something within their own kind, and for that reason they are good. Demons, too, insofar as they are of an angelic nature, are good. Since it is therefore established that each of these subsists in goodness, it necessarily follows that God, who alone is goodness, is in all things.

[Note: [Col. 1019] See *Elucidarium*, book 1, chapter 5.]

Moreover, every creature in some way senses that God is within it. Angels, indeed, and all living things sense that God is within them. For God is life, and everything that lives lives by life. An angel does not live more than a worm, although the one is immortal and the other mortal. Nor does an angel subsist more than a worm, although the substance of the former is eternal and that of the latter perishable.

The heavenly bodies also—that is, the sun, moon, and stars—sense God within themselves, since through him they shine and subsist. [Col. 1020] Trees and grasses sense God within themselves, since through him they grow and subsist. Stones, too, sense that God is within them, since through him they subsist. Demons sense that God is present to them, since through him they live and perceive; but they also sense that God is present in this respect: by God’s just judgment they suffer punishment for their evils. For God is justice, and wherever justice is exercised, God is believed to be present. Thus the emperor is present to a robber when he condemns him, just as he is present to a soldier when he rewards him.

And no one should suppose that God abhors the filth of the world; let him know that God execrates only the filth of sinners, and that nothing can in any way defile him, just as no impurity can soil a ray of the sun.

## CHAPTER XXV. Creatures also exist in God. An objection resolved. A carnal conception of God and the world. A purer understanding.

That every creature exists in the Creator is recognized from the fact that nothing is believed to exist outside God. Yet a creature is not in him in such a way that it is his substance or part of his essence, as the heart is in an animal or is part of the animal; rather, it is as the light of a lamp is in the sun: the light is not the sun’s substance, nor part of its essence.

[Note: [Col. 1020] These words are absent from the manuscripts: “as the heart … part of its essence.”]

But here some fool bursts forth and says: “If a stone is in God, and God is in the stone, then the stone is God.” This does not follow. Everything that is in another is not necessarily that in which it is. Wine is in a jar, yet it is not the jar; the sun is in a mirror, and the mirror is in the sun, yet neither is the other.

Suppose someone standing in Rome were to survey the whole city in thought: by imagining the entire city together with its people, he would enclose the whole city within his mind. It would rightly be said that Rome is in his soul and his soul in Rome, yet Rome would not thereby be his substance. So, likewise, it is entirely correct to affirm that God is in every creature and every creature in him, yet neither is the other. Rather, God the Creator is immutable, while this creature is most truly mutable.

But because we were born in darkness, we cannot see the light of truth. We imagine this world founded upon the abyss, while God, together with the angels, is situated in heaven, and we suppose that outside this world there is nothing but darkness. Rather, the sight of our mind is dazzled by the greatness of the true light, just as the bodily eye is struck back by the brightness of the sun. Our darkness cannot comprehend such clarity, and the clouded vision of the heart prevents us from contemplating it.

Indeed, this entire world is gathered within God like a very small point, while the most serene light of his majesty is diffused without limit in every direction. God fills all things essentially—above and below, within and without, and all around—and no creature’s understanding surpasses his boundless substance by any thought. Again, this scandalizes the weak intellect, which silently turns the matter over within itself: “If everything is in God, then wolves and serpents, indeed demons, are also in him.” Here, as above, no inconsistency is established, provided that good is found in all these things. Every good is in God, outside whom nothing exists.

## CHAPTER XXVI. Why every creature does not enjoy the good equally, although everything is in God. What it means to suffer evil.

But it is asked why any creature suffers anything evil, rather than the whole of creation enjoying the good equally, if God, who is the supreme good, is declared to be in every creature.

It must be understood that, just as the soul, diffused throughout the whole body, is wholly present in each individual member, yet does not assign all the functions of its administration to each member—for it grants sight to the eye but not hearing, hearing to the ear but not sight, and so on with the others—but a member from which it withdraws the gift of vegetative life will remain dull and useless in the body, and is said to suffer evil—or to suffer nothing—because it is deprived of good.

In the same way, God, diffused through all things, is wholly present in each, yet does not grant all the gifts of his grace to each one. Rather, he grants to each as he pleases: to a stone merely to exist and not to live; to a tree to live by growing but not to perceive; to beasts to perceive but not to discern; [Col. 1021] to angels and souls to discern and to exist immortally. Whatever of these gifts he withdraws from something, it immediately becomes useless within the body of the universe.

And when the good that is congenial to its nature is withdrawn from it, it is immediately and necessarily afflicted by the bitterness opposed to it—as human beings are in the world and demons in hell. Thus it is said to suffer evil when it is deprived of good, just as a blind man placed in the sun is said to suffer darkness because he does not enjoy its light.

But why God presents one creature with the sweetness of his presence to enjoy and withdraws it from another—reason cannot penetrate this with any acumen; it stands in awe of God, terrible in his judgments.

## CHAPTER XXVII. Why things change although they are in the immutable.

It is also asked: if God is in every creature and every creature is in him, how can anything perish, rather than everything remaining in one and the same state, especially since the immutable God contains all things?

It must be understood that by this the Creator is distinguished from the creature: he is immutable, whereas the creature is seen to be exceedingly unstable. Yet all things imitate eternity, continually revolving as if in circles of existence, failing and then growing again. Because they took their origin from nothing, they desire to return to nothing and, as it were, to go out from God. But because they find no exit, they are rolled around as if in circles and return again to being.

The heavens and the stars, for example, are always revolved in their circles. The waters, continually flowing, return to their springs as if after completing a circle. Trees, grasses, and animals, growing, aging, decaying, and growing again, are in a certain manner turned around in a circle. In this way, all things of themselves tend toward nothing, but through the one who continually contains them they strive to return to the nature given them. [Note: [Col. 1021] One manuscript: “bright.”]

It is also asked whether, if humanity had remained in paradise, all these things would have been mutable as they now are. Without doubt, all things would preserve their changes, as now, with unstable time—growing, declining, being born, and dying—while humanity itself would remain stable in one condition and continue as lord of all things. But because humanity became unstable through sin, it began to fall along with time and perishable things.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. Whether things would have been mutable if humanity had not sinned. That God is everywhere, and how.

Now that the darkness has been driven from the structure of the sacred building, let us gird ourselves to dismantle the engines erected against it.

To say that God is substantially somewhere but potentially everywhere is contrary to the solidity of the entire argument already developed, and it is overthrown by the force of the clearest reasoning. If he is substantially somewhere and not everywhere, then he is bounded and local; and if he is local, then he is a body; and if he is a body, it follows that he is not God.

Furthermore, if God is contained by a place, then the place that contains him is greater and better than he: greater because it encloses God, and better because it contains so great a good. Moreover, if he is substantially in heaven but potentially in the world, then his essence is one thing and his power another; and it follows that this power has come to him accidentally, something reason earlier rejected from the presence of truth.

But if he is half in heaven and half in the world, then the creature contains the Creator and encloses within itself its maker. If he is sometimes in heaven and sometimes in the world, then he is proved mutable, because he moves from place to place.

Furthermore, if God is sometimes in heaven and not in the world, then something exists only where he is, while elsewhere there is nothing; for where God is not, there is nothing.

If he is divided among individual places, then he consists of parts; and it follows that he is subject to suffering, since what is divisible by places is also dissoluble.

[Note: [Col. 1021] See Anselm, *Monologion*, chapter 20.]

For everything that consists of parts can be dissolved.

[Note: [Col. 1021] See Anselm, *The Faith of the Trinity*, chapter 4, and *Monologion*, chapter 21.]

But if he is wholly present in each individual place, then there are as many wholes as there are places. For whatever is wholly enclosed in one place is shown to have no part of itself in another place. It follows that God is confined by a place, [Col. 1022] although he is said to enclose all things in his fist.

And if he changes with the successive periods of time, dwelling yesterday in one place, today in another, and tomorrow in a third, then he is temporal. He has already lost the past and does not yet possess the future, and all accidents converge in him.

## CHAPTER XXIX. Conclusion of the questions concerning God’s presence. A comparison.

The instruments of this sacred tower easily dismantle the devices of that utterly false opinion.

[Note: [Col. 1022] See Anselm, *Monologion*, chapter 20.]

God’s power is nothing other than his essence. Therefore God is not essentially in some determinate place, but everywhere. God is also immeasurable. A place, however—that is, the space occupied by any body—is measured by height, breadth, and length; and whatever is local is bounded by front and back, right and left, above and below.

Therefore God is neither partly in heaven nor partly in the world; neither sometimes wholly in heaven and sometimes wholly in the world; neither divided among individual places nor wholly present in each place separately. Rather, he exists outside every place, in and through himself, filling every place and containing it within himself, penetrating the whole of creation and joining all things together by his substance. He is everywhere—that is, wholly in all things and outside all things—and he is distant from no place.

As the light of a lamp shines wholly in the eyes of all who stand around it, while remaining wholly in itself, so that it does not depart from itself in order to reach those present, nor leave one person in order to shine for another, but shines wholly and simultaneously for each and for all, while remaining wholly in itself—so God is wholly everywhere and in all things, and remains wholly in himself. He does not depart from himself, but gathers all things into himself.

## CHAPTER XXX. How Christ is wholly in heaven and wholly in the Virgin’s womb.

Here the question arises: since God is not enclosed by a place, how can Christ be said to be wholly in the Virgin’s womb and wholly in heaven, when there is no doubt that the Virgin’s womb is a place?

In heaven he was wholly in the essence of the Father, as all wisdom is in the soul; in the Virgin’s womb he was wholly, as the whole word is in the voice.

For God has neither beginning nor end, and therefore remains eternal. He has no past and does not receive a future [Note: [Col. 1022] Erasmus, Lyons, Venice, and Louvain: “Therefore nothing has been past for him, nor does he receive a future.” M.], but is present outside all time and exists always everywhere. Hence he is also called “I Am” (Exod. 3:14), because, existing as eternity and ordering all times, he is changed by no time.

Behold, the engine of your manifold proposition has collapsed, because no accident converges in God.

**DISCIPLE.** We do not grieve at its ruin; rather, we applaud its supporters at the sound of its destruction, because through its fall we hope for entrance into the tower. But now that this engine has been dismantled, behold, another stands erected against the tower.

## CHAPTER XXXI. How God alone is immortal. How he alone is invisible.

It was said above that God alone is immortal and alone invisible. Are angels or souls mortal? Or is God invisible to the angels, of whom it is said that they always see the face of the Father (Matt. 18:10)?

**MASTER.** Mutability is a kind of mortality. For when something moves from the past into the future, it dies, as it were, to the past. God alone is immutable, because nothing past departs from him and nothing future arrives; rather, whatever is, was, or will be is always present to him in its entirety. And just as one cannot think that he ever had a beginning, so one cannot think that he could ever come to an end.

Angels, however, are mutable, because they move from the past into the present and from the present into the future. They lack the past and do not yet possess the future. It is clear that they do not have the angelic companions whom they once lost, and that they still lack the fellowship of the saints who are pilgrims on earth. They recall past things through memory and understand future things through foreknowledge. And just as it can be conceived that they once began, so it can also be conceived that they could come to an end.

Moreover, when they contemplate a creature mutable in itself, they [Col. 1023] in a certain way degenerate from the state of immutability. Such mutability is for them a kind of mortality.

Souls, however, just as they are mutable in all respects, are likewise almost entirely mortal. God is the life of the soul, just as the soul is the life of the body. But just as the body is dead when it has no soul, so the soul is dead when it lacks God; or, just as a blind eye is called dead when it is deprived of light, so the soul is dead when it does not enjoy the blessed life that is God.

Therefore God alone possesses immortality, because he receives no mutability. He alone is also invisible, because he is not fully intelligible to any creature. The angels and the souls of the blessed always see him in their own manner, not in ours. They do not see him through intervals of space, as we see bodily things; rather, they behold him within themselves and outside themselves, in every creature and outside every creature, and no gaze of their understanding surpasses the greatness of his brightness. Because he is not seen or understood by them as fully as he is by himself, he is therefore called alone invisible.

## CHAPTER XXXII. To what extent humanity was created in the image and likeness of God. Every thing possesses some likeness of God. That souls are eternal.

**DISCIPLE.** Now that the divine nature, together with the angelic nature, holds the scepter in this tower, behold, human nature brings forward a legion and raises an engine to attack it. For it is asked how humanity can be said to have been formed in the image and likeness of God, since no correspondence to God’s likeness is seen in a human being.

**MASTER.** Things that attack are conquered by things that oppose them, as what precedes is rendered impregnable by what follows.

Two human beings are described: the inner and the outer. The inner is the soul, the outer the body; the inner is invisible, the outer visible. The invisible, therefore, was created in the image and likeness of the invisible God, while the visible was formed according to the visible world.

God is invisible: in substance, unity; in persons, Trinity. The inner human being—that is, the soul—was therefore created in the image of unity, because it is not composed of parts like the body, but is a simple nature and immortal essence.

[Note: [Col. 1023] In B: “but is of a simple nature, and immortal essence.” We have followed Erasmus, Lyons, Venice, and Louvain, which were themselves followed by the Antwerp edition of the Benedictine Fathers.]

[Note: [Col. 1023] See Anselm, *Monologion*, chapters 59, 69, and 72; see *Elucidarium*, book 1, chapters 11 and 31.]

God is also memory, which remembers itself and all things that exist; this is called the Father. From it arises understanding, which understands itself and all things that exist; this is called the Son. From both proceeds love, which loves itself and all things that exist; this is called the Holy Spirit.

The soul is created in the image of this Trinity, since memory, understanding, and the reasoning faculty of love are implanted in it. It remembers past things, understands invisible things, rejects evil, and loves good.

God’s essence is also light, life, justice, goodness, and blessedness. The soul was made according to this likeness, so that it might be luminous, living, just, good, and blessed.

The outer human being—that is, the body—is formed in a certain way after the pattern of the world, since it is composed of the four elements. Hence it is also called *microcosmus*, that is, “the smaller world.” In this respect too the soul bears a likeness to God, since it governs the smaller world in the way God governs the greater.

Every creature also possesses God’s likeness in some respect, and the more excellent one creature is than another, the more like God it is. God exists, lives, perceives, and distinguishes through reason. Stones, therefore, approach him in likeness because they exist. Trees draw nearer to his likeness because they exist and live by growing. Animals express his likeness much more fully because they exist, live, and perceive. In human beings and angels, the likeness of God shines forth most greatly, because they exist, live, perceive, and distinguish through reason.

It is established that souls are eternal. For if they are said to have been made in order to see God, it necessarily follows that, just as God is believed to have no end, so souls that are to see him must undoubtedly live without end.

[Col. 1024] But it is asked whether those souls that are not to see God are immortal. It is established that all souls are of one nature; and if some souls are immortal, then all souls are immortal. Therefore all souls that are to see God will always be blessed, and those that are not to see him will always be miserable.

[Note: [Col. 1024] Erasmus, Lyons, Venice, and Louvain read this passage as follows: “It is established that all souls are of one nature, and if some souls are immortal, therefore all souls that are to see God will always be blessed, and those that are not to see him miserable.”]

## CHAPTER XXXIII. From where the soul sees so many things in dreams. Why it does not see itself.

**DISCIPLE.** From where does the soul see so many things in dreams?

**MASTER.** The soul is seized by an insatiable desire to know the truth, and therefore it is always wandering among thoughts. Accordingly, when the bodily senses are asleep, it foresees future things through certain enigmas, with God revealing them; at times it languishes anxiously concerning probable matters, with the devil deceiving it; sometimes it converses with angels or souls; sometimes it is mocked by demons. In the manner of an eye it sees everything else, but it cannot see itself.

**DISCIPLE.** Why does it not appear to us?

**MASTER.** Because its nature is said to be so subtle that it does not permit itself to be seen by bodily eyes. As water is subtler than earth, so air is subtler than water; and as ethereal fire surpasses air in subtlety, so the soul surpasses heavenly fire in subtlety. This is why no spirit is perceived by us: the subtlety of their nature is believed to exceed our sight.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. How the soul is wholly in each member.

**DISCIPLE.** How is the soul said to be diffused throughout the whole body and yet not to be more in the largest members or less in the smallest, but wholly in each? Are there as many wholes as there are members?

**MASTER.** As was said above, if a light is placed in the midst, it does not shine less in my eyes or more in another’s eyes, but shines wholly in each and remains wholly in itself. So the soul is everywhere in the body and is wholly in each member. Hence, when one member is touched, the whole soul suffers.

There are not, however, as many wholes as there are members, because it remains wholly in itself. It is like the voice in the ears of all: it does not sound in portions, but wholly, and remains wholly in itself.

## CHAPTER XXXV. Why one soul is more capable of learning than another.

**DISCIPLE.** If all souls are of one nature, what is the reason that one is more able to learn and another slower?

**MASTER.** The soul resembles wax or a candle. Wax is capable of receiving an image if a seal is impressed upon it; similarly, a candle is capable of giving light if it is lit. In this way the soul receives the image of knowledge if the seal of instruction is impressed upon it, and it receives the light of truth if it has been kindled by the fire of wisdom.

If it neglects to make itself capable through study or practice [Note: [Col. 1024] The manuscript does not have “capable,” nor, below, “capable.”], then, like wax without an image and like an unlit candle without light, it will remain in the darkness of ignorance without knowledge and truth.

The more each soul adapts itself to instruction, the more capable of knowledge it will be. But why the fire of the Holy Spirit kindles certain souls that do not make themselves capable—or rather, that are negligent—with the light of knowledge, while it does not kindle others; indeed, why it withdraws knowledge from some who labor while not withdrawing it from others who are similar—the reason, unable to penetrate this, cries out in wonder: “How incomprehensible are the judgments of God, and how unsearchable his ways!” (Rom. 11:33).

## CHAPTER XXXVI. That there is one teacher for us.

**DISCIPLE.** Since everything is learned from teachers, how is it written that there is one teacher in heaven (Matt. 23:9), from whom each person is taught in a special way?

**MASTER.** If the matter is rightly considered, absolutely nothing is learned through a human being. Teachers plant and water outside merely by reminding us; but the truth that dwells in the soul gives growth by teaching within (1 Cor. 3:7).

[Col. 1025] A fool does not understand this, but reason, which distinguishes all things, will easily prove that it is so.

Whatever is learned is grasped better through sight than through hearing. For however much I tell someone born blind about the sun, he still does not know what the sun is, since he has never seen it. He merely believes my words that there is something called by that name, or perhaps doubts that there is anything in reality bearing that name. But if he suddenly sees it, by sight itself he proves that the sun exists—something he could not know through hearing.

In the same way, many blind people know the Scriptures, yet do not know what a book or a letter is. If their eyes were suddenly opened and a book were placed before them, they would wonder what it was they saw and would distinguish by sight what they could not know through hearing.

Moreover, if I tell one of them, “This letter is called A, and that one is called B,” he immediately turns inward, consults the truth, and proves that what he hears is true. What, then, have I taught him? Neither previously through hearing nor afterward through sight could he have known what a letter was, unless he learned it by truth teaching within and sight proving it outside.

I merely uttered the sounds of words. He, however, recognized the words and the things signified by the words, while truth examined them within. Likewise, if I tell you much about an elephant, you do not know what an elephant is unless you have seen one. We read much about David and know him, as it were, as a ruddy and handsome man. If he were to enter here now, would we recognize him? I think not.

Why? Because we were unable to learn from teachers what we had not proved through the truth of sight. Teachers merely utter the sounds of words; hearers, with truth teaching within, learn the words through the mind and the things through sight.

Thus we learn letters, unfamiliar languages, and various arts: we receive the sounds of words from our instructors, while truth teaches us to consider the things themselves within. But what should be said about singing, which is not seen but learned only through hearing? When the singer’s voice sounds outside, does not truth within form, as it were, certain ascents of the voice in the soul?

Therefore nothing at all is learned through a human being except sound alone. Words and things are distinguished through the truth dwelling in the inner human being.

[Note: [Col. 1025] The same manuscript reads “are learned.”]

And thus, in the truest sense, one teacher is proclaimed, by whom each person is instructed inwardly. Things that are not seen by us, such as God and the angels, are believed merely to exist.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. What difference there is between believing God and believing in God. True faith.

**DISCIPLE.** Is there any difference between believing God and believing in God?

**MASTER.** A great difference. Demons and pagans believe God, but they do not believe in God. They believe that God exists, that he created all things, and that he is powerful over all things. But only those believe in God who, by loving him, move toward him.

True faith is to believe that God is unity in essence and Trinity in persons; that he created all things from nothing by his Word; that he restored what had fallen through that same incarnate Word; and that on the last day he will renew all things through his Spirit. To those who believe this, he will give the supreme good, namely himself, as their reward.

This faith is the life of the soul, and through it the righteous person lives. Faith is nourished by hope as the body is restored by food; it is animated by love as the body is given life by the soul. Love is proved by action, and therefore faith without works is declared to be dead (James 2:17).

Thus through faith the soul turns away from evil and does good; through hope it rejects all transitory things and desires invisible things like itself; through love it endures whatever is difficult, restrains the impulses of the flesh, distributes necessities to its neighbors, and continually longs for the supreme good. Therefore the soul that by believing and hoping thus moves toward God will possess the supreme good without end.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. That souls separated from the flesh perceive nothing bodily.

**DISCIPLE.** If souls are naturally luminous, is the light of day of any benefit to souls stripped of their bodies? Or, conversely, does the darkness of night hinder them in any way from seeing?

[Col. 1026] **MASTER.** Just as the body is seen to perceive nothing without the soul, so the soul without the body is believed to perceive nothing bodily.

Joined to the body, it perceives colors through the eyes, voices through the ears, odors through the nostrils, flavors through the palate, and tangible things differing in softness or hardness through touch or movement. Separated from the body, it perceives nothing bodily in a bodily manner; it sees things in the proper character of their substance, with the accidents of color removed, and it perceives spiritual things in its own manner.

Therefore, just as the light of a candle contributes nothing to the sun’s ability to shine, so the light of the sun contributes absolutely nothing to the soul’s ability to see. And just as night does not hinder the sun’s radiance but rather flees from it, so it does not hinder the soul in any way, since the soul does not perceive it.

Moreover, the soul either enjoys spiritual light, itself exceedingly brighter than the sun, or, darkened by the dreadful gloom of sins, is enveloped not in the darkness of night but in its own darkness, like a blind person.

That a soul separated from the flesh does not bodily see physical light is established by this: when we wish to dictate something or plan to do anything, the soul immediately withdraws from the external senses, gathers itself inward, and considers within itself the matters with which it is occupied. The sunlight contributes nothing to this activity; indeed, it impedes it. While attending to other things, the soul does not hear loud voices close beside it.

Therefore, outside the body the soul neither sees nor hears anything bodily. If it does so, then it has assumed an aerial body.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. How the saints hear our prayers.

**DISCIPLE.** If souls do not hear bodily voices, how have many people experienced the souls of the saints—Peter, Martin, or another—hearing their prayers?

**MASTER.** It is the prayer of the heart, not of the mouth, that ascends into heaven. Souls hear not the cry of the voice but that of the heart, and they aid those who faithfully call upon them.

They do not hear loud prayers more than prayers made without a voice, whether on the tongue or only in the heart. For we too hear not words but merely sounds; words themselves are seen by the mind.

When, therefore, our souls desire something according to God and ask that it be given to them by God through the saints—whether in the heart, on the tongue, or by the voice—the souls of the saints, for whom hearing is the same as seeing and conversely, do not attend to voices but behold the words, and obtain from God what is desired for those who ask. Hence you have it written: “The Lord has heard the desire of the poor” (Ps. 10:17, according to the Hebrew).

## CHAPTER XL. How souls are understood to be separated from the body, return again, and report what they have seen. Whether hell is incorporeal, or condemned souls assume bodies.

**DISCIPLE.** Is it not written that many souls, often led out of the body, have seen many places of punishment, and likewise many pleasant and flourishing places, and in both kinds of places many souls in human form; and that, after returning to the body, they have reported that they heard many things from them?

**MASTER.** It must be understood that these souls had not completely left the body. They had merely deprived the bodily senses of their functions, while the body had not been entirely deprived of its vital spirit. Therefore the things they had heard were not bodily realities but likenesses of bodily things, which, after returning, they could report for the edification of others who remained in the body.

Once they had wholly stripped off the body, however, matters were entirely different, and they could no longer see as before. It is like our sometimes standing beside a wall and seeing not the approaching person himself but his shadow; when the obstruction of the wall is removed, we see the person as he is.

The souls of the dead also appear to the living by assuming an aerial body, in which body they produce a bodily voice or audible words.

From this it follows that hell is incorporeal: a spiritual substance resembling a bodily one, whose punishment is all the more intolerable because spirit is subtler than body. For every body fails through age and, dissolved by duration, perishes.

Therefore, if the infernal fire is bodily, it must be nourished by bodily fuel, and it follows that when that fuel is consumed, the fire itself must perish. But it is established that the fire of Gehenna does not fail; therefore it is spiritual.

If, however, it is bodily but was created without decay, then it is necessary [Col. 1027] that souls and spirits assume some kind of body in which they can experience bodily fire.

## CHAPTER XLI. Proof of the resurrection of the dead drawn from God’s promises. Another proof drawn from the eternity of souls. “New creation” is spoken of in three ways.

**DISCIPLE.** Can the resurrection of the dead be proved by reason?

**MASTER.** If those things stand firm which were proved above by arguments of the greatest truth, then, once every contradiction has been removed and every necessity established, the resurrection will take place.

It was established that God is truth. The words of truth must be fulfilled. If they are not fulfilled, it follows either that God is mutable or that he is not truth. If they cannot be fulfilled, then God is no longer omnipotent. It is clear how utterly absurd all these alternatives are when applied to God.

Therefore God, immutable truth, promised his lovers complete joy and his despisers complete punishment. Neither can be possible unless it exists in soul and body. Therefore bodies must rise and receive their souls, so that, in accordance with the promises of Truth, the former may possess complete joy in soul and body, while the latter may likewise receive complete punishment.

Furthermore, if bodies do not rise, then souls were not made eternal. But it was proved above that souls were made eternal, specifically so that they might always see God with the angels and live blessedly in that vision without end.

They do not live blessedly if they see their garments—that is, their bodies—rotting in filth without hope of recovering them. It follows, therefore, that the garments of holy souls, which are called “stoles,” must be renewed through the resurrection and changed into incorruptible glory. Clothed in these, souls will contemplate God forever in blessedness. Conversely, the wretched must put on their filthy garments again, and grieve forever over their foulness.

Therefore not only must bodies be renewed, but the common nature that served the saints must also necessarily be changed for the better. Hence you have it written: “Behold, I make all things new” (Rev. 21:5).

**DISCIPLE.** Since God has created nothing new from the beginning of the world until now, how can there be said to be a new creation?

**MASTER.** “New creation” is spoken of in three ways, ordered in this manner through the Trinity.

God the Father created every creature from nothing, and this is called the new creation.

God the Son, having become incarnate, established the Church in a new religion, and this is called the new creation. Hence you have the Apostle’s words: “We are a new creation” (2 Cor. 5:17); and elsewhere: “That we should be a kind of firstfruits of his creation” (James 1:18).

God the Holy Spirit will also yet give life to bodies and renew the whole world. This too is called the new creation. Hence you have it written: “The Lord will make a new heaven and a new earth” (Isa. 65:17).

## CHAPTER XLII. How Christ or the saints are in heaven. What is commonly understood by the name “heaven.” That the eyes do not reach the firmament.

DISCIPLE. Now that the tower has been nobly brought to its summit, it remains for it to be surrounded with battlements, and thus for its pinnacle to be completed at the highest point of the heavens. It is read concerning the Lord that, with his hands raised, he was carried into heaven, and that he sits at the right hand of God (Luke 24:50; Mark 16:19); and Stephen, in his speech, saw him standing at the right hand of God (Acts 7:55). Whoever is carried from one place to another is moved; and whoever sits or stands is contained by a place. Since, then, the Lord ascended bodily into heaven, we greatly desire to know how he is now to be believed to be there, how the souls of the saints are now there, and how they will be there once they have received their bodies. For if some place contains Christ or the saints sitting or standing so that they do not fall, then that place is proved to be better than they, since it contains so many excellent beings. And if the saints rejoice and glory in some visible and sensible creature [Note: [Col. 1027] Manuscript of Saint-Ouen here and shortly afterward: “insensible.”], as we take delight in this visible and sensible light, then again that thing is shown to be better than a rational creature, since the rational creature itself rejoices in possessing it, just as we rejoice in possessing money; and it seems a wretched kind of joy if an intellectual creature takes pleasure in nothing but a stupid thing.

MASTER. Let us climb together to the summit of this tower and, with reason investigating, let us discern how these matters stand. By the customary name we call “heaven” what we see above our heads. Above us, however, we see nothing except clouds or air illumined by the sun. Yet we see the sun, moon, and stars, which are far removed from us, just as, standing on the open sea, we see mountains at a distance; all around us we perceive nothing except the air poured out around us. Hence it is clear that no human sight penetrates the whole expanse of this air, since it can scarcely even reach the horizon. Therefore, when the Apostles could no longer see the Lord after he had been taken upward, it is said: “A cloud received him from their eyes” (Acts 1:9).

Stephen likewise did not see the Lord in heaven beyond the firmament with bodily eyes, since no human sight can in any way reach as far as the firmament. Moreover, the assembly in which Stephen saw Christ standing (ibid. 7:55) was in some house, whose roof his bodily eye could by no means penetrate to its summit. It is therefore established that he saw Christ not with the eye of the body, but by the perception of the inner man—not in a bodily heaven, but in an intellectual heaven.

But perhaps some contentious people object here that the stars are fixed in the firmament and that our sight reaches the firmament when we see them. Do our eyes therefore reach the firmament because they look at the stars? Do they therefore penetrate the entire expanse of air in the sea because they observe mountains, solid bodies as it were? For just as, when mountains are removed from view at sea, nothing but air is seen everywhere, so too, when the heavenly bodies—that is, the solid bodies—are removed, nothing but air is perceived. Whatever extends from the air up to the firmament, and the firmament itself, is not seen by us at all, both because of the great distance of that space and because of the subtlety of its nature.

## CHAPTER XLIII. The three heavens in the historical sense. Three visions signified by the three heavens. The Apostle’s rapture to the third heaven. Why angels and the just are called heaven, and demons darkness.

If it should perhaps be objected that the Apostle is said to have been caught up to the third heaven, it must be understood that three heavens are called such historically, and again that three are named symbolically.

This air is historically called the first heaven, as in the words: “The birds of heaven,” because they are seen to fly in heaven—that is, in the air. The second heaven is called the ether, as in: “The stars of heaven,” because the planets are carried through it on their wandering course. The third heaven is called the firmament, as in: “The heavenly stars,” because the stars are said to be fixed in it.

Three heavens are also read of symbolically, because learned people recognize three visions: sensory, spiritual, and intellectual. Sensory vision occurs when we perceive externally the colors and forms of things, while understanding inwardly that something is concealed, just as in written letters we understand a meaning. This vision is therefore called the first and sensory [Note: [Col. 1028] Printed editions: “substantial.”] heaven, because understanding is concealed in the Scriptures. Heaven, in fact, is named from “concealing.”

The second vision is spiritual: by it we see not things themselves, but images spiritually resembling things, as we commonly do in dreams, and as we know that John in the Apocalypse and the Prophets saw many things. This vision is called the second heaven, because realities are truly concealed in these likenesses.

The third vision is intellectual. It occurs when, neither externally seeing things nor inwardly seeing images of things, we behold with the intellect the substances themselves as they truly are, with their colors abstracted, and discern by reason the quality by which each differs from the others. This vision is called the third heaven, because in it the truth of things is concealed from fools as though in heaven.

Therefore, if the Apostle was caught up in the body, he was brought to the bodily heaven, namely, the firmament. But if he was outside the body—which seems more likely—then he is believed to have been caught up to the intellectual heaven, in which he is understood to have seen the essence of the Godhead as it is and the angelic substances as they are—not sensorially, which cannot occur except through the body, nor spiritually, which occurs only through images resembling things, but truly, which occurs only through the intellect itself.

Angels and the just are called heaven by a certain likeness, because they are concealed from human sight in the secret place of God’s presence. Conversely, demons and the impious are called darkness, because they are hidden from us in torments.

## CHAPTER XLIV. What the kingdom of heaven is, and that it is everywhere. Why we are not now in heaven. What it means to enter it. What it means to be brought into it. The purpose of bodily visions granted to some who are dying.

The kingdom of heaven—that is, the kingdom of the just—is believed to consist not in the walls of cities, not in estates of land, not in an abundance of gold and gems, and not in varied furnishings, but in justice, peace, and every kind of glory in complete joy, which comes from the vision of eternal brightness and from fellowship with the angels and saints.

God, eternal light, has been proved to be in the world and outside the world, beneath, above, and all around it—in every direction and everywhere. Therefore, if the kingdom of heaven, as reason demonstrates, is nothing other than the vision of God, who is the fountain of all good things, it necessarily follows that the kingdom of heaven is in this world and outside the world, in every creature and outside every creature. Hence the words: “The kingdom of heaven is within you” (Luke 17:21), because, abiding in God, we behold him within ourselves, in every creature, and outside every creature, as he is.

We are now called outside God, or outside the kingdom of heaven, because we are deprived of this vision. In the same way, the wretched are said then to be excluded from the kingdom of heaven, because they will be deprived of that same vision as blind people are deprived of the light of the sun.

The just are said to enter this kingdom of heaven, or this joy, because, unable to contain the ineffable joy, they are in a certain manner enveloped in it. When souls are said to be carried upward to heaven, or even to be brought into it, this is said with reference to our sight: the upper regions are known to us as brighter than the sun, and those who still remain in the flesh cannot otherwise understand this matter.

In truth, souls released from the flesh are not moved from place to place, nor are they led to some bodily location from which to contemplate God. Rather, as soon as they are separated from the body, they are joined to the angels and saints and, without delay, enjoy the kingdom of heaven—which is the vision of God—within the world, outside it, and everywhere; just as a blind person placed in the sun would immediately enjoy the sunlight if his eyes were opened.

When, however, light or the forms of angels or saints are seen by some who are dying, and harmonies of song are heard, and they are seen to be led upward, this is unquestionably done for the sake of the living, so that they may be strengthened in the Christian religion.

Moreover, it seems foolish to assert that souls, being without a location, are led from this world beyond the firmament, as though it were more beautiful there or God were more present there, since it is beyond doubt that God exists equally above and below, within and outside, and that his vision is equally present everywhere to the just.

Since souls are incorporeal spirits, it seems utterly absurd to enclose them in bodily places, especially since every place is measured by height, length, and breadth, and it is well known that spirits lack all these dimensions. They are thought to remain in it without occupying a place and to enjoy its vision in the same way that knowledge dwells without occupying a place in the soul.

## CHAPTER XLV. The glory and place of the blessed bodies. The blink of an eye.

The bodies of the saints will rise spiritual, because they will be equal to spirits in lightness, swiftness, and transparency, and every solid thing will be penetrable by them. The Lord’s body likewise rose when the stone was closed around it and entered through closed doors.

Therefore, just as the spirit is now supported by no bodily place, so it will not then be necessary for the spiritual body to be supported by any place. It is not an insensible body that gives life to the spirit, but the spirit that gives life to the body. Thus no place supports the spiritual body, which will be subtler than every element; rather, just as a spirit exists without occupying a place in the supreme Spirit, God, so will it be—unless perhaps what is substantially and personally circumscribed is accepted as its “place.”

Further, either the saints, remaining in this bodily world, will see God, or they will be outside the world. If they are outside the world, they are not supported while standing or sitting by any elemental matter, since no element is found outside the world. Whoever believes that earth or water exists there is foolishly too earthly and fluid-minded; whoever supposes that air or fire exists there is rightly judged unstable and ridiculous because of the mobility of air and fire. Therefore, outside the world they are supported by no material thing, since none is found there.

But if they are in this world, they will likewise not adhere locally to any element by standing or sitting, because they will be equal to the angels (Matthew 22:30). Since, then, they are spiritual, they will remain spiritually, not locally, in the supreme Spirit.

The glory of those bodies must be contemplated not by reason but by faith alone. [Note: [Col. 1030] Thus the *Elucidarium*, book 3, chapter 16.] Those bodies will then be as nimble as the mind and as transparent as the sun. For as quickly as the mind now reaches from east to west in thought, so quickly will that body then be able to reach there.

This is inferred from the fact that the resurrection is read to occur in the blink of an eye (1 Corinthians 15:52). The blink of an eye does not mean that the eye is opened, but that, once the eye is open, a ray of light falling upon it is seen. Yet the speed of that body will truly exceed the blink of an eye by as much as the agility of the mind exceeds that of the body.

The brightness of this body will likewise be as great as that of the spirit. This body will not be a burden to the soul but an adornment, for no corruptible mass will weigh it down; rather, its equality with the angelic nature will make it light.

Its brightness will also surpass the sun by as much as the sun surpasses our body in brightness. For the sun is an insensible body, and although it is changed, it will never be made alive; but that body will be sensible, living, and intellectual. Therefore, to the extent that the intellectual spirit differs from insensible air, to that extent the splendid brightness of that body differs from the brightness of the sun.

## CHAPTER XLVI. The common and particular glory of the saints.

At this point a considerable question arises. Since the Lord says, “The just will shine like the sun” (Matthew 13:43), while the Apostle says, “There is one glory of the sun, another glory of the moon, and another glory of the stars. Star differs from star in glory; so also is the resurrection of the dead” (1 Corinthians 15:41), the Apostle seems to think contrary to the Lord: the Lord asserts that they will shine like the sun, whereas the Apostle affirms that some will shine like different stars, others like the moon, and others like the sun.

It must be understood, however, that the Lord expressed the glory of the saints in general, while the Apostle distinguished the glory of individuals according to their merits. Thus the least in the kingdom of heaven will shine like the sun, which will then be seven times brighter than it is now (Isaiah 30:26). In this brightness each person will differ from another according to merit, just as star differs from star in brightness.

Others, in turn, will surpass these with a glory of different brightness, just as the morning star surpasses the Pleiades, the moon surpasses the morning star, and the sun surpasses the moon in brightness. But the body of Christ will surpass all of us in brightness as much as the Creator surpasses the creature. Hence he is also said to sit at the right hand of God the Father (Colossians 3:1), because he is believed to shine in the glory of divine majesty.

This vision and this glory are therefore called the kingdom of heaven, because only the heavens—that is, the just—enjoy this vision. Their highest reward is the supreme Good, in which they possess complete joy from the fullness of all good things.

## CHAPTER XLVII. That the saints will delight not in sensible things but in the supreme Good. The heaven of heavens. The chain of virtues.

It is therefore concluded that the saints will not delight in sensible things, but will glory in being in the supreme Good and in enjoying the supreme Good by seeing it in every creature and outside every creature.

For if they received as their reward anything less than the supreme Good, they would still desire something more, and it would follow that they did not possess complete joy. But since it is certain that they will possess complete joy, it necessarily follows that they will possess God, the supreme Good, and abound through his overflowing fullness in the fullness of all good things.

When the heaven of heavens is read of, God himself is understood, because the heavens, or the just, are hidden from the disturbance of human beings in the concealment of his presence (Psalm 30:21). Hence it is written: “Having treasure in heaven” (Matthew 19:21)—that is, in God.

The just are drawn to this supreme Good by a kind of chain, which is joined together from the virtues in the following way. First, faith embraces the soul like a circle; hope is attached to faith; hope is held by love; love is completed in action; action is drawn by intention toward the supreme Good; intention is closed by perseverance in the Good; and to perseverance is given God, the fountain of all good things.

Therefore, whoever, drawn by this chain, climbs this tower and reaches its summit will rejoice in knowing not only the true life but also in living blessedly in it forever, because in it he will share in this glory.

DISCIPLE. May God make you a participant in the true life and in all those who live blessedly, and may he lead us all to the supreme Good. Amen.

[ON THE CHRISTIAN LIFE.]

[Col. 1031]

## NOTICE CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING BOOK.

The book *On the Christian Life* had already been restored to its parent through Lucas Holstenius, who arranged for a new and distinctive edition of the same book, based on an old exemplar from the monastery of Monte Cassino, in which he found it inscribed under the name of Fastidius, to be printed at Rome in 1663. Gennadius lends credibility and authority to the Cassinese exemplar when, speaking of Fastidius and his works in chapter 56 of his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, he says: “Fastidius the Briton wrote to Fatalis a book *On the Christian Life*, and another, *On the Preservation of Widowhood*, of sound and worthy doctrine.”

The words of Gennadius were copied from a most ancient Corbie manuscript. In the printed editions, however, they are not read in so pure a form, but have been badly interpolated in two or three places: namely, in the printed Gennadius the book is said to have been written “to a certain Fatalis”; yet it is clear that it was addressed not to a man but to a certain widow. Moreover, in those same printed books Gennadius’s judgment is rendered much more distinguished—or, if one may say so, more foolish—by the addition of a single word, thus: “Of sound doctrine worthy of God.” Indeed, learned men not without reason suspect that Fastidius was devoted to the heresy of his fellow countryman Pelagius. For in chapter 13 of this book he speaks thus concerning Adam: “I find that there was no unbelief in him, except disobedience alone, for which he was condemned, and all are condemned by his example.” This is Pelagius’s very error: that Adam’s sin harmed his descendants by example, not by transmission, as in the letter to Demetrias in the appendix to Augustine’s works; Augustine often rebukes this Pelagian error.

Likewise, the words found here in chapter 11—“For he rightly lifts his hands to God, he pours forth prayers from a good conscience, who can say: ‘You know, Lord, how holy, how innocent, how pure from every fraud, injury, and robbery are the hands which I stretch out to you; how unstained and free from every lie are the lips with which I pour out prayers to you, that you may have mercy on me’”—are the very words which Augustine testifies, in chapter 6 of his book *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, occurred in Pelagius’s book to a widow. Jerome also attests this in the third book of his *Dialogues*, where, having quoted these words, he exclaims: “Is this the prayer of a Christian, or of a boastful Pharisee?” Trithemius wrote that Fastidius, bishop of the Britons, flourished under the emperors Honorius and Theodosius in the year of Christ 420. But the Corbie exemplar of Gennadius praised above did not have the title “bishop,” which the printed editions assign to Fastidius, written by the first hand; rather, “bishop” was added in a later hand after the word “Briton.” We have compared this book with the old Corbie manuscript, with the Remigian, Michaelinian, and Victorine manuscripts, with two Sorbonne manuscripts, and with Holstenius’s Roman edition.

[Col. 1031]

# ONE BOOK ON THE CHRISTIAN LIFE. (C, G, S)*

The author’s humble opinion of himself. That I, a sinner [Note: [Col. 1031] The printed editions add here “first,” which is absent from the manuscripts and from Holstenius’s edition.] and the last, more foolish than the rest and more unlearned than all, should dare by rather frequent letters to urge you to continue in the way of holiness and justice, is compelled in me not by confidence in my own justice, not by skill in wisdom, not by the glory of knowledge, but solely by the cause of charity toward you which I have conceived in heart and mind according to God. This charity so exhorts and prompts me, a sinner and an ignorant man, to speak that, although I do not know how to speak, I cannot be silent.

I would indeed wish, and gladly desire, that you might know those whose wisdom is more abundant, eloquence greater, knowledge fuller, and conscience freer from every contagion of sins, who might instruct you rightly by words and examples. For we, besides having the darkness of foolishness and ignorance so blinded our mind that it cannot perceive or say anything divine, are further rebuked by the consciousness of all our sins, so that, even if it can possess any light, it conceals it. Thus it comes about that, besides having nothing to say, conscience prevents us from uttering even what we have with confidence.

Yet, until one more learned and better can appear to you, be content for the time being with our unpolished admonitions, dearest sister, and pardon charity. Charity does not consider what it offers, nor seek what it does not have; but gladly imparts all that it has. Look not so much to the appearance of its gift as to the intention of its mind, and carefully consider what that charity can deny you which was able to give all that it had [Note: [Col. 1032] Printed editions: “wished.”]. It would have offered even what it did not have, if it could, since it was able to offer all that it had [Note: [Col. 1032] Thus the manuscripts. But Holstenius: “gave all that it was able to offer.” Other printed editions: “offered all that it was able to offer.”].

He thirsts, then, but only a little, [Col. 1033] who cannot be content for the time being with the water of a running stream until he reaches a fuller and purer spring. Nor do I think that he is sufficiently hungry who, though he has ordinary loaves for food, waits for fine white ones. So you too, most beloved sister, whom I am sure thirsts and hungers exceedingly for heavenly things, eat ordinary loaves for the time being until you find white wheaten bread; drink the water of a small and turbid stream until you draw from one that is more abundant and purer. Nor meanwhile let our bread displease you, though it may seem rustic. Rustic bread appears rougher, but it is stronger and more quickly satisfies the hungry stomach and restores the weary than bread which seems wheaten and fine.

Now, therefore, I shall speak as I am able, and shall explain, as best I can, what it is fitting for a Christian to do. I find no more proper beginning for this matter, or point from which to begin, than first to discuss the very name “Christian” and explain why anyone is called a Christian.

## CHAPTER I. The name and dignity of Christians. The duty of a Christian.

No wise or faithful person is ignorant that Christ is interpreted “anointed.” It is manifest that only holy men and men very worthy of God were ever anointed, and that they were none other than prophets, priests, or kings. So great was the mystery of that anointing that among the Jewish people not all, but very few out of the many, deserved to receive it; and this continued until the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, whom God anointed with the oil of gladness—that is, with the Holy Spirit—above his fellows (Psalm 44:8).

From that time, those who believed and were purified by the sanctification of that baptism are anointed not as only some had formerly been under the law, but all as prophets, priests, and kings. We are warned by the example of this anointing what sort of persons we ought to be: that where the anointing is so holy, the conduct may be no less holy. From the sacrament of this anointing derive both the designation and name of Christ and of all Christians—that is, of those who believe in Christ. He receives that name in vain who does not imitate Christ at all.

For what can you be called that you are not, or why usurp a name not your own? But if you delight to be a Christian, do what belongs to Christ and rightly assume for yourself the name Christian. Or perhaps you wish not to be one but to be called one? That is very foul and wretched: to wish to be called what you are not. For no one so comes to Christ that he is called a Christian and is not one. Whoever is called a Christian professes that Christ is his Lord. And he truly has him, if he obeys and serves him in all things. If not, he is not Christ’s servant but his mocker and derider: he calls himself the servant of one whom he pretends not to serve.
