A double judgment, therefore, is reserved for him: one for mocking God, whom he called Lord without cause, and another according to the character of his sin.

## CHAPTER II. Sinners. Why God does not immediately punish for a double reason. God’s kindness toward humankind.

But the long patience of the merciful God makes many unbelieving, shameless, and faithless people bold in sinning [Note: [Col. 1033] Printed editions: “permits.”], so that from this they suppose God is not the avenger of their sins because he does not immediately wish to punish sinners. Wretched and ungrateful people, heedless of their own salvation: they even charge God with the fact that their destruction is delayed [Note: [Col. 1033] Holstenius: “who.”], unaware that they are preserved by God’s providence for a double reason: both that his long patience may provide for the human race, and that he may not be judged impatient if he wished immediately to condemn sinners [Note: [Col. 1033] Most manuscripts: “punish.”].

For if he were not so patient, the origin of the human race would long ago have ceased; nor would we have righteous persons from among sinners if God wished to punish those who sin at once. We know and read of some who were formerly liable to many various kinds of sin, deceived either by the blindness of ignorance, the cause of unbelief, or the vanity of youth, and who afterward, through the most merciful patience of God who sustained them, were converted from error and performed works [Note: [Col. 1034] Printed editions: “work”; against the manuscripts.] of justice greater than the sins they had previously committed.

For God does not pardon sins, but delays; nor does he free the persevering sinner from death, but patiently waits for him to be converted, even late, and live. As the blessed apostle Peter says: “The Lord is not slow concerning his promises [Note: [Col. 1034] Corbie manuscript: “to fulfil promises.”], but acts patiently for your sake, not wishing any to perish but all to be converted to repentance” (2 Peter 3:9). For as one pious, kind, and merciful, he does not immediately strike you, so that you may recognize how great is his mercy toward you, how great his clemency: he prefers to wait for you, a sinner and impious person, and save you when converted, rather than punish you while sinning.

Thus the Lord himself speaks through the prophet and declares in the kindness of his own voice how much mercy and loving-kindness he wishes to bestow on humankind, saying: “And if the wicked man turns away from all his iniquities which he has done, and keeps my commandments, and performs judgment, justice, and mercy, he shall live and shall not die. None of the transgressions which he has committed shall be remembered; in his justice, which he has performed, he shall live. Do I will the death of the unjust, says the Lord Adonai, rather than that he should turn from his evil way and that I should cause him to live?” (Ezekiel 18:21–23). And elsewhere: “The iniquity of the wicked shall not harm him on whatever day he turns from his iniquity” (ibid. 33:12). And again: “Return, returning children, and I will heal your contrition” (Jeremiah 3:22).

See how God urges and invites you to turn, even late, from your sins and be able to be saved. See how he exhorts one already liable to death to live; how gently, how mercifully he invites, so that he does not deny a father’s loving-kindness even to sinners. He still calls them children, though by sinning they have lost God as Father. So too, elsewhere, he testifies in a mournful voice and with a certain miserable lamentation that sinners have caused him loss, saying: “I have become without children; I have lost my people because of their sins” (Jeremiah 15:7).

Learn, then, from this how God loves you: he prefers you to live rather than perish. And do you scorn and despise him who loves you more than you love yourself, who wishes you to live when you desire to die? “I do not will,” says the Lord, “the death of sinners [Note: [Col. 1034] Holstenius: “of those dying.” Sorbonne and Remigian manuscripts: “of those who die.” Michaelinian: “of those sinning.” Corbie: “of sinners who die.”], but that they should be converted and live” (Ezekiel 18:23). You therefore wished to die by sinning; he wishes to make you live by converting you [Note: [Col. 1034] Manuscripts: “to give you life.”]. O foolish, irreverent, and ungrateful person, who do not even agree with God when he wishes to have mercy on you; he prefers to save you by his mercy rather than allow you to perish by your sin!

## CHAPTER III. Those who abuse God’s mercy are punished even here. Unjust judges.

Let no one, then, flatter himself for this reason; let no one deceive himself by a foolish and vain supposition; let no one therefore sin freely and securely because God’s wrath and judgment do not immediately come upon sinners. Let no one suppose that he has sinned with impunity because he is not at once destroyed; rather, let him recognize that God delays rather than overlooks, and that his wrath will come suddenly and unexpectedly upon sinners, rather than pardon [Note: [Col. 1034] Printed editions: “although late, suddenly.”], as it is written: “Do not say, ‘I have sinned, and what grievous thing has happened to me?’ For the Most High is a patient requiter.” And elsewhere: “Do not delay to turn to the Lord, nor put it off from day to day; for his wrath will come suddenly” (Ecclesiasticus 5:4, 8).

This is fulfilled in many people upon whom, because of excessive sins, God’s wrath comes even in the present life and is reserved in the life to come. But no one understands this, no one recognizes it; no one suffering adversity thinks it inflicted for his evils, but regards what he suffers as a matter of custom rather than guilt. Therefore God does not seem to punish sinners in the present, because when he punishes, it is not recognized.

[Col. 1035] For there are many whom no one recognizes as already judged in the present life before the day of judgment because of the multitude of their sins. Let someone say whether he can see, even in the present time, any sacrilegious, bloodthirsty, rapacious, deceitful, murderous, thieving, fraudulent, adulterous person, or one guilty of other crimes, living to old age. For we see very many examples through which we can sufficiently prove that wicked and impious people, when the measure of their sins is complete, are judged even in this time and are denied present life no less than future life.

But this can be understood more easily by one who, through various times, has observed the death of different judges who lived impiously and wickedly [Note: [Col. 1035] For “observed.”]. The higher their power, the greater their boldness in sinning, since they think that everything they can do is permitted to them; and, because they judge others and do not fear another’s judgment, they rush headlong into sin. Thus it happens that those who do not fear human judgment in wrongdoing experience God as judge and avenger.

Some of these, having frequently shed the blood of innocent souls, experienced the wrath and judgment of God so that afterward they themselves were compelled to shed their own blood, though they had willingly shed that of others. Others who had committed like acts were so overthrown by God’s indignation that they lay unburied and became food for beasts and birds of the air. Others, who had unjustly slain an innumerable multitude of people, were cut to pieces limb by limb, so that the number of limbs severed was no less than the number of those whom they had caused to be killed.

By their judgment many wives had been made widows through the unjust killing of their husbands, and many orphans had been left behind when their fathers were killed; beyond bereavement, beggary and nakedness were inflicted upon them. For they added to their impiety and cruelty what was lacking: they robbed even the children of those whom they had caused to be killed. But now their own wives are widows and their children daily lack the bread of others. Does it not seem to you that the testimony is fulfilled in them of God’s threat: “You shall not afflict widow and orphan. But if you afflict them and, crying out, they cry to me, I will hear their cry, and I will be angry in my soul, and I will destroy you by the sword; and your wives shall be widows and your children orphans” (Exodus 22:22–24)?

O shameful wickedness! O criminal deed! O excessive and intolerable cruelty! Two most savage and atrocious acts are committed at one time: murder is committed so that robbery may follow; husbands and fathers are killed so that widows and orphans may more easily be plundered. Thus each rejoices in another’s death, as if he himself were never to die. Rightly, therefore, is God moved by cruelties and impieties of this kind. Rightly does he display his judgment in some even before the time. Rightly is neither present nor future life granted to such persons. By their example we are warned not to suppose that wicked and impious people can escape God’s judgment even in the present life.

## CHAPTER IV. God punishes the sinner when the fixed number of sins is completed.

But we ought rather to understand this: that each person is sustained by God’s patience only so long as he has not yet filled up the limit and measure of his sins; once it is completed, he is immediately struck, and no pardon is thereafter reserved for him. That there is a fixed number and measure of sins is declared by the testimony of God himself. It is most clearly shown that each person is judged sooner or later according as he has filled up the measure of his sins, when God speaks to Abraham concerning the destruction and burning of the Sodomites and Gomorrites, who had already filled up their sins, saying: “The outcry of Sodom and Gomorrah has been filled up, and their sins have been filled exceedingly greatly” (Genesis 18:20).

But what does he say concerning the Amorites, who had not yet completed their sins, and whom it is certain were destroyed many years after the aforesaid cities were burned? “The sins of the Amorites have not yet been filled up” (ibid. [Col. 1036] 15:16). By this example we are most plainly instructed and taught that individuals are brought to an end according to the fullness of their sins, and are borne with so long that they may be converted as they have not filled up the heap of their transgressions.

Let no one, I say, deceive or mislead himself: God does not love the wicked; he does not love sinners; he does not love the unjust, the rapacious, the cruel, or the impious. But he loves the good, the just, the pious, the humble, the innocent, and the gentle. As it is written: “For you are not a God who wills iniquity. The evil one shall not dwell beside you, nor shall the unjust remain before your eyes. You hate all who work iniquity; you will destroy all who speak falsehood” (Psalm 5:5–7).

## CHAPTER V. Early death for the wicked as punishment; for the good as security.

But someone says [Note: [Col. 1036] Er. Lugd. and Lov., “but someone will say.” M.], “What, then, is the meaning of what we see—that even the good perish along with the wicked?” They do not perish, but escape: they are freed from the company and persecutions of the wicked and transferred to rest. Those plainly die and perish whom, after departing this world, a punishment and penalty of still greater judgment awaits. The good are called away before their time, so that they may not be harassed longer by the harmful; but the wicked and ungodly are removed so that they may not persecute the good any longer. The righteous are called from pressures, tribulations, and afflictions to rest; the ungodly, however, are snatched from luxury, wealth, and pleasures to punishment. The former go in order to judge, the latter in order to be judged; the former in order to be vindicated, the latter so that vengeance may be carried out against them, as it is written:

“But the righteous person, if he is overtaken by death, will be in refreshment”; and again, “He was taken away while living among sinners”; and again, “His soul was pleasing to God, and therefore he hastened to remove him from the midst of iniquity”; and again, “Their path is with the ungodly toward death, but they are in peace” (Wis. 4:7, 10, 14; 3:3).

You see, therefore, that for the righteous and worshipers of God this dissolution of the body is rest, not punishment; and when they are released from the body, they are freed rather than destroyed. For this reason the faithful neither fear nor dread that release, but rather desire and long for it [Note: [Col. 1036] Three manuscripts: “await.”], since they understand that through it rest, not punishment, is being granted to them. The unrighteous and ungodly, however, conscious of their crimes, rightly dread it by natural foresight, since they know that through it they will be judged. Therefore, once this explanation has been given and accepted, we ought not to sin at all—especially since we know that judgment is both present for sinners and reserved for the future.

## CHAPTER VI. It is disgraceful to allow oneself to claim the Christian name. Who is a true Christian?

Let us not flatter ourselves merely because we are called Christians; rather, for this very reason let us believe that we will be judged if we falsely claim for ourselves a name that does not belong to us. Or if anyone is so unbelieving, so faithless, so obstinate, so stubborn, and so bold that he does not fear the anger and indignation of God the Judge—which will one day come—or is ashamed of human custom, let him see how brutish, foolish, and stupid he would be judged even by the pagans, whose vanity and madness are so great that he acquires for himself a name that is not his own.

Who is so vain and wretched that he would dare to present himself as a lawyer when he does not know letters? Who is so insane and senseless as to claim to be a soldier when he does not know how to bear arms? No one takes any name without reason. To be called a shoemaker, one must make shoes; expertise in a craft makes someone a smith or an artisan; someone is called a merchant when he sells at a higher price what he bought more cheaply. From such examples we recognize that no name exists without action, but that every name derives from action.

How, then, are you called a Christian when there is no Christian action in you? “Christian” is the name of justice, goodness, integrity, patience, chastity, prudence, humility [Note: [Col. 1036] The manuscripts lack the word “humility.”], humanity, innocence, and piety. How, then, do you defend and claim that name for yourself when, among so many qualities, scarcely a few remain in you? A Christian is one who is a Christian not merely in name but in deed; one who imitates and follows Christ in everything; one who is holy, innocent, undefiled, and untouched; one in whose heart wickedness has no place, but in whose heart piety and goodness alone abide; one who knows how to harm or injure no one, but to help everyone.

A Christian is one who, following Christ’s example, knows not how to hate even his enemies, but rather to do good to those who oppose him and to pray for his persecutors and enemies. For anyone who is prepared to injure or harm another is lying when he says that he is a Christian. A Christian is one who can say in a just voice, “I have harmed no one; I have lived justly with everyone.”

## CHAPTER VII. God has always been pleased by justice and offended by injustice. Enoch carried off to immortality.

But lest anyone suppose or believe that I am speaking merely from my own opinion, or think that what I say may easily be disregarded because I speak according to my own will rather than on the authority of the Law, I shall now begin to bring forward examples from the Law itself, whose commands open for us the way to life—examples from both the old and the new Law—and show what God commanded the human race to observe from the beginning of the world, and by what things he has always been pleased or offended.

For I read that after Adam, who was first formed by God (Gen. 1:27)—the reason for whose case need not be discussed now—Cain and Abel were full brothers at the beginning of the world. One of them pleased God because he was innocent and just; the other, because he was unjust and guilty, could not please God (Gen. 4).

Then, as time passed, Scripture identifies Enoch as exceedingly just. Justice brought him such distinction that he did not even experience present death, but was uniquely carried away from the midst of all mortals to immortality (Gen. 5:22–24). His example shows that one just person is dearer to God than many sinners.

We also know what Noah, that just man, gained from the merit of his justice: life was granted to him and his family alone when the whole world was condemned through the flood (Gen. 6–8). Scripture testifies what Abraham attained through the merit of faith and justice: at that time he alone was God’s friend on earth, because he alone had been found just (Gen. 15:5–6). And when Lot was rescued from the fire of the Sodomites while all the others perished, what was this other than the reward of justice (Gen. 19:12–29)? It would take too long to go through each person and recount the merits of all.

## CHAPTER VIII. For this reason God afflicted the Israelites with many hardships: to train them in works of piety. The fulfiller of the Law.

It is fitting for us to know how God instructed the Jewish people, whom he first chose from Abraham’s offspring to belong to himself before all other nations; what he commanded them to do and observe in order to please him.

First, I do not think it happened without cause or without God’s providence that he made them leave the region in which they had always wished to dwell, abandon their homeland, and migrate to a foreign province, namely Egypt [Note: [Col. 1037] Absent from the better manuscripts is “migrate”; in the Sorbonne manuscript, “to go”; in Holsten, “a journey.”]. But I think the reason was this: because God had chosen his people and desired to train them in mercy, piety, justice, and the other good works, he wished them for a time to be foreigners and captives in a foreign land, so that they might learn the misery and hardship of captivity and exile. Thus afterward they would more readily know how to show mercy to foreigners and those who labor, if they themselves had first learned the miseries of exile.

No one shows mercy so willingly to a foreigner or stranger except one who knows the experience of exile. No one so receives a guest without shelter into his own lodging except one who has previously needed another’s. No one feeds the hungry so readily, or gives drink to the thirsty, except one who has suffered hunger and thirst. No one covers the naked with his own clothing so readily as one who knows the hardship of nakedness and cold. No one comes to the aid of the afflicted, miserable, and suffering so readily except one who has experienced the vicissitudes of tribulation, misery, and labor.

Rightly, therefore, God—the teacher of mercy and piety, who was afterward to issue the Law through which he would deliver to his people the commands of mercy, piety, and every good work—wished them first to endure every pressure, tribulation, and affliction in a foreign land, so that afterward they might more easily show mercy to those who suffered such things and obey his commands.

You may think him a good farmer who, before sowing the seed, long breaks and subdues the earth with plows and harrows, lest the seed entrusted to it perish. In the same way God first long disciplines and subdues his people before giving them the seed of saving commands.

Finally, so that it may be clearer that they endured these things for this reason, let us consider the commands of the Lord himself, who says: “You shall not mistreat or oppress a foreigner, for you too were foreigners in the land of Egypt” (Exod. 22:21). And again we read: “The great God, who shows no partiality and accepts no bribe, executes justice for the convert, the orphan, and the widow. Love giving bread and clothing, because you too were once in the land of Egypt” (Deut. 10:17–19).

And elsewhere he says: “When you reap your harvest in your field and forget a sheaf [Note: [Col. 1038] Elsewhere, “a bundle”; the manuscripts reject this reading.], you shall not return to take it; it shall belong to the convert, the orphan, and the widow, so that God may bless you in the works of your hands. You shall remember that you were a servant in the land of Egypt; therefore I command you this word” (Deut. 24:19, 24).

From this it is easily seen and recognized that God afflicted that people with all these hardships for the purpose of teaching them, by their own example, to show mercy to another, as it is written: “For through such works you taught your people that the righteous must be humane” (Wis. 12:19). What kind of people he wants his people to be is, I think, broadly evident, and by what works they can please him is demonstrated by very many examples.

But lest what we have said seem insufficient for making his will clear, let us also join to it the precepts of the Law and the Prophets, and confirm by testimonies from both the old and the new Law what pleases God and has always pleased him, and what he has most frequently commanded to be done and observed [Note: [Col. 1038] Most manuscripts: “I shall begin to bring forward examples from the new Law: ‘You shall love,’ etc.”]:

“You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, with all your mind, and with all your strength, and you shall love your neighbor as yourself.”

That this is the chief commandment of the Law and the Prophets is confirmed by the testimony of our Lord and Savior, who says: “On these two commandments the whole Law and the Prophets depend” (Deut. 6:5; Lev. 19:18; Matt. 22:40).

Since this cannot be abolished or changed, the whole commandment of both the Law and the Prophets consists in these two commands, and the one who can fulfill them has fulfilled the Law. For nothing else is sought in the old Law except that you love God and your neighbor. Truly, the fulfiller and doer of the Law is the one who sins neither against God nor against his neighbor.

## CHAPTER IX. Who loves God. What sort of people God’s people ought to be.

But I must not pass over or conceal what it means to love God and what it means to love one’s neighbor. He loves God who obeys all his commands. He loves God who keeps his laws and precepts. He loves God who sanctifies himself just as God is holy, as it is written: “Be holy, because I, the Lord your God, am holy” (Lev. 19:2).

He loves God who fulfills the words of the prophet: “You who love the Lord, hate evil” (Ps. 96:10). He loves God who thinks of nothing but heavenly and divine things. For God is a lover only of holiness, justice, and piety; and the one who loves God does nothing other than what God appears to love.

What it means to love God is made clear by the teaching of our Lord and Savior, who says: “The one who hears my words and does them is the one who loves me” (John 14:21). If, then, the one who does what God commands loves God, the one who does not do it does not love him. Everyone who does not love hates. Therefore it is clear and manifest that those who do not keep God’s commands hate him. Of them, I think, the prophet said: “Do I not hate those who hate you, Lord, and do I not loathe your enemies? I hate them with perfect hatred; they have become my enemies” (Ps. 139:21–22).

The righteous prophet hates sinners, adulterers, and unjust people who despise God’s commands, as he says elsewhere: “I saw the transgressors of the covenant, and I loathed them.” And again: “I hated the wicked, but I loved your law” (Ps. 119:158, 113).

See, therefore, how just, upright, and holy we ought to be. We are not only forbidden to live wickedly; we are not even permitted to acknowledge those who live wickedly. Blessed Paul also clearly demonstrates this: he does not command us even to break bread with sinners, saying, “If anyone is called a brother among you who is sexually immoral, or greedy, or serves idols, or is abusive, or is drunk, or is rapacious, with such a person do not even eat” (1 Cor. 5:11).

God wished his people to be holy and removed from every contagion of injustice and iniquity. He wished them to be so just, pious, pure, spotless, and simple that the nations would find nothing in them to condemn, but rather something to admire and say: “Blessed is the nation whose God is the Lord, the people whom he chose as his inheritance” (Ps. 33:12).

Such ought the worshipers and servants of God to be: gentle, serious, prudent, pious, blameless, untouched, and spotless. Whoever sees them should be astonished and admire them, saying, “Truly these are men of God, whose conduct is such.” A person of God ought to present and conduct himself so that there is no one who does not wish to see him or long to hear him; no one who, when he sees him, does not believe that he is a son of God. Thus the prophetic saying may truly be fulfilled in him: “His mouth is sweetness itself, and he is altogether desirable” [Note: [Col. 1039] Er. Lugd. Ven. Lov.: “His mouth is full of sweetness, and he is altogether desirable.” M.] (Song 5:16).

But if a Christian presents himself in such a way, if a servant of God presents himself in such a way, that by his conduct he becomes like those who serve demons and idols, God will begin to be blasphemed through him, and people will say: “What a Christian servant of God—what evil actions, what shameful deeds, what wicked conduct he has; how impious, criminal, luxurious, and filthy his life is!” He will then be liable to that prophetic saying: “The name of God is blasphemed among the nations because of you” (Isa. 52:5; Rom. 2:24).

But woe to those through whom the name of the Lord is blasphemed. For God desires and requires nothing from us more than that his name be glorified by all through our actions, as it is written: “Offer a sacrifice of praise” [Note: [Col. 1039] Thus the manuscripts. Elsewhere: “A sacrifice of praise has honored me.”] (Ps. 50:14). This is the sacrifice that God seeks and loves above all sacrifices: that through the works of our justice his name may everywhere be praised, and that God may be proved to be true by the conduct and deeds of his servants. Those love God who do nothing except what will glorify his name.

## CHAPTER X. Love of one’s neighbor. He avoids doing harm and takes care to do good. Praise of innocence.

How God ought to be loved, I have explained as well as I could. Now let us explain as best we can what it means to love one’s neighbor as oneself, although the explanation of this matter is briefly discussed elsewhere, where it is said: “What you do not wish to be done to you, do not do to another” (Tob. 4:16).

Our Lord and Savior also says: “Whatever you wish people to do to you, do the same to them” (Matt. 7:12). No one wishes another to do evil to him. Therefore, the one who loves his neighbor as himself does not wish any evil to be done to him, since he does not wish it for himself; but if there is anything good, he gladly grants it to him, just as he himself desires and hopes to receive it from everyone.

For this alone is not required of a Christian: that he be free from evil, but also that he practice good. Even if someone has done neither evil nor good, he is not admitted to the reward of eternal life, but is consigned to the fires of Gehenna. Thus we read that the Lord said in the Gospel concerning those who do no evil but also perform no good:

“Depart from me, you accursed, into the eternal fire that my Father prepared for the devil and his angels” [Note: [Col. 1040] Holsten here and below, in chapter 13: “which your father the devil and his angels prepared.”]. “For I was hungry, and you did not give me food; I was thirsty, and you did not give me drink; I was a stranger, and you did not welcome me; I was naked, and you did not clothe me; I was sick, and you did not visit me; I was in prison, and you did not come to me” (Matt. 25:41–43).

They are condemned not because they did evil, but because they did not do good. From this every prudent and wise person may recognize what hope those who live in evil can have, when even those who have done no evil are denied life unless they have also done some good. For God does not ask this only of us: that we not be evil, but that we become good.

People are called evil because of evil works; conversely, they are called good because of good works. There are two beings whom the good and the wicked seem to serve: the good God, whom all who live well serve; and the evil devil, whose servant is everyone who does evil.

For we are not asked merely to cease being servants of the devil by living badly; we must also appear to serve God by living well. I do not know whose servant anyone seems to be who appears to do neither evil nor good, or how he will be able to hope for everlasting life from God when he has not earned it by doing good.

Let no one, I say [Note: [Col. 1040] In the same manuscripts, “he says.”], deceive and mock himself by his own judgment; let no one mislead himself through a vain opinion. Whoever is not good does not possess life. Whoever has not performed works of justice and mercy cannot reign with Christ. Whoever is not humane, pious, hospitable, kind, and merciful will not escape the fire of Gehenna. God does not love the wicked; he does not love sinners. Whoever does evil is an enemy of God. Whoever is not free from deceit cannot have a share with Christ.

For a Christian ought to seek and desire nothing more, and strive with all his strength for nothing more, than to exclude wickedness from his heart, to admit no evil into the conscience of his breast, to retain goodness, preserve justice, and guard purity of mind.

Be innocent if you wish to live with God. Be simple if you wish to reign with Christ. What benefit is wickedness, which drags one to death? What benefit is evil, which prevents one from reigning with Christ and destroys the one who possesses it? As it is written: “A wicked soul destroys the one who possesses it” (Sir. 6:4).

If you wish to live, hear what the prophet says; if you love Christ’s kingdom, hear how you may deserve to attain it: “Who is the person who desires life and wishes to see good days? Keep your tongue from evil, and let your lips not speak deceit. Turn away from evil and do good; seek peace and pursue it” (Ps. 34:13–15).

God honors and loves such people: those who do not know evil, who do not know how to lie, whose lips do not speak deceit, and in whom nothing but goodness and purity is seen.

Innocence is what commends us to God; simplicity is what makes us reign with Christ. That God loves only the innocent and wishes them to be joined to himself is declared by many testimonies, as it is written in the Psalms: “The innocent and upright have clung to me” (Ps. 25:21).

And elsewhere it is commanded and said: “Guard innocence and observe equity, for there are descendants for the peaceful person” (Ps. 37:37).

How much innocence benefits and contributes to a person, even when it is preserved late in life, is confirmed by the testimony of the prophet David. Although he had previously sinned gravely, afterward he did not fear being judged, once he had begun to know innocence, as he himself says: “Judge me, God, for I have walked in my innocence” (Ps. 26:1). He therefore knew that he no longer needed to fear judgment, because, even if late, he had come to know innocence.

And elsewhere he says: “But you received me because of my innocence” (Ps. 41:13). God afterward received the one whom he had earlier rejected because of his wickedness.

That the innocent cannot be put to shame before God is also clear from the statement: “As long as the innocent preserve justice, they will not be put to shame” (Prov. 13:6). Nothing can be more worthy or dearer to God than that innocence be preserved with complete observance.

Even if someone appears devoted in other works, if he does not possess innocence, he vainly flatters himself about his devotion. If the Jews living under the old Law were commanded to observe it—even when they were still permitted to hate their enemy—what ought you to do now as a Christian, when you are commanded to love your enemy? When, then, will you not be innocent? Or to whom could you be evil, when you are commanded to be good even to your enemies (Matt. 5:44)?

But perhaps you hate even your neighbor, although you are not permitted to hate an outsider; you persecute your brother, although you are commanded to love your enemy; and you believe yourself to be a Christian, although you keep the commands of neither the New nor the Old Testament.

But so that you do not consider yourself a Christian without cause or flatter yourself over the name alone, hear from the Apostle what you ought to be:

“Let the one who was stealing steal no longer; rather, let him labor, working with his hands at what is good, so that he may have something to give to the person in need. Let no evil word come from your mouth, but only one that is good for building up the faith, so that it may give grace to those who hear. And do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption. Let all bitterness, anger, indignation, shouting, and blasphemy be removed from you, along with all malice. Be kind and merciful to one another, forgiving one another, just as God in Christ forgave you. Be imitators of God [Note: [Col. 1041] The manuscripts, except Michael’s, read “of me.”], as beloved children, and walk in love, just as Christ loved us and gave himself for us as an offering and sacrifice to God, for a fragrant aroma. But sexual immorality, every impurity, and greed must not even be named among you, as is fitting for saints; nor obscenity, foolish talk, or coarse joking, which are improper, but rather thanksgiving. For you know this: no sexually immoral or impure person, or greedy person—which is idolatry—has an inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and God” (Eph. 4:28–5:5).

Let the one who keeps these commands rightly judge himself a Christian: the one who is holy, humble, modest, and just, and who lives by works of mercy and justice.

## CHAPTER XI. Whose prayers God does not hear. The one who prays must be just.

Do you consider him a Christian in whom there is no Christian action, whose conduct contains no justice but only wickedness, impiety, and crime? Do you consider him a Christian who oppresses the miserable, burdens the poor, covets other people’s possessions, makes many needy in order to make himself rich, rejoices in unjust profits, feeds on the tears of others, grows wealthy through the destruction of the wretched, whose mouth is constantly defiled by lies, whose lips speak nothing but unworthy, obscene, criminal, and shameful things, and who, although commanded to distribute his own possessions, seizes those belonging to others?

Such a person boldly approaches the church and rashly and shamelessly spreads out impious hands, defiled by unlawful seizure and the blood of the innocent. With that polluted and sacrilegious mouth, with which he had just spoken either falsehoods or obscenities, he pours out prayers to the Lord as though conscious of no evil.

What are you doing, shameless and wretched man? Why do you burden yourself with the weight of greater sins? Why do you inflict injury on God beyond mere contempt? Why, to provoke his anger more quickly, do you extend to God, as evidence of your punishment, criminal hands on which he does not look, since he commanded that only holy and undefiled hands be offered to him? Why do you ask God with that mouth with which you have just spoken evil?

However numerous they may be, he abhors such prayers, as it is written: “When you stretch out your hands, I will turn my face away from you; and if you multiply your prayers, I will not hear you, for your hands are full of blood. Wash yourselves; be clean; remove your wickedness from your souls” (Isa. 1:15–16).

The one who stretches and raises his hands to God ought to be fully conscious and certain of his own innocence, trusting in it, since the Apostle says: “I want men to pray in every place, lifting pure hands” (1 Tim. 2:8). [Note: [Col. 1042] These are Pelagius’s own words, according to Jerome, near the end of Dialogue 3.]

That person rightly raises his hands to God and pours out prayers with a good conscience who can say: “You know, Lord, how holy, innocent, and pure from every deceit, injury, and robbery are the hands that I stretch out to you; how just and undefiled, free from every lie, are the lips with which I pour out prayers to you, asking for your mercy.”

Such a person quickly deserves to be heard, and before he has fully poured out his prayers [Note: [Col. 1042] In place of the words from “Such a person” through “poured out,” one word occurs in a single manuscript: “he”; Holsten has “that man.”], he can obtain what he asks.

## CHAPTER XII. Almsgiving from unjust profits.

For I know that some have been so blinded by the deep darkness of wickedness and greed that when things have gone well for them—whether they have bound a poor person through their power, crushed an innocent person with false testimony, overcome a weak person by force, committed theft, or engaged in robbery—they give thanks to God, believing that they perpetrated such deeds with his assistance, and judge God so unjust that they think he participated in their crimes.

They are fools and wretches, blinded by their iniquities to such a degree that they do not understand that what God forbids cannot please God. As though one crime were not enough, they add another by thinking wickedly about God.

Others think they are justified because they give a small alms from the substance of the poor; from what they have taken from many, they give a little to one person. One person is fed from what leaves many hungry, and from the spoils of many scarcely a few are clothed.

God does not seek such almsgiving, nor does he wish piety to be provided to one person through another’s cruelty. It is better for you not to give alms than, by clothing a few, to strip many; and, in clothing one person, to rob many who are already clothed.

God approves the almsgiving that is supplied from honest labor, as it is written: “Honor God from your honest labors, and offer him from the fruits of your justice” (Prov. 3:9). But he abhors and rejects almsgiving provided from the tears of others.

What benefit is it if one person blesses you while many curse you? Or what does that almsgiving contribute to you which is provided from another person’s substance? Truly, must we fear that God has no means by which you can feed his poor unless you seize what belongs to someone else?

## CHAPTER XIII. Faith without works is of no benefit. The Apostle’s passage cited for faith without works is explained. Another passage of the same Apostle. Faith is not sufficient.

I know others whom the dark ignorance of folly and imprudence so misleads and deceives that they think the faith they pretend to possess will benefit them before God without works of justice. Through this kind of error they commit unspeakable crimes without fear, believing that God is the avenger not of crimes but only of faithlessness.

Nor are they content merely to have brought about their own ruin; they also try to entangle others who have no light of divine knowledge in their snares. In them is fulfilled the saying of our Savior: “If the blind lead the blind, both will fall into a pit” (Matt. 15:14).

For if no crime is condemned, but only faithlessness, then we sin securely and freely. And God gave his commands concerning justice without purpose if faith alone, without works of justice [Note: [Col. 1042] Er. Lugd. Ven. Lov.: “works.” M.], is beneficial.

We cannot know where this impious, criminal, and faithless error of ignorance has crept in, unless perhaps it comes from those who, by this example, were seducing the people under the old Law and handing them over with themselves to eternal death and everlasting destruction. Of them it is written:

“Do not listen to the words of the prophets who prophesy to you, for they are vain; they speak visions from their own heart and not from the mouth of the Lord. For they say to those who reject the words of the Lord, ‘Peace will be yours’; and to everyone who walks according to his own desires, to everyone who walks in the error of his heart, they say, ‘No evil will come upon you’” (Jer. 23:16–17).

We have many testimonies—indeed, testimonies from the whole Law—with which we could destroy and bury such a pernicious error. But so that we do not weary the reader by going on longer, let a few of the many suffice.

Let the person whose opinion is such answer me: Was Adam, the first human being made by God in the world's first state [Note: [Col. 1043] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions: “immediately at the beginning of the world.”], condemned on account of faithlessness or sin (Gen. 3:17)? I find no unbelief in him except disobedience alone; for this he was condemned, and all are condemned through his example.

Cain likewise was condemned not because of faithlessness, but because he had killed his brother (Gen. 4:11). Why say more? I read that the whole world perished in the flood not because of faithlessness, but because of crimes (Gen. 6:13).

When Sodom and Gomorrah were suddenly consumed by fire, I find no cause of unbelief, but only sins and crimes; Scripture demonstrates this most clearly, saying: “The men of Sodom were wicked and sinners before God exceedingly” (Gen. 13:13).

When that Jewish people so frequently seemed to perish and be punished, was it not because of sins?

But someone says [Note: [Col. 1043] Er. Lugd. Ven. Lov.: “but someone will say.” M.], “I accept only the testimonies of the old Law if you also bring me examples from the New Testament.”

Consider Ananias and Sapphira, whom the apostolic judgment condemned not for the crime of faithlessness, but because of theft and lying (Acts 5:4, 9).

Perhaps you will say to me, “What, then, does the Apostle mean when he says, ‘For we hold that a person is justified by faith apart from works of the law’” (Rom. 3:28)?

I read that the very person who says this also condemned an absent man because he had taken his father’s wife (1 Cor. 5:1). Scripture must be understood in a way that makes it consistent in every respect for those who understand it, and divergent only for those who understand it least.

The Apostle says that a person is justified by faith apart from works of the Law; but not apart from those works concerning which I hear another apostle say: “Faith without works is dead” (James 2:20). The Apostle Paul was speaking about the works of the Law—that is, bodily circumcision, the new moon, the Sabbath, and other such things that the Law had previously commanded to be done but that were no longer necessary in the time of Christ. The other apostle, however, is speaking about works of justice; whoever does not perform them is dead, even if he pretends to be faithful.

But someone says [Note: [Col. 1043] Er. Lugd. Ven. Lov.: “but someone will say.” M.] that passage of the Apostle in which he says: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. 10:10).

Fool, this is fulfilled at the time of Baptism, when, in order for someone to be baptized, only confession and faith are required. For what benefit does the washing of Baptism provide if faith alone, without justice, is sought? Everyone holds that sins are washed away by Baptism through faith. But if one must sin afterward, what benefit is there in having been washed?

Hear what the Lord says to the man who has once been healed: “See, you have become well; sin no more, lest something worse happen to you” (John 5:14). Blessed Peter the Apostle also teaches this most clearly: something worse happens to the person who sins after recognizing the way of justice, when he says:

“For if, after escaping the defilements of the world through the knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, they are again entangled in them and overcome, the latter state has become worse for them than the former. For it would have been better for them not to have known the way of justice than, after knowing it, to turn back from the holy commandment delivered to them. For what is said in the true proverb has happened to them: ‘A dog returns to its own vomit,’ and, ‘A washed sow returns to wallowing in the mud’” (2 Pet. 2:20–22).

Blessed Paul the Apostle also testifies and says that a person who sins after the sanctification of Baptism through his former error is not preserved without great repentance:

“For it is impossible for those who have once been enlightened, who have tasted the heavenly gift, who have become participants in the Holy Spirit, who have tasted the good word of God and the powers of the coming age, and who have fallen away, to be renewed again to repentance, since they crucify the Son of God for themselves again and hold him up to contempt” (Heb. 6:4–6).

A certain man approached the Savior and asked what he should do to receive eternal life, as the Evangelist bears witness; and the Lord answered him: “If you wish to have life, keep the commandments” (Matthew 19:17). He did not say, “Keep faith alone.” For if faith alone is required, the commandments are needlessly ordered to be kept. But far be it from me to say that my Lord commanded anything needless.

Yet this is what those say who, by sinning, have already become sons of perdition; and they think they have this one consolation, if they can consign others along with themselves to everlasting death. For if God does not punish the sinner, where is the prophetic statement: “If the righteous will scarcely be saved, where will the sinner and the ungodly appear?” (Proverbs 11:31; 1 Peter 4:18); and elsewhere: “Because sinners will perish” (Psalm 36:20)? And again: “Let sinners perish from the earth, and the wicked be no more” (Psalm 103:35); and again: “As smoke vanishes, so may they vanish; as wax melts before the fire, so may sinners perish before the face of God” (Psalm 68:3)?

Here I hear not merely the unbelieving and faithless condemned, but sinners. And I read that our Savior said in one place: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of my Father, who is in heaven” (Matthew 7:21). Surely these people believed in Christ, since they even called him Lord; yet for that reason the gate of the heavenly kingdom is not opened to them, because they confess with their mouths the one whom they deny by their deeds. The Apostle said that God can be denied by deeds no less than by words: “They profess to know God, but by their deeds they deny him” (Titus 1:16).

And the Lord says in the Gospel: “Many will say to me on that day, ‘Lord, Lord, did we not cast out demons in your name, and in your name perform many mighty works?’ And I will say to them, ‘I never knew you. Depart from me, all you workers of iniquity’” (Matthew 7:22). They are said to have believed to such an extent that they even performed mighty works in the Lord’s name; nevertheless, their faith will not benefit them, because they did not perform works of righteousness.

Therefore, if faith alone is beneficial, why are those handed over forever with the angels of Satan to the fires of Gehenna—those who are judged not because of treachery, but because they had done nothing good? As it is written: “And the King will say to those on his left, ‘Depart from me, accursed ones, into the eternal Gehenna, which my Father prepared for the devil and his angels. For I was hungry, and you did not give me food,’” and so forth (Matthew 25:41–42). He certainly did not say, “Because you did not believe in me.” From this it is evident that they are to be condemned not because of unbelief, but because of the barrenness of good works.

## CHAPTER XIV. Who Is Truly a Christian

Therefore let no one deceive or mislead another: unless one is righteous, one does not have life [Note: Er., Lugd., Ven., Lov.: “unless one is righteous, one will not have life” (Lov.: “life”); M.]. Unless someone has kept Christ’s commandments in all things, he cannot have a share with him; unless someone has despised earthly things, he will not grasp heavenly things; unless he has scorned human things, he cannot possess celestial things.

Nor should anyone consider himself a Christian unless he both follows Christ’s teaching and imitates his example. But do you think that person a Christian whose bread has never satisfied any hungry person, whose drink has refreshed no thirsty person, whose table no one knows, beneath whose roof neither a stranger nor a traveler has ever found lodging, whose garments have covered no naked person, whose assistance has comforted no poor person, whose goodness no one experiences, whose mercy no one knows, who imitates nothing good in anyone but rather mocks and derides it, and never ceases to persecute the poor?

Far be this from the minds of all Christians; far be it that such a person should be called a Christian; far be it that one who is such could be called a son of God.

A Christian is one who follows Christ’s way, who imitates Christ in all things, as it is written: “Whoever says that he remains in Christ ought himself to walk as he walked” (1 John 2:6). A Christian is one who shows mercy to everyone, who is not at all moved by injury, who does not allow a poor person to be oppressed in his presence, who helps the miserable, who assists the needy, who mourns with those who mourn, who feels another’s pain as his own, who is moved to tears by the tears of others, whose house is shared by all, whose door is closed to no one, whose table no poor person is unaware of, whose food is offered to everyone, whose goodness all know, and no one experiences injury from him.

He is one who serves God day and night, who continually meditates upon and contemplates his commandments; who becomes poor to the world so that he may become rich before God; who is held inglorious among human beings so that he may appear glorious before God and the angels; who seems to have nothing feigned or fabricated in his heart, whose soul is simple and undefiled, whose conscience is faithful and pure; whose entire mind is in God, whose whole hope is in Christ; who desires heavenly things rather than earthly things, who despises human things so that he may possess divine things.

For hear what is said to those who love this world and glory and take pleasure in the present age: “Do you not know that friendship with this world is enmity with God? Therefore whoever wishes to be a friend of this world makes himself an enemy of God” (James 4:4).

## CHAPTER XV. Three Kinds of Widows. What Christ’s Widow Should Be

I have explained to you, dearest sister, as far as I could, what it is fitting for a Christian to do. If, then, all generally who are called Christians ought to be such, it is now for your prudence to consider what kind of widow you ought to show yourself to be, since you ought to be an example to all who live well.

I believe you are not unaware that there are three kinds of widows. One is the most perfect, destined for a heavenly reward: following the example of that widow in the Gospel, she serves God day and night with prayers and fasts (Luke 2:37). Another is said to care for children and a household; she is not worthy of as much honor, yet she is not subject to sins. The third kind is devoted to banquets and pleasures; she is reserved for eternal death and punishment.

As it is written: “Honor widows who are truly widows.” These are the first, who are called both widows and true widows, and whom so great a priest—that is, Timothy—is commanded to honor. The second are those whom he is no longer commanded to honor, though their life is not denied them; concerning them it is said: “But if any widow has children or grandchildren, let them first learn to manage their own household piously” [Note: In many manuscripts, “well”] “and to repay an equal gratitude to their parents.” The third are those of whom it is written: “But the widow who lives in pleasures is dead while she lives” (1 Timothy 5:3, 4, 6).

From this it can be understood that not all widows are equal, nor do those please God who appear widows only in body, not in conduct.

But what Christ’s widow ought to be, the Apostle says: “She who is truly a widow hopes in the Lord and persists in prayers day and night.” Nor do I want you to overlook the fact that when the Apostle names true widows, he shows that there are also false ones—that is, false in action, mind, and manner of life, not in body.

Elsewhere the same Apostle describes the conduct and way of life of a true and chosen widow, saying: “Let a widow be chosen who has a testimony of good works: if she has raised children”—understood, for God—“if she has received strangers, if she has washed the feet of the saints, if she has supplied what was needed by those suffering tribulation, if she has pursued every good work” (ibid. 5:10). He judged her to be a true widow whose works are such.

But how can that woman call herself Christ’s widow who has never done anything of this kind? Yet there are some women who are rich, noble, and powerful, to whom it perhaps seems beneath their dignity either to raise children for God and not for the world, or to receive a stranger as a guest, or to wash the weary, muddy, filthy feet of the saints and touch them with delicate and clean hands. [Note: See Sermon 149, no. 1, in the Appendix to volume 5.]

But such women will not be worthy in the future to share the company of the saints whom they so despised in the present; nor will they be able to have a share with Christ, whom they were unwilling to receive and whose feet they recoiled from touching with their own hands. For whoever despises Christ’s servants despises Christ, as he himself says: “Whoever despises you despises me” (Luke 10:16).

Mary had an abundance of tears with which to wash Christ’s feet; but among the women of our time there is not even enough water with which to wash the feet of travelers.

Therefore, most holy and prudent woman, do not wish to imitate such women, who, although they have boldly done evil, are ashamed to do good; who are ashamed to live rightly, though they were not ashamed to sin; and who have voluntarily offered themselves to death and do not return to life even when invited. They fear human laughter, mockery, and gossip more than God’s judgment, and they value pleasing miserable human beings more dearly than pleasing Christ.

But be such as the Lord commanded you to be, such as the Apostle orders Christ’s widow to show herself. Be holy, humble, and quiet; practice works of mercy and righteousness without ceasing. Let anyone hold you up to reproach, let anyone mock and deride you: only please God and do what belongs to Christ.

Above all, meditate incessantly on the commandments of your Lord; devote yourself earnestly to prayers and Psalms, so that, if possible, no one may ever find you except either reading or praying.

And when you are such, remember us, who love you so much that what we cannot provide while present, we offer while absent.

## [ON SALUTARY INSTRUCTIONS]

### [Column 1045]

## NOTICE CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING BOOK

This book will at last be restored to Paulinus of Forum Julii, or Aquileia, on the authority of a certain Colbertine codex of excellent quality and very ancient script.

Paulinus of Forum Julii wrote it toward the end of the eighth century and perhaps died in the second or third year of the ninth century. Yet we see that the work was soon taken from him, in that same ninth century, and attributed to Augustine. For there exists, unless we are mistaken, an eight-hundred-year-old Theoderician copy bearing this title, written by the first hand at the beginning of the book: *Book of exhortation of Saint Augustine to a certain count, his dearest friend*.

It is cited by Gratian, *On Penance*, distinction 2, chapter *Si quis*; there, as also in Trithemius, it is called Augustine’s letter to Count Julian. Under this title it also had a place among Augustine’s letters in the first Amerbach edition of those letters.

Indeed, in nearly all the other manuscript codices that we have found—all later than the Theoderician copy—the book is headed as addressed to a certain count, his very dear friend. This title is supported by what is read in chapter 62: “No bishop, abbot, or count will be able to corrupt with gold and silver the palace of that judge, Christ.”

Yet scarcely one or two codices have the name of Count Julian written at the end of the book. We rather suspect that the book was sent to Aeric, duke or count, since you will find these titles used interchangeably of the same man in the *Life of Saint Eligius*, book 2, chapter 59, and in book 1 of the *Chronicle of Casauria*.

Alcuin prompted this suspicion in Letter 94, writing to Aeric as follows:

“I might perhaps have written more to you, venerable man, about the observance of Christian piety, if that distinguished teacher and devout instructor of heavenly life, my Paulinus, were not present with you. From his heart flows a spring of living water leaping up into eternal life. Have him as your counselor for eternal salvation.”

Paulinus had read Prosper’s—or, more accurately, Julianus Pomerius’s—work *On the Contemplative Life*, from which he drew nearly everything contained here from chapter 10 through chapter 20.

We collated this book against the old codices: the Theoderician, Pratellian, Audoenian, Cygirannian, Corbie, Victorine, and others. With their help we either removed glosses scattered here and there in the printed editions, transferred them to the foot of the pages among the variant readings, or at least separated them by enclosing marks.

But above all, the outstanding codex of the Colbert Library was useful for wiping away errors. It appears to have been written in Paulinus’s own age. In this codex the book is entitled as follows:

“Sermon of the blessed Paulinus, bishop of Forum Julii. To a certain friend of his serving in the world, he wishes peace and prosperity, health and everlasting joy in the Lord Jesus Christ our Savior.”

### [Column 1047]

# BOOK OF EXHORTATION, COMMONLY CALLED *ON SALUTARY INSTRUCTIONS*

To a Certain Count. (G,S)*

## CHAPTER I. Justice and Blessedness: Loving God

O my brother, if you desire to know—although I do not know—what justice is most perfect and complete [Note: Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions, however, read: “what the most perfect and complete justice is. For justice is God,” and so forth], it is to love God with one’s whole heart and to cleave to him with one’s entire will, since he is the highest good. To love the highest good is the highest blessedness.

Whoever loves God is good; if good, then also blessed. The more ardently one loves him, the better one will become. May he himself, who is this good, cause you to abound in this most blessed good, dearest brother. With daily prayers and an undivided desire of heart, though unworthy, I strive to implore him [Note: The German manuscript reads, “I strive”].

## CHAPTER II. Humanity’s Privileges in Creation

But you, dearest brother, understand [Note: See *On Spirit and Soul*, chapter 35] that you were created by the counsel of the Holy Trinity and by the work of divine majesty. From the first honor of your creation, understand how much you owe your Creator, since the eternal Creator immediately granted you, in your very creation, so great a privilege of dignity that you would love him more ardently the more you understood that he had created you in so wondrous a manner.

## CHAPTER III. The Same Subject Continued

It is not only that you were so excellently created by the Creator through the counsel of the Holy Trinity; it is also that the Creator of all things created you according to his own image and likeness—something he granted to no other creature except humanity alone.

Your soul bears within itself this image of the unity and Trinity of almighty God: first, because by God’s gift it lives and possesses understanding; second, because it was created in the image of its Creator; third, although you are called one human being, you nevertheless possess three dignities granted by the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—that is, understanding, will, and memory.

The same thing, though in other words, is indicated in the Gospel when it is said: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your strength” (Matthew 22:37). In these three things our inner human being wondrously bears the image of our Creator in its nature. From these, as from the soul’s nobler dignities, we are commanded to love our Creator, so that he may be loved to the extent that he is understood; and to the extent that he is loved, he should always be held in the memory that has received him [Note: Some manuscripts read: “so that they may be held in the memory that he commanded”].

Nor is it enough for us merely to understand God, unless our will is made active in his love; indeed, even this is not enough unless action is added together with memory and will.

## CHAPTER IV. Turning to God

But, dearest brother, may spiritual knowledge be added to your mind, illuminating it and leading you, as I desire and pray, to eternal life. With all the affection of my heart I desire, and I beseech God, that you may always press forward toward what lies ahead until you reach the lofty crown of everlasting blessedness. Do not allow the nobility of your spirit—which I know to be excellent in you—to be changed by the counsel of any friends or by the ambition of any worldly desires.

Do not obscure your goodness through the wickedness of others; but everywhere, as far as you are able, appear lovable before God and all the people [Note: The printed editions alone add: “Do not think that one who at some time displeases human beings displeases God in every respect”].

The grace of God, who helps you, will not be lacking if the will for holy admonition is present in you, to which your good mind has often attended in the divine Scriptures.

## CHAPTER V. The Same Subject Continued

Be, I beg you, though a layman, ready for every work of God; devoted to the poor and the sick [Note: The printed editions read: “moderate toward offenders, merciful toward the infirm of God”]; a comforter of the grieving; compassionate toward everyone’s miseries; generous in almsgiving, remembering the Gospel widow’s two small coins (Luke 21:2) and the prophet who says, “Break your bread for the hungry” (Isaiah 58:7).

And carefully foresee the proper discernment of almsgiving, so that it may be a consolation to both parties—to the giver, that is, and to the recipient [Note: The printed editions read, “carefully”].

## CHAPTER VI. Choosing Counselors

Therefore meditate not only on your own salvation but also on the progress and prosperity of many. Choose for yourself the best counselors, fearing God and loving truth.

For flatterers often deceive the souls of those who listen to them with a pleasing appearance and destroy them with everlasting death. Concerning such people the Psalmist says: “For God has scattered the bones of those who please human beings; they were put to shame, because God despised them” (Psalm 53:6). And the Apostle says: “If I were still pleasing human beings, I would not be Christ’s servant” (Galatians 1:10).

Let every friend be pleasing to his neighbor for edification, not for destruction; for not every friend can be a counselor, as Scripture says: “Let your friends be many, but your counselor one.”

## CHAPTER VII. True Friendship

Although a change of clothing has carried me far from you in body, it has not carried me away in charity; for charity that can be abandoned was never true [Note: Thus Alcuin, Letter 113, to Paulinus, following Jerome, Letter 41].

Therefore, through the intimate charity of friendship, let us be joined as closely as we can to the Lord Christ, for he says: “You are my friends if you do what I command you.” And again he says to his disciples: “I shall no longer call you servants, but my friends” (John 15:14–15).

## CHAPTER VIII. Observing God’s Commandments. The Two Evils God Hates in Humanity

If we wish to earn the rewards of eternal life, let us strive with all our strength to keep his commandments. For his commandments are burdensome to those unwilling, but light to those willing, as he himself says: “For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light” (Matthew 11:30); and again: “Upon whom shall I rest, except upon the humble and quiet one who trembles at my words?” (Isaiah 66:2).

The friendship of the world consists either in profit, favors, or various honors; but the Savior’s friendship consists in loving him and one’s neighbors. Therefore, whenever we fulfill Christ’s commandments through good works, we are called Christ’s friends.

He continually invites us to his friendship, while the devil, envious, seeks to plunge us into hell. The Savior loves us, and the betrayer hates us. Therefore let us not abandon the Redeemer or follow the robber. Let the one who restored us to freedom be dearer to us than the one who captured us and subjected us to slavery.

Always place before the eyes of your heart the fact that neither a crowd of friends nor the multitude of one’s household, neither a heap of gold and silver nor shining gems, neither an abundance of vineyards nor the density of crops, neither the pleasantness of expansive meadows can bring any aid to a soul departing from the body. Rather, those who love such things more greatly grieve more greatly.

Therefore our true friend, the Lord Jesus Christ, must be loved, for he will grant us present happiness and eternal blessedness. Our Redeemer is so called because he redeemed us from the captivity of the devil; Savior, because he saves us from our sins; Helper, because he helps us in times of need and tribulation; Protector, because he protects us so that we may remain unharmed among our enemies; Receiver, because he receives us into eternal dwellings.

Therefore let us fulfill with all our strength the charity, commandments, and love of so great a friend, and preserve within us the nobility of his image. Let us always remember how renowned and most glorious our emperor and friend is. He asks no other gift from us except a spiritual one.

Let us take every possible care that he find nothing that offends his eyes. And if perhaps—as human frailty ordinarily permits—the evil spirit impresses upon us some stain of negligence, let us hasten with every effort to wash it away through confession, repentance, and a fountain of tears [Note: The manuscripts do not have “and a fountain of tears”], lest we remain long without the embrace of our friend, since he is more ready to receive us than to destroy us—provided only that we do not delay returning to him from day to day [Note: The manuscripts read, “to receive us”].

For these are the two evils that almighty God hates in all human beings: negligence in returning, and despair of salvation. Let these be far removed from our thoughts, and then he will be near to our souls.

I beg you, let us not trust while boasting in earthly happiness; rather, let us give thanks to him who, although he wished human beings to be rational, asked them to follow him not in pride but in humility.

What greater glory, or what higher honor, can be ours than to be friends of that emperor who is above all emperors? And the higher he is in the power of omnipotence, the more diligent we ought to be in righteousness, holiness, humility, and observance of his commandments.

## CHAPTER IX. Justice. Study of the Scriptures

### [Column 1050]

Holiness consists in works of righteousness. Righteousness, in turn, is fulfilled in two ways: we must not do what he has forbidden, and we must do what he has commanded, according to the Prophet: “Turn away from evil and do good” (Psalm 34:15).

For the entire sequence of the holy Books was written for our salvation. Above all, it resounds in our ears and repeats again and again what human beings must avoid and what they must pursue.

Your Dignity knows well how to exercise itself in these Books, because through them God himself, our Lord, speaks to us and shows us the affection of his gracious will. Let us recognize and consider with what honor his embassy ought to be received by us.

What if a diplomatic message or letter from a king came to us? Would we not immediately set aside our other concerns, receive the letter with ready willingness and complete devotion, and, after reading it, strive to fulfill it? And behold, from heaven the King of kings and Lord of lords—and indeed our Redeemer—has deigned to send us his letters through the Prophets and Apostles, not to impose upon us some service necessary for himself, but to make known what can benefit us for salvation and glory [Note: The Colbertine manuscript reads, “what he knows”].

## CHAPTER X. Let God Be Our Possession

[Note: From Julianus Pomerius, in Prosper, book 2, *On the Contemplative Life*, chapter 16.]

Therefore, if we take pleasure in possessing anything in this world, let us possess with an unencumbered mind God, who possesses all things and created all things, and in him let us have whatever we desire happily and holily.

But since no one possesses God unless he is possessed by him, let us ourselves become God’s possession, and God will become our possessor. What can be happier in the world than for someone to have his emperor and redeemer become his wealth, and for divinity itself to deign to be his inheritance?

For from him we receive all fruits; in him and from him we always live. What, I ask, is sufficient for a human being for whom the Creator himself is not sufficient? What more does one seek for whom one’s Redeemer ought to be all joy and everything?

## CHAPTER XI. The Joy of the World

[Note: From the same book, chapter 13.]

Alas, how subtly that ancient enemy deceives us by deception and draws blindness before the eyes of our minds, so that we cannot distinguish the joys of this age from the joys of the eternal King!

To rejoice is indeed good; but if the person who rejoices does not rejoice in what he ought, what he rejoices in cannot be good.

The earthly soldier rejoices in the passing honors of this world, in beautiful garments and splendid bracelets encircling his arm, in a crown placed upon his head; but such joy is not eternal—it is destined to perish.

The robber rejoices when he has seized what he desired. The drunkard rejoices when he has found an opportunity to drink. The adulterer rejoices when he has obtained the pleasure of enjoying a prostitute’s body. The perjurer rejoices if he has acquired the resources of this world by swearing falsely. The angry person rejoices if he has carried out his anger.

And there are many other things that your Goodness, dearest brother, will be able to comprehend. Although rejoicing is good, nevertheless rejoicing in such things and things of this kind is a great evil and a sin that leads to death [Note: The printed editions read “of sin.” The reading “sin” is referred to the word “is,” not to “leading”].

Nor does any crime become so abominable before God as rejoicing and exulting by recalling past sins, and continually lying in them [Note: The manuscripts read “in it”].

These are the things we mentioned above, by which the world wishes us to rejoice, so that we may perish with the lovers of this world. We must reject these joys as the poisons of the devil, because they hasten to destroy not only the body but also the soul forever.

## CHAPTER XII. Spiritual Joy

I beg you, my brother, I beg you: by striking these arrows of the devil against the rock that is Christ (1 Corinthians 10:4), take up the shield of faith, with which you can extinguish all the fiery darts of the devil (Ephesians 6:16).

Let us rejoice in the Lord’s goodness, in a pure conscience, in true confession and worthy repentance, in mourning and true sorrow, which does not produce death according to the world but eternal salvation according to God (2 Corinthians 7:10).

But the sorrow that belongs to this world the Apostle firmly forbids, saying: “Do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption. Let all bitterness and anger and indignation and clamor and blasphemy be taken away from you, together with all malice; and be kind to one another, compassionate, forgiving one another, just as God in Christ forgave you” (Ephesians 4:30–32).

As far as we can, let us correct our ways with diligent care and hasten to acquire the virtues of all good people, so that we may be able to obtain God’s piety and mercy at the appropriate time and rejoice ineffably in the promise of that future kingdom.

These are the weapons that arm us against the devil’s assault and commend us to God. These are the weapons that strengthen, fortify, and ennoble our souls. These weapons are with us and, by God’s gift, within us. These are our true riches.

For chastity makes us chaste, righteousness makes us righteous, piety makes us devout, humility makes us humble, gentleness makes us gentle, innocence makes us innocent, simplicity makes us simple, purity makes us pure, prudence makes us prudent, temperance makes us temperate, and charity makes us dear to God and to human beings. All these good things were created by God and by the good God.

## CHAPTER XIII. Contempt for the World. The Threefold Concupiscence in the Sin of the First Parents

[Note: From Pomerius’s book 2, *On the Contemplative Life*, chapters 21 and 16.]

Therefore, if we wish to be in him as we ought to be—as the holy Apostle John says, “As he walked, so let us also walk spiritually” (1 John 2:6)—what is it to walk as Christ walked except to despise the vanity and happiness of this world and not fear suffering adversity for his name?

Let us hope for what he promised and follow where he went before us. In no way should the miserable sweetness of this world separate us from the love of Christ—nor the excuse of wife or children, nor the great pleasure of possessing gold and silver—while the holy Apostle John solemnly warns us, saying: “Do not love the world or the things that are in the world, because everything that is in the world is the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the ambition of the age” (ibid. 15–16).

These are the things that cast Adam and Eve from the paradise of delights into this miserable exile. For if the love of God had not failed in them, they would never have begun to love the counsel of the serpent who gave evil advice; indeed, they would not even have believed it.

The desire of the flesh was fulfilled in them when they tasted from the forbidden tree; the desire of the eyes, when they desired that their eyes be opened; and the ambition of the age, when they believed that they could become what God is.

Therefore, wishing us all to beware of these three kinds of death, the Apostle said: “Everything that is in the world is the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the ambition of the age.”

## CHAPTER XIV. By What Steps They Fell into Sin

And so that your Goodness, my brother, may more easily understand, if you please, how those first human beings—Adam and Eve—committed so great a sin, I shall explain it, so that the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ may grant you always to avoid it. For in those two the entire human race was originally condemned.

They would not have eaten from the forbidden tree unless they had desired it; they would not have desired it unless they had been tempted; they would not have been tempted unless they had been abandoned; they would not have been abandoned by God unless they themselves had first abandoned God; nor would they have abandoned God unless they had become proud and had damnably neglected the likeness of God in whose image they had been made.

As a result, their diseased bodies contracted death, and according to the Lord’s sentence they are believed to have died on the day when the necessity of dying was imposed upon them as punishment.

## CHAPTER XV. What It Means to Imitate Adam or Christ

We said these things a little earlier about the first human beings so that we might escape their fall and condemnation, whether as an example or as a punishment [Note: From the same book, book 3, chapter 1]. For although we were born bodily from Adam, we ought not to imitate him, but Christ our Lord, in whom we have been reborn through Baptism and live [Note: From Pomerius’s book 2, *On the Contemplative Life*, chapters 20 and 21].

What is it to imitate Adam except to allow ourselves to be killed by everlasting death through bodily desires and passions? And what is it to imitate Christ except to put to death within ourselves bodily desires and passions, and to reign happily with him who redeemed us at the price of his blood?

And if, when we were in Adam, we all fell in him, so now, because we have begun to be in Christ, let us all rise spiritually with him. To state the whole matter: Adam took paradise away from us, while Christ granted us the kingdoms of heaven and handed over his body for us sinners.

For Christ died for sin—not his own, but ours. Each of us, however, dies not for everyone’s sin, but for his own.

## CHAPTER XVI. What It Means to Die to Sin

What is it to die to sin except to condemn evil works within us and flee this miserable age?

Just as a person dead in the flesh within a tomb detracts from no one, acts violently toward no one, slanders no one, oppresses no one, does not envy the good, does not insult the wicked, does not serve the lust of the flesh, does not kindle his thirst more and more by drinking, does not burn with the flame of hatred, does not flatter the powerful and rich of this world [Note: The printed editions add, “as many do in our time”], is not carried away by restless curiosity, does not concern himself with a very large crowd standing around him, is not stretched out and encumbered by being surrounded with gold, silver, or purple garments [Note: Better manuscripts read “purple garments”], does not take pleasure in the greetings of the powerful or of relatives, does not wear himself out over injuries; pride does not inflate him, the ambition of this world does not destroy him, empty glory does not shamefully exalt him, gold or bracelets or all the false riches of this world do not inflame him, the fury of mad rage does not drive him, the stoutness and love of horses do not entice him, the most beautiful appearance of women does not make him desirous, the words of miserable actors do not provoke him to laughter, the contentions of this world do not disturb him, boldness does not exalt him, and the joys of this world do not delight him.

Anger does not make him angry, perversity does not make him suspicious, vanity does not make him talkative, malice does not make him a mocker, and the fickle love of this world does not make him changeable and unstable [Note: The manuscripts lack “makes him”].

I have extended the enumeration of these and similar things so that your most affectionate Fraternity may understand that a person dead in the flesh [Note: The Colbertine manuscript reads “mortal”] can neither do nor suffer the things I have mentioned.
