And so that we do not grow sluggish in such matters, let us strive as far as we can, with God’s help, to put our bodies to death together with their vices and desires (Galatians 5:24), and let us put on the new person, who was created according to God in righteousness and holiness of truth (Ephesians 4:24).

Let us not take pleasure in human praise, willingly lend an ear to detractors, or believe our flatterers. Let us not be at odds with one another [Note: The printed editions add, “with our subjects and brothers”]; rather, let us invite to concord those whom we are able to influence. For according to the Gospel, “Blessed are the feet that run toward peace” (Matthew 5:9).

## CHAPTER XVII. What It Means to Live According to the Flesh
Let us not be carnal—that is, let us not live carnally in this world—for the Apostle says, “If you live according to the flesh, you will die” (Rom. 8:13). Therefore, he lives according to the flesh who lives according to himself: for he is merely a human being, and he lives according to himself; that is, he goes wherever he wishes, sleeps whenever and for as long as he wishes; speaks whatever he wishes, to whomever he wishes [Note: [Col. 1052] Manuscripts: “and whatever he wishes.”], and wherever he wishes; eats and drinks whenever and as much as he wishes; laughs and jokes disgracefully among whomever he wishes and whenever he wishes. Finally, whatever is pleasant to his nostrils he seeks; whatever is soothing to the touch, whatever delights the eyes, whatever is pleasing to his body, he practices and pursues as he wishes and whenever he wishes, because he desires all things carnally, whether lawful or unlawful. He delights in the most beautiful clothing, in horses, and in weapons, as he wishes and whenever he wishes; and thus he lives and delights, not according to God, but carnally. He fulfills all the desires of his flesh as he wishes and whenever he wishes.

## CHAPTER XVIII. Remedies for Vices. Praise of Humility.

Therefore, dearest brother in Christ, we must beseech divine mercy that spiritual delight may diminish carnal desires [Note: [Col. 1053] From Book 3 of Pomerium on the Contemplative Life, chapters 3, 2, 4.], that godliness may resist anger’s cruelty within us, that patience may restrain wickedness, that chastity may conquer lust, that tranquility may endure irascibility, that moderated silence may check buffoonery and talkativeness, that spiritual devotion in vigils, prayers, and almsgiving may take the place of curiosity, that sobriety may master drunkenness, that gentleness may rule anger and fury, that maturity may govern frivolity, that true chastity may exclude wantonness, that love of God and neighbor may restrain desire for the world, and that profound humility may trample down boasting and pride. For humility makes human beings like the holy angels, whereas pride made demons out of angels.

## CHAPTER XIX. No Sin without Pride. Pride and Desire Are Always One.

And so that we may show clearly that pride itself is the beginning, end, and cause of all sins: pride is not only itself a sin, but no sin could, can, or will exist without pride. For every sin is nothing other than contempt of God, by which we despise his commandments; and nothing else persuades a human being to this except pride.

Moreover, pride and desire are so entirely one evil that desire can exist neither without pride nor pride without desire. From pride arise heresies, schisms, slander, envy, anger, quarrels, dissensions, disputes, hostility, ambition, arrogance, presumption, boasting, talkativeness, vanity, restlessness, lying, perjury, and other things of this kind, which it would take too long to enumerate individually. Desire, too, makes people gluttonous, intemperate, drunken, greedy, rapacious, fornicators, adulterers, defilers, incestuous, criminal, and countless other things through which the devil habitually casts the human race headlong into ruin.

Through pride and desire the devil says, “I will ascend into heaven” (Isa. 14:13); Christ, in humility, says, “My soul is humbled in the dust” (Ps. 43:25). Through pride and desire the devil says, “I will be like the Most High” (Isa. 14:14); Christ, through humility, “though he was in the form of God, emptied himself, taking the form of a servant; he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the Father unto death” (Phil. 2:6–8). Through pride and desire the devil says, “Above the stars of God I will exalt my throne” (Isa. 14:13); Christ, in humility, says, “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart” (Matt. 11:29).

The devil, greedy and proud, speaks through Pharaoh, saying, “I do not know the Lord, and I will not let Israel go” (Exod. 5:2); Christ, in humility, says, “If I should say that I do not know him, I would be like you, a liar; but I do know him, and I keep his commandments” (John 8:55). The proud and greedy devil says, “The rivers are mine, and I made them” (Ezek. 29:9); Christ, in humility, says, “I can do nothing of myself; but my Father, who remains in me, himself does the works” (John 5:30; 14:10).

The proud and greedy devil says, “All the kingdoms of the world and their glory are mine, and I give them to whomever I wish” (Matt. 4:8); Christ, though rich, became poor for our sake, so that by his poverty we might become rich (2 Cor. 8:9). The proud and greedy devil says, “As eggs that have been abandoned are gathered, so I have gathered the whole earth, and there was no one who moved a wing, opened a mouth, or chirped” (Isa. 10:14); Christ, in humility, says, “I have become like a solitary pelican. I have kept vigil, and have become like a solitary sparrow on the roof” (Ps. 101:7–8).

Through pride and desire the devil says, “With the sole of my feet I dried up all the streams of the embankments” (Isa. 37:25); Christ, in humility, says, “Can I not ask my Father, and he will provide me with more than twelve legions of angels?” (Matt. 26:53).

And, to bring the matter finally to a conclusion: the devil, through pride and desire, is hurled down into hell with a great fall; Christ, through humility, is raised up to heaven.

Therefore, dearest brother, I have described for you a few snares of diabolical deceit and steps of holy humility, so that you may more easily teach those subject to you how and by what means they may escape these snares and possess the kingdom of heaven through humility. And if we wish to complete the course of our contest and reach eternal blessedness, let us first beware of evil desire and diabolical pride, and strive with all humility to follow in Christ’s footsteps. If someone serving an earthly emperor struggles to obey all his commands, how much more ought one who is to serve the heavenly Emperor guard the heavenly commandments?

## CHAPTER XX. The Spiritual Soldier and the Earthly Soldier.

My brother, my brother, rouse your soul to wakefulness, and let no sleep weigh it down. Wherever an earthly soldier is sent, he is ready and prepared, and he cannot excuse himself on account of his wife or children. Much more, then, must a soldier of Christ obey his Lord and Emperor, Jesus Christ, without the impediment of this world, since he redeemed him with his precious blood.

You, the earthly soldier, go into battle against a visible enemy; but the other does not cease fighting daily against an invisible enemy. You strive to fight against the bodies of your enemy, using carnal weapons; but his struggle is against the devil, with spiritual weapons. You carry an iron helmet on your head in battle; but Christ is his helmet. You put on a coat of mail so that you will not be wounded; but he is clothed with the love of Christ in place of a coat of mail.

You cast lances and arrows against your enemy; he strives to direct humility and words of salvation against his enemy. Until you complete the battle, you do not throw away your weapons, lest you be wounded by your adversary; he must never be without weapons, because his enemy is more cunning than yours. Your enemy fights for a time; but his enemy does not cease fighting him for as long as he remains in the body.

Your weapons are laborious and heavy to carry; his weapons are gentle and light. For your earthly labor you receive an earthly gift; but for his spiritual labor he will receive a heavenly reward. You adorn your arms with the ornament of bracelets; he receives from Christ the ornament of virtues as the beauty of his soul. For he always expects a heavenly gift from Christ who casts away the earthly pomp of this world.

Woe to us if we reject from ourselves Christ’s easy yoke and place upon ourselves whatever is grievous and burdensome to our souls to carry; and while we love danger, fall into death.

## CHAPTER XXI. Love of God. How We Are Commanded to Honor Parents. Christ’s Benefits.

Therefore, dearest brother, let us consider who it is who redeemed us with his precious blood, and what we owe him who redeemed us in such great poverty. If we love our earthly parents with such affection, although they endured labor for us for only a short time, ought not our heavenly Father to be loved much more, since he was crucified for us?

Whatever service our parents have rendered us is his benefit. Before we were born into this world, he prepared parents for us by his providence, so that we might be nourished by their service [Note: [Col. 1054] Codex Corbeiensis: “we might be born.”], and he filled our mother’s breasts with milk by which we might be nourished.

Therefore, let us love our Redeemer above all, who fashioned both us and our parents with his own hands; and let us ascribe all the good that is done toward us each day to his mercy, not to our own strength. Scripture commands us to love our parents as our own flesh [Col. 1055], provided that they do not prevent us from approaching the service of Christ; but if they do prevent us, not even burial is owed to them by us (Luke 9:59).

Christ must be loved above our parents, because our parents do not grant us what Christ does. He himself said in the Gospel, “Whoever loves father or mother or children or fields more than me is not worthy of me” (Matt. 10:37). The more anyone loves him, the happier and more blessed that person will become.

For he loved us so greatly that he even deigned to die for us. His hands, which performed very many miracles, were fastened with nails for our redemption; and gall was offered as food to his honey-flowing mouth, from which saving teaching proceeded. He who harmed no one was beaten; he who cursed no one endured insults and curses for us. He suffered all these things so that he might grant us eternal life.

And although he bestows such great benefits upon us, he asks nothing from us except that we love him and preserve our souls and bodies undefiled for him, so that he may always dwell in us and we may remain in him. He does not ask from us gold, silver, cloaks, costly garments, bracelets, fields, or anything of this sort; he seeks us ourselves and desires to rest in us.

## CHAPTER XXII. Love of Neighbor. The Peaceful and the Envious.

Let us therefore approach him so that we may have eternal life. Let us possess within us love of God and neighbor, because whoever loves his neighbor has fulfilled the law; but whoever hates him, on the contrary, is a murderer (1 John 3:15).

Whoever loves his brother has a tranquil heart; but whoever hates his brother is surrounded by a storm. A gentle and kind man, even when he suffers evils, considers them nothing; but the unjust person, hearing even a small word from his neighbor, regards it as an insult.

One who is full of love proceeds with a peaceful spirit and the most serene expression; a man full of hatred walks about in anger. But you, dearest brother, do not cause scandal for anyone in your life. [Leave matters that do not concern you for others to handle; unless asked or questioned, extricate yourself from them; judge pleasing to God alone; and, if you cannot do otherwise, avoid the unjust judgments of others and give room for mercy [Note: [Col. 1055] The words enclosed in brackets are a gloss absent from the manuscripts.].] Do not do what is useful to you, but what is pleasing to him.

What you do not wish to happen to you, do not desire for your neighbor (Tob. 4:16). If you see him conducting himself in good works, rejoice with him and regard his joy as your own; and if he suffers some adversity, consider his sorrow your own [Note: [Col. 1055] The editions add: “and not only grieve with the just, but also sympathize with sinners.”].

Never love your neighbor with a feigned heart, for by such things God is provoked to anger. Whoever embraces peace prepares a dwelling for Christ in the lodging of his mind, because Christ is peace and wishes to rest in peace.

But God utterly abhors an angry, envious, slanderous, lying, or proud man. An envious man is like a ship tossed by the waves of the sea; he is always in turmoil. Like a ravening wolf, he rages pointlessly, remains in misery, and, wasting away, is reduced to nothing. Always filled with fury, he becomes a companion of demons.

A peaceful person possesses a secure mind. He is wholly protected by the army of angels and filled with the fruit of gladness, rejoicing and delighting in the Lord. Everything in him is ordered in peace. He drives away discord and illuminates the secrets of his mind. He will merit the companionship of angels and will possess forever the kingdom of eternal blessedness.

## CHAPTER XXIII. The Virtues of the Soul.

Do not, I beg you, my brother, regard the commandments of God as fables, or as though they had been issued by me, since they have flowed forth from the fountain of our Savior. Let no adversity or prosperity of the world break your soul away from the precepts and commandments of God, or from the love that is in Christ Jesus our Lord.

The virtue of your soul is to love God and hate those things that God does not love. The virtue of your soul is to pursue patience and turn away from all impatience. The virtue of your soul is to guard the chastity both of body and of soul. The virtue of your soul is to despise the empty glory of this world, trample upon all transitory things, and labor during your bodily life for the love of him who redeemed you.

The virtue of your soul is to strive for humility and abhor pride. The virtue of your soul is to restrain and suppress anger and fury. The virtue of your soul is to turn away from all folly and embrace divine wisdom. The virtue of your soul is to subject every delight of the flesh and raise your mind to Christ.

You could easily and very easily have obtained these virtues if you had wished to avoid concern for worldly things and transitory earthly matters, and had placed nothing before the love of Christ.

## CHAPTER XXIV. Pleasing God in All Things.

O my brother, love God with your whole mind, so that you may please him in all your actions. Whoever is joined in marriage hastens to please his wife; much more must a soul redeemed by Christ’s blood please Christ its bridegroom.

For God does not wish to be loved by words alone, but by a pure heart and righteous works, because he is the hearer and examiner not of words but of the heart. Never, I beg you, my brother, let carnal love exclude heavenly love from you. Never, I beg you, let the sweetness of this wandering and wretched world deceive you. Let no bodily beauty seduce you, lest death enter your soul through the windows of your eyes.

## CHAPTER XXV. How Fleeting Are the Delights of the Flesh.

Tell me, I beg you, my brother, what benefit there is in the beauty of the flesh. Does it not wither like grass struck by the heat of summer and gradually lose its former beauty? And when death comes, tell me, I beg you, how much beauty will remain in the body?

Then you will recognize that what you previously loved vainly was empty. When you see the whole body swelling and becoming foul-smelling, will you not close your nostrils so as not to endure the most offensive stench? Where, I ask, will the sweetness of lust and the abundance of banquets then be? Where will be the words of flatterers, which softened the hearts of their hearers? Where will be the sweet speeches that poured bitterness into those who loved them? Where will be immoderate laughter and disgraceful joking? Where will be unrestrained and useless merriment?

This is the end of the beauty of the flesh and of pleasure. “The world will pass away, and its desire” (1 John 2:17).

O how supremely happy a good it is—how exceedingly happy—to love the radiant beauty of Christ, to illumine our breasts with the rays of his splendor, and to drive away every darkness from us! [Note: [Col. 1056] Manuscripts: “our breasts.”]

## CHAPTER XXVI. Slander.

Do not lend your ears to receive the words of slanderers, lest you conceive death in your soul. For the slander of the one who slanders and of the one who willingly listens is food of death for both souls. To conclude briefly, the slanderer and the willing listener carry the devil on their tongue [Note: [Col. 1056] The editions add here: “But listen to the one who complains, if he does not slander, for not every complaint is slander.”].

Avoid, I beg you, the snares of slander from your ears, through which you hear that many have been captured. Ask the Lord for a prudent heart and a vigilant understanding, so that you may discern the words of slanderers. Do not be ignorant of their deceptions and ambushes, and let your foot not enter their nets [Note: [Col. 1056] The passage has been cleansed of a gloss.].

## CHAPTER XXVII. Confession of Sins. How and When Prayer Should Be Poured Out.

All evil vices must be foreign to us, since Christ wishes to be our inheritance. Therefore, because we are uncertain in such matters, let us humbly prostrate ourselves in the sight of our merciful Father and promptly bring our sins into the open, so that our heavenly Father himself may erase them.

And when we have confessed, let us not justify ourselves while praying, lest we depart condemned like that Pharisee (Luke 18:11–12). Let us remember the Publican and pray in such a way that we may deserve to obtain forgiveness for our offenses [Col. 1057]. Let the cry of our heart strike the ears of almighty God, for he will be appeased by a pure mind at the time of prayer.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. The Nature of the Serpent. The Fruit of Prayer.

Let us cast away every wickedness of heart from ourselves and forgive those who sin against us [Note: [Col. 1057] The editions read: “not with a double heart, but with a true one.”].

There is, finally, a kind of serpent which, when it begins to go to drink water, vomits out all its poison before it reaches the spring. You too should imitate this serpent in this respect, according to the evangelical command of our Lord Jesus Christ, where he says, “Be wise as serpents” (Matt. 10:16). Vomit out all the bitter poison of anger and forgive your fellow servants, so that your sins may be forgiven you by the Lord, as the Gospel commands: “Forgive, and you will be forgiven; give, and it will be given to you” (Luke 6:37–38).

And as you wish God to be toward you, so be toward your fellow servant. Whatever work you begin to do, first invoke God and give thanks to him; and when you have completed it, do the same. Invoke God with all your heart, and you will find him; and when you have found him, do not let him go, so that your mind may be joined to him in love.

Practice this, my brother, throughout your life, and offer your pure prayer to Christ the Lord. Do not let the empty thoughts of this world disturb your heart, nor let your mind be dragged in different directions. Remember that you stand in the sight of God, who sees the hidden things of the heart and knows the secrets of your mind.

Therefore, attend watchfully and continually in the sight of God at the time of prayer, so that you may more easily escape the temptation of the devil that threatens you. For if evil and filthy thoughts of this world disturb your heart and compel you to commit something unlawful, they will be driven from your soul by pure prayers and holy vigils.

Prayer is a great defense of the soul. Through the purest prayers, the Lord grants us everything useful, and all harmful things are driven away. And, not to discuss or linger over this longer, just as the flesh is nourished by bodily foods, so the inner person is nourished and fed by divine words and prayers.

Feed your soul, I beg you, with spiritual foods—that is, with faith, hope, love, and the remaining virtues through which you may understand how to love God and keep his commandments—so that when your final day comes, the angels of peace may receive you, rescue you from the power of the devil, and grant you the privilege of enjoying blessed rest in the company of the saints and possessing eternal life with all the saints.

For you know with absolute certainty that the possession of the kingdom of heaven has been promised to you; but take care lest you become excluded from it.

## CHAPTER XXIX. Providing Care for the Household.

I beg you, my brother, I beg you: proclaim to all who are subject to you and to all of good will in your household, from the greatest to the least, the love and sweetness of the heavenly kingdom and the bitterness and fear of Gehenna; and be concerned and watchful for their salvation, because you will render an account to the Lord for all who are subject to you and are in your household.

Announce, command, order, and persuade them to guard themselves against pride, slander, drunkenness, fornication, wantonness, anger, perjury, and desire, which is the root of all evils.

## CHAPTER XXX. That He Should Beware the Evil of Desire.

A greedy man holds his soul for sale. If he finds an opportunity to covet someone’s gold or silver, beautiful garments, or even any woman beautiful in face, he commits murder for nothing; and just as someone pours out water upon the ground, so it is for him to pour out the blood of his neighbor.

Very many souls have fallen into danger of death because of desire, and many were stoned for this at the Lord’s command. Saul was alienated from God because of greed; and finally, expelled from the royal height, he was killed by his enemies (1 Sam. 15).

I could say many things about many people, but a few suffice for the wise. Our Lord and Savior wished to exclude the love of money from the hearts of the Pharisees; but because they were exceedingly greedy, they mocked the Lord’s saving words.

The rich man whom the Lord summoned to the kingdoms of heaven was not permitted to enter by his love of money (Matt. 19:22). The breast of Judas, too, burned with the flame of avarice, so that he handed over the Lord, giver of all good things, into the hands of the wicked (ibid. 26:15).

A greedy man is like hell. For however many hell devours, it never says, “It is enough”; so, even if all treasures should flow into the greedy man, he will never be satisfied.

## CHAPTER XXXI. But Let Him Give Alms from His Own Possessions.

Therefore, my brother, command all who are in your household to beware of this vice. For it is better for someone to give a little from his poverty to the needy than much from unjust acquisition. Let each person give according to what he has. For each of them is required to give only as much as God has granted him; nor does he demand more from anyone than what he himself has given.

Almsgiving from unjust acquisition [Note: [Col. 1058] That is, from things acquired unjustly.] is abominable before God, whereas what has been acquired faithfully is acceptable to him.

There are some who seize what belongs to others and pretend to give alms; while oppressing some, they feign mercy toward others. But if they give from their own labor, it will be pleasing and acceptable to God.

## CHAPTER XXXII. Let Him Do Everything Humbly and Nothing Proudly. Deterring the Household from Vices.

And ask them to act humbly before God in all their works, doing whatever they ought to do, because nothing a person does with pride will be pleasing to God. Whatever is done humbly is acceptable to him.

Let them be humble in all their works, because humility is the sublimity of the virtues; and no one will come to the kingdom of heaven except through humility. The labors, prayers, almsgiving, fasts, and vigils of many years, if they have been brought to completion with pride, are counted as nothing before God.

A humble man is acceptable to God and bears God within himself. We have already discussed the evil of pride at some length; but for the sake of those subject to you, I have found it necessary to include this passage, so that they may learn to raise the shield of humility against the arrows of the devil.

The proud man is hateful to God and like the devil. Although the humble man may be lowly in appearance, he is nevertheless glorious in virtues before God. Though the proud man may appear handsome and distinguished in appearance, he is nevertheless contemptible before God in his works; and his pride and frivolity are always recognized in his words and deeds, in his expression and his manner of walking.

He always desires to be praised by human beings and wishes to be proclaimed for virtues from which he is alien. He cannot bear to be subject to anyone, but always desires to hold the first place among his equals and to ascend to a higher rank. What he cannot obtain by merit, he wishes to seize through flattery and slander [Note: [Col. 1058] The editions read: “through flattering superiors, slandering and envying equals, and despising the humble, he wishes to seize it,” and so forth.].

Just as a ship without a pilot is tossed by the waves, so the proud and frivolous man is carried about, unstable in all his actions. But the humble man considers himself the least of all; and, looking with a gentle expression, he appears eminent before God. When he has done everything, he says, “I am an unworthy servant,” and declares that he has done nothing.

God, however, publicizes his works, brings them into the open, makes his deeds wondrous, exalts him, makes him renowned, and enables him to obtain from God what he asks at the time of his prayers. Humility alone obtains these and similar things from God, because it is the seat and delightful couch of our Lord Jesus Christ, who says, “Upon whom shall I rest, if not upon the humble, the quiet, and the one who trembles at my words?” (Isa. 66:2); and again, “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart” (Matt. 11:29).

Proclaim to your people, I beg you, and say to them: “God resists the proud” and “the anger of man does not accomplish the justice of God” (James 4:6; 1:20). “God himself will judge fornicators and adulterers on the day of judgment” (Heb. 13:4). Concerning perjury: “A man who swears many oaths will not escape sin, nor will plague depart from his house” (Sir. 23:12).

Slander is fornication of the soul. And the Psalmist says, “The one who secretly slanders his neighbor, him I pursued” (Ps. 100:5). The Lord detests discord, as Solomon sang, saying, “There is a seventh thing that my soul detests”: namely, “the one who sows discord among brothers” (Prov. 6:16, 19).

## CHAPTER XXXIII. Receiving the Eucharist. Confession Must Precede It.

These are the foods and drinks of death for our soul. May the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ free us from them and grant us himself to eat, for he said, “I am the living bread that came down from heaven. Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life in himself” (John 6:41, 55).

But before each person receives the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, let him examine himself and, according to the Apostle’s command, eat of that bread and drink from the cup in this manner. For whoever eats the body and drinks the blood of the Lord unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself, not discerning the body of the Lord (1 Cor. 11:28–29).

When we are to receive him, we must first hasten to confession and penance and examine all our actions with particular care. If we perceive in ourselves sins for which we are liable, let us hasten to wash them away through confession and true penance, lest we perish with Judas the betrayer by concealing the devil within us, dragging out and concealing our sin from day to day.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. Sins of the Heart.

If we have thought anything evil or wicked, let us repent of it and hasten to erase it swiftly from our heart. Let us not wish to say, “The sin I thought of is not a great one.” Alas, foolish people! Why do we not understand that, in the sight of the Lord, our thoughts are manifest and open before they proceed into action?

For the Psalmist says, “God searches hearts and reins” (Ps. 7:10); and again, “The Lord knows the thoughts of human beings” (Ps. 93:11). Elsewhere the same Psalmist says, “You have understood my thoughts from afar; you have investigated my path and my course” (Ps. 138:3).

Let us not, I beg you, permit wicked thoughts within us, nor neglect them as insignificant, because “the one who despises small things will gradually fall” (Sir. 19:1). Let us not disregard the serpent’s bite, lest its poison be scattered into our hearts; for although poison is the serpent’s life, it is the human being’s death.

Let us cut away the thorny shoots from the field of our heart, lest they drive deep roots into us. For we know that our heart is the field of our Lord Jesus Christ. Let us cultivate it with heavenly disciplines, and let us not allow weeds to be sown in the field of so great an emperor; rather, let us adorn it with every flower of virtue, because almighty God delights in these things, as it is written in the Song of Songs: “I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys” (Song 2:1)—that is, “I am the beauty of the world, the virginity of the humble.”

## CHAPTER XXXV. The Flesh Must Be Subdued.

Let our flesh always and continually be subject to the soul and serve it like a maidservant serving her mistress. Let us not provide our body with strength for unlawful acts, lest it wage war against our spirit; rather, let the flesh always be subject, so that it may obey the commands of the Holy Spirit.

Nor should we allow the maidservant to grow fat, lest she despise her mistress; rather, let her be devoted to all her commands and services. For just as horses must be fitted with bridles, so our bodies must be restrained by fasts and prayers.

For just as charioteers, if they loosen the reins, are carried over precipices, so the soul, together with the body, if we do not place a bridle upon it, slides down toward the precipices of hell. Let us therefore be good and trained charioteers for our body, so that we may proceed along the right path.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. Extravagance in Food Must Be Avoided.

Excessive food greatly harms not only our souls but also our bodies and brings them to illness. Excessive eagerness for food and immoderate drinking commonly weaken the strength of the stomach; moreover, an abundance of blood and bile, as well as very many illnesses, are contracted through an excess of food.

Just as these things are harmful to soul and body, so moderation in fasting is a remedy for both. Even if not throughout the whole year, at least on the most sacred days of fasting let us, as far as we can with God’s help, avoid the delights of the world and the abundance of food, lest one day—God forbid—tormented in flame, we seek a drop of water and obtain no refreshment.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. The Evils of Drunkenness.

Let us flee drunkenness, lest we fall into the crime of wantonness, because the Apostle commands us not to become drunk with wine, in which is wantonness (Eph. 5:18). God gave us wine for gladness of heart, not for drunkenness.

Let us therefore drink not as much as gluttony demands, but as much as the weakness of nature requires. Let us not, then, turn into a cause of destruction what was given for the healing of our bodies.

Proclaim, I beg you, to those subject to you in your household that many have committed murder and fornication through wine, and have not even shrunk from death; others, through wine, have been seized by demons. Drunkenness is nothing other than a most manifest demon.

The drunkard thinks that he is doing something excellent when he has been brought headlong to destruction. Through drunkenness his mind is armed for curses and insults against his neighbors, his judgment is changed, and his tongue stammers.

Such a man, when he thinks he is drinking wine, is himself being drunk by wine. Very many people have contracted the greatest weakness through wine and have been unable to regain their former strength, because they did not restrain the heat of their appetite.

For just as a fish, when it hurries with eager jaws to swallow bait, suddenly finds a hook inside its mouth, so the drunkard takes into himself wine as an enemy; and it immediately drives him within to every most abominable deed [Note: [Col. 1060] Thus the better manuscripts; they nevertheless have “death” instead of “immediately.” The German manuscript reads: “through wine he takes in an enemy which, dwelling within him, drives him,” and so forth.].

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. God’s Commandments Concern All Christians.

But you, my brother, instruct all your household and those subject to you to conduct themselves soberly, and again, on account of abstinence, not to lift themselves up in pride, but to do everything temperately, justly, piously, and religiously, according to God’s help. For Christ shed his blood not only for us clergy, but also for the entire human race who have been predestined to eternal life; and the kingdom of heaven has been promised not only to us, but also to all his laypeople who keep his commandments with their whole heart.

For it is a great disgrace to the souls of laypeople who say, “What concern is it of mine to hear or learn by reading the books of Scripture, or even frequently to visit priests and the churches of the saints? When I become a cleric, I will do what clerics ought to do.” Why does such a person not understand that he wishes equally to share in bread and wine, in all the good things of this earth, and in the happiness of the kingdom, but does not wish to bear Christ’s yoke with equal labor? What benefit is it for such people to be exalted in one respect in this world and cast down in another; to shine with gold and costly garments on one side, while on the other they are overwhelmed by the miseries and vices of this world?

Let there be no anxiety for you about the person of lay attire [Note: [Col. 1060] The better manuscripts read either “the person of lay attire” or “the person of lay status.” The German version has, “what you have in the status of a layperson.” The Corbie manuscript has, “the person of lay status,” or “to assume the person of a cleric.”], because there is no partiality with God. The heavenly palace is equally open to laypeople who keep God’s commandments, just as it is to clerics and to those endowed with a religious habit. Since there is neither Jew nor Greek, neither slave nor free, but Christ is all and in all, whoever is in his body is great.

Incorporate yourself into his holy body, so that you may be a member of the noblest head. Love your head with your whole heart, and love the members of that head. How can one hand be hostile to the other, or one foot hate the other, or the remaining members fail to rejoice together with their own joint? [Note: [Col. 1060] Most manuscripts read, “if the remaining members did not rejoice together with their joint.” Some have, “if the remaining members do not rejoice together with their joint, they ought to grow,” and so on.] They ought to grow into a perfect man, into the increase of Christ’s body.

Every cleric and layperson who has been redeemed by Christ’s precious blood and baptized with Christ’s baptism [Col. 1061] ought to walk humbly and persevere in the Holy Spirit. For it is of no benefit to answer with words that one is a Christian while denying it by one’s deeds, when one is corrupt in mind and spirit. Concerning such people, Truth itself says in the Gospel: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of my Father who is in heaven will enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew VII, 21). And elsewhere the prophet rebukingly says: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Isaiah XXIX, 13).

For if a city is fortified on one side but destroyed on another, it provides its enemies with access to it. And if a ship is strongly joined together by its timbers but has one plank pierced, it is sunk into the depths by the waves. It is equally fitting for all laypeople, clerics, and monks to have faith, hope, charity, and humility; to serve God with their whole heart; to make a true confession; and to perform worthy repentance. For the most merciful Lord forgives those who flee to repentance.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. Delayed Repentance

But let us not become so confident in the Lord’s mercy that we heap sins upon sins. Nor should we say: “As long as the vigor of our fleshly age lasts, let us pursue our desires, and finally, in old age, let us repent of our evils; for the Lord is kind and merciful, and he will no longer remember our crimes.”

Let us not, I beg you, think in such a way, because it is the height of folly to think such things. It is also impious to wish to demand such permission from God, the beginning of which is to separate from God the person who entertains these thoughts. For impious thoughts separate us from God.

Therefore, I say, let us not think such things, since we do not know on what day we shall die. No human being knows the day of his departure. Not everyone dies in old age; people depart from this world at different ages. And in whatever actions each person is found, in those same actions he will be judged when his soul leaves the body. For the Psalmist says: “No one in the underworld will confess to you” (Psalm VI, 6). Therefore let us hasten to turn to repentance.

## CHAPTER XL. The Thought of Death. The Joys of the Future Life

Let the final day always be before our eyes; and when we rise at dawn, let us not presume that we shall reach evening; and when we lay our limbs down in bed, let us not be confident of the coming of daylight. In this way we shall very easily be able to restrain our body from vices and evil desires.

Let our heart always meditate on the heavenly promises. Let us transfer all the earthly things we possess to the future dwellings of the heavenly kingdom, so that when we have advanced there, we may enjoy heavenly goods.

For we believe that when our soul has been released from the bond of the flesh, if we have lived well and rightly before God, a chorus of angels will immediately come to meet us, and the ranks of all the saints will mingle in our embraces and lead us to worship the true Judge. If, while we live in the body, we do what is pleasing to God, as I have said, then we shall have peace all around us and complete security. We shall no longer fear the fiery arrows of the devil, nor any enemy who desires to shoot at our souls [Note: [Col. 1061] The Colbertine manuscript, by a second hand, reads “to slaughter” instead.]; neither iron, nor fire, nor the fierce face of the torturer, nor hunger, nor thirst, nor any bodily illness.

The flesh will no longer oppose the spirit, nor shall we fear any danger. But when we have cast off the burden of the flesh, then the Holy Spirit will grant us a dwelling in the heavens, for whom we had shortly before made a dwelling within the lodging of our body. We shall await with joy and gladness the day of the future judgment, on which the souls of individuals will receive what they deserve for their deeds.

## CHAPTER XLI. The Punishment of the Damned

On the other hand, sinners and the impious will repent—but in vain. The rapacious and greedy, the proud and adulterous, the angry and covetous, the slanderous and perjured will weep most bitterly, but they will not obtain pardon for their evils. All who have followed the pleasures of their flesh will be held in the greatest mourning; those who have served vices and passions will be in everlasting sorrow and groaning.

And when all these are destined, on account of their crimes and offenses, for the fires of Gehenna, we, if we have pleased God while we are in this body, will receive eternal rewards with the saints. Therefore let us despise all things that are empty and fleeting, so that, through Christ’s mercy, we may deserve to attain such glory.

## CHAPTER XLII. Guarding the Tongue

Let us always turn away from vices and strive toward virtues. Let no superfluous words proceed from our mouth, because we shall have to give an account for idle words on the day of judgment. Nor should we accustom our tongue to curse anyone, since it was created to bless and praise God.

Nor should we acquire the worst habits in any action of ours, or even in our thoughts, because a habit that has been prolonged and confirmed is not avoided or expelled without considerable labor.

## CHAPTER XLIII. Compunction. Perfection Is Not in Years but in Minds

Let us be children in malice and mature men in understanding. In some respects let us show ourselves old, in others young, because it belongs to children to play, but to the mature to mourn. For present mourning produces eternal joy.

Everything immoderate, however, causes the dissolution of the soul and makes it negligent toward God’s commandments. Such a person cannot easily recall his sins to memory; and, forgetting them, he does not stir himself to repentance, and thus little by little he falls away from all good things. Compunction of heart will find no access where vices and evil desires have been immoderate. But where there are tears, there the spiritual fire is kindled, so that it may illumine the mind’s secrets.

Let no love of the world separate us from the love of Christ, and let all our thoughts strive toward the rewards of our future homeland and meditate on heavenly things. This is your glory; this is the perfection of the course of your contest. For a person is called perfect not because he is perfect in age, but because he is perfect in understanding.

A childish age is no hindrance to anyone if he is perfect in mind; nor will an old age be of benefit if a person is childish in understanding. David, when he was both a boy and perfect, had his heart and mind fixed upon the Lord, and for this reason he was chosen as king. Saul, although he was advanced in age, because he possessed malicious wickedness within himself, was expelled from the royal height (1 Kings XVI).

But our Lord and Savior is crucified by the elders, and when he entered Jerusalem he was praised together by children. A tree also, if it has been fruitless for many years, is cut down; but if it is young and fruitful, it is cultivated so that it may produce even more abundant fruit.

Therefore I set forth these comparisons so that neither a young person nor an old person in your household may trust in his salvation or even in his works; but “let the one who boasts boast in the Lord” (1 Corinthians I, 31).

## CHAPTER XLIV. Loving the Company of the Good and Fleeing That of the Wicked

Enjoy the company of mature men, do not turn your ear away from their words, and let your soul delight in their counsel. For the words of people who fear God are words of life, and they are the preservation of the soul for those who willingly hear and attend to them.

As the rising sun drives away darkness, so the teaching of the saints expels darkness from our senses. Avoid, I beg you, proud, envious, slanderous, lying, perjured men who neglect their salvation, who are dead to virtues and rejoice in their own pleasures so that they may lack divine joys.

I do not say that you should have even one such person in your household; wherever you hear that such people exist, avoid them. Have no association or intimacy with such people, and do not wish to converse with them if, through the Lord’s mercy, you are unable to recall them from their error.

For often one diseased sheep pollutes the entire flock, and a small portion of gall turns great sweetness into bitterness. If such a person appears distinguished and noble to you in appearance and speaks sweet words to you, yet acts toward you in deeds that are contrary, his conduct does you more harm than his outward form pleases you through his words. For a person is tested not by words but by virtues.

## CHAPTER XLV. Right Intention

Thus be approved by God, and willingly suffer everything for the love of Christ. When bodily tribulations come upon you, let your spirit not be broken by them, nor let the fleeting things of this world soften the strength of your patience. Rather fear God if you have drawn back from your resolve; and when you recognize that you are guilty of sin, do not be ashamed to turn to repentance, because the one who repents here will not repent at the end.

In all your actions and thoughts please God, and do not strive to please anyone else except for the building up of the soul. In every work that you plan to do, think of God first. If what you are considering is according to God, examine it carefully; and if it is right before God, complete it. But if it is found to be contrary, cut it away from your soul.

Do everything with the counsel of the wise, so that your works and your steps may be directed according to the Lord’s will. In every prayer and supplication, ask that the Lord’s will, not your own, be done in you. According to the Apostle’s command, “pray without ceasing” (1 Thessalonians V, 17), and lift holy hands to God without anger or dispute.

## CHAPTER XLVI. Being Beneficial to Everyone

The Lord is merciful, and he grants mercy to those who hope in him. He did not need mercy who had no sin, who made the angels and set the archangels over them; but so that we might obtain mercy from him, he gave alms.

Almsgiving was not necessary for him to whom all the kingdoms of heaven belong, who established Dominions, Principalities, Virtues, and Powers; rather, he gave it so that by our almsgiving he might make us participants in the kingdom of heaven.

The Lord is patient and peaceable, so that through his patience and peace he might reconcile to God the entire world, which lay in wickedness. Let us also be patient and peaceable, without anger or dispute, if we wish to reach God.

Let us do good to all people—to all, I say, not partially, not to one or two or three, but to all people. For Christ did not suffer only for the saints; he went up onto the cross for sinners, the impious, and the wicked, and by his passion he recalled all of us to life.

God gave the sun, the moon, and the rain, all that grows from the earth, and all the fruits that arise on the land not only to the saints, but commonly to all human beings. He makes his sun rise upon the good and the wicked, and sends rain upon the just and the unjust (Matthew V, 45).

Therefore he gave these things commonly to all people so that our goodness, our almsgiving, our charity, our patience, and our humility might likewise be distributed commonly to all people. As long as we are in this world, let us do good to everyone, especially to those who belong to the household of faith (Galatians VI, 10); let us pray for our enemies and return good for evil.

## CHAPTER XLVII. The Rewards and Labors of the Just

Let us honor the poor and receive Christ in them, who said: “As long as you did it for one of the least of these my brothers, you did it for me” (Matthew XXV, 40). Then we shall be sons of God, heirs of God, coheirs with Christ, and participants in his kingdom (Romans VIII, 17), where we shall never die and shall not grow old; where there is no human frailty [Note: [Col. 1063] That is, fragile and miserable.], nor any pain, nor sadness after joy, nor the light of the sun, nor the splendor of the moon and stars. Rather, our Lord Jesus Christ will be light, health, life, charity, peace, joy, and every good thing for all who believe in him.

There is the land of the living, which the prophet celebrated when he said: “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living” (Psalm XXVI, 13). That is, he indicates that he will see the heavenly reward [Note: [Col. 1063] The manuscripts read this way. Perhaps “of the living.”] and live and reign with Christ forever [Col. 1064]. There no night breathes, no day will come to an end, no poverty will be seen, and no desire will appear; instead there will be everlasting joy and eternal gladness.

These are the promises made to the just, and these are the promises for which they labored and hastened, and did not cease to run in good works as long as they were in this world: in fasts, almsgiving, chastity, continence, long-suffering, patience, gentleness, goodwill, great labor, prayers, persecutions, hunger and thirst, cold and nakedness, and many vigils for the love of Christ. In every respect they avoided useless vigils.

Vigils are useless when someone remains awake over many shameful thoughts, or to undertake something contrary, or to perpetrate a crime. Such vigils they avoided and took up holy vigils. These people trampled upon the present world in order to gain the future kingdom.

They did not receive here the promises or the miserable riches of this world, which, when people use them badly [Note: [Col. 1064] The manuscripts read “them” rather than “these.”], lead them to hell. Leaving this present homeland, they sent the gaze of their soul ahead to the heavenly city whose architect and founder is God.

They avoided sin in word, deed, thought, sight, laughter, movement, the nodding of the eyes, the hands, the feet, anger, quarrel, fury, dissension, empty glory, pride, arrogance, and greed, guarding their bodies and their souls.

## CHAPTER XLVIII. Fasting and the Twofold Food

For they fasted with two fasts at once—that is, the fasting of body and soul—by abstaining from anger, fury, slander, blasphemy, and quarrel. For, as we have already explained above, these are the soul’s deadly foods; they feed it toward evil and kill it with everlasting death.

Again, the following are foods of both body and soul: gluttony, sleepiness, fornication, drunkenness, security, pleasure, and murder. These are foods of both body and soul: they nourish the body but kill and burden the soul.

Let us avoid these foods and desire heavenly nourishment that may draw and lead us to heaven—namely, divine wisdom, strong faith in Christ, kindness, goodwill, patience, humility, virtue, and divine joy.

## CHAPTER XLIX. The Punishments of the Wicked

Let good and excellent words proceed from our mouth, seasoned with divine salt, for the building up of those who hear. Let us always meditate in our minds upon the love of God and neighbor, on which the whole Law and the Prophets depend (Matthew XXII, 40), and fulfill it in our works.

These are Christ’s commandments, which he orders us to do. If we do them, we shall share in his kingdom and reign with him; but if we do not do them, he himself will not give us his kingdom. If we deny him, he too will deny us. If we do not believe, he will remain faithful, because every unbeliever acts unfaithfully, while both “it is a fault in a person to believe everything” and “it is a fault to believe nothing” [Note: [Col. 1064] Seneca, Letter 3.] [Note: [Col. 1064] The printed editions add here: “and especially always to speak evil of an enemy; for otherwise, if these words seem harsh to them, perhaps he nevertheless remembers that he is a Christian and weeps as guilty before God. Whispering, however, is always speaking evil of an enemy; but if you speak good of him, you immediately put him to shame. For such words never create concord but discord; they throw wood into the fire.”].

With the greatest care and vigilance we must ensure that on the day of judgment we do not hear from Christ, the Judge of all, what sinners will hear: “Go into the eternal fire that has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (the same, XXV, 41).

For Gehenna has truly been prepared for the devil, and not for all human beings, if we do not perform the devil’s works. Woe to those for whom have been prepared the pain of worms, the burning of flame, thirst without quenching, weeping and gnashing of teeth, tears of the eyes, outer darkness without light, and an unending punishment; where there is no honor or recognition of one’s neighbor, but continual pain [Col. 1065] and groaning; where death is desired but not granted; where there is no honor for elder or king, no master over slave, no mother loves son or daughter, and no son honors his father; where every evil, every indignation, stench, and bitterness abound.

The just feared these things and fled from them. I ask, I beseech, and again I entreat you, dearest brother, that we too may love and fear God and flee from these things, because our soul’s death is everlasting if we persevere in them.

## CHAPTER L. Three Worst Things Here, and as Many Best Things

There are three things in this world worse than every evil: the soul of a sinner persevering in sin, which is blacker than a raven; the evil angels who snatch it away; and the hell to which it is led. There are no three things worse than these.

That same soul, trembling at the fear of future judgment and looking upon its own corruption, says: “My scars have rotted and become corrupt because of my foolishness” (Psalm XXXVII, 6).

Again, there are three things than which there are no better in this world [Note: [Col. 1065] The manuscripts read: “three things in this world are not better than the soul,” and shortly afterward, “there are none better than these three.”]: the soul of a saint persevering in good works, which is more beautiful than the sun; the holy angels who receive it; and the paradise to which it is led, together with the expectation of the heavenly kingdom.

There are no better things than these three in this world. For the holy angels delight the soul with spiritual song, as the Psalmist says:

“Blessed is the one whom you have chosen and taken up, O Lord; he will dwell in your tabernacles. We shall be filled with the good things of your house. Holy is your temple, wondrous in righteousness.”

## CHAPTER LI. Here We Must Labor

Let us meditate on these things, dearest brother. Let us hold them firmly in our mind, and guard ourselves from every sin and iniquity—in word, deed, thought, hands, feet, sight, and hearing—and let us guard our body and soul.

For Christ our Lord, who is God and the Son of God, descended from heaven to earth so that he might carry us with him from earth to heaven. For us sinners he went up onto the cross so that he might free us from the devil’s torment. He accepted punishment from his enemies so that he might free us from everlasting punishment. He accepted death so that he might rescue us from death. He rose from the dead so that we might rise in soul and body on the great day of judgment.

Therefore, while we have time, let us labor and, with God’s help, always strive to do good works that please God, lest, suddenly overtaken by the day of death, we seek time for repentance and be unable to find it.

While we are in this present time, we ought to sow; for in its proper season—that is, after death or on the day of judgment—we shall reap what we ought to possess in eternal life. Here, then, let us labor and bear one another’s burdens. For where the head has gone before, the remaining members will also follow.

## CHAPTER LII. On Faith, Hope, and Especially Mutual Charity. Redeeming Sins through Charity

Through confession and the punishment received from a priest. Let us hold, as has already been inserted above, right faith, certain hope, and perfect charity, because faith is like our sense, and charity is like our health [Note: [Col. 1065] So also Sermon 105, Appendix, volume 5, sections 4 and 5.].

Faith believes, charity acts, and hope strengthens. Although different members have different functions, if all the members are held together by the unity of charity, then they will deserve to follow the head. For our head is in heaven. Truth itself, our Lord Jesus Christ, says of his faithful: “If anyone serves me, let him follow me; and where I am, there my servant will be also” (John XII, 26).

Let us beware, and beware in every respect, lest through envy, hatred, slander, anger, and quarrel we be cut off from our head, Jesus Christ. Whatever evil we and our neighbors endure for the love of Christ, let us share in it with charitable affection; and whatever good someone else receives, let us rejoice as though we had received it, and give thanks on behalf of the one who received it [Col. 1066].

Look: as we have said, someone suffers tribulation or loss in this world; or, by order of imperial authority, he is shut away in prison for his offenses; or he is saddened by the death of parents or friends. If we grieve for him, we are established in the body of the Church; if we do not grieve, we have already been cut off from the body [Note: [Col. 1066] The printed editions add here: “But alas! Sometimes we pretend to be severe, cast fuel into the flame, and when the fire has been kindled, we flee.”].

Charity, which gathers and gives life to all the members of the Church, immediately cuts us off from the body if it sees us rejoicing at another’s downfall. Perhaps, then, we do not grieve over the downfall of our neighbors because we have been cut off from the body. For if we were there, without doubt we would grieve. [Note: [Col. 1066] See Sermon 105, Appendix, volume 5, section 5.]

Let us consider, dearest brother, and attend carefully to this: a member suffers as long as it remains in the body; but if it has been cut off, it can neither suffer nor feel. When a hand or some other member has been cut off from the body, even if the entire body is then divided into many parts, that hand does not feel, because [Note: [Col. 1066] One manuscript and Sermon 105, Appendix, volume 5, read “because.”] it has already been separated from the fellowship of the remaining members.

Such is every Christian who not only does not grieve over another’s loss, affliction, or even death, but, what is worse, perhaps even rejoices. And because he is already alien from the body, he does not retain the affection of charity in his heart, although the Apostle commands: “Rejoice with those who rejoice, weep with those who weep, having the same feeling toward one another” (Romans XII, 15–16). Solomon also very clearly warns us not to rejoice at the downfall of our brothers (Proverbs XVII, 5).

But we, my brother [Note: [Col. 1066] The printed editions add: “wretched people, rejoice at the downfall of our enemies and mock them; and if he does not fall, we desire that he fall in punishment for us. But let us pray to God.”], if we wish to preserve true and perfect charity, should strive to love all people as ourselves, so that, since Christ is our head, we may deserve to be his members. Then, when Christ our glory appears, we too may deserve to appear with him in glory through the harmony of charity—that is, through love of God and neighbor—as his true and perfect members, loving all people as ourselves, without any deceit of malice or envy.

For he himself says in the Gospel: “By this all will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” (John XIII, 35). Love of neighbor does no evil.

O dearest brother [Note: [Col. 1066] From the cited sermon, section 5], if our Lord and Savior, who had no sin, deigns to love us sinners with such affection and such love that he testifies that he himself suffers what we suffer, why do we, who are not without sin and who can redeem our sins through charity, not love him with such perfect love, when he loved us so greatly that he even handed over his own Son to death for us sinners?

And since he has shown such great kindness and mercy toward us, let us keep watch lest we lose the good he has given us, and the sacrament of our baptism, in which [Note: [Col. 1066] The manuscripts read “that.”] we swore to renounce the devil, his pomps, and all sins.

And if after baptism we transgress in some sin, the merciful God has given us a second baptism—that is, a fountain of tears—and has appointed repentance for us because of our weakness. Therefore we ought truly to confess our sins and perform fruits worthy of repentance; that is, we must not repeat past sins, according to the command of the God-fearing priest.

The priest, as a wise and perfect physician, should first know how to cure his own sins and afterward wipe away and heal the wounds of others, and not make them public. [Note: [Col. 1066] These words are expressed in imitation of the Rule of Saint Benedict, chapter 46.]

Let us seek out such priests, if we can, and take counsel for our salvation with people of this kind, so that we do not lose the heavenly inheritance [Col. 1067] that the Lord prepared for us from the beginning of the world, if we serve him in justice, holiness, purity of heart, and sincere charity, crying out with the Apostle: “Who will separate us from the charity of Christ? Tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or the sword?” and the rest that follows.

As it is said: “Neither death nor life, neither angels nor principalities, neither things present nor things to come, nor any creature will be able to separate us from the charity of God that is in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Romans VIII, 35, 38–39).

For it was said of the primitive Church that “they were of one heart and one soul in the Lord” (Acts IV, 32), and that they had one will in what they desired and one will in what they rejected, because the charity of Christ had joined them together as one.

## CHAPTER LIII. The Designs of the Wicked. Almsgiving from Unjust Profits

By contrast, the worldly and lovers of this world separate and divide themselves from one another, bringing upon one another scandals, quarrels, anger, disputes, dissensions, murders, perjuries, thefts, robberies, and everything that each one loves.

Each one delights in saying in his heart: “I will do what I want and what I can” [Note: [Col. 1067] The printed editions read: “I have my lord as a friend and defender; no one opposes me; meanwhile I will do what I can.”]. “I will fulfill my thoughts and the pleasures of my body. My plans, or those of my friends or powerful relatives, support me” [Note: [Col. 1067] The printed editions add here: “I will oppress whom I wish and harm whom I wish.”]. “I have gold; silver is abundant” [Note: [Col. 1067] The printed editions add again here: “My eloquence surpasses everyone; whom should I fear?”]. “I have male and female servants, fields, and many possessions of this world—cloaks, costly garments—by which I can redeem myself. I will fulfill my desire; God will grant me time of life and repentance.”

Alas, why do we not fear what the Gospel thunders terribly, saying: “Fool, this night they will demand your soul from you; and whose will those things be that you have prepared?” (Luke XII, 20).

Let us recognize that we are human beings, and let us not become so proud against God and our neighbor that we fulfill our evil desires and put God second; nor should we strive to bend the Lord’s good will toward our evil purposes by means of gifts, while neglecting to correct our perverse will according to the Lord’s ever-righteous will.

But wherever it pleases us, we wish to avenge our injuries, saying [Note: [Col. 1067] The printed editions read: “and we do not spare our brother, saying: ‘I will take revenge on my brother or my father; I will do it,’ and so on.]: “I will commit murder, perjury, adultery, and fornication; and afterward I will give my redemption to the Lord.”

Why do we not understand that when we sin so boldly, imagining that God can be appeased by gifts, we then provoke him much more to anger than to mercy? For God does not delight in gold or silver, nor does he ask anything else from us except that our souls be presented clean in his sight.

He does not involve himself in the counsels of sinners; rather, for the sake of our salvation he always warns us and gives salutary counsel, because he himself is the counselor of our salvation, as the prophet says: “And his name shall be called Wonderful, Counselor” (Isaiah IX, 6).

Again, it is said of him in the Psalm: “Blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly” (Psalm I, 1). And again: “For there is no iniquity in him” (Romans IX, 14).

And perhaps that which we think we are doing for our own benefit—giving alms from the estates of the dead or from the plunder of the poor—appears to be almsgiving in name but not in deed [Note: [Col. 1067] The manuscripts read “which” rather than “that.”].

What sort of almsgiving is it when one person is unjustly clothed and another unjustly stripped; when one is unjustly fed and another is unjustly tormented by hunger? God does not ask these things from us. I dare to say that almighty God hates them.

Hear what he says through the prophet: “The one who offers sacrifice from robbery or from the substance of the poor is like one who sacrifices a son in the sight of his father” (Ecclesiasticus XXXIV, 24). “I will not accept these things from your hands,” he says; “for your hands are full of blood” (Isaiah I, 15).

Another prophet says: “The bread of the needy is the life of the poor; whoever defrauds him is a man of blood” (Ecclesiasticus XXXIV, 25).

Let us refuse to give unjust alms, since we wish to give just and spiritual alms. Let us give from just labors, not from robberies, or from the multiplication of crops, or from dishonest business dealings, lest many sacrileges perhaps be incurred in this [Note: [Col. 1068] The better manuscripts read “lest they incur sacraments” (or “sacred obligations”).], or, what is worse, lest blood be shed out of greed or drunkenness and the voices of those afflicted by great labor cry out against us to God.

Thus the Psalmist says: “The one who has not given his money at interest and has not accepted gifts against the innocent,” together with the rest that was mentioned above in the same psalm, which can make blessed the hearer, believer, and one who takes heed. As the same psalm concludes: “The one who does these things will not be shaken forever” (Psalm XIV, 5).

## CHAPTER LIV. Christian Happiness Is Not Earthly
Since the Creator of all things announces and impresses such teachings and others like them upon His rational creature, let us believe that the Creator loves what He created: He persecutes no one unless that person persecutes himself; He withdraws from no one unless the person first withdraws from Him; and He hates not the nature within us, but the vice we have contracted. Nor does it profit us—indeed, it harms us—to have been redeemed by Christ’s blood and voluntarily to be subject to the devil. Therefore let us think and think again that we became Christians not for earthly happiness. Not for the riches of this age, nor for the sake of this present life, do we worship Christ.

[Note: [Col. 1068] The printed editions add here: “For not all who are happy in this age will be happy in the future, nor will all who are unhappy in this age be unhappy in the future. Nor for the sake of…”]

As the Apostle says: “If in this life only we hope in the Lord, we are more pitiable than all men” (1 Cor. 15:19). For Christ, so that we would not love gold, taught us to reject offered gifts; so that we would not fear hunger, He fasted for forty days; so that we would not dread nakedness, He forbade His disciples to possess another garment besides one tunic; so that we would not be terrified by tribulations, He Himself endured everything; so that we would not fear death, He Himself accepted it. And when He had taught us all these things, He Himself went before us not only in word but also by example.

May this burn sweetly in our hearts; may the fire of the Holy Spirit make it fervent within us, so that we may follow His footsteps and not desire to remain in this world and perish with this world. Alas, how miserable we are if we refuse to believe this and do not recall our minds from love of this age, while we cannot possess these things forever and through security lose those other things! What shall we do? What shall we undertake? We must mourn if we lose the promised kingdom, and if it is suddenly said to us: “O you lovers of the world, go out to meet the Bridegroom and come to Him whom you do not wish to see, because you have put His commandments second. For you will see the very wounds that He bore in His body for you.”

What shall we say then, groaning and grieving? And what shall we answer when our merits demand retribution from Him, since we often heard and neglected what the Psalmist sang: “What shall I render to the Lord for all that He has rendered to me? I will receive the cup of salvation and call upon the name of the Lord” (Ps. 115:12–13). Let us hold firmly that the hope of good things is not placed in this world. Although worldly hope may appear to exist, it is turned into bitterness; and the world itself offers its lovers a bitter drink. Truth itself also addresses them, saying: “Where is what you loved? Where is what you considered so important?”

## CHAPTER LV. The loss of souls is greatly to be mourned.

O my brother, are our fleshly bodies made of iron, so that they do not tremble? Or is our understanding made of adamant, so that it does not soften—or even awaken—to such words of God? Why do we not say with the prophet: “Who will give water to our head and a fountain of tears to our eyes, that we may weep day and night for the wounded children of our people” (Jer. 9:1)?

[Col. 1069] The eyes of those who consider not only the deaths of bodies but also the deaths of Christian souls fail from weeping. What mourning could be more fitting, what lamentation more certain [Note: [Col. 1069] Supply, “than.”], than when each of us grieves and sorrows over a lost soul with the Apostle, who said: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I am not burning?” (2 Cor. 11:29). Again, in another passage, sympathizing with the love due to our neighbors, he says: “I could wish that I myself were accursed from Christ for the sake of my brothers” (Rom. 9:3).

Let us learn from so great an Apostle of Christ to burn with such great love for Christ, since he knew that God “did not spare His own Son, but delivered Him up for us all” (Rom. 8:32). He says, “for us all.” Therefore no layman, no cleric, no consecrated virgin, and no widow should neglect the salvation of their souls, since it is evident that so great a price of blood was poured out for us.

## CHAPTER LVI. Conversion without delay. Predestination. To merit grace through humility. To despise earthly happiness.

Therefore, all of us who remain upon the earth, let us acknowledge our sins, lest we perish with the ungodly because we do not quickly appease Him with worthy satisfaction. How quickly did the man who said the following appease His anger: “I acknowledged my sin, and I did not hide my iniquity. I said, ‘I will confess my iniquity against myself to the Lord’” (Ps. 31:5). He promises that he will confess, and he is already forgiven.

[“Pay attention, my brother: this is a great matter. He said, ‘I will confess’; he did not say, ‘I confessed, and You forgave me.’ For by the very fact that he said, ‘I will confess,’ he showed that he had not yet confessed—but he had confessed in his heart. To say, ‘I will confess,’ is itself to confess; therefore You also forgave the wickedness of my heart. My voice was not yet in my mouth; my confession, therefore, had not yet reached my lips. I had said, ‘I will confess against myself’; nevertheless God heard the voice of my heart. My voice was not yet in my mouth, but God’s ear was already in my heart.”]

[Note: [Col. 1069] The words enclosed here in brackets are a gloss absent from the manuscripts.]

And what followed? “And You forgave the wickedness of my heart.” God is always ready to forgive our sins, provided that we do not delay in returning to Him. If we delay, let us fear lest He bring His anger upon us.

[Note: [Col. 1069] The manuscripts read, “lest He bring His anger within us.”]

For He predestined some to punishment and bestowed a great benefit upon others—not unjustly, however, but according to His profound judgment. Cain committed murder, while Job, though wounded, became God’s friend; Abel, though innocent, was killed by his brother. Yet He neither allowed Job to suffer torment longer, nor granted Ananias an opportunity for forgiveness, nor abandoned Paul when buffeted, whom He made strong by His grace; nor did He accept Judas when repentant, nor abandon Peter when weeping, nor regard Saul when repentant, nor despise David when confessing.

[Note: [Col. 1069] The words “nor did He regard Saul when repentant, nor despise David when confessing” are absent from the manuscripts.]

And thus, in His profound judgment, the merciful and compassionate Lord separates the vessels of wrath from the vessels of mercy. O if only we would consider miserable Judas, once a perfected vessel, brought to destruction! He could not bear the new wine of the Holy Spirit; upon receiving it, he immediately burst, and, completely shattered, was useful for nothing.

[Note: [Col. 1069] The manuscripts read “which, having been received”; and shortly afterward, “and completely shattered.”]

Fearing these things, let us turn—let us turn while there is time. For the Psalmist says: “Seek the Lord while there is time, and be strengthened; seek His face always” (Ps. 104:4). It is time for us to be restored. And if we have been broken by some sin, we have the almighty God as potter and craftsman. Let us believe that He is able to restore what has been lost, since He created all things whole. For He Himself says: “As the potter’s clay, so are you in My hand” [Col. 1070] (Sir. 33:13).

Therefore let us humble ourselves under the hand of almighty God, so that He may exalt us at the time of visitation. Let us consider that we stand in God’s presence. Let us acknowledge what we are; let us acknowledge that we are earth and ashes, since the prophet also speaks against us: “Why is earth and ashes proud?” (Sir. 10:9). If we do not acknowledge this, we wish in vain to exalt our necks, since God resists the proud and gives grace to the humble (James 4:6).

“Be comforted, you humble,” says your God; “be comforted, you fainthearted; be strengthened, and fear no longer. Behold, your God will repay judgment; He Himself will come and save you” (Isa. 35:4).

## CHAPTER LVII. In times of distress, to flee to Christ the shepherd.

“The Lord is near; be anxious about nothing” (Phil. 4:5–6). Let the world’s unhappiness terrify us not at all, because if all the saints had feared this worldly unhappiness, they would not possess everlasting happiness. If the fleeting happiness of this world is loved, everlasting happiness is not found here. But if everlasting happiness is sought, since it is not found here, let us strive toward everlasting happiness, where we have our homeland and our parents. Let us endure with the greatest patience everything in this world for Christ’s name.

What, I ask, is there to endure in comparison with what is promised to us? The Apostle says: “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that will be revealed in us” (Rom. 8:18). Therefore let no distress terrify us; let no calamity break us. The Lord is near; our shepherd is around us. What shall we fear?

And if we are afraid, let us cry out to our shepherd, so that He may hear us. Let us cry out with contrition of heart, saying: “I have gone astray like a sheep that is lost; seek Your servant, Lord” (Ps. 118:176). Let us cry out and say: “Deliver my soul from the sword, and my only life from the hand of the flesh; save me from the lion’s mouth” (Ps. 21:21–22). Let us cry out and say: “Flight has perished from me, and there is no one who seeks my soul. Shall I look to the left? Behold, the devil roars like a wolf; like a lion, he gnashes his teeth.”

[Note: [Col. 1070] The manuscripts read, “Behold, the wolf roars like the devil.”]

“Behold, there is a wolf; the dog barks against it. I cried to You, Lord; I said, ‘You are my hope, my portion in the land of the living’” (Ps. 141:5–6). “Deliver me from the hands of my enemies and from those who persecute me.”

Surely our good shepherd, who laid down His life for His sheep, will not, if we cry out to Him, allow us to wander longer or to be torn apart and devoured by wild animals. Far from it. Indeed, leaving the ninety-nine, He went to seek the one lost sheep. And He did not go merely because He heard it crying, but before it cried out. For the Evangelist says: “Leaving the ninety-nine, he went to seek the one sheep that had perished; and when he had found it, exhausted and weary, he placed it upon his shoulders and carried it back to the flock” (Luke 15:4–5).

The shepherd graciously carried it back to the flock upon his shoulders and, by his mercy, recalled it from its wandering. Since the Lord carried this sheep back to the flock upon His own shoulders, how great is the gratitude we owe to His mercy and grace, since He humbled and bent Himself down so far toward us? He carries and refreshes; He guides and guards.

## CHAPTER LVIII. The shepherd’s aid is sought against the devil. When we shall be freed from every evil.

We beseech You, good Lord, supreme and excellent shepherd: do not let the sheep perish; fulfill the office of the supreme shepherd. Pursue the lion that has snatched the sheep from Your flock; let the lion be killed and the sheep torn from his jaws, for You are the shepherd of the sheep. Our powerful King, crush Satan beneath our feet.

And now, Lord our shepherd, our king, so many sheep are daily snatched from Your flock—why are You so silent? Answer: why are You silent? Behold, Your sheep are dragged over various precipices, and Your enemies, who hate You, lift their heads against You; yet You are silent. O Lord God, why are You silent for so long?

At this the Lord cries out through the prophet and says: “I was silent, I was silent, but [Col. 1071] I will not always be silent” (Isa. 42:14). My hand will execute judgment.

Therefore, Lord Jesus, our shepherd, our king, take up Your weapons and advance, so that You may fight against our adversary, the lion, who goes about seeking to devour us (1 Pet. 5:8). Be for us a tower of strength against the face of the enemy. We ask, and we ask most urgently, that You free us.

For the world lies in the power of evil. Behold, evils rage and the world’s lovers perish. They blaspheme, rage, and murmur against You; they not only fail to implore Your mercy, but even criticize Your judgment. Who works such things in them except the author of evil, the proud and ruined angel who desires to destroy everyone?

Deliver us, Lord God, from every evil, and let our portion be with every good thing. Deliver us from every evil, because we are delivered from every evil when we are separated from the devil and his angels. His angels are those who do his will. Let us have no portion with such people, who do the devil’s will, but with Him who said: “Whoever does the will of My Father is My brother, sister, and mother” (Matt. 12:50).

For we have been redeemed by His price.
