Fleeing the company of the wicked, let us seek what is good, cling to the supreme Good, serve Him, and do His will, so that we too may be God’s angels, of whom the prophet says: “Bless the Lord, all His angels, His ministers who do His will” (Ps. 102:20–21). For it is the will of our Father, as the Gospel says, “that one of His little ones should not perish” (Matt. 18:14), and that we should not perish and be torn from the righteous way (Ps. 2:12).

## CHAPTER LIX. The works of darkness and the weapons of light.

Let us lay aside the works of darkness and put on the weapons of light (Rom. 13:12). When the darkness of night has been driven away and the shadows of darkness expelled, let the ray of true light shine in our hearts.

[Note: [Col. 1071] The manuscripts read, “the roots of darkness.”]

In the night, let us perform not the works of night but the works of day, because we have been called children of the day. Let our understanding not grow numb through the pleasure of sleep; let our souls not be deceived by empty phantasms; and let rest not bend our bodies, weighed down by the warmth of their bedding, into deep torpor. Rather, by keeping watch, praying, fasting, and singing psalms, let us fight against the adversary, the devil, and feel the great light poured into our hearts, performing the works of day in the night.

For what should we do in the dark night of this age except drive away the devil and bring in Christ? What should we do in the blindness of this night except take captive the captor and follow the liberator? What should we do in the night except shake the devil’s darkness from our hearts and draw in the true light? What should we do in the night except uproot pride and bring in humility? What should we do in the night except drive from us the ruler of all vices and receive the fountain of all good things?

Let us receive Him, dearest brother; let us receive Him, so that we may also be received by Him and see what good things we possess, prepared by Him who calls us daily. Let us receive His yoke, which is easy, and His burden, which is light, for He lifts the burden of our sins. Let us lay aside the works of darkness and put on the weapons of light.

For what is it to lay aside the works of darkness except to renounce the devil’s pomp and his angels? And what is it for us to put on the weapons of light except to believe in God the almighty Father, who has enlightened every person coming into this world, and who also said: “While you have the light, believe in the light, so that you may be children of light” (John 12:36)?

Yet first, beloved, if you wish—indeed, because you wish—let us examine and investigate who and what the devil is.

## CHAPTER LX. Who the devil is. How many good things he took from man, and how many evils he brought upon him.

The devil is an angel separated from God through pride, who did not stand in the truth, and a teacher and father of falsehood; for falsehood was first invented by him, and he himself is falsehood (John 8:44), as our most truthful Lord Jesus Christ, Truth itself [Col. 1072] [Note: [Col. 1072] In the editions of Erasmus, Lyons, Venice, and Louvain, “most true truth.”], speaks in the Gospel of John. For he is the head and end of falsehood; deceived by himself, he hastens to deceive us.

He became the adversary of the human race, the inventor of death, the founder of pride, the king of malice,

[Note: Thus the Colbertine manuscript. Other manuscripts read, “the root.”]

the head of crimes, the prince of all vices, and also the persuader of shameful pleasures.

When he therefore looked upon that first man made by God—namely Adam, the father of us all—and, as you can frequently understand from what was said above, saw that this man had been formed from the clay of the earth in the image of God, adorned with chastity, ordered by temperance, surrounded by charity, and clothed with immortality, he—rivalrous and envious that an earthly man had received such blessedness, which he himself, while an angel, is known to have lost through pride—an insatiable murderer, immediately envied our first father, us, and our parents. He stripped us of such and so many good things and moreover killed us.

For at the very beginning the devil stripped us of many good things: chastity, continence, patience, gentleness, charity, and immortality. Thus he made us naked and wretched, mocked us as though we were wrapped in his rags, bound us under his dominion, and through that very bond subjected all our offspring to himself.

He stripped us of chastity and girded us with immodesty; he stripped us of temperance and made us intemperate; he stripped us of charity and clothed us in malice; he stripped us of immortality and offered us death. In these most shameful and foul rags he wrapped us and our descendants and left us half-alive.

## CHAPTER LXI. How willingly we must renounce him and flee to Christ.

Since the most savage enemy has acted so miserably toward us—indeed, because he has acted so—come, dearest brother, come: let us renounce this destructive inheritance. We have become orphans. Before the collector of so evil an inheritance arrives, let us renounce everything that belongs to it.

If anyone therefore neglects to renounce this inheritance, in which the devil’s rags are found—namely, his pomp and his angels—when the judge comes, he will be handed over to the creditor, as the Gospel says, and the creditor will thrust the debtor into prison. “Amen, I say to you,” says the Lord, “you will not leave there until you have paid the last quadrans” (Matt. 5:26).

Divine Scripture therefore commends the entire human race, as poor and orphaned, to God, saying: “To You the poor man is left; You will be the helper of the orphan.” And, pointing out his adversary, the devil, it adds: “Break the arm of the sinner and the wicked” (Ps. 10:14–15, according to the Hebrew).

May our Lord Jesus Christ, compassionate and merciful, be present, and show some mercy to this orphan and poor man, since he suffers a crafty and ferocious adversary and, already an orphan, is failing in his own cause. Therefore his adversary hastens to deceive him by wicked arts.

Be present, Lord Jesus Christ, as a capable defender of this orphan. Stand in the cause of the one who commanded that the children of men be judged rightly. Raise Your arm and break the arm of the sinner and the wicked. You know very well the case of this poor man and orphan—that is, of the human race—which is owed on account of the paternal bond. He has been found guilty and is held bound by the adversary. There is no other way for us to be helped except through Your counsel and most necessary aid. Judge our cause; defend us, because You are powerful.

## CHAPTER LXII. The demon as accuser in the judgment.

O my dearest brother, how happy is the soul that has so powerful a defender! Therefore, I ask, let each of us now keep watch, lest on the day of judgment the devil recognize his rags in him and the one whom Christ wished to free by His grace begin to be held perpetually guilty.

Let those who refuse to be corrected after receiving grace and return again to their former desires not flatter themselves falsely. For the day of judgment is awaited, and that most just judge will be present, who will show no regard for the person of any powerful man. [Col. 1073] No bishop, abbot, or count will be able to corrupt His palace with gold and silver.

All souls will stand there, so that each may render an account according to what he did in the body, whether good or evil (2 Cor. 5:10). The adversary, the devil, will indeed be present. The words of our profession will be recited, and he will cast into our face everything we did: on what day we sinned, in what place, and what good work we ought to have done at that time.

And if we are found to be such people, that adversary will exult in the presence of the most compassionate judge, declaring himself superior to us as he brings such a case before such a judge. For then the devil himself will have this to say:

“Most just judge, judge that this man is mine on account of his guilt, since he refused to be Yours through grace. He is Yours by nature; he is mine through misery. He is Yours because of Your passion; mine because of my persuasion. He was disobedient to You and obedient to me. From You he received the robe of immortality; from me this ragged tunic in which he is clothed. He lost Your garment and came here wearing mine.

“What business did immodesty have with him? What business did intemperance, avarice, anger, pride, and the rest of my members have with him? He abandoned You and fled for refuge to me. I see my sisters accompanying him.

“What, indeed, was he doing on that account?

[Note: [Col. 1073] Morel considers that *in circo* (“in the circus”) should be read here. See *Elementa Critica*, p. 315.]

“What was he disputing with pride? Why did he rage with anger? He is storing up wrath for himself on the day of wrath.

“Most just judge, judge,” he says, “because righteousness and judgment are the preparation of Your throne. Judge that he is mine and must be condemned with me. I recognize that all these things which he brought here are mine. He wished to be mine and desired what was mine. He must be punished with me, since the one whom You graciously chose to free at so great a price afterward willingly bound himself to me.”

[Note: [Col. 1073] The printed editions read, “Why, then, was he doing all these things?”]

Alas, alas, dearest brother! Will such a person be able to open his mouth, when he is found there in such a condition that he is justly assigned to go with the devil?

## CHAPTER LXIII. How dangerous relapse is.

Let us see what we are doing; let us see how we may be freed from him. Let us see and beware lest we receive God’s grace in vain. Rather, with an undivided heart and perfect faith, let us renounce and reject so destructive a diabolical inheritance, lest we remain orphans and poor.

Let the terrifying sentence of the blessed Apostle, uttered with terrible force, be proclaimed in our midst, so that it makes both our hearts and bodies tremble. For he says:

“If we sin voluntarily after receiving knowledge of the truth, no sacrifice for sins remains for us, but a certain terrifying expectation of judgment and the fury of a fire that will consume the adversaries. Anyone who rejects the law of Moses dies without mercy on the testimony of two or three witnesses. How much worse punishment, do you think, will be deserved by one who has trampled upon the Son of God, regarded as polluted the blood of the covenant by which he was sanctified, and insulted the Spirit of grace? For we know Him who said, ‘Vengeance is Mine; I will repay.’ And again, ‘The Lord will judge His people.’ It is terrible to fall into the hands of the living God.”

And a little later:

“Therefore do not lose your confidence, which has a great reward. For you need patience, so that, doing the will of God, you may receive the promise. For yet a little while, and He who is to come will come and will not delay in repaying each according to his work” (Heb. 10:26–31, 35–37).

These words flowed forth not from me but from Him who said: “Do you seek proof of Christ speaking in me?” (2 Cor. 13:3).

Let us extend the gaze of our heart’s eye and see; let us apply the ear of our heart to perceive and investigate the Apostle’s terrifying sentence. Let us cleanse the eye of the heart—or rather, let the very light we desire to see cleanse our heart, and, by His mercy, let it be purified from the darkness of sins. For He says: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:8).

Let this labor not be useless to our destruction but useful to our salvation. Let us run while we have the light, lest darkness overtake us (John 12:35). Again the Apostle urges us most earnestly, saying:

“Raise up your slackened hands and weakened knees, and make straight paths for your feet, so that no limping person may go astray but rather be healed. Pursue peace with all people, and holiness, without which no one will see God. Take care that no one be lacking the grace of God, lest any root of bitterness springing up cause trouble and through it many be defiled.”

And a little later:

“See that you do not refuse Him who speaks. For if those who were unfaithful to God’s word did not escape, refusing Him who spoke on earth, much more shall we not escape if we turn away from Him who speaks to us from heaven”—

[Note: [Col. 1074] Thus the manuscripts. The Vulgate reads, “if we turn away”; the printed editions, “if we heed.”]

—“whose voice then shook the earth, but now He promises, saying, ‘Yet once more I will shake not only the earth but also heaven.’ And the phrase ‘Yet once more’ declares the removal of things that can be moved, as things made, so that those things which cannot be moved may remain. Therefore, receiving an unshakable kingdom, let us have grace, by which we may serve God acceptably with fear and reverence. For our God is a consuming fire, which will consume the adversaries” (Heb. 12:12–15, 25–29).

Let us approach Him before we are consumed by Him, asking Him to burn our heart and our inward parts. Again: “For You have tested us, O God; You have examined us by fire, as silver is examined” (Ps. 65:10). For it is entirely clear that if we are not burned by Him here, there we shall be consumed like adversaries.

The Apostle says: “Let no one deceive himself; let no one mislead himself with empty words, because whatever a person sows, that he will also reap” (Eph. 5:6; Gal. 6:8). Let us not speak one thing with our tongue and another in our heart, lest we be like Judas and the Herodians: some in betrayal, some in confession, some in dissimulation.

[Note: Thus the Colbertine manuscript. Other manuscripts read, “some in destruction, some in confusion.” The printed editions read, “some into destruction, some into confusion, some into dissimulation.”]

Rather, let us be in the humility of truth. Therefore, with a true heart, let us hasten toward the fullness of faith, our hearts sprinkled clean from an evil conscience. Let us hold unwaveringly to the confession of our hope, and let us not abandon the beginning of good works, as is the custom of some. Instead, let us encourage one another—and all the more as we see the day of judgment approaching.

## CHAPTER LXIV. The flesh receives the devil. The one power he received over it. The flesh is strong for evil but pretends weakness for pious works. The flesh is like a war against the soul. It provokes every evil and prepares eternity for itself and the soul.

Let us trample down the pride of our flesh, because it is the flesh that destroys the soul and brings complete pride. As the Apostle says: “He who sows in the flesh will also reap corruption from the flesh” (Gal. 6:8).

The flesh is what receives the devil. For the devil sows his seeds in our flesh: murder, fornication, desire, lust, anger, quarrelling, drunkenness, pride, theft, and every evil suggestion. The Apostle says: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against the spirits of this flesh, against the spiritual forces in the heavenly places” (Eph. 6:12). He speaks of the devil, who is an evil spirit and is not seen.

And this most wicked spirit was cast out of heaven with his angels, of whom it is said in Revelation: “Behold, the accuser of our brothers has been cast out, who accused them day and night; and they conquered him because of the blood of the Lamb” (Rev. 12:10–11).

Of him the Apostle says: “There was given to me a thorn of my flesh, an angel of Satan, to buffet me. For this I besought the Lord three times, that it might depart from me; and He said to me, ‘My grace is sufficient for you, for power is made perfect in weakness’” (2 Cor. 12:7–9).

Again, repeating himself, he says: “I see another law in my members, fighting against the law of my mind and taking me captive in the law of sin that is in my members.” Again he says: “With my mind I serve the law of God, but with my flesh the law of sin” (Rom. 7:23, 25). And again: “There is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ” (Rom. 8:1).

It is the flesh that receives the devil, and the devil has power over the flesh, not over the soul. Therefore the Apostle says: “There was given to me a thorn of my flesh [Col. 1075]”; he does not say, “of my soul,” but “of my flesh,” an angel of Satan.

Finally, Job was tested by the devil in his flesh, as the Lord says: “And power was given him by the Lord over his possessions and his flesh.” And again: “I will give him into your power, except for his soul” (Job 1:12; 2:6).

For the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh. These oppose one another, so that you do not do whatever you wish (Gal. 5:17). The flesh is a wretched beast that weighs down the soul, as the Apostle says: “Those who are in the flesh cannot please God” (Rom. 8:8).

Again, Truth itself, our Lord Jesus Christ, says of Himself: “The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak” (Matt. 26:41). For our flesh always wishes to be powerful in wickedness, but in abstinence—that is, in fasting, vigils, prayers, and good works—it pretends to be weak.

It is our flesh that plunges us into the pit, as the Apostle says: “Put to death your members that are upon the earth”—that is, fornication, impurity, anger, quarrelling, and the other things that follow (Col. 3:5). And again: “Do not make provision for the flesh in its desires” (Rom. 13:14).

Therefore let us put our flesh to death through abstinence, fasting, vigils, and prayers, lest it bring the devil upon us with evil desires.

The flesh has been given to us as a kind of war against the soul. If it is put to death, it brings life; if it is nourished, it prepares itself for war against the soul. I praise the person who is able to have power over his flesh.

While we fear the weakness of our flesh, we neglect the salvation of our soul. O miserable soul, what do you say, when the flesh weighs so heavily upon you? Solomon says: “The corruptible body weighs down the soul”; and again he repeats: “The lying mouth kills the soul” (Wis. 9:15; 1:11).

Woe, woe to the miserable soul pursued by the flesh! Our flesh fights against the soul every day, and we must fight against the flesh every day, as the Apostle commands: “If you live according to the flesh, you will die; but if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the flesh, you will live” (Rom. 8:13).

The flesh desires and displays every evil suggestion. The flesh desires all evil; the flesh urges crimes; the flesh provokes anger; the flesh provokes murder; the flesh provokes adultery and quarrelling; the flesh inserts drunkenness; the flesh carries every evil desire of this age; and the flesh desires every evil.

O cruel beast, flesh, what do you possess? Why do you burden the soul, which would have desired nothing except to serve God if it had not joined itself to you, its enemy? But you, wretched flesh, kill not only yourself but also the soul. Your own destruction is not enough for you; you still wish to plunge the soul into hell.

Woe to you, soul, that you have received flesh as an adversary, which neither enters itself nor permits you to enter the kingdom of heaven. O evil flesh, what do you seek? What do you desire? You do not wish to endure labor; you do not wish to rest from agitation. You suffocate the soul so that, in a reversal of roles, you may be the mistress and it the slave.

I ask: why do you burden the soul, which is not troublesome to you? Nor will you escape punishment while it suffers Gehenna, for it cannot be judged on the day of judgment without you.

Why do you not consent to the spirit and to our soul, as the Gospel urges you, saying: “Be reconciled with your adversary while you are with him on the way”—that is, in this world—“lest perhaps he hand you over to the judge”—that is, to Christ—“and the judge hand you over to the officers”—that is, to the evil angels—“and the officers cast you into prison”—that is, into Gehenna. “You will not leave there until you have paid the last quadrans” (Matt. 5:25–26), that is, the smallest sin.

## CHAPTER LXV. The evils of the flesh. The soul’s prayer to God.

What are you, and what do you provide for us, except harm to our soul?

[Note: [Col. 1075] The manuscripts read, “Who are you?”]

Whoever nourishes you nourishes you for the doing of evil, because the soul does not sin except through the flesh, as it is written: “The soul that sins shall itself die” (Ezek. 18:4).

For example, you say: [Col. 1076] “How can the soul sin, since it is not seen? What can it fear, since it itself cannot be held?”

[Note: [Col. 1076] Thus the better manuscripts. Two manuscripts, together with the printed editions, read “What can it hold?”]

It is the flesh that sins, the flesh that burdens the soul; and, overcome by the flesh, the soul consents to the flesh in sins.

For the flesh is headlong toward lust, shameless toward wantonness, frequent in debauchery, immodest toward fornication, daily piling crime upon crime and sin upon sins. It does not cease joining worse things to the worst: cruel in will, vain and foolish, always inclined toward evil, but excusing and most sluggish toward good; swift toward death, difficult toward life; hating the works of light and loving darkness above all.

For it loves to fall and neglects to rise; salvation is bitter to it and destruction sweet. It is always falling from evil into worse and flowing from worse things into the worst; restless and impatient, surrounding the soul with the flames of Gehenna, thrusting itself among the shoots of greed and avarice, vanity and arrogance, anger and impatience, and the other wickednesses. It weighs itself down with what is excessive and dishonorable,

[Note: Thus the manuscripts. Perhaps the reading should be “with things overflowing and dishonorable,” or, as in a second hand in the Theoderician manuscript, “toward what is excessive and dishonorable.”]

drawing itself away from heavenly things and delighting in earthly things.

It abandons truth and hastens to drink in vanity and words of falsehood. And what more need be said? As a moth devours wool, and as fire consumes wood, hay, and straw, so rebellious and pampered flesh consumes and burns up the soul.

What do you say to these things, soul? What do you answer to these things?

“I will say to my Redeemer,” it says, “before I am stripped of the flesh: what answer should I give to these things, and toward what good should I have wished to urge the body in which I dwell?”

Let there not be in me, I beg you, O Lord, any lustful desire; but let love of the most beautiful chastity dwell within me. Let me be slow to hear evil, quick for your word, and eager to accomplish it [Note: The Colbertine manuscript has “alert.”]. Let me be solicitous in your fear, perfect in love, steadfast in faith, and in no way doubtful in hope. Let me burn with love of my neighbor, but not be consumed by the heat of hatred or waste away through the pallor of envy.

Always breathe into me the desire to think upon a holy work; compel me to do it. Persuade me to love you, strengthen me to hold fast to you, guard me lest I lose you. Let there not enter or rest in my dwelling—where your habitation ought to be—the foot of pride or the desire of gluttony, fornication or avarice, envy or anger, sadness or vainglory. But I ask from you profound humility, you who said, “Upon whom shall I rest, if not upon the humble and quiet?” and so forth (Isa. 66:2).

Give me profound humility, by which the height of the flesh and the pride that suffocates me may be bent down. Give me measured abstinence, by which the belly’s excessive greed may be restrained—the greed that destroys me. Give me purity of heart, which may render me undefiled. Give me cleanness of spirit, because the unclean lust of the flesh drags me down. Give me a willing generosity for distributing alms, by which grasping avarice may be rejected. Give me the love of charity, by which the zeal of envy may be extinguished. Grant me the patience of endurance, through which cruel anger, that savage beast, may be overcome and weakened. Grant me hope of eternal joy, by which the bitterness of sadness may be sweetened.

Make my mind inwardly glory in you because of a good work, so that no boastfulness of vainglory may proceed outwardly from me. Grant me also to maintain justice, magnanimity, and temperance in all things. Make simplicity prudent in me, so that I may live a blessed life sincerely and prudently avoid evil; so that I may be able to understand the devil’s fraudulent and deceitful cunning, lest he deceive me under the appearance of good [Note: The printed editions add, “and lest I be deceived by anyone, or deceive anyone”]; and so that I may be able to discern rationally and foresee what good I should do and what evil I should avoid.

After this, make me gentle, kind, peaceful, meek, modest, without pretense, in agreement with all good people, and constantly diligent in vigils, fasts, and prayers. Grant me also moderated speech in gentleness and the attainment of silence, so that I may speak what is fitting and keep silent about what ought not to be spoken—or whatever you may deign to bestow from the fruits of virtue.

Grant me to preserve an immaculate faith toward you without any error, and let my works be worthy in accordance with the faith [Note: The Colbertine manuscript has “worthy”]. Let me not pollute right faith by wicked conduct; let me not deny you by living badly, whom I confess by believing rightly; and let me not offend you by negligent deeds, whom I follow in action with energetic faith.

Make me, while living in a holy calling, pursue justice, love mercy, cherish truth, reject falsehood, devise or speak nothing false; fear you without ceasing, love you, cherish you, keep your commandments, and retain peace with everyone without deceit [Note: The printed editions add, “not oppress subordinates, and regard myself as a sinner above all”]. Let me summon those who are divided to reconciliation without pretense; offer sincere charity to all; scandalize no one; prefer myself to no one, but judge myself inferior to everyone; show reverence and honor not because of fear of the powerful, but for the sake of the Most High; offer obedience to elders and charity to equals [Note: The printed editions add, “resist Christian princes and authorities in nothing, but obey them in everything”]; show the grace of timely affection to the young [Note: Here again the printed editions add, “display a fatherly disposition”]; and bear the burdens or dangers of brothers with equanimity [Note: They also add here, “love a friend as my own soul and love my neighbor as myself”].

Let me benefit everyone together and harm no one; injure no one, oppose no one, slander no one, place an obstacle before no one, judge no one, speak evil of no one, be injurious to no one, criticize no one’s life, investigate no one’s path; but be concerned only for myself. Let me in no way repay evil for evil, be in no respect mindful of my injuries or seek vengeance for them; but overcome malice in every goodness. Let me prepare a blessing for one who curses me; love an enemy as a friend; endure the insults and abuse of angry people without returning them; quickly forget injuries; forgive my offender; and always be ready to grant pardon.

Let me not desire what belongs to others, nor take it on any pretext; but let me mercifully distribute what is mine to those who do not have it. For your sake, because you redeemed me, let me keep food with me for the hungry and then refresh him; give drink to the thirsty; receive the stranger; clothe the naked; visit the sick; seek out the imprisoned; console the sad; sympathize with the afflicted and mourning; provide necessities to those who lack them; and divide food and clothing with the needy. Let me embrace the native-born, cherish the member of my household, love the foreigner, ransom the captive, receive the newcomer, protect the orphan and fatherless, support the widow, aid the oppressed, provide help to the abandoned, and break the bonds of wickedness.

Let me carefully believe and hear whatever teachings your commandments declare [Col. 1078], investigate them ardently, know them wisely, practice them promptly, fulfill them eagerly, and always remain humble before you. Let me rise and not be cast down; be lifted up and not collapse; ascend and not descend, because the flesh with which I dwell always wants to lead me into sin. It wants to be crowned with me, but not to struggle alongside me. I suffer no worse enemy than the body in which I dwell. For it is like a destructive lion in my house, tearing me apart and consuming me on every side with its poisonous bite.

Therefore, drawing long sighs, I shall cry out: “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death? The grace of God. Through whom? Through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Rom. 7:24–25).

These are what I desire, O good Jesus, Savior, excellent Redeemer—these are what I desire, which up to this point I have now begged for in prayer; these and these things I entreat because I have been redeemed by your most precious blood: that because of the corruption of the flesh I may not perish forever, may not come into the second death, nor into the land of forgetfulness.

May this voice of mine sound in the ears of your mercy, so that I may do your will, not the will of the flesh; and may my entire mind meditate upon you, delight in you, follow you, and confess you, because in redeeming me your mercy is eternal, and in your mercy I, lost through the sins of my youth [Note: The printed editions and the Victorinus manuscript read, “I came back to life, having been lost, and rose from the dead, because you separated me from my sins”], came back to life and did penance before you. For you preserved for me a time of conversion; when I considered my sins, I was pierced with remorse, and by your inspiration I did penance before you.

Now and always I joyfully render innumerable thanks to you, because, in order that I might find you, you first sought me; in order that I might return to you, you compelled me; in order that I might be scourged, you looked upon me like a merciful father; in order that I might confess, you acted within me; and in order that, recognizing myself, I might weep, you gave me the gift.

“Place my tears in your sight, O Lord” (Ps. 4:9), and may my prayer reach you in heaven. Be present, I beg you, and help me; and receive me, commended to you in your hands. Deliver me from the mouth of the most savage dragon and from the hand of the most terrible hell.

When you have received me and taken me away from the midst of the shadow of death, or rather, lead me into the path of light, into the most radiant region of the living. Place me in the safest sheepfolds of your flocks, because you are the good shepherd who seeks and brings back what is lost, protects and saves what has been found, cherishes and heals what is sick.

And you are the merciful Lord, who do not put to shame those who hope in you, do not abandon those who seek you, and do not reject those who return to you; rather, you receive them with exultation and praise, and grant them to reign eternally in eternal blessedness together with your saints and elect. For to you, with the eternal Father and the Holy Spirit, belong one divinity, glory, might, dominion, and power forever and ever. Amen.

Erasmus’s edition in the preceding book differs less from the manuscripts; here we indicate no editions other than those that arose from the Louvain recension.

## [ON THE TWELVE DEGREES OF ABUSE]

[Col. 1077]

### PREFATORY NOTICE TO THE FOLLOWING TREATISE

This treatise has also been published among the works of Cyprian, on the authority of several ancient books whose false attribution deceived the early writers who cite it under Cyprian’s name: Jonas of Orléans, in book 3 of his work *On Royal Instruction*, in volume 5 of the *Spicilegium*; Ivo, book 8; and Gratian, book 23, question 5, chapter “The King.” A smaller number of manuscripts, however, attribute it to Augustine, as does a certain more recent Victorinus.

Hincmar also published a book on the same subject, still lying hidden, but very different from this treatise. This is clear from Flodoard’s words concerning it, book 3, chapter 18:

“He also wrote, for the instruction of that king, concerning the Twelve Abuses, collecting in them the sayings of the holy fathers and the constitutions of former kings; and he also admonished him concerning his promise, which before he was consecrated king he had made by word and writing to the nobles and bishops.”

Jonas, who transferred the ninth degree from the following treatise into his own book, which we have mentioned, was writing several years before Hincmar.

Pamelius testifies that he saw a book in which this treatise was attributed to Augustine, but which in the margin bore the substituted name of a certain Ebrard.

In the Victorinus and Corbie manuscripts the following is written above the treatise:

“These are the twelve abuses of the world: a wise man without works; an old man without religion; a young man without obedience; a woman without chastity; a lord without virtue; a contentious Christian; a proud poor man; an unjust king; a negligent bishop; a people without discipline; a populace without law. By these twelve abuses justice is suffocated. These are the twelve abuses of this world, through which the wheel of the world is deceived if it is caught in them, and by the just judgment of God is rolled toward the darkness of Tartarus, with no aid of justice to impede it.”

[Col. 1079]

# ONE BOOK ON THE TWELVE DEGREES OF ABUSE (C, G, S)*

## FIRST DEGREE: A WISE MAN WITHOUT WORKS

The first degree of abuse is when a wise man and preacher is without good works: he neglects to fulfill in his actions what he teaches in his speech. Hearers disdain to carry out the words of instruction when they see the preacher’s works differing from his preaching. The authority of a preacher is never effective unless he fixes it in the listener’s heart through the result of his work—especially since the teacher himself, if he has fallen into love of vices, thinks little of applying another teacher’s medicine to his own wounds.

Thus the Lord himself, wishing to instruct his disciples equally in doctrine and good works, warned them what caution they should exercise regarding these things, saying: “But if the salt has lost its savor, with what shall it be salted?” (Matt. 5:13). That is: if the teacher has gone astray, by what teacher will he then be corrected? And: “If the light that is in you is darkness, how great will the darkness be?” (ibid. 6:23). For if the eye has ceased to perform the task of seeing, who will demand that service from the hand, the foot, or the rest of the body?

Therefore teachers should consider that they may be subjected to a greater punishment if they provide an even more abundant occasion of destruction to many people [Note: The printed editions add, “of morals”]. Solomon himself, when he fell into transgression despite his great wisdom, brought about the dispersion of the kingdom of the entire Israelite people solely through his own guilt. Therefore those to whom much is entrusted lose greater things if they have not rightly administered the gifts of their ruler [Note: The Corbie manuscript reads “benefactor”] that they received. For from the one to whom more is entrusted, more is required. And the servant who knows the will of his master but does not do it will be beaten with more severe blows and heavier punishments (Luke 12:47).

## SECOND DEGREE: AN OLD MAN WITHOUT RELIGION  
### Two things in a human being that do not grow old

The second degree of abuse is when an old man is found to be without religion: although the limbs of the outer man grow old in him, the powers of the soul—that is, the limbs of the inner man—do not receive increases of strength. For it is more fitting than for anyone else that old men devote themselves to religion, since the flowering age of the present world has passed away and abandoned them.

Just as among trees that rejected tree becomes evident which does not display excellent fruit to its cultivator after its blossoms, so among human beings that man is rejected whose flower of youth has abandoned him, yet who thinks little of producing mature fruits of good works in the old age of his body. For what could be more foolish than for the mind not to hasten toward perfection when the condition of the entire body, worn out by old age, is rushing toward destruction?

While the eyes grow dim, the ears hear with difficulty, the hair falls out, the face changes to pallor, the fallen teeth diminish in number, the skin dries up, the breath smells unpleasant, the chest is constricted, [Col. 1080] the cough rattles, the knees tremble, and swelling inflates the ankles and feet, the inner man, who does not grow old, is also weighed down by all these things. All of this swiftly foretells that the house of the body is already about to collapse.

What therefore remains, except that, while the decline of this life approaches, every old man should desire to think of nothing other than how he may quickly gain access to the life to come [Note: The Corbie manuscript has “the future access to prosperity.” In Cyprian, “a future dwelling prosperously”]?

For young people the uncertain end of this life stands imminent, but for the old the departure from this light is more mature and closer. A person must therefore beware of two small members that do not grow old in his flesh and that drag the whole person with them into sin—namely, the heart and the tongue. The heart never ceases to devise new thoughts; the tongue speaks busily whatever it perceives the heart to have devised.

Let old age therefore beware lest these rejuvenated members deceive its entire harmony and mock the gravity of the rest of the body through foolish things. Everyone must consider what is worthy of an advanced age, so that he may do what makes neither life, nor age, nor office contemptible.

## THIRD DEGREE: A YOUNG MAN WITHOUT OBEDIENCE  
### In four ways “father” is used

The third degree of abuse is a young man without obedience, through whom the world is corrupted from the right order of reason. For how will one hope to be served in old age who, in youth, refuses to show obedience to his elders? Hence the ancient proverb says: “He cannot rule who first refuses to render service to someone.”

For this reason the Lord Jesus, during the time of his flesh, while he had not yet reached the lawful age of a teacher, obediently rendered service to his parents (Luke 2:51). Just as sobriety and perfection of character are required in the old, so in the young fitting service, submission, and obedience are rightly owed.

Therefore the first commandment among those that concern human beings orders the honor of father and mother (Exod. 20:12). For although one’s bodily father may no longer be alive or may have been unworthy, it is nevertheless shown that filial honor must be offered by children to any worthy and living father until they reach a mature and worthy age.

In the divine Scriptures “fathers” are called by four designations: by nature, by nation, by admonition, and by age.

Jacob speaks of his natural father to Laban: “Unless the fear of my father Isaac had been present, you would have taken away everything that is mine” (Gen. 31:42). A person is called a father by nation when the Lord spoke to Moses from the bush: “I am,” he said, “the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob” (Exod. [Col. 1081] 3:6).

A person is called a father by age and admonition when Moses says in the song of Deuteronomy: “Ask your father, and he will declare it to you; your elders, and they will tell you” (Deut. 32:7).

Therefore, if one’s natural father is not alive or is unworthy, a young man must nevertheless offer obedience to an older man who gives admonition. For how will one appear honored in old age who has not endured the labor of discipline in youth? Whatever a person has worked for, that he will also reap. All discipline, in the present, does not seem to be a matter of joy but of sorrow; afterward, however, it yields the most peaceful fruit of righteousness to those trained by it (Heb. 12:11).

Just as fruit is not found on a tree on which neither tendril nor blossom has first appeared, so one cannot attain legitimate honor in old age who has not labored in youth through the exercise of some discipline. How, then, can discipline exist without obedience? A young man without obedience is therefore a young man without discipline, because obedience itself, which is the mother of all disciplines, requires great exercise. It took its rule of conduct from Christ the Lord, who, obedient to the Father even unto death, willingly endured the shame of the cross (Phil. 2:8).

## FOURTH DEGREE: A RICH MAN WITHOUT ALMS  
### Things that cannot return love are not to be loved

The fourth degree of abuse is a rich man without almsgiving: he does not distribute to the needy and to those who possess nothing the excesses of his use, which he stores away to be preserved for the future. Thus, while he carefully guards what he has sought on earth, he loses the everlasting treasure of the heavenly homeland.

The Lord Jesus invited the rich young man who had asked him about perfection to that treasure by answering him: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell everything you have and give to the poor, and come, follow me, and you will have treasure in heaven” (Matt. 19:21).

No human being can ever possess that treasure unless he provides comfort to the poor or is himself poor. Therefore, do not let what can benefit a poor person lie dormant in your treasures. For although a rich man has amassed much, he cannot possibly enjoy it all by himself, because the nature of one human being cannot make use of many things [Note: Perhaps “cannot suffice for many things”].

What, then, is more foolish than, for the sake of one person’s food and clothing, to lose the entire delight of the heavenly kingdom and undergo the eternal torments of hell without the expectation of consolation? Whatever must at some time be lost by necessity should be distributed voluntarily in exchange for eternal recompense. For “the things that are seen are temporal, but the things that are not seen are eternal” (2 Cor. 4:18).

As long as we are temporal, temporal things serve temporal needs; when we have passed from here, eternal consolations will be provided by eternal things. Therefore we ought not to love what we will not always possess—especially since a greedy rich man without reason is revealed by his treasure, his field, and everything he has: with the whole gaze of his heart he loves things that never love him.

If someone loves gold and silver, fields and clothing, food and metals, and brute animals, the nature of things itself shows that none of these can return love in exchange. What, then, is farther from reason than to love what cannot love you, and to neglect the one who lovingly provides everything for your authority?

For this reason God commands that the world not be loved, but that one’s neighbor be loved (Matt. 22:39), because one’s neighbor can return love, whereas the world plainly cannot. Thus the Lord commanded that an enemy be loved (ibid. 5:44), so that this love might make that person a friend instead of an enemy.

Therefore, if any greedy rich man wishes to possess eternal riches, let him temporarily lose the riches that will not remain by distributing them to the needy. For if he does not sell what he loves, no one can buy what he desires.

The greedy are therefore called accursed at the judgment by the most righteous Judge, because those who passed by their dwellings did not say, “The blessing of the Lord be upon you; we have blessed you in the name of the Lord” (Ps. 128:8) [the wording as transmitted is difficult here]. Wretched, therefore, are greedy rich men, who fall into eternal damnation for the sake of transitory things. Conversely, “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matt. 5:7). Blessed is the merciful person, since in this virtue God seeks not wealth but disposition.

## FIFTH DEGREE: A WOMAN WITHOUT CHASTITY  
### Chastity is twofold: of body and of mind

The fifth degree of abuse is a woman without chastity. Just as prudence provides for and guards all good conduct in men, so chastity nourishes, fosters, and guards every honorable action in women.

Chastity guards purity, restrains avarice, avoids quarrels, mitigates anger, checks lust, moderates desire, chastises wantonness, avoids drunkenness, does not multiply words, attacks the desires of gluttony [Note: Cyprian has “purifies”; the Corbie manuscript has “cleanses thoroughly”], and utterly condemns theft. What more need be said? It restrains all vices and nourishes every virtue and everything praiseworthy before God and good people.

An immodest life expects neither praise from human beings in the present age nor recompense from God in the future. A chaste life, however, possesses a good reputation among human beings and rejoices in hope of future blessedness. It makes itself worthy of imitation by those now living and leaves behind for posterity a beloved memory. It always delights in and agrees with good morals, and it invigorates the soul through constant meditation on and recitation of the Scriptures. It preserves the examples of those who preceded it in goodness and forms inseparable companionships with the perfect.

The practice of true chastity therefore consists in two ways: in the condition and outward appearance of the body, and in the inward disposition of the soul. Through the outward way, following the Apostle, we provide examples before human beings; through the inward way, we perform good works before God.

Chastity of body means not desiring what belongs to others; avoiding every impurity; not wishing to taste food before the proper hour; not provoking laughter; speaking neither vain nor false words; maintaining an orderly appearance in all things and a fitting arrangement of both hair and clothing; not entering into companionship with the unworthy; looking at no one with a haughty gaze; not allowing the eyes to wander; not walking with a pompous or seductive step; appearing inferior to no one in undertaking a good work; inflicting insult or shame on no one; blaspheming no one; not envying the good; not mocking the old; not disputing with one’s better; not discussing matters one does not understand; and not saying everything one knows. These things make a person lovable to neighbors and acceptable to God.

Chastity of soul means doing every good thing more for the eyes of God than for those of human beings; restraining the desires of shameful thoughts; considering everyone better than oneself; envying no one; trusting nothing in oneself; always entrusting everything to God’s help; placing oneself before God’s eyes; not defiling one’s understanding with heretical perversity; agreeing in all things with Catholics; clinging to God alone; offering the chastity of one’s inner mind to the Lord Jesus Christ; bringing every good work begun to completion only at death; thinking little of present tribulations through strength of spirit; loving nothing on earth except one’s neighbors; establishing the treasure of all one’s love in heaven; and hoping for recompense from God in the heavenly places for every good deed.

Chastity is the ornament of the noble, the exaltation of the humble, the nobility of the ignoble, the beauty of the lowly [Note: Elsewhere, “the weak”], the prosperity of those who labor, the consolation of those who mourn, the increase of every beauty, the adornment of religion, the defense against crimes, the multiplication of merits, and friendship with God, the creator of all.

## SIXTH DEGREE: A LORD WITHOUT VIRTUE  
### Three things necessary for those who rule  
### Some become better, others worse, in positions of dignity

The sixth degree of abuse is a lord without virtue, because possessing the power to rule accomplishes nothing if the lord himself does not possess the firmness of virtue. This firmness of virtue, however, requires not so much the external strength—which is itself necessary for secular lords—as the inward strength of soul, which must be exercised through good morals.

The virtue of ruling is often lost through negligence of spirit, as is shown to have happened in the case of Eli the priest. Because he did not restrain his sinful sons through the severity of judgment, the Lord did not spare him in punishing them, as though he had consented to their wrongdoing (1 Sam. 2:27–36).

Those who rule must therefore possess three necessary things: fear, order, and love. Unless a lord is loved and feared, his rule cannot stand. Through benefits and graciousness, therefore, he should ensure that he is loved; and through just punishments—not for personal injury, but for the sake of God’s law—he should strive to be feared.

Moreover, since many depend upon him, he must cling to God, who appointed him to leadership and strengthened him as though he were stronger, so that he might bear the burdens of many. A stake, unless it is well fixed and attached to something stronger, quickly lets everything hanging upon it fall; and once loosened from the firmness of its stability, it falls to the ground together with its burdens.

So too, unless a prince clings tenaciously to his Creator, both he and everything he contains quickly perish. For some draw closer to God through the office of ruling, while others become worse through the dignity imposed upon them.

After receiving leadership of the people, Moses spoke with God more familiarly (Exod. 33:11). Saul, son of Kish, however, after receiving the royal scepter, offended God through the pride of disobedience (1 Sam. 15:11). After King Solomon succeeded to the throne of his father David, God endowed him with the gift of wisdom beyond all mortals, as though for the governance of an innumerable people (1 Kings 3:12). Conversely, Jeroboam, Solomon’s servant, after seizing part of the house of David’s kingdom, diverted the ten tribes of Israel that were in the region of Samaria to the worship of idols (ibid. 12:27–30).

These examples clearly show that some grow toward greater perfection in a higher position, while others descend into worse things through the arrogance of domination. From both cases it is understood that those who rise to better things can do so through strength of spirit and God’s help, while those who turn toward worse things go astray through weakness of mind together with negligence.

Therefore it is not fitting for a lord to be without virtue, and he cannot possess virtue in any way without God’s help. Whoever protects no one, if he does not have strength of spirit, cannot accomplish this; for great persons commonly struggle with great assaults and adversities.

Everyone who presides over others should therefore first strive with the full attention of his soul not to doubt God’s help at all. If, in his actions, he begins to have the Lord of lords as his helper, no human being will be able to hold his rule in contempt: “There is no power except from God” (Rom. 13:1).

For he raises the needy from the dust and makes him sit with the princes of his people (Ps. 113:7); and he casts down the mighty from their seat and exalts the humble (Luke 1:52), so that the whole world may become subject to God and all glory may stand in need of God [Note: Elsewhere, “so that all glory may be raised up”].

## SEVENTH DEGREE: A CONTENTIOUS CHRISTIAN  
### Causes of contention  
### Whether anything in the world ought to be loved

The seventh degree of abuse is a contentious Christian: although he has received participation in the name of Christ through faith and Baptism, contrary to Christ’s words and purpose he loves the fleeting delights of the world.

Everything that is contested is sought either because of love for the thing itself that is at issue or because of love for something else hidden beneath an offensive appearance. Thus, for example, war, although it is an offensive thing because of the spirited clash of combatants, is waged for love of victory and liberty; and many other beloved things are eagerly sought beneath hateful toil or fear.

From this it is plainly understood that nothing can be contested except for the sake of love—that is, for the sake of a hoped-for and subsequently received beloved reward.

Whoever contends over the present world for any reason clearly shows that he loves it. How, then, do the words of the Holy Spirit, spoken through John, forbid the world to be loved, saying, “Do not love the world, nor the things that are in the world” (1 John 2:15)?

Love of the world and love of God cannot dwell together in one heart, just as the same eyes cannot behold heaven and earth at the same time. But we must ask whether there is truly anything in the world that ought to be loved, and what world it is that the divine words forbid us to love.

We are therefore commanded not to love the earth together with the things born from it, its metals and living creatures, the beauty of clothing, the pleasures of food, and the things pertaining to these; but we are commanded to love our neighbor, for whose sake all these things were made.

All these things mentioned above, as destined not to remain, cannot accompany those journeying toward the heavenly homeland. Neighbors, however, as co-heirs of the king who are destined to remain, may freely love one another. Whatever does not remain forever in the world and will perish together with the world—and the world itself—is commanded not to be loved.

A neighbor, however, who is a part of the heavenly kingdom on earth and among the lowest elements [Note: The printed editions have “and meanwhile from the kingdom,” etc.; the Corbie manuscript has “from the innermost parts of the kingdom,” etc.], is rightly loved by those who seek the kingdom of heaven, since in that highest homeland he will be held as a co-heir forever.

The present world is therefore commanded not to be loved so that anyone who loves the age may not become alienated from the love of God. One must not contend, then, for what one is not permitted to love.

A Christian who bears the likeness of Christ’s name must therefore also possess the likeness of his character. No one is rightly called a Christian except one who is made like Christ in conduct.

Of Christ the prophet writes:

“Behold my servant, whom I have chosen, my chosen one, in whom my soul is well pleased. I will put my Spirit upon him. He will not contend, nor cry out, nor will anyone hear his voice in the streets” (Isa. 42:1; Matt. 12:18).

Behold, Christ did not contend or cry out. If you wish to retain the likeness of Christ’s character, do not contend, lest you become a Christian who abuses his calling in the Church.

Christ commanded his followers: “Do not be called Rabbi, for one is your teacher, who is Christ; and do not call anyone your father on earth, for one is your Father, who is in heaven. For you are all brothers” (Matt. 23:8–9). He commanded them to pray, saying: “Pray in this way: Our Father, who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name” (ibid. 6:9), and so forth.

In vain, then, does one contend that he has a father on earth who professes that he has a father and a homeland in heaven. No one becomes a possessor of that homeland unless he is kept secure from contention over his earthly homeland.

## EIGHTH DEGREE: A PROUD POOR MAN  
### Poor in spirit, poor in humility  
### A noble poor man

The eighth degree of abuse is a proud poor man who, possessing nothing, is lifted up in pride, although the Apostle Paul commands the rich of this age not to be proud-minded (1 Tim. 6:17).

What, then, could be more foolish than for one who, through the deepest misery, has been cast down as though into the earth and ought to walk and grieve as one lowly and humble, to raise an inflated mind against God with the haughty swelling of pride?

Through this vice those fell who had been created at the highest summit of heaven. What, then, does one who ought to appear humbler than all human beings wish by his pride to act as though he were powerful on earth?

But lest the poor grieve over their poverty, let them consider what they will receive from God. For he himself says: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:3).

By a righteous dispensation the merciful Judge entrusts the kingdom of heaven to those from whom he has withheld participation in earthly kingdoms among mortals, so that the one who has secured nothing at all on earth may appear rich in heaven’s seat.

The poor must therefore beware lest, while they lose the earthly kingdom through poverty and need, they also lose the kingdoms of heaven through the imprudence of their mind. For when, by God’s dispensation, they have received necessary poverty, it depends upon their own choice whether they are poor in spirit.

The kingdoms of heaven are not promised to every poor person, but only to those in whom humility of soul accompanies the lack of riches. The humble poor person is called poor in spirit: although he is seen externally as needy, he is never lifted up in pride. For to attain the kingdoms of heaven, humility of mind is worth more than the temporary poverty of present riches.

Indeed, those who possess riches well but are humble may be called poor in spirit; but there is no doubt that those who possess nothing but are proud are deprived of the blessedness of poverty. Concerning both kinds, Holy Scripture says:

“There is one who is as rich though he has nothing, and there is one who is as poor though he possesses great riches” (Prov. 13:7).

The one who is poor amid great riches is therefore a rich man humble in spirit; and the one who has nothing yet is rich is a poor man in the disposition of his mind. Noble poverty, then, is humility of mind, while foolish riches are the enormity of the soul.

The poor must therefore take care to understand what they are like; and since they cannot obtain by material possessions what they seek, they must cease to be proud through swelling of mind.

## NINTH DEGREE: AN UNJUST KING  
### The justice of a king  
### How many evils come from an unjust king  
### How many goods come from a just king
## The Ninth Degree of Abuse Is an Unjust King

Indeed, a king ought not to be unjust, but a corrector of the unjust. Therefore he must preserve in himself the dignity of his name: for the name “king” intellectually retains this meaning, that he should provide the office of ruler for all his subjects. But how will he be able to correct others who does not correct his own conduct, if it is unjust? [Note: [Col. 1085] Jonas of Orléans, inserting this entire Degree as from Cyprian in *On Royal Institution*, ch. 3, reads: “if it is not unjust.”] For “the throne of the king is exalted by justice,” and “the government of peoples is made firm by the king’s truth.”

The justice of a king, moreover, consists in oppressing no one unjustly through power; judging without respect of persons between a man and his neighbor; being a defender of strangers, orphans, and widows; restraining thefts; punishing adulteries; not promoting the wicked; not supporting the shameless and actors; removing the impious from the land; not allowing parricides and perjurers to live; defending the churches; feeding the poor with alms; appointing just men over the affairs of the kingdom; having as counselors old, wise, and temperate men; not attending to the superstitions of magicians, diviners, and prophetesses; delaying anger; defending his country bravely and justly against adversaries; trusting in God in all things; not being lifted up in spirit by prosperity; patiently enduring every adversity; holding the catholic faith in God; not allowing his sons to act impiously; devoting himself to prayers at appointed hours; and not tasting food before the proper hours.

“For woe to the land whose king is a child, and whose princes eat in the morning” (Eccl. 10:16). These things bring prosperity to the kingdom in the present and lead the king to the better kingdoms of heaven. But whoever does not administer the kingdom according to this law surely endures many adversities in his rule. For this reason the peace of peoples is often broken, disturbances also arise against the kingdom, the fruits of the lands diminish, and the services of the peoples are hindered. Many and various sorrows infect the prosperity of the kingdom; the deaths of dear ones and children bring sadness; the attacks of enemies ravage the provinces everywhere; wild beasts tear apart the herds of cattle and flocks of sheep; storms of spring and winter [Note: [Col. 1085] Another reading: “and the air and the hemispheres disturb the lands,” etc.] obstruct the fertility of the earth and the services of the sea; and sometimes lightning strikes burn the crops, the blossoms of trees, and every vine-shoot.

Above all, however, the injustice of a king not only darkens the appearance of the present realm, but also obscures his sons and grandsons, so that they may not hold the inheritance of the kingdom after him. For because of Solomon’s sacrilege, the Lord scattered the kingdom of the house of Israel from the hands of his sons [Col. 1086] (3 Kings 11:31); and because of the justice of King David, he always left a lamp from his offspring in Jerusalem.

Behold how much the justice of a king is worth in this world: it is plainly evident to those who observe it. For it is the peace of peoples, the protection of the fatherland, the security of the common people, the defense of the nation, care for the sick, the joy of human beings, temperate weather, calm seas, the fertility of the earth, consolation for the poor, the inheritance of children, and hope of future blessedness for the king himself.

Nevertheless, let the king know that, just as he has been established first among human beings on the throne, so also in punishments, if he has not practiced justice, he will hold the first place. For all the sinners whom he had beneath him in the present, he will then have above him in that future punishment, in a manner that cannot be appeased.

## DEGREE X. A Negligent Bishop. What a Bishop Owes to the Flock. What He Owes to Himself.

The tenth degree of abuse is a negligent bishop, who demands among human beings the honor of his rank but does not preserve before God the dignity of his ministry, for whom he serves as an ambassador (2 Cor. 5:20).

First, the dignity signified by his name must be examined by the bishop, since *episcopus* is a Greek name interpreted as “overseer” or “watchman.” Why, however, is a watchman appointed, and what is required of a watchman? The Lord himself discloses this when, under the person of the prophet Ezekiel, he declares to the bishop the account of his office, saying:

“I have appointed you as a watchman for the house of Israel. Hearing a word from my mouth, you shall announce it to them from me. But if you see the sword coming and you do not announce that the wicked should turn back from his way, that wicked man will indeed die in his iniquity, but I will require his blood from your hand. If, however, you announce it and he does not turn back, he will indeed die in his iniquity, but you will have delivered your own soul” (Ezek. 3:17–19).

Therefore a bishop, who has been appointed watchman over all, ought to observe sins carefully; and after observing them, to correct them by word and, if he can, by deed. If he cannot, then, according to the rule of the Gospel, he should avoid workers of wickedness.

“For,” says the Lord in the Gospel, “if your brother sins against you, rebuke him between yourself and him alone. If he listens to you, you have won your brother. If he does not listen to you, take with you one or two more, so that every word may be established by the mouth of two or three witnesses. If he does not listen to them, tell the Church. If he does not listen to the Church, let him be to you as a gentile and a tax collector” (Matt. 18:15–17).

Anyone who refuses to adhere to a teacher or bishop must be expelled in this manner. And whoever has been expelled in this manner ought not to be received by any other teacher or bishop. For concerning a priest it is written in the Law: “He shall not take as wife a widow or a divorced woman” (Lev. 21:7). Therefore whoever joins himself to one excommunicated by a catholic priest, without that priest’s permission, oversteps the laws of the holy priesthood, which is the chosen race of Christians.

For this reason, a bishop must be such toward those over whom he has been appointed as watchman. As for what he ought to be in himself, the Apostle Paul explains: when he comes to the rank of bishop, he should be sober, prudent, chaste, wise, modest, hospitable, having children subject to him with all chastity, possessing a good testimony from those outside, presenting the faithful word of doctrine; before the episcopate, having no more than one wife; not violent, not double-tongued, not a drunkard, not a novice (1 Tim. 3:2–4). Thus, through his conduct, he should himself display what he teaches others in the word of doctrine.

Let negligent bishops beware of what the Lord complains through the prophet at the time of vengeance, saying: “My shepherds have demolished my people; and the shepherds did not feed my flock, but fed themselves” [Note: [Col. 1086] Corbie manuscript: “mute.” In Cyprian: “many.”] (Ezek. 34:8). Rather, let those whom the Lord has appointed over his household provide them with food at the proper time—a measure of wheat (Luke 12:42), that is, pure and tested doctrine—so that when the Lord comes they may deserve to hear:

“Well done, good and faithful servant: because you have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many; enter into the joy of your lord” (Matt. 25:23).

## DEGREE XI. A People Without Discipline. What Discipline Is.

The eleventh degree of abuse is a people without discipline. Since such a people does not submit to the exercises of discipline, it binds itself in the common snare of perdition; for without the rigor of discipline it cannot escape the anger of the Lord. Therefore the undisciplined people is admonished in the words of the Psalmist: “Embrace discipline, lest the Lord become angry” (Ps. 2:12).

Discipline is the orderly correction of conduct and the observance of the preceding rules of one’s superiors. Concerning this discipline the Apostle Paul speaks thus: “Persevere in discipline, as though God were offering himself to you as sons. But if you are without discipline, of which all have become partakers, then you are illegitimate children and not sons” (Heb. 12:7–8).

Those who are therefore illegitimate children are without discipline and do not obtain the inheritance of the heavenly kingdom. But if they are sons, they endure the correction of paternal discipline and do not despair of being able someday to receive the inheritance.

Isaiah also preaches this discipline to the undisciplined people, saying: “Cease to act perversely; learn to do good” (Isa. 1:16–17). The Psalmist likewise sings in harmony: “Turn away from evil and do good” (Ps. 33:15).

Unhappy, then, is the person who casts discipline aside. For the one who tears the discipline of Christ’s Church ventures something beyond the soldiers who crucified the Lord and did not tear his tunic. For just as the tunic covers the whole body except the head, so discipline protects and adorns the whole Church except Christ, who is the head of the Church and is not subject to discipline.

“For the tunic had been woven from above throughout” (John 19:23), because this same discipline of the Church is granted and made complete by the Lord from heaven. Concerning this, after he had risen from the dead and ascended to the Father, the Lord spoke to his Apostles, saying: “But you remain in the city until you are clothed with power from on high” (Luke 24:49).

The tunic, therefore, of Christ’s body is the discipline of the Church. Whoever is outside discipline is alien to the body of Christ. Let us not tear it, then, but cast lots for whose it shall be (John 19:24)—that is, let us not dissolve any of the Lord’s commandments, but let each person remain with the Lord in the calling in which he was called.

## DEGREE XII. A People Without Law.

[Col. 1088]

The twelfth degree of abuse is a people without law. While it despises the words of God and the decrees of the laws, it encounters the snare of transgression along various paths of error. Concerning these paths, the prophet thus laments under the person of a transgressing people, representing the human race:

“But we, like sheep, have gone astray; each one has turned aside to his own way” (Isa. 53:6).

Wisdom also speaks through Solomon concerning these paths: “There are many ways that seem right to human beings, but their ends lead to death” (Prov. 14:12).

These many paths of perdition are traveled whenever the one royal way—the law of God, which turns neither to the right nor to the left—is abandoned through negligence. Concerning this way, the Lord Jesus Christ, who is “the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Rom. 10:4), declares: “I am the way, the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me” (John 14:6).

He invites all human beings together to this way, saying: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matt. 11:28). For “there is no respect of persons with God” (Rom. 2:11): there is neither Jew nor Greek, male nor female, slave nor free, Barbarian nor Scythian, but Christ is all in all; for all are one in Christ Jesus (Gal. 3:28).

Since Christ is the end of the law (Rom. 10:4), those who are without law become without Christ. Therefore a people without law is a people without Christ.

It is therefore an abuse, in the times of the Gospel, for a people to become without law, when permission to preach was given to the Apostles among all nations (Matt. 28:19); when the thunder of the Gospel resounded through every part of the world; when the nations that did not pursue righteousness attained righteousness (Rom. 9:30); when those who had been far away were brought near through the blood of Christ (Eph. 2:13); when those who had once been “not a people” became “the people of God” in Christ (Rom. 9:25); when it is the acceptable time and the day of salvation (2 Cor. 6:2), and the times of refreshment in the presence of the Most High; when every nation has a witness to the resurrection; and when the Lord himself declares: “Behold, I am with you all days, even to the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28:20).

Let us not, then, become without Christ in this transitory time, lest Christ begin to be without us in the future.

# [ON THE SEVEN VICES AND THE SEVEN GIFTS]

[Col. 1087]

## Editorial Notice Concerning the Following Treatise

The work that Hieronymus Vignierius transferred into the first part of the Supplement, under the heading “Treatise on the Seven Vices and the Seven Gifts of the Holy Spirit,” beginning “There are seven principal vices,” will not occupy entirely the place that, according to the plan, it should hold here at the beginning of the Appendix.

Vignierius found it among the printed monuments of the holy Fathers published at Paris in 1634, under the care of William Camerarius, a Scot and priest of the Congregation of the Oratory. Camerarius says that it is attributed to Augustine, not on the basis of ancient manuscripts, but solely on the authority of many learned men.

The very same work, however, is found in Hugh of Saint-Victor’s *Book of Allegories on Matthew*, book 2, chapter 3. In the same *Book of Allegories*, chapter 19, another short work on the gifts of the Holy Spirit is also inserted, beginning: “It is written: ‘For if you, although you are evil,’” etc. On the authority of the same Camerarius, Vignierius had presented this as a sermon of Augustine in the same part of the Supplement, not far before the aforementioned treatise on the seven vices.

This short work ought properly to be joined to that treatise, since it is closely related to it and contributes somewhat to its completeness. For when the short work is separated from it, the treatise appears incomplete, or at least does not correspond at all to the title prefixed by Vignierius, insofar as it is entitled “On the Gifts of the Holy Spirit.”

Hugh’s title for the treatise is more suitable, namely: “On the Seven Mortal Sins, against which the Petitions of the Lord’s Prayer Are Effective.” For it is nothing other than an exposition of the Lord’s Prayer and of its seven petitions against the seven vices.

Let Hugh retain his treatise, which, if the matter required it, could be defended for him by many arguments. If you wish, compare his second book *On the Sacraments*, part 13, chapter 1, and the third treatise of the *Sum of Sentences*, chapter 16, where you will find the seven vices described in precisely the same manner. The vice is also defined here in general in the same words as in his first book of *Miscellanies*. What the name of God means is explained just as in another treatise of Hugh’s on the *Magnificat*; and concerning the seeking of God’s favor at the beginning of prayer, his treatise *On the Manner of Praying* contains passages similar to this little book.

Finally, the treatise he wrote *On Five Sevens*, or *On Sets of Seven*, published in the cited second book of the *Allegories*, chapter 15, clearly reports the very same author as the treatise on the seven vices.

[Col. 1089]

# TREATISE ON THE SEVEN VICES AND THE SEVEN GIFTS OF THE HOLY SPIRIT (G,S)*

### What a Vice Is, and When It Is Guilt. Its Types and the Definition of Each.

There are seven principal vices, which infect rational nature and corrupt its integrity, as though with a kind of leaven mixed into it. [Note: [Col. 1089] Thus Hugh of Saint-Victor, *Miscellanies*, book 1, title 54.]

A vice, moreover, is the corruption of a natural inclination contrary to order and beyond measure. [Note: [Col. 1089] The same author says this in *On the Sacraments*, book 2, part 13, chapter 1.]

When this is received through consent, it is sin; merely feeling it without consent, however, is punishment and not guilt. Certainly, in those who have not been regenerated, vice has no excuse at all: even when consent does not follow, the fact alone that one is moved contrary to reason is deserving of condemnation. For this reason the Apostle says: “There is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Rom. 8:1). [Note: [Col. 1089] Hugh both records and defines it thus in the place cited shortly above and in the third treatise of the *Sum of Sentences*.]

The first vice is pride; the second, envy; the third, anger; the fourth, acedia; the fifth, avarice; the sixth, gluttony; the seventh, lust.

Pride is love of one’s own excellence. Envy is resentment of another’s happiness. Anger is an irrational disturbance of the mind. Acedia is disgust with the inner good. Avarice is immoderate desire to possess. Gluttony is excessive appetite for eating. Lust is immoderate desire to satisfy sexual passion.

These, then, are the seven vices from which every corruption of the rational soul proceeds; for everything that corrupts integrity is a vice. But there is another integrity, etc.

# CORRECTIONS AND VARIANT READINGS IN THE SAME TREATISE

The older Paris edition of Hugh, published in 1526 by Badius, volume 1, folio 206, column c, *Allegories on Matthew*, chapter 3: “But corrupt love through the soul’s desire is ugliness.” Vignierius in the *Supplement*: “But corrupt love through desire removes health.” “For the clarity of knowledge is as it were a certain beauty of the soul; but sincerity,” etc.

Ibid., column e, chapter 4: “and the remaining attendant vices.” Read, following Vignierius: “the subsequent vices.”

Ibid., column h: after “but at the same time they blaspheme all things,” Vignierius adds “the Lord”; and shortly afterward has “the highest good,” where Hugh has “his own good.”

Folio 207, column l, chapter 5: after “because of this the Son of God,” add “who”; and shortly afterward, instead of “could have been rational,” read “could not have been rational.” A little later: “that which is disordered is a vice”; instead of “that which is disordered is to be a vice.”

Ibid., column m, chapter 6: “seven special antidotes”; Vignierius has “spiritual,” perhaps less suitably. Then “which nevertheless”; perhaps read “which only.”

Ibid., column n: “so that the giving of what the will requires may follow.” Vignierius: “so that the giving may follow, so that what it lost by its will it may seek by its will.”

Ibid.: add “May your kingdom come.” The third petition is set against anger; after the words, “the second petition.”

Ibid., column o, chapter 7: “as it were a seeking of favor”; and below, “these words in commendation of the seeking of favor.” Vignierius does not read the word “of favor”; Hugh commonly omits it, as may be seen in his book *On the Manner of Praying*, chapters 2 and 5.

Ibid.: instead of “from prelates,” correct to “calling upon.”

Ibid.: “For there they must be sought.” In Vignierius: “For there the inheritance must be sought.”

Ibid., column r: “we place the honor of God first.” In Vignierius: “we place your honor first”; and shortly afterward, “to you and your things,” where Hugh has “to you and to God’s.”

Page 208, column t, chapter 8: after “hear again,” Vignierius repeats the word “hear.”

Ibid.: “good for so great a good.” Vignierius: “good for the highest good.”

Ibid., column u: “not thereafter to excuse yourself on account of sloth”; correct to “on account of ignorance.”

[Col. 1090] Ibid., column x: after “the inclination of your wickedness,” Vignierius adds “not the weakness of your infirmity.”

Ibid., column z, chapter 9: “There we subjected ourselves through humility to the superior.” Vignierius: “we subject ourselves.”

Page 209, column b, chapter 10: “prayer that it may be in heaven.” Vignierius: “prayer is that it may be,” etc.

Ibid., column c: “so that your will may be done in them, let them imitate them,” etc.—the passage is confused. In Vignierius it is more confused in this form: “So that the will of God may be done in them, and may precede in their hearts what they will follow in their bodies, and let them not imitate those who still cling in spirit to the earth and are earth.” It seems that it should be corrected as follows: “so that God’s will may be done in them, and may precede in their hearts . . . . . thus let them imitate those who still,” and the rest as in Vignierius.

Ibid.: “or we shall be corrected by your power.” In Vignierius: “we shall be constrained.”

Ibid., column e, chapter 11: “feed the inhabitants.” Vignierius adds “your inhabitants.”

Ibid., column f: “and we gather no more except as much as we use.” Vignierius is better: “and we do not gather more; we gather only as much as we use.”

Ibid.: “should exceed without knowledge.” Perhaps read “should approach.”

Ibid., column g: “within you have bread.” Vignierius omits “you have.”

Ibid.: “it is hungry.” Vignierius: “for it is,” etc.
