Ibid., column h: “This is today, when.” Vignierius adds “day”: “This is the day today, when.” Vignierius has “today in which”; and shortly afterward, “is aroused toward the desire for good,” while Hugh lacks the word “good.”

Page 210, column k: “give us today, give”; read with Vignierius: “give us today. Give today.”

Ibid., column l, chapter 12: “who so faithfully sets forth the condition.” Vignierius is better: “who so confidently,” etc.

Ibid.: “we feel a good”—Vignierius adds “to be”—“mercy.”

Ibid., column m: “may you provide the disposition of virtue.” Read with Vignierius: “the effect.”

Ibid., column n: “rejoice with us.” Vignierius: “gratified with us.” Perhaps: “gratuitously with us.”

Ibid.: “we, your bowels”—Vignierius omits “of your mercy”—“overflowing,” and adds “in goodness”; consider. Perhaps all these words should be retained.

Ibid.: “to yield to your right.” Vignierius: “by right.”

Ibid., column p: “so that nevertheless we may punish them.” Vignierius: “so that we may not punish them.”

Ibid., column r, chapter 13: “not so much temptation as oppression”—Vignierius omits “is”—“if it prevails.” He then adds “or if it does not prevail.”

Ibid., column s: “when because of that which.” Vignierius: “when through that which.”

Page 211, column t: “therefore the vice tempts.” Vignierius adds “this.”

Ibid., column y, chapter 14: “nor can we go out.” Vignierius: “be rescued.”

Ibid.: “Behold, alone without you”—Vignierius adds “us.” Then, after inserting a full stop: “we have become,” etc.

Ibid.: “and it is not like the other evils.” “Is” is superfluous.

Ibid., columns y–z: “by the persuasion of deadly love.” Vignierius: “of delight.”

Ibid., column z: “he could perhaps esteem.” Vignierius: “consider.”

Ibid.: “which can no longer be concealed.” Vignierius: “this can no longer,” etc.

# ON THE GIFTS OF THE HOLY SPIRIT

## On the Words of Luke: “For if You, Although You Are Evil” (Luke 11:13), etc.

It is written: “For if you, although you are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children” (Luke 11:13), “how much more will your heavenly Father give the good Spirit to those who ask him?” Therefore the heavenly Father will give the Spirit to his sons who ask him.

For those who are sons seek nothing else; those who seek something else are hirelings, servants and not sons. Those who seek silver, those who seek gold, those who seek transitory things, those who seek earthly things, seek the service of slavery, not the Spirit of freedom.

What is sought is given. If you seek bodily things, you receive no more than you seek. If you seek spiritual things, what you seek is given, and what you do not seek is added; spiritual things are given, bodily things [Note: [Col. 1091] Hugh has “carnal things.”] are added.

“Seek first the kingdom of God, and all these things will be added to you” (Matt. 6:33). Therefore, when you are about to ask the Father, etc.

# CORRECTIONS AND VARIANT READINGS IN THE SAME TREATISE

Hugh’s Badius edition, Paris, volume 1, folio 213, column o: “to those who ask him.” Vignierius adds: “he will give the good Spirit; he will give his Spirit.” Then he continues: “he will give his Spirit,” etc.

Ibid., column p: “because he is merciful.” Perhaps read: “because he is a father.”

[Col. 1092] Ibid., column q: between the words “corruption,” “elation,” and “health,” “humility”; Vignierius inserts “that is.”

Ibid.: “and they are gifts of the Spirit.” Vignierius omits “gifts.” Page 214, column r: “he himself is”—Vignierius has “is”—“piety.”

Ibid., column s: “medicine because of you.” Vignierius is better: “medicine for you.”

Ibid.: “he has no punishment.” Vignierius: “he has no peace,” less suitably.

Ibid.: “but you, from that which is contrary,” etc. Vignierius has “you, however.”

Ibid., column t: “because you were not looking.” Vignierius: “because you were not perceiving.”

Ibid., column u: “at least in tribulation.” In Vignierius: “in retribution”; and shortly afterward, “you are affected,” instead of “you are afflicted.”

Ibid.: “something else is what you see.” Vignierius: “something else is that toward which you look.”

Ibid., column y: perhaps read “not in this evil thing that delivers”; *malum*—“evil”—rather than *malam*.

# [ON THE CONFLICT OF VICES AND VIRTUES]

[Col. 1091]

## Editorial Notice Concerning the Following Book

The book *On the Conflict of Vices and Virtues* has been attributed to four very distinguished writers: first to Augustine in all editions of his works; then to Leo in his Paris edition of 1511; afterward to Ambrose in the Roman edition of 1585, where it is prefaced as having been written to Simplicianus; and finally to Isidore of Seville in the edition of 1599, published at Madrid, and in another published at Paris under the supervision of Jacques Dubreul, a monk of our monastery at Saint-Germain, in 1601.

Sigebert of Gembloux deceived Dubreul; Sigebert himself had been deceived by a false inscription in certain ancient codices, which are said to bear the name of Isidore. The manuscripts examined by us, however, either assign it to Ambrose, Augustine, or Leo. Gratian also cites it under Augustine’s name in part 2, question 22, chapter *Nec artificioso*.

We believe the author to be Ambrose—not the celebrated bishop of Milan mentioned above, but Autpert, abbot of the monastery of Saint Vincent at Vulturnum in Benevento, whose first name was also Ambrose. The writer of his Life, which appears in the third volume of the Benedictine *Saeculum*, part 2, under the year of Christ 778, testifies that he himself composed the book *On the Conflict of Vices*.

The following book has much affinity with Ambrose Autpert’s work on the Apocalypse; it clearly bears the character of a man devoted to monastic life and writing especially for monks, as where it says, chapter 16:

“If the activity of desire is so ruinous for secular men, how much more dangerous is it for those who, by their habit and way of life, have already ceased to be secular, who have devoted everything they live to the Lord?”

And chapter 18:

“If you deliver intact everything that your superior has entrusted to you to observe, and do not consider that even the smallest thing should be held back,” etc.

These final words, and many others concerning stability in chapter 14, silence in chapter 22, and so forth, appear to have been taken from the precepts of Saint Benedict.

Nor, for confirming the matter, do we add that the Benedictine Rule is expressly commended at the end of the book—especially since the book as published under Ambrose and Isidore, as well as in certain manuscripts and in the Erasmian edition, etc., lacks the final two chapters and ends with these words from chapter 26:

“But you, man of God, attend with vigilant zeal to what I say,” usually followed by the clause, “with the help of him who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.”

The book has been collated with the Saint-Germain, Corbie, Lyre, Victorine, and other manuscripts.

[Col. 1091]

# ONE BOOK ON THE CONFLICT OF VICES AND VIRTUES (G,S)*

## CHAPTER I. Even Now the Godly Must Suffer Persecution.

[Col. 1091]

The apostolic voice cries out throughout the world and says to those placed in the battle-line of faith, lest they grow sluggish through security: “All who desire to live devoutly in Christ Jesus suffer persecution” (2 Tim. 3:12).

Behold: since Christianity in its leaders is now religious and now faithful, the bonds, blows, lashes, prisons, racks, crosses, and whatever other kinds of torments there are, are absent for those living devoutly in Christ Jesus. How, then, will what was proclaimed through the Apostle be true—that all who live devoutly suffer persecution?

Or perhaps no one wishes to live devoutly in Christ Jesus in a time of peace, and therefore these things are absent? Who, even if foolish, would say this?

In the Apostle’s statement, therefore, not the particular persecution of some but the general persecution of all must be understood. Indeed, there are many established within the bosom of Mother Church who, while living devoutly in Christ, are subjected to insults and harassed by reproaches, injuries, and mockery. Is this that general persecution which the Apostle described as suffered by all who live devoutly?

I would not readily say so, since there are certain religious persons whom none of the wicked would dare disparage to their faces. Another persecution must therefore be understood, one more savage and more harmful, produced not by the severity of a mortal person [Note: [Col. 1092] Manuscripts: “material.”] but by the opposition of vices.

For while pride fights against humility; empty glory against fear of the Lord; hypocrisy against true religion; contempt against submission; envy against fraternal rejoicing; hatred against love; detraction against the freedom of rightful correction; anger against patience; insolence against gentleness; swelling against satisfaction; secular life against spiritual joy; sluggishness or idleness against the exercise of virtue; loose wandering against firm stability; despair against confidence in hope; desire against contempt of the world; hardness against mercy; fraud and theft against innocence; deceit and falsehood against truth; greed of the belly against moderation in food; foolish joy against measured sorrow; excessive speech against discreet silence; uncleanness and lust against integrity of the flesh; spiritual fornication against purity of heart; and desire for the present world against love of the heavenly homeland—when all these thrust themselves forward [Note: [Col. 1093] Several manuscripts: “attack”] against the ordered ranks of the virtues, what else rages as a cruel persecution against those living devoutly?

O how hard, O how bitter is the assault of pride, which cast angels from heaven and drove human beings from paradise [Note: [Col. 1093] Most manuscripts: “threatened.” In Ambrose and Isidore: “expelled.”], whose army and clash of arms are the vices that we have briefly touched upon!

But let us see how the camps of heaven and hell wage war, and how the weapons of Christ and the devil, brought into collision [Note: [Col. 1093] One manuscript: “counsels.”], contend.

## CHAPTER II. Right Intention.

Pride says: “Certainly you are better than many, indeed almost than everyone—in speech, knowledge, wealth, honors, and all the spiritual or bodily gifts that are available. Therefore despise everyone; regard yourself as superior to everyone.”

But true humility responds: “Remember that you are dust (Gen. 3:19), that you are ashes, that you are decay and a worm; and if you are anything, unless you humble yourself as much as you are great (Sir. 3:20), you utterly lose what you are.

“Are you higher than the first angel? Are you more splendid on earth than Lucifer was in heaven? If he fell through pride from such great sublimity, how will you, in your pride, climb from the depths to such height, when you are held, as long as you live here, in that condition of which a certain wise man says: ‘The corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks of many things’ (Wis. 9:15)?

“How densely do we think the clay of the earth is wrapped in the darkness of pride, if in heaven the star that rose in the morning could lose the globes of its light (Isa. 14:12)? Hear, then, rather the Light of truth saying: ‘Whoever follows me does not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life’ (John 8:12).

“Elsewhere he warned in what way he should be followed, saying: ‘Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart, and you will find rest for your souls’ (Matt. 11:29).

“Hear, swelling pride; hear the teacher of humility still saying: ‘Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted’ (Luke 14:11). And this: ‘Upon whom does my spirit rest, if not upon the humble and quiet person who trembles at my words?’ (Isa. 66:2).

“Hear also what the Apostle says about the one who invites you to pursue these things. He says: ‘Although he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of human beings, and being found in appearance as a man. He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death—even death on a cross’ (Phil. 2:6–8).

“If divine majesty lowers itself with such great humility, ought human frailty to be proud of anything?”

## CHAPTER III. The Same Subject.

Empty glory says: “Do whatever good you can; display to everyone the good that you do, so that everyone may call you good, so that all may proclaim you holy and venerable, so that you may be called God’s chosen one, so that no one may despise or disdain you, but that everyone may render you the honor due to you.”

But fear of the Lord responds: “If you do anything good, do it not for transitory honors but for eternal ones. Conceal what you do as far as you can. If you cannot conceal it completely, let the will to conceal it be in your heart, and there will be no rashness of ostentation; nor will it be a crime sometimes to reveal what you always wish to keep hidden.

“Thus you will appear to have fulfilled two statements of the Redeemer that seem almost contrary to one another: ‘When you give alms, let your left hand not know what your right hand is doing; but let your alms be in secret, and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you’ (Matt. 6:3–4); and, ‘Let your good works be seen, and let them glorify your Father who is in heaven’ (Matt. 5:16).

“Take great care lest that statement concerning hypocrites apply to you: ‘They do all their works so that they may be praised by human beings. Truly I say to you, they have received their reward’ (Matt. 6:2). [Note: [Col. 1094] The printed editions add: “from human beings, the praises that they loved.” Ambrose has: “that is, only the praises from human beings that they loved.”]

“Pay attention to yourself in all that you do, lest, driven by elation, you hear with those who gloried in the signs of miracles: ‘I saw Satan falling like lightning from heaven’ (Luke 10:18).”

The fear of the Lord is glory and glorification, joy, and a crown of exultation. The fear of the Lord delights the heart, gives gladness, joy, and length of days. It will be well with the one who fears the Lord at the end, and on the day of his death he will be blessed. The fear of the Lord is the religiousness of knowledge, and religiousness will guard and justify the heart and give delight and joy. The fullness of knowledge is to fear God, and its fullness comes from his fruits. The crown of wisdom is the fear of the Lord. The root of wisdom is to fear God; for its branches are long-lived (Sir. 1:11–13, 17–18, 20, 22, 25). [Note: [Col. 1094] These words, “The fear of the Lord . . . long-lived,” are absent from the manuscripts, nor do the printed codices of Ambrose and Isidore agree among themselves.]

## CHAPTER IV. Obedience Is Due to a Human Being in the Same Measure as to God.

Simulation of true religion says: “Since you do nothing good in secret, lest you be detested when known by everyone, pretend outwardly to be what inwardly you do not desire.” But true religion replies: “Rather, strive to be what you are not; for to show people that we are what we are not—what else is that but condemnation?” Remember, therefore, what is said: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who cleanse the outside of the cup and dish, but inside you are full of plunder and uncleanness. Blind Pharisee, first cleanse what is inside the cup and dish, so that what is outside may also become clean.” Likewise, what is repeated insistently: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who are like whitewashed tombs, which outwardly appear beautiful to people, but inwardly are full of the bones of the dead and every kind of filth; so you too outwardly indeed appear righteous to people, but inwardly you are full of hypocrisy and iniquity” (Matt. 23:25–28). And also what is written concerning such people: “They come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly they are ravenous wolves” (ibid. 7:15).

## CHAPTER V. The Same Argument Is Treated.

Disobedience says: “Who are you to obey those who are worse, to render service to those who are inferior? It was more fitting for you to command than for them, since they cannot equal you in intelligence or diligence. Obey the Lord’s command, therefore, all the more, and concern yourself with no one.” But blessed submission replies: “If the Lord’s command must be obeyed, it is necessary to submit to human authority. For he himself says: ‘Whoever hears you hears me; and whoever despises you despises me’” (Luke 10:16).

“You are right,” you say, “but only if the one who commands were such as he ought to be [Note: [Col. 1094] These words, ‘such as he ought to be,’ are found neither in the manuscripts nor in Isidore.]; he is not such a person through whom God commands.” But the Apostle says otherwise: “There is no authority except from God, and those that exist have been ordained by God [Note: [Col. 1094] Two manuscripts have, as in the Vulgate, ‘have been ordained’ in the feminine plural.]. Therefore whoever resists authority resists God’s ordinance” (Rom. 13:1–2). What those who command ought to be is not for subjects to scrutinize.

Indeed, the Lord says to the first pastors of the Church: “You know that the rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them, and those who exercise authority among them are called benefactors. But it shall not be so among you; rather, whoever wishes to be greater among you shall be the servant of all, just as the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a redemption for many” (Matt. 20:25–26, 28).

Yet because he foresaw that not all would become such men, he took upon himself, in the persons of the disciples, the status of all who are subject, and gave them this warning: “The scribes and Pharisees have sat on Moses’ seat. Therefore do and observe whatever they tell you, but do not do what they do. For they bind heavy and unbearable burdens on people’s shoulders, but they themselves are unwilling to move them with their finger” (Matt. 23:2–4).

## CHAPTER VI. One Must Love a Person, Even Though He Possesses Things That Are Not to Be Loved.

Envy says: “In what respect are you inferior to this person or that? Why, then, are you not equal or superior to them? How much do you possess that they do not? Therefore they ought not to be superior or even equal to you.” But rejoicing in a brother’s progress replies: “If you surpass others in virtues, you preserve yourself more safely in a lowly position than in a high one. For a fall from a height is always worse. But if, as you claim, certain people are superior or equal to you, what harm or injury do they cause you? Take great care lest, while you envy others their lofty position, you imitate the one of whom you retain this written testimony: ‘Through the envy of the devil death entered the world, and those who belong to his party imitate him’” (Wis. 2:24–25).

## CHAPTER VII. The Same Argument Is Treated.

Hatred says: “Far be it from you to love one who is opposed to you in everything: one who disparages you, insults you, provokes you with abuse, reproaches you with your sins, and always strives to get ahead of you in words, deeds, and honors. For if he did not envy you, he would never place himself above you in this way.”

But true charity replies: “Are the things you have described hateful in a person simply because of that, so that the image of God in a person is not to be loved? Christ loved his enemies even while he hung on the cross, and before the torment of the cross he warned us, saying: ‘Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who persecute and slander you, so that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven’” (Matt. 5:44–45).

And as it is said through Solomon and the Apostle: “If your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him drink; for by doing this you will heap burning coals on his head” (Prov. 25:21; Rom. 12:20). To this statement the same Apostle added from his own teaching: “Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good” (Rom. 12:21).

In contrast, concerning those known to hate their brothers, John says: “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer. And you know that every murderer does not have eternal life abiding in himself.” And again: “Whoever hates his brother walks in darkness and remains in darkness until now, and does not know where he is going, because darkness has blinded his eyes” (1 John 3:15; 2:11).

“But,” you say, “it is enough for me that I love those who love me.” But the Lord replies: “If you love those who love you, what reward will you have? Do not even the tax collectors do the same?” (Matt. 5:46). What else can you bring forward against this? Certainly, “whoever hates his brother remains in death; and whoever loves remains in God, and God remains in him” (1 John 4:16).

Therefore, vomit out every bitterness of gall, and by whatever means you can, take in the sweetness of charity. Nothing is sweeter, nothing happier than it. “God,” John says, “is charity” (ibid. 4:8). And the outstanding [Note: [Col. 1095] The printed editions add “Paul,” although all the manuscripts resist this reading.] preacher says: “The charity of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us” (Rom. 5:5). Hence charity is rightly said to cover the offenses of sins, as it is written: “Charity covers all offenses” (Prov. 10:12).

## CHAPTER VIII. The Neighbor’s Faults Must Be Corrected, but Discreetly.

Detraction says: “Who can endure, or cover in silence, how many wrongs this person or that commits—unless perhaps he is an accomplice?” But the freedom of just correction replies: “The neighbor’s wrongs must neither be kept silent nor condoned; rather, the neighbor must be rebuked to his face with fraternal charity, not secretly slandered.”

If it is objected that one therefore does not wish to rebuke a brother before his eyes, lest, being provoked, he should gain nothing from correction but instead take scandal from it, divine Scripture responds and, reversing the matter, declares that this is even more scandalous, saying: “You sat and spoke against your brother; you placed a stumbling-block against the son of your mother” (Ps. 49:20). For he takes greater scandal who realizes that someone is slandering him than one who endures correction.

And because the faults of sinners sometimes ought to be covered in silence for a time, so that they may be corrected at a more suitable moment, it is therefore added: “You did these things, and I was silent.” But lest detractors applaud themselves because of this discreet silence—those who, preferring always to disparage secretly, never advance to open rebuke—the text continues: “You thought wickedly that I would be like you.” As though it said: “It is wicked to think that I should appear like a detractor on that account; for I remain silent for a time without disparaging, while I await the opportunity for open correction.”

Hence it immediately adds: “I will rebuke you and set you before your own face” (Ps. 49:21). As though it said: “Not secretly, as is your custom, but openly, as is my concern, I will await the suitable time for correction, rebuke the sinner, and set his offenses before his face.”

“But,” you say, “I do not hate him; I love him, and therefore I judge and rebuke him in secret.” Rather, this is precisely how you hate him and do not love him: you slander him and do not correct him.

How detestable the slander of one’s neighbor is, divine utterances testify in many places. Hence there is this: “The one who secretly slandered his neighbor, him I persecuted” (Ps. 100:5); and this: “The one who slanders his brother slanders the law” (James 4:11); and this: “The one who slanders his brother shall be uprooted”; as well as the statement of the Apostle Paul: “See that, while biting one another, you are not consumed by one another” (Gal. 5:15).

## CHAPTER IX. Prayer Must Not Be Offered While One’s Neighbor Is Offended and Unreconciled; Yet His Anger Must Not Be Without Cause. Concerning Those Whose Duty It Is to Avenge Injuries against God.

Anger says: “What is done against you cannot be endured calmly; indeed, it is a sin to tolerate such things, because, if they are not resisted with great exasperation, they will thereafter accumulate against you without measure.” But patience replies: “If the suffering of the Redeemer is recalled to mind, nothing is so harsh that it cannot be endured with an even spirit. For Christ, as Peter says, suffered for us, leaving us an example so that we might follow his footsteps” (1 Pet. 2:21).

He himself says: “If they called the master of the household Beelzebul, how much more his household? If they persecuted me, they will also persecute you” (Matt. 10:24; John 15:20). Yet how small are the things we suffer in comparison with his sufferings? [Note: [Col. 1096] Thus Autpertus, in Book 1 on the Apocalypse, chapter 7.] He endured insults, mockery, abuse, slaps, spitting, scourging, a crown of thorns, and the cross; while we wretches, to our own shame, are wearied by a single speech and cast down by a single word. And what shall we do with the statement: “If we do not suffer with him, neither shall we reign with him” (2 Tim. 2:12)?

Therefore the goads of anger must be blunted, and its condemnation feared. Hence we read: “Whoever is angry with his brother shall be liable to judgment. Whoever says to his brother, ‘Raca,’ shall be liable to the council. Whoever says, ‘Fool,’ shall be liable to the fire of Gehenna.” Yet a remedy is found here [Note: [Col. 1096] In the printed editions and in Ambrose, “is indicated.”] in what follows: “If you offer your gift at the altar, and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar, and go first to be reconciled to your brother; then come and offer your gift” (Matt. 5:22–24).

As though it were plainly said: “Do not pour out even a silent prayer in your heart until, by making satisfaction to your offended neighbor, you have brought him to gentleness and meekness.” Our gift is our prayer, and our altar is our heart.

Whoever makes a practice of doing this whenever anger has been aroused without cause between two people does not incur the condemnation mentioned above. But there are many who do not forgive the sins of those who ask them for pardon. Against them comes that sentence of the Lord which says: “If you do not forgive people their sins” [Note: [Col. 1096] Only the printed editions add here, “from your hearts.”], “neither will your heavenly Father forgive you your sins” (ibid. 6:14).

“There are many things he commits,” you say, “and he repeatedly offends me.” To this it is not I but the Lord who responds. For when Peter said to him, “Lord, how often will my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? As many as seven times?” he replied: “I do not say to you seven times, but seventy times seven” (Matt. 18:21–22).

How many people are slow to forgive injuries done to themselves but quick to forgive those done against God! It sometimes happens that, under the pretext of avenging the Lord’s injuries, angry people avenge their own.

What else should be said about those who, blinded by fury, rush even to words of cursing, except what the Apostle says: “Nor will those who curse inherit the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 6:10)? James, detesting and emphasizing this, says: “No human being can tame the tongue: a restless evil, full of deadly poison. With it we bless God the Father, and with it we curse human beings, who are made in the likeness of God. From the same mouth come blessing and cursing. My brothers, this ought not to be so. Does a spring pour forth sweet and bitter water from the same opening?” (James 3:8–11). For this reason it is also said elsewhere: “Death and life are in the power of the tongue” (Prov. 18:21).

## CHAPTER X. Arrogance Must Be Avoided in Correction.

Arrogance says: “Are gentle words, rather than the harshest words—as suits such creatures when they offend—really to be directed at fools, at brutes, and at senseless animals?” But gentleness replies: “In this matter you must follow not your own persuasion but the Apostle’s instruction. He admonishes his beloved disciple concerning this judgment, saying: ‘Do not rebuke an older man, but entreat him as a father; younger men as brothers; older women as mothers; younger women as sisters, in all purity’” (1 Tim. 5:1–2).

And again: “The servant of the Lord must not quarrel, but must be gentle toward all, an apt teacher [Note: [Col. 1097] In Isidore and Ambrose, “teachable”; and after the word “resist,” they add “the truth.”], patient, correcting with modesty those who resist” (2 Tim. 2:24–25). And again: “Reprove, exhort, rebuke, with all patience and teaching” (ibid. 4:2).

This evil of arrogance harms subjects even more than it harms those in authority. For it often happens that they reject correction offered gently and with the sweetness of charity, and answer words of humility with arrows of contempt. Hence it is written: “Whoever rebukes a scoffer brings injury upon himself.” In contrast, concerning one who profits from rebuke, it is said: “Rebuke a wise man, and he will love you” [Note: [Col. 1097] Some material is added here in Ambrose.] (Prov. 9:7–8).

## CHAPTER XI. No Opportunity Must Be Given to Detraction.

Pride says: “You have God as your witness in heaven; do not concern yourself with what people on earth suspect about you.” But humble self-defense replies: “No opportunity for slander or suspicion of whispering should be given. If there are things requiring correction, they should be made known; but if there are no such things, they should be denied by a humble declaration. For the Apostle also warns us not to give the devil any opportunity through defamatory accusation” (1 Tim. 5:14).

He likewise detested this in those who, professing the Christian faith [Note: [Col. 1097] Namely, that the idol is nothing. This is better in some manuscripts than the printed reading, “agreeing with the Christian faith”; in Ambrose and Isidore, “registered under the Christian name.”], reclined in an idol-shrine to eat. Although they themselves, considering the idol nothing, ate the sacrificed food as though it were harmless, by this action they were drawing the weak consciences of their brothers toward the impious rites of idols (1 Cor. 8:4–13).

## CHAPTER XII. Twofold Sorrow.

Sorrow says: “What have you from which to rejoice, when you bear so many evils from your neighbors? Consider with what grief all those who are involved in such bitter hostility against you must be regarded.” But spiritual joy replies: “I know that sorrow is twofold—indeed, I know that there are two kinds of sorrow: one that produces salvation, the other destruction; one that leads to repentance, the other that brings to despair. You are recognized as belonging to one of them, but plainly to the kind that produces death.

“Therefore one must not be saddened by the things you recommend, but rather rejoice in the things you do not yet understand. For the giver of everlasting joy said: ‘When people persecute you and speak every evil against you falsely on account of my name, rejoice on that day and exult; for behold, your reward is great in heaven’” (Matt. 5:11–12).

Remember that the Apostles of our religion went away rejoicing from the presence of the council because they had been considered worthy to suffer dishonor for the name of Jesus (Acts 5:41). There should therefore be no place for grief where such great joy follows.

## CHAPTER XIII. The Pretext of Sloth Is Refuted.

Torpor or sloth says: “If you persist in reading with uninterrupted zeal, you will bring darkness upon your eyes; if you shed tears without ceasing, you will even lose your eyes; if, by prolonging vigils, you pay the appointed measure of psalmody, you will acquire madness of the head; if you exhaust yourself by daily labor, when will you rise for spiritual work?”

But the practice of virtue replies: “Why do you propose such long spans of time for these matters? Do you know whether you will live tomorrow? Indeed, you do not even know whether you will remain in this life for a single hour. Or perhaps you have forgotten what the Savior says in the Gospel: ‘Watch, because you do not know the day or the hour’” (Matt. 25:13).

Therefore shake off [Note: [Col. 1098] Perhaps “drive away”; and, as in Ambrose and Isidore, “of torpor.”] the body’s sluggishness, and always remember that the kingdom of heaven is seized not by the lukewarm, the soft, or the idle, but by those who are violent and force their way into it (a).

## CHAPTER XIV. The Pretext of Instability Is Dissolved.

Dissolute wandering says: “If you believe that God is everywhere, why do you remain in one particular place where such great evils are committed, rather than move to another?” But firm stability replies: “If it is as you say, since you confess that God is everywhere, then this place that you wish to flee must not be abandoned either, because God is in it as well.”

“But,” you say, “I seek a better place and find one.” I answer: “Do you find one better—or even one like the place that you know the devil and man lost?” Remember, therefore, that the first angel fell from heaven, and the first man was expelled from paradise and came into the misery of this age (Gen. 3:23).

Consider that Lot, tested by the practice of evils, was holy among the Sodomites; but when torpid with security on the mountain, he became drunk and sinned with his daughters (ibid. 19).

This weariness of wandering produces yet another form of evil: while drawing certain people away from spiritual pursuits even though they remain in one place, it strives either to entangle them in earthly business or to occupy them with the most worthless matters. This is contrary to the Apostle’s teaching: “No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in secular business, so that he may please the one to whom he has given his service” (2 Tim. 2:4); and again: “Pray without ceasing; give thanks in all things” (1 Thess. 5:17–18).

## CHAPTER XV. Conversations of Despair Are Weakened by Many Examples.

Despair says: “What things you have committed, how serious your crimes, how numerous your offenses—and you have scarcely changed your life for the better, scarcely corrected your conduct usefully! For behold, as you see, you remain bound and held by an evil habit. You try to rise, but, weighed down by the burdens of your sins, you fall back again. What, then, is to be done, when certain damnation threatens because of the past and no amendment comes from the present, except that the pleasures of temporal things should not be lost while the delights of the future age cannot be attained?”

But confidence in hope replies: “If crimes and offenses are under discussion, behold David, guilty at once of adultery and murder, described as delivered from the jaws of hell by the Lord’s mercy” (2 Sam. 11). Behold Manasseh, the most impious, foul, filthy, seductive, and wicked of all sinners, returned from death to life through repentance (2 Chron. 33:12).

Behold Mary Magdalene, stained with countless filthinesses of fornication [Note: [Col. 1098] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions have “of sins.”], running anxiously to the fountain of mercy, watering the Lord’s feet with her tears, wiping them with her hair, kissing and even licking them, and anointing them with perfume; she merited cleansing (Luke 7:37–47).

Behold Peter, bound by the chains of his denial, loosening the knots of his unbelief with the bitterest tears (Luke 22:62).

Behold the thief, guilty alike of sedition and the shedding of a brother’s blood, passing in a single hour, with one word of confession, from the cross to paradise (ibid. 23:42).

Behold Saul, persecuting the Church of God, killing many for the name of Christ, and, so to speak, staining himself entirely with the blood of martyrs; he became an apostle and was changed into a vessel of election (Acts 9:1–20).

Where, then, such and so many examples precede, let the evils of despair’s conversations give way [Note: [Col. 1099] That is, “yield”; yet Ambrose has “let them not give way.”], especially since it is also written: “On whatever day the sinner turns and groans, he shall be saved” (Ezek. 18:21). And again: “I do not desire the death of the wicked, says the Lord” (ibid. 33:11).

But concerning conduct not yet changed for the better, what else shall I answer except that whatever someone did not do yesterday, he should do today, while he is still permitted to live? Let him not delay from day to day (Ecclus. 5:8), since he does not know whether he will have even a single day in which to amend. Always resisting his evil habit with the strength granted from above, let him say morning and evening: “Now I have begun; this is the change of the right hand of the Most High” (Ps. 76:11).

## CHAPTER XVI. The Evils of Avarice. The Vow of Poverty. The Remedy for Avarice.

Desire says: “You are entirely without fault when you covet certain things to possess, because you do not desire to multiply your wealth but fear to be in need, and you spend better what another holds badly.”

But contempt for the world replies: “Such things are not obtained without danger or offense even among secular people, because the more each person begins to have, the more he desires to have. The result is that he has no limit in coveting, while he hastens to serve countless concerns of this age. For, as Scripture says, ‘The miser is not filled with money’” (Eccl. 5:9).

Paul indicates how detestable this is when he says: “Avarice, which is the service of idols” (Col. 3:5). Explaining how harmful it is, he says: “Those who desire to become rich fall into temptation and a snare of the devil, and into many foolish and harmful desires that plunge people into destruction and perdition” (1 Tim. 6:9). A certain wise man declares how detestable it is when he says: “Nothing is more wicked than the miser” (Ecclus. 10:9). James reveals how harmful it is, saying: “Come now, you rich, weep and howl over the miseries that are coming upon you. Your riches have rotted, your garments have been eaten by moths; your gold and silver have corroded, and their corrosion will be a witness against you and will eat your flesh like fire” (James 5:1–3).

Nor did our Redeemer wish to pass over how harmful the evil of desire is. For he says: “It is difficult for those who possess money to enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 19:23). And again: “It is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of heaven” (Mark 10:25).

If, then, the industry of desire is so dangerous for secular men, how much more dangerous is it for those who have already ceased to be secular in habit and conduct, who have vowed their entire life to the Lord! To them in particular the Redeemer’s words apply, by which the disease of avarice can be destroyed: “Do not be anxious about what you will eat, or what you will drink, or what you will wear; for the Gentiles seek all these things. But seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you” (Matt. 6:31, 33).

O how blessed, how secure, how worthy of embrace is this sentence! No one in this life is so secure as the one who desires to possess nothing besides Christ. Under this promise he is shown to have all that is necessary, just as Paul, the richest of the poor, said: “As having nothing, yet possessing everything” (2 Cor. 6:10)—everything, certainly, not what is superfluous, but only what is necessary. He confirms this himself, saying: “Having food and clothing, let us be content with these” (1 Tim. 6:8).

You may say: “For this reason holy and religious men ought to possess more, so that Christ’s poor may receive alms from them more effectively than from ordinary people.” I agree—but this applies to those in authority, not to subjects.

The latter are especially warned by the example of Lot’s wife, who, as she was leaving Sodom, looked back and, being turned into a pillar of salt, breathed out her spirit (Gen. 19:26). Hence Christ also warns against such a thing, saying: “No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of heaven” (Luke 9:62).

For this reason Peter says: “It would have been better for them not to know the way of righteousness than, after knowing it, to turn back from the holy commandment delivered to them. What has happened to them accords with the truth of the proverb: ‘The dog returns to its own vomit,’ and ‘The washed sow returns to wallowing in the mire’” (2 Pet. 2:21–22).

This disease of avarice is never restrained better than when the day of death is contemplated without forgetfulness, when a person considers what he will shortly be like in the tomb. This remained fixed in the memory of the one who said: “Man is rottenness, and the son of man a worm” (Job 25:6). This had not departed from the mind of the one who said: “In all your works remember your end, and you will never sin” (Ecclus. 7:40).

What good, I ask, what good then will preserved riches do? Hear what they will do [Note: [Col. 1100] Here and shortly afterward, supply “will do”]: “Naked I came from my mother’s womb, and naked I shall return there.” Hear what they will do: “We brought nothing into this world, nor can we take anything away” (Job 1:21; 1 Tim. 6:7).

## CHAPTER XVII. Against Hardheartedness.

Hardheartedness says: “If you give what you possess to the needy, from where will you feed those subject to you without money?” But mercy replies: “If you follow the Apostle’s measure in this matter, you will be able to accomplish both. For he himself says to the Corinthians: ‘If the will is ready, it is accepted according to what one has, not according to what one does not have; not that there should be relief for others and distress for you, but equality: at the present time let your abundance supply their need, so that their abundance may also supply your need, that there may be equality. As it is written: “The one who had much did not have too much, and the one who had little did not have too little”’” (2 Cor. 8:12–15; Exod. 16:18).

A certain righteous man likewise admonishes his beloved child, saying: “If you have much, give abundantly; but if you have little, share even that willingly” (Tob. 4:9). The incarnate Truth also says: “Nevertheless, give as alms what remains, and behold, everything is clean for you” (Luke 11:41).

Hear this, hardened hearts: “Judgment without mercy will be for the one who has shown no mercy” (James 2:13). In contrast, through the prophet the Lord admonishes, saying: “Break your bread for the hungry, and bring the homeless poor into your house; when you see the naked, cover him, and do not despise your own flesh” (Isa. 58:7).

Remember what happened to the rich man dressed in purple. He was not condemned because he had taken what belonged to another, but because he had not given his own possessions to the needy poor; and, placed in hell, he came to ask for the smallest things, though here he had denied even small things (Luke 16:20–24).

Remember also what the Judge of heaven will say to those placed on the left: “Go into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels; for I was hungry and you did not give me food,” and the other things terribly enumerated there (Matt. 25:41–43).

## CHAPTER XVIII. Lying Is Not Avoided through Tacit Restrictions; Nor Can the Punishment of Lying Be Avoided.

Although theft and fraud have different degrees of expression, they nevertheless say the same thing.

Theft says: “If you do not take what belongs to another, you cannot be rich or even adequately supplied from your own possessions.”

Fraud says: “If you hand over intact everything that your superior entrusted to you for safekeeping, and do not consider even a little of it worth reserving, how will you provide for your own needs or please your friends and fellow soldiers?”

But innocence replies to both: “It is better to be poor and insufficient, and to please no one by what has been given, than to harm anyone through theft or fraud. For whoever unjustly seizes what belongs to another in any way closes the entrance of the heavenly kingdom to himself.”

Hence the outstanding Preacher [Note: [Col. 1100] This manner of expression is customary in Autpertus.] rebukes certain people, saying: “It is altogether a fault among you that you have lawsuits with one another. Why do you not rather suffer injustice? Why do you not rather suffer fraud? But you yourselves do injustice and defraud, and this against your brothers. Or do you not know that the unrighteous will not possess the kingdom of God?” And among other things he adds: “Neither thieves nor the rapacious will possess the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 6:7–10).

## CHAPTER XIX. The Same Argument Continues.

Deception and lying also say the same thing; deception, however, is accomplished by cleverness, whereas lying is accomplished by a simple word.

Deception, therefore, to give one example among many, when it seeks to mock someone by not giving, says to the one who asks: “Why do you delay in asking? I have nothing that I can give you”—while concealing in his heart what he has, whether to preserve for himself or to give to others if he wishes [Note: [Col. 1101] The Corbie Manuscript reads: “what.”; the Royal Manuscript reads: “when, in wishing to harm, he seeks to give.”].

Lying says: “I absolutely do not have what you are asking for,” frustrating the petitioner not by ingenious cleverness, as deception does, but by the simple word of denial.

But truth replies to both: “No one ought to deceive anyone either by ingenious cleverness or by a simple word, because, however one may lie, ‘the mouth that lies kills the soul’” (Wis. 1:11). And “their portion will be in the lake of burning fire and sulfur” (Rev. 21:8).

## CHAPTER XX. One Should Approach Food as Medicine.

Gluttony says: “God created everything clean for eating; and whoever refuses to be filled with food, what else does he do but oppose a gift that has been granted?”

But moderation in food replies: “One part of what you say is true. So that human beings would not die of hunger, God created everything clean for eating; but so that they would not exceed the measure of eating, he commanded abstinence.

“For among its other evils, Sodom perished especially through the fullness of bread, as the Lord testifies when he speaks through the prophet to Jerusalem: ‘This was the iniquity of your sister Sodom: fullness of bread’” (Ezek. 16:49).

Therefore, just as a sick person approaches medicine, so everyone ought to approach the taking of food—not seeking pleasure in it, but supplying necessity. Hence the incarnate Truth says through the Gospel: “Take heed lest your hearts be weighed down with gluttony and drunkenness” (Luke 21:34).

In contrast, concerning the insatiable greed of the Jews, the Apostle says: “Many walk, of whom I have often told you, and now tell you even with tears, that they are enemies of the cross of Christ; their god is their belly, and their glory is in their shame, who set their minds on earthly things” (Phil. 3:18–19). And again: “Food is for the stomach and the stomach for food, and God will destroy both one and the other” (1 Cor. 6:13).

He fully overcomes this vice who, in taking food, not only maintains moderation—so that he always commands refreshment while still hungry—but also, except in bodily illness and the reception of guests, despises dishes that are more elaborate and more delicious [Note: [Col. 1101] The Royal Manuscript reads, “more sumptuous.”].

## CHAPTER XXI. Joy Does Not Belong to This Age.

Inappropriate joy says: “Why do you hide your heart’s gladness within? Come out into public rejoicing; say something outside that will make either you or your neighbors laugh; make them happy with your happiness.”

But measured sorrow replies: “From where does such great joy come to you? Have you already conquered the devil? Have you already escaped the punishments of hell? Have you already come from exile into your homeland? Have you already received assurance concerning your election?

“Or perhaps you have forgotten what the Lord says: ‘The world will rejoice, but you will be sorrowful; yet your sorrow will be turned into joy’” (John 16:20). Or perhaps you have forgotten what he says elsewhere: “Woe to you who laugh now, for you will mourn and weep” (Luke 6:25); and what is said through Solomon: “Laughter will be mixed with sorrow, and mourning takes possession of the end of joy” (Prov. 14:13); and, in contrast, what is said through the Gospel: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matt. 5:5); and again through Solomon: “A person does not know whether he is worthy of love or hatred, but everything is reserved for the future in uncertainty” (Eccl. 9:1).

“Therefore restrain empty joy, because you have not yet escaped your penal misery. Is not the person judged insane by everyone who tries to rejoice while confined in the darkness of a prison?”

## CHAPTER XXII. Multitude of Speech Must Be Avoided.

Excessive speech says: “The guilty person will not be the one who speaks many things, provided they are good, but the one who is found to speak even a few things, provided they are evil [Note: [Col. 1102] The Royal Manuscript reads, “but rather the one who speaks few and evil things.”].”

But discreet silence replies: “What you say is true; yet while many good things appear to be spoken, it often happens that speech, beginning with good things, turns toward something wrong [Note: [Col. 1102] Elsewhere, “having begun.”]. Holy Scripture itself declares: ‘In a multitude of words sin will not be absent’” (Prov. 10:19).

“Perhaps criminal words are avoided amid innumerable words. But can useless and idle words be avoided, concerning which an account will have to be rendered in the future? A measure must therefore be maintained in speaking, and sometimes even useful words must be spared, as the blessed Psalmist is read to have done. For he says: ‘I was humbled, and I was silent even from good things’” (Ps. 38:3).

## CHAPTER XXIII. Against Uncleanness.

Uncleanness says: “It is no great crime to be defiled through intercourse between male and female, whether by one’s own hands or another’s.”

But purity of flesh replies: “The Apostle does not speak in that way. What, then, does he say? ‘The impure,’ he says, ‘will not possess the kingdom of God’” (1 Cor. 6:9).

## CHAPTER XXIV. Against Lust.

Luxury says: “Why do you not now indulge yourself in your pleasure, since you do not know what will follow you? Therefore you ought not to waste the time granted to you in desires, since you do not know how quickly it may pass. For if God had not wished human beings to unite in sexual pleasure, he would not have made male and female at the very beginning of the human race.”

But inviolate chastity replies: “Do not pretend that you are unaware of what you will receive after this life. If you have lived piously and chastely, you will rejoice without end; but if impiously and luxuriously, you will be subjected to everlasting fires. You ought therefore to live more chastely precisely because, as you say, you do not know how quickly the time granted to you may pass.

“As for your claim that at the beginning of the human race God created male and female for the purpose that they should unite in mutual embraces, you speak entirely truthfully. But you do not consider that permission to marry is granted to some—that is, to those who have made no profession of virginity or widow’s chastity—but is not granted to others, namely, those who have resolved to remain virgins or continent; nor do you consider that fornication is permitted to no one with impunity.

“Or do you think that what the Apostle says to the licentious should be disregarded: ‘Flee fornication, brothers: every sin that a person commits is outside the body, but whoever fornicates sins against his own body’? If you consider this of little importance, hear what you will later lament and bewail forever: ‘Neither adulterers,’ he says, ‘nor fornicators, nor men who have sex with males shall possess the kingdom of God.’ (Ibid., XVIII, 9.) Oh, how brief is the hour of intercourse, by which eternal life is lost [Note: Col. 1102. The manuscripts read “future life.”]!

“What benefit, then, does it bring to the body, or what profit does it provide, if it leads the soul so quickly to Tartarus?”

## CHAPTER XXV. On Purity of Heart

Spiritual fornication says: “Does one really do anything deserving condemnation who consents to lust in the heart but does not proceed to the act of the lust he has desired?”

But purity of heart replies: “The person who does not guard the soul’s chastity is certainly committing sin.” Hence the author of purity says in the Gospel: “Whoever looks upon a woman in order to lust after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. V, 28).

In opposition to this [Note: Col. 1102. A wording characteristic of Autpert.], blessed Job says:

“I made a covenant with my eyes, that I would not even think about a virgin. For what portion would God have in me from above, and what inheritance would the Almighty have from the heights?” (Job XXXI, 1–2.)

For if the thought of an evil consent were not displeasing to our Creator, he would certainly not have said through Isaiah: “Take away the evil of your thoughts from my eyes” (Isa. I, 16); nor would he have said to the Pharisees in the Gospel: “Why do you think evil things in your hearts?” (Matt. IX, 1.)

Nor would the Apostle Paul have said:

“Thoughts that accuse or even defend one another, on the day when God will judge the hidden things of human beings according to my gospel” (Rom. II, 15–16). [Col. 1103]

## CHAPTER XXVI. The Happiness of the Blessed Life

Love of the present age says: “What can be more beautiful, more honorable, more graceful, or more delightful than what we see every day in the present life? Oh, how marvelous is the vault of heaven—in the pleasant air, in the light of the sun, in the waxing and waning of the moon, in the variety and movement of the stars! How pleasing is the earth—in the flowers of the groves, in the sweet motions of the waves, in the loveliness of meadows and streams, in the luxuriant stalks of the crops, in the leaves and clusters of vineyards [Note: Col. 1103. The Regius manuscript reads “in clusters”], in the shadows of forests and their open clearings, in the running of horses and dogs, in the leaps of stags and does, in the flights of hawks, in the feathers and necks of peacocks, doves, and turtledoves, in the painted walls and ceilings of houses, in the ringing songs of organs and all musical instruments, in the attractive appearances of women—their eyebrows and hair, their eyes and cheeks, their throat and lips, their nose and hands—and in the gold and gems applied externally in varied necklaces, as well as in whatever else the senses do not now recall!

“But love of the heavenly homeland replies: ‘If the things beneath heaven delight you, and if the prison is so beautiful, what must the homeland, the city, and the house be like? If such are the things possessed by exiles, what must those possessed by children be like? If mortals and wretched people are rewarded in this life in such a manner, how richly must immortals and blessed people be endowed in that life?’

“Therefore let love of the present age depart, in which no one is born without being destined to die; and let love of the future age take its place, in which all are brought to life so that thereafter they do not die. There no adversity disturbs, no necessity oppresses, no distress troubles; rather, everlasting joy reigns.

“If you ask what exists there, where such great blessedness endures, it cannot be said otherwise than this: Whatever is good is there, and whatever is evil is never there.

“‘What good is that?’ you ask. Why do you ask me? It has been defined by the Prophet and the Apostle: ‘What eye has not seen, and ear has not heard, and what has not entered the human heart—these things God has prepared for those who love him’” (Isa. LXIV, 4; I Cor. II, 9).

David, surrounded by the many riches of the world, yearned for this happiness when he said: “What remains for me in heaven, and what have I desired from you upon earth?” (Ps. LXXII, 25.) [Note: Col. 1103. Thus the manuscripts; the printed editions read, “For what is there for me?”]

Abounding in many royal delicacies, he said: “I shall be satisfied when your glory is revealed” (Ps. XVI, 15). And again: “My soul thirsted for the living God; when shall I come and appear before the face of God?” (Ps. XLI, 3.) And again: “Woe is me, for my sojourn has been prolonged!” (Ps. CXIX, 5.) Hence Paul also said: “I desire to depart and be with Christ, for that is far better” (Phil. I, 23).

Having brought these matters to a close, although I have passed over much, I have nevertheless, as I think, shown you the camp of our fornicating enemy [Note: Col. 1103. Alternatively, “the strong camp.” We follow the German manuscript, which is supported by most witnesses. The Regius manuscript instead reads: “Our enemy has become a great object of fear; for the camp …”], with which he never ceases to attack those who live piously in Christ Jesus.

But the devil is not satisfied with these things. He turns to other devices: he often speaks truthfully to some in dreams, so that at some point he may lead them into falsehood; he awakens sleepers before the proper hour or time, so that during the period meant for wakefulness he may weigh them down with the heaviest sleep; and when they are singing psalms and praying, he disturbs them with hisses, screeches, barking, various discordant sounds, and even stones or excrement thrown at them, so that, dragging them away from spiritual work by whatever means he can, he may render them fruitless.

But you, man of God, attend carefully to what I say, and believe me as I tell you things still more astonishing [Note: Col. 1103. In one manuscript the passage concludes: “and believe the truth that calls you and gently admonishes you.” See another conclusion in Ambrose and Isidore.]

## CHAPTER XXVII. The Devil’s Unheard-of Temptation, and Why It Was Permitted

I recently learned what I am about to relate from the report of someone. A certain religious man, living in monastic dress, has in our own time been assailed by an unheard-of temptation from the ancient enemy. The evil spirit repeatedly defiled pieces of his clothing—even those laid out apart from him—with filthy excrement. It was so dreadful, foul, and harmful that whatever part of the garments it touched was thereafter unfit for any use, even after it had been washed.

When I was asked why almighty God had given such power over him to that crafty serpent, I replied: “So that he might display outwardly the impurity of his heart. He would never have done this in his external clothing unless he had utterly corrupted his interior—either through unbelief and blasphemy, or at least through empty and vain glory. For the internal corruption flowed outward through the clothing.”

Because he was far away, I did not see him myself; nevertheless, as I believe, I truly discerned these things in him beforehand. But even if it is not so, can the event nevertheless be thought to have happened without cause? It happened so that in him that filth might preserve purity of heart, lest the cunning enemy defile it with the stain of empty glory—just as Paul received a thorn in the flesh lest he become conceited because of the greatness of his revelations (II Cor. XII, 7).

Let either explanation stand. Or, even if neither should be the case, can what I am about to state last nevertheless be untrue? It is entirely true—what I say is true: that filth of that kind does not harm the soul externally if a person strives to preserve inward purity of heart.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. That Someone Can Be Perfect in His Homeland; Who Truly Renounces His Own; In What Sense No Prophet Is Accepted in His Homeland; Praise of the Benedictine Rule

Meanwhile, as you yourself took care to indicate, I hear that some among you say that no one can be perfect in the homeland of his birth. They take as their argument what the Lord said: “No prophet is accepted in his homeland” (Matt. XIII, 57).

First, they must be refuted by the reasoning of truth; only then should it be shown how the statement is to be understood. Let those who say these things listen patiently, because by failing to consider the meaning of sacred Scripture wisely, they almost despise all the saints.

For if their claim is true, then all those Romans who have been converted and live among Romans, all Greeks among Greeks, all Italians among Italians, all Iberians among Iberians, all Germans among Germans, all Aquitanians among Aquitanians, all Britons among Britons, and all English among English who live religiously must be imperfect.

Behold, Paul and Antony, from the Thebaids, were perfect among the Thebans. Behold, Hilarion, from Palestine, was perfect among the Palestinians. Behold, Macarius, from Egypt, was perfect among the Egyptians. Behold, the city of Oxyrhynchus was made entirely perfect from its own citizens. And, to come to our own neighbors [Note: Col. 1104. Benevento, where Autpert lived, is near Milan, if compared with Oxyrhynchus], Protasius and Gervasius, remaining in this very city of Milan and in their own home and practicing the life of monks for ten years, became so perfect that they became martyrs.

Or perhaps your province alone is to be exempted from this rule, so that it may have monks not from its own people but only from outsiders? It is therefore more important that wherever someone may be, he should live according to the rule of the perfect, and should not turn aside from the path of perfection through the allurements of parents, relatives, or in-laws.

In this way, certainly, according to the Savior’s [Note: Col. 1104. The manuscripts likewise read *Salvatoris* (“Savior”).] declaration, he will be able to renounce father and mother, brothers, sisters, wives, children, houses, fields, and everything he possesses (Matt. XIX, 29).

I say this not to deny the highest praise to those who withdraw from one kingdom to another or from public life to the desert, but to show that even those who flee their homeland more in affection than in their footsteps are blessed and perfect.

I therefore beg those who deny that such things can happen among you [Col. 1105] to consider carefully why the Lord did not say, “No prophet is perfect in his homeland.” What else, then, is to be understood there except that when he said “not accepted,” he meant “not received”? He intended this to be understood of the ancient Prophets and of himself, who were not accepted but rather despised by the unbelieving Jews. Stephen said to them: “Which of the Prophets did your fathers not persecute? They killed those who foretold the coming of the Just One, whose betrayers and murderers you have now become” (Acts VII, 52).

Who does not see how rash and presumptuous it is for anyone to assume for himself the name of prophet?

You, therefore, reprove such people with loving affection, and always strive to live according to the rule of the fathers, especially that of the holy confessor Benedict. Do not deviate from it in any way; add nothing to it, and subtract nothing from it. For it contains everything sufficient, and nowhere is it deficient. Its words and commands lead its followers to the palaces of heaven.

Behold, dearest brother, amid my other occupations I dictated and wrote this discourse for you during the night hours, though in unpolished elegance. Since I realized that it exceeded the form of a letter, I preferred to call it a little book, *On the Conflict of Vices and Virtues*. If you find anything edifying in it, you should read it and pass it on to others.

[Col. 1105]

# ONE BOOK ON SOBRIETY AND CHASTITY, BY AN UNKNOWN AUTHOR (C, G, S)

## CHAPTER I. Three Vices to Be Avoided; Praise of Sobriety; The Evils of Drunkenness; The Use of Wine; What It Is Useful For; Why It Is Forbidden to Priests; The Harms of Drunkenness; Scriptural Passages by Which This Vice Is Condemned; At Funerals, Mourning People Are Given Heavy Drinking by Friends; Drunkenness Hostile to Body and Soul

[Col. 1105]

Since the changeable mind of mortals is sometimes pleased by good intentions and sometimes by evil ones, most people are carried headlong either from evil deeds to good through remorse, or from good deeds to evil through mental sluggishness. They provide material for moralists to discuss, so that once these matters are recognized, the corrected may rejoice, while those who cannot be changed may be confounded in their wicked ways.

For you will find it more difficult to find lovers of good than deserters of evil, because for very many—and almost all—mortals, the things that nourish the flesh are sweeter than those that restrain them from vices.

And since we ought to suggest to you the benefits of the pursuit of honesty [Note: Col. 1105. Perhaps “honest things.”], we warn anyone who wishes to serve in such a campaign that he must not be sluggish, sleepy, or drunk. Unless someone has turned away from these three vices, he can never be secure or safe; indeed, he will always be subject to every danger and even to death itself.

Strength crushes the enemy; watchfulness resists those laying ambushes; sobriety prepares the human heart. Therefore our Lord God, with fatherly affection, commanded us through his Prophets and Apostles to abstain completely from all vices, and especially from drunkenness, which is the abyss of all vices.

We wish to present the reader with something concerning the evil of this vice [Note: Col. 1105. The Regius manuscript reads “concerning the subject matter.”], and we ask only that he give attentive consideration to our exhortation and pardon our discourse, even if it is less brilliant than the eloquence demanded by hearing. We advise our listeners to attend to the reasoning of what is said, rather than expect the cosmetic ornament of frothy speech or elaborate eloquence.

Accordingly, first, for the sake of the title and dignity of the little book, let us present, insofar as we can, the fruits and benefits of sobriety; afterward we shall make public the shameful troubles of drunkenness.

Sobriety is chastity of the senses and mind, protection of all the limbs and of the body, a safeguard of chastity and modesty, close to dignity, guardian of friendship and peace, always joined to honor, fugitive from every crime and vice, steadfast in right judgment, wisdom inseparable from memory and recollection, guardian of secrets, veil of hidden things, capable of reading and instruction, at once pupil and teacher of studies and the liberal arts, attendant upon the acquisition of understanding, always eager for a good reputation, creating wholesome and useful things in one’s thoughts, a singular aid to virtue [Col. 1106], arranging all things with reason, and always presenting itself among honorable company.

Sobriety flees rashness, avoids every danger, responds to mutual duties, detests pride, governs house and household with moderation, preserves faith with those who entrust themselves to it, and, to put it briefly and summarily, the perseverance of sobriety is immeasurable strength of spirit. All virtues and every title of praise desire it, because without it they cannot be adorned or pleasing.

Drunkenness, by contrast, begins with injury to the soul and is the mother of every disgrace, the material of faults, the root of crimes, the origin of all vices, the disturbance of the head, the overthrow of the senses, the storm of the tongue, the tempest of the body, and the shipwreck of chastity.

Drunkenness is loss of time, voluntary madness, disgraceful weakness, the enfeeblement of a sound mind [Note: Col. 1106. The Regius manuscript reads “the enfeeblement of an unsound mind.”], the degradation of character, the dishonor of life, the disgrace of respectability, and the corruption of the soul.

Drunkenness, as we see every day, undermines many members of wealthy households and, depriving them of the care of management, makes them sell for a cheap coin what their parents and grandparents had gathered over a long period and purchased at great cost.

Drunkenness in either sex always desires every evil and commits unspeakable acts. Drunkenness removes the fear of God and takes the future judgment of God from the hearts of those under its power. Drunkenness, as the Apostle says, denies the heavenly kingdoms to those who desire them (I Cor. VI, 10).

Drunkenness steals the drunkard’s years and snatches away his days. He does not remember what has been entrusted to him and does not see, either with mind or eyes, what has been placed before him. From a servant it takes away not only fidelity, but also makes him prone to fraud and useless for the duty of service, along with other evils that cannot be comprehended.

And since some people do not moderate their use of wine but rather seek excess, they acquire danger to their bodily condition and life, as well as the gravest damage to their reputation and good name.

Wine was provided as a bodily remedy. It is entirely forbidden to those who abuse it, and the discipline of sobriety is decreed to be preserved. Wine is indeed necessary in many human lives: it restores a weak stomach, renews failing strength, warms someone chilled by cold, heals when poured into wounds, produces health when added to antidotes and various medicines, removes sadness, dispels all the languors of the spirit, infuses joy, and enables dinner companions to exchange honorable conversation. But taken in somewhat greater quantity, it is transformed in the drinker into a kind of poison.

For this reason we read that the Lord first commanded priests and Levites to abstain from wine, because it was necessary that those who were to hand on the divine commands to other mortals—not by words but by deeds—and fulfill them through customs of chastity and holiness should first undertake to observe the measure of sobriety. The Book of Leviticus says:

“And he said to Aaron: ‘You and your sons shall not drink wine or anything that can intoxicate, when you enter the tabernacle of the testimony, lest you die; for it is an everlasting commandment throughout your generations’” (Lev. X, 9).

The prophet Ezekiel likewise says: “No priest shall drink wine when he begins to enter the inner court” (Ezek. XLIV, 21).

Very many secular authors have also published precepts of sobriety in numerous books. We do not produce their assertions against the vices of drunkenness, because human testimony ought to confirm divine testimony, not divine testimony human testimony.

Sobriety must therefore contend with priestly devotion through fitting observance, because whoever approaches the altar of the divine majesty without sobriety will experience the destruction of untimely death. Whoever, endowed with priestly honor, is close to drunkenness is close to punishment. And when those who draw near to God are drunk, the avenging forces that rage against them are not far away.

Therefore whoever, established as a priest by divine gift, approaches the celebration of the sacrament while drunk has no delay before suffering death. Excess is always contrary to every matter, and excess in whatever sex makes a vice. Therefore whatever is immoderate and undisciplined is followed closely by a fall into ruin; for where there is no measure, there is total danger. Whatever lacks moderation plunges into destruction.

Thus, when someone is immoderate and seated in the middle of a feast, having lost the reins of self-control and been overthrown by mad drunkenness, he looks at those who have turned away and staggered, whom he was unable to see while sober. Or he pours out superfluous words in a long speech and constructs empty sayings, shouting badly while sounding good to himself. With downcast face he reclines on his back, vomiting and entirely unaware of himself, offering a spectacle to the banquet.

And while he achieves nothing sound, with no one compelling him except wine, he exposes the secrets of his heart and reveals in public the confidences entrusted to him by his friends. He is found ready for every act of cruelty or shamefulness, since no reasoning of a sober mind governs him, but drunkenness rules him.

Amid his cups he takes up unjust quarrels and, when no grounds exist, provokes a bitter fight. By introducing empty words, he does not allow the sound statements of others to be heard, and he rises to insult his fellow diners and accuse those close to him.

I thought I should admonish you about these matters so that you may receive them willingly, reader. Therefore read carefully the epistle of the Apostle Peter to the Gentiles, Paul’s Epistle to the Romans, the First Epistle to the Corinthians, and those to the Ephesians, the Thessalonians, and Titus.

Moreover, hear our Lord Jesus Christ in the Gospel warning against drunkenness: “Pay attention to yourselves,” he says, “lest your hearts be weighed down with gluttony and drunkenness” (Luke XXI, 34). And the Lord is angry with the servant whom he threatens to punish with many blows at his coming.

Therefore abstain from doing or committing such things; restrain your madness; recognize that you are human beings; cast away such great disgrace from yourselves; and avoid the crimes of drunkenness with all your strength.

Pay attention to this rustic but sound saying: “Wine is medicine; taken beyond what is proper, it is known to be poison.”

Cast away such great disgrace from yourselves, therefore, and avoid the crimes of drunkenness with all your strength. The nature of wine was created for enjoyment, not drunkenness (Ecclus. XXXI, 35); through moderation, thirst is quenched, but one must not drink all the way to drunkenness.

Flee gluttony and drunkenness, speaking and doing things of which sober people would not be ashamed.

Flee the drunkenness that is administered only to mourners at funerals by comforting friends or relatives. The grief of a lost corpse cannot otherwise be tempered without some excess of wine.

But you, healthy man, desire every day to vomit because wine compels you, and you fill yourself with as much as many people could consume with pleasure and sober satisfaction. Do you not consider it shameful for a person to wish to take in more than he can contain, and not to know the measure of his own stomach? [Col. 1108]

Do you not consider that someone bound to drunkenness cannot remain master of himself? Why do you drink to excess except so that, provoked by wine, you may grow insolent and become worse?

From this unhappy practice of drinking arises a disgraceful contest between those who challenge and those who are challenged, and the winner suffers the greater disgrace.

Because of this, the limbs of many people reject food; given over to wine, they waste away through premature weakness and an unripe old age, and while still green with youth they are shaken by trembling agitation.

Hence their lungs rot from the daily burning of wine, and through their mouths they emit foul breaths like those of the dead.

In such people there is no reason, no plan for conducting life, no memory of deeds or readings, and no foresight for any art or skill. The setting sun sees them reclining at table for lunch, and the unexpected day overtakes them as they spend the night at dinner. While, in perpetual madness, they drowse or drink as they recline day and night, they are buried every day while still living in this life.

## CHAPTER II. The Lord’s Virgins Are Instructed in Rules; Funeral Vigils

But what shall I say now, or what shall I keep silent? If any of this drunkenness should befall women—drunkenness which above burdened the male sex with the weight of the crimes mentioned—nothing must be left unsaid. Rather, we must labor so that this divine admonition may correct women who are such, and so that sobriety, through fear of correction, may restrain them from drunkenness.

But since we began this little work of admonishing men with priests, Levites, and ministers, it is fitting and appropriate that we begin our admonition concerning the female sex with the Lord’s sacred virgins, so that every rank and sex may be considered without excuse before this admonition.

The Lord’s virgin must recognize which precepts she ought to follow and from how many vices she must abstain if she wishes to reign with God both while placed in this world and, after the dissolution of this life, with him in heavenly glory.

First, the Lord’s virgin must avoid public attention, shun the crowds of the streets, and, remaining at home, devote herself either to woolworking or to divine reading.

When seated or standing among gatherings of laywomen, do not give yourself over to their obscene or licentious words or songs. Rather, flee them and close your eyes and ears, lest, deprived of the fear of God, you admit demonic thoughts into your senses, by which you might quickly perish.

The Lord’s virgin must not proceed with head ornaments, elaborate hair, or raised and joyful eyes, but with her gaze lowered toward the ground and with a downcast face, lest, hardened into servile loves, she become a cause of destruction to others even if she herself does not perish. The Gospel voice tells us what destruction of the soul the desire of the eyes causes (Matt. V, 29).

The Lord’s virgin must completely abstain from every shameless word or laugh and adorn her whole life with silence and discipline.

The Lord’s virgin who stains her face with some cosmetic for the sake of enhancing the brightness of her cheeks must fear the sentence promised through the prophet Isaiah concerning the daughters of Zion (Isa. III, 16–17).

As the Apostle teaches concerning widows, the Lord’s virgin cannot be judged chaste if she is talkative in speech, verbose in loquacity, or excessively inquisitive (I Tim. V, 13); indeed, she arouses others more strongly to lust as if she were prostituted to luxury.

The Lord’s virgin, do not entrust yourself to any man, of whatever age, in a private dwelling or private conversation without the presence of highly respectable women. When you are alone in your chamber, sit with the doors closed behind you, and do not readily open your door to any man who knocks, lest you fall into the most disgraceful suspicion or suffer the shipwreck of your modesty.

The Lord’s virgin must not enter places where men sleep, lest she be thought to have offered herself like a prostitute to those who would corrupt her.

The Lord’s virgin must avoid the companionship and conversation of a woman who teaches evil and lives miserably, or who has at some time been troubled by a bad reputation, because the Apostle Paul teaches that good morals are corrupted by evil conversations (I Cor. XV, 33).

To extinguish the flames of lust and every kind of wantonness, the Lord’s virgin must devote herself to fasting and abstinence [Col. 1109] and persist in prayer by day and night, if she wishes to escape both the snares and ambushes of the devil lying in wait, and to reach the rewards promised to virginity.
