The Lord’s virgin must flee excessively every brother whom a bad reputation recommends that she avoid, and, as far as she can, keep her visits away from him and from his banquets.

The Lord’s virgin must not be unaware that the vices of lust grow out of conversation at banquets, and that from there one proceeds to the sins of fornication.

To conclude briefly, the Lord’s virgin must abstain from every enticement of gluttony, be content with sparse food and drink, and always be adorned with honorable silence.

It is a gift of God for the Lord’s virgin not to know how to become angry, but rather to know how to restrain anger, to be kind to everyone, not to signal assent with her eyes, not to fashion her tongue through deceit and malice, neither to listen to nor reveal the secrets of another household, to flee avarice and greed, not to deny what has been deposited with her, not to possess money at interest, to forgive her sister’s fault from her heart, to place a stumbling block before no one, to offer consolation to the afflicted, to minister to the sick, not to consent to one who slanders another, and to abstain entirely from slander herself.

The Apostle says that the Lord’s virgin must stand in church in silence and teach nothing from the law:

“Let women be silent in the church; for it is shameful for women to speak in churches.” Again he says: “Let women learn in silence.” Again: “I do not permit a woman to teach” (I Cor. XIV, 34–35; I Tim. II, 11–12).

If it is shameful for women to teach or speak in church, how much more is it so for virgins, whom the care and profession of chastity promised to God bind, so that other women may imitate them more in good works?

The Lord’s virgin must not speak anything wicked, scurrilous, or deceitful, and must eradicate every lie completely from her mouth. For the Lord will destroy those who speak lies, as David teaches in the fifth psalm, and his Son in the Book of Wisdom (Ps. V, 7; Wis. I, 11).

The Lord’s virgin ought to show as much faithfulness in all things as she exercises caution in swearing. Concerning the things she has done, she should perform oaths to confirm the truth [Note: Col. 1109. Supply “she should take care to do,” or something similar.]. She should recognize the Lord’s warning in the Gospel that she must not swear at all or absolutely (Matt. V, 34).

The Lord’s virgin must beware of committing theft or fraud, giving false testimony, or consenting to those who do such things, because blessed Paul rebukes those who commit them (I Cor. VI, 8; Rom. I, 32).

The Lord’s virgin must avoid attending banquets of married women at which men are present, lest she bring upon herself the sin of lust while men converse amid their cups.

The Lord’s virgin, close your ears and your heart against every sound produced by musical art, against all secular songs, and against everything that delights sweetly in the hearing, lest a demonic melody cut the love of Christ from her heart.

Turn your face away, as far as you can, from the movements and gestures of dancers, from female cymbal-players and tambourine-players, and from all masculine entertainments, lest, struck by the sudden arrow of love for any one of them, you begin to perish grievously.

The Lord’s virgin must beware not only of becoming proud or quarrelsome but also, as far as she can, withdraw from the proud and quarrelsome. “For God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble,” Solomon proclaims in Proverbs (Prov. XXIX, 24).

The Lord’s virgin must not exalt herself through boastful speech, wealth, or nobility of birth, but must remain throughout her life in the humility and poverty of spirit that are acceptable to Christ.

For at God’s judgment such things will not be weighed, but one’s own deeds; each person will receive his reward according to what he has done, not according to how he was born.

The Lord’s virgin must flee funeral vigils and other gatherings that take place in private houses, where men and women especially come together without distinction.

The Lord’s virgin who extends nothing according to her means cannot be called or believed to be a servant of God.

But, to speak briefly, the Lord’s virgin who strives to guard the modesty she has promised to the Lord must not sin in any way—not by conspicuous walking, nor by a gesture or soft word, nor by idle speech, nor in body, nor in mind.

## CHAPTER III. The Crimes of Drunkenness among Virgins and Women; The Evils of Drunkenness Summarily Reviewed; Why the Author Began with Priests

[Col. 1110]

And since we may believe that what has been said for the admonition of consecrated virgins is sufficient—and that, from these precepts, all servants of God and laypeople alike ought to observe what is appropriate—we must now proceed to enumerate the crimes of drunkenness and show that drunkenness surpasses all vices.

In consecrated virgins themselves, drunkenness first prevents them from fulfilling the chastity they have promised, since it has always been hostile to their holy vow in either sex. Therefore drunkenness cannot be the companion of modesty, since chastity has never been the companion of intoxication. Sobriety causes women to lower their gaze toward the ground; drunkenness, having lost modesty, raises shameless faces. Sobriety brings forth a blameless word with the utmost hesitation and silence; drunkenness makes both a woman’s speech and her face immodest.

For drunkenness draws out and extorts an unspeakable, shameless voice concerning everything such women do; and whoever has been overtaken by excessive eagerness for wine can retain no modesty about keeping silent. From this intoxication follows weakness of the limbs. Thus, just as a ship is shattered when it is dashed against a reef by the waves of a mighty sea, so a woman’s body and mind, struck by the great storm of wine, are undone in all their members.

For one who naturally cannot plant firm steps while walking—how will she be able to proceed when she has been struck by the immense storm of wine, stumbling in her gait and gesturing, always with twisted, upturned eyes, or with her neck bent, and with a maidservant supporting her because of the fault of her intoxication? [Note: [Col. 1110] Er., *lassabunda* (“weary,” or “exhausted”), instead of *lapsabunda* (“stumbling”).] There is then no health, no care of the household, and no management of the family. Her stammering tongue is deprived of the function of speech; or, when she tries to burst into voice, she is not merely unintelligible but is also mocked by those listening.

Her mind is deranged, and she is utterly unaware of herself. The arrangement of her headgear slips to one side and exposes her neck, partly bare, to those watching; and, with her clothing hanging loose on every side, she is ashamed in the sight of all, while she remains ignorant of what is being done in the house. In such a woman, modesty is undoubtedly endangered, and intoxication makes public every secret that sobriety preserves in women.

When she has been swept to the ground by dizziness and thrown upon her bed, she sees all the walls running around her; she thinks the roof of the house has been stretched below and the floor raised above, and she is received as though buried in sleep. The drunkenness of such a mistress is mocked by all the women and maids with open, no longer concealed laughter, while the bedclothes are defiled by the children’s insults.

As time passes in this way while the vice of drunkenness remains, all fear flies from her heart. She gives no thought to corruption, to terror, or even to the strength of a husband who often rebukes her. Hence, as the days pass, the neglected household is so deprived of its daily adornment that the husband continually longs for the death of the woman under whose rule his labor and management diminish and decline from day to day.

There is no one with whom anything can be discussed concerning the care of the household, so that arrangements might be made for improvement, because she displays only the name of wife, not the conduct of one. Since she arranges nothing, the husband’s daily care is wearied with unceasing sadness; for, like oxen yoked to a vehicle, if one ceases to pull under the burden, the other’s effort will tear him apart.

Thus, when drunkenness has taken away the household mistress’s keys, everything is put to the test. The fullness of the storerooms is daily emptied by the thefts of servants, and the entire house resounds with the shouting of an undisciplined household. Care of the wool-working is either neglected, nonexistent, or disgraceful. For such a mistress, the maidservant who offers a larger cup will be dearer and more beloved than the one who completes her assigned task before evening.

She delights in cups and in the varied Persian colours of wine, not of tunics; she seeks not the measure of cloth for making garments, but the measure of wine brought to her. She does not raise the looms for weaving in order to protect chastity; through drunkenness she has long lost the use of the loom in her household, and the looms she has taken away from idle maids she has given over to spiders. [Col. 1111]

When this woman takes food, she scarcely reaches half an ounce of bread by eating, and afterward swallows cups of wine; therefore she seeks poultice-like portions of food for herself. As long as she remains awake, she drinks; or, if she falls asleep, thirst breaks off her sleep.

But why do I delay any longer? If I wished to recount all the vices of drunkenness, time would fail me before I finished, while the Holy Spirit cries out through Solomon in Ecclesiasticus with these weightier words:

“An intoxicated woman is a great anger, and her disgrace and shame will not be concealed.”

And concerning both sexes: “Wine destroys many.”

And again: “Drunkenness swallows prudence.”

And again: “Much wine drunk brings irritation, anger, and many falls. Much wine drunk brings bitterness of soul.” (Eccli. XXVI, 11; XXXI, 30, 38–39.)

Therefore, to bring the book to an end, I shall briefly touch upon all these matters. Through wine chastity has been submerged, and very many multitudes have been deceived by seducers. Many virgins, driven by wine and forgetting the marriage bed, have surrendered their chastity to adulterers and have entered into agreements with adulterous men concerning the death of their husbands.

Very many, driven by wine, have rushed into indecent gatherings and defiled themselves; and through such wicked intercourse, as has been said, they have borne children from fathers or mothers, sons or daughters, brothers or sisters, sons-in-law or daughters-in-law.

Through drunkenness, many men and women have fallen away from a holy and devout purpose; forgetting themselves and having lost their honors, they have remained without distinction. Fugitives from their ancestral homes, they did not end their lives where they had begun them.

Through wine, the strong have been overthrown by the weak, and very many have been struck down to death by a woman’s blow. Invincible armies, when wine held dominion over them, have been destroyed and subdued beneath the yoke of slavery. Countless people who had long refused the yoke of domination have been reduced by drunkenness to another person’s control.

Through the habit of wine, very many have been driven mad; and, while their madness endured, they were separated from human society and were often consumed by the teeth of beasts. For very many, immoderate excess in wine has changed wealth into poverty and want. Innumerable people, driven by wine, have committed unjust and impious murders.

Very many cities, long besieged and never captured, have been opened to their enemies and burned with fires after their guards had been buried in sleep and wine. There are also many other unspeakable and innumerable things by which this world has long been, and still is, frequently afflicted through the vices of drunkenness. If I wished to bring forward from sacred or secular books individual examples and the persons through whom these events occurred, the book’s excessive length would weary its readers.

Nevertheless, in this work we began with the reproach of priests and Levites, as well as with an admonition, lest we should seem to make clerics or ministers of God immune from this contamination—by which, through the Lord’s rebuke, we expose all who are devoted to this vice. It is especially fitting that those who teach the people to abstain from various faults should carefully ensure that they do not fall into some vice or fault themselves. The Apostle rightly rebukes them, saying:

“But do you suppose, O man, who judge those who do such things and do them yourself, that you will escape the judgment of God? … You who teach another, do you not teach yourself? You who abhor idols, do you commit sacrilege?” (Rom. II, 3, 21–22.)

And so forth: he condemns those who do not themselves abstain from the vices they forbid to others, and who condemn themselves in the very matters by which they judge others.

Therefore we advise all clerics and laypeople placed in various such positions of dignity to read this little book frequently. When someone has advanced in good conduct and sobriety and has become pleasing to God, let him always rejoice gladly in the Lord God because of our rebuke, giving thanks to God through our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be honor and glory for ever and ever. Amen.

[ON TRUE AND FALSE POWER.]

[Col. 1111]

ADMONITION TO THE BOOK ON TRUE AND FALSE PENANCE

Almost the whole of this book was transferred under Augustine’s name into Gratian’s *Decree* and into the *Sentences* by Peter Lombard. It was later cited and attributed to Augustine by Peter of Blois in his books on Confession and on Penance; by Vincent of Beauvais in the *Moral Mirror*, book 3, part 10, distinction 12; by Thomas Aquinas in the *Summa theologica*; and by others thereafter.

Trithemius, however, considers it spurious in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, since, he says, Augustine himself is cited in chapter 17. Martin Navarrus objects, in volume 2 of his *Commentary on Distinction 5 concerning Penance*, and says that it should rather be supposed that the passage in which Augustine is cited migrated into the text from an annotation written in the margin by some learned man. For that reason, he says, Augustine’s excellent book—attributed to him for so many centuries—should not be rejected.

Navarrus’s conjecture is supported by the old books we examined, which at that place omit at least the name of Augustine. Nevertheless, both the sense and Gratian’s actual reading demand it. But whatever one may finally think about that passage, arguments are available from every side proclaiming that this work is not Augustine’s.

Bernard Vindingus collected some of these arguments in his *Augustinian Criticism* and opposed them to a certain recent theologian—“not otherwise a bad one,” as he says—who argued that the work was wholly Augustinian in style and doctrine and that Erasmus and other scholars had foolishly denied this. Vindingus points, among other things, to phrases alien to Augustine:

- Chapter 3: “Naaman lost his leprosy through water.”
- Chapter 4: “Peter denied the Lord and excommunicated Christ’s friends from himself.”
- In chapters 4, 6, and 7: “To promise punishment.”
- Chapter 9: “To be anxious toward God.”
- In the same chapter: “Let him confess to the best person he can.”
- Chapter 17: “It is necessary for the sinner to bear fruit in penance.”

In explaining Scripture, he shows that the author possesses neither Augustine’s diligence nor agreement with him. Thus, in chapter 5, the author says that the One who promised indulgence to everyone explains it through other promises:

“Whoever confesses me before men”—that is, every sinner, however great and however often he may have sinned, of whatever rank, even if he is a priest—“I also will confess before my Father.”

In chapter 9: “He healed the whole man on the Sabbath, because he freed both the body from sickness and the soul from every contagion.”

In chapter 11: “In Peter, John, and James, and in the father and mother of the girl” (Luke VIII, 51), the priests of the Church are figuratively represented. “By the tears of the widowed mother, Martha and Mary, and the crowd of Jews,” he says, “we are taught that for those who sin publicly, not their own merit but that of the Church is sufficient,” and so forth.

In chapter 14: “All this variety must be confessed, if one has sinned in a sacred place, or against one to whom one owed a special fidelity, as in the houses of lords and of many others; if during a time appointed for prayer, or on a feast of the saints, or during a time of fasting,” and so forth.

“If someone falls into avarice, he has also diminished chastity.”

Moreover, chapter 6 suggests that every good person was detained in the underworld before Christ’s coming, although Augustine, in book 12 of *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, chapters 33 and 34, disagrees on this matter or at least expresses uncertainty. Chapter 8 also mentions the deeds of Saint Andrew, which, according to learned authorities, began to circulate long after Augustine.

[Col. 1113]

We have corrected the book against the manuscripts of the Augustinian house of the greater convent at Paris, against a Cistercian manuscript, against the Vatican manuscript, and also against the *Collectanea* of Gratian and Lombard.

In the manuscripts it is entitled *On True and False Penance*, with “devoted to Christ” omitted. At the end they read: “Here ends *On Confession*.”

[Col. 1113]

ON TRUE AND FALSE PENANCE, DEVOTED TO CHRIST  
One Book. (C, G, S)

CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 1113]

1. The usefulness of penance. Errors of the age are refuted.

How greatly the grace of penance should be desired, every authority proclaims, and the whole life of the good strives to demonstrate. For penance heals illnesses, cures lepers, raises the dead, increases the health it preserves; it gives the lame their step, abundance to the withered, and sight to the blind. It drives away vices, adorns virtues, fortifies and strengthens the mind; it heals everything, restores everything, and makes everything glad. It moderates success, restrains impulses, and regulates excesses. [Note: [Col. 1113] Two manuscripts read “departures” (*egressus*).]

Through it, the person who does not know himself recognizes himself; the person who seeks himself finds himself through it. It is this that leads human beings to the angels and restores the creature to the Creator. It showed the lost sheep to the one who sought it (Luke XV, 4), and presented the tenth drachma to the one who anxiously sought it (ibid., 8). It brought the dissipated son back to his father (ibid., 11), and handed the man wounded by robbers over to the innkeeper for care (Luke X, 35). In it every good is found; through it every good is preserved. It drives away darkness, brings in light, purifies everything, and itself is a consuming fire.

2. You, prudent and courageous woman, have perceived all these things, since you have loved to hold so great a good. For scarcely can something be loved that is wholly unknown. Relying upon this good, you will be able to be strong for every good work.

Therefore I gladly assist your will, which I have recognized as directed toward this good. [Note: [Col. 1113] Two manuscripts read “with which I have met” (*conveni*), and shortly afterward, “you did not ask” (*non rogasti*).] I eagerly undertake, as you requested, the pleasant labor concerning this matter, hoping for God’s help in your merit. For I know that your intention will never be frustrated but will be enriched in everything it desires.

When you were rich, you made yourself poor for Christ, and in your soul you will be rich in a holy exchange. Hence I shall be happy if I can bring any assistance to your true riches. I therefore offer to your love whatever I understand concerning penance, on the authority of the fathers and through the illumination of the Holy Spirit.

We do not merely attack the errors of this age; by an abundance of arguments concerning the errors we have attacked, we also strive to offer you the sweetness of consolation, so that the integrity of your mind—which, by God’s gift, has rejected every falsehood—may rejoice through reasoning over those falsehoods’ defeat.

CHAPTER TWO

3. Penance must proceed from faith. The remission granted through penance does not increase sins but restrains them.

If faith is the foundation of penance, without which nothing is good, then penance should be desired, since it is established that penance is founded upon faith. For a good tree cannot produce bad fruits (Matt. VII, 18). Penance, therefore, which does not proceed from faith, is not useful.

It must be believed, moreover, that the Savior grants the remedy of penance. For if every penance were fruitless for sinners, Christ’s killers would never have been called back to penance—a penance preached by the Lord, who was gentle and meek, and by his Forerunner. For he said, “Produce fruits worthy of penance” (Matt. III, 8), showing that penance is not barren but produces worthy fruit.

He who said, “I desire mercy rather than sacrifice” (Hos. VI, 6) did not await the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live (Ezek. XVIII, 23). Who, however, can turn in order to live unless he was in a distant region? David remembers that he was conceived in iniquities and born in sins from his mother (Ps. L, 7), yet the Lord bears witness to him: “I have found a man after my own heart” (Acts XIII, 22).

This same man, praised by the Lord, presuming upon the Lord, says, “You will be merciful to my sin, for it is great” (Ps. XXIV, 11)—not because it was great, but because David considered it great, like one who was already sated and disgusted with it. For a person does not labor to be relieved of a sin that does not seem excessive to him.

How, then, would it seem great if he still took pleasure in it? How would he ask that it be removed unless he grieved to possess it? If he did not grieve to possess it, he would rejoice that he had committed it. We know that God blotted out David’s sin either because he grieved that he had sinned, or because he groaned, watered his bed with tears, and ate ashes as though they were bread. But if he had rejoiced, he would have called his sin not great but small.

4. Therefore those who object to penance on the basis of the Apostle and mock him, saying against him, “Shall we sin so that grace may abound?” (Rom. VI, 1), are deceived. He was saying, “Turn through penance; hope for pardon even if the iniquity is very great: where sin abounded, grace abounded still more” (ibid. V, 20). No sin can remain in the presence of penance.

For he preaches conversion. But from what would a person turn if he was pleased with his former condition? Whoever turns must therefore grieve to possess what he rejoices to lose.

Penance thus obtains pardon, without which no one will attain forgiveness. For if the soul could be saved without it, it would not be said, “You have sinned; cease.” Why would one cease unless it were evil to sin? How can one love, rather than hate, what condemns when retained and saves when cast away?

Whoever now ceases must therefore grieve that he did not cease earlier. Thus he is saved because he grieves; thus he is freed because he repents. From grief comes the saying, “I have sinned; what shall I do to you?” (Job VII, 20). It is as though he said: “I grieve so greatly that I have sinned that it is a burden to me that I would not want you to refrain from taking vengeance upon me. I am seeking what punishment I can devise for myself that might satisfy you. Nothing is burdensome to me if it can free me from sin.”

It remains, then, to repent for those who wish to find forgiveness.

CHAPTER THREE

5. The error of those who believe that penance is null after Baptism. The Apostle’s passage is misused. It is refuted by the Apostle’s own deeds. The Apostle’s passage must be understood of Baptism. The usefulness of penance after Baptism is indicated by Christ’s parables.

There are some who believe that penance is effective only up to Baptism—for Naaman was a Syrian, and through water he lost his leprosy (2 Kings V, 20)—but that afterward it remains null for those who sin. They rejoice in their supposed uniqueness, arrogantly boasting that they do not possess what would make them sinners, declaring themselves clean because, as they claim, they have committed nothing after Baptism over which they could rightly grieve.

Because they understand everything perversely, drawing strength from the authority of the saints and following the father of lies, they falsely interpret what agrees with the truth. For they read in the Apostle what they do not wish to understand:

“It is impossible for those who have once been enlightened, who have tasted the heavenly gift, who have become participants in the Holy Spirit, who have tasted the good word of God and the powers of the age to come, and who have fallen away, to be renewed again through penance, crucifying again for themselves the Son of God and exposing him to contempt” (Heb. VI, 4–6).

[Col. 1115]

6. But if pride had not blinded them, they would see that the Apostle was not such a destroyer of his own labor and joy. Whom did he correct through his Letters except those who had fallen after Baptism and continued in sin itself?

He visited the Gentiles in bodily presence, strengthening them with arguments and miracles. How could he have written to unbelievers who were repeatedly opposing him? They stoned him and beat him with rods, and yet he wrote to them so that they might correct themselves. Why would he announce correction to unbelievers if he despaired of their salvation? How could he write when he knowingly and necessarily would achieve absolutely nothing?

If they could not be renewed through penance, why did he preach it? Moreover, he excommunicated the Corinthian who sinned shortly after Baptism and committed fornication surpassing that of the Gentiles. How would he receive a penitent if he preached so contrary to his own command?

7. Rather, he understood this passage as referring to Baptism. For he said that it was impossible for them to be renewed through penance so as to crucify the Son of God again and expose him to contempt—that is, so as to be baptized again.

For the person who is baptized represents the death of the cross and Christ’s burial in his immersion (Rom. VI, 3). In the sign of the cross each person is submerged in water, and, once submerged, is shown to have been buried.

Those who have fallen cannot obtain forgiveness through repeated Baptism. For just as Christ was crucified once, so Baptism must not be repeated. By his one death he redeemed everyone, so that there would be no need to die again. Seeing this, the Church understood that Baptism must not be repeated.

8. Through the fruits of penance, therefore, hope of forgiveness is offered to the baptized. The son who had departed from his father into a distant region was received by his father when, confessing through penance, he said to him, “I am no longer worthy to be called your son” (Luke XV, 21)—for I did not learn such things from you, nor did I find them with you.

The father of the household received him and clothed him with a robe and a ring. He gave him the robe because he restored in him the integrity of charity; he placed the ring on his hand because he made him work through faith and secured him with the pledge of the gifts of the Holy Spirit. He also restored the sandals to his feet because he enriched his Church through his preaching.

At his banquet the fatted calf was killed, because the One in whom all the fullness of divinity dwells bodily (Col. II, 9) became food for him. Through this he also showed that the sacraments of the Lord’s body are restored through penance and confession to baptized sinners.

For if it were otherwise, Peter, head of the Church after the Lord’s Ascension, would not have persuaded Simon, who hoped to purchase the Holy Spirit, to undertake penance for the matter in which he had devoted his money to destruction (Acts VIII, 22). [Note: [Col. 1115] The Cistercian manuscript reads “after God, head of the Church.”]

The man who fell among robbers was descending from Jerusalem—not into Egypt, toward darkness; not to the bloody Idumeans, spattered with dust; but to Jericho. The man who fell among robbers had not lived with them. Although he fell among them, though he had not previously been a robber, he was not abandoned by the Samaritan. Rather, he was helped by him and restored through care and sustenance. [Note: [Col. 1115] The manuscripts read “life” instead of “sustenance.”] This would not have happened if he had left hope of forgiveness only to the unbaptized.

Lazarus was called a friend, and afterward, having died and become foul, he was raised after four days (John XI, 11–44). This showed that, however greatly a person may sin, even after having been a friend of God, his spirit can live; but by God’s mighty cry and the weeping of many, he will be called out from sin.

First, the stone above him will be removed, because he will cast the hardness of his heart out of his mind; intercessors and preachers will remove it through their labor. The Lord released the daughter of Abraham whom Satan had bound, although the Jews protested; she was a daughter, both bound and released on the Sabbath (Luke XIII, 16).

CHAPTER FOUR

9. They wrongly understand the sin against the Holy Spirit as referring only to the sins of the baptized. What it is. They do not better understand the sin unto death.

There are still others who cry out that there is no forgiveness of sins for the baptized through penance. They say that sin against the Father and the Son is forgiven, but that sin against the Holy Spirit is not forgiven at all. They suppose that sinning against the Father and the Son belongs to unbelievers, and that they receive forgiveness through Baptism.

These people sin without the Spirit, whom they have not received; the others sin against the Holy Spirit, whom they received through Baptism but whose gifts they do not retain, choosing instead the poisons of the devil. They understand these people to be unable to obtain mercy either in this age or in the age to come (Matt. XII, 32).

But this interpretation is more an error than holy faith. If the remission of sins is accomplished through Baptism alone—which must not be repeated—why would the Lord add, “nor in the age to come”? It is clear that certain sins are forgiven in the age to come, where Baptism is not performed. No one will be baptized in the age to come and thereby freed from sin. Thus the interpretation that grants forgiveness to Baptism alone is false.

It is not only unbelievers who sin against the Father and the Son, but all who commit sin. Only those sin against the Holy Spirit who remain impenitent until death.

For the Holy Spirit is the charity of the Godhead, the love of the Begetter and the Begotten Truth, who gives us his grace as a pledge of himself. Whoever sins, does not wish to recover his grace, and never cares to be loved by him who is wholly love and charity, and does not strive toward him from whom he received the pledge, sins against the Holy Spirit. After death he will never obtain forgiveness, just as he did not obtain it while alive.

Thus no one sins against the Holy Spirit who flees to him. If anyone considers the sequence of the passage in which this is read and the reason for the saying—even if he understands it differently—he will not agree with those who interpret it perversely.

For the Jews were saying, “He casts out demons by Beelzebul” (ibid., 24), attributing the work of the Holy Spirit to the devil’s power. He therefore said: “There are sins that must be endured in one way or another; there are blasphemies that will obtain mercy. But blaspheming the Holy Spirit, as you have begun to do, will lead you to death.”

Afterward he said, “A bad tree cannot produce good fruits,” as though he were saying: “It agrees with your life to speak such things about the Spirit. A good tree cannot produce bad fruits” (Matt. VII, 18). The counsel is: “Turn and pass into a good tree; then you will no longer be able to think such things about the Holy Spirit.”

10. They object to another saying of Saint John: “There is a sin not unto death, for which one may pray; and there is a sin unto death, for which one should not pray” (1 John V, 16)—as though one should pray for sins committed before Baptism but not for other sins.

Those who understand it this way are mistaken. For he would contradict himself, since he urged the Church at Pergamum to do penance (Rev. II, 16). There are, in fact, certain venial sins that are remitted daily through the Lord’s Prayer, when we say, “Forgive us our debts” (Matt. VI, 12). These, as he himself says, are not unto death.

Other sins, however, which are unto death, are not remitted in this way but through the fruits of penance. He who received Peter when he was weeping did not deny forgiveness to the baptized. Peter had already heard, “I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. XVI, 19). Although he afterward denied the Lord and excommunicated Christ’s friends from himself, he recovered forgiveness through penance and bitter tears (ibid. XXVI, 70–75).

The Lord says that he is sick, looking toward the members united to him. These members are those who have been united to God through the sacrament of Baptism. When he recalls himself as sick in them, he does not deny that people commit sins—sins that he destroys daily through penance.

CHAPTER FIVE

11. They insist that repeated penance is ineffective. They are refuted by God’s promises and by the practice of the Apostle and the Church. Why forgiveness of sins is often necessary. Despair is an insult to God. Even a priest ought not to despair.

The treacherous still insist—those who think more highly than they ought, not sober but excessive. They say: “Even if penance is effective for those who sin once after Baptism, it will not benefit those who sin repeatedly; otherwise forgiveness would become an incentive to sin.”

They say: “Who would not always sin if he could always return?” They call God an instigator of evil if he always helps penitents, and say that he approves of the sins for which grace is always available. [Col. 1117]

But they are mistaken. On the contrary, it is clear that the one who is always ready to destroy sins greatly dislikes them. If he loved them, he would not always destroy them but would preserve them and cherish them as his own gifts. He always destroys the sins he finds, so that what he created may not be undone and what he loved may not be corrupted.

These hypocrites take their opportunity from the Lord’s deeds. “Whom,” they ask, “did he illuminate twice when blind? Whom did he cleanse twice when leprous? Whom did he raise twice when dead? Not Lazarus, whom he had previously loved; not the widow’s son, whom he restored to his mother out of compassion; nor is the prodigal son said to have been received twice; nor the daughter of Abraham to have been freed twice from the demon.”

They say that he repeated his deed in no person, teaching, as they claim, that the remedy is not often given by the Lord. He said to many, “Go, and sin no more, lest something worse happen to you” (John VIII, 11), promising punishment, not forgiveness again.

12. But the fact that he illuminated many blind people at different times and strengthened many weak people shows that the same sins are often forgiven in different persons, just as the one whom he previously healed as a leper he later illuminated as a blind man.

For this reason he healed so many feverish people, so many sick, so many lame, blind, and withered people: so that the sinner would not despair of being forgiven repeatedly. Someone is recorded as having been healed only once so that each person might fear joining himself to sin.

We still see daily in the Church those repeatedly afflicted by fever, repeatedly sick, and repeatedly seized by sufferings, being repeatedly freed, so that it may be evident that the work of the merciful one is performed as often as the confession of the penitent occurs.

For how could he heal repeatedly the body, which is of lesser worth and more unlike him, yet not free repeatedly the soul, which is more worthy [Note: [Col. 1117] The manuscripts read, “the soul worthy of death,” and so forth] and redeemed?

He calls himself a physician, one useful not to the healthy but to those who are ill (Matt. IX, 12). But what kind of physician would he be if he did not know how to cure a repeated illness? It belongs to physicians to visit and treat the sick person a hundred times. A physician would be inferior if he did not know how to accomplish what is possible for others.

13. He remembers himself, who promised, “I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live” (Ezek. XVIII, 32). Whom among sinners does he exclude?

That he promised forgiveness to everyone he declares through other promises: “Whoever confesses me before men”—that is, every sinner, however great and however often he may have sinned, of whatever rank, even if he is a priest—“I also will confess him before my Father” (Matt. X, 32).

For “whoever calls upon the name of the Lord”—that is, according to what it means for him to be called Lord, whoever calls upon him by serving him and not contradicting him, as he may perhaps often have done—“every” person, that is, whatever sinner he may be, “will be saved” (Joel II, 32).

This Promiser has filled every soul with good things, even those sitting in darkness and the shadow of death, excluding no soul. That disciple understood this teacher when he wished to correct the Corinthians through his Letters and, as he himself testifies, corrected them three times in his writings (2 Cor. XIII, 1).

For whenever he saw them fall, he ought to help them rise. He remembered the One who had said, “Whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them” (John XX, 23). We know that the first fathers, and the Church of God in every age, have always forgiven sins up to seventy times seven—that is, always. They are trying to take this power away from the Church of God.

14. The Church must believe in this way, since it confesses that it often sins. Those who dare to boast that they are without sin deny the truth within themselves after having been deceived: “We all offend in many things” (James III, 2), and not even an infant of one day can be without sin upon the earth (Job XXV, 4).

Therefore this error must be removed from the Church: the error that ever denies forgiveness to penitents. Such people do not inquire what the Apostle meant when he said, “I am conscious of nothing against myself, but I am not thereby justified” (1 Cor. IV, 4). He understood that sins can also befall the righteous. He was not asserting himself to be without sin, since he knew himself to be joined to Christ by an unbreakable bond of charity.

For unless he knew that the righteous often come to forgiveness, how would he have doubted that he sinned, when he knew that he possessed the Spirit of God and served him with the purest intention?

Why would the Lord have washed Peter’s feet and taught the Church to do the same (John XIII, 5, 15), unless offense is daily and therefore forgiveness must also be daily? Why would the Lord himself have taught those who pray to say, “Forgive us our debts” (Matt. VI, 12), unless he continued to be merciful, since he does not wish us to cease making this petition?

15. No one, therefore, can ever sin so greatly that, while penitent, he may wish to despair. [Note: [Col. 1118] Perhaps, “that he should despair.”] For what else is despair than to measure oneself against God? Whoever does not presume upon forgiveness from God does not consider that God’s mercy can be greater than his sin.

If he perceived that God is more good than he is evil, whatever justice he did not find in himself he would expect from the God who is more good. He distrusts because he does not perceive the goodness of the highest Good to be greater than his own wickedness.

Let only the one despair who can sin as greatly as God is good. But since no one can do this, let whoever fears the evil in himself presume upon the One who is better. The devil and every wickedness are less than God’s mercy.

Even the devil himself, if he could hope and perceive guilt within himself, would take from God’s goodness what he could not find in himself. Whoever still distrusts and compares his wickedness with God’s kindness puts an end to God’s power, gives an end to the infinite, and takes perfection away from the Godhead—to God, who lacks nothing, even what cannot be imagined.

16. Therefore, even if a priest has sinned, he ought not to despair, although it is written, “Who will pray for him?” (1 Sam. II, 25). For the whole Church, another priest, and the entire order of the saints will pray for him, as will Christ himself, who offers himself to God for us.

But the priest must consider this: he must not fall easily, since a heavier punishment is assigned to him for this. Let him say to himself:

“If the people sin through hunger for the word of God, I shall have to bear part of the burden. I will not dare to place unbearable burdens upon them and not move them with a finger” (Matt. XXIII, 4). But if I sin, what shall I do? I shall not escape so easily; I shall have to weep over my misery. For my condition has not been established in the same way as that of the people subject to me.

Thus let a priest fear to sin—but fear despair even more.

CHAPTER SIX
### 17. The Error of Those Who Presume on Forgiveness without Repentance

There are others who are enemies of despair [Note: [Col. 1118] Manuscripts: “there are others, desperately despairing, who”], who presume so greatly and trust in God so confidently that they acquire for themselves a certain license to sin and expect forgiveness without repentance. For they believe that, because they are called Christians, they cannot be condemned, flattering themselves with the text: “Everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved” (Joel 2:32). They think that they call upon the Lord’s name because they are able to believe in Christ and receive the Church’s sacraments, not fearing that “many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. 20:16).

They think that all Christians are few amid the multitude of Gentiles and Jews; and therefore, even if all believers are saved, the elect are nevertheless few in so great a multitude. But if anyone wishes to take notice, he will judge with the Church that these people have been deceived, although they trust in Christ’s redemption.

For they say: “What benefit would there have been in Christ’s coming, if the wicked still perished just as they had before his coming? Before God became man, only the wicked were condemned; and if the same thing were still happening after his coming, what benefit would his coming have brought?” Much, I say. For every good person was saved before the Lord’s coming through the coming [Note: [Col. 1118] Thus the manuscripts; the printed editions have *per venturum*, “through the one who was to come”]. For no one could leave hell unless he had merited being drawn out by Christ when he came; nor would human beings have possessed such great power to do good and resist the devil unless Christ had resolved to suffer so greatly and rise again.

These people pay no attention either to the Apostles or to the Lord’s words, which promise punishments so repeatedly and in so many ways to fornicators and criminal persons.

## CHAPTER VII

### 18. That God Repays the Wicked with Evil

To this is now added an iniquity like the former, although contrary to it. [Col. 1119] Those who despair judge God’s mercy; these condemn his justice, blaspheming God as unjust because they do not acknowledge that he repays evil to the wicked and they exalt their sins. But I wonder why they do not believe the Apostle who says, “Hope does not disappoint” (Rom. 5:5), while they are not afraid of the punishment that the same Apostle promises to criminals [Note: [Col. 1119] Elsewhere, “who deny it”].

For if he is not truthful when he threatens, why do they trust that he speaks truth to those who hope? But he who is truthful in promising is also truthful in threatening.

Yet it is not hope to expect good in return for evil. Rather, the person who does not abhor sin is reckless. But when he sins, let him return to repentance and trust in the Lord, whom he should fear as just and as the enemy of uncleanness.

## CHAPTER VIII

### 19. That Only Original Sin Is Forgiven without Repentance

One baptized unwillingly. The constant necessity of repentance. Sin grows when neglected; nothing is small in God’s sight. What things must continually be mourned. Not every sorrow is repentance. What repentance is. It arises only from wrongly used freedom. Mortal sins.

Since repentance is effective and fruitful, leaving no one without forgiveness and raising the dead, let us discuss something about its manner and variety.

Repentance is not necessary for those who are to be baptized [Note: [Col. 1119] The manuscript of the Augustinians: “and it is necessary for those to be baptized”]; but those who have been baptized must grieve and repent for greater and lesser sins. Through the faith of the Church alone are the sins that a person contracted in his origin forgiven: just as he received condemnation from a sinning father, so through the faith of Mother Church he obtains remission.

But the person who sinned personally acquires pardon through personal sorrow and through the faith of the Church. Through Baptism these things make a person so clean and new that nothing remains which displeases God.

Without repentance Baptism benefited no one who sinned voluntarily. But if someone were baptized unwillingly and confessed falsely, when he repents he will be saved, with the faith and charity of the whole mother Church, spread throughout the world, coming to his aid.

For this reason catechumens have been established by the Church, so that while they await Baptism they may be taught what they ought rightly to repent of. This restores a person to the freedom of choice possessed by the first parent when he still stood in an abundance of virtues.

### 20. Repentance Is Always Necessary for Those Who Sin Continually

“For we all offend in many things” (James 3:2), and these offenses are forgiven daily if they are always mourned. These sins are continually driven away through the Church’s sacraments and prayers, so that they may rightly hear: “You are altogether beautiful, and there is no blemish in you” (Song 4:7).

I do not mean that such blemishes never occur, but that they cannot remain. So great is the power of your petition and of the Church’s unity that whatever foreign matter enters cannot endure.

For although “beautiful are the feet of those who preach peace, who preach good things” (Rom. 10:15; Isa. 52:7), nevertheless the dust contracted on the road must be shaken off from those who have been washed as a figure of remission.

These sins, even if they are small through God’s mercy, nevertheless become great in sinners through negligence. No sin is so small that it does not grow when neglected. For one must not consider what he has done, but whom he has offended: how good, how kind, how devout, how forgiving is the one who created him from nothing by his most sweet compassion; who brought him without merit to Baptism; who educated and nourished him as a son; for whose benefit he created heaven and earth and everything in them from nothing; to whom all things serve as to a son; who sent an angel to help him; for whose sake he conquered his ancient enemy, strong and cunning; for whose sake he endured so many sufferings that the Son might die [Note: [Col. 1119] Elsewhere, “that he might merit the Son”]; and with whom he deigns to share fellowship—God who by his majesty rules and governs all things by his power for his sake.

How cruel it is, for those who take notice and are not ignorant of themselves, to offend such a father and commit anything against his will! Therefore those who know themselves mourn continually just as they sin continually, so that throughout their whole life they may mourn the whole of [Col. 1120] their life, which is a time of testing on earth.

### 21. The Things That Must Be Continually Washed Away by Confession

These things occur whenever something is done either below or beyond the proper measure. Even good things, which are good in themselves, contract something when they exceed the proper measure. Whatever is lacking from perfection, whatever falls short in a human being, whatever belongs to us, must be erased by mourning [Note: [Col. 1120] Elsewhere, “must be grieved over”].

Whatever is done in any way without the purest intention, whatever we undertake without the purest love of God, is not free from the activity of weakness.

Whoever has loved being as miserable as a human being is, and has not abhorred human weakness but has wholly kept it for himself, and has never tolerated his own being except in order to acquire the true being that is God, undoubtedly adds something to God’s work that must be grieved over.

And whoever knows what he is should love only that which looks toward the one who is. For if anyone thinks wisely about what adheres to the most shameful weakness through the very condition of existence—how foul and base it is in the flesh, how changeable in the mind—he loves in himself only that which will lead him to God.

Even whatever good we do: if we could do it better, it is because of us that we are not at the summit of goodness. If we know some good and perform it in some lesser way, it is not entirely separate from our own activity.

Let these things, which are constant and in a certain sense necessary, be continually washed away by confession and continually restored by compunction [Note: [Col. 1120] Manuscripts, “by rejoicing”]. Let us rise utterly pure toward the purest perfection, lest, through the multiplication of these small things, we suffer ourselves to be corrupted and worn down as by a kind of scabies; lest, when the richness of charity has been diminished, we be allowed to be afflicted by emaciation and tormented by the torture of an unclean conscience.

Let us always strive toward what is better, always striving toward the purity of Baptism and preserving it with the utmost care, so that when we depart this life we may arrive pure before the one who is most pure and be received by him without delay.

### 22. The Sorrow of Exile and Mortal Life

Let us grieve that we are exiles from our homeland; let us grieve that we live in corruptible matter. Let this sorrow arise more from longing than from punishment [Note: [Col. 1120] Perhaps, “it arises”].

This is how it differs from repentance. Repentance is a certain punishment inflicted by one who grieves, punishing in himself what he grieves that he committed. But the person who grieves because he is detained in a mortal body desires what he loves, weeping because it is delayed.

All repentance concerns wrongly used freedom. This other sorrow, however, arises more from necessity. No sin is necessary. Original sin itself is evil for this reason: it was voluntary in Adam. The pleasure of his wrongly used freedom is punished in us—not because it was necessary, but because it was voluntary. Nothing is sought from us that we would have committed; nothing is now demanded from us that we would have done [Note: [Col. 1120] The manuscript of the Augustinians: “that he then did,” omitting “now” before “would have done”]. The work of the father’s pleasure remains in his children. The devil demands as slaves the children whose father’s freedom he bought.

This sorrow arises not from a sinning conscience but from charity at work; it does not punish evil but increases good; it is not endured impatiently but embraced out of longing.

Andrew was in this longing when, placed upon the cross, he asked the Lord: “It is time for you to commend my body to the earth.” The people wanted to take him down from the cross. But he himself began to beg the Lord:

“Do not permit me, Lord, to descend alive; rather, it is time for you to commend my body to the earth. For I have carried it so long; for so long I have kept watch and labored over what was entrusted to me. I would now wish to be freed from this obedience and stripped of this most burdensome garment.

“I remember how much I labored in carrying it because it was heavy, in cherishing it because it was weak, in restraining it because it was joyful [Note: [Col. 1120] Elsewhere, “sluggish”], and in disciplining it because it was proud. You know, Lord, how often it tried to draw me away from the purity of contemplation; how often it struggled to awaken me from the sleep of the sweetest [Col. 1121] repose; how much and how often it inflicted pain.

“Therefore, most kindly Father, since for so long I have resisted it in its struggle, and by your help have overcome and conquered, I ask you, my merciful and just rewarder, no longer to entrust it to me; I return what was entrusted. Entrust it to another whom it will no longer impede [Note: [Col. 1121] Manuscripts: “whom you will no longer impede in it”], and who will preserve and restore it when it rises again, so that he too may receive the merit of his labor.

“Commend me to the earth, so that I may no longer have to keep watch, and so that I may freely hasten toward you, the fountain of unfailing joy, without this thing that troubles me drawing me back or impeding me.”

He grieved that he was no longer with the Lord, but he did not regret that what had been entrusted to the Lord had risen again.

Thus not every sorrow is repentance. There are also other sins which entirely take away life unless repentance comes to the aid. For not everyone who says, “Lord, Lord,” will enter the kingdom of heaven. Therefore repentance must be practiced, so that crimes may be erased.

## CHAPTER IX

### 23. Which Repentance Is Fruitless and Which Useful

It Must Not Be Divided. Without the Love of God No One Finds Grace.

Since not every repentance is good, let us say something about what separates true from false repentance, and barren from fruitful repentance.

There are some who regret having sinned because of present punishments. A robber dislikes his sins when they bring punishment. When the punishment is absent, he returns to his crimes.

This repentance proceeds neither from faith nor from charity or unity [Note: [Col. 1121] Elsewhere adds here, “fortified”]; it remains barren and without mercy. It does not cleanse the conscience or wash away crimes. In it there is no hope of pardon and no expectation of forgiveness.

Those who confess unwillingly agree with this repentance—not out of love for what is good, but to escape worldly loss or inconvenience. They serve the world, which they love; they seek their own glory, for which they pant; they receive the reward they expect.

If anyone remains secure in such repentance and does not strive from it toward true repentance, he will perish eternally, deceived and miserable.

Repentance, therefore, will be useful if it is voluntary: seeking the Lord whom he has lost, grieving, and anxiously hastening toward him, apart from whom there is no life.

### 24. Repentance Must Not Be Partial

[Note: [Col. 1121] *On Penance*, distinction 3, chapter “There Are Many”; *Sentences*, book 4, distinction 15, chapter “Enough”; Peter of Blois, *On Confession*.]

There are many who regret having sinned, but not completely, reserving certain things for themselves in which they may take pleasure. They do not observe that the Lord freed the deaf and mute man from the demon at the same time (Matt. 12:22), thereby teaching us that we are never healed except from everything.

If he had wished sins to be retained in part, it could have benefited the man who had seven demons to have six expelled. But he expelled seven, to teach that all crimes must be cast out together.

When he expelled the Legion from another person (Luke 8:30), he left none of all those demons behind to possess the man who had been freed. This showed that even if there are a thousand sins, one must repent of them all.

The Lord was praised when, after the demon had been cast out, the mute man spoke. He never healed anyone whom he did not completely free. On the Sabbath he healed the whole person, freeing both his body from illness and his soul from every contagion, indicating that the penitent must grieve over every crime arising together in soul and body.

For I know that God is the enemy of every criminal. How, then, could someone who reserves one crime receive forgiveness for another? Would he obtain pardon without the love of God, without which no one has ever found grace? He is God’s enemy while he persists in offending him.

It is a kind of impiety arising from unbelief to hope for half-forgiveness from the one who is just and is justice itself. For it would now be possible to find grace without repentance [Note: [Col. 1121] The Vatican manuscript: “for how would he find grace without true repentance?” Gratian: “for how would he find it without true repentance?”].

True repentance strives to bring the penitent back to the purity of Baptism. For it is right that whatever filth the penitent has contracted after purification should be washed away, at least by the tears of the mind.

But he is very hard-hearted whose bodily eyes cannot reveal the sorrow of his mind. Let him know that he is culpably [Col. 1122] hard-hearted who weeps over the loss of temporal things or the death of a friend but does not show the sorrow of sin through tears.

He should not therefore excuse himself by saying that he has no fountain of tears, since he shows through tears that he grieves over temporal things.

## CHAPTER X

### 25. The Command to Confess with One’s Own Mouth

Mercy with Justice. The Power of Priests. To Whom One Should Resort for Sacramental Confession. Confession to Someone Who Is Not a Priest.

[Note: [Col. 1122] *On Penance*, distinction 1, chapter “He Who Repents”; *Sentences*, book 4, distinction 17, chapter “But What”; *On Penance*, distinction 6, chapter “He Who Wishes”; *Sentences*, book 4, distinction 17, chapter “Now”.]

Whoever repents should repent completely and show his sorrow through tears. Through the priest, let him present his life to God; through confession, let him anticipate God’s judgment.

For the Lord commanded those who were to be cleansed to show themselves to the priests (Luke 17:14), teaching that sins must be confessed through bodily presence, not revealed through a messenger or in writing.

He said, “Show your faces”—and all of them, not one on behalf of all. Do not appoint another messenger to offer on your behalf the offering established by Moses (Lev. 14:2). Since you sinned through yourselves, blush through yourselves.

Blushing itself has a share in forgiveness. In his mercy the Lord commanded this so that no one would repent in secret. For when a person himself tells the priest and overcomes his shame through fear of the offended God, forgiveness of the crime takes place. Through confession, what was criminal in its commission becomes venial; and if what he committed is not immediately cleansed, it nevertheless becomes venial [Note: [Col. 1122] In Gratian, “vital”].

He has offered a great deal of satisfaction who, mastering his shame, has concealed nothing that he committed from God’s messenger.

For God, who is merciful and just, just as he preserves mercy in justice, so also preserves justice in mercy. It is an act of mercy to forgive the sinner his sins. But the just person must show mercy justly.

One must consider not only what he grieves, but in what he grieves, and whether he is worthy—not, I say, of justice, but of mercy. Justice alone condemns. But the person who seeks grace through spiritual labor is worthy of mercy. His mind labors by enduring shame. And since shame is a great punishment, the person who blushes for Christ becomes worthy of mercy.

Hence it is clear that the more people to whom he confesses the shamefulness of his crime in hope of forgiveness, the more easily he will obtain the grace of remission.

The priests themselves can then benefit him more and spare those who confess more. For those whom they forgive, God forgives. The Lord presented Lazarus, already raised from the tomb, to his disciples to be unbound (John 11:44), thereby showing that the power of binding and loosing was granted to priests.

For he said: “Whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven” (Matt. 18:18). That is: “I, God, and all the ranks of the heavenly army, and all the saints in my glory, praise with you and confirm those whom you bind and loose.”

He did not say, “Those whom you suppose yourselves to bind and loose,” but “those upon whom you exercise the work of justice or mercy.” I acknowledge no other works of yours regarding sinners.

Therefore whoever wishes to confess his sins in order to find grace should seek a priest who knows how to bind and loose, lest, when he has been negligent toward himself, he be neglected by the one who mercifully warns him and pleads with him, and both fall into the pit that the foolish person refused to avoid.

The power of confession is so great that, if a priest is absent, one may confess to a neighbor. Often it happens that a penitent cannot overcome his shame before a priest, although his desire seeks one and neither place nor time provides him with one [Note: [Col. 1122] Thus the manuscripts, with Gratian and the Master. The printed editions have “confess”].

And although the person to whom he confesses does not possess the power of loosing, he nevertheless becomes worthy of forgiveness because of his desire for a priest, since he confesses the shamefulness of his crime to a companion.

The lepers were cleansed while they were going to show themselves to the priests, before they reached them (Luke 17:14). Hence it is clear that God looks upon the heart when necessity prevents people from reaching priests.

Often they seek priests while healthy and joyful; but while they seek them and [Col. 1123] before they reach them, they die. Yet God’s mercy is everywhere. He knows how to spare the just, even if not as quickly as if they had been loosed by a priest.

Therefore whoever confesses completely should confess to the best priest he can.

## CHAPTER XI

### 26. When Private Confession Is Sufficient

When Public Confession Is Required, and Whence Its Merit Comes.

If the sin is hidden, it is enough to bring it to the priest’s knowledge, so that the offering of the gift may be acceptable.

At the resurrection of the ruler’s daughter, only a few were present to see it. She had not yet been buried, had not yet been carried outside the city gate, and had not yet been brought outside the house into public knowledge.

Inside, he raised the one whom he found inside, leaving only Peter, John, and James, together with the girl’s father and mother (Luke 8:51). In a figurative sense these represent the priests of the Church.

But we must observe how he raised those whom he found outside. A crowd wept over the widow’s son; Martha and Mary wept as they pleaded [Note: [Col. 1123] In Erasmus’s Lyons and Venice editions, “pleading”]; and the crowd that had followed Mary wept, stirred by Mary’s tears (John 11:39).

By this we are taught that for those who sin publicly, not their own merit but the Church’s merit is sufficient.

Thus let the dead person lie, and let him show himself dead by publicly proclaiming his death and publicly displaying the fruits of repentance, so that the crowd may weep for the one who has been lost and mourn the one whom it grieves as dead.

The Lord will be moved by these tears, and he will return her only son to the mother (Luke 7:12).

If he has persevered too little, if he has not shown himself dead through the fruits of repentance, then he must add so much more that he may stir up tears [Note: [Col. 1123] The printed editions have, “that he may be stirred by tears”], not only in Martha but also in Mary.

Let him afflict himself so greatly, and show that he grieves and feels himself dead, that those who hear and behold him may pray for forgiveness while weeping, and that the Church may imitate their weeping.

For the one who offended many by sinning must appease many by making satisfaction, so that the Church, first offended by his fault, may be bent toward mercy in his conversion, praying for the one whose death it had mourned. Then God will be moved to forgiveness, he who had earlier shown mercy.

## CHAPTER XII

### 27. Repentance Is Ineffective Outside the Church

[Note: [Col. 1123] *On Penance*, distinction 6, “He Who Wishes”; *Sentences*, book 4, distinction 17, chapter “Now”.]

Let the penitent therefore labor to be in the Church and strive toward the unity of the Church. For unless the Church’s unity comes to his aid, unless it completes through its assistance what is lacking in the sinner, the soul of the dead person will not be snatched from the hands of the enemy.

We must believe—and the devotion of faith demands that we believe—that all the almsgiving, prayers, and works of justice and mercy of the whole Church come to the aid of the person who recognizes his death for the sake of his conversion.

Therefore no one can repent worthily unless the unity of the Church sustains him.

For this reason, let him not seek priests who, because of some fault, have been divided from the unity of the Church. Judas, when repentant, went to the Pharisees and abandoned the Apostles. He found no aid except an increase of despair.

For they said: “What is that to us? You see to it” (Matt. 27:4). “If you have sinned, let it be your concern. We do not come to your aid; we do not charitably receive your sins; we do not promise to bear them; we do not teach you how to lay down the burden. What have we to do with mercy, since we do not even pursue the works of justice?”

He should have gone to the brothers [Note: [Col. 1123] The printed editions: “If he had gone, if he had gone to the brothers.” The Gloss: “He ought to have gone to the brothers”]; he should have gone to those who had prayed for Peter’s feverish mother-in-law (Mark 1:30), who had most mercifully presented the Canaanite woman, despite her boldness (Matt. 15:23); he should have asked Peter, who poured out tears for him (Luke 22:62); he should not have fled from Mary and Martha, who had obtained life for Lazarus (John 11:1), nor from the crowd that wept and had won back the widow’s only son (Luke 7:12).

He went to the divided, and divided he perished.

Every worker of good sensed this unity when he said: “There was a vineyard belonging to the peaceful one, in her who has peoples” (Song 8:11). For unless he recognized peoples gathered together in the universal Church, he would not have presumed to call himself a vine.

He knows, and learns by [Col. 1124] experience—as one who had labored for the salvation of all—that he cannot stand without the Church’s aid. It is no small matter when every good thing established either in heaven or on earth comes to his aid.

If he loses this through excommunication and does not recover it through the unity or compassion of holy Mother Church, how will he ever be able to repent worthily? How will he be able to find God benevolent when he did not hesitate to offend his most holy bride, mother, daughter, and sister, and completely despise her aid?

## CHAPTER XIII

### 28. How, How Long, and for What One Must Grieve

[Note: [Col. 1124] *On Penance*, distinction 3, chapter “If the Apostle”.]

Let him repent from faith and believe that this is the remedy. Let him regard all the fruits of his repentance as small; let him never consider them sufficient; let him always grieve; let him always blush before the Lord against whom he sinned; let him bring his sorrow to an end with his life.

For if even the Apostle continually wept over sins forgiven through Baptism, what remains for us, who have been placed upon the foundation of the Apostles, except to weep? What remains except always to grieve throughout life?

For where sorrow ends, repentance also fails. But if repentance ends, what remains of forgiveness? Let him rejoice and hope in grace for as long as he is sustained by repentance.

For the Lord said: “Go, and sin no more” (John 8:11). He did not say merely, “Do not sin,” but, “Let not even the will to sin arise in you.” How can this be preserved unless sorrow is continually guarded in repentance?

Therefore let him always grieve; let him rejoice in his grief; and, if it happens, let him always grieve over the repentance of his grief. Nor is it enough that he grieve: let him grieve from faith, and let him grieve that he has not always grieved.

## CHAPTER XIV

### 29. What Must Be Mourned and Confessed

The Circumstances of Sins. How One Who Sins in One Thing Becomes Guilty of All.

Let him consider the quality of the crime: the place, the time, the persistence, the variety of the persons involved, the kind of temptation by which he did it, and the crime’s manifold execution.

For the fornicator must repent according to the excellence of his status or office, according to the character of the prostitute, according to the manner of his act, and according to how he carried out his shameful deed.

If it occurred in a sacred place, or in a place to which he owed the excellence of faith, such as the houses of lords and of many others; if it occurred at a time appointed for prayer, on a feast of the saints, or during a fast, let him consider how long he persisted, grieve that he sinned persistently, and consider how powerful was the assault by which he was overcome.

For there are some who are not merely overcome [Note: [Col. 1124] Manuscripts: “There are not merely those who are overcome”], but offer themselves willingly to sin. They do not await temptation but anticipate desire, and they consider within themselves by how many varied actions they may delightfully commit the vice.

All this variety must be confessed and mourned, so that when he recognizes that his sin is great, he may quickly find God propitious.

In recognizing the increase of his sin, let him discover what was his age, what his wisdom, what his rank, and the whole condition of another person who did not sin. Let him dwell upon each of these things and feel the measure of the crime.

Cleansing every quality of the vice with tears, let him mourn the virtue of which he was deprived for the time being. For one must grieve, and cleanse through grief, not only because he sinned but also because he deprived himself of the virtue from which he was temporarily separated.

For although he hopes to obtain forgiveness, he can nevertheless grieve because he did not earn what would give him confidence of receiving a reward.

Let him be anxious and grieve that, although he is now escaping punishment for the past, he, miserable man, does not thereby expect glory. Since all his time is exceedingly brief, he ought to have struggled to obtain the reward.

Let him also mourn because, by offending in one thing, he has become guilty of all. [Col. 1125] For he proved ungrateful: although full of virtues, he did not fear God at all. In this respect, each sinner becomes more culpable in proportion as he is more acceptable to God. Adam sinned more for this reason: he abounded in every good.

In another way also, the person who offends in one thing is guilty of all, because every virtue suffers harm from a single vice.

If someone falls into avarice, he destroys generosity and diminishes chastity. For because of his love of money he would either violate chastity or at least love it less. If, for God’s sake, he still possesses enough chastity that he does not wish to lose it, nevertheless he guards it with less joy and less affection when he sees that it causes him financial loss.

So too with other virtues: even if they are not expelled, they are nevertheless diminished, whether greatly or slightly, through the conception of one vice, or deteriorated in their intensity. Therefore every virtue must be mourned in relation to every crime, and forgiveness must be sought for all.

He must also take notice—and by taking notice mourn—the soul of his neighbor, whom the fornicator has stolen from God or, once stolen, confirmed in evil. He must also consider that he became an example of evil through the practice of his crime, whereas he would have benefited that person more if he had been the cause of another’s conversion.

Let him therefore groan over the life of others corrupted through him, or not preserved incorrupt [Note: [Col. 1125] Manuscripts: “the life of others not preserved or corrupted through him, and the benefit, etc.”], and over the benefit he ought to have given his neighbor by the example of good.

Let him grieve over the sadness he brought upon the good by sinning, and over the joy he failed to bring them.

And let him consider not only what he did and how he did it, but how unjustly, by sinning, he offended God, as we have said.

Let him fear the saying of Truth: “You cannot serve two masters” (Matt. 6:24). Let him therefore fear that, while he persisted in one sin, he lost all the good things he had done through the contamination of evil [Note: [Col. 1125] Elsewhere, “through evil association”], so that, having served the devil through crime, he lost the service of God that he had offered [Note: [Col. 1125] Gratian: “he lost the virtues that he had offered to God”].

Nevertheless, it is devout to believe that, once God’s grace has been received—the grace that destroys the evils formerly present in him—it also rewards the good, so that when it has destroyed what it did not find to be its own, it may love and cherish the good that it had planted even in the sinner.

## CHAPTER XV

### 30. How the Penitent Must Be Disposed

He Must Not Confess Half to One Person and Half to Another. Withdrawal from the Altar. Abstention from Games. The Fruits of Repentance.

[Note: [Col. 1125] *Sentences*, book 4, distinction 15, chapter “To Some”; Peter of Blois, *On Confession*; *Sentences*, book 4, distinction 16, chapter “In Perfection”.]

Grieving in all things, let him either abandon the world or at least abandon those occupations that cannot be carried on without an admixture of evil, such as trade and military service, and other things harmful to those who use them, such as the administration of secular powers—unless he uses these by permission granted through obedience.

Let him place himself entirely under the authority of the judge and under the judgment of the priest, reserving nothing for himself, so that, at the priest’s command, he may be ready to do everything to recover the life of his soul that he would do to avoid the death of his body. Let him do this with desire, because he is recovering an infinite life, like God.

With joy he ought to do, as one who will become immortal, what he would do as one destined to die in order to postpone death.

Let him always entreat God, confident of the forgiveness which he would ask in every way and without weariness from an earthly power [Note: [Col. 1125] Elsewhere, “which”]. Let him who committed unlawful things in the freedom of choice abstain from many lawful things.

Let him always offer God his mind and the contrition of his heart, and then also whatever he can from his possessions. At that point let him offer what he offers with confidence.

“The Lord looked upon Abel and his gifts.” But it says that he looked first upon Abel, and then upon his gifts. Taking account of the mind that he knew to be humble and pure, he rewarded the offerings of his generosity.

But he did not look upon Cain or upon his gifts (Gen. 4:4–5). For he had seen that Cain’s mind was not humble, and because he did not recognize it as such, he did not accept his gifts.

In judging, therefore, the almsgiving of the giver’s heart must be considered. One must no longer consider how much he gives, but with what mind and affection he gives what he can.

For the widow, generous with the two small coins she possessed, put in more than all the others (Luke 21:2). Therefore whoever wishes to redeem his sins through the offering of temporal things must take care first to offer his mind.

### 31. The Confession Must Not Be Divided

Let the penitent be careful not, led by shame, to divide his confession within himself, wishing to reveal different matters to different priests.

Some conceal from one [Col. 1126] priest what they reserve to reveal to another. This amounts to praising oneself, tends toward hypocrisy, and leaves one always without the forgiveness which they think they can reach piecemeal [Note: [Col. 1126] Manuscripts: “which they think they can find given in fragments”].

Moreover, let the person who delights in true repentance beware of approaching the Lord’s body before a good conscience gives him strength.

But during this separation let him consider God’s terrifying judgment, where the more terrible sentence will separate sinners [Note: [Col. 1126] The manuscript of the Augustinians: “penitents.” Gratian: “the unrepentant”] into the fire.

Let him groan because he does not yet dare to receive the saving food that he greatly desired.

These are the worthy fruits of repentance: they unentangle the captive soul and preserve it in freedom.

Moreover, let the person who wishes to attain the perfect grace of forgiveness restrain himself from games and from the spectacles of the world.

For if Dinah had restrained herself and remained among her own people, she would not have been violated after being carried off by a foreign ravisher (Gen. 34:1).

Therefore the soul that has often—or even once—been carried off and corrupted should take all the greater care of itself and restrain itself. Having learned by experience what the virgin does not know, let it now be afraid.

Let it choose someone to imitate; let it not follow the one whom its own mind condemns. For a person judges himself if he does not distance from himself one who lacks the fruits of repentance; he praises and loves those whom he knows bear fruit worthily.

Let him seek worthy fruits, even if they are not sufficient fruits of repentance. There are indeed worthy fruits of the virtues, but they do not suffice for penitents.

Repentance demands more burdensome fruits, so that the Church may thereby be appeased; so that, appeased by sorrow and groans, it may obtain life for the dead.

## CHAPTER XVI
### 32. Futile Excuses in Sins

Condition or nature. God’s ordination. The failure of grace, or the efficacy of the divine will. God does not will sin, yet does not restrain it. What he provides to a human being so that he may preserve grace.

Let him recognize that his guilt is his own, and let him not wish to excuse himself, lest he increase his crime, as Adam did, for whom it was not enough to have sinned; he enlarged his crime by blaming his wife and transferring the guilt to the author of his being. This sin is incurred many times, but, because it is neglected, it is not recognized.

Let us sinners therefore not say, “I could not do otherwise, since I became a thief because God made me poor.” Nor is it surprising that I am devoted to fornication, because I was created with such a nature and weakness: weakness, not the will, compels me to commit crimes.
