Whoever is deceived in this way is mistaken. Nature is such that each person can resist the evil to which he subjects himself by his own choice.

There are also those who defend guilt by appealing to God’s providence, attributing to God’s ordination and necessity what has been left to the will and freedom of choice. God knew what the one who sinned would do; but he did not ordain sin, since he leaves no one unpunished. He ordained punishment for those who love guilt. For fire is the work of justice, not of mercy, so that those who do not love to rejoice may have something over which to grieve [Note: [Col. 1126] Perhaps, “now.”]. He did not ordain sin, who wished to heal sin [Note: [Col. 1126] The Augustinian manuscripts read, “who did not wish to create.”]; but he permitted to freedom what the sinner attributed to necessity. For if he could not sin, why should the one who is wholly justice reward him? This is why he does not sanctify mute animals: they cannot commit crimes. Even the angels who remained faithful—if they had not been free, how could they have been crowned? They could sin, and their kindred fell.

Although he created all things mercifully [Note: [Col. 1126] Elsewhere, “although he may have created.”], nevertheless he who is just had to preserve justice within mercy. But the one who does not feel his guilt says:

“I can have nothing good unless grace inspires me; without it I can do nothing. If, then, he himself does not preserve me, what guilt is mine, I who can do nothing of myself? If I could avoid crime without him, I would recognize myself as guilty. Furthermore, ‘Whatever the Lord willed, he did in heaven and on earth’: what guilt, then, is mine if he does not wish to save me?”

“Much,” I reply. Although you can achieve nothing without that mercy which you reject, you can nevertheless freely hold fast to grace, and by retaining it you can, if you wish, avoid guilt. For God [Col. 1127], who once began to do good, is compelled, by the necessity of just mercy, not to be the first to abandon anyone—unless we abandon his benefit, a matter wholly ours—for he is merciful in inspiring. Abandonment is not his nature, except toward one who abandons him.

Our guilt therefore lies in driving away the grace which we can possess perpetually. It always departs unwillingly and never abandons anyone spontaneously. Yet this does not contradict the statement that he did “whatever he willed.” He created whatever he willed, and he did not create more than he willed. Yet in each person he wills the good, and in no one the evil; but he wills it in such a way that the human being whom he does not will to sin does not cease to be human.

He does not, however, will human beings not to sin in such a way that he would turn them into cattle. Otherwise he would have no one to reward, no one into whom to infuse the radiance of his glory, no one whom he could establish as a co-heir, and no one in whom he could find his image and likeness. Nor was it fitting for him who is wholly justice to form anyone so that he could not sin, unless that condition were earned through human freedom.

He wills that human beings become good while preserving the being of both parties, so that he himself remains God and the human being remains human. For if he formed a human being without freedom, he would act against justice, which is God; and if he removed freedom, human dignity would not remain. He therefore willed that human beings not sin, but not that human nature be lost.

Thus he is merciful, since he wills our salvation; and he is not powerless, since he wills this while preserving the rights of both. For he is a just king, and he ought to protect the right of each person. Grace is always present, and never fails unless it has first been expelled. Continually and necessarily it inspires what belongs to it, if there is someone to receive it; and once expelled, it returns through repentance.

So that the creature might not perish—the creature whom he created free through his goodness and endowed with freedom—he made it serve freely in order to retain the assistance of grace, which always precedes every creature. To protect this grace, and not to expel it, he added the angels and all the blessed spirits; he added all those established in eternal life; he added those living in the flesh; and he added the entire holy Church, assisting all in all its good works. And, greatest of all, he sent his Son as an aid, whom he decreed should suffer so much for us, and appointed as a perpetual intercessor. He sent him so that we might not expel, flee from, or despise the inspiration of his goodness—apart from which he created nothing and saved no one—but might hold fast to it firmly and with thanksgiving, with all these helpers assisting us.

Thus the fault is ours—not that of the creatures granted to aid us, nor that of the author who wills nothing unjustly but mercifully, and who is omnipotent in all his will. Whoever, then, recognizes this in his confession, or at least does not defend his guilt against these truths, will obtain forgiveness through repentance.

This is true repentance, fruitful in this way. May he grant it to us who is wholly true mercy.

## CHAPTER XVII

### 33. Late Repentance: What Is True and How Rare It Is

[Note: [Col. 1127] On Penance, distinction 7, chapter “Nullus.” The Sentences, book IV, distinction 20, chapter “Sciendum.”]

Let no one wait until he can no longer sin. Let him seek the freedom of choice, so that he may erase what he has committed, not necessity. Whoever is abandoned by sins before he himself abandons them condemns them not freely, but as though by necessity.

Although the thief deserved forgiveness at the end for all his crime, this did not grant baptized people permission to sin and persevere in sin. For the one who first confessed Christ on the cross was then baptized (Luke 23:43).

If repentance comes in the final breath of life, it heals and liberates through the washing of Baptism. Thus those who are baptized at the end do not experience purgatory; instead, enriched with the goods of holy Mother Church, they will receive manifold good in true blessedness.

But those who, when they could have converted, never wished to do so, and who confess when they can no longer sin, do not so easily obtain what they desire. For the sinner must bear fruit in repentance in order to obtain life for one who is dead. It is written that no one is saved without charity (1 Corinthians 13:2).

A person therefore does not live by fear alone. Whoever repents late must not only fear God as judge, but also love him as just: he must not be feared on account of punishment, but loved on account of glory. He must grieve over the crime and over every variation of it described above.

Since this is scarcely possible, Augustine was able to doubt the salvation of such a person [Note: [Col. 1128] The word “Augustine” is absent from the manuscripts.]. I believe that the one who said, “At whatever hour the sinner groans and turns, he shall live” (Ezekiel 33:12), said that the converted person lives, not one who has merely turned [Note: [Col. 1128] The manuscripts read this way. The printed editions have: “I indeed believe him.”].

I regard as merely turned the one who grieves over the crime; converted, the one who grieves over every variation of it that we have explained. One turns away from sin who now wishes to abandon sin; one is converted who now turns wholly and entirely, who no longer merely fears punishments [Note: [Col. 1128] The manuscripts omit “not.”], but hastens and strives toward the good God [Note: [Col. 1128] Gratian reads, “but hastens and strives toward the good Lord.”].

If such conversion occurs even at the end of someone’s life, there is no reason to despair of his forgiveness. But since such a just conversion scarcely or rarely occurs, we must fear for the one who repents late. A person pressed by illness and terrified by punishment will scarcely arrive at true satisfaction, especially when the children whom he loved illicitly are present, while his wife and the world call him back to themselves.

Late repentance commonly deceives many. Yet since God is always powerful, he can always help in death those whom he chooses. Since fruitful repentance is the work not of a human being but of God, his mercy can inspire it whenever he wills, and out of mercy reward those whom, in justice, he could condemn.

But since many things hinder and hold back one who is languishing, it is extremely dangerous and close to ruin to postpone the remedy of repentance until death. Great indeed is the one to whom God then inspires it.

If anyone, then, seeks true repentance at that moment, let him await God’s clemency [Note: [Col. 1128] Gratian reads: “For if anyone through true repentance awaits God’s clemency, he will experience a greater [mercy],” and so forth. But the manuscripts read: “But great is the one to whom God then inspires true repentance, when he awaits God’s mercy, experiencing the greater [goodness],” and so forth.], experiencing the greater goodness of God in contrast with his own wickedness.

## CHAPTER XVIII

### 34. Late Repentance Subject to the Fire of Purification; The Justice of Eternal Punishment

[Note: [Col. 1128] The Sentences, book IV, distinction 20, chapter “Si vero.”]

Even if a person is converted and lives, and does not die immediately, we do not promise that he will escape every punishment. The one who postponed the fruit of his conversion to another age must first be purified by the fire of purification.

Although this fire will not be eternal, it is nevertheless grievous in a remarkable way: it surpasses every punishment that anyone has ever suffered in this life. Never has such punishment been found in the flesh—although martyrs have suffered astonishing torments, and many wicked people have endured punishments—as has often been endured.

Let each person therefore strive to correct his sins in such a way that after death he will not have to endure punishment. Some sins are mortal and, through repentance, become venial [Note: [Col. 1128] The manuscripts and Gratian read, “become life-giving.”]; they are not, however, immediately healed. Often a sick person would die unless treated, yet is not immediately healed: the one who was going to die languishes, but will live.

The unrepentant person, however, dies wholly and is tortured eternally. For if the one who dies unrepentant were always to live, he would always sin; but it is the work of God’s mercy that brings the sinner’s end. For this reason he is also tortured without end. Since he is never enriched with virtue [Note: [Col. 1128] The manuscripts read, “because he is deprived of virtue.”], always full of iniquity, always without charity, he is tortured without end.

Repentance avoids all these evils, for it always exacts sorrow in punishment.

## CHAPTER XIX

### 35. The Etymology of Repentance

[Note: [Col. 1128] On Penance, distinction 2, chapter “Poenitentes”; likewise, distinction 6, chapter “Qui vult.”]

One must always grieve over sin, as the very force of the word makes clear. *Poenitere*—to repent—means *poenam tenere*, “to hold punishment”: to punish oneself continually by taking vengeance for what one committed by sinning.

Punishment properly means an injury that punishes and avenges what each person has committed. One “holds punishment” who continually takes vengeance for what he grieves to have committed. Repentance, then, is vengeance that continually punishes in oneself what one grieves to have committed.

Accordingly, the one who grieves over his guilt should seek pardon in the ways described above. Let him not be ashamed to confess his sins to a sinner. For if the priest had no sin, the one who revealed his sins to him might be ashamed.

## CHAPTER XX

### What a Confessor Should Be; When He Should Be Removed from Office and When Restored; The Authority of the Roman Pontiff

[Note: [Col. 1129] The Sentences, book IV, distinction 19, chapter “Qualem.” Peter of Blois, book *On Penance*.]

Every priest to whom a sinner is brought, before whom every sickness is set forth, must not be judged guilty of any of those things which he is ready to judge in another. For the one who judges another while himself subject to judgment condemns himself.

Let him therefore know himself, and cleanse from himself what he sees others present to him. Let him take care to cast out of himself whatever he finds harmful in another. Let him heed what is said: “Let the one who is without sin be the first to throw a stone at her” (John 8:7).

He freed the sinful woman because there was no one who could justly throw a stone at her. How could one stone her who recognized that he himself ought to be stoned? There was no one without sin; by this it is understood that all were guilty of crime. For venial sins were continually remitted through ceremonies. If, then, any sin remained in them, it was criminal.

The priests who did not first build themselves up were therefore worse in this respect than those who were plotting against the Lord. Here, then, the crime of priests is most plainly evident and detestable beyond measure: they do not first judge themselves, yet they bind others.

They ought to fear in themselves the crime which they feared in others and recognized as detestable—those who were so blind that they hoped to seize supreme Wisdom by their plots. What was evident to them, and what each person then avoided, let the priest avoid; otherwise he has become worse in this error than those Jews.

Let the spiritual judge take care that, just as he has not committed the crime of wickedness, so he does not lack the gift of knowledge. He must know how to recognize what he ought to judge. For judicial power requires that he discern what he ought to judge [Note: [Col. 1129] The manuscripts read, “what ought to be judged.”].

As a diligent examiner and subtle investigator, let him question the sinner wisely and, as it were, astutely about what the sinner perhaps does not know or wishes to conceal out of shame. Once the crime is known, let him not hesitate to investigate its variations, its place, its time, and the other circumstances mentioned above in explaining their qualities.

When these are known, let him be benevolent, ready to raise up the sinner and to carry the burden with him. Let him have sweetness in affection, compassion in the face of another’s crime, and discernment regarding its variations. Let him assist the penitent by praying, giving alms, and performing other good works on his behalf.

Let him always help him by soothing, consoling, promising hope, and, when necessary, also rebuking him. Let him teach by speaking and instruct by acting. Let him share in the labor of one who wishes to share in consolation [Note: [Col. 1130] Elsewhere, “joy.”]; let him teach perseverance.

Let him take care lest he fall, lest he rightly lose judicial power. For although repentance may obtain grace for him, it does not immediately restore him to his former authority. Although Peter was restored after his fall, and the authority of dignity was often returned to priests who had fallen, it is not necessary that this be granted to everyone as though by authority.

There is one authority that grants and, as it were, commands restoration. There is another that does not grant it at all, but forbids it. These authorities do not contradict Scripture but agree with it, provided that the time, place, and manner of repentance bring peace.

Since there are so many who fall and then use authority to defend their former dignity, thereby making for themselves, as it were, a license to sin, this hope must be cut off. But where such things do not occur, those who sin may be restored.

Thus a just and discerning pontiff is not compelled always to cast out his priests, nor immediately to restore them, unless this has been established by the Roman pontiff.

### 37. Conclusion on Repentance

From what has been said above it is evident that repentance is useful to everyone: it removes hope from no one, yet grants no presumption. When undertaken worthily and truly, it promises not only forgiveness but certain rewards.

We write these things to you, diligent seeker of truth and lover of certainty, concerning true repentance, separating the true from the false. May he grant us to know it by experience and to feel its sweetness to the end—he who, through the illumination of his light, has bestowed upon you the prerogative of goodness and, therein, of steadfastness, unto an aroma of sweetness [reading uncertain]. Amen.

# [ON THE ANTICHRIST]

[Col. 1129]

## NOTICE CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING BOOKLET

The treatise *On the Antichrist* has also been printed among the works of Alcuin and Rabanus Maurus: in Alcuin, it is complete and full; here and in Rabanus, however, it is incomplete. For some things are omitted here that are found both in Alcuin and in Rabanus, while in turn certain things are missing in Rabanus that are absent neither here nor in Alcuin.

It is cited by Rupert, abbot of Deutz, in book 8 of his *Commentary on the Apocalypse*, chapter 13, though without naming the author, in these words: “Some relate,” and so forth; “Just as, they say, our Lord and Redeemer provided Bethlehem for himself,” and so forth. Nor do we know how the theologians of Leuven learned what they noted in their assessment of this treatise—namely, that Rupert recognizes it as a work of Rabanus.

Rabanus inserted the teaching and the same views of this booklet into his work on Paul, book 22, chapter 2; he repeatedly copies Albinus himself, just as he does many earlier authors. The Thuaneus manuscript, on whose authority it was first printed under the name of Alcuin, is supported by the Royal Manuscript numbered 4411, which presents the same booklet with this inscription: “Here begins the life of the Antichrist, issued by Alcuin for Charles the Great.” Compare Alcuin’s book 3, *On the Faith of the Holy Trinity*, chapter 19.

Nevertheless, it can scarcely be doubted that it should be attributed to Adso, abbot of the monastery of Derbensis, in view of the manuscripts in which the preceding letter is preserved. It will not be inappropriate to include that letter here in full. It reads as follows:

## ADSO THE MONK TO GERBERGA, QUEEN AND WIFE OF LOUIS OVERSEAS, KING OF THE FRANKS

“To the most excellent Queen, distinguished by royal dignity, beloved by God and cherished by all the saints, Mother of Monks and Leader of the Holy Women, Lady Gerberga: Brother Adso, the least of all her servants, sends everlasting glory and peace.

“From the time, Lady Mother, when I became worthy to be a scion of your mercy, I have always been faithful to you in all things, as your personal servant. Therefore, although my prayers are unworthy before the Lord, I nevertheless implore the mercy of our God for you and for your lord, the King, and also for the safety of your sons: may he deign to preserve for you the summit of imperial power in this life, and after this life make you reign happily with him in heaven.

“For if the Lord grants prosperity to you and longer life to your sons, we know and believe without doubt that the Church of God will be exalted and that the order of our religion will multiply more and more. This is what I, your faithful servant, wish and greatly desire. If I had been able to acquire the whole kingdom for you, I would have done so most willingly. But since I cannot do that, I will implore the Lord for your salvation and that of your sons, so that his grace may always go before you in your works, and that his glory may mercifully and piously follow after you; so that, intent upon the divine commandments, you may fulfill the good things you desire, and thereby receive the crown of the heavenly kingdom.

“Since, therefore, you have a devout interest in hearing the Scriptures and frequently speaking about our Redeemer, and also in learning about the impiety and persecution of the Antichrist, as well as his power and origin, and since you have deigned to command me, your servant, I wished to write something to you and to make you partly certain about the Antichrist. You do not, however, need to hear this from me, since you have with you the most prudent shepherd, Lord Rorico, bishop of Laon, the clearest mirror of all wisdom and eloquence in our own age.”

After this Adso continues: “Therefore, wishing to know about the Antichrist,” and so forth, as it appears in the following book of our Appendix, except that at the end, after the word “appointed,” he again turns to the Queen with this brief conclusion:

“Behold, Lady Queen, I, your faithful servant, have faithfully fulfilled what you commanded; I am ready to obey whatever else you may deign to order.”

[Col. 1131]

# ONE BOOK ON THE ANTICHRIST (G, S)

[Col. 1131]

The character of the Antichrist. Many antichrists already exist. The origin of the Antichrist. Where he will be born, and where and by whom he will be raised. The beginnings of his wickedness. His preaching. His signs. They will not be genuine. Persecution in three forms. The duration of the persecution. The final Christian king of the Franks. The Antichrist’s wickedness. The end of the Antichrist.

Those who wish to know about the Antichrist should first note why he is so called: namely, because he will be opposed to Christ in all things and will do what is contrary to Christ.

Christ came in humility; he will come in pride. Christ came to raise up the humble [Note: [Col. 1131] “To raise up” is absent from the Royal Manuscript.], to justify sinners; he, by contrast, will cast down the humble, magnify sinners, exalt the ungodly, and always teach the vices that are contrary to the virtues. He will destroy the evangelical law, restore the worship of demons in the world [Note: [Col. 1131] Elsewhere, “renew.”], and, seeking vain glory, call himself almighty God [Note: [Col. 1131] The Royal Manuscript reads, “he will seek his own glory; he will call himself Almighty.” Adso’s copy reads, “seeking his own glory,” omitting “God.”].

This Antichrist, then, has many ministers of his unbelief [Note: [Col. 1131] Adso’s copy reads, “many ministers of his wickedness”]; many of them have already preceded him in the world, such as Antiochus, Nero, and Domitian. Even in our own time, we know that there are many antichrists. For whoever—whether layman, canon, or monk—lives contrary to justice, attacks the rule of his order [Note: [Col. 1131] Elsewhere it reads, “attacks the glory of his order,”], and blasphemes what is good, is an antichrist and a minister of Satan.

But let us now consider the Antichrist’s origin. I do not invent or devise what I say from my own understanding; I find all these things written in authentic books by reading them carefully [Note: [Col. 1131] Adso’s copy does not have “authentic.” In the same manuscript, “from the tribe of Dan” appears shortly afterward.].

As our authorities therefore say, the Antichrist will be born from the Jewish people, from the tribe of Dan, according to the prophet [Note: [Col. 1131] The Royal Manuscript reads, “according to the prophecy.”] who says: “Let Dan be a serpent on the road, a horned serpent on the path” (Genesis 49:17). For like a serpent he will sit on the road and be on the path, so that he may strike those who walk along the path of justice [Note: [Col. 1131] The same manuscript reads, “who will have walked”] and kill them with the poison of his wickedness.

He will be born from the union of father and mother, like other human beings—not, as some say [Note: [Col. 1131] The same manuscript reads, “as some fabulously relate,”], from a virgin alone. Nevertheless, he will be conceived wholly in sin, generated in sin, and born in sin.

At the very beginning of his conception [Note: [Col. 1131] The Royal Manuscript reads, “at the beginning of his generation,”], the devil will enter together with him into his mother’s womb, and by the devil’s power he will be nourished and strengthened in his mother’s belly; the devil’s power will always be with him. Just as the Holy Spirit came upon the mother of our Lord, overshadowed her with his power, and filled her with divinity, so that she conceived from the Holy Spirit and what was born was divine and holy, so also the devil will descend upon the mother of the Antichrist and fill her entirely, surround her entirely, hold her entirely, and possess her inwardly and outwardly, so that, with the devil cooperating through the human being, she may conceive, and what is born may be wholly wicked [Note: [Col. 1131] Adso’s manuscript adds, “wholly evil”], wholly lost.

Hence that man is called the son of perdition (2 Thessalonians 2:3), because, insofar as he is able, he will destroy the human race, and in the end he himself will be destroyed.

You have now heard how he will be born; hear now the place where he is to be born. Just as our Lord and Redeemer provided Bethlehem for himself, where he would assume humanity for us and deign to be born, so the devil knows a place suitable for that lost man called the Antichrist, from which the root of all evils is to arise—namely, the city of Babylon.

In this city [Col. 1132], which was once the famous and glorious city of the Gentiles and the capital of the Persian kingdom [Note: [Col. 1132] The words “city of the Gentiles” are absent from the Royal Manuscript], the Antichrist will be born. He is said to be raised and to live in the cities of Bethsaida and Chorazin. The Lord invokes a curse upon these cities in the Gospel, saying: “Woe to you, Bethsaida! Woe to you, Chorazin!” (Luke 10:13).

The Antichrist will have magicians, sorcerers, diviners, and enchanters, who, inspired by the devil, will nourish him, teach him, and imbue him with every wickedness, falsehood, and criminal art. Evil spirits will be his guides, companions, and inseparable attendants always.

Then, coming to Jerusalem, he will slaughter through various torments all the Christians whom he cannot convert to himself, and he will establish his seat in the holy temple. He will also rebuild the destroyed temple that Solomon prepared for God, restore it to its former state, circumcise himself [Note: [Col. 1132] In B. “and he will circumcise himself” had been omitted. M.], and falsely claim to be the Son of Almighty God.

He will first convert kings and princes [Note: [Col. 1132] The Royal Manuscript adds, “and governors”] to himself, and then, through them, the remaining peoples. The places where the Lord Christ walked he will first destroy; then he will send his messengers and preachers throughout the whole world.

His preaching and power will extend from sea to sea, from East to West, from Aquilo (the north wind) to Septentrio (the north). He will also perform many great, marvelous, and unheard-of signs: trees will suddenly bloom and wither; the sea will be thrown into turmoil and suddenly become calm; natures will be changed into different forms; the air will be stirred by winds and by disturbances of many kinds [Note: [Col. 1132] Adso’s manuscript reads: “He will also perform many signs, great and unheard-of miracles; he will make fire come marvelously from heaven; trees will suddenly bloom . . .; natures will be changed into different forms; the course and order of the waters will be altered; the air will be stirred by winds and disturbances of many kinds.” It continues shortly afterward, “and even the dead in the sight of human beings.”], along with countless other astonishing things. He will even raise the dead in the sight of human beings, so that, if possible, even the elect will be led into error (Matthew 24:24). [Note: [Col. 1132] A few omitted words should be supplied from Alcuin.]

When they see such great and extraordinary signs, even those who are perfect and chosen by God will doubt whether he is the Christ who, according to the Scriptures, is to come at the end of the world, or not. All these miracles, however, will be false in every respect, performed through diabolical enchantments; but to sinners and unbelievers they will appear to be true [Note: [Col. 1132] Adso’s manuscript does not contain the words from “All these miracles” through “appear to be true.”].

He will arouse persecution against Christians and all the elect under the whole sky. He will rise up against the faithful in three ways: by terror, by gifts, and by miracles. He will give those who believe in him an abundance of gold and silver [Note: [Col. 1132] The Royal Manuscript adds, “for in his time hidden revenues and treasures will be revealed.”].

Those whom he cannot deceive with gifts he will overcome by terror; those whom he cannot conquer by terror he will try to seduce with signs and miracles. Those whom he cannot deceive even with signs he will attempt to kill by a miserable death in the sight of all.

Then there will be tribulation such as has not been from the time when the nations began until that time. Then let those who are in the field flee to the mountains, and let those who are on the housetop not come down into the house to take anything from it (Matthew 24:17).

Then every Christian who is found will either deny God or, if he remains in the faith, will be ordered to perish—whether by the sword, by the fire of a furnace, by serpents, by beasts, or by any other kind of torment.

This terrifying and fearful tribulation will last for three years and a half in all [Note: [Col. 1132] Rabanus adds, “will last throughout the whole world for three years and a half.” The Royal Manuscript omits “also, throughout the whole.” Adso’s manuscript reads, “will last throughout the whole world for three years and a half.”]. [Col. 1133] Those days will be shortened for the sake of the elect; for unless the Lord had shortened the days, no flesh would be saved.

As for the time when the Antichrist will come, or when the day of judgment will begin to appear, Paul indicates it in his Letter to the Thessalonians when he says [Note: [Col. 1133] The manuscripts read, “he demonstrates, saying, ‘Unless the apostasy has come,’” and so forth.]:

“We beseech you by the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ.” He makes it clear in the passage where he says: “For unless the apostasy first comes and the man of sin, the son of perdition, is revealed” (2 Thessalonians 2:1, 3), and so forth.

For we know that after the kingdom of the Greeks, and also after the kingdom of the Persians—each of which flourished in its own time with great glory and prospered in the greatest power—the Roman kingdom eventually began after the other kingdoms. It was the strongest of all the preceding kingdoms, held all the kingdoms of the earth under its rule, and all the nations of the peoples were subject to the Romans and served them under tribute.

Therefore the Apostle Paul says that the Antichrist will not come into the world before the apostasy first occurs—that is, before all the kingdoms depart from the Roman Empire to which they had previously been subject.

That time has not yet come. Although we see that the Roman Empire has already been destroyed for the most part, nevertheless, as long as the kings of the Franks endure, who ought to hold the Roman Empire, the dignity of Rome will not wholly perish, because it will stand in its kings.

Some of our teachers say that one of the kings of the Franks will hold the Roman Empire in its entirety. He will exist at the end of time and will be the greatest and the last of all kings. After he has governed his kingdom successfully, he will finally come to Jerusalem and lay down his scepter and crown on the Mount of Olives. This will be the end and completion of the Roman and Christian empires. Immediately afterward, in accordance with the opinion previously stated by the Apostle Paul, they say that the Antichrist will appear.

Then the man of sin will be revealed, namely the Antichrist. Although he will be a human being, he will nevertheless be the source of all sins; and he will be the son of perdition, that is, the son of the devil [Note: [Col. 1133] The Royal Manuscript adds, “not by nature but by imitation.” Adso’s manuscript agrees with the Royal Manuscript and shortly afterward reads, “he will fulfill the devil’s will, because the fullness of diabolical power and of every evil will dwell bodily in him.”], because he will fulfill the devil’s will in all things. The fullness of diabolical power and of every evil disposition will dwell bodily in him, and in him all the treasures of wickedness and iniquity will be hidden.

He is “the one who opposes,” that is, the one who is opposed to Christ and all his members. And he is “exalted,” that is, raised up in pride, above everything that is called God (2 Thessalonians 2:4)—that is [Note: [Col. 1133] Another explanation should be supplied from Alcuin] above all the gods of the Gentiles: Apollo, Jupiter, and Mercury, whom the pagans consider gods.

The Antichrist will exalt himself above all these gods [Note: [Col. 1133] Adso’s manuscript reads: “above all the gods of the nations, namely Hercules, Apollo, Jupiter, and Mercury, whom the pagans considered to be gods; above all these gods the Antichrist will exalt himself”], because he will make himself greater and stronger than all of them.

And not only above them, but also above everything that is worshiped—that is, above the Holy Trinity, which alone ought to be worshiped and adored by every creature—he will exalt himself in such a way that he will sit in the temple, displaying himself as though he were God.

For, as we said above, after being born in the city of Babylon and coming to Jerusalem, he will circumcise himself and say to the Jews: “I am the Christ promised to you. I have come for your salvation, so that I may gather and defend you who are scattered.”

Then all the Jews will flock to him, thinking that they are receiving God, but they will receive the devil.

Or the Antichrist will sit in the temple of God—that is, in the holy Church—wishing to make all Christians martyrs [Note: [Col. 1133] Adso’s manuscript reads, “making all Christians martyrs.”]. He will be exalted and magnified [Col. 1134], because the devil, who is king over all the sons of pride, will be in him as the head of all evils.

But suddenly and unexpectedly the Antichrist will come, and at once he will deceive and destroy the entire human race through his error. [Note: [Col. 1134] Alcuin and Rabanus read: “But so that the Antichrist may not come suddenly and unexpectedly and deceive and destroy the entire human race at once through his error, before his appearance . . .” Adso’s manuscript agrees with Rabanus, except that it reads, “before his origin.”]

Before his appearance, two prophets will be sent into the world, namely Enoch and Elijah, who will arm the faithful of God with divine weapons and fortify them against the impious Antichrist [Note: [Col. 1134] The manuscripts read, “against the assault of the Antichrist.” So the codex of Adso, which shortly afterward has “for three and a half years.”]. They will instruct, strengthen, and prepare the elect for battle, teaching and preaching for three and a half years. They will convert to the grace of faith those of the children of Israel who are found alive at that time, these two greatest prophets and teachers, and will make them unconquerable among the elect, away from the oppression of so great a storm [Note: [Col. 1134] This material, from “teaching” through “will make them,” is absent from the Regius Manuscript and from Alcuin.]. Then will be fulfilled what Scripture says: “Though the number of the children of Israel be like the sand of the sea, a remnant will be saved” [Note: [Col. 1134] Adso’s Manuscript reads, “the survivors will be saved”; and shortly afterward, “the persecution of the Antichrist will immediately begin.”] (Romans 9:27).

After they have preached for three and a half years, the persecutions of the Antichrist will immediately begin to burn fiercely, and the Antichrist will first take up his weapons against them and kill them, as it is said in the Apocalypse: “And when they have finished their testimony,” it says, “the beast will descend from the abyss, make war against them, and kill them” [Note: [Col. 1134] Adso’s Manuscript reads, “the beast that will ascend from the abyss will make war against them, and will overcome them and kill them.”] (Revelation 11:7).

After these two have therefore been killed, he will persecute the remaining faithful, either making them glorious martyrs or turning them into apostates. And all who believe in him will receive the mark of his sign upon their foreheads.

But since we have spoken of his beginning, let us speak of the end he will have. This Antichrist, therefore—the son of the devil, the worst craftsman of every kind of wickedness—after he has afflicted the whole world with a great persecution for three and a half years, as has been said, and has tortured the entire people of God with various punishments; after he has killed Elijah and Enoch and crowned the others who remain steadfast in the faith with martyrdom; at last the wrath of God will come upon him, as blessed Paul wrote, saying [Note: [Col. 1134] Adso’s Manuscript reads, “the judgment of God will come upon him, as the blessed apostle Paul writes, saying.”]: “The Lord Jesus Christ will kill him with the breath of his mouth” (2 Thessalonians 2:8) [Note: [Col. 1134] What follows is supplied from Rabanus.]; whether the Lord Jesus will kill him by the power of his manifestation, or the archangel Michael will kill him through the power of our Lord Jesus Christ [Note: [Col. 1134] Adso’s Manuscript: “Whether the Lord Jesus will kill him by the power of his own might, or the archangel Michael will kill him; he will be killed through the power of our Lord Jesus Christ, not through the power of any angel or archangel,” etc.], not through the power of any angel or archangel.

The teachers, moreover, report that the Antichrist will be killed on the Mount of Olives, from which the Lord ascended into heaven [Note: [Col. 1134] Adso’s Manuscript reads, “he will be killed in his tent and in his own place, at that spot opposite which the Lord ascended into heaven.”]. You must know, however, that after the Antichrist has been killed, the day of judgment will not immediately arrive, nor will the Lord immediately come to judgment; rather, the Lord will wait for certain people, as we understand from the Book of Daniel, who were led astray, so that they may return to repentance. But after they have completed their repentance [Note: [Col. 1134] Adso’s Manuscript reads, “but as we understand from the Book of Daniel, the Lord will grant forty days to the elect so that they may do penance because they were led astray by the Antichrist. Then, after they have completed this repentance”], no one knows how long it will be until the Lord comes; it remains in God’s disposition. For at the hour which he predetermined before the ages, the world will be judged.

[Col. 1135]

# PSALTER [Note: [Col. 1135] In earlier editions it is entitled: “By Aurelius Augustine, bishop of Hippo, which he composed for his mother.” But in Regius Manuscript 4373 it reads as follows: “Here begins the Psalter of blessed Pope John [perhaps XXII], made at Vienne.”] (G,S)*

Lord God Almighty, King [Note: [Col. 1135] The Regius Manuscript reads, “God the Father, King.”] of eternal glory, who know that blessed is the man who, scorning the way of sinners, meditates day and night upon the law of your commandments [Note: [Col. 1135] “Your” is absent from the Regius Manuscript]; teach me, a sinner, faithfully to serve you with my whole heart, with fear and trembling, and hear my voice as I humbly call upon you. And most mercifully receive my words with your ears, so that [Note: [Col. 1135] The same manuscript here adds “while”; and shortly afterward reads, “you abandon [me], lest that enemy.”] you may not abandon me, a sinner, in the anger of your wrath, lest that most ancient enemy, lying in wait, seize my soul like a lion, while there is no one to redeem or save me.

But you, Lord, whose name is wondrous in heaven and on earth, turn my enemy backward in such a way that he may be weakened and perish from before your face. May he never be able to entangle my soul in fiery snares, nor heap upon me sulfur and the spirit of storms. But because of the misery of the needy and the groaning of the poor, now rise up, look upon me, and hear me, Lord, for you are the poor man’s counsel and his hope.

Make me, O God, walk without blemish and practice righteousness, so that the grace of your mercy may be my share of the inheritance. Keep me as the apple of your eye, and protect me beneath the shadow of your wings, for you are my strength, my support, and my refuge [Note: [Col. 1135] The same codex omits these words, namely, “for you are my strength … my refuge.”]. Cleanse me, Lord, from my hidden faults, and spare your servant from those belonging to others. Send me help [Note: [Col. 1135] Elsewhere, “an angel.”] from the holy place, and grant me the desire of my soul.

Deliver me from the lion’s mouth, and lead me along the paths of your righteousness, so that I may ascend your holy mountain and stand in your holy place, innocent in my hands and pure in heart. Do not remember the sins of my youth or my ignorances. Do not destroy my soul with the ungodly, and do not hand me over to the souls of those who persecute me. Hear the voice of my supplication with such mercy that you may graciously hear me as I call upon the glory of your holy name, have mercy on me, and attend to me, Lord, so that I, who hope in you, may not be put to shame forever. Rather, forgive [Note: [Col. 1135] The Regius Manuscript reads “turn away,” omitting “me.”] me the wickedness of my heart.

Let your mercy, Lord, be upon me, as I hope in you. Delivering me from all my distress, say to my soul, “I am your salvation.” And because I hope in the protection of your wings, grant me the request of my heart, and attend to my help, Lord God of my salvation.

Make known to me, Lord, my end and the number of my days, so that I may know what I lack. Hear graciously the voice of my supplication, and bring me out of the pit of misery and the mud of filth. Set my feet upon a rock, and direct my steps along a straight path.

On the evil day deliver me, Lord, so that I may enter the place of the tabernacle of the wondrous house of God, for you are my God and my strength. Do not turn my steps away from your way [Note: [Col. 1135] The same Manuscript reads “life”], so that I may love righteousness and hate wickedness. Be my refuge and strength, for you are the great king over all the earth.

You who rule all things forever, deliver my soul from the hand of the underworld when it takes hold of me. But when you are revealed in order to judge us, have mercy on me according to your great mercy, and do not take your Holy Spirit from me. Most merciful Lord, turn your face away from my sins in that hour, and blot out all my iniquities.

Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me, so that, like a fruitful olive tree in the paradise of my God, I may receive the oil of holiness and rejoice there [Note: [Col. 1135] The same Manuscript reads, “that I may receive, so that I may rejoice.”] with Jacob and rejoice forever with Israel.

Save me in your name, and deliver me by your power. Do not despise my supplication, but have mercy on me. Send from heaven and deliver me, [Col. 1136] and make those who trample me a reproach. Crush their teeth in their mouths, and break the jaws of lions.

You are my God and my mercy. May your right hand save me, and may I be protected by the shelter of your wings when you repay each person according to his works. While my soul thirsts for you [Note: [Col. 1136] The Regius Manuscript reads, “trusts in you”], protect me from the assembly of the wicked.

When all flesh comes to you, do not remove your mercy from me, nor take your Holy Spirit from me [Note: [Col. 1136] These words are omitted in the same Manuscript, namely, “and do not take your Holy Spirit from me”]; but let your face shine upon me. Make my journey prosperous, O God my savior, so that the abyss may not swallow me up, nor the pit open its mouth over me. Be my helper and deliverer, Lord; do not delay.

For in you I hope, Lord; I shall not be put to shame forever. When you judge your people, and those who distance themselves from you perish, do not let me, humbled, be turned away in shame. For you are a just judge: you humble and exalt, exceedingly terrible—and who will resist you then, when your wrath comes?

You are the God who alone performs great wonders. Just as you fed your people with bread in the desert and did not deprive them of what they desired, so may your grace refresh me when I hunger, and may your mercy quickly come before me. And you, my protector, grant me the bread of tears and the bitterness of compunctions in the time of tribulation, and grant that I may receive from the rock the sweetness of honey, the inward sweetness [Note: [Col. 1136] The Regius Manuscript reads, “that I may receive within me the sweetness.”].

O God, who distinguishes all things between the righteous and sinners, who alone are most high above all nations, have mercy on me and grant me the blessing, you who gave the law. Forgive the wickedness of my heart, and pardon all my sins, and save your servant, my God, who hopes in you.

O God, who founded your Church [Note: [Col. 1136] The same Manuscript omits “your”; and shortly afterward, “and from ruin.”] upon the holy mountains, incline your ear to my prayer. Therefore may your hand help me, so that I may not be turned away in humiliation; but deliver me from the snare of hunters, from ruin, and from the noonday demon. Thus planted in the house of the Lord, may I flourish like a palm tree, and like the cedar that is in Lebanon may I deserve to multiply through length of days.

Be my refuge and the help of my hope, my God and great king over all the earth. When you judge the world in righteousness and the peoples in your truth, may I enjoy perpetual light with the righteous and joy with the upright in heart. May your right hand save me, and your holy arm.

You who sit above the cherubim, make me be in your presence with rejoicing, so that I may walk [Note: [Col. 1136] The same Manuscript reads, “so that my soul may walk.”] in the innocence of my heart in the midst of my house. Let not a perverse heart cling to me. Rather, let my eyes be upon your holy faithful ones, so that I may sit with them, walking along the undefiled way, when by judgment you have destroyed from your city all who now [Note: [Col. 1136] “Now” is absent from the Regius Manuscript] practice wickedness.

Lord, hear my prayer, and let my cry come to you. Do not turn your face from me; on whatever day I am troubled, incline your ear to me. Be merciful toward all my iniquities, and redeem my life from destruction. Satisfy my desire with good things.

You who look upon the earth and make it tremble, who led your people out with rejoicing and your elect with joy, make me keep judgment and righteousness at all times. Lead me out of darkness and the shadow of death, so that with a ready heart I may sing and recite a psalm to you.

Give me a sign for good, because of your mercy and your name, so that in the splendors of the holy, in the council and assembly of the righteous, my righteousness may remain forever and ever, and my horn may be exalted in glory.

And when you command me, poor, to be raised from the earth, and lift me, the needy, from the dungheap, I will bless you from now and forever. Then may I please you in the land of the living. Break my bonds, and strengthen me in your mercy.

When I call upon you in tribulation, Lord, [Col. 1137] hear me in abundance. Establish your law for me, Lord, so that I may live, and may always seek the ways of your righteousness. Give me understanding, so that I may examine your law and keep it with my whole heart.

I have gone astray like a sheep that has perished; seeking me, deliver my soul. Guard my coming in and my going out, so that my feet may stand in your house, in the courts of Jerusalem.

To you I have lifted up my soul and my eyes, you who dwell in the heavens. Rescue my soul from the trap [Note: [Col. 1137] The Regius Manuscript reads, “snare.”] of hunters, so that I may not stretch out my hands toward wickedness. Fill my mouth with joy and my tongue with rejoicing. Fill my desire with what is good, and bless me from Zion, so that I may see the good things that are in Jerusalem. Keep me far from iniquity [Note: [Col. 1137] Elsewhere, “from the good things that are in Jerusalem, having been kept far from all iniquity.”].

Let your ears be attentive to the voice of the prayer of your servant, Lord. Let not my heart be lifted up in pride, nor my eyes be raised arrogantly. Rather, let me think humbly until I find a place for the Lord, a tabernacle for the God of Jacob. There you commanded blessing and life forever. There I will lift my hands toward [Note: [Col. 1137] Elsewhere, “in”; and shortly afterward, “you comfort.”] the Holy Place, and bless you, who judge your people and find comfort in your servants. [Col. 1138]

God of gods and Lord of lords, as I weep and worship toward your holy temple, test me and know my heart. Examine me and know my paths, and lead me in the everlasting way. Preserve [Note: [Col. 1138] The Regius Manuscript reads, “consecrate.”] me, Lord, and rescue me from the hand of the sinner; deliver me from all the wicked.

Let my prayer be directed like incense in your sight, Lord. Bring my soul out of prison, so that I may confess your name, Lord. Hear me in your righteousness, and do not enter into judgment with your servant, Lord. Hear me quickly, Lord, lest my spirit fail, for you are my God, my mercy, my refuge, and my protector.

For you are great and exceedingly worthy of praise, and there is no end to your greatness. Raise up the one who has been struck down, release the one in chains, enlighten the blind—you who build Jerusalem. And when you have strengthened the bars of your gates, may I be joined within with your children.

As the angels praise you, and all your Powers in the kingdom of heaven, so may I also rejoice there in glory with the choir of the saints, praising and glorifying your name with the cymbals of my lips, a name that is holy and glorious and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 1137]

# EXPOSITION OF THE CANTICLE “MAGNIFICAT” [Note: [Col. 1137] Extracted from Hugh of Saint-Victor’s treatise on the Magnificat by an unknown writer, who most shamefully corrupted Hugh’s excellent work and mutilated it in head and members.] (G,S)*

[Col. 1137] In order to proclaim the new coming of the Son of God in the flesh, when Gabriel, who entered with a new service of greeting, venerated the Virgin, saying, “Hail, full of grace,” etc., “Behold the handmaid of the Lord” (Luke 1:28, 38), the Holy Spirit immediately came upon the Virgin, and the grace of all virtues filled her, the most holy dwelling place, at the coming of God [Note: [Col. 1137] Hugh adds, “of the Son.”]. There can be no doubt what wondrous and indescribable sweetness of heavenly joys and eternal delight the Virgin herself conceived when that eternal light descended upon her with the full splendor of its majesty, and he whom the world cannot contain placed himself wholly within the Virgin’s womb [Note: [Col. 1137] Hugh reads, “which.”].

I boldly declare that she herself could not fully explain what she was able to contain. But, taught by the Holy Spirit, she had learned to conceal her possessions in humility. She immediately rises and ascends into the hill country of Judaea. There Elizabeth, filled with the Holy Spirit, recognized what kind and how great a woman she was who had come to her, and revealed how unworthy she judged herself of her visitation, saying: “And from where is this granted to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me? Behold” (ibid., 43), etc.

Then Mary said, “My soul magnifies the Lord” (ibid., 46). You saw majesty; you tasted sweetness. Therefore what you had drunk within, you poured out externally, and you rejoiced in his righteousness: “For my spirit has rejoiced.” The soul magnifies; the spirit rejoices. And again [Note: [Col. 1137] The passage is mutilated], “in God my savior” (ibid., 47).

“God” indicates power; “savior,” mercy. For there are two things which the blessed spirits of angels and human beings draw from that fountain of goodness through eternal contemplation: the incomprehensible majesty of God and his ineffable goodness. The one generates chaste fear; the other produces love. Because of his majesty they venerate God, and because of his goodness they love him, so that love may not be dissolute without reverence, nor reverence punitive without love.

For in their wonder they love, and in their love they wonder, so that love may burn unquenchably through wonder, and wonder may glow sweetly in love. Since they never suffice perfectly to comprehend him whom they see, they remain awake in him, as it were, through wonder. The more clearly they gaze upon him, the more ardently they love him; and this is true sweetness [Col. 1138] [Note: [Col. 1138] Hugh reads, “because seeing him is itself savoring, and what is seen is sweetness.”]. True sweetness, moreover, the more perfectly it is sensed, the more desirably it is sought.

Mary’s mind had been raised to this light of contemplation. In her words she expressed the sweetness of the heavenly homeland [Note: [Col. 1138] Hugh adds, “so wondrously in her own words”] which she had incomprehensibly grasped. For when she declared that she magnified the Lord, she clearly showed that in inward vision she beheld the majesty of the eternal Godhead, which must be venerated [Note: [Col. 1138] Elsewhere, “which must be rendered”; and shortly afterward, “of the gift.”] by all. But when she asserted that she rejoiced in her savior, she showed that she had perceived a taste of inward sweetness.

Thus she confessed both the Lord and the Savior, showing that because of his power, by which he rules over all his creation, he is rightly to be feared; but because of his goodness, by which he mercifully saves certain people, he is worthy of love [Note: [Col. 1138] Add from Hugh: “Since all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth, it is perfect praise to confess him as Lord and Savior, since truth in …”]. There is truth in the Lord, and mercy in the Savior. Truth belongs to the Lord, while mercy belongs to the Savior; in truth he preserves the rule of justice. But because he also freely gathers certain wanderers into life and restores them to salvation, therefore we magnify the Lord and rejoice in the savior. For to those for whom the justice of the judge is reverent, the mercy of the Savior is sweet [Note: [Col. 1138] Hugh reads, “and the mercy is to be observed with rejoicing.”]. Therefore Mary says, “My soul magnifies the Lord, and my spirit has rejoiced in God my savior.”

One and the same spirit is called “spirit” in relation to itself and “soul” in relation to the body. The spirit had a natural, spiritual wonder; the soul, a bodily one. Hence the soul is called spirit, and conversely. The human soul is called both soul and spirit because it exists in the body and outside the body. It is called soul insofar as it is the life of the body; spirit insofar as it is a spiritual substance [Note: [Col. 1138] Hugh adds, “endowed with reason.”]. In this life the soul is lost so that the spirit may be saved, when this life is despised in order that eternal life may afterward be granted by God.

But she called him “her own,” because he was “her savior.” For almighty God, by the power with which he rules over all his creation, is Lord of all; but by the piety with which he restores only some, and not all, to life, he is not the Savior of all [Note: [Col. 1139] Hugh reads, “not Savior of all.”]. His dominion indeed extends equally over all, but his goodness is directed only toward some [Note: [Col. 1139] Hugh reads, “distinguishes some for salvation.”]. Therefore the blessed Virgin, seeing that she had been singularly chosen because she had singularly received grace, as though confirmed by a certain privilege of divine election, confidently calls him whom she had conceived as the Son for the salvation of the world also her own Savior, with joy and exultation.

“For he has regarded the lowliness of his handmaid” (Luke 1:48). This is the cause of her exultation: “because he has regarded the lowliness of his handmaid.” It is as though she said: “Because I rejoice in his grace, therefore my rejoicing comes from him; and because I love his gifts for his own sake, therefore I rejoice in him.”

God’s regard is customarily understood in three ways [Note: [Col. 1139] Add from Hugh, “in Sacred Scripture”]: according to knowledge, according to grace, and according to judgment. Concerning the first, the Apostle says [Note: [Col. 1139] The passage is truncated]: “All things are naked and open to his eyes” (Hebrews 4:13). But through grace God does not regard everyone, for “the eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous” (Psalm 33:16), etc. Concerning the third it will be said at the end: “I do not know you” (Matthew 7:23).

The eyes of the Lord behold the good and the wicked. For God to see according to knowledge means that he is ignorant of none of the things that exist; to see according to grace means to bestow gifts of mercy; to see according to judgment means to assign each person, according to his works, either to glory or to punishment.

To regard is more than to see. To regard through grace [Note: [Col. 1139] This passage is corrupt] means first to visit those who have been cast down and abandoned. When, appeased by mercy, he restores the good things that had been withdrawn, he turns to that person again through a gracious regard.

Mary therefore rightly testifies that the Lord regarded only her lowliness [Note: [Col. 1139] Hugh reads, “in herself.”], because the favor of the Godhead, which human nature lost through pride in its first parents, recovered in Mary through humility. For because the Word of the Father assumed in her the substance of a body [Note: [Col. 1139] Elsewhere, “of flesh”] with which to unite himself, he regarded her through mercy, as if to exalt the nature that he had previously cast down.

Because she humbly considered what she was—a handmaid [Note: [Col. 1139] Hugh reads, “humbly”; and shortly afterward, “exalted”]—she deserved to become, in exaltation, the mother of what she was not. For she displayed the humility of servitude [Note: [Col. 1139] The passage is incomplete].

Servitude varies in four ways. The first is servitude according to condition, by which all things ought to be subject to divine service. For a work owes its Maker, according to its condition, that it obey his ordering and follow his institutions, so that, just as it was made by him, it may proceed only from him and according to him.

According to necessity, perverse wills are said to serve God. Although they strive to oppose his commands, they are nevertheless constrained by his ineffable ordering, so that they cannot bring anything to completion without his will. Those who are unwilling serve his ordering, though they are not willingly subject to his command.

Servitude with fear occurs when we fulfill divine commands not out of love but out of dread. The fourth kind of servitude occurs when we willingly obey his commands because we love the one who commands us and seek no advantage in our service apart from him, except that by walking according to him we may be able to reach him [Note: [Col. 1139] Hugh reads, “attain him.”].

Our parents in paradise refused to offer the Creator servitude according to condition when, lifted up in pride, they despised being under him, for which [Note: [Col. 1139] The same source reads, “from whom”; and shortly afterward, “perversely with him”] they had been created. In their perversity they wished to be similar in majesty to him, though they were not equal in nature [Note: [Col. 1139] Hugh adds here: “Grace therefore appropriately corresponds to guilt.”].

Eve, through pride, without considering that she was God’s creature and God’s work, wished to be equal to God. Mary, however, humbly subjecting herself to her Maker, called herself a handmaid. Therefore the former was cast down, and the latter was chosen. He despised the proud and regarded the humble; what the proud woman lost, the humble woman received.

Therefore she says, “He has regarded the lowliness of his handmaid” [Note: [Col. 1140] Some material must be supplied here from Hugh]. But servants of God sometimes possess humility without humiliation, though they never possess humiliation without humility. Those who have humility without humiliation are people who, although they do not appear outwardly contemptible before human beings, nevertheless preserve intact the merit of humility inwardly before God.

Therefore Mary, who was humble before God and despised among human beings for God’s sake, testifies that she was regarded in both respects: her humility was acceptable to God, and her humiliation among human beings was transformed into glory.

Hence it follows: “From this time all generations will call me blessed.” Until then she had borne among human beings the reproach of barrenness, because she preferred the integrity of virginity to the marriage bed. But from the very point at which in the earlier, carnal generation she endured what was almost a sentence of condemnation, she has now received, with deserved praise, blessing from every mortal generation [Note: [Col. 1140] Hugh reads, “she is praised with deserved blessing”; then some desirable material follows here], because every generation calls me blessed for the fruitfulness of my offspring.

“For he who is mighty has done great things for me, and holy is his name” (Luke 1:49). It was a great thing that a virgin should conceive a son without male seed. It was a great thing that she should carry in her womb the Word of God the Father clothed in her flesh. It was a great thing that, while confessing herself a handmaid, she should become the mother of her own Maker.

“He who is mighty.” Because his power can be believed, she confessed him to be mighty; but how great or of what kind it is cannot be comprehended. She confessed his power but did not presume to investigate it, because it is not fitting [Note: [Col. 1140] Hugh reads, “it is not possible”] to know how great it is, since it is infinite. Everything he foresaw that he would do, he does; and anything he did not foresee would happen—not merely doubtful, but necessarily must happen [Note: [Col. 1140] Hugh treats this at length; consult him.].

Mary does not say, “He did great things in her,” or “in me,” or “through me,” but says, “for me.” For what was done in her for the salvation of all was, by the privilege of love [Note: [Col. 1140] Hugh reads, “of election”], specially ordained for her glory.

Therefore she said “great things” [Note: [Col. 1140] Add from Hugh, “and she did not specify what kind”], because the mystery of the incarnation of the Word is acknowledged to be ineffable above all things. Nothing was ever done more wondrously than that God should become human, and that an incomprehensible nature should unite the substance of a body to itself in such a way that it was neither less in that body, since it was immense in itself, nor less in itself, since it existed in that body [Note: [Col. 1140] Hugh reads, “had been wholly”]. These, then, are the great things.

“And therefore holy is his name.” What is his name? His fame [Note: [Col. 1140] See the book On the Seven Vices]. His name is his knowledge; faith is his name. This name is holy among the holy; it glories with the holy [Note: [Col. 1140] Hugh reads, “because it is glorified by the holy”; then some material from him must be supplied], is blessed by the holy, and is blasphemed by the perverse. For when the Word is born in the flesh, the glory of God is made known among human beings through the Word.

“And his mercy is from generation to generation for those who fear him” (ibid., 50). He did great things for Mary, I say, but not for her alone; rather, he did them excellently for one, yet for all who fear him. No one is excluded from grace [Note: [Col. 1140] Elsewhere, “the negation is excluded from those who fear.”].

“He has shown strength with his arm; he has scattered the proud in the imagination of their hearts” (ibid., 51). This is the mercy he displayed toward those who fear him: he sent his Word into this world through the flesh he assumed, so that through him he might overthrow the aerial powers with mighty strength and redeem the human race from their power.

Those proud ones are the spirits whom God scattered, driving them out from human hearts and seizing their spoils [Note: [Col. 1141] Elsewhere, “breaking them apart”]. Through that power which previously ruled in human beings, he destroyed them [Note: [Col. 1141] Hugh reads, “for by that power which previously ruled … he destroyed them”]. And this he did with his arm—that is, through the humility of the Son he conquered the devil. His arm is his Son. That very weakness was power, because through it the devil was conquered. And he scattered them “in the mind of his heart,” that is, in the depth of his counsel.

The profound counsel was that God should become human for humanity, and that the innocent should suffer so that the guilty might be redeemed. In these things there was counsel, and the devil could not foresee it; but he was caught by Leviathan’s hook. Alternatively, by the proud we may understand the Jews, who arrogantly despised Christ’s humble coming and whom he cast down. Hence it follows:

“He has brought down the mighty from their seat and exalted the humble” (Luke 1:52). The mighty are those whom he cast down—namely, the children of the kingdom who seemed to possess it—and he took the nations into fellowship with the kingdom and into the adoption of children through humble confession. He also cast wicked spirits out of human hearts; and the humble, that is, humbled human beings, he exalted.

The mind of God’s heart is also the living and enduring disposition of eternal [Note: [Col. 1141] Hugh reads, “inward”] and hidden predestination. He himself is the book of life. “Mind,” therefore, is the same as “book.” A person is written in the book in three ways: according to foreknowledge, according to cause, and according to action.

According to the first, the predestined are written; they are never erased, although for a time someone may be permitted to stray from the way of truth as though he were about to perish [Note: [Col. 1141] Elsewhere, “may appear”]. According to cause, those are written who, by turning aside into errors, withdraw from the way of truth they had begun. Such people would sometimes be worthy of salvation if they persevered in that condition to the end. According to action, those are written whose works, according to human judgment, appear such that they seem worthy to be written in the book of life, but who nevertheless abandon the good things they appeared to be doing. According to foreknowledge, these were never in the book of life.

“He has brought down,” etc. First he cast down from heaven the angel who was proud, and from paradise the proud human being; afterward he restored to glory the human being humbled through repentance [Note: [Col. 1141] Elsewhere, “who was to be humbled”]. Every day as well he casts down and humbles the proud by withdrawing his grace; afterward, restoring their former grace to those who have been humbled, he exalts them.

But to whom does the following refer: “He has filled the hungry with good things, and sent the rich away empty” (Luke 1:53)? He calls “hungry” those who recognize that they need the true good. By “rich” he wishes us to understand those who are proud and consider themselves more abundantly endowed than others with gifts of grace. Therefore, just as the humble, thinking little of themselves, merit receiving greater grace, so the proud, presuming upon themselves, lose even what they have received.

“He has helped his servant Israel, remembering his mercy” (ibid., 54). He helped Israel his servant as a physician helps the sick: that is, he received the humble and innocent in order to heal the infirm, redeem the captive, justify the ungodly, and save the righteous.

He helped Israel—not the Israel whom he found, but in order to make Israel—remembering his mercy, which he had promised long ago but had long delayed: “As he spoke to our fathers” (or “to our ancestors”), “to Abraham and to his seed forever” (ibid., 55). Merciful in promising, truthful in providing: for he promised without obligation and fulfilled without deceit. “As he spoke to our fathers, Abraham and his seed forever.”

Note concerning “My spirit has rejoiced in God my savior”: some people rejoice neither from God nor in God. For those who rejoice in the pleasure of the flesh, or who rejoice when they have done evil (Proverbs 2:14), rejoice neither in God nor from God, and the thing in which they rejoice is evil. Because they rejoice from evil toward evil and establish their joy in wickedness, they do not rejoice in God at all.

There are others who misuse the gifts of grace they have received, turning what was given for the salvation of the soul toward the use of the flesh and the joys [Note: [Col. 1142] Hugh reads, “glory”] of the world. They rejoice in having received the gifts, because they do not love, either in God or for God’s sake, what they have received from God [Note: [Col. 1142] The passage is incomplete and must be repaired from Hugh]. But those who, having received grace, turn that very gift they received from him toward the love of God are plainly shown to rejoice both from God and in God.

Conversely [Note: [Col. 1142] Hugh reads, “Therefore Mary”], to show that her joy was solid—having arisen neither from vanity nor having been turned toward vanity—she declared that she loved God’s gifts in God and rejoiced in the Savior because of the gracious regard with which she had been anticipated, saying: “My spirit has rejoiced in God my savior.”

[Col. 1141]

# ON THE ASSUMPTION OF THE BLESSED VIRGIN MARY [Note: [Col. 1141] The manuscripts read, “and perpetual virgin Mary, mother of the Lord.”—This book is thought to have been written in the time of Charlemagne, because Book 1 of the Capitularies, chapter 158, when listing the festivals of the year, says, “We leave the question of the Assumption to be asked.” But whether this refers to the beginning of the book, or whether this is the very book which in the catalogue of Alcuin’s works in Gibab’s second century of British Writers is listed under the title “Responses to Questions,” we do not determine.] BOOK ONE. BY AN UNKNOWN AND DEVOUT AUTHOR. (G,S)

## PREFACE. A prayer for divine light in speaking worthily.

[Col. 1141]

# On the Temporal Dissolution of the Virgin and Mother of the Lord and Her Perpetual Assumption

In replying to the questions concerning the temporal dissolution of the Virgin and Mother of the Lord and her perpetual assumption, I beseech you, God omnipotent Father, with suppliant prayer: you who command the clouds, and they rain down showers; who touch the mountains, and they smoke; who open the earth, and it sprouts—command me what I should say, grant me what I should utter, and open the way toward which I should direct my discourse.

For it is venerable to me, Lord, and most deeply reverend in my heart, to speak of the mother of your Son and to occupy my tongue with words concerning her most holy body [Col. 1142]—she alone deserved, as one about to bear him, to receive God and man, having been made the throne of God and the palace of the eternal King, according to what you taught us through your holy Patriarchs, Prophets, and Apostles, by figures and by words. We have believed these things and are certain of them, because you have never deceived us—you who neither know how to be deceived nor to deceive—showing that your Son, coeternal and consubstantial with you, was to become incarnate, and that, having become incarnate through a virgin’s womb, he took from it flesh, he who together with you created all bodily things: the Author from the one who ministered [Note: [Col. 1142] Thus the Royal Manuscript. The Corbie Manuscript, however, reads “from the administering one” (*administratrice*); another Royal Manuscript, “by administration” (*administratione*); the printed editions, “from the administrator” (*administrator*).]. God became man from man; taking nature from her, not origin, while your Holy Spirit sanctified the human womb in her and purified and cleansed it for the conception of your Son. The effect of whose dignity and grace neither the heart can conceive nor the tongue [Col. 1143] express.

For no other conception and no other birth would have suited God, who had come to redeem those whom he had chosen to create: to create especially by majesty, to redeem by humility [Note: [Col. 1143] The Corbie Codex reads “by humanity” (*humanitate*).]. Taking from a sanctified and immaculate body a holy and immaculate nature of humility, he did not remove the ineffable grace of sanctification which he, when about to be conceived, had bestowed [Note: [Col. 1143] Elsewhere, “which” (*quam*).], when he was conceived and born. How greatly this sanctification prevailed in the Virgin’s body is known to him alone who received from her nature the nature that he had created.

Through him, Lord, I ask you—for through him you grant every good thing that you choose to grant—that you grant me to speak without offense about such great holiness. Even if I cannot speak of it wholly as it is, which is impossible for every human tongue, nevertheless let what it is be spoken of in part as it is. Let that which is most precious in true preciousness, most holy in certain holiness, and most inestimable in most faithful truth resound.

Since these things surpass human understanding, may your Spirit be present, and by his holy breathing lead us into all the truth of what must be said. For we must speak of that body and soul which he himself sanctified beyond the ordinary course of nature and upon which he bestowed grace. May he not permit us to say what is foreign, but what is proper: for the praise and glory of you, God omnipotent Father; for the honor of your Son, born through the Virgin; and of that same Holy Spirit, our God and Lord, with whom you possess the kingdom and dominion throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## CHAPTER ONE. The Author’s Love of Truth. Some Things in Scripture Are to Be Expounded in One Way, Others in Another.

[Note: [Col. 1143] The manuscripts prefix here: “Here begins the sermon.”]

Because I am about to answer a question of the deepest importance and highest dignity, I beseech my reader to intercede for me. If he recognizes that I have said anything fully, let him be grateful to the gifts of God; but if I have said less, let him have compassion on my humility. For although we may have little ability, nevertheless we undoubtedly desire what is true.

In undertaking to speak, insofar as the Lord grants it, about the assumption of the most holy body of Mary, perpetual virgin, and of her sacred soul, we first say this: in the divine Scriptures, after the Lord on the cross entrusted his mother to the disciple (John 19:27), so that chastity might protect chastity through chaste services, nothing is found concerning her except what Luke records in the Acts of the Apostles. After naming the same people, he says: “These all continued with one accord in prayer with the women, and Mary the mother of Jesus, and his brothers” (Acts 1:14).

We say this because the greater the things are, the more cautiously they ought to be treated when they cannot be fully confirmed by the specific testimony of authorities. But because Holy Scripture has left certain matters to be sought by diligent inquiry, they are not to be judged superfluous when they have been disclosed by truthful investigation.

For the authority of truth is fruitful: and when it is carefully examined, it is recognized to bring forth from itself what it itself is. Often, when examined, it gives birth to a true coherence that it conceals in explicit words; and often, through open expressions, it indicates matters in which it invites us to seek nothing beyond what it has uttered. Such is the passage: “Abraham begot Isaac, Isaac begot Jacob, Jacob begot Judah and his brothers” (Matthew 1:2), and other passages of this kind, in which the literal sense alone is to be retained.

Other passages it commends in such a way that they at once suggest both the letter and the mystical meaning [Note: [Col. 1143] The manuscripts read “instruct” (*instruat*).]: for example, the crossing of the Red Sea, the heavenly manna, the tabernacle of God, and the ark of the covenant, in which the figure of future things was shown—namely, the privilege of Christ’s Baptism and of the Church.

Other passages it presents only mystically, as when it says that God breathed into Adam’s face the breath of life [Note: [Col. 1143] The manuscripts read “Adam” (*Adam*).], although God has neither a mouth for breathing nor hands for working, while the prophet says: “Your hands have made me and fashioned me” (Job 10:8) [Note: [Col. 1143] The printed editions read “although” (*licet*).].

## CHAPTER TWO. There Are Truths About Which Scripture Is Silent, Though Reason Is Not. The Assumption of Blessed Mary Is Among Them.

[Col. 1144]

There are also certain matters which, although their mention has been entirely omitted, are nevertheless believed for sound reasons, since the coherence of the matter itself is believed to be both guide and precursor. For Scripture says nothing about the righteousness of Melchizedek, priest of the Most High God, although it is understood that he possessed merits worthy of such great praise. It says nothing to commend the blessed life of Enoch and Elijah after they were taken away, although everyone plainly knows that those whom the Lord wished to take from here and preserve for the future live in blessedness.

What, then, should be said about Mary’s death and about her assumption, concerning which divine Scripture commends nothing? We must seek by reason what agrees with the truth, and the truth itself must become authority, without which authority necessarily cannot prevail [Note: [Col. 1144] Thus one Royal Manuscript; in the Corbie Manuscript, “authority necessarily prevails,” with *nec* omitted. The printed editions read, “nor is it authority, nor does it prevail.”].

Mindful of the human condition, we do not fear to say that she underwent that temporal death which certainly her same Son—who is both God and man—endured under the law of the human lot. We say this because he was received and poured forth as man from her womb.

## CHAPTER THREE. Whether It Is Fitting That Blessed Mary’s Body Should Be Dissolved into Dust. It Does Not Follow from Adam’s Curse.

But if we say that she was held by the bonds of death and dissolved into common decay, worms, and ashes, it must be weighed whether this is fitting for such holiness and for the privilege of such a palace of God [Note: [Col. 1144] The manuscripts read “it must be labored over” (*laborandum*).].

For we know that it was said to the first parent: “For dust you are, and to dust you shall return” (Genesis 3:19).
