If this is said of death, it is a general sentence; but if it concerns dissolution into dust, the flesh of Christ escaped this condition—the flesh taken from Mary—which did not suffer corruption.

For concerning this it was written through the prophet David: “For you will not abandon my soul in the underworld, nor will you permit your holy one to see corruption” (Psalm 15:10). But concerning which holy one this was said, the archangel disclosed when he said to Mary: “And the holy one who will be born from you will be called the Son of God” (Luke 1:35).

Truly he is holy, and the Holy of Holies. Hence those things are also called “Holy of Holies” which preserved the things by which he was prefigured—he who alone is truly called the Holy of Holies.

For this is the one of whom the same archangel Gabriel spoke to Daniel, among the other future things that he revealed, saying: “And the vision and prophecy shall be fulfilled, and the Holy of Holies shall be anointed” (Daniel 9:24).

This Holy One did not see corruption; on the third day he rose again, returning triumphantly from the underworld. His flesh, which was taken from Mary, though it died through weakness, came to life again through the power of God.

But this was possible for him because he could die when he wished and rise again when he wished. Thus the nature taken from the Virgin is excepted from that general sentence. And if this does not belong to Mary, it nevertheless belongs to the Son whom she bore.

## CHAPTER FOUR. Mary Is Freed from Eve’s Curse.

After these things that were said to Adam, from which Mary’s Son is excepted, we must consider what was also said to Eve: whether they apply generally to all women, and whether Mary is excepted in any respect.

For it is written: “God also said to the woman, ‘I will multiply your hardships and your conceptions. In pain you shall bear children, and you shall be under your husband’s power, and he shall rule over you’” (Genesis 3:16).

Mary endured hardship, for a sword of Christ’s Passion pierced her soul (Luke 2:35). But she did not multiply conceptions, nor did she live under the power of a man—that is, of a husband. With wholly intact entrails she received Christ from the Holy Spirit, and, with the integrity of her virginity remaining, she remained a virgin.

Because she received him without the pollution of sin and without loss through male involvement, she bore him without pain and, without violation of her integrity, remained with the modesty of her virginity intact.

For this was what he could accomplish in his mother, because God chose to be born from a human being in this way. Therefore, although Mary shares Eve’s hardships, she does not share in giving birth with pain.

Her singular holiness and singular grace earned this for her, by which she was judged singularly worthy to receive God. Thus she is not without reason excepted, by true judgment, from certain general conditions [Col. 1145], since so great a grace preserves her and the privilege of her dignity raises her up.

For the whole world shows how great Christ’s power can be; Mary’s integrity shows how great grace can be. Just as she differs from nature, so she differs from ordinary usage.

What, then, if we say that amid such great difference she underwent the death of the human lot, yet that she through whom God chose to be born and to share the substance of flesh was not held by its bonds? Would that be impious? For we know that Jesus can do all things, and he says of himself: “All power has been given to me in heaven and on earth” (Matthew 28:18).

## CHAPTER FIVE. Christ Must Be Believed to Have Honored His Mother in This Matter, Since She Possessed His Own Nature. The Unity of Grace with Christ. Mary’s Special Unity with Christ.

If, then, he wished to preserve his mother’s virginity intact in its modesty, why would he not wish to preserve her incorrupt from the foulness of decay? Let him speak who has known the mind of the Lord and has been his counselor: does it not belong to the Lord’s kindness to preserve the honor of his mother, since he came not to abolish the law but to fulfill it (Matthew 5:17)?

For just as the law commands honor toward one’s mother, so it condemns dishonor. Since he honored her above others in life by the grace of his conception, it is pious to believe that in death he honored her by a singular preservation and special grace.

He could make her separate from decay and dust, who by being born from her could leave a virgin behind. Decay and the worm are indeed the reproach of the human condition. Since Jesus is free from this reproach, Mary’s nature is excepted, because Jesus is proved to have taken it from her.

For Jesus’ flesh is Mary’s flesh, and much more specially than Joseph’s relation to Judah and his other brothers, to whom he said: “For he is our brother and our flesh” (Genesis 37:27).

Although Christ’s flesh was magnified by the glory of the resurrection and glorified by a powerful ascension above all the heavens, it nevertheless remained and remains the same nature of flesh that was taken from Mary.

For he is the one who was conceived, born, and raised from the dead through the glory of the Father. He himself certainly bears witness to this after the resurrection, when he says to the Apostles: “See my hands and my feet, for it is I myself” (Luke 24:39).

For what does “it is I myself” mean except that I am not another person from the one I was when I suffered? You can recognize this, since you recognize the wounds of the nails in my hands and feet.

Therefore this same one ascended into heaven and carried above the stars the flesh that he had received from his mother, honoring all human nature, and much more especially maternal nature.

If, then, the son is the mother’s nature, it is fitting that the mother should also belong to the son, not insofar as this concerns an equal administration, but insofar as it concerns the same reciprocal substance: man from man, flesh from flesh, mother from son, son from mother—not toward unity of person, but toward unity of bodily nature and substance.

For if grace can create unity without the particularity of a special nature, how much more where there is both unity of grace and the special birth of a body?

The unity of grace exists, for example, among the disciples in Christ, concerning whom he himself said: “Holy Father, keep them in your name, whom you have given me, so that they may be one as we are.” And again, concerning all the righteous: “I pray not only for these, but also for those who will believe in me through their word, that they all may be one, as you, Father, are in me, and I in you”—that is, that they may be by grace what we are by the nature of divinity.

If this unity of grace, which is preserved among all who believe in Christ, is not removed from Mary even by the judgment of those who understand less, how much more does the special character of nature itself, together with unity of grace, make mother and son, son and mother, one?

We must also see what he subsequently added concerning those whom he wished to be one with him through grace. For he said: “Holy Father, those whom you have given me, I will that where I am, they also may be with me, so that they may see my glory which you have given me” (John 17:11, 20, and following).

O the great and inestimable goodness of God, who wishes to have his own with him in glory, so that they may enjoy his radiance—those who, joined to him here by faith, are judged worthy to be one with him!

If, then, he wishes to have them with him, and since he can do so who can do all things, what should be thought concerning his mother, where is she worthy to be, except in the presence of the Son?

## CHAPTER SIX. Mary’s Body Is Already in Heaven in Two Ways.

As far as I behold, understand, and believe, Mary’s soul enjoys Christ’s radiance and his glorious presence, always thirsting to see him and always contemplating him. While she is fed in an inestimable manner, she is honored by the Son with a certain more excellent and special privilege: possessing in Christ the body that she bore, glorified at the right hand of the Father—and, if not the body by which she bore him, nevertheless the body that she bore.

And why should it not be the body by which she bore him? Unless an authority not yet perceived should stand in the way, I truly believe that it is also the body by which she bore him, because such great sanctification is more worthy of heaven than of earth.

The throne of God, the Lord’s heavenly bridal chamber, the house and tabernacle of Christ ought to be where he himself is. Heaven is more worthy to preserve so precious a treasure than earth; such great integrity is rightly followed by incorruptibility, not by any dissolution into decay.

Therefore, when I am unable to conceive of that most sacred body—from which Christ took flesh and united the divine nature to human nature, not losing what he was but assuming what he was not, so that the Word might become flesh, that is, God might become man—being handed over to worms and destined, after the common lot of decay, to become dust for worms in the future, I fear to say it.

If I felt nothing higher about it than about my own body, I would say nothing except what I would say about my own body: that without any ambiguity it must be dissolved in death, and after death become decay, after decay a worm, and after the worm, as is fitting, the most abject dust.

But this does not seem compatible with what should be believed concerning Mary, because the gift of incomparable grace drives such an estimation far away.

## CHAPTER SEVEN. This Is Inferred from Christ’s Petition for His Ministers. Angels Served Christ on Earth.

Many considerations invite me to say this, among them what Truth himself once said to his ministers: “Whoever serves me, let him follow me; and where I am, there also shall my minister be” (John 12:26).

If this is a general sentence concerning all who serve Christ through faith and pious action, how much more does it apply specially to Mary, and in what a special way?

Everyone who thinks soundly understands that Mary was Christ’s servant through the performance of her work and through the most steadfast truth of faith. Without doubt she proved herself his minister in deed: she carried him in her womb, nourished and cherished him after he was born, and, as the Gospel says, laid him in a manger (Luke 2:7). Fleeing from Herod’s presence, she hid him in Egypt (Matthew 2:13), and she accompanied his entire infancy with a mother’s affection.

Thus, even to the cross, where she saw her son—now a fully grown man—hanging, she certainly did not withdraw from following him, not only by the steps of her feet, as though out of reverence for the Lord, but also through the affection of imitation.

Therefore Mary, as Christ’s minister in the qualities of her special works, was most devoted; and without doubt she was his follower in the faith of religion and the love of true belief [Note: [Col. 1146] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read: “because of her love for her son, and also in imitation of his conduct, as though out of reverence for God. Mary…”].

For she could not fail to believe in his divinity, since she knew that she had conceived him not from male seed according to the order of nature, but through divine inspiration announced by the archangel.

She continually saw a multitude of ministering angels present with him: at his conception and birth, when, together with the angel, the heavenly host became present, crying out and saying: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2:14); and when he fled into Egypt and later returned from there.

From these things she could plainly recognize that such services were fitting only for God. Hence the announcement of the star and the unexpected arrival of the Magi from the most distant regions were for her a very great indication of the truth.

Likewise, the extraordinary encounter with Simeon and Anna, distinguished by prophetic dignity from all others and special to this child, was such an indication. Mary preserved all these things and, strengthened in faith by all of them, pondered them in a devout heart.

Thus, entirely without hesitation but certain of her son’s power as of true divine strength, when the wine failed at the wedding she said: “They have no wine” (John 2:3), knowing clearly that he could do what he soon brought about by a divine miracle.

Behold, then, Mary, Christ’s minister in faith and deed, and his devoted follower even to his death—not more in the steps of her feet than, as we must believe, in the affection of imitation. If she is not where Christ wishes his ministers to be, where then will she be? And if she is there, will it be by equal grace? And if by equal grace, where is the equal judgment of God, who repays each person according to his merits?

If, then, grace was given to Mary above all others during her life according to her merit, will it be diminished after her death? Far from it. For if the death of all the saints is precious, Mary’s is certainly most precious, accompanied by such great grace that she is called, and truly is, the mother of God.

## CHAPTER EIGHT. Christ Could Preserve Mary without Corruption. He Willed It, Because It Was Fitting.

Having considered all these things and examined them by true reason, I judge that we must confess Mary to be in Christ and with Christ: in Christ, because in him we live, move, and exist; with Christ, because she was gloriously assumed to the joys of eternity and received with greater honor by Christ’s kindness than the others whom he honored above others here by grace.

She was not brought after death to the common humiliation of decay, worm, and dust—she who bore her own Savior and the Savior of all. If it is within his power to prevent a hair of the saints’ heads from perishing, it is also within his power to preserve her, soul and body, intact.

If no ecclesiastical person doubts Christ’s power to preserve his mother forever without corruption, why should it be doubted that he wished to do what accords with the grace of such great kindness?

If the divine will, by grace alone, chose to preserve not only the bodies of the boys unharmed amid the flames of a raging fire but even to preserve their garments unburned, why would it reject in his own mother what it chose in another’s garment?

By mercy alone he wished Jonah to remain incorrupt in the belly of the whale, beyond the ordinary course of nature (Jonah 2:1). Will grace not preserve Mary incorrupt beyond nature? Daniel was preserved from the lions’ most immoderate hunger (Daniel 6:22); shall Mary, endowed with such great merits of dignity, not be preserved?

Because we do not recognize all these things that we have mentioned as preserving nature [Note: [Col. 1147] Two manuscripts read “usage” (*usus*).], we do not doubt that in Mary’s integrity grace could accomplish more than nature [Col. 1148].

For the things we speak of are works of divinity; and therefore they are possible, because they come from the Almighty. Christ, moreover, is the Power of God and the Wisdom of God. Everything that belongs to the Father belongs to him; everything that the Father wills, he wills; and he wills all things that are just and fitting.

Accordingly, Mary seems rightly to rejoice with inexpressible joy, in soul and body, in her own Son, with her own Son, and through her own Son. No hardship of corruption ought to follow her, since no corruption of integrity followed her in bearing such a Son.

Let her always be incorrupt, whom such great grace has completely drenched; let her live whole and entire, who gave birth to the whole and perfect life of all; let her be with the one whom she carried in her womb; let her who bore, cherished, and nourished him be with him.

Mary is the Mother of God, the Nurse of God, the Minister of God, and the Follower of God. Concerning her, as I have already said, because I do not dare to think otherwise, I do not presume to say otherwise.

## CHAPTER NINE. With What Disposition the Author Asserted the Foregoing.

Let your fraternal Charity receive this understanding according to what the Spirit of Christ inspired. I have shown in part the considerations that encouraged me to speak in this manner.

But if anyone chooses to oppose these things without being willing to say that Christ cannot do them, let him explain why it would not be fitting for him to will them and, consequently, why they should not be.

If he demonstrates that he truly knows God’s counsel in these matters, I shall begin to believe him concerning matters about which I did not presume to think otherwise [Note: [Col. 1148] The printed editions read “I cannot” (*possum*).]. I shall marvel that he has investigated the depth of the divine counsel, which I seem, with the Apostle, to be obliged to admire with due reverence, saying: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and inscrutable his ways!” (Romans 11:33).

And because, according to the same Apostle, “we know in part and we prophesy in part” (1 Corinthians 13:9), I have spoken about these matters, although not as much as they are, nevertheless in the manner in which I believed I ought to speak.

If what I have written is true, I give you thanks, Christ, because concerning your holy Virgin Mother I could not think anything except what seemed pious and fitting.

If I have spoken as I ought, approve it, I beseech you, Christ, you and your own. But if I have not spoken as I ought, forgive me, you and your own.

You who live and reign with God the Father and the Holy Spirit throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

---

# ON THE VISITATION OF THE SICK (G, S)*

## BOOK ONE. OF UNCERTAIN AUTHORSHIP.

## CHAPTER ONE. When Weeping Is Effeminate and When It Is Human.

Yesterday I set out to bid a final farewell, with the grace of a visit, to my most beloved nephew who was dying. But, touched by inward grief of heart, and not without some slight moistening of my eyes, I could scarcely at last utter a word from my sobbing mouth—so that I was unable to say anything sufficiently worthy either of me or of him.

For if the mind, which is affected by no small grief—as is the case with everyone—attempted to compose words, the very attempt to compose words would increase the tears. Thus I spared words in order to spare tears.

To pour forth tears that offer no consolation is effeminate. But to shed no tears at all, when we are commanded to rejoice with those who rejoice and to weep with those who weep, is both disobedience and inhumanity.

And Jesus wept.

Therefore I shall weep, my sweetest nephew, lest I be disobedient and inhuman, or fail to imitate my Jesus. I shall also restrain my tears, lest I seem excessively effeminate.

## CHAPTER TWO. Penance Prepares One for Eternal Life. Christ Leads; God, Who Is Here Received, Receives the One Who Comes.

You too, most beloved nephew, are hastening to enter the way of all flesh [Col. 1148], where you will see your parents, the holy Patriarchs, and also the supreme blessedness of all.

For such a great journey, lest you grow faint on the way, you need substantial provisions for the road. You are to be set as a living stone in the wall of the heavenly city, in whose building no sound of clamor or hammer is heard. Here the clamor must be endured; here the hammer must be applied to the stone; here everything superfluous must be broken away from the stone being squared.

Let the clamor be the recollection of your sins, over which your most humble confession should resound in the priest’s ear, according to the saying: “Confess your sins to one another” (James 5:16). Let the hammer be repentance of the heart, more than merely striking the breast. Let both of these be moderated while you still retain some strength in this life, so that they will not be required when you are placed in God’s building.

For where are you going? To life.

By what way? Hear the Lord saying: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6).

You cannot go astray: Christ is the way. You cannot be deceived: Christ is the truth. You cannot fail to live: Christ is the life. Through Christ, the way, you will go to Christ, the true life.

Christ is the way; you are the traveler. Carry Christ as your provision for the journey; the way, the truth, and the life will lead you to himself.

But where will you find this way? Where will you find this provision? Christ is God, and God is everywhere.

If God is everywhere, then he is also in you, behind you, before you, and around you. All things are full of God. Do not think God far away; wherever you seek him, you will find him.

If you ascend into heaven, he is there; if you descend into the underworld, he is present. If you take your wings at dawn so that you may dwell at the ends of the sea, even there his hand will lead you and his right hand will hold you (Psalm 138:8 and following).

Thus you have God everywhere as your guest. Make your lodging welcome to so great a guest. Then you will safely say to your guest that, in going, he should lead you; in leading, conduct you; in conducting, bring you through; and in bringing you through, lodge you.

I tell you: if you present him with lodging that is pleasing to him, he will offer you his lodging more graciously and more gladly.

O how blessed you will be if you are God’s guest, if you receive a dwelling in his city, namely, the heavenly Jerusalem; if one day God, giving you thanks, says: “I was a guest, and you welcomed me; and insofar as you did it to one of the least of mine, you did it to me” (Matthew 25:35–40): “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom!”

I had been mistaken, for I had promised you God’s lodging in exchange for your lodging, whereas I had called one already enrolled as a citizen—indeed, already reigning with him—a guest.

God does not promise you lodging; he promises you a kingdom. You will reign with Christ; you will be an heir of God and a fellow heir of Christ (Romans 8:17).

## CHAPTER THREE. Preparation for This: To Turn Away from Evil and Do Good. The Sum of All Good Is Love. It Is God’s Gift. Love of God and Neighbor Are the Two Wings by Which One Flies to God.

But to attain such great happiness, various preparation is necessary for you, dearest. Confession and penance have already been briefly noted above. To confess and repent is to turn away from evil. To turn away from evil is, in a certain way, good.

But you have heard: “Turn away from evil and do good” (Psalm 36:27). Turning away from evil is good, but a prompt and effective gladness for doing good is necessary. For God loves a cheerful giver (2 Corinthians 9:7).

And what does it mean to do good? The rule for doing good is set forth publicly. The Teacher of teachers recounts the good deeds owed to him, saying: “I was a guest, naked, and in prison, thirsty and hungry; and you ministered to me. You did these things to me insofar as you did them to one of the least of mine” (Matthew 25:35 and following).

Great is the good that, when done to the poor, overflows to God. But generosity toward the poor is not the whole performance of goodness.

The Apostle says: “If I distribute all my possessions as food for the poor, but do not have love, it profits me nothing” (1 Corinthians 13:3).

Therefore the sum of all good is love. The distribution of your possessions to the poor does not overflow to God unless it proceeds from the root of love.

“God is love” (1 John 4:8). What proceeds from God overflows to God; what does not overflow to God does not proceed from love. Thus both proceeding from God and overflowing to God are gifts of God.

Therefore distribute what is yours to the poor in such a way that your distribution overflows to God.

But what will you distribute? Perhaps you lack something to distribute. Hear Tobit: “My son, if you have much, give abundantly; but if you have little, strive to share even that little” (Tobit 4:9).

If you give someone even a cup of cold water, you will not lose your reward (Matthew 10:42). But perhaps you lack even water. Yet you have something to distribute: you have yourself.

Give yourself to God, and you will have God himself.

How will you give yourself to God? “Set your house in order, for you shall die and not live.” Perhaps you have no house. Set yourself in order, if you do not set your house in order (Isaiah 38:1).

What kind of ordering will that be? Love God, and God will love you.

Take wings with which you may fly up to God. The wings by which you will fly are love of God and love of neighbor. Love of God and neighbor is the proper ordering of yourself.

“You shall love your neighbor as yourself.” Love of neighbor does no evil (Romans 13:9–10).

What shall I say about love of God? “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your strength” (Deuteronomy 6:5).

Let your eye love God, your mouth, your hand, your foot, and every sense of yours. Whatever you are, whatever love is in you, let all of you love God.

These are the two wings by which you will fly to the heavens, be carried to the saints, and be inserted among the angels. Your hand may be idle from work and your foot from walking, but never will a holy soul or a mind that fears God be able to be empty of love.

## CHAPTER FOUR. Correction, as God’s Gift, Is to Be Loved.

But you say: “I love God.”

Good—would that what you have promised in words were truly in you. The proof of love for God is the completion of his commandments: the voluntary fulfillment of his works, loving what God loves, and embracing with ardent desire what God does.

If, then, you love God, you love what God does. And if you love what God does, you love God’s discipline, which chastises you.

Do you endure God’s scourge? Do you suffer from coughing? Are your lungs failing? Does your stomach reject food? Are you wasting away with consumption? Do you loathe wine? Are you afflicted with dysentery? Are you affected by many kinds of illness?

These too, if you have eyes and are thoughtful, are gifts of God.

“My son, do not reject the discipline of the Father. For no son exists whom the father does not correct.” But do not grow faint under the Lord’s discipline, and do not become weary when you are reproved by him (Hebrews 12:5).

“For the Lord corrects the one whom he loves, and, like a father with his son, he takes pleasure in him” (Proverbs 3:12).

Do you wish to know that bodily illness gives birth to the soul’s salvation? Hear the Lord answering the Apostle: “Power is made perfect in weakness” (2 Corinthians 12:9). It is as though he said: Embrace the weakness that you suffer, because through it you will progress from strength to strength.

If strength is increased in weakness, and strength is the salvation of the soul, then bodily weakness, when it gives birth to salvation through the soul’s strength, is a gift of God. For the salvation of the soul comes from nowhere except God.

Therefore do not despise God’s scourge; but, when scourged, give thanks to God. Love the one who corrects you, love the one who reforms you, love the one who reproves you—not in fury or anger, but in mercy.

Open to the one who knocks; be devoted to the one who calls; give thanks to the one who has mercy.

Return to yourself. Think for a little while; think about God. Consider, if you can, that “his mercies are over all his works” (Psalm 144:9).

He is God; he is judge. He does not wish you to be condemned, nor would he wish you to be judged evil. He wishes to have mercy on you. In you he mercifully scourges what you have stubbornly committed against him.

## CHAPTER FIVE. God’s Mercy as Though Unjust.

My God, my God—I shall dare to say it; with your peace I shall say it, and I shall say it filled with great joy. In a kind of ecstatic exultation I shall say it, presuming upon you:

Unless you were God, you would be unjust. For we have sinned grievously, we cling stubbornly to sin, we rejoice in sin, we walk after sin, we proclaim our sin with outstretched necks, and we do not conceal it—and yet you are appeased.

We provoke you to anger, but you lead us toward mercy. We irritate you to fury, but you delay vengeance. You could punish sinners with just destruction and overthrow the negligent, yet your patience waits for us to be corrected through repentance.

My God, my mercy, is this not injustice?

But is there injustice with God? (Romans 9:14) Far from it.

For that God the just judge patiently endures, that just severity is mercifully bent—this is all God. You would not otherwise be God unless you were bent, unless you suffered patiently, unless you had mercy. Nor would you otherwise be bent, suffer patiently, or have mercy unless you were God.

Whatever you do, therefore, is yours. Do, then, God, what you do, because what you do is yours. What is yours is good. What you do, therefore, is good, my God, my mercy.

## CHAPTER SIX. To Receive Illness and God’s Scourges Joyfully. Death Is to Be Preferred to the Present Life.

You, therefore, my dear one, who are soon to depart from the world, must not despise so great and ineffable a kindness of the Lord your God; receive his scourging gladly. He scourges in you what you do not know, and not unjustly—for his judgments are just: this bodily illness is spiritual medicine. [Col. 1151] Moreover, consider that your illness, as the physicians say, is incurable; and reflect with yourself that, whether you wish it or not, if you presume to murmur against God, you will endure the illness and will not be healed by murmuring. Indeed, your soul will be weakened while you murmur against your God, your father, your physician, and your most gentle and peaceful teacher, who, even in scourging, is utterly calm and, when he is angry, always remembers mercy.

Yield, therefore, to my counsels; and since by murmuring you would endure two evils, be at peace and make your bodily burden a spiritual antidote. For if in your scourging you wish to recognize God, you will not be scourged in both body and soul: God does not scourge twice for the same thing. O with how joyful a breast and how glad a heart you ought to desire the divine visitation! Certainly, if you were entirely strong in body, you ought with all your wishes to seek bodily weakness as medicine from God, and to fear that bodily health might be the soul’s sickness.

I know nothing else, but because you are ill, you ought beneficially to rejoice: since the divine call is near, you ought to attend it gladly with all your strength. Come now: if God had granted you a bishopric or some other honor, as desirable to you as health is to the sick, would you not receive that gift of God with the greatest joy? Certainly, with greater exultation and more affectionate willingness, and with thanksgiving as well, you ought to regard this divine chastisement as uniquely yours, because this too is a most useful gift of God. [Note: [Col. 1151] Manuscripts: *utillimum* (“most useful”).]

Moreover, if you were thinking about the shipwreck of this life and about acquiring the exchange of a shortened death, how unspeakably you would grow weary of living, and how eagerly you would desire to die in the Lord! For “Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord” (Revelation 14:13).

To make a brief comparison, then, let us compare—if you please—the present life, which is the beginning of sorrows, and, as though in a friendly dispute, examine what ought rather to be desired: to live badly or to die well. For no one can live well in the present life: “Every human being is a liar” (Psalm 115:11). And the Apostle, seeing—more than other human beings—“another law in his members warring against the law of his mind” (Romans 7:23), desires “to depart and be with Christ” (Philippians 1:23). And we know that “every creature groans and labors” (Romans 8:22) until it is freed from slavery to corruption by him who subjected it in hope.

Finally, who can count the troubles of the present life: hunger, thirst, cold, heat, weariness? They are innumerable and, through sheer familiarity, domestic to us. Yet these are only the beginning of sorrows. But, to consider more deeply what lies within us: desire, love, hatred, fornication, adultery, killing or being killed, robbery, theft—are these not hostile passions to us? Yet who is immune, who is free from all these things? And who, being subject to so many and such great passions, will be immune from sin? And who, living under sin, lives well?

Therefore every human being lives badly, because sin too is evil. Finally, I declare boldly that the beginning of human life is the beginning of sorrows. There were philosophers who did not fail to recognize this: they mourned at the birth of children but rejoiced at their death, signifying that a human being is born for labor but dies for rest.

Even holy David was so grieved both over the birth and over the life of the son whom he had begotten from Bathsheba that, while the child was still alive, he remained mourning and fasting; but when the little child had died, he both rejoiced and ate (2 Samuel 12:16 and following).

O desirable death! O death, the end of all present evils! O death, closure of labor and beginning of rest! Who could imagine the benefits of your blessedness? For to die badly is not for Christians; but to die well is to live with Christ. And who could adequately set forth its benefits—its benefits which unite a human being to Christ, which, as has been said, are the end of evils, the nurse and beginning of secure happiness?

Farewell, my most beloved death. I confess that, if I could, I would gladly embrace you, gladly taste you, and freely undergo you. And I testify that all my thought, and the frequent reading of this present letter, urges me to love you—only do not come prematurely. But you, my flesh and my bone, whom my letter visits, and who will receive it as you are about to die, receive consolation from this same letter and from the other copies that are with you, so that, placed at the end, you may not come to the court of your God as though abandoned.

## CHAPTER VII. The prayer of one who is dying

When all these things have been completed, prayer is necessary for you. Therefore address God, and, unless you act otherwise, speak to him confidently in these words:

“My God, my God, my mercy, my refuge, I desire you; I hasten to come to you. Do not despise me, placed in this fearful crisis; be present to me with favor in these great necessities of mine. I cannot redeem myself by my works, but you redeem me and have mercy on me. I distrust my merits, but I trust in your mercies; and I trust in your mercies more than I distrust my evil deeds.

“You are my hope, my God. Against you alone I have sinned, through my own fault. I who was dear to you for redemption, let me not be worthless for destruction. And now I come to you, who fail no one. I desire to depart and be with you. Into your hands I commend my spirit, Lord.

“Look upon me, Lord God of truth, and grant me, my God, that I may sleep and rest in peace. You who live and reign as God in perfect Trinity, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.”

# BOOK TWO

[Col. 1151]

## CHAPTER I. The occasion of this work

[Col. 1151]

I had thought that I had brought the course of the preceding treatise to a close when certain of the brothers, receiving it and adhering to it attentively, praised it highly and, as they testified, reread it gladly for their own benefit; they judged it necessary for the common consolation of those departing from this age.

I, however, regarding their joy as my own fraternal joy, embraced it in such a way that my little work pleased me in their delight; and what I myself had dictated without prior deliberation, I worked through in solitary examination. [Note: [Col. 1151] Royal Manuscripts: *peragrarem* (“I might traverse”).]

What had been written was simple, but, as I believe, catholic in its teaching. Therefore, out of regard for the simplicity of the statements and for the brothers’ goodwill—for they had already praised it in this way—I spared it. Although it was a small volume, they called it *The Visitation of the Sick*; I allowed the preceding material to remain as it was.

But because I had aimed at epistolary brevity, I had omitted certain things that would have been necessary for the same visitation of the sick. These things, therefore, which I had omitted for the sake of concision, as well as those subsequently requested of me concerning the same matter, I committed to writing below. They properly belonged earlier in the order, but the useful speed of moving toward other matters placed them afterward.

## CHAPTER II. Faith necessary for one who is about to depart. It must be directed especially toward Christ. Christ has exalted the human being above the angels

My dearest one, as you are about to depart from us—for the final day presses upon you—be faithful. Without faith you cannot please God, and an unbeliever is not acceptable to God. There are therefore many things concerning God that must be believed for the salvation of the soul.

Faith, then, must be applied to the divine mysteries more than argumentation by words. For we cannot comprehend individually, through rational arguments, all that must be believed concerning God; yet we can and must believe. Indeed, we cannot speak about God without in some measure exceeding ourselves mentally. Where there is an excess of the mind, there the succession of faith is appropriate.

That wondrous mystery, therefore, concerning the unity of the Trinity and the deifying Trinity of unity, is to be believed rather than explained. [Col. 1153] Let it indeed be believed on the testimony of Holy Scripture.

There are also other things concerning God the Son that are, as it were, near and adjacent to us; through their very nearness and adjacency they are familiar to us, and through that familiarity they are delightful to us. For it is delightful and salutary for a human being, especially one who is dying, to speak and be satisfied with the humanity of Christ.

That “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14) concerns humanity; that God became human concerns humanity. Both, therefore, comprise this ineffable mystery of humanity. Since the weak human intellect, dulled by the weight of its own humanity and now seeing “through a mirror in an enigma” (1 Corinthians 13:12), cannot comprehend the divinity of God as it ought, let it turn its intellectual eye toward Christ’s humanity, which belongs to us.

Let it delight in that humanity and be satisfied by it; let it turn its face toward it, just as it is said of Hezekiah: “Hezekiah turned his face with tears toward the wall” (2 Kings 20:2). The wall is Christ’s humanity. Hence Solomon says: “Behold, he stands behind our wall” (Song of Songs 2:9). His divinity, namely, which neither bends nor is to be bent toward any sin, lay hidden beneath our flesh. For “he appeared on earth and lived among human beings” (Baruch 3:38).

To this wall Hezekiah truly turned his face at the point of death, as the prophet had foretold to him through the Spirit; and thus he recovered. With confidence in this expectation of health, Jacob finally exults:

“I saw the Lord face to face”—the face of divinity in which God existed, face to face with the humanity that he was to assume—“and my soul was saved” (Genesis 32:30).

All the saints burned with desire for this incarnation, since it was clear to them that the human race could not otherwise be saved than through the incarnate Son of God. For “there is salvation in no one else; nor is there any other name under heaven given among human beings by which it is necessary for a human being to be saved” (Acts 4:12).

Turn, therefore, your face more familiarly toward this wall of ours, our mediator; approach what belongs to you with greater confidence. He who became a companion by sharing your weakness knows how to sympathize with your weaknesses.

He carried the prerogative of our flesh upward into the heavens, because the human being who is God has been exalted above the heavens. He shared in our humanity so that we might share in his divinity. Dare, therefore, my son, to make some sharing with your human God, because God first made a sharing of your pure humanity with himself.

Salvation proceeded from divinity; redemption came through humanity; yet both came from each other. But because what is mine is mine [Note: [Col. 1153] The printed editions do not repeat *meum* (“mine”).], because I unite it to myself by a certain thought, kinship [Note: [Col. 1153] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read *agnatione* (“descent from the same family”).], and a secret affection, and claim it for myself by a kind of right of blood relationship, I speak more safely and joyfully to my Jesus than to any of the holy spirits. Christ owes more to me than to any of the heavenly spirits.

What you are, God deigned to become. He did not become what an angel is, although he is the Angel of great counsel. He exalted you above the angels, for you will judge angels. I would not wish to have the place of an angel if I could have the place assigned to a human being.

Your God, your human being, your garment—your richly colored garment, which he most fittingly adapted to himself and put on—has gone before you to the court of his God. There he continually intercedes for us, no longer made lower than the angels, but crowned with glory and honor and set over the works of God’s hands (Psalm 8:6).

Since you have him as intercessor and mediator, appoint him as your gracious helper. And “if God is for you, who can be against you?” (Romans 8:31).

The incarnation, passion, resurrection, and ascension of God above the heavens, as well as your own future transformation, must therefore be believed firmly and faithfully. Let these things be your faith, my son; let them search out and possess your heart. Let your mouth taste nothing sweeter; let it boldly confess and sing them. “For with the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Romans 10:10).

## CHAPTER III. Certain external signs to be applied to the sick. Concerning the cross

[Col. 1154]

Although these things may suffice for salvation, there are nevertheless certain outward signs that at times awaken even sluggish faith and, as it were, drive a kind of compunction into its innermost chambers. The religion of Christianity requires that these be observed, and the devotion of friends who gather around the sick rejoices to fulfill them.

Do not neglect these things either, my son. They will be salutary for you yourself and consoling to me and to those dear to you. Christians possess, as it were, a venerable memorial of that Lord’s cross, and they call it “cross” from the representation of the cross itself. We confess that it is worthy of all veneration, and we venerate it in remembrance of our Crucified One.

An image of a suffering human being is added upon the cross, through which the saving passion of Jesus Christ is renewed for us. Embrace it humbly and venerate it reverently, while recalling this to mind:

> The figure present, which I behold, is neither God nor human being;
>
> but it is God and human being whom the sacred figure signifies.
>
> Truly human and truly God, yet both are one and the same;
>
> he suffers the insults of the cross, undergoes death, and is buried;
>
> the same one lives, and through these signs of the cross he triumphs over the enemy.
>
> The inscription of this cross makes that known to us;
>
> namely, the cross and the crucified one are its own sign.
>
> This also I venerate, and I always adore Jesus.

But you, good Jesus, who, hanging for me, suffered in this way, deign to have mercy on me; and grant me—since you died for me, and died for this purpose, so that, dying to the world, I might live for you—grant me this, good Jesus.

## CHAPTER IV. The sacraments to be received by the sick. Confessing to God alone is not sufficient

Nor must that command of the Apostle James be omitted:

> “Is anyone among you sick? Let him bring in the presbyters of the Church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with holy oil in the name of the Lord Jesus; and the prayer of faith will save the sick person” (James 5:14–15).

Therefore ask that this be done for you and on your behalf, as the Apostle James—or rather, the Lord through his Apostle—said. The very anointing with consecrated oil is understood as a typological anointing of the Holy Spirit.

Do not refuse, my son, to receive that life-giving nourishment of the Lord’s body; rather, seek it most eagerly and eat it faithfully. For that incomparable and ineffable food will be the most salutary viaticum for you: the price of your redemption, the memorial of the Redeemer, and the defense of the redeemed.

In the preceding treatise I briefly reminded you about confession, since an insistent need to move on to other matters pressed upon me. Now too I intend to make a concise recapitulation of the same subject of confession.

There are some who think that it is sufficient for their salvation if they confess their sins to God alone, since nothing is hidden from him and no one’s conscience is concealed from him. They do not wish, or are ashamed, or disdain to reveal themselves to priests—yet the Lord established them as those who distinguish between leprosy and leprosy through the lawgiver (Deuteronomy 17:8–9).

But I do not want you to be deceived by this very opinion, so that you are ashamed to confess before the vicar of the Lord, wasting away from embarrassment or stiff-necked from disdain. For you must humbly submit to the judgment of one whom the Lord does not disdain to have as his vicar.

Therefore ask a priest to come to you and make him fully acquainted with the innermost recesses of your consciences. Do not let that superstition of dreamers deceive you—a superstition which, in visiting the sick, confirms that confession of sins to God saves without consulting a priest.

We do not deny that confession of sins must frequently be directed to God. For blessed is the one who “will seize and dash his little ones, or his greatest ones, against the rock” (Psalm 136:9). The rock, however, is Christ (1 Corinthians 10:4).

But we testify, and sound doctrine testifies, that you must not flatter yourself with the ears of those who applaud you: you first need a priest to act as mediator with your God through a salutary judgment. Otherwise, under both the Law and grace, how would the divine response be fulfilled: “Go and show yourselves to the priests” (Luke 17:14; Leviticus 14:2)? How would this be fulfilled: “Confess your sins to one another” (James 5:16)? [Col. 1155]

Therefore let a presbyter be brought in as the examiner of your scars, in God’s place; reveal your ways to him, and he will provide you with the antidote of reconciliation.

## CHAPTER V. A deceptive practice of confession. What confession should be like. Confession must be accompanied by penance and hatred of sin

Nor should you address the presbyter with a certain cunning, as some do, since such an address would be a deception of yourself. Deceitful people approach priests and confess in their presence as follows:

“I am a sinner, lord priest. I have sinned by swearing falsely, committing adultery, fornication, killing a human being, lying, committing sacrilege, stealing, and robbing. I have committed all these things, through my fault, either in deed or in will.”

Thus, while mocking God—although he is not mocked—they confess things they have not done, inserting falsehoods, veiling what has been revealed. The result is that, in the same offense, they both uncover their sin and overshadow what has been uncovered. The priest then departs more uncertain, after hearing uncertainly what was certain.

How well and justly would such a priest deal with these tricks if he applied his judgment to all the things he had heard and imposed suitable correction upon one who had presented himself as guilty of everything, excluding nothing and disclosing nothing specifically, defaming himself! He also dispensed good counsel out of order, and there was no proper place for these things then. A more temperate course would have been to disclose his general illness to the physician and first to lay open, one by one, his wounds, bruises, and swelling injuries according to the severity with which they pressed upon his inward parts.

You, however, my son, will not act in this way, since you will follow the sounder counsel. Regard the priest standing before you as an angel of God. “The lips of the priest,” says Malachi, “guard knowledge, and they seek the law from his mouth; for he is the angel of the Lord of hosts” (Malachi 2:7).

Address God’s minister with the reverence with which it is fitting to address both God and his angel. Open to him the most hidden recesses of your inner chambers; reveal the innermost barriers of your ashamed consciences. Do not be ashamed to say before one person what perhaps you were not ashamed to do before and with many.

“To sin is human; to desist from sin is Christian; to persist is devilish.”

Therefore reveal to the angel of God the crimes that most grievously trouble your mind. Say nothing obscure; envelop no fault in ambiguities; cover nothing true with circumlocutions.

You should also indicate, if you remember, the places and times in which you sinned; the persons with whom you sinned—not their names, so that the association may be secretly corrected even as they desist from sin; the age at which you fell; the rank in which you were then serving the Church; whether you fell once or through habit; whether through necessity or through will. For all these things have their own judgments.

If, in secular judgments, places are distinguished from places—murder committed in the king’s court receives one punishment, in a public road another, and in a rural village another; sometimes forgiveness is granted because of the time, infancy is excused, old age is sometimes spared, while middle age is restrained by a severe bridle; crimes committed on the solemn birthdays of princes are punished with fierce destruction—then other offenses too must be expelled by judgments all the stricter when committed in places consecrated to God, at times devoted to God’s festivals, in a more discerning age, against persons specially delegated to God, and in higher ranks.

Is not more required of the one to whom more has been entrusted? Is it not less to have killed one person than many? Is it not lighter to have sinned once than a hundred times? Does not one who fell through necessity obtain pardon more quickly than one who fell through will?

And although, wherever sin is committed, sin is always sin, and no time, age, person, or place protects the sinner from sin, nevertheless all these circumstances must be examined in their own manner, since all must be reproved and corrected according to their own measure.

These things, however, if they are kept silent or cleverly disguised when spoken, strangle the soul; if they are exposed, they vanish through penance. Pursue them in proper order so that they may be reduced to nothing; explain your sins without circumlocution, as far as you can—indeed, strive manfully to uproot them.

Alas! Why are you ashamed to confess what you were not ashamed to do? It is better [Note: [Col. 1156] Manuscripts: *lautius est* (“it is more richly/better”).] to endure a little embarrassment before one person than, on the day of judgment, to waste away, marked and grievously cast down, before so many thousands of human beings.

Let your confession be accompanied by penance, for in this way your iniquity will be forgiven. And: “Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven and whose sins are covered” (Psalm 32:1).

Confession of sin is also the condemnation of the sinner; but penance produces a useful confession. Hatred must also be directed against sins, since the friend of sins is the enemy of his own soul. Sins must be hated with perfect hatred, since they have become our enemies.

To be unwilling to destroy their momentary allurements—although they can be nullified by a momentary striking of the heart, and through their nullification you will possess eternal rest, whereas through storing them up you will go into infernal torment—is the height of madness.

Confess, therefore, my dear one, by name those crimes that trouble you; disclose specifically what you know to be specific. Add the daily matters from which you have not been cleansed, at least in thought, to a general collection. In this way, trust in pardon.

Now, after consulting the priest, your offenses must be referred to God; they must then be presented to him. Such a presentation will not afterward be fruitless.

And what I perhaps forgot and omitted: forgive your debtors their debts from your heart, and love all human beings in God and for God’s sake.

## CHAPTER VI. That these things were written for the less educated

Our little pages seem like cheap and contemptible instructions because they are not dressed in rhetorical breath and cothurnus-like grandeur. They also seem superfluous, since all these things were accessible to the more learned.

But it sometimes happens that learned people know many things about which they have not doubted, and think that everyone has learned the same things through the same method of study. But we were among the number of those less capable, and we know clearly how a weary ox treads.

A large number of people desiring counsel for their souls also came to us. Some spoke out of simplicity, others deliberately. We gave them counsel as seemed good to us.

But to you, for whom our heart keeps closer watch, and whom the concern of this letter visits—since the most impatient grief removes the pleasure of conversation—we have directed this treatise from what we drew from those more experienced. [Note: [Col. 1156] Manuscripts: *peritiores* (“the more experienced”).]

It is therefore yours—entirely yours—and also most necessary for you, who are placed at the point of death and, if it could be seen, would already see death itself. Thus, made more vigilant by our instruction, or made more watchful by the necessity of your own end, watch over yourself, provide for yourself, and counsel yourself.

If in our treatises I have pointed out things you did not know, or repeated things you did know, nevertheless in both cases our labor was spent on your behalf out of the utmost care for you. And if this chain of admonitory words does not benefit you because you already knew everything, it will at least benefit some who know less; and it will also benefit me, for whom it is a pleasure to admonish you, because I will have satisfied myself.

## CHAPTER VII. To which priests sins should be declared

But lest some superstition of certain presbyters be passed over by us untouched, as though unknown, let the conclusion of our discourse now turn somewhat toward presbyters, since confession must be made before them.

It would be superfluous to write this if it were not being offered as a remedy for an error already spreading among many. It is better to provide for the ignorance of priests than to leave the ignorant, uncorrected, in their ignorance. This error could harm you too, since it has harmed many.

As was stated above, you must confess before a priest and submit to his judgment. But just as star differs from star in brightness, so priest differs from priest in his manner of life.

Many are called priests, but not all are priests in reality. The administration of the presbyterate is entrusted to many, but not all serve equally in the ministry entrusted to them.

One greedily and insatiably seeks present advantages—his own interests, not those of Jesus Christ. Another is hindered by negligence. Another is suffocated by ignorance, and yet “if anyone is ignorant, he shall be ignored” (1 Corinthians 14:38). But another carefully examines the proper place and time for the guardianship entrusted to him and responds, with a tested life, to the needs of the ministry imposed upon him.

From among these, if you know them, the more experienced and more attentive should be summoned. For if the more proven physicians are sought for bodily illnesses, how much more should subtler physicians—and, if one may say so, more spiritual physicians—be applied to the spiritual corruptions of souls?

I do not say this so that you may condemn or criticize the priests of the Lord. For “the Lord knows those who are his” (2 Timothy 2:19). But I say that if you receive a prophet in the name of a prophet, or a righteous person in the name of a righteous person, you will receive the reward of a prophet or of a righteous person (Matthew 10:41). Such priests, therefore, should be summoned.

## CHAPTER VIII. The error of priests who bind even after death. Whether their judgment does harm. These priests must be instructed. What satisfaction should be imposed upon those who confess. Despair is the gravest crime. Those at the point of death are to be absolved if they ask. If they recover, they must undergo canonical discipline

Now see what results from the ignorance of the ignorant. A less educated priest has heard your confession and sees your illness, but does not know how to weigh such matters with an even balance. He does not know that swift medicine is absolutely necessary for sudden illnesses and for those at the point of death. He responds to the sick person:

“Brother, if you survive, fast in this way, give alms in this way, pray in this way.”

He has said all these things well, but observe the impious error:

“But if you die from this illness, so that your soul may not appear unrepentant before God, I enjoin you under obedience that your soul, for a whole week, or an entire year, or for whatever period of time, undergo the punishment you have deserved in penance after your death.”

O blindness of the heart, fit to be destroyed! He had come to console the sick person; yet to one upon whom the greater and more urgent necessity of absolution rests, he adds a part of bondage by denying absolution.

O occasion of the ruin of souls! Whether this priest’s address harms the one confessing—though it is certain that it does not help him—let that be reserved for God’s judgment.

But if you should ask what answer ought to be given to this consoler, or rather desolator, I say plainly: he must be instructed, not followed. There is no disobedience where there is the humble duty of instruction.

If you wish to know what poultice should be applied to such corruptions, so that at least, through your case, priests may be instructed and this too may contribute to salvation, I add what I would answer to those at the point of death who nevertheless confess:

Nothing should be imposed upon anyone that either impossibility removes from his capacity or dwindling time prevents him from fulfilling. But if his hands possess something that may benefit the poor, or if his friends wish to give from their own resources, it is lawful for his sins to be redeemed by almsgiving. We also believe that the prayers of friends will benefit him.

But if he lacks even the smallest sum of money, or if the religious devotion of friends who might pray for him is absent, and he is able to do nothing at all except confess and repent, while the enormity of his faults also weighs him down, what am I to do with him? Am I to lead him away—or even be led into despair concerning him?

But who, O good Jesus, should despair of your mercy? I declare boldly that despair of you is a greater accumulation of sin than any offense arising from human weakness.

Why did the tears of the chief of the Apostles benefit him, unless they may benefit me also? Why is the memory of that thief in the Gospel recalled to us with such reverence? By what alms, works, or prayers did you respond, my most kind, sweet, and merciful Jesus, almost under oath:

“Truly I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise”—

unless by his faith and his very brief prayer:

“Remember me, Lord, when you come into your kingdom” (Luke 23:42–43)?

Therefore I say to all—I say finally to those who confess, and I say to those who seek counsel after confessing—that those who have confessed must not despair, and that priests must not bind anyone after death. Rather, together with their Jesus, let them say: “Release him and let him go” (John 11:44).

For it is better that such an absolution benefit, or at least not harm, than that indiscriminate binding should do harm. Nor should priests offer the pretext of a deceptive security, since it is better for them to entrust the dying person to the hand of the most merciful God than to exclude a despairing person from the kingdom of God with tales of postponement.

For how will a priest say for the deceased whom he himself bound, “Absolve, Lord, the soul of your servant,” or the other formulas of absolution?

All who ask for absolution must therefore be absolved. Nor are they to be suspended from the communion of the faithful when death is feared to be imminent, and when the bitter remembrance of sins either moves them to tears or fear of death leads them to pardon, as Scripture testifies: “And the terrified will be cleansed” (Job 41:16).

If such people should nevertheless recover, they must not neglect to undergo the prolonged discipline of the canons.

Therefore, while there is no longer time for anything else, this immediate counsel must be applied to those at the point of death.

This counsel too I give you, my dearest friend: ascend in your heart to pray in the temple of the Lord, if you cannot do so in body. Say, together with that already justified sinner, “God, be merciful to me, a sinner” (Luke 18:13), so that you may ascend righteous to God, justified by him who lives and reigns throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

# [CONCERNING CONSOLATION]

[Col. 1157]

## NOTICE CONCERNING THE TWO SERMONS THAT FOLLOW IMMEDIATELY

[Col. 1157]

These two sermons exist in an old Corbie manuscript, apparently copied a thousand years ago. The first is prefaced with this title: “Here begins a sermon of Saint John concerning the consolation of death.” The second, joined very closely to the first and without a title, has nothing else at the end except: “Here ends the sermon concerning the resurrection.”

Moreover, this other sermon now appears for the first time from the praised Corbie exemplar, enlarged by a third part that was lacking in the editions previously printed. That section contains a recapitulation of what was said in the first sermon, and it is recognized as belonging to this little work through other arguments that are not uncertain.

We believe that the John designated at the beginning of the first sermon is none other than Chrysostom. Compare his forty-first homily on 1 Corinthians 15, his first homily on 2 Corinthians, his sixty-first homily on John, and finally his seventieth homily to the people of Antioch, and so forth.

[Col. 1159]

# CONCERNING THE CONSOLATION OF THE DEAD (G,S)*

## First sermon

### CHAPTER I. Two kinds of sadness

[Col. 1159]

Give me your silence, brothers, lest a useful and timely discourse pass you by. For medicine is most needed when a serious illness arises, and soothing eye-salve must be applied most carefully when the eye has been troubled by pain.

Therefore, whoever does not have this pain should not interrupt, but rather listen, because it does not hinder a healthy person to know a medicine that may be beneficial. But whoever has the eye of the mind troubled by this event and is tormented by grief should be all the more attentive to opening his eye to receive the eye-salve of saving speech, through which he may obtain not only consolation but also a remedy.

It is certain that if a person whose eye is in pain refuses to open it for the physician pouring in the eye-salve, the eye-salve is poured outside, beyond the pupil, while the eye remains in pain. So too the mind of one who grieves, if it closes itself to the word because of excessive sadness and does not receive salutary admonition, will begin to grieve more and perhaps suffer what is contained in Scripture: “The sadness of the world produces death” (2 Corinthians 7:10).

Blessed Paul the Apostle, teacher of the faithful and salutary physician, said that there are two kinds of sadness: one good and the other bad; one useful and the other useless; one that saves and the other that destroys.

And lest what I say seem doubtful to anyone, I shall recite his own words. For he says:

“Godly sadness produces repentance unto enduring salvation”—

this is that good sadness.

He then continues:

“For the sadness of this world produces death” (ibid., 11)—

this is that bad sadness.

### CHAPTER II. The causes of mourning for the dead with regard to the dead themselves. Their vanity is demonstrated.

Let us therefore consider, brothers, this grief that is now in our hands, that is now enacted in the breast and heard in the voice, and ask whether it is useful or useless, whether it can benefit or harm. Look: here lies a lifeless body; here lies upon a bier a human being without the human being, limbs, certainly, without the spirit. He is cried out to, but does not answer; he is called, but does not hear. His face lies pale, its appearance changed, through which death itself is discerned [Note: [Col. 1159] The printed editions add, “and is shuddered at.”] Moreover, his perpetual silence is pondered; the pleasure is pondered—whether the pleasure that was, or the usefulness that was to be; the necessities are pondered; the sweetest words come to mind; long familiarity is sought. These are, without doubt, the things that move the tears, provoke the wailing, and plunge the whole mind into profound grief.

Against such powerful and mighty weapons of pain [Note: [Col. 1159] The printed editions add, “we must arm ourselves with spiritual safeguards. First of all, then, etc.”], this must first of all be set forth: everything that is born in this world must die. For this is the law of God and the unchangeable sentence that the prince of the human race received after his transgression, when God said, “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Gen. III, 19). What new thing, then, has happened if a human being, born for this purpose, has fulfilled the divine law and sentence? What new thing has occurred if, born among mortals, he has answered to his own nature, since he could not excuse himself? What is ancient is not unfamiliar; what is daily is not unheard of; what is common is not peculiar. If we know that our grandfathers and great-grandfathers departed by this road of death; if, finally, we have heard that the Patriarchs and Prophets themselves, beginning with Adam the first-formed, migrated from this world not without their passing away, let us raise our spirit from the depths of grief, because he has returned what he owed. And surely, when a debt is repaid, what grief can it have? This is truly a debt that no money can redeem; this is a debt that neither virtue, nor wisdom, nor power can excuse, and which not even kings themselves will finally be able to avoid.

I would certainly urge you to increase your grief if the matter had been such that, though it could have been redeemed or postponed by your resources, it had come about through negligence or parsimony [Col. 1160]. But since God’s decree is firm and unchangeable, we grieve in vain and ask concerning ourselves why he has died, when it is written, “The issues of death belong to the Lord God” (Ps. LXVII, 21). Therefore, if this common condition of life is received into the mind, the eye of the heart, weighed down as it is, will begin to be relieved, as though by a first application of medicine.

## CHAPTER III. Other causes concerning ourselves, no more reasonable. Why excessive grief brings about death.

“But,” you say, “I know that this event is common; I know that the one who has died has paid his debt. But I think of the pleasure, I recall the necessities, I long for the familiarity.” If you are afflicted with grief on account of these things, you are being led by error, not governed by reason. You must know that the Lord, who had given this pleasure, can give another that is greater, and can supply the necessity through another occasion [Note: [Col. 1160] Alternatively: “and he who brought this necessity upon you is able to supply it sufficiently through another occasion.”]

As for usefulness, just as you see your own, you must also consider that of the one who has died, because perhaps it was advantageous for him in this way, as it is written: “He was taken away, lest wickedness should change his understanding. For his soul was pleasing to God, and therefore he hastened to lead him out from the midst of iniquity” (Wis. IV, 11–14). But what shall I say about familiarity, which time, as it passes, makes one forget, so that it seems never to have existed [Note: [Col. 1160] Perhaps, “sometimes”]? Therefore, what time and the passing days accomplish, reason and good reflection ought to accomplish much more. And this above all must be considered: the divine judgment declared through the Apostle, “For the grief of the world produces death” (II Cor. VII, 10). If both present pleasure and usefulness, or familiarity, are things of the world and passing joys of this age, beware lest casting down the spirit and grieving the soul on account of them be truly a fatal sickness.

Repeating it again and again, I shall say: “For the grief of the world produces death.” Why does it produce death? Because excessive grief is accustomed either to lead to doubt or to dangerous blasphemy.

## CHAPTER IV. Mourning for the dead was permitted to those who lived before Christ. Why Christ wept for Lazarus.

“But,” someone will say, “you forbid mourning for the dead, although the Patriarchs were mourned, as was Moses, that servant of God, and many prophets thereafter—especially since even the most righteous Job tore his garment at the death of his sons (Job I, 20)?”

It is not I who forbid mourning for the dead, but the Apostle, the illuminator of the nations, who says: “I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, concerning those who sleep, so that you may not grieve like those who have no hope” (I Thess. IV, 12). The brightness of the Gospel cannot be obscured because those who lived before the Law, or under the shadow of the Law, mourned their dead. And rightly they mourned, because Christ had not yet come from heaven, the one who dried up that fountain of tears through his resurrection. Rightly they mourned, because the sentence of death still remained. Rightly they lamented, because the resurrection had not yet been preached. All the saints indeed hoped for the coming of the Lord; but meanwhile they mourned the dead, because they had not yet seen the one whom they hoped for.

Finally, Simeon, one of the ancient saints, who had previously been anxious about his own death, after receiving the Lord Jesus, still a child according to the flesh, into his hands, rejoiced over his departure, saying: “Now you dismiss your servant, Lord, in peace, because my eyes have seen your salvation” (Luke II, 29). O blessed Simeon! Because he had seen what he hoped for, he now counted his own death as peace and rest.

“But,” you say, “it is read in the Gospel that the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue was mourned (ibid. VIII, 52), and that Lazarus was mourned by his sisters (John XI, 31).” But they still understood things according to the ancient Law, because they had not yet seen Christ risen from the dead. The Lord himself plainly wept for Lazarus, who had already been buried (ibid., 35), not in order to provide a model for weeping over the dead, but to show through his tears that he had assumed a true body [Col. 1161]. Or certainly he wept out of human love [Note: [Col. 1161] The Corbie manuscript reads, “out of human custom.”] for the Jews, because even after such a sign had been shown they would not believe in him. For Lazarus’s death could not have been the cause of the tears of the one who had himself said that Lazarus was sleeping and had promised that he would raise him, just as he did.

## CHAPTER V. Mourning for the dead is no longer permitted. On those who will be alive and will not die on the day of judgment.

The ancients therefore had their own custom and their own frailty, preceding the coming of Christ [Note: [Col. 1161] The Corbie manuscript reads, “while Christ was still…”—perhaps, “while his coming was still pending.”]. But from the time when the Word became flesh and dwelt among us; from the time when the last Adam annulled the sentence given to the first Adam; from the time when by his death he destroyed our death, and the Lord rose from the underworld on the third day—since then death is no longer terrifying to the faithful. The setting is not feared, because the Rising One has come from on high.

The Lord himself, who cannot lie, cries out: “I am,” he says, “the resurrection and the life; whoever believes in me, even if he has died, will live; and everyone who lives and believes in me will never see death” (John XI, 25–26). The divine voice is clear, dearest brothers: whoever believes in Christ and keeps his commandments, if he has died, will live.

The blessed Apostle Paul, receiving this voice and holding fast to it with all the strength of faith, instructed us: “I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, concerning those who sleep, so that you may not be sorrowful” (I Thess. IV, 12). O marvelous declaration of the Apostle! In one statement, before presenting his teaching [Note: [Col. 1161] The printed editions read, “in one statement, so as to commend both teachings.”], he commends the resurrection. For he calls those who have died “sleeping,” so that, by saying that they sleep, he may unmistakably designate that they will rise.

“Do not,” he says, “be sorrowful concerning those who sleep, as the others are.” Let those who have no hope be sorrowful; but let us, who are children of hope, rejoice together. He himself recalls what our hope is, saying: “For if we believe that Jesus died and rose again, so also God will bring with Jesus those who have fallen asleep” (ibid., 13). For Jesus is salvation for us who live here, and life for those who depart from here.

“For me,” the Apostle says, “to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (Phil. I, 21). It is plainly gain, because death, by hastening the end, makes a profit of the anxieties and tribulations that a longer life contains.

Now the Apostle describes the order and condition of our hope: “This we say to you by the word of the Lord: we who live, who remain until his coming, shall not precede those who have fallen asleep. For the Lord himself will descend from heaven with a command, with the voice of an archangel, and with the trumpet of God; and the dead who are in Christ will rise first. Then we who live, who remain, will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet Christ in the air, and so we shall always be with the Lord” (I Thess. IV, 14–16).

This is what he says: when the Lord comes, he will find many Christians in the body who have not yet experienced death. Yet they will not be caught up to heaven before the holy dead have risen from their tombs, raised by the trumpet of God and the voice of the archangel. When they have been raised, they will be caught up together with those who are living in the clouds to meet Christ in the air, and so they will reign with him forever.

Nor can there be any doubt that bodies, although heavy, can be lifted into the air, since at the Lord’s command Peter, still bearing his bodily form, walked upon the waves of the sea (Matt. XIV, 29); and Elijah, also to confirm this hope, was carried up to heaven through this air in a fiery chariot (IV Kings II, 11).

## CHAPTER VI. What we shall be like after the resurrection. Death is more to be desired than mourned. Yet it must not be self-inflicted.

“But perhaps you ask what those who have risen from the dead will be like. Hear your Lord himself saying: ‘Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father’” (Matt. XIII, 43). Why should I speak of the splendor of the sun, when the faithful must be transformed into the glory of Christ the Lord himself, as the Apostle Paul testifies: “Our citizenship is in heaven. From there also we await the Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ, who will transform the body of our humiliation into conformity with the body of his glory” (Phil. III, 20–21).

Without doubt this mortal flesh will be transformed into conformity with Christ’s splendor; it will put on immortality [Note: [Col. 1162] The manuscript reads, “it will be clothed with immortality.”], because “what was sown in weakness will immediately rise in power” (I Cor. XV, 43). The flesh will no longer fear corruption, nor suffer hunger, thirst, illnesses, or adverse accidents. For peace is secure, and firm security is the condition of life. The glory there is truly heavenly, where joy will be granted without failure.

Bearing these things in his mind and before his eyes, the blessed Paul said: “I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ, which is much better” (Phil. I, 23) [Note: [Col. 1162] So the Corbie manuscript. The printed editions read, “which is indeed much better.”]. And teaching still more openly, he says: “While we are in the body, we are away from the Lord; for we walk by faith and not by sight. But,” he says, “we have the better desire to be away from the body and present with the Lord” [Note: [Col. 1162] The Corbie manuscript reads, “and to come to the Lord.”] (II Cor. V, 6–8).

What are we doing, people of little faith, who are anxious and faint if one of our loved ones departs to the Lord? What are we doing, when we take greater delight in pilgrimage in this world than in being brought into Christ’s presence? Truly, truly, everything we live is pilgrimage. For, like pilgrims in this world, we have uncertain dwellings; we labor and sweat; we travel difficult roads full of dangers. On every side ambushes are prepared by spiritual and bodily enemies [Note: [Col. 1162] The manuscript does not contain “by bodily enemies.”]; on every side the byways of error are laid out [Note: [Col. 1162] The manuscript reads, “the accidents of the world, prepared by error.”].

And although we are pressed by such dangers, we not only do not desire to be freed ourselves, but even mourn and lament those who have been freed as though they were lost. What has God bestowed upon us through his Only-Begotten if we still fear the event of death? What does it profit us to boast that we have been reborn from water and the Spirit, if pilgrimage from this world grieves us?

The Lord himself cries out: “If anyone serves me, let him follow me; and where I am, there my servant will be also” (John XII, 26). Suppose an earthly king were to summon someone to his palace or banquet: would he not hasten with thanksgiving? How much more must we hasten to the heavenly King, who will make those whom he receives not only his banqueters but also his fellow rulers, as it is written: “If we have died with him, we shall also live with him; if we endure, we shall also reign with him” (II Tim. II, 11–12).

I do not say this so that anyone should lay hands upon himself or kill himself against the will of God the Creator, or drive his soul from the lodging of his body. Rather, I say this so that, cheerfully and joyfully, whether he himself is called or his neighbor is called, he may go himself and rejoice with those who depart.
