For this is the sum of Christian faith: to await true life after death, to hope for return after departure. Having therefore received the Apostle’s voice, let us now confidently give thanks to God, who through Christ our Lord has given us victory over death (I Cor. XV, 57), to whom are glory and power now and forever and ever. Amen.

# Second Sermon

[Col. 1161]

## CHAPTER I. Why the resurrection is doubtful among unbelievers.

In the preceding little book we briefly touched upon the consolation of mortality [Col. 1162] [Note: [Col. 1162] So the Corbie manuscript. The printed editions read, “of the dead.”] and the hope of resurrection. Now we hasten to speak more fully and forcefully about the same matters. For what I have said is certain to the faithful, but seems fabulous to unbelievers and doubters; to them we shall present a few arguments more concisely.

Certainly, whoever you are who disbelieve, you maintain complete doubt concerning the substance of the body. Some disbelieve that flesh, once changed into dust, can rise again and live again. But concerning the soul, no human being can have any doubt, since even the philosophers themselves, although pagans, do not disagree about the immortality of the soul. For what is death except the separation of body and soul? When the soul departs—the soul that always lives and does not know how to die, because it is from the breath of God [Note: [Col. 1163] The printed editions add, “inspired by him.”]—only the body dies, because one thing in us is mortal and another immortal.

But the departing soul, which cannot be seen by bodily eyes [Note: [Col. 1163] The printed editions read, “which cannot be seen.”], is received by angels and placed either in Abraham’s bosom, if it is faithful, or under guard in the prison of hell, if it is sinful, until the appointed day arrives when it receives back its body and renders an account of its deeds before the tribunal of Christ, the true Judge.

Therefore, since all the hesitation concerns the flesh [Note: [Col. 1163] The printed editions read, “contradiction”], its weakness must be defended and its resurrection established.

## CHAPTER II. The sprouting of seeds proves that resurrection is possible. Creation also proves it.

But if some doubter and unbeliever asks me, “How will the dead rise? In what body will they come?” I shall answer him in the words of the Apostle: “Fool, what you sow is not made alive unless it first dies; and what you sow, you sow a bare grain of wheat or of some other seed” (I Cor. XV, 36–37)—dead and dry, without moisture. Yet when it has rotted, it rises more fertile, becomes clothed with husks, and is armed with ears of grain.

He, therefore, who raises up the grain of wheat for your sake [Note: [Col. 1163] The printed editions add, “will he not be able to raise you yourself for his own sake?”]; who raises the sun every day, as though from the tomb of night; who restores the moon, as though from destruction; and who recalls the departing seasons for our benefit—will he not seek us ourselves, for whose sake he restores all things, but allow us, whom he kindled with his breath and animated by his spirit, to be extinguished once and for all [Note: [Col. 1163] The printed editions read “ashes” instead of “once and for all”]? Will there then no longer be a human being who has piously recognized and worshiped him?

But again you doubt that you can be restored after death, brought back after the ashes and bones have been consumed? O human being, tell me: what were you before you were conceived in your mother’s womb? Nothing, certainly. God, therefore, who created you from nothing—will he not be able more easily to restore you from something? Believe me: he who was able to create what did not exist will more easily be able to remake what already existed [Note: [Col. 1163] A later hand in the manuscript reads, “than he.”].

He who commanded you to grow from a shapeless drop of liquid in your mother’s womb into nerves, veins, and bones will, believe me, be able to generate you again from the womb of the earth.

But you fear that perhaps your dry bones cannot be clothed again with their former flesh? Do not, do not measure the majesty of God according to your own inability. That God, creator of all things, who clothes trees with leaves and meadows with flowers, will also be able at once to clothe your bones at the springtime of the resurrection [Note: [Col. 1163] The manuscript reads, “at that certain time of spring.”]

The prophet Ezekiel had once doubted this very matter. When the Lord asked him whether the dry bones that appeared scattered throughout the field would live, he replied, “You know, Lord.” But after he saw, at God’s command and while he himself prophesied, the bones running to their places and joints; after he saw dry bones bound with sinews, woven with veins, covered with flesh, and clothed with skin, he then prophesied in the spirit. The spirit of each one entered those bodies lying there, and they rose, and immediately stood [Note: [Col. 1163] The manuscript does not contain “and immediately stood.”]. Thus confirmed concerning the resurrection, the Prophet recorded the vision so that knowledge of so great a matter might reach posterity (Ezek. XXXVII, 3–10).

Rightly, therefore, Isaiah cries out: “The dead shall rise, and those who are in the tombs shall rise, and those who are in the earth shall rejoice. For the dew that is from you is healing for them” (Isa. XXVI, 19) [Col. 1164]. For truly, just as seeds moistened by dew germinate and rise, so through the dew of the Spirit the bones of the faithful will germinate [Note: [Col. 1164] The printed editions read, “so, visited by the dew of the Holy Spirit, the bones of the faithful will germinate with their bodies into eternal glory.”]

## CHAPTER III. A great flame from a small flintstone.

But you doubt how the whole human being can be restored from small bones? Indeed, you kindle a great flame from a tiny spark of fire. Will God not be able, from the small ferment of your ashes, to restore your whole little body, which has been kneaded together [Note: [Col. 1164] The manuscript reads, “kneaded”?]?

For even if you say, “The remains of the flesh itself appear nowhere; perhaps they have been consumed by fire or devoured by beasts,” know this first: whatever is consumed is contained in the bowels of the earth, from which it can again be brought forth at God’s command. Even when fire is not visible, you take a small stone and a little iron and strike out from the stone’s hidden interior as much fire as is needed.

What you therefore accomplish by your skill and wisdom, which God himself has granted you—namely, bringing forth what does not appear [Note: [Col. 1164] The manuscript omits this and the other words that follow in brackets]—will that divine majesty not be able by its own power to bring forth what for the time being is unseen? Believe me, God can do all things.

## CHAPTER IV. Christ, the Apostles, the examples of the martyrs, and the mother of the Maccabees testify that the resurrection will truly occur. Hence fear of death is excluded. The command not to mourn.

Ask only whether he promised that he would bring about the resurrection. And when you have learned that it was promised through so many testimonies—indeed, when you have the most certain pledge of Christ the Lord himself—strengthened by faith, cease now to fear death.

For whoever still fears disbelieves; whoever disbelieves contracts an incurable sin, because by his unbelief he dares to declare God either powerless or, at any rate, a liar.

But the blessed Apostles and the holy martyrs did not show themselves thus. Because of this preaching of the resurrection, the Apostles proclaim that Christ rose and announce that the dead will be raised in him; they refused neither death nor torments nor crosses. If, therefore, every word stands on the testimony of two or three witnesses, how can the resurrection of the dead be called into doubt when it has so many such competent witnesses, who bear testimony to it with the shedding of their blood?

And what of the holy martyrs? Did they have a certain hope of resurrection, or not? If they had not, they would surely not have accepted death through so many torments and punishments as the greatest gain. They did not consider the punishments of the present, but the rewards to come. They knew what had been said: “The things that are seen are temporary, but the things that are not seen are eternal” (II Cor. IV, 18).

Listen, brothers, to an example of courage. A mother encouraged seven sons and did not mourn, but rather rejoiced. She saw her sons scraped with claws, cut to pieces with iron, and roasted in a frying pan; yet she did not shed tears or raise wails, but carefully encouraged her sons to endure. For she was not cruel, certainly, but faithful. She loved her sons, not tenderly, but bravely. She encouraged them toward the passion, which she herself also joyfully accepted [Note: [Col. 1164] The manuscript reads, “which she herself also accepted” in the subjunctive; perhaps, “which she would herself also accept.”]. For she was secure concerning the resurrection of herself and her sons (II Macc. VII).

Why should I speak of men, women, boys, and girls [Note: [Col. 1164] The manuscript reads, “Why should I speak of boys, women, and girls?”]? How they made sport of this death, how they passed with the greatest speed into the heavenly army! They could certainly have continued living for the present if they had wished, because it lay within their power either to live by denying Christ or to die by confessing him. But they chose rather to cast away temporal life and take up eternal life; to be excluded from earth and dwell in heaven.

Amid all this, brothers, what room is there for doubt? Where can fear of death still remain? If we are the children of the martyrs, if we wish to be found their companions, let us not be saddened by death or mourn our loved ones who precede us to the Lord.

For if we wish to weep, the blessed martyrs themselves will mock us and say: “O faithful ones, O you who desire the kingdom of God—you who mourn and lament your loved ones when they die gently, in beds and upon feather mattresses, with sorrow: if you saw them tortured and killed by the Gentiles for the name of the Lord, what would you do? Or has no example gone before you?

“Abraham the patriarch, offering his only son as a sacrifice, slaughtered him with the sword of obedience (Gen. XXII, 10); nor did he spare the one whom he loved with such great affection [Note: [Col. 1165] The manuscript reads, “he nearly slaughtered him with the sword, nor did he spare such affection”]. He did this so that he might be proved obedient to the Lord.

“But if you say that Abraham did this because of God’s command, you also have a command: ‘Do not be sorrowful concerning those who sleep’ (I Thess. IV, 12). If, therefore, they do not keep the lesser commands, when will they keep the greater? Or do you not know that a spirit broken in such matters is found unfit for greater things? Who, fearing a stream, ever enters the sea? In the same way, whoever impatiently mourns one who has been lost—when will he be able to reach the contest of martyrdom? For whoever is steadfast and courageous in these matters is already laying down a step toward better things.”

## CHAPTER V. David’s outstanding example concerning this matter. Why it is not permitted to wear black mourning clothes. The pagan’s response upon hearing of his son’s death. Pagans, Jews, and catechumens who die are to be mourned. What kind of grief is salutary. Recapitulation of both sermons.

Let these things suffice, brothers, for contempt of death and confirmation of future hope. It remains that I produce one example from the ancients—one that may provide complete consolation and that I want everyone to hear with ears patient of heart.

David, the great king, bore with extreme impatience the illness of his beloved son, whom he loved as his own soul. When human remedies no longer helped, he turned to the Lord. Laying aside his royal glory, he sat on the ground, lay in sackcloth, neither ate nor drank, and prayed to God continuously for seven days, in case his son might be granted to him.

The elders of his household approached him and, seeking to console him, urged him to eat bread, fearing that while he wanted his son to live he himself might die first. They could neither extract this from him nor compel him, for impatient love is accustomed to disregard dangers themselves.

The king lies in the squalor of sackcloth while his son is ill; neither words provide consolation, nor does the very necessity of food summon him. His mind is nourished by grief [Note: [Col. 1165] The printed editions read, “necessity drew him away; he suffers grief; and immediately, tears flow continuously.”]; his breast is refreshed by pain; his eyes shed tears instead of drink.

Meanwhile, what God had decreed took place: the boy died. His wife was in mourning, the entire household in lamentation, and the servants were terrified and agitated about what might happen. No one dared announce the death of the son to his master [Note: [Col. 1165] The manuscript reads, “name it to him”], fearing, of course, that he who had mourned the boy’s life with such impatience would end his own life if he heard that the boy was dead.

While the servants whispered among themselves, while in their sadness one advised or forbade another to speak, David understood. He forestalled the messengers and asked whether his son had breathed his last. They could not deny it, but indicated what had happened by their tears.

An extraordinary gathering took place [Note: [Col. 1165] The manuscript reads, “an ordinary gathering”], with great expectation and fear that the devout father might do something dangerous to himself [Note: [Col. 1165] The manuscript reads, “that the father of the son himself might do something dangerous.”].

King David immediately rose from the sackcloth, cheerful, as though he had heard that his son was safe. He went to the baths, washed his body, went to the temple, worshiped God, and feasted with his friends, having restrained his sighs, laid aside all groaning, and now displaying a joyful face.

His household marveled, and his friends were astonished at this new and sudden change of conduct [Note: [Col. 1165] The printed editions read, “conversion”]. Finally, they dared to ask what this meant: why, when his son was alive, he had grieved so deeply, but when he was dead, he did not grieve.

That man, distinguished by great courage, replied: “While my son was still alive, it was necessary for me to humble myself, fast, and mourn in the sight of the Lord; for there was hope of obtaining the gift of life [Note: [Col. 1165] The manuscript does not contain “of life.”]. But after the will of the Lord [Col. 1166] had been done, it is foolish and impious to torment the mind with useless lamentation.” Thus he said: “I shall go to him, but he will not return to me” (II Sam. XII, 16–23).

Behold an example of courage and virtue. If that David, still living under the Law—under what I shall not call permission, but rather the necessity of mourning—thus separated his mind from irrational grief [Note: [Col. 1166] The printed editions read, “overcame”], thus restrained his own sorrow and that of his household, then with what face do we, who are now under grace and under the sure hope of resurrection, for whom all grief is forbidden, mourn our dead in the manner of the Gentiles? Why do we raise mad wails, as though reveling in another kind of Bacchic frenzy? Why do we tear our tunics and bare our breasts, and sing empty words and dirges [Note: [Col. 1166] The manuscript reads, “and empty words”] around the body and the tumult [Note: [Col. 1166] “Mound” must certainly be read here; M.] of the deceased?

Finally, for what reason do we dye our garments black, unless to prove that we are truly unbelieving and wretched not only by our tears but also by our clothing? These practices are alien, brothers; they are foreign and not permitted. And even if they were permitted, they would not be fitting.

But some of the brothers and sisters, although their own faith and the Lord’s command make them strong, are weakened and broken by the opinion of parents and neighbors, lest they be judged stony and cruel if they spare their clothing [Note: [Col. 1166] The manuscript does not contain, “if they spare their clothing”] and do not rave in insane mourning. How vain and foolish it is to consider the opinions of mistaken people and not fear that one may do less than the faith one has received requires!

Why does such a person not learn endurance instead? Why does the one who doubts not learn faith from me? Even if such grief fills the breast, one ought silently to work through the mourning inwardly [Note: [Col. 1166] The printed editions read, “to direct it”; and with the word “to make public” they close the treatise], not make it public through the levity of one’s spirit.

I wish to offer one further example to correct those who think that the dead ought to be mourned. The example comes from pagan history.

There was once a certain pagan leader [Note: [Col. 1166] Horatius. See Livy, book 2. Plutarch, *Laconian Apophthegms*, reports a similar saying by a Spartan], who had an only son, dearly loved. While he was sacrificing to his idols in the Capitol according to pagan error, he was informed that this only son had died [Note: [Col. 1166] Perhaps, “had passed away.”].

He did not abandon the sacred rites he was performing; he did not weep, nor did he sigh at all. But hear what he replied: “Let him be buried. I remember that I fathered a mortal son.”

Consider the answer; consider the virtue of the pagan: he did not even order them to wait for him or to hand his son over to burial in his presence.

What shall we do, brothers, if the devil brings this man before Christ on the day of judgment as a witness against us and says:

“This was my worshiper, whom I deceived through my tricks so that he would serve blind and deaf images. I had promised him neither resurrection from the dead, nor paradise, nor the kingdoms of heaven. Yet this wise man did not grieve or groan over the death of his noble only son, nor did he abandon my rites on receiving such news.

“But your Christians, your faithful, for whom you were crucified and died precisely so that they would not fear death but would be secure concerning the resurrection, not only mourn the dead in voice and dress, but are even ashamed to proceed to church. Some of your own clergy and pastors also suspend their ministry and devote themselves to mourning, as though insulting your will.

“Why? Because you called to yourself those whom you wished to call from the darkness of the world.”

What will we be able to answer to this, brothers? Will confusion not seize us when in this respect we are found inferior to the Gentiles?

And indeed, the pagan ought to be mourned: because, not knowing God, as soon as he dies he proceeds by a straight path to punishment. The Jew ought to be mourned, because, not believing in Christ, he has assigned his soul to destruction. Our catechumens are plainly to be grieved over if, through their own unbelief or through the negligence of those close to them, they depart without saving baptism.

But the one who departs from this world sanctified by grace, marked with faith, approved by his manner of life, or secure in innocence, ought to be blessed, not mourned; desired, not [Col. 1167] lamented—desired with moderation, since we know that we ourselves will follow as the times approach.

Therefore wipe away your tears, cease your sighs, restrain your groans, O faithful one. In place of this grief, put on that salutary grief which the blessed Apostle declared to be according to God and which is accustomed to produce lasting salvation (II Cor. VII, 10): namely, repentance for the sins committed.

Search your breast, questioning your own conscience. And if you find something for which you ought to repent—and you will, since you are human—draw sighs in confession, pour out tears in prayer, be concerned about that true death, about the punishment of the soul; be concerned about sin, as David says: “For I declare my iniquity, and I shall be anxious on account of my sin” (Ps. XXXVII, 19). Then you will not be terrified by the temporal dissolution of this body, which in its proper time will be restored by God’s command to something better.

See how the divine judgment has embraced both matters, saying: “The hour is coming when those who are in the tombs will rise.” Behold security; behold contempt for death. But what follows? “Those who have done good will rise to the resurrection of life; but those who have done evil will rise to the resurrection of judgment” (John V, 28–29). Behold the difference among those who rise.

All flesh must indeed rise—human flesh, that is. But the good person will rise to life, and the wicked person will rise to punishment, as it is written: “Therefore the ungodly shall not rise in judgment, nor sinners in the assembly [Note: [Col. 1167] The manuscript reads, “counsel”] of the righteous” (Ps. I, 5).

Therefore, so that we may not rise for judgment, let us set aside the grief of death and take up that repentance and grief; let us take care for good works and a better life. Let the thought of this funeral and corpse serve to make us know that we are mortal and, through this reflection, not neglect our salvation in the time while it is possible and permitted—either by bearing fruit toward improvement or by correcting ourselves if we have gone astray in ignorance.

Let us not be suddenly overtaken by the day of death and then seek time for repentance without being able to find it; let us not seek to distribute alms and make satisfaction for our offenses when what we desire is no longer granted.

Therefore, brothers, having shown that death is common [Note: [Col. 1168] Perhaps one should add: *sorte*, or *conditione* (“by lot,” or “by condition”).], having shown the prohibition of tears, having demonstrated the fragility still found among the ancients and not Christian fortitude, having displayed the Lord’s sacrament and the Apostles’ testimony concerning the resurrection, having recalled the deeds of the Apostles and the sufferings of the martyrs, having further set forth the example of David and, moreover, the deed of a Gentile, and finally having explained both harmful and beneficial sorrow—the former harmful, the latter saving through repentance—now that all these things have been so demonstrated, what else ought we to do, brothers, except give thanks and say to God the Father, “Your will be done, as in heaven and on earth” (Matt. 6:10)? You gave life; you appointed death. You bring into this age; you lead out of this age; and when you have led out, you preserve. For nothing of yours perishes, since you have said that not even a hair of their head shall perish (Luke 21:18). “You take away their spirit, and they fail, and return to their earth; but you send forth your spirit, and they are created, and you renew the face of the earth” (Ps. 103:29–30).

These words, brothers, are worthy of the faithful; this is saving medicine. With the eye wiped by this sponge of consolation, and bathed in this collyrium of reason, it will not merely fail to experience the blindness of despair, but will not even endure the dimness of sorrow. Rather, looking upon all things clearly with the eyes of the heart, it will say, in the words of that most patient Job: “The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away; as it has pleased the Lord, so it has happened. Blessed be the name of the Lord” (Job 1:21), forever and ever. Amen.

# [On the Rectitude of Catholic Conduct]

[Col. 1167]

## Editorial Notice on the Treatise *On the Rectitude of Catholic Conduct*

[Note: [Col. 1167] At this point the Benedictine Fathers read: “Having already printed the preceding page, a Remigian manuscript came into our hands, approximately eight hundred years old, containing the first of the preceding sermons under this title: ‘Here begins the little book on the consolation of the death of Saint John, Bishop of Constantinople.’” M.]

[Col. 1167] This treatise appears in Book Two of the *Life of Saint Eligius, Bishop of Noyon*, chapter 15, having evidently been collected and written down through the work of Audoin, the author of that *Life*. In this sermon he endeavored to gather together the pious bishop’s daily and principal admonitions to his people. “For every day,” Audoin says, “he tirelessly exhorted the people entrusted to him with saving admonitions . . . . . When crowds had gathered from every side at the church, he would briefly comprise in his sermon many important matters, rich in spiritual edification; raising his voice with prophetic confidence, he would address them with admonitions of this kind: ‘I ask you, dearest brothers, and with great humility I admonish you,’ and so forth.”

Audoin represents the sermon there in full; when it has ended, he adds: “It is enough to have related thus far, in summary, the familiar admonitions of so great a man. Although he did not go through them in the order in which they are arranged, as though within the space of a single day, he nevertheless always communicated such instructions to the people at different times.”

Our old Germanensis manuscript agrees with this. It presents this same treatise, written separately from Eligius’s *Life*, under the following title: “Here begin the sermons of blessed Eligius, which he delivered to the people with the utmost zeal from the abundant treasury of his heart.”

Nevertheless, nearly everything Eligius presents there was drawn from the Caesarian Sermons, which, through the efforts of Caesarius—as we have observed elsewhere—were regularly read in churches throughout Gaul and Spain. See the Appendix to the preceding volume, and compare Sermons 29, 78, 110, 116, 141, 210, 249, 258, 265, 266, 273, 275, 277, 278, 279, 289, and so forth. In them you will find both Eligius’s own words and certain passages explained more clearly than they are here.

For example, from Sermon 129, no. 2, and Sermon 130, nos. 1 and 2, you will understand the reading found here in section 5, “Let no one make *vetulas*,” where Jacobus Sirmondus thought that *vitulas* (“calves”) should be written, just as in the Council of Auxerre. Likewise, you will learn from Sermon 288, no. 5, and Sermon 289, no. 4, of the same Appendix how to understand this statement of Eligius in section 9: “Whoever presumes to have a concubine before legitimate marriage sins more seriously than one who commits adultery.” He is not considered to sin more seriously for any other reason than that his deed is an example of greater harm. Caesarius gives the reason for this interpretation: “Because the adulterer still wishes to commit so grave an evil secretly . . . . . but the man who wishes to have a concubine publicly . . . . . thinks that he may freely commit an execrable act while the whole people sees it.” Thus he gives others an opportunity to go astray, so that they believe the act is permitted with impunity. For sins, as Augustine says in the *Enchiridion*, chapter 80, “although great and dreadful, once they have become habitual are believed to be either small or nothing.”

[Col. 1169]

# Treatise on the Rectitude of Catholic Conduct (C, G, S)*

[Col. 1169] The bishop’s obligation to exhort the people. Frequently to recall the day of judgment and the vows of Baptism. The duty of a Christian. Pious practices prescribed. Christians deterred from Gentile rites. God alone to be worshiped. Pious admonitions. Against drunkenness. Against superstitions. Conduct on Sundays and in churches. What judges should do. Frequently to arm oneself with the sign of the cross. The devil’s harassment of those who live piously. Why God permits it. Giving alms to the poor. Giving tithes to God through the poor or the churches. Observing God’s commandments. Correcting one’s conduct promptly. Loving enemies. Caring for the soul. How one should fast. Nourishing the soul with divine readings. Against sexual immorality. Concubinage. Capital crimes. Pious instructions for right living. Immediately to pursue piety. To disagree with the devil. Not to swear. When to pray or converse. Avoiding scandals. Being merciful. Commendation of charity. Exhortation to repentance and vigilance. That each person has an angel of God. That no one should ever despair. Caution in speech. Maintaining sobriety. That nothing is evil in itself. Inviting the poor to one’s table. Consideration of death. The happiness of eternal life. Meditation on the final judgment. How Christ will reproach the rejected for his benefits. The punishment of the rejected. The blessed lot of the just. Not to be ashamed of public repentance. Not to despair of forgiveness. Not to presume excessively. The end of the world is near. Despising earthly things. Patiently bearing adversity for the love of God. Always reverencing God as present. Maintaining charity. Persevering in a good resolution. Repentance not to be postponed.

## 1

[Note: [Col. 1169] See Sermon 249, no. 2, in the Appendix to volume 5.]

I ask you, dearest brothers, and with great humility I admonish you, to listen attentively to what I wish to suggest to you for your salvation. For the omnipotent Lord knows that I offer these words to you with ready love; if I do not do so, I shall undoubtedly be held liable for a debt. Therefore receive what I say willingly—not on account of my insignificance, but for the sake of your salvation—provided only that what you receive with your ears you complete in your deeds, so that I may deserve to rejoice with you in the heavenly kingdom both over my service and over your progress.

If anyone is perhaps displeased that I strive to preach to you so frequently, I ask him not to take offense at me, but rather to consider my danger and hear the Lord’s terrible warning to the priest: “If you do not announce his iniquity to the wicked man, he will die in his iniquity, but I will require his blood from your hand. If, however, you announce it to the wicked man, and he is not turned from his iniquity and from his wicked way, he will indeed die in his iniquity, but you will have saved your soul” (Ezek. 33:8–9). And also: “Cry out; do not cease. Raise your voice like a trumpet and announce their crimes to my people” (Isa. 58:1).

Consider, therefore, brothers, that I must without ceasing stir your hearts toward the dreadful judgment of God and toward the desire for the heavenly reward, so that I may deserve to rejoice with you forever in the company of the angels.

## 2

[Note: [Col. 1169] From the Benedictine Rule, chapter 4.]

Therefore I ask you always to fear the day of judgment and to keep the day of death under suspicion, daily before your eyes. Consider what sort of people you will be when presented before the sight of the angels, and what recompense you will receive according to your merits: whether on that day you will be able to bring back undefiled what you promised in Baptism.

Remember that at that time you made a covenant with God, and in Baptism you promised to renounce the devil and all his works. Whoever was able to do so answered these things personally and on his own behalf; whoever was unable to do so had a sponsor promise them to God in his place—namely, the person who received him from the sacred font.

Consider, therefore, what sort of covenant you made with God, and ask yourselves whether, after that promise, you followed the works of the wicked devil whom you renounced. For you renounced the devil and all his pomps and works—that is, deceits, lots, auguries, thefts, frauds, fornications, drunkenness, and lies. These are truly his works and pomps.

In opposition to this, you promised to believe in God the almighty Father, and in Jesus Christ, his only Son, our Lord, born of the Virgin Mary, who suffered under Pontius Pilate, rose from the dead on the third day, and ascended into heaven.

Then you promised to believe in the Holy Spirit, the holy catholic Church, the communion of saints, the forgiveness of sins, the resurrection of the flesh, and eternal life. Without doubt, this pledge and confession of yours, which you then promised, is always held before God.

Therefore, dearest ones, I admonish you always to keep this confession or promise in your memory, so that the fact that you are called Christians may not be for your judgment, but rather for your remedy.

## 3

[Note: [Col. 1170] From Sermon 266, nos. 2 and 1, in volume 5 of the Appendix. Again from no. 2.]

For this reason you became Christians: that you might always perform the works of a Christian—that is, that you might love chastity, flee sexual immorality and drunkenness, maintain humility, and detest pride. For the Lord Jesus Christ both displayed humility by his examples and taught it in words, saying: “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart, and you will find rest for your souls” (Matt. 11:29).

You must also reject envy, have charity toward one another, always think about the future age and eternal blessedness, and labor more for the soul than for the body. For the flesh will remain in this world only a short time; but the soul, if it has acted well, will reign in heaven without end, whereas if it has acted wickedly, it will burn without mercy in hell.

Whoever thinks only about this present life is like the animals and beasts. Therefore, dearest ones, it is not enough for you to have received the Christian name if you do not perform Christian works. The name “Christian” benefits the person who always keeps Christ’s commandments in mind and fulfills them in deed: who does not steal, does not give false testimony, neither lies nor commits perjury, does not commit adultery, harms or hates no one, but loves everyone as himself; who does not repay his enemies evil for evil, but rather prays for them; who does not stir up quarrels, but recalls those who are at odds to harmony.

The Lord Jesus Christ himself graciously delivered these commandments in the Gospel, saying: “You shall not commit murder; you shall not commit adultery; you shall not steal; you shall not give false testimony; you shall not commit perjury; you shall not commit fraud. Honor your father and your mother. And you shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Matt. 19:18–19). And: “Whatever you wish people to do to you, you also do to them; for this is the Law and the Prophets” (Matt. 7:12).

He also gave commandments greater than these, but very demanding and fruitful, saying: “Love your enemies, and do good to those who hate you; pray for those who persecute and slander you. Behold a demanding commandment, and it seems harsh to human beings; but it has a great reward. Hear what it is: ‘So that you may be,’ he says, ‘sons of your Father who is in heaven’” (Matt. 5:44–45).

O what grace! Though we are unworthy to be servants by ourselves, through the love of our enemies we become sons of God.

Therefore, brothers, love your friends in God, and love your enemies for God’s sake. For whoever loves his neighbor, as the Apostle says, has fulfilled the law (Rom. 13:8). Whoever wishes to be a true Christian must necessarily observe these commandments; for if he does not observe them, he deceives himself.

That person is a good Christian who believes in no amulets or inventions of the devil, but places all his hope in Christ alone; who joyfully receives strangers as Christ himself, because he says: “I was a guest, and you received me”; and: “As long as you did this for one of the least of mine, you did it for me” (Matt. 25:35, 40).

I say, that person is a good Christian who washes the feet of guests and loves them as his dearest relatives; who gives alms to the poor according to what he possesses; who comes frequently to church and presents an offering to be offered to God on the altar; who does not taste the fruits of his fields until he has first offered to God; who does not possess fraudulent weights or double measures; who does not lend his money at interest; who lives chastely himself and teaches his children or neighbors to live chastely and in the fear of God; and who, whenever the holy solemnities approach, preserves chastity for several days even with his own wife, so that he may approach the Lord’s altar with a secure conscience.

Finally, he is one who knows the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer by heart, and teaches the same to his children and household. Whoever is such a person is undoubtedly a true Christian; and Christ also dwells in him, for Christ said: “I and the Father will come to him, and we will make our dwelling with him” (John 14:23). Likewise, through the prophet he says: “I will dwell in them, and I will walk among them, and I will be their God” (Lev. 26:12).

## 4

[Note: [Col. 1171] From the same sermon, no. 3; from Sermon 265, no. 2; and from Sermon 78, no. 6, of the same Appendix.]

Behold, brothers, you have heard what good Christians are like. Therefore, insofar as you can, labor with God’s help so that the Christian name may not be false in you. But in order that you may be true Christians, always keep Christ’s commandments in your minds and fulfill them in your actions.

Redeem your souls from punishment while you have the means of obtaining remedies. Give alms according to your ability; maintain peace and charity; recall those who are at odds to harmony; flee lies; dread perjury; do not give false testimony; do not steal. Offer oblations and tithes to the Church; provide lamps for holy places according to what you possess. Keep the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer in your memory, and teach them to your children.

Teach and discipline the children whom you have received from Baptism, so that they may always live in the fear of God. Know that you are their sponsors before God. Also gather frequently at church; humbly seek the protection of the saints; honor Sunday, out of reverence for Christ’s resurrection, without any servile work; and celebrate the solemnities of the saints with pious affection.

Love your neighbors as yourselves. Whatever you wish others to do to you, do the same to them; whatever you do not wish done to you, do to no one. Above all, have charity, because “charity covers a multitude of sins” (1 Pet. 4:8).

Be hospitable and humble, casting all your anxiety upon God, because he cares for you (1 Pet. 5:7). Visit the sick; seek out prisoners; receive strangers; feed the hungry; clothe the naked; flee soothsayers and magicians.

Let there be equality in your weights and measures; let there be a just balance, a just bushel, and an equal sextarius. Do not demand more than you gave, and do not exact interest from anyone for money lent at interest.

If you observe these things, you will come confidently on the day of judgment before the tribunal of the eternal Judge and say: “Give, Lord, because we gave; have mercy, because we showed mercy. We have fulfilled what you commanded; repay what you promised.”

[Col. 1172]

## 5

[Note: [Col. 1172] See Sermon 278, no. 2; 277, no. 4; 267, nos. 5 and 3; 279, no. 5; 263, no. 4; 278, no. 1; 277, no. 4; and 278, no. 5, in the Appendix to volume 5.]

Above all, however, I announce and solemnly charge you to observe none of the sacrilegious customs of the pagans: neither *caragios* [Note: [Col. 1172] Erasmus, the Lyons edition, Venice, and Louvain read *carcarios*; and shortly afterward, *carcarii*. M.], nor diviners, nor sorcerers, nor incantation-practitioners. Do not presume to consult or question them for any reason or illness, because whoever does this evil loses the sacrament of Baptism.

Likewise, do not observe auguries or sneezes, and when you are traveling do not pay attention to any little birds singing. Rather, whether you undertake a journey or any other work, sign yourselves in the name of Christ, and say the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer with faith and devotion; then the enemy will be able to harm you in nothing.

No Christian should observe on which day he leaves his house or on which day he returns, because God made all the days. No one should look to a particular day or to the moon when beginning a task.

No one on the Kalends of January should perform abominable and ridiculous rites involving old women, little deer, or *joctici* [Note: [Col. 1172] The Corbeiensis manuscript reads *jotticos*. The Germanensis reads *jotricos*.], nor should he set tables for the night, or engage in excessive gift-giving or drinking.

No Christian should believe in fires [*pyrae*] [Note: [Col. 1172] The manuscripts read *purae*, which is the same thing, from *pûr*, “fire”;] or sit in the singing, because these are works of the devil.

No one on the feast of Saint John or on the solemnities of the saints should perform solstitial rites, dances [*balationes*] [Note: [Col. 1172] The Benedictine Fathers recommend this reading; see volume 5 of the Appendix, Sermon 265, no. 4, and Sermon 266, no. 3. In B., *vallationes*. M.], or dances [*saltationes*] [Note: [Col. 1172] The *Spicilegium* adds *caraulas*, or *coraulas.], or sing diabolical songs.

No one should presume to believe in or invoke the names of demons, Neptune, Orcus, Diana, Hercules, Minerva, Geniscus [Note: [Col. 1172] Erasmus and Louvain read *Genistus*.], or other foolish figures of this kind.

No one should observe Thursday as a day of leisure apart from holy festivals, whether in May or at any other time; nor should he observe the days of *tiniarum* [Note: [Col. 1172] Elsewhere, *turmarum*.] or walls, or any day whatsoever except Sunday.

No Christian should go to shrines, stones, springs, trees, or enclosures [Note: [Col. 1172] So the Germanensis manuscript. The Corbeiensis reads *cettos*. The printed editions read *ocellos*.], or set up lights at crossroads, or presume to fulfill vows there.

No one should presume to hang amulets around the neck of a human being or any animal, even if they are made by clerics, and even if it is said that the object is holy and contains divine readings. For there is not Christ’s remedy in them, but the devil’s poison.

No one should presume to perform lustrations, enchant herbs, or make cattle pass through a hollow tree or through a hole in the earth, because by these practices he appears to consecrate them to the devil.

No woman should presume to hang amber [*succinos*] around her neck, nor, in weaving, dyeing, or any other work, mention Minerva or other ill-omened figures. Rather, in every work she should desire Christ’s grace to be present and trust wholeheartedly in the power of his name.

No one should presume to shout when the moon is eclipsed, because it is eclipsed at fixed times by God’s command. No one should fear beginning any work at the new moon, because God made the moon for marking the seasons (Gen. 1:14) and moderating the darkness of the nights—not to hinder anyone’s work or make a person insane, as fools think when they suppose that those possessed by demons suffer from the moon.

No one should call the sun or moon “lords,” or swear by them, because they are God’s creatures and serve human needs at God’s command.

No one should set before himself fate, fortune, or *genesis* [Note: [Col. 1172] The printed editions read *Genistum*.], which is commonly called “birth-sign,” so as to say, “As his birth-sign has brought him forth, so will he be.” For God wills all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth (1 Tim. 2:4), and he disposes all things in wisdom, as he ordained before the foundation of the world.

Moreover, whenever any illness occurs, do not seek enchanters, diviners, sorcerers, or *caragii* [Note: [Col. 1173] The Germanensis manuscript reads *luinos*.], and do not practice diabolical amulets at springs, trees, or crossroads. Rather, let the sick person trust in God’s mercy alone, receive the Eucharist of Christ’s body and blood with faith and devotion, and faithfully ask the Church for blessed oil with which to anoint his body in Christ’s name. Then, according to the Apostle, “the prayer of faith will save the sick person, and the Lord will raise him up” (James 5:15), and he will receive health not only of body but also of soul. In him will be fulfilled what the Lord promised in the Gospel, saying: “All things whatever you ask for in prayer, believing, you will receive” (Matt. 21:22).

Above all, wherever you are—whether at home, on a journey, or at a feast—do not utter foul or lustful words from your mouth. For, as the Lord declares in the Gospel, “People will render an account on the day of judgment for every idle word they have spoken” (Matt. 12:36).

Also forbid diabolical games, or *vacillationes* [Note: [Col. 1173] The manuscripts read *allationes*. Perhaps *balationes* should be read, as above in the preceding column.], or the songs of the Gentiles. No Christian should practice these things, because through them he becomes a pagan. It is not right that diabolical songs should proceed from a Christian mouth, from which Christ’s sacraments are administered and which ought always to praise God.

Therefore, brothers, reject all the inventions of the enemy with your whole heart, and flee the sacrileges mentioned above with utter horror. Show veneration to no creature except God and his saints. Cut down the springs and trees which they call *sacrivos* [“sacred”]; forbid the making of representations of animals [Note: [Col. 1173] So the Germanensis manuscript. The Corbeiensis reads “representations of feet.” The printed editions read “plants or hoofs of feet, which,” etc.], which people place at crossroads [Note: [Col. 1173] The Germanensis manuscript reads *luinos*.], and burn them with fire wherever you find them.

Do not believe that you can be saved by any other means than by invoking the Lord and by the cross of Christ. For what sort of practice is it that, if those trees where wretched people fulfill their vows fall, they do not carry their wood home for the fire? See how great is human folly: they honor a tree, an insensible and dead thing, while they despise the commandments of almighty God.

## 6

Therefore let no one believe that heaven, earth, or any creature whatsoever, apart from God, is to be worshiped, because he alone created and ordered all things.

Heaven is indeed lofty, the earth immense, the sea boundless, and the stars beautiful; but the one who created these things must necessarily be more beautiful and more immense. For if the things that are seen are so incomprehensible—namely, the varied fruits of the earth, the beauty of flowers, the diversity of fruits, the kinds of animals, some upon the earth, others in the waters, and others in the air; the intelligence of bees; the blowing of the winds; the dews of the clouds; the crashes of thunder; the changes of the seasons; and the varying return of days and nights—all of which the human mind cannot in any way grasp by estimation—if, then, the things we see are such, and we cannot comprehend them at all, what must we judge those heavenly things to be which we do not yet see? Or what must the craftsman of all these things be like, at whose will all things are created?

Therefore, brothers, fear him above all things; worship him among all things; love him beyond all things; hold fast to his mercy; and never despair of his kindness.

## 7

[Note: [Col. 1173] From Sermon 266, no. 3; Sermon 278, no. 5; and Sermon 265, no. 3, in the Appendix to volume 5.]

Imitate those whom you see to be good. Correct and rebuke those whom you see to be bad, so that you may receive a double reward.

Whoever is known to have lived free from the evils mentioned above until now should rejoice, give thanks to God, and henceforth remain vigilant, hastening to persevere in good works. But whoever has practiced evil works until now should correct himself quickly and repent with his whole heart before he departs from this light. For if he dies without repentance, he will not go to redemption, but will be plunged into the fiery Gehenna, from which he will never emerge, forever and ever.

Therefore I address everyone; I speak to men and women [Col. 1174]: let each person correct himself, amend his vices while he can, and expiate by repentance the evil works he has committed.

Let no one get drunk, and let no one at a feast compel another to drink more than is appropriate, because the Apostle severely rebukes those devoted to much wine, saying: “Nor will drunkards possess the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 6:10).

Let no one, even for the slightest reason, follow the devil’s inventions. As was said, let no one observe, when leaving or entering a house, what encounters him, whether some voice of an objector is heard, what kind of bird’s song is chattering, or even what he sees someone carrying. For whoever observes these things is recognized as pagan in part.

Whoever despises them should rejoice that the prophet cries out for him: “Blessed is the man whose hope is the Lord, who has not turned toward vanities and false insanities” (Ps. 39:5). The Apostle also admonishes us: “Whatever you do in word or deed, do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ” (Col. 3:17).

All such observances must therefore be abandoned completely. Astrologers must be despised, auguries dreaded, and dreams disregarded, since Scripture testifies that they are vain. Hence Moses also commands: “You shall not practice augury; you shall not observe dreams; you shall not turn to magicians” (Lev. 19:26, 31).

You must therefore observe these things with your whole mind. If you know that anyone secretly practices amulets of any kind, it is best neither to take food with him nor to have any association with him (1 Cor. 5:11).

Despising all these things, therefore, turn yourselves to God’s help, and never despair of his mercy.

Gather at church every Sunday, and there do not conduct business, quarrels, or idle conversations. Rather, listen silently to the divine readings, and pray for the peace of the Church and for your sins. Whoever is not afraid to chatter in churches will have to render an account both for himself and for others, since he neither hears the word of God himself nor permits others to hear it.

Concerning such people the Lord says in the Gospel: “Woe to you, hypocrites, who shut the kingdom of heaven before people; you yourselves do not enter, nor do you permit those entering to enter” (Matt. 23:13).

You judges who preside, judge with complete justice. Do nothing unjustly in judgment; do not accept gifts against the innocent; do not regard a person’s status; and do not seize the property of others with predatory force, because you do not know what may happen concerning your own things, even overnight.

Do not oppress the poor or the stranger in judgment in any way, fearing what the Truth says: “In the judgment with which you judge, you will be judged; and in the measure with which you measure, it will be measured back to you” (Matt. 7:2).

Always beware lest the prophet say of you: “Woe to you who are powerful in this world, who justify the wicked for gifts and take justice away from the just. Woe to you who call good evil and evil good” (Isa. 5:22–23, 20). “Your lips speak lies, and your hands are full of iniquity; truth has become forgotten among you, and justice has fled from you” (Isa. 59:3, 15, 14).

## 8

Considering these things together, brothers, both those who preside and those over whom they preside, strengthen yourselves in the fear of God. Retain what has been said; do what has been commanded. Always have Christ in your mind and his sign on your forehead.

Know that you have many adversaries who hasten to impede your course. Therefore, in every place and at every hour, arm yourselves with the sign of the cross; fortify yourselves with the banner of the cross. For this alone they fear; this alone they dread. It has also been given to you as a shield, by which you can extinguish the flaming arrows of the evil one [Note: [Col. 1174] From Sermon 265, no. 1, in the Appendix to volume 5.]

Indeed, the sign of Christ and the cross of Christ are great things; but they benefit only those who keep Christ’s commandments. Therefore, in order that they may benefit you, strive with all your strength to fulfill his commandments.

Whether you sit, walk, eat [Note: [Col. 1174] It would be better to read *sedeatis* . . . *ambuletis* . . . *manducetis*, as is said shortly afterward, *ascendatis*, *surgatis*. M.], ascend to bed, or rise from your couch, may the sign of Christ continually guard your forehead, so that it may protect you always—keeping you vigilant through remembrance of God and guarding you in sleep.

Whenever you are awakened at night and sleep has fled from your eyes, immediately make the sign of the cross. Let your mind also be occupied with prayers, and let God’s commandments be turned over in your heart, lest the enemy suddenly creep into a sluggish breast, or the greedy adversary spread into your soul through foolish negligence.

When he suggests an indecent thought to your mind, set before yourselves the future judgment of God, the punishment of hell, the pains of Gehenna, and the darkness of Tartarus, which the wicked will suffer. If you do this, the shameful thought will immediately vanish, and the power of Christ will not abandon you, because what the prophet sings is true: “Mercy will surround the one who hopes in the Lord” (Ps. 31:10).

## 9

[Note: [Col. 1175] From Sermon 278, nos. 2, 3, and 4.]

But when, with the Lord’s help, you have fulfilled all these things, know that the devil will take it badly when he sees you withdrawing from his fellowship. For this reason he may perhaps inflict upon you certain evils or illnesses.

Do not despair because of this. God permits it to happen in order to test you, so that it may become known whether you hold fast to his mercy with your whole heart and whether you truly believe in him.

You, however, must endure everything patiently and bless God in all things, so that what is written may be fulfilled in you: “Blessed is the man who endures temptation, because when he has been tested, he will receive the crown of life” (James 1:12).

Let this also console you, which the Apostle says: “When we are afflicted, we are disciplined by the Lord, so that we may not be condemned with this world” (1 Cor. 11:32). Likewise: “God scourges every son whom he receives” (Heb. 12:6). And again: “The Lord reproves and disciplines those whom he loves” (Prov. 3:11).

If once or twice you have endured courageously and faithfully, for the love of God, the evils he inflicts, God will afterward deign to drive him so far from harassing you that he will never again be able to harm you.

Therefore, if you are true and not false Christians, flee and despise all the devil’s stratagems, and hold fast to God with your whole mind, so that whatever adversity the enemy brings upon you, you may endure patiently and bravely.

Even if he has predicted something through sorcerers or diviners, and it then comes to pass, do not be astonished. Spirits flying through the air can easily foresee certain future events. Concerning this matter divine Scripture testifies, saying: “Even if they tell you the truth, do not believe them; for the Lord your God is testing you, to determine whether or not you fear him” (Deut. 13:3).

Know also that the enemy can harm neither you nor anything belonging to you except insofar as God permits it. God permits this because human sins demand it. He permits it for two reasons: either to test whether you are good, or to chastise you if you are sinners.

But whoever patiently endures God’s dispensation, so that when he has lost something he says, “The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away; as it has pleased the Lord, so it has happened. Blessed be the name of the Lord” (Job 1:21), will, for this patience, receive either a crown if he is just or forgiveness if he is a sinner.

But if he murmurs or despairs, he will suffer the loss both of his possessions and of his soul.

Believe me, brothers: if you always remain with your whole heart in the fear of God and keep his commandments, refusing to observe any inventions derived from pagan custom, the enemy will be able to harm you in nothing, and everything belonging to you will prosper.

For no auguries or any other fabrications can harm an upright Christian. Where the sign of the cross has gone before with faith and the fear of God, the enemy can harm nothing there.

They can harm the lukewarm and negligent, however, because, abandoning God’s commandments and practicing evil works through negligence of their way of life, they themselves willingly hand themselves over to the power of demons. If they persevered in Christ’s service and relied solely upon his help, they would suffer absolutely no evil.

10. [Note: [Col. 1175] From Sermon 78, §§ 6, 5, 2, in the Appendix to Volume 5.] Knowing these things, therefore, cling to God’s mercy with all your strength, always perform good works, and distribute from your possessions to the poor. Let the one who has more give more; but let the one who has less give cheerfully and gladly from that very little. Let each person give whatever he is able to give, for there is surely something from which he will gain joy. Certainly, the one who gives little will receive much, as the Lord promises to the Apostles, saying, “He will receive a hundredfold and will possess eternal life” (Matt. 19:29). He gives, I say, a single coin and acquires the heavenly kingdom; he gives a small sum of money and purchases eternal life.

Hold fast, then, to almsgiving, because, as it is written, “Almsgiving delivers from death, and whoever practices it will not go into darkness” (Tob. 4:11). Let each person extend as much as he is able. Whoever has gold, let him give gold; whoever has silver, let him give silver; but whoever has no money, let him give the poor a piece of bread with a good disposition; and if he does not have a whole one, let him break off part of what he has and give a portion to the needy. Let him know that, however little he gives with a good disposition, it will be acceptable to God. For the Lord is pleased and nourished not by the abundance of the gift but by the generosity and devotion of the giver.

And so that no poor person may excuse himself from almsgiving, the Lord himself promised that he would repay a reward even for a cup of cold water (Matt. 10:42). For the one to whom God has given greater resources will certainly face the greater danger at the judgment. God could indeed have made everyone rich; but he wished there to be poor people in this world so that the rich would have a means by which to redeem their sins.

Redeem yourselves, therefore, beloved, while you have the price within your power. Give alms from honest and just labor, not from another person’s plunder. Listen now to the poor begging at your doors, so that they too may plead for you on the day of judgment. Attend to the prophet crying out: “Whoever turns his ear away from the needy will himself call upon the Lord, and he will not answer him” (Prov. 21:13).

Give, therefore, from what God has given you, because he himself receives what you give to the poor. You give to them, certainly, but you send it ahead for yourselves into the future—not something with which to fill your stomach, but something with which to extinguish flames; for just as water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sin (Ecclus. 3:33). Hence the Lord says through the prophet: “Each will give the ransom for his soul, and there will be neither sickness nor disaster among them.” Give, therefore, while it is permitted, the ransom for your souls. Redeem yourselves while you live, because after death no one can redeem you.

11. [Note: [Col. 1176] See Sermon 277, §§ 1, 3, in the Appendix to Volume 5.] Let each person give God, through the poor or through churches, a tenth of whatever craft or skill provides his livelihood. Let him consider that everything by which he lives belongs to God—whether earth, rivers, seeds, or all that is beneath the heavens and above the heavens—and that, if God himself had not given it, he would possess nothing. For our God, who condescends to give everything, condescends to ask a tenth of what is his from us—not for his own benefit at all, but for ours.

Thus he himself promised through the prophet, saying: “Bring the whole tithe into my storehouses, and test me in this, says the Lord: whether I will not open for you the floodgates of heaven and pour out for you the fruits of the earth in abundance” (Mal. 3:10). Freely return, therefore, a tenth of everything you possess on earth, which you know is pleasing to God: of grain, wine, legumes, hay, gold, silver, cattle, and also wool from the shearing of sheep.

Do not defraud the tenth from your entire property, lest nine parts be taken away from you and only the tenth remain. “Turn back to this,” says the Lord, “that I may open for you the floodgates of heaven and pour out my blessing upon you” (ibid. 7). If, therefore, you give willingly, the Lord will always give you more; but if you do not give, then, however many poor people may die of hunger in the places where you live, you will be guilty of that many murders. Moreover, the Lord will send pestilence and famine upon you, and you will lose everything you possess—and even your souls.

So that these things may not come upon you, hasten to give with a good disposition what will enable you to redeem your souls. Do not choose to whom you will show mercy, lest you pass by someone who deserves to receive it, for you do not know to whom Christ may deign to come. Know that what you give on earth to a poor person or a stranger, you give to the one seated in heaven, who said, “Whoever receives you receives me” (Matt. 10:40), and, “As long as you did it for one of the least of mine, you did it for me” (ibid. 25:40).

12. Amid all these works of goodness that the Lord has commanded to be practiced, he asks nothing else of you except the salvation of your souls—and that you always fear him and keep his commandments. If you do this, he will give you, as he promised through Moses, rains at the proper time, and your land will produce its growth. There will be an abundance of fruits, orchards, vineyards, and crops, and you will abound in every good thing. He will give you peace all around; you will be without fear, and he himself will dwell among you.

But, on the other hand, if you do not keep his commandments, the plagues foretold by that same Moses will come upon you: pestilence, famine, and the sword. The sky will be like iron and the earth like bronze; the earth will not produce its growth, all the crops will be destroyed, and all your labor will be consumed in vain. Moreover, your enemies will rise against you, the sword will devour you, and your land will become deserted and desolate (Lev. 26:3–45).

Then you will cry out in distress, and the Lord will not answer you, as he threatens through the prophet, saying: “I spoke, and they did not listen; and they will cry out, and I will not answer” (Zech. 7:13). The prophet also cries out: “The hand of the Lord is not shortened, so that he cannot save or hear; but your iniquities have made a division between you and your God, and your sins turn his face away, so that he does not hear” (Isa. 59:1–2).

So that these things may not happen to you, keep what has been commanded. Fulfill God’s commandments, so that you may live and fare well, and so that no calamity may befall you. For he himself consoles us through the prophet, saying: “If they repent of their iniquities, I too will repent of the evil that I said I would do to them; and I will not do it, says the Lord” (Jer. 18:8).

Keep these things, therefore, brothers, always in mind; tell these words to your children and neighbors. Recall them while you sit in your houses and while you walk, and do not forget them when things go well for you. Always fear God and serve him alone, lest his anger be aroused against you. Know that he keeps his covenant and mercy with those who love him and keep his commandments, and that he will remove every sickness from them.

Consider that, as the Apostle John foretells, “It is the last hour” (1 John 2:18). Therefore, do not love the world any longer (ibid. 15, etc.), because it passes away quickly, and all its desire passes away with it. But do the will of the Lord, so that you may remain forever, have confidence when he appears, and not be put to shame at his coming.

Let no one deceive you. Whoever does righteousness is righteous; and whoever commits sin is of the devil. Indeed, every sin—whether theft, adultery, or lying—is not committed without the devil’s activity. Consider, I beg you, how destructive it is to practice the devil’s works and to become his accomplice—not in rest, but in the punishment of Gehenna.

Therefore, whenever you sin, do not wait with deadly complacency for the wounds themselves to fester, nor add other wounds to them; rather, hasten immediately to apply medicine to yourselves through a confession of repentance. In great works as well, strive continually to make progress: let the one who has been proud until now now become humble; let the adulterer become chaste; let the one who used to steal or take away other people’s property now begin to distribute his own to churches or to the poor; let the envious become kind; let the drunkard become sober; let the angry become patient. Let the one who has wronged another quickly ask forgiveness; and let the one who has been wronged forgive without delay, so that he too may be forgiven. Or why should he not forgive his brother a little, so that God may deign to forgive him everything?

13. [Note: [Col. 1177] Approximately Sermon 308, § 3; Sermon 210, § 5; Sermon 273, § 1.] For this too is a kind of almsgiving: that a person forgive with all his heart the one by whom he has been injured. But if someone is so poor that he has nothing with which to perform bodily almsgiving—since it cannot happen that he suffers no injury from anyone—if he forgives with all his heart everyone who sins against him, holds hatred toward no one in his heart, and loves everyone as himself, this will undoubtedly be counted for him as the greatest almsgiving.

To enable us to forgive more freely those who sin against us, the Lord exhorts us in the Gospel, saying: “If you forgive people their sins, your heavenly Father will also forgive you your sins; but if you do not forgive, neither will your Father forgive you” (Matt. 6:14–15).

Let no one deceive himself; let no one mislead himself. For whoever harbors hatred in this world even against one person will lose everything he offers to God in good works, because the Apostle does not lie when he cries out terrifyingly: “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer, and he is a liar and walks in darkness” (1 John 3:15).

Here “brother” must be understood as every human being, because we are all brothers in Christ. Therefore, brothers, I exhort you to love your enemies because I know of no stronger medicine for healing the wounds of sins. Although it is a great labor to love enemies in this world, the reward in the future will be great. Whoever loves his enemies here will be God’s friend—not only his friend, but also his son, as he himself, as we have already mentioned above, promises, saying: “Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who slander you, so that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 5:44).

Whoever loves will possess rest; for whoever does not love, as the Apostle says, “remains in death” (1 John 3:14).

14. Since these things are so, beloved, have true love for one another, not false love. Always direct your actions toward God, and labor for whatever you can do out of love for God and for eternal life. Run while you have the light, before darkness overtakes you (John 12:35). When you labor for the flesh, labor also for the soul. If you run for the sake of the flesh, which after a short time worms will devour in the grave, run all the more for the soul, so that, adorned with good works, it may rejoice forever in heaven.

[Note: [Col. 1178] From Sermon 141, §§ 4, 5, 2.] Above all, whenever you fast, give to the poor what you ought to have eaten; and, as the Lord teaches in the Gospel, “When you fast, do not become like the hypocrites, sorrowful, so that you may be seen by people,” but be seen by the one who alone sees in secret. And again he warns: “Take care not to practice your righteousness before people, in order to be seen by them” (Matt. 6:16, 18).

Always think more about the food of the heart than the food of the body; and while you live in the world, purchase eternal life for yourselves by living well. Listen willingly to the divine readings in church, and continually recall at home what you hear, so that just as the body is nourished by food, so the soul may be refreshed by God’s word. For it is certain that what the flesh is like when it receives food only after many days, such is the soul that is rarely nourished by God’s word.

Therefore, beloved, whether you walk, sit, work, or do anything at all, always bring to mind what you have heard from the divine reading, and continually turn over the evangelical commandments in your heart.

15. Above all, flee sexual excess and avoid evil desire, fearing what the Lord says in the Gospel: “Everyone who looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. 5:28).

Love your lawful wives without any pretense, as the Apostle commanded, saying: “Husbands, love your wives, just as Christ also loved the Church.” And according to the same Apostle: “Wives should be subject to their husbands and fear them as God” [Note: [Col. 1178] Er., Lugd., Ven., Lov.: “Wives should be subject to their husbands, as is fitting in the Lord.” M.] (Eph. 5:25, 22).

Let no husband presume to dismiss his lawful wife for any reason, because, according to the Lord’s judgment, “Whoever dismisses his wife, except on account of fornication, makes her commit adultery” [Col. 1179] (Matt. 5:32).

We prohibit the keeping of concubines, whether before marriage or after marriage, because it is entirely illicit. For whoever intends to marry a lawful wife ought to preserve his virginity until marriage, and after marriage know no other woman besides his one lawful spouse, as the Apostle Paul commanded. Let him keep faith with her, just as he wishes her to keep faith with him; and let him not sin with another woman, just as he does not wish his own wife to sin with another man, fearing what the same Apostle proclaims so solemnly: “God will judge fornicators and adulterers” (Heb. 13:4).

[Note: [Col. 1179] See Sermon 289, §§ 3, 4; Sermon 288, § 5, in the Appendix to Volume 5.] For whatever is not permitted to women by the law of marriage is also entirely forbidden to men. Whoever presumes to keep a concubine before lawful marriage sins worse than one who commits adultery, and for this reason deserves to be separated from the fellowship of Christians. If he does not repent, eternal fire will torment him without remedy.

16. Therefore, Christian, flee fornication; now be ashamed to sin under the eyes of God and the angels. Detest with every effort the capital crimes, which are sacrilege, murder, adultery, false testimony, theft, robbery, pride, envy, greed, anger, and drunkenness. These are the crimes that plunge people into eternal punishment. Whoever recognizes that he has even one of them within himself, if he does not repent, will burn in the fire of Gehenna without any remedy.

Therefore, Christian soul, keep watch, pray, and always beware of the crimes mentioned above; and whatever good you are able to do, do it for eternal life. Open your hand to the poor, so that Christ may open his door to you and you may enter into the joys of paradise. Do not hand yourself over to destruction, because Christ poured out his blood for you. He considered you sufficiently dear, since he purchased you at so great a price.

Let fear of Gehenna terrify you, so that you may abstain from wicked works. Expect death to be present at every hour, and continually fear God’s future judgments over you, so that what is written may apply to you: “Blessed is the person who is always fearful” (Prov. 28:14).

Correct what you have done badly while you can, while you have permission to repent. Do not despair of forgiveness if you turn toward better things, because despair is worse than every sin.

[Note: [Col. 1179] Likewise Sermon 258, § 2.] Therefore, never despair of God’s mercy—not after a hundred sins, nor after a thousand crimes—for there is no guilt so great that repentance cannot obtain forgiveness for it.

However much someone provokes you, however much he insults you, however much injury he does to you, remain silent and be patient; do not return the insult. By remaining silent, you will overcome the injury more effectively. When you are cursed, bless; and you will have great grace if you do not injure the one by whom you have been injured.

Despise no one—not a servant, not a needy person—for perhaps he is better regarded by God than you are; and because, according to the Apostle, we are all one in Christ Jesus (Gal. 3:28); and because God is not a respecter of persons (Acts 10:34). Rather, as it is written, “Each person will receive from the Lord whatever good he has done, whether slave or free” (Eph. 6:8).

Do not slander your brother, do not bring an accusation against your neighbor, and do not oppress him by force. Rather, as it is said through Moses: “If your brother, compelled by poverty, sells himself to you, you shall not oppress him in the manner of slaves through your power, but deal with him in the fear of God. Remember that you are a servant” (Lev. 25:39, 43, 41).

Do not hate your brother in your heart; rather, rebuke him openly, so that you may not bear sin because of him (ibid. 19:17). Hence the Lord also says in the Gospel: “If your brother sins against you, rebuke him between you and him alone” (Matt. 18:15). And again: “If he sins seven times in a day, and turns back seven times, forgive him” (Luke 17:4). And again: “If you offer your gift at the altar, and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar, and go first to be reconciled to your brother; then come and offer your gift” (Matt. 5:23–24).

Let these commandments, Christian, call you back to harmony; let these sweet medicines of Christ heal the wounds of hatred. If you despise them, you turn back upon yourself the terrible sentence that says: “Everyone who is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment; and whoever says to his brother, ‘Raca,’ or ‘Fool,’ will be liable to the fire of Gehenna” (ibid. 22).

Behold, beloved, you have heard what you must fear and what you must observe. Therefore have charity, hold fast to patience, flee discord, and put a bridle on your tongue, lest it drag your soul to Gehenna. For according to Scripture, “Death and life are in the power of the tongue” (Prov. 18:21), and “The talkative person will not be established on earth” (Ps. 139:12).

17. Weighing these things with careful consideration, beloved brothers, bring your words and conduct into harmony. Always pursue righteousness; love Christ’s commandments. Let the impious abandon his way, and the unjust man his thoughts; and let him return to the Lord, as the prophet cries out, and he will have mercy on him, because he is gracious in forgiving (Isa. 55:7).

For he himself exhorts us, saying: “Turn back to me, and I will heal your wounds” [Note: [Col. 1180] Manuscripts: “your apostasies.”] (Hos. 14:3, 5). And again: “Seek good and not evil, so that you may live; and the Lord of hosts will be with you.” And again: “Hate evil and love good, so that the Lord may have mercy on you” (Amos 5:14–15).

Behold, the Lord himself cries this out through the prophet; and if you disdain to listen to me, at least listen to him. He also consoles sinners in the Gospel, saying: “I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance” (Luke 5:32). Again he exhorts us, saying: “Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you” (Matt. 6:33). And again: “Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you” (ibid. 7:7).

Now, because of his ineffable compassion, the Lord not only exhorts us but even begs us to turn back to him.

[Note: [Col. 1180] From Sermon 29, § 3, in the Appendix to Volume 5.] Let us listen to him while he begs, lest, if we do not act, he fail to hear us when he judges. Let us also listen to Scripture saying: “Son, have compassion on your soul, pleasing God” (Ecclus. 30:24).

What does human weakness answer to this? God begs you to have mercy on yourself, and you refuse. How will he hear you supplicating him on the day of necessity, when you do not listen to him begging you for your own sake?

If you neglect these things now, brothers, what will you do on the day of judgment, or to whose help will you flee? If, I say, you now neglect such exhortations from God, then you will not escape the torments of hell. Neither gold nor silver will be able to free you, nor the riches that you now hide in corners and through which, having become arrogant, you have forgotten your salvation.

Hence the Lord says through the prophet: “I will visit evil upon you, bring the pride of the impious to rest, and humble the arrogance of the mighty” (Isa. 13:11). And again he exhorts us, saying: “Return, transgressors, to your heart” (ibid. 46:8): cease acting perversely, learn to do good, assist the oppressed, defend the poor, and do not slander the widow, the stranger, or the orphan (ibid. 1:16–17).

18. Keep these things, therefore, brothers, in your minds, and hasten to guard them with the greatest care. Fight so that, separated from the devil, you may be joined to God, who redeemed you. Let the nations be astonished at your way of life. And if they slander you, or even mock you for pursuing Christian practices, do not be disturbed by this; for they will give an account of it.

Place all your hope, therefore, in Christ’s mercy. Guard your souls not only from immoral acts but also from filthy thoughts, because the Lord God, the just judge, judges thoughts as well.

I also warn you, brothers, to lay aside pride completely, through which the devil fell from heaven. For, as the Apostle testifies, “God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble” (James 4:6). Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke 14:11). And again: “Unless you turn and become like little children, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 18:3).

Abandon entirely the habit of swearing, because in this respect you greatly violate God’s commandments, since the Lord forbids it in the Gospel: “I say to you, do not swear at all—neither by the earth, nor by your head, nor by anything else. Let your speech be, ‘Yes, yes; No, no.’”

When people injure you, bring forward the commandments of God, which say: “I say to you, do not resist evil; but if anyone strikes you on the right cheek, offer him the other also”; and, “Whoever wishes to take your tunic, let him have your cloak as well”; and again, “Give to the one who asks you, and do not demand back what is yours from the one who takes it” (ibid. 5:34–37, 39–40, 42).
