You must certainly hold to the manner of prayer that the Lord commanded, saying: “When you pray, do not pray with many words, but in the secrecy of your heart; and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you. For your Father knows what you need before you ask him” (ibid. 6:5–8).

Recall these words, therefore, beloved; continually remember these commandments. Wherever you are, introduce the remembrance of Christ into your conversation, because he says: “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there I am in the midst of them” (ibid. 18:20).

Also flee occasions of stumbling, because the Lord severely marks the one who provokes conflicts, saying: “Woe to that person through whom the stumbling block comes” (ibid. 7).

In showing compassion to your neighbor, hold to the saying that is found in the Gospel: “Whoever has two tunics, let him give to the one who has none; and whoever has food, let him do likewise.” And also: “Give, and it will be given to you” (Luke 3:11; 6:38).

Always remember the Lord’s words, which say: “If you remain in me and my words remain in you, whatever you ask will be done for you” (John 15:7). Listen also to the Apostle crying out: “The time is short. It remains that those who have wives should be as though they had none; those who weep as though they were not weeping; those who rejoice as though they were not rejoicing; and those who use this world as though they were not using it. For the form of this world is passing away” (1 Cor. 7:29–31).

So that we may desire heavenly things more than earthly things, let us hear the Lord saying: “What does it profit a person if he gains the whole world but suffers the loss of his soul?” (Matt. 16:26).

To teach us to love charity, the evangelist John exhorts us, saying: “If we love one another, God remains in us, and his charity is perfected in us.” And again: “God is charity, and whoever remains in charity remains in God, and God in him” (1 John 4:12, 16).

Paul likewise sets forth the excellence of charity, saying: “If I distribute all my possessions as food for the poor, and if I hand over my body so that I may burn, but do not have charity, it profits me nothing” (1 Cor. 13:3). Hence again he exhorts us, saying: “Let all your things be done in charity” (ibid. 16:14). And again: “Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ” (Gal. 6:2).

The same Apostle, gently restraining the wicked and directing them toward perfection, says: “Let the one who used to steal steal no longer” (Eph. 4:28). And this: “Flee fornication. Every sin that a person commits is outside the body; but the one who commits fornication sins against his own body.” And again: “Neither the greedy nor fornicators, adulterers, drunkards, thieves, revilers, or extortioners will possess the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 6:18, 8–10).

The same Apostle restrains greed, saying: “Greed is the root of all evils” (1 Tim. 6:10). Therefore, brothers, cast away greed, pursue charity, lay aside impiety, support one another in humility, and take every precaution against what the Apostle, writing to the Romans, adds: “The wrath of God will be revealed from heaven against all impiety and injustice of human beings” (Rom. 1:18).

Also beware of what the Voice of Truth threatens in the Gospel: “Those who practice iniquity will be thrown into the furnace of fire; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matt. 13:50). Consider, therefore, how fierce and terrifying that fire is; and let the one who now cannot bear to put even a single finger into fire fear being tormented there with his whole body forever.

19. I therefore beg you: if you wish to be freed from that fire or from that punishment, cease henceforth from sinning. Attend to the Lord crying out through the prophet: “Return, you who depart from your iniquities, and I will heal you” (Ezek. 18:32). And again: “I do not desire the death of the impious, but that he should turn back and live” (ibid. 33:11). Through Isaiah also he cries out, saying: “When you have turned back and groaned, you will be saved” (Isa. 45:22). Through Joel likewise he admonishes us, saying: “Turn back to me with all your heart, with fasting and weeping and mourning” (Joel 2:12).

Behold how many testimonies from the divine oracles have been brought forward for your conversion. Watch carefully, therefore, because the nearer the end of the world the devil sees, the more cruelly he rages against Christians, so that, knowing that he will soon be condemned, he may multiply companions for himself in punishment, with whom he will certainly be tormented without end.

Be more attentive in guarding yourselves, therefore, and continually live in the fear of God, knowing that each one of you has an angel of God who continually observes what he does. If he acts well, he produces joy for the holy angel who is attached to him; but if he practices evil works, he drives the holy angel away from himself and joins himself to a wicked demon.

Therefore, beloved, while I say these things, return inwardly to yourselves and examine your consciences. Consider whether you possess minds worthy of the fellowship of angels. And if you see yourselves to be good and worthy of God, never presume upon your merits with a proud mind; rather, from now on, beware with humility.

But if you see yourselves subject to sins, do not despair in any way. Make only this agreement with God in your heart: that you will sin no more. Hope confidently for forgiveness, because the Lord continually opens the bosom of his compassion and seeks, through repentance, to receive everyone to himself.

For even if someone has been an adulterer, prostitute, thief, drunkard, liar, or even a murderer of children, let him henceforth take care as a penitent, and God will forgive him. Take as examples the tax collector from the Gospel, the thief, the prostitute, and also Paul, who says of himself: “Formerly I was a blasphemer, a persecutor, and an insolent man; but I obtained the mercy of God because I acted ignorantly in unbelief” (1 Tim. 1:13).

You too, therefore, if perhaps you committed such things in ignorance, reform yourselves, I beg you, while it is permitted, through repentance. Confess to the Lord with all your inmost heart, for he is good. Let it grieve you that you have not done what is good. And let the one who repents repent in such a way that he no longer commits what must be lamented.

And you who are poorer in this world, do not be saddened on that account, because if you act well, you will be richer in heaven.

20. Finally, beware lest anyone utter shameful speech from his mouth. And, according to the Apostle, “Do not be led astray by various fables and teachings” (Heb. 13:9). Rather, correct the disorderly, console the fainthearted, and be patient toward everyone (1 Thess. 5:14). Let no evil speech proceed from your mouth (Eph. 4:29), fearing what is written: “Bad conversations corrupt good morals” (1 Cor. 15:33).

Also abhor gluttony and drunkenness, because the Lord himself rebukes this, saying: “Beware lest your hearts be weighed down by gluttony and drunkenness” (Luke 21:34). And the Apostle forbids it, saying: “Do not become drunk with wine, in which there is debauchery” (Eph. 5:18).

Without doubt, whoever eats or drinks more than is appropriate both incurs sin and cannot preserve his health [Note: [Col. 1182] Manuscripts: “satiety.”], because when the stomach or veins have been filled with excessive fullness, lust must immediately be generated in the limbs.

Hence it is also written elsewhere: “Wine drunk in excess is bitterness of soul, a ruin that multiplies offense for the foolish, diminishes strength, and causes wounds” (Ecclus. 31:39–40).

I say these things not to assert that God’s creature is evil or to judge it worthy of condemnation, but to make you more cautious and more sober. Indeed, I also warn you not to call any creature of God evil, because God created everything very good (Gen. 1:31). For whatever seems evil or harmful to us is evil to us because of our fault, not by its nature.

Therefore, brothers, detesting only the devil, who became evil through pride, glorify the Lord, the creator of so many good things. Always beware of the broad road that leads to destruction; seize the narrow one through which eternal spaciousness is found.

Invite the poor and strangers to your banquet, and attend to the Lord commanding this matter: “When you make a lunch or dinner, do not invite the rich who may dine with you; rather, invite the poor, the weak, the blind, and the lame, and you will be blessed, because they have nothing with which to repay you; for you will be repaid in the resurrection of the righteous” (Luke 14:12–14).

[Note: [Col. 1183] See Sermon 116, § 4, in the Appendix to Volume 5.] For it is not just that, in a Christian people who were redeemed at one price and serve one Lord, some should walk about drunk with their bellies distended by lavish feasts, while others waste away in danger from hunger.

It is altogether a sin that our surplus should be devoured by moths while the poor are not considered worthy to receive even the most ancient garments. Why do you not consider that you came into this world on equal terms, that you are servants of one Lord, that you will depart from the world by a similar exit, and that, if you act well, you will come to one blessedness?

Why should the poor person not receive food with you, when he will receive fellowship with the angels together with you? Why should he not receive even an old tunic, when together with you he will receive the robe of immortality?

Considering these things, brothers, care for the poor in such a way that you may receive an exceedingly abundant repayment for them in heaven.

Always flee lying, because it is no small crime, Scripture saying: “The mouth that lies kills the soul” (Wis. 1:11). And: “A false witness will not go unpunished” (Prov. 19:5). And David says to the Lord: “You will destroy all who speak lies” (Ps. 5:7). And the Apostle says: “Putting away lying, speak the truth, each one with his neighbor” (Eph. 4:25).

### 21. [Note: [Col. 1183] What follows formed a treatise *On the Vanity of the World*.]

Therefore, while you are placed in this life, live in such a way that, when you have departed from here and your flesh has begun to be devoured by worms in the grave, your soul, adorned with good works, may rejoice in heaven with all the saints. Let the destruction of sinners also restrain you from evil works. Consider the misfortunes of those whom you have already sent ahead. Consider the tombs of the rich, or of those who were with you a short time ago: what they were and what they are, and what their riches or worldly desire profited them. Behold, nothing remains of them except ashes. If they could speak, they would doubtless say this to you:

“Why, unhappy people, do you run about so much for the desire of the world? Why do you fill yourselves with vices and crimes? Consider our bones, so that at least in this way your desire—or your misery—may fill you with horror. What you are, we were; what we are, you will be.”

Weigh all these things, brothers, with careful reflection; and, considering them, be afraid. Always set the day of death before your eyes, and hasten as much as you can toward amendment. Do not disregard the fact that the merciful Lord sustains you while you are sinners, for the longer he waits for you to amend, the more severely he will avenge your neglect.

If perhaps you think that the end of the world will come late, let each person at least consider his own end. [Note: [Col. 1183] From this point the passage was transferred into Bernard’s *Book of Meditations*, chapter 2.] Behold, while a person willingly and most happily lingers in the world and plans many things to be done over a long period [Note: [Col. 1183] Another reading: “over long periods.”], he is suddenly snatched into death and unexpectedly taken from the body. But blessed is the person who has always kept that hour before his eyes and hastened to be found prepared at the hour of death, so that he may escape the terror of so great a fear.

If you wish to know, dearest ones, it is with great fear and great pains that the soul is separated from the body. For angels come to take it up, so that they may lead it before the tribunal of the dreadful Judge. Then, remembering its evil deeds, which it performed day and night, it trembles and groans, and seeks to flee from them and ask for a delay, saying, “Give me at least the space of one hour.”

Then, as though speaking together, all its deeds say:

“You performed us; we are your works. We will not abandon you, but will always be with you, and with you we will proceed to judgment.”

This is what the soul of the sinner does. It is separated from the body with dreadful fear and proceeds weighed down by its sins and immense confusion. But when the soul of the just person is separated from the body, it does not fear or tremble; rather, it departs with joy and proceeds with exultation, while holy angels lead it to God.

Fear that hour now, brothers, so that you will not fear it then. Take precautions against it now, so that then you may be secure. Remember continually that you walk amid the devil’s snares; therefore always be ready, so that when the Lord’s command is sent, you may be able to pass free from every stain of sin into rest.

Do not suppose that you will remain long in this world. For surely it will happen that, after the Lord’s command has been sent, you will not be granted even the space of one hour—or even a moment—to remain in this life. Beware, therefore, lest your departure bring sadness to the holy angels and joy to your enemies.

Know, moreover, that when the soul is torn away from the body, it is immediately cast either into paradise for its good merits or, certainly, into hell for its sins. [Note: *Continuo*—“immediately”—is absent from the Corbie manuscript and from the *Book on the Vanity of the World*.]

Therefore choose now what you wish, and arrange it here, during your life: either to rejoice forever with the saints or to be tormented without end with the ungodly. Thus, at least, let punishments frighten you if rewards do not attract you; and if you cannot despise the present world, at least possess it with justice.

Let the person who went astray in youth come to his senses at least in old age, and let him now cleanse through repentance the evils he committed by sinning. Behold, the world is gradually failing, and everything that appears passes swiftly like mist or like an evening shadow. Behold, what was once foretold is now plainly seen in the present time: all good things are being withdrawn, and evils are increasing daily.

Do not, therefore, brothers, continue to love the world, which you see passing so swiftly. Do not now fasten the anchor of your heart in love of it, when you see it declining in this way toward its end—especially since the Apostle cries out that friendship with this world is hostility toward God. [Note: The words “which you see passing so swiftly” through “fasten the anchor of your heart” are added from the *Book on the Vanity of the World*.]

### 22.

Therefore love eternal life with all your strength, I beseech you—a life which you will never bring to an end throughout the ages. [Note: So too in Bernard’s *Meditations*, chapter 17, and sermon 110, no. 4, in volume 5 of the Appendix.]

Hasten there, where you will live forever and where you will never again fear dying. For if you love this wretched and fleeting life in which you live with so much labor, and in which you scarcely satisfy the body’s necessities by running, striving, sweating, and sighing, how much more ought you to love eternal life, where you will never endure any labor, where there is always perfect security, secure happiness, happy freedom, free blessedness; where that saying of the Lord in the Gospel will be fulfilled: “Human beings will be like angels” (Matthew 22:30)—like them, certainly, not in substance but in blessedness. And also this: “Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (the same, 13:43).

What do you think the splendor of souls will be then, when the light of bodies possesses the brightness of the sun? There will then be no sadness, no labor, no pain, no fear, no death; but perpetual health will always endure. No evil will arise there, no misery of the flesh, no sickness, no necessity of any kind. There will be no hunger, no thirst, no cold, no heat, no weariness from fasting, and no temptation of the enemy; no desire to sin, no possibility of wrongdoing. Everything will be exultation, everything joy; and human beings, joined to the angels, will flourish like springtime, without any weakness of the flesh.

There, therefore, will be certain joy, secure rest, true peace, infinite delight—there, where, if there is any possibility of gaining a place, there will be no possibility of losing it throughout the ages. [Col. 1185] In that blessedness, whatever is gained once is held forever. [Note: Another reading has *qui*—“who”—instead of *quod*—“whatever.”]

Nothing is more magnificent than that place, nothing more glorious, nothing brighter, nothing more beautiful, nothing truer, nothing more generous, nothing more sincere than that goodness, nothing richer than that abundance. There is always peace and the highest solemnity; there is true and certain happiness.

There the fiercest enemy, who continually desires to slaughter souls, will no longer be feared; nor will the devil’s fiery arrows or any temptations of the enemy be feared. The savagery of barbarians will not inspire terror, nor will any adversity thereafter be feared. Iron will not be feared there, nor fire, nor the altogether savage face of any torturer.

No one in that glorious place needs clothing, because there is neither cold nor heat there, nor any irregularity of the air. No one there hungers, no one is sad, no one is a stranger; rather, all who have been deemed worthy to reach that place will live securely as in their homeland.

The flesh will no longer oppose the spirit, nor will any danger be feared. Instead, Christ will bestow upon them unspeakable and eternal rewards with the angels; and they will receive what, as the Apostle says, “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart, what God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Corinthians 2:9).

Behold the kind of blessedness he will lose who refuses to amend himself now, while it is permitted. Therefore, brothers, with the Lord’s help, let us disdain any longer to serve sin, since so great a blessedness is prepared for us in heaven.

### 23.

Therefore, while there is time, let us hasten to make God favorable toward us; let us despise earthly things so that we may attain heavenly things. Let us consider ourselves pilgrims in this world, so that we may hasten more freely toward heaven. For everything seen here passes swiftly and soon goes by like a shadow.

Let us consider what we shall be on the day of judgment, when we are to be brought before the sight of God and the angels and our deeds are to be placed before our eyes. What will that confusion be like for the person who must blush for his sins in the sight of God and of all human beings—the person who here does not even wish to look upon a single person who sins against him? Or what terror will there be then in seeing God angry, whom, even when reconciled, the whole universe cannot comprehend?

Let us always fear that day, which now we are wholly unable to foresee. Let us continually dread that day, and at least in this way withdraw our actions from evil. Let us consider what terror there will be on that day, when the Lord comes from heaven to judge the world. What fear there will be in seeing God, at whose coming all the elements will be shaken, heaven and earth will tremble, and the powers of heaven will be disturbed!

Then, when the angels’ trumpets sound beforehand, all the nations that are beneath heaven and every human being—both male and female, each in the sex in which he or she was born in the world—the good and the wicked, the holy and sinners, and everyone who from the beginning of the world has been born and died, whether devoured by beasts, consumed by fire, or swallowed by waters—all will rise together in a moment of time and in the twinkling of an eye (1 Corinthians 15:52), undoubtedly in the very bodies and in the very flesh that they had here; namely, as a perfect man and according to the measure of the fullness of Christ’s age (Ephesians 4:13), in which the Lord himself also rose from the dead.

And all will come before Christ’s judgment, and both the elect and the rejected will see him with their own eyes, just as the Lord himself also says in the Gospel:

“Then they will see the Son of Man coming in the clouds of heaven with great power and majesty, surrounded by ranks of angels. And all the nations will be gathered before him, and all the tribes of the earth will mourn over themselves. He will separate them from one another as a shepherd separates sheep from goats, and he will place the righteous at his right hand and the ungodly at his left.

“Then he will say to those who will be at his right hand: ‘Come, blessed of my Father; possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world. For I was hungry, and you gave me food; I was thirsty, and you gave me drink; I was a stranger, and you welcomed me; naked, and you clothed me; sick and in prison, and you visited me. Whatever you did for one of the least of mine, you did for me’” (Matthew 24:29; 25:32–36, 40).

Then, while all are looking on, he will display the bruises and the marks of the nails in that very body which was wounded for our sins. And so, addressing the sinners, he will say: [Note: From sermon 249, nos. 4–5, in volume 5 of the Appendix.]

“I formed you, human being, from the clay of the earth with my own hands, and I placed you amid the delights of paradise, which you did not deserve. But you, scorning me and my commands, preferred to follow the deceiver; and therefore, condemned by a just punishment, you have been assigned to the torments of hell.

“Afterward I took pity on you. I assumed flesh and dwelt on earth among sinners. For you I endured insults and blows. To rescue you, I accepted slaps and spittle; to restore to you the sweetness of paradise, I drank vinegar with gall. For you I was crowned with thorns, fastened to the cross, and wounded with a lance. For you I died and was placed in the tomb; I descended to the underworld.

“To lead you back to paradise, I entered the prison of Tartarus; so that you might reign in heaven, I penetrated the depths of hell. Recognize, therefore, what I, human wickedness, endured for you. Behold the bruises I received for you; behold the holes of the nails by which I hung fastened to the cross.

“I took upon myself your pains so that I might heal you; I took upon myself punishment so that I might give you glory; I took upon myself death so that you might live without end. I was placed in the tomb and lay hidden so that you might reign in heaven. I endured all these things for you.

“What greater things than these ought I to have done for you, and did not do? Tell me now, or show me, what you have suffered for my sake, or what good you have done for yourselves. When I was invisible, I willingly became incarnate for you; when I was incapable of suffering, I deigned to suffer for you; when I was rich, I became poor for you.

“But you, always rejecting my humility and my commandments, followed the deceiver rather than me. Behold, now my justice cannot judge otherwise than that you receive what your deeds deserve. Therefore hold what you yourselves chose. You despised the light—possess the darkness. You loved death—go into destruction. You followed the devil—go with him into eternal fire.” [Note: The *Book on the Vanity of the World* adds: “your master.”]

What, do you think, will the grief be then, what mourning, what sadness, what anguish, when this sentence has been pronounced against the ungodly? For then there will be a harsh separation from the sweet fellowship of the saints; and, handed over to the power of demons, they will go in their own bodies with the devil into eternal punishment and will remain forever in mourning and groaning.

Driven far away as exiles from the blessed homeland of paradise, they will be tormented in Gehenna, never to see the light, never to obtain relief, never to end their punishments, never to receive rest. They will be tormented in hell for thousands upon thousands of years and will never throughout the ages be freed.

There, the one who tortures is never at any time wearied, and the one who is tortured never dies. For there fire consumes in such a way that it always preserves; torments are inflicted in such a way that they are always renewed. Each person will suffer there the punishment of Gehenna according to the character of his guilt.

Nothing will be heard there except weeping, lamentation, and the gnashing of teeth. There will be no other consolation except the flame and terrors of punishment. Miserable sinners will burn forever in eternal fire, throughout the ages of ages.

But the righteous will go into eternal life, undoubtedly in the very flesh that they had here. They will be joined to the holy angels, assigned to everlasting joys in the kingdom of God, never again to die, never to see corruption, but always filled with the joy and sweetness of Christ. They will shine like the sun in the glory and splendor that God has prepared for those who love him.

And the more one person has obeyed God in this life than another, the greater reward he will receive there; and the more someone has loved God here, the more closely he will see him then. [Note: Here the treatise *On the Vanity of the World* concluded with ten additional verses.]

### 24. [Col. 1187]

Behold, dearest ones, I have foretold these things to you plainly, so that you may understand what is destined for each person. No one will now be able to excuse himself on the ground of ignorance, since death and life, the punishments of the ungodly and the glory of the righteous, have been foretold to you.

Now it rests in your own choice to select what you will hold. For whatever each person desires and obtains here, that is what he will possess. Therefore desire eternal life with all your strength, and do not delay your amendment any longer. To gain the heavenly kingdoms, willingly abandon what must be lost at the end of this light.

Let anyone who is held bound by the chain of sin now rise, I ask, and, awakened from the sleep of his death, awake. Let him return to confession and do penance. Let him not be ashamed to repent publicly for the impurities he has committed, because it is truly far better to repent here for a short time than to endure the punishments of hell for thousands upon thousands of years.

If he repents with his whole heart, the Redeemer who raised Lazarus, already stinking after four days, will quickly come to his aid (John 11:43). That bosom of mercy is always ready, and he mercifully waits to receive the penitent.

For, as we find written, one must never despair of God’s mercy in forgiving even very great crimes, since he himself cries out daily through the prophet:

“On whatever day the sinner turns from his impurity, all his iniquities will be forgotten before me” (Ezekiel 18:21).

And again, through another prophet, he says:

“I am the Lord your God, who blots out your iniquities” (Isaiah 43:25).

And this saying from the Gospel:

“There will be joy in heaven over one sinner who repents, more than over ninety-nine righteous persons who have no need of repentance” (Luke 15:7).

And also:

“I do not desire the death of the sinner, but rather that he turn and live” (Ezekiel 33:11).

Consider, dearest brothers, how abundant is the goodness of our God and how unspeakable his mercy. He is despised every day, and every day, in his most kind compassion, he invites us to repentance.

His loving generosity gives us confidence, so that we neither despair of Christ’s mercy nor presume that forgiveness has been granted to us without the fruit of repentance. For the Lord is as indulgent and merciful in the tenderness of a father as he is severe and to be feared in the majesty of a judge.

He can indeed grant pardon to the guilty; he can turn aside his own sentence; he can bestow grace upon the penitent. [Note: The Corbie manuscript has “he can bestow the grace of repentance”; *Spicilegium* has “he can freely grant time for repentance.”] Yet he cannot judge except with complete justice, since with God there is no alteration or shadow of change (James 1:17).

For he judges with perfect equity and repays each person equally according to his deeds—good things to the good and evil things to the evil. Therefore, dearest ones, remember what you have done; and if you recognize that you have sinned, flee without any delay to the remedies of repentance.

Hear the prophet’s admonition:

“Do not delay turning to the Lord, and do not postpone it from day to day” (Sirach 5:8),

because you do not know what will happen tomorrow.

Always remember that you live in the presence of almighty God, who observes not only the deeds but also the thoughts of all human beings, as the Apostle says:

“No creature is invisible in his sight, but all things are naked and open to his eyes” (Hebrews 4:13).

### 25.

Thinking continually about these things, guard yourselves with the greatest vigilance, and always prepare yourselves for the coming of the last day with good works.

Behold, as we hold with complete certainty, the end of the world is at hand; the end of the age is already approaching. And what must be mourned is that so many evils are committed daily and so many tribulations are increasing that, through these very things, the world itself seems in some way to proclaim its end.

Behold, nearly everything that the Prophets foretold and that the Apostles predicted has already been fulfilled. Only the day of judgment and the dreadful coming of Antichrist still remain. Behold: war upon war, tribulation upon tribulation, famine upon famine, pestilence upon pestilence, and nation rises against nation. Everything that was foretold long ago we now see fulfilled.

Why, then, are we made of stone and possess an iron breast, so that amid so many evils we give no thought at all to the remedy of our souls? For a long time now the divine voice has threatened, but human obstinacy is in no way changed. Heavenly vengeance was once announced, yet no satisfaction is offered by human beings. God’s anger draws near, yet repentance is practiced lukewarmly. The Prophets testify that punishment will come, yet rarely do human beings implore God’s help.

Therefore, beloved ones, I urge you: now, while the world is ending, let human wickedness at least come to an end, and let the mercy of God alone be sought with all your strength.

Let the burdens of riches no longer press you down to the earth, since soon we shall leave everything here. Let us not wish to possess both Christ and the world at once; but, having spurned the world, let us hasten freely toward heaven.

### 26.

Let us remember how grave are the crimes we have committed and how dreadful are the punishments of hell that we fear; and, according to the character of our guilt, let us apply the remedy of repentance.

Let us consider that, according to the Apostle, “we brought nothing into this world, and we can take nothing out of it when we die” (1 Timothy 6:7). We were born naked, and naked we shall certainly die. Whatever has been found here will undoubtedly be left here.

Only good works, if we have performed them here, will be carried with us to heaven; indeed, they will carry us to heaven. Therefore, like pilgrims content with what is sufficient, let us acquire here for ourselves those riches that we may carry with us to our homeland in paradise.

Let us love God above all things, because it is truly wicked not to love the one to whom we cannot repay what is owed, even when we love him. For what can we, the wicked, repay to the good Lord for all that he has repaid to us (Psalm 115:12), since, without any merits of ours preceding, he granted such things to us undeserving, so that he might redeem us from the yoke of cruel domination?

He descended to us from the seat of the Father’s majesty; he endured insults on earth; he bore abuse; he underwent an undeserved death. He patiently endured all these things in order to show us examples of humility and patience. Hence he also said to his disciples who followed him:

“Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart” (Matthew 11:29).

Therefore, just as he acted for us, so we too ought to tolerate calmly all adversities that befall us because of our sins, so that we may be able to receive the fruit of patience in eternal life.

Let us press forward, brothers, along our course while we have time. Let us hate this world, which we cannot possess for long. Let no contagion of evil works pollute us any longer, but let the divine presence always restrain us from sins.

For if we are ashamed when sinful human beings like ourselves, formed from the same clay, see us sinning, how much more ought we to reverence and fear the eternal and only sinless almighty God, who considers and sees not only deeds but also thoughts?

Let us fear him daily and always carry his reverence with us. Let the hope of forgiveness lift us up in such a way that the fear of Gehenna always afflicts us.

Above all and before all things, let us have charity, remembering the Lord’s command, which says:

“Have salt in yourselves, and have peace among yourselves” (Mark 9:49).

And also:

“I give you a new commandment: that you love one another” (John 13:34).

For elsewhere it is said:

“Have charity, which is the bond of unity” (Colossians 3:14).

And again:

“Be imitators of God, as beloved children, and walk in love” (Ephesians 5:1–2).

And again:

“Let all bitterness and anger and indignation be removed from you, together with all malice” (the same, 4:31).

And:

“Let not the sun go down upon your anger” (ibid., 4:26).

Indeed, just as medicine accomplishes nothing for a wound if iron remains inside it, so the prayer of a person in whose breast deadly hatred dwells accomplishes nothing.

Let us have charity, brothers, because if we have it, we shall be filled with every virtue. But if we do not have charity, whatever good we seem to possess, we lose entirely.

Nor should we grow completely weary in the undertaking of living well, especially since the Lord says that no one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is worthy of the kingdom of heaven (Luke 9:62).

To look back means nothing other than for someone to regret the good he has begun and to become bound once more by worldly desires.

Finally, let no amount of evil turn us away from hope of forgiveness, because however grave human guilt may be, divine mercy is nevertheless greater. Hence the Psalmist says:

“With the Lord there is abundant mercy, and with him there is plentiful redemption” (Psalm 129:7).

And again:

“A contrite and humbled heart God does not despise” (Psalm 50:19).

### 27.

Let these things refresh us, brothers, in memory by day and by night; let these commands frequently urge us onward. Let us consider the end of life as already, already approaching; let us expect the day of death as near, since we do not know it to be far away.

Let us amend what we have done wrong now, lest we begin to repent then, when we will no longer be able to do so. There will indeed be repentance in hell, but entirely fruitless. There will be repentance there that has pain but no remedy; and there the person who refused here to hear what God commanded will in no way be able to obtain from God what he asks.

Therefore, dearest ones, let us obey God’s commands in all things as much as we can, so that there we may receive the reward of his gift.

Let us ourselves chastise ourselves here, while it is permitted; let us ourselves reckon with ourselves concerning our deeds; let us ourselves accuse ourselves before our Judge; and let us not postpone our amendment until the end of life. Rather, whenever we fall into sins, let us rise again through repentance.

With all our strength let us overcome the worst pleasures and enticements of the flesh, and let us take every precaution against this: that we are hastening daily toward death, and that while we are unaware and stand secure, death suddenly comes.

Let us therefore hasten there where death is no longer feared, where all the saints desire to receive us or see us, where Christ, the heavenly King, and the angels, the citizens above, await us with arms extended in love.

There, I say, let us hasten, where we may live without end and where we may be companions of the angelic ranks.

Finally, let us live in the exile of this world in such a way that we may come to the future judgment with a secure conscience, adorned with good works. There let us offer our souls to God as a most acceptable gift, so that in exchange for this he may grant us the blessedness of eternity and we may glorify him throughout the ages of ages.

Until now, dearest ones, we have offered you these commands to taste, as it were, like milk. And now, in the presence of God and of the holy angels who hear us speaking, we have discharged our obligation by handing on heavenly commands to you.

From now on it is your responsibility to consider how our admonition may produce the effect of salvation, and how, always doing God’s will, you may guard yourselves from every evil and finally arrive, rejoicing and free from every contagion of sin, at the heavenly kingdoms.

By the favor of our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 1189]

## SERMON ON THE CREED [Note: [Col. 1189] Formerly in volume 10, *On Time*, sermon 181, and subsequently in Appendix 59. Compiled from Rufinus, Caesarius, Gregory, Ivo of Chartres, etc.; moreover, it contains, section by section, the entire sermon 242 of the Appendix to volume 5.] (S)

### PREFACE. The necessity of inward and outward faith. The Creed as the rule of faith. The manner of its institution. What it contains.

[Note: [Col. 1189] Ivo of Chartres, sermon on the Creed, and the prologue of Fulgentius, *On Faith*.] It is known, beloved, to your Charity that soldiers of this world, when they are about to receive temporal benefits from temporal lords, are first bound by military oaths and profess that they will keep faith with their lords. How much more, then, ought those who will serve the eternal King and receive eternal rewards to be bound by heavenly sacraments and publicly profess the faith by which they will please him? For the Apostle says: “Without faith it is impossible to please God” (Hebrews 11:6). He who searches hearts and reins recognizes this faith in our hearts (Psalm 7:10). Yet, for preserving the unity of the Church, together with faith of the heart there is, under the dispensation of this time, a necessary confession of the mouth: for “with the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Romans 10:10)—not only for preachers, but also for hearers. For otherwise one brother could not think well of another, nor could the peace of the Church be preserved, nor could teaching another or learning from another, as necessary for salvation, be possible, unless what one holds in the heart were conveyed to other hearts by signs of the voice, as though by its own vehicles. Faith, therefore, must be kept in the heart and expressed by the mouth.

For faith is the foundation of all good things and the beginning of human salvation. Without it no one can attain the number of the children of God, because without it one receives neither the grace of justification in this world nor possesses eternal life in the world to come. And if anyone does not walk by faith, he will not attain sight. Observing this, the holy Apostles handed down a sure rule of faith, which, comprised in twelve statements according to the number of the Apostles, they called the Creed (*Symbolum*): by it believers might maintain Catholic unity and refute heretical perversity. Thus our forebears said that the Creed was instituted for this reason.

[Note: [Col. 1190] From Rufinus’s Creed and sermon 242 in the Appendix to volume 5.] For they relate that, after the ascension of our Lord and Savior to the Father, when his disciples, inflamed by the coming of the Holy Spirit, spoke in the tongues of all peoples, and were about to depart from one another for the several nations in order to preach the word of God, they first established among themselves a common standard for their future preaching, lest, having departed from one another locally, they should preach something diverse or discordant to those invited to faith in Christ. Therefore, all being assembled in one place and filled with the Holy Spirit, each contributed what he believed, combining into one brief summary of their preaching; and they ordained that this rule should be given to believers. The Creed is brief in words but great in mysteries. For whatever was prefigured in the Patriarchs, whatever was proclaimed in the Scriptures, whatever was foretold in the Prophets—whether concerning God unbegotten, or God born from God, or the Holy Spirit, or the reception of every sacrament, or the mystery of the Lord’s death and resurrection—this Creed contains all in brief, and contains it in confessing it. Therefore, once he has reached an age of understanding, let everyone who has professed the apostolic faith learn it from the mouths of those who recite it at Baptism. Let us now come to the sacrament and text of the profession of this Creed, which begins as follows:

### CHAPTER I. To believe God, to believe God, and to believe in God. The faith of the devil. “Almighty.”

“I believe in God the Father Almighty.” [Note: [Col. 1190] From sermon 242, no. 2, in the Appendix to volume 5; and from Rufinus’s Creed.] First, beloved, attend carefully to the kind of statement found at the head of the Creed. Thus it begins with: “I believe.” See that our Lord does not command us to investigate divine judgments, but to believe; not to demand an explanation, but simply and unwaveringly to offer faith. He does not say, “I believe God,” or “I believe God”; although these too are necessary for salvation. For it is one thing to believe him, another to believe that he exists, and another to believe in him. To believe him is to believe that what he says is true; to believe that he exists is to believe that he is God; to believe in him is to love him. Many even wicked persons can believe that what he says is true: for they believe it to be true, yet refuse to make it their own, because their feet are too sluggish for that. Demons, too, can believe that he himself is God. But only those who love God know how to believe in God: those who are Christians not merely in name, but also in deeds and life, because without love faith is empty. Faith with love is the faith of a Christian; faith without love is the faith of a demon. Whoever, therefore, will not believe Christ does not yet even imitate demons.

One already believes Christ, but hates Christ; he has [Note: [Col. 1191] Perhaps: “who has.”] a confession of faith in fear of punishment, not in love of the crown: for they too feared punishment. Finally, when blessed Peter confessed to the Lord, saying, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matthew 16:16), he seems to utter from his mouth almost the same words as the demons; but their confession, because it was uttered with hatred of Christ, was deservedly condemned, whereas his, because it proceeded from inward love, was rewarded with eternal blessedness. Therefore we, who are children of God by adoption of grace (Romans 8:15), in saying, “I believe in God the Father Almighty,” should believe him in such a way that we cleave to him through love.

“In God the Father Almighty.” Observe that, when the Creed joins the name of God the Father, it shows that God did not first begin to be and afterward become Father; rather, without any beginning he is always both God and Father. When you hear “Father,” recognize that he has a Son truly begotten, just as one is called a possessor who possesses something, and a lord who rules someone. God the Father, therefore, is the designation of a hidden mystery, whose Son is truly the Word. Nor should anyone ask how he begot the Son: even angels do not know it, and it is unknown to the Prophets. Hence it was said: “Who shall declare his generation?” (Isaiah 53:8). God is not to be investigated by us, but believed. But, to speak briefly, it suffices for us to know that light begot splendor. He says “Almighty,” moreover, because he is almighty, to whom nothing is impossible, who created heaven and earth, sea, human beings, and all animals and creeping things, not by any laborious act, but by the command of his word alone. Therefore let it not enter our thoughts to ask how this or that could have happened, when we are commanded to confess him almighty.

### CHAPTER II. Jesus, Christ, Only-Begotten. On account of the manner of his conception, Christ compares himself to a worm. This manner of birth is neither injurious nor impossible for God.

And in Jesus Christ, his only Son, our Lord.

[Note: [Col. 1191] From Sermon 242 in Appendix, volume 5; see also Ivo of Chartres, sermon on the Creed, and the Creed of Rufinus.]

Observe that, just as one must believe in the Father, so also one must believe in the Son. And because he is equal to the Father in majesty, we know that we owe him as much honor and dutiful service as we owe the Father.

Jesus is interpreted as “Savior.” He is called Jesus because he saves the people. Christ is named from chrism, because just as ancient kings were anointed with sacred oil, so our Lord Jesus Christ was filled through the outpouring of the Holy Spirit.

He is called “Only-begotten” because he admits neither comparison nor likeness with creatures, since he himself is the supreme Creator of all things. Human beings are called sons of God by grace; he alone is the Son begotten by nature.

These things show that he is rightly to be believed in: because he is equal to the Father, he is our Savior, redeeming us; he is Christ, our King, ruling us; and he is our only Lord, who, having stripped the ancient enemy, incorporates us into his singular dominion.

Who was conceived from the Holy Spirit—that is, the Holy Spirit alone was the author of his conception. For just as a worm is formed from pure mud when the sun warms it, so, when the Holy Spirit illumined and sanctified the Virgin’s heart, Christ’s flesh was conceived from the Virgin’s flesh alone, without the operation of any generative origin of flesh.

Therefore, comparing himself to a worm through the Psalmist, he says, “I am a worm and not a man” (Psalm 21:7)—that is, “not conceived in the human manner.”

Born of the Virgin Mary.

He who came to renew the nature of human beings, grown old through sins, willed to have a new mode of birth. Thus the only-begotten Son of God became the son of a human being, so that he who was the Creator of the world might also become its Redeemer.

That God of majesty was incarnate from Mary does not mean that he was defiled by being born of a Virgin, any more than he was polluted when, from dust, he formed the human being. Indeed, if the sun or fire touches mud, it purifies what it touches while remaining itself undefiled.

Nor was God dishonored by the cause of mercy. It should not be considered unbelievable that he himself was born of a Virgin, since he was able to form Adam from virginal dust and the first woman from a rib.

God gave to Mary his Son, whom he alone loved as begotten equal to himself from his own heart, as his very self, so that he might naturally be one and the same common Son of God and of Mary.

All nature was created by God, and God was born from Mary. God created all things, and Mary gave birth to God. God, who made all things, made himself from Mary; and thus he remade everything that he had made. He who was able to make all things from nothing did not will to remake them, once violated, without Mary.

## CHAPTER III. Why the Lord Willed to Be Crucified. The Power of the Cross

Suffered under Pontius Pilate, was crucified, died, and was buried.

[Note: [Col. 1192] See Sermon 242 in Appendix, volume 5, and the Creed of Rufinus.]

Pilate was the judge appointed in Judaea at that time by the emperor, under whom the Lord suffered. His mention concerns the indication of the time, not the dignity of his person.

Crucified.

The Prophets foretold many things concerning this: how, crucified on the cross, he would hang before the eyes of the wicked people with his hands extended. To state it briefly, he was suspended on the cross so that he might release us from the condemnation of the forbidden tree and free us from death.

But one asks what the cross signifies, and why the Lord chose to suffer on the gibbet. A threefold explanation is given.

First, so that Christ might be offered as redemption for the guilt of the world, and the ancient enemy might be caught as though by the hook of the cross—that is, so that he might vomit out those whom he had swallowed, defeated not by power but by justice.

The second reason is that he might provide human beings who follow him with instruction in life. For this purpose he ascended the cross: to offer us an example of suffering and resurrection.

The third reason for undertaking the cross was that the pride of the world and its inflated wisdom might, through the supposedly foolish preaching of the cross, be humbled and collapse, and might learn that what is foolish in God is wiser than human beings.

But we must still consider why the Lord chose this particular kind of death. We read in the Gospel that the Pharisees wanted to throw him down from the mountain; “but he, passing through their midst, went away” (Luke 4:29–30). Elsewhere also we read that the Jews took up stones to throw at him; but he hid himself and went out of the temple (John 8:59).

Why did the Lord refuse to be thrown down, stoned, or even beheaded by the sword? He certainly did this for the sake of our salvation. The death of Christ is the sign of our salvation.

He therefore refused to be stoned or struck by the sword, because we cannot always carry with us stones or iron with which to defend ourselves. Instead, he chose the cross, which is represented by a slight movement of the hands and by which we are also protected against the enemy’s deceptions.

For by this sign of the cross the Lord’s Body is consecrated, the baptismal font is sanctified, priests and the other ecclesiastical orders are initiated, and everything that is sanctified is consecrated by this sign of the Lord’s cross together with the invocation of Christ’s name.

## CHAPTER IV. The Mystery of the Cross. The Depth of the Mystery of the Cross

The cross itself also contains a great mystery: its arrangement is such that its upper part seeks the heavens, its lower part clings to the earth, and, fixed in place, reaches the depths of the underworld, while its breadth extends toward the regions of the world.

For through the passion of the cross Christ benefited the angels in heaven, whose number, diminished through the apostate angel, is daily completed from the souls of the faithful; he benefited us who are on earth; those who, because of original sin, were being held in the underworld; and also those who lived in the different regions of the world.

When lying horizontally, the cross extends toward the four quarters of the world: east and west, north and south. For through his passion Christ draws all nations to himself and has subjected all things to himself, according to what he himself says after rising from the dead: “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matthew 28:18).

[Note: [Col. 1193] Words of Ivo of Chartres; see Sermon 247 in Appendix, volume 5, sections 4 and 5.]

This figure of the cross also contains a deeper sacrament, which must be considered with greater care the deeper it is.

In the breadth of the cross is understood love of neighbor, which must extend not only to friends but also to those who are to be loved as enemies.

In its length is understood the long and persevering endurance of labors and persecutions, which our pilgrimage, longing for its homeland, must patiently bear both for love of our neighbors and for the performance of every good work.

Likewise, its height represents the eminence of hope, penetrating to the interior of the veil, where those who are here subjected to manifold trials by the citizens of Babylon enjoy the vision of peace, until they are freed from slavery to corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God.

The depth of the cross must also be considered, because the mystery of the cross is profound. In it the understanding of many who are called wise has failed: they dared to criticize what they could not comprehend by human reasoning—namely, how the Word coeternal with God the Father, containing all things and filling all things, enclosed himself wholly in the human being he assumed, and yet did not cease to rule, fill, and contain the whole world.

## CHAPTER V. Why Christ Chose the Punishment of the Cross. Through the Death of the Flesh He Merited a Twofold Resurrection for Us

Therefore, let us feel no shame because of the cross of Christ, since through his passion we possess victory. For just as the eternal Son of God was born not for himself but for us, so the immaculate Lamb of God suffered not for himself but for us.

Who would not recognize this as a wondrous mystery, in which the very one who is God is proclaimed to be human, and the same Lord who is announced is described as crucified? Nor was it unforeseen or unexpected for him that he would be slain, since by the counsel of his divinity he assumed humanity precisely so that he could be killed on humanity’s behalf.

He chose the punishment of the cross so that a more exalted victory might be prepared through a more degrading penalty; and so that he who suffered for the good of the universe might die raised up on high, as though before the eyes of the world. At the same time, those who saw the crucified one might behold the wonders of the Crucified.

The sudden darkness of the sun, the trembling of the earth, the splitting of the rocks, and the resurrection of the dead sufficiently and abundantly displayed the glory of the one who suffered.

And what testimony could be greater than that the thief who was crucified alongside him asked his fellow sufferer that he might be remembered in the heavenly kingdom?

Therefore, beloved, although Christ endured mockery and insults, we do not lament his cross and death with sighs; rather, we celebrate them with continual praises.

The death of our Lord Jesus Christ was not in the soul but in the flesh alone. Our death, however, is not only in the flesh but also in the soul: in the soul because of sin, and in the flesh because of the punishment of sin.

But because he committed no sin, he did not have sin in his soul and did not die except in the flesh alone—and this through the likeness of sinful flesh, which he drew from Adam.

Thus his single death benefited our double death, and his single resurrection benefited the resurrection of soul and body. For his resurrection dissolved our two deaths and shaped our two resurrections.

Nor without reason did he lie in the tomb for one day and two nights, since he joined the light of his single death to the darkness of our double death. He came to us, who were held in the death of flesh and spirit, and brought his one death of the flesh, thereby dissolving our two deaths. For if he had assumed both, he would have freed us from neither.

## CHAPTER VI. What Christ Accomplished for Us through His Weaknesses

[Col. 1194]

He was buried, so that, for the consolation of the buried, the earth might also receive the blessing of his body.

The weaknesses of the incarnate Word are recounted, concerning which the Apostle says, “What is weak in God is stronger than human beings” (1 Corinthians 1:25).

He was born of a Virgin, so that we might be born from the virgin womb of the Church. He was tempted, so that he might free us from temptation. He was seized, so that we might be released. He was bound, so that we might be freed from the knot of the curse. He was mocked, so that he might free us from the mockery of demons. He was sold, so that he might redeem us. He was humbled, so that he might exalt us. He was captured, so that he might take us away from captivity to demons. He was stripped, so that the nakedness of the first human being, through which death entered, might be covered.

He was crowned with thorns, so that he might free us from the thorns of sins—or rather, so that he might show that those who were thorny because they loved vices would be crowned with him and would become the head and crown of the Church.

He was given vinegar to drink, so that he might intoxicate us with the sweetness of heavenly desire and eternal joy.

Finally, he was sacrificed on the altar of the cross, so that he might erase the sins of the whole world. He died, so that he might make death’s dominion captive. He was buried, so that he might bless the burial of the saints and bury us to himself, dead to vices and desires.

This weakness of Christ, therefore, overcame all the strength of the world.

## CHAPTER VII. What He Did in the Underworld

He descended to the underworld so that he might free Adam the first-formed human being, the Patriarchs, the Prophets, and all the righteous who were being held there because of original sin; and so that, released from the bonds of sin, redeemed by his blood from that captivity and from the place of the underworld, he might recall them to the heavenly homeland and the joys of perpetual life.

The others who, in addition to original sin, committed personal guilt remained in the punitive Tartarus, as Scripture asserts. Thus it was said through the Prophet in the person of Christ: “I shall be your death, O death”—that is, through his death Christ killed death, the enemy of the human race, and gave life. “I shall be your sting, O underworld” (Hosea 13:14).

He partly “stung” the underworld, insofar as he liberated some; and partly left it, insofar as those who remained in torment for their principal crimes were concerned.

On the third day he rose from the dead.

If you have believed concerning Christ what belongs to dishonor, believe also what belongs to glory. If you have believed what belongs to death, believe also what belongs to life.

For just as in the passion there is the mystery of piety, so in the resurrection there is the exercise of power, as he himself says: “I have authority to lay down my life, and I have authority to take it up again” (John 10:18).

[Note: [Col. 1194] From Sermon 242, section 3, and afterward from Sermon 177, section 1.]

He ascended into heaven—that is, he placed above the heavens, at the right hand of God the Father, the condition of our nature that he assumed when he was born from a human mother.

Let us also ascend with Christ meanwhile in our hearts, so that, when his promised day arrives, we may follow him in our bodies as well.

Yet we must know, brothers, that pride did not ascend with Christ, nor avarice, nor lust; none of our vices ascended with our physician. Therefore, if we desire to ascend after our physician, we must lay aside our vices and sins.

For they all press upon us like fetters and strive to bind us in the nets of sins. Therefore, with God’s help, let us do as the Psalmist says: “Let us break their bonds” (Psalm 2:3), so that we may confidently say to the Lord, “You have broken my bonds; to you I will sacrifice a sacrifice of praise” (Psalm 115:16–17).

He sits at the right hand of God the almighty Father.

To sit belongs to one who judges. And because our Redeemer, taken up into heaven, now judges all things and will come at the end as judge of all, he is described as sitting.

## CHAPTER VIII. All Human Beings Will Be Judged by Christ

From there he will come to judge the living and the dead.

[Note: [Col. 1194] Again from the cited Sermon 242; Sermon 110, sections 1, 2, and 3, from which the material omitted here should be supplied.]

He will come to judgment in the very body in which he ascended into heaven, to judge Christians and pagans, the righteous and sinners, the faithful and the impious.

For, as the Apostle says, “We shall all stand before the tribunal of Christ, so that each may receive what was done through his body, according to what he has done, whether good or evil” (2 Corinthians 5:10).

The Lord also announces this in the Gospel, saying [lacuna].

## CHAPTER IX. How They Ought Already to Prepare for the Last Judgment

Let us ourselves chastise ourselves; let us ourselves reckon with ourselves concerning our daily conduct; let us ourselves accuse ourselves daily before our judge; and, while we are in the flesh, let us fight daily against the flesh itself, with the Lord’s help.

Whoever does this will be freed from hearing evil. But whoever despises it—[Note: [Col. 1195] From Sermon 249, sections 4, 5, and 6, from which the omitted material here should also be supplied.]—what will he do on that fearful day of judgment, when, while the world trembles and the trumpets of the angels sound before him, the Lord, surrounded by the light of the heavenly host, will sit upon the throne of his majesty [lacuna]?

## CHAPTER X. We Must Flee to the Remedies of Repentance

The end of one’s life, which is always uncertain, must not always be delayed as a remedy for salvation, because the one who makes us secure by saying, “On the day when the sinner turns, all his iniquities will be consigned to oblivion” (Ezekiel 18:21–22), also wished to make us cautious by saying, “Do not delay turning to the Lord, and do not defer it from day to day” (Sirach 5:8).

Let us therefore turn to better things while the remedies remain in our power. Here let us extinguish death by dying to sins; here let us acquire life through the merits of life.

Therefore, beloved brothers, wisely and faithfully considering these things, let us hasten to flee to the remedies of repentance, and through chastity or humility, through works of justice and mercy, let us obtain eternal things for ourselves with God.

But, to return to the point from which we digressed, the following occurs in this holy Creed:

## CHAPTER XI. The Mystery of the Trinity Is Explained through Comparisons

I believe in the Holy Spirit.

[Note: [Col. 1195] From Sermon 242, section 4; see Appendix, volume 5, Sermon 245, section 2.]

Observe that, just as one must believe in the Father, so also one must believe in the Son and in the Holy Spirit. For whoever does not believe in one person of the Trinity will gain nothing from believing in the other two.

The Catholic faith is this: that we venerate, believe, worship, and confess one God in Trinity and the Trinity in unity.

In this Trinity there is nothing earlier or later, because just as the Father never existed without the Son, nor the Son without the Father, so the Father and the Son never existed without the Holy Spirit.

The Holy Trinity is therefore coeternal, and the unity is inseparable, without beginning and without end. Nothing is greater or lesser.

The equality of the persons is indicated, because the Holy Trinity is equal and there is one divinity. The Apostle says and teaches, “Through the things that have been made, the unseen things are perceived” (Romans 1:20), and through the creature the Creator is understood, according to these and many other comparisons.

The sun, its radiance, and its heat are three names, yet the three are one. What shines is what is hot, and what is hot is what shines: these three names are recognized as one reality.

So the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are three persons, yet one in divinity, and the undivided unity is rightly believed.

Likewise, from earthly things: vein, spring, river—these are three names, yet the three are one in their nature. So also the substance and divinity of the three persons—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—are one.

Neither the person of the Father nor that of the Holy Spirit, but only the person of the Son, assumed flesh.

To make this understood, I shall use comparisons. Certainly, if you wish to understand the Creator through the creature, in the soul there are both soul and reason; and although they are one, the soul does one thing and reason another: we live by the soul, and we understand by reason.

So, although the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one substance, the whole Trinity made the human being whom the person of the Son alone, not the whole Trinity, assumed.

And although the Son of God himself was God and human, only the human was subject to suffering.

For example, we see a tree containing within itself the radiance of the sun. When it is cut, we see that the blow of the striking iron receives the sun’s radiance before it reaches the wood. Yet, although the radiance is there, it can neither be cut nor separated from the woodcutter. So also the divinity can neither be separated nor cut; but what was subject to suffering was that which, like wood, could be both bound and held.

Therefore, just as we must believe in the Father and the Son, so also must we believe in the Holy Spirit.

This, beloved, is the unviolated rule of truth: that those who are one and are one should not be separated by us on earth. For just as nothing created can be made equal to the divinity, so the nature of divinity excludes every division and inequality.

According to evangelical truth, just as the Son came forth from the Father, so also the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father. And just as the only-begotten Son is God, so also the Holy Spirit is God.

Just as the Father has mercy on whom he wills, and the Son reveals the Father to whom he wills, so also the Holy Spirit is read to inspire whom he wills and to distribute the gifts of heavenly graces as he wills.

Therefore the sevenfold grace of the same Spirit is rightly described by the Prophet (Isaiah 11:2–3), because through his inspiration one arrives at rest, and in the full reception and vision of him true rest is possessed.

Concerning him it is rightly promised, “He himself will teach you all things” (John 14:26), because unless that same Spirit is present in the heart of the hearer, the teacher’s speech is useless.

Let no one attribute to the human teacher what he understands from the teacher’s mouth, because unless the one who teaches is within, the teacher’s tongue labors outwardly in vain.

Therefore, since without him we can do nothing good, let us, with his help, make ourselves such that the Holy Spirit may deign to come to us and dwell within us.

## CHAPTER XII. The Catholic Church. No Greater Riches Than Faith. The Church Is One

The holy catholic Church.

[Note: [Col. 1196] From Sermon 243, section 4; the words of Gregory, Moralia, book 35, chapter 7; Cyprian, On the Unity of the Church, near the middle.]

It must be understood that we are to believe the Church, but not to believe in the Church, because the Church is not God but the house of God.

He calls it “catholic,” meaning spread throughout the whole world, because the churches of the various heretics are not called catholic: they are confined to particular places and to their respective provinces. This Church, however, is spread from the rising to the setting of the sun in the splendor of one faith.

There are no greater riches, no treasures, no honors, and no greater substance in this world than the catholic faith, which saves sinners, enlightens the blind, heals the sick, baptizes catechumens, justifies the faithful, restores penitents, increases the righteous, crowns martyrs, ordains clerics, consecrates priests, prepares people for the heavenly kingdoms, and shares eternal inheritance with the holy angels.

Whoever he is, and whatever sort of person he is, is not a Christian if he is not in the Church of Christ.

For it alone is the Church through which the Lord willingly accepts sacrifice; it alone confidently intercedes for those who have gone astray.

Therefore the Lord also gave this command concerning the sacrifice of the Lamb: “You shall eat it in one house, and you shall not carry any of its flesh outside” (Exodus 12:46).

The lamb is eaten in one house because in the one catholic Church the true sacrifice of the Redeemer is offered. The divine command forbids carrying its flesh outside because it forbids giving what is holy to dogs.

It alone is the place where good work is fruitfully performed; hence those who had labored within the vineyard alone received the payment of a denarius.

It alone preserves those within it by the strong bond of charity. Thus the water of the flood lifted the ark to higher places, but destroyed all whom it found outside the ark.

It alone is the place where we truly contemplate the heavenly mysteries. Therefore the Lord says to Moses, “There is a place with me, and you shall stand upon the rock”; and shortly afterward, “I will take away my hand, and you shall see my back” (Exodus 33:21, 23).

Because truth is seen only from the catholic Church, the Lord declares that there is with him a place from which he may be seen.

Moses is placed upon the rock so that he may contemplate the appearance of God, because unless someone holds firmly to the solidity of faith, he does not recognize the divine presence.

“Take away,” he says, “the ray of the sun from the body: unity does not admit division of light. Break a branch from a tree: once broken, it cannot bear fruit. Cut off a stream from its spring: once cut off, it dries up.”

In these words of Cyprian we understand that light does not admit division except among the holy who are predestined for the kingdom of God and cannot in any way be separated from the Church. We understand that a broken branch does not sprout with the shoot of eternal salvation. We recognize the dryness of the stream cut off from its spring in the fact that those who are separated from unity are emptied of the Holy Spirit.

## CHAPTER XIII. Who Becomes a Participant in the Merits of the Saints

The communion of saints—

[Note: [Col. 1197] From Sermon 242, section 4; Sermon 224, section 1; Sermon 209, sections 5 and 1; Gregory, Homily 37 on the Gospels; and the final words of the above-cited Sermon 209 in Appendix, volume 5.]

—that is, we are held in fellowship and communion of hope with those saints who died in the faith that we have embraced.

If, therefore, we wish to have communion with the saints in eternal life, let us think about imitating them. They ought to recognize something of their virtues in us, so that they may deign to intercede with the Lord on our behalf.

For if we cannot endure the torments that the saints endured, let us at least, with their intercession, resist evil desires.

Neither Abraham, Isaac, nor Jacob was killed, yet they were honored for the merits of faith and justice and were deemed worthy to be first among the Patriarchs. Whoever is found faithful, just, and praiseworthy is gathered to their banquet.

Therefore, beloved brothers, even if we suffer nothing of that kind—if we endure no chains, scourging, imprisonment, bodily punishment, or human persecution for the sake of justice—we can nevertheless obtain fellowship with the saints if we take care to chastise our body and subject it to service; if we become accustomed to entreating the Lord in a spirit of humility and with a contrite soul; if we strive to receive injuries inflicted by our neighbor with a tranquil mind; if we love those who hate us and inflict injuries upon us, do good to them, and gladly pray for their life and welfare; and if, together with the virtue of patience, we strive to adorn ourselves with the fruits of good works.

For when we conduct ourselves in this way and, in the Apostle’s words, present our bodies as a living, holy, and acceptable sacrifice to God (Romans 12:1), we shall be granted, through heavenly favor, to receive the same glory as those who gave their members over to death for the Lord.

Then, just as their death is precious in the sight of the Lord, so also may our life be precious. When the bonds of the flesh have been broken, we too shall be deemed worthy to enter the courts of the heavenly city and, among the choirs of blessed martyrs, render vows of thanks to our Redeemer.

These are the footprints that all the saints, returning to their homeland, left for us, so that by clinging to their paths we might follow them to joy.

Why do we not hasten and run, so that we may be able to see our homeland? A great number of beloved ones awaits us there. A frequent and abundant crowd of parents, brothers, and children longs for us—already secure concerning their own safety, yet still concerned for our salvation.

What joy there will be in common for them and for us when we come into their embrace and presence!

There is the glorious choir of the Apostles. There is the distinguished number of rejoicing Prophets. There the innumerable people of martyrs are crowned for victory in their struggles. There the most radiant crowd of virgins rejoices; there also the strength of confessors is praised.

The reward of those who, keeping the Lord’s commandments, transferred earthly possessions to heavenly treasures is also reckoned there.

What tongue is sufficient to speak, or what understanding to grasp, how great are the joys of the heavenly city: to take one’s place among the choirs of angels, to stand with the blessed spirits in the glory of the Creator, to behold the face of the present God, to see the unbounded light, to suffer no fear of death, and to rejoice in the gift of perpetual incorruption?

Let us hasten with eager desire toward these chosen ones of God, so that we may soon be with them and soon come together with Christ—to him whom we have as the guide of this journey, the author of salvation, the prince of light, and the giver of joy.

## CHAPTER XIV. The Remission of Sins. The Novatians Are Refuted

The remission of sins.

Above all, brothers, the remission of sins must be believed, because this is the one remedy that releases the human race from the sentence of perpetual death.

For this reason the only-begotten Son of the Most High deigned to assume flesh and was content with the cross, so that indulgence might make you innocent, though you could not escape your crimes.

Therefore the immaculate Lamb was slain, so that the stain of the human race might be wiped away by his blood.

I am amazed that some are so obstinate that they think repentance should not be granted to those who have fallen, or that forgiveness should be denied to those who repent, although it is written, “Remember from where you have fallen, and repent, and do the works you did at first” (Revelation 2:5).

This is certainly said to one who is known to have fallen and whom the Lord urges to rise again through works, because it is written, “Almsgiving delivers from death” (Tobit 4:11). This does not mean the death that Christ’s blood once extinguished, from which the saving grace of Baptism and of our Redeemer freed us, but the death that later crept in through offenses.

For since it is written, “The Lord did not make death, nor does he rejoice in the destruction of the living” (Wisdom 1:13), he who wishes no one to perish certainly desires sinners to repent and through repentance return again to life.

Therefore through the Prophet Joel he also cries out and says, “And now, says the Lord your God, return to me with all your heart, with fasting and weeping and mourning; tear your hearts and not your garments, and return to the Lord your God, for he is merciful and gracious, patient and rich in mercy, and one who relents from the evil he has decreed” (Joel 2:12–13).

The Lord also, displaying the piety of God the Father in the Gospel, says, “Which one of you is there who, if his son asks him for bread, will give him a stone? Or if he asks for a fish, will give him a serpent? If you, then, although you are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father from heaven give the good Spirit to those who ask him?” (Matthew 7:9–11).

Here the Lord compares an earthly father with the eternal and generous piety of God the Father.

If an evil father on earth, when gravely offended by a sinful and wicked son, nevertheless rejoices and gives thanks when he later sees him reformed, having laid aside the sins of his former life and, corrected through the pain of repentance, returned to sober and good conduct and to the discipline of innocence; if he embraces with paternal exultation the one whom he had previously lost and now received back—how much more does that one true Father, good, merciful, and compassionate, indeed goodness, mercy, and compassion itself, rejoice in the repentance of his children?

He does not threaten the penitent, the weeping, or the lamenting with anger or punishment; rather, he promises forgiveness and pardon.

For if the devil was powerful enough to lead you from the lofty heights of virtue into the depths of evil, how much more will God be able to restore you to the highest summit of goodness—and not merely restore you to what you were, but make you far more blessed than you previously appeared?

## CHAPTER XV. We Must Not Despair, and From Where Despair Proceeds. We Must Not Cease Entreating Forgiveness

Only do not lose heart, nor cut off your hope of good things, lest, I beg you, what usually happens to the impious happen to you.

It is not the multitude of sins that leads to despair, but impiety. Therefore Solomon did not say, “Everyone who comes into the depths of evil despises”; rather, he says, “The impious person, when he comes into the depths of evil, despises” (Proverbs 18:3).

It is therefore characteristic of the impious to despair of salvation and to despise when they have come into the depths of evil, not of sinners as such.

For impiety does not allow them to look toward God or return to the place from which they have slipped away.

This thought, then, which cuts off hope of conversion, descends from impiety. Like a very heavy stone resting upon the neck of the soul, it always forces the soul to look downward toward the earth and does not allow it to raise its eyes to its God.

But it is the mark of a manly spirit and an excellent mind to cast the enemy’s burden from the neck of one’s soul—or rather, to cast away the devil who presses one down—and to command one’s soul to sing these prophetic words to the Lord:

“As the eyes of servants are upon the hands of their masters, and as the eyes of a maidservant are upon the hands of her mistress, so our eyes are upon the Lord our God, until he has mercy on us. Have mercy on us, Lord; have mercy on us, because we are filled exceedingly with contempt” (Psalm 122:2–3).

There is excellent and heavenly philosophical teaching in these words.

“We are filled,” he says, “with contempt.” This is what he wished to teach us: even if we are filled with the multitude of our sins and covered with contempt and reproaches, nevertheless our eyes must be upon the Lord our God until he has mercy on us.

Nor should we cease from supplication before we deserve to obtain forgiveness for our sins.
