For this is truly the mark of a steadfast and persistent soul: not to be driven away from perseverance in asking by despair of obtaining, but to continue and persist in supplication until mercy is shown.

And lest you perhaps think that you incur greater offense before God if, when you do not deserve to be heard, you persist importunately in prayer, remember the Gospel parable. There you will find that the Lord did not present persistent and importunate petitioners as ungrateful to him.

For he says, “Even if he will not give him anything because he is his friend, yet because of his persistence he will rise and give him whatever he needs” (Luke 11:8).

Understand, beloved, therefore, that the devil introduces despair of obtaining precisely in order to cut off from us hope in God’s goodness, which is the guide of the journey by which one goes to heaven.

But just as it is philosophical to moderate one’s tears over ordinary death, so I consider it both foolish and irreligious to receive consolation in the death of the soul.

## CHAPTER XVI. However Guilty One May Be, Hope of Life Remains. God Never Despises Sincere Repentance. God Created Us for Heaven, Not for Hell. Through Repentance Any Sins Whatever Can Be Washed Away Here
Moreover, I think that we ought to be accused of negligence if, while those who lament the bodies and common death of the departed perform this act with such severity and vehemence, knowing and being certain that their tears contribute nothing to the life of the deceased, we do nothing comparable in lamentation for the soul, although we know that through repentance it can be restored to its proper condition. For we know that many have fallen away from the straight path and been hurled from the entrance of the narrow way, and yet have been restored in such a manner that they surpassed their former achievements by their later ones, attained the palm and the crown, and were once again believed to have been enrolled among the number and choir of the saints.

And I do not want you to think that I am speaking only about those who sinned in a few and minor matters. I am speaking about one who succumbed to every evil, who by the enormity of his crimes shut the way to the kingdom of heaven against himself; and not about unbelievers, but about one who had been among the faithful, indeed among those who had previously pleased God, but afterward fell either into adultery or into every form of impurity which, as the Apostle says, is shameful even to mention. God never despises repentance if it is offered to him sincerely and simply. He receives it, gladly accepts it, embraces it, and does everything to restore the person to his former condition. What is still more excellent and remarkable is that, even if someone has been unable to complete the entire order of making satisfaction, God nevertheless does not reject repentance, however slight or briefly practiced it may have been. He receives even that and does not allow the reward of so small a conversion to perish.

This, it seems to me, is what Isaiah indicates when he says concerning the Jewish people: “Because of sin I grieved you for a little while, and I struck you, and I turned my face away from you; and you were grieved, and you walked sorrowfully, and I consoled you” (Isaiah 54:7–8). Since, then, we have these examples of repentance, let us not persist in evil, nor despair of reconciliation. Rather, let us say, “Let us also return to the Father and draw near to God.” Believe me: he will never turn away one who turns back to him. For he himself says, “I am God who draws near, and not God who is far away” (Jeremiah 23:23). And again, through the same prophet: “Sins,” he says, “separate between me and you” (Isaiah 59:2).

If, then, sins are what separate us from God, let us remove this obstacle from between us, and nothing will prevent us from being joined to God. For this reason God created us and brought us into being when we did not exist: so that he might bestow eternal goods upon us and grant us the kingdoms of heaven. [Col. 1200] [Note: [Col. 1200] See Appendix to volume 5, Sermon 77, no. 2.] He did not make us for the purpose of handing us over to Gehenna and everlasting fire. The kingdom of heaven was made for us; Gehenna was made for the devil.

I shall demonstrate from the Gospels that this is so. The Lord himself will say to those who will be at his right hand: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.” But to those who will be at his left he will say: “Depart from me, accursed ones, into the eternal fire that has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matthew 25:34, 41).

If, then, the fire of Gehenna was prepared for the devil, while the kingdom of heaven was prepared for humanity from the foundation of the world, our only concern must be not to exclude ourselves from entering into these blessings by stubbornly persisting in evil. For as long as we remain in this life, whatever sins may befall us, it is possible for all of them to be washed away through repentance. But when we have been taken away from this world, even if we shall then repent—for we shall repent greatly, but our repentance will be of no benefit—and even if there is gnashing of teeth, wailing and weeping, and even if we pour out prayers and cry aloud with countless supplications, no one will hear us, no one will come to our aid, and no one will pour even water from the tip of a finger onto our tongue, laid in the flames. Rather, we shall hear what that rich man heard from Abraham: “A great chasm has been fixed between us and you, and no one can cross from here to there, nor from there to here” (Luke 16:26).

## CHAPTER XVII. Pleasures Quickly Pass Away. They Lead to Everlasting Torments. We Enjoy Them Now as Though in a Dream.

Let us therefore at last come to our senses and remember what benefited those who remained until their final day in bodily luxury and the pleasures of the present life. Look now upon their tombs and see whether any trace of their former ostentation remains there, or whether you recognize any sign of their riches or luxury. Search now for the garments and foreign perfumes, for the pleasure of the spectacles, for the crowds of attendants, and for the lavishness of banquets. Where have their laughter, their jokes, and their immoderate and unrestrained merriment gone? Where have they withdrawn? Where are those things now, and where are the people themselves? What is the end of both?

Look more carefully and approach the tombs of each one. See only ashes and the foul remains of worms, and remember that this is the end of bodies, whether they have spent their lives in delights and joy or in toil and self-restraint. If everything—the whole matter and its entire cause—ended in ashes and worms, these losses would be small and could easily be excused as part of the condition of nature. But now turn your eyes away from these ashes and tombs, and recall your thought to that dreadful tribunal of divine judgment, which a burning river surrounds with fiery currents: where there are weeping and gnashing of teeth, where there is outer darkness, where there is that worm of conscience which will never die, and the fire which will never be extinguished.

Remember the parable of Lazarus and that rich man, who was master of such great wealth, clothed in purple and fine linen, yet at that time could not find even a single drop of water when he was placed in the necessity of burning thirst. Tell me, I ask you, what more does this life have than a dream? For just as those who are confined in mines, whether condemned there or subjected to some other punishment, when after a long period of harsh existence they are perhaps briefly released into sleep, see themselves placed among abundant dishes and enjoying sumptuous banquets, but when they rise find that none of the pleasure of their dream has remained with them, so that rich man also had this life as though it were a dream. When he departed, nothing remained with him except regret for the past and punishment in the present.

## CHAPTER XVIII. Everlasting Punishments. The Power of Repentance.

Remember these things, and set the fire of Gehenna against those flames of lust and desire that harass you now. The fire that exists in the present life consumes everything it receives; but that fire torments forever those whom it takes in and always preserves them whole for their punishment. For this reason it is also called unquenchable—not only because it itself is not extinguished, but because it will neither extinguish nor destroy those whom it receives. [Col. 1201] Scripture says that sinners too will put on incorruption—not, of course, for the honor of life, but for the duration of punishment.

No voice can set forth the power of this punishment and that fire; no speech can explain it. For among corruptible things there is nothing that can be compared with incorruptible things, whether good or evil. What shall we do there? What shall we answer? Nothing will remain except gnashing of teeth, wailing and weeping, and late repentance, while every source of help has ceased on all sides and punishments grow stronger everywhere; there will be no consolation at all. No one will meet our eyes there except the ministers of punishment and the dreadful faces of the torturers.

Yet we can not only escape these punishments and these torments, but also acquire eternal blessedness, provided that we repent of our evils.

## CHAPTER XIX. How It Is Corrupted. Yet Even Then It Was Not Entirely Fruitless. It Must Be Read Carefully.

Do you see how great is the power of repentance? Do you see how much merit conversion restores? Repentance, however, is corrupted if someone again becomes entangled in the same evils for which he confessed.

“For,” he says, “if one builds and another destroys, what do they gain except toil? And if one who has been baptized from the dead again touches the dead, what benefit does he receive from his washing?” So also, “if a person fasts for his sins, and then goes and does the same things again, who will hear his prayer?” (Sirach 34:28, 30–31). And again he says: “The one who turns back from righteousness to sin, the Lord casts into the sword. And just as a dog, when it returns to its vomit, becomes hateful, so also a fool, when he returns to his sin” (Proverbs 26:11).

But now listen to what we must say. It often happens that someone has corrected many and great faults through repentance, yet amid the good things that he has corrected through repentance has also committed sins. This is [Col. 1202] what most strongly brings despair into the mind, because the person seems to have destroyed what he built and poured out all those labors in vain. This is the thought that especially places the burden of despair upon the soul.

But we must again consider the thought by which this worst and life-destroying idea may be driven away: namely, that if the good things we performed and that amendment sought through repentance had not existed, and if they had not stood as a counterweight against the weight introduced into us by sin, there would have been nothing to prevent us from falling into the depths of evil. But now, like a strong breastplate, they have not permitted a heavy and bitter missile to penetrate as far as the vital organs, but have broken the greater part of the force of the deadly weapon.

It is certain that the one who carries more good works with him there, as well as more evil works, will have some refreshment even amid the punishments. But the one who has no good works and brings with him a great abundance of evil works—what awaits him need not be stated. There will unquestionably be a balancing of good and evil there, as though both sides had been placed on a scale. Whichever side sinks will claim as its worker the one toward whom the balance inclines. If, then, the multitude of evils prevails, it drags its worker into Gehenna. But if the good works are greater, they will resist and oppose the evils with all their strength and will call their worker back from the very border of Gehenna to the region of the living. [Note: [Col. 1202] From Sermon 29, no. 4; Appendix to volume 5.]

Therefore, dearest brothers, if we are willing to consider these things attentively, let us acquire remedies for ourselves on the day of necessity, so that when the day of judgment comes we may not be punished with the impious and sinners, but may come happily with the righteous and those who fear God to eternal rewards. Amen.

[Col. 1201]

# SERMON ON THE EVE OF EASTER: ON THE EATING OF THE LAMB

It is also found among the spurious works of Jerome. (C, S)*

The mystery of Easter is fulfilled in us. When it is to be celebrated. Where. Christ is a lamb for some and a kid for others. Why the lamb was killed in the evening rather than during the day. What it means to eat unleavened bread with bitterness. Why raw or boiled meat is not to be eaten. What the lamb’s head, feet, and entrails signify. Why the lamb’s bones are not to be broken. What the girded loins at the eating of the lamb teach us. Why sandals and a staff are required.

Today the people of Israel—and truly the people who see God, for this is what “Israel” means—are commanded to depart from Egypt. Today the Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world (John 1:29), is slaughtered for the salvation of all. Today the doorposts of our houses—that is, our foreheads—are marked with his blood. Today the Egyptians are killed, and God’s people are freed from the slavery of Pharaoh (Exodus 12). Today the firstborn of the Egyptians are struck, while not only the Israelites but also their irrational animals are preserved. “You will save humans and beasts, Lord” (Psalm 35:7).

Let us prepare ourselves, dearest brothers, for the sacrifice of the lamb, and let us take hold of him—not when the light is uncertain and the horns of the moon are not yet full, nor when it is beginning to wax or wane, but on the fourteenth day, that is, when its light is complete and perfect, when the whole world is filled with the fullness of its lamp.

Nor should we think that this year-old lamb may be eaten just anywhere. We are commanded to eat it in one house; that is, we should understand that the lamb is to be sacrificed in one Church. [Note: [Col. 1201] In Jerome: “lest it be outside the Church.”] From this it is evident that the Jews and heretics, and all the gatherings of perverse doctrines [Note: [Col. 1201] Jerome: “and doctrines.”], who do not eat the lamb in the Church, are not eating the flesh of the lamb but of the dragon, which, according to the Psalmist, was given as food to the peoples of Ethiopia (Psalm 73:14).

For just as in the Flood no one was saved except the one who was in Noah’s ark (Genesis 7:24), and when Jericho collapsed the house of only Rahab the prostitute—that is, of the believing Church from the nations—was preserved (Joshua 6:23), so in the sacrifice of the lamb the lamb is truly killed only when it is slaughtered in one house.

“You shall have,” he says, “an unblemished lamb. You shall take it from the lambs or from the kids” (Exodus 12:5). It is also commanded elsewhere that whoever could not celebrate the Passover in the first month should celebrate it in the second. Accordingly, it is now commanded that whoever cannot have a lamb should at least have a kid.

For Christ is sacrificed in the house of the Church in two ways: if we are righteous, we feed on the flesh of the lamb; if we are sinners and practice repentance, a kid is killed for us. This is not because Christ is one of the kids whom he taught would stand on the left [Note: [Col. 1202] In Jerome: “For Christ does not become from the kids whom [he places] on the left,” etc., with other words omitted.], but because, according to the diversity of merits, he becomes for each person either a lamb or a kid.

It is also asked why this lamb is not sacrificed during the day but in the evening. The reason is clear. Our Lord and Savior suffered at the consummation of the ages. Hence John also says in his Epistle, “Little children, it is the last hour” (1 John 2:18). But when it is the last hour, the beginning of night follows the end of day.

We must also understand that as long as we are in this world—that is, as long as we remain in Egypt—we are not in bright light but in darkness and gloom. And although the Church, that is, the moon, shines as though in the night, we are nevertheless unable to possess the perfect radiance of the true Sun.

“In one house,” he says, “you shall eat the flesh roasted by fire, and you shall eat unleavened bread with bitterness. You shall not eat any of it raw or boiled in water, but only roasted by fire” (Exodus 12:9–10).

We are commanded to eat bread without the old leaven of malice and wickedness (1 Corinthians 5:8). Concerning this leaven the Lord also warns his disciples in the Gospel, saying, “Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees,” and afterward explains that the leaven of the Pharisees is their doctrine [Note: [Col. 1203] In Jerome, “perverse” is absent.] (Matthew 16:6, 12). [Col. 1203] And so, if we wish to be alienated from the doctrine of this age and to make ourselves, as it were, strangers to worldly conduct, let us be subject to persecutions and pressures, and, according to the Apostle, let us eat the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth (1 Corinthians 5:8).

Do you wish, hearer, to understand what I am saying? Say what is true; speak what is sincere; show partiality to no person—not to the rich, not to the powerful. However powerful or noble the sinner may be, rebuke him, and you will have eaten the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth in bitterness. Hence the Apostle says, “I have become your enemy by telling you the truth” (Galatians 4:16). And a proverb of the pagan world, expressed also by a poet, says: “Obsequiousness creates friends; truth creates hatred” (Terence, *Andria*, act 1, scene 1, line 41).

As for what follows, that we should not eat the lamb’s flesh raw or boiled: this means that we should neither understand the divine Scriptures—which truly are the flesh of the lamb—only according to the history, as the Jews do, and consume them raw as food, nor, following the heretics, weaken them by directing them through certain allegories and the cloudiness of interpretation toward every perverse doctrine, removing the truth of their nourishment and encountering only shadows and images [Note: [Col. 1203] Jerome: “pour them out.”]. Rather, we should understand them according to the history in which they were written, and at the same time cook them in the fire of the Holy Spirit; and whatever in them appears incongruous or obscure according to the letter, we should open through spiritual exposition.

“You shall eat the head with the feet and the entrails” (Exodus 12:9). The head of the lamb seems to me to be what is written in John’s Gospel: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God; he was in the beginning with God” (John 1:1–2). The feet are the human nature which he deigned to assume for our salvation.

But it can also be understood in another way: the head is spiritual understanding; the feet are the simple narrative according to the history; and the entrails are whatever lies hidden within the letter [Note: [Col. 1203] Elsewhere: “shines.”], whatever does not appear on the surface but is brought forth by teachers after careful examination, grinding, and rumination. What was thought to be foul and unbecoming will be discovered to be life-giving.

For example, what could appear more shameful in Scripture than that Hosea should be commanded to take a prostitute as his wife (Hosea 1:2), that Judah should lie with Tamar, his daughter-in-law (Genesis 38:16), that David should be stained by adultery with Bathsheba (2 Samuel 11:4), and that Onan, the son of Judah, should spill his seed upon the ground so as not to beget children (Genesis 38:9)? If these things are understood according to the letter, are they not condemned and mocked by pagans and unbelievers as though they were dung from the Scriptures? But if you examine them, wash them, and cook them in the fire of the Holy Spirit, they are transformed into food, and what was thought useless is found to be a mystery.

“You shall leave none of it until morning, and you shall not break any of its bones; whatever remains of it until morning you shall burn with fire” (Exodus 12:10). Let us not reserve any of the lamb’s flesh for the age to come; let us eat as much as we can. But if there are matters in it that are strong—namely, the Church’s doctrines concerning the Trinity, the resurrection, the soul, the angels, and other such matters—let us not discuss them according to our own opinions [Col. 1204] with perverse interpretations, and let us not break them. Rather, let us proclaim them as they are, in their strength.

If something should escape us as human beings, and we should be unable to eat it from the lamb’s flesh, we must know that in the age to come the teaching of the Holy Spirit will open it to us, and we shall eat it.

“You shall eat it in this manner: let your loins be girded, your sandals on your feet, and your staffs in your hands; and you shall eat it in haste, for it is the Passover of the Lord your God” (Exodus 12:11).

Up to this point the command has concerned what kind of flesh of the lamb we ought to eat. Now we are told in what manner we should eat it. “Let your loins,” he says, “be girded.” The Apostles are also told, “Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning in your hands” (Luke 12:35). John is girded with a leather belt (Matthew 3:4), and Elijah is described as having a belt, possessing nothing soft or womanish in himself but being entirely manly and austere—for he was a hairy man (2 Kings 1:8).

Therefore, if we wish to eat the flesh of the lamb, let us put to death our loins and the works of the flesh. Let what is said in Job concerning the devil—“His strength is in his loins, and his power in the navel of his belly” (Job 40:11)—be killed in us, so that the flesh may not lust against the spirit, but so that by the spirit we may put to death the works of the flesh; and, having been purified, may feed on the flesh of the lamb.

But so that you may know, dearest brothers, that whoever renders the marital debt to his wife cannot devote himself to prayer or eat the flesh of the lamb: Moses was commanded that the people who were about to ascend Mount Horeb should be purified beforehand for three days (Exodus 19:10), and when David came to the priest Ahimelech and was asked whether the young men were clean, he replied that they had been purified since yesterday and the day before yesterday (1 Samuel 21:4–5).

If the bread of the Presence could not be eaten by those who had touched their wives, how much more can that bread which came down from heaven not be violated or touched by those who shortly before had remained in marital embraces? We are not saying this to condemn marriage, but to say that at the time when we are going to eat the flesh of the lamb we ought to abstain from the works of the flesh.

As for what follows—“and your sandals on your feet, and your staff in your hands”—this commands that, as long as we walk through the wilderness of this age, we should be shod with the sandals of peace, lest a scorpion or serpent creep upon us in the desert, lest a snake attack the heel of one who walks. And if one should perhaps rise against us, let us have a staff in our hands, strike it, and say, “Your rod and your staff have themselves consoled me” (Psalm 22:4).

See the mystery of the Scriptures. As long as we walk through the solitudes, we need sandals to cover our feet. But when we enter the promised land, it is said to us with Joshua: “Remove the strap of your sandal, for the place on which you stand is holy” (Joshua 5:16).

Therefore, when we enter the kingdoms of heaven, we will have no need of sandals—not of those protections by which we are guarded in this world—but, to speak in a new way, we shall follow that lamb who was killed for us.

But see what John says about us: “These are the ones who did not defile their garments, for they remained virgins; they follow the Lamb wherever he goes” (Revelation 14:4)—Jesus Christ, to whom be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 1203]

# SERMON ON PSALM 41, FOR THE NEWLY BAPTIZED

This too is falsely attributed to Jerome in printed editions. (C, S)

The sons of Korah sing joyful things. Deer are enemies of serpents. The Church’s threefold fountain. The Trinity. The exercises of those to be baptized. The changed nature of the baptized.

Surveying the entire Psalter with an attentive mind, I nowhere find that the sons of Korah sang anything sorrowful. [Col. 1204] Their psalms are always joyful and pleasant; always despising earthly and lowly things, they desire heavenly and eternal things, corresponding to the interpretation of their name, since “Korah” means “Baldness.”

Therefore, because our Lord was crucified [Col. 1205] and buried in the place of Calvary (Matthew 27:33), all who believe in his cross and resurrection are called the sons of Korah—that is, the sons of Calvary. Upon that Calvary our Lord, the true Elisha, after his resurrection ascended to the kingdoms of heaven. He is mocked by the little children of the Jews, but bears devour the mockers (2 Kings 2:23–24). This brief statement about the title is sufficient; let us now return to the beginning of the Psalm.

“As the deer longs for the springs of water, so my soul longs for you, O God” (Psalm 41:2). It is the nature of deer to despise the venom of serpents. Indeed, they draw them out of their caves with their nostrils in order to kill and tear them apart. When the poison begins to seethe within them, although it cannot kill them, it nevertheless arouses the heat and burning of thirst. Then they long for springs and extinguish their burning poisons in the purest waters.

Therefore, just as those deer long for springs of water, so our deer, who departed from Egypt and from the world, killed Pharaoh in his deeds [Note: [Col. 1205] In Jerome: “in the waters.”] and drowned his entire army in Baptism. After killing the devil, they long for the Church’s springs: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

That the Father is a fountain is written in Jeremiah: “They have abandoned me, the fountain of living water, and have dug for themselves cracked cisterns that cannot hold water” (Jeremiah 2:13). Concerning the Son we read in one place: “They have abandoned the fountain of wisdom” (Baruch 3:12). Concerning the Holy Spirit: “Whoever drinks of the water that I shall give him will have within him a fountain of water springing up into eternal life” (John 4:13–14). The Evangelist immediately explains that the Savior was speaking of the Holy Spirit (John 7:39). From these passages it is most clearly demonstrated that the three fountains of the Church are the mystery of the Trinity.

The soul of the believer longs for these; the soul of the baptized longs for these [Note: [Col. 1205] In Jerome: “of the baptizer.” Perhaps it should be read: “of the one to be baptized.”] and says, “My soul thirsted for God, the living fountain” (Psalm 41:3). He did not wish merely to see God lightly or casually; he desired him with his whole ardor and thirsted with his entire burning desire.

Before they received Baptism, they spoke among themselves and said, “When shall I come and appear before the face of God?” (Ibid.) Behold, dearest brothers, what they were asking has been fulfilled. They have come and stood before the face of God; they have appeared before the sight of the altar and before the mystery of the Savior. [Note: [Col. 1205] In Jerome: “and they understood this mystery,” etc.]

They deserve to see this only if, from conscience and from the depths of their hearts, they say in remembrance, “My tears have been my bread day and night” (Ibid. 41:4). Throughout Lent they devoted themselves to prayer and fasting; they slept in sackcloth and ashes, seeking the future life through confession of their sins. But because they shed tears and were sorrowful, it is said to them, [Col. 1206] “Those who sow in tears will reap in joy” (Psalm 125:5), and, “Blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted” (Matthew 5:5).

While the devil was taunting them all on account of these things and saying, “Where is your God?”, now that they have been admitted to the body of Christ and reborn in the life-giving fountain, they speak confidently and say, “I will pass into the place of the wonderful tabernacle, even to the house of God” (Psalm 41:5).

The house of God is the Church; it is the wonderful tabernacle, because in it dwells the voice of rejoicing and confession and the sound of those feasting. The angels in heaven and all the powers rejoice over the faith and attainment of eternal life which our brothers now have deserved to receive. For if the angels rejoice and exult over one sinner who repents and over one sick little sheep carried on the shepherd’s shoulders, how much more do all the kingdoms of heaven exult over so many brothers reborn and cleansed in the life-giving flood, seeing human beings purified from the old stain of sins and prepared for their citizenship in heaven?

Therefore, you who have now put on Christ, and who, following our guide, are lifted from the abyss of this world by the word of God like little fish on a hook, say: “The nature of things has been changed in us.” Fish that have been drawn from the sea die; but the Apostles drew and fished us from the sea of this world so that we might become alive from the dead.

As long as we were in the world, our eyes were in the depths and our life moved about in filth. After we were rescued from the waves, we began to see the sun; we began to look upon the true light. And, overwhelmed by such great joy, we say to our soul, “Hope in God, for I shall confess him, the salvation of my countenance and my God.”

And afterward: “Therefore I shall remember you from the land of the Jordan and Hermon, from the little mountain. Deep calls to deep” (Psalm 41:6–8).

Let us also cry out to the Lord from the land of the Jordan—that is, from the river in which the Lord was baptized—and from Hermon, that is, from the curse of this world, since “Hermon” means “Anathema,” and from the little mountain of this world. For although someone may be holy, as long as he struggles in this world, he is not on a great and lofty mountain but on a small and lowly one. [Note: [Col. 1206] In Jerome: “moves about.”]

Let us cry out to the Lord, and let us interpret the depths of his Scriptures through other testimonies of Scripture. Whatever we cannot find in the deep of the Old Testament [Note: [Col. 1206] In Jerome: “the hidden [thing].”], we resolve from the hidden things of the New Testament in the voice of God’s waterfalls—that is, of his Prophets and Apostles. All the heights of the Lord, his waves, and the rush of the river that gladden the city of God (Psalm 45:5) have passed over us in Christ Jesus, to whom be glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 1205]

# SERMON ON WHY THE PRIESTS ANOINT THE EARS AND NOSTRILS OF THE NEWLY BAPTIZED WITH HOLY OIL

(C, G, S)

## Editorial Notice

Jacobus Sirmundus published this sermon together with the two that immediately follow it in an appendix after forty Augustinian sermons, judging that these three were certainly not Augustine’s, although the manuscript from Floriacum, from which he extracted them, attributed them to him. Their style is by no means unlike that of the sermons formerly numbered *On Time* 192, 193, and 194, now numbered 237, 238, and 239 in the Appendix to volume 5. In the manuscript they follow not only the Floriacum codex but also the very ancient Remigius codex, and in both codices they are likewise attributed to Augustine.

Ivo of Chartres also cites the three that follow under Augustine’s name in his decree *On Baptism*. But Ivo calls the sermon beginning “We promised” the third homily, and subsequently calls the one beginning “Thus far” the fourth homily; in the manuscripts mentioned above, however, they are fifth and sixth in order. In the Remigius manuscript, nevertheless, the sermon “We promised”—which is indeed fifth there—has near its beginning the following: “In the first and second preaching, therefore, we spoke only about these things . . . . . but now we are going to speak about the interior mysteries,” etc.; these words clearly support Ivo’s arrangement.

Leidrad, bishop of Lyon, transferred a considerable portion of the subsequent sermon, which begins “Everyone indeed,” into a book on Baptism that he published at the command of Charlemagne. The book was recently published in volume 3 of the *Analecta*, but Leidrad himself omits the author’s name.

The sermon beginning “Thus far” concerns the rite of washing the feet after Baptism. Ambrose is reported to say in book 3 of *On the Sacraments*, chapter 1, that this rite is not observed by the Roman Church.

[Col. 1207]

The mysteries are not entrusted to catechumens. What the anointing of the ears signifies. Who possesses ears for hearing. Why the nostrils are also anointed. Another interpretation of this mystery.

Every word of God, dearest brothers, ought to be heard with complete attention and care of mind, but especially the word that we are to address to your Charity today. For this reason, after the catechumens had already been dismissed, we retained only you to hear it. Beyond those things which all Christians together ought commonly to observe, we are going to speak specifically about heavenly mysteries, which cannot be heard except by those who, through the Lord’s gift, have already received them.

You ought therefore to hear what we say with all the greater reverence, insofar as these matters, entrusted only to the baptized and faithful hearers, are greater than those which even catechumens are accustomed to hear. But you should not be surprised, dearest brothers, that amid the mysteries themselves we said nothing to you about the mysteries, and that we did not immediately interpret what we had handed on. We did this not through negligence—for in matters so sacred and divine, negligence would be sacrilege—but through reverence.

We honored such sacred and divine things with the silence due to them, and amid those holy arrangements of the mysteries we ceased from the task of teaching, so that by remaining silent we might venerate more greatly the majesty of divine grace, which no human words can adequately explain.

But because it is necessary that your Dilection be instructed and taught in all things, now that the order of the mysteries has been completed we explain to you what we previously handed on, lest, because you do not understand the dignity of the divine mystery, you should consider it less precious. If you understand it, you will see that everything believed precious in this world is utterly insignificant in comparison with so great a sacrament. [Note: [Col. 1207] Ivo cites this under Augustine’s name, *On Baptism*, chapter 193.]

Let each one of you therefore recall the several forms of the mysteries which, through our ministry, by the Lord’s gift, you have received. What you then received simply [Note: [Col. 1207] In Ivo: “humbly.”] and faithfully, understand now wisely, so that you may better preserve what you have understood.

First, certainly, we anointed your ears with the oil of blessing. But recognize why, according to ecclesiastical tradition, this is done by all the Catholic priests of Christ. [Note: [Col. 1207] Leidrad, *On Baptism*, chapter 2, in volume 3 of the *Ancient Analecta*.]

The entrance of faith and of the whole sacred teaching is admitted into the soul through the ears, and understanding arises from hearing. No one can know the mysteries of faith unless he hears the one who preaches, as the blessed Apostle affirms when he says, “How will they hear without a preacher?” and again, “Faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of God” (Romans 10:14, 17).

Rightly, therefore, the organs of this sense are sanctified by that oil, without which faith cannot reach the soul. At the same time, those coming to Baptism are instructed to guard their ears undefiled by every evil and shameful word until the end, and, like the deaf, not to hear one who slanders his neighbor or one who speaks obscenely or immodestly. Thus they fulfill the statement of divine Scripture: “Fence your ears with thorns, and do not listen to an evil tongue” (Sirach 28:28); and elsewhere, “Do not believe every empty report”; and again, “Give your heart to discipline and prepare your ear for words of wisdom.” [Note: [Col. 1207] Ivo also cites these passages in the place mentioned above.]

The holy anointing applied to the ears therefore signifies that they should turn away from and flee every word outside the discipline of Christ, as though it contradicted his teaching, and should turn themselves to hearing only the words of God, because by that oil they have consecrated their hearing to the words of Christ.

The Savior himself speaks to the Father and glories in the obedience of the people who believe in him, saying, “You did not desire sacrifice and offering, but you perfected ears for me” (Psalm 39:7). The ears of Christ’s faithful are perfected when they desire to hear nothing except Christ and the things that belong to Christ.

[Col. 1208] Hence also in the Gospel the same Lord, when speaking about the mystery of the heavenly kingdom, said: “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear” (Matt. 13:9, 43). For although it is common to all to have ears, ears for hearing are not common to all. Whoever despises the words of God, although he cannot despise them unless he first hears them, nevertheless, because he despises what he hears, is said not to have heard; for he disdains what he has heard as though he had not heard it. And therefore such people have ears—not those called ears for hearing, but ears that hear in order not to hear, that is, so that they may despise what they have heard as though they had never heard it, as we said. Only those are said by Christ to have ears for hearing who, when they hear with their ears, firmly commit what they hear to their minds; and what they have entrusted to their minds, they carry out in their deeds. Of such hearers the Lord speaks in the Gospel: “Blessed are your eyes, because they see, and your ears, because they hear” (ibid., 16); and again: “Everyone who hears these words of mine and does them will be like a wise man who built his house upon rock. And the rain fell, and the rivers came, and the winds blew, and they beat upon that house, and it did not fall, for it had been founded upon rock.” Again, concerning those who hear badly, who indeed have ears but not for obedience, he declares: “Everyone who hears these words of mine and does not do them will be like a foolish man who built his house upon sand. And the rain fell, and the rivers came, and the winds blew, and they rushed upon that house, and it fell, and its fall was great” (Matt. 7:24–27). You see, therefore, how great is the difference between one who hears well and one who hears badly—that is, between the person who keeps the words of God and the person who, after hearing them, despises them as though they had never been heard. The one who obeys and acts is reckoned wise; the one who despises is reckoned foolish. The former builds upon a solid foundation; the latter’s vain building, without a foundation, is described as easily falling. There is stability in the one case; in the other, ruin—and great ruin. No one falls more grievously than the person who, after hearing the word of God, turns to the sins for which eternal punishments have been prepared. [Note: [Col. 1208] Ivo, *On Baptism*, chap. 193.]

But you, after your ears have been anointed with blessed oil, have been marked out among the number of wise hearers, so that, rightly retaining the words of God—that is, fulfilling what you hear—you may on the day of judgment hear Christ saying to you: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (ibid. 25:34).

Do not, however, think that it was done idly or without a definite sacramental meaning that we also anointed your nostrils with the oil of blessing. [Note: [Col. 1208] Leidradus, *On Baptism*, chap. 2, in volume 3 of the *Veterum Analectorum*.] This is understood to be done so that those who come to Baptism may be admonished to preserve the sacrament of so great a mystery inviolate and intact until death: so that, as long as they draw the breath of this life through their nostrils, they may not depart from the worship and service of Christ our Lord. Hence the holy man Job says: “The Lord lives, who has taken away my judgment, and the Almighty, who has brought bitterness upon my soul; for as long as breath remains in me, and the spirit of God is in my nostrils, my lips shall not speak iniquity, nor shall my tongue utter deceit. Far be it from me to judge you righteous; until I expire, I shall not depart from my innocence; I shall not abandon the justification which I once began to hold” (Job 27:2–6).

But an even subtler understanding is signified by this anointing of the nostrils. The fragrance of that oil, which has been blessed in the name and power of Christ, summons you to spiritual perception of fragrance, so that you may be able to sense Christ—not with the senses of the body but of the mind—with inestimable sweetness; and, delighted by knowledge of his fragrance, following his footsteps, you may be able to say what the chorus of believers says to God: “We shall run after you in the fragrance of your perfumes” (Song 1:3). The Apostle commends this fragrance to Christians when he says: “But thanks be to God, who always leads us in triumph in Christ Jesus, and manifests through us the fragrance of the knowledge of himself in every place; [Col. 1209] for we are the good fragrance of Christ to God” (2 Cor. 2:14–15). Consider how greatly the Apostles advanced in perceiving the fragrance of Christ and in commending it to others through the urgency of their preaching and the holiness of their life. [Note: [Col. 1209] Perhaps, “it” (*eum*).] While they [Col. 1210] spread everywhere the fragrance of Christ’s sweet perfume, they themselves also became a good fragrance to God. This too we desire to be fulfilled in you, most beloved brothers: that when you yourselves have received the good fragrance of the knowledge of Christ, a most sweet fragrance to God may also rise from the holiness of your life. Through the Lord.

[Col. 1209]

## SERMON ON THE MYSTERY OF BAPTISM (C, G)

The caution required of those being baptized. The grace of baptismal water. Those being baptized are questioned concerning faith in the Trinity. What faith is required concerning other matters. Faith in the resurrection. Triple immersion and its reason. Baptism is not repeated.

In our first treatise we promised that we would speak about all the mysteries which, through our ministry and the grace of Christ, you have received, lest some negligence arising from ignorance be born in you. But we had regard for your labor and memory, taking precautions lest either your mind, wearied by listening, should be unable to understand everything, or your memory, burdened by learning many things at once, should quickly lose even what it had understood. Therefore, in our first preaching [Note: [Col. 1209] The Remigian manuscript and Ivo, *On Baptism*, chap. 194, add: “and second.”] we spoke only about those things which, before you came to the holy font, we handed on to you according to the ordinances of the Catholic rule; and we interpreted what the anointing signified, which, applied to different parts of your bodies, indicates different meanings, insofar as the Lord has deigned to grant it. We showed that through the oil of sanctification you had been prepared for hearing with complete faith, and that, called to possess the good fragrance of Christ, you had been admonished to renounce the devil with your whole heart.

Now, however, we are going to speak about the inner mysteries that were celebrated in the holy font itself. After you had made the most solemn pledge, by which you promised to renounce all his pomp and works, and every fornication of the devil, you descended into the font—the sacred font, the font of life, the font of redemption, the font sanctified by heavenly power; sanctified in such a way that, by washing away the sins of human beings, it sanctifies them after many transgressions. You must not judge those waters with your eyes but with your mind. For although the substance of that water belongs to the common nature of waters, its effect is nevertheless special and proceeds from the grace and power of God, who created the waters by which bodily impurities and visible stains are washed away. He himself therefore sanctified the waters, so that by the hidden power of his might he might wash away through them sins that are not seen. For the Holy Spirit works in that water, so that those who before Baptism were held guilty of various crimes and were destined to burn with the devil in the hell of eternal fire might, after Baptism, deserve to enter the kingdom of heaven. Hence, expressing the power of so great a sacrament, the Lord says in the Gospel: “Unless someone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” (John 3:5).

In this font, therefore, before we immersed you with your whole body, we asked: “Do you believe in God the almighty Father?” You answered: “I believe.” Again we asked: “Do you also believe in Jesus Christ, his Son, who was born of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary?” Each of you answered: “I believe.” Again we asked: “And in the Holy Spirit?” You answered likewise: “I believe.” We did this according to the command of our Lord Jesus Christ the Savior. When he was ascending to the Father in heaven, he charged his disciples—that is, the Apostles—saying: “Go, baptize all nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe all things whatsoever I have commanded you” (Matt. 28:19).

But when someone hears “Father and Son and Holy Spirit,” let no one suppose that we confess three gods. Far be such sacrilege from our faith, for we have learned from his own testimony that there is one God: “I am God, and there is no other besides me; a just God and a Savior, there is none besides me. Turn to me, and you shall be saved, for I am God from the ends of the earth, and there is no other besides me” (Isa. 45:21–22). And in another book: “Hear, O Israel: the Lord your God is one God.” And again: “The Lord your God is God in heaven above and on earth below, and there is no other besides [Col. 1210] him” (Deut. 6:4; 4:39).

We therefore hold and believe in three persons: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—of one power, one substance, one eternity, one will, and also one deity; and we venerate the whole Trinity under the designation of one God. To believe in several gods is pagan impiety; and, again, not to believe in three persons of one substance in one deity and equality, or coeternity, is heretical madness. For manifest is the authority of Christ that we have cited: “Baptize all nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.”

[Note: [Col. 1210] Ivo, *On Baptism*, chap. 194.]

When we asked, “Do you believe in the holy Church, and the forgiveness of sins, and the resurrection of the flesh?” we did not ask in such a way that you should believe in the holy and catholic Church as you believe in God. It is holy and catholic because it rightly believes in God. We therefore did not say that you should believe in the Church as though you were to believe in it as in God; rather, understand that we say—and said—that, while living in the holy and catholic Church, you should believe in God; and that you should also believe in the resurrection of the flesh, which is to come. Therefore, just as you believed in the mystery of the Trinity and received the one God in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; just as you believed that your sins were to be forgiven, and now through Baptism believe that they have been forgiven; so also believe that the resurrection of the flesh is to come—which indeed you promised to believe.

For the whole hope of Christians consists in this: that we believe in truth that this same body, not another, will rise; and that, just as we now stand in the church before the altar of God, so we shall stand on the day of judgment before the tribunal of God, as the blessed Apostle Paul says: “For we must all be manifested before the tribunal of Christ, so that each may receive what belongs to his own body, according to what he has done, whether good or evil” (2 Cor. 5:10). This is what faithless souls do not believe will happen. And there are some who promise with their lips that they believe, but despair in their hearts. They do great injury to almighty God, since they do not believe that human beings can be raised and brought to life after death.

But we, who give credence to the divine utterances, cannot doubt our resurrection. For we believe that the God who made human beings when they did not previously exist can easily restore those who once existed. He who made heaven, earth, and the seas, and what is in them, and all the elements, from nothing—how could he not restore human beings, whom he made for the purpose that in this life they should do what would be judged in another, and should deserve either rewards for a good will or punishments for an evil one?

This is the faith of Catholic Christians: that we believe we shall rise with this same soul with which we now live, possessing a sufficient example of resurrection in Christ himself, our Lord, the Word of the Father. Although he is God and the Son of God, God the Word, and according to the substance of his divinity coeternal and consubstantial with the Father, he therefore assumed a human being from our nature—according to which he willed to be born of a Virgin and afterward to suffer and die, and on the third day to rise and ascend into heaven—in order to kindle us to the hope of resurrection. Thus we believe that we shall be raised from the dead just as we confess that Christ rose from the dead.

[Col. 1211] Hence the blessed Apostle rebukes the minds of unbelievers, saying: “But if Christ is preached as having risen from the dead, how do some among you say that there is no resurrection of the dead?” (1 Cor. 15:12). Hold this, therefore, firmly and believe what is affirmed by the divine utterances: that there will be a resurrection in which glorious immortality will be given to all the saints who love Christ and do his will, so that they may rejoice forever in the presence of God with the angels and heavenly Powers. But unbelievers and sinners, and those who do not do the commandments of God, will rise for this purpose: that their flesh, made immortal, may be assigned to eternal fires; that it may burn forever and never be consumed by burning. For this too is attested by the word of our Lord Jesus Christ, who pronounced in the Gospel concerning sinners: “Then the wicked will go into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life” (Matt. 25:46).

These, then, are the things we have said up to this point. [Note: [Col. 1211] Ivo, *On Baptism*, chap. 194.] After you promised to believe, we immersed your heads three times in the sacred font. This order of Baptism is celebrated with a twofold sacramental meaning. You were rightly immersed three times because you received Baptism in the name of the Trinity. You were rightly immersed three times because you received Baptism in the name of Jesus Christ, who rose from the dead on the third day. That repeated threefold immersion expresses the type of the Lord’s burial, through which you were buried with Christ in Baptism and, with Christ, [Col. 1212] rose in faith, so that, washed from sins, you might live by imitating Christ in the holiness of virtues.

Hence the blessed Apostle says: “Do you not know that all of us who have been baptized in Christ Jesus have been baptized into his death? For we were buried with him through Baptism into death, so that just as Christ rose from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too might walk in newness of life. For if we have been planted together in the likeness of his death, we shall also be so in the likeness of his resurrection; knowing this, that our old man was crucified together with him, so that we might destroy the body of sin, and that we might no longer serve sin” (Rom. 6:3–6).

Consider, most beloved brothers, under what condition the Apostle said that the baptized exist: “so that we might no longer serve sin.” What greater thing is there—not negligence, but madness—than, after receiving the forgiveness of sins through Baptism, to wish to be bound by sins; so that one who had been made holy from a sinner should wish once again to become a sinner from a holy person; and after that sacred font, in which one may be washed only once, to return again to the filth of vices?

Pay attention, therefore, most beloved, so that what you have received—what you can no longer receive again—may be preserved by you whole and undefiled to the end; and, once made without sin, so that you may depart from all sins forever. For Christ, who in his mercy cleansed you when you had been polluted and stained by the devil’s persuasion, does not wish those whom he has cleansed to be stained again. To him be glory and honor, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, forever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 1211]

## SERMON ON THE ANOINTING OF THE HEAD AND THE WASHING OF THE FEET (G)

What the pouring of chrism upon the baptized signifies. That the promises made in Baptism should be diligently fulfilled.

Up to this point we have spoken about the mysteries celebrated either before the sacrament of Baptism or in Baptism itself. [Note: [Col. 1211] Ivo, *On Baptism*, chap. 195: “which are completed through the sacrament in Baptism itself,” etc.] Now, however, we shall treat of those things which, by holy institution, are completed for those who have already been baptized.

After Baptism has been completed, we pour chrism—that is, the oil of sanctification—upon your heads. This demonstrates that, through the Lord, royal and priestly dignity is conferred upon the baptized. For in the Old Testament those who were chosen for the priesthood or kingdom were anointed with holy oil; and by the anointing of the head some received from the Lord the power to reign over the people of God, others the power to offer sacrifices. Just as we read that holy David and the other kings were anointed by the Prophets and transformed from private persons into kings through the oil of sanctification, so also we read that holy Aaron was anointed by Moses and consecrated from a layman into a priest of the Lord with holy oil. Hence it is sung in the Psalm: “Like ointment upon the head, which descended upon the beard, the beard of Aaron” (Ps. 132:2).

But that oil in the Old Testament conferred a temporal kingdom and a temporal priesthood, for these had to be administered in this life, which ends within the course of a few years. This chrism, however—that is, this anointing which has been placed upon you—has conferred upon you the dignity of that kingdom and that priesthood which, once conferred, will never end.

Perhaps you are surprised that we have said that through that chrism you have obtained the kingdom of future glory and the priesthood. It is not I but the Apostle Peter—or rather, Christ speaking through the Apostle—who declares that this dignity has been conferred upon you. For he speaks in this way to the faithful, that is, to those who have been washed in Baptism and consecrated with chrism: “But you are a royal and priestly race, a holy nation, a people of acquisition, so that you may proclaim the virtues of him who called you from darkness into his marvelous light” (1 Pet. 2:9).

Consider, therefore, the honor which you have received in that mystery, and take care lest, after being made sons of the kingdom through Baptism following your sins, you should, by sinning again—God forbid—wish to become sons of hell. [Col. 1212] For how do you suppose that God will not be angry if, after his benefits and the forgiveness of sins, you wish to return to sinning; and if, after being adopted as sons of God, you wish once again, like slaves, to despise God and do the devil’s will?

When all the sacraments had been completed, we also handed on to you a commandment both by example and by word. For we washed the feet of each of you, [Note: [Col. 1212] This rite was still observed in certain churches in the twelfth century, as Hugh of Saint-Victor testifies in his commentary on John 13, where he says that some wished original sin not to be forgiven except through the washing of the feet after Baptism, and claimed Ambrose, bishop of Milan, as the authority for this. See his *On the Initiation of the Catechumens*, chap. 6.] urging you to imitate us—or rather, our Lord and Savior himself—so that, just as we washed your feet, so you too should wash the feet of your brothers and guests. We teach you not merely to be hospitable, but also humbly to honor those guests whom you have received into your lodgings, so that you are not ashamed to fulfill toward them the duty of servants.

But if anyone considers this degrading and, puffed up with diabolical pride, disdains to carry out the Lord’s command; if, although noble in this world, he is ashamed to wash the feet of poor Christians and of those who are despised in this world—he who both commanded this and did it, or rather, who deigned to do it before commanding it, since he set the example beforehand so that he might more easily commend the command—then let him hear what we read in the Gospel concerning the Lord Jesus:

“Knowing,” he says, “that the Father had given all things into his hands, and that he had come from God and was going to God, he rises from supper, lays aside his garments, and, having taken a towel, girds himself. Then he pours water into a basin and begins to wash the feet of the disciples and to wipe them with the towel with which he was girded.” And again: “After he had washed their feet, he took his garments; and when he had reclined again, he said to them: ‘Do you know what I have done to you? You call me Teacher and Lord, and you speak rightly, for so I am. If I, then, Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, how much more ought you to wash one another’s feet? For I have given you an example, so that just as I have done to you, you also should do. Amen, amen, I say to you: a servant is not greater than his lord, nor an apostle greater than the one who sent him. If you know these things, blessed are you if you do them’” (John 13:3–5, 12–17).

Consider, therefore, most beloved brothers, how great an unhappiness and how great a madness it is for a servant to disdain washing the feet of a fellow servant, or a disciple the feet of a fellow disciple, when the Lord and Master of all deigned to wash the feet of servants and disciples. He humbled himself before his inferiors; we, however, disdain to humble ourselves before equals and often before those who are better than we are. This arises from nothing other than unbelief concerning the future. For if we truly and wholeheartedly believed that through these commandments of the Lord, which we observe during the brief period of our life, we shall attain eternal and heavenly rewards, we would not merely be unashamed to fulfill every work of humility—we would even glory in doing so.

Commit firmly, therefore, to your memory what you have heard from us, and what you promised to us—or rather, to the Lord. [Note: [Col. 1213] The promise concerning the washing of the feet in Baptism is found in the appendix to volume 5, sermons 168, no. 3, and 257, no. 2.] Let no tribulation of the present life ever take away from you the memory of your pledge. Fulfill all the commands you have heard; fulfill all that you promised.

Do not become like the Jewish people. When they had heard the commandments of God, they rightly said: “Everything that the Lord has commanded us, we shall hear and do.” But they neglected what they had promised well. They pleased God when they promised that they would keep his commandments. Thus we read that the people of Israel said to Moses: “Come near, and hear all that the Lord our God says to you; and you shall speak to us all that the Lord our God says [Col. 1214] to us, and we shall hear and do it.” And the Lord said to Moses: “I have heard the words of the speech of this people, all that they have spoken. Who will grant that their heart may be such within them, that they may fear me and observe my commandments all their days?” (Deut. 5:27–29).

They pleased God, as we said, when they promised that they would do his commandments; but they displeased him when they transgressed the commandments given to them, which they had promised to keep. Of them the Prophet says: “They loved him with their mouth, and with their tongue they lied to him” (Ps. LXVII, 36). For this is to love God with the mouth and not with the heart: they promise that they will do God’s will, they lie with their tongue, and they flee back to doing the devil’s will, provoking almighty God to anger, since he does not allow himself to be mocked.

He sees the deeds of human beings, even when they are done in secret; he hears every word, even when it is whispered secretly; he understands and recognizes the thoughts of everyone. He will judge with the utmost severity. Here he does not always punish those who despise him because he has determined that there will be a judgment in the future, where eternal condemnation and everlasting punishment are reserved for sinners. There will be the weeping of the eyes and the gnashing of teeth. There, as the Lord himself says: “Their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be extinguished” (Isa. 66:24).

But you, most beloved brothers, we believe in the name of the Lord, do not hear our words—or rather, divine words—only superficially, because what we say to you we borrow from the holy and divine utterances. We hope in the Lord that you will do all that you have promised, with God assisting you in holy works through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ himself, to whom be glory and honor with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 1213]

## TREATISE ON THE CREATION OF THE FIRST HUMAN BEING (S)

### ADMONITION

In Ambrose it is entitled *On the Dignity of the First Human Being*. In Alcuin, however, *Sayings of the Blessed Albinus the Levite on the passage of Genesis: “Let us make man in our image and likeness.”* Paulinus of Aquileia, in the above-mentioned book *On Salutary Instructions*, chapters 2 and 3, borrowed several things from this very treatise. Moreover, it is inserted in its entirety in the book *On the Spirit and the Soul*, chapter 35. Here, therefore, it is enough to give the first and last words.

The dignity of the human condition is recognized as being so great that the human being was created not merely by the word of command, as were the other works of the six days, but by the counsel of the holy Trinity and the work of the divine majesty [lacuna]. [Note: [Col. 1213] Repeat the omitted material from the book *On the Spirit and the Soul*.]

Therefore let everyone attend more carefully to the excellence of his first condition, and recognize in himself the venerable image of the holy Trinity; and let him strive to possess the honor of the [Col. 1214] divine likeness, for which he was created, through nobility of conduct, the practice of virtues, and the dignity of his merits. Thus, when what he is has been revealed, he may then appear like the one who wondrously fashioned him according to his likeness in the first Adam and more wondrously restored him in the second.

[Col. 1213]

## SERMON ON THE VANITY OF THE WORLD

It is found above, in Eligius’s treatise *On the Uprightness of Catholic Conduct*, §§21, 22, and 23, apart from approximately ten verses at the end beginning with the words, “Let us therefore bless the Lord,” etc.

Placed in this life, brothers, act in such a way that, when you have departed from here and your flesh has begun to be devoured by worms in the grave, your soul, adorned with good works, may rejoice in heaven with all the saints. Let the death of those whom you have sent ahead restrain you from evil works or sins [lacuna]. [Note: [Col. 1213] Repeat the omitted material from Eligius’s treatise *On the Uprightness of Catholic Conduct*.]

And then, the more obedient anyone here has been to God than another, the greater reward he will receive there; and the more anyone here has loved God, the more closely he will see him. Let us therefore bless the Lord our God, brothers, who has gathered us for spiritual joy. Let us always be humble [Col. 1214] in heart, and let our joy be with him. Let us not be puffed up by any prosperity of this world; but let us know that our happiness exists only when these things have passed away. Now, brothers, let our joy be in future hope; let eternal life be our entire desire; let all our sighs breathe toward Christ. Let us desire that one supremely beautiful one, who loved the ugly in order to make them beautiful; let us run toward him alone, sigh for him, and always say: “Let the Lord be magnified, who desire the peace of his servant” (Ps. 35:27).

[Col. 1215]

## SERMON ON CONTEMPT FOR THE WORLD

[Note: [Col. 1215] The manuscripts add: “to Clerics.”]

By an unknown author. (G, S)

### CHAPTER ONE. Some commandments are special, others common.

Hear, most beloved brothers, the life-giving teaching of our Father—you who desire not an earthly but an eternal inheritance; who do not wish to receive a portion in the land of the dying, but to sing with the Psalmist: “My portion in the land of the living” (Ps. 142:6); who have left Egypt and are hastening toward the land of promise.

Hear, then, possessing ears for hearing, the loving Father calling us to the inheritance of heaven and saying: “Come, children, hear me; I will teach you the fear of the Lord. Who is the person who desires life?” (Ps. 34:12–13). Who are you who desire to enter into life? Keep the commandments of God.

Some of these commandments are special, while others are common. The special ones belong properly to canons or clerics and to monks; the common ones belong to all Catholics. The special commandments are these: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell everything you possess and give to the poor, and follow me.” And again: “Everyone who has left house, or field, or father, or mother, or brothers, or sisters, or children, or fields for my sake will receive a hundredfold and will possess eternal life.” And to the disciples: “You who have followed me, in the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits upon the throne of his majesty, you also will sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. 19:21, 29, 28). These commandments, therefore, the more singular they are, the more excellent; the more severe, the more pleasing to God.

### CHAPTER TWO. Clerics should possess nothing as their own.

Our Savior says again, among other things: “Whoever does not renounce all that he possesses cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14:33). By saying “all,” he intended that his disciples should possess nothing as their own. Whoever possesses anything on earth is removed from the discipline of Christ. But if he is not a disciple of Christ, how does he presume to have the power of binding and loosing?

Pay attention, brothers, to the words of the Gospel: “Jesus entered through closed doors to the disciples, and, breathing upon them, said: ‘Receive the Holy Spirit. Whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them; and whose you retain, they are retained’” (John 20:22–23). Did those men possess anything as their own, to whom the Master had commanded: “Carry nothing on the road” (Luke 9:3), and concerning whom Luke the evangelist reports: “Everything was common to them” (Acts 4:32)?

See what Peter said to Jesus: “Behold, we have left all things and followed you” (Matt. 19:27). Those who had left everything had kept absolutely nothing for themselves. How, then, do those who presume to possess property on earth arrogate to themselves the power of binding and loosing? How are they not ashamed to say: “The Lord is the portion of my inheritance” (Ps. 16:5)?

Where is that apostolic saying: “What agreement is there between Christ and Belial?” (2 Cor. 6:15). Those who do not wish to leave earthly possessions—why do they eat the sins of the people? If they receive tithes with the sons of Levi, how will they receive a portion among the other tribes? If they attend to the etymology of their name, why are clerics called *clerici*—from *cleros*, “lot”—unless because the Lord is their lot or inheritance?

### CHAPTER THREE. Why they are shorn. The seat of wisdom is in the brain.

Why do they not at least consider the signs of their clerical status, by which they are distinguished from laymen? For their heads are not shaved and tonsured without reason, but for a most perceptive and evident purpose. By these signs they are separated from the way of life of laymen. Since this may, with God’s favor, benefit many, we have thought it most useful to insert it into this admonition.

We have learned from the authority of many Fathers that the brain is the seat of wisdom; and that Christ, as Paul testifies, is the Power and Wisdom of God (1 Cor. 1:24). Since, therefore, the brain is in the head, and wisdom, according to the authority of the Fathers, has its seat in the brain, and since through the wisdom infused into it all the members are governed from the head, which is so through the brain, the seat of wisdom, we cut the hair on that part of the head in which we recognize the new Wisdom—that is, Christ—to be present, in order to show that no obstacle stands between ourselves and the true [Col. 1216] Wisdom. As we have said, this Wisdom is Christ, who according to the Apostle is also our head—for he said: “The head of a woman is the man, but the head of a man is Christ, and the head of Christ is God” (1 Cor. 11:3). By this we signify that the evil preoccupation with earthly things hinders the eyes of our mind from contemplating God.

For we know that the more anyone becomes entangled in earthly occupations, the more he is hindered from seeing his Creator. Hence the Apostle says: “No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in secular affairs” (2 Tim. 2:4). Likewise: “The unmarried person thinks about the things of God” (1 Cor. 7:32).

For this reason Moses says: “Let the Levites shave the hair of their flesh” (Num. 8:7). *Levite* is interpreted as “one who has been taken up.” Whoever, therefore, has been taken up into divine offices ought to shave the hair of his flesh—that is, the superfluous thoughts of his heart. To shave the head, therefore, signifies cutting away earthly and superfluous thoughts from the mind.

Nor is it inappropriate that superfluous thoughts are signified by hairs and locks. For just as hairs are not a part of the body but a kind of excess proceeding from the body’s moisture, so temporal goods are not natural to us but foreign and superfluous. Therefore the faithful of Christ, who yearn from the depths of their being for eternal life, who trample the world and its pleasures beneath their feet, who do not wish to possess anything on earth but say with the Apostle, “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. 3:20), retain only a very small portion of hair upon their heads, signifying through its removal that they have only a minimal concern for earthly things.

For this reason they also retain that small portion of hair, because while they are in this world they cannot be entirely free from earthly thoughts. Therefore, whatever cleric, called to the lot of the Lord, grows his hair and is ashamed to shave or cut it, plainly testifies that he belongs not to the lot of God but to the lot of the world. For the more anyone loves, fosters, and nourishes the hairs of his flesh, the more he shows that his heart is fixed not in heaven but on earth; but the more he shaves and subdues them, the more he proves that he loves not earthly things but eternal ones.

### CHAPTER FOUR. They should not cover their heads while praying.

If, as we said earlier, we shave our hair for this reason—that we may demonstrate that nothing intervenes between us and God—it is clearly established that, when we persist in prayer, we ought not to place foreign coverings upon our heads, especially since the Apostle says: “A man ought not to pray with his head covered, for he is the image of God” (1 Cor. 11:7).

Let clerics, therefore, who devote themselves to psalmody and spiritual hymns cease to wear hair, miters, and other coverings upon their heads, lest, while we speak with God, hiding the signs of his service, we be judged unworthy of the favor of the one whose salutary teaching we presume not to obey. For whoever does not obey the Apostle contradicts the Gospel. And according to the voice of that same Apostle: “Do you seek proof of Christ speaking in me?” (2 Cor. 13:3). Likewise: “If an angel from heaven should preach to you a gospel other than the one you have received, let him be anathema” (Gal. 1:8).

Let such presumption therefore be completely uprooted from the clergy, lest—God forbid—its prayer be driven away by God.

### CHAPTER FIVE. They should despise the world and worldly things. The weapons of the world; earthly estates.

[Source ends here.]

Having thus prefaced these clerical signs, by which we ought to be distinguished from laypeople, let us return to the admonition proposed. Let us hear the apostle John saying, “Do not love the world, nor the things that are in the world” (1 John 2:15). Let us also hear the Psalmist rebuking lovers of the world: “Sons of men, why do you love vanity and seek falsehood?” (Psalm 4:3). Solomon likewise follows, saying, “Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity” (Ecclesiastes 1:2).

[Col. 1217]

It is pleasing to observe how harmoniously the instruments of the Holy Spirit sound together. The Apostle admonishes us not to love the world; the Psalmist attacks its lovers; Solomon cries out that everything is subject to vanity. Why we should not love the world—or pursue falsehood [Note: [Col. 1217] The Royal manuscript reads “lest” (*ne*).]—Ecclesiastes explains, as though he were saying: “For this reason the things below are not to be loved: because they are transient falsehoods; because the things they promise they do not bestow, and therefore are not good.” For since God is the author of every good thing, and commands his faithful to seek and love all that is good, if worldly things were true goods, he himself would not despise them, nor command his followers to despise them.

What, then, does the Truth testify about himself? Let us hear: “Foxes have dens, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head” (Matthew 8:20). Again, if the glory of the world were not vain, he would not have hidden himself when the crowds wanted to make him king. Again, if the glory of the world were not vain, and if earthly riches were true goods, the Lord would not reproach their possessors, saying, “Woe to you who are rich,” and so forth (Luke 6:24). And elsewhere: “It is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 19:24).

Let us also hear what he says to those who imitate him: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell everything you have, and give to the poor” (ibid., 21). Again: “Unless someone renounces everything that he possesses, he cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14:33). Again: “No one can serve two masters—that is, God and Mammon” (Matthew 6:24).

The skillful teacher saw that his disciples would struggle with the world and that, if they possessed something by which they could be held, they would be thrown down more easily. Therefore he took weapons away from our enemies and his own, when he deprived us of earthly possessions. For a naked man is not usually afraid of robbers; but whoever entangles himself in worldly things prepares weapons by which he may be pierced. Whoever, therefore, does not wish to be pierced should proceed naked along the road of this exile.

## CHAPTER VI. Let them desire the kingdom of God. Let them love God and their neighbor. Let them receive the cup of Christ.

Perhaps someone will ask: Since God commands his followers to set worldly things aside, what does he command them to desire? Hear him himself saying: “Seek the kingdom of God.” Again: “Lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven” (Matthew 6:33, 20).

Someone will ask again: If God wishes people to hate earthly things, what ought they to love? These are the things he commanded us to love when, through Moses, he replied: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and your neighbor as yourself” (Deuteronomy 6:5). We are commanded to love our neighbor only on earth, because he shares with us the inheritance of the heavenly kingdom.

There, filled with divine love, as Scripture testifies—for it says that we should love our fellow citizens as ourselves (Leviticus 19:18)—with God’s favor we shall accomplish this through him by whom we were redeemed and shall live without end. He also loved us first when, because of our evil works, we were his enemies; and when we were useless servants, he adopted us as his sons and heirs, handing over his only-begotten Son for us, so that he might rescue us from the snare of eternal death.

What child could worthily love so kind a father? Who could repay anything worthy of such great benefits? Amazed at these immense benefits, the Psalmist says: “What shall I repay the Lord for all that he has repaid me?” Then he adds to this very question: “I will take the cup of salvation” (Psalm 115:12–13), and so forth.

However small this repayment may be—namely, to receive the Lord’s cup—nothing else seems so worthily to correspond to the Lord’s passion. This is the meaning: just as he gave his blood for our redemption, so we should pour out our own blood in confession of his name.

[Col. 1218]

But how will someone give his blood for Christ who is unwilling to cast away the vanity of the world for him, when we love our possessions less than ourselves? How will someone surrender his life for Christ who possesses these vain and false things contrary to his commands? For he himself says: “If you love me, keep my commandments” (John 14:15). The apostle John also says: “Whoever says that he loves God and does not keep his commandments is a liar” (1 John 2:4). Therefore the person who refuses to keep his commandments is proved to love himself and not God.

## CHAPTER VII. Let them pursue poverty. The blessedness of poverty.

Since Christ became poor and needy for us, why are we ashamed to be poor for him? Does his poverty not make us rich, since the Truth testifies that the kingdom of heaven belongs not to the rich but to the poor? For he says to the poor: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 5:3).

If the kingdom of heaven belongs to the poor, it remains that hell belongs to the rich.
