Therefore have peace with everyone, while hating the vices of all. Have peace in heart, mouth, and deed. For if Cain had had peace in his heart, he would not have attacked his brother. If Absalom had had peace in his mouth, he would not have despised his father. If Judas had had peace in his deed, he would not have fled to the noose.

O how good, how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together, so that there may be one heart, one will, one soul of all, and one manner of life! For the devil cannot enter a house or mind in which peace reigns.

O how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together! So great is the excellence of this virtue that the prophet first expressed his wonder at it before showing what it was or what benefit it possessed. What great amazement he placed first when he said, “Behold!” What wonderful benefit he proclaimed when he added, “How good and how pleasant” (Psalm 132:1)!

But you must know, my brothers, that some things are good but not pleasant, and some things are pleasant but not good. For example, fasts, vigils, mortifications, and similar practices are good. They are good but not pleasant, because the flesh does not rejoice in them but is harmed. Feasts and drunkenness are pleasant, but they are not good. Those who do such things rejoice when they have done evil and exult in the worst deeds.

O monk, you will scarcely be able to find in the present life one thing that is both good and pleasant. Do you nevertheless desire to find that one thing? Seek peace and embrace it. For this is the sole virtue that possesses both goodness and pleasantness.

This is that goodness which makes us dwell with one manner in the house, so that we may always desire to live and die together. In the present we dwell together, and in the future we shall receive the reward of eternal joy.

O peace, serenity of mind, tranquility of spirit, simplicity of heart, bond of love, fellowship of charity! This is that highest happiness which removes enmities, restrains wars, curbs anger, tramples the proud, loves the humble, calms the discordant, reconciles enemies, pleases everyone, and is desired by everyone. Yet by all evil people that peace which is good is fled and hated like death.

O peace, you do not know how to be exalted; you do not know how to be puffed up. Blessed is the one who has you; accursed is the one who hates you and who obstructs and breaks you among human beings, for he is the Antichrist and the son of perdition.

O peace, whoever has you, let him hold you; whoever does not have you, let him seek you; whoever has lost you, let him search for you, if he greatly desires to be a son of God.

O peace, you are such a good among created things, so wondrous and so glorious, that nothing sweeter is usually heard, nothing more delightful desired, nothing more useful possessed. For just as the human spirit never gives life to the members unless they are united, so the Holy Spirit never gives us life unless we are united in peace.

Yet, as we have said, no one exists who does not wish to have peace. Ask everyone whether they desire peace: all with one voice will say, “This we love, this we desire, this we long for, this we want.”

If therefore, brothers, people love peace, let them love justice also, because these are two most beloved friends. Justice and peace kiss one another; but if you do not love the friend of peace, will peace itself love you and wish to dwell with you? Far from it.

Therefore love peace by loving justice. For this peace is given by the angels to people of good will. Do the angels also offer peace to people of perverse will? Far from it. And who are people of perverse will more than those who, with proud eyes and insatiable hearts, never say, “Enough”? Such people can never have peace.

Therefore, my brothers, since we have begun to trample upon the world and despise all earthly things, let us not desire riches; nor let us who are poor in the desert be lifted up into pride by riches. For it is in no way fitting that in this solitary life, where senators become laborers, laborers should become idle; and that we who came after leaving riches, who were masters of estates, should become pampered peasants.

In the end, the one who desires to possess nothing from the world has peace. He is tranquil; he rejoices in all good things, as that pagan said:

> Human beings would lead a most peaceful life on earth if these two words—“mine” and “yours”—were removed from the nature of all.

O blessed poverty, everywhere full of peace, everywhere secure, everywhere unharmed, everywhere the friend of all! For whoever loves you loves true peace; and whoever does not love you knows nothing of complete tranquility.

But some servant of God may say: “Behold, I see rich men who are proud, haughty, impious, and lacking every perfect goodness; yet one thing is apparent: they have peace among themselves.” What then? Should I rejoice in their wicked concord? I do not know whether I should grieve.

O monk, know that just as discord among the good does great harm, so it is greatly to be lamented when there is peace among the wicked. For all the worst things that can be done or imagined among human beings increase when the wicked live peacefully; but when they quarrel, the world is somewhat calmed.

For just as the concord of the wicked is contrary to the concord of the good, so it is to be desired that the good have peace and that the wicked be at odds. For through discord the wicked are sometimes made very good, recognizing what they are and what they will be. While they are afflicted and their faces are filled with disgrace, they sometimes seek the name of the Lord, which nevertheless had never been loved in their hearts in a time of peace.

Yet we must pray that the good may also be held in goodness to the end, and that the wicked may be converted before they reach the end.

But you, brothers, love peace with one another; and may that peace guard your hearts and your understanding, which surpasses all sense.

## SERMON THREE. ON SILENCE

Silence, dearest brothers, is supremely necessary for you in the desert among all other things. Everything that does not build up becomes a danger to those who speak and those who hear. Our tongue must follow both our understanding and reason, not our will.

We must not merely keep our eyes closed, but also preserve our tongues unharmed within our teeth. For empty speech is an indication of an empty conscience. As you are, such are the speeches you utter; and such as your mind is, so it is proved to be. As you have been in your deeds, so you are proved to be in your words.

Very foolish is the one who does not first bring a word to the tongue of reason before bringing it out to the tongue of the mouth. The verbosity of the mouth portrays in speech what a person is in mind. Verbosity turns a person into a jester, lays aside the dignity of human nature, seizes honors for itself, and acquires innumerable enemies.

Finally, the restlessness of the tongue inflames adolescence toward frivolity, mature age toward deceit, and old age toward slander. This little spark must therefore be extinguished, lest it turn into a great flame; the sapling must be cut off, lest it grow into a forest; the drop must be stopped, lest it swell into a spring.

It is greater, brothers, to restrain the tongue than to capture a city, because the latter attacks from outside, whereas the former attacks within. Here weapons are taken up against yourself, while there they are taken up against another.

The greatest shame and humiliating disgrace is to be unable to restrain the tongue and to be unable to bind a lowly member. Behold, the tongue seeks to go out and searches for movement. But you, O monk, restrain it through temperance; fasten upon it the bolt of reason; circumcise it with the maturity of discernment.

O tongue, you introduce danger, you produce mourning, you often create discord, you give birth to the poison of detraction, and you lead those who trust you to hell. O monk, recognize the wicked tongue; flee it, despise it, and, if you can, put it to shame.

But I wish to teach your tongue to speak well. Do you wish to speak well? Give it measured movement [Note: [Col. 1239] Elsewhere, “measure.”]; for a precious tongue knows only how to construct divine words continually. O how holy is the mouth from which heavenly utterances always burst forth!

O monk, consider that you will render an account for every idle word, and all the more because you are less bound to the world. You ought not to live in the marketplace but in a cell; you ought not to nourish a household, but the souls of households through prayer.

It is therefore not necessary for you to speak much, to associate among people, or to conduct trade by which you may live. For we regard trade in a monk as hidden usury.

Therefore love solitude, O monk; flee the crowd, lest you be caught in your speech and put to shame in your deed. And if you are questioned, it is better to answer briefly to each question than, by lingering longer, to extend your curious words at greater length.

For what else is verbosity than seed that produces no fruit? O verbose man, blush and consider your great misery. For what else are you than tasteless salt, which is useful for no seasoning? You are truly fruitless, and you make fruitless those who hear you.

O verbose liar, who have rarely wished to speak the truth; O chatterer, know yourself. You are never ashamed to speak, nor do you consider what you can say, but only how much; you do not measure the meaning of your words, but only seek to satisfy yourself.

O verbose man, blush, because you are entirely recognizable by what you do. For your habit is to disclose hidden things and proclaim what is known in gatherings. But if you do not know, you dream up unheard-of things and pretend to know what you do not know, so that everyone may gladly listen to you.

O craftsman of lies, O maker of tales, read what is said: “For the man of many words shall not be directed” (Psalm 139:12), nor shall he be directed into the promised land.

O monk, you too must pay careful attention. For the one who does not bridle his tongue has a vain religion. Whoever does not guard his tongue is not a monk; but whoever moderates his tongue is most prudent and is a monk.

Come, then, my brothers: love silence; place a guard over your mouth. Be solitary, so that you may be joined to the angels. Be rustic, so that you may be citizens of the saints and members of God’s household. Be mute, so that you may be eloquent. Speak to God, so that you may be truthful. Contemplate in the desert, so that you may be contemplated by the saints in heaven. Lift up your heads, so that you may be lifted up in heart. Extend your arms, so that, flying toward heaven with your whole body, you may be extended upward. May Christ our God lead us there. Amen.

## SERMON FOUR. ON PRUDENCE
Dearly beloved brothers, you must not only maintain silence in the desert, but also seize prudence. For prudence is necessary for you, because it teaches what must be avoided and what must be held fast. Prudence teaches you not to be proud, not to rely on temporal things, and not to marvel at transitory things, since they are fleeting; it teaches you to understand that you should possess what you have as though it belonged to another. Prudence teaches you to let go profitably of what you cannot keep forever. Prudence teaches you always to remain the same in all things, in prosperity as well as in adversity, just as the hand is the same both when it is extended into a palm and when it is clenched into a fist. It teaches you how excessive praise is blameworthy, and excessive condemnation likewise: the former because of flattery, the latter because of suspected malice. Prudence gives its testimony to truth, not to friendship. Prudence promises with discretion, hastens to fulfill its promises, and gives more than it had promised. Prudence teaches how you should order the present, how you should remember the past, and how you should foresee the future.

O blessed is the prudent person, happy—and truly happy—is the one who is found prudent! For if he loses everything he possesses, he cries out, “All my things are with me.” What are these things that are mine, except justice, temperance, fortitude, and prudence? O truly prudent person! For you do not consider as good anything that can be taken away. Since the prudent person is therefore content within himself, he has everything with him and is sufficient to himself in all things. But nothing is enough for the imprudent person, because he is content with nothing; since he hopes to possess everything without end, he therefore lacks everything.

Be prudent, then, brothers, as serpents, and innocent as doves. For these two qualities are joined to one another, so that without the other either one accomplishes little or nothing at all. Innocence without cunning is considered foolishness; cunning without innocence, however, is judged arrogance.

The serpent’s cunning is divided into four parts. The first is that it gathers the venom of its entire body in its throat, and there, prudently instructed by nature, strives to keep it, so that if need should ever arise, it may have at hand the means by which it can defend itself. But in this respect the serpent is sometimes deceived. For the weasel is always hostile to the serpent, and stations itself before the opening of the serpent’s cave; provoking it, it skillfully mocks it for a long time with the shadow of its tail, until it observes the serpent coming out. Then the weasel climbs above it and lays an ambush, so that when it sees the serpent’s head it may exact a deadly revenge from the enemy whom it could never love. Thus provoked, the serpent thrusts its head outside the opening of the cave; and, seeing nothing below, it turns its throat and looks upward. But when the weasel sees the desired moment, it sinks its teeth in below the venom, and so kills its enemy without danger.

This is the first cunning of the serpent. In it, my brothers, the wise men of the world are signified—those whose prudence is concerned wholly not with heavenly things but with earthly things [Note: [Col. 1241] Manuscripts: *conversatur* (“is occupied with”).]—and the devil mocks them in the shadow of changeable things: by mocking, he deceives them; by deceiving, he kills them. And lest they should perhaps be able to aspire upward, he often compels them to breathe their last amid those very earthly desires.

The serpent’s second prudence is that, when it wishes to descend into water, it lays down its venom in a very safe place; but when it departs from the water, it takes up the venom again. There are some who follow these tracks of the serpent: after renouncing worldly conduct, after assuming the habit of holy religion, and after taking the oath of holy profession, they first embrace the knowledge of holy truth, and then return to the venom of depraved custom. For such people it would have been better not to have known the truth than, after knowing it, to turn back. In this, my brothers, we must not imitate the serpent, because it takes up its venom again.

The serpent’s third prudence is that it has learned to cast off its old skin every year. When it is about to lay it aside, it seeks a narrow opening through which it may pass, abandoning its skin there with pain, knowing that once the skin has been shed it will appear more beautiful. By this, my brothers, we are taught that we too must lay aside the skin of our vices, pass through the opening of Christ’s wounds, and then appear more beautiful.

Through this opening the rich man Zacchaeus entered when he distributed all his goods to the poor. In this opening that prostitute Mary, in the house of Simon the leper, laid aside the garment of her former way of life; and, weeping at the Savior’s feet, she renewed her clothing for herself.

The serpent’s fourth nature is that, when it suspects that its head is about to be injured, it arranges its whole body to receive the blow, so that, although the body may be struck, if it can preserve its head unharmed it suffers no loss of life. So too let us not fear to endure everything that opposes us for love of our Head, so that we may be able to rest in blessed life.

Thus did Peter act, suspended on the cross for him; so too Bartholomew, flayed alive; so too Paul, beheaded; so too Stephen, wounded by stones; so too Lawrence, roasted on a gridiron; and so too that most holy virgin [Note: [Col. 1241] Agatha.], tortured in the breast. She, gloriously mutilated, wounded, and afflicted in this way, was being led to prison, and, as though invited to a banquet, was entreating the Lord with prayers and solemnly commending her contest to him.

Be prudent, then, my brothers, and let us be vigilant in prayer, patiently bearing all torments for love of him in whom our salvation, life, and resurrection consist. Let us stand prudently in prayer. For just as the angels praise God purely in the land of the living, so we who sing psalms to the Lord day and night must possess purity together with the holy angels. For just as the angels act in heaven, so we monks must act on earth.

Therefore, my brothers, established in this solitude, we must pray and suffer with all our devotion. We must patiently bear each thing and must not presume to say: [Note: [Col. 1241] Bernard, *On the Song of Songs*, sermon 30, no. 11.] “Behold, the vegetables are windy, cheese weighs down the stomach, milk harms the head, the chest cannot endure water as a drink, cabbages nourish melancholy, leeks kindle choler, fish do not suit my taste.”

Do not say these things, my brothers; do not even think them. For we did not leave the world [Col. 1242] so that we might be delicately fed in the desert. And although in the desert you do not always eat milk, butter, cabbages, or vegetables—although you take these only on feast days and on those days when you are visited by the holy old bishop Valerius—but on all other days take raw herbs, barley bread, and water, still it is not enough merely to restrain the body; we must also preserve the mind unharmed.

Come, then, my dearest brothers, whose life, as I think, is holy, as many of you have seen and heard. I came to the city of Hippo and arrived there safely, because that holy man Valerius was bishop. I did not expect to become a bishop, and so I arrived safely with my dearest friends Evodius, Simplicius [Note: [Col. 1242] “Who is this Simplicius,” says Lupus, “of whom Augustine nowhere makes mention? As for Nebridius, it is clear from *Confessions* 9.3.6 that, serving God among his own people and not with Augustine, he was released from the flesh shortly after Augustine’s conversion.”], Nebridius, and Alypius, carrying no wealth with me. With the grace of God assisting me, I received considerable favor from the aforesaid old bishop Valerius, because he gave me a small garden, separated from the pagans in the desert [Note: [Col. 1242] “It is false,” says Lupus, “that Valerius’s garden was in the desert, etc. For it was in a suburban field.”]. There, wearied by much labor, I began to build a monastery; and, after longer anxiety, I gathered together the servants of God living in the woods [Note: [Col. 1242] “That too is false,” says the same Lupus. “For Africa had seen no monks at all down to Augustine’s time.”]. Thus I began to live together with you according to the apostolic rule, having and possessing everything in common.

Then it pleased him who had separated me from my mother’s womb to say to me, “Go up higher”; and, with great distress, I became a bishop-priest. And because I could not be here with you, I wished to have priests with me in the bishop’s house, and I began to live together with them in the same way.

But I found you to be such as I had desired: chaste, kind, restrained, humble, poor in every desire, obedient, solitary, merciful, trampling the world with all its pomp. But what are all these things without perseverance? Be prudent, then, persevering in goodness, and keep watch in prayers, because the adversary, the devil, reigns. May the almighty Lord deign to free you from him. Amen.

I beg you, my brothers, not to be disturbed by my departure. For I had decided to remain among you for a long time in consolation and to live with you until the feast of the Lord’s Ascension. But our adversary Fortunatus has arrived in the region, and therefore I am compelled to return to Hippo without fail, eager to see him and to dispute together with him [Note: [Col. 1242] Manifest falsehood: for, according to *Reconsiderations* 1.16, Fortunatus departed from Hippo after holding a disputation with Augustine while the latter was still a priest; nor, as Possidius testifies in chapter 6, did he ever return.]. For with all his devotion he tries to scatter the sons whom I begot in the depths of charity. Pray for me, brothers, and do not cease, so that, just as Fortunatus openly lies in wait for the holy faith, so we too, with the grace of God assisting us, may openly overcome him and his followers and bring them back to the way of truth.

## SERMON V

### On Obedience, to His Priests

In all your works, dearest priests of God, always remember God’s commandments, and be obedient in everything, so that by his grace you may be found worthy of the promise; knowing that without obedience everything is empty, while with obedience everything is found full of charity.

It is therefore necessary for you to obey not only the good and restrained, but also the unruly and wicked—not because they are wicked, but because they command the observance of good things, and these we must obey.

O venerable and holy obedience, salvation [Col. 1243] of all the faithful, guardian of all virtues: you open heaven and close hell; you also brought the Son of God down to earth, and he came among human beings, not to do the will of a human being, but the will of his Father who sent him. For the Father’s will was that he should redeem the human race and reconcile to himself his creation, which had perished. And so that this will might be accomplished, the Son was obedient unto death.

Therefore, so that obedience might not be burdensome for us, the Savior brought the present life to its end through obedience. Obedience is rightly placed above every sacrifice, because it rescued us from the power of the devil—something that no legal sacrifice could accomplish.

Nor is it surprising that we sinners are subjected to obedience in this life, when the Mediator of God and human beings did not abandon it even in death and, though equal to the Father in all things, subjected himself to it. We, however, because of sin, are subject to other human beings. For nature gave birth to all people equal; but the inequality that arose through vice has been ordered by God’s judgment, and therefore we must obey human beings.

Yet evil must never be done through obedience, even if an angel or archangel, a cherub or seraph, commands you. Not even God himself, who is blessed forever, can command us not to love him with all our devotion.

But you must know, priests of God, that on account of disobedience the good we are doing must sometimes be interrupted. Since at times the prosperity of this world is commanded to us, and at other times adversity, it must therefore be understood that obedience is sometimes nothing if it contains something of one’s own will, and sometimes is very little if it contains nothing of one’s own.

For when the prosperity of this world is commanded, when a higher position is ordered, the person who obeys in order to receive these things empties the virtue of obedience for himself if he longs for them out of his own desire. Again, when contempt for the world is commanded, when insults and reproaches are ordered, unless the mind itself desires these things, it diminishes the merit of obedience for itself, because it descends unwillingly and reluctantly to what is despised in this world.

Obedience must therefore have something of its own in adversity, and must have nothing of its own in prosperity.

We can demonstrate this well if we bring forward the deeds of two friends of God. When God commanded Moses to govern the Israelite people, he was humble in himself; considering and fearing the glory of such great rule, he humbly excused himself so as not to accept it. But when the apostle Paul was warned by a revelation from God to go to Jerusalem, he was not unaware of what he would have to suffer there. Thus, when the faithful wished to restrain him, he exclaimed, “I am ready not only to be bound, but also to die for the name of Jesus” (Acts 21:13).

Behold: Paul goes to Jerusalem, learns by revelation about the coming adversity, and yet eagerly embraces it. Moses, however, had nothing of his own in regard to prosperity, because he pleaded in prayer that he should not govern the people. Paul, too, accepted adversity by his own choice, because he knew the evils that threatened and prepared himself for harsher ones. Moses wished to avoid the glory of power, while Paul wished to endure hard and difficult things.

Therefore, through the virtue of both servants of God we are instructed that, if we strive to grasp the palm of obedience, we should accept the prosperity of the world solely at command, and embrace adversity out of devotion.

But I, priests of the most high God—as many of you have seen and been able to hear—came to this city with my dearest friends Evodius, Simplicius, Alypius, Nebridius [Note: [Col. 1243] Here and below, the errors already noted in the preceding sermon.], and Anastasius.

I came safely in the end, because I knew that the holy old man Valerius was bishop. For that reason I approached confidently—not in order to have power over you, but to be cast aside in the house of the Lord all the days of my life; not in order to be served, but to serve. I desired to live peacefully in solitude, and I brought no wealth with me. But with the grace of God assisting me, and having also received favor from the holy old bishop, I built, after much labor and exhaustion, a monastery in the desert, separated from the pagans [Col. 1244], and, after longer anxiety, gathered together the servants of God living in the woods. I began to live together with them according to the manner and rule established under the holy Apostles, having and possessing everything in common, and living in vigils and prayers beyond what we are able to express.

Their reputation reached the ears of the holy bishop Valerius, and he was pleased to visit us in the desert. He stayed with us for thirteen days, giving me a garden full of delights, situated on level ground. Since the place was separated from the pagans, I gladly accepted it, so that I might also build a monastery for brothers whom I had found to be such as I had desired to find.

When it had been built, it pleased him who had separated me from my mother’s womb and called me by his grace to say to me, “Go up higher”; and so, with distress and great anxiety, I became a bishop-priest. And because I could no longer dwell bodily with my brothers, as I had previously done, I therefore wished to have you clerics within the bishop’s house, and at once began to live with you according to the apostolic form.

It pleased all of you to think as one in God and to possess everything in common. You wished to do these things not under compulsion but voluntarily, and you wished to profess that you would live without private property until death.

O priest, pay attention—pay careful attention: it was yours to promise, but it is not yours to abandon. You are bound to a wife; do not now seek release. You have been released from a wife; do not now seek a wife, because you have a case with me. You bound yourself to me—did I compel you? Did I ask you to come? Did I flatter you by promising this and that? Far from it.

Therefore be faithful, and I will give you the crown of life. Do not resist me, but be obedient unto death. Do not resist me, because all authority is from God, and whoever resists authority resists God.

Yet I did not come in order to have authority over you, but only to live in solitude with my brothers. Behold, now I am a bishop, and I am not ashamed to be poor. Why? Because I promised to preserve poverty. Therefore take care that you do not abandon me as a poor man. You wished to be poor with me; take care that you are not seized by riches. It was my will that we should always be poor with all our devotion. And if we are not, this poverty that we display outwardly must be judged not poverty but great misery.

Do not resist me, then, because all authority is from God. Nor are authorities to be despised, whether they belong to the world or to the Church, because all have been ordained by God. For when the Lord had healed the lepers, he sent them to the authorities, saying, “Go, show yourselves to the priests” (Luke 17:14). And when the Jews rejected Samuel, the Lord said to him, “They have not rejected you, but me” (1 Samuel 8:7). And to Moses: “Anyone who acts proudly against the priest or against the judge shall die” (Deuteronomy 17:12).

Take care, therefore, priests, that none of you dare rise up against the superior or priest who has charge of all of you. For they have been placed in the Church for our benefit, to determine what we ought to do, to render an account to God on our behalf, and to preserve the unity of the Church [Note: [Col. 1244] Lupus observes that subsidiary prefectures of this kind were unknown in those times; but that Augustine directly presided over his clerics is inferred from Possidius, chapter 24, and from the Acts concerning the appointment of Heraclius, now Letter 113.]. The Lord wished us to be concerned for this unity, lest, like sheep without shepherds, we should be divided from the unity of the faith through various errors.

For just as there is one Lord and one shepherd, so he wished there to be one sheepfold. Therefore the Lord did not wish the seamless tunic, which was whole, to be torn, because he does not permit the unity of the Church to be violated. For this reason Paul says: “I beseech you, brothers, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that there be no schisms among you; but preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (1 Corinthians 1:10).

For just as many rays proceed from one sun, and yet there is one light, so we, proceeding as many from one head, must possess everything peacefully and in common.

For storms of enemies frequently arise among us, wishing to destroy our harmony and, by sowing discord, extinguish the union of peace. Most terrifying lions frequently attack us, so that, by striking the head, they may at least cause the members to move in terror. And what is more grievous to me, we often suffer evil not only from malignant spirits but are also torn apart by those of our own household. Internal wars, against which no precaution is taken, are frequently worse than external wars, which are foreseen.

Behold: righteous Abel is killed by his own brother; Esau pursues his fleeing brother; Joseph is sold by his brothers; and the Savior is betrayed by a disciple. All these evils occurred because they neglected to obey.

The same thing happened to our Januarius, who seemed among us to be a pillar of obedience and poverty, and whose destruction we must often bewail and lament. For he came to us with tears and promised to preserve poverty as long as he lived; yet, without our knowledge, he possessed a vineyard and a field in the world [Note: [Col. 1245] Rather, only “money which he said belonged to his daughter,” says Augustine, sermon 355, no. 3.].

O deadly profession! O treacherous promise! With his mouth he said what he hated in his heart. We thought him holy, though he was worse than everyone else. And thus for eleven years and more, as you saw and heard, our Januarius lived badly and dies badly.

Why, or in what way, did he live badly? Because he secretly kept what was his own [Note: [Col. 1245] The printed editions add: *non* (“not”).]. And how does he die badly, except because in the end he did not acknowledge himself, and, obstinate in his own opinion, made a will for us and enriched the son he had in the world [Note: [Col. 1245] Two errors. For according to the same sermon, no. 3, “his son is in the monastery,” not in the world; and “he made the Church his heir,” while he disinherited this son.]?

If only he had said this to us at the end, so that he might have obtained pardon through our prayers. But he neither confessed nor repented of having done it; therefore he is not one of mine, nor was he one of mine while he lived. Bind his corpse’s hands, placing one hundred and eleven shekels, tied up in a cloth, that he kept in the wall of his little cell, weeping and saying, “May your money perish with you” (Acts 8:20).

For it is not permitted for us, servants of God, to place or use it for food, clothing, or the work of the monastery, because it is the price of damnation.

Come, then, priests of God, take care that you do not fail in temptations; take care that you do not rebel against me openly or secretly. Be faithful to me, and be obedient to me. And if this is burdensome and troublesome to you, go outside, go to my brothers, and learn from them, because they are meek and humble of heart, poor in spirit, and sons of obedience.

Go outside, and I want you to consider what you are and what they are. Are you also such as they are? Would that you were such as they are! You are gluttons, while they are models of the highest sobriety; you roam about the city, while they flee the sight of human beings; you are unchaste, while they are chaste; you are mockers, while they are most fervent in prayer; you walk about adorned in rabbit or squirrel skins, while they are clothed in the blackest and roughest sheep’s wool, apart from what lies within.

You take the greatest care to be delicately fed, longing for various meats; but after they entered the desert they never ate meat. You seek choice and intoxicating wines; they take only a little water. You desire to appear splendid in soldiers’ belts; they are adorned with camel-hair girdles around their waists, after the manner of Elijah and John [Note: [Col. 1245] Whether these things suit Augustine’s clerics is clear from sermon 356, no. 3, where he testifies that he found them such as he had desired; and from no. 13, concerning whether there was anything improper in their clothing.].

O my chosen vineyard, I planted you; take care that you are not turned into bitterness. I beg you, do not leave me poor and follow Januarius, who was rich. O happy vineyard, whose cluster I greatly fear may at the end be most bitter! O what shall we do then on that day of calamity when God the Father says to the Son, “Call the laborers and give them their wages” [Col. 1246] (Matthew 20:8)?

Then, before the judge, the voice of your rebellion will be heard: what you promised and how you wished to keep those promises. You promised to flee the world and despise the things that belong to the world; and behold, now you are rebels, wholly preoccupied with worldly things in all your desires.

Why, then, did you murmur if I was not bodily present with you during these Paschal days [Note: [Col. 1246] Days on which the bishop’s presence was especially necessary. Yet, when Augustine asked that the people grant him five days’ freedom from the Scriptural duties imposed on him by the councils, they did not grant it, as he says in Letter 213, no. 5. Furthermore, in Letter 122 he says: “Let Your Love know that I was never absent with wanton freedom, but under necessary servitude.”]?

For it pleased me to separate myself from you and go to my brothers in solitude, whom, as I have often said, I found to be such as I had desired to find. Why, then, are you disturbed? Are they not truly poor? Are they not obedient? Have they not trampled upon the world and its pomp? Have they not preceded you for a long time in their manner of life? Are they not truly my brothers and fathers? Did I not reach the way of truth through their examples? Have I not always loved them and always desired their holy way of life? Was I not also instructed in the faith through Simplicianus of Liguria?

Why, then, do you murmur? Why do you show that you are grieved by my absence? Do what pleases me, and then, wherever I may be, I shall be with you until the end of the age.

For I had decided to live humbly in charity with these rustic companions of mine until the feast of the holy Ascension of the Lord, and I did not wish to return to you until I knew that you had been reformed. But since I now perceive that Fortunatus, the adversary, has secretly arrived in the region like a wolf, I have therefore been compelled to return to you, eager to see him, dispute with him, and, with the Lord’s help, trample him underfoot—him who strives with all his strength to scatter and slaughter the sons whom I begot in the depths of charity.

Pray, then; and we too wish to pray with you. Stop quarreling any further about my absence. Pray and do not cease, so that, just as Fortunatus, the Manichaean priest, openly lies in wait for the holy Christian faith, so we too, with the grace of God assisting us, may openly overcome him and his followers.

Pray without ceasing, so that you may be worthy to remain in the calling of clerics to which you have been called by the grace of God; so that, when you are called to your reward on the last day, you may not be cursed and cut down like a fig tree without fruit and cast into the fire, as destroyers of the law who occupy the land and perish in your iniquities.

May God himself help you to accomplish marvelous things from his law—he who is blessed forever. Amen.

## SERMON VI

### On Mercy
Brothers most dear, I announce to you great joy: by God’s grace we have overcome Fortunatus, the Manichaean presbyter, and he, obstinate in his opinion like another son of perdition, withdrew from our people in confusion [Note: [Col. 1246] The lie has now been repeated for the third time.]. After his departure I baptized nearly sixty pagans who had adhered to him to some extent. And behold, I have now returned to you, wishing to complete the work I began.

“Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matt. 5:7). Oh, if only we carefully considered God’s mercy, we could possess within ourselves the pattern of showing mercy. O brothers, what caused Christ to become incarnate except mercy? What subjected him to our misery except sheer compassion? O blessed mercy, which alone recognized the exchange by which we were saved! For mercy alone directs a human being to God, mercy alone leads a human being to God, mercy alone brings God down to the human being. This alone is the mediatrix who comforts those in adversity; this joins those who are separated; this alone, by humbling God, exalts us. How loving was God’s descent, so that from it our glorious assumption might proceed! O great mercy, O infinite mercy, you alone were able to draw God from heaven to earth and raise us from exile to [Col. 1247] the kingdom. O great bond of mercy, by which God was bound [Note: [Col. 1247] The printed editions add: “willed to be bound.”] and could be bound, while the bound human being breaks his bonds!

O monk, if you considered your misery, in God’s work toward you you would find nothing but mercy. It is mercy when he scourges in order to correct; when through tribulation he frees from sin; when he permits hypocrites and tyrants to reign. God does all these things in mercy, desiring to give us eternal life.

Pay attention, therefore, brothers—pay attention: for in a shepherd or judge mercy and justice must exist together. Mercy without justice is destroyed and turns into cruelty. And is justice without mercy acceptable to God? Certainly not. The Almighty always exercises mercy together with justice toward the just and unjust, the blessed and the condemned: to the blessed he gives a glory which they do not deserve to possess for any good works they may have performed; and to the wicked he gives a punishment which, for the evils they have committed, they deserve to receive even greater.

Be merciful, therefore, my brothers, as your merciful Father is merciful. Be merciful, considering how greatly Moses flourished in mercy on behalf of the people, for whose salvation he asked to be erased from the book of life; and again, with what zeal for rectitude, when he had obtained pardon, he said to the people, “Let each man place his sword upon his thigh” (Exod. 32:27). Behold: the one who had asked for the life of everyone at the cost of his own life destroyed the lives of a few by the sword—within, kindled by the fire of love; outwardly, inflamed by zeal for justice and severity, strong in both respects. As the people’s ambassador before God, he pleaded in prayer; and as God’s advocate before human beings, he brought forward the charge to be enforced by swords.

Let us therefore, my brothers, strive to seize mercy while we live. Let the hungry be fed by us, the naked clothed by us, the stranger received by us, the orphan consoled through us, the sick visited by us, and the dead buried by us. These are the works of mercy about which we must be questioned on the last day.

But you will say: “Behold, we are in the desert; we cannot see the poor or the orphans. How can we console the fatherless and widows? How can we bury the dead?”

O my brothers, I know well that you are in the desert. I do not believe that you see the poor, nor do I wish you to leave the monastery so that you may console mothers or relatives. For I have known many who left the monastery for this very reason, yet never returned to the monastery. Under the appearance of good, many evils are committed.

For behold, the devil says: “O monk, do you not know that your mother is grieving? See, she has recently lost her husband, buried her son, lost her property, and is sick unto death; perhaps she does not wish to confess. What are you doing in the desert? What are you thinking? Rise quickly, leave the monastery, enter the city, penetrate the homes of your relatives, and perform works of mercy among them. For this is what God wills; this is what he commands to be done.”

While the servant of God is thinking this, he sometimes leaves the monastery, believing that he is doing good. And behold, when he approaches, his mother kisses her son, his father embraces him, and his brothers applaud, saying: “Do not abandon us. We are brothers; our father is elderly; it is your responsibility to govern the household. Why, then, do you presume to return to the monastery?”

And so, by listening, he consents; by consenting, he remains; by remaining, he becomes worse than all the others, and loses whatever good he had done.

Beware, therefore, my brothers—beware the devil’s malice. Nevertheless, I want you to perform works of mercy. Even if you do not live in the world or among the nations, you can still perform works of mercy well by praying, pleading, and supplicating for orphans and the fatherless.

If this does not seem sufficient to you, you must consider how a hundred or more of you live together in the monastery, how you are often sick, often afflicted by the devil, and often suffer. Surely you also often die? You can therefore perform works of charity among yourselves as well.

But one of you may say: “I have a father in the world, and I have promised God that I will live in the monastery until death. Now my father is sick and cannot live without me. What should I do? What should I choose? If I leave, I break my vow; if I stay, I allow my father to die.”

What, then? O brothers, pay attention to what you ought to do, as it occurs to me for the present. If someone’s father cannot in any way live without his monk-son, the son must arrange for the father to be supported from the monastery’s goods. And if the monastery is unable to do so, the son must make every effort to see how his father may not be left without help. If he cannot find a way, then, with God’s blessing and with the permission of his superior, he should leave the monastery and assist his father in word and deed, so that his father does not fail through neglect. He should not think that he has broken his vow: for if he remains alive after his father’s death, he should not hesitate to return at once to his former life, living holily and justly as he had begun, and all the more firmly in proportion as he has felt himself burdened beyond necessity by serving his father.

No one, therefore, will be able to excuse himself from mercy: neither the rich, because he possesses resources; nor the poor, because he is not without a cup of cold water; nor the monk, because at the very least he must pray.

O human being, who are cruel with respect to another’s righteousness, first recognize yourself. For if you are good, O monk, you can easily fall; if you are rich, it is a gift of fortune, not of nature; if you are healthy, behold, sickness is close at hand; if you are wise, you do not possess constancy.

Therefore show mercy toward everyone: toward the wise and the foolish, toward the healthy and the sick, toward the noble and the ignoble. O human being, what will become of you if your master is compassionate and kind, while you have ignored mercy?

Let mercy be nourished among you, my brothers—not through negligence, not through faintheartedness, not through indiscretion, and not through weakness of spirit; rather, let it be watchful in every respect, so that it retains what properly belongs to it without taking away what justice requires.

O monk, look upon the mercy of holy Joseph, who forgot the injury done by his brothers. Choose, my brothers, the clemency of David, who mourned the madness of his pursuing son.

O monk, if you close the bowels of mercy to one in need, the door of Christ will be entirely closed to you. For this is the Lord’s gate, and the righteous shall enter through it. This illuminates the New Testament and abolishes the rigor of the Old. This is the wood by which Moses sweetened the waters; this is the salt by which Elisha removed the barrenness of the waters; this is the flour by which Elisha eradicated the death that was in the pot. This is the oil which the Samaritan poured upon the wounded man. This is the Jordan by which Naaman the Syrian was cured of leprosy.

This virtue alone distinguishes the cruel from the compassionate, and the king from the tyrant. O monk, where would you be if God’s mercy had not come to your aid? For if God dealt with you according to a strict judgment, you could not imagine a punishment corresponding to your offenses.

Attribute everything, therefore, to God’s mercy, and in like manner expend mercy for the benefit of your neighbor, so that you are not stingy in showing mercy when you have experienced God’s generosity.

Love mercy, therefore, my brothers, because I have never seen a pious person end in an evil death. May God show such mercy toward you. Amen.

## SERMON VII. ON OBEDIENCE

[Note: [Col. 1248] The manuscripts add: “and its discernment.”]

My dearly beloved brothers, we must obey God in everything if we wish to be saved in the desert. And if this seems difficult to us, we ought to consider the obedience of the Son of God and not delay in laying aside our defiance.

For the Son of God himself was obedient unto death, even death on a cross. And do we refuse to obey his commands? Christ was obedient unto death, not for his own benefit but for ours. Be obedient to him, therefore, not for his benefit but for your own.

Behold, brothers: the angel obeys God in everything; and you, who are dust, contradict God? Things without reason obey God, while you, a rational being, resist God? The sun does not depart from its path, nor the moon, nor the stars. For all heavenly things fulfill their appointed duties [Note: [Col. 1248] The manuscripts read “need” instead.]; yet you seem to resist God’s will in everything.

At God’s command [Col. 1249] the fields are adorned with flowers, the earth is made fertile by rains, the forest is curled with leaves, and the little bird sings like a harp in the grove. Everything obeys God, and human beings alone resist God’s will.

O monk, read what is said: “Obedience is better than sacrifice” (1 Sam. 15:22). What is the reason, unless it is that in sacrifices another person’s flesh is slaughtered, whereas in obedience one’s own will and flesh are put to death?

Be obedient, therefore, my brothers, so that you may be able to appease God for the sins you have committed. A person appeases God all the sooner when, having repressed the pride of his own will, he sacrifices himself with the sword of the commandment.

Nevertheless, be cautious in obedience, my brothers. Beneath it the dragon’s gall may lie hidden under the appearance of honey, and a wolf beneath a sheep’s skin. Poison often lies concealed in sweet drink, and death is often placed in a pot.

Let the one who commands, therefore, and the one who intends to obey, pay attention that the obedience be honorable and adorned with complete discernment. For if it is not discerning, it must be considered cruelty; if it is not honorable, we must not obey it at all.

For example, if we are commanded not to love God, or to hate God, should we obey? Could God himself even command such a thing? What is commanded must therefore be honorable and just, brothers. If it is not honorable or just, we must not obey it at all, even if an apostle should have indicated it to us.

Hold fast, therefore, my brothers, and bind this in your hearts: obedience without discernment is empty, and the fault lies not with the obedient party but with the one who commands. Obedience deprived of honor is pride, and the fault lies with both parties—with the one who consents and the one who commands—and on the last day they will be punished with equal punishment.

Be careful what you command; beware and weigh what you impose. Indeed, whenever obedience has not been honorable and just, let shepherds recognize that they have proceeded into irregularity.

Obedience, therefore, my brothers, is true, holy, and meritorious when it is enriched with discernment, honor, justice, and humility. These are the companions of holy obedience, without which all obedience is vain and useless.

This is that obedience which preserves harmony among angels, nourishes peace among monks, and produces tranquility among citizens. This is that obedience without which the state cannot stand, without which no household can be governed.

O how enormous was the vice opposed to obedience! Through it the devil lost heaven; through it humanity lost paradise; through it Saul lost his kingdom; through it Solomon lost divine love.

O holy bride of God, Obedience! You are the perfect ladder by which heaven is climbed; you are the chariot by which Elijah was carried into paradise; you are the gate of paradise for the faithful and the enclosure of the condemned [Note: [Col. 1249] The printed editions read: “and the enclosure of their hell.”].

O holy obedience, you nourish humility, test patience, and examine gentleness. Be obedient, therefore, brothers, together with Abraham, rendering to Caesar what belongs to Caesar and to God what belongs to God.

We render to Caesar what is owed to him when we render *dulia*—the service of reverence—to our superiors. This *dulia* consists in the demonstration of reverence and love. We must show this not only to shepherds but also to God’s saints; and then, through obedience, we render to Caesar what belongs to Caesar.

But we render to God what belongs to God when we persevere in *latria*, for this belongs to God alone. It consists in prayer, thanksgiving, the offering of outward worship, and the devotion of the inward mind.

May God, blessed forever, deign to grant us both to do this and to persevere in it. Amen.

## SERMON VIII. ON PERSEVERANCE

My brothers, as the Apostle says, “No one can be crowned unless he has competed lawfully” (2 Tim. 2:5). For no one competes lawfully except the one who competes in the arena to the end; and if he competes to the end, he competes lawfully [Col. 1250] [Note: [Col. 1250] The words “and if he competes … he competes lawfully” are absent from the manuscripts]. Therefore he is rightly crowned.

It is not, then, a great good merely to begin what is good; to bring it to completion—this alone is perfection. Many undertake many things, but fail along the way. Many go out into the desert, but few reach the promised land.

O my brothers, let it not weary you to begin great things, nor let it disgust you to hold fast to what you have begun. Know that perseverance shapes merit, gives color to a good intention, rewards the runner, crowns the fighter, leads to the prize, and brings everyone to the harbor.

This is the long robe of holy Joseph, reaching all the way to the end. This is the priestly tunic extending to the feet. This is the tail of the sacrifice which we are bound to return and offer to God. This is the heel of good action which we must guard against the serpent’s bite.

This is the virtue that binds God. This is what gives form to every good thing. This is perseverance, by which martyrs are crowned with laurel, virgins crowned, priests and confessors exalted. This is a garment without wrinkle, a tunic without stain, goodness without evil.

O monk, who have begun to live well, beware lest you flourish only for a time. Beware lest you be compared to grass, which is born today and immediately withers.

Let us labor, therefore, brothers, and while laboring let us persevere. Let us labor so that we may possess perseverance. Let all monks labor in order to retain it; let virgins labor in order to give it form; let widows labor so that they may persevere in it.

Pay attention, however, brothers, for the devil sometimes invites and leads God’s servants toward good so that he may extract evil from the good all the more severely. Against this assault of the devil perseverance alone is effective, so that good beginnings may be brought to a good conclusion: so that the beginning does not differ from the middle, nor the middle from the end.

To conclude a good beginning with an evil end—what else is this than producing monstrous things? Such an action is like a chimaera, which has its beginning in reason but its end in sensuality. For when this happens, the painter joins a horse’s neck to a human head and adds unfruitful feathers above it.

Beware, therefore, O monk, lest your action give birth to a monster. The offspring of the womb will be monstrous if the end does not correspond to the head.

Some have a good beginning, but their life is a remarkable monster, displaying what seems to be a human head; then the middle descends into lust and has a sheep’s belly; and finally it shows the feet of a wolf in rapacity.

O monk, what does it profit you to begin something good and not include its completion? If you lose the good of virtue, you incur loss and deserve a great punishment.

O how much better it would have been for you not to recognize the way of truth than, after recognizing it, to turn back through inconstancy! O monk, through your apostasy you are regarded as fickle; with Judas you fall into instability of mind; you put God second, lose your friends, forfeit hope, are hated by everyone, and in life are proved to be an apostate worse than all others.

O monk, pay attention: unless you persevere, you will die the death. Therefore, if you have begun to build, complete the work; if you have not begun, begin.

If you have offered the flower of your youth to the devil, at least do not delay in sacrificing the dregs of your old age to Christ. For he is merciful; he will gladly receive you, give you a white robe, a ring for your hand, and sandals for your feet. Then, after you have grown old in evil days, your youth will be renewed like the eagle’s, enduring forever.

Begin, therefore, my brothers, and persevere. Bring back to your memory how much good Judas abandoned. I could not possibly express to you in words how fervently he began to act well; but how he persevered, you know.

Behold, Solomon fell through inconstancy; so did Saul, and so did many others. For many began, but the number of those who persevered is small.

Beware, therefore, how carefully you walk, considering that the one who thinks he is standing should take care lest he fall.

Blessed, then, is the one who perseveres in doing good to the end. May he who deigned to die for us grant us this gift. Amen.

## SERMON IX. ON ANGER AND HATRED

[Col. 1251]

My dearly beloved brothers, just as remembering everything and making no mistake belongs not to humanity but to divinity alone, so also being disturbed, suffering, and forgetting belong only to humanity, not to divinity.

For God does not lie as a human being does, nor is he provoked like a son of man. It is human, therefore, my brothers, to be disturbed and to become angry; and falling into anger is a condition common to the good and the wicked alike. But persevering in anger or hatred is diabolical.

Therefore you who are spiritual must pay the greatest attention, lest anger rest in the bosom of fools. A fool immediately reveals his anger. Yet firmly restraining the irascible spirit is a mark of great prudence and perfection.

O monk, do not become angry. For we bear the name and habit of holy religion in this vast solitude. Guard yourselves, therefore, from every disturbance; for it is not fitting for God’s servants to fall into disturbance.

Will your fasts, your abstinence, and your sacrifices benefit you? From anger, finally, comes resentment; from resentment, hatred, which is anger grown old in the soul. From this arises murder, if not in deed, at least in intention; from this, insult; from this, detraction; from this, suspicion and injury—works of the flesh and of the devil.

O monk, lay aside anger, destroy resentment, and calm your fury, lest you become a son of perdition.

How much better it would be for a monk to live peacefully in the world than to quarrel in anger and fury in a monastery adorned with every good thing, while keeping hatred in his heart!

The one who preserves hatred in his heart deserves neither to praise God nor to be heard by him. With what face, O monk, with what feeling and devotion can you ask God for forgiveness if, while hating your brother, you ask God to forgive you as you forgive your own debtors?

Believe me, then: he will forgive you only as much as you forgive another. Let us therefore put aside anger, my brothers, which is rightly signified by foul-smelling Lazarus on the fourth day, because the one who carries anger in his heart is immediately corrupted by the stench of infamy.

If anger therefore arises in the soul, restrain it at once; strike it against the rock; suffocate it by the example of your Savior, who, struck on one cheek, immediately offered the other [Note: [Col. 1251] Rather, Augustine observes in *On Lying*, chapter 15, no. 27, that he offered it only in the preparation of his heart.]. For if he had not first done this himself, he would not have commanded me to do it.

Come, then, my brothers: learn from him who said that he was humble and gentle. Learn by deeds what you have often read from his lips.

“Let not the sun go down upon your anger.” If your brother sins against you, go to him, invite him to peace, give him a kiss, and you have won your brother. But you who have caused offense must not delay in going; do not delay in reconciling with your brother. Go to him and ask forgiveness.

If you offended him by word, reconcile him by word; if by deed—which may God avert it—appease him by deed. For this is what befits God’s servants; this is how they should drive out demons and bring in the holy angels.

For wherever anger has reigned, there the devil will certainly be prince, and nothing good will be able to come forth from there.

Let us therefore flee anger, my brothers: it suffocates reason, ignores the measure of justice, does not know the sun of justice, breaks friendships, easily takes away peace, tramples the wisdom of the mind, makes the wise foolish, causes monks to go astray [Note: [Col. 1251] The manuscripts read “conquers.”], suffocates priests, empties chastity of its force, and tears apart the dignity of shepherds.

Nor can one filled with anger be capable of counsel.

O monk, look upon your head: for while placed upon the cross, he prayed for his crucifiers. And the chief martyr Stephen, kneeling for those who were stoning him, cried out, “Lord, do not hold this sin against them” (Acts 7:59).

But if we are not of such perfection that we can return good for evil, at least let us not return evil for evil. Injuries should not, however, be forgiven through faintheartedness, but through the wisdom that is in Christ Jesus.

O how great, my brothers, is the stain of this sin! O how great and broad is the misery it brings upon both body and soul! For the body loses rest and cheerfulness [Col. 1252], while the soul loses eternal life.

Through anger, former sins come and return to us [Note: [Col. 1252] The manuscripts omit “sins.”], and thus we are confounded and condemned.

But let us, brothers, who are truly Christians, leave vengeance to the one who says, “Vengeance is mine, and I will repay” (Heb. 10:30). Whatever pertains to you, forgive him.

Does he himself not carry out more wondrous acts of vengeance than we can imagine? We must not ask or desire this for ourselves, however, but pray for them with mind and pure heart.

For when we seek to have our wrongs avenged, we usurp what belongs to God. Nevertheless, we must pray without ceasing that he avenge the blood of his servants—not for condemnation but for correction—he who is blessed forever. Amen.

## SERMON X. ON PURITY OF CONSCIENCE [Note: [Col. 1252] The printed editions read: “On purity of conscience, love of tribulations, and the hope by which through them one is invited to heavenly things.”], AND THE VIRTUE OF HOPE

Today, dearly beloved brothers, I intend to invite you to spiritual joy. This joy is produced neither by an abundance of riches, nor by the world’s deceptive glory, nor by the fruitfulness of offspring, nor by bodily health, but by purity of conscience.

O happy delight of a holy conscience! O happy purity of conscience, which excludes the inward worm, frees reason from the prison of pain, and purifies the mind from every impurity!

O holy mind, paradise of delights, planted with varied shrubs of good works, purpled with various flowers of the virtues, and gently watered by heavenly grace!

This is, my brothers, the paradise in which the tree of heavenly wisdom is planted. This is God’s bridal chamber, Christ’s palace, the dwelling place of the Holy Spirit. This is Solomon’s throne, the bed of the heavenly bridegroom, in which the good conscience itself delights most fully and rests with the bridegroom.

O conscience, in you and for you Rebecca meets Isaac when he comes from the field. In you Jacob delights in his marriage with Rachel. In you the Shunammite Abishag warms King David in joyful embraces.

O holy conscience, you are still on earth, yet you dwell in heaven! Rejoice, O holy soul, adorned with a holy conscience; rejoice in heavenly and eternal glory.

In this conscience, my dearest brothers, that fiery Magdalene offers perfumes precious to Christ. There Mary chose the better part, which shall not be taken away from her.

Come, then, my brothers: if we wish to reach this glory, let us now carefully examine the conscience mentioned above. Let us read there the letter of lust and observe the mark of pride, as well as of greed and envy. Let us erase them through confession, through contrition of heart, and through true satisfaction. Then by grace we shall deserve to attain that glory which “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man,” which God has prepared for those who love him.

O my brothers and joy of my heart, let us hasten to enter this holy of holies. Then we shall possess a good that we shall not lose, a perfect good that we shall not forfeit.

Nevertheless, if we wish to reach this glory, we must love temptations, hunger, and every kind of tribulation. For just as gold is purified in a furnace, iron is cleansed by a file, and a flail separates chaff from grain, so in the furnace of tribulations patience is exercised, courage strengthened, constancy solidified, and hope invited to heavenly things.

O hope of the saints and tower of their strength, you do not bring shame but pour grace into those who await you; you do not blind but enlighten; you do not leave hungry but refresh.

O blessed heavenly hope, you conquer the fear of the world and uproot worldly consolations. Through you fear does not increase; through you false desire is not dreamed of; through you lust is shattered; through you pride is humbled; through you envy does not rule; through you all vices are brought to an end.

O hope of the heavenly court, in you charity reigns, which believes everything that pertains to salvation and hopes for everything that has been promised.

O my brothers, what human being can weaken the mind of God’s servants if the heavenly court [Col. 1253] pleads for him before God? What harm will the thunderbolts of tyrants do him? What will the precipices of fortune accomplish?

O hope, you direct thoughts; in charity you establish height, so that we may persevere in it unto death; in charity you extend breadth even to the enemy [Note: [Col. 1253] The manuscripts read: “unto death.”].

O hope of heavenly glory, through you the patriarchs patiently endured evils; through you the prophets bore all evils; through you the apostles joyfully advanced toward death; through you the martyrs were afflicted; through you virgins were burned; through you confessors were reviled; through you priests were clothed; through you widows bind themselves to chastity; through you married women gird their loins; through you fatherless children and orphans hope to smile; through you the poor hope to rejoice; through you travelers hope to reach the goal and end of their labor.

O hope, you make everything bearable sweetly and gently.

Come, then, my brothers: love this hope, hold fast to it, but not without fear. For the one who hopes and does not fear is negligent; but the one who fears and does not hope is crushed and descends into the depths like a stone.

May he free us from that descent who descended from heaven in order to give us life and ascent—our God himself. Amen.

## SERMON XI. ON TEARS, COMPUNCTION, AND PENITENCE

[Note: [Col. 1253] The manuscripts read: “On weeping and penitence.”]

Know, my dearest brothers, that eternal lamentations will follow the joys of the world; for no one can rejoice both here and in the world to come. Therefore, whoever wishes to possess the one must lose the other. If, then, O monk, you wish to rejoice here, know that you are already an exile from your homeland; but if you have wept here, you will be constituted a citizen of the heavenly homeland. “Blessed,” he says, “are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matthew 5:5).

But someone will say, “What ought we to weep for, and why must we weep?” I, however, my little sons and brothers, say that we must weep for the sins we have committed. Let this weeping be our bread, which we ought to eat every day, day and night. We must also weep for the sins of peoples, as though they were our own wounds. For this is what Paul did when he cried out, “Who is weak, and I am not weak?” (2 Corinthians 11:29). We must also weep over the delay of the eternal kingdom, as that prophet David clearly showed when he said, “Woe is me, for my sojourn has been prolonged!” (Psalm 119:5).

These, then, are the three miseries with which the book of Jeremiah is woven: the soul’s lamentation for sins, the assault of misery, and the delay of the homeland. With the rains of these tears we must irrigate the soil of our mind, so that it may bring forth the fruits of good works and various flowers of the virtues.

These tears are also the three waves through which the children of Israel passed into the promised land. Truly, sinners come out of the Egypt of vices, crossing the Red Sea while their enemies are submerged and their vices drowned. Truly, they sing gloriously to the Lord when, entering the heavenly Jerusalem, they lay aside their corruptible garment and are joined to the holy angels.

O monk, therefore make your mind the book of Ezekiel, in which lamentations and woe were written (Ezekiel 2:9). O monk, turn yourself toward these lamentations; embrace these sorrows throughout all the days of your life, weeping for your own sins and not only, as we have said, for your own, but also for those of your neighbor.

Take care, however, not to weep over anyone’s bodily death, nor over the loss of possessions, nor over bodily illness. All these things must occur; all of them are very common. Therefore place yourself in God’s will, leaving everything to him, and he himself will lead you back and guide you. Whatever happens to you, receive it willingly; praise God in all things and render him every honor, giving him thanks.

Every day weep for the sins you have committed and for those you see your neighbors committing, as though they were your own wounds. This is what that sinful woman Mary did, not only in the Pharisee’s house but also after the coming of the Holy Spirit: she always grieved and throughout her life wept for what she had committed.

So too did Mary, the mother of the Lord [Col. 1254]. When she stood beside the cross, she was not weeping for her own sins, since she had none; but she wept not only over her Son’s Passion, but also over the condemnation of the Jews.

But you will say: “I see a dead brother or friend; natural weakness invites me to lament.” I say to you, monk, restrain your grief. It is not your part to weep for the dead, but the world’s. Yet I do not forbid natural tears, which natural necessity draws forth. For many shed tears, and although nature often invites us to do so, the mind of the wise nevertheless remains unmoved.

O you who appear to be wise in the world, take care that your mind not consent to mourn the dead. Strive for grief to be overcome by the mind. Take care that your mind not be swallowed up by weakness. Let the Spirit weaken the flesh, and reason weaken sensuality.

O monk, if death is approaching, do not grieve; prepare yourself so that you cannot fear death, so that after death you may begin to live—you who, before death, were living by dying, or dying by living.

Do you wish, then, O monk, to live forever? Lay aside weeping for earthly things; do not mourn what belongs to the world and what must necessarily occur. Lay aside entirely weeping for earthly things, and take up lamentation for heavenly things. “Blessed,” he says, “are those who mourn” (Matthew 5:5); “Blessed are you who weep, for you shall laugh” (Luke 6:21).

Let us love tears, I say, because they are sweet to those who love God. Let us always delight in this life in weeping and lamentation. Let us be as ready for lamentation and weeping as we were bold in sin. In whatever measure our intention was directed toward sinning, in that same measure let our devotion be directed toward repentance.

Grave sins require the gravest lamentations. Receive, my brothers, compunction; for it is the health of souls, the remission of sins, and a spiritual sacrifice that is supremely pleasing to God: a rich holocaust, the sinner’s heart humbled and watered by daily tears.

O monk, prick the eye of your mind, so that a tear of compunction may come forth. O compunction, how holy and wondrously are you proclaimed! You are a spiritual bath; you are God’s scourge, by which God is changed; you are the goad by which God is inclined toward humanity; you are the bond by which God is strongly constrained.

O holy and immaculate compunction, without which Baptism is of no avail to adults, without which the body is received for the Lord’s judgment, without which every confession is fruitless, without which all satisfaction is empty.

O tearful compunction! O tear that purifies the mind, makes intention fruitful, waters confession, and sanctifies the soul! This is the tear, the sister of holy compunction, which extinguishes illicit impulses, opens paradise, closes hell, and makes us despise the world in all things.

O blessed tear! You extinguish carnal thought, drive out the diseases of sins, and vomit forth the venom of guilt. O blessed plank, O life-giving little ship, by which the shipwrecked person can return to the harbor of salvation! O saving water, through which every sin is destroyed! O way by which we climb to paradise! O spiritual passage by which one passes from a trackless place onto the road!

O blessed bath of the repentance of tears, which is effective for cleansing as often as the human heart needs purification! This is, my brothers, the heavenly fuller’s herb, with which he daily cleanses the soiled garments of his servants from filth. This is heavenly natron, boiled from the dew of divine grace, which wipes away the stains of sins. This is the lye with which the head of the inner person is thoroughly washed.

O tear, you are a sweet consolation against the ruin of human beings, a substitute for Christ’s Passion, placing a remedy against sin, so that through you Christ is compelled to die as often as a person falls into the abyss of sins.

O monk, who, then, can restrain himself from tears? Let us enter, I beg you, into our consciences and examine them. And if we laughed in youth, let us at least weep in old age, considering what we paid to Christ and what we paid to the devil during the time of our youth.

And if, before we reached the desert, sight bent us through lust; if the throat was corrupted through gluttony; if hearing was corrupted by excessive speech or by willingly listening to slander; if the tongue stumbled in speech; if the sense of smell went astray in smelling; if touch was deceived by sensual pleasure; if the feet went toward theft—if you find guilt in these things or in any one of them, wash away the guilt through a tear. Measure your tears according to the amount of filth, taking up repentance, which is the mother of all good things.

Fear, however, which conceives repentance, gives birth to compunction. That repentance is worthy and good which mourns sins already committed in such a way that, once mourned, they are not committed again. For what is repentance except to weep over what has been done and not to commit again what must be mourned?

For whoever mourns sins in such a way as to commit sins again still does not know how to repent. Is not the person who dissimulates a mocker—and not a penitent—if he continues to do what he regrets?

Repent, therefore, my brothers, and as penitents practice repentance in weeping and lamentation, so that you may worthily laugh in the glory of the blessed. Amen.

## SERMON XII. ON PRIDE AND HUMILITY

Dearest brothers, wherever pride has been, there contempt and discord will also rule. It is therefore not fitting for the servants of God established in the desert to be proud, but humble; not haughty, but gentle, chaste, kind, and adorned with every virtue.

Take care, my brothers, and watch attentively, lest you be puffed up with pride over the good things entrusted to you, knowing that pride made demons out of good angels, whereas humility made human beings like angels. Pride cast angelic glory down from heaven, but humility made human weakness ascend to heaven.

O my brothers, take care lest, while praying, reading, standing, sitting, or keeping vigil, you say with mouth or heart, dwelling in ash and sackcloth with the Pharisee, “I thank you, Lord, that I am not like the rest” (Luke 18:11). Those leading the solitary life often think this under the devil’s prompting; the enemy of God’s servants often tries to make them say this.

Indeed, I would rather have you leave the desert than say or think such things. But when you are tempted to assert this or to think it about yourselves, cry out immediately, howl immediately, and say, “I am a worm and not a man, the reproach of men and the outcast of the people” (Psalm 22:6). And with the Publican say, whatever virtues may adorn you, “God, be merciful to me, a sinner” (Luke 18:13).

Let your Charity therefore attend to what our Truth said: “Let the greater among you become as the lesser, and the leader as the servant” (Luke 22:26).

O monk, the greater you are, the more humble yourself in all things, and you will find grace before God and human beings.

O holy and venerable humility, you made the Son of God descend from the Father’s bosom into the womb of the holy Virgin Mary. You made him be wrapped in cheap little cloths, so that he might clothe us with the ornaments of the virtues. You circumcised him in the flesh, so that he might circumcise us in mind. You made him be scourged bodily, so that he might free us from the scourge of sin. You crowned him with thorns, so that he might also crown us with his eternal roses. You made him, who was the physician of all and heals everything by a single word, become weak, so that he might heal us who are weak.

O holy humility, how unlike pride you are! Pride itself, brothers, cast Lucifer from heaven, but humility made the Son of God incarnate. Pride expelled Adam from paradise, but humility introduced the thief into paradise. Pride divided and confused the tongues of the giants, but humility gathered together all who had been scattered. Pride transformed Nebuchadnezzar into a beast, but humility made Joseph ruler of Israel. Pride drowned Pharaoh, but humility exalted Moses.

This is that holy humility which made us strangers to the world, which made us flourish in every perfected virtue within the solitary community. This is that holy humility which handed philosophers over to a reprobate mind, blinded the Jews, suffocated the pagans, set Christians aflame, destroyed the obstinate, cast down the powerful from their thrones, and exalted the humble.

But pride, my brothers, does not act thus. What does it do? It strikes down leaders, makes the rich swollen with arrogance, and deceives the religious. It blinds human beings so that they do not recognize what they are. It destroys the fruit of their work and binds the human mind, because every evil is opened by it.

This is that boiling pot which Jeremiah saw (Jeremiah 1:13), in which all the princes and shepherds of darkness are boiled: the pursuers of temporal goods, the hunters of riches, those who desire the first seats in the synagogues, to be greeted in the marketplace, and to be called Rabbi.

The devil kindles this pot when he inflates the hearts of fathers toward higher things. These are the four winds that blow through the whole world: arrogance, attributing to itself what it does not have; insolence, appropriating to itself what it owes to another; pride, believing much about itself beyond what is true; and stubbornness, raising itself up as a superior.

These are the four smiths who shake the whole world and scatter the hearts of God’s children. May God protect us from them. Amen.

## SERMON XIII. ON THE FORTITUDE THAT MUST BE MAINTAINED

Because by God’s grace we have been gathered together in this vast solitude, so that we may dwell together with one mind in one house and have everything in common, we ought therefore, among the other virtues, to seize, follow, and imitate fortitude.
