For if we embrace this virtue, brothers, we will not fear the darts of Fortune [Note: [Col. 1256] The fact that Augustine found the name Fortune, so often celebrated here, displeasing in his earlier works is clear from Book 1, chapters 1 and 2, of the Retractations.]; we will mock the devil’s blandishments and despise his threats.

O my brothers, bind this in your hearts, for whoever is strong is free. He does not serve Fortune, nor worldly vanity.

O my brothers and joy of my heart, consider how great was the fortitude of the martyrs, who, as though incapable of suffering, despise torments, confound tyrants, and scorn everything that belongs to the world. Though flayed, though burned, though afflicted in every limb, though thrown down bodily in every way, we do not nevertheless read that they were changed in mind.

But you must know, brothers, that fortitude is spoken of in many ways: namely, the fortitude of hypocrites, of philosophers, and of good believers.

The hypocrite, indeed, endures much, bears much, and appears strong in all things. But woe to the hypocrite, for by hunting after the glory of the world he earns eternal punishment. Here he pursues glory in such a way that he has no glory. This fortitude is not virtue but vice; it is called not greatness of soul but weakness, not goodness but infirmity.

Heretics display this fortitude; false brothers seize it. By God’s grace, I have never known you to belong to their number.

There is also a fortitude belonging to philosophers, who trampled riches, honors, display, dignities, and sometimes even the limbs of their own bodies. But this fortitude is insufficient for the merit of eternal life. Why? Because they lacked charity and the fear of God. Charity itself, after all, is the form of every good action.

O how great was Plato’s severity of fortitude! O how many and how great adversities he endured! But because he lacked the foundation of faith, hope did not raise up that fortitude; and because he did not advance in charity, he entirely lost the merit of virtue.

But there is another fortitude by which good people struggle every day unto death. Such people are founded upon God. Therefore we said above, brothers, that they fear neither the words nor the blows of the wicked.

This is that wondrous fortitude [Note: [Col. 1256] The Regius Manuscript reads: “This is that munificent fortitude.”] by which Moses overcame the harshness of the desert road. This is the heavenly bread that fed Elijah in the desert. This is the fortitude that despises death. This is the key by which God’s house is opened and laid bare. This is what compels the reins of pleasure to lie beneath the bridle of reason. This is the fortitude with which John is adorned in the desert. This is the fortitude by which Paul, the model of hermits, is blessed.

It is the armor and belt of Antony and the other holy fathers [Col. 1257], girded and armed with which they never cease to cry out daily in the heights with tireless voice.

O fortitude, staff of hermits, girdle of cenobites, and sacrament of all monks! You avail against poverty, so that the spirit of one who loves poverty is not broken, but becomes inwardly greater and grows richer in mind. The less one abounds in Fortune’s goods, the more fortitude prevails against the world’s assault.

O fortitude, if you suffer pain, you give thanks in all things; in tribulation you find spiritual riches and delights, so that illnesses may contribute to the mind’s advantage rather than to the body’s detriment.

O fortitude, you empty out all cruelty, reject prison, do not fear the cross, embrace the rack, desire chains, and always run willingly toward death.

O monk, the course of your contest is worth nothing, nor your work, unless it is strengthened by the pillar of fortitude. No building of good work exists unless you embrace the pillar of fortitude. But if the pillar of fortitude is broken, the whole building of good works collapses.

If David had held fast to this, he would not have committed homicide and adultery. If Samson had preserved it, a woman would not have handed him over to his enemies. If Solomon had loved it, he would not have worshiped idols. If Peter had held fast to it, he would not have denied the faith at the voice of a maidservant. If the children of Israel had possessed it, they would not have murmured in the desert.

Come, then, brothers: be strong in the battle of temptations, tribulations, illnesses, and injuries; fight with the ancient serpent, and you will receive the eternal kingdom. Amen.

## SERMON XIV. ON JUSTICE AND FRATERNAL CORRECTION

As you know well, dearest brothers, by God’s grace I have deserved to build three monasteries near Hippo, laudably, in honor of the holy Trinity.

The first of them is this one, in which for many years you have lived cheerfully, content with scant nourishment, associated with beasts, served by birds, scorning the delicacies of food, and fleeing the sight of human beings [Note: [Col. 1257] “It is false,” says Lupus, “that Augustine built a monastery in some unknown solitude near Hippo and lived in it. This is clear from Possidius: for he says that Augustine, having returned to Africa with his friends from Italy, lived for three years on the estate at Thagaste, until at Hippo—where he was seeking to win an Agent in the Imperial Service into his society—he was seized by the people, made a presbyter, and built a monastery on the Valerian estate.”].

And therefore I am not the wretched one; rather, you have often been accustomed to angelic conversations. Another monastery was also built in the garden that our holy father Valerius gave me. And since, after I became a presbyter and then a bishop, I could not always live here with you or with the brothers who are in the aforesaid monastery, I therefore wanted to have a monastery of clerics with me below the bishop’s house, and I began to live together with them according to the apostolic tradition [Note: [Col. 1257] The printed editions add here: “rule.”].

Therefore this word must be heard, understood, and fulfilled in deeds by you alone, who have chosen to live laudably in the desert: “Love justice.”

But to our brothers and the clerics who live in the city—and who are also bound to preach the word of God daily—it pertains not only to love justice with regard to themselves, but also to judge, rebuke, beseech, and reprove the chosen people of God with all patience and instruction.

And although our brothers who have been placed in the garden of the holy Bishop Valerius are sufficiently distant from the city [Note: [Col. 1257] Lupus, as above at Sermon 4, falsely accuses this place of being fictitious], nevertheless, since their reputation has been spread abroad by God, I appointed them to preach the word of God profitably to the people, so that the souls of the faithful, hearing and seeing their life and examples, might willingly return to him who created all things from nothing [Note: [Col. 1257] “That Augustine appointed brothers to the ministry of the word and to hear the confessions of the faithful is a mere ecclesiastical fable, plainly contrary to the discipline of those times, and therefore to be laughed at rather than refuted,” says Lupus.].

See, then, how they judge the earth and bind and loose whatever they wish, always with God’s favor. But you who have been separated from the world, and who also wished to choose the safer life, hear that above all you must love justice in all things.

O my brothers and joy of my heart, do you wish to know how you solitaries ought to love justice? Take care not to remove the speck from another’s eye while failing to see the beam in your own eye; nor should you wish to lift up another’s fall in such a way that you do not see your own.

You must not care for another’s illness in such a way that you neglect yourselves when sick, lest it be said to any one of you, “Physician, heal yourself first” (Luke 4:23). Heal yourself first, then, O monk, so that, once healed, you may be able to heal another’s wounds.

Hear, my brothers, hear what the Lord said to the Pharisees who accused the adulterous woman: “Let the one among you who is without sin be the first to throw a stone at her” (John 8:7).

O monk, in whatever matter you judge another, you condemn yourself. With what face, my brothers, shall we rebuke others for what we find more seriously in ourselves?

Therefore it is our responsibility, brothers, to be pure and holy. And if then we see our brother sinning, we must rebuke him with all gentleness, lest he perish through our negligence. For charity, not hatred or resentment, but zeal for justice, must draw the sword of correction.

Let mercy always be bound in your hearts, lest, like Judas, the one who has sinned go in despair to hang himself.

This, however, pertains especially to you, brothers. But let us hear what pertains to the brothers living in the city. Certainly it is not only this: they must also take care that they do not embitter judgment through hatred, inflame it through cruelty, or soften it through love of money. For we are truly poor and have become a spectacle to angels and human beings. They must not abandon justice through fear; they must not be moved by a purple garment or by a rich man’s gifts. Rather, the sackcloth of the poor man, the orphan, and the fatherless should move them to exercise God’s justice with labor.

Those who judge the earth must walk the royal road, turning neither to the right by making judgment soft nor to the left by making punishment harsh. It is not cruelty to punish guilt, but justice; it is not tyranny, but the judgment of divine rectitude.

We do not, however, wish or advise them to judge immediately. Rather, let them proceed with all deliberation, and, after finding and examining the cause of the matter, let them judge the offenders in Christ’s name. If they have sinned publicly, let them be punished publicly, so that others who love justice may love it more strongly, those who fear justice may fear it, and they may take care not to offend.

O holy and praiseworthy justice! Under you and through you chastity reigns; through you peace and security triumph; through you dignity flourishes and bears fruit in patience.

O justice, whoever loves you and grasps you will cross with Moses, on dry ground, the sea of the world reddened with the blood of vices. This is the rod by which, when the rock is struck, water pours forth; for when the stony hearts of subjects are touched by the judgment of justice, rivers of virtues overflow.

This is Aaron’s rod, which put forth leaves, blossomed, and bore fruit: for justice is like a leafy branch when conceived in the mind; it blossoms when exercised manfully; it bears fruit when a subject is corrected.

This is the winnowing fan by which grain is separated from chaff and pus is driven out from a disease. For against the disease of sin a biting plaster must be applied, lest corruption, left untreated, swell into a greater vice and unpunished iniquity result in an increase of crime.

This is the measure by which we must measure punishments and weigh merits.

Yet attend, my brothers and shepherds who must judge the earth: sometimes justice must be relaxed because of the scandal of many; sometimes it must be intensified, so that it may serve as a safeguard for the rest.

Then justice is truly called a sword sharp on both sides, because it defends the human body from external injuries and the soul from spiritual afflictions. It is the medicine of vices and the antidote of sins. It is the dagger with which Phinehas pierced the Jew who was consorting with the Midianite woman, and the plague ceased. It is the stone with which David struck the Philistine and freed Israel from servitude.

But without discernment this is a sword in the hand of a madman. Without prudence it is death and the persecution of the good. Without mercy it is a sword in the hand of a tyrant.

Justice, my brothers, must be held with the greatest discernment, and punishment must be inflicted with the greatest deliberation—not judging from suspicion, but from complete certainty of the truth.

Attend, my brothers: first investigate, and afterward judge rightly—not according to appearance, but with a righteous judgment. O how easy it is to judge! But O how bitter it is to withdraw what has been judged!

Therefore neither a boy nor a senseless person ought to preside over you, but a man of years, prudent, chaste, and sober, so that in his conduct and station he may appear to all as the salt of the earth and the light of the world. Such a person will not be able to ignore justice.

For the Roman kingdom continued peacefully for as long as it permitted the wise to reign. But when it permitted young and inexperienced men to reign, as though they knew nothing of justice, they became respecters of persons; and thus, losing justice, they lost dominion over the whole world.

Young and imprudent men, therefore, must not be appointed leaders or shepherds of churches, lest they perish together with the people. For when such men preside, they think neither of past nor future things; they even stop their ears against hearing what is good and true.

We do not doubt that not only young men but also those grown old [Note: [Col. 1259] Manuscripts read “the aged”; and shortly afterward they omit “by no means.”] frequently do these things in evil days. For the life of a shepherd ought to be beneficial every day.

But how can anyone do this if he has ignored justice and believes that he will reign forever? Such people cannot remember their last things, because they believe they will live forever.

O brothers, as we have frequently said, the shepherds and princes of the Romans possessed knowledge of past events, by which they could be thoroughly informed, and they always sought to learn something about the future. Their practice consisted in this: they pursued justice unto death and thought themselves happy to die for it.

But you, O monk who preside, I beg you, remember what you are, what you were, and what you will be. Then you will be reckoned just by God, and you will not sin forever.

This, my brothers, must always be our practice. If we do this, we shall always be faithful and just.

But there are some—by God’s grace, not among us—who wish to live in the spirit of liberty: proud, greedy, disorderly, gluttonous, adulterous. If anyone rebukes them, they bark like dogs, bite like serpents, devour like lions, and suffer like women in labor, saying that evil is good and good is evil.

Such men openly and with living speech presume to deny justice, saying, “See how the hypocrite who appears to uphold justice persecutes me.”

Such a person, brothers, is worse than all others; and it would have been better for him if he had remained in the world. Therefore, if we should find anyone like this in our congregation—which God forbid—who wishes to trample justice in such a way, he must not be retained but expelled, as one who wishes to live in the spirit of his own liberty.

From such people may God free us, as he has done until now by his grace, so that our holy and immaculate religion may continually increase from good to better, through Jesus Christ our Savior. Amen.

## SERMON XV. ON THE FAITH OF THE TRINITY, WHICH SIMPLE PEOPLE MUST NOT INVESTIGATE, AND ON THE SEVEN GIFTS OF THE HOLY SPIRIT AGAINST THE SEVEN VICES

[Note: [Col. 1259] Manuscripts: “Against those who speak sublime things and the wise of this world.”]

It is written, dearest brothers, that we must not speak of lofty matters as though we were glorying as the wise men of this world. For the prophet says: “Do not multiply lofty words” (1 Samuel 2:3). This saying is directed especially to you, who are rustic people living in the forests, although you must in no way doubt that you are fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household.

Do not, therefore, multiply lofty words. What are these lofty matters about which we must not speak at length, except the omnipotence of God, the coeternity of his Only-Begotten, and the magnificence of the Holy Spirit? O my brothers and joy of my heart [Col. 1260], if we wish to know how immense the Father is, we cannot grasp it. If we desire to imagine how the Son is coeternal and consubstantial, the whole natural human mind collapses. If we wish to know how the Holy Spirit contains all things and is contained by none, all human reasoning fails. Therefore, let us not concern ourselves with investigating all these things.

Why not—except because we are in no way capable of it? Therefore, my brothers, know that wherever the unity of the Trinity is being investigated, great caution must be exercised [Note: [Col. 1260] Augustine, Book 1, chapter 3, *On the Trinity*], because nowhere is error more dangerous, nothing is sought with greater labor, and nothing more fruitful is found.

Let that holy Solomon, then, come against those who wish to know more than is necessary, and let him rebuke and instruct them, saying: “Do not seek what is too high for you, and do not investigate what is too strong for you” (Ecclesiasticus 3:22). Let Paul also arise, the pillar of the faithful and the light of the world, and by his voice confound all those who philosophize while bearing the name of Christ, wishing to be wiser than one ought to be.

Yet I do not say, brothers, that you should not inquire at all. But you who are unsophisticated should not multiply discussions of divine matters. Ask, you who are spiritual, how you may keep God’s commandments; how you ought to overcome the devil in the wilderness; how you may embrace the patience that Christ taught. These are the things that the servant of God must always read and fulfill.

Our nature, finally, is fragile; and yet it cannot be comprehended by reason. The philosopher Aristodemus also labored for many years investigating the nature of the bee, but ultimately he could not understand it. How, then, can we grasp the Trinity? Why are we surprised, brothers, if we are unable to know the nature of God, when we are made of clay and carry about a belly filled with dung? Can even the angels investigate it in heaven? Certainly not. For what do they know except that God is three and one, and that he created and governs all things without labor or suffering?

Do not, therefore, brothers, speak of lofty matters; do not be wiser than one ought to be wise. On the day of judgment Christians will not be condemned, nor will they have to give an account because they were ignorant of philosophy, dialectic, astrology, or music; nor because they were unable to know the nature of God. They will be condemned for neglecting to obey God.

Therefore know, brothers, that it is better humbly to confess ignorance than rashly to claim knowledge, because rashness incurs punishment, whereas ignorance merits pardon. Let it suffice for us to know of the mystery of the Trinity only as much as the Lord explained to his disciples. No one knows how to speak about his own nature as does the one who himself said: “Baptize the nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19).

He plainly declares three persons, but he indicates their unity by saying “in the name”; for he did not say, “in the names.” The Trinity is not divided: indivisibly and individually, each person is God, and the life or deity is undivided in action, harmonious in will, equal in power, and equal in glory; it is neither diminished in the individual persons nor increased in the three.

The Holy Trinity, therefore, is one God: from whom all things exist, through whom all things exist, in whom all things exist. And so that we would not think there are three gods, the Apostle says, “To him be glory,” not “to them.” To him, indeed, may glory always belong, who said: “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Genesis 1:26).

For when he says “image” in the singular, he shows that the nature in whose likeness man was to be made is one. But when he says “our” in the plural, he demonstrates that God is not one person, in whose image man was being made. If the essence of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit were one person, he would not have said “our,” but “my”; nor “let us make,” but “let me make.” If, however, there were three essences in those three persons, he would not have said “our,” but “our images.” And therefore, when he says, “in our image,” he indicates the trinity of unity, in whose image our inner man was made, retaining the likeness of the Holy Trinity.

Just as the Father is God, the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God, yet we do not believe in three gods but in one God possessing three persons, so there are soul as understanding, soul as will, and soul as memory. Yet there are not three souls in one body, but one soul which, although it is of one substance and nature, nevertheless has three dignities: understanding, will, and memory.

And just as the Son is generated from the Father, and the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, so the will is generated through the understanding, and memory proceeds from these two. Without these three the soul cannot be perfect, nor can any one of the three exist as an integrated whole without the other two. Understanding alone is not enough unless there is will in love; nor are these two enough unless memory is added, which always remains in the mind of one who understands and loves, making its choice.

For God, the creator of the universe, directs all the movements of the soul toward the good: understanding, so that we may understand what he commands; will, so that it may be in his love; and memory, so that we may not forget what he orders.

Come, therefore, my brothers and crown of my mother; do not investigate except as much as is necessary for your salvation. Do not be wise except as much as one ought to be wise. What ought we to know except that God is three and one? What else is necessary for us except to turn away from evil and do what is good? What else is necessary except that we know good and evil—the good so that we may know how to seize it, and the evil so that we may know how to avoid it?

It is not, then, evil to know evil; for unless you have recognized it, how will you be able to avoid it? “Through the law I came to know sin,” says the Apostle (Romans 7:7), because before the law I did not know sin; but through the law that was given I learned what was to be observed and what was to be avoided.

To know evil, therefore, is not evil. But who among the pagans has ever doubted that doing what is evil is evil?

It is necessary, therefore, to know that pride is the mother and head of all vices. From it descend vainglory, envy, anger, sadness, greed, and the pleasure of the flesh, which includes gluttony and lust.

Someone ascends, my brothers, to the wisdom of the world. As he considers the honors displayed to him by his disciples, he stretches his wings to the ends of the earth, presumes upon himself, and glories in himself. Thus, by becoming proud and presumptuous, he is soon attacked by vainglory, when he seeks to appear glorious to others.

While seeking this, he notices and sees that some people despise him, saying, “He is not what many believe him to be.” For we do not doubt that many are sharper than he and many better than he.

But when that inflated man, who thinks he knows everything or possesses everything, sees some who are greater than himself, envy immediately attacks him. Anger follows in its footsteps; and when he is unable to carry his anger into action, he becomes sad. Seeking consolation for his sadness, he is touched by greed, so that he may acquire the means to surpass everyone.

And behold, while he gathers and acquires riches, he immediately falls into the pit of gluttony and lust.

But O the great mercy of the Savior! The Spirit of piety, through contempt for the world, was appointed to drive out greed. Yet because, once greed has been cast aside, one is often oppressed by evil sadness, the spirit of knowledge is given, so that it may show what kind of sadness is good and what kind is evil.

If knowledge therefore brings about good sadness, which arises from sorrow for sins, worldly sadness, which produces death, is driven out. But because many lack all these virtues, as do angry people, the spirit of fortitude is given, which restrains anger through self-control.

Such a person is strong—indeed, stronger—who conquers his own spirit than one who captures a city. But because he still envies the one who commands with greater strength, the spirit of counsel is given, which expels envy through love of neighbor.

But because he often wishes to be praised for such great merits, the spirit of understanding is given, through which he understands what he is. And because he discovers that he is nothing, he is humbled before God; thus, through humility, the spirit of understanding expels vainglory.

But because at times he does not care about outward things, yet often continues to glory inwardly in himself, the spirit of wisdom is given, through which he begins to know God. Whoever knows God’s goodness and mercy loves him with the whole affection of his heart; and thus wisdom, through charity, expels [Col. 1262] pride. Once pride has been expelled through grace, we become the temple of God and the dwelling place of the Holy Spirit. Amen.

## SERMON XVI. ON DISOBEDIENCE, NEGLIGENCE, PATIENCE, AND CHASTITY

[Note: [Col. 1262] Manuscripts: “On remembrance of the final judgment.”]

My most beloved brothers, in all your works always remember that we shall all stand before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each person may give an account according to what he has done in the body. We must take care not to appear before that terrible tribunal empty or stripped bare.

For then the saints will not help us, because there will be no time for mercy or for obtaining mercy, and Mary will already flee from the gate of paradise. For then all will be against us: Abraham against the disobedient, Isaac against the impatient, Jacob against the negligent, and Joseph against the incontinent.

O how harshly the disobedient will be rebuked, my brothers, by the venerable father of obedience, Abraham—how forcefully and how shamefully! Therefore, my brothers, pay attention and always be ready for obedience to God’s commandments, always having ears prepared for hearing and a tongue prepared for speech. Hasten with feet ready to go; prepare your hands for work without delay; with joyful heart, tranquil face, smiling mouth, and eyes adorned with the splendor of holiness.

Yet I wish you to keep holy obedience not through servile love or fear, but with every affection of charity. Then, before the judge’s tribunal, Abraham will not condemn you but commend you; he will not drive you away from himself but summon you; he will not curse you but exalt you in the eternal homeland.

I beg you, brothers, to lay aside all negligence, lest holy Jacob rise against you on the last day while Abraham is commending you. Flee, brothers, flee negligence. For just as diligence is the mother of every good work, so negligence is the stepmother of all teaching and discipline.

But even if we have obedience and are entirely free of negligence, that is still not enough unless we also possess patience with Isaac. For just as through impatience all good things are destroyed and all that is excellent is suffocated, so through patience all good things are generated and all iniquities are plunged into the depths.

Whoever is not patient, my brothers, is not a monk.

But even if we have obedience with Abraham, patience with Isaac, diligence with Jacob, and do not preserve chastity with Joseph, what benefit will all these things bring us? We must therefore love chastity above all, without which our works are worthless.

O chastity, ornament of the noble, exaltation of the humble, nobility of the ignoble, beauty of the lowly, consolation of the sorrowful, increase of beauty, glory of our holy religion, diminution of sins, multiplication of merits, friend of God, kindred of the angels, life of the patriarchs, crown of the prophets, belt of the apostles, aid of the martyrs, vehicle of confessors, mirror of virgins, refuge of widows, and joy and consolation of all the good!

Yet there are some, my brothers, who wish to live lustfully in their youth. If they reach old age, they boast, saying that they are continent. They choose to serve chastity only when lust disdains to have them as its servants.

Are such people to be called continent? Far from it. They will have no reward, because they have not engaged in the contest of labor. But eternal glory truly awaits those who have been strong enough to endure glorious struggles. Amen.

## SERMON XVII. ON VIGILANCE AND THE AVOIDANCE OF IDLENESS

[Note: [Col. 1262] Absent from the manuscripts: “and vigilance.”]

The Apostle Peter, dearest and most beloved brothers, concerned for your salvation, gently admonishes you and exhorts you to keep watch, saying among other things: “Keep watch, brothers, because your adversary the devil seeks someone to devour; we must resist him through faith” (1 Peter 5:8).

But faith seeks prayer, and prayer desires prudence [Col. 1263]. What follows, then, except that we should be prudent, founded in faith, and vigilant in our prayers?

Why must we keep watch in vigils, brothers, except because if we do not watch and remain idle, what else will we appear to be in this solitude but lukewarm? And if we are lukewarm, the Savior will begin to vomit us out of his mouth, from his fellowship, and from his holy people, because we are neither hot nor cold.

Keep watch, therefore, brothers, laying aside idleness in everything. For what is idleness except the burial of a living person, as that pagan, the dearest friend of the most holy Apostle, said [Note: [Col. 1263] Seneca, so called on the basis of apocryphal sources]?

Through idleness, dearest brothers, we grow weary of the rigor of holy solitary religion. Through it we are often tempted to leave this wilderness; through it we are frequently inflamed toward lust; through it we are stirred to pride; through it we are led toward the glory of the world; through it we are tempted to feed delicately; through it we are suffocated by the desire to dress expensively; through it we are dragged into excessive sleep; through it we are willingly led to listen to worldly speech.

This is that most evil idleness which frequently destroys the gatherings of the saints: giving birth among them to lust, nourishing gluttony among them, sowing weeds among them, generating murders among them, and producing all the works of the flesh.

What, then, do you say, brother? What can you do in idleness except the works of the flesh? No one will ever be a citizen of heaven if he has loved idleness.

Therefore, brother who live in the wilderness, if you wish to be perfect, flee idleness, because nothing worse is found among the servants of God.

Rise, then, you who sleep, my dear rustic brother. Rise, you who live in the wilderness, if the eyes of your mind are closed. Rise, you who neither stretch the eyes of your mind toward the heights of the virtues nor are able to open them to see what is necessary for you. Flee idleness, and remember to do something.

O my brothers, I wish you always to be occupied, so that by grace you may deserve to receive the prize of salvation. Wishing to flee this, the holy father of monks, Antony, cried out to the Lord in the wilderness and said:

“O Lord my God, Samaritan, true guardian of souls and bodies, awaken your grace in me; pour mercy into your servant, so that, placed in the wilderness, I may not remain idle in your sight.”

And Antony heard:

“Antony, do you wish to please God? Pray. And when you cannot pray, work with your hands, and always do something. Do what is within you; do what you can, and help from the holy one will not fail you.”

Why, then, do you despair, brother? Is the same God not still God? Was the same one not also crucified for you? Do, therefore, what is good.

Flee idleness, which is death, and open the eyes of your mind and body. You will see that each creature has been assigned to its own task. Behold, the sun completes the course of the year; the moon likewise moves through the months and their changes, as do the other stars. All perform without rest the tasks assigned to them.

Do even brute animals flee idleness through the industry of their nature? Do we not see them always laboring to preserve themselves in existence? Do we see them failing or growing sluggish in their necessities? Far from it. All are obedient; all do what they ought to do.

Only wretched man, lulled to sleep by acedia, frequently withdraws from his duty, and, disfiguring the image of God in himself, persists in acedia.

Be ashamed, Christian, and hide yourself from the face of your Savior, since you are shown today to have become more foolish than beasts and ants. Go to the ant and consider its paths. Learn from it, wretched man, who walks with head held high and already seeks to ascend above the stars of heaven. Consider its paths: although it has no teacher, it does not cease, as though concerned for its salvation, to gather grain in summer by which it may live in winter.

This must be observed not only by secular people but also by us who by God’s grace are in the wilderness and dwell in this vast solitude [Note: [Col. 1263] An error frequently noted]. We must attend to the ways of ants and imitate them in their work.

For we must labor without interruption [Col. 1264], so that we may acquire the good fruit of our works in the summer of the present life, as carefully and diligently as possible, so that in the wintertime, in the season of cold and judgment, we may not perish from hunger but may be adorned with every good thing and eternally refreshed in our homeland.

Come, therefore, my most beloved brothers, my crown and my joy, which you are: drive out all idleness, always do something good, and let anyone who is weary of praying or singing psalms not delay in working with his hands.

Consider that as long as David occupied himself in warfare, lust did not insult him. But after he remained idle in his house, he labored in adultery and committed murder.

While Samson fought with the Philistines, he could not be captured by his enemies. But after he slept in the lap of a woman and remained idly with her, he was immediately captured and blinded by his enemies.

While Solomon was occupied in building the temple, he did not experience the assault of lust. But after withdrawing from his work, he soon felt lust’s attack; and, failing, with a woman urging him toward idols, he worshiped the golden calf in the chamber.

Keep watch, therefore, my brothers, keep watch, and do not fail. For I have not known you to be holier than David, stronger than Samson, or wiser than Solomon.

Lay aside all acedia, which leaves speech bare, deprives you of every good thing, and strips you of the garments of the virtues.

O my brothers, I wish you always to be occupied in honorable work, and that what you lost in the world in the past you may recover by laboring in the wilderness in the future.

And if there are some among you who have lived most holily in the wilderness for eighty years or more [Note: [Col. 1264] What exceedingly old sons Father Augustine had, of whom it is said below, Sermon 21, “both head and beginning”! Lupus thus argues the author’s lack of learning], adorned with the yoke of holy obedience, poverty, and chastity, let them now rejoice as they await the blessed hope and the coming of the Lord.

For these men, as we see, can no longer devote themselves to fasts, prayers, and the works of the monastery as they once did—they did these things while they were able. Therefore, my little sons, if they now do not do what they were accustomed to do, let it not trouble you.

If they rest, do not be surprised. If I honor them as fathers, do not grieve, because they are worthy. You ought not to be saddened, for charity does not think evil but rejoices in what is good.

Therefore we wish, and in the name of Christ we order, that those who are a hundred years old or more should say “Our Father” while sitting on their little beds, and that they should be served carefully and without murmuring, so that they too may intercede for us in heaven, since their dwelling is already there.

May he grant us to obtain it, who is blessed forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON XVIII. ON AVOIDING ENVY

My most dearly desired brothers, do not envy one another; rather, let each person strive to please God in everything. Envy burns up all virtues, scatters every good thing, and generates every evil.

But you will say: “We are indeed unsophisticated; we know very well how to sin. But we are ignorant and weak when it comes to avoiding sins or rising again from sins. How, then, will we be able to recognize someone who has envy, or recognize it in ourselves?”

O my brothers, do you wish to recognize whether you yourselves are envious? Do you also wish to recognize whether your brother possesses envy? Pay attention: the envious person is one who makes another’s good his own evil; and when he cannot do so, he cries out through streets and squares, barking and burning like a dog. But first he kills himself, in the manner of the phoenix.

For what does the phoenix do except this? When it grows old, it flies to the hottest regions, gathers very dry wood, and, once the wood has been gathered, beats it with its wings, thereby kindling a fire. It then allows itself to be burned in that same fire. From these ashes a little worm is born, and afterward becomes another phoenix.

So the hypocrite acts, and so the envious person behaves throughout all the days of his life, burning himself inwardly and outwardly, attacking himself, and first wounding and tormenting himself.

O envious person, how few friends you have—perhaps you have no one whose good does not grieve you and whose evil does not make you rejoice! You rightly deserve to be deprived of every friend, since you are shown to rejoice in the good of none of your friends.

O envy, worse than every vice and more destructive than every plague! O envious one, who can never rest, do you not know that every wickedness has some shadow of happiness? But you, most evil envy, always seem to possess torment without refuge, illness without remedy, labor without respite, punishment without interruption, and hunger without satisfaction.

O envious, deadly worm, who are born each day in Jonah’s ivy! O fiery serpent by which the people of Israel are bitten! This is, dearest brothers, the locust by which the fruits of the earth are consumed.

For we read, my most beloved brothers, that manna was given from heaven to the children of Israel, and when it was kept, a multitude of worms burst forth from it. Thus, from grace bestowed by God upon the faithful, envy sometimes arises in the heart of the proud. And the more heavenly grace is strengthened in the faithful person, the more the mind of the proud is dissolved into the worm of envy.

We also read of a worm born from the ivy whose shade protected Jonah from the heat. At last the ivy collapsed and was utterly destroyed.

Through the worm of envy, too, we understand that the children of Israel in Egypt were bitten by fiery serpents.

So you also, worshipers of the sacred wilderness, true children of Israel, when you hear your envious detractors whispering against you, rejoice, because you have deserved to become children of God and of the holy fathers. Rejoice, praying for them, so that you may deserve to have them as companions in the fellowship of the saints.

Rebuke them and show them that envy itself is that most evil moth which destroys the purple garments of the virtues; the rust which plunders the treasure of wisdom; the locust which burns the green things of the earth. For whatever good work grows green in a person, the plague of envy almost completely destroys.

This is what cast the angel out of heaven; what exiled man from paradise; what struck the children of Israel in the wilderness; what armed Joseph’s brothers against him; what sent Daniel into the lions’ den; what nailed our Head to the cross; what caused Judas to hang himself.

Know and learn, my brothers, and proclaim it from the rooftops: envy is that most savage beast which removes faith, scatters concord, multiplies the third tongue, destroys justice [Note: [Col. 1265] The manuscripts omit the words “the third tongue ... destroys”], and generates every evil.

It is what killed Abel, burdened Adam, hanged the Shepherd, slaughtered Peter when he denied Christ, beheaded Paul and John, stoned Stephen, struck down Goliath, and deceived David. It is what overturned the walls of Jerusalem, ravaged Rome, destroyed Carthage, and devastated Troy. Many evils have been done through this most savage beast.

O my beloved brother, O dear rustic, O half of my soul, why do you not lay aside envy? Why do you love it? Do you love death? Are you going to the gallows? Are you throwing yourself into the lions’ den?

O envious one, who never rests but always persecutes the servants of God with Saul, leading them bound to the chief priest: behold, you labor to hold others, but you are held by them. You seek to bind others, but behold, as you fall to the ground, you hear with Saul, “Why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9:4).

You are anxious to hold others, but behold, blinded, you are held by everyone. You seek to defraud others, but behold, wickedly defrauded yourself, you are immediately carried away to the ground.

Come, therefore, brothers, lay aside envy. And if you see that you have envious people among you, pray for them, because they die as many times as they see you shining with every good work.

Do you wish, then, to torment them? You will never be able to torment the envious more effectively than by serving virtue and glory. Then they bark like dogs, devour like lions, grow pale in the face, threaten with their heads, make their eyes sparkle like stars, clench their hands into claws, and gnash their teeth; thus they die in soul and body.

But do good yourselves—not in order to inflame them to madness, but to please God. Pray for those who persecute and slander you, grieving over the evil affecting their bodies, but grieving more deeply over the destruction of their souls.

May Christ grant us contrition for sins and love of neighbor—he who is blessed forever and ever [Col. 1266]. Amen.

## SERMON XIX. ON THE VIGIL OF THE NATIVITY OF CHRIST

Gird yourselves, powerful sons, and be ready. For tomorrow the iniquity of the earth will be wiped away, and the Savior of the world will reign over us.

Tomorrow the darkness of shadows will be diminished. Tomorrow light will be restored to the eyes of the faithful and of believers. Tomorrow the world will embrace its restoration.

Tomorrow the Creator of the stars and Redeemer of all will hang at the breasts of the holy virgin Mary. Tomorrow he who eternally precedes the revolving ages will begin to be borne along by the courses of years.

Tomorrow, with the laws of nature set aside, the womb of the virgin Mary will be made fruitful by the power of divinity alone; from her little stream a great river will arise, the finest fruit will appear, and from her shoot the root of perfect goods will proceed, like a bridegroom from his bridal chamber.

Tomorrow, monk, you will receive the little infant Jesus, who nevertheless was made before all the ages. Prepare yourself, therefore, because he deigns to see you, kiss you, embrace you, and never release you unless you first release him.

Look, therefore, brothers, with the eyes of mind and body, and you will see God’s power coming, proceeding from the Father like a bridegroom from his bridal chamber. Him whom you will see, whom you will hold, whom you will adore, hold firmly with a pure mind and clean heart: wholly in the world and wholly in heaven; wholly in the world for justification, wholly in heaven for glorification; wholly in the world to lead forth those who are wandering, wholly in heaven to receive those who have arrived; wholly on the Father’s throne, wholly in the lap of his glorious mother.

For tomorrow the seals of the figures will be opened, the oracles of the prophets will shine, the miracles of nature will appear, and the channels of grace will drip; because Jesus Christ, the Son of the living God, will be born in Bethlehem of Judea.

When he comes, we shall see the bush burning but not consumed; Aaron’s rod flowering and producing fruit.

Gird yourselves, therefore, powerful sons, and be ready, so that with Ezekiel we may see the most sacred gate perpetually closed. For tomorrow, with the holy boy Daniel, we shall also see the cornerstone.

Tomorrow we shall see the King of kings with the eyes of the mind and of the body: beneath the form of visible bread, the invisible bread—heavenly nourishment, blessed refreshment, food of eternal life, pledge of our redemption, and saving sacrifice. Tomorrow we must eat it with our whole affection.

This is that bread and food given to the Israelite people, the sweetest manna, containing every delight and the sweetness of every flavor. This is the food that Pharaoh saw, in which there were beautiful and lovely ears of grain. This is the bread given to Elijah, in whose strength he walked for forty days and forty nights and reached the mountain of God.

This is the bread by which the angels are fed, by which the apostles are nourished, by which the martyrs are refreshed, by which confessors are fed, by which virgins are nourished, and by which all the elect are satisfied.

Whoever eats this bread worthily will not die forever, because it is the spirit of life and life itself.

This is the bread that descended from heaven, which the virgin will present to us tomorrow, which she will carry in her lap, which she bore in her womb without burden, which she gave birth to without corruption. His mother was found to be a virgin before childbirth, a virgin in childbirth, and a virgin after childbirth.

She worshiped the one whom she bore, but first in her mind rather than in her womb, and before the Son was conceived in her womb.

Lift up your heads, my brothers, lift them up in this vast solitude. Behold, your redemption is already at the gate.

O how great are the mighty works God performs for us! Behold how he has loved us. God himself became man; the Creator became a creature; the richest became poor. The giver of the law is called, for our sake, the destroyer of the law.

He loved us so that he might receive us; he humbled himself so that he might exalt us in himself. He bent down so that he might raise us up to himself [Col. 1267]. Behold how he loved us: he descended so that he might exalt us; he emptied himself so that he might grant us power.

Gird yourselves, therefore, powerful sons, and be ready, because tomorrow you will see, with the unshaken gaze of faith, in the one and same God and Lord [Note: [Col. 1267] Manuscripts: “and man”], divinity incarnate, majesty subjected, liberty enslaved, power weakened, eternity bounded, virginity made fruitful, and life weakened.

Gird yourselves, therefore, and be ready with a pure mind, complete faith, and sincere charity, so that when that Holy of Holies comes and knocks, you may immediately open to him.

Do not, then, be weary of subduing your flesh for a short time through fasts and abstinence from food and drink, because behold, the rewarder will come, rendering to each person according to his works.

Therefore, while awaiting the Savior, let us live soberly, justly, and chastely in this age, awaiting the blessed hope and the coming of the Lord, so that we may be worthy to rejoice with him in heaven. Amen.

## SERMON XX. ON THE NATIVITY OF THE LORD
Beloved brothers, man was made not only by the Wisdom of God so that he might exist, but also for the wisdom of God, so that he might be blessed and enjoy it in the manner in which wisdom could be apprehended. But because, by sinning, he lost the faculty by which he ought to have enjoyed wisdom—because he forgot to eat his bread, and changed that nourishment by which souls live into bodily pleasure—he became immersed in earthly and bodily things in sense and desire. He could not raise himself to knowledge of spiritual things without love, but recognized only the things of the flesh and did not recognize the delight of spiritual things.

Therefore that very Wisdom of God, while it was above, came down today to where man was, in order to recall him from where he had fallen. And behold, the Word became flesh, so that God and man might be among human beings. Thus that bread was changed into milk, so that it might be received by little human beings. Wisdom itself above was bread, and that same Wisdom below was milk. In its divinity Wisdom was bread; and in its humanity, the bread descending from heaven became milk today, so that human beings, nourished like infants by milk and strengthened, might be able to approach the bread of divinity; and that same bread might refresh them and, by refreshing the weak, restore them to incorruption.

Thus he gave those being restored to incorruption the nourishment of incorruption: to the little ones, the undefiled flesh that he had taken from his virgin mother; to the perfect, the incorruptible divinity that he had from the eternal Father. To the former, so that they might not fail on the way; to the latter, so that they might be refreshed and perfected in their homeland; to the former for consolation, to the latter for glorification.

For this reason, then, the Son of God became man today for the redemption of human beings, so that flesh might be liberated through flesh; so that the price of redemption might be taken from what belonged to the human race; so that the remedy might arise from the place where the defect had been contracted; and so that in the same reality both the physician’s skill and the justice of the redeemed might be displayed, when from his own substance a remedy is found for healing and a price for redemption. Since, therefore, what was to be redeemed had to be liberated from corruption, the price of redemption ought to have been incorruptible.

For this reason Mary was chosen as mother and preferred above all creatures, filled with every grace and completed in her mother’s womb with every virtue and holiness, so that an utterly pure Son might be born from an utterly pure mother; and just as in heaven the Son had an immortal and eternal Father, so on earth he might have a mother free from every corruption.

Therefore, in heaven the Son is such as the Father is; and on earth, according to the flesh, the Son is such as the mother is. In heaven, with the Father, he is eternal and immeasurable; on earth, with his mother, he is undefiled and gentle. In heaven, with the Father, he is exalted and incorruptible; on earth, with his mother, he appears today humble and corruptible in a manger. In heaven the image of the Father appears; on earth he is shown as Mary’s son. In heaven he is shown as the maker of the stars and of all things; but on earth today he is placed between an ox and an ass.

The virgin mother rejoices in humility [Col. 1268]; but today her Son commends humility by deed. Through a virgin [Note: [Col. 1268] Another reading: “Through fire.”] he came to us today; and through a virgin he went before us. Through incorruption he came, in order to take away sin; through incorruption he went before us, in order to display virtue. Jesus of Nazareth came to us today to bring a remedy; he went before us to give an example.

For a good tree could not produce bad fruit, since every tree is known by its fruit. The root is sound, and its fruit is incorrupt. Therefore Gabriel was sent as the messenger of our Savior’s advent, to proclaim the Son of God’s new birth in the flesh. In him the form of a servant, joined to the Lord, powerfully defeated the enemy: strong in him, yet not violent for the infliction of injury, but effective for the attainment of justice.

For this reason Gabriel, one of the greater Angels of heaven, was sent; but he is called Gabriel because he was stronger than all the rest. Gabriel is interpreted as “Strength,” because that very weakness was also strength, since in it the enemy was overcome and the spoil, taken by violence, was brought back.

For three had perished, and a fourth followed as their redeemer, God. The first was without male or female, like Adam. The second was from a male without a female, like Eve from Adam, because he took one of Adam’s ribs and filled the place with flesh. The third was from male and female, like Abel. The fourth was from a female without a male, like the Savior of the world, who today deigned to be born for us from the blessed virgin Mary.

And because the first author of guilt was cast down through a woman, therefore a woman, Mary the virgin, conceived and today gave birth to the author of grace without a male. This woman is the mother and mistress of the whole world, who, remaining a virgin, gave birth today to a son. The star brought forth the sun; the creature gave birth to the Creator; the daughter conceived the Father and the Son, at once the rich one and the poor one. She is daughter and mother; maidservant and mistress; begetter and begotten. She gave birth in integrity, conceived in virginity, and after giving birth, as we said above, remained a virgin; she immediately adored the one whom she had borne.

May he make us participants in that adoration and grace, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON XXI. ON THE THREE KINDS OF MONKS IN EGYPT

[Note: [Col. 1268] Manuscripts: “On the three kinds of monks and on holy poverty.”]

As the holy father Jerome declared to us in writing, beloved brothers, there are three kinds of monks in Egypt. Two of them are excellent, but the third is altogether lukewarm and must be avoided with every inclination of the heart.

What are those two kinds praised as excellent, if not the kind and order of the Hermits and the Coenobites, whose renowned life and holy community took its beginning in the time of the apostles’ preaching? These are those perfect men to whom I often clung during the time of my errors [Note: [Col. 1268] But before Ponticianus’s account, Augustine knew nothing of monasteries; see Book 8 of the *Confessions*, chapter 6, sections 14 and 15.], through whom I also deserved to be enlightened. When the fame of their holiness reached my ears, I did not long delay being baptized.

When my devout mother was urging me at Milan to return to my homeland, and I desired to have them in the depths of charity and to live together with them, I went with all charity to that man Simplicianus, who from his youth had lived most devotedly for God. With weeping and groaning I begged him to give me some servants of God from among his own. He gave them to me as a father would.

Why did he give them to me as a father? Because he knew that I wished to build a monastery in Africa. And taking with me Anastasius, Fabianus, Severus, Nicolaus, Dorotheus, Isaac, Nicostratus, Paulus, Cyrillus, Stephanus, Jacobus, and Vitalis the little poor man [Note: [Col. 1268] Possidius, chapter 3, says that Augustine returned “to Africa with other fellow citizens and friends.” Augustine names no others besides Navigius, Adeodatus, Alypius, Evodius, and Nebridius in the *Confessions*. Nothing is said of these Italians. “Therefore,” says Lupus, “this company must be counted among the fables.”], [Col. 1269] who found a money-pouch at Milan and did not steal it—we have already spoken of him, because he found it and did not steal it, nor did he wish to depart after the gold.

Thus, having taken these men with me, I wished to imitate, together with my dearest friends Evodius, Alypius, and Pontianus, who had long been with me, and with the other twelve whom I had recently taken in, those whose fame the holy presbyter Jerome had also described to me [Note: [Col. 1269] Lupus also observes that this is false, since Augustine says that his first friendship with Jerome began during his own presbyterate, through the agency of Alypius, who was traveling in the Holy Land.].

And so I reached Africa after my devout mother had died, and I built—as you see—the monastery in which we now are, separated from the peoples in the wilderness. It pleased God to give me a hundred brothers, enlightening our hearts not only to imitate the most holy solitary fathers, but also, in this wilderness, to possess everything in common after the manner of the Apostles.

God wished us to preserve these things, afterward to teach them, and through me to command them to you. For you see that many fathers existed before me, whom we ought to follow and imitate; yet they did not, as I have done, teach others to live according to the apostolic life. Therefore I do not blush to call myself the head and beginning of all of you.

Nevertheless, do not be reluctant to follow and imitate them in everything, observing that we must have and possess everything in common, since those who live in the height of poverty may do nothing except be of one heart and one soul and possess everything in common. Hence the prices of the fields were placed before the Apostles’ feet, as though to be trampled underfoot, because those holy Apostles and friends of God considered the prices of fields unworthy to be handled with their hands.

Hence also, in the old law, the Levites were commanded to possess nothing on the earth. Therefore we ought not to possess temporal goods as property. Nor should I, who am a bishop, possess anything except for the purpose of distributing it, because the goods of the Churches are the patrimony of the poor.

For this reason I, who am a bishop, must take the greatest care that the possessions of the poor, which the Church of Hippo appears to preserve, not be given to the rich; and this I have done until now. For I have relatives, and they are not ashamed to call themselves nobles [Note: [Col. 1269] Augustine says in Sermon 356, section 13, that he was not “born of nobles,” but “of the poor”; and in Book 2 of the *Confessions*, chapter 3, he calls himself “the son of a very humble citizen of Thagaste.”].

They come to me as bishop, sometimes with threats, sometimes with flattery, saying: “Give us something, father; we are your flesh.” Yet, by God’s grace and through your prayers, I do not recall having enriched any relative. I consider the poor dearer to me than the rich, because all the faithful ought to be content with food and clothing, especially we clergy. As a sign of this we ought to have our heads tonsured and shaven, lest the hairs of riches occupy the minds of God’s servants.

Come, then, brothers: be poor, not only in word but also in deed and in truth. Consider what he says to us who made himself our price on the altar of the cross, who is also our advocate in heaven and intercessor at the right hand of God the Father.

For that God of gods said to his disciples, whom he had chosen before all the world to be the salt of the earth, the light of the world, rulers of the Church militant, and teachers and senators of the Church triumphant: “Blessed are the poor in spirit” (Matthew 5:3)—not, “Blessed are those who endure harsh things under great necessity.”

Such people murmur, slander, envy those who have possessions, seize and steal; or, if not in deed, they at least try to fulfill these things in will. Therefore the Savior does not call them blessed, because they must be considered not poor but wretched. Why? Because, having been led out of temporal hardships, they have been assigned to eternal miseries, where they will not only be unable to possess blessedness but will not even find a drop of water.

Blessed, therefore, are the poor in spirit, but not those who pretend to poverty. Such are hypocrites, proclaiming poverty outwardly but unwilling to bear any necessity. In all their works they hope for the respect of honor, the glory of praise, to be feared by their superiors and revered as God, and to be called holy by everyone. They preach poverty and abstinence only with their voice, but do not think of moving them with their finger. Outwardly they cover their bodies with despised clothing, but inwardly, next to the flesh, they are clothed in purple. They proclaim that they lie in ashes, but do not despise lofty palaces. Outwardly they display an angelic face, but we do not hesitate to believe that inwardly they have a wolf’s.

Such were those Sarabaites of whom the father Jerome wrote to us in the third place, whose kind must be avoided with every inclination of the heart. They were in Egypt, living in the holes of rocks, clothed only in the skins of pigs and oxen, girded with palm ropes, and carrying thorns tied to their belts at their heels. Barefoot and bloodied, they would leave their caves and go to Jerusalem for the feast of Tabernacles. Entering the Holy of Holies, they preached that poverty and abstinence should be observed with every devotion; afterward they hurried to pluck out their beards publicly, without redemption [perhaps: compensation]. Thus, having acquired reputation and profit, they returned to their own places, rejoicing and feasting in solitude beyond anything we can explain.

Do not imitate these men, my brothers and my little children, whom I give birth to daily in the depths of charity. I beg you, do not imitate them, because we proclaim that they are already not blessed but condemned.

Love poverty, then; love it with every inclination of the heart, and do not fail, so that you may be an elect race, not a rejected one; a holy nation, not a stubborn one; a people acquired for possession, not for destruction; a royal priesthood, not a saleable price.

You are that apostolic form and holy community, separated from the world in heart and deed. By God’s power you have already struck down the leaders of Moab, and you have already wounded to death the satraps and tyrants of Jerusalem and the hypocrites of Egypt.

You are my chosen vineyard, planted in the midst of the paradise of the Church, redeemed and watered with Christ’s blood. To this vineyard I alone, by God’s power, gathered you and made you my laborers, so that, working in it to the end, you may receive worthy fruit in its season.

To this vineyard I chose you; to this inheritance of God I summoned you, although I was favored by the holy bishop Valerius, who gave me many things from the goods of the bishopric so that I might build a monastery in the wilderness. For it was not enough for me to sell my patrimony [Note: [Col. 1270] Augustine distributed his patrimony not to the monastery but to the poor, as is clear from Sermon 355, section 2. See Letter 126, section 7.], unless he himself also assisted me.

To this community, therefore, I chose you. You did not choose me, but I chose you. And behold, after I became bishop, I frequently asked Vitalis, Nicolaus, Stephanus, Dorotheus, Paulus, Jacobus, and Cyrillus not to leave me alone in the episcopate. For although I was a bishop, I did not believe that I ought to despise poverty; rather, I wished to live with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob amid riches while preserving true poverty, so that I might belong to the number of those of whom the Apostle says, “As having nothing, yet possessing everything” (2 Corinthians 6:10).

I frequently asked them to come, not so that they might be rebels against the wilderness, but so that, living solitarily even in the city, we might dwell in a holy palace. But behold, they did not wish to come, fearing for themselves lest they be captured by the world. Why did they refuse? Not because they were unworthy, but because they wished not only to be poor; they also wished to do more than we have set forth in our *Mirror*, trampling upon the world and all its pomp in every respect.

For this gift we ought all to possess the greatest joy, because they wished to do what they had promised to God and to me. And because I could not stand alone as bishop, I asked the holy old man Valerius, who had already given me authority to preach to the people, to establish a monastery of clergy within the bishop’s house [Note: [Col. 1270] Lupus says that “it is quite probable that Augustine did not establish the monastery of clergy until after Valerius’s death,” when he perhaps first obtained the use of the episcopal residence [Col. 1271].].

It pleased the holy bishop to accommodate me. Thus I began to live with them in complete poverty [Col. 1271], eating no meat except when guests came, but only vegetables and legumes without oil or butter, as I had previously been accustomed to do joyfully with you.

Therefore, my brothers, although you see me in the episcopal chair, I rejoice that I hold poverty as my dear bride, because she is also Christ’s bride, the possession of the saints, the life of the blessed, the security of the faithful, the adornment of the clergy, the life of monks, the beauty of nobles, and the magnificence of the rich.

This is that holy poverty which, when possessed and loved, cannot suffer any want. Nor is this surprising, brothers, because it is granted the possession of the Lord of all. For he is a treasure to those who hope in him amid poverty, a consolation in solitude, glory in humiliation, honor in contempt, and shelter in every protection.

Be poor, then, my brothers, because the Lord has heard the desire of the poor, and his ear has heard the preparation of their heart. Then you will truly be poor in spirit, truly blessed, kind, obedient, truthful, not hypocritical, and ignorant of every evil—if you are found to be poor in heart and deed.

May the blessed Stephen, first among the martyrs, who prayed to our Lord Jesus Christ for his persecutors, deign to obtain this grace for us. He lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON XXII. ON THE CONSOLATION OF THE BROTHERS IN THE WILDERNESS, FROM WHOM SAINT AUGUSTINE DEPARTED, WITH AN EXHORTATION TO PRAYER AND TEARS

[Note: [Col. 1271] Manuscripts: “On prayer.”]

My brothers and joy of my heart, it is time for me to return to him who sent me to you. But do not be saddened, and let not your hearts be troubled. For I shall ask the Father, and he himself will keep you, and the Spirit of truth will remain with you forever.

Again I say: do not be further saddened by my departure, but always pray for one another, so that you may be saved. Prayer is exceedingly necessary for God’s servants and solitaries. Through it God is appeased; through it God bends down toward us.

The Jewish people had worshiped a molten calf, and the Lord said to Moses, “Let me alone, so that my anger may burn against them.” Moses replied, “I beg you, Lord, let your anger cease, and be appeased toward the wickedness of your people” (Exodus 32:10–12). And behold, the Lord was appeased.

Oh, how great is the cause of prayer itself! Oh, how great a mystery! Behold, Moses prayed on the mountain, and Joshua defeated Amalek. Through prayer Hezekiah was healed and obtained salvation of soul and body. Through prayer Saul became Paul, teacher of the Gentiles and preacher of the whole world.

Therefore I beg you, my brothers, pray for one another, so that you may be saved. With the Apostle I entreat you that, before all else, supplications, prayers, petitions, and thanksgivings be made. Pray and do not grow weary; and, if possible, pour out tears.

Oh, what a great evening sacrifice you have offered to God: to pour out tears with prayer! For divine Scripture sometimes invites us to tears and sometimes to joy. The Savior often said to his disciples, “Blessed are those who mourn in this life, because they shall rejoice in eternal life.” First there must be sorrow; but after sorrow joy follows, because blessed are those who mourn.

But afterward the Savior says, “Rejoice and exult, because your reward is abundant in heaven” (Matthew 5:5, 12). This reward is acquired through tears and prayers.

Pray, therefore, my brothers, in the wilderness; pray and do not grow weary. For just as barking belongs to dogs, so praying belongs to the inhabitants of the wilderness. The prayer of the good is speech directed to God. When God’s servants read, God undoubtedly speaks fervently to them; but when they pray, they speak sweetly with God.

He himself is wise, because under few words he comprehends many things; and whatever is necessary he grants cheerfully, more abundantly and more perfectly than human beings know or are able to think.

O my most beloved brothers, cry out in the wilderness, howl in this vast solitude, do not cease to shout. Cry out in prayer and do not grow weary—not only with your voice, but especially with your mind.

For behold, you always hear the birds singing in the desert and praising God their maker. And if you cannot sing, since you are already very old, at least do not be silent in your mind. For even those who are silent with their mouths but pray in their minds are heard by the Lord.

In prayer, what is sought is not so much speech as understanding. Behold, Jeremiah is strengthened in prison; Daniel rejoices among lions; the three young men dance in the furnace; Job triumphs on the dung heap; the thief finds paradise from the cross; Susanna is defended among the elders; Stephen is received into heaven from the torrent and is heard praying for Saul among those who stone him.

There is therefore no place in which we ought not to pray, because God is everywhere and everywhere deigns to hear us. Pray, then, always and in every place, so that you may be saved.

We must pray not only for ourselves but for everyone. For, as the venerable father Ambrose says: “If you ask God only for yourself, you possess only your own merit; but if you ask for everyone, everyone will ask for you.”

Holy prayer, pillar of holy virtues, ladder to divinity, husband of widows, kin of Angels, foundation of faith, crown of monks, relief of married women. Blessed is the one who loves you; more blessed the one who practices you. Blessed the one who binds himself to you; more blessed the one who perseveres in you.

Blessed is the one who loves you; more blessed the one who practices you. Blessed the one who binds himself to you; more blessed the one who perseveres in you.

Blessed is the one who pours out tears with you, because we do not hesitate to offer to God a holy and undefiled holocaust.

Weep, therefore, my brothers, while praying, and do not cease, so that you may be made worthy of God’s grace.

But you will say: “Behold, we are many, and except for Evodius, Alypius [Note: [Col. 1272] Alypius, who obtained the episcopate before Augustine, is imagined here to have been left in the monastery, on the basis of letters 24, 27, 28, and 29 in Augustine.], and Pontianus [Note: [Col. 1272] “Of this Pontianus,” says Lupus, “these sermons—namely, this one, 36, and 48—report wondrous tricks and fables, and excessively gross lies. Therefore I believe that he is an invented companion.”], who know many things from Holy Scripture, we are all crude and uneducated [Note: [Col. 1272] Yet those in the monastery at Hippo were not so uneducated; as Lupus observes, “ten of them were simultaneously and at one time advanced to the episcopate.”]. Teach us, then, to pray.”

O my brothers, although you are crude and do not grasp subtle matters, I do not therefore consider you weaker; rather, I hold you dearer as ignorant and humble than the learned who are puffed up and proud.

Nevertheless, by God’s grace, what you have is sufficient for your salvation. Although you do not understand the marrow of the Scriptures as Evodius, Alypius, and Pontianus do, who lived with me for a long time at Rome [Note: [Col. 1272] The claim that Evodius lived with Augustine at Rome is understood to be false on the basis of Book 9 of the *Confessions*, chapter 8], we do not doubt that you understand the bark of the Scriptures.

For we told you first that you ought to sing psalms, pray, and work with your hands whenever necessary; and if you have time remaining, do not delay saying, “Our Father.”

That prayer is called the Lord’s Prayer. In it there are seven petitions, in which all kinds of prayer are included—prayers by which we appeal to God for desirable goods, for the avoidance of evils, or for the removal of sins.

The first three petitions concern eternity; the remaining four appear to concern this temporal life. For daily bread—that is, spiritual bread—although it is everlasting, also belongs to this life insofar as it is supplied to the soul through certain signs, spoken words, or writings. It is therefore called bread because it is learned by working and explaining, and thus is, as it were, swallowed by eating.

Now also our sins are forgiven us, and we forgive others; this is the second of the four petitions. The temptations that now trouble our life, and deliverance itself from evil, belong to this life, because through God’s justice we incur death, from which we are to be delivered by God’s mercy.

Since these things are so, the words of the petitions themselves must be treated more carefully, so that, once understood, they may produce a greater affection of the heart, and what is requested may be brought more quickly to fulfillment.

Pray, therefore, brothers, saying, “Our Father,” giving thanks to the giver of all good things, who is our sweetness, our life and resurrection, our hope, and the light of our eyes, the staff of our old age. He gives us understanding so that we may recognize him and understand the secrets of his secrets.

For he has given us effectiveness in our work, grace among the elect, accomplishment in his commandments and those of his servants, consolation and steadfastness in adversity, caution and fear in prosperity; and wherever we turn, his great mercy goes before us.

O my brothers, let us not neglect to pray, to discipline the flesh, or to keep vigil. Yet what shall we render to him who did not permit us to be submerged when we were on the great sea?

Behold, we were consumed, and he liberated us; we were wandering in the world, and he led us back to the way; we were ignorant, and he taught us the truth.

Therefore, brothers, let us not grow weary of praying, since we ought not to govern a household but only to please God.

And so that you may be able to sing psalms and pray without great bodily hindrance, I have ordered one hundred and forty garments, with footwear, to be brought from the goods of the bishopric of the Church of Hippo for you, my beloved brothers. In the cold season, each of you is to receive as much as necessary, returning and carefully preserving the garments in the common wardrobe with complete diligence and charity.

Know that true charity does not seek what is its own but what belongs to God. Acting thus, do not fail.

May the God of peace, who brought back from the dead the great shepherd of the sheep through the blood of the eternal covenant, our Lord Jesus Christ, make you fit in every good thing, so that you may do his will, accomplishing in you what is pleasing before him through Jesus Christ. To him be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

Pray for us, brothers, and before my departure I wish to greet you with a holy kiss. Amen.

## SERMON XXIII. ON FASTING

You have often heard, beloved brothers, that fasting is a holy thing, a heavenly work, the gate of the kingdom, and the form of the future age. Whoever performs it rightly will be considered God’s companion, joined to him, and made spiritual.

Through fasting, my brothers, vices are thrown down, virtues are increased, the flesh is humbled, and demonic powers are conquered.

O sacred fast, you restrain the body so that it does not rise; you stir up the virtues so that they may rise again; you enlighten and heal the guilty person so that he may live.

O fasting, you are sweet to the good, hateful to the wicked, delightful to the holy, but detestable to the perverse.

O sacred fast, you disclose divine mysteries; you recognize the things of wisdom and prudence; you make us remember the past; you do not neglect to order the present; and you hasten to foresee the future.

But beware, my brothers, lest by fasting you become proud, greedy, or filled with avarice or hypocrisy.

For you have often heard that Babylon is a great and populous city, hostile to Christians, serving idols and enslaved to various errors. They say that certain giants built it, but, puffed up with pride, they constructed in its midst a tower called Babel.

Afterward Nebuchadnezzar came, enlarged it, enriched it, and, puffed up with pride, cried out and said: “Is this not Babylon the city which I built as a royal house, by the strength of my power and the glory of my splendor?”

And while the king was crying out in this way, a voice came upon him, saying: “To you it is spoken, O king: Your kingdom shall pass from you; you shall be driven out from human beings, and your dwelling shall be with beasts and wild animals. You shall eat grass like an ox, and seven periods shall pass over you, until you know that the Most High rules in the kingdom of human beings” (Daniel 4:27–29).

Thus you see that, through pride, he lost his earthly kingdom and his understanding, because he wished to dwell with beasts [Col. 1274].

This Babylon, my brothers, is this world, which is full of confusion, full of errors, iniquities, and the poison of malice. Behold now how the whole world lies in evil. Behold how the devil reigns in it, while ambition reigns, while treachery dominates, and while simplicity is trampled underfoot.

Therefore, brothers, recognizing all these things, let us beware of every evil, knowing that by humility alone we are able to overcome all evils, without which our fasts will not benefit us.

This is the way by which we shall be able to enter life. We ought not therefore to be exalted if we live well; rather, preserving humility, let us never cease to philosophize. For what is philosophizing except meditating beforehand upon death?

The glory of the world does not lead us to the kingdom of heaven; neither does an abundance of riches, nobility of lineage, knowledge, wisdom, or eloquence of words; but only the grace of Christ, virtues, and works.

Come, then, brothers: consider why you came here, what you desired in the wilderness, what you wished to do, and what office you desired to hold. With one voice you will all say, “We desire to serve God.”

And because this is so, you must frequently attend to the fact that your office is not merely to afflict the flesh with fasts and abstinence from food and drink, insofar as bodily health permits, but also to despise the world and mourn your sins. We ought not to seek the teacher’s chair, but to persevere in ashes and sackcloth in the wilderness until death.

May Christ, the Son of God, whom we believe to have fasted forty days and forty nights, help us. He is blessed forever. Amen.

## SERMON XXIV. ON THE EXHORTATION TO SOLITUDE, AFTER THE EXAMPLE OF SAINT JEROME; AND ON FASTING

For we read [Note: [Col. 1274] “Here the author sins against the ancient rule of cautious liars, ‘A liar ought to remember himself.’ For he says, ‘We read,’ and by that word sufficiently indicates that he was not Jerome’s contemporary but lived much later.” Lupus.] beloved brothers, that the holy father Jerome was a Cardinal [Note: [Col. 1274] Lupus proves at length that this is false from the dispute that arose between Jerome and John of Jerusalem, because Jerome refused to be enrolled in the list of clergy of the Church of Jerusalem.
