Nor should anyone say that he became a Cardinal after this controversy, for it occurred after the death of Damasus.], in the church of Saint Lawrence the martyr.

And because he strongly reproached the Romans for avarice and foul luxury, they wished, as you have already heard, to denounce him publicly in women’s clothing [Note: [Col. 1274] “This is a fable and imposture, exceedingly insulting both to this most holy teacher and to the Roman Church,” says Lupus. “Oh, how dearly Rufinus would have bought this, if anyone had devised such things in his own time!” exclaims Cardinal Baronius.].

But, with God’s help, the reputation of his holiness not at all diminished, he eventually left Rome and, at the request of Paula and Eustochium, whom he had nurtured in the faith of Christ, he led an extremely austere life with them, as the holy father Jerome wrote to us in a letter. Indeed, I have never heard that any of the faithful of our own time was more austere.

Therefore, brothers, we too, as you have seen, wished to abandon the world, desired to flee with Jerome to the forests, and desire to persevere according to the apostolic life. For this reason let us carefully attend to living holily and justly in the wilderness.

You must know that fasting is exceedingly necessary for those who dwell in solitude. But first let us see what fasting is. For what is fasting except the proper satisfaction of all the limbs? The limbs ought to make satisfaction for the sins they have committed.

Therefore, if someone has sinned through gluttony, let him make satisfaction by fasting; for whoever alone is without guilt is alone without punishment. But since no one is without guilt, no one ought to live without punishment.

My eye has often sinned, because through it death entered my soul. Let the eye therefore be closed and suffer, so that it may not see what delights it.

The same must be done with each of the body’s members, brothers. Then we offer a great fast, one acceptable to God and devoted to him, when we abstain from iniquities and pleasures. This is the great and perfect fast.

Acting in this way, we are said to live holily, justly, and piously. Piety is rendering to God the worship that is owed to him. A person is said to live justly when he renders to God what he ought to render, and to Caesar what belongs to Caesar.

What else is impiety than committing idolatry? Yet many say that impiety occurs when someone does not distribute his possessions to the poor.

Therefore, my brothers, I want you to know that one thing is a disgraceful act, another a crime, and another impiety. A disgraceful act occurs when, by sinning, we offend ourselves; a crime, when we offend our neighbor; impiety, when we commit idolatry.

Likewise, one thing is mercy, another clemency, and another piety. Mercy concerns nature; clemency concerns justice; piety concerns God.

And because you are uneducated, brothers, let an example be given. Mercy occurs when someone sees a person being justly condemned and led to the gallows, is naturally moved and sympathizes with him, and, moved in this way, frees him from the gallows.

Likewise, if someone steals something good from a poor person, and another person comes, takes it away from the thief, and restores it to the poor person, we say that the latter has mercy.

Clemency, however, occurs when someone sees a person unjustly punished and exposes himself to danger in order to rescue him. We say that such a person possesses clemency.

Piety, on the other hand, is nothing else than worshiping God with a pure mind, which by another name is called *latria*.

We are rightly said to fast when we flourish in piety, mercy, and clemency.

May Christ help us, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON XXV

[Note: [Col. 1275] This sermon too is filled with many errors when it discusses feasts, vigils, and fasts according to present practice. Yet even after Augustine, the Carthaginian Calendar records no feast of the Apostles except those of Peter and Paul, Andrew and James, and no feast of Blessed Mary.] 

ON FASTING, AND WHERE IT WAS INSTITUTED
You should know, dearest brothers, that this solemn fast, which our nurturing mother the Church commands us to observe today, God commanded from the creation of humanity, at the very beginning of the world, in paradise to Adam and Eve: they were to abstain from the fruit of the tree. The holy Moses also observed this before the Law and received the Law. Under the Law, Elijah imposed this discipline upon himself and flew to heaven in a chariot.

As long as Eve abstained, she remained a virgin and stayed in paradise; but when she violated the fast, she fell into misery, experienced the corruption of lust, remained subjected to a master, and was expelled from paradise. Moses too, after fasting, spoke face to face with God, although before fasting he had not dared either to see God or to approach him. Jerusalem was delivered from Sennacherib in the time of King Hezekiah and Isaiah through fasting; and 185,000 men were slain from heaven in a single night. So that their bodies would not stink, they were burned and reduced to ashes and dust.

In the time of Jonah, too, when he preached fasting, the people obtained pardon in ash and sackcloth. Did not Joshua, son of Nun, also fast before he regulated the course of the day, the sun, and the moon, and defeated his enemies?

O fast, banquet of souls! Blessed is the one who loves you, but more blessed is the one who practices you frequently. For the person who fasts in order to appear good, to preserve himself, to become healthier, or to keep his body from growing excessively fat is not blessed. The fast he practices is not a virtue but presumption; it is not a virtue but emaciation. Therefore we must fast not for the world but for God; for this is how the holy fathers acted under the Old Law. They gave tithes to God and the firstfruits of all their goods; so we too must give God the firstfruits.

We give God these firstfruits when, while abstaining from food in the body, we also give alms, and when we fast from vices in the mind. Such firstfruits are now acceptable to God.

[Col. 1276] But know, my brothers, that in ancient times our faithful fathers were accustomed to fast during the vigils of the great solemnities until nightfall [Note: We find no fast of vigils in Augustine except that of the Nativity of the Lord, which perhaps was ended at the ninth hour; at that hour such fasts were subsequently ended in the Church. But even in Bernard’s time people fasted until evening during Lent, as is clear from his third sermon on Lent.]. This was praiseworthy and good. But they did not do only this: they also kept watch through the night and gathered in the church, playing and dancing in chorus. That was detestable and evil.

Such people were not only Romans, nor only Papians and Ravennates, but also Milanese. The mother at Milan who regenerated me in Christ in flesh and spirit grieved over that shameful custom; and, at her urging, our holy father Ambrose decreed that the vigils should be abolished [Note: Since this is described in book 9 of the *Confessions*, chapter 7, no. 15—“holding the chief place among the vigils”—Augustine also teaches in sermon 311, no. 5, that singing and dancing had yielded to the institution of vigils made by Aurelius.], or at least cease everywhere, so that murders and fornications might be abandoned by the faithful.

The Church of Milan, however, left the faithful only the fast of mind and body together with almsgiving. But you will say: “Must we always fast throughout our life?” O my brothers, you have received my rule, and you have frequently heard among other things that you should discipline your flesh through abstinence from food and drink, as far as health permits. I do not wish to bind myself. I did not wish to carry your burdens; but I wished to place this one thing upon you: that you fast and abstain as much as, with God’s favor, you are able.

I do not, however, want you to fast on Sundays; heretics and unbelievers do that. Every fast, except on Sundays, is good and praiseworthy if it is properly undertaken.

There is, however, a fast of devotion, such as fasting on the vigils of the saints Cyprian, our fellow countryman, and Gervasius and Protasius, and others like them. There is another fast prescribed by institution, such as that of the Assumption of holy Mary; the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist; and the feasts of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, Simon and Jude, Matthew, Andrew, and James the Greater. We must always fast on the vigils of these saints, so that, just as by fasting we suffer together with them, so in the future we may likewise be glorified together with them.

But immediately you will say to me, brothers: “Why do we celebrate the feast of the Nativity of Saint John? Was he conceived in sin?” Therefore pay attention. First a human being is sown; afterward he is conceived in the womb, and there the flesh is formed. Then, after forty-seven days [Note: Even the aged Augustine hesitated concerning the origin of souls, *Retractations* 1.3.] the soul is created and infused into the body, according to the holy father and martyr Cyprian [Note: You will not find even a word on this question in Cyprian, says Lupus.], whom I am compelled to believe in all things [Note: Yet immediately afterward he does not believe him, sermon 28.], because he spoke most excellently through the Holy Spirit.

Nevertheless, the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist is celebrated not as his first birth but as his second. His first birth was in the womb, when the soul was infused into the womb. The other was from the womb, when he came into the light; and this was without sin, because he had been sanctified in the womb.

This festival has a vigil not only among the faithful but also among unbelievers. At this feast especially, the pagan unbelievers used to gather at their church and keep vigil, as we said above. But although those vigils have been abolished [Note: We read that they were prohibited around the thirteenth century because of the scandals arising from them.], we still retain the ancient name: because when we fast, we call it a vigil.

Or let us explain it another way, brothers. While that holy Elizabeth, who was the daughter of holy Ismara—and Ismara was the biological sister of holy Anna, the mother of our Lady—was pregnant with John, John had not yet been sanctified before the Virgin’s arrival. But when Elizabeth was greeted by the Virgin, John was immediately sanctified in the womb. Rightly, therefore, we ought to celebrate his birth.

But now let us speak about the apostles whose vigils are not observed. The feast of Philip and James has no fast because it falls between Easter and Pentecost [Note: The feast of James is placed immediately after the Nativity of the Lord in the Carthaginian calendar.], a period of joy, gladness, and exultation, because the Savior rose from the dead.

James the apostle, the son of Zebedee, also has no vigil among some people because he was killed during the days of Unleavened Bread. Nor do we celebrate the day of his death, but rather the day of his translation [Note: As Lupus observes, this first became known toward the end of the eighth century, under the reign of Alfonso the Chaste.].

Bartholomew also appears to have no vigil because he was flayed on one day and died on the following day; thus, if he had a vigil, it would have to fall on the third day, which is contrary to the rule governing the other fasts.

Thomas has no vigil because he came during Advent [Note: The name and celebration of Advent were unknown in Augustine’s time.]. Barnabas has no fast because he was not one of the Twelve. Matthias has no fast because his feast falls during a time of fasting. John the Evangelist has no fast because we are in the *Gloria in excelsis* and ought to sing, “Glory to God in the highest.”

Nevertheless, I ask you, brothers: although you are not obliged to observe these fasts for the remission of your sins, or to fast because of the danger posed by enemies, do not cease fasting, disciplining your flesh as much as you are able to bear.

May Christ, the Son of God, who deigned to be born and die for us, help us. Amen.

## SERMON XXVI. ON MURMURING AND DETRACTION, AND ON THE PUNISHMENTS OF THE DAMNED

[Note: In the manuscripts this sermon occurs immediately before Sermon 19 and is entitled “On Murmurers and the Punishments of Hell.”]

While we remain in the desert, dearest brothers, we must in no way be murmurers, detractors, or whisperers, knowing that such people will not inherit the kingdom of God. Therefore let us not speak foolishly with a deceitful tongue; but, with God’s help—for without his will and command not even a leaf of a tree is moved—let every murmuring and detraction be far from us, as we consider what happened to Mary, the sister of Aaron and Moses, because she murmured.

She murmured because Moses had taken an Ethiopian wife. The Lord became exceedingly angry with her for murmuring, since Moses was the meekest of all the people who dwelt on the earth. And the Lord said to Aaron and Mary, “Go out to the tent of the covenant.” When they had come there, the Lord said, “Why were you not afraid to speak against my servant Moses, with whom I speak face to face? He is indeed my servant, and he is most faithful in my house.” And behold, Mary was filled with leprosy, which fell upon her like snow.

When Moses saw this, he cried out to the Lord, saying, “My God, I beg you, heal her.” The Lord answered him, “Let her be separated outside the camp for seven days, and afterward Mary shall be restored to her former health” (Num. 12:4, 8, 14).

Therefore pay attention, brothers: this Mary who sinned signifies the soul of subjects and disciples when it refuses to obey its superior or presbyter; by refusing, it murmurs, and by murmuring it becomes leprous. This becomes apparent when its guilt is made public.

But the good shepherd, who cares for all of you and seeks the health of souls, has compassion on the sinner and asks through prayers for the help of divine medicine for the sick person. Every day, in an unwearied voice, the good shepherd cries out—the shepherd who does not cease to lay down his life for his sheep—saying: “I beg you, Lord, heal her; heal her wounds, for she has been shaken. Heal her, for she is full of the leprosy of murmuring. Restore her, for she has been separated from the fellowship of your faithful.”

Therefore, brothers, take care not to be murmurers. For just as leprosy devours its own body and infects those who cling to it, so the murmurer not only destroys himself but also kills all who listen to him.

Therefore, brothers, take care not to be murmurers [Col. 1278] or talkative, but truthful; for in excessive speech sin cannot be absent, nor can truth be wholly present. O what a great danger it is—not only to speak falsehoods, but also to proclaim truths! It is painful and dangerous. In short, I do not dare to praise the talkative; but I presume to call the silent blessed.

Pay attention, my brothers; pay attention, lest you be seized together with my murmuring presbyters. For I came to you and wished to be with you in this solitude during the Paschal days [Note: See the final note to Sermon 5], because the presbyters murmured against Augustine and spoke against him. They did not wish to obey the Lord’s commands; therefore they became leprous through murmuring, were struck by the uncleanness of their sins, and were expelled from my house, because they were not worthy to remain with me when called.

Therefore they were separated and expelled because they could not remain without murmuring. But you, whose duty is always to pray, I beg you to pray more fervently now, so that we may joyfully restore to communion with the Church of Hippo those whom I believed I would find such [Note: Rather, the aged Augustine says in sermon 356, no. 3: “I found them as I desired.” And in sermon 355, no. 7: “All obey me willingly.” In these sermons he makes every effort to free the clergy from every evil suspicion.] but whom I could not find so.

This expulsion, however, is for salvation, not destruction; for correction, not condemnation. Thus Adam was expelled from paradise so that he might be corrected in this exile of misery and, through this temporal punishment, obtain the eternal promise by grace.

Although Adam sinned, the Lord nevertheless did not abandon him, but always invited him and his descendants to repentance. After Adam sinned, he wished to hide and concealed himself from the face of the Lord; this was a sign of grief and shame.

I want you to do likewise, brothers. If you have ever murmured or sinned—for this is the condition of all living beings—be ashamed and hide your face in humility from the face of the Savior. Then, when he visits you in the solitude of paradise and calls you, saying to each one, “Adam, where are you?” (Gen. 3:9), consider in what misery of sins you have been placed.

By calling you by your own name he gives a sign that he is calling you to repentance. By saying, “Where are you?” he shows that he does not know the sinner’s way—not that he is ignorant of it, but that he rejects it. He appears in the afternoon, showing that the Lord grows cold toward the love of sinners, because through sin the love of charity has grown cold in the human being.

Consider this, recognize that you have sinned with Adam, and say: “Lord, I heard your voice in the desert and was afraid, because I was naked of good works, and I hid myself” (ibid., 10) “in humility, recognizing that I have sinned against heaven and before you.”

But those who act in the opposite way—murmuring, speaking against their neighbor, and carrying evil in their hearts—the Lord will expel from paradise. Yet, moved by mercy, the Lord will make tunics of skins for them, so that they may not die forever in the time of cold.

O great mercy of God! O infinite clemency of God! O his great and wonderful love toward us! Behold, every day we sin and frequently offend him; yet he does not wish to abandon us. Instead, every day he gives and bestows on us tunics of correction [Note: Elsewhere, “of contrition”] and forgiveness.

Behold how great is the mercy of our Savior. Therefore, my brothers and joy of my heart, let us return to our senses and examine our minds carefully, knowing that we are now placed in the paradise of repentance and delights, and that we have been set and established in his Church.

He gave us commandments so that we might love him with our whole heart and whole mind, and love our neighbor. But how can we love him if we have become whisperers and detractors in the desert?

O how wretched and deadly a plague is murmuring itself! O how poisonous it is, for it has destroyed gatherings of clergy and many cities! And because it is a great danger to live among murmurers, such people must be expelled, lest the others be corrupted by them.

“For the third tongue commits many evils” (Ecclus. 28:16). Therefore, if after being corrected once they do not reform, let them be expelled from your holy and distinctive fellowship. Do not think this cruel, nor should those who have been expelled for a time grieve over their expulsion. Rather, let them accept it with complete humility, grieving and weeping that they have not yet understood the Apostle, who says: “If anyone thinks that he is religious, yet does not bridle his tongue, his religion is worthless” (James 1:26).

It is better to be expelled temporarily from the present congregation than permanently from the heavenly kingdom. Thus, as we said above, Adam was expelled from paradise not for condemnation but for correction.

But when the brother who has sinned and spoken against his neighbor has been corrected and reformed, I want him to be received fraternally among you. It is better for us to be reproached for mercy than for cruelty on the last day. For when we read that a devout person perished, I do not know of such a case; but I frequently hear that an impious and cruel person perished.

Therefore, my brothers and joy of my heart, I beg you not to sin, so that on the last day you may be found neither cruel nor excessively merciful. Put away murmuring; close your tongue behind your teeth; set a guard over your mouth; and be silent. It is praiseworthy to be silent not only from evil but sometimes even from good.

For the holy prophet says, “I was silent from good things” (Ps. 38:3). We must not bring every good thing forward everywhere; rather, let us recognize the proper time for bringing each thing forward.

Therefore, brothers, be not talkative but truthful. Trample down murmuring and flee from it as from death. For murmuring, detraction, and contempt are the condition of hypocrites and ignorant people.

The hypocrite is never satisfied with murmuring and detraction, cursing everyone so that he alone may be proclaimed blessed by all. He judges everything so that no one may dare to judge him. He despises everything so that he alone may be gazed upon by everyone.

O hypocrite, beware lest you reach my table. For there, before you take anything, my reading will first be read to you. What did I first inscribe on my table? What do I first desire to have or hear there? What do I first command to be kept there, except this:

> Whoever loves to gnaw at the reputation of the absent through his words  
> must know that this table is unworthy of him [Note: Possidius reports that this was placed on Augustine’s table in his *Life*. Also Odo of Cluny, book 3 of the *Collationes*, no. 5.]?

Therefore, brothers, if anyone desires to murmur, let him presume to approach not only our congregation [Note: The printed editions add, “apostolic”], but not even our table.

We did not come to the desert in order to murmur, but so that, after trampling upon all worldly things, we might be able to live piously, holily, and justly in the desert. If we do not do this—God forbid—it would have been better if we had never been born.

Why, my brothers, would it have been better? Is it not because it would have been better not to exist than to exist badly? Is it not better to lack existence than to be perpetually tortured while existing? For I know of nothing that nonexistence could harm. But to possess existence and be perpetually tortured—what else is that than always to have death without death?

I dare to say to you, my brothers, truly and beyond doubt: it would be better not to exist than to be perpetually afflicted or eternally tortured while existing [Note: A lengthy note was placed in the margin of Jordan’s copy, reconciling this passage with another passage of Augustine, *On Free Choice of the Will*, book 3, chapter 6, no. 18; in the Royal and Victorine manuscripts it was rashly transferred into the text itself.].

Let us therefore strive always to live well, so that we may also always possess well-being. We know that by God’s grace we have existence, but we are entirely ignorant of perpetual well-being. Therefore let us restrain our tongue and the other members of our body in such a way that, through divine grace, we may not arrive at perpetual evil existence.

Nor should it be said of us what is said of Judas the betraying disciple: “It would have been better for that man if he had not been born” (Matt. 26:24). Why would it have been better for him if he had not been born, except because it is better to be entirely without existence than to lie in hell?

There will indeed be a sting of pain and remorse there, but there will be no correction of the will, so that the damned can in no way love or desire righteousness. Therefore, although that rich man who was tormented in hell seemed to care for his living brothers, he did not truly care about righteousness, because those who are in hell cannot love righteousness in any way.

The rich man lay buried in hell [Note: From Augustine’s book *On the Care to Be Had for the Dead*, chapter 14], and he entirely did not know or understand what had happened to his brothers. Yet he seemed to care for them, just as we who are alive care about the dead, although we certainly do not know what they are doing.

Therefore, brothers, let us beware lest we sin and reach that flame [Note: Gregory, *Moralia*, book 9, chapter 38]. That flame has burning but no light. Why? Because those whom the flame of Gehenna torments are blinded by it from the vision of the true light. Thus, while the pain of burning torments them outwardly, the punishment of blindness darkens them inwardly, so that those who had offended their Creator in heart and body may be punished in both body and heart, and may feel punishment in both places—those who, while they lived, served perverse pleasures.

Behold, brothers, how sinners are punished. There is one fire for all, but not all are tortured in the same way. The longer someone has remained in pleasures, the more severely he will be tortured forever.

There is therefore one fire for each person, and it is bodily. Yet, in order that it may torture the most savage sinners bodily, it is not kindled by human skill, nor fed with wood, pitch, or oil. Once kindled after sin, it will endure forever; of this we must have no doubt.

O hell, how broad you are, and you have no measure; you are deep, and I know that you have no bottom; you are insatiable, for I hear that you gladly receive all, both poor and rich; full of incomparable burning, full of intolerable stench, full of every immeasurable pain.

There is every misery there; there is darkness; there is no fragrance; there is eternal horror; there is no hope of good; there is no despair of evil. Rather, every evil that can be imagined will be there forever for the damned.

There, my brothers, the demons never cease weeping and crying out; they never stop striking sinners—now the proud, now the arrogant, now the person full of worldly glory, now the lustful, now the traitor, now the murderer, now the usurer, now the verbose, now the flatterer, now the liar, now the detractor.

Behold how they will cry out. But what will they cry except: “Strike, tear apart, kill; kill without death; strip swiftly; hasten to plunder; bring coals; prepare pitch; melt gold and silver”?

Because, while they lived, they did not wish to understand God, and if they had lived forever they would always have wished to do evil, they will therefore justly be tortured forever without redemption.

Therefore, brothers, I beg you not to sin. Guard your tongue; preserve it; shut it with an iron bar, for a vain word will not go into emptiness. We shall have to give an account for every idle word on the last day.

May Jesus Christ our God help us to persevere in every good thing, he who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON XXVII. ON THE PRODIGAL SON

Peace to you, dearest brothers, who have chosen the better part with Mary, since you wished to despise the world and its pomp. You wished to scorn earthly things. With the sounder counsel of the holy fathers Ambrose and Simplicianus, we have undertaken a safer life with Paul, who fled from the world, fearing lest we be captured by it.

In short, we are in the desert, understanding the joy of fellowship and the breaking of bread, crying out with the prophet: “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity!” (Ps. 132:1).

This life is safer and sweeter: here one person encourages another, and one is inflamed by the example of another. O holy eremitical life, solitary life, life of the perfect, angelic rather than human life, life of penitents, life of those who fight against the world, life of those who flee to God, deifying rather than human life, life of sons who have gone astray and are returning to the father!

This is the house where the son is reconciled to his father—the son who had squandered his portion of the substance by living luxuriously. If our Januarius had known this, my brothers, he would not have withheld gold from us who did not know it. If he had loved it, he would have been ashamed to possess a vineyard, a field, and money [Note: The same error as above, Sermon 5.].

Why? Because he would have seen you voluntarily embracing harsher poverty than my presbyters. For just as that son who departed into a distant region squandered his substance by living luxuriously, so he himself, or any sinner, while loving carnal pleasures, lives as an exile from the Lord; and the more unlike God he becomes by sinning, the farther he is removed from God.

The substance of a human being is everything that lives, thinks, understands, and speaks; and God distributes this equally. The sinner consumes this substance when he spends his conscience, life, thoughts, and words on evil deeds.

It is also said of this son that he began to be in need. Therefore he attached himself to one of the citizens of that region, who sent him into the fields to feed pigs. He longed to fill his belly with the carob pods (*siliquae*) that the pigs ate, and no one gave him any.

The sinner is in need when he desires to fill his belly not with the bread of eternal life but with acorns, which are food for pigs. Therefore he attached himself to one of the rulers of the world, under whose favor he might feed pigs—that is, demons.

For the pig is an unclean animal; it is filled and takes pleasure in filth. The carob pods are not only acorns but also everything shameful and unclean that the pig enjoys eating. These carob pods are fornication, drunkenness, and gluttony. These are the demons’ foods, with which the sinner desires to be filled, but no one gives them to him in sufficient measure.

The sinner is always hungry; he always seeks to devour; he always desires to take pleasure, now in wantonness, now in something else. But when the Lord the Father visits him through the grace of his Passion, the wretched sinner repents. He is sorry that he is already feeding pigs; he reflects, and through reflection rises and goes to the father, saying:

“Father, I have sinned against heaven, because I have frequently taken your name and the names of your saints in vain. I have also sinned before you, because I have sinned against your humanity, because I did not recognize in my deeds the weakness you suffered for me. I have sinned before you because you are God and human being. I have sinned against heaven, because I have sinned against the Father and the Holy Spirit. Therefore I am not worthy to be called your son” (Luke 15:21).

But let us hear, read, and proclaim what the merciful father did; let us not be silent. Moved by mercy, when he saw him alive, he ran to meet him; when he saw him weeping, he wept; when he saw him stripped, he ordered a robe to be prepared; when he saw him barefoot, he ordered shoes to be put on him; believing him weak and hungry, he ordered the fattened calf to be killed.

O how great is the mercy of such a father! O how infinite his compassion! O how sweet and devout his pity!

Behold, the son fled into a distant country, yet the father patiently waits for him. He destroyed all his goods, yet the father hastens to call him back. He feeds pigs, yet the father now prepares a calf for him. He is almost dying of hunger, yet the father already cries out that a feast should be held. He appears naked, deprived of good works, and behold, he is clothed in the former robe of the Savior’s grace, which he received in Baptism, and he is given the ring of the faith of betrothal.

Thus he can no longer feed pigs, since he has fled to the father’s house; rather, as a citizen of the saints and a member of God’s household, he is established forever and beyond in the house of divine majesty.

The merciful father demonstrated this well: when he saw him, he was moved by mercy and ran to meet him; stretching out his arms around his neck, he kissed him and said to his servants, “Bring the calf, and let us eat. This son of mine [Col. 1282] was dead and has come to life again; he was lost and has been found” (Luke 15:23–24).

The Savior did the same for Peter when Peter denied him: when he looked at him, when he looked upon his mind, then Peter wept bitterly. The Savior runs to the sinner, because the sinner cannot approach God by himself unless the Savior helps him, unless he looks upon his mind.

But after he has looked upon him, he bends over his neck, because he places his light burden upon his neck, saying, “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart” (Matt. 11:29).

Then the sinner is clothed in the robe, when the soul is clothed in the garment of virtues. There are two robes: one, namely, when the soul is clothed in the garment of virtues in the present; the other is the robe of immortality, when the body too will be resurrected at the end of the age.

Therefore, my brothers, although you are in the desert, you must nevertheless know that the two robes are the two resurrections. One is of the soul, when it is resurrected from the vices in which it lay dead; the other is of the body, when the body is conformed to the body of Christ’s glory, when it will be restored on the day of judgment.

Come, then, my brothers and crown of my mother: know that we have already fed pigs, since for a long time we pleased demons by sinning. We frequently desired their carob pods when we wished to please the world, when we longed to flourish in it, and when we clung to its pleasures with our whole desire.

But now, by God’s grace, we are servants of Christ. Let us not cease crying out: “I have sinned, Lord; I am no longer worthy to be called your son.”

Hearing our cry, he runs to us, kissing us and giving us his peace. He gave us the robe when he stripped the soul of its vices. He gave us the ring when he strengthened us in his faith. He gave us shoes when he impressed upon us the remembrance of death. He killed the calf when, in the sacrament of the altar, he renewed in our minds the remembrance of his Passion.

Then the father eats and feasts with us, when we take delight in persevering in his works. Then, when we have been so adorned, God commands the angels to prepare a banquet, because we were dead and have risen; we were lost and have been found.

Consider, therefore, brothers, why we have come. Behold, we are in solitude; we have been separated from the world, and for a long time now we have remained in solitude, so that we may be able to live more peacefully according to the apostolic pattern.

A place does not make people holy; rather, good conduct will sanctify both the place and us. An angel sinned in heaven; Adam sinned in paradise; yet neither had a holier place than that. For if places could make their inhabitants blessed, neither human being nor angel would have fallen from his dignity.

Consider, therefore, what the black garment, the leather belt, and the crown of the head signify. The black garment, which is of little value, announces to us contempt for the world and remembrance of death. The leather belt signifies restraint of the loins. The hair shaved from the crown of the head signifies the removal of the excess of sins from the mind.

Thus the holy father Ambrose answered me when he regenerated me in Christ in the thirtieth year of my life [Note: Rather, in the thirty-third year, the year in which Monica died; book 9 of the *Confessions*, chapter 11, no. 28], when I asked him.

Consider, therefore, brothers, how blameworthy it would be if pride or lust were concealed beneath such a habit. Humility itself is therefore supremely necessary for us who remain in the desert; it is signified by the garment. Chastity is signified by the girding of the loins; obedience is understood through submission.

We also carry staffs, by which discipline is understood—a discipline under which we must always be ready to remain.

But may God, who has recalled us from the darkness of the nations to grace, also strengthen us in every good thing, so that we may abound in hope and in the virtue of the Holy Spirit. Amen.

## SERMON XXVIII. ON THE LORD’S SUPPER
We have heard, dearest brothers, that when the Lord dipped the bread and gave it to Judas, Satan entered into him after the morsel. And Jesus said: “What you are doing, do quickly” (John 13:26). When he had received the morsel, he immediately went out. It was night.

When he had gone out, the Lord said to his disciples: “Rise.” And afterward he said: “Little children, I am with you only a little while longer. Before I depart from you, however, I give you a new commandment: that you love one another, just as I have loved you” (ibid., 33–34).

For your Charity knows well that the whole perfection of our life and edification is received from the Gospel. Its words were given to us by our supreme Master; therefore they are more precious, and every day they sufficiently exhort and edify us. We now present them to you and recall them to your memory—not because you do not understand them well, although you remain in the desert [Note: [Col. 1283] See the note to Sermon 4], and are also bodily separated from the nations, before I became a priest and bishop, as you were able to see together—but for this reason I recall them to you: not to teach you, but to admonish both myself and you, brothers.

In the Gospel passage that concerns the present day, we are instructed concerning patience, love, and humility. Therefore, brothers, so that I too may be more fully corrected and taught together with you, I wished to leave behind my priests, whose apostolic life is one with yours and theirs; and I did not hesitate to leave behind, even bodily on this day, the holy old man Valerius, desiring to teach you and to be taught by you, so that together we may worthily offer some fruit to God on the day of so great a solemnity.

Therefore, brothers, as we approach the exposition of the holy Gospel, I first want you to hear and know that the Lord Jesus, wishing to correct his disciple Judas in many ways—by threats, sacraments, examples, and lamentation—and inviting him to correction by these means, finally revealed that he was already prepared for condemnation and ruin when he said at supper: “He who dips his hand with me in the dish is the one who will betray me” (Matthew 26:23).

When Judas had thought that his wicked life was known to no one, he was ashamed while listening to the Master, but he did not repent. For long before the Passion he had said: “Did I not choose twelve, and one of you is a devil?” (John 6:71). And after supper he said: “You are clean, but not all” (ibid. 13:10). The Master said this wishing to correct the disciple by a word. See how he corrected him with words of fear.

But when the Lord saw that he could not correct him by words, since Judas was unwilling, he endeavored to correct him and to instill eternal fear in him, saying: “Woe to that man by whom I am betrayed! It would have been better for him if he had not been born” (Matthew 26:24).

But the Lord gently invited the disciple, whose heart had been wickedly hardened, to the love of the sacrament, saying to him after Peter and to the others: “Take and eat; this is my body” (ibid., 26). For that sacrament is given to human beings so that the body may be joined on earth to its head. Just as many grains make one bread and many clusters produce one wine, so the body of Christ is formed from many human beings.

The Lord offered the disciple the sacrament of unity in order to invite him to the humility of love. Although he also offered an example of humility for the sake of the other disciples, he nevertheless greatly desired to recover the lost sheep.

But when he saw that Judas was wickedly obstinate, he rose from supper, laid aside his garments, girded himself with a towel, and came first, as I think, to the prince of the Apostles. Before him the incarnate God knelt: God before a human being, the Creator before his creature, the Master before his disciple, the King before a fisherman, the learned before the unlearned, wisdom before ignorance, beauty before deformity.

Therefore, when Peter saw the incarnate God bending down before him, he was terrified and horrified. He ran through the dining room like a madman and cried out: “You shall never wash my feet” (John 13:8). For Peter said: “Lord, I have already said that you are the Christ, the Son of the living God; and you are washing my feet?”

But you ought to observe, brothers who live in the desert, why, I ask, the supper is said to have taken place when, after the washing of the feet, the Lord is said to have handed Judas a morsel of bread. We must not understand that the supper had ended when bread is said still to have been on the table. They were still eating when the Lord rose from the table, and yet the supper is already said to have taken place. You must understand that it had not yet been eaten, but had been prepared and brought to the table for the use of the guests.

Therefore John, the great eagle, calls this the supper, attending carefully to everything. First he wished to commend the majesty of our Savior, saying: “Jesus, knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands, and that he had come forth from God and was going to God” (John 13:3).

John expresses Christ’s great power when he affirms that the Father had given everything to him. He proclaims Christ’s great majesty when he asserts that he came forth from God. Yet today we have heard that the one who has everything in his hand also lays aside his garments.

But what wonder is it if he lays aside his garments for his disciples, when he also gave his flesh for his enemies? What wonder is it if he girded himself with a towel in the manner of a servant, when, taking the form of a servant, he was found in appearance as a man? What wonder is it if he poured water into a basin, when he deigned to pour out his blood for our redemption?

And John says: “Then he came to Simon Peter” (ibid., 6). Some, among them that most holy martyr and teacher Cyprian, appear to think that the Lord washed Judas before Peter, wishing to recall the aforesaid disciple.

But the reasoning does not seem weighty [Note: [Col. 1284] The author has now forgotten that in Sermon 25 he claimed to believe Cyprian in everything]. Since he had already made Peter the head of all, he approached him first in honor, so that the others might afterward do likewise. Therefore this should be understood as follows: after summarizing the matter well by saying, “He began to wash the feet and wipe them with the towel,” he returns afterward to the order of events by saying: “Then he came to Simon.”

What, moreover, does the Lord mean when he later says: “He who has bathed does not need to wash except his feet, but is completely clean” (ibid., 5, 6, 10)? If he is completely clean, why is it necessary for him to wash his feet?

Therefore, brothers, you must observe that the Lord makes this statement concerning the washing of Baptism. Whoever has been completely bathed in Baptism needs only to wash the feet of venial sins, from which the human mind cannot remain free—not even an infant whose life upon earth lasts only one day.

Finally, when the sacraments of the sacred supper had been performed and completed, when the Apostles had been made priests in that same supper, had received Communion, and their feet had been washed, he returned to the table and said: “Do you know what I have done to you? If I, the Lord and Master, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet” (ibid., 12, 14).

If I am the Master, learn from the Master. If I am the Lord, let the servant be ashamed to despise this. If I have already spared the traitor, strive also to spare. If I knelt before him, be humble before your adversaries. If I permitted myself to be kissed by him, deign also to offer your cheek. If I called the traitor “friend,” do not disdain to call your enemy “friend” in heart and deed, because “a servant is not greater than his lord.”

A little later, showing his grief over and grieving for the son of perdition, troubled in spirit and sorrowful, he said: “One of you will betray me” (ibid., 21).

O how deeply the Lord grieved over his lost disciple! O how earnestly he strove to recall him to himself! He grieved because he could not correct him. He grieved because he knew that Judas was already obstinate with the devil. He grieved because he was about to pronounce upon him the sentence of eternal condemnation.

And when the disciples saw that the face which the angels long to behold was troubled, they asked who it was, wondering which of them was the greater. But why was this? Only because, judging as human beings do, they thought that the one who was greater, so that he might exercise dominion, was arranging to betray the Master.

Some perhaps suspected Peter, because he had already promised that he would do more and much more for the Master, suspecting that he spoke so often with a feigned heart when he said, “You are the Son of God.” But because Peter knew himself to be innocent, he signaled to John to ask. The Lord said to him: “It is the one to whom I shall give the dipped bread; but take care not to tell Peter.” And when Jesus had dipped the bread, he gave it to Judas (John 13:26).

Therefore it must not be believed that the Lord said this in a loud voice, because if Peter had known it, he would have torn the traitor apart with his teeth. Nor should it be thought that Judas then received the body of Christ, because the Lord had already given Communion to all the disciples, including Judas, as Luke clearly shows. Nevertheless, the Lord wished to hand the dipped bread to the disciple in order to signify that his heart had been dipped in poison.

“And after the morsel, Satan entered into him.” Had Satan not already entered his heart before the morsel? Certainly, brothers, before the morsel Satan had entered Judas’s heart, but only in affection and will; after the morsel Satan entered in affection and deed.

Yet the morsel that Christ gave the disciple was good. The sacrament that he bestowed upon him was also good. But sometimes good things do harm, and sometimes bad things are beneficial. For the body of the Lord, which is good, is bad for the wicked. The sting of the flesh is bad, and yet it was good for Paul; and we know that what was bad proved beneficial to him.

As we said above, brothers, this bread, handed by Christ and unworthily received by Judas, caused Christ, by reason of his merit, to allow the devil greater license over him after his manifestation, and therefore he inflicted a heavier vengeance upon him. For when grace had been withdrawn, the Lord abandoned him to evil; he abandoned him according to the desires of his heart, and he went after his own devices.

And permitting him to remain in his own will and judgment, he said to the disciple: “What you are doing, do quickly” (ibid., 27). It was as if the Lord were saying: “Because I cannot recall you by the fear of shame, or of eternal death, or by love, I give you power to carry out in deed what you have already done in your will.”

O Judas, what are you doing? Take heed before you act; for after the deed you may perhaps be unable to have the grace of repentance. Why do you desire to betray [him], who forgave you many sins? Did he not often free you from death? Did he not, out of love for you, heal your father of leprosy and also free your mother, with whom you had committed incest, from paralysis? [Note: [Col. 1285] Vinding rightly rejects these as fabrications.] Did he not appoint you as a disciple? Did he not make you keeper of the purse? Did he not often catch you in theft and always spare you? Did he not honor you, for the most part, after Peter? [Note: [Col. 1285] John and James also seem to have been preferred to him, since at the Transfiguration, and at the raising of the ruler of the synagogue’s daughter, and elsewhere, they alone were beside Christ, not Judas.] Did Christ not always wish to have you near him? Did he not often recall you to peace after he knew that you would betray him? Did he not give you his sacred body? Did he not kneel before you? Did he not wash your feet? Did he not kiss you?

Why, then, do you wish to betray the Master from whom you have received so many good things?

But considering none of these things, he immediately went out after receiving the morsel. And he went out appropriately, because he truly went out from God and from the fellowship of God’s disciples. And, the Evangelist says, it was night (ibid., 30). Night was fittingly given to the betraying disciple, because blindness had darkened his mind.

After that disciple had departed from them into the night, the Master immediately gathered the eleven and said: “Little children, I am with you only a little while longer; therefore I give you a new commandment: that you love one another, just as I have loved you” (ibid., 33–34).

For he was a new man, because human beings are generated in four ways: without a mother, as Eve; without a father and mother, as Adam; from a father and mother, as human beings; or without a father, from a mother alone, as Christ. He was therefore rightly new, because he was God and man.

He also promised a new kingdom, which no one had ever dared to promise; therefore he gave a new commandment. In the Old Law it had been said: “You shall love your friend, and you shall hate your enemy” (Matthew 5:41). But Christ gave a new commandment, because he commands us to love enemies as friends.

For the other virtues—faith, prayer, almsgiving, virginity, and the other virtues of the body—may be shared by both believers and unbelievers [Note: [Col. 1285] How can faith belong to unbelievers?]. But loving an enemy is a virtue belonging only to Christians. Therefore the Master of truth said: “By this people will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” (John [Col. 1286] 13:35).

Know, however, brothers, that this order must be observed in loving. First we must love God above ourselves and above all things; then our soul, which is our nearest possession; then the body, because it is God’s creation. Therefore the Apostle said: “No one ever hates his own flesh” (Ephesians 5:29).

We must therefore nourish the body, not kill it, but sustain it with food and drink as health permits. God wills this; the Apostle wills this; and so I too, brothers, have commanded you. Therefore I exhort and admonish you, and command that you discipline the flesh only as much as nature can bear.

For when I see among you some who are sixty, some seventy, and some a hundred years old [Note: [Col. 1286] See above, Sermon 17], and see them fervent with the love of God, crucifying their bodies and not even drinking wine, I fear that they may offend God rather than please him. To such men I command in the name of Christ that at least on Sundays and feast days they drink wine or beer.

But let the young men who are strong and have already begun to triumph over the enemy do penance in the name of Christ, lest they be overcome by the enemy. For this is what I wish, and what I have often commanded to be observed; thus we shall not kill our bodies, but they shall serve their Creator.

Next we must love our neighbor as our brother, our friend, or our enemy. Therefore take heed: if you see your enemy hungry, feed him; give him drink; cover him; and do not despise your own flesh.

Spiritual love belongs to the good, because everyone who possesses it is good. Has anyone ever entered paradise with hatred? I remember often reading of someone going to hell while harboring hatred, but I shall never admit that such a person flies to heaven.

Do we therefore wish, brothers, to be citizens of the heavenly city? Let us observe the new commandment of the new city. That city, I say, has peace, commands peace, and loves those who love peace. Let us therefore pursue peace, without which no one can see God. Let us seek peace, and afterward follow peace. God dwells in it; in it he rests and is at peace, because “his place has been made in peace.”

Let us not, then, have a heart dipped in hatred, lest we be sons of Judas the traitor, lest we be hanged with him and, together with him, be dragged by the devil into the depths. Whoever carries hatred in his heart is a second devil; whoever obstructs peace is an antichrist; and whoever establishes peace among brothers is truly a son of God.

Consider Mary, brothers, because, having loved greatly, many sins were forgiven her. What else did the Lord say to Peter but, “Peter, do you love me?” And because he loved, he deserved also to be loved; he deserved to hear: “Feed my sheep; feed my lambs” (John 21:15).

He even said to the disciple who loved Christ and whom Christ loved: “My beloved, come to me, because it is time for you to feast.”

Let us therefore have peace, brothers, if we wish to have peace with Christ. If you wish to be loved by Christ, love your enemy for Christ’s sake. If you wish to be loved, then love.

Embrace this peace, love it, and preserve this peace and concord until death, if you wish to have peace with God. For peace is the guardian and care of all the virtues.

At his birth he commanded the angels to announce it. He often announced peace to the Apostles; he commanded human beings to preach peace; he left peace to the Apostles as a testament; while hanging on the cross he asked for peace; and in the sacrifice he so often wished peace to be proclaimed among the people.

In the end, no pardon will be given except to the peaceful person. Therefore drive from you this deadly poison of hatred, and have peace among yourselves, because you are brothers who have been gathered together here in this vast solitude.

For together we all share one bread, one garment, one black color, and one water. Let us therefore recall, brothers, that the Lord was kissed by an enemy and nevertheless called that betrayer “friend”: “Friend,” he said, “why have you come?” (Matthew 26:50).

Give, then, the peace of reconciliation, but not the kiss of betrayal. For who could doubt that one who falsely kisses an enemy or flatters him with words is the brother, companion, and likeness of Judas the traitor? [Col. 1287] But whoever does so out of love is a true son of Christ.

For you, brothers, whose life is the light of the world, although the world does not see you, I nevertheless call you the light of the world and the salt of the earth. Therefore, because you are light, let your good works shine.

We who appear to bear upon our bodies, in our habit, the figure of the cross, and who bear the name of holy religion; we who also wear the black garment of humility and appear girded with leather belts—let us beware lest we be whitewashed tombs, which appear beautiful and splendid outwardly but inwardly are full of hidden bones of the dead.

Let us take care lest it be said to us: “Woe to you who shut the kingdom of heaven before human beings” (Matthew 23:13). For I greatly fear that we may not enter paradise [Note: [Col. 1287] Perhaps, “that we may enter paradise”—i.e., the manuscript may have omitted non], and may not permit others to enter.

But why do I say this, brothers? Not because I believe you to be evil, but because I grieve over our lost brother Simplicius [Note: [Col. 1287] Lupus had already observed that this Simplicius was an unknown and fictitious man, in the note to Sermon 4]. He came to this place and to this holy community with such fervor, but when he heard that his father had been killed, he departed from us and entered the world so that he might avenge his father.

Therefore, whoever thinks that he stands must watch carefully and see that he does not fall. When people see those who appeared to be pillars of holiness falling so wickedly, they not only shut the kingdom of heaven against those very men, but also against those who remain in the world.

Finally, brothers, for us who bear the name and habit of holy religion, an evil life is shown to be more dangerous than it is for those who remain in the world. Let us therefore weep for our sins and for our lost brother. Let us love one another, because love is from God.

Let no one be ashamed to ask forgiveness from another, because Christ was not ashamed to recall his enemies to peace upon the cross. Let the servant not be ashamed to do what the Lord first did.

May the Lord, who makes us dwell together in one way of life in a house, who is true peace, and who has made both one, cause us to persevere in true peace.

## SERMON XXIX. ON THE DECEITFUL TONGUE

I wish you to know, dearest brothers, what the deceitful tongue is—the tongue from which David, the most excellent of the Prophets, asked the Lord to deliver him when he said: “Lord, deliver my soul from lying lips and from a deceitful tongue” (Psalm 119:2).

Therefore know, brothers, that the deceitful tongue is not only the one that sows discord among brothers, stirs up quarrels, incites rages, and even disturbs assemblies. We also call that tongue deceitful which seeks to praise you by flattering you, saying to your face that you are what you are not.

We must pray to God concerning such people, that he may free us from them, and so we may be freed. Why must we ask to be freed from them? Why must we flee from them as from death? Because they are flatterers; because they love and practice lies; because they are inventors of falsehood; because they are brothers of the devil; because they destroy truth; because they lead purity astray; because they invent hatreds; because they are the devil’s javelin-throwers; because they are Satan’s mediators; because they persecute God; because they assail souls [Note: [Col. 1287] Perhaps “killers”]; and because they are inventors of every evil, carrying honey in their mouths while spitting the incurable poison of asps into human hearts.

Behold why we must ask the Lord to deliver us. O wicked and deceitful tongue! O wicked betrayal! O most evil cunning of the devil! O great malice! It seeks to ensnare human beings not only through bitter words but also through sweet ones, so that it may lead them with itself into the depths.

For if one person is harmed by another, suffers reproaches, insults, and injuries, he regards that person as an enemy. “I believe he does not love me; I must certainly guard myself against him,” a person will say. But if I wish to please God, I must offer him the other cheek, bear everything with patience, and not return evil for evil.

See what remedy there is for such things. But if someone proclaims me blessed, and I do not recognize the words as flattery, what remedy will I have? Therefore, brothers, the deceitful tongue is not only the one that causes evil among brothers, but also the one that flatters.

If someone does not offend by word, he is a perfect man. But because no one is perfect on the journey, we must therefore bear one another’s burdens. Yet no one can bear another’s burdens unless he has love.

But whoever does not have love cannot bear not only the burdens of his neighbor, but even his own. What should one who has no love do? Immediately he makes a beam out of a splinter, regarding a word as a deed and thinking that the deed has been committed. Thus he grieves, cries out, becomes sorrowful, threatens to tear his neighbor’s life apart. In this way the one who lacks love is consumed, unable to bear another’s burdens, often desiring even to die but unable to do so.

But we, brothers, must not act in this way. If you are struck by a deceitful tongue, say, not with a troubled spirit, not with an inflated heart, but with humility and tranquility: “Lord, deliver my soul from lying lips and from a deceitful tongue.”

Thus, in a person who possesses love, the love of charity is stirred more frequently. The heart is inflamed and burns; the inward parts of compassion revive; and thus those who are touched by a deceitful tongue do not cease to cry out: “My life is spent with grief, and my years in sighing” (Psalm 31:10).

## SERMON XXX. ON THE CONFESSION OF SINS

People commonly say, dearest brothers: “God knows everything; with him there is neither past nor future. He sees and weighs everything; all things are naked and open to him. Why, then, does he wish us to confess to human beings the sins we have wickedly committed? Is it not better to keep all evils silent than to proclaim them from the rooftops?”

For someone may say: “I have sinned more than all human beings.” But if I proclaim all my sins to human beings, I shall be regarded by everyone as worse than all others, and many will commit many evils by my example. How, then, should a person confess his sins to another?

O human being, do you not know that we are all sinners? If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us. We all sin; we are all born with sin; we are all submerged in sins—even the infant whose life upon earth is only one day old.

Why, then, are we afraid to confess our sins? Nevertheless, we ought to confess to God, because he is good and his mercy endures forever. God wishes us to confess—not because he is unaware of our sins, but so that the devil may hear that we confess and repent of having sinned; and when our sins have been confessed with grief and tears, he may no longer have grounds on which to accuse us.

For, brothers, the devil wants us to remain silent, while God wants us to confess. And whom should we obey more? Certainly God, who has commanded what leads to salvation.

It is not enough to cease from evil unless we confess with grief the sins we have committed. Nor is it enough to confess to God alone; we must confess our sins to one another.

Do not delay confessing to God; do not delay turning to God; do not put it off from day to day. For the wrath of God will suddenly come, and at the time of vengeance it will destroy you.

O my brothers, who until now have slept, turn to God with all your heart, with fasting, mourning, and weeping (Joel 2:12). For when he says “with all your heart,” the prophet teaches us that the heart is the source of repentance; weeping belongs to the eye; mourning to the mouth; and fasting pertains to the whole body.

O human being, do not delay turning to God. Examine your mind; look carefully into each secret place of your heart; consider, before you approach confession, that the heart sinned by desiring evil, the eye by seeing vanity, the mouth by speaking falsehood, the ear by hearing lies, and the hand by committing beatings and murders—or, if not in deed, at least in will. Who will be able to excuse himself? The feet, too, are swift to evil.

Therefore, my brothers, just as you presented your members to serve impurity and iniquity leading to iniquity, so now present your members to serve God in sanctification. First, let the heart that thought and desired evil repent and grieve. Let the eye weep; let the mouth pray without ceasing; let the ears hear the word of God; let the hands extend alms, receive strangers, care for the sick, and clothe the naked; let the feet come to church; let the knees bend and labor.

For just as there was no member that did not displease God by sinning, so let there be no member that does not suffer a fitting punishment. God gave us members so that we might serve him, not the world.

But alas, brothers! Those who have become citizens of heaven and members of God’s household have become lovers of the world, loving earthly things more strongly than heavenly things, transitory things more than eternal things, and their possessions more than themselves.

Not so, my brothers, not so! For behold, the time is already near; behold, it is already threatening us. Rise, then, you who eat the bread of sorrow, and let us hasten to go to church and confess our sins with grief and tears.

But first this order must be observed: we must consider our sins beforehand, so that in declaring them we may confess to God and to the priests their nature and circumstances, and so be able to depart from their feet not burdened but relieved.

And do not, my brothers, delay confessing your sins. For whoever postpones confession until the final day of Lent or of his life gives a sign that he does not do it willingly—not graciously, not with a pure heart, but apparently under compulsion. Consider, then, how much compelled service pleases God or human beings.

Let us not therefore delay from day to day revealing the secrets of our hearts [Note: [Col. 1289] A similar sentence occurs in Prosper, Sentence 71, but not the same words]. For God promised forgiveness to the repentant, but he did not promise it to one who postpones until tomorrow.

Therefore let us not delay. When you approach confession, whether you are a man or a woman, take care not to laugh or walk about adorned; do not begin by telling stories. Rather, with head bowed and back covered with ashes and sackcloth, confess your sins to one another.

But I beg you, O human being, do not be afraid to confess. Frequently the devil binds your heart so that you will not confess, saying: “How shall I confess this and that?” O human being, whenever you perceive this, do not doubt that it is the devil’s temptation. He wishes wickedly to bind you so that, remaining in your sins, you may always do without great resistance what pleases him.

Therefore do not be afraid to confess your sins, brothers. For what I know through confession I know less than what I do not know. Why are you afraid to confess your sins? The one who hears your sins is a sinner, just as you are, and perhaps a greater one. He is a human being; he differs from me in nothing; he possesses nothing foreign to me.

Why, then, do you fear, O sinful human being, confessing to a sinful human being? Choose what you wish: if you hide without confessing, you will be condemned without confession. For this reason God requires confession: to free the humble. For this reason he condemns the one who does not confess: to punish the proud forever.

Confess, my brothers, and do not delay. Hasten to approach the sacred harvest of confession. For this is the salvation of souls, the disperser of vices, the restorer of virtues, the assailant of demons, the terror of hell, the obstacle of the devil, the garment of angels, the confidence of the churches, the salvation, guide, staff, light, and hope of all the faithful.

O holy and wondrous confession! You close the mouth of hell and open the gates of paradise. O confession, without you the righteous is judged ungrateful, and the sinner will be regarded as dead. O confession, life of the righteous and glory of sinners, you alone are necessary for the sinner; nevertheless, if anyone is regarded as righteous, he too ought to bind himself to you and practice you frequently.

In the judgment nothing will remain that has been cleansed through confession. O undefiled confession! It was weighed with such weight and availed so much before God that a man knows how to attribute to the thief who confessed the crucified Lord on the cross as much as if he had been crucified for the Lord [the wording is textually corrupt].

Behold how much the brief confession of the sinner accomplished.

But we who are priests—and would that we were good priests—must keep watch over ourselves carefully and diligently, so that we may implant the word of fear and contrition in the hearts of those who sin with such moderation that we do not frighten them away from the word of confession; so that they may open their hearts and we may not close their mouths.

Nor should we absolve even a contrite person unless we have seen that he has confessed, because “with the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Romans 10:10).

Therefore whoever has the word of confession in his mouth but not in his heart is either deceitful or empty. But whoever has it in his heart and not in his mouth is either proud or fearful.

It is therefore fitting that priests should be such as to recognize and know what kind, what quality, and what quantity of medicine they ought to offer to the sick, with the help of our Lord God, who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON XXXI. ON THE DECEITFULNESS OF THE WORLD AND ITS DETESTATION, BECAUSE OF THE THREE CHIEF EVILS THAT ARE IN IT.

It is written, dearest brothers, that we should not love the world, because the world is passing away, and its desire as well (1 John 2:15, 17). O unclean world, which never ceases to ensnare human beings, does not permit them to rest, seeks to seize everyone, and seeks to kill everyone! Woe to the one who trusts you; blessed is the one who resists you; but more blessed is the one who departs from you unharmed.

O unclean, treacherous world, you promise every good thing, but inflict every evil; you promise life, but give death; you promise joy, but bestow sorrow; you promise rest, but behold, turmoil; you promise a flower, but it quickly withers; you promise permanence, but quickly depart. You are therefore not to be loved, because you pass away altogether, and your desire vanishes like smoke.

Let all your lovers address you, O unclean world, you who once wished to grant them the flower of their most serene youth, long life, abundance of riches, a multitude of dependents, and the pleasantness of peace. Let them all speak; let everyone declare; let venerable father Adam rise with all his sons, and let them speak with one voice whether in this life they had joy without sorrow, peace without discord, rest without fear, health without illness, light without darkness, bread without suffering, laughter without weeping.

Do not therefore love the world, brothers, because it passes away, and its desire with it. O unclean world, deceitful and treacherous! Are you not more dangerous when flattering than when afflicting? Are you not more to be feared when you entice than when you reject? Are you not more to be hated when you pretend to love than when you show that you hate? O unclean world, to dwell in you and not grieve is impossible; to hope in you and not fear is vain; to love what is yours in you and not be endangered is impossible.

O my brothers, do not therefore love it, because it passes away, and its desire with it. But behold, the world passes away and troubles us, yet it is loved; it deceives, yet is considered faithful; it kills, yet is desired as though it were life; it bends us, yet is embraced.

O unclean world, even if you flourished, what would your lovers do? But in truth you do not flourish, and possess no stability; your honey and sweetness have harshness, false delight, certain pain, uncertain joy, harsh labor, fearful rest, a reality full of misery, and an empty hope of blessedness.

Do not therefore love the world, because everything that is in the world is either the desire of the flesh, or the desire of the eyes, or the pride of life (ibid. 16). Let us speak today, brothers, if we can, about each of these in turn.

The desire of the flesh is the pleasure that wretched flesh seeks in an illicit manner, such as gluttony, drunkenness, lust, excessive sleep, and empty laughter. And because the flesh is closer to us, it first attacks us through its vices. For the more familiar the world is, the more dangerous it is, and many fall through its vices. Behold: Adam through gluttony, Lot through drunkenness, Solomon through lust.

Therefore, brothers, we must hasten to meet gluttony with abstinence. Consider that man first found death not because of drink, but because of fruit. Esau did not lose his birthright because of a chicken, but because of lentils. For I know that Noah was permitted to eat every kind of flesh that appeared suitable for food; we read that Elijah was refreshed with meat; and we praise the marvelous abstinence of John. Thus we [Col. 1291] ought to act—but not like Esau, deceived by his desire for lentils; not like David, reproved because of his desire for water (2 Samuel 23:55); but like our King, who, tempted not with meat but with bread, overcame the most dreadful tempter.

O great and wondrous virtue of abstinence, through which human beings are made sons of the Most High God; through which vices and demons are driven out; through which not only the salvation of souls is achieved, but also bodily health is possessed!

Behold, brothers, how great and what sort the desire of the flesh is. It is the fuel and mother of other pleasures: for whoever eats well frequently feels the lusts of the flesh and seeks sleep. From this come loquacity and quarrels, which are works of the flesh; from this comes the squandering of money. Do not therefore love the world, brothers, because in it the desire of the flesh is supreme.

But what else is there except the desire of the eyes, my brothers? God made eyes for us that see, and he performed great works so that with our whole heart we might praise him, weeping if we have done anything evil. Behold, we are in misery, and in our miseries we ought not to laugh but to weep. For when a child is born, it does not laugh but cries. Why does it cry, unless because by its voice it bears witness and confesses through its weeping that it has come into misery?

For the children of Adam are born for labor and sorrow, because a heavy yoke has been placed upon the children of Adam from the day they leave their mother’s womb until the day of their burial. We ought therefore not to laugh but to weep, observing and knowing that we never read that the Lord laughed, but that he wept.

But how we should weep for sins, and how we should raise our eyes toward the mountain from which help will come, let us hear from John. For what does he say except that everything in the world is the desire of the eyes? It is called the desire of the eyes because through the eyes the desires for gold and silver, for possessions and for all earthly things, are secretly conveyed into the depths of the soul.

Therefore the eye must be guarded with the utmost care, because it is the gate and messenger of the heart. Close the eye, and the will to possess will not exist; let the will cease, and behold, hell is closed.

Behold, brothers, as many evils as are done through the eyes, so many good things can be obtained through those same eyes. If David had closed his eyes, he would not have seen the woman and would not have committed adultery. If Judas had not seen the money, he would certainly not have betrayed the Master. And if the Sodomites had closed their eyes, they would not have seen the young men and would not have perished.

Let us therefore close our eyes so that they may not see vanity; let us guard the gate of our heart, lest the thief who daily seeks to enter come and be able to plunder all our goods. Close the eye, and you lose the vice; close the gate, and you kill the thief; close the eye, and the will to possess will not exist; close the eye, and you will have closed hell for eternity.

Although many blind people are nevertheless evil, we do not doubt that they would be worse if they saw the things that belong to the world. Vision itself is the cause of greed and the beginning of desire. Let us therefore close the gate, lest death be able to enter through our windows.

For what else do we read is in the world except the pride of life? O pride, stepmother of all virtues, who created you, who sent you to us, who introduced you so miserably into the gathering of rich and poor? I know that God did not make you, nor send you to us, nor introduce you into the gathering of poor or rich monks; nor, when he assumed flesh, did he wish to assume you. Rather, with humility, your enemy, he deigned to dwell among an ox and an ass, and wished to be subject to Mary and Joseph.

What, then, are you doing among us? Nature does not display you, for all are begotten in one way, live in one way, and die in one way. What, then, are you doing among the servants of God? What do you display to them? Why do you inflate them? Why do you show that you inflate them? You know that you cannot grant them eternal life. What do you display to them for which they should be raised above the stars of heaven, desiring to be like God and wishing, if they could, to ascend above him?

O pride, stepmother of virtues, mother of vices, gate of hell, teacher of error, head of the devil, beginning of vices, what are you doing among human beings? What do you promise them, that they show themselves to love you so greatly?

Behold, your lovers fall so quickly from the heights. Behold Nebuchadnezzar, whom you appeared to love so greatly and who loved you so greatly; you bound him to yourself so firmly [Col. 1292] that you made him believe that there was no one greater than he in the world. And behold, soon he is bent down and falls, plunged into the depths, and eats grass like an ox. Behold what happens to those who love you!

But those who do not love you are lifted entirely from the dung and placed with the princes of the Lord’s people, holding a throne of glory, honor, and dignity in knowledge.

Come, then, brothers: learn to possess humility; learn to trample down pride; learn also to avoid it. To trample it down as death—how difficult for the rich, how painful, how meritorious! Be poor, then, if you truly desire to be humble. For when riches have been destroyed and trampled down, holy and perfect humility is more easily acquired, and with it they will truly be able to dwell.

O riches, you appear exceedingly sweet and pleasant to foolish people, but you are altogether more deadly than every poison. For who could take poison unless it had been joined with some sweetness? But when mixed with sweetness, it is easily swallowed; and thus the one who receives it dies.

So the one who loves riches appears to taste sweetness; but behold, death hidden among riches attacks the proud, exalted, wealthy, and inflated person. Once attacked, he is killed; once killed, he is led to hell.

Behold how much the riches of this world benefit us: through them we are killed; through them we are changed daily; through them we are frequently ambushed; through them we are lifted into vanity; through them we are falsely honored; through them the devil always awaits the opportunity to lead the proud soul to hell.

Take away riches, therefore, my brothers, so that you may more easily take away pride; take away riches, and hell will not exist. Give alms, and all things will be clean for you.

O my brothers, do you not know that not giving to the poor is the same as taking from them? And rightly so: when someone can assist the hungry, if he does not feed them, he rightly extinguishes life and permits them to die. Let a Christian be ashamed and blush to take from the poor, to whom we are always commanded to give.

It is beyond every injustice to wish to become rich from the scant resources of the poor or of widows. Therefore, brothers, honest profits are to be loved, but harmful gains are to be abhorred. Let no one dare to take from the place where he ought to distribute what has been collected. The one who gathers by retaining loses by adding; the one who does not repel the poverty of those who demand money draws poverty toward himself instead.

O my brothers, that day will come—it will come, and it will not delay—when it will be said to us: “I was hungry, and you did not give me food.” And finally it will be said to them: “Go, accursed ones, into the eternal fire” (Matthew 25:42, 41).

O brothers, if those who did not give generously, and did not give to the poor what they had acquired through labor, will be sent into the fire, what will be said to those who were not afraid to seize what belonged to others? They burn with the devil who did not clothe the naked; where do we suppose those will burn who stripped widows and orphans?
