We ought not therefore to strip the poor so that, stripped bare, we may abound in the pride of life; rather, let us not delay in giving alms, so that we may be poor and humble.

But it is not enough for us merely to do these things; let us also hasten to lead our neighbor to them, saying to those who possess power and to rulers of lands that they should not only extend alms, but also preserve their kingdoms in peace, knowing that when justice is removed, kingdoms become robberies.

For there are many rulers, but few lovers of justice will be found. When Socrates was asked, while laughing, why he laughed so heartily, he replied: “I see great robbers causing little ones to be led to the gallows.” And he is reported to have cried out in a loud voice: “How much more deserving of hanging you are, who live in chairs and houses while committing greater robberies, than those who appear to dwell trembling every day in the forests!”

Therefore, brothers, do not rob; do not lend at interest, so that you may abound in the pride of life. But if riches abound, do not set your heart upon them; scatter them, so that you may be humble and may be able to imitate the one who will say to those who follow him: “Come, blessed of my Father, possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (ibid. 34). Amen.

## SERMON XXXII. TO LEPERS, THAT THEY SHOULD MAINTAIN PATIENCE

[Col. 1293]

My dearest brothers, I know that God has struck you and that you have become lepers until the day of your death. Therefore I beseech you in our Lord Jesus Christ, by whose precious blood you have been redeemed, not to fail amid the tribulations that are for your glory, knowing that through the affliction of the flesh we put to death the weakness of the mind.

For the spirit fails while wretched flesh rests in pleasure. Therefore, if poverty presses you, if mourning saddens you, if your stomach aches, if your chest or belly swells, if pain throughout your body disturbs you, if calamity vexes you on every side, may your love of God, devout patience, and certain hope of heavenly things always gladden you amid all the labors and dangers of this life.

Let us despise riches in our hearts, and we shall be rich. Let us despise the punishments inflicted by enemies, and we shall always be victorious. Let us despise bodily health, and we shall receive eternal rest and health.

Patience is therefore supremely necessary for you who are weak and ill. No one can be blessed, no one becomes a citizen of heaven, no one is established as a friend of God, who is not found patient amid evils.

O patience, you conquer every adversity—not by struggling, but by enduring; not by murmuring, but by giving thanks in all things. Patience is the one that wipes away the dregs of every pleasure; the one that restores pure souls to God; the ship that brings all its lovers to harbor. It is the means by which hell is closed and paradise opened to those who love it. It is the means through which everyone is justified, and without which no one is justified.

O if it is grievous to you that you are lepers, have patience in all things. Lift up your heads, and behold with your heart the wounds of our Savior hanging upon the wood, the sufferings of him who is dying, the price of him who is redeeming, and the scars of him who is rising again.

What else shall we be able to see except a head bowed down to call and to spare; a heart opened to love; arms extended to embrace; and the whole body exposed for redemption? Consider how great these things are, you who suffer; weigh them on the scales of your heart, so that he who was wholly fastened to the cross for you may be wholly fixed in your heart.

And what more [Note: [Col. 1293] Perhaps here and immediately below, “what more.”] did our Savior endure for us? What more did he bear patiently? His entire life was full of sorrow. And at last, coming to the cross through his passion, he who is truly the palm of victory is exposed to mockery; he who came to break the thorns of sins is crowned with thorns; he who without labor or pain releases those in chains is bound; he who raises up the fallen is hung upon wood; the fountain of eternal life is given vinegar to drink; discipline scourges him; salvation is wounded; life dies.

For a time death killed Life, so that death might be killed by Life forever.

Behold, brothers, the patience of Christ; behold the goodness and mercy of Christ. And if you are pleased to hear still more, we can preach yet more about Christ. Do not therefore grow weary of listening. If you were becoming tired, I would preach no more to you. For I desire to console you, not to sadden you. If it is wearisome, say so; but if it is joyful, listen.

Behold, the Savior who rules the stars came and wished to suck at the breast. He who is bread itself wished to hunger; he who is the fountain wished to thirst; he who is light wished to sleep; he who is rest wished to grow weary; he who is truth wished to be hidden; he who is judge of the living and the dead was condemned by a mortal judge; he who is justice was judged by the unjust; he who is unity was changed.

Nothing is more beneficial to us than to think every day how much God and man endured for us.

Behold, the Savior suffered; he became a leper upon the cross; he became patient, leaving us an example so that we might follow his footsteps. If you do this, you will not only bear your illness without resentment, but you will also not cease to cry out with the prophet in voice and deed: “Let my life fail in sorrow, and my years in groaning” (Psalm 30:11).

But you will say: “O how grievous, how inhuman, how harsh it is to be unable to live among human beings!” Behold, we are separated [Col. 1294] from the cities; the nations despise us; our parents hate us; our relatives flee us; our friends abandon us; we are separated from the camps, as though we had not been born from human beings.

O my brothers, consider this patiently, and do not be troubled. What you say is true, but I do not want you to be ignorant of what you read. For the Lord said to Moses: “The one full of leprosy shall not dwell in my house” (Leviticus 13:46).

Why, then, are you troubled if you cannot live among human beings? Could the citizens of the world have provided this for us? Could they have opened the house of God to you? Will you become better through their company? Or do you not know what was said to the holy man Anthony: “If you wish to be saved, flee human beings; flee the world and its pomp”?

Why, then, are you troubled if you cannot associate with human beings? Behold, holy Job, righteous, wise, rich, upright, and fearing God, nevertheless becomes a leper [Note: Scripture does not call him a leper; nor is this any less contradicted by what is said immediately afterward: “he is cast outside the camp.”]. Yet he does not complain. He is cast outside the camp, despised and abandoned by human beings. His wife blasphemes him; yet he does not complain, nor does he speak mortally against God with his lips, considering that another life would soon come.

Do not therefore be troubled, but consider that God has struck you because of your sins, or in order to test you. Behold, Mary, because she murmured against her brother Moses, became leprous. King Azariah, because he presumed, became leprous; and so did Gehazi, because he committed simony, and Naaman, because he glorified himself.

You too have now been struck [Note: Perhaps *quandoquidem*, “since indeed.”]. Be patient, and receive it with a joyful spirit, lest you suffer eternal torments both here and in the future. Take courage, therefore, and do not fear.

I had believed that I would be with you on the third day of Easter; but because our Valentinus departed from this world, I was unable to be with you. Now, however, after breaking up silver vessels from the goods of the church of Hippo, I wished to provide for you in your needs and for the captives.

May God console us, he who consoles his own in every tribulation. Amen.

## SERMON XXXIII. ON THE DETESTATION OF DRUNKENNESS, WITH AN ACCOUNT OF A TERRIBLE CALAMITY

Do not be surprised, dearest brothers, if today, with God’s help, I complete three sermons. A terrible calamity occurred today, as you have all heard. Because of it I wished not only to have all the elders come to the church of Hippo, but also ordered all the women and children to be gathered together.

Now that they have been gathered, I intend to relate to you with grief and anxiety, before it becomes known among the people, what happened to our distinguished citizen of Hippo, Cyrillus.

For, as you know, he was powerful among us in deed and speech and was loved by almost everyone. He had a son, as you know, and possessed him as his only child. Because he was his only child, he loved him excessively and above God. Therefore, drunk with excessive love, he neglected to correct his son, even giving him permission to do whatever pleased him.

O deceitful freedom! O great destruction of sons! O deadly paternal love! Behold, they say that they love their sons whom they contrive to slaughter. They say that they love those for whom they are already preparing the gallows. Fathers say that they are raising their sons; but behold, father and son are both already falling into the pit.

Why does the father fall into the pit with his son, unless because the father is blind, because he is evil, and because he appears to neglect his own salvation and that of his sons? In what way could the father have neglected these things except when he granted his son freedom, when he neglected to correct him, when he spared the rod, and when he always showed him a cheerful face?

Do you wish to hear now how father and son fall into the pit? Although you know it, because it is necessary for you to fear as long as you live, I am not ashamed to say again what happened today.

Behold, your Cyrillus had a son, as you know, whom he neglected to correct; and by living luxuriously he consumed part of his possessions. But behold, today, after becoming drunk, he wickedly assaulted his pregnant mother, attempted to violate his sister, killed his father, and wounded two sisters to death [Note: [Col. 1295] Vindingus lists this among the fables.].

O great dominion of the devil! He killed the father whom he ought to have revered after God; he assaulted his pregnant mother, by whom he had been carried; he wished to violate the sisters whom he ought to have loved most tenderly, and wounded two of them to death.

O grievous drunkenness, mother of all evils, sister of every lust, father of every pride! O drunkenness, you blind the mind, lack sound judgment, possess no counsel; you are a flattering demon, sweet poison, pleasant sin.

O drunkenness, does not the stomach swell because of you? Does not the breath putrefy because of you? Do you not blind the eyes? Do you not weaken all the limbs? Do you not hasten death? Do you not empty the purse? Do you not take control of a human being? Do you not lead with you the one who loves you, turned into a bestial and irrational creature?

O drunkenness, let those who love you learn to recognize you; let them learn to avoid you; let them learn again to avoid you; let them flee you as death, because whoever loves you will not obtain the kingdom of God.

Therefore, faithful ones, abstain and do not become drunk with wine. For it is not enough to abstain: you must teach others who abstain to abstain as well, teaching them how Lot, when drunk, lay with his daughters; and how Samson, filled with wine, was handed over to his enemies through a prostitute.

Hear, faithful ones; hear Isaiah saying: “Woe to those who rise early to pursue drunkenness and drink until evening, so that they may burn with wine” (Isaiah 5:11)!

In the Old Law it was also commanded that when priests entered the temple to minister to the Lord, they should not drink wine at all. If this was so when they merely entered the temple, what ought we wretched people to do?

O how many of you visit the tavern before the temple; refresh the body before the soul; follow the devil before God! O faithful who are not faithful, what have you to do with wine? Was wine made so that you might fail while cursing the name of the Lord?

Abstain, therefore, from excessive drinking, lest you become rebellious. For as long as Adam abstained, so long was he obedient; so long did he remain good, holy, and righteous. Thus Elijah also performed miracles as long as he was refreshed with bread and water; but after he ate meat and drank wine to satiety, he is not read to have performed miracles [Note: How recklessly this is said! For he ate meat brought to him miraculously by a raven (1 Kings 17:6), and this was the beginning of his miracles, whose grace he did not lack until his being taken up.].

Come, then, faithful ones: considering among other things the calamity mentioned above, fear God, and in fearing him earnestly beseech him to free us always from these and from every evil. Amen.

## SERMON XXXIV. ON THE TWO TYPES OF PEOPLE WHO ABANDON THE WORLD, REPRESENTED BY THE HOLY LOT AND HIS WIFE

You have heard, dearest brothers, that Lot, Abraham’s nephew, lived holily and righteously among the worst of the Sodomites and Gomorrhans. When the Lord wished to destroy those cities, he sent angels to his servant Lot so that he would not perish with the wicked. As he was leaving, the angels said to him: “Save your life” (Genesis 19:17).

But because Lot’s wife looked back, she was immediately changed into a pillar of salt.

Therefore, my brothers, whatever things have been written were written for our instruction, so that we might derive some fruit from them. In Lot and his wife two types of people who abandon the world are represented: one abandons it perfectly; the other comes to death lukewarmly, looking back.

Sodom, which is interpreted as “blindness,” or “mute,” or “harshness,” is likewise the world, in which there are mute and blind people. To them holy angels and holy preachers are sent, so that they may say: “Save your life, and save yourself on the mountain.”

For what else is fleeing Sodom than fleeing [Col. 1296] the fire of lust, luxury, pride, and avarice? We are also commanded not to look back at these things, because one who has conquered the world and entered the mountain of holy religion ought not to look back.

Why? Because it would be better not to recognize the way of truth than to turn back after recognizing it. What does this mean except that it would have been better for someone to have remained in secular and lay life than afterward to abandon the solitary life?

For apostasy is evil; it is mortal; it is to live always under condemnation. Such women are compared with Lot’s wife, because as they die, looking back, they are changed into a pillar of salt.

Lot is commanded to save himself on the mountain, by which the contemplative life is signified. You, however, human being, climb the mountain of repentance; climb the mountain of divine contemplation. Save yourself on this mountain; fly across to this mountain like a sparrow, and there save your soul, stripped of the cares and dignity of the world.

Thus did that glorious young man Nathanael [Note: Since Scripture is silent about this name, Augustine would not have guessed it], of whom we read. For he said: “Teacher, what shall I do to have eternal life?” The Lord said to him: “If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments.” The young man said to him: “Which commandments?” The Lord said: “You shall love the Lord your God with your whole heart; you shall not commit murder; you shall not commit adultery; you shall not steal; you shall not bear false witness; honor your father and your mother; and your neighbor as yourself.”

All these things pertain to your way. The young man said to him: “Lord, I have kept all these things from my youth; what do I still lack?” The Lord said to him: “If you wish to be perfect, sell everything you possess, give it to the poor, and follow me” (Matthew 19:16–21).

And that young man followed Jesus [Note: Scripture suggests the contrary], and afterward, never looking back, left his father and mother, his wife, children, sisters, and his own life. Then the prudent young man climbed God’s mountain, left Sodom and Gomorrah, fled the fire of lust, suffocated worldly care, and, climbing the mountain of supreme contemplation, bought the hidden treasure in the field, holding it dear throughout his life.

Peter did the same when he voluntarily abandoned everything, leaving all things and following Jesus. So also did Mary, the sister of Lazarus, together with her brother Lazarus and the most prudent virgin Mary, when they sold everything and placed the price at the apostles’ feet.

Elijah also wished to do this, and John, the son of Zechariah, when they entered the desert. So did Paul with Antony, when they cultivated the desert for many years. So did my brothers who wished to imitate and follow the life and examples of the holy fathers.

Do we also desire to do this? Indeed, we are in the world; nevertheless, as we began, we always desire to be with you in solitude, and we demonstrated this in deed when we were not burdened by the episcopal Church.

Come, then, brothers: for God’s sake you have submitted yourselves to God’s yoke, so that, once permission to sin has been removed, you may be held in a good purpose by the chain of obedience.

But pay attention, my brothers and joy of my heart: it does no good to act well under compulsion unless you do so of your own free will. For those who do good deeds under compulsion are not pleasing to God in what they do, and they are aptly compared to Simon of Cyrene, whom the Jews compelled to carry Christ’s cross.

Behold, Simon carries the cross with sorrow because he does not carry it willingly. He is compelled, but he does not remain in it; therefore, because he does not persevere, he flees and departs from the cross without fruit. For nothing is called good unless one perseveres in the good unto death.

Thus let us crucify our bodies with blows, vigils, and abstinence from food and drink. But I fear that we may do this under compulsion and, while mortifying ourselves to the world, live at least in our will for the world.

Therefore, brothers, let us climb this mountain of obedience, and let us attend to what we have promised God. Nothing is greater than obedience; nothing is worse than disobedience.

Adam perished because he was disobedient; Christ rose because he obeyed the Father. [Col. 1297] Jonah, being disobedient, was swallowed by a fish. Saul, being disobedient, was seized by a demon.

May Christ himself free us from such seizure, so that we may be able to fly worthily to the mountain of contemplation. Amen.

## SERMON XXXV. TO JUDGES, THAT THEY SHOULD BEWARE OF BEING CORRUPTED BY HATRED, LOVE, MONEY, PRAYERS, OR FEAR, AND SHOULD AVOID OTHER VICES AND PRESERVE JUSTICE
Asked by you, O judges, although burdened by a lengthy disputation with Fortunatus, the presbyter of the Manichaeans [Note: [Col. 1297] See above, near the end of Sermon 4.], we have not delayed, with God’s help, to deliver a sermon out of affection for you. For behold, you are now gathered in the bishop’s house; you have all assembled together, not to hear sophistries, not to understand the cleverness of poets, nor for me to proclaim that you are blessed, but solely to hear what is necessary for your salvation and, after hearing it, to fulfill it in your deeds.

For you are regarded by men as leaders of the people, judges of the earth, fathers of orphans, husbands of widows, zealots for justice, lovers of the commonwealth. Beware, therefore, lest you be corrupted by hatred, love, money, entreaties, or fear. It is fitting, then, that judges not merely fulfill what we have said, but, with God’s help, trample down pride, abhor luxury, detest falsehood, and despise greed, which is said to be the stepmother and chief enemy of justice. For greed is the thing that knows neither father nor mother, destroys friends, and abandons even itself.

It is fitting, then, that judges pursue generosity rather than greed, and love little children; that they show a cheerful face to the small and to orphans, not only in word but also in deed. They must not turn their face away from the poor, nor should those set over others disdain to protect the faithful, nor lift up their necks by looking down on certain people, knowing that learned and unlearned alike die together.

It is fitting, then, that judges carefully guard in a vigilant mind the grace they have received from God, show faithfulness, and preserve zeal for righteousness. It is also fitting that judges be devoted to clemency, haters of cruelty, kind toward all, slow to anger, swift to mercy, steadfast in adversity, humble and cautious in prosperity; and, however greatly elevated by dignities, let them recognize themselves as they are and beware of despising those beneath them.

It is also fitting that judges be wise and exceedingly learned in the law, so that they may not be able to say, as though ignorant of the holy law, “good is evil” and “evil is good.” It is also fitting that judges fear God more than other men, care more for the salvation of souls than for the body, and love the honor of God more than full purses.

But woe to you, O judges, woe to you forever and beyond; because there is no truth in you, no mercy, no piety, no justice, nor can the knowledge of God be found in you. For what reigns among you? Greed, falsehood, shouting, outward show, and the perversion of the sacred law, saying “evil is good” and “good is evil.” Behold the acceptance of persons. There is no truth in you. Truths have been diminished by you.

O fathers of the poor—indeed, not fathers, but plunderers! Why are you not fathers? Because everywhere the poor are oppressed through you, and there is no one who takes pity on God’s little ones. But if a rich man speaks, you immediately fall silent and carry his cases up to the clouds.

O judges who love the knowledge and justice of the world, consider what you are doing. For you are full of worldly knowledge, and in that knowledge you will die. For what is worldly knowledge except to amass treasure, acquire earthly profit, deceive one’s neighbor, lie, swear oaths, carefully pervert justice, and do similar things in every respect? This is the wisdom of this world. In these things nearly your entire life consists. Therefore consider, you who judge the earth, that the wisdom of this world is folly before God.

But you say, “O bishop, we do not love this knowledge; we do not commit theft; we neither deceive nor injure our neighbor.” Why? “Because we receive nothing except as much as he may wish to give us.” But I say to you that you have done as much as you were able to do. You were not given more; therefore you did not receive more. You did as much as you could. You made small cases great.

For even if you did not seize by force, and did not rob your neighbor on the road, you can nevertheless be thieves. A thief fears evil and, where he cannot act, does not act; yet he is still a thief. For God examines the heart, not the hand.

A wolf often comes to the sheepfold and seeks to seize the sheep, seeks to tear them apart, seeks to devour them. Yet the shepherds keep watch and the dogs bark, and so the wolf, in fear, flees. Do we therefore say that he is not a wolf? Far from it. So you too do as much as you can; if you could do more, you would do more.

Come, then, O judges; take care lest you be confounded with the false judges of Susanna. For the Lord will stir up the spirit of Daniel, place his spirit and the wisdom of his boy Daniel in the mind of some young man, and, as he did with Susanna’s judges, he will confound all the false witnesses together with the judges. Then they will know what their knowledge has profited them.

Consider, therefore, O judges of the earth, what God speaks through his servant Hosea. For he says: “I will visit my people, and the judges, and I will repay them according to their ways and their thoughts” (Hos. IV, 9).

O how dreadful it is to fall into the hands of the Lord! O how great will be the vengeance, how great the misery of the wicked on the last day! For evil merchants and false judges will be expelled from the house of the Lord; they will be exiled from the house of God, expelled from paradise, and they will go to the place where there will always be weeping and gnashing of teeth.

Therefore heed my counsel; open the doors of your hearts. Rise, you who sleep; read the prophet Isaiah, follow him—not tomorrow, but today; yet not merely today, but even now. For the Prophet says: “Let the wicked abandon his way, and the unjust man his thoughts, and let him return to the Lord, and he will have mercy on him, because he is merciful” (Isa. LV, 7).

Run, judges, lest you be judged, to the Father of mercies; seek pardon; return what you have unlawfully received. Seek pardon, for he is near to all who call upon him in truth. He is the one who heals the brokenhearted and saves the humble in spirit and those troubled in heart.

Walk while you have the light, while it is day. Behold, O judges, night will already come, because death has already come, in which it will not be permitted to walk. Consider what you are and where you are going. Your parents, dead, proclaim it; the grave cries out; hell howls; demons await; priests proclaim it: “Why are you proud, earth and ashes?”

O judge who did not acknowledge God: while you pass beside the tombs of your fathers, know that the dead cry out, “You are earth, and to earth you will go” (Gen. III, 19). They were human beings, just as you are, possessing riches. Where they are now, so shall we be. Where is their pride, where their conscience, where the teacher’s chair, where the honor of their disciples, where their garments adorned with silk and leather? O ash and dust! O judge, consider what you are and what you will be.

Do not, then, delay turning to God, and do not put it off from day to day. For his anger suddenly comes, because the day of destruction is near; indeed, it must be present, and the times are hastening.

Nevertheless, let none of you despair; let none distrust God’s mercy. But consider that no fault is so great that it cannot have pardon. And lest anyone despair, take as an example that sinful woman Mary, mistress of luxury and mother of vainglory, the sister of Martha and Lazarus, who afterward deserved to be called the apostle of the Apostles.

May God himself, who for our sake deigned to be born and to die, help us. Amen.

## SERMON XXXVI. TO HIS PRESBYTERS, REPROVING THEIR EVIL LIFE

Dearest brothers, as Your Charity knows, the hand that must cleanse the stains of a polluted vessel ought to be clean, lest, being itself polluted, it soil the vessel still more when filth handles filth. Therefore, priests of the Most High God, it is said to you: “Be clean, you who carry the vessels of the Lord” (Isa. LII, 11).

For you are the ones who must carry the vessels of the Lord, to whom it has been given to know the mysteries of the kingdom of God. You are the salt of the earth, the light of the world, the lamp that is lit, the city set on a mountain, the pillars of the temple, the tree of knowledge planted in the midst of paradise, the patrons and rulers of the earth, citizens of the angels and of paradise, sons of the Prophets, kinsmen of the Patriarchs, successors of the Apostles.

Be clean, therefore, so that, together with the fathers, you may worthily carry the vessels of the Lord; for these vessels are not only golden and silver ones, but also those for whose redemption the Lord deigned to die.

Therefore let Your Charity consider what sort of men you ought to be, so that you may worthily carry the vessels of the Lord. For the Apostle says: “It is necessary that a bishop be without reproach, as God’s steward; not arrogant, not angry, not addicted to wine, not violent, not greedy for shameful gain” (Tit. I, 7).

I, the bishop, must observe these things, but not I alone: you also, together with me, must observe them, with God’s help. In every respect, just as he commands a bishop to be without reproach, so he commands a presbyter to be irreproachable—that he should not seek wives, riches, or honors, lest he be called worldly. For one who cares for souls ought not to go from house to house, nor frequent the marketplace with peasants, nor acquire commercial ventures, nor seek godmothers, nor dig with a hoe, nor enter taverns, nor run about unless compelled by necessity. Those who act in this way are irreproachable before men. Thus they will be able worthily to carry the vessels of the Lord.

But if the contrary should be the case—which may the Lord avert—how will he be able to remove evil from the midst of the sheep if he himself falls into a similar or greater offense? Such a man is not called a steward but rather a dissipator. For a steward is one thing, and a master another. A steward is a servant. It is not permitted for a steward to strike servants, to kill, or to harbor anger, because his master is humble, kind, and merciful. Therefore it is not permitted for a steward to be raging. Nothing is more foul, more harmful, more frivolous, or more disgraceful in a shepherd than rage.

Let the shepherd, then, take heed; let the steward also take heed of what is written: “The servant of God must not quarrel, but be humble toward all, patient, a teacher, instructing with gentleness those who oppose him” (II Tim. II, 24–25).

Let shepherds learn, when they are offended, to be patient. And if I am to deserve patience, presbyters must not only abstain from quarrels but also beware of drunkenness. It is not permitted for a cleric to drink or eat outside the proper hour, or to go from house to house and arrange a lunch or dinner.

Take heed, my presbyters, take heed; and if I speak the truth, do not be disturbed. For a cleric is greatly despised who, when often invited to a meal, does not refuse, even when compelled by some necessity. Frequently, at dinner or lunch, where a great crowd gathers, quarrels and drunkenness arise, along with the works of the flesh.

Therefore a cleric must be exceedingly careful not to dare to dine outside his own house or the bishop’s house, or even to dare to prepare such a meal there for worldly people. For what else ought we to have except that we are not greedy for shameful gain? All profit must be far removed from presbyters. For we are not merchants of worldly things but of the things that belong to God.

Worldly people cannot come to us—can they even understand? Far from it. You wished to hear our sermon, and, setting aside the pain of my teeth, I wanted to have you here, not so that you might hear that you are good, but so that, by speaking the truth, you might understand your misery.

What are you? You will say, “We are shepherds.” I say that you are shepherds, and what you say is true. But what sort of shepherds, or of what quality, I do not dare say, because I would be a liar together with you.

We are all sinners; we were all born and conceived in sins; we all live in sins. Yet it is necessary that I speak the truth, because I am a bishop, because I am a shepherd, because I am prepared to lay down my life for you. Therefore I ought not to remain silent. Although I am a sinner, I have already decided and prepared myself to lay down my life for your salvation.

Nevertheless, I will speak. Everything that is true, whoever says it, is from God—from the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. It is necessary to speak it, not conceal it. [Col. 1300] For if I were to remain silent about the truth, I would be like you in every respect; and I do not wish that.

If God is with me, who can be against me? Fortunatus or Arius with his plots? [Note: [Col. 1300] “First, it is a great falsehood and a remarkably inept trick that Augustine disputed with Arius; and, second, that he disputed with Fortunatus when he was already a bishop.” Lupus. See Sermon 4.]

Because I told them the truth, they therefore laid ambushes for me in the desert, wishing to seize and kill me; yet God delivered me. I would nevertheless gladly have accepted martyrdom, and I am always prepared to die for the truth.

Hear, then, rebels [Note: [Col. 1300] More correctly, Augustine says of his priests in Sermon 355, no. 7, vol. 5: “They all willingly obey me.”]; hear, ravening wolves; hear, you mockers. Let that holy Ezekiel also come, who had seen a closed gate in the house of the Lord (Ezek. XLIV, 1); let him rise and open to you the vision that he saw and touched.

Speak, speak, O holy Ezekiel; speak to my presbyters. Say to them what the Lord says: “Son of man, prophesy against the shepherds of Israel, and say to them: Woe to the shepherds who fed themselves. Are not flocks fed by shepherds? You ate the milk and clothed yourselves with the wool; you killed what was fat, but you did not feed my flock. You did not strengthen what was weak, nor heal what was sick. You did not bind up what was broken, nor bring back what was cast away; you did not seek what had perished. Rather, with harshness you ruled them and with power. And my sheep were scattered. But I will require my flock from the shepherds’ hand” (Ezek. XXXIV, 2–5, 10).

Behold how the Lord complains against you: you are not shepherds but ravening wolves, because nearly everything you do, you do for profit. You seek not only what belongs to the churches but also what belongs to worldly people.

Behold, let us examine the mind; let us investigate the truth. Do you deign to sing Mass, baptize, or bury the dead without payment or a promise? Do you not desire to see the death of the rich more quickly than the health of the body? Behold how you are wolves; behold how you are infected with every kind of simony.

O priests, what are we doing? What are we? Why do we sleep so much? Behold, a thief steals once; once he takes or exacts his neighbor’s usury. But if he is caught, he is cursed, beaten, accused of theft, and judged to death as a thief.

O my priests, if usury is judged a crime in a layman, if for this he ought to die and is condemned to death, what will become of you on the last day? What would the world do to us if it had power over us?

Therefore hold fast to justice; do not pursue profit. Having food and clothing, you ought to be content in every respect. But whoever celebrates, preaches, or baptizes in order to acquire profit thereby deprives himself in fact of heavenly goods.

For behold, the Roman princes received from their riches as much as they needed, distributed the rest to the poor, and preserved remarkable justice in all things. Because of these and the other good deeds they performed and wished to be observed, they deserved to be elevated to a magnificent empire and feared by all throughout the world.

Behold, they were pagans, and they considered it utter folly to worship a crucified god; yet they feared their god. And we, who bear the name of Christ on our foreheads, what else do we pursue daily except simony and robberies?

I too was once an unbeliever, and not only among the Carthaginians but also among the Romans I was considered by everyone exceptionally astute. A large crowd often surrounded me; when they saw and heard me passing, they placed their hand over their mouth. They had made me a Roman citizen and head of the tribunes, and had arranged for me to marry the daughter of Pontianus, a woman equal to me in rank. [Note: [Col. 1300] Many passages here are refuted as false by Book 6, chapter 6 of the Confessions: “I was eager,” Augustine says, “for honors, profits, and marriage.” Hence Lupus: “How, then, would he not have seized that highest tribunate with both hands?”]

For I dare to say—and I dare to assert this—that I had not been changed in any respect: I despised everything, rejected all that they had promised, abhorred riches, cautiously left the city, fled to Milan [Note: [Col. 1301] He traveled to Milan by public transport; Confessions, Book 4, chapter 13.], did not seek a wife, and thought that nothing was worse than the company and association of women [Note: [Col. 1301] On the contrary, Alypius was unable to dissuade him from pursuing marriage; Confessions, Book 6, chapter 12. His mother sought a wife for him, chapter 13. A concubine was succeeded by another, chapter 15.].

As a servant of my iniquities, I did not want to do any of these things; yet now, as a servant of Christ, I am frequently tempted to have the things we have mentioned, and even greater ones [Note: [Col. 1301] “Plainly,” says Lupus, “it is blasphemous that Augustine, a bishop, was assailed by the impulses of such temptations. This is clear from Book 1, chapter 10 of the Soliloquies and Book 10, chapter 30 of the Confessions, and elsewhere.”].

But we, brothers, who are always in combat, although we are tempted to return to the world, marry, engage in commerce, live delicately, and even ascend the teacher’s chair, let us beware lest we be condemned with the world.

For you are exalted gods, in whose assembly the God of gods desires to stand. You are his vicars, acting in his place. You are all sons of the Most High, to whom is given the power of binding and loosing, even of opening heaven and closing hell.

Come, then, priests of the Most High God; open the ears of your hearts. Cease now from acting perversely; learn to do good. Feed the sheep by word and example; do not close heaven to them. You close it when you do not correct; you close it when you show them how to live badly.

Be an eye to the blind and a foot to the lame. You are an eye to the blind when you drive away the darkness of their ignorance; you are a foot to the lame when you show them the way of truth or strengthen their faith. But if you do not know how to strengthen your own faith for your own sake, how will you be able to strengthen the faith of others?

Therefore take heed, and do not be disturbed if I tell you the truth. For I know—and know well—that the truth is bitter to you. Why else do you not believe me when I tell the truth, and why are you not changed for the better?

The truth is therefore bitter, and those who love or proclaim it are often filled with bitterness and sorrow. Nevertheless, I do not dare to remain silent, nor do I intend to please you; for if I pleased evil men, I would not be God’s servant.

You want me to please you; you desire me to love you; yet you do not want me to correct you. Nevertheless, I beg you to amend your lives: trampling down greed, despising luxury, avoiding pride, hating simony, loving the poor, rejecting the pomp of this age, interceding for us, and praying without ceasing, so that I too, together with you, may by grace deserve worthily to carry the vessels of the Lord.

And if anyone has murmured against me, let him know that he has murmured against his father, the bishop. Let him be spared, and let prayer be made for him.

## SERMON XXXVII. THAT PRIESTS OUGHT TO PRESENT THEMSELVES AS MINISTERS OF GOD AND BEWARE OF SEEKING TO SELL THE GIFTS OF THE HOLY SPIRIT; ALSO ON PRESERVING PATIENCE AND CHASTITY, AND ON DETESTING FORNICATION

Dearest brothers, as the history of the Acts of the Apostles relates, when Judas defected from the company of the Apostles, divine providence, providing the foundations for the structure of the Church—which according to John are the twelve names of the Apostles—called the blessed Matthias to the apostleship. And just as Matthias assumed the leadership and rose in Judas’s place, so we too have assumed leadership in the Church of God. By his grace he wished to make us his ministers, established us in his palace, and chose us to be a holy nation, the people of God, the salt of the earth, the light of the world, and angelic men without sin.

We too are ministers and servants of God. For those are called servants who do not serve merely for outward appearance, but faithfully obey the Lord’s will in all things; and then they are brought into such intimacy with the Lord that they are no longer called servants but friends.

Therefore let us present ourselves with our whole mind in great tribulation, in knowledge, in sincere love, in vigils, in prisons and scourging, in the word of truth. And thus, possessing nothing, let us possess all things by possessing Christ.

For this is the life of the blessed; this is the salvation of priests; this is the rest of God’s servants; this is the will of his friends. This is our sanctification: that in all things we present ourselves as God’s ministers—in great patience, in tribulation, in need, in chastity, in abstinence, in knowledge, in gentleness, in sincere love, in the word of truth, giving no one any occasion for offense, so that our ministry may not be blamed. For we are servants of Christ.

The ministry of Christians is then blamed and our service despised, when we despise the things that belong to Christ and neglect to fulfill them in our deeds. But woe to us, my brothers, woe to us, because we bear the false name of Christ and carry the false name of God, since we do not fulfill in our deeds what we ought to fulfill.

Let us examine our minds, priests, and know whether we are servants of Christ. For let us know what we ought to do, lest we be useless servants. What is it? Certainly nothing else except that we present ourselves as God’s ministers in great patience.

But woe to us, because we seem to have no patience at all. We ought to be poor, because we are members of Christ and ministers of God. But if poverty assails us, or we are disturbed and afflicted by some bodily necessity, we seek to sell the gifts of the Holy Spirit.

O my priests, do not commit this evil. Rather, remember that you received freely, and therefore give freely, lest you be condemned with Simon Magus, to whom Peter said: “Your money be with you unto perdition” (Acts VIII, 20).

Whoever also receives a price for the sacraments is a Gehazi and full of leprosy. For when Elisha had cleansed Naaman, the commander of Syria, of leprosy in the Jordan, Naaman returned and offered the Prophet many gifts; but he refused to accept them. When Naaman had departed, Gehazi, the Prophet’s disciple, spoke to him, asking the commander of Syria for gifts. After he had received them, the Prophet knew everything through the Spirit, and, seeing him, rebuked him and struck him with leprosy (IV Kings V, 15–27).

So also all who ask money for the sacraments are struck down. But you will say: “Does not Scripture say, ‘He who serves the altar should live from the altar’?” (I Cor. IX, 13).

O priests, I do not dare entirely to deny what you say. But you know that God looks into the hearts of men. If you delay giving a sacrament, even if you are surrounded by every kind of poverty, you are not a shepherd, you are not a minister of Christ, but a merchant.

Therefore do not ask, and do not receive even so much for Baptism, if you do not wish to perish with Simon. For by making an agreement you have sold the sacrament and betrayed your Savior with Judas.

Present the sacraments with spontaneous and sincere willingness, asking nothing, expecting nothing, desiring nothing from what has been promised. But if something is given to you, you receive it justly and may justly possess it.

Remember, however, that a priest ought to lead a poor life. Therefore, if he has pride, if he rejoices in a great benefit [Note: [Col. 1302] This word indicates that the author is of more recent date.], let him not delay giving to the poor whatever remains beyond food and clothing, because everything belongs to the poor.

That saying, however, which the faithful ought not to deny—“He who serves the altar should live from the altar”—is entirely true, because it is not permitted for priests to work with their hands, to dig with a hoe, to forge iron, or do similar things [Note: [Col. 1302] Augustine, in his book On the Work of Monks, and the ancient canons teach otherwise.]. This is on account of the reverence and dignity of so great a sacrament.

But that principle applies more to worldly people than to priests, so that the priests of God do not perish from hunger or nakedness. Therefore it is right that he who serves the altar should live from the altar.

Likewise, brothers, whoever buys a sacrament, or a church, or prebends [Note: [Col. 1302] Another word scarcely understood in this sense before the tenth century.], or the revenues of churches, or has obtained these things for himself through secular power, should know that he has already been condemned with Gehazi and Judas, has already become leprous, and must already be expelled from the temple of the Lord.

Why is this so? Because “he who does not enter the sheepfold by the door, but climbs in by another way, is a thief and a robber” (John X, 1). [Col. 1303] Therefore he must be reproved, because the Lord drives buyers and sellers from the temple; he must be driven away, because lepers are commanded to be expelled.

He does not enter the Church by the door who enters through a lay entrance. For spiritual gifts were not entrusted to laymen but to the vicars of the Lord. The Lord’s vicars are those who hold the place of the Apostles.

Let laymen administer their own castles and estates; but let them take care not to touch the goods of the Church of Hippo. For the rich rarely or never provide prebends for poor priests; and if they do provide them, they do not do so for the love of God, but so that they may be able to enjoy the Church’s goods with their wife and household.

Therefore let the priest who allows himself to be defrauded by a rich man through fear or affection know that he will not remain unpunished; and if not in the present life, at least in the future he will not escape eternal fire.

Let us return, then, brothers, to our subject, and let us know how we can present ourselves as ministers of God—for you wish to know.

Behold: if persecutions come, let us not fail, but have patience. If the necessity of poverty occurs, let us not despair, but trust in the Lord. If we are slandered, let us not answer, but spare our adversaries. If we are struck with fists or blows, let us not delay offering the other cheek. If we are struck by a word or a murmur, let us remain silent. If we are killed, let us go joyfully to death.

Why? Because “a servant is not greater than his master. If they persecuted me, they will also persecute you” (John XV, 20), says the Lord.

Thus we ought to be adorned with patience if we desire to be ministers of Christ. But what else is required except that we present ourselves in chastity? This is that virtue without which a person becomes guilty of everything. This is that virtue that commends us to God, makes us like angels, and leads us by flight above the ether. This is that virtue without which we cannot carry the vessels of the Lord.

This is the holy virtue that the Apostle teaches us to embrace: “Fornication and every uncleanness must not even be named among you” (Eph. V, 3), lest your mind be corrupted by evil conversations.

Therefore, brothers, take heed: not only must fornication be removed from you, but also every false suspicion. It is not fitting for a cleric to sit with women, converse with them, or frequent their houses, lest an evil suspicion arise from this.

O how vile, how wretched and faint-hearted is the cleric who frequently associates with women! He is exceedingly foolish and inexperienced who seeks women’s friendships.

Therefore, you who are the light of the world and the city situated on a mountain, ought to guard your reputation in such a way that those who praise you are not put to shame by slanderers.

Take heed also, brothers; take heed of what the Apostle says: “Fornication and uncleanness.” Fornication is natural intercourse with women, but illicit. Fornication is intercourse with prostitutes. A woman, whether adulteress or concubine, is called a prostitute.

Fornication is forbidden to clerics because, since we are ministers of the Lord, we must not become members of a prostitute. O how shameful it is for a cleric to be led captive by a prostitute! For whoever clings to a prostitute becomes one body with her.

Therefore we must know that it is evil to fornicate. For if marriage is forbidden to priests, how much more will the crime of fornication be judged in us?

Behold, brothers: married laymen are commanded to abstain for a time so that they may devote themselves to prayer; yet priests, who ought every day to consecrate the Lord’s body, are not ashamed to keep concubines in their homes.

Behold how you ought to know how to possess your vessels in sanctification. For you know, brothers, that one day David came to the priest Ahimelech and, being hungry, said: “Give me something to eat.” And he replied: “I have no ordinary bread at hand, but only holy bread; therefore tell me, O David, are your servants clean from women?” And he said: “They have been so since yesterday and the day before.” Thus the priest gave them the consecrated bread (I Kings XXI, 3–6).

If, then, the priest asked whether David’s servants were clean in order that they might receive the bread of the Presence, what ought we, wretched priests, to do in order to receive the Lord’s body?

O my brothers, even the priests of the pagans, when they ought to offer incense to their gods, abstain from every evil as far as they can.

Behold, I was already bishop of Hippo, and I traveled with certain servants of Christ to Ethiopia [Note: [Col. 1304] Here Lupus observes that Augustine never traveled to pagan Mauretania, but only to Christian territory, and not for the sake of preaching, but as Zosimus’s envoy to settle certain affairs. He says that this supposed apostleship is manifestly an imposture, as the letter now numbered 199, no. 46, indicates—all the more certainly because it was written when he was an old man.], in order to preach the holy Gospel of Christ to them; and there we saw [Note: [Col. 1304] “Behold,” says Lupus, “Augustine, in Book 16 of The City of God, chapter 8, written by him in old age, says that he saw such monstrous human beings not in Ethiopia but in a Carthaginian mosaic. Nor does he say that they exist, but ‘they are said to exist,’ and ‘the history of the nations relates it,’ a history naturally teeming with falsehoods.] many men and women [Note: [Col. 1304] Note the words “men and women.” From them one might not incorrectly infer that this author was a Gaul or a Walloon, since these peoples call males “men.” Lupus.] who had no heads, but large eyes fixed in their chests, while the rest of their limbs were like ours.

Among them we saw their priests married. Yet they practiced such great abstinence that, although all the priests had wives, they nevertheless wished to touch them only once a year; on that day they abstained from every sacrifice.

We also saw, in the lower regions of Ethiopia, men who had only one eye in their forehead. Their priests withdrew from the company of men and abstained from every desire of the flesh. During the week in which they were to offer incense to their gods, they abstained from every stain of the flesh; they consumed nothing except a metreta of water per day. Remaining content in this way, they worthily offered sacrifice to their gods.

O the great misery of Christians! Behold, pagans have become teachers of the faithful, and sinners and prostitutes have gone before the faithful into the kingdom of God. [Note: [Col. 1304] From the books of The City of God, on the contrary, it is clear how firmly Augustine believed that the entire pagan rite was occupied with [lacuna]ditiis [the surviving reading is uncertain].]

Let us not be like this, brothers, let us not be like this. Let us love the Lord not merely with our mouths, but in deed and in truth. Then we shall be his true ministers, if we live soberly, justly, and chastely—he who is blessed forever. Amen.

## SERMON XXXVIII. ON THE GREAT PRAISES OF SACRED SCRIPTURE, WITH AN EXHORTATION TO DILIGENT READING OF IT

[Note: [Col. 1304] Manuscript: “On Reading Sacred Scripture.”]

It is written, dearest brothers, that Moses placed in the tabernacle a bronze basin in which Aaron and his sons were to wash when they entered the Holy of Holies (Exod. 40:28). Therefore pay attention, because whatever was carried out under the ancient Law in the temple of God foreshadowed something that was to come, which was concealed in our Church under a figure, as the Apostle says: “Whatever was written was written for our instruction” (Rom. 15:4). For the holy fathers would not have taken care to commit so many and such great writings to memory unless they might edify some by reading and others through examples.

Read, therefore, my brothers, read Sacred Scripture; read it, lest you be blind and leaders of the blind. Read Sacred Scripture, in which you will clearly find what must be held to and what must be avoided. Read it, because it is found to be sweeter than every honey, more pleasant than every bread, and more cheerful than every wine. Take hold of it, and you will find how the God of gods is length because of eternity, how he is breadth because of charity, how he is height because of majesty, and how he is depth because of the immensity of wisdom [Note: [Col. 1304] Manuscripts: “depth.”].

Seek Sacred Scripture, and you will find how this God of gods, born from the Virgin Mary and made man, loves us as charity, knows as truth, sits [Note: [Col. 1304] Elsewhere, “strikes.”] as equity, and rules as majesty. Read Sacred Scripture, and you will find how that Nazarene, Jesus, governs as the beginning, protects as salvation, acts as power, is revealed [Col. 1305] as light, and is present as piety.

And therefore, my brothers, as long as we remain in this frail and vain life, let us take the utmost care with all our mind to learn and savor this wisdom. For what is a man reckoned to be without letters? What is he? Is he not perhaps a beast or a kid? Is he not an ox or an ass? Is he not a horse or a mule, which have no understanding?

Come, therefore, brothers, who are called shepherds of rational sheep: hasten to seize—not the sophistries of the pagans, not the songs of poets, not the deceits of philosophers, for which teachers and hearers will have to give an account—but that most sweet Wisdom of wisdoms, which is called God’s inheritance and the dear possession of his children.

This is that teaching to be loved above all, which the Prophets foretold, which the Patriarchs drew from God, which the Son of God, after appearing on earth and dwelling among human beings, opened and declared, showing most clearly what must be held to and what must be avoided, and enlightening us by teaching this very thing through his Apostles.

This is what teaches us to love heavenly things and despise earthly things. This is the mother of the faithful, who daily teaches us how to believe that God is omnipotent, how we shall see him coming in the seat of his majesty, and how we shall see him giving good things to the good and evil things to the wicked.

This is the lamp for our feet and the way of our salvation, in which we are instructed how first to love God above all things; afterward our own soul, as something nearer to us; afterward the soul of our neighbor; afterward our own body; and afterward the body of our neighbor as our own. For this is the perfect order of loving God, ourselves, and our neighbor.

This is that sacred wisdom which came forth from the mouth of the Most High, hidden from philosophers, sophists, astrologers, curious investigators, and dialecticians, but revealed to uneducated and simple fishermen. Is it not even today revealed only to little ones?

This is the teacher and mistress of all wisdoms and teachings, which also teaches us to recognize those who are outwardly charming but inwardly deceitful. This is the science of sciences: the food of Angels, the dish of Archangels, the glory of Apostles, the confidence of Patriarchs, the hope of Prophets, the crown of martyrs, the strength of virgins, the refreshment of monks, the leisure of bishops, the storeroom of priests, the beginning of children, the instruction of widows, the beauty of married people, the resurrection of the dead, and the everlasting protection of the living.

This is through which we are adorned with faith, strengthened by hope, and fortified by charity. This is what, when someone finds it, he will find life and draw salvation from the Lord.

This is the basin of the laver that Moses placed in the tabernacle, in which Aaron and his sons were to wash when they entered the Holy of Holies. But you will say: What are we to understand by the high priest Aaron? I tell you, brothers, that by Aaron we are to understand the high priest, and by his sons the other, lesser priests. By the bronze basin I understand the Law of the Lord, in which all priests, both great and small, ought to study—by reading it, teaching it, and fulfilling it in their works. By bodily cleanliness let us understand compunction, by which we must be cleansed, so that through purification we may be found worthy to enter the Holy of Holies—that is, to penetrate the secrets of God and of the Scriptures.

And therefore, my brothers, pay attention and consider that we have a vessel prepared in which the filth of the mind must be washed away and purity of mind prepared. For behold, the holy Law and spotless Scripture are ready, so that we may be adorned with virtues. But woe to us, who ought to be an example of correction, and behold, we are an example of error. Whence does this come, except that we are blind and ignorant, knowing nothing of the Law, and disdain to read it, while nevertheless we daily strive to occupy the chair and take charge of souls?

What wonder, then, if a priest falls? What wonder if he does not lift up those who sin? What wonder if he is a leader of the blind? Behold how he has trampled upon the Law of the Lord and despised it as death. But what did he love? What did he pursue? [Col. 1306] What did he desire with all his affection? To keep a wife or concubine discreetly, to possess horses in the stable like a soldier, to raise dogs for the hunt, and to guard falcons; and yet, like a horse and a mule without understanding, he desires to be honored at banquets and to be called Rabbi by human beings.

Behold how a priest falls; behold how he lives. But if he falls who seemed to himself to be a pillar in the temple, how much more will the people perish? If God found perversity in his Angels, how much more in those who dwell in houses of clay and have an earthly foundation?

Learn the Law, therefore, priests, lest you curse the deaf. You curse the deaf when, through ignorance, you do not know how to give counsel. You place a stumbling block before the blind when you present falsehoods as truths.

Therefore, brothers, do not now grow sluggish, but read Scripture. Learn it, little children; read it often, because it is gentler than oil, higher than gold, and purer than silver. This is what especially calls us toward God and invites us to love God; it enlightens hearts, purifies the tongue, tests the conscience, sanctifies the soul, confirms faith, drives away the devil, despises sin, warms cold souls, shows the light of knowledge, expels the darkness of ignorance, extinguishes worldly sadness, kindles the joy of the Holy Spirit, and gives drink to the thirsty.

This is our holy and spotless Law, Scripture, which makes the wise out of the foolish, places the first in the position of the last, makes the great out of the small, changes the noble from the ignoble, restrains nature, forbids frivolity, tempers sorrow, brings hope, crowns the old, teaches the young, softens the disdainful, instructs the erring, heals the sick, strengthens the weak, makes the brutish sensible, grants stability of mind, rouses the sleepy, rebukes the idle, incites the sluggish, gives grace to believers, humbles kings, exalts the humble, points out straight paths, and commands almsgiving.

This is the science of sciences, which gives wisdom, exalts glory, multiplies honor, and teaches humility, charity, gentleness, obedience, and meekness. It is good understanding for all who do good and love God. This is what preserves abstinence, chastity, generosity, and voluntary poverty. Finally, it gives instruction to all, happiness, sweetness, joys, stability of heart, sobriety of body, compunction of mind, and true humility; it fulfills brotherly charity and kindles the fear of the Lord.

Therefore, my brothers, whoever loves this wisdom and diligently fulfills the Law will be called great in the kingdom of heaven, will possess authority in the Church, and will receive abundant rewards and gifts on the last day. Amen.

# SERMON XXXIX. ON THE SOLITARY AND CONTEMPLATIVE LIFE

Peace be with you, brothers, and may charity with faith not fail you. Peace be with you, brothers, because you were chosen before the foundation of the world in this vast solitude, so that you might be with Elijah, Paul, Hilarion, Antony, and John, holy and blameless in the sight of God.

Peace be with you, because you are not a rejected race but an elect one; not a venal priesthood but a royal priesthood; not an obstinate nation but a holy one; not a people destined for destruction but for acquisition. Peace be with you, who love not the company of human beings but that of Angels in woods and groves. Peace be with you, and may the true charity of the Apostles be with you: as though possessing nothing, and possessing all things.

Peace be with you, my brothers and my dearest sons, whom daily I bring to birth in Christ within the depths of charity. May that peace of Christ, I say, which surpasses all understanding, guard—as we desire—our hearts and our minds.

Peace be with you, brothers, who have trampled upon the world, despised it, and until now have not loved the world’s praise; you have fled human laughter so that you might devote yourselves to holy companies and angelic conversations. Peace be with you, whom I have chosen as sons and brothers, so that I might have you as companions and participants in my temptations.

Now, you who wish to live this life according to the apostolic pattern did not choose me, but I chose you. I separated you from this wicked age [Col. 1307] and led you through the various places of the desert, through caves and cells, so that, like the Apostles themselves, you might remain content with scanty food.

Let us stand here, therefore, brothers, fighting daily in battle with the ancient serpent. Let us stand firm in battle, tightening and girding our loins and holding burning lamps of charity, justice, peace, and tranquility. For you did not choose me for this, but I chose you, and I placed you in the vineyard of repentance; whoever presumes to destroy it will be bitten by the most dreadful serpent of hell.

This is that fertile vineyard which I planted in the thirty-third year of my life, like God’s servant Noah. With all our mind, and with God as our guide, we desire to adorn it with the holy examples and teachings of the saints and to guard it, once adorned, in such a way that none of those passing by may be able to harvest it; nor may the boar from the forest be able to destroy it; nor may strangers be able to tear away its labors and fruits.

This is the vineyard that I planted like a master of a household, and which I surrounded with the hedge of poverty, charity, obedience, and chastity, as I learned from Simplicianus, that most dear man. Like a master of a household going out early in the morning, I brought you into it as laborers, so that you might bring forth the fiftieth-, sixtieth-, and hundredfold fruit, according to the abundance of the glory of the Lord Christ.

This is that spotless religious life whose holiness is proclaimed throughout the whole world, whose manner of life is admired by all, and whose life is regarded as more angelic than human not only by Christians but even more by Jews and pagans.

This is that most delightful paradise which God planted in the beginning, in which, by grace and gift through the merits of my mother, he placed the human being, so that he might practice the virtue of patience, instruction in doctrine, bodily chastity, perseverance in prayer, confession of sins, and abundance of tears.

This is that paradise from which flow rivers of wisdom and truth, continence and chastity, in which God delights as in all riches.

This is that apostolic rule, the rod of direction and equity, which began in the time of the apostolic preaching. Its members had one soul and one heart in the Lord, and none of the things they possessed did they say was their own; everything was held in common and distributed to each according to his need.

Have we not also, my brothers, promised to live in this way until death?

This, then, is the apostolic religious life, separated from the world in heart and body, which strikes down the leaders of Moab, kills the satraps and tyrants of Jerusalem, and wounded the hypocrites of Egypt unto death.

This is the vineyard of God’s servant Noah, situated in the midst of paradise, redeemed and watered by the blood of Christ. The leaders of the Sarabaites and the shepherds of heretics, like a boar from the forest in the time of those great monks and hermits—Paul, namely, and Antony—tried to destroy it. They tried to burn its hedge, overthrow its stone enclosure, cut down its fruits, vines, and flowers, and sow tares in and fill its plain of virtues; but, surrounded by God’s power, they were completely unable to do so.

To this vineyard, my brothers, I have brought you and made you my laborers, so that, laboring until the end, you may receive worthy fruit in its season.

For this you did not choose me, as we said above, brothers, but I chose you. But after a year I became a bishop, though I did not abandon you. Compelled to dwell among the peoples, I organized a monastery of priests and clerics and entered the bishop’s house so that I might live in common with them, just as I had formerly lived with you.

Therefore, you did not choose me, but I chose you. You know from whom, brothers, this saying was chiefly spoken: it was spoken by the Lord and spoken to the Lord’s disciples. Nevertheless, it was spoken not only to them but also to us, whom he called to share in their responsibility and glory. Just as he graciously called us through grace and made us participants in his exhortation, so also did he call you.

For he is delicate who wishes to enjoy a share but evades the administration of that share [the concluding phrase, ex rata, is uncertain]. He rightly deprives himself of honor who seeks honor without burden.

Therefore, to you, who are shepherds only of your own souls, the good shepherd speaks—the one who on the third day, as you heard, laid down his soul for his sheep—saying, “You did not choose me, but I chose you” (John 15:16). This does not mean merely abandoning this deserted dwelling, but proceeding from virtue to virtue and bearing fruit, so that your fruit may remain.

In these four matters, my brothers, we must pay attention: dignity, duty, caution, and steadfastness. Dignity, because he says, “I chose you”; duty, so that you may go; caution, so that you may bear fruit; steadfastness, because your fruit may remain (ibid.). Thus there is dignity in election, duty in labor, caution in fruitfulness, and steadfastness also in fruitfulness.

For it is a great thing that the one who does not err chose us when he chose; greater still that the work to which he chose us is God’s work; but greatest of all that among the elect he chose us beforehand. The meaning is this: “You did not choose me, but I chose you by every manner of choosing.”

There are three modes of choosing: election, sub-election, and pre-election. Election is when the good is chosen from a multitude of good and evil, just as oil is separated from the winepress. Sub-election is when the better are chosen from among those already chosen as good. After that, when the best are chosen from among the better, it is pre-election.

In this order Aaron and his sons were chosen to exercise the priesthood before the Lord. First, the Lord chose Israel from every nation under heaven as a people specially belonging to him. From among these he sub-chose the sons of Levi, who, like spiritual ministers, were to serve perpetually in the Lord’s tabernacle. From among these he also pre-chose the sons of Aaron as priests, who by their prayers and offerings would appease the Lord’s indignation against the people.

In this same manner he chose us when he washed us through the water of Baptism. He sub-chose us when he called us to the lot of the saints and into the order of the clergy. But when he advanced us to the state of hermits and made us stewards of his ministries in the administration of his household, he pre-chose us.

It is a great thing, brothers, that he chose us; greater that he sub-chose us; but greatest that he pre-chose us. Truly, then, the Lord chose us and pre-chose us as an inheritance for himself. For at the raising of our hands the heads of kings bow down, they offer gifts, and they even profess themselves our fathers, awaiting our being with Elijah and the hermit Paul as intercessors before God.

Yet woe to those who dwell in the desert if they are cast out among the wicked fish on the last day. Woe to the shepherds of sheep if they are to be counted among the goats.

What more is to be said, brothers? Listen. “I appointed you to go” (ibid.). For there are four positions of human beings: reclining, sitting, standing, and walking. Every human being is positioned in a place in such a way that he either lies down, sits, stands, or walks.

These differ among themselves in the following way. When a person lies down, all parts of the body rest. But when he sits, the lower parts of the body rest, because they appear to be sitting, while the upper parts labor. When he stands, the whole person labors to raise himself, because he generally struggles against his own weight. But when he walks, a heavy weariness caused by movement is added to the labor.

In this manner, brothers, there are four grades and states of human beings in the Church of God. Among the faithful some are good and some are evil. We do not distinguish the number of the evil, brothers, because they have multiplied beyond the number of the sand of the sea. But the good receive both order and distinction.

Some of the good are active, some contemplative, and some are superior to both. Thus there is one class of the wicked and three classes of the good. For there are four classes of the faithful.

The wicked are those who lie down, resting in the world. Such people place all their hope and trust in the amount of their riches; their god is their belly. Lying in bed, they speak to their soul and often say: “O my soul, you have many good things stored up; feast and drink, oppress the poor, despise your neighbors, reject your offspring, enlarge yourself, spread your wings, rise above the stars. Let there be no meadow that your luxury does not pass through.” Say this to your soul [Note: [Col. 1308] See Bernard, Sermon 2 on the Assumption, no. 2.].

He guards the fortress who preserves himself from every evil. O brothers, such people lie prostrate, sleep at night, and are drunk; and behold, death soon attacks them as they lie and sleep, and they vanish at once like a spark.

To such people the Apostle cried out daily when he said: “Brothers, knowing that it is already the hour for us to rise from sleep” (Rom. 13:11).

Among the good are the good married people, who make good use of permitted things. But such people are divided, because in part they serve God and in part the world. Of them the Apostle says: “They honor God with their substance,” being intent on works of mercy; nevertheless, they are excessively concerned with wife, possessions, brothers, children, and relatives (Prov. 3:9; 1 Cor. 7).

And because these people take pleasure in the world in part, they are said to sit, because they labor in the upper parts and rest in the lower.

There are also contemplatives, whose manner of life, as we said above, is in heaven. I believe, by God’s grace, and am certain, that you are among their number. Such people place all their hope in God. They always desire to endure reproaches, hunger, nakedness, and afflictions for the love of Christ. For them to live is to die, and to die is gain, as they cry out with the Apostle: “Who will free me from this body of death?” (Rom. 7:24).

Such people are like soldiers and citizens of heaven. They labor upon the earth and are daily sustained by Angels.

There are also others who walk. It is incumbent upon these to walk—not merely, like us, from virtue to virtue, but to walk, travel among, and examine the various classes of human beings more than we do, to see what is being done.

These are the shepherds and superiors, whose duty it is now to exhort, now to rebuke, now to threaten, now to console, now to teach, now to preach, now to read, now to pray; to laugh with some, weep with others, applaud some, flee from others, visit some in mind and in writing, and look upon others in person.

Such are the superiors, truly shepherds, walking like the Teacher Jesus, who, walking beside the Sea of Galilee, called his disciples and said to them: “Go into the whole world and preach the Gospel to every rational creature” (Mark 16:15).

Such are all the shepherds of the Churches, to whom Christ says, “Go,” because it is dangerous for shepherds and physicians of souls merely to stand still. Go, therefore, because it is destructive to sit, and fatal to lie down.

Go, awaken those who lie down, and say: “Rise now from sleep, because you have slept for a long time.” Cry out, shepherds and preachers of truth, and raise your voices so that the sound of your correction, rebuke, charity, and holiness may be heard throughout the whole earth.

Did not the Teacher, wishing to raise a dead man who had been dead four days, cry out in a loud voice? Keep watch, therefore, awaken those who sleep, and apply threats and terrors to them.

Then go to those who sit, and exhort them to advance toward better things. Say: “Upon the rivers of Babylon sit and weep as you remember Zion; stretch out your hand to the poor, lest your right hand be given over to oblivion.” For the person who stretches out his hands to God but does not, to the best of his ability, stretch out his hands to the poor stretches them out in vain.

But if someone who sits should at some time wish to stand, place your hand beneath him and say: “Rise after you have sat, you who have eaten the bread of sorrow.”

To those who stand, say what was promised: “You will sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. 19:28). These people need consolation, because they labor greatly. Therefore it must be said to them: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. Blessed are you who weep now, for you shall laugh. Blessed are you who hunger now, for you shall be filled. Blessed are you who flee human beings, for you shall be joined to Angels. Blessed are the solitary, for you shall be made citizens of heaven.”

Act courageously, therefore, my brothers; let your heart be strengthened, and wait for the Lord, because he will come and will not delay. It will be a little while, and you will see the one who rewards your military service, for which you endured hardships and anxieties. For the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and many violent people will seize it.

For this is the labor of our office [Note: [Col. 1309] See Bernard, Sermon 35, On Various Matters, new edition.].

This world, my brothers, is often compared with the sea, across which there are many ways of passage. Some cross by a ford, some by a boat, some by a bridge, and some, submerged, swim in the waves. These are the four [Col. 1310] states that we have named.

Those who lie down are submerged and descend into the depths like a stone. Married people cross the sea by a ford, and these will be saved amid the waves, purified by fire. Contemplatives cross the sea’s water by a bridge, choosing the safer way, for whom the world is dead.

These are those who despise the world, because, as we have learned by experience and proved by eyewitness faith, they cross the great sea with dry foot and step amid hunger and thirst, nakedness and cold, many vigils, and very numerous labors.

You, my brothers, are those who have remained with me in my temptations, and we cross the great sea by a bridge. It is truly our duty to help the others, lest they descend into the depths like a stone.

Help us all with your prayers; all of you fast as you cross this great sea, because all are placed in danger—the sailors as well as those who are submerged, and even those who cross this sea by a ford are in danger.

Are we not also in danger, we who cross by the bridge? Does a bridge not sometimes collapse? We must pray earnestly, brothers, lest we fall from the bridge. For if we were to fall from the bridge—which God forbid—we would die more quickly, because we would fall from a higher place.

Let us therefore stretch out our hands from the bridge toward those who are submerged, lest they die; and let us labor lest the well of hell also be opened and close its mouth over us.

Now, brothers, let us hear about caution. As you hear, pay attention and see how cautiously you must walk. You must walk cautiously so that you may bear fruit.

For the Lord mentions three fruits in the Gospel: the thirtieth, the sixtieth, and the hundredfold. The hundredfold is that of virgins, the thirtieth that of subjects, and the sixtieth that of superiors—that is, a doubled fruit.

For it is not enough for a superior to preserve himself spotless; rather, he must make the good shine forth, insofar as he is able, through his life and example. To signify this, the full-length tunic has been given to us, so that, doing good and holding the lamps of good works, we may persevere until the day of our calling, lest it be said to us: “This man began to build and was not able to finish” (Luke 14:30).

Our canons and priests ought to pay attention to this: the greater the dignity they have in honor above others, the greater the difficulty in rendering an account, because as many steps as they ascend toward the summit, by so many bonds of accountability will they be bound.

Who is bound by as many bonds as a priest, whether ox or ass, thief or captured lion? O priest, when you put on your vestments, first you are bound around the throat by the amice; afterward you put on the alb; with the undergirding or belt you tighten your loins, as if it were being said to you: “Bind your throat by setting a guard over your mouth; bind the cord of mixed drink; let your heart not meditate on evil. Tighten your loins; crucify your flesh through abstinence from food and drink, insofar as health permits.”

Doing these things, my most beloved brothers, you will live, you will be well, and it will be well with you. Nevertheless, pray to him without whom you can do nothing, so that, just as he chose you from the world and brought you to this singular apostolic life and fellowship, so he may help you to eat at the table in the kingdom of his Father.

Consider, however, my brothers, that as long as we live we are placed in great danger. Therefore let no one trust in his good works; rather, let him consider, as the Apostle says, that “whoever thinks that he stands must beware lest he fall” (1 Cor. 10:12).
