Did not Lucifer fall in this way, though adorned? Did not Peter also, or Judas, who was more familiar with Christ than the other disciples? And because he did not confess concerning himself and did not persevere in what was good, he fell, burst apart, and died.

Ask, therefore, brothers, him without whose will not even a leaf of a tree is moved, to rule and direct you in this solitude in such a way to the very end that you may go and bear fruit, and that your fruit may remain. Amen.

Do not be troubled, dearest brothers, if I compel you to drink wine and to eat wheat bread together with beets mixed with butter. For today we believe that the Son of Man rose from the dead; therefore it is right to rejoice and feast, because our brother had been dead and has come back to life; he had been lost and has been found.

Approaching the table, therefore, feast with [Col. 1311] joy, because I am Jacob, your father.

# SERMON XL. ON THE OBSERVANCE OF THE CLERGY
You heard at table, dearly beloved brothers, how the Lord commanded his servant Abraham to take his son Isaac, whom he loved above all earthly things, and offer him upon one of the mountains that the Lord had shown him. Some say that this was the mountain of Calvary, on which that God and man was crucified.

The sequence of the story, recently understood in its simple sense, first builds up the sons of obedience. For “the word is faithful, living and effective, and sharper than any two-edged sword.” But something must now be said to you about the manner and power of obedience. For just as one must obey willingly, so also cheerfully, and likewise swiftly. Obedience must be without delay. Slow and disputatious obedience does not please God: when it is commanded, it asks why, for what reason, and on what account it is commanded.

An exemplary form of this obedience is set before us today. Abraham is our father; for so he is called, an old man faithful and the first path of belief. Let holy father Abraham, therefore, be considered among all people the first rule and model of obedience and of true obedience.

Behold, brothers: God commanded him to sacrifice his son. But which son? Hear, and marvel as you hear: his beloved son, his firstborn son, the son of the great promise, the son of the great generation. For it had been said to Abraham: “In Isaac shall your offspring be called” (Gen. XXI, 12), and in him shall your offspring be like the stars of heaven and like the sand of the sea, in the extreme of your old age.

Abraham was a hundred years old when he begot Isaac from Sarah, his own barren wife; from Hagar, his maidservant, he had Ishmael the archer. He had received the promised child wondrously, and more wondrously still he religiously brought up the child he had received. Yet amid all this Abraham did not contradict, nor murmur, nor hesitate, nor trouble his face. Rather, rising like a father, he armed himself with a pious cruelty against his son, so that he might obey at once.

Attend, you sons of obedience, who have made a vow and profession. Go, brother, and do likewise. Think always of fulfilling these things; always do this with a joyful face, and you shall live, and your offspring shall be blessed beyond the offspring of Abraham.

Nevertheless, I do not know what greater thing this voice murmurs, or what more affectionate thing it whispers in our ears, although these matters were written so long before us and were spoken allegorically. Let us therefore examine the leaves of the vine so that we may find the fruit of spiritual understanding—like the kernel beneath the shell, the grain beneath the chaff, and the treasure beneath the earth.

But, in order to satisfy today’s solemnity of Christ, let us consider whether we can apply what was said about the time of Abraham to me, Augustine, your father. Let us attempt to say something on this subject to the praise of God and for our partial edification.

According to the Hebrews, Abraham received three names at three different times. At first he was called Illam [Note: [Col. 1311] In Genesis, chapter XI, verse 26, he is called Abram immediately from his birth.], which there signifies “the Exalted,” while he was still in Chaldea, in his land and kindred, in the house of his father. But when he ascended into the land of Canaan at God’s call, he was called Abram, which is interpreted “Exalted Father.” Finally, at the time of his circumcision [Note: [Col. 1311] Rather, before the command concerning circumcision, Gen. XVII, 5.] he was then called Abraham, that is, “Father of many nations.”

Pay attention, brothers, and see yourselves in your father. For at first I was called an exalted philosopher. I was renowned above all the great, and a most discerning investigator of the liberal arts. I was exalted, I say, with the height of knowledge that puffs up, not with the charity that builds up. For the Roman princes called me a fragrant cedar, abundant in leaves; but I had no fruit. I was exalted and impious above all my contemporaries, raised up and lifted higher than the cedars of Lebanon.

And behold, there came to me a mother full of piety; the preaching of the holy [Col. 1312] bishop; and the life and examples of the holy fathers Paul, Antony, and Simplicianus. Together with all these, the voice of the Lord, breaking the cedars, shattered the cedar of Lebanon, and I, a victim prepared for sacrifice as a sweet-smelling offering, thus became an exalted father.

Afterward I came to Africa, bringing with me nineteen of my brothers, living together in a holy palace and desiring to separate ourselves from the world. Holy father Valerius, wishing to share in the fruits and prayers, gave us this secluded place in which we are now; many of us saw it. But when this place had been built, in the name of Christ and of the holy Trinity I was made bishop of Hippo, and I was called “exalted father of many.”

For bishops, my brothers, just as they are called shepherds of the flock, are also fathers of the people because of their care and paternal solicitude. Then I became like a fruitful olive tree in the house of God. Bishops are compared to the olive because of the threefold power of oil. For oil first gives light, nourishes, and comforts weary limbs. So bishops ought to give light by their word, nourish by their example, and comfort the needy by temporal beneficence.

I do not say, brothers, that I do this; yet I strive to explain Holy Scripture, to fortify the tower of David with the strongest shields, to make it known once fortified, and to order it once made known. For what do I understand by the tower of David except the Church of the saints? Thus our teaching and exposition now flourishes from east and west, from north and south.

Yet it does not proceed from me, but from the house of God. Thus I am called not only the father of nations, but also an abundant vine on the sides of the house of God. The sides of that house are the readers and those who pray, and the married people among the readers, those who pray, and those who marry.

For you who read and pray, we have abundantly poured out instruction, to whom I have handed down apostolic discipline. To the married we have also poured out the cup of life. To you, however, I have poured the wine of fervor, charity, and equity; to them we have given peace and patience.

Let us therefore return to the story mentioned above, which suggests three things to us: regular discipline, progress, and outcome. For the Lord says to us, “Take your son” (Gen. XXII, 2), as though the Lord were saying: You who are a monk, take your son Isaac, whose name is interpreted “Laughter”; that is, take your own will, in the execution of which a person laughs and delights.

And this is the first offering that a person ought to return and offer to God upon one of the mountains that God shows us. For the Lord points out many kinds of mountains. But among these four, the mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, is called a mountain; he will be “the mountain of the house of the Lord at the top of the mountains in the last days” (Isa. II, 2). And again: “The mountain of God is a rich and thick mountain” (Ps. LXVII, 16). From this mountain, moreover, dew and ointment descended for the beard of Aaron. For all of us can receive ointment from Christ’s fullness.

The apostles too, brothers, are called mountains, because his foundations—that is, the Church—are upon the holy mountains. Are not the angels also called lofty mountains? Moreover, Jesus, who is called a mountain, sits upon Mount Tabor and delivers a sermon to his disciples, enumerating the seven beatitudes of the Spirit.

O brothers, consider how great an impediment and how serious a loss the excess and abundance of possessions bring to holy religion. We read this much more clearly in the book of our conscience than we can express in words.

Is it not written that the sin of the Sodomites was abundance of bread and pride of life? Did not the angels, seeing themselves abound in beauty, fall because they grew proud in their wisdom? Were not our first parents expelled from paradise for virtually the same reason? Was not the world drowned when people, abounding in possessions and not knowing God amid their abundance, perished? Were not the Egyptians, abounding and filled with anger, drowned? Were not idols made on earth because of abundance? Did not Amalek, because he abounded—that is, because he was full of envy—fall by the hand of Saul? Were not many thousands killed in the time of David? Did not Saul, abounding in pride, become proud [Col. 1313] and get cast out? Was not Herod the Ascalonite slaughtered? Did not Herod the tetrarch, hoping through his abundance to satisfy the people who believed John to be holy and righteous, nevertheless behead him?

Consider, brothers, what happened to Holofernes, to Caesar, to Nero, to Valentinian, to Constantine, to Decius, and to Julian. What, then, did abundance profit Caesar and Nero? What did money profit Ahasuerus? What did feigned and disguised repentance profit Antiochus?

Let us therefore honor Christ, poor in the present, so that we may be rich in the future. For pride and luxury accompany riches. Let us therefore love, brothers, the supreme poverty of Christ and the apostles, lest the fairest color of our holy religion be changed and the stones of our sanctuary be scattered.

Indeed, my brothers, the commendation of voluntary poverty shines among us more fully when it is compared with other kinds of poverty. For there are five kinds of poverty: the first is misfortune; the second is the poverty of covetousness; the third, the poverty of excess; the fourth, of deceit; the fifth, the poverty of the will.

The first is possessed by a beggar, the second by a miser, the third by a spendthrift, the fourth is a whitewashed wall, and the fifth is possessed by a shackled man. The first is a scourge, the second a poison, the third a winnowing fan, the fourth a shelter, and the fifth a building. The first is miserable because it torments; the second poisonous because it kills; the third windy because it puffs up; the fourth deceitful because it conceals; the fifth glorious because it crowns.

Nor is it surprising that Christ, a lover of moderation, commends moderation of spirit, since Epicurus, the teacher of pleasure, also commended it, saying: “How happy poverty is, if it is cheerful!”

The devout person makes an offering of his own will, and this takes place especially in the profession of obedience.

Next, brothers: “Abraham saddled the donkey, taking two boys with him. Isaac carried cedar wood, while Abraham carried fire and a sword. When they came to the mountain, Isaac was bound and placed upon the wood; and, knowing God’s will from his father, he did not open his mouth. But when Abraham stretched out his hand, he heard: ‘Do not stretch out your hand against the boy’ (Gen. XXII, 3–12); instead, take a ram for Isaac from all your best possessions, which I have prepared for you among the thorns.”

Let us now pay attention, brothers. For what do I understand by the donkey except our flesh, which must be disciplined like a donkey by the rod, by burdens, by fodder, by ashes, and by sackcloth, lest, fattened, thickened, and enlarged, it kick back like a donkey that wanted to play with its master like a puppy?

The two boys are the five senses of the human being. Yet we call them two because two are assigned within the limbs for their use and execution. Like Abraham, I have joined you to two boys, in you and in our canons, so that the flesh may not grow wanton and death may not enter through the windows: namely, to poverty and prayer. Through these two, you will be able to extinguish the five bodily senses.

Through these things we shall forget past evils; evil thoughts will not rise into your hearts; affection for relatives will not rule over you. These are the things that sift monks daily like wheat. These are the biting cares that have weakened the holy purpose of the man. Among these the holy man is cooked and tormented. These are the biting and dying flies of monks, which destroy the sweetness of the ointment. These are the flying things that eat the grain sown in the soul.

But you, brothers, whenever these things rise into your hearts, turn back to prayer or to the occupations of work, lest the serpentine flies swallow you. Did not holy father Antony do this? When he had received letters from his loved ones living in the world, he did not wish to read any of them, but threw the letters he had received into the fire, saying: “You are deceptive papers, even full of lies; I burn you so that I may not be burned by you.”

Next, brothers: Isaac is bound. So you too must be bound in this solitude so firmly that you no longer know the customs of secular life and may grasp the sweetness of holy religion. Let the sobriety of sleep, tranquility of mind, cleanliness of body, severity toward death, and every expectation of salvation please you.

Isaac is released and joyfully returns to his mother in Beersheba. So may you, released, turn back to the mother who is above, Jerusalem. When you have reached her, she will give you a dwelling of refreshment, the blessedness of rest, and the splendor of light.

## SERMON XLI. ON THE OBSERVANCE OF THE LENTEN FAST

“When you fast, anoint your head and wash your face, so that you may not appear to people to be fasting” (Matt. VI, 17–18).

The duty of one who fasts is to sit in ashes and sackcloth, not to keep filthy garments, to mortify the flesh, to make the face thin, to remain pale, not to wash it, not to approach a lavish table, not to visit banquets and festivals, and not to walk with bowed head; but rather, giving alms, preserving chastity, and living justly, holily, and devoutly, he should rejoice while awaiting the holy resurrection of Christ.

Do all these things, however, not so that you may be seen by people, but only by him who sees everything in secret. But if it should happen that the smoke of your fasts is scattered among people, wash your face at once, so that you may not appear to people to be fasting.

Three things, brothers, are set before us today: to fast, to wash the face, and to anoint the head. These three are the things in which our whole life ought to consist. What are these things, brothers, except turning away from evil, doing good, and contributing everything you have to God? Behold what our holy Christian religion contains.

For what does fasting mean, brothers, except turning away from evil; washing the face, doing good; anointing the head, giving everything to God?

But someone may say, “This exposition is brief; and you have not offered us living water as we desire.” Pay attention, then, brothers. For the ancient enemy first persuaded your first parents in paradise to offend the Lord; second, to hide their faces from God after midday; third, to eat from the forbidden tree. There, it is said, he was to prick the head; here, to anoint the head. There, by hiding the face, he was to lie concealed; here, he was to wash it. There, he was to eat; here, he was to fast.

Let us believe the one who has now commanded these things, but not the one who persuaded the contrary. For the Father says: “This is my beloved Son; listen to him” (Matt. XVII, 5). For today he says: “When you fast.”

There is, brothers, a praiseworthy fast and a condemnable fast. Condemnable is the fast that people see, which is performed for the sake of people; praiseworthy is that which is performed solely for the sake of God.

Some fast as sick people, some as those who are surfeited, some as misers, and some as hypocrites. The sick person fasts in order to recover; the surfeited person, in order to regain appetite; the miser, in order to save; the hypocrite, in order to appear. The fast of the sick person is one of health; the fast of the surfeited person is one of gluttony; the fast of the miser is one of frugality; the fast of the hypocrite is one of pretence.

Although these fasts are not dangerous, as in the case of the sick person, they are nevertheless fruitless. Fast, therefore, brothers, for God’s sake. Let us break the nut so that we may receive the kernel; let us cast away the leaves so that we may find the fruit; let us cleanse the well so that we may draw water from the fountains of the Savior.

For the Savior says: “Come, you who thirst, to the waters” (Isa. LV, 1). There are three kinds of the Savior’s water, brothers: the water of tears, when he wept over Lazarus and over the city; the water that he placed in the basin when he washed the feet of the disciples; and the water that flowed from his side.

We ought to possess the first, brothers, if we desire to fast rightly. The first water is therefore that of contrition, the second of confession, and the third of satisfaction. The first heals the mind, the second refreshes, and the third makes fruitful.

Therefore, faithful one, if you wish to fast rightly, receive these waters, wash yourself, and you will be cleansed from leprosy. For unless you have these waters, your fast will be of little value.

Today, therefore, dearly beloved brothers, summoned to the wedding of the great King, let us adorn ourselves with garments, trumpets, and well-sounding cymbals. Let us praise the master of the household himself, who has deigned to call us to his wedding.

What is the wedding prepared today, brothers, except the righteous days that God has deigned to consecrate? These are the days that we ought to observe, in which we shall deserve to receive the law. These are medicinal days, which bring health to soul and body. These are wedding days [Col. 1315], on which we ought to be adorned with garments and sound cymbals, trumpets, and well-sounding instruments.

These are the instruments that we ought to sound at the Lenten wedding. First, we ought to clothe ourselves with holy virtues, having stripped off vices. Second, by striking our breasts in contrition, we ought to make the cymbal sound. Third, like heralds we ought to cry out, calling little ones who suck at the breast to learn to fast and old people to teach them to fast: “For behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now are the days of grace and salvation; behold, the days of remission; behold, the days of satisfaction.”

You, therefore, wicked one, who have slept for a long time, arise; remember from where you have fallen, and do penance while you have time, while you are healthy, while you are able to sin, so that you may be seen to repent not from fear but from love.

For everyone, my brothers, who through penance has wiped away his sins is already a sharer in angelic blessedness. For penance itself is the medicine of the wound, the hope of salvation, through which sinners are saved and through which God is inclined to mercy.

When you have done penance, brothers, pour out tears of heart and body for your sins. Was it not by weeping, my brothers, that Peter was regarded by Christ? Did not Mary obtain forgiveness? Was not Martha healed by tears? Was not the Canaanite woman heard? Was not Lazarus recalled to life?

Wash your face, therefore, you who begin to fast today; strike your breast with tears; raise your voice by confessing and announcing your sins to the priest.

Hear, brothers, what David obtained through confession. What did he say except, “I have sinned against the Lord”? And the prophet Nathan said, “God has taken away your sin from you” (II Kings XII, 13).

Beware, brothers, however, lest your confession be like Saul’s. When rebuked by Samuel, he said in pride, “I have sinned.” He immediately deserved to hear, “God has taken away the kingdom from you” (I Kings XV, 24, 28).

So Judas also said, “I have sinned” (Matt. XXVII, 4), not in sorrow but in despair. So Cain said, “My iniquity is greater than that I should deserve forgiveness” (Gen. IV, 13).

Therefore, brothers, when you fast, wash your faces with tears; anoint the head—Christ, who is the head of all. Anoint him, then, with the oil of mercy, by giving alms and crying out words of contrition: “We have sinned, Lord, but have mercy.”

Thus we shall be anointed by Christ with the oil of gladness. So we read that David was anointed; so we see Peter and Mary anointed; so we have always wished to behold the brothers anointed.

But someone will say, “How is God to be anointed?” O sinner, go first to Mary the sinful woman. For she anointed the feet, and afterward the head—that is, the soul—and afterward was able to approach the head. For if she had not first washed Christ’s feet with tears, she would not have dared to approach Christ’s head in order to anoint it.

It is therefore necessary first to pour out tears upon the feet and afterward to approach Christ’s head.

Know, however, my brothers, that unless you forgive your enemies from your heart, everything you do—whether you fast, give alms, or perform every good deed—is vain, and you are useless servants, unless you forgive your neighbor.

But you will say, “I cannot forgive my enemy. Since, then, the good I do is of no value to me without this, I no longer wish to afflict myself by fasting or distributing goods.”

But I say to you: “Forgive, and you will be forgiven.” Yet no evil will remain unpunished, nor any good unrewarded, before God, who knows the hidden things of everyone’s heart.

## SERMON XLII. ON THE LIFE AND CONDUCT OF CLERICS

Dearly beloved brothers, that holy man Jeremiah, considering the negligence of priests and prelates, uttered lamentable words and said: “The little ones asked for bread, and there was none; nor was there anyone to break it for them” (Lam. IV, 4).

Jeremiah therefore cried out, seeing the destruction of the holy City; he wept and lamented the cruelty of mothers, fathers, and shepherds who devour their children unto perdition.

“Woe to you, shepherds of Israel, who ate what was fat, but did not strengthen what was broken; you did not bring back what had gone astray; you did not heal what was sick; you did not clothe what was naked” (Ezek. XXXIV, 2–4).

O brothers, today we have become ravening wolves, setting justice aside and ignoring truth and mercy. Beware, therefore, lest the Lord say to you today: “I appointed you steward over my household, and you did not break bread for them.”

You are therefore not a steward but a squanderer; not a watchman but a killer.

“O wicked servant, I shall cast you into the outer darkness, because your little ones asked you for bread, and there was no one to break it for them.”

Therefore, brothers, bread must be distributed and broken for subjects before they perish from hunger. For if they die, their blood will be demanded from your hands.

Bread of every kind of holiness must therefore be distributed to the hungry. There is, brothers, pure bread, which must be distributed and broken for the children. There is also another, impure bread, which must be distributed to servants.

These breads are joined in the house of God, just as chaff is joined to grain on the threshing floor. Yet we read in Scripture of three breads: the breads of Pharaoh, of offering, and of presentation. The first are the laity, the second are the priests, and the third are the shepherds.

Pharaoh’s breads are divided into three parts: the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the pride of life. The first is lust, which weakens; the second is greed, which torments; the third is pride, which puffs up like a bladder.

Lust produces impurity; greed generates envy; pride gives birth to injustice. Lust presses a person within himself through pollution; greed draws him outside himself through emptiness; pride lifts him above himself through arrogance.

Lust depresses a person within himself, because although he was made in the image of God, he seeks to live like a pig in the mud. Greed drags a person outside himself, because for the sake of earthly things he abandons heavenly things. Pride lifts him above himself, so that he puts his mouth in heaven.

And thus, fathers and brothers, through lust a person desires to delight in empty things; through greed, to find consolation in passing things; through pride, to glory in impiety.

These are the shepherds whom the Lord drove from the temple, selling and buying. These are the captains of fifty whom Elijah burned. These are the false prophets clothed in goatskins, who inwardly also are ravening wolves.

Therefore, let us who are called shepherds break lust through abstinence, drown greed through almsgiving, and flee pride through humility and patience.

For just as it is impossible for a demon obstinate in evil to enter paradise, so it is impossible for lustful, greedy, and proud shepherds to make their subjects chaste, humble, and good. For the flock must be such as its ruler is.

There is also another bread, the bread of offering, which we must not only break but also offer to God. David said: “Let my prayer enter like incense in your sight” (Ps. CXL, 2).

This is a threefold bread, because prayer ought to be abundant, devout, and pure. It ought to be abundant so that you may pray for everyone, even for those who accuse and persecute you; devout, so that you may not ask carelessly but devoutly, and it will be given to you if you persevere.

But someone may say: “What kind of person should the one who asks be? What should he ask? For whom should he ask? And from whom should he ask?”

If you ask what kind of person you ought to be, we say: good, because we know that God does not hear sinners [Note: [Col. 1316] Augustine contradicts this, Tractate 44 on John, no. 13, where he says that these words belong to one not yet enlightened: “For,” he says, “God also hears sinners.”].

But if you ask what you ought to request, I say: life, or the merit of life, or the attaining of the merits of life.

But if you ask for whom you ought to pray, I say: for those living well and badly, so that the good may persevere and the wicked may be converted—not for the saints, nor for the damned. For whoever prays for a martyr does an injury to the martyr; and whoever prays for the damned will obtain nothing.

Yet God is powerful enough to make bread from these stones.

But if you ask further from whom you should ask, it is said that we ought to ask everything from the Father in the name of the Son. Thus we shall be true shepherds.

There is also another bread, namely the bread of propitiation. And this is threefold [Col. 1317]: the bread of angels, of which a person eats at the altar; the bread of children, that is, the words of holy doctrine.

This is the bread that descended from heaven together with the first bread. This is the bread that it is not good to take and give to heretical dogs, because it is the bread of children.

This is the bread requested: “Friend, lend me three loaves” (Luke XI, 5)—namely, of life, doctrine, and example.

This is the bread given to Peter, so that he might feed the lambs. For three times the Lord said to Peter that he should feed the sheep, so that you, as a shepherd, may understand that the sheep are to be fed by doctrine, life, and example—or by the Eucharist, doctrine, and holy life.

And just as the Lord said this to Peter, so also he said it to his other apostles.

Therefore, let us feed our sheep; let us break bread for our little ones, lest they fail on the way. Let us feed them with angelic bread; let us feed them with the word; let us feed them by example, lest the whole people perish.

For we are the heads of the nations, guides of the blind and ignorant, staffs of the lame, princes of the lands, attendants of kings, superior to angels—but worse than demons when we carelessly neglect these things.

Brothers, let us therefore feed the people, lest they be like sheep without a shepherd, so that Jesus Christ our Lord may lead them from the pastures of solitude to the pastures of fellowship.

## SERMON XLIII. ON THE EPIPHANY AND SEEKING CHRIST
You have heard, dearest brothers, that the most holy kings diligently sought the Lord; and we do not doubt that, in seeking God and man, they found him, and we firmly believe and proclaim that they offered him precious gifts. Therefore, brothers, seek Christ; seek the Nazarene; seek him who is flowering, white, and ruddy. Seek Christ, and him crucified; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you; cry out, and call upon the beloved, announcing that you languish with love.

O you lovers of the world, who set your minds on earthly things, whose god is your belly and whose life is in confusion: what are you doing without Christ? What do you desire, what do you esteem, what do you hope for? Can you have peace without Christ? Can happiness or victory, dignity or security, faith or charity, hope or confidence, steadfastness or temperance, prudence or knowledge, beauty or strength, smell or touch, sight or hearing exist without Christ? O my brothers, certainly not.

Seek Christ, therefore, while he may be found; call upon him while he is near. For in him are all virtues, and the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden. Seek Christ, and you will find Christ; knock at Christ, and it will be opened to you through Christ. Direct your way toward Christ, so that Christ may direct you. Guard Christ, so that Christ may guard you. Love Christ, so that Christ may love you. Seek Christ in poverty, and you will find Christ in riches. Feed Christ’s hungry, so that Christ may feed you. Visit Christ’s sick, so that Christ may visit you. Keep peace with your neighbor for the love of Christ, so that Christ may make peace for you.

Let us seek this Christ, then; let us truly desire him; let us always acknowledge him as best we can. Let us continually search for him, and, once found, hold him so firmly, so gently, and so lovingly that we do not lose him.

Christ must be sought—but not in the public square, where there is supreme vanity. Christ must be sought—but not in the marketplace, where there is great hostility. Christ must be sought—but not in the tavern, where there is supreme drunkenness. Christ must be sought—but not in the secular court, where there is the greatest falsehood. Christ must be sought—but not in the schools of worldly philosophers, where there is boundless perversity.

O you lovers of the world, who set your minds on earthly things and do not cease rushing about for earthly honors and spectacles, flying across mountains and the Alps, wishing to investigate the heights of heaven, the breadth of the earth, and the depths of the sea, in heat and cold, hunger and nakedness: why do you not seek Christ, in whom all these things—and greater things—are found perfectly? Stop now acting perversely; learn to do good, you who take pains continually to investigate the movements of the heavens—not, however, so that you may know God more perfectly, but so that you may appear distinguished before the world.

[Col. 1318] Wise and foolish alike, seek Christ—but not with lust, in which hidden ugliness lies; not with pride, in which eternal calamity lies hidden; not with greed, in which there is slavery to sorrows and eternal unhappiness.

But alas, brothers, alas! Today there is no one who does good; there is no one who seeks to worship Christ in deed; nor is there anyone who hopes in him. The soldier hopes in his sword, the king in riches, the child in an apple, the servant in his master, the wife in her husband, the husband in his wife, the old woman in a little money, and the peasant in his hoe.

Behold, brothers, behold how each person departs from God our Savior. Behold how we hope in vanity, abandoning God our creator and departing from God our Savior. Not so, then, my brothers, not so. Even if riches and honors abound, do not set your heart upon them; set your heart only upon Christ, always hope in him, because he cares for each one of you.

Let us seek Christ, then, my brothers, and never rest until we find him. Seek him while he may be found; call upon him while he is near.

But how shall we seek him? For today Christ is being sought: the pagans seek him, and the Jews seek him. O Christian, take care not to seek Christ with the Jews, but do not cease seeking him with the pagan kings. For the pagans seek to worship Christ, whereas the Jews already seek to overthrow Christ. The pagans come to Christ, whereas the Jews despise Christ. The pagans labor by coming to Christ, whereas the Jews, by remaining inactive, fail to know Christ. The pagans worship Christ, offering him gifts; whereas the Jews are already plotting Christ’s death. The pagans, worshiping Christ and seeing miracles there, magnify him with their whole heart; whereas the synagogue of the Jews is already crowning Christ with thorns. The pagans return by another road, rejoicing; whereas the Jews are already beginning to fear lest the Romans come and take away their place and nation.

Be ashamed, faithless Jews, be ashamed; for the time will come when not one stone upon another will remain in you, because you did not recognize the time of your visitation. Be ashamed, for behold, strangers are already entering upon your inheritance and are being led by a star to your king who has been born—he whose precious birth was predestined before the ages, foretold by the prophets, announced to the shepherds, and revealed to the wise kings.

O Jews, ever rebellious against God, blind and obstinate, why do you not consider the wonders that God performs in the midst of your land? Why do you not seek Christ? Why do you not recognize God and man? Why do you not worship him as the true Son of God?

O my brothers, it is not only the Jews: wicked Christians also seek to kill Christ today. When do they seek this, if not when they disdain to keep his commandments?

The Magi did not act in this way. Rather, as soon as Christ was born, they believed and began to labor along the road; thus, persevering, they eventually deserved to find him—not amid costly clothing, not amid a multitude of servants, not in a painted bedchamber, not on an ivory couch, not in a royal hall. Instead of a bedchamber, he wished to recline in a stable; instead of a bed, he wished to have hay; instead of servants, [Note: [Col. 1318] This expression supports Lupus’s conjecture concerning a Gallic or Valonian author, as does the preceding phrase, “flying across the Alps.”] the Savior wished to have an ox and an ass.

Come, then, my brothers: seek Christ; seek the Nazarene; seek this flowering, white, and ruddy one, at whose birth the angels sing, the saints rejoice, the barren woman cries out, the widow prophesies, the old man Simeon waits, Joseph reflects, Mary the mother lays him down, the ox recognizes him, the ass carries him, the star points him out, and the Magus worships him.

This is the God of gods in Zion, who appears terrible among the Cherubim, wondrous among the Seraphim, and incomprehensible in the powers. This is he who was recently born from the Virgin Mary and became man: he became man in order to make us gods. This is he who hungered in order to refresh us; who thirsted in order to serve us the drinks of eternal life. This is he who was tempted for us in order to free us from temptations; who was bound for us, [Col. 1319] in order to release us; who was humbled for us, in order to exalt us; who was stripped for us, in order to cover us; who was crowned for us, in order to crown us; who was given gall and vinegar to drink, in order to open for us honey-flowing fountains.

He accepted death in order to give us eternal life; he was buried in order to bless the burial of his own; he ascended into heaven in order to open for us the gates of heaven; he sits at the right hand of God the Father in order to hear the prayers and petitions of believers.

Behold, then, for what purpose Christ was born; behold why Christ descended to us.

What, then, are you doing, O lovers of the world? What have you to do with the flesh, venerable old men? O delicate young men, what do you think you are doing, when you can do nothing without Christ, no matter what earthly goods adorn you?

Seek Christ, therefore, young men, so that you may remain young. Seek Christ, you old men, so that you may be able to live in every prosperity. Seek Christ and do not cease seeking that Christ, that Jesus, who healed the centurion’s servant, restored the paralytic, raised Lazarus, gave sight to the blind, blessed the sinful woman, answered the Canaanite woman, spared the thief, and granted him paradise.

Seek this Christ in faith, hope, and charity. Seek Christ and do not cease. Seek Christ and do not place your hope in the length of your life, for its end is uncertain.

But take care not to be deceived, because many evils are done under the appearance of good. For the ancient enemy never ceases to assume the form of an angel of light, spreading snares of deception everywhere. The wicked one knows the dispositions of human beings, and knows to whom he should apply the heat of greed, the voracity of gluttony, the foulness of lust, or the calamity of envy. He knows very well whom to disturb with sorrow, whom to deceive with joy, whom to oppress with fear, and whom to seduce with admiration. He examines the dispositions of all and never ceases to sift and scrutinize everyone’s affections; and wherever he discovers what pleases, there he places his exercise [Note: [Col. 1319] Manuscript: “army” (*exercitum*).].

You, therefore, faithful one, when you sense temptations, seek Christ immediately; call upon Christ immediately. Then he himself will immediately help you, because he is faithful and does not permit us to be tempted beyond what we are able to bear.

He is blessed forever. Amen.

## SERMON XLIV. ON PIETY, CHARITY, AND SUFFRAGES FOR THE DEAD

Dearest brothers, I do not remember ever reading that a person who willingly practiced works of charity or piety in this life perished by an evil death. For a pious person has many intercessors, as does the one who cheerfully practices works of charity.

What else can we say about pious people except what we frequently read: “For their works follow them” (Rev. XIV, 13)? Why is this? Because they have many intercessors; therefore it is impossible that the prayers of many should not be heard.

Consider, therefore, O man, who it is who meets you on the road. Notice that he is a human being made in the image of God, and yet he is poor, naked, wretched, a beggar, perhaps an orphan and a fatherless child. Take care, however, not to despise such a person, not to strike him, not to drive him away. For although he may appear poor, naked, hungry, wretched, suffering, and ashamed, the poor person must nevertheless not be driven away.

Do not despise them, brothers, nor, even if they ask insistently, ever murmur about them, because the poor and needy do not cease praising God.

Consider, you rich man, as you walk along roads and streets with head and neck held high, that you were born together with the poor man from a woman and will live for only a short time. Although you are rich, you are often filled with bitterness and pains. You were conceived in filth, nurtured in darkness, and your mother gave birth to you amid pains. Before your departure you heavily burdened your mother; at your departure you shamefully tore your mother apart. You wept together with the poor man and beggar when you entered the valley of tears.

We were therefore born as equals; together we live, together we shall all die. Consider, then, O rich man, that poor and rich alike are born and [Col. 1320] die in the same way. Do not despise them, then; do not turn away the hand of blessing from them. Receive them with a serene face; refresh them by word and example.

Let mercy, therefore, my brothers, be our mother. For the person who refreshes the hungry with the bread of the word, who cools the thirsty with the drink of wisdom, who calls the one who has gone astray back into the father’s house, who protects the innocent, who instructs the sick in faith and patience, and who helps the oppressed in tribulation by consoling them or sharing their suffering—this person is truly pious, truly merciful, truly a friend of God. No one should dare to say that such a person will perish by an evil death.

O mercy, safeguard of salvation, ornament of faith, expiation of sins! You test the just, strengthen the saints, and lead the wicked to goodness. Let the one who appears to abound in every good thing or to be adorned with chastity never cease saying, “I am an unprofitable servant.”

But attend also, my brothers; attend, because we must not show mercy only to the poor on the road. We should also strive with all diligence to show mercy and offer assistance to the dead, considering what Judas Maccabaeus did. For he said that it was a holy thought to pray for the dead, so that they might be released from their sins (II Macc. XII, 46).

Judas himself knew that no one could boast of having a pure heart. He also considered that the stars were not clean in God’s sight. For the angels fell from heaven; therefore the stars were not clean. Nor is even an infant, whose life upon earth is one day long, without sin.

What, then, shall we say about ourselves? Can we boast of having a pure heart? Certainly not. Why? Because we are all sinners; we were all conceived and born in sins; we all lead a life capable of sin; we live in sins; and perhaps we die in venial sins.

Therefore we need mercy, because we are all going to depart from this life. Even if we severely mortify the flesh with fasts and abstinence, even if we patiently endure every evil for the love of Christ, nevertheless “the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory that is to be revealed in us” (Rom. VIII, 18).

Therefore we need mercy, because we cannot acquire eternal life by our own merits.

Do you wish, O man, that God should have mercy on you? Make sure that you have mercy on your neighbor. For God will have mercy on you to the extent that you have mercy on your neighbor; you will receive in the other life to the extent that you do in the present life.

Pray, then, for the dead, so that, when they are in eternal life, they will not neglect to pray for you. For they await us, so that they may be helped through us; the time for working has already fled from them.

Those who lie in torments cry out every day. They cry out, and few there are who answer; they howl, and there is no one to comfort them. O what great cruelty, my brothers! O what great inhumanity! They cry out to us every day—those who, while they lived, wished to endure many evils for our sake—and we take no care to help them. O truly great inhumanity!

Behold: a sick person lies and cries out, and is comforted by physicians; a pig cries out, and everyone does not cease crying out with it; an ass falls, and everyone hastens to lift it up. But a believer cries out in torments, and there is no one to answer.

Behold our inhumanity, brothers. Come, then, let it not be so. Remember, brothers, that it is a holy, health-giving, pious, and blessed thought, pleasing to God and the angels, to pray for the dead so that they may be released from the punishments they suffer for their sins.

But someone may say: “Behold, I had a pious and good father, merciful and chaste, humble and adorned with every virtue. For if what I read is true, I have no doubt that he is blessed. Why, then, should I wish to pray for him, give alms, fast, or visit the bodies of the saints? It is not necessary to pray for him, because he was faithful, pious, chaste, humble, patient, and adorned with every good thing; he did not pursue gold, nor did he hope in treasures of money. He could have transgressed, but he did not transgress; he could have done evil, but he did not. What, then, should I believe except what I read? For what do I read or hear preached except that whoever does good will be well rewarded?”

O man, I dare not deny you in any way what you say. For what believer doubts that the one who has done good will receive good in return? Nevertheless, I advise you not to cease praying for the dead.

For I said above that no one lives without guilt; no one can boast of having a pure or clean heart. What, then, do I advise, what do I wish, or what do I entreat, except that you abandon the uncertain and accept the certain?

What is uncertain except that you do not know whether your father is being tormented or whether he was worthy of hatred or love? For many have been regarded as saints and yet have been found in God’s sight to be not good but evil.

Accept, therefore, what is certain, and abandon what is uncertain. It is certain that he was a sinner; and although he may have been adorned with good works, we nevertheless do not know whether he deserved to possess eternal glory.

Read, therefore, O man, and hasten to fulfill in deed what it is: a holy and health-giving thought to pray for the dead, to give alms, to afflict the flesh, to practice works of piety, and to make pilgrimages, so that they may be released from their sins.

For even if those for whom you pray are blessed or condemned, provided that you do not know this and it has not been revealed to you by God, you cannot wrong the blessed or the condemned, nor offend God. If they are blessed, they do not need your good; and if they are condemned, they cannot obtain it.

Therefore, as long as you are not certain that they are neither condemned nor blessed, do not delay praying for them. For, as we said above, those who are blessed do not need your good works; and the wicked do not obtain them because they are condemned.

Know, nevertheless, and believe without doubt, that even if you plead for blessed or condemned dead persons, the good works performed for the good are not lost. For we have often preached and often taught with complete faith that no evil will remain unpunished and no good unrewarded before him with whom there is no partiality.

Your prayer will return into your own bosom. Therefore one must always pray for the dead; and if it does not benefit them because they are blessed or condemned, the prayer will return into our own bosom.

Thus we shall be good, thus pious and merciful; thus we shall not be able to perish by an evil death, because the Lord will guard us throughout our whole life. Afterwards, when we depart from it, he will give us that which “neither eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of a living human being.”

Let us hasten, then, brothers, to pray for the dead, so that they too may hasten to call us to themselves. For they see the holy Trinity to be as truly one as the three are together; two are not more than one thing; they are infinite in themselves, each in each, all in each, each in all, and all in all, and the one is all things.

If you cannot understand how the holy Trinity is three and one, take an example. There is one sun running, warming, and shining in the sky. There is one fire on earth, likewise possessing three things: motion, light, and heat; nor can you divide the light from the motion and the heat.

So it is with the holy Trinity of God. And if we cannot grasp its mystery, let us hasten to do good, so that, as it is, we may deserve by grace to see the holy Trinity.

For it is inhuman to abandon one’s homeland, to despise one’s homeland, or to be unwilling to dwell in it. Let us therefore not be sluggish in doing good, so that we may be able to dwell in our homeland and return to it.

[Note: [Col. 1321] Augustine, *On Free Will*, book 3, no. 77.]

For so great is the beauty of justice, so great the delight of eternal light—that is, of unchangeable truth and wisdom—that even if it were not permitted to remain in it for longer than one hour or half an hour of a single day, for this reason alone the innumerable years of this life, filled with delights and overflowing with temporal goods, would rightly and deservedly all be despised. [Note: [Col. 1321] The words “all these things” appear to be redundant or to have been transposed. M.]

O glorious kingdom of God! O desirable homeland of ours! You are worth as much as I possess. For the widow bought as much of you with two small coins as Peter did by leaving everything, as Zacchaeus did by giving half his patrimony, and as Mary, the sister of Lazarus, did when she sold everything and placed it at the apostles’ feet.

Why, then, are we sluggish in doing good? Why do we neglect to pray for the dead? [Col. 1322]

Let us contemplate, then, brothers, our homeland, gathered not only from human beings but also from angels and archangels, thrones and dominions, principalities and powers. There a human being will also see the holy and undivided Trinity as it is; he will see it more clearly—in proportion to how much more he has deserved through working on the way.

Yet, no matter how heavily laden we are with good works, we cannot purchase it on that account, unless we possess it through grace. Nevertheless, there we shall all be content, all happy, all rejoicing.

For this is that better portion which Mary chose by resting and sitting at the Lord’s feet. She contemplated God and man; therefore she chose the better portion (Luke X, 42). Why does he call it the better portion, except because eternal life is signified through contemplation?

It is the best life because it is secure, because it is eternal, because it is true. Our happiness is to have God, to see God, and to contemplate God. Therefore it is the better portion, and we cannot possess this portion on the way.

Why? Because as long as we live, we are pilgrims away from the Lord; we are always in danger and always in labor in this life, growing weary with Martha. Here we are with Martha, laboring, receiving guests, and ministering to the servants of God whatever is necessary.

Martha chose this portion, and it was good, but not the best, because it was not eternal. Nevertheless it was good, because by persevering in works of charity she deserved, together with her sister, to sit at the Lord’s feet in eternal life.

Let us hasten, then, to practice works of piety and to pray for the dead, so that we may be able to see and reverently greet the most holy prophets and true patriarchs. These are the ones whose names remain forever, because they are worthy of God, distinguished in faith, outstanding in hospitality, shrewd in understanding, wise in action, rich in secular possessions, restorers and renewers of the world, trusting in the promises, and receivers of angels. They see God face to face; they are prudent and victorious, and the power of their rule did not cease until Christ, born in the world from their offspring through the womb of the blessed Virgin, who is the hope of all nations, appeared in the world in splendor.

These are the holy men with whom God spoke and to whom he showed his secrets, so that, illuminated by the Holy Spirit, they might recognize as present the things that were to come.

Let us hasten, then, brothers, to leave this age, so that we may also be able to greet and see the holy apostles, whose blessed eyes deserved to see God living in the flesh [Note: [Col. 1322] Manuscript: “coming.”], whose fruit remains forever in the homeland.

Let us also hasten, my brothers, to enter the holy of holies, so that we may be able to see the holy martyrs of God, who subdued the flesh, strengthened the spirit, commanded demons, shone with virtues, despised present things, and proclaimed by voice and conduct that homeland of which we are now speaking.

Let us also hasten, brothers, to enter the holy of holies, so that we may be able to see the holy confessors of God. Although they did not experience the sword of persecutors, they are not deprived of the reward of martyrdom, being worthy of God through the merit of their life; for martyrdom is accomplished not only by the shedding of blood but also by abstaining from sins and practicing the divine commandments.

Let us therefore hasten to enter the holy of holies, so that we may deserve to see and reverently greet the holy Mother of God, together with her holy virgins, whom multitudes of both sexes follow in her footsteps by their example [Note: [Col. 1322] The sense is defective; something is missing or redundant. M.]. They abandoned marital unions and renounced the propagation of children, and deserved to devote themselves in mind, action, dress, and bearing to the eternal Bridegroom who is in heaven.

These were sacred virgins, devoted to God, who in their life persevered in prayers, adhered to fasts, gave alms, refreshed the poor, rejoiced in tribulation, were powerful in battle, and gave thanks to God amid the losses of temporal [Col. 1323] possessions.

Let us hasten, then, my brothers, to imitate these saints. Let us learn from them to practice works of charity courageously and without interruption; and by practicing them we shall, through grace, deserve to see God face to face, as he is. May he grant this to us who is the strength and salvation of all the saints. Amen.

## SERMON XLV [Note: [Col. 1323] The style of this sermon is very concise and unlike that of the preceding sermons.] ON THE NEED TO DO PENANCE AND AVOID DETRACTION

Blessed is the person toward whom God will show mercy. Let us confess, brothers, and he will show mercy to us. Our sins are great; nevertheless, since the Lord is great, let us do penance [Note: [Col. 1323] Perhaps one should read: “but because the Lord is great, let us do penance.”]. For “his mercy endures forever” (Ps. CV, 1).

See, brothers, what he says: “forever.” In hell, who will confess to you? No one can do penance in hell; such penance is fruitless. Here he shows mercy to the penitent; here he extends his hand to the fallen. In heaven sits the Judge, who urges us to conversion.

Blessed are those who practice justice. The just person falls seven times a day through his thoughts or his words, and rises again. On whatever day the sinner is converted and does penance, God will have mercy on him.

Nor should the just person be secure, nor should the sinner despair. In both there should be fear and hope.

Fortunate is the person to whom Christ has made this life known; he is both father and mother. The one who acts in this way frees himself and leads others to eternal life by his example.

For there is a law that shares in the Gospel. If a baptized person sins and performs true penance, his sins are quickly forgiven. The ungodly person is one who denies Christ; neither in this age nor in the future will he be forgiven.

We have spoken of ungodliness; let us speak of piety. The first step is humility and perseverance in good works. The second step is to fast and give alms. The third step is to pursue charity and possess patience. The fourth step is to abandon everything for the love of Christ. The fifth step is to renounce vices.

It is a greater virtue to renounce vices than possessions. It does no good to abandon earthly goods if we do not abandon vices. Many abandon riches but do not abandon vices.

It is good to fast and give alms. Fasting without almsgiving is of little value; fasts, however, together with other virtues, will be beneficial.

What does fasting profit me if I am lustful, if I am angry, if I am a detractor? The wounds of the tongue are greater than those of the sword. The sword kills the body, but it does not kill the soul.

See, brothers, how many evils the tongue contains. In good things it is great; in evil it is death.

From where did the devil fall? Did he commit theft? Did he commit murder? Did he commit adultery? The devil did not fall because of these things, but because of the tongue, because he said: “I will ascend into heaven; above the stars I will set my throne, and I will be like the Most High” (Isa. XIV, 13).

What does Solomon say? “In the hands of the tongue are death and life” (Prov. XVIII, 21).

Detraction is a great vice. The prophet says: “Woe to me, miserable man, because I have unclean lips” (Isa. VI, 5). Therefore the one who has unclean lips cannot prophesy.

Woe to me, miserable man, if I have abandoned mother, brothers, sisters, perishable possessions, and the world, yet here I am anxious over perishable things.

We promise peace with our lips, but do not keep it in our heart. The weapon of Christians is the peace of Christ. I kill myself if I slander others.

“Solomon” is interpreted as “Peaceful,” distinguished by the work of holy conduct. Your wife is called wisdom, your sister and bride. The devil has many snares: murder is the devil’s snare; greed is the devil’s snare; detraction is the devil’s snare.

As long as we are in holiness, our souls are engaged in the work of God. As long as we direct our will toward sinning in sins, our souls are disturbed. For where there is greater punishment, there is greater victory.

But what ears of flesh do not understand, the ears of Christ in heaven understand.

The just person and the sinner have flesh in equal measure and suffer an equal shipwreck; their ends are alike, but their rewards are different. The just are led to eternal rewards; sinners to everlasting Gehenna.

One must not consent to the detractor. For there is so great a difference between the fornicator and the detractor that the one who fornicates kills only himself, whereas the one who detracts destroys both himself and the one who listens.

“Cursed is the person who does the work of God negligently” (Jer. XLVIII, 10), as the prophet says.

There are children of Gehenna, children of perdition, children of the devil, and children of God, because each person is called the child of the one whose works he performs.

And in another place he says: “Come, children, hear me; I will teach you the fear of the Lord. Turn away from evil and do good; seek peace and pursue it. The eyes of the Lord are upon the just, and his ears are toward their prayers” (Ps. XXXIII, 12, 15, 16).

Through the favor of our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON XLVI. ON ANGELS AND HOSPITALITY
Because we are always defended by the angelic natures lest we be overwhelmed, dearly beloved brothers, let us not be reluctant to speak about them for their honor. But what shall we say about the angelic spirits, when we are impure to speak about them? Nevertheless, we firmly believe and hold with unwavering faith that, blessed through the divine presence and vision, they rejoice forever in the Lord’s good things, “which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart.” What, then, shall I, a wretched sinner, dust and ashes, say to you? For I am unable to conceive their glory, nor are you sufficient to hear of it. Yet surely, if “the mouth speaks from the abundance of the heart,” let us say what we can to the praise of God, who deigns to inflame us with love for himself.

In the heavenly spirits there is not merely an admirable dignity and a lovable condescension, but such glory that no human tongue or heart can in any way express or conceive it. For they always stand in attendance upon God; they are God’s household, citizens of heaven, princes of paradise, teachers of knowledge, instructors in wisdom, illuminators of souls, their guardians, zealous protectors of bodies, and defenders of the good.

This is well attested by that teacher of teachers and preacher of truth, when he was caught up to the third heaven, was deemed worthy to take part in that blessed court, and saw God as he is, and was granted knowledge of secrets beyond all other human beings. Then he said, then he declared and exclaimed, that they were all “ministering spirits sent forth for service on our behalf” (Hebrews 1:14).

They are the guardians of the provinces, carefully preserving all our dignities, both spiritual and temporal. They obtain victory for us against the fuel of sin; they secure victory for us against the devil; they are the means by which we are led to tears of contrition, penitence, and prayer. They are the means by which our deeds and thoughts are joyfully carried to heaven. They are our brothers, who love us greatly, instruct us everywhere, protect us in all things, await our arrival in heaven, and desire that the seats of paradise be filled through us.

These are the most holy spirits who are present as guardians while we sleep and present in triumph while we pray. Who, then, brothers, would lack the memory of the angels in his mind? Who would not love them? Who would not venerate those who always stand in God’s presence? They are the means by which we are sustained; through them we are helped on sea and land; through them we are enlightened in mind and body; through them we are comforted in tribulations and distress; through them we are frequently delivered from sicknesses; through them, and by them, at the end we are contemplated [Note: [Col. 1324] Perhaps, “we are strengthened.”]; we are made firm in faith and defended from the evil spirit; and, once victory has been obtained, through these same angels we are carried to paradise or to purgatory. While we are being purified, we do not doubt that they often visit and console us, promising that we shall enter the heavenly city of Jerusalem.

Come, then, brothers, let us strive to imitate the holy angels, and not only them, but also the friends of the angels. Let us look around with an undivided mind and read through the Scriptures as best we can, so that we may find the friends of the angels. Once we have found them, let us ask what they did, how they pleased the angels, and in what matters they imitated them confidently.

Let the holy father Abraham come, and let what he did be made known. Let his nephew Lot also come and say why and how he deserved to be rescued from Sodom by the angels. Let Tobias come, leading his son with him, and let him teach why he deserved to be enlightened through an angel and his son to be protected [Note: [Col. 1325] Perhaps, “his son.”]. Let the three youths come and write how, when active and passive agents are brought near one another, action does not necessarily follow. Let Peter also come, and let us hear how he deserved to be freed through an angel, so that, hearing the great and wonderful deeds performed by the holy angels, we may be able to follow and imitate them.

Tell us, holy father Abraham, what did you do, or what did you teach people to do, so that you pleased the holy angels so delightfully? Tell us, so that we may learn from you; teach us, so that we may be capable of being taught by you. For you are a father, and because we are all your children, it is fitting that you should teach us.

O brothers, what else could he say, what else could he teach, except that he always wished to preserve hospitality? O holy and true hospitality, which deserved at times to receive not only angels but God himself! Behold why Abraham pleased God’s angels; behold why Lot deserved to be rescued; behold why Tobias was enlightened and his son preserved unharmed; behold why the three youths and Peter were preserved unharmed in prison.

Learn, then, Christians; learn to show hospitality to everyone, lest perhaps the one whose door you have closed and to whom you have denied hospitality should be God himself. Lot went out to meet the angels as though they were travelers, and by his praiseworthy custom he had already been freed from the Sodomite vice. Among the worst he was preserved as the best; he was snatched from the city’s danger, escaped the bodily fire, and was preserved for an eternal reward.

Did Abraham not see God when he saw three and adored one? Therefore, brothers, hurry to receive travelers. You do not know whether Christ may deign to visit you, although Christ is always present in the guest. Let your door be open to travelers; receive them gladly; wash their feet; wash their heads; cleanse their impurities; and do not withdraw your hand from any poor person. And if you are unable to help everyone, at least let your goodwill be directed toward them.

Receive travelers, then, brothers, because the reward we receive for traveling will be the reward we shall receive for welcoming travelers. For the one who refreshes another for God’s sake and the one who labors for God’s sake become equals.

O holy hospitality, friend of the angels, sister of charity, crown of humility! Whoever possesses you possesses true humility; and whoever possesses you, O humility, possesses true hospitality, for without you hospitality is nothing.

Let us learn, then, brothers, not only from the fathers to preserve hospitality, but from Christ to embrace humility. [Note: [Col. 1325] From Augustine, Sermon 69, no. 2.] Let us learn from him not to fashion the world, not to create all visible and invisible things, not to perform miracles in the world itself, not to raise the dead, not to walk upon the waters with dry feet—not any of these things—but only that he is gentle and humble of heart. This is the perfect foundation of hospitality.

O holy humility, sister of hospitality and its sweet friend! Whoever possesses you [Note: [Col. 1325] Perhaps something should be added: “possesses you.” M.] considers himself in all things more unworthy than others; he never desires to appear superior, flees all primacies and seats of honor, abhors every form of domination, embraces hospitality alone, and desires to possess that alone.

Come, then, brothers: our homeland is lofty, but the way is humble. Let us measure it, seek it out, and walk upon it. Thus Abraham and Lot acted when they received travelers; thus Tobias acted when he buried the dead; and thus also did the angels of whom the Savior says that they always behold the face of the Father who is in heaven (Matthew 18:10). Amen.

SERMON XLVII. ON THE VEHEMENT DETESTATION OF THE SODOMITE SIN

[Col. 1326]

Hear, not dearly beloved brothers, but princes of Sodom; receive with your ears the law of your God, people of Gomorrah. Hear, and make it heard to your sons, O nation full of sin, burdened with iniquity, wicked offspring, criminal children.

Behold, you have abandoned God, blasphemed the Holy One of Israel, and have already turned away backward. From the sole of the foot to the crown of the head there is no soundness in you. Therefore your land is desolate, your cities are burned with fire, foreigners devour your country in your presence, and the city will be laid waste as in an enemy’s devastation.

Why do you suffer these things, unless because you have already become like the Sodomites? Hear, then, princes of Sodom; hear Isaiah speaking to you: “I am full of your sacrifices, because you offer them to me unworthily. Do not offer sacrifice any longer, for my soul has hated your Sabbaths, your incense, and your solemn festivals, and all these things have become burdensome to me. When you stretch out your hands, I will turn my eyes away from you; and when you multiply your prayers, I will not hear, because you practice shamefulness” (Isaiah 1:4–15).

What is that shamefulness except the impurity which the Apostle calls it (Romans 1:24)? It is indeed that shamefulness, that supreme impurity, that supreme misery from which the angels flee and at which the demons close their eyes. It is the impurity and misery that males practice with males.

Of them the Apostle says: “Not only those who do these things, but also those who consent to those who do them, are worthy of death” (ibid., 32). This is rightly called impurity, because it is excessive filthiness of mind and body. And this filthiness is not only sin but also the punishment of sin. For when God sees people wholly despising him and trampling upon his commandments, he turns them over to a debased mind, so that they practice that abomination and neither understand nor take notice. As the Apostle says: “Because they did not approve of having God in their knowledge, the Lord handed them over to disgrace; for the males, abandoning the natural use of the female, burned with desire for one another” (ibid., 28, 26–27)—that is, males practicing shamefulness with males.

O how abominable a vice! O how detestable a crime! O how deadly a loss! O how wicked a sin! O how unheard-of an evil! Behold, a member of Christ not only commits fornication but even becomes a prostitute. This is that impurity which God supremely hates, which the saints detest, which the blessed hate, which those who attain the eternal kingdom of God flee, and which those who are to be tormented and cursed with the devil and his angels love.

O most wicked Sodomites and sinful men! O most wicked ones, as Scripture bears witness: “The Sodomites were exceedingly wicked and sinful before the Lord” (Genesis 13:13). A sinner is said to be “before the Lord” when God does not leave his sin unpunished and, though he postpones punishment, does not defer it indefinitely. Hence he says: “The cry of Sodom and Gomorrah has multiplied, and their sin has become exceedingly grave” (ibid., 18:20).

A sin is called a cry when it is not only conceived in thought but brought into action without any fear and multiplied through habitual practice. Then the Lord stretches out the sword of his fury, rains fire and sulfur from heaven, and the cities are burned and overwhelmed.

The cities were rightly overwhelmed and destroyed by sulfur, because both their women and their men were burning with foul lust. O most wicked lust, destruction of virtues, increase of vices, conflagration of pleasure, diminution of charity, emptying of purses! You are sweet, but behold, all your sweetness is soon turned into great bitterness.

O lust, through you peace was destroyed; through you murder was committed; through you cities were burned; through you kingdoms were lost; through you almost every evil was done. Through you David was estranged from God; through you Samson died; through you Solomon was expelled; through you Lot suffered, abandoning his homeland and losing his wife.

Therefore, transgressors of the law, pay attention; read the law. O followers of the people of Gomorrah, cease now to act perversely; learn now to do good; learn now to fear God. Flee the Sodomites as death. Do not associate with them, lest you perish with them.

For the time will come—and it will not delay—and that holy Joseph will rise up, who was not afraid to accuse his brothers of this most wicked crime before his father. Let this example of chastity now arise and slay all who practice such iniquity. Let that great saint Paul, the vessel of election, come and put to shame all who love such things, so that none may be found anywhere in the world. Let that beloved of God, the image of virginity, Saint John, come and put such people to shame by his virginal presence. Let that lamp of the world and beloved forerunner also come and, with his great boldness, slay all such people by the breath of his mouth. Let Lot, the nephew of Saint Abraham, come with his nephews and drive all such people from the land of the living. Let all the holy angels come and burn all who practice the iniquity of Gomorrah.

Come, then, cease now to act perversely; learn with Lot and Joseph to do good, before what we have said is fulfilled.

Remember frequently, and do not forget, what that Roman woman Tarpeia did. What did she do? Great lust reigned in her, yet she, though a pagan, wished to live chastely. What did she do? She wished and ordered that her eyes be torn out; and, having set aside all delicacies, she wished to take only bread with water, in measured quantity.

O brothers, what an astonishing condition of the woman, what astonishing goodness, what astonishing strength! For by doing this she did not expect paradise, nor did she desire to be praised for it, nor did she seek to be proclaimed blessed—for we do not know why she did it, since we declare that she was a pagan. Yet I know one thing: if she had asked Augustine for advice, I, as a faithful man, could have said nothing other than that she should take only bread and water according to a determined weight and measure.

We, then, brothers, must know and in no way doubt that chastity cannot coexist with abundance and prosperity. But if you do not believe me, believe the people of Gomorrah. They abounded greatly in all good things, and after they had eaten and drunk, they rose up to play.

So I see you also acting: for you have an abundance of bread, wine, and every good thing that you need. Therefore I fear that you may perish. Why? Because there is no evil that does not reign among you. Are you not proud? Are you not greedy? Are you not gluttonous? Are you not corrupters of boys?

O wretched men, members of the devil, why are you not ashamed? Why do you not cease to do such things? I, a bishop, am ashamed to speak of such things; I am ashamed also to recount others. But if I remain silent, it is death for me; and if I preach this, I will not escape your tongues.

Therefore I will preach boldly, because you are not ashamed to practice these things publicly. Reform your lives, then, and I will reform my words; cease to act perversely, and I will cease to reproach you for your evils. The Lord acts in the same way, for when life is changed, he changes his judgment: to those who do good he promises glory; to those who do evil, eternal punishment.

Let us therefore instruct ourselves, brothers, in knowledge and chastity, so that by studying and understanding we may be agreeable, approachable, and gentle in sincere charity. For if you wish to indulge in lust, you will never be able to have charity. Charity is a virtue called the consummation and perfection of the other virtues, and lust is likewise their destruction. No virtue, no goodness, no wisdom can coexist with lust; neither justice nor praise can do so. Rather, every perversity and partiality reigns in it.

Therefore consider how necessary chastity itself is. For if we live chastely, there will be no quarrels within, no evil words. And if you do not believe me, read what happened to Lot. The holy angels entered his house; after this, the Sodomites surrounded his house and perhaps entered not only through the door [Note: [Col. 1327] Rather, as Augustine observes in *Against Lying*, no. 34, with Scripture as witness, Genesis 19:11: “they could not even find the door of the house.”], but through the windows.

Did they also beat Lot and his nephews [Col. 1328]? Certainly, in my judgment, they received not only words but blows. And perhaps Lot’s wife was turned into a pillar of salt because she did not arrange to resist the Sodomites.

Women too were involved in a similar crime and the same sin, and perhaps to a greater degree, because in those cities women were the beginning of so great a crime, and afterward those most wicked women taught the men.

O women, mothers of lust, was it not enough that you had deceived the first man?

Let us therefore turn to the Lord; let us be penitents, united in the love of God, and let us labor together as united members. For just as hatred disperses the Church, so the bond of love builds it up. Hatred generates detraction and envy, which are the plague and destruction of the Church. Through hatred that holy usefulness and joyfulness are lost of which it is said: “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is when brothers dwell together in unity” (Psalm 132:1).

Through hatred Christ is expelled, and he is true wisdom, because “wisdom will not enter into a malevolent soul” (Wisdom 1:4). Therefore I beg you to amend your lives, teaching your sons and daughters how to live chastely and walk modestly; let them abstain from food and drink; let their speech be modest, their walk honorable, their faces lowered, their tongues approachable, their minds full of love, and their hands full of good works.

If you do this, brothers, you will be rescued from hell with holy Lot as you flee, and by grace you will fly toward glory. Amen.

SERMON XLVIII [Note: [Col. 1328] Lupus of the *Origin of the Hermit Saint Augustine*, p. 378, after examining this sermon, says: “Far be it that these most fabulous and mendacious sermons should be those of Saint Augustine. Thus our teacher Basil of León went astray when, from this utterly mendacious Sermon 48, he thought that the final sentence of Saint Prosper had been taken.” This teacher’s error was not perceived clearly enough by Charles Morel, who here also followed him badly.] ON THE CARE OF THE SOUL

The human soul, dearly beloved brothers, participates in, encompasses, and contains the nature of all creatures—and all the more so because it is more gloriously marked with the image of God. For everything spiritual belongs to it: it has heaven as a dwelling place, angels as companions in rejoicing, glory as something to possess, and the Trinity as something to enjoy.

Indeed, in the human being bodily creation had also been placed, and the nature of all bodily and natural things was in him, directed toward him, and operating through him; and this was all the more perfect because he was more marvelous than every bodily thing. For he possessed everything, and everything obeyed him, because everything was subject to him: the stars, so that they might give light; the elements, so that they might nourish; animals, so that they might submit; and foods, so that they might sustain. Sheep and oxen, lions and birds—everything obeyed the human being without any rebellion.

And what more? Even that which is greater. What is greater except what is divine? For what is divine in the human being except that the human being himself is adorned with the image of the holy Trinity? “Let us make,” says the holy Trinity, “the human being in our image and likeness” (Genesis 1:26).

What is the image of God in us except that which is found to be better in us? And what is found to be better in us except reason, understanding, memory, and will?

O human being, you have heard your glory; now hear your misery. O human being, born of woman, living for a short time, filled with many miseries, who come forth and are crushed like a flower of the field, and flee like a shadow, never remaining in the same condition—now rich, now poor; now healthy, now sick; now joyful, now sad; now knowledgeable, now ignorant; now seeing, now blind; now a citizen, now an exile; now good, now evil—behold how stable you are, behold how enduring!

O human being, do you not know that you could have avoided dying? For both possibilities were in your power: to be able and not to be able to die. You despised the first and chose the second; you despised life and chose death; you despised sweetness and chose bitterness; you despised eternal life and wished to choose eternal death.

And how did this happen, human being? Were you not created good, upright, holy, and beloved by God [Col. 1329]? Yet, most wretchedly grown fat, made rich, and enlarged, you rebelled against God your creator.
