And behold, lifted up in pride, ignorant of God’s grace [Note: [Col. 1329] Perhaps, “ignorant concerning grace.”], unaware of justice, you fell into the pit of misery, into the mire of filth, and into the shadow of death.

Therefore consider what follows. Do you think that God lies, or that the son of man can be changed? He himself established it and pronounced the sentence: whenever you ate from the tree, you would have to die. Did he decree this in jest, or assert it while laughing? This does not appear so to me at all. Why does it not appear so? Because experience has taught me, and I have tested it with eyewitness faith.

Do I not experience that, after sin, the elements—which had been in the highest and best condition—immediately began to fight because of sin? There is the principle of earth in the flesh, the principle of moisture in the blood, the principle of air in the spirit, and the principle of fire in heat. These four immediately began to battle one another after sin; and thus our first parents were weighed down by illnesses and afflicted by pain of the head, stomach, liver, and all their members. Thus they die; thus they are led to the graves.

But someone may say: What is a human being after death? It is certain that he is not a human being; and yet he is something, insofar as two parts remain. What are those parts except soul and body, matter and form? The soul does not die or succumb through death, since it is entirely immortal. Nor does the matter of the body perish, since it is one in number; for although the body is dissolved, it does not reach such a degree of dissolution that it becomes entirely nothing or passes into non-being.

The same soul always remains, as something divine; yet the human being is diminished insofar as being is concerned. For all souls are spirits, and all bodies are earth, and they will remain so until the soul clothes itself again in its body, so that the whole human being may be glorified, body namely and soul.

If, then, you ask what a dead human being is, what else can we say except that he is earth, decay, a corpse, and stench? If you ask about his being, you see that it has ceased. If you ask about the body, ask the earth.

Go, you young and powerful men, to the graves of your fathers; consider what they were and what they are. Let us open their monuments and see who among them was master and who servant, who handsome and who ugly, who upright and who bent. Let us open the eyes of mind and body, and let us not be reluctant frequently to consider our great misery. Let us enter the graves and learn what we find.

What, brothers, do we find, and what things? For if we look, we find the heads, loins, and bellies of the dead. Truly and undoubtedly truly—believe me, who have experienced it—you will find in the heads toads leaping about, generated from the brain; in the loins, serpents generated in the lower back and moving about; in the belly, worms gushing forth, generated from the entrails.

Behold what we are and what we shall soon be; behold into what we are dissolved. Why, then, do you puff yourself up, rich man? Why do you not pay attention to what you hear? Why are you troubled when you look upon it? Why do you not turn back when you experience this every day?

Remember all these things, brothers, and do penance with weeping and lamentation before those bitter days arrive, full of misery and sadness.

You have now heard what a dead human being is. It remains to say what becomes of the soul. O my brothers, what can we say about this except that we agree with our old women? What do they say except that the soul is either in paradise with those who rejoice or in hell with those who suffer; but if it is in purgatory, it is on the way to its homeland. These souls are already well situated, because they are secure.

Nevertheless, we must pray for them and assist them with our whole devotion through prayers, almsgiving, sacrifices, fasts, and mortifications. These, finally, are those afflicted ones who cry out daily to the Lord and have recourse to him, whose knowledge is invoked everywhere, whose wisdom is demonstrated, whose mercy is weighed everywhere, and whose power is proclaimed everywhere.

They cry out daily, each one pleading for his own mercy and lamenting his own misery, saying:

“Lord, know that I am suffering violence; therefore I have recourse to you [Col. 1330], not despising your knowledge, not turning away from your wisdom, but appealing to your mercy. For I do not suffer unjustly, Lord, because I suffer not for another’s wrongdoing but for my own. I suffer violence, Lord, because I suffer severely, and I suffer justly.

“I sinned, Lord, by gathering possessions and riches and by not distributing enough to the poor, as you commanded. But in my unhappiness I gathered many things with pain and sorrow, not knowing to whom I would leave them, whether friend or relative.

“O unhappy human being, consider and carefully observe what you are doing and thinking, while you do not cease gathering throughout all the days of your life.

“O human being full of greed, do you not know that there are three things that are insatiable, and that the fourth never says, ‘Enough’? And what is that which never says, ‘Enough,’ except the human mind, which never says, ‘It is sufficient’?

“O human being, do you not know that greed is the root of all evils and the service of idolatry, the mother of usury, the begetter of simony, the fuel of guilt, the way to eternal punishment, and the nurse of hell?

“O greed, insatiable abyss, you never say, ‘Enough.’ You are always hungry, always in pain, always grieving over everything. If the sun rises every day, you say sorrowfully, ‘There will be drought.’ If rain descends, you declare that everything is in danger. If you see mild weather approaching, you will desire either sun or rain to be present.

“O interminable plague, O ravenous madness! Everything else is enclosed within its limits; greed alone is bounded by no limit. In a human being all vices grow old; greed alone grows young.

“O madness without any limit! Is the earth not bounded by its boundaries, water limited by its confines, air enclosed within its own limit, and heaven constrained by its boundaries, while greed alone knows no limit?

“O greedy man, if the whole earth is given to you, you seek the sea. But if you possess earth and sea, you seek the air. But if you possess earth, sea, and air, you still aspire to heaven and desire to penetrate it. And if you have penetrated heaven, you still will not rest until you have made yourself equal to God or become higher than the Most High.

“O plague more savage than the devil! For the devil wished to be like the Most High; but the greedy man would wish to ascend above God, if he could.

“Rightly, on the last day the Lord will speak to the greedy, saying: ‘O human being, you entered the world without honor, covered in a bloody membrane; you were born without riches, generated without greed. Yet you lived in greed, expanded yourself in gold and silver, and forgot God your creator. Where, then, is the fruit and profit of your labors? Go, therefore, accursed ones, into eternal fire, and as you wished, so let it be done.’

“Behold the sentence of the supreme King.”

Therefore, brothers, do not love the body more than the soul, nor your children more than yourselves. Behold, the day of death is at the door. Then each person is shut out by his own household, abandoned by his wife, separated from his relatives, and carried by those same people to the grave.

O great cruelty! O great wonder! O astonishing faithlessness! Behold, the beloved husband is abandoned by his beloved wife; the son is cast away by his mother; the father by his children; and the children by their father are buried beneath the earth. The dead man alone is abandoned, while each person returns to his own affairs; and soon he is handed over to oblivion, as though dead from the heart.

Behold, brothers, what the friendship of the world is like and how much it is worth. For there is no one who loves a friend or relative so greatly that he wishes to remain with him for a single night. See, then, O human being, what sort of friends you have, for whose sake you lose your soul and offend God. Everyone will abandon you; everyone will hide himself; everyone will quickly flee from you; and they will place you in a pit three cubits deep.

For when we were at Ostia on the Tiber, joined by a mother of charity, awaiting calm weather because of our return to Africa, and compelled by Ponticianus the prefect [Note: [Col. 1330] “When Augustine went from Rome to Milan to take up the teaching of rhetoric, Symmachus was prefect of the city, as is said in *Confessions* 5.13; and he held that office for many years thereafter. Indeed, he still held it when Saint Boniface was appointed to the apostolic see and vigorously supported the Eulalian schism against him.” Lupus.], a most distinguished man who had come from Rome to visit us, we returned with him once more to Rome to inspect more carefully the magnificent buildings and works of the pagans.

I was led with the others to see Caesar’s corpse in the tomb, and I saw that it was entirely marked by a livid color and surrounded by decay. His belly had burst open, and I observed swarms of worms passing through it. Two hungry creatures were feeding in the hollows of his eyes; his hair no longer clung to his head; his teeth appeared after his lips had been consumed; and the foundation of his nostrils had been exposed.

Looking at my most Christian mother, I said:

“Where now is Caesar’s splendid body? Where is the greatness of his riches? Where is the display of his pleasures? Where is the multitude of his lords? Where is the crowd of his barons? Where is the line of his soldiers? Where are his hunting dogs? Where are his swift horses? Where are the singing birds? Where is the painted bedchamber? Where is the ivory couch? Where is the royal bed? Where is the imperial throne? Where are the changing garments? Where are the sun-bright locks of hair? Where is the beautiful face? Where is everything beneath heaven?

“For people respected you; princes feared you; cities worshiped you; everyone feared you. Where, I ask, are all these things? From whom has so much arrogance departed? Where has your magnificence gone?”

And the mother, full of piety, replied:

“Son, everything failed him together when his spirit failed, and they left him imprisoned in a grave three cubits deep, full of stench and decay.”

Come, then, faithful followers of Christ; consider what we are, take notice of what we have come to, and look carefully at what we already are.

Do penance, then, my little children, whom I am again bringing to birth until Christ is formed in you. Do penance before death, the enemy of nature, attacks you. Establish for yourselves a confession that is simple, humble, useful, private, frequent, ready, bitter, tearful, and urgent, since we are entirely ignorant of the hour of death.

For when you are in the final illness, brothers, how difficult, how harsh, how painful, how tearful it will be for you to repent and grieve over the evils you have committed and the good deeds you have omitted! Why will this happen except because the whole attention of the mind is seized where the force of pain is present?

Many impediments confront the heart. The body is in pain; suffering afflicts it, because death is approaching to enter. Fathers gaze with darkened eyes upon the children they loved most, for whose sake they even consider themselves condemned. They look upon their wives, already weeping. The world still gives them confidence; the devil gives them assurance that they should not grieve over their sins and provides a promissory note to those who are failing. The flesh still hopes sufficiently that it will not fail; the physicians still encourage the sick man so that they may profit; relatives applaud; priests entice. And thus the rich die in hell.

O human being, you have heard what I have said; I firmly believe that you will soon experience all these things. Therefore I beg you: before you are weighed down by illness, do penance and set your house in order. Do what must be done; make your will while you are healthy, while you are wise, while you are still your own master. For if you wait for illness, you will certainly be led by threats or flatteries where you do not wish to go.

O human being, while you are young, set your house in order; do penance; love God not only in word but in deed and truth. And if you have offended your neighbor by word, appease him by word; if by deed, appease him by deed, because we will be spared according to the same measure by which we have spared others.

O human being, do penance. “Remember your last things, and you will never sin” (Ecclesiasticus 7:40). Return to yourself, remembering that you were liquid seed, that now you are a vessel of dung, and that you will be food for worms [Note: [Col. 1331] See the *Meditations* attributed to Bernard, chapter 3.]. These are the last things that the faithful person ought to think about every day.

O human being, remember your last things, because after death a worm will be born for you from your tongue on account of the sin of the tongue; from your stomach, on account of the sin of gluttony; from the semen of your loins, scorpions on account of the sin of lust; from your brain, toads on account of the sin of pride.

Remember your last things, O young man, who move about in splendor with your head held high, despising all that belongs to God [Col. 1332]. Remember your last things, because you are earth and to earth you will go. Remember your last things, because you were conceived in guilt, born in punishment, living in misery, and necessarily you will die in anguish.

O human being, why do you boast of your strength? Behold, in a little while you will fall ill and fail. Why do you puff yourself up with the wisdom of the world? Behold, it is foolishness, and you will lose it; “I will reject your prudence,” says the Lord. Why do you puff yourself up with knowledge? Has not the heart of the philosophers been darkened, and have they not become futile in their thoughts? Have they not been handed over to a debased mind?

Why do you boast of the nobility of your lineage? Is not the condition of everyone’s birth the same? Is not the conclusion of everyone’s death the same? Which noble person was ever born without the shedding of blood? Does not the noble person pass through the same passage as the poor person when he is born? Is the rich person spared from the rule of death?

Why do you boast of riches? They are snares for you rather than friendships. For the poor person is almost never sought for killing, whereas the rich person is always plotted against.

Remember, O human being, your last things. You feast every day, yet consider how naked you came from your mother’s womb and how naked you will return.

Come, then, brothers: open your homes to the poor; give alms; subject your pleasures to reason; and in all things remember your last things, so that you may not sin mortally for eternity.

May God help us—without whose will not even a leaf of a tree is moved—to accomplish what pleases him, who is blessed forever and ever. Amen.

SERMON XLIX. ON THE MISERY OF THE FLESH AND THE FALSEHOOD OF THE PRESENT LIFE [Note: [Col. 1332] In the Germanensis manuscript, approximately four hundred years old: “On the miserable life of this age.” In the others, much has been interpolated and altered, as we have already noted. Sermons 62, 64, 65, 66, and 67 were likewise fabricated by the same method.]

[Note: [Col. 1332] From the first letter of Abbot Columbanus.]

O life, which deceives so many, has led so many of your own astray and blinded so many! While you flee, you are nothing; while you appear, you are a shadow; while you exalt, you are smoke! You are sweet to fools and bitter to the wise. Whoever loves you does not know you; those who despise you understand you. You are to be feared and fled. Woe to those who trust you; blessed are those who despise you. You are not truly life, as you present yourself.

To some you show yourself as long, so that you may destroy them at the end; to others as short, so that, while they wish to repent, you may not permit them to do so; to some as generous, so that they may do whatever they wish; to others as constrained, so that they may not do what is good. Therefore, O wise one, flee what flees. For our life is like a man in another’s house, not knowing at what hour or on what day the master will say, “Go outside, because the house in which you are is not yours.”

O vain world, why do you promise us so much while deceiving us? Whoever wishes to be your friend will be made an enemy of God. Friendship with the world is enmity with God.

[Note: [Col. 1332] See the book *On Saving Precepts*, chapter 64.]

It is the flesh that destroys the soul; it is the flesh that receives the enemy together with vices. It sows murders, sows fornication, sows desire, sows quarrels, sows lust, sows theft, sows idolatry, sows greed, sows pride and discord among brothers; it sows envy, sows blasphemy against God, provokes schisms, stirs up heresies, and introduces divisions within the Church of God; it places stumbling-blocks among Christian peoples, wars among nations, enchantments among kinsmen; and, what is worse, it casts various kinds of thoughts into the hearts of God’s servants, together with all the things that are evil in this fallen, most wicked, and unspeakable world—which, as though born, passes away with all speed.

The devil also has power over the flesh, but not over the soul, as the Lord says to the devil concerning blessed Job: “I give him into your power, but not his soul” (Job II, 6). Wretched flesh burdens the soul; wandering flesh sinks it into hell. The flesh is hostile to the soul: if it were not hostile, it would certainly not have loved the vanity of this age or enjoyed a vain life.

O most dreadful life, [Col. 1333] which is swollen by bodily humors, fevered by pains, made diseased by the air, bloated by food, weakened by fasting, relaxed by amusements, consumed by sadness, constricted by anxiety, dulled by security, made proud by riches, driven out by poverty, exalted by youth, bent down by old age, broken by illness, consumed by grief—and above all these things, most dreadful death descends in a fury.

O flesh, weighed down by deformity, you ought to have embraced that life which consists in eternity: where there is life without death, youth without old age, light without darkness, joy without sadness, nobility and will without injury, and a kingdom without change. These are the seven things you ought to have obtained.

O miserable flesh, why did you refuse them while you lived? If you had persevered in good and had not been deprived of every good, if you had acted well, you would have remained there where everlasting joy is, where glory does not wither, where delight is incorruptible and incomparable, where Christ is the joy of the Apostles, Prophets, and all the saints, and where there is also supreme gladness with the holy Angels singing praises to God—where there is the delight of every good thing.

You despised all these delightful goods through the wickedness of this age. Behold: after the end, although you are confined in the clay of the earth, you have enmity—that is, corruption, stench, and worms—and you suffer the dissolution of stench, so that the living may learn from you what you were and what you are: for you are consumed by worms. Finally, at the end, because of the last things and because of the returning soul—that is, the life that was previously in the body—you will be handed over to eternal punishments and condemned together with the soul.

[Note: [Col. 1333] See the book *On Saving Precepts*, chapter 64.]

O wretched soul, which the flesh persecutes! The flesh desires; the body acts. When the flesh is satisfied with abundant foods and drinks and pleasures, it urges the doing of every evil. The flesh provokes murders; the flesh perpetrates adulteries; the flesh commits quarrels and scandals; the flesh introduces drunkenness; the flesh carries every desire of this age.

O miserable flesh, what do you have, what do you do, why do you burden the soul so greatly, when it desires nothing except to serve God? You, O miserable flesh: is your own destruction not enough for you, that you still try to sink the unhappy soul with you? Woe to you, soul, because you have received flesh opposed to you.

Wicked flesh, what do you seek, what do you desire? For the soul cannot be judged without you on the day of judgment. Miserable and rotting flesh, filled with every filth of sins, when you were alive you were beautiful as the sun, radiant as the moon, and your eyes glittered like stars; your hair was long, and you anointed yourself with precious perfumes; you used the finest garments, and in your foods and drinks you placed a multitude of spices.

And know this, soul: while you restored and nourished the dark and stinking body, you were preparing food for worms. You ought to have remembered what you heard from your Maker and Craftsman when you first committed sin: “You are earth,” he said, “and you shall return to earth” (Gen. III, 19). And hear Job saying: “Naked I came forth from my mother’s womb, and naked I shall return there” (Job I, 21). Hear also Isaiah prophesying: “Truly, the people are grass” (Isa. XL, 7).

Miserable and unspeakable flesh, hear the excellent preacher, the Apostle Paul, saying: “We brought nothing into this world, and we can take nothing out of it” (I Tim. VI, 7). Miserable flesh carries nothing else with it except the burden of sins. The soul sins only through the flesh. Let the soul see how it can.

Our soul suffers imprisonment; the flesh keeps it shut in. The soul cries out to the Lord, not the flesh, which persists in wickedness. The soul has no other remedy unless it is taken away from the flesh and the flesh is reduced to dust; unless wine is taken from it and water given to it; unless blood is removed from it and earthly moisture given to it.

O miserable flesh, what will be done with you when I depart from you and life withdraws from you? You alone will lie in the womb and bosom of the earth, and you will never again be handed over to anything else. You will possess within yourself the worst inheritance, [Col. 1334] namely, corruption, stench, and worms. Behold what you acquired while alive; behold what you possess while lying in the tomb.

Could you not weaken yourself with fasts, and humble yourself through fasting in ashes and sackcloth? You would have been saved forever together with the soul if you had believed it, because you cannot do good unless you do good to others: that is, unless you afflict the body through abstinence, you cannot save the soul.

Hear what our Creator says to the flesh:

“O my creature,” he says, “I took you, beautiful and shining, from the clay of the earth; I placed my image in you; I gave you the breath of life; I granted you an invisible soul; I clothed you with the garment of immortality; I placed you in the paradise of delight. You enjoyed an angelic life; you contemplated foods and delights of gladness; I subjected to your rule everything that I created; and I gave you abundant riches.

“Moreover, all the trees of paradise were subject to you; and for the sake of one forbidden thing that you ate there, behold where you have fallen: from paradise into hell, from light into darkness, from a place of pleasantness and delight into chaos and every kind of darkest evil. In place of delightful fragrance, you are now handed over to rottenness and stench; in place of angelic food, you will lie beneath worms as their food; in place of the garment of immortality, you are clothed in a corrupted garment.

“Behold, I have taken away and withdrawn the life that I granted, so that you, miserable and rotting flesh, may be handed over to hell, where there is weeping and groaning and wailing, and also the gnashing of teeth and the most horrible torments; and, what is worse, after death you will be reduced to corruption, and after worms, stench, and decay, finally to dust.”

O flesh that will be handed over to unquenchable fire, hear the soul saying to the body:

“I came from heaven, granted to you by God. You are from the earth; it is better that you ascend with me to heaven than that you drag me to hell. While we live and are together, let us work with our hands at what is good—that is, almsgiving and fasting in chastity, hospitality toward the needy, clothing for the naked poor, and every good work—so that through the good work we perform we may be able to ascend to the heavenly places.

“There we will no longer be clothed in the dissolution of the body, but in the garment of incorruption; there there will no longer be stench, but the sweetest fragrance; there there will no longer be darkness, but perpetual light will shine; there there will no longer be a multitude of worms, but a host of angels, countless thousands of saints, and the chorus of all the Prophets, together with the holy Angels, will continually sing a hymn to God.”

May Christ make us share eternal joys with them—he who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON L

[Note: [Col. 1334] Compiled from various sayings of Caesarius of Arles.]

### ON THE SALVATION OF THE SOUL

As far as concerns the desire of our soul, dearest brothers, it is our wish to come frequently to visit you; but, by the necessity of the time, we have now deserved to come to you safely. And therefore, because we rejoice in the common health of our bodies, let us speak, insofar as the Lord grants, about the salvation of souls, which is the true salvation.

For this reason, brothers, we were made in the image of God, so that, by God’s gift, we may understand what homeland is to be desired, what true blessedness is, what true life is, what perfect health is, and what eternal happiness is. But let us recognize these things inwardly in the heart, by God’s inspiration.

No one will be able to excuse himself by saying, “I do not know letters; therefore I cannot understand God’s commandments,” because even one who does not know letters ought to understand what is or is not.

Let a man question his conscience, address himself, and say to himself in his own words: “O man, who are you, or where are you, and from where did you come?” And answer yourself: “I am a human being, and I recognize that I am God’s creature.”

Ask again and say: “What do you possess within you, or from what things do you recognize that you were made?” Answer and say: “I recognize that I consist of soul and flesh.”

“What do you possess within you that is better of these two things?” Answer: “Without a doubt, I possess a soul better than the flesh.”

You have answered most excellently and in due order, and you have said that you possess a soul better than the flesh. Tell me further: “Where are you, O man?” You will answer: “In the world.”

“And afterward, where will you be?” “In heaven.”

“How long will you be there?” “Forever and ever.”

You have answered most justly and spoken the truth. Now take account of your life and be a just judge. From all the things that God has given you, preserve for your flesh what will sustain it in the world, and set aside for your soul what will enable it to live forever in heaven.

Pay close attention to your conscience and see whether you have set aside as many things for your soul in heaven as you have for your body in the world; whether you have set aside as many solidi in heaven as you have kept for yourself in the world. See whether through almsgiving you have stored in paradise, where your soul may live, as many modii of wheat and as many amphorae of wine as you have reserved for yourself so that your flesh may live in the world.

When you have carefully attended to these matters and wisely considered them, you see that you have kept almost the whole pound for your flesh in the world and stored one ounce in heaven. Be ashamed and quickly flee to the remedies of repentance, because you have judged the judgment begun within yourself.

You said one true thing, but accomplished another by your works: for you assigned everything to the flesh, not only faithfully but also unfaithfully. I do not know whether your judgment is in danger before you, when your judgments between your soul and your flesh are unjust. And where will I be able to find you just, when I know that you are unjust toward yourself?

Then, certainly, we nourish the flesh, adorn the flesh, sometimes make ourselves drunk, and feed the flesh with excessive delicacies—the flesh that, whether we wish it or not, worms will devour in the tomb after a few months or years—and we despise the soul that is presented by Angels to God in heaven.

O how harsh it will be for the sinful soul, and how unbearable that hour will be, when it sees a good soul receiving rest in paradise, while it itself is tortured in eternal punishment!

Therefore, dearest brothers, consider that we should give the soul not merely a greater share, but at least an equal one. For we were made in the image of God not outwardly in the body, but inwardly, in the inner person. Our flesh was formed from the clay of the earth. Is it just, then, that the clay of the earth should be preferred to the image?

The flesh ought to serve, and the soul to command. The one ought to exercise authority, and the other to submit in service. In all good Christians the soul rules, and the flesh is compelled to serve. But in sinners and lovers of this world, in an inverted—indeed, perverted—order, the flesh is raised up and the soul humbled. The flesh is fed with delicacies, while the soul is tortured by hunger; the flesh luxuriates in costly garments, while the soul is scarcely wrapped in old rags. And if it has been burdened with sins, it is presented to the eternal Judge, and then its true disgrace will appear.

For since the soul ought to be the head in its body, whoever excessively exalts, nourishes, cherishes, and pampers the flesh with delicacies or pleasures, while despising and disregarding the soul, raises the feet high and presses the head into the depths. And just as a person who seems to walk on inverted feet appears in the eyes of men, so is the person in the eyes of the Angels whose own flesh rules over him.

As I said above, therefore, God made us in his image and likeness. Although the inner person ought to rule in us, we despise God to such an extent that we make the image of God serve miserable clay. This is an unjust judgment: to prefer our flesh to the soul.

But not all people do this with sound judgment. For there are many who are upright, sober, humble, merciful, and chaste, in whom the soul holds authority and the flesh serves in submission.

And so I ask you, brothers: let each person attend to his conscience. If the flesh is ruling, let him quickly raise up its mistress and spur on its maidservant, so that the flesh may not conquer the soul and drag it into lust; rather, let the mistress govern her flesh and lead it along the paths of chastity and justice.

But whoever feels that the soul rules within him should, with God’s help, maintain the discipline of self-restraint and, across the straits of this world’s sea, steer his bodily vessel in such a way that, with truth as its guide, it may press onward and not, through carelessness, suffer shipwreck amid the waves of justice.

For this is how it may be recognized that the soul truly rules in us: let us reserve from our substance sufficient food and simple clothing for ourselves, [Col. 1336] and whatever more God gives, let us store up for the soul’s eternal blessedness through almsgiving to the poor. Otherwise, when we adorn our flesh with ornaments and fatten it with many delicacies, we may have a share with that rich man dressed in purple, and not with Lazarus.

For you know, as you have often heard in the Gospel, that the rich man who feasted splendidly every day and wore purple and fine linen went out from his body, was buried in hell, and there, amid the flames, sought a drop of water and a place of refreshment, but did not deserve to find one. Behold what riches the flesh that luxuriates and feasts in this world will find in hell!

But Lazarus, who possessed neither riches nor adornments in this world, rested after death in the bosom of holy Abraham.

As I said above, therefore, dearest brothers, let us restrain our appetite and prepare simple food and clothing for our flesh in this world, so that something may remain for us to store up for the soul in the world to come.

Let what the perishing appetite desires be reserved for almsgiving. Let the ornaments that luxury and indulgence demand in the world be stored in heaven by mercy and truth.

If we wish to be adorned, let us seek ornaments by which no one is adorned unworthily. If we desire delicacies, let us not seek bodily and passing delicacies, from which excrement is produced in this world, but rather spiritual and eternal ones, from which the Angels feast in heaven.

And if you perhaps ask what those delicacies are, hear the Apostle saying: “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man—what God has prepared for those who love him” (I Cor. II, 9).

Do you still ask and inquire what this is? If you wish to recognize the truth, God is your delicacy, your rest, your health, your joy, your happiness, your refreshment, your delight; and whatever your soul can rightly desire, God will be all of it for you.

Thus the blessed Apostle says: “And God will be all in all” (ibid. XV, 28).

O covetous man, hear me: what is sufficient for you if God is not sufficient for you?

If, then, you desire all these things, seek the rest of paradise; sigh for eternal blessedness, from which no friend departs and into which no enemy enters; from which the good can never depart, and into which the wicked can in no way enter.

Let us therefore hasten to that homeland adorned with good works, so that, when we have given alms to the poor, we may be able to reach the heavenly kingdoms. May he lead us there who is blessed forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON LI

[Note: [Col. 1336] It appears in the Appendix to volume 5 as sermon 53, with nine verses removed from the beginning here.]

Let no one, dearest brothers, deceive himself with false security and think that he will not come before the tribunal of Christ, etc.

## SERMON LII

[Note: [Col. 1336] This is sermon 355 of volume 5.]

For this reason I wished and asked yesterday that you should gather more frequently today; this is what I am going to say, etc.

## SERMON LV

[Note: [Col. 1336] The style of this sermon is no different from that of the preceding sermons.]

### ON THE DEATH OF VALENTINUS, BISHOP OF CARTHAGE

[Note: [Col. 1336] “There is an intolerable error in this heading,” says Lupus. “For in the time of Augustine we know of no Valentinus among the bishops of the Church of Carthage. When Augustine was taken into the presbyterate, Saint Aurelius presided over the Church of Carthage, and he remained in office almost until the death of Saint Augustine. Capreolus succeeded him immediately; Quodvultdeus succeeded Capreolus; Deogratias succeeded Quodvultdeus; Eugenius succeeded Deogratias: there was no Valentinus at all.”]

The Book of Wisdom, dearest brothers, commends the wisdom of the name in many ways: first, because it frees a person from danger; second, because it preserves the one who has been freed; third, because it crowns the one who has been preserved.

How it frees is clear from the example of Noah, whom it saved in the ark when the waters destroyed the earth. How it preserves is clear from Jacob: the Lord led him along straight paths and showed him the kingdom of God while he was sleeping. When he awoke, he said: “Truly, this is the house of God and the gate of heaven” (Gen. XXVIII, 16–17).

As for the glory of God that crowns, it is added: “God will repay his holy ones for their labors and will lead them along a wondrous way” (Wis. X, 17).

These are the three states of the Church: namely, the state of repentance, of righteousness, and of glory. In the first the Lord frees; in the second he preserves; in the third he crowns. In the first we are afflicted; in the second restored; in the third perfected. In the first there are labor and sorrow; in the second taste and beauty; in the third glory and honor.

Nevertheless, because reading and exhortation concerning these states have so often been offered to our brothers, the canons, and have been discussed daily at table, perhaps you will say in your hearts: “It is wearisome for us to hear so much about this, because we must also render the service that is fitting to us by honoring Bishop Valentinus.”

But do not begrudge me your support, brothers. And if this should weary you, I shall take refuge with my brothers, who desire with their whole mind and whole affection to hear me. For a familiar and ancient word can sometimes become new. Food that has long been chewed is also digested more quickly.

Therefore, brothers, so that the distinction of the three states may shine forth more clearly, let us adapt our efforts to them in this way.

In the state of repentance, the Lord brings the blind man back along hard paths and promises him the kingdom of God his Father. In the state of righteousness, the Lord leads the righteous man along straight paths and shows him the kingdom of God. In the state of glory, the Lord brings the righteous and holy man out along a wondrous way and introduces him into the kingdom of God.

Behold, brothers, how the blind man is brought back from the trackless place to the road, from exile to his homeland, from one dwelling to another, from virtue to virtue, from the prison of the body to eternal glory.

Behold how the blind man is brought back so that he may not be without Christ; the righteous man is led so that Christ may be with him; the holy man is brought out so that he himself may be with Christ.

O my brothers, behold how miserable it is to be without Christ, how safe it is to have Christ with oneself, and how blessed it is to be with Christ. For we must not think that having Christ with oneself is the same as being with Christ.

The Apostle had Christ with him when he said, “I am not alone, but the grace of God is with me” (I Cor. XV, 10). He was not yet with Christ when he desired to depart and be with Christ. The thief has Christ with him, to whom Christ promised, “Today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke XXIII, 43).

The blind man is therefore brought back along hard paths. Certainly, it is hard to abandon one’s customary ways, harder to undertake what is unfamiliar; but hardest of all is to be cooked continuously in a furnace, in which one must be so thoroughly boiled that one can be cut like meat and twisted in every direction like a rod.

These are the paths that are harder than all hardships for sinners, more bitter than all bitterness, and hateful as death. What are these paths, brothers, except abandoning the things that belong to the world?

O how hard, how deadly it seems, how bitter it seems, to abandon the things that belong to the world! But because they are hard, bitter, and painful, “you will receive a hundredfold and will possess eternal life.”

Come, soldiers, rise now, because you have slept long enough. Arm yourselves with contrition of heart, confession of mouth, and affliction of the flesh, because behold, the Savior will come and will not delay. Behold, he is already at the door; behold, he is already calling you; behold, he compels you to come.

But you will say, O wretch: “In contrition there is pain, in confession shame, in affliction labor. What, then, shall I do?”

Come, O soldier of Christ! You are already being proclaimed a citizen of heaven by the one who is above you, the very one who considers your labor and pain. Nevertheless, the harder they are, the more useful they will be to you. Fight bravely while you can, for a crown of righteousness has been laid up for you, which the Lord, the just Judge, will give you on that day.

After the blind man has become seeing and the wicked man righteous, then, brothers, we shall be able to sing: “The Lord led them along straight paths” (Ps. CVI, 7).

There are, brothers, so that our students may not depart empty-handed, three kinds of straightness. One thing is to be ruled, another to be directed, another to be corrected [Note: [Col. 1338] Perhaps, “to be raised up.”]

For the Prophet said, “The Lord rules me, and I shall lack nothing” (Ps. XXII, 1). And again, “Direct my way in your sight” (Ps. V, 9). And again, “In what way does a young man correct his path?” (Ps. CXVIII, 9). And again, Isaiah says, “Morning by morning he raises up my ear” (Isa. L, 4).

An inanimate thing, brothers, is properly said to be ruled, such as a wagon or a ship. A sentient thing without reason is directed, such as a horse or a mule, which have no understanding. A rational thing is corrected—that is, ruled by the heart—such as a human being. But the righteous person is raised up, so that he may understand and seek the things that are above.

Thus Jeremiah wished this when he said, “Stand in your ways and consider which is the eternal way” (Jer. VI, 16). Daniel, prostrate before the vision of majesty, heard the Angel say, “Stand upon your feet” (Dan. X, 11).

If you do not believe the Prophet, however, believe the poet, you perverse student, to whom God gave a lofty face and commanded him to see the heavens (Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, book 1, lines 85–86). When a tyrant asked him, “Why did God make you?” he replied, “So that I might contemplate heaven and the gods of heaven.”

Human beings were made on earth not for the earth, but for heaven; they were made from the earth not for the sake of the earth, but for the sake of heaven.

I do not know whether any of the faithful, brothers, could have said more, or offered a more convincing argument. Does even a mute and irrational animal know the cause of its illness? Does the sick lion seek the animal called the ape, which, once devoured, immediately restores it to health? Does even a sick ape seek a dog’s blood, a bear seek ants, a leopard seek does, or a vine seek serpents as food?

Yet a human being, worn down by the study of medicine, seems to know none of these things. Every creature strives after happiness; but if a human being strives after it, he nevertheless does not appear to strive for it in his actions.

Seek, therefore, O man, heaven, for which you were made. Do not seek philosophy, since you were not made for philosophy. Nor is it useful for you to know what is on the earth, but only what is above.

Stand, then, upon your feet; stand in your natural ways, for which you were made, and direct them, if necessary, in giving and forgiving. “Give, and it will be given to you.” Then the Lord will say to you, “Friend, come up higher; enter into the joy of your Lord.”

But someone may say, “How and in what manner will the spirit depart from the body?” Does Solomon seem to be ignorant of this when he confessed that he was utterly ignorant of the way of the eagle in the heavens (Prov. XXX, 18–19)?

How, then, does he see God, how an angel, how himself, how another spirit, whether good or evil? On this point that magnificent philosopher marvels today. For in his books *On Animals* he stated that the five bodily senses are common to us and to irrational animals for use, not for pleasure.

A human being finds pleasure in everything; a beast, however, finds pleasure only in two things, namely taste and touch. In the other senses it is sometimes moved and aroused, but does not take pleasure.

How, then, is it that, once the spirit has departed from the body, it entirely loses the two senses that it shares with beasts? It neither uses nor enjoys taste or touch, but retains the other three for use and pleasure.

This nevertheless seems marvelous to him: that a spirit without a body should use bodily senses. Yet even if the philosopher perhaps did not fully understand this, it is nevertheless true—entirely true and indisputable—that the free spirit sees God and delights in God, so that it may not always have to be told, “O soul, where is your God?”

It will also hear the Angels singing and rejoicing. It will also see and hear: “Be over five cities,” that is, blessednesses, and so to each according to his works.

And if we should say, “Lord, what will you do when we have deserved to receive all these things from your generosity?” that great master of the household will answer, as Alexander is said to have answered a soldier asking for a gift, to whom he had given a city: “Even if you are not worthy to receive so great a thing, I am nevertheless worthy and able to give so great a thing.”

The Angels, brothers, will marvel greatly at God’s works: at the joining of soul and flesh in the human being, at the joining of humanity and the Word in Christ, and at the joining of humanity and God in heaven.

For the Lord will say, “Father, I will that they be one with us, just as you and I are one” (John XVII, 11). At the first they marvel, where one is joined to one; at the second, more greatly, where one will be joined to two; but at the third, most greatly of all, where one will be joined to three in the Trinity.

Although these matters have been explained generally, they can nevertheless be applied spiritually to the commemoration of this holy Bishop Valentinus. When he was a catechumen of nineteen years, he came to Baptism; and thus the Lord brought him back along straight paths. afterward he led him, as a bishop, along the hard paths of repentance; afterward he brought him out along the path of wonder and glory.

Let us therefore run after him, brothers, so that we may seize the prize of the eternal calling on that day when Jesus, the Son of God, comes—he who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON LVI

[Note: [Col. 1339] In two manuscripts that are not particularly old, it is attributed to Augustine. It is the work of an author imitating Caesarius.]

### AN ADMONITION SHOWING THAT IT IS GOOD TO READ SACRED SCRIPTURE.

With Christ’s favor, dearest brothers, always receive divine reading with eager and thirsting hearts, so that your most faithful obedience may bring us spiritual joy. But if you wish the words of Holy Scripture to become sweet to you, and if you wish the divine commandments to advance in you as they ought, withdraw yourselves for certain hours from worldly occupations. Even within your homes, rereading the divine utterances, devote yourselves entirely to God’s mercy, so that this may happily be fulfilled in you which is written of the blessed man: “He will meditate on the law of the Lord day and night” (Ps. 1:2); and this: “Blessed are those who search out his testimonies and seek him with their whole heart”; and this: “I have hidden your words in my heart, that I may not sin against you” (Ps. 118:2, 11).

For, as you yourselves have heard, just as the one who hides God’s words in his heart does not sin, so the one who does not hide them does not cease to sin. If merchants are not satisfied to seek profit from only one kind of merchandise, but purchase several goods by which they may increase their wealth; and if farmers try to plant various kinds of seed, so that they may prepare sufficient food for themselves and their families—how much more, in spiritual profits, ought it not be enough for you to hear divine readings in church! In your homes and at your meals, and when the days are short, even for certain hours during the nights, you ought to devote yourselves to divine reading, so that you may gather spiritual wheat in the granary of your hearts and store the pearls of Scripture in the treasuries of your souls. Thus, when we come on the day of judgment before the tribunal of the eternal Judge, we may be found, as the Apostle says, “clothed and not naked” (2 Cor. 5:3).

And carefully attend to this also, dearest brothers: the divine Scriptures are like letters sent to us from our homeland. [Note: [Col. 1339] Caesarius, in the Appendix to volume 5, sermon 69, no. 2.]

For our homeland is paradise; our parents are the Patriarchs, Prophets, Apostles, and martyrs; its citizens are the angels; and our king is Christ. When Adam sinned, we were cast out in him, as it were, into the exile of this world. But because our king is more kind and merciful than can be thought or expressed, he deigned to send us the divine Scriptures, like letters of invitation, through the Patriarchs and Prophets, by which he might invite us to our eternal and sovereign homeland.

And when human frailty, with a rebellious spirit, despised his Scriptures, he deigned to descend in person, to free us from the tyranny and pride of the devil, and by the example of his gentleness to summon us to true humility; also to free us from the power of the ancient serpent through the outrage of his Passion [Note: [Col. 1340] Manuscripts: “also to free us from the power of the ancient enemy through the mercy of his Passion.”]; to descend to the realms below and rescue the ancient saints who were held liable under original sin; to ascend on high; to send the Holy Spirit from heaven, who would strengthen us against all the devil’s snares; and to dispatch his Apostles, who would proclaim the kingdom of God throughout the whole world.

And although he found us not only proud but also impious, liable not only to original sins but also to actual sins, he nevertheless forgave everything, without anyone pleading for us. He did not, as we deserved, drag us—oppressed by many chains and fetters—to perform laborious tasks; rather, in his ineffable goodness, he mercifully and compassionately invited us to reign with him.

Since these things are so, dearest brothers, what do those servants think of themselves who presume so greatly to despise the commands of their Lord that they do not even deign to reread the letters of invitation themselves, by which he invites them to the blessedness of his kingdom? For if one of us sent a letter to his administrator, and that man not only failed to carry out what was commanded but also disdained to reread the very order, he would deserve not indulgence but punishment, not freedom but imprisonment. So the person who neglects to read the divine Scriptures sent from our eternal homeland must fear lest he receive not eternal rewards but fail even to escape everlasting punishment.

For it is so dangerous for us not to read the divine commandments that the prophet cries out mournfully: “Therefore my people have been led into captivity, because they had no knowledge; but the one who is ignorant will himself be ignored” (Isa. 5:13). Without doubt, the person who neglects to seek God through divine reading in this age will be disdained by God, who will not acknowledge him in eternal blessedness. He must fear lest, when the doors have been closed, he deserve to be shut out with the foolish virgins and hear: “I do not know you” (Matt. 25:12); and: “I do not know you; depart from me, workers of iniquity” (Luke 13:27).

What does “I do not know you,” “I do not know you,” mean? How does he not know those whom he sends into the fire? Precisely because, as has already been said, those who do not wish to understand him in this age by reading will be disdained by God and not acknowledged on the day of judgment.

And we must hear, not carelessly but with great concern and fear, what is written in Solomon: “The one who stops his ear so as not to hear the law—his prayer will be accursed” (Prov. 28:9). The one who wishes to be heard by God must first hear God. With what confidence does he wish God to hear him, when he despises him to such an extent that he neglects to read his commandments?

And what of this, dearest brothers? Some Christians—and, what is worse, sometimes even clerics—when they are about to undertake a journey, arrange to have bread, wine, oil, and various provisions prepared for themselves. Yet while each person makes such extensive preparations for an earthly journey, so that his flesh may have food, he does not care to read even one little book, by which his soul might be refreshed here and forever.

Although each person has two human beings within him—the inner person made in the image of God and the outer person formed from the mud of the earth—he appears to take such great care for the body, which worms will devour in the grave, while the inner person, made in God’s image, is recognized as being tortured by hunger and thirst like a worthless slave, without the nourishment of God’s word. For he neglects God to such an extent that he despises and scorns his image within himself.

Therefore, dearest brothers, wisely and profitably considering these things, let us strive, as far as we can, to put an end to all idle tales, slander, and buffoonery. Let us flee the obstacles of this world with all our strength and seek certain hours in which we can devote ourselves to prayer or reading for the salvation of our souls. Thus this may be fulfilled in us which is written: “Those who are learned will shine like the stars for everlasting ages” (Dan. 12:3).

May he himself deign to grant this, who, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, lives and reigns as God throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON LVII

[Note: [Col. 1341] This has already been treated above, col. 1213.]

Placed in this life, brothers, live in such a way that, when you have departed from here and your flesh has begun to be devoured by worms in the grave, etc.

## SERMON LVIII

[Note: [Col. 1341] We give it in a more correct form, as it appears in the Michaeline manuscript, approximately five hundred years old, in which it too is attributed to Augustine.]

### ON THE FACT THAT THE GLORY OF THE WORLD IS NOTHING

The apostolic reading has sounded this message, dearest brothers: “The time is short. It remains that those who have wives should be as though they had none, and those who use the world as though they did not use it; for the outward form of this world is passing away” (1 Cor. 7:29, 31), and like a thief, the day of the Lord will come.

Therefore, O soul, whoever you are who hear and read, may the counsel of the most holy Daniel help you, who says: “Accept my counsel and redeem your sins with almsgiving” (Dan. 4:24). If you neglect this counsel, you knock at heaven without purpose.

O soul, who dwell within the fragile walls of the flesh, “watch and knock,” he says; “ask and pray.” “To the one who knocks and asks, it will be opened,” says the Lord. And “if you pass through fire, I am with you, and the flame will not burn you.” If you seek something by praying, you will find it; when you knock by asking, Christ will open the doors for you, so that you may enter as the possessor of paradise.

If you still think, brother, that something remains for you at the end of the world, consider at least your own end. It is written: “Naked I came from my mother’s womb, and naked I shall also go beneath the earth” (Job 1:21). Therefore, brother, you brought nothing with you when you entered the world, and you will take nothing with you when you leave the world.

[Note: [Col. 1341] Here sermon 75 began.]

Hear, then, all you foolish among the people, and at last come to know your negligence. Go to the graves of the dead and see examples for the living. Bones lie there; the human being perishes [Note: [Col. 1341] Elsewhere, “the flesh.”], and yet his case is reserved for the day of judgment.

That man too was once like us, living in vanity and devoting himself in this world to riches. He multiplied his fields, planted vineyards, filled his barns and many storehouses, and rejoiced in his abundance. And behold, suddenly everything was taken from his sight.

He applauded himself in many forms of display, dressed in silken garments, indulging himself in pageantry and luxury, cultivating the lavishness of banquets, displaying dances and amusements amid drunkenness, mingling his lunches with dinner, and scarcely putting an end to his merriment. And behold, everything was taken from his sight.

Where, then, did all those things go? Where is the pageantry, where the finery, where the elaborate banquets? Where now are those who crowded around him in frenzied throngs, who praised him at home [Note: [Col. 1341] Elsewhere: “Where now are those who saw him in the forum, standing far above everyone? Where are those who praised him at home,” etc.] and in the marketplace? Where are the adornments of his houses and the costly luxury of his clothing? Where is the ostentation of gems and the immense weight of silver? Where, finally, is that very greed which, while daily doing whatever it wishes with everything, does not know when it will lose it all?

Where is that wisdom and eloquence devised for public display? Where are the applause of praise and the constant flattery of friends? Where are the submissive throngs of servants and the radiant lights of lamps? Where is the crowd of clients going before him?

All these things have passed from his sight, and there will be no further memory of him. He lies in the grave, reduced to dust. His flesh, nourished by indulgence, has fallen away; his sinews have separated from their joints. Only the bones remain, preserved as examples for the living, so that the remains of the dead may be recognized.

His body is thought to be resting, but his soul dwells in hell and will see the light no more. For many shadows surround him; trembling and affliction seize him; worms and fire consume him, and weeping will not cease from his eyes. The gnashing of teeth torments him continually, because the worst pains press upon him, and punishments do not cease for his soul.

Now he regrets having lived wickedly in this world, having been negligent, and having failed to love piety and mercy. Now he seeks them and does not find them. He regrets having possessed and stored up great riches without distributing them to the needy; having wasted the time of repentance and failed to reform his days, so that he would not fall into such punishments.

A great resurrection therefore awaits him, to deliver him to a worse judgment. There the angels will trouble him, reproaching him because he did not love almsgiving; therefore mercy is denied him. A burning Gehenna awaits him, because during his life he did not extinguish its fire among the poor. Everlasting worms will consume his belly, because he did not feed the hungry poor.

O how valuable before the Lord is the mercy shown in the life of this world! When it delights in being shown here, it is found again to be gathered up at the judgment, as the Gospel says: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matt. 5:7).

Run, therefore, while you have the light of this life, lest the darkness of death overtake you. Show mercy in this world, so that it may wipe away sins and come to your aid on the day of judgment. For what you eat, you lose; what you labor for, you leave behind; but what you distribute to the poor, that you will possess securely.

May your mercy go before you on the day of judgment and itself plead for you in the presence of the Lord, so that, being merciful, you may obtain mercy, through the favor of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom belong honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON LIX

[Note: [Col. 1342] It appears above, col. 1215.]

Hear, dearest brothers, the saving teaching of our father, who does not concern himself with earthly things, etc.

## SERMON LX

[Note: [Col. 1342] In the Library of the Fathers it was published among the homilies of Caesarius under Augustine’s name, and several manuscripts also attribute it to him. Others, however, attribute it to Caesarius. But whether in the printed editions or in the manuscripts, the variety is astonishing. We now give this version corrected from the Floriac manuscript, which agrees in no small measure with the preceding treatise on Obedience, col. 1221.]

### ON THE PERSECUTION OF CHRISTIANS

We have often said, dearest brothers, that Christians always suffer persecution. This world lies in evil. Our adversary, the devil, reigns in the world—and do we suppose that we do not suffer persecution?

What thing does not persecute the Christian? Everything that is in the world persecutes the Christian. Do we wonder if others persecute us when we wish to serve Christ? Even our parents persecute us. Whoever is unlike us persecutes us and hates us. Do we wonder if others persecute us?

Our very body persecutes us. If I eat a little and my small body becomes strong, the health of my body persecutes my soul. Wherever I turn, there is persecution for me. If I see a woman, my eye persecutes me, for it desires to kill my soul. If I see riches, gold, silver, or possessions, whatever I see and desire persecutes my soul.

Let us not think that martyrdom consists only in the shedding of blood. For Christians and religious people there is always martyrdom [Note: [Col. 1342] The manuscript does not contain “for Christians and religious people.”]. Lust persecutes the young man; lust wishes to pour out the blood of the soul. When your soul is endangered and, as it were, placed in peril, then the Lord Jesus stands at the Father’s right hand and fights for his young man.

If, therefore, there are martyrdoms in a time of peace, there are also denials. Let no one say, then, that this is not martyrdom. It is both martyrdom and denial. I, who today appear to be a monk, if I break my commitment, have denied Christ. And if I deny Christ in peacetime, what would I do in persecution? I am not tortured or burned, yet I deny him. If I were tortured and burned, what would I do?

The one who denies during persecution receives pardon for his wound; the saints pray for him. For what does he say? “I wanted to fight, but my flesh failed in the struggle. My spirit did not yield, but my body yielded. My mind thought one thing, but my body compelled another.” Yet he has no excuse. For no wound ought to separate anyone from the love of Christ.

What does Christ say to you? “You were burning in the fire; you were hanging on the torture stake; you were tortured for my sake,” and you say, “I could not endure the torments.” How, then, did Peter endure? How did Paul, how did the other martyrs endure? Did they have bodies different from the one you have?

O monk, who flee fasting, do you think you will escape fire? This, then, is what I say: at all times there are martyrdoms, and there are also persecutions [Note: [Col. 1343] The manuscript reads, “transgressions.”].

Finally, what does the Apostle say about widows who married a second husband? What does he say? “They incur condemnation because they have rejected their first pledge” (1 Tim. 5:12).

What does he say to the widow? “O widow, before you promised me that you would remain a widow, it was in your power to marry. From the time you professed that you would remain mine, from that time you began to belong to me. If you wish to take a second husband, you have despised me; you are an adulteress, because you had already been joined to me” [Note: [Col. 1343] The manuscript omits: “you are an adulteress, because you had already been joined to me.”].

So too, monk, before you made your promise, it was in your power to do what you wished. Your voice bound you to me. Who compelled you? Did I impose necessity upon you? Were you not free? It was in your power to make the promise. You promised, and you began to belong to me. I do not wish to lose what is mine; you may not abandon what you promised.

Making the promise was yours; abandoning it is not yours. If you abandon me, I will not have you in the rank in which I previously had you. At first you were free. You were indeed part of my household; you were not before my eyes, nor were you among my servants, but you were nevertheless part of my household. You were not with me, but you were nevertheless mine. From the time you began to serve as my soldier, if you withdraw, I will not regard you as part of my household but as a fugitive.

Why do I say all this? Because it was in our power to promise the service of God and to obey; it is not in our power to abandon it. You promised? You have your reward. You denied? You have your punishment. Both are yours, to your shame. We have said, and we say again: You promised? You have your reward. You abandoned it? You have your punishment. Both are yours; choose whichever you wish. You have the way of death and of life; enter whichever you choose.

I say all this to you, dearest brothers, lest anyone among you think that he has unrestricted freedom and say: “Then those who have wives, who live in cities, who serve as soldiers, who conduct business—in short, the whole world—is in danger, and only monks are saved.”

Our condition is not the same as theirs. They knew their weakness and did not promise to do what they could not do. They are indeed Christians. But one Christian is like a secular person and like a merchant; another Christian is like a soldier. Cornelius too was a soldier, a centurion, yet he was saved.

I, who am a monk, who have ceased to be secular and have become a monk, will either be saved as a monk or else I will not be saved: there is no other middle way. If I wish to abandon the life of a monk and follow a secular life, the Lord will not regard me as secular but as a transgressor.

Therefore we may not abandon what we have undertaken. Someone may say: “What shall I do if I have sinned in this undertaking and have become neither a secular person nor a monk? Has someone sinned by a greater sin? Does he desire to amend?”

This, then, is what I say: we may not abandon what we undertook, even if you have lost the dignity of your undertaking [Note: [Col. 1343] The manuscript does not contain: “This, then, is what I say … even if you have lost the dignity of your undertaking.”].

If you have sinned while established in the monastic life, be repentant as a monk—not as a secular person, but as a monk.

Someone may say: “I fled my master so that he would not beat me. Must I always flee?” If you regret that you fled, you must return to your master. Let no one say, “I regret that I fled, and therefore I must always flee.”

Whether we are saints or sinners, we may not change our undertaking. If you are holy, you are a blessed monk; if you are a sinner, you are a wretched monk. You may not change your undertaking, even if you have lost the dignity of your undertaking.

I speak these things generally; and what I say to you, I also say to myself, lest anyone think that he has the power to change his undertaking [Note: [Col. 1344] This is where the Floriac manuscript ends; the printed editions differ greatly.]

I am telling you something new—as a comparison, not as a command. Suppose that two monks have fallen; that is, each has sinned. One of them, for example, took a secular wife and said, “I cannot endure this; I cannot continue as a monk.” The other, who had sinned, understood his sin. He confesses it to no one, yet he grieves over what he did and day and night implores the Lord’s mercy.

I do not say that he did well to sin. Yet in comparison with the one who is publicly wicked, this man is holy.

Why do I say all this? Not to give sinners hope, or through that hope to provide an occasion for sinning, but to say that even whoever has sinned may not change his undertaking.

The Lord, however, is powerful to free both me and you entirely from all the devil’s snares. To him be honor and glory throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON LXI. ON OBEDIENCE

If we wish to earn the rewards of eternal life, let us strive with all our strength to keep God’s commandments. God’s commandments are heavy for those unwilling to obey, but light for those who desire it, as he himself says: “My yoke is easy, and my burden is light” (Matt. 11:30).

Let us hear our Lord and Savior commanding us and admonishing us by his example. “Take my yoke upon you,” he says, “and learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart” (ibid., 29).

What does it mean to take God’s yoke upon oneself except to subject oneself, for God’s sake, to the commandment of holy obedience?

A gentle person is one who bears with equanimity all injuries and insults inflicted upon him, who keeps in practice that apostolic judgment which says: “Do not repay evil for evil or abuse for abuse, but on the contrary, bless” (1 Pet. 3:9); and again: “Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good” (Rom. 12:21).

A humble person is one who chooses to be lowly in God’s house and prefers everyone to himself; who always considers himself dust and ashes; and in everything he does, continually abases and despises himself as an unworthy servant, not merely in word but in deed, thought, and his entire conduct.

Such a person is unquestionably fit to preserve discipline and obedience. He cannot perish from the way of righteousness, nor turn aside to the right or the left, because in being gentle he is broken by no adversity, and in being humble he is lifted up by no prosperity or glory.

The greatness of obedience’s fruit is shown when it adds: “And you will find rest for your souls.” The discipline of obedience is labor now, but in the future it has the most peaceful fruit.

We must understand also that the more obedient we are now to our fathers, the more God will be obedient to our prayers; and the more his yoke will be easy for us and his burden light.

We must know too that a proud person, impatient of discipline, cannot submit to the rules of obedience. Because he lives arrogantly, he despises others and wants to obey his own decisions rather than another’s. Because he is impatient, he judges even small and light matters to be harsh and intolerable, and considers correct only what he has conceived with an obstinate heart; he uses his own judgment as the standard for everything.

Such brothers often disturb those who are united in fellowship, stir up quarrels, refuse to live according to the measure of others, and are not content with the things with which religious poverty ought to be content. Although they live more carelessly than the others, they wish to be honored more than the others.

Such rebellious and disobedient souls frequently fall into the passions of their flesh and slide into shameful deeds. Many of them miserably and damnably depart from the fellowship of the brothers and from their holy undertaking.

The Apostle Peter cries out terribly concerning such people: “If, having escaped the pollutions of the world, they are again entangled in them and overcome, their latter state has become worse than their former. For it would have been better for them not to have known the way of righteousness than, after knowing it, to turn back from the holy commandment delivered to them” (2 Pet. 2:20–21). Hence the Lord says: “Woe to the one through whom scandal comes!” (Matt. 18:7).

Whoever recognizes himself as such a person, while he still has time to correct himself, should quickly return to tears and repentance. Let him conquer pride with humility, condemn impatience with gentleness, and turn vices into virtues, lest, if he persists in evil, he reach eternal punishments.

We must therefore preserve the obedience we have professed both in virtue and in deed. We do this when we honor and love the one who presides over us for the love of God, and when we hasten willingly to fulfill whatever he commands us, as though it had been commanded by the heavenly Lord himself.

For the superior takes Christ’s place in the monastery. Hence Christ says to his shepherds: “Whoever hears you hears me, and whoever despises you despises me” (Luke 10:16).

Just as those who willingly obey ought to rejoice and expect a great reward from the Lord—for what they do at the command of their superiors they render to God himself, the author of all—so those who despise the commands of their superiors ought to fear and expect a great judgment from God. For when a superior is despised, it is not he himself but the one in whose place he has been set who is held in contempt.

God cannot be honored by us without great benefit, nor despised without great harm.

Obedience must be without delay, not with murmuring or sadness of spirit, but with joy and cheerfulness. “God loves a cheerful giver.” A good deed performed with sadness is not acceptable to God, because he is more an examiner of the heart than of the body.

Obedience must also continue unto death, because Christ obeyed his Father for us unto death. Our Redeemer himself admonishes us by his example to this holy commandment, saying: “Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart.”

## SERMON LXII. ON THE FEAR OF THE LORD AND THE AVOIDANCE OF GREED

[Note: [Col. 1345] In the German manuscript it is entitled: “A book of Saint Augustine on the fear of the Lord.”]

The fear of the Lord drives out sin. Through the fear of the Lord many good things are born. Solomon says: “The beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord”; and elsewhere he says: “Blessed is the person who is always afraid” (Prov. 9:10; 28:14).

Through the fear of the Lord souls escape the punishments of hell, and through love of him everlasting joy is found, because the fear of the Lord and love of neighbor are charity.

Whoever has charity has God; and whoever has God flees worldly things. Whoever loves Christ fears hell and desires paradise: he longs to reach it, hopes to remain in it, and there is no fear of death or trembling before the enemy there.

Whoever has God within him drives away the devil. Therefore, through love of God and neighbor, eternal life is acquired. Love of God causes one to remain in God. The Apostle says: “Love of neighbor does no evil” (Rom. 13:10). Let each person not do to another what he does not wish done to himself; whoever acts in this way does not incur sin.

Whoever entangles himself in earthly things distances himself from the love of God. In this world riches are never acquired without sin. If one person does not lose, another does not acquire; the one who acquires rejoices, while the one who loses grieves.

Many hope to make alms from the tears of others: they strip one person and clothe another. They make one person destitute and restore another with what belongs to someone else. Almsgiving acquired through iniquity is an abomination before God. Whoever thinks he can show mercy from iniquity is nothing before God.

What shall we say, dearest brothers, about those rich people who store up treasures and do not know for whom they gather them (Ps. 38:7); who acquire earthly things and lose heavenly ones; who gain money and lose their souls; who pay attention to what they acquire and do not weigh what they lose?

Many think they walk in the light and imagine that they are outwardly radiant, while inwardly they remain dark, full of the mud of sins.

O blind greed, which separates souls from Christ! Such was the rich man who feasted splendidly every day, while Lazarus lay as a beggar at his gate. When the rich man died, he fell into hell, while Lazarus was raised to Abraham’s bosom (Luke 16).

Why, wretched rich people, are you not terrified, since you desire earthly riches and lose heavenly ones? Whoever does not fear such an example walks blindly.

The Apostle James says: “Come now, you rich, weep and howl over the miseries that are coming upon you. Your riches have rotted, and your garments have been eaten by moths. Your gold and silver have rusted, and their rust will be a testimony against you” (James 5:1–3).

Woe to those who are such. The greedy person has no mercy; the covetous person is like hell. The more hell devours, the more it desires and craves; so too the greedy person will never be satisfied.

Empty power grows, and punishment grows as well. “The mighty will suffer mightier torments” (Wis. 6:7). The greater the honor given, the greater the danger.

Such people are boastful, proud, full of vanity, luxurious, gluttonous, and more eager to please human beings than God. They love themselves, serve their appetites, attend more to the flesh than to spiritual things, adorn the body and defile the soul, assent to carnal things, and neglect spiritual ones.

Outwardly they adorn themselves, though inwardly they are corrupted. They consider themselves wise, though they are fools, because “the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God” (1 Cor. 3:19).

Gathering worldly friendships, they lose eternal ones. For the Apostle says: “Whoever wishes to be a friend of this world makes himself an enemy of God” (James 4:4).

The proud person neglects to serve God and serves the devil. He is useless to God [Note: [Col. 1346] Perhaps, “unlike”], and like the devil.

Woe to those who despise the divine words and love false suggestions! While they reject the truth, they desire the devil’s vanities; while they pursue earthly things, they lose heavenly ones. Woe to those whom hell snatches away in such a state.

While they have time and are in their own power, they do not correct or amend themselves. When death comes, their power will remain behind, and will not their wretched soul alone go into hell?

O dearest brothers, what shall we say about those who made vows and did not fulfill them? It is better not to make a vow than, after making one, not to fulfill what was promised; it is better not to promise than not to keep the pledged faith.

It will be much worse for you if you do not give God what you promised than if you had never made the vow. For the prophet says: “Make vows to the Lord your God and fulfill them” (Ps. 75:12). And in Wisdom it is said: “The mouth that lies kills the soul” (Wis. 1:11). Elsewhere the Psalmist says: “You will destroy all who speak lies” (Ps. 5:7). And elsewhere: “By your words you will be justified, or by your words you will be condemned” (Matt. 12:37).

Many, which is worse, abandon God’s promises, deceived by the devil’s fraud, and follow evil works.

Consider yourselves, therefore, dearest brothers, and reflect on where the kings are, where the powerful, where the friends, where the parents are. See how from such great power or joy there comes such misery and anguish; from such great riches, so much poverty; from such great satiety, such hunger; from such brief delight, such prolonged sadness; from such a brief life, such a long death; from such little health, such prolonged illness; from such brief light, such lengthy darkness; from such slight pleasure of scent or luxury, such great pains and stench; and from the abundance of our clothing, from which we ought to have given to the poor, such great nakedness will come upon us.

I urge you, dearest brothers: while the Lord grants you spiritual understanding, do not love everything that is destined to die. Give a little, and you will receive much. Those who have left everything for Christ will receive a hundredfold and possess eternal life.

And although few—alas!—are willing to seize this way of salvation, since “many are called, but few are chosen,” it is nevertheless better to enter eternal life with the few than to go to Gehenna with the many.

“A little that the righteous has is better than the great riches of the wicked” (Ps. 36:16), with the assistance of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom belong honor and dominion forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON LXIII

[Note: [Col. 1347] It is sermon 251 in the Appendix to volume 5.]
