O dearest brothers, how fearful is that day on which our Lord Jesus Christ has determined to come with flaming fire, etc.

## SERMON LXIV

[Note: [Col. 1347] In addition to the customary variants of the German manuscript, this further point is to be observed: in that same manuscript, the final part of the following sermon is joined together here.]

### ON EXHORTING PRIESTS TO TEACH WHAT THE CHRISTIAN PEOPLE OUGHT TO KNOW AND OBSERVE
Listen, my little children, and understand how Holy Scripture admonishes us and invites us to the kingdom of heaven, and shows us the way by which, with Christ’s help, we may escape the evils of this world and attain eternal life. For the Lord cries out through the prophet to the priests who preside over the people, that they should teach and admonish them and announce the way of truth. He says: “Cry out, do not cease; raise your voice like a trumpet, and announce to my people their crimes” (Isaiah 58:1). And again: “If you do not announce his iniquity to the wicked man, I will require his blood at your hand” (Ezekiel 3:18). There is therefore a great obligation upon all priests to show the people the way of salvation, by which they may acquire eternal life.

First of all, they must explain that every Christian ought to know and firmly keep in his heart the first commandment, as the Lord says: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your strength, and with all your mind; and your neighbor as yourself” (Matthew 22:37). If you place these things—that is, love and fear of God, and love of your neighbor—in your heart, and if you are willing to receive these precepts with the greatest reverence, then, with God’s generosity, you will be able more easily to attain to every other good intention.

For he has promised those who love him resurrection after death, the delights of paradise, fellowship with the angels, and everlasting life. After this, neither adversity troubles you, nor illness burdens you, nor old age overtakes you, nor death confronts you; instead there are perpetual peace and security, most welcome health of souls and bodies, beautiful youth, and the eternal life of the heavenly kingdom. These things are promised to those who do good and restrain themselves from evil.

Let each person therefore consider how he may attain to that goodness. Let him be well-disposed, devout, kind, merciful, sober, chaste, ready for every good work, and slow to evil. Let him flee idleness in the practice of virtue [Note: [Col. 1347] Perhaps, “of vice.” M.] and strive to please God by every exercise of virtue. Let him not be a slanderer, fornicator, plunderer, or miser; not a drunkard, glutton, or participant in vulgarity that has no bearing on the matter. Let him flee both these things and those who are engaged in them as he would a serpent, lest he defile his soul with vices and evils of this kind.

Let him love justice, seek peace, love his parents, and show affection toward his neighbor. Let him receive strangers with joy, visit the sick, and, insofar as he is able—with God’s help and as God supplies him with an abundance of temporal goods, so that he has something from which to give—let him gladly distribute to the poor and with the greatest joy assist their needs. Let him believe that God is his recompense-giver, who sees and considers all things; concerning this he also said: “Whatever you have done for one of these least ones, you have done for me” (ibid. 25:40).

And, my little children, always stretch out your hand to the poor with joy and a glad heart, insofar as you are able. If there is a laborer who cultivates the earth, let him not defraud the Church of a tenth from his fruits and from all that the Lord gives him, and let him not neglect to give a portion of it to the poor. If he is a merchant and works at this, but does not serve God from his labor, or is unwilling to pay the tithe, and does not take care to provide the poor with a portion of his goods, he himself, together with his money, will be reduced to nothing.

Whatever skill at making a profit the Lord has granted to anyone, by which he can feed and clothe himself and his family, and by which he can gain something beyond the tithe, let him gladly give from the portion that remains to him for the redemption of his soul and those of his family. In all these matters one must live chastely, soberly, and devoutly, so that the good work you do may become acceptable to God.

Laypeople, gladly assemble at church; make your confessions to the priests with a humble and pure heart; and ask them to deign to pray to God for your sins, so that he may forgive you. On Sundays you ought to offer oblations to God for yourselves and your families, according to the means permitted by your condition.

For it is a worthy and acceptable sacrifice to God that Christians should hasten to appease, through sacred offerings and the generosity of almsgiving, whatever they have done negligently, and that through true confession, as stated above, contrition of heart, complete satisfaction, pure prayer, fasting, and abstinence, they should wish to wash away their sins.

And you likewise, acting in all these ways, consider yourselves carefully: why were you born in this valley of misery, that is, in this world? Why, except that, stripped of everything on account of the sin of our first parents and banished from paradise into this present exile, we might return to our homeland by doing good?

If, therefore, through ignorance or foolishness you have sinned against God in any way, do not delay to amend it through your good works. Bring this carefully to mind: if someone has entered marriage, let him live peacefully and quietly in his household, as befits a good Christian; let him honor his parents; let him love his wife; and let him instruct his sons and daughters in the Catholic faith and the law of God with the greatest discipline, so that they may know how to love, fear, and honor God. For this is pleasing to God.

Above all, abstain from obscene speech, dearest ones, and do not slander your neighbors. If something in someone displeases another in any respect, follow that evangelical teaching: rebuke and admonish him in charity; and if you win him over, you will save yourselves (Matthew 18:15).

Avoid drunkenness in everything. For this is a great ruin of the soul. Just as fire easily sets straw ablaze and lightly consumes dry chaff, so drunkenness corrupts the body and casts both soul and body into a great conflagration of sins, especially in the young. Wine and youth are a double fire. Therefore whoever does not guard against drunkenness will not escape sin.

When you come to church, you must enter with the greatest reverence and the utmost fear, considering that you are going to the Lord and ruler of every creature, to ask him there for forgiveness of your negligences. While we also stand in church, pouring out prayers to the Lord for our sins, let us first, insofar as possible justified by works of faith, raise the eyes of our mind to God, always attending to how consolation from above may be bestowed upon us by God [Note: [Col. 1348] The manuscript reads, “consolation” (consolatium).].

For the eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and his ears are turned to their prayers. If you do these things frequently and keep God before your eyes, the enemy will flee from you. For the good angel of the Lord will be your helper if he sees that your mind remains firm in these things.

Consider that God is kind and merciful, and mercifully receives those who beseech him with a pure heart. He does not delay his promises, and he lifts up and heals those who are contrite in heart.

This also, dearest ones, must not be hidden from us: the words of Christ, announced to us through Holy Scripture, tell us that the end of this world is drawing near. Through the daily signs that were foretold in the Gospel and that occur every day, I hope that his coming is near, when he will judge the whole world by fire.

For behold, the Lord will come [Col. 1349], and all his angels with him, and the powers of heaven will be shaken. Then our Redeemer, the king of all, will sit upon the seat of his majesty, and all nations will be gathered before him. He will separate them from one another, as a shepherd separates sheep from goats. He will place those who are good at his right hand, but the wicked at his left.

And to those who will be at his right he will say: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world. I was hungry, and you gave me food; I was thirsty, and you gave me drink; I was naked, and you clothed me; I was sick and in prison, and you visited me,” and so forth.

Then the righteous will answer, saying: “Lord, when did we see you hungry, thirsty, naked, sick, or in prison, and minister to you?” Then he will answer them, saying: “As long as you did it for one of my least ones, you did it for me.”

But to those who will be at his left he will say: “Depart from me, accursed ones, into the eternal fire, which has been prepared for the devil and his angels. For I was hungry, and you did not give me food,” and so forth for each matter. “And these will go into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life” (Matthew 25:34–42, 46).

Consider therefore, my little children, the great mercy of God, with what patience he bears us in our sins. Let us reflect upon that future judgment, lest he reproach us for our sins. Therefore, dearest ones, this must be considered by us in everything. While each person is able, while he has time, while he holds the price in his hands, let each one redeem himself insofar as he is able, lest he remain a debtor to sin and in slavery to the devil [Note: [Col. 1349] What follows is taken verbatim from a homily entitled in the German manuscript “For Preaching,” whose beginning is: “We ought to consider.”].

And from that point onward, laypeople, after penance has been performed and reconciliation made, receive Communion according to the priest’s counsel, especially at the times appointed for this by the Church. Beforehand, however, abstain for several days even from your own wives, so that you may receive the holy sacrifice with a pure heart and chaste body.

Show honor to your priests, and obey them for God’s sake. For the Lord himself says to them: “Whoever hears you hears me, and whoever despises you despises me” (Luke 10:16). Let children honor their parents; likewise, let all Christians honor one another. For it is written: “Anticipating one another in honor” (Romans 12:10).

Feed the hungry; offer drink to the thirsty; receive guests and travelers, especially the poor; show them whatever kindness you can; wash their feet; clothe the naked; assist those in tribulation; console the sorrowful; visit the sick; bury the dead; seek out those in prison; and from your goods, insofar as the means granted you by the Lord permit, assist and minister to them.

Help widows and orphans who are in tribulation. Assist the poor and oppressed against wicked men or unjust judgment insofar as you can, or provide them with aid. Maintain right judgment and justice; show mercy in everything; keep peace among yourselves; and recall those who are in discord to the path of concord.

Keep the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer, and teach your sons and daughters so that they too may keep them. Instruct in the faith the children whom you received at Baptism, and know that you stand as their guarantors before God. Therefore always teach, constantly discipline, and correct them.

Admonish all your subjects, as you are bound to do, to live soberly, chastely, devoutly, and justly in this world. Speak the truth in heart and mouth; preserve chastity and continence; practice sobriety and moderation in food and drink; observe the fast; honor your elders; love the younger in the love of Christ; be patient toward everyone; do good to those who hate you.

Let charity and joy, patience, kindness, goodness, hope, faith, modesty, gentleness, continence, chastity, and love continually be in your heart. Preserve these things in holy thoughts, speech, and pious works. Above all, guard and hold fast humility [Note: [Col. 1349] This sentence is excerpted from the Rule of Benedict, chapter 4.].

Place all your hope in the Lord. When you find anything good in yourselves, do not ascribe it to yourselves for your empty praise, but to God for his glory, since he gave it to you. But when you see evil in yourselves, know that it came about not because of God, but through your own fault and negligences.

Fear the day of judgment; dread Gehenna; desire eternal life; guard your thoughts, works, and words alike for good, day and night. Every day hope for your departure from this world, which is always drawing near. Fulfill God’s commandments, and never despair of his mercy.

What one does not wish done to oneself, one should not do to another. And just as you wish people to do good to you, do the same to them. Preserve charity—which is love of God and neighbor—in everything and before all things.

Let no one deceive himself, brothers: every person who, after Baptism, has committed mortal sins—whether murder, adultery, fornication, theft, false testimony, perjury, or similar mortal sins—if he has not done true penance, given proper alms, and persevered in good works, will never enter the kingdom of heaven or possess eternal glory, but will descend into hell with lamentation. For those who do such things will not possess the kingdom of God (Galatians 5:21).

Therefore it is written: “God will by no means spare the transgressors” (Job 9:28), because a sinner will either suffer a temporal scourging, or undergo purification in this world, or be left to be punished by eternal judgment, or be punished in this world for the evil he has committed and which must be punished. This is why God does not spare transgressors.

And elsewhere it is written: “God permits no sins to go unpunished,” that is, without vengeance, because either we shall avenge our sins here through penance, or God will avenge them through the severity and justice of judgment.

Know this most certainly and believe it firmly: every person, however criminal or sinful he may have been, if he has performed true penance, given proper alms, and persevered in good devotion with righteous works, will not taste eternal death and will never descend into hell. Instead, after this present life, he will be lifted by holy angels into heaven and will possess eternal glory.

Therefore God said: “A person will not be judged twice for the same thing.” And the Apostle says: “If we judged ourselves, we would certainly not be judged by the Lord” (1 Corinthians 11:31, 9). This means that those who judge themselves in this present life through true penance will not be judged concerning these matters at the final judgment, because their judgment is thus concluded in this life.

Hence it is also written elsewhere that if we perform perfect penance, God not only forgives our faults but, after our faults, also promises rewards.

Therefore, dearest brothers, let us hasten to amend our life in the present life; let us mourn whatever evil we have done against God’s commandments; let us cease from sinning any further; and let us preserve ourselves in good will, right thought, and holy words and works, with the help and governance of our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns as God forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON LXV

### On General Instruction for the Human Race, in Desire for the Heavenly Life and Contempt for the Present Life

[Note: [Col. 1350] In the German manuscript this sermon has the following heading: “Homily for Instructing People.”]

Dearest brothers, each person ought to amend his sins insofar as he is able, with God’s help. Every Christian ought to desire the heavenly homeland and God the almighty Father who dwells in heaven, so that he may be worthy to say: “Our Father, who are in heaven” (Matthew 6:9). That is, we ought to desire to reach the place where the heavenly Father is, where our heavenly homeland is; there we should hope to arrive, so that there also we may remain.

This life is not heavenly but earthly, not a homeland but an exile, neither everlasting [Col. 1351] but temporary, since it inclines daily toward its end. But that heavenly homeland, in which God dwells with his holy angels and elect, has no end.

Truly, then, he is foolish who does not desire to reach such a Father, such a homeland, and such fellowship with the citizens of heaven. Who, having been led into captivity, would not wish to return thereafter to his homeland? Who, placed in a dark prison, would not wish to leave it and see the light? Who, suffering hunger until death, would not eat if the opportunity to do so were available? Who, suffering thirst, would not drink if the opportunity to drink existed?

For us, dearest ones, this world is truly not a homeland but Babylonian captivity, because we are entangled in many ways in the snares of various enemies—namely, the world, the flesh, and the enemy of the human race. This present life is also not freedom for us, but a prison of sins.

Let us therefore labor to be rescued from this captivity and from this prison of darkness. Let us not, as slaves, anxiously and laboriously desire this food and drink of present vanity, but, as free children, desire the heavenly food and drink—namely, that which is the complete satisfaction of the citizens above.

For this food and this heavenly life we ought to ask and pray to our Creator and Governor, that he may deign to guard and govern us in this valley of misery, or present exile, so that with his help we may be able to reach the harbor of salvation.

For this world resembles the sea. The sea stinks, and likewise the world. With God’s help we must draw ourselves out of this stench. We must pray to God our Creator with the greatest humility and beseech his saints, that, rescuing us from the valley of tears, he may make us companions of those heavenly citizens [Note: [Col. 1351] See below, Sermon 67.].

For we ought to hasten there with the greatest zeal, where we hope to remain without interruption, where there is no fear of death and no uncertainty concerning the enemy. There is life without end, youth without old age, light without darkness, joy without sadness, will without trouble, rest without labor, fullness without weariness, brightness without cloud.

But this life is dreadful and laborious, fragile and wearisome, fleeting and miserable, deceptive and deceitful, and full of hardships and scandals. In mourning we are born, in labor we live, and in sorrow we die.

And what is worse, and more grievous than all else, certain people, departing this life without confession or contrition because of their sins, are not only punished by temporal death but, led into hell, die an everlasting death. They have lived their lives without any mercy, and because of this they will suffer many torments and will never attain eternal life.

While they had time, they did not wish to amend their lives. They loved gluttony more than they pursued abstinence, lust more than chastity, earthly things more than heavenly things, and the creature more than the Creator.

Abstinence leads to chastity; chastity leads to glory; and fornication plunges one into punishment. Chastity lifts one to heaven, while lust sinks one into hell. Chastity unites one with the holy angels, while fornication joins one to demons.

Sobriety forms holy thoughts, but drunkenness, even when it hears holy words, does not receive them in the heart.

Therefore every true lover of the soul ought not merely to love the body by nourishing it, but also to nourish the soul by feeding it. We see naturally that when the body is hungry, it seeks food; when it is thirsty, it desires drink; when it is naked, it wants clothing; when it labors, it asks for rest; when sleep oppresses it, it seeks sleep; and so it is with the body’s other necessities.

The soul, however, needs all these things. The Lord’s commandment is its bread; holy prayer is its drink; truth and justice are its clothing; humility and obedience are its rest.

At this banquet of eternal fellowship many are called, but few are chosen. Some receive thirtyfold fruit, others sixtyfold, and others a hundredfold (Matthew 22:14; 13:8).

O how blessed is that soul to which the Lord God has deigned to grant a dwelling in eternal [Col. 1352] rest! And whoever wishes to enter this dwelling, namely the heavenly kingdom, must not be proud or avaricious, envious or wrathful, gluttonous or drunken, greedy or lustful, perjured, murderous, a falsifier, or an adulterer—and so with each of the other vices.

Although he may have committed innumerable evils, he must not despair of God’s mercy. Rather, he ought to place hope in God’s mercy and confidence in recovering salvation through the amendment of his life and the practice of good works.

He ought willingly to hear God’s words, diligently to assemble at church, to confess very frequently to priests, and to maintain firm charity toward all people. For whoever does not have charity will not be able to enter eternal life.

A person lives only a short time in this world. Therefore, while we have time, let us do good to everyone and prepare good paths for the Lord. Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation.

Christ is the salvation of humanity. If we ought to love our parents and friends, how much more are we bound to love him who made and created both us and our parents? Let us love him who rules over every creature, namely God. Let us love our neighbor as ourselves, because our neighbors, like us, were formed from the earth, so that by this we may be worthy of eternal life, with the help of him who lives and reigns, and so forth.

## SERMON LXVI

[Note: [Col. 1352] In the German manuscript this sermon is called “A Homily of Saint Augustine.” The author imitated Caesarius of Arles.]

### On Doing Penance

The kind and merciful God exhorts us, dearest brothers, to compunction and penance, saying: “Turn to me with all your heart, in fasting and weeping and mourning” (Joel 2:12); “For I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live” (Ezekiel 18:23). And again the prophet says: “Do not delay to turn to the Lord, and do not put it off from day to day” (Sirach 5:8). And again: “When you have turned and groaned, you will be saved” (Ezekiel 18:27).

Turn therefore, dearest ones, to the Lord our God, as good servants to a faithful master. Let us humble ourselves in God’s sight and weep before God who made us. Let us not disdain to do penance in this world and to ask forgiveness for our sins, so that we may escape infernal punishment and reach eternal joy.

Let us therefore amend ourselves through fasts, vigils, and other devout works, knowing that “God does not despise a contrite and humbled heart” (Psalm 50:19). For the Apostle says: “I chastise my body and bring it into servitude” (1 Corinthians 9:27).

If we labor for our flesh, let us labor also for our soul, which is more worthy. If we care for the fellowship of our miserable flesh, which worms will devour in the tomb after a few years, how much more ought we not to despise the soul that is presented to God and his angels in heaven?

Consider, dearest brothers, that an abundance of fodder produces lust. When the flesh is filled with such abundant delights and the mind is soothed by such riches, the fatness of the flesh provides food for worms.

Again I ask you, brothers: whenever you pass beside the tomb of a rich man, inspect carefully where his riches or ornaments are [Note: [Col. 1352] Here and shortly afterward, “his” would be better read. M.], where his glory is, where his vanity is, where his luxuries and pleasures are, or where his spectacles are.

Consider carefully, look, and recognize that nothing remains in them except ash, stench, and worms.

O man, look upon the tombs of the dead and speak to yourself. Speaking with yourself, you can say: “Behold, from that wretched man who was laid here, nothing remains except bones and dust.”

And truly, man, if you wish to hear those dry bones themselves, they will be able to preach to you and say: “O wretched one, how much you run about for the desire of this world, or how you submit your unhappy neck to pride and lust! Why have you attached yourself to serve the cruelest masters, namely vices and crimes?

“Pay attention to me and understand; consider me, and perhaps even thus your lust or [Col. 1353] avarice will horrify you. What you are, I once was; and what I now am, you will be afterward. If vanity remained in me, let iniquity not consume you. If lust defiled me, let chastity adorn you. Look upon my dust and abandon your evil desire,” and so forth.

Therefore, insofar as we can, let us labor with God’s help so that the wounds of others may provide us with medicines, and the death of others may benefit us unto life. This can be done most effectively if we are more concerned for the soul than for the body, so that when our flesh has been placed in the tomb, our soul may be lifted into heaven adorned with good works.

O soul, if the beauty of another woman or the desire of the flesh, which is the ruin of the soul, has deceived us, know that body and soul together will suffer punishments. For when our flesh has rotted in the tomb, our soul will be plunged into the abyss of hell to be tortured.

Behold what sermons the bones and ashes of the dead proclaim daily to the Lord. Truly I say, dearest brothers: whoever is lustful or negligent, if he is willing to receive what I say with great fear, hastens to the remedies of penance, and departs this life in penance, will possess the joys of paradise.

But if he does not do penance and sudden death overtakes him, he will suffer the torments of eternal punishment without any remedy.

Let us therefore, beloved brothers, fight manfully against carnal desires insofar as we can, with God’s help, so that, having conquered the pleasures of this world, we may be worthy to attain eternal reward throughout endless ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON LXVII

### On Fleeing Vanity and Attaining Virtues

[Note: [Col. 1353] The heading in the German manuscript is: “Homily for Preaching.”]

Beloved brothers, we ought to possess humility, keep God’s commandments, maintain charity, follow truth, and flee vanity. For truth cleanses [Note: [Col. 1353] The German manuscript reads: “Blessed Augustine said, ‘Truth cleanses.’”], while vanity defiles.

Christ is the truth, as he himself says: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6)—the straight way, the true light, and everlasting life.

Those who speak truthfully are children of God, while liars are children of the devil. For each person is called the child of the one whose works he does. Those who follow God are always in the light; but those who imitate the devil walk in darkness and will never have the light.

O most beloved children, how evil and perverse it is to abandon the light and follow darkness; to flee life and approach death; to abandon truth and follow falsehood; to delight in empty glory and despise eternal things; to rejoice in present pain and punishment and lose everlasting joy and rest!

For Scripture says: “Do not seek glory, and you will not be confounded when you have become glorious” [Note: [Col. 1353] The same codex reads: “Jerome says, ‘Do not seek glory, and you will not be saddened when you are without glory.’”].

Blessed are those who have spiritual eyes, contemplate heavenly things, and reject earthly things. From this fragile, miserable, and brief life they hasten to that blessed rest of the saints, which will never end [Note: [Col. 1353] Thus above, Sermon 65.]. They hasten there, where they hope always to remain, where there is no fear of death and no dread of the enemy.

There is life without death, youth without expectation of old age, light without darkness, joy without sadness, will without injury, a kingdom without change, rest without labor, fullness without weariness, and brightness without cloud. There is an angelic life, always joyful.

Although the joy of this world often appears to be happiness, it very frequently turns into sadness. The kingdom of God has no end. The life of this world is dreadful; that life, however, is to be loved and desired.

For this present life is miserable and fleeting, indeed uncertain, deceptive, and insatiable. In punishment and mourning we are born; in misery and distress we are raised; in labor we live; in pain we die; and at the end—which is more grievous still—if we depart without repentance, we will suffer everlasting torments.

For afterward they will not obtain forgiveness who, while they had time here [Col. 1354], did not perform worthy penance. Those who do not possess Christ’s commandments, or who, possessing them, do not keep them, and who despise the heavenly promises; those who love gluttony more than abstinence and pursue lust more than chastity—without doubt they will not possess the kingdom of God.

Fornication drives the soul toward punishment; chastity lifts the mortal person to glory. Chastity raises the path to heaven; lust makes one fall into hell. Chastity joins the dying person to the holy and everlasting angels; fornication associates him with Satan and the demons.

A fattened pig rolls in the mud. If you place pearls before a pig, it will trample them in the mire without noticing. So also a drunken and gluttonous person, filled with wine and sated with food, plunges himself into various lusts. Rolling in the filth of vices, he neither utters the words of Holy Scripture with his mouth nor receives them in his heart.

Fornicating is sweet to him, while preserving continence is bitter. That wretched man walks about inflated and proud, and desires to be better than others in this world, although before God he is worse. He considers himself higher than the rest, even though he is lower than everyone.

And so, while he thinks he stands better and more firmly, he falls into a precipice and goes into the eternal abyss. May almighty God rescue you from it, he who lives and reigns without end. Amen.

## SERMON LXVIII

### How Vices Are to Be Opposed through Virtues; and on Infernal Misery
Brothers, we ought to fear sufficiently on account of three things: the belly, desire, and pride. For the devil ensnared our father Adam through these three, saying, “On whatever day you eat from this fruit, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like gods” (Gen. 3:5). Let us therefore keep these three most evil things in mind and fear them, lest, like Adam, naked, we be expelled from paradise.

Against the belly and gluttony, let us practice abstinence; against desire and greed, poverty of spirit and generosity in almsgiving; against pride and arrogance, true humility and complete submission. We know that we have God’s angels as guardians, just as the Savior himself says: “Amen, I say to you: their angels always see the face of my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 18:10). Therefore we can certainly believe that all our works, whatever we do by day and by night, whether good or evil, will be reported by them in God’s presence.

For a good angel urges us toward good counsel [Note: [Col. 1354] Add: “of the work.”], because when we do something good, we should believe that he is at our right hand. But when we think or do something evil, whether small or great, no one should doubt that we have a wicked angel as our instigator. He rejoices in this and mocks us, while the holy angel is saddened and grieves. And so, whenever we speak idle words or do anything evil, it is the devil’s counsel. But when we groan and sigh over our sins, or perform works of virtue, then we have the holy angel of God as our minister and counselor.

Let us therefore carefully guard ourselves against those three things mentioned above, which the devil supplied to Adam through the prompting of evil counsel. These three—namely, gluttony, desire, and pride—generate many and boundless evils. For from these evil and principal roots of vices arise sacrilege, homicide, fornication, theft, greed, lust, false testimony, anger, discord, perjury, and things like them.

Therefore, dearest brothers, let us set true humility against pride and arrogance; abstinence against gluttony; almsgiving against desire; perfect repentance against sacrilege; love of God and neighbor against homicide; kindness against theft; charity against greed; chastity against lust; truth of heart and mouth against false testimony; peace against anger [Note: [Col. 1354] The Germanensis manuscript reads: “against anger, true patience.”]; true concord and the firm bond of peace against discord [Col. 1355]; fear of the Lord against perjury—and above all, firm hope, right faith, and perfect charity.

By thus confronting vices with virtues and healing opposites with opposites, let us live before God and human beings with justice and fairness. These are the weapons of the angels: the breastplate and bow of the virtues, the strongest shield of faith, and the helmet of salvation. Whoever carries these weapons with him, unwavering in faith, can be harmed by no devil.

O dearest brothers, we must arm ourselves so completely against the worst enemy—the most merciless foe of the human race—that we may be able to overcome him manfully. He is always ready, like a robber, to steal our good works by supplying evil counsels.

Certainly many are deceived by the devil’s boldness and by the false security they imagine for themselves. They say, “I am young. While I have time, and while youth still flourishes in me, I will enjoy the world. When I reach old age and can no longer pursue what I desire, then I will repent and abstain.” But that wretched man does not consider that he has no certainty of even an hour or a moment, nor any power over his own life.

Come, dearest brothers: let this most evil security neither deceive nor seduce you. It cannot be called security, but rather danger. Therefore let us always keep the day of death in our memory; let us always stand in the fear of the Lord and do penance, because our passing—namely, the life of this age—is brief, and this miserable temporal power of the present world is fleeting and fragile.

Where are the emperors and kings? Where are the generals, princes, or barons [Note: [Col. 1355] The Germanensis manuscript omits “barons”]? Where are their gold, silver, and ornaments? It is written: “The powerful will suffer powerful torments” (Wis. 6:7).

Woe to that gloomy dwelling! Woe to that feeble pit! Woe to that cavern so dark, so deep, and so obscure! Let us consider, dearest brothers, how from such slight consolation comes such long calamity; from such brief joy, such long sadness; from such little light, such great darkness; from such meager profit, such grievous loss; from such empty security, such mighty danger; from the slight power of this age, such long torments destined to remain without end; from such brief pleasure, such long and yet bitter tears; and from the vain pomp of this world, such dreadful punishment in Gehenna.

From this punishment a father will not free his son, nor will a son stand surety for his father. There no friend will be found to redeem anyone, nor brother to come to his aid. Those who are there wish to die, but cannot obtain death. There bitter repentance is undertaken too late, and the repentant person is not thereby helped. There is no life, but a harsh dwelling and eternal death; there is dark fire and a terrible place; there is the flame of Gehenna, unquenchable; there are immeasurable torments and powerful sighs; there are mournful groans and prolonged weakness.

There the wretched are with the wretched, the proud with the proud, murderers with murderers, adulterers with adulterers, the greedy with the greedy, thieves with the wicked, false prelates with false subjects, dissolute religious persons with dissolute companions and wanton female companions, and so it is with each kind. All of them together will be tortured indescribably and tormented without end in the prison of hell.

May almighty God deign to rescue us from this, once we have been corrected from our vices—he who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON LXIX

[Note: [Col. 1355] It bears the style of the preceding sermons.]

### ON THE EXHORTATION TO PRAYER, WITH THE EXAMPLE OF A CERTAIN DECEASED MAN IN EGYPT; AND ON THE MISERY OF THE SOUL

Dearest brothers, when you wish to pray or mourn your sins, close the door upon yourselves and pray to the Lord your God with your whole heart. Then the Lord, looking upon you, will be gracious and compassionate toward you, like a loving mother toward her son when she finds him grieving and weeping.

Write these things, dearest ones, in your hearts and understand them. Those who do not understand should question those who possess sound understanding.

Acquire for yourselves, dearest ones, a heavenly treasure, setting aside the vanities of this world [Col. 1356]. Consider and greatly fear the following dreadful example. A certain holy man, placed in an ecstasy of mind, saw and heard about a certain soul departing from Egypt and struggling against its body.

The man whose soul is now being discussed was exceedingly robust in body and possessed of abundant temporal goods. Established in such bodily and worldly prosperity, he thought of nothing except accomplishing every evil within his power. He gave no thought at all to the salvation of his soul and lived wholly in sins.

It happened that, suffering from illness, he drew near to death. And behold, his spirit, knocking at the door of the body, was greatly shaken by terror and sorrow and delayed for a very long time in coming out. For it saw demons prepared before it, muttering among themselves and saying: “Why is he delaying? Why is this happening? Why is he making so many delays? Let us hurry; perhaps Michael and his companions will overpower us and take that soul from us, the soul that we have bound with our chains for many years.”

Then one of the demons replied: “Do not be afraid. He is ours. I know his deeds; I was always with him, day and night.”

When that wretched soul heard this, it said: “Woe is me! Why was I ever born or created? Woe is me! Why did I ever enter this body? Woe is me, that I ever existed in this most evil prison of flesh!

“Woe to you, miserable body! Why did you seize other people’s money? You gathered the resources of the poor and their possessions into your own house. You nourished yourself with delicate foods, while I hungered for our salvation. You drank flavorful wine, while I thirsted for the fountain of life. You adorned yourself with costly garments, while I remained naked of virtues.

“You were stout, while I was thin; you were ruddy, while I was pale; you were cheerful, while I was sad. You laughed, while I wept; you rejoiced, while I grieved. You always acted against me. Now you are food for worms, rot, and dust.

“You will rest for a little while in the earth, and afterward you will be led with me into hell, destined to suffer eternal torments just as I too shall.”

After these words, the body began to sweat and give up its spirit. Then that devil, the angel of Satan, who had remained not as his good guardian but as his evil guardian and instigator, seized the soul and said:

“Do not delay, companions; do not waste time. Take hold of the sharpest tridents and drive them painfully into his eyes! For whatever he saw, whether beautiful or shameful, he desired entirely.

“Pierce his mouth, because in eating, drinking, or speaking he never spared either the just or the unjust, whatever he desired.

“Pierce also his deceitful and false heart, in which there was neither piety nor mercy nor charity nor goodness.

“Pierce as well his grasping hands, which were ready for theft, robbery, and plunder, but slow to perform works of piety.

“And likewise his feet, which were swift toward every evil path.”

Then, punishing that wretched soul, expelled from the body, limb by limb, they lifted it upon their black, dark, bat-like wings and led it to hell.

As it was traveling in this manner, the soul saw a great brightness and said: “Where—or what—is that brightness?”

The demons replied: “Do you not recognize the homeland from which you departed when you came into this exile? Once you renounced our pomps and drove us out through Baptism and the sign of the cross. You heard the prophets and apostles; you also heard your priests and parish priests [Note: [Col. 1356] Note.], who never ceased preaching to you the way of life and praising the name of your Savior. But your heart was far from their teaching.

“Now you are passing beside that homeland from which you first came, yet you will neither turn aside there nor enter it. You hear the choirs of angels, not for your consolation but for your perpetual desolation. You will see the brightness of the saints, yet you will not dwell there, just as we do not, for we were cast out of paradise. As we were and are in perdition, so you also will be with us.

“Until now you were in exile; now you will remain with us in damnation, where we have many companions” [Col. 1357].

Then that wretched soul began to say with pain, weeping, and immense groaning:

“Woe to me, wretched creature, that I was ever created and born, or placed in this defiled body! Woe to me, that, placed in this damnation, I have lost eternal brightness, from which I once departed without stain!

“Now I see the spacious road that leads to the homeland, yet I will not travel along it.”

Then the enemies led her, weeping and groaning in this manner, to the gates of perdition. There the devil was prepared to receive her in the likeness of a dragon. He opened his most foul jaws, swallowed her, and vomited her into a most burning place of fire, where those like her await judgment.

Instructed and warned by this example, dearest ones, let the savage wounds of others be certain medicines for us. While we are able, let us amend our lives here for the better, renouncing carnal things and pursuing spiritual ones, so that, departing joyfully from this little body, we may be able to say:

“My soul has clung to you, because my flesh has been chastened for you, my God. For this reason, O my Lord, may your right hand receive me.”

May he deign to grant this to us, who saves all who hope in him and who lives and reigns as God forever and ever. Amen.

The true death that people do not fear [Note: [Col. 1357] It should read: “do not fear.”] is the separation of the soul from God. And for the most part people fear this death, etc.

## SERMON LXXIII

[Note: [Col. 1357] It is a fragment not inconsistent with Augustine’s character. It appears in Vignier’s *Supplement*, p. 2, sermon 27.]

### ON THE ONE WHO RETAINS ANGER IN HIS HEART FOR A LONG TIME AND DOES NOT WISH TO HUMBLE HIMSELF

Everyone who wishes to avenge himself on his enemy calls down God’s vengeance upon himself. But do what the Apostle says, brothers: “Returning no one evil for evil.” For this is to conquer evil by good [Note: [Col. 1357] Vignier has “to conquer.”].

When you wish to avenge yourself, you undoubtedly wish to conquer. Take care lest, while you wish to conquer a person, you are conquered by anger. Because he injured you, you also wish to injure him; because he harmed you, you also wish to harm him—and, so that you may conquer, to harm him more than he harmed you.

How do you conquer evil with evil? The Apostle did not say this; you did not hear this. Rather, you heard: “Do not be conquered by evil.” Perhaps you will reply, “That is also what I want. But no one conquers me.”

The Apostle said: “Conquer evil with good.” This means that the one who injured you through his anger, conquer him through your patience; the one who injured you through his greed, conquer him through your mercy.

Look: the one who stripped you through his greed is in need; look, he is hungry. Take your revenge—he is your enemy. But if he is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him drink. “For by doing this you will heap burning coals upon his head” (Rom. 12:21, 20).

If you think that by this he urged us toward wickedness, as though he had said that you should harm him more by piling coals upon his head, then you wish to conquer evil with evil. And even if you perform that almsgiving, you wish to perform it out of a desire for vengeance.

But you say: “What does ‘You will heap burning coals upon his head’ mean?” The burning coals are those in which he is burned so that he may repent of having been hostile toward you.

You are a human being, and he is a human being. He wished to injure you; do you wish to injure him? Behold, you are both evil. How then do you say, “I hate evil,” when you increase the number of evil people? Do you wish to conquer your enemy? Look within yourself and see whether you have there someone whom you ought to conquer.

When you have considered this, you will say to yourself: “The one who injured me is a human being. Let me pray to the Lord for him, that he may repent.” If you do this, you will have both lost an enemy and gained a friend, since the one who injured you has been made good through your prayers.

And let us not, as servants [Note: [Col. 1358] Vignier has “his own servants.”], hasten to defend ourselves before the Lord with shameless haste, so that, when that day of vengeance arrives, we may not be punished with the impious and sinners, but may be honored with the just and those who fear God forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON LXXVI

[Note: [Col. 1358] In a Remigian manuscript of approximately seven hundred years, it is attributed to Augustine.]

### ON THOUGHTS

First of all, we must resist evil thoughts. When the adversary whispers something carnal or filthy, it must be destroyed and shaken off before it stains and wounds the mind. For he is accustomed to bring sadness, to inspire doubts about one’s purpose, to breathe despair of good things, to introduce various desires, and to sharpen every kind of arrow, so that, as it is written in the tenth Psalm, “They may shoot in secret at the upright in heart” (Ps. 10:3).

Therefore, as soon as such a thought begins, turn your mind to the Lord with a doubled sigh, and do not permit the counsel that could defile your understanding to approach.

For just as a white garment, when sprinkled with blood, regains its whiteness if it is washed immediately, but if the stain remains and becomes baked in, it is scarcely washed clean, so the human mind, if it immediately destroys an arising thought, can retain its own brightness; but if it permits the thought to remain longer, it is scarcely cleansed except with great effort.

This is the first victory of our secret battle, which the Lord and the angels await: when the human mind faithfully confronts evil thoughts and overcomes wicked thoughts with good reasoning. From this praise arises; from this glory grows, as the Apostle says: “When he comes,” he says, “the Lord will bring to light the hidden things of darkness and will disclose the counsels of hearts; then each person will receive praise from God” (1 Cor. 4:5).

For it is clear among the more faithful that from God the Judge a person receives either praise or blame not only for deeds but also for thoughts.

Likewise, brothers, let it not escape us that we frequently suffer thoughts against our will, and that we frequently endure evil thoughts. We learn when this happens from the Apostle, who says: “I do not do the good I want, but the evil I hate, that I do”; and, “I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind and taking me captive under the law of sin” (Rom. 7:15, 23).

Indeed, it is Satan’s one particular concern to burden the human mind with wicked counsels. For from the beginning we received this injury: we watch the serpent’s head, while he watches our heel—not, certainly, the heel of our feet, but of our mind—so that, if somehow he can, he may hold back with his bite the soul running toward heavenly things and keep it among earthly things.

Therefore, if we are to live with sincere minds against these dark forces of evil, the eyes of the heart must be carefully tended. And, if we are to conquer, weapons are absolutely necessary for us. “The weapons of our warfare,” he says, “are not carnal, but powerful through God for the destruction of strongholds,” destroying evil counsels (2 Cor. 10:4). Amen.

Saint Aurelius Augustine, Bishop of Hippo, *Two Books on Diverse Questions to Simplicianus*. 101–102

### Book One

Two questions from Paul’s Letter to the Romans are treated, as proposed by Simplicianus. Same page.

**Preface.** Same page.

**Question One.** For what purpose the Law was given. Desire increased through the Law. How sin was dead without the Law. How it came to life again. Who makes bad use of the Law. The Law is fulfilled only by spiritual people. “Carnal” used in two senses. The punishment of original sin. What the law of sin in the members means. Passages in which the Law may seem to be called evil. The Law is good. The Manichaean error concerning the Old Law. The testimonies are explained by which the Law may seem not to be good. 103

**II.** The argument of the Letter to the Romans. The grace of faith precedes good works. The grace of faith is lesser in catechumens and greater in the regenerate. The Apostle’s purpose in the examples of Jacob and Esau. Good works arise from grace, not grace from works. How Jacob’s election and Esau’s rejection are just. Whether Jacob was elected on the foreknowledge of future faith. Election from grace and God’s purpose. Whether faith is to be counted among the gifts of grace. How Esau’s rejection is just. Faith is the gift of the merciful God. Why the gift of faith was withheld from Esau. Whether Esau was rejected and Jacob approved on the foreknowledge of their future will. Good will comes to exist in us through God’s action. Whether calling produces good will. Effectual calling. Why Esau was not called effectually. What God’s hardening is. Resolution of the question concerning Esau’s rejection. All human beings are one mass of sin. How God hated Esau, although he hates nothing that he has made. What sin is. The vessels of destruction are made for the correction of others. Not all are called, but people from among all—both Jews and Gentiles. The Apostle’s purpose in the Letter to the Romans. How hidden the election of grace is. 111

The remaining five or six questions proposed by Simplicianus from the Books of Kings. 127–128

How the Spirit of God in Saul was both good and evil. Saul, while pursuing David, was checked by a prophetic and good spirit. Certain gifts of the Holy Spirit can be possessed without charity. How wisdom and knowledge differ. How repentance can be attributed to God. Why repentance and jealousy seem less suitable to God than foreknowledge, anger, and similar terms. 138

## Notice concerning the Book on Christian Combat

289–290

Saint Aurelius Augustine, Bishop of Hippo, *One Book on Christian Combat*. It exhorts and instructs people to fight the Christian struggle against the devil. [Col. 1366] He teaches that the devil is conquered and subdued by us when desires are conquered and the body is brought into servitude; but that the body itself is subjected to servitude if we submit ourselves to God, whom every creature serves either willingly or by necessity. He shows that human weakness is fortified by the aid of faith, and that through the Son of God made flesh it has been given a remedy suited to its need. He then goes through the individual articles of the faith contained in the Creed, exposing the various heresies that have arisen against it and commanding that they be avoided. 289–290

**Chapter One.** A crown promised to those who conquer. The adversary, the devil, is conquered through Christ’s aid. Same page.

**V.** “Spiritual wickedness in the heavenly places”: in what sense this is said. 293

**VIII.** All things are governed by divine providence. 295

**IX.** Exhortation to taste the sweetness of God. 296

**XV.** Nor should those who introduce three gods be listened to. Same page.

**XVI.** Nor should those who deny the equality and eternity of the persons be listened to. 300

**XVII.** The faith of Christ’s incarnation. Those who deny that Christ is God must not be listened to. Same page.

**XVIII.** Nor should those who deny that Christ had a true body be listened to. Same page.

**XIX.** Nor should those who deny that Christ had a human mind be listened to. 301

**XX.** Nor should those who say that he was assumed by the Wisdom of God in no other way than the other saints, who become wise, be listened to. Same page.

**XXI.** Nor should those who say that only the body was assumed by the Word be listened to. 302

**XXII.** Nor should those who deny that Christ’s body was formed from a woman, and say that it was made in the same way as that in which the Spirit appeared in a dove, be listened to. Through a woman came death; through a woman, life. Same page.

**XXIII.** Those who say that the Son of God is a creature because he suffered must not be listened to. The Son of God suffered without any change in his divinity. 303

**XXIX.** Nor should the Donatists be listened to, who deny that the Church is spread throughout the world. Donatus himself was divided from his own followers. Donatus’ case against Caecilianus at Rome proves nothing. The Donatists want Baptism to be useless unless they themselves have administered it. 306

**XXX.** The Luciferians must not be listened to. Although they do not rebaptize, they cut themselves off from the Church because the Church received those who repented of the Arian heresy. 307

**XXXI.** Nor should the Cathari be listened to, who deny that the Church can forgive all sins and forbid widows to marry. 308

**XXXII.** Nor should those who deny the resurrection of the flesh be listened to. 309

**XXXIII.** When we are little, we should be nourished by the simplicity of faith. Perfect charity allows neither worldly desire nor fear. Knowledge of the truth comes in a cleansed heart. Same page.

Saint Aurelius Augustine, Bishop of Hippo, *One Book on Catechizing the Uninstructed*. Requested by a Carthaginian deacon, he undertakes to teach the art of catechizing. First he gives instructions so that this duty may be fulfilled not only by a definite method and suitable procedure but also without weariness and with cheerfulness. Then, applying the instructions in practice, he offers as examples two discourses prepared for instructing someone who wishes to become a Christian: one longer and the other very brief. 309–310

**Chapter One.** At the request of a Carthaginian deacon, he writes about catechizing the uninstructed. Same page.

**II.** A discourse that often pleases the listener displeases the speaker; why this happens. Whoever gives a discourse should take care to speak without tediousness and cheerfully. 311

**III.** What a complete narrative for the person being catechized should be. The narrative must be directed toward the goal of charity. The ancient Scriptures are presented in order to commend Christ’s coming, whose end is charity. 313

**IV.** The chief reason for Christ’s coming: the commendation of charity. What is narrated from Scripture about Christ in catechesis must be related to love. 314

**V.** The person approaching catechesis must be examined concerning the purpose for which he wishes to become a Christian. 316

**VI.** The opening of catechesis, and the narrative from the history of the creation of the world up to the Church’s present time. 317

**VII.** The resurrection, judgment, and certain other matters to be conveyed after the narrative. Same page.

**VIII.** How educated people are to be catechized. 318

**IX.** How grammarians and orators are to be treated. The voice directed to God’s ears; the emotions of the soul. 320

**X.** Now concerning the acquisition of cheerfulness. Six causes that bring weariness to the catechist. Remedy for the first cause of weariness. Same page.

**XI.** Remedy for the second cause of weariness. 322

**XII.** Remedy for the third cause of weariness. 323

**XIII.** Remedy for the fourth cause of tediousness. How a listener exhausted either by listening or by standing is to be refreshed. In which Churches the practice of listening to the word of God while seated has been adopted. 324

**XIV.** Remedy against the fifth cause of weariness. Remedy against the sixth cause of weariness. Again, against the sixth cause. 326

**XV.** The discourse must be adapted to the diversity of persons. 328

**XVI.** A model discourse for the catechist. An opening based on the praiseworthy purpose of undertaking the Christian religion for the sake of future rest. Rest must not be sought in restless things. Nor in wealth or honors. Those who seek rest in bodily pleasures and spectacles. 329

**XVII.** The person who wishes to become a Christian for temporal advantage is reproved. The true Christian is one who professes the religion for the sake of future rest. He proceeds to narrate what must be believed. Why the Son of God became human. 330

**XVIII.** What is to be believed concerning the creation of human beings and other things. Man placed in paradise. Why the one whom God foreknew would sin was created. The fall of man and the angel did no harm to God. 332

**XIX.** The good and the wicked in the Church, to be separated at the end. Two cities from the beginning of the human race. The Flood and the ark as a sacrament. Abraham and the people of Israel. Their words and deeds were prophecy. 333

Of the Israelites…
slavery in Egypt, and liberation and the passage through the Red Sea. Baptism represented in figure. The sacrifice of the sheep as a figure of Christ’s Passion. The Law written by the finger of God. Jerusalem as a type of the heavenly city. 335

**XXI.** The Babylonian captivity and what the events in it signify. What kind of freedom was restored after the Babylonian captivity. 336

**XXII.** The six ages of the world. The sixth age from Christ’s coming. Christ, revealing the New Testament of the eternal inheritance, teaches by his example that earthly things are to be despised. His birth, life, and death. 338

**XXIII.** The Holy Spirit sent on the fiftieth day after Christ’s resurrection. The Jews converted through the preaching of the Apostles and burning with zeal for the evangelical life. Churches established among the Gentiles through Paul. 339

**XXIV.** The Church sprouts and is pruned like a vine. From those things that are seen to have been fulfilled, let the things still remaining to be fulfilled be believed—especially the future judgment. 341

**XXV.** Faith in the resurrection commended. Everlasting death in torments. The eternal life of the saints. We must beware not only of pagans, Jews, and heretics, but also of bad Christians. Association should be with the good, yet hope must not be placed in them. 342

**XXVI.** The initiation of the catechumen, with an exposition of the signs. A shorter discourse is sometimes to be used. Another, shorter discourse begins. The Son of God was sent down so that we might be freed from the death that entered through Adam. 344

**XXVII.** The prophecies of the Old Testament are seen to have been fulfilled in the Church. Hence faith is strengthened in those things that remain to come: the final judgment and the resurrection. Temptations from the wicked, even those found within the Church, must be avoided. Association with the good. All hope in God. 346

[Col. 1368]

## NOTICE ON THE BOOK ON CONTINENCE

347–348

**OF ST. AURELIUS AUGUSTINE, BISHOP OF HIPPO, ONE BOOK ON CONTINENCE.**—He explains two verses of Psalm 140: “Set, O Lord, a guard over my mouth, and a door of continence around my lips; let not my heart incline to wicked words, to make excuses for sins.” Taking his subject from this, he teaches that the virtue of continence must, in accordance with its office, restrain the lusts both of body and of mind, and must generally keep watch over the restraint of the pleasures of desire that oppose the pleasure of wisdom. He commands us not to trust in our own powers when fighting against desire, which is indeed recognized through the Law but overcome only through grace. He censures the proud who offer various excuses for their sins; in this connection he refutes at greater length the Manichaeans, who attributed their sins to an inborn nature of evil within themselves. He also proves from the same Apostle that the passage in Galatians 5:17, “For the flesh desires against the spirit,” and so forth—by which they wished to demonstrate two natures, one good and one evil—was wrongly understood by those heretics.

349–350

**CHAPTER ONE.** Continence from the lust of the flesh is a gift of God. Continence of the mouth is itself also a gift of God. The mouth of the body and the mouth of the heart. Ibid.

**II.** The mouth of the heart, through which consent is expressed as an inward word. Continence of the heart commended by Christ under the name of the mouth. The continence of the heart is sometimes violated without violation of the body. When continence of the heart is preserved, one does not sin against bodily continence. Ibid.

**III.** The struggle of continence against lusts so long as we are in this life. The inner struggle of desires is experienced only by those who fight for the virtues. Desire is recognized through the Law, but overcome only through grace. We must fight lest the desire for sin reign. The works of the flesh must be put to death. 352

**IV.** Presumption concerning one’s own powers must be avoided if continence is to be preserved. To live according to man and to live according to the flesh are the same thing. 355

**V.** Whoever wishes to overcome the desire for sin must not trust in himself. The excuse of sins must be restrained through continence. Various excuses for sins. The accusation of fate, fortune, and the devil—and, among the Manichaeans, of God himself. 356–357

**VI.** Against others who, in order to excuse themselves, say that sins please God. God brings good even from evil things. Man was created with the power to sin, but is to receive as his reward the inability to sin. 358

**VII.** The duties of continence and justice alike tend toward peace. Against the madness of the Manichaeans concerning two natures fighting one another. There is war in man because of the weakness contracted through guilt; peace will come when that weakness has been healed. 359

**VIII.** The flesh desires against the spirit, not because it is an inimical nature, but because it is corrupted. The desires of the flesh arise from corruption; they can be diminished here, but cannot be entirely removed except in the life to come. The desire of the flesh is here the punishment of sin; when the flesh has been healed, it will not exist among the blessed. 361

**IX.** The flesh is not evil by nature, since the Apostle urges husbands to love their wives by its example. Three unions are indicated by the Apostle, all of them good, the third being that of flesh and spirit. Why no example of the woman’s subjection is given from the flesh. 363

**X.** The Manichaean heresy denies that Christ possessed true flesh. It says that souls belong to Christ, bodies to the devil, and that both sexes are from the devil. 365

**XI.** The comparison of flesh and Church, and the respects in which it holds. 366

**XII.** The false continence of the Manichaeans and certain others, especially heretics. Likewise the unclean continence of certain people, who resort to magical arts in order to obtain other men’s wives. 367

**XIII.** Continence restrains and governs not only bodily lusts but also the desires of the mind. The evil movements of the soul must be restrained by withholding consent and rejecting even the pleasure of thought. 369

**XIV.** Faith without works does not save. The vices of the flesh must be steadily conquered. In the battle of continence, strength and victory must be ascribed to God. 370

## NOTICE ON THE BOOK ON THE GOOD OF MARRIAGE

371–374

**OF ST. AURELIUS AUGUSTINE, BISHOP OF HIPPO, ONE BOOK ON THE GOOD OF MARRIAGE.**—Augustine teaches that marriage is honorable in many respects, and is good not only by comparison with fornication but in its own kind, being in itself free from every sin. He demonstrates that continence is far superior [Col. 1369]; and therefore, although in former times the saints had to make use of marriage as necessary for propagating the people of God through whom Christ was to be prophesied and born, now, after the saying, “Let him accept it who is able to accept it,” marriage should be embraced only by those who are unable to remain continent. In other respects, he shows that our continent men and women can scarcely be compared in any way with those ancient married people—Abraham and Sarah in particular—much less preferred to them, since those people, although married, possessed the virtue of continence in the disposition of their minds and excelled above all in the praise of obedience, which contains all the virtues as though it were their matrix.

373–374

**CHAPTER ONE.** The first association of husband and wife. Ibid.

**II.** On the propagation of children, if man had not sinned: differing opinions. Ibid.

**III.** The good of marriage is manifold. The first and second good of marriage. The third good of marriage. 375

**IV.** The fourth good of marriage. What adultery is. Faith must be preserved even in lowly matters and preferred to this life. 375–376

**V.** When the union of a man and woman is marriage, and when it is not. 376

**VI.** On the demanding and rendering of the marriage debt. 377

**VII.** The marriage covenant is not annulled by the separation of the spouses. Whether, after dismissing an adulterous wife, it is permitted to marry another. The taking of another wife is forbidden according to Roman custom. 378

**VIII.** The practice of divorce among the Gentiles and among the Jews. Marriage is wholly good, not good merely by comparison with fornication. 379

**IX.** Marriage is to be desired only for another reason. The saints ought to have used marriage in the earliest times; now continence is to be preferred. 380

**X.** An objection against continence. Now only those should marry who cannot remain continent. Marriage is not a sin. The only marital intercourse is that undertaken for the purpose of procreation. 380–381

**XI.** The use contrary to nature is more detestable in a wife than in a prostitute. The greater holiness of the unmarried is commended, not the holiness of the married denied. 382

**XII.** Married women who think only about how to please God are exceedingly rare. 383

**XIII.** Marriage was formerly to be embraced even by the continent, but now only by those who cannot remain continent. How rare it is to use marriage solely for the sake of offspring. Ibid.

**XIV.** To use a concubine for the sake of children is a greater sin than to use a wife because of lack of continence. 384

**XV.** Marriage cannot be dissolved on account of infertility. Whether, with the wife’s consent, it is permissible to take another woman so that children common to both may be born: he does not dare to decide. 385

**XVI.** In intercourse and in the use of food, the principle of virtue and vice is similar. Ibid.

**XVII.** The married people of the present time are not to be compared with the holy married people of the earliest age. It was at some time permitted for one man to have several wives, but never for one woman to have several husbands. 386

**XVIII.** The sacrament of marriage has now been reduced to one husband and one wife. A bishop may not be ordained unless he is the husband of one wife. 387

**XIX.** Whether at least our continent people are to be compared with the ancient married saints. 388

**XX.** The law of purification after intercourse does not show that intercourse is a sin. Whether any of the continent of the present time can be compared with the ancient married fathers. 389

**XXI.** Continence, like the other virtues, must be distinguished as disposition and action. It is taught by Christ’s example that a virtue can exist in disposition even when it is not expressed in action. 390

**XXII.** In the ancients continence was to be held in disposition, but now in action. The inquiry of the Jovinianists is rejected. 391

**XXIII.** Continence is better than marital chastity; yet married people can be better than continent people. The good of obedience is greater than that of continence. A married woman who is more obedient is to be preferred to a virgin who is less obedient. Obedience is the mother of all virtues. 392

**XXIV.** The good of marriage among Christians is threefold. The ancient married people possessed obedience in action and continence in disposition. 394

**XXV.** The calumnies of the Manichaeans against the fathers of the Old Testament are refuted. 395

**XXVI.** The continent of the present time should not think disparagingly of the ancient married fathers. Virginity must be protected by humility. Ibid.

**OF ST. AURELIUS AUGUSTINE, BISHOP OF HIPPO, ONE BOOK ON HOLY VIRGINITY.**—He first discusses the excellence of sacred virginity consecrated to God, demonstrating that no marital fruitfulness can now be compared with it [Col. 1370]. He then confronts two opposed errors: one condemning marriage, the other equating it with virginity. The former consists in thinking that marriage is indirectly and tacitly condemned by the Apostle when he says to the Corinthians, “Nevertheless such shall have trouble in the flesh; but I spare you”; the latter in arguing from his writing to the same people, “I think therefore that this is good because of the present necessity,” that perpetual continence is commended for the sake of the life of this world, not the life to come. Thereafter he commands Christ’s virgins to possess the humility by which so excellent a gift is preserved, and exhorts them with the greatest earnestness and gravity to pursue it above all.

395–398

**CHAPTER ONE.** Virgins should not despise the holy married fathers. 397

**II.** Christ, son of a virgin and bridegroom of virgins. The Church, like Mary, is both mother and virgin. Ibid.

**III.** Spiritual kinship with Christ is to be preferred to his bodily kinship. Ibid.

**IV.** Mary’s virginity was dedicated to God by a vow before she heard that she would conceive Christ. 398

**V.** The birth of one Virgin is the glory of all virgins. Virgins themselves are mothers of Christ in spirit. Ibid.

**VI.** Mary alone is simultaneously virgin and mother in body and spirit. 399

**VII.** No marital fruitfulness can be compared with virginity. Ibid.

**VIII.** Virginity is honored because it is dedicated to God. 400

**IX.** Lost virginity is compensated by no fruitfulness of the flesh. Ibid.

**X.** Marriage is not to be compared with virginity because it bears children. 401

**XI.** Virgins are praised because they are dedicated to God. Ibid.

**XII.** Sacred virgins are born for the Church not through bodily but through spiritual fruitfulness. The good of marriage is inferior to the good of holy virginity. Ibid.

**XIII.** Against those who think that continence is useful only for the present life. Ibid.

**XIV.** Virginity is commended not by commandment but by counsel, for the attainment of a singular glory in the life to come. 402

**XV.** Counsel, not commandment, is given not to marry. 403

**XVI.** What the trouble of the flesh in marriage is. Ibid.

**XVII.** Against those who think that the Apostle condemned marriage there. How harmful it is to attribute a lie to Scripture. 404

**XVIII.** Virginity is to be preferred in such a way that marriage is not condemned. Ibid.

**XIX.** Two opposing errors concerning virginity and marriage. 405

**XX.** The Apostle’s saying, “But I spare you,” is wrongly applied to the condemnation of marriage. Ibid.

**XXI.** The praise and merit of virginity are greater when marriage is not avoided as though it were evil. 406

**XXII.** It is shown from the Apostle that virginity is to be loved not for this life but for the life to come. 407

**XXIII.** The same is proved from the words of the Lord. 408

**XXIV.** Likewise from the words of Isaiah. Why the Church is called the kingdom of heaven. Ibid.

**XXV.** Isaiah speaks of the eternal reward promised to eunuchs. 409

**XXVI.** The objection concerning the denarius given to all, against the diversity of rewards. 410

**XXVII.** The future glory of virgins is greater, and they have certain distinctive joys in heaven. To follow the Lamb wherever he goes belongs particularly to virgins. Ibid.

**XXVIII.** How far all can follow the Lamb. 411

**XXIX.** Where they follow him, virgins alone do so. There is no envy in heaven because of the difference of rewards. 411–412

**XXX.** He exhorts to virginity as a work beyond obligation, not as a commandment. 412

**XXXI.** Humility is especially commended to virgins. The measure of humility given to each person. Pride is the mother of envy. Ibid.

**XXXII.** The Lord’s commandments and examples concerning humility. 413

**XXXIII.** Humility must be guarded by Christians, but especially by virgins. 414

**XXXIV.** The present exhortation to humility does not concern unmarried women living contrary to their purpose. 415

**XXXV.** Christ commands that humility be learned from him. 416

**XXXVI.** The teaching of humility is readily heard by sinners. Virgins should hear it much more. Ibid.

**XXXVII.** The example of humility set before virgins in the Lord himself. 417

**XXXVIII.** Fear is necessary even for virgins—not worldly or servile fear, but the chaste fear of God. 418

**XXXIX.** The Holy Spirit’s dwelling is a humbled heart. A reason for the just to humble themselves arises from the danger of falling. 419

[Col. 1371]

**XL.** Those who will fall are mixed among the just, so that fear may be increased by their fall. Let the just person not think that little has been forgiven him and therefore love little. Let him count as forgiven whatever evil has not been committed by him. 420

**XLI.** The first thought of humility: that virginity is possessed as a gift of God. Commandments are fulfilled only by the one who gives them when he commands. Obedience and penitence are alike gifts of God. Ibid.

**XLII.** Continence and wisdom likewise are provided only by God. 421

**XLIII.** Virgins must not exalt themselves over this very gift of God. 422

**XLIV.** What a virgin should consider, so that she may not truly dare to prefer herself to a woman, even a married woman. Ibid.

**XLV.** The hundredfold, sixtyfold, and thirtyfold fruit understood in various ways. 423

**XLVI.** The superior character of the common life of consecrated women. Ibid.

**XLVII.** So that a virgin may not become inflated, let her consider that perhaps she cannot suffer for Christ what a married woman can. 424

**XLVIII.** Another occasion for humility: no one here is without sin. Ibid.

**XLIX.** Virgins are irreproachable through the cleansing of sins and humble confession. The deadly security of sinning in the hope of the forgiveness promised to those who confess. 425

**L.** The small sins that creep upon watchful people grow through pride and are destroyed through humility. If anyone here happens to be without sin, the greater he is, the more he humbles himself. 425–426

**LI.** God, who gave virginity and guards it, dwells among the humble. 426

**LII.** The manner in which humility is to be practiced by virgins. Ibid.

**LIII.** The holier virgins are, the more humble they should be. 427

**LIV.** Let them love the bridegroom with their whole heart. Ibid.
