## NOTICE ON THE BOOK ON THE GOOD OF WIDOWHOOD

429–430

**OF ST. AURELIUS AUGUSTINE, BISHOP OF HIPPO, THE BOOK ON THE GOOD OF WIDOWHOOD, OR A LETTER TO THE WIDOW JULIANA.**—Here he teaches and exhorts widows. First, by teaching, he proves that the profession of holy widowhood is to be preferred to marriage, while second marriages, indeed even third and subsequent marriages, are lawful and never evil; and that women who marry after a vow of widowhood or virginity are rightly condemned, but that the marriages themselves are neither to be regarded as adulteries nor to be dissolved. He wishes the merits of widows to be assessed from the very strength of their continence and piety, and therefore demonstrates that a widow who has had two husbands may sometimes rightly be preferred to a widow who has had one. Then, by exhortation, he urges Juliana above all to attribute her continence to the benefit of God and to beware of the rumors that have begun to spread among certain enemies of the grace of Christ. He commands her to devote all her efforts, together with her virgin daughter and widowed mother-in-law, to pleasing God; to have spiritual delights in place of carnal pleasures; and finally not to neglect guarding her reputation.

429–432

**CHAPTER ONE.** Having been asked by Juliana, he writes about the profession of widowhood. He explains the Apostle’s teaching on this matter. 431

**II.** Among the Apostle’s unmarried women are not virgins alone, but widows also. Ibid.

**III.** The good of widowhood is greater than that of marriage, although marriage is truly good. The fidelity of marriage and its other goods, though inferior to widowhood. 432

**IV.** The profession of widowhood does not condemn second marriages. The error of the Cataphrygians and Novatians, disclosed by Tertullian. 433

**V.** The good of widowhood is called honorable because it is more honorable, not because marriage is considered shameful. 434

**VI.** Married women are also holy in body, although less so than unmarried women. The good of widowhood is not diminished when the good of marriage is praised, but increased. Whether the widow Anna was more blessed than Ruth, who married twice. Ibid.

**VII.** Holy women in the time of the Law married not because of desire but under the compulsion of obedience. 435

**VIII.** At the present time both second and first marriages are to be rejected unless lack of continence stands in the way. In former times marriage was obedience to the Law; now it is a remedy for weakness and a consolation of human nature. 436

**IX.** To marry after a vow of continence is condemnable; yet such marriages are not to be condemned. 437

**X.** Against those who say that the marriages of women who have fallen from a holy purpose are adulteries. The whole Church is a virgin. 438

**XI.** The fall from a holy purpose is evil, but the marriages of those who have fallen are nevertheless good. 439

**XII.** No marriages, however numerous, are to be condemned. Ibid.

**XIII.** A widow who has had two husbands may sometimes be preferred to one who has had one. The merits of widows are to be assessed from the strength of their continence itself. 440

**XIV.** Another comparison among threefold widows. He wishes for Juliana the widow the three goods that belonged to Anna. 440

[Col. 1372]

**XV.** Recapitulation of the preceding. 441

**XVI.** The second part of the little work, concerning exhortation. Continence is a gift of God. 442

**XVII.** Against the Pelagians, who defend free choice in such a way as to deny the grace of God. 443

**XVIII.** The strength of exhortation comes from grace. 444

**XIX.** He exhorts to the good of widowhood. Let Juliana the widow direct all her attention to pleasing God. He wishes the virgin Demetrias, her grandmother, and her mother likewise to have one pursuit: pleasing God. 445

**XX.** The worldly allurements that so quickly fail are to be despised. 447

**XXI.** Spiritual delights should take the place of carnal pleasures for widows. Ibid.

**XXII.** Care for a good reputation. 448

**XXIII.** Those who practice continence should persevere and persuade others to practice continence. Conclusion. 449

**OF ST. AURELIUS AUGUSTINE, BISHOP OF HIPPO, TWO BOOKS ON ADULTEROUS MARRIAGES, TO POLLENTIUS.**

451–452

**BOOK ONE.**—Two questions in particular are treated. The first concerns the passage in the First Letter to the Corinthians, “But to those who are in marriage I command . . . the woman . . . if she departs, let her remain unmarried,” and so forth. Pollentius thinks that the Apostle’s command applies to women who leave their husbands for a reason other than fornication, and that only these women are forbidden to marry another man. Augustine, on the contrary, maintains that it concerns only those who have left their husbands because of fornication, and that departure is not permitted for any other reason. The second question concerns the other passage in the same letter: “But to the rest I say, not the Lord,” and so forth. Augustine teaches that the Apostle said this as an admonition, namely, that believing spouses should not use the permission granted to them to leave unbelieving spouses. Pollentius, on the contrary, holds that Paul there forbade believing spouses to dismiss even unbelieving spouses. Finally, the question is touched upon whether catechumens lying at the point of death benefit from being baptized when they neither request it nor can answer on their own behalf.

Ibid.

**CHAPTER ONE.** The disagreement between Pollentius and Augustine concerning Paul’s passage: whether a spouse who wishes to remain unmarried may depart without the cause of fornication. Ibid.

**II.** A spouse may not depart except because of fornication. Ibid.

**III.** The Apostle’s passage is to be understood of a woman who departs from a fornicating husband. 453

**IV.** The Apostle is wrongly understood as speaking of a woman who departs out of a preference for continence. Ibid.

**V.** That interpretation of the Apostle is refuted. 454

**VI.** Pollentius’s opinion: a woman who departs from an adulterer is not forbidden by command to marry another, but should avoid it only because of reproach. 454

**VII.** The command that even a woman who departs from an adulterer should remain unmarried. 455

**VIII.** The same rule applies equally to man and woman in this matter. Ibid.

**IX.** Pollentius’s objection from a passage in Matthew. It is refuted from a similar passage in James. The sins of the ignorant. Matthew is to be understood from Mark and Luke. 456

**X.** How the passage in Matthew stands in the books read by Pollentius. 457

**XI.** Another somewhat obscure passage in Matthew, clarified by the other Evangelists. 458

**XII.** A woman dismissed because of fornication does not cease to be the wife of the man who dismissed her. 459

**XIII.** Pollentius holds that unbelieving spouses may not be dismissed; Augustine says that this is permitted, though not advantageous. Ibid.

**XIV.** Many things not commanded by the prescription of law are to be done on the advice of charity. Ibid.

**XV.** Certain things are lawful but not advantageous. 460

**XVI.** What is lawful but not advantageous differs from what is unlawful, so that if the former is done it is not a sin, although it ought not to be done. 461

**XVII.** How what is permitted but not advantageous differs from what is not advantageous because it is not permitted. Christ neither forbids nor commands the dismissal of an unbelieving spouse; Paul advises that it not be done. Ibid.

**XVIII.** Why, just as the Israelites were commanded to abandon foreign wives, Christians are not similarly commanded to abandon unbelieving spouses. Paul’s advice is to be received as Christ’s. What is permitted is sometimes advantageous and sometimes not. Departure from an unbelieving spouse is not prohibited by a command of the Law but by the advice of charity. 462

**XIX.** The advice not to marry concerns what is more advantageous; the advice not to dismiss an unbeliever concerns something whose opposite is not advantageous. 464

**XX.** Concerning not dismissing unbelieving spouses: the Apostle’s statement is advice, not command. A warning here that the matter is discretionary; other statements of the Apostle, however, concern a matter commanded. [Col. 1373]

**XXI.** Pollentius’s opinion concerning marriages with unbelievers is examined. The question concerning those already joined is different from that concerning those who are to be joined. The cited passage of the Apostle concerns those already joined, not those who are to be joined. What is unlawful and forbidden by the Lord is never advantageous to do. 465

**XXII.** A man who dismisses an adulterous wife and marries another in order to make her a Christian commits adultery. 467

**XXIII.** It is not permitted to enter an adulterous marriage in order to make the woman a Christian. Ibid.

**XXIV.** The vow of continence must not be broken in hope of compensation. 468

**XXV.** The Apostle’s advice in matters that are not commanded is to be heeded. The question concerning marriages is extremely difficult. Another question raised by Pollentius. Ibid.

**XXVI.** Whether baptism should be given to catechumens at the point of death when they do not request it and cannot answer on their own behalf. The opinion of some denying this is rejected, though not condemned. 469

**XXVII.** How the Lord’s saying, “Do not give what is holy to dogs,” is to be understood. 470

**XXVIII.** In the proposed case baptism is to be given even to catechumens who retain adulterous marriages. The same principle applies to reconciliation granted to a penitent in danger of death. Ibid.

**BOOK TWO.**—Pollentius is refuted for thinking that adultery dissolves a marriage just as death does, and for applying to it the Apostle’s statement in the First Letter to the Corinthians, “But if her husband has died, she is free,” wishing “died” in this passage to mean an adulterer as well. His remaining arguments are then dissolved, and the various difficulties which he fears would arise unless a man were permitted to marry another after repudiating an adulterous wife are refuted.

471–472

**CHAPTER ONE.** The occasion of this book. Ibid.

**II.** Pollentius’s opinion: a spouse is forbidden to marry another if he or she has departed from a spouse who was not fornicating, but not if the departure was from a fornicating spouse. He holds that “dead” in Paul’s passage is also to be understood as “fornicating.” Ibid.

**III.** Pollentius is refuted. Ibid.

**IV.** How absurd it is to count fornication as death that dissolves the marital bond. Ibid.

**V.** The marital bond is dissolved by death, but not by fornication and the separation of the spouses. 473

**VI.** How fitting reconciliation after adultery is for a Christian with a repentant spouse. Ibid.

**VII.** Husbands who rage against adulterous wives, although they themselves are adulterers. 474

**VIII.** Adulterous husbands should be punished more severely than adulterous wives. The law of Antoninus, which wished dissolute men to be condemned equally with women. The dissolute conduct of men is worse. 474–475

**IX.** A man unwilling to be reconciled with his adulterous wife cannot marry another. 476

**X.** Complaints by incontinent people against Christ’s law, which forbids marrying another after dismissing an adulterous wife, are made in vain. If the complaints of the incontinent were admitted, adultery would have to be permitted in many cases. The complaint of a woman dismissed for a reason other than fornication and wishing to marry another will seem more just. Ibid.

**XI.** Another objection of Pollentius: that, at least for the purpose of begetting children, it should be permitted to marry another after dismissing an adulterous wife. 478

**XII.** At the present time marriage for the sake of children should be chosen only by those who cannot remain continent. Ibid.

**XIII.** Those unwilling to be reconciled with adulterous spouses should preserve continence. 479

**XIV.** Another objection: that this view excludes kindness, since husbands would wish adulterous wives to be punished, after whose death they could marry others. 480

**XV.** Husbands should be led to spare adulterous wives not by license for lust but by concern for piety. 481

**XVI.** It is objected that an incontinent man who secured his adulterous wife’s death by accusing her would obtain forgiveness through baptism or reconciliation, which would otherwise be denied to him as a perpetual adulterer. More serious objections can be devised against Pollentius’s view than the difficulties he raises. 482

**XVII.** Another difficulty against Pollentius’s position. 483

**XVIII.** Either marital continence or the more excellent continence must be preserved. 484

**XIX.** He exhorts spouses separated from their spouses by divorce to continence. 485

**XX.** Men ought to lead women in chastity. He proposes the continence of clerics who were chosen unwillingly to men unwilling to remain continent after divorce. 486

**OF ST. AURELIUS AUGUSTINE, BISHOP OF HIPPO, ONE BOOK ON LYING.**—He investigates what a lie is and whether it is ever to be admitted, weighing examples and the force of arguments on both sides [Col. 1374]. Eight kinds of lies are presented; after they have been examined and altogether rejected, it is established that one must never lie.

487–488

**CHAPTER ONE.** The difficulty of the subject to be treated. Ibid.

**II.** Jokes are not lies. Ibid.

**III.** What a lie is. Whether a will to deceive is required in a speaker for there to be a lie, or whether something less is sufficient. Ibid.

**IV.** Whether lying can ever be useful or permissible. 489

**V.** The opinion affirming that one should sometimes lie. The opinion denying that one should ever lie. The examples advanced for lying from the Old Testament are examined. No example of lying is available from the New Testament. Timothy’s circumcision was not performed by pretense. Peter was willingly corrected by Paul. Authority for lying cannot be established by examples from ordinary life any more than from Scripture. 491

**VI.** Lying is iniquity and brings death to the soul; it therefore must not be admitted for anyone’s temporal salvation. 494

**VII.** One must not lie even for the sake of bodily chastity. What lust is. 495

**VIII.** Nor should one lie with the aim of preserving others for eternal life. 496

**IX.** Some think that lying should be employed to prevent a man from suffering sexual violation at another’s hands. Their argument and example are refuted. The sins of others are not to be imputed to someone who could have prevented them by a lesser sin of his own. Whoever does not wish to restrain sinners by sinning must not consent to their sins. Each person should avoid the lesser sin that is his own rather than the greater sin of another. Whether one should lie to avoid bodily impurity. Lies that harm others are not to be admitted in order to avoid bodily impurity. 497

**X.** Lying is never to be used in religious teaching. 500

**XI.** Lies are also to be avoided when they harm another person or the liar himself. “Lying” and “being a liar” differ. 501

**XII.** Whether a lie that harms no one and benefits someone should be used. Whether there are honorable lies that benefit some and harm no one. Whether to lie is always to give false testimony. Ibid.

**XIII.** Whether one should lie in order not to betray either a murderer or an innocent person sought for execution. Firmus, bishop of Thagaste, neither wishes to lie nor can be induced by torture to betray a man being sought for execution. What a person who is questioned and knows where the man sought for execution is should answer. 503

**XIV.** The eight kinds of lies. 505

**XV.** Divine authorities by which lying is prohibited, and other commandments to be understood from the deeds of the saints. The command to offer the other cheek to one who strikes. The command not to swear at all. The command not to think about tomorrow. The command that the Apostles carry nothing with them on the journey. 506

**XVI.** The double mouth, of voice and heart: which mouth is meant by the saying, “The mouth that lies,” and so forth. The mouth of the heart is also shown in the Gospel. Whether only that lie is forbidden by which someone is slandered. Three interpretations of the passage in Ecclesiasticus (chapter 7, verse 14). 508

**XVII.** Verse 7 of Psalm 5 likewise understood in three ways. How the command forbidding the giving of false testimony is to be understood. 510

**XVIII.** How another passage of Scripture is to be understood. What has so far been discovered on both sides in the preceding investigation. Error that measures evil by desire and habit. Our life is twofold. Whether lesser sins may be admitted, if not for temporal benefit, at least to preserve holiness. 511

**XIX.** Three things to be preserved for the sake of holiness: bodily chastity, purity of mind, and truth in teaching. 514

**XX.** One must not lie for the sake of bodily chastity. The origin of the word “faith.” Purity of mind. 515

**XXI.** Recapitulation of the preceding. One must never lie by any of the eight kinds of lies listed. How blind the defenders of lying are. 516

**OF ST. AURELIUS AUGUSTINE, BISHOP OF HIPPO, ONE BOOK AGAINST LYING, TO CONSENTIUS.**—Augustine responds to writings that Consentius sent him for consideration concerning the use of lying to expose the Priscillianists in hiding, who falsely claim to be Catholics. He teaches that liars are not to be drawn from their hiding places by means of lies, nor blasphemers by means of blasphemies. He refutes the error of the Priscillianists, found especially in Dictinius’s book entitled *The Scales* [Col. 1375], in which they dogmatize that religious people ought to lie in order to conceal their religion. He argues that the testimonies and examples they produce from the divine books in support of this error are partly not lies and partly, even when they are, not to be imitated. He resolves the difficulty concerning compensatory sins, rejecting even a lie that might seem useful or necessary for preserving anyone’s temporal or eternal salvation. Finally, he firmly instructs Consentius never to lie at all, especially in matters pertaining to religious teaching, and to defend this position against heretics.

517–518

**CHAPTER ONE.** Those who abuse lies in order to remain hidden are not to be drawn from their hiding places by our lies. Ibid.

**II.** The Priscillianist error concerning the use of lying to remain hidden from others. This opinion of the Priscillianists abolishes martyrdom altogether. 519

**III.** A lie by Catholics to capture heretics would be more harmful than a lie by heretics to conceal themselves from Catholics. The matter is demonstrated by an example. To wish to capture Priscillianists through lying is to be corrupted along with them. 520

**IV.** One who lies in one matter is not trusted in others. 523

**V.** It is more tolerable for a Priscillianist to lie while concealing his heresy than for a Catholic to lie while concealing the truth. Catholics who falsely claim to be Priscillianists act worse than Priscillianists who falsely claim to be Catholics. 523

**VI.** It is never permitted to deny Christ before men, even deceitfully and fictitiously. Objection. Response. The possible objections are likewise refuted. Believing in the heart is not enough unless Christ is also not denied with the mouth. How Psalm 14, verse 3, is to be understood, where the person who speaks truth in his heart is praised. Likewise the Apostle’s command that we speak truth with our neighbor. Those who preach the truth without truthfully doing so are tolerated, but those who proclaim falsehood are not. 525

**VII.** A lie is not to be admitted under any supposedly good intention. Some acts are made good or evil by their end; others are sins in themselves and are not to be done for any apparently good end. 527

**VIII.** One sin may be lighter than another because of the intention; nevertheless the lighter sin is not to be done, since it is often more serious than a sin of another kind. 529

**IX.** Compensatory sins themselves are not to be admitted. Lot’s act in offering his daughters to the Sodomite violators. Lot’s example, disturbed as he then was by fear, is not to be imitated. Nor is David’s example of swearing in anger. What David and Lot ought to have done. How Lot can scarcely be defended from sin. The deeds of the saints are not all to be transferred into our conduct. 530

**X.** The examples sought in Scripture in support of lying are to be weighed. Concealing the truth is one thing; uttering a lie is another. Abraham and Isaac are defended from lying. Jacob’s act was not a lie. Tropes are not lies. Metaphor. Antiphrasis. Why tropes occur in Scripture. 532–533

**XI.** The threefold method of arguing against those who use the divine Scriptures to support their lies.
wish to enlist female patrons. 535

XII. Certain examples of lying from the Old Scriptures are genuinely such; from the New Testament, however, none can be produced. Peter’s and Barnabas’s dissimulation rightly reproved by Paul. Certain ceremonies of the Law observed by Paul were not observed deceitfully. Paul became all things to all people, not by lying but by showing compassion. What lying is. 536

XIII. Passages of the Gospel that seem to lend support to lying are examined. Christ figuratively pretended not to know what he knew. Likewise, prophetically and figuratively, he pretended that he was going farther. 537

XIV. Examples in the Old Scripture, if human lies are narrated there, are not to be imitated. Just as Judah’s fornication is not to be imitated, so neither is Tamar’s lie. 538

XV. Lying is always unjust, since it is a sin and contrary to truth. In the case of the Hebrew midwives and Rahab, it was not deceit that was rewarded, but benevolence. 539

XVI. Whether a good person may at some time lie for another’s salvation. 541

XVII. Whether the Hebrew midwives and Rahab would have acted better by refusing to lie. The rule by which those passages brought forward from Scripture as examples of lying are to be assessed. Ibid.

XVIII. Whether one should lie in order to conceal from a sick person something that would bring about his death. Truth must not be feared lest it be called homicide [Col. 1376]. If lying is permitted in the proposed case, how difficult it is to set limits to lies so that they do not grow into perjuries and blasphemies. A sharp argument against teachers of lying. 543

XIX. Just as sexual violation must not be committed in order to rescue someone in danger, so neither should a lie be spoken. If lies are permitted in some way, one must fear that they will advance as far as perjuries and blasphemies. How perjury and blasphemy differ. 544

XX. Whether one should at least lie for a person’s eternal salvation. In danger concerning eternal salvation, just as a person should not be aided through sexual violation, so neither through lying, which is truly sin. 546

XXI. Epilogue. 547

# ST AURELIUS AUGUSTINE, BISHOP OF HIPPO, ONE BOOK ON THE WORK OF MONKS

At the urging of Aurelius, bishop of Carthage, Augustine defends the cause of those monks who supported themselves by the work of their own hands against certain others of the same profession. These latter wished to live from the offerings of religious people, boasting that, while doing no work, they were fulfilling the evangelical commands by caring nothing for food and clothing. First he demonstrates that the apostle Paul gave God’s servants both a command and an example of performing bodily work by which they might provide themselves with food and clothing. Next he shows that those evangelical commands, by which those monks fostered not only their idleness but also their arrogance, are not contrary to the apostolic command and example. Finally, he censures the long-haired monks and entreats and exhorts them not to continue growing their hair contrary to the apostolic command. 547–548

I. The writing of this work was prompted by Aurelius. The opinion of monks who refuse to work concerning the meaning of the Apostle’s command to work. They oppose the Gospel command not to be concerned about bodily food. Ibid.

II. They are refuted because, just as they derive the meaning of the Gospel from various sayings of the Lord, so they fail to consider that the Apostle’s passage must be understood from his other sayings. 550

III. Paul’s command concerning bodily work is proved from the circumstances of the passage. By his own example Paul taught what he commanded. 551

IV. Paul’s meaning is clarified from his other Epistles. 552

V. The apostles were permitted, following Christ’s example, to have women who ministered to them accompany them. Ibid.

VI. Christ granted the right to live from the Gospel not only to the apostles but also to others. 553

VII. The authority not to work given to the apostles is to be understood as concerning bodily work. 554

VIII. The Apostle plainly speaks of the work of the hands. 555

IX. This is shown more openly and clearly by what follows. 556

X. Why Paul did not live from the Gospel. Ibid.

XI. In this matter, as in others, Paul accommodates himself through compassion to the weak. How, without pretense or deceit, he became as one under the Law and as one without the Law. He fears that, if he lives from the Gospel, the weak may think the Gospel is being sold. 557

XII. Shaken by the dangers threatening the weak, he chooses to work rather than live from the Gospel. 558

XIII. What the Apostle’s bodily work consisted of. Honest occupations for obtaining a livelihood. 559

XIV. When the Apostle used to work against the monks’ idleness. 560

XV. Although Paul commands God’s servants to work, he nevertheless does not wish their necessities to be cared for less by the faithful. Work is to be chosen by God’s servants so that it may be carried out with a free mind, without anxiety and greed. 561

XVI. Paul wishes the necessities of God’s servants who cannot provide themselves with food because of their occupations or illnesses to be supplied by the faithful. Ministry to the saints, by which material things are supplied to those from whom spiritual things are received in return. Let both God’s servants obey Paul by working and good believers by supplying their necessities. 562

XVII. The idle allege that they devote themselves to prayer, psalms, reading, and the word of God. It is permissible to sing psalms while working. Reading is of no benefit unless one does what is read. 564

XVIII. Those who refuse to work under the pretext of distributing the word of God are chastised. Paul appointed definite times for distributing the word and others for working. The best administration is that everything be done in its proper order. 565

XIX. Paul truly performed bodily work. 566

XX. The objection: did the other apostles sin by not working and living from the Gospel? The answer. The command to work applies to those who do not preach the Gospel. 567

XXI. Those who wish to be idle have for the most part been converted from a poor and laborious life. Ibid. [Col. 1377]

XXII. Against the idle and talkative, who by example and speech draw others away from work. 568

XXIII. The Gospel is not rightly understood by the idle. The useless are mockingly ridiculed. Monks shutting themselves in so that no one sees them for many days. The evangelical command not to think about tomorrow is shown to agree with the Apostle. 569

XXIV. The Gospel does not forbid storing something up for tomorrow. 571

XXV. What benefit is there in having left one’s former occupations if one must still work? The charity of common life. Even those who are converted from a higher way of life ought to work, but much more those converted from a lower one. Ibid.

XXVI. How the command not to be anxious about food and clothing is to be understood. How the saying about the birds of heaven and the lilies of the field is to be received. 573

XXVII. We must use our diligence, lest we seem to tempt God. 574

XXVIII. He vividly describes idle and wandering monks. 575

XXIX. Augustine’s occupations. He would prefer to work according to the monks’ custom at fixed hours. 576

XXX. He fears that good people may be corrupted by growing idle through the indolence of the wicked. 577

XXXI. Against long-haired monks. 578

XXXII. The perverse interpretation of Scripture by the long-haired monks. The apostle Paul professed the highest chastity. The command to men not to cover the head. The mind signified by the man, desire by the woman. 579

XXXIII. He asks certain good long-haired men to shave their hair. 580

# ST AURELIUS AUGUSTINE, BISHOP OF HIPPO, ONE BOOK ON THE DIVINATION OF DEMONS

The divinations of demons and the practices pertaining to their worship are not therefore rightly performed because they do not occur unless God permits them. Whence those divinations of demons arise, and why they are sometimes true, although for the most part false. 581–582

I. The occasion for writing this book. What God permits is not immediately right. Even in matters pertaining to religious worship, God permits things that displease him. Ibid.

II. Pagan sacrifices should not therefore be considered good because God did not prevent them from being performed. Things permitted by the almighty God, although condemned by that same just God. The pontifical books of profane rites. What has so far been established and what is to be treated next. 583

III. The divination of demons arises from three causes. They excel in keenness of perception, speed of movement, and long experience of things. Demons are not therefore to be placed above human beings. 584

IV. Even though demons perform certain marvelous things, they are to be despised. 585

V. From where demons foretell future events. 586

VI. How far the divination of demons is removed from the sublimity of divine prophecy. Demons are usually deceived and deceive others. How they are deceived. How they deceive. Ibid.

VIII. Demons were able to foretell certain truths from the oracles of the prophets, yet dared to say nothing against the true God. 588

IX. It was foretold by the prophets that the worship of demons would yield to the worship of the one God. 589

# ST AURELIUS AUGUSTINE, BISHOP OF HIPPO, ONE BOOK ON THE CARE TO BE TAKEN FOR THE DEAD, TO PAULINUS

When asked by Paulinus, bishop of Nola, whether burial in the memorial shrines of martyrs benefits the spirits of the dead, he first shows that the dead themselves suffer no harm even if burial is entirely denied to their bodies. The place of burial, however, is not in itself of any benefit, but only incidentally, insofar as the memory of it moves and increases the affection of those praying for the departed. The care of burial arises from the human heart’s affection for its own flesh, and was rightly despised by the holy martyrs, since it makes no difference to happiness or misery. From this he proceeds to discuss the dead who are said to have appeared to the living so that burial might be provided for their bodies. He explains by various examples how such apparitions occur. Finally, he asks whether the dead take an interest in care for and affairs of the living. 591–592

I. Paulinus’s question: whether it benefits a dead person to be buried near the memorial of a saint. His own opinion is that it does benefit him. The difficulty raised by the same person is discussed. According to the kind of life each person has led, the things done for the dead either benefit them or do not. Ibid. [Col. 1378]

II. What honor paid to burial contributes. If the burial of Christians’ bodies is denied, it takes nothing away from them. 593

XII. Apparitions of the delirious. The apparition experienced by Curma the municipal official. 602

# ST AURELIUS AUGUSTINE, BISHOP OF HIPPO, ONE BOOK ON PATIENCE

At the beginning Augustine distinguishes true patience from false. He then exhorts us to embrace the patience that is true, by which evils are endured for eternal life and out of love for God. Finally, he teaches that this virtue of patience is to be attributed not to the powers of free choice but to the assistance of divine grace. 611–612

II. What true patience is and how useful it is. Ibid.

VIII. The use of patience in mind and body. 614

IX. Patience of mind. Ibid.

X. Patience in external hardships. Both kinds of patience in martyrs. The greater contest of patience when the devil rages. 615

XVIII. Just as charity comes from God, so true patience, which flows from charity, comes from him. 619

XIX. If desire comes from the world, how does it come from human will? That a person is not of the world is not a matter of nature but of grace. 620

1151–1152 **CHAPTER ONE.** The occasion of this subject. Ibid. II. Faith is necessary for one who is about to depart from this life. It must be directed especially toward Christ. **ADMONITION ON THE TWO SERMONS THAT FOLLOW IMMEDIATELY** 1157–1158

**SERMON ONE: ON THE CONSOLATION OF THE DEAD** 1159–1160

**CHAPTER ONE.** There are two kinds of grief. Ibid. II. The causes of mourning for the dead, with respect to the dead themselves. They are shown to be vain. Ibid. III. Other causes, with respect to ourselves, and no more reasonable. Why excessive grief brings about death. Ibid. IV. Mourning was permitted to those who lived before Christ. Why Christ wept for Lazarus. Ibid. V. It is no longer permitted to mourn the dead. Those who are alive on the day of judgment will not die. 1161 VI. What we shall be like after the resurrection. Death is to be desired rather than mourned. Yet it is not to be inflicted upon oneself.

**SERMON TWO** 1161–1162

**CHAPTER ONE.** Why the resurrection is doubtful among unbelievers. Ibid. II. The sprouting of seeds proves that it is possible. Creation also proves it. 1163 III. And the immense flame that comes from a small flint. 1164 IV. Christ, the apostles, the examples of the martyrs, and the mother of the Maccabees testify that the resurrection will truly take place. Hence fear of death is banished. The command not to mourn. Ibid. V. David’s excellent example concerning this. It is not permissible, therefore, to wear black garments for mourning. The answer of a pagan upon hearing of his son’s death. Pagans, Jews, and catechumens who are dying are to be mourned. What sort of sadness is salutary. Recapitulation of both sermons.

1165 **ADMONITION ON THE TREATISE ON THE RIGHT CONDUCT OF CATHOLIC LIFE**

1167–1168 **TREATISE ON THE RIGHT CONDUCT OF CATHOLIC LIFE.** That a bishop is bound to exhort the people. To recall frequently the day of judgment and the vows of baptism. The duty of Christians. Pious exercises are prescribed. Christians are warned away from the rites of the Gentiles. God alone is to be worshiped. Pious admonitions. Against drunkenness. Against superstitions. How one should conduct oneself on Sundays and in churches. What judges ought to do. To fortify oneself frequently with the sign of the cross. That the devil harasses those who live piously. Why God permits this. To distribute alms to the poor. To give tithes to God through the poor or the churches. To keep God’s commandments. To correct one’s character quickly. To love one’s enemies. To care for the soul. How one should fast. To nourish the soul with sacred readings. Against lust. Concubinage. Capital crimes. Pious instructions for right living. To pursue piety without delay. To disagree with the devil. Not to swear. How one should pray or converse. To avoid scandals. To be merciful. Commendation of charity. Exhortation to repentance and vigilance. That each person has an angel of God. That no one should ever despair. On caution in speech. On maintaining sobriety. That no thing is evil in itself. That the poor are to be invited to the table. Consideration of death. The happiness of eternal life. Meditation on the final judgment. How Christ will reproach the reprobate with his benefits. The punishment of the reprobate. The blessed lot of the righteous. Not to be ashamed of public penance. Nor to despair of pardon. Nor to presume excessively. That the end of the world is imminent. To despise earthly things. To endure adversity patiently for the love of God. Always to revere God as present to oneself. To preserve charity. To persist in a good purpose. Repentance is not to be postponed.

1169–1170 **SERMON ON THE CREED**

1189–1190 **INTRODUCTION.** The necessity of inward and outward faith. The Creed as the rule of faith. How it was instituted. What it contains. Ibid. **CHAPTER ONE.** To believe God, to believe God’s word, and to believe in God. The faith of the devil. Almighty. Ibid. II. Jesus, Christ, the Only-Begotten. Christ compares himself, in respect of his conception, to a worm. This manner of birth is neither injurious to God nor impossible. 1191 III. Why the Lord wished to be crucified. The power of the cross. 1192 IV. The mystery of the cross. The depth of the mystery of the cross. Ibid. [Col. 1394] V. Why Christ chose the punishment of the cross. Through the death of the flesh he obtained for us a double resurrection. 1193 VI. What Christ accomplished for us through infirmities. 1194 VII. What he did in hell. Ibid. VIII. All human beings will be judged by Christ. Ibid. IX. How one ought to prepare oneself for the final judgment. 1195 X. We must flee to the remedies of repentance. Ibid. XI. The mystery of the Trinity is explained by means of comparisons. Ibid. XII. The Catholic Church. Through faith there are no greater riches. The Church is one. 1196 XIII. How one becomes a participant in the merits of the saints. 1197 XIV. The remission of sins. The Novatians are refuted. Ibid. XV. That one must not despair, and from where despair proceeds. One must not cease begging for forgiveness. 1198 XVI. However guilty one may be, hope remains during life. God never rejects sincere repentance. Through repentance, sins of whatever kind can here be washed away. 1199 XVII. Pleasures quickly pass away. They lead to eternal torments. At present we enjoy them as though in a dream. 1200 XVIII. Eternal punishment. The power of repentance. Ibid. XIX. How repentance is corrupted. Yet even then it was not entirely fruitless. It must be read cautiously.

1201 **SERMON ON THE EVE OF EASTER, ON THE EATING OF THE LAMB.** (Also found among the spurious works of Jerome.)—The mystery of Easter is fulfilled in us. When it is to be celebrated. Where. Christ is a lamb to some and a kid to others. Why the lamb was killed in the evening, not during the day. What it means to eat unleavened bread with bitterness. Why raw or boiled flesh is not to be eaten. What the lamb’s head, feet, and entrails signify. Why the lamb’s bones are not to be broken. What our girded loins at the eating of the lamb teach us. What the footwear and staff signify.

1201–1202 **SERMON ON PSALM XLI, TO THE NEWLY BAPTIZED.** (Also falsely attributed to Jerome.)—The sons of Korah sing joyful things in the psalm. Deer are enemies of serpents. The Church’s threefold fountain. The Trinity. The exercises of those about to be baptized. The changed nature of the baptized.

1203–1204 **SERMON ON THE ANOINTING OF THE EARS AND NOSTRILS OF THE NEWLY BAPTIZED WITH HOLY OIL BY THE PRIESTS.**—The mysteries are not entrusted to catechumens. What the anointing of the ears signifies. Who has ears for hearing. Why the nostrils are also anointed. Another interpretation of this mystery.

1205–1207 **SERMON ON THE MYSTERY OF BAPTISM.**—The care required of those about to be baptized. The grace of baptismal water. Those about to be baptized are questioned concerning faith in the Trinity. What faith is required concerning other matters. Faith in the resurrection. Triple immersion, and why baptism is not repeated.

1209–1210 **SERMON ON THE ANOINTING OF THE HEAD AND THE WASHING OF THE FEET.**—What the pouring of chrism upon the baptized signifies. That the promises made in baptism should be diligently fulfilled.

1211–1212 **TREATISE ON THE CREATION OF THE FIRST HUMAN BEING**

1213–1214 **SERMON ON THE VANITY OF THE WORLD.** Ibid. **SERMON ON CONTEMPT FOR THE WORLD.** (By an uncertain author.) 1215–1216 **CHAPTER ONE.** Some commandments are particular, others common. Ibid. II. Clerics should possess nothing as their own. Ibid. III. Why they are tonsured. The seat of wisdom is in the brain. Ibid. IV. They should not cover their heads while praying. Ibid. V. They should despise the world and worldly things. The weapons of the world; earthly estates. Ibid. VI. They should desire the kingdom of God. They should love God and neighbor. They should receive the cup of Christ. 1217 VII. They should pursue poverty. The happiness of poverty. 1218 VIII. Epilogue.

**SERMON ON THE GOOD OF DISCIPLINE** 1217–1218

**CHAPTER ONE.** Authority and pride. The praise of discipline. 1219 II. All things are contained and ordered by discipline. Ibid. III. By discipline all vices are restrained. Ibid. IV. Human discipline serves the law of God. What severity must be avoided. How it is to be avoided. 1220 V. Those are guilty to whom discipline has not yet come, but less so than those whom it has abandoned. For whom discipline is burdensome, and for whom light. Ibid. VI. Discipline in animals. 1221 VII. How the Lord may be found or known. Ibid. VIII. One should strive for a religious life and a good reputation. The crowd is accustomed to judge good people badly. One must give suspicion no opportunity. Ibid. IX. To what extent a good conscience is sufficient. 1222

**SERMON ON OBEDIENCE AND HUMILITY.** (It is a fragment by an uncertain but ancient author.) 1221–1222 **CHAPTER ONE.** How pleasing obedience is to God. Without obedience there are no virtues. Where obedience is absent, pride is present. Ibid. II. Pride is the worst of all sins. With pride, there can be the appearance of virtue without its reality. 1223 III. It is better to be devoted to all vices than to be proud. Those who withdraw from a monastery into the desert should not despise the brothers’ assembly. Those who act otherwise are compelled to do so. Hence those who visit brothers from the deserts in a coenobium [Col. 1395] are not to be reproved.

1223–1224 **TREATISE ON CHARITY, OR ON THE WORDS OF THE PSALM: “THE EARTH HAS GIVEN ITS FRUIT.”**—The fruit of the blessed earth is charity, that is, cleaving to God. To return the fruit of charity. Whoever does not love God loves neither himself nor his neighbor. Love of the world is not love.

1223–1224 **TREATISE ON PRAYER AND ALMSGIVING.**—To give alms freely to the poor. Mercy itself prays. Mercy has no limit. Prayer should accompany mercy. The praise of prayer.

1225–1226 **SERMON ON THE UNIVERSALITY OF ALMSGIVING.**—The Manichaeans deny alms to sinners, and the reason why. Others fear that by giving to sinners they may offend God. Alms must be distributed to everyone. The righteous are to be preferred. Yet enemies are not to be despised. Not because they are sinners, but because they are human beings. Christ did not deny alms to sinners.

1229–1230 **TREATISE ON THE TWELVE STONES** of which Revelation 21:19–20 speaks.

**MISCELLANEOUS SAYINGS** (by an uncertain author).—To be simple and prudent. The thief and robber. Dangers everywhere. Rulers. Degrees of sin. An obscure reading. The fornicator and adulteress. Old age. The sick body. Truth. Scripture. Judgments at the gate. Hatred of the one who reproves. The transience of the world. The sadness that is forbidden. To practice judgment and mercy. The perversity of the world. A friend. The soul of Jerusalem. Offered to God. From where the heart is taken away. To God. The natural conversation of each person.

1231–1232 **ADMONITION ON THE SERMONS TO THE BROTHERS LIVING IN THE DESERT**

1233–1234 **SERMONS TO THE BROTHERS LIVING IN THE DESERT**

1235–1236 **SERMON ONE.** On the establishment of the regular life. Ibid. **SERMON II.** On peace. 1237—**SERMON III.** On silence. 1239—**SERMON IV.** On prudence. 1240—**SERMON V.** On obedience. 1242—**SERMON VI.** On mercy. 1246—**SERMON VII.** On obedience. 1248—**SERMON VIII.** On perseverance. 1249—**SERMON IX.** On anger and hatred. 1251—**SERMON X.** On purity of conscience and hope. 1252—**SERMON XI.** On tears, compunction, and repentance. 1253—**SERMON XII.** On pride and humility. 1255—**SERMON XIII.** On fortitude. 1256—**SERMON XIV.** On justice and fraternal correction. 1257—**SERMON XV.** On faith in the Trinity, which simple people are not to investigate, and on the gifts of the Spirit against the seven vices. 1259—**SERMON XVI.** On disobedience, negligence, patience, and chastity. 1262—**SERMON XVII.** On watchfulness and idleness. Ibid. **SERMON XVIII.** On envy. 1264—**SERMON XIX.** On the vigil of Christ’s Nativity. 1266—**SERMON XX.** On the Nativity of the Lord. 1267—**SERMON XXI.** On the monks in Egypt. 1268—**SERMON XXII.** On the consolation of the brothers in the desert, with an exhortation to prayer and tears. 1271—**SERMON XXIII.** On fasting. 1273—**SERMON XXIV.** On the exhortation to solitude, and on fasting. 1274—**SERMON XXV.** On fasting, and where it was instituted. 1275—**SERMON XXVI.** On murmuring and detraction, and on the punishments of the condemned. 1277—**SERMON XXVII.** On the prodigal son. 1280—**SERMON XXVIII.** On the Lord’s Supper. 1282—**SERMON XXIX.** On the deceitful tongue. 1287 [Col. 1396] **SERMON XXX.** On the confession of sins. 1288—**SERMON XXXI.** On the world’s deceitfulness and its detestation, because of the three principal evils that are in it. 1290—**SERMON XXXII.** To lepers, that they should maintain patience. 1293—**SERMON XXXIII.** On the detestation of drunkenness, with an account of a terrible incident. 1294—**SERMON XXXIV.** On the two classes of people who abandon the world, represented by the holy Lot and his wife. 1295—**SERMON XXXV.** To judges, that they should beware lest they be corrupted by hatred, love, money, prayers, or fear, and that they should avoid the other vices and preserve justice. 1297—**SERMON XXXVI.** To his own presbyters, reproving their wicked life. 1298—**SERMON XXXVII.** That priests ought to present themselves as ministers of God and beware lest they attempt to sell the gifts of the Holy Spirit; also on maintaining patience and chastity, and on the detestation of fornication. 1301—**SERMON XXXVIII.** On the immense praises of Sacred Scripture, with an exhortation to read it diligently. 1304—**SERMON XXXIX.** On the solitary and contemplative life. 1306—**SERMON XL.** On clerical observance. 1311—**SERMON XLI.** On the observance of the Lenten fast. 1314—**SERMON XLII.** On the life and morals of clerics. 1315—**SERMON XLIII.** On the Epiphany and seeking Christ. 1317—**SERMON XLIV.** On piety, charity, and suffrages for the dead. 1319—**SERMON XLV.** On practicing repentance and avoiding detraction. 1323—**SERMON XLVI.** On angels and hospitality. 1324—**SERMON XLVII.** On the detestation of sodomy. 1326—**SERMON XLVIII.** On care of the soul. 1328—**SERMON XLIX.** On the misery of the flesh and the falsity of life. 1332—**SERMON L.** On the salvation of the soul. 1334—**SERMONS LI–LIV–LV.** On the death of Valentinus. 1336—**SERMON LVI.** That it is good to read sacred Scripture. 1339—**SERMON LVII.** 1341—**SERMON LVIII.** On the fact that the glory of the world is nothing. Ibid. **SERMONS LIX–LX.** On the persecution of Christians. 1342—**SERMON LXI.** On obedience. 1344—**SERMON LXII.** On fear of the Lord and avoiding greed. 1345—**SERMON LXIII.** 1347—**SERMON LXIV.** An exhortation to priests, that they should teach the people what they ought to know and observe. Ibid. **SERMON LXV.** An exhortation to instruct people, motivated by the desire for heavenly life and contempt for the present life. 1350—**SERMON LXVI.** On practicing repentance. 1352—**SERMON LXVII.** On fleeing vanity and acquiring the virtues. 1353—**SERMON LXVIII.** How vices are to be opposed through the virtues; and on infernal misery. 1354—**SERMON LXIX.** An exhortation to pray, with the example of a deceased man in Egypt; and on the misery of the soul. 1355—**SERMONS LXX–LXXII–LXXIII.** On the one who retains anger in his heart for a long time and refuses to humble himself. Ibid. **SERMONS LXXIV–LXXV–LXXVI.** On thoughts. 1358

[Note: [Col. 1395]]

The final volume of the Benedictine edition contains a supplement to the various volumes. From it we have transferred here the material relating to Volume Six, where it will be read more conveniently:

1. Column 255: In place of Note 2 substitute:

“Those same words, spoken by the Father over Christ after his baptism, are read by the author of the *Questions from the Old and New Testament*, Question 54, in the appendix to Volume 3 of this edition; by Hilary of Poitiers, in *On the Psalms*, no. 291, as well as in Book 8 of *On the Trinity*, no. 25, and in his *Commentary on Matthew*, chapter 2, no. 6; and by Justin Martyr, *Dialogue with Trypho*. Indeed, Augustine himself, in Book 2 of *On the Harmony of the Gospels*, no. 31, confirms this reading. Therefore Danaeus has rashly and entirely without any manuscript authority added here: ‘You are my Son.’”

2. Column 783, Note 2, add:

“These are excerpted in summary from Augustine, *On the Trinity* 6, no. 11, where he explains Hilary’s words.”

3. Column 863, penultimate line of the *Admonition on the Book of Soliloquies*, after the words “he is filled,” add:

“Certainly, many phrases occur here that are foreign to Augustine—for example, these in chapter 18: ‘when I was breaking your commandments,’ or those in chapter 26: ‘in the secret place of your council,’ and so forth. Nor does the allusion occurring in chapter 22 to the acts of Saints Andrew, Bartholomew, and Agatha suggest the age of that same Doctor any more strongly. Moreover, a somewhat different view of hell seems to be expressed in chapter 22, especially if by ‘our fathers’ the ancient righteous are meant, than the view Augustine holds in *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, Books 12, chapters 33 and 34.”

4. Column 877, eight lines before chapter 16, above the words “there is no sin,” it should be noted that these words are taken from Augustine, Sermon 99, no. 6.

5. Column 1066, line 60: The words “so that we may not repeat what has passed, etc.” are illustrated by what is found in Alcuin’s *On the Divine Office*, in the chapter on the Lord’s Supper. After the entire rite for reconciling a penitent has been briefly described, the following is added:

“After this, the priest should admonish him that what he has washed away through repentance he must not repeat by doing it again.”

This agrees with the ancient Victorine manuscript cited by Morinus, *On Penance*, Book 8, chapter 11, no. 21. At the end of the reconciliation of penitents it prescribes:

“After this, the penitents shall rise and be admonished by the bishop not to undo again, by repeating it, what they have washed away through repentance.”

That the same practice was customary among the Greeks is proved by the fact that John the Faster, after absolution has been given to the penitent, wants the following to be said to him:

“You have been freed, upon confessing, from your former evils; therefore do not, through negligence concerning the divine commandments, subject yourself to later evils, so that, according to the Gospel, the last things may be worse for you than the former things from which, through God’s mercy, you have been freed.”

6. Column 1077, line 3 of the *Admonition*, before the words “But as for Augustine,” prefix:

“The Oxford editors point out that, in a very ancient manuscript volume of Saxon homilies, it is found under this title: ‘On the Twelve Abuses, according to the Disputation of Saint Cyprian, Bishop and Martyr’; and they accordingly allow the view, which some had already held, that it may be the work of Saint Patrick, the apostle of the Irish. If this were so, the Saxon translator ought to have indicated that he was translating according to Patrick, not according to Cyprian.”

7. Column 1227, below the title of the sermon *On the Universality of Almsgiving*, note:

“This sermon is cited under Augustine’s name and copied out to a large extent by Hincmar, in the book *On the Non-Trinal Deity*, p. 445.”

END OF VOLUME SIX.
